# Patrologia Latina, volume 71 — English translation

# Patrologia Latina, Volume 71

## Complete Course of Patrology

Or Universal Library—complete, uniform, convenient, economical—of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with numerous manuscript codices, and most diligently corrected; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the very extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with separate analytical indexes following each volume and each author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of every page and indicating its subject matter; augmented with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and with others possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever any Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance, and another of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers, and in which passages of their works, commented on the individual texts of the several books of Scripture.

The most accurate edition, and one easily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of its type, the quality of its paper, the integrity of its text, the perfection of its correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the exceptionally convenient format of the volumes, consistently alike throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection itself—single, systematic, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works relating to every period, place, language, and form.

## First Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church, from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of complete series in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

The Patrology was printed in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. The Latin edition is sold at 1,200 francs for the thousand volumes; the Greek-Latin at 1,300 francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the Eastern authors, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

# The Complete Works of Saint George Florentius Gregory, Bishop of Tours

Together with the Epitome and Chronicle of Fredegar the Scholastic, with its continuators and other ancient monuments, collated with manuscript codices and old editions, corrected and enlarged, and illustrated with notes and observations, through the work and study of Dom Thierry Ruinart, priest and Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint-Maur.

In this latest revision of the edition, we have arranged the material in a better order: the fuller notes, which under the title “Addenda” had occupied many pages almost secretly at the end of Ruinart’s edition, have been restored among the notes of that most learned man, so that each may readily be read beneath the particular passage it illustrates.

Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of complete series in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

# In the Year of Our Lord 595

## Saint Gregory, Bishop of Tours

*(Ruinart’s Paris edition, 1699.)*

[Col. 0009]

# To the Most Illustrious Lord, Lord Achille de Harlay, Supreme President of the Senate of France

## Dedication

If the heavenly powers possess any awareness of human affairs, if any concern for their own works touches them, I do not doubt, most illustrious President of the Senate, that our Gregory will regard it as a distinguished favor that you allow a new edition of his works to appear under the auspices of your most renowned name.

While he lived, he especially desired that his writings should reach posterity complete and unaltered. He besought the priests of the Lord who would govern the Church of Tours after him not to permit these books to be destroyed or rewritten in abridged form, with certain passages omitted according to someone’s discretion, but to ensure that they were copied exactly as they had been left by the author himself, untouched and complete in all their parts and divisions.

How grateful, then, must he now be to the man who preserves the integrity of his books, protects that integrity by his authority, or, finally, rescues it from the judgment of unjust men! You therefore act nobly toward Gregory, since you have not disdained to have your illustrious name prefixed to this new revision of his works. For surely no one will be so bold or reckless as to inflict even the slightest injury upon Gregory’s writings when he sees them approved by the judgment of so wise and equitable an arbiter.

You, most distinguished man, also make this undertaking worthy of your name—and, if I may say so, of your rank and dignity—by extending your protection to our Gregory. Since you sincerely love religion, and always keep before your eyes the history of our nation and the customs of your ancestors, you cannot fail to approve an author whom everyone venerates as the father of Frankish history, from whom we have learned the beginnings and progress of the Christian religion in Gaul, and likewise the deeds of our earliest kings.

Even if Gregory, now placed above the lot of mortals, cares little for his writings, we may not therefore abandon concern for what he published during his life for our use. It is in the interest of the Frankish and Christian commonwealth not merely to preserve them from destruction, but also to maintain their authority unimpaired against those who either diminish the author’s credibility because of what seems to them his excessive simplicity and credulity, or remove a substantial portion from his genuine works as though it had been rashly sewn on by interpolators.

I have attempted to do both these things for Gregory. If the weight of your judgment is added to this work, I shall consider myself to have received no small reward for my undertaking and to have secured its approval by all. For such is your insight, such your fairness, and finally such your authority among everyone, that your judgment is equivalent to that of all, and no one who disagrees with you can rightly be considered wise.

I would therefore call our Gregory fortunate to have obtained such a patron and defender—upright, wise, incorruptible, worthy of the judgment of a great and most wise king—one who, after having performed with perfect integrity the office of chief examiner of royal causes, now gives judgment as supreme arbiter over all matters; a man, I say, who brings nothing from the law courts into his own household, but is himself the father and provider of the poor; who regards knowledge of law and statutes not as a display of learning but as the rule of his life; who shows other judges, by his example, a model not less of speaking well than of living well; and who finally embodies in himself the Harleys, Brularts, Thuaneuses, Bellevres, and other heroes of his lineage, embracing them all in his great and exalted spirit.

Protected by such patronage, Gregory will look down upon certain men of such refined fastidiousness that they consider reading him beneath them and reject him altogether as unworthy of their taste. They will begin to judge more correctly when they see that you think very differently from them about our Gregory—namely, that he is a man whose natural and entirely unaffected eloquence reaches the level of those ancient masters of Roman expression.

I remember a distinguished man, deeply conversant with good literature, who, on returning recently from the royal court, where he had heard you congratulate the king, amid a large company of senators and members of every order, on the peace granted to Europe, said that he seemed to himself to have heard not an orator of our own time but, as it were, a toga-clad prince of that golden age.

Since this outstanding power of speech lies not in an empty sound of words but chiefly in the matters themselves, I have no fear that the discourse of our Gregory, however rough and uncultivated, will offend you. In a historian, if he possesses eloquence, you do not indeed disdain it; but if he does not possess it, you do not demand it very urgently—provided that he reports matters worthy of knowledge, as Gregory certainly does when he records genuinely and sincerely the religion, customs, and earliest deeds of the ancient Franks.

For this reason, those who are unfamiliar with Gregory’s reading seem to me not merely insufficiently educated but complete strangers in the history of their own country. If such severe critics were to place before their eyes the period in which Gregory wrote, they would certainly understand that he could not have written otherwise, since, as he himself says, culture and the study of literature were perishing throughout Gaul; nor ought he to have done so, since at that time few understood a philosophizing rhetorician, whereas very many understood a rustic speaking plainly.

Moreover, I am convinced, most illustrious man, that Gregory will please you for the reasons already mentioned and for others as well: as the guardian of the ancient discipline that you love so greatly; as a reconciler of priesthood and empire; and, finally, as a vigorous defender of equity and justice, of which you are an exceptionally devoted champion. This became clear in the judgment concerning Bishop Praetextatus, in which Gregory firmly rejected fabricated canons, without fear of human power, which he opposed.

This is the Gregory whose scattered works, gathered into a single body, we now dedicate to you: a man illustrious in the splendor of his birth, and no less distinguished in holiness than in episcopal dignity; a candid, sincere, and wholly unvarnished author; finally, one endowed with the ancient customs that you love and diligently follow.

Nothing more opportune or fortunate could have happened to us than, through Gregory as our interpreter, to offer this public testimony of our respect for you and at the same time of our gratitude for that singular love with which you pursue literature and all literary men. We, a very small part of those who strive to shed light upon or restore ancient authors, shall consider ourselves truly fortunate if, with the kindness that is your custom, you accept this little work and continue hereafter to encourage and protect us with your patronage.

I earnestly and repeatedly beg you to grant this favor to us—  
the most devoted and obedient servant of Your Highness,

**Fr. Thierry Ruinart, M.B.**

[Col. 0011]

# Preface to the New Edition of Saint Gregory, Bishop of Tours

[Col. 0013]

### 1

[Col. 0013A]

No one who is a stranger to history is unaware of how celebrated Saint Gregory, Bishop of Tours, has always been among learned men. By the nobility of his family, the holiness of his life, and the variety of his many writings, he stood out greatly among the other bishops of his age.

Since I am about to speak chiefly about his works, I do not intend to linger over an extended account of the distinction of his lineage or a fuller narration of his illustrious deeds, since these are sufficiently and abundantly known both from his writings and from the *Life* that we shall present below together with various testimonies about him by distinguished men.

In connection with this new edition of his works, however, four matters occur to me in particular, concerning which I think it worthwhile to give an account. First, what was the necessity or usefulness of this edition? [Col. 0013B]

Second, which works are Gregory’s, and at what time or in what order were they written? Third, should several chapters be removed from his *History*, as the distinguished scholar Charles Cointius thought? Fourth, what have I accomplished in this edition?

After these matters concerning Gregory have been explained, I shall say a few words about Fredegar’s *Epitome*, his *Chronicle* and its continuators, and our Appendix.

### 2

I would rightly be considered rash if, without the testimony of learned men, I had dared to assert that a new edition of Gregory’s works was necessary after so many others had already been published, at various times, by men of the greatest learning and scholarship.

But since I have as witnesses to my assertion all those learned men who in our own time have devoted their efforts to illuminating the history of our nation, I do not doubt that I shall be excused by sensible men—especially since I did not undertake this work without the advice of many friends, who encouraged me when I was hesitating and discouraged by the magnitude of the labor.

Although I do not consider myself more learned or more diligent than those who prepared the earlier editions—for I willingly revere and honor them as masters—no one will deny that I have been more fortunate in possessing more manuscript codices, which at that time lay hidden in the drawers of libraries and by which it was possible to correct Gregory’s works. I have also had at hand innumerable observations by learned men concerning the deeds of our kings, Gallic chronology and geography, and other matters relating to the history of our nation, so that it was not excessively laborious to illuminate Gregory with various notes and observations.

### 3

[Col. 0014A]

That it was necessary to review Gregory’s published works against manuscript codices can readily be proved, not in my own words but in those of others, since learned men have repeatedly complained that these works were not published with sufficient accuracy or in accordance with the author’s intention, owing to the lack of ancient codices.

The procession will be led by the ever-praiseworthy Jerome Bignon, who states several times in his preface to the *Formulas of Marculf* that many things occur in Gregory of Tours, and almost countless passages have been altered by those who published them.

[Col. 0014B]

Hadrian Valesius, the most accurate historian of the Franks, frequently made the same observation. Since he had often noticed errors in Gregory’s published works, he was compelled to return to the manuscript codices. “Since,” he says in the preface to his second volume, “I had observed that Gregory was more corrupt than all the others, I took care to obtain volumes of his writings on parchment.”

After reviewing the manuscript codices that had come into his hands, he declares that he gained much from their accurate reading and from carefully collating them with the printed books—both in the notation of years, in the proper names of persons and places, and in the narration of events. Finally, he explains individually the principal passages that, with the aid of those codices, he restored after they had previously been corrupted and damaged.

### 4

[Col. 0014C]

Valesius wrote this even after the completion of Andrea Chesne’s edition, although Chesne had testified that he had prepared it by collating numerous manuscript codices.

The Reverend Father Charles Cointius, a priest of the French Oratory renowned for learning and piety, agrees with Valesius. In his immense work entitled the *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks*, he repeatedly complained that Gregory’s works were corrupted, but especially under the year 617, where he first begins to discuss Gregory. There he adopts the words of Valesius quoted above.

This induced him, in addition to the codices used by Valesius, to seek out others for use in praising Gregory’s works and illuminating the more difficult passages of our history.

Those learned men knew how necessary it is to possess thoroughly corrected editions of ancient authors, by which later historians may be assisted in writing history. For this reason Valesius produces many examples showing that either he himself or others had previously gone wrong because they had encountered codices that had not been copied or edited with sufficient accuracy.

[Col. 0015A]

Although this is especially important for those who labor to illuminate history from ancient monuments—that they obtain them pure and genuine—it is most important when there are no other authors of the same age whose assistance could easily correct the errors that may have entered the codices.

Such is our Gregory: the sole surviving author who deliberately committed to writing the deeds of the earliest kings of our nation, in whose time he lived. Valesius therefore rightly calls his books “the foundation of our history,” from which the first knowledge of Frankish origins and affairs must chiefly be derived. That learned man valued Gregory so highly that he considered the books of his own history, which he prepared with immense labor and uncommon diligence, deserving to be called nothing other than commentaries on Gregory of Tours.

[Col. 0015B]

Gregory was no less useful to Cointius in composing the ecclesiastical annals of the Franks, which we see largely woven together from Gregory’s books.

One may infer how highly Jerome Bignon valued our Gregory from the fact that he had resolved to publish in one volume Gregory’s *History*, the ancient book of laws, and Marculf’s corrected formulas, adorned with notes, as a single body of ancient law. For this purpose he had already borrowed several codices, as the learned man who prefixed the preface to the posthumous edition of Marculf’s formulas testifies. We have copied his words here.

### 5

Such is the fortune of our Gregory that, however rustic the language in which he wrote, no one can write about the beginnings of the Frankish kingdom without his assistance.

[Col. 0015C]

He is also worthy of praise because he did not sprinkle the origin of the Franks with fables, as the historians of our history who came later did. He says nothing about Trojan exiles, whom those writers invented as the ancestors of the Franks; nothing about other such empty tales or fictions with which our history was later stuffed, while the first dynasty of our kings still endured, as is clear from Fredegar’s *Chronicle* and from the fragments of the same work that we published after its continuators.

When Gregory is about to discuss the origin of the Franks, he first consulted authors earlier than himself. After reporting their testimonies, he added a few words about matters that were commonly circulating at the time.

He cites three authorities on this subject: Sulpicius Alexander, Renatus Profuturus Frigeridus, and the historian Orosius. Everyone knows the last of these; the other two are known only from our Gregory. [Col. 0015D]

Yet what they relate about the Romans agrees so closely with the other monuments of Roman history that scarcely anyone can deny that they also wrote truthfully about the Franks, especially since they seem to have flourished around that period.

### 6

Their testimonies show that the Franks long remained in the region situated beyond the bank of the Rhine. For this reason, I have no doubt that it was called Francia on the Peutinger Map and in other descriptions of ancient Germany.

Sulpicius Alexander, whom Gregory cites, explicitly gave it that name. From him we also infer that the Ampsivarii, Chatti, Bructeri, and Chamavi were offshoots of the Frankish nation.

[Col. 0016A]

When Arbogastes crossed the Rhine into Francia to avenge the violation of the majesty of the Roman Empire by the Franks, he devastated the Bructeri nearest the river and the district inhabited by the Chamavi without anyone coming to oppose him, says that author, except that a few Ampsivarii and Chatti appeared on the farther ridges of the hills under the leadership of Marcomer.

For, as Valesius astutely observes, if Marcomer had not ruled these peoples—Marcomer whom the same Sulpicius had earlier called a Frankish king—he would neither have been obliged to defend the first two peoples nor have been able to command soldiers from the latter two.

Gregory asks whether the Franks at that time had kings, or merely leaders, or whether their rulers were called by some other name—princes, sub-kings, or royal leaders—and he appears to leave the matter undecided, since among those authors no Frank before the time of the tyrant Eugenius is found bearing the title of king.

[Col. 0016B]

For this he is severely criticized by Valesius, who maintains that kings always existed among the Franks. Yet although I do not intend to dispute about the name “king,” I do not think it can be proved from any ancient monument that all the Franks at that time obeyed a single king.

Although it seems certain that one family was foremost among them, as Gregory puts it, and more noble than the others, from which the rulers of the people were customarily selected—rulers whom Roman writers, according to the custom of other peoples and their own manner of speech, called kings or petty kings—who would wish to guess what they were called among the Franks themselves?

[Col. 0016C]

I would not deny, however, that one king among them was superior to the others, since this seems to follow from Gregory himself, not only in the case of Chlodio but also of Chlodovechus. We read that Chlodovechus had several of his kinsmen as Frankish kings, whom, seized by a desire for monarchy, he destroyed one after another.

Indeed, since after his death his sons divided the kingdom among themselves, scarcely anyone can deny that this was an ancient custom of the nation.

### 7

The Franks therefore had their settlements on the farther bank of the Rhine. But as a warlike people impatient of peace, they often crossed the Rhine and devastated the Roman provinces. Thus opportunities arose everywhere for many battles, in which the Franks were at times checked and defeated, and at other times victorious.

Meanwhile, when the affairs of the Empire were thrown into confusion by the appearance of usurpers, both sides summoned them to provide assistance. They had not long been among the Romans before many of them, through their own valor and greatness of spirit, earned the first ranks of military honor and even civil offices.

Indeed, the Romans had entered into treaties with the Franks long before; Gregory testifies from the words of Sulpicius Alexander that these treaties were merely renewed in the time of Eugenius.

[Col. 0016D]

And not without reason, if what the emperor Constantine Porphyrogenitus writes to his son Romanus is true: namely, that Constantine the Great had decreed that the Romans should never enter into a treaty with barbarian nations except with the Franks.

This was in fact the only way of restraining the Franks: to compel them, by treaties or by some other means, to abstain from their customary plundering.

Thus Libanius, in the panegyric addressed to the emperors Constantius and Constans, congratulates these rulers on the heavy yoke imposed upon the necks of the Franks. He adds that this yoke was nothing other than the fact that, through the valor of those rulers, the Franks were confined within their own boundaries and thereafter did not attack the Roman provinces; for to defeat excited Franks and to prevent them from becoming excited must be regarded as precisely the same thing.

[Col. 0017A]

“The Franks,” he says, “submitted to so heavy a yoke. For this is their slavery: to have no one whom they may plunder.”

### 8

When the majesty of the Roman Empire had entirely declined and no one was any longer capable of resisting Frankish arms, they crossed the Rhine not merely to plunder the provinces but to acquire a permanent settlement.

[Col. 0017B]

After first attempting this by various incursions, they gradually succeeded through various advances, acquiring now one city, now another, and now one province, now another.

The common authorities call Pharamond the first man to lay the foundations of a kingdom in Gaul. Yet both in Gregory and in Fredegar, his epitomator and the earliest continuator, there is everywhere a profound silence concerning him.

If we believe Gregory, that honor seems rather to belong to Chlodio—or, as Gregory calls him, Chlogio. Chlodio lived at the fortress of Dispargum on the border of the Thuringians, or, as others write, of the Tungrians. He first sent scouts to Cambrai and afterward occupied that city and the entire region as far as the River Somme.

This is all that Gregory records about him.

[Col. 0017C]

Of King Merovech he says only that he is said to have been born from the stock of Chlogio. His son was Childeric. Gregory alone relates his varying fortunes—namely, his expulsion from the kingdom and his restoration several years later, during which Aegidius is said to have ruled the Franks as master of the Roman soldiery.

More certain, however, are Gregory’s accounts of the expeditions of that king into Gaul, in which he is said to have captured the famous cities of Orleans and Angers.

Childeric died in Belgica Secunda, where in our own time his burial mound was discovered near Tournai. Anyone wishing for an accurate description of it should read the book on the subject published by Chifflet in 1655. The precious objects found there are kept in the Royal Library at Paris.

Gregory nowhere explicitly states whether those kings had fixed settlements in Gaul. Nevertheless, scarcely anyone can doubt that they extended their kingdom into the territory of Belgica Secunda, from which they made excursions into the other provinces of Gaul.

[Col. 0017D]

I infer that this was Gregory’s opinion from the replacement of Childeric by Aegidius. Aegidius lived in Belgica Secunda, whose royal seat, Augusta Suessionum, was still held by his son Syagrius when Chlodovechus finally expelled him from it and had him put to death after his defeat.

Chlodovechus himself, having become heir to his father’s kingdom, left nothing undone to invade the regions of Gaul, or Roman territory, that were still subject to the Romans, and to bring neighboring kingdoms under his rule as well. This gave him the occasion to put many of his kinsmen to death.

[Col. 0018A]

After killing those of the Frankish nation who were kings, destroying Syagrius, commander of the Roman forces, repeatedly defeating the Burgundians, and finally conquering the Visigoths who ruled Septimania and the neighboring provinces, he brought almost the whole of Gaul under his rule.

Establishing the seat of his kingdom at Paris, he raised that flourishing kingdom, which to this day continues by the favor of God Almighty, to the highest greatness—a kingdom whose predecessors had labored so long to lay its foundations.

### 9

It is extremely difficult to explain what form of government prevailed among the Franks before that time, what their laws or customs were, in what order kings succeeded their fathers or were chosen from the royal family, and what authority the kings ultimately possessed over their subjects.

Gregory indicates their religion in a single word when he says that they had been held by the errors of fanatics—that is, pagans—before Chlodovechus embraced the Christian religion.

[Col. 0018B]

We nevertheless infer from the same author that some of them were Arians, since he records that Lantechild, the sister of Chlodovechus, was an Arian. She had not absorbed the errors of this sect from the Gauls or Romans, who were entirely free from them, but either from her fellow tribesmen or certainly from other barbarians, almost all of whom, as everyone knows, had been infected with this poison.

Such was the Franks’ passion for fighting and their inclination toward war that, according to Libanius, the height of happiness among them lay in times of war, and even those who had lost one limb fought with the rest of their bodies intact.

[Col. 0018C]

At least once each year they assembled in one place to discuss matters of greater importance: that is, whether to advance the war against their enemies, or at least to make an incursion against neighboring peoples.

After the booty had been captured, each man received his share by lot or by some other method. We infer from Gregory himself that this was observed so scrupulously that even the king usually received nothing other than what fell to him under the common law of distribution.

### 10

These assemblies were called the Campus Martius, either after Mars, the god of war, or after the month of March, in which they were usually held. When they were later transferred by Pippin to the month of May, they were commonly called the Campus Maii, or Campus Madii.

Gregory records an assembly of the Campus Martius summoned by Chlodovechus in Book II, chapter 27, when he ordered everyone to come equipped with weapons so that they might display their splendor.

[Col. 0018D]

There is no doubt that if disputes or quarrels had arisen among any of the Franks, they too would have been settled in such assemblies.

At first these arrangements were easy. But when the kingdom had later been extended through several provinces, other assemblies, in addition to the general assembly, were summoned by the king whenever the needs of affairs required them.

Although these were sometimes called the Campus Martius or Campus Madius, they are generally designated in ancient authors by the name *placita*.

When, because of the multitude of affairs or the length of journeys, it became extremely difficult to settle every matter in one place or within the space of a few days, assemblies were established in the larger cities at fixed times. These were held by counts or other officials, and even by bishops and abbots. Matters that were not important enough to be brought before the royal palace were settled by their judgment.

[Col. 0019A]

Later, smaller assemblies were also established in villages and towns. They were presided over by officials appointed by the count, who are therefore often called vice-counts or vicars.

### 11

From this arose various ranks of officials and dignities among the Franks, whose names and duties were for the most part borrowed from the Romans.

Those who came from the most noble families but were not designated by any special title of dignity were called brave men, elders, men of greater age, leading men, foremost men, chief men, nobles, magnates, and grandees. The king was accustomed to use their counsel in the assemblies.

[Col. 0019B]

Others, having attained courtly dignities, were chancellors, referendaries, household officers, chamberlains, chamberlains, and counts of the stable. The chief among them were the princes or mayors of the palace, and so forth.

Nor should the king’s fosterers be omitted; they were commonly called *bajuli* and possessed the greatest authority with princes.

Those entrusted with the care of cities were called counts. They too had their own officials in the cities, who are frequently listed in the formula collections.

Dukes, placed over many counties, were chiefly placed in command of armies, although they also had their own soldiers, with whom they advanced to war when necessity pressed.

Those called patricians in Burgundy or Provence were distinguished from dukes in Frankish administration only by name.

Gregory mentions a tribune in one place, and elsewhere speaks of tribunitian authority.

[Col. 0019C]

Counts who saw to it that tribute and other revenues of the fisc owed in the provinces were conveyed to the ruler sometimes purchased their counties, or obtained them by gifts and money so as to remain in office.

This was why certain men of low birth were raised to such dignities.

There were also fiscal officials besides these, so called because they had charge of the royal estates. They too had under them fiscal officials and servants of various ranks, who are frequently mentioned by Gregory.

## 12

Here would be the place to inquire what distinction existed among the ancient Franks between families, and whether there was some intermediate social condition between nobles and slaves. But this question cannot be resolved without some historical record, and I have found none concerning the Franks before they established themselves in Gaul. I find only this certain: the name “Frank” designated a free man, exempt from every form of servitude.

[Col. 0019D] When, however, the Franks united with the ancient Gauls—or, as they then called them, Romans—into a single people, I find that some men were descended, as Gregory says, from the noblest and senatorial families; others were enslaved; others were born free; and still others, through the favor of their masters, were wholly or partly released from the yoke of servitude.

Those among the ancient Gauls who were distinguished either by wealth or by descent from ancient families obtained dignities, even the highest, just as the ancient Franks did, and became counts and dukes. For this reason we often read in Gregory that they are designated by the expressions “Frank” or “Roman” by origin. [Col. 0020A] We may also infer that the privileges of certain cities were preserved for their citizens, since, when a king took possession of them, the citizens required him to swear that their particular privileges would be maintained intact.

## 13

The laws used by the Frankish people before they established their permanent settlement in Gaul are no less unknown. In the panegyric mentioned above, Libanius records laws among the Franks by which it had been ordained that those who dared greater undertakings among them should also enjoy greater honors.

The Salic Law was always famous among our ancestors, and learned men have written widely about its origin and various additions. But since it is certain that the law was not transmitted to later generations in the form in which it was originally established and dictated by the still-pagan Franks, we cannot from it investigate the customs of the ancient Franks, especially in matters relating to religion.

[Col. 0020B] Fredegar, in his *Epitome*, chapter 18, describes the manner in which the envoys betrothed Chlotild to Chlodoveus. “Offering,” he says, “a solidus and a denarius, as was the custom of the Franks, they betrothed her on behalf of Chlodoveus.” In the ancient formulas preserved by Bignon, no. 5, this is said to have been done according to the Salic Law.

Our Gregory says nothing about these matters. But in Book IX of his *History*, chapter 20, he reports a copy of an agreement dealing with the dowry and the *morganegiba*—that is, the gift which a husband offered his wife on the morning of the first day of their marriage.

Theodoric was the first to purge the ancient Frankish laws of paganism; his brothers Childebert and Chlotar completed the work; and Dagobert published them, enlarged and amended, in the year 630, as is clear from the preface to that king’s capitularies, which we shall provide in the appendix.

[Col. 0020C] Gregory nowhere expressly mentions the Salic Law or any other law by name, apart from the ecclesiastical canons and Roman law. Yet from what he relates we can easily infer that the provisions of the Salic Law concerning government were always observed by the Franks with the greatest constancy.

Such is the provision in chapter 62, no. 6, which declares that no portion of Salic land should pass to a woman, but that the whole should devolve upon the male sex. From Gregory’s *History* we learn that this was carefully observed in royal successions. Nowhere do we read in him that women received a share in divisions of the kingdom. Indeed, if a king died without male children, it was not his daughters but either his brothers or his nephews who succeeded to the kingdom.

[Col. 0020D] This was the first method of dividing the kingdom among the four sons of the great Chlodoveus; and the same method was observed among the sons of Chlotar the monarch after his death. When the kings Charibert or Childebert died without male offspring, they were succeeded not by their daughters but by their brothers.

## 14

Nevertheless, such was the dignity of the daughters of kings that in reliable authors one nowhere finds any of them married to anyone other than kings. Indeed, even while they remained unmarried in their father’s house, they were called “queens”—perhaps so that they might remember that they were destined to be betrothed only to kings and joined to no other men, lest so illustrious a name be dishonored.

We likewise read that the sons of kings were often called kings, because they were destined to succeed to their father’s kingdom. For it was then an established custom among the Franks that, when a king died, the kingdom was divided according to the number of his sons. Each son was so independent in his own kingdom that none possessed any authority in the government of his brother’s kingdom.

[Col. 0021A] This is evident from what happened in the case of Guntram. He had no sons, and although he was commonly called the father of his nephews—that is, of his brothers’ sons—when he sent bishops into the kingdom of the young Chlotar to investigate, together with the leading men of that kingdom, the murder of Praetextatus in a holy place, Chlotar’s leading men declared that they would not permit it. They said that, as guardians of their king, they possessed authority, by royal sanction, to suppress wrongdoing.

In fact, Guntram was never able to prevent Melantius, who had been intruded into the see of Praetextatus by Fredegund’s action, from taking possession of the Church of Rouen.

[Col. 0021B] Kings who were underage and not yet competent or capable of governing the kingdom remained under the guardianship of their mother, if she survived, and of the kingdom’s leading men. Gregory makes this clear in the cases of Childebert, the son of Sigibert, and Chlotar, the son of Chilperic.

When Childebert had passed his fourteenth year, his uncle Guntram declared him a king—that is, capable of governing peoples by himself, or, in our language, of full age—in Book VII of the *History*, chapter 33. From the same chapter we also learn the manner in which a king was formally established. Guntram, placing a spear in Childebert’s hand, said: “This is the sign that I have handed over to you my entire kingdom.” Certainly, ancient coins teach us that the spear was among the Franks an emblem of royal power.

[Col. 0021C] Chlodoveus, however, after the killing of Sigibert, king of Cologne, and of his son, was raised upon a shield and established as their king. Sigibert, when accepted as king by the Neustrians, was placed upon a shield. We likewise read that Gundobad-Ballomer was raised up as king by his people.

Gregory repeatedly records that the supreme dominion of our kings was subject to God alone, warning them that, unless they exercised justice, God’s judgment threatened them. We have an excellent example of this in Book V of the *History*, chapter 19. There Gregory, addressing Chilperic, testifies that all bishops were indeed subject to the king, but that the king himself was subject only to God, who avenges every human crime:

“If one of us goes astray, you can correct him; but if you go astray, who will correct you? We speak to you, but if you wish, you listen; if you do not wish to, who will condemn you, except the one who has declared himself to be Justice?”

[Col. 0021D] Chlotar, the father of Chilperic, likewise acknowledged no human being above himself. After becoming sole monarch following the deaths of his brothers and their sons, and when he was near death and suffering greatly from the violence of fever, he exclaimed: “Alas, what kind of king is that heavenly one who kills such great kings?”

For this reason the Frankish kings never tolerated even the slightest appearance of subjection that might obscure their authority. In this connection, the deed of Theudebert, king of the Austrasians, is memorable. According to the Greek author Agathias, when Theudebert heard that the emperor Justinian had adopted among his other titles the name “Frankish,” as though he had at some time conquered the Franks, he mobilized his army so that, by capturing Constantinople and subjugating the empire, he might dispel the emperor’s arrogance.

[Col. 0022A] The emperor Anastasius, moreover, recognized Chlodoveus as no lesser than himself. Gregory testifies that Anastasius sent him consular letters as a token of honor and friendship. Chlodoveus should not, however, be thought to have received any authority from the emperor on this account, since at that time he already surpassed the emperor himself in power.

Nevertheless, Chlodoveus thereafter appeared in public wearing a diadem in the imperial manner and dressed in *blattea*, that is, purple clothing; he was also honored with the name of Augustus.

## 15

[Col. 0022B] Our kings did not acquire the great authority they possessed by displaying arrogance toward their peoples, like the eastern kings who were accustomed to being worshiped by their subjects, nor by the abundance of gold and riches. They won it through their love for their peoples and through the reciprocal love of their subjects for the king, which seems naturally implanted in Frankish hearts.

Hence it happened that the other nations which, as the empire declined, had established themselves in various provinces could not long retain them, because they abused their power. The Franks, however, not only preserved unharmed the provinces they acquired through their valor, but either subjected the neighboring provinces to themselves or, content with their own boundaries, made those provinces tributary.

Who does not know that, after destroying the Alans, the Vandals held Africa for scarcely a century, and that shortly afterward the Suebi in Galicia were compelled to submit to the yoke of the Visigoths? The Burgundians did not last much longer in Gaul, nor the Ostrogoths in Italy, nor the Visigoths in Septimania.

[Col. 0022C] The Franks, however, still endure in Gaul. From the very beginnings of their established kingdom they either subjected to themselves or made tributary the Alamanni, Bavarians, Thuringians, Saxons, Wends, Slavs, and other peoples. They expelled the Visigoths from Septimania, completely extinguished the kingdom of the Burgundians, terrified the Ostrogoths in Italy, and imposed tribute upon the Lombards, who had succeeded the Goths in Italy. The Lombards were so dependent upon the Franks that they did not dare appoint a king for themselves without Frankish permission.

In a word, nothing failed to obey the Franks. Even the emperors valued their friendship so highly that they sought it through frequent embassies, gifts of money, and cessions of provinces; and it came very near to the point of their paying tribute to the Franks. They would undoubtedly have done so had shame not prevented them.

[Col. 0022D] When the envoys of King Theodoric demanded such a payment from the emperor, Theophylact Simocatta says in Book VI of his *Histories* that the emperor courteously rewarded the envoys and urged the Franks to enter into an alliance without payment, since he could not endure that barbarians should exact tribute from Romans.

## 16

So great even then was the fame of the Franks, and so great was the prosperity of peoples under those rulers, that neighboring nations which had been subjected by barbarians from the remnants of the Roman Empire desired, according to Gregory’s testimony, to have the Franks as their kings. Under them, they hoped both that the Catholic religion, which they had recently embraced, would flourish and that the peoples might enjoy their freedom.

[Col. 0023A] This occurred after the conversion of Chlodoveus, when he took not only Remigius—his own apostle and that of the entire nation—but also other bishops, many of whom were then celebrated for their holiness in Gaul, as his advisers.

A letter of the blessed Remigius on this subject survives. In a few words, but with extraordinary force, it sets forth the duties of a ruler.

From that time onward the authority of the bishops began to become so great that scarcely anything was done without their advice. Gregory is witness that several of them served as envoys to foreign rulers. If disagreements arose among brothers after the division of the kingdom, they were settled through the bishops; without their intervention, scarcely anyone who had fallen from the king’s favor recovered it.

[Col. 0023B] It does not seem worthwhile to collect examples of these and similar matters, since they meet the reader everywhere in Gregory’s *History*. Certainly, when Guntram’s army performed badly in the Spanish expedition because it was eager for plunder, the king summoned four bishops together with the other leading men of the kingdom and began to investigate the conduct of the army’s commanders, as Gregory reports in Book VIII of the *History*, chapter 30.

Likewise, after the death of Praetextatus, the same ruler sent three bishops to the leading men of Chlotar’s kingdom to investigate the matter. Finally, when that same Guntram appeared to doubt the legitimacy of Chlotar’s birth—Chlotar being the son of Chilperic and Fredegund—the queen summoned, above all, the leading men of the kingdom, that is, the bishops, and confirmed by oath that her son’s birth had been legitimate.

[Col. 0023C] No one, therefore, should find it at all surprising that the bishops judged the cases of private persons in their cities, together with the counts and other officials assigned to them. This is certain from the ancient formulas and other old records, and indeed from our Gregory himself, especially when the bishops delivered judgments on the greater affairs of the kingdom.

## 17

For in their kingdoms our kings recognized no one as greater than the bishops. They knew that the bishops were Christ’s vicars and dispensers of the mysteries of God. Hence they sat first in the royal assemblies, and their names were recorded before those of anyone else.

The bishops themselves received the sons of kings from the sacred font. They were also frequently invited to the royal table, and the kings themselves asked to be fortified by their blessings. Thus King Chilperic once declared that he would not release our Gregory, just as Jacob once refused to release the angel, until he had first received a blessing from him.

[Col. 0023D] The religious devotion and piety of our kings moved them not only to confirm the ancient immunities of the clergy and of the churches that had been granted by the emperors, but also to add new privileges to the old ones.

The Church of Reims, in which they had been spiritually born in Christ, together with the basilica of the blessed Remigius, their apostle, enjoyed complete immunity, as Frodoard testifies.

Gregory relates in Book III of the *History*, chapter 25, that everything which the churches of Auvergne had customarily paid to the treasury was granted to them by King Theudebert. Childebert II is said to have confirmed this in Book X, chapter 7.

At Tours, however, not only the clergy but all the citizens were exempt from every tribute out of reverence for Saint Martin. If at any time the greed of the treasury’s officials, or any other consideration, persuaded the rulers to act otherwise, they yielded to the warnings and intercessions of the bishops.

[Col. 0024A] Chlotar I had gone somewhat further than the others in this matter. He had enacted by decree that all churches should pay part of their revenues to the treasury. While the other bishops, through fear or flattery, indulged the king’s will, Injuriosus, bishop of Tours, unwilling to tolerate so unusual a measure, departed without taking leave of the king.

Moved by this action and led to repentance, the king asked the bishop to return. He then tore up the decree with his own hands and honored Injuriosus with gifts, praising him for having inspired such salutary advice.

[Col. 0024B] Gregory writes in Book IX, chapter 30, how religiously our kings observed these matters. But the action of King Charibert deserves eternal remembrance. When Bishop Euphronius warned him that tributes had been exacted from the people of Tours by his officials, the king groaned; then, after consigning the tax registers to the flames, he sent back to the people of Tours the gold that had already been collected. He feared that what the officials had exacted in his name, even without his knowledge, might bring upon his own head the indignation of God and of Saint Martin.

## 18

How devoted our kings always were to the profession of the Catholic religion is especially clear from the fact that they never wished to marry women infected with heresy.

Sigibert took Brunichild as his wife, and his brother Chilperic took Galeswintha; both women were daughters of Athanagild, king of the Visigoths, and both were contaminated by the Arian heresy. Yet neither was admitted to the king’s bed until she had first renounced her heresy.

[Col. 0024C] Conversely, the daughters of our kings, when married to foreign kings who were alien to the Catholic faith, preserved their own religion inviolable and undefiled. The first and principal condition of their marriage agreements was that those queens should have freedom to practice their religion.

When Amalaric, who had married Chlotild, the daughter of the great Chlodoveus, attempted to violate this agreement, he paid for his treachery with the death inflicted upon him by Chlotild’s brothers. Chlotild herself remained steadfast in the Catholic faith.

Under the same conditions, Chlotsinda married Alboin, king of the Lombards; Ingund married Hermenegild, king of the Visigoths in Spain; and Bertha married the king of Kent in England. All these queens not only persevered in cultivating the Catholic faith but also inspired it in their husbands and, through them, in the peoples among whom they lived.

[Col. 0024D] Nicetius, the most holy bishop of Trier, urges Chlotsinda to this effect in a letter included here in the appendix. He exhorts her not only to preserve the integrity of her religion through virtue and holiness of life, but also to try to persuade her husband, King Alboin, and all the Lombards subject to him, of its truth.

Although Chlotsinda’s efforts were unsuccessful in Alboin’s lifetime, what she had then sown later produced growth, as one may reasonably suppose, when Agilulf, at the urging of another queen of Frankish descent—Theodelinda, as our Gregory testifies—embraced the confession of the Catholic faith together with the people subject to him.

[Col. 0025A] The same thing occurred among the Visigoths. Chlotild sowed the seed, and even by the shedding of her blood she asserted the truth of the Catholic faith during the reign of Amalaric. Ingund watered it when her husband Hermenegild, having renounced the Arian heresy, joined the Catholic faith. But the harvest was gathered in full when, under King Reccared, the entire Visigothic nation entered the Catholic Church.

Bertha’s efforts in England were no less successful. She had the good fortune to see her husband first softened by the gentleness of her character and afterward made a Christian through the preaching of Saint Augustine and the other monks sent from Italy by Gregory the Great.

Thus, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying, unbelieving husbands sanctified by believing wives enlarged the Catholic Church throughout almost the whole of Europe.

[Col. 0025B] The Burgundians had already embraced the Catholic faith, having been led to it by the example of the Franks and by the fame of the miracles of Remigius, their apostle. Avitus himself attests this in a debate against the Arians held in the presence of King Gundobad.

Thus no province in the entire West remained which did not owe its salvation to the Franks. Not without reason, therefore, did Gregory—far greater in deed than in name—offer this illustrious judgment concerning the Frankish kings in Book V, Letter 6:

“As much as royal dignity surpasses other men, so much does the summit of the Frankish kingdom surpass the kingdoms of all other peoples.”

## 19

The reverence both of the kings and of the kingdom for the Roman pontiff was so great that, although in accordance with the custom then prevailing all bishops were called apostolic men or [Col. 0025C] popes, no one among them except the Roman pontiff was called simply “pope,” that is, “father of all.”

Likewise, the name “apostolic see” designated, by way of eminence, the Roman Church, as is clear both from our Gregory and from various councils of those times.

For this reason, and because most barbarians were infected with the corruption of heresy, Catholics were designated by the name “Romans,” even by the heretics themselves.

## 20

Such, according to our Gregory, was the condition of Gaul under the great Chlodoveus and his sons and grandsons. But from this same author we must now inquire what ecclesiastical discipline prevailed among the Franks at that time.

[Col. 0025D] First, no one who is even slightly willing to examine the canons of the councils of that age will deny that episcopal elections were free and unrestricted. We also repeatedly read that these canons were approved and confirmed by the kings, lest they should appear to lack the authority due to them.

Nevertheless, if we examine Gregory’s *History* and his other works, some may think that a custom entirely contrary to these canons prevailed at that time, since we often read there that episcopal successions took place at the king’s command.

“This man,” he says, “was appointed in the place of the deceased bishop by the king’s order”; or, “That man, having obtained the king’s order after the bishop’s death”; or another, “having previously obtained a royal mandate, attained the episcopate of the widowed city, all others having been passed over.”

When Gregory uses these or similar expressions, he seems to imply that bishops were appointed not by the free election of the citizens or clergy but solely by royal authority.

[Col. 0026A] Yet if we consider Gregory’s words and the events he narrates somewhat more carefully, we shall see that the discipline of those times was such as to safeguard royal authority without undermining the force of the ecclesiastical canons.

Since, as we have observed from Gregory, the authority and dignity of bishops in the kingdom were then so great, nothing could have been more reasonable or equitable than that no one should attain this rank without the king’s consent and authority. On the other hand, if, according to the discipline of those times, churches enjoyed the freedom to elect a bishop for a vacant see, it was equally just that they should retain their legitimate rights.

[Col. 0026B] The procedure was as follows. When a bishop died, the election of a successor immediately took place in the city that had been deprived of its shepherd. The person upon whom the votes had converged—or someone acting on his behalf, or others chosen by the church itself—then brought the documents of the election to the king.

If the king judged them legitimate and detected nothing defective in the election, he accepted it; but if the citizens had agreed upon someone whom he or the kingdom regarded with suspicion, he declared the election invalid.

After accepting the election, the king wrote to the metropolitan, granting him and the bishops of his province authority to ordain the new bishop.

The fathers of the Fifth Council of Orléans expressed all this briefly in canon 10 in the year 549:

“With the king’s consent, in accordance with the election of the clergy and people, as is written in the ancient canons, the bishop shall be consecrated by the metropolitan—or by one whom he has sent in his place—together with the bishops of the province.”

[Col. 0026C] That this rule was put into practice is demonstrated by the almost innumerable passages in Gregory in which he calls the document produced by the citizens for the election their “consent,” while he calls the king’s document a *diploma*, *order*, *mandate*, or *note*.

Gregory himself shows that the expression “mandate” must not be understood as excluding an election, since he repeatedly states that the king issued his mandate after the citizens’ consent had been brought to him.

Indeed, although the royal letters or mandate made no mention of a preceding election or consent, as we infer from the formulas of Marculf, the citizens’ consent had nevertheless actually preceded it. This we learn not only from Gregory but also from the *Life of Saint Desiderius of Cahors*.

[Col. 0026D] In that *Life*, royal letters addressed to the bishops are reported, together with a note sent to Sulpicius the metropolitan. In the note the king says not a word about the election or consent of the clergy or people. Yet in the royal letters mentioned immediately above he testifies that the promotion had taken place with the consent of the abbots and of the entire clergy.

## 21

I do not, however, deny that elections made by the clergy and people were sometimes annulled by the kings—either because the electors’ votes were divided and each party approached the king with its own electoral document, or because the person elected displeased the king.

Nor would I deny that on some occasions men were appointed from the palace by the king in place of deceased bishops, even without awaiting the election of the clergy or people. [Col. 0027A] The metropolitans consecrated them after the king himself had informed them of their learning and upright conduct; but when these men first arrived in their own cities, the consent of the citizens or clergy was requested.

This custom greatly weakened the freedom of elections. Unknown to the councils and introduced gradually and imperceptibly, it was first inserted at Chlotar II’s direction into the edict confirming the Fifth Synod of Paris, in the year 615, so that thereafter it might have the force of law:

“When a bishop dies, the person who is to be ordained in his place by the metropolitan together with the bishops of the province shall be elected by the clergy and people; and if he is a suitable person, he shall be ordained by the ruler’s command.”

[Col. 0027B] This later rule adds a new provision to the first rule concerning ordinations which we saw in the Fifth Council of Orléans: “or indeed, if he is chosen from the palace, let him be ordained on account of the merit of his character and learning.”

This new custom, however, became the occasion of many evils in the Church. It favored the efforts of ambitious men, especially royal officials, who later grasped the wealthier bishoprics. They were immediately made bishops from among the laity and caused no small diminution of the holiness of the Gallican Church.

Others obtained royal mandates through money and gifts, others through flattery, and still others through the offices of royal ministers whom they had corrupted. In this way they introduced what was called the Simoniacal heresy. Hence we read of so many canons against neophytes and Simoniacs enacted in the Gallican councils of that period. Yet these canons, like the letters of the Roman pontiffs—especially those of Gregory the Great—were never adequate to eradicate so wicked a plague.

I omit certain particular examples. Since they were contrary to the rules, they ought not to have become law.

[Col. 0027C] Thus, in certain distant provinces, several bishops were consecrated without the king’s permission, either because the king overlooked the matter or because, owing to his youth or to disturbances in the kingdom, he paid no attention to it.

The boldness of the bishops of Aquitaine II was greater. They expelled Eumerius, bishop of Saintes, from his seat because he had been consecrated by royal command without the metropolitan’s advice. But when Charibert learned of this, he ordered Eumerius to be restored to his see and, as Gregory reports, imposed a penalty upon the bishops who had undertaken such an act.

Charibert did not, however, become so enraged with the bishops because they had wished to examine Eumerius’s ordination—for the canons permitted them to do so—but because they had expelled from his see, without the king’s judgment, a man who had long held the episcopate with royal authority.

## 22

[Col. 0027D] In Gregory’s books one nowhere finds the transfer of bishops from one see to another, except in the case of those who, expelled from their own cities by order of heretical rulers, came into the Frankish kingdom and were placed over vacant churches—a practice the Church always approved.

There are several instances of coadjutors being appointed while the incumbent bishop was still living. They were ordained either through royal favor or for some other reason, with the expectation that they would eventually succeed to a particular church.

But they were not appointed under the empty title used today, nor were they ordained in the very church that they were eventually to obtain. Rather, as though a new bishopric were being established, they held office in a fortress belonging to their future diocese, with jurisdiction assigned to them over several neighboring villages.

Thus Munderic was ordained at Tournus, Aventinus at Châteaudun, and Austrapius at the fortress of Sellensis.

[Col. 0028A] Our Gregory refused to ordain Burgundio as coadjutor, although Burgundio was the nephew of Felix, bishop of Nantes—first because he was a neophyte, and second because the sacred canons forbade anyone to be substituted for a bishop while the latter was still alive, as Gregory himself relates in Book VI, chapter 5.

For this reason, what the same Gregory reports concerning the bishops Theodore and Proculus, driven from Burgundy, should seem altogether unusual. They are said to have governed the Church of Tours jointly after the death of Licinius or Leo. I therefore think that they should be called administrators rather than bishops of Tours.

Sometimes, however, bishops—even very holy ones—designated as their successor someone from their own clergy whom they knew to be more suitable than the others for that ministry.

Thus Sacerdos, bishop of Lyon, when near death, appealed to King Childebert to arrange for Nicetius to be substituted for him in the see of Lyon.

[Col. 0028B] Maurilius, bishop of Cahors, afflicted with gout and foreseeing serious future disputes concerning his successor, pleaded that Ursicinus be substituted for him while he was still alive.

The same had been done, as we just mentioned, by Felix, bishop of Nantes. He had drawn up a document on the matter and arranged for it to be strengthened by the signatures of the bishops of the province.

Gregory mentions not a single chorepiscopus, unless that name is given to those who, as we have just said, were ordained in fortresses. For Munderic, whom we said had held office at the fortress of Tournus, was ordained, Gregory says, “so that, while Saint Tetricus, who was then bishop of Langres, was alive, he might govern the fortress of Tournus as archpriest and reside there.”

## 23

[Col. 0028C] Ordinations belonged to the metropolitans within each of their respective provinces.

Thus Gregory, in Book IV of the *History*, chapter 35—a passage lacking in earlier printed editions—relates the ordination of Avitus, bishop of Auvergne, which took place at Metz by order of King Sigibert, and observes that the canonical rigor was not observed in this matter.

Gregory himself, however, was consecrated at Reims by Aegidius, the metropolitan of that city, as Fortunatus sings; neither of them was ever reproached for this act.

When the same Aegidius attempted not only to ordain bishops but also to establish a bishopric at Châteaudun, which lies within the diocese of Chartres, he was severely rebuked by the bishops of the Fourth Council of Paris, because he had undertaken so unusual an act beyond the boundaries of his own city and province.

[Col. 0028D] And rightly so, since even he himself was not permitted to do this by virtue of the vicariate of the apostolic see granted to his church in the time of Saint Remigius. Such privileges were granted only with the rights of the metropolitans preserved intact.

Hence the bishopric of Châteaudun, which had been established by a rash act contrary to the provisions of the canons, soon fell. The Church of Laon, however, which had been established by Saint Remigius, remained and continues to this day, because when he established it in a fortress of his own diocese he wronged no one.

[Col. 0029A] King Childebert I likewise attempted to establish a new bishopric at the fortress of Melun. But when Leo, bishop of Sens, whose diocese included that place, protested, the matter came to nothing.

The bishopric of Arisitum likewise disappeared. The Goths had established it by removing several villages from the diocese of Rodez—villages that obeyed them—and assigning them to the new see.

## 24

The canons never permitted anyone to be promoted from the lay state to the priesthood without first passing through the several grades of ministry. Although this rule was frequently violated, more religious bishops nevertheless always observed it.

Gregory gives an illustrious example from his own conduct in the passage already cited from Book V of the *History*, chapter 15. Burgundio, the nephew of Bishop Felix, approached him with the support of his uncle and of the other bishops of the province, seeking to be consecrated bishop. Gregory replied:

[Col. 0029B] “We have it written in the canons that no one may advance to the episcopate unless he has first regularly received the ecclesiastical orders.”

He then instructed Burgundio about what he had to do to show himself worthy of episcopal honor.

From the same Gregory, in Book IV, chapter 6, we learn through what grades one was canonically required to ascend in order to attain so great a dignity. Cato the priest explains that he had received the clerical grades according to canonical institution in these words:

“I was a lector for ten years; I served in the office of subdeacon for five years; I was devoted to the diaconate for fifteen years; and for twenty years now I have enjoyed the honor of the priesthood.”

Nicetius, who later became bishop of Lyon, was not ordained priest until he was thirty years old.

These were the requirements of the rule. In practice, however, the contrary custom prevailed to a considerable extent, introduced by various circumstances.

[Col. 0029C] Some of those circumstances were legitimate: the needs of the Church, or the remarkable holiness of certain men, demonstrated by illustrious deeds or even miracles.

The readiness of certain bishops, however, was rightly disapproved, as is clear from the example of Burgundio, mentioned more than once. The bishops of the province of Lyon III had agreed to his promotion while he was still a layman, but our Gregory, a vigorous defender of the canons, prevented it by his authority.

The ambition of others was likewise condemned. These men obtained bishoprics through royal authority and tried to command others before they had learned, as Gregory the Great says, to obey.

[Col. 0029D] I believe, nevertheless, that men of this kind were tested for some days in the clerical state before being consecrated. Gregory our author observes this concerning Badegesil: after being tonsured and ascending the grades through which clerics pass, he became, forty days later, the successor of the deceased Domnolus, bishop of Le Mans.

### 25

As regards councils, some were provincial, consisting of the bishops of a single province; others comprised the entire nation or kingdom. The former were convened by each metropolitan at fixed times, according to the prescriptions of the canons. The summons to the latter, however, belonged to the king; and although their bishops might perhaps belong to different kingdoms, they were nevertheless readily compelled by the mutual consent of all the kings. At these councils matters of faith and more important affairs were dealt with, or at least peace was negotiated between kings. We learn this from Gregory, Book IX of the *History*, chapter 20. When King Guntram had said that a synod ought to be convened from all the provinces of Gaul, Gregory—who was then an envoy of King Childebert—replied that the celebration of so great a synod seemed unnecessary, since no new heresy had then arisen and no danger threatened the faith; it was enough, therefore, for each metropolitan to meet, according to the custom of the canons, with those subject to him.

Mapinius, however, bishop of Reims, refused to go to the Council of Toul, summoned by King Theudebald, because the king had not disclosed to him the reason for the summons. From this we infer that bishops, at least those of the principal sees, ought to have been informed beforehand of the matters to be treated in such councils. Indeed, on that occasion Mapinius reproved Nicetius of Trier because, instead of appealing to him, he had gone to the king to restrain the insolence of certain wicked men. We shall give his letter in the appendix, together with another letter of King Sigebert, in which he orders Desiderius of Cahors not to attend a synod that had been summoned without consulting him.

### 26

Moreover, from Guntram’s response to the words of Gregory cited above, it is clear that the cases of bishops were among the principal reasons why councils of all the bishops of the nation were to be convened. “That matter of God,” he says, “stands above all others: you must inquire why Bishop Praetextatus was killed by the sword in a church, and then investigate the dissensions among the bishops and the various crimes of which some of them are accused.”

Indeed, even kings themselves referred to councils the cases of bishops whom they believed to have been disloyal to them. This is clear in the case of Praetextatus, whom King Chilperic accused at the Council of Paris as though he were guilty of treason. Our own Gregory likewise, when accused by Count Bladaste of spreading malicious rumors against Queen Fredegund, cleared himself by an oath at the Council of Brennac.

Nor may we omit the distinguished deed of Childebert II. He had ordered Aegidius, bishop of Reims, to be brought to Metz. Aegidius was indeed guilty of many crimes, but had not yet been heard at any synod. When other bishops rebuked the king, he ordered Aegidius to be restored safely to his city. Later, however, Aegidius was found guilty of lèse-majesté at a synod of bishops held at Metz, deprived of his episcopal see, and sent by the king into exile at Strasbourg.

Furthermore, not every man was admitted as a witness against bishops. Thus, when certain witnesses of inferior rank had been heard against Gregory at the Council of Brennac, the bishops complained about the matter. Since Gregory could not be convicted of any crime by the testimony of the witnesses, and the case seemed to remain undecided, after Mass had been said at three altars, he cleared himself by an oath. Yet he declared that he had done this not without suffering an affront, since it was contrary to the canons.

If those condemned at these councils refused to accept their sentences, they still had recourse to the Apostolic See. Thus, when Bishops Sagittarius and Salonius complained that they had been unjustly deposed at the Council of Lyon, they first obtained permission from King Guntram and then went to Rome with his letters of recommendation. There they were heard by Pope John and, at his command, restored to their sees, as Gregory relates in Book V of the *History*, chapter 21.

### 27

From Gregory’s words and actions we may gather how great was the reverence then shown by the Gallican Church toward the sacred canons. Aegidius, bishop of Reims, was driven from his seat only after the sanctions of the canons had been read, once he had been found guilty of conspiracy against the king.

Everyone knows with what courage and constancy Gregory defended the authority of the canons against the king himself and his queen in the case of Praetextatus. Neither threats, flattery, nor gold or silver could ever move him away from observing them. Accordingly, whenever some difficulty arose in the conduct of affairs, he thought it should be resolved by producing the words of the canons.

Thus he refuted the obstinacy of Bertegundis, who had abandoned her husband and fled to the monastery of Tours, by rereading the Nicene canon. In the same way he responded to the petition of Burgundio, who insistently demanded that he be installed in the see of Nantes while Bishop Felix was still living.

We infer that the code of canons then used by the Gallican Church was different from the collection of Dionysius Exiguus, both from the Nicene canon—which, although cited by Gregory, is not found in Dionysius—and from the new gathering of leaves sewn into the codex by King Chilperic against Praetextatus. Gregory states that in this gathering there were canons described as apostolic, which occupy a place in the codex of Dionysius; consequently, they were absent from the genuine code of the Gallican canons.

### 28

At that time the bishops carefully visited their dioceses, traveling through the villages and towns subject to their authority, as is certain from numerous passages in Gregory. Most of them were accustomed at fixed times to withdraw to monasteries or solitary places, so that, refreshed there by prayer and spiritual exercises, they might return more vigorous to the care of the souls entrusted to them. In some places they used to do this with solemn ceremony on the day of the Lord’s Supper.

Although those holy bishops always endeavored to be present among the churches entrusted to them, they took particular care to remain with their people whenever those communities were afflicted by some calamity. Thus, when a bubonic plague was devastating the city of Albi, Salvius, then the most holy bishop of that church, “like a good shepherd,” says Gregory, refused ever to leave the city. Theodorus, bishop of Marseille, on learning while absent that a very severe plague was raging in his city, immediately returned and, devoting himself to prayers and vigils at the tomb of Saint Victor, tried to incline God toward mercy.

### 29

The resources of the churches were chiefly entrusted to the administration and authority of the bishops, and were to be distributed at their direction. Hence they were also called nour­ishers of the poor and widows. When a certain Goth had seized the property of the Church of Agde, Bishop Leo warned him not to invade “the possessions of the poor, which,” he said, “God has entrusted to our administration,” if he did not wish to be killed by their tears, since they were to be supported from those revenues.

For this purpose there were catalogues in the churches, called *matriculae*, in which the poor of the church were registered and sustained from ecclesiastical property and the offerings of the faithful. Bishops sometimes also gave others letters signed in their own hand, so that the faithful, moved by them, might more readily give alms to those who requested them.

Finally, such was the reverence shown by everyone toward the bishops—“whom the Holy Spirit has placed to govern the Church of God”—that the following saying became universally accepted: “For even this cannot be accepted without heresy,” says Gregory in Book II, chapter 23, “that in the church the priest should not be obeyed.” By this title, here and elsewhere, he designates the bishop.

### 30

The distribution of the Church’s resources belonged to the archdeacons. Their care extended not only to the support of the poor but also to that of the clergy, who, at least in most churches, lived a common life. This, unless I am mistaken, is what Gregory calls the “canons’ table.” In the final book of the *History*, chapter 30, section 16, he writes that this had been established by Baudinus at Tours.

The same is understood from chapter 9 of the *Life of the Fathers*. Patroclus, who then resided at Bourges, neglected to join the other clerics at the meal of the canonical table. While the others refreshed their bodies, he preferred to devote himself to prayer and sacred reading. The archdeacon severely rebuked him and warned him either to eat with the other brothers or at least to leave the place. He did not consider it right for one man to pretend to share no food with those with whom he was thought to be fulfilling an ecclesiastical office.

The same book shows that the archdeacon was charged with the instruction of the clergy and served as head of the school, as Gregory frequently implies. We nowhere read, however, that the cleric whom Aetherius had placed over the school of Lisieux was a deacon. The archdeacons, although in charge of the schools, were distracted by many responsibilities and therefore arranged for younger clerics to be instructed by others.

### 31

Those placed in charge of rural churches, which we today call parishes or pastoral districts, were called presbyters. Gregory sometimes calls them archpresbyters, either because they presided over neighboring presbyters, as happens today, or because they had several clerics under their discipline in their own church.

There were also other lesser clerics placed over certain churches. One such was Cautinus, later bishop of Clermont, who, in Book *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 30, is said to have governed the Church of Issoire during his diaconate. Urbanus, a deacon, became the keeper of the shrine of Saint Julian of Brioude.

Indeed, in Book I *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 66, Gregory mentions a small oratory consecrated to Saint Patroclus at Troyes, served by only one cleric, whom he shortly afterward calls a lector. The same author also mentions men who lived alone, or at least with very few companions, in sacred places. There is no opportunity to discuss them at greater length here.

### 32

Clerics, at least those of the lower orders, did not necessarily have to be assigned to this office by their own bishops. Some, depending on the circumstances of time or place, were admitted to the clergy by any bishop or abbot, in accordance with their own wishes or those of their parents. Thus Gregory himself relates that he ordained Winnoc, who had recently been brought from Britain into his diocese, as a presbyter, so that he might keep him with him.

Those who had once been ordained in any church could not transfer to another, nor could they remain for any considerable length of time in another diocese without the permission of the bishop who had ordained them. Thus, when Theodulf, who had been ordained a deacon at Paris, moved to Angers, he was repeatedly excommunicated by Ragnemod, bishop of Paris, as Gregory relates in Book X of the *History*, chapter 14, because he delayed returning to the church in which he had been ordained a deacon.

Abbots also trained clerics in their monasteries, as Gregory attests frequently, especially in his books of miracles. From this arose the custom by which the names “monk” and “cleric” were used interchangeably of monks. The learned Louis Thomassin proves this at length.

Indeed, those destined for ordination, even to the priesthood, were educated in monasteries. This is clear from the example of Meroveus, son of King Chilperic, who was placed in the monastery of Aninsola to be instructed in the priestly discipline.

### 33
