The clerical state was often a convenient refuge from impending death, especially for men of rank whom suspicious kings feared might stir up disturbances. Certainly King Chararic, captured by Chlodovech together with his son, escaped the danger of death in no other way. They were later compelled to undergo it when, having abandoned the clerical state, they wished to return to secular life.

This is why Chlodoald, son of Chlodomer, was no longer sought out for death by his uncles: he had had his hair cut and had been ordained a presbyter. Nor had those same kings demanded anything else from Chlotilde except that she allow her grandsons to become clerics, if she wished them to be rescued from death.

No one should suppose that such men were ordained by bishops against their will and while protesting. The Church never permitted this. Rather, as Thomassin aptly observed, they were ordained willingly—indeed, most eagerly—because they were certain that no other way remained to secure their own lives.

Several such men are encountered in various places who, for the rest of their lives, devoted themselves so diligently to pious exercises that they ultimately deserved to be counted among the saints. Yet we admit that there were others who later regained their former liberty and, abandoning their undertaking, married or returned to their own wives. They argued that, having been ordained by force, they were not bound by any laws of continence. The Church, however, never tolerated this with impunity; through various canons it condemned such presumption.

Our Gregory calls this crime apostasy in Book IV of the *History*, chapter 4, where he recounts the deed of Macliavus, count of the Britons. When Macliavus had been ordained bishop of Vannes in the extremity of his distress and later, after Chanao’s death, took back his wife, he was excommunicated by the other bishops.

Gregory frequently mentions bishops who had been married before their ordination, but immediately adds that, according to the prescriptions of the canons, they had been separated from one another. In Book *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 78, he calls this “the order of Catholic institution,” intending to show that the practice was observed uniformly throughout the entire Catholic Church, not merely in one region or another.

Hence great scandal arose among the people if a bishop was thought to have had any relations with his own wife. Bishop Aetherius of Lisieux had many small beds for clerics around his own bed, plainly so that they might serve as witnesses to his continence.

Bishops slept in houses that Gregory commonly calls “the houses of the Church” or “ecclesiastical houses.” These stood beside the church, so that bishops and clerics might have easier access to it. Women were more rarely permitted to enter such houses. Indeed, it had long been the custom in the Church of Lyon that a woman should not enter the church house. When the wife of Bishop Priscus violated this prohibition, she was punished by divine judgment, as we learn from Book IV of Gregory’s *History*, chapter 36. We supplied this passage from the Casinensis manuscript, since it was missing from earlier editions.

### 34

At that time, clerics were distinguished from secular men no less by their clothing and outward appearance than by their morals. Meroveus had for some time been held under guard by his father Chilperic. Later, after he had been tonsured and had changed into the clothing customarily worn by clerics, “he was ordained a presbyter,” says our Gregory in Book V, chapter 14. Hence, when he later abandoned the clerical state and fled, he is said to have been dressed in secular clothing.

Elsewhere, Saint Martin is said to have appeared to someone dressed in black. No one will deny that clerics, like monks, were tonsured at that time. Louis Thomassin, however, believes that the first evidence for the clerical crown belongs to our Gregory. He admits that clerics had previously been tonsured but not marked by a crown of hair.

Gregory’s passage occurs in the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 17, where he relates that Nicetius, later bishop of Trier, emerged from his mother’s womb with the hairs on his head arranged in such a way that one might think a clerical crown had been marked out by them.

### 35

By Gregory’s time the monastic order was so closely joined to the clerical state that to be a monk and to be a cleric were effectively the same thing. Louis Thomassin proves this at length and, as is his custom, learnedly. Indeed, as we observe in various places, those whom Gregory calls clerics at the beginning of a chapter he later calls monks.

This is not surprising, since in those times, and already long before them, monks performed all clerical duties and devoted their principal attention to the celebration of the divine offices. Abbots even ordained clerics, as we have just said. Whenever something solemn had to be done in the Church, the bishops immediately summoned the abbots and presbyters of their dioceses, as Gregory frequently records.

The holiest bishops of that age held monks in such high regard that scarcely one of them can be found who did not establish some monastery. When traveling, Gregory was accustomed to turn aside to monasteries so that he might enjoy the holy conduct of the monks living there and learn the distinguished deeds of their predecessors. From these visits he gathered the many remarkable deeds of holy men that he later published both in the books *On the Glory of the Confessors* and in the *Lives of the Fathers*.

He also did not think it unworthy of the history of our people to insert the deaths and miracles of holy monks, so that the minds of his readers might be refreshed by this variety of events and encouraged by such narratives to imitate examples of their virtues.

### 36

The monks’ reverence and obedience toward bishops were no less great. This may be confirmed by the single example of the monk Ulfilaicus. Gregory relates in Book VIII of the *History*, chapter 15, that when the bishops ordered him to descend from the column on which he sat in imitation of the Stylites, he immediately obeyed, saying that it was a crime not to obey priests. He preferred to lead a common life with the other monks rather than strive for perfection while acting contrary to the commands of priests.

Gregory nowhere explains whether certain monasteries at that time were exempt from episcopal jurisdiction. We nevertheless learn from him that, in monasteries under royal protection, bishops had no authority without a special command of the prince.

When Maroveus, bishop of Poitiers, refused to take charge of the monastery of Saint Radegund, which had been built in his own city, and declined to perform the translation of the Holy Cross, which was being urgently requested of him, Radegund went to King Sigebert. He entrusted this responsibility to Euphronius, bishop of Tours.

Once the monastery had been placed under the king’s protection, the bishop of Poitiers could govern it regularly, like the other monasteries of his diocese, only after obtaining a special royal directive from Childebert, as Gregory states in Book IX of the *History*, chapter 40.

After Radegund’s death, when Bishop Maroveus was absent from the city, Gregory, who was present, could scarcely be persuaded to conduct her funeral, because the monastery cemetery had not yet been consecrated by priestly blessing. Only after everyone present had earnestly requested it did he presume, out of affection for his brother, to consecrate the altar; even then, however, he did not cover the body with earth in the cemetery, reserving that act for the local bishop.

### 37

The abbots and abbesses were elected by the common votes of the monks or nuns, but they had to receive their blessing from the bishops. That the clothing of consecrated women differed from secular clothing is also demonstrated by the fact that Gregory frequently records, when recounting the conversion of women religious and monks, that both went off to monasteries after changing their clothing.

Whether all sacred virgins were completely tonsured, however, is not entirely clear. Certainly, when Gregory recounts that men were sent by Chrodielde and her followers into the monastery of the Holy Cross to drag away the abbess by force, he says that they fell upon the superior Justina, whom he affirms was seized by those assassins with her hair unbound.

Other monuments of that period could also confirm that consecrated virgins then kept their hair. Yet there are also sources that suggest the contrary view. On this question one may consult Hugh Menard in his observations on the Gregorian sacramentary, or Mabillon in his notes on the *Life of Saint Gertrude, Abbess of Nivelles*, found in the eleventh volume of the Benedictine *Acta Sanctorum*. There he also discusses the little caps of consecrated virgins, which seem to have been succeeded by the linen coverings that Gregory records Justina as having worn on her head.

The virgin Papula, however, in Book *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 16, bade farewell to the world by cutting off her hair, but she did so in order to disguise herself as a man. It is certain that monks did not grow long hair; Papula spent the rest of her life among them in male dress.

That consecrated women were distinguished from laywomen may also be understood from a passage in Gregory where Radegund declares that she had been freed from lay bonds and had passed over to the religious rule. It is also clear there that the word “religion” already designated the monastic order at that time; this could easily be demonstrated from many other passages. From this usage arose the terms “religious men” and “religious women.”

Gregory also frequently calls the sacred virgins who lived in monasteries *sanctimoniales*, or nuns. Just as men were forbidden to enter the convents of nuns, so women were barred from men’s monasteries. In most monasteries they were not even allowed access to the church. This is clear in the case of Condat, from the *Life of Saint Romanus*, that is, chapter 1 of the *Lives of the Fathers*.

Although monks who were not recluses were permitted to leave the monastery, this was so strictly forbidden to the nuns of the Holy Cross at Poitiers by the rule of Saint Caesarius that they were not even allowed to go to the cemetery to bury the body of blessed Radegund.

We learn this from Gregory in *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 106. In describing the funeral of the blessed queen, he presents the clerics as escorting the body with psalmody, while the nuns followed only with their eyes and tears, lamenting and weeping from the windows and battlements of the walls.

We also infer from Book X, chapter 29, that several rules coexisted in monasteries of men. Gregory writes that in the monastery of Agaune the rules not only of Cassian but also of Basil and of the other abbots who established monastic life were in force.

### 38

Although everyone admits that the principal occupation of clerics and monks was always prayer and the study of the sacred Scriptures, some have nevertheless believed that the custom of reciting the divine office publicly or privately at fixed hours was not very ancient.

Our Gregory, however, traces its origin to the very beginnings of the Gallican Church. In Book I of the *History*, chapter 29, speaking of a certain holy man who is said to have established the Church of Bourges shortly after the time of Decius, he says:

> “The clerics ordained by him undertake the rite of psalmody, and they are instructed in how they should build the church and celebrate solemn rites for almighty God.”

Once peace had been granted to the Church, who could deny that the divine offices were celebrated publicly in the churches? The same was done in monasteries, not only the larger ones but also those in which only a few monks lived, as is certain from various passages in Gregory. He sometimes calls this daily obligation of psalmody the “office of the Lord.”

He frequently mentions night vigils celebrated both by himself and by others. From these passages we understand that Matins, or Lauds as we now call them, was separated from the vigils by some interval of time. This is clear from one passage in Book I *On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 33. After spending the night vigils in the church, he says that he withdrew when the signal for Matins was given.

In this passage and in chapter 2 of Book II he implies that the office of Matins was customarily celebrated in the morning—that is, when the sky was growing light, as he says in the *Life of Saint Gall*, among the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 6. From that *Life* we also learn that nearly the same psalms which we sing today at Lauds were already recited at that hour.

When the holy man, near death, asked what was being sung in the church, he was told that the clerics were singing the blessings. Then, after the fiftieth psalm and the blessing had been sung, and the Alleluia with its brief conclusion had been completed, he finished Matins.

I would not deny, however, that Gregory sometimes also called the night vigils Matins. In chapter 23 of Book III *On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, he says that a signal was given at the morning hours and that the people celebrated the vigils.

He says that Terce and Sext were instituted in the Church of Tours by Bishop Injuriosus, in Book X, the final chapter of the *History*. He calls it “the course of the third hour” in chapter 96 of *On the Glory of the Confessors*.

He mentions Vespers, which some writers of his age called the *Lucernarium*, in *On the Miracles of Saint Julian*, chapter 20. There he recounts the story of a certain thief who, after the people had left following the evening grace, remained hidden in the basilica. Night had come and was already covering the world with darkness when the clerics of Saint Peter of Bordeaux entered the church, recited the appointed sections of the psalms, and departed.

No specific mention of the other hours occurs in this author, but he commonly includes them all under the general term “the course of the divine office.” He states in *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 47, that the office was performed in the church by alternating choirs.

### 39

We would, as may reasonably be conjectured, possess a full and complete account of the course of the Gallican Church if the treatise that our Gregory wrote on that subject had survived to us.

Walafrid Strabo, in *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 25, testifies that the psalms, according to the revision which Father Jerome had made from the Septuagint edition, were introduced into the churches of Gaul from the Roman regions by Gregory, bishop of Tours.

But Peter Pithoeus called this into question, since it was written by Strabo alone. Our Mabillon, however, altogether denies it in his *Treatise on the Gallican Office*, chiefly because Gregory himself consistently praises another version, particularly in the books of the *History* that he composed last, where he frequently cites several passages from the psalms that were read in the ecclesiastical office.

The same is confirmed by the preface of Gregory himself to the psalms, a fragment of which has been appended to this edition. In it, the headings of the psalms that Gregory undertakes to explain all follow the edition of the Septuagint translators.

We may infer from the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 12, that the divine office was not then celebrated in the vernacular. There it is said of Brachio, who had submitted himself to Aemilianus for conversion, that he did not know what he was singing because he did not know letters—that is, the Latin language.

### 40

We shall demonstrate from various passages and examples in Gregory how diligent ecclesiastics of every rank were in performing these offices at the appointed hours even in private, whenever they could not be present with the others.

While staying at Paris, Gregory himself lived near the church of Saint Julian, which he visited at midnight in order to complete his course. Similarly, Gregory, bishop of Langres, had a house at Dijon adjoining a baptistery in which relics of many saints were kept. He visited this sacred place every night and, after completing his course there, returned to bed.

The diligence of the most blessed Germanus, bishop of Paris, in performing such offices is altogether worthy of remembrance and praise. Even while riding on journeys, if he could not do otherwise, he recited the course bareheaded, as Fortunatus records in his *Life*, even when snow or rain was pressing upon him.

Gallus, bishop of Clermont, near death asked, as we have just said, what office was being sung in the church. When he was told that the clerics were completing the blessings, he himself recited the office. After completing the morning course, he died.

Those holy men did not think that they were permitted to omit the divine office. Certainly, when Portianus—whose *Life* Gregory included among the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 5—was being pressed by a nobleman at the court of King Theoderic to taste a little wine, the most holy abbot refused, chiefly because he had not yet paid the Lord the debt of psalmody.

Elsewhere a certain presbyter is praised because, according to the custom of priests, he rose at night from his bed and prayed.

Finally—and it is not possible to produce all Gregory’s passages relevant to this subject—Bishops Salonius and Sagittarius, notorious for their crimes, are severely rebuked by Gregory in Book V, chapter 21, because there was no mention of God among them and absolutely no remembrance of the divine office.

This concerns the obligations of clerics. Although laypeople were exempt from such a burden, they nevertheless attended the divine offices, especially the nocturnal vigils, at least on Sundays and feast days. Thus, in the book *On the Virtues of Saint Julian*, Fedamia is rebuked because, while the others were celebrating the night watches, she alone lay in bed devoted to sleep.

At such solemn celebrations, banquets were prepared for the clerics and for the poor registered in the *matricula*, or catalogue, and sometimes also for distinguished men, especially in the larger churches where the bishop celebrated. Gregory testifies more than once that these banquets took place in the church house.

### 41

Our Gregory is no less useful for discovering the rite of the Gallican liturgy than for explaining the parts of the divine office. We cannot help regretting the loss of the book *On the Masses Composed by Saint Apollinaris Sidonius*, to which our Gregory had added a preface, as he himself testifies in Book II of the *History*, chapter 22. From it we would have learned the entire sequence of our liturgy.

This passage of Gregory refutes the opinion of those who have written that the Gallican liturgy was borrowed from the Mozarabic rite. Other passages in Gregory make it certain that the Gallican liturgy had been established long before Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, whom they consider the author of the Mozarabic rite.

One example will suffice here, from the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 17. Speaking of the lessons that were recited during the solemn celebration of Mass in the presence of King Theudebert, Gregory says:

> “After the lessons had been read which the ancient canon prescribed.”

That rite of celebrating Mass in the Gallican Church was therefore already ancient at that time, before Isidore occupied the see of Seville.

This was the constant tradition of our fathers, which Hilduin, abbot of Saint-Denis, confirmed in the ninth century when writing to Louis the Pious. He asserts that a particular order of the Mass, according to Gallican custom, had been used from the beginning of the received faith in these regions of Gaul.

What that order was may be understood from the ancient liturgies edited by the very distinguished Joseph Thomas, a regular priest, and by our Mabillon. On the basis of numerous testimonies from our Gregory, as well as other ancient monuments and compelling arguments, they established that these liturgies were genuinely Gallican.

What the parts of the liturgy were, and what rite was used in celebrating it, must be determined from Gregory’s writings.

### 42

We learn chiefly from Book IV of the *History*, chapter 16, that three readings from various books of Sacred Scripture were read at the beginning of Mass. The first was ordinarily taken from the Prophets, the second from the canonical Epistles, and finally the third from the Gospel. Bishop Palladius himself was reading the prophecy during the celebration when King Guntram, who was present, forbade him to continue the Mass.

Gregory indicates more than once that the passions of martyrs and the lives of confessors were sometimes read during the solemnities of Mass, though nowhere does he state clearly enough at what point this reading took place. Nevertheless, we infer that it was performed in place of the first reading from the Gallican Lectionary of Luxeuil, edited by Mabillon, where, on the feast of Saints Peter and Paul, the prophecy is omitted and the passion of the apostles is prescribed for reading.

This is made still clearer by the Bobbio Sacramentary, likewise edited by Mabillon in volume I of the *Museum Italicum*. There, in Masses for the liturgical season, three readings are everywhere given, [Col. 0040A] whereas on the birthdays of the saints only two are recorded. We conjecture that, in place of the first reading, lives of such saints were read from another codex.

Gregory himself suggests the same in chapter 86 of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, where he says:

> After the passion of Saint Polycarp, whose feast was being celebrated, had been read together with the other readings introduced by the priestly canon, the time came for the sacrifice to be offered.

That such Acts of the Saints were recited by a lector is attested by Gregory in Book II of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 49. I would not deny that by the term “lector” a cleric specially appointed for this purpose is to be understood, although they could also have been read by other senior clerics.

The same Gregory mentions, in Book VIII, chapter 3, a psalm of response that had been sung by a deacon during Mass before [Col. 0040B] the king. We have no doubt that this took place between the two readings, at the time when the gradual is sung today.

When these things had been completed, the deacon solemnly proceeded to read the Gospel, as reported in Book VIII, chapter 4. When he announced the Gospel reading, the entire people responded by giving glory to God, perhaps in the same words that we still use today. For Guntram, in the passage of Gregory just cited, relates that the people’s response to the deacon announcing the Gospel reading was the same as their response to a man who had announced to King Sigibert that a son had been born to him. “Hence,” he says, “it happened that the whole people proclaimed alike at both announcements: ‘Glory to almighty God.’”

### 43

When the readings had been completed, the deacon enjoined silence upon the people so that they might listen to the Mass, as we learn from Gregory’s Book VII, chapter 8. The celebrant then briefly instructed those present concerning the solemnity being observed; after giving this admonition, he added a prayer, or collect, which in the old Bobbio Sacramentary is commonly called the *Missa*.

Taking advantage of this silence, as Gregory relates in the same passage, King Guntram once adjured those present not to kill him, as had happened to his brothers. Immediately the entire people poured forth a prayer to the Lord for the king’s safety.

### 44

“When the time for offering the sacrifice had arrived,” Gregory says in Book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 86, “the deacon brought from the sacristy the tower in which the mystery of the Lord’s body was contained,” as it seems to me.

The people made the offering of bread and wine. The gifts, after the offering, were placed upon the altar and covered with a cloth or pall, which had to be sufficiently large to cover both the altar and the offerings at once.

Gregory calls it a silk pall in Book VII, chapter 22. In the *Life of Saint Nicetius of Lyons*, however, a Sarmatian covering is said to have been offered for this purpose. The holy bishop refused to accept it because it was not large enough to cover the altar together with the sacred gifts, and because it was so thinly woven that the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood could not adequately be covered by it.

The pall that covered the altar outside the solemnities of Mass was different from these. We learn this from Book X, chapter 15, where Justina is said to have been covered with an altar cloth [Col. 0041A] at the time when furious men entered the monastery at Poitiers and attempted to carry off the abbess.

The passage of Gregory that we have just cited is presented somewhat differently in the printed editions: there the word *ministerium* appears instead of *mysterium*, as though the tower customarily brought by the deacon contained nothing other than vessels and other things necessary for celebrating Mass. But, apart from the arguments that we have presented in the notes to this passage, the authority of all manuscript codices entirely supports preferring our reading.

Indeed, it is especially well suited to elucidating canon 22 of the First Council of Orange, which has greatly perplexed the minds of learned men. For when that canon prescribes that the chest and chalice are to be offered, and that the chalice is to be consecrated by the admixture of the Eucharist, the Fathers intended nothing other than this: after the chest containing the bread and the chalice containing the wine had been offered to God, a particle of the Eucharist brought from the sacristy in the tower was to be placed in the chalice, as our Mabillon explains in his commentary on the *Roman Order*, paragraph 20.

### 45

After the offering of the bread and wine, those who had been excluded from communion with the Church were compelled to leave. When King Theodebert had entered a church at Trier, Nicetius, bishop of that city, who was celebrating the sacred mysteries, addressed the king after the sacred readings had been read and the gifts had been placed upon God’s altar. He declared that he would not complete the solemnity of Mass unless the excommunicated persons whom the king had in his retinue first withdrew from [Col. 0041C] the church, as is related in the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 17.

Cautinus, bishop of Auvergne, however, permitted the excommunicated Eulalius to watch the solemnity of Mass with the others, as Gregory relates in Book X of the *History*, chapter 8. Those whom Nicetius wished to expel were obstinate in their crimes; Eulalius, on the other hand, clung to the bishop’s feet and protested that he had been suspended from communion without a hearing and without deserving it. Consequently, he was later restored to communion, while punishment for the hidden crime was reserved for God’s judgment, if he had in fact committed it, as rumor alleged.

Gregory relates in Book II of *The Miracles of Saint Martin* that, after seeing a miracle performed by the holy bishop, the entire people burst into acclamations and sang the hymn “Glory to God in the highest.” But since by that time the sacred gifts had already been placed upon the altar, nothing can perhaps be inferred from this except that, because of this extraordinary favor, the people sang the hymn on that occasion outside the customary order. For Eberegisilus, bishop of Cologne, filled with similar joy when the body of Saint Mallosus was discovered, raised his voice and caused the whole clergy to sing the *Gloria in excelsis Deo* with him, as Gregory himself writes in Book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 63.

### 46

Gregory mentions a *contestation* in Book II of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 14. It contained an account of the virtues of the blessed confessor and corresponds to our present preface. From this we learn that it was sung by the bishop himself, that is, by the celebrating bishop. When it had been completed, the entire people proclaimed “Holy” in praise of the Lord, as is still done today.

He also mentions the same hymn in the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 16, where he further reports that the holy gift was blessed with the sign of the cross, in accordance with Catholic custom. By these final words he indicates that the Catholic Church, spread throughout the whole world, used this blessing, made with the sign of the cross, in the consecration of the Eucharist. Thus, although the particular rites of the various churches sometimes differed from one another, in the act of consecration itself there was everywhere uniformity—not only in the recitation of the words of Christ the Lord but also in the manner of blessing.

He cites the sacred words in Book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 87, and there mentions the breaking of the Lord’s body before communion.

We have evidence in the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 16, that the Lord’s Prayer was sung at Mass. We infer from Book II of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 30, that it was likewise sung by everyone, including women. In this respect, as Mabillon observed, the Gallican Church agreed with the Greek Church and differed from the Roman rite. For, as we learn from Letter 67 of Gregory the Great, Book VII, Indiction 11, addressed to John, bishop of Syracuse, among the Greeks the Lord’s Prayer was recited by the entire people, whereas in the Roman Church it was said by the priest alone.

### 47

After the sacrament of the Lord’s body had been broken, as our Gregory says in Book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 87, the priest himself received the Eucharist and distributed it to the others for eating.

This passage might seem to imply that both the priest and all those present communicated from the same host, unless it were certain that the individual faithful, or at least very many of them, were accustomed to bring their own offering to the altar, from which they later communicated.

The solemnities of Mass were considered completed before communion was distributed, at least to the laity, as can easily be inferred from several passages of Gregory. Certainly King Guntram, in Book IX of the *History*, chapter 3, approached the altar to receive communion after the solemnities had been completed.

To prevent anyone from twisting the word “solemnities” into another meaning, we shall cite other passages free of all ambiguity. One is from Book II of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 47, where we read:

> When, after the Masses had been completed, the people began to receive the most holy body of the Redeemer, etc.

Furthermore, a widow, in chapter 65 of the book *The Glory of the Confessors*, approached the saving cup after the Masses had been completed and celebrated.

Everyone approached the altar to receive holy [Col. 0042D] communion. Indeed, all drank the blood of Christ from a single chalice. This was the difference between Catholics and Arians, as Gregory himself observes in Book III of the *History*, chapter 31. For among the Arians it was customary that, when they came to the altar, kings received communion from one chalice and the lesser people from another.

This passage also makes clear that communion under both kinds was ordinarily given to everyone, although some were content with one kind alone. For when Bishop Cautinus said to Eulalius, in Book X, chapter 8, “Take for yourself a particle of the Eucharist and place it in your mouth,” Eulalius received the Eucharist, communicated, and departed.

Here the word “Eucharist” plainly designates a single kind. It was divided into several particles—or into the offerings—and distributed to those who were to communicate, not placed in the mouth as is done today. Rather, each person, including laypeople, took it in his own hand and placed it in his own mouth.

Women, however, did not receive the Eucharist with an uncovered hand, as we learn from other monuments. Instead, they received it from the priests in a veil, commonly called an *orarium*, and then communicated.

If any of those present were not excommunicated but nevertheless, in Hincmar’s words, were not prepared to communicate, *eulogiae* were distributed to them—that is, something from the offered loaves that had not been consecrated, as the same author continues in the *Capitula* of the year 852—and this was given as a token of communion.

Thus, when Meroveus, son of Chilperic, had fled from the monastery of Saint Carilefus and gone to the basilica of Saint Martin, where Gregory was then celebrating the sacred mysteries, he asked Gregory, after the Masses, to give him *eulogiae*. When Gregory refused, Meroveus complained that he had been unjustly suspended from communion and threatened to inflict many evils upon the city of Tours unless he deserved to receive communion from the bishop.

The distribution of blessed bread, as it is called, followed these *eulogiae*. This practice is still observed today, especially in parish churches, on Sundays.

These, then, are the points that can be gathered concerning the celebration of Mass from various passages of Gregory. Mabillon, adding numerous testimonies from other authors, used them to illuminate the Gallican liturgy extensively. We, for our part, so that it may more readily be clear to everyone what that rite was at the time, shall present in the appendix to this volume, insofar as is permissible, a specimen of a complete Mass drawn from the liturgies and other monuments edited by Mabillon himself [Col. 0043C].

### 48

Gregory reveals in many passages the great reverence with which people approached either the celebration or the reception of the divine mysteries.

In Book *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 87, he relates that the presbyter Epachius was divinely punished because he rashly presumed to perform what he was unworthy to perform. He reproves him because, although he had drunk after cockcrow, he had nevertheless dared to celebrate the sacred mysteries:

> This, he says, a person who is fasting can perform only with fear, as conscience terrifies him.

In the preceding chapter he warns that crimes must be lamented and mourned when one is about to approach the altar, lest, while polluted in deed, we receive the body and blood of the Lord for judgment rather than for the obtaining of forgiveness.

It was not even considered lawful to look upon the sacred gifts placed upon the altar. Thus Nicetius, bishop of Lyons, is said to have appeared in a vision to a certain presbyter in the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 8, in order to prevent him from placing upon the altar a covering that was too thin and did not fully cover the sacred mysteries.

Gregory commonly calls the vessels used for the sacred ministry “consecrated,” and, as occasion requires, he mentions various kinds of them: chalices, patens, towers, crosses, and so forth. He considered it a grave sacrilege to adapt them to human uses, and by various miracles he shows that God punished the audacity of transgressors.

All these vessels were called by Gregory and by the other authors of his age by the single term *ministerium*, sometimes *sacrum ministerium*. But he calls *ministerium quotidianum* only those vessels that were absolutely necessary for celebrating Mass: namely, a small paten with a chalice, which the presbyter Maximus, while traveling, carried suspended around his neck together with a Gospel book.

For otherwise the chalice used in solemn Masses was very large, as was the paten, since, as we have just said, everyone communicated from a single chalice. The paten also had to be large enough to contain all the offerings of those present. Maximus carried this small paten with the chalice so that he could celebrate the sacred mysteries every day.

Mass could indeed be celebrated every day. A widow is said to have celebrated the solemnities of Mass daily for an entire year, in chapter 65 of *The Glory of the Confessors*, solely because she supplied what was necessary for offering the sacrifice and also attended it, as can easily be inferred from the context.

The presbyter Severus celebrated two Masses every Sunday, according to chapter 50 of the same book: one in each of two estates situated twenty thousand paces from one another.

Finally, we are told in the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 8, that the people assembled for solemn Mass at the third hour, which we now call the ninth hour.

### 49

We learn from canon 12 of the Council of Narbonne, held in the year 589, that the ministers of the altar were clothed in white when the sacred rites were being performed.

Gregory suggests the same in *The Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 20, where he praises the considerable choir of priests and levites in white garments who attended the dedication of his oratory.

In chapter 44 of the *History*—chapter 38 in other editions—an archdeacon clothed in white is said, as was customary, to have invited the bishop to the altar to celebrate the solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity.

A crowd of white-robed deacons was also present at the funeral of blessed Nicetius, bishop of Lyons, according to *The Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 61.

He mentions priestly vestments in other passages as well. In the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 8, we find *candidae*, that is, white and ample garments, as they are described there, which it was customary for priests to place upon their shoulders during the Easter festivals. This is, if I am not mistaken, the same vestment that Saint Remigius calls the white Easter *amphibalus* in his testament, which he left to the bishop who would succeed him.

The vestments used for performing the sacred rites were taken up in the sacristy, where they were customarily removed after the solemnities had been completed. For when Guntram was displeased that Palladius, bishop of Saintes, who had supported Gundobald, was performing the sacred rites in his presence, Palladius—who had already begun the readings— withdrew into the sacristy.

### 50

The faithful offered gifts so that Masses might be celebrated for them. Gregory suggests this in Book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 75, where the Frigoritans are said to have recovered their health after arranging for Masses to be celebrated in honor of Saint Sigismund and offering a gift to God for his repose.

He expresses the matter more clearly in Book I of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 12, where Queen Ultrogotha is said to have come to the church of Saint Martin and, after offering many gifts, requested that a Mass be celebrated in honor of the holy confessor.

In *The Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 65, a widow offered wine every day for the sacrifice on behalf of her deceased husband, although she herself approached communion less frequently.

It is also certain from chapter 2 of the same book that various kinds of objects were offered to the churches by the faithful, and indeed placed upon the altar, as is clear from numerous other passages.

Because the peoples had neglected the payment of tithes, blessed Hospicius threatened the devastation of the region, in Book VI of the *History*, chapter 6.

The devotion of the people of Limoges is especially noteworthy. They were accustomed to offer gifts to the church of Saint Junianus not merely once or twice, or whenever they wished, but, having in a sense become its tributaries, they bound themselves to pay tribute to it every year on fixed days.

### 51

Gregory describes the form and magnificence of churches or basilicas in more than one passage. From this one can understand the extent of our fathers’ piety: when the matter concerned founding and adorning houses consecrated to God, they spared neither expense nor labor.

Read chapters 14 and 16 of Book II of the *History*. In the former, the basilica of Saint Martin at Tours is described; in the latter, the older church of Auvergne.

Gregory frequently mentions marbles, paintings, gold and silver ornaments, curtains, small palls, and roofs themselves made of bronze, all used to adorn churches.

From the same author we learn that churches had two principal parts: the *capsum*—which we interpret as the nave—and the presbytery, so called because the presbyters customarily stood there. It was also called the altar area, because the principal altar stood there.

Gregory testifies in Book *The Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 37, that an *analogium* existed in the Church of Saint Venerandus among the Arverni. Elsewhere he seems to designate it by the name *tribunal*. The bishop preached there, and in the same place the Epistles and Gospels were read at public gatherings of the faithful.

Mabillon gives a precise description of the old *analogium* from the Church of Saint Clement in Rome in his preliminary commentary on the *Roman Order*, where he also represents its ground plan.

Churches additionally had porticoes, crypts, and sometimes oratories attached to them, which also possessed their own altars. Indeed, it could easily be demonstrated from many passages of Gregory that several oratories sometimes existed within a single basilica. Read Book V of the *History*, chapter 50, and elsewhere.

In Book X, the final chapter, Gregory writes that he consecrated numerous churches, oratories, and altars. But he explains the ceremonies of a church’s dedication individually in *The Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 20, where he describes the dedication of his oratory.

It was unlawful to consecrate altars without the relics of saints. Therefore Palladius, bishop of Saintes, asked Pope Gregory for such relics to place in the altars he had built.

### 52

Gregory calls the following things “relics of the saints”: a piece of the tomb covering of some saint, or a pall placed upon the same tomb; wax or oil from the lamps and candles that customarily burned there; dust gathered from the site; herbs or flowers placed there; and other things of this kind.

The bones of certain saints, especially Eastern ones, were also kept, and Gregory likewise designates them by the name “relics.” Such relics, enclosed in a hollow stone or in a small bottle or box, were deposited within the very structure of the altar, as Gregory testifies that he found them at the end of Book X.

In Book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 34, he calls *loculus* that part of the altar in which such relics were enclosed. We now call it a *sepulchre*, since it seems to represent the tombs of the saints, over which altars were customarily erected in antiquity.

For in former times it was not permitted to erect altars except over the relics of holy martyrs. Consequently, in the larger churches the principal altar was generally built on an elevated site, with a crypt beneath it furnished with the relics of the saints. That crypt also had its own altar.

In some places those crypts constructed above the tombs of the saints were called *confessiones*, following the example of the Roman Church. The “confession of Saint Peter” in Rome was already the name of that part of the Vatican in which the bodies of the blessed Apostles rest.

Likewise, the “thresholds” of Saint Martin or Saint Hilary were the names given to the basilicas of those saints, because pilgrims customarily visited them, just as they visited the thresholds of the Apostles located at Rome.

We also read in Gregory that relics of the saints were kept in baptisteries. But those baptisteries should not be considered different from oratories, since not only was the sacrament of baptism administered there, but the sacred mysteries and the daily offices were also celebrated.

A certain Syrian named Eufronius kept the relics of Saint Sergius the martyr enclosed in a small box high in the wall opposite the altar, in his own house. Gregory relates in Book VII of the [Col. 0046C] *History*, chapter 31, that Eufronius converted this house, located near Bordeaux, into a church.

Tombs of the saints enclosed in the walls of churches are also frequently encountered elsewhere—or rather, in arches constructed within the walls themselves.

It was never lawful to place the relics of saints upon the altar except, perhaps, for a very brief interval. This was scarcely permitted except during their translation or during public processions.

### 53

The tombs of the saints were customarily covered with palls and enclosed by railings when large crowds of people gathered around them. Ciboria were also constructed over them, as well as *fredae*, that is, canopies. These sometimes ended in the form of a pyramid, with a cross placed at the top, as Gregory observes concerning the tomb of Saint Julian the martyr in chapter 20 of his *Miracles*.

In place of a cross, some tombs had a dove, such as is said to have existed above the sepulchre of blessed Dionysius in Book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 72.

Gregory relates in Book I of *The Miracles of the Same Saint*, chapter 2, that the crown of the tomb of blessed Martin, which proclaimed his merit, was stolen by a certain Chuno.

This appears to have been a mark of sanctity: that a pall was placed upon someone’s tomb. Hence Gregory observes that due honor had not been shown to a certain holy presbyter because his tomb, adjoining another, could not, owing to the narrowness of the site, be adorned with a pall or illuminated with candles.

This was then the solemn rite of canonizing, as we would say today, a saint: that his body should be lifted from the earth by the bishop and placed beneath an altar.

Those who believed that they had been freed and preserved unharmed through the saints’ intercession hung chains, fetters, and other votive offerings of this kind upon the saints’ tombs, as we learn from the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 8.

Those who had been accused of serious offenses and were required to clear themselves by oath also customarily came there. Such oaths, we read, were sometimes given in the porticoes of churches, sometimes in the sacristy, and sometimes after touching the tomb itself or the altar.

But the oath that Chilperic required from our Gregory was altogether unusual: after the Masses had been celebrated, Gregory was to prove his innocence by oath at three altars. The holy bishop nevertheless performed this, although it was contrary to the canons, so that he would not be regarded by the king as guilty of an offense against majesty.

### 54

Gregory defended the right of asylum granted to churches and sacred places by examples and written statements.

The inviolable immunity of churches appeared so secure even to kings that they considered it impossible to execute persons accused of treason, even after those persons had been dragged from sacred places.

A certain assassin had been discovered in the church of Saint Marcellus near Chalon. He had been prepared to kill King Guntram in the very church, as is related in Book IX of the *History*, chapter 3. Nevertheless, the king ordered him to be led out and released alive, because he considered it sacrilegious to cut down a man who had been led out of a church.

With similar clemency, Childebert, king of the Austrasians, promised to spare certain persons—even those accused—who had been charged with conspiring against him, because they had fled to a church. “Have this promise,” the most pious king says in Gregory, Book IX, chapter 38, “concerning your lives, even if you are found guilty. For we are Christians; it is sacrilegious to punish even criminals after they have been led out of a church.”

From that time, refuges at the basilicas of the saints became famous. Not only did the basilicas themselves enjoy this immunity, but also many buildings and places attached to them, where the accused were permitted to live in safety.

Among the more celebrated were the churches of Saint Hilary at Poitiers, Saint Martin at Tours, Saint Germanus at Auxerre, Saint Remigius at Rheims, and many others, which Gregory mentions on various occasions.

### 55

Gregory lists the ornaments of churches in more than one passage: curtains hung on the walls and doors, or curtains separating the sacristy from the other parts of the church; paintings that instructed the faithful—especially the uneducated—no less than they adorned the temples; ceilings or coffered roofs coated with gold and silver; and roofs cast from bronze or tin.

There were also very rich palls, with which altars and the tombs of saints were customarily covered and adorned. On the principal festivals the ornaments were richer and more splendid than those used daily.

In chapter 20 of *The Miracles of Saint Julian*, Gregory describes the basilica of that holy martyr shining with immense ornaments on his feast day.

I omit the sacred vessels—chalices, patens, Gospel books, and other copies of Sacred Scripture—as well as the books called *sacramentaries*, that is, missals, ritual books, penitentials, and others necessary for daily use.

There were also crosses sometimes adorned with gems and precious stones, lamps hung in the churches, candlesticks, and banners or standards carried in public supplications or processions—or at least carried when the clergy and people went out to meet a king or bishops arriving in a city.

Pious devotion regarded all these things as holy and dedicated to God. The faithful therefore considered that they could not be used for profane purposes without sacrilege, and they often believed that healing could be brought to them by merely touching them.

They even counted among such sacred things the ropes of bells or signals, and the keys with which the doors of churches were opened, to say nothing of those keys brought from Rome that Gregory mentions in one place.

They sometimes pressed the keys of basilicas upon animals, either to free them from a disease they had contracted or at least to avert an impending one.

### 56

Anyone can also easily detect, from reading our Gregory, the ancient customs of the Gallican Church.

Among them were the feasts of saints, including confessors, which were celebrated in Gaul at that time. The observance of Sunday was maintained so carefully that it began with first vespers—that is, on the preceding Saturday afternoon. When some people violated this observance, they were punished by God.

The same author praises the holy Lent more than once. His words in the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 15, are especially noteworthy, where he mentions the forty days that the authority of the Fathers established should be spent in the strictest abstinence before the Easter festivals.

He describes the rites of the Rogations or Litanies. Some of these were performed on fixed days; others when some public calamity occurred. On such occasions public prayers, solemn vigils, and fasts were also proclaimed.

Certainly, the people of Rheims carried a pall taken from the tomb of Saint Remigius throughout all the places of their region, and not in vain. For not a single person within their borders was afflicted by the plague that was devastating the other regions.

We also learn from the same author that supplications or processions were held from one church to another on the solemn festivals of the saints.

In the books of the *History*, Gregory frequently explains the solemn receptions of bishops or kings. These were conducted by the clergy and people of the cities with crosses, banners, and candles carried in advance. He also mentions the public acclamations of the people on such occasions, in which they offered good wishes to the arrivals, sometimes in various languages, to increase the solemnity.

Elsewhere he mentions the funeral rites of the dead, including changes of clothing, mourning garments, and other practices of this kind.

We learn from chapter 6 among the *Lives of the Fathers* that bishops of the same province customarily came to celebrate the funeral of a deceased bishop. There Gregory describes the funeral procession of Saint Gallus. In the following chapter he gives a similar account concerning Gregory of Langres.

Chapter 106 of *The Glory of the Confessors* should also be read on this subject, for there he gives a fuller account of the ceremonies surrounding the burial of blessed Radegund.

From that chapter we further learn that cemeteries intended for burying the faithful already had to be consecrated by priestly—that is, episcopal—blessing. An altar was customarily erected there for offering propitiatory sacrifices for the repose of the dead, as the same Gregory shows to have been done frequently elsewhere.

The bodies of the dead were first washed and then clothed before burial, and quite often they were buried in churches. At this time in Gaul, this was permitted to others besides bishops and princes.

The corpses of excommunicated persons and unbelievers were excluded not only from churches but also from the common cemeteries of the faithful. Indeed, Count Palladius, who had killed himself, was not placed beside the bodies of Christians.

Gregory proves in more than one passage, by miracles and by examples of holy men, that the use of blessed water to drive away illnesses was legitimate. He also frequently speaks of other things fortified by priestly blessing.

We have already discussed blessed bread, or *eulogiae*, which were distributed toward the end of Mass.

Gregory also calls *eulogiae*, or “blessings,” any small gifts given or received by priests as a sign of friendship, because they served as a kind of token of communion and were customarily blessed by the priests themselves.

It was unlawful, in the presence of a priest, to take any food or drink unless it had first been blessed by him. God often chose to confirm this practice by miracles, as we learn from our Gregory and from other ancient authors.

There are almost as many testimonies concerning the efficacy and powers of the sign of the cross as there are pages.

### 57

Gregory also has much to say about the administration of the sacraments. We have already explained above the rite by which the sacrament of the Eucharist was distributed. We likewise observed above, from chapter 86 of the book *On the Glory of the Martyrs* in our edition, that at that time it was kept in the sacristy in a tower, from which it was customarily brought to the altar [Col. 0049C]. This is supported, besides Fortunatus’s passage concerning the tower built by Bishop Felix, by the blessing of the tower, which you will find transcribed from an ancient sacramentary in the appendix to this volume.

Gregory describes in the books of the *History* the penance of King Chlothar when he approached the tomb of Saint Martin. In the *Life of Saint Nicetius of Lyons*, a certain man, when close to death, is said to have implored penance from a presbyter with many tears. Elsewhere Gregory mentions a man condemned to death who asked a priest for penance—secretly, perhaps because even then civil laws prevented those condemned to the extreme penalty from receiving penance.

Nor are examples of indulgences lacking in our author [Col. 0049D]. Bishop Victor, who had been suspended from communion because he had rashly reconciled certain criminals, was restored to communion before the appointed time through the king’s intercession. Likewise, at the Synod of Metz, Basina and Chrodieldis, who had been excommunicated on account of their crimes, were absolved at Childebert’s request by the fathers of the Council.

Gregory indicates that times were appointed for conferring baptism when he recalls Guntram’s complaints against those who had repeatedly delayed the baptism of Chlothar II. He also defended the unity of baptism, and indeed its unity in the name of the most holy Trinity, on many occasions. From the same author we infer that baptism was then administered by immersion, at least in Spain; he also frequently reports the names given in baptism [Col. 0050A].

He praises more than once the blessing of chrism performed by bishops, as well as the anointing with chrism that was used in receiving heretics returning to the Church. He also praises those who, marked with the standard of the cross, proved their faith by their works; and he testifies that King Clovis was not only baptized by Remigius, the apostle of the Franks, but was also anointed with sacred chrism bearing the sign of Christ’s cross.

Among the episcopal duties which the fathers of the Fourth Council of Paris forbid the improperly ordained Bishop Promotus to exercise is the confirmation of infants. Gregory likewise explains more than once the power of exorcisms over demons. Whenever the occasion arises, he mentions tonsured clerics, lectors, doorkeepers, candle-bearers, subdeacons, and the other higher clerical orders. We have already explained above, from the words of the presbyter Cato, the intervals that ought to be observed for receiving these orders properly [Col. 0050B]. He also repeatedly implies that the ordinations of bishops were celebrated on Sundays.

He frequently praises the anointing of the sick. Certainly, in Book I, chapter 41, the envoy Artemius, passing through Auvergne and falling ill with fever, was visited by Bishop Nepotianus and, after being anointed with holy oil, recovered his health.

That marriages were contracted with a priestly blessing is clear from King Chilperic’s complaint against Bishop Praetextatus in Book V of the *History*, chapter 19. There the king reproaches him for an obvious violation of the canons, because he had joined Merovech in marriage to the widow of his uncle. Elsewhere, too, Gregory repeatedly condemns, with episcopal freedom, incestuous marriages and women brought in as additional wives, even among princes [Col. 0050C].

### 58

Examples of ecclesiastical censures are not lacking in Gregory’s books. Thomassinus finds in Gregory’s action, reported in Book VI of the *History*, chapter 10, some indication of an irregularity incurred through a lack of leniency. Gregory recalls that he had written in favor of the thieves who had broken into the basilica of Saint Martin, reminding the king that these thieves had not been accused by the clerics to whom the matter belonged. The pious bishop says that he did this because he feared that the men might die on his account, since, while living in the body, he had often pleaded for the lives of the lost.

A certain presbyter mentioned in Book I of *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 73, considered himself liable to great reproach if a thief were condemned to death through his accusation. That priest had accused the man of stealing a horse [Col. 0050D], and therefore left no stone unturned to rescue the defendant from death. When the judge refused to do so, he obtained from God, through the merits of blessed Quintinus, the salvation of the condemned man.

In Book VI of the *History*, chapter 8, Ursicinus, Bishop of Cahors, was suspended from the order he had received because he had publicly supported Gundovald Ballomer. He was forbidden, for a full three years, to celebrate Masses, ordain clerics, or bless churches and chrism, and so forth.

Palladius, who had violently taken his own life, was deprived of ecclesiastical burial, as we have already observed. Maroveus, bishop of that same city, threatened to place the city of Poitiers under interdict unless Chrodieldis, abandoning her wickedness, restored the abbess to the monastery of the Holy Cross, from which she had been abducted [Col. 0051A].

When the church of Saint Dionysius near Paris had been polluted by a slaughter committed there, it lost its liturgical office, and no sacred rites were celebrated there until it had been reconciled by the bishop. I pass over the depositions of bishops on account of crimes committed, the excommunications of incestuous persons and of those guilty of other crimes, since these matters are too well known to require more extended treatment.

### 59

From all this it is clear that Gregory’s works are exceedingly useful for investigating the discipline of the Gallican Church. A few points should now be added from which it may be understood that they are no less suitable for confirming our faith.

From the same author we learn that this was the very faith which our fathers had received from the disciples of the Apostles. Indeed, Gregory never spoke more carefully than when he treated matters of faith, nor did he investigate anything throughout his life with such diligence as those things pertaining to the integrity and purity of the faith.

He expressly testifies to this at the beginning of Book I of the *History*. After confessing that he was not fully trained in the rules of grammar, he adds that he had always endeavored to possess a pure and sincere understanding of matters of faith: “Seeking only this,” he says, “that I may retain without any disguise or hesitation of heart what is proclaimed to be believed in the Church,” and so forth.

He then sets forth his profession of faith, which he made more extensive than the Nicene or Constantinopolitan Creed, in order to declare that he was alien to the heresies that had later arisen [Col. 0051C].

He proposes excellent rules of faith in Book X of the *History*, chapter 13—namely, the authority of Sacred Scripture and apostolic tradition—which he uses to refute the obstinacy of a certain heretic who had dared to call the future resurrection into question. Elsewhere, in Book V, chapter 45, he praises the authority of the holy Fathers whom God left to the Church after the Apostles.

Finally, our forefathers valued so highly the disputations that Gregory had committed to writing against heretics that they assigned them a place among the rules of faith in books later prepared for the instruction of priests. We possess such a collection, compiled from the Fossatensian manuscript in the time of Charlemagne. In it, the canons of the councils are preceded by the Athanasian Creed, confessions of faith by Augustine and others, and then disputations against heretics excerpted from Gregory’s *History* [Col. 0051D].

And rightly so. Gregory was so devoted to the faith that he omitted no opportunity to defend it. He repeatedly demonstrated and confirmed the mystery of the most holy Trinity and the truth that the persons subsist equally in one nature and divinity, adducing testimonies from Sacred Scripture and various miracles performed in this connection—miracles that he had either witnessed himself or learned from others.

He refuted King Chilperic, who wished to revive the errors of Sabellius, by explaining the Catholic doctrine concerning the distinction of the persons and the unity of the nature, so effectively that the king, although he raged against him, was forced to remain silent [Col. 0052A].

Against a certain Sadducee presbyter, he asserted the future resurrection of bodies by appropriately cited testimonies from Sacred Scripture, with such force that the man, thoroughly convicted, promised never again to oppose it. In the same place he also discusses learnedly the truth of the final judgment and proves that the condemned must suffer eternal punishments.

He treats of these same punishments, as well as of the temporary punishments suffered by the souls of the dead, in the final chapter of Book I of *On the Glory of the Martyrs*. In his profession of faith he acknowledged the truth of original sin against the Pelagians, professing that fallen humanity had been liberated by Christ. There, and elsewhere, he praises Mary’s perpetual virginity. He also repeatedly confirms, not merely in words but by examples, the necessity of divine assistance for acting rightly.

Accordingly, in the chapter of the book *On the Glory of the Martyrs* just mentioned, he teaches that good deeds must be attributed not to one’s own powers but to God’s strength; while in chapter 41 he considers right faith, animated by good works, necessary for salvation [Col. 0052B].

When occasion arose in his historical narratives, he declared the true and real presence of the Lord’s body and blood in the Eucharist so plainly that he might seem deliberately to have wished to express that Catholic doctrine after the rise of the Berengarian heresy. “Boldly,” he says in Book *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 86, “although we are actually defiled, we receive the holy body and blood of the Lord for judgment,” and so forth. In chapter 10 of the same book he relates the story of a Jewish boy who had approached with Catholics to partake of the glorious body and blood of the Lord [Col. 0052C].

“After the Masses had been completed,” he says in Book II of *On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 47, “the people received the most holy body of the Redeemer,” and so forth. He frequently mentions the celebration of Masses and the offering of the sacrifice. Masses celebrated to obtain rest for the dead are found in *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 65; and Palladius, who had killed himself, was not deemed worthy of the solemn rites of Mass.

Elsewhere Masses are said to have been celebrated at the funerals of the dead in the presence of the body. Likewise, continuous psalm-singing around the body of the deceased before burial is mentioned, along with other practices of the same kind that readers encounter throughout his works.

The veneration of sacred relics, the invocation of the saints, their sacred images, and other such practices—things which more recent heretics have attacked so vehemently, attending perhaps more to popular abuses than to the Church’s doctrines—are supported by almost as many arguments as there are pages in the books of the *Miracles* [Col. 0052D].

In Book I of *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 22, Gregory says that the custom of keeping images of Christ among the faithful arose from love for the prototype: namely, so that they might possess the image of him whose law they retain on the tablets of their hearts, painted and displayed throughout churches and houses on visible tablets as a memorial of virtue.

On the same occasion Rufinus says in Book VII of the *History*, chapter 14: “The preservation of the insignia of former times is for the memory of posterity: it is a sign of their honor, but of our love.”

### 60

Although the principal usefulness of our Gregory’s works lies in learning both the ecclesiastical and secular history of the Frankish kingdom, they also contain material concerning the affairs of other nations that should not be despised. Writers of the proper histories of those peoples have likewise drawn from them.

To prove this by examples, Gregory himself described for us the fortunes of the Burgundians and Thuringians. From him we have the succession of the Visigothic kings in Septimania and Spain. He also narrates many things concerning the Ostrogoths and Lombards, in connection with the expeditions undertaken by our kings against them in Italy.

This gave him occasion also to discuss the Greek emperors, who repeatedly attempted to secure and restore their faltering power in Italy with Frankish assistance. Hence the various embassies from Greece to Gaul and from Gaul to Greece that Gregory frequently mentions.

There is no space to enumerate what he records about the Huns, Saxons, Bavarians, and other peoples of Germany [Col. 0053B]. Add also what he reported from Orosius and other authors concerning the tyrants or emperors of the Roman Empire in the West during its final period, or at least concerning their military commanders. He interspersed these accounts with certain things that he had received by tradition or from authors now unknown.

He did the same in the narrative that he composed chiefly from the *Chronicle* of Eusebius or Jerome and the history of Orosius, concerning events from the creation of the world to the fifth century.

In Book I of the *History*, chapter 10, he reviews various opinions concerning the crossing of the Red Sea, and there praises travelers who had visited the monasteries of Egypt. Then he speaks about the ancient nations: “Lest we seem,” he says in chapter 16, “to have knowledge only of the one Hebrew nation, the remaining kingdoms,” and so forth [Col. 0053C]. He lists the kings of ancient peoples who ruled before Christ’s coming.

He explains at somewhat greater length what happened after Christ was born. He reviews the persecutions against the Church and records certain matters concerning the condition of Gaul, from which we learn what the beginnings of the Church were in those regions—or at least what opinion concerning the matter prevailed while Gregory was alive.

### 61

Some people think that it can be inferred from his writings that two traditions then existed in Gaul concerning the first apostles of the Gallican Church. According to one, their mission was traced back to the age of the Apostles themselves; according to the other, it was assigned to the time of Decius, or at least of Marcus Aurelius.

They even accuse Gregory of lacking consistency in this matter, since they say that he embraced the former opinion in the books of the *Miracles* and the latter in the *History*. Although I do not intend to revisit these questions concerning the missions of the saints, which have been debated so vigorously in our own time and which I consider outside the scope of my undertaking, I venture to affirm that Gregory nowhere contradicted himself when the opportunity arose to write about these missions.

Those are mistaken who think that he spoke of the martyrs of Lyons, or of the seven bishops whom he says were sent under Decius, in such a way as to deny that martyrs or other preachers of the divine word had entered Gaul before them.

For, as the highly learned Jacques Sirmond wisely observed, Gregory did not hold the error of supposing that no bishops in Gaul were older than these seven [Col. 0054A]. His own words make this certain. “In Gaul,” he says in Book I, chapter 26, speaking of the persecution of Antoninus, “many were crowned through martyrdom for the name of Christ.” Then, in chapter 28: “Under Decius . . . During his reign seven men were ordained bishops and sent to preach in Gaul,” and so forth.

He therefore does not say that martyrdoms were first seen in Gaul at that time, as Sulpicius Severus had earlier written. He does not exclude other preachers of the divine word who had spread the Gospel in Gaul before those seven bishops. Nor, consequently, did he contradict himself when he wrote in Book *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 56, that Eutropius had been sent by Saint Clement.

Indeed, he is consistent with himself concerning those seven bishops when he writes in *On the Glory of the Confessors*: in chapter 4, concerning Saint Gatianus, “whom we know to have been sent by the Roman bishops”; in chapter 27, “Martial, sent by the Roman bishops”; and in chapter 30, “Stremonius, himself also sent by the Roman bishops with Gatianus and the others whom we have mentioned” [Col. 0054B].

Nor is it useful to object that Saturninus is said in chapter 48 of Book I of *On the Glory of the Martyrs* to have been ordained by disciples of the Apostles. Gregory could call those who professed the faith disseminated by the Apostles at Rome “disciples of the Apostles.”

He likewise speaks of Ursinus, the apostle of Bourges, in chapter 80 of *On the Glory of the Confessors*, although in Book I of the *History*, chapter 29, he implies that Ursinus was a disciple of the seven bishops. Some, however, think that another Ursinus is meant here—namely Senicianus, who is listed second in the catalogue of the bishops of Bourges.

In the passage cited, Gregory says that after the death of Ursinus the Christian faith declined among the Bituriges. This could scarcely have happened after the death of a disciple of the seven bishops, at the end of the third century. Gregory himself testifies that at that time the Christian faith had died out among the Bituriges, although the faithful in that city had built a church with remarkable workmanship.

Gregory also wrote frequently about the miracles of other saints, such as Timothy and Apollinaris of Reims, Memmius of Châlons, Valerius of Couserans, and several others. But he was silent about their missions because, as may be conjectured, he had learned nothing certain about them.

### 62

Although what we have reported is more than sufficient to establish the usefulness of Gregory’s works, certain people, including learned men, are accustomed to criticize various things in them. It has therefore seemed worthwhile to discuss these criticisms briefly, so that it may be clear that they are not important enough either to diminish the authority of so eminent a man or to deter pious and learned readers from reading his works.

These are the charges brought against Gregory. They say that he wrote in such a rustic style that he can scarcely be read without weariness; that he sometimes praised apocryphal writings of the ancients; that he occasionally presented not only uncertain things as certain but even false things as true; that he fell into various errors; and finally that he was so simple and credulous that he regarded every sort of ordinary event indiscriminately as a miracle.

But the rusticity of his style was a defect not of Gregory but of his age. At that time, after the various disasters that Gaul had suffered under the repeated incursions of the barbarians, letters had become so uncultivated that no one could be found capable of committing historical events to writing, as Gregory himself testifies in the prologue to the *History* [Col. 0055A].

Or, if someone had attempted to describe them in a more polished style, his writing would have been useless, since most people would not have understood it; Gregory himself states this more than once. This was also why the laws and even the diplomas of our kings were composed in precisely the same rustic style.

Thus, in order to accommodate himself to the character of his age, Gregory knowingly and deliberately used the accusative where an ablative absolute would ordinarily have been expected. This barbarous mode of expression was therefore not peculiar to Gregory; anyone can easily detect it in other trustworthy documents of his age [Col. 0055B].

Moreover, although Gregory, being a man of exceptional modesty and humility, frequently professes himself ignorant of the Latin language and a simple man, he should not be considered so unlearned as to have possessed no literary education. On the contrary, it can be inferred that he was deeply familiar with the reading of ancient authors from the various passages of their works that he occasionally interwove with his own narrative.

He also implies that he possessed some knowledge of Greek words when he explains the force of Latin terms from their etymology. Fortunatus, who certainly knew him well, may likewise be called as a witness in this matter, since he repeatedly praises Gregory’s eloquence and learning.

And indeed, however simple the language in which Gregory wrote, he describes historical events with a certain sincerity and natural eloquence, so that his narrative is neither unpleasant nor tedious [Col. 0055C].

### 63

I would not deny, however, that Gregory was sometimes mistaken. This is a special prerogative of the sacred books: they alone are immune from error.

Gregory sometimes followed apocryphal writings and, I admit, used false records. He employed chronological calculations that were not sufficiently consistent. Yet these matters scarcely detract from the usefulness of his works, since they concern chiefly the ancient histories that he drew from other authors and can therefore easily be corrected from other sources.

Accordingly, such errors do not impair the history of our nation—which is the principal usefulness of his works—whether ecclesiastical or secular, and especially that which comes closest to Gregory’s own age [Col. 0055D]. For the most part he wrote what he had seen or heard himself, and no one would say that he ever used bad faith in reporting it.

### 64

“But,” you will say, “Gregory was so credulous and simple that he seems to have inserted anything whatsoever into his writings without discrimination and to have attributed nearly every event to miracles.”

I would not deny that Gregory may at times have been too ready to believe miracles. Nevertheless, since it is certain from other authors of his age that many miracles occurred at that time, I would not judge that they should be rejected merely because they are miracles, unless some serious reason advises this.

In this matter the rule of Saint Augustine should be followed. When he learned that many miracles were circulating among the people, miracles commonly reported by pious men, he said: “I would rather confess that these matters are too lofty for me to grasp than rashly decide that they are false miracles or inventions of an excessively credulous person” [Col. 0056A].

For the working of miracles is the mark of the true Church, by which the Fathers and Doctors of the Church of every age have always asserted that it was distinguished from the sects of heretics.

From the time when our Lord promised in the Gospel that those who would believe in him would perform greater and more numerous works than he himself had performed, miracles have not been lacking in the Church whenever they were necessary either for the conversion of unbelievers or for confirming the faithful in the true faith.

Peter professed that he possessed this power in the *Acts of the Apostles*. When a lame man asked him for alms, Peter replied that he had no silver, but “what I have,” he said, “I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ, rise and walk.” Even the shadow of Peter’s body alone cured diseases.

I say nothing of Paul’s miracles. But according to his testimony, this grace passed from the Apostles to the faithful: he writes that to some were granted various kinds of tongues, to others the grace of healing, and to others different gifts of the charisms [Col. 0056B].

Ignatius, a disciple of the Apostles, when he was near martyrdom, feared that the beasts might spare him through a miracle, as had happened to other saints. Justin reproaches the pagans for the impotence of magicians and enchanters, whereas Christians, by invoking the name of Jesus Christ alone, could accomplish anything.

Irenaeus, who flourished in the second century and suffered at the beginning of the third, has especially remarkable things on this subject. In Book II of *Against Heresies*, chapter 57, he does not merely list one or two, or even several, miracles performed by Christians. Rather, he proves that this itself is a prerogative of the Catholic Church: while the sects of heretics could accomplish nothing by their tricks except perhaps to harm the unwary, the faithful confirmed their faith through miracles—miracles both certain and frequent.

Thus, he says, the lame very often received the power to walk, the blind their sight, the deaf their hearing, and even the dead their life through the prayers of the faithful. In the following chapter he observes that those who had been raised from the dead lived for a long time afterward among the other mortal inhabitants, lest malicious people dare to attribute such great miracles to magic [Col. 0056C].

The same matter is attested in the third century beyond all possibility of exception by Cyprian, bishop of Carthage and martyr of Christ. He treated this subject more than once, especially in his books *On the Vanity of Idols* and *To Demetrianus*.
