I omit Eusebius, Lactantius, and others who lived toward the end of the third century and the beginning of the fourth. The same power continued after peace had been granted to the Church, as is witnessed by Jerome, Rufinus, Sulpicius Severus, and others who wrote the lives of the Fathers and other saints.

The same is attested by Paulinus and by Theodoret, who among the Greek Fathers was scarcely inferior to anyone in learning and who published a separate book on this subject under the title *Religious History*.

Augustine narrates very many miracles performed in his own time, especially in the books *On the City of God*. As many heralds proclaimed the miracles of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, discovered by Ambrose, as there were writers of that age: Ambrose himself, Paulinus, Augustine, Gaudentius, and others [Col. 0057A].

The miracles of Saint Stephen, whose relics had recently been discovered, were no less celebrated; two books concerning them are included among Augustine’s works. Shortly afterward Victor of Vita described the miracles performed by Catholics during the persecution unleashed by the Vandals in Africa.

At approximately the same time Basil, bishop of Seleucia, composed two books about the miracles of Saint Thecla.

This concerns the centuries that preceded our Gregory. We shall prove below that miracles were no less frequent in the sixth century, in which Gregory lived. To treat of later times does not belong to our undertaking; those who desire more on the subject may consult the complete books of the *Miracles* found in collections of the lives of the saints.

### 65

From what we have brought forward it is now evident that no ecclesiastical author can rightly be blamed for inserting miracles throughout his works, or at least for publishing separate books concerning the miracles of the saints. Gregory therefore should by no means be despised for the very reason that he narrated miracles throughout his books.

Nor should anyone say that miracles were performed by God, the Most Good and Greatest, when they were necessary to establish the faith among the nations, but that this cannot be applied to Gregory’s times. Miracles never seem to have been more necessary, whether for bringing about the conversion of unbelievers or for confirming the faithful in the true faith, than at the end of the fifth century and throughout the sixth, when our Gregory wrote.

At that time barbarian nations had so overrun Europe that scarcely any region remained in which they did not rule [Col. 0057C]. They were either pagans or, at any rate, so infected with the Arian heresy that, although Christian in name, they retained most pagan superstitions together with false doctrines. All were so fierce and barbarous that anyone who attempted to persuade them of the true religion by arguments and the authority of Sacred Scripture would have labored in vain.

Miracles were therefore necessary, since this alone was the means of convincing them.

Certainly, as long as Clovis, the first Christian king of our people, enjoyed success, he did not even wish to consider changing his religion. But when he was placed in the utmost danger during a battle and had been rescued from such great perils only through a miracle, he embraced the faith of his own accord.

In the same way, a miracle of the holy father Benedict performed before Totila, king of the Goths in Italy, moved him—a man whom previously neither the authority of priests nor the misfortunes of the wretched had ever been able to turn toward compassion [Col. 0057D].

The uneducated faithful also had great need of miracles. They were oppressed by various forms of extortion at the hands of heretics, sometimes even tortured with punishments or enticed by inducements to change their religion.

There was another particular reason for miracles being performed in the sixth century: the error of certain people who denied the resurrection of the dead. It was chiefly to refute this error that Gregory the Great composed the books of the *Dialogues* concerning the virtues and miracles of the saints of Italy.

### 66

We also possess illustrious men of those times, beyond all possibility of exception, who testified that miracles frequently occurred then [Col. 0058A].

Gregory the Great published four books of *Dialogues* concerning the miracles of the saints of Italy. Bishop Victor of Vita did the same in his books *On the Vandal Persecution*, where he narrates the things that God displayed in Africa for the confirmation of the Catholic faith.

In Gaul, besides the lives of the saints written by serious and contemporary authors, we have witnesses whom no one could ever contradict without being charged with rashness. Among them were several bishops distinguished for holiness and learning, especially the metropolitans Avitus of Vienne, Stephen of Lyons, and Aeonius of Arles.

After they had overcome the Arians in a disputation held before the king of the Burgundians by arguments and testimonies from Scripture, they also promised to prove their faith by miracles if the Arians were willing to agree to it.

“If our arguments,” said Avitus on behalf of them all to King Gundobad, who was present at the disputation, “cannot convince them, I do not doubt that God will confirm our faith by a miracle. Let Your Highness order that both they and we go to the tomb of a just man of God and ask him about our faith; and let Boniface do the same concerning his. The Lord will pronounce through the mouth of his servant in which faith he is pleased.”

Thus those holy men trusted God so greatly because they knew that they possessed the faith which, when God’s cause required it, could even move mountains.

The same bishops also imply that they undertook this disputation in imitation of the most blessed Remigius, the apostle of the Franks, who at that time confirmed the Catholic faith among that people by almost countless wonders [Col. 0058C]:

“By the providence of the Lord for his Church, and by his inspiring the heart of our lord Remigius for the salvation of the whole people, he destroyed the altars of idols everywhere and powerfully strengthened the true faith with a multitude of signs,” and so forth.

Saint Nicetius, bishop of Trier, places the miracles of that same Saint Remigius and of Saint Medard before Chlotsinda, exhorting her to recount them to her husband, Alboin, king of the Lombards, so that by the example of Clovis he might be moved to embrace the faith.

“What can we say about our lords, Bishops Remigius and Medard, whom I believe you have seen? We cannot set forth things as great as the wonders we see God performing through them.”

The holy bishop continues with these words concerning the miracles that were then frequent at the tombs of the saints:

“Where today so many wonders appear that I am unable to express them in words” [Col. 0058D].

He immediately adds that similar things did not occur in the churches of the heretics, because they professed a faith different from that of the saints who performed the miracles.

How confidently Nicetius spoke concerning the truth and certainty of so many and such great miracles is clear from his writing that King Alboin himself ought to be challenged to send some trustworthy men from his own people to the tomb of Saint Martin, so that they might investigate the truth of the matter for themselves.

“Let him send to our lord Martin on his feast day . . . where today we see the blind receive sight . . . where the deaf recover hearing and the mute health. For why should I speak of lepers or of the very many others? Whoever is afflicted by any weakness, there each year one person after another is healed” [Col. 0059A].

The Arian king Theodemir—whom Gregory calls Chararic—sent people to this feast and, moved by such great miracles, embraced the faith together with the entire nation of the Suevi, over whom he then ruled in Galicia.

Add to these other witnesses distinguished for learning and holiness: Fortunatus, who wrote many lives of the saints; Cyprian, bishop of Toulon, in the *Life of Saint Caesarius*; Hilary of Arles; Eucherius; Dynamus the patrician, a man distinguished by birth, rank, and the testimony of Gregory the Great; blessed Audoenus in the *Life of Saint Eligius*; the monk Jonas; and others who at that time published lives of the saints, constructing them almost in their entirety from narratives of miracles.

67. Therefore no one can deny that in the time of our Gregory miracles frequently occurred at the tombs of the saints, and that this was believed not merely on the opinion of the common people or the report of little women, but was also accepted on the authority of learned men and holy bishops, who judged that our faith could be confirmed by the certainty of such miracles and the errors of heretics refuted. It is also certain that those miracles were so clear and well attested that not even the heretics dared call them into question or were ever able to obscure them by any sophistry. Hence it came about that many, having renounced heresy, embraced the Catholic faith—and indeed not ordinary people, nor one or two obscure men of no reputation, but kings themselves and entire nations: the Franks, Burgundians, Suevi, Visigoths, Angles, Lombards, and others.

No one, therefore, should find it surprising that Gregory, who burned with the desire to advance the orthodox faith and was aflame with the greatest devotion toward the holy friends of God, devoted such great attention to collecting miracles. At that time he saw them as highly effective for instilling the faith in heretics and most useful for correcting the morals of the faithful. The miracles Gregory relates cannot be called into doubt merely because of their number. For concerning most saints he relates only one miracle or perhaps two; in this respect he was more sparing than those who wrote the Lives of such saints, which, as I was saying shortly before, they generally composed almost entirely from miracles. He does have more to say about Saint Martin or Saint Julian. But we have just cited the passage of Saint Nicetius, which sufficiently attests that many more miracles occurred at Saint Martin’s tomb than our Gregory reports.

What he wrote he knew extremely well, either because the events had happened to him personally or because he had received them from others. Who would say that the miracles which he acknowledges had occurred to himself were false? Gregory cannot be described as so deceitful and depraved in mind that he deliberately wished to pass off falsehoods as truths, nor as so dull-witted that, while well, he considered himself sick, or that, though not sick, he thought himself divinely healed at the ashes of the saints. The same must be said of most of the other sick people, especially serious and well-known men, who confessed that they had been healed through the merits of the saints, either openly before everyone or at least to Gregory himself.

There is, I admit, one respect in which he was more credulous than was appropriate: namely, in believing what he found written by the ancients or had received from old traditions. But this neither detracts from his good faith nor creates any prejudice against what he reports as having seen or heard himself; on the contrary, it strongly proves the candor and sincerity of his character.

68. “But how many and how great,” you may say, “are the lesser events that Gregory assigns to miracles, although they in no way surpass the natural efficacy of causes?” Yet the character and religion of men distinguished for piety are such that they attribute to the heavenly efficacy of prayers and to the intercession of the saints what otherwise does not exceed the power of nature. Such were Cyprian, Augustine, Theodoret, and the other great men whom we mentioned above.

Gregory, then, may have been simple—but in the sense that, without disguise and always with an open mind and sincere heart, he expressed the truth in straightforward language. “This is Gregory’s praise, not his reproach,” says Sirmondus, reproving Hilduin, who called Gregory a man of remarkable simplicity, although Hilduin himself, if the word is taken negatively, was much simpler than Gregory.

69. For we should not suppose that all the miracles circulating publicly were immediately admitted by Gregory without selection or examination, since he repeatedly calls upon God as witness to the truth of what he narrates in his books. Indeed, he found reports from others difficult to believe, as he himself testifies in Book I of the *Miracles*, chapter 5.

He had often heard that oil before the cross in the monastery at Poitiers was accustomed to increase so greatly that, although vessels were continually carried away full from it, it nevertheless never diminished. But he could never be brought to believe this until he had investigated the truth of the matter with his own eyes over the course of an hour. Someone boasted that he had received the cloth with which the venerable cross at Jerusalem had long been wrapped; but Gregory did not believe him until he had observed that the matter had been confirmed by certain miracles.

When he had received accounts of events from others, he named the people who had reported them, lest he appear to impose uncertain matters as certain. Sometimes, moreover, he wished such miracles to be confirmed by oath, or he produced many witnesses to the reported event, lest anyone should think that he was mocking the pious credulity of simple people. He says this himself in Book II of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 32, and implies it repeatedly elsewhere.

70. Perhaps some will attribute to Gregory’s allegedly excessive simplicity the fact that he repeatedly counted among the relics of the saints dust collected from their tombs, cloths laid upon them for some time, flowers or herbs scattered there by the faithful or fastened to the walls, oil taken from lamps burning there, water drawn from nearby springs or wells, and other things of this sort.

But this objection will disappear when a sensible reader observes that examples of the same practice occur everywhere in the works of the most serious Fathers and authorities. Witnesses to this custom include Jerome, Augustine, Paulinus, Leo, and Gregory, each of them Great and Roman pontiff, Bede, and many others, whose passages we have more than once cited in the notes to Gregory’s text.

Anyone wishing to know more about the subject should consult the special book on the relics of the saints by Ferrandus, a priest of the Society of Jesus, or should read the learned investigation of Ludovico Antonio Muratori on this topic in Volume II of the *Anecdota*. There he also presents a list of the oils that Gregory the Great sent to Theodelinda through John, written in Gregory’s own age on Egyptian papyrus, as our Mabillon testifies in *Itinerarium Italicum*, p. 14.

71. Finally, I wish to draw attention to one point concerning Gregory’s books on the miracles of the saints: namely, that he related only those miracles of the saints that had not been written down by other authors. It is therefore not surprising that he sometimes passes over more famous deeds of the saints and records instead certain obscure events.

This also shows how carelessly some acted when they called certain deeds of the saints into question merely because Gregory did not mention them. For, as he himself testifies, it was outside his purpose to discuss such matters. We learn from his own statement that this was indeed his intention, in the general preface to these books: “Desiring to disclose certain miracles of the saints that have until now remained hidden,” and so forth.

He states the matter even more explicitly in chapter 45 of *The Glory of the Confessors*, the last book he revised:

> Although we have already said in the prologue to this book that we would write only those things which God was pleased to perform after their death … nevertheless, I do not think it absurd to recall some things about their life, when we know that nothing has been written about them.

He therefore did not write about the deeds of saints that were already known from elsewhere or whose Lives were available. But now we must pass to the second part of our preface.

## II

72. There is scarcely any difficulty in compiling a catalogue of Gregory’s works, since he not only listed them throughout his books but also enumerated them individually at the end of Book X of the *History of the Franks*:

> I have written ten books of Histories, seven of Miracles, and one on the Lives of the Fathers. I have composed one book as a commentary on the Psalter; I have also produced one book on the ecclesiastical courses.

What he means by the seven books of miracles he explains in the prologue to *The Glory of the Confessors*:

> In the first little book we have inserted certain things about the miracles of the Lord, the holy apostles, and the remaining martyrs, which have until now remained hidden, and so forth. In the second we have set down the miracles of Saint Julian the Martyr. Four little books concern the miracles of Saint Martin; the seventh concerns the life of certain Religious—or, as most manuscript codices read, of certain *Feliciosi*; this eighth book we are writing concerning the miracles of the Confessors.

There is no difficulty concerning these books. The work which he calls, in second place, the life of the Religious or *Feliciosi* is the one called at the end of the *History* the book on the Lives of the Fathers.

All these works survive except the book on the ecclesiastical courses, which has entirely perished, and the commentary on the Psalms, of which only a few fragments remain. For some time we were persuaded that this commentary was preserved at Rome, having received letters stating that a manuscript from the Vatican Library, originating in the monastery of Fonte Avellana, was entitled *The Commentary on the Psalms of Florentius, Georgius, and Gregory*.

But when our Stephanotius, the Procurator General of our Congregation in the Roman Curia, investigated the matter more carefully, he discovered both that this title had been written into the codex by a later hand and that the commentary repeatedly cited authors later than our Gregory, such as Haymo and Remigius. Finally, the author of this commentary uses the Vulgate version of the Psalms, whereas Gregory does not ordinarily use it when citing the Psalms.

Indeed, in the preface to the Gregorian commentary that we have just mentioned, the titles of the Psalms are given according to the version of the Seventy translators. The person who prefixed Gregory’s name to that codex was misled by a fragment of Gregory’s preface on the titles of the Psalms, which the author of the commentary placed before his work together with other patristic prefaces.

We shall present this fragment, transcribed from the codex by the pious and learned Thomas, after the books on the miracles of the saints, together with two fragments of the commentary published by Mabillon.

73. Gregory also praises, in Book II of the *History*, chapter 22, the book of Apollinaris Sidonius entitled *On the Masses*, to which he says that he added a preface. But that work is known to us only by name.

Of lesser importance is the *Passion of the Seven Holy Sleepers Resting at Ephesus*, which Gregory admits that he translated into Latin with the aid of a certain Syrian interpreter. He gives an epitome of it in chapter 95 of *The Glory of the Confessors*. Whether this very translation prepared by Gregory exists anywhere is uncertain.

We infer that the version found in Surius is not Gregory’s from the single fact that most of the names of the Sleepers given there differ from those which Gregory himself lists in *The Glory of the Confessors*. The very same names appear in a history of these Sleepers that we found in certain manuscript codices. But since it contains much of doubtful reliability, and it is not established that it can be called Gregory’s work, we did not think it appropriate to assign it a place among his works. We shall speak below of the history of the other Seven Sleepers.

While examining manuscript codices, we also encountered various short works under Gregory’s name, entitled *Sermon*, *Life*, *Passing*, or *Miracles*, concerning certain saints whom Gregory praises. But since these are nothing other than Gregory’s own chapters dealing with such saints, excerpted from his works, it would have been superfluous to investigate them at greater length.

74. Besides the books listed above, many writers enumerate among Gregory’s works several separate little books on the lives of certain saints whom Gregory himself praises in various books of the *History of the Franks* or of the *Miracles*.

Among these are the book on the life of Saint Illidius, which he praises in Book I of the *History*, chapter 40; and the book on the life of Saint Quintianus, mentioned in Book II, chapter 36. Elsewhere he mentions books written by himself on the lives of Saint Monegundis, Saint Nicetius, Saint Friardus, Saint Caluppa, Saint Senoch, and Saint Patroclus. Vossius and others list these individually in their catalogue of Gregory’s works.

Although it is certain that these are not separate from the chapters of the *Lives of the Fathers* that have been published under the titles of the lives of these saints, so far as I know there is no controversy among learned men about this point. Whether these little books should in fact be separated from the *Lives of the Fathers*, as Margarinus Bignius, the Cologne scholars, and others did in their editions, is of little importance.

Certainly, as I understand the matter, Gregory first gathered into a single book the lives of certain saintly Fathers of his own age, which he entitled *The Life of Certain Feliciosi or Religious*. Later, when he had learned the deeds of other saints as well, he issued separate little books about them, which he or others subsequently joined to the rest under the single title *Lives of the Fathers*.

Certainly, in all the manuscript copies that I have been able to see, all these Lives—that is, twenty chapters—are found together under one and the same title, *Lives of the Fathers*. It is certain that he prefixed this title to his book, otherwise called *The Lives of the Feliciosi*.

There would be greater difficulty concerning the Life of Saint Nicholas, which the Sammarthani praise in *Gallia Christiana*, if there were not an obvious error of the copyists—or at least a lapse in the memory of the authors themselves—who introduced the name Nicholas in place of Nicetius. For the Sammarthani, who alone list a Life of Saint Nicholas among Gregory’s works, copied the passage from Vossius’s book *On Latin Historians*. But Vossius does not have a Life of Saint Nicholas; he has one of Saint Nicetius, which the Sammarthani omit.

75. Barrius, the author of the *Christian History of the Ancient Fathers*, Bignius, the Cologne scholars, and others also listed among Gregory’s works a book entitled *On the Miracles of Saint Medard*. Gerardus Johannes Vossius followed them in Book II of *On Latin Historians*, as did several others, because of the following passage of Gregory in chapter 95 of *The Glory of the Confessors*, where, concerning Saint Medard, he says:

> After a book had been written concerning his miracles, a certain woman …

They attributed this book chiefly to Gregory because it was different from the Life of the same saint written by Fortunatus. For that Life was not published until after Gregory’s death. There Fortunatus invites his readers to pray, as he says, for the safety of “our king Theodebert”; and Theodebert succeeded his father Childebert II only after Gregory had died.

But even if we admitted that the book on Saint Medard praised by Gregory was not the work of Fortunatus, it would nevertheless not follow that Gregory published it. Gregory’s words cited above do not prove this: he praises the book, but does not say that he wrote it himself. Yet he regularly does so when he mentions his own little works.

Cointius argues that this book was composed by the very woman who is said to have been healed there by Gregory. But since the work, if it is distinguished from Fortunatus’s book, exists nowhere, it is pointless to investigate its author—no ancient writer praised it, and no modern writer has ever seen it.

As for the antiphon in honor of Saint Medard, which Surius published under the name of our Gregory, scarcely anything certain can be said, since it contains nothing by which its author can be identified. It contains nothing contrary to the truth, provided that what it reports about the death of Saints Medard and Gildard is said to have occurred on the same day, not in the same year. We shall present it in its proper place.

76. Among the innumerable little works of the Fathers and other ancient writers listed in the catalogue of the manuscript codices of England, Freherus notes a *Little Book on the Passion of the Lord* attributed to Gregory of Tours.

But Freherus himself, together with other learned men, judges that this book should not be distinguished from the commonly circulated *Acts of Pilate*. We readily agree, provided that someone gives us more certain information from the English codex itself or from some similar source.

The words in Book I of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 23, may have given that writer—whoever he was—the opportunity to attribute this book to Gregory:

> Pilate sends the Acts to Tiberius Caesar, and reports to him both the miracles of Christ and his passion and resurrection. These Acts are preserved in writing among us today.

But Gregory admits that those Acts were preserved in writing among them; he does not say that he himself wrote them. Hence they have not yet been assigned a place among his works, nor should they be.

77. We found a book entitled *The Miracles of Saint Andrew* under the name of Gregory of Tours in a codex of our library at Saint-Germain-des-Prés, written approximately six hundred years ago. The book is also found in other codices, but without Gregory’s preface.

That preface, as well as the brief epilogue of the work, can scarcely be doubted to be Gregory’s, given the style and manner of composition, even though he made no mention of this book in his catalogue of works. Nor should this seem surprising, since he likewise did not list there the *Masses* of Apollinaris Sidonius, to which he elsewhere recalls having added a preface, nor the *Passion of the Seven Ephesian Sleepers*, which he himself testifies elsewhere to have translated from Greek into Latin.

We shall publish that preface and epilogue to *The Miracles of Saint Andrew*, together with the table of contents and several chapters that have not been published. We shall not publish the book itself, since it is none other than the apocryphal Life of this saint, commonly attributed to Abdias of Babylon.

78. I shall say no more about the *Passion of Saint Julian*, which we found inserted in certain manuscript codices into a book of the miracles of that same saint written by our Gregory. Whether it was inserted by Gregory himself or by someone else cannot be determined.

Some may perhaps think that the *Passion* itself is Gregory’s work. But no one will easily persuade himself that Gregory first wrote it and himself prefixed it to the account of the miracles, and that later generations removed it. On the contrary, it is much more likely that it was attached to the book of miracles so that both works could be read together on the feast of the holy martyr.

If anyone nevertheless says that Gregory himself did this, I shall not strongly object. The short preface prefixed to it has the flavor of Gregory’s style. For this reason we have thought it appropriate to present the book without that *Passion* in its proper place, as it appears in most manuscripts and in all published editions; we shall present the *Passion* itself, together with the beginning of that book, after the other works of Gregory, as it appears in other manuscript codices.

79. Besides the published versions, certain manuscript codices that we have seen attribute to Gregory the history of the Seven Sleepers resting at the Major Monastery.

Certainly Alberic, monk of the Three Fountains in Campania, admitted this book among Gregory’s genuine works. In his *Chronicle*, under the year 319, he writes that the genealogy of Saint Martin was briefly set forth by Gregory of Tours; he then adds the very words found on this subject in the book of the Seven Sleepers, praises the seven brothers, and lists their names.

The same work is praised and regarded as a genuine production of Gregory by a monk of Saint-Sulpice in the patriarchal church of Bourges, chapter 27.

Cointius, however, rejects it as Gregory’s work under the year 595, no. 51, because it is not listed among Gregory’s works in the epilogue to the Gregorian *History*. Yet he had proposed the matter as uncertain under the year 591, no. 2, where, from the letter prefixed to this little book, dedicated to Saint Sulpicius, he acknowledged that the sanctity of that saint was highly commended.

The title “archbishop,” which is attributed to Sulpicius in that letter and to Briccius, bishop of Tours, in the *History* itself, creates difficulty, since we cannot deny that metropolitans in these regions were either never called archbishops before the ninth century or were so called only very rarely.

Nevertheless, we read that Canon VI of the First Council of Mâcon decreed that an archbishop should not presume to celebrate Mass without the pallium.

Nor would I wish to conceal the fact that this *History* is preserved in a codex of the College of the Society of Jesus in Paris, in a much fuller form than the published version, but without the author’s name and even without Gregory’s dedicatory letter to Sulpicius. Briccius is there called not an archbishop but a prelate. We note all these matters in their proper place.

There are other considerations that might perhaps be brought forward on either side of this controversy, but there is no opportunity to pursue them at greater length. I wish only to observe that, even if the letter prefixed to the work is attributed to Gregory, it does not follow that the *History* itself was written by that same author. On the contrary, the writer of the letter expressly states that he found this narrative at the Major Monastery and sent a transcript of it to Sulpicius, as he had requested.

80. In a codex of the monastery of Saint-Patrice, written eight hundred years ago, there is a *Life of Saint Albinus, Bishop of Angers*, ending with the words:

> Here ends the Life of Blessed Albinus, composed by Blessed Gregory, bishop of the city of Tours.

In very many codices—namely, those of the Church of Reims, Saint-Germain-des-Prés, Vendôme, the Royal Library, and several others—there is also a *Life of Saint Maurilius*, likewise bishop of Angers, attributed to our Gregory. But since these Lives are none other than those circulated under the name of Fortunatus, we do not think that they were written by Gregory; perhaps they were merely revised and corrected by him.

The letter prefixed under Gregory’s name to the *Life of Saint Maurilius*, which we shall give at the end of this volume, states this explicitly. There Gregory—or, if it is certain that he was the author of the letter—testifies that he corrected the Lives of Saints Albinus and Maurilius, which had been corrupted by scribal errors.

If we admit that Gregory was the author of this letter, it seems necessary to distinguish the Fortunatus who wrote these Lives from the celebrated poet Venantius Fortunatus. The latter was flourishing in the time of Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, to whom the letter is dedicated, and of our Gregory, and survived them both.

For how could Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, while Fortunatus was still alive and frequently residing in Paris and Tours, have invited Gregory of Tours to purge from scribal errors the Lives of the saints when Fortunatus himself—the author of those Lives, who was present and was regarded as the friend and disciple of both bishops—could have corrected them more easily?

Weighty arguments prove that another Fortunatus existed, distinct from the poet Venantius, but it is not our purpose to pursue them here.

Even if it were established that the *Life of Saint Maurilius* was at some time corrected by Gregory of Tours, we nevertheless maintain that it is not the same Life that commonly circulates in printed books and certain manuscripts, even though Gregory’s letter is read before it.

For the author of this letter says that he undertook to correct that Life chiefly in order to remove from it many things that seemed incredible to people. Among these, surely, should have been counted the resurrection of Renatus, who had been dead for seven years. Yet in the Life itself this miracle—which, as it says there, had been omitted by Fortunatus—is read as an addition to the others.

We prove the same from two manuscript codices: one written approximately six hundred years ago in the monastery of Vendôme, and another of five hundred years in our library at Saint-Germain-des-Prés. There, after Gregory’s letter and the transcription of the table of contents of the Life, we read that it was written at the command of Raino, who is listed thirty-fifth in the catalogue of the bishops of Angers compiled in the time of Bishop Eusebius. It reads as follows:

> Raino, once the daily disciple of Saint Martin and always a canon, and afterward, after a short time, the thirty-third (elsewhere thirty-fifth) humble bishop from the beginning of Christianity of the holy Church of Angers, ordered this Life of Blessed Maurilius to be written and sought out for the honor of almighty God and of that same Saint Maurilius, and for the remission of his soul’s sins, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 905 and in the twenty-fifth year of his episcopal ordination. Archanaldus, disciple and deacon of Saint Martin, wrote and sought it out at the command of the aforesaid Lord Raino.

What that Life was is indicated by Lord Hadmerus in the book on the miracles appended to it. He says that in modern times, during the translation carried out under Bishop Nifingus, this Life—which he had presented under the title of Book I—had been polished by the successors of Saint Maurilius with considerable wit and elegance.

Moreover, this Life contains many things that cannot belong to the age or character of Gregory or Fortunatus, as Launoy has proved at length.

From the same book of Hadmerus we learn that the Life of the same Saint Maurilius written by Magnobodus, bishop of Angers, must also be distinguished from both of the preceding Lives. This Life is entirely different from the first two in the previously mentioned Vendôme codex, where it bears the following title:

> In the name of Christ, I, Magnobodus, bishop—though a sinner—of the Church of Angers, have explained, as my rusticity permitted, simply and plainly, as I was able, according to the writings of the presbyter Justus, the Life of Saint Mauritionus, bishop and confessor, in the tenth year of my ordination and the thirty-sixth year of our prince, Lord King Chlothar, son of King Chilperic.

That is, in the year 619 of the Christian era, shortly after the death of our Gregory.

I have treated these matters at somewhat greater length because the letter published under Gregory’s name is commonly prefixed to the *Life of Saint Maurilius*, which contains many things contrary to the truth and became famous because of the controversy that arose in our own time concerning the resurrection of Saint Renatus.

Some have attempted to confirm this miracle by Gregory’s authority, although it was omitted by Fortunatus, as we have just said, and is not reported by Magnobodus. The latter nevertheless relates that a certain barren woman, through the intervention of blessed Maurilius—for this is how he always calls him—obtained from God a son who, after serving for a long time as a priest in the Church of Calonna, where Maurilius lived, eventually succeeded him in the episcopate.

81. Our Dom Mabillon extracted from an ancient codex of Saint Gall in Switzerland a *Life of Saint Aredius, Abbot of Attanum*, attributed to Gregory of Tours and different from the one published in Volume I of the *Acta Sanctorum* of the Benedictine Order. It seems not unworthy of Gregory and not far removed from his character, except that certain phrases drawn from Gregory the Great, and even from the Rule of Blessed Benedict, occur throughout it, contrary to Gregory’s usual practice.

Moreover, Gregory frequently praises the miracles and deeds of Aredius, but nowhere does he mention, as he otherwise usually does, that he himself wrote Aredius’s Life.

It might be answered that Gregory wrote this Life after returning from his Roman journey, and that it is therefore not surprising that he made no mention of the Life of Saint Aredius in other works written earlier, nor used the expressions of Gregory the Great. After returning from Rome, where—as one may infer of that exceptionally diligent investigator of ecclesiastical matters—he could have seen Gregory the Great’s books, as well as the Rule of Blessed Benedict, which was already famous at that time, he might have imitated their manner of expression.

There are, however, other indications suggesting that this Life should not be attributed to Gregory, but rather to some monk of Attanum who composed it chiefly from Gregory’s works, thereby providing later generations with the opportunity to attribute it to Gregory.

Gregory himself repeatedly praises Aredius and gives a summary of his life near the end of Book X of the *History*. Moreover, the miracles appended to the *Life of Saint Aredius* do not bear the stamp of Gregory’s style.

The author speaks as though a certain bishop had sat in the village of Brioude; elsewhere he writes about the bishop of Tours, who at that time was Gregory, in a manner in which Gregory himself would not have written.

Finally, as is clear from its prologue, this Life was written so that it might be read in the assembly of the faithful on the annual feast of Saint Aredius. All these things, and others that will occur to readers, suggest that the author of this Life was someone other than Gregory.

We nevertheless infer from the events related and from the final chapter that the author wrote it shortly after Aredius’s death. There he testifies that the events he has written occurred within a short time. He therefore concludes that far more numerous events will be written in the future, over the long stretches of time that will follow, since miracles were occurring frequently at the saint’s tomb.

From all this we may conclude that the Rule of Saint Benedict had already been received in the monastery of Attanum at that time—that is, toward the end of the sixth century or at the beginning of the following one—and that the author was thoroughly familiar with it.

82. One question remains: namely, whether our Gregory composed some chronicle distinct from the *History* that we possess from him, as certain medieval authors seem to testify. Following Sigebert of Gembloux, they say that Gregory first abridged the history in a short book, which he later arranged more fully in nine books, and that he also wrote a *Chronicle*, and so forth.

But those authors, as Valesius observes in Book XV of *Frankish Affairs*, carelessly judged one and the same work to be two different works because of the variety of titles in different codices.

Gregory’s *History* is the same work that in some ancient parchment manuscripts is called *Ecclesiastical History* under his name, while in others it is called a *Chronicle*.

Certainly, authors of that age used to call histories *Chronicles* or *Chronica*, even when they were more extensive, if they had been arranged according to the sequence of years. This could easily be proved by six hundred examples.

The *Breviary*, or abridged *History of the Franks*, which some say was published by Gregory, is none other than the *Epitome of Fredegar*. It is not surprising that it was attributed to Gregory, since its wording is entirely drawn from his, and it bears his name, as well as the same preface as the *History*, under Gregory’s name.

Much the same fate befell the book entitled *The Deeds of the Franks*, written by an anonymous author. In nearly all codices it bears Gregory’s name, since for the most part its composition is drawn from his very words.

It is nevertheless entirely certain from the sequence of events that its author reached the principate of Theodoric *Calensis*.

Indeed, in a codex of Saint-Remi at Reims, the anonymous Dionysian book *On the Deeds of Dagobert* also seems to be counted among Gregory’s works. There *The Deeds of the Franks* is called “Gregory’s first book,” while the anonymous Dionysian work is simply called “the second book.” Perhaps by this name Count Ecchard, who founded the monastery of Saint-Patrice, referred in his testament to the *Chronicle that Gregory of Tours composed in two books*.

83. It is not so easy to determine the time at which Gregory composed each of the books he published, [Col. 0069A] or, at any rate, to explain which were published by him earlier and which later. In my opinion, he did not ordinarily complete and write out one book after another in sequence; rather, having sometimes interrupted the composition of one work, he would begin another or continue one already begun. Indeed, even after a work seemed to have been completed, when an opportunity arose he enlarged it with new additions.

Certainly, since he wished to arrange most of his books according to subject-matter rather than chronology, whenever he first found something in some ancient document, heard it reported by others, or himself observed it with his own eyes, he immediately took care to record it in its proper place in those books that he had either already written or was preparing to write on a similar subject. Almost no one can deny that this is especially certain of the books of the *Miracles*, [Col. 0069B] although we do not deny that some order may also be discerned among them.

We infer that Gregory composed the first two books on the miracles of Saint Martin before the others, since no other books of the *Miracles* are cited in them. The book on the *Life of the Fathers* seems to have been written—or rather begun—afterward, under the title *The Life of Certain Blessed Men* (*Feliciosorum*), or, as other manuscripts have it, *The Life of Certain Religious Men* (*Religiosorum*). At first it consisted of fewer chapters, but eventually grew to twenty chapters, or Lives, which it still contains today.

Then he undertook the book on the *Glory of the Martyrs*, to which he added the book on the *Virtues of Saint Julian*, which some call the second book of the *Glory of the Martyrs*, as we learn from its prologue, in which he cites the preceding book. The second book on the virtues of Saint Martin is also mentioned there.

[Col. 0069C] We cannot determine when he began the book on the *Glory of the Confessors*. But we infer that by at least the year 588 it had been extended as far as chapter 95, because there he mentions Charimeres, “who now,” he says, “is Childebert’s referendary.” For in the thirteenth year of Childebert—that is, in the year of Christ 588—Charimeres succeeded Agiricus as bishop of Verdun, as Gregory himself testifies in book IX of the *History*, chapter 23.

Perhaps at the same time he was writing the third book on the *Miracles of Saint Martin*. In its chapter 24 Aredius is praised as still living, although according to Gregory himself, book X of the *History*, chapter 29, he died in the sixteenth year of King Childebert—that is, in the year of Christ 591.

Finally, it is clear that the fourth book on the miracles of the same saint had not been completed before the year 594, [Col. 0069D] since in its fifth chapter a miracle is related that occurred in that very year, namely the nineteenth year of King Childebert.

After all these books, he revised the book on the *Glory of the Confessors*, whose prologue cites the other books entitled *On Miracles*. As for several Lives of saints that he had written separately, we infer that he added them to the book on the *Lives of the Blessed Fathers* only in the final years of his life, because he regularly praises them under the titles of individual little books. Eventually, however, he included them all under the single title *Lives of the Fathers*, adding the prologue that is still read at the beginning of the book today; in that prologue the book on the *Glory of the Confessors* is mentioned.

84. There was disagreement among certain authors of this age [Col. 0070A] as to whether Gregory’s *History* should be regarded as the final product of his mind. Those who wish it to have been written before the books of the *Miracles*, at least before those books were revised, appeal to the text of the *History* itself, which extends only to the sixteenth year of the younger Childebert—that is, to the year of Christ 591. By contrast, certain events are related in his other writings that occurred three years later, namely in the nineteenth year of the same King Childebert, and even after Guntram’s death.

Yet although Gregory’s *History* ends in the sixteenth year of Childebert, it does not follow that it was written in that very year. It could have happened that, while laboring over this work in the final year of his life, he died before reaching the current year.

Certainly, in the epilogue to the *History*, which he perhaps wrote while constrained by illness, he reviews all his other works; [Col. 0070B] but in other books, when he lists the works he had published, he does not cite the *History*. Indeed, in the *History* he repeatedly cites the books of the *Miracles* and the Lives of the saints that he had published, whereas nowhere, so far as we read, does he mention the *History* in his other books. This, it seems to me, is a most powerful argument that Gregory composed the other books before the *History*.

Nor does it help to cite chapter 30 of the book on the *Glory of the Confessors*, where Gregory, praising Stremonius, says that he was sent into Gaul by the Roman bishops together with Gatianus and the others whom we have mentioned. For a little earlier, in chapter 27, he had discussed Martial, bishop of Limoges, whom he records as having been sent by the Romans. He had already mentioned Dionysius of Paris and Saturninus in book I of the *Glory of the Martyrs*.

[Col. 0070C] Moreover, many believe that Gregory published the *History* not once but in stages. They suppose that he first wrote six books, extending to the death of King Chilperic, and later added four others, intending to publish more if God had granted him a longer life. Gregory himself seems to suggest this in the prologue to book VII, where he indicates his intention of continuing the *History*, which, having been brought in the earlier books he published as far as Chilperic’s death, he appeared to have left incomplete.

Fredegarius, in fact, had known no more than those first six books. When he decided to continue Gregory’s *History* in his *Chronicle*, he began with Chilperic’s death. Nor did the Anonymous author who wrote the *Gesta Francorum* possess more than those books. Thus, although he carried his narrative as far as the reign of Theuderic of Châlons, [Col. 0070D] after relating Chilperic’s murder—the point at which Gregory’s sixth book ends—he describes the war between Childebert and Chlotar, both of them the second of that name, omitting the other events recorded in the four following books of Gregory’s *History*. It is certain that this war took place after King Guntram’s death and after Gregory’s complete *History* had ended.

For this reason, in certain manuscript codices, even some of considerable antiquity, only six books of Gregory’s *History* are found. The Corbie and Beauvais codices, however, which seem to have been written not long after Gregory’s death, contain a fragment of book VII.

85. A few observations should be made concerning the titles of Gregory’s books. [Col. 0071A] The books of the *Histories* are entitled *Ecclesiastical History of the Franks* in the most ancient codex of the monastery of Corbie. Learned men have judged this title, as the authentic one and one especially appropriate to the contents of the books, preferable to the others; we have therefore adopted it in our edition.

Most of the other manuscript codices, as well as the printed editions, simply call it the *History of the Franks*; some manuscripts likewise call it the *Deeds of the Franks*. More frequently, however, later authors cite it under the title *Chronicle* or *Chronicles*, as we have already observed.

Gregory himself calls the following seven books by the common designation *the seven books of the Miracles* at the end of the *History*. Some add the *Lives of the Fathers* to them under the title of an eighth book of the *Miracles*. Gregory, however, distinguishes this work from the others under the special title *Lives of the Fathers* in the passage cited above, where he also mentions a book on his exposition of the Psalter and another on the ecclesiastical offices (*cursus ecclesiastici*) that he had published.

[Col. 0071B] In addition, Gregory assigns a particular title to each of the books of the *Miracles* in the prologue to the book on the *Glory of the Confessors*. There the first is said to concern the miracles of the Lord, the holy Apostles, and the other Martyrs, which had previously lain hidden; the second concerns the virtues of Saint Julian the Martyr, whom he sometimes calls his special patron because he had been brought up for some time in Julian’s basilica at Brioude. The next four are called books on the virtues of Saint Martin; the seventh concerns the life of certain Blessed Men (*Feliciosorum*), or, as some manuscripts have it, of certain Religious Men (*Religiosorum*); and the final book concerns the miracles of the Confessors.

[Col. 0071C] Other manuscripts give these same books somewhat different titles. They sometimes call the first book *On the Glory of the Martyrs* or *The Glory of the Martyrs*; some also call it the first book, and call the following book, on Saint Julian, the second book of the *Glory of the Martyrs*. Likewise, a book called *The Glory of the Confessors* appears in some copies; in the *Chronicle of Saint Benignus* it is cited under the title *The Book of Illustrious Men*.

Some, setting aside Gregory’s own division of his books, have introduced another division with new titles. We observed this in a codex of Fleury written approximately six hundred years ago. There the first work appears under its title, the book on the *Glory of the Martyrs*; then the *Lives of the Fathers* appears under the title *The Second Book*; after this comes the book on the *Glory of the Confessors*, which is called there the third book of Gregory of Tours. Whether there were more, we were unable to determine, since the following leaves had been torn from the codex.

[Col. 0071D] Similarly, in a codex of the monastery of Saint-Ouen at Rouen, of the same period, there is a single book stitched together from several chapters of the books on the *Glory of the Martyrs* and the *Glory of the Confessors*, together with several Lives of the Fathers, under this title: “Here begins the book of George Florentius Gregory, bishop of Tours, on the Miracles of the Saints.”

In much the same way, books—or rather several chapters—of the works on the *Glory of the Martyrs* and the *Glory of the Confessors* are intermixed in a codex of the Paris College of the Society of Jesus, under this single inscription: “Here begins the book of the Miracles of George Florentius Gregory, bishop, on the Glory of Many Martyrs or Confessors.”

These matters, however, are of too little importance to deserve fuller treatment. Nor should we linger longer [Col. 0072A] over investigating the names of our Gregory, who is known to have been called Florentius by his father and George by his grandfather. Owing to the errors of copyists, these names are sometimes found written somewhat differently in the manuscripts.

### III

86. Charles Cointius, a priest of the French Oratory, a man renowned for piety and learning, published some years ago his *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks*. In the first and second volumes he used the books of our Gregory in such a way that he not only cited various passages to illuminate the history of our people or to lend authority to the events he narrated, but also frequently transcribed entire chapters.

But when he encountered certain manuscript codices, and indeed very ancient ones, in which some [Col. 0072B] chapters found in the common editions were missing, he persuaded himself that those chapters had been added to Gregory’s *History* by some interpolator. Therefore, whenever an opportunity arose, he rejected them as spurious, or, if some of them suited his purposes, presented them under the name of an interpolator, whose authority, he maintained, must be far less than Gregory’s.

Since this learned man believed and wrote that not merely one or two chapters, but many chapters scattered throughout Gregory’s *History*, had been interpolated in this way, it seemed important to investigate the matter more fully and carefully, lest false works be imposed as genuine works of Gregory, or true and authentic material lose the authority properly due to it.

[Col. 0072C] To prevent confusion in examining the arguments on this subject, the reasons he brings forward in defense of his opinion must be considered one by one. There are altogether three: first, he derives his argument from the authority of the manuscript codices; second, from Fredegarius, the seventh-century epitomator of Gregory; and third, from differences of style and from various events related in such chapters, which he regards as foreign to historical truth and wholly opposed to Gregory’s genuine productions. If we demonstrate that these arguments are worthless, the learned man’s opinion will collapse, while the integrity of Gregory’s works will stand unshaken.

87. Cointius says that he had seen altogether five manuscript codices of Gregory’s *History*, none of which represents the complete *History* as it exists in the printed editions. [Col. 0072D] He regards this as clear evidence of interpolation, since he considers it much more probable that certain material was added by copyists than that anything was removed from a complete and authentic work.

Although this argument may reasonably have seemed extremely strong to Cointius, since he knew of no other codex containing Gregory’s *History* complete as it appears in the printed editions, it will nevertheless, I hope, seem to learned men entirely without force. We can oppose codices to codices, and we can also demonstrate that the codices containing the complete *History* possess much greater authority than those that, as we shall prove even from Cointius himself, are mutilated and defective, since they do not present Gregory’s genuine *History* in its entirety, as he himself admits. Let us therefore come to the matter itself.

88. First, [Col. 0073A] we have before us a codex of excellent quality from the library of the monastery of Bec in Normandy, elegantly and accurately written approximately seven hundred years ago. Not a single chapter of Gregory’s printed *History* is missing from it.

We have also had another codex from the monastery of Royallieu of the Cistercian Order in the diocese of Beauvais, no less complete except for one or two chapters of the final book, which are absent because several leaves have been removed from the codex.

We present a third from the famous library of the holy monastery of Monte Cassino in Italy. It was written in Lombard script approximately seven hundred years ago or more, according to our Mabillon. From it we received not only various [Col. 0073B] readings but also the complete sequence of all the chapters, sent to us by the pious and learned Dom Erasmus of Gaeta, librarian and vicar general of that holy place. From this sequence and from the various readings we discovered what had already been established for me: not a single chapter is missing from that codex.

We likewise have two codices from Roman libraries as witnesses to the same fact, brought from Gaul to Rome by Queen Christina of Sweden. One is preserved in the Vatican Library, the other in the library of His Eminence Cardinal Ottoboni. Dom Claude Stephanotius, the procurator general of our Congregation in the Roman court, carefully inspected and examined them and observed that they were entirely complete, except that the final chapter of book X is absent from the Ottobonian codex.

[Col. 0073C] A sixth codex was supplied to us by Father Modestus of Saint-Amable, of the Order of Discalced Carmelites. In the *Holy Monarchy* he praises the Clermont codex, in which Gregory’s *History* is no shorter by even one chapter than the printed editions. Our own Peter Laurence, a monk of Illiers, inspected and carefully collated that same codex—or at least a similar one—which is still kept by the Discalced Carmelites at Clermont, and found it entirely complete.

We owe knowledge of a seventh, and indeed ancient, codex to Guillaume Morel. He admits that he obtained it from the library of Saint Martin of Tours. From it we learn that all the disputed chapters were present, not only from the correction of the text but also from the various readings taken from that codex, which Morel himself reported in the appendix to his edition. Among these readings there are frequent references to chapters that Cointius believes should be excised.

[Col. 0073D] I saw an eighth codex in the library of the monastery of the Holy Trinity at Vendôme. It contains no more than the first five books of the *History*, with the title of book VI, but it represents every chapter of those books, which is the central point at issue.

Add to these Gregory’s published editions, which unquestionably were based on complete codices. Certainly Guillaume Parvus, who first published Gregory’s *History*, did not add these “interpolations,” as Cointius calls them, on his own—although [Col. 0074A] Cointius seems to imply this. But it is certain that, even if they were interpolations, they are found in manuscripts much older than his edition.

After him Matthias Flacius Illyricus, Marquard Freher, and other learned men published the same *History* in complete form, corrected and illustrated from manuscript codices, as they themselves assert. Yet they nowhere warned that many passages were missing from their codices and should be considered stitched onto Gregory’s work.

The same must be said of the edition of André Duchesne, who declares that he carefully corrected it from five manuscript codices.

Besides these codices in which Gregory’s *History* is transcribed complete, we have many others, including some of great antiquity, that support our cause no less, since they contain, under the name of Gregory of Tours, chapters that Cointius calls interpolated. Such is the Life of Saint Brictius, attributed to Gregory of Tours in the most ancient lectionaries; the deeds of Saint Salvius, bishop of Albi, in the codex of Marmoutier; and various other examples that there is no time to list individually.

[Col. 0074B] We cannot, however, omit an old collection of canons and professions of faith copied from the Fossatensis codex, now Colbert’s. In it several fragments of our Gregory are cited in such a way that it cannot be denied that they were taken from the complete *History* as we defend it.

There Gregory’s discussion of the Catholic faith with Agilanus, an envoy of King Leuvigild, is cited under the title *Disputation on the Faith of the Trinity*, “which Gregory, bishop of Tours, composed,” and is said to be in book V, chapter 43. Shortly afterward, another discussion that he held with Opila, [Col. 0074C] likewise an envoy of Leuvigild, is said to have been excerpted from book VI, chapter 40. These statements cannot be true if those chapters are removed from Gregory’s books as Cointius wishes to have done.

According to Cointius’s reckoning, the first of these disputations occupies chapter 31 of book V in the Corbie codex, while the second occupies chapter 26 of the following book.

89. We therefore oppose codices to Cointius’s codices, and complete, wholly uncorrupted codices to mutilated and defective ones. The codices praised by Cointius must be considered inferior to ours in authority for this purpose, since all of them lack many passages that, even according to Cointius’s own admission, belong to Gregory’s *History*.

The Beauvais codex should rather be called a fragment of Gregory’s *History* [Col. 0074D] than Gregory’s *History* itself, since it begins at chapter 3 of book II and ends at chapter 23 of book V.

The Corbie codex is not mutilated, but it presents only the first six books, omitting the rest except for a fragment of book VII, which, as in the Beauvais codex, is placed near the end of book IV.

The Colbert codex, which Valesius calls the Thuaneus and Cointius calls the Saint-Michael codex, is wholly on our side, if it deserves any confidence. Several quires having been torn from it, it begins at chapter 17 of book VI and thereafter omits no chapter whatever.

The other Thuaneus, or Colbertinus, which Cointius calls the Saint-Arnulf or Metz codex, is defective at the beginning owing to a fault in the codex and subsequently omits many passages. [Col. 0075A] This was done deliberately, and indeed so carelessly that it confused books IX and X of Gregory’s *History* in order to make room for Fredegarius’s *Chronicle* among Gregory’s works under the title of book X of Gregory’s *History*.

Finally, the fifth Cointian codex, from the royal library, contains scarcely four books, copied so carelessly that there is no agreement between the chapters listed in the index and the chapters actually written in the book. Indeed, book IV ends at chapter 17, although all the chapters of that book are listed in the table placed before it.

The codex is not, however, mutilated: after these books of the *History*, Ado’s *Chronicle* follows in the same hand.

90. Another argument likewise proves that the Cointian codices do not possess sufficient authority [Col. 0075B] for excising numerous passages from Gregory’s *History*: namely, the fact that the missing chapters are not the same in all those codices but vary from one to another.

There are passages in the Corbie or Beauvais codex that do not occur in the Metz, Saint-Michael, or Royal codices; conversely, other passages occur in those codices, or in one or the other of them, that are absent from the Beauvais or Corbie codex. Thus no certain rule can be established from any of these codices.

If the Corbie codex is preferred to the others because it is much older and more complete than they are, the authority of the others will immediately become unstable, since they will have been mixed with various interpolations. The same must be said of the Corbie or Beauvais codex itself if the authority of the Royal or, at any rate, the Metz codex is judged preferable to that of the others.

[Col. 0075C] Indeed, whether the learned man wishes it or not, neither the Corbie nor the Royal codex, nor any other of Cointius’s codices, can escape criticism, since none of them represents Gregory’s genuine works with sufficient accuracy: some admit interpolated material, while others reject genuine material.

The Corbie codex itself contains only six of Gregory’s books, although even Cointius does not deny that there were more books, which were already known at the time when that codex was written. For it contains, like the Beauvais codex, a fragment of book VII.

Furthermore, the Beauvais codex passes in book II from chapter 19 to chapter 32. Yet not everything in between can be called interpolated, even according to Cointius’s own admission, and the Corbie codex would contradict him on this point.

Certain passages, therefore, and indeed entire books, were removed from Gregory’s works in these codices deliberately and by the copyists’ own choice. Why, then, should they not also have omitted certain chapters that the copyists, or at any rate the epitomators, did not consider relevant to their purpose?

[Col. 0075D] The reason those writers had for not copying the later books of Gregory’s *History* was the same as their reason for omitting numerous chapters from the earlier books. If my conjecture is not mistaken, they wished to possess a history of the Frankish kings separated from foreign narratives and particular events. Thus they had those things that Gregory had written on that subject copied, while omitting other matters that did not belong to their purpose.

[Col. 0076A] For the chapters absent from the codices praised by Cointius concern certain individual persons, or present a succession of bishops, especially bishops of Clermont and Tours, or treat other matters of the same sort, about which lovers of Frankish history—particularly those living in provinces far removed from Auvergne or Tours—cared little.

Fredegarius certainly did the same. In composing an epitome of the *History of the Franks* from Gregory’s writings, he omitted most such material because it did not concern Frankish affairs. The Anonymous author who wrote under King Theuderic, Aimoinus, and the other historians of the Franks who followed them did the same.

The copyists of these codices may also have had another reason for omitting certain chapters: the events narrated in those passages were repeated in the books of the *Miracles* published by Gregory.

[Col. 0076B] I have found the same thing in various copies of the *Miracles*. When these codices had presented separately, under Gregory’s name or under some other title, the passing of Saint Martin, the passing of Saint Radegund, or other stories of that sort, these very chapters were omitted in their proper places from the books of the *Miracles*. Yet no one would say that they had not been excerpted from those works.

Indeed, we shall see below that the books of the *Miracles* published by Gregory suffered the same fate as his *History*, since there are certain manuscript codices in which many chapters are regularly omitted while the rest are represented, as though those books in fact contained nothing more.

91. These particular events, the successions of bishops, and the deaths of distinguished men—all of which Cointius considers interpolated and which the epitomators omitted—Gregory nevertheless rightly admitted into his *History*. As he observes in the prologue, he had undertaken not only to describe the deeds of kings and princes, but also to relate to the faithful [Col. 0076C] how the Churches had been defended, how the faith of Christ had languished in some and burned fervently in many, what conflicts belonged to the wicked, or what manner of life to those who lived rightly, and other matters of the same kind. These subjects will be difficult to find in Gregory’s *History* if the chapters that Cointius insists should be rejected are removed.

Furthermore, as the Corbie codex also indicates in its title, Gregory wrote an ecclesiastical history. It therefore required accounts both of episcopal successions and of the deaths of great men, together with narratives of their distinguished deeds.

The earlier writers of ecclesiastical history whom Gregory had proposed to imitate had done the same, especially Eusebius of Caesarea. In addition to the deeds of distinguished men, Eusebius inserted in his *History* lists of bishops not only [Col. 0076D] of the patriarchal sees, but also of the Church of Caesarea, over which he presided, and of Jerusalem, which at that time was subject to his metropolitan see.

92. In my view, a decisive argument can also establish that Gregory’s *History* was abbreviated in the Cointian codices and cut down from a fuller form, such as is found in other codices, if it can be shown that numerous chapters found in Cointius’s copies have a necessary connection with the very chapters missing from them.

Moreover, the passages that Cointius calls interpolated are sometimes explicitly cited in those codices, such as the Corbie codex, in which the sense is occasionally incomplete and defective unless it is supplemented from other codices.

[Col. 0077A] Several examples of this must be presented.

In the Corbie codex, which alone with the Royal codex contains book I, chapters 26 and 27 are missing. Thus Gregory’s account of the Roman emperors who persecuted Christians in the early centuries of the Church is interrupted. He passes from the persecution of Trajan to that of Decius, omitting the persecutions of Hadrian, Antoninus, and Severus. Yet Gregory, who professed to follow the chronicles of Eusebius, Orosius, and Severus, cannot be said to have omitted them.

He would also have omitted several emperors in presenting their succession, although he had nonetheless resolved to carry that succession intact from Julius Caesar to the establishment of the Frankish kingdom in Gaul.

In the same Corbie codex, chapter 31 and the following four chapters are missing. [Col. 0077B] Yet chapter 36, which it calls chapter 30, begins, as it does in the other codices, with the words: “Then our light also rises . . . Martinus”—a thoroughly erroneous reading. For in that case Martin’s birth would be assigned to the time of Valerian and Gallienus, unless five chapters are supplied from other codices, chapters in which Gregory carries the succession of emperors from Gallienus to Constantius. He actually relates that Martin was born while Constantius was emperor, which is entirely consistent with the truth.

93. In book II, chapter 3, Gregory describes the persecution stirred up by the Vandals in Africa. On that occasion he gives the complete letter of Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, as it appears in the printed editions and in our codices.

But after relating the history of the persecution, the Corbie codex omits the letter, although [Col. 0077C] it is plainly evident that it was deliberately passed over. For it reads as the other codices do: “But when Eugenius saw that he was being led away, he sent a letter to the citizens . . . in this manner”; then, with the letter omitted, it continues the history.

A little farther on, the Beauvais codex omits twelve verses that completely interrupt the sense, as may be seen in their proper place.

Likewise, the Royal codex omits chapters 5 and 6 of the same book, in which Attila’s invasion of Gaul is narrated, although it contains chapter 7, which continues the account of that same invasion.

94. Book III is exactly the same in all the codices, and therefore there is no controversy concerning it.

But [Col. 0077D] in book IV, chapter 13, in the Corbie codex, as also in ours and in the printed editions, Gregory, speaking of the litany or supplication instituted by Bishop Gallus to Saint Julian of Brioude, says: “According to the institution of Saint Gall, as we wrote above.”

The passage to which he refers appears above in chapter 5. Yet that chapter is missing from the Corbie codex itself, as it is from the other Cointian codices.

In chapter 14 of the same book, which all the manuscripts contain, the Saxons are said to have rebelled against King Chlotar in renewed madness. Their first rebellion, however, is described in chapter 10, which the Royal and Saint-Arnulf codices omit.

Likewise, these same two codices, like all the others, contain the statement concerning Chramn in chapter 16: “He was perpetrating various evils, as we have said.” Gregory had spoken at greater length of these evils in chapter 13 of the same book IV, which is not found in those codices.

[Col. 0078A] 95. Chapter 21 of book V, in which Gregory described various crimes of the bishops Sagittarius and Salonius, is missing from the Corbie, Beauvais, and Colbert—or Saint-Arnulf—codices. Yet those same codices contain chapter 28 of the same book, which plainly presupposes chapter 21.

For Gregory, reviewing the case, writes as follows: “Against the bishops Sagittarius and Salonius that ancient calamity is repeated. Crimes are brought against them,” and so forth.

But in the final chapter of the same book, which no codex lacks, these words are read: “Therefore, when farewell had already been said after the aforesaid synod, . . .” These words concern the Synod of Berny-Rivière, whose proceedings and occasion Gregory narrated in chapter 48 and the following chapters of the printed editions and of our manuscripts. Yet the Cointian codices do not contain these chapters at all.

Moreover, chapter 32 of the following book, which is likewise found in all the printed and manuscript copies, including the Cointian ones, plainly presupposes these very chapters omitted here.

## 96

Now, since we have reached the sixth book, several examples must also be brought forward from it; these will leave the supporters of Cointius no loophole, however slight, if they maintain that the authority of his manuscripts should be followed in distinguishing genuine chapters of Gregory’s *History* from interpolated ones.

Gregory begins chapter 12 with these words: “Then King Chilperic, seeing these disputes between his brother and his nephew”—disputes which are plainly no different from those Gregory had narrated in the preceding chapter, as Cointius himself admits. Yet the two Cointian codices, namely the Corbie and Metz manuscripts, omit chapter 11, although they possess [Col. 0078C] chapter 12.

Indeed, these same two codices also contain chapter 24 of the same book, which begins as follows: “New wars again arise against Theodore, etc.” These words plainly and necessarily presuppose the whole of chapter 11, which, as we have already observed, is absent from Cointius’s manuscripts—something Cointius himself is compelled to admit. Fredegar also supports us, since in his epitome he treated both chapters, namely the eleventh and the twelfth.

Accordingly, these two passages placed Cointius in such difficulties at the year 581, number 9, that, on the one hand, he refused to admit chapter 11 because it was absent from his manuscripts, while, on the other, because of its close—indeed, as he himself admits, necessary—connection with chapters 12 and 24, he did not dare wholly to reject it. He therefore preferred to leave the matter unresolved [Col. 0078D], judging it sufficient to say that this eleventh chapter deserved greater credence than the other chapters missing from the Corbie manuscript, “since,” he says, “there are no arguments by which it can either be proved or disproved.”

But if the words of this learned man are accepted, those arguments which elsewhere he regarded as especially powerful for proving the interpolation of many chapters in Gregory’s *History* must collapse—namely, the testimony of manuscript codices. For when, despite the authority cited from the Corbie and another manuscript, and even from Fredegar himself, he answers that there are no arguments by which the authority of this passage can either be proved or disproved, he undermines his own position.

Chapters 34 and 35 of the same book are no less closely connected. In the former, the death of one of King Chilperic’s sons is described; this death provides the foundation for the latter chapter, which begins: “While these things were taking place, the queen was informed that the child who had died, etc.” Yet the first chapter is absent from Cointius’s manuscripts, which contain the second.

Chapter 15 of the same sixth book placed Cointius in still greater difficulty. He says that it is so closely joined to the following chapter that he admits the two to be connected by an indissoluble bond. Yet the Cointian manuscripts omit the former and contain the latter.

Thus, becoming bolder against his own manuscripts, Cointius admits at the year 582, number 4, that their authority is very great for rejecting certain chapters, but not equally weighty for retaining them. “The other chapter,” he says—namely chapter 16—“although it is found in the Corbie and Metz manuscripts, appears to be spurious, because it is very closely connected with the preceding chapter” [Col. 0079B], which cannot be admitted.

He explains in a single word why the preceding chapter cannot be admitted: namely, because it falsely, as may be conjectured, censures Bishop Felix. By these words he deprives his own manuscripts of all authority, including the Corbie manuscript, which, as Cointius himself affirms, like the others admitted fables and slanders against a bishop; these alone provided him with an occasion for detecting interpolation.

It is therefore not surprising that, elsewhere, when discussing the chronological calculations found at the end of the fourth book of Gregory’s *History*, Cointius wholly rejects them as wrongly attributed to Gregory, although they are found in every codex, both printed and manuscript, including the Corbie and Beauvais manuscripts, which were written not long after the lifetime of our Gregory.

Cointius therefore argues in vain that those codices support him, when he himself is compelled to admit that they are interpolated and offer uncertainties as certainties. On the contrary, everyone can see that those very codices are much more favorable to our position. For once it has been admitted—as the passages we have cited irrefutably prove—that they were copied from the complete *History* by someone who wished to collect only the principal events, they do not oppose the integrity of Gregory’s *History*, which we defend, and they retain their full authority. Their conformity with the other manuscripts and their antiquity ought certainly to secure this authority for them.

No one who has examined them can deny that some of them, such as the Beauvais and Corbie manuscripts, were written not long after Gregory’s time.

## 97

Thus far we have discussed the first six books of Gregory’s *History*. Regarding the remaining books, there is less to be said from the manuscript codices, since thereafter Cointius possessed no sufficiently authoritative manuscript by which he could distinguish—using his own expression—the interpolations from Gregory’s genuine text.

Nevertheless, his inclination to cut down the books of Gregory’s *History* was so strong that whenever an opportunity arose to cite chapters missing from the Metz manuscript, he immediately declared them, solely because they were absent from that codex, either interpolated or at least doubtful. He did this even though he himself acknowledged that the manuscript was incomplete and defective, and although he had another manuscript at hand—not to mention the others—from the monastery of Saint Michael, much older and of better quality, in which all the chapters are contained, as they are in the printed editions.

“But this manuscript,” Cointius says, speaking of the Saint-Michael manuscript, “relates exactly the same things as the printed editions and therefore cannot help in detecting interpolations.”

In these words, however, the learned man assumes what he was obliged to prove. He speaks as though it were certain that many passages in Gregory’s later books had been interpolated. Yet this is precisely the matter under investigation, and it was he himself who wished to investigate it.
