If anyone wishes to know what authority should be assigned to the two manuscripts, or which of them should be preferred to the other, this must be judged from the condition of the manuscripts themselves.

As we have already observed, the Metz manuscript, incomplete and defective through the carelessness of its scribe, contains ten books which it attributes to Gregory. Yet it patches together several genuine chapters from the ninth and tenth books into a single book, which it calls the ninth, in order to make room among Gregory’s works for Fredegar’s *Chronicle*, which it placed under the title of the tenth book.

At the beginnings of the books, indices of the chapters are sometimes prefixed in this manuscript, but they are so defective that for the most part they do not correspond to the chapters transcribed in the book itself. Some chapters are omitted, others divided into several chapters, and sometimes two are compressed into one.

The same manuscript contains chapter 7 of book X, which begins, as it does in the printed editions: “In the aforesaid city, namely Clermont,” although it says nothing about that city. The two preceding chapters have been omitted and must therefore be supplied from other copies.

The Saint-Michael manuscript, however, lacks its beginning [Col. 0080C], owing to the ravages of time. For from the numerical letters placed along the lower edge of the manuscript it is discovered that, out of twenty gatherings, ten are missing from the portion of the manuscript that contained the first part of the *History*, that is, the first five books.

It begins, accordingly, with chapter 7 of book VI, and thereafter nothing is missing from that manuscript. It is written in a plain and even script, which appears to be at least seven hundred years old, and in a style that unmistakably bears the mark of antiquity—precisely the kind of style Cointius repeatedly says he seeks in Gregory. That is, it frequently contains changes of case; one letter is used in place of another; men’s proper names are formed barbarously; and all the other features are found which Cointius commonly praises in the Corbie manuscript in the earlier books of Gregory’s *History*.

These two manuscripts are still preserved in the Colbert Library, where anyone can readily consult them.

But if the Saint-Michael manuscript possesses such authority over the Metz manuscript, everyone can see that Cointius wrongly regards those chapters as interpolated—or at least relegates them to the category of doubtful passages—merely because they are omitted from the Metz manuscript while being found in the Saint-Michael manuscript.

But enough has been said about the manuscript codices. We must now turn to the argument drawn from Fredegar.

## 98

Cointius repeatedly proclaims that Fredegar’s authority is so great in this controversy that he has sometimes asserted that the entire dispute could be settled by it alone, since it supplies, as he puts it, the strongest arguments for refuting the boldness of the interpolator.

We prove, however, that Fredegar’s authority favors us much more than Cointius by this fact alone: as Cointius himself admits, Fredegar accepted many of those chapters which are missing from the Royal and Metz manuscripts, and even from the Beauvais manuscript; yet he omitted many passages from Gregory’s genuine works which all the manuscripts, including the Cointian ones, contain.

For Fredegar wholly passed over the first and the four last books of Gregory’s *History*, except for two or three chapters of book VII. From the remaining books he did not touch chapters 3 and 4 of book II; he omitted several chapters from book III, which is found complete everywhere; and from book IV he does not contain chapters 4, 12, 31, 34, and 41. From book V he omits chapters 11, 14, 21, 22, 30, and 32; from book VI, chapters 5, 17, 28, 29, 30, 32, and 33. Yet all these chapters [Col. 0081B] are found in the Corbie manuscript and are accepted by Cointius as genuine and authentic offspring of Gregory.

It is therefore clear that Fredegar’s authority is not very useful to the learned man for proving, from Fredegar’s silence, that many passages were added to Gregory’s *History*, since it is certain that this author freely and deliberately omitted many passages from Gregory’s genuine text.

## 99

“But,” you will say, “when Fredegar was composing an epitome of Frankish history, he judged it contrary to his purpose to insert foreign matters, even if they had actually been related by Gregory. Thus no one should be surprised if he omitted some chapters from Gregory’s genuine *History*.

“Yet he cited none of the passages missing from the Corbie manuscript. It is therefore probable that they did not yet exist at that time, but were later stitched into Gregory’s works by an interpolator.”

But Cointius’s whole argument collapses—and will entirely favor us—if it is true that Fredegar followed the same principle in omitting the passages absent from the Corbie manuscript as he did in omitting those which he did not report from Gregory’s genuine *History*. We have already observed that this was indeed his principle, and we have demonstrated it again.

Fredegar omitted chapters from Gregory’s *History*, even genuine ones, which had little relevance to the general history of the Frankish people. The scribe of the Corbie manuscript did the same; so did those who copied the other manuscripts cited by Cointius. And they did so with the same purpose as Fredegar.

For, just like Fredegar, wishing to preserve only a general history of the Franks, they omitted the individual histories of private persons or particular places as useless to their purpose.

The variety of omissions in the various manuscripts suggests the same thing. As we have already observed more than once, such was the fortune of our Gregory that, since he was the first and only ancient writer to record with distinction the great deeds of our people, later writers copied from his works, each according to his own inclination, whatever seemed useful to him: some copied more, others less.

Hence some manuscripts present four books of the *History*, others five, others six, and still others nine or ten. Even within those books, some copied more chapters and others fewer, according to their preference; while some reduced them to an epitome.

Anyone who has even slightly studied the history of our people knows all this—anyone who has read the works or chronicles of Fredegar, Aimoin, Rorico, Adhemar, and many other authors. Nor do manuscript codices fail to prove that similar freedom was exercised in dividing up the books of the *Miracles*. Some contain one or two books of Gregory, others several, while some contain only fragments, with titles added as the scribes thought appropriate.

There is no opportunity to discuss all these matters more fully, lest we seem merely to repeat what has already been said.

## 100

After examining the arguments which Cointius has drawn against numerous chapters of Gregory’s *History* from the authority of certain manuscript codices or from Fredegar’s silence, several others remain to be examined. These he derives either from style or from the contents of the chapters, alleging that they are foreign to Gregory’s manner of writing or at least appear contrary to other works of Gregory himself or to the testimony of other reliable authors of the Gregorian age.

Although we have discussed these matters in their proper places, as far as the brevity of our notes permitted, they must nevertheless be examined here somewhat more fully.

First, as regards the harshness of style or rusticity of language—which Gregory himself repeatedly admits to be found in his works—I appeal to all who have read Gregory’s writings and who are willing to compare the chapters Cointius calls interpolated with the others: could one egg be more like another than these passages are like those?

For in the former, just as in the latter, there are changes of case—that is, accusative cases, as grammarians call them, used in place of ablatives. There are also feminine nouns used as masculines, and masculine nouns joined with adjectives in the feminine gender. There occur exotic words and wholly barbarous modes of expression. The evidence itself prevents us from bringing examples of these matters forward.

I readily admit that in the Corbie and Beauvais manuscripts, which Cointius is rightly pleased to imitate in transcribing Gregory’s text, certain names are written somewhat more barbarously, so to speak, than in the other, less ancient manuscripts; and that changes of case, letters, and genders are more frequent in them.

But this results from the different character and preference of scribes belonging to different periods. Such diversity may indeed prove the antiquity of the manuscripts, but not a diversity in the works themselves.

The same persons are written in sixth- or seventh-century manuscripts as Chlotovechus, Chlothacharius, and Chrochtichildis, while in writings of a later age they are called Hlodoveus, Hlotarius, and Hlotildis—or Chlodoveus, Chlotarius, Chlotildis, and so forth.

The same thing happened with several other words, which copyists altered at will. Thus they changed *equites*—a word the ancients used to designate a horse—into *equos*; *intentionem* into *contentionem*; and, when they found *indignate* or *exsequere* written in their exemplars, they replaced them with *indignamini* and *exsequi*. There are countless similar examples.

These changes certainly gave rise to many variant readings, but they have never caused learned men to call into question ancient monuments, since otherwise it would have to be said that perhaps not a single one had reached us entirely uncorrupted.

Thus the works of Gregory that are no less certain than those called interpolated by Cointius have likewise undergone such changes at the hands of copyists.

But if anyone insists that those ancient and barbarous words or changes of case are absolutely necessary for restoring authority to the chapters Cointius regards as interpolated, and for restoring the native form of Gregory’s works, there are ancient manuscripts which display all of them. We have frequently restored them as they actually occur in our edition, or noted them in the annotations, whenever such unusual forms of expression would have caused excessive difficulty for readers.

The same chapters also contain certain distinctive words that bear the stamp of Gregory’s style and character. Among these are approximately the following: *intentio* used for *contentio*; *equites* for *equi*; *species* for merchandise or things offered for sale; *consensus* for an instrument of election; *cicindelus* for a candle or wax taper; *satellites* for companions; *manicis apprehensus*, “seized by the sleeves”; *Barbarus* for a Frank; and many other expressions of the same kind, which anyone can observe. We have collected them in the onomastic index at the end of this volume.

## 101

Cointius’s argument is no more substantial when he maintains that many things are frequently found in the interpolated chapters which do not accord well with Gregory’s genuine works, or even contradict them.

He then produces several passages in which that author—or, as he calls him, the interpolator—seems not to have sufficiently protected the reputation of certain holy men, and others in which he reports statements opposed to the testimony of contemporary authors. If these passages are admitted, he says, either those authors or Gregory himself must be acknowledged to have departed from the truth. Consequently, none of these passages ought to be regarded as genuine offspring of Gregory.

To all this one could answer in a single word: even if some such things were found in the disputed chapters, their authority would not immediately be overthrown, since many things are also found in Gregory’s genuine chapters which do not agree with Gregory himself or with other records.

Cointius is compelled to admit this more than once in his *Annals*, and Valesius demonstrated it with many examples in the preface to volume II of his *Frankish Affairs*.

Thus, in book II, at the final chapter, Gregory writes that King Chlodovech died in the eleventh year of Licinius’s episcopate at Tours. Yet it is certain that Leo, Licinius’s successor, attended the Council of Agde through his representative five years before Chlodovech’s death.

Gregory says in book IV, chapter 42, that war broke out between Guntram and Sigibert, although, as Cointius himself asserts, this is not true.

In book V, chapters 2 and 3, Chilperic is said to have been at Soissons, although these very passages presuppose that he was absent from there.

I omit other examples, which can easily be supplied from Cointius’s own works—examples of a kind that cannot be found in the chapters Cointius regards as interpolated.

We shall examine in their proper places the particular passages which the learned man brings forward for this purpose.

If Gregory sometimes appears to have shown insufficient concern for the reputation of holy men, this should be attributed to his candor and sincere mind. He presented human actions genuinely, as he knew them, without regard for persons.

Nor should anyone believe that all the deeds even of the holiest men were praiseworthy. Gregory sometimes disagrees with ancient authors and with other writers of his own age. This is not surprising, since even the more ancient records are not always consistent with one another, and daily experience shows that one and the same event may be narrated differently by various authors, even by experienced men who took part in it.

Let us now proceed to unravel Cointius’s particular difficulties.

## 102

Cointius criticizes absolutely nothing in the whole of the first book of the *History*. Since the events narrated in it did not concern his purpose, he did not undertake to examine it.

Nor does he say anything about all those chapters in which Gregory repeats matters that he had treated in other books. He does admit most of the other chapters, since they narrate true and certain events, but regards them as interpolated for the sole reason that they are absent from certain written codices.

These matters have just been discussed, and it would be useless to say more about them. The remaining chapters, which he rejects for some particular reason, remain for us to examine here.

The learned man thinks that chapter 36 of book II was added by an interpolator because the events concerning Saint Quintian reported there are related in an improper chronological order. For the passage narrates the expulsion of the holy man from his see by the Goths, although this had happened much earlier.

I do not deny the point; but nothing follows from it. Gregory does not say here that Quintian was expelled in that very year, which would indeed have been false. Rather, speaking of the great inclination of the Gauls toward the Franks, he says that this aroused the envy of the Goths, who for that reason had driven several bishops from their sees. On this occasion Gregory offers the distinguished example of Saint Quintian, although the saint had left his see and departed from the city long before that time.

## 103

There is no matter of controversy in the third book, since all codices, both printed and manuscript, reproduce it in full.

Chapters 5, 6, 7, 11, and 12 of book IV are missing from certain manuscripts because, as we are convinced, they did not concern the general history of the Franks.

Cointius maintains, however, that these chapters were fabricated and deserve no credence because, if they are admitted, the bishops of Aquitaine Prima—including several who are still honored today with the title of saint, such as Probianus, bishop of Bourges, and Dalmatius, bishop of Rodez—would have to be judged guilty of the gravest offense. They had decided to ordain a bishop without consulting the king, and one entirely unworthy of such dignity: namely Cato, who was so swollen with pride that he considered no one more worthy of the episcopate than himself.

Cautinus, too, who was promoted to the episcopate, is portrayed in these chapters in such colors that he ought rather to have been punished with the extreme penalty than granted an episcopal see.

This is Cointius’s argument. But these considerations in no way overthrow the authority of the events reported in the chapters.

The audacity of the bishops of Aquitaine must indeed be condemned: without consulting the king, they had resolved to ordain a bishop, even though he had been elected by clergy and people. But the unusualness of the act does not diminish the truth of the event, which could also be confirmed by other examples.

Certainly, the attempt of the bishops of another Aquitaine—namely, the province of Bordeaux—was far more audacious. They had driven Eumerius, bishop of Saintes, from his see, after Heraclius had already been substituted in his place, because Eumerius had been ordained at the king’s command without the presence of the metropolitan.

The action would have succeeded had not the threats of King Charibert intervened. Out of reverence for his father, he rendered the bishops’ attempt void.

Cato was indeed swollen with pride, but because of his other qualities, especially his compassion toward the poor, he was so well liked by the people that everyone wished to have him as bishop. Both facts are certain from Gregory himself, namely from chapter 31, which even Cointius accepts as indisputable.

There, speaking of Cato’s death, which he suffered while caring for the poor during a time of plague, Gregory says: “He was a man of great humanity and a considerable lover of the poor; and I believe that this was, for him, if he possessed any pride, a remedy.”

As for Cautinus, we readily admit that he is presented in these chapters as extremely savage and wholly unworthy of episcopal rank. But unless Cointius proves from trustworthy authors that he was not such a man, he will establish nothing at all against the truth of this *History*.

Nor does it help that Cautinus was never expelled from his see, since everyone knows that in Gregory’s time several bishops entangled in various crimes remained in their sees until death. If only this could not be proved by so many examples! It is enough to mention Melantius, who was intruded into the place of Praetextatus of Rouen.

He rejects chapter 19 of the same fourth book because it is missing from two manuscripts and does not assign the year of Saint Medard’s death with sufficient accuracy.

But since Gregory did not intend there to designate any precise year for the death of the blessed Medard, this objection contributes nothing to undermining the authority of the chapter. No one disputes Gregory’s statement that Saint Medard died during the reign of Chlothar.

## 104

The learned man attempts to undermine chapter 5 of book V. Although it generally reports true events, he says, it contains several matters that appear open to criticism.

First, it contains much against Felix, bishop of Nantes, whom the Church honors as a holy man. Second, the Gregory whose text is commonly read—or, as Cointius says, the interpolator—there calls Gregory, bishop of Langres, his great-grandfather, and Nicetius, bishop of Lyon, his maternal uncle. This is contrary to the practice of the genuine Gregory, who, when speaking elsewhere of these same holy men, never mentions such kinship. The clerics of Tours likewise remained silent about it in the *Life of Gregory of Tours* himself.

Of these two parts of the objection, Cointius himself resolves one. He admits and defends the kinship between our Gregory and those holy men. Indeed, he confirms by an example that an argument from silence—which might otherwise be extremely strong—must be entirely rejected in this matter.

“For Gallus, bishop of Clermont,” he says, “was certainly the paternal uncle of our Gregory, as Gregory himself testifies in his book *On the Virtues of Saint Julian*, chapter 23. Yet Gregory neither in Gallus’s life nor anywhere else, although he very frequently mentions Gallus and his parents, calls Saint Gall his paternal uncle.”

Cointius adds that anyone who carefully compares the lives of Saints Gregory of Langres, Nicetius of Lyon, and Gallus of Clermont will easily discover that these holy men were related, although Gregory did not state this openly.

As for the sanctity of Felix of Nantes, which forms the second part of Cointius’s objection, I have no intention of detracting from it. But we cannot deny that holy men have had their blemishes, which Gregory perhaps in good faith judged greater in Felix than they really were. This must be pardoned to human weakness.

Certainly, as Cointius himself admits at the year 582, number 4, Gregory openly accuses this same Felix of anger and deceit in book VI, chapter 16. Yet this chapter is found in all the manuscripts, including the Corbie manuscript; indeed, it is joined to the preceding chapter, which is not much more favorable to Felix.

## 105

The objection against chapter 9 of book V is trivial: namely, that the person is called Caluppa here, whereas the genuine Gregory called him Caluppan in the *Lives of the Fathers*.

Who does not know that such names are often written in different ways not only in different manuscripts but also in one and the same copy? It would be entirely pointless to offer examples of this.

Indeed, there is no variation in this name in Gregory. The person called Caluppa in the nominative case in the *History* is the same person who appears in the ablative case as Caluppane in the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 11. Everyone knows that names ending in this way are variously declined, so that we commonly find forms such as Attilanem from Attila and Agilanem from Agila.

## 106

The arguments which the learned man brings against chapter 21 of the same fifth book are, in his view, stronger. They must indeed be very weighty, since they ought to undermine the authority of all the manuscript codices, including the Corbie manuscript, which is believed to have been written not long after Gregory’s time.

For, as Cointius himself admits, this chapter 21 is explicitly cited in chapter 28 of the same book, which all manuscripts possess, and possess complete.

Cointius nevertheless considers it interpolated, and he believes that many things prove this.

First, the title of Patriarch is bestowed there upon Nicetius, bishop of Lyon, contrary to the practice of those times and of Gregory himself.

Second, the fathers of the Council of Lyon are said there to have judged that the bishops Sagittarius and Salonius should be expelled from their sees on account of murders and adulteries, although, as Gregory himself states below in chapter 28, the bishops assembled at Chalon decided that those same bishops should be cleansed of those very crimes by penance alone.

Third, he objects that the Council of Lyon is silent on the matter, since nowhere in the surviving canons of that synod is it stated that the case of Sagittarius and Salonius was discussed there.

Finally, he considers it highly implausible that the interpolator reports that Sagittarius once said that the sons whom Guntram had fathered by Austrigild would never succeed their father in the kingdom because of the lowliness of their birth.

This is Cointius’s argument, and each point must be answered.

First, as regards the name Patriarch, with which Nicetius is honored in this chapter, there is nothing surprising. His successor Priscus had the same title of honor at the Second Council of Mâcon in 585.

The title is also given to Chelidonius, bishop of Besançon, in the *Life of Saint Romanus, Abbot of the Jura*, written by an author contemporary with our Gregory. There the author reproves Hilary, bishop of Arles, for having cast Chelidonius, patriarch of the metropolitan see of Besançon, from his throne.

Saint Desiderius, bishop of Cahors, called Sulpicius of Bourges a patriarch in the following century, in a letter addressed to him.

Although these examples are unusual in each of the authors concerned, they are entirely free from suspicion of falsity or doubt, and so is Gregory’s text.

## 107

Cointius next argues—this is the second part of his objection—that Gregory’s supposed interpolator wrote that a sentence of deposition had been pronounced against the bishops Sagittarius and Salonius, who were guilty of murder and adultery.

“This could not have happened,” Cointius says, “since according to the genuine Gregory, in chapter 28 of the same book, these same bishops were summoned again before the court for precisely the same crimes and were subjected only to penance at the Council of Chalon, but were not deprived of office.”

I readily admit that the fathers of Chalon did not act with the same severity as those of Lyon. But I maintain that the bishops of Lyon pronounced sentence in accordance with the prescriptions of the canons, whereas those of Chalon refrained from enforcing the canons for just reasons, as it is reasonable to suppose.

No one with even a slight knowledge of the canons is unaware that among both Greeks and Latins persons guilty of such crimes were, by a single judgment and with one voice, declared unworthy of an episcopal see.

If, therefore, one of the two chapters—21 or 28—had to be rejected because of the matters contained in them, chapter 28 should rightly be rejected, since it is contrary to ecclesiastical discipline; not chapter 21, which is entirely consonant with the sacred canons and the rules of the Church.

As a witness to this matter, whose authority among all men is of the greatest weight because of his extraordinary learning and sincere candor, I cite Louis Thomassin, a priest of the French Oratory like Cointius himself. Discussing this matter, without rejecting either of Gregory’s chapters, he says in part II, book I, chapter 58, number 11, of his *Ecclesiastical Discipline*:

“The judgment of the Council of Lyon agreed with the canonical decrees, by which criminals of this kind are irrevocably deposed. But the judgment of the Council of Chalon, which was more concerned with leniency, was not so much a judgment as an attempt to obtain favor from the pontiff and king, who were more inclined toward mildness. The bishops judged that these matters should be cleansed by penance; by these words a more lenient and accommodating opinion of the bishops is suggested, not a definitive sentence, etc.”

This author, in the following number, counts the leniency of the Council of Chalon among those rare dispensations which could never obscure the most brilliant light of the canons followed by the fathers of Lyon. Consequently, it cannot undermine the authority of Gregory’s *History* in reporting the matter.

As for Cointius’s objection against the authenticity of chapter 21—namely, the silence of the Council of Lyon concerning the case of Sagittarius and Salonius, since it is not mentioned in the surviving canons of that council—it proves nothing at all unless the learned man demonstrates that absolutely every case discussed in councils was expressed in their canons. No one would assert that.

Nor was this necessary or useful to posterity in the present case. The canons concerning the deposition of these bishops were not then being promulgated, since the ancients already had such canons in abundance. Nor was it appropriate to insert an isolated event into the canons, where it would have served no purpose.

If anyone wants examples of matters discussed in synods which nevertheless do not appear in their acts or canons, I shall offer one or two from Gregory himself.

Gregory relates that a certain bishop was so simple-minded that at the Council of Mâcon he was not ashamed to assert that, under the word “man” in the sacred Scriptures, women were not included. Yet no trace, however slight, of this matter survives in the acts of the Council of Mâcon.

The same author mentions in the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 6, a certain Bishop Marcus who was unjustly expelled from his see. His case was discussed at the Fifth Council of Orléans, as Cointius himself admits, and he was restored to his see. Yet the acts of the Fifth Council of Orléans say nothing about the matter, although Gregory himself writes that the council was summoned by Childebert chiefly for this reason.

## 108

The final part of the objection is that it is not plausible that Sagittarius reproached Austrigild for the lowliness of her birth or said that her sons should not be admitted to the succession.

But this accomplishes nothing unless Cointius proves either that Austrigild did not in fact come from a lowly station—which cannot be done, since Fredegar himself testifies that she was Mercatrudis’s maidservant—or else that Sagittarius was an exceptionally prudent and discreet man, so that he could never be said to have exceeded the bounds of propriety in speech.

Whether that is true, I appeal even to Cointius himself as judge. Who does not know that this man, to say nothing of his other offenses, was frivolous and extremely proud? After various reversals of fortune, he attacked Guntram and his sons not merely with words but also with arms, supporting Gundovald Ballomer’s cause among the Convenae (Comminges), where he miserably perished.

[Col. 0088D] **109.** The learned man brings forward several arguments to undermine the authority of chapter 48 of the same fifth book. Although that chapter contains some true material, he says, it nevertheless seems unacceptable in other respects, since certain details do not sufficiently accord with Gregory’s genuine chapters. For Gregory there portrays Leudastes as a man born in a humble station, who eventually rose from the lowest ranks to the highest summit of dignity and power; yet Gregory never elsewhere reproached him with such things, although he more than once discussed his vices and wicked character.

Next, Cointius says that the interpolator erred by stating that the city of Tours had remained under Sigibert’s authority for two years after it had been wrested from Chilperic’s hands [Col. 0089A]—something Cointius considers false, since Sigibert did not recover that city before the year 574, and lost it, together with his life, at the beginning of the following year.

There is, however, an entirely easy answer to these objections. Gregory did indeed discuss Leudastes’ vices more than once elsewhere, but only in connection with other actions of his; it is therefore not surprising that he said nothing there about his birth or the beginnings of his fortunes. Here, on the other hand, he deliberately undertook to discuss his origin and homeland in detail, and therefore ought to have explained somewhat more carefully his parents and the circumstances of his earliest actions, and to have narrated at somewhat greater length matters that he had elsewhere omitted or touched on only lightly.

Sigibert, moreover, could be said to have held Tours for two years, even though neither year was complete. Who could deny that, among ordinary authors, the final part of one year [Col. 0089B] and the beginning of the next are commonly called simply two years? Gregory certainly does not say here that Tours remained continuously under Sigibert’s authority for two full years.

**110.** Cointius considers chapter 49 of the fifth book—which is chapter 50 in our edition—deserving of rejection because Gregory is there portrayed as imprudent in defending his innocence, answering the king’s questions with matters that he ought to have concealed. He also objects that Chilperic and Fredegund are represented there as much milder than they usually were. Finally, he objects that the interpolator makes disgraceful accusations against Felix, bishop of Nantes, whom he does not hesitate to make a participant in a conspiracy against the king.

As to the first point, Gregory admits that he had heard evil rumors about the queen, but denies that he himself had invented them. This answer may indeed have been imprudent, if the question had not required it. Gregory may have been asked about the rumor that was circulating among the people, and he answered in the manner most consistent with the candor evident in all his other works. I know that this answer seemed imprudent to Valesius; nevertheless, he does not on that account deny that it belonged to Gregory, nor do the other learned men who have never supposed Gregory to have been entirely free from human error.

Of no greater weight is the learned man’s statement that Chilperic’s and Fredegund’s innate savagery is not found in this passage. They were not always and everywhere so cruel that they ordered every person who incurred their displeasure to be put to death by fair means or foul. Certainly this was an affair of great importance: it was being handled in a public synod. The question itself, moreover, was delicate, and Fredegund may not have been pleased that her life and character were being investigated so carefully. She knew Gregory to be a most holy man, whom neither threats nor blandishments could ever turn from the right path. It was therefore more expedient to soothe the king’s anger than to inflame him against the accused.

But once Gregory had cleared himself by oath, and Leudastes and Riculfus had been declared guilty of the calumny, violence was inflicted upon them. When Leudastes escaped by flight, the other was ordered to be killed. Although he obtained his life through Gregory’s intercession, he was nevertheless subjected to intolerable tortures, which Gregory describes.

Finally, as for Felix the bishop, he had indeed received Riculfus into his household, but he was never guilty of, or a participant in, the conspiracy conceived against the king and his sons. Indeed, as we observed in the notes on this passage, this conspiracy against the king and his sons entered the printed text through a change in a small word, but never existed at all.

The printed text reads as follows:

> He said that the queen was accused of this crime so that, once she had been expelled from the kingdom, and her brothers and father had been killed, Chlodovecus might receive the kingdom.

These words represent a wicked conspiracy. But if one reads, as we restored it from the Regiomontanus manuscript, “her brothers having been killed, Chlodovecus by his father,” and so forth, the genuine sense of the passage is recovered: namely, that the queen was accused of adultery at Chlodovecus’s instigation, so that, after she had been expelled on account of that crime, he himself—his brothers having been killed, namely those whom Chilperic himself had already killed at the prompting of that same Fredegund—might, as the sole survivor, receive the kingdom from his father.

**111.** Against chapter 8 of book VI Cointius raises a chronological error, which he considers sufficient to diminish the authority of the chapter. Gregory—or, as Cointius would have it, the interpolator—is said there to state that Eparchius died in the forty-fourth year of his confinement. The learned man proves this false from the Life of that same saint, written by a contemporary author, where Eparchius is expressly said to have lived in confinement for only thirty-nine years.

Furthermore, Aptonius, during whose episcopate Eparchius began to be confined, did not assume the governance of the Church of Angoulême before the year 541. Yet Eparchius unquestionably died in the eighty-first year of that same century, and consequently could not have spent more than forty years confined in his cell [Col. 0090C].

We agree with Cointius that Eparchius died in the thirty-ninth year of his final confinement, as the Life records. But if “confinement” is understood to include the whole period during which Eparchius, after abandoning the world, lived in a monastery or in a deserted place to which he had withdrawn out of a desire for greater solitude, then every difficulty disappears. For it is certain from his Life that he first donned the monastic habit in the monastery of Sedecia (Sedeciano), then lived for some time separated from the others in a solitary place, before he was confined by episcopal authority. Gregory, bringing all these periods together, could therefore, without violating historical truth, say that Eparchius spent forty-four years in confinement.

**112.** As for the matters we considered against chapter 9 of the same book, where Saint Domnolus, bishop of Le Mans, is discussed [Col. 0090D], we dealt with them in the notes to that passage; it would be superfluous to repeat them here.

We must proceed to chapter 15, which Cointius rejects because it contains much damaging to the reputation of Felix, bishop of Nantes, and because it is so closely joined to the following chapter that the one cannot be admitted without the other. The learned man also rejects this chapter, although it appears in absolutely all the manuscripts, including the Corbeiensis, which he does not deny to have been written shortly after Gregory’s time. He must therefore admit that there existed some author either contemporary with Gregory or nearly so, from whom the interpolator—who himself also lived in those times—drew this and many other materials that he reports.

Since, however, this author has never been known to anyone, it seems better for us frankly to admit that Felix did have certain blemishes, but either expiated them through repentance or possessed them to no such degree that they could obscure the charity of Christ, which covers a multitude of sins.

**113.** The learned man considers chapter 22 deserving of rejection because it represents King Chilperic as someone else—namely, milder than he really was. In Cointius’s view, Chilperic would immediately have crushed Charterius, who was accused of having written insulting letters against him, or at least his accuser, the deacon who was said to have planted those letters upon his own bishop.

But Chilperic was not so savage or so incapable of controlling himself that one could say he refrained from cruelty on any occasion only because he was an impostor. Certainly, as learned men have more than once observed, Chilperic was more uxorious than savage, and sinned more by obeying his wife—who incited him to kill men whom she herself suspected—than through innate cruelty.

On this matter we should hear the distinguished Hadrian Valesius in book XI of *The Frankish History*. After criticizing Chilperic for indulging his enraged wife too much, he adds:

> Clearly, whenever she did not incite him, you would have thought Chilperic changed and unlike himself: so approachable, accessible, mild, and even patient of insult was he.

Fortunatus praised his gentleness at length; yet no one has on that account said that this author’s poems were invented by an impostor. And although Fortunatus may perhaps seem to some to have exceeded the bounds of poetic praise in commending Chilperic, no one would say that he chiefly praised gentleness in a most savage man.

Finally, Cointius himself elsewhere reproaches our Gregory for having attacked Chilperic too harshly at the end of book VI of the *History*, as though he were entirely unworthy of praise, although Cointius insists that no one can deny that Chilperic performed notable deeds.

**114.** The often-mentioned learned man considers chapter 34 of the same book interpolated, although it is praised in the following chapter—which all manuscripts and printed editions possess—and contains much that is true. His reason is that, as he says, it contains several matters remote from probability.

The first is that, at the beginning of the chapter, an embassy from the Spaniards is mentioned; if this is admitted, it will be the third embassy that the Spaniards sent to Gaul that year. Second, at the beginning of the chapter the envoys are called *legati* [Note: [Col. 0091] It should perhaps be read: “Second, because at the beginning of the chapter the envoys are called *legati*.”], which indicates that several were sent on that occasion; yet as the speech proceeds, mention is made of only one envoy [Col. 0091D]. Finally, Chilperic is said there to have considered giving Basina in marriage to Reccared, king of the Goths, although she had been violated and confined in a monastery.

The first two objections are very easily answered. It is not impossible that three embassies came from Spain to Gaul in that year, since negotiations were underway for a marriage between Leuvigild’s son and Chilperic’s daughter, something the Goths especially desired. As for Gregory’s having written “envoy” or “envoys” on one occasion or another, that matter is wholly irrelevant to either affirming or denying the authenticity of this chapter.

The plan reported by Gregory—to substitute Basina for Rithgunt and give her to the son of the Gothic king—reveals the mind of a man wavering between alternatives, who both wished and did not wish to give his daughter in marriage to Reccared. The same is proved by the repeated postponements of this marriage, which Gregory himself records. In the end matters proceeded so far that, although she had often been promised and had even set out for that purpose, she never married Reccared.

Thus Chilperic did not dare entirely to reject the request of the Goths, nor indeed did he wish to do so. Yet he found it difficult to part with his daughter, whom he had fathered by Fredegund and loved above the others, especially fearing that she might be badly treated by the Goths, as had happened to Chlotild and Ingund. He proposed substituting Basina for Rithgunt for no other reason, perhaps, than to delay Rithgunt’s departure.

**115.** Cointius adds chapter 36 of the same book to the spurious chapters because Gregory, in discussing Aetherius, bishop of Lisieux, whom we mentioned above, refers to him even though Gregory himself had made no previous mention of him. He also objects that Aetherius is represented in this chapter as insufficiently prudent, since he entrusted the education of his city’s boys to a thoroughly wicked man.

The first part of this objection may indeed suggest either that Gregory had suffered a lapse of memory, or that something concerning Aetherius once existed in Gregory’s writings but is no longer preserved, or at least that these words were added by scribes. It does not, however, establish that the entire chapter was interpolated. Similar words concerning Tetricus, bishop of Langres, in book IV, chapter 16, persuaded neither Cointius nor anyone else that that chapter had been inserted by an interpolator. Gregory says there:

> At that time Saint Tetricus was bishop there, whose memory we mentioned in the preceding book;

yet no trace of him remains in the preceding books.

Aetherius’s indulgence toward a wicked man does indeed show that Aetherius was excessively accommodating and imprudently merciful, but it does not prove that the account of what happened is either false or rashly sewn into Gregory’s text.

**116.** There is no greater reason for rejecting the following chapter, even though it attributes the killing of Lupentius the abbot to Innocentius, count of Gévaudan, who is later said in chapter 38 to have succeeded Theodosius as bishop of Rodez after Theodosius’s death.

It would not have been easy to prevent Innocentius from becoming a bishop, given the great favor he enjoyed with the queen, unless this crime had been publicly known. Yet nowhere do we read that Innocentius was declared guilty of so serious a crime, or even publicly accused, although rumor may perhaps have attributed it to him.

But at that time this was not a lawful—or at least sufficient—reason for preventing an ordination, which otherwise, according to the prescriptions of the canons, was sought through the votes of the clergy and people, or at least by royal command. Nor are there lacking examples of wicked men who for a long time held episcopal sees obtained through crimes during that period. Melantius alone, intruded into the place of Praetextatus of Rouen, can furnish an example of this, as we have already observed [Col. 0093A]. It would not be difficult to add many others, if the matter required it.

**117.** These are Cointius’s principal arguments for diminishing the authority of many chapters in the first six books of Gregory’s *History* that are absent from certain manuscript codices. Concerning the later books he says little, claiming that this is because of the lack of manuscripts.

Yet, while disregarding the excellent manuscript of Saint-Mihiel, he frequently denies various passages to Gregory solely because, as we have already said, they are absent from the manuscript of Metz or are lacking in Aimoinus. It is nevertheless certain, as we have demonstrated above—and Cointius himself cannot deny—that many passages were deliberately omitted from that manuscript.

The authority of Aimoinus in this matter can be shown to be worthless by this single argument: according to Cointius’s own testimony, Aimoinus both admitted interpolated material and omitted genuine material. Aimoinus himself, moreover, in chapter 18 of book I, admits that he encountered a manuscript utterly corrupted by the fault of its scribe.

But Cointius, imbued with the belief that many passages in Gregory’s books had been added by an interpolator, rejects those very authors or manuscripts whom he praises most highly because they omit certain chapters whenever they happen to preserve passages omitted by others.

Enough has been said above concerning the manuscript codices. We must now say a little about one or another passage of Gregory that Cointius contends was interpolated on the basis of the events it narrates.

**118.** The first, and certainly a very celebrated, passage concerns Saint Salvius, bishop of Albi, whose life, remarkable vision, and death our Gregory describes at the beginning of book VII. Cointius considers this passage to have been added by an interpolator, not only because it is absent from the manuscript of Metz, but also because, if it is admitted, Gregory must be judged contradictory to himself: here he records Salvius’s death under the year 584, whereas in book VIII, chapter 22, he writes that it occurred in the following year.

The same author, under the year 686, where he discusses Salvius, bishop of Amiens, does not hesitate to attribute to the interpolator what he calls “impudence,” asserting that he was a liar and perjurer who swore an oath that he had learned from Salvius of Albi the things he dared to insert under Gregory’s name, although he had actually excerpted them from the deeds of another Salvius, who was bishop of Amiens in the following century.

So much for his claim. But these arguments can easily be shown to have no force. First, the authority of the manuscripts is entirely on our side, as we have often said, since we can set against Cointius’s single mutilated, carelessly corrupted, and later manuscript many complete manuscripts of excellent quality and greater antiquity.

Second, there is no contradiction in Gregory between chapter 1 of book VII and chapter 22 of the following book. Although in the first passage he says that Salvius died “this year,” that is, in 584, and in the other says that Desideratus was given to the people of Albi as bishop “this year,” that is, in 585, nothing at all can be inferred from comparing the two chapters except that Salvius died in 584, indeed in the month of September, and that in the following year—that is, after several months—Desideratus was given as his successor. Whether these statements conflict with one another I leave to fair-minded readers to judge.

Certainly, even if the interval between the two events had been somewhat longer, Gregory’s account would not thereby be unacceptable, since it is plausible that after Salvius’s death some disturbances arose over the appointment of his successor. On that occasion, some writers say, the see of Albi was occupied by a certain Theotfridus.

Thus there is no contradiction in Gregory, even if chapter 1 of book VII is admitted among his genuine works.

“But,” says the learned man, “the interpolator, whoever he may have been, inserted into Gregory’s historical text many passages from the deeds of Saint Salvius, bishop of Amiens, who lived much later than Gregory” [Col. 0094B].

Cointius’s entire objection will collapse, however, if we demonstrate that the deeds of Salvius of Amiens were for the most part stitched together from Gregory’s text, rather than that material was added to Gregory from those deeds. This will certainly not be difficult once the two accounts are compared.

Gregory’s narrative contains no contradiction whatsoever. It has nothing that could not have been said by an eyewitness and a contemporary writer. On the contrary, it contains many details which, as Cointius himself admits, belong so specifically to Salvius of Albi that they cannot be attributed without error to the other Salvius.

That author calls God as witness that he is writing the truth—things that he had either seen himself or received from Salvius himself. He must therefore be judged a perjurer and guilty of a most serious crime if he told falsehoods, something that cannot be imagined of anyone without the greatest and clearest reason. Indeed, all these considerations show that the narrative is true and genuine.

Add to this the presence of Gregory’s characteristic spirit and style, together with his genuine modes of expression. The contrary is true of the *Deeds* that bear the name of Salvius of Amiens. They were compiled by an author ignorant of the facts, who did not know the succession of the bishops of Amiens, confused the chronology, reported falsehoods, and, as Cointius himself indicates, rashly attributed to his own Salvius events certainly performed by our Salvius of Albi.

He wrote that Salvius succeeded Honoratus, although Cointius himself admits that four bishops intervened between them. He makes Honoratus contemporary with the monarch Theodoric, contrary to Cointius’s own calculation, according to which the final year of Honoratus was 580 and Theodoric did not obtain the Frankish monarchy until a hundred years later; yet, in the thirteenth year of Theodoric’s reign, Salvius ascended the throne of Amiens.

The same author then relates that Mummolus the Patrician, after capturing a city and demolishing its walls, sent many captives to Spain, and that these were returned to Salvius at the king’s command. But the circumstances of time, persons, and places forbid these events from being understood as referring to the city of Amiens or to Salvius its bishop.

Everything fits perfectly if the reference is to the city of Albi. It is certain that Mummolus occupied that city while Saint Salvius was alive, as Cointius himself wrote after our Gregory. He is therefore forced to admit that his author transferred certain passages from the deeds of Salvius of Albi into the acts of Salvius of Amiens.

If, then, the author of the Life of Salvius of Amiens is shown, by Cointius’s admission, to have attributed certain deeds of Salvius of Albi to his own Salvius, he must have been either guilty of bad faith or—what I would more gladly believe—ignorant: a man who confused the succession and chronology of kings and bishops, transferred cities from one province to another, and finally turned everything upside down in order to fabricate the life of his Salvius.

I now appeal to all who have read this passage: should such an author be preferred to the writer of chapter 1 of book VII of Gregory’s *History*, who composed the deeds of Salvius of Albi in an unimpeachable manner and according to the laws of history?

We have said nothing about the vision shown to Salvius, which may perhaps displease some people, because Cointius admits that it really occurred, whether to Salvius of Amiens or to Salvius of Albi. But reliable witnesses, beyond all exception, frequently report that such visions occurred in those times to holy men, whether they were in the body or outside the body, as the Apostle says of himself: Augustine in his book *On Care for the Dead*, Gregory the Great, the author of the *Passion of Saints Perpetua and Felicity*, and many other authors of great renown.

**119.** It remains for us to say something about the epilogue to Gregory’s *History*, which Cointius partly rejects and partly accepts at his pleasure. He divides it into three parts.

He concludes the first with the words *inlibata permaneant* (“may they remain unimpaired”), and admits it because it is found in the manuscript of Saint-Mihiel. He also admits the second, although it is absent from the Michaelinus manuscript, because, he says, Gregory permitted his works to be described in verse in the prologue to the *History*, and this part of the epilogue contains nothing other than what could have been made from the prologue.

But he entirely rejects the third part, where various calculations are found, because in his view it does not sufficiently agree with Gregory’s reckoning.

In this matter he pays no attention to the authority of the manuscripts, in which these same calculations are found at the end of book IV, even in the Corbeiensis manuscript. Nor does he think we should listen to those who reconstructed the life of our Gregory from his writings, although Cointius admits that this third part of the epilogue was known to them as well.

To refute all this, a single argument suffices for him: the discrepancy among these calculations. Yet no one would say that this alone is sufficient to diminish the authority of a work supported elsewhere by many nearly certain arguments. Who does not know that in such calculations not only did most medieval authors depart from the truth, but scribes also generally added further errors to their errors, either through their own carelessness or because, relying too much on themselves, they wished to correct the calculations of the ancients?

Consequently, in the transmission of such numbers there are almost as many variant readings as there are manuscripts—not only in Gregory’s works but also in other authors of excellent quality, whom no one has on that account considered false or interpolated. This could easily be demonstrated by the six hundred examples supplied by Cointius himself.

**120.** It is now time to bring this discussion to an end, although some may complain that it has been too lengthy. It was necessary to pursue it somewhat more carefully, since the issue concerned the rejection or acceptance of a not insignificant portion of the sole *History* of our people—a portion that a man among the most distinguished of scholars judged should be denied to Gregory, whereas we defend it as his genuine offspring.

I wish everyone to be convinced that I undertook this not out of a desire for dispute, nor because I arrogantly presumed to contend with so great a man, but solely out of devotion and love for the truth, in order to assert and defend the integrity of the works of that author whose restoration and elucidation I had undertaken.

This matter would not have displeased Cointius himself, whose memory I honor deeply, since he was a sincere lover of truth. He adopted his opinion because of the authority of the manuscript codices that he possessed, which were incomplete and defective; he would easily have accepted the contrary view if, in revising Gregory’s history, he had been aided by other manuscripts superior in number, completeness, and authority.

**IV.**

**121.** We have now reached the third part of our preface, in which an account must be given of what we have accomplished in this new edition of Gregory’s works.

We collected Gregory’s works, which had been divided into parts and mixed together with the works of various authors, into a single volume. With the help of manuscript codices, we attempted to purge them of the almost countless errors that had entered the text here and there through defects in the manuscripts or editions, or from any other cause; and in fact, as readers will see, we removed very many such errors.

We then added certain material anew and supplied, on the authority of some copies, several chapters that had been indicated in earlier editions but had not yet been found. In addition, we asserted the integrity of Gregory’s *History*, which had nearly been lost from the minds of certain learned men because of the defects of some manuscripts, by appealing to the authority of manuscripts of better quality and entirely free from suspicion, as well as to other arguments.

We also added marginal notes presenting variant readings from manuscript codices and from old and new editions; indicating the dates of events; elucidating the events themselves; describing the locations of places; and supplying information about persons. Where necessary, we have also cited or quoted passages from other authors.

And lest the text should sometimes appear, so to speak, overwhelmed by the length or multitude of such notes, we added several more extensive notes at the end of the volume [Note: [Col. 0095] We preferred to place the more extensive notes below the text as well. EDIT.], referring to them those matters that required fuller discussion. In these notes we have also inserted certain monuments of antiquity and included other material that had escaped us or that we received after this edition had already been begun, material suitable for elucidating Gregory [Col. 0097A].

Besides this preface, which we place before Gregory’s works, we shall publish a Life collected from his writings by Odo the abbot, compared with many manuscripts. We shall append to it testimonies concerning our Gregory by distinguished men.

After these will follow the Frankish Annals—that is, passages from all the ancient authors who preceded Gregory—and other ancient monuments in which mention is made of France or the Franks, arranged in chronological order. The distinguished Carolus Bultellus, a devoted student of Frankish history, carefully collected these materials and generously communicated them to me for the purpose of illuminating the history of our Gregory.

We append to these a chronological index of those matters in Gregory’s or Fredegarius’s works that chiefly concern Frankish history. For we have not published only Fredegarius’s *Epitome*, which is an abridgment of Gregory’s *History*; we have also thought it appropriate to append his *Chronicle* itself and its continuators, down to the death of King Pippin and the inauguration of his sons Carloman and Charles. We shall discuss these matters specifically below.

We have also added an appendix containing certain ancient monuments of both the ecclesiastical and civil history of our people—namely, those that our Gregory cites or that contribute in any way to elucidating his writings or those of Fredegarius.

I omit the various indexes. Since all these materials will be apparent to every reader, it does not seem worthwhile to explain them at greater length.

But since the quality of the manuscripts from which ancient monuments have either been extracted or emended contributes greatly to establishing their authority and correcting their errors, it is useful to set out individually the number and condition of the manuscripts that we used in preparing this edition of Gregory.

**122.** First, we compared the books of the *History* with two codices of venerable antiquity, which, according to the unanimous judgment of all the learned men who have examined them, were written not long after the time of our Gregory.

They formerly belonged to Antonius Oyselius of Beauvais, a man who rendered distinguished service to literary studies. From him they passed to the distinguished Claudius Jolius, cantor and canon of the Church of Paris, his daughter’s grandson. Through the favor of that venerable and most learned old man, we were able to inspect and examine those very ancient codices conveniently and at leisure, and even to take them home for as long as we wished.

The first of them, which, as we were informed—and as is indicated more than once by an inscription written in the margin of the book—belonged to the Church of Saint Peter of Beauvais, was formerly kept in the library of the principal church of Beauvais. It is written most elegantly on parchment, in large Roman letters of the kind commonly called uncial or majuscule letters. Yet it has been damaged in many places by rain, damp, or mildew, or eaten away by age, so that it is incomplete in many passages.

It lacks its beginning and end because several leaves were torn from the codex. It begins in the middle of chapter 2 of book II and ends in chapter 15 of book V, which corresponds to chapter 23 of the commonly printed editions [Col. 0098A].

The second codex, which, as its inscription testifies, once belonged to the famous monastery of Corbie in the territory of Amiens, should not be considered later in date. Except for its titles and the beginnings of several books, which are written in majuscule Roman characters, it is written, as Valesius says, in thoroughly barbarous letters of medium size. The letters are so interconnected, and so many are represented by certain abbreviated symbols, that the reader must almost guess what is written.

This difficulty of reading, as I suppose, so discouraged André Duchesne that although he testifies that he had seen the codex, he does not say that he collated it. Indeed, the few remarks he makes about it differ so much from the codex that one could scarcely say that he had seen it.

The codex, however, is complete, and its writing has remained intact. The difficulty of reading it did not deter me from the task, so that I even collated it word for word in its entirety against the printed editions. It is written in the letters commonly called Merovingian or Frankish. Anyone who wishes to see its characters as they are actually written should consult Mabillon’s *De re diplomatica*, where, in book IV, page 349, he will find a specimen of them engraved from the codex itself.

We also possessed two other codices from the Colbert Library. Because they once belonged to the distinguished de Thou, Duchesne and Valesius commonly call them the Thuanean codices.

Cointius preferred to call one of them the manuscript of Saint-Mihiel because, as its inscription indicates, it was written in some monastery of that name; he called the other the manuscript of Saint-Arnulf, or the Metz manuscript, after the famous monastery to which it once belonged [Col. 0098C].

The former appears to have been written about seven hundred years ago, in an old script and without any division of the chapters, although an index of them precedes each book. But after the first ten quires had been removed from the codex, it begins only in the middle of chapter 17 of book VI.

The latter is about one hundred years more recent. It too lacks its beginning because the codex is defective, since it begins with chapter 7 of book II. Many chapters, however, are missing here and there, either through the scribe’s carelessness or by design. Some have been added by another hand, and there are also frequent interlinear variant readings, or explanations of words, which were either supplied from another codex or added by the copyist himself.

Finally, it stitches book IX and book X—or rather, several chapters from each—into a single book under the title of book IX, and calls Fredegarius’s *Chronicle* Gregory’s book X, as we have already observed above.

From the Royal Library we had a single codex of Gregory’s *History*, written about five hundred years ago, which, as its inscription states, once belonged to Saint Mary’s at Ottemburg in the diocese of Mainz. It nowhere gives Gregory’s name, but it does contain his preface. It omits many chapters here and there, as is proved to have been done deliberately by the indexes prefixed to the individual books.

The index of the first book, for example, lists only twenty-six chapters, although the book itself contains many more: its last chapter is chapter forty, which corresponds to chapter thirty-eight of the printed editions [Col. 0099A]. The index of book II lists thirty-two chapters, whereas the book itself contains thirty-six, in addition to others without any title prefixed. The index of book IV lists thirty-five chapters with their summaries, yet the book itself ends in the middle of chapter 11, corresponding to chapter 16 of the printed editions.

Nor is the codex mutilated or incomplete. Immediately after Gregory comes Regino’s *Chronicle*, written by the same hand.

These, then, are the five codices consulted by Cointius. The learned man therefore has good reason to complain that he saw only incomplete codices of Gregory’s *History*.

123. The sixth codex, then, against which we collated Gregory’s works, is that of the monastery of Bec in Normandy, written about 700 years ago. Nothing at all is missing from it except Gregory’s first preface; [Col. 0099B] its script is plain, uniform, and of the finest quality. The seventh we had from the monastery of Mont-Royal in the diocese of Beauvais, of the Cistercian Order. It contains absolutely all the books of Gregory’s *History*, except for several final chapters of the last book, which are missing because some leaves were torn from the codex. We saw an eighth codex in the library of Vendôme, written on paper and more recent than the others, since it does not seem to be more than 200 years old. It contains only the first five books, but these are entirely complete, except for Gregory’s first preface. The chapters of Book VI are appended to Book V. The scribe complains that he was unable to obtain the book itself, and testifies that it is a work most worthy, alike by the dignity of its author and of its subject matter.

[Col. 0099C] 124. Nor was it enough to examine the Gallican codices; it seemed appropriate also to consult the Italian ones. In this matter R. P. D. Claudius Stephanotius, procurator general of our Congregation at the Roman Curia, came to our assistance. As is his custom, he generously sent from Rome various readings and other materials relevant to our undertaking.

The first of the Italian codices of which we received information and variant readings is the Casinensis itself, which our Mabillon praises in his *Itinerarium Italicum*, p. 123. He says that he and his companion Michael, his brother, saw it at Monte Cassino, and that it contains Gregory of Tours’ *History*, differing in certain respects from the printed editions. We give these differences in their proper places, together with the four chapters that had previously been known only by their titles.

To this must be added two codices carried from Gaul to Italy by Queen Christina of Sweden, [Col. 0099D] to which our Stephanotius had access. The first, written in the tenth century and apparently in the monastery of Saint-Laumer at Blois, is now preserved in the Vatican Library through the gift of Alexander VIII. It contains the whole *History*, except for the preface and the final chapter of Book X. Some passages are also missing from Book IV, owing to the negligence of the copyist, who left several pages blank; a few others are absent because one or two leaves were torn out.

The second codex, formerly belonging to the monastery of Fleury, is held in the library of His Eminence Cardinal Ottoboni. Through his favor, the distinguished scholar Franciscus Blanchinus supplied us with this codex and with anything else we needed. [Col. 0100A] Readily complying with the eminent cardinal’s zeal for learning, he never misses an opportunity to assist us and our studies.

Finally, the most illustrious D. Laurentius de Zaccagnis, first prefect of the Vatican Library, lent us the last codex from the Vatican Palatine Library. He is known to all learned men for his published works and deserves our particular commendation for his generosity toward our studies. This codex, formerly belonging to the monastery of Saint Nazarius at Lorsch and apparently written about 800 years ago, is missing many chapters throughout—namely, precisely those that we noted above as missing from the Thuaneus, or Colbertinus. In it, Book IX is also confused with Book X, and Fredegar’s *Chronicle* is presented under the title of Book X of Gregory’s *History*. [Col. 0100B] We had observed nothing on this matter in the marginal notes to Gregory’s text in the earlier books, since at that time we had not yet received information about this codex from Rome.

A codex from the monastery of Saint-Trond in Hesbaye appears to resemble this one. In it, as Godefridus Henschenius observes in the material prefixed to the *Life of Saint Sigibert*, many chapters are missing. In addition, we saw several other codices, some of them extremely ancient, containing fragments of Gregory’s *History* under various titles. It will be enough to discuss them in their proper place if anything noteworthy should occur in them, or otherwise to mention them below in the catalogue of manuscript codices.

125. No one, moreover, will say that these fragments should be despised, since, on the contrary, they are of great value for [Col. 0100C] confirming the genuine text of Gregory. Because they were excerpts intended to be read in public services, they contain as many witnesses to the truth of the events narrated in them as there were churches that adopted them in the readings of the divine office.

Thus, since in most such fragments the title *Sermon on the Passing of Saint Martin* is found, and since in all of them the holy bishop is consistently said to have departed to heaven when Atticus and Caesarius were consuls—as is found absolutely everywhere, both in the printed and in the manuscript codices of Gregory’s *History*—who will deny that this is Gregory’s true and genuine reading, which various churches have used for more than 900 years?

Besides the other codices, we saw two of such antiquity: one from the library of Corbie, the other in the archives of the cathedral church of Angers, [Col. 0100D] both written in characters almost Merovingian toward the end of the eighth century. Although in the notes to this passage of Gregory we had thought it sufficient to confirm the text by the authority of all the manuscripts and otherwise to leave undecided the question of the final year of Saint Martin, which different writers assign to different years, nevertheless, after more carefully examining Gregory’s passages, we came to regard this as certain: in Gregory’s view Martin died when Atticus and Caesarius were consuls, and therefore in the common era 397, in which it is established that Atticus and Caesarius were consuls. [Col. 0101A]

Gregory repeats this in his book *On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, and confirms the date by other chronological indications. He writes that Saint Martin died in the second year of the emperor Honorius, which likewise corresponds to the year 397; and he records that Perpetuus ascended the throne of Tours in the sixty-fourth year after Martin’s death. This would certainly not be true if Martin’s death were postponed beyond the year mentioned, since Perpetuus presided over the Council of Tours in 461. I pass over the other arguments found in published authors.

“But,” you may say, “Gregory, in his books of *Miracles*, when calculating once and again the years from Saint Martin’s death to his own time—that is, to the regnal year of King Childebert in which he was writing—clearly indicates that Martin went up to heaven in the year 400.”

I admit that this was Gregory’s view if we follow this calculation of his, as many writers of later and more recent [Col. 0101B] times did. Among them Albericus of the Three Fountains, a monk in Champagne, undertakes to prove it at any risk and employs, among other arguments, those two statements of Gregory: one concerning the consulship of Atticus and Caesarius, and the other concerning the second year of the emperor Honorius. He brings both of them down to the year 400 of the Christian era.

Yet it is certain that both belong to the year 397. We should therefore rely rather on the chronological indications derived from the aforesaid consulship and the second year of Honorius than on the other indication Gregory gives from the years of King Childebert. The former method of calculation, based on the consulship, is much more certain and demonstrable. It is hardly credible that Gregory invented it; rather, he must have taken it from ancient records of his own church or from other public documents.

[Col. 0101C] When he wished to compare this indication of the consulship with the regnal years, he could easily have made a mistake amid the obscurity of those times, just as even today, in this age of learning, establishing the correspondence is not without difficulty. Therefore, if Gregory erred in one of the two calculations, he should by no means be thought to have erred in assigning the consulship. Accordingly, I have no hesitation in believing that Saint Martin’s death should be placed in the year 397, to which, according to the accepted opinion among scholars, the consulship of Atticus and Caesarius belongs.

But let us now continue with the preface.

126. We used no smaller number of codices in preparing Gregory’s books *On the Miracles of the Saints*. Among them were three, written about 800 years ago, containing all the books, copied throughout in an excellent hand.

The first, together with others mentioned above and below, [Col. 0101D] was communicated to us from the Colbert Library by the distinguished scholar Stephanus Baluzius. The second, from the library of the principal church of Beauvais, was supplied to us, with the consent of the venerable Chapter, by D. de Neuilly, a canon of that church.

Finally, we borrowed the third from the church of Laon through the agency of the most learned D. Leleu, with the consent of the other venerable canons. At its end are written these words:

> Here ends happily the eighth book. Adalard, subdeacon, wrote this codex in honor of the blessed archangel Michael.

On another leaf the following inscription is read:

> This book was offered to God and Saint Mary by the unworthy levite Odalricus . . . . . If anyone should remove it by any contrivance, may he incur the anger of almighty God and be condemned under the anathema of perpetual [Col. 0102A] malediction.

The worn words, I suspect, identified the church of Reims, to which Odalricus presented many other codices, as is evident from similar inscriptions in codices that are still preserved in the metropolitan library of the church of Reims. The church of Saint Michael also still stands there, in the canons’ cloister.

127. Besides the Colbertinus codex mentioned above, we had three others from the same library containing several of the books of *Miracles* published by our Gregory. One of them, brought from the church of Tulle, contains all the books except the *Lives of the Fathers*.

An ancient codex of Saint Martin at Tours [Col. 0102B] contains the same number, with the exception of the book *On Confessors*. We received variant readings from it and from another codex in the library of the cathedral church of Saint Gatianus from our Edmund Martenne. R. P. Joannes Harduinus, with his customary kindness, communicated to us two codices from the library of the Clermont College of Louis the Great in Paris.

The distinguished Herovallius, a regular canon of that place and heir no less to his father’s love of letters than to his name, supplied us with one codex from the celebrated library of Saint-Victor in Paris.

We likewise received one from the library of Jumièges, another from Fleury, a third from Bec, and a fourth from Saint-Vincent at Le Mans; we also had four from our library of Saint-Germain.

We saw no complete codex from the Royal Library, but we saw many fragments of various books, together with one copy [Col. 0102C] of all the books *On the Miracles*. This copy is printed, but its margins contain numerous variant readings transcribed by the distinguished scholar Petrus Pithoeus.

We also had variant readings collected from two manuscript codices by the late distinguished Jacobus Sanbovius, priest and doctor of the Sorbonne, famous in his own right. Other variant readings we owe to our Stephanotius, who took them from a Roman codex belonging to Queen Christina of Sweden. This codex contains nearly all the books of the *Miracles*.

To it must be added a Vatican codex from the Palatine Library, about 800 years old, formerly belonging to the monastery of Weingarten in Swabia. It contains the book *On the Glory of the Confessors*.

We shall mention the others in their proper places as occasion requires, as well as those that contain only a few individual lives or certain [Col. 0102D] particular chapters. Below, in the detailed Index, we shall state against which codices each individual book was collated.

128. We also investigated and examined with no less care the various editions of Gregory’s works, since it is certain that much can sometimes be obtained from collating such books with one another for the elucidation of ancient works.

The earliest edition of Gregory known to us appeared at Paris in 1511 from the workshop of Joannes Parvus, under the care of Hieronymus Clichtoveus of Nieuwpoort, who dedicated it to Guillelmus Parvus. It contains, after a Life of our Gregory, two books *On the Glory of the Martyrs* and four books *On the Virtues of Saint Martin*, together with a letter *On the Seven Sleepers*. This letter is also attributed to our Gregory in other printed editions. [Col. 0103A]

In the following year, the remaining works of the same author were published under the supervision of Guillelmus Parvus, then confessor to King Louis XII, from the types of Jodocus Badius.

129. In 1561 Guillelmus Morelius, the king’s printer, undertook a new edition of Gregory. Under his care Gregory’s *History* appeared, as he himself testifies, corrected against a manuscript codex of the library of Saint Martin at Tours; several variant readings were also added at the end.

Later, in 1563, Morelius published in another volume the two books *On the Glory of the Martyrs* and the book *On the Glory of the Confessors*, based, as he says, on ancient and manuscript codices.

130. Not long afterward Gregory’s edition was seen for the first time in Germany. Mathias Flacius Illyricus states that he prepared it from an ancient codex of Saint Nazarius at Lorsch. [Col. 0103B] It appeared at Basel from the press of Petrus Perna, not in 1558, as the first page incorrectly states, but in 1568, as may be inferred from the dedicatory letter. Indeed, at the end of the book the printer praises Morelius’s edition, which appeared in 1561.

In the same century, seven books—that is, all the books except the *Lives of the Fathers*—of the *Miracles* were published at Cologne in 1583 from the types of Maternus Cholinus.

131. In the same year, 1583, R. Laurentius de la Barre published at Paris, from the press of Michael Sonnius, a collection of ancient authors under the title *Christian History of the Ancient Fathers*. Among other brief works he inserted our Gregory’s *History*, together with three books of the *Miracles*: the two books *On the Glory of the Martyrs* and the book [Col. 0103C] *On the Glory of the Confessors*.

But six years later, in 1589, Margarinus de la Bigne, a Parisian doctor of the Sorbonne, published a much enlarged *Library of the Holy Fathers*, which he had previously edited several years earlier. In it he included all the works of our Gregory.
