From then on they occupied a place in the subsequent editions of the *Library of the Fathers*, namely the Cologne edition of the doctors of Cologne in 1618 and the Lyons edition of 1677.

132. In the tenth year of the present seventeenth century, two further editions of Gregory’s *History* appeared at Paris. One was in Latin, from the library of Laurentius Bochellus, with variant readings from the Oiselian manuscript and other papers of Bochellus appended at the end of the book. The other was in French, based on the translation of Claudius Bonetus of the Dauphiné. This edition was prepared by the distinguished scholar d’Hemery d’Amboise, master of requests, with a lengthy preface to Gregory’s *History*, in which he chiefly demonstrates the usefulness of this author for refuting the errors of the new heretics. [Col. 0103D]

These were followed in 1613 by the edition of Marquardus Freherus, prepared against a codex of the Palatine Library and included in the collection of historians of France that he caused to be printed at Hanau by the Wechel press.

Finally, at the beginning of our century, Andreas Duchesne, a man celebrated for his learning and deserving well of the history of our nation, undertook a very extensive collection [Col. 0104A] of all authors who had written anything about the Frankish people. He published its first volume in 1636, in which, among other things, he gave the leading place to the works of various authors, including Gregory’s *History*, collated against five manuscript codices. This edition appears more accurate and more carefully corrected than the others.

Four years later, namely in 1640, Joannes Balesdens, an advocate in the Paris Parlement, published at Paris eight books of the *Miracles*, together with the history of the Seven Sleepers. In his preface he testifies that he had purged and corrected these books against manuscript codices.

To all these editions must finally be added the French edition of all Gregory’s works translated into our language and furnished with notes. It appeared under the care of Michael Marollius, abbot of Villalupes, at Paris from the workshop of Frederic Leonard in 1668, in two volumes.

133. These, then, are the various [Col. 0104B] editions, both Latin and French, of the works of Gregory of Tours that we were able to see and that we used, after collating them with manuscript codices, in preparing our own edition.

Besides these, we also consulted the works of distinguished men who, either when opportunity arose or expressly for that purpose, have illuminated the books of our Gregory, especially in this century.

Among others, Hadrianus Valesius is famous. He spent almost his entire life elucidating the history of our nation, and published three volumes entitled *History of Frankish Affairs*. No less useful is his *Description of the Gauls*, filled with monuments and testimonies of ancient authors.

Carolus Cointius, a priest of the French Oratory, undertook to illuminate the affairs of the Franks, especially ecclesiastical matters, and comprised them in seven volumes [Col. 0104C] under the title *Annals of the Franks*. A distinguished scholar, Gerardus du Bois, published an eighth volume from his papers; we had hoped that he would publish more, if his life had permitted it.

The late Carolus Fresnius Cangius explained obscure words and matters of that kind in his highly praised *Glossary*. The illustrious Hieronymus Bignonius explained many things in his notes on the formulas of the monk Marculf.

The distinguished Stephanus Baluzius likewise elucidated and corrected many passages, both in the capitularies of the kings and in other works that testify to his profound learning.

What pertains to ecclesiastical discipline under the first dynasty of our kings he chiefly clarified from Gregory’s works: this was done by Ludovicus Thomassinus.

We also owe much to Joannes Savaroni of Clermont, president of the court of aids in his native city, who frequently cites and explains the works of our Gregory in his notes on Apollinaris Sidonius and in his *Origins of Clermont*.

Nor should the distinguished Antonius Dadinus Alteserra be omitted, the renowned professor at the academy of Toulouse, who published at Toulouse in 1679 a separate work containing notes and observations on Gregory of Tours’ *History* and Fredegar’s *Chronicle*. [Col. 0104D]

No one who has even once examined the outstanding work of D. Joannes Mabillon, *On Diplomatics*, can be unaware of how useful it can be for illustrating Gregory. But the modesty of my excellent teacher forbids me to say more. In his work on the Gallican liturgy and in his other studies, he has greatly enhanced the history and ancient customs of our nation by means of Gregory’s words.

If anything useful to scholarship is found in this edition or in my other little works, I openly confess that I owe it all to him.

I shall not list the remaining authors individually; each is praised in the appropriate place. We must now say a few words about Fredegar. [Col. 0105A]

V.—On Fredegar and His Works.—134. It is difficult to say who Fredegar was, since even his name is not certain. Nevertheless, he is commonly called Fredegar and is frequently cited under that name; but learned men confess that they have been unable to discover the origin of it. No known codex, indeed, bears this name.

Hadrianus Valesius even praises one codex that attributes the works commonly ascribed to Fredegar to another person, namely a certain Idatius. But this codex is none other than the Sirmondianus, in which the name Adatius does occur, although it was written about 200 years later—that is, apparently in about the ninth century, judging from the form of its script. [Col. 0105B]

The title, added to the codex by I know not whom, reads as follows:

> An abridged excerpt from the *Chronicle* of Eusebius, Jerome, and other authors, by a certain Adatius.

This writer, whoever he was, was deceived, as Valesius himself also observes, by the *Chronicle* of Idatius, which forms part of Fredegar’s collection, together with the letter prefixed to it under the name of Udacius or Idacius. In that letter the writer claims to have collected the preceding material from Eusebius and Jerome, while stating that the following material was composed by himself.

But those statements had been made by Idatius about his own *Chronicle*, which occupies a place in Fredegar’s collection; a later writer nevertheless extended them to the entire collection.

Nor can anything else be inferred from Rigordus, who writes in his *Life of Philip Augustus* that he verified the genealogies of the kings according to the chronicles of Idacius and Gregory of Tours. This is easily confirmed from Rigordus’s own writings. A little earlier, while discussing the origin of the Franks, he says that he carefully investigated the matter from Gregory of Tours’ *History*, from the *Chronicles* of Eusebius, from the *Chronicles* of Idatius, and from the writings of many others. He then reports the material concerning the Frankish origin from the Trojans and other [Col. 0105C] matters that are found in Fredegar’s collection, partly under the name of Eusebius or Jerome and partly under other titles.

That Idatius is different from Fredegar, or from the author of the collection circulated under Fredegar’s name, can be demonstrated by this single argument: the latter professes in his preface to follow Idatius, repeatedly praises his work, and even makes an epitome of his *Chronicle*; moreover, he inserts into his own collection epitomes of Gregory and Isidore, who lived after Idatius. He must therefore unquestionably be distinguished from Idatius. [Col. 0105D]

All this is done by the author of the collection, as his writings testify, and he himself declares in the preface to the *Chronicle*:

> Therefore, diligently traversing the chronicles of blessed Jerome, Idatius, and a certain Wise Man, or also Isidore, and even Gregory, from the origin of the world until the kingdom of Guntram was passing away, I inserted these five chronicles into the volume of this little book . . .

If anyone wishes to introduce some Idacius or Adacius as the author of this collection, distinct from Idatius the writer of the *Chronicle* and later in age than our Gregory, let him produce arguments sufficient to establish it, and we shall willingly agree with him.

Meanwhile, following the example of learned men, we shall continue to call our compiler Fredegar the Scholastic, especially since, without some serious reason, it should not be thought that this name was rashly assigned to him by the learned men whom Josephus Scaliger praises without naming. Scaliger himself and Marquardus Freherus are found to have been the first to call him so.

135. Valesius and Cointius believe Fredegar was a Burgundian. We readily agree with them, and the conclusion can indeed be supported by his writings. [Col. 0106A]

In the earlier parts of his collection he narrates the arrival of the Burgundians in Gaul and includes several noteworthy and distinctive details about this people that are found neither in Gregory nor in other authors.

In the *Chronicle*, which is properly his own work, [Col. 0106B] he treats matters concerning the kingdom of Burgundy much more carefully and at greater length than the rest. He begins his book with praise of Guntram, king of Burgundy, adds much concerning his virtues, and traces the succession of years through the kings of Burgundy.

First, he marks events by the years of Guntram; he does not enumerate Childebert’s years until, after Guntram’s death, Childebert had succeeded to the kingdom of Burgundy. From that point, omitting the years in which the same Childebert had reigned in Austrasia, he reckons his years from the beginning of his Burgundian reign.

Thus, after Childebert’s death, he passes over Theudebert, king of the Austrasians, although he was the elder, and records the years of Theoderic, to whom Burgundy had fallen. [Col. 0106C] Nor does he give the years of Chlothar until, after the sons of Childebert had been killed, Chlothar had received Burgundy.

Valesius suspects that Fredegar’s homeland was Aventicum, because of certain distinctive details concerning that city, which he reports at greater length. At that time the city was considered part of Burgundy. It had first been the capital of the Helvetii, as is clear from ancient notices; it was then assigned to the Transjurans and finally became part of the kingdom of Burgundy.

Fredegar frequently mentions the Transjuran dukes and sometimes describes their deeds. He then develops at length the praises of Aventicum. As he himself writes, after suppressing the rebellion of the Germans, Flavius Vespasian ordered the city to be built—or rather restored—and entrusted its completion, after it had been begun, to his son Titus. When Titus had gloriously carried this out, the city became adorned and most distinguished in Gaul. Finally, Fredegar alone narrates the disaster it suffered at the hands of the Germans in the time of Gallienus. [Col. 0106D]

136. The date of this author must be derived from his own writings. But first his genuine writings must be separated from additions, and this must be done especially on the authority of the manuscript codices. It is therefore useful to examine what each codex contains.

From the manuscript and printed codices it is clear that Fredegar—or whoever else is now known under that name—made a historical collection from various excerpts of ancient authors and added to it an account of events occurring in his own time.

But since this collection contains different brief works in different codices, it is not very easy to determine with certainty which materials were collected by the first author.

Nevertheless, it seems entirely beyond doubt that Gregory’s epitome and the *Chronicle* [Col. 0107A] appended to it are genuine works of this author, since these brief works are found in every copy, even though the *Chronicle* is longer in some codices and shorter in others.

Something must be said about the other parts of the collection.

137. The codex of the distinguished Jacobus Sirmondus, now called the Claromontanus because it is kept in the Clermont College of Louis the Great in Paris, was written in the seventh century—that is, while the author of the collection was still alive.

It first presents a chronological work under the title *Book of Generations*, from the creation of the world to the kingdom of the Assyrians. Various catalogues follow, namely those of the Roman [Col. 0107B] emperors from Augustus to Alexander, surnamed Severus; of the Hebrew kings; and so forth. Then follow computations of the years from Adam to the birth of Christ.

Next comes a catalogue of the Roman pontiffs from Saint Peter to Theodore, continued thereafter in a somewhat more recent hand to Hadrian I. Finally, a brief *Chronicle* is appended, from the beginning of the world to the thirty-first year of the emperor Heraclius. These catalogues and computations are listed in the index prefixed to the beginning of the book.

The same book is found in one of Canisius’s codices, which is called the lesser codex; we shall use that designation from now on. The catalogues and other calculations are absent from it, however, and it is clear from the preface that they were all omitted through the copyist’s fault. In the preface, as also in the Sirmondian codex, the author promises that he will discuss many matters of this kind. [Col. 0107C]

This book is entirely absent from the greater Canisian codex and from the Boherian codex. In its place those codices contain the little book of Quintus Julius Hilarion, which has been published in the *Library of the Fathers*.

138. The second book of the Fredegarian collection is found in the Sirmondian codex without any other title:

> Here begins the chapter-list of Jerome’s Chronicle, excerpted.

It contains sixty-two chapters, from the reign of Ninus to the death of Belisarius. [Col. 0107D]

This same book is found in the lesser Canisian codex under the title:

> Here begin the chapters excerpted from Jerome’s Chronicle,

and in the Boherian codex under the title:

> Here begin Jerome’s Chronicles.

In both codices, however, the *History of Dares the Phrygian on the Origin of the Franks* is inserted. It is entirely fabulous, though different from the work under this author’s name that we recently saw in the manuscript codex of Saint-Albin at Angers.

The lesser Canisian codex divides this book into two parts. It calls the first *Book II of the Generations*, which is concluded by the letter of Idatius; the second it calls *Book III of the Chronicle*.

139. The third book has no title in any manuscript. In the Sirmondian codex it begins simply:

> Here begins Gregory’s preface. As . . .

Then follows:

> Here begins the chapter-list of Book IV, excerpted from the Chronicle of Gregory, Bishop of Tours; in the name of Christ, let it begin.

Next comes Chapter 1, *On the Huns*, and so forth.

This book is the epitome of Gregory’s *History* that has been published. [Col. 0108A]

It appears to be a copyist’s error that he wrote “Book IV” here instead of “Book III,” as is evident from the preceding and following books—unless the error arose from the negligence of the same writer, who carelessly and without sufficient attention to the division established by the author in the earlier books sometimes called the subsequent books the second and third, and sometimes the third and fourth. [Col. 0108B]

According to the reckoning of the lesser Canisian codex, this book is in fact the fourth. The Ambrosian codex cited by Lambecius in volume II of the *Bibliotheca Vindobonensis* agrees with this, reading:

> Here begins the Greek preface of Book IV.

The Boherian codex, however, which at the end of the preceding book reads:

> Here ends Book I,

also appends to this book:

> Here ends Book II.

At its beginning it had prefixed:

> Here begins the Greek preface.

Then:

> Chapters of the book, which is excerpted from the Chronicles of the Greek bishop of Thoronacis. Here begins the book. When the Vandals . . .

We infer that a similar title existed in the lesser Canisian codex because, following its usual practice, it prefixed a title to the book while omitting the chapter-list:

> Here begins the preface of Book IV, excerpted from the Greek Chronicle of Bishop Thoromachus.

The copyist believed that this book had been excerpted and translated into Latin by a ninth-century author from the chronicle of some Greek bishop named Thoromachus. No one now fails to know that this is false.

140. After the epitome of Gregory’s *History*, the lesser Canisian codex contains the book of Julian Hilarion, which, as we observed above, some codices place first.

In the Boherian codex, the *Chronicle* follows immediately after the epitome under the title of Book III [Col. 0108C] of the *Chronicle*.

The Sirmondian codex, however, reads:

> Here begins the prologue of a certain Wise Man,

although neither the prologue itself nor anything else appears in its place. Instead, with no space left between, Fredegar’s *Chronicle* is presented under this title:

> Here begins the chapter-list of Book IV of the Chronicle, in the name of Christ.

But after the list of chapters and the prologue it has:

> In the name of Our Lord Jesus Christ, XI. Here begins the sixth Chronicle. Guntram . . .

and so forth, as in the printed editions, where the account reaches the death of Flaccus in Chapter 90. We shall demonstrate below that this chapter is the last of Fredegar’s *Chronicle*, although some other codices contain more. [Col. 0108D]

The other codices contain nothing after this *Chronicle* and its continuators. The Sirmondian codex, however, presents the following book under this title:

> In the name of the Holy Trinity, here begins Book III. ΚΡΩΝΗΚΩΡΩΜ, that is, of Isidore, Bishop. The first [book] is by Julius Africanus, under the emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, and so forth.

At the end it reads:

> Here ends the book, an abridgment of times collected by Saint Isidore according to the truth of history, from the beginning of the world to the fortieth year of King Chlothar.

And thus the codex ends.

441. It seemed worthwhile to pursue these matters at greater length so that Fredegar’s genuine works might be clearly recognized. From this we infer that he composed a historical collection from the very beginning of the world to the time of Guntram, drawing on various authors’ chronicles, and later added an account of the history of his own time. [Col. 0109A]

He himself professes this in the preface prefixed to the *Chronicle*, which we published in col. 586 [Note: [Col. 0107D] Here and below, whenever the parenthesis is absent, the reader is referred back to the numbers printed in heavier type within the text. EDITOR]. He says:

> Therefore, traversing the chronicles of blessed Jerome, Idatius, and a certain Wise Man, or also Isidore, and even Gregory, from the origin of the world until the kingdom of Guntram was passing away, I inserted these five chronicles into the volume of this little book . . . . .
>
> After Gregory’s volume had been completed, I did not remain silent about the events of the times . . . which later became known to me . . . through reading and hearing, and also through seeing everything that I learned with certainty; I wrote them in the volume of this little book.

That the author of the entire collection was one and the same person is proved, apart from the preface and the ancient codices, by the uniformity of style everywhere: the same epitomizer’s character, language everywhere equal and similar to itself—that is, plainly uncultivated and barbarous whenever the author speaks in his own voice and does not use another’s words.

The variations found even in the very oldest codices in the assignment of the individual books seem to have arisen from the carelessness of copyists, as we have already said. [Col. 0109B]

Although this author names no writer older than Jerome from whom he could have assembled his collection, the matters he narrates prove that he excerpted earlier sources. For it seems beyond doubt that he included Julius Africanus—whose material Eusebius excerpted—under the name of Jerome or Eusebius, whom Jerome continued.

Therefore, it does not seem necessary to admit another ancient author besides Africanus, one who lived in the time of Alexander Severus, as several learned men have thought after Henricus Canisius and Marcus Welserus. Hadrianus Valesius, however, believes that, besides Julius Africanus, other more recent Greek authors were also collected by this writer. [Col. 0109C]

Only this can be established with certainty: this author composed his collection chiefly from Jerome’s *Chronicle* and the other authors whom we cited from his preface, while here and there mixing in narratives from other authors whose works had come into his hands.

142. The difficulty concerning the collector’s date would be greater—and indeed more consequential—had it not already been elucidated by Valesius, Cointius, and other learned men. Since Fredegar’s Chronicle extends to different periods in different manuscripts, it is not surprising that scholars have not all held the same opinion concerning the date of its author. In most printed editions, where it appears under the title of Book XI of the *History of the Franks*, or at least as an Appendix to Gregory’s *History*, it reaches the death of Charles Martel. Three manuscripts agree with this: as we have often said, they present it under the title of Book X of Gregory of Tours’s *History*. They are the Colbertine manuscript, famous among Cointius’s works under the name of the Thuaneus; another from the Vatican Library; and a third—if it should nevertheless be distinguished from the Vatican manuscript—the Nazarianus from the Archipalatine Library, which Marquard Freher testifies that he used. To these, unless I am mistaken, one from the Canisian manuscripts should be added.

But when Canisius himself found this Chronicle extended to the death of Pippin in one of his manuscripts, he not only inserted this addition in volume II of his *Antique Reading*, but also took the opportunity to attribute the whole Chronicle, indeed the entire Fredegar collection, to an anonymous author who lived under Charlemagne; and he actually published it under this title. Following him, Marquard Freher published the Chronicle, continued to the same period, under Fredegar’s single name.

Andreas Chesnius, however, followed a different course. In volume I of the *Writers of Frankish History* he inserted the same Chronicle under Fredegar’s name, saying that it had been written at the command of Childebrand, Pippin’s uncle, and continued to Pippin’s death under the supervision of Nibelung, Childebrand’s son. He thus supposed that the original writer, Fredegar, had written the entire Chronicle at Childebrand’s command up to Pippin’s accession, and that afterward either Fredegar himself or someone else had extended it, at Nibelung’s command, to the death of that king.

But the learned man was mistaken, deceived by the inscription of the Petavian manuscript, which we gave in column 685. From that inscription it could indeed be inferred that Fredegar’s Chronicle had been continued through Childebrand’s efforts, or at least that its continuators had been brought together into a single body; it could not be inferred that the work had first been composed at that time. Learned men have already proved by the strongest arguments that Fredegar—or whoever else may be the author of this Chronicle—was older than Childebrand, and that he concluded his Chronicle in the year 641. We shall briefly touch upon those arguments here, adding several further considerations which, as I think, will settle the matter.

143. That Fredegar’s Chronicle did not extend beyond the fourth year of Chlodoveus the Younger—that is, the year 641 of the common era—and consequently ended at chapter 90, is demonstrated by the Sirmondian, or Claromontane, manuscript, which was written around that time. This is proved not only by the form of its square script and its capital letters, in which it is written, but also by the material contained in it.

For the catalogue of Roman pontiffs, which, as we said above, is inserted in the first book of the collection, ends with Theodore, who governed the Roman Church from 642 to 649. The succeeding pontiffs are listed down to Hadrian I, but in a different hand, and one somewhat more recent. The series of Roman emperors agrees with this: it is carried down to the thirty-first year of Heraclius’s reign—that is, to the year 641 of the common era—and thus to the fourth year of Chlodoveus the Younger, at which we maintain that the Chronicle ended.

Spanish affairs are likewise described from approximately the same period on the basis of Isidore’s Chronicle. Its concluding statement, which we reproduced above from the same manuscript, indicates the fortieth year of King Chlothar, that is, A.D. 623.

The manuscript’s antiquity is further demonstrated by an old inscription placed on its final page in Merovingian characters. The letters, however, have nearly been worn away by age; it seemed worthwhile to transcribe here what remains:

> Lucerius the presbyter-monk found dom . . . . tuma . . . . through this chronicle, and through another chronicle . . . . . that there are seven hundred years . . . . . . . . . . . he reckoned that six thousand d . . . . . . . . . . . had been completed, he reckoned those years in upen . . . . . . . . . . . in the thirteenth indiction, d . . . . . . . . . . . with Dagobert reigning in his fourth year.

From these fragments we gather that that monk Lucerius calculated the total of the years in the fourth year of Dagobert, in the thirteenth indiction. This must undoubtedly be understood of Dagobert not the First but the Third, whom others call the Second; his fourth year coincides with A.D. 715. Therefore the Claromontane manuscript had already been written in that very year—that is, before Fredegar’s Chronicle was continued.

Moreover, Philippus Labbeus had seen the same inscription in the Claromontane manuscript, or at least in another similar manuscript. In his chronological epitome under the year 715, he testifies that he had seen an ancient manuscript in which the thirteenth indiction, in the month of August, was reconciled with the fourth year of King Dagobert.

144. There are also numerous other indications which clearly suggest that the genuine Fredegar Chronicle ends at chapter 90. The other manuscripts containing the entire Fredegar collection, although they present continuators appended to the Chronicle, nevertheless bear certain marks indicating that these are separate works. In the Boherian manuscript, for example, a certain space has been left between chapter 90 and the continuators. Nor does the table of chapters list more than ninety.

The same is true of Fredegar’s edition prepared by Marquard Freher. Aimoin had seen no more, as Henschenius observes in volume I of the February *Lives of the Saints*, in which he also praises a manuscript of Melchior Goldast written about the year 600. In that manuscript Fredegar’s Chronicle ends with exactly ninety chapters, and the common concluding formula *explicit* is added, indicating a completed work.

The continuators also differ from the first writer of the Chronicle in other respects. Fredegar had arranged the deeds of the kings of Burgundy by years, reporting each event in its proper place and time. But the first person to continue the work after chapter 90, omitting many matters and setting aside the sequence of years and kings, heaps many events together. He entirely omits the deeds of Sigibert, which Fredegar had begun, and does not say a single word about Sigibert’s death or about the fortunes of his son Dagobert, who, having been transported to Scotland through Grimoald’s faction and later recalled by the nobles of the kingdom, held his father’s kingdom for some time.

Furthermore, he compressed nearly one hundred years of important events into four or five pages. Other continuators followed him, each narrating events in his own manner. The strong inclination some of them display toward the kings and princes of Austrasia proves that certain of them were from Austrasia. Finally, they say nothing about the kings of the Lombards and Goths, or about the rulers of other neighboring peoples, whose succession and more notable deeds Fredegar nevertheless used to report.

145. Since it must therefore be clear that the genuine Fredegar Chronicle cannot extend beyond ninety chapters, we thought it appropriate in this edition to separate it from its continuators and also to distinguish the several continuators who had previously been confused together. We judge that the continuation of Fredegar’s Chronicle should be divided into four parts. This is evident from the difference of style, from the different manner of narrating events, and even from the age of the writers, which is sometimes indicated.

The first part comprises chapter 91 and the five chapters following it. It is the least authoritative of all, since it appears to have been added after the other parts by a compiler in order to fill the gap lying between Fredegar’s Chronicle and the author of the second part. For this purpose that author used ancient but fabulous sources; hence the events between the years 642 and 680, which he covers, are reported very confusedly.

The second part begins with chapter 97 and ends in the middle of chapter 109, with these words: “The kingdom of the Franks.” Its author principally narrates events that took place in Austrasia from 680 to 736, and does so with considerable accuracy. He reveals his own date in chapter 109, where, going over the course of the years, he indicates that he is writing on the very Kalends of January in the year 735. According to our method of reckoning, however, that year, beginning in January, must be counted as 736.

The third part continues from chapter 109 through chapter 118—that is, from the time at which the preceding part ended to the accession of King Pippin, which took place in the year 752. We have already noted that it was written at the command of Childebrand, the uncle of that king; this is shown by an old inscription, from which we also infer that it was written by a contemporary author.

The remaining material, which follows down to Pippin’s death, with which the entire collection concludes, is indicated by the same inscription to have been written at the command of Nibelung, Childebrand’s son. Whether the same author wrote at the command of both Childebrand and Nibelung cannot be determined from the inscription, nor does it matter greatly to know. Perhaps he was the very person who brought all these continuations together into one body, adding material from the *Deeds of the Franks* and from the Dionysian Anonymous to the first part, so that there would not be a gap of thirty-nine years between Fredegar and the second continuator. Certainly the frequently mentioned inscription seems to suggest this.

It is clear that all these parts of the chronicles had already been made into a single historical body in the ninth century from the Jurensian manuscript, which was offered by Mannon, provost of that place, toward the end of the ninth century at the tomb of Saint Eugendus. In that manuscript all these continuators are joined together. They are likewise presented together in two other manuscripts: the Boherian, of the finest quality, written about the year 600, and another of those from which Canisius prepared his edition.

Nevertheless, we have published Fredegar’s Chronicle separately from its continuators, and also each part of the continuation under its own title, so that the confusion of so many authors would not create difficulty for readers. The final part, which until now had not been distinguished by any division into chapters, we thought best to divide into several chapters for the convenience of readers.

146. From everything we have said, it will not be especially difficult to determine Fredegar’s date. Since his Chronicle concludes in the year 641, and since he repeatedly—especially in the preface—asserts that he is going to write what he himself had heard and seen, or at least had read or learned elsewhere with certainty, no one can deny that he flourished toward the end of the seventh century.

We infer from chapter 48 that he lived at least until the year 658. There he relates that a certain Frankish merchant named Samo went into Sclavonia in the fortieth year of Chlothar—that is, A.D. 623—and was there elected king and ruled for thirty-five years.

From what we have also said about Fredegar, it must be concluded that this author is to be held in high esteem by learned men, since, after Gregory is lacking, he is the oldest, eyewitness, and sole historian of our people. Thus, if some authors happen to appear who were reluctant to praise him, they must either be understood as speaking of the earlier books of his collection, or they paid attention to the barbarism of his style and to his wholly unpolished manner of narrating events, or finally they believed that his Chronicle extended to Pippin’s death.

For if we are speaking of his genuine Chronicle—which, as we have proved, does not extend beyond the death of Flaocatus, related in chapter 90—there is no one who ought not to approve him. Hadrianus Valesius held this view. Since he initially failed to distinguish the continuators of the Chronicle from Fredegar, he was offended by the barbarism of the style and the brevity of the written material. He therefore pronounced Fredegar not merely unlearned, but also, as one ignorant of the grammar of the Latin language and utterly barbarous, held him hateful to the point of wearying and horrifying his readers.

Later, however, after examining the matter more carefully and, with the aid of the Sirmondian manuscript, separating the genuine Fredegar Chronicle from the rest, he immediately broke into praise of Fredegar, attributing the brevity of the author’s expression and narration to the defects of the age:

> “Fredegar,” he says, “is so necessary to our history that, if we wish to know the times of the younger Chlothar, Dagobert, and Chlodoveus II, we simply cannot do without him.”

Elsewhere he admits that there was no historian of our people who did not transfer Fredegar’s words into his own commentaries. Finally, when he had reached the year 641 in his *History of Frankish Affairs*, and was deprived of Fredegar, he complains:

> “The scholastic Fredegar abandoned us in that year: a diligent historian, within the capacity of those times, as close to Gregory in authority as he is in age, useful and necessary amid the great scarcity of good authors, and by no means to be despised. His brevity and all his other faults must be attributed to the times.”

So wrote Valesius, and every sincere lover of the ancient history of the Franks will readily agree with him.

147. In correcting Fredegar, we made particular use of four manuscript codices. The first is commonly called the codex of Jacob Sirmond. It is now preserved in the library of the Paris College of the Society of Jesus, Louis the Great. The Reverend Father Joannes Harduinus, with his customary kindness, allowed us to use it as freely as we wished. Since, as we said above, it was written in the author’s own age, we compared it most diligently word for word.

The second came from the library of the most illustrious Boherius, mitred president of the senate at Dijon. Our Dom Odo Clergerius first compared this manuscript with the printed editions at Dijon, at Saint Benignus. Later, through the kindness of the distinguished D. Boherius of Saviniacum, we were able to inspect and examine the manuscript itself. He, inheriting his father’s and grandfather’s love of letters no less than their other qualities, brought it to Paris and lent it to us for use.

The third, preserved in the Colbertine Library, we obtained through the most courteous permission of the distinguished Stephanus Baluzio. The fourth, brought from the monastery of Saint Nazarius at Lorsch to the Vatican Library, was compared with the printed editions by our Dom Claudius Stephanotius, the indefatigable helper of our studies.

To these manuscripts must be added two from which Canisius published his historical and chronological collection of Thoromagus, as he calls it, and a third from the Palatine Library, collated by Freher. We shall list all these manuscripts, together with the various editions that we consulted, below in a separate catalogue of codices.

148. Only a few things remain to be said about the monuments added in the Appendix at the end of this volume, since their complete catalogue will be presented in its proper place. We selected from ancient authors and various collections of histories those materials that are either praised by our Gregory or greatly useful for illuminating his works. A few of them were newly recovered from manuscripts, but most were collated with ancient codices and corrected in various places. One of these manuscripts is Corbeiensis, written in Gregory’s own age.

Finally, we appended a brief history of the condition of our monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. It is the distinguished monument of the piety and munificence of King Childebert, and in its basilica he himself, together with several other kings, has his burial place. We also had an image of the tomb of Queen Fredegund engraved on copper, along with other remains of that age, which greatly contribute to the illumination of the history of those times.

149. At last our preface, perhaps somewhat lengthy, must be brought to an end, and the *Life of Saint Gregory, Bishop of Tours* must be presented. It has already been published without the author’s name, though in some ancient manuscripts it is attributed to Odo the abbot. Thus it is entitled in the manuscript of Saint Sergius of Angers:

> “Prologue of Dom Odo the Abbot. Of all . . . . The Life published by Odo the Abbot begins.”

The same statement is repeated at the end.

We think that this Odo was none other than Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny. He was educated and lived for a long time at Tours, and could readily have been led to write the *Life of the holy bishop*, who at that time was already buried at the feet of Saint Martin in his basilica. Perhaps Odo compiled it from Gregory’s own writings before becoming a monk, while he was still precentor and master of the schools of the Martinian basilica.

# LIFE OF SAINT GREGORY, BISHOP OF TOURS, BY ODO THE ABBOT

## Prologue

All the saints are rightly honored in memory, but the faithful first honor those who shone more brightly than the rest either through teaching or through example. Among these, blessed Gregory, archbishop of the see of Tours, was certainly one, and the fact that he shone with this twofold gift is demonstrated by no small number of proofs.

Some account of his deeds must necessarily be given, lest the reputation of so great a man should at some time be obscured by a cloud of doubt. It is certainly enough for his glory that he has Christ, whom he sought to please, as his witness in heaven. Yet it would be wrong here to remain silent about the praises of one who devoted himself to proclaiming the praises of so many saints.

How small, indeed, will this account be, and how little will it present his excellence as it truly was? For, omitting many things commonly reported, we touch upon only a few that are confirmed by his books. But if someone, seeking signs in the Jewish manner, measures any saint by the number of his signs, what will he think of the blessed Mother of God, or of John the Forerunner? [Note: [Col. 0115B] Germ.: “they think” (*censent*); Serg.: “he will be thought” (*censebitur*). The sound reading is “he will think” (*censebit*).]

Let him therefore make a sounder judgment: on the terrifying day, when many who performed signs have been rejected, those who pursued works of righteousness alone will be gathered at the right hand of the heavenly Judge. We do not therefore commend our bishop by the performance of miracles, although these too will by no means be lacking; rather, we shall undertake to show that he imitated Christ, who was gentle and humble of heart. [Note: [Col. 0115B] Ed. and Cor.: “we show” (*demonstramus*); Germ.: “we would show” (*demonstraremus*).]

## I

Gregory arose from the Celtic region of Gaul, a native of the territory of Auvergne, born of his father Florentius and his mother Armentaria. If earthly nobility contributes anything to divine nobility, his parents were not only wealthy in possessions but also illustrious in birth. More important, they appeared to be so devoted to the duties of divine service that anyone among them who proved irreligious would rightly be branded degenerate.

To establish this, let us insert something concerning his nearer relatives. Thus Georgius, once a senator, took Leocadia as his wife. She descended from the line of Vettius Epagathus, whom Eusebius, in the fifth book of his *Histories*, reports as having suffered at Lyon and as having endured martyrdom there more gloriously than the others of that time. Leocadia gave birth to Saint Gallus, bishop of the see of Auvergne, and to Florentius, the father of this child. Concerning this Florentius, and also Armentaria his mother, as well as his brother Peter, Justinus’s wife, his sister, and his two nieces, namely Heustena and Justina, the disciple of blessed Radegund, the books of miracles report such things as show that their faith and merits were of no small importance.

Auvergne (*Arvernis*; Ed.: *Arvernia*), the native soil of the boy, had once raised its head exceedingly high, so that it surpassed the senators like the Tarpeian city [i.e. Rome]. From it Gregory’s family had sprung; it produced senators, judges, and whatever else I might mention from the order of the foremost citizens.

Let this much be said about his parents, so that, since the Lord is found in a righteous generation, it may contribute to Gregory’s praise that his ancestry appears to have been a pillar adorned with the title of holiness. [Note: [Col. 0116B] Germ.: “that his [lineage] appears to be joined with him as a column” (*quod sua . . . eo colluminata videtur*).]

Fortunatus, recalling his family and homeland (*Book VIII, poem 17*), writes:

> “Perhaps the glory of his race, the summit of Tours,  
> Coming from the Auvergne Alps, a mountain higher than the Alps themselves.”

And concerning his mother (*Book X, poem 21*):

> “Twice blessed in merits, a Maccabean woman for herself and the world,  
> Who sent seven palms from her womb to heaven:  
> You too, Armentaria, blessed in your powerful offspring,  
> Glorious in your child, surrounded by the fruit of your womb;  
> Gregory is for you a new palm, a crown.”

Thus a most noble offspring emerged from a noble stock, like a rose made more pleasing by its own stem, and reflected the increased honor of its nobility back upon its parents.

Although the majesty of a mystery is no longer sought in names, Gregory is nevertheless here appropriately named, as the facts themselves confirm. For the Greek word calls a person “watchful.” Gregory observed not only the third watch, but—what is greater—the second as well, and, something rarely seen, even the first. Because he bore the Lord’s yoke from adolescence, he “sat alone,” as Jeremiah says—or at least near Martin. [Al.: “he will sit” (*sedebit*).]

As soon as his youthful strength permitted, he was devoted to the study of letters. In these studies, under Bishop Gallus, his uncle, the tenderness of his intellect first grew firm.

## II

While he was still occupied with learning the shapes of letters, divine providence initiated him under the auspices of virtue and ennobled his holy infancy by the manifestation of signs.

His father was lying sick in bed, seized by an excessive illness. A fever raged in his innermost bones; gouty fluid swelled outward; a dry vapor began to press upon his face. Then a man appeared to the boy in a vision and said:

> “Have you read,” he said, “the book of Joshua?”

He replied:

> “Nothing,” he said. “I am attending to no letters except the characters with which I am now constrained and afflicted. I do not know at all whether this book exists.”

The man said:

> “Go and make a little rod of wood capable of receiving this name, and, after writing it in ink, place it beneath the support of your father’s head. If you do this, it will be his protection.”

When morning came, he told his mother what he had seen. The holy boy had evidently perceived that the matter was to be accomplished not by his own judgment but by his mother’s. She then ordered the vision to be fulfilled. It was done, and his father recovered immediately.

What could be more reasonable than that the name of Jesus, or wood, should be suitable for restoring health?

## III

His parents were truly noble and possessed extensive estates spread throughout Burgundy. When Saint Nicetius, a man of complete religious devotion who governed the city of Lyon, lived near the parents mentioned above, he ordered the boy Gregory to be summoned. [Note: [Col. 0117D] Germ.: “his” (*ejus*); Serg.: “lived near him” (*ei vicinarentur*).] The holy man contemplated him for a while as he stood before him, and, having divined in him I know not what divine quality, ordered the boy to be lifted up to him—for he was lying in bed. [Note: [Col. 0117D] Serg.: “to come to him, for he lay in bed, as though . . . foreseeing.”]

As though foreseeing that the boy would become his fellow citizen in paradise, he embraced him and began to cherish him in his arms. Yet, something that must not be passed over, he covered himself entirely with a cloak so that he did not touch the boy’s naked body even with his fingertips. When the boy had grown up, he often impressed this example of chastity upon his hearers, urging them to infer from the caution of this perfect man how much all fragile persons ought to avoid the touch of sensual pleasure. [Note: [Col. 0118D] Ed., “ought to avoid touches.”]

He therefore blessed the boy, wished him prosperity, and sent him back to his parents.

## IV

About two years after the miracle we have described, the aforementioned Florentius was seized by a recurrent illness. Fever burned; his feet swelled; an excruciating pain twisted them. The disease, having lasted through the intervening day, had exhausted the man, and he now lay almost shut up in his chamber. [Note: [Col. 0118D] Other manuscripts, “seized by a renewed illness.” Ed., “seized by renewed pain.”]

Meanwhile the boy again saw in a dream a person who asked him whether he knew the Book of Tobit. He replied, “Not at all.” The person said:

> “Know that Tobit had been blind and was healed through his son, with the angel accompanying him, by means of a fish’s liver. You therefore do likewise, and your father will be saved.”

He reported this to his mother. She immediately sent the boys to the river. A fish was caught, and what had been commanded to be taken from its entrails was placed upon the coals. The result of the power did not fail: as soon as the first odor of the smoke entered the father’s nostrils, all that swelling and pain immediately departed. [Germ., “the odor of the smoke.”]

If it is a great thing that the mouth of Zechariah was rightly opened for John, it is certainly not a small thing that Florentius was healed twice through his son.

From this the parents recognized that he would rely especially upon the right foot; nor could they fail to understand that divine providence had appointed him for more honorable duties. Nevertheless, they did not immediately tonsure him, awaiting, as I think, his own consent to undertake the clerical state. He was, however, applied with greater diligence to his literary studies.

## V

He was still a layman, but had grown both in mind and body, when suddenly he was seized by a very severe attack of fever and stomach phlegm. He began to suffer gravely; his illness grew worse day by day, and medical skill accomplished nothing. His uncle Gallus visited him frequently, while his mother, as a mother, continually attended him with laments.

But when all human help was despaired of, it was suggested from heaven to the young man that he should turn to divine assistance. He therefore asked to be carried to the tomb of Saint Illidius, which was nearby. But this did him little good, because the purpose sought through that affliction was being postponed.

When he had been carried home again, he shortly began to be tormented so severely that it was thought he was being driven toward death. At last his suffering made the purpose understood. He consoled those who mourned for him, saying:

> “Carry me once more to the tomb of blessed Illidius. I have faith that he will soon grant health to me and joy to you.”

When he had been carried there, he poured forth a prayer in whatever voice he possessed, promising that, if he were freed from this disease, he would assume the clerical habit without delay. He had spoken, and immediately felt the fever depart. A quantity of blood flowed from his nostrils, and the entire illness disappeared, as though some messenger, having obtained the matter for which he had come, were hastening away.

He therefore cut off his hair and devoted himself entirely to divine service.

## VI

When Saint Gallus was called to receive the long-earned crown of a blessed life, the man of God Avitus took charge of the young man. After examining his intelligence and disposition, Avitus applied the diligence of teachers and advanced him toward the citadel of wisdom with all the speed permitted by the young man’s industry and the teachers’ assiduity. You will find this in the *Life* of the aforementioned Illidius.

In the study of letters, Gregory exercised himself with such discernment that he avoided both extremes. He did not altogether shudder at the fables of the poets, nor, as is the custom of many, did he cling to them improperly and make his mind their servant through their seductive charm.

He did what was sufficient: he sharpened the edge of his heart as though against a whetstone, and, as if borrowing golden vessels from the Egyptians and departing for the wilderness where he might eat manna [mss.: *quo*, “whither”], he entered into the investigation of the powers of the divine Scriptures.

He himself shows this when speaking about himself:

> “I do not recall Saturn’s flight, Juno’s anger, or Jupiter’s adulteries.”

He goes on there to append the other monstrosities, until he says:

> “Despising all these things as though they were soon to collapse, I shall turn rather to the divine and evangelical writings; for I do not wish either to be bound in my own nets or to be entangled in them.”

In this he shows that he knew these things but rejected them with sounder judgment.

## VII

At the appointed time he was ordained deacon.

At that period there was a man from Auvergne who had brought away a piece of wood from the most holy tomb of blessed Martin. But because he carelessly neglected the reverence due to the wood, his entire household began to suffer grievously. As the illness grew worse and he, unaware of the cause of the punishment, made little effort to amend himself, he saw in a dream a terrifying person asking why he was being treated in this way.

When he said that he did not know, the person replied:

> “The wood that you brought from the bed of Dom Martin you are keeping here negligently, and for that reason these things have befallen you. But go now and take it to Gregory the deacon.”

The Levite was already worthy, as I think, to whom this Dom Martin might entrust the precious possessions of his flock.

At that time many men shone in Auvergne in the religious habit. The young man visited them, sometimes with blessed Avitus and sometimes alone, so that he might either receive examples of piety from them or, through mutual charity, provide them with what they perhaps lacked.

In them he was truly worshiping Christ. Like the sun’s radiance shining (*refulgens*, Ed.) from the mountain peaks, he looked upon Christ in these men while Christ could not yet be seen in himself. With this purpose he directed his mind, proclaiming for Christ’s praise whatever Christ deigned to accomplish through them or through those who had already gone before him to heaven.

## VIII

Among the others in whom, as we said, Christ shone like a light upon the mountains, he discovered the glorious Dom Martin. Martin surpasses the rest like a certain Olympus and, being nearer to the ether, reflects the heavenly splendors more brightly than the very stars. The whole world had long ago rightly conspired in his veneration, and Gregory, burning with desire for him, was inflamed with devotion. [Note: [Col. 0119D] Here the *Life* ends in the Cormaric manuscript.]

Always carrying Martin in his heart and on his lips, Gregory spread his praise everywhere. But while he fixed himself too intensely upon the exercise of virtues (*mentis*, printed thus [sic]), his flesh was weakened by its own powers—for such is its nature.

Thus Daniel, after being lifted up by contemplation of an angelic vision, became weak in bodily strength and was ill for many days. Gregory too, advancing in virtue but wasting away in bodily strength, at one time contracted an illness accompanied by fever and pustules. At length he was so exhausted that, unable to eat or drink, he lost all hope of this life.

One thing nevertheless remained: his confidence, resting upon Martin, did not waver at all. Indeed, burning more fervently, he became so inflamed with desire for Martin that, when death had almost risen above his head, he did not hesitate to set out on a journey to visit Martin’s tomb. His illness could not dissuade him, because the fever of the body was overcome by the fever of love.

After traveling two or three stages, the illness grew stronger because of the journey. But even then he could not be compelled to abandon his purpose or cease hastening toward Martin in confidence. He adjured those who sought to dissuade him in the name of the divine majesty to place him before Martin’s tomb, whether alive or, if it should happen so, dead.

What more is there to say? He reached the place somehow; his faith was tested, and he obtained the salvation he had hoped for. Nor was he alone healed: a certain Armentarius, one of his clerics, who had been entirely without consciousness, was also healed through the merit of the aforementioned faith. Giving thanks both for himself and for him, satisfied—or rather, more greatly inflamed—with love for Martin, Gregory returned to his homeland.

## IX

Once, while traveling from Burgundy to Auvergne, a great storm arose against him. Dense air gathered in the clouds; the sky began to flash with frequent lightning and resound with powerful peals of thunder. Everyone grew pale and trembled at the danger that threatened.

But Gregory, calmer in spirit, drew from his breast the relics of the saints—for he carried them continually around his neck—and steadfastly held them out against the threatening clouds. Immediately the clouds divided, passing on the right and left, and provided an unharmed road for those traveling.

But pride, which is often nourished by virtues, immediately crept into the young man’s spirit. He rejoiced privately and arrogantly attributed the event to his own merits. Yet what is as close to pride as a fall? The horse on which he was seated immediately slipped and threw him violently to the ground, so that, bruised throughout his body, [Germ., “shaken throughout his body”] he could scarcely rise.

Understanding the cause of his fall, he thereafter took sufficient care never to cast himself down, on any pretext, through the goadings of vainglory. Whenever divine power accomplished something through him, he attributed it not to his own merits but to the power of the relics, which, as we have said, he carried with him. If you consider the matter carefully, correcting pride was more remarkable than dividing a cloud.

## X

He was accustomed to prayer, especially during the hours of quiet. The solemnity of the Blessed Virgin Mary arrived, and her relics were preserved at a village called Marciac in Auvergne. Gregory happened to be present there. While the others were sunk in deep sleep, he went out according to his custom to pray in secret, and from a distance saw the oratory shining with immense brightness.

He therefore believed that some of the devout had already gone ahead to celebrate the vigils. Astonished by the sight of the light, he proceeded there and found everything silent. He sent someone to the sacristan, but meanwhile the door opened of its own accord.

He entered reverently into the angelic watch and immediately recognized the divine visitation. The brightness that he had admired from outside immediately disappeared, and he could see nothing except the power of the glorious Virgin. [Note: [Col. 0120D] Serg., “And he could see nothing more.” Al., “through the power.”]

### XI

In the one hundred and seventy-second year after the passing of the lord Martin, in the twelfth year of King Sigibert’s reign, blessed Euphronius—who, growing old amid miracles, had been endowed with such grace that he seemed to possess the spirit of prophecy—was gathered to his fathers. The time had come when Gregory, long ardently devoted to blessed Martin and suited to the ministry of pastoral office, ought to undertake the governance of Martin’s chair in his place.

When blessed Euphronius had died, the people of Tours assembled to deliberate about his successor; and without difficulty all were persuaded that Gregory should be preferred in the election. They had long known him to be a person highly popular for this position and had recognized many of his deeds as worthy of such a man. [Note: Ed.: “in this place.” Serg.: “for they had long recognized that he was worthy of so great an office. Then indeed, etc.”] Then, when all united in harmonious agreement, one could see the matter prospering with God’s [Al.: “the Lord’s”] favor. For the company of clergy [Ed.: “crowd”], joined by noblemen, and the rural and urban populace alike, with one accord shouted that Gregory should be chosen: distinguished by clear merits, likewise eminent in nobility, outstanding in wisdom, foremost in lineage, known to princes, revered for his integrity, and capable of every office.

An embassy was sent to the king, and by the Lord’s dispensation Gregory himself happened to be present. When the assembly dealt with this matter, with what humility he tried to excuse himself, and in what ways he attempted to withdraw! But since it is the Lord’s will [Note: Germ.: “But because it is God’s will here.” Ed.: “thence”], everything else was bent in this direction. The king compelled him by authority; Queen Brunhild pressed him insistently. But because well-ordered humility does not refuse obedience, at last he consented.

As I believe, lest he flee after being delayed on any pretext, Archbishop Giles of Reims immediately ordained him. Thus the poet Fortunatus writes (*Poems* V.2):

> Julian sends his foster-son to Martin,  
> and offers to his brother what had been dear to himself.  
> The gracious hand of Father Giles consecrated him to the Lord,  
> so that he might govern [Al.: refresh] the people whom Radegund loves.  
> Sigibert, rejoicing, favors him, and Brunhild honors him.

Thus the see of Tours received Gregory on the eighteenth day after it had lost Euphronius. When the people of Tours leapt up in triumph for their new pastor, the aforesaid poet composed this panegyric poem (*ibid.*):

> Clap your hands, happy peoples, holding new vows:  
> behold, with the bishop’s arrival, the hope of the flock has come.  
> Let the vigorous youth celebrate this; let stooping old age celebrate it;  
> let every person proclaim this common good.

And other verses, by which he shows that Gregory was celebrated by the people of Tours and entered the chair lawfully.

### XII

Once he had obtained the episcopate, what sort of man and how great he was may be stated briefly: the many churches that he newly built, or whose roofs and fabric he restored, make it clear; and the books published in praise of the saints or in exposition of the sacred Scriptures demonstrate it even more fully.

For he repaired the mother church that the lord Martin had built, since it had been weakened by extreme age, giving it an arched form; and he adorned its decorated walls with the deeds of that same Martin. Our versifier did not leave this unmentioned, saying among other things (*Poems* X.2):

> Gregory, working with Martin’s aid, restored this church anew—  
> what the former man had been, the latter had become old.

And again (*ibid.*):

> Therefore this excellent priest, repairing these ancient foundations,  
> raised it higher than it had shone before.

But there were many others, as we have said, as is found in his own chronicles—for example, the church of the Holy Cross, or at the estate of Martiensis [Note: Serg.: “Martensian.” Ed.: “at Artensian.” Is this the village or estate of Arton, or the estate of Marciac? Fortunatus praises the church of the Holy Cross founded by Gregory in *Poems* II.3; it still exists today and is distinguished by its parochial title.]

### XIII

As for building spiritual temples—that is, guarding the flock—how zealously he devoted himself may also be observed from the fact that he did not restrain his preaching even from holy men themselves. To say nothing of those whose sins, as the Apostle says, are manifest, about whom anything we might say would be superfluous, let at least two men be brought forward to show how greatly he concerned himself with those who were more perfect—men whom, because of the distinction of their holiness, scarcely anyone except Gregory would have dared to rebuke.

Not long after his ordination, the holy abbot Senoch came out of his cell and set out to greet him. The holy man received him with great reverence and gradually examined him through mutual conversation; he soon perceived that Senoch was infected with the plague of pride [Ed.: “heat”]. But the grace supplied to Gregory for discerning spirits completely purged him of that same pride.

He was no less vigilant with blessed Leobard, whom an evil spirit so harassed with sinister thoughts that, because of a certain insult in words, he had decided to leave the cell in which he had long enclosed himself. But this man too could not suffer the disaster, since he deserved to have Gregory as his helper. For when he customarily went to the Great Monastery, as though to kiss the sacred footsteps of Martin, the solicitous pastor turned aside to his hut to see how the sheep bound by Christ’s love was conducting himself.

Leobard immediately disclosed to him the secret thoughts which the devil had fabricated as though they were reasonable. Gregory, whose intelligence was exceptionally keen, at once detected the devil’s inventions; sighing with no small sorrow, he began to rebuke the man and exposed the devil’s cunning in appropriate words. On returning home, he sent him, with pious concern, books suitable for the purpose of the monks. After reading them again, Leobard was not only cured of the attack he had been suffering but also made great progress in the acuity of his understanding.

Therefore, seek nothing more magnificent now, and expect nothing more distinguished in praise of Gregory. If the soul is better than the body, even a liar cannot deny that it is better for someone to be raised up in the soul. How commanding his voice was, and how authoritatively his way of life impressed upon his subjects the things he taught, the diligent reader will discover in his books.

### XIV

Yet, as we related above, he was frequently wearied by bodily weakness because of his neglect of the flesh. Whenever illness more harshly assailed his little body, exhausted by excessive exercise of virtue, he turned to his Martin and was quickly healed. This happened very often.

When and how it happened is arranged in the account of the miracles in such a way [Note: Serg.: “This often happened, whenever …,” and in the account of the miracles it is arranged in the same way, so that, etc.] that it rightly delights the reader. For, as a prudent and humble man, he first applied bodily remedies to himself; but the more humbly he sought them, judging himself unworthy to receive healing through a miracle, the more divine generosity reserved him for the medicine of its own power.

On one occasion he was healed, by blessed Martin’s customary power, of a pain in one temple. Soon afterward, a thought was planted in him by the tempter: that the throbbing of his blood vessels might be calmed by bloodletting. While he was turning this over in his mind, the veins of both temples sprang out, the renewed pain broke in more fiercely, and he hurried to the basilica. First he asked forgiveness for the thought; then he touched his head to the cloth of the saint’s tomb, and immediately departed healthy.

### XV

I confess that he had already set down many things in praise of various people. Yet, although he burned with an even greater love for Martin, he considered himself in no way worthy to write what had to be written about his miracles—until, twice and three times during sleep, he was warned that he would incur guilt if he remained silent.

Finally, he had ordered that the oratory of Saint Stephen in the suburb be lengthened, and that the altar, which was intact, be moved forward as before. But because he found none of the relics there, he sent one of the abbots to the bishop’s residence to bring out the relics of that martyr, although he had forgotten the key. Finding the chest locked, the abbot did not know what to do: returning to the bishop for the key would cause delay; but if he displayed the chest, he knew that it would trouble him because it contained the relics of many saints.

While he was thus at a standstill, so that divine grace might show itself Gregory’s collaborator, he saw the chest opened, its bolts springing apart. Giving thanks, he brought the relics to Gregory, amid the great wonder of many people. When Gregory returned, he found the chest locked as he had left it.

### XVI

Gregory performed many deeds in the healing of the sick, too many to pursue here. Yet he tried to exclude his own merits from them, attributing them instead to the saints whose relics he likewise carried. In fact, these things happened through him all the more truly because he attributed them more humbly to others.

There is the following example. Once, as he was walking along the road and carrying around his neck a golden cross with relics of blessed Mary, ever-virgin, or of blessed Martin, he saw not far from the road a poor man’s little dwelling burning in a fire. It was covered, as poor people’s shelters commonly are, with leaves and bundles of brushwood—fuel for the flames. The wretched man ran about here and there with his wife and children, shouting and bringing water, but in vain. The flames had already gained the upper hand and could not be subdued.

Then Gregory rushed up and raised the cross against the balls of flame. Immediately, at the sight of the holy relics, the entire fire was so stunned that it could neither burn further what it had already seized nor scorch anything even slightly.

### XVII

There had been a reason why he had to visit the town of Reims. After being courteously received there by Bishop Giles, he rested during the night. At dawn on the following Sunday he came to the church to converse with the bishop.

While he was awaiting the bishop’s arrival in the sacristy—for he did not wish to speak in the church—Sygo, once the treasurer of King Sigibert, approached him. Gregory kissed him and made him sit beside him. While they were conversing for a little while and Sygo hung upon Gregory’s words, his ear, which had long been deaf, suddenly opened with a kind of crack [Germ.: “noise”].

Sygo began to give thanks and to proclaim what had been done for him through Gregory. But the man of God, mindful of his customary humility and trying to draw him away from this opinion, said:

> Do not, dearest son, give me any thanks; give them to blessed Martin, through whose relics—which, although unworthy, I carry—your hearing has been restored and your deafness driven away.

### XVIII

The virtue of charity so predominated in him that he extended the affection of love even to his enemies, as the following example will show.

Once it happened that he was hurrying to visit his venerable mother in Burgundy. In the fir woods beyond the river Verberis [Note: Papyrius Masso read *Araris*, but our reading is better, based on Gregory himself, who calls this river *Berberis*], he encountered robbers. They attacked his company with such force that they seemed intent not only on stripping them but also on killing them.

Gregory could not be terrified by their assault, for he was traveling surrounded by Martin’s protection. Soon he called upon Martin’s help and experienced it present with him, so that the robbers took flight more quickly than they had emerged.

Gregory, however, exercising his customary compassion [Note: MSS. 2: “making use of his customary compassion”], was not thrown into confusion even in the disturbance. He called the fleeing men back and invited his enemies to food and drink. But one would have thought they were being driven by clubs, or that unwilling horses were being forced against their capacity by spurs, so that they could not even hear the man calling them back.

Thus Gregory was shown to be near to the heavenly ears and devoted to works of charity.

### XIX

The faith and devotion of the people grew greatly through Gregory, while the malignant enemy was tormented by no small grief. Therefore, unable to bear the force of his own malice, he tried, in open words, to drive either the pastor’s confidence or that of the flock into madness.

On Christmas Day itself, when Gregory was proceeding to solemnize the pontifical festival in the principal basilica, as was customary [Note: Serg.: “when he was proceeding to solemnize the principal festival …”; Germ.: “when Gregory was proceeding to solemnize in the principal basilica, as is customary”], one of the possessed, more savage than the others, began to rave violently. Pushing his way among the crowds who followed or encountered him, and who had surrounded Gregory, he thrust himself in their path and said:

> In vain you seek Martin’s threshold; you approach his church to no purpose, because he has abandoned you on account of your many crimes. Behold, abhorring you, he performs miracles at Rome.

The devil whispered these and many other words to all the people, crowded together as they were. At the sound of them not only were the hearts of the peasants thrown into turmoil, but the clergy too, and Gregory himself, were shaken with fear.

Entering the basilica with great weeping, they all prostrated themselves on the pavement, praying that they might be worthy of the holy man’s presence. A certain man whose two hands and one foot had contracted three years earlier lay prostrate with the others before the holy altar, praying for blessed Martin’s help. Suddenly he was seized by a severe fever and tortured as though stretched upon a rack.

Meanwhile the sacred solemnities were being conducted. As the holy bishop continued in tears, awaiting the arrival of blessed Martin, and as, by the divine mystery, the pall had already been spread according to custom, the sick man was completely restored to health.

Gregory therefore rejoiced greatly and gave thanks to almighty God. With his eyes drenched in a flood of tears, he burst forth to the people in these words:

> Let fear depart from your hearts, brothers, because the blessed confessor dwells with us. And do not believe the devil at all: he was a liar from the beginning and did not stand in the truth.

As he offered these and other words of consolation to those present, everyone’s mourning was released into joy; and they returned home through Martin and Gregory much more joyful than they had come.

### XX

Since we have mentioned Christmas, let us recall what once happened to our bishop on that day.

On the sacred night of this solemnity [Al.: “of this Nativity”], wearied by the vigils of the preceding day, he had lain down for a short while on his elbow when a certain man hurried to him, saying:

> Rise and return to the church.

He awoke, made the sign of the cross over himself, and went to sleep again. The man did not stop but warned him a second time. Yet when he awoke and still felt himself weighed down, he went to sleep again.

Then the man came a third time and struck him on the cheek, saying:

> Here you are, supposed to remind the others about the vigils, and you are so long held down by sleep!

Struck by this voice, Gregory returned to the church with swift speed. He proved so pleasing to the heavenly eyes that, even when human weakness pressed upon him, he was not permitted to neglect his salvation.

### XXI

It seemed appropriate to insert this account of how God wished to rebuke him, lest he sin through the frivolity of others.

When blessed Martin had healed Gregory from a desperate illness so completely that he hurried to the church on the following day, Gregory instructed one of the priests to celebrate the solemn Masses in his place, so that he himself would not be exhausted.

But when the priest uttered certain festive [Al.: “hasty”] words in a rustic manner, some of those standing nearby began to mock him, saying that it would have been better to remain silent than to speak so inelegantly.

During the following night, however, Gregory saw a man saying to him that one must never dispute about the mysteries of God. From then on he was sufficiently resolved not to permit foolish and shallow people in his presence to disparage the sacred solemnities.

### XXII

The man of God often went farther afield, as a true counselor both of the flock and of himself, either for the benefit of his subjects or for the sake of his own salvation.

On one occasion he went to pray at the tomb of blessed Hilary and also turned aside to visit holy Queen Radegund. It happened that, while these two—like inhabitants of paradise—were conversing with one another about heavenly things, the oil that ordinarily trickled there, drop by drop, before the relics of the holy cross increased at the bishop’s arrival to such an extent that within the space of one hour more than one sextarius overflowed.

Later, when blessed Queen Radegund was summoned to the King of heaven, the man of God Gregory received news of her death. When he arrived, she had already departed; he placed her holy remains in the tomb. At that time he solemnly blessed the altar but reserved its cover for the bishop, who happened to be absent.

### XXIII

There had been a reason why he had to cross the river Garonne near the fortress of Biavium. At that time, however, the river had swollen so greatly that it inspired considerable terror in those who looked upon it.

Not far away the holy priest Romanus rests; according to his Life, our Martin buried him. When a storm of winds on one side and mountains of waves on the other threatened enormous danger to the traveler, Gregory raised his eyes to heaven and repeatedly looked toward the church of the aforesaid Romanus. Immediately he smoothed the entire sea to such an extent that, once the crashing had been stilled, he was carried without danger to the opposite bank.

### XXIV

Gregory had spent sixteen years in the episcopate when his namesake, the great Gregory, was installed in the apostolic see. It is an accepted tradition that the two had long been bound to one another by a special friendship.

Nor is this surprising, since Fortunatus compares this Gregory with Gregory of Nazianzus: the latter, as it were, had been given to the East, the Roman Gregory to the South, and our Gregory to the West.

When our Gregory sought the sacred thresholds of the Apostles [Note: It seems that Gregory undertook this journey in the year 594. For the preceding three years, during which Gregory the Great was already pope, he had spent in Gaul, according to the *Lives of the Fathers*, etc.], the holy pope received him with great reverence. Introducing him to the Confession of blessed Peter, he stood beside him and waited for him to rise.

Meanwhile, being a man of profound intelligence, he marveled at God’s hidden dispensation and considered how such great grace had flowed from heaven upon a man of this kind—for Gregory was short in stature.

Gregory immediately perceived this divinely and, rising from prayer, looked calmly at the pope and said:

> The Lord made us, and not we ourselves; he is the same in small things as in great.

When the holy pope realized that this was an answer to his own thought, he rejoiced at the discovery and began thereafter to hold in great veneration the grace he had until then admired in Gregory. He so ennobled the see of Tours that he gave it a golden chair, which was to be preserved thereafter in that see [Ed.: “city”].

### XXV

Blessed Martin had magnified his foster-son Gregory in every way and shown himself favorable to him by many signs. But on one occasion, to show that he too cooperated in Gregory’s works, Martin deigned to make his presence known—although invisible—through the splendor by which he was accustomed to be seen.

Gregory was about to consecrate an oratory from the storehouse of his predecessor at Tours. He carried with great reverence relics of the holy martyr Saturninus and of the lord Martin, which had been received from the basilica.

There was a considerable choir of priests and Levites in white garments, a distinguished company of honored citizens, and also a great assembly of the secular people [Germ.: “of the worldly order”]. Ceremonially shining candles were carried, and crosses were raised aloft.

As they approached the doorway, a terrifying brightness suddenly flooded the little chamber and struck everyone’s eyes with an overwhelming radiance. It continued for some time, darting here and there like lightning. All were struck with excessive fear and lay prostrate on the ground.

But Gregory, conscious of so great a power, steadfastly encouraged them, saying:

> Do not be afraid. Remember how a ball of fire came forth from the head of blessed Martin and was seen to ascend into heaven; and for that reason believe that he has visited us with these holy relics.

Then everyone glorified God, and the elder, together with the clergy, said:

> Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; God is the Lord, and he has shone upon us.

### XXVI

Let these few things be said about our bishop. We do not commend him by the abundance of miracles, which are sometimes granted even to the reprobate; nor do we show that even this grace was lacking to him. [Note: What follows to the end is condensed into a few words in the Germ. manuscript.]

For the commendation of his glory, let this suffice: he followed Christ with a humble heart and did not put his trust in treasures of money. This truly is to have performed wonders: as is shown in part above, he was guarded from the snare of sins. Protection from sins is superior to every glory.
