In the twenty-first year of his episcopate, as though the number seven had been completed three times in faith in the holy Trinity, he was gathered to his fathers—not so much full of days, since he had been ordained at nearly thirty years of age, as full of perfection.

Yet he does not seem to be entirely shut away in the tomb, since at least his tongue remains alive in the world. And because, as we believe, he has been joined to blessed Martin in heaven, he is also near him in the tomb through his holy body.

The people of Tours, so that they may not seem ungrateful for divine gifts, must always recall how greatly they have been supported by God. For they were given a patron not of an ordinary kind, but Martin. What first or special thing can be said in his praise, when, as it is written, it is clear that his least deeds are greater than the greatest deeds of others? Nevertheless, all the nations of the world, so to speak, testify how highly he must be esteemed. They love him with such personal devotion that even in our own time, when charity has already grown exceedingly cold, we see many people unknown to us in both race and language flocking to his most holy tomb. Truly it may be said of Martin:

> Whose face the whole earth longs to see.

Their devotion rightly and severely rebukes the apathy of those of us who live nearby. Yet it is plainly by divine governance that his love has penetrated the hearts of all, so that his memory is as sweet to everyone as that of another Josiah, and that it has spread through all the earth, so that wherever Christ’s name is found, Martin is honored.

They were also given Gregory, a man distinguished not only by holiness but by learning, lest the city of Tours seem obscure because it lacked the service of a writer. Indeed, just as Rome, the city of Romulus, is made illustrious after the Apostles by another Gregory, so Tours, after Martin, is adorned by this Gregory.

We trust that we have him as a kind of advocate and mediator with God and with blessed Martin, and that we may entrust our needs to him for resolution. He, however, will not forget either his own mercy or Martin’s mercy, which he took such care to commend to us. For he arranged these miracles in order to commend that mercy, so that all who would hear in the future how many and how great things Martin visibly accomplishes, and what desperate illnesses he heals, might have no doubt at all about his power. And if, by the dispensation of the times, bodily miracles should cease, let us nevertheless always believe that he works the medicine of his power in our souls.

Therefore, may Gregory, conscious of Martin’s mercy, always commend to him his flock [Note: Ed.: “may he always increase from his flock”]; may he always intercede with him for the condition of his holy place and for the welfare of the entire kingdom.

Nor should we pass over how he preserved his customary humility even in his burial. He had himself buried in a place where he would always be trampled under everyone’s feet, and where the very conditions of the place would ensure that he could never be held in any special reverence.

But the flock of blessed Martin could not endure this. They lifted their lord’s friend from that place and, having erected a beautiful mausoleum, placed him with due reverence to the left of the holy tomb [Note: We have discussed the tomb and relics of blessed Gregory in fuller notes, column 1391. His feast is commemorated on this very day in the older calendars and martyrologies. He died in the year 595.]

He died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December, that is, during Martin’s week, so that, joined to Martin in heaven, he might complete the solemnity of Martin which, already ill, he had begun to celebrate here, through the agency of the Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God, forever and ever. Amen.

*[Column 0127] Here ends the Life of Saint Gregory, Archbishop of Tours.*

## Genealogical Table of Saint Gregory of Tours

## Testimonies of Distinguished Men concerning Saint Gregory, Bishop of Tours

*[Column 0129A] Venantius Fortunatus, in the letter prefixed to his works and addressed to Saint Gregory, Bishop of Tours.*

> To the holy lord, Gregory, pope, endowed with the gift of merits and admitted and raised up to the sacred altars: Fortunatus.  
> The brilliant utterances of your acumen, etc. Therefore, apostolic man worthy to be proclaimed, Pope Gregory, since you personally insist that I bring forth certain passages from the little works of my incompetence for transfer to you, I marvel that you allow yourself to be led astray by love of my trifles, etc. But since … etc.

He praises him repeatedly in his poems; it is enough to select a few passages.

### From Book V, Poem 7

> Honored summit, life-giving glory, abundant light,  
> a pastor pleasing through love of the apostolic see.  
> Sacred Gregory, ever to be embraced by me from the lofty height, etc.

### Book V, Poem 13

> Flourishing in studies and faithful in sacred law,  
> always bringing forth the future gifts of your soul.

### Book VIII, Poem 16

> Gracious, blessed father, universal light, Gregory,  
> rightly the head who rules from the summit of priestly dignity, etc.

### Book VIII, Poem 17

> Happily coming from the fields of Auvergne,  
> you are a beacon scattering light over the peoples with your voice.  
> Hurrying from those Alps, your mind is higher even than they.

### Book VIII, Poem 23

> Sweet, dear, gracious, eloquent, kindly Gregory,  
> father of your country, sacred here and dear there.  
> Equal in gifts, merits, minds, and character,  
> honored by everyone in every capacity.

### From Book IX, Poem 7

> With joyful heart and graceful pen  
> you send letters, as my eager wish desires,  
> composing gentle words of earnest salvation,  
> dear Gregory.

### Baudonivia, a nun, in the Life of Saint Radegund, Queen, no. 27

> The messenger went to the apostolic man, the lord Gregory, bishop of the city of Tours, and arrived. But what he saw with his own eyes while present, before he buried her, he inserted concerning her virtues in the Book of Miracles which he composed. When he came to the place where the holy body lay, he later said under oath, weeping, that he had seen an angelic face in human form. Her face shone like a rose and a lily; he was so shaken and struck with fear that he seemed to stand as a devout man, full of God, before the presence of the blessed Mother of the Lord.

### Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, Book III, chapter 1, where he speaks of the holy recluse Hospitius of Nîmes

> Through this man the Lord deigned to perform great miracles, which are recorded in the books of the venerable man Gregory, Bishop of Tours.

### Agobard, Archbishop of Lyon, in *Against Jewish Superstitions*, chapter 4

> How great a holiness and truth Saint Gregory, bishop of the Church of Langres, possessed is attested by his Life, written among the *Lives of the Fathers* by Gregory of Tours, chapter 7, by the end of his life, and by the honor bestowed upon him by the Church down to the present day.

### Florus of Lyon, in his Martyrology, 4 November

> On the fourth day before the Nones: at Bourges, the deposition of Saint Lusor, a boy who was the son of a certain senator, etc., as is written in the Book of the Miracles of Gregory, Bishop of Tours. Ado and the other authors of martyrologies also used the words of that same Gregory.

### From the calendar of the Sacramentary of Saint Gatianus, the cathedral church of Tours, written about 800 years ago, and from another of the Great Monastery, written about 600 years ago

> On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December: Saint Gregory of Tours.

On the same day he is praised in various ancient martyrologies, especially those of the churches of Tours, as well as in the Roman, Gallican, and other martyrologies.

### From the old Lectionary of the Church of Chalon, concerning Saints Sylvester and Agricola, bishops, and Desideratus, priest, in Perard and the Bollandists, 17 March

> Although briefly, the magnificent man Gregory, Bishop of Tours, writes splendidly about them in his Books of Miracles: “But the most blessed Sylvester …,” from the Book on the Glory of the Confessors, chapters 85–86.

### Hericus the monk, *Miracles of Saint Germanus, Bishop of Auxerre*, Book I, chapter 29

> Gregory, bishop of Tours, a curious investigator and most diligent editor of miracles, records certain things performed by this blessed Father and through his memory. We preferred to make them known in his words rather than ours, lest, by exchanging one work for another, we detract something from the credibility of a matter not without worth. “Germanus …,” as Gregory has it in the Book on the Glory of the Confessors, chapter 41.

### From the second Life of Saint Medard, written in the ninth century, volume VIII of the *Spicilegium*

> At that time, among the Gallican bishops, Gregory the historian was held in distinction at Tours in speech and conduct, etc.  
> Setting aside our own material, we considered it right to attach to this little work what Gregory the historian reports concerning the virtue of this most holy bishop: “Medardus, the glorious confessor …,” from *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 95.

### From the Testament of Ecchard, Count and founder of the monastery of Patriciacum (Persy), ninth century, in Perard’s *History of Burgundy*, p. 26

> Give to Enschise, archbishop, one tapestry of the better kind, one book of the *History of the Lombards*, and the *Chronicle* which Gregory of Tours made, book two. (So in the text.)

### From Saint Odo, in a sermon in which blessed Martin is said to be equal to the Apostles

> Likewise, when Gregory of Tours was bringing his [Saint Martin’s] relics into a new basilica, he appeared to him, etc.; Odo took this from chapters 20, 59, and 104 of the Book on the Glory of the Confessors. He also praises Gregory’s words repeatedly elsewhere.

### Letaldus the monk, in the prologue to the Life of Saint Julian, Bishop of Le Mans

> I have inferred from the book of Gregory of Tours, by conjecture, the period in which that great man flourished. In Book I of his Histories, under the consulship of Decius and Gratus, he says of Sixtus, etc. … since blessed Dionysius is said to have been among their number by Saint Gregory, etc.

### Frodoard, *History of Reims*, Book II, chapter 2

> Gregory relates in the *History of the Franks* what happened concerning this bishop [Aegidius], etc.

### Book IV of the same History, chapter 59

> Our city is also said to have been distinguished by several other miracles of this blessed Father [Saint Martin]. Among them we have thought it appropriate to insert here those which Saint Gregory of Tours recounts in his Books of Miracles, etc.

The same author repeatedly praises these and other works of Gregory.

### Aimoïn, *History of the Franks*, Book III, chapter 41

> When Gregory of Tours at that time surpassed the other bishops in holiness, etc.

In the same work, chapter 66:

> For these reasons he brought accusations against the holy bishop Gregory.

He repeatedly calls the same man blessed Gregory.

### Hugh, Archdeacon of Tours, in the Dialogue addressed to Fulbert, from volume I of Mabillon’s *Analecta*

> Martin has outstanding interpreters of his miracles … He has Gregory, Bishop of Tours, who recounts wonderful miracles about Martin after his death.

### Fulbert, Bishop of Chartres, Letter 97, addressed to Robert, King of the Franks

> Prompted by your sacred command, I have hastened to investigate and write to you whether any history reports that blood rained down, and, if the event occurred, what it signified. I found Livy, Valerius, Orosius, and many others who report this matter. For the present it is enough to produce Gregory, Bishop of Tours, as a witness, on account of the authority of his religion. Thus that same Gregory says in the sixth book of his Histories, chapter 14: “In the sixth year …”

### Adhemar, *Chronicle*, Part I, chapter 30

> At that time Saint Gregory, Archbishop of Tours, shone with great miracles. During the same period Saint Germanus, Bishop of Paris, sent by King Charibert, consecrated at Angoulême the basilica of Saint Eparchius, where he himself had recently been buried. The venerable Gregory, Bishop of Tours, was present with him, and they dedicated the basilica under the authority of that same blessed Martin, placing in it many relics of blessed Martin the bishop. Finally, on the altar consecrated by that same Saint Germanus and Gregory, the marks of the holy cross are still seen impressed. Likewise, in honor of Saint Peter, they consecrated the church of the episcopal see which Clovis had built, etc.

### The same author, in the little book on the miracles of Saint Eparchius, abbot of Engoulême, from the manuscript of Saint Cyprian of Poitiers and Labbe

> Gregory, Bishop of the city of Tours, while undertaking to describe the virtues of saints whom other writers had passed over, also remembers among the others this patron of ours, saying: “Eparchius, a recluse of Engoulême, died …,” from Gregory’s *History*, Book VI, chapter 8.

### From the Life of Charlemagne, Chesne, volume II, p. 68

> At that time [of Childebert] Saint Gregory the First, pope, and Gregory, Bishop of Tours, flourished, etc.

### From the metrical Life of Saint Melanius, Bishop of Rennes, from a manuscript

> Certainly Melanius of Rennes, as the Gregory of Tours  
> writes, who writes many such things,  
> shone in the world with countless signs,  
> worthy of a perfect bishop, etc.

He praises him in chapter 55 of *On the Glory of the Confessors*.

### Rodulfus Glaber, in the Life of Saint William, Abbot of Dijon
For there was, as the blessed Gregory, bishop of Tours, the eminent recorder of the miracles of many saints, reports, a very large chest, etc., from chapter 51 of *The Glory of the Martyrs*. Because of his disbelief in it, the same saint relates that another Gregory, bishop of Langres, who bore that holy name, was once rebuked rather sharply.

An anonymous author who wrote the *Acts of the Archbishops of Rouen* in the eleventh century, in volume II of Mabillon’s *Analecta*.

Thus, as the blessed Gregory of Tours relates in his writings, on the holy night of Easter, in the episcopal place where he was accustomed to stand, they struck him with swords and killed him.

How great his holiness was is attested by the frequent healings granted to the sick from his tomb,” as Gregory of Tours reports, having experienced it himself.

The author of the *Life and Miracles of Saint Solemnis, bishop of Chartres*, from a royal manuscript.

“The blessed Gregory, then bishop of Tours, spoke in this way of the blessed Solemnis, bishop of Chartres: ‘Although from the city of Tours,’” etc. This saint spoke of that saint as a testimony.

From the *Life of Saint Maximus of Chinon, Confessor*, from a manuscript of the monastery of Marmoutier.

Gregory, bishop of Tours, a man of great nobility and simplicity, wrote much in plain language. He wrote two books on the life or memory of certain confessors; he wrote one book of *Miracles of the Saints*, one book of the miracles of Julian, martyr of Brioude, and four books of the miracles of Saint Martin displayed in his own time. He abridged the *History of the Franks* in a small book and afterward arranged it more fully in nine books. He also wrote a *Chronicle of Ecclesiastical History*.

The *Chronicle of Liège*, written in the year 1132, in Labbe, volume I of the *Bibliotheca*, p. 335.

In the year 572 Gregory, bishop of Tours, flourished in Gaul. Other chroniclers everywhere say the same, and it would be superfluous to list them individually.

Hugh, or the anonymous author of Saint-Marien of Auxerre.

In the seventh year of Justin, Gregory was ordained bishop of the people of Tours, a man renowned in every respect. Among other works that he wrote, he recorded many miracles and wonders of Saint Martin, which occurred most abundantly in his days.

[Col. 0133C] *Deeds of the Bishops and Counts of Angoulême*, by an Angoulême canon, about the year 1159, chapter 4.

Gregory, archbishop of Tours, and Germanus . . . consecrated the cathedral church, etc., and with the king’s approval consecrated as bishop Mererius, who had been the king’s chaplain, etc.

Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, against his detractors.

“You praise Gregory, illustrious through his Auvergne birth,

to whom the lofty chair of Martin grants a place.”

Peter of Poitiers, a monk, in the panegyric of Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny.

“From here too came Julian’s beloved pupil,

who governed the Church of Tours well.”

He speaks of the men of Auvergne. Also in his letter to a detractor:

[Col. 0133D] We are not unaware how splendidly Fortunatus exalted Gregory of Tours, together with many other bishops, in a most laudatory panegyric.

From an anonymous author who wrote the *Deeds of the Bishops of Tours and the Abbots of Marmoutier*, cited by Bochel.

“This Eustochius lived in the time of the blessed Gregory of Tours.” He frequently copied many passages from Gregory himself.

From the *Life of Lord Garnerius, provost of Saint Stephen of Dijon*, in Perard and Fiot’s history of that place.

“Concerning this church, the *Life of Saint Gregory, bishop of Langres*, states that those carrying his body, taking him from Langres,” etc. *On the Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 7. And below: “There is another basilica, concerning which it is written in the aforesaid *Life of Gregory* that his house adjoined the baptistery,” etc.

[Col. 0134A] Rigord, in the *Life of Philip Augustus*, under the year 1184.

“Having taken care, as we were able to gather from the history of Gregory of Tours, etc., we have determined this sufficiently clearly in our own history.” And under the year 1185: “Proving this from the chronicles of Hydatius and Gregory of Tours,” that is, of Fredegar.

Alberic, a monk of the Three Fountains, in his *Chronicle*.

“Martin was born in Pannonia. Gregory, bishop of Tours, briefly summarized his genealogy as follows: ‘A certain king,’” etc., from the book *On the Seven Sleepers*. In the year 593: “Thus far Gregory of Tours.”

Vincent of Beauvais, in the *Historical Mirror*, book XXI, chapter 124.

“Concerning Saint Gregory, archbishop of Tours . . . He is renowned in every respect. He was a native of the region of Auvergne,” etc. Saint Antoninus says the same, etc.

Matthew of Westminster, in the *Flowers of History*.

[Col. 0134B] In the year of grace 572 Gregory, bishop of Tours, was ordained and shone forth conspicuous in holiness.

In the year of grace 598 Gregory, bishop of the city of Tours, flourished in Gaul; he brought from the territory of Auvergne, etc.

Bernard Gui, bishop of Lodève, *On the Saints of Limoges*, in Labbe, volume I, p. 629.

“Saint Pelagia . . . whom Saint Gregory of Tours, in his book *On the Miracles of the Saints*, places among the saints,” etc. He praises the same man repeatedly, as do Peter Equilinus in *On the Births of the Saints* and others who compiled the Lives of the Saints.

Robert Gaguin, book II of his *History of France*.

“Gregory was a man especially distinguished for holiness,” etc. He praises his works frequently.

From Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

Gregory, bishop of Tours, formerly a monk and disciple of Saint Avitus, bishop of the Auvergnese, was a learned and noble man, gentle and humble as well. He was of such holiness and purity that even during his life he shone with miracles, etc.

The same author, book III of *On the Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, chapter 51. Gregory . . . whose father Florentius, son of the senator Georgius, was himself a praiseworthy man who shone in holy conduct. Therefore the good father, instructing his son Gregory in the fear of the Lord, entrusted to his memory the deeds of the saints, by which he always advanced toward better things . . . He was a man of the greatest charity and humility, so that in his time he scarcely had an equal on earth . . . He became renowned through many miracles both during life and after death; his feast is celebrated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December. His Life is preserved in writing.

The same author, book II, chapter 10. Gregory . . . a holy man beloved by God and human beings, thoroughly skilled in the sacred Scriptures, was most diligent in investigating the deeds of the saints . . . Since he was a learned and educated man, he wrote many short works in straightforward language, etc. He compiled a catalogue of Gregory’s works, as did later authors: Possevinus, Bellarmine, Vossius, the author of his brief Life, Labeus, Cavius, and others.

Hieronymus Chlictoveus of Nieuwpoort, in his edition of various short works.

We reserved the last place in human eloquence, as the most eminent of all the others, for Gregory of Tours, without any hesitation in granting him the palm above the rest and in judging that it ought not to be taken from him.

Preface to the edition of Josse Bade.

Since the commentaries of the blessed bishops Gregory of Tours and Ado of Vienne possess the greatest authority, etc., for they are conspicuous in the holiness of their lives and shine with the summit of episcopal Christian piety, and they transmit many events that they themselves saw and discovered, not indeed with studied elegance but with sincere truth. Their piety—especially that of Gregory of Tours—could by itself win over the reader.

Mathias Flacius Illyricus, in the letter prefixed to his edition.

Gregory of Tours deserves to be read . . . No ancient historian exists who knew the affairs of those times so certainly or embraced them so fully. He praises him frequently in the *Magdeburg Centuries*.

From the *Patriarchate of Bourges*, chapter 27, volume II of Labbe’s *New Bibliotheca*, p. 32.

“This will become clear from the writings of the divine Gregory of Tours, certainly a man most learned in the knowledge of historical events.” He is praised frequently in the same book.

Preface to the *Lives of the Saints* extracted from the volumes of Aloysius Lippomanus.

Gregory, surnamed Florentinus, a man distinguished for learning and nobility, governed the Church of Tours with the greatest holiness. His writings are accorded the faith customarily accorded to a most holy man who has deserved exceedingly well of the Christian faith, etc.

Joannes Mariana, book V of *Spanish Affairs*, chapter 10.

The silence of Gregory of Tours adds a weightier argument. Will you think that this was granted as a favor by a Gallic writer and a man of great authority?

Papirius Masson, in *Notice of Gaul*.

Once the kingdom of the Franks had been established, I would rather learn from the books of Gregory of Tours how great a change occurred than from my own speech.

Joseph Scaliger, book VI of *On the Correction of the Chronology*.

Great thanks are due to Gregory, who amid such neglect of history applied his mind to writing these things. Without him, one would have had to fear that the fabulous Hunibald would gain possession of that history, etc. We have neither a better nor an older authority in the history of the Franks.

[Col. 0135C] Nicolas Faber, tutor of Louis XIII, king of France, in a *Schediasma*, etc.

Gregory, bishop of Tours, was the most diligent and most ancient writer of our history.

Hieronymus Bignonius, in the preface to the *Formulas of Marculf*.

Gregory of Tours himself, than whom we have no more worthy historian, receives light from Marculf in many places and is altogether illuminated by him.

Jacques-Jean Chifflet, in his *Investigation*, etc.

Saint Gregory, the most ancient and most faithful historian of the Franks.

The Sammarthani, in *Gallia Christiana*.

Saint Gregory, the light of the Gallican Church, illustrious in the glory of virtue, wisdom, and exceptional holiness, who deserved well of ecclesiastical history and of the affairs of the Franks.

[Col. 0135D] Jean Launoy, doctor of Paris, in his *Discussion*, etc.

Gregory of Tours pursued with the greatest diligence the beginnings of the Christian religion among the Gauls and events worthy of remembrance. He praises Gregory and his works everywhere.

Hadrian Valesius, in the preface to volume II of *Frankish Affairs*.

Gregory, whom I acknowledge as a pious and wise man and the foremost of our historians, and whom I judge most worthy of praise.

[Col. 0136A] Jean de Bonne, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, in *Notice of Authors*.

Gregory of Tours, a faithful historian, but one of simpler eloquence.

Charles Cointius, *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks*, under the year 544.

We ought not to have omitted the birth of this illustrious man, whom one might rightly call the father of Frankish history. He says the same frequently elsewhere.

Antoine Dadin d’Alez, professor of civil and canon law and dean of the University of Toulouse, in his letter concerning the notes, etc., on the books of Gregory.

I devoted my efforts to preserving the memory of the greatest bishop and to dispelling the error and slander of malicious men, by whom the most expert writer on our affairs, and in part a witness, is treated as an inept author of fables and dreams. My labor will not be in vain if I restore the reputation of the bishop, successor in the see and merits of the divine Martin.

[Col. 0136B] The Bollandists, under 17 March and elsewhere.

Saint Gregory of Tours, to whom Frankish history owes as much alone as it owes to all the other writers before him taken together.

Jean Balesdens, in his edition.

I would not unjustly say that, although the simplicity of a dove seems visible in Gregory’s writings, the prudence of a serpent is nevertheless not absent, since in selecting and examining matters he was especially attentive to their usefulness and evidential value. Nor would I hesitate to assert that in this respect he surpassed later writers, etc.

## ON FREDEGAR

From the *Life of Saint Pippin, Mayor of the Palace of Austrasia*, in Chesne’s volume I of *Frankish History*.

But lest I seem to have introduced something new from the Life of the most blessed Duke, it will not be inappropriate to place before the eyes, collected in one place, the same words inserted at various points in the *Deeds of the Franks* as testimony to his holiness. They run as follows: “Up to that time, from the beginning when Dagobert began to reign, through the counsel of the most blessed Arnulf,” etc. He produces excerpts from Fredegar, from chapter 58 of the *Chronicle* through chapter 86.

Rigord, praised above, in the *Life of Philip Augustus*. Joseph Scaliger, book VI of *On the Correction of the Chronology*.

Several years ago an appendix to Gregory appeared, which some say was written by Fredegar. That appendix contains many excellent things, which one would not easily find elsewhere.

Valesius, in the later part of his *Defense*, chapter 8.

Believe me: if Fredegar had not written them, or if we had suffered the loss of Fredegar, we could safely and without danger of error remain ignorant of the deeds of the two sons of the younger Childebert, of the younger Chlothar, of Dagobert, and of the later Chlodovech up to the fourth year of his reign. Fredegar committed these matters to writing with the greatest diligence and accuracy possible for his age . . . Nor will you find any one of our ancient historians who did not transcribe almost word for word book V of Fredegar’s *Chronicle*.

Charles Cointius, under the year 584, no. 21.

He is the most ancient of all who wrote Frankish affairs after Gregory.

[Col. 0137]

# FRANKISH ANNALS FROM THE YEAR 255 TO CHARLEMAGNE, FROM THE ANCIENT WRITERS, SAINT GREGORY OF TOURS, FREDEGAR, ETC.

Some preliminary material is given concerning France and the peoples of the Franks.

[Col. 0137A] The region of the Franks is called **FRANCE**; it lies in Germany between the Saxons and the Alemanni.

“What shall I say again of the innermost nations of France?” Eumenius, in the *Panegyric of Constantine the Great*, chapter 6.

“You have punished the kings themselves of France for their rashness.” The same author, chapter 10.

“FRANCE, the joy of the Romans.” A coin of Constantine the Great, in Spanheim, *On the Excellence of Coins*.

“FRANCE AND ALEMANNIA, the joy of the Romans.” A coin of the same emperor, in Morel’s *Specimen of Antiquities*, no. 2 of the edition.

“Let the forces of France and of the Chamavi come;

let Germany tremble.” Ausonius, *Mosella*.

“. . . Where France, mingled with the Suebi,

strives for obedience.” The same author, *On the Consulate*.

France is shown on the right bank of the Rhine in the Peutinger Map.

[Col. 0137B] “. . . The province will expel

the standards sooner than France the kings

whom you give it.” Claudian, book I of *On the Praise of Stilicho*.

“Between the Saxons and the Alemanni lies a people not so extensive as it is powerful, once called Germany, now France.” Saint Jerome, in the *Life of Saint Hilarion*.

“When the question was asked about the outcome, whether they ought to cross into France.” Sulpicius Alexander, book III of the *Histories*, cited by Gregory of Tours, book II of his *History*, chapter 8.

“Believing that all the hidden places of France could safely be penetrated.” The same author, book IV of the *Histories*, in the same place.

## THE PEOPLES OF THE FRANKS

The Salii, Attuarii, Bricteri or Bructeri or Burcturi, Chamavi, Ampsivarii, Chatti, Chauci, Cherusci, Tencteri, Usipetes, and Sicambri.

“Having made these preparations, he first sought the Franks of all, namely those whom custom called the Salii.” Ammianus Marcellinus, book XVII of the *Deeds*.

“Julian, etc., suddenly invaded the region of the Franks, whom they call the Attuarii.” The same author, book XX.

“Believing that all the hidden places of France could safely be penetrated,” etc. “After assembling an army, he crossed the Rhine, laid waste the Bructeri nearest the bank, and also the district inhabited by the Chamavi, with no one appearing anywhere to oppose him, except that a few Ampsivarii and Chatti, under the leadership of Marcomer, appeared on the farther ridges of the hills.” Sulpicius Alexander, book IV of the *Histories*, cited by Gregory of Tours, book II, chapter 8.

“Chauci, Cherusci, Chamavi, who are also Franks; France; Bructeri.” The Peutinger Itinerary Map.

The Franks were called Sicambri because they possessed the territory of the ancient Sicambri, from whom that land received the name of France. For, as Tacitus testifies in book XII of the *Annals*, the Sugambri were destroyed and transported into Gaul; and Cluverius, in book III of *Ancient Germany*, chapters 9, 10, and 20, writes as follows: “The Tencteri and Usipetes succeeded to the lands of the Sicambri, and those peoples, together with the Ampsivarii, Attuarii, Bructeri, Chamavi, Chatti, Chauci, and Salii . . . afterward joined together into one body and established for themselves the new name of Franks.”

## YEAR 253

Valerian and his son Gallienus, Augusti.

[Col. 0138A] 255. Aurelian defeats the Franks invading Gaul.

The same Aurelian, then tribune of the Sixth Gallic Legion at Mainz, so crushed the Franks invading Gaul and roaming throughout it that, after capturing three hundred of them and killing seven hundred, he sold them under the crown. Hence the following song was again made about him: “A thousand Franks, a thousand Sarmatians—we killed at once.” Vopiscus, *Life of Aurelian*, p. 211.

259. Gallienus wages war against the Franks in Gaul.

Gallienus, seeing that the Germanic peoples were more hostile than the others and were harassing the Celtic nations along the Rhine with greater violence, undertook to defend this region against the enemy. He ordered commanders, together with the armies of those regions, to make war against the others who were intent on plundering Italy, Illyricum, and Greece. He himself, stationed across the Rhine and guarding it as far as he could, sometimes prevented the enemy from crossing, and at other times set his prepared forces against those who had crossed. But because he was conducting war against an enormous multitude while himself possessing only very small forces, his affairs had already been reduced to straits, when he seemed to have lessened the danger somewhat by making a treaty with one of the leaders of the Germanic people. For that leader restrained the other barbarians from continually crossing the Rhine and opposed those who were invading. Zosimus, *History*, book I. Zonaras, likewise describing this war in book XII of the *Annals*, says that it was fought against the Franks.

260. Valerian is captured by the Persians; Gallienus rules alone.

262. Gallienus crosses into Gaul against Posthumus. Posthumus is aided by the Franks.

Gallienus therefore began war against Posthumus with Aureolus and the commander Clodius, who later obtained the imperial power and was a prince of the family of our Caesar Constantine. Posthumus, supported by many Celtic and Frankish auxiliaries, went to war with Victorinus, with whom he had shared the imperial power. Gallienus’s party was victorious. Trebellius Pollio, *Life of Gallienus*, p. 178.

[Col. 0138C] 264. Gallienus celebrates an enemy triumph at Rome, with disguised Franks among the captives.

There also went peoples in disguise, such as Goths, Sarmatians, Franks, and Persians, so that no fewer than two hundred were led in each group. The same author, p. 179.

265. Frankish pirate raids. Tarragona is plundered by the Franks.

The Franks themselves, fierce beyond the others, whose strength boiled over toward war, carried the heat of their fury beyond the Ocean itself and kept even the shores of Spain hostile with their arms. Nazarius, *Panegyric of Constantine the Great*, no. 17.

After these events had gone favorably and beyond expectation, he, becoming—as men do—more relaxed in prosperity, nearly delivered the Roman state to destruction, together with his son Saloninus, whom he had honored with the title of Caesar, so that . . . the Juthungi of the Alemanni possessed Italy, and the peoples of the Franks, after plundering Gaul, possessed Spain, while the town of Tarragona had been ravaged and almost destroyed. Aurelius Victor, *On Gallienus*.

[Col. 0138D] 268. Gallienus is killed; Claudius becomes Augustus.

270. Death of Claudius; Aurelian becomes Augustus.

273. Aurelian defeats Tetricus in Gaul and celebrates a triumph at Rome. Franks among the captives.

Goths, Alans, Roxolani, Sarmatians, Franks, Suebi, Vandals, and Germans, their hands bound, went before him as captives. Flavius Vopiscus, *Life of Aurelian*, p. 220.

274. Probus defeats the Franks in Gaul.

“Let the Franks, thrown down in impassable marshes, bear witness; let the Germans and Alemanni, driven far from the banks of the Rhine, bear witness . . . You are Frankish, Gothic, Sarmatian, Parthian—you are everything, and previously you were always worthy of imperial power and worthy of triumphs.” Flavius Vopiscus, *Life of the Emperor Probus*, p. 237.

275. Aurelian is killed; Tacitus becomes Augustus.

276. Death of Tacitus; Florian becomes Augustus and is killed after sixty days. When the statues of Tacitus and Florian were struck down by lightning, the haruspices gave an oracle concerning the Franks.

At Interamna the statues of Tacitus and Florian were struck down by lightning. At that time the haruspices gave the following response: At some time an emperor of Rome would come from their family, whether through a woman or through a man, one who would impose judges upon the Parthians and Persians and keep the Franks and Alemanni under Roman laws. Flavius Vopiscus, [Col. 0139B] *Life of Florian*, p. 231.

[Col. 0139B] Probus becomes Augustus.

277. Probus decisively defeats the Franks in Gaul through his commanders.

He fought a second battle against the Franks. After they had been decisively defeated by the efforts of his commanders, he himself fought with the forces of the Burgundians and Vandals. Zosimus, *History*, book I, p. 664.

280. Frankish pirate expedition from the Pontus, where settlements had been assigned to them, through the Mediterranean Sea. Greece and Asia are ravaged, Syracuse is captured, and they return to France.

The incredible audacity and undeserved success of a few Frankish captives under the emperor Probus repeatedly returned to people’s minds. Seizing ships in the Pontus, they had ravaged Greece and Asia and, not without punishment, had put in at many shores of Libya; finally they had captured Syracuse itself, once famous for naval victories. Then, carried across an immense distance, they entered the Ocean where it breaks through the lands and thus demonstrated, by the outcome of their recklessness, that nothing was closed to pirate desperation wherever access by ship was open. Eumenius, *Panegyric to Caesar Constantius*, chapter 18.

Likewise, when the Franks had approached the emperor and received settlements from him, a certain part of them attempted revolt. Having obtained a large number of ships, they threw all Greece into confusion. They were carried to Sicily, attacked the city of Syracuse, and inflicted a great slaughter there. At last, when they had also landed in Africa and had been repulsed after troops were brought from Carthage, they were nevertheless able to return home without suffering any loss. Zosimus, *History*, book I.

Proculus, rebelling in Gaul and betrayed by the Franks, is defeated and killed by Probus.

Probus pursued him even to the farthest lands. Proculus wished to seek the aid of the Franks, from whom he himself claimed to derive his origin; but when the Franks betrayed him—for it is characteristic of them to break faith while laughing—Probus defeated and killed him. Flavius Vopiscus, *Life of Proculus*, p. 246.

[Col. 0139D] 282. Probus is killed. Carus becomes Augustus; his sons Carinus and Numerian become Caesars.

283. Carus dies after being struck by lightning. Carinus and Numerian become Augusti.

284. Numerian is killed. Diocletian becomes Augustus; Maximian Herculius becomes Caesar.

285. Carinus is killed.

286. Maximian Herculius becomes Augustus, enters Gaul, and restrains and crushes the rebellious peasants who called themselves Bagaudae.

287. Maximian defeats the Burgundians, Alemanni, Chabiones, and Heruli who had poured into Gaul.

He sets Carausius against the Franks and Saxons. He orders Carausius to be killed; when Carausius learns of this, he occupies Britain.

After these events Carausius, who was of very low birth but had gained an outstanding reputation in the active ranks of the army, had been assigned, at Boulogne and along the coast of Belgica and Armorica, the task of pacifying the sea, which the Franks and Saxons were troubling. He had often captured many barbarians, but had neither returned the booty intact to the provincials nor sent it to the emperors. When suspicion began to arise that he was deliberately allowing the barbarians to pass so that he could intercept them with their booty and enrich himself by this opportunity, Maximian ordered him to be killed. Carausius then assumed the purple and occupied Britain. Eutropius, book IX.

The Franks invade Batavia.

He killed many thousands of Franks who had invaded Batavia and other lands on this side of the Rhine, etc. An anonymous author, *Panegyric to Maximian and Constantine the Great*, chapter 4, concerning the victory of Constantius, father of Constantine the Great.

He cleansed the land of Batavia of every enemy, after it had once been occupied under Carausius, his former fosterling, by various peoples of the Franks. Eumenius, *Panegyric to Constantine the Great*, chapter 5, concerning the victory of his father Constantius.

288. Maximian defeats the Germans beyond the Rhine and maintains a military station in France. Athech and Genobaudes, kings of the Franks. Athech obtains peace from him, and Genobaudes receives back his kingdom. The Franks cease their pirate warfare.

“Since Genobaudes has recovered his kingdom through you, while Athech has received a gift, what else did he seek by coming into your presence with all his people except that he might then reign with unimpaired authority, once he had appeased you, Maximian? He repeatedly displayed you, as I hear, to his countrymen and ordered them to gaze upon you for a long time and learn obedience, while he himself served you.” Claudius Mamertinus, *Panegyric to Maximian*.

“I pass over the Franks who came to the king to ask for peace.” Claudius Mamertinus, *Birthday Speech for Maximian and Diocletian*, chapter 5.

“Victory beyond the Rhine, and pirate wars crushed after the Franks had been subdued.” The same author, chapter 7.

289. Maximian wages an unsuccessful war against Carausius.

When war had been unsuccessfully attempted against Carausius, a man highly experienced in military affairs, peace was finally agreed. Eutropius, *History*, book IX.

[Col. 0140C] 291. Maximian transfers Franks into Gaul.

“Thus, just as earlier, at your command, Diocletian Augustus, he replenished the deserted lands of Thrace with inhabitants transferred from Asia; and just as afterward, at your command, Maximian Augustus, the abandoned fields of the Nervii and Treveri were joyfully restored by return and the Frank, received under Roman laws, cultivated them.” Eumenius, *Panegyric to Caesar Constantius*, chapter 21.

292. Constantius and Galerius become Caesars. Gaul is assigned to Constantius. Boulogne is captured by him.

293. Constantius recovers Batavia, occupied by the Franks, and leads them away into Gaul.

He killed, drove out, captured, and led away many thousands of Franks who had invaded Batavia and other lands on this side of the Rhine. Anonymous author, *Panegyric to Maximian and Constantine*, chapter 4.

“Having captured that same army through valor and preserved it through clemency, while preparations were being made to recover Britain by building fleets, he cleansed the land of Batavia—once occupied under his former fosterling by various peoples of the Franks—of every enemy. Not content merely to conquer, he transferred the inhabitants themselves into Roman territories, so that they were compelled to lay down not only their weapons but also their savagery.” Eumenius, *Panegyric to Constantine Augustus*, chapter 5.

“Or does this very Batavia, which has just ceased to be barbarian, miss the savagery of the Franks as though it had swallowed it no more than if the surrounding rivers and the sea washing its shores had covered it?” The same author, *Oration for the Restoration of the Schools*, chapter 18.

“Thus, just as earlier, at your command, Diocletian Augustus, he replenished the deserted lands of Thrace with inhabitants transferred from Asia; just as later, at your command, Maximian Augustus, the abandoned fields of the Nervii and Treveri were joyfully restored by return and the Frank, received under Roman laws, cultivated them; so now, through your victories, unconquered Caesar Constantius, whatever remained sparsely inhabited in the lands of the Ambiani, Bellovaci, Tricasses, and Lingones is flourishing again under a barbarian cultivator.” Eumenius, *Panegyric to Caesar Constantius*, chapter 21.

[Col. 0141A] Allectus, the associate of Carausius, kills him and holds Britain for three years after him.

296. Constantius brings war to Britain. Allectus is defeated and killed by Asclepiodotus, prefect of the praetorian guard. Some Franks in Allectus’s army are killed and others captured.

“For indeed, unconquered Caesar, victory over all the enemies whom you attacked has been granted to you by the unanimous consent of the immortal gods, but especially the destruction of the Franks. Even those soldiers of yours who, by mistake, as I said shortly before, had been separated by the foggy sea and reached the town of London, slaughtered throughout the city whatever remained of that mercenary multitude of barbarians after the battle, when they were thinking of fleeing after the town had been plundered. They not only brought safety to your provincials through the slaughter of the enemy but also gave them pleasure as spectators. O manifold victory, worthy of innumerable triumphs, by which Britain was restored and the strength of the Franks utterly destroyed!” Eumenius, *Panegyric to Caesar Constantius*, chapter 17.

[Col. 0141B] 305. Diocletian and Maximian lay down the purple and name Constantius and Galerius Augusti.

Constantius obtained Gaul, Spain, and Britain.

Constantine, recalled by his father from Galerius, set out for Gaul and joined him at the time when Constantius was crossing to Britain.

306. Constantius dies at York.

Constantine, proclaimed Caesar by Galerius, crossed into Gaul, suppressed the invasion of the Franks, and took the kings themselves captive. After crossing the Rhine and entering France, he ravaged the Bructeri and built a bridge at Cologne.

“You punished the very kings of France for their rashness, because they had violated the peace during the absence of your father. You did not hesitate to punish them with the most extreme tortures, fearing neither the perpetual hatred nor the inexpiable anger of that people.” Eumenius, *Panegyric to Constantine the Great*, chapter 10.

[Col. 0141C] “This is your daily and eternal victory, Constantine, in the execution of Ascaricus and Ragaisus.” The same author, chapter 11.

“Yet, so that the savagery of the barbarians might be broken in every way and the enemies might not mourn only the punishments inflicted upon their kings, you also brought devastation upon the Bructeri, unconquered emperor. In this your first purpose was that, having suddenly crossed with your army, you should attack them unawares—not because you distrusted open battle, since you preferred to meet them openly, but so that this nation, accustomed to frustrate war through the refuge of forests and marshes, might lose the opportunity for flight. Countless numbers were therefore slain and very many captured; all the livestock that was found was either captured or slaughtered; every village was consumed by fire. The adult males who fell into your hands—whose treachery was unsuited to military service and whose ferocity was unfit for slavery—were given over as a spectacle to punishments and exhausted the raging beasts by their numbers.” The same author, chapter 12.

“Moreover, by constructing the bridge at Cologne, you insult the remnants of the afflicted people, so that it may never lay aside its fear but always tremble and always stretch out suppliant hands. Yet you do this more for the glory of your empire and the adornment of the frontier than to make it possible for you to cross into enemy territory whenever you wish, since the entire Rhine is equipped with armed ships and soldiers are stationed along every bank as far as the Ocean.” The same author, chapter 13.

Constantine instituted Frankish games for that victory and celebrated it every year for six days, with at most twenty-four circus races.

“On the Ides: Frankish games.”

“On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, and on the sixteenth, fifteenth, fourteenth, and thirteenth: Frankish games, twenty-four races.”

The ancient Roman Calendar, in Bucherius’s commentary on Victor of Aquitaine.

[Col. 0142A] 307. Maximian made Constantine Augustus instead of Caesar and gave him his daughter Fausta in marriage.

308. The Franks disturb Gaul. Constantine sets out against them with a small force, at the urging of Herculius, who meanwhile resumes the purple and solicits the army to revolt. Constantine returns with admirable speed and crushes him.

The people of the Franks were under arms. Herculius persuades Constantine, who suspects nothing, not to take the whole army with him, saying that the barbarians could be defeated with a few soldiers. In this way Herculius himself would have an army that he could seize, while Constantine could be overwhelmed because of the small number of his troops. The young man trusts him as an experienced elder, obeys him as his father-in-law, and departs, leaving behind the greater part of the soldiers. Herculius, after waiting a few days, when he thought that Constantine had already entered the territory of the barbarians, suddenly assumed the purple, seized the treasury, gave gifts lavishly as was his custom, and fabricated accusations against Constantine that immediately recoiled upon himself. The emperor was quickly informed of what had happened. He flew back with the army at admirable speed; Herculius, caught by surprise and not yet adequately prepared, was overwhelmed, and the soldiers returned to their emperor. Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 29.

310. Constantine defeats the Franks, Alemanni, and other peoples of Germany.

“Why should I mention the Bructeri? Why the Chamavi? Why the Cherusci, the Vangiones, the Alemanni, and the Tubantes? Their names resound with war; the savagery of barbarism brings horror even through the words themselves. All these peoples, first separately and then armed together, had risen in a conspiracy of united alliance. Yet you, emperor, when you saw such a mass of war, feared nothing so much as that you might be feared. You approach the barbarians and, disguising your princely appearance, draw near as closely as you can with two companions . . . Innumerable peoples had been gathered together for war, but they were routed by your single attack while they were assembling their combined strength, and they afforded you a swift victory.” Nazarius, *Panegyric to Constantine the Great*, chapter 18.

[Col. 0142C] **313. Constantine, having defeated Maxentius, returns and routs the Franks in Gaul.**

For, not wearied by battles and sated with victories—as nature dictates—you gave yourself to leisure and rest, but with the same forcefulness with which you had returned to your Gaul, you proceeded to the lower frontier of Germany: after a great interval of time, indeed, but with only a short distance between places, immediately after your year-long campaign you began a new war from the Tiber to the Rhine. *Panegyricist uncertain, Panegyric on Constantine the Great*, chapter 21.

The fickle and unreliable tribe of the barbarians had broken faith, and it was being reported that, having selected leaders for an outbreak on the basis of strength and boldness, they had taken up positions on the Rhine. At once you were present to meet them, and your presence terrified them from daring to cross. You even seemed to have acted contrary to your own hopes, since, by forestalling their outbreak, you would have no occasion for victory; but, employing an unexpected plan, you withdrew, having simultaneously spread a fabricated report of a greater disturbance on the upper frontier. Thus you offered those foolish and bestial minds an opportunity to come into our territory, while leaving commanders in concealment to attack them when they were off their guard. When they came there, fortune followed your plan. Filling the entire channel of the Rhine with ships, you sailed across and ravaged their lands and their sad, mourning homes; you inflicted such slaughter and devastation upon that perjured people that scarcely will it retain a name after that disaster. *Ibid.*, chapter 22.

It is easy to conquer the timid and unwarlike, such as pleasant Greece and the luxuries of the East produce—men scarcely enduring a light cloak and protecting their silken folds from the sun by avoiding it, and, whenever they come into danger, forgetting their freedom and begging to be permitted to serve. But the Roman soldier, whom discipline orders to be whatever it makes him, or the savage FRANK, swollen only with the flesh of wild animals, who despises life because of the meanness of his food—how difficult is it to overcome or capture such men? Yet this you, Emperor, recently did both in Italy and, shortly before, in the very sight of the barbarian lands. *Ibid.*, chapter 24.

**Imperator Caesar, son of the divine Constantine, Flavius Constantinus Maximus, victorious and triumphant, pious, fortunate, unconquered Augustus, Germanicus, Sarmaticus, Francicus, Gothicus, Vandalicus.** From Onuphrius.

**320. Crispus Caesar defeats the Franks in Gaul.**

The FRANKS themselves, fiercer than the rest, fell beneath your arms in such a way that they could have been utterly destroyed, had you not, by the divine impulse by which you rule all things, preserved for completion those sons whom you yourself had struck down […] while they fought with the memory of the defeat they had suffered not broken but sharpened. Nazarius, *Panegyric on Constantine the Great*, chapter 17.

What joy flooded your gentle heart, greatest Constantine, when after so long an interval you were permitted to see your son—and to see victory as well? He certainly reported that the wars had been brought to an end, and did so to win his father’s favor, not to display himself: how gracious in receiving an enemy, how fierce toward one who resisted, how merciful toward one who pleaded. *Ibid.*, chapter 37.

[…] Greater is your glory throughout the lands,

Behold, Augustus, present among your own people and everywhere so great

In your commands; auspiciously, fertile Crispus, you now prepare

The untouched shores of Ocean, where the FRANKS have been uprooted;

Behold, a distant land gives them over, a land whose trackless spaces

Are wholly open across broad fields beneath the victorious boundary.  
P. Optatianus Porphyrius, *Panegyric*.

**325. Crispus Caesar was preparing to make war on the Franks.**

The Caesars granted peace its leisure, indulging their sons

With golden ages, in the honor of filial devotion to their homeland,

A merciful God by right. But Crispus’ strength, destined for brave deeds,

Prepares to guard the Rhine and Rhône on their farther banks,

And to impose grim laws upon the FRANKS.  
P. Optatianus Porphyrius, *Panegyric*.

**337. Constantine the Great dies on 22 May. His three sons, Caesars Constantine, Constantius, and Constans, become Augusti.**

Constantine holds Gaul.

**340. After Constantine is killed, Constans rules in Gaul.**

**341. Constans fights the Franks in Gaul.**

Constans fights against the FRANKS with varying success. St. Jerome, *Chronicle*.

[Col. 0143C] At the same time it also happened that the state was thrown into disorder. For the tribe of the FRANKS, having made an incursion into Gaul, devastated Roman lands. Socrates, *History*, book I, chapter 10.

**341. In the consulship of Marcellinus and Probinus, a battle was fought in Gaul between Constans Augustus and the tribe of the FRANKS.** Idatius.

**342. The Franks are defeated and pacified by Constans.**

The FRANKS were subdued by Constans, and peace was made with them. St. Jerome, *Chronicle*.

In the third consulship of Constantius and the second of Constans: at that time Constans, after overcoming the FRANKS in war, made them allies and confederates of the Roman people. Socrates, book I, chapter 13.

In the third consulship of Constantius and the second of Constans: in their consulship the FRANKS were defeated or pacified by Constans Augustus. Idatius.

**350. Magnentius, a Frank by birth, seizes the imperial power and kills Constans Augustus near the Pyrenees, at the fort of Helena, through the Frank Gaiso.**

**351. Magnentius is defeated in battle at Mursa by Constantius Augustus. Franks and Saxons are in Magnentius’ army.**

There were also present, under the name of kinship, the very eager allied FRANKS, and the Saxons, peoples living beyond the Rhine and the western sea, the most warlike nations of all. Julian, in his first oration, *In Praise of the Emperor Constantius*.

**353. Magnentius kills himself at Lyons; his brother Decentius Caesar hangs himself at Sens.**

**355. Silvanus, master of the infantry, seizes power at Cologne and is killed after twenty-eight days. A multitude of Franks is at the court of Constantius Augustus.**

While Gaul, through long neglect, endured bitter slaughter, plunder, and fires as the barbarians rampaged, with no one coming to its aid, Silvanus, commander of the infantry, was sent by order of the emperor to correct these conditions, as one effective for that task. Arbetio pressed for this to be expedited by every means available, so that he might place upon his absent rival—whose continued survival still distressed him—the burden of a dangerous enterprise. Ammianus describes more fully the plots contrived against Silvanus, and then continues:

Malarichus, commander of the gentiles, enraged by the injustice of the affair and joined by his colleagues, loudly protested, declaring that men devoted to the Empire ought not to be surrounded by factions and deceit. He asked that he himself, leaving his relatives behind as hostages while Mallobaudes, tribune of the arms, pledged that he would return, be ordered to go more swiftly and lead Silvanus; that he should attack a man who had attempted nothing of the sort that the most determined conspirators had provoked. Or, if Mallobaudes would make a comparable pledge on his behalf, he asked that Mallobaudes be permitted to hasten, promising to accomplish what he himself had undertaken. For he asserted that he knew beyond doubt that, if an outsider were sent, Silvanus—timid by his own nature and made still more fearful by nothing at all—might perhaps disrupt an arrangement. Although he offered useful and necessary advice, he was speaking to the winds in vain. For Arbetio, and so forth.

Malarichus, having suddenly obtained this opportunity, still disheveled and mournful, and grievously lamenting the plight both of himself and of his countryman Silvanus, called in the FRANKS, whose multitude at that time flourished in the palace, and now spoke more boldly. When the plot had been exposed and the deceit revealed by which, as was openly acknowledged, their safety was being pursued, he began to raise an uproar, and so forth.

Meanwhile Silvanus, acting at Cologne and learning through the constant reports of his men what Apodemi­us was doing to undermine his fortunes, and knowing the tender disposition of the fickle emperor, feared that, while absent and without trial, he might be condemned. Placed in the greatest difficulty, he was considering entrusting himself to barbarian loyalty. But Laniogaisus, then a tribune, objected and explained that the FRANKS, from whom the danger arose, would either kill him or betray him after receiving a reward. Judging nothing among those present to be safe, Silvanus was driven toward desperate counsels. Gradually he conferred more privately with the highest officers, and, having inflamed them with the magnitude of the promised reward, he rose to imperial power, temporarily taking a purple garment from the standards of the dragons and military banners, and so forth.

[Col. 0144C] The matter having thus been arranged through certain subordinate soldiers, who were suitable for carrying it out precisely because of the darkness and were inflamed by expectation of rewards, a sudden band of armed men burst forth at sunrise. As usually happens in uncertain affairs, when boldness prevails, they killed the guards, entered the palace, dragged Silvanus from the little chapel where he had fled in terror, and butchered him with repeated sword blows as he was making his way to a Christian assembly. Thus the commander, who had deserved no exile, met this kind of death: fearing the accusations by which, through the faction of wicked men, he had been ensnared while absent, he had advanced to the ultimate means of preserving his safety. Although Constantius had retained him in gratitude because of his timely betrayal with the armed forces before the battle of Mursa, Silvanus nevertheless feared him as uncertain and changeable, even though he could point to the brave deeds of his father Bonitus—Franks, indeed, but men who, on Constantine’s side, had often fought fiercely against the followers of Licinius in the civil war. Ammianus Marcellinus, book XV.

**355. The Franks plunder Cologne. Julian is made Caesar by Constantius Augustus and sent to Gaul.**

Julian reached Turin by the direct roads. There, when news was brought […] It reported that Cologne, a city of great renown in Lower Germany, had been seized after a stubborn barbarian siege by great force and destroyed. Ammianus, *History*, book XV.

**356. Julian recovers Cologne, captured by the Franks, and makes peace with their kings.**

Since no one resisted, he decided to go to recover Cologne, which had been destroyed before Caesar’s arrival in Gaul, and so forth […] Accordingly, having entered Cologne, he did not move away from there until, when the kings of the FRANKS had been terrified and their fury had abated, he secured a peace that would meanwhile benefit the state and recovered the extremely well-fortified city. Ammianus, *History*, book XVI.

Having found Gaul afflicted and crushed by these disasters, I first recovered Cologne, a city situated on the Rhine, which about ten months earlier had fallen into the power of the enemy. Julian, letter to the Athenian Council and People.

**357. Six hundred Franks are besieged by Julian in a fort of the Menapii and compelled to surrender.**

Severus, master of the cavalry, proceeding through Cologne and Jülich toward Rheims, encountered very strong bands of FRANKS—six hundred light-armed troops, as later became clear—ravaging places left without garrisons. This opportunity encouraged them to commit the crime, since, with Caesar occupied in the retreats of the Alamanni and no one preventing them, they thought they could satisfy themselves with abundant plunder. But now, fearing the return of the army, they occupied two fortifications that had formerly been emptied and defended themselves as far as possible. Julian, struck by the novelty of the situation and conjecturing what would happen if he passed them by unharmed, kept his troops and decided to surround them, and so forth […] Worn down by hunger, sleeplessness, and utter despair, they voluntarily surrendered themselves. They were immediately sent to the emperor’s court. When a multitude of FRANKS came out to rescue them from danger, and discovered that they had been captured and carried away, it dared nothing further and returned home. Having completed these operations, Caesar returned to Paris to spend the winter. Ammianus, *History*, book XVII.

**358. Julian makes war on the Salii and Chamavi and accepts into surrender that part of the Salii which had invaded Gaul.**

Having prepared these reinforcements, he attacked first of all the FRANKS, namely those whom custom has called SALIANS, who had once dared to establish dwellings for themselves boldly on Roman soil at a place called Toxiandria. When he had reached Tongeren, an embassy of the people mentioned above came to meet him, and so forth. Suddenly attacking them all, he struck them as a whirlwind of lightning. Since they were now praying rather than resisting, victory turned them toward the proper sphere of mercy, and he received them in surrender together with their possessions and children. Ammianus, *History*, book XVII.

Moreover, moving an army against those barbarians—that is, the FRANKS, SALIANS, and CHAMAVI—with the gods favoring me, I received part of the SALIANS and expelled the Chamavi, and so forth. Julian, letter to the Athenian Council and People.

Julian kills some of the Chamavi and captures others alive, binding them in chains together with their king Nebiogastes. He makes peace after returning to him his captured son and taking only the king’s mother as a hostage.

He attacked the CHAMAVI as well, who had dared similar acts; with the same speed he killed some, while others, who resisted fiercely but were captured alive, he bound in chains, and so forth. When their ambassadors had prostrated themselves on the ground before him, he granted peace on these terms: that they should return unharmed to their own country. Ammianus, *History*, book XVII.

When Julian had broken into hostile territory and the CHAMAVI begged him to spare their people as his own, he agreed and ordered their king to come to him. When he came, and so forth, they supposed […] He therefore made peace and asked only for Nebiogastes’ mother; the barbarians, approving the treaty, immediately gave her to him together with the same king’s son, who had been captured in battle. These matters completed, with autumn drawing to an end and winter beginning—for it was already cold—he departed. From excerpts of Eunapius of Sardis, *On Embassies*.

**360. Julian Caesar is proclaimed Augustus at Paris. After crossing the Rhine, he invades the territory of the Frankish Attuarii, routs them, and, when they beg for peace, grants it on his own terms.**

Julian […] went out to the frontier of Lower Germany […] Then, having crossed the Rhine, he suddenly invaded the territory of the FRANKS whom they call ATTUARII, restless men who were still roaming too freely through the outermost parts of Gaul. Attacking them suddenly while they feared no hostile action, he defeated them with little difficulty. After many had been captured and killed, he granted peace on his own terms to the others who survived and begged for it. Ammianus, *History*, book XX.

**A Frank from the court of Constantius Augustus is freed from a demon through St. Hilarion.**

A certain candidate of the emperor Constantius, with red hair and a complexion indicating his province—for among the Saxons and Alemanni his people are not so extensive as they are powerful, and among historians the region is called Germany but is now called FRANCIA—had been possessed by a demon from ancient times, that is, from childhood. The demon forced him to howl at night, groan, and gnash his teeth. In secret he asked the emperor for leave to travel, simply explaining the reason. Having also received letters to the governor of Palestine, he was escorted to Gaza with great honor and a retinue, and so forth.

At that time the old man was walking on the soft sands and murmuring something to himself from the Psalms. Seeing such a great crowd approaching, he stopped, returned everyone’s greeting, and blessed them with his hand. After an hour he ordered the others to leave but instructed that the man remain with his servants and attendants. From his eyes and expression he recognized why he had come. At once the man was suspended for questioning, scarcely touching the ground with his feet and roaring horribly, and answered in the Syrian language in which he had been questioned. You could see words of pure Syriac resounding from the mouth of a barbarian who knew only the FRANKISH and Latin languages, so that no rasping sound, aspiration, or idiom of Palestinian speech was absent. He therefore confessed the manner in which the demon had entered him. Since his interpreters understood only Greek and Latin, Hilarion also questioned him in Greek so that they might understand. The man likewise answered in the same words and produced many pretexts for enchantments and necessities of magical arts. “I do not care,” he said, “how you entered, but I command you, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, to come out.” When he had been cured, he offered ten pounds of gold in rustic simplicity and received from Hilarion barley bread, hearing that those who were nourished by such food regarded gold as dirt. St. Jerome, *Life of St. Hilarion*.

**363. Julian dies. Jovian Augustus.**

**364. The Frank Malarichus refuses to accept the command of the army in Gaul.** From Ammianus, *History*, book XXV.

Jovian Augustus dies. Valentinian becomes Augustus; a few days later he creates his brother Valens Augustus and entrusts him with the empire of the East.

**366. The Frank Charietto, while fighting as commander in both Germanies against the Alamanni, is killed.** From Ammianus, *History*, book XVII.

**367. Gratian Augustus.**

**368. Franks and Saxons ravage Gaul.**

The FRANKS and Saxons, who bordered on the Gallic territories, violated them with bitter plunder, fires, and the deaths of captives, wherever each was able to break through by land or sea. Ammianus, *History*, book XXVII.

Emperor Caesar Flavius Valentinianus […] greatest Germanicus, greatest Alamannicus, greatest FRANCICUS, greatest Gothicus, holding tribunician power for the seventh time, emperor for the sixth time, consul for the second time. Onuphrius.

**369. Peace between the Romans and the Franks.**

**370. The Saxons are defeated by the Romans in Frankish territory; the Franks offer no assistance because of their peace with the Romans.**

The Saxons were slaughtered at Uson, in the territory of the Franks. St. Jerome, *Chronicle*, 377.

[Col. 0146D] Valentinian crushed the Saxons, and so forth, within the very territory of the FRANKS. Orosius, book VII, chapter 32.

**374. Macrianus is killed by the king of the Franks.**

Macrianus, king of the Alamanni, perished in FRANCIA. While he was greedily breaking through it and devastating it with wholesale slaughter, he was surrounded and killed by the stratagems of the warlike king Mellobaudes. Ammianus, *History*, book 30.

**375. Valentinian Augustus dies. Valentinian the Younger becomes Augustus; Gratian Augustus gives him Italy and Africa while retaining Gaul for himself.**

**377. Gratian Augustus. The Frank Merobaudes is consul. Richomeres, commander of the household troops, is sent by Gratian into Thrace against the Goths.**

Richomeres, the FRANK, commander of the household troops, was joined to Profuturus, and so forth. With stubborn contest the two sides, not yet wearied, afflicted each other on equal terms; neither relaxed his native firmness, while the vigor of their spirits was aroused by their ardor. The day, yielding to evening, brought the savage, deadly struggles to an end […] after which Richomeres returned to Gaul, in order to bring reinforcements from there for the greater tumult of battle that was expected. Ammianus, *History*, book XXXI, chapters 7–8.

**378. Gratian, through Mellobaudes, king of the Franks and commander of the household troops, defeats the Lentienses.**

The Lentienses, a people of the Alamanni, […] having gathered the peoples of all their districts into one body, boldly attacked us in their pride with forty thousand armed men—or seventy thousand, as some vaunted in exaggerating the emperor’s praise. Gratian, and so forth, entrusted the task to Nannienus, a commander of sober courage, and joined Mallobaudes to him as a colleague of equal authority, commander of the household troops and king of the Franks, a warlike and brave man. Nannienus, weighing the changeable fortunes of war and therefore judging that they ought to delay, was troubled, while Mallobaudes, seized by a great desire for battle, was impatient of postponement and, as was his custom, was eager to go against the enemy. Accordingly, when the terrible clash of opposing cries had first inspired fear, battle began near Argentaria at the signal given by the trumpeters […] no more than five thousand, it was estimated, escaped; among many other brave and daring men, King Priarius too was killed, the instigator of destructive wars, and so forth.

Gratian, having turned there with his army, sought the paths leading to the heights with the same courage as before. The Lentienses, seeing him intent upon their destruction with every determination to persevere, obtained a surrender through humble entreaty. After offering, as ordered, their vigorous young men to be mingled with our recruits, they were permitted to return unharmed to their native lands. Ammianus, *History*, book XXXI, chapter 10.

Valens Augustus is burned alive by the barbarians while fighting the Goths.

**379. Bauto and Arbogastes, Franks, are sent by Gratian Augustus with forces to Theodosius in Macedonia and Thessaly against the barbarians.**

But Gratian, greatly disturbed by the report of these events, sent away a fairly large force entrusted to the commander Baudonius. He also sent Arbogastes with him. Both were FRANKS by birth, extremely well disposed toward the Romans, entirely free from greed and the pursuit of gifts, and equally distinguished in military matters for intelligence and strength. After they had reached Macedonia and Thessaly with the army, the Scythians who were conducting affairs there, and so forth, sent to the emperor Theodosius, promising goodwill and alliance and that they would do whatever he commanded. Zosimus, *History*, book IV.

Theodosius is made Augustus by Gratian Augustus.

**382. Priam reigns in FRANCIA.** Prosper’s *Pithaean Chronicle*.

**383. Merobaudes II and Saturninus are consuls. Maximus seizes the imperial power. He captures Gratian by deceit at Lyons and kills him through the commander Andragathius.**

**384. Richomeres the Frank and Clearchus are consuls.**

**385. Arcadius Augustus. Bauto the Frank is consul.**

When I came to Milan before the consul Bauto, and on the Kalends of January recited a panegyric to that consul, before such a great gathering and in the sight of so many people, in accordance with my profession as a rhetorician at that time. St. Augustine, *Against the Letters of the Priscillianists*, book III, chapter 30.

**388. After Maximus is defeated and killed at Aquileia, the Franks and Saxons who had served Maximus in the naval forces join the victors.**

That man, Maximus, was immediately defeated by the FRANKS and the Saxon people in Sicily, at Siscia, at Poetovio, and everywhere throughout the world. St. Ambrose, Letter 40 to Theodosius.

Victor, the son of Maximus, is removed from power and killed by Arbogastes.

Genobaldus, Marcomeres, and Sunno invade Gaul. Nannius and Quintinus, commanders of the army, lead an army against them. Quintinus enters FRANCIA and suffers a great defeat.

At that time, under the commanders Genobaldus, Marcomeres, and Sunno, the FRANKS broke into Germany, and so forth. When their ranks had consequently been thrown into confusion, the legions were slaughtered, Heraclius, tribune of the Jovinians, and nearly all who commanded the soldiers were killed; night and the hiding places of the forests gave a safe escape to the few survivors. Sulpicius Alexander, book III of the *Histories*. Read the complete passage in Gregory of Tours, book III of the *History*, chapter 8, column 57.

**380. The Franks harass Gaul. Arbogastes incites the Romans against them. Valentinian makes peace with them.**

At that time Charietto and Syrus, appointed in place of Nannienus, were staying in Germany with an army deployed against the FRANKS, and so forth. Sulpicius Alexander, book IV of the *History*, in Gregory of Tours, book II, column 59.

**392. Valentinian Augustus is killed at Vienne. Arbogastes raises Eugenius to the imperial power.**

While various events were taking place in the East through the Thracians, the condition of the state was disturbed in Gaul, and the emperor Valentinian was shut up in the palace at Vienne, and so forth. Sulpicius Alexander, in Gregory, book II of the *History*, column 59.

Arbogastes, descended from the tribe of the FRANKS, whom the emperor Gratian had ordered to hold the position second to the commander Bauto, after Bauto had departed this life, relying on his own ability, transferred the command of the army to himself without imperial authorization, and so forth. At last Valentinian […] handed him a document removing him from office. After reading it, Arbogastes said: “You gave me no power, and you will not be able to take it away.” Having spoken these words, he tore up the document, threw it on the ground, and departed, and so forth. Therefore Arbogastes attacked the emperor, who was staying at Vienne in Gaul, mortally wounded him, and killed him. Although all bore the crime in silence because of the man’s dignity and military courage, and also because the soldiers were devoted to him with great affection, since he despised money, they proclaimed Eugenius emperor, and so forth. Zosimus, book IV of the *History*.

**Arbogastes makes war on the Franks and later makes peace with them.**

In the same year Arbogastes pursued Sunno and Marcomeres, subordinate kings of the FRANKS, with the hatred proper to kinsmen, and so forth. Sulpicius Alexander, in Gregory, book II of the *History*, column 60.

At about the same time the commander Arbogastes prepared for war against his own people, that is, the FRANKS, and in battle killed a considerable multitude with his own hand; with the survivors, however, he made peace. But when, at a banquet, he was asked by the kings of his people whether he knew Ambrose, and had replied that he knew the man, that Ambrose loved him, and that he was accustomed to dine frequently with him, he heard this answer: “That is why you conquer everyone: because you are loved by that man who says to the sun, ‘Stand,’ and it stands.” Paulinus, *Life of St. Ambrose*.

**393. Franks in the army of Eugenius.**

Then the tyrant Eugenius, having undertaken the preparations for a campaign, made for the Rhine frontier, in order, according to custom, to renew ancient treaties with the kings of the Alamanni and FRANKS and display to the savage peoples the enormous army of that time. Sulpicius Alexander, in Gregory of Tours, book II of the *History*, column 60.

[Col. 0148D] **394. Theodosius Augustus defeats and kills Eugenius. Arbogastes kills himself.**

Theodosius’ victory has always depended upon the power of God, not human confidence. This Arbogastes is the clearest proof of both points: he […] having gathered the forces of Gauls and FRANKS, he poured forth, relying also upon the special worship of idols, yet he succumbed with great ease. Eugenius and Arbogastes had drawn up their battle lines across the plains, and so forth. But Theodosius, stationed on the highest Alps, without food or sleep […] with his body spread upon the ground and his mind fixed upon heaven, prayed. Then, after passing the sleepless night in continuous prayer, and so forth, he alone seized his weapons. Knowing that he was to be protected by the sign of the cross and also to gain victory, he fortified himself with the sign of the cross and gave the signal of victory—or, by the sign of the cross, gave the signal for battle—and entered the war, certain that he would be victorious even if no one followed him, and so forth. Eugenius was captured and killed. Arbogastes struck himself with his own hand. Thus here too the civil war was extinguished by the blood of two men. Orosius, *History*, book VII.

[…] It did not benefit the enemy Cauto

To cling to fortified positions. The hope of the rampart collapsed,

And the barriers lay open when the rocks were torn away, and so forth.

But the savage inventor of crimes had pierced his deep

Side with more than one sword; a double blade grew warm,

And at last the avenging hand turned its anger

Against him. Claudian, *Panegyric on the Third Consulship of Honorius Augustus*.

**395. Theodosius Augustus dies at Milan. Arcadius rules the East, Honorius the West; through Stilicho, Honorius makes peace with the Franks.**

Yet above all you order him to calm the savage peoples

And pacify the Rhine. He flies, borne on swift horses […]

You would see the kings, struck with terror, bowing their necks.

Before our commander the Sicambri scattered their blond hair,

And the FRANKS, praying in fearful murmurs,

Lay prostrate upon the ground. Though Honorius is absent,

An oath is sworn in his name, and Alemannia

Humbly implores your name.

The fierce Bastarnae came; the inhabitant of the forest,

The Bructerus of Hercynia, came; the Cimbrian emerged
