From his broad marshes, and the Cherusci left the mighty Elbe.

He receives their various prayers and, though asked only slowly,

Gives his assent, granting peace as a great gift, and so forth.

This journey of Stilicho is your achievement. Claudian, *Panegyric on the Fourth Consulship of Honorius Augustus*.

We marvel that the enemy falls in rapid wars,

When they collapse through terror alone. We brought no trumpets

Against the FRANKS; nevertheless they lay prostrate, and so forth.  
The same author, book I, *On the Praises of Stilicho*.

Arcadius married Eudoxia, daughter of the Frank Bauto or Baudo.

Eudoxia was conspicuous for exceptional beauty and was being raised in the household of Promotus’ son. Zosimus, book V of the *History*.

Eudoxia was not made according to the illegitimate nature of her husband; rather, she possessed no small share of barbarian nature. Philostorgius, book II of *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 6.

[Col. 0149C] **397. The Frankish kings Marcomer and Sunno are punished.**

[…] The province will expel the rods

More quickly than FRANCIA will expel the kings

Whom you have given it; no longer is it permitted

To strike rebels in battle, but to punish them in chains.

Under our judge, the Roman prison investigates royal crimes.

Marcomeres and Sunno teach this lesson: one of them endured

Exile in Etruria, while the other, promising

To avenge the exile, fell beneath the sword of his own people—

Brothers eager to stir up new troubles,

Furious with hatred of peace and, by nature,

Desiring crimes. Claudian, book I, *On the Praises of Stilicho*.

**399. The Roman Empire was feared by the barbarians.**

[…] At that time, handsome in appearance,

When Stilicho’s son-in-law gave answers to the Germans

Who voluntarily begged for peace, and to the Cauci, and so forth.

I delight in seeing the humble FRANK and sorrowful Sueve at my feet,

And, Germanicus, our Rhine. Claudian, *Against Eutropius*, book I, verses 377 ff.

The same author, book II, *On the Praises of Stilicho*, introduces Gaul complaining that Stilicho, victor over the Franks, refuses the consulship.

He alone subdued the Germans and the FRANKS for me;

Why is he not yet read in the official lists? Claudian, book II, *On the Praises of Stilicho*.

**400. Flavius Stilicho and Aurelian are consuls.**

**406. On the last day of December, after the Vandals have crushed the Franks, they cross the Rhine and invade Gaul.**

Two years—or three years—before the Roman invasion, the peoples stirred up by Stilicho, the Alans, as I have said, the Sueves, the Vandals, and many other tribes with them, crush the FRANKS, cross the Rhine, and invade Gaul. Orosius, book VII, chapter 40.

Salvianus describes the vices and customs of the Franks and other peoples in book IV of *On Providence*, chapter 14, and in book VII, chapter 15.

**407. In Britain, Constantine is acclaimed emperor; he crosses into Gaul and places Justinianus and Neviggastes the Frank in command of Celtic armies.**

A fierce battle takes place between Constantine and the barbarians devastating Gaul; the Romans gain the victory. Zosimus, *History*, book VI.

**408. The Franks defeat the Vandals.**

Meanwhile Respendial, king of the Alans, and so forth. Frigeridus, book II, chapter 9, in Gregory of Tours, column 61.

Arcadius dies at the age of thirty-one. Theodosius, his son, is Augustus. Sarus is sent by Stilicho against Constantine; he defeats and kills Justinianus and, after violating his oath, kills Neviggastes. Edobinchus the Frank and Gerontius are appointed in their place by Constantine; they compel Sarus to flee to Italy. At the same time Sarus, Stilicho, and so forth. Zosimus, book VI of the *History*.

**409. Honorius admits Constantine into partnership in the empire. Vandals, Alans, and Sueves occupy Spain. The city of Trier is plundered by the Franks.**

The city of Trier was plundered and burned by the FRANKS in a second incursion. Frigeridus, book II, chapter 9, in Gregory of Tours, column 62.

**410. Rome is captured by Alaric.**

Franks in the army of Constans, son of Constantine.

After Edobeccus had been sent ahead to the Germanic peoples, Constans and the prefect Decimius Rusticus, who had already been master of the offices, went to Gaul with the FRANKS, Alamanni, and the entire body of troops, intending to return immediately to Constantine. Frigeridus, book II, chapter 9, in Gregory of Tours, column 62.

Gaiso the Frank, count of the sacred largesses of Honorius Augustus, then master of the offices and afterward master of the army. Books VII and IX of the Theodosian Code.

**411. Count Constantius is sent against Constantine and besieges Arles.**

Edobichus, the Frank, master of the army under Constantine, came to his aid with enormous forces; he was defeated by Constantius and killed by his treacherous friend Edicius. Meanwhile the army of Honorius was surrounding Arles, and so forth. Sozomen, book IX, chapter 14.

Jovinus, master of the Roman army in Gaul, assumes the purple. Franks in his army.

The fourth month of Constantine’s siege had scarcely begun when suddenly messengers arrived from farther Gaul announcing that Jovinus had assumed the imperial insignia and, with the Burgundians, Alamanni, FRANKS, Alans, and the whole army, was threatening the besiegers. Advancing with such speed, he forced Constantine to surrender after the city had been opened. Frigeridus, in Gregory of Tours, book II, chapter 9, column 61.

Constantine is handed over alive by the people of Arles to Constantius and killed by order of Honorius Augustus.

**412. The tyrants Jovinus and Sebastianus, brothers, are killed in Gaul.**

Apollinaris, grandfather of Sidonius Apollinaris, was prefect of the praetorium of Gaul. Sidonius Apollinaris, book III, letter 12.

**413. Trier is plundered by the Franks.**

[Col. 0150D] The chief city of the Gauls was destroyed through three successive devastations. Salvianus, book VI, chapter 15.

**414. At the same time Count Castinus of the household troops is sent to Gaul on an expedition undertaken against the Franks.** Frigeridus, in Gregory of Tours, book II, chapter 9, column 62.

**415.**

For in the consular records we also read that Theodomer, king of the FRANKS, son of Richimer, formerly [king], and his mother Ascyla were killed by the sword. Frigeridus, ibid., in Gregory of Tours.

Trier is destroyed by the Franks.

The subject is not being treated as the most excellent city of Trier, but because it has been overthrown by four devastations. Salvianus, book VI, chapter 8.

Finally, the wealthiest city of the Gauls was stormed four times. *Ibid.*, chapter 13.

Since three destructions had not corrected you, you deserved to perish at the fourth. *Ibid.*, chapter 15.

[Col. 0151A] **416. The Franks occupy the part of Gaul nearest the Rhine. See below under the year 428.**

**420. Constantius is made Augustus by Honorius Augustus.**

Pharamund reigns in FRANCIA. Prosper’s *Pithaean Chronicle*.

**421. Constantius Augustus dies in the seventh month of his reign.**

**423. Joannes seizes the Western Empire.**

**424. Valentinian, son of Constantius Augustus, is made Caesar by Honorius Augustus and sent to the West against the tyrant Joannes.**

**425. The tyrant Joannes is captured and killed. Valentinian is proclaimed Augustus by Theodosius Augustus.**

**428. Chlodio, king of the Franks.**

In the consulship of Felix and Taurus: the part of Gaul near the Rhine which the FRANKS had occupied for possession was recovered by the arms of the commander Aetius. Prosper’s *Chronicle*, attached to Jerome’s *Chronicle*.

**431. 8. Theodosius Augustus, son of Arcadius Augustus. The FRANKS are defeated by Aetius in battle and received into peace.** Idatius, *Chronicle*.

[Col. 0151B] **437. Chlodio, king of the Franks, sends scouts ahead, crosses the Rhine, routs the Romans, captures Cambrai, and occupies all the places as far as the River Somme.** Gregory of Tours, book II, chapter 9, column 63.

**445. Battle between Chlodio, king of the Franks, and Aetius and Majorian, Roman commanders.**

[…] After a short time

You fought together, where the FRANK Cloio had overrun

The broad lands of Arras, and so forth. Sidonius, *Panegyric on Majorian Augustus*.

**Description of the Franks from Sidonius, in the same work.**

Here too he subdues monsters whose red hair, drawn from the crown

Of the head toward the forehead, lies there, while the bared neck

Shines through its loss of bristles. Then, beneath pale blue eyes,

The watery gaze gleams white; and on faces shaven everywhere,

Instead of a beard, thin crests are drawn by the comb.

Closely stitched garments restrain the men’s tall limbs;

In them the knee is exposed beneath the raised covering,

And a broad belt hangs across the narrow waist.

To hurl swift double axes through the vast empty air,

To anticipate the place of the blow, to whirl shields—

This is their sport—and to leap ahead of their twisted spears,
And had earlier come against the enemy. From childhood years

There is a mature love of war. If perchance they are pressed,

Whether by numbers or by the advantage of position, death overwhelms them;

They remain steadfast, fearless, and survive in spirit,

Already almost beyond life.

448. The death of Chlodio; dissension among his children concerning the kingdom. Whether Meroveus was his son and successor is uncertain.

But the death of their king supplied Attila with an opportunity to harass the Franks in war, and the dissension that arose among his children over the kingdom. The elder of them had decided to call Attila to his aid, the younger Aetius. We saw the latter while he was carrying out an embassy at Rome, still beardless: his blond hair was so long that it flowed around his shoulders. Aetius, who had adopted him as his son and had honored him with many gifts, both from himself and from the emperor, sent him away, calling him a friend and ally of the Roman people. From the history of Priscus the rhetorician and sophist.

449. Apollinaris, the father of Sidonius, praetorian prefect of the Gauls.

451. Attila, king of the Huns, invades Gaul; the Franks are in his army. He is defeated by Aetius; Meroveus, king of the Franks, took the Roman side. Gregory of Tours, *History*, book II, chapter 7, column 55.

. . . . Suddenly, when, amid the uproar,

The barbarian world had poured all its forces into you,

Gaul, with the warlike Rugian accompanied by the Gelonian,

The savage Gepid followed, while the Burgundian drove on the Scirian;

The Hun, the Bellonotus, the Neurus, the Bastarna,

The Thuringian, the Bructerian, whom even the Nicer washes

With its wolf-haunted wave—

The Frank bursts forth; the Hercynian forest, felled swiftly by the double-headed axe,

Fell into boats, and the alder formed a bridge across the Rhine.

And now Attila had spread himself with his terrifying hordes

Across your fields, Belgic Gaul. Sidonius, *Panegyric on Avitus Augustus*.

[Col. 0152A] For the Franks were auxiliaries to these Romans. Jordanes, *On the Deeds of the Goths*, chapter 36.

In this most famous battle . . . the Franks fought on the Roman side, and the Gepids on the side of the Huns. The same author, chapter 41.

454. Aetius is killed by Valentinian Augustus.

455. Valentinian Augustus is killed at the instigation of Maximus, who seizes the empire. The Franks ravage Gaul, and so forth. Maximus appoints Avitus master of the soldiers in Gaul; the barbarians flee from fear of him.

The Frank was laying low first the German and then the Belgian,

And so forth.

As soon as he assumed the burden of the honor conferred,

You would say that the Alamannian was asking pardon for his madness, and so forth. Sidonius, *Panegyric on Avitus Augustus*.

Maximus, torn to pieces by his own men and thrown into the Tiber on the seventy-seventh day of his reign. Rome is captured by Genseric. Avitus Augustus.

FROM SAINT GREGORY OF TOURS.

[Col. 0152B] YEAR 458. Childeric, king of the Franks, succeeds his father Meroveus, column 63. Aegidius becomes master of the Roman soldiers in Gaul; when Childeric is expelled by the Franks because of his debauchery, Aegidius is appointed in his place, 66.

464. The Franks recall Childeric and expel Aegidius, 66.

477 to 481. Childeric fights at Orleans; Adovacrius comes to Angers, 70. Paulus, master of the Roman soldiers, fights against the Goths; after Paulus is killed, Childeric takes Angers, 70. The islands of the Saxons are captured by the Franks, 71. Childeric, joined with Adovacrius, subdues the Alamanni, 71.

481. Clovis succeeds his father Childeric after his death.

486. Clovis marches against Syagrius, the son of Aegidius, and routs him; after he has been demanded back from Alaric, he kills him, 78.

487. At the Campus Martius Clovis kills a Frank who, in the preceding year, had refused him a vessel belonging to the church of Rheims, 79, 556.

[Col. 0152C] 491. Clovis’s expedition against the Thuringians, whom he subjects to his rule, 79.

493. Clovis takes Clotilde as his wife, 80.

496. Having invoked the name of Christ, Clovis defeats the Alamanni, after killing their king, 82. Remigius instructs Clovis, learned in the faith, and baptizes him; balsams are poured out, the church is sprinkled with divine fragrance, and those standing by are granted such grace that they thought themselves placed amid the fragrances of paradise, 83. More than three thousand Franks and Clovis’s sister are baptized, 84.

497. Albofledis, Clovis’s sister, dies. On this matter Saint Remigius consoles Clovis by letter, 84, 1326.

498–499. Godegisel, king of the Burgundians, conspires against his brother Gundobad, the other king of the same people; joining himself to Clovis, he drives Gundobad away, 85–86 and following.

500. After killing Godegisel and expelling the Franks from Vienne, Gundobad asserts his sole rule over Burgundy, and establishes laws, in the same place.

[Col. 0152D] 502. Clovis subdues the cities of Armorican Brittany, 144.

503. A conference between Clovis and Alaric, king of the Visigoths, near Amboise, 90, 91.

507. Having defeated the Visigoths in battle near Poitiers and killed their king Alaric, Clovis extends the Frankish kingdom as far as the Pyrenees, 92–95.

508. After spending the winter at Bordeaux, Clovis subjects Angoulême and Toulouse to himself. Having received the insignia of the consulship at Tours in the basilica of Saint Martin, he is called Augustus; then he establishes the seat of his kingdom at Paris, 95.

509. Sigibert, king of the Franks at Cologne, is killed by his son Chloderic, who is himself also killed; Clovis adds Cologne and the neighboring regions to his dominion, 96, 97.

After Chararic, a Frankish petty king, and his son are killed, Clovis takes possession of their kingdom, 97.

510. Ragnachar, king of the Franks at Cambrai, is killed by Clovis together with his brother Richar; Clovis occupies their kingdom, 98, 99. Rignomer at Le Mans is ordered to be killed by Clovis, 99. The Namnetes, besieged by Chillo, commander of Clovis’s army, are miraculously freed, 791.

[Col. 0153A] 511. After defeating the neighboring kings and killing his own relatives, Clovis, monarch of the Franks, dies at Paris on the fifth day before the Kalends of December and is buried in the basilica of the Apostles, 100. The Frankish kingdom is divided into a tetrarchy among Clovis’s four sons: Theodoric has his seat at Rheims, Chlodomer at Orléans, Childebert at Paris, and Chlotar at Soissons, 105.

516. Chochilaicus, king of the Danes, enters Gaul; he pays for this crime with his death and the destruction of his men, who are defeated in a naval battle, 106. Hermenefrid, after killing his brothers, rules alone in Thuringia, having deceived Theodoric, whom he had summoned to his aid, 106, 107.

Sigismund obtains the kingdom of Burgundy after the death of his father Gundobad, 107.

522. Theodoric takes Sigismund’s daughter as his wife, [Col. 0153B] 108.

523. At Clotilde’s instigation, the Franks take up arms against the Burgundians, 108. After Godomar has been driven away, his brother Sigismund is led away captive with his wife and children by Chlodomer, 109.

524. Godomar, having recovered his strength, regains the kingdom of the Burgundians. As Chlodomer is preparing to march against him, he kills Sigismund with his wife and children, 109. Chlodomer is killed in battle, and the kingdom of the Burgundians is destroyed by the Franks. Godomar regains the kingdom once more, 110.

525. Chlotar and Childebert undertake an expedition into Burgundy. Theodoric, refusing to go there, ravages the Auvergne, 114, 1161, 1166.

526. Childebert and Chlotar kill Theodebald and Chlotar, their nephews by their brother Chlodomer; Chlodoald is rescued by brave men, 123.

528. Theodoric prepares an expedition against Hermenefrid, king of the Thuringians, 110.

[Col. 0153C] 529. The Thuringians are defeated by the Franks. Chlotar brings Radegund back from there as a captive, 112.

530. Childebert, while his brother is occupied in Thuringia, attempts unsuccessfully to seize the Auvergne, 113. Theodoric kills Hermenefrid by treachery and occupies the kingdom of the Thuringians, 112. Munderic, a rebel against Theodoric, is suppressed, 117.

531. Childebert attacks the Visigoths to avenge the wrongs done to his sister Clotilde. After killing Amalaric, he returns to Frankish territory laden with spoils, together with his sister, 114.

533. An expedition of the Franks against the Visigoths, 127.

534. Theodebert succeeds his father Theodoric after his death, 128.

537. Childebert and Theodebert undertake an expedition against Chlotar; but that civil conflict was miraculously restrained by Clotilde’s prayers at the tomb of Saint Martin, 129.

539. Theodebert’s expedition into Italy. He leaves Buccellinus there as commander of the army; after defeating Belisarius and then Narses, Buccellinus occupies a large part of Italy, 133, 134.

[Col. 0153D] 542. Childebert and Chlotar undertake an expedition into Spain against the Visigoths. Zaragoza, besieged by them, is relieved through the prayers of Saint Vincent, 130, 131.

544. Gregory of Tours is born on the feast of Saint Andrew, 1264, about 545. Queen Clotilde departs to the heavenly realms and is buried by her sons in the basilica of the Apostles, 141.

546. The groin plague, which is checked in various places through the intercession of the saints, 144, 959, 1174, and so forth.

548. Theodebald succeeds his father Theodebert, 138.

553. After Theia is killed, the Gothic kingdom in Italy comes to an end. Around this time Chanao, count of the Bretons, kills his brothers, 143.

555. Chlotar occupies the kingdom of the deceased Theodebald, 148. Chramn, sent by his father Chlotar into the Auvergne, behaves very badly there, 151, 797. Chlotar suppresses the rebellious Saxons and devastates Thuringia because of the assistance it had provided them, 148. After Buccellinus, commander of the Franks in Italy, is killed and his army destroyed, Narses drives the Franks out of Italy, 567.

556. Forced by his own men to fight against the Saxons, Chlotar is unsuccessful, 154. Chramn rebels against his father and joins Childebert, and so forth, 155 and following.

557. The Saxons burst into Frankish territory; Chlotar undertakes a third expedition against them. Childebert ravages the Champagne of Rheims, 158.

558. Childebert dies and is buried in the basilica of Saint Vincent, which he had built. Chlotar obtains sole rule, 160.

559. Chramn, brought before his father, escapes and flees to Brittany, 160.

560. Chlotar undertakes an expedition against Chramn and the Bretons; he orders him to be killed together with his wife and children, 161, 162. He visits the tomb of Saint Martin, 285. He orders its basilica, burned by Wilichar, to be restored, 160.

561. Chlotar dies and is buried in the basilica of Saint Medard, 162. The kingdom is divided among Chlotar’s four sons: Charibert has Paris as his seat, Guntram Orléans, Chilperic Soissons, and Sigibert Rheims, 162, 163.

562. Charibert receives Gundovald, who claimed to be the son of Chlotar. Sigibert has him tonsured and forces him into exile; he takes refuge with Narses in Italy, receives a wife, and departs for Constantinople, 163. Charibert, devoted to vices, 1026. Sigibert routs the Huns who burst into Gaul and later makes a treaty with them, 163.

564. While Sigibert is occupied against the Huns, Chilperic invades Rheims and other cities. From this arose civil war. Chilperic is driven away; Sigibert recovers what he had lost, and so forth, 163.

564. Synod of Saintes, 165.

565. Peace is restored between Sigibert and Chilperic, 163. Guntram takes Austrigild as his wife, 164.

566. Sigibert takes Brunhild as his wife, 168. Sigibert’s second expedition against the Huns, 169. When war breaks out between Sigibert and Guntram, Arles is besieged by Sigibert, 169 and following.

567. Sigibert sends an embassy to Justin, the successor of Justinian, 180. Council of Lyon, at which Salonius and Sagittarius are deposed, 232. Chilperic takes Galswintha as his wife and later kills her, 168. Charibert dies, 167, 908. Civil war and a new division of the Frankish kingdom follow, 187, 574.

569. Alboin migrates into Italy with the Lombards, 182.

571. Portents and a great plague, 172. The Lombards burst into Gaul; after the patrician Amatus is driven away and killed, they are subsequently utterly destroyed by Mummolus, 183.

572. The Saxons, bursting from Italy into Gaul, are routed by Mummolus, 183, 573.

573. The Saxons return to their homeland with Sigibert’s permission, 184. Gregory is consecrated at Rheims by Aegidius and, while sick, is healed through the merits of Saint Martin, 1038. Fourth Council of Paris, to settle the dispute between Guntram—or Chilperic—and Sigibert, 190. Bishop Pappolus of Chartres presented the fathers of the synod with a petition against Aegidius of Rheims, who had ordained the bishop of Dourdan, 343.

574. After Cleph’s death, the Lombards again invade Gaul but are slaughtered to the point of annihilation, 186, 574. Civil war between Chilperic and Sigibert grows fierce, 190 and following, 802. Peace is somehow made, 1043.

575. After almost driving his brother Chilperic from the kingdom and winning Guntram over to himself, Sigibert is killed, 195. Childebert II, rescued from Chilperic’s hands, succeeds his father, 201. The people of Tours are harassed by Ruccolen, count of Le Mans, 1056.

576. Brunhild, the widow of Sigibert, marries Meroveus, the son of Chilperic, 201. From this arise serious disputes between father and son, 215 and following. Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, departs to heaven, 211.

577. Guntram, deprived of his sons, adopts Childebert, 221. Council of Paris against Praetextatus, [Col. 0155A] 222 and following. Dissension among the counts of Brittany, 220. Uncertainty concerning Easter, 221. Meroveus is killed, 229.

578. Chilperic overruns Poitiers, 235. He sends an expedition against the Bretons, 237.

579. Council of Chalon in the case of Sagittarius and Salonius, 238. Incursions of the Bretons, 240.

580. Chilperic falls into the heresy of Sabellius. Reproved first by Gregory and then by Salvius, he repents, 256. Council of Berny, at which Gregory is cleared, 264. A severe plague in Gaul, 243. Chilperic falls ill; at Fredegund’s urging he devotes himself to pious works, 243, 244. He kills his son Chlodoveus, 249. King Leovigild begins a persecution in Spain, 247. Gregory’s discussion of the faith with Agilan, an Arian, 255.

581. Childebert makes a treaty with Chilperic, abandoning Guntram, 271. Gregory visits Chilperic at Nogent, where Chilperic receives gifts from the emperor, 272. Aegidius, bishop of Rheims, is Childebert’s envoy to Chilperic, 273. Gregory’s debate concerning the faith with Priscus the Jew before the king, 274. Chilperic enters Paris, 277. On the following day a paralytic is healed at the tomb of Saint Germanus, 972. While Guntram and Childebert are at odds, Chilperic invades Guntram’s cities, 289.

583. Aegidius, bishop of Rheims, is again Childebert’s envoy to Chilperic. Civil war, 304.

584. Gregory disputes about the faith with Oppilan, an Arian, 315. After making peace with Guntram, Childebert undertakes an expedition into Italy against the Lombards, and so forth, 318, 319. Rigunthis is sent to Spain, betrothed to Reccared, 321. After her father is killed, the matter remains unfinished, 357. Chilperic is killed at Calae [place-name uncertain], 324. He is buried at Paris in the basilica of Saint Vincent, 326. Guntram comes to Paris at Fredegund’s invitation. He corrects his brother’s errors. Chlotar II is named as his father’s successor, 325, 326, 597. Gundovald is hailed as King Ballomer at Brives, 338. Various embassies from Childebert to Guntram, and civil disturbances, 335, 339, 340.

585. Civil war, 349. Guntram marches with an army against Gundovald, 350, 840. He receives an embassy from him, 357. Gundovald is besieged at Comminges, 361, and killed, 365, 597. Famine grows severe in Gaul, 369. Guntram is received at Orléans, 375, where he visits Gregory, 376, and entertains him at a banquet, 377. At Paris he arranges for the bodies of his nephews to be transferred to the basilica of Saint Vincent, 381 and following. He founds the monastery of Saint Marcellus at Chalon, 595. Gregory is sent as envoy to Childebert, 385 and following. Childebert’s expedition into Italy against the Lombards, at the emperor’s instigation, 390. The Council of Mâcon is held, 392. Childebert’s assembly at Besançon, 392.

586. After Hermenegild is killed by his father, Ingund, while fleeing, dies in Africa. Guntram, seeking to avenge his niece, marches into Septimania, 397, 399, 597. Praetextatus, bishop of Rouen, is killed through Fredegund’s agency, 402. The Goths seek peace; Reccared invades Gaul once and again, 402, 408, 409.

587. Reccared succeeds his father Leovigild, 416, [Col. 0155D] 598. He seeks peace from the Franks, 419. Saint Radegund dies, 420. Gregory oversees her funeral, 985. The incursions of the Basques are suppressed, 425. Rauching rebels, 426. He is killed, 427. A conference and peace between Guntram and Childebert at Andelot, 429, 430, 439, 598. Childebert’s expedition against the rebels, 431. Reccared and the Gothic people become Catholic, 433. He seeks peace from the Franks, 435, 445. The disturbances of the Bretons are settled, 436.

588. Gregory is sent as envoy to Childebert, 439. The Franks are routed by the Lombards, 450.

589. The Lombards seek peace from Childebert, 852. Guntram’s expedition into Septimania, 454, unsuccessful, 455, 600. Theodebert, Childebert’s son, is granted to the people of Soissons, and so forth, 460. A great scandal begins in the monastery of Sainte-Croix at Poitiers, 463 and following.

590. A great plague at Rome. Saint Gregory is elevated to the papacy, 479. Childebert’s expedition against the Lombards, [Col. 0156A] 485. Maurice satisfies the Franks concerning the envoy killed in Africa the preceding year, 483 and following, 488. Council concerning Tetradia, 490. The Breton war, 493, 600. Gregory refutes a Sadducee priest, 497. The disturbances of the nuns of Poitiers increase, 502. Uncertainty concerning Easter, 516. Council of Metz, at which Aegidius of Rheims is deposed, 511 and following; there also the nuns of Poitiers are acquitted, 514.

591. Chlotar II is baptized, 522.

FROM THE CHRONICLE OF FREDEGAR, ETC.

YEAR 593. Guntram dies, and Childebert obtains his kingdom, 601. He comes to Orléans, 1135. Chlotar drives away Quintrio, duke of Champagne, 601.

594. The Breton war, 601. Gregory sets out for Rome. His *Life*, p. 24.

595. Childebert routs the Varni, 601. Gregory, bishop of Tours, dies piously on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December. *Life*, no. 26.

596. Childebert II dies. His sons succeed him: Theodebert II in Austrasia and Theodoric II in Burgundy, 601. Chlotar routs the armies of both, 602.

597. Queen Fredegund dies, 602.

598. Wintrio, duke of Champagne, is killed through Brunhild’s agency, 602.

599. Brunhild is disgracefully expelled from Austrasia, 602.

600. Defeated by Theodebert and Theodoric, Chlotar accepts peace on unjust terms, 603.

602. The Basques are subdued by the same kings and receive a duke, 604.

603. Desiderius, bishop of Vienne, is deprived of office at the assembly of Chalon, 605.

604. Chlotar is driven away by Theodoric and makes a treaty with Theodebert, 605.

605. At Brunhild’s instigation, Theodoric marches against Theodebert, [Col. 0156C] 607. They make peace, 608.

607. Brunhild rages against Saint Aredius and others, 608. The conspiracy of the four kings against Theodoric comes to nothing, 509.

608. An assembly between Theodebert and Theodoric concerning peace, 611.

610. An assembly at Saloissa between the same parties, 617.

611. After making a treaty with Chlotar, Theodoric prepares an expedition against his brother Theodebert, 618.

612. After twice defeating and capturing Theodebert, and killing his son, Theodoric invades Austrasia, 618 and following. He marches against Chlotar, 619.

613. While preparing to march against Chlotar, Theodoric dies. SIGIBERT II succeeds him; Chlotar, after defeating and capturing Sigibert with his brothers, orders them killed, and then Brunhild as well. Thus he obtains sole rule, 620 and following, 1351.

616. Assembly at Bonneuil, 624.

617. Chlotar, remitting the tribute that the Lombards had been paying, makes peace with them, 626.

618. Queen Bertrude dies, 626.

[Col. 0156D] 622. Dagobert is appointed king of the Austrasians by his father, 626.

623. Samo, a Frankish merchant, becomes king of the Slavic Wends, 626.

625. At Clichy, Dagobert takes Gomatrude as his wife, 630.

628. Chlotar dies and is buried in the basilica of Saint Vincent at Paris. DAGOBERT obtains the entire kingdom, excluding his brother, 633. Dagobert grants his brother Charibert part of Aquitaine, where he rules, 634.

629. Peace is made between the Franks and the emperor Heraclius, 637. Charibert, after defeating the Basques, enlarges his kingdom, 634.

630. Charibert II dies, and then his son Chilperic. From that time Dagobert rules alone in Francia, 641. The Franks are routed by the Slavs and Wends, 641, 642. Dagobert builds the church of Saint Denis near Paris, and so forth, 651. At Dagobert’s command, the Bulgarians are killed in one night by the Bavarians, 645. Dagobert assists Sisenand, king of Spain, 646.

631. The Wends ravage Thuringia, 646. Dagobert remits tribute to the Saxons so that they may restrain them, 647.

632. The Wends continue to harass the Frankish territories, 647. SIGIBERT III is appointed king of Austrasia by his father Dagobert, 647.

633. After another son, Chlodoveus, is born to him, Dagobert designates a division of his kingdom between them, 648. Radulf, duke of Thuringia, meditates rebellion because of the victory he has won over the Wends, 648.

635. The rebellious Basques are suppressed, 648. Judicael, king of Brittany, comes to Dagobert and promises submission to him, 650.

636. The Basques swear obedience to Dagobert, 650.

638. Dagobert dies and is buried in the basilica of Saint Denis, 651. His son CHLODOVEUS II obtains the kingdoms of Burgundy [Col. 0157B] and Neustria, 651.

640. The treasures of his father are divided between Sigibert and Chlodoveus, 655. Sigibert’s expedition against the rebel Radulf, 656, is unsuccessful, 657. This occurred in the eighth year of Sigibert; if his reign began in 632, this would be the year 639.

641. Civil disturbances in Burgundy, 658 and following. Queen Nanthildis dies, 659.

654. King Sigibert dies. Grimoald, mayor of the palace, sends Dagobert, Sigibert’s son, away to Scotland and raises his own son Childebert to the kingship. After both are deposed, Chlodoveus obtains sole rule, 657, note.

656. Chlodoveus II dies, 663.

656. CHLOTAR III alone of his brothers succeeds his father, under the guardianship of his mother Balthildis, 663.

660. CHILDERIC II is appointed king of Austrasia, 664.

669. Chlotar III dies. His brother THEODERICUS III succeeds him; shortly afterward, when Ebroin is exiled to the monastery of Luxeuil, Theodoric is thrown from the throne and Childeric becomes monarch, 664, 665.

673. After Childeric II and his pregnant wife are killed, 665, Theodoric III is restored through Ebroin’s agency and obtains sole rule, 666. Civil disturbances, in the same place.

674. Ebroin raises Chlodoveus to the throne of Austrasia, falsely claiming that he was the son of Chlotar III, 665, note. After Chlodoveus is expelled, DAGOBERT II, the son of Sigibert III, returns from Scotland and obtains part of the Austrasian kingdom, 665, note.

678. Saint Leodegarius is killed by Ebroin, 666. Civil disturbances, 667.

680. After the deaths of Dagobert II and his son Sigibert, Theodoric once again obtains sole rule, 667.

681. Ebroin is killed, 668.

687. Pippin of Herstal, mayor of the palace of Austrasia, routs King Theodoric and Berthar, the mayor of the palace, 670. From that time he obtains control of the palace.

690. CHLODOVEUS III succeeds his deceased father Theodoric III as monarch, 670.

[Col. 0157D] 694. CHILDEBERT III succeeds his brother Chlodoveus, who died without children, as monarch, 670.

About 697. Pippin’s victory over the Frisians at Dorestad, 671.

710 or 711. DAGOBERT III succeeds his deceased father Childebert as monarch, 671.

714. Pippin dies shortly after the killing of his son Grimoald, 672. Civil wars, in the same place.

715 or 716. Dagobert dies, leaving the young Theodoric. The Franks appoint Daniel, the son of Childeric II, king under the name CHILPERIC III, 672. Charles is driven away by the Frisians, 672.

[Col. 0158A] 717. Battle of Vincy, in which Chilperic is defeated by Charles, 673.

718. CHLOTAR IV, the son of Theodoric III, is appointed king by Charles to oppose Chilperic, 673.

719. Chilperic, having summoned Eudo, duke of Aquitaine, to his aid, is defeated by Charles, 673. King Chlotar dies, in the same place.

720. After making a treaty with Duke Eudo, Charles receives Chilperic from him as king, 674.

721. THEODERICUS IV, son of Dagobert III, becomes king after Chilperic’s death, 674.

724. Charles ravages Angers and then suppresses the rebellion of the Saxons, 674.

725. The Bavarians are subdued by Charles, 674.

731. Duke Eudo, after making a treaty with the Saracens, is defeated by Charles, 674.

732. The Saracens, summoned by Eudo, ravage Francia and are routed by Charles, whom Eudo joined. From this he was afterward called Martel, 675.

733. Charles provides for the defense of Burgundy against the Saracens, [Col. 0158B] 675, 677. He strikes down the Frisians, 676.

734. Charles’s expedition against the Saxons, 677.

735. After Eudo’s death, Charles occupies Aquitaine, 675.

736. Through the treachery of Duke Maurenti, the Saracens capture Avignon, 678.

737. After defeating the Saracens, Charles occupies Septimania and other territories, 678 and following. King Theodoric IV dies; interregnum.

738. Charles’s expedition against the Saxons, 677.

739. The Saracens are again driven away by Charles, 680.

741. Charles receives the keys of Saint Peter from Gregory III, 680. After dividing his principality between his sons, he dies, 681, 682.

742. CARLOMANN and PIPPIN, princes, wage war against the Basques and Aquitanians and defeat them, 682. Then they crush the Alamanni, 683.

745. Expedition against Odilo, duke of Bavaria, 683. CHILDERIC III, thought to be the son of Theodoric IV, is appointed king.

[Col. 0158C] 744. Carlomann defeats the Saxons, 683. Pippin defeats Duke Theudebald, 684.

745. The rebellion of the Basques is suppressed by Pippin, 684.

746. Carlomann suppresses the rebellion of the Alamanni, 684.

747. Carlomann abandons his principality and becomes a monk, 684. Pippin defeats the Saxons and makes them tributaries, 684.

749. Pippin’s victory over the Bavarians, 685, 686.

750. Peace in Francia this year and the following year, 686.

752. After Childeric is deposed, PIPPIN is appointed king, 686, and anointed, 991, note.

753. Pippin punishes the rebellion of the Saxons, 687. His brother Grifo is killed, 688. He sends his son Charles to meet Pope Stephen, 688.

754. Pope Stephen is received with the greatest honor by King Pippin, 688. Pippin’s expedition into Italy against the Lombards, 689.

755. After breaking their pledge and harassing Rome, the Lombards are again defeated by Pippin and made tributaries of the Franks, [Col. 0158D] 691.

756. Desiderius is established and consecrated as king of the Lombards with Pippin’s approval, 692.

757. Treaty between Pippin and the emperor of the East, 693.

758. Peace in Francia this year and the following year, 693.

760. Pippin begins a war against Waifarius, duke of Aquitaine. It continues until the year 768, when, after Waifarius is killed, Aquitaine is completely subjected to Pippin, 693 and following.

768. After dividing the kingdom between his sons Charles and Carlomann, Pippin dies, 703. CHARLES and CARLOMANN are inaugurated as kings, 704.

[THE HISTORY OF THE FRANKS BY SAINT GREGORY OF TOURS.]

[Col. 0159]

[HISTORY OF THE FRANKS.]

Preface.

[Col. 0159]

1–2. As the cultivation of liberal letters was declining—or rather, perishing—from the cities of Gaul, while some events were being conducted rightly and others wickedly, while the savagery of peoples raged, the fury of kings grew sharper, the churches were attacked by heretics and protected by Catholics, the faith of Christ burned fervently in many and grew cold in some, and the churches themselves were either enriched by the devout or stripped by the faithless—and no learned grammarian skilled in the art of dialectic could be found who might depict these things either in prose or in metrical verse—many people repeatedly groaned, saying: “Woe to our days, because the study of letters has perished among us, and no one is found among the peoples who can publish the deeds of the present in written pages.”

[Note: Some have *recedente*, “declining”; the Casinensis manuscript has *decedente itaque*, “as it was declining, therefore.” Moreover, this preface is absent from most printed editions and manuscripts. Fredegarius nevertheless transmitted it in full.]

For, continually observing that these and similar things were being said, I was unable—so that the memory of past events might reach those to come—to conceal, despite my uncultivated speech, either the struggles of the wicked or the life of those living rightly.

[Note: Fredegarius’s printed edition has *clerici*, “clerics”; in the manuscript, however, *cleriique* was found, but an ancient hand corrected it to *clerici*.]

And especially impelled by this consideration, since I have often marveled that among our people few understand a rhetorician speaking philosophically, while many understand a rustic who speaks, I resolved in my mind that, as an accounting of the years from the very beginning of the world, the first book should begin. Its chapters I have set out below.

[Note: The Casinensis manuscript has *duxi*, “I led,” and below, instead of *illicitus*, “unlawful,” it has *illectus*, “enticed.”]

THE TEN BOOKS OF THE ECCLESIASTICAL HISTORY OF THE FRANKS BY SAINT GEORGE FLORENTIUS GREGORY, BISHOP OF TOURS.

THE CHAPTERS OF BOOK ONE BEGIN.

[Col. 0159]

I. On the creation of Adam and Eve, and on Adam as a type. II. How Cain killed his brother Abel. III. Enoch the righteous: how he was translated by God. IV. On the Flood, Noah, the ark, the wrath of God, and the reckoning of the generations. V. On the descent of Noah and his sons, especially Cush, son of Ham, the beginner and inventor of magic and idolatry, and of the statue. VI. On the tower of Babylon and the confusion of languages. VII. On Abraham’s origin, birth, and interpretation, and on Nimrod. VIII. On Isaac, Esau and his sons, and Job. IX. On Jacob and his sons, and Joseph in Egypt. X. On the nature of the Nile and the crossing of the Red Sea. XI. On the children of Israel in the wilderness, their entry into the Promised Land, and Joshua. XII. On the kings of the Jews. XIII. On Solomon and the building of the Temple. XIV. How the kingdom of Israel was divided because of Rehoboam’s harshness, and on the Babylonian captivity and the prophets of that time. XV. On the return of the Jews from Babylon up to the birth of Christ. XVI. On the kings and kingdoms of the remaining peoples. XVII. On the Roman emperors. At what time Lyon was founded. XVIII. On the birth of our Savior, the gifts of the Magi, and the slaughter of the infants. XIX. On Christ’s preaching, miracles, and passion. XX. On Joseph of Arimathea, who buried him. XXI. On the vow of the apostle James. XXII. On the day of the Lord’s resurrection. XXIII. On the Lord’s ascension, and on the death of Pilate and Herod. XXIV. On Peter, who came to Rome and bore martyrdom for Christ, and on Nero; on James, Mark, and John the Evangelist. XXV. On the persecution under the emperor Trajan. XXVI. On the origin of heresies and schisms. XXVII. On the martyrs Photinus and Irenaeus. XXVIII. On the persecution under Decius and the seven men sent into Gaul to preach. XXIX. On the conversion of the people of Bourges. XXX. On the persecution under Valerian and Gallienus. On Chrocus and the shrine of the Auvergne. XXXI. On other martyrs. XXXII. On the martyr Privatus and the tyrant Chrocus. XXXIII. On the persecution under Diocletian. XXXIV. On Constantine the Great, blessed Martin, and the discovery of the Lord’s Cross. XXXV. On the reign of Constans. XXXVI. On Saint Martin’s arrival. On the matron Melania. XXXVII. On the death of the emperor Valens. XXXVIII. On Theodosius and his reign. On the death of the tyrant Maximus. XXXIX. On Urbicus, bishop of the Auvergne. XL. On Saint Illidius and his successor in the episcopate. XLI. On Saint Nepotianus, also bishop of the Auvergne. XLII. On the chastity and burial of the Two Lovers. XLIII. On the passing of blessed Martin.

BOOK ONE.

Prologue.

[Col. 0161A] 5. As I am about to write of the wars of kings with hostile peoples, of martyrs with pagans, and of churches with heretics, I first wish to set forth my faith, so that anyone who reads may not doubt that I am Catholic.

It also seemed appropriate, for the sake of those who despair as the end of the world approaches, to explain openly, by gathering together the total recorded in chronicles or histories of earlier years, how many years there have been from the beginning of the world.

[Note: Thus have the manuscripts of Bec and Reg; others have *chronica*, “chronicle.” Certainly below all have *chronicae Eusebii*, “the chronicles of Eusebius.”]

But first I ask pardon from my readers if I should depart from grammatical usage in letters or syllables, since I have not been thoroughly instructed in that art.

[Note: The Regius manuscript has *de qua plene*, “in which I have not been fully instructed”; the Casinensis has *adprime non sum instructus*, “I have not been instructed at all well.”]

My sole concern is to retain, without any embellishment or hesitation of heart, what is proclaimed as being believed in the Church; for I know that a person subject to sins can, through pure belief, obtain forgiveness from our merciful Lord.

[Note: The manuscripts and several printed editions have *apud Deum*, “with God.”]

[Col. 0161B] 6 I therefore believe in God the Father almighty. I believe in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord and God, begotten of the Father, not made; not after the ages, but existing always with the Father before all time. For the Father could not have been called Father unless he had a Son; nor would he be Son if he did not, in turn, have a Father. But those who say, “There was when he was not,” I reject with execration and declare must be separated from the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0161C] The Nicene Fathers added this against the Arians in their creed; hence, if I am not mistaken, after these words, “There was when he was not,” one should add, and so forth.]

I believe this Christ to be the Word of the Father, through whom all things were made. I believe this Word became flesh, through whose passion the world was [Col. 0162A] redeemed; and I believe that it was his humanity, not his divinity, that was subject to suffering. I believe that on the third day he rose again, liberated the lost human race, ascended into heaven, sits at the Father’s right hand, and will come to judge the living and the dead.

I believe that the Holy Spirit proceeded from the Father and the Son,

[Note: [Col. 0161C] All the printed editions and manuscripts, together with the Corbie manuscript, have this phrase, “and the Son” (*Filioque*). Indeed, from the fifth and sixth centuries it is found in professions of faith in the synods of Spain. Nevertheless, in the ninth century disturbances arose when it was first added to the Constantinopolitan Creed, which was sung during the solemn celebration of Mass.]

not as inferior, or as though he had not existed previously, but as the equal and coeternal God, always with the Father and the Son, consubstantial in nature, equal in omnipotence, coeternal in essence, so that he was never without the Father or the Son, nor inferior to the Father or the Son. I believe that this holy Trinity subsists in the distinction of persons: one person being the Father, another the Son, and another the Holy Spirit. In this Trinity I confess that there is one deity, one power, and one essence.

[Col. 0162B] I believe

[Note: [Col. 0162C] From this point through chapter 1, the passage is absent from the Royal manuscript.]

blessed Mary to have been a virgin before childbirth and likewise a virgin after childbirth. I believe the soul to be immortal, yet not to possess any share in divinity. And I faithfully believe everything established at Nicaea by the three hundred and eighteen bishops.

Concerning the end of the world, I hold what I learned from those who came before. The Antichrist

[Note: [Col. 0162C] The Casinensis manuscript reads: “I learned that the Antichrist will first come, claiming that he is Christ,” and so forth. In the Corbie manuscript, after “will come” there is a worn half-line, after which appears “then, but first, circumcision.”]

will first introduce circumcision, claiming that he is Christ; then he will set up his statue in the temple at Jerusalem, to be worshiped, just as we read that the Lord said: “You will see the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place” (Matthew 24:15).

[Note: [Col. 0162C] Among others, two most illustrious fathers of the Gallican Church understood this passage about the Antichrist in this way: Irenaeus, near the end of Book V, and Hilary in his Commentary on Matthew, chapter 25.]

But that day is unknown to all human beings, as the Lord himself makes clear when he says: “But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven nor the Son, but the Father alone” (Mark 13:32). Here too we shall answer the heretics who attack us, asserting that the Son is inferior to the Father because he does not know this day. Let them understand, therefore, that this Son is the Christian people, so named by God, concerning whom it is said: “I will be a father to them, and they shall be sons to me” (2 Corinthians 6:13). For if he had spoken this about the only-begotten Son, he would never have placed the angels before him. Thus he says, “Neither the angels of heaven nor the Son,” showing that he spoke not about the Only-Begotten but about the adopted people.

[Note: [Col. 0163D] The holy Fathers offer various other interpretations of this passage. The more common one is that the Son of Man, according to the nature of his humanity, did not know that day, although as God-man he knew it perfectly. Or he did not know it in the capacity in which he had been sent as envoy to humanity. For it was not among those truths that he was to communicate to human beings, concerning which he said elsewhere: “I have made known to you everything that I have heard from my Father”—that is, everything that I was to make known to you on his behalf. So Augustine and Gregory the Great.]

But our end is Christ himself, who, if we turn toward him, will in his abundant kindness grant us eternal life.

[Col. 0163B] Concerning the reckoning of this world, the *Chronicles* of Eusebius of Caesarea, bishop, and of Jerome, presbyter, speak clearly and set forth the calculation of the succession of all the years. Orosius, too, after investigating these matters most diligently, gathered into one total the entire number of years from the beginning of the world to his own time. Victor likewise did this when he was investigating the order of the Paschal celebration. Therefore, following copies of the writings mentioned above, we too wish—if the Lord deigns to grant his assistance—to calculate the entire accumulation of years from the creation of the first human being down to our own time. We shall accomplish this more easily if we begin with Adam himself.

## I

In the beginning the Lord formed heaven and earth in his Christ, who is the beginning of all things—that is, in his Son. After creating the elements of the world, he took a clod of fragile mud

[Note: [Col. 0163D] So the Casinensis manuscript; others read “the most fragile.”]

and fashioned the human being in his own image and likeness. He breathed into his face the breath of life, and he became a living soul. While he slept, a rib was taken from him, and the woman Eve was created.

There is no doubt that this first man, Adam, before he sinned, prefigured our Lord the Redeemer. For while he slept in the slumber of his passion, he brought forth water and blood from his side and presented to himself the immaculate virgin Church, redeemed by blood and cleansed by liquid, having neither spot nor wrinkle—that is, washed by the waters because of the spot, and stretched out upon the cross because of the wrinkle.

Thus these first human beings, living happily amid the delights of paradise,

[Note: [Col. 0163D] The printed editions read, “in the delightful paradise.”]

were enticed by the serpent’s cunning and transgressed the divine commandments. Cast out from the angelic dwelling, they were assigned to the labors of the world.

## II

When the woman was recognized by her companion

[Note: [Col. 0163D] So the manuscripts, as also more than once below. The printed editions, however, read, “When the woman was recognized by her consort.” The Corbie manuscript, as elsewhere, frequently uses the accusative for the ablative; it reads, “the woman recognized the companion.”]

she conceived and gave birth to two sons. But when God graciously accepted the sacrifice of one, the other swelled with burning envy and, rising up as a new murderer in the shedding of his brother’s blood, overcame, defeated, and killed his brother.

[Note: [Col. 0164D] The printed editions read, “in the blood against his brother … rising up as a fratricide.”]

## III

From that point onward the whole human race plunged into accursed crime, except for righteous Enoch, who walked in the ways of God and was taken up by the Lord himself because of his righteousness, and so was delivered from the midst of the sinful people. For thus we read: “Enoch walked with God, and he was not found, because God took him” (Genesis 5:24).

## IV

Therefore, angered against the iniquities of a people who did not walk in his paths, the Lord sent a flood and, as the waters inundated the earth, destroyed every living creature from its surface. Only Noah, most faithful and specially belonging to him, who bore the image of his own type, did he preserve in the ark, together with his wife and the wives of his three sons, for the restoration of the human race.

Here the heretics reproach us, asking why sacred Scripture said that the Lord was angry. Let them understand, then, that our Lord is not angry as a human being is angry: he is stirred up in order to terrify; he drives away in order to recall; he becomes angry in order to correct.

Nor do I doubt that the form of the ark bore the type of the mother Church. Passing through the waves and reefs of this age, she nurtures us in maternal care amid the evils that threaten, and protects us with loving embrace and defense.

From Adam, therefore, to Noah there are ten generations: Adam, Seth, Enos, Cainan, Malaleel, Jared, Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech, and Noah. In these ten generations there are found 1,242 years. The book of Joshua son of Nun clearly explains that Adam was buried in the land of Enachim, which was formerly called Hebron (Joshua 14:15).

## V

After the flood Noah had three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. From Japheth, likewise from Ham, and from Shem, peoples went forth. And, as the ancient history says, from them the human race was scattered beneath the whole heaven.

Ham’s firstborn was Cush. Under the instruction of the devil, he was the originator of every magical art and the first inventor of idolatry. At the devil’s instigation, he first set up a little statue to be worshiped,

[Note: [Col. 0164D] Others read *stratunculam*. The Bec, Royal, and Regium manuscripts read “a little statue to be worshiped”; the Corbie manuscript reads *staticolam*. Morel, likewise using the manuscript of Saint Martin of Tours, reads *statunculum*, and observed that this neuter form had recently been found in an edited fragment of Petronius. Alteserra reports his words: “Thus the craftsmen took from this mass and made little bowls and dishes, little statues, and so forth.”]

and by a false power he showed human beings stars and fire falling from heaven. He crossed over to the Persians. The Persians called him Zoroaster,

[Note: [Col. 0164D] Pliny has more to say about Zoroaster, whom they consider to have been the first king of the Bactrians.]

that is, “living star.” Since then, the Persians, accustomed to worshiping fire, honor as a god the very one whom they say was divinely consumed by fire.

## VI

As human beings multiplied and scattered throughout all the lands, they came out from the East and found a grassy plain in Shinar. There they began to build a city and tried to construct a tower reaching to the heavens. God, refuting their vain thought, their language, and themselves, scattered them widely throughout the whole earth. The city was therefore called Babel, that is, “Confusion,” because there God confused their languages.

This is the Babylon built by the giant Nimrod,

[Note: [Col. 0165C] The Corbie manuscript reads “built by Hebron.”]

son of Cush. As the history of Orosius relates, it was laid out as a square on a remarkably level plain. Its wall, made of baked brick poured with bitumen, was fifty cubits wide and two hundred cubits high; its circuit measured 470 stadia. One stadium

[Note: [Col. 0165C] The Badius edition reads: “One stadium contains 125 paces.” Pliny likewise says in Book I, chapter 23: “A stadium amounts to 125 of our paces, that is, 625 feet.” Ancient authors frequently say more about Babylon’s extent; they wrote that it ought to be designated as a province rather than a city. The editions of Orosius vary in describing its circuit, Book II, chapter 6, some reading 480 stadia, others 470. The authority of our Gregory persuades us that the latter reading is preferable. Quintus Curtius, Book V, section 1, gives Babylon’s circuit as 358 stadia and provides further noteworthy information about the city.]

contains five *aripennes*. Twenty-five gates were placed along each side, making one hundred in all. The doors of these gates, of astonishing size, were made of cast bronze.

The same historian relates many other things about this city,

[Note: [Col. 0165D] Orosius describes all these matters in *History* II.7.]

adding: “Although the beauty of the construction had been so great, it was nevertheless conquered and destroyed.”

## VII

Noah’s first son was Shem. From him, in the tenth generation, Abraham was born: Noah, Shem, Arphaxad, Sale, Heber, Peleg, Reu,

[Note: [Col. 0165D] So the Bec, Royal, and Regium manuscripts; others read “Peleg, Ragau.”]

Serug, Terah, who begot Abraham. In these ten generations—from Noah to Abraham—942 years are found.

[Note: [Col. 0165D] The Corbie manuscript has 900; the Bec manuscript, 945.]

At that time Ninus was reigning. He built a city that he called Nineveh; the prophet Jonah determines the extent of its area in three days’ journey.

Abraham was born in the forty-third year of Ninus’s reign. This is Abraham, the beginning of our faith. He received the promises; to him Christ our Lord showed that he would be born and suffer for us as a sacrificial offering, saying in the Gospels: “Abraham rejoiced that he was to see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John 8:56).

Severus relates in his *Chronicle* that this holocaust was offered on Mount Calvary,

[Note: [Col. 0165D] The author of Sermon 6 of the Appendix to Augustine, formerly Sermon 71 *de tempore*, says the same and praises Jerome. The statement is actually found in chapter 15 of the Commentary on Mark incorrectly attributed to Jerome.]

where the Lord was crucified,

[Note: [Col. 0166D] Gennadius, in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, lists a *Chronicle* among the works of Sulpicius Severus; I think this refers to the *Sacred History* published by him. Yet I do not read there that Isaac was led by his father to be sacrificed on the summit of Calvary.]

just as it is still famously said today in the city of Jerusalem itself. On this mountain stood the holy cross to which the Redeemer was fastened, and from it flowed that blessed blood.

Here, then, Abraham received the sign of circumcision, showing that what he bore on his body we should bear in our heart, as the Prophet says: “Circumcise yourselves for your God, and circumcise the foreskin of your heart” (Deuteronomy 10:16), “and do not follow foreign gods” (Jeremiah 35:15). And again: “No one uncircumcised in heart shall enter my sanctuary” (Ezekiel 44:9).

After a syllable had been added to his name,

[Note: [Col. 0166D] In Genesis 17, he is called Abraham instead of Abram.]

God called this Abraham “father of many nations.”

## VIII

When he was one hundred years old, he begot Isaac. Isaac, in the sixtieth year of his life, had twin sons born to him by Rebekah. The first was Esau, also called Edom, that is, “earthly”; because of his appetite he sold his birthright. He was the father of the Idumeans. In the fourth generation from him Jobab was born: Esau, Reuel, Zerah, Jobab, who is also Job.

Job lived 249 years. In his eightieth year he was freed from his illness; after the illness, he lived 170 years, and, with all his possessions restored twofold, he rejoiced with as many children as he had lost.

[Note: [Col. 0166D] The Book of Job, chapter and final verse, nevertheless says that Job lived 140 years after this. The Syriac and Arabic versions have 146; so too the Greek version, which also says that Job’s entire life lasted 240 years. The other versions do not have this.]

## IX

Isaac’s second son was Jacob, beloved by God, as he says through the Prophet: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Malachi 1:3). After wrestling with an angel, he was called Israel, from whom came the Israelites.

He begot twelve patriarchs, whose names are: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher. After these he begot Joseph by Rachel, in the ninety-second year of his life. He loved Joseph more than his other sons. By her he also had Benjamin, the last of all.

When Joseph was sixteen years old, bearing the image of the Redeemer, he saw dreams that he told to his brothers: as though he were gathering sheaves

[Note: [Col. 0166D] The Regium manuscript reads, “gathering his own sheaf, while the sheaves of his brothers,” and so forth; the Royal manuscript reads, “binding his own sheaf,” and so forth, which conforms more closely to the text of Genesis.]

which the sheaves of his brothers worshiped. And again: as though the sun and moon, together with eleven stars, were falling down before him. This provoked great hatred against him among his brothers.

Inflamed by envy, they sold him for twenty pieces of silver to Ishmaelites traveling into Egypt.

[Note: [Col. 0166D] So the Regium manuscript, as also in Genesis; others read “thirty.”]

When famine threatened and they had gone down into Egypt, Joseph recognized them, but they did not recognize Joseph. After causing them much distress and having Benjamin brought to him, he revealed himself to them. Benjamin too had been born of Rachel, their mother.

After this all the Israelites went down into Egypt and, through Joseph, enjoyed Pharaoh’s favor. Jacob, after blessing his sons, died in Egypt and was buried in the tomb

[Note: [Col. 0167D] The Regium manuscript reads, “in his tomb by Joseph.” Both readings are true according to Genesis.]

of his father Isaac in the land of Canaan. After Joseph and Pharaoh had died,

[Note: [Col. 0167D] The Regium manuscript adds “by Pharaoh,” which is also the correct reading.]

the whole nation was subjected to slavery. Through Moses it was liberated after the ten plagues of Egypt, Pharaoh having been drowned in the Red Sea.

## X

Since many have said much about this crossing of the sea, it seemed appropriate to insert into this account something about the site and the crossing itself.

The Nile flows through Egypt, as you know very well, and irrigates it with its current; hence the Egyptians are called “Nile-dwellers.” Many explorers of places now say that its banks are filled with sacred monasteries.

On its bank stands not the Babylon mentioned above but another city called Babylon,

[Note: [Col. 0167D] This is now called Cairo, the principal city of Egypt on the Nile; formerly the seat of the sultans of Egypt, it is now subject to the Turks.]

in which Joseph built granaries of squared stones and mortar with marvelous workmanship. They are broader at the bottom and narrower at the top, so that grain could be poured in through a small opening; these granaries can still be seen today.

From this city the king set out with chariot forces and a large body of infantry to pursue the Hebrews.

The river mentioned above, coming from the East, runs toward the western region and the Red Sea. From the West, however, a lake or branch of the Red Sea extends toward the East, measuring about fifty miles in length and eighteen in width.

At the head of this lake the city of Clysma was built,

[Note: [Col. 0168D] Ptolemy describes it as a fort situated in the Arabian Gulf. Simler, in Ortelius, thinks it is the Lismum of Antoninus.]

not because of the fertility of the place, since nothing is more sterile, but because of its harbor. Ships arriving from India rest there because of the harbor’s convenience, and goods purchased there are carried throughout Egypt.

As the Hebrews traveled through the desert toward this lake, they came as far as the sea itself. Finding fresh water, they encamped. In this narrow place, bounded both by the desert and by the sea, they settled, as it is written: “When Pharaoh heard that the sea and the desert had closed them in, and that they had no way by which they could proceed, he sent out to pursue them” (Exodus 14:3).

When the people, with the Egyptians threatening, cried out to Moses, a staff was cast over the sea at the divine command, and the sea was divided. They walked across dry ground and, as Scripture says, “were surrounded on every side by a wall of waters” (Exodus 14:22). They crossed unharmed to that shore which lies opposite Mount Sinai, while the Egyptians were drowned, with Moses as their leader.

Much is related about this crossing, as I have said. But we have taken care to insert into this page what we learned to be true from wise people, and certainly from those who had themselves visited that place.

They say that the tracks made by the wheels of the chariots remain to this day and can be seen in the depths as far as the range of human vision reaches. If a slight disturbance of the sea covers them, when the waters become calm they are divinely renewed again as they had been.

Some say that the Israelites, after making a small circuit through the sea, returned to the very shore from which they had entered. Others assert that there was one entrance for all. Some say that a separate path was opened for each tribe, citing this testimony from the Psalter:

“He divided the Red Sea into divisions” (Psalm 135:13),

[Note: [Col. 0168D] The Tours manuscript, used by Morel, reads *testimonium psalterii abutentes*, apparently using the fourth case for the sixth. Gregory seems not to approve the opinion of which he is speaking here.]

which divisions we ought to understand spiritually, not literally.

For there are also many divisions in this age, which is figuratively called the sea. Not all can cross to life equally or by one road. Some cross at the first hour—that is, those who, reborn through baptism, are able to remain undefiled by every pollution of the flesh until the end of the present life. Others cross at the third hour, namely, those who are converted at a more advanced age. Others at the sixth hour, those who restrain the heat of lust. At each of these hours, as the Evangelist records (Matthew 20), they are hired according to their own faith to work in the Lord’s vineyard. These are the divisions by which the sea of this life is crossed.

But the claim that, after reaching the sea and keeping to the shore of the lake, they returned means what the Lord said to Moses: “They shall turn back and encamp before Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea, opposite Baal-zephon” (Exodus 14:2).

There is no doubt that this crossing of the sea and the pillar of cloud prefigured our baptism, as blessed Paul the Apostle says: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:1–2). The pillar of fire, however, prefigured the Holy Spirit.

From Abraham’s birth, therefore, to the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt and their crossing of the Red Sea—which occurred in Moses’ eightieth year—462 years are reckoned.

## XI

From that point the Israelites spent forty years in the wilderness. They were instructed in the laws, tested, and fed with angelic food. After receiving the Law and crossing the Jordan with Joshua son of Nun, they then received the promised land.

## XII

After this crossing, whenever they set aside the divine commandments, they were often subjected to the service of foreigners. But when they repented and groaned, the Lord granted them deliverance through the arm of brave men.

Afterward, when they asked the Lord for a king through Samuel, as the other nations had, they received Saul first and then David.

From Abraham to David there are fourteen generations: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Judah, Perez, Esrom, Aram, Amminadab, Nahshon, Salmon, Boaz, Obed, Jesse, and David.

David begot Solomon by Bathsheba. He was raised to the kingship by the prophet Nathan, his brother, and by his mother.

## XIII

After David died and Solomon began to reign, the Lord appeared to him and promised to grant whatever he requested. But Solomon set aside earthly riches and sought wisdom above all. This pleased the Lord, so that he heard from him: “Because you did not seek the kingdoms of the world or its riches, but asked for wisdom, you shall receive it. No one before you was so wise, nor will anyone after you be so” (1 Kings 3:12).

The judgment he later pronounced between two women disputing over one infant confirmed this (ibid. 3:16 and following).

This Solomon built a temple for the name of the Lord with marvelous workmanship, bringing into it a great quantity of gold, silver, bronze, and iron, so that some said that no similar building had ever been constructed in the world.

From the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt to the building of the temple, which occurred in the seventh year of Solomon’s reign, 480 years are found,

[Note: [Col. 0169D] The Corbie manuscript has 280, but this is erroneous, as is clear from the Third Book of Kings, chapter 6.]

as the history of Kings testifies.

## XIV

After Solomon’s death, his kingdom was divided into two parts because of Rehoboam’s harshness. Two tribes remained with Rehoboam; this was called Judah. Ten tribes went to Jeroboam; this was called Israel.

Afterward they turned to idolatry. Neither the prophets’ predictions, nor their deaths, nor the disasters of their homeland, nor even the destruction of their own kings subdued them. At last the angry Lord raised up Nebuchadnezzar against them. He led them captive to Babylon together with all the ornaments of the temple.

During this captivity the outstanding prophet Daniel went into exile unharmed among hungry lions, and three youths went into captivity while bedewed amid the flames. Ezekiel also prophesied during this captivity, and the prophet Ezra was born.

From David to the desolation of the temple and the migration to Babylon there are fourteen generations: David, Solomon, Rehoboam, Abijah, Asa, Jehoshaphat, Joram, Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, Hezekiah, Manasseh, Amon, and Josiah.

In these fourteen generations 361 years are found.

[Note: [Col. 0169D] So the manuscripts and the Badius edition; others, with the Bec manuscript, have 340. The Corbie manuscript has 390.]

They were liberated from this captivity through Zerubbabel, who afterward restored both the temple and the city.

But this captivity, I think, prefigures that captivity in which the sinful soul is led away. Unless Zerubbabel—that is, Christ—liberates it, it will wander in exile terribly. For the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free” (John 8:36).

May he himself establish within us a temple for himself, in which he may deign to dwell: a temple in which faith may shine like gold, in which the word of preaching may gleam like silver, and in which all the ornaments of that visible temple may shine in the integrity of our thoughts. May he himself also grant a saving fulfillment to our good will. For “unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Psalm 126:1).

This captivity is said to have lasted seventy-six years.

[Note: [Col. 0169D] So the Corbie manuscript; others have 70.]

## XV

After returning through Zerubbabel, as we have said, sometimes murmuring against God, sometimes falling after idols, sometimes committing abominations and imitating what the nations practiced, and despising God’s prophets, they were handed over to the nations, subjected, and destroyed.

At last the Lord himself, promised through the voices of the patriarchs and prophets, deigned to come into the world for redemption, entering through the Holy Spirit into the womb of the Virgin Mary and being born for the salvation both of that nation and of all nations.

From the migration to the birth of Christ there are fourteen generations: Jeconiah, Shealtiel, Zerubbabel, Abiud, Eliakim, Azor, Zadok, Achim,

[Note: [Col. 0169D] The same manuscript has “Joachim.”]

Eliud, Eleazar, Matthan, Jacob, Joseph the husband of Mary, from whom our Lord Jesus Christ was born. Joseph is counted as the fourteenth.

[Note: [Col. 0169D] Here only thirteen are listed, unless a double Jeconiah is admitted—that is, father and son, who were also both called Joachim, as Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, and other Fathers observe.]

## XVI

Therefore, lest we seem to know only one Hebrew nation, we shall mention the other kingdoms and when, or during what period, they existed in relation to the Israelites.

In Abraham’s time Ninus reigned over the Assyrians; among the Sicyonians, Europs; among the Egyptians, the sixteenth ruler, whom they called *dynastes* in their own language.

In Moses’ time Tropas was the seventh king among the Argives;

[Note: [Col. 0170D] The Corbie manuscript has “Trophas.”]

in Attica, Cecrops was first; among the Egyptians, Cenchris was twelfth, and he too was drowned in the Red Sea; among the Assyrians, Agatadis was sixteenth; among the Sicyonians, Maratis.

In Solomon’s time, when he reigned over Israel, Silvius was fifth among the Latins; among the Lacedaemonians, Festus;

[Note: [Col. 0170D] The Regium manuscript has “Sistus”; others, together with the printed editions, have “Fistus.” We have preferred the Corbie manuscript’s reading.]

among the Corinthians, Oxion was second; among the Egyptians, Thephei.

[Note: [Col. 0170D] So the same Corbie manuscript; others have “Thebei.”]

In the 126th year

[Note: [Col. 0170D] The Corbie manuscript has “in the 120th year.” The Badius edition has “in the 76th year.”]

over the Assyrians, Eutropes was reigning; among the Athenians, Agasastus was second.

When Amon reigned over Judea, at the time when the captivity went to Babylon, Argeus ruled the Macedonians; Gyges the Lydians; Vaphres the Egyptians; Nebuchadnezzar Babylon; he led the Jews captive; and Servius Tullus was sixth among the Romans.

[Note: [Col. 0170D] The manuscripts—the Corbie, Royal, Bec, and Regium—omit the word “Tullus.”]

## XVII

After these came the emperors. The first was Julius Caesar, who obtained the monarchy of the entire empire. The second was Octavian, the grand-nephew of Julius Caesar, whom they call Augustus; from him the month of August also received its name.

In the nineteenth year of his reign, we find it most clearly recorded that Lugdunum, a city of Gaul, was founded.

[Note: [Col. 0171C] Valesius considers both statements made here by Gregory to be false in his *Notice of Gaul*. For, as Dio testifies—and as this author observes—Lugdunum was founded by Lucius Plancus at the command of the senate, which feared that Plancus, armed, might join Antony, who had been declared an enemy of the state. Second, Lugdunum was not called “Most Noble” because of the multitude of martyrs, but because of the splendor and power of the colony, which even contributed senators to the curia. Claudius Augustus was also born in that city.]

Later, having been made illustrious by the blood of martyrs, it was called “Most Noble.”

## XVIII

In the forty-third year of Augustus’s reign,

[Note: [Col. 0171D] The Corbie manuscript has “in the forty-fourth year of his reign,” and so forth. The other manuscripts have “forty-third,” as do the printed editions.]

our Lord Jesus Christ, as we have said, was born according to the flesh from the Virgin Mary in Bethlehem, the town of David. The Magi saw his immense star in the East, came with gifts, and worshiped the child, humbly presenting their offerings.

But Herod, zealous for his kingdom and attempting to persecute Christ God, killed the infant children. He too was later struck down by divine judgment.

## XIX

When our Lord and God Jesus Christ was preaching repentance, granting the grace of baptism, promising the heavenly kingdom to all nations, and working wonders and signs among the peoples—bringing wine from water, extinguishing fevers, giving sight to the blind, restoring life to the dead, freeing those possessed by unclean spirits, and restoring lepers miserably disfigured by their skin—by performing these and many other signs he most clearly declared himself to the peoples as God.

Among the Jews anger was kindled and envy was stirred up. Their minds, nourished on the blood of the prophets, plotted unjustly to kill the Righteous One. Thus, so that the oracles of the ancient prophets might be fulfilled, he was betrayed by a disciple, unjustly condemned by the chief priests, mocked by the Jews, crucified with criminals, and guarded by soldiers after he had given up his spirit.

After these things had occurred, darkness fell over the whole world, and many, converted and groaning, confessed Jesus as the Son of God.

## XX

Joseph too was seized—the man who embalmed him with spices and placed him in his own tomb—and was shut up in a small chamber,

[Note: [Col. 0171D] Gregory took this from the apocryphal Gospel of Nicodemus, or from some author of the same sort. The *Acts of Pilate*, which Pope Gelasius classified among the apocrypha in his catalogue of apocryphal books, deserve no greater credibility.]

and guarded by the very leaders of the priests, who showed greater cruelty toward him than toward the Lord himself, as the *Acts of Pilate* sent to the emperor Tiberius report.

[Note: [Col. 0171D] Tertullian likewise testifies to this in the *Apology*, and Eusebius derives it from him in Book II, chapter 2, of his *History*. Orosius has more in Book VII, chapter 2, where he says that Pilate reported to Tiberius and the senate concerning Christ’s passion and resurrection, his miracles, and the things that were being done through his disciples in his name.]

Thus, while Christ was guarded by soldiers, Joseph was guarded by the priests themselves.

But when the Lord rose again, the guards were terrified by an angelic vision. Since he was not found in the tomb, the walls of the little chamber in which Joseph was being held were lifted up into the air during the night. Joseph himself was released from custody by an angel, and the walls were restored to their place.

When the chief priests reproached the guards and insistently demanded the holy body from them, the soldiers said to them: “Return Joseph to us, and we will return Christ to you. But, as we recognize the truth, neither you are now able to return God’s benefactor, nor we the Son of God.”

Then, while the priests stood confounded, the soldiers were released under this pretext.

## XXI

It is said that the Apostle James, when he had seen the Lord already dead on the cross, solemnly declared

[Note: [Col. 0172C] The printed editions read “is said to have detested.” Jerome cites this story from the Gospel of the Hebrews in his Catalogue of Illustrious Men. The widely circulated Abdias also relates it in Book VI.]

and swore that he would never eat bread unless he saw the Lord rising again.

On the third day the Lord returned, having despoiled hell in triumph. He appeared to James and said: “Rise, James, and eat, for I have already risen from the dead.”

This is James the Just, whom they call the Lord’s brother,

[Note: [Col. 0172D] The material following this point through chapter 22 is absent from the Royal manuscript. Most Greek and Latin Fathers say that James was Joseph’s son by another wife; Jerome attacks them. Indeed, the mother of James who is mentioned in the Gospel had not yet died at the time of Christ’s passion. Thus Joseph would have had either to divorce her in order to marry Mary or to have had two wives simultaneously. Everyone can see that both alternatives are entirely false.]

because Joseph is said to have had him by another wife.

## XXII

We believe that the Lord’s resurrection took place on the first day, not on the seventh, as many suppose. This is the day of the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, which we properly call “the Lord’s Day” (*Dominicam*) because of his holy resurrection. This was the first to see the light in the beginning, and this was the first to be granted the privilege of beholding the Lord rising from the tomb.

From the captivity of Jerusalem and the desolation of the temple [Col. 0172C] until the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, until the seventeenth year of Tiberius—668 years are reckoned [Note: [Col. 0172D] This reckoning of the years is not found in the Corbie manuscript.].

## XXIII

When the Lord had risen, he disputed with the disciples about the kingdom of God for forty days. While they watched, he was received into a cloud and carried up into the heavens, where he sits gloriously at the right hand of the Father.
