Pilate sent a report of the proceedings to Tiberius Caesar, informing him both of Christ’s miracles and of his passion and resurrection. These proceedings [Note: [Col. 0172D] Justin Martyr praises the Acts of Pilate in *Apology* 2; in his time they were in everyone’s hands. Those, however, which have reached us and are now commonly circulated ought to be reckoned among spurious documents.] are still preserved in writing among us today.

Tiberius reported this to the senate [Note: [Col. 0172D] The Corbie manuscript reads “to the senators”] [Col. 0173A]; but the senate rejected it angrily because the report had not first come to it. From this, indeed, the first seeds of hatred against Christians began to sprout.

Pilate, however, did not remain unpunished. For the crime of his office—that is, for the death he inflicted upon our Lord Jesus Christ—he killed himself with his own hands [Note: [Col. 0173D] He was banished to Vienne, a city of Gaul, as Ado of Vienne writes in his *Chronicle.*]. Many think that he was a Manichaean, in accordance with the passage read in the Gospel: “Some people came from Galilee and reported to him that Pilate had mingled their blood with their sacrifices” (Luke 13:1).

King Herod likewise, while raging against the Lord’s apostles, was divinely struck for such great crimes. His body swelled and teemed with worms; and, taking a knife to cleanse the evil, he directed a blow of his own hand against himself [Note: [Col. 0173D] So read the Regius manuscript; others read, “he freed himself by a blow from his own hand.” The Corbie manuscript reads, “by blows.” Concerning the death of Herod Agrippa, besides Acts 12, Josephus should be consulted, *Jewish Antiquities*, book 7. Gregory, however, here confuses the Ascalonite with Agrippa. What he relates here happened to the Ascalonite, as Josephus reports in book 2 of *The Jewish War*, and after him Eusebius and Rufinus in book 1, chapter 8 of their *History.*].

## XXIV

[Col. 0173B] Under the emperor Claudius, the fourth after Augustus, the blessed apostle Peter came to Rome. Preaching there, he most clearly proved by many miracles that Christ is the Son of God. From those days onward, Christians began to exist in the city of Rome.

When the name of Christ spread increasingly among the peoples, the ancient serpent’s envy arose against it, and savage wickedness poured itself into every recess of the emperor’s heart. For that lustful, vain, and proud man Nero—who was both the sexual partner of men and again a pursuer of men, and the most filthy violator of his mother, sisters, and every woman related to him—in order to complete the mass of his wickedness, was the first to raise persecution against the worship of Christ and against those who believed.

He had with him Simon Magus, a man of every kind of wickedness [Col. 0173C] and a master of every magical art. When the Lord’s apostles Peter and Paul had overthrown him, Nero was stirred against them because they preached Christ as the Son [Note: [Col. 0173D] All printed editions have this reading. Nevertheless, one should read “preached Christ as the Son of God,” which is the reading of the Bec manuscript.] and despised the worship of idols. He ordered Peter to be killed by crucifixion and Paul by the sword. While attempting to flee the uprising he had himself provoked, he too killed himself with his own hand at the fourth milestone from the city.

At that time James, the brother of the Lord, and Mark the evangelist were also crowned with glorious martyrdom for Christ’s name. Yet the first of all to enter this way was the Levite and martyr Stephen.

After the killing of the apostle James, great calamity overtook the Jews. For when Vespasian arrived, the temple was burned, and six hundred thousand Jews were afflicted in that war by sword [Note: [Col. 0173D] The Corbie manuscript reads, “by war and sword.”] and famine.

Domitian, the second after Nero, raged against the Christians [Col. 0173D]. He exiled the apostle John to the island of [Col. 0174A] Patmos, and inflicted various cruelties upon the peoples. After his death, the blessed apostle and evangelist John returned from exile. An old man and full of days, having lived a life perfected in God, he descended alive into the tomb.

It is said [Note: [Col. 0173D] This was the opinion of certain ancients, which Tertullian and most of the other Fathers refuted. Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus, who had seen John’s disciples, affirms in a letter reported by Eusebius, book 5, chapter 24, that John was buried at Ephesus and lay there awaiting the final resurrection.] that he would not taste death until the Lord came again to judge, since he himself says in the Gospel: “I want him to remain thus until I come” [Note: [Col. 0174D] This is the reading of the Bec, Regius, and Regius manuscripts, together with the Bad and Ill printed editions; our Vulgate still retains this reading. Others read, “If I want him,” as the Greek reads and as appears in several Latin manuscripts.] (John 21:21).

## XXV

Trajan, the third after Nero, began a persecution against the Christians. Under him the blessed Clement, the third bishop of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0174D] The Corbie manuscript reads, “was bishop of the Church. He suffered,” etc.], suffered martyrdom; and the holy Simeon, bishop of Jerusalem and son of Cleophas, is said to have been crucified for Christ’s name. Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, was taken to Rome and handed over to the beasts. These events occurred in the time of Trajan [Col. 0174B].

## XXVI

After him Aelius Hadrian was made emperor [Note: [Col. 0174D] This chapter and the following one are absent from the Corbie manuscript.]. Hence Jerusalem was called Aelia after Aelius Hadrian, the successor of Domitian, because he restored it.

After these sufferings of the saints, it was not enough for the opposing party to stir unbelieving nations against the worshipers of Christ; it also had to stir up schisms among the Christians themselves. It incited heresies, and the divided Catholic faith was expounded in different ways.

Under the rule of Antoninus, the insane Marcionite and Valentinian heresy arose [Note: [Col. 0174D] The Regius manuscript reads, “the insane heresies arose.”]. Justin the Philosopher, after writing books for the Catholic Church, was crowned with martyrdom for Christ’s name.

In Asia, when persecution arose, the most blessed Polycarp, a disciple of the apostle and evangelist John, was consecrated to the Lord through fire at the age of eighty, like a most pure burnt offering [Col. 0174C]. In Gaul also many were crowned with heavenly jewels through martyrdom for Christ’s name; the accounts of their sufferings are faithfully preserved among us to this day [Note: [Col. 0174D] Namely, in the letter of the martyrs of Lyon, which Eusebius reports in his *Ecclesiastical History.* We have included it, together with the sufferings of the martyrs mentioned above, among the genuine Acts of the Martyrs.].

## XXVII

Among these was Photinus, the first bishop of the Church of Lyon. Full of days and subjected to various punishments, he suffered for Christ’s name.

The most blessed Irenaeus, successor of this martyr, who had been sent to that city by the blessed Polycarp, shone with admirable virtue. Within a short time, through his preaching, he restored the city to the Christian faith almost in its entirety.

When persecution came, however, the devil waged such wars there through the tyrant, and so great a multitude of Christians was slaughtered for confessing the Lord’s name [Col. 0174D], that rivers of Christian blood flowed through the streets [Col. 0175A]. We could gather neither their number nor their names, for the Lord has written them in the book of life.

The executioner, in the presence of the blessed Irenaeus, subjected him to various torments and dedicated him to the Lord Christ through martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0175C] Saint Gregory the Great complains in book 9, letter 50, that he could not find the writings and deeds of Saint Irenaeus together. We possess most of his writings, but no one has yet produced an authentic account of his deeds. Jerome gives Irenaeus the title of martyr.].

After him forty-eight martyrs suffered [Note: [Col. 0175C] They suffered not after Irenaeus, but before him, together with Bishop Photinus. Gregory himself gives their names in book 1 of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 49.], among whom we read that Vettius Epagathus was the first.

## XVIII

Under the emperor Decius, many wars arose against the Christian name, and such slaughter took place among the believers that they cannot even be counted.

Babylas, bishop of Antioch, with three children [Note: [Col. 0175D] This is the reading of all the manuscripts and the Bad printed edition; others, together with the Bec manuscript, read “brothers.” Chrysostom and others mention three boys killed with Babylas.], namely Urbanus, Prilidanus, and Epolonus; Sixtus, bishop of the Roman Church; Laurentius the archdeacon; and Hippolytus were brought to completion through martyrdom for confessing the Lord’s name [Col. 0175B].

Valentinian and Novatian, then the chief leaders of the heretics [Note: [Col. 0175D] The Corbie manuscript reads, “then especially heretics, whose leaders,” etc.], raged against our faith at the urging of the enemy.

During his reign, seven men who had been ordained bishops were sent to preach in Gaul, as the account of the passion of the holy martyr Saturninus relates [Note: [Col. 0175D] The Acts of Saint Saturninus indicate the time of his mission to Gaul, but say nothing about the others listed here; different writers assign their arrival in Gaul to different periods. Gregory, however, believing that they came to Gaul together, derived the dates of the others as well from the certain chronological point given in the Acts of Saint Saturninus.].

For it says:

“Under the consuls Decius and Gratus, as faithful memory preserves it, the city of Toulouse first began to have the holy Saturninus as its chief priest.”

They were sent as follows: to Tours, Bishop Gatianus [Note: [Col. 0175D] The Regius manuscript reads *Gazianus*, and so below. The printed editions, together with the Regius manuscript, read *Gratianus*.]; to Arles, Bishop Trophimus; to Narbonne, Bishop Paul; to Toulouse, Bishop Saturninus; to Paris, Bishop Dionysius; to Clermont, Bishop Stremonius; and to Limoges, Bishop Martial.

Among these, the blessed Dionysius, bishop of Paris, after being subjected to various punishments for Christ’s name, ended his present life by the sword.

Saturninus, already secure in his martyrdom, said to his two priests:

“Behold, I am now being sacrificed, and the time of my release is at hand. I ask you not to abandon me completely until I fulfill the appointed end.”

When he was seized and led to the Capitol, he was left alone and dragged along. Therefore [Note: [Col. 0175D] Gregory reported what follows from popular tradition. These details are not found in the Acts of Saint Saturninus, which you may see among the genuine Acts of the Martyrs, p. 109. I imprudently assigned them there to about the year 245, around which time Saturninus came to Gaul, although he was not established as bishop of Toulouse until the consulship of Decius and Gratus, that is, in the year 251.], when he saw that he had been abandoned by them, he is said to have prayed:

“Lord Jesus Christ, hear me from your holy heaven, so that this Church may never deserve to have a bishop from among its citizens.”

We know that this has continued to happen in that very city to the present day.

He was then tied to the feet of a raging bull, hurled down from the Capitol, and ended his life.

Gatianus, Trophimus, Stremonius, Paul, and Martial, living in the highest holiness [Note: [Col. 0176C] The Regius manuscript reads, “in the highest religious devotion.”], after gathering peoples for the Church and spreading the faith of Christ everywhere, departed in a blessed confession. Thus both those who left the earth through martyrdom and those who left it through confession were united together in heaven.

## XXIX

Of these men’s disciples, one came to the city of Bourges and announced Christ, the Savior of all, to its peoples [Note: [Col. 0176C] This chapter is absent from the Corbie manuscript. Gregory calls this man Ursinus in *The Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 80, and says there that he was ordained by the apostles’ disciples and sent to Gaul. He speaks in the same way about Saturninus in *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 48. It is clear that Bourges was the name of the city itself, while the inhabitants or citizens were called Bituriges, from a sermon by Sidonius Apollinaris delivered for the election of the bishop of Bourges, book 7, letter 9, where he says, “Previously I knew the Bituriges before I knew Bourges”—that is, he knew Simplicius, the citizen for whom he was pleading, before he had ever gone to Bourges.].

Thus a very few believers from among them were ordained clerics, undertook the practice of psalmody, and were instructed in how they should build a church and celebrate solemn rites for almighty God.

Since they still had little ability to build, they sought the house of a certain citizen, so that they might turn it into a church. The senators and other leading men of the place were then bound to pagan rites; those who had believed were poor, in accordance with the Lord’s saying reproaching the Jews: “For prostitutes and tax collectors will go before you into the kingdom of God” (Matthew 21:31).

When they had not obtained the house from the person they had asked, they found Leocadius, the first senator of Gaul, who was descended from Vettius Epagathus, whom we mentioned above as having suffered for Christ’s name at Lyon [Note: [Col. 0176D] Above, chapter 27.] [Col. 0176C]. When they had explained their request and their faith to him, he replied:

“If my house, which I have at the city of Bourges, were suitable for this work, I would not refuse to provide it.”

When they heard this, they fell at his feet and, after offering three hundred gold pieces together with a silver dish, declared that it was fully suitable for this ministry [Note: [Col. 0176D] Thus read the Bec, Regius, and Regius manuscripts; the others read, “suitable.” The Tours manuscript, cited by Morel, reads: “For if my house … I would not refuse to provide it … to be suitable for this mystery.” Observe that this chapter, which is absent from the Corbie manuscript, is found in the Tours manuscript.].

Then, accepting three gold pieces from them as a blessing and kindly waiving the rest, he—although still entangled in the error of idolatry—became a Christian and made his house into a church [Col. 0177A]. This is now the first church in the city of Bourges, splendidly constructed and illuminated by the relics of the first martyr Stephen [Note: [Col. 0177C] Even today the principal church of Bourges, dedicated to Saint Stephen, yields to few sacred buildings in Gaul.].

## XXX

[25] In the twenty-seventh place, Valerian and Gallienus obtained the Roman Empire. During their time they stirred up a severe persecution against the Christians.

At that time Cornelius at Rome [Note: [Col. 0177C] Cornelius nevertheless died in the year 252, during the reign of Decius, and, as is more probable, at Centumcellae, where he received his glorious repose, as is recorded in the oldest Bucherian *Pontifical.* Some nevertheless insist that he suffered at Rome; but there is no disagreement concerning the time of his martyrdom. Cyprian was beheaded near Carthage in the year 258, under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus.], and Cyprian at Carthage, glorified those places with their blessed blood.

During their time that Chrocus, king of the Alamanni, also invaded Gaul with an assembled army. Chrocus is said to have been a man of great arrogance. After committing various injustices, and acting, as they say, on the advice of his wicked mother, he gathered the Alamannic people, as we have said [Note: [Col. 0177C] The Bec and Regius manuscripts read, “the people having been gathered”; although this reading is better, it is not necessarily more authentic. Gregory, as he himself admits, frequently used the accusative for the ablative. This single warning should suffice. Others date Chrocus’s invasion to the beginning of the fifth century.], and ravaged all Gaul, overthrowing from their foundations all the buildings that had been constructed in ancient times [Col. 0177B].

When he came to Clermont, he burned, demolished, and overturned that shrine which the Gauls call *Vasso Galatae* in the Gallic language [Note: [Col. 0177D] The Regius manuscript reads *Vasa*. They maintain that by this name the ancient Gauls designated the god Mars.].

It had been built and reinforced with remarkable workmanship, and its wall was double. On the inside it was constructed of small stones; on the outside, of squared and carved blocks. That wall was thirty feet thick. On the interior it was decorated with varied marble and mosaic [Note: [Col. 0177D] The following material, through the next numbered section, is absent from the Regius manuscript. Alteserra conjectures that this same temple was dedicated to Mercury, since Pliny, book 3, chapter 7, writes that in his own time an enormous statue of Mercury had been made by Zenodorus among the Arverni. Pliny’s words are: “Indeed, the whole grandeur of statues of that kind was surpassed in our age by Zenodorus, who made a Mercury in the Gallic city of the Arverni, over ten years, at a cost of four hundred thousand sesterces, by his own hand.”]. The pavement of the building was also laid with marble, while its roof above was covered with lead.

## XXXI

Near this city [Note: [Col. 0177D] This chapter and the following four are absent from the Corbie manuscript.] the martyrs Liminius and Antolianus rest. There, Cassius and Victorinus, joined in brotherly affection through their love of Christ, attained the kingdom of heaven together by the shedding of their own blood.

For antiquity reports that Victorinus had formerly been the slave of the priest of the aforesaid temple. When he often went through the district called the Christians’ quarter to persecute Christians, he encountered Cassius, a Christian [Col. 0177C]. Moved by Cassius’s preaching and miracles [Col. 0178A], he believed in Christ. Abandoning his filthy pagan rites and being consecrated through baptism, he shone greatly in the working of miracles.

Not long afterward, as we have said, they were joined together on earth through martyrdom and departed together for the heavenly kingdoms [Note: [Col. 0177D] Ancient martyrologies commemorate the feasts of these martyrs. The passions of Saints Cassius, Victorinus, Antholianus [Col. 0178C], and Astrebundius, together with those of the other saints crowned in that city, are said to have been written by the blessed Praejectus, according to the second author of the Life of Praejectus in the second Benedictine century. Gregory also writes about them elsewhere. Saints Cassius and Victorinus rested in the church of Saint Cassius, which is now a parish church; Antolianus rested in the church of Saint Gall, according to book 1 of Savaron’s published *Book of the Churches of Clermont*, chapters 9 and 8. Liminius, according to Gregory himself in *The Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 36, was preserved in the church of Saint Venerandus.].

## XXXII

When the Alamanni invaded Gaul, Saint Privatus, bishop of the city of Gabala [Note: [Col. 0178C] His feast is celebrated on August 21. The seat of the bishop of Gabala, formerly at Anderitum, was transferred to Mende around the tenth century and remains there today.], was found in the crypt of Mount Memmat, where he was occupied with fasting and prayer, while the people of the fortress of Gredon were shut up in its defenses [Note: [Col. 0178D] So reads the Regius manuscript; the others, together with the printed editions, read, “shut up in the defenses of the people of the fortress of Gredon.” Gredo is thought to be a village situated at the foot of the mountain, commonly called Greze. There is, however, a viscounty of Credon in Gévaudan, and the Regius manuscript together with the Bad printed edition reads *Credonensis*.].

But since the good shepherd would not consent to hand over his sheep to wolves, he was compelled to sacrifice to demons. Abominating and rejecting this profane act, he was beaten with clubs until he was thought to be lifeless. From the very blows, however, after a few days, he breathed out his spirit.

Chrocus was captured near the Gallic city of Arles and, subjected to various punishments, died after being struck with the sword, deservedly paying the penalties for the injuries he had inflicted upon God’s saints [Col. 0178B].

## XXXIII

Under Diocletian, who was the thirty-third to rule the Roman Empire, a severe persecution against the Christians was carried on for four years [Note: [Col. 0178D] Diocletian’s persecution cannot in any way be restricted to four years. See our preface to the *Genuine Acts of the Martyrs* on this matter.]. Thus, on one occasion, on the very sacred day of Easter, large crowds of Christians were killed for the worship of the true God.

At that time Quirinus, priest of the Church of Siscia [Note: [Col. 0178D] The manuscripts Bec, Regius, and Regius correctly read this. The printed editions mistakenly read *Sistiensis*. Siscia was an episcopal city in Upper Pannonia, where Quirinus suffered; Prudentius mentions him in hymn 7 of *The Crowns*. See his Acts among the genuine martyrs, p. 552, under the year 309.], endured glorious martyrdom for Christ’s name. The pagans tied a millstone around his neck and hurled him violently into the whirlpool of a river.

When he had fallen into the whirlpool [27], he was carried for a long time upon the waters by divine power; the waters did not swallow the man whom the weight of guilt did not oppress [Col. 0178C].

The crowd standing around marveled at this event and, despising the fury of the pagans, hurried to rescue the priest. Seeing this, he did not allow himself to be removed from martyrdom [Col. 0179A], but, raising his eyes to heaven, said:

“Lord Jesus, who in glory sit at the right hand of the Father, do not allow me to be removed from this arena. Rather, receive my soul and graciously join me with your martyrs in everlasting rest.”

After saying this, he gave up his spirit. Christians took his body and reverently committed it to burial.

## XXXIV

Constantine, the thirty-fourth Roman emperor, obtained the Empire and ruled prosperously for thirty years.

In the eleventh year of his reign, after peace had been restored to the Churches following Diocletian’s death, the most blessed bishop Martin was born at the city of Sabaria in Pannonia [Note: [Col. 0179C] Today, as is thought, it is a town in Hungary called Szombathely, formerly Stain am Angern, in the county of Eisenburg. Cluverius, however, believes that ancient Sabaria once existed where the castle of Sarwar now stands, which the Germans call Rothenturn, three leagues below the aforesaid town, at the confluence of the Sabaria River with the Arrabo.], to pagan parents, though not of the lowest rank.

In the twentieth year of his reign, Constantine killed his son Crispus with poison and his wife Fausta in a heated bath [Col. 0179B], allegedly because they had wished to betray his rule.

During his reign, the venerable wood of the Lord’s cross was discovered through the efforts of his mother Helena, as revealed by the Hebrew Judas, who after baptism was called Quiriacus.

Up to this point, the historian Eusebius writes in his *Chronicles*. From the twenty-first year of Constantine’s reign, the presbyter Jerome added an account, stating that the presbyter Juvencus composed the Gospels in verse at the request of the emperor mentioned above.

## XXXV

Under the reign of Constans, Jacob of Nisibis [Note: [Col. 0179C] Some printed editions mistakenly read *Niebenus*. This is the famous James, bishop who freed the Mesopotamian city of Nisibis from the siege of Sapor, king of the Persians, in the year 350. Unless Gregory himself has erred, one should read “Constantius” instead of “Constans.”] lived. At his prayers the ears of divine mercy inclined, and they drove many dangers away from his city.

Maximinus, bishop of Trier, was also found to be powerful in every form of holiness.

In the nineteenth year of the younger Constantius [Note: [Col. 0179D] So reads the Regius manuscript. Others read “Constantine,” but this is erroneous, for Constantine the Younger was killed in the fourth year of his reign. Gregory here calls Constantius “the younger,” perhaps to distinguish him from Constantius Chlorus.], Antony the monk died, in the one hundred and fifth year [Note: [Col. 0179D] The printed editions, together with the Regius manuscript, read “in the hundredth year,” but this is erroneous.] of his life.

The most blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, was sent into exile at the urging of the heretics. There, writing books in defense of the Catholic faith, he sent them to Constantius, who in the fourth year of his exile ordered him released and allowed him to return home.

## XXXVI

Then our light also arose [Note: [Col. 0179D] Everything up to “Melania,” however, is absent from the Regius manuscript.] and Gaul was illuminated by the rays of new lamps [Col. 0180A]. That is, at that time the most blessed Martin began to preach in Gaul. By many miracles he declared Christ, the Son of God, to be the true God among the peoples and turned away the unbelief of the pagans.

He destroyed shrines, suppressed heresy, built churches, and, while shining with many other virtues, completed the summit of his praise by restoring three dead persons to life.

In the fourth year of Valentinian and Valens, Saint Hilary, full of holiness and faith, after displaying many miracles on every side, departed to heaven from Poitiers [Note: [Col. 0179D] Authors disagree concerning the day and year on which Saint Hilary died. The matter is discussed more fully in his Life, recently published by our people before his works, no. 113 and following. His feast is celebrated on the Ides of January in ancient and recent martyrologies; it is more probable that he died on that day in the year 368 [Col. 0180C]. Fortunatus reports that he raised a dead infant in book 1, no. 12 of his Life. Gregory also discusses this saint in *The Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 2. Besides Jerome, other holy Fathers describe Melania’s praises at length. During Valens’s time she was especially distinguished for supporting and concealing the confessors whom he persecuted. On one occasion she fed five thousand monks for three days while they were fleeing the tyrant’s ambushes. See Saint Paulinus’s letter to Severus, formerly letter 10, in the new edition, 29. Rosweyd notes, in his annotations on Rufinus and Melania’s pilgrimage, that Gregory erred here by calling Urbanus Melania’s son. He misunderstood a passage in Jerome’s *Chronicle*, where Jerome says that the little son of Melania had been praetor *Urbanus*, that is, praetor of the city of Rome; Gregory interpreted this as though *Urbanus* were the child’s name.]. For he too is said to have raised the dead.

Melania, a noble matron and resident of Rome, went to Jerusalem out of devotion, leaving her son Urbanus in Rome. She displayed herself to everyone in such complete goodness and holiness that the inhabitants called her Thecla.

## XXXVII

After Valentinian’s death, Valens, his successor in the undivided Empire, ordered monks to be compelled into military service and commanded that those who refused be beaten with clubs.

Afterward the Romans fought a most savage war in Thrace [Note: [Col. 0180D] Several manuscripts read *Thraciae*; some, together with the printed editions, read *Thraces*. Gregory of Nyssa, Sozomen, Theodoret, and others describe at length the persecution of Valens and the glorious confessions of the orthodox. The law against monks is found in book 26, *On the Decurions*. Valens died on August 9 in the year 378, after reigning a little more than fifteen years.], in which there was such slaughter that the Romans, having lost the support of their horses, fled on foot.

When they were being cut down in a tremendous massacre by the Goths, and Valens, wounded by an arrow, was fleeing, he entered a small hut. As the enemies approached, the hut was set on fire over him, and he was deprived of the burial he desired.

Thus divine vengeance, because of the blood shed by the saints, finally came forth.

Up to this point Jerome has written; from this time onward the presbyter Orosius wrote more.

## XXXVIII

[Col. 0180C] Therefore, when the emperor Gratian saw that the state had been abandoned [Note: [Col. 0180D] The Regius manuscript reads “destroyed.”], he made Theodosius his colleague in the Empire.

Theodosius placed all his hope and confidence in God’s mercy. He subdued many peoples not so much by the sword as by vigils and prayer, restored the state [Note: [Col. 0180D] The Regius manuscript reads, “and, restoring the state,”], and entered Constantinople as a victorious ruler.

Maximus, however, after winning a victory through tyranny over the oppressed Britons [Col. 0181A], was proclaimed emperor by the soldiers. Establishing his seat at Trier [Note: [Col. 0181C] The same manuscript reads, “establishing a seat for himself.”], he surrounded the emperor Gratian with treachery and killed him.

The blessed Martin, already a bishop, came to Maximus.

In Gratian’s place, Theodosius—who had placed all his hope in God—assumed the entire Empire. Then, relying upon divine inspiration, he killed Maximus, stripped of his imperial power [Note: [Col. 0181C] Here book 1 ends in the Regius manuscript. Everything up to book 2 is absent except the closing formula: “Here ends book 1, from the beginning of the world to the passing of Saint Martin; 5,546 years are reckoned.” In the Corbie manuscript the next four chapters are omitted, but the final one is present. In the Vatican manuscript those same four chapters, which the Corbie manuscript lacks, are absent. It should also be noted here that certain other chapters are missing from the Vatican manuscript in the earlier books of Gregory; since their catalog has not yet been received, it has not been possible to assign them to their proper places. Thus, besides the four chapters mentioned above that are absent from book 1, book 2 lacks chapters 14, 15, 16, 17, 21, 22, 23, 26, and 39; chapters 1 and 4 do not appear in their proper places but are found at the end of the book. Book 4 lacks four chapters, namely 5, 6, 7, and 12. Book 5 lacks thirteen: 5, 7, 9, 10, 12, 33, 37, 38, 41, 43, 46, 47, and 49. The remaining omissions are noted in their proper places.].

## XXXIX

Among the Arverni, after Bishop and preacher Stremonius, the first bishop was Urbicus, a convert from the senatorial class. He had a wife who, according to ecclesiastical custom, lived religiously, withdrawn from association with the priest [30]. Both of them devoted themselves to prayer, almsgiving, and good works.

While they were engaged in these things, the envy of the enemy, who is always hostile to holiness, was stirred against the woman. Setting her ablaze with desire for her husband, he made her a new Eve. Inflamed by lust and covered by the darkness of sin, the woman went through the darkness of night to the church’s house.

When she found everything locked, she began to knock on the doors of the church and to cry out in words such as these:

“How long will you sleep, priest? How long will you fail to open the closed doors? Why do you despise your wife [Note: [Col. 0181D] The Bec and Regius manuscripts read, “Why do you despise your attendant … why do you stop your ears,” etc. Above, in chapter 2, a husband is called an attendant. The Tours manuscript also reads, “Why do you despise your attendant,” etc.]? Why, with your ears stopped, do you not hear Paul’s command? For he wrote: ‘Return to one another, lest Satan tempt you.’ Behold, I return to you—not to a stranger, but to my own vessel I return.”

After she had declaimed these and similar words for a long time [Note: [Col. 0181D] The Regius manuscript reads, “while she was declaiming,” and continues: “At last the priest’s religious devotion grew lukewarm, and he ordered her to enter the bedroom and, after intercourse, to depart.”], the priest’s religious devotion at last grew weak. He ordered her to be brought into the bedroom, and after having intercourse with her, ordered her to leave.

Then, returning to his senses only later and grieving over the crime he had committed, he went to the monastery of his diocese to do penance. There, washing away what he had done with groaning and tears, he returned to his own city and, having completed the course of his life, departed from this world.

A daughter was born from this intercourse [Note: [Col. 0181D] The printed editions and the Bec manuscript read “from this conception.” It should be observed that the word *religion* is used here to express a state of holier life, as Gregory often does elsewhere.], and she remained in religious devotion.

The priest himself, together with his wife and daughter, was buried in the crypt of Cantobennum [Note: [Col. 0181D] The Regius manuscript reads *Catabennum*; the Bad printed edition reads *Cantobonum*, commonly Chantoin. A convent for women later existed there, whose church was dedicated to Saint Peter, as recorded in Savaron’s catalogue of the churches of Clermont, book 1, chapter 26. The regular canons of the cathedral church withdrew there; when the secular chapter of Clermont had been given secular dress, they refused to renounce the Rule [Col. 0182C]. In the same little book, chapter 8, Saint Urbicus is said to have been buried in the church of Saint Gall, though perhaps he had already been moved from that place. Indeed, he was later transferred again to the church of Saint Illidius. The monastery of Cantobennum is discussed below, book 2, chapter 21. Robert, abbot of Cantinobum, is mentioned in the appendix to the *History of the Translation of Saint Austremonius* in Labbe, volume 2 of the *New Library*, p. 506.], beside the public embankment [Note: [Col. 0182C] Two printed editions read “Publianum.” The term “public embankment” designates public or military roads.].

In his place Legonus [Note: [Col. 0182C] Is this Saint Linguinus, who is said to be buried in the church of Saint Venerandus in chapter 10 of book 1 of the *Churches of Clermont*? Savaron thinks that this is rather the martyr Liminius. In book 2, chapter 18, he mentions a church of Saint Leogontius, where the same saint—whom Savaron considers to be Gregory’s Legonus—is said to rest [Col. 0182D].] was appointed bishop.

### XL

When he had died, Saint Illidius succeeded him, a man of extraordinary holiness and distinguished virtue. He shone with such sanctity that his fame reached even foreign lands. Thus he was sought out by the daughter of the emperor of Trier and cured her of an unclean spirit—as we recorded in the book that we composed about his Life. [Note: The Regius manuscript and the edition of Bad. read this way; the others have: “so that, being sought by the daughter of the emperor of Trier, he cured her in spirit,” etc.]

According to report, he was very old, full of days, and rich in good works. Having happily completed the course of this life, he departed to Christ and was buried in a crypt in the suburb [Note: The edition of Bad. has *suburbio* (“in the suburb”); the Regius manuscript has *suburbana*.] of that city. He also had an archdeacon named Justus, both in name and in merit, [Note: He is mentioned among the saints who rested in the church of Saint Illidius, in Book I *On the Churches of Clermont*, chapter 2, although he is mistakenly called a bishop in the heading. Unless, perhaps, there were two Justuses, one an archdeacon and the other a bishop. For in the same book, chapter 14, Justus is said to rest in the church of Saint Cyricus. See Sirmond on Letter II, Book IV, of Sidonius. The feast of Justus is mentioned in the Illidian tables on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November. We shall say more about Saint Illidius in his Life, which is among the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 2.] and who, completing the course of his life in good works, was buried beside his master’s tomb.

After the passing of the blessed confessor Illidius, such great miracles appeared at his glorious tomb that they can neither be fully written down nor retained in memory. Saint Nepotianus succeeded him.

### XLI

Accordingly, among the Arverni Saint Nepotianus was regarded as the fourth bishop. [Note: Even according to Gregory’s reckoning Nepotianus is the fifth bishop of the Arverni. See the book *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 37, concerning his tomb.]

At that time envoys were being sent from Trier to Spain. Among them was a certain Artemius, remarkable for wisdom and beauty and flourishing in the prime of life; he was seized by a violent fever. Since the others went on ahead, he was left behind sick among the Arverni. [Col. 0182C] For at that time he was bound by an engagement among the people of Trier.

Saint Nepotianus visited him, anointed him with holy oil, and, by the Lord’s gift, restored him to health. After receiving from that same saint the word of preaching, Artemius forgot both his earthly bride and his own possessions. He was joined to the holy Church and became a cleric, advancing in such holiness that he succeeded the blessed Nepotianus in governing the sheepfolds of the Lord’s flock. [Note: The church of Saint Artemius is mentioned in the little book *On the Churches of Clermont*, chapter 29. Savaro laments in his notes on this book that it was destroyed and profaned, and that the stone coffin which once contained the bones of the blessed man was trampled under the feet of passersby. His feast is celebrated on 24 January.]

### XLII

At that time a certain Injuriosus, one of the Arvernian senators, sought, with his great wealth, a girl of equal rank as his wife; after giving a pledge, he appointed the day of the wedding. Each was an only child of his father.

When the appointed day arrived and the marriage ceremony had been celebrated, they were placed in one bed according to custom. [The number 32 appears here in the edition.] But the girl, deeply saddened, turned toward the wall and wept most bitterly. He said to her:

“Why are you troubled? Please tell me.”

When she remained silent, the man added:

“I beg you by Jesus Christ, the Son of God, to explain wisely to me what grieves you.”

Then she turned toward him and said:

“If I weep throughout all the days of my life, will my tears ever be so abundant that they can wash away the immense sorrow of my heart? For I had resolved to preserve my little body undefiled for Christ, untouched by a man. But woe is me, who have been so abandoned by him that I could not accomplish what I desired, and have lost on this final day—which I ought never to have seen—what I preserved from the beginning of my life.

“For behold, abandoned by immortal Christ, who promised me paradise as my dowry, I have been allotted the companionship of a mortal man; and instead of unfading roses, the withered spoil of roses adorns me not but disfigures me. [Note: The Regius manuscript reads: ‘they do not adorn but disfigure the bridal garments … beside the four-streamed river.’]

“And when I ought to have put on the robe of purity above the four-streamed river of the Lamb, this garment has brought me a burden, not an honor.

“But why prolong our words? Wretched am I, who ought by my lot to have earned the heavenly realms, but today am plunged into the abyss. Oh, if this was to be my future, why was not the very day of my life’s beginning also its end? Oh, if only I had entered the gate of death before I received nourishment from milk! Oh, if only the kisses of gentle nurses had been spent at my funeral!

“For earthly appearances fill me with horror, because I behold the pierced hands of the Redeemer for the life of the world. I do not gaze upon diadems glittering with splendid jewels, since in my mind I contemplate that crown of thorns. I reject the broad spaces of your land, extending far and wide, because I long for the beauty of paradise. Your upper chambers fill me with horror [Note: Bign. and others have *solatia* (“comforts”); *solaria* is more correct, meaning the upper parts of buildings.], when I behold the Lord seated above the stars.”

Moved by compassion when she uttered these words with great weeping, the young man said:

“Our most noble Arvernian parents, each of us an only child, wished us to be joined so that, when they departed from the world, a stranger heir might not succeed them.”

She replied:

“The world is nothing; riches are nothing; the pomp of this age is nothing; the very life that we enjoy is nothing. Rather, that life must be sought which is not closed when death brings it to an end, which is not dissolved by any stain, nor terminated by any decline; where a person, remaining in eternal blessedness, lives in light that does not set.

“And, greater than all these things, rejoicing in the Lord’s own presence and enjoying continual contemplation, translated into an angelic state, he delights in imperishable joy.”

He answered:

“Through your sweetest words, eternal life has shone upon me like a great radiance. Therefore, if you wish to abstain from carnal desire, I shall become a participant in your mind.”

She replied: [Col. 0184B]

“It is difficult for women to expect such conduct from the male sex. Nevertheless, if you will act so that we remain undefiled in this world, I shall grant you a share of the dowry that has been promised to me by my bridegroom, the Lord Jesus Christ, to whom I have vowed myself both as servant and as bride.”

Then, armed with the banner of the cross, he said:

“I shall do what you urge.”

They gave each other their right hands and lay down. For many years afterward they lived reclining in one bed, with praiseworthy chastity. This was later revealed at their deaths.

For when the girl, having completed the contest, departed to Christ, the man performed the funeral rites. As he placed the girl in the tomb, he said:

“I give you thanks, eternal Lord our God, because just as I received this treasure entrusted by you, so I restore it undefiled to your mercy.”

At this she smiled slightly and said: [Col. 0184C]

“What are you saying when no one has asked you?”

After she had been buried, he himself followed her not long afterward. [The number 34 appears here in the edition.]

When the tombs of both had been placed against different walls, a novel miracle appeared that revealed their chastity. For at dawn, when the people came to the place, they found the tombs together, although they had left them far apart—clearly so that, since heaven holds them as companions, the monument of their buried bodies might not separate them here.

To this day the inhabitants of the place have wished to call them “the Two Lovers.” We also mentioned them in the book of the *Miracles*. [Note: In the book *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 32. These Two Lovers were buried in the church of Saint Illidius. The girl’s name, which is not expressed here, may be gathered from Book I *On the Churches of Clermont*, where, in chapter 11, Saint Injuriosus and Scholastica are said to rest bodily in the church of Illidius. Since Gregory calls Injuriosus one of the two here, there is no doubt that the woman was Scholastica, who had been given to him in marriage.]

### XLIII

In the second year of the reign of Arcadius and Honorius, [Note: The Clermont manuscript, in which this chapter is read under the title of a sermon by Gregory of Tours, as also in many other manuscripts, has: “When Arcadius and Honorius were emperors, Saint …” The Corbie manuscript, nine hundred years old, likewise has this under the title *Letter on the Passing of Saint Martin*.] Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, full of miracles and holiness and granting many benefits to the sick, departed happily from this world to Christ in the eighty-first year of his life and the twenty-sixth of his episcopate, at Condat, a village of his diocese. [Note: It is commonly called Candes. It lies on the boundary of the territories of Tours and Angers, at the confluence of the Vienne and Loire, from which it took its name. For the ancient Gauls called the confluence of two rivers *Condatum*.]

He passed away at midnight, on what was counted as Sunday, during the consulship of Atticus and Caesarius. [Note: So the Corbie and German manuscripts; others have *Caesarico*, and some *Caesareo*. These consuls designate the year 397 of the common era, which Cointius, in volume I of the *Ecclesiastical Annals of France*, under the year 498, thinks and argues was Martin’s final year. Scaliger, in Book VI of *The Correction of the Times*, insists that he died in 395. Others assign another year, as may be seen in the distinguished Joseph Antelmius’s special dissertation on this matter. Indeed, since neither Severus Sulpicius nor Gregory himself is consistent in identifying chronological markers, each preferring his own calculation, they have gone off into differing opinions. For us it is enough to reproduce Gregory’s text as it appears in the manuscripts and printed editions, leaving each person free to choose.]

Many heard choirs singing in heaven at his passing, as we explained more fully in the first book of his miracles, chapters 4 and 5. When the holy man of God first began to fall ill at Condat, as we have said, the people of Poitiers gathered for his passing just as the people of Tours did.

When he departed, a great dispute arose between the two peoples. The people of Poitiers said:

“He is our monk; he was our abbot; we demand what has been entrusted to us. You may be satisfied that, while he was a bishop in the world, you enjoyed his conversation, shared his table, were strengthened by his blessings, and were also delighted by his miracles. Let all these things be enough for you. Allow us at least to take away the lifeless corpse.” [The number 35 appears here in the edition.]

The people of Tours answered:

“If you say that the deeds of his miracles are enough for us, know that, while he was with you, he performed more miracles than he did here. To pass over many examples, he raised two dead men for you, but one for us; and, as he himself often used to say, [Note: Severus Sulpicius bears witness to the same in Dialogue 2 *On the Miracles of the Same Saint*.] his power was greater before his episcopate than after it. Therefore it is necessary that what he did not complete with us while alive, he should complete at least when dead. He was taken away from you, but given to us by God.

“Yet if the ancient custom is observed, he will have his tomb in the city where he was ordained, by God’s command. Certainly, if you wish to claim him by the privilege of the monastery, know that his first monastery was with the people of Milan.” [Note: The Clermont manuscript, two Corbie manuscripts, the German manuscript, and the Vincentian manuscript read this way. Others have “by the privilege of the monastery.”]

While they were arguing, the sun declined and night closed in. The body, placed in the midst, was guarded by both peoples, the doors having been secured with bars, since it was expected that the people of Poitiers would carry it away by force at daybreak. But almighty God did not wish to deprive the city of Tours of its own patron.

At midnight, therefore, the entire Poitevin company was overcome by sleep, and no one remained awake from that multitude.

When the people of Tours saw that they were asleep, they seized the clod of the most holy body. Some threw it out through a window; others received it outside. They placed it in a boat and, with all the people, descended the river Vienne. [Note: Also *Vigenna*; some manuscripts have *Vincenna*, “la Viane,” or “la Vignanne”; it is commonly called the Vienne. It rises in Limousin, waters several towns of that region as well as of Poitou, and finally flows into the Loire near Condat.]

Entering the channel of the Loire, they proceeded toward the city of Tours with great praise and abundant psalmody. Awakened by their voices, the people of Poitiers, having nothing of the treasure they had been guarding, returned to their own country in great confusion.

If anyone should ask why, after the passing of Bishop Gatianus, only one bishop—namely Litorius [Note: Several manuscripts and printed editions have *Lidorius*. Sulpicius Severus, in the book *On the Life of Saint Martin*, chapter 8, suggests that several bishops ought to be placed between Gatianus and Martin. There, speaking of an altar of a certain pseudo-martyr which Martin overturned, he says that it had been established by earlier bishops. Since it would be impious to attribute this to Saint Gatianus, the first bishop, other intermediate bishops appear to have to be admitted.]—had been bishop until Saint Martin, let him know that, because of pagan opposition, the city of Tours remained for a long time without priestly blessing. For those who appeared to be Christians at that time celebrated the divine office secretly and in hiding. If any Christians were discovered by the pagans, they were either beaten or beheaded with the sword.

From the Passion of the Lord until the passing of Saint Martin, 412 years are reckoned. [Note: Scaliger, in Book VI of *The Correction of the Times* and at the end of Books IV and VI, thinks that 362 should be read here; adding the thirty-three years of Christ’s life to that number yields the year 395.]

The first book is completed. It contains 5,546 years, reckoned from the beginning of the world until the passing of Saint Martin the bishop.

# BOOK TWO

## Prologue

Following the order of times, we recount together, in confused interweaving, both the miracles of the saints and the slaughter of nations. For I do not think it unreasonable to recall the blessed life of the saints amid the disasters of the wretched, since this is produced not by the writer’s facility but by the sequence of events.

For the attentive reader, if he searches diligently, will find among those histories of the Israelite kings that, under the just Samuel, the sacrilegious Phinehas perished, and that under David, whom they call “Strong of hand,” [Note: So the Corbie manuscript; others have “strong in hand.”] Goliath the foreigner fell.

Let him also remember that in the time of Elijah, that outstanding prophet who took away the rains whenever he wished and poured them upon the parched lands whenever he pleased, and who enriched the poverty of the widow by prayer, there were great slaughters of peoples, great famines, and a drought that oppressed the afflicted earth.

Let him remember what evils Jerusalem endured in the time of Hezekiah, to whom God added fifteen years of life. And under the prophet Elisha, who restored the dead to life and performed many other miracles among the peoples, how many massacres and what miseries oppressed the Israelite people.

Thus Eusebius, Severus, and Jerome in their Chronicles, as well as Orosius, wove together the wars of kings and the miracles of martyrs. So we too have written in this manner, in order that the sequence of the ages and the reckoning of the years might more easily be found in its entirety down to our own times.

Proceeding, therefore, through the histories of the authors mentioned above, we shall, with the Lord’s help, discuss what was done afterward. [Note: So the Casinensis manuscript; others have “with the Lord’s command.”]

### I

[Note: This chapter is absent from the Corbie and Regius manuscripts. Moreover, some learned men of our time who do not approve Gregory’s account think that he was mistaken here in confusing Brictio, about whom Sulpicius wrote at the end of Dialogue 3, with Brictius of Saint Martin, whom they maintain were entirely different people.

First, neither Sulpicius nor Fortunatus, who also mentions Brictio, says that he succeeded Martin. Second, it does not seem likely that a man so criminal as Brictio is described by those authors would have succeeded so great a man in the episcopate. Third, if Brictio had succeeded Martin, Sulpicius, who wrote the Dialogues while Brictio was seated at Tours, would either have concealed his many crimes or at least suppressed his name.

Finally, Sulpicius and Fortunatus called him Brictio, whereas Martin’s successor is called Briccius even by Gregory himself. Some also maintain that this entire chapter of Gregory’s History was added by an interpolator, since it is absent from the oldest manuscripts, namely the Corbie and Beauvais manuscripts, and since it contains many things that are not sufficiently consistent with one another to be regarded as written by Gregory: namely, that a vain man succeeded Martin; that, at least seventy years old, he was accused of adultery; and that he remained in Rome for seven years to defend his case.

They add that the name of the Roman pontiff, who was nevertheless well known to Gregory, has been suppressed; that no other memory of these events exists; and other arguments of the same kind, which the distinguished Joseph Antelmius advances in a letter to the Reverend Father Antoine Pagi, published at Paris in 1693.

Against all these arguments, however, may be set the ancient and constant tradition of the Church of Tours, which has always venerated its Brictius as Gregory represents him and still honors him today with public worship.

The objections brought against this tradition may perhaps not seem strong enough to overturn it altogether. For what is surprising if Brictius, a man not entirely lacking in other good qualities, whose crimes Saint Martin had concealed, and whom Martin himself had educated from childhood in his monastery and ordained priest, was appointed his successor?

Sulpicius did indeed report his insults against the holy man, but he did so at the very time when Brictius, harassed by his own people, openly confessed those things, declaring—as Gregory himself reports—that these calamities had justly befallen him because he had repeatedly attacked the holy man with slanders.

Nor does that slight difference in names cause difficulty, since even the martyrologies, including the most ancient ones, as we have observed in many places, sometimes call this blessed man Brictius and sometimes Brictio.

What is said about Fortunatus does not strengthen the objection, since it is certain that he expressed in verse only what Sulpicius had said in prose.

The arguments offered for denying this history to Gregory are even less significant. It is indeed absent from the Corbie manuscript, but many other passages are missing from that manuscript which are nevertheless certainly written by Gregory, as we prove in their proper places.

Nor can anything be established from the Beauvais manuscript, since, after several leaves had been torn away, the first surviving leaf begins at the end of the third chapter.

Moreover, this history is found in other manuscripts, including ancient and reputable ones, both in Gregory’s own History and in other manuscripts under the title *Life of Saint Brictius*, and indeed under Gregory’s own name.

That a vain man, raised to the episcopate, should have been accused of adultery at the age of seventy; that he should have remained in Rome for seven full years either to defend his case or for any other reason; that Gregory should have suppressed the pontiff’s name; and arguments of this sort are not so strong that they can uproot a tradition hitherto unshaken, since examples are not lacking even in our own times by which Gregory’s account may be approved.

Indeed, Pope Zosimus, in Letter 4 to Aurelius and the African bishops, testifies that Brictius, bishop of the city of Tours, was falsely accused by Lazarus. That Lazarus, as the same pope reports in Letter 6, was condemned at the Council of Turin because he had attacked the life of the innocent bishop Brictius with false accusations.]

After the death of the blessed Martin, bishop of the city of Tours, a supreme and incomparable man whose virtues are preserved in great volumes among us, Brictius succeeded to the episcopate.

But when this Brictius was a young man in the first stage of life, he laid many snares for Saint Martin, who was still living in the body, because Martin often rebuked him for being too ready to pursue frivolous matters. [Note: Latinius thinks that *futiles* should be read in Latin. The Regius, German, and Clermont manuscripts have *cor facile* (“an easy heart”). The first reading should be retained. Gregory uses the word *faciles* in the same sense in Book II of the *Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 1, and frequently elsewhere.]

One day, when a sick man was seeking medicine from blessed Martin, he met the still-deacon Brictius in the street and said to him simply:

“Behold, I am waiting for the blessed man, but I do not know where he is or what he is doing.”

Brictius replied:

“If you are looking for that madman, look into the distance. There he is, gazing at the sky in his usual manner like a lunatic.” [Note: So the Regius manuscript with the two printed editions; others have *solite* (“in the usual manner”), from which Latinius conjectures that *sollicite* (“anxiously”) should be restored.]

When the poor man, after returning to him, obtained what he had requested, the blessed man addressed the deacon Brictius:

“Behold, Brictius, do I seem mad to you?”

When Brictius, embarrassed by these words, denied that he had said them, the holy man replied:

“Were my ears not at your mouth when you were speaking these words at a distance? Truly I tell you: I have obtained from God that after my passing you will attain the honor of the episcopate. But know that you will suffer many adversities in the episcopate.”

When Brictius heard this, he mocked him, saying:

“Was I not right to say that this man utters delirious words?”

Even after he had been ordained a priest, he often provoked the blessed man with insults.

Having obtained the episcopal office with the consent of the citizens, he devoted himself to prayer. For although he was proud and vain, he was considered chaste in body.

In the thirty-third year of his ordination, [Note: The Clermont, German, and Regius manuscripts have “in the thirtieth year.”] a lamentable charge arose against him concerning a crime. A woman to whom his chamberlains customarily brought his clothing for washing, and who had changed her dress under the appearance of religious devotion, [Note: Observe the change of clothing by those who adopted a religious life; this occurs frequently in Gregory, but it is enough to note it once. See the Second Council of Arles, canon 25.] conceived and gave birth.

Because of this, all the people of Tours rose in anger and laid the entire crime at the bishop’s door, wishing unanimously to stone him. They said:

“For a long time the mercy of the holy man concealed your lust. God does not allow us any longer to be defiled by kissing your unworthy hands.” [Note: The Regius manuscript reads: “May God not allow us to be defiled any longer by kissing your unworthy hands.” It is an ancient and thoroughly commendable custom to kiss the hands of bishops, since through the laying on of their hands the Holy Spirit is given. This may be seen in Paulinus’s *Life of Saint Ambrose*, in Ferrandus’s *Life of Saint Fulgentius*, and elsewhere. Kings also regarded it as an honor, as Gerbert—or whoever the ancient author under the name of Saint Ambrose may have been—testifies in *On the Dignity of Priests*, chapter 2: “When you see the necks of kings and princes submit to the knees of priests, and, having kissed their right hand, believe that they are fortified by their prayers,” and so forth.]

But he vigorously denied the charge and said:

“Bring the infant to me.”

When the infant was brought—thirty days old from birth—Briccius the bishop said to him:

“I adjure you by Jesus Christ, the Son of almighty God: if I fathered you, declare it before everyone.”

The infant replied:

“You are not my father.”

When the people asked that the child be questioned about who his father was, the priest said:

“This does not concern me. As far as I was concerned, I took care. If you have anything further, investigate it yourselves.”

Then, insisting that these things had been brought about by magical arts, they rose against him in a single conspiracy. Dragging him along, they said:

“You will no longer rule over us under the false name of shepherd.”

Still wishing to satisfy the people, he placed burning coals in his *birrus*, [Note: The name *birrus* designates a garment in the *Acts of Saint Cyprian*. We have discussed it further in *Genuine Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 218. Add the passage from Book II of the *Life of Saint Odo*, in the fifth volume of the Benedictine series, where, in section 5, that saint is said to have been seized by the fringe of the *birrus*, by which cloaks were customarily covered.] drew it tightly around himself, and went with the crowds of people to the tomb of blessed Martin.

When he had cast the coals before the tomb, his garment appeared unburned. He continued:

“Just as you see this garment unharmed by these fires, so my body is undefiled by the touch and intercourse of a woman.”

But since they did not believe him and contradicted him, he was dragged away, accused, and expelled, so that the holy man’s statement might be fulfilled: “Know that you will suffer many adversities in the episcopate.”

After he had been expelled, they appointed Justinian to the episcopate.

Finally, Brictius sought the pope of the city of Rome, weeping and lamenting and saying:

“I suffer these things deservedly, because I sinned against the holy man of God. I often called him mad and demented, yet, although I saw his miracles, I did not believe him.”

After his departure, the people of Tours said to their priest:

“Go after him and pursue your case, for if you do not pursue him, you will be humbled to the contempt of us all.” [Note: The Tours manuscript cited by Morel has: “Go after him and pursue your case; for if you do not pursue him, you will be humbled by the contempt of all of us.” From this it may be inferred that this chapter on Saint Brictius existed in the Tours manuscript. If examples are needed to support his History—as it was not possible to give them in their proper place because the notes had already grown too extensive—we first offer the example of Victor II, Roman pontiff, from Book IV of Papirius Masson’s *Lives of the Pontiffs*. He relates that Victor, who had caused trouble for his predecessor Leo IX, was accustomed, whenever adversity befell him, to say: “What Saul did, Paul suffers.”

“Infants who have spoken by divine inspiration to avert accusations from the innocent occur frequently in ecclesiastical history; it will be enough to offer one or two examples. Saint Broon, bishop and disciple of Saint Patrick, was cleared of a similar accusation when the infant Brigid commanded that her father be identified, in the *Life of Saint Brigid* by Surius and Bollandus, on 1 February. Saint Sergius, pope of Rome, was likewise declared innocent by a similar miracle, through Saint Adhelelmus, later bishop of Sherborne, as is related in his Life by the same authors on 25 May and in the *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, volume III. Finally, the elderly monk Daniel was freed from suspicion of adultery by the public declaration of an infant twenty-five days old, in the *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 114.

“As for those who handled fire unharmed to prove their chastity, examples among authors are more numerous than need to be cited here as evidence.”]

Justinian, however, leaving Tours, attacked the Italian city of Vercelli and, struck by God’s judgment, died in exile.

When the people of Tours heard of his death and persisted in their wickedness, they appointed Armentius in his place.

Briccius the bishop came to Rome and reported to the pope everything he had suffered. There, residing at the apostolic see and frequently celebrating the solemnities of Mass, he washed away by weeping whatever offense he had committed against the holy man of God.

After seven years, therefore, he returned from Rome with the authority of that pope and planned to go back to Tours. When he came to a village called Laudiacum, [Note: This same place is called Mons-laudiacus below, in Book X, chapter 31; it is commonly called Montlouis. The Regius manuscript has *Claudiacum*.] six miles from the city, he took up lodging there.

Armentius was seized by a fever and breathed out his spirit at midnight. This was immediately revealed to Bishop Brictius in a vision, and he said to his companions:

“Rise quickly, so that we may hasten to Tours to bury our brother, the bishop.”

When they entered the city through the gate, behold, the dead man was being carried out through another gate.

After he had been buried, Brictius returned to his own chair and afterward lived happily for seven years.

When he died after the forty-seventh year of his episcopate, Saint Eustochius succeeded him, a man of magnificent holiness. [Note: See also Book X, chapter 31, concerning both men.]

### II

After this, [Note: The Regius manuscript begins abruptly with “The Vandals.”] the Vandals left their own region and rushed into Gaul with King Gunderic. After devastating it severely, they turned toward Spain.

The Suebi followed them—that is, the Alamanni—and seized Galicia. Not long afterward, a quarrel arose between the two peoples, because they were related to one another.

When they came out armed for battle and were already prepared for the conflict, the king of the Alamanni said:

“How long shall war be stirred up against the entire people? Let the companies of both peoples not perish, I beg you. Instead, let two of our men go out into the field with weapons of war and fight each other. Then the one whose boy wins shall possess the region without a battle.”

All the people agreed to this, so that the entire multitude would not fall by the edge of the sword.

In those days King Gunderic had died, and Trasamund had obtained the kingdom in his place. [Note: The Corbie manuscript always has *Trasamund*. The Regius, Beauvais, and Regius manuscripts, together with several printed editions, have *Transimundus*; others have *Trasimundus*. These events, however, took place not under Trasamund but under Genseric, as we stated in the *History of the Vandal Persecution*, where we described this people’s invasions first of Gaul, then of Spain and Africa.]

When the boys fought, the Vandal side was defeated and yielded. After the boy had been killed, Trasamund promised that they would withdraw, namely that, after preparing the necessities for the journey, he would remove himself from the borders of Spain.

At that same time Trasamundus persecuted the Christians and compelled all Spain, by tortures and various kinds of death, to consent to the perfidy of the Arian sect.^45 Consequently, a certain religious girl was brought before this tribunal: she was exceedingly wealthy, flourishing in senatorial nobility according to the dignity of the world, and—nobler than all these things—strong in the Catholic faith and serving Almighty God blamelessly.

When she had been brought before the king, he first began to entice her with flattering words to be rebaptized. But when she drove back his poisoned dart with the shield of faith, the king ordered her possessions to be taken away—possessions which she already possessed in her mind as the kingdoms of paradise—and then, after subjecting her to punishments, ordered her to be tortured without hope of preserving her present life.

What more need be said? After many interrogations, after the treasures of earthly riches had been taken from her, when she could not be broken so as to rend the blessed Trinity, she was unwillingly led to be rebaptized. When she was being forcibly compelled to plunge into that muddy bath, she cried out:

> “I believe that the Father with the Son and the Holy Spirit are of one substance and essence.”

With a fitting pollution she infected all the water—that is, she sprinkled it with a discharge of the bowels. Thereafter she was brought to the lawful tribunal and, after the racks, flames, and claw-like instruments, was beheaded for Christ the Lord.^46

**[Col. 0192C, note]** The Spaniards call this girl Vincentia, and they maintain that she suffered at Coria in Lusitania. We discussed her in the aforementioned book on the Vandal persecution, chapter 2.

After this, when the Alamanni pursued them as far as Traducta,^47 and the sea had been crossed, the Vandals were scattered throughout all Africa and Mauretania.

**[Col. 0192C] III.** Since persecution against Christians grew strong in their time, as has been mentioned above, it seems appropriate to recall some of the things they inflicted upon the Churches of God, and how they were expelled from the kingdom. After Trasamundus had died, following the crimes he had committed against the saints of God, Hunericus, more savage in mind, seized the African kingdom and was placed over the Vandals by their own choice. How many Christian peoples were slaughtered under him for the most sacred name of Christ cannot be comprehended by human beings. Africa, which sent them forth, is nevertheless a witness, as is the right hand of Christ, which crowned them with unfading jewels.

We have nevertheless read the passions of some of those martyrs, from which certain episodes must be repeated so that we may come to what we promised. Cyrola, falsely called a bishop, was then regarded as the chief champion of the heretics. When the king was sending persecutors to various places to harass the Christians, the persecutor found the holy Bishop Eugenius, a man of indescribable holiness who was then reputed to possess great wisdom, in the suburb of his city. He seized him so violently that he did not even permit him to go and exhort the Christian flock.^48

When Eugenius saw that he was being led away, he sent the citizens a letter for the preservation of the Catholic faith, as follows.^49

> “To the beloved sons and daughters, most sweet in the love of Christ, of the Church entrusted to me by God, Eugenius, bishop.

> “Royal authority has issued an order and has commanded us to come from Carthage for the exercise of the Catholic faith. Therefore, lest, when I depart from you, I leave the Church of God in uncertainty—that is, in suspense—or abandon Christ’s sheep in silence without being their true shepherd, I have considered it necessary to send these substitutes for me to your holiness. In them, not without tears, I ask, exhort, admonish, and earnestly and abundantly entreat you, by the majesty of God, by the dreadful day of judgment, and by the terrible splendor of Christ’s coming, to hold the Catholic faith more firmly, asserting that the Son is equal to the Father and that the Holy Spirit possesses the same divinity as the Father and the Son.^50

> “Therefore preserve the grace of the one baptism, guarding the anointing of chrism.^51 Let no one who has been reborn from water return to the water. For by God’s command salt is made from water; but if it is reduced again to water, all its character immediately disappears. Hence the Lord rightly says in the Gospel: ‘If the salt has lost its savor, with what shall it be salted?’ (Matthew 5:13). To lose its savor means, certainly, to wish to be salted a second time, when having been salted once is sufficient.

> “Have you not heard Christ saying: ‘He who has been washed once has no need to wash again’ (John 13:10)? Therefore, brothers, and my sons and daughters in the Lord, do not let my absence grieve you. For if you adhere to Catholic discipline, I shall neither forget you because of any distance nor be separated from you by death.^52

> “Know that wherever they cause me to be divided by ordeals, the palm of victory is with me. If I go into exile, I have the example of the blessed John the Evangelist; if I go to the end of death, ‘For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain’ (Philippians 1:21). If I return, brothers, God will fulfill your desire.

> “Nevertheless, what I have not concealed from you is sufficient for now: I have admonished and instructed you as I was able. Therefore I am free from the blood of all who perish; and I know that these letters will be read against them before the tribunal of Christ, when he comes to repay each person according to his works.

> “If I return, brothers, I shall see you in this life; if I do not return, I shall see you in the life to come. Yet I say to you: Farewell, pray for us, and fast, because fasting and almsgiving have always inclined the Lord toward mercy.

> “Remember that it is written in the Gospel: ‘Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who, after killing the body, has power to destroy both soul and body and cast them into Gehenna’ (Matthew 10:2).”

The holy Eugenius was then led to the king, and he contended with that Arian bishop on behalf of the Catholic faith. When Eugenius had completely defeated him concerning the mystery of the Holy Trinity, and Christ had moreover displayed many miracles through him, the same bishop, inflamed by envy, was kindled to still greater madness.

At that time there were with the holy Eugenius two men of the greatest wisdom and holiness, the bishops Vindemialis and Longinus, equal in rank and not unequal in virtue. It was said that the holy Vindemialis had raised a dead man; Longinus, meanwhile, had restored health to many sick people. Eugenius likewise drove away not only blindness of the visible eyes but also blindness of the mind.

When that wicked Arian bishop saw this, he summoned a certain man who had been deceived by the error in which the bishop himself lived and said:

> “I cannot endure that these bishops display many signs among the people and that everyone follows them while disregarding me. Now obey what I command. Take fifty gold pieces, sit in the street through which we shall pass, place your hand over your closed eyes, and, when I pass by with the others, cry out with a loud voice: ‘You, most blessed Cyrola, chief priest of our religion, I beseech you: look upon me and manifest your glory and power, so that, when you open my eyes, I may be worthy to see the light which I have lost.’”

The man carried out the order and sat in the street. When the heretic passed by with the saints of God, the man who had intended to mock God cried out in a loud voice:

> “Hear me, most blessed Cyrola; hear me, holy priest of God. Look upon my blindness. I shall try the remedies which the other blind have often received from you, which lepers have experienced, and which even the dead themselves have perceived. I adjure you by the power which you possess to restore to me the light I desire, for I have been struck by grievous blindness.”

Without knowing the truth, he was nevertheless speaking truly: greed had blinded him, and for money he thought he could mock the power of Almighty God.

Then the bishop of the heretics turned aside for a little while, as though he were about to triumph by his power. Inflated with vanity and pride, he placed his hand over the man’s eyes and said:

> “According to our faith, by which we rightly believe in God, let your eyes be opened.”

As soon as this crime had burst forth, laughter was changed into lamentation, and the bishop’s deceit was exposed publicly.^53 For such pain seized the wretched man’s eyes that he could scarcely restrain them with his fingers, lest they burst.^54

At last the wretched man began to cry out and say:

> “Woe to me, wretched man that I am, for I have been deceived by the enemy of divine law. Woe to me, because I wished to mock God for money and accepted fifty gold pieces to commit this crime.”

He said to the bishop:

> “Here is your gold; restore my sight, which I lost through your deceit.”

And to the Christians he said:

> “I beg you, most glorious Christians, do not despise a wretched man, but quickly come to the aid of one who is perishing. For I have truly learned that ‘God is not mocked’ (Galatians 6:7).”

Then the saints of God, moved by compassion, said:

> “If you believe, all things are possible for one who believes” (Mark 9:22).

But he cried out in a loud voice:

> “Whoever does not believe that Christ the Son of God and the Holy Spirit possess a substance and divinity equal to God the Father, let him suffer today what I am suffering.”

And he added:

> “I believe in God the Father Almighty. I believe in Jesus Christ, the Son of God, equal to the Father. I believe in the Holy Spirit, consubstantial and coeternal with the Father and the Son.”

When they heard this, and each of them anticipated the others in mutual honor, a holy contention arose among them as to which of them should make the sign of the blessed cross upon the man’s eyes. Vindemialis and Longinus urged Eugenius to do it; but Eugenius, for his part, entreated them to lay their hands upon the blind man.

When they had done so and were holding their hands over his head, the holy Eugenius made the sign of the cross over the blind man’s eyes and said:

> “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, the true God, whom we confess as three in one equality and omnipotence, let your eyes be opened.”

Immediately the pain was removed, and the man returned to his former health.

It was made perfectly clear through this man’s blindness how the bishop of the heretics covered the eyes of hearts with the wretched cloak of his assertion, lest anyone be permitted to contemplate the true light with the eyes of faith.

O wretched man, who did not enter through the door—that is, through Christ, who is the true door—but became more a wolf to the flock than a guardian! The torch of faith which he ought to have kindled in the hearts of believers, he was attempting to extinguish by the perversity of his heart.^55

The saints of God performed many other signs among the people, and there was one voice among the people saying:

> “The Father is true God, the Son is true God, the Holy Spirit is true God: to be worshiped in one faith, feared with one fear, and venerated with the same honor.”

For it was clear to everyone that the things Cyrola asserted were false.

When King Honoricus saw that his assertions were thus stripped bare by the glorious faith of the saints, that his sect of error was not being raised up but rather destroyed, and that his bishop’s fraud had been exposed in this crime, he ordered the saints of God to be killed after many tortures, after the racks, after the flames, and after the claw-like instruments.^56

He ordered the blessed Eugenius to be beheaded, but under such a pretext that, if at the hour when the sword rested upon his neck he did not return to the sect of the heretics, he would not be killed—lest the Christians honor him as a martyr—but would instead be condemned to exile. It is clear that this was what happened. For when death was imminent and he was asked whether he was resolved to die for the Catholic faith, he replied:

> “For this is eternal life: to die for justice.”

Then, with the sword suspended, he was assigned to exile at Albi, a city of Gaul, where he also ended his present life.^57 Many miracles are now very frequently displayed at his tomb.
