He ordered the holy Vindemialis to be struck with the sword. This was carried out in the course of this struggle. Octavianus the archdeacon, together with many thousands of men and women who asserted this faith, were killed or disabled.

But for the love of glory, these punishments were nothing to the holy confessors, who knew that, having been afflicted in little, they would be rightly ordered in much (Wisdom 3:5), according to the Apostle’s saying:

> “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in the saints” (Romans 8:18).

At that time many who had been wandering from the faith, receiving riches, entangled themselves in many sorrows. Thus, at that time, the unhappy bishop named Revocatus was drawn away from the Catholic faith.^58

Then the sun appeared dark, so that scarcely a third of it seemed to shine; I believe this was on account of so many crimes and the shedding of innocent blood.^59 After such a crime, Honoricus was seized by the demon that had long been nourished by the blood of the saints, and he tore himself with his own bites. In this torment he ended his unworthy life by a fitting death.

Hildericus succeeded him,^60 and after Hildericus died, Gelesimer took possession of the kingdom. He too was defeated by the Roman state^61 and ended his life and sovereignty. Thus the Vandal kingdom fell.

**[Col. 0196C] IV.** Many heresies were attacking the Churches of God at that time, and divine vengeance was often inflicted upon them. Athanaricus, king of the Goths, also aroused a great persecution. He mutilated many Christians with the sword after subjecting them to various punishments; he also sent some into exile and killed them by hunger and diverse tortures.^62

Thus, when God’s judgment was impending, he was expelled from the kingdom for shedding righteous blood and became an exile from his homeland—the man who had attacked the Churches of God.

But now let us return to what came before.

**[Col. 0197A] V.** There was a rumor that the Huns^63 intended to burst into Gaul. At that time, in the town of Tongeren, there was a bishop named Aravatius,^64 a man of exceptional holiness. He devoted himself to vigils and fasts, was frequently drenched by a rain of tears, and prayed for the Lord’s mercy, asking that he never permit this unbelieving people, which was always unworthy, to come into Gaul.

But perceiving through the Spirit that, on account of the people’s sins, this request had not been granted to him, he resolved to seek the city of Rome,^65 so that, with the protection of apostolic power added to him—the protection which he humbly implored from the Lord—he might more easily deserve to obtain what he sought.

Accordingly, he approached the tomb of the blessed apostle and begged for the assistance of his goodness, consuming himself through great abstinence and extreme hunger, so that he remained for two or three days without food or drink, and no interval passed in which he ceased from prayer.

When he had remained there for many days in such affliction, he is said to have received this answer from the blessed apostle:

> “Why do you trouble me, most holy man? For it has been entirely decreed in the Lord’s deliberation that the Huns will come into Gaul and lay it waste with the greatest devastation. Do not therefore make further plans; hurry quickly, put your household in order, prepare your burial, and seek clean linen. For you will depart from the body, and your eyes will not see the evils that the Huns will inflict in Gaul, as the Lord our God has spoken.”

Having received this answer from the holy apostle, the bishop hastened his journey and quickly returned to Gaul. Coming to the city of Tongeren, he quickly took with him what was necessary for his burial. Then, bidding farewell to the clergy and the other citizens of the city, he announced with weeping and lamentation that they would not see his face again.

They followed him with great wailing^66 and tears, humbly entreating him:

> “Do not abandon us, holy father; do not forget us, good shepherd.”

But when they could not call him back with their tears, they received his blessing with kisses and returned.

He then approached the city of Maastricht,^67 where he departed from the body after being struck by a slight fever. After being washed by the faithful, he was buried beside the public road itself. How his blessed body was later transferred, after a long period of time, we have written in the book of *Miracles*.^68

**[Col. 0198A] VI.** The Huns, having departed from Pannonia, arrived, as some relate, at the city of Metz on the very vigil of holy Easter. Devastating the rest of the country, they handed the city over to flames, slaughtered the people by the edge of the sword, and killed the priests of the Lord before the holy altars.^69 No place in it remained unburned except the oratory of the blessed Stephen, the first martyr and deacon.

I have not refrained from relating what I heard from certain people about that oratory. They say that, before these enemies came, a faithful man saw in a vision the blessed deacon Stephen conversing with the holy apostles Peter and Paul about this destruction and saying:

> “I beg you, my lords, do not permit, through your intercession, the city of Metz to be burned by its enemies, because there is a place in it containing the pledge of my small remains.^70 Rather, let the people learn that I possess some power with the Lord. But if the people’s crime has grown so great that nothing else can happen except that the city be given over to fire, at least let this oratory not be burned.”

They answered him:

> “Go in peace, dearest brother. Your oratory alone will be spared the fire. But we shall not obtain the city’s preservation, because the sentence of the Lord’s decree has already gone forth against it. The people’s sin has prevailed, and the cry of their wickedness has risen before God. Therefore this city will be consumed by fire.”

There is no doubt, then, that when the city was devastated, the oratory remained unharmed through their intercession.

**[Col. 0198C] VII.** Attila, king of the Huns, departing from the city of Metz and crushing many cities of Gaul, attacked Orléans and attempted to capture it by the most powerful blows of battering rams.

At that time the most blessed Anianus was bishop in the aforementioned city, a man of exceptional wisdom and praiseworthy holiness, whose virtuous deeds remain faithfully preserved among us.^71 When the besieged people called out to their bishop, asking what they should do, he trusted in God and instructed everyone to prostrate themselves in prayer and, with tears, continually implore the Lord’s help, which is ever present in times of need.

When they had prayed as he had commanded, the priest said:

> “Look from the city wall and see whether God’s mercy has already come to your aid.”

He suspected that, through the Lord’s mercy, Aetius was approaching; he had earlier gone to Arles because he feared what was to come. But when they looked from the wall, they saw no one.

He said:

> “Pray faithfully. The Lord will deliver you today.”

While they were praying, he said:

> “Look again.”

When they looked, they saw no one bringing aid.

For the third time he said:

> “If you ask faithfully, the Lord will quickly be present.”

Then they implored the Lord’s mercy with weeping and great wailing.^72 After the prayer had ended, they looked from the wall for the third time, according to the old man’s command, and saw in the distance what seemed to be a mist rising from the earth.

When they reported this, the priest said:

> “It is the Lord’s help.”

Meanwhile, the walls were already trembling from the battering rams and were on the point of falling. Then, behold, Aetius arrived, together with Theodorus,^73 king of the Goths, and his son Thorismodus, with their armies. They rushed to the city and drove out and repelled the enemy.

Thus, through the intercession of the blessed bishop, the city was liberated, and they put Attila to flight. Attila then went to the field of Mauriacum^74 and prepared himself for battle. When the Goths heard this, they prepared themselves manfully against him.

During those days news reached Rome that Aetius was in the greatest danger amid the enemy ranks. When his wife heard this, anxious and sorrowful, she continually visited the basilica of the holy Apostles and prayed that her husband might be returned safely from this campaign.^75

While she was doing this day and night, one night a very poor man, drunk with wine, fell asleep in a corner of the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter. When the doors had been closed according to custom, the guards did not throw him out. Rising during the night, when lamps were shining throughout the building, he was terrified and sought an exit by which he might escape outside.^76

But when he struck the barriers of the first and second doors and realized that everything was locked, he lay down alone, trembling and awaiting an opportunity to leave when the people gathered for the morning hymns.

Meanwhile, he saw two persons greeting each other reverently and concerned about one another’s welfare. Then the older of them began as follows:

> “I can no longer endure Aetius’s wife’s tears. She continually asks that I bring her husband back safely from Gaul, although something else had been predetermined concerning him in the divine judgment. Nevertheless, I have obtained immense mercy for his life. And behold, I am now hastening there to bring him back alive.

> “But I adjure you: whoever hears this must remain silent and must not dare to make God’s secret public, lest he quickly perish from the earth.”

But the man who heard this could not remain silent. As soon as dawn broke, he disclosed everything he had heard to the mistress of the household, and when he had finished speaking, he lost the sight of his eyes.

Aetius, therefore, joined by the Goths and Franks, fought against Attila. When Attila saw that his army was being destroyed to the point of annihilation, he fled and vanished. Theodorus, king of the Goths, fell in this battle. No one should doubt that the army of the Huns was put to flight through the intercession of the bishop mentioned above.

Nevertheless, the patrician Aetius won the victory together with Thorismodus and destroyed the enemy. When the war was over, Aetius said to Thorismodus:

> “Hurry quickly back to your homeland, lest, while your brother is present, you be deprived of your father’s kingdom.”

When Thorismodus heard this, he departed swiftly, as though he intended to forestall his brother and be the first to obtain his father’s throne.^77

By a similar deception he drove away the king of the Franks.^78 When they had withdrawn, Aetius, after stripping the battlefield, returned victoriously to his homeland with great spoils.

Attila returned with only a few men. Not long afterward the Huns captured, burned, and destroyed Aquileia, and Italy was overrun and devastated.

Thorismodus, whom we mentioned above, subdued the Alans in war.^79 Later, after many disputes and wars, he was overcome and killed by his brothers.^80

[Editorial notes]

[Col. 0192D, on Traducta] In Book V, chapter 1 of his *Natural History*, Pliny records, among other names formerly given to the Tingitanian city in Africa now commonly called Tangier, that Claudius Caesar, when making it a colony, called it Julia Traducta. Others maintain, and substantiate from authors’ testimony, that Julia Traducta lay on the other shore, namely on the Spanish coast; indeed, our Gregory appears to place Traducta in Spain. Hardouin believes that there was one Traducta on each shore, thereby readily reconciling the authors’ disagreement. See what he himself says on this matter in his notes and emendations on this passage of Pliny.

[Col. 0192D, on Hunericus] The printed editions read “Honoricus.” He succeeded his father Genseric; Guntabund succeeded him, and Trasamund succeeded Guntabund.

[Col. 0193D, on “Christian flock”] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions, with Bec, read *Christi ullum* (“any [flock] of Christ”).

[Col. 0193D, on the letter] The entire letter is absent in Corbie, but was evidently omitted deliberately, since that manuscript has “he sent a letter … as follows.”

[Col. 0193D, salutation] Manuscript 1 reads *commissis* (“entrusted [ones]”).

[Col. 0193D, on Carthage] Regm. reads *Carthaginem* (“to Carthage”) and, below, adds *litteras* (“letters”) after *vicarias* (“substitutes”).

[Cols. 0193D–0194D, Trinitarian variant] The same manuscript and Bec read: “asserting that the Father and the Holy Spirit possess the same divinity as the Son.”

[Col. 0194D, chrism] Salvian, an author of the same age, lists baptismal grace and the anointing of chrism among the goods bestowed by God upon Christians, *On the Governance of God*, Book III.

[Col. 0194D, on Eugenius’s absence] Thus manuscripts 2; others read: “indeed, if you adhere to Catholic discipline, I neither forget you … nor am separated [from you].”

[Col. 0195D, on the exposure of the fraud] The Beauvais manuscript, with the preceding matter lost, begins at “was exposed publicly.” What follows through “Then the saints of God” is absent from that manuscript. Moreover, an occurrence resembling this one took place in Spain in Leovigild’s time, as Gregory himself recounts in *The Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 13.

[Col. 0195D, on restraining the eyes] Regm. reads “he restrained [them] by force”; Casin. reads “he restrained [them] with his own fingers.”

[Col. 0195D, on the torch of faith] Bell. reads *faciem* for *facem* (“torch”), unless I am mistaken.

[Col. 0195D, on Eugenius and the others] On Eugenius and the others praised here by Gregory, consult our edition of the *History of the Vandal Persecution*, chapter 8, where we discuss them at length and Eugenius’s tomb near the city of Albi.

[Cols. 0195D–0196D, on the darkened sun] In the year 450; Scaliger proves in Book VI of *On the Correction of Chronology* that the Huns’ incursion into Gaul occurred in the following year.

[Col. 0196D, on Hildericus and Gelesimer] Reg. reads *Hildericus*, which is the same name, since in those times H had the sound that Ch has for us. In fact, Hildericus succeeded not directly to his father Huneric, but after Guntabund and Trasamund; Gelisimer seized the kingdom not after Hildericus’s death, but after his expulsion. Procopius and others describe their fortunes. See our edition of the *History of the Vandal Persecution*, chapter 12.

[Col. 0196D, on “the Roman state”] That is, by Belisarius, the celebrated general of the emperor Justinian.

[Col. 0196D, on Athanaricus] This passage through “whence” is absent from manuscripts 2. Athanaricus’s persecution is described in the *Sincere Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 670, under St Saba, in the year 372.

[Col. 0197C, on “Huns”] Several manuscripts and printed editions read *Hunos* or *Hunnos*, which are equivalent. In the Royal manuscript this chapter and the following one are absent.

[Cols. 0197C–0198D, on Aravatius/Servatius] Nearly all printed editions, with the Bec manuscript, read Servatius; Corbie reads Asavatius. Because common authors supposed him to be Servatius, bishop of Tongeren, praised by Athanasius, Sulpicius Severus, and others, who attended the councils of Sardica, Ariminum, and even Agrippina—if the acts of that council are genuine—they attempted to refer the calamity of Gaul which Gregory here attributes to the Huns to Vandal incursions. But since, among all manuscripts available for inspection, only Bec here and only the Clermont manuscript in *The Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 72, read Servatius, I readily agree with those who distinguish the two: the former Servatius lived in the fourth century; the latter, Gregory’s Aravatius—also Asavatius in Corbie, and Arvatius in *The Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 72, and in Fredegar even in old manuscripts—lived in the following century. Valesius discusses the question at length in the preface to volume II of the *History of the Franks* and accepts two men. Henschenius, however, attempts at greater length to prove, under 13 May in the Bollandists, that there was only one.

While occupied with elucidating this difficulty, I found among the Corbie manuscripts transported to our library of Saint-Germain one manuscript, partly in Merovingian and partly in Roman script, written at least 900 years ago. It contains this entire Gregory narrative, and indeed a somewhat longer version, under the title of the Life of St Servatius. In this manuscript the holy man is never called anything but Servatius, whether in the Life itself or in the ancient hymn appended to it. It must therefore be inferred either that he himself bore two names, or at least that by that time the name Aravatius had been transferred to Servatius. In the Vatican and Vendôme manuscripts he is likewise called Aravatius.

[Col. 0198D, on his resolve] Several manuscripts read “he began to seek.”

[Col. 0198D, on the mourners] Thus Corbie and Beauvais; the others, with the printed editions, read “with great lamentation.”

[Col. 0198D, on Maastricht] That is, Trajectum on the Meuse, mentioned below and commonly called Maastricht. Shortly after Attila destroyed Aduatuca, the episcopal see of Tongeren was transferred there; it later moved to Liège.

[Col. 0198D, on the *Miracles*] Namely, in *The Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 72.

[Col. 0198D, on Stephen’s relics] Even now several relics of the holy Protomartyr are preserved in the principal church of Metz dedicated to St Stephen.

[Cols. 0198D–0199C, on Anianus] His feast is observed on 17 November. On this siege see Sidonius Apollinaris, Book VIII, letter 15, to Prosper, Anianus’s successor. Surius included in volume II Anianus’s acts, pieced together by Saussaye from diverse authors; but we found the acts as composed by an ancient author in manuscript codices, where his journey to Arles and the miracles worked on it are recounted more fully. See Chesne, volume I, p. 521. Sidonius Apollinaris’s poem 7 on the same matter should also be read.

[Cols. 0199C–0200C, on Theodorus and Thorismodus] Thus the manuscripts and most printed editions read *Theodorus*, whereas Sidonius calls him Theodoris or Theodoricus; others read Theudo. Thorismodus is called Thurremodus in Corbie, Thursimodus in Beauvais, Thursimundus in Regm., and Thorismondus in Bec. They are Theuderic or Theodoric, king of the Visigoths from 419 to 452, and his son Thurismund, who held the same kingdom for one year after his father’s death and was killed by his brothers in 453, as will be said below.

We learn this king’s correct name from an ancient inscription recently moved to the convent of the Minims at Narbonne from an old oratory of St Lupus, not far from the city. It had formerly been consecrated under the title of St Vincent, the saint of Agen celebrated in those parts. The inscription is the epitaph of a certain Palenops, carved upon white marble; it seemed proper to reproduce it there in full, since it supplies both the true name of the Gothic king and a certain indication of the date of his rule, correlating the tenth year of that reign with Indiction IV. The line which appears to divide the inscription into two parts marks a fracture in the marble which has almost obliterated the line by hand.

The antiquity of the same oratory may also be inferred from another monument. On an old portion of its stone altar an inscription of Rusticus, fifth-century bishop of Narbonne, may be seen, in which he asks the faithful to intercede with God for himself—perhaps because he had consecrated this altar. In Roman letters it reads: “PRAY FOR ME, YOUR RUSTICUS.” These inscriptions, together with a third written in Leovigild’s time and printed below, were sent to me by the distinguished Monsieur Peche, canon of the principal church of Narbonne.

[Cols. 0200C–0200D, on Mauriacum] Authors do not agree on this matter. Blondel thinks Mauriacum is the village called Heiz le Mauru in the diocese of Châlons; indeed Jordanes does not distinguish the Mauriac fields from the Catalaunian ones. Isidore writes that the battle occurred in the Catalaunian fields in era 452, as does Hydatius, who places them not far from Metz. In notes on Sidonius’s poem 7, Savaron cites some of his countrymen who wished the fields to be named from Mauriacum, a town of Auvergne. Valesius, following Fredegar, places the Mauriac fields among the Tricasses and thinks they took their name from Mauriacum, commonly Mery, a town on the Seine between Troyes and Ponts-sur-Seine; he maintains that there Attila was first lightly engaged, and that a great battle followed shortly afterward in the Catalaunian fields. We pass over several others who force into the text the Secalaunian fields—La Sologne near Orléans—in place of the Catalaunian fields, or Catallani among the Tectosages, since their opinion is now rejected by everyone.

[Col. 0200D, on Aetius’s wife] Thus Corbie, Bec, Colb. a., and Regm.; others read “that she might receive him safe from this expectation.”

[Col. 0201D, on the exit] Thus the older codices; others read, “he sought an entrance through which he might escape outside.”

[Col. 0201D, on the Frankish king] Was it King Merovech? Sidonius testifies in the panegyric delivered for his father-in-law that, after Aetius’s death, Merovech made war upon First Germany and Second Belgica in order to extend his kingdom’s boundaries. Prosper writes that Merovech reigned in Francia in 447. For the cause of Attila’s war, see the *History* of Priscus the rhetorician and Jordanes, *On Gothic Affairs*, chapter 35 and following.

[Col. 0201D, on the Alans] Thus the Corbie, Beauvais, Colbert, Regm., Royal, and Palatine manuscripts, together with the editions of Basle and others. Most printed editions, with Bec, read Alamanni. Certainly the Alans then had their seat beyond the Loire. On them consult Valesius, Book IV of *Frankish Affairs*.

[Cols. 0201D–0202D, on Thorismodus’s death] He was killed in 453, as Valesius likewise proves, by his brothers Theoderic and Frideric; the former seized the kingdom, according to Hydatius and others.

## VIII

Accordingly, when these matters had been arranged and completed in due order, I considered it wrong to remain silent about what Renatus Frigeridus’ *History* relates concerning the Aetius mentioned above [Note: This author is known to us solely through Gregory]. For when, in the twelfth book of his *Histories*, he reports that after the death of the divine Honorius, Valentinian, still a boy, was made emperor by his cousin Theodosius after only a single five-year period had elapsed, and that at Rome the tyrant John had risen to imperial power, and says that his envoys had been despised by Caesar, he adds:

> “While these things were thus taking place, the envoys returned to the tyrant, bringing back more dreadful orders [Note: Most manuscripts read *atrociora*, ‘more dreadful’; others have *atrocia reportantes*, ‘bringing back dreadful orders’]: moved by these, John sent Aetius, who at that time was managing the palace, to the Huns with a great weight of gold. Aetius knew them from the time when he had been held hostage and was bound to them by close friendship. He sent him with instructions of this kind: as soon as the opposing forces had entered Italy, they were to attack them from the rear, while he himself would come from the front.

> “Since many things about this man must subsequently be recorded, it seems fitting to begin with his family and character. His father Gaudentius, a man of the highest rank in the province of Scythia [Note: *Sciciae* in the Bellovacensis manuscript; *Scyciae* in Beccensis], began his military career in the household service and advanced to the highest office of master of the cavalry. His mother was Itala, a noble and wealthy woman. His son Aetius, a praetorian from childhood, was a hostage of Alaric for three years, and thereafter of the Huns. Later, having married Carpilio’s daughter, he passed from being count of the household troops to managing the palace for John.

> “Of medium height, well formed with a manly bearing, so that he was neither weak nor burdensome; lively in spirit, vigorous in body, a most capable horseman, skilled in shooting arrows, energetic with the spear, eminently suited to warfare, and renowned in the arts of peace; free from greed, possessed of very little ambition, endowed with excellent qualities of mind, and not even by wicked instigators diverted from his purpose; extraordinarily patient under injury, eager for toil, fearless in danger, and exceptionally enduring of hunger, thirst, and sleeplessness. From his earliest age it was plainly foretold how great a power fate had destined for him, and that he would be celebrated in his own times and places.”

This is what the aforesaid historian relates about Aetius. When the emperor Valentinian had reached adulthood, however, he feared that Aetius might overthrow him through tyranny and killed him without any grounds existing. Later, while the emperor himself was seated on the tribunal in the Campus Martius and addressing the people, Occylla, Aetius’ *buccellarius*, came from the opposite direction and pierced him with a sword. Such was the end of both men [Note: For the murder of Aetius and Valentinian, and for the other affairs of the declining empire reported here and in what follows, see Orosius, book VII; Procopius, book I of the *Vandalic History*; Marcellinus Comes; Prosper; and others. It seems unnecessary to treat these matters at length in the notes. We have nevertheless placed them in their proper locations in the chronological index prefixed to Gregory’s works, so that the sequence of Frankish affairs, with which they are interwoven, might be more readily understood.].

## IX

As for the kings of the Franks, many do not know who the first of them was. For although Sulpicius Alexander’s *History* relates much about them [Note: We know this author, and his *History*, from no source other than Gregory], it nowhere names their first king, but says that they had leaders. What it relates about them, however, seems worth recalling.

For when he says that Maximus, having lost all hope of the empire, was sitting inside Aquileia as though out of his mind, he adds:

> “At that time, under the leadership of Genobaud [Note: Most printed editions have *Genobaldo*; Beccensis, *Genebaudo*; Badianus has *Sansone* for *Sunnone*; Reginensis, *Sumsone*], Marcomer, and Sunno, the Franks burst into Germany. After breaching the frontier and killing many people, they ravaged especially the fertile districts and struck fear even into Agrippina, the city of Cologne.

> “When this report reached Trier, Nannenus [Note: This is how the ancient manuscripts name him. The Colbertinus and Reginensis have *Namninus*; most printed editions, *Nannius*] and Quintinus, masters of the soldiery, to whom Maximus had entrusted the defense of Gaul and the care of his young son, gathered an army and assembled at Agrippina. But the enemy, laden with booty and having ravaged the richest parts of the provinces, crossed the Rhine, leaving many of their own men behind on Roman soil, prepared to renew the devastation. The Romans engaged them successfully, killing many Franks in the Carbonarian Forest [Note: The Carbonarian Forest lay between the Rhine and the Scheldt and formed part of the Ardennes].

> “When a council was held to decide whether they should cross into Francia, Nannenus opposed the proposal, because he knew that they were not unprepared and would undoubtedly be stronger and safer in their own territory. When this displeased Quintinus and the other military men, Nannenus returned to Mainz. Quintinus crossed the Rhine with his army near the fortress of Nivisium [Note: Others have *Novesium*. This variation also occurs in other authors; it is commonly called Neuss, a town not far from Cologne], setting up camp on the far side of the river. He encountered empty huts and great villages abandoned by their inhabitants. For the Franks, pretending to be afraid, had withdrawn into more remote forests, having prepared ambushes at the edges of the woods.

> “Thus, after all the houses had been burned—upon which foolish cowardice had placed the completion of its victory—the soldiers spent an anxious night under the burden of their arms. At first light they entered the woods under Quintinus as commander of the battle. Becoming entangled in the maze of the paths, they wandered about until nearly midday. At last, when they found everything closed off by enormous fences and solid barriers, they burst into marshy fields adjoining the forests. As they were attempting to break out [Note: Two manuscripts read: ‘as they were attempting to break out’], a few of the enemy appeared. Joining tree trunks together and standing upon them or upon felled trees, as though from the tops of towers, they poured forth arrows in the manner of artillery, smeared with the poisons of plants, so that even wounds inflicted on the surface of the skin, though not in vital places, would be followed by certain death.

> “Then, surrounded by a larger multitude of enemies, the army poured greedily into the open fields which the Franks had left unobstructed. The first cavalrymen sank into the abysses, and, their human and animal bodies becoming mixed together, were crushed in the fall by one another. The infantry, whom no burden of horses had trampled, became entangled in the mud and could scarcely extricate their steps; they again hid themselves trembling in the woods, from which they had barely emerged a moment before.

> “Thus the ranks were thrown into confusion, the legions were cut down, and Heraclius, tribune of the Jovians [Note: Valesius reads *Jovianorum*. The Jovian soldiers were indeed famous; see Toinard’s notes on Lactantius. Others may be mentioned here, so called after Jovinus, whom the text will mention below], together with nearly all who commanded the soldiers, was killed. Night and the hiding places of the forests provided a safe escape for only a few.”

This he narrated in the third book of his *History*.

In the fourth book, when relating the killing of Victor, the son of the tyrant Maximus, he says:

> “At that time Carietto and Syrus had been substituted for Nannenus and were stationed in Germany with an army opposed to the Franks.”

A little later, when the Franks had carried booty away from Germany, he added:

> “Arbogastes, wishing to delay nothing, urges Caesar to exact the penalties due from the Franks unless they immediately restore everything they had plundered the previous year after killing the legions, and surrender the instigators of the war, so that the violation of the peace might be punished in them.”

He reported these events while they were still leaders; thereafter he says:

> “After a few days, Marcomer and Sunno, the Frankish royals, having quickly concluded a conference and obtained hostages according to custom [Note: The Reginensis reads: ‘The emperor, having received hostages from them according to custom, withdrew to Trier for the winter’; and instead of *pro an vices*, the same manuscript has *an per vices tenuerint regnum*, ‘whether they held the kingship in turns.’ The Bellovacensis, Beccensis, and Turonensis manuscripts read *imperatorisque ex more obsidibus*, which Morel suggests should be restored as *imperatisque ex more obsidibus*, ‘and having demanded hostages according to custom’], withdrew to Trier for the winter.”

Since he calls them royals, we do not know whether they were kings or held the kingship in turns.

The same writer, when recalling the difficulties of the emperor Valentinian, adds:

> “While various events were occurring in the East throughout Thrace [Note: Beccensis has *Thracas*], the public order in Gaul was disturbed. With the emperor Valentinian shut up in the palace at Vienne and reduced almost below the condition of a private citizen, the administration of military affairs was entrusted to Frankish guards, while civil offices also passed over into the conspiracy of Arbogastes. No one among all those bound by military oaths could be found who dared obey either the familiar conversation or the commands of the emperor.”

He then reports that in the same year Arbogastes, pursuing Sunno and Marcomer, the Frankish sub-kings, out of ethnic hatred [Note: Arbogastes himself was a Frank by birth, as Paulinus writes in his *Life of Saint Ambrose*, and other writers of the same period also imply], attacked Agrippina in the depth of winter, believing that all the retreats of Francia could safely be penetrated and burned, since the leafless and dry forests could not conceal those lying in ambush.

Accordingly, after gathering an army and crossing the Rhine [Note: In the Bellovacensis manuscript, after the words ‘crossing the Rhine,’ the two following leaves are missing through chapter 12], he ravaged the district nearest the river inhabited by the Bricteri [Note: The Corbey manuscript reads: ‘the district nearest the bank of the Bructeri.’ These, unless I am mistaken, are the Bructeri mentioned by Velleius Paterculus, Tacitus, and others, whom Sidonius joins with the Thuringians, Franks, and others in poem 7. They lived, as H. Junius thinks, in modern Westphalia]. He also ravaged the district inhabited by the Chamani [Note: Two printed editions have *Aetiam* instead of *etiam*, by which name Ortelius thought a district was designated, inhabited by the Chamani, or Chamavi, as other manuscripts read. Below, for *Ampsuariis*, Chesnius and others have *Ampsivariis*; likewise, for *Chattis*, the Corbey manuscript has *Chatis*. These are the famous Catti, a people of Germany], without anyone ever appearing to oppose him, except that a few Ampsuarii and Chatti appeared on the more distant ridges of the hills under the leadership of Marcomer.

Again, leaving aside both the titles of leaders and royals, he plainly indicates that the Franks had a king [Note: Is this the man whom writers of our own history call Pharamund or Faramund, whom they wish to be the father of Chlodion and the progenitor of the Frankish monarchy? The author who wrote the *Deeds of the Franks* under King Theuderic II calls Chlodion the son of Faramund; Rorico and others followed him. In Prosper’s *Chronicle*, under the twenty-sixth year of Honorius—that is, A.D. 420—Faramund is said to have reigned in Francia; and above, under the fourth year of Theodosius—that is, A.D. 382—we read: “Priam reigns in Francia.” Yet Eugenius, of whom Gregory speaks here, was killed in 394. It is remarkable that nothing about Faramund occurs in Gregory or Fredegar. Moreover, in book II of his *Frankish History*, p. 87, Valesius charges Gregory with ignorance for interpreting Sulpicius Alexander’s words “under the leadership of Genobaud,” etc., and “under the leadership of Marcomer” as titles of the office of duke, as though the Franks at that time had only leaders and not kings—a mistake which, he says, most ancient and modern writers carelessly followed. Yet, as Valesius thinks certain, Sulpicius meant by *duces* there nothing other than the instigators or leaders by whom the Franks carried out the wars recounted here; and these princes were truly kings of the Franks, as is established from Claudian, Paulinus’ *Life of Saint Ambrose*, and Sulpicius himself, who calls them not only *regales* but also *subreguli*, titles by which, Valesius maintains, that author designated kings. In additions to volume I, Valesius likewise observes that Priscus sometimes calls Attila and Bleda, kings of the Huns, *regales*]. Omitting his name, he says:

> “Afterward the tyrant Eugenius, having assumed the military expedition, made for the Rhine frontier, so that, after forming the customary ancient treaties with the kings of the Alamanni and Franks, he might display to the savage peoples the enormous army which he then possessed.”

This is what the aforementioned historian discussed concerning the Franks.

Renatus Profuturus Frigeridus, whom we mentioned above, when reporting that Rome had been captured and destroyed by the Goths, says:

> “Meanwhile Respendial, king of the Alamanni [Note: Valesius and Cointius read ‘king of the Alans’], when Goar had crossed over to the Romans, turned his own forces away from the Rhine, while the Vandals were being hard-pressed in war by the Franks, their king Godegisil having been killed and nearly twenty thousand having been slain by the sword in battle, and all the Vandals being destined for extermination, had not the strength of the Alans come to their aid in time.”

This point troubles us: when he names the kings of other peoples, why does he not name the king of the Franks?

Nevertheless, when he says that Constantine, having assumed tyranny, ordered his son Constantius to come to him from Spain, he writes as follows:

> “The tyrant Constantine summoned his son Constans from Spain, likewise a tyrant, so that they might deliberate together in person about the supreme affairs of state. It was therefore arranged that Constans, leaving behind the court establishment and his wife, a Caesar-Augusta, and entrusting everything within Spain to Gerontius, hastened by an uninterrupted journey to his father. When they had come together, and many days had passed without any fear from Italy, Constantine, devoted to his throat and belly, advised his son to return to Spain.

> “After sending his forces ahead, while he remained with his father, messengers arrived from Spain announcing that Gerontius was preparing Maximus, one of his dependents, invested with imperial power and girded about with bands of barbarian peoples against him. Terrified by this, they sent Edobecus [Note: Beccensis has *Odobecus*] to the Germanic peoples. Constans and the prefect Decimus [Note: So read the Corbey, Badian, and other manuscripts, as also below; others have *Decimius*. He was Rusticus, as Sirmond notes; Apollinaris Sidonius praises him in book V, letter 9], now master of the offices, set out for Gaul with the Franks and Alamanni and with every military force, intending to return at once to Constantine.”

Again, when he writes that Constantine was under siege, he says:

> “Scarcely had the fourth month of Constantine’s siege begun when suddenly messengers arrived from farther Gaul announcing that Jovinus had assumed the royal insignia and was approaching the besiegers with the Burgundians, Alamanni, Franks, Alans, and the entire army. Thus, with events hastened, the city was opened and Constantine surrendered. He was immediately sent toward Italy and, when the emperor dispatched assassins to meet him, was beheaded above the river Mincius.”

A little later he reports the same:

> “In those same days the prefect of the tyrants, Decimus Rusticus, Agroetius, formerly chief of the notaries of Jovinus [Note: The Reginensis reads *Jovinus*, followed by many others. The Corbey manuscript has ‘formerly of the chief notaries of Jovinus’], and many nobles were captured among the Arverni by the generals of Honorius and cruelly put to death. The city of Trier was plundered and burned by the Franks in a second incursion.”

When Asterius had received the rank of patrician through imperial letters, he adds:

> “At the same time Castinus, count of the household troops, was sent to Gaul after undertaking an expedition against the Franks.”

This is what these writers said about the Franks.

Orosius, himself a historian, also records the following in the seventh book of his work [Note: Namely chapter 28, or the penultimate chapter of the entire work]:

> “Stilicho, having gathered the peoples, crushes the Franks, crosses the Rhine, traverses Gaul, and advances as far as the Pyrenees.”

The historians mentioned above have left us this information about the Franks, without naming their kings.

For many report that the Franks had migrated from Pannonia. At first, they say, they inhabited the banks of the Rhine [Note: The Colbertinus and other manuscripts have ‘settled upon’]. Then, after crossing the Rhine, they crossed into Thuringia [Note: All the manuscripts that I have been able to inspect have *Thoringiam* here and *Thoringorum* below, except the Reginensis, which on the second occurrence has *Tungorum*, and the Badianus, *Tongrorum*. Since Thuringia lies beyond the Rhine in relation to Gaul, Valesius thinks that one should read *transacto Moeno*, ‘after crossing the Main,’ the river that those traveling from Pannonia toward Thuringia would have had to cross. R. P. Daniel of the Society of Jesus took another path in his French *History of France*, where he says that the word *Rhine* should be retained because Gregory’s passage must be understood of the Franks who, after receiving settlements from the emperor Probus near the Black Sea, wandered through various provinces and finally returned through Gaul to their homeland; in this way they crossed the Rhine, which they ought in fact to have encountered on their way. But this interpretation seems contrary to Gregory’s words. William Morel says that he saw an ancient manuscript in which the same hand had written *Thoringorum vel Tungrorum*, ‘of the Thuringians or Tungri.’ Hence some more recent writers think that, after crossing the Rhine, the Franks inhabited the region of the Tungri. But not only the printed and manuscript copies, but also Fredegar, the author of the *Deeds of the Franks*, and others oppose this reading].

There, near the districts or cities, they set up over themselves long-haired kings from the first—and, so to speak, nobler—family of their people. This was later confirmed by the victory of Chlodovech [Note: The Reginensis has *Hludouvichi*. Gregory implies that Chlodovech’s victory granted him sole kingship and that royal dignity thereafter remained with his descendants. Valesius demonstrates from Claudian and Eumenius that Frankish kings had been long-haired well before Chlodion]. We shall set this out in the following account.

For in the consular records we read that Theodomer, king of the Franks, son of the late Richimer [Note: Valesius thinks that *quondam* should be read as *cons.*, that is, ‘consul’; the Reginensis does not contain this word, and when Valesius cites the same passage in additions to volume I of the *History*, he omits it. Some have thought that Aschila, mentioned here, was the daughter of the emperor Anthemius, because Ricimer was Anthemius’ son-in-law. But they have confused two Ricimers, different in time and homeland, as Sirmond notes in his annotations on Ennodius’ *Life of Saint Epiphanius*. Furthermore, as Scaliger observes in book VI of *On the Correction of Time*, chronicles were written among the ancients in two ways: some by a succession of consuls, which were called *Consularia*, such as Gregory cites here; others in which the consuls were not arranged, which were called *Chronica*], and his mother Aschila, were killed by the sword.

They also relate that Chlogio, an able and very noble man among his people, was at that time king of the Franks. He lived at the fortress of Dispargum [Note: Since there is no agreement about the location of Thuringia praised by Gregory, there is likewise disagreement about the fortress called Dispargum. Some think it was Duisburg on the Rhine in the duchy of Cleves; others, with Ortelius, Asciburgium, commonly Asbourg, in the county of Moers; others, including Cointius, Duisborch, still a town between Brussels and Leuven; Wendelinus and others believe it was Diest], which lies in the territory of the Thuringians.

In these regions—that is, toward the south—Romans lived as far as the river Loire. Beyond the Loire, the Goths ruled. The Burgundians, also following the Arian sect, lived across the Rhône, which adjoins the city of Lyon.

Chlogio sent scouts to the city of Cambrai, and after inspecting everything, followed them himself. He crushed the Romans and seized the city. Having remained there for a short time, he occupied the territory as far as the river Somme [Note: From Apollinaris Sidonius’ *Panegyric on Majorian* we learn that Chlodion, who had overrun Arras, was driven away by Majorian:

> “After a short time  
> You fought together with the Franks, when Cloio had overrun  
> The lands of Arras …”

Sirmond reads *Francus qua*, ‘the Frank when,’ etc. Prosper, in his *Chronicle* under the fifth year after Honorius’ death—that is, the year 427—says that Clodius ruled in Francia. Twenty years afterward, that is, in 447, Meroveus is said to have ruled in Francia].

Some assert that a certain Merovech was of his line and that Childeric was Merovech’s son.

## X

This nation, however, always seemed to give obedience to superstitious rites and did not acknowledge God at all. They fashioned for themselves forms of forests, waters, birds, beasts, and the other elements as well, and were accustomed to worship them as gods and offer sacrifices to them.

Would that the terrible voice which spoke through Moses to the people had touched the innermost fibers of their hearts when it said:

> “You shall have no other gods besides me. You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor worship any likeness of what is in heaven, or on earth, or in the waters; you shall not make such things, nor worship them”  
> (Exodus 20:3–5).

And:

> “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve, and by his name shall you swear”  
> (Deuteronomy 6:13).

What if they had been able to understand what punishment followed upon Israel’s veneration of the molten calf? After the feast and songs, after their debauchery and dances, when with unclean mouths they spoke of that image, saying, “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exodus 32:4), twenty-four thousand of them fell.

What of those who had been initiated into the worship of Baal-peor and, mingling with the Moabite prostitutes, were struck down and laid low by their own people? In that plague Phinehas the priest, after killing the adulterers, appeased the wrath of God (Numbers 25:1, 5), and it was reckoned to him as righteousness (Psalm 105:31).

What if those words had also been brought to their ears which the Lord thunders through David:

> “For all the gods of the nations are demons, but the Lord made the heavens”  
> (Psalm 96:5).

And:

> “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands. May those who make them and all who trust in them become like them”  
> (Psalm 115:4, 8; Psalm 135:15, 18).

Or this:

> “Let all who worship carved images and boast in their idols be put to shame”  
> (Psalm 97:7).

And again what the prophet Habakkuk testifies:

> “What benefit is a carved image that its sculptor has carved? He fashioned it, a molten image, a phantom of the mind [Note: Beccensis and Colbertinus, together with Morel’s manuscript, Chesnius, and Freher, read: ‘A phantom, a lie.’ But other printed editions give the passage entirely differently: ‘What benefit is a carved image to its maker, who carved it? A molten image and a false likeness … Behold, he is covered with gold and silver, and there is no breath in it.’ This reading conforms more closely to our version. The other seems rather to convey the sense than the words of the sacred text]. This is the product of gold and silver, and there is no spirit in it. But the Lord is in his holy temple; let all the earth be silent before him”  
> (Habakkuk 2:18–20).

Another prophet also says:

> “Let the gods who did not make heaven and earth perish from the earth and from beneath the heavens” [Note: The same manuscripts have ‘from beneath heaven’]  
> (Jeremiah 10:11).

And in the same place:

> “Thus says the Lord, who creates the heavens, he himself is God; who forms the earth and the things in it, he himself is its fashioner. He did not establish it in vain; he formed it to be inhabited”  
> (Isaiah 45:18).

> “I am the Lord; this is my name. I will not give my glory to another, nor my power to carved images, which have passed away from the beginning”  
> (Isaiah 42:8).

And elsewhere:

> “Are there among the carved images of the nations any that can bring rain?” [Note: Beccensis has: ‘Is there a God among the carved images … who brings rain?’]  
> (Jeremiah 14:22).

And again through Isaiah he says:

> “I am the first and the last” [Note: The Reginensis has: ‘and I am the last’], “and besides me there is no God, and no creator whom I do not know. All the makers of idols are nothing, and their most cherished things will not benefit them. They are their own witnesses, because they neither see nor understand, and they shall be put to shame” [Note: The same manuscript and Beccensis have ‘they shall be put to shame’. From “Who has fashioned” through “with burning coals” is absent in the Corbey, Reginensis, and Beccensis manuscripts]. “Behold, all their associates shall be put to shame; for they are craftsmen among men. Who has fashioned a god or cast a carved image for no useful purpose? He formed it with burning coals and hammers, and worked it with the strength of his arm. Likewise the woodworker shaped it with a compass and made the image of a man, like a handsome man dwelling in a house. He cuts down a tree, works it, and makes a carved image, and worships it as a god. He fastens it with nails and hammers so that it will not fall apart. They carry it because they cannot walk [Note: The Reginensis and Beccensis have ‘they shall carry them’]. But the remainder of the wood is made into fuel for people, and they warm themselves. From another part he makes a god and a carved image for himself; he bends before it and worships it [Note: The Reginensis has ‘and he worships and beseeches it’], and beseeches it, saying: ‘Save me, for you are my god.’ I have burned half of it in the fire, and on its coals I baked bread; I cooked meat and ate it, and from what remains I will make an idol. Before a block of wood I shall fall down [Note: The Corbey, Beccensis, and Reginensis manuscripts, together with Morel’s manuscript, have ‘I shall worship’]. Its other part is ashes. A foolish heart worshiped it, and it did not save its soul [Note: The Reginensis has ‘it did not save him’], nor does he say, ‘Perhaps there is a lie in my right hand’”  
> (Isaiah 44:6–20).

But this nation of the Franks did not understand these things at first; afterward, however, they did, as the following history relates.

## XI

Avitus was one of the senators and, as is abundantly clear, a citizen of Arvernia. When he had sought the imperial power and wished to live in luxury, he was cast out by the senators [Note: So read the Corbey and Colbertinus manuscripts; others have ‘expelled’]. At the city of Placentia he was ordained bishop [Note: Placentia is the well-known city of Italy. Gregory devotes the entire second book of *The Glory of the Martyrs* to Saint Julian, who rests at Brioude, formerly Brivas, in Arvernia].

When he learned that the senate, still hostile to him, wished to deprive him of his life, he made for the basilica of Saint Julian, the Arvernian martyr, with many gifts. But, having completed the course of his life on the journey, he died; he was carried to the village of Brioude and buried at the feet of the aforementioned martyr. Martianus succeeded him [Note: Perhaps Majorianus].

In Gaul, Aegidius, one of the Romans, was appointed master of the soldiers [Note: Several manuscripts and printed editions read ‘was called.’ He had received this office from Avitus. Idatius calls him count of both military commands.].

## XII

Childeric, however, being exceedingly abandoned to luxury and ruling over the nation of the Franks, began to dishonor their daughters outrageously. Therefore they became indignant and expelled him from the kingdom. When he learned that they also wished to kill him, he went to Thuringia, leaving there a man dear to him [Note: The Colbertinus adds, in a hand nearly contemporary: ‘named Viomadus.’ He is so called by Aimoinus in book II, chapter 7], who could soften the minds of the furious men with gentle words. He also gave a sign indicating when he might return to his homeland.

They divided a single gold coin between them: Childeric carried one half away with him, while his friend kept the other, saying: “When I send this half to you, and the two halves joined together make one solidus, then you may return to your homeland with a secure heart.”

Childeric therefore departed for Thuringia and hid with King Bisinus [Note: The Reginensis and Badianus have *Basinus*; the Reginensis and Beccensis, *Bissinus*] and his wife Basina. Finally, after they had expelled him, the Franks unanimously chose as their king Aegidius, whom we previously said had been sent by the state as master of the soldiers.

When he had ruled over them for eight years, that faithful friend secretly reconciled the Franks and sent messengers to Childeric with the half of the divided solidus that he had retained. Childeric, recognizing the sure signs that he was desired by the Franks, returned from Thuringia at their own request and was restored to his kingdom.

While they were ruling together, that Basina whom we mentioned above left her husband and came to Childeric. When he anxiously asked why she had come to him from so distant a region, she is said to have replied:

> “I know your worth, that you are exceedingly capable; therefore I have come to live with you. For you should know that if I had known anyone more worthy than you in the lands across the sea, I would certainly have sought to live with him.”

He rejoiced and took her as his wife. She conceived and bore a son, and they named him Chlodovech. He was a great man and an excellent warrior.

## XIII

At Arvernia, after the death of Saint Artemius, Venerandus, a bishop from the senatorial class, was ordained. What sort of pontiff he was, Paulinus testifies [Note: The printed editions, together with several manuscripts, read ‘the presbyter Paulinus.’ The editor of the new edition of his works insists that this was Paulinus, the famous bishop of Nola, in chapter 49 of his *Life*, against Chiffletius, who denies it. Rosweydus leaves the matter undecided. Certainly, even if Gregory calls this Paulinus ‘presbyter,’ as several manuscripts do, nothing follows from that, since the letter could have been written by Paulinus while he was still a presbyter, and Gregory may have read the title as it was then prefixed to it. But whoever this Paulinus was, nothing survives from him apart from the words quoted here by Gregory], saying:

> “For if you see these priests worthy of the Lord—Exsuperius [Note: Saint Jerome praises Exsuperius in his letter to the monk Rusticus and elsewhere. Pope Innocent I also wrote to him. His feast is observed on September 28. Pope Zosimus mentions Simplicius in letter 7. The Colbertinus and Badianus call him *Supplicius*. See book *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 45, concerning Amandus. In the Corbey, Reginensis, and Badianus manuscripts, Dynamius is written *Damianus*. Beccensis has *Dinamium Engolesinae*], of Toulouse; Simplicius of Vienne; Amandus of Bordeaux; Diogenianus of Albi; Dynamius of Angoulême; Venerandus of Arvernia; Alithius of Cahors; or now Pegasius of Périgueux—whatever the evils of the age may be, you will certainly see men most worthy to be guardians of all holiness, faith, and religion.”

He is reported to have died on the very vigil of the Lord’s Nativity [Note: Gregory discusses the church of Saint Venerandus in *The Glory of the Confessors*, chapters 35 and following. He is mentioned in the little book *On the Saints of Clermont*, chapter 10, where it is said that the bodies of several holy martyrs were buried there. It now stands in the gardens of the monastery of Issoire. See Savaron’s notes. The feast of Saint Venerandus is celebrated on January 18].

When morning came, the procession of the solemnity was the observance of his funeral. After his death, a shameful dispute among the citizens arose over the bishopric [Note: All the manuscripts read *intentio*, ‘purpose’ or ‘contention’; the printed editions have *contentio*, ‘dispute,’ both here and below. It is nevertheless certain that Gregory and similar authors commonly use *intentio* to express contention]. Since the factions had divided among themselves and each wished to elevate one candidate or another, there was great conflict among the people.

Nevertheless, while the bishops were seated on Sunday, a certain veiled woman, devoted to God, boldly entered among them and said:

> “Hear me, priests of the Lord. Know that those whom these men have chosen for the priesthood do not please God. For behold, the Lord himself will today provide a bishop for himself. Therefore do not disturb or quarrel with the people, but be patient for a little while. The Lord is now guiding the one who will govern this Church.”

While they were marveling at these words, a presbyter named Rusticus arrived. He belonged to the diocese of the city of Arvernia itself, and he had already been indicated to the woman in a vision.

When she saw him, she said:

> “Behold the one whom the Lord has chosen; behold what sort of bishop the Lord has appointed for you. Let this man be ordained bishop.”

As she spoke, the whole people, setting aside every dispute, cried out that he was worthy and just. He was placed in the cathedra and, amid the joy of the people, received the honor of the seventh episcopate in that place [Note: His feast is celebrated on September 24; he is commonly called Saint Rotiri].

## XIV

[Note: [Col. 0211B] This chapter and the following three—that is, 14, 15, 16, and 17—are absent from Bell. and Corb. In Colb. a., this chapter and the following one were added in another but ancient hand.]

In the city of Tours, after Bishop Eustochius had died in the seventeenth year of his priesthood, Perpetuus was ordained as the fifth bishop after blessed Martin [Note: [Col. 0211B] Below, in Book X, chapter 31, he is called the sixth bishop of Tours, because Justinian and Armentius, who were appointed between him and Briccius, are not counted there. Apollinaris Sidonius, however, in Book IV, Letter 18, counts him as the sixth from blessed Martin, including the two mentioned above; in this sense he can here be called fifth after Saint Martin, so that Briccius is first, followed by Justinian, Armentius, and the fourth, Eustochius, whom Perpetuus succeeded.].

When he saw that miracles were continually taking place at Martin’s tomb, he judged the small chapel that had been built over it, on seeing how tiny it was, unworthy of such miracles. After removing it, he built there the great basilica that remains to this day [Note: [Col. 0211C] After the blessed bishop had died at Condat, the people of Tours, although the people of Poitiers protested, brought his sacred body back to their city by placing it on the Loire. It was first deposited beside the riverbank at a place that was thereafter called the Station of the Body of Blessed Martin; an oratory dedicated to his name can still be seen there today. It was subsequently transferred elsewhere, and as miracles at his tomb multiplied, Brictius, his successor, built a church over the holy body in the eleventh year after Martin’s death, as Gregory relates. Perpetuus later demolished it in order to build a more magnificent one. Gregory described this new basilica in Book II of his History, chapter 14, and the transfer of the sacred body into it in Book I of The Miracles of Saint Martin, chapter 6. Apollinaris Sidonius, then bishop of Clermont, also discusses the same basilica, which he adorned with verses at Perpetuus’s invitation; these are found in Letter 18 of Book IV, addressed to Lucontius. Our Gregory praises other verses composed by Martin, the apostle of the Galicians or Suebians, in Book V of his History, chapter 38; he also published others composed by Paulinus of Périgueux, which had been inscribed in various places in the basilica. How famous Saint Martin’s tomb subsequently became is evident from various passages of Gregory, which there is no time to cite individually. Certainly our kings always venerated Martin as the special patron of their kingdom and enriched his basilica with various gifts and privileges. After it had been burned by Willicharius, Chlothar I restored it and had it covered with tin. Saint Odo briefly describes the various ornaments with which it once shone in his sermon on its burning: “Inside it was covered with marble plaques. For sometimes the reddish wall presented a varied and very beautiful design in Proconnesian marble, sometimes white in Parian marble, and sometimes green in Spartan marble; outside, it gleamed with golden, sapphire-colored, and mosaic stones, and its roof was covered with tin plates.” Saint Audoenus relates that the tomb of the same holy man was made and adorned with gold, silver, and precious gems by Saint Eligius. Herbernus, who, after being abbot of Marmoutier, became archbishop of Tours toward the end of the ninth century, after the sacred body had been brought back from Burgundy, describes the apse as it had been constructed by blessed Perpetuus. We reproduce his words here, which the Anonymous author adopted in the Deeds of the Counts of Anjou, from two manuscript codices:

“Indeed, the apse in which the body of blessed Martin was contained, which they had also brought from Auxerre, was cast from gold and silver—what is called electrum—and was two fingers thick. The craftsman had designated blessed Perpetuus as the author of the work by means of letters and verses carved upon it. It had no crack, opening, window, or door. Blessed Perpetuus had made it when he raised his body from the ground, first wrapped in red purple and carefully sewn together, and placed it in this apse. He also made a square, hollow altar from cut stones, covered it with a large slab, and cemented it with the others. He also made inside it another apse, cast from orichalcum, copper, and tin, a palm in thickness, with a cast door fastened by bolts, hinges, and four keys; within it he placed this electrum apse. Finally, he made above it a canopy adorned with the finest gold and precious stones, worthy of so great a priest.”

At the beginning of the eleventh century, the church of Saint Martin, which the Normans had burned, was not merely restored but entirely rebuilt from its foundations by Herveus the treasurer, in approximately the form in which it is seen today. Glaber Rodulfus writes that the dedication of this basilica was solemnly celebrated. The body of the blessed bishop was then restored to its proper place, where, as Sigebert of Gembloux writes in the following century, it shone forth in miracles, decently placed beneath a ciborium covered with gold, silver, and gems. That ciborium was destroyed and dismantled by the Calvinists in the preceding century; but its former appearance can be seen from the glass window of a chapel situated in the northern aisle of the major basilica, where Louis XI, king of France, is depicted twice kneeling in prayer before Saint Martin’s tomb beneath the ciborium. Other reliquaries of the saints can also be seen there, which before that calamity had been kept around the tomb of the blessed bishop. Although the tomb of the holy man had been moved from its place so many times, it had not yet been opened after the first translation carried out by blessed Perpetuus. This is evident from an old document, which we thought it worthwhile to transcribe here from a manuscript codex of Saint Martin:

“With Charles the Fair present, together with his wife and many bishops and princes, and by permission of John XXII, in the year 1323, on 1 December, the head of Saint Martin was transferred by Robert, bishop of Chartres, after Saint Martin’s tomb had been opened.

“Within that tomb they found one silver chest, and in it a little willow basket, wonderfully white and fresh, in which blessed Perpetuus had honorably placed the body of that most blessed confessor. Perpetuus had assumed the dignity of the cathedral see of Tours in the sixty-fourth year after the passing of the most glorious Martin. When that venerable bishop of Chartres opened with devotion and trembling the basket in which the most blessed body lay hidden, he found the head, together with the rest of the body, wrapped and bound like that of a little child, and found attached to it a label on which was written: ‘THIS IS THE BODY OF BLESSED MARTIN, BISHOP OF TOURS.’ On seeing this, and rejoicing together in the Lord over so precious a treasure found there, the same bishop of Chartres began to unwrap the holy body, which at the time of its translation had been bound with a certain white band by blessed Perpetuus and sealed with his own seal. When it had been unbound and uncovered, the same bishop informed the king that he should receive the head of the most blessed confessor and place it in a golden vessel, which had immediately been prepared. But the king, unwilling and not presuming to touch the most holy head, told the bishop that he himself should receive and transfer it.”

Such was the condition of the Martinian church until the year 1562, when the Calvinist heretics, having gained possession of the city of Tours, completely stripped all the churches of the city and province, burning the relics of the saints in an immense act of sacrilege. The place where Saint Martin’s body was burned can still be visited today at the southern door of the church. In the following year, when the disturbances had been somewhat calmed, the few things that had been rescued from the fury of the heretics were identified by order of the venerable chapter and placed in a reliquary. We copied the chapter’s decree on this matter from its registers; it reads as follows:

“In the year 1563, on 1 July, my lords ordered that one of the large bones of the arm of the most blessed Martin, and another from his head, as well as the silk cloth in which the body of that most blessed Martin had been placed, together with the other relics from the heads of the blessed Briccius and Gregory that remained and had not been burned by the heretics in the previous year, should be placed in a small wooden chest made for this purpose, which should be covered with some beautiful silk cloth; and that an inscription identifying each such relic should be placed upon it, and that it should be signed by me, the notary, for the perpetual remembrance of the matter.”

The same register indicates that all these things were done on the following 3 July. In the year 1564, on 5 July, those same relics, placed in the chest, were deposited upon the altar standing behind the high altar, where the chest of Saint Martin had formerly been. On 11 September 1636 they were solemnly examined by the entire chapter. That altar, raised by many steps, can still be seen today; beneath it lies the stone of blessed Martin’s tomb. On the greater festivals, the priest celebrating Mass begins there, and at the words after the Confession, “We beseech you, Lord, by the merits of your saints, whose relics are kept here,” he kisses that stone and then proceeds to the high altar to celebrate Mass in the customary manner.

A tablet bearing the following inscription was affixed by order of the chapter to a column near the tomb:

“Names of the bodies of the saints of this church that were buried here: Saint Martin, Saint Briccius, Saint Spanus, Saint Perpetuus, Saint Gregory of Tours, Saint Eustochius, Saint Eufronius. In the midst of these lay the body and tomb of the most blessed Martin, whose venerable relics were kept in chests.”

This, then, is the present condition of the church of Saint Martin. To discuss its privileges and jurisdiction, which it still exercises over many other churches, is not part of my purpose. What we have presented here we owe for the most part to the distinguished Gatianus Galiczonus, doctor of the Sorbonne, canon and cantor of that church, who, when we were staying at Tours, showed us everything in detail.]

It stands five hundred and fifty paces from the city [Col. 0213A]. It is one hundred and sixty feet long [Note: [Col. 0214C] The Reg., Colb., and Chesn. manuscripts read “one hundred and fifty-five feet long.”], sixty feet wide, and forty-five feet high up to the vault. It has thirty-two windows in the presbytery [Note: [Col. 0214C] Here, by “altar,” the presbytery is probably meant, while by “capso” the nave is understood. Consult Mabillon’s Gallican Liturgy, Book I, chapter 8, no. 1 and following. Gregory discusses this church again in Book I of The Miracles of Saint Martin, etc. See also Letter 18 of Book IV of Apollinaris Sidonius, which includes verses that he himself composed for adorning the same church.], twenty in the nave, and forty-one columns. Throughout the entire building there are fifty-two windows and one hundred and twenty columns; eight doors, three in the presbytery and five in the nave.

The solemnity of this basilica possesses a threefold significance: the dedication of the church, the translation of the saint’s body, and his ordination to the episcopate. You shall observe this on the fourth day before the Nones of July [4 July]; but know that his deposition is celebrated on the third day before the Ides of November [11 November]. If you celebrate these faithfully, you will deserve the protection of the blessed bishop both in the present age and in the age to come.

And because the vault of the former chapel had been constructed with elegant workmanship, the priest considered it unworthy that its work should perish. Instead, in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, he built another basilica and incorporated that vault into it. He also built many other basilicas, which still stand in the name of Christ to this day [69].

## XV

At that time the basilica of the blessed Symphorianus, martyr of Autun, was also built by the priest Eufronius. Eufronius himself subsequently obtained the episcopate of that city [Note: [Col. 0214D] He presided over the Church of Autun toward the end of the fifth century. He took part in the ordination of John, bishop of Chalon, as Apollinaris Sidonius testifies in Book IV, Letter 25; the same author wrote to him in Letter 8 of Book VII and Letter 2 of Book IX. There is also an excellent letter of his and of Lupus, bishop of Troyes, concerning ecclesiastical discipline, in Sirmond, volume I of the Councils; Idatius praises another letter of his to Count Agrippinus in his Chronicle.]. He sent with great devotion the marble that is found above the holy tomb of blessed Martin.

## XVI

Saint Namatius, after the death of Bishop Rusticus, was at that time the eighth bishop among the people of Clermont [Note: [Col. 0214D] This chapter and the following one are absent from the Regius and Colbertinus manuscripts.]. He built by his own efforts the church that still stands [Note: [Col. 0214D] This is the cathedral church, about which Savaro makes many observations in his notes on chapter 1 of The Churches of Clermont. Hence it is called “the older” in Mor. s. and Regm.; the printed editions instead have “the very ancient.” See Mabillon’s Gallican Liturgy, Book I, chapter 8.], and is regarded as the older church within the city walls. It is one hundred and fifty feet long, sixty feet wide, and fifty feet high inside the nave up to the vault. In front it has a rounded apse, with side chapels constructed in elegant workmanship on either side, and the entire building is arranged in the form of a cross [Col. 0214B]. It has forty-two windows, seventy columns, and eight doors.

The fear of God and great splendor are seen there; and very often the religious perceive a most sweet fragrance, like that of spices, coming forth there. Its walls at the presbytery are adorned with *opus sarsurium*, made from many kinds of marble [Col. 0215A] [Note: [Col. 0215C] Altaserra observes that *opus sarsurium* is the same as plasterwork, which is varied and multiform, so called from the verb *sarcire*, “to patch” or “join.” The walls of temples and public buildings were covered or encrusted with marble, as is described here of the church constructed by Saint Namatius.].

When the blessed bishop had completed the building in the twelfth year, he sent priests to Bologna, a city of Italy, asking them to provide him with relics of Saints Vitalis and Agricola, whom we know with complete certainty to have been crucified for the name of Christ our God [Note: [Col. 0215C] He did indeed obtain relics of these martyrs, as Gregory himself relates in Book I of The Glory of the Martyrs, chapter 44. Saint Ambrose describes the passion of these same martyrs in Book I, chapters 1 and 2, of his work On the Exhortation to Virginity.].

## XVII

His wife built a basilica of Saint Stephen outside the city walls [Note: [Col. 0215C] Today it is a parish church, its name having been changed about two hundred years ago; it is called Saint Eutropius Suburbicarius. Saint Namatius was buried there with other saints, as indicated by the booklet On the Saints of Clermont, chapter 13.].

When she wished to adorn it with painted colors, she held a book in her lap, reading the accounts of the deeds of the ancients [Note: [Col. 0215D] Thus the Regm. manuscript. The printed editions instead have “accounts of ancient action”; Mor. s. has “of ancient action.” Gregory frequently mentions paintings in churches, for example in Book VII, chapter 36, and Book X, final chapter, etc.], and indicating to the painters what they ought to depict on the walls.

One day, as she sat in the basilica reading, a poor man came in to pray. Seeing her in a black garment and already advanced in age, he thought she was one of the needy. He brought out a piece of bread, placed it in her lap, and departed. She, not disdaining the gift of the poor man, who did not recognize her identity, accepted it and gave thanks. She set it aside, preferring it to her own feasts, and each day took a blessing from it until it was consumed.

## XVIII

At that time Childeric fought battles at Orléans; Adouacrius [Note: [Col. 0215D] So Bell., Corb., Reg., and Regm., together with several printed editions. Others have Odouacrius, while Colb. has Odoacrius. Bec. has Adouacius.] came with the Saxons to Angers. A great plague then devastated the people. Aegidius died and left a son named Syagrius. After his death, Adouacrius took hostages from Angers and other places.

The Britons were expelled from Bourges by the Goths [Note: [Col. 0215D] Corb. and Bec. read “from Bourges.”], and many were killed near the village of Dol [Note: [Col. 0215D] A monastery of our Order, which at the beginning of this century was transferred to secular canons, still exists there. It is commonly called Bourg de Déols, separated from Châteauroux by the intervening River Indre.]. Count Paulus, however, with the Romans and Franks waged war against the Goths and carried off plunder [Note: [Col. 0215D] Here he calls those Gauls “Romans” who had not yet been subjected to foreign kings. Indeed, not only in Gaul but also in Italy, Spain, Africa, and elsewhere, even after these provinces had been completely subdued by the barbarians, the peoples were divided into two classes, as it were. Some were called Romans, namely the ancient inhabitants, because they had been subject to Roman rule and generally continued to live under Roman laws even when subject to foreign rulers, and adhered to the Catholic faith. Others were called barbarians, a term they considered honorable. See Valesius, Book VI of Frankish Affairs, p. 289, for more on this matter.], and plundered them.

When Adouacrius came to Angers, King Childeric arrived on the following day; after Count Paulus had been killed, he took possession of the city. On that day a great fire burned the church building [Note: [Col. 0216C] In the Bell. manuscript, after several lines at the end of the page had been worn away, the following page of the same leaf begins with the words “the region.” The words “so that what concerns you,” etc., belong to chapter 32.].

## XIX

After these events, war was waged between the Saxons and the Romans. But when the Saxons turned their backs, they left many of their own people dead by the sword as the Romans pursued them. Their islands, together with the great number of people killed there, were captured and destroyed by the Franks [Note: [Col. 0216C] These islands were situated in the Loire, as Cointius believes. The Saxons had fortified them so that, if matters went badly for them, they would have an open route of escape by sea. Cointius also thinks that *Alanos* should be read instead of *Alamannos*, since they had invaded a part not of Italy but of Gaul. The observations made above on chapter 7 of this book support his conjecture.].

In that year, in the ninth month, the earth shook. Adouacrius made a treaty with Childeric, and together they subdued the Alamanni, who had invaded part of Italy.

## XX

Eorichus [Note: [Col. 0216C] Regm. has Theodericus and below Teddricus; Corb. and Bec. have Eoricus or Euricus. Below, in chapter 25, he is called Evarix. Gregory relates the death of Victorius in Book I of The Glory of the Martyrs, chapter 45, and in The Life of Saint Abraham. Apollinaris Sidonius also discusses him in Book VII, Letter 17. This chapter is absent from Bell.] the king of the Goths appointed the general Victorius over seven cities in the fourteenth year of his reign.

Upon arriving immediately at Clermont, Victorius wished to add to the city. Hence he ordered that those crypts, which still remain today at the basilica of Saint Julian, and the columns now standing in the church, be set in place [Note: [Col. 0216D] Three manuscripts have “written.” Moreover, this does not refer to the basilica of Brioude, as Fredegar thought, but to the one situated within the city of Clermont in honor of Saint Julian, as Savaro observes in his notes on chapter 33 of Book I, On the Churches of Clermont. Consult Cointius under the year 554, no. 4.].

He ordered the basilica of Saint Lawrence and of Saint Germanus of the village of Licaniacum to be built [Note: [Col. 0216D] The Casinensis manuscript has “Saint Martin of Lecaniacum”; Regm. has “Saint Germanus in the village of Licaniacum.” Marollius observes that this place is now commonly called Saint-Germain de Lambron.].

He remained at Clermont for nine years. He brought accusations against the senator Eucherius [Note: [Col. 0216D] He is thought to be the man to whom Sidonius writes in Book III, Letter 8.]. After having him placed in prison, Victorius ordered him brought out at night and tied beside an ancient wall; he then ordered the wall itself to be thrown down upon him.

Because Victorius was excessively licentious in his love of women and feared that the people of Clermont would kill him, he fled to Rome. There, while attempting to practice similar excesses, he was pelted to death with stones. After his death, Eorichus reigned for four years; he died in the twenty-seventh year of his reign. There was also then a great earthquake.

## XXI

After Namatius, bishop of Clermont, had died [Note: [Col. 0216D] This chapter is absent from Corb., Bell., Reg., and Colb.], Eparchius succeeded him, a most holy and devout man. Since at that time the church possessed only a small estate within the city walls, the priest himself had a dwelling there, in the place now called the *Salutatorium* [Note: [Col. 0217C] The *Salutatorium*, otherwise called the *secretarium*, is now known as the sacristy. This is clear from Gregory the Great’s Letter 54 of Book IV to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna, and from canon 2 of the First Council of Mâcon.
