It received this name because bishops customarily sat there before the celebration of Mass to receive the greetings of the faithful who wished to commend themselves or some business to their prayers. Saint Martin appears to have left this to the priests, according to Sulpicius Severus, Dialogue 2, where Martin is said to have devoted himself to prayer while the priests, sitting in another sacristy with his permission, were occupied with receiving greetings or hearing business.], and rose from it to the church altar to give thanks to God during the night.

One night, as he entered, he found the church full of demons, and their chief seated in the bishop’s chair in the form of an adorned woman. The bishop said to him:

“O accursed harlot, is it not enough for you to infect every place with various pollutions? Must you also defile the chair consecrated by the Lord with the foul addition of your sitting? Depart from the house of God, lest it be polluted by you any longer.”

The demon replied:

“Because you call me a harlot, I shall prepare many snares for you through the desires of women.”

Having said this, he vanished like smoke.

Nevertheless, the priest was tempted by a bodily agitation toward lust [Note: [Col. 0217D] Mor. s. reads “from lust.”]; but, fortified by the sign of the holy cross, he suffered no harm from the enemy.

They also say that he established a monastery on the fortress of Mount Cantobennus [Note: [Col. 0217D] For this monastery, see above, Book I, chapter 39. Savaro considers the monastery of Cantobennus to be the very one that Saint Genesius, bishop of Clermont, is said to have established not far from the city for nuns, according to his Life. Others do not distinguish it from the monastery of Candidinum, which Felix, bishop of the same city, entrusted to Praejectus, then abbot and later his successor and martyr, as is related in the second Life of Praejectus. This site, later destroyed, was restored in the eleventh century by a certain Aldefredus, whom Robert, bishop of Auvergne, subjected to the monastery of Pibrac in the final year of the following century. After various vicissitudes, however, it was donated in our own age to the Discalced Carmelites. See the notes on Book I, chapter 39.], where there is now an oratory. During the days of Lent he used to shut himself in there; but on the day of the Lord’s Supper, accompanied by the clergy and townspeople with great psalmody, he returned to his own church.

When Eparchius departed this life, Sidonius was appointed in his place. He was a man of the highest nobility according to worldly rank and one of the foremost senators of Gaul, so much so that he took the daughter of the emperor Avitus as his wife.

During his episcopate, while Victorius, whom we mentioned above, was still living in the city of Clermont, there was in the monastery of blessed Cyricus [Note: [Col. 0218C] Thus Regm. with Bad.; the other printed editions and Bec. have Cyriacus. Our reading, however, is the correct one. This is Cyricus the boy, who suffered martyrdom together with his mother Julitta. See Savaro’s notes on the booklet On the Churches of Clermont, no. 14, which concerns the church of Saint Cyricus. Gregory also discusses it in The Life of Saint Abraham, Book of the Lives of the Fathers, chapter 3.] in that city an abbot named Abraham, who shone with the faith and works of the earlier Abraham, as we have written in the book of his Life [73].

## XXII

Saint Sidonius [Note: [Col. 0218D] This chapter is absent from Corb., Bell., Colb., and Regius. Sidonius is too illustrious a figure for us to make further observations about him here. His works were first published by Savaro and later by J. Sirmond. He was called Caius Sollius Apollinaris Sidonius; Savaro compiled his Life and prefixed it to his works. Sidonius himself wrote Letter 16 of Book V to his wife Papianilla, daughter of the emperor Avitus. After he received the priesthood, he treated her as a sister, as Sirmond demonstrates in his notes on that letter, where he also discusses further the celibacy of senior clergy. See above, Book I, chapter 39, and Jerome’s letter to Pammachius.] possessed such eloquence that he could often compose, extemporaneously and with brilliant clarity, whatever he wished, without any delay obstructing him.

One day he was invited to attend the festival of the basilica of the monastery mentioned above [Col. 0218A]. When the little book that he customarily used to conduct the sacred solemnities was wickedly taken away from him, he nevertheless, relying on the moment, delivered the entire service so skillfully that everyone marveled, and those standing there thought that it was not a man but an angel who had spoken. We have explained this more fully in the preface to the book that we appended concerning the Masses composed by him.

Although he possessed magnificent holiness and, as we have said, belonged to the foremost senatorial families, he would often, without his wife’s knowledge, take silver vessels from the house and distribute them to the poor. When she discovered this, she was offended with him; nevertheless, after giving the value to the needy, she restored the household objects.

## XXIII

When he had been devoted to the service of the Lord and was leading a holy life in the world [Note: [Col. 0218D] This chapter is absent from Corb., Bell., Colb., and Regius.], two priests rose up against him. They stripped him of all authority over the affairs of the Church, left him only a narrow and meager means of support, and reduced him to the utmost humiliation.

But divine mercy did not wish to leave his injury unpunished for long. One of those utterly wicked men, unworthy of being called a priest, had threatened before nightfall that he intended to drag him from the church [Note: [Col. 0218D] Regm. reads “intended to be dragged out”; Chesn. and Freh. read “intended either to drag him out.”]. When he heard the signal being given for Matins, he rose, boiling with anger against the holy man of God, intending to carry out in his wicked heart what he had planned the previous day.

He entered his privy, and while attempting to relieve his bowels, breathed out his spirit. A boy was waiting outside with a candle for his master to come out. Day had already dawned [Col. 0218C], and his companion, that is, the other priest, sent a messenger saying:

“Come; do not delay, so that together we may carry out what we agreed upon yesterday.”

But when the dead man delayed giving an answer, the boy lifted the curtain of the doorway and found his master dead on the little seat in the privy.

It is therefore certain that this man was guilty of no lesser crime than that Arius, whose internal organs were similarly expelled in portions through his lower parts [Col. 0219A] [Note: [Col. 0219D] Regm. has “the discharge of the lower part,” and below “let the priest be obeyed.” Bec. has “the discharge of the lower part … let the priest be obeyed.” For this cannot be understood without heresy: that in the Church the priest of God, to whom the sheep have been entrusted for feeding, should not be obeyed, while someone assumes authority that has been entrusted to him neither by God nor by human beings.].

Thereafter the blessed priest, although one enemy still remained, was restored to his authority. Later, when he began to fall ill after being seized by a fever, he asked his people to carry him into the church. When he had been brought there, a multitude of men, women, and children gathered around him, weeping and saying:

“Why are you abandoning us, good shepherd? To whom are you leaving us like orphans? Will there be life for us after your departure? Will there afterward be anyone to season us with the salt of wisdom, or to rebuke us with such prudence regarding fear of the Lord’s name?”

While the people said these and similar things with much weeping, the priest at last, as the Holy Spirit flowed into him, replied:

“Do not be afraid, O people. Behold, my brother Aprunculus is alive, and he will be your priest.”

They did not understand him, however, and thought that he was saying something in a state of ecstasy.

When he had departed [Note: [Col. 0219D] He died in the year 484, according to Savaro, specifically on 21 August; nevertheless, his feast is celebrated on 23 August in the Roman Martyrology. He was buried in the church of Saint Saturninus, as is stated in Book I, On the Churches of Clermont, chapter 22. This church, having changed its name, is now called Saint Amandinus. The body of blessed Sidonius was later transferred to the church of Saint Genesius.], the wicked priest—the surviving one of the two—immediately seized all the Church’s property, driven by greed as though he were already bishop. He said:

“At last God has looked upon me, recognizing that I am more righteous than Sidonius, and has granted me this authority.”

As he was carried proudly throughout the city, the Sunday that was approaching after the holy man’s death arrived. He prepared a banquet and ordered all the citizens to be invited into the church house [Note: [Col. 0219D] Gregory frequently mentions the “church house.” The name undoubtedly seems to designate the episcopal buildings adjoining the major church of the city, that is, the cathedral.]. Disregarding his elders, he reclined first upon the couch.

When the cupbearer offered him a cup, he said:

“My lord, I had a dream. If you permit me, I shall relate it. Last night, on this Sunday, I saw a great house, and in the house there was a throne on which sat someone like a judge, superior to all in authority. Many priests in white garments stood around him, together with exceedingly innumerable crowds of people.

“While I was gazing at these things in fear, I saw in the distance blessed Sidonius standing among them and attentively disputing with that priest who was most dear to you and who departed this world a few years ago. After defeating him, the king ordered him to be thrust into the deepest confines of the prison. After that man had been removed, Sidonius rose up against you again [Note: [Col. 0219D] The printed editions have “suggests to you,” or “reports to you.”], saying that you had shared in the crime for which the former man had been condemned.

“But when the judge began anxiously to inquire whom he should send to you, I began to hide myself among the others and stood behind them, thinking to myself that perhaps I, who am known to the man, would be sent. While I was silently turning these thoughts over in my mind, everyone else was removed, and I remained alone in public. Summoned by the judge, I approached him. As I contemplated his power and splendor, I became numb and began to falter from fear.

“He said to me: ‘Do not be afraid, boy. Go and tell that priest: “Come to answer your case, because Sidonius has asked that you be summoned.” But do not delay in going, for that king, under a solemn charge, commanded me to say these things to you, declaring: “If you remain silent, you will die the worst of deaths.”’”

As he spoke, the priest was terrified. The cup slipped from his hand, and he gave up his spirit. He was taken dead from the couch and committed to burial, destined to possess hell [76] with his companion.

The Lord displayed such a judgment against rebellious clerics in this world: one received the death of Arius; the other, like Simon Magus, was hurled headlong from the lofty tower of pride by the prayer of the holy apostle. There is no doubt that both possess Tartarus, since together they acted wickedly against their holy bishop.

Meanwhile, as the terror of the Franks was already resounding in these regions and everyone earnestly desired them to reign, Saint Aprunculus, bishop of Langres [Note: [Col. 0220D] He is mentioned again below in chapter 36 and in Book III, chapter 2; several letters of Ruricius, bishop of Limoges, to him survive. Sidonius wrote Letter 10 of Book IX to him while he was still bishop of Langres. He was buried in the church of Saint Stephen, according to Book I, On the Churches of Clermont, chapter 13, where he is called a saint. He is commemorated in Saussay’s Gallican Martyrology on 14 May.], began to be suspected by the Burgundians.

As their hatred increased day by day, orders were given that he should be secretly struck down with a sword. When news of this reached him, he was lowered at night from the fortress of Dijon by the wall and came to Clermont. There, in accordance with the word of the Lord that he had placed in the mouth of Saint Sidonius, he was appointed the eleventh bishop.

XXIV. But [Note: This chapter is lacking in Bell. In three others it begins without qualification, “In the time of Sidonius,” etc.] in the time of Bishop Sidonius a great famine afflicted Burgundy. As the people were scattered through various regions, and there was no one to distribute food to the poor, a certain Ecdicius, one of the senators and a kinsman of this man [Note: Ecdicius, or, as others write, Hecdicius, was the son of the emperor Avitus and the brother of Papianilla, Sidonius’s wife. Of him there survive Sidonius’s poem 20, Letter 1 of Book II, and Letter 3 of Book III. He was made Patrician by the emperor Julius Nepos, according to Letter 16 of Book V.], is said, trusting in God, to have performed a great deed at that time. For, when the famine was growing severe, he sent his servants with horses and wagons through the neighboring cities, so that they might bring to him those who were being afflicted by this want. Going forth, they brought to his house [Note: Most printed editions, with Bec, read “to his houses.”] all the poor whom they were able to find. There he fed them throughout the whole period of the barren season [Col. 0220D] and rescued them from death by famine. There were, as many say, more than four thousand people of both sexes indiscriminately. When abundance returned, he once again arranged their departure and restored each person to his own place.

After they had departed, a voice descended to him from heaven and said: “Ecdicius, Ecdicius, because you have done this deed, bread will never be lacking for you and your offspring, because you have obeyed my words and satisfied my hunger by feeding the poor.” Many also record that Ecdicius possessed extraordinary speed: for on one occasion he is reported to have put a multitude of Goths to flight with ten men [Note: Sidonius relates this in Letter 3 of Book III, where it is said that scarcely eighteen horsemen were with Ecdicius.].

It is also said that Saint Patiens, bishop of Lyon, bestowed a similar benefit upon the people during that same famine. A letter of blessed Sidonius still exists among us on this subject [Note: This is Letter 12 of Book VI. He praises the same man for constructing a church at Lyon in Book II, Letter 10. His memory is commemorated in the ecclesiastical calendars on the third day before the Ides of September.], in which he praised him in grand rhetorical style.

[Col. 0221B] XXV. At this time Evarix [Note: This is the same man who above, in chapter 20, is called Eorichus or Eurichus. In the chapter headings, even those of the older manuscripts, “of King Euva” is read. This chapter is lacking in Bellov.] too, king of the Goths, extending beyond the Spanish frontier, inflicted a severe persecution upon the Christians in Gaul. He beheaded indiscriminately those who did not consent to his wickedness; he confined clerics in prisons; priests he sent into exile, or killed by the sword. He had even ordered the entrances of the sacred temples themselves to be blocked with thorns, evidently so that the infrequency of entering might cause people to forget the faith.

At that time especially, the cities of Novempopulana and the two Germanias [Note: Aquitania must undoubtedly be read. For Evarichus did not launch a persecution in Germania; on the contrary, it raged most fiercely in Novempopulana and in both Aquitanias, as is clear from Sidonius’s own letter to Bishop Basil, which Gregory praises below; it is Letter 6 of Book VII. In it the cities of these three provinces in which the persecution raged are listed: Elusa, Auscius, Vasates, and Convenae in Novempopulana; Rutheni, Lemovicae, and Gabali in Aquitania Prima; Burdigala and Petrocorii in Aquitania Secunda. Nevertheless, it was not permissible to alter Gregory’s text without the authority of some manuscript. Valesius indeed thinks that Gregory’s name Germania should be understood as Aquitania, because Euricus reigned there, whom Gregory here believed to have originated in Germania. In the same way Lugdunensis Germania is called so by Sidonius in Book V, Letter 7. Janus a Costa, in Book II of the Decretals of Gregory IX, Title I, considers that “geminaeque germanae” should be read here. For, as he continues, he elegantly calls the twin, or double, Aquitania—First and Second—the sister and blood-relative of Novempopulana, that is, of Third Aquitania, as though provinces divided into two, three, or more parts were sisters to one another by virtue of this division, having as their common mother the city of Rome, the capital of the empire, from which the provinces were established and, as it were, born. Thus, in Tertullian’s book On the Cloak, the Roman colony of Utica is called the sister of Carthage. This opinion of his can be confirmed from the Testament of Saint Remigius and other ancient documents, in which the churches of Rheims and Trier are called sisters because each was a metropolis in Belgica and the chief city of its province. It is also supported by the manuscript of Königsberg, which reads “geminaeque germanae.”] were devastated by this calamity. There still exists, written on this very subject to Bishop Basil, a distinguished letter of Sidonius himself, which speaks as follows. But the persecutor, struck down by divine vengeance, died not long afterward.

XXVI. After this [Note: This chapter is lacking in the Corbie and Bellov manuscripts. In Colbert, however, it was added by another hand, though an ancient one. Concerning Perpetuus, Volusianus, and Verus, see below, Book X, chapter 31.] blessed Perpetuus, bishop of the city of Tours, having completed thirty years in the episcopate, rested in peace. In his place Volusianus, one of the senators, was appointed. But, being regarded with suspicion by the Goths, he was taken to Spain almost as a captive in the seventh year of his episcopate; he soon afterward died. In his place Verus [Note: Thus Colbert and Regius, together with some printed editions; others, with Bec and Königsberg, have Virus.] succeeded him and was ordained the seventh bishop after blessed Martin.

XXVII. After these events [Note: This chapter is lacking in the Bellovac manuscript.], when Childeric died, his son Chlodovechus reigned in his place. In the fifth year of his reign, Syagrius, king of the Romans and son of Aegidius, had his seat at the city of Soissons [Note: Corbie has Saxonas; nevertheless, as also below, Soissons is written by another hand of nearly equal age. Bec has Suessiones, and below Sessionas. These variant readings occur frequently in the manuscripts.], which the aforementioned Aegidius had once held.

Chlodovechus came against him with his kinsman Ragnacharius [Note: The same manuscript has “Ragnarius, his kinsman, who also held [a kingdom], came and prepared a battlefield for fighting”; Königsberg has “Racanarius ... had held,” etc.; Colbert has “Raghenarius,” etc. The Palatine manuscript and, throughout, another hand in Königsberg use Hludouvichus for Chlodovechus; another hand in Königsberg has Clodoveus. It is enough to have noted this once and again.]—for he too held a kingdom—and demanded that a field be prepared for battle. Nor did the other delay or fear to resist. Thus, when the two sides fought one another, Syagrius, seeing his army routed, turned his back and hastened at a swift pace to Alaric, king of Toulouse.

Chlodovechus sent to Alaric, demanding that he hand Syagrius over; otherwise, he should know that war would be waged against him because of his detention. Fearing that on Syagrius’s account he might incur the wrath of the Franks, as is the custom of the Goths when they are afraid [Note: See Salvian, Book VII, On the Government of God.], Alaric handed him over in chains to the envoys. Chlodovechus, having received him, ordered him to be committed to custody and, after taking possession of his kingdom, secretly commanded that he be struck down with the sword.

At that time many churches were plundered by Chlodovechus’s army, because he was still entangled in pagan errors. The enemy had carried away from a certain church a vessel of extraordinary size and beauty, together with the other furnishings of ecclesiastical service. The bishop [Note: This was Saint Remigius, bishop of Rheims, as Fredegar, chapter 16, Hincmar, Frodoard, and other authors testify. By “furnishings of ecclesiastical service” they understood the sacred equipment of the church, as is clear from numerous passages in Gregory himself and in other authors; see Book I, chapter 7, of Mabillon’s Gallican Liturgy. On this subject one should read the Testament of Saint Aredius, which we shall present in full in the Appendix.] of that church sent messengers to the king, asking that, if he did not deserve to receive anything else from the sacred vessels, at least his church might receive back its vessel.

When the king heard this, he said to the messenger: “Follow us to Soissons, because there all the things that have been acquired will be divided. When the lot gives me that vessel which the bishop requests, I shall fulfill his request.”

When he arrived at Soissons, and the entire burden of the booty had been placed in the middle, the king said: “I ask you, bravest warriors, not to refuse to grant me this vessel—he was speaking of the vessel mentioned above—outside my share.” When the king said this, those whose minds were sounder replied: “Everything that we see, glorious king, is yours; and we ourselves are subject to your authority. Now do what seems good to you, for no one is able to resist your power.”

When they had said this, one rash, envious, and hot-tempered man [Note: Chesne, together with Colbert, has “one rash Frank.” Other printed editions have “hot-headed.”] raised his battle-axe and struck the vessel with it, saying: “You will receive nothing from here except what the true lot grants you.”

At this, while everyone was stunned, the king restrained his injury with the mildness of patience, took the vessel, and returned it to the ecclesiastical messenger, keeping the wound hidden in his heart.

After a year had passed, he ordered the entire phalanx to appear with its weapons, so that it might display the splendor of its arms in the Field of Mars [Note: This was the name given to the assembly of the Franks because it ordinarily took place every year on the Kalends of March in a field where all had to attend equipped with weapons. Later it was called the Field of May, after Pippin transferred it to the Kalends of May.].

When he had decided to inspect them all, he came to the man who had struck the vessel and said to him: “No one brought weapons as neglected as yours. Neither spear, sword, nor axe is useful to you.” He seized the man’s axe [Note: Most printed editions have “battle-axe,” and so below wherever the word axe occurs.] and threw it onto the ground.

When the man bent down slightly to pick it up, the king raised his hands and drove his own axe into the man’s head. “This,” he said, “is what you did at Soissons to that vessel.” After the man had died, he ordered the others to depart, thereby instilling great fear in them because of this deed.

He fought many wars and won many victories. In the tenth year of his reign he made war upon the Thuringians and subjected them to his rule [Note: Corbie has “Many wars thereafter”; other copies have “Many wars thereafter, and so on.” Chlodovechus made the defeated Thuringians tributary, as the author of the Deeds of the Franks reports; afterward, as Gregory himself also testifies, the Thuringians still had their own kings.].

80 XXVIII. There was also Gundeuchus [Note: This chapter is lacking in Bellov. Gundeuchus is written in Corbie and others. Some have Gundivicus. In some manuscripts his sons are called Gundobaldus, Gothesilus or Godegisilus, Hilpericus, and so forth. Bec has Gundobaudus. Concerning Athanaric’s persecution, see above, chapter 4.], king of the Burgundians, descended from Athanaric, the persecuting king whom we mentioned above. He had four sons: Gundobadus, Godegiselus, Chilpericus, and Godomarus.

Gundobadus killed his brother Chilpericus with the sword and drowned his wife in the water with a stone tied around her neck. He condemned his two daughters to exile. The elder, having changed her clothing, was called Chrona [Note: She is so called in Corbie, the Palatine, and Colbert, which agree with the Life of Saint Chlotildis, where Chrona is read in section 2 of the first volume of the Acts of the Benedictine Saints. Bec and Königsberg, however, together with most printed editions, have Mucuruna; others have Corona. In Fredegar’s Epitome, chapter 17, she is called Sedeleuba. She is discussed in chapter 22 of the Chronicle. Savaro observes that Chlotildis and Chrona’s mother was called Agrippina, about whom Sidonius writes in Book V, Letter 7.], and the younger Chrotechildis [Note: Also Chrotchildis, Chrotigeldis, Rodieldis or Chrodieldis, and Chrotildis. Today she is commonly written Clotildis.] was so named.

Now, when Chlodovechus repeatedly sent an embassy to Burgundy, his envoys found the girl Chrotechildis. When they saw that she was graceful and intelligent and learned that she was of royal lineage, they reported this to King Chlodovechus. Without delay he sent an embassy to Gundobad, asking for her in marriage. Fearing to refuse, Gundobad handed her over to the men; and they, taking the girl, brought her quickly before the king. When he saw her, the king was greatly pleased and joined her to himself in marriage. He already had a son by a concubine, named Theodoric.

XXIX. Thus the king had a firstborn son by Queen Chrotechildis. When the woman wished to have him consecrated in baptism, she continually preached to her husband, saying:

“The gods whom you worship are nothing; they can help neither themselves nor others, for they are carved either from stone, wood, or some kind of metal. The names you have given them belonged to human beings, not gods [Note: The Bad edition has this reading; the others have “they were human beings, not gods.”]. Consider Saturn, who is said to have escaped by flight from his son lest he be driven from the kingdom; and Jupiter himself, the foulest perpetrator of every sexual outrage, the violator of men, the mocker of relatives, who could not even abstain from intercourse with his own sister, as she herself says: ‘Jove’s sister and wife’ (Virgil, Aeneid, Book I). What could Mars and Mercury do? They are endowed with magical arts rather than possessing the power of divine majesty.

But he should be worshiped who created heaven and earth, the sea, and everything in them by his word from things that did not exist; who made the sun shine and adorned heaven with stars; who filled the waters with reptiles, the earth with living creatures, and the air with flying things; at whose command the earth is adorned with crops, the trees with fruits, and the vineyards with grapes; by whose hand the human race was created; by whose generosity all creation itself serves the human being whom he created, both in obedience and in benefit.”

But while the queen said these things, the king’s mind was in no way moved to believe. He replied: “By the command of our gods all things are created and come forth. Your God, however, is shown to be able to do nothing; and, what is more, he is proved not even to belong to the race of gods.”

Meanwhile the faithful queen presented her son for baptism. She ordered the church to be decorated with veils and curtains, hoping that by this mystery he might more easily be drawn to belief, since preaching could not bend him. After the boy was baptized, and they had called him Ingomer [Note: Cassine and some printed editions have Ignomer.], he died in the very white garments [Col. 0225A] in which he had been regenerated [Note: “In white garments,” that is, within the week during which the newly baptized appeared dressed in white.].

Moved to anger by this, the king vehemently rebuked the queen, saying: “If the child had been dedicated in the name of my gods, he would certainly have lived. But now, because he has been baptized in the name of your God, he could not live at all.”

The queen replied: “I give thanks to God almighty, the creator of all things, who has not judged me wholly unworthy, but has deemed the one born from my womb worthy to be received into his kingdom. As for me, my heart is not touched by grief over this matter, because I know that those who are called from this world in white garments are to be nourished under God’s gaze” [Note: Others have “who has been called ... is to be nourished under God’s gaze.”].

After this she bore another son, whom she named Chlodomer after he had been baptized. When he began to fall ill, the king said: “Nothing else can happen except that the same thing will occur with this child as with his brother: baptized in the name of your Christ, he will immediately die.” But at his mother’s prayer, by the Lord’s command, he recovered.

XXX. But the queen did not cease preaching to the king that he should recognize the true God and disregard idols. Yet he could in no way be moved to believe these things, until at last war broke out against the Alamanni. In that war he was compelled by necessity to confess what previously he had denied by choice.

It happened that, when the two armies engaged, they were struck down with great violence, and Chlodovechus’s army began to fall in large numbers toward destruction. Seeing this, he raised his eyes to heaven, and, pierced in heart and moved to tears, said:

“Jesus Christ, whom Chrotechildis proclaims to be the Son of the living God, who are said to give help to those in distress and grant victory to those who hope in you, I devoutly implore the glory of your aid: if you grant me victory over these enemies, and I experience that power which the people dedicated to your name proclaims that it has proved in you, I shall believe in you and be baptized in your name. For I called upon my gods, but, as I discover, they have withdrawn far from my aid. Therefore I believe that they possess no power, since they do not come to the aid of those who obey them [Note: Thus four manuscripts; the others, together with the printed editions, have “come to the rescue.”]. Now I call upon you, and I desire to believe in you; only rescue me from my adversaries.”

As he said these things, the Alamanni turned their backs and began to slip away in flight. When they saw that their king had been killed, they submitted themselves to Chlodovechus’s authority, saying: “We beg you, let the people perish no further; we are now yours.”

He then stopped the war, restrained the people, and returned in peace. He told the queen how, by invoking Christ’s name, he had deserved to obtain victory [Note: Bec, the Morin manuscript in another hand, and another manuscript cited by Henschenius, together with Chesne, have here: “This took place in the fifteenth year of his reign, that is, in the year 496.” These words seem to have been taken from the Book of the Deeds of the Franks. They are absent from all the other manuscripts and printed editions that we were able to consult. Corbie and Bellov, however, have “in the fifteenth year of Chlodovechus” in the middle of chapter 37, as will be noted below. The battle mentioned here is believed to have been fought near the town of Tolbiac, as can be inferred from the same chapter 37.].

XXXI. Then [Note: This chapter is absent from the Bellov manuscript.] the queen secretly ordered Saint Remigius, bishop of the city of Rheims, to be summoned, asking him to teach the king the word of salvation. When the priest had been summoned, he began to explain to him privately [Note: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions have “he began to urge him.”] that he should believe in the true God, creator of heaven and earth, and disregard idols, which can benefit neither themselves nor others.

The king replied: “I shall gladly listen to you, most holy father. But one thing remains: the people who follow me will not allow me to abandon their gods. I shall go and speak to them according to your word.”

When he assembled his people, before he spoke, the power of God went before him, and the entire people acclaimed together: “We cast away mortal gods, pious king, and we are ready to follow the immortal God whom Remigius proclaims.”

This was reported to the bishop. Filled with great joy, he ordered the baptismal bath to be prepared. Painted veils shaded the streets of the church; the baptistery was adorned with white curtains; the baptismal font was arranged; balsams were spread; wax candles gleamed, fragrant with scent; and the whole temple of the baptistery was sprinkled with divine fragrance [Note: Hincmar and the writers who followed him assert that on this very occasion chrism was brought down from heaven in a flask by a dove. Although Gregory does not say this explicitly, he nevertheless suggests that something extraordinary occurred when he says that the place was sprinkled with divine fragrance, so that all, by the grace granted by God, thought themselves to be placed in Paradise. Certainly Hincmar not only described this miracle in the Life of Saint Remigius, but also spoke of it publicly, as a matter known to all, before a large assembly of prelates, princes, and peoples at Metz, when he was inaugurating Charles the Bald as king in the principal church there. Some trace of the event is also visible in the Life of Saint Chlotildis, which seems to have been written before Hincmar. As for the claim that the Magdeburg Centuriators had seen a manuscript of Gregory in which the flask was mentioned, and that heterodox opponents later tore it apart, this does not seem plausible. Perhaps they had before them the Book of the Deeds of the Franks, edited by Chesne in volume I, which is attributed to our Gregory in certain manuscripts and in which this story was written. One such copy is preserved in the library of the archmonastery of Saint Remigius at Rheims and was written about five hundred years ago. The flask itself is still carefully preserved at Rheims in the archmonastery of Saint Remigius for the consecration of our kings [Col. 0226D] [Col. 0225: Only a stranger to our history does not know that the sacred flask was destroyed and lost by the agents of the Convention; but a portion of the chrism was reverently gathered by a certain honorable man, kept hidden for a long time, and finally, when Clodovechus’s throne had been restored, was entrusted to a new flask used in the consecration of Charles X as king.].].

God granted such grace to those standing by that they thought themselves placed amid the fragrances of Paradise. The king, therefore, was the first to ask to be baptized by the bishop.

The new Constantine approached the baptismal bath, about to wipe away the disease of the ancient leprosy [Note: Colbert has the following note in the margin, added about four hundred years ago: “Behold, this historian agrees with the History of Saint Sylvester concerning Constantine’s leprosy being cleansed in the baptismal font.” It certainly seems that, by the time of this passage—in which Chlodovechus is compared with Constantine and Saint Remigius with blessed Sylvester—the belief had already become widespread that Constantine was baptized at Rome by blessed Sylvester and cleansed of his leprosy. The Acts of Saint Sylvester are also included in the Gelasian Decree. In the Regius manuscript, after the words “to be baptized by the bishop,” nearly a page is left blank; the following section then begins as though continuing the text with the words “This new Constantine approaches,” which are joined to the middle of the following chapter and continue with “he said, with my army I shall bring you aid,” etc.] and to wash away with fresh water the filthy marks borne from ancient times [Note: Thus Corbie and Regius; others have “the marks of ancient deeds.”].

When he entered for baptism, the holy man of God addressed him in eloquent speech:

“Bend your neck gently, Sicamber [Note: Brower discusses the people of the Sicambri at greater length in his notes on Fortunatus’s poem 4 of Book VI.]; worship what you burned, burn what you worshiped.”

For Saint Remigius was a bishop of outstanding learning and thoroughly trained in rhetorical studies [Note: See the letter of Apollinaris Sidonius, Book IX, Letter 7, addressed to Remigius himself. Avitus also speaks of him in the Assembly of Bishops before King Gundobad: “Because the Lord was providing for his Church and inspiring, for the salvation of the whole people, the heart of our lord Remigius, who everywhere destroyed the altars of idols and powerfully increased the true faith with a multitude of signs, it came to pass that the bishops,” etc. Thus Remigius’s apostolate was also beneficial to outsiders. Nothing of his writings survives except a few letters; the commentaries on Sacred Scripture commonly attributed to him are much later than his lifetime. His Life, praised here by Gregory and believed to have been composed by Fortunatus, still exists, but it is too brief to be adequate for describing the deeds of so great a man, the apostle of kings and of our people; it does not contain even a single word about the conversion of the Franks or the baptism of Chlodovechus. It is therefore not surprising that Gregory said no more about these matters. Hincmar wrote a longer account, and scarcely any author failed to praise this most holy man.].

He was also so distinguished in holiness that he was equal to the virtues of Saint Sylvester. There is now a book of his Life which reports that he raised a dead man.

Thus the king, confessing the almighty God in the Trinity, was baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and was anointed with sacred chrism together with the sign of Christ’s cross. More than three thousand of his army were baptized as well.

His sister Albofledis [Note: Colbert has Albfledis, both here and below. The letter praised here, from which it is clear that Albofledis consecrated her virginity to God, will be presented in full in the Appendix.] was also baptized; not long afterward she departed to the Lord. When the king grieved over her, Saint Remigius sent him a consolatory letter, which began as follows:

“Your cause of sorrow troubles me, and troubles me greatly: your sister Albofledis, of blessed memory, has departed. But we may take comfort in this matter, because she departed from this world in such a way that she ought rather to be received with reverence than mourned.”

Another sister of his, named Lanthechildis [Note: Thus Corbie; others have Lantildis. Gregory frequently mentions only chrismation in the reconciliation of Arians, just as even today, in conferring the sacrament of confirmation, scarcely any mention is made of the imposition of hands, although it is altogether necessary. Thus it seems beyond doubt that at that time the imposition of hands was also administered in addition to chrismation, lest, if anyone coming from heresy were received without it, he be judged, as Augustine says in Book V of On Baptism against the Donatists, chapter 23, to be entirely without guilt. See Morinus, On Penance, Book IX, chapter 10, and Cointius, volume I of the Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks.], was also converted. She had fallen into the heresy of the Arians, but confessed that the Son and the Holy Spirit were equal to the Father and was anointed with chrism.

XXXII. At that time the brothers Gundobadus and Godegiselus held the kingdom around the Rhône or Saône, together with the province of Marseille. Both they and their peoples were subject to the Arian sect.

When they were attacking one another, Godegiselus, hearing of King Chlodovechus’s victories, secretly sent an embassy to him, saying: “If you provide me assistance in pursuing my brother [Note: Thus Corbie and Bec; the others have “aid.” In the oldest manuscripts, solatium, “comfort” or “assistance,” is very often used instead of auxilium, “aid.”], so that I may kill him in war or drive him from the kingdom, I shall pay you each year whatever tribute you yourself wish to impose.”

Chlodovechus gladly accepted this and promised to provide him assistance wherever necessity demanded it. At the appointed time he moved his army against Gundobadus.

When Gundobadus heard this, unaware of his brother’s treachery, he sent to him, saying: “Come to my aid, because the Franks are taking up arms against us and are approaching our territory to seize it. Let us therefore be united against the hostile nation, lest, separated from one another, we suffer what other peoples have endured.”

Godegiselus replied: “I shall go with my army and provide you aid.”

Thus all three moved their armies and arrived at the fortress called Dijon: Chlodovechus against Gundobadus and Godegiselus [Note: Thus Corbie, Bec, and Regius read “Godegiselum,” better than the others, which have “Godegiselus.” At that point the two brothers appeared to be joined together against Chlodovechus, since Godegiselus’s treachery had not yet been revealed.] with all the equipment of war.

They fought beside the river Ouche [Note: The Bad edition incorrectly has Isère. The Ouche is a river of Burgundy, commonly called the Ousche; after flowing past Dijon and other places, it empties into the Saône at Saint-Jean-de-Losne. Marius writes that this occurred during the consulship of Patricius and Hypatius, that is, in the year 500.]. Godegiselus joined Chlodovechus, and together their armies crushed Gundobadus’s people. When Gundobadus perceived the treachery of his brother, which he had not suspected, he turned his back and fled, traversing the banks of the Rhône and the marshes until he entered the city of Avignon.

Godegiselus, having won the victory, withdrew in peace after promising Chlodovechus a portion of his kingdom, and entered Vienna in triumph, as though he already possessed the whole kingdom.

King Chlodovechus, having further increased his strength, pursued Gundobadus in order to drag him from the city and kill him. When Gundobadus heard this, terrified with fear, he was afraid that sudden death would overtake him. Yet he had with him an illustrious man named Aridius [Note: Nearly all the manuscripts have this form; most printed editions, together with Bec, have Aredius. This is, unless I am mistaken, the man mentioned in the assembly of bishops before King Gundobadus, discussed below in chapter 34. See Fredegar’s Epitome, chapter 18.], energetic and wise. Summoning him, he said:

“Distress surrounds me on every side, and I do not know what to do, because these Barbarians have come upon us to destroy the entire region after killing us.”

Aridius replied: “You must soften this man’s ferocity, lest you perish. Therefore, if it pleases you, I shall pretend to flee from you and cross over to him. When I have approached him, I shall ensure that he destroys neither you nor this region. Only make every effort to fulfill whatever he commands you through my counsel, until the Lord in his mercy grants success to your cause.”

He replied: “I shall do whatever you command.”

As he said this, Aridius took his leave and departed. Going to King Chlodovechus, he said: “Behold, I, your humble servant [Note: Bellov and Bec omit “servant.”], most pious king, come to your power, abandoning that wretched man Gundobadus. If your mercy deigns to look favorably upon me, both you and your descendants shall have in me a wholehearted servant and faithful man” [Note: Some manuscripts and printed editions have “receive me” instead of “look favorably upon me.”].

Chlodovechus received him most readily and kept him with him. For Aridius was pleasant in conversation, energetic in counsel, just in judgment, and faithful in any trust committed to him.

Finally, while Chlodovechus was encamped with his entire army around the city walls, Aridius said: “If your lofty majesty, O king, would graciously accept a few words from my humility, although you do not lack counsel, I shall offer them with complete fidelity. They will be useful both to you and to the cities through which you intend to pass.

“Why,” he said, “do you retain your army when your enemy is stationed in a very strong position? You devastate the fields, graze down the meadows, cut up the vineyards [Note: All the manuscripts except Colbert have this reading; the printed editions, together with Bec, have ‘destroy the vineyards.’], cut down the olive groves, and ruin all the produce of the region, while in the meantime you are unable to harm him. Send an embassy instead and impose upon him a tribute to be paid to you every year, so that the region may remain safe and you may rule perpetually over one who pays tribute. If he refuses, then you will do whatever you please.”

Accepting this counsel, the king ordered the enemy [Note: Thus the Bellov and Corbie manuscripts; others have “ordered the enemy of the fatherland to return,” etc. Here, however, the army is designated by the word hostis, “enemy,” which our people in later centuries commonly used in the vernacular form l’host.] to return to his own country.

Then he sent an embassy to Gundobadus and ordered him to pay the tribute imposed upon him every year. Gundobadus paid what was due at once and promised that he would continue to pay thereafter.

### XXXIII

After this, having recovered his strength, he now scorned to pay the tribute promised to King Chlodovechus and raised an army against his brother Godegisel, shut him up in the city of Vienne, and besieged him. But when provisions began to fail the lesser people, Godegisel, fearing that the famine might extend even to him, ordered the lesser inhabitants to be expelled from the city. Once this had been done, among the others there was expelled from the city that craftsman who was responsible for the aqueduct. Angered that he had been expelled from the city along with the others, he went furiously to Gundobad, explaining how, by entering the city, he could exact vengeance upon his brother.

With that man as guide, Gundobad sent his army through the aqueduct, many men carrying iron bars in front. The entrance to it had been closed by a large stone; when the craftsman’s skill had enabled them to dislodge it with those bars, they entered the city. While the men on the wall were shooting arrows at them, these soldiers came up behind them. [Note: Some manuscripts and editions read “press upon them.”] When a trumpet sounded from the middle of the city, the besiegers seized the gates and, having opened them, entered together. While the citizens of the city were being slaughtered between these two forces, Godegisel fled for refuge to the church of the heretics and was killed there together with the Arian bishop.

Finally, the Franks who had been with Godegisel gathered into a single tower. Gundobad ordered that not one of them should be harmed; instead, after seizing them, he sent them into exile at Toulouse to King Alaric. He put to death the senators and the Burgundians who had supported Godegisel. He himself restored the entire region now called Burgundy to his own dominion. He established milder laws for the Burgundians, so that they would not oppress the Romans.

[Note: Those laws still bear the name of their institutor, commonly called the “Gombette Laws.” Gundobad’s law is praised in the Capitularies of Charlemagne and by Agobard. They are contained in the code of ancient laws published for public use by Friedrich Lindenbrog.]

### XXXIV

When he had learned from the holy bishop Avitus of Vienne that the arguments of the heretics were worthless, he confessed Christ the Son of God and the Holy Spirit to be equal to the Father and secretly asked to be anointed with chrism. [Note: That is, in the public conference between Catholic bishops and Arians, held at Lyons in the presence of the king and the magnates of the realm, which we shall report below in the Appendix. See also Letter 2 of the same Saint Avitus in Sirmond.] The priest said to him: “If you truly believe what the Lord himself taught us, you must carry it out.” [Note: Thus Corb., Bell., Cas., and Bec.; Regm. has “you must carry it out” (*debes exsequi*). The other witnesses omit the word *debes* (“you must”).] He replied: “Whoever acknowledges me before men, I too will acknowledge him before my Father who is in heaven. But whoever denies me before men, I too will deny him before my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 10:32–33). [Note: This passage through “Thus also [to] his holy and beloved blessed apostles” is absent from Regm. and Bec., where passages of this sort from Scripture are for the most part omitted.] [Note: Colb., with most editions, reads: “Thus also [he instructed] his holy and beloved blessed apostles.”]

“Thus also he instructed his holy and beloved blessed apostles, when he taught them about the trials of the persecution to come, saying: ‘Beware of men. For they will hand you over to councils, and in their synagogues they will scourge you; and you will stand before kings and governors because of me, as a testimony to them and to all nations’” (Matthew 10:17). [Note: The word “all” is absent from most manuscripts and editions, but is found in the older witnesses.]

“But you, although you are a king and fear being seized by no one, fear the rebellion of the people, lest you confess the Creator of all in public. Abandon this foolishness, and proclaim with your mouth among the people what you say you believe in your heart. For blessed Paul likewise says: ‘With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation’” (Romans 10:10). [Note: Bellov. reads “unto salvation.”]

“So also the Prophet says: ‘I will confess you, Lord, in the great church; in a weighty people I will praise you’” (Psalm 34:18). “And again: ‘I will confess you among the peoples, Lord; I will sing a psalm to your name among the nations’” (Psalm 56:10).

“For, fearing the people, O king, do you not know that it is better for the people to follow your faith than for you to favor the weakness of the people? You are the head of the people, not the people your head. If you set out for war, you lead the enemy bands, and they follow wherever you have gone. Therefore it is better that, with you going before them, they should recognize the truth, than that, while you perish, they should remain in error. For God is not mocked” (Galatians 6:7); nor does he love one who, for the sake of an earthly kingdom, does not confess him in this world.”

Confounded by this reasoning, that man continued in this madness until the end of his life and did not wish publicly to confess the equality of the Trinity.

At that time the blessed Avitus was a man of great eloquence. When the heresy had arisen in the city of Constantinople—both that which Eutyches taught and that which Sabellius taught, namely, that our Lord Jesus Christ possessed no divinity—he wrote against them at the request of King Gundobad. [Note: Some have “Eutices” or “Euticis”; most have “Euthicus.” Bell. and Bec. read “both that, and Eutyches, and Sabellius.” “Nestorius” may perhaps be read instead of “Sabellius.” Yet no mention of Nestorius occurs in Letter 2 to Gundobad, which is entirely concerned with this matter, although there Avitus extensively refutes errors that he sometimes also attributes to Eutyches; see also Letters 3 and 28. Certainly the orthodox zeal of the Fathers of the Gallican Church persisted: at the Fifth Council of Orléans, in 549, canon 1, they condemned and anathematized the depraved doctrines of Eutyches and Nestorius with execrations.]

From that time there remain among us admirable letters which, just as they then suppressed the heresy, so now build up the Church of God. [Note: Besides the eighty-eight letters, the distinguished scholar Jacques Sirmond published several works of Saint Avitus, including the homily on the Rogations mentioned here, which we also found in an old manuscript. His Life is contained in volume 1 of Labbe’s *Bibliotheca nova*. His feast is celebrated on February 5; on that day the Bollandists provide further material about him.]

For he wrote one book of Homilies on the beginning of the world, and six books on various other subjects, composed in verse; and nine books of Letters, among which the letters mentioned above are included.

In one homily that he wrote on the Rogations, he relates that these very Rogations—which we celebrate before the triumph of the Lord’s Ascension—were instituted by Mamertus, bishop of that city of Vienne, who was then presiding over it, while the city was being terrified by many portents. [Note: The same is attested by Sidonius, book 5, Letter 14, and book 7, Letter 1; Caesarius of Arles, Homily 33; and many subsequent authors. See also the First Council of Orléans, canon 27, etc. How often and by what rite they were performed, and what was read in church on those days, is explained by our Mabillon in book 2 of *Gallican Liturgy*, p. 152, in the notes on no. 55 and following, and in the two Gallican lectionaries, which are wholly concerned with the Rogations. Mamertus’s feast is kept on 11 May. See below, book *On the Miracles of Saint Julian*, chapter 2.] For it was frequently shaken by earthquakes; and the fierceness of deer and wolves, having entered through the gates, wandered throughout the city, as he wrote, fearing nothing.

When these events continued throughout the year, and the days of the Paschal solemnity arrived, the whole people devoutly awaited the mercy of God, hoping that at least the day of so great a solemnity would put an end to this terror. But during the vigil of that glorious night, while the solemn celebration of the Mass was taking place, the royal inner palace was suddenly set on fire by divine flame. Everyone was terrified and left the church, fearing that either the whole city would be consumed by this fire or that the earth, splitting open, would swallow it. The holy priest prostrated himself before the altar and, with groaning and tears, implored the mercy of the Lord.

Why say more? The prayer of the renowned bishop penetrated the heights of heaven, and a river of flowing tears extinguished the fire of the house.

When these things had occurred, and the Ascension of the Lord’s majesty was approaching, as we have already said, he imposed a fast upon the people, established a manner of prayer, a sequence of eating, [Note: Freherus thinks that “a sequence of reading” should be read. Here Gregory notes three conditions of religious fasting by which it becomes beneficial. Avitus himself calls the Rogations a “most laborious festival.”] and a cheerful distribution of alms. When the terrors had thereafter ceased, the report of what had happened spread through all the provinces and urged all priests to imitate what the priest had done in faith. This is celebrated to the present day in the name of Christ throughout all the churches, with compunction of heart and contrition of spirit.

### XXXV

At that time Alaric, king of the Goths, seeing King Chlodovechus continually defeat nations, sent envoys to him, saying: “If my brother wishes it, it has been in my mind that, God being favorable, we should see one another together.”

[Note: It is an ancient custom, confirmed by Holy Scripture and ancient authors and still continuing today, for kings to call one another brothers. Learned men have observed this more than once. The distinguished scholars Étienne Baluze and Gisbert Cuper provide examples in their notes on chapter 8 of Lactantius’ *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, and Mabillon in book 2 of *De re diplomatica*, chapter 2, section 15. For my part, speaking only of our own people, I will cite the ninth formula in book 1 of Marculf, which is an introductory letter sent when an embassy is dispatched to another king. It begins: “To the glorious and most excellent brother, that king, in the name of God, from that king.”]

Chlodovechus did not reject this proposal and went to him. They met on an island in the Loire near the village of Ambacia, in the territory of the city of Tours. [Note: Chesn. reads “Ambaciacensis.” This town is still famous, commonly called Amboise, situated at the confluence of the Loire and the Amasse. Severus Sulpicius speaks of it in *Dialogues* 3: “In the village of Ambatia, that is, in that old fortress which is now densely inhabited by brothers,” and so forth. This is believed to be the same island that is still seen near Amboise, planted with trees and commonly called the island of Saint John.]

They spoke together, ate and drank together, promised one another friendship, and departed in peace.

### XXXVI

Already at that time many people in Gaul greatly desired to have the Franks as their lords. [Note: The words beginning “And so” through the following chapter are absent from Corb. and Bell. Valesius argues in book 6 of *Frankish History* that Quintianus was not driven from his see until after Chlodovechus’ death; consult him if desired.] Thus it happened that Quintianus, bishop of Rodez, was driven from the city because of this hostility. For they said to him: “It is your desire that Frankish rule should possess this land.”

A few days later, when a quarrel arose between him and the citizens, suspicion fell upon the Goths who lived in that city. The citizens reproached them, saying that Quintianus wished to subject himself to the Frankish dominion; and after taking counsel, they planned to stab him with a sword.

When this was reported to the man of God, he rose during the night with his most faithful attendants, departed from the city of Rodez, and came to the Auvergne. There he was kindly received by Saint Euphrasius, who had once succeeded Aprunculus as bishop of Dijon. Euphrasius gave him houses, fields, and vineyards, and kept him with himself, saying: “The resources of this Church are sufficient to support both of us, provided that the charity preached by the blessed Apostle remains among the priests of God.”

The bishop of Lyon also gave him some property belonging to his church which he possessed in the Auvergne.

The rest concerning Saint Quintianus—both the ambushes he endured and the things that the Lord graciously worked through him—has been written in the book of his Life. [Note: This is chapter 4, *Lives of the Fathers*.]

### XXXVII

King Chlodovechus therefore said to his men: “I greatly regret that these Arians possess part of Gaul. With God’s help, let us go and, having overcome them, bring the land under our authority.”

[Note: King Theodoric of the Ostrogoths testifies that this war arose from slight causes. He moved heaven and earth to prevent it, sending letters and embassies to Chlodovechus and other kings. See Cassiodorus, book 3, Letters 2–4.]

When everyone approved this proposal, he mobilized his army and directed it toward Poitiers, for Alaric was then staying there.

But since part of the army was passing through the territory of Tours, out of reverence for Saint Martin he issued an edict that no one from that region should take anything except grass and water for sustenance. One of the soldiers, finding a poor man’s hay, said: “Did not the king order that only grass, and nothing else, should be taken? And this,” he said, “is grass. We will not be transgressors of his command if we take it.”

Having used force against the poor man and taken the hay by violence, the matter reached the king. The soldier was immediately killed with the sword, and Chlodovechus said: “Where will there be hope of victory if Saint Martin is offended?” [Note: Corb. reads: “if we offend Saint Martin,” reflecting Gregory’s familiar variation in case.] It was enough to make the army refrain from taking anything further from that region.

The king himself sent messengers to the basilica of Saint Martin, saying: “Go, and perhaps you will receive some sign of victory from the holy shrine.” Then, giving them gifts to present at the holy place, he said: “If you, Lord, are my helper, and have determined to deliver into my hands this unbelieving people, always hostile to you, graciously reveal at the entrance of the basilica of Saint Martin that you will be favorable to your servant, so that I may know it.”

As the young men hurried to the place in accordance with the king’s command, and were entering the holy basilica, the principal cantor who was there suddenly began this antiphon:

“You have girded me, O Lord, with strength for war; you have subdued beneath me those who rose up against me; you have given me the backs of my enemies, and you have destroyed those who hate me” (Psalm 17:40–41).

[Note: The older manuscripts read *imposuit* (“intoned”); the others read *incoepit* (“began”). In the Roman Church the *primicerius* was the head of the lower choir; that this office was also in use in the Gallican Church in Chlodovechus’s time may be inferred from Saint Remigius’s letter to Falcon, bishop of Tongeren, in which the most holy man complains that Falcon had established at the Church of Mouzon levites, presbyters, archdeacons, and a *primicerius* of the most distinguished school and body of readers. See Du Cange’s *Glossary* and Thomassin, book 2, part 1 of *Discipline of the Latin Church*, p. 103. Moreover, the practice of seeking knowledge of future events through readings of Holy Scripture was customary in those times, as is clear from several other passages of Gregory. The same was done at the election of Saint Martin in Severus Sulpicius, *Life*, chapter 7. See also the Life of Saint Consortia, no. 9, century 1 of the Benedictines, under the year 578.]

When they heard those singing the psalm, gave thanks to the Lord, and promised vows to the blessed confessor, they joyfully announced the news to the king.

When he arrived with his army at the river Vigenna, [Note: On this river, see book 1, chapter 43.] he had no idea at all where he ought to cross it, for it had swollen from the rains. That night he prayed to the Lord to deign to show him a ford by which he could cross. At daybreak, by God’s command, a doe of extraordinary size entered the river before them; as it forded the stream, the people recognized where they could cross.

When the king reached Poitiers and was staying at a distance in the tents, a fiery beacon appeared to him to emerge from the basilica of Saint Hilary and move toward him, as though he were to be aided by the light of the blessed confessor Hilary to defeat more freely the heretical ranks against which that same priest had often fought for the faith. [Note: See Venantius Fortunatus, book 2 of the *Life of Saint Hilary*, section 7.]

He charged the entire army not to strip anyone there or on the road, nor to seize anyone’s property. [Note: Some editions and Bec. read “not to plunder anything.”]

In those days there was a man of admirable holiness, Maxentius the abbot, shut up in his monastery for fear of God within the territory of Poitiers. We have not supplied the monastery’s name to the reading, because that place is still called the Cell of Saint Maxentius.

When the monks of the monastery saw a band of the enemy approaching the monastery, they begged the abbot to leave his cell and go out to pray to them. [Note: Bec. reads “to pray to them”; the other manuscripts and some editions read “to console them”; the remaining editions read “to consult with them.”]

When he delayed, they were struck with fear and brought him out of his cell through the open door. He went fearlessly to meet the enemy, as though he were going to ask for peace. One of them drew his sword and raised his hand to strike at the holy man’s head; his hand stiffened at his ear, and the sword fell backward. The attacker himself fell at the blessed man’s feet and begged forgiveness.

When the others saw this, they returned to the army in great fear, afraid that they too might perish. The blessed confessor touched the man’s arm with blessed oil, made the sign of the cross over it, and restored it to health. Through his intercession the monastery remained unharmed.

He performed many other miracles as well; whoever carefully seeks them will find them all by reading the book of his Life. [Note: A Life of Saint Maxentius, edited from two manuscript codices, is found in volume 1 of the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, page 578; consult it. The monastery still exists, together with the town of the same name, subject to our Order under the Congregation of Saint Maur. It was destroyed by the Calvinists and restored a few years ago. Saint Leodegarius, martyr and bishop of Autun, was its abbot and for a long time lay there after his death.]

[Note: In Corb. and Bellov. the following words are inserted here, in the first hand: “In the fifteenth year of Chlodovechus.” It nevertheless seems clear that this battle was fought in the twenty-sixth year of Chlodovechus, that is, in A.D. 507. See the notes above on chapter 30.]

Meanwhile King Chlodovechus met King Alaric of the Goths on the field of Vogladum, ten miles from the city of Poitiers. [Note: The text reads “the greatest part of the people of the Auvergne, who had come with Apollinaris, and the foremost [perhaps “very many,” *plurimi*] among the senators, fell.”] [Note: Some manuscripts and editions read “Vocladum.” It is commonly called Vouillé, a town on the river Clain, three leagues from Poitiers. Colb. reads “Dubiacum.”] When they had engaged one another at a distance, they came to close quarters. When, according to their custom, the Goths turned their backs, King Chlodovechus, with the Lord’s help, obtained the victory.

He had as his ally the son of Sigibert the Lame, named Chloderic. This Sigibert, fighting against the Alamanni near the town of Tolbiac, had been struck in the knee and walked with a limp. [Note: Sigibert had his seat at Cologne, from which Tolbiac—today Zülpich or Zülch—is about four leagues distant. There the famous battle between the Alamanni and Chlodovechus was fought, which provided the occasion for the conversion of the Franks. Henschenius nevertheless thinks that this war was fought near Strasbourg, since Chlodovechus then proceeded to Rheims and crossed the Tulle. But after defeating the Alamanni, Chlodovechus pursued them, so that, when he was already hastening to Rheims, he must have crossed the Tulle. See Valesius, book 6 of *Frankish History*.]

After the Goths had been routed and the king had killed Alaric, two men suddenly came from opposite directions and struck both his sides with spears. He escaped death, however, thanks both to his armor and to the speed of his horse.

At that time most of the people of the Auvergne, who had come with Apollinaris, and the leading senators were killed. [Note: This was the son of Saint Apollinaris Sidonius, born before his episcopate from a lawful marriage. Gregory mentions him in book 3, chapter 2, and book 1 of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 45, and elsewhere.]

Concerning this battle, Amalaric, the son of Alaric, fled to Spain and shrewdly seized his father’s kingdom. [Note: After Alaric was killed, his son Gesalec seized part of his father’s kingdom, while Theodoric the Great, king of the Ostrogoths, ruled the other part. After Theodoric’s death, Amalaric—also called Amalric or Almaric—son of Alaric by Theudicusa, or Theodogotha, daughter of that same Theodoric, began to reign.

The anonymous author of the *History of the Caesars*, from Constantius Chlorus to Theodoric, king of Italy, says of this Theodoric: “Afterward he took as his wife a woman from the Franks, named Audofleda. For before his reign he had had a wife by whom he had daughters: one, named Arevagni, he gave to Alaric, king of the Visigoths in Gaul; and his other daughter, Theodegotha, to Sigismund, son of King Gundobad.” On the other hand, Jordanes, chapter 58, and the *Miscellaneous History* say: “Before he had offspring by Audefleda, daughter of Lodoin, king of the Franks, he had natural daughters by a concubine, whom he had fathered while still in Moesia: one named Theudicoda and the other Ostrogotho. As soon as he came to Italy, he joined them in marriage to neighboring kings, one to Alaric of the Visigoths and the other to Sigismund of the Burgundians.” Procopius, in book 1 of *The Gothic War*, says that Theodoric betrothed his virgin daughter Theudicusa to Alaric.

Shortly after the passage cited above, the Anonymous calls Amalaberga the wife of Hermenefrid, king of the Thuringians, and the sister of that same Theodoric. Yet according to Procopius, the *Miscellaneous History*, and even Cassiodorus himself, book 4, Letter 1, Amalaberga was the daughter of Theodoric’s sister Amalafrida.]

King Chlodovechus sent his son Theuderic through the cities of Albi and Rodez to the Auvergne. [Note: The older manuscripts spell the name “Theudericus”; others have “Theodericus” or “Theodoricus.”] As he went, he subjected those cities—from the borders of the Goths to the boundary of the Burgundians—to the dominion of his father.

Alaric reigned for twenty-two years. Chlodovechus, spending the winter near Bordeaux, took all of Alaric’s treasures from Toulouse and came to Angoulême. [Note: Some write “Encolisma,” “Ecolisina,” or “Engolisma.” It is an episcopal city, commonly called Angoulême, well known.] The Lord granted him such favor that, at his presence, the walls collapsed of their own accord. He then expelled the Goths and subjected the city to his dominion.

After accomplishing this victory, he returned to Tours, offering many gifts to the holy basilica of the blessed Martin. [Note: Regm. reads “he entered.” Moreover, while preparing for this war, Chlodovechus was warned by Saint Remigius and ordered everyone inviolably to abstain from sacred objects. This won him victory over his enemies from God. The letter of Saint Remigius and the letter that Chlodovechus himself wrote to the bishops after the war on this subject still survive; we shall present them in the Appendix, together with the charter concerning the establishment of the monastery of Micy, which the same king testifies that he granted in the name of the holy, equal, and consubstantial Trinity.]

### XXXVIII

King Chlodovechus received from the Emperor Anastasius documents concerning the consulship. In the basilica of the blessed Martin he dressed himself in a purple tunic [Note: Bec. and Mor. read “a tunic and belt.” Our reading is to be retained. The term “purple tunic” denotes a purple garment, especially appropriate to a consul and an Augustus. That *blata* or *blatta* signifies purple is clear from ancient glossaries and writers; see Savaro’s notes on book 9, Letter 13 of Sidonius, and elsewhere; Brouwer’s notes on book 2, poem 3 of Fortunatus; Hugo Menard’s notes on Saint Gregory’s sacramentary; and others.] and a military cloak, placing a diadem on his head.

Then, mounting a horse [Note: So read Corb., Bell., and other older manuscripts, which here and almost everywhere else call horses intended to carry men “horsemen.” The editions and some manuscripts read “on horseback.”], he scattered gold and silver with his own hand along the route between the gate of the atrium of the basilica of the blessed Martin and the church of the city, distributing it with the greatest generosity before the assembled people. From that day he was called Consul or Augustus. [Note: The editions read “Consul and Augustus.” Cointius argues, under the year 508, that Gregory intended by these words that Chlodovechus had been admitted by Anastasius into the imperial dignity, since from the time of Justinian it was the same thing to be consul and emperor. Theophanes, in the *Miscellaneous History*, chapter 15, testifies that Zatus, king of the Lazes, having obtained from Emperor Justin a share in the imperial title, afterward wore the imperial crown and cloak.

Valesius, in book 6 of *Frankish History*, thinks that the title “consul” here means the dignity of patrician, which was later conferred upon Charlemagne. The title of the chapter in even the oldest manuscripts supports this view: “On the Patriciate of Chlodovechus.” Moreover, near the principal door of our basilica of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, several ancient statues of the early line of kings still survive. They were sculpted under the grandsons of Chlodovechus; among them is one representing Chlodovechus clothed in consular garments and wearing the *baculus hypaticus*, which he holds in his hand.]

After leaving Tours, he came to Paris and established the seat of his kingdom there. Theuderic also came to him there.

### XXXIX

Finally, when Eustochius, bishop of Tours, had died, Licinius was ordained bishop of Tours, the eighth after Saint Martin. [Note: This chapter is absent from Bellov. and Corb. In Colb. it is written in another, though ancient, hand in the margin. Regm. reads: “Finally, at the eighth place after Saint Martin, Theodorus …” Yet in other passages, as in the other manuscripts, the name is Licinius.]

During his time the war described above was fought. During his time also King Chlodovechus came to Tours. He is said to have been in the East and to have visited the holy places, including Jerusalem itself, and to have repeatedly seen the places of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection that we read about in the Gospels.

### XL

While King Chlodovechus was staying at Paris, he secretly sent word to the son of Sigibert: “Behold, your father has grown old and limps on a weak foot. If he were to die, his kingdom would rightly be restored to you in friendship with us.”

Seduced by this ambition, the son plotted to kill his father. [Note: Other witnesses, here and below, read “Burconia.” The forest of Buconia later became famous for the monastery of Fulda, founded there on the river Fulda by Saint Boniface, apostle of Germany, archbishop of Mainz, and martyr, in the eighth century. There was also a forest of Buronia not far from Cologne Agrippina, nearer the river Scheldt than Buconia.] When Sigibert had left the city of Cologne, crossed the Rhine, and was preparing to travel through the forest of Buconia, he fell asleep at midday in his tent. His son sent assassins upon him and killed him there, intending to possess his kingdom.

But by God’s judgment he fell into the pit that he had treacherously dug for his father.

He therefore sent messengers to King Chlodovechus to announce his father’s death and to say: “My father is dead, and I have his treasures and kingdom in my possession. Send your men to me, and I will willingly send you whatever you desire from his treasures.”

Chlodovechus replied: “I thank you for your goodwill, and I ask you to open everything to my men when they arrive, since you will afterward possess it all.”

When they arrived, the son displayed his father’s treasures to them. As they examined various objects, he said: “My father used to heap gold coins into this little chest.”

“Put your hand all the way to the bottom,” they said, “so that you may find everything.”

When he had done so and was bent far over, one of them raised his hand and struck him in the brain with a battle-axe. Thus he deservedly suffered what he had done to his father.

When Chlodovechus heard that Sigibert and his son had been killed, he came to the same place and summoned all the people, saying:

“Hear what has happened. While I was sailing along the river Scheldt, Chloderic, the son of my kinsman, was pursuing his father, telling him that I wanted to kill him. When his father fled through the forest of Buconia, Chloderic sent bandits against him, handed him over to death, and killed him. He himself, while opening his father’s treasures, perished when someone whose identity I do not know struck him.

“But I am in no way an accomplice in these events. I cannot shed the blood of my relatives; that would be a crime. Since these things have happened, however, I offer you counsel: if you approve, turn to me, so that you may be under my protection.”

When they heard this, they applauded him with their shields [Note: Most editions, following Bec., read “with their palms.” Valesius observes from book 7 of Julius Caesar’s *Commentaries on the Gallic War* that the Gauls used to strike their weapons together when approving their commander’s speech. Tacitus says the same of the Germans, and Ammianus Marcellinus of the Romans.] as well as with their voices, lifted him upon a shield, and made him their king.

Having received the kingdom of Sigibert together with its treasures, he also brought the people themselves under his authority. For God daily prostrated his enemies beneath his hand and increased his kingdom, because he walked with an upright heart before him and did what was pleasing in his sight.

### XLI

After this he sent to King Chararic. [Note: Nearly all the manuscripts omit the word “king”; Regm. includes it. Yet below Chararic is said to have possessed a kingdom. Malbrancus, book 2, chapter 38, calls Chararic king of the Morini.]

When Chlodovechus fought against Syagrius, Chararic had been summoned to provide assistance [Alternative: aid], but stood at a distance, helping neither side and waiting to see how the matter would turn out, so that whichever side won, he might form a friendship with it.

For this reason Chlodovechus became angry with him, went against him, and captured him by treachery together with his son. He had their hair cut off and ordered Chararic to be ordained a presbyter and his son a deacon.

When Chararic complained and wept over his humiliation, his son is said to have remarked: “These branches have been cut from green wood; they do not wither at all but quickly sprout again so that they may grow. Would that the man who did this might perish just as quickly.”

These words reached Chlodovechus’ ears. He understood them to mean that they threatened to let their hair grow again and kill him. He therefore ordered both of them to be put to death. When they were dead, he acquired their kingdom, treasures, and people.

XLII. At that time Ragnacharius [Note: [Col. 0238D] Bell. has *Ragnarius*; Reg., *Ranacharius*; Colb., *Ragenharius*; Reg., *Regnacharius*.] was king at Cambrai, so unrestrained in debauchery that he scarcely spared even his close relatives. He had as his counselor Farron [Note: [Col. 0238D] Others, with Corb., have *Faronem*; some, *Pharronem*. Concerning the Farrones, see below the notes on chapter 41 of Fredegar’s Chronicle.], befouled with similar filth. It is said of him that whenever food, a gift, or anything of any kind had been brought to the king, he habitually said: “This is sufficient for him and for his Farron.” For this reason the Franks were swelling with the greatest indignation.

Accordingly, Chlodovechus, having given them golden bracelets [Note: [Col. 0239D] Thus Colb. and Chesn.; other editions and manuscripts have *sive armillis* [“or bracelets”].] or belts—that is, things entirely made to resemble gold (for they were bronze, deceitfully gilded)—gave these to his *leudes* [Note: [Col. 0239D] Thus Chesn. and all the manuscripts except Regm., which has *legatis* [“envoys”]. Most printed editions have *proditoribus* [“traitors”]. The word *leudibus* should be retained.
