Our kings called their vassals, especially the more noble ones who were subject to no one except the prince, their *leudes*, or faithful men; later they were called barons. See Bignonius on the *Formulae of Marculf*, book I, chapter 40, who had already observed in chapter 18 that these same men were also called *Anstrustiones*. Finally they were called *Vassi* or *Vassalli*. See Cangius’s Glossary.] so that they might be incited against him [Note: [Col. 0239D] All editions have *inimicarentur* [“might become enemies”].].

When he had set an army in motion against him, and Ragnacharius repeatedly sent scouts to find out what was happening, he asked the messengers on their return how strong this force was. They replied: “It is a very great reinforcement for you and your Farron.” Chlodovechus then came and drew up for battle against him. Seeing his army defeated, Ragnacharius prepared to flee; but he was seized by the army and, with his hands bound behind his back, was brought before Chlodovechus together with his brother Richarius [Note: [Col. 0239D] The Regm. manuscript has *Rachanarius*.].

Chlodovechus said to him: “Why have you humiliated our family by allowing yourself to be bound? It would have been better for you to die.” He raised an axe and drove it into his head. Then, turning to his brother, he said: “If you had given your brother assistance, he surely would not have been bound.” He struck and killed this man with the axe in the same way.

After their death, their traitors learned that the gold they had received from the king was counterfeit. When they told the king this, he is said to have replied: “Rightly does one receive such gold who of his own will leads his lord to death. What they owed these men while they lived ought to be enough for them, lest, while paying the penalty for their wicked betrayal of their lords, they should perish amid tortures.” When they heard this, they hoped to obtain mercy, asserting that it would be sufficient for them if they deserved to remain alive.

The kings mentioned above were his relatives. Their brother, named Rignomeris [Note: [Col. 0239D] Others, with Bell., have *Regnomeris*; shortly below some manuscripts have *Cinomannis*. Four printed editions have *Cenomanniam*.], was killed at the city of Le Mans by Chlodovechus’s command. After their death, Chlodovechus took their entire kingdom and treasures. Having also killed many other kings and his closest relatives, toward whom he was jealous lest they take his kingdom from him, he extended his own kingdom throughout all Gaul.

Yet on one occasion, after assembling his men, he is said to have spoken of the relatives whom he himself had lost: “Woe is me, who have remained like a stranger among foreigners and have no relatives who could help me in adversity, should it come.” But he said this not out of grief for their deaths; rather, he spoke deceitfully, in case he might still find someone whom he could kill.

XLIII. After these events had taken place, he died at Paris and was buried in the basilica of the holy Apostles [Note: [Col. 0240D] It is now called Saint Geneviève, because the most holy virgin was buried there and became renowned for many miracles. It is a celebrated abbey of Regular Canons of the Order of Saint Augustine; Abbot Suger of Saint-Denis brought them there from the Abbey of Saint-Victor and settled them there.], which he himself had built together with Queen Chrotechildis.

He died in the fifth year after the battle of Vouillé. The total duration of his reign was thirty years. His entire lifetime [Note: [Col. 0240D] The words “his entire lifetime, forty-five years” are absent from the Corb. and Regm. manuscripts. Chlodovechus died in the common era in the year 511. That was neither the 112th year after Saint Martin’s death, if it is true that he departed to heaven in 397, nor the eleventh year of Bishop Licinius, since Leo, a deacon acting in the name of Bishop Verus, Licinius’s predecessor, subscribed to the Council of Agde in 506.] was forty-five years.

From the passing of Saint Martin, therefore, until the passing of King Chlodovechus—which occurred in the eleventh year of the episcopate of Licinius, priest of Tours—one counts 112 years.

Queen Chrotechildis, after her husband’s death, came to Tours. There, serving at the basilica of Saint Martin, she remained in that place all the days of her life with the greatest chastity and kindness, rarely visiting Paris.

[Col. 0240C] Here ends the second book.

THE THIRD BOOK.

[Col. 0241]

PROLOGUE.

103 I should like, if it pleases you, to set forth briefly what favorable events befell Christians who confess the blessed Trinity, and what destruction befell heretics who divide that same Trinity.

Let us omit how Abraham venerates it beneath the oak, Jacob proclaims it in the blessing, Moses recognizes it in the thorn bush, the people follow it in the cloud, and fear it on the mountain; or how Aaron bears it on the breastplate, or David prophesies of it in the psalm, praying that he may be renewed by the right Spirit, that the Holy Spirit may not be taken from him, and that he may be strengthened by the sovereign Spirit (Psalm 50 [51]:12–14). Here too I perceive a great mystery: the one whom the heretics assert to be lesser, the prophetic voice proclaimed to be sovereign.

But, as we have said, setting these matters aside, let us return to our own times. Arius, the first and wicked inventor of this wicked sect, with his inward parts cast into the privy, is subjected to the infernal fires. Blessed Hilary, however, defender of the undivided Trinity, because of this was sent into exile and is restored to the paradise of his homeland. King Chlodovechus confessed this faith; with its help he crushed the heretics and extended his kingdom throughout all Gaul. Alaric, denying it, was deprived of his kingdom, his people, and—what is greater—eternal life itself.

The Lord restores a hundredfold in this life to those who truly believe in him, even if, while the enemy lies in wait, they lose certain things. Heretics, however, neither acquire anything [Note: [Col. 0241B] Corb., Bel., and Casin. have: “nor do they acquire anything better.”], but what they seem to possess is taken away from them.

The deaths of Godegisel, Gundobad, and Godomar proved this: they lost both their homeland and their souls [Note: [Col. 0241B] As Valesius observes, Gundobad long possessed a very flourishing kingdom and, departing by a natural death, left it to his son Sigismund.].

But we confess one invisible, immense, incomprehensible, glorious, everlasting, and eternal Lord—one in Trinity because of the number of persons, that is, of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and three in unity because of the equality of substance, divinity, omnipotence, and power—who is the one supreme and almighty God, reigning forever and ever.

105 I. After King Chlodovechus had died, his four sons—that is, Theuderic, Chlodomer, Childebert, and Chlothacharius [Note: [Col. 0241C] Thus the ancient manuscripts, although they sometimes vary; others have *Hlotharius* or *Chlotarius*, which is the same name. In any case, the sons of Chlodovechus did not receive equal portions of their father’s kingdom. Theuderic’s share was much larger than the others’. Nevertheless, it could be called equal, because, having accompanied his father on campaigns while the boundaries of the paternal kingdom were being extended, he could already be considered to have acquired something for himself.]—received his kingdom and divided it among themselves in equal measure.

At that time Theuderic already had a son named Theudebert, handsome and capable. Since they possessed great courage and had abundant military strength, Amalaric, son of Alaric and king of Spain, asked for their sister in marriage. They graciously granted this request and sent her to him in the region of Spain with a great quantity of splendid ornaments [Note: [Col. 0242B] See below, chapter 10.].

II. After Licinius [Note: [Col. 0242B] This chapter is absent from the Regio manuscript. Moreover, Gregory himself, book X, chapter 31, places between Licinius and Dinifius the bishops Theodore and Proculus, from Burgundy, who, having been expelled from their see, were appointed in Licinius’s place after his death by order of Queen Chlothildis.] had died as bishop of the city of Tours, Dinifius ascended the episcopal chair.

At Auvergne, after the death of blessed Aprunculus [Note: [Col. 0242C] Corb. has *Abroncoli*; Bell., *Abrunculi*; Colb., *Patrunculi*. Concerning him, see book II, chapters 23 and 36. Eufrasius subscribed to the Council of Orléans I, and the priest Paulinus attended the Council of Agde in his name. He is commemorated on January 14. Gregory frequently discusses Saint Quintianus. See *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 4.], the holy Eufrasius was regarded as the twelfth bishop. He lived four years after Chlodovechus’s death and departed this life in the twenty-fifth year of his episcopate.

When the people had chosen Saint Quintianus, who had been expelled from Rodez, Alchima and Placidina [Note: [Col. 0243C] Regm. has *Althima*; Corb. and Bell., *Placidana*. Concerning these women, see below, chapter 12. Corb. has *Apollonaris*. He was the son of Saint Apollinaris Sidonius, who had been commander of the Auvergnates in the battle of Vouillé, and the father of Arcadius, concerning whom see below, chapter 12 and elsewhere. Saint Apollinaris Sidonius had by Papianilla, daughter of the emperor Avitus, Alcima and Apollinaris; this Apollinaris, by Placidina, had Arcadius, and Arcadius had another Placidina, who married Leontius the Younger, later bishop of Bordeaux. Fortunatus speaks of her in book I, poem 14. See Valesius, book VII of *Frankish History*, p. 324, and Sirmond’s notes on Sidonius’s *Letters*, book III, letter 13.]—the wife and sister of Apollinaris—came to Saint Quintianus and said:

“Holy lord, let it be enough for your old age that you have been ordained bishop. Let your piety,” they said, “permit your servant Apollinaris to obtain the place of this honor. When he has ascended to this rank, he will obey you as you wish; you will also command, and he will obey your order in everything. Only lend the ear of your kindness to our humble petition.”

He replied to them: “What can I provide, when nothing is subject to my authority? It is enough that, devoting myself to prayer, the Church provide me with my daily sustenance.”

When they heard this, they sent Apollinaris to the king. He went, offered many gifts, and succeeded to the bishopric. After abusing that office for four months, he departed this world.

When this was reported to Theuderic, he ordered Saint Quintianus to be installed there and all authority over the Church to be entrusted to him, saying: “He was expelled from his own city because of his zeal for our love.” Messengers were immediately sent, and, after summoning the bishops and the people, they placed him in the chair of the Church of Auvergne. He was the fourteenth bishop appointed over that Church.

The other deeds he performed, both his miracles and the time of his departure, are written in the book we composed about his Life [Note: [Col. 0243D] Chapter 4 of the *Lives of the Fathers*.].

III. After these events, the Danes, with their king named Chlochilaichus [Note: [Col. 0243D] Colb. has *Hrodolaico*; Bec., together with the printed editions, *Chochilaico*.], came by sea in a naval expedition against Gaul. Going ashore, they ravaged one district of Theuderic’s kingdom and took its people captive. Having loaded their ships with captives and the remainder of the plunder, they wished to return to their homeland.

Their king, however, remained on the shore until the ships reached the open sea, intending to follow afterward. When this was reported to Theuderic—that a region of his had been ravaged by foreigners—he sent his son Theudebert to that area with a powerful army and a great supply of weapons. After killing the king, Theudebert overcame and crushed the enemy in a naval battle and restored all the plunder to the land.

IV. At that time three brothers held the kingdom of the Thuringian people: Baderic, Hermenefridus [Note: [Col. 0243D] Thus Corb. and Bellov.; others have the slightly different form *Herminefredus*. Colb. has *Ermenfredus*. Bertharius is once called *Bertecarius* in the Corb. manuscript.], and Bertharius.

Finally, Hermenefridus violently overpowered and killed his brother Bertharius. When Bertharius died, he left his daughter Radegund an orphan; he also left other children, concerning whom we shall write below.

Hermenefridus’s wife, however, an evil and cruel woman named Amalaberga [Note: [Col. 0243D] Thus the older manuscripts; others have *Amalberga* or *Almaberga*. According to Procopius, book I of the *Gothic History*, she was the daughter of Amalafrida, sister of Theodoric, king of Italy; a little farther below he calls her the sister of King Theudat.], sowed civil war among these brothers.

One day her husband came to a banquet and found the middle of the table left uncovered. When he asked his wife what this meant, she replied: “A man who is deprived of half his kingdom ought to have the middle of his table left bare.”

Moved by this and similar words, he rose against his brother and, through secret messengers, invited King Theuderic to pursue him, saying: “If you kill him, we will divide this region equally between us.”

Theuderic was delighted when he heard this and went against him with an army. When they had joined forces and pledged faith to one another, they set out for battle. Engaging Baderic, they crushed his army and cut him down with the sword. After securing the victory, Theuderic returned home.

Hermenefridus immediately forgot his pledge and neglected to fulfill what he had promised to grant King Theuderic. Great hostility consequently arose between them.

V. After Gundobad had died [Note: [Col. 0244C] During the consulship of Peter, that is, in the year 516, according to Marius of Aventicum.], his son Sigimund obtained his kingdom. With diligent care he built the monastery of Agaunum, together with houses and basilicas [Note: [Col. 0244D] Marius of Aventicum reports that the monastery of Agaunum was built by Sigismund during the consulship of Florentius and Anthemius, that is, in the year 515. Avitus’s homily, delivered at the renewal of that monastery, suggests that Marius’s statement should be understood as referring to its restoration. It is situated in the diocese of Sion, at the foot of Mount Saint Bernard. At first it flourished under a private rule, then for a long time under the Benedictine rule, and finally passed to Regular Canons. We discussed it in the Preface to the Passion of Saints Maurice and his Companions, in the *Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 288. These men are commonly called the Agaunum martyrs; Gregory discusses them in *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, book I, chapters 75 and 76.].

After losing his first wife [Note: [Col. 0244D] Her name was Ostrogotha. The title of Homily 8 of Saint Avitus, *From the Lost Works*, reads: “On the conversion of our lord Sigisricus, on the day after his sister was received from the Arian heresy.”], the daughter of Theodoric, king of Italy, by whom he had a son named Sigiricus, he took another wife. She began, as stepmothers commonly do, to act maliciously against and to provoke his son.

It happened, therefore, that one day during a solemn festival, when the boy recognized his mother’s garments upon her, he was stirred by anger and said to her: “You were not worthy that these garments should touch your back [Note: [Col. 0244D] Bochel. has *contegerent* [“should cover”].], garments known to have belonged to your mistress—that is, my mother.”

Inflamed with fury, she incited her husband with deceitful words, saying: “This wicked man desires to possess your kingdom and, after killing you, intends to extend it as far as Italy, so that he too may possess the kingdom which his grandfather Theodoric of Italy held. He knows that he cannot accomplish this while you live; and unless you fall, he will not rise.”

Stirred by these and similar words, and following the advice of his wicked wife, he became a wicked parricide. He ordered his son, made drowsy by wine, to sleep in the afternoon. While the boy slept, an *orarium* [Note: [Col. 0245C] The printed editions have *lorum* [“strap”], but the word *orarium* should be retained. Although it has various meanings, it properly denotes a certain elongated linen cloth made in the form of a band. See Cangius’s Glossary, or Cardinal Bona, *On Liturgical Matters*, book I, chapter 24.] was placed beneath his neck and tied under his chin; two boys pulled it toward one another, and he was strangled [Note: [Col. 0245C] Here too the printed editions have *suffocatus est* [“was suffocated”], a word perhaps more suitable for expressing the event, though it occurs less frequently in authors of the later period. *Occisus est* [“was killed”] is found in the Chronicle of Marius, during the consulship of Symmachus and Boethius, that is, in the year 522.].

After this had been done, the father, repenting only afterward, threw himself upon the lifeless corpse and began to weep most bitterly. An old man is said to have spoken to him as follows:

“From now on, weep for yourself, who through wicked counsel have become a most savage parricide. There is no need to weep for this innocent boy who has been slaughtered.”

Nevertheless, he went to the saints of Agaunum and remained there many days in tears and fasting, seeking forgiveness. Establishing there continuous psalmody [Note: [Col. 0245C] Reg. and Regm. have “establishing there a continual choir of psalm-singers,” which is also added by a second hand in Colb. The reading of the other manuscripts and editions is better. Here the continuous chanting instituted day and night in the Church of Agaunum is intended; our Mabillon proves this at length against Cointius in the second Preface to the fourth Benedictine century.], he returned from Lyon, with divine vengeance pursuing him immediately afterward.

King Theuderic took this man’s daughter [Note: [Col. 0245C] She was Suavegotta, concerning whom Frodoardus writes in book II of his *History of Rheims*. See below the notes on chapter 26 of book IV.].

VI. Queen Chrotechildis then addressed Chlodomer and her other sons, saying:

“Let me not regret, my beloved, that I raised you with tenderness. I beg you, resent my injury and avenge with vigilant zeal the death of my father and mother.”

When they heard this, they went into Burgundy and marched against Sigimund and his brother Godomar. Their army was defeated, and Godomar turned his back.

While Sigimund was attempting to flee to the saints of Agaunum [Note: [Col. 0245D] Thus all the manuscripts; Chesn. has *sanctos Agaunenses* [“the saints of Agaunum”]; the other editions have *saltus Agaunos* [“the Agaunum forests”]. Marius reports that, during the consulship of Maximus, that is, in the year 523, Sigismund was handed over to the Franks by the Burgundians and brought into Gaul in monastic dress. In the following year his brother Godomar succeeded him, and Chlodomer was killed. Compare the Life of Saint Sigismund in volume I of the Bollandists.], Chlodomer captured him with his wife and sons and led him away as a prisoner. He was placed under guard and kept within the territory of the city of Orléans.

When these kings had departed, Godomar, having regained his strength, gathered the Burgundians and recovered the kingdom.

Chlodomer, preparing to march against him again, resolved to kill Sigimund. At that time the blessed Avitus, abbot of Micy [Note: [Col. 0245D] The printed edition incorrectly has *Nutiacense*; the manuscripts do not specify the place, but they have *Avito*, and some read *Adjuto*, “a great abbot.” An anonymous writer who composed the deeds of the Frankish kings under Theuderic says in chapter 20: “The blessed Avitus, who was then a holy man and abbot in the city of Orléans, begged Chlodomer not to kill them,” and so forth. Micy was a celebrated abbey of our order, commonly called Micy; it is also called Saint-Mesmin after its founder, namely Saint Maximin, the successor of Avitus. It lies about two leagues from Orléans and is now occupied by the Feuillants. The feast of Saint Avitus is celebrated on June 17, on which day his Life is found in Surius.], then a great priest, said to him:

“If, with your eyes turned toward God, you amend your plan and do not allow these men to be killed, God will be with you and you will depart victorious. But if you kill them, you yourself will be delivered into the hands of your enemies and will perish by a similar fate. What you do to Sigimund, his wife, and his children will be done to you, your wife, and your children.”

But Chlodomer refused to heed his advice and said: “I think it foolish advice to leave enemies at home and march against the others, while they rise behind me and the others before me, so that I fall between two enemy formations. Victory will be achieved more safely and easily if one group is separated from the other; once one has been killed, the other too can readily be consigned to death.”

Immediately, after killing Sigimund, his wife, and his children, he ordered them thrown into a well at Columna [Note: [Col. 0246C] Cas. and Regm., together with Bad., have *Colonia*. Here they think that Columella, commonly called Coloumelle, or certainly a village near it, commonly called Coulmiers, is intended. Near both villages, as Valesius observes in his *Notitia*, is a place called in old charters the Well of Saint Sigismund, in the vernacular Saint-Sigismond, or, by contraction, Saint-Simond. Sigismund is honored not only among confessors but also among martyrs, in accordance with the custom of those times, when innocent people killed for whatever reason were called martyrs. His feast is celebrated by the older martyrologies on the Kalends of May; on that day the Bollandists published his Life. In it his sons, killed together with him at Belsa, are called Giscladus and Gundebaudus. Three years after their death, Venerandus, abbot of Agaunum, with the approval of King Theudebert, arranged for their bodies to be exhumed and transferred to his monastery. See book I of *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 75. Marius writes in his Chronicle that Sigismund was killed during the consulship of Maximus, that is, in the year 523.], a village of the city of Orléans. He then went into Burgundy, calling King Theuderic to his assistance [Note: [Col. 0246D] The printed editions have *suppetias* [“aid”], and likewise in many places.].

Theuderic, unwilling to avenge the injury done to his father-in-law [Note: [Col. 0246D] Thus Bell.; the others have *volens* [“willing”], but incorrectly. Theodoric, while promising assistance to Chlodomer, did not wish to avenge the death of his father-in-law. He had married Sigismund’s daughter. Nevertheless, Fredegar, in his epitome, chapter 36, seems to have read *volens*, since he says that Chlodomer was deceived by Theodoric, as though Theodoric had indeed sent troops, but troops that joined the Burgundians during the battle.], promised to go.

When they had joined one another at a place called Virontia [Note: [Col. 0246D] Thus Corb. and Bell.; Labbe interprets the place as Voiron in Dauphiné. Bec. has *Visoronitom*; the other manuscripts and printed editions have *Visorontiam*, which Valesius in his *Notitia* and Cointius think is Veseronce. [Col. 0247D] This place lies on the Rhône between the cities of Vienne and Belley.], within the territory of the city of Vienne, they engaged Godomar.

When Godomar had turned his back with his army and Chlodomer was pursuing him, Chlodomer became separated from his men by a considerable distance. The enemy, imitating his insignia, shouted to him: “Turn here, turn here! We are your men.”

Believing them, he went toward them and rushed into the midst of his enemies. They cut off his head, fixed it upon a spear, and raised it aloft. When the Franks saw this and recognized that Chlodomer had been killed, they recovered their strength, drove Godomar away, crushed the Burgundians, and brought the country under their own power.

Immediately afterward, Chlothacharius took his brother’s wife, named Guntheuca, in marriage. Queen Chrotechildis, after the days of mourning had passed, took his sons into her household and kept them with her. One of them was called Theodoualdus [Note: [Col. 0247D] Others have *Theotbaldus*. Agathias is therefore mistaken when he writes in book I that Chlodomer perished without children and that, after his death, the Franks, despairing, accepted terms from the Burgundians. Chlodomer died during the consulship of Justinus II and Opilio, that is, in the year 524, according to the Chronicle of Marius.], the second Guntharius, and the third Chlodoualdus. Godomar again recovered the kingdom.

VII. Afterward, Theuderic, mindful of the perjury of Hermenefridus, king of the Thuringians, summoned his brother Chlothacharius to his aid and planned to march against him, promising King Chlothacharius a share of the spoils if God should grant them the gift of victory.

Having therefore summoned the Franks, he said to them:

“I beg you, resent both my injury and the death of your relatives [Note: [Col. 0247D] The Regm. manuscript has “my relatives.” See above, chapter 4.], and remember that formerly the Thuringians came violently against our relatives and inflicted many evils upon them. Our people wished to make peace with them after giving hostages [Note: [Col. 0247D] The same Regm. manuscript has “did not wish to make peace with them.”], but they put the hostages to death by various forms of execution. Then they attacked our relatives, carried away all their property, hung the children by the sinews of their thighs from trees, and killed more than two hundred girls with cruel slaughter. They tied the women by their arms to the necks of horses; the horses, driven in different directions by the sharpest goads, tore the women apart and divided them into separate pieces.

“They stretched others across the wheel-ruts [Note: [Col. 0247D] Ancient glossaries call the public roads themselves *orbitae*. An *orbita* is the rut formed on roads by the wheels, or circles, of wagons. In French we say *des ornières* [“ruts”].], drove stakes into the ground, and made loaded wagons pass over them. When their bones had been crushed, they gave them as food to dogs and birds.

“Now Hermenefridus has deceived me concerning what he promised and wholly refuses to fulfill it. Here we have a lawful undertaking [Note: [Col. 0247D] This expression occurs frequently in Gregory to indicate that something may be undertaken lawfully and with justification. Even today the French say *avoir droit d’entreprendre une chose* [“to have the right to undertake something”]. See book IV, chapter 14.]. Let us go against them with God’s help.”

When they heard this and were indignant at so great a crime, they went to Thuringia with one mind and one purpose.

Theuderic, taking his brother Chlothacharius and his son Theudebert with him as allies, went away with an army.

The Thuringians prepared traps for the approaching Franks. In the field where the battle was to take place, they dug pits. Covering their openings with thick turf, they made the field look level. When the Franks began to fight, many of their horsemen fell into these pits, and this greatly hindered them. After discovering the trick, however, they began to guard against it.

Finally, when the Thuringians saw that they were being slaughtered in great numbers, they put their backs to the enemy and, after their king Hermenefridus had fled [Note: [Col. 0248D] The printed editions add *prae timore* [“out of fear”].], reached the river Onestrude [Note: [Col. 0248D] The Colb. manuscript has *Unstrondem*. This is a river of Eichsfeld, commonly called Unstrudt by the inhabitants, as Browerus observes in his notes on Fortunatus.].

There such a great slaughter of the Thuringians took place that the riverbed was filled with a heap of corpses, and the Franks crossed over them to the farther bank as though over a bridge. After accomplishing the victory, they took possession of that region and brought it under their authority.

Chlothacharius, returning, took Radegund, daughter of King Bertharius [Note: [Col. 0248D] He was Hermenefridus’s brother. See above, chapter 4. Fortunatus describes the destruction of Thuringia and laments it in the first book of the Supplement to his poems, where he also writes about her brother, who was unjustly killed. Fortunatus wrote the first book of the Life of Saint Radegund, and the nun Baudonivia wrote the second; both are found in the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, first century, p. 319. The monastery founded by her still flourishes under the title of the Holy Cross and belongs to the Benedictine Order. These matters are discussed below more than once, especially in book IX.], captive with him and took her as his wife. Later he unjustly had her brother killed by wicked men.

She, turning to God, changed her clothing and built a monastery for herself within the city of Poitiers. Through prayers, fasts, vigils, and almsgiving she shone so brightly that she was held in great esteem among the people.

While the kings mentioned above were still in Thuringia, Theuderic wished to kill his brother Chlothacharius. He secretly prepared armed men, summoned Chlothacharius to him as though he wished to discuss something privately with him, and, having spread a tent across part of the house from one wall to the other, ordered the armed men to stand behind it.

Because the tent was too short, the soldiers’ feet appeared below it. Chlothacharius recognized this and entered the house armed with his own men. When Theuderic realized that Chlothacharius had discovered the plot, he invented a story and spoke of one thing after another. Finally, not knowing how to conceal his deception, he gave him a large silver dish as a favor.

Chlothacharius took his leave, thanked him for the gift, and returned to his quarters. Theuderic complained to his men that he had lost his dish without any apparent reason. Then he said to his son Theudebert: “Go to your uncle [Note: [Col. 0248D] The printed editions have “your father.”] and ask him to give you willingly the gift I gave him.”

Theudebert went and obtained what he requested. In such deceits Theuderic was extremely crafty.

VIII. After he had returned to his own country, Theuderic ordered Hermenefridus to come to him under the protection of a pledged promise; he also enriched him with honorable gifts.

One day, while they were conversing on the wall of the city of Tolbiac, Hermenefridus fell from the height of the wall to the ground, pushed by someone unknown, and there breathed out his spirit. But who threw him down from there, we do not know. Many nevertheless assert that Theuderic’s deceit was unmistakably involved in this [Note: [Col. 0249D] Procopius, book I of the *Gothic History*, reports that after killing Hermenefridus the Franks subjected Thuringia to themselves.].

IX. While Theuderic was still in Thuringia, word spread in Auvergne that he had been killed. Arcadius, one of the senators of Auvergne, invited Childebert to take possession of that region. Childebert did not delay but went to Auvergne.

On that day so dense a fog gathered that nothing could be distinguished beyond two *jugera* [approximately half a hectare]. The king used to say: “I would like,” he said, “to see with my own eyes the Auvergne Limagne, which is said to shine with such delightful fertility” [Note: [Col. 0249D] Bec. has this reading; Bell. and Bad. have *unicam* [“only”]; the others have *unquam* [“ever”]. Gregory is speaking of that part of Auvergne which is still called the Limagne of Auvergne, where Clermont, the capital of the province, is situated. Savaro collected much concerning Auvergne’s fertility and pleasantness from various authors in his notes on letter 21 of book IV of Sidonius. Consult him if you wish.].

But God did not grant this to him.

When the city gates were shut and there was no broad passage by which he could enter, Arcadius cut through the bar of one gate and admitted him into the city. While these things were taking place, word was announced that Theuderic had returned alive from Thuringia.

### X.

Childebert, learning this with complete certainty, returned from the Arverni and set out for Spain [Note: By the name Spain they here intend Septimania, and they hold that Amalaric was killed not at Barcelona or Toledo, as some prefer, but at Narbonne. For the territories subject to the Visigoths, even within the ancient boundaries of Gaul, were frequently designated at that time by the name Spain, as could be proved by six hundred examples. Read Valesius, book VII of *The History of the Franks*.] on account of his sister Chrotechild [Note: Others have Chrotilde or Crotigelde. Bec and Regm. have Chlocchilde. See the note on book II, chapter 28.].

She suffered many attacks from her husband Amalaric because of the Catholic faith. For very often, when she proceeded to the holy church, he ordered dung and various foul substances to be thrown upon her [Col. 0249C]. Finally, he is said to have beaten her with such cruelty that she sent her brother a handkerchief stained with her own blood. Greatly provoked by this, he set out against Spain.

When Amalaric heard this, he prepared ships for flight. As Childebert approached and Amalaric was about to board ship [Note: Corb. and Bellov. have Alaric; likewise in the table of contents, although elsewhere they always call him Amalaric.], he remembered that he had left a quantity of precious stones in his treasury. When he returned to the city to fetch them, he was shut out by the army from the harbor [Note: Colb., together with nearly all printed editions, has “from the gate.”]. Seeing that he could not escape, he began to take refuge in the church of the Christians [Note: Notice that Catholics are called Christians, in distinction from the Arians.] 114. But before he touched the holy threshold, someone thrust out a hand and wounded him with a mortal blow from a spear; dying there, he gave up his spirit.

Then Childebert wished to take his sister away with him, together with the great treasures. But she died on the road, I know not by what accident, and was later brought to Paris and buried beside her father Chlodovech. Childebert carried away, among the remaining treasures, the most precious vessels of the churches. For he carried away sixty chalices, fifteen patens, and twenty Gospel-books in jeweled covers, all made of pure gold and adorned with precious gems; but he did not allow them to be broken up. He distributed and handed everything over to the churches and basilicas of the saints for ecclesiastical service [Note: Thus Casin.; the others do not have *in ministerium*, nor do the printed editions.].

### XI.

After this, Chlothacharius and Childebert resolved to march against Burgundy. Theuderic was summoned, but he refused to go in their support [Note: Regm. has “support”; the printed editions have “assistance.”]. The Franks who looked to him said: “If you refuse to go with your brothers into Burgundy, we shall leave you and prefer to follow them instead.”

But, considering them faithless to him, he said: “Follow me to the Arverni, and I shall lead you into a country where you will receive as much gold and silver as your desire can crave, and from which you will take cattle, slaves, and clothing in abundance. Only, do not follow them.”

Enticed by these promises, they promised to do his will. He then planned to cross into that region, promising the army again and again that he would permit all the spoil of the country, together with its inhabitants, to be carried into their own territories.

Chlothacharius and Childebert, however, marched into Burgundy and, besieging Augustodunum, drove out Godomar and occupied the whole of Burgundy [Note: In the consulship of Justinian IV and Paulinus, if we trust Marius—that is, in the year 534.].

### XII.

Theuderic, coming with his army 115 to the Arverni [Col. 0250C], devastated and ravaged the whole region. Meanwhile Arcadius, the author of that crime, through whose negligence the region had been laid waste, made for the city of Biturica. At that time this city belonged to the kingdom of King Childebert.

His mother Placidina and his father’s sister Alchima [Note: These women were already mentioned in chapter 2 of this book. Here Reg. reads *Archidima* for *Archima*. In any case, they do not seem to have been captured at Cahors, as the printed editions imply; rather, they were captured among the Arverni and sent into exile at Cahors. Arcadius was the nephew of Saint Sidonius, namely the son of Apollinaris, Sidonius’s son.] were arrested, stripped of their possessions, and condemned to exile at the city of Cahors.

King Theuderic therefore advanced as far as the city of Arverna and pitched camp in the suburb of that city [Note: Several manuscripts have the feminine form *suburbana*]. Blessed Quintianus was bishop at that time. Meanwhile the army traversed the entire wretched region, destroying everything and conquering all before it.

Some of them reached the basilica of Saint Julian, broke down the doors, removed the bolts, and plundered the possessions of the poor that had been gathered there. They perpetrated many evils in that place [Col. 0251A]. Nevertheless, the perpetrators of these crimes, seized by an unclean spirit, tore themselves with their own teeth in savage bites, crying out: “Why do you torture us so, holy martyr?”—as we have recorded in the book of his Miracles [Note: Namely, chapter 13 of book II of *The Miracles*, which concerns Saint Julian. Gregory is speaking here of his basilica near the city of Brioude.].

### XIII.

The enemies stormed the fortress of Lovolautrum [Note: Codex Reg. has *Novolautrum*, whose location is uncertain. Valesius, in his *Notitia*, thinks it was a place called Volorre, near Tigernum, the town of Thiers, among the Arverni. Compare this chapter with the life of Saint Quintianus in the book *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 4.], and they pitifully killed the presbyter Proculus at the altar of the church, because he had once inflicted an injury upon Saint Quintianus.

I believe that, on account of this man, the fortress itself was delivered into the hands of the wicked, although it had been defended up to that day. For when the enemies were unable to storm it and were already preparing to return to their own country, the besieged, hearing this, were deceived by premature joy and security, just as the Apostle says: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come” (1 Thessalonians 5:3).

Finally, through the servant of that presbyter Proculus [Note: Codex Corb. has *stuprum*; Bell. has the erroneous reading *struum*], the people, now secure, were delivered into the hands of the enemy. When the captives were being led away after the fortress had been destroyed, a violent rain—which had been withheld for thirty days—began to fall.

Then the besieged inhabitants of the fortress of Meroliacum [Note: Valesius likewise thinks this place was Oliergue, a fortress not far from Thiers. Others, however, more plausibly believe that the place called Chastei Merliac is intended here. It lies about two miles from the town of Mauriac, famous for its Benedictine abbey, on the slope of a very high hill, from which one descends through meadows into a deep valley.] were freed by paying a ransom; but their cowardice brought this about, for the fortress was naturally well defended.

It was enclosed by sheer-cut rock a hundred feet or more high, not by the construction of walls [Note: Thus the older manuscripts; others, with the printed editions, have “without walls.”]. In the middle was a vast pond of water, of most agreeable quality; on the other side were abundant springs, so that a stream of fresh water flowed out through the gate [Note: Corb. has “through the whole fortification”; the word *fortification* was written by another but very ancient hand.].

The fortification extended over so large an area that those dwelling within its enclosure could cultivate the land and gather crops in abundance [Col. 0251C]. Trusting in the protection of this stronghold, the besieged went outside to seize some booty and then hide themselves again within the fortress. But they were captured by the enemy.

There were fifty men [Note: The second printed edition has five hundred; all the manuscripts, however, have fifty, except Corb., which has *quinquaginti*]. Then, brought before the eyes of their parents with their hands bound behind their backs, and with the sword already threatening them, the besieged consented that each man should pay three *trientes* as his ransom [Note: Here and frequently below the printed editions always write *trientes*. Francis Pithou therefore observed in his notes on title XXXVII of the Salic Law that Gregory always uses *triens*.].

As Theuderic departed from the Arverni, he left his kinsman Sigivald there, as if to guard the region [Note: Compare chapter 14 of *The Miracles of Saint Julian*]. At that time a certain Litigius, one of the royal summons-officers [Note: Thus Corb. and Bellov.; others have “the lesser ones.” As Valesius observes in the preface to volume II of *The History of the Franks*, the *monitores* were those who announced military expeditions to the Franks in the king’s name and compelled them to go to war. In Visigothic laws they are called *compulsores*; our people sometimes expressed their office by the Germanic phrase “to ban into the host.”], was there and was preparing great plots against Saint Quintianus.

Although the holy bishop prostrated himself at Litigius’s feet, the man was never moved to submit to him. On one occasion he even reported to his wife, as a joke, what the saint had done. She, moved to better understanding, replied: “If you have been brought so low today, you will never rise again.”

On the third day, messengers arrived announcing the king’s presence, and they led away Litigius, bound, together with his wife and children. After departing, he never returned to the Arverni.

### XIV.

Munderic, who claimed to be of royal kin [Note: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions have “of the kings.”], was swollen with pride and said: “What have I to do with King Theuderic? The royal throne is owed to me just as it is to him. I shall go out, gather my people, and exact an oath from them, so that Theuderic may know that I am a king just as he is.”

He went out and began to seduce the people, saying: “I am the prince; follow me, and it will go well with you” [Col. 0252B]. A rustic multitude followed him, as human weakness commonly inclines people to do, swearing an oath of loyalty and honoring him as king.

When Theuderic learned this, he sent him a message, saying: “Come to me, and if any portion of the rule of our kingdom is owed to you, take it.” Theuderic spoke deceitfully, intending that Munderic should come to him and be killed.

But Munderic refused, saying: “Go and report to your king that I am a king just as he is.”

Then the king ordered an army to be mobilized, so that Munderic might be overcome and punished by force. When Munderic learned this and realized that he could not defend himself, he sought the walls of the fortress of Victoriacum [Note: Aimoinus understood this place as Victoriacum among the Arverni in book II. Although it is true that a fortress called Victoriacum existed in that region, not far from Brioude, we nevertheless think, with Valesius, that Gregory is speaking here of Victoriacum in Champagne, commonly called Vitry, in the diocese of Châlons.], fortified himself there with all his possessions, and gathered around him those whom he had seduced.

The army was therefore mobilized, surrounded the fortress, and besieged it for seven days. Munderic resisted with his followers, saying: “Let us stand firm and fight together to the death; let us not submit to our enemies.”

When the army shot arrows against them from all sides without achieving anything, they reported this to the king. He sent one of his men, named Aregisilus [Note: Colb. has *Archisilus*, and so consistently thereafter], and said to him: “You see how this traitor prevails in his defiance. Go and give him your oath, so that he may come out safely. When he has come out, kill him and erase his memory from our kingdom.”

Aregisilus went and did what he had been ordered. First, however, he gave a signal to the people, saying: “When I have said such and such things, immediately rush upon him and kill him.”

Entering, Aregisilus said to Munderic: “How long will you remain here like one of the foolish? Will you really be able to resist the king for long? Behold, once your food has been taken away, when hunger has overcome you, you will come out of your own accord, be delivered into the hands of your enemies, and die like one of the dogs.”

“Listen instead to my advice and submit to the king, so that you and your sons may live.”

Munderic, softened by these words, replied: “If I come out, the king will seize and kill me, my sons, and all the friends who have gathered here with me.”

Aregisilus said to him: “Do not be afraid. If you wish to come out, receive an oath regarding this offense and stand securely before the king. Do not fear; you will be with him as you were before.”

Munderic replied: “Would that I might be sure that I shall not be killed” [Col. 0253B].

Then Aregisilus placed his hands upon the holy altar [Note: Several manuscripts and the printed editions have “the holy altar”] and swore to him that he would come out safely.

After the oath had been given, Munderic came out through the gate of the fortress holding Aregisilus’s hand. The people watched him from a distance [Note: Chesn., with Bec., has “waited for him.”].

Then Aregisilus gave the signal, saying: “Why are you looking so intently, people? Have you not seen Munderic before?” [Note: Reg. has, “Have you not seen him before?” Several editions, with Bec., have, “Have you seen Munderic before?”]

Immediately the people rushed upon him. Understanding what had happened, Munderic said: “I recognize most clearly, by this word, that you have given the people a signal to kill me. Nevertheless, I tell you this: because you deceived me by perjury, no one will ever see you alive again.” He thrust a spear through Aregisilus’s shoulders, and Aregisilus fell and died.

Munderic then drew his sword and, together with his men, inflicted great slaughter upon that people [Col. 0253C]. Until he breathed out his spirit, he did not cease killing anyone he could reach. After he was killed, his possessions were transferred to the royal treasury.

### XV.

Theuderic and Childebert then entered into a treaty. They swore to one another that neither would move against the other, and exchanged hostages so that the agreements might be more firmly secured.

Many senators’ sons were given as hostages at this time [Note: That is, they were delivered as hostages]. But when discord again arose between the kings, they were assigned to public servitude. Whoever received one of them for custody made him his own slave.

Many escaped by flight and returned to their homeland; some were retained in servitude. Among these was Attalus, the grandson of blessed Gregory, bishop of Langres, who was assigned to public service and appointed keeper of horses.

He was serving a certain barbarian [Note: That is, a Frank. Just as the ancient inhabitants were called Romans, so the others, as we have already observed, were called Barbarians. This usage occurs frequently in Gregory.] within the territory of the Treveran frontier.

Blessed Gregory sent servants to search for him. When they found him, they offered gifts to his master, but he rejected them, saying: “This boy must be redeemed from such a lineage for ten pounds of gold.”

When they returned, a certain Leo, from the kitchen staff of his master Gregory, said: “Would that you would allow me to go; perhaps I could bring him back from captivity.”

His master rejoiced, and Leo was sent to the place. He wanted to steal the boy away secretly, but could not. Then, taking a man with him, he said: “Come with me and sell me in that barbarian’s house. Let the price paid for me be your profit; only grant me freer access to do what I have determined.”

After receiving his oath, the man went away and, having sold Leo for twelve gold pieces, departed.

The buyer asked the inexperienced servant what work he knew. He replied: “I am highly skilled at preparing everything that is to be eaten at my masters’ tables [Note: The printed editions, with Bec., have “everything that is to be consumed.”]. I do not fear that anyone equal to me in this skill can be found. I tell you the truth: even if you wished to prepare a feast for a king, I could arrange royal dishes, and no one could do it better than I.”

The master replied: “The day of the sun has arrived”—for this is what the barbarians were accustomed to call the Lord’s Day—“and on this day my neighbors and relatives will be invited to my house. I ask you to prepare a meal for me that they will admire and say, ‘We have never seen a better one, even in the king’s house.’”

He replied: “Let my master order a multitude of young chickens to be gathered, and I shall do what you command.”

When the things the boy had requested had been prepared, Sunday dawned, and he made a great feast filled with delicacies. When everyone had eaten and praised the meal, the master’s relatives departed.

For the Lord granted this boy favor, and gave him authority over everything his master kept in readiness. His master loved him greatly, and he himself distributed food and dishes to everyone who was with him.

After a year had passed, when the master had become entirely confident in him, Leo went out into a meadow near the house with Attalus, the boy who kept the horses. Lying on the ground with him at a distance, with their backs turned so that no one would know what they were saying to one another, he said to the boy:

“It is time for us now to think about our homeland. Therefore I advise you that tonight, when you have brought the horses in to be shut up, you must not be overcome by sleep. As soon as I call you, come to me, and we shall depart.”

The barbarian had invited many of his relatives to a feast, including his son-in-law, who had married his daughter. At midnight, when they rose from the banquet and went to rest, Leo followed his master’s son-in-law to his lodging with a drink and offered it to him, saying:

“Tell me, creditor of my father-in-law, if you can: when will you decide to take his horses and ride them to your own homeland?”

He said this for amusement. The other, likewise answering truthfully in jest, replied: “Tonight, if it is God’s will.”

The first said: “Would that my servants guard me, so that you do not take any of my possessions.”

They laughed and departed.

When everyone was asleep, Leo called Attalus. After saddling the horses, he asked whether he had a sword [Note: The printed editions have, “Attalus from his bed; he asks,” and so forth]. Attalus replied: “I have none, only a small spear.”

Leo entered the dwelling of his master and seized his shield and sword. When his master asked who he was and what he wanted, he replied: “I am Leo, your servant. I am waking Attalus so that he may rise more quickly and lead the horses out to pasture, for he is held by sleep as if drunk.”

The master said: “Do as you please.” Saying this, he fell asleep.

Leo went outside, armed the boy, and found the courtyard gates miraculously opened. At the beginning of the night he had secured them with wedges driven in by a hammer, to guard the horses. Giving thanks to the Lord, they departed with the remaining horsemen [alternative reading: horses], taking also one *volucrum* with clothing [Note: Codex Bellov. has *voluclum*; Corb. has “taking a *voluclum* of clothing.”].

When they came to the river Mosella [Note: It can scarcely be doubted that *Mosa* should be read, as Valesius remarks in the *Notitia of Gaul*. For the Meuse flows between the cities of Rheims and Trier and separates their two dioceses; after crossing the Meuse, one immediately reaches Champagne. None of these circumstances can be fitted to the Moselle. Indeed, wherever they had crossed the Moselle, it would scarcely have been possible for them to reach Rheims on that same day. Since, however, all the manuscripts and printed editions have *Mosella*, Gregory’s text has not been altered, especially because it seems certain that they did not follow the direct road. For there were not three days’ journey from Trier to the Meuse, since the river is no farther from Trier than from Rheims—about eighteen leagues.], 121 while they were crossing it, some men detained them. Leaving behind the horsemen [alternative reading: horses] and clothing, they floated across the river on a shield and emerged on the farther bank.

Entering a forest in the darkness of night, they hid themselves. The third night had arrived, and they had continued their journey without tasting any food. Then, by God’s providence, they found a tree full of fruit, commonly called a plum tree [Note: Bell. and others have *pruna*, “plums”]. They ate from it and, thus sustained for a little while, entered upon the road to Champagne.

As they continued, they heard the sound of horses’ hooves running. They said: “Let us lie flat on the ground, so that we will not be seen by the men who are coming.”

Suddenly a great thornbush appeared. Passing behind it, they threw themselves to the ground with drawn swords, so that, if noticed, they might immediately defend themselves against the wicked men with their swords [Note: Corb. and Bell. do not have *framea*, “sword.”].

When they had reached that place, however, they stopped before the thornbush. One of the riders, while the horses urinated, said: “Woe to me, for these detestable fugitives have escaped and cannot be found. But I swear by my life that, if they were discovered, I would order one to be condemned to the gallows and the other to be cut to pieces by sword blows.”

The barbarian who said this was their master, coming from the city of Rheims and searching for them. He would certainly have found them on the road if night had not prevented it. Then, having set the horsemen [alternative reading: horses] in motion, they departed.

The fugitives reached the city that same night. Entering, they found a man and asked him where the house of the presbyter Paulellus was. He showed them. As they passed through the street, the signal for Matins sounded; for it was Sunday. They knocked at the presbyter’s door and entered.

The boy explained what had happened to his master. The presbyter said to him: “My vision has indeed come true. For this night I saw two doves flying toward me and settling upon my hand; one of them was white and the other black.”

The boys said to the presbyter: “May the Lord forgive us for violating His holy day [Note: For in those times it was not permitted to eat or drink anything on Sundays before Mass]. We ask you to provide us with some food, for the fourth day is dawning since we tasted any bread or stew.”

He concealed the boys, gave them bread soaked in wine, and went to Matins. The barbarian also followed, searching for the boys again, but the presbyter deceived him and he returned. The presbyter had long been a friend of blessed Gregory.

Then, having regained their strength from the meal, the boys remained for two days in the presbyter’s house and departed. In this way they were brought safely to Saint Gregory.

When the bishop saw the boys, he rejoiced and wept upon the neck of his grandson Attalus [Note: He apparently later became count of the Aedui, to whom Sidonius wrote letter 18 of book V].

He freed Leo from the yoke of servitude, together with all his family, and gave him his own land. There he lived as a free man with his wife and children for all the days of his life.

### XVI.

While Sigivald [Note: He had been left above, in chapter 13, by King Theuderic to guard the city.] was living in the Arverni, he committed many evils there. He seized the property of various people, and his servants did not cease from thefts, murders, raids [Note: The printed editions have “beyond measure”], and various other crimes. No one dared even mutter in their presence.

Thus it happened that he rashly seized the estate of Bulgiacum, which the blessed Bishop Tetradius had once left to the basilica of Saint Julian [Note: This Tetradius was bishop of Biturica, as we learn from Gregory himself in book II of *The Miracles*, chapter 14. Gregory calls him “blessed”; this should be understood not as a surname but as an honorific epithet. Thus, in the book *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 86, we find “blessed Agricolaus,” and in Tertullian, book *On the Prescription of Heretics*, “blessed Eleutherus.” For further examples, see Sirmond’s note on letter 9 of book I of Sidonius Apollinaris.].

When Sigivald entered that house, he immediately became insane and fell upon a bed. Then the woman, instructed by the priest, had him lifted into a litter and carried to another estate, where she received him restored to health. He approached the woman and explained everything he had suffered.

When he heard this, he made vows to the blessed Martyr and restored, doubled, everything he had taken [Note: The edition with Bec. has “everything he had taken by force”]. We have also recalled this miracle in the book of the Miracles of Saint Julian (chapter 14).

### XVII.

When Bishop Difinius [Note: Several printed editions have Dionysius. Moreover, when this chapter is compared with the final chapter of book II and the end of book X, where Gregory enumerates the bishops of Tours, it becomes clear how little consistent he is both in assigning the dates of the bishops’ pontificates and in the order in which they occupied this see. Nevertheless, this chapter is found in all the manuscripts.] died at Tours, Ommatius presided for three years. He had been ordained at the command of King Chlodomer, whom we mentioned above.

When Ommatius also departed this life, Leo served for seven months [Col. 0257A]. He was an energetic and useful man in the construction of wooden works.

After Leo’s death, the bishops Theodorus and Proculus, who had come from the region of Burgundy, governed the Church of Tours for three years, having been appointed by Queen Chrotechild. When they had died, Francilio, one of the senators, was substituted.

In the third year of his episcopate, when the holy night of the Lord’s Nativity had shone upon the people, this bishop, before descending to the vigils, ordered a cup to be brought to him. A boy arrived and immediately handed it to him. After drinking it, he at once gave up his spirit. It is therefore certain that he was killed by poison.

After his death, Injuriosus, one of the citizens, became the fifteenth to obtain the episcopal see after blessed Martin.

### XVIII.

While Queen Chrotechild was staying at Paris, Childebert saw that his mother loved the sons of Chlodomer, whom we mentioned above, with undivided affection. Driven by envy and fearing that, with the queen’s support, they might be admitted to the kingdom, he secretly sent to his brother, King Chlothacharius, saying:

“Our mother is keeping our brother’s sons with her and wants to give them the kingdom [Note: Thus Corb. and Bell. Nearly all the others, together with the printed editions, have “wants them to be given the kingdom.”]. You must come quickly to Paris, and after taking common counsel we must decide what should be done with them: whether, after their hair has been cut, they should be treated like the rest of the people [Note: Hotomannus discusses the law concerning royal hair in chapter II of *Franco-Gallia*. Agathias, a Greek, gives a notable testimony on this subject in book I: “It is customary for the kings of the Franks never to be shorn . . . their entire hair hangs becomingly down upon their shoulders, while the hair at the front, parted from the forehead, falls to either side. Nor, as with the Turks and Barbarians, is their hair matted, filthy, and dirty, or indecently curled through being tangled; rather, they apply various cleansers to it and carefully tend it. This is assigned to the royal line among them as a kind of distinction and an exceptional prerogative of honor. Their subjects, on the other hand, are shorn in a circular fashion, and are scarcely permitted to grow their hair long.” He praises the customs and civility of the Franks at greater length. Procopius is more sparing in his praise, because the Franks often opposed the enterprises of the emperors. Gregory repeatedly praises the custom of growing the hair among princes of the royal line, as in book VI, chapter 24, and book VIII, chapter 10, and elsewhere. See the notes of Savaro and Sirmond on the letters of Sidonius Apollinaris, book I, letter 2.], or, after they have been killed, the kingdom of our brother should be divided among ourselves on equal terms.”

Chlothacharius was greatly pleased by these words and came to Paris. Childebert had spread it among the people that the two kings were joining forces in order to raise the little boys to the kingdom.

The kings then joined together and sent to the queen, who was staying in the city, saying: “Send the boys to us, so that they may be elevated to the kingdom.”

She rejoiced, unaware of their deceit. After giving the boys food and drink, she sent them to the kings, saying: “I do not think that I have lost a son if I see you installed in his kingdom.”

As soon as they departed, they were seized and separated from their servants and nurses. Both groups were kept under guard separately: the servants apart and the little boys apart.

Childebert and Chlothacharius then sent Arcadius, whom we mentioned above (chapters 9 and 12), to the queen with a pair of shears and a drawn sword. When he arrived, he displayed both objects to the queen and said:

“Your sons, our lords, most glorious queen, ask to know your will: what do you think should be done with the boys? Shall they be allowed to live with their hair cut, or shall both be put to death?”

The queen was terrified by the message and exceedingly inflamed with anger, especially when she saw the drawn sword and the shears. Overcome by bitterness and, in the midst of her grief, not understanding what she was saying, she simply replied:

“It is better for me to see them dead than shorn, if they are not to be raised to the kingdom.”

Arcadius, taking little account of her grief and not investigating what she might later have considered more fully, hurried back and reported:

“With the queen’s approval, complete the undertaking you have begun; she wishes your plan to be carried out.”

Without delay, Chlothacharius seized the elder boy by the arm, dashed him to the ground, and cruelly killed him by driving a knife into his armpit [Note: Corb. has “and, after fixing the knife”; Colb., together with Reg. and several editions, has “armpit” rather than “axilla”; Regm. has “under the armpit”; Reg. and Bec. have “in the armpit.”].

As the boy cried out, his brother fell at Childebert’s feet, clasped his knees, and said with tears:

“Come to my aid, most merciful father, so that I too may not perish like my brother.”

Then Childebert, his face drenched with tears, said:

“I beg you, dearest brother, by your generosity grant me his life. I will give whatever you command for his soul; only let him not be killed.”

But Chlothacharius, driven by insults [Note: Thus Corb., Bell., Bec., and Colb. The others have “driven by rage.”], replied:

“Either drive him away from you, or you will certainly die for him. You are the instigator [Note: These same manuscripts, together with Chesnius, have “instigator of this cause.” Reg. has “investigator”; Regm. has “inciter.” The printed editions generally have “originator.”] of this affair, and so quickly do you withdraw from your loyalty?”

Hearing this, Childebert thrust the boy away from him toward Chlothacharius. Chlothacharius seized him and, as he had done with his brother, killed him by driving a knife into his side.

Then they killed the servants together with the nurses as well. After they had been killed, Chlothacharius mounted his horses [Note: *Equis*, “horses,” in the alternative reading] and departed, caring nothing for the murder of his nephews. Childebert, meanwhile, withdrew into the suburb.

The queen arranged the little bodies upon a bier and, with great chanting and immense mourning, accompanied both of them together to the basilica of Saint Peter [Note: Today the basilica of Saint Geneviève, as we have already noted. This crime seems to have been committed around the year 526, although Valesius argues that it occurred later, in 532 or the following year.], where she buried them. One of them was ten years old, the other seven.

They could not capture the third, Chlodouald, because he was rescued through the aid of brave men [Note: Valesius, book VII of *The History of the Franks*, considers that the “brave men” who helped Chlodoald escape death were those later commonly called barons.]. He renounced the earthly kingdom, turned to the Lord, and, cutting his hair with his own hand, became a cleric. Devoting himself to good works, he departed this world as a presbyter [Note: He died around the year 560, on 7 September, the day on which his feast is celebrated. He founded a monastery in a village called Novientum, three miles downriver from Paris on the Seine, now commonly called Saint-Cloud. A collegiate church now stands there, the monastery having long since been destroyed, and his sacred body is preserved in it. His life, taken from a manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, is found in the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, volume I, where it is stated, number 8, that he assumed the habit of holy religion from Saint Severinus, who was not the abbot of Agaunum. John, abbot of Saint Flodoald, subscribed to the assembly at Attigny under King Pepin in the year 765; we do not doubt that he presided over this monastery. For the ancients sometimes changed *ch* into the letter *f*.].

These two kings divided Chlodomer’s kingdom between themselves in equal shares.

Queen Chrotechild, however, conducted herself so nobly and magnificently that she was honored by everyone. Constant in almsgiving and wakeful through the nights in vigil, she always displayed herself pure in chastity and every form of virtue. She generously and willingly distributed estates to churches, monasteries, and every holy place that needed them, so that people might think that at that time she was not a queen but the very handmaid of God, diligently serving Him [Note: That is, a nun. See below, book IV, chapter 1.] 126.

Neither the kingdom of her sons, nor worldly ambition, nor power raised her up toward ruin; rather, humility lifted her to grace.

### XIX

At that time the blessed Gregory was also at the city of Langres, a great priest of God, renowned for signs and miracles [Note: Our Gregory wrote his life, which you will find below among the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 7.]. But since we have mentioned this bishop, I have thought it worthwhile to insert into this account a description of the site of Dijon, where he was especially often present.

It is a fortified settlement built with extremely strong walls, situated in the middle of a quite pleasant plain, possessing very fertile and productive lands [Note: Thus Bel. and Regm.; but the other manuscripts and printed editions have: “a land very fertile and productive.”], so that when the fields have once been cut by the plow, seed is sown and great abundance of crops follows.

To the south it has the river Ouche, exceedingly rich in fish; to the north another little stream [Note: This is here called the Suzon. It rises in the valley of that name three miles above Dijon. On the Ouche, see above, book II, chapter 32.] enters through one gate and, flowing beneath the bridge, emerges again through another, surrounding the whole fortified site with its gentle current. Before the gate, however, it turns aside toward the mills with remarkable speed.

There are four gates, placed on the four quarters of the world. The entire structure is adorned with thirty-three towers. Its wall is built of squared stones up to a height of twenty feet; above that it is constructed of small stones. It is thirty feet high and fifteen feet wide. Why it is not called a city, I do not know [Note: Even today Dijon does not possess the legal status of a city—that is, it is not distinguished by an episcopal see—although it was the seat of the dukes of Burgundy and the capital of the entire province, and still remains the seat of the supreme senate.].

It has precious springs around its circuit. On the western side there are very rich mountains, filled with vineyards, because they provide the inhabitants with such noble Falernian wine that they reject the wine of Chalon [Note: Corb. has this reading. Bellov. and Colb. read *Scalononum*; Regm., *Calonum*; Bec. and the others, together with the printed editions, *Scalonum*. We have preferred the reading of Corbeiensis, for the sense is that such excellent wines are produced at Dijon that its citizens have no need of the wines of Chalon. Savaro, however, interprets *Scalonum* as *Ascalonum*, that is, wine brought from the Palestinian city of Ascalon. Ascalon was close to Gaza, whence came the Gazan wines mentioned below, book VII, chapter 29. Claudius Robert, at the end of the *Gallia Christiana* published in 1626, discusses Dijon at greater length, and there, column 59, thinks that in this passage of Gregory one should read *Chalybonium*. For, as he reports, Chalybonian wine—wine of the sort used only by the kings of Persia, just as the water of the Choaspes was used only by them—is commended after the Syrian city of Chalybon.], for the ancients report that it was built by the emperor Aurelian.

### XX

At that time King Theuderic had betrothed Uvisigard, the daughter of a certain king, to his son Theudebert [Note: Namely, Waccho, king of the Lombards, as Paul the Deacon reports in book I, chapter 21, of his *History of the Lombards*.].

### XXI

After the death of Chlodovech, when the Goths had seized much of what he had acquired [Note: King Theodoric of Italy, having heard of Chlodovech’s victory at Vouillé, sent the general Ibba, or Ebban, with forces into Gaul to resist the Franks, who were invading the kingdom of the Visigoths. This was why the Franks, after abandoning the siege of Arles and being driven away, acquired nothing beyond Aquitaine. Theodoric, however, leaving the Visigoths the remaining part of their kingdom, occupied the regions beyond the Rhône that Odoacer had granted to Euric, the father of Alaric. From then on there was almost continuous war between Chlodovech and Theodoric and their successors. The circumstances by which that part of Gaul finally came under Frankish rule will be discussed in the notes to chapter 31.], Theuderic sent Theudebert, while Chlothacharius sent his elder son Guntharius, to reclaim these territories.

Guntharius reached the region of Rodez but, for some reason—I do not know what caused it—turned back. Theudebert, however, proceeding as far as the city of Béziers, captured the fortress of Deas [Note: Blondel and others think this place was Montadié. Valesius prefers to understand by this name Diou, in Septimania.] and plundered the surrounding territory. Then he sent envoys to another fortress called Capraria [Note: Capraria still exists, now commonly called Cabrière. It lies at approximately equal distances from Lodève, Agde, and Béziers, but belongs to the diocese of Béziers, as Valesius observes.], declaring that unless its inhabitants submitted to him, he would burn the entire place and take captive those who lived there.

### XXII

At that time there was there a noblewoman named Deuteria [Note: Some manuscripts, and indeed the older ones, have *Deoteria*. Valesius nevertheless considers *Deuteria* the correct reading and consequently conjectures that this woman was Gallic by birth—or, as people then said, Roman. He accuses Fredegar of ignorance for writing *Deoteria*, or *Teoteria*. But writers of that period used the letters *u* and *o*, as well as *d* and *t*, interchangeably, so that scarcely anything certain can be established from such changes.], a very capable and wise woman, whose husband had withdrawn to the city of Béziers [Note: This is the reading of all the manuscripts, together with Chesn.; most printed editions have *Biternas*.].

She sent messengers to the king, saying:

> “No one, most merciful lord, can resist you. We acknowledge our lord: come and do whatever is pleasing in your eyes.”

Theudebert came to the fortress and entered peacefully. Seeing that the people had submitted to him, he did them no harm. Deuteria came out to meet him; but when he saw that she was beautiful, he was seized with love for her and took her to his bed.

### XXIII

In those days Theuderic killed his kinsman Sigivald with the sword and secretly sent word to Theudebert that he too should put Givald [Note: Corb. and Bellov. have *Sigivald*; Regm. has *Gilvald*.], his son, to death, since he had him with him at the time. But because Theudebert had received him from the sacred font, he did not wish to destroy him.

He gave him the letter his father had sent, saying:

> “Flee from here, because I have received my father’s command to kill you. But if he has died and you hear that I am reigning, then return to me without fear.”

When Givald heard this, he gave thanks, said farewell, and departed. The Goths had by then seized the city of Arles, from which Theudebert held hostages; Givald fled there. But seeing that he was insufficiently protected there, he set out for Italy [Note: The Corbeiensis manuscript has *Italiam*, which is the same place meant by *Latium*.] and concealed himself there.

While these events were taking place, Theudebert was informed that his father was seriously ill and that, unless he hurried to him and found him alive, he would be excluded by his uncles and would not return there afterward. On hearing this, he set everything else aside and hastened there, leaving Deuteria with her daughter in Auvergne.

Not many days after he had departed, Theuderic died, in the twenty-third year of his reign. Childebert and Chlothacharius then rose up against Theudebert and attempted to take away his kingdom. But he appeased them with gifts [Note: Regm. has “having appeased them with gifts.” The printed edition and the manuscripts, except Corb. and Bell., have *Leodibus*.] and was defended by his leudes, and so was established in his kingdom. Later he sent to Auvergne and summoned Deuteria from there, taking her as his wife.

### XXIV

When Childebert saw that he could not prevail against Theudebert, he sent an embassy to him and ordered him to come to his presence, saying:

> “I have no sons; I desire to have you as a son.”

When Theudebert came, Childebert enriched him with so many gifts that everyone marveled. From valuable possessions—arms, clothing, and the other ornaments suitable for a king—he gave him three sets of each; likewise, he gave him three sets of horsemen and of *catini* [Note: Manuscript 1 has *catenis*. The printed edition has *equis et catenis* (“horses and chains”). Valesius therefore thinks that *catenarum* refers to torques, with which, according to Florus Annaeus, book IV, the Germanic peoples used to adorn their necks. Mor. interprets *catinis* as “vessels.”].

When Givald heard that Theudebert had obtained his father’s kingdom, he returned to him from Italy. Theudebert rejoiced at his return and kissed him; he gave him a third of the gifts he had received from his uncle and ordered that everything his father had placed in the treasury from the property of Givald’s father, Sigivald, should be restored to him.

### XXV

Once established in his kingdom, Theudebert made himself a great man and outstanding in every virtue. He ruled his kingdom with justice, honored priests, endowed churches, relieved the poor, and bestowed many benefits upon many people with pious and most gracious generosity.

He graciously remitted every tax that was paid into his treasury by the churches situated in Auvergne [Note: See the letter written to him by Aurelian, bishop of Arles, below in the Appendix, and Fortunatus, book II, poem 12. Marius, bishop of Avenches, and other authors call him “the Great.” His greatness of spirit was such that, unable to tolerate the vanity of the emperor Justinian, who had himself styled “Frankish” in his titles as though he had conquered the Franks, he prepared an expedition to the East so that, after subjugating the empire and capturing the royal city of Constantinople, he might avenge the injury done to his people. Prevented by death, however, he left the enterprise unfinished. Agathias, a Greek author of that period, reports this in book I of his *History*.].

### XXVI

When Deuteria saw that her daughter had grown fully mature, she feared that the king, desiring her, might take her for himself. She therefore placed the girl in a cart, yoked it to untamed oxen, and hurled her from a bridge; the girl died in the river itself. This happened at the city of Verdun.

### XXVII

When seven years had already passed since Theudebert had been betrothed to Uvisigard, and he refused to marry her because of Deuteria, the assembled Franks became extremely indignant with him, asking why he was abandoning his betrothed.

Then, moved by this pressure, he left Deuteria—by whom he had a small son named Theodobald [Note: Bell. and Corb. have this form; the others have *Theodovaldus*.]—and took Uvisigard as his wife. He did not have her long, however: when she died, he took another wife. He never again took Deuteria.

### XXVIII

Childebert and Theudebert assembled an army and prepared to march against Chlothacharius. When Chlothacharius heard this, believing himself unable to withstand their army, he fled into a forest [Note: The author who wrote the *Deeds of the Franks* under King Theuderic gives the name of the forest in these words: “He fled into the forest of Arelaunus and made barricades.” Some printed and manuscript copies incorrectly have *Aurelianus* for *Arelaunus*, which misled Aimoinus, who thought that *combros*, that is, the cutting down of trees in forests, was the name of some village in the district of Orléans. The forest of Arelaunus will be discussed below, at chapter 24 of Fredegar’s *Chronicle*.] and made great barricades in those woods, placing all his hope in God’s mercy.

When Queen Chrotechildis heard this, she went to the tomb of the blessed Martin, prostrated herself there in prayer, and kept vigil throughout the night, praying that civil war might not arise between her sons.

When the two kings arrived with their armies and surrounded Chlothacharius, intending to kill him the following day, a storm arose at dawn in the place where they had gathered. It tore down the tents, scattered the possessions, and overturned everything; lightning mixed with thunder and hailstones descended upon them.

They themselves fell face-first upon the ground, which had been covered with hail, and were violently beaten by the falling stones.
