No covering remained for them except their shields, for they were especially afraid of being burned by the heavenly fires. Their horses also [Al. *their horsemen*] were scattered so widely that scarcely one could be found every twenty stadia; many of them were not found at all.

Then, struck by the stones and prostrate upon the ground, as we have said, they did penance and begged God’s forgiveness because they had wished to undertake such an act against their own blood.

But not a single drop of rain fell upon Chlothacharius, nor was any sound of thunder heard. They did not even feel the breath of any wind in that place. They therefore sent messengers to him and asked for peace and reconciliation. When peace was granted, they returned to their own territories. No one should doubt that this was a miracle of the blessed Martin, obtained by Queen Chrotechildis.

### XXIX

Afterward King Childebert went to Spain. When he entered it with Chlothacharius, they surrounded and besieged the city of Zaragoza with their army.

But the inhabitants turned to God with such humility that, clothed in hair shirts and abstaining from food and drink, they circled the city walls while singing psalms with the tunic of the blessed martyr Vincent. The women, too, wearing black cloaks, with their hair loosened and ashes placed upon them, followed weeping, so that one would have thought they were mourning at the funerals of men.

Thus that entire place placed its hope in the Lord’s mercy [Note: The Bell. and Regm. manuscripts, together with most printed editions, have “placed it with the Lord of mercy.” Boch. has “the merciful Lord.”], so that it was said that the fast of the Ninevites was being celebrated there. It was thought that nothing else could be done except to bend divine mercy through their prayers.

Those who were besieging the city did not know what the besieged were doing. When they saw them circling the walls in this manner, they thought that they were practicing some kind of magic. They seized a peasant from the city and asked him what this action meant.

He replied:

> “They are carrying the tunic of the blessed Vincent, and with it they are praying that the Lord may have mercy on them.”

Fearing this, the besiegers withdrew from the city. Nevertheless, after acquiring a large part of Spain, they returned to Gaul with great spoils [Note: The anonymous author who wrote the *Deeds of the Franks* under King Theuderic reports that Childebert summoned the city’s bishop and asked him for something from the relics of the blessed Vincent. “He gave him,” he says, “his stole. Then, having acquired [the territory], etc.” When Childebert returned to Paris, he built a church in honor of the blessed martyr Vincent. This occasioned the construction of the celebrated basilica, also called Holy Cross in Fortunatus’s book on the *Life of Saint Germanus*. It later became the burial place of our kings and of princes of the royal line, as Gregory often records. It is now known by the name of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and will be mentioned more than once below. Victor of Tunnuna, in his account of this expedition, does not disagree with Gregory. Later Spanish authors, however, write that on this occasion a great defeat was inflicted upon the Franks by the commander Theudisclus. See Cointius under the year 542.].

### XXX

After Amalaric, a king named Theoda [Al. *Theuda*] was appointed in Spain. When he was killed, they raised Theudegisel to the kingship. While he was dining with his friends and was in high spirits, suddenly, after the lights had been extinguished during the meal [Note: Bell. and Corb. have this reading; the others, together with the printed edition, have: “after the candles had suddenly been extinguished during the meal,” and so forth. The bishops of Spain attempted to abolish this most wicked license for killing kings through various councils, as Cointius observed under the year 584.], he was struck down by his enemies with a sword and died. After him Agila took the kingdom.

The Goths had adopted this detestable custom: if one of their kings displeased them, they attacked him with the sword, and whoever pleased them, they set up as king.

### XXXI

Since Theodoric, king of Italy [Note: Theodoric, surnamed the Great, king of the Ostrogoths, died during the consulship of Olybrius, according to Marius—that is, in the year 526. By his marriage to Audofleda, the sister of Chlodovech, not his daughter as some maintain, he had Amalasuntha, famous among the writers of that age. She married Eutharic, a noble prince of the illustrious Amal line. After the death of both her father and her husband, she assumed the guardianship of her son Athanagild, who was not yet capable of administering the kingdom, and after his death arranged for the scepter to pass to Theodahad, or Theodatus, who belonged to the royal line. Forgetful of the favor he had received, he forced Amalasuntha into exile on an island in Lake Bolsena and shortly afterward ordered her to be strangled. Justinian made war upon the Goths under the pretext of avenging her death. Procopius and other authors describe this war at greater length, and in the end it proved fatal to the Goths. From this it is clear how far Gregory departed from the truth in this chapter, which is nevertheless preserved in full in all the manuscripts and printed editions.], had married the sister of King Chlodovech, he died leaving behind a young daughter with his wife.

When the girl had grown up, she abandoned her mother’s advice—for her mother was arranging a royal son for her—and, in the frivolity of her mind, took a slave named Traguilan [Note: Colb. and some editions have *Trauvillanem*; Bell. has *Traquillanem*; Regm. has *Straguilonem*. See Fredegar, chapter 44.] and fled with him to a city where she could find protection.

Her mother was extremely angry with her and urged her not to continue humiliating her noble lineage, but to dismiss the slave and marry a man of royal birth like herself, whom her mother had chosen for her. She refused absolutely to agree.

Her mother then, still raging against her, raised an army. When they came upon them, they killed Traguilan with the sword, beat the girl, and brought her back to her mother’s house.

They were living under the Arian sect. Since it was their custom that, when they came to the altar, the king should receive communion from one chalice and the lesser people from another [Note: In the eighth century this custom still prevailed in the Roman Church: communion was given to everyone from a single chalice, as may be gathered from the ninth letter of Gregory II to Saint Boniface of Mainz, where the pope writes that it was not appropriate to place two or three chalices on the altar when the solemnities of Mass were being celebrated.], she placed poison in the chalice from which her mother was to receive communion.

After the mother had drunk from it, she died immediately. There is no doubt that such an evil deed came from the devil’s side.

What will those wretched heretics say in reply to this, so as to explain how the enemy can have a place in their *Holy* [Note: All the manuscripts except Bell. have *Sancta*. Bell. initially has *Scam*, while another hand has *sectam*; the first edition has that reading as well. The word *Sancta* should be retained, since it refers to the sacred Eucharist, here under one species. See Mabillon’s preliminary commentary on the *Roman Order* in volume II of the *Museum Italicum*.] sacrament?

But we, confessing the Trinity in one equality and one omnipotence, even if we drink something deadly in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, the true and incorruptible God, will suffer no harm.

The Italians, therefore, enraged against this woman, invited King Theodahad of Tuscany and set him up as their king. When he learned what this harlot had done—how, because of the slave she had taken, she had become a parricide against her own mother—he had a bath heated to a fierce temperature and ordered her to be shut inside it with a young girl.

Without delay, entering amid the intense heat, she collapsed upon the floor, died, and was consumed.

When her kinsmen, Kings Childebert and Chlothacharius, as well as Theudebert, learned this, and learned that she had been killed by so shameful a punishment, they sent an embassy to Theodahad, reproaching him for her death and saying:

> “Unless you settle with us what you have done, we shall take away your kingdom and condemn you to a similar punishment.”

Then, fearing them, he sent them fifty thousand gold pieces [Note: Theodatus did not give money to the Frankish kings on the occasion described here, which is fictional, as we have said. He had nevertheless promised them a huge sum, together with Provence and the other regions that the Ostrogoths possessed in Gaul, in order to obtain their aid against Justinian. While the matter was still unfinished, Vitiges succeeded Theodatus and not only handed over to the Franks the money and territories that had been promised, but also subjected to their rule the Alamanni who, after the battle of Tolbiac, had fled to Italy and received settlements from Theodoric, as Agathias writes.].

Childebert, however, who was always envious and crafty toward King Chlothacharius, joined with his nephew Theudebert. Dividing this gold between themselves, they refused to give any of it to King Chlothacharius. He therefore attacked the treasures of Chlodomer and took from them much more than they had defrauded him of.

### XXXII

Theudebert went to Italy [Note: Marius likewise records this under the year 539, when Apio was consul. Procopius gives a fuller account of this war and accuses the Franks of violating their oath: after accepting embassies and gifts from Justinian, they nevertheless joined the Goths; or rather, while the Goths and Romans were fighting one another, the Franks, hostile to both sides, plundered and invaded the greater part of Italy.].

He acquired much there. But because those regions are said to be unhealthy, his army was afflicted by various fevers and collapsed. Many of his men died in those places.

Seeing this, Theudebert returned from there, carrying many spoils himself or having them carried by his men. It is said, however, that at that time he reached the city of Pavia, where he again sent Buccellinus [Note: Reg. and nearly all the printed editions have *Buccilenus*. Procopius and Agathias call him Butilinus. He was an Alemannian by birth. Since Franks and Alemanni were mixed together in his army, and most of the latter were not yet Christians or were still devoted to various superstitions, Procopius frequently writes against Frankish customs. Agathias, book I, is much fairer, saying: “For the Franks are not savage like many of the barbarians, etc. They are Christians of the most orthodox beliefs, etc.”].

After Buccellinus had conquered that lesser Italy [Note: Gregory calls Liguria and Venetia “lesser Italy,” as Valesius observes in book VIII of his *History of the Franks*.] and reduced it under the authority of the aforementioned king, he sought the greater Italy. There he fought many times against Belisarius [Note: The printed editions and the Regm. manuscript have this form once. Other manuscripts, including the oldest, always have *Belsuarius*. The famous Belisarius is intended, and it would be superfluous to say more about him or about the eunuch Narses.], winning the victory.

When the emperor saw that Belisarius was being defeated repeatedly, he removed him and appointed Narses in his place. He made Belisarius master of the household, as though restoring him to the humbler office he had held previously.

Buccellinus fought great battles against Narses. After conquering all Italy, he extended his dominion as far as the sea. He sent great treasures from Italy to Theudebert. When Narses brought this to the emperor’s attention, the emperor, hiring foreign troops for money, sent reinforcements to Narses. Afterward he engaged in battle, was defeated, and withdrew.

Afterward Buccellinus occupied Sicily and, exacting tribute from it, sent it to the king. He was very fortunate in these undertakings.

### XXXIII

At that time Asteriolus [Note: Reg. has *Etteriolus* once and then *Atteriolus*. Secundinus appears to be the man whom Jonas, in book II, chapter 1, of the *Life of Saint John of Réomay*, says was divinely punished for scorning a letter from John, abbot of Réomay; there Secundinus is called a patrician.] and Secundinus were held in high regard by the king. Both were wise and trained in rhetorical learning.

Secundinus was often sent by the king on embassies to the emperor, and because of this he had acquired an inflated sense of pride and undertook various actions contrary to reason. For this reason a bitter quarrel arose between him and Asteriolus. It proceeded so far that, forgetting the verbal accusations between them, they tore at one another with their own hands [Note: Thus Corb. and Bellov. The others, together with the printed editions, have “they beat one another.”].

When the king had reconciled the matter and Secundinus was still puffed up over his own violence [Note: The same manuscripts, together with Bec., Reg., Regm., and Colb., have *tumuerat*. The printed editions have *timeret*, “was afraid.”], another dispute arose between them [Al. *contentio*, “conflict”].

The king took Secundinus’s side and handed Asteriolus over to his power. Asteriolus was greatly humiliated and removed from office, but through Queen Uvisigard he was restored. After she died, Secundinus rose against him again and killed him.

Asteriolus left behind a son. When the son grew up and reached adulthood, he began to seek revenge for the wrong done to his father. Secundinus, terrified, fled from estate to estate before him. When he saw that, with his pursuer close at hand, he could no longer escape, he killed himself with poison, as is said, so as not to fall into the hands of his enemy.

### XXXIV

Desideratus, bishop of Verdun [Note: He succeeded Saint Vitonus and signed the Council of Clermont in 535 and the Fifth Council of Orléans in 549. He died in 550. Wasseburg calls him a saint.], had suffered many injuries at the hands of King Theuderic. After enduring many calamities, losses, and hardships, he had at last, by the Lord’s command, returned to his own freedom and, as we have said, obtained the episcopate in the city of Verdun.

Seeing that its inhabitants were extremely poor and destitute, he grieved for them. Since Theuderic had left him dispossessed of his own property and he had nothing of his own with which to comfort them, he observed the goodness and clemency that King Theudebert showed toward everyone and sent an embassy to him, saying:

> “The fame of your goodness is spread throughout the whole world, for your generosity is so great that you provide assistance even to those who do not ask. I ask that, if your mercy possesses any money, you lend it to us so that we may relieve our fellow citizens. When those conducting business have returned an undertaking in our city, as the other cities possess, we shall repay your money with lawful interest.”

Moved by compassion, Theudebert then lent him seven thousand gold pieces. Desideratus distributed the money through his fellow citizens. By conducting business with it, they became wealthy and remain prosperous to this day.

When the bishop offered the king the money owed, the king replied:

> “I have no need to receive it. It is enough for me that, through your administration—or through my generosity—the poor who were oppressed by poverty have been relieved.”

He demanded nothing and thus made the aforementioned citizens wealthy.

### XXXV

After the aforementioned bishop had died in the city just mentioned, a certain Agericus, one of its citizens, was appointed to his see.

His son Siagrius [Note: Reg., Colb., and Bad. have *Siacrius*. Below, for *Sirivaldo*, some printed and manuscript copies have *Sirivuldo*. Siagrius was the son of Desideratus, and he avenged the injuries mentioned in the preceding chapter, which his father had suffered under Theuderic. More about Agericus will be found below.] remembered the injuries inflicted upon his father—how he had been accused before King Theuderic by Sirivald and not only stripped of his property but also subjected to punishments—and he attacked Sirivald with an armed force and killed him in this manner.

At dawn, when a dense fog prevailed and one could scarcely yet discern anything through the darkness as it began to break, he came to Sirivald’s estate in the territory of Dijon, called Floriacum [Note: A village on the river Ouche in the diocese of Langres, commonly called Florey. It belongs to the monastery of Saint Marcellus at Chalon.].

One of his companions came out of the house. Thinking that he was Sirivald, they killed him. As they were returning [Note: Regm. has “as they rejoiced.”], as though they had won a victory over their enemy, one of the household told them that they had not killed their lord but a subordinate.

They returned and searched for him. When they found the small cell in which he was accustomed to sleep, they attacked it. They fought for a very long time at its entrance but could not overcome him. Then, breaking through the wall on one side, they entered and killed him with the sword.

He was killed after Theuderic’s death.

### XXXVI

After these events, King Theudebert began to fall ill. The physicians devoted great efforts to him, but nothing helped, because the Lord was already ordering him to be called away. After suffering from the illness for a very long time, he finally succumbed to it and gave up his spirit.

The Franks, however, hated Parthenius intensely because he had imposed the aforementioned king’s taxes upon them. They began to pursue him. Seeing himself in danger, he fled from the city and earnestly begged two bishops to escort him to the city of Trier [Col. 0268A] and to suppress the uprising of the enraged people by their preaching.

While they were on their way, Parthenius was lying in his bed one night when suddenly, in a dream, he uttered a loud cry, saying:

> “Alas, alas! Help, those who are here, and bring aid to one who is perishing!”

Those present were awakened by the cry and asked what had happened. He replied:

> “My friend Ausanius and his wife Papianilla [Note: Colb. has “Papia, his wife,” but incorrectly; the following makes clear that Papianilla was Parthenius’s own wife, whom he had killed because he was consumed by jealousy], whom I once killed, were summoning me to judgment, saying: ‘Come to give an account, because you are to plead your case with us before the Lord.’”

Driven by jealousy, he had killed an innocent wife and a friend several years earlier.

When the bishops reached the aforementioned city and found themselves unable to withstand the uproar of the raging people, they wished to hide Parthenius in the church. They placed him in a chest and spread over it the vestments used for the church.

The people entered and searched every corner of the church. Finding nothing, they went out in anger. Then one of them, speaking from suspicion, said:

> “There is the chest in which our enemy has not been sought.”

When the custodians said that it contained nothing except the church’s ornaments, the people demanded the key, saying:

> “Unless you unlock it immediately, we ourselves will break it open.”

At last the chest was unlocked. They removed the linens, dragged out the man they found inside, and applauded, saying:

> “God has delivered our enemy into our hands.”

They beat him with their fists and spat upon him [Note: Thus the manuscripts; most printed editions have *perungentes*, “anointing” or “smearing.”]. They tied his hands behind his back and stoned him against a pillar.

He was extremely gluttonous at table. But whatever he ate, he digested rapidly by taking aloe, so that he could be moved more quickly to eat; he also publicly emitted the sounds of his belly without any regard for the dignity of those listening.

Thus he met his end and died.

### XXXVII

That year brought a severe winter, harsher than usual [Note: This is a Gallic expression, found in all the manuscripts except Bec., which, together with the printed edition, has: “There was a severe and harsher winter.”], so that torrents, bound by frost, provided people with a passable road just like the rest of the ground.

Birds, too, overcome by the cold or hunger, could be caught by hand without any human trickery, since the snows were so deep.

From the death of Chlodovech to the death of Theudebert, thirty-seven years are reckoned [Note: Col. has thirty-six.].

After Theudebert died in the fourteenth year of his reign, his son Theodobald [Note: Bec. has this form; the others have *Theodovaldus*. See above, chapter 27.] reigned in his place.

**The Chapters of Book Four Begin**

[Col. 0269]

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0269]

## I

Accordingly, Queen Chrothechildis, full of days and endowed with good works, died near the city of Tours, during the episcopate of Injuriosus. She was carried to Paris with great psalmody [Note: Thus all the manuscripts; except Reg. which has *psallentium chloro*, and Bec., together with the printed edition, *psallentium praeconio*. The feast of Saint Chlotildis is celebrated on 3 June. Her Life was published from a manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in the *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Benedictini*, volume II, under the year 545. She must have died approximately in that year according to Cointius’s reckoning, if Injuriosus’s death is to be assigned to the year 546], and was buried by her sons, Kings Childebertus and Chlothacharius, in the sanctuary of the basilica of Saint Peter, beside King Chlodovechus. For she herself had built that basilica [Note: The basilica of Saint Peter in Paris, where the monastic order flourished, is said to have been built by her in the Life of Saint Balthildis. Bell., *S. Genoveva*. Thus the ancients wrote. See Mabillon, *Gallican Liturgy*, book II, §16], and in it the most blessed Genovefa was also buried.

## II

Finally, King Chlothacharius had ordered that all the churches of his kingdom should pay a third of their revenues into the treasury. Although all the bishops consented and signed, unwillingly, blessed Injuriosus courageously rejected the measure and disdained to sign, saying:

“If you wish to take away God’s property, the Lord will quickly take away your kingdom; for it is unjust that the poor, whom you ought to feed from your granary, should have your granaries filled from their support.”

Angry with the king, he departed without bidding him farewell. Then the king, moved and also fearing the power of blessed Martin, sent after him with gifts, begging pardon and condemning what he had done, while at the same time asking him to pray to Saint Martin the bishop for him.

## III

King Chlothacharius himself had seven sons by different women: by Ingundis, Guntharius, Childericus, Charibertus, Guntchramnus, Sigibertus, and a daughter, Chlotsindis; by Aregundis, Ingundis’s sister, he had Chilpericus; and by Chunsena [Col. 0271B] he had Chramnus.

Let us explain why he took his wife’s sister. After he had taken Ingundis in marriage and loved her with an exclusive affection, he received this request from her:

“My lord has done with his servant what pleased him and has admitted me to his bed. Now, to complete my reward, let my lord the king hear what his handmaid suggests. I beg you to deign to arrange for my sister, your servant, a suitable and prosperous husband [Note: That is, a wealthy one. Reg. and the printed editions have *habilem*, ‘suitable’], so that I may not be humbled but rather, being exalted, may serve you more faithfully.”

When he heard this—for he was exceedingly lustful—he was inflamed with love for Aregundis. He went to the estate where she was staying [Italian: “he goes”], and joined her to himself in marriage. After taking her, he returned to Ingundis and said:

“I have considered how to fulfill that reward which your sweetness requested of me. In seeking a wealthy and wise man whom I ought to join to your sister, I found no one better than myself. Know, therefore, that I have taken her as my wife; I do not believe this will displease you.”

But she replied:

“Let my lord do what seems good in his eyes; only let your servant live with the king’s favor.”

Guntharius, Chramnus, and Childericus died while their father was still alive. We shall write later about Chramnus’s end.

Alboinus, king of the Langobards [Note: Corb. has *Albuenus*, Bell. *Alboenus*. Paulus gives a fuller account of him in books I and II of *The Deeds of the Langobards*. Blessed Nicetius, bishop of Trier, wrote to Chlotsindis; we shall present his letter in the Appendix], also took Chlotsindis, the king’s daughter, as his wife.

Bishop Injuriosus of the city of Tours died in the seventeenth year of his episcopate. Baudinus, formerly one of King Chlothacharius’s household, succeeded him, the sixteenth bishop after the death of blessed Martin.

## IV

Chanao, count of the Britons, killed three of his brothers. Wishing also to kill Macliavus, he seized him, loaded him with chains, and kept him in prison; but Macliavus was saved from death through Felix, bishop of Nantes. Afterward he swore to his brother that he would be faithful to him; but, I do not know by what accident, he tried to break his oath. When Chanao perceived this, he again pursued him.

Seeing that he could not escape, Macliavus fled to another count of that region, named Chonomor [Note: Regm. has *Clonomor*. He is discussed by the author of the Life of Saint Gildas, found in Surius, in Bollandus under 19 January, and in the first Benedictine century].

When Chonomor perceived that Macliavus’s pursuers were approaching, he hid him underground in a small chamber, constructing a mound above it in the customary fashion and leaving him a small opening through which he could draw breath. When his pursuers arrived, they said:

“Look: Macliavus lies here dead and buried.”

Hearing this, they rejoiced, drank upon the mound, and reported to Chanao that Macliavus was dead. When Chanao heard it, he took possession of Macliavus’s entire kingdom. For the Britons had always been under Frankish authority after the death of King Chlodovechus, and they were called counts rather than kings [Note: Valesius discusses at length, *Frankish History*, book VI, pp. 281 ff., whether the Britons had their own kings and at what time. He reports that they crossed from greater Britain into Armorica, or Third Lyons, under the emperor Placidius Valentinianus, subdued the inhabitants, and imposed their own laws and name upon the region. Yet he thinks it possible to question whether the region obeyed the Frankish kings, since it is clear that it always existed under its own princes, whom various writers called at times counts, at times dukes, and sometimes even kings. Writers commonly used the name “kingdom” for the territory of the Britons, as did Gregory himself here and elsewhere. Indeed, the princes of the Britons often waged war against the Franks, always used their own laws, and lived under hereditary rulers, whereas in other regions counts or dukes were frequently changed at the will of our kings. This is said in defense of royal dignity among the Britons. Others oppose Gregory’s passage, which we are explaining, and the authority of other ancient writers, who explicitly assert that the Britons obeyed the Frankish kings. After weighing these and the other passages of ancient authors which Valesius discusses more fully, he concludes that, although the Britons were often subdued by arms, they nevertheless never submitted, by any definite acknowledgment of sovereignty, either to the Merovingian family or to the Carolingian kings of the Franks].

Macliavus, rising from underground, went to the city of Vannes, where he was tonsured and ordained bishop. After Chanao died, however, he apostatized; letting his hair grow, he took both the kingdom of his brother and the wife whom he had left after entering the clergy. The bishops excommunicated him. We shall write below what kind of death he suffered (book V, chapter 16).

Bishop Baudinus died in the sixth year of his episcopate. The abbot Guntharius was appointed in his place, the seventeenth bishop after the passing of Saint Martin.

## V

Finally [Note: This chapter is absent from Corb., Bell., Colb., and Reg. Saint Gallus’s Life is found among the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 6], after blessed Quintianus, as we stated above, had departed this world, Saint Gallus was appointed to his see with the king’s assistance.

During his time, when that plague which they call the bubonic plague [Note: Thus it was called because, when an ulcer arose in the groin or armpit, it killed in the manner of a serpent] raged through various regions and was then especially devastating the province of Arles, Saint Gallus was anxious not so much for himself as for his people. Since he prayed to the Lord day and night that he might not, while alive, see his people ravaged, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a nocturnal vision. The angel’s hair and clothing were white like snow, and he said to him:

“You do well, O priest, to pray thus to the Lord for your people, for your prayer has been heard. Behold, you will be delivered from this disease together with your people, and while you live no one in this region will perish in this devastation. But do not be afraid now; after eight years, be afraid.”

Thus it became clear that after those years he would depart from this world.

When he awoke, he gave thanks to God for this consolation, because God had deigned to strengthen him through a heavenly messenger. He instituted the Rogation observances, so that in the middle of Lent the people would come on foot, singing psalms, to the basilica of the blessed martyr Julianus. The distance on this journey is approximately 360 stadia [Note: Brivate is about twelve leagues from the city of Clermont].

At that time, during a sudden vision, the walls of houses and churches also seemed to be marked with signs. For this reason the peasants called this inscription “Tau.”

When, as we said, the plague was consuming other regions, it did not reach the city of Arvernia, through the intercession of Saint Gallus’s prayer. I therefore consider it no small grace that he deserved this: that, while appointed shepherd, he did not see his sheep devoured, because the Lord defended them.

When he had departed this world and, after being washed, had been carried into the church, Cato the presbyter immediately received praise from the clergy concerning the episcopate. He took control of all the church’s property as though he were already bishop. He removed the administrators [Note: From this passage one may understand the office of the *ordinatores*. Bertefridus, bishop of Amiens, in the privilege of Corbie, forbids any bishop among his successors, or archdeacon, or any administrator of the church of Amiens, to approach the monastery mentioned above or presume to do so unless invited by the abbot], rejected the ministers, and arranged everything himself.

## VI

The bishops [Note: This chapter is absent from Bell., Corb., Colb., and Reg.] who had come to bury Saint Gallus, after they had buried him, said to the presbyter Cato:

“We see that the greater part of the people has chosen you. Come, consent to us, and we shall bless and consecrate you to the episcopate. The king is a child; and if any fault is charged against you, we shall take you under our protection and, together with the nobles and leading men of King Theodobaldus’s realm, act so that no injury may be brought upon you. Trust us so fully that we may stand surety for you: even if some loss should occur, we shall repay everything from our own resources.”

But he, puffed up with the high-heeled buskin of vain glory, said:

“You know—for rumor has spread it—that from the beginning of my life I have always lived religiously, devoted myself to fasts, delighted in almsgiving, frequently kept prolonged vigils, and persevered in continuous psalmody through regular night watches. My Lord God does not permit me to be deprived of this ordination, since I have rendered him such service. I have always obtained the grades of the clergy according to canonical institution. I was a lector for ten years; I served in the office of subdeacon for five years; I was devoted to the diaconate for fifteen years; and I have now enjoyed the honor of the presbyterate for twenty years. What remains for me now except to receive the episcopate, which faithful service has earned? Return, therefore, to your cities and perform whatever belongs to your responsibilities; for I shall canonically assume this honor.”

Hearing this, the bishops departed, cursing his vain glory.

## VII

When he had been elected to the episcopate with the consent of the clergy, although he had not yet been ordained and was already presiding over everyone, he began to direct various threats against the archdeacon Cautinus, saying:

“I shall remove you; I shall humble you; I shall order many deaths to be inflicted upon you.”

Cautinus replied:

“I desire your favor, most gracious lord. If I deserve it, I shall render you one service. Without any effort or deceit on your part, I shall go to the king and obtain the episcopate for you, asking nothing except that I may earn your favor.”

But Cato, suspecting that Cautinus wished to mock him, despised these words greatly.

When Cautinus saw himself being humiliated and subjected to accusation, he feigned illness, left the city during the night, and went to King Theodobaldus, announcing the death of Saint Gallus. When the king and those with him heard this, they summoned priests to the city of Metz, and Cautinus the archdeacon was ordained bishop.

When the messengers of the presbyter Cato arrived, Cautinus was already bishop. Then, by the king’s command, the clergy were handed over to him, as were all the things they had brought from the church’s property. Bishops and chamberlains who were to accompany him were appointed, and they sent him to the Arvernians.

He was gladly received by the clergy and citizens and was given as bishop to the Arvernians. Later great enmity arose between him and the presbyter Cato, because no one could ever bend Cato to submit to his bishop. A division also arose among the clergy: some were subject to Bishop Cautinus, others to the presbyter Cato. This was their greatest detriment.

When Bishop Cautinus saw that Cato could in no way be bent to submit to him, he took away all the church’s property from him, his friends, and everyone who supported him, leaving them empty and destitute. Yet whenever any of them turned back to him, they received again what they had lost.

## VIII

While Agilanus was reigning in Spain and oppressing the people under the most grievous yoke of his rule, the emperor’s army entered Spain and seized several cities. After Agilanus was killed, Athanagildus received the kingdom [Note: Regm., together with Bad., incorrectly has *Athanagel dux*, “the duke Athanagel.” With the assistance of the patrician Liberius, whom Justinian had sent to Spain, he defeated Agilanus; but afterward he labored greatly to expel the Greeks, who had occupied several cities].

Afterward Athanagildus fought many battles against that army and usually defeated them, partly taking from their power the cities which they had wrongfully occupied.

## IX

When Theodobaldus had reached adulthood, he took Uvaldetrada as his wife [Note: Thus Corb., Bell., Bec., and Reg.; others have *Waldetrudam* or *Uldotradam*. She was the second daughter of Wacho, king of the Langobards, and sister of Wisegardis, the wife of Theodebertus. See Paulus, book I, chapter 21].

They say that Theodobaldus was of an evil disposition. Thus, being angry with someone whom he suspected concerning his affairs, he invented this fable:

“A serpent found a flask full of wine. Entering through its mouth, it greedily drank what was inside. Inflated with wine, it could not get out by the opening through which it had entered. The owner of the wine arrived, and when the serpent tried but could not escape, he said to it: ‘First disgorge what you have swallowed, and then you will be able to depart freely.’”

This fable prepared for him great fear and hatred.

Under his rule Buccellinus, after bringing all Italy back under the Frankish kingdom, was killed by Narses, Italy having been captured for the emperor’s side; and there was no one who afterward recovered it [Note: Concerning Buccellinus’s expeditions into Italy, besides other authors, one should especially read Procopius and Agathias, who wrote at length about the wars fought in Italy between Justinian and the Goths, in which the Franks repeatedly intervened. They also discuss the embassies sent by both sides for this reason. Valesius thinks that Buccellinus was killed in 554, and Hamingus, the other commander of the Frankish army, in the following year, when Leutharius, Buccellinus’s brother, died between Trent and Verona while hastening home laden with booty. These Frankish disasters are mentioned by the appendix to Marcellinus Comes, Marius in his *Chronicle*, the deacon Paulus, and other authors, though in different years. Although on that occasion the Franks entirely lost what they possessed in Italy, and no one was then sent to recover it, it is nevertheless certain that Chlothacharius later possessed something in Italy, as his son Sigibertus himself testifies below, book IX, chapter 20; and the Langobards living in Italy paid tribute to the Frankish kings, according to book X, chapter 3].

During his time we saw grapes growing on a tree which we call the elder [Note: Mor. s. has *saucum*], without any connection with vines. The flowers of those trees, which—as you know—normally produce black berries, produced grains like those of grapes.

At that time a fifth star also seemed to enter the circle of the moon, coming from the opposite side [Note: Thus Corb. and Regm.; most others have “a star of the fifth moon”; others, “the star”]. I believe these signs announced the king’s death.

He himself became very ill and could not roll himself from the waist downward [Note: Regm. has “for a long time he could not stand”; Bec. and Bell. have “could not move himself”]. Gradually wasting away, he died in the seventh year of his reign. King Chlothacharius took possession of his kingdom and took his wife Vuldetrada to his bed. But, rebuked by the priests, he abandoned her, gave her to Duke Garivaldus, and sent his son Chramnus to the Arvernians [Note: Regm. has “sending her to the Arvernians, to his son Chramnus”].

## X

That year, when the Saxons rebelled, King Chlothacharius mobilized an army against them and destroyed a great part of them. He marched through all Thuringia and devastated it because its inhabitants had given assistance to the Saxons [Note: Some manuscripts have “had furnished aid.” In place of “all Thuringia,” others have “Tournai, Thuringia.” Marius reports that the devastation of Thuringia, because it had supplied aid to the Saxons, occurred after Chlotharius’s second expedition, in the fifteenth year after the consulship of Basilius, that is, 556; he assigns the first expedition to the preceding year, in which Theodebaldus died].

## XI

When Bishop Guntharius died in the city of Tours, Cato the presbyter was, as they say, sought for the governance of the Church of Tours at the instigation of Bishop Cautinus. Accordingly, the clergy, together with Leubastes the martyrarius [Note: The Second Council of Orléans, in 533, canon 13, decreed that abbots, *martyrarii*, and others should not presume to issue *apostolia*, that is, letters of release. *Martyrarii* were so called because they presided over oratories of the martyrs. From the Angevin formula, no. 48, in volume IV of Mabillon’s *Analecta*, it may be inferred that a *martyrarius* presided over a matricula, or hospital for the poor] and the abbot, hastened with great ceremony to Arvernia.

When they had made the king’s will known to Cato, he kept them waiting for an answer for several days. Wishing to return, they said:

“Make your will known to us, so that we may know what we ought to follow; otherwise we shall return to our own people. We did not seek you of our own will, but at the king’s command.”

But he, being desirous of vain glory, gathered a crowd of the poor and ordered them to cry out in these words:

“Why do you abandon us, good father—your children, whom you have raised until now? Who will refresh us with food and drink if you depart? We beg you not to leave us, whom you have been accustomed to feed.”

Then, turning to the clergy of Tours, he said:

“You see now, dearest brothers, how this multitude of poor loves me. I cannot leave them and go with you.”

Receiving this answer, they returned to Tours.

Cato had meanwhile formed a friendship with Chramnus and received a promise from him that, if King Chlothacharius should happen to die at that time, Cato would immediately be placed over the Church after Cautinus had been expelled from the episcopate. But he who had held the see of blessed Martin in contempt did not obtain the one he desired. What David sang was fulfilled in him:

“He did not desire blessing, and it shall be far from him” (Psalm 108:18).

For he was raised up on the buskin of vanity, thinking that no one surpassed him in holiness. On one occasion he hired a woman with money to cry out in the church as though possessed, confessing that he was a great saint and beloved by God, while Bishop Cautinus was guilty of every crime and unworthy to attain the priesthood.

## XII

Finally [Note: This chapter is absent from Corb., Bell., Reg., and Colb.], after Cautinus had assumed the episcopate, he made himself such that everyone detested him. He was excessively devoted to wine, for he was often so drenched in drink that he could scarcely be carried from a banquet by four men.

As a result he became epileptic afterward; this was frequently revealed to the people. He was also so intent upon avarice that, whenever the boundaries of any property adjoined his own boundary, he considered himself ruined if he did not diminish something belonging to it. From the great he took things with quarrel and scandal; from the lesser he seized them by force. Of him and of such men our Sollius says: “He neither gave prices, because he despised them, nor accepted documents, because he had no hope” [Note: Bad. has *Solinus*, but our reading is better. The reference is to Gaius Sollius Apollinaris Sidonius. The passage cited by Gregory is found in Letter 1 of book II, addressed to Hecdicius, where he speaks of Serenatus’s vices: he invaded the property of others without offering a price because he despised them, and did not accept documents—that is, letters or deeds of sale].

At that time there was a presbyter named Anastasius, freeborn by descent, who possessed some property by documents belonging to Queen Chrotechildis, of glorious memory. The bishop repeatedly summoned him and humbly and submissively begged him to give him the queen’s documents and surrender this property to him.

But Anastasius delayed fulfilling the priest’s wish. The bishop alternately enticed him with flatteries and terrified him with threats; finally he ordered that Anastasius be brought unwillingly to the city and detained there shamelessly, and that, unless he surrendered the documents, he be abused and killed by hunger.

But Anastasius resisted with manly spirit and never handed over the documents, saying that it was better for him to waste away from hunger for a time than to leave his descendants in misery in the future.

Then, by order of the bishop, he was handed over to guards, so that unless he disclosed those documents he would be killed by hunger.

There was at the basilica of the martyr Saint Cassius [Note: Concerning this basilica, see book I, *On the Churches of Clermont*. It still exists, as Savaro notes, designated as a parish church. See above, book I, chapter 31. The Bollandists discuss Saint Cassius and his companions under 15 February, the day on which their feast is celebrated] an extremely ancient and deeply hidden crypt. In it stood a great sarcophagus of Parian marble, in which the body of a very old man appeared to have been placed.

The presbyter was buried alive in this tomb above the dead man and covered with the stone that had previously covered the sarcophagus, while guards were stationed before the entrance. But the guards, confident that he was held down by the stone, since it was winter lit a fire and, overcome by warm wine, fell asleep.

The presbyter, like a new Jonah, as though from the belly of the underworld, pleaded for the Lord’s mercy from inside the sealed tomb. Since the sarcophagus was spacious, as we have said, although he could not turn his whole body, he could freely extend his hands toward whichever side he wished.

As he himself was accustomed to relate, a deadly stench issued from the dead bones. It shook not only his external senses but also the inward organs. When he blocked the entrance to his nostrils with his cloak, he smelled nothing evil for as long as he could hold his breath. But whenever he thought he was nearly suffocating, he moved the cloak slightly away from his mouth and breathed in the pestilential odor not only through his mouth and nostrils but also, so to speak, through his very ears.

What more need be said? When, as I believe, the divine mercy took pity on him, he stretched his right hand toward the side of the sarcophagus and found a bar which, when the covering had shifted, had remained between it and the rim of the tomb. Moving it little by little, he perceived, with God’s help, that the stone was being displaced.

When it had been moved far enough for the presbyter to thrust his head out, he widened the opening so that he could more freely escape with his whole body.

Meanwhile, the darkness of night was covering the day, though it had not yet spread everywhere. He went toward another entrance of the crypt. It was secured with very strong bolts and firm locks, but it had not been smoothed so tightly that a person could not see between the boards.

The presbyter leaned his head toward the opening and noticed a man passing along the road. Although his voice was faint, he called to him. The man heard him, and without delay, holding an axe, cut through the wooden stakes that held the bolts and opened the way for the presbyter.

The presbyter rose by night and went home, earnestly begging the man not to tell anyone anything about him.

Entering his own house, he found the documents which the aforesaid queen had given him, and carried them to King Chlothacharius, explaining how he had been handed over alive to burial by his bishop.

Everyone was astonished, saying that neither Nero nor Herod had ever committed such a crime: that a living man should be confined in a tomb. Bishop Cautinus came before King Chlothacharius; but when the presbyter accused him, he withdrew defeated and confounded.

The presbyter, having received royal orders, defended and possessed his property as he pleased and left it to his descendants.

In Cautinus there was nothing holy and nothing worthy of regard. He was wholly ignorant of every kind of writing, ecclesiastical as well as secular. He was very dear and submissive to the Jews—not out of concern for salvation, as a shepherd’s care ought to be, but in order to purchase spices. While he flattered them and they made themselves plainly known as flatterers, they sold them to him at a price greater than their value [Note: Chesn. and Freh. have *venumdabat*, “he sold”; the plural reading is preferable].

### XIII

Chramnus [Note: This chapter is absent from the Regius and Colbertinus manuscripts. Compare it with chapter 66 of Book I, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*.] was residing at that time at Arvernum. Many matters were then being handled by him irrationally, and for this reason he was hastened from the world [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions instead have: “he was removed more quickly.”]; for the people were cursing him greatly. He loved no one from whom he could receive good and useful advice; instead, after gathering worthless young men of unstable character, he loved only them [Note: Thus the same manuscripts. The printed editions read: “He cherished and loved worthless persons, unstable in youthful age.”], listening to their counsel, so that, by issuing orders, he commanded the daughters of senators to be dragged away in their very sight [Note: Thus the Corbeiensis. Other manuscripts have: “he ordered them to be forcibly taken away in their sight.” The printed edition reads: “having issued predatory orders,” or “giving them to robbers, he ordered them to be forcibly taken away,” and so forth. The Firminus mentioned here belonged to the noble family of the Firmini, who were praetorian prefects and patricians, as is clear from the Novels of Valentinian and Marcian. Savaro thinks that they originated among the Arverni, in his notes on Sidonius, Letter 2 of Book IX, which is addressed to Firminus.].

He drove Firminus, who had been gravely wronged, from the office of count of the city, and substituted Salustius, son of Evodius [Alternative reading: Euvodius]. But Firminus went with his mother-in-law to a church. It was then the days of Lent; and Bishop Cautinus had decided to go to the diocese of Brivas [Note: Here *diocese* designates a district, for Brivas, where the celebrated church of Saint Julian is located, belonged to the diocese of Arvernum. Elsewhere this word sometimes designates a province subject to metropolitan jurisdiction, and sometimes several provinces subject to a patriarch, primate, or exarch. It also had a place in the civil administration of the state. Hence “the diocese of the East,” and so forth. Sometimes it designates a village or district, as here and below in Book VII, chapter 38; now it is commonly used for the jurisdiction of a bishop, which medieval writers frequently called a parish. See Cangius’s *Glossary* and Sirmond on Letter 16 of Book IX of Sidonius. The institution of the Litanies, which Gregory mentions here, is found above in chapter 5, although that chapter is absent from four manuscripts.], singing psalms, according to the institution of Saint Gall, as we wrote above.

The bishop therefore left the city amid great weeping, fearing that he might suffer some misfortune on the journey; for King Chramnus was also directing threats against him [Note: Observe that Chramnus is here called “king,” because he was the king’s son. You will find other examples of this kind throughout Gregory.]. While he was traveling, the king sent Imnacharius and Scaptharius, chief men of his household [Note: We also find the expression “sent from the king’s side” in the final formula of Book I of Marculf. The name remains in use for papal legates sent from the Roman curia into the provinces.], saying: “Go and forcibly drag Firminus and his mother-in-law Caesaria out of the church.”

When the bishop had departed with the psalm-singing procession, as we mentioned above, those sent by Chramnus entered the church and tried to soothe Firminus and Caesaria with various deceptive conversations. But after they had wandered about the church for a very long time, talking of one thing after another, while those who had taken refuge there listened attentively to what was being said, they approached the royal doors [Note: That is, the doors. The Corbeiensis has *ad reias*. The royal doors were also the gates or screens by which the presbytery was enclosed. See Mabillon’s commentary on the *Roman Order*, no. 20, and the Orders themselves, *Museum Italicum*, volume II.] of the sacred building, which had then been opened.

Then Imnacharius and Scaptharius [Note: In the Becianus the first is once called Imnacrius, while the other is always called Captarius.] seized Firminus and Caesaria in their arms and threw them out of the church, with boys ready to receive them; they immediately sent them into exile. But on the following day, when the guards had been overcome by sleep, the two, finding themselves free, fled to the basilica of blessed Julian and were thus freed from exile. Their property, however, was confiscated to the treasury.

Bishop Cautinus, suspecting that he too would be subjected to injury, had nevertheless set out on the journey and had a saddled horse. He saw behind him men approaching on horseback, coming to meet him, and said: “Woe is me, for these are the men whom Chramnus has sent to seize me.” Mounting his horse [Alternative reading: “horseman”], leaving the psalm-singing procession, he galloped alone as far as the portico of the basilica of Saint Julian, spurring the animal with both heels, almost dead from exhaustion.

But as we relate these events, we recall Sallust’s judgment concerning those who disparage historians. He says [Note: At the beginning of his book *On the War with Catiline*]: “It seems difficult to write of deeds: first, because words must be made equal to actions; and then because most people think that the faults which you criticize have been mentioned out of malice and envy.”

But let us follow what we have begun.

### XIV

After the death of Theodobald, Chlothacharius had received the kingdom of the Franks [Note: Observe that Theodobald’s portion is here called the kingdom of the Franks. See Cointius under the year 558, where he discusses the name “France” at length and proves that the kings of each part of the kingdom of France were called kings of the Franks. He collects much material on this subject there.] and was touring it. He heard from his men that the Saxons were again boiling over with madness, rebelling against him, and refusing to pay the tribute which they had been accustomed to provide every year.

Provoked by these words, he marched against them. When he was already near their territory, the Saxons sent ambassadors to him, saying: “We are not contemptuous of you, and we do not deny the payments which we have been accustomed to render to your brothers [Note: Valesius thinks that *brother* should be read, since it could be said that the Saxons paid tribute only to Theodoric, his son Theodebert, and his grandson Theodobald, who are here called Chlothacharius’s grandsons.] and nephews; indeed, if you demand anything greater, we will pay it. We ask only one thing: let there be peace, so that your army and our people may not clash.”

When King Chlothacharius heard this, he said to his men: “These men speak well. Let us not advance against them, lest perhaps we sin against God.”

But they said: “We know them to be liars, and they will certainly not fulfill what they have promised. Let us march against them.”

Again the Saxons offered half of their property, asking for peace. King Chlothacharius said to his men: “Desist, I beg you, from these men, lest God be stirred up against us in this way.” But they did not agree.

Again the Saxons offered their clothing, livestock, and all their property, saying: “Take all these things, together with half our land. Only leave our wives and little children free, and let no war be waged between us.”

But the Franks refused to agree even to this. King Chlothacharius said to them: “Desist, I beg you, desist from this purpose. We have received no justified cause; do not go to a war in which you will be destroyed. Yet if you wish to go there of your own free will, I will not follow.”

Then, angered against King Chlothacharius, they rushed upon him, tore his tent apart, assailed him with insults, and, dragging him away by force, wanted to kill him if he delayed departing with them.

Seeing this, Chlothacharius went with them unwillingly. They joined battle, but were cut down by their adversaries in a tremendous slaughter. So great a multitude fell from both armies that it could neither be estimated nor counted.

Then Chlothacharius, greatly ashamed, asked for peace, saying that he had not come against them of his own will. Having obtained it, he returned to his own lands.

### XV

[Note: This chapter is absent from the Bellovacensis and Corbeiensis manuscripts.]

When the people of Tours heard that the king had returned from the slaughter of the Saxons, they reached an agreement [Note: A *consensus* was a public document by which the king was informed that a church had been deprived of its bishop, and was asked to permit the man chosen as his successor to be consecrated. Its form is found in Book X of Marculf, chapter 7. The *praeceptio*, mentioned at the end of this chapter, or, as it is otherwise called, the *praeceptum*, was sent by the king to the metropolitan, instructing him to ordain as bishop a man approved and chosen by the king. Its form is found in the same book, chapter 5. An *indiculus* was also sent by the king for the same purpose, as appears from formula 6 of that book. Bignonius thinks that the distinction between the *indiculus* and the *praeceptum* was that the *praeceptio* was a diploma of greater authority, signed by the king and perhaps secured by the impression of his ring, whereas the *indiculus* was a simple letter without a seal. See the Appendix on these matters.] concerning the presbyter Eufronius, and went to the king. Having submitted their petition, the king replied: “I had ordered that Presbyter Cato be ordained there. Why has our command been disregarded?”

They answered him: “We did ask him, but he refused to come.”

While they were saying this, Presbyter Cato suddenly arrived, begging the king to order that, after Cautinus had been expelled, he himself should be installed at Arvernum. When the king laughed at this, he asked again to be ordained at Tours, the place he had previously despised.

The king said to him: “I first ordered that you be consecrated to the episcopate at Tours. But, as I hear, you held that church in contempt; therefore you will be kept far from its authority.” And so he departed in confusion.

When the king inquired about Saint Eufronius, they said that he was the nephew of blessed Gregory [Note: Namely, Gregory, bishop of Langres, whom we mentioned above in Book III, chapter 19, and among the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 7, and elsewhere.].

The king replied: “This is a first and noble lineage. Let the will of God and of blessed Martin be done. Let the election be completed.” And when the royal order had been issued, Saint Eufronius was ordained bishop, the eighteenth after blessed Martin.

### XVI

Chramnus was carrying out various evil deeds at Arvernum, as we have said, always harboring hatred against Bishop Cautinus. At that time he fell gravely ill, so that his hair fell out from the severity of the fever.

He then had with him a distinguished man, conspicuous in every virtue, an Arvernian citizen named Ascovindus [Note: Thus all the manuscripts except the Becianus and the printed editions, which have *Anscovindus*.], who earnestly tried to turn him away from this wickedness, but could not.

He also had Leo of Poitiers, a grievous stimulus toward the perpetration of every evil, who, according to the interpretation of his name, was like a lion, savage in every form of greed. It is said that on one occasion he declared that the confessors of the Lord, Martin and Martial [Note: The first bishop and apostle of the Lemovices.], had left nothing useful to the rights of the treasury.

But immediately he was struck by the power of the confessors, became deaf and mute, and died out of his mind. The wretched man came to the basilica of Saint Martin at Tours, kept vigil, and gave gifts; but the saint’s accustomed power did not regard him. He returned with the very illness with which he had come.

Chramnus, having returned from Arvernum, came to the city of Poitiers. While he was residing there in great power, deceived by the counsel of evil men, he desired to cross over to his uncle Childebert, intending to lay snares for his father.

Childebert deceitfully promised to receive him, although he ought rather to have admonished him spiritually not to become his father’s enemy. Then, through secret messengers, they conspired with one another and united against Chlothacharius.

But Childebert did not remember that whenever he had acted against his brother, he had always departed in confusion.

After making this alliance, Chramnus returned to the Lemovician territory and brought under his own authority the region through which he had previously traveled in his father’s kingdom. Meanwhile the people of Arvernum were confined within the walls and were perishing miserably, oppressed by various illnesses.

King Chlothacharius sent two of his sons, Charibert and Guntchramnus, against him. They came through Arvernum and, hearing that Chramnus was in the Lemovician territory, advanced as far as the mountain called Black Mountain and found him there.

They pitched their tents and encamped opposite him, sending an embassy to demand that he return the paternal possessions which he had wrongfully seized; otherwise, they said, he should prepare a battlefield.

Although he pretended to be subject to his father, he said: “I cannot relinquish everything that I have taken possession of, but I wish to retain it under my authority, with my father’s favor.”

They asked that battle decide the matter between them. When both armies had been set in motion and had assembled for battle with a great display of arms, a storm suddenly arose with violent flashes of lightning and thunder and prevented them from fighting.

As they returned to their camps, Chramnus deceitfully announced through a stranger that their father had died. At that time, as we said above (chapters 10 and 14), war was being waged against the Saxons. The brothers, fearing the report, returned with the utmost speed to Burgundy.

Chramnus sent his army after them, came as far as the city of Chalon, and captured it by siege. From there he proceeded as far as the fortress of Dijon. When he arrived there on a Sunday, I shall tell what happened.

Saint Tetricus, the bishop, was then there, whose memory we mentioned in the preceding book [Note: Nothing concerning Saint Tetricus appears in the preceding book as we now possess it. Yet in the manuscript table of contents of the book *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 105 is entitled “On Saint Tetricus, Bishop of Langres,” although nothing about him is found in that book, either in the printed editions or the manuscripts. More about him is read in the following book, chapter 5, and in the *Book of the Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 7, where he is called the son and successor of Saint Gregory. He attended the Council of Orléans V in 549, the Council of Paris II in 555, and the council held by Piolus, presbyter of Lyon, II in 567. Fortunatus wrote his epitaph in Book IV, poem 3. His feast is celebrated on March 18. He was buried at Dijon in the church of Saint John, beside Saint Gregory.].

The clergy placed three books upon the altar—the Prophets, the Apostle, and the Gospels—and prayed to the Lord that he might reveal what would happen to Chramnus: whether success would come to him, or whether he would be able to reign, let divine power declare it. At the same time they made an agreement [Note: The Corbeiensis, Becianus, and Bellovacensis have *conhibentiam*.] that each should read at Mass whatever passage he first opened in his book.

When the first book, that of the Prophets, was opened, they found:

> “I will remove its hedge, and it shall be laid waste; instead of producing grapes, it produced wild grapes” (Isaiah 5:5, 2).

When the book of the Apostle was opened, they found:

> “For you yourselves know very well, brothers, that the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” [Note: Thus the Corbeiensis and Bellovacensis. The others, together with the printed editions, have: “in the night, thus he will come.”]. “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them, like labor pains upon a pregnant woman, and they will not escape” [Note: Here the Regius manuscript ends, although at the beginning of this book it contains a table of all its chapters and is not mutilated. Regino’s *Chronicle*, written in exactly the same hand as Gregory’s books, follows immediately.] (1 Thessalonians 5:2–3).

The Lord said through the Gospel:

> “Whoever does not hear my words will be like a foolish man who built his house upon sand: the rain descended, the rivers came, the winds blew, and they struck that house; it fell, and its ruin was great” (Matthew 7:27).

Chramnus was received into the basilicas [Note: The Colbertinus and Reginensis have “the basilica,” perhaps that of Saint Benignus or Saint John, which are now enclosed within the walls of the city.] by the priest mentioned above. After eating bread there, he proceeded to Childebert. Yet he was not permitted to enter within the walls of Dijon.

At that time King Chlothacharius was waging a vigorous war against the Saxons. For the Saxons, as was reported [Note: Thus the Corbeiensis and Bellovacensis; most of the others have “when they asserted.”], having been stirred up by Childebert and angered against the Franks in the preceding year, left their own country, entered Frankish territory, and plundered as far as the city of Divitia [Note: Thus the Corbeiensis and Bellovacensis. It is commonly said to be Deutz, near Cologne. It is strange, however, that this place should be called a city; today it is called Tuitium and is famous for its abbey, governed by Abbot Rupert. Ammianus Marcellinus mentions the people of Divitia in Books XXVI and XXVII. Here, as often above, Gregory simply calls the trans-Rhine region “France.” The Colbertinus has *Mustia*. The printed editions generally have *Nutia*.], and committed an exceedingly grievous crime.

### XVII

Then Chramnus, having already received the daughter of Wiliacharius [Note: Others, together with the Colbertinus, have *Willicharius*. He was the duke of Aquitaine; his daughter, whom Chramnus married, is called Chalda in the *Book of the Deeds of the Franks*.], approached Paris and bound King Childebert to himself by an oath of loyalty and affection, swearing that he was utterly hostile to his father.

While Chlothacharius was fighting against the Saxons, King Childebert entered the Reims region of Champagne. Hurrying as far as the city of Reims, he devastated everything with plunder and fire. For he had heard that his brother had been killed by the Saxons, and, believing that everything was being subjected to his kingdom, he seized whatever he could reach.

### XVIII

At that time Duke Austrapius, fearing Chramnus, also fled to the basilica of Saint Martin. Divine assistance did not fail him in his great tribulation.

For when Chramnus had ordered him to be so strictly confined that no one dared provide him with food, and he was guarded so closely that he was not even allowed to draw water, so that, compelled by hunger, he might leave the holy basilica of his own accord and perish, someone came and brought the half-dead man a little vessel of water to drink.

After he had accepted it, the local judge rushed up, snatched it from his hand, and poured it onto the ground. Swift divine vengeance and the power of the blessed bishop followed this act. On that very day the judge who had done this was seized by fever and died in the middle of the night; he did not live until the hour of the following day at which he had knocked the cup from the fugitive’s hand in the basilica.

After this miracle, everyone brought him whatever was necessary in great abundance.

When King Chlothacharius returned to his kingdom, Austrapius was held in high honor with him. In his time Austrapius entered the clerical order at the fortress of Sellense [Note: It is still known by its ancient name, commonly Selle or Celle, where there is an abbey of regular canons.], which lies in the diocese of Poitiers, and was ordained with the expectation that, when Bishop Pientius, who then governed the Church of Poitiers, died, Austrapius himself would succeed him.

But King Charibert changed this plan. When Bishop Pientius had departed from this life [Note: If Pientius, as Beslius observes, died at Metulum, commonly Melle, within his own diocese, Gregory’s words “at Paris” should refer to Pascentius, not Pientius. Pientius and Austrapius, mentioned here, had been entrusted with the construction of the monastery of Saint Radegund, as Baudonivia herself attests. Fortunatus dedicated to Pascentius the Life of Saint Hilary which he had written. Pientius, commonly Saint Pien, is commemorated on March 13.], Pascentius, then abbot of the basilica of Saint Hilary at the city of Paris, succeeded him by order of King Charibert.

Austrapius protested that this place should be restored to him [Note: The Reginensis has “should be given back.” The Becianus has “should be re-given.”], but his loudly proclaimed words accomplished little. He himself returned to his fortress, where a revolt of the Theifali [Note: The Teifali or Taifali were one of the barbarian peoples who flooded Gaul at the beginning of the fifth century. Some of them established settlements among the Pictones and gave their name to a village called Teifalia, which still exists under the name Tifaugia, commonly Tiffauges, between Clisson and Mortagne, on the river Sèvre. There were also pagan Taifali who, together with the Sarmatians, maintained a garrison among the Pictones, according to the *Notitia Dignitatum* of the Roman Empire. See Valesius, Book VIII of *The Frankish History*, or his discussion of the matter in the *Notitia Galliarum*.] whom he had often oppressed arose against him. Wounded by a spear, he ended his life cruelly.

The Church of Poitiers, however, recovered its dioceses.

### XIX

During the reign of King Chlothacharius [Note: This chapter is absent from the Corbeiensis and Bellovacensis; it is present in the others and is listed among the chapters of Book IV in the Regius manuscript. Saint Medard is also discussed in the book *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 95. Cointius dates his death to 545; Valesius to 560. His basilica, with a notable Benedictine monastery under the Congregation of Saint Maur, still stands near Soissons, and his tomb is visible in the underground crypt. In addition to his Life, Fortunatus wrote poem 17 of Book II about him, where he discusses the basilica completed by Sigibert.], Saint Medard, bishop of God, having completed the course of a good work and being full of days, distinguished in holiness, died.

King Chlothacharius buried him with the greatest honor at the city of Soissons and began to build a basilica over him. His son Sigibert later completed and adorned it.

At his blessed tomb we saw the fetters and chains of prisoners lying broken and shattered. They are preserved there to this day as testimony to his power.

But let us return to what came before.

### XX

King Childebert began to fall ill. After lying on a sickbed at Paris for a very long time, he died and was buried in the basilica of blessed Vincent [Note: This is the basilica called Saint-Germain-des-Prés, discussed above in Book III, chapter 29. The tomb of King Childebert is still seen in the middle of the choir, although it is not of such great antiquity. His burial is recorded in the original Usuard Martyrology on December 23; on that day his anniversary is still celebrated every year with solemn ceremony. “You will not easily find,” says Valesius in Book VIII of *The Frankish History*, “a man whose piety and concern for the highest affairs of the Church were attested by more and greater proofs than Childebert’s.” This is demonstrated by the holy places which he built, endowed, and protected; by the councils which were frequently held under his care; by the letters of Roman pontiffs and other bishops; and by the testimony of nearly all the writers of his age. Because of his piety toward divine worship, Fortunatus calls him both king and priest, and praises him repeatedly, both in the Life of Saint Germanus and in his poems. See Valesius in the work cited and other authors throughout. We shall give his Constitution against the remnants of paganism in the Appendix.], which he himself had built.

King Chlothacharius received his kingdom and treasures, while he sent Ultrogotha [Note: That is, the wife of King Childebert, together with his two daughters, Chrotberga and Chrotesinda.] and her two daughters into exile.

Chramnus was brought before his father, but afterward proved faithless. Seeing that he could not escape, he went to Britain, where he and his wife and daughters hid with Chonober, count of the Britons [Note: Others have *Coonober*; the Bellovacensis has *Chonoo*, and likewise below. The Corbeiensis has *Chonoo*. In this chapter the name is twice written *Chonober* and *Chonobro*. Above, in Book IV, chapter 4, column 144, line 20, the same Corbeiensis has *Chonoone* for *Chanaone*, although elsewhere the name is *Chanao*.].

His father-in-law Wiliacharius [Note: The Corbeiensis and Bellovacensis have “Wiliacharius the priest.” The Corbeiensis and several printed editions have *Willicharius*, as above.] fled to the basilica of Saint Martin.

Then the holy basilica was burned by Wiliacharius and his wife because of the sins of the people and the mockeries committed there—a deed which we recall with deep sorrow. The city of Tours too had already been consumed by fire the previous year, and all the churches built within it had been abandoned.

At once, by order of King Chlothacharius, the basilica of blessed Martin was covered with tin and restored with the same elegance that it had previously possessed.

Then two swarms of locusts appeared. Passing through Arvernum and the Lemovician territory [Note: The Bellovacensis has “the Lemajecinian … Romanician plain.”], they are said to have reached the plain of Romaniacum, where they engaged in a great battle among themselves and suffered enormous losses.

King Chlothacharius, roaring against Chramnus, marched with an army against him into Britain. But Chramnus did not fear to come out against his father.

When the two armies had gathered and encamped on the same field, and Chramnus had drawn up his line against his father with the Britons, night came on and brought the battle to an end.

That night Chonober, count of the Britons, said to Chramnus: “I consider it unjust that you should go out against your father. Permit me tonight to fall upon him and overthrow him together with his entire army.”

But Chramnus, as I believe, prevented by the power of God, did not permit this to happen.

In the morning, both armies were put in motion and hurried to battle against each other. King Chlothacharius went forth as a new David about to fight against his son Absalom, mourning and saying:

“Look down, Lord, from heaven, and judge my cause, for I suffer unjust injuries from my son. Look down and judge justly, and impose the judgment which you once imposed between Absalom and his father David.”

When they had joined battle, the count of the Britons turned his back and fell there.

Chramnus then fled, having ships prepared at sea. But while he was trying to rescue his wife and daughters, he was overtaken by his father’s army, captured, and bound.

When this was reported to King Chlothacharius, he ordered that Chramnus be burned with his wife and daughters. They were shut into the hut of a poor man [Note: Others have: “and he shut them into the hut of a poor woman.” Marius records that he was burned with his wife and children in the year 560.]. Chramnus was stretched out upon a bench and strangled with a neck-cloth; then the hut was set on fire over them, and he perished with his wife and daughters.

### XXI

In the fifty-first year of his reign, King Chlothacharius went with many gifts to the shrine of blessed Martin [Note: Blessed Germanus, bishop of Paris, accompanied him. On this occasion he proceeded to Poitiers to ask Radegund’s forgiveness on the king’s behalf, as Baudonivia relates in the Life of Saint Radegund. At that time he undoubtedly blessed Abbess Agnes, as is said below in Book IX, chapter 42.].

When he arrived at Tours at the tomb of the aforementioned bishop, he reviewed all the actions which he might have performed negligently and prayed with deep groaning that the blessed confessor of the Lord would ask mercy for his sins and, through his intercession, cleanse away the things he had committed irrationally.

Afterward he returned. In the fifty-first year of his reign, while hunting in the forest of Cuise [Note: It still retains its name, *la forêt de Cuise*, near Compiègne. Cointius proves at length that Chlothacharius died in the fiftieth year of his reign; Valesius considers it probable that he exceeded the year by several days. On that view, at least at the beginning of this chapter, one should read “the fiftieth year.” Henschenius thinks that “the fifty-second” should be written. According to Marius, Chlothacharius died in the twentieth year after the consulship of Basilius, that is, in the year 561, indiction IX.], he was seized by fever and then returned to the estate of Compiègne.

As he was suffering severely from the fever there, he said: “Alas! What do you think? What kind of king is that heavenly King, who kills such great kings in this way?”

In this state of distress he breathed out his spirit. His four sons carried him with great honor to Soissons and buried him in the basilica of blessed Medard.

He died one day after the completion of the year in which Chramnus had been killed.

### XXII

After his father’s funeral, Chilperic took the treasures that had been gathered at the estate of Brinnacum [Note: Others have *Brannacum*, commonly Braine, a town about three leagues from Soissons, toward Reims, where there is a distinguished Premonstratensian abbey dedicated to Saint Evodius.], and went to the more influential Franks. Having softened them with gifts, he brought them under his authority.

He soon entered Paris and occupied the seat of King Childebert, but he was not permitted to hold it for long. His brothers joined together and drove him out. Thus the four of them—Charibert, Guntchramnus, Chilperic, and Sigibert—made a lawful division among themselves.

The lot [Note: It is called a *lot* because they divided the portions of the kingdom by lot, as Valesius observes at the beginning of Book VII of *The Frankish History*. Some, however, maintain that this division was made while their father was still alive.] gave Charibert the kingdom of Childebert and Paris as his seat; to Guntchramnus it gave the kingdom of Chlodomer and Orléans as his seat [Note: Valesius argues that Guntchramnus never resided at Orléans.]; to Chilperic, the kingdom of his father Chlothacharius and Soissons as his royal seat; and to Sigibert, the kingdom of Theuderic and Reims as his seat [Note: Thus all the manuscripts and printed editions except one, that of Chesnius, which has “Metz.” It is true that the Colbertinus manuscript, formerly belonging to the monastery of Saint Arnulf at Metz, now reads “Metz,” but this was inserted by some rascal who substituted the word after the original had been worn away. It is certain that Sigibert had a royal residence at Reims, which Chlodoveus had assigned to his eldest son Theodoric as the capital of his kingdom. Theodbert, son of Theodoric, fell ill at Chalon and died on the journey while returning to Reims, as Fortunatus testifies in the Life of Saint Germanus.
