Hence the ancient author who wrote the deeds of Saint Quinidius, bishop of Vaison, to show that he was famous everywhere as one who lived under Chlodoveus’s sons and grandsons, says: “His fame was not hidden from Rome. The kingdoms of the Franks, finally at Reims with their Germanic peoples … did not cover it.” He attributes the Germans to Reims because they were subject to the kings of Austrasia, whose kingdom had Reims as its capital. This agrees with the ancient author who wrote the *Deeds of the Franks* under the first dynasty of our kings, as well as with Rorico and many others who attest that Reims was the royal seat. I omit Baronius, Petavius, Cointius, and other more recent writers. Scaliger, Hadrian Valesius, and others write that Reims, or Reims together with Metz, was the seat of the kingdom, and call them the kings of Metz and Reims. No one can deny, however, that most of the later kings of Austrasia resided chiefly at Metz.]. 

### XXIII

After the death of King Chlothacharius, the Chuni [Alternative reading: Huns] attacked Gaul. Against them Sigibert led an army, fought them, and defeated and routed them. Later their king secured friendship with him through ambassadors.

While Sigibert was occupied with them, his brother Chilperic seized Reims and took away the other cities that belonged to Sigibert. From this there arose among them, what is worse, a civil war.

Returning victorious from the Huns, Sigibert occupied the city of Soissons. There he found Theodbert, son of King Chilperic, seized him, and sent him into exile.

Then he advanced against Chilperic and provoked a battle. After defeating and routing him, he restored his cities to his own authority.

He ordered Chilperic’s son Theodbert to be guarded for a full year at the estate of Ponticon [Note: A royal estate on the river Aisne, in the district of Pertensis, not far from Victoriacum Incensum in Champagne. Papirius Massonus wrongly confused it with Pont-à-Yonne near Sens. See Book IV of *On Diplomatic Affairs*, where palaces are discussed, no. 118.].

Later, being merciful, he returned Theodbert to his father, enriched with gifts and in good health, after obtaining from him an oath that he would never act against him. This oath was later broken through the working of sins.

### XXIV

When King Guntchramn had obtained part of the kingdom, like his brothers, he removed the patrician Agroecula [Note: Bell. and Bec. have *Agroecula*, as does the printed edition; but Corb., Regm., and Colb. have *Agricola*. Celsus is mentioned more than once below. According to the Chronicle of Marius, he died in the fourth consulship of Justin the Younger, that is, in the year 570. Chesnius records the epitaph of Silvia, his mother, in volume I, p. 517. The dignity of patrician in Guntchramn’s kingdom derived from the Burgundian kings. Since they had received it from the emperors and were often pleased to be called by that title, even after those emperors had died, the men who were later appointed prefects over those provinces under our kings generally bore the name “Patrician.” See Valesius, book VI of *Frankish History*, and Bignonius on book I of Marculf’s *Formulary*, no. 35.] and bestowed upon Celsus the honor of the patriciate. He was a man tall in stature [Note: *Status* is found in the sense of “stature” even among authors who are by no means obscure, both sacred and secular. See Du Cange’s *Glossary* and note 273 in the new edition of Saint Paulinus.], strong across the shoulders, robust in the arm, inflated in his speech, apt in his replies, and learned in the study of law. Thereafter such a desire for possessing property arose in him that, repeatedly taking away the property of churches, he brought it under his own authority.

For once, when he heard a reading from the prophet Isaiah being read in church, in which it says, “Woe to those who join house to house and add field to field, until there is no room” (Isaiah 5:8), he is said to have exclaimed: “This ‘Woe’ applies incongruously to me and my sons.” Yet he left behind a son who, having died without children, left the greater part of his wealth to the churches that his father had despoiled.

### XXV

King Guntchramn was a good man. First he took Veneranda, one of his household’s female slaves, as a concubine, and by her he had a son, Gundobad. Later he married Marcatrud [Note: Colb. has *Mercatrudem*. Magnarius, or Magnacharius, is mentioned below, book V, chapter 17.], the daughter of Magnarius. He sent his son Gundobad [Note: Bell. and Bec. have *Gundobadum*; Regm. has *Gundebaudum*; Colb. has *Gundebadum*; others have *Gundebaldum*.] to Orléans.

[Note: What follows, up to the words “after exacting a thousand gold pieces from Bishop Leontius” in the following chapter, is absent from Bec., Colb., Regm., and Bad. But no one should call the material found here interpolated, since, if it is omitted, the text is plainly altogether mutilated and interrupted.]

But Marcatrud, jealous after having borne a son, plotted against the boy’s life and, as they say, sent poison into his drink and killed him [Note: Corb. has this reading, *transmisso ... veneno*, “the poison having been sent.” Bell., together with the *od.* edition, has “she arranged for it to be given to him in his drink.”]. After he had died, by God’s judgment she herself lost the son she had, incurred the king’s hatred, and, having been dismissed by him, died not long afterward.

After the king took Austrechild [Note: Corb. has this form; others have *Austrigildem*. Another manuscript in Chesnius has the additional name Bobilana. Bell. has *Bobillam*.], surnamed Bobila, by whom he again had two sons, the elder was called Chlothar and the younger Chlodomer.

### XXVI

King Charibert [Note: Corb. erroneously has *Sigibertus*; others have *Haribertus*.] took Ingoberg as his wife, by whom he had a daughter who was later taken to Kent [Note: This was Aldeberga, or Bertha, who was married in England to Ethelbert, king of Kent, and worked diligently with Saint Augustine and the other monks sent by Gregory the Great for the conversion of her husband and the whole nation. She had with her Letaldus, bishop, as some believe, of Senlis, whose memory is celebrated on February 24. For *Cantia*, the Bell. manuscript and others used by those who prepared most of the editions before Chesnius have *Gantia*. By joining the word’s first syllable to the preceding word, they made the name *Ingantia*, as though this had been the queen’s name. See Bede, book IX, chapter 25; William of Malmesbury; and others; and compare below, book IX, chapter 26.], taking a husband there.

At that time Ingoberg had in her service two girls, daughters of a certain poor man. The first was called Marcovefa [Note: Bell.’s manuscript has *Marocovefa*.], and wore a religious habit; the other was Merofled. The king was very much captivated by their love, for they were, as we have said [Note: This is the reading of all the manuscripts and printed editions except Chesnius, who has “as was said.”], the daughters of a wool-worker.

Ingoberg, jealous because the king loved them, secretly arranged for their father to work, intending that when the king saw this he would hate his daughters. While he was working, she summoned the king. He, hoping to see something new, watched the man from a distance arranging royal wool [Note: Corb. and Bell. have this reading; most printed editions have *lascias*.]. When the king saw it, he was angered, abandoned Ingoberg, and took Merofled.

He also had another girl, the daughter of a shepherd—that is, one who pastured sheep [Note: The words “that is, one who pastured sheep” are absent from the printed editions, but are found in the Corb., Bellovac., and Palatine manuscripts. In Bell. she is called *Teudegildis*; Regm. has *Teotigildis*; the printed editions have *Theudegildis* or *Teodegildis*.]—named Theudechild. It is also said that he had a son by her, who, as soon as he emerged from the womb, was immediately carried to the tomb.

During this king’s reign, in the city of Saintes, Leontius [Note: This was the bishop of Bordeaux, of whom Fortunatus writes in book IV, poem 10, and elsewhere. He must be distinguished from another bishop of the same name, Leontius of Arles, somewhat earlier, about whom the same Fortunatus writes in book IV, poem 9. The same author praises Leontius and Emerius in book I, poem 12. Leontius took part in various councils. The people of Bordeaux celebrate his feast on November 15.] gathered the bishops of his province and expelled Emerius from the episcopate, asserting that he had not been lawfully invested with that honor.

For he had obtained a decree from King Chlothar that he should be consecrated without the advice of the metropolitan, who was not present. After he had been expelled, they agreed upon Heraclius [Note: On the agreement, see above, chapter 15.], then a presbyter of the city of Bordeaux, and sent their agreement, subscribed with their own hands, to King Charibert through the presbyter Nuncupatus.

When Nuncupatus came to Tours, he disclosed what had happened to the blessed Euphronius, asking him to subscribe to this agreement. The man of God plainly refused.

After the presbyter had entered the gates of Paris and approached the king’s presence, he said:

“Hail, glorious king. The apostolic see sends abundant greetings to your eminence.”

The king replied: “What? Have you visited the city of Rome [Note: Bell. has this reading; the others, together with the printed edition, have “the city of Tours.” Although other episcopal sees were also then called apostolic, as is clear even from this passage, and all bishops were called apostolic, as everyone knows, nevertheless, when the term was used absolutely, without the accompanying name of a see or bishop, it was understood chiefly of the Roman see and its pontiff. The same is to be said of the title “pope,” which before the time of Gregory VII was common to all bishops. See Cointius on the year 562, where he discusses this matter. Below, in place of “your father ...,” the edition with Bec. has “your father’s ...”.], so that you might bring us greetings from its pope?”

“Your father,” said the presbyter, “Leontius, together with his provincial bishops, sends you greetings. He informs you that Aemulus—for that was the name by which they customarily called Emerius in his infancy—has been expelled from the episcopate because, contrary to the sanction of the canons, he sought the bishopric of the city of Saintes. Therefore they have sent you their agreement that another should be appointed in his place, so that, while transgressors of the canons are regularly reproved, the power of your kingdom may be prolonged through ages.”

As he said this, the king, gnashing his teeth, ordered him to be dragged from his presence, placed upon a cart filled with thorns, and driven into exile. He said:

“Do you suppose that no one remains among the sons of King Chlothar who will uphold his father’s actions, since these men have expelled a bishop whom his will had chosen, without our judgment?”

Immediately he sent religious men and restored the bishop to his position. He also sent some of his chamberlains, who, after exacting a thousand gold pieces from Bishop Leontius, were to impose fines upon the remaining bishops according to their means. Thus he avenged the prince’s injury [Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts. The printed editions have *patris*, “the father’s injury.” Corb. and Regm. have *principis est ulta injuria*, “the prince’s injury was avenged.”].

Afterward he married Marcovefa, that is, Merofled’s sister [Note: Some manuscripts and editions have the erroneous form *Marcovei Famero fledis*.]. For this reason both of them were excommunicated by Saint Germanus the bishop. But since the king was unwilling to abandon her, she was struck down by divine judgment and died.

Not long afterward, the king himself also died after her.

Charibert [Note: Gregory repeatedly records Charibert’s vices, whereas Fortunatus gives a fuller account of his praises in book VI, poem 4, which therefore seems to have been written at the beginning of his reign. What follows concerns Theudechild, but not Charibert’s wife, as does Fortunatus’s poem 25 in book IV. Brouverus suspects that she was the wife of Theodoric and mother of Theodebert. Yet Valesius, book VII of *Frankish History*, proves that what Fortunatus writes there cannot be attributed to Theodoric’s wife. He therefore thinks that she was rather the daughter of that same Theodoric and the sister of Theodebert—this very woman who, as Procopius reports in book IV of the Gothic War, although he does not mention her name, after marrying first Hermegisclus and then Radiger, kings of the Varni, was finally forced to return to Gaul. Gregory also speaks of the same woman, as Valesius thinks, in the book *On the Glory of the Confessors*. He conjectures that she was also the same as Theodechild, who is said to have built the monastery of Saint Peter of the Living near Sens. Finally, Frodoard praises Queen Suavegottha, the mother of Queen Theudechild, in book II of the *History of Rheims*. She gave to the church of Rheims part of the estate of Virisiacum, where hermits were then living. Marlotus also, in book II of the *Metropolis of Rheims*, chapter 20, together with Valesius, considers them to have been the wife and daughter of Theodoric. Cointius, however, on the year 564, maintains that Theodechild, whom Procopius records as having married the king of the Varni, was a daughter of Clovis by an earlier wife, and the sister of Theodoric and Theodebert’s aunt. On Charibert’s death, see the book *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 19.] having died, Theudechild, one of his queens, sent messengers to King Guntchramn, offering herself voluntarily in marriage to him.

The king gave them this reply:

“Let her come to me with her treasures; I shall receive her and make her great among the peoples, so that she may enjoy greater honor with me than with my brother, who has recently died.”

She rejoiced at this, gathered everything together, and set out for him. When the king saw her, he said:

“It is better for these treasures to remain with me than with this woman, who unworthily entered my brother’s bed.”

Then, after taking away many things and leaving her only a few, he sent her to a monastery at Arles.

She, however, submitting unwillingly and being afflicted by fasts and vigils, secretly summoned a certain Goth [*Gothum*; Al. “visited”], promising that if he would take her to Spain and marry her, she would leave the monastery with her treasures and follow him gladly. He, without hesitation, promised to do so.

When she had gathered her possessions, packed them into bundles [Al. *volucris*], and was preparing to leave the convent, the abbess’s vigilance anticipated her intention [Note: This was Liliola, the third abbess of the place; she had been preceded by two women named Caesaria.]. Her deception was discovered, and the abbess ordered her to be severely beaten and committed to custody. There she remained until the end of her present life, worn down by no ordinary sufferings.

### XXVII

King Sigibert, seeing that his brothers were taking wives unworthy of themselves and, through their degradation, even joining slave women to themselves in marriage, sent an embassy to Spain and sought Brunichild, daughter of King Athanagild, with many gifts.

She was a girl elegant in her accomplishments, beautiful in appearance, honorable and distinguished in character, prudent in counsel, and gracious in conversation. Her father did not refuse, but sent her to the aforementioned king with great treasures.

He, after gathering his nobles around him and preparing a banquet, received her as his wife with immense joy and delight.

Because she was subject to the Arian faith, she was converted through the preaching of the priests and the exhortation of the king himself. She believed in and confessed the blessed Trinity in its unity, and was anointed with chrism. She remains Catholic in the name of Christ [Note: This is the reading of Corb., Bec., and Bell., and rightly so, for when Gregory wrote this she was still alive; she was torn to pieces in 614. The printed editions have *perseveravit*, “she remained”; Colb. has *permansit*, “she continued.” Sigibert’s and Brunichild’s marriage was celebrated by Fortunatus in book VI, poem 2.].

### XXVIII

When King Chilperic saw this, since he already had several wives, he sought her sister Galsuinth [Note: Corb., Bell., and Freh. have *Galsuintham*; others have *Galsuendam* here and below. Galsuintha was older in age than Brunichild.], promising through his messengers that he would abandon the others, provided that he might obtain a woman worthy of himself and of royal offspring.

Her father, accepting these promises, sent his daughter to him with great wealth, just as he had sent the elder sister [Col. 0292A]. Galsuintha was older in age than Brunichild.

When she came to King Chilperic, she was received with great honor and joined to him in marriage. He also loved her greatly, for she had brought great treasures with her.

But because of his love for Fredegund, whom he had previously possessed, a great scandal arose between them. She had already been converted to the Catholic faith and had been anointed with chrism [Note: Fortunatus sang of her marriage, conversion, and death in book VI, poem 7.].

Since she continually complained that she was suffering injuries from the king and said that she had no dignity with him, she asked him to permit her to return freely to her homeland, leaving behind the treasures she had brought with her.

He concealed his intentions by various devices and soothed her with gentle words. Finally, he ordered a servant to strangle her and found her dead upon her bed.

After her death, God displayed a great miracle. The lamp that burned suspended by a cord before her tomb fell to the pavement when the cord broke, although no one had touched it. The hardness of the pavement fled before it, as though it had descended into some soft substance; it sank halfway in, yet was not at all shattered. Those who saw this regarded it as a very great miracle [Note: Some, together with the printed edition, have *magno*, “great,” instead of *grandi*.].

After the king had mourned her death, he received Fredegund in marriage a few days later.

After this, her brothers, thinking that the aforesaid queen had been killed through his dismissal of her [Bell. has “to him”], deposed him from the kingdom.

At that time Chilperic had three sons by his former queen Audovera: Theodebert, whom we mentioned above (chapter 23), Merovech, and Chlodovech.

But let us return to what we had begun.

### XXIX

The Huns [Note: See above, chapter 23, and Paul the Deacon, book II of *The Deeds of the Lombards*, chapter 10, where the Huns are also called Avars. Valesius discusses the Huns or Avars more fully in book IX of *Frankish History*; consult him.] were again attempting to come into Gaul. Against them Sigibert marched with an army, taking with him a great multitude of brave men.

When they were about to engage in battle, the Huns, trained in magical arts, displayed various illusions to them and greatly overcame them. When Sigibert’s army fled, Sigibert himself was held enclosed by the Huns. But afterward, being an elegant and resourceful man, he overcame by the art of gift-giving those whom he could not overcome by the strength of battle.

For after giving gifts, he made a treaty with their king [Note: The Regm. manuscript has *foedus iniit*, “he made a treaty.”], that for all the days of his life they would never wage war against one another. This was rightly judged to bring him more praise than reproach. The king of the Huns also gave many gifts to King Sigibert.

The king was called Gagan [Note: This is the reading of Corb. and Bec., together with several printed editions; Regm. has *Garganus*; others have *Chaganus* or *Caganus*. It was not peculiar to the Huns that all their kings should bear the same name. Thus the Egyptian kings were once called Pharaohs and later Ptolemies; the Persians, Arsacids; the Athenians, Cecropids; the Ethiopians, Candaces; the Lombards, Flavii—not to mention Caesars and Augustuses. Even today “Prester John” is said to be the king of the Ethiopians, and so forth.], for all the kings of that people are called by this name.

### XXX

King Sigibert, wishing to capture the city of Arles, ordered the Arvernians to rise up. At that time Firminus was count of that city, and he went at their head.

From the other side Audouarius [Note: This is the reading of the older manuscripts; Regm. has *Adovagrius*; the printed editions have *Adouarius* or *Eudouarius*.] also arrived with an army. They entered the city of Arles and exacted oaths of allegiance on behalf of King Sigibert.

When King Guntchramn learned this, he sent the patrician Celsus there with an army. Celsus went and took the city of Avignon [*Avennicam*].

Then he approached Arles, surrounded it, and began to attack Sigibert’s army, which was confined within the walls.

At that point Bishop Sabaudus said to them:

“Go out and enter the battle, because while you remain shut up beneath the walls you will not be able to defend either us or the subjects of this city. If, with God’s favor, you defeat them, we shall keep the faith we promised. But if they prevail against you, behold, you will find the gates open; enter, lest you perish.”

Deceived by this trick, they went out and prepared for battle. But after being defeated by Celsus’s army, they fled. When they came back to the city, they found the gates barred [Note: What follows, almost to the end of chapter 38, is absent from Regm.].

As the army was struck from behind by javelins [Note: Several manuscripts, together with the printed edition, have *foderetur*, “was pierced.”] and pelted with stones by the townspeople, they made for the Rhône River. There, placing their shields beneath them, they sought the farther bank.

But the violence of the river swept away and killed many of them. At that time the Rhône did to the Arvernians what the Simois is said once to have done to the Trojans:

> [Lacuna] snatched beneath the waves,  
> It rolled the shields of men, helmets, and mighty bodies.
>
> Rare swimmers appeared in the vast whirlpool.  
> *(Virgil, Aeneid, book I.)*

The few who, as we have said, managed to swim across with the help of their shields reached the level ground of the opposite bank. Stripped of their possessions and deprived of their horses [Al. “deprived by horses”], they were restored to their homeland amid no small humiliation.

Permission to depart was nevertheless granted to Firminus [Note: Some printed editions have *Firmino ... tantum*, “to Firminus alone”; Corb. and Bellovac. have *Magni ibi tunc viri*, “men of great standing were there at that time.”] and Audouarius.

Many men from the Arvernians were then struck down there, not only carried away by the torrent but also felled by sword blows.

171 Thus King Guntchramn, having recovered that city, restored Avignon to the possessions of his brother [Note: This is the reading of all the manuscripts; most printed editions have *patris*, “of his father.”], in accordance with his customary goodness.

### XXXI

In Gaul there then appeared a great portent [Note: This passage is fully illuminated by the Chronicle of Marius of Avenches, where he speaks of the same event as follows: “In this year (563), a powerful mountain called Tauredunum, in the territory of Valais, suddenly collapsed, crushing the fortress near which it stood and the villages, together with all their inhabitants. It moved the lake, which was 69 miles long and 20 miles wide, so completely that, overflowing both banks, it devastated ancient villages with their people and animals. It also demolished many holy places together with those serving them, violently threw down the bridge of Geneva, mills, and people, and, entering the city of Geneva, killed many people.”] at the fortress of Tauredunum, which was situated on a mountain above the Rhône River.

For more than sixty days it gave out some sort of bellowing. At last that mountain split and separated from another mountain near it and, together with people, churches, wealth, and houses, plunged into the river. Blocking the riverbank, it drove the water backward.

That place was enclosed on both sides by mountains, between whose narrow confines the torrent flowed. The water therefore flooded the upper region, which lay along the bank [Note: Most printed editions have *insidebant*, “lay along the banks”], and covered and destroyed it.

The accumulated water, bursting downward, found people unaware, killed them as it had done those above, overturned houses, destroyed animals, and violently and suddenly swept away and overturned everything situated along those banks as far as the city of Geneva [Note: Corb. and Bell. have *Jenubam*; most printed editions, together with Bec., have *Janobam*; Colb. and Chesnius have *Genuam*. It is clear that Geneva, commonly called Genève, is intended here; the event indeed occurred in Valais.].

Many report that such a mass of water accumulated there that it entered the aforementioned city over the walls. There is no doubt about this, because, as we have said, the Rhône flows through those places between narrow mountain passes and, when it was blocked, had nowhere to divert on either side. The displaced mountain, which had descended, burst out all at once and thus destroyed everything.

After this had happened, thirty monks came from the place where the fortress had collapsed. Digging through the earth that remained after the mountain’s destruction, they found bronze or iron. While they were doing this, they heard the mountain bellowing as it had before.

But while they were held back by savage greed, the part that had not yet fallen collapsed upon them, covering and killing them. They were never found again.

Similarly, before the disaster in the territory of the Arvernians, great portents terrified that region. Often three or four great bright lights appeared around the sun. The peasants called them “suns,” saying, “Look, there are three or four suns in the sky.”

On one occasion, however, on the first day of October, the sun appeared so darkened that not even a quarter of its light remained. It appeared foul and discolored, like a sack.

A star also, which some call a comet, appeared over that region for a whole year, bearing a ray like a sword. The sky seemed to burn, and many other signs appeared.

In the church of Clermont, while the morning vigils were being celebrated on a certain feast, a bird called a corydalus [Note: Corb. and Bec. have *Coredallus*; Colb. has *Coradallus*. See Alteserra.], which we call a lark, entered and extinguished all the lamps that were burning by placing its wings over them, with such speed that you would have thought they had been placed in one man’s hand and submerged in water.

Then, passing beneath the veil in the sacristy, it attempted to extinguish a lamp [Note: Corb. and Bell. have *cicindelum*; others and most printed editions have *cicindelem*. Our reading is confirmed by the *Life of Saint Eligius*, published by Saint Audoenus, chapter 47, where the meaning of this word is explained, volume V of the *Spicilegium*. On the veils of churches, see Cardinal Bona, book I of *Liturgical Matters*, chapter 25, and Mabillon, book I of *Gallican Liturgy*, chapter 8.], but the doorkeepers prevented it and killed it.

A similar thing was done by another bird with the burning lamps in the basilica of the blessed Andrew [Note: On this church, see the little book *On the Churches of Clermont*, chapter 34. In 1149 it was restored by Count William and the Dauphin of Auvergne and handed over to the Premonstratensians, as Savaro observes.].

When the disaster itself arrived, such slaughter was made of that population throughout the entire region that it is impossible to count how many multitudes fell there. When coffins and boards had already run out, ten or more were buried in a single pit in the ground.

On one Sunday, three hundred bodies of the dead were counted in one basilica of Saint Peter [Note: There were formerly several basilicas dedicated to Saint Peter at Clermont. This passage must be understood of the parish church, mentioned in the cited book, chapter 6.]. The death itself was sudden. For when a wound arose in the groin or armpit, shaped like a serpent, those people were so infected by the poison [Note: Bell. has this reading; Corb. and Bec., together with most printed editions, have “the person was so infected.” Others have “was killed.” Marius mentions this disaster in his Chronicle under the year 571. See also the book *On the Miracles of Saint Julian*, chapter 45.] that they breathed out their spirit on the following or the third day.

The power of the poison also robbed a person of his senses.

At that time the presbyter Cato also died [Note: On this presbyter, see above, chapter 6 and following chapters.]. Although many had fled from this plague, he remained, burying the people and saying Masses for them individually [Note: Bell., Colb., and several printed editions have *viriliter*, “manfully,” which has the same sense here], and never left that place.

This presbyter was a man of great humanity and much loved by the poor. I believe that this was a remedy for him, if he had possessed any pride.

Bishop Cautinus, however, after traveling through various places out of fear of this disaster, returned to the city and, contracting the disease, died on the Friday of the Lord’s Passion. At the same hour his cousin Tetradius also died.

At that time Lyon, Bourges, Chalon [Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts and Chesnius; most editions have *Cavallonum*. Bad. has *Cabilo*, which in fact is the city intended here, not Cavaillon in Provence.], and Dijon were also severely devastated by this disease.

### XXXII

[Note: This chapter and the five following are absent from the printed editions and manuscripts, although they are listed in the chapter index in the Beccensis and Regiomontanus manuscripts and in the edition prepared by Jodocus Badius. In old editions and manuscripts, chapter 47 occurs after chapter 41 or 42. We have these chapters from a manuscript codex of the holy monastery of Cassino, written seven hundred years ago. Indeed, its style and turns of speech, its shifts of cases, and its contents bear the stamp of our Gregory’s genius; in chapter 36 he cites the *Life of Saint Nicetius* written by himself. The monastery of Randan has been destroyed, but the village, commonly called Randan, retains the name; it lies among the Arverni near the confluence of the Dore and the Allier.]

At that time, in the monastery at Randan in the territory of Clermont, there was a presbyter of outstanding virtue named Julianus, a man of great abstinence. He used neither wine nor any cooked food, always wearing a hair shirt beneath his tunic. He was first at the vigils and constant in prayer. By invoking the Lord’s name and making the sign of the holy cross, he easily cured the possessed, gave sight to the blind, and drove away other illnesses.

Since he stood constantly and his feet had become infected by dampness, someone asked him why he always stood contrary to the limits of his body’s strength. He was accustomed to reply with a spiritual joke:

“They are doing their work while life remains my companion, and, by the Lord’s command, their support does not abandon me.”

We ourselves once saw him cure a possessed man merely by his word in the basilica of the blessed martyr Julian. He often brought relief through prayer to those suffering from quartan fevers and other fevers.

At this time, full of years and virtues, he was taken from this world into rest.

### XXXIII

The abbot of that monastery also died at that time. He was succeeded by Sunniulfus [Note: Bad., in the title, has “On the abbot Symnulphus.” Regm. and Bec. have “On the abbot Sumniulfus.” Visions of this sort occur in the *Acts of Saints Perpetua and Felicitas*.], a man of complete simplicity and charity.

Often he himself washed the feet of guests and dried them with his own hands. There was only this about him: he governed the flock entrusted to him not by fear, but by supplication.

He himself was also accustomed to relate that in a vision he had been led to a certain river of fire. On one side of the bank, crowds of people—or bees—were rushing together and being plunged into the hives. Some were immersed up to the waist, others up to the armpits, and some up to the chin. They cried out weeping that they were being burned terribly.

There was also a bridge over the river, so narrow that it could scarcely accommodate the width of one foot. On the other side of the bank a large house appeared, white on the outside.

Then he asked those who were with him what these things meant. They replied:

“He will be thrown from this bridge who is found negligent in disciplining the flock entrusted to him. But whoever has been diligent crosses without danger and is led joyfully into the house you see beyond.”

Hearing this, he was shaken from sleep and thereafter appeared much stricter to the monks.

### XXXIV

I shall also reveal what happened at a certain monastery at that time. I do not wish to name the monk [Note: In the chapter index of the manuscripts and in Bad., it is called “On a monk from Bordeaux.” A similar event appears in the first Dialogue of Sulpicius Severus, chapter 5, where an abbot ordered a boy to be beaten with rods because he had carried an asp in his cloak unharmed. The boy was to learn to serve God in humility rather than glory in signs and virtues, since awareness of weakness was better than vanity about virtues.], because he is still alive; I do not want him, when these writings reach him, to fall into empty glory and thereby become diminished.

A certain young man came to the monastery and commended himself to the abbot so that he might live in God’s service. The abbot put many things before him, saying that the service of that place was difficult and that he could not possibly fulfill everything imposed upon him. The young man promised that he would fulfill everything in the name of the Lord, and so the abbot accepted him.

After a few days, while he was conducting himself in all things with humility and holiness, the monks removed grain from the granary—about three measures—and set it in the sun to dry. They ordered this young man to guard it.

While the others were eating and he was sitting on guard over the grain, the sky suddenly became cloudy. Behold, a heavy rainstorm, driven quickly by the roar of the wind, was approaching the pile of grain.

Seeing this, the monk did not know what to do. But reasoning that if he summoned the others, they would be unable to put everything away in the granary because of the quantity, he set everything else aside and turned to prayer, begging the Lord not to allow a drop of that rain to fall upon the wheat.

As he prostrated himself on the ground and prayed, the cloud divided, and very heavy rain fell all around the grain without wetting a single grain of wheat, if such a thing may be said.

When the other monks and the abbot came quickly, intending to gather up the grain, they saw this miracle. Looking for its guardian, they found him—not far away, thrown down upon the ground—praying [Al. “they found him”].

When the abbot saw this, he prostrated himself after him. After the rain had passed and the prayer was complete, he called him to rise. Then he ordered that the monk be seized and beaten, saying:

“It is necessary, my son, for you to grow humbly in the fear and service of God, not to glory in prodigies and virtues.”

He shut him in a cell for seven days and ordered him to fast as one guilty, so that he might turn him away from empty glory, lest it become any impediment to him.

Now, as we have learned from faithful men, this same monk is devoted to such great abstinence that during the days of Lent he takes no bread as food, except that on the third day he drinks a full cup of *thisina* [tisane]. May the Lord, in answer to the prayers of the faithful, deign to preserve him in a manner pleasing to himself until the completion of his life.

[Col. 0297C] **XXXV**

[Note: Caput istud...]: This chapter, together with those that follow and that we are now publishing for the first time, was praised as an authentic work of Gregory by the ancient author of the *Life of Saint Avitus, Bishop of Clermont*, who began his narrative with this chapter and added some material from the following one. It is sufficient to report the variant readings. It begins as follows:

“Thus, in the city of Arverna, according to the dignity of the world, the blessed Avitus was born of no lowly noble stock. During his boyhood, by God’s providence, he was advanced to the rank of archdeacon. When Bishop Cautinus had died, many were seeking the episcopate ... He received valuable goods from Ennodius [Col. 0297D] ... He promised the Church many good things according to God; nevertheless ... but if he should wait ... to receive blessings. For this grace ... may come ... chastity. At the same time, at Lyon, a city of Gaul, Saint Nicetius was elected and consecrated bishop.”

Thus far Gregory of Tours. This author wrote, as may be inferred from the antiquity of the manuscript from which these passages were first copied, about six hundred years ago. Avitus is frequently praised by Gregory. He built a church at Thigernum, as appears from Book I, chapter 67, of the *Miracles*; he repaired the church of Saint Antolianus, as appears from chapter 65. He died in the year 594, on September 20, the day on which his feast is celebrated. He was buried in the church of Saint Mary of Portus, which he had built. Although it was called the principal church, learned men maintain that it must nevertheless be distinguished from the cathedral. See Savaron’s notes on Book II of *The Churches of Clermont*, chapter 2.

After, as we have said [Note: Namely, above, chapter 31 of this book.], Bishop Cautinus had died at Arverna, many were competing for the episcopate, offering much and promising still more. For the presbyter Eufrasius, formerly the son of the senator Ennodius [Note: Savaro reads *Euvodius*. This name frequently occurs in old manuscripts written in this form instead of *Evodius*.], sent the king, through his kinsman Beregesilus, splendid articles obtained from the Jews, so that what he could not obtain by merit he might obtain by gifts. He was indeed elegant in his manner of life, but he was not chaste in his conduct. He often intoxicated barbarians, but rarely refreshed the needy. And, I believe, this was the reason that he did not succeed: he wished to attain these honors not through God but through men.

Nor could what the Lord had spoken through the mouth of Saint Quintianus be altered [Note: In the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 4, where more is said about Hortensius.]: “For no one of the stock of Hortensius shall arise to govern the Church of God.”

Accordingly, the archdeacon Avitus assembled the clergy in the church at Arverna. He promised nothing [or, according to the variant, “promised much”], but after receiving their consent [Note: Gregory more than once calls the instrument of election by this name in chapter 26. Gregory often discusses Saint Avitus below and in the books of the *Miracles*. See also Fortunatus, Book III, poem 24 and the following two poems. At Gregory’s invitation he sang Gregory’s praises in Book V, poem 4, preceded by a letter to Gregory himself. Savaro, in *The Origins of Clermont*, pp. 137 ff., praises this chapter of Gregory’s Book IV of the *History* and wrote an epitome of it. From this it is clear that the chapters we are publishing here for the first time from the Cassinese manuscript also existed in other manuscripts, at least one of which was known to Savaro.], he petitioned the king. Firminus, who had formerly been appointed count in this city, wished to prevent him, but he did not go away.

His friends, who had been sent in this matter, begged the king that at least one Sunday might pass without Avitus being blessed, so that he might not be consecrated. If this could be brought about, they would give the king a thousand gold pieces; but the king did not agree to their request.

Thus, when the citizens of Arverna had assembled together, the blessed Avitus—who at that time, as we have said, was archdeacon—was elected by clergy and people and received the episcopal chair. The king loved him so greatly in this high office that, temporarily setting aside canonical strictness [Note: The rule was that ordinations should be performed by the metropolitan within his own province, according to the prescriptions of the canons. Gregory himself was likewise consecrated at Rheims by Aegidius.], he ordered him to be blessed in his own presence, saying: “May I deserve to receive a blessing from his hand.” He did this as a favor, so that Avitus might be blessed at Metz.

After receiving the episcopate, Avitus showed himself great among men, granting justice to the peoples, help to the poor, consolation to widows, and the greatest assistance to orphans. If a stranger came to him, he was so loved that the stranger recognized in him both a father and a homeland. Though Avitus flourished in great virtues and kept with all his heart everything pleasing to God, he uprooted sinful lust in every respect and planted the just chastity of God.

**XXXVI**

When Bishop Sacerdos of Lyon died at Paris after that synod which expelled Saffaracus [Note: Saffaracus, bishop of Paris, was deposed at the Second Synod of Paris, dated by Sirmondus to 555 and by Cointius to 551.], Saint Nicetius was elected by him and received the episcopate, as we have written in his *Life* [Note: In the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 8; compare that chapter with this passage.]. He was an outstanding man of complete holiness and chaste conduct.

The love which the Apostle commanded us to maintain toward everyone, if possible (Romans 12:17), he practiced toward all so effectively that the Lord himself, who is true love, could be seen in his breast. For even if he became angry with someone because of negligence, he immediately received the person after correction as though he had never been offended. He was a chastiser of offenders and a pardoner of penitents, generous in almsgiving and energetic in labor. He devoted himself most diligently to raising churches, repairing houses, sowing fields, and planting vineyards.

Yet these activities did not distract him from prayer. After serving in the priesthood for twenty-two years, he departed to the Lord, who now grants great miracles at his tomb to those who pray. From the lamp oil that is lighted daily before his tomb, he restores sight to the blind, drives demons from possessed bodies, restores health to contracted limbs, and is in this age regarded as a great protection for all the sick.

The bishop Priscus, who had succeeded him, began, together with his wife Susanna, to persecute and kill many of those whom the man of God had held as friends—not because they had been overcome by any fault, convicted of any crime, or caught in theft, but solely because malice had inflamed him with envy that they had been faithful to Nicetius.

Priscus and his wife uttered many blasphemies against the holy man of God. Although earlier bishops had long observed the rule that a woman should not enter the church building, Susanna entered even the little cell where the holy men had rested, together with young girls.

At last divine majesty was stirred against the household of Bishop Priscus because of these acts. His wife, seized by a demon, wandered madly throughout the city with her hair loose. She confessed that the saint of God, whom while sane she had denied, was a friend of Christ, and cried out that he should spare her.

That bishop was seized by an attack of quartan fever and incurred trembling. When the fever itself had passed, he remained continually trembling and senseless. His son and the whole household likewise appeared discolored and stupid, so that no one could doubt that they had been struck by the power of the holy man.

For Bishop Priscus and his household were always barking against the saint of God with wicked words, while claiming that anyone who spat insults against him was their friend.

At the beginning of his episcopate, Priscus had ordered the building of the ecclesiastical house to be raised. A deacon whom the holy man of God, while still alive, had often removed from communion because of adultery, and whom he had repeatedly ordered to be beaten, yet could never bring to amendment, climbed onto the roof of that building. When he began to uncover it, he said: “I thank you, Jesus Christ, that after the death of the most wicked Nicetius I have deserved to tread upon this roof.”

The words were still hanging in his mouth when the timber beneath his feet suddenly gave way. He fell to the ground; it cracked, and he died.

When the bishop and his wife were committing many acts contrary to reason, the saint appeared to someone in a dream and said: “Go and tell Priscus to amend his evil works and let his works become good. Tell the presbyter Martin also: Because you consent to these works, you will be chastised; and if you do not wish to correct your perversity, you will die.”

When the man awoke, he spoke to a certain deacon, saying: “Go, I beg you. Since you are a friend in the bishop’s household, say these things either to the bishop or to the presbyter Martin.”

The deacon promised to speak, but afterward, having changed his mind, refused to say them. When he had gone to sleep that night, the saint appeared to him and said: “Why did you not say what the abbot told you?” He then clenched his fists and began striking the deacon’s throat.

In the morning, with his throat swollen and in great pain, the deacon approached the men and reported everything he had heard. But they paid no attention to what they had heard and said that it was merely a dream fantasy.

The presbyter Martin, however, immediately fell into fever and, while ill, recovered; [Note: It may perhaps be read: “He fell into a fever and, while ill, recovered.” But since he always consented in a flattering manner to the bishop ...] he continued to speak privately with the bishop in the oratory and to agree with him in the evil deeds and blasphemies which they uttered against the saint. He was again struck by fever and breathed out his spirit.

**XXXVII**

At this same time Saint Friardus also died, full of days, outstanding in holiness, eminent in action, and noble in life. We have recounted some of his miracles in the book which we wrote about his life [Note: In the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 10.]. When Bishop Felix arrived at the time of his passing, the entire cell trembled. I therefore have no doubt that something angelic was present there, since the place shook as he passed away. The bishop washed him, wrapped him in suitable garments, and committed him to burial.

**XXXVIII [Al. XXXII]**

To return, then, to the history [Note: Because the number of chapters has increased through the additions from the Cassinese manuscript, we shall place Chesne’s numbers in the margin alongside ours through the end of the book, for the convenience of citation. All manuscripts except the Beccensis read: “To return, or go back, to the history.” Most printed editions instead read: “At that time, when he had died.” Below, the Corbeiensis has “Athanieldus ... Leuveldus”; several printed editions have “Athanoldus.” We learn that “Leuvigildus” is the authentic name, and the period of his reign, from an ancient inscription placed on the tomb of a certain Goth. The inscription can still be seen in the church of the village called Truillas, two leagues from Narbonne. Ancient ruins of buildings and remains of aqueducts from the earliest period survive there. We give the inscription here in full:]

After King Athanagild had died in Spain, Leuva and his brother Leuvigild received the kingdom. When Leuva died, his brother Leuvigild seized the entire kingdom. After his wife had died, he took as wife Gunthsuentha [Note: The printed editions, together with the Beccensis, read “Gunsventha”; others have “Grandiswintha.”], the mother of Queen Brunichildis. He had two sons by his first wife; one of them married the daughter of Sigibert, and the other the daughter of Chilperic [Note: Hermenegild married Ingund; Reccared became betrothed to Rigunth, the daughter of Chilperic, but never married her, as will be said below.]. He divided the kingdom equally between them, killing all those who had been accustomed to kill kings and leaving none of them alive—not even one who “urinated against a wall.”

**XXXIX [Al. XXXIII]**

After the Emperor Justinian had died at Constantinople, Justin sought the imperial power. He was devoted to excessive greed, despised the poor, and plundered senators. His avarice was so great that he ordered iron chests to be made in which he could pile up talents of gold coins [Note: Thus the printed editions; the Colbertine and Corbeiensis manuscripts read “gold coin.”]. He is also said to have fallen into the Pelagian heresy. For not long afterward, having become deranged [Note: Thus the Corbeiensis, Beccensis, and Bellovacensis; this is a word familiar to Gregory. The printed editions and Paul the Deacon, Book I, chapter 11, read “having become insane.”], he appointed Tiberius Caesar as his associate to defend his provinces. Tiberius was a just, charitable, impartial man who exercised discernment and won victories; and, what surpasses all other good qualities, he was also a most genuine Christian.

Finally, King Sigibert sent envoys to the Emperor Justin [Note: Thus the Corbeiensis and Bellovacensis. The printed editions, together with the Colbertine and Beccensis, read “to Justinian.”], seeking peace—Uvarinarius the Frank and Firminus of Arverna. They traveled by sea, entered the city of Constantinople, spoke with the emperor, and obtained what they had requested. In the following year [Note: The Corbeiensis and Bellovacensis read “in another year.”] they returned to Gaul.

After this, Antioch in Egypt and Apamea in Syria, great cities, were captured by the Persians, and the people were led away captive. The basilica of Saint Julian, the martyr of Antioch, was then burned in a destructive fire.

Persian-Armenians came to the Emperor Justin [Note: Thus the Colbertine; the Corbeiensis has “the Persians.” The Beccensis reads “to Justinian ... the Persarmenians.” The other printed editions have “to the Emperor Justinian ... with a great quantity of gold.” Procopius mentions the Persarmenians in Book IV of *The Gothic War*. Valesius says that Greater Armenia was called Persarmenia because it was subject to the Persians.] carrying a great quantity of woven silk. They sought his friendship and said that they were hostile to the Persian emperor.

His envoys had come to them and said: “The imperial concern asks whether you are keeping inviolate the treaty made with him.”

When they replied that everything promised by them was being preserved intact, the envoys said: “You will show that you are keeping his friendship if you also worship fire, as he worships it.”

When the people replied that they would certainly not do this, the bishop who was present said: “What divinity is there in fire, that it should be worshiped? God created it for human use. It is kindled by fuel, extinguished by water, burns when applied, and grows cold when neglected” [Note: Others read: “and when neglected, where will it be?”].

As the bishop continued with these and similar words, the envoys, inflamed with fury, struck him with clubs amid their insults. When the people saw their priest covered in blood, they rushed upon the envoys, laid hands on them, and killed them. Then, as we have said, they sought the friendship of this emperor.

**XL [Al. XXXIV]**

Palladius, the son of the late Count Brittianus and Caesaria [Note: The Bellovacensis manuscript has “Britani”; others have “Britanni.” The older printed editions have “Brictianus.” This chapter is absent from the Beccensis and Badensis, although it is mentioned in their chapter lists.], obtained from King Sigibert the countship of the city of Gabalis [Note: Most printed editions misleadingly have “Gallicana”; the Colbertine has “Callitana.” But here the city of Gabalis is meant, now the village of Javoulz, while the episcopal see has been established at Mende.]. A dispute then arose between him and Bishop Parthenius, greatly setting the people against one another. For Palladius often overwhelmed the bishop with insults, various reproaches, and accusations, invading the property of the Church and despoiling his people.

As this dispute grew, they came into the presence of the aforesaid ruler and brought various charges against one another. Palladius repeatedly called the gentle bishop effeminate: “Where are your husbands, with whom you live in disgrace and shame?”

But divine vengeance immediately followed these words spoken against the priest and wiped them out. In the following year Palladius was removed from the countship and returned to Arverna, while Romanus sought the countship.

It happened one day that the two men met in the city of Arverna. As they quarreled over the matter of the countship, Palladius heard that King Sigibert intended to have him killed. But this was discovered to be false and to have been spread chiefly by Romanus.

Then Palladius, terrified by fear, was reduced to such a state of anguish that he threatened to kill himself with his own right hand. His mother and his kinsman Firminus watched him closely so that he would not carry out what he had conceived in his embittered mind. Yet, slipping away from his mother’s sight during an interval, he entered a room and obtained a period of solitude.

He drew his sword, stepped on the hilt, and raised the point toward his chest. Pressing down upon it, he drove the sword in beneath one breast and out through the shoulder blade of his back. Raising himself again, he was pierced through the other breast in the same way, fell, and died. We were astonished that this crime had been accomplished not without the work of the devil. The first wound could have killed him if the devil had not provided support by which he could complete this wicked act.

His mother ran up in terror and, bereaved, collapsed over her son’s little body; the whole household raised cries of lamentation.

Nevertheless, he was carried to the monastery of Chronon [Note: This is the form found in the Bellovacensis and Corbeiensis. The Colbertine and Chesne have “Chronensium”; most other printed editions have “Dironensium.” Saint Gallus, later bishop of Arverna, withdrew to this place, as is said in his *Life* among the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 6. It is now commonly called Cornon or Cournon, where there is a college of canons under the title of Saint Martin.] and committed to burial. He was not placed beside the bodies of Christians, nor did he deserve the solemn celebration of Masses [Note: Observe that Masses for the dead were formerly customarily celebrated when it was hoped that they would be useful to the deceased. See Mabillon, Book II of the *Gallican Liturgy*, no. 70.]. It is clear that these things happened to him for no other reason than the injury he had inflicted upon the bishop.

**XLI [Al. XXXV]**

Alboin, king of the Lombards, who had taken Chlothosind, the daughter of King Chlothachar, as his wife, abandoned his own country and set out for Italy with the entire Lombard people [Note: Several printed editions have “with four thousand Lombards.” Marius dates Alboin’s migration into Italy to the year 569 and his death to 572.].

After raising an army, they departed with their wives and children, intending to settle there. Once they had entered the region, they roamed through it for about seven years, reducing it to their power by plundering churches and killing priests.

When Alboin’s wife Chlothosind died, he took another wife whose father he had killed a short time before. Therefore, the woman, always hating her husband, waited for an opportunity at which she could avenge her father’s injuries.

It happened that, desiring one of the household servants, she killed her husband with poison [Note: This was Rosemund, daughter of Cunimund, king of the Gepids. First she arranged for her husband Alboin to be killed; then, when she attempted to kill her adulterous lover Helmigis with poison, she was forced to drink the remaining poison after he had already drunk half of it, and they died together. See Paul’s *History of the Lombards*, Book I, chapter 27, and Book II, chapters 28–29.]. After he died, she departed with the servant, but they were captured and killed together. The Lombards then appointed another king over themselves.

**XLII [Al. XXXVI]**

Eunius, also called Mummolus, obtained the patriciate from King Guntchramn. I have thought it appropriate to trace somewhat further back the origin of his military career.

He was born of a father named Peonius [Note: Several printed editions have “Poenius”; the Colbertine has “Pionius.”] and was a citizen of the city of Auxerre. Peonius governed the countship of that municipality.

When he sent gifts to the king through his son in order to renew his office [Note: That is, so that his tenure as count might be extended. At that time our kings customarily appointed judges or prefects, who were called counts, over cities or towns for a fixed period. If these officials provided gifts and no one complained about them, their office was easily granted to them for the same period again. This was also sometimes a path to higher dignities, as happened in Mummolus’s case. The word “office” often signifies a function. See Bignon on Book I of Marculf, form 11.], the son, having given away his father’s property, sought his father’s countship and displaced the parent whom he ought to have supported.

From that point he advanced step by step and was raised to a higher summit. When the Lombards burst into Gaul, the patrician Amatus, who had recently succeeded Celsus, went out against them, engaged in battle, turned his back, and fell [Note: Most printed editions have “Armatus Pericius, who had recently succeeded Celsus. They met there.” But Paul the Deacon, Book III, chapter 3, also calls him the patrician Amatus.].

The Lombards are said to have inflicted such slaughter upon the Burgundians that the number of the slain could not be counted. Laden with plunder, they withdrew again into Italy.

After they had departed, Eunius, who was also Mummolus, was summoned by the king and obtained the dignity of patrician.

When the Lombards again invaded Gaul and advanced as far as Mustias-Calmes [Note: This is the reading of the Bellovacensis. The Corbeiensis has “Musticascalmes”; the Beccensis, “Mutias-Calmes”; several printed editions have “Musciascalmes.” Our reading is found in Paul, Book III of the *History of the Lombards*, chapter 4, where this Lombard invasion is also described.], which lies near the city of Embrun, Mummolus moved his army and marched there with the Burgundians.

After surrounding the Lombards with his army and making barricades of felled trees, he fell upon them through the trackless parts of the forests. He killed many [Col. 0304C], captured some, and sent them to the king. The king ordered them to be kept scattered in various places, while a few escaped by flight, so that they might report the events to their homeland.

**XLIII [Al. XXXVII]**

Among those in this battle were the brothers and bishops Salonius and Sagittarius [Note: Some printed editions have “Salvinus,” because they read that form instead of “Salonius,” as in the Colbertine. Salonius of Embrun and Sagittarius of Gap were bishops.]. They are said to have killed many with their own hands—which is worse—not armed with the heavenly cross but equipped with secular helmet or breastplate.

This was Mummolus’s first victory in battle.

Afterward the Saxons who had come into Italy with the Lombards again burst into Gaul. Within the territory of Riez, that is, at the village of Stablon [Note: Thus the old manuscripts; Chesne has “Staplon.” The place is now commonly called Stoblon or Establon, in the diocese of Riez in Provence.], they pitched camp and ranged through the villages of neighboring cities, carrying off plunder, taking captives, and laying everything waste.

When Mummolus learned of this, he moved his army and fell upon them. He killed many thousands of them and did not stop slaughtering until evening, when night brought an end to the fighting. He had found them unprepared and unaware of what had happened.

At daybreak the Saxons drew up their army and prepared for battle. But messengers intervened, and they made peace. After giving gifts to Mummolus, they departed, leaving behind all the region’s plunder and the captives [Note: The printed editions place the comma in such a way that the Saxons appear to have departed with the captives. But from Paul the Deacon, Book III, chapter 5, it is clear that the words “with the captives” belong with what precedes, since he reads: “leaving behind the captives and all the plunder, they returned to Italy.” See also chapters 6 and 8 of the same Paul.]. First they swore that they would return to Gaul in submission to the kings and as auxiliaries [Also: “as helpers”] of the Franks.

Thus the Saxons returned to Italy, taking with them their wives, children, and all their property, intending to return to Gaul so that King Sigibert might gather them together and settle them in the place from which they had departed.

They divided themselves, as they say, into two groups. One came by way of the city of Nicea, the other by way of Embrun, following the same route that they had taken the previous year. They joined one another in the territory of Avignon [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions, together with the Beccensis, have “in the territory of Arverna.” But the manuscript reading is preferable, since below they were intercepted by Mummolus while crossing the Rhône. This could not have happened if they had already been in the territory of Arverna, which lay far from the banks of the Rhône. The territory of Avignon is therefore meant here. Fredegar supports us, chapter 68.].

It was then the harvest season. That place had an abundance of the earth’s produce lying in the open air, for the inhabitants had stored none of it at home. At last, when they came to the threshing floors, they divided the crops among themselves. Gathering and threshing them, they ate the grain, leaving nothing for those who had done the labor.

But after they had consumed the produce and reached the bank of the Rhône River, intending to cross the stream and proceed to the kingdom of King Sigibert, Mummolus met them and said:

“You shall not cross this stream. Behold, you have ravaged the regions of my lord the king, gathered the crops, devastated the herds [Note: Most printed editions add “slaughtered them”], delivered the houses to the flames, and cut down the olive groves and vineyards. You shall not go up from here unless you first make satisfaction to those whom you left behind in small numbers. Otherwise you will not escape my hands unless I set the sword upon you, and I shall avenge the injury done to my lord, King Guntchramn, upon your wives and children.”

Then, greatly afraid, they gave many thousands of gold coins as their ransom [Note: The Corbeiensis manuscript has “gold coins”], and they were permitted to cross. Thus they reached Arverna.

It was then spring. There they put forward strips of cut bronze [Note: Others have “tiles”] in place of gold. Anyone who saw them had no doubt that they were tested and assayed gold. For they had been colored by some unknown trick. Deceived by this fraud, some gave gold and received bronze and were reduced to poverty.

They then crossed to King Sigibert and were settled in the place from which they had previously departed.

**XLIV [Al. XXXVII]**

This chapter is absent from the Corbeiensis and Bellovacensis manuscripts.

In the kingdom of King Sigibert, Jovinus, governor of Provence, was removed from office, and Albinus was appointed in his place. This caused great hostility between them.

When overseas ships arrived at the harbor of Massilia [Note: Most printed editions have only “When the overseas ships arrived,” omitting the rest. It is clear from the title of the chapter that these events took place at Massilia, and that the chapter concerns the archdeacon of Massilia. “Harbor” is frequently used for a port by Sidonius. See Joseph Laurentius’s *Amaltheon*.], the men of the archdeacon Vigilius stole seventy vessels of oil and fish sauce, commonly called *orcae* [Note: The Colbertine has “arcae,” but our reading should be retained. An *orca* is a customary type of vessel.], without their owner’s knowledge.

When the merchant discovered that his property had been stolen, he began diligently investigating where the stolen goods had been concealed. While making inquiries, he heard from someone that the men of the archdeacon Vigilius had committed the theft.

The report reached the archdeacon. He investigated and discovered the matter, but instead of making it public he began to excuse his men, saying: “No one has ever gone out from my house who would dare to commit such an act.”

While the archdeacon was making this sort of excuse, the merchant went to Albinus, explained his case, and accused the archdeacon of involvement in this fraudulent crime.

On the holy day of the Lord’s Nativity, when the bishop arrived at the church, the archdeacon appeared dressed in white. As was customary [Note: It was customary that when a bishop came to the church to celebrate, the archdeacon and the rest of the clergy, dressed in white and carrying smoking censers, should meet him. See Paul of Mérida in Mabillon, Book I of the *Gallican Liturgy*, chapter 7, and elsewhere.], he invited the bishop to proceed to the altar and celebrate the solemnity of the holy day at the proper time.

Without delay, Albinus leapt from his seat, seized the archdeacon, dragged him away, beat him with fists and feet, and confined him in prison [Note: Most printed editions have only “he confined the archdeacon,” omitting the other words.].

Neither the bishop, nor the citizens, nor any person of rank, nor even the voice of the entire people crying out could ever obtain that the archdeacon be allowed, after giving sureties, to celebrate the holy day with the others and that his accusation be heard later. Nor did Albinus, because of the sacred solemnity itself, feel any fear that he should not seize a minister of the Lord’s altar on such a day.

What more is there to say? He condemned the archdeacon to pay four thousand solidi. The archdeacon appeared before King Sigibert and, with Jovinus pursuing the matter, settled it by paying four times the amount.

**XLV [Al. XXXIX]**

After this, three Lombard leaders—Amo, Zaban, and Rhodanus [Note: They were among the leaders who ruled the Lombards after the murder of King Cleph in the year 574.]—invaded Gaul.

Amo took the road through Embrun and advanced as far as Machovilla [Note: This is the reading of the two old manuscripts, the Corbeiensis and Bellovacensis. The others, together with the printed editions, have “Machao-villa,” except the Colbertine, which lacks the word “villa.” Paul the Deacon, Book III, chapter 8, agrees with the old manuscripts and reads “Machovilla.”], in the territory of Avignon, which Mummolus had received as a royal gift. There he pitched his tents.

Zaban, descending by way of Die [Note: Some printed editions have “Dea,” which amounts to the same thing. Dia or Dea was a bishop’s city of the Vocontii and remains famous today. The Bellovacensis has “Verdunensis,” and the Corbeiensis “Virdunensis,” although its first hand had written “Vinsunensis.” The correction is from the same period as the manuscript itself. Freherus notes in the margin that the Palatine manuscript has “Virdunensis.” Valesius therefore thinks that this city had two names: one Latin, namely Dea, and another Gallic, namely Virdunum. The same author observes elsewhere that there is a river in Provence called Verdun, commonly Verdon, from which some place mentioned here may perhaps have received its name. Paul the Deacon, who recounts all these expeditions of the Lombards and Saxons in almost the same words as Gregory, has “Diensem” in chapter 8, where he describes this invasion.], came to the city of Valence and set up camp there.

Rhodanus attacked the city of Grenoble and spread out his tents there. Amo also ravaged the province of Arles, together with the surrounding cities. Advancing as far as the very Stony Plain [Note: Commonly called La Crau, as Cointius notes.], which lies beside the city of Massilia [Note: The Bellovacensis has “and receiving as much”;], he stripped it both of livestock and of people. He laid siege to Aix and withdrew after receiving twenty-two pounds of silver from its inhabitants.

Rhodanus and Zaban acted similarly in the places to which they had come.

When this was reported to Mummolus, he moved his army and went to meet Rhodanus, who was ravaging Grenoble. But while the army was laboriously crossing the river Isère [Note: Thus the Corbeiensis and Bellovacensis. Others have “Esera,” “Isara,” or, with aspiration, “Hesera” and “Hiser.” These variant readings also occur in other writers, but they designate the same river, commonly called the Isère, which rises in Savoy and joins the Rhône somewhat above Valence.], by God’s command an animal entered the stream and showed them a ford. Thus the people reached the farther bank.

When the Lombards saw this, they did not delay but drew their swords and attacked them. Battle was joined, and so many Lombards were slaughtered that Rhodanus, wounded by a spear, fled to the high mountains.

From there, with the five hundred men who remained to him, he burst through the trackless forest and reached Zaban, who was then besieging the city of Valence. He told him everything that had happened.

They then gave everything over to plunder and returned to the city of Embrun. There Mummolus met them face to face with a countless army. Battle was joined; the Lombard phalanxes were cut down to the point of annihilation, and the leaders returned to Italy with only a few men.

When they had reached the city of Susa [Note: Others have “Siosium”; the name of Segusium is still preserved today, commonly called Susa, on the Dora River.], the inhabitants received them harshly, especially because Sisinnius, the master of the soldiers on the emperor’s side, was stationed in that city.

A boy pretending to be Mummolus’s messenger, in Zaban’s presence, brought a letter to Sisinnius and offered him greetings in Mummolus’s name, saying: “He himself is close at hand.”

When Zaban heard this, he quickly withdrew from the city and passed on.

When Amo heard these things, he gathered all the plunder along the route and departed. But when the snows resisted him, he abandoned the plunder and could scarcely escape with a few men.

For they had been terrified by Mummolus’s prowess.

## XLVI [Alternative XL]

For Mummolus fought many wars, in which he emerged victorious. For after the death of Charibert, when Chilperic had taken possession of Tours and Poitiers—which had fallen by agreement to Sigibert’s share—the king himself, together with his brother Guntram, chose Mummolus to restore these cities to their [alternative: “true”] lord. Coming to Tours, he drove out Chlodovech, Chilperic’s son, and, having exacted oaths from the people in favor of King Sigibert, proceeded to Poitiers. But Basilus and Sigharius, citizens of Poitiers,

[Note: Other editions have *Siagrius*. The *Regm.* manuscript has *Pasilius ac Siagrius*. Fortunatus’s poem 18 in Book IV is an epitaph for a certain distinguished Basilus of Poitiers, who may perhaps be the same man Gregorius mentions here.]

gathered a multitude and wished to resist. He surrounded them from different directions, overwhelmed them, buried them, and killed them; and thus, advancing to Poitiers, he exacted the oaths. Let what has been said meanwhile about Mummolus suffice

[Note: The remainder, and so forth, to the end of the chapter is missing in almost all manuscripts.]

and let the rest be deferred to a later time.

## XLVII [Alternative XLI]. The Death of Andarchius

Since I am about to speak of the death of Andarchius, I think it appropriate first to begin with his family and homeland. He was, as they report,

[Note: The *Colb.* manuscript, together with most printed editions, reads *Facilis*.]

a slave of the senator Felix. Assigned to serve his master and placed with him for literary studies, he emerged well educated. For he was thoroughly instructed in the works of Virgil, the books of the Theodosian Code, and the art of calculation.

Puffed up by this learning, he began to despise his masters. When he was traveling to the city of Massilia by order of King Sigibert, he commended himself to Duke Lupus.

[Note: He was duke of the region of Champagne around Rheims, whom Gregorius mentions more than once below. Fortunatus continues his praises in Book VII, poems 7, 8, and 9.]

On returning from there, Lupus ordered him to accompany him and carefully commended him to King Sigibert, handing him over for service. The king, sending him to various places, gave him an opportunity to serve in military affairs. Thus treated almost as an *honoratus*

[Note: That is, almost as one of those who administered civil and public affairs in the prince’s name, to whom the title *Honoratus* was granted. On this title, see Valesius’s notes on Ammianus Marcellinus and Du Cange’s *Glossary*.]

he came to Auvergne. There he formed a friendship with Ursus, a citizen of that city.

Meanwhile, being of keen intelligence and wishing to marry his daughter, he hid a breastplate, as they say, in a document case, the sort in which papers are usually kept. He said to the woman, the wife of Ursus:

“Because I entrust to you, hidden in this document case, more than sixteen thousand gold pieces of mine, which may become yours if you give me your daughter to marry.”

But—

> What can you not compel mortal hearts to do,  
> accursed hunger for gold?  
>   
> *(Virgil, Aeneid, Book III.)*

The woman, believing this ingenuously, promised, in her husband’s absence, to give the girl to him in marriage. But Andarchius returned to the king and presented an order to the local judge that the girl should be joined to him in marriage, saying:

“I gave a pledge at her betrothal.”

But the man denied it, saying:

“I neither know who you are nor where you come from, nor possess anything of yours.”

As the dispute spread and grew more intense, Andarchius requested that Ursus be summoned into the king’s presence. When he had come to the estate of Brennacum,

[Note: The *Colb.* manuscript has *Brinna*.]

he sought out another man named Ursus, brought him secretly to the altar, and made him swear and say:

“By this holy place and the relics of the blessed martyrs: if I do not give my daughter to you in marriage, I will not delay to pay you sixteen thousand solidi.”

Witnesses were standing in the sacristy, secretly listening to the speaker’s words, but not seeing at all the person who was speaking. Then Andarchius soothed Ursus with gentle words and caused him to return to his homeland without the king’s presence. Having made this oath, he produced before the departing king a written record of the sworn statements, saying:

[Note: Thus the *Colb.*, *Bec.*, and *Regm.* manuscripts. But *Chesn.* has “he presented it to him”; other editions have “he presented it to him while he was departing.” *Bellov.* more briefly has “he presented it, saying.”]

“Ursus wrote this and this to me; and therefore I request an order from Your Glory that he give me his daughter in marriage. Otherwise, let me be permitted to possess his property until, after receiving sixteen thousand solidi, I withdraw from this case.”

Having obtained the royal orders, Andarchius returned to Auvergne and showed the judge the king’s command. Ursus, however, withdrew into the territory of Velay.

[Note: Most printed editions, together with *Bec.* and *Colb.*, have *Villavum*. *Regm.* and *Bad.* have *Villanum*, as also below. It is certain that Velay is intended, still commonly called *le Velay*. See the notes on Book X, chapter 25.]

When his property was being handed over to this man, Andarchius also came into Velay. Entering one of Ursus’s houses, he ordered dinner to be prepared for him and commanded that water be heated for his bath. But when the household servants failed to obey their by-no-means uncouth master, he beat some with clubs and others with rods, striking several on the head and drawing blood.

The household was thrown into confusion. Dinner was prepared, Andarchius washed in hot water, became drunk with wine, and settled down upon a bed. Only seven servants were with him. When they had fallen into deep sleep, buried no less in sleep than in wine, Ursus gathered his household and closed the doors of the house, which were made of wooden boards. Taking the keys, he broke up the heaps of grain that were there;

[Note: The word *metae* is used for a heap of sheaves, as Alteserra proves with many examples in his notes on this passage. See Hincmarus, *Life of Saint Remigius*.]

then he piled these heaps of grain, which at that time was in sheaves, around and over the house, so that the house could be seen entirely covered by them. Having then set fire to them in various places, when the building’s timbers, already burning above the unfortunate men, began to collapse, they awoke and raised their voices.

[Note: Other editions have “they were awakened to cries that had been uttered.”]

But no one was there to hear them, until the entire house had burned down and the fire consumed them as well. Ursus, fearing what might happen, sought the basilica of Saint Julian; and, having given gifts to the king, he recovered all his property.

## XLVIII [Alternative XLII]

Chlodovech, the son of Chilperic, having been driven from Tours, went to Bordeaux. Finally, while he was staying in the city of Bordeaux with no one troubling him at all, a certain Sigulf, on Sigibert’s side, set himself against him. He pursued him as he fled, with trumpets and horns, as though he were pursuing a staggering stag; and Chlodovech scarcely had a free route by which to return to his father. Nevertheless, passing back through Angers, he returned to him.

When a dispute arose between the kings Guntram

[Note: Valesius, followed by Cointius, thinks *Chilpericum* should be read. Gregorius is speaking here and in the following chapters of the war that broke out between Chilperic and Sigibert; to reconcile them, Guntram arranged for the bishops under his rule to assemble at Paris. Nevertheless, it was thought improper to alter the reading, since all printed editions and manuscripts have *Guntchramnum*. Cointius believes that the Fourth Council of Paris, held in 573, is being praised here.]

and Sigibert, King Guntram assembled at Paris all the bishops of his kingdom, so that they might declare where the truth lay between the two. But because their sins caused the civil war to grow more dangerous, they delayed hearing them.
