King Chilperic, however, moved by anger, invaded through his elder son Theodobert—the same son who had once been captured by Sigibert and had sworn loyalty to him

[Note: Above, chapter 23. Most printed editions, together with some manuscripts, have “once captured,” and so forth.]

—the cities belonging to Sigibert, namely Tours and Poitiers, and the other cities situated this side of the Loire. Coming to Poitiers, Theodobert fought against Duke Gundobald.

[Note: *Bel.* and *Corb.* have *Gundoaldum*; *Regm.*, *Gundobaudum*; another version, *Guntwaldum*.]

When Gundobald’s army turned its back, Theodobert inflicted a great slaughter upon that people. He also burned a large part of the region of Tours; and, unless they had surrendered in time, he would immediately have conquered the whole of it. Then, after moving his army, he invaded, devastated, and destroyed the Limousin, the Quercy, and the other provinces of those people;

[Note: *Corb.* and *Bell.* have “the neighboring provinces of those regions”; *Bad.*, “the remaining provinces”; *Regm.*, “the remaining cities of those regions”; *Bec.*, “the provinces of those cities.”]

he burned churches, stripped them of their sacred vessels, killed clerics, demolished men’s monasteries, and violated the girls,

[Note: So the manuscripts; most printed editions have “violated the girls,” *Freh.* “the girl,” and below, together with *Bec.*, “of the persecutor.”]

and devastated everything. At that time there was a worse groaning in the churches than during the persecution of Diocletian.

## XLIX [Alternative XLIII]

[Note: This chapter is absent from *Bell.* and *Corb.*.]

We are still astonished and amazed that such great blows had fallen upon them. But let us return to what their ancestors did and what these men are perpetrating. After the preaching of priests, their ancestors turned from shrines to churches; these men daily plunder churches. Their ancestors venerated and obeyed the priests of the Lord with all their hearts; these men not only do not listen, but even persecute them. Their ancestors enriched monasteries and churches; these men demolish and overthrow them.

What shall I say about the monastery of Latta, in which the relics of blessed Martin are kept?

[Note: *Colb.* has *Lata*; *Bec.*, “the monastery of Lettat.” Perhaps the monastery mentioned here stood in the village that is still called Siran-la-Late, or la-Latte, not far from Severiacum, Sivré, Bellismum, and Noviliacum, Neuilli.]

When one band of enemies approached it and planned to cross the nearby river in order to plunder the monastery, the monks shouted:

“Do not cross over here, barbarians, do not! This is the monastery of blessed Martin.”

When many of them heard this, they were moved by fear of God and turned back. Yet twenty of them, who did not fear God and did not honor the blessed confessor, boarded a ship and crossed over. Spurred on by the Enemy, they beat the monks, overturned the monastery, and plundered its property. Making bundles of the goods, they loaded them onto the ship.

When they entered the river, the keel immediately veered this way and that. As they had lost the assistance of their oars and tried to return by driving the shafts of their spears into the riverbed, the ship split open beneath their feet, and each man’s iron weapon, which he was holding against himself, was driven into his breast. Thus all of them were pierced through and killed by their own weapons.

Only one of them remained unharmed—the man who had rebuked them and warned them not to commit these deeds. If anyone judges that this happened by chance, let him observe that one innocent man escaped among many guilty men. After the others were killed, the monks pulled them and their goods from the riverbed, buried the men, and restored the goods to the monastery.

## L [Alternative XLIX]

While these things were happening, King Sigibert stirred up those peoples who live beyond the Rhine

[Note: *Chol.* has “Sigibert stirred up three peoples,” and so forth.]

and, beginning a civil war, prepared to march against his brother Chilperic. When Chilperic heard this, he sent envoys to his brother Guntram. They joined together and made a pact that neither would allow his brother to perish.

But when Sigibert arrived bringing those peoples, and Chilperic was stationed on the other side with his army, King Sigibert, intending to march against his brother, found no place where he could cross the river Seine.

[Note: All manuscripts have this reading except *Colb.* and *Chesn.*, which have *Segona*, as though the Saône—perhaps the river Sagona or Arar, now called the Saône—were intended here. The old printed editions also have *Sequanam*. Gregory’s *Book II of the Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 7, makes it clear that *Sequanam* should be read here. See also Book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 72.]

He sent a message to his brother Guntram, saying:

“If you do not permit me to cross this river through your territory, I will march against you with my entire army.”

Fearing this, Guntram made a pact with him and permitted him to cross.

When Chilperic learned that Guntram had abandoned him and gone over to Sigibert, he moved his camp and went as far as the village of Avallocium near Chartres.

[Note: This village is on the Lidericus River and was later called Allocium or Alogium, now Alluye. Most manuscripts and editions write *Alocium*; *Bec.* has *Valocium*.]

Sigibert pursued him and asked that a battlefield be prepared for him.

[Note: At that time blessed Germanus, bishop of Paris, wrote to Brunechildis, Sigibert’s wife, asking her to avert the destruction threatening the whole region. This letter, worthy of so great a bishop exhorting Christian rulers to peace, remains; we shall include it in the Appendix.]

But Chilperic, fearing that the two armies might clash and that their kingdom might consequently collapse, sought peace. He returned the cities that Theodobert had unjustly invaded, begging that their inhabitants should not be blamed in any way, since Theodobert had acquired them by unjustly oppressing them with fire and sword.

The villages around Paris were also largely consumed by flames at that time, and both houses and the remaining property were plundered by the enemy, so that captives too were carried away. The king protested that these things should not be done, but he could not overcome the fury of the peoples who had come from the farther side of the Rhine. He endured everything patiently until he could return home.

Then some of those foreign peoples murmured against him, asking why he had withdrawn from the contest. But he, being fearless, mounted his horse and went toward them, soothing them with gentle words, while later ordering many of them to be stoned to death.

Nor is there any doubt that this too occurred through the power of blessed Martin, so that they might be brought to peace without war. For on the very day on which they made peace, three paralytics were brought to the basilica of blessed Martin.

[Note: Gregory recounts the healing of these three paralytics in Book II of the *Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapters 5, 6, and 7.]

With the Lord’s help, we shall discuss this in the books that follow.

## LI [Alternative XLV]

It is painful to the mind to recount these civil wars. For a year later Chilperic again sent envoys to his brother Guntram, saying:

“Let my brother come with me; let us meet, make peace, and pursue our enemy Sigibert.”

When this had been done, and they had seen one another and honored each other with gifts, Chilperic moved his army as far as Rheims, burning and conquering everything.

When Sigibert heard this, he again summoned those peoples whom we mentioned above, came to Paris, and prepared to march against his brother. He sent messengers to the people of Dunois and Tours, ordering them to march against Theodobert. When they ignored this, the king sent the dukes Godegisel and Guntram

to lead the campaign. They raised an army and marched against him.

But abandoned by his own men, Theodobert remained with only a few; nevertheless, he did not hesitate to go out to battle. When they engaged, Theodobert was defeated and fell on the field. His enemies stripped his lifeless body—a thing painful to say.

Then a certain Arnulf gathered the body, washed it, and clothed it in suitable garments. It was buried in the city of Angoulême.

[Note: *Corb.*, *Bell.*, and *Freh.* have *Colosinensem*; *Colb.*, *Ecolunensem*; *Bec.* and *Mor. 5*, *Ecolinensem*.]

King Chilperic, however, learning that Guntram had again made peace with Sigibert, fortified himself within the walls of Tournai with his wife and children.

## LII [Alternative XLVI]

In that year a flash was seen to pass across the sky,

[Note: So *Corb.*; the others, together with the printed editions, have “lightning was seen.”]

just as we had once seen happen before the death of Chlothar. Sigibert, having obtained the cities situated this side of Paris, advanced as far as Rouen, wishing to surrender those same cities to the enemy. His own men prevented him from doing so.

Returning from there, he entered Paris; and Brunechildis came to him there with her sons. Then the Franks who had formerly looked to Childebert the elder sent an embassy to Sigibert, asking him to come to them, abandon Chilperic, and establish himself as king over them.

Hearing this, he sent men to besiege his brother in the city mentioned above,

[Note: That is, in Tournai, as appears from the preceding chapter.]

intending to hurry there himself. Saint Germanus the bishop said to him:

“If you go and refuse to kill your brother, you will return alive and victorious; but if you entertain another plan, you will die. For the Lord said through Solomon: ‘The pit that you prepare for your brother, you will fall into yourself’ (Proverbs 26:27).”

But because of his sins he neglected to heed this.

When he came to an estate called Victoriacum,

[Note: As Miraeus observes, this village lies between Douai and Arras on the Scarpe River and is still called Vitry. Hariulfus, in his *Chronicle of Centula*, calls it a royal estate situated in the suburb of Arras.]

his entire army gathered around him, and they placed him upon a shield and proclaimed him king.

Then two young men, carrying powerful knives commonly called *scramasaxes*,

[Note: *Corb.* has *scrumasaxos*; *Regm.*, *scramaxos*; *Colb.*, *chramasaxos*. The word is barbarian and means knives for wounding, or short swords, from the Saxon *sax* or *sachs*. See Vossius, *On the Latin Language*, Book II, chapter 17.]

which had been smeared with poison, and pretending that they were engaged in another matter,

[Note: *Bell.*, *Mor. s.*, and others have “were suggesting another matter.” Marius records the murder of Sigibert under the year 576, although learned scholars believe it occurred in the preceding year.]

having been bewitched by Queen Fredegund, struck him in both sides. Crying out and falling, he gave up his spirit shortly afterward.

There too his chamberlain Charegisilus fell. There also was Sigila, who had once come from Gothia; he was badly mutilated and was later captured by King Chilperic. Chilperic burned every one of his joints with red-hot cauteries, separated him limb from limb,

[Note: *Corb.* has “having separated his limbs.”]

and brought his life to a cruel end.

That Charegisilus was as frivolous in his work as he was weighty in his greed. Rising from humble beginnings, he became great with the king through flattery; he was a claimant to other people’s property and a breaker of wills. His life ended in such a way that, as death approached, he did not deserve to fulfill his own wish, since he had often destroyed the wishes of others.

King Chilperic, meanwhile, was caught in an uncertain situation and did not know whether he would escape or perish, until messengers came to him announcing his brother’s death. Then he departed from Tournai with his wife and sons and buried him at the village of Lambres, having clothed him there.

[Note: This village lies on the Scarpe River between Cambrai and Arras. Cognatus, in his *History of Tournai*, places it near Douai, on the road to Arras. Fortunatus discusses this change in Chilperic’s fortune in Book IX, poem 1.]

From there Sigibert was later transferred to the basilica of Saint Medard at Soissons, which Chilperic himself had built, and was buried beside his father Chlothar.

Sigibert died in the fourteenth year of his reign, at the age of forty. From the death of the elder Theudibert to the death of Sigibert, twenty-nine years are reckoned.

[Note: *Corb.* and *Colb.*, together with *Bad.*, have twenty-eight.]

Between the death of Sigibert and that of his grandson Theodobert there were eighteen days. After Sigibert died, his son Childebert reigned in his place.

From the beginning up to the Flood: 2,242 years. From the Flood to Abraham: 942 years. From Abraham to the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt: 462 years.

[Note: *Colb.* has 452; *Bec.*, 442.]

From the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt to the building of Solomon’s Temple: 480 years. From the building of the Temple to its destruction and the migration into Babylon: 390 years.

[Note: This is the reading of the *Bell.* and *Corb.* manuscripts, which write the number as CCCLXL. *Regm.*, *Bec.*, and *Bad.* have 340; *Colb.* and *Chesn.*, 361; other printed editions, 360.]

From the migration to the Passion of the Lord: 668 years.

[Note: *Colb.*, *Chesn.*, and *Bad.* have 648. The *Regm.* manuscript has no number.]

From the Passion of the Lord to the death of Saint Martin: 412 years. From the death of Saint Martin to the death of King Chlodovech: 112 years. From the death of King Chlodovech to the death of Theudibert: 37 years.

[Note: The *Colb.* manuscript has 34.]

From the death of Theudibert to the death of Sigibert: 29 years. These together amount to 5,774 years.

[Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts, together with *Bad.* The calculation agrees with the individual figures as given in our text. The other printed editions, however, have 5,744.]

# BOOK FIVE

## Prologue

It wearies me to recount the various civil wars that severely afflict the Frankish people and kingdom. What is worse is that we now see the time which the Lord foretold at the beginning of sorrows:

“Father rises against son, son against father, brother against brother, and neighbor against neighbor” (Matthew 10:21).

The examples of earlier kings ought to frighten them, for as soon as they were divided, they were killed by their enemies. How often even the City of cities, the head of the whole world, has fallen after entering into civil wars, and, when they ceased, risen again as though from the dust!

Would that you too, O kings, were exercised in those wars in which your ancestors labored, so that peoples, terrified by your peace, might be subdued by your strength. Remember what Chlodovech, the head of your victories, did: he killed hostile kings, crushed harmful peoples, and subjected native nations, whose kingdom he left to you intact and unharmed.

And when he did this, he possessed neither gold nor silver, as there is now in your treasuries.

[Note: This shows that Chlodovech and his sons did not accumulate much silver. Hence above, Book III, chapter 7, Theodoric was distressed at the loss of a silver dish.]

What are you doing? What are you seeking? What do you not have in abundance? Luxuries multiply in your houses;

[Note: *Corb.* and *Bell.* have “In the houses, military affairs.”]

wine, grain, and oil overflow in your storerooms; gold and silver are heaped up in your treasuries. One thing is lacking to you: because you do not have peace, you need the grace of God.

Why does one take away another’s property? Why does one covet what belongs to another?

[Note: Others have “Why does one take away another’s property, when he covets what belongs to another?”]

Beware, I beg you, of the Apostle’s words:

“If you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another” (Galatians 5:15).

Examine carefully the writings of the ancients, and you will see what civil wars produce. Consider what Orosius writes about the Carthaginians,

[Note: Book IV, especially from chapter 6 onward, is almost entirely about the Carthaginians.]

who, after saying that their city and territory were destroyed after seven hundred years, added:

“What preserved it for so long? Concord. What destroyed it after so many years? Discord.”

Beware discord; beware civil wars, which attack both you and your people. What else can be expected except that, when your army has fallen, you too, left without support and immediately overwhelmed by hostile peoples, will collapse?

If civil war delights you, O king, wage the war that the Apostle says is waged within a human being (Galatians 5:17): let the spirit desire against the flesh, let vices yield to virtues, and, being free, serve your Head—that is, Christ—you who once had been bound in slavery to the root of evils.

## I

After King Sigibert had been killed at the estate of Victoriacum, Queen Brunichildis remained at Paris with her children. When news of this deed reached her, and she, confused by grief and mourning, did not know what to do, Duke Gundobald

[Note: The printed editions, together with *Regm.*, have *Gundobaldus*; most manuscripts have *Gundovaldus*. *Corb.* has “King Gundovaldus.”]

secretly seized her little son Childebert, rescued him from the imminent danger of death, gathered the peoples over whom his father had ruled, and established him as king. The child had scarcely completed one lustrum of life—that is, five years—and began to reign on the day of the Lord’s Nativity.

In the first year of his reign, King Chilperic came to Paris, seized Brunichildis, and sent her into exile at the city of Rouen. He also took away her treasures, which she had brought to Paris. He ordered her daughters to be held in the city of Meaux.

[Note: *Regm.* and *Bad.* have *Meldis*; *Bec.*, *Meledum*; three other manuscripts, *Meledus*. Most printed editions have *Meledis*, now commonly Meaux.]

Then Roccolenus

[Note: Others have *Rucculenus*; *Regm.*, *Rotolenus*; *Bec.*, *Ruccolenus*. Below, in chapter 4, it has *Ruccolinus* or *Rutulenus*.]

came to Tours with the men of Le Mans, plundered, and committed many crimes. How, for the many evils he perpetrated, he was struck down by the power of blessed Martin and died, we shall recount in what follows.

[Note: Below, chapter 4, and Book II of the *Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 27.]

## II

King Chilperic sent his son Merovech with an army to Poitiers. But Merovech abandoned his father’s arrangements, went to Tours, and there even kept the holy days of Easter. His army greatly devastated that region.

Pretending that he wished to go to his mother, he himself went to Rouen, where he joined Queen Brunichildis and took her as his wife. When Chilperic heard this—that Merovech had taken his uncle’s wife contrary to divine law and canon law—he was deeply angered and immediately marched to the town mentioned above.

When the two learned that he had decided to separate them, they fled for refuge to the basilica of Saint Martin, which was built of wooden boards above the city walls. When the king arrived and tried by many stratagems to remove them from there, while they suspected that he was acting deceitfully and did not believe him, he swore to them, saying:

“If it is God’s will, I myself will not attempt to separate you.”

[Note: Most printed editions, together with *Bec.*, have “if it should be God’s will”; *Bad.* has “if it should be God’s will, I myself would not attempt to separate you.”]

Hearing this oath,

[Note: Others have “receiving this oath.” The *Colb.* manuscript below has “he feasted with them.”]

they left the basilica. He kissed them, received them graciously, and dined with them. A few days later, taking Merovech with him, the king returned to Soissons.

[Note: Another reading has *Sessiones*, and below as well. *Regm.* and *Bec.* have *Sessionis*.]

### III

While they were staying there, some men from Campania assembled and attacked the city of Soissons [Col. 0317C]. After driving Queen Fredegund and Chlodevich, the son of Chilperic, out of it, they intended to bring the city under their own control. When King Chilperic learned of this [Note: [Col. 0317D] Valesius observes that Gregory here seems to contradict himself: he says that Chilperic was staying at Soissons, yet speaks of him as though he had not been there.], he marched there with an army, sending messengers to warn them not to wrong him and thereby bring about the destruction of both armies. But they disregarded this and prepared for battle. When the battle was joined, Chilperic’s side prevailed and put the opposing force to flight, striking down many brave and useful men among them. After routing the survivors, he entered Soissons.

After these events, because of Merovechus’s marriage to Brunichild, the king began to regard his son Merovechus with suspicion, saying that this battle had arisen through his wickedness. He ordered that Merovechus be disarmed and, with guards assigned to him, be kept under honorable custody [Note: [Col. 0317D] Distinguished men were always entrusted to the custody of honorable persons, as Jerome notes in Book II *Against Vigilantius*. See also Book I of *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 45. Pontius calls it “delicate custody” in the *Life of Saint Cyprian*, no. 15.], while he considered what arrangement to make concerning him in the future.

Godinus [Col. 0318A], who had transferred himself from Sigibert’s party to Chilperic and had been enriched by him with many gifts, had been the leader of this war. But, defeated in the field, he was the first to flee. The king confiscated the estates that he had granted him from the royal treasury in the territory of Soissons and gave them to the basilica of Saint Medard. Godinus himself also died not long afterward, overtaken by a sudden death.

His wife was taken by Rauchingus [Note: [Col. 0318D] Others read *Rauchinchus*], a man filled with every kind of vanity, swollen with pride, and insolent in his arrogance. He treated his subjects in such a way that he seemed not to recognize any humanity in himself; raging against his own people beyond the limits of human wickedness and folly [Note: [Col. 0318D] Corb. and Bell. read, “beyond measure and folly.”], he committed unspeakable evils.

For if, as is customary [Note: [Col. 0318D] Thus in Book II of Saint Gregory’s *Dialogues*, chapter 20, a certain monk held a lamp for Saint Benedict while he was sitting at table.], a servant held before him at a banquet a burning candle, he would have the servant’s legs stripped bare and would press the candle against them until the servant was deprived of its light. Then, when the candle had been relit, he would do the same again, until the entire lower legs of the servant holding it had been burned. If the servant tried to cry out or to move from that place to another, an unsheathed sword immediately threatened him. Thus, while the servant wept, Rauchingus would exult with great delight.

Some said that at that time two of his servants, as often happens, had come to love each other: a man and a girl. When this affection had continued for two years or more, they went together to a church. When Rauchingus learned of this, he approached the priest of the place and immediately asked that his servants, under ecclesiastical protection, be returned to him. Then the priest said to him:

“You know what reverence must be shown to the churches of God. You will not be able to take them unless you give assurance that their union will continue and likewise promise that they shall remain free from every bodily punishment” [Note: [Col. 0318D] A formula concerning this matter is preserved in Bignonius among the ancient works of uncertain authorship, no. 22. See also that distinguished man’s notes.].

But after remaining silent for a long time in uncertainty, he finally turned to the priest, placed his hands upon the altar with an oath, and said:

“Since they will never be separated by me; rather, I shall ensure that they remain in this union. For although it has displeased me that such things were done without the concurrence of my counsel [Note: [Col. 0318D] Colb., with some printed editions, reads *convenientia*; Bec. reads *conhibentia*.], nevertheless I gladly accept the fact that this man has not taken another’s maidservant, nor this woman a stranger’s servant.”

That priest, trusting the promise of the cunning man in his simplicity, returned the servants to him under protection. He accepted them, gave thanks, and withdrew to his house. At once he ordered a tree to be felled; its trunk, cut into sections and split with a wedge [Note: [Col. 0319C] Corb. reads, “its sections with wedges.” Chesn. reads, “its section with a wedge.” Bec. reads, “the trunk … hollowed out,” and so forth.], he ordered to be hollowed out. After earth had been dug to a depth of three or four feet, he ordered a vessel to be placed in the pit. There he arranged the girl as though dead and ordered the boy to be thrown on top of her. After a covering had been placed over it, he filled the pit with earth and buried them alive, saying:

“I have not violated my oath, since these two will never be separated.”

When this was reported to the priest, he ran there quickly and rebuked the man; with difficulty he obtained permission for them to be uncovered. Nevertheless, he brought the boy out alive, but found the girl suffocated. In such deeds he was exceedingly wicked, having no other usefulness [Note: [Col. 0319C] Regm. reads, “having absolutely no other usefulness.” In Corb. and Bell. the words from “exceedingly wicked” through “perverse deeds” are absent.] except in laughter, deceit, and every perverse action. Therefore, it was not undeserved that he departed from life in such a manner—he who, while enjoying this life, had done such things—as we shall relate later (Book IX, chapter 9).

Siggo, too, the *referendarius* [Note: [Col. 0319D] The *referendarius* was then what is now called a chancellor. On his office and privileges, see Mabillon, *On Diplomatics*, Book II, chapter 11, and Bignonius on formula 25 of Book I of Marculf. Below, *provocatus* means “promoted.”], who had held King Sigibert’s ring and had been summoned by King Chilperic to obtain the service that he had held during his brother’s time, abandoned Chilperic and went over to Childebert, King Sigibert’s son. His possessions in the territory of Soissons were obtained by Ansoaldus [Note: [Col. 0319D] Thus the manuscripts; most printed editions have *Ansovaldus*. Bec. has *Ansolvaldus*.]. Many others also who had transferred themselves from Sigibert’s kingdom to Chilperic withdrew from him. Siggo’s wife also died not long afterward [Note: [Col. 0319D] Regm. reads, “not after a long period of time.”]; but he took another wife.

### IV

In those days Roccolenus, sent by Chilperic, arrived at Tours with great arrogance. He pitched his camp beyond the Loire and sent messengers to us, demanding that we remove Guntchramnus, who at that time was being accused of Theodobert’s death, from the holy basilica. If we did not do so, he ordered that both the city and all its suburbs be burned.

When we heard this, we sent an embassy to him, saying that what he was demanding had never been done in ancient times here, and that even now the violation of the holy basilica could not be permitted. If it were done, it would bring prosperity neither to him nor to the king who had issued such commands. He should fear rather the holiness of the bishop, whose power on the previous day had restored a woman suffering from paralysis [Note: [Col. 0319D] Colb., with Chesn., reads “paralyzed limbs”; but the woman is called paralyzed in Book II of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 27, where this same story is related.].

Fearing none of this, while he was staying in the church’s house beyond the Loire, he broke open the house itself, which had been fastened with bolts [Note: [Col. 0319D] Thus Corb.; others read “cut apart.”]. The men of Le Mans, who had then arrived with him, even carried off the bolts themselves in filled leather bags [Note: [Col. 0319D] *Folles* are leather bags, that is, made of hide. See Juvenal, Satire 13.], overturned the grain stores, and devastated everything.

But while Roccolenus was doing these things, he was struck by God and became yellow with jaundice. He sent back his harsh commands, saying:

“Unless you cast Duke Guntchramnus out of the basilica today, I shall crush all the growing things around the city [Note: [Col. 0319D] Thus Corb., Bell., and Bec.; others, with Chesn., read “I shall devastate them.”], so that the place may become fit for the plow.”

Meanwhile, the holy day of Epiphany arrived, and he began to be tortured more and more. Then, taking counsel from his men, he crossed the river and approached the city. Finally, when the people were leaving the church singing psalms [Note: [Col. 0320C] By the institution of Perpetuus, the vigils of Epiphany were held in the cathedral church below, in Book X, chapter 31. From the present passage we learn that a procession then proceeded to the basilica of Saint Martin. At its head were first carried the standards or banners, then the cross, and sometimes also sacred relics, and so forth. This is also clear from other passages of Gregory; the custom still continues today in processions of the Catholic Church.], and hastening toward the holy basilica, he was carried on horseback behind the cross, with the standards preceding him.

But when he entered the holy basilica, the fury of his threats immediately cooled [Note: [Col. 0320D] Colb. reads “flared up.” Bell. and Corb. read “became fearless.”]. Returning from the church, he was unable to take any food that day [Col. 0320B]. From there, being very short of breath, he departed for Poitiers. For it was during the days of holy Lent, when he often ate the offspring of rabbits. After arranging the measures by which he intended either to oppress or condemn the citizens of Poitiers on the Kalends of March, he died the day before. Thus his pride and arrogance came to rest.

### V

At that time Felix, bishop of the city of Nantes [Note: [Col. 0320D] This chapter is absent from Corb., Bell., and Colb.; it is found in Casin., Bec., Regm., and others. Gregory often speaks of Felix, as does Fortunatus, who celebrated his praises at length, especially in Book III, poems 3, 4, and following. Felix subscribed to the Second Council of Tours in 567 and the Fourth Council of Paris in 573.], wrote me a letter full of insults, also writing that my brother had been killed because, being greedy for the episcopate, he had killed a bishop. But the reason he wrote these things was that he coveted a church estate. When I refused to give it to him, he vomited upon me, as I said, a thousand insults in the fullness of his rage.

On one occasion I replied to him:

“Remember the prophetic saying: ‘Woe to those who join house to house and add field to field. Will they alone inhabit the earth?’ (Isaiah 5:8). Oh, if Massilia had had you as its priest! Its ships would never have brought oil or other commodities, but only paper [Note: [Col. 0320D] Brought, of course, from Egypt. See the notes on Book VI, chapter 6.], so that you might have had greater opportunity to write against and defame good men. But the poverty of paper puts an end to verbosity.”

For he was possessed by immense greed and arrogance. But, setting these matters aside lest I appear like him, I shall explain how my brother [Note: [Col. 0320D] He was called Peter, and was a deacon, as is clear from what follows. See Book II of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 24.] departed this life and how swiftly the Lord brought vengeance upon his killer.

As blessed Tetricus, bishop of the church of Langres, grew old, he had deposed the deacon Lampadius, who had been his creditor. My brother, wishing to assist the poor whom Lampadius had unjustly despoiled, agreed to his humiliation, and thereby incurred his hatred.

Meanwhile, blessed Tetricus was struck by an attack involving the blood [Note: [Col. 0321C] That is, he was seized by apoplexy, which arises from an effusion of blood.]. When no medicines were of any use to him, the clergy, disturbed and deprived of their shepherd, sought Mondericus [Note: [Col. 0321C] As the Bollandists note under 18 March, he was Mundericus, or, as others write, Modericus, son of Ansbert, the famous senator, and brother of Saint Arnulf, bishop of Metz. He is said to have died renowned for miracles.]. Granted by the king and tonsured, he was ordained bishop, under the arrangement that while blessed Tetricus lived he would govern the fortress of Ternodorum [Note: [Col. 0321D] The town of Tornodorum, commonly called Tonnerre, distinguished by the dignity of a county. There is no doubt that bishops of such fortresses, who served in the place of archpriests, were called *chorepiscopi* by many authors.] as archpriest and reside there; when his predecessor died, he would succeed him.

While he lived in this fortress, he incurred the king’s anger. It was alleged against him that he had supplied food and gifts to King Sigibert when Sigibert was advancing against his brother Guntchramnus. Accordingly, he was taken from the fortress and confined in exile on the bank of the Rhône, in a narrow, roofless tower, where he remained for almost two years in great torment.

Through the intervention of blessed Nicetius, bishop of Lyon, he returned to Lyon and lived with him for two months. But when he could not obtain from the king restoration to the place from which he had been removed, he escaped by night and went over to King Sigibert [Note: [Col. 0321D] Thus Casin.; others read “to Sigibert’s kingdom.” Sigibert had not yet been killed when these events occurred.]. At the village of Arisitum [Note: [Col. 0321D] Regm. reads *Aritensem*, but incorrectly. Valesius lists several other bishops of Arisitum from various authors in his *Notice of the Provinces of Gaul*. That see, however, did not last long. It is uncertain what place this was; from Gregory’s passage we learn that it lay within the boundaries of the diocese of Rodez. There is a village called Ariat, which could have been called *Arisitum* in Latin. There is also a mountain village called Aire. Most, however, think that *Arisitensis* designates a district or territory about six leagues long, still called l’Arsat.], he was appointed bishop, having under him approximately fifteen dioceses [Note: [Col. 0322C] That is, parishes; this usage is also familiar to other authors, as Savaro observes in his note on Letter 16 of Book IX of Apollinaris Sidonius. These parishes had formerly belonged, together with Septimania, to the Visigoths, who had established a bishop there.]. These had first been held by certain Goths, but were then claimed by Dalmatius [Note: [Col. 0322D] Regm. reads “Saint Martin the bishop”; Bad. reads “Bishop Matius.” Moreover, instead of *nunc vero* (“but now”), one should read *tunc vero* (“but then”), or at least *vindicat* (“claims”), not *vindicabat* (“claimed”). Valesius reads *tum* in his *Notice*.], bishop of Rodez.

When he departed, the people of Langres again sought Silvester, a relative either of ours or of blessed Tetricus, as bishop [Note: [Col. 0322D] Regm. reads “of Bishop Tetricus.” See above, Book IV, chapter 16.]. Nevertheless, in seeking him they acted at the instigation of my brother. Meanwhile, after blessed Tetricus had died, Silvester was tonsured and ordained priest, receiving full authority over the church’s property. He then prepared to travel to Lyon to receive episcopal consecration.

While these things were taking place, because he had long been epileptic, he was seized by the disease, became violently insensible, and continually uttered a moaning sound for two days. On the third day he breathed out his spirit.

After these events, Lampadius, as we said above, deprived of honor and property, joined himself to the son of Silvester out of hatred [Ed. *odio* (“out of hatred”)] for the deacon Peter [Col. 0322A]. He contrived and asserted that his father had been killed by Peter’s magic. The young man, light-minded because of his age, was stirred against him and publicly accused him of parricide.

When Lampadius heard this, after a legal hearing had been held in the presence of Saint Nicetius, my mother’s uncle, he was sent to Lyon. There, in the presence of Bishop Siagrius [Note: [Col. 0322D] This is the celebrated bishop of Autun mentioned by Saint Gregory, who obtained from that holy pontiff the honor of the pallium for his see and the privilege of sitting in the first place.], who was present with many other priests and secular leaders, he cleared himself by oath, declaring that he had never been involved in Silvester’s death.

Two years later, again incited by Lampadius, Silvester’s son overtook the deacon Peter on the road and killed him after wounding him with a lance. When this had been done, Peter’s body was lifted from that place and carried to the fortress of Dijon, where he was buried beside Saint Gregory, our great-grandfather [Note: [Col. 0322D] In the basilica of Saint John, now designated as a parish church.].

The murderer fled and went over to King Chilperic, leaving his property to the treasury of King Guntchramnus [Note: [Col. 0322D] Regm. reads, “leaving to the royal treasury the property that belonged to him.”]. As he wandered through various places because of the crime he had committed, with no secure place in which to remain, at last—so I believe, because innocent blood was crying out against him to divine power—while traveling through a certain region, he killed an innocent man with a drawn sword [Note: [Col. 0322D] The same manuscript reads, “he killed a man, perhaps with a sword.”].

The man’s relatives, grieving over the death of their kinsman, raised a riot, drew their swords, and cut him to pieces, scattering his limbs. By the just judgment of God [Note: [Col. 0322D] The printed editions read, “according to the judgment of God.”], the wretched man met such an end: he who had killed an innocent kinsman did not remain guilty for long. This happened to him in the third year.

After Silvester’s death, the people of Langres again demanded a bishop and received Pappolus [Col. 0322C], formerly archdeacon of Autun. Many, they say, were the wicked things he did; we pass them over lest we appear to be detractors of our brothers. Nevertheless, I shall not omit the kind of end he had.

In the eighth year of his episcopate [Col. 0322C], while he was traveling around the dioceses and church estates [Note: [Col. 0322D] Severus Sulpicius calls the customary episcopal practice of visiting the diocese, in Letter 1 to Eusebius, a solemn custom, as is fitting for bishops. Gregory and other ancient authors frequently mention it.], blessed Tetricus appeared to him one night as he slept, with a threatening expression, and said:

“What are you doing here, Pappolus? Why are you polluting my see? Why are you invading the church? Why are you scattering the sheep entrusted to me in this way? Leave this place; abandon the see; depart far from the region.”

As he said this, he struck Pappolus’s chest forcefully with the staff he held in his hand. At this he awoke, and while considering what it might mean, a pain was fixed in that spot [Note: [Col. 0323D] Thus Regm. The printed editions, with Bec., read *ficta*, a word Gregory likewise uses in Book III of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 10. According to Alteserra, *ficta* means a sudden pain, as though a nail had been driven in; physicians call it *pleuritis*, “a dart.” Our reading expresses the matter more clearly.], and he was afflicted with the greatest pain.

Remaining in this anguish, he abhorred food and drink and awaited his death, which he already expected to be near. Why say more? On the third day, while he was expelling blood from his mouth, he expired. He was then carried to Langres and buried.

In his place Mummolus, an abbot called Bonus by surname, was appointed bishop [Note: [Col. 0323D] He was abbot of Saint John of Réomay in the territory of Tonnerre and had succeeded Saint Silvester; he himself was succeeded by Leopardinus. Mummolus, already a bishop, subscribed to the First and Second Councils of Mâcon.]. Many praise him highly, saying that he was chaste, sober, moderate, exceedingly ready for every good work, a lover of justice, and devoted to charity with all his purpose.

After receiving the episcopate, he learned that Lampadius had defrauded the church of much property and had amassed fields, vineyards, and slaves from the spoils of the poor. He ordered him stripped of everything and driven from his presence [Col. 0323B]. Lampadius now lives in extreme poverty and seeks his food with his own hands. Let this suffice concerning these matters.

### VI

In the same year as above—that is, the year in which Sigibert died and his son Childebert began to reign—many miracles appeared at the tomb of blessed Martin. I wrote of them in the little books that I attempted to compose about his miracles. Although in a rustic style, I did not allow myself to conceal what I had either seen myself or learned from reports of the faithful.

Here I shall relate only what happened to those who, after a heavenly miracle, sought earthly medicines, since his power is shown not only through the grace of healings but also through the chastisement of fools.

Leonastes of Bourges [Note: [Col. 0323D] Becc. and Colb. read *Leonastis*. Regm. reads *Leonastis Bituricensis*. Freh. reads *Leuvastis*. The printed editions, except Chesn., read *Leonastes Biturigis*.], an archdeacon, lost the sight of his eyes when cataracts descended upon them. After visiting many physicians without being able to recover any vision at all, he came to the basilica of blessed Martin. There he remained for two or three months, fasting continually and imploring that he might recover his sight.

When the feast arrived, his eyes were restored and he began to see. After returning home, he summoned a certain Jew and placed cupping glasses upon his shoulders, hoping by their benefit to increase the light in his eyes. When the blood flowed, he was again reduced to his former blindness.

After this had happened, he returned once more to the holy church. There he remained for a long time again, but did not deserve to recover his sight. I believe that this was not granted him because of his sin, in accordance with the Lord’s saying:

“To him who has, more will be given, and he will have abundance; but from him who has not, even what he has will be taken away” (Matthew 13:12).

And also:

“See, you have been made well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5:14).

For he would have remained in good health if he had not brought the Jew upon the divine power. The Apostle admonishes and reproves such people, saying:

“Do not be yoked together with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? [Note: [Col. 0323D] Regm. reads, “light with darkness … with Belial.”] What agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what share has a believer with an unbeliever? What agreement has the temple of God with idols? For you are the temple of the living God. Therefore, ‘Come out from among them and separate yourselves from them,’ says the Lord” [Note: [Col. 0323D] The same manuscript reads, “says the Lord.”] (2 Corinthians 6:14–17).

Let this cause teach every Christian that, when he has been deemed worthy to receive heavenly medicine, he should not seek earthly remedies.

### VII

[Note: [Col. 0324D] This chapter is absent from Corb., Bellov., and Colb.]

I also wish to recall which men, and what sort of men, were called by the Lord in this year. Hence I consider him great and acceptable to God who is placed from our land in his own paradise [Note: [Col. 0324D] Regm. reads, “and therefore.” Below, others read, “who placed such men …”].

For blessed Senoch the priest, who lived near Tours, thus departed from the world. He was of Theifalian origin. Having become a cleric in the territory of Tours, he withdrew into a cell that he had constructed himself between ancient walls. After gathering monks, he restored an oratory that had long lain in ruins. He also performed many miracles among the sick, which we have recorded in the book of his Life [Note: [Col. 0324D] Among the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 15. On the people of the Theifali, see above, Book IV, chapter 19.].

### VIII

In that year blessed Germanus, bishop of Paris, also died [Note: [Col. 0324D] Corb. and Bellov. read, “At that time blessed …”]. At his funeral, this miracle confirmed the many miracles that he had performed during his life. When the prisoners called out, the body became too heavy to carry in the street; but when they were released, it was again lifted without difficulty. The men who had been released themselves proceeded freely in the funeral procession as far as the basilica in which he was buried.

At his tomb [Note: [Col. 0324D] That is, the basilica of Saint Cross and Saint Vincent, which for many centuries has commonly been designated by the name of the holy confessor. He died on 28 May, the day on which his feast is celebrated.], believers experience many miracles through the Lord’s granting, so that anyone who asks justly quickly carries away what he desires. If anyone diligently wishes to investigate the miracles he performed during his life, he will find everything by reading his Life, composed by the priest Fortunatus [Note: [Col. 0324D] It is preserved in Surius and Bollandus under 28 May, and in the first volume of the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*.].

### IX

In the same year Caluppa the recluse also died [Note: [Col. 0324D] This chapter is absent from Corb., Bellov., and Colb.]. From his childhood he had always been religious. At the monastery of Melit [Note: [Col. 0324D] Regm. and Bad. read *Meletense*.], in the territory of Auvergne [Col. 0324D], he became a convert and presented himself to the brothers in great humility, as we have written in the book of his Life [Note: [Col. 0324D] It is among the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 11.]

### X

There was also, in the territory of Bourges, a recluse named Patroclus [Note: [Col. 0325C] This chapter too is absent from the same three manuscripts], invested with the dignity of the priesthood, a man of extraordinary holiness and religion, and of great abstinence. He was often afflicted by various ailments caused by fasting.

He drank neither wine, beer, nor anything that could intoxicate, except water lightly flavored with honey; nor did he use any kind of broth. His food was bread soaked in water and sprinkled with salt [Col. 0325A]. His eyes never became dim. He was constant in prayer. If he interrupted it even briefly, he either read something or wrote.

He often provided remedies through prayer for those suffering from fevers [Note: [Col. 0325C] Gregory frequently mentions *frigoritici*, that is, people suffering from fever, because a fever attack begins with a chill. Most printed editions have *pustulae*, while the manuscripts have *pusulae*. Strictly speaking, *pustulae* are swellings or vesicles of the skin, whereas *pusulae* are a type of disease commonly called “sacred fire” or “Saint Anthony’s fire.”], pustules, or other illnesses. He also performed many other signs, which would take too long to recount in detail.

He always wore a hair shirt next to his bare body [Col. 0325B]. At the age of eighty he departed from the world and migrated to Christ. We have also written a little book about his Life [Note: [Col. 0325D] Among the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 9.].

### XI

Since our God always deigns to glorify his priests, I shall disclose what happened to the Jews of Auvergne in this year.

Although blessed Avitus [Note: [Col. 0325D] Regm. reads *Adjutus*. Fortunatus praises him in Book III, poem 24. See above, Book IV, chapter 35. Fortunatus described in verse this conversion of the Jews brought about by Bishop Avitus in Book V, poem 4, at the urging of our own Gregory, to whom the poem was dedicated together with a prefatory letter. He begins by commending the grace of Christ the Lord:

> Among your venerable servants, excellent creator,  
> It is fitting, Christ, that your praise should always resound,  
> Inspiring the mind, granting both desire and fulfillment,  
> Without whom no good can prevail.]

often admonished them to abandon the veil of the Mosaic Law, understand it spiritually, and contemplate in the sacred Scriptures Christ, the Son of the living God, promised by prophetic and royal authority [Note: [Col. 0325D] Thus Corb. and Bell.; this passage is understood as referring to David. The other printed and manuscript witnesses, however, read *legali* (“legal”), in which case the passage would express the Law and the Prophets.]. Yet there remained in their hearts—not merely that veil by which the face of Moses was overshadowed, but a wall as well—while the priest prayed that, when they turned to the Lord, the veil of the letter might be torn away from them [Note: [Col. 0326C] On Good Friday, when the Church publicly prays for the Jews that the veil may be removed from their eyes. See Mabillon’s note on no. 29 of the *Gothic Missal*, Book III of the Gallican Liturgy.].

One of them came to Saint [Col. 0325C] Easter to be baptized. Reborn to God through the sacrament of baptism, he proceeded in white with the other newly robed believers. As the people were entering the city gate, one of the Jews, at the devil’s instigation, poured foul-smelling oil over the head of the converted Jew. When the whole crowd, filled with horror, wanted to drive him away with stones, the bishop did not permit it.

On the blessed day when the Lord, after redeeming humanity, gloriously ascended to heaven, the priest proceeded singing from the church to the basilica [Note: [Col. 0326C] At Tours, by the institution of Perpetuus, vigils were held in the basilica of Saint Martin on that day.]. The entire crowd following him rushed upon the synagogue of the Jews [Col. 0326A], destroyed it from its foundations, and reduced it to the level of a field [Note: [Col. 0326D] Thus Corb. Others read, “destroying it … the place is made level.” Regm. reads, “and reduced it to the level of a field.”].

On another day the priest sent messengers to them, saying:

“I do not compel you by force to confess the Son of God, but I proclaim him and place the salt of knowledge [Note: [Col. 0326D] Cod. Regm. reads, “the sun of justice.”] in your hearts. For I am a shepherd set over the Lord’s sheep, and that true Shepherd who suffered for us said of you that he has other sheep who are not of his fold, whom he must bring in, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd (John 10:16). Therefore, if you wish to believe as I do, become one flock, with me set over you as guardian; but if you choose otherwise, leave this place.”

After long wavering and doubting, on the third day, as I believe through the bishop’s influence, they joined together and sent him this reply:

“We believe in Jesus, the Son of the living God, promised to us by the voices of the prophets; and therefore we ask to be washed in baptism, lest we remain in this sin” [Note: [Col. 0326D] The words from “and therefore” through “remain” are absent from Corb. and Bellov.].

The bishop rejoiced at the message. On the holy night of Pentecost, after the vigils had been celebrated, he went out to the baptistery beyond the walls. There the entire multitude prostrated itself before him and asked for baptism. Weeping for joy, he washed them all with water, anointed them with chrism, and gathered them into the bosom of Mother Church.

Candles blazed, lamps shone, and the whole city gleamed white with the white-robed flock. The city’s joy was no less than that which Jerusalem once deserved to witness when the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles. More than five hundred were baptized.

Those who refused to receive baptism [Note: [Col. 0326D] *Percipere* is absent from Corb. and Bell. Below, instead of *redditi sunt* (“were sent back”), Colb. has *redierunt* (“returned”). It seems that afterward Jews in Massilia were also compelled to receive baptism, as appears from Saint Gregory the Great’s Letter 45 of Book I, addressed to Virgilius of Arles and Theodore, bishop of Massilia.], departing from that city, were sent back to Massilia.

### XII

After this, Brachio, abbot of the cell of Menat, also died [Note: [Col. 0326D] This chapter is absent from Corb., Bell., and Colb.]. He was of Thuringian origin and had practiced hunting in the service of Duke Sigivald, as we have written elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0326D] In chapter 12 of the book *On the Lives of the Fathers*. In Regm. he is called Braco. The monastery of Menat still exists in the diocese of Clermont, under the Order of Saint Benedict.].

### XIII

Therefore, to return to the matter at hand, King Chilperic sent his son Chlodovech to Tours. After assembling an army, he passed through the territories of Tours and Angers as far as Saintes [Note: [Col. 0326D] Thus Corb. and Bell. The others read, “between the territory.”], and overran it.

Mummolus, patrician of King Guntchramnus, advanced with a large army as far as Limoges [Col. 0327A] and fought against Desiderius, Duke of King Chilperic. In that battle five thousand of Mummolus’s army fell; but twenty-four thousand of Desiderius’s men [Note: [Col. 0327D] The words “but of Desiderius, twenty-four thousand” are absent from Bellov.]. Desiderius himself fled and barely escaped.

Mummolus the patrician returned through Auvergne and devastated it in various places with his army, and thus proceeded into Burgundy.

### XIV

After this, while Merovech was being held under close guard by his father, he was tonsured, and, having changed into the clothing customarily used by clerics, was ordained a presbyter. He was sent to the Cenomannian monastery called Aninsula [Note: Colb. has *Cenoniacum, which is called Annisola*. It still exists, named popularly Saint-Calais after its founder and first abbot, Saint Carilefus, under the Rule of Saint Benedict and the Congregation of Saint Maur. Observe here that Merovech stayed in the monastery so that he might be instructed in clerical duties, and that clerical dress differed from secular clothing. Indeed, Gregory the Great ordered in Letter 10 of Book V that English boys be instructed in the faith in monasteries of Gaul.], so that there he might be trained in the priestly discipline.

When Gunthchramn Boso heard this—he was then residing in the basilica of Saint Martin, as we have said—he sent the subdeacon Riculfus [Al. *Rigulfus*] to give him secret advice that he should seek refuge in the basilica of Saint Martin. When he had gone, Gailenus [Note: So Corb., Bell., and Regm.; the others have *Gaulenus*.], his servant, arrived from another direction. Since those who were escorting him had only slight assistance, Gailenus himself carried Merovech off on the road; Merovech then covered his head, put on secular clothing, and made for the church of Saint Martin. While we were celebrating Mass, he found the doors of the holy basilica open and entered.

After Mass he asked us to give him *eulogiae* [Note: The use of *eulogiae* for any little gift, especially one sent by devout persons, is well known; in sacred usage it otherwise means blessed bread. Hence Hincmar, *Capitula* of the year 852, no. 7: “So that from the offerings presented by the people and remaining after the consecration, or from the loaves, etc., after the solemnities of Mass, those who were not prepared to receive Communion may receive from them every Sunday and on feast days,” etc.]. At that time Ragnemodus, bishop of the see of Paris, who had succeeded Saint Germanus, was with us. When we refused his request, he himself began to cry out and say that we were wrong to suspend him from communion without the consent of the brethren. While he was saying this, and with the agreement of the brother who was present, after the canonical case had been formally stated [Note: Regm. has *contestatus causam canonicam*.], he received the *eulogiae* from us.

I feared that, while suspending one person from communion, I might become the murderer of many. For he threatened to kill certain members of our people if he did not obtain our communion. Nevertheless, because of this affair, the region of Tours suffered many disasters.

During these days Nicetius, the husband of my niece, having a personal case of his own, went to King Chilperic with our deacon, who was to report Merovech’s flight to the king. When they saw them, Queen Fredegund said: “They are spies. They have come to find out what the king is doing, so that they may know what to report to Merovech.” Immediately she ordered them stripped and thrown into exile; after seven months had elapsed, they were released from it.

Accordingly Chilperic sent messengers to us, saying: “Drive that apostate out of the basilica; otherwise I shall set the whole region on fire.” When we wrote back that it was impossible for what had not been done in the time of the heretics to be done now, in the time of Christians, he raised an army and sent it there.

In the second year of King Childebert, when Merovech saw that his father was intent upon this course of action, he decided to go to Brunichild with Duke Gunthchramn, saying: “Far be it that, on my account, the basilica of Saint Martin should suffer violence, or that his region should be subjected to captivity because of me.”

He entered the basilica and, while keeping vigil, brought the possessions he had with him to the tomb of Saint Martin. He prayed that the saint would help him and grant him his favor, so that he might be able to obtain the kingdom.

At that time Count Leudastes, while laying many snares for him out of affection for Fredegund, finally surrounded his servants, who had gone out into the countryside, and slaughtered them with the sword; he also wished to kill Merovech himself, if he could find him in a suitable place. But Merovech, following Gunthchramn’s advice and desiring to avenge himself, ordered Leudastes seized when the chief physician Marileif [Note: Others have *Mareleif*; Regm. has *Marilefius*.] returned from the king’s presence. After having him beaten with extreme severity, and taking away his gold, silver, and the other possessions he had brought with him, Merovech left him naked. He would certainly have killed him, had Leudastes not slipped from the hands of those beating him and sought refuge in a church. Later, after we had clothed him and obtained his life, we sent him back to Poitiers.

Merovech, however, spoke of many crimes committed by his father and stepmother. Although some of these were true, I believe that it was not pleasing to God that they should be made public by the son, as I learned from what followed.

One day I was invited to his banquet. While we were sitting together, he humbly asked that something be read for the instruction of his soul. I opened the Book of Solomon and seized upon the first verse that met my eyes. It contained these words: “The eye that looks askance at his father, let the ravens of the valleys pluck it out” (Prov. III, 17) [Note: Corb. has *exasperat*; Colb. has *qui aversus dispexerit*.].

Since he did not understand this, I reflected that the Lord had prepared this verse. Then Gunthchramn sent his servant to a certain woman, already known to him from the time of King Charibert, who possessed a pythonic spirit, so that she might tell him what was going to happen. He further asserted that, before this time, she had foretold to him not only the year but also the day and hour in which King Charibert would die.

Through her servants she sent him this reply:

“It is destined that King Chilperic will die this year, and that Merovech, after excluding his brothers [Note: So Corb., Bell., and Colb.; the others, along with the printed editions, have *Merovechus inclusis fratribus*. The word *rex* appears only in Bell.], will seize the entire kingdom. You, however, will hold the government of his whole kingdom for five years. In the sixth year, in one of the cities [Note: Valesius understood this as the bishopric of Tours; but the city of Tours lies on the left bank of the Loire. On the right bank are Nevers, Orléans, and Nantes. Cointius thinks that the last of these is more likely intended; Gregory’s text does not contradict him.] situated on the right side of the channel of the Loire, with the support of the people, you will obtain the dignity of the episcopate, and, as an old man full of days, you will depart from this world.”

When the servants returned and reported this to their master, he was immediately lifted up by vanity, as though he were already sitting in the chair of the church of Tours, and brought these words to me. I laughed at his foolishness and said: “These things must be sought from God; what the devil promises must not be believed. He was a liar from the beginning and never stood in the truth” (John VIII, 44) [Note: The words that follow, up to *stetit*, are absent from Corb. and Bell.].

When he departed in confusion, I laughed heartily at the man who thought such things should be believed.

Finally, one night, after the vigils had been celebrated in the basilica of the holy bishop, I fell asleep while lying on my little bed and saw an angel flying through the air. As he passed over the holy basilica, he cried out in a loud voice:

“Alas, alas! God has struck down Chilperic and all his sons; none of those who have come forth from his loins will remain to rule his kingdom forever.”

At that time he had four sons by different wives, apart from his daughters. When these things were later fulfilled, I then recognized with complete clarity that what the fortune-tellers had promised was false.

While Merovech and his companions were staying at the basilica of Saint Martin, Queen Fredegund—who had already secretly supported Gunthchramn Boso because of the death of Theodobert—sent to him, saying: “If you can drive Merovech out of the basilica so that he may be killed, you will receive a great reward from me.”

Thinking that killers were already at hand, Gunthchramn said to Merovech: “Why do we sit here like sluggish and timid men, and hide around this basilica like fools? Let our horses come; taking our hawks, let us exercise ourselves in hunting with the dogs and amuse ourselves with open-air spectacles.”

He said this craftily in order to separate Merovech from the holy basilica. Gunthchramn was otherwise a good man. He was, however, exceedingly ready to commit perjury; nevertheless, he never gave any of his friends an oath that he would not immediately abandon.

Accordingly, as we have said, they left the basilica and proceeded to the house at Jocundiacum [Note: This place is near the river Cher opposite Tours, popularly called Jouay.], close to the city. But no one harmed Merovech [Note: So Corb. and Bec.; the others have *noscitus est*; Casin. has *notus est*.].

Since Gunthchramn was then being accused, as we have said, of the death of Theodobert, King Chilperic sent messengers and a letter written to the tomb of Saint Martin. It contained a request that Saint Martin should write back to him whether it was lawful or not to remove Gunthchramn from his basilica.

But the deacon Baudegilus [Note: So Corb. and Bell.; Regm. and Bad. have *Baudigisilus*; Colb. *Baidegisilus*; Bec. *Baudegisilus*; several printed editions *Baudinus*.], who delivered this letter, sent a blank sheet of paper, together with the letter he had brought, to the holy tomb. After waiting three days and receiving no written reply [Note: Corb. and Bell. have “began to write back.”], he returned to Chilperic.

The king then sent others to demand an oath from Gunthchramn that he would not leave the basilica without the king’s knowledge [Note: Regm. has “consent.”]. Swearing solemnly, Gunthchramn gave the altar cloth as surety [Note: That is, by touching it.] and declared that he would never leave the place without royal command.

Merovech, however, not believing the pythoness, placed three books upon the saint’s tomb: the Psalter, the Books of Kings, and the Gospels. He kept vigil throughout the night and asked that the blessed confessor show him what would happen to him, and whether or not he could obtain the kingdom, so that he might know what the Lord revealed [Note: This custom, especially when secular matters were concerned, greatly displeased Saint Augustine. The Gallic councils condemned the “Lots of the Saints” and similar forms of divination—Agde, canon 42; Orléans I, canon 30; and others. They were finally abolished completely in the Third Capitulary of 789, where chapter 4 reads: “That no one presume to cast lots in the Psalter, the Gospel, or other things, nor observe any divinations.” For the manner in which this sortilege was performed with sacred books, see the notes of the distinguished scholar Étienne Baluze on that passage. See also the note above on Book II, chapter 37. This custom had likewise become established among the pagans. Thus Hadrian, according to Spartianus, divined the future from whatever verse happened to be the first to meet his eyes in Virgil.].

Afterward, having continued for three days in fasting, vigils, and prayers, he again approached the blessed tomb and opened the Book of Kings. The first verse on the page he opened was this:

“Because you have forsaken the Lord your God and walked after foreign gods, and have not done what is right in his sight, therefore the Lord your God has delivered you into the hands of your enemies” (III Kings IX, 9).

This verse was found in the Psalter:

“Nevertheless, because of their treachery you set evils before them; you cast them down when they were lifted up. How have they become a desolation? Suddenly they have failed; they have perished because of their iniquities” (Psalm LXXI, 18–19).

In the Gospels this was found:

“You know that after two days the Passover will take place, and the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified” (Matthew XXVI, 2).

Confounded by these responses, he wept for a very long time at the tomb of the holy bishop. Then, taking Duke Gunthchramn with him, he departed with five hundred men or more.

After leaving the holy basilica and traveling through the territory of Auxerre, he was seized by the duke Erpo [Note: Regm. has *Herpo*; Bec. *Herbonem*.] of King Gunthchramn. While Erpo was holding him, Merovech somehow slipped away and entered the basilica of Saint Germanus [Note: Beside the city of Auxerre, where it still exists, though now within the city, with a very celebrated Benedictine monastery under the Congregation of Saint Maur.].

When King Gunthchramn heard this, he was enraged. He condemned Erpo to pay seven hundred gold pieces [Note: Corb. has seventy.] and removed him from office, saying: “You detained, as my brother says, his enemy. If you intended to do this, you should first have brought him to me; otherwise, you should not even have touched the man whom you pretended to hold.”

The army of King Chilperic, advancing as far as Tours, subjected that region to plunder, burned it, and devastated it. It did not spare the possessions of Saint Martin but seized whatever it touched, without any regard for God or fear of him.

Merovech stayed for nearly two months in the aforementioned basilica, then fled and reached Queen Brunichild. But the Austrasians did not receive him. His father, meanwhile, raised an army against the Champenois, thinking that Merovech was hiding there; but he harmed no one and was unable to find him.

### XV

At the time when Alboin entered Italy, Chlothar and Sigibert settled the Suebi and other peoples in that place [Note: Compare this chapter with Book IV, chapter 43. As Valesius and Cointius point out, however, Sigibert alone gave the Suebi a place to inhabit, since Chlothar was already dead at that time. Paul the Deacon must also be corrected, for, following Gregory carelessly, he fell into this error.]. Those who returned in Sigibert’s time—that is, those who had been with Alboin—rose up against them, wishing to drive them from that region and destroy them.

But the Suebi offered them a third of the land, saying: “We can live together without conflict.” They, however, were angry with them because they themselves had previously held the land, and they absolutely refused to make peace.

Then the Suebi again offered them half; afterward, two-thirds, leaving themselves one-third. When the others refused, they offered them, together with the land, all their cattle, provided only that they cease from war. But the others would not agree even to this and sought battle.

Before the battle they discussed among themselves how the wives of the Suebi should be divided, and who should take which woman after the Suebi had been destroyed, thinking that they already possessed them as though they had been killed. But the mercy of the Lord, which establishes justice, turned their intention in another direction.

When they clashed, there were twenty-six thousand Saxons, of whom twenty thousand fell. Of the Suebi, six thousand four hundred and eighty were likewise struck down [Note: So Corb. and Bellov.; Colb. also had this reading. Later, however, the words *ex quibus* were added after *millia*, so as to produce: “six thousand, of whom four hundred and eighty,” etc. Bec. and the printed editions have this reading, which is supported by Paul the Deacon, Book III, chapter 7.]. The survivors obtained the victory.

Those who remained of the Saxons swore that none of them would cut his beard or hair until they had first taken vengeance on their adversaries. When they fought again, they fell in an even greater slaughter, and thus the war came to an end [Note: Witichind, a monk of Corvey in Saxony who flourished under Otto the Great, observes that the Transalpine Suebi occupied the region inhabited by the Saxons who migrated to Italy. For this reason, even in his own time, they used laws different from those of the Saxons, although they had settlements in Saxony.].

### XVI

These events took place in Brittany.

Macliavus and Bodicus, formerly counts of the Bretons [Note: Regm. has “dukes, and counts.” Macliavus had been ordained bishop of Vannes; see above, Book IV, chapter 4. Although an apostate, he nevertheless never allowed another to be ordained while he was alive.], had sworn an oath between themselves that whichever of them survived would defend the sons of the other party as his own.

When Bodicus died, he left a son named Theoderic. Macliavus, however, forgot his oath, expelled Theoderic from his homeland, and seized his father’s kingdom.

Theoderic remained for a long time an exile and wanderer. At last God took pity on him [Note: The printed editions have “who, when God had taken pity.”]. He gathered men from Brittany, attacked Macliavus, killed him and his son Jacob with the sword, and restored to his own power the portion of the kingdom that his father had once held. The other portion was claimed by Warochus [Note: Bell. has *Varrocus*], the son of Macliavus.

### XVII

King Gunthchramn killed two sons of the former Magnacharius [Note: Colb. has *Magnarius*; Colb. and several printed editions have *Maginharius*. A note in Colb.: “Gunthchramn had married Marcatrude, daughter of the duke Magnacharius. Because she had poisoned and killed Gundobad, his stepson, whom Gunthchramn had had by the venerable [woman], he divorced her and married Austrigild, her servant. Guntio and Wiolicus, the sons of Magnacharius, could not endure this, and it ultimately became the cause of their destruction. Marius of Avenches records the death of Magnacharius in the year 566.”] with the sword because they were uttering many detestable and abominable things against Queen Austrechild [Note: Others have *Austrigild*.] and her children. He confiscated their property for his treasury.

He himself also lost his two sons, who were struck down by a sudden illness [Note: Namely Chlodomer and Chlothar, whose epitaphs Chesnius reports in volume I of the *History of France*, p. 512. Marius calls them “royal and excellent young men” under the year 577.]. He was deeply saddened by their death because he remained bereft and without children.

That year there was uncertainty concerning the date of Easter. In Gaul, together with many cities, we celebrated Holy Easter on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May [Note: Colb. has March, but this is erroneous.]. Others, along with the Spaniards, observed this solemnity on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April. Nevertheless, as they say, those springs in Spain that are filled by God’s command were filled at the time of our Easter [Note: Concerning these springs, see Cointius under the year 497, no. 3. This uncertainty arose because the Franks followed Victorius’s calendar, as had been established in the Council of Orléans IV, canon 1, in the year 541, whereas the Spaniards followed the ancient Latin canon. See Cointius under the year 339, no. 15.].

### XVIII

At Chinon [Note: This is a fortress situated on the Vienne, popularly called Chinon, from which later writers incorrectly formed *Chinon­ium*.], a village in the territory of Tours, while Mass was being celebrated on the very glorious day of the Lord’s Resurrection, the church trembled. The terrified people, overcome with fear, cried out with one voice that the church was collapsing. All fled from it, even breaking through the doors as they escaped.

After this, a great plague devastated the people.

King Gunthchramn then sent ambassadors to his nephew Childebert, asking for peace and requesting to see him. Childebert came to him with his nobles. They met at the bridge called Pierre [Note: Many villages in Gaul bear this name and are popularly called Pierre-Pont. The one mentioned here is said to be Pont-Pierre, situated in the Vosges forest on the Meuse between La Mothe and Neufchâteau; it is scarcely known today.]. They greeted and kissed one another.

King Gunthchramn said:

“It has happened through the impulse of my sins that I have been left without children [Note: Gunthchramn had two daughters, Chlodoberga and Chlothild; but he counted them as nothing because, under the Salic Law, which had always applied in all divisions of the kingdom and continued to do so, they were incapable of inheriting the kingdom. Never, since the Frankish empire came into existence, had women been admitted to succeed to royal dignity.]. Therefore I ask that this nephew of mine be my son.”

He placed Childebert upon his own chair and handed over to him his entire kingdom, saying:

“May one shield protect us, and one spear defend us. If I have sons, I shall nevertheless regard you as one of them, so that the affection I promise you today before God may remain between them and you.”

Childebert’s nobles likewise made this promise on his behalf.

They ate and drank together, honored each other with worthy gifts, and departed in peace.

Then they sent an embassy to King Chilperic, demanding that he restore what he had taken from their kingdom. If he delayed, they said, he should prepare the field for battle. He disregarded this and ordered circuses to be built at Soissons and Paris, providing them as a spectacle for the people [Note: Regm. has “and offered them to the people to be watched”; Bad. “intending to provide a spectacle for the people in them.” The manuscript Bellov. is worn here, continuing through the words “and, pressing his mouth with his finger,” in the following chapter.].

### XIX

After these events, Chilperic heard that Praetextatus, bishop of Rouen, was giving gifts to the people against the king’s interests. He ordered him summoned to his presence.

After examining him [Note: Corb., Bec., and others have *quem discussum*, with a change of case, a construction Gregory acknowledges elsewhere as familiar to him.], he discovered that possessions belonging to Queen Brunichild had been entrusted to him. He ordered these possessions taken away and Praetextatus held in exile until an ecclesiastical hearing.

When the council had assembled, Praetextatus was brought before it. The bishops who had come to Paris—forty-five in number [Note: See Book VII below, chapter 16.]—were in the basilica of the apostle Saint Peter.

The king said to him:

“What did you think you were doing, bishop, when you joined my enemy Merovech, who ought to have been my son, to his aunt, that is, to his paternal uncle’s wife? Were you unaware of what the decrees of the Canons had established concerning this matter? You are shown to have transgressed not only here, but also to have acted with him, giving gifts so that I might be killed. You made a son an enemy of his father; you seduced the people with money so that no one would keep faith with me; and you wished to deliver my kingdom into another’s hands.”

As he said this, the crowd of Franks roared and wanted to break down the doors of the basilica, as though they would drag the priest outside and stone him. But the king prevented them.

When Bishop Praetextatus denied that he had done the things the king alleged, false witnesses appeared. They displayed certain objects and said:

“You gave us these and those things so that we would have to promise our allegiance to Merovech.”

He replied:

“You are indeed telling the truth that you were often given gifts by me, but the purpose was not that the king should be driven from his kingdom. When you gave me excellent horses and other things, could I do anything other than repay you with gifts of the same kind?”

The king withdrew to his lodging [Note: The ancients used *metatum* for a place where guests or soldiers were lodged; writers of a later age used it for any dwelling.]. We gathered together and sat in the basilica of Saint Peter’s secretariat.

While we were conversing, Aetius, archdeacon of the church of Paris, suddenly arrived. After greeting us, he said:

“Listen to me, priests of the Lord, who are gathered here together. Either you will raise your name at this moment and shine with the glory of a good reputation, or no one hereafter will regard you as priests of God, if you do not wisely assert your own standing or allow your brother to perish.”

When he had said this, none of the priests answered him. They feared the fury of the queen, at whose instigation these things were being done.

As they sat absorbed and pressing their lips with a finger, I said:

“Please attend to my words, most holy priests of God, and especially you who appear to be closer to the king. Give him holy and priestly counsel, lest, raging against a minister of God, he perish through God’s anger, lose his kingdom, and lose his glory.”

While I was saying this, they all remained silent. As they kept silent, I continued:

“Remember, my lords and fellow priests, the prophetic word that says: ‘If the watchman sees a man’s wickedness and does not report it, he will be guilty of the soul of the one who perishes’ (Ezekiel XXXIII, 6). Therefore do not remain silent. Preach, and place his sins before the king’s eyes, lest some evil befall him and you be held guilty for his soul.
