“Do you not know what happened in recent times? How Chlodomer seized Sigimund and shut him in prison? Avitus, the priest of God, said to him [Note: Regm., as elsewhere, has *Adjutus*. See above, Book III, chapter 6. Here Gregory does not mean a bishop by the word “priest,” as often elsewhere, for Saint Avitus was only abbot of Miciacum.]: ‘Do not lay hands upon him, and when you go against Burgundy, you will gain the victory.’ But Chlodomer rejected what the priest had told him, departed, and killed Sigimund together with his wife and children. He then invaded Burgundy, where he was overwhelmed by the army and killed.

“What of the emperor Maximus? Did he not compel Saint Martin [Note: Corb., Bell., and Colb. have *Germanum*. We have retained the reading of the other witnesses because Sulpicius Severus reports in *Dialogue* 3 that this same thing happened to Saint Martin, where he says that Saint Martin took part in the ordination of Felix.] to communicate with a certain murderous bishop, and did Saint Martin, in order more easily to free those condemned to death, consent to the impious king? Yet, as the judgment of the eternal King pursued him, Maximus was expelled from the empire and condemned to a most wretched death?”

When I had said this, no one answered anything. They were all attentive and astonished.

Two flatterers among them—something grievous to say of bishops—nevertheless informed the king, saying that he had no greater enemy in his affairs than I.

Immediately one of the royal attendants was sent at a rapid run to bring me before him. When I arrived, the king was standing beside a tent made of branches. Bishop Bertchramnus stood at his right, and Ragnemodus at his left [Note: Bertramnus was bishop of Bordeaux, and Ragnemodus bishop of Paris. Both are frequently praised by Fortunatus; more will be said of them below.]. Before them stood a low bench [Note: That is, a low table, called in French *un banc*, from which the word “banquet” was derived to designate a feast], covered with bread and various dishes.

When the king saw me, he said:

“O bishop, you ought to distribute justice to everyone, and here I do not receive justice from you. Instead, as I see, you consent to iniquity, and the proverb is fulfilled in you that ‘the raven does not pluck out the eye of the raven.’”

I replied:

“If one of us, O king, wishes to depart from the path of justice, you can correct him. But if you transgress, who will correct you? We speak to you, but if you wish, you listen; if you do not wish, who will condemn you except the one who declared himself to be Justice?”

Since the flatterers had inflamed him against me, he replied:

“With everyone else I have found justice, but with you I cannot find it. But I know what I shall do, so that you may be marked out before the people and everyone may clearly see that you are unjust. I shall summon the people of Tours and say to them: ‘Cry out against Gregory, that he is unjust and grants justice to no one.’ When they have shouted these things, I shall answer: ‘I, who am king, cannot find justice with him; and you, who are lesser, will find it?’”

I answered:

“You do not know that I am unjust. He knows my conscience, to whom the secrets of the heart are manifest. As for the false outcry by which the people insult me at your command, it means nothing, because everyone knows that these words have come from you. Therefore it is not I but you who will be marked out by the acclamation.

“But why say more? You have the Law and the Canons. You must examine them carefully. Then, if you fail to observe what they command [Note: Regm. has “if you wish to observe them.”], know that God’s judgment hangs over you.”

He then pretended to flatter me, thinking that, by doing so deceitfully, he would prevent me from understanding him. Turning toward the broth that had been set before him, he said:

“For your sake I prepared this broth, containing nothing except fowl and a little chickpea.”

Recognizing his flattery, I replied:

“Our food ought to be to do the will of God, not to take pleasure in such delicacies, so that under no circumstances do we neglect what he has commanded. You, however, who blame others for injustice, first promise that you will not disregard the Law and the Canons. Then we shall believe that you are pursuing justice.”

He extended his right hand and swore by almighty God that he would in no way fail to do what the Law and the Canons taught.

Afterward I took some bread, drank some wine, and departed [Note: Regm. has *discessit*, “he departed.”].

That same night, after the nocturnal hymns had been sung, I heard the door of our lodging being struck repeatedly with heavy blows. I sent a servant and learned that messengers from Queen Fredegund were standing outside.

After they had been admitted, I received the queen’s greeting. Then the servants begged me not to oppose her interests, and at the same time promised two hundred pounds of silver [Note: Cod. Regm. has “marks.”] if Praetextatus were overthrown with my opposition. They said:

“We already have the promise of all the bishops. Only you must not proceed against us.”

I replied:

“Even if you gave me a thousand pounds of gold and silver, could I do anything other than what the Lord commands? I promise only this: I shall follow whatever the others agree upon in accordance with the decrees of the Canons.”

They did not understand what I was saying, and departed after thanking me.

When morning came, some of the bishops came to me bearing a similar message. I gave them a similar reply.

When we had assembled in the basilica of Saint Peter, the king arrived in the morning and said: “For the authority of the Canons has decreed that a bishop caught in theft should be removed from episcopal office.”

When we replied, “Who was the priest against whom the charge of theft was being brought?” the king answered: “You yourselves saw the articles that he stole from us.” For three days earlier the king had shown us two bundles [Note: [Col. 0336D] Thus Corb., Bell., and Colb.; this word is elsewhere used in these manuscripts for *involucra*, as we have already observed. They likewise have *species* instead of *speciebus*, with the case changed.], filled with articles and various ornaments, which were valued at more than three thousand solidi. He also had a sack containing gold coins, weighing nearly two thousand [Note: [Col. 0336D] Colb. has *numismate*, “with a coin.” But Gregory here, as elsewhere, uses *numismatis* for *numismatibus*, “with coins.”]. The king said that these things had been stolen from him by the bishop.

The bishop replied: “I believe you remember that, when Queen Brunhild was leaving the city of Rouen, I came to you and told you that I had been entrusted with her property—that is, five bundles—and that her servants had come to me repeatedly so that I might return it, but that I did not wish to do so without your advice. You, however, said to me, O king: ‘Remove these things from your possession, and let her property be returned to the woman, lest hostility on account of these matters arise between me and my nephew Childebert.’

“Accordingly, when I returned to the city, I handed one bundle over to her servants, for they were unable to carry any more. They returned again asking for the rest, and once more I consulted Your Majesty [Note: [Col. 0336D] Other manuscripts and printed editions read *consiliatus sum*, “I took counsel.”]. But you ordered me, saying: ‘Remove these things, remove them from your possession, O priest, lest this matter cause a scandal.’ Again I handed them two of the bundles; two others, however, remained with me. Why, then, are you now bringing an accusation against me and charging me with theft, when this matter ought to be regarded not as theft but as safekeeping?”

To this the king replied: “If this deposit was entrusted to you for safekeeping, why did you undo one of the bundles, cut into pieces a border woven with golden threads, and distribute it through men who wished to drive me from the kingdom?”

Bishop Praetextatus replied: “I already told you above that I had received gifts from those men; and since I had nothing at hand to give them, I took this from the deposit and offered them gifts in return. It seemed to me that what belonged to my son Merovechus was my own, since I had received him from the baptismal font of regeneration.”

When King Chilperic saw that he could not overcome him by these accusations, he departed from us, utterly astonished and confounded by conscience [Alternative reading: “and”]. He summoned some of his flatterers and said to them: “I admit that I have been defeated by the bishop’s words, and I know that what he says is true. What shall I now do so that the queen’s will concerning him may be fulfilled?”

Then he said: “Go, approach him, and say—as though you were offering counsel on your own initiative—‘You know that King Chilperic is a pious and penitent man, and that he is quickly moved to mercy. Humble yourself before him and say that you committed the acts of which he has accused you. Then, prostrating ourselves at his feet, we shall obtain forgiveness for you.’”

Deceived by this, Bishop Praetextatus promised that he would act accordingly.

When morning came, we assembled at the customary place. The king arrived and said to the bishop: “If you gave gifts in return for gifts to these men, why did you demand oaths from them that they should remain faithful to Merovechus?”

The bishop replied: “I confess that I asked that they maintain friendship with him. Indeed, I would have summoned not merely a man but, if it had been lawful, an angel from heaven to be his helper. For he was my son, as I have often said, spiritually, through the baptismal font.”

As this dispute grew more heated, Bishop Praetextatus prostrated himself on the ground and said: “I have sinned against heaven and before you, O most merciful king. I am a wicked murderer. I wished to kill you and to raise your son to your throne.”

When he had said this, the king prostrated himself at the feet of the priests and said: “Listen, O most holy priests, to the guilty man confessing an execrable crime.”

When weeping, we raised the king from the ground, he ordered Praetextatus to leave the basilica. The king himself withdrew to his lodging, sending a book of Canons, in which a new quire had been inserted containing canons said to be apostolic [Note: [Col. 0337C] These are the canons still commonly called the Apostolic Canons, whose authority at that time was entirely absent from the Gallican Church. Hincmar discusses them in *Opusculum* 24. [Col. 0337D] The canon cited here is number 21, but it was not reported accurately by the opponents of Praetextatus. It says nothing about homicide; in the canon itself the reading is “theft.” Concerning the collection of Canons praised here by Gregory, and concerning the Apostolic Canons, see Cointius under the year 577, where he discusses them more fully. From this passage the distinguished Paschasius Quesnel, in Dissertation XVI on the works of Pope Leo, proves that the collection of Dionysius Exiguus had not yet been received in Gaul at that time. Dionysius places the Apostolic Canons before the others; but Gregory’s words, criticizing the king for inserting a new quire containing canons said to be apostolic, show that they were not then present in the Gallican codex. Indeed, we have before us a very ancient codex of the Canons of the Gallican Church, copied from the Corbie manuscript in the time of Pope Vigilius. In it these canons are absent, and the translation of the other Greek Canons [Col. 0338C] is different from the one elaborated by Dionysius Exiguus. See the learned man’s dissertation, mentioned above [Col. 0338D], on the ancient codex of the Gallican Church.], which contained the following:

“Let a bishop caught in homicide, adultery, or perjury be removed from the priesthood.”

When this had been read, and Praetextatus stood in astonishment, Bishop Bertchramnus said: “Listen, brother and fellow bishop: since you do not possess the king’s favor, you will not be able to enjoy our affection either, until you have obtained the king’s pardon.”

After these proceedings, the king demanded either that Praetextatus’s tunic be torn, or that the hundred and eighth psalm, which contains the curses against Iscariot [Note: [Col. 0338D] The words of this psalm, “and let another take his episcopate,” were applied by Peter against Judas Iscariot in Acts III, to show that Judas had fallen from the apostolate.], be recited over his head, or at least that a judgment against him be written so that he might never again communicate [i.e., participate in communion]. I resisted these conditions, in accordance with the king’s promise that nothing should be done outside the Canons.

Then Praetextatus was snatched from our sight and placed in custody. Attempting to escape from there at night [Alternative reading: “when he was fleeing”], he was severely beaten and driven into exile on an island in the sea adjoining the city of Coutances [Note: [Col. 0338D] This is a Norman episcopal city, commonly called Coutances, known to everyone. Not far from it lies the island of Caesarea, commonly called Jersey, formerly belonging to Normandy but now part of the English county of Southampton; together with its neighboring island Guernsey, it is the only remnant possessed by the English of the ancient Norman inheritance.].

After this, it was reported that Merovechus was again attempting to reach the basilica of Saint Martin. Chilperic ordered the basilica to be guarded and all its entrances closed. The guards left one doorway through which a few clerics could enter for the service, while keeping the other doors shut; this was a source of great annoyance to the people.

While we were staying at Paris, signs appeared in the sky: twenty rays from the northern quarter, rising in the east and hastening toward the west. One of them, longer than the others and towering above them, as though raised aloft, soon faded; and in the same way the remaining ones that followed vanished. I believe that this foretold the death of Merovechus.

While Merovechus was hiding in the territory of Rheims and did not dare entrust himself openly to the Austrasians, he was surrounded by the men of Tarvanna [Note: [Col. 0338D] Tarvanna, the city of the Morini, was destroyed in the immediately preceding century; its episcopal see was divided among three bishoprics: Boulogne, Saint-Omer, and Ypres.]. They said that, if he came to them, they would abandon his father Chilperic and submit themselves to him. He quickly gathered the bravest men around him and went to them.

When they revealed the treachery they had prepared, they shut him inside a certain estate and, surrounding him with armed men, sent messengers to his father. When Chilperic heard this, he decided to hasten there.

But Merovechus was being held in a small lodging and feared that, in revenge for his enemies, he would suffer many punishments. He summoned his companion Gailenus and said: “Until now we have shared one soul and one counsel. I beg you not to allow me to be delivered into the hands of my enemies; instead, take up your sword and attack me.”

Without hesitation, Gailenus stabbed him with a dagger. When the king arrived, Merovechus was found dead [Note: [Col. 0338D] Marius reports his death under the year 578. His body was later brought to Paris, as is related below, Book VIII, chapter 10.].

At that time some asserted that the words of Merovechus, which we related above, had been fabricated by the queen, and that Merovechus had secretly been killed at her command.

Gailenus was captured, and after his hands and feet, his ears, and the tips of his nose had been cut off, he was subjected to many other tortures [Col. 0339A] and miserably killed. They also hoisted Grindio, fastened to a wheel, into the air. Gucilio [Note: [Col. 0339C] Corb. has *Guciolonem*; Bell. has *Ciucilonem*. He had once been a palace count of King Sigibert. The palace count was placed in charge of the royal court, administered justice, and reported matters of greater importance to the prince. As archchaplain, he judged ecclesiastical matters brought before the palace; in the same way, this official judged secular affairs. See Bignonius’s notes on Book I of Marculf, formula 25.], who had once been palace count of King Sigibert, they killed by cutting off his head. They also inflicted cruel deaths of various kinds on many others who had come with him.

People were also saying at that time that Bishop Egidius [Note: [Col. 0339D] Egidius, or Aegidius, bishop of Rheims, was notorious for both his good and his evil deeds. Fortunatus praises him in Book III, poem 18. Frodoard, Book II of his *History of Rheims*, has more about him, as does our Gregory in various places.] and Guntchramnus Boso had been the principal leaders in this ambush: Guntchramnus because he enjoyed a secret friendship with Queen Fredegund on account of the murder of Theodobert; Egidius because he had long been dear to her.

## XX. 

When the emperor Justin [Note: [Col. 0339D] See chapter 31 below. Paul the Deacon copied all these matters in Book III of *On the Deeds of the Lombards*, chapters 11 and 12.] had lost his senses and become deranged, and his empire was governed solely by the empress Sophia, the people, as we have already related in the preceding book (Book IV, chapter 33), chose Tiberius Caesar, a useful, energetic, and wise man, generous in almsgiving and an excellent defender of the poor.

When he distributed generously to the poor from the treasures Justin had amassed, and the empress repeatedly rebuked him for reducing the commonwealth to poverty, saying, “What I gathered over many years you are recklessly scattering in a short time,” he replied: “Our treasury will not be impoverished, provided that the poor receive alms or captives are ransomed. For this is the great treasure, as the Lord says: ‘Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not break in and steal’ (Matthew 6:20). Therefore, from what God has given, let us gather treasure in heaven through the poor, so that the Lord may deign to increase it for us in this world.”

And because, as we have said, he was a great and true Christian, while he supplied aid to the poor with joyful generosity, the Lord provided him with ever more.

As he was walking through the palace, he saw a marble slab in the pavement of a room, on which the Lord’s cross had been carved. He said: “By your cross, Lord, we protect our foreheads and breasts; yet behold, we are trampling the cross beneath our feet” [Note: [Col. 0339D] Theodosius and Valentinian had forbidden the sign of the cross to be engraved on a floor, or on a stone or marble laid upon the ground. Single law, Code *Neminem licet signum*. See also canon 6 of the Council in Trullo.]. Immediately he ordered it removed. When the slab had been dug up and set upright, they found another beneath it bearing the same sign. He ordered that one removed as well. After it had been taken away, they found a third, which was also removed at his command. When it had been taken away, they found a great treasure containing more than one thousand hundredweights of gold. He removed the gold and, as was his custom, supplied it even more abundantly to the poor; nor did the Lord allow anything to be lacking for him according to his good will [Note: [Col. 0339D] Thus Corb. and Bell.; Bec. has “will provide”; others have “permitted.”].

I shall not omit what the Lord later bestowed upon him.

That famous Narses, the commander of Italy [Note: [Col. 0339D] A most celebrated eunuch, who succeeded Belisarius and completely destroyed the Ostrogoths in Italy; but, badly treated by the empress, he invited the Lombards into that same region. Valesius, Book IX of the *History of the Franks*, considers this story an unfounded invention.], having a large house in a certain city, departed for Italy with many treasures [Note: [Col. 0340C] Thus the ancient manuscripts and the printed editions. Chesne has “entered”; Colb. has “returned.”] and arrived at the city mentioned above. There, in his house, he secretly dug a large cistern, in which he deposited many thousands of hundredweights of gold and silver. After killing those who knew of it, he entrusted the hidden treasure under oath to one old man alone.

After Narses died, these riches lay concealed beneath the earth. When the old man repeatedly observed Tiberius’s almsgiving, he went to him and said: “If it will benefit me, I shall tell you, Caesar, of a great matter.”

He replied: “Tell me whatever you wish. It will benefit you if you report something that may benefit us.”

The old man said: “I possess knowledge of a treasure hidden by Narses, which, now that I am at the end of my life, I can no longer conceal.”

Then Caesar Tiberius rejoiced and sent his servants to the place. The old man went ahead, while they followed in astonishment. When they reached the cistern, uncovered it, and entered, they found so much gold and silver that those carrying it away could scarcely empty it over many days. From this wealth he distributed still more generously and joyfully to the needy.

## XXI. 

Accordingly, a disturbance arose against the bishops Salonius and Sagittarius [Note: [Col. 0340C] This chapter is absent from Corb., Bell., and Colb. It is preserved in Casin. and others. Compare chapter 28 below. Here Gregory relates events that had happened to these two bishops—Sagittarius and Salonius—at least a decade earlier.].

They had been brought up by Saint Nicetius, bishop of Lyons, and had received the office of deacon. In his time Salonius was appointed priest of the city of Embrun, and Sagittarius priest of the Church of Gap [Note: [Col. 0340D] Ebrodunum, Embrun, and Vapingum or Vapincum, Gap, are cities in the Dauphiné situated not far from one another, though belonging to different ecclesiastical provinces. The former is the metropolitan see of the Maritime Alps; the latter is subject to the archbishop of Aix in the province of Narbonne II.].

After they had assumed the episcopate and been left to their own discretion, however, they began to rage with insane fury in invasions, assaults, murders, adulteries, and various crimes. Thus, on one occasion, when Bishop Victor of the Tricastini was celebrating the solemnity of his birthday [Note: [Col. 0340D] Most printed editions, together with Regm. and Bec., have *Tricassinorum*. Our reading should nevertheless be retained. The city of Troyes is *Tricassina* in Champagne; here, however, the city of the Tricastini in the Dauphiné is meant, commonly called Saint-Paul-Trois-Châteaux. Eusebius the presbyter, mentioned here under Victor’s name, attended the Second Council of Lyons and himself subscribed the First Council of Mâcon. The birthday solemnity he was celebrating was the anniversary of his consecration as bishop. Even today, in the Roman Pontifical, the day of a bishop’s consecration is counted among the more solemn feasts; this is an ancient custom, as is clear from old sacramentaries.], they sent out a troop armed with swords and arrows and attacked him.

They came and tore his clothing, beat his servants, and carried off the vessels and all the equipment of the meal [Note: [Col. 0341D] Regm. omits “of the meal.”], leaving the bishop in great disgrace.

When King Guntchramnus learned of this, he ordered a synod to be assembled at the city of Lyons. The bishops gathered with the blessed patriarch Nicetius [Note: [Col. 0341D] Cointius objects to the title “patriarch,” given here to Nicetius, in order to prove that the account of Sagittarius and Salonius was added to Gregory’s *History* by an interpolator. But the same title is given to Priscus, Nicetius’s successor, at the Second Council of Mâcon. Sulpicius, bishop of Bourges, is called patriarch in a letter of Desiderius of Cahors, printed by Chesne, volume I, page 880; nor does the title appear to have been granted to any other metropolitan in the other Gallican synods of that period. The Council of Lyons mentioned here is commonly called the Second Council of Lyons, held in 567.], examined the case, and found that the two men were thoroughly convicted of the crimes of which they had been accused. They therefore ordered that those who had committed such acts be deprived of the honor of the episcopate.

But because they still knew that the king was favorable to them, they approached him and pleaded that they had been removed unjustly. They also asked that permission be granted them to go to the pope of the city of Rome. The king granted their requests and, after giving them letters, permitted them to depart.

When they appeared before Pope John [Note: [Col. 0341D] John III, surnamed Catellinus, to whom, as Gregory observes, they went with the king’s permission.], they declared that they had been removed for reasons having no validity [Col. 0341B] [Note: [Col. 0341D] Regm. has “removed from their honors.”].

The pope sent letters to the king ordering that they be restored to their sees. The king fulfilled this without delay, though he first rebuked them at length.

But, what is worse, no reform followed. Nevertheless, they sought peace from Bishop Victor by handing over the men whom they had sent to cause the riot. Remembering the Lord’s command that evil should not be repaid to enemies with evil (Romans 12:17), Victor did them no harm and allowed them to depart free.

For this reason he was later suspended from communion: although he had publicly accused the men, he had secretly spared his enemies without the counsel of the brothers whom he had accused. But through the king’s favor he was again restored to communion.

These two men continued daily to involve themselves in greater crimes. In the battles that Mummolus fought against the Lombards, as we have already mentioned above (Book IV, chapter 37), they armed themselves like laymen and killed many with their own hands. In anger they also attacked some of their own citizens, beating them with clubs until blood flowed.

As a result, the outcry of the people again reached the king, and he ordered the two men to be summoned. When they arrived, he did not wish them to be brought into his presence, intending first to hold a hearing and then, if they were found qualified [Note: [Col. 0341D] That is, “free from accusation,” as Gregory commonly uses the word; [Col. 0342D] hence in the *Capitularies* one finds the expression *se idoneare*, “to prove oneself qualified.” See Alteserra’s notes.], to allow them to deserve an audience with the king.

But Sagittarius, enraged and taking this arrangement harshly, began, being a light-minded and frivolous man, and fluent in irrational speeches, to declaim at length against the king. He said that the king’s sons could not inherit the kingdom because their mother, formerly taken from the household of Magnachar [Note: [Col. 0342D] That is, she had been a maidservant in Magnachar’s house. See the note above on chapter 17.], had entered the king’s bed, not understanding that, setting aside the rank of women, those who are born of kings are called the king’s children.

When the king heard this, he was greatly enraged. He confiscated both their horses and their servants, and ordered them shut up in monasteries far removed from him, where they were to do penance. He left each of them no more than one cleric. He also issued a stern warning to the local judges that they were to guard them with armed men and allow no one access to visit them.

The king’s sons were still alive in those days, and the elder of them began to fall ill. The king’s attendants approached him and said: “If the king would graciously listen to the words of his servants, they would speak in your presence.”

He replied: “Speak whatever you wish.”

They said: “Perhaps these bishops have been condemned to exile though innocent, and the king’s sin may thereby be increased, so that our lord’s son may perish.”

He replied: “Go at once and release them, asking them to pray for our children.”

When they had gone, the bishops were released. Leaving the monasteries, they came together and kissed one another, since they had not seen each other for a long time, and returned to their own cities.

They became so penitent that they seemed never to cease chanting psalms, to observe fasts, and to give alms. They completed the book of David’s song during the day and spent the nights meditating in hymns and readings [page 234].

But this holiness did not remain uncorrupted for long. They turned back again, and often spent the nights feasting and drinking to such an extent that, while the clerics were celebrating Matins in the church, the bishops called for cups and sampled wines.

There was absolutely no mention of God, and they had no thought at all for the daily course of prayer [Note: [Col. 0342D] This is what the canonical hours were called. Today we would say: “They had no concern for reciting the Breviary.” The diligence with which clerics, including bishops, fulfilled this duty in those times is evident from numerous other passages of Gregory. See Mabillon’s discussion of the Gallican course, paragraph 6.].

At dawn, they rose from supper, covered themselves with soft garments, and, buried in sleep and wine, slept until the third hour of the day. Nor were there lacking women with whom they might defile themselves.

When they arose, they bathed and reclined at the banquet. Rising from it in the evening, they longed for supper until the hour of daylight mentioned above. They did this every day, until the wrath of God came upon them—a matter that we shall recall later (Book VII, chapter 39).

## XXII. 

Then Vuinnochus [Note: [Col. 0342D] Colb. has *Wanochus*; Bad. has *Munochus*. His death is related in Book VIII, chapter 34.], a Breton, came from Brittany to Tours in the strictest abstinence, wishing to go to Jerusalem. He wore no clothing except garments made from woolless sheep hides. Since he seemed to us very religious, and so that we might retain him more easily, we honored him with the dignity of the priesthood [Note: [Col. 0343D] Colb. and Regm. have “we burdened him.” In most printed editions Ingitrudis is called Ingetrudis. Regm. reads: “Ingiltudis, moreover, had a religious custom,” and so forth. Ingiltrudis is discussed below in Book IX, chapter 33, and Book X, chapter 12.].

Ingiltrudis had the religious custom of collecting water from the tomb of Saint Martin. When the water ran out, she asked that a vessel of wine be carried to the blessed man’s tomb. After the night had passed, she ordered that it be taken from there in the presence of this priest. When it was brought to her, she said to the priest: “Remove the wine from here and pour in only one drop of the blessed water, of which very little remains” [Note: [Col. 0343D] Regm. has “pour in from it what little remains.” Cointius thinks that from this and similar miracles arose the custom of invoking Saint Martin’s name over wine and then drinking it among the guests as a symbol of mutual charity; later, he believes, corrupt usage perverted the custom. I would rather suppose that formerly the faithful were accustomed to prepare banquets on the feast of Saint Martin, as on other more important festivals, and that although this was abolished on other feast days, it continued on this one because of the saint’s renown. Gregory, however, is not discussing that custom here, but the water with which the holy man’s tomb was washed and which was often given to the sick to drink for their healing.].

When she had done this, astonishingly, the vessel, which had been half full, became full again as the single drop descended. The same vessel, emptied in this manner two or three times, was filled again by only one drop. There is no doubt that in this too the power of blessed Martin was at work.

## XXIII. 

After these events, Samson, the younger son of King Chilperic, was seized by dysentery and fever and departed from this life.

He had been born when King Chilperic was being besieged at Tournai by his brother (Book IV, chapter 52). His mother, fearing that he would die, abandoned him and wished him to perish. But when she could not bring this about, the king rebuked her and ordered that he be baptized. After he had been baptized and received by the same bishop [Note: [Col. 0344D] This appears to have been Chrasmarus, bishop of Tournai and at the same time of Noviomagus or Vermandois. The Beauvais manuscript ends here; the remainder has been torn away.], he died before completing a single five-year period.

His mother Fredegund also fell seriously ill in those days, but recovered.

## XXIV. 

After this, during the night that fell on the third day before the Ides of November, a great portent appeared to us while we were celebrating the vigils of blessed Martin. In the middle of the moon a shining star was seen to gleam, and other nearby stars appeared above and below the moon. The circle that generally signifies rain also appeared around it.

But what these things signified, we do not know. For this year we often saw the moon turn black, and before Christmas there were severe thunderstorms. Those radiances around the sun, which, as we have already mentioned, appeared before the disaster at Clermont (Book IV, chapter 31), and which peasants call “suns,” also appeared [Note: [Col. 0344D] The chapter ends here in Corb.]. They also report that the sea rose beyond its proper bounds, and many other signs appeared.

## XXV. 

Guntchramnus Boso came to Tours with a few armed men and forcibly carried away his daughters, whom he had left in the holy basilica. He took them as far as the city of Poitiers, which belonged to King Childebert.

King Chilperic also invaded Poitiers, and his men drove away the men of his nephew. They brought Ennodius from the county into the king’s presence. When he had been condemned to exile, they handed over his property to the treasury. [Col. 0344A] But after a year he was restored both to his country and to his property (Book VIII, chapter 26).

Guntchramnus Boso left his daughters in the basilica of Saint Hilary and went on to King Childebert.

## XXVI. 

In the third year of King Childebert, which was the seventeenth year of Chilperic and Guntchramnus, Dacco, formerly the son of Dagaric [Note: [Col. 0344D] Corb. has *Dacolenus*; Colb. has *Taceo Tagarici*; Bad. has *Dargo Godarici*; Regm. has *Dago Gadarici*; Bec. has *Dacco Gadarici*.], having abandoned King Chilperic and wandering here and there, was treacherously captured by the commander Dracolenus [Note: [Col. 0344D] Corb. has *Dragoleno*, who is called *Dratglenus* in the list of chapters.], who was called Industrius.

Dracolenus led him in chains to King Chilperic at Brannacum, after giving him an oath that he would secure his life with the king. But he forgot his oath and approached the ruler, making wicked accusations so that Dacco would be put to death.

While Dacco was being held in chains and saw that he would certainly not escape, he secretly sought penance from a priest, without the king’s knowledge [Note: [Col. 0344D] Observe that a man placed in danger secretly sought penance from a priest; in France this was denied to condemned men before death until the time of Charles VI. See Mabillon, preface to the Third Benedictine Century, part I, no. 24.]. After receiving it, he was killed.

When Dracolenus was quickly returning to his homeland, Guntchramnus Boso was at that time attempting to take his daughters away from Poitiers. When Dracolenus heard this, he confronted him. But the others, being prepared, resisted and tried to defend themselves.

Guntchramnus sent one of his friends to Dracolenus and said: “Go and tell him: ‘You know that we have made a pact with each other. I ask you to withdraw from your ambush against me. I do not forbid you to take as much of my property as you wish; only let me, even if stripped bare, be permitted to go wherever I choose with my daughters.’”

But Dracolenus, being frivolous and light-minded, replied: “Behold the rope by which other guilty men, bound and led by my hand, have been sent to the king. This man too shall be bound with it today and taken there.”

Having said this, he drove his horse forward with blows of his heels and directed it at Guntchramnus at a rapid pace. As he struck at him with a futile blow, the shaft of his spear broke and the sword fell to the ground.

When Guntchramnus saw death hanging over him, he invoked the name of the Lord and the great power of blessed Martin. Raising his pole, he seized Dracolenus by the throat and lifted him upward, hanging from his horse [Note: [Col. 0344D] Regm. has “from the horse, again.”]. One of Guntchramnus’s companions then struck him in the side with a lance and finished him. After Dracolenus’s companions had been put to flight and Dracolenus himself stripped, Guntchramnus departed freely with his daughters.

After this, his father-in-law Severus was bitterly accused before the king by his sons. When he heard this, he went to the king with great gifts. He was captured and stripped on the way, led into exile, and ended his life by a most wretched death.

His two sons, Bursolenus and Dodo, were also condemned to death on a charge of treason. One was forcibly killed by the army; the other was captured while fleeing and died after his hands and feet had been cut off. All their property, as well as their father’s, was transferred to the treasury. For they possessed great treasures.

## XXVII. 

Then the men of Tours, Poitiers, Bayeux, Le Mans, Angers, and many other places went to Brittany at the command of King Chilperic. They took up position against Warochus [Note: [Col. 0345C] Colb. has *Voracium*, and below *Varadium*.], formerly the son of Macliau, at the river Vilaine [Note: [Col. 0345C] It cuts across the peninsula of Brittany and flows into the British Ocean between the cities of the Veneti and the Namnetes. In the vernacular it is called *la Vilaine*.].

But Warochus treacherously attacked the Saxons of Bayeux during the night [Note: [Col. 0345C] The Regm. manuscript reads “the Saxons and the men of Bayeux.” The other reading is preferable. The reference is to Saxons originally from Germany who, as the power of the Roman Empire declined, invaded Great Britain and Gaul. Some of them settled in the Armorican region and in the territories of Bayeux [Col. 0345D] and Nantes, mingling with the ancient inhabitants and sharing the name of both peoples. Hence Fortunatus, Book III, poem 8, praises Felix, bishop of Nantes, for bringing the Saxons under the yoke of Christ. Charles the Bald calls their region “the Saxon tongue” in his laws at Savonnières.], killing a very large number of them.

Three days later, after making peace with the commanders of King Chilperic and giving his son as a hostage, he bound himself by oath to remain faithful to King Chilperic. He also surrendered the city of Nantes [Col. 0345B] on the condition that, if he were deemed worthy to govern it by the king’s command, he would pay every year, without anyone having to remind him, all the tribute or other dues owed from it.

When this had been done, the army was withdrawn from the place.

After this, King Chilperic ordered that fines be exacted from the poor and from the *juniores* of the churches or basilicas [Note: [Col. 0345D] Here *juniores* means servants of the Church, as Cointius holds under the year 586; elsewhere the term designates clerics below the rank of subdeacon. See the First Council of Mâcon, canon 8, and Bignonius’s notes on Marculf, Book I, formula 3. Here *bannum* means a fine imposed on those who had not come when summoned to the *bannum*, that is, to the assembly, military service, or levy.], because they had not gone on campaign. It was not customary for such men to perform any public service.

After this, Warochus forgot his promise and wished to violate what he had done. He sent Eunius, bishop of Nantes, to King Chilperic. But the king, moved to anger, ordered him to be rebuked and condemned to exile.

## XXVIII

In the fourth year of Childebert, which was the eighteenth year of the reigns of Guntram and Chilperic, a synod was held at the city of Chalon, at the command of King Guntram. After various cases had been examined, that ancient calamity was renewed against the bishops Salonius and Sagittarius.[^c0035-1] Crimes were brought against them: they were accused not only of adulteries but also of murders. But the bishops judged that these matters could be cleansed through penance, and it was added that they were guilty of treason against the majesty of the ruler and of betraying their country.[^c0035-2] For this reason they were stripped of the episcopate [another reading: deposed] and thrust under guard into the basilica of Saint Marcellus. Escaping from there, they wandered away in different directions until others were installed in their cities.[^c0035-3]

## XXIX

King Chilperic ordered new and severe assessments to be made throughout his entire kingdom. Consequently, many people abandoned those cities [another reading: their cities], or their own possessions, and sought other kingdoms, preferring to live as exiles elsewhere rather than be subjected to such danger. For it had been decreed that a landowner should pay one amphora of wine for each aripennis.[^c0035-4] Many other levies were also imposed, both on the remaining lands and on slaves; but it was impossible to fulfill them.

The people of Limoges, seeing themselves burdened with such a load, assembled on the Kalends of March and attempted to kill Marcus the referendary, who had been ordered to carry out these measures. They would certainly have done so had Bishop Ferreolus not rescued him from the danger threatening him.[^c0035-5] The crowd also seized the assessment registers and burned them together in a fire. The king, therefore, greatly angered, sent agents from his own retinue, afflicted the people with enormous losses, terrified them with punishments, and imposed the death penalty.[^c0035-6] It is also reported that at that time abbots and priests were stretched out upon stakes and subjected to various tortures, because the royal agents accused them of having been present as followers [another reading: helpers] in the people’s rebellion to burn the registers; thereafter they imposed even harsher taxes.

## XXX

The Britons also laid waste to the region of Rennes with fire, plunder, and captivity. Fighting their way forward, they advanced as far as the village of Cornutium.[^c0035-7] Bishop Eunius [another reading: Eonius], brought back from exile, was assigned to Angers as pastor, and was not permitted to return to his own city of Vannes. The duke Bippolenus [the manuscripts also read Bypolenus, Dipolenus, and Beppolenus] was sent against the Britons and overwhelmed certain places in Brittany with sword and fire. This action provoked an even greater disturbance.

## XXXI

While these things were taking place in Gaul,[^c0035-8] Justin, having completed the eighteenth year of his reign, ended his life together with the madness that had seized him. After he was buried, Tiberius Caesar seized the imperial power that he had earlier undertaken.[^c0035-9] But when the people, according to the custom of the place, were awaiting his appearance at the circus spectacle and were planning an ambush for him on behalf of Justinian, who was then regarded as Justin’s nephew, he proceeded through the holy places. After completing his prayer, he summoned the pope of the city and entered the palace with the consuls and prefects. Then, clothed in purple, crowned with the diadem, and placed upon the imperial throne, he confirmed his rule amid immense acclamations.[^c0035-10]

When the factionalists waiting at the circus learned what had happened, they returned in confusion and shame, having accomplished nothing, for they were unable to oppose a man who had placed his hope in God.[^c0035-11] A few days later Justinian arrived and threw himself at the emperor’s feet, bringing him fifteen hundredweights of gold as a token of gratitude. Following his customary clemency, Tiberius received him and ordered him to remain in the palace.

The empress Sophia, forgetting the promise she had once made to Tiberius, attempted to lay a trap for him. When Tiberius went to a country estate, in order to enjoy the imperial vintage festival for thirty days,[^c0035-12] Sophia secretly summoned Justinian and wished to raise him to the imperial throne. When Tiberius learned of this, he swiftly returned to Constantinople, seized the empress, and stripped her of all her treasures, leaving her only the provisions necessary for her daily sustenance. He separated her children from her and appointed others from among his own loyal servants, expressly ordering that none of the former attendants should have access to her.

But he later loved the reprimanded Justinian with such great affection that he promised his own daughter to Justinian’s son and in turn sought Justinian’s daughter for his own son; the arrangement, however, did not come to fruition. Tiberius’s army defeated the Persians and returned victorious, carrying away such a vast quantity of booty that it was thought sufficient even for human greed. Twenty elephants were captured and brought before the emperor.[^c0035-13]

## XXXII

In that year the Britons were very hostile around the city of Nantes [the manuscript Colbertinus reads: Vannes] and around Rennes.[^c0035-14] Carrying away immense booty, they ravaged the fields, stripped the vineyards of their produce, and carried off captives. When Bishop Felix sent an embassy to them, they promised to make amends but were unwilling to fulfill any of their promises.

## XXXIII

At Paris a certain woman fell under accusation, many asserting that she had abandoned her husband and had intercourse with another man. Her relatives therefore went to her father and said: “Either declare your daughter innocent, or let her die, lest this disgrace bring a stain upon our family.”

The father replied: “I know my daughter to be entirely innocent, and what evil men are saying is not true. Nevertheless, lest the accusation grow further, I shall establish her innocence by oath.”

They answered: “If she is innocent, affirm this by an oath upon the tomb of the blessed martyr Dionysius.”

He replied: “I shall do so.”

Then, once this had been agreed, they came together at the basilica of the holy martyr. The father raised his hands over the altar and swore that his daughter was not guilty. Others, however, from the husband’s side, declared that he had sworn falsely [the manuscript Reginensis reads: openly].

While they were arguing, they drew their swords, rushed upon one another, and slaughtered one another before the very altar. They were men of rank and leading persons in the service of King Chilperic. Many were wounded by swords; the holy basilica was sprinkled with human blood; its doors were pierced by spears and swords; and wicked weapons raged as far as the tomb itself.

When the violence had scarcely been brought under control, the place lost its liturgical function,[^c0035-15] until all these events reached the king’s knowledge. The men hurried into the ruler’s presence, but they were not received back into favor. Instead, they were ordered to be sent to the bishop of that place, so that, if they were found guilty of this crime, they might not properly be admitted to communion [thus the manuscript Reginensis; other copies read: so that they might not be found and admitted].

Then Bishop Ragnemodus, who presided over the Church of Paris [other readings: Reginmodus, Raimundus, and Regnamodus], brought together those who had acted wickedly [another reading: those things which had been done wickedly], and they were received into ecclesiastical communion.

The woman, however, when she was summoned to judgment not many days later, ended her life by hanging.

## XXXIV

In the fifth year of King Childebert, great floods afflicted the region of Auvergne, so that the rain did not cease for twelve days. The Limagne was flooded with such an inundation[^c0035-16] that it prevented many people from sowing their seed. The rivers Loire and Flavaris—the latter called the Elaver [the manuscripts and printed editions read Elacrem, except for Colbertinus, which has Ilacrem, and Chesnius, Elaurem; some manuscripts cited by Altessera read: “and the Elaver, which they call the Melacer”][^c0035-17]—together with the other torrents flowing into it, rose so high that they passed beyond boundaries they had never previously exceeded. They caused great destruction among livestock, damage to cultivated land, and ruin to buildings.

Likewise, the Rhône, joined by the Saône and overflowing its banks, inflicted severe damage upon the inhabitants and partly demolished the walls of the city of Lyon. When the rains had ceased, the trees blossomed again; it was then the month of September.[^c0035-18]

In the territory of Tours, before daybreak, a flash of light was seen to run across the sky and fall toward the eastern region. A sound like that of a falling tree was also heard throughout the whole land. It should not, however, be attributed to a tree, because it was heard over fifty miles or more.

That same year the city of Bordeaux was violently shaken by an earthquake, and the city walls were in danger of collapsing. The entire population was so terrified by fear of death that, unless they fled, they thought they would be swallowed up together with the city. Many therefore moved to other cities. The tremor [another reading: fear] extended to neighboring cities and reached as far as Spain, though with less force. Nevertheless, enormous stones were dislodged from the Pyrenees Mountains and struck down both animals and human beings.

Fire of apparently divine origin also consumed the villages of Bordeaux. They were suddenly caught by the flames, and houses and courtyards, together with their stores of grain, were burned. The fire had no external fuel whatsoever, unless perhaps it was kindled by divine command.

The city of Orléans also burned in a severe conflagration, so completely that nothing at all remained to the wealthy. If anyone rescued anything from the fire, it was seized by the thieves who pressed in upon him. Near the boundary of Chartres, genuine blood flowed from a broken loaf of bread [the manuscript Corbeiensis reads: “from the city’s broken bread”]. At that time the city of Bourges was also severely battered by hail.

## XXXV

These most grievous portents were followed by a terrible plague. Since the kings were at odds and were again preparing civil war, a dysenteric illness seized almost all Gaul. Those who suffered from it had a severe fever accompanied by vomiting, excessive pain in the kidneys, and heaviness in the head or neck. What was expelled from the mouth [the manuscript Corbeiensis omits “from the mouth”] was saffron-colored or else green. Many claimed that it was a hidden poison.

The more rustic people called these pustules “corales.”[^c0035-19] This is not implausible, because when cupping glasses were applied to the shoulders or legs, many people were relieved as blisters developed and burst, allowing the accumulated pus to drain away. Herbs that counteract poisons, taken as a drink, also provided relief to many.

This illness began in the month of August and first seized children and adolescents, carrying them off to death. We lost our sweet and dear little children, whom we had cherished in our laps, carried in our arms, or painstakingly nourished with food supplied by our own hands. But, wiping away our tears, we said with blessed Job: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be his name forever” (Job 1:21).

During those days King Chilperic fell seriously ill. When he recovered, his younger son, who had not yet been reborn through water and the Holy Spirit, began to fall ill. Seeing him near death, they washed him in baptism. When he showed some improvement, his elder brother, Chlodobert by name, was seized by the same disease.

His mother Fredegund, seeing him in danger of death, repented too late and said to the king:

“For a long time divine mercy has sustained us while we acted wickedly. Often he has struck us with fevers and other evils, but no amendment followed. Look: now we are losing our sons. The tears of the poor, the lamentations of widows, and the sighs of orphans are already destroying them; nor does any hope remain for whom we might gather possessions. We store up treasures without knowing for whom we are gathering them. Look: the treasures remain empty of their owner and full of plunder and curses.

“Were not the storerooms overflowing with wine? Were not the granaries filled with grain? Were not the treasuries packed with gold, silver, precious stones, necklaces, and the other ornaments of royalty? Look: we are losing what we possessed that was most beautiful.

“Now, if it pleases you, come and let us burn all the unjust assessment registers. Let what was sufficient for our father and king Chlothar be sufficient for our treasury.”

After speaking these words, the queen struck her breast with her fists and ordered the registers brought out—the ones that had come from her cities through Marcus. She threw them into the fire and then turned again to the king:

“Why do you hesitate?” she said. “Do what you see me doing, so that, even if we lose our beloved children, we may at least escape everlasting punishment.”

Then the king was pierced in his heart and handed over all the assessment registers to the fire. When they had been burned, he sent men to prevent future assessments.

After this the younger child, wasting away under excessive suffering, died. With the greatest mourning they carried him from the estate at Brennac to Paris and ordered him buried in the basilica of Saint Dionysius.[^c0035-20] They placed Chlodobert in a coffin and carried him to Soissons, to the basilica of Saint Medard. They laid him before the holy tomb and made vows for him. But at midnight, already gasping and emaciated, he breathed out his spirit. They buried him in the basilica of the martyr saints Crispinus and Crispinianus.[^c0035-21]

There was great mourning throughout the whole people. The grieving men and the women dressed in mourning garments, as is customary at the funeral of a spouse, followed this funeral in the same manner. Afterwards King Chilperic gave many gifts to churches, basilicas, and the poor.

## XXXVI

During these days Austrechildis, queen of King Guntram, was consumed by this illness. Before she breathed out her wicked spirit, however, seeing that she could not escape death, she drew deep sighs and wished to make others participants in her death, arranging that the funerals of others should be mourned at her own funeral.

It is said that, following the example of Herod,[^c0035-22] she petitioned the king, saying:

“There would still have been hope of living if I had not perished in the hands of wicked physicians. The potions I received from them violently took away my life and caused me quickly to lose this light. Therefore, so that my death may not pass unavenged, I beg you, and with the interposition of an oath I implore you: when I have departed from this light, let them immediately be slain by the sword, so that, just as I can no longer live, neither may they glory after my death; let there be one grief equally for our friends and theirs.”

After saying this, she surrendered her unhappy soul.

The king, having completed the funeral rites according to custom [the manuscript Corbeiensis reads “after the funeral,” while others read “after the public mourning,” except the Casinensis, which has “after the duty of the funeral”],[^c0035-23] found himself bound by the oath of his wicked wife and fulfilled the command of iniquity. He ordered two physicians who had attended her to be struck down with the sword.[^c0035-24] Many prudent people judge that this was not done without sin [the manuscript Reginensis reads: “which prudent judgment knows was not without command…”].

## XXXVII

Thus the count Nantinus of Angoulême also died, exhausted and consumed by the illness. But what he did against priests and the churches of God must be traced from an earlier point.[^c0035-25]

His uncle Maracharius had long exercised the office of count in that city. After completing that office, he joined the Church, became a cleric, and was ordained bishop. He was very diligent in building up and repairing both churches and church buildings. In the seventh year of his episcopate, however, enemies introduced poison into the head of a fish. He innocently accepted it and was cruelly killed.

Divine mercy did not long allow his death to remain unavenged. Frontonius [the manuscript Beccensis reads Frontimius], by whose counsel this crime had been carried out, was immediately appointed to the episcopate. After living there for one year, he died under the advance judgment of God.

After his death Heraclius, a priest of Bordeaux who had once been an envoy of the elder Childebert, was ordained bishop. Nantinus, wishing to avenge his uncle’s death, sought the countship in that same city. After receiving it, he inflicted many injuries upon the bishop.

He said to the bishop: “You keep with you the murderers who killed my uncle, and you receive at table the priests who were involved in this crime.”

As his hostility increased, he gradually began to seize by force the estates of the Church that Maracharius had left by written testament. He claimed that the Church ought not to obtain the property of a man who had been killed by its clergy.

After killing some laymen, he went further and had a priest seized, bound, and pierced with a spear. While the priest was still alive, with his hands twisted behind his back and himself fastened to a stake, they tried to force him to say whether he had been involved in the matter. When he denied it, he gave up his spirit as blood poured from the wound.

The bishop, angered by this, ordered Nantinus to be barred from the doors of the Church. When priests assembled at the city of Saintes,[^c0035-26] Nantinus begged to deserve the bishop’s peace, promising that he would return all the Church’s property that he had unjustly taken and would present himself humbly to the priest.

The bishop, seeking to obey the command of the brethren, granted everything that was requested. Entrusting the priest’s case, however, to almighty God, he received the count back into charity.

After returning to the city, Nantinus stripped, battered, and demolished the houses that he had wrongfully seized, saying: “Even if this is recovered by the Church, it will be found deserted.” The bishop was therefore again moved to anger and suspended him from communion.

While these things were happening, the blessed bishop completed the course of his life and departed to the Lord. Nantinus, through the intervention of certain bishops, who were won over by rewards and flattery, was admitted to communion.

A few months later he was seized by the illness mentioned above. Burned by an excessive fever, he cried out:

“Alas, alas! I am being burned by Bishop Heraclius; by him I am tormented; by him I am summoned to judgment. I recognize the crime; I remember that I unjustly inflicted injuries upon the bishop. I beg for death, lest I be tortured by this torment any longer.”

As he cried this out in the midst of a raging fever, his bodily strength failed and he poured out his wretched soul, leaving unmistakable evidence that this had happened to him in vengeance for the blessed bishop. His lifeless body became so black that one might have thought he had been burned after being placed upon live coals.

Let everyone, therefore, be astonished, wonder, and fear lest they inflict injuries upon priests, because the Lord is the avenger of his servants who hope in him.[^c0035-27]

## XXXVIII

At this time the blessed Martin, bishop of Galicia, also died, and that people mourned him greatly.[^c0035-28] He was born in Pannonia. From there he hastened eastward to visit the holy places and so thoroughly immersed himself in learning that in his own times he was considered second to no one.

He then came to Galicia, where, when the relics of the blessed Martin were being carried, he was ordained bishop. Having completed approximately thirty years in that priestly office, he departed to the Lord full of virtues.[^c0035-29] He himself composed the verses that are above the southern door of the basilica of Saint Martin.

## XXXIX

In that year there was a great persecution of Christians in Spain. Many were sent into exile, deprived of their possessions, destroyed by hunger, confined in prison, afflicted with blows, and killed by various punishments.

The chief author of this crime was Goisvintha,[^c0035-30] whom King Leuvichild had taken as wife after her marriage to King Athanagild.[^c0035-31] But the disgrace of humility that she had inflicted upon God’s servants was pursued by divine vengeance, and she herself became notorious among all peoples. A white cloud covered one of her eyes and drove away from her eyelid the light that her mind did not possess.[^c0035-32]

King Leuvichild had two sons by another wife. The elder had married the daughter of King Sigibert, and the younger had married the daughter of King Chilperic. When Ingundis, the daughter of King Sigibert, was sent to Spain with great retinue, her grandmother Goisvintha received her with great joy. But she did not allow her to remain long in the Catholic religion. Instead, by gentle words she began to entice her to be rebaptized into the Arian heresy.

Ingundis resisted courageously and began to say:

“It is entirely sufficient that I have once been washed in saving baptism from original sin and have confessed the Holy Trinity to exist in one equality. I confess that I believe this with my whole heart, and I shall never turn back from this faith.”

When Goisvintha heard this, she was inflamed with the fury of anger. Seizing the girl by the hair of her head, she dashed her to the ground, beat her for a long time with kicks until she was covered in blood, ordered her stripped, and plunged her into a pool.[^c0035-33] Yet, as many assert, she never turned her heart away from our faith.

Leuvichild gave them one of the cities in which they were to reside and reign.[^c0035-34] After they had gone there, Ingundis began to preach to her husband that he should abandon the deception of heresy and recognize the truth of Catholic law. For a long time he rejected her preaching, but at last, moved by it, he converted to the Catholic faith. When he was confirmed, he was called John.

When Leuvichild heard this, he began to look for ways to destroy him. Understanding what was happening, Hermenegild joined the emperor’s side and formed an alliance with the emperor’s prefect, who was then attacking Spain.

Leuvichild sent messengers to him, saying: “Come to me, because there are matters that we should discuss together.”

Hermenegild replied: “I shall not come, because you are hostile to me on account of my being Catholic” [the Casinensis reads: “because you are hostile to me”].

Leuvichild then gave thirty thousand solidi to the emperor’s prefect to withdraw him from Hermenegild’s support, and, having mobilized an army, came against him.

Hermenegild, summoning Greek forces, went out against his father, leaving his wife in the city. When Leuvichild approached from the opposite direction, Hermenegild, abandoned by his support and seeing that he could achieve nothing, sought refuge in a nearby church, saying:

“Let my father not come against me. For it is wrong either for a father to be killed by his son or for a son to be killed by his father.”

When Leuvichild heard this, he sent Hermenegild’s brother to him.[^c0035-35] After giving an oath that he would not be humbled, the brother said:

“You yourself come, fall at the feet of our father, and he will forgive you everything.”

Hermenegild asked that his father be summoned. When Leuvichild entered, Hermenegild prostrated himself at his feet. Leuvichild seized and kissed him, softened him with gentle words, and led him to the camp. Then, forgetting his oath, he signaled to his men. They seized Hermenegild, stripped him of his clothing, dressed him in a worthless garment, and returned to the city of Toledo. After taking away his children, Leuvichild sent him into exile, accompanied by only one little boy.[^c0035-36]

[^c0035-1]: They had already been accused and condemned in the Council of Lyon II, as stated above in chapter 20, but were restored by a decree of Pope John. They had attended the Fourth Council of Paris in 573 with the other bishops. This chapter, found in all the manuscripts, also establishes that chapter 20 of this book—although missing from several copies—is genuinely Gregory’s work. Marius treats their deposition in this same year.

[^c0035-2]: The charge added was that they were guilty of treason against the ruler’s majesty and of betraying their country.

[^c0035-3]: Specifically, Aridius was substituted for Sagittarius at Gap, and Emeritus for Salonius at Embrun. Both attended the Second Council of Mâcon in 585; Aridius attended the Second Council of Valence in 584. Gregory the Great wrote three letters to him, in which his name appears as Aregius, as it also does in his Life, written by a contemporary author and printed by Labbe in volume I of the *Bibliotheca nova*. His feast is celebrated in his own church on 1 May.

[^c0035-4]: The ancient Gauls called an aripennis, as Valesius notes, a half-*jugerum*, containing 120 feet.

[^c0035-5]: This bishop is discussed below in Book VII, chapter 10.

[^c0035-6]: The manuscripts Reginensis and Beccensis read “crushed” instead of “afflicted.” Valesius observes in Book X of his *Frankish History* that this is the first mention among our historians of royal agents (*missi*). Later they became famous under the name *missi dominici*.

[^c0035-7]: Cointius calls this place Cornuz. Valesius says that it is commonly thought to be Saint-Aubin-le-Cormier. The manuscript Reginensis reads Tornuntium.

[^c0035-8]: The manuscript Colbertinus has no division here; it reads: “they provoked a greater disturbance, and when they returned to Gaul…”

[^c0035-9]: Gregory actually reports above, in chapter 20, that Justin had been made Caesar in the year 577. See the Chronicle of John of Biclaro. Paul the Deacon copied Gregory in Book III, chapter 12. Marius writes that Tiberius succeeded Justin in 579 after Justin’s death. Others maintain that Tiberius was proclaimed Augustus by Justin in September 578 and that Justin died in the following month, having nearly completed the twelfth year of his reign.

[^c0035-10]: That is, with the acclamations customarily offered to kings.

[^c0035-11]: The manuscript Corbeiensis reads: “Nevertheless, he who had placed his hope in God did not fear his enemies.”

[^c0035-12]: The vintage festivals were famous among ancient Christian and pagan writers. They report that the emperors observed them; see Capitolinus on Antoninus and Lampridius on Heliogabalus, among others.

[^c0035-13]: John of Biclaro and Evagrius, Book V of his *History*, say that this occurred while Justin was still alive.

[^c0035-14]: The manuscript Colbertinus reads Vannes. The reading adopted here should nevertheless be considered preferable, both because of the manuscripts and printed editions and because Felix was bishop of Nantes.

[^c0035-15]: The church was placed under interdict because blood had been shed there. See Audoenus, Book II of the *Life of Saint Eligius*, chapter 20.

[^c0035-16]: Gregory had already called this part of Auvergne the Limagne in Book III, chapter 9. It is still called Limagne, probably named from *limus*, “mud,” on account of its fertility, according to Altessera. Sidonius discusses it in Book III, Letter 1, saying: “Let the Goths judge its worth, since they disdain even their own Septimania provided that, by possessing this envious corner, they may enjoy its desolate ownership.”

[^c0035-17]: This is the river Elaver, commonly the Allier, which rises in the Cévennes, passes through Auvergne, and below the city of Nevers flows into the Loire.

[^c0035-18]: Marius writes that this occurred in October of the year 580.

[^c0035-19]: The manuscript Colbertinus reads: “the Coriales, that is, pustules.” The manuscript Beccensis reads: “Corales, that is, pustules.” They were, unless I am mistaken, pustules arising in the heart and therefore called *corales*, or perhaps the sputum was purple in color, like coral.

[^c0035-20]: Fortunatus calls him Dagobert and wrote epitaphs for him and for his brother Chlodobert in Book IX, poems 4 and 5. They died after the Council of Brennac, as is clear from the final chapter of this book.

[^c0035-21]: This is now a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict under the Congregation of Saint Maur, with a notable basilica whose nave was destroyed by the Calvinists in the preceding century. Some think that an episcopal see formerly existed there.

[^c0035-22]: Herod of Ascalon, near death, requested that the most distinguished Jews be killed immediately after his own death. See Josephus, Book I of *The Jewish War*, chapter 21.

[^c0035-23]: The manuscript Corbeiensis reads “after the funeral”; others read “after the public mourning,” except the Casinensis, which has “after the duty of the funeral.” Chesnius prints Austrechildis’s epitaph in volume I of the *Frankish Historical Writers*, p. 517; she lived thirty-two years.

[^c0035-24]: Marius calls them Nicolaus and Donatus in his *Chronicle*, where he says that Austrechildis died in September 581.

[^c0035-25]: This chapter is absent from the manuscripts Corbeiensis and Colbertinus. The manuscript Reginensis reads “Thus, after this plague…” In Beccensis, Nantinus is called count of Angoulême. The name of this city is written variously as Ecolesina, Egolisma, and, today, Inculisma. It is enough to have noted this once and again. Maracharius attended the dedication of the church at Nantes by Bishop Felix, as Fortunatus reports in Book III, poem 4.

[^c0035-26]: Sirmond dates this synod to 579 in volume I of the *Councils of Gaul*.

[^c0035-27]: The final portion of the chapter is absent from the manuscript Reginensis.

[^c0035-28]: This chapter is absent from the manuscripts Corbeiensis and Colbertinus. The manuscript Reginensis reads: “leaving great mourning among his people.” The older writers used *Callaecia* for Galicia.

[^c0035-29]: He was first bishop of the monastery of Dume and then of Braga. He held the latter dignity for approximately twenty years, not thirty. His feast is celebrated on 20 March. See his eulogy in volume I of the *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, p. 257. A letter of Fortunatus, with a poem, Book V, poem 1, is also extant to him. Compare Book I of the *Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 11. Sirmond published the verses mentioned here; they are also found in volume XV of the Cologne edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, and elsewhere.

[^c0035-30]: Goisvintha was the mother of Queen Brunhild, the wife of Sigibert, whom she had borne to King Athanagild, her former husband; she was therefore Ingundis’s grandmother. Leuvichild married her after the death of his first wife, Theodosia, daughter of Severianus, duke of Cartagena. By Theodosia he had two sons: Hermenegild, Ingundis’s husband, and Reccared, to whom Rigunthis, Chilperic’s daughter, was betrothed. After his brother’s death and his father’s death, Reccared obtained the kingdom, converted from Arianism to Catholicism, and brought the entire Visigothic people to the true faith. These details are supplied to clarify this whole chapter and the later passages concerning the same matter. For the persecution mentioned here, see also Isidore’s *Chronicle* under the year 606 of the Spanish Era.

[^c0035-31]: Other manuscripts read Athanagildus and Atanachildis. Leuvichildus is likewise written variously as Leuvihildus, Leuvichildis, Levieldus, and Leviheldis. These variant readings occur in different manuscripts whenever the names are repeated.

[^c0035-32]: The manuscript Casinensis reads: “but she who had inflicted disgrace upon many.”

[^c0035-33]: On this occasion, apparently, Leuvichild convened a synod of Arian bishops at Toledo. It was decreed there that anyone who passed from the Roman religion to their party should not be rebaptized, but should be admitted by the laying on of hands, reception of communion, and the recitation of “Glory to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit.” This is taken from John of Biclaro under the year 581.

[^c0035-34]: Specifically, Seville, the capital of Baetica, where Hermenegild was later besieged by his father. He was captured at Córdoba, sent from there into exile at Valencia, and finally killed at Tarragona, according to John of Biclaro; other authorities prefer Seville as the place of his death. Gregory discusses these matters repeatedly below.

[^c0035-35]: Reccared, as noted above.

[^c0035-36]: His father ordered him killed because he refused to receive communion from an Arian bishop on the holy day of Easter, as Saint Gregory the Great narrates more fully in Book III, chapter 31 of the *Dialogues*, and Paul the Deacon in Book III, chapter 21 of his *History of the Lombards*. This occurred at Tarragona in 586, according to John of Biclaro’s *Chronicle*; John says that Hermenegild’s killer, Sisbert, was punished by an ignominious death two years later. Hermenegild’s feast is celebrated under the title of martyr on 13 April. His wife Ingundis, fleeing but captured, was taken to Sicily, where she is said to have died. Gregory nevertheless writes below, in Book VIII, chapter 28, that she died in Africa while the Greeks were taking her to Constantinople. Their son Athanagild lived at the court of the Emperor Maurice. In an appendix we shall provide several letters written to him, or on his account to others, by King Childebert and Queen Brunhild.

[Col. 0355A] **XL.** Therefore, after Chilperic’s sons had died, the king, filled with grief, was staying with his wife in the forest of Cotia in the month of October. [Note: [Col. 0355C] In Regm. this chapter has been displaced from its proper place and appears as no. 42. Concerning the forest of Cotia, see above, Book IV, chapter 22.] Then, at the queen’s instigation, he sent his son Chlodovech to Brennac, so that he too might perish in this destruction. In those days the disease that had killed his brothers was raging violently there; nevertheless, he suffered no harm in that place. For the king himself came to Calam, a villa of the city of Paris. [Note: [Col. 0355C] There Saint Bathildis, wife of Chlodovech II, built a very famous convent, where, after living for some time as a nun, she died piously. The place retains its ancient name, commonly Chelles, four leagues from the city, on the river Marne. Concerning it, see Bede, Book III of the *History*, chapter 8.] After a few days he ordered Chlodovech to come to him; it will not be burdensome to relate what sort of death he met.

While therefore he was living with his father in the aforesaid villa, he began prematurely to boast, or to say: “Behold, with my brothers dead, the whole kingdom has been left to me; all Gaul will be subjected to me, and fate has granted me universal rule. Behold, with my enemies placed in my hands, I shall inflict whatever I please.” [Col. 0355B] He also spoke disparagingly and improperly about his stepmother, Queen Fredegund. When she heard this, she was greatly terrified.

After several days, someone came and said to the queen: “The reason you sit bereaved of your sons is Chlodovech’s deceit. For, desiring the daughter of one of your maidservants, he killed your sons by magical arts through their mother. Therefore I warn you not to expect anything better for yourself, since the hope by which you were to reign has been taken from you.”

Then the queen, terrified by fear, inflamed with rage, and pierced by this new bereavement, seized the girl whom Chlodovech had looked upon with desire, had her severely beaten, ordered the hair of her head to be cut off, and commanded her to be fastened and nailed before Chlodovech’s tent upon a split stake. [Note: [Col. 0355D] So Bad.; but Corb. and Chesn. read *abscissam sudi*, “cut off from the stake”; Colb. has *abscisso sude*, “the stake having been split”; Bec. has *scissa sudi*, “split from the stake.”]

After the girl’s mother had also been bound and long tortured, [Col. 0355C] she extracted from her a confession that confirmed the truth of these statements. [Note: [Col. 0355D] Regm. reads: “confirmed it to the king.” Then: “The king, leaving the other matters aside….”] Having reported this and other things of the same kind to the king, she demanded vengeance against Chlodovech.

Then the king, having gone hunting, ordered him to be summoned [Col. 0356A] more secretly. When he arrived, he was seized by order of the king, placed in fetters by the dukes Desiderius [Note: [Col. 0355D] This is the man who, according to Gregory, Book IX, chapter 33, married Tetradia while her husband Eulalius was still alive. He is mentioned elsewhere, especially in Book X, chapter 8. Bobo was the son of the duke Mummolinus, concerning whom see Book VI, chapter 45.] and Bobo, stripped of his armor and clothing, covered with a cheap garment, and brought bound to the queen. [Note: [Col. 0355D] *Vinctus* is absent in Corb.]

She ordered him to be kept in custody, wishing to learn from him whether matters were as she had heard, whose advice he had followed, at whose instigation he had done these things, and with whom he had formed his closest friendships. He denied the other matters but revealed the friendships of many people.

Finally, after three days, the queen ordered him, still bound, to be taken across the river Marne and kept under guard in a villa called Nuceto. [Note: [Col. 0355D] Valesius judges that this should be written *Nuceto* in his *Notitia Galliarum*; Corb. agrees. Colb. has *Nocito*, while others have *Noceto*, commonly Noisy, not far from Cala but on the opposite bank of the Marne.] While he was held there, he was struck with a knife and died; he was buried in that very place. [Note: [Col. 0356C] From there his body was later transferred with solemn ceremony to Paris, to the basilica of Saint Vincent; see below, Book VIII, chapter 10.]

Meanwhile messengers came to the king to report that Chlodovech had pierced himself with a blow of his own hand; they asserted that the very knife with which he had struck himself was still standing in the wound. By these words King Chilperic was deceived, and did not weep for the man whom he himself, so to speak, had delivered to death at the queen’s instigation. His servants were also dispersed in various directions.

His mother, however, was killed by a cruel death. [Note: [Col. 0356C] This was Audovera, whom Chilperic had dismissed because she had taken his own daughter from the sacred font, if we are to believe the Anonymous author who wrote the *Deeds of the Franks*. Cointius, under the year 565, no. 4, considers this story fictitious.
