His sister, Chlodovech’s sister Basina, later caused disturbances in the monastery of the Holy Cross at Poitiers.] His sister was sent to a monastery, deceived by the queen’s servants; [Note: [Col. 0356C] So Corb. and Colb.; the printed editions instead read, “confined in a monastery.” The manuscript reading is found in Aimoinus, Book III, chapter 43.] she remains there now, having changed her clothing. All their wealth was transferred to the queen.

The woman who had spoken against Chlodovech was condemned to be burned to death. As she was being led away, the wretched woman began to protest that she had spoken lies; but her words accomplished nothing. She was bound to a stake and burned alive in the flames.

Chlodovech’s treasurer, dragged back by Cuppan, count of the stable, [Note: [Col. 0356D] Gregory narrates his crimes in Book X, chapter 5.] was sent bound to the queen, to be subjected to various tortures. But the queen ordered him to be released both from his punishments and from his chains, and, at our intercession, allowed him to depart free.

**XLI.** After these events [Note: [Col. 0356D] This chapter is absent from Corb. and Colb. We read the instrument of Saint Elafius the bishop concerning estates that he gave to Saint Stephen together with his brother Leudomirus the deacon. It was executed publicly in the city of Châlons, in the church of the aforesaid martyr, on the fifth day before the Ides of June, in the fourth year of King Sigebert of the Franks. After the donors, Egidius, metropolitan of Reims, and Beatus, whose see is not specified, subscribed the document. Beatus, as I believe, was the same Bishop Beatus of Amiens who took part in the Council of Orléans V in the year 549. It is therefore not possible that Saint Honoratus, whom Cointius says succeeded Beatus around the year 554, should have been placed in charge of the Church of Amiens before the fourth year of King Sigebert, before 565. Elafius—Badius has *Elaphius*, most editions *Elasius*—is commemorated at Châlons on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September. His sacred body is preserved in the monastery of Saint Peter in the same city, [Col. 0357C] of the Order of Saint Benedict, under the Congregation of Saint Vanne. The instrument by which Elafius bequeathed certain property to the church of Saint Stephen, [Col. 0357D] that is, the cathedral church, is confirmed by his Life, which in a manuscript breviary of the Abbey of All Saints at Châlons reads as follows: “When the church of Châlons had been deprived of its pastor, Sigebert, son of Chlothar and grandson of the great Chlodovech, summoned Elafius from Limoges and arranged for him to be elevated to that see. After reluctantly accepting the episcopal office, Elafius devoted himself entirely to the Lord, giving generous alms, persevering in prayer, and omitting nothing that belonged to the duty of a good shepherd. Led by love and longing for such a brother, Leodemirus left his homeland and went to Châlons. Their fraternal harmony greatly benefited the church of Châlons; they also gave it their hereditary estates near the city of Limoges, and so forth.” Concerning him, the Necrology records under the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September: “At Châlons, the natal day of the most glorious prelate Elafius, brother of Blessed Leudomirus.” Furthermore, Beatus, who wrote Saint Elafius’s instrument, was not a bishop, as is clear from his own words: “I, although unworthy, am nevertheless called Beatus; at the command of Elafius, the venerable bishop, and with the consent of Leudomerus the deacon, I wrote this charter in the place of Ernoldus the notary.” Thus what I said in the notes about Beatus, whom I suspected of having been Bishop of Amiens, falls.] Elafius, bishop of Châlons, was sent to Spain on an embassy on account of matters involving Queen Brunichildis. He was seized by a severe fever, breathed his last, and was then carried dead to his own city and buried there.

Bishop Eonius also, whom we mentioned above as an envoy of the Britons, [Note: [Col. 0358D] Above, chapter 30, where Eunius is called bishop of Vannes.] was not permitted to return to his own city; instead, the king ordered that he should be maintained at public expense at Angers. When he came to Paris and was celebrating the sacred solemnities on the Lord’s Day, he uttered a cry with a neighing sound and fell to the ground. As blood burst from his mouth and nostrils, he was carried away in people’s arms, but recovered. He was excessively devoted to wine and was often so shamefully drunk that he was unable to walk.

**XLII.** Miro, king of Galicia, sent envoys to King Guntram. As they were passing through the territory of Poitiers, which King Chilperic then held, this was reported to him. He ordered them to be brought under guard before him and kept in Paris.

At that time, at the city of Poitiers, a wolf came from the forests, entered through the gate, and, after the gates had been closed, was trapped within the city walls and killed. Some people also asserted that they had seen the sky on fire.

The river Loire was greater than in the preceding year, after the torrent Caris had joined it. [Note: [Col. 0358D] Corb. has *estoreus*; Colb. has “the torrent Duricarus joined it.” The printed editions, together with Bec., have *Caris* or *Cares*. Cod. Regm. reads “greater from the river … cares.” In my opinion, the river Caris is meant here, commonly called the Cher, which flows into the Loire.]

The south wind blew with extraordinary violence, so that it felled forests, tore down houses, carried away hedges, and hurled people themselves about until they were destroyed. Its breadth was about seven *jugera*; its length could not be estimated. Roosters often gave their call at the beginning of the night. The moon was darkened, and a comet appeared. A severe plague then followed among the people.

After a year the envoys of the Suebi were dismissed and returned to their own country. [Note: [Col. 0358D] These are presumably the envoys said above to have been sent by Miro; he ruled over the Suebi living in Galicia. Hence, in the chapter index of Cod. Regm., they are called “Galician envoys.”]

**XLIII.** Maurilius, bishop of the city of Cahors, [Note: [Col. 0358D] This chapter is absent from Colb. and Corb. Bad. has *Maurilius*, and in the chapter index, “Concerning Maurilius.” Bec. has *Marilius*.] was seriously ill from gouty humors. In addition to the pains caused by that humor, he inflicted great torments upon himself; for he often drove red-hot iron into his shins and feet, in order to increase his suffering still further.

Since many people desired his bishopric, he chose Ursicinus, [Note: [Col. 0358D] Concerning him, see below. He subscribed the acts of the Second Council of Mâcon.] who had once been Queen Ultrogotha’s *referendarius*. While he was still alive, Maurilius asked that Ursicinus be blessed, and then departed from this world.

He was exceedingly generous in almsgiving and very well instructed in the ecclesiastical Scriptures, so that he often recited from memory the sequence of the various genealogies described in the books of the Old Testament, a matter that many people find difficult to retain.

He was also just in judgments and defended the poor of his church from the hands of wicked judges, in accordance with what is written in Job:

“I rescued the needy from the hand of the powerful;  
I helped the helpless, who had no one to assist him.  
The mouth of the widow blessed me,  
when I was the eye of the blind,  
the foot of the lame,  
and the father of the weak.”  
(Job 29:12–16)

**XLIV.** King Leuvichild, for his part, sent Agila as an envoy to Chilperic, a man of no particular ability or practical intelligence, but perverse in his will alone with regard to the Catholic faith. When the journey had brought him through Tours, he began to challenge us concerning the faith and to attack ecclesiastical [Col. 0358B] doctrines.

“For,” he said, “the sentence pronounced by the ancient bishops was unjust, since it asserted that the Son was equal to the Father. For how,” he said, “can he be equal to the Father in power who says, ‘The Father is greater than I’ (John 14:28)? It is therefore not right that he should be considered like the one to whom he declares himself inferior, before whom he laments the sorrow of death, and to whom, finally, as he dies and as though endowed with no power, he commends his spirit. Hence it is clear that he is inferior to the Father both in age and in power.”

To this I asked whether he believed Jesus Christ to be the Son of God, and whether he confessed him to be the Wisdom of God, the Light, [254] the Truth, the Life, and Justice.

He replied: “I believe that all these are the Son of God.”

And I said: “Then tell me: when was the Father without wisdom? When without light? When without life? When without truth? When without justice? For just as the Father could not exist without these, so he could not exist without the Son. These things in particular correspond to the mystery of the Lord’s name.” [Note: [Col. 0358D] Regm. reads, “which correspond to the Lord’s words.”] “Indeed, the Father would not be the Father if he did not have a Son.

“As for your claim that he said, ‘The Father is greater than I,’ know that he said this from the humility of the flesh he had assumed, so that you might understand that you were redeemed not by power but by humility. For you who say, ‘The Father is greater than I’ ought to remember that elsewhere he says, ‘I and the Father are one’ (John 10:30). The fear of death and the commending of his spirit must likewise be referred to the weakness of the body, so that he may be believed to be true God and likewise true [Col. 0359A] man.”

He replied: “Whoever fulfills another’s will is inferior to that one.” [Note: [Col. 0359D] Corb., Bec., and Colb. c. read, “is younger than he.”] “The Son is always inferior to the Father, because he does the Father’s will, whereas the Father is not shown to do the Son’s will.”

To this I replied: “Understand that the Father exists in the Son and the Son in the Father, always in one divinity. To recognize that the Father does the will of the Son, if evangelical faith remains in you, hear what Jesus himself, our God, said when he came to raise Lazarus: ‘Father, I thank you because you have heard me. I knew indeed that you always hear me; but because of the crowd standing around I said it, so that they may believe that you sent me’ (John 11:41–42).

“And when he came to his passion, he said: ‘Father, glorify me with the glory that I had with you before the world existed’ (John 17:5). The Father answered him from heaven: ‘I have glorified him, and I will glorify him again’ (John 12:28). The Son is therefore equal in divinity—not inferior, nor lacking anything. For if you confess him to be God, you must necessarily confess him to be complete and in need of nothing; but if you deny that he is complete, you do not believe him to be God.”

He replied: “The Son of God began to be called so after he assumed a man; for there was a time when he did not exist.”

And I said: “Hear David speaking in the person of the Father: ‘From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you’ (Psalm 109:3). And the evangelist John says: ‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God’ (John 1:1). This Word therefore became flesh and dwelt among us, and through him all things were made (John 1:14, 3). For you, blinded by the poison of persuasion, think nothing worthy of God.”

He replied: “Do you also call the Holy Spirit God, or do you declare him equal to the Father and the Son?”

To him I said: “In the three there is one will, one power, and one operation: one God in Trinity, and threefold in unity. Three persons, but one kingdom, one majesty, one power, and omnipotence.”

He said: “The Holy Spirit, whom you present as equal to the Father and the Son, is understood to be inferior to both, because he was promised by the Son and is read to have been sent by the Father. No one promises anything except what is subject to his own dominion, and no one sends anyone except one who is inferior to him, just as he himself says in the Gospel: ‘Unless I go away, that Paraclete will not come; but if I go away, I will send him to you’ (John 16:7).” [Note: [Col. 0359D] Regm. reads, “the Paraclete will not come.”]

To this I replied: “The Son rightly said this before his passion: unless he returned victorious to the Father and, having redeemed the world by his own blood, prepared for God a dwelling worthy of him from the human race, the Holy Spirit, who is the same God, could not descend into a fanatical breast infected with the stain of original sin. For, says Solomon, ‘The Holy Spirit will flee from deceit’ (Wisdom 1:5). But if you have any hope of resurrection, do not speak against the Holy Spirit, because, according to the Lord’s judgment, blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come (Matthew 12:32).” [Note: [Col. 0359D] Corb. and Regm. have *effugiet*, “will flee”; the printed editions, together with Bec. and Colb. c., have *fugiet*, “will flee.” The wording in Corb., Regm., Bec., and Colb. c. is “for blaspheming in the Holy Spirit”; the printed editions have “for blaspheming the Holy Spirit.”]

He said: “He who sends is God; he who is sent is not God.”

To this I asked whether he believed the teaching of the apostles Peter and Paul. When he answered, “I do,” I added:

“When the apostle Peter rebuked Ananias for defrauding the estate, see what he says: ‘Why has it entered your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit? You have not lied to human beings but to God’ (Acts 5:3–4). And when Paul distinguished the degrees of spiritual gifts, he said: ‘All these things are accomplished by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each as he wills’ (1 Corinthians 12:11). Whoever does whatever he wills is subject to no one’s power. For, as I said above, you think nothing correctly about the Holy Trinity; and how wicked is the perversity of this sect was shown by the death of its founder, Arius himself.”

He replied: “Do not blaspheme the law that you do not observe. As for us, although we do not believe what you believe, we do not blaspheme it, because it is not considered a crime if both this and that are worshiped. Thus, in common speech, we say: ‘It is not harmful if someone passing between the altars of the pagans and the church of God venerates both.’” [Note: [Col. 0359D] It should be observed from this passage that, once the faith of the Catholic Church has been abandoned, no true religion is acknowledged. This Arian, while recognizing all good religions, showed that he possessed none.]

Seeing his stupidity, I said: “As I see it, you show yourself both a defender of the pagans and an advocate of heretics, since you stain ecclesiastical doctrines and preach that pagan impurities should be worshiped.

“It would be better,” I said, “if you armed yourself with the faith that Abraham saw in the oak, Isaac in the ram, and Jacob in the stone; that Moses saw in the thornbush; that Aaron carried on the *logion*; [Note: [Col. 0360D] That is, on the high priest’s breastpiece, where *logos*, or the name of God, was written.] that David celebrated on the timbrel; that Solomon proclaimed in understanding; the faith that all the patriarchs and prophets, and the Law itself, proclaimed either through oracles or represented through sacrifices; the faith that our present advocate Martin either possessed in his heart or displayed in his works—so that you too might be converted and believe in the inseparable Trinity, and that, after receiving our blessing and having your breast cleansed of the poison of evil belief, your iniquities might be wiped away.”

But, moved to fury and growling something like a madman, he declared: “Before my soul departs from the bonds of this body [Note: [Col. 0360D] Regm. reads, “is separated.”], I shall receive a blessing from none of your priests.”

And I said: “May the Lord never allow our religion or faith to grow so lukewarm [Note: [Col. 0360D] The same reading is found in Colb.: *tabescere*, “to waste away.”] that we should distribute his holy things to dogs and expose the sacred pearls of great price to filthy swine.”

At this he abandoned the dispute, rose, and departed. But afterward, when he had returned to Spain, weakened by illness, he was converted to our religion by necessity.

**XLV.** At about the same time King Chilperic wrote a short treatise declaring that the Holy Trinity should be named not with a distinction of persons but simply as God. He asserted that it was unworthy for God to be called a person, like a human being composed of flesh; he also affirmed that the Father himself was the Son, and likewise that the Holy Spirit himself was the Father and the Son. “Thus,” he said, “he appeared to the prophets and patriarchs; thus the Law itself announced him.”

When he had ordered this to be read to me, he said: “This is what I want you and the other teachers of the churches to believe.”

I replied: “Having abandoned this belief, pious king, you ought to follow what other teachers of the Church left to us after the apostles; what Hilary and Eusebius taught; [Note: [Col. 0361C] Namely, Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, who fought brilliantly with Hilary of Poitiers against the heretics who attacked the Holy Trinity. Chilperic was reviving the false doctrines of Sabellius.] and what you confessed in baptism.”

Then the angry king said: “It is clear to me that Hilary and Eusebius are powerful enemies in this matter.”

I replied: “You ought to take care not to offend God or his saints. For you should know that in person the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another. [Note: [Col. 0361C] So Corb., Bec., Colb. c., and the old editions. Colb. a. also originally had this reading, but someone placed a mark beneath the letter *i* to produce: “one is the Father, another the Son, another the Holy Spirit.” This is the reading of Regm. and Chesnius.]

“It was not the Father who assumed flesh, nor the Holy Spirit, but the Son, so that he who was the Son of God might himself, for the redemption of humanity, be considered the son of man and of the Virgin. It was not the Father who suffered, nor the Holy Spirit, but the Son, so that he who had assumed flesh in the world might himself be offered for the world. As for what you say about persons, this must be understood spiritually, not bodily. In these three persons there is one glory, one eternity, and one power.”

Moved by this, he said: “I shall explain these matters to wiser men than you, who will agree with me.” [Note: [Col. 0361C] Regm. reads, “I have decided to explain these matters.”]

And I replied: “He who wishes to follow what you propose will never be wise but foolish.”

At this he growled and fell silent.

Not many days later, when Salvianus, bishop of Albi, arrived, the king ordered these things to be read to him, asking him to agree with him. When Salvianus heard them, he rejected them so completely that, had he been able to touch the sheet on which they were written, he would have torn it to pieces. Thus the king abandoned this undertaking. [Col. 0361C]

The same king also wrote other books in verse, as though imitating Sedulius; but those little verses conform not at all to the rules of meter. [Note: [Col. 0361C] Corb. has “conform in no way to meter.” Fortunatus praises Chilperic’s eloquence and his inclination toward literature in Book IX, poem 1. Nothing of his works survives except several verses in honor of Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, which Aimoinus transmits. Brouverus nevertheless thinks that Fortunatus composed them, and others do not consider them to be of such great antiquity. Sedulius flourished at Rome under Theodosius, and Christian poets sought to imitate him. See Bede, Book V of the *History*, chapter 19.]

He also added letters to our alphabet: namely, ω, as the Greeks have it, and *ae*, *the*, and *uui*, whose characters we have written below. They are these: ω ψ Ζ Δ. [Note: [Col. 0361D] We have represented these characters as they appear in the oldest of all the manuscripts, Cod. Corb. In Colb. they are: ω ο, Ψ *ae*, y, which is cut through the middle by a transverse stroke, z, Δ *uui*. Regm. has: o u, y *the*, z, y *uui*. Bec. has: Θ *ccc*, Ψ *ae*, z *the*, and after the unknown letters, *vui*. The same chapter of Gregory appears in an old collection of canons and professions of faith from a Colbertine manuscript written about eight hundred years ago, where the same letters are written in nearly the same form as in Cod. Corb., except that the final letter is *a, uiui*. Most printed editions have represented these characters with Greek letters: ω or Ο, Ψ, Ζ, Π. In Aimoinus’s edition, Book III, chapter 41, they are χ *ch*, θ *th*, φ *ph*; but a manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, written about four hundred years ago, has Ψ *ae*, T *the*, *am u*. In any event, these letters suffered the same fate as those once invented by the emperor Claudius: together with their author, they perished.] He sent letters to all the cities of his kingdom, so that children might be taught in this way and anciently written books might be smoothed with pumice and rewritten.

**XLVI.** At this time Agroecula, bishop of Chalon, died. [Note: [Col. 0362C] This chapter is absent from Corb. and Colb.] He was a very refined and prudent man, of senatorial origin. In that city he constructed many buildings, arranged houses, and built a church, which he supported with columns, adorned with varied marble, and decorated with mosaic. [Note: [Col. 0362C] Regm. reads, “which he decorated with varied ornament.” He was a man of great abstinence, so that he never ate during the day except once, and this meal was called supper, at which in springtime he sat in such a way… Perhaps, instead of *temporive*, one should read *temporius*, as the written manuscripts have it in the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 11. The *musivum* mentioned here and often by Gregory is work composed of tesserae arranged to represent various figures; among the ancients it was highly valued and is called in French *ouvrage à la mosaïque*. On this subject the illustrious Joannes Ciampinus published an excellent volume at Rome. See also Bergerius, Book II, *On the Public Roads of the Empire*.]

He was a man of great abstinence, for he never took lunch, but only supper; and he sat down to it at such a time that he rose while the sun was still standing. He was small in stature but of great eloquence. He died in the forty-eighth year of his episcopate and the eighty-third year of his life. [Note: [Col. 0362D] His feast is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology on March 17. He took part in the Third, Fourth, and Fifth Councils of Orléans, the Second Council of Clermont, the Second Council of Paris, and the Third Council of Lyon. See the *Book on the Glory of the Confessors*, chapters 85 and 86, and Bollandus under March 17. Fortunatus praises Agricola in Book III, poem 22, although Cointius understands this to refer to Agricola, bishop of Nevers.] Flavius, *referendarius* of King Guntram, succeeded him.

**XLVII.** At that time Dalmatius also, bishop of the city of Rodez, departed from this world. [Note: [Col. 0362D] This chapter is absent from Corb. and Colb. Dalmatius subscribed the Council of Clermont in 535 and the Fourth Council of Orléans in 541; he is commemorated in the Gallican Martyrology on November 13.] He was a man outstanding in every holiness, abstaining both from food and [or, according to the correction] from the desires of the flesh; extremely generous in almsgiving and kind to everyone, steadfast enough in prayer and vigils.

He built a church, but because he repeatedly demolished it for renovation, he left it unfinished. After his death many people, as usually happens, sought the bishopric.

The presbyter Transobadus [Note: [Col. 0362D] Regm. and Bec. have *Transobaldus*. “Trusting … with Gogo.” Concerning Gogo, see Book VI, chapter 1.] was especially intent on obtaining it. He was confident because he had commended his son to Gogo, who at that time was the king’s fosterling.

The bishop had drawn up a will in which he indicated who was to receive, after his death, the king’s gift [Note: [Col. 0362D] The same manuscripts, together with Bad., have this reading, and correctly; the others have *regi Sexenium*. The bishop had not chosen Sexenius as his successor; rather, he indicated the conditions under which the bishopric—which he calls the king’s gift, or *xenium*—ought to be conferred.] He adjured them by terrible oaths that no outsider, no covetous man, and no one bound by marriage should be ordained in that church, but that a man freed from all these things, who lived solely for the praises of the Lord, should be appointed in his place.

The presbyter Transobadus prepared a banquet for the clergy in the city itself. While they were seated, one of the presbyters began to slander the aforesaid bishop with indecent words. [Note: [Col. 0363D] From this passage comes our French word *blâmer*, “to blame,” which here and often elsewhere in Gregory has this meaning.] He went so far as to call him demented and foolish.

As he was saying this, the cupbearer arrived to offer the cup. But when the presbyter had taken it and brought it near his mouth, he began to tremble; then, loosening the cup from his hand, he leaned his head upon the man beside him [another reading: “upon someone else”] and gave up his spirit. He was carried from the banquet to the grave and covered with earth.

Afterward, the bishop’s will was read again in the presence of King Childebert and his nobles, and Theodosius, [Note: [Col. 0363D] Regm. has *Theodus*. Concerning him and the others mentioned here, see Book VI, chapter 38.] who at that time held the archdeaconate of that city, was ordained bishop.

**XLVIII.** When Chilperic heard of all the evils that Leudastes was committing against the churches of Tours and against the entire people, he sent Ansoualdus there. [Note: [Col. 0363D] Regm. has *Ansoaldus*.] When he came for the feast of Saint Martin, he gave us and the people the choice, and Eunomius was appointed count.

Finally, when Leudastes saw that he had been removed, he sent to Chilperic, saying:

“Until now, most merciful king, I have guarded the city of Tours. But now that I have been removed from office, see how it is being guarded. For you should know that Bishop Gregory intends to hand it over to the son of Sigebert.”

When the king heard this, he said: “Not at all; but since you have been removed, you are making these accusations.”

He replied: “The bishop says even greater things about you. He says that your queen is involved in adultery with Bishop Bertchramn.”

Then the angry king ordered Leudastes, after beating him with fists and kicks and loading him with chains, to be confined in prison.

XLIX. [This chapter, which in most manuscripts is not distinguished from the preceding one, is absent from Corb. and Colb.] But since the book calls for an ending, I would like to relate some matters concerning his actions; first, however, it seems appropriate to begin with his origin, homeland, and character.

He was born on the island of Cracina [Regm. and Bad. read *Gracina*. Alteserra holds that *Eracina* should be read, as denoting the island of Radina, l’île de Ré, as Papirius Massonus wrote in his description of rivers. Valesius would prefer *Cratina* or *Ratina*. It was formerly called the island of Herus or Herio, and lies adjacent to the coast of Poitou], off Poitiers, to a slave of a fiscal vine-dresser named Leocadius [Bad. reads “of a fiscal tax-gatherer”; Regm., “a slave of the fiscal vineyard”]. From there he was summoned into service and assigned to the royal kitchen. But because in his youth he had bleary eyes, which did not tolerate the harshness of smoke, he was removed from the pestle and promoted to the kneading basket [that is, he was made a baker instead of a cook]. But while pretending to delight in the fermented doughs, he deserted his service and fled. When, after being brought back twice or three times, he could not be restrained from fleeing, he was punished by the cutting off of one ear.

Since he could not conceal the mark inflicted upon his body by any authority, he fled to Queen Marcovefa, whom King Charibert, loving her excessively, had taken to his bed in place of his sister. She gladly took him in, advanced him [that is, promoted him, as is clear from other passages of Gregory], and appointed him keeper of the best horses. From this point, already possessed by vanity and devoted to arrogance, he sought the office of count of the stables [the count of the stable had charge of the prince’s horses; this dignity later became military and grew greatly in importance. Cangius sets out its duties and development at length in his *Glossary*, which no one will ever regret consulting]. Having obtained it, he despised and subordinated everyone; he was puffed up with vanity, dissipated by luxury, inflamed by greed, and, in the lawsuits of his patroness, her own protégé was carried here and there. After her death, stuffed with plunder, he began, by means of gifts, to retain that very position with King Charibert.

Afterward, when the sins of the people were pressing upon them, he was appointed count at Tours. There he displayed himself even more arrogantly in the splendor of his honors; there he showed himself rapacious in plunder, swollen with quarrels, and befouled with adulteries. By sowing discord and bringing accusations, he amassed no small treasures. After Charibert’s death, when that city had fallen to Sigibert’s portion, and he passed over to Chilperic, the faithful men of the aforesaid king seized everything that he had unjustly accumulated.

When King Chilperic was passing through the city of Tours with his son Theodbert, and I had already arrived at Tours, Theodbert strongly commended him to me, so that he might obtain the countship that he had previously held. He made himself very humble and submissive to us, repeatedly swearing over the tomb of the holy bishop that he would never act contrary to the order of justice, and that he would be faithful to me in every matter, both in his own lawsuits and in the needs of the Church. For he feared—and this later came to pass—that King Sigibert might again recall that city under his own dominion.

When Sigibert died and Chilperic again succeeded to the kingdom, this man entered upon the countship. When Merovech arrived at Tours, he plundered all his property everywhere. But while Sigibert held Tours for two years, he lay hidden in Brittany. After he had assumed the countship, as we have said, he was lifted up by such frivolity that he would enter the church’s house wearing breastplates and coats of mail, girded with a quiver and carrying a spear in his hand, his head helmeted. He trusted no one, because he was hostile to everyone [Regm. reads “contrary” or “opposed.” For—].

Whenever he sat in judgment with elders, whether laymen or clerics, and saw someone pursuing justice, he immediately flew into a rage. He belched out insults at the citizens; he ordered presbyters dragged out by their sleeves and soldiers beaten with clubs. He practiced such cruelty that it can scarcely be related [the same manuscript reads, “can scarcely be endured”].

When Merovech departed—the man who had plundered his property—he became our accuser, falsely asserting that Merovech had used our counsel to seize his goods. But after the damage had been inflicted, he renewed his oaths and gave as guarantor the covering of the tomb of blessed Martin [that is, a carpet with which the holy bishop’s tomb was covered; Gregory frequently uses this word], swearing that he would never again oppose us.

L. [This chapter is absent from Corb. and Colb.] But since it would be lengthy to relate in order his perjuries and other evils, let us come to the matter of how he wished to overthrow me by unjust and abominable accusations, and how divine vengeance descended upon him, so that this might be fulfilled: “Everyone who lays a snare will himself be ensnared” (Jeremiah 9:4); and again, “He who digs a pit will fall into it” (Proverbs 26:27).

Thus, after the many evils he had inflicted upon me and mine, and after the many plunderings of ecclesiastical property, he joined himself to the presbyter Riculfus, a man perverted by similar wickedness, and went so far as to say that I had uttered a charge against Queen Fredegund. He asserted that, if my archdeacon Plato or our friend Gallienus [the Regm. manuscript reads “Ioislenus”; below, however, the same manuscript has “Gallienus”] were subjected to punishment, they would certainly convict me of having spoken these things.

Then the angry king ordered him, as we have said above (chapter 48), beaten with fists and kicks, loaded with chains, and confined in prison. For he said that he had a cleric, Riculfus [Regm. reads “presbyter”], through whom he had spoken these things. This Riculfus, however, was a subdeacon, exceedingly pliable in the same frivolous manner. In the year before this [Bad. reads “before this year,” using a change of case familiar to Gregory], after consulting with Leudastes about this matter, he sought reasons for offense by which, once I had been offended, he might pass over to Leudastes. At last he found his opportunity, approached him, and, after preparing every kind of deceit and snare for four months, returned to me with Leudastes, begging that I should receive him with his excuse.

I did so, I confess, and received a secret enemy publicly into my house. When Leudastes had departed, Riculfus threw himself at my feet, saying: “Unless you quickly come to my aid, I shall perish. Look: at Leudastes’ urging, I said what I ought not to have said. Now send me into another kingdom; if you do not, I shall be seized by the royal authorities and suffer a death penalty.”

I replied: “If you have uttered anything contrary to reason, your words will fall upon your own head. I will not send you to another kingdom, lest I be regarded with suspicion before the king.”

After this, Leudastes became his accuser, saying that he had heard the aforesaid speeches from the subdeacon Riculfus. Riculfus was again bound, while Leudastes was released, and he was consigned to custody. He said that Gallienus and Plato the archdeacon had been present on the day when the bishop had uttered these things [so Regm.; Bad. has “archdeacon”; the other manuscripts, with Bec., have “archdeacons.” Yet Gallienus is not called an archdeacon above; hence this passage cannot establish that there were then several archdeacons in the church of Tours. Saint Remigius mentions archdeacons in his letter to Falcon. Plato later became bishop of Poitiers; concerning him, see Book IV of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 32].

But the presbyter Riculfus, who had already received a promise of the episcopate from Leudastes, had been lifted up to such an extent that he equaled the arrogance of the magician Simon. Three times, or even more, he had given me an oath over the tomb of Saint Martin. On the sixth day of Easter he treated me with such insults and spitting that he scarcely restrained his hands, being confident in the deceit he had prepared.

On the following day, that is, Saturday during Easter itself, Leudastes came into the city of Tours, and, pretending to be engaged in another matter, seized Plato the archdeacon and Gallienus and bound them in chains. He ordered them, chained and stripped of their clothing, to be led to the queen.

When I heard this, as I sat sorrowfully in the church’s house, disturbed and entering the oratory, I took up the book of David’s songs, so that when it was opened it might offer some verse of consolation. In it the following was found: “He led them out in hope, and they did not fear; and the sea covered their enemies” (Psalm 77:53).

Meanwhile, when they had entered the river upon a bridge supported by two boats, the vessel carrying Leudastes sank. Unless he had been rescued by the aid of swimming, he might perhaps have perished with his companions. But the other vessel, which was fastened to it and carried the prisoners, was lifted above the waters by God’s assistance.

Those who had been bound were then brought before the king and vigorously accused, so that they might be condemned to death. But the king reconsidered and, releasing them from their bonds, kept them unharmed in open custody [“open custody” was the term used when an accused person was not kept in prison but entrusted to a magistrate for safekeeping, or when he was treated more leniently].

At the city of Tours, Duke Berulfus [Fortunatus still mentions Berulfus as count in Book VII, poem 15], together with Count Eunomius, fabricated a story that King Gunthram had wished to seize the city of Tours. “Therefore,” he said, “lest any negligence occur, the city must be entrusted to a guard.” They deceitfully placed guards at the gates, pretending to protect the city but in fact guarding me. They also sent men to advise me that I should secretly take the Church’s better possessions and withdraw in flight to Auvergne; but I did not consent.

The king therefore summoned the bishops of his realm and ordered the matter to be carefully investigated. While the cleric Riculfus was repeatedly examined in secret and brought forward many falsehoods against me and mine, a certain Modestus, a carpenter, said to him: “Unhappy man, who plots these things so obstinately against your bishop! It would have been better for you to remain silent and obtain the bishop’s favor by asking pardon.”

At this he began to shout loudly and say: “There he is—the man who orders me to be silent so that I may not pursue the truth! There he is—the enemy of the queen, who does not allow her criminal case to be investigated!”

This was immediately reported to the queen. Modestus was seized, tortured, flogged, loaded with chains, and consigned to custody. While he was held between two guards, bound in chains and fastened in a stocks, the guards fell asleep at midnight. He poured out a prayer to the Lord, asking that by his power he might deign to visit the wretched man, and that he who had been bound though innocent might be released through the visitation of Bishops Martin and Medard.

At once his bonds broke, the stocks were shattered, and the door was unlocked. He entered the basilica of Saint Medard while we kept vigil at night [this took place at Soissons, from which city Brennacum is about three leagues distant. Fortunatus composed poem 1 of Book IX in praise of Chilperic at the very time when this synod of Brennacum was held].

The bishops therefore gathered at the estate of Brennacum and were ordered to sit together in one house. When the king arrived, he greeted everyone and, after receiving their blessing, took his seat.

Then Bertchramnus, bishop of Bordeaux, against whom the charge involving the queen had been brought, presented the case and addressed me, saying that I had made the accusation against him and the queen. I denied truthfully that I had spoken these things, though others had heard them; I had not devised them. For outside the house there was a great rumor among the people, who said: “Why are such accusations being brought against the priest of God? Why does the king pursue such matters? Could a bishop have said such things, or even such things about a servant? Alas, alas! Lord God, grant help to your servant!”

The king, however, said: “The crime of my wife is regarded as my disgrace. If, therefore, you think that witnesses should be brought against the bishop, here they are. But if you think that this should not be done and that the matter should be entrusted to the bishop’s sworn word, say so; I will gladly hear what you command.”

Everyone marveled at the king’s prudence and patience alike. Then, when all said, “An inferior person cannot be believed against a priest,” the matter nevertheless proceeded to the point that, after Masses had been celebrated, I cleared myself by oath before three altars of the words in question [from this passage some infer that Gregory celebrated Mass three times in one day. Others interpret it to mean that, after celebrating Mass, Gregory cleared himself of the accusation by giving an oath concerning his innocence at three altars. Gregory did this because, according to the canons, a subdeacon or lesser cleric ought not to be admitted as a witness against a bishop. Laymen likewise were by no means admitted to accuse bishops, according to the prescriptions of the canons]. Although this was contrary to the canons, it was nevertheless carried out because of the king’s case.

Nor do I omit this: Queen Rigunthis [this was Rigunthis, daughter of Chilperic and Fredegund, of whom Gregory speaks frequently. She is called “queen” according to the custom of those times, when the daughters of kings were called queens. Indeed, the old poet known under the name of Alcuin, describing the hunting of Charlemagne, writes that the daughters of that king wore crowns on their heads] sympathized with my sufferings and observed a fast with her entire household until a boy announced that I had fulfilled everything just as it had been prescribed.

The priests then returned to the king and said: “Everything that was commanded has been fulfilled by the bishop, O king. What remains for you now except to be deprived of communion together with Bertchramnus, the accuser of his brother?”

He replied: “No; I merely reported what I had heard.”

When they asked who had told him these things, he answered that he had heard them from Leudastes. But Leudastes, in accordance with the weakness of his plan and intention, had already taken flight.

Then all the priests agreed that the sower of scandal, the defamer of the queen, and the accuser of the bishop should be excluded from all churches, because he had withdrawn himself from the hearing. They therefore sent a letter, signed by them, to the other bishops who had not been present. And so each man returned to his own place.

When Leudastes heard this, he sought the basilica of Saint Peter at Paris. But when he heard the king’s edict that no one in his kingdom should receive him—and especially when he learned that the son whom he had left at home had died—he came secretly to Tours and transferred to that place the finest possessions he had in Bourges. When the royal officers pursued him, he slipped away in flight.

His wife was captured and confined in exile in the district of Tournai. As for the cleric Riculfus, an order was given for his execution. I scarcely obtained his life, though I could not excuse him from torture. For no substance, no metal, could endure blows as great as this wretched man sustained. From the third hour of the day, with his hands bound behind his back, he hung suspended from a tree. At the ninth hour he was taken down, stretched upon the rack, and beaten with clubs, rods, and doubled leather straps—not by one or two men, but by as many beaters as could approach his miserable limbs.

When he was already in danger of death, he disclosed the truth and exposed publicly the secret plans of the deceit. He said that the accusation against the queen had been brought so that, once she had been expelled from the kingdom and her brothers killed, Chlodovechus would receive the kingdom from his father [so the Regm. manuscript reads. Chlodoveus wanted nothing other than to drive his stepmother Fredegund from the kingdom; and once her brothers Theodbert and Merovech had been killed, he would thus have gained the kingdom. The editions with Bec. read “with her brothers and father killed,” as though he had contemplated killing his own father, which is scarcely plausible. If Chilperic had been killed, Chlodoveus would have had no reason to deliberate about expelling Fredegund, since he himself would already have been master of everything and could have expelled her at will]. Leudastes would obtain the dukedom, while the presbyter Riculfus—who had already been Chlodovechus’s friend since the time of blessed Bishop Euphronius—would seek the episcopate of Tours, with the archdeaconate promised to this cleric Riculfus.

When, by God’s grace, we returned to Tours, we found the church disturbed by the presbyter Riculfus. Under Bishop Euphronius, having been accused on account of the poor, he was ordained an archdeacon. Thereafter, when he was advanced to the presbyterate, he withdrew to his own property, always arrogant, puffed up, and presumptuous [Regm. reads: “always the same in arrogance, full of every wickedness. For …”].

While I was still staying with the king, he entered the church’s house shamelessly, as though he were already bishop. He inventoried the church’s silver and brought the remaining property under his own control. He enriched the senior clerics with gifts, gave away vineyards, and distributed meadows; but he afflicted the lesser clerics with clubs, many blows, and even with his own hand, saying: “Recognize your lord, who has won victory over his enemies, whose ingenuity has cleansed the city of Tours of the Arverni people” [the edition of Chesne reads “corrected.” Gregory was in fact an Arvernian].

The wretch did not know that, apart from five bishops, all the rest who had held the episcopate of Tours were related by descent to our family. He was accustomed to say repeatedly to his intimates that no one could deceive a prudent man except through perjuries.

But when I had returned and he still despised me, neither coming to greet me as the other citizens had done, but rather threatening to kill me, I ordered, with the counsel of the bishops of the province, that he be removed to a monastery. When he was being held there under stricter restraint, messengers of Bishop Felix intervened—Felix had been a supporter of the aforementioned cause—and, after Riculfus had ensnared the abbot with perjuries, he escaped in flight and went to Bishop Felix, who eagerly took him in, though he ought to have abhorred him.

Leudastes, meanwhile, went to Bourges, taking with him all the treasures he had extracted from the spoils of the poor. Not long afterward, when the people of Bourges and the local judge attacked him, they carried off all the gold and silver and whatever else he had brought with him, leaving him nothing except what he wore. They would also have taken his life, had he not escaped by flight.

Afterward, having recovered his strength, he again attacked his plunderers with some men from Tours. Having killed one of them, he recovered some of the property and returned to Tours. When Duke Berulfus heard this, he sent his men with weapons to capture him. Seeing that he was on the point of being seized, Leudastes abandoned his possessions and sought the basilica of Saint Hilary at Poitiers.

Duke Berulfus sent the captured property to the king. Leudastes, however, would leave the basilica and burst into the houses of various people, carrying out open plundering. He was also often caught in adulteries within the very holy portico [Regm. reads: “in the basilica itself, before the portico”]. The queen was angered that a place consecrated to God should be polluted in this way and ordered him expelled from the saint’s basilica.

After his expulsion, he went again to his hosts in Bourges, begging them to conceal him [for the manner in which he eventually perished miserably, see the following book, chapter 32].

LI. Although I ought to have mentioned above, in chapter 45, the conversation with blessed Bishop Salvius, since it escaped my mind, I do not think it sacrilegious to write it afterward.

When, after the aforementioned synod, we wished to take leave of the king and return to our own places, we decided not to depart until we had left this man after exchanging kisses with him. I found him when I sought him in the courtyard of the house at Brennacum.

I told him that I was already about to return home. Then, withdrawing a little, while we conversed with one another, he said to me: “Do you see what I perceive above this roof?”

I replied: “I see the roof covering that the king recently ordered to be put up.”

He said: “Do you see nothing else?”

“Nothing else,” I answered.

I supposed that he was speaking jokingly. I added: “If you see something more, tell me.”

Drawing deep sighs, he replied: “I see the unsheathed sword of divine wrath hanging over this house.”

Yet the priest’s statement did not deceive him: twenty days later, the king’s two sons, whom we recorded above as having died (chapter 35), died.

The fifth book is completed, having been finished in the fifth year of King Childebert.

## The Chapters of Book Six Begin

Book six begins, commenced in the sixth year of the same Childebert.

[Col. 0369]

I. How Childebert went over to Chilperic, and concerning Mummolus’s flight.  
II. Concerning Chilperic’s envoys returning from the East.  
III. Concerning Childebert’s envoys to Chilperic.  
IV. How Lupus was driven from Childebert’s kingdom.  
V. A dispute with a Jew.  
VI. Concerning Saint Hospitius, who was confined, and his abstinence and miracles.  
VII. Concerning the death of Ferreolus, bishop of Uzès.  
VIII. Concerning Eparchius, who was confined at the city of Angoulême.  
IX. Concerning Domnolus, bishop of Le Mans.  
X. Concerning the breaking into the basilica of Saint Martin.

XV. Concerning the death of Bishop Felix.

XIX. Concerning Chilperic’s men at the River Ouvèze.

XXVII. How King Chilperic entered Paris.

## Book Six

[Col. 0371]

### I

In the sixth year of his reign, King Childebert, rejecting the peace of King Gunthram, joined himself to Chilperic. Not long afterward Gogo died [he is the man called the king’s foster-father in Book V, chapter 47. Indeed, in Book VIII, chapter 22, Wandelinus is said to have died as the king’s foster-father. See also the letter of Duke Chamingus to that same Gogo, published by Freher. It is clear from his own letter to Trasericus that he was devoted to literary studies; other letters of his were also published by Freher and Chesne. As Fortunatus makes clear, he brought Brunichild into Gaul; Fortunatus devoted the first four poems of Book VII to her praises], and Wandelinus was appointed in his place.

Mummolus fled from the kingdom of Gunthram and shut himself within the fortifications of the walls of Avignon. A synod of bishops was convened at Lyon [this appears to be the Third Council of Lyon, although its inscription says that it was convened in the twenty-second year of Gunthram, that is, in 583, the eighth year of Childebert. Six canons were enacted there, which are found in the collections of the Councils. Mummolus’s flight in this same year, 581, is mentioned by Marius]. Disputes concerning various cases arose, and it condemned those who were negligent in judgment. The synod returned to the king, dealing at length with the flight of Duke Mummolus and to some extent with the disagreements.

### II

Meanwhile, the envoys of King Chilperic, who had gone to the Emperor Tiberius three years earlier, returned, not without grave loss and hardship. Since they had not dared to approach the port of Marseille because of the discord between the kings, they came to the city of Agde [so Corb. and Colb. read; others have Agathen. It is a very well-known episcopal city, commonly called Agde, under the metropolitan see of Narbonne, in Septimania], which lies in the kingdom of the Goths.

But before they reached the shore, the ship, driven by the wind and thrown upon the land, was smashed to pieces. The envoys, seeing themselves and their servants in danger, seized planks and were scarcely carried back to shore; many of the servants were lost, but most escaped. The local inhabitants seized the goods that the waves had carried onto the shore, taking what was better among them and bringing it back to King Chilperic. The people of Agde nevertheless kept much of it for themselves.

At that time I had gone to the estate of Novientum to meet the king [there are several royal estates of this name, commonly called Nogent. From chapter 5 it is clear that Gregory is speaking here of one in the Parisian district; consequently, either of the one situated on the Seine below Paris, today Saint-Cloud, or of the one above the same city, near the confluence of the Marne with the Seine, near Vicennes, and still called Nogent].

There the king showed us a large *missorium*, which he had made of gold and jewels and which weighed fifty pounds [a *missorium* was a basin or disk. Some wish the word to designate a bowl; others, a table with all its furnishings]. He said: “I made this to adorn and ennoble the Frankish people. I shall make many more, if life accompanies me.”

He also showed us gold coins weighing a pound each, which the emperor had sent. On one side they bore a painted image of the emperor and the inscription in a circle:

**TIBERII CONSTANTINI PERPETUI AUGUSTI**

“Of Tiberius Constantine, the Eternal Augustus.”

On the other side they bore a four-horse chariot and its driver, together with the inscription:

**GLORIA ROMANORUM**

“Glory of the Romans.”

He also showed many other ornaments that had been presented by the envoys [see Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, Book III, chapter 13].

### III

Finally, while he was staying at the same estate, Egidius, bishop of Reims, came with the principal nobles of Childebert on an embassy to King Chilperic. After a discussion had taken place, concerning how they ought to unite in peace once King Gunthram’s kingdom had been taken away, King Chilperic said:

“My sons have not remained for me, as my sins increase, and now I have no other heir except the son of my brother Sigibert, namely King Childebert. Therefore, in everything I am able to accomplish, let him be my heir. Only, as long as I live, let me be permitted to retain everything without scruple or dispute.”

They thanked him, confirmed what had been said by signing agreements, and returned to Childebert with great gifts. After they had departed, King Chilperic sent Bishop Leudovaldus [Corb. has Leodoaldus; apparently the bishop of Bayeux, concerning whom see below, Book IX, chapter 13, or else the bishop of Avranches, who was also still living at that time] with the chief men of his kingdom. After an oath had been given and received [the other manuscripts, except Corb., read “after the oath of peace had been received”] and the agreements had been confirmed, they returned with gifts.

### IV

Duke Lupus of Champagne [Regm. has Campaniensis, and Bad. Campaniae; all designate the same well-known province. Below, instead of *adversis*, which is the reading of Corb. and Colb., they have *diversis*], having long been harassed and continually stripped by his enemies, especially Ursio and Bertefred [Colb. has Berahtfrid], was finally attacked by an army after an agreement had been made that he should be killed.

When Queen Brunichild saw this, grieving over the unjust persecution of her faithful man, she girded herself like a man and burst into the midst of the enemy ranks, saying:

“Do not, men—do not do this evil! Do not persecute an innocent man! Do not engage in battle for one man, so that the region’s protection may perish.”

While she was speaking, Ursio replied:

“Withdraw from us, woman. Let it be enough for you that you held the kingdom under your husband. Now your son reigns, and his kingdom is preserved not by your protection but by ours. Withdraw from us, lest the hooves of our horses pin you to the ground.”

After they had exchanged these and other words for a very long time, the queen’s ingenuity prevailed in preventing them from fighting.

Nevertheless, when they withdrew from that place, they attacked Lupus’s houses and seized all his reserve funds [a reserve fund was money set aside for assistance, or a more secluded place where such money was kept. Plautus often uses *praesidium* for money; compare *Digest* 30.1, “Si chorus,” §1]. Pretending that they were depositing it in the king’s treasury, they brought it into their own houses, threatening Lupus and saying: “Alive, he will not escape our power.”

Seeing himself in danger, after securing his wife within the walls of the city of Laon [today called Laon, a city commonly known by that name, situated on the summit of a very high hill; it long remained impregnable and was made an episcopal see by Saint Remigius], he fled to King Gunthram. Received kindly by him, he remained in hiding with him, waiting for Childebert to reach the legitimate age.

### V

Accordingly, while King Chilperic was still staying at the aforesaid estate, he ordered the baggage to be moved and planned to come to Paris. When I approached him to take my leave, a certain Jew named Priscus arrived; he was on familiar terms with the king for purchasing various articles. The king gently took him by the hair with his hand and said to me:

“Come, priest of God, and lay your hand upon him.”

When Priscus resisted, the king said:

“O hard heart and ever-unbelieving generation, which does not understand that the Son of God was promised to it through the voices of the prophets; which does not understand the ecclesiastical mysteries prefigured in its sacrifices.”

[Note: In the Corbie manuscript, the words “the Son of God” are absent, and below the word “conjugio” (“marriage”) is also missing. The Bec manuscript reads “divine mysteries” instead of “ecclesiastical mysteries.”]

When he had said this, the Jew replied:

“God has no need of marriage, is not enriched by offspring, and does not tolerate having any associate in his kingdom—he who said through Moses: ‘See, see that I am the Lord, and besides me there is no god’ [Note: The Casinensis manuscript reads: “there is no other.”]. ‘I kill, and I make alive; I strike, and I heal’” (Deuteronomy 32:39).

At this the king said:

“God begot an eternal Son from a spiritual womb—not younger in age, nor lesser in power—of whom he himself said: ‘From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you’ (Psalm 109:3). Having therefore been born before the ages, he sent him into the world in the last ages as its healer, as your prophet says: ‘He sent his Word, and healed them’ (Psalm 106:20).

“As for your claim that God does not beget, hear your prophet speaking from the voice of the Lord: ‘Shall I, who cause others to give birth, myself not give birth?’ (Isaiah 66:9). He said this concerning the people who are reborn in him through faith.”

The Jew replied:

“Could God become man, or be born from a woman, be subjected to blows, and be condemned to death?”

While the king remained silent, I inserted myself into the discussion and said:

“The reason that God’s Son became man was not his own necessity but ours. For he could not redeem man, who was captive to sin and subjected to the slavery of the devil, unless he assumed humanity.

“But I shall provide you with testimonies from your own books—not from the Gospels and the Apostle, which you do not believe—and with your own weapon I shall pierce you, just as David is once said to have slain Goliath.

“That God would become man, hear your prophet:

> ‘He is God and man, and who has known him?’

“And elsewhere:

> ‘This is our God, and no other shall be accounted beside him;  
> he found the whole way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant  
> and to Israel his beloved.  
> After this he appeared on earth and lived among human beings’” (Baruch 3:36–38).

“As for his being born of a Virgin, likewise hear your prophet saying:

> ‘Behold, a Virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son,  
> and his name shall be called Emmanuel,’  
> which is interpreted, ‘God with us’” (Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23).

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “which is interpreted, ‘God is with us.’” The Reginensis reads “shall receive” instead of “shall conceive.”]

“As for his being subjected to blows, being fastened with nails, and being exposed or subjected to other insults, another prophet says:

> ‘They pierced my hands and my feet;  
> they divided my garments among themselves’” (Psalm 21:17), and so forth.

“And again:

> ‘They gave me gall for food,  
> and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink’” (Psalm 68:22).

[Note: In the same manuscript, the words “and in my thirst” are absent.]

“And that through the very gibbet of the cross he would restore the fallen world, which had been subjected to the dominion of the devil, to his kingdom, the same David says:

> ‘The Lord reigned from the wood’” (Psalm 95:10).

[Note: Some have complained that the rabbis erased the words “from the wood,” and indeed they are not found in the Vulgate. Nevertheless, the authority of the Septuagint translators and most of the ancient Fathers retains them. Certainly they were accepted in the Gallican churches in antiquity, as is proved not only by this text of Gregory and by Fortunatus’s hymn on the Holy Cross, but also by a Psalter written on purple parchment in silver and gold letters, once used by Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, and preserved in our monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés among the precious relics of antiquity; in it the same words are read.]

“This does not mean that he had not previously reigned with the Father, but that he received a new kingdom over the people whom he had liberated from the slavery of the devil.

[Note: The Reginensis reads: “he had liberated the uncultivated people,” instead of “he had liberated the people,” followed by “a kingdom.”]

The Jew replied:

“What necessity did God have to suffer these things?”

I answered him:

“I have already told you: God created man innocent, but, deceived by the cunning of the serpent, he became a transgressor of the commandment. Therefore he was expelled from the seat of paradise and assigned to the labors of this world; through the death of God’s only-begotten Christ he was reconciled to God the Father.”

The Jew said:

“Could God not send prophets or apostles to recall him to the way of salvation, unless he himself had been humbled in the flesh?”

I replied:

“From the beginning the human race has continually sinned. It was never terrified either by the drowning of the flood, the burning of Sodom, the plagues of Egypt, the miracle of the sea, or the division of the Jordan. It always resisted God’s Law and did not believe the prophets; indeed, it not only failed to believe them but also killed the very preachers of repentance.

“Therefore, unless he himself had descended to redeem it, no other could accomplish these things. Through his birth we have been reborn, through his baptism washed clean, through his wound healed, through his resurrection raised up, and through his ascension glorified.

“As for his coming to heal our diseases, your prophet says:

> ‘By his bruise we were healed’” (Isaiah 53:5).

“And elsewhere:

> ‘He himself will bear our sins  
> and will pray for the transgressors’” (Isaiah 53:12).

“And again:

> ‘Like a sheep he was led to slaughter,  
> and like a lamb before its shearer is silent,  
> so he did not open his mouth.  
> In his humiliation his judgment was taken away.  
> Who will declare his generation?’” (Isaiah 53:7–8).

“‘The Lord of hosts is his name’” (Isaiah 54:5).

“Jacob too, from whose lineage you boast that you have come, speaking as though to Christ himself, the Son of God, in the blessing of his son Judah, said:

> ‘Your father’s sons shall worship you.  
> Judah is a lion’s cub.  
> From the shoot, my son, you have risen;  
> lying down, you have slept like a lion,  
> like a lion’s cub.  
> Who will rouse him?’” (Genesis 49:8–9).

> “His eyes are more beautiful than wine,  
> and his teeth whiter than milk” (Genesis 49:12).

“‘Who,’ he says, ‘will rouse him?’ Although he himself said:

> ‘I have power to lay down my life,  
> and I have power to take it up again’” (John 10:18),

the apostle Paul nevertheless says:

> ‘Whoever does not believe that God raised him from the dead  
> cannot be saved’” (Romans 10:9).

Although we and others were saying these and many other things, the wretched man was never moved to believe. Then, when the king saw that he was not touched by these arguments, he turned to me and requested that he depart after receiving a blessing.

[Note: Kings were blessed by bishops, as Gregory frequently records. Hence Saint Hilary, writing against Constantius, reproaches him with these words: “You receive priests with a kiss; you submit your head to a blessing, so that you may trample upon the faith.”]

For he said:

“I shall say to you, priest, what Jacob said to the angel who spoke with him: ‘I will not let you go unless you bless me’” (Genesis 32:26).

Having said this, he ordered water to be brought to him. After washing his hands and offering a prayer,

[Note: Jerome, writing to Eustochium, says: “Food should not be taken without prayer first being offered, nor should one leave the table without giving thanks to the Creator.” Each dish was marked with the sign of the cross, as is related below in Book I, On the Glory of the Martyrs, chapter 80. Likewise, according to Gregory the Great, Book I of the Dialogues, chapter 4, a certain servant of God, having forgotten to bless lettuce with the sign of the cross, bit it and was seized by a demon.]

we took bread, giving thanks to God, and received it ourselves and offered it to the king. After drinking unmixed wine, we took our leave and departed. The king, mounting a horse [Variant: “mounting his horse”], returned to Paris with his wife, his daughter, and his entire household.

### VI

At that time there was near the city of Nice a recluse named Hospitius, a man of great abstinence. Bound with iron chains close against his bare body and wearing a hair shirt over them, he ate nothing except plain bread with a few dates. During the days of Lent, he was sustained by the roots of Egyptian herbs, which merchants brought to him for the use of hermits.

[Note: From this passage it may be inferred that Egyptian merchants frequently visited Gaul. They brought not only herbs but also that famous papyrus paper. Thus Gregory, above, in Book V, chapter 5, writing in reply to Felix of Nantes, who had attacked him with insults, says that Felix would have been fortunate if he had had Gregory as bishop of Marseilles, since in that case he would have had enough paper for writing down his insults; Egyptian merchants were evidently often arriving there and bringing such paper into Gaul. See Mabillon, Book I, On Diplomatics, chapter 8, and Alteserra on Book V, chapter 5, of this History.]

At first he drank the broth in which they had been cooked and thereafter ate the roots themselves.

For through him the Lord deigned to perform great miracles. Once, when the Holy Spirit revealed to him the coming of the Lombards into Gaul, he foretold it in these words:

“The Lombards will come into Gaul and devastate seven cities, because their wickedness has increased in the sight of the Lord. For there is no one who understands, no one who seeks God, no one who does good in order to appease God’s anger. The whole people is faithless, devoted to perjury, given to theft, ready for murder; from them no fruit of justice grows in any way.

“No tithes are given; the poor are not fed; the naked are not clothed; travelers are not received as guests or sufficiently supplied with food. Therefore this plague is coming upon you.

“Now I say to you: Gather all your property within the enclosure of the walls, so that it may not be plundered by the Lombards, and fortify yourselves in the strongest places.”

While he was saying these things, everyone was astonished. Taking their leave, they returned home in great wonder.

He also said to the monks:

“You too, depart from this place, taking with you what you possess; for behold, the people whom I foretold is approaching.”

When they said to him, “We will not leave you, most holy father,” he replied:

“Do not fear for me. It will happen that they will inflict injuries upon me, but they will not harm me unto death.”

After the monks had departed, that people arrived. While devastating everything it found, it came to the place where the holy man was enclosed. He showed himself to them through the window of the tower. They went around the tower but could not find an entrance by which they could reach him.

Then two of them climbed up, uncovered the roof, and, seeing him surrounded by chains and clothed in a hair shirt, said:

“This man is a sorcerer, and he has committed murder; that is why he is kept bound in these chains.”

They called an interpreter and asked him what evil he had done to be confined in such punishment. He admitted that he was a murderer and guilty of every crime.

Then one of them drew his sword and raised it to strike his head. At the very moment of the blow, his right hand remained suspended and stiffened, and he could not draw it back. He then released the sword and threw it to the ground.

When his companions saw this, they raised a cry to heaven, begging the holy man mercifully to explain what should be done. He placed upon the man the sign of salvation and restored his arm to health.

The man was converted in that same place, had his head tonsured, and is now regarded as a most faithful monk. The two leaders

[Note: The Reginensis reads: “the two who approached him.” Paul, however, in the cited book, chapter 2, has “two leaders.”]

who had listened to him returned unharmed to their homeland. Those who had despised his command died miserably in that very province.

Many of the Lombards were also seized by demons and cried out:

“Why do you torture and burn us in this way, holy and blessed man?”

But he laid his hand upon them and cleansed them.

After this there was a resident of Angers who, through an excessive fever, had lost both speech and hearing. When he recovered from the fever, he remained deaf and mute.

Accordingly, a deacon from that province was sent to Rome to bring back relics of the blessed apostles or of the other saints who protect that city. When he reached the parents of the sick man, they asked him to be willing to take the man as his companion on the journey, trusting that, if he visited the tombs of the most blessed apostles, he might immediately obtain a cure.

As they traveled, they came to the place where blessed Hospitius lived. After greeting him and kissing him, the deacon explained the reason for the journey and announced that he was setting out for Rome. He asked to be commended to the holy man’s friends among the shipmasters.

While he was still there, the blessed man perceived through the Spirit of the Lord that a healing power was present. He said to the deacon:

“I ask you to bring before me the sick man who is now your traveling companion.”

Without delay the deacon hurried to the lodging and found the sick man full of fever, indicating by a gesture that he heard a ringing in his ears. He took him and brought him to the holy man.

Hospitius grasped him by the hair and drew his head toward the window. Taking oil sanctified by a blessing, he held the man’s tongue with his left hand and poured the oil into his mouth and upon the crown of his head, saying:

“In the name of my Lord Jesus Christ, let your ears be opened, and may that power which once cast out the harmful demon from a deaf and mute man unlock your mouth.”

Having said this, he asked his name. The man replied in a clear voice:

“My name is thus.”

[Note: The Colbertine and Chesne manuscripts read: “My name is Pir.”]

When the deacon saw this, he said:

“I give you immense thanks, Jesus Christ, who deign to display such things through your servant. I was seeking Peter; I was seeking Paul and Laurence, and the other saints who illumine Rome with their own blood. Here I have found them all; here I have discovered them all.”

When he said this with the greatest weeping and wonder, the man of God, carefully avoiding empty glory, replied:

“Be silent, be silent, dearest brother. I do not perform these things; rather, he does who created the world from nothing, who, assuming humanity for our sake, grants sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, and speech to the mute; who restores the original skin to lepers, life to the dead, and abundant healing to all the sick.”

Then the deacon departed joyfully with his companions, taking his leave.

After they had gone, a certain man named Dominicus—for that was the man’s name—who had been blind from birth, came to test the power of this miracle. After he had remained in the monastery for two or three months, devoting himself to prayer and fasting, the man of God finally summoned him and said:

“Do you wish to receive sight?”

He replied:

“My desire was to see things unknown.”

[Note: The Reginensis reads: “to see things unseen.”]

“For I do not know what light is. I know only one thing: everyone praises it.”

[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads: “it is praised by human beings.”]

“But I have never deserved to see from the beginning of my life until now.”

Then, making the holy cross with blessed oil upon his eyes, Hospitius said:

“In the name of Jesus Christ, our Redeemer, let your eyes be opened.”

Immediately his eyes were opened. He was filled with wonder, seeing the great works of God that he now beheld in this world.

Afterward a certain woman was brought to him who, as she herself proclaimed, had three demons. When he had blessed her with a sacred touch and placed a cross from the holy oil upon her forehead, the demons were expelled and she departed cleansed.

He also healed another girl who was tormented by an unclean spirit, by means of a blessing.

When the day of his death was already approaching, he summoned the monastery’s superior and said:

“Bring a tool, break through the wall, and send messengers to the bishop of the city, so that he may come to bury me. For on the third day from now I shall depart from this world and go to the rest prepared for me, which the Lord has promised me.”

When he had said this, the superior of the monastery sent messengers to the bishop of the city of Nice to report these things to him.

Afterward a certain Crescens came to the window and, seeing him bound with chains and covered with worms, said:

“O my lord, how can you endure such severe tortures so bravely?”

He replied:

“He strengthens me for whose name I suffer these things. But I tell you that I am already being released from these chains and am going to my rest.”

When the third day arrived, he removed the chains with which he was bound and prostrated himself in prayer. After praying for a very long time with tears, he placed himself upon a bench, stretched out his legs, raised his hands toward heaven,

[Note: The Reginensis reads: “with his feet and hands raised, and his eyes lifted toward heaven.”]

and, giving thanks to God, surrendered his spirit.

Immediately all the worms that had pierced his holy limbs vanished.

Then Bishop Austadius

[Note: It is strange that Austadius is omitted from the catalogues of the bishops of Nice. The place where Hospitius lived is seen near Villefranche. It is a peninsula, as Petrus Joffredi writes, about three miles from the city of Nice, near the mouth of the harbor of Hercules, or Villefranche, toward the east. From the corrupted name of Saint Hospitius it is commonly called San-Sospir. The ruins of the monastery that existed there in the saint’s time still remained; but the tower and the remains of the church dedicated under his name were destroyed about sixty years ago, when a fortress was built there by order of Victor Amadeus, duke of Savoy. The church of Saint John, built there, was later placed under the authority of Ebrard, abbot, and the monks of Saint-Pons, when the monks had died out; this was done by Archinbald, bishop of Nice, toward the end of the eleventh century.]

arrived and most carefully committed the blessed body to burial.

[Note: It is said that his body is still preserved in the cathedral church of Nice, where he is venerated on October 15. He is also commemorated in the Roman Martyrology on May 21. Gregory speaks of him again in On the Glory of the Confessors, chapter 97.]

I learned all these things from the mouth of the man whom I previously described as having been healed by him from muteness and deafness. He told me many other things about Hospitius’s virtues, but forbade me to speak of the matter, because I had heard that his Life had been written by many people.

### VII

[Note: This chapter is absent from the Corbie and Colbertine manuscripts. Ferreolus is venerated by most people as a martyr. Marc-Antoine Dominici published his Life from a Toulouse manuscript, where it is said that his feast is celebrated on January 4. He founded a monastery and wrote a Rule, which has been published more than once and is found in the Codex of Rules and in the Concordia of Benedict of Aniane.]

At that time Ferreolus, bishop of Uzès, a man of great holiness, died, full of wisdom and understanding. He composed several books of letters, apparently following Sidonius.

After his death, Albinus, a former governor, received the episcopate through Dynamius,

[Note: Gregory mentions Dynamius more than once below. He is the same man who wrote the Life of Saint Marius, abbot of Bodan, in the diocese of Sisteron, the Life of Saint Maximus, bishop of Riez, and other works. Gregory the Great sent him letters with several small gifts. Fortunatus sang his praises in Book VI, poems 11 and 12; there he also speaks of Albinus, Jovinus, and Theodore, whom Gregory mentions here and below in chapter 11.]

who was governor of Provence, without the king’s approval. He held it for no more than three months and, when a cause arose that resisted his removal, he died.

Jovinus, who had formerly been governor of Provence, again received the king’s order concerning the episcopate. But the deacon Marcellus, son of the senator Felix, forestalled him. Having summoned the bishops of the province, Marcellus was ordained bishop through the influence of Dynamius. But Jovinus later drove him out by force in order to remove him. Shut up in the city, Marcellus tried to defend himself by force, but when he could not prevail, he won through bribes.

### VIII

[Note: This chapter, absent from the Corbie and Colbertine manuscripts, is cited in the Book of the Miracles of Saint Eparchius, whose words we have included among the Eulogies of various authors dedicated to our Gregory.]

Eparchius, a recluse of Angoulême, also died. He was a man of magnificent holiness, through whom God displayed many miracles. Passing over the greater number of them, I shall briefly relate a few.

He was a native of Périgueux, but after his conversion became a cleric. Coming to Angoulême, he built a small cell for himself. Having gathered a few monks there, he remained constantly devoted to prayer. If anyone offered him gold or silver, he distributed it either for the needs of the poor or for the redemption of captives.

No bread was ever baked in that cell while he was alive; when necessity required it, devout people brought it in. For he redeemed a great multitude of people from their offerings.

He often suppressed the venom of evil pustules

[Note: The Reginensis reads: “pustules.”]

by the sign of the cross; by prayer he drove demons from possessed bodies; and he frequently commanded judges—with an outpouring of sweetness, rather than merely asking them—to forgive the guilty. For his speech was so gentle that they could not refuse him when he had begged for mercy.
