On one occasion, a man was being led away to be hanged for theft. The local people also accused him of many other crimes, both thefts and murders, making him a notorious criminal. When this was reported to Eparchius, he sent his monk to plead with the judge that the guilty man’s life be spared.

[Note: Gregory later calls this judge the “count.” In fact, counts were appointed to administer justice in the cities.]

But the crowd mocked and shouted that, if the man were released, neither the region nor the judge could be safe. Therefore he could not be released.

Meanwhile,

[Note: So the Casinensis and Bec manuscripts; others read: “He is stretched out upon the ground,” followed by “toward.”]

he was stretched out upon the rack, beaten with rods and clubs, and condemned to the gallows.

When the sorrowful monk reported this to the abbot, he said:

“Go and watch from a distance, for know that the Lord by his gift will grant what a human being refused to grant. When you see him fall, immediately seize him and bring him to the monastery.”

The monk fulfilled the command. The abbot prostrated himself in prayer and poured out prayers to the Lord in tears for so long, until the support was broken and the man, hanging in chains, was restored to the earth.

Then the monk seized him and presented him alive and unharmed to the abbot.

Giving thanks to God, the abbot ordered the count to be summoned and said:

“You had always been accustomed to listen to me with a kindly disposition, dearest son. Why, then, did you harden yourself today and not release the man whose life I had requested?”

The count replied:

“I gladly listen to you, holy priest; but when the crowd rose up, I could do nothing else, fearing that a riot would be stirred up against me.”

The abbot said:

“You did not listen to me, but God deigned to listen. The man whom you handed over to death, he restored to life. Behold, he stands before you alive and well.”

When he had said this, the count, astonished,

[Note: So the Reginensis manuscript; others read: “at the feet of the astonished count.”]

fell at his feet, since he saw alive the man whom he had left in the grip of death.

I learned these things from the mouth of the count himself. He performed many other deeds as well, but I thought it would take too long to pursue them.

After forty-four years of enclosure, he was briefly stricken by a fever and surrendered his spirit. He was carried out from his cell and committed to burial.

A great assembly of those whom he had redeemed, as we have said, accompanied his funeral procession.

[Note: He died in the year 581, on July 1, the day on which his feast is celebrated. His Life is found among the Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, First Era, p. 267. It is also found in Gonon and, together with the book of his virtues, in volume I of Labbe’s New Library; from these it appears that Eparchius lived as a recluse for only thirty-nine years. Perhaps Gregory intended to designate the entire period from the time Eparchius had taken the monastic habit from Martin, abbot of the monastery of Sedacium. Gregory speaks of him again in On the Glory of the Confessors, chapter 101. He is commonly called Saint Cybar, under whose name a monastery of our Order exists near the city of Angoulême; but his relics were burned by the Calvinists in 1558.]

### IX

[Note: This chapter is absent from the Colbertine and Corbie manuscripts. The Reginensis, however, has “Mummolus” here, while below, like the others, it has “Domnolus.” He subscribed to the Second Council of Tours in 567.]

Domnolus, bishop of Le Mans, began to fall ill. In the time of King Chlothar, he had presided over the monastic community at the basilica of Saint Laurence in Paris.

[Note: This basilica still exists, bearing a parish title. A few years ago ancient gypsum sarcophagi were discovered there, dating back approximately nine hundred years. When they were opened, black garments and figures of monks were seen, but as soon as they were exposed to purer air they crumbled into dust. This was often attested to us by the distinguished Nicolas Gobillon, doctor of the Sorbonne, pastor of that church, and vicar general of the most illustrious archbishop of Paris. The Basilica of Saint Martin, also mentioned here, lies not far from Saint Laurence and is now famous under the name Saint-Martin-des-Champs. Gregory discusses it in Book I of the Miracles of Saint Martin, chapter 19.

“Cointius, however, under the year 655, denies that Domnolus was ever abbot of Saint Laurence and rejects this entire chapter of Gregory’s History as having been added by an ignorant interpolator, chiefly for two reasons: first, because it is absent from the Corbie and Colbertine manuscripts; second, because it contains many details wholly contrary to the Life of Saint Domnolus, written by a serious and contemporary author.

“We do not deny that this chapter is missing from certain manuscripts. But since it is found in others, including ancient and excellent manuscripts—the Bec and Casinensis, among others—and since nothing occurs in it that is contrary to Gregory’s character or style, we maintain that it should not be rejected from Gregory for this reason.

“As for the author of the Life of Saint Domnolus, we do not intend here to debate whether his authority should be considered so great that it could invalidate Gregory’s text as it now stands. We say only that these authors relate different things about Domnolus, but not contradictory things. What our Gregory relates about Domnolus as bishop and about his death is not inconsistent with the truth and is not opposed to the author of the Life, as Cointius himself admits.

“Gregory indeed assigns Domnolus only a little more than twenty years in the episcopate, which does not agree with Cointius’s calculation; but this does not conflict with the author of the Life, which is the only point we are investigating, since he specified neither the date when Domnolus assumed the see nor the year of his death.

“Nor do ancient documents contradict it. Indeed Papebrochius, who refers to the same Life under May 16 in the Bollandists, and suspects that Gregory was interpolated on the basis of the manuscript copies, nevertheless admits that Domnolus could have obtained a successor after twenty-two years in the episcopate, since no mention of Domnolus, bishop of Le Mans, appears in public records before the Second Council of Tours in 567, and since it is certain that the church of Le Mans remained vacant for a long time after the death of Innocentius, and was even occupied for several years by Scienfredus, a pseudo-bishop.

“Now our Gregory wrote that, before becoming bishop, Domnolus had been abbot of Saint Laurence in Paris and had been highly esteemed by King Chlothar. The king intended him for the see of Avignon, but Domnolus rejected it and later became bishop of Le Mans.

“The author of the Life says nothing at all about these matters, but neither will one find anything contrary to them. Indeed, he himself testifies that he would write the Life of the blessed man only from the time when he began to preside over the see of Le Mans: ‘From that time,’ he says, ‘we shall begin, when by his glorious arrival he was commanded by God’s providence to illumine us and remain with us.’

“He therefore relates that Domnolus came to Le Mans after many journeys, already consecrated as bishop, and that he was immediately elected by the clergy and people. But he says nothing whatsoever about his earlier deeds, and nothing prevents us from repeating them from Gregory’s text.

“Indeed, the great intimacy between Saint Germanus of Paris and Domnolus—which continued throughout their lives, as the author of the Life himself attests—supports our Gregory, who wrote that Domnolus was abbot in the city of Paris at precisely the time when blessed Germanus presided over that city as bishop.

“We have treated this matter at somewhat greater length because necessity required us to vindicate Gregory’s text.

“Saint Domnolus founded a celebrated monastery in the suburbs of Le Mans in honor of Saint Vincent, where he was buried. It still exists under the Order of Saint Benedict and the Congregation of Saint Maur, enjoying the privilege of a regular abbey. The body of the holy bishop was raised from the earth in 1124 by Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, in the presence of Fulk the Younger, count of Anjou, as we learned from the charter of that monastery. It is now preserved in a silver reliquary lined with gold, of exquisite workmanship, which Cardinal Luxemburg had made.”]

Since, while the elder Childebert was alive, he had always remained faithful to King Chlothar and frequently concealed the king’s messengers who had been sent to spy, the king was waiting for an opportunity to confer upon him the honor of the episcopate.

When the bishop of the city of Avignon died, the king had decided to send Domnolus there. But when blessed Domnolus heard this, he went to the basilica of Saint Martin the bishop, where King Chlothar had then come to pray. He kept vigil throughout the night and, through the leading men who were present, made a petition to the king that he should not be removed from the king’s presence like a captive, nor allow his simplicity to be wearied among sophisticated senators and philosophizing judges, asserting that this position was for him one of humility rather than honor.

The king agreed. When Innocentius, bishop of Le Mans, died, he appointed Domnolus bishop of that church.

Once he had assumed the episcopate, he proved himself so great and so worthy that, raised to the summit of holiness, he restored the use of walking to a disabled man and sight to a blind man.

[Note: The lame man was called Rainarius, and the blind man Siagrius, according to the author of the Life.]

After twenty-two years in the episcopate, when he saw himself grievously afflicted by the royal disease and by a stone, he chose the abbot Theodulf to succeed him. The king agreed to his choice. But shortly afterward, changing his mind, the king transferred the election to Badechisilus,

[Note: The Reginensis reads “Baldechilus.” He is Badegisilus, as the Chesne manuscript has it, whom Gregory mentions more than once below. He subscribed to the Second Council of Mâcon in 585. It is strange that nothing at all is recorded about him in the acts of the bishops of Le Mans published in volume III of Mabillon’s Analecta. See Book III of the Miracles of Saint Martin, chapter 35. This is, unless I am mistaken, Gregory’s first mention of the mayor of the palace.]

the chief officer of the royal household. After being tonsured and ascending through the ranks that clerics occupy, he succeeded Domnolus forty days later, when the bishop died.

### X

[Note: This chapter is absent from the Corbie and Colbertine manuscripts, but it is found in Fredegar, chapter 87.]

In those days the basilica of Saint Martin was broken into by thieves. They placed at the window of the apse a lattice that had been above the tomb of a certain deceased person. Climbing up by means of it, they broke through the glass and entered. After taking a large quantity of gold and silver and silk garments, they departed, not fearing to place their feet upon the holy tomb, where we scarcely dare even to apply our lips.

But the power of the saint wished to expose this outrage also through a terrible judgment. After committing the crime, the thieves came to the city of Bordeaux. When a quarrel arose, one killed the other. Thus the deed was revealed, the stolen property was found, and the silver pieces and garments were recovered from their lodging.

[Note: So the Reginensis and Badian manuscripts; others read: “the silver was secured.”]

When this was reported to King Chilperic,

[Note: The Reginensis reads “Chlothar.”]

he ordered them bound in chains and brought before him.

Then, fearing that men might die on account of that saint, who, while living in the body, had often pleaded for the lives of criminals, I sent the king a letter of entreaty, asking that, since our people—the persons to whom prosecution belonged—had not accused them, they should not be put to death.

[Note: So the Casinensis and Reginensis manuscripts; the printed editions, together with the Bec manuscript, read: “since we had not accused them.”]

He received the request kindly and restored them to life. He carefully gathered together the articles that had been scattered and ordered them returned to the holy place.

## XI

At Massilia [Note: Missing in Corbie and Colbert, but it was not added by an interpolator. See the notes on the following chapter and on chapter 24 of this book.], Dynamius, governor of Provence, began to plot grievously against Bishop Theodore. But when Theodore was preparing to hasten to the king, Dynamius had him seized in the middle of the city, held him there, and subjected him to severe insults before finally releasing him. The clergy of Massilia, meanwhile, were conspiring with Dynamius to expel Theodore from the episcopate. But while Theodore was traveling to King Childebert, he was ordered to be detained, together with Jovinus, the former prefect, by King Guntram.

When the clergy of Massilia heard this, they were filled with great joy: Theodore was now detained, now being assigned to exile, and matters had reached the point where he would never return to Massilia. They seized the church’s houses, inventoried its sacred vessels [that is, the sacred vessels; it should be noted that the custom had already become established that, when a bishop died, the clergy plundered whatever they could], unlocked the storerooms, stripped the supply rooms, and seized all the church’s property as though the bishop were already dead, spreading various accusations against the bishop that, by Christ’s favor, were proved false [elsewhere: “he proves them false”].

After Childebert had made peace with Chilperic, he sent envoys to King Guntram, demanding that Guntram return the half of Massilia that Childebert had given him after the death of his father. If he refused, he should know that he would lose much because of retaining that territory. But since Guntram refused to return it, he ordered the roads closed, so that no passage through his kingdom would be open to anyone.

Seeing this, Childebert sent Gundulf, made duke from among the *domestici* [the *domestici* kept watch in the prince’s palace, and their chief was called the count of the *domestici*. Under our kings they administered royal estates; see Marculf, Book II, formula 52. Gregory indicates in Book X, chapter 28 that they supplied provisions for the king travelling to judicial assemblies. They are numbered among the great men of the kingdom in the preface to the Burgundian laws and in the Ripuarian laws, chapter 90; see also the assemblies of Chlodovech III and Childebert III in *De re diplomatica*, Book VI, nos. 19 and 24. “Senatorial family,” here and elsewhere in Gregory, denotes families admitted to the Roman senate. Many provincials, especially from Gaul, had received citizenship and some had been enrolled in the senate; such persons were called foreign senators, though most had never even seen Rome. Gregory may sometimes, however, call men senators because they were among the leading men of their own city; see Cange, *Glossarium*.], a man of senatorial family, to Massilia. Gundulf, however, no longer daring to travel through Guntram’s kingdom, came to Tours. I received him graciously and recognized him as my mother’s maternal uncle [namely, the brother of Saint Nicetius, bishop of Lyons, as Cointius observes]; I kept him with me for five days, supplied him with what he needed, and allowed him to depart.

But after he had gone on, he was unable to enter Massilia because Dynamius opposed him. Nor was the bishop, who had already come with Gundulf, received into his own church. Dynamius, together with the clergy, kept watch over the city gates, insulting and despising both men alike—the bishop and Gundulf.

At last, summoned to meet the duke, Dynamius came to the basilica of Saint Stephen, which is close to the city. The doorkeepers were guarding the entrance to the building so that, when Dynamius entered, the doors would immediately be closed. Once this had been done, the armed crowd following Dynamius was unable to enter behind him. Without understanding what had happened, while they were discussing various matters among themselves over the altar, they withdrew from the altar and entered the *salutatorium*. When Dynamius entered with them, already stripped of the support [or: assistance] of his followers, they rebuked him terribly.

After driving away the retainers who had been making a commotion around the man brought there with their weapons [elsewhere: “led there”], the duke, together with the bishop, gathered the city’s leading citizens around him so that he could enter the city. Dynamius, seeing all this, asked forgiveness, gave the duke many gifts, and, having also sworn that he would henceforth be faithful to the bishop and to the king, put on his own clothing.

Then, once the gates of both the city and the sacred buildings had been opened, the duke and the bishop entered the city with banners, acclamations, and various insignia of honor.

The clergy who had been involved in this crime—whose leaders were Abbot Anastasius and the presbyter Proculus [Regm.: “and Abbot Proculus”; Bad.: “the presbyters of Proculus.” Anastasius was abbot of Saint Victor’s, the still very celebrated Benedictine monastery at Massilia, founded by John Cassian in the fifth century]—took refuge inside Dynamius’s house, asking from him the protection of refuge whom they had urged on. Many of them, however, were released upon the provision of suitable guarantors and were ordered to go to the king.

Meanwhile Gundulf, having brought the city under King Childebert’s authority and restored the bishop to his position, returned to King Childebert. But Dynamius, forgetting the oath of loyalty he had promised King Childebert, sent envoys to King Guntram, saying that he was losing through the bishop the portion of the city that belonged to him, and that he would never possess Massilia under his authority unless the bishop were removed from it.

Enraged by this, Guntram ordered—against the law of religion—that the bishop of the supreme God be brought before him in chains. He said: “Let the enemy of our kingdom be driven into exile, lest he be able to harm us any longer.”

But since the bishop was suspected and could not easily be dragged out of the city, the feast of the dedication of an oratory in the countryside outside the city arrived. As he was leaving the city to hasten to this celebration, armed men suddenly poured forth from hidden ambushes with a great uproar. They surrounded the holy bishop, threw him from his horse, drove away all his companions, bound his servants, beat the clergy, placed the bishop himself upon a miserable nag, allowed none of his men to follow him, and led him into the king’s presence.

As they passed through the city of Aix, Bishop Pientius of the place, sympathizing with his brother, gave him clergy for consolation, supplied him with necessities, and allowed him to depart [Bec. and Regm., with Bad.: “Pientius”; others: “Piencus.” Pientius, bishop of Aix—*Aquae Sextiae*, Aix-en-Provence—sent a representative who subscribed to the Second Council of Mâcon in 585].

While these events were taking place, the clergy of Massilia again opened the church’s houses, searched its secrets, inventoried some things, and carried others into their own homes. But when the bishop had been brought before the king and was found not to be guilty, he was permitted to return to his city and was received by the citizens with great acclaim.

From this there arose a serious enmity between King Guntram and his nephew Childebert; after breaking their treaty, they plotted against each other.

## XII

King Chilperic, seeing these quarrels springing up between his brother and his nephew [namely, those mentioned in the preceding chapter, as Cointius acknowledges; yet this chapter cannot be rejected, since it is found in all the manuscripts. The preceding chapter must therefore also be admitted, although it is missing in two manuscripts; nor does its absence from the Corbie and Colbert manuscripts prove that either chapter was interpolated. Fredegar in chapter 87 made an epitome of both chapters], summoned Duke Desiderius and ordered him to bring some mischief upon his brother.

Desiderius, having assembled an army, routed Duke Ragnovald [Corbie, Bec., and Regm., with some printed editions: “Ragnovald”; Colb. and Chesn.: “Regnovald” and “Reginovald”], invaded Périgueux, exacted an oath of submission, and proceeded to Agen.

When Ragnovald’s wife heard that, with her husband routed, this city would be brought under King Chilperic’s power [Corbie: “this city”; others: “these cities … would be brought under …” The Corbie reading is preferred. After Agen was captured, Ragnovald’s wife, who had taken refuge in the basilica of Saint Caprasius situated in that city, fell into the hands of the enemy. Saint Caprasius, bishop of Agen, suffered martyrdom with the virgin Fides under Maximian. We have called Caprasius a bishop on the basis of the present, and indeed more recent, tradition of the people of Agen, which is supported neither by the Acts nor by other ancient monuments. A basilica still exists under this saint’s name, distinguished by a college of canons; his sacred head is preserved there. His feast is celebrated throughout the diocese on October 20. The basilica of Saint Saturninus at Toulouse, to which this woman later fled, is today an important college of secular canons], she sought the basilica of Saint Caprasius the martyr. But she was dragged from there, stripped of her property and the assistance of her servants, and, after guarantors had been provided, was sent to Toulouse. There she again entered the basilica of Saint Saturninus and remained there.

Desiderius, meanwhile, took away all the cities in that region that belonged to King Guntram’s sphere and subjected them to King Chilperic’s authority.

When Duke Berulf heard the Bituriges muttering that they would enter the territory of Tours, he mobilized his army and took up position on their borders. At that time the districts of Isiodorensis and Berravensis in the territory of Tours were severely devastated [Corbie has “the district of Stodunensis”; Regm. incorrectly has “Autisiodorensis.” The traditional reading should be retained, for Iciodorum or Isidiorum is a village on the River Crosa, commonly called Iserre or Isure, bordering the Bituriges Cubi. Berravensis is Barou near the same river, not far from Iciodorum, as Valesius observes in his *Notitia Galliarum*. Gregory notes that churches had been built in both places]. Later, those who had been unable to be present during this siege were also cruelly punished. Duke Bladastes [others: “Blandastes” or “Bladastis”; Corbie: “Baudastis”] went into Vasconia and lost the greater part of his army [Vasconia here means the ancient seat of the Vascones in the Pyrenees; after abandoning it, they later occupied Novempopulania].

## XIII

This chapter is missing in Corbie and Colbert.

Lupus, a citizen of Tours, wishing to enter the clergy after losing his wife and children, was prevented by his brother Ambrosius, who feared that, if Lupus joined the clergy, he would make the Church of God his heir. Ambrosius instead arranged another marriage for him and, having been badly advised, appointed the day on which Lupus was to be joined to his bride and give the marriage gifts.

Afterward they came together at the fortress of Cainon, where they had lodgings. But Ambrosius’s wife was an adulteress: she loved another man with the passion of a brothel, hated her husband, and plotted against him.

While the brothers were dining together and, during the night, had become drenched with wine to the point of drunkenness, they lay down together on a single bed. Then the lover of Ambrosius’s wife came at night, while everyone was sleeping and overcome by wine. He lit straw with fire in order to see what they were doing [elsewhere: “what he was doing”], drew his sword, and struck Ambrosius on the head, so that, descending through his eyes, the sword severed the neck of his head.

Awakened by the blow, Lupus saw himself rolling in blood and cried out loudly: “Alas, alas! Help! My brother has been killed.”

The lover, who had already committed the crime and was leaving, heard this, returned to the bed, and attacked Lupus. When Lupus resisted, he overpowered him after tearing him with many blows and, having inflicted a mortal wound, left him half alive. No one in the household noticed.

When morning came, everyone was astonished at so great a crime. Lupus, however, was found still alive; he recounted what had happened and gave up his spirit. Nor did the adulterous woman take long to mourn: after a few days had passed, she joined the adulterer and departed with him.

The adulterer, named Vedastes Avo, later came to a bad end; see Book VII, chapter 3.

## XIV

In the seventh year of King Childebert—which was the twenty-first of Chilperic and Guntram—[this whole chapter is quoted by Fulbert in letter 97 to King Robert, where he reads “in the sixth year,” etc.] there were heavy rains, flashes of lightning, and thunder in the month of January. Flowers appeared on the trees. The star that I mentioned above as a comet appeared, with such great darkness around it that it seemed to be placed in some opening; it shone through the darkness, sparkling and scattering its hair. From it there projected a ray of extraordinary size, which appeared from a distance like the great smoke of a fire.

It was seen in the western quarter during the first hour of the night. On the holy day of Easter, at the city of Soissons, the sky appeared to burn, so that two fires were visible: one larger, the other smaller. After the space of two hours they joined together; becoming one great flame [elsewhere: “fire”], they vanished.

In the territory of Paris, true blood flowed down from a cloud, fell upon the clothing of many people, and stained it so foully that the people themselves shrank from and rejected their own garments. This portent appeared in three places within the territory of that city. In the territory of Senlis, when a certain man rose in the morning, his house appeared to have been splashed with blood from within.

There was therefore a great epidemic among the people that year: various malignant illnesses, with pustules and blisters, afflicted many people with death [Bad.: “various illnesses, or diseases”; others: “malignant illnesses”]. Many, nevertheless, escaped by applying diligent care. For we heard that in the city of Narbonne a disease of the groin was raging severely that year, so that there was no respite once a person had been seized by it.

## XV

This chapter is missing in Corbie and Colbert.

Bishop Felix of the city of Nantes, having fallen ill with this disease, began to suffer severely. He then summoned the bishops who were nearby and begged them to strengthen with their signatures the agreement he had made concerning Burgundio, his nephew. When this had been done, they sent Burgundio to me.

At that time Burgundio was about twenty-five years old. When he came, he asked me to go to Nantes and consecrate him, after he had been tonsured, as bishop in place of his uncle, who was still alive. I refused, because I knew that this did not conform to the canons [this is prohibited by canon 8 of the Council of Nicaea, later confirmed by many others].

I nevertheless gave him this advice: “My son, we have it written in the canons that no one may attain the episcopate unless he has first regularly passed through the ecclesiastical ranks [the Council of Sardica states this in canon 13, canon 10 in the Greek text; thereafter the supreme pontiffs and other Fathers confirmed it in various synods. See Gratian, distinctions 52 and 59]. Therefore, dearest son, return there and ask the man who chose you to tonsure you himself. When you have received the rank of presbyter, be constant in attendance at the church; and when God wills him to depart this life, you will then easily ascend to the episcopal rank.”

But when Burgundio returned, he neglected to carry out the advice he had received, because Bishop Felix appeared to be recovering somewhat from his illness. After the fever had gone away, however, his shins developed pustules from the fluid. Then, when he applied an excessively strong cantharides poultice [that is, one made from the poisonous insect *cantharis*, just as medicines are prepared from vipers and similar creatures for the treatment of diseases], his shins became gangrenous, and in the thirty-third year of his episcopate, at the age of seventy, he ended his life [he died on the eighth day before the Ides of January; he is venerated as a saint among the people of Nantes. See above, Book V, chapter 5].

His cousin Nonnichius succeeded him by order of the king.

## XVI

This chapter, which is necessarily connected with the preceding one, appears in the Corbie and Colbert manuscripts in precisely these words. It must therefore be inferred that both are Gregory’s work. Yet Cointius called both spurious; since the Corbie manuscript was written shortly after Gregory’s time, he must consequently admit that the interpolator was almost Gregory’s contemporary.

When Pappolenus heard of Felix’s death, he took back his niece, from whom he had been separated. He had previously been betrothed to her; but when Bishop Felix was evading the marriage, Pappolenus came with a large company, carried the girl away from the oratory, and took refuge in the basilica of Saint Albinus.

Then Bishop Felix, angered, separated the girl from her husband by deceitful stratagems. He changed her clothing and placed her in a monastery near the city of Bazas [a city of Novempopulania, or modern Gascony, commonly called Bazas. It was the birthplace of the noble poet Ausonius, who, after attaining several high offices of the Empire, was made consul by the emperor Gratian, his own pupil].

But she secretly sent boys as messengers [Corbie and Colbert: “boys”; the printed editions with Bec.: “boy”; in Regm. the word is absent. Both readings are possible. *Puer* is rarely used for a man, more often for a servant, even one advanced in age; as Jerome says, it expresses not age but status], asking him to receive her after she had been taken from the place where she had been put. He did not refuse; he took the girl from the monastery, joined her to himself in marriage, and, protected by royal orders, ceased to fear her parents’ threats.

## XVII

That year King Chilperic ordered many Jews to be baptized, and I received several of them from the holy font. Some of them, however, washed only their bodies and not their hearts [it seems that at that time Jews in Gaul were being compelled to accept the faith, a practice Gregory the Great disapproves in Book I, letter 45. See Cointius’s discussion of the matter under the year 591, sections 12 and following, and Launoius’s separate book on the subject]. Having deceived God, they returned to the very unbelief they had previously held, so that they appeared both to observe the Sabbath and to honor the Lord’s Day.

Priscus, however, could not be diverted in any way from discovering the truth. The king, angered, ordered him to be handed over to custody, intending that the man who could not believe voluntarily should at least be made to believe against his will.

But Priscus, having given certain gifts, asked for time until his son should take a Jewish woman of Massilia in marriage; he deceitfully promised that thereafter he would fulfill what the king had ordered.

Meanwhile hostility arose between Priscus and Phatir [Corbie and Colbert, with Chesn.: “Phatir”; Bec.: “Pathir”; some editions: “Pathirem”; Regm., another Colbert manuscript, and Bad.: “Patrem,” and below “Pater”], a convert from Judaism who had already become the king’s son through baptism.

On the Sabbath day, Priscus, girded with a stole and carrying no tool in his hands, went into the more secluded places as though he were about to fulfill the Mosaic laws. Suddenly Phatir arrived and slaughtered him with a sword, together with the companions who were present.

After killing them, he fled to the basilica of Saint Julian with his sons, who were at the nearby street [this is the church now called Saint Julian the Poor, or Saint Julian the Old, discussed below in Book IX, chapter 6. Launoius had questioned this identification, suggesting that Gregory might have meant another church of Saint Julian, called the Church of the Mimes or Fiddlers, situated on the Martinian Way. Valesius rightly rebuked him for ignorance, since the latter church was built by two cantors only in the year 1330. See Brollius, our *Antiquities of Paris*, Book III].

While they were staying there, they heard that the king, the lord having departed this life [Corbie and Bec.: “the lord having died”; Colbert: “the lord having been killed,” and in another hand, “he ordered that their lord be killed, but the servants …”; others: “the lord having been killed.” Cointius, who reports this chapter, has “the lord was killed,” instead of “when the lord was killed.” Yet the narrative itself makes clear that Priscus, here called “lord,” escaped unharmed], had ordered the servants to be dragged from the basilica and killed as criminals.

Then one of the servants, drawing his sword, killed his companions after his master had already fled [Corbie, Bec., and some printed editions omit “his”]. He himself afterward left the basilica with his sword; but when the crowd rushed upon him, he was cruelly killed.

Phatir, having received permission, returned to the kingdom of Guntram, from which he had come. But not many days later he was killed by Priscus’s relatives.

The conclusion of this chapter is missing in the Colbert manuscript.

## XVIII

The envoys of King Chilperic—namely Ansouldus and Domegiselus [others: “Ansoaldus” and “Domichisilus.” Here observe, with Valesius and others, the ancient custom of the Franks in Gaul and the Goths in Spain, which was also that of the ancient Germans: not the wife but the husband offered the dowry to the wife. Cornelius Tacitus praises this custom in chapter 18 of his *On the Customs of the Germans*, where he explains the manner in which it was performed and what possessions the husband was accustomed to receive from the wife]—returned from Spain, where they had been sent to inspect the dowry.

In those days King Leuvichildus was stationed with his army against his son Hermenegild, from whom he had also taken the city of Mérida. We have already explained above how Hermenegild had allied himself with the generals of the Emperor Tiberius [Book V, chapter 39]. This matter also caused the envoys to delay, so that they returned later than expected.

When I saw them, I was concerned to know how the faith of Christ was flourishing among those Christians who had remained there, since they were few. Ansoualdus then answered me:

“The Christians who now live in Spain preserve the Catholic faith intact. But the king is now attempting by a new device to drive it out, while deceitfully pretending to pray at the tombs of the martyrs and in the churches of our religion. For he says: ‘I have clearly recognized that Christ is the Son of God, equal to the Father; but I do not at all believe that the Holy Spirit is God, since he is not read to be God in any books.’

“Alas, alas! What an impious judgment, what a poisonous belief, what a perverse mind! Where is the saying of the Lord: ‘The Spirit is God’ (John 4:24)? And where is Peter’s saying to Ananias: ‘Why has it seemed good to you to tempt the Holy Spirit?’ (Acts 5:9) ‘You have not lied to men but to God’ (Acts 5:4). And where is Paul’s saying, when he lists the spiritual gifts: ‘All these things are activated by one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one as he wills’ (1 Corinthians 12:11)? For he who works whatever he wills is known to be subject to no one.”

When Ansoualdus approached King Chilperic, a delegation from Spain followed [Cointius thinks this embassy was carried out by Florentius and Exsuperius, mentioned in Book III of the *Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 8]. It proceeded from Chilperic to Childebert and then returned to Spain.

## XIX

At the Bridge of Urbienus in the territory of Paris [that is, the bridge situated on the River Urbia; hence this chapter is described in the Index as “Concerning the men … at the River Urbia,” which separated Chilperic’s kingdom from Guntram’s. Valesius believes this Urbia to be the river now called the Orge, or l’Orge. It waters several villages in the territory of Paris and flows into the Seine near Juvisy], King Chilperic had stationed guards so that raiders from his brother’s kingdom might be prevented from doing harm.

Asclepius, who had learned this in advance from a former duke [Corbie and Bec.: “When Asclepius learned this”; Bad.: “when he learned this from a former duke”], attacked by night, killed them all, and severely devastated the district nearest the bridge.

When this was reported to King Chilperic, he sent messengers to the counts, dukes, and other agents [that is, royal officials; among the Romans these had succeeded the *frumentarii*. See Gothofredus on the Theodosian Code], ordering them to assemble an army and invade his brother’s kingdom.

But he was restrained by the counsel of good men from doing so. They said to him: “They have acted perversely; you act wisely. Send messengers to your brother, and if he wishes to correct your injury, seek no evil [Corbie: ‘do no evil’; literally, ‘conduct no evil’]. If he does not, you will afterward consider what course to pursue.”

Thus, having accepted this counsel, he restrained the army and sent an embassy to his brother. But Guntram corrected everything and sought his brother’s full affection.

## XX

That year Chrodinus died, a man of magnificent goodness and piety, exceedingly generous in almsgiving, a provider for the poor, an abundant benefactor of churches, and a nourisher of clergy.

For he would often establish estates from the beginning, plant vineyards, build houses, and lay out fields. Then he would summon bishops whose resources were small, provide a banquet, and generously distribute to them the houses themselves with their cultivators and cultivated lands, together with silver, tapestries, household equipment, servants, and attendants. He would say: “Let these things be given to the Church, so that, while the poor are refreshed by them, they may obtain forgiveness for me from God.”

We heard many other good things about this man, but it would take too long to pursue them. He died at the age of seventy [Colb. a. and Chesn.: “eighty”; Chrodinus’s praises were celebrated by Fortunatus in Book IX, poem 16].

## XXI

The following signs appeared again that year. The moon suffered an eclipse. In the territory of Tours, true blood flowed from a broken loaf. The walls of the city of Soissons collapsed. The earth trembled near the city of Angers. Within the walls of the town of Bordeaux, wolves entered and devoured dogs, showing no fear whatever of human beings. Fire appeared to run across the sky.

The city of Bazas was also consumed by fire, so that its churches and ecclesiastical buildings were devastated. We learned, however, that all its church furnishings had been rescued.

## XXII

This chapter is missing in Corbie and Colbert *a*.

King Chilperic, having overrun his brother’s cities, appointed new counts and ordered all the urban taxes to be brought to him. We learned that this was carried out as ordered.

In those days two men were seized by Nonnichius, count of the city of Limoges [Colb. *m*: “Nunnichiolemo”; below, however, it has “Nonnichius.” Carterius subscribed to the Second Council of Mâcon in 585]. They were carrying, in the name of Carterius, bishop of Périgueux, letters containing many insults against the king. Among other things, the letters said that the priest complained that he had descended from paradise into hell—namely, because he had been transferred from King Guntram’s kingdom into Chilperic’s authority.

The count mentioned above sent these letters and the men carrying them to the king under strict guard. The king, however, showed patience for the bishop’s sake and sent for men who would present him before the king, so that he might investigate whether the accusations brought against him were true.

When the bishop arrived, the king presented the men and the letters to him and asked whether they had been sent by him. The bishop denied that he had sent them. The men were then asked from whom they had received them. They named the deacon Frontunius [the printed editions and Bec.: “Frontonius”].

The bishop was asked about the deacon. He replied that the deacon was his principal enemy and that there could be no doubt that the mischief was his, since he had often brought unjust charges against him.

The deacon was brought without delay. The king questioned him, and he confessed against the bishop, saying: “At the bishop’s command, I dictated this letter” [that is, “I wrote it”; see Mabillon’s notes on letter 304 of Saint Bernard].

The bishop protested, saying that the deacon had often sought *ingenia* [that word denotes deceit or any device for circumventing another in Gregory and in the ancient writers of our people; see Bignonius on Book II of Marculf, chapter 36, and Alteserra on Book IV of this History, chapter 28] in order to discover how he might remove him from the episcopate.

The king, moved by mercy and commending his case to God, yielded to both sides. He kindly begged the bishop to pardon the deacon and asked the priest to pray for him. Thus the bishop was sent back to his city with honor.

Two months later, however, Count Nonnichius, who had sown this scandal, died struck down by blood; and because he had no children, the king granted his property to various persons.

## XXIII

After many funerals among his sons, a son was born to King Chilperic. Because of this, the king ordered all prisons to be opened, prisoners to be released, and the compositions owed to the treasury by negligent persons not to be demanded at all.

But afterward this infant caused great mischief [the reading should, I think, be *dolorem*, “grief.” See below, chapters 34 and 35; Valesius, however, explains this *dolum*, “mischief,” as referring to the death of Mummolus, which Fredegund, hostile to him, brought about on the occasion of this son’s death, below in chapter 35. Marculf’s Book I contains formula 39: “That on the birth of the king, just as at the birth of our kings’ sons, free persons should be released.” His baptism is discussed below in chapter 27].

## XXIV.

New wars again arose against Theodore the bishop. For Gundovald, who claimed that he was the son of King Chlothacharius, came from Constantinople and was conveyed to Massilia; concerning his origin, I have thought it worthwhile to say a few things briefly.

[Note: He had previously reported above, in chapter 11, more about the things he had suffered at the hands of Dynamias. Therefore, although the eleventh chapter is absent from the Corbie and Colbertine manuscripts, it is nevertheless clear from this twelfth chapter, which exists in both codices, that it was not added by an interpolator. Moreover, we have consistently written *Gundovaldus*, the reading of the manuscript codices, although the printed editions have *Gundobaldus*.]

When he had been born in Gaul and brought up with careful attention, as is the custom of these kings—

[Note: See below, Book VIII, chapter 10, and elsewhere.]

—his mother presented him to King Childebert, with his hair hanging down his back in locks, and educated in letters, saying: “Behold,” she said, “your nephew, the son of King Chlothacharius. And because he is hated by his father, receive him, since he is your flesh.”

He received him and kept him with himself, because he had no sons. These things were reported to King Chlothacharius, and he sent messengers to his brother, saying: “Send the boy, so that he may come to me.” He did not delay, but sent the young man to his brother. When Chlothacharius saw him, he ordered the hair of his head to be cut, saying: “I did not beget this boy.”

Therefore, after the death of King Chlothacharius, he was received by King Charibert. Sigibert, however, summoned him and again cut the hair of his head, and sent him to the Agrippine city,

[Note: That is, to the elder Childebert, the uncle of the then-reigning Childebert.]

[Note: The Franks are said to have called Cologne by this name—according to Rorico, Hincmar, and other still older writers—because perhaps they were the first simply to call it *Colonia*, omitting the word *Agrippina*, its proper name, as it seems; previously it was called *Colonia* only as an adjunct, for example, Colonia Traiana, Colonia Augusta, and other cities into which the Romans led colonies. It was the city of the Ubii, in which Julia Agrippina, the mother of Nero, was born. After she had married the emperor Claudius, she ordered a Roman colony to be led there; hence, from her name, it was called Colonia Agrippina, as Tacitus relates in Book XII of the *Annals*.]

which is now called Cologne. He too, having escaped from that place, let his hair grow again and went to Narses, who at that time governed Italy. There, having taken a wife, he fathered sons and went to Constantinople.

From there, as they say, after many years, he was invited by someone to come to Gaul. He landed at Massilia and was received by Bishop Theodore. Having also received horsemen from him [variant: horses],

[Note: From “And from him also having received” up to “he was associated” is absent from the Corbie manuscript.]

he joined Duke Mummolus. At that time Mummolus was in the city of Avignon, as we have already said above (chapter 1).

Duke Guntchramnus, however, seized Bishop Theodore and threw him into custody for this reason, judging that he had admitted a foreigner into Gaul and had wished by this means to subject the Frankish kingdom to imperial authority.

[Note: Yet this same man had summoned Gundovald, below, chapter 26; but he was a man of no loyalty.]

But Theodore produced, as they say, a letter bearing the signatures of the leading men of King Childebert, saying: “I have done nothing on my own except what was commanded me by our lords and superiors.”

The priest was therefore guarded in a small cell and was not permitted to approach the church. One night, while he was praying to the Lord with particular attention, the cell shone with an extraordinary brightness, so that the count who was guarding him was terrified by great fear. A globe of immense light appeared above him for the space of two hours.

When morning came, that count related these things to the others who were with him. Afterward Theodore was brought before King Guntchramnus with Bishop Epiphanius,

[Note: Cointius conjectures that this man governed the church of Fréjus; he was still a priest when he subscribed to the Council of Orléans in the name of his predecessor Exspectatus. Alteserra interprets him as Epiphanius, patriarch of Grado, mentioned by Paul the Deacon in Book IV, chapter 34. But the chronology is against this.]

who was then staying at Massilia while fleeing from the Lombards—especially since he too was alleged to have been an accomplice in this affair.

When examined by the king, they were found guilty of no crime. Nevertheless, the king ordered them to remain under guard; after many punishments, Bishop Epiphanius died there.

[Note: What happened to Theodore, you will learn from Book VIII, chapter 12.]

Gundovald, however, withdrew to an island in the sea, awaiting the outcome of events. Duke Guntchramnus, together with the duke of King Guntchramnus, divided Gundovald’s property and carried away with him to Auvergne, as they say, an immense weight of silver, gold, and other possessions.

## XXV.

In the eighth year of King Childebert, on the day before the Kalends of February, when on Sunday the signal had been sounded at the morning office in the city of Tours and the people, rising, were gathering in the church,

[Note: From this and several other passages of our Gregory, to which other authors also bear witness, we learn that formerly the entire people customarily gathered together with the clergy in the church to celebrate the morning office, at least on Sundays and feast days.]

in cloudy weather and with rain, a large ball of fire—or, according to another reading, a fiery ball—fell from heaven and traversed the air over a considerable distance. It gave such great light that everything could be seen as though it were midday. When it was again received into the cloud, night followed.

The waters also rose beyond their usual level. For the Seine—

[Note: The Corbie manuscript has *Sigona*, a name by which the Seine is sometimes designated in ancient writings, as is clear from other passages.]

—and the Marne caused such a great flood around Paris that shipwrecks frequently occurred between the city and the basilica of Saint Laurence.

[Note: We have already spoken of this basilica at chapter 9 of this book. Certain more recent writers gratuitously wished to distinguish it from the present parish church of Saint Laurence; this is decisively disproved in Book IV of *Diplomatic Affairs*, no. 110, against those who think that Gregory’s basilica of Saint Laurence stood near the smaller bridge, not far from the Seine. Certainly, even if we had no other arguments besides the ordinance of Childebert III, published in Book VI of *Diplomatic Affairs*, no. 28, no difficulty would remain in this matter, since the location of the basilicas of Saint Laurence and Saint Martin is clearly indicated there. Moreover, since the same charter shows that the basilica of Saint Dionysius, where his sacred body rested, then stood in a village outside the city of Paris, at the very place where it still stands, and since some more recent writers deny this, it seemed worthwhile to reproduce the charter in full from the Dionysian original in the Appendix.]

## XXVI.

Duke Guntchramnus also returned to Auvergne with the treasures mentioned above and went to King Childebert. When he subsequently returned with his wife and sons, King Guntchramnus seized and detained him, saying to him:

“Your invitation brought Gundovald into Gaul, and for this reason you went to Constantinople some years ago.”

He replied: “Your own duke Mummolus received him and kept him with himself at Avignon. Now allow me to go, and I will bring him to you; then I shall be free of the charges brought against me.”

The king said to him: “I will not allow you to leave until you have suffered a fitting penalty for what you have done.”

But seeing that he was near death, Guntchramnus said: “Behold my son; receive him, and let him be a hostage for what I promise my lord the king. If I do not bring Mummolus to you, I will forfeit my little son.”

Then the king permitted him to leave, keeping his child with him. Guntchramnus, taking with him the men of Auvergne and Velay, went to Avignon.

Through Mummolus’s stratagem, however, frail boats had been prepared on the Rhône. The men boarded them unsuspectingly, but when they reached the middle of the river, the boats filled with water and sank. Some escaped by swimming; others, seizing the planks of the boats themselves, reached the bank. Most of those whose cunning was less effective were drowned in the river.

Duke Guntchramnus arrived at Avignon. For after he had entered within the walls of that city, Mummolus had arranged that, since only a small part of it remained unfortified by the Rhône, that entire area should be protected by diverting water from the river. There he dug trenches of great depth, and the flowing water covered the traps he had prepared.

When Guntchramnus arrived, Mummolus said from the wall: “If faith is sincere, let him come to one side of the bank and I to the other, and let him say whatever he wishes.”

When they had met there—for an arm of the river lay between them—Guntchramnus said in reply: “If it is permitted, I will wade across, since there are certain matters that should be discussed more privately between us.”

Mummolus answered: “Come; do not be afraid.”

Guntchramnus entered the water with one of his companions, being weighed down by the weight of his coat of mail. As soon as that companion reached the river’s pit, he sank beneath the water and disappeared. Guntchramnus, too, was sinking and was being carried away by the swift current, when one of those standing nearby extended a spear to his hand and brought him back to the bank.

After exchanging insults, Guntchramnus and Mummolus withdrew. While Guntchramnus was besieging the city itself with the army of King Guntchramnus—

[Note: Valesius thinks that *Childeberti* should be read here. The men of Auvergne and Velay were indeed subject to Childebert.]

—these events were reported to Childebert. Angered that Guntchramnus was acting without orders, he sent there Gundulf, mentioned above (chapter 11). Gundulf lifted the siege and brought Mummolus to the men of Auvergne; but after a few days he returned to Avignon.

## XXVII.

The day before Easter was to be celebrated, King Chilperic went to Paris. In order to free himself from the curse written into the agreement between him and his brothers, namely that none of them should enter Paris without the consent of another (see Book VII, chapter 6), he entered the city preceded by the relics of many saints. He celebrated Easter with great joy and delivered his son to baptism. Ragnemodus, the priest of that city, received him from the sacred font and ordered that he be called Theodoric.

## XXVIII.

Marcus the referendary, whom we mentioned above (Book V, chapter 29), after having gathered treasures from the unlawful assessments, was suddenly seized by a pain in his side. He shaved his head, received penance,

[Note: Those who were given monastic clothing at the point of death were called “monks for assistance.” That penitents in Gaul were formerly tonsured is clear from canon 12 of the Council of Agde and elsewhere. See Sirmond on Book IV of Apollinaris, Letter 24.]

and breathed out his spirit. His possessions were transferred to the treasury, for great treasures of gold and silver, together with many kinds of goods, were found there. He carried nothing else away with him from that place except the loss of his soul.

## XXIX.

The envoys who had returned from Spain reported nothing definite, because Leuvichild was encamped with the army against his elder son.

At the monastery of the blessed Radegund—

[Note: At Poitiers, dedicated to the holy Cross; it still exists under the Rule of Saint Benedict. More will be said about it below.]

—a certain girl named Disciola,

[Note: The Colbertine manuscript has *Discila*. She is venerated as a saint together with Abbess Agnes on the third day before the Ides of May. She is included in the *Poitevin Litanies*, published by Henri-Louis Castanet, bishop of Poitiers.]

who was the niece of the blessed Salvius, bishop of Albi, died in the following manner.

When she had begun to fall ill and the other sisters were continually serving her, the day arrived on which she was to depart from the body. Around the ninth hour she said to the sisters:

“Behold, I already feel lighter; behold, I feel no pain. Now there is no need for your concern to provide me with any care. Rather, leave me, so that I may relax more easily into sleep.”

Hearing this, her sisters withdrew for a short time from the cell and returned after a little while. Finally, as they stood before her, they waited to hear what words she would speak.

She, however, extending her hands and asking a certain person for a blessing, said: “Bless me, holy servant of the Most High God. For behold, you have already been wearied three times today on my account. And why, holy one, do you endure repeated insults for the sake of a weak little woman?”

When those present asked to whom she was speaking these words, she gave no answer at all. Then, after a short interval, she uttered a loud cry with laughter and thus surrendered her spirit.

And behold, a possessed man who had then come to be cleansed at the glory of the blessed Cross seized his hair in his hands and struck himself against the ground, saying:

“Alas, alas, alas for us, who have suffered such a loss! If only we had been permitted to inquire into the causes beforehand; then this soul would have been taken from our power!”

When those who were present asked him what the words he had spoken meant, he replied:

“Behold, the angel Michael has received the girl’s soul and is carrying it up to heaven. Our prince, whom you call the devil, has no share in her.”

Afterward the body was washed with water and shone with such snowy whiteness—

[Note: The Corbie manuscript has: “They said that the body, by whom it was washed, shone with such whiteness …”]

—that the abbess could not find any linen at hand that appeared whiter than the body. Nevertheless, dressed in clean linen, she was committed to burial.

Another girl of this monastery also had a vision, which she related to the sisters. “I thought,” she said, “that I was making a journey, and I desired to reach a living spring as I walked toward it. Since I did not know the way, a man appeared before me and said: ‘If you wish to approach the living spring, I will be the guide of your journey.’

“I thanked him and followed the one who went before me. As we walked, we came to a great spring whose waters shone like gold.

[Note: The same manuscript has: “The water … shone.”]

The grasses, however, radiant with fresh light, glittered like different kinds of jewels.

“The man said to me: ‘Behold the living spring that you sought with such great labor. Now satisfy yourself from its streams, so that it may become for you a spring of living water leaping up into eternal life.’

“When she eagerly drank from these waters, behold, the abbess came from the other side. She clothed the naked girl in royal garments, which shone with such light, gold, and necklaces that they could scarcely be looked upon. The abbess said to her: ‘Your Bridegroom is sending you these gifts.’

“When the girl had seen this, she was pierced in her heart, and a few days later she asked the abbess to prepare for her a cell in which she might be enclosed.

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads: “When she had asked this, the abbess quickly prepared the cell and then said to her: ‘Behold the cell …’”]

“When it had quickly been completed, the abbess said: ‘Behold the cell; what do you desire now?’

“The girl asked to be permitted to be enclosed. When this had been granted, the virgins gathered with much singing of psalms and lamps burning. With the blessed Radegund holding her hand, she was led all the way to the place. Thus she said farewell to everyone, kissing each one individually, and was enclosed.

“When the entrance through which she had entered had been sealed, she now devotes herself there to prayer and reading.”

## XXX.

In this year the emperor Tiberius departed from the world, leaving the peoples in great mourning at his death. For he was of the highest goodness, ready in almsgiving, just in judgment, and extremely cautious when judging. He despised no one but embraced everyone with goodwill. He loved everyone, and he too was loved by everyone.

When he had begun to fall ill and had already despaired of continuing to live, he summoned the empress Sophia and said:

“Behold, I feel that the time of my life is already fulfilled. Now, with your advice, I shall choose who ought to govern the state. For a vigorous man must be chosen, one who may succeed me in this authority.”

[Note: Thus read the Corbie and Colbertine manuscripts; the Regius manuscript has: “For we must provide someone worthy to be joined to so great a dignity.” The other manuscripts omit this verse.]

She chose a certain Maurice, saying:

“This man is very vigorous and shrewd; for he has often fought against the enemies of the state and won victories.”

She said this because, after Tiberius’s death, she intended to be joined to Maurice in marriage.

But when Tiberius learned that the empress had agreed to this choice, he ordered his daughter to be adorned with imperial ornaments. He summoned Maurice and said:

“Behold, with the consent of the empress Sophia, you have been chosen for the empire. To make you more secure in it, I shall give you my daughter.”

When the girl came forward, her father gave her to Maurice, saying:

“May my empire be granted to you together with this girl. Use it—or, according to another reading, her—happily, and always remember to take delight in equity and justice.”

Maurice received the girl and led her to his house. After the wedding ceremony had been completed, Tiberius died.

Therefore, after a public suspension of legal business was proclaimed—

[Note: Other authors also use *justitium* to designate mourning, because during public mourning a *justitium*—that is, a suspension of the administration of justice—was proclaimed, as though legal proceedings were brought to a standstill. Paul the Deacon adds in Book III of his *History of the Lombards*, chapter 17, that Maurice was the first of Greek origin to be confirmed in the empire.]

Maurice, dressed in the diadem and purple, proceeded to the circus. After acclamations of praise had been offered to him and gifts had been distributed to the people, he was confirmed in the empire.

## XXXI.

At last King Chilperic received the envoys of his nephew Childebert. The first among them was Egidius, bishop of Reims. When they had been admitted to the king and had presented their proposal, they said:

“He asks that the peace which you made with our lord, your nephew, be preserved by you in every respect. He cannot have peace with your brother, because after the death of his father he took away from him a part of Massilia, and he retains his fugitives, refusing to return them to him. Therefore your nephew Childebert wishes to preserve intact the affection that he now maintains with you.”

Chilperic replied:

“My brother has become guilty in many ways. For if my son Childebert investigates the course of events, he will immediately discover that his father was killed through this man’s collusion.”

While he was saying this, Bishop Egidius said:

“If you unite with your nephew, he too will unite with you. Once the army has been mobilized, the vengeance that is owed him will be inflicted more quickly.”

After they had confirmed this by oath and exchanged hostages with one another, the envoys departed.

Trusting in their promises, Chilperic mobilized the army of his kingdom and came to Paris. When he had settled there, he inflicted great loss upon the inhabitants.

Duke Berulf, with the men of Tours, Poitiers, Angers, and Nantes, came to the border of Berry. Desiderius and Bladastes, with the entire army of the province entrusted to them,

[Note: The Colbertine manuscript has *commissum* instead of *commisso*. The Corbie manuscript reads: “with the common army of the province entrusted to him.”]

besieged Berry from the other side, greatly ravaging the regions through which they came.

Chilperic ordered the army that had joined him to pass through Paris. When it had passed through, he too crossed over and went to the fortress of Melodunum,

[Note: Thus read the Corbie manuscript here and in the following chapter. The written manuscripts vary. Some have *Mecledonense*, as do most printed editions; in the Colbertine manuscript, however—and indeed in an ancient hand—the reading is *Medolonense*. Bécan and the Regius manuscript have *Mededonense*. All these names designate Melodunum, a town of the Senones situated on an island in the Seine, commonly called Melun. It was already famous in the time of Julius Caesar. King Childebert, the son of the great Clovis, established an episcopal see there, had not Leo, metropolitan of Sens, opposed him; the place still belongs to the diocese of that city. We possess a letter of Leo in which the town is called *Medeclonense* and, in the sixth case, *Medeclone*.]

burning and devastating everything. Although his nephew’s army had not come to him, his nephew’s dukes and envoys were nevertheless with him.

Then he sent messengers to the dukes mentioned above, saying:

“Enter Berry and, approaching as far as the city, demand oaths of loyalty in my name.”

The people of Berry, numbering fifteen thousand, gathered at the fortress of Mediolanum,

[Note: Thus read the Corbie, Bécan, and Colbertine manuscripts, although the printed editions have *Mecledonense*. Here Mediolanum is designated: today Magdunum on the River Yèvre, within the borders of Berry, commonly called Mehun-sur-Yèvre, as the learned Valesius and Cointius have observed. It already bore both names in the time of Aimoinus, who notes this in Book III, chapter 50.]

and there engaged Duke Desiderius in battle. A great slaughter took place, so that more than seven thousand men fell from the two armies.

The dukes, together with the remaining part of the people, reached the city, plundering and devastating everything. Such destruction was inflicted there as had never, even in ancient times, been heard of: no house, vineyard, or tree remained, but everything was cut down, burned, and destroyed. They even removed the sacred vessels from the churches and burned the churches themselves.

King Guntchramnus came with an army against his brother,

[Note: That is, near Melodunum, where Guntchramnus defeated Chilperic’s army. Their dukes were fighting among the people of Berry, near Mediolanum, or Magdunum, which must be distinguished from Magdunum on the Anger and Magdunum on the Loire.]

placing all his hope in God’s judgment. One day, already toward evening, he sent out his army and killed the greater part of his brother’s army.

In the morning, when envoys came together, they made peace, promising one another that whichever party had exceeded the limits of the law would make compensation to the other according to whatever the priests or the leading men of the people judged. Thus they departed in peace.

King Chilperic, unable to restrain his army from plunder, slaughtered the count of Rouen with a sword and then returned to Paris, abandoning all the booty and releasing the captives.

As for those who had been besieging Berry, when they received the order to return to their own lands, they carried away such great booty that the entire region from which they had departed was thought to have been greatly emptied, both of people and of livestock.

The army of Desiderius and Bladastes also entered the territory of Tours and committed such great burnings, plundering, and killings as are usually inflicted upon enemies. They also led away captives, many of whom they later stripped and released.

A disease among the livestock followed this devastation, so that scarcely one animal remained. It would have been a novelty if anyone saw a beast of burden—

[Note: The Colbertine manuscript has *juvencum*, “a young ox,” instead.]

—or even a young cow.

While these things were taking place, King Childebert was stationed with his army in one place.

[Note: Apparently not far from his brothers, so that he might send assistance to Chilperic according to the agreement, or at least observe the outcome of the war.]

One night, when the army had been mobilized, the lesser people raised a great murmur against Bishop Egidius and the king’s dukes. They began to shout and proclaim publicly:

“Let those who sell the king’s kingdom be removed from his presence—those who subject his cities to another’s rule and hand over the people of this prince to the dominion of another.”

While they shouted these and similar things, morning came. They seized their weapons and hurried to the king’s tent, intending to seize the bishop and the leading men, overpower them by force, beat them, and tear them apart with swords.

When this became known, the priest took flight. Mounting a horse—

[Note: Another reading has *equo*, “horse,” instead of *equite*, “horseman.”]

—he made for his own city. That people followed him with shouting, throwing stones after him and pouring out insults.

At that time he was protected by the fact that they did not have horses ready.

[Note: Another reading has *equos*, “horses,” instead of *equites*, “horsemen.”]

Nevertheless, when the horses of his companions had grown tired, the bishop continued alone. He was so terrified that he did not trouble to retrieve one of the shoes that had slipped from his foot. Thus he reached the city and shut himself inside the walls of Reims.

## XXXII.

A few months earlier, Leudastes had come into the territory of Tours with a royal order to receive his wife and remain there.

[Note: He had previously contrived many things against Gregory, in Book V, chapters 49 and 50, accusing him of saying that the queen was polluted by adultery.]

He also brought me a letter signed by the hands of priests, asking that he be received into communion. But since I had not seen a letter from the queen, whose cause had chiefly led to his exclusion from communion, I delayed receiving him, saying:

“When I receive the queen’s command, I shall not delay receiving him.”

Meanwhile I sent to her. She returned a written reply, saying:

“Pressed by many people, I could do nothing else except permit him to depart. Now I ask that he not receive your peace or accept the eucharistic gifts from your hand until we have considered more fully what ought to be done by us.”

As I reread this letter, however, I feared that he might be killed. I summoned his father-in-law and made these matters known to him, urging him to act cautiously until the queen’s anger should be softened.

But he deceitfully received the advice that I had offered in simplicity for the sake of God, and, although he was still hostile to us, he refused to do what I had instructed. Thus the proverb was fulfilled that I heard a certain old man reciting:

“Always give good counsel to friend and enemy alike: the friend accepts it, the enemy rejects it.”

Having rejected this advice, he went to the king, who was then staying with his army in the district of Melodunum.

[Note: The Colbertine manuscript has *Melodonnense*; Bécan has *Megledunense*. See the preceding chapter.]

He begged the people to offer prayers to the king so that he might be permitted to appear before him. When all the people had pleaded on his behalf, the king allowed himself to be seen by him.

He fell at the king’s feet and begged forgiveness. The king said to him:

“Keep yourself cautious for a little while, until I have seen the queen and learned how you may return to her favor, since you are found to be greatly at fault with her.”

But he was imprudent and frivolous. Trusting in the fact that he had been granted an audience with the king, he fell at the queen’s feet in the holy church on Sunday, when the king had returned to Paris, and begged forgiveness.

She trembled and, abhorring the sight of him, pushed him away from her. With tears flowing, she said:

“Since there is no one among my children who can investigate the causes of my accusation, I entrust them to you, Lord Jesus, to investigate.”

Then, falling at the king’s feet, she added:

“Woe to me, who see my enemy and have no power against him!”

He was then driven away from the holy place, and the solemn celebration of Mass took place.

When the king and queen had left the holy church, Leudastes followed them as far as the marketplace, unaware of what would happen to him. He went around the merchants’ houses, inspecting their wares, weighing silver, and looking at various ornaments, saying:

“I shall buy this and that, because a great deal of gold and silver has remained for me.”

While he was saying these things, the queen’s servants suddenly arrived and wished to bind him with chains. He drew his sword and struck one of them. The others, inflamed with rage, seized shields and swords and attacked him.

One of them, delivering a blow, stripped the greater part of his head of its hair and skin. As he was fleeing across the city bridge, his foot slipped between the two beams that formed the bridge. His shin was crushed, and, with his hands tied behind his back, he was handed over to custody.

The king ordered that he be attended by physicians—

[Note: Thus reads the Corbie manuscript. The Colbertine manuscript has “that he be healed”; most printed editions, with Bécan, have “that attention be given to him,” that is, “that he be treated.”]

—until he had been healed of these wounds and could be tortured by prolonged punishment.

When he had been taken to a royal estate and, as his wounds putrefied, was passing his final days, the queen ordered him to be thrown face-up onto the ground. A huge bar was placed against his neck, and another man struck him on the throat.

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads: “With a huge sword they pierce his throat … carrying his treacherous life to its end, he thus ended it.”]

Thus, after living a life of treachery, he met a fitting death.

## XXXIII.

In the ninth year of King Childebert, King Guntchramnus restored to his nephew Childebert the portion of Massilia.

The envoys of Prince Chilperic, returning from Spain, reported that the province of Carpitania

[Note: Carpitania was part of the ancient province of Tarraconensis, in the region of New Castile, where there are now parts of the Alcarria and La Mancha, toward the Tagus and the Guadiana. Its chief city was Toledo, a city famous in its own right.]

had been severely devastated by locusts, so that no tree, vineyard, forest, fruit, or anything green remained that had not been destroyed by the locusts.

They said that the hostility that had arisen between Leuvichild and his son was growing greatly. A plague, raging more fiercely in those regions, was also devastating many places—

[Note: Thus reads the Regius manuscript. Others have: “For his plague was devastating throughout the regions.”]

—but it was raging most violently around the city of Narbonne.

[Note: Narbonne and the other cities of Septimania were then assigned to Spain because they were subject to the Visigoths.]

It was now the third year since it had seized that place and then subsided—

[Note: The Colbertine manuscript has “had raged”; the Regius manuscript has “had arrived.”]

—and the people, returning from flight, were again consumed by the disease. The city of Albi was also suffering especially from this affliction.

In those days, many rays appeared from the north in the middle of the night, shining with extraordinary brilliance. They came together and then separated again until they vanished. The sky itself also shone from the northern quarter, so that it seemed to be producing the dawn.

## XXXIV.

[Note: This chapter is absent from the Vatican, Corbie, and first Colbertine manuscripts, although they contain the following chapter, to which it is necessarily connected. The *placitum* mentioned here was a day appointed for hearing envoys. More generally, *placita* were assemblies in which public matters, whether of the kingdom or of private persons, were considered. Just as there were royal *placita*, so there were those of counts, judges, and others; they were later called parliaments. Public instruments issued after matters had been concluded in such assemblies were also called *placita* or judgments. See Bignon on Book I of Marculf, formula 37, and Mabillon, *De re Diplomatica*.]

Envoys again came from Spain, bringing gifts and receiving a formal appointment with King Chilperic, so that, in accordance with the earlier agreement, he might give his daughter in marriage to the son of King Leuvichild—

[Note: That is, to Reccared, the brother of Hermenegild. The girl, namely Rigunth, had been promised to him some time earlier.]

After the appointment had been granted and everything had been arranged, the envoy returned.

But when King Chilperic had left Paris to go into the district of Soissons, a new grief arrived. His son—

[Note: Theodoric, mentioned above in chapters 23 and 27 and below in the following chapter.]

—the one whom he had washed in sacred baptism the previous year—was seized by dysentery and breathed out his spirit.

This was what the fiery sign we mentioned above, which had fallen from the cloud, prefigured.

Then, amid immense weeping, they returned to Paris and buried the boy. They sent after the envoy so that he might return, in order to postpone the formal agreement that had been made. The king said:

“Behold, I am suffering mourning in my household; how shall I celebrate my daughter’s wedding?”

At that time he wished to send another daughter there—

[Note: Basina, who later caused many disturbances in that monastery together with Chrodield; Gregory gives a full account of them below.]

—the daughter he had by Audovera, whom he had placed in the monastery at Poitiers.

But she delayed, especially because the blessed Radegund resisted, saying:

“For it is not fitting that a girl dedicated to Christ should return again to the pleasures of the world.”

[Col. 0401C] **XXXV.** While these events were taking place, word was brought to the queen that the boy who had died had been carried off by magical arts and enchantments, and that Mummolus the prefect—whom the queen had long hated—was privy to the matter.

[Note: [Col. 0401D] Valesius investigates why Mummolus is called “the prefect” here. For although it is certain that the governors of the Province of Massilia were at that time given the title of prefect, he observes that the title cannot therefore be attributed to Mummolus, since Chilperic, in whose dominion Mummolus lived, had never possessed anything in that province. Rejecting Falcetus’s opinion—who, imprudently applying the customs of his own age to ancient times, wrote that Mummolus was so called because he was prefect of the city of Paris—he finally concludes that Gregory called Mummolus “prefect” because he had in fact been prefect of the court, or chief officer of the royal household.]

Accordingly, while Mummolus was dining in his own house, one of the king’s courtiers lamented a boy dear to himself, who had been seized by dysentery. The prefect replied to him: “I have an herb at hand; if a dysenteric person [310] drinks it, he is immediately cured, however desperate his condition may be.” When this was reported to the queen, she was inflamed with still greater fury.

Meanwhile she seized the women of the city of Paris, subjected them to torture, and compelled them by blows to confess what they knew. But they confessed that they were sorceresses and declared that they had caused many people to die, adding something that I cannot believe by any means: “Your son, O queen,” they said, “we sacrificed in exchange for the life of the prefect Mummolus.”

Then, after subjecting the women to more severe tortures, the queen killed some, handed others over to the flames, and bound others to wheels after their bones had been broken. Thus she withdrew with the king to the estate of Compendium, and there revealed to him everything she had heard about the prefect.

The king then sent attendants and ordered Mummolus to be brought before him. After examination, they loaded him with chains and subjected him to punishments.
