With his hands bound behind his back, he was hung from a beam and questioned about what magical practices he knew. But he confessed nothing of the things we mentioned above.

[Col. 0402B] Yet he repeatedly stated that he had received from these women ointments and potions intended to win him the favor of the king and queen. Accordingly, when he had been removed from the punishment, he summoned the lictor and said: “Tell my lord the king that I feel no harm from the things inflicted upon me.”

When the king heard this, he said: “Can it really be true that this man is a sorcerer, if he has suffered no injury from these punishments?”

[Note: [Col. 0402D] Regm. reads: “Do you think it is true that this man is a sorcerer, and that he has not been harmed by these punishments? Let him be stretched upon the pulleys and beaten with triple-thonged whips until the torturers themselves grow tired.”]

Then he was stretched upon the pulleys and beaten with triple-thonged whips until the torturers themselves grew weary. After this, stakes were driven beneath the nails of his hands and feet. When the proceedings had reached the point at which a sword was poised to sever his neck, he obtained his life from the queen; but the humiliation that followed was scarcely less than death.

Placed upon a wagon, he was sent to the city of Bordeaux, where he had been born, stripped of all his property; [311] on the way, bleeding from the blows inflicted upon him, he could scarcely reach the place to which he had been ordered to go.

[Note: [Col. 0402D] Bad. reads *ictus* (“struck”); Colb. m., *ictu actus* (“driven by a blow”).]

[Col. 0402C] But not long afterward he breathed his last. After this, the queen seized the boy’s treasure and burned all his clothing and other possessions that she could find, whether of silk or of any other fabric. They say that these filled four wagons. She melted the gold and silver in a furnace and stored them away, so that nothing might remain intact to recall to her the memory of her son’s lamentation.

**XXXVI.** Aetherius, bishop of Lisieux, whom we mentioned above, was expelled from his city—or restored to it—in the following manner.

[Note: [Col. 0402D] This chapter is absent from Vat., Colb. a., and Corb. Regm. has *Aethericus vero Luxoviensis*. The printed editions have *Lyxoensis* or *Lixoensis*, commonly Lisieux in Normandy. Moreover, the passage in which Gregory is supposed to have mentioned Aetherius above does not exist. Hence Cointius infers that this chapter was attached to Gregory’s history by another author. Gregory himself, however, in Book IV, chapter 16—which is found in the Corb., Bellov., and all the other manuscripts—similarly says of Saint Tetricus, bishop of Langres, “whose memory we have mentioned,” although nothing about him is found elsewhere in Gregory.]

There was a certain cleric from the city of Le Mans, exceedingly lustful, a lover of women, and greatly devoted to gluttony, fornication, and every kind of impurity. He had repeatedly had intercourse with a certain woman as with a prostitute. He shaved the hair of his head, changed his male clothing [Note: [Col. 0403D] Regm. reads: “and changed feminine clothing into masculine clothing.”], and took her with him to another city, so that suspicion of adultery might be removed when they arrived among strangers.

For the woman was freeborn and descended from good parents. After many days had passed, her relatives learned what had happened. They hastened to avenge the dishonor done to their family, found the cleric, bound him, and handed him over to custody; but they burned the woman to death.

And, as the accursed hunger for gold compels, they arranged for the cleric to be sold for a price, in such a way that either someone would appear to redeem him or he would certainly be condemned to death. When these matters were reported to Bishop Aetherius, he was moved by mercy and, giving twenty gold pieces [Note: [Col. 0403D] The same codex reads “silver pieces.”], rescued him from the death that threatened him.

After he had thus been granted his life, the man declared that he was a teacher of letters, promising the priest that, if he entrusted boys to him, he would make them proficient in learning. The priest was pleased by what he heard, gathered the boys of the city, and assigned them to him for instruction.

Eventually, when he was already honored by the citizens, and when the bishop had bestowed upon him some land and vineyards, and he was invited into the homes of the parents of those whom he taught, [312] he returned to his vomit and, forgetful of his former offense, lusted after the mother of one of the boys.

When the chaste woman disclosed this to her husband, her relatives joined together and, subjecting the cleric to the severest tortures, sought to kill him. But the priest, again moved by mercy, freed him after reproving him with gentle words and restored him to his position of honor.

His perverse mind, however, could never be inclined toward goodness. Rather, he became the enemy of the man who had repeatedly saved him from death. He joined himself to the city’s archdeacon and, presenting himself as worthy of the episcopate, plotted to kill the bishop.

They engaged a cleric to strike him with a double-headed axe. They went about everywhere, whispering, secretly forming alliances, and offering rewards, so that, if the priest died, the cleric himself might succeed him.

But the mercy of the Lord forestalled their treachery and, by swift compassion, restrained the cruelty of these wicked men. On the day when the priest had gathered workers in the field to plow, the aforesaid cleric pursued him with an axe, while the priest knew absolutely nothing of these plans.

At last, noticing this, the priest said: “Why are you following me so intently with that double-headed axe?”

Terrified by fear, the man fell at the priest’s knees and said: “Be strong, priest of God. For you should know that I was sent by the archdeacon and ordered to strike you with an axe. Although I repeatedly wished to do this, whenever I raised my right hand and poised the blow, darkness covered my eyes, my ears were stopped, and my whole body was shaken with trembling. My hands, moreover, were without strength, and I could not accomplish what I wished. But whenever I lowered my hands, I felt no evil at all. I realized that the Lord is with you, because I was unable to harm you in any way.”

When he had said this, the priest wept, imposed silence upon the cleric, and returned home to dine. After the meal he rested upon his bed, with many little beds for clerics arranged around it.

[Note: [Col. 0403D] In accordance with the prescription of the canons, which require bishops always to have with them witnesses of their private conduct; see the canon *Cum pastoris*, 2, q. 7. Compare Gregory the Great, Book IV, Letter 44. The Roman synod in the case of Symmachus calls such companions *concellanei*; the Greeks call them *syncelli*.]

Finally, [313] these men, despairing of carrying out their wickedness through the cleric himself, devised new schemes by which either they might kill him by force or bring against him some charge that would remove him from the priesthood.

Meanwhile, while everyone was sleeping, at about midnight they burst into the priest’s chamber, shouting loudly and saying that they had seen a woman leaving his room and had therefore dismissed her while they hurried to the bishop.

And indeed this was the devil’s doing and counsel: to bring such a charge against a priest who was nearly seventy years old.

Without delay, joining the aforesaid cleric to themselves once more, they bound the priest with chains by the hands of the very man from whose neck he had often shaken off bonds, and handed him over to strict confinement by the man whom he had often freed from filthy prisons.

But when the priest realized that his enemies had gained great power against him, he prayed amid his tears for the mercy of the Lord while bound in chains. Immediately the guards were overcome by sleep, and, when his chains had been divinely broken, he came out of custody unharmed—the frequent liberator of the guilty. Then he escaped and crossed into the kingdom of King Guntram.

After he had departed, the joined accomplices proceeded more freely to King Chilperic, seeking the episcopate. They made many accusations against the bishop and added: “By this, most glorious king, recognize that what we say is true: fearing death for his crimes, he has fled to the kingdom of your brother.”

The king did not believe them and ordered them to return to the city. While these events were taking place, the grieving citizens, distressed by the absence of their shepherd and learning that everything done against him had been perpetrated through envy and greed, seized the archdeacon together with his accomplice, subjected them to punishment for their offense, and petitioned the king to restore their priest to them.

The king then sent envoys to his brother, asserting that he had found no crime in the bishop. King Guntram, who was kind and generous in showing mercy, gave him many gifts and also sent letters to all the bishops of his kingdom, asking them, for God’s sake, to give the exile some consolation.

[Note: [Col. 0404D] Bec. reads *aliquid* (“something”).]

[314] He then traveled through the cities, and the priests of God bestowed so much upon him, both in clothing and in gold, that he could scarcely bring it all into the city that had deserved him. The saying of the Apostle was fulfilled: “For those who love God, all things work together for good” (Romans 8:28).

For this man’s pilgrimage brought him wealth, and his exile introduced abundant riches. Afterward, when he returned, the citizens received him with such honor that they wept for joy and blessed God, who had at last restored so great a priest to the church.

**XXXVII.** Lupentius, abbot of the basilica of Saint Privatus the martyr in the city of Gabala, came after being summoned by Queen Brunichilde.

[Note: [Col. 0405C] This chapter is absent from Vat., Corb., and Colb. a. The body of Saint Lupentius was brought to Catalaunum and preserved in the cathedral church until the year 1667, when the church, struck by lightning on January 19, burned down, and the sacred relics kept there were consumed with it. What remained—namely, half-burned bones and ashes—was collected together and is preserved in a chest behind the high altar. The feast of Saint Lupentius is celebrated there on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November, and he is commonly called Saint Louvent.]

He had been accused, as they say, by Innocentius, count of the aforesaid city, of having spoken something profane about the queen. But when the charges had been examined and he was found to have no knowledge of any crime against the majesty of the queen, he was ordered to depart.

Yet as soon as he began his journey, he was again seized by the aforesaid count and taken to the estate of Ponticon, where he was subjected to many tortures. He was then released and ordered to return. When he had pitched his tent beside the river Axona, his enemy again attacked him.

Overwhelming him by force, the enemy cut off his head, placed it in a sack weighted with stones, and gave it to the river. He bound the rest of the body to a stone and submerged it in the depths.

After a few days, he appeared to certain shepherds; the body was drawn from the river and buried. But while the funeral arrangements were being made, and no one knew who the dead man was—especially since the severed head had not been found—an eagle suddenly arrived, lifted the sack from the bottom of the river, and placed it on the bank.

Those present were astonished. They seized the sack, and, while carefully investigating what it contained, found the severed head. Thus it was buried with the remaining limbs.

For they say that even now a light divinely appears there, and that if a sick person faithfully prays at this tomb, he departs restored to health.

[Col. 0405C] **XXXVIII.** Theodosius, bishop of Rodez, who had succeeded Saint Dalmatius, [315] died.

[Note: [Col. 0405D] This chapter is also absent from Corb., Vat., and Colb. a. Concerning Saint Dalmatius, the election of Theodosius, and Transobadus, see above, Book V, chapter 47. In Colb. m. Transobadus is called Trusobaldus; in Regm., Teusobaldus; in others, Trasobadus.]

In that church, disputes and scandals concerning the episcopate became so strong that it was almost stripped of its sacred ministry vessels and all its better property. Nevertheless, the priest Transobadus was rejected, and Innocentius, count of the Gabali, was elected to the episcopate with the assistance of Queen Brunichilde.

[Note: [Col. 0405D] The same man as the one mentioned in the preceding chapter and in Book X, chapter 8.]

After assuming the episcopate, he immediately began to challenge Ursicinus, bishop of Cahors, saying that he was retaining dioceses belonging by right to the Church of Rodez.

As the dispute grew through prolonged contention, after several years the metropolitan, seated with his provincial bishops at the city of Clermont, issued a judgment, namely that he should recover the parishes that it was remembered the Church of Rodez had never possessed. This was accordingly done.

[Note: [Col. 0405D] Thus Colb. m. and Regm.; this is the genuine reading. Gregory and other authors of his age likewise use the word in the form *metropolitanus*. See the Third Council of Paris, canon 8, and the formulas of Marculf. Hence the reading *metropolitanis* in Chesne and several other printed editions is incorrect; some others more correctly have *metropolitanus*. [Col. 0406C] This was Sulpicius, as appears from the following chapter and from Book X, chapter 26. The parishes over which the dispute arose were, as Valesius suspects, those that had been assigned to the bishopric of Arisitum; see above, Book V, chapter 5.]

[Col. 0406A] **XXXIX.** Remigius, bishop of Bourges, died. After his death, the greater part of the city was destroyed by a severe fire, and there perished those things that had survived the attacks of the enemy.

[Note: [Col. 0406D] The words from “and there” through “perished” are absent from Colb. m. Cas. has: “had resisted the attacks.”]

Afterward Sulpicius was preferred to the priesthood in that very city, with King Guntram’s support. For when many people were offering gifts, the king is said to have replied as follows to those seeking the episcopate:

“It is not the custom of our rule to sell the priesthood for a price, nor is it proper for you to purchase it with gifts. Otherwise we would be marked by the disgrace of shameful profit, and you would be compared with Simon Magus. But in accordance with God’s foreknowledge, Sulpicius will be your bishop.”

And so, having been brought into the clergy, he assumed the episcopate of the aforesaid church. He was a man of very noble birth, one of the foremost senators of Gaul, well educated in literature and rhetoric, and second to no one in the art of verse. He had urged the holding of the synod mentioned above concerning the parishes of Cahors.

**XL.** An envoy named Oppila arrived from Spain, bringing many gifts to King Chilperic.

[316] For the king of the Spaniards feared that Childebert might mobilize an army to avenge the wrong done to his sister, because Leuvigild had seized his son Hermenegild, who had married Childebert’s sister, and had confined him in custody, while the woman herself had been left with the Greeks.

[Note: [Col. 0406D] Ingund, the daughter of Sigibert.]

Accordingly, when this envoy arrived at Tours on the holy day of Easter, we asked whether he belonged to our religion. He replied that he believed what Catholics believe. Then he went with us to the church and attended the solemn celebration of Mass; but he neither exchanged the kiss of peace with our people nor received communion from the sacrifices.

[Note: [Col. 0406D] Observe that the man was present at the sacred rites but did not participate in them or receive the peace from the other faithful. To “hold Masses” means to attend them, according to canon 47 of the Council of Agde, or, if the subject is a priest, to celebrate them, as in the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 60. See Cardinal Bona, Book I of *Liturgical Matters*, chapter 2, no. 6.]

It therefore became clear that he had lied when he said that he was a Catholic. Nevertheless, he attended when invited to the banquet.

When I earnestly asked him what he believed, he replied: “I believe that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are of one power.”

I answered him: “If you believe what you assert, what prevented you from receiving the sacrifices that we offer to God?”

He replied: “Because you do not render the *Gloria* correctly. For, following Paul, we say: ‘Glory to God the Father through the Son’; but you say: ‘Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit,’ although the teachers of the churches teach that the Father was announced to the world through the Son, just as Paul himself says: ‘To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, to God alone, be honor and glory forever and ever, through Jesus Christ our Lord’ (1 Timothy 1:17).”

I replied: “I think that it is unknown to no Catholic that the Father was announced through the Son. But he preached the Father in the world in such a way that he also showed himself to be God by his mighty works.

“It was necessary for God the Father to send the Son to earth to reveal God: since the world had not believed the patriarchs, the prophets, or even the one who delivered the Law, it might at least believe the Son.

“Therefore glory must be given to God with distinction according to the persons. [317] We say: ‘Glory to God the Father, who sent the Son; glory to God the Son, who redeemed the world with his blood; glory to God the Holy Spirit, who sanctifies the person already redeemed.’

“For you, who say ‘Glory to the Father through the Son,’ take glory away from the Son, as though he were not glorious with the Father merely because he announced the Father in the world.

“The Son announced the Father in the world, as we have said, but many did not believe, as the Evangelist John says: ‘He came to his own, and his own did not receive him. But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name’ (John 1:11–12).”

[Note: [Col. 0407D] Thus Corb., Bec., Colb. a., Colb. c., and Regm.; the others do not have *sua*. Below, Corb. and Regm. read *quotquot eum*, and so forth.]

“For you who disparage the Apostle Paul and do not understand his meaning, notice how carefully he speaks, and, according to what a person can receive [Alternative: rightly], observe how he preaches among unbelieving peoples, so that he may not impose a burden that seems too heavy upon anyone. Thus he says to some: ‘I gave you milk to drink, not solid food; for you were not yet able, and even now you are not able’ (1 Corinthians 3:2).

[Col. 0407C] “Solid food belongs to the mature (Hebrews 5:14). But he also says to others: ‘I determined to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified’ (1 Corinthians 2:2).

[Note: [Col. 0407D] These words, through “nothing among you,” are absent from Corb.; this is an omission by the scribe.]

“Now, you heretic, because Paul preached only Christ, and him crucified, do you doubt that he rose again? Rather, observe his caution and see his wisdom in what he says to others whom he saw to be stronger in faith: ‘Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, now we no longer know him in that way’ (2 Corinthians 5:16).

[Note: [Col. 0407D] The printed editions have “Jesus Christ.”]

“Deny, then, you accuser of Paul—if such madness has seized your mind—that he was even crucified. But, I beg you, abandon such things and hear better counsel: apply eye salves to your bleary eyes and receive the light of apostolic preaching.

“For Paul spoke in human terms, and more humbly, in order to raise them to the heights of a more exalted faith, as he says elsewhere: ‘I have become all things to all people, that I might save all’ (1 Corinthians 9:22).

“Will a mortal man not give glory to the Son, whom the Father himself glorified from heaven not once, but twice and three times? Listen to what he says from heaven when the same Son was being baptized under John’s hand as the Holy Spirit descended: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’ (Matthew 17:5).

“Surely, if you have stopped-up ears so that you cannot hear these things, believe what the apostles [318] heard on the mountain when Jesus was transfigured in glory and spoke with Moses and Elijah. Indeed, from the bright cloud the Father said: ‘This is my most beloved Son; listen to him’ (2 Peter 1:17).”

The heretic replied: “In none of these testimonies does the Father speak of the glory of the Son; he merely points out the Son.”

I answered: “If you accept these things in that way, I will offer you another testimony in which the Father made the Son glorious. When the Lord was approaching his Passion, and he said, ‘Father, glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you’ (John 17:1), what did the Father answer him from heaven? Did he not say: ‘I have glorified him, and I will glorify him again’ (John 12:28)?”

[Col. 0408B] [Note: [Col. 0407D] Regm. reads *clarificet*—“may glorify”—and below, *clarificavi … clarificabo*—“I have glorified … I will glorify.”]

“Behold, the Father glorifies him with his own voice, and you try to deprive him of glory? You show your will, but you have no power.

“For you who present yourself as an accuser of the Apostle Paul, hear Paul himself—or rather, Christ speaking through him: ‘Let every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father’ (Philippians 2:11).

“If his glory is now shared with the Father, and he dwells in the very glory in which the Father now is, how do you dishonor him as though he were without glory? Or why should glory not be rendered to him among human beings, when he reigns in heaven with glory equal to the Father’s?

“We therefore confess Christ, the Son of God, to be true God. Accordingly, since the deity is one, the glory also will be one.”

After this, silence was imposed and the dispute came to an end. The envoy then approached King Chilperic, presented the gifts that the king of the Spaniards had sent, and returned to Spain.

[Col. 0408C] **XLI.** When King Chilperic learned that his brother Guntram had made peace with his nephew Childebert and that they both wished to take away from him the cities he had seized by force, he withdrew with all his treasures to the city of Cambrai and took with him everything he had been able to preserve of greatest value.

He sent messengers to the dukes and counts of the cities, ordering them to repair the walls of their towns, to bring their property, wives, and children within the fortifications, and, if necessity required, to fight bravely themselves, so that the opposing side might not harm them. He added: “If you lose anything, when we take vengeance upon our enemies [319] you will acquire greater things”—not knowing that the accomplishment of victories rests in the hand of God.

Then he repeatedly mobilized the army and again ordered it to rest within the frontier. During these days a son was born to him. He ordered the child to be raised at the estate of Victoriacum.

[Note: [Col. 0408D] In Belgium, where Sigibert had been killed, as stated in Book IV, at the end of the last chapter. The son of Chilperic mentioned here was later called Chlotar and succeeded his father in the kingdom.]

He said: “Perhaps, while he is publicly seen, he may suffer some misfortune and die.”

**XLII.** King Childebert went into Italy. When the Lombards heard this, fearing that they might be slaughtered by his army, they submitted themselves to his authority, gave him many gifts, and promised that they would be faithful and subject to his side.

[Note: [Col. 0408D] Concerning Childebert’s various expeditions into Italy, see Paul the Deacon, Book III, chapters 17 and following. Several letters on this matter have been published by Chesne and Freher, in which Maurice and his prefects complain of the Franks as men guilty of violating their allegiance. Authari, son of Cleph, was then reigning among the Lombards; he was called Flavius on account of his dignity, and he transmitted this praenomen to the later kings of his people, as Paul the Deacon reports in Book III, chapter 16.]

After carrying out with them everything the king wished, he returned to Gaul and ordered the army to be mobilized. He commanded it to be directed into Spain, but it remained at rest.

Fifty thousand solidi had been received from the Emperor Maurice fifty years earlier, so that Childebert might drive the Lombards out of Italy. When the emperor learned that Childebert had made peace with them, he demanded the money back. But Childebert, relying on his resources, did not even wish to give an answer on this subject.

[Note: [Col. 0409D] Regm. reads: “but for some reason I do not know, it remained behind.” For *ab.*]

**XLIII.** New events also took place in Galicia, which will be related below.

[Note: [Col. 0409D] In French, “below”; hence Colb. a. has “below.”]

When Hermenegild, as we said above, was hostile to his father and was living with his wife in a certain city of Spain, relying upon the support of the emperor and of Miro, king of Galicia, he learned that his father was coming against him with an army. He considered how he might repel or kill his approaching father, in his misery unaware that divine judgment threatened him because he was contemplating such actions against his parent, however heretical that parent might be.

[Note: [Col. 0409D] Book V, chapter 39, which should be consulted. The city mentioned here is Seville, whose bishop at that time was Saint Leander, envoy to the Emperor Tiberius, seeking aid against Leuvigild. Miro was a Catholic; his father, together with the whole Suevic people over whom he ruled, had been brought to the true faith through Martin of Dumio. John of Biclarum and the commonly circulated Isidore write in the Chronicle that Miro went to Leuvigild’s aid and died at Seville.]

After deliberation, he selected three hundred armed men from among many thousands and shut them inside the fortress of Osset, [320]

[Note: [Col. 0410C] Others have *Osset* or *Oser*; it was a fortress opposite Seville, formerly called Julia Constantia by the Romans.]

in whose church the fonts are filled by divine power. His plan was that, at the first assault, his father would be frightened and exhausted by these men and would more easily be defeated by the lower force, which was much larger.

When King Leuvigild learned of these stratagems, he was greatly troubled in thought. “If I go there with the entire army,” he said, “the opposing army, massed together, will be cruelly wounded by javelins. But if I go with a few men, I shall be unable to overcome the band of brave men. Nevertheless, I will go with everyone.”

[Col. 0409C] [Note: [Col. 0410C] Corb. has *ibit*—“will go”—instead of *ivit*—“went.”]

Approaching the place, he crushed the men and burned the fortress, as has already been mentioned above. After achieving victory, he learned that King Miro was stationed against him with an army. Having surrounded him, he demanded an oath that Miro would remain faithful to him in the future.

Thus, after they exchanged gifts with one another, each returned to his own country. But after Miro had returned home, he took to his bed a few days later and died; for he had been weakened by the unhealthy waters and harmful climates of Spain.

After his death, his son Eurich sought the friendship of King Leuvigild. Having given an oath, as his father had done, he assumed the kingdom of Galicia.

In that same year, his kinsman Audica, to whom his sister was betrothed, came with an army. He seized a cleric and ordered him to be invested with the dignity either of the diaconate or of the priesthood.

[Note: [Col. 0410D] Isidore writes in his Chronicle that Audica condemned Euboricus, who had become a monk, to the monastery. He also reports that Leuvigild waged war against the Suevi; Audica was defeated and compelled to assume the office of priest, by which means the rule of the Suevi in Spain was destroyed. See the Chronicle of John of Biclarum.]

Audica himself, having taken the wife of his father-in-law,

[Note: [Col. 0410D] Namely Siseguntia, the wife of Miro, according to the Chronicle of John of Biclarum.]

obtained the kingdom of Galicia.

But Leuvigild captured his son Hermenegild and brought him with him as far as Toledo, condemning him to exile. He was unable, however, to rescue Hermenegild’s wife from the Greeks.

[Col. 0410B] **XLIV.** Locusts from the province of Carpitania, which they had devastated for five years, advanced this year, [321] following the public embankment, and moved into another province adjacent to it.

Thus the swarm extended for a length of one hundred and fifty miles; its width reached one hundred miles.

[Note: [Col. 0410D] The word “one hundred” is absent from Cod. Corb.]

This year many omens appeared in Gaul, and there was much devastation among the people. For roses were seen in the month of January. A great circle also appeared around the sun, mixed with various colors, such as the rainbow in the celestial arch usually appears when the rain has departed.

[Note: [Col. 0410D] Cod. Colb. has “when the rain is descending.”]

A severe frost scorched the vineyards. A storm followed and devastated vineyards and crops in many places, while extreme drought consumed what remained after the hail. Only a small harvest appeared in some vineyards, and none at all in others, so that people, angered against God, opened the entrances of the vineyards and let in their livestock and beasts of burden, mingling harmful prayers with their misery and saying: “May a vine shoot never grow in these vineyards forever.”

Trees that had produced fruit in July produced other fruit in September. A recurring disease among livestock grew so strong that scarcely anything remained.

## XLV.

Meanwhile, when the Kalends of September arrived, a large Gothic embassy came to King Chilperic. He himself, having already returned to Paris, ordered many households to be removed from the fiscal estates [Note: On this passage concerning the fiscal estates, see Valesius, *Rerum Francicarum*, book XI. He says that the ancient Germans were accustomed to live not in cities but in estates and villages, in which each man maintained his household and as much livestock as he could. Our kings, retaining this custom, possessed many such estates scattered throughout the kingdom, so that they almost never stayed outside their own estates, even while traveling. From these, nearly everything needed by them and their people was supplied. For there were farmers, vine-growers, shepherds, cooks, bakers, and so forth, each performing his own work; these were called fiscal or royal slaves. Some called them the lord’s household, others the king’s servants. The king’s domestic officers, sometimes also called mayors of the palace, presided over these estates and their inhabitants. They were more powerful according to the number of estates over which they were placed. Each estate had its own administrator, called the lord’s agent, who was subject to the domestic officer and obliged to render an account to him. Such were the households of our kings; and Chilperic, exercising his right, compelled many unwilling people to go to Spain.] and have them loaded onto wagons. He also ordered many who wept and resisted departure to be confined, so that he might more easily send them across with his daughter. For it is said that many, fearing that they would be taken away from their own parents, ended their lives by hanging themselves because of this bitterness. A son was separated from his father, a mother from her daughter, and they departed with deep groans and curses. Such was the lamentation in the city of Paris that it was compared with the Egyptian lamentation.

Many of the leading men [Note: This was said of those who possessed some rank or wealth; sometimes they were also called the older-born or elders. Conversely, the lower-born were those who had nothing above the condition of commoners. See Du Cange’s *Glossary*.], who were being forced to leave, drew up wills and assigned their possessions to churches, asking that, once the girl had entered Spain, those wills should immediately be opened, as though they were already buried.

Meanwhile, ambassadors of King Childebert arrived in Paris and formally warned King Chilperic not to remove anything from the cities that he held from his father’s kingdom, nor to give his daughter any part of his treasures, and not to dare touch any slaves, horsemen [Alternative: horses], yokes of oxen, or anything of that kind. One of these ambassadors, it is said, was secretly killed, but it is unknown by whom. Suspicion, however, fell upon the king.

King Chilperic promised that he would touch none of these things. Then, having summoned the leading Franks and his other loyal men, he celebrated his daughter’s wedding [Note: See chapter 9 of the following book]. He handed her over to the Gothic ambassadors and gave her great treasures. Her mother also brought forth an immense quantity of gold, silver, and clothing, so that, when the king saw these things, he thought that nothing had been left for him.

When the queen saw that he was upset, she turned to the Franks and said: “Do not suppose, men, that anything from the treasures of the earlier kings is kept here. Everything you see has been offered from my own property, because the most glorious king has bestowed many gifts upon me. I too gathered some things through my own labor [Note: The Corbie manuscript omits “labor”] and restored many things from the estates granted to me, both from their produce and from their revenues. You yourselves have often enriched me with your gifts, and these things that you now see before you come from them. Nothing here comes from the public treasuries.”

Thus the king’s mind was deceived. There was such a quantity of goods that the gold, silver, and other ornaments loaded fifty wagons.

The Franks also offered many gifts: some gold, some silver, some horsemen [Manuscript variant: horses], most clothing; and each gave a present according to his means.

When the girl was finally taking her leave, after tears and kisses, and was going out through the gate, one axle of the wagon broke, and everyone exclaimed, “A bad omen!” Some accepted this as an augury.

At last, after departing from Paris, she ordered tents to be pitched eight miles from the city. During the night, fifty men rose, seized one hundred excellent horses [Alternative: horsemen], as many golden bridles, and two great chains, and fled to King Childebert. Moreover, throughout the entire journey, anyone who could slip away escaped, carrying with him whatever he had been able to seize.

A great supply of provisions for the journey was also collected from various cities. The king ordered that nothing be supplied from his treasury for it, but that everything come from contributions exacted from the poor [Note: That is, contributions or collections, especially those made extraordinarily. Otherwise such contributions were called *conjecta*, as Bignonius observes in his notes on Marculf, book I, chapter 3].

Because the king suspected that his brother or nephew might set some ambush for the girl along the road, he ordered her to proceed surrounded by an army.

The distinguished men accompanying her were Bobo the duke, son of Mummolenus, with his wife, acting as her escort; Domegisilus; and Ansoualdus. The mayor of the palace was Waddo [Note: The Colbertine manuscript and another copy have *Watdo*; Regm. has *Wardo*; Bec. has *Waldo*. In the table of chapters of Colb. A, *Walado*], who had formerly governed the county of Saintes. The remaining common people numbered more than four thousand.

The other dukes and chamberlains [Note: Bignonius considers the chamberlains to have been the same as the bedchamber officers in Marculf, book I, formula 25. Hincmarus explains their duties in these words: “The care of the dignity of the palace, and especially of royal ornament, as well as the annual gifts of the soldiers, apart from food, drink, and horses, belonged chiefly to the queen and, under her, to the chamberlain,” and so forth. See Tilius, Falcetus, *Origins*, book I, chapter 11, and Du Cange’s *Glossary*.], who had traveled with her, turned back from Poitiers; the others continued onward as best they could.

Along the road such great plunder and so great a quantity of booty were taken that they can scarcely be described. They stripped the poor people’s little dwellings; they ravaged the vineyards, cutting the trunks and carrying away the vines with their grapes [Note: Corbie has “with all the stems”]; they seized livestock and whatever else they could find, leaving nothing along the road by which they passed.

What was spoken through the prophet Joel was fulfilled: “The caterpillar has eaten what the locust left; the grasshopper has eaten what the caterpillar left; and the rust has eaten what the grasshopper left” (Joel 1:4) [Note: Corbie has *erugo*, “rust,” for *brucus*]. So it also happened at that time: the storm destroyed what the frost had left, drought consumed what the storm had left, and hostility carried away what the drought had left.

## XLVI.

While these people were proceeding with this booty, Chilperic—our age’s Nero and Herod—went to the Calense estate, which lies about one hundred stadia from the city of Paris, and there devoted himself to hunting.

One day, having returned from the hunt, as night was already growing dark, he was being helped down from his horse and was resting one hand upon the shoulder of a servant when someone approached and struck him beneath the armpit with a knife. With a second blow he pierced his belly. Immediately, a great quantity of blood poured from his mouth and from the opening of the wound, and he breathed out his wicked spirit.

The evil he had committed is shown by the preceding account. For he repeatedly devastated and burned many regions; and he felt no sorrow for them, but rather rejoiced, like Nero once did when he sang tragedies amid the burning of the palace [Note: In Suetonius, book VI, chapter 38].

He often punished people unjustly because of their wealth. In his time, scarcely any clerics deserved to become bishops. He was devoted to gluttony, and his belly was his god. He claimed that no one was wiser than himself. He composed two books, as though he had taken Sedulius as his model, whose feeble verses cannot stand on any meter. In them, because he did not understand the subject, he put short syllables where long ones belonged and treated long syllables as short. He also composed other little works, hymns, and Masses [Note: That is, collects or prayers, as learned men interpret it; no one is unaware of the various meanings that the word *Missa* can bear], which cannot be accepted on any reasonable grounds.

He detested the lawsuits of the poor and constantly blasphemed the priests of the Lord. When he was in private, he found no subject for mockery or jokes more readily than the bishops of the churches. He called one frivolous, another proud; one wealthy, another lustful; one arrogant, another swollen with pride. He hated nothing more than the churches [Note: Thus Corbie and Bec.; other manuscripts have “no thing” rather than “no one”].

He often said: “Look, our treasury has become poor; look, our riches have been transferred to the churches. No one rules at all except the bishops; our honor has perished and has been transferred to the bishops of the cities.”

While constantly saying these things [Alternative: doing these things], he often tore up the wills that had been written in favor of the churches. He also frequently trampled upon the commands of his father, thinking that no one would remain to carry out his wishes.

As for lust and debauchery, nothing that could be conceived of had he not perpetrated in action. He was always devising new methods of harming the people. If he found anyone guilty in those days, he ordered his eyes to be torn out. In the orders he sent to judges for his own advantage, he added this: “If anyone disobeys our commands, let him be punished by the removal of his eyes.”

He never loved anyone sincerely, and no one loved him. Therefore, when he breathed out his spirit, all his own people abandoned him [Note: Corbie omits “his own people.” Moreover, Mallulfus—called Malulfus by others, Madulfus in the Colbertine and Regm. manuscripts, and Madalulfus by Aimo—was honored as a saint among the people of Senlis on the fourth day before the Nones of May, the day of his translation].

Mallulfus, bishop of Senlis, had already been staying in his tent for three days and had been unable to see him. When he heard that Chilperic had been killed, he came, washed the body, clothed it in better garments, spent the night in hymns, placed it in a boat, and buried it in the basilica of Saint Vincent in Paris [Note: A monument of King Chilperic can still be seen in the basilica of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, but it does not appear to be of such great antiquity. The inscriptions reported by Valesius near the end of book XI of the *Rerum Francicarum* must be attributed to another Hilperic, apparently a prince of royal descent, as may be inferred from the name. For it is certain, even from Gregory himself, that not only kings but also other Frankish princes were customarily buried in that basilica. Chilperic is said to have built it anew, according to the Testament of Bertrannus, bishop of Le Mans, where the same king is called illustrious and “of good memory.” Concerning his death, see the notes on the final chapter of Fredegar, who did not include the remaining books of Gregory in his epitome].

Queen Fredegund remained abandoned in the church [Note: Here the Corbie manuscript ends, except that near the end of book IV, both in that manuscript and in the Beauvais manuscript, a fragment from chapters 7 and 8 of book VII is included. We have copied the words “The book ends,” and so forth, from Corbie].

The sixth book of Georgius Florentius, or Gregory, bishop of Tours, ends. Thanks be to God.

## 327–328. BEGIN THE CHAPTERS OF THE SEVENTH BOOK

[Col. 0413]

1. On the death of Saint Salvius, bishop.  
2. On the conflict between the people of Chartres and the people of Orléans.  
3. On the death of Vedast, surnamed Avo.  
4. That Fredegund took refuge in a church; and concerning the treasures brought to Childebert.  
5. That King Guntchramn came to Paris.  
6. That the same king brought under his control the possessions that had belonged to Charibert’s kingdom.  
7. That Childebert’s ambassadors demanded Fredegund.  
8. That the king appealed to the people not to kill him as they had killed his brothers.  
9. That Rigunthis was detained by Desiderius after her treasures had been taken.  
10. That Gundovald was raised to kingship; and concerning Rigunthis, daughter of King Chilperic.  
11. On the signs that appeared.  
12. On the burning of the territory of Tours, and the power of Saint Martin.  
13. On the burning and plundering of the city of Poitiers.  
14. On Childebert’s ambassadors sent to King Guntchramn.  
15. On Fredegund’s wickedness.  
16. On the return of Bishop Praetextatus.  
17. On Bishop Promotus.  
18. On what was said to the king, that he should make himself cautious lest he be killed.  
19. That the queen was ordered to withdraw to an estate.  
20. That the same woman sent someone to kill Brunichild.  
21. On the flight and custody of Eberulf [Other manuscripts: Berulf].  
22. On his wickedness.  
23. On a Jew killed with his family.  
24. On the plunder of the city of Poitiers.  
25. On the spoils of Marileifus.  
26. That Gundovald traveled around the cities.  
27. On the injury done to Bishop Magnulfus [Other manuscripts: Aginulfus].  
28. That the army approached.  
29. On the death of Eberulf.  
30. On Gundovald’s ambassadors.  
31. On the relics of Saint Sergius the martyr.  
32. On other ambassadors of Gundovald.  
33. That Childebert came to his uncle Guntchramn.  
34. That Gundovald went to Comminges.  
35. On the destruction of the basilica of Saint Vincent, martyr of Agen.  
36. On Gundovald’s conference with the army.  
37. On the battle against the city.  
38. On the death of Gundovald.  
39. On the death of Bishop Sagittarius and Mummolus.  
40. On Mummolus’s treasures.  
41. On a giant.  
42. On the power of Saint Martin.  
43. On Desiderius and Waddo.  
44. On a woman diviner (pythoness).  
45. On the famine of the present year.  
46. On the death of Christopher.  
47. On the civil war among the citizens of Tours.

# BOOK SEVEN

## I.

Although it is my purpose to continue the history where the order of the preceding books left it, devotion nevertheless first demands that something be said about the death of Blessed Salvius, bishop, who is shown to have died in this year [Note: He is commemorated on September 10. Gregory says below, book VIII, chapter 22: “After the death of Saint Salvius, Desideratus was given to the people of Albi as bishop in this year”—namely, 585. It must therefore be said that the see was vacant for at least several months. Some writers say that Theofridus sat between the two].

For, as he himself was accustomed to relate, after spending a long time in secular clothing and handling the worldly affairs of the age together with judges, he nevertheless never became entangled in those desires in which the minds of young men are accustomed to be ensnared.

When the fragrance of divine inspiration had touched the inner depths of his being, he abandoned secular service and sought a monastery. Then, as a man already devoted to God, he understood that it was better to live in poverty with the fear of God than to pursue the profits of the passing world. In that monastery he remained for a long time under the rule established by the fathers.

When he had advanced in strength both of understanding and of age, and the abbot who presided over the monastery had died, he undertook the duty of feeding the flock. But the man who ought, on account of correction, to have made himself more publicly available to the brothers became more withdrawn after assuming the office. Immediately he sought a more secluded cell.

For, as he himself said, in the former cell he had changed the skin of his body more than nine times, being consumed by excessive abstinence. Finally, after receiving the office, while devoting himself more earnestly to prayer and reading in this strict frugality, he often reflected that it would be better for him to remain hidden among the monks than to have taken the name of abbot before the people.

What more is there to say? He enclosed himself, bidding farewell to the brothers, while they also bade farewell to him. In this enclosure he remained in complete abstinence, even more strictly than before. Out of charitable service, he took care that whenever a stranger came he would offer prayer and provide blessings with the fullest measure of grace; these frequently brought complete healing to many sick people.

At one time, exhausted by a severe fever, he lay gasping on his little bed. Suddenly the cell was illuminated by a great light and trembled. Then, stretching his hands toward heaven with thanksgiving, he breathed out his spirit.

The monks, together with his mother, mingling their wailing, removed the body of the deceased, washed it with water, clothed it, placed it upon a bier, and passed the night in psalmody and weeping. When morning came and the funeral rites had been prepared, the body began to move on the bier.

Then, with his cheeks reddening, the man was shaken as though awakened from a deep sleep. Opening his eyes and raising his hands, he said: “O merciful Lord, what have you done to me, that you have permitted me to return to this dark place of worldly dwelling, when your mercy in heaven was better for me than the utterly wretched life of this world?”

His companions were astonished and asked what such a prodigy meant, but he gave no answer to their questions. Rising from the bier and feeling no harm from the illness with which he had suffered, he remained for three days without food or drink.

On the third day, having summoned the monks and his mother, he said: “Listen, dearest ones, and understand: what you see in this world is nothing; rather, as the prophet Solomon sang, ‘All is vanity’ (Ecclesiastes 1:2). Blessed is the one who can live in this world in such a way as to deserve to behold the glory of God in heaven.”

As he said these things, he began to doubt whether he should continue speaking or remain silent. While he was silent, the brothers pressed him with prayers to explain what he had seen. He said:

“When four days ago you saw me lifeless, while the cell trembled, I was seized by two angels and lifted into the heights of the heavens, so that I thought I had beneath my feet not only this squalid world, but also the sun, the moon, the clouds, and the stars.

“Then I was brought through a gate brighter than this light into that dwelling. Its entire pavement was like gleaming gold and silver; the light was ineffable and its vastness indescribable. A multitude of both sexes covered it so completely that the length and breadth of the throng could not be seen.

“When the angels who went before us made a way for us through those pressing around us, we reached a place that we had already been viewing from afar. A cloud brighter than every light hung above it. There the sun, the moon, and the stars could not be seen; rather, above all these things something shone with a splendor brighter than natural light [Note: The older manuscript, the Colbertine manuscript, and Regm. have *splendidus*, ‘splendid,’ rather than the printed reading].

“A voice came forth from the cloud, like the voice of many waters. There men in both priestly and secular clothing humbly greeted me, a sinner. Those who went before me explained that they were martyrs and confessors, whom we honor here with the highest service.

“Standing in the place where I had been ordered to stand, I was covered by an extraordinarily sweet fragrance, so that, refreshed by this sweetness, I still desired no food or drink.

“And I heard a voice saying: ‘Let this man return to the world, because he is necessary to our churches.’ The voice was heard, but the speaker could not be seen at all.

“Prostrate upon the pavement, I said with tears: ‘Alas, alas, Lord! Why have you shown me these things, if I was to be deprived of them? Behold, today you cast me from your presence, so that I must return to the frail world and can never come back here. Please, Lord, do not take your mercy away from me; rather, I beg you to permit me to dwell here, lest I fall there and perish.’

“And the voice that spoke to me said: ‘Go in peace. I am your guardian until I bring you back to this place.’

“Then, abandoned by my companions, I descended weeping and returned here through the gate by which I had entered.”

As he spoke these things, everyone present was astonished. Then the holy man of God again began to say with tears: “Woe to me, for I have dared to reveal such a mystery. Behold, the sweet fragrance that I drew from the holy place, by which I was sustained for these three days without any food or drink, has departed from me.

“My tongue is also covered with severe wounds and so swollen that it seems to fill my entire mouth. I know that it was not pleasing to my Lord God that these secrets should be made public. But you know, Lord, that I did this in simplicity of heart, not in the pride of my mind.

“I beg you to forgive me and not to abandon me, according to your promise.”

Having said this, he fell silent and took food and drink.

As I write these things, I fear that they may seem unbelievable to some reader, in accordance with what Sallustius says when writing history [Note: At the beginning of his book on the Catilinarian War], where he recalls the virtue and glory of good men: “What each person considers easy to do, he accepts calmly; what lies beyond that, he regards as fictitious and counts as false.”

For I call Almighty God to witness that I know I heard everything I have related from the man’s own mouth.

After a long time, this blessed man was taken from his cell and elected to the episcopate; he was ordained against his will. When he had spent, as I believe, his tenth year in that office, a groin disease became severe in the city of Albi, and most of its people had already died. When only a few citizens remained, the blessed man, like a good shepherd, never wished to leave that place. He continually urged those who remained to devote themselves to prayer, to persist earnestly in vigils, and always to occupy themselves with good things, both in their actions and in their thoughts. He said:

“Do these things so that, if God should wish you to depart from this world, you may enter not into judgment but into rest.”

When, as I believe, the Lord had already revealed to him that the time of his calling was near, he prepared his own sarcophagus, washed his body, put on his clothing, and thus breathed out his blessed spirit, always intent upon heaven.

He was a man of great holiness and very little desire for possessions, never wishing to keep gold. If he was compelled to accept it, he immediately distributed it to the poor.

During his time, when the patrician Mummolus had taken many captives from that city, Salvius pursued them all and redeemed them. The Lord granted him such favor with that people that even those who had taken the captives both made concessions to him concerning the price and, beyond that, rewarded him [Note: The older manuscript has “and rewarded him with due honor”]. Thus he restored the captives of his homeland to their former freedom.

I have heard many good things about this man, but as I wish to return to the history I began, I leave many of them aside.

## II.

After Chilperic had died, and the death he had long sought had been found [Note: The words “and the death he had long sought” are absent from Regm.], the people of Orléans, joined by the people of Blois [Note: This is the first mention of the people of Blois among ancient authors, as Valesius notes in his *Notitia*. Like the people of Châteaudun, they belonged to the diocese of Chartres. The people of Châteaudun unsuccessfully attempted to withdraw from it under King Sigibert. Promotus, who had been installed as bishop of Châteaudun by Aegidius, bishop of Reims, was removed from his position, as will be said below in chapter 17. But the people of Blois were more successful in this century: through the agency of Louis the Great, Innocent XII, Roman pontiff, granted them an episcopal see when the diocese of Chartres was divided into two. Accordingly, the first bishop of this see, the most illustrious Lord David Nicolas de Bertier, was consecrated on September 15 of the present year, 1697, in which we are writing], attacked the people of Châteaudun and overthrew them while they were unsuspecting. They committed their houses, stores of grain, and whatever could not easily be moved [Note: Bec. and two Colbertine manuscripts have “could not easily be moved”] to the flames; they plundered the livestock and carried away whatever goods they could lift.

After they departed, the people of Châteaudun joined with the rest of the people of Chartres and pursued them immediately, treating them with the same fate that they themselves had suffered, leaving nothing in the houses, outside the houses, or belonging to the houses.

While they were still raging against one another and stirring up quarrels, and the people of Orléans were brandishing weapons against them, the counts intervened. Peace was granted until the hearing—namely, so that on the day when judgment was to take place, the party that had unjustly risen against the other might settle the matter through justice. Thus the war came to an end.

## III.

Vedast, surnamed Avo [Note: This chapter is absent from Colb. A and Vat. Other manuscripts have *Vedastus*, and Bec., Colb. M, and Regm. have “surnamed Grandfather.” Compare chapter 13 of the preceding book], who a few years earlier had killed Lupus and Ambrosius because of his love for Ambrosius’s wife, and had taken her—she was said to be his cousin—as his wife, was committing many crimes within the territory of Poitiers.

At a certain place he joined Childeric the Saxon. While they were provoking one another with insults, one of Childeric’s servants [Note: Colb. M has “one of Chilperic’s servants”] pierced Avo with a spear. Falling to the ground, and wounded by many additional blows, he poured out his wicked soul as his blood flowed. Thus divine majesty avenged the innocent blood that he himself had shed with his own hand.

The wretched man had often committed many thefts, murders, and adulteries, which I think it better to pass over in silence. That Saxon, however, settled the matter of his death with his sons.

## IV.

Meanwhile Queen Fredegund, now widowed, arrived in Paris and, with the treasures that she had shut up within the enclosure of the walls, took refuge in a church [Note: From this passage Valesius, in chapter 1 of his book *On the Parisian Basilicas*, argues against Launoius that the principal or cathedral church of Paris existed within the city under the first dynasty of our kings. It is indeed certain that Gregory commonly uses the word “church” to designate the cathedral church]. She was protected by Bishop Ragnemod.

The remaining treasures, which had been left at the estate of Celles, including the golden serving dish that he had recently made (book VI, chapter 2), were taken up by the treasurers and carried swiftly to King Childebert, who was then staying in the city of Meaux [Note: Bec. has “at Meldes”].

## V.

Queen Fredegund, having taken counsel, sent ambassadors to King Guntchramn, saying:

“Let my lord come and receive the kingdom of his brother. I have a little child, whom I desire to place in his arms, and I humble myself before his authority.”

When King Guntchramn learned of his brother’s death, he wept most bitterly. After moderating his lamentation, he mobilized his army and headed for Paris. When he had been received within the walls, his nephew King Childebert arrived from another direction.

## VI.

But when the people of Paris refused to receive him, he sent ambassadors to King Guntchramn, saying:

“I know, most merciful father, that your piety is not unaware of how, until the present time, an enemy faction has oppressed us both, so that no one can obtain justice concerning what is owed to him. Therefore I now humbly beg that the agreements made between us after my father’s death be observed.”

Then King Guntchramn said to his ambassadors:

“O wretched and ever-faithless men, who possess nothing true within you and do not remain faithful to your promises! Behold, abandoning everything you had promised me, you drew up a new pact with King Chilperic, so that, after driving me from the kingdom, you might divide my cities among yourselves.

“Here are the agreements themselves; here are your own signatures by which you confirmed this conspiracy [Note: Compare chapter 3 of book VI, where the plan to drive out Guntchramn was discussed. At that time he had the agreements in his possession, taken from Chilperic’s archives]. And with what face do you now ask me to receive my nephew Childebert, whom by your perversity you wished to make my enemy?”

The ambassadors said to him:

“If anger has seized your mind so completely that you will grant your nephew none of what you promised, at least cease taking away what is owed from the kingdom of Charibert.”

He replied:

“Here are the agreements made between us: whoever entered the city of Paris without his brother’s consent would lose his share, and the martyr Polyeuctus [Note: He had been chosen above the others because he was renowned for punishing perjurers, as Gregory himself testifies in book I of *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 103], together with the confessors Hilary and Martin, would be his judge and avenger.

“After this, my brother Sigibert entered it, and, dying by God’s judgment, lost his share. Chilperic acted likewise. Through these transgressions they lost their shares. Therefore, because they perished according to God’s judgment and the curses of the agreements, I shall, with the law assisting me, bring the whole kingdom of Charibert, together with his treasures, under my authority. From then on I shall grant nothing to anyone except according to my own will.

“Withdraw, then, you ever-lying and faithless men, and report these words to your king.”

## VII.

After they departed, Childebert’s ambassadors came again to the king mentioned above, demanding Queen Fredegund and saying:

“Hand over the murderess who attacked my aunt, who killed my father and my uncle, and who also slew my cousins with the sword” [Note: Fredegund was accused of having ordered the strangling of Galswintha, Childebert’s maternal aunt, and of having arranged the deaths of Sigibert, his father; Chilperic, his uncle; and Chlodoveus and Meroveus, his cousins].

But he replied: “In the hearing that we are to hold, we shall decide everything, considering what ought to be done.”

For he was protecting Fredegund under his patronage. He often invited her to dinner and promised to become her greatest defender [Note: Chesn. and Colb. A, in another hand, have “he promised that he would become her greatest…”; Regm. has “that he would become her greatest…”].

One day, while they were dining together, the queen rose and took her leave, but the king detained her, saying: “Take a little more food.”

She replied: “Forgive me, my lord, I beg you. In accordance with women’s custom, it has happened to me that I must rise because I am pregnant.”

When he heard this, he was astonished, knowing that it was only the fourth month since she had given birth to another son. Nevertheless, he allowed her to rise.

The leading men of Chilperic’s kingdom, including Ansoualdus and the others, gathered around his son, who, as we said above, was four months old. They called him Chlotharius [Note: He had the same name as his uncle. We have written the earlier one as *Chlothacharius* from the oldest manuscripts; the manuscripts of our text commonly call this one *Chlotarius*, *Chlottharius*, or *Hlotharius*, forms that we follow].

They demanded oaths throughout the cities that had previously belonged to Chilperic, requiring that the people remain faithful to King Guntchramn and to his nephew Chlotharius.

King Guntchramn restored, through the intervention of justice, everything that the faithful men of King Chilperic had unjustly taken from various people. He also gave much to the churches and restored the wills of the deceased who had appointed churches as their heirs but whose wills had been suppressed by Chilperic. He showed himself kind to many and gave much to the poor [Note: The Colbertine manuscript, in another hand, has “and to all”; Regm. has “and in many things”].

## VIII.

Because he was not trusted by the people among whom he had come [Note: Thus Corbie, Beauvais, Bec., and Colb. A; the other manuscripts have “by everyone”], he armed himself. He never went to a church or to any other place he wished to visit without a large guard.

It happened, therefore, that one Sunday, after the deacon had ordered silence so that the people might listen to the Mass, the king turned to the assembled crowd and said:

“I adjure you, men and women who are present, to deign to keep faith with me inviolate, and not to kill me as you recently killed my brothers. Allow me at least three years [Note: After three years Childebert would have reached eighteen years of age and would consequently have been able to protect both himself and the little Chlotharius] to raise my nephews, who have become my adopted sons. Otherwise it may happen—may eternal divinity not permit it—that, when I am dead, you perish together with these little children, since there will be no strong man left from our family to defend you.”

When he had said this, the entire people offered a prayer to the Lord for the king.

### IX

While these things were taking place, Rigunthis, daughter of King Chilperic, proceeded as far as Toulouse with the treasures mentioned above. Seeing that she was now close to the territory of the Goths, she began to delay, since her attendants were also telling her that she ought to remain there: exhausted as they were from the journey, they had unkempt clothing, torn footwear, and the equipment of the horses and wagons was still scattered separately, just as it had been when they were transported in carts. All these things, they said, ought first to be carefully put in order, and only then should she proceed on the journey and be received by her bridegroom with every mark of elegance; for fear that, if they appeared unkempt among the Goths, they might be mocked by them.

While she was therefore being delayed for these reasons, news of the death of King Chilperic reached Duke Desiderius. He too gathered the bravest men around him, entered the city of Toulouse, seized the treasures he found from the power of the queen (Rigunthis), and confined them in a certain house under the protection of seals and the guard of brave men, assigning the queen a meager allowance until he should return to the city.

### X

He himself, however, hurried to Mummolus, with whom he had made a treaty two years earlier. At that time Mummolus was staying within the walls of the city of Avignon with Gundovald, whom we mentioned in the preceding book (chapter 24). Gundovald, joining the aforementioned dukes and proceeding to Limoges, arrived at the village of Briva Curretia [Col. 0421D], where Saint Martin, said to have been a disciple of our Martin, rests.

**[Note: [Col. 0421D]** That village was so called from the bridge built over the river Curretia. *Briva* means “bridge” in the ancient Gallic language. It is now a fairly elegant town in Limousin, called Briva Hilaris, commonly Brive-la-Gaillarde, near the confluence of the Curretia, the Corrèze, and the Visera, the Vézère, in the present-day diocese of Tulle. Martin, whom Gregory praises here, is commemorated among the people of Limoges on 18 September. **[Col. 0422C]**]

There he was raised upon a shield as king. But when they had gone around with him for the third time, he is said to have fallen, so that he could scarcely be supported by the hands of those standing nearby. Then he proceeded through the surrounding cities.

Meanwhile Rigunthis was staying in the basilica of Saint Mary at Toulouse, to which the wife of Ragnovald, whom we mentioned above [Col. 0422B], had fled in fear of Chilperic.

**[Note: [Col. 0422C]** She is said in the preceding book, chapter 12, to have taken refuge in the basilica of Saint Saturninus. Perhaps, after spending some time in the basilica of Saint Saturninus, she had moved to Saint Mary. The basilica of Saint Mary praised here is still famous under the title of Blessed Mary of the Gilded, commonly Notre-Dame de la Daurade. It belongs to the Benedictine Order and the congregation of Saint Maurus, and there remain there relics of a very ancient image of Blessed Mary in mosaic work, from which the place takes its name. Some think that the title “of the Gilded” was not given to the basilica of Saint Mary until relatively recently, but only from the time when another church was built at Toulouse in honor of Blessed Mary, which was called the Whitened Church, Notre-Dame de la Dalbade. To distinguish it from that church, the old basilica of Blessed Mary began to bear the name “of the Gilded,” on account of the mosaic or tessellated work representing various images of the saints with which the walls of this church were covered. **[Col. 0422B]**

Ragnovald, returning from Spain, was restored to his wife and property. He had gone to Spain on an embassy, sent by King Guntram.

At that time, the basilica of the blessed Martin at the village of Briva was burned in a great fire by an approaching enemy, so that both the altars and the columns, which had been constructed from various kinds of marble, were destroyed by the fire. But afterward the church was repaired by Bishop Ferreolus [Col. 0422D], as though it had suffered no harm.

**[Note: [Col. 0422D]** This bishop was Ferreolus of Limoges, mentioned above in Book V, chapter 29. He took part in the Second Council of Mâcon in 585. He buried Saint Aredius, as is related in his Life. **[Col. 0422D]**]

For the inhabitants greatly admire and venerate this saint, because they frequently experience his miracles.

### XI

For when these things were taking place, it was the tenth month [339]. Then new shoots with misshapen grapes appeared on the trunks of the vines, and flowers appeared on the trees. A great fiery torch moved across the sky and illuminated the world over a wide area before daylight came. Rays also appeared in the sky. On the northern side, a fiery column, as if hanging from heaven, was seen for the space of two hours, and a great star was set above it. At Angers the earth trembled, and many other signs appeared which, in my opinion, foretold the destruction of Gundovald himself.

### XII

King Guntram therefore sent his counts to seize the cities that Sigibert had once received from the kingdom of his brother Charibert [Col. 0423A], so that, after exacting oaths of allegiance, they might subject them to his authority.

The people of Tours and Poitiers, however, wished to transfer their allegiance to Childebert, the son of Sigibert. But the people of Bourges, aroused against them, prepared to march against them and began setting fires within the territory of Tours.

Then they burned the church of Maroialum [Col. 0423D], in the territory of Tours, where relics of Saint Martin were kept.

**[Note: [Col. 0423D]** Maroialum is a village adjoining the bank of the Cher, on the boundary of the territories of Tours, Bourges, and Blois. It is now commonly called Mareuil-sur-Cher. The church of this village is still dedicated to Saint Martin and, besides being the parish church, is adorned with a Benedictine priory dependent on the abbey of Villeloin, as Marollius notes. **[Col. 0423D]**]

But the power of the blessed man was present, so that in so great a fire the small cloths that had been placed upon the altar were not consumed by the flames. Not only they, but also little herbs previously gathered and placed on the altar, were not burned at all.

**[Note: [Col. 0423D]** The faithful used to collect such little herbs after they had been placed for some time on altars or the tombs of saints, for the treatment of illnesses. **[Col. 0423D]**]

When the people of Tours saw these fires, they sent an embassy, saying that it was better for them to submit for a time to King Guntram than for everything to be devastated by fire or sword.

### XIII

Immediately after Chilperic’s death, Duke Gararic had come to Limoges and received oaths in the name of Childebert. From there he came to Poitiers, where the inhabitants received him, and he remained there.

When he heard what the people of Tours were suffering, he sent an embassy, urging them that, if they wished to act prudently, they should not surrender themselves to the side of King Guntram, but should rather remember Sigibert, who had once been the father of Childebert [340].

We, however, sent the bishop and citizens this reply: unless they submitted for a time to King Guntram, they would suffer the same things. We asserted that Guntram was now a father over two sons, namely Sigibert and Chilperic, who had been adopted by him, and that he held the chief power of the kingdom just as King Chlothar, his father, had once done.

When they still did not agree, Gararic left the city, as though he were going to bring an army, but left Eberon, Childebert’s chamberlain, in the city.

Sicharius, however, together with Willacharius, count of Orléans, who had recently received Tours [Col. 0423D], mobilized an army against Poitiers, so that the people of Tours on one side and those of Bourges on the other, once aroused, might devastate everything.

**[Note: [Col. 0423D]** Codex Reginensis has *Willichario*; Colbertinus a has *Willario*. **[Col. 0423D]**]

**[Note: [Col. 0423D]** Another hand in Colbertinus a has: “who was staying at Tours.” **[Col. 0423D]**]

When they had drawn near the boundary and begun to burn houses, the people of Poitiers sent envoys to them, saying:

“We ask you to hold back until the settlement which Kings Guntram and Childebert are to make between themselves. If it is agreed that good King Guntram will receive these districts [Col. 0423D], we do not resist; if not, we acknowledge our lord, whom we ought to serve more fully.”

**[Note: [Col. 0423D]** The manuscripts vary considerably. Colbertinus a, Reginensis, Chesnensis, and Freherus have: “that the good king may receive these districts.” Colbertinus m, Beccensis, and Illyricus have: “that the good king of peace may receive these districts.” Coloniensis and Bignonius have: “that the king may receive these districts as a sign of peace” [Col. 0424D]. Badianus has: “that the king may receive us peacefully.” **[Col. 0423D]**]

They replied: “This matter does not concern us at all [Col. 0424D], except that we must carry out the commands of our prince. For if you refuse, we shall devastate everything as we have begun.”

**[Note: [Col. 0424D]** Others have, “It does not concern you”; Beccensis, “It does not concern us.” **[Col. 0424D]**]

While the matter was thus proceeding toward the surrender of everything to fire, plunder, and captivity, the people of Childebert were expelled from the city and gave their oath to King Guntram, though they did not keep it for long.

### XIV

When the appointed settlement arrived, King Childebert sent Bishop Egidius, Guntram Boso, Sigivald, and many others to King Guntram. When they had entered his presence, the bishop said:

“We give thanks to almighty God, most merciful king, that after so many labors he has restored you to your territories and your kingdom.”

The king replied:

“Thanks ought to be given to him who is King of kings and Lord of lords, who in his mercy has deigned to bring these things about—not to you, whose treacherous counsel and perjuries caused my territories to be burned in the preceding year; you, who have never kept complete faith with anyone, whose treachery is spread everywhere, and who show that you are not a priest but an enemy of our kingdom.”

At these words the bishop, moved to anger, fell silent.

One of the envoys said: “Your grandson Childebert begs you to order that the cities which his father held be restored.”

He replied: “I already told you earlier that our agreements confer these things upon me; therefore I do not wish to restore them.”

Another of the envoys said: “Your grandson asks you to order that the sorceress Fredegund, through whom many kings have been killed, be handed over, so that he may avenge the death of his father, uncle, and cousins.”

He said: “She cannot be handed over to his power, because she has a son who is king. Nor do I believe that the things you assert against her are true.”

After this, Guntram Boso approached the king, as though he intended to make some proposal. Since it had become publicly known that Gundovald had been raised up as king, the king anticipated his words and said:

“O enemy of our territory and kingdom, who years ago attacked the East for this reason: to bring a certain Ballomer [Col. 0424D]—that is what the king called Gundovald—against our kingdom. You are always treacherous and never keep what you promise.”

**[Note: [Col. 0424D]** That is, a false lord or pseudo-prince. **[Col. 0424D]**]

He replied: “You, lord and king, sit upon the royal throne, and no one dares answer you concerning what you say. I declare myself innocent in this matter. But if there is someone like me who secretly brings this charge against me, let him come forward now and speak openly.

“You, most merciful king, committing this to God’s judgment [Col. 0424D], let him decide when he sees us fighting on the level ground of a single field.”

**[Note: [Col. 0424D]** Beccensis has: “Then, O king, [I commit it] to judgment.” Another hand in Colbertinus a has: “I, O king, will commit this,” and so on. Below, the same hand has inserted *faithful men of this kingdom* in place of *hearts*. For a long time that wicked custom persisted of settling doubtful lawsuits by single combat; it frequently applied even to disputes concerning ecclesiastical property. See Ansegisus, *Collection*, Book IV, chapter 23. The Church never approved such combats, although they were often carried out by public authority. Moreover, every form of judicial combat has now been suppressed by the edicts of Louis the Great and completely abolished in Gaul. **[Col. 0424D]**]

When everyone was silent, the king added:

“Everyone ought to be stirred by this matter to drive from our borders a foreigner whose father managed mills; and, to speak plainly, his father sat among combs and arranged wool.”

Although it could happen that one man was skilled in both crafts, one of the envoys nevertheless replied to rebuke the king:

“Then, as you claim, this man had two fathers here, both a wool-worker and a miller. Far be it from you, O king, to speak so crudely. For it has never been heard that one man could have two parents at the same time, apart from a spiritual relationship.”

**[Note: [Col. 0425D]** Namely, one natural father and another spiritual father in baptism. **[Col. 0425D]**]

Then, when many burst out laughing, another of the envoys replied:

“We bid you farewell, O king. Since you refused to restore the cities of your grandson, we know that the axe fixed above the heads of your brothers is safe; it will more swiftly swing down upon your brain.””

And so they departed amid scandal.

Then the king, inflamed by these words, ordered horse dung, rotten sticks, straw, and hay dissolved by decay, together with the foul mud of the city, to be thrown over the heads of those departing. Covered with these things, they went away only after suffering immense insult and abuse.

### XV

While Queen Fredegund was staying in the church at Paris, Leonard, a member of the household who had then arrived from Toulouse, entered her presence and began to relate the insults and injuries suffered by her daughter, saying:

“Since I went with Queen Rigunthis at your command, I saw her humiliation and how she was stripped of her treasures and all her possessions. I myself escaped by flight and have come to report to my lady what happened.”

When she heard this, she was moved by fury and ordered him to be stripped in the church itself. She commanded him to leave her presence naked, without the clothing and belt that he had received as a gift from King Chilperic.

She also had the cooks, bakers, and anyone else whom she discovered had returned from this journey beaten, stripped, and mutilated.

She attempted to overwhelm Nectarius, the brother of Bishop Baudegisil [Col. 0425D], with wicked accusations before the king, asserting that he had carried away much of the dead king’s treasure.
