**[Note: [Col. 0425D]** This was Baudegisil, bishop of Le Mans, mentioned above in Book VI, chapter 9. Nectarius, a distinguished man, is mentioned in the *Miracles of Saint Aredius*. **[Col. 0425D]**]

She also said that he had taken away much leather and wine from the storerooms, and asked that he be thrown bound into the darkness of prison. But the king’s patience and his brother’s assistance prevented this from happening.

While carrying out many empty acts there, she did not fear God, in whose church she was seeking help.

At that time she had with her Judge Audo, who, during the king’s reign, had agreed with her in many evil deeds. For he, together with the prefect Mummolus, had subjected many Franks who in the time of the elder King Childebert had been free men of noble birth to a public tax.

After the king’s death, those men stripped and denuded him, so that nothing remained to him except what he was able to carry upon himself. They burned his houses; indeed, they would have taken his life as well, had he not sought refuge in the church with the queen.

### XVI

She received Bishop Praetextatus reluctantly. After the king’s death, the citizens of Rouen had sought him from exile and restored him to his city with great joy and praise.

After his return, he came to the city of Paris and presented himself to King Guntram, begging him to investigate his case carefully.

The queen maintained that he ought not to be received, since by the judgment of forty-five bishops he had been removed from priestly office [Col. 0426B].

**[Note: [Col. 0425D]** See above, Book V, chapter 19, concerning the Council of Paris convened for this reason. There Praetextatus had not actually been removed from the priesthood, because our Gregory of Tours resisted; but when Melanius had been substituted in his place through the faction of certain men, Fredegund said that he had been deprived of the priesthood. It had always been forbidden by the canons for two bishops to preside simultaneously over the same church. **[Col. 0425D]**]

When the king wished to convene a synod on this matter, Ragnemodus, bishop of that city, answered on behalf of all, saying:

“Know that the priests imposed penance upon him, but did not remove him entirely from the episcopate.”

Thus he was received by the king, admitted to his banquet, and returned to his city.

### XVII

Promotus, who had been appointed bishop at the fortress of Dunum by order of King Sigibert, and had been removed after the king’s death because that fortress belonged to the diocese of Chartres, had been subjected to a judgment requiring him to perform only the office of a priest [Col. 0426B].

**[Note: [Col. 0426D]** This chapter is absent from Reginensis. Dunum is the fortress commonly called Châteaudun, a town on the river Lidericus, the Loir. Aventinus, brother of Saint Solemnis, is said to have lived there for some time before Promotus; both were bishops of Chartres. See the Bollandists under 4 February. **[Col. 0426D]**]

**[Note: [Col. 0426D]** This occurred at the Council of Paris held in 573. Letters concerning the matter to King Sigibert and to Aegidius, metropolitan bishop of Reims, who had laid hands on Promotus, are preserved. **[Col. 0426D]**]

He came to the king, asking that he receive the episcopal ordination at the aforementioned fortress.

But Bishop Pappolus of Chartres opposed him, saying, “It belongs to my diocese,” and especially pointing to the judgment of the bishops. He could obtain nothing else from the king except permission to receive the property he possessed within the boundaries of that fortress, where he continued to live with his mother, who was still alive [344].

**[Note: [Col. 0426D]** Nevertheless, in the following year he subscribed the Second Council of Mâcon together with bishops who had no see. **[Col. 0426D]**]

### XVIII

While the king was staying at the city of Paris, a certain poor man came and said:

“Listen, O king, to the words of my mouth. Know that Faraulf, formerly the chamberlain of your brother, is seeking to kill you. For I heard his plan: when you went to the church for morning prayer, he would attack you either with a knife or pierce you with a spear.”

The king was astonished and sent for him. When Faraulf denied it, the king, fearing the matter, strongly armed himself. He did not go even to holy places, or anywhere else, except surrounded by armed men and guards.

Faraulf died not long afterward.

### XIX

When a great outcry arose against those who had been powerful with King Chilperic—namely, that they had taken estates or other possessions belonging to others—the king ordered everything that had been unjustly taken to be restored, as has already been indicated above (chapter 7).

He also ordered Queen Fredegund to depart for the estate of Rhotoialum [Col. 0427D], situated in the territory of Rouen. All the older and more distinguished women of King Chilperic’s kingdom followed her.

**[Note: [Col. 0427D]** Reginensis has: “The older and more distinguished women all followed her,” and so forth. **[Col. 0427D]**]

There they left her with Bishop Melanius [Col. 0427D], who had been removed from Rouen, and went over to her son, promising that he would be carefully raised by them.

**[Note: [Col. 0427D]** Melanius had been substituted for Praetextatus when the latter was sent into exile. **[Col. 0427D]**]

**[Note: [Col. 0427D]** Rhotoialum was a village not far from the confluence of the Autura and the Seine, commonly called Rueil or Rueuil. Its name is omitted by Colbertinus m and Reginensis. Beccensis has *Rethojalensim*. **[Col. 0427D]**]

### XX

After Queen Fredegund had gone to the estate mentioned above, she was very sad because her power had been diminished in part. Thinking that Brunichild had received a better lot than she had [Col. 0427D], she secretly sent a cleric close to her, who might kill Brunichild after deceiving her by trickery: he was to insinuate himself subtly into her service, win her confidence, and then strike her secretly.

**[Note: [Col. 0427D]** This is the reading of the two Colbertine manuscripts and Beccensis. That is, she thought that Brunichild had received a better fortune than she had, as Valesius observed, although in Colbertinus m a second hand corrupted the reading by restoring the form found in printed editions: “thinking himself better than Brunichild.” **[Col. 0427D]**]

The cleric came and commended himself to her by various devices, saying:

“I am fleeing from the presence of Queen Fredegund and asking your help.”

He also began to make himself humble, agreeable, obedient to everyone, and the queen’s intimate.

But after a short time they realized that he had been sent deceitfully. After being bound and beaten, he revealed the hidden matter and was permitted to return to his patroness. When he explained what had happened and declared that he had been unable to carry out the orders, he was punished by the amputation of his hands and feet.

### XXI

After these events, when King Guntram had returned from Chalon and was attempting to investigate his brother’s death, the queen accused Eberulf the chamberlain [Col. 0428D]. She had asked him to remain with her after the king’s death, but had been unable to obtain this.

As this hostility grew, she asserted that the king had been killed by Eberulf himself, that he had taken much of the treasure, and that he had then fled to Tours [alternative: crossed over]. Therefore, if the king wished to avenge his brother’s death, he should know that Eberulf was the leader of this crime.

**[Note: [Col. 0428D]** The manuscripts, except Beccensis, have *Berulfus* in the chapter index. Chamberlains sat with the other nobles of the palace in royal assemblies, as is clear from Book I of Marculfus, formula 25. Others call them household officials. **[Col. 0428D]**]

Then the king swore to all the nobles that he would destroy not only Eberulf himself but also his offspring to the ninth generation, so that by their deaths this wicked custom might be removed and kings might no longer be killed.

When Eberulf learned this, he sought the basilica of Saint Martin, whose property he had often invaded.

Then, under the pretext of guarding it, the people of Orléans and Blois came in turn for these watches. After fifteen days had passed, they returned with much booty, bringing pack animals, cattle, and whatever they had been able to seize.

Those who had driven away the animals of Saint Martin, however, became involved in a quarrel and pierced one another with spears.

Two men who were stealing mules approached the house of a neighbor and began asking for a drink. When he denied having any, they raised their spears to pierce him. But he drew his sword and pierced both of them; they both fell and died. The animals of Saint Martin, however, were restored.

So many evils were then committed there by these men of Orléans that they cannot be described.

### XXII

While these things were taking place, Eberulf’s possessions were distributed among various people. His gold, silver, and other valuable goods, which he had kept with him, were displayed publicly [Col. 0428D].

**[Note: [Col. 0428D]** Colbertinus a, in a second hand, has this reading. The others have: “he displayed them.” Below, *entrusted* means “deposited with others.” **[Col. 0428D]**]

Whatever he had entrusted to others was confiscated [Col. 0428B]. Herds of horses, pigs, and pack animals were also plundered.

His house within the walls, which he had taken from the control of the church, was filled with grain, wine, hides, and many other things; it was completely stripped, and nothing remained there except bare walls.

For this reason he regarded us with particular suspicion—we who faithfully attended to his affairs—often promising that, if he ever regained the king’s favor, he would avenge upon us the sufferings he had endured.

God knows, to whom the secrets of the heart are revealed, that with a pure heart, insofar as we could, we offered him consolation. Although he had previously laid many snares for us concerning the property of Saint Martin, there was nevertheless a reason for me to forget these things: I had taken his son from the sacred font.

But, I believe, that matter was a great obstacle to the unhappy man, because he showed no reverence toward the holy bishop. For he often committed killings within the very courtyard that stands at the feet of the blessed man, constantly engaging in drunkenness and frivolity.

When he saw a certain presbyter already drunk, because the man had delayed giving him wine, he beat him with his fists and various blows, smashing him against a bench, so that he seemed almost to give up his life. He would perhaps have died if medical cupping devices had not come to his aid.

**[Note: [Col. 0428D]** Two Colbertine manuscripts have *solatia*, “remedies.” **[Col. 0428D]**]

Because he feared the king, he had a dwelling in the very *salutatorium* [Col. 0428D] of the blessed basilica.

**[Note: [Col. 0428D]** Colbertinus m has *salutario*, and below *salutarii*; Casinensis has *sacrario* and *sacrarii*. The word *salutatorium* should be retained; see the note above on Book II, chapter 21. **[Col. 0428D]**]

When the presbyter who held the keys of the doorway had locked the other doors and withdrawn, girls entered through the door of the *salutatorium* with his other children. They gazed at the paintings on the walls and examined the ornaments of the blessed tomb. This was highly criminal in the eyes of religious people.

When the presbyter learned of it, he drove the keys into the door and fitted bars on the inside.

When Eberulf noticed this after dinner, drenched in wine, and we were singing psalms in the basilica at the beginning of the night for the sake of prayer, he entered in a fury and began to assail me with insults and curses. Amid his abuse he reproached me for wanting to separate him from the fringes of the holy bishop.

Amazed at the madness that had seized the man, I tried to soothe him with gentle speech. But when I could not overcome his fury with mild words, I decided to remain silent.

Seeing me silent, he turned to the presbyter [Col. 0429D] and poured out many insults against him. He attacked that man with insolent words and me with various reproaches.

**[Note: [Col. 0429D]** Beccensis has *presbyterium*, by which all the presbyters present would be designated; but our reading is better. **[Col. 0429D]**]

When we saw that he was, so to speak, being driven by a demon, we left the holy basilica and brought the scandal and the vigil to an end. We regarded it as especially disgraceful that he had begun this quarrel without reverence for the saint, before the very tomb of the bishop.

During those days I had a dream, which I related to him in the holy basilica. I said:

“I thought that I was celebrating the solemn rites of the Mass in this sacred basilica. When the altar, with the offerings, had already been covered by a silk cloth, suddenly I saw King Guntram entering. In a loud voice he was crying:

‘Drag out the enemy of our race; tear the murderer away from God’s sacred altar.’

“When I heard this, I turned to you and said:

‘Seize the altar cloth, unhappy man, with which the sacred gifts are covered, lest you be thrown out from here.’

“When you seized it, you relaxed your hand and did not hold it manfully. I, however, stretched out my hands and pressed my chest against the king’s chest, saying:

‘Do not drive this man from the holy basilica, lest you suffer danger to your life; lest the holy bishop pierce you with his power. Do not kill yourself with your own spear, because if you do this, you will be deprived of both the present life and the eternal one.’

“But when the king resisted me, you loosened your hold on the cloth and came after me. I was very troublesome to you. When you returned to the altar, you seized the cloth but again let it go.

“While you held it half-heartedly and I resisted the king manfully, I awoke terrified with fear, not knowing what the dream meant.”

After I had told him these things, he said:

“The dream you saw is true, and it agrees very closely with my own thought.”

I asked him: “What did your thought foresee?”

He replied:

“I had decided that, if the king ordered me to be dragged from this place, I would hold the altar cloth with one hand, and with the other, after drawing my sword and first killing you, I would strike down in death as many clerics as I found afterward.

“Nor would it have been an injury to me to succumb to death after taking vengeance upon the clerics of this saint.”

When I heard this, I was astonished and marveled at what had happened, because the devil was speaking through his mouth. He had never possessed any fear of God.

For while he was at liberty, his horses and cattle were released into the fields and vineyards of the poor. If those whose labors they were destroying drove them away, Eberulf’s men immediately beat them.

In the distress in which he now found himself, he often recalled that he had unjustly taken the property of the holy bishop.

Finally, in the preceding year, he caused a certain lowly man named Commotus to summon the agents of the church [Col. 0429D].

**[Note: [Col. 0429D]** Alteserra thinks that *Commotus* was the man’s proper name. **[Col. 0430D]**]

Then, setting justice aside, he took away properties formerly possessed by the church under the pretext of a purchase, giving that man part of his golden belt.

But he committed many other such perverse deeds until the end of his life, which we shall explain later.

**[Note: [Col. 0430D]** Most printed editions have *quae in*. See chapter 29. **[Col. 0430D]**]

### XXIII

In this same year [Col. 0430D], the Jew Armentarius came to Tours with one fellow adherent of his sect and two Christians, to collect bonds that Injuriosus, as deputy-governor, and Eunomius, as count, had deposited with him for public taxes.

**[Note: [Col. 0430D]** This chapter is absent from Colbertinus a and Vaticanus. **[Col. 0430D]**]

After summoning the men, he received a promise that the money would be repaid with interest. They also said to him:

“If you come to our house, we will pay what is owed and honor you with other gifts, as is fitting.”

When he went there, Injuriosus received him and placed him at a banquet. When the meal was over and night was approaching, they moved from that place to another.

Then, as they say, the Jews and the two Christians were killed by Injuriosus’s men and thrown into a well near his house.

When their relatives heard what had happened, they came to Tours. After informing certain men, they discovered the well and pulled out the bodies, while Injuriosus strongly denied that he had been implicated in the matter.

Afterward he came to court. But since, as we said, he denied the charge vigorously [Col. 0430D], and they had no means by which they could convict him, it was judged that he should clear himself by oath.

**[Note: [Col. 0430D]** See Marculfus, Book I, formula 38. **[Col. 0430D]**]

When they did not agree even to this, they brought the case before King Childebert’s assembly.

Nevertheless, neither the money nor the bonds of the dead Jew were found.

Many people were then saying that the tribune Medardus [Col. 0430D] had been involved in this crime, because he too had borrowed money from the Jew.

**[Note: [Col. 0430D]** That is, a collector of taxes, as Alteserra interprets it. **[Col. 0430D]**]

Injuriosus nevertheless came to the assembly in the presence of King Childebert and observed the proceedings for three days, until sunset.

**[Note: [Col. 0430D]** It was customary for assemblies to end at sunset; Bignonius observes that this was also customary among other peoples in Book I of Marculfus, formula 37. Concerning the assembly, *les plaids* or assizes, see Du Cange’s *Glossary*, and the note above on Book VI, chapter 34. **[Col. 0430D]**]

But when the others did not come and no one summoned him concerning the case, he returned home.

### XXIV

In the tenth year of King Childebert, King Guntram therefore mobilized the peoples of his kingdom and assembled a great army.

But the greater part, together with the people of Orléans and Bourges, marched against Poitiers, for they had departed from the allegiance they had promised the king.

They first sent an embassy to learn whether the people of Poitiers would receive them or not. But Maroveus, the bishop of the place, received the envoys harshly.

**[Note: [Col. 0431D]** Reginensis has *Meroveus*. **[Col. 0431D]**]

They entered the territory and committed plunder, arson, and murder.

Those who returned with booty, passing through the territory of Tours, did the same to those who had already given their oaths, so that even the churches were burned and whatever they could find was plundered. This happened repeatedly while the people of Tours were reluctant to return to the king.

But when the army drew nearer to the city, and they saw that most of the region had already been devastated, they sent messengers, declaring that they were faithful to King Guntram.

When they were received within the walls of the city, they attacked the bishop, saying that he was unfaithful.

When he saw himself being hard pressed by them, he broke up one of the golden chalices used in the sacred ministry and reduced it to coins, thereby ransoming himself and the people.

**[Note: [Col. 0431D]** Examples of this are praised in Book I of *Gallican Liturgy*, chapter 7. **[Col. 0431D]**]

### XXV

They attacked Marileifus with the greatest ferocity. He had formerly been regarded as the chief of the physicians in King Chilperic’s household and had already been thoroughly stripped by Duke Gararic. Now these men stripped him again, so that no property remained to him.

They also took away his horses, gold and silver, and the valuable goods he possessed, and subjected him himself to ecclesiastical authority.

His father’s service had been of such a kind that he devoted himself to the church’s mills, while his brothers, cousins, and other relatives were subject to the lord’s kitchens and bakery.

**[Note: [Col. 0431D]** Casinensis and Reginensis have *colonis*, “tenant farmers”; Colbertinus m has *colinis*. **[Col. 0431D]**]

### XXVI

Gundovald wished to approach Poitiers [Col. 0431C], but he was afraid. For he had already heard that an army was being mobilized against him.

In the cities that had belonged to King Sigibert, he received oaths in the name of King Childebert. In the others, which had belonged either to Guntram or to Chilperic, the people swore in his own name that they would keep faith.

After this he came to Angoulême. Having received oaths and presented gifts to the leading men, he attacked Périgueux and seriously maltreated the bishop because the latter had not received him.

**[Note: [Col. 0431D]** This was Carterius, mentioned above in Book VI, chapter 22. In that same year he subscribed the Second Council of Mâcon, as did Nicasius of Angoulême. **[Col. 0431D]**]

### XXVII

From there he departed for Toulouse and sent messengers to Magnulfus [Note: Colb. a. has *Maginulfum*; Colb. m. and Regm. have *Manulfum*. In the table of contents in the manuscripts he is called Aginulfus. Magnulfus is named in the Council of Mâcon, to which he subscribed through a legate.] 351, the city’s bishop, asking to be received by him. But the bishop, not forgetting the earlier injury that he had suffered at the hands of Sigulfus [Note: Is this the Sigulfus who, standing on behalf of Sigibert shortly before the latter was killed, expelled Chlodoveus, Chilperic’s son, from Bordeaux and pursued him as he fled, as Gregory relates in Book IV, chapter 48, or, in other editions, 42? A duke Sigulfus is mentioned below in Book VIII, chapter 18, but he is a different man if events are being narrated in their proper chronological order.], who had once tried to raise himself to the kingship, said to his fellow citizens:

“We know that Guntchramn is king, and his nephew Childebert; but as for this man, we do not know where he comes from. Therefore be ready, and if Duke Desiderius wishes to bring this calamity upon us, let him perish by a fate like Sigulfus’s, so that all may have an example and no foreigner dare violate the kingdom of the Franks.”

While they resisted him in this way and prepared for war, Gundovald arrived with a large army. When they saw that they could not withstand him, they received him.

Afterward, while the bishop was seated at a banquet in the episcopal house together with Gundovald, he said:

“You claim to be the son of King Chlothacharius, but we do not know whether this is true or not. And if you are able to vindicate the undertaking you have begun, it is regarded in our minds as incredible.”

He replied:

“I am the son of King Chlothacharius. At present I am about to receive a portion of the kingdom, and I shall hasten to Paris and establish the royal seat there.”

The bishop said to him:

“Is it true, then, that no one of the Frankish line remains, if you fulfill what you say?”

During this dispute, when Mummolus heard what was being said, he raised his hand and struck the bishop in the face, saying:

“Are you not ashamed to answer so great a king in such a degenerate and foolish manner?”

But when Desiderius learned from the bishop’s counsel what had been said, he was moved to anger and laid hands upon him, and, after beating him together with the others with spears, fists, and kicks, bound him with a rope and condemned him to exile. They took away all his property, both personal and ecclesiastical, without leaving anything behind. Waddo, who was Queen Rigunthis’s major-domo, joined them; the others who had departed with him scattered in flight.

### XXVIII

Afterward, the army withdrew from the city of Poitiers and advanced farther [Note: That is, farther on; Regm. has: “the army withdrew from Poitiers and advanced farther,” and so forth] in pursuit of Gundovald. Many from Touraine followed him for the sake of profit; but when the people of Poitiers fell upon him, some were killed and very many were plundered and returned. Those who had earlier joined the army from among them departed together with it [Note: Bad. has “had joined themselves,” and Colb. a., in a later hand, has “had been joined.” But Gregory and other authors of his period frequently use *jungo* passively or intransitively.]

Thus the army approached the river Dordogne [Note: Or *Duranium*, commonly the Dordogne, a notable river that rises in Auvergne, passes through many cities, and joins the Garonne shortly before the latter flows into the sea. Colb. m. and Regm. have *Dononiam*.] and began to wait, to learn what had happened to Gundovald. As stated above, Duke Desiderius and Bladastes had already joined him, together with Waddo, Rigunthis’s major-domo. Sagittarius the bishop and Mummolus were with him as his principal supporters. Sagittarius had already received a promise of the bishopric of Toulouse.

### XXIX

While these things were happening, King Guntchramn sent a certain Claudius, saying:

“If you go and either kill Eberulfus, expelled from the basilica [Note: The basilica of Saint Martin, of course; compare chapters 21 and 22], with a sword, or bind him in chains, I shall enrich you with great gifts. Nevertheless, I warn you most emphatically not to inflict any injury upon the holy basilica.”

But Claudius, being devoted to vanity and greed, hurried to Paris. He had a wife from the territory of Meaux. He began considering whether he should see Queen Fredegund, saying:

“If I see her, I may be able to extract some gift from her. For I know that she is hostile to the man to whom I have been sent.”

When he approached her, he immediately received great gifts from her and extracted many promises: either to kill Eberulfus after dragging him from the basilica, or to ensnare him by deceit and bind him in chains, or at least to butcher him in the very atrium.

Returning to the fortress of Dune, he urged the count to add three hundred men, supposedly to guard the gates of the city of Tours, so that when Claudius arrived he could use their assistance to overpower Eberulfus. When the count was mobilizing these men, Claudius came to Tours.

As he traveled, he began, as is customary among barbarians, to observe omens and to say that they were unfavorable to him. At the same time he asked many people whether the power of blessed Martin was at that moment being manifested against the treacherous; or whether, if someone had inflicted an injury upon those who trusted in him, vengeance would immediately follow.

Thus, having dismissed the men who, as we have said, were supposed to come to his assistance, he himself approached the holy basilica. Immediately joining the unfortunate Eberulfus, he began giving assurances and swearing by all that was sacred, and by the power of the present bishop, that no one would be more faithful in Eberulfus’s affairs, and that he could plead his case with the king [Note: Regm. and Chesn. and others have “could conduct his case.”]

The wretched man had formed this plan in his mind: “Unless I deceive him by perjuring myself, I shall not overcome him.”

When Eberulfus saw that Claudius was making such promises to him with oaths, in the very basilica, throughout the porticoes, and in every venerable place of the atrium, the miserable man believed the perjurer.

The next day, while we were staying in a villa about thirty miles from the city, Eberulfus was invited to a banquet at the holy basilica with Claudius and the other citizens. There Claudius would have struck him with a sword if his servants had not stood farther away. Yet Eberulfus, being as foolish as he was, never noticed this.

After the banquet ended, Eberulfus and Claudius began walking together through the atrium of the basilica’s house, promising each other faith and affection with oaths exchanged between them.

As they spoke in this way, Claudius said to Eberulfus:

“I should like to drink at your lodging, if wines mixed with spices were available, or at least if your generosity would call for a draught of stronger wine.”

When he said this, Eberulfus was pleased and replied that he had such wine:

“You will find everything you wish for at my lodging; only let my lord deign to enter my little dwelling.”

He sent his servants one after another to look for stronger wines, namely Laticine and Gazitine [Note: It should perhaps be read *Latina*, that is, Falernian, so called from Mount Falernus in Campania Felix, as above in Book III, chapter 19. Alteserra nevertheless thinks that *Laticina* referred to white wines because they resembled the color of water; hence Virgil, *Aeneid* I, joins “Latician Lyaeus” with royal dishes. Gazitine wines were also famous at that time, as is clear from this and other passages of Gregory. Sidonius praises the same wines in poem 17, as does Cassiodorus in Book XII, letter 12, and others. Isidore, Book XXIII, says that they were so called because they were brought from Gaza in Palestine. See the *Life of the Confessors*, chapter 65.]

When Claudius saw that the servants had left him alone, he raised his hand toward the basilica and said:

“Most blessed Martin, grant that I may soon see my wife and my parents.”

For the wretched man, placed in danger, was thinking both of killing Eberulfus in the atrium and of fearing the power of the holy bishop.

Then one of Claudius’s servants, who was stronger than the others, seized Eberulfus from behind, squeezed him tightly with his powerful arms, and, throwing him backward, prepared his chest for the throat-cutting. Claudius drew his sword from his belt and directed it at him. But the other, while he was being held, adjusted the iron drawn from his belt so as to strike Claudius.

When Claudius, raising his right hand, drove his dagger into the man’s chest, the latter, without hesitation, thrust his own dagger beneath Claudius’s armpit and, drawing it back toward himself with a measured stroke, cut off Claudius’s thumb.

At this, Claudius’s servants came together with their swords and wounded Eberulfus with repeated blows. When he slipped from their hands and, already half-dead, tried to flee, they drew their swords and struck his head with great violence. His brain spilled out, and he fell and died. He did not deserve to be saved by the saint whom he had never understood how faithfully to invoke.

Claudius, terrified by fear, then sought the abbot’s cell, wishing to be protected by the man toward whose patron he had not known how to show reverence [Note: Colb. a., in a later hand, has “in whose Father’s atrium.” The abbot then in charge of the monastery of Saint Martin was Eustachius, or Eustochius, as Cointius observes; he is mentioned below in *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 20. Alteserra wrongly understands this passage as referring to the Major Monastery, which he does not distinguish from the monastery of Saint Martin, now a distinguished collegiate church.]

When the abbot had seated himself, Claudius said:

“An immense crime has been committed, and unless you help us, we shall perish.”

While he was speaking, Eberulfus’s servants rushed in with swords and spears. Finding the door barred, they broke the glass windows of the cell and thrust spears through the openings in the wall, impaling Claudius, who was already half-dead from the blows. His attendants hid behind the doors and beneath the beds.

The abbot was seized by two clerics and, with difficulty, rescued alive from among the sword blades. When the doors were opened, a crowd of armed men entered.

Some of the matricularii [Note: The *matricularii* were poor people supported by the resources of the church, because their names were written in a register, or *matricula*, as may be seen in Frodoardus, Book II of the *History of Reims*, chapter 5; Hincmar, and others. The name was also given to those who cared for such poor people and for the house in which they were housed, which was likewise called a *matricula*, as appears from formula 11 of the Roman law in Bignon; the learned man’s notes on this passage should also be consulted. From this usage the term was transferred to those who cared for any church, who were called the churches’ custodians, or *matricularii*. The name is still retained by those who administer the property of parish churches, commonly called *marguilliers*. Alcuin also repeatedly calls himself Saint Martin’s *matricularius*, that is, its fosterling. See Du Cange’s *Glossary*.] and other poor people tried to tear down the roof of the cell because of the crime that had been committed.

The possessed and various needy people also went forth with stones and clubs to avenge the violence done to the basilica, indignant that such things—things that had never before occurred—had been perpetrated there.

What more need be said? The fugitives were dragged from their hiding places and cruelly butchered; the floor of the cell was stained with gore. After they had been killed, they were dragged outside and left naked on the cold ground.

The assassins, having seized the spoils, fled during the following night.

God’s vengeance immediately came upon those who had polluted the blessed atrium with human blood. Yet the crime of the man who allowed the blessed bishop to suffer such things was not considered a small one either.

The king was greatly angered by this, but when he learned the circumstances, he calmed down. Nevertheless, he gave the unfortunate man’s property, both movable and immovable, whatever had been left to him from his own possessions [Note: This is how Colb. a., in a later hand, reads. The others have: “whatever had been left by the former owners.” Bad. has: “and whatever had belonged to the former owners,” and so forth. Freh. and others have: “whatever had been left from his own possessions.” The same Colb. manuscript, in a later hand, reads below: “his wife, stripped of all her possessions.”], to his own faithful men, who left his wife severely despoiled in the holy basilica.

The nearest relatives took the body of Claudius and the others to their own region and buried them.

### XXX

Accordingly, Gundovald sent two clerical envoys to his friends. One of them, the abbot of the city of Cahors, concealed the letters he had received beneath the wax in a hollowed-out writing tablet. But he was seized by King Guntchramn’s men; when the letters were discovered, he was brought into the king’s presence, severely beaten, and thrown into custody.

### XXXI

At that time Gundovald was in the city of Bordeaux, greatly loved by Bishop Bertchramn. While Gundovald was seeking what might provide support for his cause, someone related that a certain king in the East had fastened the thumb of the martyr Saint Sergius [Note: Saint Sergius was famous in the East. He is said to have suffered martyrdom together with Bacchus under the Emperor Maximian at Rosapha in Commagene, or Augusta in Euphratesia, a city later called Sergiopolis after him. Chosroes, king of the Persians, unsuccessfully tried to capture this city under the Emperor Justinian. Another Chosroes, under the Emperor Maurice, regarded the same martyr as a special patron and enriched his basilica with a golden cross and various gifts, as related by Evagrius, Book IV, chapter 28, and Book VI, chapter 21; Theophylact Simocatta, Book V, chapter 13; Nicephorus, and others. See Baronius under the year 593. From this it is clear that the name of Sergius was famous among Christians and barbarians alike. Justinian dedicated one basilica to him at Constantinople and another at Ptolemais, according to Procopius. Pilgrimages to Saint Sergius at Araphas, or Saraphas, are praised in the Second Council of Nicaea, from John Moschus, *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 180. See also our Gregory, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, Book I, chapter 97.] from the right arm of his body.

Whenever necessity arose to drive off enemies, the king trusted in this aid; and when he raised his arm after lifting the forearm of his right arm, the multitude of the enemy immediately slipped into flight, as though overcome by the martyr’s power.

When Gundovald heard this, he began to investigate carefully who in that region had been worthy to receive relics of Saint Sergius the martyr.

Meanwhile, a merchant named Eufronius [Al. *Eufron*] was betrayed by Bishop Bertchramn out of hostility, because Eufronius had once forcibly tonsured him, and because he coveted his property [Note: Perhaps this is because bishops at that time claimed for themselves the possessions of clerics, at least of deceased clerics; this was later forbidden in 615 at the Fifth Council of Paris, canon 8.]. Disregarding this, Eufronius went to another city and returned after his hair had grown back.

The bishop therefore said:

“There is a certain Syrian here, named Eufronius, who converted his house into a church and placed the relics of this saint there. He has witnessed many signs through the assistance of the martyr’s power. For when the city of Bordeaux was once burning in a great fire, this house, surrounded by flames, was not burned at all.”

As he said this, Mummolus immediately hurried with Bishop Bertchramn to the Syrian’s house. Surrounding the man, he ordered him to display the holy relics.

The man refused. Yet, thinking that some treacherous plot had been prepared against him because of some wrongdoing, he said:

“Do not trouble an old man or inflict an injury upon the saint. Take one hundred gold pieces from me and depart.”

When Mummolus continued insisting that he wished to see the holy relics, Eufronius offered two hundred gold pieces, but still could not persuade him to leave unless the relics themselves were shown.

Then Mummolus ordered a ladder to be raised against the wall. The relics had been stored high up in a small container in the wall opposite the altar. He ordered his deacon to climb. As the deacon went up the ladder’s steps and grasped the object, he was so shaken by trembling that he seemed unlikely, even alive, to return to the ground.

Nevertheless, after receiving the container, which hung from the wall, he brought it down, as we have said. When Mummolus examined it, he found a bone from the saint’s finger, which he did not hesitate to strike with a knife. He placed the knife upon it and struck it from the other side as well.

Although it could scarcely be broken after many blows, the little bone split into three parts, which scattered in different directions. I believe that it was not pleasing to the martyr that Mummolus should handle these things.

Then Eufronius began to weep bitterly, and everyone fell to the ground in prayer, asking God to deign to reveal what had been removed from human sight.

After the prayer, the fragments were found. Mummolus took one of them and departed, but, as I believe, not with the martyr’s favor, as was made clear in what followed.

While they were staying in this city, they ordered the presbyter Faustianus [Note: Colb. a. and Regm. have *Faustinianus*. The city of Aquae mentioned here was otherwise called Aquae Tarbellicae, commonly Acqs or Dax, and Vicus Julii, or Adura, commonly Aire; these were cities of Novempopulania and had always been subject to the metropolitan of Elusa, or Auch, as was also Vasates. Because of the disturbances of that time, however, their bishops were compelled to obey the bishop of Bordeaux, who was metropolitan of the neighboring province, namely Aquitania II.] to be ordained bishop of the city of Aquae.

The bishop of Aquae had recently died, and Nicetius, the count of that place, brother of Rusticus, bishop of Vicus Julii, had extracted from Chilperic an order that a tonsured priest should be assigned to that city. But Gundovald, attempting to overturn his decree, summoned the bishops and ordered that Faustianus be consecrated.

Bertchramn, the metropolitan bishop, concerned about the future, instructed Palladius of Saintes to consecrate him, for Bertchramn’s eyes were then afflicted with ophthalmia. Orestes, bishop of Vasates, was also present at this ordination, but he denied this before the king.

### XXXII

Afterward Gundovald again sent two envoys, Zotanus and Zabulfus, to the king with consecrated rods [Note: Greek envoys carried a *caduceus*, according to the passage in the Digest, Book L, under *On the Division of Property*. Hence Mercury, the messenger of the gods, carried a *caduceus* in his hand, which Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, calls a rod. Only Colb. a. gives the names of the envoys.], according to Frankish custom, so that no one might touch them, but that, after presenting their embassy, they might return with the reply.

But these men, imprudent, explained many things they were asking for before they saw the king’s presence. The report immediately reached the king, and they were therefore brought before him bound in chains.

Then, when asked what they sought, to whom they had been sent, and by whom they had been dispatched, they did not dare deny it and said:

“Gundovald, who recently came from the East, says that he is the son of your father, King Chlothacharius. He sent us so that he may receive his rightful portion of the kingdom. But if it is not restored to him by you, know that he will come into these regions with an army.

“All the bravest men of that region, which lies beyond the Dordogne and belongs to Gaul, have joined him.” And he says:

“Then God will judge, when we have joined battle on the level ground of a single field, whether I am the son of Chlothacharius or not.”

The king, inflamed with fury, ordered them to be stretched upon the rack and beaten with the utmost severity, so that, if what they said were true, they might prove it more clearly; and if they still concealed any deceit in the secret recesses of their hearts, the force of torture might extract it against their will.

As the punishments increased, they said that he had assigned his niece—that is, King Chilperic’s daughter [Note: Rigunthis, betrothed to Reccaredus]—to exile with Magnulfus, bishop of Toulouse; that Gundovald himself had taken away all the treasures; and that Gundovald himself had been sought by all the leading men of King Childebert’s kingdom. They added especially that, when Guntchramn Boso had gone to Constantinople some years earlier, he had invited Gundovald himself to Gaul.

### XXXIII

After they had been beaten and thrown into prison, the king ordered his nephew Childebert to be summoned, so that they might hear these men together.

When the two kings questioned the men jointly, they repeated before both kings what King Guntchramn alone had previously heard. They also firmly asserted that, as we have already said, this matter was known to all the senior men in the kingdom of King Childebert.

For this reason, some of King Childebert’s former officials feared attending this assembly, since they were thought to have been involved in the matter.

Afterward King Guntchramn placed a spear in King Childebert’s hand and said:

“This is the sign that I have handed over my entire kingdom to you [Note: That the spear was a royal emblem among the Franks is clear from the ring of King Childeric I, found in his tomb together with other treasures. On it the king is represented with his hair flowing over his shoulders and holding a spear in his hand like a scepter. See Chifflet, p. 96, in the book published on this subject under the title *Anastasis Childerici*.].

“From now on, go and subject all my cities, as though they were your own, to the authority of your rule. For, because of their sins, no one of my line remains except you, who are my brother’s son. You are to succeed as heir throughout my entire kingdom, with the others disinherited.”

Then, after dismissing everyone else, he took the boy aside and spoke with him privately, first earnestly charging him not to reveal the secret conversation to anyone.

He then told him whom he should include in his counsels and whom he should exclude from conversation; whom he should trust, whom he should avoid, whom he should honor with gifts, and whom he should remove from honor.

In particular, he warned him never to trust Egidius, bishop of Reims, or to keep him with him, because Egidius had repeatedly perjured himself against both Childebert and his father [Note: This is how Colb. a., in a later hand, reads; the others have “or keep him with him.” Regm. has “have him as a counselor.”].

Afterward, when they had assembled for a banquet, King Guntchramn exhorted the entire army, saying:

“See, men, that my son Childebert has now become a grown man. See this, and take care not to regard him as a child [Note: Childebert had passed his fourteenth year and, as we would now say, having been declared of age, began to administer his kingdom himself. In the same way, Balthildis later handed over the administration of the kingdom to her son Chlothar when he entered puberty. See Valesius, Book XII of the *History of the Franks*.].

“Now abandon the perversities and presumptions you practice, because he is king, and you must now serve him.”

After saying these and similar things, he allowed them to feast and rejoice for three days, enriched them with many gifts, and sent them away in peace.

Then King Guntchramn restored to Childebert everything his father Sigibert had possessed, charging him not to approach his mother, lest someone provide an opportunity for her to write to Gundovald or receive letters from him.

### XXXIV

When Gundovald heard that the army was approaching him, and after being abandoned by Duke Desiderius, he crossed the Garonne with Bishop Sagittarius, the dukes Mummolus and Bladastes, and Waddo, making for Comminges [Note: Among the ancients this was called Lugdunum Convenarum, both because of its situation—for among the ancient Gauls *dunum* means a mountain—and because of the circumstance of its foundation, namely that many people gathered in that place. Jerome explains the matter in his work against Vigilantius, who was born in that city: “He answers his own race, being born from the seed of robbers and Convenae, whom Gnaeus Pompey, after conquering Spain, placed in the Pyrenees and gathered into one town; hence the city of the Convenae.” They were Vascones, who then inhabited the Pyrenean ranges. See Valesius, *Notitia Galliarum*. This city was destroyed by Guntchramn in 585, as Gregory relates below, and for a long time lay in ruins, its episcopal seat having been transferred elsewhere. But it was repaired to some extent by Bertrand, who died in 1120, and began again to be cultivated and inhabited. Taking its name from its restorer, it is now commonly called the city of Saint-Bertrand of Comminges, *Saint-Bertrand de Comminges*, under the metropolitan of Auch in Gascony.]

It is a city situated on the summit of a mountain and touching no other mountain. A great spring bursts forth at the foot of the mountain, surrounded by a very secure tower. The inhabitants descend from the city to it secretly through a passage and draw water.

When Gundovald entered the city at the beginning of Lent, he spoke to the citizens, saying:

“Know that I have been chosen king by all who are counted among King Childebert’s realm, and that I have no small support with me. But since my brother King Guntchramn is raising an immense army against me, you must enclose provisions and all your goods within the protection of the walls, so that, while divine mercy increases our strength, you may not perish from want.”

Believing him, they gathered and stored in the city whatever they were able to possess and prepared to resist.

At that time King Guntchramn sent a letter to Gundovald in the name of Queen Brunichildis, in which it was written that, after abandoning the army and ordering it to return to its own regions, Gundovald himself should spend the winter farther away, near the city of Bordeaux. He had written this deceitfully, so that he might learn more fully what Gundovald was doing.

While Gundovald remained in the city of Comminges, he spoke to the inhabitants, saying:

“Look, the army is already approaching. Go out to resist it.”

When they had gone out, Gundovald’s men seized and closed the gates, excluded the people outside, and, together with the bishop of the place [Note: This was Rufinus, who subscribed to the Second Council of Mâcon in that same year], subjected to their own use everything they could find in the city.

So great a quantity of grain and wine was discovered there that, if they had stood firm courageously, they would not have lacked food for many years.

### XXXV

At that time the commanders of King Guntchramn had heard that Gundovald was staying beyond the Garonne, on its bank, with a huge multitude of warriors, and that he was keeping with him the treasures that he had taken from Rigunthis.

They therefore made a sudden attack and crossed the Garonne by swimming with their horses [Edition: *equis*; that is, “with horses”], while some of the army were drowned in the river.

The rest came out onto the bank and, searching for Gundovald, found camels carrying a huge weight of gold and silver, as well as horses [For *equites*, read *equos*: “horses”] that he had left exhausted along the roads.

Afterward, when they learned that Gundovald and his men were staying within the walls of the city of Comminges, they left behind the wagons and various impediments, together with the smaller contingent of people, and the stronger men resolved to pursue him, just as they had crossed the Garonne.

As they hurried on, they came to the basilica of Saint Vincent, which stands near the boundary of the city of Agen, where the martyr is said to have completed his contest for Christ. They found it filled with various treasures belonging to the inhabitants.

The people had believed that Christians would not violate the basilica of so great a martyr, and its doors had been firmly barred with the greatest care. But the army approached, and when it could not open the doors of the church, it kindled a fire. After the doors had been consumed, the soldiers carried away all the property and every possession they could find there, including the sacred vessels.

But divine vengeance terrified many of them [Note: Joseph Scaliger, Book VI of *On the Correction of the Times*, maintains that this basilica stood in the Capraria valley near Lugdunum Convenarum. He therefore thinks Gregory was mistaken in writing that it stood near Agen, confusing the place where the blessed martyr suffered with the basilica consecrated in his memory. Scaliger himself, however, is mistaken. The basilica plundered by Guntchramn’s soldiers was indeed near Agen, specifically at Pompeiacon, where Saint Vincent suffered. The sequence of events presents no difficulty. Since Gundovald was at Bordeaux, Guntchramn’s army advanced from Poitiers to the Dordogne. Terrified by this news, Gundovald withdrew to Comminges. As Guntchramn’s army pursued the enemy there, it passed through the territory of Agen, as the route required; on that occasion the soldiers plundered Saint Vincent’s church. They then continued their march and reached the foot of the mountain on which Lugdunum Convenarum stood, as Gregory relates. See *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 105. Fortunatus speaks of this basilica, and of another dedicated to the same saint, which Leontius, bishop of Bordeaux, had built or adorned, in Book I, poems 8 and 9. The feast of this saint is celebrated on 9 June.]

For many of them were divinely burned in their hands, emitting a great cloud of smoke, as usually rises from a fire. Some, seized by a demon and raging in their possession, loudly proclaimed the martyr. Many others, separated from their companions [Note: This is how Colb. a., in a later hand, reads. The others have “separated from the rebellion”], wounded themselves with their own weapons.

The rest of the common people advanced farther, not without great fear.

What more need be said? Everyone gathered at Comminges—for that is the name we have given the city—and the entire phalanx encamped in the city’s suburban plain, remaining there with its tents spread out.

The whole surrounding region was devastated. Some soldiers, whom the sharper spur of greed drove farther from their comrades, were killed by the inhabitants.

### XXXVI

Many climbed the hill [Note: Thus Colb. a. and Regm.: “But very many of them acted secretly and spoke with Gundovald.” The other manuscripts, with Bec., have: “For many concealed themselves,” and so forth.] and repeatedly spoke with Gundovald, heaping insults upon him and saying:

“Are you that painter who, in the time of King Chlothacharius, scratched figures upon the walls and ceilings of oratories [Note: From this came the term *charaxaturae*, meaning erasures or cancellations of writing and ink stains. See the testament of Saint Remigius and Marculf, Book II, formula 17]?

“Are you that man whom the inhabitants of Gaul so often called by the name Ballomer?

“Are you that man who, because of the presumptions you make, was repeatedly tonsured and sent into exile by the kings of the Franks?

“Or who, most wretched of men, brought you into these regions? Tell us. Who gave you such audacity that you dared approach the territories of our lords and kings? Certainly, if someone summoned you, declare it in a loud voice.

“Look: death lies before your eyes. Look: here is the very pit of destruction that you have long sought, into which you may be thrown headlong. Name your attendants one by one, or announce by whom you were invited.”

But when Gundovald heard this, standing close to the gate, he said:

“That my father Chlothacharius regarded me with hatred is unknown to no one. But that I was tonsured by him and afterward by my brothers is known to all.

“This circumstance brought me into association with Narses, the prefect of Italy. There I took a wife and fathered two sons. After she died, I went to Constantinople with my children.

“The emperors received me most graciously, and I lived there until this time. Some years ago, when Guntchramn Boso had gone to Constantinople and I was carefully investigating the affairs of my brothers, I learned that our family had become greatly reduced and that no one remained of our line except Childebert and Guntchramn—my brother’s son and my brother.

“For the sons of King Chilperic had perished with him, with only one little boy left behind [Note: Yet from Book VI, chapter 24, it appears that Gundovald had come to Gaul before Chilperic’s death. See above, chapter 32]. My brother Guntchramn had no sons, and our nephew Childebert was not at all strong.

“After Guntchramn Boso had carefully explained these matters to me, he invited me, saying:

“‘Come, for you are being invited by all the leading men of King Childebert’s kingdom, and no one has dared to murmur against you. We all know that you are the son of Chlothacharius, and no one remains in Gaul who can govern that kingdom unless you come.’

“But after giving him many gifts, I received oaths from him at twelve holy places, so that I might approach this kingdom securely.

“I came to Marseilles, where the bishop received me with the greatest kindness; he possessed the writings of the elders of my nephew’s kingdom.

“From there I went to Avignon in accordance with the arrangements made by Patrician Mummolus. But Guntchramn, forgetting his oath and promise, took away my treasures and subjected them to his own authority.

“Now recognize that I am king, just as my brother Guntchramn is. Yet if your minds are driven by such great hatred, let me be brought before your king; and if he recognizes me as his brother, let him do what he wishes.

“Certainly, if you are unwilling even to do this, at least let me return to the place from which I first came. I shall depart and inflict injury upon no one.

“Nevertheless, so that you may know that what I say is true, question Radegund of Poitiers and Ingetrud of Tours [Note: Colb. a. and Bec. have *Ingotrud*; Colb. m. has *Introgunda*; Regm. has *Intragunda*. This is Ingeltrudis, who founded the monastery in the atrium of Saint Martin’s basilica and whom Gregory mentions several times]. They will affirm to you that what I am saying is certain.”

When he had said this, many responded to his words with insults and reproaches.

### XXXVII

The fifteenth day of the siege had dawned, and Leudegisilus was preparing new machines for destroying the city. Wagons had been constructed with battering rams, pack-saddles, and axles, under which the army might advance to demolish the walls. [Note: Thus Bec and the printed editions; others read tecta (“covered”), and Colbertinus a, second hand, has tecta erant (“were covered”).] But when they had drawn near, they were so overwhelmed with stones that all who approached the wall fell. They threw upon them burning vessels filled with pitch and fat, while others, filled with stones, they hurled down upon them. But when night stopped the fighting, the enemy returned to the camp.

Gundovald was accompanied by Chariulfus, a very wealthy and powerful man, whose storerooms and supplies had greatly replenished the city; it was chiefly from his resources that these men were fed. [Note: Colbertinus m and Chesnianus and others read Ariulfus; below, Hariulfus; Bec has Mariulfus, but below Cariulfus.]

When Bladastes saw what was happening, fearing that, after gaining victory, Leudegisilus would put them to death, he set fire to the church building. While those shut inside were rushing together to quench the fire, he slipped away in flight. [Note: Colbertinus a reads “he was shut in,” and, after “rushing together,” a second hand adds “all.”]

When morning came, the army again rose for battle and made bundles from branches, as though to fill the deep valley situated on the eastern side. But this machine was of no use. Bishop Sagittarius frequently went around the walls in arms and often threw stones from the wall at the enemy with his own hand.

### XXXVIII

Finally, those who were attacking the city, seeing that they could accomplish nothing, sent secret messengers to Mummolus, saying:

“Recognize your lord and finally desist from this perversity. What madness surrounds you, that you should submit yourself to an unknown man? Your wife has already been captured with your sons; your sons, as I think, have already been killed.” [Note: Colbertinus a reads ut puto (“as I think”); Regmius has “and, as I believe, your sons have already …”]

“Where are you rushing? What are you waiting for, except that you should fall?” Where are you rushing? What are you waiting for, except that you should fall?”

When he received this message, he said:

“Now, as I see, our kingdom is coming to an end, and our power is falling. One thing remains: if I could know that I would have security for my life, I could spare you much trouble.”

When the messengers had departed, Bishop Sagittarius, together with Mummolus, Chariulfus, and Waddo, went to the church. There they exchanged pledges with one another that, if they received assurances concerning their lives, they would abandon Gundovald’s cause and hand him over to the enemy.

The messengers returned and promised them security of life. Mummolus said:

“Let only this be done, and I will hand him over into your power. Recognizing my lord the king, I will hasten into his presence.”

Then they promised that, if he fulfilled this, they would receive him favorably; and if they could not excuse him to the king, they would place him in a church so that he would not be punished with the loss of his life.

After making these promises with the interposition of an oath, they departed.

Mummolus, however, going with Bishop Sagittarius and Waddo to Gundovald, said:

“You yourself, who are present, know what pledges of fidelity we gave you. But now accept wholesome advice: depart from this city and present yourself to your brother, as you have often sought to do. For we have already spoken with these men, and they said that the king does not wish to lose your support, since little of your family remains.”

But Gundovald, understanding their deceit and overcome with tears, said:

“By your invitation I was brought into these Gauls. Some of my treasures, containing an immense weight of silver and gold and various kinds of goods, are being held in the city of Avignon; some Guntchramnus Boso has seized. Trusting in God’s help, and placing all my hope in you, I entrusted my counsels to you and always desired to reign through you. Now let your reckoning be with God, if you have spoken any falsehood to me: let him himself judge my cause.”

When he had said this, Mummolus replied:

“We are speaking no deceit to you. But look: very brave men are standing at the gate, awaiting your arrival. Now remove my golden belt, with which you are girded, so that you may not appear to go forth ostentatiously; gird on your own sword and return mine.”

He replied:

“I do not accept these words simply, that the things of yours which I have until now enjoyed in friendship should be taken away from me.” [Note: The Cassino manuscript has “in the city.”]

Mummolus insisted with an oath that nothing unpleasant was being done to him.

They therefore went out through the gate, and he was received by Ollo, count of Bourges, and Boso. Mummolus, however, returned to the city with his followers and firmly secured the gate.

When Gundovald saw that he had been delivered into the hands of his enemies, he raised his hands and eyes toward heaven and said:

“Eternal Judge and true avenger of the innocent, God, from whom all justice proceeds, who does not delight in falsehood and in whom there is no deceit or crafty malice, to you I entrust my cause. I beseech you to avenge swiftly those who, though I am innocent, have delivered me into the hands of my enemies.”

After saying this, he signed himself with the Lord’s cross and began to depart with the men mentioned above.

When they had moved some distance from the gate, where, as is usual around the city, the entire valley falls away precipitously, Ollo pushed him, and he fell. Ollo also shouted:

“Here is your Ballomer, who calls himself both the king’s brother and his son!”

He thrust a spear at him, wishing to pierce him, but it was deflected by the rings of his armor and did no harm. Finally, when Gundovald tried to rise and return to the mountain, Boso hurled a stone at his head; he fell and died.

The entire crowd then came, fixed their spears in him, tied his feet with a rope, and dragged him through all the army camps. They tore out his hair and beard and left him unburied in the very place where he had been killed.

On the following night, those who were first—[Note: Cassino has “those who had been sent”—secretly carried away all the treasures they could find in the city, together with the church vessels.

In the morning, when the gates had been opened and the army admitted, they delivered the entire population shut inside to the edge of the sword. They also slaughtered the priests of the Lord with their ministers at the very altars of the churches. After killing everyone, so that not even one who urinated against a wall would remain, they set fire to the whole city, together with the churches and the remaining buildings, leaving nothing there except bare ground.

### XXXIX

Leudegisilus therefore returned to the camp with Mummolus, Sagittarius, Chariulfus, and Waddo, and secretly sent messengers to the king to ask what should be done with them. The king ordered that they be put to death.

Waddo and Chariulfus then departed from them, leaving their sons as hostages.

When news of their destruction was brought, Mummolus realized what had happened, armed himself, and went to Leudegisilus’s hut. Seeing him, Leudegisilus said:

“Why are you coming like a fugitive?”

Mummolus replied:

“As I see, the promised faith is not being kept, for I perceive that I have been placed on the brink of death.”

Leudegisilus answered:

“I will go outside and settle everything.”

When he had gone out, the house was immediately surrounded at his command, so that Mummolus might be killed there. But Mummolus resisted the fighters for a very long time and then came to the doorway. As he was going out, two men struck him on both sides with spears; thus he fell and died.

When Bishop Sagittarius saw this, he was terrified and trembled with fear. One of those standing nearby said to him:

“Look with your own eyes, bishop, at what is happening. Cover your head so that you will not be recognized, and make for the forest to hide for a while; when their anger has passed, you may escape.”

He accepted this advice and tried to flee with his head covered, but someone drew a sword and cut off his head together with his hood.

Then each man returned to his own place, committing great plunder and murder along the way.

During these days Fredegund sent Cuppan to Toulouse, in order that he might rescue her daughter from there by whatever means he could. Many claimed that he had been sent for this reason: if he found Gundovald alive, he was to lure him to her with many promises. But since he could not do this, he brought Rigunth back from that place, not without great humiliation and disgrace. [Note: She never married Reccaredus, nor, it seems, did Chlodosvinda, daughter of Sigibertus. See below the notes on Book IX, chapter 25. Therefore Reccaredus, undoubtedly weary of so many delays, eventually joined Baddo, a woman of his own people, to himself in marriage.]

### XL

Leudegisilus the general therefore came to the king with all the treasures mentioned above. The king later distributed them among the poor and the churches.

After Mummolus’s wife had been seized, the king began to inquire what had become of the treasures they had gathered. When she learned that her husband had been killed and that all their boasting had utterly fallen to the ground, she disclosed everything. She said that a great quantity of gold and silver still remained at Avignon and had not come to the king’s knowledge.

The king immediately sent men to bring these things, together with a boy whom Mummolus had trusted greatly and to whom he had entrusted them. When they went away, they took everything that had been left in the city.

They say that there were two hundred and fifty talents of silver and more than thirty of gold. But, it is said, he had taken these from an ancient treasure that he had discovered.

The king divided it with his nephew, King Childebert, and gave his own share chiefly to the poor. To the woman he left nothing beyond what she had received from her parents.

### XLI

At that time a man of enormous stature, one of Mummolus’s associates, was brought to the king. He was so great in body that he was thought to stand two or three feet taller than the tallest men. He was a carpenter and died not long afterward.

### XLII

After this, the judges issued an edict that those who had been slow to join this expedition should be condemned.

The count of Bourges also sent his men to plunder such people in the house of blessed Martin, which was situated in that district. But the steward of that house began to resist them vigorously, saying:

“These are men of Saint Martin. Do not inflict any injury on them, because they have not been accustomed to go out on such undertakings.”

They replied:

“We have nothing to do with your Martin, whom you are always bringing forward pointlessly in legal matters. You and they will pay the penalties because you neglected the king’s command.”

As he said this, one of them entered the courtyard of the house. Immediately he was struck with pain, fell, and began to suffer severely.

Turning to the steward, he said in a lamentable voice:

“I ask you to make the Lord’s cross over me and invoke the name of blessed Martin. Now I have learned how great his power is. For as I entered the courtyard of the house, I saw an old man holding a tree in his hand; it immediately spread its branches and covered the whole courtyard. One of its branches touched me, and, shaken by its blow, I fell down.”

He signaled to his companions, asking that he be carried out of the courtyard. Once outside, he began more earnestly to invoke the name of blessed Martin. Thereafter he was in better condition and was healed.

### XLIII

Desiderius protected himself and his possessions within the fortifications of the camp.

Waddo, Rigunth’s chief steward, went over to Queen Brunichild. She received him and dismissed him with gifts and favor.

Chariulfus sought the basilica of Saint Martin. [Note: This is thought to designate the church of Saint Martin at Lériac, still distinguished today by a college of canons near Bourges, under the jurisdiction of Saint Martin of Tours.]

### XLIV

At that time there was a woman who possessed a pythonic spirit [another reading, here and below: “phytonic”]. By divining, she brought considerable profit to her masters; and she advanced so far in their favor that, once set free by them, she was allowed to follow her own wishes.

If anyone suffered a theft or some other misfortune, she immediately declared where the thief had gone, to whom he had delivered the stolen goods, or what he had done with them. Every day she gathered gold and silver and went about in ornaments, so that among the people she was thought to possess something divine.

But when these things had been reported to Agericus, bishop of Verdun, he sent men to arrest her. After she had been seized and brought before him, he recognized in her, in accordance with what we read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 16:16), an unclean pythonic spirit.

When he pronounced an exorcism over her and anointed her forehead with holy oil, the demon cried out and revealed to the priest what it was. But since it was not driven out of the girl through him, she was allowed to depart.

When the girl saw that she could not live in that place, she went to Queen Fredegund and hid there.

### XLV

In this year a great famine almost overwhelmed all Gaul. Many made bread from grape seeds and hazelnut blossoms; some dried fern roots, ground them into powder, and mixed in a little flour to make bread. Many also cut the grass among the crops and prepared it in the same way.

There were also many who had no flour at all. They gathered various herbs and, after eating them, became swollen and perished. Very many, consumed by hunger, died.

At that time merchants grievously plundered the people, so that they would scarcely sell even a modius of grain—or, in Colbertinus a, even a small quantity—or half a modius of wine for one triens. The poor submitted themselves to servitude so that they might receive even the smallest amount of food. [Note: Here Book VII ends in the Vatican and Colbertinus a manuscripts; in them the next two chapters are absent.]

### XLVI

During these days the merchant Christophorus went to the city of Orléans. For he had heard that a great quantity of wine had been brought there. He went, purchased wine, and transported it in small boats. Having received a large sum of money from his father-in-law, he traveled on horseback with two Saxon boys.

The boys had long hated their master and had often run away from him, because they were beaten very severely and very frequently.

When they came to a certain forest, their master going ahead, one of the boys hurled a spear with great force and pierced him. When he fell, the other tore his head apart with a sword. Thus, cut into pieces by both of them, he was left lifeless.

They took the money and fled.

Christophorus’s brother buried the body and sent his men after the boys. They captured the younger one and bound him, while the older escaped with the money.

When the men returned, they had left the prisoner too loosely bound. He seized a spear and killed one of those who were bringing him back. But he was taken by the others as far as Tours, subjected to various punishments, mutilated, and hung from the gallows, completely lifeless. [Note: Regmius has “was hung upon the gallows.”]

### XLVII

At that time serious civil wars broke out among the citizens of Tours.

Sicharius, son of the late John, was celebrating the solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity at the village of Montalomagus with Austregisilus and the other country people. [Note: This is a well-known place near Tours, commonly called Mantelan. Perpetuus built a church there, as is said below in Book X, at the end.] The priest of the place sent a boy to invite certain men, so that they should come to his house for drinking.

When the boy arrived, one of those who had been invited did not fear to draw his sword and strike him. He immediately fell and died.

When Sicharius heard this—he maintained friendship with the priest because the boy had been his servant—he seized his arms and went toward the church, waiting for Austregisilus.

When Austregisilus heard this, he took up his weapons and advanced against him. When both sides came together and clashed, Sicharius was rescued among the clergy and fled to his own estate. Four wounded boys were left in the priest’s house, together with silver and clothing.

After Sicharius had fled, Austregisilus attacked again, killed the boys, and carried away the gold, silver, and the remaining goods.

Afterward, when they had assembled before the civic court, it was ordered that Austregisilus, who was a murderer and had plundered the property after killing the boys without a hearing, should be condemned by legal judgment. [Note: Marculf, Book I, chapter 28, contains a “hearing formula” by which someone was compelled to appear before the prince for the examination of any matter.]

A few days after the judgment had begun, Sicharius learned that the property seized by Austregisilus was being held by Auno, his son, and his brother Eberulfus. Abandoning the legal proceedings, he joined Audinus and, raising a revolt, attacked them at night with armed men. They battered down the house in which they were sleeping, killed the father together with his brother and son, and carried away their property and livestock, after killing their slaves.

When we heard this, we were greatly distressed. We joined a judge to the embassy we sent to them, so that they might come into our presence, settle the matter reasonably, and depart in peace, lest the quarrel grow further.

When they came and the citizens had assembled, I said:

“Do not, men, advance further in crimes, lest evil be extended still farther. We have lost sons of the Church; now we fear that we may also lose others through this hostility. I beg you to be peaceful, and let the one who has committed the wrong settle it while charity remains, so that you may be sons of peace and, with the Lord granting it, be worthy to receive the kingdom of God.

“For he himself says: ‘Blessed are the peacemakers, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven’ (Matthew 5:9).

“Look: even if the means of the man [the transmitted phrase following this is materially uncertain] are small, he will be redeemed by the Church’s silver. Meanwhile, let the man’s soul not perish.”

As I said this, I offered the Church’s silver. But Chramnisind’s party, seeking vengeance for the death of his father, brother, and paternal uncle, refused to accept it. [Note: This chapter and various other passages of Gregory provide very bad examples of the custom of pursuing private enmities by arms, a practice that among the Franks was not entirely forbidden by royal command or legal authority, although it was restricted within certain limits. Thus, if anyone had been wounded or killed, his relatives and connections, or even his friends, would assemble to avenge the wrong by force of arms. See Marculf, Book I, formula 18, and Bignonius’s notes. This evil custom, called the feud, was later more often forbidden in the kings’ capitularies.]

After they departed, Sicharius prepared to travel to the king and therefore went to Poitiers to see his wife.

When he warned a slave to perform his work and struck him with a raised staff, the man drew the sword from his belt and did not fear to wound his master. When Sicharius fell to the ground, his friends ran up, seized the slave, cruelly beat him, cut off his hands and feet, and condemned him to the gallows.

Meanwhile, a report spread through Tours that Sicharius had died.

When Chramnisind heard this, he summoned his relatives and friends and hurried to Sicharius’s house. After plundering them and killing some of the slaves, he burned all the houses—both Sicharius’s and those of the others who shared ownership of the estate—carrying away with him the livestock and whatever he could move.

The parties were then brought by the judge to the city and stated their respective cases. The judges decided that the man who, because he did not wish to accept the earlier settlement, had burned the houses should lose half the compensation that had been awarded to him.

This was done contrary to the laws, so that they might merely be reconciled; Sicharius, however, was to pay the other half of the compensation.

Then, with silver supplied by the Church, and after receiving security for what had been judged, they settled the matter. The parties gave each other pledges that neither side would ever again mutter against the other, and thus the dispute came to an end. [Note: A formula for such security is found in Marculf, Book II, chapter 18.]

## The Chapters of Book Eight Begin

1. How the king came to Orléans.  
2. How the bishops were presented to him, and how he himself prepared a banquet.  
3. Concerning the singers and Mummolus’s silver.  
4. Praise of King Childebert.  
5. Concerning the visions that the king or we saw about Chilperic.  
6. Concerning those whom we presented.  
7. Concerning Bishop Palladius and how he celebrated Mass.  
8. Concerning the signs that were shown.  
9. Concerning the oath given for Chilperic’s son.  
10. Concerning the bodies of Merovech and Chlodovech.  
11. Concerning the doorkeepers and the death of Boant.  
12. Concerning Bishop Theodore and the plague upon Ratharius.  
13. Concerning Guntchramnus’s embassy sent to Childebert.  
14. Concerning the danger in the river.  
15. Concerning the conversion of the deacon Ulfilaic.  
16. What he reported concerning the miracles of Saint Martin.  
17. Concerning the signs that appeared.  
18. That Childebert sent an army into Italy, and which generals or counts were appointed or removed.  
19. Concerning the death of Abbot Dagulf.  
20. What was done at the synod of Mâcon.  
21. Concerning the legal proceeding at Belsonnacum and the violated tomb.  
22. Concerning the deaths of bishops and of Wandelinus.  
23. Concerning floods.  
24. Concerning islands of the sea.  
25. Concerning the island on which blood appeared.  
26. Concerning Eberulfus, who was a general.  
27. That Desiderius went to the king.  
28. Concerning Hermenegild and Ingund, and concerning the Spanish envoys secretly sent to Fredegund.  
29. That Fredegund sent someone to kill Childebert.  
30. That the army went into Septimania.  
31. Concerning the killing of Bishop Praetextatus.  
32. Concerning the death of Domnola, wife of Nectarius.  
33. Concerning the burning of the city of Paris.  
34. Concerning recluses who were assailed.  
35. Concerning the Spanish envoys.  
36. Concerning the death of Magnovaldus.  
37. That a son was born to Childebert.  
38. That the Spaniards invaded Gaul.  
39. Concerning the deaths of bishops.  
40. Concerning Pelagius of Tours.  
41. Concerning those who killed Bishop Praetextatus.  
42. That Bippolenus was appointed general.  
43. That Nicetius was appointed governor of Provence, and concerning what Antistius did.
