44. Concerning the man who tried to kill King Guntchramnus.  
45. Concerning the death of the general Desiderius.  
46. Concerning the death of King Leuvichild.

# BOOK EIGHT

### I

King Guntchramnus, in the twenty-fourth year of his reign, set out from Chalon and approached the city of Nevers. He had been invited to come to Paris so that he might receive Chilperic’s son—whom he was already calling Chlothar—from the sacred font of regeneration.

After departing from Nevers, he came to the city of Orléans and at that time presented himself magnificently to its citizens. For he went about visiting their houses when invited and tasted the meals they provided. They gave him many gifts, and he distributed gifts to them with lavish generosity.

When he came to the city of Orléans, it was the feast of blessed Martin, namely the fourth day before the Nones of the fifth month. [Note: This was the feast of his Translation, which is still celebrated on this very day, 4 July.]

An immense crowd of people came out to meet him with standards and banners, singing praises. On one side the language of the Syrians, on another that of the Latins, and on another that of the Jews themselves resounded in various praises, saying:

“May the king live, and may his kingdom be extended among diverse peoples for countless years.”

The Jews, who appeared to share in these praises, said:

“May all nations worship you, bend the knee to you, and be subject to you.”

Therefore, after Masses had been celebrated, when the king was seated at the banquet, he said:

“Woe to the Jewish nation, evil and faithless, and always living with a deceitful mind. For this reason, it said flattering praises to me today, so that all nations might worship me as lord and so that I might order their synagogue, which was formerly destroyed by Christians, to be restored at public expense. But, since the Lord forbids it, I will never do this.”

O king distinguished by admirable prudence! He understood the deceitfulness of the heretics so well that they could not at all steal away from him what they would later have proposed.

Already, during the banquet, the king spoke to the priests who were present, saying:

“I ask that tomorrow, in my house, I may deserve your blessing, and that your entrance may bring me salvation, so that from this moment I may be saved when the words of your blessings have flowed over me in my humility.”

When he had said this, we all gave thanks, and when the meal was finished, we rose.

### II

When morning came, while the king was visiting holy places for the sake of prayer, he came to our lodging. There was the basilica of Saint Avitus the abbot, whom we have mentioned in the Book of Miracles. [Note: In the Book on the Glory of the Confessors, chapter 99. The Basilica of Saint Avitus still stands today with a college of canons, beside which a seminary for the education of younger clerics has recently been established.]

I confess that I rose joyfully to meet him. After offering a prayer, I begged him to deign to accept in my dwelling the eulogiae of blessed Martin. He did not reject this; entering in kindly spirit, he drank a cup, invited us to the banquet, and departed happily.

At that time Bertchramnus, bishop of Bordeaux, was very hostile to the king, together with Palladius of Saintes, because they had received Gundovald, whom we mentioned above (Book VII, chapter 31). Bishop Palladius had especially incurred the king’s anger because he had repeatedly deceived him.

A little earlier, the other bishops and the king’s nobles had questioned them about why they had received Gundovald and why they had ordained Faustianus, bishop of Aix, at his slightest command. [Note: Colbertinus a and Regmius have “Faustinianus.” Compare Book VII, chapter 31.]

Bishop Palladius took the responsibility for the ordination away from Bertchramnus, his metropolitan, and placed it upon himself, saying:

“The eyes of my metropolitan were greatly afflicted with pain, and I, stripped and despised, was unwillingly brought by him to that place. I could do nothing except what he ordered—he who claimed to receive all authority over Gaul.”

When this was reported to the king, he was greatly provoked, so that it could scarcely be obtained that he would invite to the banquet men whom he had not previously seen.

When Bertchramnus entered, the king asked:

“Who is this? It has been a long time since he was seen by me.”

They replied:

“This is Bertchramnus, bishop of the city of Bordeaux.”

He said:

“We give thanks that you have thus guarded faith toward your family. You ought to have known, dearest father, that you had a relative through our mother and that you should not have introduced a foreign plague [Gundovald] among your people.”

When Bertchramnus had heard such words and others like them, the king turned to Palladius and said:

“Nor to you, Bishop Palladius, should excessive thanks be given. For the third time you have perjured yourself before me—which is an unjust thing to say of a bishop—sending notes full of deceit. You excused yourself to me by letters, while with other writings you invited my brother.” [Note: Colbertinus a has “and you excused yourself by letters.”]

“God has judged my cause, since I always sought to summon you as fathers of the Church, while you have always acted deceitfully toward me.”

To Bishops Nicasius and Antidius he said:

“You, most holy fathers, tell me what you have considered for the welfare of the province or the safety of our kingdom.”

When they too remained silent, the king washed his hands, received a blessing from the priests, and sat down at the table with a joyful expression and cheerful face, as though he had said nothing about his contempt.

### III

Meanwhile, when the meal was already half over, the king ordered me to have our deacon sing—the one who had sung the responsorial psalm at Mass the previous day. [Note: This corresponds to the Gradual or Gradale of today. Augustine frequently mentions the psalm that was sung after the Epistle. See Menardus on the Gregorian sacramentary, p. 368.]

When he had sung, the king again ordered me to have all the priests who were present, through my admonition, command the individual clerics belonging to their offices to sing before the king.

Warned by me according to the king’s command, each one sang the responsorial psalm in the king’s presence as best he could. [Note: The first hand of Colbertinus m has “sang.” After the bishop had recited the verse of the psalm, the cleric added the antiphon or response, in the manner in which we still sing the Song of the Three Children at the Ember Masses.]

When the dishes were being brought out, the king said:

“All the silver that you see belonged to that perjurer Mummolus (see Book VII, chapter 40). But now, by the grace granted by the Lord, it has been transferred into our possession. For I have already had fifteen dishes, as large as this larger one you see, cut up; and of it I have retained no more than this one and another, of one hundred and seventy pounds.

“What more than what is necessary for daily use should I retain? I have no other son, which is the worse, except Childebert, who has enough from the treasures his father left him—and what I have already arranged to send him from the property of that most wretched man, which was found at Avignon.

“The rest must be given to meet the needs of the poor and the churches.”

### IV

“There is only one thing I ask of you, priests of the Lord: pray for the mercy of the Lord upon my son Childebert.

“For he is a wise and useful man, so cautious and energetic that in a life of many years one could scarcely find his equal.

“If God deigns to grant him to these Gauls, perhaps there will be hope that through him our nation, which has been greatly emptied, may rise again.

“I do not doubt that this will happen according to his mercy, because such was the omen of the boy’s birth. For on Holy Easter Day, while my brother Sigibert was standing in the church and a deacon was proceeding with the holy book of the Gospels, a messenger came to the king. At the same moment there was the voice of the one announcing the Gospel reading and of the messenger saying: ‘A son has been born to you.’ As a result, all the people, at both announcements, proclaimed together: ‘Glory to almighty God.’

“But he received baptism on Holy Pentecost, and the king was nevertheless elevated on the holy day of the Lord’s Nativity.

“Therefore, if your prayer accompanies him, he may, with the Lord’s favor, reign.”

When the king had said this, they all poured out a prayer to the Lord that his mercy might preserve both kings.

The king added:

“Yet because his mother Brunichild threatens to kill me, I have no fear of this. For the Lord, who rescued me from the hands of my enemies, will also free me from her plots.”

### V

At that time he spoke many hostile words about Theodore. [Note: He was the bishop of Marseille, concerning whom more is said in the preceding book.] He declared that, if Theodore came to the synod, he would again be driven into exile, saying:

“For I know that he caused my brother Chilperic to be killed. Indeed, we should not even be regarded as men if we are unable to avenge his death this year.”

I replied:

“And who killed Chilperic, if not his own wickedness and your prayer? He laid many plots against you contrary to justice, and they brought him to his death.”

To speak plainly, I had examined this very closely in a dream vision. I saw Chilperic with his head tonsured, as though being ordained a bishop by you; then he was carried and placed upon a clean chair covered only with soot. [Note: Fredegar and others have “covered with no cloths.”] Lamps and candles shone before him.

When I had related this, the king said:

“I too saw another vision that foretold his destruction. He was brought bound in chains into my presence by three bishops, one Tetricus, another Agricola, and the third Nicetius of Lyon. [Note: Tetricus was bishop of Langres; Agricola was bishop of Chalon. For Tetricus, Colbertinus a, second hand, has Theodoricus, and so below.]

“Two of them said: ‘Release him, we beg you, and allow him to depart after he has been chastised.’

“But Bishop Tetricus answered them bitterly: ‘It shall not be so; he will be burned with fire for his crimes.’

“While they argued for a long time and exchanged these words, I saw at a distance a bronze vessel placed over a fire and boiling violently.

“Then, while I wept, they seized the wretched Chilperic, whose limbs had been broken, and threw him into the bronze vessel. Immediately, amid the steam of the boiling liquid, he was so dissolved and melted that no trace of him remained at all.”

When the king had said this, we marveled, and when the meal was finished, we rose.

### VI

The next day the king went out hunting. When he returned, we presented Garacharius, count of Bordeaux, and Bladastes to him. As we said above, they had taken refuge in the basilica of Saint Martin because they had joined Gundovald.

Previously I had pleaded their case but had been able to obtain nothing. Then I said:

“Let your power hear, O king. Look, I have been sent to you on an embassy by my lord. But what shall I report to the one who sent me, when you are unwilling to give me any answer?”

The king, astonished, said:

“And who is your lord, who sent you?”

I replied with a smile:

“Blessed Martin sent me.”

Then he ordered the men to be brought before him.

When they came into his presence, he reproached them for many acts of treachery and perjury, repeatedly calling them “clever foxes.” But he restored them to his favor and returned what had been taken from them.

### VII

[Note: [Col. 0453D] Those were said to “observe Masses” who attended the sacred mysteries but did not communicate, as Mabillon concludes in his *Gallican Liturgy* from chapter 8 of book X of this history. Canon 29 of the Third Council of Orléans (538) forbade anyone to observe the morning sacrifices of Mass or the evening ones while bearing weapons of war.]

When Sunday came, the king went to the church to observe the solemn celebration of the Masses. Those who were called “observers of the Masses” were present at the sacred mysteries but did not receive Communion, as our Mabillon concludes in his *Gallican Liturgy* from chapter 8 of book X of this history. Canon 29 of the Third Council of Orléans, held in 538, forbade anyone to observe the morning or evening sacrifices of the Mass while carrying weapons of war.

The brothers [bishops] and fellow priests who were present gave Bishop Palladius a place from which to conduct the festival. When he began the prophecy, the king asked who he was. When they announced that Bishop Palladius had begun it, the king immediately became agitated and said:

“Will the man who has always been faithless and treacherous to me now preach the sacred words? I shall leave this church altogether, lest I hear my enemy preaching.”

Saying this, he began to leave the church. Then the priests, disturbed by their brother’s humiliation, said to the king:

“We have seen him present at your banquet, and you receive a blessing from his hand; why, then, does the king now reject him? If we had known that he was hateful to you, we would certainly have turned to another who ought to have performed these rites. Now, if you permit it, let him complete what he has begun; but if hereafter you raise any objection, let the matter be settled by the severity of canonical sanction.”

Bishop Palladius had already withdrawn into the sacristy with great humility. Then the king ordered him to be recalled, and thus he completed what he had begun.

For when Palladius and Bertchramnus had again been invited to the king’s banquet, they became angry with one another and reproached each other with many adulteries and fornications, and also with certain perjuries. Many people laughed at these matters; but some of more discerning understanding lamented that the devil’s tares should grow in such a manner among the priests of the Lord.

Accordingly, when they departed from the king’s presence, they gave written guarantees and sureties that they would assemble at the synod on the tenth day before the Kalends of the ninth month.

### VIII

Then signs appeared: rays from the northern quarter, as they often tend to appear. A brightness seemed to pass across the sky, and flowers appeared on the trees. It was the fifth month.

### IX

[Note: [Col. 0453D] Baptism was administered not only at the Nativity of the Lord and of Saint John, but also on the feast-days of martyrs in certain churches. The fathers of the Second Council of Mâcon, held in 585, attempted to abolish this custom in accordance with the older canons.]

After this the king came to Paris and began to speak before everyone, saying:

“My brother Chilperic is said to have died leaving a son. The child’s guardians, at the mother’s request, asked that I receive him from the holy font at the solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity, but they did not bring him. Afterwards they asked that he be baptized at holy Easter, but even then the infant was not brought. A third time they pleaded that he be presented at the festival of Saint John, but even then he did not come.

“They therefore moved me, during a season of hardship, from the place where I was living. I came, and behold, the child was hidden and not shown to me. Hence, as far as I understand, there is nothing in the promise made to me; rather, I believe he is the son of one of our *leudes*. For if he had been of our lineage, he would certainly have been brought to me.

“Therefore know that I shall not receive him unless I learn certain proofs concerning him.”

When Queen Fredegund heard this, she gathered the leading men of her kingdom—namely, three bishops and three hundred of its best men—and they swore that this child had been fathered by King Chilperic. Thus suspicion was removed from the king’s mind. [Note: All manuscripts except Bad. read “from the king’s minds.”]

### X

Finally, since he often lamented the deaths of Merovech and Chlodovech, and did not know where they had been thrown after they were killed, a man came to the king and said:

“If it is not held against me hereafter, I will indicate the place where Chlodovech’s body lies.”

The king swore that no harm would be done to him, but rather that he would be increased with gifts. Then the man said:

“The truth of what I say will be confirmed by the very circumstances of the deed. When Chlodovech was killed and buried beneath the eaves of a certain chapel, the queen, fearing that he might someday be found and buried with honor, ordered him to be thrown into the river Marne.

[Note: Colb. m., with Bec., correctly reads *lapsum*, “net,” the word used for a fishing-net; in Colb. a. *lampsum* has “net” supplied by a second hand; Regm. reads *lacum*, “pool”; the printed editions read *capsum*. On Chlodovech’s death see above, book V, chapter 40; on Merovech’s killing, chapter 19 of that book. Both were brought back to Paris and buried in the basilica of Saint Vincent, now called Saint-Germain-des-Prés.]

“Later I found him in a net which I had prepared by my own labor for the purpose of catching fish. Since I did not know who he was, I recognized Chlodovech by his long hair. I seized him, carried him on my shoulders to the bank, and there buried him beneath a covering of turf.

“Here he is, his limbs preserved; do with him as you wish.”

When the king learned this, he pretended to go hunting. After the grave had been opened, he found the little body whole and unharmed. Only one part of the hair, which had been underneath, had already fallen away; the other part, with its locks of hair, remained intact.

It was recognized that this was the man whom the king had been earnestly seeking. The bishop of the city was therefore summoned, together with the clergy and people, and, amid an innumerable display of candles, the body was carried to the basilica of Saint Vincent to be buried. The king wept no less for his dead nephews than when he had seen his own sons already buried.

After this he sent Pappolus, bishop of the city of Chartres, who, having searched for Merovech’s body, buried it beside Chlodovech’s tomb.

### XI

[Note: This chapter is absent from Vat. and Colb. a.; Bec. reads: “Postarius . . . of another hostarius [doorkeeper].”]

A certain doorkeeper, however, spoke about another doorkeeper, saying:

“Lord king, this man accepted a reward and agreed that you should be killed.”

This doorkeeper was seized, beaten, and subjected to many tortures, but revealed nothing concerning the matter about which he was questioned. For many people were then saying that the affair had been brought about by intrigue and envy, because the doorkeeper against whom this crime had been alleged was greatly loved by the king.

Ansoualdus, touched by some suspicion—I do not know what kind—left the king without even saying farewell. The king, however, returned to Chalon and ordered Boantus, who had always been faithless to him, to be struck with the sword. Boantus barricaded himself in his house, but was killed by the king’s men; his possessions were brought under the authority of the fisc.

### XII

[Note: Regm. reads “as duke, on the side [of King Childebert]”; Colb. m. reads “led, as if,” perhaps for *dux*, “duke.”]

Finally, when the king was attempting with the greatest determination to persecute Bishop Theodore again, and when Massilia had already been restored to the dominion of King Childebert, Ratharius was sent there, as if as duke, on King Childebert’s behalf to hear legal cases.

But setting aside the business which had been assigned to him by the king, he surrounded the bishop, demanded sureties, and sent him to the presence of King Guntchramn, so that he might appear at the synod to be held at Mâcon, as though he were to be condemned by the bishops.

Yet divine vengeance was not absent; it is accustomed to defend its servants from the mouths of raging dogs. For as soon as the bishop had departed from the city, Ratharius immediately plundered the property of the church, claiming some of it for himself and locking up the rest under the protection of seals.

When he had done this, a most savage illness immediately attacked his servants and killed them, exhausted by fever. His son was overcome by the same affliction, and Ratharius buried him in the suburb of Massilia amid deep lamentation. Such a plague fell upon his household that, when he departed from that city, he was scarcely thought likely to return to his homeland.

Bishop Theodore, meanwhile, was detained by King Guntchramn. But the king did him no harm. He was a man of extraordinary holiness and constant in prayer. [Note: He is venerated as a saint in the Gallican Martyrology on 2 January; see above, book VI, chapter 24.] Concerning him Bishop Magneric of Trier related the following to me.

Some years earlier, when Theodore was being taken under such strict guard to the presence of King Childebert that, whenever he arrived at any city, he was not permitted to see either the bishop or any of the citizens, word was brought to the bishop, upon Theodore’s arrival at Trier, that he had already been put aboard a ship and was being secretly taken away.

The priest rose sadly and followed swiftly. He found Theodore on the bank and reproached the guards, asking why their impiety was so great that a brother was not permitted to see his brother. At last he saw him, kissed him, gave him some clothing, and departed.

[Note: Colb. m. and Regm. read “Martin.” Although Trier also has a basilica of Saint Martin, founded by Magneric himself, Saint Martin’s tomb was never there. Saint Maximin was buried in the suburban church which still bears his name; it is, like Saint Martin’s basilica, a celebrated Benedictine abbey.]

He then came to the basilica of Saint Maximin and prostrated himself at the tomb, retaining the words of the Apostle James: “Pray for one another, so that you may be saved” (James 5:16).

After pouring out a long prayer with tears, asking that the Lord deign to help his brother, he went outside. And behold, a woman whom a spirit of error was tormenting began to shout at the priest and say:

“O wicked and ancient man, who pours out prayer to the Lord for our enemy Theodore! Behold, every day we seek a way to drive him from these Gauls, for he consumes us with daily fires, and you do not cease praying for him! It would have been better for you to investigate carefully the property of your own church, lest anything be lost to the poor, than to plead so earnestly for this man.”

She kept saying:

“Woe to us, for we cannot overcome him!”

Although demons ought not to be believed, the sort of priest Theodore was became clear from the fact that the demon, in its grief, cried out these words against him. But let us return to the matter begun.

### XIII

[Note: Confluent, now commonly called Coblenz, remains a celebrated and strongly fortified place under the diocese and temporal jurisdiction of the archbishop of Trier.]

The king therefore sent envoys to his nephew Childebert, who was then staying at the fortress of Confluent, which received that name because the Moselle and the Rhine, flowing together from every direction, join there in the same place.

Since it had been agreed that the city of Troyes in Champagne should be joined to the two kingdoms, this arrangement did not seem suitable to the priests of Childebert’s kingdom. Felix, the envoy, first offered a greeting, displayed the letters, and said:

“Your uncle, O king, asks carefully who has drawn you away from this promise, so that the priests of your kingdom are delaying their arrival at the Council which you had jointly decided to hold. Or perhaps evil men are causing a root of discord to grow between you?”

While the king remained silent, I replied:

“It is no wonder if tares are sown among peoples, for among these men it cannot immediately discover where it may take root. [Note: Col. and Bign. read “who may take root”; a second hand in Colb. m. reads “where two”; Regm. reads “whom the root binds . . . can be found.”] Nothing is hidden: King Childebert has no other father than his uncle, nor does he intend to have any other son than this man, in accordance with what we heard him say this present year. [Note: See above, chapter 4, and book VII, chapter 33.] Far be it, then, that a root of discord should sprout between them, since they ought alike both to protect and to love each other.”

Then King Childebert called the envoy Felix aside and said to him:

“I beg my lord and father not to inflict any injury upon Bishop Theodore. If he does so, a scandal will immediately sprout between us, and we shall be separated by discord, although we ought to be peaceful by preserving love.”

After receiving answers concerning other matters as well, the envoy departed. [Note: After this, Vat. and Colb. a., omitting fourteen chapters, pass to chapter 28, concerning Hermenegild and Ingund.]

### XIV

While we were staying with the king in the aforementioned fortress, we were kept at the prince’s banquet until the night was dark. When the meal was finished, we rose and came to the river. There we encountered a boat on the bank which had been prepared for us.

As we boarded, a crowd of various people rushed upon us, and the boat was filled with both people and water. But the power of the Lord was present, with no small miracle: although the boat had been filled up to its rim, it could not sink.

We had with us the relics of blessed Martin and those of other saints, and we believe that we were saved by their power. When the boat returned to the bank from which we had departed, it was emptied of both people and water, and the outsiders were driven back. We crossed without hindrance.

The next day, after bidding the king farewell, we departed.

### XV

[Note: Eposium is also called Epusum; in the Antonine Itinerary, Epoisum; it is now commonly Ivois, a town in Luxembourg territory on the little river Chiers, called Ivois by the French and Ipsch by the Germans, and in recent years also Carignan. The monastery of Saint Martin praised here by Gregory, formerly on a neighboring hill, has been entirely destroyed. As Brower relates in the *Annals of Trier*, book X, around the year 979, Archbishop Egbert of Trier transferred the bones of Blessed Wulfilaic into the town. The same saint is commemorated in the Benedictine Fasti, under the name of Saint Wulf the convert, on 21 October; he was wrongly divided into the two names Wulfilaic and “layman,” although this passage proves that he was a deacon.]

We then set out on our journey and came to the fortress of Eposium. There, meeting the deacon Ulfilaicus, we were led to his monastery and received with the greatest kindness.

This monastery is situated about eight miles from the aforementioned fortress, on the summit of a mountain. On that mountain he built a large basilica, which he adorned with the relics of blessed Martin and of the other saints.

While we were staying there, we began to ask him to tell us something about the benefit of his conversion, or how he had entered the clerical office, since he was by birth a Lombard. But he could not explain it, for he was wholly intent on avoiding empty glory.

I adjured him with solemn oaths, first promising that I would not disclose to anyone what he told me, and began to ask him to conceal nothing from me of the matters about which I questioned him. After he had resisted for a very long time, he was finally overcome by both my prayers and my entreaties and spoke as follows:

“When I was a very small boy, I heard the name of blessed Martin. I did not yet know whether he was a martyr or a confessor, what good he had done in the world, or what region had deserved to receive his blessed limbs in a tomb. Yet I was already celebrating vigils in his honor, and, if any money came into my hands, I gave alms.

“As I advanced into greater age, I applied myself to learning letters. Through them I was able to write before I knew the order of the written letters.

“Then I joined Abbot Aredius, and, instructed by him, I visited the basilica of blessed Martin. On our return, he took up a little dust from the blessed tomb as a blessing. After placing it in a capsule, he hung it around my neck. [Note: Colb. m. and Bec. read “which, placed in a capsule, I hung . . . around [my neck].”]

“We were taken to his monastery in the territory of Limoges. [Note: The monastery of Attane, now distinguished by the name of its founder, Saint Aredius.] When he received the capsule in order to place it in his oratory, the dust increased so greatly that it not only filled the entire container but also spilled outside through the joins wherever it found an opening.

“From the light of this miracle my spirit was kindled more strongly to fix all my hope upon his power.

“Afterwards I sought the territory of the city of Trier, and by my own labor built the dwelling which you see on the mountain where you now are.

“Here, however, I found an image of Diana, which the unbelieving people worshiped as a god. I also erected a column upon which I stood amid great torment, without any covering for my feet.

“When winter arrived, as it usually does, [Note: Colb. m. and Bec. read *solite*, that is, “as usual,” as Bad. has; the others read *solitae*, referring it to “winter.”] I was so scorched by icy cold that the force of the cold often shook the nails from my feet, and water frozen into ice on my beard hung down like candles. That region is often said to endure a severe winter.

“But when we carefully asked what food or drink he had, or how he had overturned the images on that mountain, he said:

“‘My drink and food were a little bread and vegetables, and a small amount of water. But when a crowd from the neighboring villages began to gather around me, I continually preached that Diana was nothing, that the images were nothing, and that the worship which they seemed to practice was nothing; that those things were themselves unworthy, since they produced songs amid drinking and unrestrained revelry. Rather, a sacrifice of praise should be offered to almighty God, who made heaven and earth.

“‘I often prayed that the Lord, after the image had been destroyed, would deign to free the people from this error. The mercy of the Lord bent the rustic mind, causing it to incline its ear to the words of my mouth, so that, abandoning the idols, it might follow the Lord.

“‘Then I summoned some of them. With their help I later succeeded in uprooting this enormous image, which I could not overthrow by my own strength; for I had already broken the remaining images, which were easier.’”

That is, the other signs or images.

Already in the time of the emperor Domitian, the worship of Diana was famous in those regions, so that she was called Diana Arduinna, from the name of the celebrated forest, as is clear from an ancient inscription preserved by Browerus in his *Antiquities of Trier*. It seemed worthwhile to reproduce here the inscription itself, which proves that the worship of Diana was famous in the forest of the Ardennes:

> To the spirits of the departed. Quintus Caesius, son of Quintus, of the Claudian tribe, Atilianus, priest of Diana Arduinna, made this for himself and his heirs: twelve feet in front, fifteen feet in depth. On the fourth day before the Ides of October, during the consulship of the emperor Caesar Flavius Domitian, for the eighth time, and Gaius Valerius Messalinus.

From the same Browerus we learn that below a grove in the same region, near Echternach—a town distinguished by its Benedictine monastery—there is an ancient monument of Diana carved with varied ornamentation into solid rock. It is almost worn away, but bears this inscription:

> To the goddess Diana, Quintus Posthumus Potens fulfilled his vow willingly and deservedly.

Did Diana Arduinna derive her name from this? Certainly, in Gruter, chapter 49, there is an ancient inscription consecrated to five gods: Arduinna, Camulus, Jupiter, Mercury, and Hercules. The figure inscribed “Arduinna” is represented in the form of Diana.

“When many people had gathered at this statue of Diana, they cast ropes around it and began to pull. But all their labor was unable to accomplish anything.

“Then I hurried to the basilica, prostrated myself on the ground, and with tears implored divine mercy: since human effort could not overthrow it, might divine power destroy it.

“After the prayer I went outside and approached the workmen. We seized the rope, and as soon as we began to pull at the first effort, the image immediately fell to the ground. We smashed it with iron hammers and reduced it to dust.

“At that very hour, when I came to take food, my entire body, from the crown of my head to the sole of my foot, became so filled with malignant pustules that no spot large enough for a single finger could be found unoccupied.

“I entered the basilica alone and stripped myself before the holy altar. I had there a flask filled with oil, which I had brought from the basilica of Saint Martin. With my own hands I anointed all my limbs with it and then lay down to sleep.

“When I awoke around midnight and rose to recite the office, [Note: That is, to recite the divine office.] I found my entire body healthy, as though no ulcer had appeared upon me.

“I recognized that these wounds had been inflicted only through the envy of the enemy. Since that envious one always tries to harm those who seek God, when the bishops arrived—though they ought rather to have encouraged me to carry out the work I had begun with skill—they said to me:

“‘This is not a proper way for you to live, nor can you be compared with the lowly Simeon of Antioch, who sat upon a column. [Note: The celebrated Saint Simeon Stylites, of whom Gregory himself writes in *The Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 26.] Nor does the situation of this place allow you to endure such torment. Come down instead and live with the brothers whom you have gathered around you.’

“Because refusing to obey priests is reckoned a crime, I confess that I came down at their words. I walked with those same men and took food with them.

“Then one day the bishop, testing me, sent workmen farther away to the village with shields, hammers, and axes. They smashed the column upon which I had been accustomed to stand.

“On the following day I came and found everything destroyed, and I wept bitterly. But I could not erect what they had demolished, lest I be called opposed to the commands of the priests. Thus, as I now live, I am content to live with the brothers.”

### XVI

When I asked him to recount something of the miracles of blessed Martin which the saint had performed in that place, he related the following.

A certain Frank, a man of the highest nobility among his people, had a son who was mute and deaf. His parents brought him to this basilica, and I ordered him to rest on a little bed inside the holy temple with my deacon and another minister. During the day he devoted himself to prayer; at night he slept in the same church, as I have said.

One day, when God took pity on him, blessed Martin appeared to me in a vision and said:

“Cast the lamb out of the basilica, because he has now been healed.”

When morning came, while I was considering what this dream might mean, the boy came to me and, uttering his voice, began to give thanks to God. Then he turned to me and said:

“I give thanks to almighty God, who has restored both speech and hearing to me.”

Having thus been restored to health, he returned home.

Another man, who was frequently involved in thefts and various crimes and was accustomed to swear falsely, was once accused by certain people of theft. He said:

“I will go to the basilica of blessed Martin, and, clearing myself by oaths, I shall be declared innocent.”

When he entered, the axe slipped from his hand and fell at the door. Struck by severe pain of heart, the wretch confessed in his own words what he had come to excuse by perjury.

Another man, similarly accused of setting fire to his neighbor’s house, said:

“I will go to the church of Saint Martin, and, after giving my oath, I shall be declared innocent of this crime.”

It was clear that he had burned that house. As he went to give his oath, I turned to him and said:

“According to the testimony of your neighbors, you will not be innocent of this crime. Yet God is everywhere, and his power is outwardly present in the same way that it is inwardly present. Nevertheless, if empty confidence has so seized you that you think God or his saints do not punish perjuries, behold the holy church opposite you; swear as you please. But you will not be permitted to tread upon the sacred threshold.”

Then, raising his hands, he said:

“By almighty God and by the power of blessed Martin, his bishop, I did not commit this fire.”

After he had given his oath and was departing, it seemed to him that he was surrounded by fire. He immediately fell to the ground and began to cry out that he was being fiercely burned by the blessed bishop.

The wretch kept saying:

“I call God to witness: I saw fire fall from heaven, and, surrounding me with powerful vapors, it is consuming me.”

As he said this, he breathed out his spirit. This event became a lesson to many, so that they no longer dared to swear falsely in that place.

The deacon related many other miracles of this kind, but I thought it would take too long to follow them all.

### XVII

While we were staying in that place, we saw signs in the sky for two nights: rays from the northern quarter, shining so brightly that none had previously been seen to appear in this manner. On both sides, from the east wind and the west wind, there were blood-red clouds.

On the third night, around the second hour, these rays appeared again. And behold, while we gazed at them in astonishment, other rays like them rose from the four regions of the world. We saw the entire sky covered by them.

There was a bright cloud in the middle of the sky, toward which these rays gathered in the form of a tent. The tent began below with broader bands and narrowed upward, often gathering into a single peak like the crown of a hood. Among the rays there were also other clouds, flashing like a powerful lightning storm.

This sign inspired great fear in us (see above, chapter 24). For we expected some affliction from heaven to be sent upon us.

### XVIII

[Note: See Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book III, chapter 22; the chronicle of John of Biclaro; and, below, book X, chapter 3, on Wintrio. Fredegar’s Chronicle, chapter 14, calls him Quintrio, duke of Champagne. By Gudila he had a daughter, Saint Glodesind, abbess, who founded the nunnery at Metz still celebrated under her name; her Life is in the second Benedictine century, p. 1087.]

Meanwhile King Childebert, urged by imperial envoys who demanded the gold that had been given the previous year, sent an army into Italy. There was a report that his sister Ingund had already been transferred to Constantinople.

But when the commanders quarreled among themselves, they returned without acquiring any profit. Duke Wintrio, driven away by his own countrymen, lost his dukedom and would have ended his life had flight not provided him assistance. Later, however, after the people had been pacified, he recovered the dukedom.

Accordingly, Nicetius, removed from the county of Auvergne through the expulsion of Eulalius, sought a dukedom from the king, giving immense gifts for it. Thus he was appointed duke in the cities of Auvergne, Rodez, and Uzès. [Note: From this and similar passages Bignon argues that dukes ranked above counts, and that a duke need not have twelve counties subject to him; see below, book IX, chapter 7, and the notes of that learned man on book I of Marculf’s *Formulae*, no. 8, as well as Alteserra’s special book on the matter and Cange’s *Glossary*.] He was a man very young in years but sharp in judgment, and he established peace in the region of Auvergne and in the other places under his authority.

Duke Childeric the Saxon, having incurred the anger of King Guntchramn for the reason mentioned above, sought the basilica of Saint Martin, leaving his wife in the kingdom of the aforesaid king. The king had warned her not to presume to see her husband unless he had first been reconciled to royal favor.

After we had repeatedly sent embassies to the king on his behalf, we finally obtained permission for him to receive his wife and remain on this side of the Loire, [Note: Colb. m. and Regm. read “around the Loire.”] though he was not to presume to cross over to King Childebert.

But after receiving permission to take back his wife, he secretly crossed over to Childebert. Having been appointed duke over cities beyond the Garonne that were held under the power of the aforementioned king, he went there.

King Guntchramn, wishing to govern the kingdom of his nephew Chlothar, the son of Chilperic, decided that Theodulf should be count of Angers. When Theodulf was brought into the city, the citizens—and especially Domigisil—rejected him respectfully.

Returning to the king and receiving a second order, he was admitted by Duke Sigulf and governed the county of that city.

Gundobald, receiving the county of Meaux over Guerpin, entered the city [Note: Bec. reads thus; other witnesses read “Guerpin (or Vuerpin), and having entered,” whence Bignon conjecturally added “invaded”; Ches. reads “obtained.”] and began to conduct legal business. As he traveled through the district of the city in this capacity, he was killed by Guerpin in a certain village.

Gundobald’s relatives gathered and attacked Guerpin. They killed him after he had been shut up in a *pessile* of the house. [Note: The printed editions read “a hanging house”; Bec. “of a hanging house.” Valesius judges the reading *pessilem domus*, found in Colb. m., preferable, although he confesses that its meaning escapes him unless *pessile* is a part of a house whose significance is now unknown.] Thus both men departed from the county under the threat of death.

### XIX

[Note: Bec. omits “abbot”; nevertheless its chapter index has “Concerning Abbot Daulf.” Another witness reads “the adulterous husband, who ought to be killed on the land of this monastery.”]

Since Abbot Dagulf was often accused of his crimes—for he frequently committed thefts and murders and was also excessively unrestrained in adulteries—on one occasion, desiring the wife of his neighbor and having intercourse with her, he sought various opportunities by which he might kill the woman’s husband within the precincts of this monastery.

He had warned the husband, saying that if he approached his wife, he would be punished. After the man had departed from his lodging, Dagulf came by night with one cleric and entered the prostitute’s house.

After they had drunk for a very long time and become intoxicated, they lay down on one bed. While they were sleeping, the husband arrived, set fire to the straw, raised a double-bladed axe, and killed both of them.

Let this event therefore be a lesson to clerics, so that they do not, contrary to the statutes of the canons, enjoy the company of foreign women, since both the canonical law itself and all the sacred Scriptures forbid this—except in the case of those women whose conduct cannot be considered criminal.

### XX

[Note: For the canons of this synod and the names of those present, see Sirmond, vol. I, p. 381.]

Meanwhile the appointed day arrived, and the bishops, by order of King Guntchramn, gathered at the city of Mâcon.

Faustianus [Note: Other witnesses read Faustinianus; see above, book VII, chapter 31, where his ordination is described and Nicetius is discussed.], who had been ordained bishop of the city of Aix by order of Gundovald, was removed on the condition that Bertheramnus, Orestes, and Palladius, who had consecrated him, should support him in turn and provide him with one hundred gold pieces each year.

Nicetius, however, formerly a layman who had earlier obtained an order from King Chilperic, acquired the episcopate in that same city.

Bishop Ursicinus of Cahors was excommunicated because he openly confessed that he had received Gundovald. The settlement imposed on him was that, while doing penance for three years, he should cut neither his hair nor his beard, abstain from wine and meat, and be entirely forbidden to celebrate Masses, ordain clerics, bless churches and chrism, or distribute *eulogiae*. Nevertheless, he was to exercise the administration of the church’s temporal affairs and possessions as he ordinarily had. [Note: That is, he was to retain charge of the temporal affairs and possessions of his church. He nevertheless subscribed to the council among the other bishops; Faustianus also subscribed, although he is said there not to have a seat. Nicetius neither subscribed nor is listed among the other fathers, perhaps because the former count had not yet been ordained bishop.]

A certain bishop at this synod maintained that a woman could not be called a human being. But, after receiving a reasoned answer from the bishops, he fell silent, since the sacred book of the Old Testament teaches that, when God created humanity in the beginning, it says: “Male and female he created them, and he called their name Adam” (Genesis 5:2). This is explained as “earthly human being.” Thus he called the woman by the same name as the man, for he called both of them human beings.

The Lord Jesus Christ, too, is therefore called “the Son of Man,” because he is the son of a Virgin, that is, of a woman. When he was preparing to turn water into wine, he said: “Woman, what is that to me and to you?” (John 2:4), and so forth.

This case was settled after being refuted by many other testimonies as well.

Bishop Praetextatus of Rouen recited before the bishops the prayers which he had composed while in exile. Some were pleased with them; others criticized them because he had not followed the rules of the art. His style, however, was ecclesiastical and rational in many passages.

At that time there was a great slaughter between the servants of Bishop Priscus and those of Duke Leudegisil. [Note: Priscus was bishop of Lyons and held first place in the synod; see above, book IV, chapter 36, and *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 8.] Priscus, however, offered a large sum of money to purchase peace.

During these same days King Guntchramn fell seriously ill, so that some thought he could not survive at all. I believe this happened by God’s providence [Note: Another reading is “was.”], for he was considering driving many of the bishops into exile.

Bishop Theodore therefore returned to his own city and was received with praise, with the entire people welcoming him favorably.

### XXI

While this synod was being held, King Childebert [Col. 0463B] joined his retinue at the estate of Belsonancum, situated in the midst of the Ardennes Forest [Note: Ortelius suspects that the town of Bastonacum is meant here, which the inhabitants commonly call Bastoigne. Indeed, the *Deeds of the Bishops of Auxerre*, as Valesius himself attests, mention the estate of Bastonia, situated in the Ardennes Forest; today it lies not far from the River Ourthe and the Ardennes Forest, in the Duchy of Luxembourg.]. There Queen Brunichildis complained before everyone about her daughter Ingundis, who was still being held in Africa, but obtained little consolation.

Then a case arose against Guntram Boson. A few days earlier, a female relative of Boson’s wife had died without children and had been buried in the basilica of the city of Metz with great ornaments and much gold. A few days later the feast of Saint Remigius occurred [Note: Colb. manuscript and Regm., *Remedius*], which is celebrated at the beginning of October.

When many people were leaving the city with the bishop, and especially the leading citizens with the duke, Guntram Boson’s men came to the basilica where the woman had been buried. They entered, closed the doors over themselves, opened the tomb, and removed and carried away all the ornaments of the dead woman’s body that they could find.

When the monks of that basilica learned of this, they came to the door, but were not allowed to enter. Seeing this, they informed their bishop and duke. Meanwhile, the men, having taken the objects and mounted their horses, began to flee. But fearing that, if caught on the road, they would be subjected to various punishments, they returned to the basilica. They placed the objects upon the altar, but did not dare go outside; instead they shouted and said, “We have been sent by Guntram Boson.”

When Childebert had assembled with his nobles at the estate mentioned above, and Guntram, questioned about the matter, had given no answer, he secretly fled. Thereafter all the possessions that he had acquired in Auvergne as a grant from the treasury were taken from him [Col. 0464A]. He also abandoned in disgrace the property of various people whom he had wrongfully dispossessed.

### XXII

This year Laban, bishop of Elusa [Note: That is, the Elusan bishop. Elusa, commonly called Eause, was formerly the metropolis of Novempopulania [Col. 0464D]. After its destruction, this dignity was transferred to the city of Auch. Laban subscribed the Council of Paris IV in 573 and the Second Council of Mâcon through his representative in 585.], died. Desiderius, a layman, succeeded him. For the king had promised under oath that he would never ordain a bishop from among the laity. But what can the accursed hunger for gold not compel in human hearts?

Bertchramnus, returning from the synod, was seized by a fever. He summoned the deacon Waldo, who had himself also been called Bertchramnus at baptism, entrusted him with the whole substance of his episcopal office, and committed to him all the provisions of both his will and his benefactions. When Waldo had departed, Bertchramnus died [Note: Fortunatus, in the manner of poets, continues the praises of this Bertchramnus, bishop of Bordeaux, in Book III, chapters 20 and 21.].

The deacon returned with the gifts and the consent of the citizens [Col. 0464B] and hurried to the king, but obtained nothing. Then the king issued an order that Gundegisil, count of Saintes, surnamed Dodo, should be ordained bishop; and this was done.

Because many of the clergy of Saintes had, before the synod, supported Bishop Bertchramnus and had written certain hostile things against their priest Palladius, intended to humiliate him, they were seized by the priest after Bertchramnus’s death, severely beaten, and stripped.

At this time Wandelinus, the tutor of King Childebert, also died. No one was appointed in his place, because the queen mother wished to retain personal charge of her son. Whatever he had acquired from the treasury was restored to the treasury’s rights.

During these days Bodegisilus [Note: Fortunatus wrote his eulogy, Book VII, poem 5.], a duke full of years, died, but none of his property was diminished for his sons.

Fabius [Note: In the Colb. and Regm. manuscripts, *Sabius*; Bec. has *Saius*. Faustus attended the Second Council of Mâcon in 585.] was appointed in place of Faustus, bishop of Auch.

After the death of Saint Salvius, Desideratus was appointed bishop of Albi this year [Note: Some place Theofridus between the two; he may have occupied the see for some time. This is why Gregory records Salvius’s death in the preceding year, Book VII, chapter 1.].

### XXIII

There were great rains this year, and the rivers rose so high that shipwrecks frequently occurred. Overflowing their banks, covering the nearby crops and meadows, they caused severe destruction. The spring and summer months were so wet that winter seemed more likely to have arrived than summer.

### XXIV

This year two islands in the sea were divinely consumed by fire. For seven days they burned and collapsed, together with their people and animals. Those who had fled into the sea and plunged into its depths were consumed in the very water in which they submerged themselves; and those who did not immediately give up their spirit were burned by a more grievous punishment. When everything had been reduced to ash, the sea covered it all.

Many also reported that the signs which, as we related above in the eighth month, we had seen in the sky—apparently as though the heavens were burning—had been caused by the brightness of this fire (Chapters 8 and 17).

### XXV

On another island, situated near the city of Venice, there was a deep pond filled with fish. It was changed into blood to the depth of one cubit. For many days an immeasurable multitude of dogs and birds gathered there, licking this blood, and returned satiated at evening.

### XXVI

Ennodius was appointed duke over Tours and Poitiers. Berulfus [Note: Above he is called Eberulfus, as also in some manuscripts here and by others in the title of this chapter.], who had previously governed those cities, was suspected, together with his associate Arnegisil, of having secretly stolen the treasures of King Sigibert.

When he sought this duchy in the aforementioned cities, the duke Rauchingus [Note: Some printed editions have *Rochingus* and understand *ingenium* to mean an instrument, as though he had been bound together with another person by some sort of artfully constructed machine. But our reading, found in the Colb. manuscript, is better. They called an artifice by which they deceived someone acting incautiously an *ingenium*.] captured him and his companion by means of a trick. Without delay, servants sent to their houses plundered everything. Much of their own property and some of the aforesaid treasures were found there; all of it was brought to King Childebert.

When the matter had reached the point that the sword was about to sever their necks, their lives were obtained through the intervention of the bishops, and they were released. They received nothing, however, of what had been taken from them.

### XXVII

Duke Desiderius hurried to King Guntram with certain bishops and with Abbot Aredius, or Antestius. Since the king was reluctant to receive him, he was overcome by the priests’ petitions and restored Desiderius to his favor.

Then Eulalius appeared there, supposedly to bring a complaint concerning his wife, who had rejected him and gone over to Desiderius [Note: See below, chapter 45, and Book X, chapter 8.]. But he was reduced to ridicule and humiliation and remained silent.

Desiderius, having been rewarded by the king, returned with his favor.

### XXVIII

Thus, as we said above, Ingundis, abandoned by her husband with the emperor’s army while she was being led to that ruler with her little son, died and was buried in Africa.

Leuvichildus handed over to death his son Hermenegildus, whom the aforementioned woman had borne [Note: On 13 April, the day on which his feast is celebrated in the Church as that of a martyr. See above, Book V, chapter 39, and the notes.].

Moved by these events, King Guntram sent an army into Spain, intending first to subject Septimania—which is still considered within the boundaries of Gaul—to his rule, and then to advance farther.

While this army was on the move, a little document was found with some rustic people—I do not know who they were [Note: The printed editions have *a quibusdam nescio quibus*; Bec. has *cum nescio quibus hominibus*; Regm. has *Breviculum a*, and so forth.]. They sent it to King Guntram for reading. It was written as though Leuvichildus were writing to Fredegundis, urging her by whatever means she could to prevent that army from going forward, saying:

“Quickly kill our enemies, that is, Childebert [Note: Guntram had nevertheless declared war. Perhaps Leuvigildus thought that Guntram had undertaken it at the instigation of Childebert, Ingundis’s brother, or of their mother Brunichildis. Or perhaps Childebert himself had moved into Spain, as Paul the Deacon testifies, *History of the Lombards* III, chapter 21, where he says that the Spaniards were defeated by Childebert on that occasion. What Gregory relates here in several chapters, John of Biclaro compresses into one account under the year 586.] and his mother, and make peace with King Guntram, purchasing it with many rewards. And if you perhaps have too little money, we shall secretly send it; only fulfill what we ask.

“When we have taken revenge on our enemies, then give property to Bishop Amelius and the noblewoman Leuba [Note: The Colb. manuscript, in a second hand, has *retribuite*, ‘return’; Amelius was bishop of Bigorre and attended the Second Council of Mâcon.], through whom access will be opened for our messengers to come to you. For Leuba is the mother-in-law of the duke Bladastus.”

### XXIX

Although this letter had been brought to King Guntram and made known to his nephew Childebert, Fredegundis nevertheless ordered two iron knives to be made. She also ordered them to be sharpened more deeply and dipped in poison, so that, if the mortal attack did not dissolve the vital fibers, the poison itself might more quickly tear life away.

She handed these knives to two clerics with the following instructions:

“Take these swords and go as quickly as possible to King Childebert, pretending to be beggars. When you have thrown yourselves at his feet as though asking for alms, stab him through both sides, so that Brunichildis, who derives her arrogance from him, may fall when he falls and be subjected to me. But if the boy is so carefully guarded that you cannot approach him, kill the enemy woman herself.

“Your reward for this deed will be that, if you die in carrying it out, I shall give property to your parents and enrich them with gifts, making them foremost in my kingdom. Meanwhile, cast away all fear, and let there be no dread of death in your hearts. For you know that this fate overtakes all human beings. Arm your spirits with manly courage, and consider how often brave men have fallen in war. Their parents have consequently become noble, risen above everyone through immense wealth, and surpassed them all.”

As the woman spoke, the clerics began to tremble, thinking it difficult to fulfill these orders. Seeing them uncertain, she sent them, drugged with a potion, to the place she had ordered them to go;անակ immediately their courage increased, and they promised to carry out everything she had commanded.

She also ordered them to take a small vessel filled with this potion, saying:

“On the day when you carry out what I command, drink this potion in the morning before beginning the deed [Note: The printed editions have *incipiatur*, ‘before it is begun’; from this point, drink the potion.]. It will give you great firmness for accomplishing it.”

After instructing them in this way, she dismissed them.

They proceeded and, as they approached the city of Soissons, were captured by Duke Rauchingus [Col. 0466D]. Under examination, they disclosed everything and were then bound and confined in prison.

A few days later Fredegundis, now uncertain whether the orders had been carried out [the manuscript reading is *certa*, “certain,” but *incerta*, “uncertain,” is evidently intended], sent a boy to investigate what rumor the people were spreading, or whether he might find anyone saying that Childebert had already been killed.

The boy left her and came to the city of Soissons. Learning that the men were being held in prison, he approached the door. But when he began speaking with the guards, he too was captured and handed over to the custody.

Then all of them were sent together to King Childebert. Under examination, they revealed the truth, declaring that Fredegundis had sent them to kill him and saying:

“We received the queen’s orders to pretend to be poor. When we had thrown ourselves at your feet and asked for some payment, we intended to stab you with these swords. And if the sword had been driven in with a weaker attack, the poison with which the iron had been treated would quickly have penetrated your soul.”

After they had said this, they were subjected to various punishments: their hands, ears, and noses were cut off, and they were killed by different forms of execution.

### XXX

King Guntram therefore ordered an army to be mobilized against Spain [Note: Valesius, Book XIII of the *History of the Franks*, thinks that this expedition was completed in 585, before the Council held at Mâcon. But since above it is said to have been undertaken on account of the killing of Hermenegildus, and since John of Biclaro agrees in his *Chronicle*, it should rather, in my opinion, be assigned to the following year, that is, 586, in which Saint Hermenegildus was killed at his father’s command. Valesius’s error arose from his assigning to 585 the seventeenth year of Leuvigildus, which John of Biclaro calls the third year of Maurice; yet according to Biclaro’s reckoning that is the year 586.], saying:

“First subject the province of Septimania, which is near Gaul, to our authority. It is disgraceful that the boundary of the savage Goths should extend as far as Gaul.”

Then, having mobilized his entire royal army, he directed it there.

The peoples living beyond the Saône, Rhône, and Seine [Note: The Colb. manuscript has *Segona*.], joining with the Burgundians, devastated the banks of the Saône and Rhône, plundering both crops and livestock. They committed many murders, burnings, and acts of plunder in their own territory. They also stripped the churches and killed the clergy themselves, together with the priests and the rest of the people, at the very altars consecrated to God. They advanced as far as the city of Nîmes.

Likewise, the people of Bourges and Saintes, together with those of Périgueux, Angoulême, and the other cities that were then subject to the aforementioned king’s authority, traveled as far as the city of Carcassonne and committed similar crimes.

When they approached the city, the inhabitants voluntarily opened the gates. They entered without resistance, but, stirred by some quarrel with the people of Carcassonne, they left the city.

Then Terentiolus, formerly count of the city of Limoges, was struck by a stone thrown from the wall and died. His head was cut off in revenge against the enemy and carried into the city.

At this the entire population was terrified. Intending to return to their own country, they abandoned everything they had either seized along the way or brought with them.

The Goths also killed many of them after ambushing and stripping them. Then they fell into the hands of the people of Toulouse, whom they had inflicted with many injuries as they went; stripped and beaten by them, they scarcely managed to reach their own territory.

Those who had attacked Nîmes devastated the entire region, burning houses, setting crops on fire, uprooting olive groves, and cutting down vineyards. Unable to harm those inside the fortified towns, they advanced to other cities. These were strongly fortified and abundantly supplied with food and other necessities; although the attackers ravaged their surrounding districts, they were less able to break into the cities.

Duke Nicetius of Auvergne also set out on this expedition with the Auvergnates and besieged the cities with the others. When he was not succeeding, he reached a certain fort. After giving their word, the people inside voluntarily opened the gates, and, trusting them as peaceful men, received them. But after entering, the invaders disregarded their oath, plundered all the defenses, and reduced the inhabitants to captivity.

Then, after taking counsel, each man returned to his own country. Along the way they committed such crimes—murders, plunder, and pillage—through their own territory that it would take too long to recount them all.

Nevertheless, since we say that they burned the crops of Provence, people were left lifeless along the roads, perishing from hunger and starvation. Some were drowned in rivers, and many were killed in riots. It was reported that more than five thousand had been killed in these massacres.

Yet the deaths of the others did not restrain those who remained. At that time the churches of the Auvergne region that stood near the public roads were stripped of their sacred furnishings. There was no end to their wrongdoing until each man reached his own home.

When they had returned, great bitterness of heart took possession of King Guntram. The commanders of the army mentioned above went to the basilica of Saint Symphorian the Martyr. When the king came for the saint’s festival, they were brought before him under the condition that a hearing would take place later.

Afterward, when four bishops had been summoned [Note: So Bec., together with most printed editions. Colb. a. has, “After four days, when they had assembled”; Colb. m. has, “After three or four …”; Regm., “After three days, when four had assembled”; Bad., “After three or four days, when they had assembled,” and so forth.], together with the leading laymen, he began to question the commanders, saying:

“How can we obtain victory at this time, when we do not preserve what our fathers acquired? They built churches, placed all their hope in God, honored the martyrs, and revered the priests; with divine help they often subdued hostile peoples by sword and shield.

“But we not only fail to fear God; we even devastate his sacred places, kill his ministers, and tear apart and destroy the very relics of the saints as objects of mockery. Victory cannot be obtained where such things are committed. Therefore our hands are weak, the sword grows cold, and the shield no longer defends and protects us as it once did.

“Thus, if this is attributed to my guilt, may God now return it upon my head. But if you despise the royal commands and delay fulfilling what I order, the axe should already be sunk into your heads. It will be an example to the whole army when one of the leading men has been killed.

“Nevertheless, we must now determine what ought to be done. If anyone intends to follow justice, let him do so now; if anyone despises it, let public vengeance now hang over his neck. It is better that a few stubborn men perish than that God’s anger descend upon the whole innocent region.”

When the king had spoken, the commanders replied:

“Your Majesty, the greatness of your goodness cannot easily be described: your fear of God, your love for the churches, your reverence for priests, your compassion for the poor, and your generosity toward the needy.

“But because everything uttered by Your Glory is considered right and true, what shall we do when the whole population has fallen into vice and everyone delights in doing wrong? No one fears the king, no one fears the duke, and no one reveres the count. If anyone happens to dislike these things and attempts to correct them for the sake of your long life, rebellion immediately arises among the people, and immediately a tumult breaks out. Each person attacks his superior with such savage determination [Col. 0469B] that, if he cannot finally remain silent, he scarcely believes he will escape.”

The king replied:

“If anyone follows justice, let him live. If anyone rejects our law and command, let him perish now, so that this blasphemy [Gallic: *blâme*, ‘blame’] may no longer be directed against us.”

As he spoke, a messenger arrived and said:

“Richaredus, son of Leuvichildus, has come out of Spain and seized the fortifications of Caput Arietis [Note: It is commonly called Cabaret. Alteserra identifies it with Castelnaudary, which, he says, Peter of Vaux-de-Cernay calls *Castrum Novum Arii* in his *History of the Albigensians*, in the district of Lauragais.], devastated a large part of the territory of Toulouse, and carried away people as captives. He stormed the fortress of Ugernum near Arles [Note: This fortress is famous in ancient authors; according to Sidonius, Avitus was hailed there as emperor. Today, however, because the name has changed, it is uncertain whether it was Beaucaire, commonly called *Bellum Quadrum*, or the island of Guernica, commonly called La Vergne, a name that corresponds fairly well to Ugernum. Both places, though separated by the Rhône, are near Tarascon, from which the ancient Ugernum is certainly known to have been not far distant, as it was also from Arles, according to the *Life of Saint Caesarius*. Biclaro calls the modern place Ugernum in his *Chronicle.]; he carried off all its property and inhabitants, and then shut himself inside the walls of Nîmes.”

When the king heard this, he chose Leudegisil to replace Calumniosius, surnamed Aegilanis [Note: The Colb. manuscript, Regm., and Chesn. have *Agilanis*.], as duke, entrusted to him the entire region of Arles in Provence [Col. 0469C], and stationed more than four thousand guards along its borders.

Duke Nicetius of Auvergne likewise set out with guards and surrounded the boundaries of the region.

### XXXI

While these things were taking place, and Fredegundis was staying at the city of Rouen, she exchanged bitter words with Bishop Praetextatus. She said that a time would come when he would return to the places of exile in which he had been detained.

He replied:

“I have always been, am now, and shall remain a bishop both in exile and outside exile. For you will not always enjoy royal power. We are raised from exile into a kingdom by God’s gift; but you will be plunged from this kingdom into the abyss.

“It would have been better for you to abandon your folly and wickedness and turn now toward better things, and to withdraw from this boastfulness with which you are always inflamed. Then you might obtain eternal life and bring the little one whom you bore to legitimate age.”

After he had spoken these words, and the woman had taken them very badly, she withdrew from his presence, boiling with rage.

When the day of the Lord’s Resurrection arrived [Note: That is, Sunday, which authors of the later period commonly call “the day of the Lord’s resurrection.” If it is true that Praetextatus died on 24 February 586, the sixth day before the Kalends of March, this is the day on which he is commemorated in the Roman Martyrology; in a recently written copy of Usuard’s calendar from the church of Rouen, he is commemorated on the following day. Henschenius, however, understands this passage to refer to the Easter festival, in the entry for 24 February in the *Bollandists*, and the anonymous author cited below supports him. He therefore writes that Praetextatus died on 14 April, the day on which Easter was celebrated in 586. Praetextatus subscribed the Third Council of Paris, the Second Council of Tours, and finally the Second Council of Mâcon in 585; from this it is clear that his murder must be assigned to 586, as must the events Gregory relates in these chapters.], the priest went early to the church to perform the ecclesiastical offices. He began, as customary, to lead the antiphons in order.

While he was singing the psalms and was reclining upon the form [or platform], a cruel murderer appeared and struck the bishop, who was resting upon it, beneath the armpit with a knife drawn from his belt.

The bishop cried out for the clerics present to help him, but, though many stood around, no one came to his aid. Stretching his hands, covered with blood, toward the altar [Note: An anonymous author who wrote the *Acts of the Archbishops of Rouen* in the eleventh century, published in volume II of Mabillon’s *Analecta*, has: “As soon as he felt the wounds, he ran to the altar, embraced it, and fortifying himself with the viaticum of the Lord’s body and blood, gave his soul back to God.”], he offered a prayer and gave thanks to God. He was carried into his room in the hands of the faithful and placed upon his bed.

Immediately Fredegundis arrived with Duke Beppolenus and Ansovaldus, saying:

“It should not have happened to us and to the rest of your people, holy priest, that such things should befall your office. If only the identity of the man who dared to commit such a deed were revealed, so that he might endure punishments worthy of this crime.”

Knowing that she was uttering these words deceitfully, the priest replied:

“And who did this except the one who has killed kings, who has so often shed innocent blood, and who has committed various evils in this kingdom?”

The woman answered:

“We have very skilled physicians who can cure this wound. Permit them to come to you.”

He replied:

“God is already ordering me to be summoned from this world. You, who have proved yourself the chief author of these crimes, will be accursed in this age, and God will avenge my blood upon your head.”

When she departed, the bishop put his household in order and breathed his last.

Romacharius, bishop of the city of Coutances, came to bury him. At that time great grief seized all the citizens of Rouen, especially the leading Franks of that place.

One of the leading men came to Fredegundis and said:

“You have committed many evils in this world, but you have never yet done anything worse than ordering a priest of God to be killed. May God swiftly avenge innocent blood; for we shall all be investigators of this evil, so that you may no longer be permitted to commit such cruelties.”

As he departed from the queen’s presence after saying this, she sent someone to invite him to a banquet. When he refused, she asked that, if he did not wish to partake of her banquet, he would at least drink a cup, so that he would not leave the royal house fasting.

While he waited, he accepted the cup and drank wormwood mixed with wine and honey, as is customary among the barbarians [Note: Gregory repeatedly calls the Franks barbarians. Wormwood wine was used at banquets not only by barbarians but also by Romans, as is clear from Capitolinus’s *Life of Gordianus*, Lampridius’s *Life of Heliogabalus*, Saint Ambrose’s *Book on Tobit*, and other authors. Jonas also discusses it in the *Life of Saint Columbanus.]. But this drink had been poisoned.

As soon as he drank it, he felt a powerful pain attack his chest. As though he were being cut open internally, he cried out to his attendants:

“Flee, wretched men, flee this evil, lest you perish together with me.”

Although they had not drunk from it and hurried to depart, he immediately became blind. He mounted his horse, fell at the third milestone from that place, and died.

Afterward Bishop Leudovaldus [Note: He was the bishop of Bayeux, as appears from Book IX, chapter 13. His see was the first in Lower Lyon after the metropolitan see; therefore he then undertook responsibility for the widowed church of Rouen.] sent letters to all the priests and, after taking counsel, closed the churches of Rouen, so that the people would not attend the divine solemnities there until the author of this crime had been discovered through a common investigation.

He also arrested certain men and, after subjecting them to punishment, extorted the truth from them concerning how these things had been carried out through Fredegundis’s counsel. But because she defended them, he could not avenge the deed.

It was also reported that assassins had come against him because he was determined to investigate the matter diligently. But, protected by the guard of his people, he suffered no harm.

When these events had been reported to King Guntram and the accusation had been directed against the woman, he sent three bishops to the child who was said to be Chilperic’s son, whom we stated above was called Clotharius (Book VII, chapter 6): namely, Artemius of Sens, Veranus of Cavaillon [Note: So the manuscripts, and correctly. At that time Flavius governed the church of Chalon, while Veranus governed the church of Cavaillon, also called Cavellion or Cavellicum. Both subscribed the Council of Mâcon in 585. The *Life of Veranus* appears in volume II of Labbe’s *Bibliotheca nova*, p. 690. He died on the third day before the Ides of November, although his feast is celebrated in his city on the Ides themselves. Artemius of Sens subscribed the First and Second Councils of Mâcon and is commemorated at Sens on 23 April. Finally, Agroecius of Troyes subscribed the Second Council of Mâcon through his representative [Col. 0472C]. This has been noted because, for some reason unknown to me, the names of this bishop and of Felix of Belley are missing from their proper places in the subscriptions of the Council of Mâcon, as Sirmondus notes in his errata.], and Agroecius of Troyes.

He sent them so that, together with those who were raising the child, they might investigate the person responsible for this crime and bring him before the child.

When the priests had spoken, the leading men replied:

“We are utterly displeased by what has happened, and we desire more and more to avenge it. For it cannot be that, if someone guilty is found among us, he should be brought before your king, since we are able to restrain the crimes of our own people by royal authority [Note: They recognized no king other than the younger Chlotarius, whose nobles and counselors they were; because of the king’s infancy, the administration of affairs lay with them. Consequently, Guntram had no jurisdiction over them. Hence, with Fredegundis’s support, Melantius again obtained the see of Rouen; Gregory the Great commended him, together with Augustine and the other monks traveling to England, in Book IX, letter 52.].”

Then the priests said:

“Know that, unless the person who committed this deed is brought forward publicly, our king will come here with his army and lay waste to this whole region with sword and fire. For it is clear that the woman who ordered the Frank to be killed by magic has killed the bishop with the sword.”

After saying this, they departed without receiving any reasonable answer, earnestly warning that Melantius—who had previously been appointed in Praetextatus’s place—should never perform the priestly office in that church.

### XXXII

Many evils were committed at this time. Domnola, the former wife of Burgolenus and daughter of Victorius, bishop of Rennes [Note: He subscribed the Second Council of Tours in 567 and is praised by Fortunatus, Book III, poem 4.], whom Nectarius had married, had a dispute over vineyards with Bobolenus, Fredegundis’s referendary [Note: Regm. has *Bodoleno*. In the preceding chapter and below, chapter 42, he is called Beppolenus. See chapter 43. Here, as often in Gregory, *intentio* denotes a dispute or lawsuit.].

When he learned that she had come to these vineyards, he sent messengers warning her not to presume to enter the property. She disregarded this and proclaimed that the property had belonged to her father; then she entered.

The man, having stirred up a riot, attacked her with armed men. After she had been killed, he harvested the grapes and plundered the property. He also killed with the sword both the men and the women who were with her. None of them survived except those who managed to escape by flight.

### XXXIII

In those days there was a woman near the city of Paris who said to its inhabitants: “Flee from the city, and know that it is destined to be consumed by fire.” When many mocked her, supposing that she was saying this either from some prophetic omen, or because she had dreamed some empty dream, or certainly because she was uttering it under the inspiration of the noonday demon (see Book IV, *On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 36), she replied: “It is not at all as you say. For I am speaking the truth, because in a dream I saw a radiant man coming from the basilica of Saint Vincent, holding a candle in his hand and setting the houses of the merchants alight one after another.”
