[Col. 0472C] Finally, on the third night after the woman had spoken these words, at the beginning of dawn, one of the citizens entered a storeroom with a light burning. Having taken oil and the other things that were necessary, he went away, leaving the light beside a small vessel of oil.

[Note: [Col. 0472D] So the Casinensis manuscript; the others have *assumptoque eo* or *ab eo*.]

This house was the first one beside the gate that opens an exit toward the south. From that light the house caught fire and was consumed, and the other houses also began to catch fire. Then, when the fire collapsed upon the prisoners in the jail, blessed Germanus appeared to them. Breaking the beam and the chains by which they were held, and opening the door of the prison, he allowed the prisoners to leave unharmed. They went out and made their way to the basilica of Saint Vincent, where the tomb of the blessed Bishop is located.

Thus, while the wind carried the flames here and there throughout the entire city, and the fire raged with all its force, it began to approach another gate where there was an oratory of Saint Martin. This had once been built because there he had driven away the leprosy that disfigured a man by curing his skin with a kiss.

[Note: [Col. 0473D] Sulpicius Severus relates this miracle in the *Life of Saint Martin*. Valesius, in his *Dissertation on the Basilicas*, chapter 2, believes that the oratory mentioned here stood on the island in the Seine itself, by the northern gate of the city, far from the place where the church now called Saint-Martin-des-Champs is seen. King Philip I of the Franks assigned that church, built by his father King Henry, to the Benedictine monks of Cluny toward the end of the eleventh century. Henry nevertheless believed that he was building the church on the site where the old oratory had stood; but, says Valesius, he was mistaken, though this is not surprising, since no trace of the earlier building remained. It is nevertheless certain from a charter of Childebert III, which we shall publish in the Appendix, that under the first dynasty of our kings a basilica of Saint Martin existed at the place where the church of Saint-Martin-des-Champs now stands. Whether it is the same basilica that Gregory praises here we leave others to investigate.]

The man who had built it aloft among interwoven branches, trusting in the Lord and not doubting the power of blessed Martin, enclosed himself and his possessions within its walls, saying: “For I believe—and this is my faith—that the one who so often commanded fires to retreat, and who in this place cleansed a leper’s skin by a healing kiss, will drive the fire away from this place.”

As the fire approached, great balls of flame were carried toward it. Striking the wall of the oratory, they immediately grew lukewarm. The people shouted to the man and woman: “Flee, wretches, so that you may escape! Look, the weight of the fire is already falling upon you; look, the ashes of the fire with its embers are extending all the way to you like a violent rain. Leave the oratory, lest you be burned up in the same fire.”

But they continued to pray and were never moved by these words. Nor did the woman ever move away from the window through which the flames sometimes entered; she was fortified by the firmest confidence in the power of the blessed Bishop.

So great was the power of the blessed Bishop that he not only saved this oratory together with the house of his own fosterling, but also did not allow the flames, despite their dominance, to harm the other houses that surrounded it. There the fire fell, having begun to rage from one side of the bridge. On the other side it consumed everything with such force that the river brought it to an end. Nevertheless, the churches and their houses were not burned.

People used to say that this city had been consecrated in ancient times, so that neither fire nor serpent nor dormouse had ever prevailed there. But recently, when the channel beneath the bridge was being cleaned and the mud with which it had been filled was removed, they found a bronze serpent and dormouse. After these had been removed, dormice appeared there in numbers beyond counting, as did snakes; and afterward the city began to endure fires.

### XXXIV

Since the prince of darkness has a thousand ways of causing harm, I shall reveal what recently happened to certain recluses and devotees of God.

Vennocus the Briton, a priest distinguished by his office, whom we mentioned in another book,

[Note: [Col. 0474D] Above, Book V, chapter 22, where he is called *Vuinnochus* or *Vinnochus*.]

devoted himself to such strict abstinence that he wore only clothing made of skins and ate food consisting of uncooked wild herbs. He merely placed a vessel of wine to his mouth, so that it seemed more as though he were touching his lips to it than drinking from it.

But when the generosity of the devout frequently supplied him with vessels full of this liquid, he learned—which is worse—to drink beyond measure and to become so unrestrained through drinking that he was often seen drunk. As his drunkenness grew stronger, he was eventually seized by a demon and tormented by demonic possession, to such an extent that whenever he could seize a knife, any kind of weapon, a stone, or a club, he would run after people in mad fury. Necessity therefore required that he be kept chained in a small cell. After raging in this condition for two years, he breathed his last.

Another man, Anatolius of Bordeaux, a boy—so they say—of twelve years, was serving as an attendant to a certain merchant when he asked that permission be granted him to become a recluse. His master resisted for a long time, thinking that the boy would grow lukewarm in this undertaking and would be unable, at that age, to accomplish what he was attempting to pursue. At last, overcome by the attendant’s pleas, he granted him permission to carry out what he requested.

There was an ancient crypt there, vaulted [in French, *voûté*] and constructed with elegant workmanship. In one corner was a small cell enclosed by squared stones, large enough to admit scarcely one standing person. The boy entered this cell. He remained there for eight years or more, content with meager food and drink, and devoted himself to vigils and prayers.

Afterward, having suffered a powerful terror, he began to cry out that he was being tormented within. It happened that, aided—as I believe—by the forces of the diabolical party, he knocked out the squared stones by which he had been enclosed, smashed the wall down to the ground, beat his palms together, and cried that he was being burned by God’s saints.

When he had been kept in this madness for a very long time, and repeatedly invoked the name of Saint Martin, saying that he was being tormented by him rather than by the other saints, he was brought to Tours. But, I believe, the evil spirit was restrained by the power and greatness of the saint and did not mutilate the man. After remaining there for a year without suffering any harm, he returned; but once again he fell into the condition from which he had been free.

### XXXV

Envoys from Spain came to King Guntram with many gifts, asking for peace, but they received no definite answer. For in the preceding year, when the army had subdued Septimania, the ships that had gone from Gaul to Galicia were ravaged by order of King Leuvichild; their goods were taken, their men were beaten and killed, and some were carried away captive.

[Note: [Col. 0474D] John of Biclaro intended to designate this same event in his *Chronicle*, where, under the seventeenth year of Leuvigild, he reports that the province of Galicia—one should read, from this passage of Gregory, *Gallecia* or *Callaecia*—was freed from Frankish attack.]

A few of the survivors escaped in small boats and reported to their homeland what had happened.

### XXXVI

Thus, at the court of King Childebert, Magnovaldus was killed by royal order for secret reasons, in the following manner.

The king was standing inside the palace of the city of Metz and watching a spectacle, observing how an animal surrounded by a pack of dogs was being harried. Magnovaldus was summoned. He came, unaware of what was to happen, and, laughing freely with the others, began to watch the animal.

But the man who had been ordered to do it, seeing him absorbed in the spectacle, swung an axe and struck him on the head. He fell and died. His body was thrown out through a window of the house and buried by his own people; his possessions were immediately seized, and whatever was found was brought into the public treasury.

Some, however, maintained that the reason for his execution was that, after his brother’s death, he had killed his brother’s wife by inflicting various wounds upon her and had taken his brother’s wife to his bed.

### XXXVII

After this, a son was born to King Childebert. He was received from the sacred font by Magneric, Bishop of Trier,

[Note: [Col. 0475D] He is commemorated on 25 July and was buried in the monastery of Saint Martin, which he himself founded and which still exists under Benedictine observance. Ebervinus, its abbot, wrote his *Life*. He is praised by Fortunatus, Book III, poem 11, and frequently by our Gregory.]

and was named Theodobert. King Guntram felt such joy at this that he immediately sent envoys and sent him many gifts, saying: “Through this child God, by the particular mercy of his majesty, will raise up the kingdom of the Franks, if his father, or he himself, should live to succeed his father.”

### XXXVIII

In the eleventh year of the reign of King Childebert, envoys again came from Spain, asking for peace; but obtaining no definite answer, they returned. Richared, the son of Leuvichild, came as far as Narbonne, raided within the boundaries of Gaul, and secretly withdrew.

### XXXIX

In that year many bishops died.

[Note: [Col. 0475D] This chapter and the four following are absent from Colbertinus a. and the Vatican manuscript. Concerning Badegisilus, see above, Book VI, chapter 9; he subscribed the Second Council of Mâcon in 585. His wife is called Magnatrudis below, Book X, chapter 5. He must be distinguished from Bertegisilus, who twice invaded the same see, as Saint Bertramnus complains in his Testament.]

Badegisilus, Bishop of Le Mans, was a very savage man toward the people, unjustly taking away or plundering the property of various persons. His wife, who was even more savage, joined herself to his harsh and pitiless disposition and goaded him into committing crimes with the wickedest counsels.

No day or moment passed in which he was not engaged either in plundering citizens or in various disputes. Every day he continued to hear cases with judges, exercise secular military authority, rage against some people, and drive others to slaughter. He even proceeded to beat many with his own hands and to say: “Just because I have become a cleric, shall I not avenge my injuries?”

But what shall I say about the rest, when he did not even spare his own brothers and sisters, but plundered them more than others? They were never able to obtain justice from him concerning their paternal or maternal property.

After completing the fifth year of his episcopate, as he was entering the sixth, he prepared a banquet for the citizens with immense rejoicing. But after he was seized by a fever, he promptly ended the year he had begun, death overtaking him. In his place Bertchramnus, an archdeacon of Paris,

[Note: [Col. 0475D] His *Acts* are found in volume III of Mabillon’s *Analecta*. Among other many gifts that he made to various churches, his Testament records that he left the estate of Bobane, in the territory of Étampes on the river Cala, to the basilica of blessed Vincent, where the body of blessed Germanus, by whom he had been nourished, rests. He asked the abbot of that distinguished place to have his name recited in the book of life. He took part in various councils. His feast is celebrated in the *Gallican Martyrology* on 3 February. Papebrochius discusses him under 6 June in the *Acta Sanctorum*.]

was appointed.

He is reported to have had many disputes with the widow of the deceased, because she retained as her own the property that had been given to the church during the episcopate of Badegisilus, saying: “This was my husband’s office.” Although unwilling, she nevertheless restored everything.

She was of unspeakable wickedness. For she often cut away from men everything shameful, together with the skin of their bellies, and burned women’s more private bodily parts with red-hot metal plates. She also committed many other wicked acts, which I have thought it better to leave unmentioned.

Sabaudus, Bishop of Arles, also died,

[Note: [Col. 0476D] He was discussed above, Book IV, chapter 30; he is commonly called Sapaudus. He took part in various councils and received from Pope Pelagius the vicariate in Gaul. Licerius is discussed below, Book IX, chapter 23.]

and Licerius, King Guntram’s referendary, was appointed in his place. At that time a severe plague devastated the province of Provence.

Evantius, Bishop of Vienne, also died,

[Note: [Col. 0476D] Evantius subscribed the First Council of Mâcon in 581, the Third Council of Lyon in 583, the Second Council of Valence in 584, and the Second Council of Mâcon in 585. Some commemorate his feast on 13 January, others on 3 February.]

and Virus, a priest from the senatorial class, was appointed to his see by the king.

Many other priests also departed from this world in that year; I have chosen to pass over them,

[Note: [Col. 0476D] The Reginensis manuscript has *nolui* (“I did not wish to”).]

since each left memorials of himself in his own city.

### XL

There was also in the city of Tours a certain Pelagius, practiced in every kind of wickedness and fearing no judge because the keepers of the royal draft animals were under his authority. For this reason he never ceased committing thefts, sudden and unforeseen robberies or acts of violence,

[Note: [Col. 0476D] That is, robberies or sudden and unforeseen acts of violence.]

seizures, murders, and various crimes, both on the rivers and on land.

I often summoned him and tried, with threatening as well as gentle words, to restrain him from this wickedness. But from him I received hatred rather than any benefit of justice, in accordance with that saying from the Wisdom of Solomon: “Reprove a fool, and he will add to his hatred of you” (Proverbs 9:8).

For the wretched man hated me so greatly that, after frequently robbing and beating people, he often left them lifeless and sought ways to bring charges against the church or the basilica of Saint Martin.

It happened once that he beat and trampled our men as they came carrying a hedgehog in vessels, and seized the vessels themselves. When I learned of this, I suspended him from communion—not as an avenger of my own injury, but so that I might more easily bring him back from this madness in a reformed condition.

But he came with twelve men whom he had chosen in order to swear falsely concerning this crime. Since I was unwilling to accept any oath, he or our fellow citizens compelled me; after dismissing the others, I accepted only his oath and ordered him to be received back into communion.

At that time it was the first month. When the fifth month arrived, in which meadows are usually mown, he invaded the meadow of the nuns, which adjoined the boundary of his own meadow. As soon as he put the sickle to it, he was seized by a fever and breathed his last on the third day.

He had prepared a tomb for himself in the basilica of Saint Martin at the village of Condat. When it was uncovered, his people found it broken open and smashed to pieces.

[Note: [Col. 0477D] The Reginensis manuscript has “uncovered,” or “broken open.”]

He was therefore buried afterward in the portico of that basilica. The vessels containing the hedgehog, concerning which he had sworn falsely, were also taken from his storeroom after his death.

The power of blessed Mary was made manifest,

[Note: [Col. 0477D] The Badian manuscript has “of Saint Martin.”]

in whose basilica the wretched man had uttered his false oath.

### XLI

When the report spread throughout the whole land that Bishop Praetextatus had been killed by Fredegund, she, in order more easily to clear herself of the crime, ordered the boy who had been seized to be beaten severely, saying: “You have brought this slander upon me, claiming that you attacked Praetextatus, Bishop of the city of Rouen, with a sword.”

She handed him over to the priest’s nephew. When he had subjected him to torture, the boy revealed the entire matter clearly and said: “For I received one hundred solidi from Queen Fredegund to do this; from Bishop Melantius, fifty; and from the city’s archdeacon, another fifty. In addition, I had been promised that I would become a free man, as would my wife.”

At these words, the man drew his sword and cut the accused into pieces. Fredegund then appointed Melantius, whom she had previously made bishop, to the church.

### XLII

While Duke Beppolenus was being severely harassed by Fredegund and was not receiving the honor due to his rank, he saw that he was despised and went to King Guntram. From him he received authority over the duchy comprising the cities that belonged to Chlothar, the son of King Chilperic. He proceeded there with a large force, but was not received by the people of Rennes.

When he came to Angers, he committed many evils there. He devastated the grain, hay, wine, and whatever else he could find in the houses of the citizens he visited, breaking down the doors without waiting for the keys. He killed and trampled many of the inhabitants of the place. He also struck fear into Domigisilus, but was reconciled with him.

When he approached the city and was dining with various people in a *tristega*,

[Note: [Col. 0477D] Colbertinus m. and Reginensis have *tristico*; the Bec manuscript has nothing. *Tristega* are buildings divided into three stories; a *pulpitum* is the roof of a single-storied building.]

the roof of the house suddenly broke through, and he barely escaped half alive, while many others were crippled. Nevertheless, he continued in the same evil actions that he had previously committed.

At that time Fredegund also overturned much of his property in her son’s kingdom. He himself returned to Rennes, wishing to subject its people to King Guntram, and left his son there. Before much time had passed, the people of Rennes attacked and killed the son together with many distinguished men.

Many signs appeared in that year. In the seventh month trees were seen to flower, and many trees that had previously borne fruit produced new fruit, which remained on the trees until the time of the Lord’s Nativity. A flash of light was seen to run across the sky in the form of a serpent.

### XLIII

In the twelfth year of King Childebert, Nicetius the Auvergnian was appointed governor of the Province of Marseille and of the other cities in those regions that belonged to that king’s kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 0477D] Under the sons of Chlothar I, Provence was divided into two parts. One was called the Province of Arles, comprising Arles, Riez, and other cities, and was assigned to Guntram; the other, called the Province of Marseille, comprising Marseille, Avignon, Aix, and other towns, was obtained by Sigibert. The governors of the former are often called patricians by the ancient historians, and sometimes also dukes. The prefects of the latter were occasionally called patricians; here Nicetius is called governor.]

Antestius was sent by King Guntram to Angers. There he inflicted many injuries on those who had been involved in the death of Domnola, the wife of Nectarius. He confiscated the property of Beppolenus,

[Note: [Col. 0478D] Several editions have *Bobolenus*, as above in chapter 32; the Reginensis has *Bobellinus*.]

because he had been the chief author of this crime. He then went to Nantes and began to challenge Bishop Nonnichius, saying: “Since your son was involved in this crime, justice demands that he suffer a punishment worthy of his offenses.”

But the boy, terrified by the accusation of his conscience, fled to Chlothar, the son of Chilperic. Antestius, after receiving sureties from the bishop that he would appear in the king’s presence, went to Saintes.

A report had meanwhile spread that Fredegund was secretly sending envoys to Spain, that they had been secretly received by Palladius, Bishop of Saintes, and then sent onward. At that time it was the season of holy Lent, and the bishop had withdrawn to an island in the sea for the sake of prayer.

[Note: [Col. 0478D] It was the custom of holy men to withdraw into the wilderness during the days of Lent. See the Preface to the first century of the Benedictines, no. 111.]

According to custom, while he was returning to his church, where the people were awaiting him for the celebrations of the Lord’s Supper, Antestius surrounded him on the road. He said—perhaps the text should read *cui* (“to whom”) rather than *qui*—without having investigated the truth of the matter: “You shall not enter the city, but shall be condemned to exile, because you received envoys of the enemy of our lord the king.”

The bishop replied: “I do not know what you are talking about. Nevertheless, since the holy days are approaching, let us go to the city. When the celebrations of the holy solemnities have passed, bring forward whatever charges you wish, and you will receive an answer from me, because what you allege is nothing.”

But Antestius said: “By no means. You shall not reach the threshold of your church, because you have proved disloyal to our lord the king.”

What more is there to say? The bishop was detained on the road, the church’s house was inventoried, and its property was plundered. The citizens could not persuade the man

[Note: [Col. 0479D] That is, “could not prevail against the man,” namely, Antestius.]

to allow the matter to be investigated at least after the Easter celebration. When they pleaded and he resisted, he finally disclosed the wound hidden in his heart.

“If he sells to me the house that he is known to possess within the boundaries of the territory of Bourges, and places it under my control, I shall do what you request,” he said. “Otherwise he will not escape my hands unless he is driven into exile.”

The bishop was afraid to refuse. He wrote, signed, and handed over the estate. After giving sureties for his appearance before the king, he was thus permitted to enter the city.

When the holy days had passed, he went to the king. Antestius was also present, but was unable to prove any of the charges he had brought against the bishop. The bishop was ordered to return to his city, and the matter was deferred until the next synod, so that perhaps some of the charges brought against him might be established more clearly.

[Note: [Col. 0479D] He is praised by Fortunatus, Book I, poem 3, for having built a church to Saint Stephen. He had also built another in honor of Saints Peter, Paul, Lawrence, and Pancratius. It contained thirteen altars, but four of them had not been consecrated because he had no relics to place in them, as is clear from Saint Gregory the Great’s Letter 50, Book V. There the blessed pontiff states that he sent Palladius the relics he had requested from him; in Letter 52 of the same book he also commended to Palladius Augustine and other monks traveling to England. His name appears in the calendars of the Church, and he is honored as a saint in his own church. He subscribed the Fourth Council of Paris in 573 and the Second Council of Mâcon in 585.]

Bishop Nonnichius was also present, and he departed after giving many gifts.

[Note: [Col. 0479D] He was the Bishop of Nantes and successor to Felix, as stated above, Book VI, chapter 15; he is also praised in Book IV, *On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 26. Another bishop of the same see was Nonnichius, or Nunichius, who subscribed the Council of Vannes in the preceding century and to whom Apollinaris Sidonius wrote Letter 13 of Book VIII.]

### XLIV

Fredegund, supposedly in the name of her son, sent envoys to King Guntram. After their request had been disclosed and they had received a response, they took their leave and departed; but for some reason they lingered for a while near his lodging.

When morning came, as the king was proceeding to Matins with a candle carried before him, a man appeared to be sleeping like a drunkard in a corner of the oratory. He was girded with a sword, whose blade rested against the wall.

When the king saw this, he exclaimed that it was not normal for a man to rest in such a place under the terror of night. The man was seized, bound with thongs, and questioned about the meaning of his actions.

Without delay he was subjected to torture and said that he had been sent out by the envoys who had arrived, so that the king might be killed. The envoys of Fredegund were then seized, but when questioned they confessed nothing about the matter, saying: “We were sent for no other purpose than to deliver the embassy that we have presented.”

The king therefore ordered the man to be beaten with various wounds and confined in prison, and ordered the envoys to be condemned to exile in different places. It became entirely clear that Fredegund had sent them under this plot so that they might kill the king.

[Col. 0480A] The mercy of the Lord did not permit this. Among them Baddo was considered the senior.

[Note: [Col. 0480D] The Colbertinus a. manuscript has *Batto*.]

### XLV

When envoys from Spain repeatedly came to King Guntram and were unable to obtain any favor of peace, while hostility instead continued to grow, King Guntram restored the city of Albi to his nephew Childebert.

When Duke Desiderius saw this—he had established the best of his property in the territory of that city—he feared that vengeance might be exacted from him because of his former hostility, since he had once severely afflicted the army of the glorious King Sigibert in that same city. He therefore crossed into the territory of Toulouse with his wife Tetradia, whom he had formerly taken from Eulalius, then Count of Auvergne, and with all their possessions. He raised an army and prepared to march against the Goths, after first dividing his property, as they say, between his sons and his wife.

Taking with him Count Austrovald, he headed for Carcassonne. When the citizens of that city heard this, they prepared themselves as though intending to resist; they had learned of his plans beforehand.

When the battle was finally joined, the Goths began to flee, and Desiderius and Austrovald struck the enemy from behind. When the Goths had also fled, Desiderius approached the city with a few men, for the horses of his companions had been exhausted.

As he approached the city gate, surrounded by the citizens who were inside the walls, he was killed together with all who had followed him. Only a few somehow escaped and reported what had happened.

When Austrovald heard that Desiderius was dead, he turned back from the road and went to the king, who immediately appointed him duke in Desiderius’s place.

### XLVI

After this,

[Note: [Col. 0480D] This chapter is absent from Colbertinus a. and the Vatican manuscript.]

Leuvichild, King of the Spaniards, began to fall ill. But, as some assert, he did penance for his heretical error, urged that no one be found to support this heresy, and passed over into the Catholic faith. After continuing for seven days in tears over the things he had wickedly attempted against God, he breathed his last.

[Note: [Col. 0480D] He did indeed recognize the truth, according to Gregory the Great, Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 31: “But, terrified by fear of his people, he did not deserve to arrive at the Catholic faith.” Neither John of Biclaro nor Isidore, under the year 606 of the era, writes of Leuvigild’s conversion, although they provide much information about him. Paul of Mérida says that he departed this life to everlasting punishment, chapter 16 of *The Lives of the Fathers of Mérida*.]

His son Richared succeeded him as king.

XXVIII. On the gifts that Queen Brunichild sent.  
XXIX. That the Lombards asked King Childebert for peace.  
XXX. On the surveyors of the cities of Poitiers and Tours.  
XXXI. That King Guntram sent an army into Septimania.  
XXXII. On the hostilities between Childebert and Guntram.  
XXXIII. That the devout woman Ingeltrudis went to Childebert to bring a complaint against her daughter.  
XXXIV. On Fredegund’s hostility toward her daughter.  
XXXV. On the death of Waddo.  
XXXVI. That King Childebert sent his son Theodobert to Soissons.  
XXXVII. On Bishop Droctigisilus.  
XXXVIII. On the attempt of certain men to act against Queen Brunichild.  
XXXIX. On the scandal that arose in the monastery at Poitiers through Chrodield and Basina. — Letter of the bishops to Saint Radegund.  
XL. On the first cause of the scandal.  
XLI. On the slaughter in the basilica of Saint Hilary. — Rescript of the bishops.  
XLII. Copies of the letter that Saint Radegund sent to the bishops.  
XLIII. That the priest Theutarius came to calm this scandal.  
XLIV. On the unseasonable weather of the year.

# BOOK NINE

[Col. 0481]

### I

[Col. 0481A] Thus, after the death of Leuvichild, King of the Spaniards, his son Richared made a treaty with Goisvintha, his father’s widow, and received her as his mother.

[Note: [Col. 0481B] Nevertheless, she later joined herself to Uldila, an Arian bishop, and plotted against Reccared, as John of Biclaro reports under Reccared’s third year.]

For she was the mother of Queen Brunichild, the mother of the younger Childebert. Richared, however, was Leuvichild’s son by another wife.

After conferring with his stepmother, Richared sent envoys to King Guntram and to Childebert, saying: “Be at peace with us, and let us enter into a treaty, so that, supported by your protection, whenever necessity demands, we may in like condition, with affection intervening, protect one another.”

[Note: [Col. 0481B] All printed and manuscript witnesses read this way. Nevertheless, unless I am mistaken, it should read: “So that we may protect you in like condition,” or else: “So that we may protect one another in like condition …”]

The envoys who had been sent to King Guntram were ordered to remain at the town of Mâcon.

[Note: [Col. 0481B] So all the manuscripts and most editions. Colbertinus and Bignonius have *Matescense*. In either case Mâcon must be understood. Fortunatus certainly has *Matasconem* for *Matisconem* in the *Life of Saint Germanus*.]

There the king learned the reasons for their mission through the men who had been sent to him, but he refused to receive their words. Hence afterward such hostility grew up between them that they did not allow anyone from his kingdom to pass into the cities of Septimania.

Those who came to King Childebert, however, were received with goodwill. After gifts had been given and peace had been obtained, they returned with gifts.

### II

In that year the most blessed Radegund departed from this world. She left great mourning in the monastery that she had founded. I too was present at her burial.

She died in the sixth month, on the thirteenth day of the month, and was buried three days later. The miracles that appeared there on that very day, and the manner in which her funeral took place, I have tried to describe more fully in the *Book of Miracles*.

[Note: [Col. 0482B] *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 106. He also discusses her in Book I, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 5. She died on 13 August, in the year 587, as follows from this passage of Gregory. She was buried in the basilica of Saint Mary, where at that time there was a cemetery for nuns and which is now occupied by secular canons. Most of her sacred relics, together with the remains of Saint Hilary, were burned by the Calvinists in 1562. See the note on Book III, chapter 7.]

### III

[Col. 0483A] Meanwhile, the feast of Saint Marcellus arrived. It is celebrated in the city of Chalon in the seventh month, and King Guntram was present.

When, after the solemn rites had been completed, he approached the most holy altar in order to receive communion,

[Note: [Col. 0483D] The ancient custom of the Gallican Church should be noted here: holy communion was administered only after the Mass had been completed. See *Gallican Liturgy*, Book I, chapter 5.]

a certain man came forward as though he wished to present a petition. As he hurried toward the king, a knife slipped from his hand. When he was suddenly seized, they found another unsheathed knife in his hand.

Without delay he was led out of the holy basilica, bound, and subjected to torture. He confessed that he had been sent to kill the king, saying: “This is how the man who sent me instructed me.”

Because the king knew that many hatreds had gathered against him and feared that he might be struck down, he ordered himself to be completely surrounded by his men. No way could be found for anyone with swords to approach him except that he might be stabbed in the church, where he was known to stand safely and without fear.

When those about whom the man had spoken were also seized and many had been killed, the king released the man alive after he had been beaten with blows, because he considered it sacrilegious

[Note: [Col. 0483D] The Fathers assert that the right of asylum had been granted to churches from the earliest centuries of the Church, once Christian rulers had arisen. The First Council of Orléans, under the great Clovis in 511, established it; it was later confirmed repeatedly both by various conciliar canons and by edicts of our kings.]

to put to death one who had been led out of a church.

## IV

[Note: This chapter is absent from the Colbertine and Regius manuscripts, although it is listed in their table of contents for this book.]

That year another son was born to King Childebert, whom Bishop Veranus of Chalon, receiving him from the font, named Theodoric. For at that time the bishop himself was endowed with great virtues, so that, often making the sign of the cross over the sick, he immediately restored them to health, with the Lord’s aid.

[Note: The Bec and Colbertine manuscript A correctly read *Cavillonensis* rather than *Cavellionensis*, as observed above at Book VIII, chapter 31; the printed editions have *Cabillonensis*. Fredegar records Theodoric’s birth in the following year.]

## V

[Note: This chapter, together with the following three, is absent from the Colbertine manuscript A and the Vatican manuscript.]

Many portents also appeared afterward. For vessels throughout the houses of various people were marked with certain signs, I do not know what kind, and this marking could in no way ever be scraped away or erased. This portent began in the territory of the city of Chartres and, passing through the territory of Orléans, advanced as far as the boundary of Bordeaux, omitting no city that lay in between. In the vineyards, after the vintage had ended in the eighth month, we saw new shoots bearing deformed grapes. On other trees new leaves and new fruits appeared. Rays appeared in the northern quarter. Some claimed that they had seen serpents falling from a cloud. Others asserted that a village, with its cottages and inhabitants, had suddenly vanished in total destruction. Many other signs also appeared, which usually announce either the death of a king or the ruin of a region. The vintage that year was scanty, the waters violent, the rains immense, and the rivers greatly swollen.

## VI

That year there was in the city of Tours a man named Desiderius, who claimed to be some great personage and asserted that he could perform many signs. He even boasted that messengers passed to and fro between him and the apostles Peter and Paul. Since I was not present, a great multitude of country people flocked to him, bringing with them blind and infirm persons. He sought not to heal them by holiness but to mock them through the delusion of necromantic art.

For those who were paralyzed or impeded by some other infirmity he ordered to be stretched out violently, so that, since he could not set them upright through the gift of divine power, he might appear to restore them by his own skill. Finally, his assistants seized the people’s hands, while others seized their feet, and they dragged them in different directions, so that it seemed their sinews would be torn apart. When they were not healed, they were dismissed lifeless. Thus it happened that many breathed out their souls in this torture.

The wretch had become so puffed up that he called blessed Martin his inferior and likened himself to the apostles.

[Note: The Bec and Casinensis manuscripts read *juniorem*, “younger.”] Nor is it surprising that this man should call himself like the apostles, since the author of the wickedness from which such things proceed will, at the end of the world, confess himself to be Christ. For, as we said above, it was observed that this man had been steeped in the error of necromantic art. According to those who saw him, whenever someone had spoken some evil of him at a distance and in secret, he would reproach the person in the presence of the assembled crowd, saying: “This is what he said about me, and that—things unworthy of my holiness.” And how could he have learned this except from demons acting as informants?

He wore a hood and tunic made of goat hair. In public he abstained from food and drink; but secretly, when he had entered an inn, he stuffed so much into his mouth that the servant could not keep up with bringing him what he demanded. When his deceit was exposed and discovered by our people, he was driven beyond the city’s boundary. We never learned where he went afterward; nevertheless, he said that he was a citizen of Bordeaux.

Seven years before this there was also another very great deceiver who misled many through his trickery. He was dressed in a sleeveless tunic

[Note: A *colobium* was a garment without sleeves, such as Egyptian monks customarily wore; see Cassian, *Institutes*, Book I, chapter 5.]

with a linen cloth thrown over it, and carried a cross from which little flasks hung; he claimed that they contained holy oil. He said that he had come from Spain and was presenting relics of the most blessed martyrs Vincent the Levite and Felix the martyr.

[Note: Felix suffered at Gerona; see Book I, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 92.]

But when he arrived at the basilica of Saint Martin at Tours toward evening, while we were seated at a meal, he sent word, saying: “Let them come out to meet the holy relics.” Since the hour had already passed, we replied: “Let the blessed relics rest upon the altar until morning, when we shall go out to meet them.”

But he rose at first light and, without waiting for us, came with his cross and appeared in our little chamber. Astonished and wondering at his presumption, I asked what this meant. He replied in a proud and inflated voice: “You ought to have provided a better reception for us. I shall report this to King Chilperic, and he will avenge my insult.”

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads “Childebert”; both kings were then reigning.]

He entered the oratory, disregarded me, and himself recited one lesson, then another and a third; he himself delivered the prayer and himself concluded it. Then, raising his cross again, he departed. His speech was rustic, and the breadth of his tongue was ugly and obscene; nor did any rational discourse proceed from him. He went as far as Paris.

In those days the public Rogation processions were being celebrated, which customarily take place before the holy day of the Lord’s Ascension. It happened that, while Bishop Ragnemod was proceeding with his people and going around the holy places, this man also arrived with his cross, displaying to the people an unusual garment. He gathered tax collectors and country women around him, formed his own chorus, and attempted to go around the holy places as though accompanied by his own multitude.

When the bishop saw this, he sent his archdeacon, saying: “If you are presenting relics of the saints, place them for a while in the basilica and celebrate the holy days with us. When the solemnity is over, you may continue on your way.”

But he disregarded what the archdeacon said and began to assail the bishop with insults and curses. The priest, recognizing that he was a deceiver, ordered him confined in a small cell. When everything he possessed had been searched, a large sack full of the roots of various herbs was found with him, along with moles’ teeth, mice’s bones, and bears’ claws and fat. Seeing that these were instruments of magic, the bishop ordered everything to be thrown into the river. He took away the man’s cross and ordered him expelled beyond the boundary of the city of Paris.

But after making another cross, the man began again to practice what he had done before. He was captured by the archdeacon, bound in chains, and ordered to be kept under guard.

In those days I had come to Paris and was lodging at the basilica of the blessed martyr Julian.

[Note: On this basilica, see above, Book VI, chapter 17.]

On the following night the wretch broke out of custody and, still wearing the chains with which he had been bound, hurried to the aforementioned basilica of Saint Julian. He collapsed on the pavement at the place where I was accustomed to stand and, overcome by sleep and wine, fell asleep.

Unaware of what had happened, we rose in the middle of the night to render thanks to the Lord and found him sleeping. Such a stench came from him that it surpassed the foulness of every sewer and privy.

[Variant: *paedor*, “stench.”]

Because of this stench we could not even enter the holy basilica.

One of the clerics approached and tried to rouse him while holding his nose, but he could not do so, for the wretch was thoroughly soaked in wine. Then four clerics came, lifted him among them, and threw him into one corner of the basilica. After bringing water, washing the pavement, and sprinkling it with fragrant herbs, we entered and completed the service.

[Note: The piety of our forefathers in rendering the praises owed to God at the appointed hours deserves notice, since even bishops rose at night to perform the customary office. Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, recited the office during journeys with his head uncovered, even when snow or rain pressed heavily upon him, as Fortunatus relates. Mabillon discusses this matter more fully in his *Disquisition on the Gallican Office*, section 6.]

Even while we were chanting, he could not be awakened, until daylight had been given to the earth and the sun’s lamp had risen higher. I then returned him, with an apology, to the priest.

When the bishops gathered near the city of Paris and we related these events at a meal, we ordered that he himself be brought in for punishment. When he stood there, Bishop Amelius of the city of Bigorre lifted his eyes and recognized him as his own servant, who had escaped from him by flight. He therefore received him back under guard and returned him to his homeland.

[Note: The name of this fortress is written differently in different authors. Caesar, in Book III of the *Gallic War*, calls the people Bigerrones. The city that was the capital of the tribe was formerly called Turba or Travia; today it is Tarbes. In the ancient *Notitiae*, the city of Turba, where the fortress of Bigorra stood, occupies the tenth place in Novempopulania. Amelius signed the acts of the Second Council of Mâcon in 585.]

There are many who practice such deceptions and do not cease to lead the rustic people into error. Of them, I think, the Lord says in the Gospel: “False Christs and false prophets will arise in the last times, and, by giving signs and portents, they will lead even the elect into error” (Matthew 24:24).

Let this suffice concerning them; let us rather return to our subject.

## VII

When Ennodius was administering the governorship of the cities of Tours and Poitiers, he also received authority over the cities of Vieux-Juliers and Béarn.

[Note: The Regius manuscript has *Bernanae*; the Colbertine manuscript M and the Bec manuscript have *Bernarnae*. In the ancient *Notitiae* it occupies the seventh place among the cities of Novempopulania. Today, with the name Béarn transferred to the region, it is called Lescar, commonly Lascura.]

But when the counts of the cities of Tours and Poitiers went to King Childebert, they prevailed upon him to remove Ennodius from office.

[Note: Counts governed individual cities, whereas dukes presided over several. See the notes above on Book VIII, chapter 18.]

When he learned that he had been removed from these offices, he hurried to the cities mentioned above. But while he was staying there, he received orders to withdraw from them. Having thus obtained leisure, he returned home and devoted himself to private work.

The Basques, bursting out of the mountains, descended onto the plains, ravaging vineyards and fields, setting houses on fire, and carrying away some people as captives together with their livestock. Duke Austrovald often marched against them, but exacted little vengeance from them.

[Note: Above, at Book VIII, chapter 45, Austrovald is called a count. Variant: *exercuit*, “exercised,” for *exegit*, “exacted.”]

[Note: The Basques, living in the Pyrenean Alps, after various incursions, eventually gained possession of Novempopulania as the Frankish kingdom declined; from them it was also called Vasconia. See Alteserra, Book I of *Aquitanian Affairs*, chapter 16.]

The Goths, because of the devastation inflicted the previous year by King Guntram’s army in Septimania, burst into the province of Arles. They carried off plunder and captives as far as ten miles from the city. They also laid waste a fortress called Ugernum, together with its goods and inhabitants, and returned without opposition.

[Note: The Regius manuscript has *Rigernum*. See above, Book VIII, chapter 30.]

## VIII

Since Guntchramn Boso was hated by the queen, he began to go about among bishops and nobles and beg the wretched woman for forgiveness from the one whom he had formerly despised.

[Note: This is how the manuscripts and printed editions read. It nevertheless seems that the text should be understood as: “the wretched man begged forgiveness from her,” or “the wretched man begged her forgiveness.”]

When King Childebert was still young, he had often harassed Queen Brunichild with insults and reproaches, and he had also supported those who inflicted injuries upon her. The king therefore ordered him pursued and killed in order to avenge the injury done to his mother.

When Boso saw himself placed in danger, he sought the church of Verdun through Bishop Ageric, who was the king’s godfather, trusting that he would obtain forgiveness. The bishop then hurried to the king and pleaded for him. Since the king could not refuse what the bishop requested, he said: “Let him come before us, and, once sureties have been given in the presence of my uncle, let us carry out whatever judgment he decrees.”

He was then brought to the place where the king was staying. Stripped of his weapons and held by his sleeves, he was presented to the king by the bishop. Falling at the king’s feet, he said: “I have sinned against you and your mother by not obeying your commands, but acting against your will and the public interest. Now I ask you to forgive the wrongs I have committed against you.”

The king ordered him raised from the ground and placed him in the bishop’s hands, saying: “Let him remain with you, holy priest, until he comes into the presence of King Guntram.” He then ordered him to depart.

## IX

After this, Rauchingus joined the leading men of the kingdom of Chlothar, Chilperic’s son, pretending that he wished to negotiate peace so that no hostility or plundering would arise between the borders of the two kingdoms. They took counsel that, once King Childebert had been killed, Rauchingus would hold the kingdom of Champagne with Theodobert, his elder son; while Ursio and Berthefredus, taking to themselves the younger son, recently born and called Theodoric, and excluding King Guntram, would hold the rest of the kingdom.

[Note: The Colbertine manuscript A has *Bertfredus*, and so below.]

They also raged against Queen Brunichild, intending to bring her into disgrace, as they had previously done during her widowhood.

Rauchingus, puffed up with supreme power and, so to speak, boasting that he was approaching the glory of the royal scepter itself, prepared to go to King Childebert so that he might carry out the plan he had formed. But the mercy of God first placed these words in King Guntram’s ears. He secretly sent messengers to King Childebert and made all these schemes known to him, saying: “Hurry quickly, so that we may meet one another; there are matters that must be dealt with.”

Childebert carefully investigated what had been reported to him and, discovering that it was true, ordered Rauchingus summoned. When Rauchingus arrived, before the king ordered him to appear in his presence, he issued letters and sent servants with public transport, who were to seize his property at each place. He then ordered Rauchingus admitted to the chamber and, after speaking with him about various matters, ordered him to leave the chamber again.

As he was leaving, two doorkeepers seized him by the feet, and he fell on the steps of the doorway, so that part of his body lay inside and part extended outside. Then those who had been ordered and prepared for this task rushed upon him with swords and smashed his head into such small fragments that his whole brain seemed to have been reduced to pulp. He died immediately. He was then stripped, thrown out through a window, and given burial.

He was fickle in character, greedily coveting the possessions and wealth of others beyond what was human, and exceedingly proud of his own riches—so much so that even at the moment of his death he admitted that he was the son of King Chlothar. Nevertheless, a great deal of gold was found with him.

After he was killed, one of his servants immediately flew off at swift pace and announced to his wife what had happened. She, dressed in finery and covered with magnificent ornaments, jewels, and the glitter of gold, mounted a horse and was carried through the street of the city of Soissons, with servants preceding and others following her. She was hurrying to the basilica of Saints Crispinus and Crispinianus, as though to attend the Masses, for that was the day of the blessed martyrs’ passion.

[Note: Their feast is celebrated on 25 October. Their memory was adorned with distinguished ornamentation by blessed Eligius, as Saint Audoenus relates in Book II, chapter 7 of his *Life*. Rauchingus’s wife had previously been married to Godinus; see Book V, chapter 3.]

When she saw the messenger, she turned back through another street, threw her ornaments on the ground, and fled into the basilica of Saint Medard the bishop, thinking that she would be protected by the confessor’s safeguard.

The servants sent by the king to search for Rauchingus’s property found such riches in his treasuries that not even in the inventory of the public treasury could such wealth have been found. They presented all of it to the king.

[Note: The printed edition has *potuerant*; the Casinensis manuscript reads: “such things could have been found in the king’s own public treasury.”]

On the day he was killed, many men from Tours and Poitiers were with the king. They had formed this plan: if they could accomplish this evil, they would subject these men to punishment and say, “One of you killed our king.” After slaughtering them with various punishments, they would boast that they had avenged the king’s death. But almighty God, because their plans were wicked, scattered them and fulfilled what is written: “You will fall into the pit that you dig for your brother” (Ecclesiasticus 27:29).

Magnoualdus the duke was appointed in Rauchingus’s place.

Ursio and Berthefredus were already certain that Rauchingus would be able to carry out what they had discussed. They therefore came with an army. But when they heard that he had suffered such a death, they gathered an even greater multitude of men who appeared to belong to their party and fortified themselves within the fortress of Vabre, which was near Ursio’s estate, together with all their possessions, as men conscious of their conspiracy. They planned that, if King Childebert wished to act against them, they would defend themselves by force against his army.

[Note: This fortress gave its name to a district situated between the Meuse and Moselle, on the banks of the rivers Alisontia, Orne, and Chiers. The district comprised two or three counties, namely those of Scarpone, Verdun, and Chastel-sur-Moselle. It is still called *le pays de Vaivre*. See Book IV of *Diplomatic Affairs*, number 128. Do not confuse this place with the fortress of Vabre in Rouergue, now called Vabres, where John XXII enlarged a monastery into an episcopal see after detaching several parishes from the diocese of Rodez.]

Queen Brunichild sent instructions to Berthefredus, saying: “Separate yourself from that wicked man, and you will live; otherwise you will perish with him.”

[Note: The Regius manuscript has “that unjust man.”]

The queen had received Berthefredus’s daughter from the font and therefore wished to show him mercy. He replied: “Unless I am separated from him by death, I shall never leave him.”

[Note: The Colbertine manuscript A has: “I shall never depart from him.”]

## X

While these things were happening, King Guntram again sent word to his nephew Childebert, saying: “Let all delay cease and come, so that I may see you. There is a matter of certain necessity, both for the safety of our lives and for the public interest, so that we may meet one another.”

When Childebert heard this, he took his mother, his sister, and his wife and set out to meet his uncle.

[Note: At Andelot. See below, chapter 20.]

Bishop Magneric of the city of Trier was also present. Guntchramn Boso also came, whom Bishop Ageric of Verdun had received under his protection. But that bishop, who had given surety for him, was not present, because it had been arranged that Boso should be presented to the king without anyone’s protection. Thus, if the king himself decided that he ought to die, the priest would not be able to excuse him; but if the king granted him life, he would depart free.

When the kings had met, Boso was judged guilty of various *facilitates* (“compliances” or concessions) and ordered to be killed.

[Note: The Bec and Morin manuscripts read *facilitatibus*; the printed editions have *falsitatibus*, “falsehoods.”]

When he learned this, he fled to the residence of Bishop Magneric. He closed the doors, separated the clerics and servants from him, and said: “I know, most blessed priest, that you possess great honor with the kings, and now I flee to you so that I may escape. Look: the executioners are at the door. You must clearly understand that, if I am not rescued from them, I shall go out after killing you and die. Know most certainly that either one death will seize us both or one life will defend us both.

“Holy priest, I know that you are a common father to the king and to his son, and I know that whatever you ask of him you will obtain. He will absolutely be unable to refuse whatever you request from your holiness. Therefore either obtain forgiveness for me or let us die together.”

He said this while drawing his sword. The bishop was disturbed when he heard it and said: “What am I to do if you hold me here? Release me, so that I may go and beg the king’s mercy; perhaps he will have pity on you.”

Boso replied: “By no means. Send your abbots and trusted men, so that they may report what I am saying.”

[Note: That is, faithful clerics or other household members whom he trusted.]

Yet they did not report the matter to the king as it actually was. They said that Boso was being defended by the bishop. The king was therefore provoked and said: “If the bishop refuses to come out of there, let him perish together with the author of this treachery.”

When the bishop heard this, he sent messengers to the king. After they had related the matter, King Guntram said: “Set fire to the house, and if the bishop cannot get out, let them both be burned together.”

When the clerics heard this, they violently broke down the door and forced the priest outside. The wretched man, seeing himself surrounded on both sides by fierce flames, approached the doorway with his sword at his side. But as soon as he stepped over the threshold and planted his foot outside, one of the crowd hurled a spear and struck him in the forehead.

Stunned by the blow, he tried, as though mad, to draw his sword. But those standing around wounded him with such a multitude of spears that, with the points fixed in his sides and the shafts supporting him, he could not fall to the ground. The few who were with him were also killed and exposed together in the field. It was only with difficulty that permission was obtained from the rulers for their bodies to be buried.

He had been fickle in conduct, greedy for wealth, immoderately covetous of other people’s property, swearing to everyone and fulfilling his promises to no one. His wife and children were sent into exile, and his property was transferred to the treasury. A great quantity of gold, silver, and various goods was found in his inventories. Nor did the things he had hidden underground remain concealed; his guilty conscience brought them to light. He frequently used diviners and lots, wishing through them to learn the future, but he remained deceived.

## XI

King Guntram made peace with his nephew and the queens, exchanging gifts with them and settling public affairs. They then feasted together. King Guntram praised the Lord, saying:

“I give you the greatest thanks, almighty God, who have granted me to deserve to see the sons of my son Childebert. Therefore I do not think that I have been wholly abandoned by your Majesty, since you have granted me this: to see my son’s sons.”

King Childebert then received Dynamias and Duke Lupus after they had been restored to him, and he handed Cadurcus back to Queen Brunichild.

Thus, with peace and joy, they gave thanks to God again and again. After the agreements had been written down,

[Note: They are reported below, chapter 20.]

and after rewarding and embracing one another, each returned to his own city.

## XII

[Note: This chapter and the following two are absent from the Vatican manuscript and the Colbertine manuscript A.]

King Childebert gathered an army and ordered it sent to the place where Ursio and Berthefredus were shut up. It was an estate in the district of Vabre, above which rose a steep mountain. On its summit he built a basilica in honor of the holy and most blessed Martin.

[Note: The Regius manuscript reads: “a basilica ... was built.” Valesius thinks this was the basilica that Ulfilaicus, mentioned above in Book VIII, chapter 15, is said to have built near Eposium, a town in the county of Vabre.]

They said that a fortress had formerly stood there; but at that time the place was fortified not by construction,

[Note: The same Regius manuscript reads: “not by structure but only by nature.”]

but solely by nature.

The men mentioned above had shut themselves inside this basilica with their possessions, wives, and household. King Childebert therefore, as we have said, ordered his army to be sent there. Before the troops reached them, however, the enraged soldiers, wherever they were able to find either their estates or their property, gave everything over to fire and plunder.

When they approached the place, the soldiers rushed up the mountain and surrounded the basilica with weapons. They had as their commander, it seems, Godegisilus, the son-in-law of Duke Lupus.

[Note: Chesn. omits “it seems.” Fortunatus praises the duke Godegisilus in Book I, poem 6, but that man had married the daughter of Gallimagnius. Perhaps, if this is the same person, he had two wives.]

Since the soldiers could not draw Ursio and Berthefredus out of the basilica, they tried to set fire to it. When Ursio saw this, he girded on his sword and went outside. He slaughtered those who were besieging the basilica with such carnage that none of those who came within his reach could remain alive.

There Count Trudulfus of the royal palace also fell, and many of that army were struck down.

[Note: The Regius manuscript has *Tridulphus*; the Bec manuscript has *Tridulfus*.]

When no one seemed able to escape Ursio’s slaughter,

[Note: This is how the Badian manuscript and others read; others have *cerneretur*, “was seen.” The Regius manuscript reads: “when it was seen that no one was striking Ursio.”]

he was suddenly struck in the thigh by someone, disabled, and fell to the ground. Others then rushed upon him and ended his life.

When Godegisilus saw this, he began to shout: “Let there now be peace! Look, the greatest enemy of our lords has fallen. Let this Berthefredus live.”

While he was saying this, the whole people were eager to plunder the goods gathered in the basilica. Berthefredus mounted a horse and made for the city of Verdun. There, thinking that he would be protected in the oratory located in the ecclesiastical residence, especially since Bishop Ageric himself was staying in that house, he took refuge.

But when it was reported to King Childebert that Berthefredus had escaped, he was struck with grief and said: “If this man has escaped death, Godegisilus will not escape my hands.”

[Note: The name Godegisilus is absent from the Colbertine manuscript M and the Regius manuscript.]

The king did not know that Berthefredus had entered the bishop’s house, but thought that he had fled to another region.

Godegisilus, fearing for himself, again gathered an army and surrounded the ecclesiastical residence with armed men. Since the bishop could neither surrender Berthefredus nor defend him successfully, the soldiers climbed onto the roof and struck him with the very tiles and masonry—or, according to another reading, materials—with which the oratory was covered. They killed him there together with three servants.

The bishop grieved deeply over this, because he had not only been unable to defend Berthefredus but had also seen the place in which he was accustomed to pray, and in which the relics of the saints had been gathered, polluted with human blood.

King Childebert sent gifts to recall him from his grief, but he refused to be consoled.

Many people, fearing the king in those days, withdrew to other regions. Some were also removed from the rank of dukes, and others succeeded to their offices.

## XIII

King Guntram ordered Baddo, whom we said above had been bound for the crime of treason,

[Note: Book VIII, chapter 44.]

to come into his presence. He sent word as far as Paris, saying: “If Fredegundis can establish, with suitable witnesses, that he is free from the charge brought against him, let him depart free and go wherever he wishes.”

But when he came to Paris, no one from the party of the woman mentioned above appeared who could establish his innocence. He was therefore bound, loaded with chains, and brought back under strict guard to the city of Chalon.

Later, however, after messengers had intervened—especially Leudovald, bishop of Bayeux—he was released and returned home.

At that time a severe dysenteric illness was raging in the city of Metz. While we were traveling in those days to meet the king, we encountered on the road, near the city of Reims, a citizen of Poitiers named Wiliulf, suffering from this disease and consumed by fever. He had left Reims greatly weakened. When he came to the city of Paris with his wife’s son, he made his will and died at the estate of Rigoialum.

[Note: Elsewhere it is called Rotoialum or Ruolium, commonly Rueil, a royal estate that Charles the Bald gave to the monastery of Saint-Denis. A villa called Richeliana, distinguished by especially celebrated springs, is still visited there. It must be distinguished from the estate of the same name in Normandy, Rueil, mentioned above in Book VII, chapter 19.]

The boy, who was also suffering from this illness, died as well. Their bodies were brought together into the territory of the city of Poitiers and buried.

Wiliulf’s wife was then married to a third husband, the son of Duke Beppolenus, who, as is commonly reported, had himself already left two living wives behind. He was fickle and lustful. When he was pressed by an excessive passion for fornication, he abandoned his wife and slept with female servants, rejecting lawful marriage and seeking another woman. He did the same to his second wife and to this woman, to whom he was married as his third, not knowing that “corruption will not possess incorruption” (1 Corinthians 15:50).

## XIV

After this, since Egidius, bishop of the city of Reims, was suspected of the treason concerning which those mentioned above had been killed,

[Note: Chapter 12.]

he approached King Childebert with great gifts and begged forgiveness. First, however, he received oaths in the basilica of Saint Remigius, so that he would suffer no harm on the journey.

[Note: The Regius and Colbertine manuscripts M have “Saint Remedius.” According to Frodoard, this basilica, formerly called that of Saint Christopher, became distinguished and famous through the tomb and frequent miracles of the most blessed Remigius, apostle of the Franks. The holy chrism used for the consecration of our kings is kept there. [See above the note appended to page 225. EDIT.] Some kings, and also several queens, were solemnly inaugurated there. In this basilica were buried not only many archbishops of Reims and other noblemen and princes, but also Carloman, brother of Charlemagne, and several other Frankish kings and queens. Because of its fame and privileges, it has enjoyed the title of archmonastery for approximately six hundred years; it still continues under the rule of Saint Benedict and the Congregation of Saint Maur. For more information, consult Frodoard or Marlot, *Metropolis Remensis*, volume I, Book III, chapters 2 and following.]

The king received him peacefully, and he departed. He also obtained peace with Duke Lupus, whom, as we mentioned above, he had driven from the dukedom of Champagne at his instigation.

[Note: Book VI, chapter 4.]

King Guntram was therefore greatly stirred to bitterness, because Lupus had promised him that he would never make peace with Egidius, since Egidius was known to have been an enemy of the king.

### XV

At that time, therefore, in Spain King Reccared, moved by divine mercy, summoned the bishops of his religion and said:

“Why does continual scandal spread between you and those priests who call themselves Catholics? When they display many signs through their faith, you are unable to perform anything of the kind [Note: This was at all times the distinction between Catholics and heretics: the former confirmed their faith by miracles, whereas the latter could not do so, as we have observed from Irenaeus, Tertullian, Eusebius, Cyprian, and others in the notes to the *Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 131. Nicetius of Trier used this argument in his letter to Chlodosinda against the Arians.] Therefore, I ask you, meet together, and, after examining the beliefs of both parties, let us discover what is true; then either let them accept the reasoning you give and believe what you say, or, recognizing the truth proclaimed by them, let you believe them.”

When this had been done, and the bishops of both parties had assembled, the heretics put forward the arguments that they had often advanced, which we have already set down [Col. 0493B]. The bishops of our religion likewise answered with the arguments by which we demonstrated in the preceding books that the heretical party was for the most part defeated. In particular, when the king said that no sign of healing the sick had been shown by the heretical bishops, and recalled how, in the time of his father, a bishop who boasted that through the rightness of his faith he could restore sight to the blind through an incorrect faith had touched a blind man and departed in confusion, leaving him condemned to perpetual blindness—a matter that we have explained more fully in the *Book of Miracles* [Note: Namely, in the book *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 13. See also above, Book II, chapter 3. John of Biclarum mentions this discussion under the year 588.]—he summoned the priests of God privately.

After questioning them, he learned that one God is worshiped in the distinction of three persons, namely, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; that the Son is not lesser than the Father and the Holy Spirit, nor the Holy Spirit lesser than the Father or the Son; but that this Trinity is confessed to be the true God in one equality and omnipotence.

Then, understanding the truth, Reccared laid aside dispute, submitted himself to the Catholic faith, and, having received the sign of the blessed cross together with anointing with chrism, believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, equal to the Father with the Holy Spirit, reigning for ever and ever. Amen.

Next he sent messengers to the province of Narbonne. When they reported what he had done, that people too was joined to the same faith [Note: *Colb. a.*: “who, reporting what he had done, is joined …”].

At that time there was a bishop of the Arian sect named Athalocus. Through empty propositions and false interpretations of Scripture he so disturbed the churches of God that he was thought to be Arius himself—Arius himself, whom the historian Eusebius relates to have gone into seclusion [the wording is corrupt or uncertain] [Col. 0494A] [Note: Rufinus added two books to the books of Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History*; but since Gregory and other similar authors knew Eusebius’s *History* from no other source than Rufinus’s translation, they praised the whole work under Eusebius’s name. The death of Arius is described in Book X, chapter 14.].

But when the people of his sect would not allow him to impose these beliefs, and the flattery of a few encouraged him to give his assent, he was inflamed with anger. He entered his cell, bent his head over his bed, and breathed out his wicked spirit [Note: *Regm.*: “But when this people would not follow his sect,” etc. Paul the Deacon of Mérida reports in *Lives of the Fathers of Mérida*, chapter 19, that Athalocus, an Arian bishop, raised a revolt against Reccared near Narbonne with twelve companions, but that their efforts failed, although they had called the Franks to their aid. John of Biclarum, in the first year of Reccared, records a victory won against the Franks by Reccared’s commanders, in which he says that the duke Desiderius died with many Franks. This was, unless I am mistaken, a different conspiracy—that of the Arian bishop Sunna and others against Reccared—which the same John of Biclarum assigns to the following year. Likewise, in Reccared’s third year, the bishop Uldila and Goswintha were discovered plotting against the same king, as we said above in chapter 1 of this book.].

Thus the people of the heretics, remaining within that province itself, confessed the indivisible Trinity and abandoned their error.

### XVI

After this, Reccared sent an embassy to Guntram and Childebert for the sake of peace, so that, just as he asserted that he was one with them in faith, he might also show himself united with them in love.

But they were rebuffed by King Guntram, who said:

“What faith can they promise me, or how ought I to be believed by those who handed over my niece Ingund to captivity, through whose treachery both her husband was killed and she herself died in exile? Therefore I do not receive Reccared’s embassy until God commands me to take vengeance on these enemies.”

When the envoys heard this, they proceeded to Childebert, by whom they were also received peacefully, saying:

“Our lord, your brother Reccared, wishes to clear himself of the crime laid against him, as though he had been involved in the death of your sister. If you wish, he can be cleared by an oath or by any other suitable condition. Moreover, by giving your Grace ten thousand solidi, he desires to possess your affection, so that he may enjoy your support and you his benefits whenever necessity requires.”

When they had said this, King Childebert and his mother promised that they would preserve peace and affection with him in full.

After gifts had been both received and given, the envoys added:

“Our lord has also commanded us to put before you a proposal concerning your daughter or sister Chlodosinda [Note: Below, chapter 20, she is called Chlodoswinda. See the notes to chapter 25], that she be given to him in marriage, so that the peace promised between you may more easily be confirmed.”

They replied:

“Our promise in this matter will be made favorably, but without the advice of our uncle, King Guntram, we do not dare to do this. We have promised that in matters of greater importance we will do nothing without his counsel.”

Having received this answer, the envoys returned.

### XVII

In that year, during the spring, there were heavy rains. When the trees and vines had already put forth leaves, falling snow covered everything. Then, in the ensuing frost, both the shoots of the vines and the other visible fruits were scorched. So severe did the cold appear that even swallows and other birds that had come from foreign regions were killed by its force.

This too was astonishing: where frost had never caused harm, it then destroyed everything; and where it had usually caused damage, it did not reach.

[Note: This chapter, together with the following one, is absent from *Colb.*.]

### XVIII

The Bretons, invading the territory of Nantes [Note: This chapter and the following two are absent from *Vat.*], carried off booty, overrunning estates and taking captives. When this was reported to King Guntram, he ordered an army to be mobilized and sent a messenger there to tell them that they must make amends for everything they had done wrong, or else know that they would fall by the sword of his army.

Fearing this, they promised that they would correct everything they had done wrong.

When the king heard this, he sent an embassy there: namely, Namatius, bishop of Orléans [Note: He attended the First Council of Mâcon in 581 and the Second in 585], and Bertchramn, bishop of Le Mans, together with counts and other distinguished men. Distinguished men from the kingdom of Chlothar, son of King Chilperic, were also present. Going to the territory of Nantes, they spoke with Warocho and Vidimaclo [Note: *Regm.*: “Indimacle.” *Colb. m.*: “Vidimacle.” *Cod. Bec.*: “Vidinacle.”] about everything the king had commanded.

They said:

“We too know that these cities are to be restored to the sons of King Chlothar, and that we ought to be subject to them. Nevertheless, we do not delay in making amends for everything we have done contrary to justice.”

After giving sureties and signing bonds, they promised that they would pay King Guntram and Chlothar a thousand solidi apiece as compensation, and promised never again to invade the boundaries of those cities.

When these matters had been settled, the others returned and reported to the king what had been done.

Bishop Namatius, however, while remaining there after recovering within the boundaries of the city of Nantes the estates that his parents had formerly lost, developed three malignant pustules on his head. Greatly weakened and wishing to return to his own city, he breathed out his spirit within the territory of Angers. His little body was carried to his city and buried in the basilica of Saint Anianus the Confessor [Note: It still exists, distinguished by a college of canons. On its antiquity and privileges, the highly esteemed Hubert, cantor of that church, published a separate treatise.]. Austrinus, son of the late Pastor [Note: Pastor was also the father of Aunacharius, bishop of Auxerre, and of Austregildis, mother of Saint Lupus, bishop of Sens, as we learn from the Life of that same Lupus], was appointed to his see.

Waroch, however, forgetting his oath and his bond, set aside everything he had promised. He seized the vineyards of the people of Nantes and, gathering the vintage, transported the wine to Vannes. Because of this King Guntram again became extremely angry and ordered an army to be mobilized, but then stopped.

### XIX

The war between the citizens of Tours, which we said above had been concluded [Book VII, chapter 47], again rose into renewed madness.

Sicharius, after the killing of Chramnisindus’s parents [Note: Some have *Chramisindus*, and so below], had made a great friendship with him. They loved each other with such mutual affection that they often ate together and lay together in the same bed.

One day Chramnisindus prepared a dinner at night and invited Sicharius to his feast. When Sicharius arrived, they sat down together for the meal. Sicharius, intoxicated with wine, made many boastful remarks to Chramnisindus. Finally he is said to have said:

“You owe me great thanks, dearest brother, because I killed your parents. From the compensation received for them, gold and silver abound in your house; you would now be naked and needy if that matter had not somewhat strengthened you.”

Hearing this, Chramnisindus received Sicharius’s words bitterly and said in his heart:

“If I do not avenge the death of my parents, I ought to lose the name of a man and be called a weak woman.”

Immediately he extinguished the lights and split Sicharius’s head with a dagger. Sicharius uttered a small cry at the very threshold of death, fell, and died. The boys who had come with him fled.

Chramnisindus stripped the dead body of its clothing and hung it on a stake of the hedge. Then, mounting Sicharius’s horses, he went to the king. Entering the church, he prostrated himself at the king’s feet and said:

“I ask for my life, glorious king, because I killed men who secretly killed my parents and seized all their possessions.”

When he had explained the circumstances in order, and Queen Brunhild had taken the matter seriously—because Sicharius had been placed under her protection [that is, on the basis of her pledged word]—she began to rage against him.

When he saw that she was hostile to him, he asked for the district of Vosges in the territory of Bourges [Note: *Regm.*: “the district of Vosges in the territory.” *Colb. m.*: “the district of the territory of Bourges.” Marollius, cited by Valesius, thinks that this Vosges is the place called *Besage* in French, situated within the boundaries of Bourges. If the reading of the Regiomontanus manuscript is genuine, the name Vosges could refer to the famous forest of the Vosges between Alsace and Lorraine, commonly called *Vosge*, at least most of which belonged to Childebert’s kingdom. From what follows, however, it seems possible that a district of Bourges is intended here.], where his parents lived, because he was hated in the kingdom of King Guntram.
