Sicharius’s wife, Tranquilia, leaving her children and her husband’s property in the territory of Tours or Poitiers, sought the village of Mauriopes among her parents [Note: This is the district of Mauripensis, commonly called Hurepoix, lying between the Seine, the Yonne, and the Loing, beginning not far from Paris. The village mentioned here, however, cannot apparently be assigned to it.], and there she was married again.

Sicharius died at about forty years of age [Note: *Colb. m.* and *Regm.*: “twenty.”]. In life he was frivolous, a drunkard, and a murderer; while drunk, he injured a number of people.

Chramnisindus returned to the king, and it was judged that he should establish against himself that he had killed Sicharius. He did so.

But because, as we have said, Queen Brunhild had placed Sicharius under her protection, she ordered Chramnisindus’s property to be confiscated. Later it was restored to him by Flavianus, the domesticus.

Chramnisindus then hurried to Agen and obtained a letter from her that no one should molest him. The queen herself had granted Chramnisindus’s property to him [Note: *Colb. m.* and *Bad.*: “The property was granted.”].

### XX

In the thirteenth year of King Childebert, when we had hurried as far as the city of Metz to meet him, we were ordered to go on an embassy to King Guntram. We found him near the city of Chalon and said:

“Your most glorious nephew Childebert sends you the fullest greeting, illustrious king, and returns immense thanks for your affection, because you continually admonish him to do what pleases God, is acceptable to you, and is fitting for the people. He promises to fulfill everything that you discussed together, and promises that he will violate nothing of the agreements written between you.”

The king replied:

“I do not return thanks in the same way, because what was promised to me is being violated in such a manner. My share of the city of Senlis is not returned [Note: Or perhaps the share of Rosson, as is stated below in the agreement]. The men whom, for my benefit, I wished to migrate because they were hostile to me were not permitted to do so. How, then, do you say that my dear nephew wishes to transgress nothing of the written agreements?”

We replied:

“He wishes to do nothing contrary to those agreements, but promises to fulfill everything. Thus, if you wish now to send someone to divide Senlis, do not delay; you will immediately receive what is yours. As for the men you mention, written names will be handed over, and everything promised will be fulfilled.”

While we were saying this, the king ordered the agreement itself to be reread in the presence of those standing there.

### Copy of the Agreement

“When, in the name of Christ, the most excellent lords Guntram and Childebert, kings, and the most glorious lady Brunhild, queen, had met at Andelot [Note: A fortress in the diocese of Langres, commonly called Andelot, between Langres itself and Nasium, the fortress of the Leuci. It should be distinguished from another fortress and monastery of the same name in the Vosges forest toward Alsace, commonly called Andelaw; and also from Andelot, or Andeleis and Andilegius, commonly called Les Andelys, a town in the diocese of Rouen, with an ancient Benedictine nunnery and a collegiate church], out of a desire for affection, so that they might settle with fuller deliberation everything that could in any way generate discord between them, the following was decided, agreed, and accepted between them, through the mediation of priests and nobles, with God as mediator and out of a desire for affection:

As long as almighty God wills that they survive in the present world, they shall preserve pure and simple faith and affection toward one another.

Likewise, since the lord Guntram, according to the agreement that he had made with the late lord Sigibert, had obtained in full the portion of Charibert’s kingdom, he said that it should be restored to him in full; and the party of the lord Childebert [Note: That is, those who spoke on Childebert’s behalf. This manner of speaking is still used in court] wished to recall to itself from all sides what his father had possessed. It was therefore fixed by firm deliberation between them that, in the third portion of the city of Paris with its boundaries and people, which by written agreement had come to the lord Sigibert from the kingdom of Charibert, together with the castles of Duno and Vendôme, and whatever the aforesaid king had received from the district of Étampes or Chartres along that route, with its boundaries and people, all this should remain perpetually in the right and dominion of the lord Guntram, together with what he had previously held from Charibert’s kingdom while the lord Sigibert was still alive.

Under the same condition, the cities of Meaux [Note: Some editions have *Meldonenses*; Chesne and others have *Medus, Turonus, Pictavus*. The cities listed here are well known and still possess episcopal sees: Meaux in Brie; Senlis; Avranches in Normandy; Vicus-Julius, today Aire in Gascony; the district of Couserans, whose city lies on the Salat, called Saint-Lizier after Saint Licerius, bishop of Couserans, who subscribed to the Council of Agde; Lapurdum, or the city of the Tarbelli, today Bayonne, as Valesius proves in his *Notice of the Gauls*; and Albi, which, after six cities were detached from the province of Bourges, was made a metropolitan see by Innocent XI. The papal document concerning this was issued on 3 October 1678], and two portions each of Senlis, Tours, Poitiers, Avranches, Aire, Couserans, Bayonne, and Albi, with their boundaries, shall from this day be claimed by King Childebert for his own authority.

The following condition shall be preserved: whichever of these kings God decrees will survive, the kingdom of the one who dies without sons shall, by perpetual right, be recalled in its entirety to the survivor, who shall leave it, with the Lord’s help, to his descendants.

It was specifically agreed that everything which King Guntram has granted to his daughter Chlothild [Note: She is mentioned, together with her sister Chlodeberga, who had already died, in the Second Council of Valence in 584, where the girls are called dedicated to God], or may hereafter grant, by God’s favor, in all properties and persons, whether in cities, lands, or revenues, shall remain in her right and dominion. If she wishes, according to her own judgment, to dispose of anything from fiscal lands, goods, or a reserve [Note: As we have already said, authors of this age called *praesidium* money deliberately set aside for necessities. See the Fifth Council of Paris, canon 8. Hugo Menard interprets *praesidium* in his notes to Gregory’s *Holy Sacramentary* as movable property], or to grant anything [variant: to grant to anyone], it shall be preserved forever, with the Lord’s help, and shall never at any time be taken away by anyone. Under the protection and defense of the lord Childebert, together with everything that she is found to possess when her father dies, she shall possess it securely, with all honor and dignity.

The lord King Guntram likewise promises that if—as human frailty permits, though divine mercy forbid and he himself does not wish to see it—it should happen that the lord Childebert dies from this life while Guntram survives him, he will receive under his protection and defense his sons, the kings Theudebert and Theuderic, or any others whom God may still grant him, as a dutiful father, so that they may possess their father’s kingdom in complete security. He will also receive under his protection and defense, with spiritual affection as though they were a good sister and daughters, the mother of the lord Childebert, the lady Queen Brunhild, and her daughter Chlodoswinda, sister of King Childebert, for as long as she remains within the region of the Franks, and also his queen Faileuba [Note: *Colb.*: “Fagileiba.”], together with all their property, cities, lands, revenues, titles, and the entire body of their possessions, both what they presently appear to possess and what, under Christ’s protection, they may justly increase. They shall possess everything in complete security and peace. If they wish, according to their own judgment, to dispose of anything from fiscal lands, goods, or a reserve, or to grant anything to anyone, it shall be preserved forever with firm stability, and their will shall never at any time be taken away by anyone.

Concerning the cities—namely Bordeaux, Limoges, Cahors, Béarn, and Bigorre—which it is established that Galswinth, sister of the lady Brunhild, acquired on coming into Francia, both as dowry and as *morganegiba* [Note: Since the word was unfamiliar to copyists, they wrote it in various forms. *Regm.* and *Colb. m.* have *Morganeliba*; *Colb. a.*, *Morgungeba*; Freher and Chesne, *Morgangeba*. It was a gift that the bridegroom gave the bride on the morning of the wedding day. Cangius explains its etymology and various meanings at greater length from numerous authors in his *Glossary*]—that is, a morning gift—and which the lady Brunhild is known to have acquired by judgment of the most glorious lord King Guntram and the Franks while Chilperic and Sigibert were still alive, it was agreed as follows:

The lady Brunhild shall receive the city of Cahors at once as her own property, with its boundaries and entire people. The remaining cities named above shall be possessed by the lord Guntram for as long as he lives, so that after his death they shall return, with complete security, to the dominion of the lady Brunhild and her heirs, with God’s favor. While the lord Guntram is alive, neither the lady Brunhild nor her son King Childebert or his sons shall reclaim them by any device or at any time.

Likewise, it was agreed that the lord Childebert shall hold Senlis in its entirety, and that the third portion due therefrom to the lord Guntram shall be compensated from the third portion of the lord Childebert, which is in Rosson [Note: *Colb. m.* and other editions: *Rosontisse*; *Bec.*: *Rossontisse*. This may perhaps designate Ressons-le-Long, a village between Soissons and Vic-sur-Aisne. Others, however, think that the reference is to Resson in the district of Beauvais, commonly called Resson, which gives its name to one of the nine archdeaconries of the church of Beauvais].

Likewise, according to the agreements made between the lord Guntram and the late lord Sigibert, those *leudes* who first gave their oaths to the lord Guntram after the death of the lord Chlothar, and who are later convicted of having transferred themselves to the other side, shall be removed from the places where they are found to reside.

Similarly, those who, after the death of the lord Chlothar, are convicted of having first given their oaths to the lord Sigibert and then transferred themselves to the other side shall likewise be removed.

Likewise, whatever the aforesaid kings have granted to churches or to their faithful [Note: Thus all manuscripts; the printed editions have “whatever they will have granted”], or may still wish to grant justly, with God’s favor, shall be preserved securely. Whatever is restored by law and justice to any of the faithful in either kingdom shall cause him no prejudice; he shall be permitted to possess and receive what is owed to him.

If anything was taken from anyone without fault during the interregna, it shall be restored after a hearing.

Whatever each person possessed through the generosity of the preceding kings up to the death of the glorious-memory lord King Chlothar, let him possess securely; and whatever was taken from faithful persons after that time, let him receive now.

Because pure and simple concord has been bound between the aforesaid kings in the name of God, it was agreed that in both kingdoms a road shall at all times be open to the faithful of either king, for both public and private business, to whomever wishes to travel.

Likewise, no one shall solicit another’s *leudes*, nor receive those who come over. If, however, someone should think that one side ought to be approached because of some loss, let redress be rendered according to the gravity of the offence.

It was also agreed to add the following to this pact: if either party should, through any deceit, at any time transgress the present provisions, he shall lose all benefits, both those promised and those presently granted, and they shall accrue to the one who has inviolably observed everything written above; and he shall be released in every respect from the obligation of the oaths.

When all these matters had been settled, the parties swore by the name of almighty God, by the indivisible Trinity, by all divine things, and by the terrible day of judgment that they would inviolably observe everything written above, without any evil deceit or fraudulent contrivance.

The pact was made on the fourth day before the Kalends of December [Note: *Colb. m.* and *Regm.* with *Bad.*: “the third day”], in the twenty-sixth year [I.e., 587] of the reign of the lord King Guntram, and in the twelfth year of the lord Childebert’s reign.

[Note: The material that follows to the end of the chapter is absent from *Colb. a.* and *Vat.*.]

After the agreement had been read, the king said:

“May I be struck by God’s judgment if I transgress anything contained here.”

Then, turning to Felix, who had come with us as an envoy, he said:

“Tell me, Felix. By now you have completely joined in friendship my sister Brunhild and Fredegund, the enemy of God and men.”

When Felix denied this, I said:

“Let the king have no doubt that the friendship between them is being preserved—the friendship that was established many years ago. For you should know that the hatred once fixed between them still sprouts; it has not withered. Would that you, most glorious king, had less affection for her. For, as we have often discovered, you receive her embassy more favorably than ours.”

He replied:

“Know, priest of God, that I receive her embassy in such a way that I do not abandon my affection for my nephew King Childebert. I cannot bind friendship with one from whom those who would take away my present life have repeatedly emerged.”

While he was saying this, Felix said:

“I believe it has reached Your Glory that Reccared sent an embassy to your nephew [See above, chapter 16], seeking your niece Chlodoswinda, the daughter of your brother, in marriage. But he wished to promise nothing concerning this without your advice.”

The king said [Note: Badius’s edition has the following: “To this the king, recalling in his mind what he had heard concerning his treachery, answered after mature deliberation: ‘It does not seem prudent for me to consent to sending there my niece, whom I ought to love uniquely, where her innocent sister is commonly said to have been killed by the most shameful treachery. Nor does it befit royal majesty, or do I consider it honorable to our family, not to exact some vengeance or punishment for the wicked death of my dearest niece Ingund.’ Felix the envoy replied: ‘The tongues of wicked men often assert many things that are far from the truth. Therefore no one ought to believe them before a just inquiry has been made. Reccared, moreover, is ready to clear himself by every proper means, whether by oaths or by whatever other conditions you command, and to show himself innocent of the things imputed to him by depraved men, who would be grieved if they saw between you the true and sincere affection that is fitting. Therefore be pleased to admit his lawful purgation; and if he is found to be such, then allow Chlodoswinda to be betrothed to him, as he asks.’ The king, hearing so firm an offer to undertake Reccared’s purification, and considering that if he were innocent of the charges then made against him, what was being requested from Reccared would benefit the kingdom and honor his niece and should therefore by no means be rejected, began to incline his mind and said: ‘If what you say is true, and if my nephew Childebert [I think this should be read instead of “Reccared”] fulfills what he wished to have written in the agreements, etc.’”]:

“It is not best for my niece to go there, where her sister was killed. Nor does it reasonably please me that the death of my niece Ingund should go unavenged.”

Felix replied:

“They wish to clear themselves of this in every way, either by oaths or by whatever other conditions you command. Only give your consent that Chlodoswinda be betrothed to him, as he requests.”

The king said:

“If my nephew fulfills what he wished to have written in the agreements, I too will do his will in these matters.”

When we promised that he would fulfill everything, Felix added:

“He also implores Your Piety to grant him assistance against the Lombards, so that, once they have been driven from Italy, the part that his father recovered while alive may return to him, while the remaining part may, through the support of you and him, be restored to the emperor’s authority.”

The king replied:

“I cannot send my army into Italy and voluntarily hand them over to death; for Italy is now being devastated by a very severe plague.”

I said:

“You have instructed your nephew that all the bishops of his kingdom should assemble, because there are many matters that ought to be investigated. But according to the custom of the canons, your most glorious nephew wished each metropolitan to assemble with his provincials [*Ch.*: “with his comprovincials”], so that whatever was being done irrationally in his own region might be corrected by priestly decree. What reason is there for so great a multitude to assemble in one place? The faith of the Church is not shaken by any danger; no new heresy has arisen. What necessity is there for so many priests of the Lord to gather together?”

He replied:

“There are many matters that must be distinguished, matters that have been unjustly handled, both concerning incest and concerning the cases being conducted between us. But above all there is this cause of God, greater than all others: you must investigate why Bishop Praetextatus was killed by the sword in a church. There must also be an inquiry concerning those accused of lust, so that, if defeated, they may be corrected by priestly decree, or, if found innocent, the public error of the accusation may be removed.”

Then he ordered that this synod be postponed until the Kalends of the fourth month [Note: No mention of this synod is found anywhere; hence it may be doubted whether it was ever convened].

After these things had been said, we proceeded to the church, for that day was the solemnity of the Lord’s Resurrection [Note: In *Bad.*, with the intervening material omitted, this is joined to the middle part of the following chapter as follows: “A solemnity on account of which everything was conducted with greater devotion and affection; and, as though whatever the king did were done religiously, it happened at that time in this manner: For three days …”].

After the Masses had been celebrated, he invited us to a banquet. It was no less lavish in its dishes than rich in joy. The king always spoke of God, the building of churches, and the defense of the poor; at times he laughed and delighted in spiritual joking, adding things by which we too might enjoy some happiness.

He also said these words:

“Would that my nephew kept his promises. Everything I have belongs to him. Yet if he is offended because I receive the envoys of my nephew Chlothar, am I so foolish that I cannot restrain matters between them, lest scandal spread? I know that this is more likely to occur than to proclaim it among the *Tongins* [reading and sense uncertain]. If I discover that Chlothar is truly my nephew, I will give him either two or three cities in some region, so that he will not appear to be disinherited from my kingdom, nor will the things I leave to him prepare trouble for this other one.”

After saying these and other things, he treated us with gentle affection, weighed us down with gifts, and ordered us to depart, instructing us always to report to King Childebert whatever would contribute to the prosperity of his life.

### XXI

The king himself, as we have often said, was generous in almsgiving and zealous in vigils and fasts. For at that time it was reported that Massilia was being severely devastated by the bubonic plague, and that this disease had rapidly spread as far as a village in the territory of Lyon called Octavum. But the king, like a good priest providing remedies by which he might heal the wounds of the sinful populace, ordered all the people to assemble at the church, the Rogation ceremonies to be celebrated with the greatest devotion, and nothing else to be consumed as food except barley bread with pure water. He also urgently commanded everyone to attend the vigils. This was accordingly done at that time.

For three days, with his almsgiving flowing more abundantly than usual, he feared deeply for the whole populace, so that he was then regarded not merely as a king but also as a priest of the Lord, placing all his hope in the Lord’s mercy and casting upon him the thoughts that came to him, believing with complete faith that he would bring them to fulfillment. For it was then commonly reported among the faithful that a certain woman, whose son was suffering from quartan fever and lay anxiously in bed, made her way through the crowd as far as the king’s back. Secretly tearing off the fringes of the royal garment, she put them into water and gave it to her son to drink; immediately the fever was extinguished and he was healed.

I do not doubt this, since I myself have often heard people invoking his name while a demonic apparition was tormenting them, and confessing the deeds of their own crimes when his power compelled them to recognize them.

[Note: That is, the possessed or demoniacs. Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book IV, chapter 35, relates a vision of this same king, through which he discovered a treasure that he later used to adorn the tomb of Saint Marcellus. See also Aimoin, book III, chapter 3.]

### XXII

As we said above, since the city of Massilia was suffering from a most grievous contagion, I have decided to recount in greater detail what it endured. In those days Bishop Theodorus had gone to the king, ostensibly to bring some accusation against the patrician Nicetius.

[Note: Two manuscripts read “Theodorus [went] to the king,” omitting “bishop.”]

But when King Childebert refused to hear him at all concerning this matter, he resolved to return home.

Meanwhile, a ship from Hispania arrived at his port with its customary cargo; it wickedly carried with it the source of this disease. When many of the townspeople purchased various goods from it, a single house, in which there were eight persons, was immediately left empty after all its inhabitants had been killed by the contagion. The conflagration of the plague did not at once spread through all the houses of the city. But after a certain interval, and as though a flame had been kindled in a field of grain, it set the entire city ablaze with the fire of disease.

The bishop of the city, however, went to the site and confined himself within the enclosure of the basilica of Saint Victor, together with the few who had remained with him at that time. There, throughout the devastation of the city, he devoted himself to prayers and vigils, imploring the mercy of the Lord so that, once the destruction had ceased, the people might at last be permitted to rest in peace.

[Note: Gregory also discusses Saint Victor of Massilia, the martyr, in *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, book I, chapter 77.]

After this plague had ceased for two months, when the people had already returned to the city in security, the disease broke out again, and those who had returned died. Thereafter, too, the city was afflicted by this destruction on many occasions.

### XXIII

Bishop Agericus of Verdun, suffering severely from the gall of that prolonged bitterness because Guntchramnus Boso, for whom he had stood surety, had been killed—or also because of the hidden bitterness that Berthefredus had been killed inside the oratory of the church’s house—and especially because he kept Guntchramnus’s sons with him and wept every day, saying, “You were left orphans because of my hatred,” was inflamed by these causes, as we have said. Weighed down by the bitterness of his gall and, above all, consumed by severe fasting, he died and was placed in a tomb.

[Note: The feast of Saint Agericus is celebrated on 1 December. Fortunatus praises him in book III, poems 27 and 28. He was buried at Verdun in the oratory of Saint Martin that he himself had built; it is now called Saint Agericus after him, together with the monastery attached to it, belonging to the Order of Saint Benedict and having a regular abbot from the congregation of Saint Vanne.]

His abbot Buciovaldus also sought the episcopate but obtained nothing. For the royal authority, with the consent of the citizens, decreed that Charimer, the *referendarius*, should be made a priest, while Abbot Buciovaldus was passed over. They said that he was proud, and for this reason some called him Buccusvalidus.

Licerius, bishop of Arles, also died. In his church Virgilius, abbot of Autun, was installed as his successor with the assistance of Bishop Syagrius.

[Note: Between the two, Saxius places Paschasius, who occupied the see for a very brief interval; indeed, in the ancient diptychs of the church of Arles edited by our Mabillon in volume III of the *Analecta*, Paschasius is listed in the same order. The same author argues from the *Life of Virgilius* himself that Virgilius was made bishop after having been abbot of Lérins. But Gregory’s authority seems preferable, since he was contemporary with Virgilius. Accordingly, Barralis, who published his life in the *Chronologia Lirinensis*, records that he was first a monk of Lérins, then abbot of Autun, and finally, after being abbot, bishop of Arles. Gregory the Great wrote several letters to Virgilius. The Bollandists discuss him on 5 March, when his feast is celebrated among the people of Lérins, and at Arles on 7 October.]

### XXIV

Deutherius, bishop of Vence, also died, and Fronimius was appointed in his place.

[Note: Bec has *Deotharius*; Colb. m. and Regm. have *Deotherius*. He took part in the Fourth Council of Orléans in 541 and in several subsequent councils down to 585, when his envoy attended the Second Council of Mâcon together with Fronimius, his successor, who subscribed among the bishops who did not possess a see.]

This Fronimius was a native of the city of Bourges, but for some reason went to Septimania. After the death of King Athanagild, he was magnificently received by his successor Leuva and was ordained bishop in the city of Agde.

After Leuva’s death, however, while Leuvichild was raging in that heretical perversity, and Ingundis, the daughter of King Sigibert whom we mentioned above (*Book V*, chapter 39 and following), was being taken to Hispania for marriage, Leuvichild heard that this bishop had advised her never to mingle herself with the poison of heretical belief. For this reason he continually harassed him and laid snares of injury for him, until he drove him from the episcopate.

When he could find no traps with which to ensnare him, at last he sent someone to attack him with a sword. Fronimius learned of this through intermediaries, abandoned the city of Agde, and came to Gaul. There he was received and honored by many bishops, and then went on to King Childebert. Thus, when the opportunity became available, he received episcopal authority in the aforesaid city, by the king’s grant, in the ninth year after his deposition.

That year the Britons subjected the territories of Nantes and Rennes severely to plunder: they harvested the vineyards, devastated the cultivated land, carried off the rural population into captivity, and kept none of their former promises. Indeed, they not only failed to keep their promises but also spoke ill of our kings.

### XXV

Therefore, when King Childebert had promised, in response to the request of the Lombards, that his sister would become the wife of their king, after accepting gifts he nevertheless promised her to the Gothic envoys when they arrived, because he knew that that people had been converted to the Catholic faith.

[Note: This king was Authari, called Aptacharius by our Gregory below, book X, chapter 3. He later married Theodelinda, daughter of Garibald, duke or king of the Bavarians, as Paul the Deacon relates at greater length in book III, chapter 31, of *The Deeds of the Lombards*. Several letters of Gregory the Great to her survive.]

[Note: This was Chlodosuinda, who, it seems, married neither king; or at least she must be considered to have died shortly after the marriage contracted with Reccared. For Reccared, together with Queen Baddo, his wife, subscribed to the profession of the Catholic faith in the year 627 of the era, the fourth year of his reign. From this one may infer that Reccared, weary of having so often suffered rejection from the Franks, took a wife from among his own people. Indeed, his son and successor Liuba is said in Isidore’s *Chronicle* to have been born of a mother of lowly rank, in the year 639 of the era.]

He also sent an embassy to the emperor, so that what he had not previously done—namely, to defeat the Lombard people and, with the emperor’s support, drive them from Italy—might now be accomplished. Nevertheless, he also sent his own army to undertake the conquest of that region.

[Note: To this should be referred what Gregory wrote above on this matter, *Book VI*, chapter 42. This embassy will be discussed more fully in *Book X*, chapter 2 and following. Compare also chapter 30 of book III of Paul the Deacon’s *History of the Lombards*, where he describes the slaughter of the Franks in almost the same words as our Gregory, quoting his words under the title *History of the Franks*.]

When the dukes departed for that place with the army, the forces engaged one another. But our men were severely beaten: many were struck down, some were captured, and very many escaped by flight and scarcely returned to their homeland. So great was the slaughter of the Frankish army there that no similar one was remembered from former times.

### XXVI

In the fourteenth year of King Childebert, Queen Ingoberga, the widow of the former Charibert, departed from this world. She was a very prudent woman, endowed with a religious way of life, and not negligent in vigils, prayers, or almsgiving.

[Note: Regm., together with the printed editions, has *cordata*, “wise.”]

I believe that, warned by God’s providence, she sent messengers even to me, so that I might assist her in what she was planning according to her wishes—that is, for the remedy of her soul—and yet in such a way that, when I came to her, she would set down in writing what she had decided should be done after taking counsel.

I came, I confess, and saw a person who feared God. After she had received me kindly, she summoned a notary and, as I have said, after taking counsel with me, assigned certain properties to the church of Tours and the basilica of Saint Martin, and certain others to the church of Le Mans.

After a few months, worn down by a sudden illness, she departed from this world, leaving many free persons behind through written instruments.

[Note: Colb. m. has “a few days.” Bertramnus, bishop of that same city, attests in his testament that Ingoberga left something to the church of Saint Mary of Le Mans; see volume III of the *Analecta*, page 114.]

She was, I believe, in the seventieth year of her life. She left behind one daughter, whom the son of a certain king in Kent joined to himself in marriage.

[Note: Namely, Ethelbert; see above, *Book IV*, chapter 26.]

[Col. 0506A]

### XXVII

The duke Amalo, while sending his wife to another estate to attend to business, fell in love with a certain freeborn girl. One night, drunk with wine, he sent his servants to drag the girl away and bring her to his bed.

Although she resisted, she was forcibly taken to his residence. While they beat her with slaps, a stream of blood flowed from her nostrils and drenched her. Thus it happened that the bed of the aforementioned duke himself was also stained by this stream. He took the girl, beaten with fists, blows, and other strikes, into his arms, and immediately, overcome by sleep, began to sleep.

She stretched out her hand beyond the man’s head and found a sword. Drawing it, she struck off the duke’s head with a manly blow, like Judith striking Holofernes. When he began to cry out, the servants came running.

When they wanted to kill her, he exclaimed, saying, “Do not do it, I beg you. I am the one who sinned, because I attempted to violate her chastity. Since she strove to preserve her modesty, let her by no means perish.”

Having said this, he breathed out his spirit.

When his household gathered around him and mourned, the girl, by God’s help, left the house. During the night she reached the city of Chalon, which lies about thirty-five miles from that place.

[Note: Colb. a. has “fifteen miles.”]

There she entered the basilica of Saint Marcellus, fell at the king’s feet, and disclosed everything she had suffered. Then the most merciful king not only granted her life but also ordered a written warrant to be given to her, so that, once she was placed under his protection, none of the dead man’s relatives would ever cause her any trouble.

Nevertheless, by God’s favor we learned that the girl’s chastity had not in any way been violated by the savage ravisher.

[Col. 0506C] **Variant:** [Al. *suo*, “by his own.”]

### XXVIII

Queen Brunichildis ordered a shield of extraordinary size to be made of gold and gems. She sent it to the king in Hispania together with two wooden bowls, commonly called *bacchinon*, likewise decorated with gems and gold. She dispatched Ebregisil, who had often gone to that region on an embassy.

[Note: Colb. m. has *baecchinon*; Regm. has *baethinon*. In German, *Becken*; in French, *bassin*.]

When he had departed, a report was brought to King Guntchramnus by someone who said that Queen Brunichildis was sending gifts to the sons of Gundovald.

[Note: Namely, to the man who, claiming to be the son of Chlothar, was killed; see above, *Book VII*, chapter 38.]

On hearing this, the king ordered strict guards to be established throughout the roads of his kingdom, so that absolutely no one could pass without being searched. They even examined people’s clothing, footwear, and other belongings to see whether letters were being carried secretly.

Ebregisil, as he approached Paris with these objects, was arrested by Duke Ebrachar and brought before Guntchramnus. The king said to him:

“Is it not enough, most wretched of men, that by your shameful counsel you summoned that Ballomer, whom you call Gundovald, to marriage—he whom my hand subdued, who wished to subject the power of our kingdom to his own dominion—and now you are sending gifts to his sons so that you may summon them again into Gaul to slaughter me?” Therefore you shall not go where you wish, but shall die by death, because your embassy is hostile to our people.”

[Note: Regm. has “to subject the power.”]

When Ebregisil denied this, saying that the matter did not concern him and that the gifts were instead being sent to Richared, who was supposed to marry Chlodosuinda, the sister of King Childebert, the king believed his statement and released him. He then proceeded on the route to which he had been sent, carrying the gifts with him.

### XXIX

Accordingly, when King Childebert was invited by Sigibert, the priest of the town of Momociacum, to celebrate Easter in the aforesaid city, he fixed the date for the celebration there.

[Note: The manuscripts, except Bec, have *Sigiberto*; Bec and the editions preceding Chesnius have *Sigimundo*. Chesnius prints both readings. There is no less difficulty concerning the name of the see. Bad. has *Noviociacensis*; Regm., *Noviomensis*. If this reading is genuine, there is no remaining difficulty. Valesius and Cointius think that *Moguntiacensis* should be read. No light is shed on this difficulty by the published catalogues of the bishops of Mainz or Noviomagus. Sidonius governed the church of Mainz around that time, according to Fortunatus, book IX, poem 9, but perhaps had already died, as Cointius believes. Cointius writes that Gregory’s Sigimundus, or Sigibertus—or, as Serarius calls him, Wilibertus—succeeded him. Thaumastus, or Theomastus, bishop of Momociacum, is also praised in *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 53.]

At that time his elder son Theodobert suffered severely from a swelling of the throat, but recovered.

Meanwhile King Childebert mobilized an army and prepared to go with it into Italy to make war against the Lombard people. But when the Lombards heard this, they sent envoys with gifts, saying:

“Let there be friendship between us, and let us not perish. We shall pay a fixed tribute to your authority, and whenever it is necessary to fight against enemies, we shall not be reluctant to bring assistance.”

When King Childebert heard this, he sent envoys to King Guntchramnus to report to him what the Lombards were offering. But Guntchramnus, not opposing this agreement,

[Note: Casin. has *convenientia*, “agreement.”]

gave counsel for confirming peace.

King Childebert nevertheless ordered the army to remain where it was. He sent envoys to the Lombards, saying that if they confirmed what they had promised, the army would return home. But this was by no means fulfilled.

### XXX

King Childebert ordered assessors to go to Poitiers at the invitation of Bishop Maroveus—namely, Florentianus, *maior domus regiae*, and Romulfus, count of his palace—so that the people might pay the census which they had rendered in the time of his father, after the reassessment had been carried out.

[Note: Colb. a. has *Domus Reginae*, “the Queen’s household.” Regm. calls him Romulfus, vice-count of the palace. See *Book IV*, *Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 6, and Fortunatus, book X, poems 16 and 18.]

Many of those formerly liable had died, and for this reason the burden of the tribute had fallen upon widows, orphans, and the infirm. The assessors, examining the matter in order, released the poor and infirm, but placed under the public census those whom the requirements of justice made liable to tribute; they then proceeded to Tours.

When they wished to impose the tributary obligation upon the people, saying that they had a book in their hands showing how the people had paid under the earlier kings, we replied:

“It is evident that the city of Tours was assessed in the time of King Chlothar, and that the books were brought before the king. But when the king was moved by fear of Saint Martin the bishop, they were burned.

“After the death of King Chlothar, this people swore allegiance to King Charibert. He likewise promised under oath that he would impose no new laws or customs upon the people, but would keep them in the condition in which they had formerly lived under his father’s rule. He promised that he would impose no new ordinance upon them that would amount to plunder.

“Gaiso, the count at that time, having obtained a capitulary—the kind of document we have mentioned that earlier officials had produced—began to exact tribute. But Bishop Eufronius prohibited him. Gaiso nevertheless sent the matter, together with the unlawful exaction, to the king’s presence, displaying the capitulary in which the tribute was contained.

“The king, groaning and fearing the power of Saint Martin, committed the document to the flames. He returned the gold pieces that had been exacted to the basilica of Saint Martin, charging that no one from the people of Tours should ever pay any public tribute.

“After his death, King Sigibert held this city and imposed no burden of tribute. So now, in the fourteenth year of his reign after his father’s death, King Childebert has exacted nothing, nor has this city groaned under any burden of tribute.

“It is now in your power to decide whether you consider a tribute due or not. But see to it that you do not cause harm by deciding to act against his oath.”

When I had said this, they replied:

“Here is the book we have in our hands, in which a census has been imposed upon this people.”

I answered:

“This book was not brought from the king’s treasury, nor has it ever been valid for so many years. It is not surprising if, because of the enmities of these citizens, it has been preserved in someone’s house. God will judge those who, for the sake of plundering our citizens, have produced it after so long an interval.”

While these things were being done, Audinus’s son, who had produced the book, was seized by fever that very day and died on the third day.

Afterward we sent messengers to the king, asking him to send instructions concerning what he ordered to be done in this matter. They promptly sent a letter with an official royal warrant, ordering that the people of Tours should not be assessed out of reverence for Saint Martin.

[Note: An *auctoritas* was a diploma or royal order that took precedence over other documents and therefore seems to have been signed by the king’s own hand and sealed with his ring, as may be inferred from the letter of Saint Radegund below, chapter 42. See Bignonius’s notes on book I of Marculf’s *Formulas*, formula 4.]

When this had been read, the men who had been sent for this purpose immediately returned home.

### XXXI

King Guntchramnus mobilized an army against Septimania.

[Note: Regm. has *Hispaniam*, “Hispania.” Since Septimania was subject to the Visigothic kings in Hispania, Gregory elsewhere more than once calls it Hispania.]

Beforehand, Duke Austrowald had approached Carcassonne and received the oaths of allegiance, subjecting the people themselves to royal authority. The king sent Boso and Antestius to capture the remaining cities.

When Boso arrived arrogantly, despised and condemned Duke Austrowald for daring to enter Carcassonne without him, he proceeded there with the men of Saintes, Périgueux, Bordeaux, Agen, and Toulouse.

[Variant: *perrexit*, “went.”]

As he advanced in this boastful fashion, the Goths were informed of his movements and prepared an ambush. Boso pitched his camp beside a small river near the city, sat down to banquets, devoted himself to drunkenness, and provoked the Goths with insults and blasphemies.

They fell upon the men, finding them dining and unsuspecting. The latter shouted and rose against them. The Goths resisted for a short time and then pretended to flee. When the pursuers rose after them, those who had been waiting in ambush emerged, enclosed the pursuers in the middle, and cut them down to the last man.

Those who managed to escape fled, scarcely mounting their horses, abandoning all their equipment on the open plain and taking nothing of their own property with them. They counted it a great gain if only their lives were spared.

The pursuing Goths found and plundered all their possessions, carrying away all the infantry as captives. About five thousand men fell there, while more than two thousand were taken captive. Many, however, were released by the Goths and returned home.

[Note: Regm. has “after the horsemen had mounted.” The printed editions have “after mounting a horse.” Isidore states in his *Chronicle*, year 624 of the era, that some sixty thousand Franks were routed in this battle, adding that the Goths had never before won a greater victory. John of Biclar also records the same event in his *Chronicle*. The commander of Reccared’s army was Claudius, duke of Lusitania, to whom Saint Gregory the Great commended the monk Cyriacus. Paul the Deacon praises Claudius, as well as his expedition first into Septimania and then into Francia, in his *Book of the Lives of the Fathers of Mérida*.]

### XXXII

The king, angered, ordered the roads throughout his kingdom to be closed, so that no one from Childebert’s kingdom could have passage through the territory of his kingdom. He said:

“Because of the treachery of the man who made a treaty with the king of Hispania, my army has been destroyed. And if those cities do not submit to my authority, this is caused by his instigation.”

Another fire of bitterness was added to this matter. King Childebert was planning to send his elder son, Theodobert, to Soissons. This had aroused suspicion in King Guntchramnus, who said:

“Since my nephew is sending his son to Soissons for this purpose, he intends to make him enter Paris and wishes to seize my kingdom.”

Childebert could never have held such a thought, even in imagination, if it is permissible to say so. Guntchramnus also hurled many insults against Queen Brunichildis, saying that these actions were being carried out by her counsel through her son. He further added that she wished to invite the former son of Gundovald and unite him to her in marriage.

For this reason he ordered a synod of bishops to assemble on the Kalends of November. Many bishops hurrying to this gathering from the remotest parts of Gaul turned back on the way because Queen Brunichildis cleared herself of this accusation by oaths. Thus, once the roads had again been opened, he made passage available to those wishing to approach King Childebert.

### XXXIII

In those days Ingeltrudis, who had established a monastery in the atrium of Saint Martin, came before the king as though she were going to accuse her daughter.

[Note: This monastery long stood within the enclosure of Saint Martin and was called Saint Mary of Scriniolum. Around the beginning of the eleventh century it was transferred by Herveus the treasurer to a nearby hill, which, because of its pleasant location and agreeable view, is called Bellusmons. It can still be seen there, dedicated to the Rule of Saint Benedict.]

Berthefledis, the former daughter of King Charibert, lived in that monastery. But as Ingeltrudis was leaving, Berthefledis entered the monastery at Le Mans.

[Note: Regm. has “the monastery at Le Mans”; several printed editions, together with Bec, have “returned.”]

She was devoted to gluttony and sleep and had no concern for the service of God.

I think the matter involving Ingeltrudis and her daughter should be traced back further. Some years earlier, when Ingeltrudis had begun, as we said, to establish a monastery for girls within the atrium of Saint Martin, she sent instructions to her daughter, saying:

“Leave your husband and come, so that I may make you abbess over this flock that I have gathered.”

When the daughter heard this frivolous advice, she came to Tours with her husband. After entering her mother’s monastery, she said to her husband:

“Go back from here and manage our property and our children, for I shall not return with you. No one joined in marriage will see the kingdom of God.”

He came to me and reported everything he had heard from his wife. Then I went to the monastery and reread the decrees of the canons of Nicaea, in which it is written:

“If any woman leaves her husband and rejects the marriage bed in which she has lived well, saying, ‘There is no share in the glory of the heavenly kingdom for anyone who has been joined in marriage,’ let her be anathema.”

[Note: Regm. has: “If any married woman leaves her husband.” This seems to be canon 14 of the Council of Gangra, which the ancients commonly appended to the Council of Nicaea; this is indicated by the title in the ancient manuscripts.]

When Berthegundis heard this, she feared that she would be deprived of communion by the priests of God. She left the monastery and returned with her husband.

After three or four years had passed, her mother again sent instructions to her, asking her to come to her. Berthegundis then loaded ships with both her own property and that of her husband, took one son with her while her husband was absent, and arrived at Tours.

But her mother could not retain her because of the husband’s wickedness—namely, lest she suffer the legal charge that had been contrived through his deceit. She therefore sent Berthegundis to her brother Bertchramnus, her own son and bishop of the city of Bordeaux.

Her husband followed her. The bishop said to him:

“Since you joined her to yourself in marriage without the counsel of her relatives, she will not be your wife.”

They had already been joined together for almost thirty years. Her husband frequently went to the city of Bordeaux, but the bishop refused to restore her to him.

When King Guntchramnus arrived at the city of Orléans, as we mentioned in the preceding book, her husband began to assail the bishop more fiercely with words, saying:

“You took away my wife together with her servants. And behold—an action unbecoming a priest—you have committed the disgrace of adultery, you with my maidservants and she with your servants.”

[Note: *Book VIII*, chapters 1 and 2, where Guntchramnus acknowledges Bertchramnus as his maternal relative. Valesius believes that Ingeltrudis, who was Bertchramnus’s mother, was a sister of Ingundis and Aregundis, wives of Chlothar I, and therefore Guntchramnus’s maternal aunt.]

The king, moved to fury, compelled the bishop to promise that he would return her to her husband, saying:

“She is my relative. If she has done anything wrong in her husband’s house, I shall avenge it. But if not, why should her husband be deprived of his wife after being reduced to such disgrace?”

[Note: Colb. m. and Bec. have *redactus vir*; the printed editions have *redacta viro*; Regm. has *redactus vir conjux ei auferatur?*]

Bishop Bertchramnus then promised, saying:

“I confess that my sister came to me after many years. Out of affection and longing I kept her with me as I wished. But now she has left me. Let him now seek her and call her back wherever he wishes; he will find no opposition from me.”

Having said this, he secretly sent messengers to her, ordering her to change her clothing, undertake penance, and go to the basilica of Saint Martin. She did not delay in doing so.

Her husband came with many men following him, intending to drive her from that holy place. She was wearing religious clothing and asserted that she had undertaken penance.

[Note: After penance had been undertaken, it was not permitted to return to the allurements of the world, as the Fathers of the First Council of Tours say, canon 8. For this reason the Third Council of Orléans forbade anyone, in canon 24, to impose penance upon married persons without the consent of both parties.]

But she refused to follow her husband.

Meanwhile Bishop Bertchramnus died at Bordeaux. Berthegundis, having returned to her mother, said:

“Woe is me, who listened to the counsel of an evil mother! Behold, my brother has died; behold, I have been abandoned by my husband and separated from my children. Where shall I go, unhappy woman, or what shall I do?”

After taking counsel, she then went to Poitiers. Her mother wished to keep her with her but was completely unable to do so.

From this arose hostility, as they repeatedly went before the king. The mother wished to defend the property of the father, while the daughter wished to defend that of her husband. Berthegundis produced a gift from her brother Bertchramnus, saying:

“My brother gave me this and that.”

But her mother did not accept the gift. Wishing to claim everything for herself, she sent people who broke into her house and carried off all her property, together with the deed of gift.

Thus the mother proved herself guilty, when she later restored some of those very possessions under compulsion to the daughter, who demanded them.

But after I and our brother Bishop Maroveus had repeatedly received royal letters ordering us to reconcile them, Berthegundis came to Tours. When she appeared in court, we compelled her, as far as we could, to submit to reason; but her mother could not be swayed.

Then, inflamed by anger, the mother went to the king, intending to disinherit her daughter from the paternal property. In the king’s presence, she set forth the case, while her daughter was absent, and judgment was given that, after the daughter had been restored one quarter, the mother should receive three quarters together with her grandchildren, whom she had by one son.

The priest Theutharius, who had recently been converted from the office of *referendarius* under King Sigibert and had received the honor of the priesthood, attended in order to carry out this division according to the king’s command. But because the daughter resisted, neither was the division made nor was the quarrel brought to an end.

[Note: See the following book, chapter 12.]

### XXXIV

Rigunthis, the daughter of Chilperic, repeatedly brought accusations against her mother. She said that she herself was the mistress and that her mother should be reduced to servitude. She abused her with many and frequent insults, and at times they struck each other with fists and slaps.

Her mother said to her:

“Why are you troubling me, my daughter? Here are your father’s possessions, which are in my keeping. Take them and use them as you wish.”

She entered the storeroom and opened a chest filled with necklaces and precious ornaments. For a long time she took various objects from it and handed them to her daughter, who was standing nearby. Then she said to her:

“I am tired now. Put your hand in and remove whatever you find.”

When the daughter inserted her arm and began taking objects from the chest, her mother seized the chest’s lid and struck it down upon her neck. Pressing it with all her strength, she crushed her throat against the lower edge of the chest, so that her eyes seemed ready to burst.

One of the young women inside cried out loudly:

“Run, please, run! Behold, my mistress is being grievously strangled by her mother!”

Those who had been waiting outside the door rushed in, broke into the room, and dragged the girl away from the impending death.

[Note: Codex Regm. has: “But those who were outside, rushing in quickly, dragged the girl from the room,” and so forth.]

After this, hostility between the two of them grew more violently, chiefly and almost exclusively because Rigunthis was pursuing adulterous affairs. Quarrels and beatings therefore continually took place between them.

### XXXV

Beretrudis [Note: This chapter is absent from Vat. and Colb. a. Beretrudis was the wife of the duke Launebod, whom Fortunatus praises for constructing the church of Saint Saturninus at Toulouse in Book II, poem 9; there he also extols Beretrudis’s piety at length.] when she was dying appointed her daughter her heir, leaving various things either to the convents of women that she herself had founded, or to the churches and basilicas of holy confessors. But Waddo, whom we mentioned in the preceding book [Note: Gregory has already discussed Waddo several times. For his sons, see the following book, chapter 21.], complained that his son-in-law had plundered his horses. He therefore planned to go to one of his estates, which he had left to his daughter and which lay within the territory of Poitiers, saying:

“Since this man, coming from another kingdom, has carried off my horses, I shall take away his estate.”

Meanwhile he sent word to the estate-manager [Note: The *agens*, also called an *actor* below, was the person responsible for the estate and the properties dependent upon it.] that, when he arrived, he should have everything necessary for his expenses prepared. On hearing this, the manager gathered the men of that household [Col. 0513A] and prepared for battle, saying:

“Unless I die, Waddo shall not enter my master’s house.”

When Waddo’s wife heard that preparations for war were being made against her husband, she said to him:

“Do not go there, dear husband. If you go, you will die, and I shall be miserable with the children.”

She grasped him and tried to hold him back. Her son also said:

“If you go, we shall all die together, and you will leave my mother a widow and my brothers orphans.”

But when these words could not restrain him, he was inflamed with rage against his son, calling him timid and weak. He threw down his axe and nearly struck the boy’s brains out. The boy, however, being knocked partly aside, escaped the blow.

At last they mounted their horses and departed. Waddo again ordered the manager to clean the house with brooms and cover the benches with coverings [Col. 0513B]. But the manager disregarded his order and, together with the crowd of men and women mentioned above, stood before his master’s door awaiting his arrival.

When Waddo came and immediately entered the house, he said:

“Why are these benches not covered with coverings, or the house cleaned with brooms?”

Then, raising his hand with a dagger, he aimed at the man’s head. The man fell and died.

When the dead man’s son saw this, he cast a spear from the opposite side and hurled it at Waddo. The *falarica* [Note: The *phalarica*, or *falarica*, was properly a missile weapon used by defenders of towers; it was so called from *phala*, a word denoting a wooden tower.] pierced the middle of Waddo’s belly and emerged from his back. As he fell to the ground, the crowd that had gathered began to bury him under stones.

Then one of those who had come with him approached amid the shower of stones, covered him with a cloak, and, after calming the crowd, lifted him onto a horse while his son lamented. He brought him home alive. But immediately, amid the tears of his wife and children, Waddo breathed his last.

Thus, after his life had ended so unhappily, his son went to the king and obtained his property.

### XXXVI

In the year mentioned above, King Childebert was staying with his wife and mother within the territory of the city called Strasbourg [Note: Gregory was the first, according to Valesius, to call Argentoratum “Strataburgum.” Hence below, Book X, chapter 19, he says: “the city of Argentoratum, which they now call Strasbourg.” The name perhaps means a town on a road, that is, situated on a public or military road that was then much frequented.].

Then the more powerful men who were in the city of Soissons or Meaux [Note: Regm.: “who were in the city of Meaux.”] came to him and said:

“Give us one of your sons, so that we may serve him; that is, by keeping a pledge of your dynasty among us, we may more easily resist our enemies and strive to defend the boundaries of your city” [Note: Colb. a.: “the boundaries of your world.”].

The king was pleased by this request and decided to send his elder son Theodobert there. He assigned him counts, household officers, officials, tutors, and everyone necessary for the performance of royal service, and in the sixth month of that year sent him according to the wishes of the men who had asked the king to dispatch him. The people received him joyfully and prayed that divine mercy might grant him and his father a long life.

### XXXVII

[Note: In Vat. and Colb. a. the remainder of this book, together with the first chapter of the following book, is absent.] At that time Droctigisilus [Note: Regm.: Doctigisilus.] was at the city of Soissons. Because of excessive drinking, as they say, he had lost his reason with the fourth year approaching. Many of the citizens maintained that this had come upon him through sorcery, brought about by the dismissal of an archdeacon whom he had removed from office. Thus, within the city walls, he was more afflicted by this madness; but if he went outside the city, he functioned more normally.

When the aforementioned king came to the city and Droctigisilus was behaving better, he was not permitted [Note: So Bec. and Regm.; the others, conversely, read “he was permitted to enter.”] to enter the city because of the king who had arrived.

Although he was greedy for food and drank wine beyond measure, and beyond what priestly caution permitted [Col. 0514B], no one accused him of adultery. Nevertheless, later, when a synod of bishops had assembled at the estate of Sauriciacum [Note: Commonly called Sourci or Saurci, a village situated not far from the river Aisne.], it was ordered that he should be allowed to enter his city.

### XXXVIII

When Queen Faileuba, the wife of King Childebert, fell ill after giving birth to a child who immediately died, she heard that certain people were attempting to act either against her or against Queen Brunichild. Once she had recovered from her illness, she approached the king and disclosed to him and to his mother everything she had heard.

The report was as follows: Septimina [Note: Regm. and Colb. m.: Septimana; nevertheless, they call her both Septiminia and Septimina.] the nurse of her children wished, by her counsel and persuasion, to induce the king, after expelling his mother and abandoning his wife, to take another wife, so that with the king they might carry out whatever they wished or obtain it by entreaty [Col. 0514C].

If the king refused to comply with what she advised, then, after he had been killed by sorcery, his sons would be elevated to the throne; their mother and grandmother would nevertheless be rejected, and the conspirators themselves would rule the kingdom.

She declared that the partners in this plan were Sunnegisilus [Note: Colb. m.: Somnigisilus and Gallomanus. Regm.: Domnigisilus … Gallomagus; and likewise below. Gallomagnus was the father of Palatina, who married Godegisilus, as Fortunatus reports in Book VII, chapter 6.] the master of the horse, Gallomagnus the referendary, and Droctulf, who had been assigned to Septimina as her companion in raising the king’s children.

At last Septimina and Droctulf were seized. Before long, when they were stretched between posts and beaten more violently, Septimina confessed that she had killed her husband Jovius by sorcery out of love for Droctulf, and that she had engaged in sexual relations with him. They also confessed to the matters mentioned above and identified the men named as participants in the plot.

The men themselves were then sought. But, terrified by their consciences, they took refuge in hiding within the precincts of the churches.

The king himself went to them and said:

“Come out to judgment, so that we may determine whether the charges brought against you are true or false. For, in my opinion, your consciences would not have terrified you into fleeing into this church if you had not been guilty. Nevertheless, you have a promise of your lives, even if you are found guilty. We are Christians; it is unlawful to remove criminals from a church and punish them.”

They were then brought outside and came with the king to judgment. When questioned, they protested, saying:

“Septimina and Droctulf disclosed this plan to us. But we rejected and fled from it, and never wished to consent to such a crime.”

The king replied:

“If you had given no assistance, you would certainly have reported it to our ears. Is it true, then, that you gave your consent in this matter, while you wished to conceal it from our knowledge?”

They were immediately expelled and again sought refuge in the church.

Septimina and Droctulf were beaten severely. Her face was wounded with heated cauteries, and after everything she possessed had been taken from her [Col. 0515B], she was led to the estate of Marilegium [Note: Commonly called Marleim today, in Alsace, approximately halfway between Molsheim and Saverne. The ruins of a royal estate may still be seen between the town of that name and the village of Kirkem, which also once had its own royal palace. Gregory discusses both places in Book IV of *On Diplomatic Affairs*.], so that, turning a mill, she might prepare each day the flour necessary for the provisions of the women stationed in the women’s quarters.

Droctulf, with his hair and ears cut off, was assigned to cultivate the vineyard. After a few days he fled. The estate-manager [Note: That is, the procurator of that royal household.] searched for him and brought him back to the king. There he was beaten severely and sent again to the vineyard he had abandoned.

Sunnegisilus and Gallomagnus, however, were stripped of the property they had received from the royal treasury and thrust into exile. But when envoys came, among them bishops, from King Guntchramn and pleaded on their behalf, they were recalled from exile. Nothing was left to them except what they appeared to possess as their own.

### XXXIX

In the monastery at Poitiers, a scandal arose when the devil lay in the heart of Chrodieldis, who claimed to be the daughter of the former King Charibert. Relying, as she imagined, upon royal relatives, she exacted oaths from the nuns that, after charges had been brought against the abbess Leubovera and the abbess had been expelled from the monastery, Chrodieldis herself should be installed as superior.

She left with forty girls or more and with her cousin Basina, the daughter of Chilperic, saying:

“I am going to my royal relatives, so that I may make them aware of our disgrace: here we are humiliated not as daughters of kings, but as though born of wicked servants.”

The wretched and foolish woman [Note: So the manuscript copies read. The printed editions have *fatua*, “foolish,” which has the same meaning in Gregory.] did not remember the humility in which the blessed Radegund, who had founded this monastery, conducted herself.

Having left it, she arrived at Tours. After greeting us, she said:

“I beg you, holy priest, to take care of these girls, who have been reduced by the abbess of Poitiers to great humiliation, and to provide them with food until I go to our royal relatives, explain to them what we are suffering, and return.”

I replied:

“If the abbess has committed an offense or omitted anything prescribed by canonical rule, let us go to our brother Maroveus, the bishop, and together accuse her. Once the matter has been corrected, return to your monastery, lest the abundance gathered by holy Radegund through fasts, frequent prayers, and abundant almsgiving be scattered.”

She answered:

“By no means; we shall go to the kings.”

And I said:

“Why do you resist reason [Note: The printed editions read “Why do you resist the reply?” Regm. below has “Why do you despise the admonition?”]? Why do you refuse to heed priestly admonition? I fear that the priests assembled from the churches will remove you from communion.”

For the same thing was inserted by our predecessors in the letter they wrote to the blessed Radegund at the beginning of this community. I have thought it appropriate to include a copy of it in this account.

#### COPY OF THE LETTER

[Col. 0516B]

“To the most blessed Lady Radegund, daughter in Christ of the Church: Eufronius, Praetextatus, Germanus, Felix, Domitianus, Victorius, and Domnolus, bishops [Note: They were Eufronius of Tours, Praetextatus of Rouen, Germanus of Paris, Felix of Nantes, Domitianus of Angers, Victorius of Rennes, and Domnolus of Le Mans.].

“The immense providence of the Godhead is continually concerned with providing remedies for the human race, and it never appears at any place or time to withdraw from the unceasing benefits it bestows. The merciful Ruler of all things everywhere plants in the inheritance of ecclesiastical cultivation people who, cultivating his field with the hoe of devoted faith and strenuous labor, enable the harvest of Christ, by divine moderation, to reach the blessed return of a hundredfold.

“So widely does the distribution of his goodness extend, bringing benefit everywhere, that he nowhere denies what he recognizes as beneficial to many. When he comes as judge, he will have among the many such persons as he may crown. Accordingly, when the beginnings of the venerable faith began to breathe in the regions of Gaul with the rise of the Catholic religion [Note: It is remarkable that here the beginnings of the Christian faith in Gaul are traced back to the time of Saint Martin.], and when the ineffable mysteries of the Lord’s Trinity had then reached the knowledge of only a few, divine mercy, taking counsel for our salvation, deigned to send blessed Martin from a foreign stock for the illumination of this land, so that it might obtain nothing less here than it received from the apostles preaching throughout the circle of the world.

“Although he was not present in the time of the apostles, he did not fail to receive apostolic grace. For what was lacking in rank was supplied by reward, since a later position takes nothing away from one who surpasses others in merits.

“Likewise, most reverend daughter, by God’s favor we rejoice to see in you examples of heavenly love rising again. As the age of the world declines through old age, faith renews itself in the flower of your mind’s struggle; and [Perhaps: so that] what had grown lukewarm in the sluggish chill of old age may at last grow warm again through the ardor of a fervent spirit.

“Since you have come almost from the same part of the world from which we know that blessed Martin came here [Note: Radegund was the daughter of Berthachar, king of the Thuringians, as Gregory himself relates above, Book III, chapter 4. Martin, as everyone knows, was born at Sabaria in Pannonia.], it is no wonder if you appear to imitate in your work the one whom we believe to have been appointed your guide on the journey. Since you have followed his footsteps, may you fulfill his examples with a blessed vow, and make that most blessed man your companion to the same extent that you refuse to retain a share in the world.

“Because the radiance of this conviction shines forth, you return the hearts of your hearers suffused with heavenly light. Thus, everywhere awakened, the minds of girls, kindled by a spark of divine fire, hasten eagerly and swiftly to be watered by the fountain of Christ’s love in your heart; and, abandoning their parents, they choose you for themselves rather than their mother. This is accomplished by grace, not by nature.

“Therefore, seeing the desires of this devotion [Note: Regm.: ‘Therefore, remaining in this devotion, and having learned this…’], we give thanks to the compassion of heaven, which makes human wills adhere to its own will. For we are confident that those whom it commands to be gathered among you, it wishes to preserve in its embrace.

“And because, by God’s favor, we have learned that certain women from our territories have eagerly flown to the establishment of your rule, and because we have also examined the letter of your petition, which we gladly received, we affirm this with Christ as author and healer: although all those who enter there must equally preserve inviolably in the love of the Lord whatever they appear to have accepted with the greatest willingness, since a faith promised to Christ, with heaven as witness, must not be defiled—and it would be no slight crime to pollute the temple of God, God forbid, so that it might be scattered by his burning anger—we nevertheless establish the following specifically.

“If any woman, as has been said, from places sacerdotally entrusted to our governance by the providence of the Lord, should be deemed worthy to join your monastery in the city of Poitiers [Note: Bec., Colb. m., and Chesn.: Pictavina.], then, according to the Constitutions of blessed Caesar, bishop of Arles, no further permission to depart shall be granted to her, since, as the rule states, she appears to have entered of her own will [Note: So Casin.; others have *prodita*. The passage cited here occurs in chapter 1 of Saint Caesarius’s Rule for Nuns.]. This is so that, because of the shameful disgrace of one woman, that which shines honorably among all should not be brought into accusation [or: ‘into disgrace’].

“Therefore, if—God forbid—any woman, inflamed by the enticement of an unsound mind, should wish to plunge her discipline, glory, and crown into the stain of so great an outrage, and, following the counsel of the enemy, should endure departure by whatever means from the cloisters of that monastery—or rather from the kingdom of heaven—like Eve expelled from paradise, she shall be struck with the wound of a terrible anathema, separated from our communion, and plunged into and trampled underfoot in the mud of the streets.

“If, moreover, abandoning Christ and being taken captive by the devil, she should wish to marry a man, not only she herself, who refuses the rule, but also the man joined to her, that shameful adulterer, more truly a sacrilegious offender than a husband, and anyone who supplied poison rather than counsel so that this might occur, shall be struck by a similar punishment and heavenly judgment, as has been said concerning her, with our prayers, until, after separation has taken place and suitable penance has been performed for the accursed crime, she may deserve to be received and restored to the place from which she departed.

“We add also that the priests who will at some time succeed us shall be bound by guilt under a similar condemnation. If, contrary to what we believe, they should wish to relax anything in a manner different from what our decision contains, let them know that, by the judgment of the eternal Judge, they will have to answer for it together with us. For the instruction of our common salvation is this: whatever is promised to Christ must be observed inviolably.

“We believe that this decree of our determination, for the sake of its permanence, must be strengthened by the subscription of our own hands, and that, with Christ as our guide, it will remain perpetually observed by us [Note: The printed editions read ‘will endure.’].”

After this letter had been read, Chrodieldis said:

“No delay will hold us back from going to the kings, whom we know to be our relatives.”

They had come on foot from Poitiers and had received the assistance of no horseman [I. horse]; hence they were breathless and extremely weak. Nor had anyone provided them with any food for the journey. They reached our city on the first day of the first month. There had been heavy rains, and the roads had been broken up by the excessive quantity of water.

### XL

They also spoke against the bishop, saying that through his treachery both these women had been disturbed and the monastery had been abandoned. But it seemed appropriate to recall the origin of this scandal more fully.

In the time of King Chlothar, when the blessed Radegund had founded this monastery, she and her entire community had always been subject and obedient to the earlier bishops. In the time of Sigibert, however, after Maroveus had obtained the bishopric of the city, the blessed Radegund sent clerics to the East, having received letters from King Sigibert concerning her faith and devotion, to obtain a piece of the Lord’s cross and relics of the holy apostles and other martyrs [Note: These words imply that Maroveus, having received letters from Sigibert, sent to the East to obtain relics in order to satisfy Saint Radegund’s devotion. Nevertheless, it is certain that the clerics were sent by Radegund herself; therefore I think the text should be restored as follows: ‘The blessed Radegund sent clerics to the East,’ and so forth. See the *Life of Saint Radegund* written by Baudonivia, sections 18 and following. Fortunatus also expressed the same event in verse in the supplement to poem 2, addressed to the emperor Justin and the empress Sophia; the hymns and other poems that he composed on this occasion are found in Book II.].

When they returned, they brought these relics. After they had been delivered, the queen asked the bishop that they be placed in the monastery with due honor and solemn psalmody [Note: Those relics were brought to Tours and for some time lay in the monastery of men founded there by Saint Radegund, until finally they were carried to Poitiers. This occasioned Gregory, who was not yet a bishop, to build the oratory of the Holy Cross, concerning which see Fortunatus, Book II, poem 3. See Brouverus’s notes on that poem and the *Life of Saint Radegund* by Baudonivia, section 19.].

But he disregarded her request and, mounting his horse, withdrew to an estate.

The queen then again sent to King Sigibert, asking that by his command one of the bishops should place these relics in the monastery with the honor that was fitting and fulfill her desire. For this work Saint Eufronius, bishop of Tours, was appointed.

He came to Poitiers with his clerics and, amid solemn psalmody and an array of shining candles and incense, brought the holy relics into the monastery while the bishop of the place was absent.

Afterward, when she repeatedly sought the favor of her own bishop and could not obtain it, necessity moved her, and she and the abbess whom she had appointed went to the city of Arles. There they received the rule of Saint Caesarius and of the blessed Caesaria and secured themselves under royal protection [Col. 0519A], since they could find no care for their defense in the man who ought to have been their shepherd.

As this scandal spread from day to day, the time came for the blessed Radegund’s death. After she had died, the abbess again asked to live under the authority of her priest. When he initially wished to refuse, he promised, on the advice of his associates, to become their father as was proper and to provide his protection wherever necessity required.

Accordingly, when he went to King Childebert, he obtained an order permitting him to govern this monastery according to ecclesiastical rule, just as he governed the other parishes [Note: Our kings always took special care of this distinguished place, as is clear from a capitulary of Louis the Pious dating from around 822, preserved by Baluzius, which is entirely concerned with this monastery. It held a place among the monasteries that, free from every military service and payment, owed the emperor only their prayers, as is clear from the notice concerning the matter drawn up at the assembly of Aachen in 817.].

But, as these girls claim, I do not know what still remained in his mind—perhaps something that would stir up scandal.

While they were intent on hastening to the king’s presence, as we have said, we gave them this advice:

“You are acting contrary to reason, and by no means can the sort of argument that prevents blasphemy be inserted into your case. But if, as we have said, you disregard reason and refuse to accept salutary advice, at least consider this in your hearts: once the winter season has passed and the spring that has followed it has come, when the breezes are more favorable, you may go wherever your will leads.”

They accepted this advice as suitable. The following summer Chrodieldis left Tours, entrusting the other nuns to her cousin [Note: The printed editions read: ‘having entrusted the other nuns to her cousin Chrodieldis, she went to the king,’ and so forth.], and went to King Guntchramn.

He received her and honored her with gifts, and she returned to Tours, leaving Constantina, the daughter of Burgolinus, in the monastery at Autun while she awaited the bishops whom the king had ordered to come and investigate their case with the abbess.

Many of the others, however, were deceived by various men and married before she returned from the king.

When they had waited for the bishops’ arrival and realized that none was coming, they returned to Poitiers and took refuge within the basilica of Saint Hilary. They gathered thieves, murderers, adulterers, and people guilty of every kind of crime around them, prepared themselves for battle, and said:
