“We are queens, and we shall not enter our monastery until the abbess has been expelled.”

At that time a certain woman was confined there who, a few years earlier, had thrown herself from the wall and fled to the basilica of Saint Hilary, spewing out many accusations against the abbess, though we learned that these were false.

Afterward, she was drawn into the monastery with ropes through the place from which she had thrown herself. She asked to be confined again in a private cell, saying:

“I have greatly sinned against the Lord and against my lady Radegund, who was still alive in those days. I wish,” she said, “to remove myself from the gatherings of the whole community and do penance for my negligence. For I know that the Lord is merciful and forgives those who confess their sins.”

She entered the cell.

When this scandal had arisen and Chrodieldis had returned from King Guntchramn, the woman broke open the door of her cell during the night, left the monastery, and went to Chrodieldis, again bursting out with many accusations against the abbess, as she had done before.

### XLI

While these things were happening, Gundegisilus of Bordeaux, accompanied by Nicasius of Angoulême [Note: Another reading is Ecolesinensis. He subscribed to the Second Council of Mâcon, where he is called Nicasius of the Aquilinenses. Gundegisilus of Bordeaux is praised by Fortunatus, Book VII, poem 31.], Saffarius of Périgueux, and Maroveus himself, bishop of Poitiers, came to the basilica of Saint Hilary, since Gundegisilus was metropolitan of that city. He rebuked these girls and wished to bring them back to the monastery.

But when they resisted with greater obstinacy, and he, together with the others, pronounced excommunication against them according to the letter mentioned above, a mob of buffoons [Note: *Muriones*, or, as Saint Augustine has it in Letter 143 to Marcellinus, *moriones*, meaning fools; the word is derived from the Greek μορός, “foolish.”] rose up and assaulted them with such violence in the very basilica of Saint Hilary that, when the bishops fell to the pavement, they could scarcely rise. The deacons and the other clerics, drenched in blood and their heads split open, also left the basilica.

So immense was the terror that had seized them, with the devil, I believe, cooperating, that when they left the holy place they did not even say farewell to one another. Each made his way back by whatever road he could take.

Desiderius, the deacon of Syagrius, bishop of Autun, was also present at this disaster. Without looking for the ford of the Clain [Note: The printed editions, together with Bec., read *Cleni*, commonly the Clain, a river flowing into the Vienne.], he entered the river at the first bank he reached and, with his horse swimming, was carried out onto the field on the farther bank.

After this, Chrodieldis chose administrators, invaded the monastery’s estates, and subjected to her service anyone from the monastery whom she could seize, treating them with blows and beatings. She threatened that, if she could enter the monastery, she would throw the abbess from the wall and cast her to the ground.

When this was reported to King Childebert, he immediately sent an authoritative order commanding Count Macco to suppress the affair with all diligence.

Gundegisilus, having suspended these women from communion together with the other bishops, as we have said, wrote a letter in his own name and that of the bishops present to those priests who at that time were assembled with King Guntchramn [Note: Valesius thinks they were assembled at Autun.]. From them he received the following reply.

#### COPY OF THE REPLY

“To their ever-lordly and most worthy of the apostolic see [Note: Regm.: ‘To their lords, and …’ Perhaps the reading should be ‘To the holy lords and …,’ and so forth. This is the customary formula.] Gundegisilus, Nicasius, and Saffarius [Note: Lalandus, in the *Supplement to the Councils of Gaul*, adds ‘and Maroveus.’ In Colb. m. and Regm., Aunacharius is absent below; indeed, he does not appear among those who subscribed, any more than Agroecula does. The others also did not subscribe in the order in which their names are listed here. The bishops were Aetherius of Lyon, Syagrius of Autun, Aunacharius of Auxerre, Hesychius of Grenoble, Agricola of Nevers, Urbicus of Riez, Felix of Béziers, Veranus of Cavaillon, Felix of Châlons, and Bertramnus of Le Mans.], Aetherius, Syagrius, Aunacharius, Hesychius, Agroecola, Urbicus, Felix, Veranus, Felix again, and Bertchramnus, bishops.

“We received the letter of your blessedness with as much joy at the report of your health as we are bound by no small sorrow at the injury that you indicated you had suffered, since the rule has been transgressed and no reverence has been shown to religion.

“But because you reported that the nuns who, at the devil’s instigation, departed from the monastery of the blessed Radegund had refused to heed any correction from you and had not wished to return within the walls of their monastery, from which they had left—and, moreover, that they had inflicted injury upon the basilica of Saint Hilary through the slaughter and outrage committed against you and your companions—you therefore appeared to have suspended them from the grace of communion and, for this reason, chose to consult our humility concerning the matter.

“Since we know very well that you have reviewed the decrees of the canons [Note: This shows that *percurrere* is not used here for reading carried out hastily. See Mabillon, *Defense of Monastic Studies*, article 19.] and possess the fullness of the rule, so that those found guilty of such excesses must be restrained not only by excommunication but also by the satisfaction of penance, we therefore add, with reverent devotion and the impulse of the highest affection, that we declare our concordant agreement with what you have decided. This agreement shall remain until we are all present together in synodal council on the Kalends of November and can deliberate with a common mind how the temerity of such people may be brought under the bridle of discipline, so that hereafter no one may commit similar acts through boastful presumption of such a lapse.

“Nevertheless, because the blessed apostle Paul appears in his own words to admonish us unceasingly that we must correct all who transgress by diligent preaching, in season and out of season (II Tim. 4:2), and because he declares that godliness is useful for all things (I Tim. 4:8), we therefore urge you further to implore the Lord’s mercy with constant prayer, so that he may deign to kindle in them the spirit of contrition and cause them to repent through worthy satisfaction for what they appear to have incurred by their offense.

“May the souls that have in some manner perished return, through your preaching, to their monastery, with Christ’s favor; may he who carried the wandering sheep upon his shoulders back to the fold deign, at the return of these transgressors, to rejoice as over a flock regained.

“We ask this especially: that, as we trust you will do, you may continually grant us the support of your intercessions.

“Your special friend, Aetherius the sinner, ventures to send greetings.

“Your dependent, Hesychius, reverently dares to send greetings.

“Your friend, Syagrius, reverently sends greetings.

“Your devotee, Urbicus the sinner, humbly sends greetings.

“Your venerable servant, Veranus the bishop, reverently sends greetings.

“Your servant Felix ventures to send greetings.

“Your humble friend Felix dares to send greetings.

“Your humble and obedient servant, Bertchramnus the bishop, ventures to send greetings.”

### XLII

The abbess also read the letter that the blessed Radegund had wished to send to the bishops who were present in her time. Now the abbess herself again sent copies of it to the priests of the neighboring cities. This is the copy.

#### COPY OF THE LETTER
«To the holy lords and those most worthy of the apostolic see, fathers in Christ, to all the bishops, Radegund, a sinner.

A fitting undertaking of prudent provision then advances firmly toward completion when the matter of the flock entrusted to the general fathers, physicians, and shepherds is brought to their ears and commended to their judgment; their participation can provide the contribution of charity, their counsel that of authority, and their support the intervention of prayer. And since long ago, by divine providence and the inspiration of mercy, I was released from secular bonds and seemed voluntarily, with Christ as my guide, to have been transferred to the rule of religion, I have also considered with an inclined mind the advancement of others, so that, with the Lord announcing it, my desires might become profitable to the rest.

Therefore, under the direction and reward of the most excellent lord King Chlothar, I established a monastery for women in the city of Poitiers, and, once founded, endowed it by a deed of gift to the extent that royal generosity had granted me. Moreover, for the community gathered by me through Christ’s favor, I adopted the rule under which holy Caesaria lived [Note: Thus the manuscripts. Most printed editions, however, read *degit*, “lived.”], which the diligence of the blessed Caesarius, bishop of Arles, suitably compiled from the institution of the holy Fathers. With the agreement of the most blessed bishops both of this city and of the other places, and also by the choice of our community, I appointed as abbess my lady and sister Agnes, whom from her earliest age I cherished and raised as a daughter [Note: Thus Badius and others; others read *eduxi*, “brought up”], and I entrusted myself, after God, to obey her governance according to the rule.

Observing the apostolic model, both I and the sisters transferred by written deeds the earthly property that we appeared to possess, reserving nothing as our own within the monastery, through fear of Ananias and Sapphira. But because the moments and times of the human condition are uncertain, since the world is hastening toward its end, and since some prefer to serve their own will rather than the divine will, moved by zeal for God I present this page of my petition, offered in the name of Christ to your apostolic authority, which I trust will outlive me.

And because I could not be present, I prostrate myself by the substitution of this letter, as though cast at your feet, adjuring you by the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and by the day of the fearful judgment, that, when you are thus represented, no tyrant may attack you, but a legitimate king may crown you. Thus, if after my death—although we do not believe this can happen—any person, or the bishop of that place, or princely authority, or anyone else should attempt to disturb the community, whether by malicious persuasion or judicial compulsion; or to break the rule; or to appoint as abbess anyone other than my sister Agnes, whom the most blessed Germanus consecrated with his blessing in the presence of his brothers; or if the community itself, which cannot happen, should attempt amid murmuring to change her; or if anyone—whether a person or the bishop of the place—should seek by a new privilege to claim for himself any authority in the monastery or over the monastery’s property beyond what the preceding bishops or others exercised while I was alive; or if anyone should attempt to depart from the rule; or if anyone should seek to take away anything from the possessions which the most excellent lord Chlothar, or the most excellent lords the kings, his sons [Variant: *regis*, “of the king”], bestowed upon me, and which, with his permission, I transferred to the monastery for it to possess, and which I obtained confirmed by the authority of the most excellent lords the kings Charibert, Guntram, Chilperic, and Sigibert, with the imposition of an oath and the subscriptions of their own hands; or from those things which others, for the remedy of their souls, or the sisters there, from their own possessions, have contributed—if any prince, bishop, powerful person, or any of the sisters should dare to diminish any of these things or attempt by some contrivance to convert them to private ownership, let them be struck by the perpetual sword of anathema [Note: Regm. reads: “or any one of the sisters should attempt by any contrivance to diminish these things and convert them to her own property.”].

Let such a person incur, after God, the anger of your holiness [Note: I think we should read “the anger of your holiness,” and so forth] and of your successors, on account of my supplication and Christ’s will, so that, just as robbers and despoilers of the poor are held outside your grace, no one may, while you oppose it, diminish or alter anything from our rule or from the monastery’s possessions.

I also ask this: when God wills to call the aforesaid lady, our sister Agnes, from this world, that she who pleases God and her, from our community, may be appointed abbess in her place, preserving the rule and diminishing nothing from the purpose of holiness. For let no private will, nor anyone else’s will, ever precipitate matters [Note: Regm. reads: “for sometimes one’s own will … precipitates …”].

But if—which God forbid—anyone should wish to act against God’s command and the authority of the kings concerning any of the conditions written above and solemnly commended before the Lord and his saints, or should wish to diminish anything from the person or property involved, or should attempt to inflict any trouble upon my aforesaid sister Agnes, the abbess, let that person incur the judgment of God, of the holy cross, and of blessed Mary; and let him have as opponents and persecutors the blessed confessors Hilary and Martin, to whom, after God, I entrusted my sisters for protection.

You also, blessed bishop, and your successors, whom I diligently claim as patrons in God’s cause: if—which God forbid—anyone should arise who attempts to contrive anything against these provisions, do not hesitate, for the purpose of repelling and confuting God’s enemy, to hasten to the king whom that place shall obey at that time, or to the city of Poitiers, on behalf of the matter commended to you before the Lord, and to labor as executors and defenders of justice against the injustice of others. Thus may the Catholic king in no way permit such wickedness to be committed during his reign, nor allow what has been established by the will of God, myself, and the kings themselves to be overturned.

Likewise I adjure the princes whom God, for the governance of the people, shall command to survive after my death, by the King whose kingdom shall have no end and at whose nod kingdoms stand, who granted them life and kingship: let them order the monastery—which, with the permission and support of the lord kings, their father or grandfather, I have appeared to build, organize according to the rule, and endow—to be governed under their protection and authority together with Agnes the abbess. Let them permit neither the aforesaid abbess nor anything belonging to our monastery to be harassed, disturbed, diminished, or changed by anyone. Rather, for God’s sake, together with the lord bishops, and at my supplication before the Redeemer of the nations, let them order it to be defended and fortified, as I commend it to them, so that, for protecting the handmaids of God in whose honor they act, they may be joined eternally in the kingdom with the defender of the poor and the Bridegroom of virgins.

I also adjure you, holy bishops, most excellent lord kings, and the entire Christian people, by the Catholic faith in which you were baptized and by the churches that you preserve, that in the basilica which we began to build in honor of holy Mary, the Mother of the Lord and God, where many of our sisters have also been laid to rest, whether it is completed or unfinished, when God commands me to depart from this light, my little body should be buried there.

If anyone should wish or attempt to have anything else done in this matter, let him incur divine vengeance, with the cross of Christ and blessed Mary prevailing; and, with your intervention, may I deserve to obtain a burial place in that basilica together with the community of sisters.

And so that this supplication of mine, which I have signed with my own hand, may be preserved in the archive of the universal Church, I beseech you with streaming tears: whenever necessity demands action against wicked persons, may your pious consolation, through pastoral concern, provide assistance by your protection to my sister Agnes, the abbess, or to her community, whenever they ask to be helped by you [Note: Mansi, correctly, omits the little word *quo* when he inserted this letter into his collection of Councils, vol. IX, col. 810]; and let them not proclaim themselves abandoned by me, for God has prepared for them the protection of your grace.

In all things recall this before your eyes, through him who, from the glorious cross, commended his virgin Mother to the blessed apostle John: just as the Lord’s command was fulfilled by him, so may there be among you what I, unworthy and humble, commend to my lords, the fathers of the Church and apostolic men. When you have graciously preserved this trust, may you rightly restore the example, sharing in the merits of the one whose apostolic command you fulfill [Note: At the end of the *History of Aquitaine*, this testament of blessed Radegund was published together with the subscriptions of several bishops; these, however, appear to have been added by someone else.»]

### XLIII

After this, when Bishop Maroveus heard various reproaches from them, he sent Porcarius, abbot of the basilica of blessed Hilary, to Bishop Gundegisel and his other provincial colleagues, asking them to grant the girls permission to come to a hearing once communion had been given to them. But he could obtain nothing.

King Childebert, however, suffering continual trouble from both sides—that is, from the monastery and from the girls who had left—sent the presbyter Theutharius to settle the disputes that were taking place among them. When he summoned Chrodechild [Note: Thus Bec.; others read *qui provocatae Chrodieldis*] and the other girls to a hearing, they said:

“We have not come because we have been suspended from communion. If we deserve to be reconciled, then we will not delay coming to the hearing.”

When he heard this, he went to the bishops. After he had spoken with them about the matter, he could obtain no result concerning their communion, and so he returned to the city of Poitiers.

The girls, separated from one another, returned—some to their parents, some to their own homes, and some to the monasteries in which they had previously been. For, having been gathered together, they could not endure the severe winter because of the shortage of firewood. A few, however, remained with Chrodechild and Basina. For there was then also great discord among them, because each of the two wished to place herself above the other.

### XLIV

That year, after Closed Easter [Note: “Closed Easter,” that is, Low Sunday or the first Sunday after Easter, is commonly so called in the old lectionaries and Gallican missals edited by our Mabillon. It is likewise popularly called *Pâque close* among our people], there was such an immense rain accompanied by hail that within two or three hours enormous rivers seemed to be rushing even through the smaller channels of the valleys. Trees flowered in autumn and produced fruit, just as they had previously done. In the ninth month roses appeared. The rivers, moreover, rose beyond measure, so that overflowing their banks they covered places which they had never customarily reached, causing no small damage to the crops.

## 477–478 BEGIN THE CHAPTERS OF BOOK TEN

### Chapters

I. Gregory, pope of Rome. The prayer of Saint Gregory to the people.  
II. The return of Grippo, envoy from the emperor Maurice.  
III. That the army of King Childebert went into Italy.  
IV. That the emperor Maurice sent the murderers of his envoys into Gaul.  
V. That Cuppa [Variant: Chuppa] invaded the frontier of Tours.  
VI. The imprisoned Auvergnats.  
VII. That in that city King Childebert granted the clergy exemption from paying tribute.  
VIII. Eulalius and Tetradia, who had been his wife.  
IX. The army of King Guntram, which went into Brittany.  
X. The death of Chundo, his chamberlain.  
XI. The illness of the younger Chlothar.  
XII. The wickedness of Berthegund.  
XIII. A disputation concerning the resurrection.  
XIV. The death of Theodulf the deacon [Note: Colb. manuscript and Regm. read *Gundo*. Nevertheless, the chapter itself discusses Theodulf, as in the printed editions].  
XV. The scandal of the Poitiers monastery.  
XVI. The judgment pronounced against Chrodechild and Basina. The text of the judgment.  
XVII. Their excommunication.  
XVIII. The assailants sent to King Childebert.  
XIX. The expulsion of Aegidius, bishop of Reims.  
XX. The aforesaid girls reconciled at this synod.  
XXI. The death of Waddo’s sons.  
XXII. The death of Childeric the Saxon [Note: The Colb. manuscript and Regm. read *Chilperic*, and in the chapter itself they call him *Chuldericus* or *Childericus*].  
XXIII. Signs and uncertainty concerning Easter.  
XXIV. The destruction of the city of Antioch.  
XXV. The death of the man who called himself Christ.  
XXVI. The death of the bishops Ragnemod and Sulpicius.  
XXVII. Those whom Fredegund ordered to be killed.  
XXVIII. The baptism of her son Chlothar.  
XXIX. The conversion, miracles, and death of Aredius, abbot of Limoges.  
XXX. The weather conditions of the present year and the observance of the Lord’s Day.  
XXXI. A recapitulation concerning the bishops of Tours.

# BOOK TEN

## [Col. 0527]

### I

In the fifteenth year of King Childebert, therefore, our deacon, returning from the city of Rome with relics of the saints [Note: Compare Book I, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 83], reported the following: in the preceding year, during the ninth month, the river Tiber had risen in such a flood [Note: Gregory the Great himself records this flooding of the Tiber in *Dialogues* III.19, and Paul the Deacon in *History of the Lombards* III.24 and following chapters. In his *Life of Saint Gregory*, published in the first Benedictine volume among the acts of the saints of our order, Paul also copied almost this entire chapter of our Gregory] that it covered the city of Rome, and ancient buildings were destroyed. The church’s granaries also collapsed, in which several thousand *modii* of wheat perished.

A multitude of serpents, together with a great dragon as massive as a beam, descended through the bed of that river into the sea; but the beasts, suffocated amid the salty waves of the turbulent sea, were cast upon the shore. Immediately afterward there followed the disaster that they call the groin disease. For, arriving in the middle of the eleventh month, it first struck Pope Pelagius—according to what is read in the prophet Ezekiel, “Begin from my sanctuary” (Ezekiel 9:6)—and swiftly killed him. After his death, a great slaughter of the people was caused by this disease.

But because the Church of God could not be without a ruler, the whole people elected Gregory the deacon. He was from one of the leading senatorial families and, devoted to God from his youth, established six monasteries in Sicily from his own property and founded a seventh within the walls of Rome. Assigning to them such an abundance of land as was sufficient to provide daily sustenance, he sold the remainder, together with all the household goods, and distributed it to the poor.

He who had formerly been covered in silk, accustomed to proceed through the city in a robe glittering with gems, was now consecrated to the ministry of the Lord’s altar, covered in a cheap garment [Note: A monastic garment, namely the one he adopted after renouncing everything in the monastery of Saint Andrew, which he himself had founded at Rome, where the Benedictine Rule was in force. Mabillon published a dissertation on this subject in volume II of the old *Analecta*]. He was also appointed as the seventh levite [Note: That custom long prevailed at Rome, that there should be only seven deacons, namely regional deacons, in memory of the seven deacons instituted by the apostles at Jerusalem. On these see Mabillon, commentary on the *Roman Order*, chapter 3], to assist the pope.

His abstinence in food, his vigilance in prayer, and his diligence in fasting were so great that, with his stomach weakened, he could scarcely remain standing. He was so trained in grammar, dialectic, and rhetoric that no one in the city itself was thought to equal him.

Seeking more intently to flee this eminence [Note: What follows is abridged at the end of the chapter in Regm., which also omits Saint Gregory’s prayer], lest the vanity of the honor he had attained in the world should again steal upon him—an honor he had previously rejected—he sent a letter to the emperor Maurice, whose son he had received from the sacred font. He adjured him, and begged him with many prayers, never to consent to the people’s request to exalt him with the glory of this office.

But Germanus, prefect of the city of Rome, anticipated his message and, having intercepted him and torn up the letters, sent the consent that the people had given to the emperor. The emperor, giving thanks to God for the deacon’s friendship, because he had found an opportunity to confer this honor upon him [Note: Paul the Deacon, in the *Life of Saint Gregory*: “because he had found an opportunity to confer the honor upon him”], issued an order that he should be appointed.

When all that remained was for him to be blessed, and the plague was devastating the people, he began to address the people concerning the performance of penance in the following manner.

## THE PRAYER OF GREGORY TO THE PEOPLE

“O most beloved brothers, we ought to fear the scourges of God that we should have feared were coming; at least let us fear those that are now present and experienced. Let sorrow open for us the way of conversion, and let the punishment itself that we suffer dissolve the hardness of our hearts. For, as the prophet foretold, ‘The sword has reached even to the soul’ (Jeremiah 4:10).

Behold, the entire people is struck by the sword of heavenly anger, and individuals are laid waste by sudden slaughter. Sickness does not precede death; rather, as you see, death outruns the delays of sickness. Each person who is struck is carried away before he can turn to the lamentation of repentance. Consider, therefore, what sort of person arrives before the sight of the strict Judge when he has no time to weep for what he has done.

The inhabitants are not taken away in part, but fall together. Houses are left empty; parents look upon the funerals of their children, and their own heirs precede them to destruction. Let each one of us therefore flee to the lamentation of repentance while there is time to weep before the blow. Let us call before the eyes of our mind whatever we have committed through error, and punish by weeping what we have wickedly done.

‘Let us go before his face in confession’ (Psalm 94:2), and, as the prophet admonishes, ‘Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to the Lord’ (Lamentations 3:41). To lift our hearts with our hands to God is to raise the devotion of our prayer by means of meritorious good works.

He certainly gives confidence to our trembling who cries out through the prophet: ‘I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live’ [Ezekiel 33:11]. Let no one despair because of the enormity of his sins. For a three-day repentance wiped away the long-standing sins of the Ninevites [Jonah 3:10], and the converted thief earned the rewards of life even in the sentence of his own death [Luke 23:43].

Let us therefore change [Variant: lift up] our hearts, and confidently believe that we have already received what we ask. The Judge is more quickly bent toward prayer if the petitioner is corrected from his wickedness.

Since the sword of so great a punishment is hanging over us, let us devote ourselves to unremitting weeping. For what is commonly an unwelcome persistence to human beings pleases the judgment of Truth: the gracious and merciful God wishes forgiveness to be demanded from him by prayers, though he does not wish to be angry with us according to what we deserve. For he says through the psalmist: ‘Call upon me in the day of your tribulation, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me’ (Psalm 49:15).

He is therefore his own witness: he desires to show mercy to those who call upon him, since he commands that he be called upon. Therefore, dearest brothers, with contrite hearts and corrected conduct, beginning at first light on Wednesday, let us come with a mind devoted to tears for the sevenfold Litany, according to the arrangement set out below, so that the strict Judge, when he sees that he must punish us for our sins, may himself spare us from the sentence of the condemnation he has proposed [Variant: proposed].

Let the clergy go out from the church of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian, together with the priests of the sixth region. Let all the abbots with their monks go out from the church of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, together with the priests of the fourth region. Let all the abbesses with their communities go out from the church of the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, together with the priests of the first region. Let all the children go out from the church of the holy martyrs John and Paul, together with the priests of the second region. Let all the laymen go out from the church of the holy protomartyr Stephen, together with the priests of the seventh region. Let all the widowed women go out from the church of Saint Euphemia, together with the priests of the fifth region. Let all married women go out from the church of Saint Clement the martyr, together with the priests of the third region [Note: Gregory himself, in Book II, letter 2, and John the Deacon, in Book I of the *Life of Saint Gregory*, no. 42, give the order of persons and places somewhat differently. Perhaps there were several such litanies, as Baronius thinks. Paul the Deacon, in Book III of his *History of the Lombards*, agrees with our Gregory].

Thus, coming out from the individual churches with prayers and tears, let us gather at the basilica of blessed Mary, ever-virgin, Mother of our Lord and God Jesus Christ, so that there, praying earnestly to the Lord with weeping and lamentation, we may deserve to obtain forgiveness for our sins.”

When he had said this, he ordered the gathered ranks of the clergy to sing psalms and to entreat the Lord’s mercy for three days. At about the third hour, both choirs of those singing came to the church, crying through the streets of the city, “Lord, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison*).

Our deacon, who was present, asserted that within the space of one hour, while the people were uttering supplicating voices to the Lord, eighty men had fallen to the ground and breathed out their spirits. Yet that great priest did not cease preaching to the people, urging them not to stop praying.

Our deacon also obtained the relics of the saints from this priest, as we have said, while he was still living as a deacon. While he was preparing hiding places for flight, he was seized, dragged away, and brought to the basilica of blessed Peter the apostle. There he was consecrated to the office of pontifical grace and given as pope to the city.

But our deacon did not depart until he returned from Porto to his bishopric [Note: Bec. reads *de Portu*, “from Porto”; the editions read *de porta*, “from the gate.” Is the place indicated here where Gregory, while fleeing the pontificate, sought hiding? Or is the reference to Gregory of Tours’ own deacon, who is said to have been led as far as Porto in Book I, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 83], and with attentive observation saw how he had been ordained.

## II

When Grippo [Note: Colb. A reads *Gripho*, and likewise below] returned from the emperor Maurice, he reported the following: in the preceding year, after securing a ship, he and his companions reached a port in Africa and entered great Carthage.

While they were staying there, awaiting the order of the prefect who was present [Note: Thus Colb.; the others read *qui aderant*, “who were present”], concerning how they should approach the emperor’s presence, one of the boys—Evantius’ boy, that is, who had gone with him—carried to the camp an article snatched from the hand of a certain merchant.

The merchant, whose property it was, pursued him and demanded that his own possession be returned. But when the boy delayed, and the quarrel grew from day to day, the merchant one day found the boy in the street. Seizing his garment, he began to hold him, saying:

“You will not get away from me until you return to my possession the things you violently stole.”

The boy tried to wrench himself from his hands, and did not hesitate to kill the man with a sword he had drawn. He immediately returned to the camp and did not reveal to his companions what had happened.

As we have said, the envoys were then there: Bodegisil, son of Mummolenus, from Soissons [Note: Fortunatus praises Mummolenus in Book VII, poem 14]; Evantius, son of Dynamius of Arles; and Grippo, a Frank by birth. They had risen from the meal and had given themselves over to sleep for the sake of rest.

When what the boy had done was reported to the city’s senior official, he gathered soldiers, surrounded the entire populace with weapons, and sent them against the envoys’ camp. They, awakened unexpectedly, were bewildered when they saw what was happening.

Then the official who was in charge cried out:

“Lay down your arms and come out to us, so that we may learn peacefully how the homicide occurred.”

Hearing this, they were terrified with fear. Still unaware of what had happened, they asked for a pledge that they might come out without weapons in safety. Those men swore that they would protect them, but impatience did not permit them to keep their word.

As soon as Bodegisil came out, they struck him with a sword, and likewise Evantius. When the two had been thrown down before the entrance of the camp, Grippo seized his weapons and, with the boys who were with him, went out to them, saying:

“We are not ignorant of what has happened. Behold, my traveling companions, who had been sent to the emperor, have been struck down by the sword. God will judge our injury, and their death will be avenged by your destruction, because you have slaughtered us, innocent men who came in peace. There will no longer be peace between our kings and your emperor. We came for peace and to provide assistance to the Roman state. Today I call God as my witness: your wrongdoing has caused the peace promised among the rulers not to be preserved.”

As Grippo spoke these and similar words, the Carthaginian army’s battle array was dissolved [Note: Badius reads *Carthaginenses*, “the Carthaginians”], and each man returned to his own place.

The prefect, however, approached Grippo and began to soothe his anger over what had happened, arranging how he should approach the emperor’s presence. When Grippo arrived, he reported the embassy for which he had been sent and explained the destruction of his companions.

For this reason the emperor was greatly troubled and promised to avenge their death, according to the judgment that King Childebert would issue. Then, after receiving gifts from the emperor, Grippo returned in peace [Note: Gregory discussed this embassy above, in Book IX, chapter 25. It is greatly illuminated by various letters of Childebert and Brunhild edited by Freher and Chesnius in volume I, which Grippo had carried to Constantinople. In these letters, which King Childebert and his mother Brunhild wrote separately not only to the emperor and the empress Anastasia but also to the patriarch and other leading men of the empire, they declare that they will omit nothing to ensure that peace between the Romans and the Franks always remains firm and unshaken. This embassy also dealt with providing the Romans assistance against the Lombards in Italy, which we learn from Gregory and Paul the Deacon was supplied by Childebert. But, if I am not mistaken, Childebert’s chief purpose was to recover from the emperor’s hands Athanagild, his nephew through his sister Ingund, who had been taken to Constantinople after the death of Hermenegild; this is clear from the letters cited. Whether he ever achieved this, however, is unknown to us.].»
### III

When these matters had been reported by Grippo to King Childebert [Note: In Vat., “These things were reported by Grippo to King Hildebert.” Compare this chapter with chapter 32 of Book III of Paul the Deacon’s *History of the Langobards*.], he immediately ordered an army to be mobilized into Italy and sent twenty commanders to defeat the Langobard people. I have not thought it necessary to insert their names in order.

The commander Audoualdus [Note: Paul calls him Andualdus. Below, Colb. m., Regm., and Chesn. read *Victrione*; concerning him, see above, Book VIII, chapter 18.] with Vinthrione, having roused the people of Campania, approached the city of Metz, which lay on his route, and committed such extensive plundering, murders, and massacres that he was thought to be bringing an enemy upon his own country. Other commanders likewise acted in the same way with their troops [Col. 0531B], so that they harmed their own territory or the population living there before accomplishing anything resembling a victory over the enemy.

As they approached the boundary of Italy, Audoualdus with six commanders turned to the right and reached the city of Milan; there, at a distance, they established a camp on the plain. The commander Olo, approaching the fortress of this city at Bilitio, situated in the Caninian fields, 486 [Note: Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XV, and Apollinaris Sidonius, poem 5, line 177, praise the Caninian fields; but they were in Raetia, since in reality they lay between Raetia and Liguria, where Bilitio is still found today, as Paul has it together with Gregory—or Belincio or Berinzona, which is a fortress of Cisalpine Lombardy commonly called Bellinzona. Colb. m. reads, “situated close by in the Caninian fields.”] rashly, was wounded by a spear beneath the nipple [Note: Others, following Paul, read “beneath the breast”], fell, and died.

When these men had gone out to plunder in order to obtain some provisions, they were struck down everywhere by attacking Langobards. There was a certain lake in the territory of the city of Milan called Coresium [Note: Regm. and Colb. m. read *Ceresium*; Bec., *Cerasium*], from which a small but deep river flows. They had heard that Langobards were stationed along the shore of this lake.

When they approached it, before crossing the river we have mentioned, one of the Langobards, standing on the shore, protected by a cuirass and helmet and carrying a spear in his hand, raised his voice against the Frankish army, saying: “Today it will become clear to whom the divine power grants victory.” From this it may be understood that the Langobards had prepared this sign for themselves [Col. 0532A].

Then a few men crossed over and, engaging this Langobard in combat, struck him down. At once the entire Langobard army passed by in flight. These men too crossed the river, but found none of them, recognizing only the remains of their camp, where they had either kept fires or pitched tents. Since they had found no one, they returned to their own camp. There the emperor’s envoys came to them [Note: Paul says that they came to Audoualdus while he was near Milan. Freher published a letter from the commander of the Roman army to Childebert, in which he explains the course of this expedition and accuses Chenus—whom I believe to be the Cedinus mentioned below—of violating the peace made with the Langobard king. In another letter he explains to Childebert how much progress he had made against the Langobards. Nevertheless, Childebert is said not to have undertaken any further expedition into Italy; Maurice seems to reproach him for this in a letter written to him. Those portions of these letters that contribute to the elucidation of our Gregory will be presented in the Appendix.], announcing that an army had arrived to assist them and saying:

“After three days we shall come with them, and this shall be your sign: when you see the houses of this village, which is situated on the mountain, burning in flames and the smoke of the fire rising to the heavens, know that we are present with the army we promise.”

But after waiting six days according to the agreement, they saw that none of them had come. Ced[in]us [Note: So Bec. together with Paul. Colb. a. reads *Chedinius*, Regm. *Cedinius*, and the printed editions *Chedinus*. On this occasion, as Paul relates, the Franks reached as far as Verona; he also lists the names of the camps destroyed by them in the territory of Trent.] entered Italy on the left with thirteen commanders and captured five fortresses, from which he also exacted oaths of allegiance.

A severe illness of dysentery afflicted the army, because the air was unsuitable and unfamiliar to those men; many consequently died. When the wind arose and rain fell, and the air began to cool somewhat, it brought relief to the illness.

What more need be said? After wandering through Italy for nearly three months without accomplishing anything and without being able to avenge themselves on their enemies, since the latter had fortified themselves in extremely strong positions, and without being able to capture the king, upon whom vengeance might be taken, since he had secured himself below the walls of Pavia, the army—weakened, as we have said, by the unhealthy air and worn down by hunger—decided to return to its own country.

They also subjugated, after receiving oaths of allegiance, the king’s territories which his father had previously possessed [Note: From this passage it may also be inferred that Sigibert possessed some part of Italy, namely the regions nearest Raetia, as Valesius judges in Book XV of his *Frankish History*, around the territory of Trent and the river Adige in Venetia.] From these places they carried away both captives and other plunder. Thus, as they returned, they were so consumed by hunger that before reaching their native land they stripped themselves of weapons and clothing in order to buy food [Col. 0533A].

King Aptacharius of the Langobards [Note: Paul the Deacon calls him Authari; he discusses this embassy in Book III, chapter 35 of his *History of the Langobards*.] sent an embassy to King Guntchramn with the following words:

“Most merciful king, we are subject and faithful to you and to your people, just as we were to your fathers, and as we desire to remain. Nor do we depart from the oath which our predecessors swore to your predecessors. Now cease your persecution of us, and let there be peace and harmony between us, so that whenever necessity arises we may provide assistance against our enemies. Thus, when both your people and ours have been preserved and our peaceful disposition is known, the adversaries who surround us and make hostile noise will fear our friendship more than they rejoice in our discord.”

King Guntchramn received these words peacefully and sent the envoys to his nephew, King Childebert. While they remained there recounting these matters, others arrived announcing that King Aptacharius had died and that Paul had been appointed in his place [Note: Paul is not mentioned by Paul the Deacon. Rather, as he relates in Book III, chapter 36, Agilulf, also called Ago, duke of the Taurinians, succeeded Authari. The succession was arranged by Theodelinda, Authari’s widow, who took him as her partner in the kingdom and in marriage; this was approved by all the Langobards at a general assembly held at Milan in the following year, in May. Gregory the Great wrote several letters to both of them and dedicated his *Dialogues* to Theodelinda. Agilulf eventually converted to the Catholic faith and established peace with the Franks, perhaps when Athanagild had by then died, or at least when no hope remained that Childebert would recover him. He is never mentioned again. See Paul the Deacon, Book IV of the *History of the Langobards*, chapter 1.] They brought words of the same kind as those stated above.

But King Childebert made an agreement with them that he would inform them of what would be appropriate for him in the future, and ordered them to withdraw.

### IV

Maurice sent to King Childebert’s presence those Carthaginians who had killed his envoys in the preceding year (above, chapter 2), their hands bound and loaded with chains—twelve men in all—with this condition: if Childebert wished to kill them, he would have permission; but if he chose to release them for ransom, he should accept three hundred gold pieces for each and be satisfied, so that he might choose whichever course he wished. In this way, once the scandal had more easily been quieted, no occasion for enmity would arise between them.

But King Childebert delayed accepting the prisoners and said:

“It is uncertain among us whether these are the murderers whom you bring, or others, or perhaps slaves belonging to someone, since those of ours who were killed among you were men free by birth. Moreover, Grippo is standing here, for at that time he had been sent as an envoy with those who were killed. He says: ‘The prefect of that city, together with two or three thousand men whom he had gathered, attacked us and killed my companions. I too would have perished in that slaughter if I had not been able to defend myself courageously.’

“When I approach the place, I shall be able to identify the men. If your emperor, as you say, has decided to preserve peace with our lord, he ought to exact vengeance.”

Thus the king gave his decision that he would send them afterward to the emperor, and ordered the prisoners to withdraw.

### V

[Note: This chapter and the following one are absent from Vat. and Colb. m.; they do, however, contain chapter 7, which is chapter 5 there and begins with the words, “In the aforementioned city of Auvergne,” etc., presupposing the preceding chapter. We have already spoken of Cuppa above, Book V, chapter 40; in most printed editions he is called Chuppa.]

In those days Cuppa, formerly master of the horse of King Chilperic, invaded the territory of the city of Tours and sought to carry off its cattle and other property as booty. But when the inhabitants became aware of this, they gathered a multitude and began to pursue him. They recovered the plunder, killed two of his servants, and caused him himself to flee naked; two other servants were captured and sent bound to King Childebert. The king ordered them thrown into prison and directed that they be questioned as to whose assistance had enabled Cuppa to escape without being captured by those who were pursuing him [Col. 0534B].

They replied that it had been done through the treachery of the vicarius of Animodi [Note: These vicarii are still commonly called *viguiers*. They were appointed over particular territories in the name of the counts to administer justice to the lower classes, just as the counts’ office was to administer justice in the cities. There were also greater vicarii, who were later called viscounts. See Bignon’s notes to the old formulas of an unknown author, no. 1.], who governed that district with judicial authority.

The king immediately sent letters to the count of the city, ordering him to send Cuppa bound into the king’s presence. If he attempted to resist, the count was even to kill him by force, if he wished to obtain the prince’s favor.

But Cuppa did not resist. Having given sureties, he went where he was ordered. When he found Flavianus, the *domesticus* [Note: That is, “having found Flavianus, the *domesticus*.”], he pleaded that, together with his companion, he was not guilty; he was reconciled with him and ordered to return home, after first giving gifts to that *domesticus*.

Cuppa himself again gathered some of his men and sought to seize and marry the daughter of Badegisilus, formerly bishop of Le Mans. He attacked at night with a band of companions the estate of Maroialia [Note: Some editions read *Marogalia*. It was mentioned above, Book VII, chapter 12. There was also another estate of the same name, as Valesius observes, near Orléans, now commonly called Marolle.], intending to accomplish his purpose. But Magnatrudis, the mother of the household—namely, the girl’s mother—detected him and his treachery. She came out with her servants, drove him back by force, and killed most of his men; thus he withdrew, not without shame.

### VI

At Clermont, the prisoners’ chains were broken during the night by God’s will. When the entrances of the prison had been opened, they came out and entered a church. When Count Eulalius ordered additional chains to be fastened upon them, the chains, once placed upon them, were immediately shattered like fragile glass. Thus, through the intervention of Bishop Avitus [Note: Gregory says nothing about the death of blessed Avitus. Cointius conjectures that he died after the year 591, the final year of Gregory’s *History*, namely in 594, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, when his feast is celebrated. He was buried in the church of Saint Mary the Principal, called Saint Mary of Portus in the life of that holy man. Savaro notes that this church must be distinguished from the cathedral. Another Avitus rests in the church of Saint Venerandus, according to the cited book, chapter 10; he was the brother of Saint Bonitus.], they were rescued and restored to their own freedom.

### VII

In the aforementioned city, King Childebert generously granted all tribute owed by churches, monasteries, and the remaining clergy who appeared to belong to the Church, or who in any way exercised ecclesiastical office. The collectors of this tribute had already suffered considerable losses, since, after a long period and successive generations, and because the properties themselves had been divided into many portions, the tribute could scarcely be collected.

With God’s inspiration, he ordered the matter to be corrected in such a way that whatever was owed to the treasury beyond this would neither inflict losses upon the collector nor cause delay to withdraw any servant of the Church from his duty.

### VIII

[Note: This chapter is absent from both Colbertine manuscripts and from Vat.]

At the boundary of the territories of Auvergne, Gévaudan, and Rouergue, a synod of bishops was held against Tetradia, formerly the wife of Desiderius, because Count Eulalius sought from her the property which she had carried away with her when she fled from him [Note: Regm. reads, “Eulalius the count sought her and the property.”]

I have thought it worthwhile to recall in greater detail the circumstances of this case: how she left Eulalius and how she took refuge with Desiderius. Eulalius, as is characteristic of youthful age, behaved irrationally in certain matters. Consequently, after he had often been rebuked by his mother, he conceived hatred for the woman whom he ought to have loved.

At length, while she frequently remained in prayer in the oratory of her house and very often completed the night watches in prayer with tears while her servants slept, she was found bruised while praying in the hair shirt in which she prayed. Since no one knew who had done this, the crime of parricide was nevertheless attributed to her son. When Bishop Cautinus of Clermont learned of it, he removed Eulalius from communion.

When the citizens gathered with the priest for the feast of the blessed martyr Julian, Eulalius threw himself at the bishop’s feet, complaining that he had been removed from communion without being heard. The bishop then permitted him to watch the solemn rites of the Mass with the others [Note: Gregory often uses this expression, which also occurs in canon 29 of the Third Council of Orléans. From this passage our Mabillon, in Book I, chapter 6 of *Gallican Liturgy*, conjectures that those who “watched the Mass” were present but did not communicate.].

But when the time came for communion and Eulalius approached the altar, the bishop said:

“Popular rumor proclaims you a parricide. I do not know whether you committed this crime or not; therefore I leave the matter to the judgment of God and of the blessed martyr Julian. If, as you claim, you are innocent, come closer, take for yourself a portion of the Eucharist, and place it in your mouth [Note: From this passage of Gregory, our Mabillon derives four conclusions in Book I, chapter 5 of *Gallican Liturgy*: first, that the word Eucharist designates only the form of bread; second, that communion was given from a portion rather than from an entire formula; third, that communion was received under the form of bread alone; and fourth, that the ancient custom continued into Gregory’s time by which men placed in their own mouths the Eucharist they had received in their hands. Women, however, as is clear from canon 42 of the Council of Auxerre, received it not with the bare hand but on a linen cloth called the *Dominical*. From the same text we learn that laypeople were permitted to approach the altar for holy communion. Our Hugh Menard discusses at greater length the manner of receiving holy communion customary in the earliest centuries of the Church, in his notes to the Gregorian Sacramentary, pages 378, 379, and 391.]. For God will regard your conscience.”

He took the Eucharist, received communion, and departed.

He had a wife, Tetradia, noble on her mother’s side but of lower birth on her father’s. But when the man began consorting in his own house with female servants, he began to neglect his wife; and when he returned from a prostitute, he repeatedly inflicted severe blows upon her. He had also incurred many debts on account of his crimes, and repeatedly squandered his wife’s jewelry and gold to pay them.

At last, when the woman had been placed in these difficulties, had lost all the honor she had possessed in her husband’s house, and he had gone to the king, she was desired by a man named Virus [Al. Verus], who was the nephew of her husband. The intention was that, since Eulalius had lost his wife, she should be joined in marriage to this man.

But Virus, fearing the hostility of his uncle, sent the woman to Duke Desiderius, so that in due course she might be married to him. She took with her the whole of her husband’s property—gold, silver, clothing, and everything that could be moved—together with her elder son, leaving the younger one in the house [Col. 0536B].

When Eulalius returned from his journey, he learned what had happened. After his grief had subsided somewhat, he attacked his nephew Virus and killed him among the narrow valleys of Auvergne.

When Desiderius, who himself had recently lost his wife, heard that Virus had been killed, he took Tetradia as his wife. Eulalius, meanwhile, seized a girl from a monastery at Lyon and took her as his wife. But, at the instigation of his concubine, as some say, jealousy closed his understanding through sorcery.

After a long time, Eulalius secretly attacked and killed Emerius, the girl’s cousin. Likewise, he killed Socratius, the brother of his sister, whom his father had fathered by a concubine [Note: Some printed editions, with Bec., read “the brother of his mother-in-law.”]. He committed many other evil deeds, which would take too long to recount.

His son John, who had departed with his mother, escaped from Desiderius’s house and came to Auvergne. When Innocentius had already assumed the bishopric of Rouergue, Eulalius sent him a request that, through his assistance, he might recover the property owed to him in the territory of that city.

Innocentius replied: “If you give me one of your sons, whom I may make a cleric and retain as my assistant, I shall do what you ask.”

Eulalius sent him the boy, named John, and recovered his property. Bishop Innocentius received the boy, cut the hair of his head, and gave him to the archdeacon of his church. John subjected himself to such strict abstinence that he took barley instead of wheat, drank water instead of wine, and used a donkey instead of a horse; he wore extremely poor clothing.

Thus, when the priests and distinguished men mentioned above had gathered at the boundary of the aforementioned cities, Tetradia was brought forward by Aginus, and Eulalius appeared to bring a charge against her. When he sought the property she had taken from his house when she departed for Desiderius, it was judged that Tetradia should restore what had been taken fourfold and that the sons she had conceived by Desiderius should be regarded as illegitimate [Note: Bec. reads, “it was judged that Tetradia should…”; Regm. and Bec. read *incestos*, and Colb. m. *incesti*. *Incertos* means illegitimate.].

They also decreed that, if she discharged what she had been ordered to pay Eulalius, she would be permitted to enter Auvergne and enjoy without dispute the property that had come to her through her father’s inheritance. And so it was done.

### IX

While these things were taking place, and the Britons were raging violently around the cities of Nantes and Rennes, King Guntchramn ordered an army to be mobilized against them. He chose Beppolenus and Ebracharius as commanders.

Ebracharius, however, suspecting that if victory were achieved with Beppolenus he himself would obtain Beppolenus’s command, formed a hostile relationship with him. Throughout the entire journey they provoked one another with insults, abuse, and curses. Along the road they traveled, they committed arson, murders, plunder, and many crimes.

Meanwhile they came to the river Vicinonia. After crossing it, they reached the river Ulda [Note: It rises near Rohannia in the diocese of Vannes and flows into the Vicinonia—or, as it is called today, the Vegelania—not far from Ponte Corbino. It is commonly called the Aoust. Hence some more recent writers have altered the ancient name and called this river the August.]. There they destroyed the huts in the surrounding area, built bridges over it, and thus the entire army crossed.

At that time a certain priest had joined Beppolenus and said: “If you follow me, I shall lead you as far as Waroch and show you the Britons gathered together in one place.”

When Fredegundis heard that Beppolenus was setting out on this campaign, because he had already been hateful to her for some time, she ordered the Saxons of Bayeux, tonsured according to the custom of the Britons [Note: This was presumably because they had first invaded Great Britain, from which they had borrowed this custom. The Saxons too, as is evident from Letter 9 of Book VIII of Apollinaris Sidonius, were tonsured in the British manner. On the tonsure of the Britons, see Mabillon’s preface to the third century of the *Acts of the Saints* of our order, Part I, where he discusses the matter at greater length.], and dressed in an appropriate style, to go to Waroch’s assistance.

When Beppolenus arrived with those who had chosen to follow him, he engaged in battle and killed many Britons and the aforementioned Saxons over the course of two days. Ebracharius had withdrawn from him with a larger force and did not wish to approach until he heard that Beppolenus had been killed.

On the third day, when the men who were with Beppolenus were already being killed and he himself was resisting despite having been wounded by a spear, Waroch and the forces mentioned above attacked and killed him. For Waroch had enclosed them among narrow roads and marshes, where they were more likely to be trapped in mud than cut down by the sword.

Ebracharius, however, proceeded as far as the city of Vannes. The royal bishop had sent his clerics with crosses and psalmody to meet him, and they escorted him to the city.

At that time some people also reported that Waroch, wishing to flee to the islands with ships laden with gold, silver, and his other possessions, had gone out into the open sea; but when the wind arose and the ships sank, he lost the property he had loaded onto them.

Nevertheless, when he came to Ebracharius, he sought peace and handed over hostages together with many gifts, promising that he would never act against the interests of King Guntchramn.

After Waroch had withdrawn, the royal bishop, together with the clerics and the inhabitants of his city, gave similar oaths, saying:

“We are not guilty before our lords the kings, nor have we ever arrogantly acted against their interests. Rather, we have been held captive by the Britons and subjected to a grievous yoke.”

When peace had thus been established between Waroch and Ebracharius, Waroch said:

“Now depart and report that I shall willingly carry out everything the king orders. So that you may believe this more fully, I shall give my nephew as a hostage.”

And he did so, and the war ceased [Note: So the Casinensis manuscript; the others read, “and the war against him ceased.” Bec. reads, “and the war against him ceased.”]

Nevertheless, a great multitude was killed, both from the royal army and from the Britons.

When the army departed from Brittany and the stronger men crossed the river, the lower-ranking and poorer men who were with them were unable to cross at the same time. When they remained on the bank of the river Vicinonia, Waroch, forgetting the oath and the hostages he had given, sent his son Canao with an army. Canao seized the men he found on that bank and bound them; he killed those who resisted. Some who attempted to cross the torrent with their horses were thrown into the sea by the force of the current.

Later Waroch’s wife released many of them with candles and tablets, as though they were free men [Note: The word *multi* is absent in Regm.], and they returned to their own homes.

The army itself, which had crossed earlier, feared to return by the route it had come, lest it suffer the evils it had inflicted. It therefore headed toward the city of Angers, seeking a bridge over the torrent of the Mayenne [Note: The Mayenne is a river which Gregory calls a torrent because of its rapidity. It rises in the territory of Le Mans, and, swollen by several other rivers, joins the Loire below Angers.].

But the small force that had crossed earlier was stripped, beaten, and reduced to every kind of disgrace at the very bridge we have mentioned.

As they passed through the territory of Tours, they plundered and stripped many people, having found the inhabitants of the area unprepared.

Many of this army nevertheless came to King Guntchramn and said that the commander Ebracharius and the count Uviliacharius, having accepted money from Waroch, had caused the army to perish.

For this reason Ebracharius was brought before the king. After being subjected to many insults by him, he was ordered to withdraw from his presence, while Count Uviliacharius hid himself by flight.

### X

In the fifteenth year of King Childebert, which was the twenty-ninth of Guntchramn [Note: This is the year 590. This chapter is absent from Colb. a. and Vat.], while King Guntchramn was hunting in the Vosges forest, he discovered the tracks of a slain buffalo. When he pressed the forest keeper more closely about who had dared to do this in the royal forest, the keeper revealed the name of Chundo, the king’s chamberlain.

When the forest keeper had said this, the king ordered Chundo to be seized and taken to Chalon in chains.

When the two men brought their charges before the king [Note: That is, “contended,” as Regm. has it], and Chundo said that he had never presumed to do what was alleged against him, the king adjudicated the matter in the field [Note: Such combats took place in a field; hence the combatants were called *champions*. Concerning duels, see the notes above on Book VII, chapter 14.].

Then the chamberlain gave his nephew in his place to undertake the combat, and the two stood in the field. The boy threw a spear at the forest keeper and pierced his foot, whereupon the man immediately fell backward.

As the boy attempted to cut the fallen man’s throat with a knife hanging from his belt, the wounded man pierced him through the belly with his knife. Both fell and died.

When Chundo saw this, he fled to the basilica of Saint Marcellus. The king shouted that he should be seized, and before he could reach the sacred threshold he was captured, bound to a post, and buried beneath stones.

Afterward the king deeply regretted this, since his anger had driven him to act rashly, causing him to kill so quickly a man faithful and necessary to him for the sake of such a trivial matter.

### XI

Chlothar, the son of the former King Chilperic, fell seriously ill and was considered so near death that his death was reported to King Guntchramn. Consequently, Guntchramn left Chalon, apparently wishing to travel to Paris, and proceeded as far as the boundaries of the city of Sens.

But when he heard that the boy had recovered, he turned back from his journey.

When Fredegundis, the boy’s mother, saw him regarded as beyond hope, she vowed a large sum of money to the basilica of Saint Martin, and the boy appeared to improve.

She also sent messengers to Waroch, asking that those from King Guntchramn’s army who were still being held in Brittany be released for the sake of the boy’s life. Waroch fulfilled this request. Thus it became clear that through this woman’s collusion Beppolenus had been killed and the army had been destroyed.

### XII

[Note: This chapter and the following five are absent from Colb. a. and Vat. Ingeltrudis was discussed at length above, Book IX, chapter 33.]

The devout Ingeltrudis, who, as we explained in the preceding books, had established a monastery for women in the atrium of Saint Martin, appointed her niece abbess when she began to fall ill. The rest of the community murmured loudly about this, but when we rebuked them, they ceased their quarrel.

Ingeltrudis was at odds with her daughter because the daughter had taken away her property, and she begged that the daughter not be permitted to pray either in the monastery she had founded or over her grave.

She died, as I believe, in the eightieth year of her life and was buried on the seventh day before the Ides of the first month [March].

Her daughter Berthegundis then came to Tours. Since she was not received there, she went to King Childebert and requested permission to govern the monastery in her mother’s place.

The king, forgetting the judgment he had pronounced against her mother, granted Berthegundis another charter authenticated by his own signature. It stated that she was to bring under her control all the property that her mother or father had possessed, and that everything Ingeltrudis had left to the monastery was to be taken away.

When she came with this charter, she removed all the monastery’s furnishings so completely that she left nothing inside except bare walls. She gathered around her people guilty of various crimes and prepared for seditions; if anything remained from the estates that devotion had donated [Note: Colb. m. reads, “from the remaining estate-properties, whatever the devout had given”; Bad., “from the remnants of the estates.”], they carried off the produce.

She committed so many evils there that they could scarcely be recounted in order.

After receiving the possessions we have mentioned, she returned to Poitiers, uttering many false accusations against the abbess, who was her close relative [Col. 0540B].

### XIII

In those days there arose one of our presbyters, infected with the poison of Sadducaean wickedness, saying that there would be no resurrection. [Note: A little earlier, Eutychius, bishop of Constantinople, had called the future resurrection of the flesh into question; Saint Gregory, who was then residing there, refuted him. Others in various regions likewise followed this heresy. On this matter, see the preface to the French translation of the *Dialogues* of Saint Gregory, published in 1689 by one of our congregation of Saint-Maur.]

When we affirmed that the resurrection had been foretold in the sacred writings and demonstrated by the authority of apostolic tradition, he replied:

“It is clear that this is commonly proclaimed, but we are not certain whether it is true or not, especially since the Lord, angry with the first man whom He had formed with His holy hand, said: ‘In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return’ (Gen. III, 19). What answer will you give to this, you who proclaim that the resurrection is to come, when the Godhead does not promise that a man reduced to dust will rise again?”

To him I replied:

“I think that no Catholic is unaware of what the words of the Lord and our Redeemer, or of the fathers who preceded us, say concerning this matter. For in Genesis, when the patriarchs died, the Lord said: ‘But you shall go to your people. You shall be buried in a good old age’ (Gen. XXV, 8). And to Cain it is said: ‘The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth’ (Gen. IV, 10). Hence it plainly appears that souls live after departing from the body and await the future resurrection with eager expectation.

“It is also written concerning Job that he will rise in the resurrection of the dead. And the prophet David, although speaking in the person of the Lord, nevertheless foreseeing the resurrection, says: ‘Will he who sleeps not add to rise again?’ (Ps. XL, 9)—that is, ‘Will the one oppressed by the sleep of death not come to the resurrection?’

“Isaiah also teaches that the dead will rise from their graves (Isa. 66). The prophet Ezekiel likewise, when he described dry bones covered with skin, strengthened with sinews, filled with veins, animated by the breath of the spirit, and the man restored, most clearly taught that the resurrection is to come (Ezek. 37).

“There was also this clear sign of the resurrection: when a dead body touched the bones of Elisha, it revived through the effect of their power (IV Kings XIII, 21). This was manifested by the resurrection of the Lord Himself, who is ‘the firstborn of the dead,’ who brought death upon death and restored life to the dead from the grave (Apoc. I, 5).”

The presbyter replied:

“I do not doubt that the Lord died and rose again in the man He had assumed. Nevertheless, I do not admit that the rest of the dead will rise.”

And I said:

“What necessity was there for the Son of God to descend from heaven, assume flesh, undergo death, and enter the underworld, unless it was so that He would not allow the man whom He had formed to remain abandoned in perpetual death? Moreover, the souls of the righteous, which until His Passion had been confined in the prison of the underworld, were released when He came. For, descending to the lower regions and flooding their darkness with a new light, He led their souls out with Him, so that they would no longer suffer in that place—according to the saying, ‘And in his grave the dead shall rise.’”

The presbyter said:

“Can bones reduced to ashes be animated again and produce a living man?”

I replied:

“We believe that, even if a man is reduced to dust and scattered by the violent force of water, earth, and wind, it is not difficult for God to restore these things to life.”

The presbyter answered:

“Here especially I think you are in error, attempting with gentle words to assert an exceedingly dangerous deception when you say that one carried away by beasts, submerged in water, devoured in the throats of fish, reduced to excrement and expelled through the secret process of digestion, or cast away by flowing [or hidden] waters, or destroyed by decaying earth, will come to the resurrection.”

To this I replied:

“You have forgotten, I think, what the evangelist John, reclining upon the Lord’s breast and searching out the secrets of the divine mystery, says in the Apocalypse: ‘Then,’ he says, ‘the sea will give up its dead’ (Apoc. XX, 13). Hence it is clear that whatever part of a human body a fish has swallowed, a bird has carried off, or a beast has devoured will be gathered together by the Lord and restored for the resurrection. For it will not be difficult for Him to restore what has been lost, since He created from nothing things that had not existed. He will restore these things to such solid integrity as they previously possessed, so that the body that existed in the world may receive either punishment according to its merits or glory.

“For the Lord Himself says in the Gospel: ‘The Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father with his angels, to repay each one according to his works’ (Matt. XVI, 27).

“Martha also, when she doubted concerning the present resurrection of her brother Lazarus, said: ‘I know that he will rise in the resurrection on the last day’ (John XI, 24). The Lord said to her: ‘I am the resurrection, the way, the truth, and the life’ (ibid. XI, 25).”

The presbyter said:

“But how is it said in the psalm, ‘For the ungodly shall not rise in judgment’ (Ps. I, 5)?”

I replied:

“They will not rise in order to judge, but they will rise in order to be judged. For the Judge cannot sit with the ungodly when He is to render an account of their deeds.”

He said:

“The Lord said in the Gospel, ‘He who does not believe is already judged’ (John III, 18), plainly because he will perish without resurrection.”

I replied:

“He has been judged so that he may come to eternal punishment, because he did not believe in the only-begotten Son of God; nevertheless, he will rise in the body, so that he may suffer in that very body in which he sinned. Judgment cannot take place unless the dead rise first.

“For just as heaven, as we believe, holds those saints who have died, from whose graves that power frequently proceeds by which the blind are enlightened, the lame receive the use of their legs, lepers are cleansed, and other benefits of healing are granted to the sick who ask for them, so we believe that sinners too are kept in that infernal prison until the judgment.”

The presbyter said:

“But in another psalm we read: ‘The spirit has passed from the man, and he shall be no more; and he shall no longer know his place’ (Ps. CII, 16).”

I said:

“This is what the Lord Himself said in a parable to the rich man who was tormented in the flames of Tartarus: ‘You received good things in your lifetime, and likewise Lazarus evil things’ (Luke XVI, 25). That rich man no longer recognized his purple garments and fine linen, nor the pleasures of the banquet that air, earth, or sea had provided for him; nor did Lazarus recognize the wounds or the corruptions that he had endured while lying before the rich man’s gates, when Lazarus rested in Abraham’s bosom but the rich man was tormented in the flames.

The presbyter said:

“In another psalm we read: ‘Their spirit goes forth, and they return to their earth; on that day all their thoughts perish’ (Ps. CXLV, 4).”

I replied:

“You speak correctly. When the spirit has gone forth from a man and the body lies dead, it no longer thinks about the things it left in the world. Thus, for example, it does not think about building, planting, or cultivating a field; it does not think about gathering gold, silver, or the other riches of the world. This thought has perished from the dead body, because the spirit is no longer in it.

“But why do you doubt the resurrection, which the apostle Paul—within whom, as he says, Christ Himself spoke—clearly expresses when he says: ‘We have been buried with Christ through baptism into death, so that, just as he died and rose again, we too may walk in newness of life’ (Rom. VI, 4)?

“Again: ‘We shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed. The trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed’ (I Cor. XV, 51).

“And again: ‘As one star differs from another in glory, so also is the resurrection of the dead’ (ibid. XV, 41).

“Again, in the same place: ‘It is sown in corruption; it will rise in incorruption’ (ibid. XV, 42), and what follows.

“Again, in the same place: ‘We must all be presented before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to his own body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil’ (II Cor. V, 10).

“To the Thessalonians he most plainly indicates the future resurrection, saying: ‘I do not want you to be ignorant concerning those who sleep, so that you may not grieve like the others who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so also God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus.

“For this we say to you by the word of the Lord: we who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord, will not precede those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead who are in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and thus we shall always be with the Lord. Therefore comfort one another with these words’ (I Thess. IV, 12 and following).

“There are very many testimonies concerning these matters that confirm this truth. But I do not know why you doubt the resurrection, which the saints await according to their merit and which sinners fear according to their guilt.

“For even those elements that we see demonstrate this resurrection: trees covered with leaves in summer are stripped when winter comes; but when spring returns, they rise, as it were, and are clothed again with the covering of leaves they previously possessed.

“The seeds also show this. When they are cast into the earth and entrusted to the furrows, if they die, they rise again with abundant fruit, as the apostle Paul says: ‘Fool, what you sow is not brought to life unless it first dies’ (I Cor. XV, 36).”

All these things have been made manifest to the world for belief in the resurrection. For if there is no future resurrection, what benefit will it be for the righteous to act well, and what harm will it be for sinners to act wickedly? Let everyone therefore follow his own wills, and let each person do what pleases him, if there will be no future judgment. [Note: Colb. m. reads *voluntatibus suis* (“their own wills”); Regm., *voluntates suas* (“their own wills”). The printed editions, with Bec., read *voluptatibus suis* (“their own pleasures”).]

Or do you not, wicked man, fear what the Lord Himself said to the blessed apostles?

“‘When the Son of Man comes in the seat of his majesty,’ He says, ‘all nations will be gathered before him, and he will separate them from one another as a shepherd separates sheep from goats. He will place the sheep at his right hand, but the goats at his left. And he will say to the former: “Come, blessed ones, receive the kingdom”; but to the latter: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity”’ (Matt. XXV, 31 and following).

“And as Scripture itself teaches: ‘These will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life’ (ibid. XXV, 46).
