“Do you think there will be a resurrection of the dead or a judgment of deeds when the Lord does these things? Let the apostle Paul answer you, as he answered other unbelievers: ‘If Christ has not risen, our preaching is vain, and your faith is also vain’ (I Cor. XV, 14).”

At this the presbyter, saddened, departed from our presence, promising to believe in the resurrection according to the order of the Holy Scriptures that we have mentioned above.

### XIV

At that time there was a certain Theodulf, a deacon of the city of Paris, who thought himself somewhat learned. [Note: Regm. reads: “who seemed to be alone at the altar, so that, approaching it frequently, he stirred up disputes.” Bad. reads: “who frequently stirred up disputes in the same church,” and so forth, as in Regm. Colb. m. has almost the same reading, except that instead of “in the same church” it has, corruptly, “the same access.”]

He frequently stirred up disputes concerning this matter. Leaving the city of Paris, he came to Angers and placed himself under Audoveus, bishop of that city, [Note: Regm. and Colb. m. read Audoenus, by which name he is also called in the Chartulary of Saint Sergius of Angers, as the Sammarthani note in *Gallia Christiana*.] on account of the ancient friendship they had shared when they lived together in Paris. For this reason he was frequently excommunicated by Ragnemodus, bishop of the city of Paris, because he delayed returning to his own church, in which he had been ordained a deacon.

He had attached himself to the aforementioned bishop of Angers in such close familiarity that he could not free himself from his importunity, since the bishop was a man of good morals and pious affection.

It happened that the bishop had built a sunroom above the city walls. After finishing his evening meal, he descended from it, supporting himself with one hand upon the deacon, who was so drunk with wine that he could scarcely place one foot before the other. Becoming angry for some unknown reason with a boy who was walking ahead with a light, he struck him on the neck with his fist.

At this blow [or: through this impulse], unable to control himself, the deacon was thrown from the wall by the same force. He seized the bishop’s handkerchief, which hung from his belt, and would almost have fallen away with it, had not the abbot quickly embraced the bishop’s feet. Falling upon a stone, with his bones and rib cage shattered, he vomited blood mixed with ruptured bile and breathed out his spirit.

He was devoted both to wine and to a dissolute life of adultery.

### XV

Meanwhile, the scandal which, through the sowing of the devil, had arisen in the monastery at Poitiers was daily growing into greater iniquity. [Note: Bec., Colb. m., and several printed editions read *in ampliori quotidie iniquitate* (“into a greater daily iniquity”).] Chrodieldis, having gathered to herself, as we said above, murderers, sorcerers, adulterers, fugitives, and persons guilty of other crimes, remained prepared for sedition. She ordered them to burst into the monastery at night and drag the abbess outside.

When she sensed the tumult of those who were coming, the abbess asked to be carried to the chest of the holy Cross; for she was weighed down by the pain of gout, so that she might at least be relieved by its help.

But when the men entered, lit a candle, and wandered here and there through the monastery with weapons, searching for her, they entered the oratory and found her lying on the ground before the chest of the holy Cross. Then one man, fiercer than the others, who had undertaken this crime in order to cut down the abbess with a sword, was struck with a knife by another, as I believe through the cooperation of divine providence. Lying on the ground as his blood flowed, he did not accomplish the intention he had conceived with his rash mind.

Meanwhile the superior Justina, together with other sisters, covered the abbess with the altar cloth that lay before the Lord’s Cross, after the candle had been extinguished. [Note: Fortunatus wrote to Gregory on her behalf (Book VIII, poem 15, and the letter prefixed to that poem). In Book IX, poem 7, he calls her the niece of our Gregory. I therefore infer that she was the daughter of Justin, said in Book II of the *Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 2, to have been Gregory’s sister’s husband.] But the men came with drawn swords and spears; tearing the clothing and almost lacerating the nuns’ hands, they seized the superior, mistaking her for the abbess because of the darkness. They pulled away the linens, loosened the hair from her head, dragged her off, and carried her in their hands as far as the basilica of Saint Hilary, to be committed to custody.

As they approached the basilica, when the sky had begun to grow slightly light, they realized that she was not the abbess. They immediately ordered the girl to return to the monastery. Returning there, they seized the abbess, dragged her out, and shut her up in custody near the basilica of Saint Hilary, in the place where Basina had taken up residence. They stationed guards at the door so that no one might offer any assistance to the captive.

Afterward, in the half-darkness of night, they attacked the monastery. Since they had no light from any burning lamp, they took from the storeroom a cup which, having long ago been coated with pitch, had remained dry, set it on fire, and made a great torch from the blaze. They then carried off all the monastery’s property, leaving only what they could not carry.

These things took place seven days before Easter.

When the bishop bore all this heavily and was unable to calm the devilish sedition, he sent to Chrodieldis, saying:

“Release the abbess, so that she may not be held in this prison during these days. Otherwise I will not celebrate the Lord’s Pasch, nor will any catechumen in this city receive baptism, unless the abbess is ordered to be released from the bond by which she is held. But if you are unwilling to release her even then, I will gather the citizens and take her away.”

When he had said this, Chrodieldis immediately appointed assassins, saying:

“If anyone attempts to take her away by force, strike her at once with the sword.”

At that time Flavianus, recently appointed *domesticus*, was present. Through his help the abbess entered the basilica of Saint Hilary and was hidden there. [Thus Bec.; other copies read “was released.”]

Meanwhile murders were committed at the tomb of Saint Radegundis, and before the chest of the holy Cross itself certain men were mutilated during the sedition.

When this fury increased with the coming of day through Chrodieldis’s arrogance, and the seditionists continued to commit the repeated killings and other injuries mentioned above, her arrogance became so swollen that she looked down upon her cousin Basina with an even loftier bearing. Basina began to do penance, saying:

“I have gone wrong in following Chrodieldis’s arrogance; and now I am held in contempt by that same woman, and I stand rebellious against my abbess.”

Then she turned and humbled herself before the abbess, seeking her pardon, and the two were together with one mind and one will.

Finally, when the scandal had arisen, the boys who were with the abbess, while resisting the sedition stirred up by Chrodieldis’s faction [or: group], struck Basina’s boy, who fell and died. The boys then fled after the abbess to the basilica of the Confessor, and for this reason Basina left the abbess and departed. But when the boys again slipped away in flight, the two women returned to the peace they had previously shared.

Afterward many hostilities arose between these factions. Who could ever explain in words such great wounds, such great slaughter, and such great evils, where scarcely a day passed without murder, an hour without quarrelling, or even a moment without weeping?

When King Childebert heard this, he sent an embassy to King Guntram, so that the bishops joined from both kingdoms might correct these events by canonical authority.

For this reason King Childebert ordered that our humble person, together with Ebregisilus, bishop of Agrippina, and Maroveus, bishop of the city of Poitiers itself, should be present. [Note: Regm. reads *Eberegisilo*. He is so called in Book I of the *Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 63. Cointius proves from Fortunatus that he succeeded Charentinus, although in the usual catalogues Ebregesilus is placed before Charentinus.] King Guntram, however, ordered Gundegisil, bishop of Bordeaux, to attend with his provincial bishops, since he himself was the metropolitan of that city. [Note: Most editions and Casin. read “metropolitan”; the meaning is the same.]

But we began to object, saying that we would not go to that place unless the savage sedition that had arisen through Chrodieldis were restrained by the severity of a judge.

For this reason an order was issued to Macco, who was at that time count, commanding him to suppress the sedition by force if they resisted.

When Chrodieldis heard this, she ordered these assassins to stand armed before the entrance of the oratory, so that, if they wished to resist the judge and he attempted to use force, they too would resist together with them.

It was therefore necessary for the count to proceed there with armed men. Some of those who resisted were beaten with clubs, others pierced by weapons, and those who resisted more fiercely were subdued by blows of swords.

When Chrodieldis saw this, she came out to meet them carrying the Lord’s Cross, whose power she had previously despised, saying:

“Do not, I beg you, use force against me, for I am a queen, the daughter of a king, and the cousin of another king. Do not do this, lest a time should come when I avenge myself upon you.”

But the crowd paid no attention to what she said. As we have related, they rushed upon the resisters, dragged them bound from the monastery, stretched them out upon stakes, and beat them severely. Some had their hair cut off, others had their hands cut off, and some had their ears and noses severed. Thus the sedition was suppressed and came to an end.

Then, while the priests who were present were seated upon the tribunal of the Church, Chrodieldis appeared, hurling many insults and accusations against the abbess. She asserted that the abbess had a man in the monastery who, dressed in women’s clothing, was thought to be a woman, although he had plainly been shown to be a man, and who continually served the abbess. She pointed at him, saying: “There he is.”

When he had stood before everyone in the woman’s clothing, as we have said, he declared that he could perform no manly work and had therefore adopted this garment. He professed that he knew the abbess only by name, had never seen her, and had never spoken with her—especially since he lived more than forty miles from the city of Poitiers.

Thus, when Chrodieldis could not convict the abbess of this charge, she began to bring forward other savage accusations:

“What holiness is found in this abbess, who makes men eunuchs and orders them to live with her in the imperial manner?” [Note: Regm. reads “in the nuptial manner.” Our reading is better. She was alluding to the ancient custom by which eunuchs used to serve empresses.]

Questioned about this, the abbess replied that she knew nothing of the matter.

Meanwhile, when this woman had mentioned the name of the eunuch boy, Reovalis, the chief physician, appeared and said:

“When this boy was little and suffered from an illness in his thigh, he was considered beyond hope. His mother approached Saint Radegundis and asked her to order that some treatment be provided for him. She summoned me and ordered me to help him if I could. Then, just as I had once seen physicians practice at Constantinople, I cut the boy’s testicles and restored him healthy to his sorrowful mother. I have learned that the abbess knew nothing whatever about this matter.”

But when the abbess could not be found culpable in this matter either, Chrodieldis began to bring forward other savage accusations. Since the assertions and responses concerning them are included in the judgment written against these women, we have preferred to insert the text itself for reading.

## Text of the Judgment concerning the Same Women

### XVI

“*To the most glorious lords, the kings: the bishops who were present.*

“By the favor of God, religion most rightly lays its causes before pious and Catholic princes, given to the people as rulers, to whom sovereignty has been granted, recognizing that, through the participation of the Holy Spirit, it is associated with and strengthened by the decree of those who rule.

“And because, at the command of your authority, we assembled in the city of Poitiers concerning the affairs of the monastery of Saint Radegundis, of blessed memory, so that we might learn, by hearing the parties dispute, the disagreements between the abbess of that monastery and the nuns who had departed from that same flock without sound deliberation, we summoned the parties and questioned Chrodieldis and Basina [Note: Regm. and Colb. m. read Sabina] why they had so boldly departed from their rule after breaking the monastery doors, and why on this occasion the gathered community had been divided.

“They replied and declared that they could no longer endure the danger of hunger, nakedness, and even murder. [Note: Regm. and Bad. read *diversae* (“various women”), and likewise express the corresponding following allegations in the feminine gender; Bec. reads *diversi eorum* (“various of them”).] They added that various persons among them washed improperly in the bath, that the abbess herself had played at the gaming board, that laypeople dined with the abbess, and that betrothals had taken place in the monastery; that she had rashly made clothing for her niece from a silken altar cloth; [Note: All witnesses except Bec. and Regm. read *neptis* in place of *nepti* (“for her niece”).] that she had thoughtlessly removed the little gold leaves that had been arranged around the edge of the altar cloth and criminally hung them around her niece’s neck; that she had needlessly made a gold-adorned ribbon for the same niece; and that she had celebrated *barbatoria* indoors.” [Note: Two manuscripts read *barbaturias*, and Regm. reads *inique* instead of *intus eo quod*. “To celebrate *barbatoria*” means to perform masks or roles by attaching beards to oneself. In this sense, as Alteserra observes, Petronius says in a fragment: “Today my slave is performing a bearded role.” Hence the satyric games, because the actors wore beards in the manner of satyrs and fauns as they are commonly depicted by painters; the sacred canons repeatedly proscribed such abuses. Cointius, however, interprets the word as referring to the barber’s art.]

“We asked the abbess what she had to say in response. She said concerning the hunger of which they complained that, insofar as the poverty of the times permitted, they had never suffered excessive want. Concerning clothing, she said that if anyone searched their chests, they would find that they possessed more than necessity required.

“Concerning the bath, she reported that what was alleged had taken place during the days of Lent [Note: At that time the custom was not to bathe, because of the mourning of penitence], and that, because of the bitterness of the lime, so that its new construction would not harm those who washed, Lady Radegundis had ordered the monastery’s servants to inspect it publicly until all harmful odor had departed. This remained in use for the servants from Lent until Pentecost.

“Chrodieldis replied: ‘Afterward many others washed there at various times in the same way.’

“The abbess replied that she neither approved what they alleged nor knew whether it had happened. Yet she further blamed them, saying that if they had seen it, why had they not reported it to the abbess?

“Concerning the gaming board she replied: ‘Even if I had played while Lady Radegundis was alive, I would regard myself as less culpable; nevertheless, it is not prohibited by written rule or by the canons.’ She promised, however, at the bishops’ command, with her head bowed in penitence, to fulfill whatever should be ordered.

“Concerning banquets also she said that she had introduced no new custom, but only what had been done under Lady Radegundis; that she had offered blessed bread (*eulogiae*) to faithful Christians, and that it could in no way be proved that she had dined with them.

“Concerning the betrothals, she said that before the bishop, clergy, and elders she had received betrothal payments on behalf of her orphaned niece. Nevertheless, if this were a fault, she declared before everyone that she sought pardon for it; yet she had not held a banquet in the monastery on that occasion.

“Concerning what they counted as an offense regarding the altar cloth, she produced a noble nun who had given her a silken *maforte*—a type of larger garment peculiar to women, covering the head and shoulders—which she had brought from her parents as a gift. She had cut off a portion from it, from which she made whatever she wished; but from the remainder, insofar as it was suitable, she properly prepared an altar cloth for the adornment of the altar. From the piece left over after that cut, she placed purple cloth on her niece’s tunic. She said that she had given it there for the benefit of the monastery; the donor Didimia fully confirmed this.

“Concerning the little gold leaves and the gold-adorned ribbon [Note: These used to be arranged and worn in the form of a crown by a bride; the custom still survives in certain regions], she called upon your servant Macco, who was present, as a witness: through his hands she had received twenty solidi from the bridegroom of the aforementioned girl, her niece, and from this money she had publicly done these things; nothing belonging to the monastery had been mixed into it.

“When Chrodieldis and Basina were asked whether they perhaps attributed to the abbess, God forbid, adultery, murder, sorcery, or any capital crime for which she should be punished, they replied that they had nothing to say except to proclaim that she had committed these acts against the rule, which they had already mentioned.

“Finally, because the monastery’s enclosures had been broken open and the unfortunate women had been permitted, without discipline from their abbess, to do whatever they wished for so many months, they brought before us as pregnant women those whom we had believed to be innocent nuns.

“After these matters had been examined in order, and no crime had been found that would depose the abbess, we solemnly admonished the abbess, with paternal correction concerning the lesser matters, that she should in no way repeat them hereafter so as to incur reproach. [Note: Other copies read *cognosceret* (“might recognize [them]”).]

“Then, when we questioned them about the cause of the opposing party, who had committed greater crimes—that is, those who had despised the admonition of their priest not to go outside the monastery, trampled upon the bishop, and left him in the monastery in utter contempt; who had broken bars and doors, departed after making the bishop’s warning void, and drawn other women into their sin and transgression; and who, when Bishop Gundegisil with his provincial bishops had come to Poitiers for this very matter at the command of the kings and summoned them to the monastery for a hearing, had disregarded the admonition and, when the bishops came to the basilica of the blessed Confessor Hilary where they were staying, had, in a sedition, beaten both bishops and ministers [Note: That is, deacons] with clubs and shed the blood of the Levites inside the basilica—

“thereafter, when the venerable presbyter Theutharius had been sent on the lords’ command in this case and a date had been established for the judgment, without waiting for the appointed time they attacked the monastery with great sedition. They set cups on fire in the courtyard, broke the rear doors with clubs and axes, kindled a fire, beat and wounded the nuns within the enclosures and in the very oratories, plundered the monastery, stripped the abbess and tore loose her hair, dragged her brutally and mockingly through the streets, and shut her away in a place where, although not bound, she was not free.

“When the feast of Easter came—a festival observed *per saeculum* (“in the world”; the sense is uncertain)—the bishop offered a ransom for the condemned woman, so that she might at least witness the baptism; but no pleading voice could obtain this by persuasion. Chrodieldis replied that they had neither known of nor ordered such a crime, still asserting that this had been obtained at her signal, lest she be killed by her own people. [Note: Regm. reads *festivo scilicet per omne saeculum* (“indeed, festive for all time”).]

“Hence it is clear that this requires consideration: their cruelty was further increased in that they killed a servant of their own monastery who had fled to the tomb of the blessed Radegundis and, as their crime grew, remedied nothing by petitioning. Rather, having themselves entered the monastery afterward, they seized it; and when, at the lords’ command, they were to produce those seditious persons publicly, they refused to comply, instead holding weapons in defiance of the kings’ commands and angrily taking up arrows and spears against the count and the populace.

“Then the women again went out to the public hearing and secretly removed the holy and most sacred Cross, treating it with indignity and disgrace; afterward they were compelled to restore it to the church.” [Note: This is the Cross which Saint Radegundis had arranged to have brought to the monastery with such great ceremony, and which also gave the monastery its name. The Regm. manuscript is somewhat fuller: “They removed it and, dragging them indecently and insultingly to their disgrace, as they deserved—for they had acted violently and against their own modesty in their church against the ministers of the Church—while they were being dragged with such insult, as they indeed deserved, they were moved by penitence for their crimes and asked that pardon be granted them by the abbess, promising that they would amend whatever they had done wrong. Repeatedly pretending this and fleeing repentance, they were instead plotting the abbess’s death, as they publicly confessed. Then, when the doors had been opened,” and so forth.]

“When these many capital crimes had been recognized, yet not restrained, but rather continually increased by further offenses, and when we told them to ask the abbess’s pardon for their fault or to correct what had been wrongly directed, they refused to do this and instead plotted her death, as they publicly confessed. [Note: The printed editions, with Colb. m., read *directum* (“directed”).] After we had opened and reviewed the canons, it seemed most just that they should be deprived of communion until they performed worthy penance, while the abbess should be restored to her place.

“These are the measures we have undertaken at your command, insofar as they concern ecclesiastical order, after carefully consulting the canons and without any respect of persons. [Note: Thus Bec. and Regm.; others read “after restricting ourselves.”]

“As for the property of the monastery and the documents of your royal fathers, which were stolen from the place and which they have admitted possessing, but which, in their disobedience to us, they will in no way voluntarily return: in order that the eternal reward of your piety and that of your former princes may endure, it belongs to your piety and authority to compel, by royal command, their restoration for the rebuilding of the place. [Note: Regm. reads: “But it will be for your piety to confirm this by a firm judgment: that you not allow them to return to the place which they have so impiously destroyed, nor permit them further to aspire to it, so that …”] Do not permit them to return to the place which they so impiously and profanely destroyed, nor allow them to aspire to it again, lest worse things occur. Thus, when these things have been restored in full, with the Lord’s help, may everything be acquired for God under Catholic kings, and may religion lose nothing; may the preserved order of the fathers and the canons benefit us in worship and increase for you in fruitfulness.

“May Christ the Lord nourish and govern you, grant your kingdom extended duration, and bestow a blessed life upon you.””

### XVII

Afterward, when they had been suspended from communion by the issuance of the judgment and the abbess had likewise been restored to the monastery, these women appealed to King Childebert, adding evil to evil. They named to the king certain persons who, they alleged, not only committed adulteries with the abbess herself but also carried daily messages to her enemy Fredegundis.

When the king heard this, he sent men to bring them bound. But when they had been examined and no crime was found in them, they were ordered to depart.

### XVIII

A few days before this, when the king entered the chapel of the Marilegis estate, his young men saw an unknown man standing at a distance [Col. 0550C] and said to him: “Who are you, and where do you come from, or what is your business? For we do not recognize you as one of us.” When he replied, “Because I am one of you,” he was immediately thrown out of the chapel and questioned. Without delay he confessed, saying that he had been sent by Queen Fredegund to kill the king. He added:

“We are twelve men sent by her; six of us came here, while the other six remained at Soissons to deceive the king’s son. And I, while waiting at [the] place, intending to strike King Childebert in the chapel, was overcome by fear and did not resolve to carry out what I had intended.”

When he had said this, he was immediately subjected to savage punishments and named various accomplices. After these had been sought out in their several places, some were committed to prison, some were left with their hands cut off [Col. 0550D], and some, after their ears and noses had been amputated, were released to be mocked. Most of those in bonds, however, fearing the kinds of torture, stabbed themselves with their own swords; some also died amid the tortures, so that the king’s vengeance might be accomplished.

### XIX

Sunnigisilus [Note: [Col. 0551D] The Regm. manuscript has *Domnigisilus*, as in the preceding book, chapter 38.] was again handed over to tortures and beaten daily with rods and leather thongs. When his wounds became putrid, and the wounds themselves had just begun to close as the pus drained away, they were reopened again for punishment.

Amid these tortures he confessed not only concerning the death of King Chilperic [Note: [Col. 0551D] So read all the manuscripts and printed editions; Valesius nevertheless thinks that *Childeberti* should be read. He attributes this, as he supposes an error, to a lapse in Gregory’s memory, since it seems quite impossible to him that a nobleman from Austrasia, honored at Childebert’s court, could have been selected by Fredegund—who is thought to have arranged Chilperic’s death—to inflict death upon Chilperic himself, especially since she had many assassins in Neustria who were her most faithful instruments in crime. Childebert had not yet died, however, when Gregory wrote this. Therefore, if Valesius’s opinion is correct, this passage must be understood of the death which Rauchingus and the others mentioned here had planned to inflict upon Childebert.], but also that he had committed various other crimes. Among his confessions he further added that Egidius, bishop of Rheims, had been an accomplice in the conspiracy of that Rauchingus [Note: [Col. 0552D] Other copies have *Ravingus* or *Ravincus*. He is the same Rauchingus of Book VIII, chapter 29, and Book IX, chapter 9, where the conspiracy mentioned here is described.], Ursio, and Berthefred to kill King Childebert.

Without delay the bishop was seized and brought to the city of Metz, exhausted as he was by a very long illness. While he remained there under guard, the king ordered bishops to be summoned for his examination, specifically so that they should be present at the beginning of the eighth month in the city of Verdun [Col. 0551B]. Then, rebuked by the other priests for ordering a man to be dragged from the city and thrown into custody without a hearing, he allowed him to return to his own city, sending letters, as we have said above, to all the bishops of his kingdom, ordering them to be present in the aforesaid city in the middle of the ninth month for his examination.

There were heavy rains, immense waters, intolerable cold, roads dissolved into mud, and rivers overflowing their banks; yet they could not resist the royal command. Finally, when they had assembled, they were dragged as far as the city of Metz, and there the aforementioned Egidius was also present.

The king then declared him to be his enemy and a traitor to the region, and selected Ennod(i)us, formerly a duke, to prosecute the case. His first statement was this:

“Tell me, bishop, what made you think that, abandoning the king, in whose city you enjoyed the dignity of the episcopate, you should submit yourself to the friendship of King Chilperic—who is known always to have been an enemy of our lord the king, who killed his father, condemned his mother to exile [Note: [Col. 0552D] The Regm. manuscript has *equuleo* (‘rack’), but the other reading is better. In fact, Chilperic, as Gregory himself relates in Book V, chapter 1, ordered Brunichild to be deported into exile after Sigibert’s death.], seized the kingdom, and subjected to his own rule the cities which, as we have said, he conquered by an unjust act of usurpation—and that you should receive fiscal estates from him as possessions?”

He replied:

“I shall not be able to deny that I was a friend of King Chilperic; nevertheless, this friendship did not arise against the interests of King Childebert. As for the estates you mention, I acquired them through charters of that king.”

When he produced those documents publicly, the king denied that he had granted them. Otto [Ed. *Otho*], who had then been referendary and whose purported subscription appeared there, was summoned and denied that he had signed them [Col. 0551D]. For his hand had been forged in the document containing this order.

Thus, in this case, the bishop was first found to be a deceiver. After this, letters were produced containing many insults against Brunichild, letters that had been written to Chilperic; likewise, letters from Chilperic to the bishop were brought forward, in which, among other things, this had been inserted:

“For if the root of any matter is not cut off, the stalk that has risen from the earth will not wither.”

From this it is entirely clear that these writings had been composed so that, once Brunichild had been overcome, her son might be crushed.

The bishop denied either having sent these letters in his own name or having received them from Chilperic’s reply. But his familiar servant appeared, and he had preserved these matters under headings of notes throughout volumes of documents. Therefore, it was beyond doubt to those present that the letters had been sent by him [513].

Next, agreements were produced, supposedly in the names of Childebert and King Chilperic [Col. 0552B]. They contained a provision that, after King Guntchramn had been expelled, the two kings should divide his kingdom and cities between themselves. But the king denied that this had been done with his knowledge, saying:

“What have you done to set my uncles against one another, so that civil war might arise between them?”

This caused the army to ravage and lay waste the city of Bourges, the district of Étampes, and the fortress of Mediolanum [Note: [Col. 0552D] This is how the Bec. and Colb. manuscripts read. Colb. *a* has *Mediolanensem*; the printed editions have *Miliodunense*. Here, I think, Mediolanum, or Magdunum Biturigum, is intended rather than Melodunum, which is a town of the Senones on the Seine. Both places were attacked in this war. See above, Book VI, chapter 31.]—and in that war many were killed. “Their souls,” he continued, “as I think, will have to be required from your hands at God’s judgment.”

The bishop could not deny these things. For the documents had been found together in one of the chests in the register of King Chilperic. They had come into the bishop’s possession when, after Chilperic had been killed, his treasures had been removed from the estate of Chelles in the district of Paris and brought to him.

While the dispute over such matters continued for a long time, Abbot Epiphanius of the basilica of Saint Remigius also appeared, saying that he had received two thousand gold pieces and many objects in order to preserve King Chilperic’s friendship. Envoys also stood forth—men who had gone with him to the aforementioned king—and said:

“After leaving us behind, he spoke alone with him for a long time. We understood nothing of those words, except that later we learned of the planning of the destruction mentioned above.”

When the bishop denied this, the abbot, who had always been a participant in the secret counsels, identified the place and the man who had brought the gold pieces we mentioned; and he narrated in due order how the agreement concerning the destruction of the region and of King Guntchramn had been made. When confronted with this, the bishop subsequently confessed it.

When the bishops who had been summoned heard these things and saw that a priest of the Lord had been an accomplice in such great evils, they sighed and begged for a period of three days to deliberate [Col. 0553A]—perhaps Egidius, coming to his senses, might find some means by which he could excuse himself from the offenses charged against him [514]. But when the third day dawned, they assembled in the church and asked the bishop to declare whether he had any defense.

Ashamed, he replied:

“Do not delay in pronouncing judgment upon the guilty. For I know that I am liable to death for the crime of treason, since I have always acted against the interests of this king and his mother. I know that, on my advice, many conflicts were waged, by which certain regions of Gaul were devastated.”

When the bishops heard this and lamented the disgrace of their brother, they obtained his life but removed him from the priestly order after reading the canonical decrees [Col. 0553B]. He was immediately taken to the city of Argentorate, which they now call Strasbourg [Note: [Col. 0553D] See above, note b, column 513. Ed.], and condemned to exile.

In his place Romulfus [Note: [Col. 0553D] Frodoard praises him in Book II, chapter 4, where he says that he was the brother of John, duke of Champagne, who succeeded his father Lupo. His piety is attested by the devout donations which, according to the same author, he made to the Church of Rheims and elsewhere.] was installed as bishop. He was the son of Duke Lupus and already possessed the dignity of the priesthood. Epiphanius, who presided over the basilica of Saint Remigius, was removed from the office of abbot.

For many weights of gold and silver were found in the bishop’s register. Those which came from that wicked campaign [Note: [Col. 0553D] The Bad. and Colb. manuscripts have *malitia* (‘wickedness’), as does Colb. *a*. But *militia* (‘campaign’) was later written by another hand; Gregory uses this word elsewhere.] were transferred to the royal treasures; those found to have come from taxes or from the remaining property of the Church were left there.

### XX

At this synod Basina, daughter of King Chilperic, whom we said above had been removed from communion together with Chrodieldis [Note: [Col. 0553D] This chapter and the following three are absent from the Vat. and Colb. *a* manuscripts.], prostrated herself on the ground before the bishops and begged forgiveness, promising that she would enter the monastery with affection for the abbess and transgress none of the rule [Col. 0553C].

Chrodieldis, however, protested that, so long as Abbess Leobovera remained in that monastery, she would never enter it. But the king pleaded that forgiveness be granted to both, and so, having been received back into communion, they were ordered to return to Poitiers: Basina, as we have said, to return to the monastery, while Chrodieldis was to reside in the estate that had formerly belonged to the Waddo mentioned above, which the king had granted to her.

### XXI

The sons of Waddo [515], wandering through the territory of Poitiers, committed various crimes, including murders and several thefts. For some time earlier they had attacked merchants under cover of night, slaughtered them with the sword, and carried off their goods. They also ensnared by trickery and killed a man of tribunitian authority, plundering his property.

When Count Macc(o) tried to suppress them, they sought an audience with the king. While the count was going to render to the treasury the service customarily owed to it [Note: [Col. 0553D] From this and other passages of Gregory and other authors, Bignonius infers in his notes on Book I, chapter 8 of Marculf that the Counts were responsible for conveying taxes to the treasury.], they too appeared before the king, offering a large belt ornamented with gold and precious stones, as well as a remarkable sword whose hilt was set with Spanish gems and gold.

When the king learned with complete clarity that they had committed the crimes he had heard about, he ordered them bound in chains and subjected to torture. While they were being tortured, they began to reveal the treasures of their father that had been hidden—treasures which their father [Note: [Col. 0553D] Waddo, major-domo, had joined himself to Gundovald Ballomer, concerning whom Gregory has spoken repeatedly above.] had seized from the property of the aforementioned Gundovald.

Without delay, men were sent to investigate, and they found an immense quantity of gold and silver, together with various objects adorned with gold and gems [Col. 0554B]. These they brought into the royal treasury. After the elder had been beheaded, they condemned the younger to exile.

### XXII

Childeric the Saxon [Note: [Col. 0554D] Bec., Colb. *m.*, and several editions have *Chuldericus*.], after committing various crimes, murders, seditions, and many other wicked deeds, went to the city of Auch, where his wife possessed an estate.

When the king, having heard of his wickedness, ordered him killed, he became so drunk with wine one night that he was found dead in his bed, suffocated by it. They asserted that, in the earlier crime already mentioned, in which the priests of the Lord were massacred by Chrodieldis in the basilica of Saint Hilary [Note: [Col. 0554D] See above, Book IX, chapter 41.], he had been the standard-bearer. And if this was so, God avenged the injury done to his servants.

### XXIII

In this year such a great brilliance shone upon the earth during the night [Col. 0554C] that one might have thought it was midday. Fiery globes likewise appeared repeatedly to run across the sky during the nights and illuminate the world.

There was uncertainty concerning Easter because, in Victor’s cycle, the fifteenth moon was written as the date on which Easter should be celebrated [Note: [Col. 0554D] Casin. has “the twelfth.”]. But lest Christians celebrate these solemnities under that moon like the Jews, he added [another date]; the Latins, however, used the twenty-second moon. For this reason many in Gaul celebrated on the fifteenth moon. We, however, on the twenty-second [Note: [Col. 0554D] Colb. *m.*, Regm., and Bad. have “the twenty-first.” Besides, the custom prevailed in the Catholic Church of celebrating Easter at the full moon, or on the fifteenth moon, when it fell on a Sunday. In Gregory’s time some objected to this, lest Christians and Jews, as it seemed to them, celebrate part of the Easter festival together. When some attempted to renew these complaints during the Gregorian reform of the calendar in the immediately preceding century, Clavius refuted them in his defense of that calendar, since Easter had been forbidden on the fourteenth moon for the sole reason that Christians should not celebrate the festival on the day when the Jews sacrificed the lamb.].

Nevertheless, we investigated diligently; but the springs of Spain, which are filled by divine providence, were filled for our Easter.

There was a great earthquake on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of the fifth month, on the fourth day [Note: [Col. 0554D] Regm. has “on the fifth day.”], early in the morning, when the light had begun to return. The sun suffered an eclipse in the middle of the eighth month, and its light diminished so greatly that it scarcely had as much power to shine as the horns of the fifth moon [Col. 0555A]. There were heavy rains, severe thunder in autumn, and the waters rose excessively. A severe epidemic of the groin devastated the city of Viviers and the city of Avignon.

[Note: [Col. 0555D] The ancients more often called this city Alba Helviorum; today it is called Vivarium or Vivaria, commonly Viviers, where the episcopal see is under the metropolitan see of Vienne.]

### XXIV

In the sixteenth year of Childebert and the thirtieth of Guntchramn’s reign, a certain bishop from overseas regions came to the city of Tours, named Simon. He announced to us the destruction of the city of Antioch, asserting that he had been captured in Armenia, in Persia.

For the king of the Persians, after invading the frontier of Armenia, carried off booty and burned the churches with fire. He led this priest and his people captive, as we have said. At that time they also attempted to burn the basilica of the forty-eight holy martyrs, about whom I have spoken in the Book of Miracles [Note: [Col. 0555D] In Book I, On the Glory of the Martyrs, chapter 96.], who suffered in that region. They piled up wood, mixed in pitch and swine hides, and placed beneath them blazing torches [517]. But the fire did not take hold of the prepared fuel, and so, seeing the mighty works of God, they withdrew from it [Note: [Col. 0555D] Here the Regm. manuscript ends, the remaining leaves having been torn out. According to the table of chapters, however, nothing was missing except perhaps the final chapter on the bishops of Tours, which is not mentioned in the table.].

When a certain bishop heard of the capture of the aforementioned priest, he sent payment to the king of the Persians through his own men. After receiving it, the king released this bishop from the bond of slavery.

Departing from those regions, he came to Gaul so that he might receive some consolation from the devout. He reported these things to us, as we said above.

There was a very devout man in Antioch in the giving of alms. He had a wife and children, and, after he began to possess anything of his own, no day in his entire life ever passed without his having first tasted a meal that he shared with a poor person [Col. 0555C].

One day he had gone throughout the city until evening but had been unable to find a needy person with whom he might take food. Going outside the gate as night fell, he found a man in a white garment standing with two others. Seeing him, and terrified—as that ancient Lot is said to have been in the story [Note: [Col. 0556D] In Sacred History, namely Genesis, chapter 19.]—he said:

“Perhaps my lord is a stranger. May he deign to come to the house of his servant; and, after taking a meal, rest on the bed. In the morning you may set out on whatever road you wish.”

The one who was senior, holding a handkerchief in his hand, replied:

“Could you not, man of God, save this city with your Simon, so that it would not be destroyed?”

Then he raised his hand and shook the handkerchief he was holding over half the city. Immediately all the buildings collapsed, and everything that had been built there; old men and infants, men and women, were crushed there, and both sexes perished [Col. 0555D].

[Note: [Col. 0556D] Evagrius described this disaster at Antioch at length in Book VI, chapter 8; Henri Valesius demonstrates in his *Annotations* that it occurred in the year 589.]

Seeing this, and rendered senseless both by the sight of the man and by the sound of the ruin, he fell to the ground and became as though dead. The man then raised his hand again with the handkerchief [Col. 0556A], as if over the other half of the city. His two companions seized him and entreated him with dreadful oaths to spare half the city so that it would not collapse. His anger was appeased, and he restrained his hand. Then, raising the man who had fallen to the ground, he said:

“Go to your house; do not be afraid. Your children, your wife, and your entire household are safe, and none of them has perished. For the constant prayer and the alms that you daily give to the poor have protected you.”

After saying this, they disappeared from his sight and were never seen by him again.

When he returned to the city, he found half of it demolished and overturned, together with its people and animals. Some of these were later dragged out dead from the ruins; a few, weakened, were found alive. Nevertheless, the things spoken to this man by that very angel of the Lord, so to speak, were not void. When he came, he found his whole household unharmed; he mourned only the funerals of relatives who had died in other houses. The right hand of the Lord protected him and his household in the midst of the wicked, and he was saved from the dangers of death, like that aforementioned Lot once was in Sodom (Genesis XIX).

### XXV

In Gaul, however, the often-mentioned disease invaded the province of Marseille. A severe famine oppressed the people of Angers, Nantes, and Le Mans.

These are the beginnings of sorrows, in accordance with what the Lord says in the Gospel:

“There will be pestilences and famines and earthquakes in various places” (Matthew XXIV, 7); “and false Christs and false prophets will arise” (ibid. XXIV, 11); “and they will give signs and wonders in heaven, so as to lead the elect into error” (Mark XIII, 22).

Just as has happened in our own time.

For a certain man from Bourges, as he later admitted himself, entered the forest while cutting wood to meet the needs of some task. A swarm of flies surrounded him, and for this reason he was considered insane for two years. From this it may be understood that the affliction was the wickedness of a demonic assault.

After passing through the neighboring cities, he went to the province of Arles. There he clothed himself in skins and prayed as though he were a religious. In order to deceive through him, the adverse power granted him the ability to foretell the future. To advance in an even greater crime, he was moved from that place and, leaving the aforementioned province, entered the territory of Gévaudan [Note: [Col. 0556D] Today Le Gévaudan. Its principal city was formerly Anderitum, but for many centuries Mimate, Mende, and today the episcopal see have held the chief position.].

He proclaimed himself to be great and did not fear to profess himself Christ. He took with him a certain woman as his sister, whom he caused to be called Mary. A multitude of people flocked to him, bringing the sick, whom he touched and restored to health. Those who came to him presented him with gold, silver, and clothing.

To make his deception easier, he distributed these things to the poor. He prostrated himself on the ground and poured out prayers with the aforementioned woman; then, rising, he ordered himself to be worshiped again by those standing around him.

He foretold the future, announcing to some that illnesses and to others that losses would come, while promising health to a few. But he did all these things by demonic arts and by certain deceptions of which I know not what kind.

An immense multitude of people was deceived by him—not only the more rustic, but also ecclesiastical priests. More than three thousand people followed him.

Meanwhile, he began to strip and plunder those whom he encountered on the road; yet he gave the spoils to those who possessed nothing. He threatened bishops and citizens with death because they scorned to worship him.

When he entered the territory of the city of Velay, he came to the place called Anicium [Note: [Col. 0557C] Here the city of Velay is clearly distinguished from Anicium. Anicium, which today is an episcopal see, commonly called *Podium*, Le Puy, is named from its situation. For *podium*—a *puy*, *Peu*, or *puech*—designates a mountain in those regions, not only in antiquity but also now. That place is famous for its cathedral church, dedicated to blessed Mary and situated on a lofty mountain. Its bishop styles himself the immediate suffragan of the Roman pontiff, and he was at one time granted the privilege of the pallium. We shall discuss the site of the ancient city of Velay in the Appendix.

Some people call the ancient city of the Vellavi *Revessio*. Mabillon proves by many arguments, in his appendix to Part I of the fourth century of the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, p. 758, that it stood where the town of Saint-Paulien is now seen. There he also produces several inscriptions relevant to the matter. It is enough to present one here, recovered from the ancient road leading from that town to Gergovia:

“Caesar, prince of the youth, restored the roads and bridges that had collapsed through age.”]

He approached the nearby basilicas with his entire army and took up position, arranging his battle line to wage war against Bishop Aurelius [Note: [Col. 0558C] Aurelius is venerated as a saint among the people of Le Puy.] who was then stationed there. He also sent messengers ahead of him—men naked, dancing and playing—to announce his arrival.

The bishop, astonished, sent brave men to him to ask what he meant by these actions. One of them, the eldest, bent down as though to kiss his knees and inquire into his course; he was then ordered to be seized and stripped. Without delay, the man drew his sword and cut him to pieces. Thus fell this “Christ”—who ought rather to be called Antichrist—and he died. All who had been with him were scattered.

That woman Mary, however, was handed over to punishment and made public all his fantasies [Col. 0557C] and deceptions. For the men whom he had drawn into believing in him by the devil’s deception never returned to sound understanding. They continued to profess him as Christ and to say that this Mary possessed a share of divinity.

Throughout Gaul, many others also emerged who, by means of such deceptions, attached certain little women to themselves. These women, behaving wildly, acknowledged them as saints, and they presented themselves as great before the people. We saw many of them and, rebuking them, attempted to call them back from their error.

### XXVI

Ragnemodus [Note: [Col. 0558C] This chapter and the following one are absent from the Vat. and Colb. *a* manuscripts. Faramodus, who yielded his place to Eusebius, became his successor after Eusebius’s death, as we learn from the commonly circulated lists.] also, bishop of the city of Paris, died.

When his brother Faramodus, a priest, competed for the episcopate, a certain Eusebius, a merchant of Syrian origin, was substituted in his place after giving many gifts. Once he had received the episcopate, he dismissed the entire *schola* [Note: [Col. 0558D] That is, readers, singers, and others who were under the discipline of the archdeacon.] of his predecessor and appointed Syrians of his own family as ministers of the church.

Sulpicius, bishop of the city of Bourges, also died, and his chair was obtained by Eustasius [Note: [Col. 0558D] Colb. *m.*, Bad., and Ches. have *Eustachius*. He is also called this in the *Patriarchate of Bourges*, chapter 28, where he is given the title of saint. His predecessor Sulpicius, mentioned here, was surnamed Severus, to distinguish him from the other Sulpicius, bishop of Bourges, who was called Pius. The feast of Severus is celebrated on the fourth day before the Kalends of February. He had been buried in the church of Saint Julian, from which he was transferred to Saint Ursinus, where he now rests. A book on the Seven Sleepers is circulated under his name and attributed to our Gregory. See above, Book VI, chapter 39, and the Bollandists’ entry for 29 January.], a deacon of Autun.

### XXVII

Among the Franks of Tournai a considerable dispute also arose because the son of one man repeatedly rebuked the son of another, who had married his sister, in anger, asking why he visited a prostitute after abandoning his wife.

When this anger did not result in the correction of the crime, it rose to such a degree that the first youth attacked his kinsman and killed him together with his companions; then he himself was struck down by those who had come with the other man. No one remained alive from either side except one man, whom the killer had not reached.

As a result, the parents of both sides raged against one another. Queen Fredegund repeatedly rebuked them, urging them to abandon their hostility and become reconciled, lest the obstinacy of the quarrel grow into a greater scandal.

But when she could not appease them with gentle words, she restrained both sides with a double axe.

She invited many people to a banquet and made the three men sit together on a single bench. When the meal had been prolonged for some time, until night covered the earth, the table was removed [Note: [Col. 0558D] Casin. has “when the table had been brought in.”]. As was the custom of the Franks, they remained seated on their benches just as they had been placed.

After drinking a great deal of wine, they became so drunk that their young men, soaked with wine, fell asleep in the corners of the house wherever each had collapsed [Col. 0558C]. The men appointed by the woman, carrying three axes, then stood behind the three men. While they were conversing, the youths’ hands were swung in a single attack, as it were, and the men were struck down. The banquet ended.

The men’s names were Chariualdus, Leodoualdus, and Waldinus.

When this was reported to the parents, they began to guard Fredegund more closely and sent messengers to King Childebert so that she might be seized and killed. But the people of Champagne, stirred by this affair, delayed matters; meanwhile, she escaped with the help of her supporters and hurried to another place [Col. 0559A].

### XXVIII

After this she sent envoys to King Guntchramn, saying:

“Let my lord the king proceed as far as Paris, summon my son, his nephew, and order him to be consecrated by the grace of baptism. When he has received him from the holy font, may he deign to regard him as his own foster-son.”

When the king heard this, he summoned the bishops—namely Aetherius of Lyon, Syagrius of Autun, Flavius of Chalon, and the others whom he wished [Note: [Col. 0559D] Aetherius, who is also praised below, and Syagrius are well known from the letters of Saint Gregory the pope. Gregory mentioned Flavius above, Book V, chapter 46. All three attended various councils.]. He ordered them to go to Paris, indicating that he would follow later.

Many from his kingdom, both household officials and counts, also attended this assembly to prepare what was necessary for the royal expenditure.

After deliberating that he ought to attend, the king was prevented by pain in his feet [Col. 0559B]. When he recovered, he went to Paris [522]. From there he hastened to the estate of Rotojalum belonging to that city. After summoning the child, he ordered a baptistery to be prepared in the village of Nemptodorum [Note: [Col. 0559D] The village of Nemptodorum was near Rotojalum; today it is called Nanterre, famous for the birth of blessed Genevieve, patroness of the city.].

While these things were being done, envoys of King Childebert approached him and said:

“You did not recently promise these things to your nephew Childebert, so that you would form friendships with his enemies, did you? But, as far as we can see, you observe nothing of your promise; rather, you abandon what you promised. And you are setting this boy up as king in the chair of the city of Paris. God will judge you, because you do not remember what you freely promised.”

When they had said this, the king replied:

“I am not abandoning the promise I made concerning my nephew, King Childebert. He ought not to be offended if I receive from the holy font his cousin, my brother’s son; for no Christian ought to reject this request.

“As God most clearly knows, I wish to undertake this not through any cunning but in the simplicity of a pure heart, because I fear incurring divine displeasure. It is no humiliation for our people if he is received by me. If masters receive their own servants from the sacred font, why should I not be permitted to receive a close relative and make him my spiritual son through the grace of baptism?

“Go now and report to your lord: I wish to preserve unaltered the pact I made with you. If the offense of your condition does not cause you to abandon it, it cannot be abandoned by me.”

After saying this, the envoys departed. The king approached the holy font and presented the boy for baptism. Receiving him, he wished him to be called Chlothar, saying:

“May the boy grow and prove himself worthy of this name, and may he possess such power as did the one whose name he has received” [Note: [Col. 0559D] This was Chlotarius, Guntram’s father, whom, following the older manuscripts, we have written as Chlothacarius in Gregory’s text. Both Chlotarii possessed the monarchy of the Franks.].

When the ceremony had been completed [Col. 0560A], he loaded the little boy, who had been invited to the feast, with many gifts. Likewise, the king, invited by him, departed laden with many presents and resolved to return to the city of Chalon [Note: [Col. 0560D] In the Vat. and Colb. *a* manuscripts, Fredegar’s Chronicle is appended to this chapter under the title of Book X of Gregory’s History.].

### 523

**XXIX.** In this year also Aredius, leaving the earth at the Lord’s summons, departed to heaven. He was a native of the city of Limoges, born not to parents of ordinary standing in his region, but to parents of very noble birth. He was delivered to King Theudebert and attached to the royal courtiers. At that time there lived in the city of Trier a man of outstanding holiness, Nicetius the bishop, who was regarded among the people as remarkable not only for his admirable eloquence in preaching but also for his good and miraculous works. When he saw the boy in the royal palace, discerning—I do not know what divine quality—in his face, he ordered him to follow him. Leaving the royal palace, the boy followed him.

When they had entered the little cell and were conversing about matters pertaining to God, the young man asked the blessed priest to correct him, instruct him, educate him, and train him in the divine books. While he was living with the aforementioned bishop in the fervor of this study, and his head already tonsured, one day, while the clerics were singing psalms in the church, a dove came down from the upper chamber. It flew gently around him and settled upon his head, indicating, as I believe, that he was already filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit. When he tried, not without embarrassment, to drive it away, it flew around for a little while and again settled either upon his head or upon his shoulder. It accompanied him continually—not only there, but also whenever he entered the bishop’s cell. The bishop observed this for many days with no little astonishment.

Afterward, the man of God, filled with the Spirit as we have said, returned to his homeland, his father and brother having died, in order to console his mother Pelagia, who looked to no relative other than this child. Then, while he devoted himself to fasts and prayers, he begged her to take responsibility for all the affairs of the household—that is, the discipline of the servants, the cultivation of the fields, and the care of the vineyards—so that no impediment might befall him and cause him to cease from prayer. He claimed for himself only this privilege: that he should supervise the building of churches.

What more need be said? He built temples of God in honor of the saints, sought their relics, and made tonsured monks from his own household. He founded a monastery [Note: [Col. 0560D] Namely the monastery of Atane, which, after having long been subject to the Benedictine Rule, passed to secular canons subject to the chapter of Saint Martin of Tours. It gave its name and origin to the surrounding town, which is still called Saint-Yrieix, in Limousin.] in which the rules not only of Cassian but also of Basil and of the other abbots who established the monastic life are observed, while the blessed woman supplied each monk with food and clothing.

Yet, although burdened with this responsibility, she did not cease to resound with praises of God. Rather, continually—even while carrying out some task—she always offered prayer to the Lord like the acceptable fragrance of incense.

Meanwhile, the sick began to flock to Saint Aredius. Laying his hands upon each one with the sign of the cross, he restored them to health. If I wished to write down their names individually, I could neither go through their number nor recall their names. I know this one thing, however: everyone who came to him sick departed in good health.

Of the greater miracles, we shall present a few. Once, while he was traveling with his mother and hurrying toward the basilica of Saint Julian the martyr, they arrived in the evening at a certain place. The place was dry and barren, without flowing streams. His mother said to him: “My son, we have no water; how can we rest here tonight?” He prostrated himself in prayer and poured out prayers to the Lord for a very long time. Then, rising, he planted in the earth the staff he was carrying in his hand. After turning it around twice or three times, he happily pulled it toward himself. Immediately a stream of water followed, so abundant that it supplied plentiful drink not only for them at once but afterward also for their animals.

More recently, while traveling, a rain cloud began to approach him. Seeing it, he bent his head slightly over the horse on which he was sitting and stretched out his hands to the Lord. When his prayer was completed, the cloud divided into two parts, and an enormous rain descended all around them; yet over them—not to say what seems impossible—not a single drop fell.

Wistrimundus, also called Tatton, a citizen of Tours, was suffering severe pain in his teeth, so severe that his jaw had also swollen. When he had complained of this to the holy man, Aredius placed his hand upon the place of pain, and immediately the pain was driven away and never again arose to trouble the man. The sufferer himself reported this.

Of the signs that the Lord worked through the power of Saint Julian the martyr and Saint Martin the blessed confessor, in Aredius’s hands, we have written many in the Books of Miracles, as he himself related.

After these and many other acts of power, which he accomplished with Christ’s cooperation, he came to Tours after the feast of Saint Martin and remained there for a short time. He told us that he would remain in this world for only a short while longer, or would certainly soon be released from it [Note: [Col. 0561D] Thus the Becensis manuscript; others read, “that he himself, or the long-lived, …” Moreover, understand the feast of Saint Martin mentioned here as the Translation, celebrated on 4 July, since Aredius died on 25 August.]. Then he bade us farewell and departed, giving thanks to God that, before he died, he had been deemed worthy to kiss the tomb of the blessed bishop.

When he had returned to his cell, after drawing up his will [Note: [Col. 0561D] We shall give it in the appendix from volume II of Mabillon’s *Analecta*. Gregory wrote about Aredius in Book II of the *Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 39, and Book II of the *Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 40. We shall give his Life below, in addition to that published among the *Acts of the Saints of our Order*, Benedictine Century I, p. 349. Fortunatus wrote to him in poem 20 of Book V.], arranging everything, and appointing the bishops Saint Martin and Hilary as his heirs, he began to fall ill and to suffer from dysentery. On the sixth day of his illness, a woman who was often tormented by an unclean spirit and could not be cleansed by the saint began, with her hands tied behind her back, to cry out:

“Run, citizens! Leap up, people! Go out to meet the martyrs and confessors who are coming to the burial of blessed Aredius. Behold, Julian from Brioude is here; Privatus from Gévaudan; Martin from Tours; and Martial from his own city [Note: [Col. 0562D] Namely Limoges, whose people regarded Martial as their apostle.]. Saturninus from Toulouse is here; Dionysius from the city of Paris; and several others whom heaven holds, whom you worship as confessors and martyrs of God.”

When she began shouting these words at the beginning of the night, her master bound her again. But she could not be restrained. Breaking her bonds, she began to hurry toward the monastery, still crying out these words.

Immediately the blessed man gave up his spirit, with a testimony to the truth that he had been received by angels. At his funeral he also cleansed this woman, together with another woman tormented by a more evil spirit, from the wickedness of the hostile demon, after he had been covered by the tomb [Note: [Col. 0562D] The Casinensis manuscript reads “tormented.” The note continues: “After the funeral had been celebrated, when he had been covered,” etc.].

I believe that, by God’s will, he was unable to cleanse these same women while he was still in the body so that his funeral might be glorified by this power.

After the funeral had been celebrated, a certain woman approached his tomb with her mouth gaping open and without the use of her voice. Having touched the tomb with her kisses, she was granted the gift of speech.

**XXX.** In the second month of this year, a severe plague afflicted the people both in the region of Tours and in the region of Nantes, so that anyone who fell ill, even if struck only by a slight headache, gave up his soul. But when rogation prayers had been performed with great abstinence and fasting, and almsgiving had also been added, the force of the divine anger was appeased [Col. 0562C].

In the city of Limoges, however, many were consumed by heavenly fire because they had performed public labor on the Lord’s Day, thereby violating that day. This is a holy day, the first to behold the light created in the beginning and to shine forth as a witness to the Lord’s resurrection. Therefore Christians ought to observe it with complete faith, so that no public work may be performed on it.

In the region of Tours, some were also burned by this fire, but not on Sunday. There was an immense drought, which destroyed all the fodder of the grasses. As a result, a severe disease grew among the sheep and beasts of burden, leaving little stock from which replenishment could arise, just as the prophet Habakkuk foretold: “The sheep shall fail from the fold, and there shall be no cattle in the stalls” (Habakkuk 3:17).

This plague spread not only among domestic animals but also among the very kinds of savage beasts. For throughout the clearings of the forests, a multitude of deer and other animals, struck down, were found in pathless places. The hay perished because of the rainwater that fell upon it and the flooding of the rivers [Note: [Col. 0562D] The Badian manuscript reads: “when the hay had been found,” etc.]. The crops were scanty, while the vineyards were abundant; but the acorns that appeared did not mature.

**XXXI.** Although I seem to have written something about the bishops of Tours in the preceding books [Note: [Col. 0563C] This chapter is absent from the Alexandrian manuscript.], I have decided to repeat the account for the sake of their succession and chronology, so that it may be known when the first preacher came to the city of Tours.

1. The first bishop, Gatianus [Note: [Col. 0563C] Most editions read Gratianus; the Colbertine manuscript reads Catianus.], was sent from the pope of the Roman See in the first year of the reign of Decius [527]. The city was inhabited by a multitude devoted to pagan idolatries, and by his preaching he converted some of them to the Lord. At times, however, he concealed himself because of the opposition of the powerful: whenever they found him, they often afflicted him with insults and abuse. With a few Christians whom he had converted, as we have said, he secretly celebrated the solemnity of the Lord’s Day in crypts and hiding places [Col. 0563B].

He was very devout and feared God. Had he not been such, he certainly would not have left his home, his parents, and his homeland out of devotion to the love of the Lord. He is said to have lived in this city under such conditions for fifty years. He died in peace and was buried in the cemetery of the very settlement, which belonged to the Christians. The episcopate then remained vacant for thirty-seven years [Note: [Col. 0563C] The Casinensis manuscript has “thirty-eight,” as does the Badian. But since above it has “eight,” I infer that “seven” should be read here and that the final i was carelessly added by a copyist. The feast of Saint Gatianus is celebrated on 18 December. His sacred body, together with the relics of other saints, was burned by the Calvinist heretics in 1562. Saint Gatianus is said to have been buried in the cemetery of the settlement, which is thought once to have stood on the site where a church was later built in honor of the blessed Mary. That church still survives, distinguished by its parochial title under the name of Saint Mary the Rich. No trace of the blessed Gatianus’s burial remains there, however. Perhaps, as is stated below in §3, Saint Martin later transferred him to the church of Saint Litorius, where he was deposited near Litorius himself. Hence that church—which is believed to be the oldest of the entire city and bears cathedral status, although it recognizes other patrons, especially Saint Maurice—is still better known today under the name of Saint Gatianus.].

2. The second, Litorius [Note: [Col. 0563D] The Colbertine manuscript and the Badian read Littorius; the Becensis manuscript and others read Lidorius. His feast is celebrated on 13 September. See the note on Book I, final chapter.], was ordained bishop in the first year of the reign of Constans. He was a citizen of Tours and was also very devout. He built the first church within the city of Tours, when there were already many Christians. The first basilica was made by him from the house of a certain senator. In his time Saint Martin began to preach in Gaul.

He held office for thirty-three years [Note: [Col. 0563D] The Casinensis manuscript reads “thirty-eight.”], died in peace, and was buried in the aforementioned basilica, which is still called by his name.

3. The third, Saint Martin, was ordained bishop in the eighth year of Valens and Valentinian [Note: [Col. 0563D] The Colbertine and Regius manuscripts read: “in the ninth year of Valens, he was ordained bishop.” Valentinian’s eighth year began in February 371; Saint Martin’s ordination should therefore be assigned from this passage to that year, since his feast was already being celebrated under Bishop Perpetuus on 3 July.].

He was from the region of Pannonia, from the city of Sabaria. Out of love for God, he first established a monastery near the Italian city of Milan. But because he fearlessly preached the Holy Trinity, he was beaten with rods and expelled by the heretics from Italy; he then came to Gaul. He converted many pagans, destroyed their temples and statues, and performed many signs among the people. Before becoming bishop he even raised two dead people; after becoming bishop, however, he raised only one.

He transferred the body of blessed Gatianus and buried it beside the tomb of Saint Litorius, in the aforementioned basilica bearing his name. He prevented Maximus from sending the sword into Spain to kill the heretics [Note: [Col. 0564C] Namely the Priscillianists, whom Maximus, at the instigation of Bishop Ithacius, had ordered to be punished by the sword. This affair caused great disturbances in the Church. See Dialogue 3 of Sulpicius Severus, who describes the origin and development of the same heresy more fully near the end of Book II of his Sacred History.]. Martin judged that it was enough for them to be removed from communion with the Catholic churches.

When he had completed the course of this present life, he died at the settlement of Condatensis in his own region, in the eighty-first year of his age. His body was taken from that settlement by boat and buried at Tours, in the place where his tomb is now venerated [the Becensis manuscript reads “adorned”]. We have read the three books written by Sulpicius Severus about his life. Even in the present age he continues to reveal himself through many miracles.

In the monastery now called the Major Monastery, he built a basilica in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. In the settlements also—that is, at Alingavia [Note: [Col. 0564D] Alingavia, now a settlement enclosed within the walls of the city on the Loire, is also called Langesium, commonly Langeais, where a council was held in 1270 under John of Monsonau. Salonacum, as Valesius thinks, is Sonnay or Sonné, between the rivers Andria and Clasia and between two forests, not far from Île-Savary and Châtillon-sur-Indre. There is, however, another settlement of the same name between the forest and the castle of Reginald. Marollius, the abbot, in the French edition thinks it is Sully or Sougé. Ambaciacum was discussed above, Book II, chapter 35. Cisomagum is, for Marollius, Charnisay, between the forest and the river Clasia, or perhaps Cicongné. But more plausibly, as Valesius thinks, Maanus in his History of the Metropolitan Church of Tours identifies it as Chisseau, a settlement on the river Cher, not far from Montrichard. Tornomagus is commonly Tournon on the river Creuse. Condate is discussed in Book I, chapter 43.], Solonacum, Ambaciacum, Cisomagum, Tornomagus, and Condate—after destroying pagan shrines and baptizing the Gentiles, he built churches.

He held office for twenty-six years, four months [Note: [Col. 0564D] The Regius manuscript reads “three months and seventeen days.” The Bede, Colbertine, and Badian manuscripts read “four months and seventeen days.”], and twenty-seven days, and the episcopate remained vacant for twenty days.

4. The fourth, Briccius, was ordained bishop in the second year of Arcadius and Honorius, when they were reigning jointly. He was a citizen of Tours. In the thirty-third year of his episcopate, the citizens of Tours accused him of adultery. After expelling him, they ordained Justinian bishop. Briccius, however, went to the pope of the City [Rome] [Note: [Col. 0565C] This is the reading of the Regius manuscript; others read: “Briccius went to the pope of the City.” See the notes on Book II, chapter 1. His feast is celebrated on 13 November.].

Justinian, following him, died near the city of Vercelli. The people of Tours, acting wickedly again, appointed Armentius. Briccius, after spending seven years with the pope of the City, was found free of the accusation and was ordered to return to his own city.

He built a small basilica over the body of blessed Martin, in which he himself was also buried. As he entered through one gate, Armentius was being carried out dead through another. After Armentius had been buried, Briccius recovered his see.

He is said to have established churches in the settlements, namely at Catalonnum [Note: [Col. 0565C] The Colbertine manuscript reads Calatonnum, and the Châlons and other manuscripts Catolonnum. Marollius thinks this place is Chaumont, in the territory of Tours and Blois; Valesius rejects this and prefers to identify it as Clion, on the river Andria between Paludellum, Paluau, and Châtillon. Bricca may be Bray or Bré on the river Cher or Indre. There is also a place on the border of the territories of Tours and Angers commonly called Brèche. Marollius thought Rothomagus was the settlement called la Rouë or Saint-Antoine-du-Rocher. Maanus prefers to interpret it as Ruam, a place not far from Montbazon, commonly called Pont de Ruam, after the bridge there over the river Indre. Briotreidis is, for Marollius, Autrèche, three leagues from Amboise. Maanus thinks it is Brisay, a castle mentioned in the deeds of the lords of Amboise; Valesius insists that it is Le Bridoré on the Indre.], Bricca, Rothomagus, Briotreidis, and Caino. The total duration of his episcopate was forty-seven years. He died and was buried in the basilica that he had built over Saint Martin.

5. The fifth, Eustochius, was ordained bishop. He was a holy man who feared God and came from a senatorial family. He is said to have established churches in the settlements of Brixis [Note: [Col. 0565D] For Valesius, Brixis is Brisay, discussed in the preceding note. Iciodorum, as we said in Book VI, chapter 12, is Iseure, on the border of the territories of Tours and Poitiers. Luccae—or, as the Colbertine and Bede manuscripts have it, Lucae, or as Gregory elsewhere has it, Lociae—is commonly Loches, a celebrated place on the Indre, where blessed Senoch founded a monastery. Dolus is the name of a settlement not far from the river Indre.], Iciodorum, Luccas, and Dolus.

He also built a church within the walls of the city, in which he placed the relics of the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius. These had been brought from Italy to Saint Martin [Note: [Col. 0565D] This is the reading of the Becensis manuscript; others read “by Saint Martin,” but that is erroneous. Compare Book I of On the Glory of the Martyrs, chapter 47. Saint Ambrose discovered the relics of Gervasius and Protasius in 386, when Saint Martin was already bishop. The letter of Saint Paulinus mentioned here is not extant. Even today, beside the church of Saint Mary the Rich, an oratory with a small hospital dedicated to Saints Gervasius and Protasius can be seen, but it lies in the suburb. Yet a church of Saints Gervasius and Protasius is said below, in §12, to have existed within the city walls.], as Saint Paulinus mentions in his letter.

He held office for seventeen years and was buried in the basilica that Bishop Briccius had built over Saint Martin [Note: [Col. 0566C] The feast of Eustochius is celebrated in the Roman Martyrology on 19 September. He attended the Council of Angers in 453. Together with Leo and Victurius, he wrote a letter against clerics who had recourse to secular tribunals.].

6. The sixth, Perpetuus, was ordained bishop. He too was, they say, of senatorial stock and was a relative of his predecessor. He was very rich and possessed estates in many cities. After removing the basilica that Bishop Briccius had previously built over Saint Martin, he constructed another, larger one, with marvelous workmanship [Note: [Col. 0566C] A detailed description of this church is given above, Book II, chapter 14. See also Book I of the Miracles of Saint Martin, chapter 6.]. He transferred the blessed body of that venerable saint into its apse.
