He established fasts and vigils, specifying how they were to be observed throughout the course of the year; this practice is still recorded among us. Their order is as follows.

#### On the fasts

After Pentecost [Note: [Col. 0566C] That is, beginning at Pentecost. The ancients called the period between Easter and Pentecost “the Fifty,” during which fasting was not permitted.], fast on Wednesday and Friday until the Nativity of Saint John.

From the kalends of September until the kalends of October, fast twice a week.

From the kalends of October until the deposition of Saint Martin, fast twice a week.

From the deposition of Saint Martin until the Nativity of the Lord, fast three times a week [Note: [Col. 0566C] This article is absent from the Regius manuscript.].

From the Nativity of Saint Hilary until the middle of February, fast twice a week.

#### On the vigils

At the Nativity of the Lord, in the church [Note: [Col. 0566C] That is, in the cathedral church.].

At the Epiphany, in the church.

At the Nativity of Saint John, at the basilica of Saint Martin.

At the Nativity of Saint Peter’s episcopate [Note: [Col. 0566C] That is, the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter, as it is called in the Second Council of Tours. It was so celebrated in Gaul that from it the Sundays leading up to Lent were called the first, second, and so forth after the Chair of Saint Peter. See Mabillon’s observations on §24 of Book II of Gallican Liturgy. The word “episcopate” is absent from the Châlons manuscript.], at his basilica.

On the sixth [another reading: fifth] day before the kalends of April, at the Resurrection of Our Lord Jesus Christ, at the basilica of Saint Martin.

At Easter, in the church [Note: [Col. 0566D] In the oldest calendars the feast of Easter is distinguished from the feast of the Resurrection. In them the feast of the Resurrection is celebrated on 27 March, whereas Easter, as everyone knows, has always been celebrated in the Church on varying dates according to the variation of the moon.].

On the day of the Ascension, in the basilica of Saint Martin.

On the fiftieth day [Note: [Col. 0566D] That is, Pentecost. It is also called this in canon 25 of the First Council of Orléans.], in the church.

At the Passion of Saint John [Note: [Col. 0566D] In the Gallican Sacramentary, which our Mabillon published from an ancient manuscript in volume I of the *Museum Italicum*, between the Nativity of Saint John and the feast of Saints Peter and Paul, there is a Mass for the Passion of Saint John.], at the basilica, in the baptistery.

At the Nativity of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, at their basilica.

At the Nativity of Saint Martin, at his basilica.

At the Nativity of Saint Symphorianus, at the basilica of Saint Martin.

At the Nativity of Saint Litorius, at his basilica.

Also at the Nativity of Saint Martin, at his basilica [Note: [Col. 0566D] This feast appears only in the Regius manuscript. It is certain from Gregory himself that by this time the feast of Saint Martin was already celebrated twice: once in July and once in November, the latter being expressed here.].

At the Nativity of Saint Briccius, at the basilica of Saint Martin.

At the Nativity of Saint Hilary, at the basilica of Saint Martin.

Perpetuus built the basilica of Saint Peter, in which he placed the chamber of the earlier basilica; it survives to our own time. He himself also built the basilica of Saint Lawrence on Mount Laudiacum [Note: [Col. 0567B] Mentioned above, Book II, chapter 2. Laudiacum is said to be six miles from the city. The place still survives, commonly called Mont-Loïs, about three leagues above Tours, situated on the left bank of the Loire.].

In his time churches were built in the settlements of Evena [Note: [Col. 0567B] Evena is Enevoc in the Regius manuscript and is today Avoine, between the Loire and the Vienne, as Maanus and Valesius believe; they do not agree with Marollius, who thinks it is Eve-le-Montier. See *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 19. Mediconnum is Metray for Marollius and Monnoye for Maanus; Valesius does not disagree with the latter and thinks it could also be Mosne, on the Loire near Amboise. Berrao is the name given to the district of Berray, discussed above in Book VI, chapter 12, where we said it was Barou, between the Creuse and the Claise. Hesitating here, Marollius proposes three other settlements: Bourray on the Cher near Montrichard; Berray not far from Loudun; and Bretenay on the Loire below Tours. The Regius manuscript has Herrardum instead of Berrao. Valesius derives Balatedine—or Balacedina, as the Regius manuscript has it—from Balatedum, Balatedinis. Following Maanus, he thinks it is Balan, not far from the river Cher. Marollius translates it as Vaune, a place otherwise called Roches-Corbon. Finally, Vernadum—or Vernao, as the Châlons, Bede, and Colbertine manuscripts have it, or Ernaldum according to the Regius manuscript—is still represented by the modern name Vernou, says Valesius: a castle belonging to the archbishop, famous as a barony, on the river Cisse.], Mediconnum, Berrao, Balatedine, and Vernadum.

He drew up a will [Note: [Col. 0567D] Perpetuus’s will, together with his epitaph, will be given in the appendix from volume V of the *Spicilegium*. He presided over two councils: the First Council of Tours in 461 and the Council of Vannes in 465. Apollinaris Sidonius wrote to him in Letter 9 of Book VII, where he reports in full the speech he had delivered at Bourges for the election of Bishop Simplicius. See also Letter 18 of Book IV. See above the note on Book II, chapter 14. Paulinus also dedicated a book on the life of Saint Martin to him. His feast is celebrated on 8 April, though in ancient calendars it appears on 30 December.], and assigned what he possessed in each city to the churches in those same cities, while also granting a substantial endowment to the church of Tours.

He held office for thirty years and was buried in the basilica of Saint Martin.

7. The seventh, Volusianus, was ordained bishop. He was of senatorial stock, a holy man, very rich, and himself a relative of his predecessor, Bishop Perpetuus. In his time Chlodovech was already ruling in certain cities of Gaul. For this reason the Goths suspected this bishop of wishing to submit himself to Frankish rule. He was condemned to exile at the city of Toulouse and died there [Note: [Col. 0567D] The memory of Saint Volusianus is especially celebrated among the people of Foix, where he is venerated under the title of martyr, as also in the Roman Martyrology on 18 January. They say that he was beheaded by the Visigoths at a place called Petrosa, commonly Corona, in the county of Foix. His sacred body was brought to Foix and long preserved in the church of Saint Nazarius, now commonly called Saint Volusianus, until it was reduced to ashes by the raging Calvinists, together with the basilica itself, which was later restored to some extent. The canons regular of Saint Augustine possess this place; the counts of Foix enriched it with various gifts, as is related at greater length in their history. At the prayers of Volusianus, Apollinaris Sidonius composed verses to be inscribed in the church of Saint Martin; they are found in Book IV, Letter 18. He also wrote to Volusianus in Book VII, Letter 17, as did Ruricius of Limoges in the final letter of Book II.].

In his time the settlement of Mantolomaus was built [Note: [Col. 0568C] The same place is called Mantelomagus in Book VII, chapter 47; it is commonly Mantelan.], as was the basilica of Saint John in the Major Monastery [Note: [Col. 0568C] Its ruins still survived, but buildings erected several years ago completely destroyed them.].

He held office for seven years and two months.

8. The eighth, Verus, was ordained bishop [Note: [Col. 0568C] Most manuscripts read Virus. He signed the acts of the Council of Agde in 506 through the deacon Leo.]. He too was suspected by the Goths because of his zeal in the aforementioned matter, was led into exile, and died there. He left his possessions to the churches and to those who had deserved well.

He held office for eleven years and eight days [Note: [Col. 0568C] This is the reading of the manuscripts and editions. Cointius and other learned men, however, who assign the death of Saint Martin to the year 397, think that the reading should be “eight years and eleven months.” Otherwise, according to their reckoning, the death of Verus would have to be postponed beyond the year 508, which cannot be the case. For Gregory says in the following chapter that, after defeating the Goths, Clodovech came to Tours, where Licinius was bishop. But Clodovech’s return from that expedition cannot be placed later than 508. See Cointius under the year 507, §10.].

9. The ninth was Licinius, a citizen of Angers. Out of love for God he went to the East and visited the holy places. Departing from there, he established a monastery on his own estate within the territory of Angers. Later, after serving as abbot in the monastery where Saint Venantius was buried [Note: [Col. 0568C] The monastery of Saint Venantius, converted into a college of canons, still survives and is subject to the church of Saint Martin. Licinius signed the acts of the First Council of Orléans in 511.], he was chosen for the episcopate.

In his time King Chlodovech returned to Tours victorious from the slaughter of the Goths.

He held office for twelve years, two months, and twenty-five days, and was buried in the basilica of Saint Martin.

10. In the tenth place, Theodorus and Proculus were appointed [Note: [Col. 0568D] Above, in Book III, chapter 17, they are said to have been appointed after the death of Leo. The canons forbade two bishops to sit simultaneously in one church. They should therefore rather be regarded as administrators of the widowed church than as bishops of Tours. At the end of the same century, when the Lombards were ravaging Italy, many bishops were driven from their sees and assigned to other churches with the authority of the emperor as well, but only, as Gregory the Great says, so that they might receive sustenance if the church already had its own bishop—not so that the dignity of the episcopal throne might be divided through the sharing of communion. See his Book I, Letter 43, and elsewhere.], at the command of the blessed Queen Chrotechildis. They had been ordained bishops in Burgundy, followed her, and had been expelled from their cities by enemy attacks. Both were very old. They governed the church of Tours together for two years and were buried in the basilica of Saint Martin.

Arnulfus, a disciple of Saint Remigius and, as they say, from the counts of Rheims, is said to have succeeded them. He was ordained an exorcist and, after various pilgrimages, was killed at Rheims by the servants of Scariberga, his betrothed, whom he had consecrated to God; he is venerated as a martyr on 18 July [Note: [Col. 0569D] His life is found in the Floriacensian Library edited by Boscius. He is also discussed by Frodoard and Marlot in their History of Rheims. A cross erected at the place where he suffered can still be seen at Rheims on the Caesarean Way. His relics were brought to the diocese of Chartres and gave their name to a settlement in the Aquiline Forest, where a priory subject to the monastery of Fosses exists. Another place of the same name, belonging to the Cluniac order, is famous near the town of Crespy, where his relics are also kept. Maanus places Saint Arnulfus between Ommatius and Leo. Gregory seems to have omitted him because he held the see for only seventeen days.].

11. The eleventh was Bishop Dinifius, who also came from Burgundy. He entered the episcopate through the election of the aforementioned king [Note: [Col. 0569D] Namely Chlodomer. The Colbertine manuscript reads: “through the election of the brothers,” and so forth. In the Bede he is called Dinisius; in some printed editions, Dionysius. See Book III, chapters 2 and 17.]. The king granted him something from the royal domain and gave him authority to dispose of these goods as he wished. Dinifius left the best of what he possessed to his church and also gave something to those who had deserved well.

He held office for ten months and was buried in the basilica of Saint Martin.

12. The twelfth was Ommatius [Note: [Col. 0569D] The Regius manuscript reads Ommarius. He was the son of Saint Ruricius the elder, bishop of Limoges, by Iberia, daughter of Ommatius; Sidonius sang their wedding in Poem 2. The same author frequently praises the nobility of the Ommatian and Rurician families. Fortunatus praises the Ruricii as descended from the family of the Anicii in Book IV, Poem 5. Canisius published the letters of this Ruricius.], from the senators and citizens of Auvergne, and very rich in estates. Having drawn up his will, he distributed his possessions among the churches of the cities in which he owned property.

He enlarged the church within the walls of the city of Tours, consecrated by the relics of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, which adjoins the wall. He began to build the basilica of Saint Mary within the walls of the city but left it unfinished.

He held office for four years [Note: [Col. 0569D] The Colbertine manuscript reads “three years.”] and five months. He died and was buried in the basilica of Saint Martin.

13. The thirteenth, Leo, was ordained bishop after having been abbot of the basilica of Saint Martin. He had been a carpenter and also made towers covered with gold leaf; some of these are still preserved among us. He was also skilled in other works.

He held office for six months and was buried in the basilica of Saint Martin.

14. The fourteenth, Francilio, was ordained bishop from among the senators. He was a citizen of Poitiers and had a wife named Clara, but they had no children. Both were very rich in agricultural lands, most of which they gave to the basilica of Saint Martin; they also left some property to their relatives.

He held office for two years and six months [Note: [Col. 0569D] The Regius manuscript reads “five months.” See Book III, chapter 17.]. He died and was buried in the basilica of Saint Martin.

[Col. 0569C] **15.** The fifteenth was Injuriosus, a citizen of Tours, indeed from the lower ranks of the people, but nevertheless freeborn. During his episcopate Queen Chrotechildis died. He completed the church of Saint Mary within the walls of the city of Tours. In his time the basilica of Saint Germanus [Note: It is commonly called Saint-Germain-sur-Loire.] was also built. The villages Noviliacus [Note: Noviliacus, or Nobiliacum, is a name common to several places. Among these, in the territory of Tours, are Noviliacus Nobilis (Neuilly-le-Noble), Noviliacus on the Eder (Neuilly-le-Lierre), and Noviliacus on the river Braena (la Branle). There is also Noviliacus at the Stone Bridge (Neuilly-Pont-Pierre), situated on the boundary between the Touraine and Anjou. Luciliacus, commonly called Lusillé, is a village between the rivers Care and Anger, well known enough. Gregory praises Injuriosus’s zeal above, Book IV, chapter 2. He attended the Second Council of Orléans in 533 and the Fourth in 541; in 538, however, the priest Campanus signed on his behalf.] and Luciliacus were founded. He instituted the saying of Terce and Sext in the church, which practice continues in God’s name to the present day. [Col. 0570A] He was bishop for sixteen years, eleven months, and twenty-six days; he died and was buried in the basilica of Saint Martin.

**16.** The sixteenth was Baudinus, ordained bishop from the office of referendary to King Chlothar. He had a son [Note: Colbert manuscript: sons.] and was distinguished by many acts of charity. He also distributed to the poor the gold left by his predecessor, more than twenty thousand solidi. During his episcopate another village called Noviliacus was built. He established the canons’ common table. He was bishop for five years [Note: The same manuscript: ten years. See Book I of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 9, where he is called a saint. According to Maanus, his body is preserved today in the castle of Lucacum (Loches).], ten months; he died and was buried in the basilica of Saint Martin.

**17.** The seventeenth was Guntharius, ordained bishop from the abbacy of the monastery of Saint Venantius [Note: The Colbert manuscript and Bad edition have “Saint Evantius.” On Guntharius, see the Book *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 8.], a very prudent man while he held the office of abbot, and one who frequently carried embassies between the Frankish kings. After he had been ordained bishop, however, he became devoted to wine and appeared almost senseless. This made him so demented that he could not recognize guests whom he knew well; nevertheless, he often assailed them with insults and reproaches. He was bishop for two years, ten months, and twenty-two days. He died and was buried in the basilica of Saint Martin, and the episcopate remained vacant for one year [Note: See above, Book IV, chapter 11.]

**18.** The eighteenth was Eufronius, a priest ordained bishop, from that class which we earlier called senatorial; a man of exceptional holiness, he had been a cleric from early youth. During his episcopate the city of Tours, together with all its churches, was consumed by a great fire. Of these churches he later restored two, leaving a third, the oldest [Col. 0570C] [Note: The Regius, Beccian, and Colbert manuscripts have “the third, the older one.”], abandoned. Later the basilica of Saint Martin itself [536] was burned by Wiliacharius, when it had provided refuge during the former plot against Chramnus (see Book IV, chapter 20); afterward the same bishop roofed it with tin, with the assistance of King Chlothar. During his episcopate the basilica of Saint Vincent was built. Churches were built in the villages Tauriaco [Note: Marollius is uncertain whether Tauriacum is Turé or Truye, between the Care and the Andria. Maanus says nothing about this place, nor does Valesius provide further information. Cerate, in Beccian, Cerente, is likewise a village situated between Andrès (the Indrois) and the Care, commonly called Céré. In the same district is Orbiniacum, commonly Orbigny. The Colbert manuscript and Bad edition, however, have Tausire, Uscerate, and Orbaniacum. Orbaniacum is also read in the Book *On the Glory of the Martyrs*. Note that the basilica of Saint Vincent still exists in the city of Tours and serves as a parish church.], Cerate, and Orbigniacum. He was bishop for seventeen years, died at the age of seventy, and was buried in the basilica of Saint Martin [Note: His feast is celebrated on 4 August. He attended the Third Council of Paris in 557 and presided over the Second Council of Tours in 567. Fortunatus praises him in Book III, poem 4.]. The episcopate remained vacant for nineteen days.

**19.** The nineteenth was Gregory. I, unworthy as I am, found the church of the city of Tours—in which blessed Martin and the other priests of the Lord were consecrated to the office of bishop—dismantled and shattered by fire. I rebuilt it on a broader and higher scale and dedicated it in the seventeenth year of my episcopate. In it, as I learned from aged priests, the relics of the blessed martyrs of Agaunum [Note: Namely, Saint Maurice and his companions, whom he calls below the witnesses of the blessed legion. They are treated at length in the *Acts of the Genuine Martyrs* under the year 286. Fortunatus praises this church, restored by Gregory, at length in Book X, poem 2.] had formerly been placed. I also found in the treasury of the basilica of Saint Martin the little chest in which their sacred relic had been preserved, although it had been dissolved by extreme decay, a relic brought there because of the power of their holiness [Note: The Colbert manuscript and Bad edition read: “in which, through extreme decay, the relic had been dissolved, brought there through the grace of their virtues because of their power.”]

While vigils were being celebrated in their honor, I wished once more, by the light of a candle, to inspect these things. As we examined them carefully, the caretaker of the building said: “There is here a stone covered by a lid. I have absolutely no idea what it contains, nor have I discovered that the earlier custodians of this charge knew. I will bring it, and examine carefully what is enclosed within.” I had it brought down and opened it—I confess it—and found inside a silver chest containing not only the relics of the witnesses of the blessed legion but also those of many other saints, both martyrs and confessors [537]. We also discovered other hollow stones, just like this one, in which relics of the holy apostles together with those of the remaining martyrs had been kept. Admiring this divinely granted gift and giving thanks, after celebrating the vigils and also saying Masses [Note: The Colbert manuscript and Bad edition: “and also singing hymns at the Masses.”], I placed these relics in the church.

In the small chapel of Saint Martin adjoining the church itself, I placed the relics of the holy martyrs Cosmas and Damian. I found the basilicas of Saint Perpetuus burned by fire, and ordered them, by the work of our craftsmen, to be painted or decorated with the same splendor they had possessed before. I ordered a baptistery to be built beside that basilica, in which I placed the relics of Saint John together with those of the martyr Sergius; and in the former baptistery I placed the relics of the martyr Saint Benignus. In many places within the territory of Tours I dedicated churches and oratories and adorned them with the relics of the saints. I have judged it tedious to enumerate them in order.

I wrote ten books of *Histories*, seven of *Miracles*, [Col. 0572A] one on the *Lives of the Fathers*, and one book of commentary on the Psalter; I also composed one book on the ecclesiastical Offices. Although I wrote these books in a rather rustic style, I nevertheless adjure all the priests of the Lord who will govern the humble church of Tours after me, by the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and by the terrible day of judgment for all the guilty: if you are not to depart from that judgment ashamed, condemned with the devil, never have these books destroyed or rewritten, reading some passages and omitting others. Rather, let everything remain with you complete and undefiled, just as it was left by us [Note: Here the Colbert manuscript ends, and nothing has been torn away. Hence Cointius judges that what follows was added by some later writer.]

But if you, whoever you are, priest of God, have been instructed by our Martianus [Note: The Regius manuscript has Martinianus. Here, however, he alludes to Martianus Capella, the famous author, although his date is uncertain; see Vossius, Book III, part II, *On Latin Historians*.] in the seven disciplines [538]—that is, if he taught you in grammar to read, in dialectic to discern the propositions of disputations, in rhetoric to recognize the kinds of meters, in geometry to gather the measurements of lands and lines, in astrology to contemplate the courses of the stars, in arithmetic to collect the parts of numbers, and in harmonics to combine the modulations of pleasing accents in songs—if you have been so trained in all these subjects that our style seems rustic to you, nevertheless I do not ask you to tear out what I have written. But if anything in it pleases you, I do not object to your writing it in verse, provided that our work remains intact.

We prescribed these books in the twenty-first year of our episcopate. Although [alternative: “namely”] in the preceding sections we wrote about the bishops of Tours [alternative: “have written”], recording their years, the chronological number does not thereby follow or add up [Col. 0572C] [Note: Beccian: “of the chronicles.” Casinensis: “recording their years, although this reckoning does not produce the chronological number.”], because we were not able to discover the intervals between the ordinations in their entirety.

The total of the years of the world is therefore as follows: From the beginning to the Flood, 2,242 years; from the Flood to the passage of the children of Israel through the Red Sea, 1,404 years; from that passage through the sea to the Lord’s resurrection, 1,538 years; from the Lord’s resurrection to the passing of Saint Martin, 412 years; from the passing of Saint Martin to the year mentioned above—that is, the twenty-first year of our episcopate, which was the fifth year of Gregory, Roman pope, the thirty-first of King Guntram, and the nineteenth of the younger Childebert—168 years [Note: This is the reading of the Regius and Chesne editions; another reading has 178. Other printed editions have 218; Beccian has 118, perhaps for 198, which would agree with the end of Book IV.]

The total of all these years is 5,814 [Note: The Regius and Chesne editions have this reading. Other printed editions have 864. Neither number agrees with the sums of the individual parts. Our duty is to reproduce the genuine readings of the manuscripts; but how this sequence of years is to be reconciled with the ancient authors, or even with Gregory himself, learned men—Scaliger, Petavius, Menander, Maanus, Valesius, and others—have investigated at greater length. Since they did not follow the same method, however, they reached differing conclusions. Cointius maintains that these calculations, like those given above, are interpolations.]

[Col. 0571] **Here ends the Ecclesiastical History of the Franks of Gregory, Bishop of Tours.**

[Col. 0573]

## RUINART’S NOTICE CONCERNING THE PITHOUEAN MANUSCRIPT, WHICH HE HAD IN HAND AFTER COMPLETING THE EDITION

[Col. 0573]

We had already brought our appendix to an end when, through the kindness of the illustrious Claude Peleterius, administrator of the kingdom, we were permitted to examine the manuscript codices of the Pithou Library. Among others, one came into our hands which contained, besides Gregory’s account of the death of Saint Martin—reported under the title *Sermon of Gregory, Bishop, on the Passing of Saint Martin*—a catalogue of the bishops of Tours, that is, the final chapter of Gregory’s *History*, together with the various calculations of years reported there.

In that codex, however, the years from the passing of Saint Martin are counted in such a way that, except for the years of Guntram, which all the manuscripts and printed editions give incorrectly, all the calculations establish that the final year of the holy bishop was 397. For there one reads:

“From the passing of Saint Martin to the year mentioned above—that is, the twenty-first year of our episcopate, which was the fifth of Gregory, Roman pope, the thirty-first of King Guntram, and the nineteenth of the younger Childebert—197 years.”

“The total of all these is 4,747 years.”

Thus all the numbers of years converge upon the year 594; if 197 years are subtracted from this, the year 397 is obtained, in which we believe Martin died, and which we established on Gregory’s authority in our preface. Perhaps Gregory assigned the current year 614 because he added the epilogue to his *History* when he was preparing to travel to Rome. He is believed to have undertaken that journey in that year and to have died the following year, as Cointius proves.

Moreover, the names of the bishops following the catalogue of the bishops of Tours given by Gregory are appended in the Pithouean manuscript up to Landramnus, in whose time—that is, in the ninth century—the codex was written. They are listed in this order: Latinus, bishop; Charegiselus, bishop; Medegesilus, bishop; Sigilaicus, bishop; Rigobertus, bishop; Chrodobertus, bishop; Bertus, bishop; Guntramnus, bishop; Ibbo, bishop; Gausbertus, bishop; Dido, bishop; Rangabertus, bishop; Austaldus, bishop; Eusebius, bishop; Herbernus, bishop; Joseph, bishop; Landramnus, bishop.

[Col. 0573B]

## EPITOMES OF THE HISTORY OF THE FRANKS OF SAINT GEORGE FLORENTIUS GREGORY, BISHOP OF TOURS, BY FREDEGARIUS THE SCHOLASTIC (C, S)*

[Col. 0573]

## GREGORY’S PREFACE BEGINS

541–542 “As the cities of Gaul were declining, or rather perishing altogether,” etc., as above, columns 1 and 2. The Claromontane codex has precisely this wording. But the Boherian and Ambracian manuscripts, in Cambecius, volume II, have: “The Greek preface begins. As the cities were declining,” etc.

I call this epitomizer Fredegarius, following learned men who designated him by this name, although I have never seen a written codex in which he was called by that name. The learned men who wrote about Frankish affairs in this century testify to the same regarding themselves, calling this author Fredegarius the Scholastic and following Joseph Scaliger and Freher, who were the first to call him so, evidently on the basis of some manuscript codex.

We copied the following title, *Capitularies*, etc., from the same Claromontane codex, in which the Boherian manuscript reads: “The chapters of the book begin, which is excerpted from the Chronicles of the Greek Bishop of Thoronacis.” From a similar codex, as I conjecture, Canisius, in volume II of *Ancient Readings*, considers a bishop of Thoromacus to be the author of this work, one who wrote in Greek. It is called the fourth book because, among the various chronicles which that author collected into one body, Gregory’s epitome appears in the fourth place. We have said more about these matters in the general preface to this volume.

## EPITOME OF THE HISTORY OF THE FRANKS

[Col. 0575]

[Col. 0575D] **547 I.** When the Vandals had passed through Gaul and, not long afterward, the Huns were preparing to enter Gaul (Gregory of Tours, Book II, chapters 2 and 5), blessed Arvatius [Note: This is the reading of the Claromontane and Ambracian codex, cited in volume II of Lambecius’s Imperial Library. The printed editions have Servatius. The Boherian manuscript has “when blessed Arvatius, bishop of the Tungri.” See the notes to Book II of Gregory, chapter 5.] the bishop of the city of Tongeren heard of it and went to Rome, to the threshold of the apostle Saint Peter. There, continually fasting and keeping constant vigils, he received in a dream a response from the apostle that the Most High had decreed that the Huns should enter Gaul. He immediately returned to his city, predicting his own death so that he would not see this evil.

The deeds of the patrician Aetius [Note: This is the reading of the Claromontane, Boherian, and Freher editions. Chesne has Agetius; Canisius has Aetius, the familiar form of the name.] are praised in this chronicle. He was manly in appearance, lively in spirit, vigorous in body, exceptionally swift on horseback, skilled with arrows, energetic with the spear, highly suited to warfare, renowned as a seeker of peace, no pursuer of avarice, endowed with spiritual goods, extremely patient of injuries, eager for labor, fearless of dangers, and exceedingly tolerant of hunger, thirst, and vigils. At the beginning of his life it was clearly foretold what great power fate [alternative: deeds] had destined for him, and he was to be celebrated in his own and future times (chapter 6).

The historian mentioned above relates these things about Aetius. What he accomplished when he entered into conflict with the Huns, Idatius narrates in this volume of his history [Note: As stated in the preface, Fredegarius published a collection of chronicles divided into five or six books. The third book is excerpted from Idatius, who is cited here; there Aetius is said first to have deceived Attila and then Thorismund, after receiving money from each of them.] (chapter 7).

For in those days, while his wife’s prayers were being offered at the thresholds of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul amid fasts and vigils, Aetius was freed from danger through the apostles’ intercession. This was revealed to a certain poor man, who announced that Aetius had been saved through his wife’s prayers. When the poor man disclosed this, he was struck with blindness.

**II.** Concerning the kings of the Franks, blessed Jerome wrote about those who had existed long ago [Note: Jerome, in the *Life of Saint Hilarion*: “Among the Saxons and Alamanni there is a people, not so extensive as it is powerful, called Germany by historians but now called Francia.” Procopius likewise frequently designates the Franks by the name Germans.].

The history of the poet Virgil first relates that Priam was their king when Troy was captured through the treachery of Ulysses, and that they then departed from there. Later they had Friga as king. By a twofold division, one part of them set out for Macedonia; others, called Phrygians after Friga, wandered through Asia and settled on the shore of the Danube and the Ocean Sea.

Again, by a twofold division, the middle part of them entered Europe with Francio as their king. Wandering through Europe, they occupied the banks of the Rhine with their wives and children and attempted to build, not far from the Rhine, a city modeled on Troy. The work was begun but remained unfinished.

The remainder of them, who had stayed on the shore of the Danube, chose a king named Turchot [Note: Aimoin, Book II, chapter 2, with the Boherian manuscript, has Torchot . . . Torchi. Rorico, Book I, has Torcat.], from whom they were called Turchi, while the others were called Franks after Francio. For many generations afterward they had dukes and continually refused foreign domination [Chesne: ruled foreign dominations].

**III.** We learn that the Franks continued down to the dukes Marcomer, Sunno, and Genebaud (chapter 9). In their time, during the reign of the emperor Theodosius, they broke into Germany and ravaged the districts, even causing fear at Cologne. When this was reported at Trier, Nanninus [alternative: Nannius] and Quintinus, master of the soldiers [Note: The Boherian and Canisius editions have “masters of the soldiers.”], gathered an army and drove the Franks out of Germany. At Carbonaria there was a slaughter of the Franks.

Later, when Heraclius and Jovianus [Note: The printed editions have Jovinianus; and below the Claromontane index has Juvinianus. The Boherian manuscript below has “Heraclius and Juvinianus with a few men.” This is Jovinus, as the alternate reading of the Claromontane has it, one of those who assumed tyranny during the reign of Honorius. It is false, however, that Constantine was killed by Jovinus’s envoys. On Arbogast, who was a Frank by birth, see the *Life of Saint Ambrose*.] crossed beyond the Rhine with an army, intending to bring the Franks to destruction, such a slaughter of soldiers was inflicted by the Franks that Heraclius and Jovianus could scarcely escape from the same battle. They did not dare thereafter to take up arms against the Franks.

A short time later, Arbogast, puffed up with pride, took up arms against the Franks. Fighting with them, he was defeated and fled.

**IV.** The Franks dared to remain for the winter at Trier (ibid.). When the emperor Valentinian had been reduced below the status of a private citizen, responsibility for military affairs was entrusted to Frankish guards [Col. 0578B]. They also overstepped their civil offices and, bound by oaths, entered into Arbogast’s conspiracy.

Arbogast, pursuing the dukes Marcomer and Sunno with hatred, attacked the Franks—deceived by a stratagem of the army and to be burned, with the leaves stripped from the bare and withered forest—while they lay in ambush [the corrupt reading is uncertain]. After crossing the Rhine, he ravaged the district inhabited by the Chamavi [Note: The Claromontane has Amavi; the Boherian, Amogi.].

**V.** Then, after the dukes had been destroyed, kings were again created among the Franks from the same stock as before (ibid.).

**VI.** At that time Jovianus assumed royal ornaments. Constantine turned to flight and headed for Italy. Jovianus, the ruler, sent assassins to meet him [Note: Fredegarius carelessly attributes to Jovinus here what Frigeridus wrote about Honorius.]; Constantine was beheaded on the river Mincio [Note: The Boherian has Mentia. It is called the Mincius, commonly Mencio or Menzo, an Italian river that flows past the city of Mantua and empties into the Po.].

Many nobles were captured among the Arverni on Jovianus’s orders and cruelly killed by the generals of Honorius (ibid.).

**VII.** The city of Trier was captured and burned by the Franks through the faction of one of the senators, named Lucius. When the emperor Avitus was devoted to luxury, and this Lucius had the most beautiful woman of them all, Avitus, pretending that bodily weakness confined him to bed, ordered all the wives of the senators to visit him [Note: The margin of the Claromontane has: “He sent orders to all the wives of the senators that they should visit him.”].

When Lucius’s wife came and was violated by Avitus, Avitus rose from his bed the next day and said to Lucius: “You have beautiful baths, and you wash in cold water” [Note: The Claromontane and Boherian have: “For you wash in cold water.” Freher has: “in cold water.”].

Lucius, angered by this, had the city seized by his faction and burned by the Franks.

**VIII.** Castinus, count of the household troops, received command of an expedition against the Franks. He crushed them, crossed the Rhine, traversed Gaul, and reached as far as the Pyrenees [Note: Gregory, Book IX, chapter 2, recalls these events concerning Stilicho from Orosius. Fredegarius carelessly attributes them to Castinus—Gastinus in the Claromontane—of whom Gregory had spoken shortly before.].

**IX.** The Franks diligently sought a long-haired king of their own choosing, as had previously been the case, from the line of Priam, Friga, and Francio, and set over themselves a man named Theudemer [alternative: Theodomir], son of Richemer, who had been killed by the Romans in the battle mentioned above (ibid. and chapter 10).

His son Chlodeo [Note: This is the reading of the Claromontane, although a different and indeed ancient hand wrote Clodoveus. Canisius likewise has this form. The Boherian has “his son Chloveus.” Others have Chlogio. Gregory, chapter 9, discusses Theudemer and Chlodio, but nowhere writes that Chlodio was Theudemer’s son. Aimoin and Rorico say that Marcomer was a son of Priam and that Pharamund sprang from Marcomer; when Pharamund was elected king and later died, his son Chlodio succeeded him.] succeeded to the kingdom. He was a very capable man among his people and lived at the fortress of Esbargem [Note: The printed edition has Hespergum. Others, with the Anonymous author, Rorico, and Aimoin, have Dispargum . . . All have “of the Thuringians” below.], which lies in the territory of the Thuringians.

The Burgundians, too, followed the sect of the Arians and were settled in Cisalpine territory. Chlodeo sent scouts to the city of Cambrai, inspected everything, then followed himself, crushed the Romans, captured the city, and from there occupied the land as far as the river Somme.

This people was devoted to fanatical practices. It is said that, while Chlodeo [Boherian: Chlodeveus] was sitting with his wife on the seashore at midday in summer, his wife went into the sea to bathe and was terrified by a beast of Neptune, which had attacked her in the likeness of a Minotaur. When immediately afterward she had been touched either by the beast or by a man [Note: The Boherian adds: “she conceived and gave birth.” Chesne has: “when she had immediately been touched by the beast.” Cointius judges this story to have been added by an interpolator in the year 426, during the Carolingian dynasty, so that, as he says, the Merovingian rulers who had been deprived of the kingdom might be held in lower esteem among the people. But the falsity of this learned man’s conjecture is evident from the fact that the passage is found in full in the Claromontane codex, which was copied a thousand years ago under the first dynasty of our kings.], she conceived and bore a son named Meroveus, from whom the Frankish kings were afterward called Merovingians.

**X.** The luxurious emperor Avitus was ordained bishop at the city of Piacenza and afterward fled to the church [Note: The Boherian has “basilica,” and calls it that below.] of Saint Julian, where he lost his life (chapter 11).

XI. Childeric, son of Meroveus, succeeded his father in the kingdom but, corrupted by excessive lust, subjected the daughters of the Franks to sexual violation (Chapter 12). The Franks, indignant at this, expelled him from the kingdom. Wiomadus, a most loyal Frank to Childeric—for when Childeric was being led captive with his mother by the Huns, Wiomadus had freed him by flight—divided a single gold coin with Childeric. When he saw that the Franks were trying to kill Childeric, he said to him:

“Flee to Thuringia and hide there for a while. If I can reconcile the Franks to you, I shall send you half of this gold coin as a sign; and if I cannot, wherever you are attacked, let me know the route by which you have gone. Whenever I am able, and send you this half, and the two halves joined together make one solid coin, then you may safely return to your homeland.”

Childeric lived concealed in Thuringia with King Bisinus and his wife Basina [Note: Claromontanus has *Bysinum*, and below once *Bysinam*. Bollandus has *latuit Francis* (“he was hidden from the Franks”). Then.] The Franks unanimously elected Aegidius king. Wiomadus, Childeric’s friend, was appointed sub-regulus by Aegidius and the Franks [Note: So Claromontanus; but the printed editions have: “They again appointed Wiomadus, Childeric’s friend, sub-regulus under Aegidius.” *Iterum* (“again”) is absent from Canisius, but Chesnaye and Aimoinus have *Winomadum*. Bollandus has: “Wiomadus … the Franks appointed under the rulers through Aegidius … single gold coins.”]. On Wiomadus’s advice, Aegidius imposed a tax of one gold coin on every Frank. They submitted and paid it.

Wiomadus again said to Aegidius: “This exceedingly hard people, whom you ordered me to govern, have contributed too little. They are raging in their pride; order them to pay three solidi each.” When this had been done, the Franks, submitting, said: “It is better for us to pay a tax of three solidi each than to endure an exceedingly harsh life with Childeric.”

Wiomadus said again to Aegidius: “The Franks are rebelling against you. Unless you order many of them to be slaughtered, you will not tame their pride.” He selected one hundred men who were useless and unsuitable in times of need [Note: So Claromontanus and Bollandus. The printed editions instead have “useful … suitable”] and sent them to Aegidius. Following Wiomadus’s advice, Aegidius ordered them to be killed.

Wiomadus said secretly to the Franks: “Are the taxes you pay not enough? How long will you endure this evil, allowing your parents to be slaughtered like cattle?” Then the Franks unanimously said: “If only we could find Childeric somewhere, we would gladly receive him again as king over us; perhaps through him we might be rescued from these afflictions.”

Then Wiomadus went immediately to Aegidius and said: “Now the Frankish people have been completely subdued under your discipline.” He advised him to send envoys to the emperor Mauricius and, if possible, to draw the neighboring peoples into the undertaking, so that fifty thousand solidi might be sent by the emperor [Note: Freher has “to the emperor”], and that the peoples, having received this as a gift, might more readily submit to imperial rule.

He added: “At your prompting I have served for a few solidi, but I, your servant, have little silver. I wanted to send a boy with your envoys, so that he might buy silver for me more advantageously at Constantinople.”

Then, having received from Aegidius five hundred gold coins as a gift, which he was to send for purchasing this commodity, he sent a boy in whom he had confidence, together with half of the gold coin that he had divided with Childeric, and a little sack full of lead pieces, which the boy was to carry with him as solidi.

When it had already been discovered that Childeric was at Constantinople, the boy approached him, instructed to go ahead of Aegidius’s envoys and immediately inform Childeric, before the envoys came into the emperor’s presence, that Aegidius—who was obliged to pay taxes into the public treasury—was seeking taxes to be paid to the emperor.

When Childeric had reported this to the emperor Mauricius, the emperor was filled with fury and indignation. When Aegidius’s envoys were presented to him and made this allegation, he ordered them to be thrown into prison.

Childeric said to the emperor Mauricius: “Order me, your servant, to go to Gaul. I shall avenge the fury of your indignation upon Aegidius.”

Mauricius enriched Childeric with many gifts, and Childeric returned to Gaul by sea. When Wiomadus learned of his arrival from the boy, he went to him at the fortress of Bar [Note: There is more than one fortress of this name, commonly called Bar, to which this passage might refer. It could refer equally to Bar on the Aube or Bar on the Seine. Valesius thinks that Bar-le-Duc, now apparently the more famous, had not yet been built at that time. But since the district of Bar is mentioned nearly a thousand years ago in Count Wolfaudus’s testament establishing the monastery of Saint Michael in the region of Verdun, and in other documents of the same period, the place must already have been famous enough to give its name to the neighboring district. It may therefore be designated here, although it was later called Bar-le-Duc.] He was received by the people of Bar. As the initial payment for their reception of him, he generously granted them all their public revenues, following Wiomadus’s advice.

Afterward he was again elevated to the kingship by all the Franks and fought many battles with Aegidius. He inflicted numerous defeats upon the Romans.

XII. Basina, who had King Bisinus as her husband in Thuringia, heard that Childeric had been elevated to the kingship by the Franks. She quickly left Bisinus and went to Childeric (Chapter 12). When he had carefully asked her why she had come to him from so far away, she is said to have replied:

“I know your worth, that you are exceedingly vigorous; therefore I have come to live with you. If I knew of anyone more worthy beneath the heavens, I would have sought him.”

Childeric rejoiced and, admiring her beauty, took her in marriage. When they had lain together on their marriage-bed throughout the first night, the woman said to him:

“Tonight we shall abstain from intercourse. Rise secretly, and whatever you see before the palace halls, tell your maidservant.”

When he had risen, he saw figures of a lion, a unicorn, and a leopard walking about [Note: Cointius thinks that these visions were added by an interpolator. But, as we have already observed at Chapter 9, the authority of the Claromontanus manuscript contradicts this view.]

He returned and told the woman what he had seen. The woman said to him:

“My lord, go again and tell your maidservant what you see.”

He went outside and saw animals resembling bears and wolves walking about. After reporting this also to the woman, she compelled him a third time to go and report what he saw.

When he had gone out for the third time, he saw smaller animals resembling dogs and smaller beasts tearing one another apart and rolling about [Col. 0581D].

When he had told Basina all these things, they chastely abstained until the following day. Rising from the bed, Basina said to Childeric:

“The things you visibly saw exist in reality. They have this interpretation: a son will be born to us who will bear the sign and likeness of a lion in strength; his sons will bear the sign of the leopard and unicorn in strength. From them will then be born descendants who will resemble bears and wolves in their strength and voracity. And the third things that you saw at the end will be the pillars of this kingdom. They will rule like dogs, and their strength will resemble that of the smaller beasts. The multitude of smaller beasts that tore one another apart and rolled about signifies peoples, without fear of their rulers, laying waste to one another.”

Basina conceived and bore a son named Chlodoveus. He was great and an outstanding warrior, exceedingly strong like a lion in comparison with the other kings.

Childeric fought King Odouacer of the Saxons at Orléans and, victorious, advanced to Angers. When Aegidius died, he left a son named Syagrius (Chapter 18).

At the same time the Britons were expelled from Biturica [Variant: *Betorica*] by the Goths, and many were killed at Dol [Note: Some printed editions have “Toulouse,” or a variant of it, falsely. It is a village of the Bituriges. See the notes to Gregory, Book II, Chapter 18.]

Count Paul, with the Romans and Franks, made war upon the Goths and carried off booty. After defeating Odouacer, Childeric killed Count Paul and seized Angers (Chapter 19). After these events, war was waged between the Saxons and the Romans. When the Saxons turned their backs and many of them had been killed, their island, together with a great number of its people, was captured and destroyed by the Franks [Note: Freher’s edition has “on the mainland.” Bollandus has “on the mainland … captured and destroyed.”].

XIII. In that same year there was an earthquake. In the fourteenth year of his reign, Eoricus, king of the Goths, magnificently built the church of Saint Julian at Brioude, adorned with columns [Note: Fredegarius is mistaken. For, as we have already observed, it was not Euricus but Victorius, appointed over the Auvergne by Euricus, who adorned with columns—not built—the basilica of Saint Julian, not at Brioude but in the city of Auvergne itself, which we now call Clermont]. Eoricus reigned for twenty years (Chapter 20).

XIV. Excessive famine came upon Burgundy (Chapter 24). When the people were dispersed by hunger into various regions and no one could provide them with food, a certain senator named Aedicius is said to have performed a great work before God.

He sent his servants with horses and wagons [that is, with animals and carts] through the neighboring cities, so that they might bring to him those afflicted by want. They brought to his house all the poor whom they could find, and there, feeding them during the time of scarcity, he freed them from hunger. They numbered more than four thousand, and he nourished them until the time of abundance.

After they had departed, a voice from heaven descended and reached Aedicius, saying: “Because you have done this deed, bread will never be lacking for you or your descendants.”

Aedicius possessed extraordinary speed. Several times he put large numbers of Goths to flight with only a few men. Evatrix [Variants: *Evarix*; Bollandus and another witness have *Evagrus*], king of the Goths, crossed the frontier of Spain and inflicted a severe persecution upon Gaul (Chapter 25).

XV. After Childeric died, his son Chlodoveus ruled in his place (Chapter 27). In the fifth year of his reign, Syagrius, the Roman patrician, had his seat at the city of Soissons [Note: Canisius has “Saintes.” But it is clear that Soissons is meant here; in old writings it is commonly written *Sessonas*, *Sexonas*, or *Saxonas]. His father had formerly held it.

Chlodoveus attacked him with Ragnacharius. When Syagrius saw that their army had been defeated, he turned his back and hastened to King Alaric at Toulouse. Chlodoveus sent envoys to Alaric, ordering him to surrender Syagrius; otherwise, he should know that war would be waged against him.

Fearing this—as is customary among the Goths when they are terrified—Alaric handed Syagrius over in chains to the envoys. Chlodoveus imprisoned him and, having obtained his kingdom, ordered him to be killed by the sword [Bollandus: “beheaded”]. Because Chlodoveus was a pagan, he permitted churches to be plundered.

XVI. Accordingly, an enemy had taken a large vessel from the church of the city of Reims, together with the remaining sacred vessels (same source). Saint Remigius, the bishop and apostolic leader of that city, came to Chlodoveus and asked that, if he did not deserve to receive anything else from the sacred vessels, he might at least receive that vessel.

The king heard him and said: “Send a messenger to Soissons. There the things that have been acquired will be divided. If the lot gives that vessel to me, I shall fulfill your request.”

When the booty had been placed in the middle for division, the king said: “I ask you at least to grant me this vessel outside my portion.”

When the king had said this, the Franks replied: “Glorious king, the things we see are yours; but we too are yours, lord. Do what pleases you.”

Then one frivolous, envious, and rash man struck the vessel loudly, saying: “You will receive nothing from here except what the true lot grants you.”

The king softened this insult through patience. After the lot had been cast, he sent the vessel he had received to blessed Remigius, while concealing the wound in his heart.

On the Kalends of March he ordered all the armed companies to come forth for inspection. As he went around among them, he came to the man who had struck the vessel and said to him: “Your armor is neglected, and your axe is not serviceable.”

He seized the man’s axe and threw it to the ground. When the man had bent down slightly, the king raised his hands and drove the axe into his head.

“So,” he said, “you did to the vessel at Soissons, imposing great fear upon yourself on that account” [Note: Chesnaye and Freher have “he caused fear.” Canisius has “the Franks caused fear on account of this.”].

XVII. There was a king of the Burgundians named Gundiochus, descended from King Athanaric, the persecutor (Chapter 28). He had four sons: Gundobadus [Note: Other witnesses have *Gundebadus*, *Gunthegiselus*, and *Gotemarus*; we have retained the reading of the Claromontanus and Bollandus manuscripts, and so below], Godegiselus, Chilpericus, and Godemarus.

Gundobadus killed his brother Chilpericus with the sword. He drowned Chilpericus’s wife by tying a stone around her neck. He killed their two sons with the sword. He condemned their two daughters to exile. The elder, named Saedeleuba [Note: Other witnesses have *Chrona*, and below *Chrothildis*. Bollandus has *Chrotechildis*. See the notes to Gregory], changed her clothing and devoted herself to God; the younger was called Chrotechildis.

XVIII. Chlodoveus repeatedly sent an embassy to Burgundy and sought Chrotechildis (same source). Since it was not permitted for him to see her, Chlodoveus sent a certain Roman named Aurelianus to gain access to Chrotechildis by whatever ingenuity he could employ.

Aurelianus went to that region alone, like a beggar, carrying a bag on his back and wearing shabby clothing. He carried with him Chlodoveus’s ring, so that he would be more readily believed.

When he came to the city of Geneva [Note: So Claromontanus has it, not “to the gate of the city,” as Bollandus, Canisius, and Freher have. It is Geneva, which the ancients wrote as *Januba*. Chesnaye has *Genovam*], where Chrotechildis was sitting with her sister Saedeleuba, the women—who practiced hospitality toward travelers—received him for the sake of the reward. Chrotechildis washed his feet.

Aurelianus bent toward her and spoke privately:

“My lady, I have a great message to deliver to you, if you would graciously grant me a place where I can speak with you more secretly.”

She consented and said: “Speak” [Note: Claromontanus, Bollandus, and Canisius have: “Having consented and heard him privately, she said…”].

Aurelianus said: “King Chlodoveus of the Franks sent me to you. If it is God’s will, he wishes to join you to him in marriage. So that you may be certain, he has sent you this ring.”

She accepted it and rejoiced greatly. Then she said to him:

“Take one hundred solidi as a reward for your labor, and this ring of mine. Hurry back to your lord and tell him: If he wishes to join me to himself in marriage, he must immediately request me through envoys from my uncle Gundobadus. When the envoys come, once security has been obtained for the present, let them promptly establish the agreement.

“If they do not hasten to complete the matter, I fear the arrival of a certain wise man, Aridius, from Constantinople. If he arrives first, all these plans will be scattered.”

Aurelianus returned home in the same clothing in which he had come. When he was already approaching the territory of Orléans, and had come near his house, he had a certain poor beggar traveling with him as a companion on the road [Note: Canisius has “he had.” Chesnaye has: “a certain poor beggar whom he had with him on the road … had stolen the bag from his companion”].

When Aurelianus, now secure, had been overcome by sleep, his companion stole his bag containing the solidi. When he awoke, Aurelianus, full of grief, hastened home and sent servants to look for the beggar who had carried his bag.

They seized him and brought him before Aurelianus. Aurelianus had the beggar severely beaten for three days, then allowed him to go.

Aurelianus immediately reported every detail to King Chlodoveus, announcing the sequence of events and the messages [Note: Freher omits *successionem* (“sequence”). Claromontanus has: “reporting … he announces to Soissons.” Bollandus has: “reporting that the messages had been honorable, he announces them.”].

When Chlodoveus approved of Chrotechildis’s worth and counsel, he sent envoys to Gundobadus, asking him to give him his niece Chrotechildis in marriage.

Gundobadus, fearing that he could refuse and hoping to enter into friendship with Chlodoveus, promised that he would give her. The envoys, offering a solidus and a denarius, as was the custom of the Franks, betrothed her to Chlodoveus [Note: Bollandus, Canisius, and Chesnaye have “married her to him.” This custom of the Franks is described according to the Salic Law in an old formula in Bignon’s work, after the formulas of Marculfus, p. 219. See also his notes on the various formulas, no. 5, p. 364], requesting an immediate agreement that he should give her to Chlodoveus in marriage.

Without delay, once the agreement had been made at Chalon [Note: Canisius and other witnesses have *Cavallonum*; Bollandus has *Cavilonno*], the wedding preparations were made. The Franks came quickly, took Chrotechildis from Gundobadus, lifted her into a *basterna* [Note: A *basterna* was a type of vehicle proper to married women. It was covered, as Altaserra infers from Jerome’s commentary on Isaiah 66, with awnings, which we may interpret as “sleeping compartments” or *basternae], and sent her to Chlodoveus with many treasures.

When Chrotechildis learned that Aridius had arrived back from the imperial court, she said to the Frankish elders:

“If you wish to present me to your lord, remove me from the *basterna*, lift me onto a horse, and hasten toward that region as quickly as you can. I cannot come into his presence in this *basterna*.”

The Franks lifted Chrotechildis onto a horse and hurried toward Chlodoveus.

XIX. When Aridius heard of these events and came at swiftest speed from Marseille to Gundobadus, Gundobadus said to him:

“Have you heard that we have entered into friendship with the Franks and that I have given my niece as a wife to Chlodoveus?”

Aridius replied:

“This is not the cultivation of friendship but the beginning of perpetual discord. You ought to have remembered, my lord, that you killed Chrotechildis’s father, your brother Chilpericus, with the sword; that you ordered her mother to be killed by tying a stone around her neck; and that you had her two brothers beheaded and thrown into a well. If Chrotechildis prevails, she will avenge the injury done to her parents. Immediately send an army after her, so that she may be brought back. You will more easily bear the quarrel of one woman than that you and your people be continually troubled by the Franks” [Note: Claromontanus and Bollandus have *scandalizeris* (“you will be offended”). Canisius, Freher, and other witnesses have *vexentur* (“they will be harassed”)].

Hearing this, Gundobadus sent an army after Chrotechildis to hold her back [Note: Canisius has “to bring her back.” Bollandus has “to be held back … they hold back”], so that, pursuing her, they might seize the treasures and the *basterna* and hold everything back.

When Chrotechildis had approached Villariacum [Note: Two places among the people of Troyes may be referred to here: Villers, not far from Arcy and Troyes itself, and Villori, a village somewhat farther from Troyes and near Bar on the Aube. Or perhaps Villa Riaco?], where Chlodoveus was residing in the territory of Troyes, and before Chrotechildis had yet crossed the borders of Burgundy, she asked those escorting her to plunder and burn twelve leagues on both sides within Burgundy [Note: Canisius has *leucas*. Claromontanus, in another hand, explains it as *leugas*].

When this had been carried out with Chlodoveus’s permission, Chrotechildis said:

“I give thanks to you, almighty God, because I see the beginning of vengeance for my parents and brothers” [Col. 0585D].

XX. Then she was immediately brought into Chlodoveus’s presence [Note: The printed editions have “brought into the presence of Chlodoveus”], and Chlodoveus took her in marriage and loved her greatly with all royal honor (same source, Chapter 29).

Chlodoveus already had a son by a concubine, named Theuderic. When Chrotechildis had borne her first son and wished to consecrate him in baptism, she continually urged her husband to become a Christian [Note: The printed edition has “so that he might become a Christian”], but the king’s mind was in no way moved to follow her counsel. He said:

“Everything is created at the command of our gods; your God is shown to be able to do nothing.”

The queen presented her son for baptism. After the child had been baptized, the boy, whom they called Ingomer [Variant: *Ingomerus*], died in his white baptismal garments.

The king, inflamed with anger, rebuked the queen, saying: “If the boy had been baptized in the name of my gods, he would have lived” [Note: Freher has “if the boy had been named.” This word is omitted in the Claromontanus manuscript].

But the queen gave thanks to almighty God that from her womb she had received a firstborn son into His kingdom [Col. 0586A].

After this she bore a son whom she named Chlodomer. When he had been baptized and began to fall ill, the king said: “This one too, like his brother, is dying.”

At his mother’s prayer, with the Lord’s help, he recovered. Nevertheless, the queen continually urged the king through flattering words to worship Christ (Chapter 30) [Note: Canisius has *blandis* (“gentle” or “persuasive”). Claromontanus and Bollandus have *blandiciis* (“flatteries”)].

XXI. When King Chlodoveus made war against the Alamanni, at the queen’s urging he vowed that, if he obtained victory, he would become a Christian (same source).

When the two armies joined battle and there were great massacres, Chlodoveus said:

“I call upon the God whom Queen Chrotechildis worships. If he helps me in this battle so that I defeat these enemies of mine, I shall be faithful to him.”

The Alamanni turned their backs and fled. When they saw that their king had been killed, they remained exiles from their homes for nine years [Note: Freher and another witness have “one hundred and four years.” The passage is obscure, and other authors do not explain it], nor could they find any people who would provide them aid against the Franks. At last they surrendered themselves to Chlodoveus’s power.

For when Chlodoveus had returned from the battle mentioned above to Reims [Note: Claromontanus has *Remus*. Bollandus has *Remus … entered*], he was secretly consecrated through baptism at Easter, together with six thousand Franks, by Saint Remigius, bishop of the city of Reims (Chapter 31), with Queen Chrotechildis also urging him on [Note: Hincmarus, Flodoardus, and others followed this account. Others, however, relying on a letter of Saint Avitus, maintain that Chlodoveus was baptized on the Nativity of the Lord].

When Saint Remigius was announcing to Chlodoveus, in the white garments of baptism, the Gospel reading describing how our Lord Jesus Christ had come to his passion, Chlodoveus said:

“If I had been there with my Franks, I would have avenged his injury.”

Already demonstrating his faith through these words, he declared himself to be a true Christian.

XXII. Godegiselus, the brother of Gundobadus, sent envoys to request Chlodoveus’s assistance, having learned that Chlodoveus was exceedingly strong in battle. He promised that, if Chlodoveus expelled Gundobadus from the kingdom with his assistance, he would pay tribute to Chlodoveus’s side [Note: Rohart has “promising that, if he …, he would pay tribute”] (Chapter 32).

Gundobadus, unaware of his brother Godegiselus’s treachery, sent to him and said:

“Come, so that we may resist the Franks together and not suffer what other peoples have endured.”

Godegiselus replied: “I shall come and give you aid.”

Chlodoveus marched with the Franks against the two kings and drew up for battle in the plain of Dijon [Note: So Claromontanus has it. The meaning, unless I am mistaken, is either “he led the army through the fields of Dijon” or “in the plain of Dijon”; likewise, Chapter 25 speaks of the plain of Vouillé. The printed editions have “he led the army to the fortress of Dijon, to the plain…”].

Godegiselus joined Chlodoveus, and the two armies crushed Gundobadus’s people. But when Gundobadus recognized his brother’s treachery, he turned his back, followed the bank of the Rhône, and entered the city of Avignon.

Godegiselus, having won the victory, fulfilled in part his promise to Chlodoveus and entered Vienna in triumph [Note: Freher has “he triumphs.” Canisius and Chesnaye have “he entered Avignon in triumph, and Chlodoveus … sent men who could drive him from the city.”].

King Chlodoveus sent word after Gundobadus and ordered that he be driven from the city.

XXIII. Aridius, a most prudent man, was sitting with Gundobadus inside the fortress and said to him (same source):

“You must soften this man’s ferocity. I shall pretend to flee from you and go over to him, so that I may do what will harm neither you nor this region. Whatever he commands you through my advice, promise to do, until the Lord prospers your cause.”

XXIV. Aridius took leave of Gundobadus and went to Chlodoveus, saying:

“Leaving that treacherous man Gundobadus, I offer myself to your glory” [Note: Claromontanus, Bollandus, and Freher have *expeti*, meaning “I sought your glory.” In this author the manuscripts frequently use the sixth case for the fourth; noting this once is sufficient] (same source).

Chlodoveus received him kindly. He was agreeable in conversation, energetic in counsel, just in judgment, and faithful in the trust committed to him [Note: Other witnesses have “in commissions”].

He said to Chlodoveus:

“This region is yours. Why do you permit it to be laid waste? Order Gundobadus to pay you tribute, and you will rule both him and the region. If he refuses, complete what you have begun.”

Gundobadus promised to carry out what Chlodoveus had commanded. Chlodoveus returned to Francia, leaving five thousand Franks with Godegiselus.

Gundobadus left Avignon, gathered his forces, and surrounded Godegiselus at Vienna. He entered the city through an aqueduct and killed Godegiselus. He slaughtered with the sword the Franks gathered in a single tower and afterward resolved to return nothing to Chlodoveus (Chapter 33).

XXV. King Alaric of the Goths had entered into a fraudulent friendship with Chlodoveus. When Chlodoveus recognized this through his envoy Paternus, he took up arms against Alaric and, in the plain of Vouillé, ten miles from the city of Poitiers, killed Alaric. After slaughtering a great number of Goths, Chlodoveus occupied his kingdom, extending from the Tyrrhenian Sea, the Loire River, and the Pyrenees Mountains to the Ocean Sea (Chapters 35, 37).

He removed Alaric’s treasures from Toulouse and brought them with him to Paris. He enriched the churches of Saint Martin and Saint Hilary with many gifts; supported by their aid, he is seen to have accomplished these things.

When he went to Paris, he established the seat of his kingdom there (Chapter 38).

XXVI. His son Theuderic captured cities along the coast. At his father’s command, the son returned to him (same source).

Chlodericus [Variant: *Chlodoveus*], son of King Sigibert, whom Chlodoveus [Variant: *Theodoricus*] had kept with an army as his ally against the Goths, was incited by flattering [Note: Canisius has “light” or “frivolous”; other witnesses have “gentle” or “light”] words while sailing along the River Scheldt.

He treacherously killed his own father Sigibert in the forest of Bochonia [Note: The printed editions have *Burconia*; other witnesses have *Burgundia*, *Burgunia*, or *Burchonia*], and he himself was killed by Chlodoveus’s assassins. Chlodoveus took over Sigibert’s kingdom, together with its treasures, without any battle.

XXVII. Chlodoveus killed King Chararicus, his relative, and subjected his kingdom to himself (Chapter 41).

XXVIII. Chlodoveus treacherously killed King Ragnacharius, his relative, with his own hand, and similarly slaughtered his brother Richarius with his own hand (Chapter 42).

He subjected to his power the kingdom of Ragnacharius, who had his seat at Cambrai. Chlodoveus’s kingdom was greatly extended throughout Gaul. He carefully arranged matters so that none of his relatives would survive who might rule, except those descended from his own seed.

XXIX. When Chlodoveus died, he was buried in the church of the apostle Saint Peter, which he had built through his own work (Chapter 43). He died in the fifth year after the battle of Vouillé [Note: Bollandus has “the battle of Vouillé”; other witnesses have “the battle of Vouillé” with variant spellings]. He held the kingdom for thirty years.

From the passing of Saint Martin until the passing of Chlodoveus there were one hundred twelve years.

Queen Chrotechildis devoted herself to prayers and vigils at the threshold of Saint Martin at Tours.

XXX. Chlodoveus’s four sons—Theuderic, Chlodomer, Childebert, and Chlotar—divided his kingdom among themselves by equal arrangement (Book III, Chapter 1). Theuderic received Metz as his seat, Chlodomer Orléans, Childebert Paris, and Chlotar Soissons.

Theuderic already had a son named Theudebert, useful and energetic.

XXXI. Amalricus, son of Alaric, married their sister; through her, Barcennona [Reading corrupt; editorial correction: “because of … at Barcinona”] was killed by Childeric [Read *Childebert*. Barcino was an episcopal city of the province of Tarraconensis and the capital of modern Catalonia. See the passage in Gregory] and the Franks (same source, Chapters 2 and 3).

XXXII. The Danes sailed to Gaul, invaded Theuderic’s kingdom, and were defeated by Theudebert [Note: So Claromontanus, Bollandus, and Canisius. Freher and Chesnaye instead begin Chapter 32: “The Alans were defeated by Theudebert…” Certainly the table of contents, even in Claromontanus, has: “Concerning the Alans, how they … in the kingdom…” Nothing is said there about the Danes, who may perhaps be the same people, since Gregory mentions only Danes. Bollandus, instead of “the Danes sailing,” has “the Alamanni sailing,” and so forth] son of Theuderic, and lost both all their booty and their lives.

XXXIII. Three brothers ruled the Thuringians: Badericus [Variant: *Baldericus*], Ermenfridus, and Bertharius (Chapter 4). Ermenfridus killed Bertharius at the instigation of Ermenfridus’s wicked wife, named Amalberga. He also killed his brother Badericus with the aid of Theuderic [Note: Bollandus, other witnesses, Freher, and Canisius have “with his counsel”].

Ermenfridus himself was killed by Theudebert, son of Theuderic. The kingdom of the Thuringians was brought under the power of the Franks.

XXXIV. Gundobadus’s son Sigimundus was elevated to the kingship at the town of Quatruvium, near Geneva [Note: Canisius and another witness have “at the town of Ardegavum”; another witness has “at Agaunum”], by command of his father. He had as his wife the daughter of Theuderic, king of Italy, by whom he had a son named Sigiricus (Chapter 5).

When she died, he took another wife. At the instigation of his stepmother, he ordered his son Sigiricus to be killed. Afterward, therefore, he performed severe penance and built the monastery of the holy martyrs of Agaunum, a work of extraordinary beauty [Note: In fact, it had already been built; he enlarged it and established there a continual service of psalm-singing. See Gregory and the notes], and built several other monasteries.

Chrotechildis continually urged her sons to avenge the deaths of their father and mother and of their brothers (Chapter 6). For this reason they attacked Burgundy and defeated Sigimundus and Godemarus in battle [Note: Above he is called *Gotemarus*; here Bollandus has *Godemarus*].

XXXV. Chlodomer captured Sigimundus as he was fleeing to the monastery of the holy martyrs of Agaunum and brought him, together with his wife and children, to Orléans (same source). Godemarus turned his back and went into hiding.

Godemarus regained his strength and retained the kingdom of Burgundy. Chlodomer again moved his army against Godemarus, after having killed Sigimundus with his wife and children.

XXXVI. The abbot Avitus foretold to Chlodomer that he would suffer on that very journey what Sigimundus had done [Variant: “the same thing”] (same source). When the Franks and Burgundians joined battle at Veserontia [Note: Chesnaye and Freher have *Vesontia*. It is a place near Vienne in the territory of the Allobroges, according to Gregory], Chlodomer was beheaded, deceived by the auxiliaries of Theuderic, who had Sigimundus’s daughter as his wife.

XXXVII. The Franks, however, regained their strength during that same battle. After defeating and annihilating the Burgundians at Veserontia, they subjected their homeland to their power (same source).

Chlotar took as his wife Chlodomer’s wife, named Guntiucha, and Chrotechildis raised Chlodomer’s three sons: Theudoaldus, Gunthacharius [Variant: *Guntharius*], and Chlodoaldus.

Childebert treacherously invaded the Auvergne against Theuderic. Chlotar and Childebert attacked Burgundy, but Theuderic refused to join them. Childebert and Chlotar drove Godemarus into flight and occupied Burgundy. Theuderic ravaged the Auvergne with an army (Chapters 9, 11, and 12).

Mundericus, who claimed to be related to the king and said that the kingdom was owed to him, was killed by Theuderic’s retainers after being deceived (Chapter 14). His property was placed under the royal treasury.

### XXXVIII

Peace was made between Childebert and Theuderic with an oath, and hostages were given (ch. 15). But it was broken very soon, and many sons of senators were subjected to servitude on this account. [Note: Among the Romans, if faith was broken, hostages were originally condemned to death, as appears from Livy; later it was sufficient to reduce them to slavery.] The nephew of blessed Gregory, bishop of the city of Langres, who was serving a certain barbarian at Trier, was freed and brought back through the ingenuity of a certain Leo, one of that bishop’s cooks.

### XXXIX

Queen Chrotechildis was living at Paris with the sons of Chlodomer whom she was raising, and loved them with unique affection. Childebert, moved by envy of them, persuaded Chlotar that they should be killed (ch. 18). Of these, two—Theudoald and Gunthar—were killed by Chlotar’s own hand. Chlodoald was tonsured for the clergy and, leading a worthy life, died; at his tomb the Lord deigns to display miracles.

[Col. 0590B] Theuderic betrothed to his son Theudebert Wisigard, the daughter of a certain king. [Note: Clar. together with Can. and Freh. reads “Theuderic betrothed his son Theudebert to Wisigard,” where Wisigard is understood; and below, “he married Roman” [or “a Roman woman”]. Nevertheless, between these two words something had been written in Clar. which has been deliberately rubbed away.] (ch. 20). Theudebert, abandoning Wisigard, took Theotheria [Note: Ches. and others, and Boh., read Deotheria.] as his wife, a Roman by birth (ch. 22).

### XL

Theuderic died in the twenty-third year of his reign [Note: Thus Clar. and Boh., together with the anonymous author of the *Deeds of the Franks* and the printed editions, except Chesn., which, with Aimoïn, reads “twenty-fourth.”], and his kingdom was taken up by Theudebert, who showed himself great and outstanding in every virtue (ch. 23). Theotheria, jealous of Theudebert, deceitfully killed her own daughter. Theudebert, abandoning Theotheria, married Wisigard (chs. 25–27).

### XLI

Childebert and Theudebert, having entered into an alliance, marched with an army against Chlotar (ch. 28). But through the prayers of Chrotechildis at the threshold of Saint Martin, and by divine direction, they were separated when hail and a violent storm of thunder and lightning came upon them. They made peace and returned to their own residences.

### XLII

After this, Childebert and Chlotar attacked Spain and devastated most of it (ch. 29). They killed Amalric, king of Barcelona (ch. 10). The city of Zaragoza was delivered through prayers and fasts. [Note: The epitomator confuses into one event the war which Childebert undertook against the Visigoths and another which, eleven years later, Childebert and Chlotar together waged against the same people. Gregory discusses the former in Book III, chapter 10, and the latter in chapter 29 of the same book.] (ch. 29).

### XLIII

After Amalric, Theudo [Note: In the index of Clar. and in Boh., here and in the index, the name is Theuthacadus; Chesn. has Theudahadus.] reigned in Spain (ch. 30). After he was killed, Theudegisel assumed the kingdom. While he was sitting happily at dinner, his own men extinguished the candles and killed him. Agila succeeded him in the kingdom. The Goths have long had this vice: when a king does not please them, he is killed by them.

### XLIV

Since Theuderic, king of Italy, had Chlodoveus’s sister as his wife, and left by her a young daughter with his wife, when the girl’s mother was arranging for her to be joined in marriage to the king’s son, the girl was seized by a servant named Tranquilla. [Note: Chesn. and Freh. read Tranquillianos; Can. and Boh. read Traquillane; Valesius has Trauvillane, believing him to be Triquilla, prefect of the royal household, mentioned by Boethius in Book I of the *Consolation*. For at that time many names ending in *a* were rendered in the plural as names ending in *anis*, such as Attilanis and Melanis. Trivva is called prefect of the bedchamber in the extracts from the history edited by Henri Valesius, appended to Ammianus Marcellinus.] (ch. 31).

Tranquilla was captured with an army by the girl’s mother and beheaded. After recovering her daughter, the mother imposed discipline on her and took her away with her. The daughter killed her mother with poison. Theodatus [Note: Clar. and Boh. have Theothadus; below, Theuthado. Ch. and others have Theuhadus. On these matters see the notes on Gregory, to which should be added what Procopius says about Amalasuntha’s murder in his *Secret History*. There he admits that, out of fear of the empress Theodora, he concealed the matter in his *History of the Goths*.
