He writes here that Theodora, fearing that if Amalasuntha came to Byzantium, as she herself had decided, the emperor Justinian might fall in love with her and neglect Theodora, instructed the envoy Peter to arrange for her death through Theodatus; this was done shortly afterward.] sought the kingdom of Theuderic and ordered the daughter, who had become her mother’s murderer, to be shut in a fiercely heated bath so that she would be burned there.

For this crime, as a settlement, fifty thousand solidi were sent to Childebert, Chlotar, and Theudebert. Childebert and Theudebert divided the money between themselves and gave nothing from it to Chlotar. After Theodatus died, Totila succeeded to the kingdom, but the patrician Narses killed him, and the kingdom of the Goths in Italy was destroyed. [Note: In Clar., this has been transferred by another, ancient hand.]

### XLV

Afterward Theudebert entered Italy with an army and devastated it throughout its maritime districts (ch. 32). The patrician Narses was put to flight. Later the duke Buccellinus, by order of Theudebert, occupied Sicily and, ruling all Italy, enjoyed great success in these circumstances. [Note: Ch. and others read “great misfortune”; Boh. reads “great misfortune.” Gregory of Tours mentions Buccellinus’s arrival in Campania in Book I of the *Dialogues*, chapter 2.]

### XLVI

At the petition of Desideratus, bishop of Verdun, Theudebert mercifully gave eight thousand solidi to the citizens of Verdun for its recovery (chs. 34, 36). Theudebert, afflicted by a fever, died in the fourteenth year of his reign.

### XLVII

Queen Chrotechildis, full of days and good works, died and was buried in the sacristy [Note: In another manuscript of Clar., the letters *at* have been added, producing *sacratario*.] of the basilica of Saint Peter (Book IV, ch. 1). Chlotar ordered all churches to pay one-third of their revenues to the treasury; but when Bishop Injuriosus resisted, this evil was abolished (chs. 2, 3).

By Ingund, Chlotar had Gunthar, Childeric, Aribert, Guntram, Sigibert, and a daughter, Chlodesinda. By Aregund, Ingund’s sister [Note: Ch. and Freh. in some copies read Radegund; below, Gunsina. In the next chapter: Aquilana, Spain.], he had Chilperic, and by Unsina he had Chramn.

### XLVIII

While Angilane was reigning in Spain, and was unjust toward his people, the imperial army entered Spain. Agila was killed (ch. 8).

### XLIX

Athanagild succeeded to the kingdom. He expelled the imperial army from Spain (ibid.).

### L

Theudebald, son of Theudebert, married Waldetrada. [Note: The editions, and below, have Valderada; others have Vuldotrada and Vuldodrada.] He was very unjust toward his people. During his time grapes grew in a vessel [Note: Freh. reads *Cauro*; Can. and others read *Sambuco*; Clar. has *in pauco*. The first letter, however, is almost worn away; below, instead of “moon,” Boh. has *limina*]. A star coming from the opposite direction entered the moon.

In Italy, Buccellinus repeatedly fought bravely against the patricians Belisarius and Narses, put them to flight, and crushed their armies. At last, weakened by a flux of the bowels, and with his army likewise worn down by the same illness [alternative: perished], he was defeated and killed by Narses, after Belisarius had already died. In that same year Theudebald died, and Chlotar received his kingdom, taking Waldetrada as his wife.

### LI

In that year, when the Saxons rebelled, Chlotar mobilized an army and destroyed most of them, devastating Thuringia because they had dared to assist them. [Note: Boh. reads, “because they had dared to assist them.”] Not long afterward, when the Saxons rebelled again, Chlotar marched an army against them (ch. 14).

The Saxons offered to make amends for everything they had done wrongly and offered half of all their possessions as compensation, except for their wives and children. The Franks scorned accepting this and tried to kill them, saying to Chlotar: “You will not make peace with them; rise, let us fight and avenge ourselves on them.” When he refused, the Franks, wishing to kill Chlotar, compelled him to go unwillingly into battle. There such a great slaughter of the Franks was inflicted by the Saxons that it would have seemed incredible.

### LII

Childebert plotted an ambush against Chlotar together with Chramn (ch. 16). Aribert [Note: Below he is called Charibert. Clar. has Airibertus; others, Chairibertus.] and Guntram, by order of their father, marched with an army against Chramn. But, by divine providence intervening [Note: *Sicediti*. Clar. reads *temperate*, instead of *tempestate*, unless I am mistaken.], they were separated from the battle when a severe lightning storm arose. Chramn continued with Childebert (ibid.).

The Saxons, coming into Francia through Childebert’s faction, carried off booty as far as the city of Divicia. [Note: Can. and Ch. and others read Duucia; others, Devicia.] Chramn bound himself firmly to Childebert. Childebert devastated the Campania of Reims (ch. 17). The duke Austrapius, fearing Chramn, fled into the basilica of Saint Martin (ch. 18).

### LIII

King Childebert died at Paris and was buried in the basilica of Saint Vincent, which he himself had built. Chlotar took possession of its treasures and kingdom (ch. 20).

### LIV

He sent Waldetrada and her two daughters into exile (ibid.). [Note: Can. and Boh. join these words to the preceding chapter, and with better arrangement. Moreover, one should read Ultrogotha, who had been Childebert’s wife. See Gregory.]

Chramn fled to Britain to Conober, count of the Britons. [Note: Ch. and Freh. read “to Cunobert, king.” Below, instead of Willacharius, Clar. and Boh. have Quillacharius; this name is carelessly divided in Can. as “Quia Lacharius.” Below, Ches. and Freh. read “because of him.”] His father-in-law Willacharius took refuge in the church of Saint Martin. Through him this basilica [alternative: church] was burned. Later it was suitably restored by Chlotar and covered with tin.

Chramn was captured by his father Chlotar and burned alive in Britain with his wife and children; Conober, count of the Britons, was killed. [Note: Thus the printed editions, except Ches., which, with Boh., reads “was killed”; Clar. has “with him killed.”]

### LV

For the sins he had committed or negligently failed to correct, Chlotar hurried to the threshold of blessed Martin the Confessor to seek pardon (ch. 21). From there, coming to the estate of Compendium, he died in the fifty-first year of his reign, afflicted by a fever.

Chilperic, after seizing Chlotar’s treasures at the estate of Brennacum, occupied Childebert’s seat at Paris; but he was soon driven out from there (ch. 22). Charibert, Guntram, Chilperic, and Sigibert divided their father’s kingdom by lot.

The lot gave Charibert the kingdom of Childebert, with his seat at Paris; Guntram the kingdom of Chlodomer, with his seat at Orléans; Chilperic the kingdom of his father Chlotar, with his throne at Soissons; and Sigibert the kingdom of Theuderic, with his seat at Metz. [Note: Gregory has Reims.]

At the same time the Huns attacked Gaul. Sigibert marched against them with an army, defeated them [alternative: killed them], and put them to flight (ch. 23). Later he made peace with them. Chilperic invaded Reims and seized other cities belonging to Sigibert, whereupon civil war arose between them.

Sigibert occupied Soissons. He captured Theudobert, Chilperic’s son, and sent him into exile. After Chilperic was defeated and put to flight, Sigibert recalled the cities to his own rule. After a year [Boh. reads “after years”], he restored Theudobert, Chilperic’s son, after they had exchanged oaths concerning peace. [Note: Can. and Ches. read, “after exchanging peace, hostages, and oaths.”]

Guntram, reigning in Burgundy, appointed Celsus in place of the patrician Agricolanus—a man ready in speech and exceedingly eager in greed. [Note: Can. and Ch. and others read, “most prudent in civic affairs.”] (ch. 24).

### LVI

Guntram was a good king, fearing God (ch. 25). First he took a concubine named Veneranda, by whom he had a son named Gundobad. Later he married Marchitrud, daughter of Magnachar. [Note: Clar. has Magnicharus; Boh. has Magnichari.] After she had borne Guntram a son, she deceitfully killed Gundobad with poison.

By God’s judgment she lost the son she had, and incurred the king’s hatred through her gluttony. After dismissing her, Guntram married Austrechild, her own maidservant, also called Bobilane. By her he had two sons, named Chlotar and Chlodomer.

This was the occasion for dismissing Marchitrud. After Magnachar’s death, her mother had married one of Magnachar’s retainers, a man of humble origin. At the instigation of Gunthio and Wioticus [Note: Clar. has Cinccio and Wiolicus; Can. has Cumtio and Vivolicus; others, Convention; Ch. and others, Uncio and Vivolicus; Boh., Quintio and Vinoticus.], the mother was separated from him by order of Guntram, and the boy himself was killed.

The sons cried out, calling their mother a sorceress and a harlot. [Note: *Herbaria* refers to a woman who prepares magic spells from herbs or potions.] This was the reason the daughter was expelled from the kingdom.

King Charibert married Ingoberga. After leaving her, he took Merofled, the daughter of a wool-worker, and another wife, Theudechild, the daughter of a shepherd of sheep. By the latter he had a son, but the child died immediately (ch. 26).

### LVII

Now when Sigibert saw that his brothers were taking low-born wives, he sent Gogo as an envoy to Athanagild, king of Spain. [Note: Clar. and others, except Ches., have Anagild; the same occurs below. In chapter 63, however, Athanagildo is read.] He asked that the king give him his daughter, named Bruna, in marriage. Athanagild sent her to Sigibert for marriage with many treasures (ch. 27).

To adorn and augment her name, it was decided that she should be called Brunechildis. [Note: The Clar. manuscript reads, “to adorn her, it was increased so that she might be called …”; Boh. has Brunechildes.] Sigibert received her as his wife with great joy and delight.

### LVIII

Earlier, during Sigibert’s childhood, all the Austrasians, when they were choosing Chrodin as mayor of the palace, because he was energetic in everything, feared God, and was imbued with patience, so that nothing except what pleased God and men could be found in him, chose him for that honor.

But he rejected the honor and said:

“I cannot establish peace in Austrasia, especially since all the leading men, together with their children, throughout Austrasia are my relatives. I cannot discipline them, nor can I kill anyone among them. They themselves would then rise up against me and act superstitiously. May God not permit their deeds to deliver me into the prison of hell. Choose another from among yourselves, whomever you wish.”

[Note: Since the words Austrasia, Neustria, and so forth occur frequently in Fredegar and his continuators, it is useful to observe that the Frankish empire under the sons and grandsons of Chlodoveus was often divided into various regions or kingdoms. The more famous division, which lasted until the end of the first dynasty, divided Francia into three kingdoms: Burgundy, so called because it comprised in its entirety that part of Gaul which had been subject to the Burgundians; eastern Francia; and western Francia. In the Germanic language these were called *Ooster riich* and *Wester riich*, that is, the eastern kingdom and the western kingdom.

Eastern Francia was later called Austrasia, and finally Austrasia in its Latinized form; western Francia was called Wester, then, through some unknown development, Neuwester—“New Wester”—then Neptricum, Neptria, Neustria, and finally Neustrasia. Although certain cities and regions of Francia consistently belonged to Austrasia and others always to Neustria, some belonged to different kingdoms at different times. This must be especially observed when reading the records of these periods.]

### LIX

But when they could not find another, they then elected Gogo, their fosterling mentioned above, as mayor of the palace, on Chrodin’s advice. On the following day Chrodin was the first to go to his residence for service, holding Gogo’s arm about his own neck. [Note: Can. and others read *Bracibe*. Aimoïn, Book III, chapter 4, says that he placed Gogo’s arm around his own neck, giving a sign of future domination.] When the others saw this, they followed the same example.

This was favorable to Gogo’s administration, until he brought Brunichildis from Spain. Brunichildis immediately made him hateful to Sigibert, and, at her instigation and through her counsel, Sigibert killed him. [Note: Aimoïn likewise writes this in Book III, chapter 4, although it appears false on the evidence of Gregory, Book VI, chapter 1.]

So many evils and bloodshed were brought about in Francia through Brunichildis’s counsel that the prophecy of the Sibyl was fulfilled:

“Bruna will come from the regions of Spain; before her face many peoples will perish.”

But she was torn apart by the hooves of horses. [That is, by the hooves of horses.] [Note: On her punishment, see chapter 41 of the *Chronicle* below and the appendix to the *Chronicle of Marius*. We shall give the passage in full below in our appendix.]

### LX

Chilperic took Gachilosoinda, Brunichildis’s sister, as his wife, abandoning Fredegund and the other wives he had. [Note: The edition has Gachilisinda; others have Galsonta or Valsonta.] Later, breaking the oath he had given to the envoys of the Goths never to degrade Gachilosoinda from the dignity of queen, he had her beaten. After her death, he again took Fredegund as his wife.

Her brothers judged that Gachilosoinda had been killed through his contrivance and drove him from the kingdom. Chilperic had three sons by his former queen Audovera: Theudobert, Meroveus, and Chlodoveus.

### LXI

The Huns [alternative: Chuni] attempted to come into Gaul. Against them Sigibert advanced with a large army (ch. 29). The Huns, trained in magical arts and displaying many illusions, struck fear into Sigibert’s army, and it turned its back.

Sigibert was surrounded by the Huns, but he was freed through his prudence by offering gifts; this circumstance brought him no disgrace. He established an everlasting peace with the Huns and was honored by the king of the Huns with fitting gifts.

### LXII

Sigibert ordered the citizens of Auvergne to occupy Arles (ch. 30). At Guntram’s command, the patrician Celsus massacred the Auvergnats at Arles.

### LXIII

After King Athanagild died in Spain, Leuva and his brother Leuvild assumed the kingdom (ch. 32; others, 38). Leuva died. Then Leuvild held the whole kingdom of Spain, having Gadsuinda, Brunechildis’s mother, as his wife. [Note: Boh., here and in chapter 83 below, has Geresvinda; others have Gaisvinda.]

### LXIV

At the same time, after the emperor Justinian died at Constantinople, Justinus seized [alternative: held] the empire—a wicked and greedy man (ch. 33; others, 39). Sigibert sent envoys to him: the Frank Warmacharius [alternative: Warmarius] and the count Firminus. They established peace with the emperor. [Note: The printed editions read, “that they might establish peace.”] After this was done, they returned in the second year.

### LXV

Before it assumed this name, the people of the Lombards, departing from Schatanavia [Note: Can. has Schandavia; others, Schatanagia. Paul the Deacon calls it Scandinavia in Book I of *The Deeds of the Lombards*, chapter 2. He says that it was an island situated not so much in the sea as surrounded by marine waves which, because of the flatness of their margins, encircled the land. It was also called Baltia; the kingdoms of Sweden and Norway are there today. See Ortelius.], which lies between the Danube and the Ocean Sea, crossed the Danube with their wives and children.

When the Huns discovered them crossing the Danube, they tried to make war upon them and asked why their people presumed to enter their territory. The Lombards then ordered their women to tie the hair of their heads to their cheeks and chins, so that, pretending to be men, they might appear to display a very large number of warriors. For their women’s hair was very long around the cheeks and chin, like a beard.

It is reported that a voice from above spoke to both battle lines: “These are the Lombards.” Their god, whom the superstitious call Wodan, was reported to have spoken these words. [Note: Can. and others have Wisodan. He is the Romans’ Mercury, according to Paul the Deacon, who gives much information about these matters and about the origin and progress of the Lombards in Book I, chapter 8 and following; consult him if you wish.]

Then the Lombards cried out: “May he who established the name grant victory!” In this battle they defeated the Huns and invaded part of Pannonia.

Not long afterward, the patrician Narses, terrified by the threats of the emperor Justinus and his empress Sophia—for the empress had sent him a woman’s gold distaff, with which he was to spin because he was a eunuch—and ordered him to govern spinners [Note: That is, effeminate men who occupied themselves with spinning like women. A *pensum* is a bundle of wool or hemp that hangs from a distaff and is drawn out by the spindle. From the same word comes the expression that someone has “finished his task,” meaning that he has completed the matter entrusted to him. On this deed of Narses, see Paul the Deacon, Book II of *The Deeds of the Lombards*, chapter 5; Valesius considers the story fabulous, Book IX of *The History of the Franks*, vol. II, p. 36], not peoples, replied:

“I shall spin a thread such that neither the emperor Justinus nor the empress will be able to bring it to their heads.”

Then, inviting the Lombards from Pannonia, he brought them into Italy with their king Alboin. Alboin had Chlodesinda, daughter of King Chlotar, as his wife. After she died, he took another wife, whose father he had killed (ch. 33; others, 41).

### LXVI

He himself perished through the treachery of that woman, by poison (ch. 35; others, 41). Later she and a certain Lombard, with whom she was making her way swiftly to Ravenna from the city of Verona, where she had killed her husband, were captured together on the road [Note: Chesn. and Freh. read, “she perished together with him,” for they were captured there] and killed.

### LXVII

The Lombards chose a king over themselves named Clip [alternative: Calip] (ch. 36; others, 42). When the Lombards burst into Gaul, the patrician Amatus was killed by them, and many of the Burgundians suffered slaughter there. After Amatus, Mummolus assumed the patriciate.

### LXVIII

When the Lombards again invaded Gaul, Mummolus fought them bravely and crushed them almost to annihilation; only a few of them returned to Italy (ibid.).

The Saxons whom Theudebert had sent into Italy burst into Gaul, setting up camp at Stuplon. [Note: Others have Stipholon; Boh. has Staplon. See Gregory.] They inflicted much slaughter throughout the neighboring regions. Mummolus defeated them, and they fled back to Italy, having lost everything they had plundered (ch. 37; others, 43).

The Saxons again planned to come into Gaul with their wives and children, so that, having been received by King Sigibert, they could return to the place from which they had departed. When they came into the territory of Avignon, Mummolus immediately went to meet them and prevented them from crossing the Rhône. Later, after receiving gifts, he permitted them to cross. Proceeding to Sigibert, they were settled in the place from which they had previously come.

Later, after Clip died, the Lombard dukes Chamo, Zaban, and Rodanus invaded Gaul (ch. 39; others, 45). Mummolus came against them with an army and destroyed the three dukes and their army almost to annihilation.

In another year, Mummolus, with an army and by order of Guntram, took Tours and Poitiers from Chilperic’s power and restored them to Sigibert’s side (ch. 40; others, 46). Many of Chilperic’s army and the Poitevins themselves were there slaughtered by the sword. [Note: Others read “and the Poitevins themselves.”]

The Lombard dukes Taloardus and Nuccio [Note: The printed editions have Nuntio; Ches. has Thaloardus] entered the territory of Sion [Note: That is, the territory of Sedunum. Sedunum is an episcopal city in those regions, subject to its own bishop, who is confederated with the Rhaetians; it is commonly called Sion.] through small gates with an army and inflicted enormous slaughter at the monastery of the Agaunian saints.

At the village of Bex [Note: A place commonly called Bex, situated not far from the monastery of Agaunum. Marius records this disaster under the year 574.], not far from that monastery, the dukes and their army were killed by Wiolicus and Theudofred, dukes of Guntram. Only forty of them returned in flight to Italy. [Note: Freh. and Can. and others erroneously read “forty thousand.”]

### LXIX

Chlodoveus, son of Chilperic, invaded Bordeaux. Defeated by the duke Sigulf, he fled back to his father. [Note: Others read, “defeated and put to flight.”] (ch. 42; others, 48).

### LXX

Chilperic invaded Poitiers and Tours, which belonged to Sigibert’s kingdom; he put the duke Sigulf to flight and overthrew his army (ibid.). Chilperic restored to Sigibert the cities he had invaded. After a year, Chilperic entered Sigibert’s kingdom with a large army; but envoys intervened and they were reconciled.

### LXXI

Afterward, having reached a common agreement, both marched with an army, wishing to kill Guntram and seize his kingdom (ch. 44; others, 50).

Sigibert remained with his army at Arciaca. [Note: This is a village five leagues north of the city of Troyes, situated on the Aube River; hence it is called Arcis-sur-Aube. Duodecim Pontes was once a small town named from the number of its bridges; it is now simply called Pontes-sur-Seine. On this place see Valesius, *Notitia Galliarum*.] Chilperic remained at Duodecim Pontes.

When Guntram heard this, he quickly moved his army and, coming to the estate of Veriaco [Note: Perhaps Villariacum, mentioned above in chapter 19], while envoys intervened, these three brothers—Sigibert, Guntram, and Chilperic—joined together at Troyes and, in the church of Saint Lupus, swore oaths against Guntram to preserve peace. Guntram likewise confirmed peace with them by oath.

Returning to the Austrasian camp, they raised a rumor against Sigibert, saying: “As you promised, give us a place where we may become rich, or let us fight; otherwise we shall not return to our homeland.”

He wished [Note: Freh. and Chesn. read “he did not wish”] to go against Guntram, compelled by his men. The Austrasians, with great cunning [Note: Can. has “treacherously”], said to him: “You confirmed peace with Guntram by oath; how can we attack him?” Then, unanimously crying out that they wished to march against Chilperic, they immediately advanced against him.

His army was already hurrying homeward and was far away. When Chilperic learned this, he turned his back and reached Tournai. [Note: Can. has Tours. But, according to Gregory, Tornacum—Tournai—should be read, since Chilperic withdrew there.] (ch. 45; others, 51).

Sigibert followed him and came to Paris. There, when Sigibert saw the most holy and blessed Germanus, bishop of the city of Paris, he heard these prophetic words from him:

“If you intend to pursue your brother in such a way as to kill him and take away his kingdom, it is written: ‘The pit that you prepare for your brother, you will fall into.’” (Proverbs 26:27).

Unwilling to heed his correction, Sigibert continued to plan the accomplishment of his desire (ch. 46; others, 52).

When he had reached Vitry, all the Neustrians [Note: Chesn. and Freh. have Neustrasii] came to him and subjected themselves to his authority. Only Ansoald remained with Chilperic.

Fredegund sent two boys deceitfully, and they killed Sigibert; they themselves too were killed. Chilperic recovered his strength and regained his kingdom.

### LXXII

Brunechildis and her son Childebert were being held under guard at Paris. But through the faction of the duke Gundoald, Childebert was placed in a basket [alternative: a hamper], received through a window by a boy, and the boy alone presented him at Metz. There he was raised to his father’s kingdom by Gundoald or by the Austrasians (Book V, ch. 1).

By order of Chilperic, Brunechildis was confined in exile at Rouen. [Note: Chesn. and Freh. have Rothomerem; Canis. has Rotomagi; Ch. and others have Ratomum. The reading of Clar. and Boh., which we follow, is the best, since the ancients called Rouen Rodomum or Rotomum.]

In that year a radiance appeared to move across the sky. Sigibert was buried in the church of Saint Medard, at the age of forty, in the fourteenth year of his reign (ch. 46; others, 52).

### LXXIII

From the death of the elder Theudebert to the death of Sigibert: twenty-nine years (ibid.). [Note: Can. and others have nineteen.]

From the beginning to the Flood: 2,242 years.

From the Flood to Abraham: 942 years.

From Abraham to the exodus of the children of Israel from Egypt: 462 years.

From the exodus of the children of Israel from Egypt to the building of Solomon’s Temple: 480 years. [Note: Can. has no number here.]

From the building of the Temple to its destruction [Note: Boh. and Can. have “desolation”; Freh. has “dissolation.”] and the Babylonian captivity: 370 years. [Note: Chesn. has 370; Canis. 350; Clar. and Freh. 340, that is, 390.]

From the Babylonian captivity to the Passion of the Lord: 648 years. [Note: Chesn. has 647.]

From the Passion of the Lord to the death of Saint Martin: 412 years.

From the death of Saint Martin to the death of King Chlodoveus: 112 years.

From the death of King Chlodoveus to the death of Theudebert: 37 years. [Note: Chesn. has 27.]

From the death of Theudebert to the death of Sigibert: 29 years.

Together these amount to 5,774 years.

### LXXIV

Chilperic sent his son Meroveus to Poitiers with an army. On his return from there, Meroveus went to Rouen and married Brunichildis (Book V, ch. 2). Chilperic immediately separated him from her.

The people of the Campania invaded Soissons. [Note: That is, they invaded Suessiones.] Chilperic prevailed against them with an army and recovered Soissons (ch. 3).

He had his son Meroveus tonsured and burdened with the clerical state, and Meroveus was ordained a priest. [Note: Chesn. reads, “He had Meroveus tonsured as a cleric and ordained as a priest.”] (ch. 14).

He sent the duke Roccolenus, and likewise the duke Guntram, to Tours to pursue them (ch. 4). Roccolenus, afflicted by illness, accomplished nothing there.

### LXXV

At that time Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, departed to the Lord (ch. 8). Chilperic sent his son Chlodoveus to Tours [that is, to Turones], so that he might invade the cities of Childebert beyond the Loire (ch. 13).

The patrician Mummolus of Guntram fought against Chlodoveus and Desiderius, Chilperic’s duke, and defeated them. Five thousand were killed by Mummolus’s army, but twenty thousand by Desiderius.

### LXXVI

War arose between the Suebi and the Saxons (ch. 15). Twenty thousand were killed by the Saxons, and only six thousand of them remained. Six thousand four hundred and eighty-eight of the Suebi were also overthrown. The survivors, however, won the victory.

The Saxons vowed that they would cut neither hair nor beard until they had avenged this injury, but their anger proved false.

### LXXVII

At that time Magliavus and Bodecus were counts among the Britons, and they entered into friendship with one another by oath (ch. 16). After Bodecus died, Magliavus expelled his son, named Theuderic, from the kingdom.

But at last, having regained his strength, Theuderic killed Magliavus and his son Jacob and recovered his father’s kingdom. Waroch, Magliavus’s son, was made count in his father’s place (ch. 17).

King Guntram, at the instigation of Queen Austrechildis, killed the two sons of Magnachar with the sword and reduced their possessions to the treasury. Guntram’s two sons died immediately afterward.

### LXXVIII

Guntram adopted Childebert, Sigibert’s son, as his own son (ch. 18).

Chilperic drove Praetextatus, bishop of Rouen, into exile, charging him with having acted against Chilperic on the advice of Brunechildis; this charge was true (ch. 19).

Meroveus was again made a layman. Fleeing from Tours [that is, from Turones], he came through Auxerre to Dijon and proceeded into the Campania of Reims. He was surrounded by the people of Thérouanne and confined in a certain estate by Gailenus [alternative: Gaulenus], his retainer (ch. 14).

At Meroveus’s own request, he was killed with a knife. Gailenus, whose hands and feet, nose and ears were cut off, ended his life shamefully.

## LXXIX

At that same time the emperor Justin became insane (Chapter 20). His Augusta Sophia governed the empire together with Caesar Tiberius. Tiberius was exceedingly generous in almsgiving. But when Sophia reproached him for wasting the treasury, Tiberius ordered a stone to be lifted in the middle of the Palace, where a cross had been found. Beneath it—printed editions read “above it”—two crosses were found on another stone. When that stone too had been lifted, a thousand *centenaria* of gold were discovered beneath it—according to some copies, *centenarii*; Chesne gives “a hundred talents.” Tiberius distributed this wealth generously among the poor for the love of God.

## LXXX

After Narses had died, Tiberius found his treasure buried beneath the earth, betrayed by a certain old man—*senece* as in Claromontanus, where the sixth case is formed from *senex*, instead of *sene*; Bohier has *senice*. The printed editions incorrectly read *prudente alloquio Senecae*, or *Senicae*. The treasure consisted of an enormous quantity of gold and silver by weight, as well as precious stones (same chapter). Tiberius likewise distributed it generously as provisions among the poor.

Samson, son of Chilperic, died, and Chilperic mourned him deeply (Chapter 23). In that year a star was seen shining in the middle of the moon (Chapter 24). Gunthramn Boso, leaving his daughters in the church of Saint Hilary, went over to Childebert (Chapter 25).

In the third year also of King Childebert—which was the seventeenth year of Chilperic and Gunthramn—according to Chesne and Freher, “sixteenth,” erroneously—Gunthramn Boso, wishing to take his daughters away from Poitiers, was attacked by Dracolene (Chapter 26). Gunthramn offered Dracolene many gifts; but Dracolene, being arrogant, said: “I have a rope ready, with which I usually bind others; today Gunthramn too shall be bound with it.”

When the battle had begun, Gunthramn, invoking the name of the Lord and the power of Saint Martin, raised his spear, slaughtered Dracolene by striking him in the throat, and, hanging him from his horse, threw him dead upon the ground. Afterwards he successfully completed what he had begun.

Then the people of Poitiers, the Bajocassini—Canus and Freher have *Bagassinitae*, and below *Baigassini*, as does Claromontanus; but the reading should be *Bajocassini*, following Gregory, whom one should consult. Those same editions have *Romani*; Claromontanus, *Teromanni*; Bohier, *Bagassinitae, Rotmanni*. Below, Chifflet has *Baicassinis*, and others *Bagasinis*—the Cenomani, and the people of Angers, together with many others, marched into Brittany against Waroch. Waroch fell upon them by night and inflicted a great slaughter upon the Saxon Bajocassini (Chapter 27).

In the fourth year of Childebert—which was the eighteenth year of Gunthramn and Chilperic—Bishops Salonius and Sagittarius were degraded from the episcopate at a synod in Chalon (Chapter 28). Chilperic ordered very burdensome assessments to be made throughout the whole population of his kingdom (Chapter 29).

Marcus the referendary, who was carrying out this assessment and had all the *poleptici* with him, was killed by the people of Limoges on the Kalends of March; all the *poleptici* were burned in the fires. According to the note, he escaped death in Gregory, who mentions him under the year 580 and reports his death under the ninth year of Childebert, Book VI, chapter 28.

While these things were taking place, the emperor Justin ended his life in the eighteenth year of his reign, in the insanity into which he had fallen (Chapter 31).

## LXXXI

Tiberius seized the empire (same chapter). The Augusta Sophia, forgetful of her promise, plotted against Tiberius; she wished to raise Justinian, Justin’s nephew, to the imperial power. When Tiberius perceived this, he seized Sophia, stripped her of her treasures, separated the children from her, and ordered her to be confined under guard.

After rebuking Justinian, he later loved him with such affection that he promised his daughter to Justinian’s son and sought Justinian’s son for his own daughter. Canus and Chesne have “and his son for his daughter”; Freher has “and his daughter for his son.” It should be read, as in Gregory: “and he sought his daughter for his own son.” But the arrangement did not come to pass.

Tiberius’s army defeated the Persians and, returning victorious, brought back such an immense quantity of booty that it was thought sufficient to satisfy human greed. Twenty elephants were brought back from there.

## LXXXII

At that same time, in the fifth year of King Childebert, such great calamities occurred throughout the entire region that it would have seemed exceedingly astonishing (Chapter 34). All the rivers passed beyond boundaries they had never previously exceeded; livestock perished, and buildings suffered great destruction from the floods. But when the rains ceased, the trees blossomed again.

It was the month of September. A radiance seemed to run across the sky. A sound like trees being torn down was heard throughout the whole earth. The city of Bordeaux was shaken by an earthquake. Immense stones were torn from the Pyrenees Mountains, and they struck down livestock and people.

The settlement of Bordeaux, suddenly seized by a divinely kindled fire, burned many people; houses and yards with their stores of grain were consumed by the fire. The fire had no visible fuel; perhaps, however, it was a divine command. The city of Aureliana was devastated by this fire (Chapter 35).

At the boundary of Chartres, blood flowed from broken bread. But these portents were followed by an exceedingly severe pestilence and by discord among the kings. When they were again preparing civil war, a dysenteric disease—Claromontanus and Canus have *besentericus*, and so below—overran all Gaul.

In those days Austrechild, Queen of the prince Gunthramn, was consumed by this disease. She accused the physicians before Gunthramn—Chesne has “with the physicians accused before Gunthramn”; Canus, “the physicians … accused.” Canus and Freher commend another reading: “the physician of Gunthramn, accusing the Christians in this matter, by order …”—and, by Gunthramn’s command, the physicians, subjected to various punishments, departed from this world. All the printed editions below read “departed to heaven” (Chapter 36).

In that year there was a great persecution of Christians in Spain, instigated by Goaesinda, whom King Leubildus had taken after King Athanagild. He had two sons by another wife (Chapter 39). One of them, named Ehermengildus, took as his wife Sigibert’s daughter, named Sedegundis. The manuscripts and printed editions all have this form, from which it appears that the words *sed Ingundis*, taken by the epitomator from Gregory, were originally substituted for a single name.

## LXXXIII

She was sent to Spain with great treasures and elaborate furnishings and was kindly received by her grandmother Goaesinda, who later mistreated her (same chapter). But since she absolutely refused to consent to her grandmother’s wicked counsel, she was ordered to live with her husband in one of the cities. Immediately, by preaching to her husband, she converted him to the worship of Christ, and after being baptized he became a Christian. Canus has this reading; others have “baptized in the worship, he became.”

Her father Leubildus pursued him and wished to kill him; finally, in the course of this pursuit, the son was killed, through whom the opportunity was provided.

After the death of Mirion, king of Galicia, his son Euric and his son-in-law, named Audegane, contending for the kingdom, the Suebi and all Galicia were subjected to the power of the Goths by Leubildus. Chesne and Canus have “the Suebi of Suavia”; Freher, “the Galicians.” Our reading, that of the better Claromontanus manuscript, indicates that the Suebi and all Galicia, which they occupied, subsequently obeyed Leuvigildus.

## LXXXIV

Thus Chilperic lost, in a single year, his three sons, already grown, through an illness of dysentery. He had them by Fredegund. Valesius observes, in Book X, that Fredegarius was mistaken here when he wrote that three grown sons of Chilperic by Fredegund died of dysentery in one year. Only two died: one after completing fifteen years, the other an infant immediately after receiving baptism, according to Fortunatus.

His son Chlodoveus still remained. Later, at Fredegund’s instigation, Chilperic had him bound and confined under guard; there, through Fredegund’s conspiracy, he was struck with a knife and died (Chapter 40).

## LXXXV

After this, the patrician Mummolus fled from the kingdom of Gunthramn and sought the fortress of Avignon for his protection. Claromontanus and Bohier have *Avennionem*; the printed editions incorrectly have *Avencionem* (Book VI, chapter 1).

The envoys of Chilperic, who had gone to the emperor Tiberius, returned from him at that time without delay. Another reading is “were immediately removed” (Chapter 2).

## LXXXVI

Childebert, abandoning his peace with Gunthramn, joined himself to Chilperic so that they might take away his kingdom together. Chilperic, while he was without sons, promised to leave Childebert as heir to his kingdom (Chapters 1 and 3). But, as usual, he proved to be a liar.

Duke Lupus of Champagne was pursued by Ursio and Bertefredus and by the army with intent to kill him; but, through Brunichild’s intervention, he was freed, and his protection was transferred by the men mentioned above. Claromontanus and Canus have “was transferred by the men mentioned above”; others have *scalatus*.

## LXXXVII

At that time Hospicius was shut up near the city of Nice. He was bound with iron chains directly against his bare body, with a hair shirt over them, and ate nothing except plain bread and a few dates; during Lent he ate the roots of plants (Chapter 6). While he continued in the body, many miracles were displayed through him, by the Lord’s favor (Chapter 12).

Chilperic sent Duke Desiderius with an army to invade Périgueux and Agen. After putting Duke Ragnoald to flight, he invaded these cities and stripped his wife of all her possessions.

Duke Baudastus died in Gascony and lost the greater part of his army (same chapter). Chesne has *Blaudastus*. Gregory, however, tells more about this same Bladastus below: two years later he besieged Bourges and afterwards joined Gundovaldus.

In the seventh year of King Childebert—which was the twenty-first year of Chilperic and Gunthramn—another reading in the printed editions is “the twentieth”; below Chifflet has “a comet”—a comet appeared on the day of holy Easter (Chapter 14).

At the city of Soissons the sky was seen to burn. In the Parisian region blood flowed again and fell upon the clothing of many people. Various illnesses and a great mortality afflicted the population that year (Chapter 18).

At that time the envoys of Chilperic, Ansoaldus and Domegiselus, who had been sent to Spain to inspect the dowry, returned. King Leubildus was encamped with an army against his son Ermenchildus. Then he killed his son and could not free his son’s wife from the Greeks; she remained there until death (Chapter 43).

## LXXXVIII

That year Duke Rodinus died, a charitable man, full of goodness, just in all things, and most compassionate toward the poor. Once, as was his custom, he had ordered a dead man to be buried. While boys were digging a grave near a certain monument, he lifted a stone and discovered a treasure of extraordinary size and a great quantity of solidi (Chapter 20).

He considered this treasure truly his own. Bohier and Claromontanus have “he considered it his by right”; Freher, “he considered it as a man”; Chesne, *censivit*. He distributed it faithfully among the poor without interruption. With equal faith he returned the treasure to the one from whom he had received it.

Many signs and portents were seen in the sky that year (Chapter 21). A son was born again to Chilperic, and he ordered all prisoners to be released (Chapter 23).

## LXXXIX

Gundoaldus, who claimed to be the son of Chlotarius, returned from Constantinople and was sent by Childebert to Chlotarius, his uncle (Chapter 24). Fredegarius seems to have thought that this was Childebert I, who, according to Gregory, sent Gundovaldus to Chlotarius, and that he was Chlotarius’s uncle; this is false, for they were brothers. Or perhaps Childebert calls himself Gundovaldus’s uncle, in which case his words should be understood as follows: “He was sent by Childebert to his father Chlotarius,” which is not contrary to the truth. For Gundovaldus was first presented to Childebert I when he was sent to Chlotarius. Compare Gregory, Book VI, chapter 24.

When Chlotarius saw him, he ordered the hair of his head to be cut. Sigibert summoned him and sent him to the city of Agrippina, now called Cologne. From there he slipped away and went to Narses. Canus and Chifflet have “he was sent”; our reading is better, meaning “he went.” Narses then sent him to the emperor Maurice (Chapter 26).

When he had returned from there, he was received by the patrician Mummolus through the conspiracy of the bishops Syagrius and Flavius, so that they might depose Gunthramn from the kingdom and raise Gundoaldus. Syagrius was bishop of Autun and Flavius bishop of Chalon. Valesius thinks that they had always been loyal to Gunthramn and that Mummolus accused them of treason maliciously because he found their influence burdensome.

For this reason Mummolus was killed. Gundoaldus was hurled from the top of a cliff by Duke Boso, through the conspiracy of the city of Comminges; dashed to pieces there, he died (Chapter 38).

Cariatto, Gunthramn’s sword-bearer, who revealed this affair, received the bishopric of Geneva in return for this act of reciprocal recompense. Chifflet has *Cariatus*; others have the same form. He subscribed to the Second Council of Valence in 584 and likewise to the Second Council of Mâcon in the following year.

## XC

At that time Chilperic entered Paris, contrary to the agreement he had made with the Franks; for this reason he justly lost his portion thereafter (Book VI, chapter 27). Claromontanus has *Gunthramnus*; the printed editions incorrectly have *Guntramno*. See the passage in Gregory.

Gunthramn returned Childebert’s share of Marseille (Chapter 33). The king ordered Mummolus to be disgraced through Fredegund’s conspiracy, because they accused him of having killed her son by magic; and many women were killed by Fredegund on account of that false accusation (Chapter 35).

## XCI

Fearing Gunthramn and Childebert, Chilperic advanced against Cambrai with his treasures and his entire military force (Chapter 41). Because of this fear he often mobilized the army and made it encamp.

## XCII

Childebert went into Italy, and the Lombards commended themselves to his authority (Chapter 42). Childebert returned from there in glory.

He had previously received fifty thousand gold pieces from the emperor Maurice to conquer the Lombards in Italy. But he not only did them no harm; he also entered into friendship with them. As mentioned above, King Leubildus killed his son Ermenchildus.

## XCIII

Chilperic and Fredegund sent their daughter to Spain, with great—or, in another reading, many—treasures and a large household, to serve him; Leubildus’s son took her as his wife (Chapter 46).

Soon afterwards Chilperic was killed at the estate of Cala, not far from Paris, by a man named Falco, who had been sent by Brunichild. The author of the *Deeds of the Franks*, followed by Aimo, attributes Chilperic’s murder to Fredegund, supposedly because she feared that the king himself would punish her illicit love affair with Landeric. Sunnigisilus, however, who confessed from Gregory’s *History*, Book X, chapter 19, that he was guilty of Chilperic’s death, did not transfer the crime to Fredegund. Childebert appears to accuse Fredegund of the deed when, according to Gregory, Book VII, chapter 7, he demanded her from Gunthramn and said that she had killed his father and uncle. Fredegund herself shifted the blame to Eberulf, Chilperic’s chamberlain (Book VII, chapter 21).

Thus he ended his most cruel life by a fitting death (Chapter 46).

**The excerpted book of the Chronicle ends here.**

# Chronicle

## Notice concerning the following Chronicle

We append to the *History* of our Gregory the Chronicle which, in the collection attributed to Fredegarius, occupies the fourth or sixth place, because it is, as it were, a continuation of that work.

Hence certain manuscript copies, in which the ninth and tenth books of Gregory’s *History* are combined into one and called the ninth, present this very Chronicle under the title of the tenth book of Gregory of Tours’s *History*. In most printed editions it has been published under the title of an Appendix or of the eleventh book of Gregory’s *History*.

Most learned men have thought that its author wrote under the reign of King Pippin or, at any rate, of his son Charlemagne, because in all the commonly printed editions and in nearly all the manuscripts events are described down to the times of those rulers. But they did not sufficiently distinguish the continuators from the first author of the Chronicle.

After the matter was examined more carefully, and with the aid of ancient manuscripts, learned men concluded that the work of the first author did not extend beyond the fourth year of Chlodoveus II, A.D. 641; the events that follow were added by various authors. All of these will be distinguished in their proper places in our edition.

If anyone wishes to know more about these matters, let him read, if he pleases, the preface that we have placed before this volume.

# The Chronicle of Fredegarius Scholasticus with Its Continuators, or Appendix to the History of Saint Gregory, Bishop of Tours, Concerning the Franks

## Prologue

Since I have nothing to offer with the exact propriety of a single word unless it has been granted by the Most High, and while I seek to complete a sentence I scarcely accomplish, through a long circuit, the distance of a short road, the interpreter of this language’s vernacular word sounds absurd—Chesne and Freher have “the interpretation of the words of this vernacular language is absurd.” If necessity causes me to alter anything in the order of the words, I seem to have departed from the office of an interpreter.

Therefore, having carefully read through the chronicles of blessed Jerome, Hydatius, a certain Wise Man, Isidore, and even Gregory, from the origin of the world down to the decline of the kingdom of Gunthramn, I inserted individually into this little book’s five chronicles the matters corresponding to them, omitting very little—perhaps the phrase should be in the ablative, “with very little omitted”—that they most skillfully composed without reproach.

Since this is so, I considered it necessary to pursue the truth more diligently. For that reason, in these earlier chronicles, as though in a future work, I marked out beforehand for myself the kingdoms and periods of all things. In the present work, however, setting down those periods, I fitted together in the most careful order the deeds of each people.

The very prudent men whom I mentioned above composed these chronicles with the utmost rigor—this word is a Greek noun, which in Latin means “deeds of the times”—dictating them as they flowed forth like a perfectly pure and abundant spring. I too had wished that such eloquence of speech might fall to my lot, so that mine might be at least somewhat comparable. But water is drawn more dearly where the stream’s continuity is not assured.

The world is already growing old; therefore the sharpness of wisdom grows dull in us. No one can, nor does anyone presume to, be like the orators—or, in another reading, the prudent men—of earlier times. Nevertheless, insofar as the rusticity and extremity of my understanding permitted—Chesne and Freher have *externitas*, “outwardness”; Canus has *tenuitas*, “meagerness”; Bohier has *strenuitas*, “energy”—I ventured to adapt these same books with the greatest diligence and with as much brevity as I could.

Let no reader doubt anything here: if the name of each book is referred back to its author, he will find that everything rests upon truth.

After completing Gregory of Tours’s book, I did not refrain from writing in this volume all the deeds of the times that I was able to find written anywhere, and all that I later came to know: the deeds of kings and the wars fought by peoples. By reading, hearing, and even seeing, I carefully strove to insert everything that I had learned with certainty, beginning my account at the time when Gregory’s ending ceased and fell silent, when he wrote that the life and deeds of Chilperic had ended.

Some printed editions read: “at the point where Gregory’s *History* reached its end.” The Vatican manuscript has: “when its ending ceased and was silent.” In these versions the prologue ends. Freher and Chesne instead have: “when the deeds of the story ceased and fell silent”; Bohier has: “when his life had ended, I wrote.” Chesne and Freher add: “In the present work, setting down those periods …” The scribe had written these words at the end of the page, and we have restored them above in their proper place.

# Chronicle

## In the year 583

### I

When King Gunthramn had already ruled the kingdom of Burgundy for twenty-three years—another reading has “year”—with great goodness and prosperity, he showed himself among priests as a priest ought to do. He was also exceedingly well disposed toward the *leudes*, generously giving alms to the poor. He held his kingdom in such great prosperity that all the neighboring peoples as well sang the highest praises of him.

## AN. DLXXXIV

In the twenty-fourth year of his reign [Note: Fredegarius places Gregory of Tours’ chronology one year earlier; this is useful to note for reconciling the two authors. What follows should, however, be compared with Gregory’s History under the year 592.], out of love for God he ordered the church of blessed Marcellus—where the saint himself rests bodily—in the suburb of Cabillonum, although the site is nevertheless in the territory of the Sequani, to be magnificently and skillfully built; and, gathering monks there, he founded a monastery [Note: Gregory, under the year 579, Book V, chapter 28, mentions the basilica of Saint Marcellus, which had an abbot, as is clear from Book I, chapter 53, of *On the Glory of the Martyrs*. That monastery still exists, although its abbatial title has been diminished since it was made subject to Cluny. It lies beyond the Arar, which is why it is here said to be situated in the territory of the Sequani. Ch. and Freh. have, in a single reading, *sed tamen est in Segonum* for *Sequanum*.], and endowed the church itself with very many possessions.

He ordered a synod of forty bishops to be held; and, following the model of the institution of the monastery of the holy Agaunian martyrs—which, in the time of King Sigismund, had been confirmed by Avitus and the other bishops at the command of that ruler [Note: This, as may be conjectured, took place on the feast of the Holy Martyrs in this very year, when Saint Avitus delivered the homily entitled “In the Basilica of the Holy Agaunian Martyrs, at the Renewal of That Monastery or the Passion of the Martyrs.” Sirmond published a fragment of it.]—Guntchramnus saw to it, through the joining of this synod, that the constitution of the monastery of Saint Marcellus was established [Note: Several editions, together with Colb., read: “the monastery … was established by its institution.” Vat. has “was confirmed.” Valesius and the others think that this was done at the Second Synod of Mâcon in 585, where, as may be gathered from the subscriptions, forty-three bishops were present, together with three others who had no sees, and representatives of twenty absent bishops. It might, however, perhaps better be referred to the Second Synod of Valence, which Cointius assigned to 585, although Sirmond judges that it was held in May of this very year, 584. At that synod, indeed, everything that the king and the others had donated, or would later wish to donate, to the basilica of Saint Marcellus, Saint Symphorianus, or any other sacred place, was confirmed. Lalandus, in his supplement to the Councils of Gaul, maintains that this council was held in the basilica of Saint Marcellus itself in 594, and that no more than eleven bishops attended it; hence he thinks that an error entered Fredegarius’ text, which reads XL for XI. Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, Book III, chapter 35, reports that a treasure was miraculously discovered by King Guntram, in which, he says, “immeasurable treasures that had long ago been deposited there were found.” From that gold the king later made a solid ciborium of marvelous size and great weight, decorated it with many precious gems, and intended to send it to the Lord’s Sepulchre in Jerusalem. But when he was quite unable to do so, he ordered it to be placed above the body of blessed Marcellus the martyr, which was buried in the city of Cavallonus, where his royal seat was; and it remains there to the present day. Nowhere is there any work made of gold that can be compared with it.], and he took care of it.

### II

In this year Gundoaldus [Note: Vat. has *Gundwaldus*. He is discussed at length by Gregory, especially in Book VII, chapter 26, and elsewhere.] attempted, with the support of Mummolus and Desiderius, to invade part of Guntchramnus’ kingdom in November and to overthrow its cities. Guntchramnus sent the count of the stables, Leudegiselus [Note: Others read *Leudiselus, Leudichildus, Leudisium,* or *Leudigildus*.], and the patrician Aegilanus with an army against them. Gundoaldus turned his back and took refuge in the city of Conbana [Note: That is, Convennae. See Gregory.]; from there he was hurled from a cliff by the commander Boso [Note: Others read “by Oso,” perhaps for “Ollo”; Gundobaldus was driven out by the latter and killed by Boso, according to Gregory, Book VII, chapter 38.] and perished.

### III

When word was brought to Guntchramnus that his brother Chilperic had been killed, he hastened to Paris. There he ordered Fredegundis and Chilperic’s son Chlotharius to come to him; he ordered the boy to be baptized at the villa of Rioilus [Note: Ch. and Freh. read *Riogilo*; others, *Riolo*, commonly Ruel. Guntram did indeed come to Paris in this year for Chlotharius’ baptism, but the latter was not baptized until six years later.], and, receiving him from the sacred font, confirmed him in his father’s kingdom.

## AN. DLXXXV

### IV

In the twenty-fifth year of Guntchramnus’ reign, Mummolus was killed at Senuvia [Note: Others read *Senovia*. Below, Ch. and others have *Sinodia*.] at Guntchramnus’ command. His wife Sidonia, together with all his treasures, was presented to Guntchramnus by Domnolus, a member of the household, and Wandalmarus, the chamberlain.

## AN. DLXXXVI

### V

In the twenty-sixth year of his reign, Guntchramnus’ army entered Spain; but, weakened immediately by the unhealthy conditions of the place, it returned to its own territory.

## AN. DLXXXVII

In the twenty-seventh year of the same reign, Leudisclus [Note: So Clar. This is, I think, the man mentioned above in chapter 2. For in Colb. and Ch. and others he is called *Leudigisilus*, as he is by Gregory, Book VIII, chapter 30. Others have *Leudiselus, Leudisius, Leugisistus,* or *Leudistus*.] was appointed patrician over the region of Provence by Guntchramnus. It was announced that Theodobertus, son of King Childebertus, had been born.

### VI

That year there was such a great flooding of the rivers in Burgundy that they greatly exceeded their banks. In the same year the count Syagrius went to Constantinople on an embassy at Guntchramnus’ command, and there, through deception, was appointed patrician [Note: Syagrius was sent to Constantinople to negotiate peace and received the dignity of patrician from the emperor; this is what is here called “deception.” For he ought not to have accepted something by which he seemed to submit himself to the emperor’s authority. Valesius, for his part, interprets this as referring only to the title of patrician, or imperial counselor; but since Fredegarius says that Syagrius was appointed patrician and that the deception had begun but was not completed, this may perhaps be understood as the patriciate of the province of Massilia, a region which Maurice may have attempted to restore to the Empire, or at least to retain some shadow of dominion over. Maurice may also have attempted this for another reason: before the Franks occupied their kingdom, the Burgundian kings customarily obtained the name of patrician from the emperors; and Maurice may have very much preferred that this practice continue through ambassadors even among the Franks who possessed the same region.].

The deception did indeed begin, but did not proceed to completion. In that year a portent appeared in the sky: a fiery globe fell to the earth amid sparks and roaring. In the same year Levildus [Note: Others read *Leupildus, Leuvichidus,* or *Leupoldus*. The same variations occur for his son: *Richardus, Richarius,* or *Richaricus*.], king of Spain, died, and his son Richaridus obtained the kingdom.

## AN. DLXXXVIII

In the twenty-eighth year of the reign of Lord Guntchramnus, it was announced that another son of Childebertus, named Theudericus, had been born.

### VII

Guntchramnus joined Childebertus, confirming peace at Andelaus. There the mother, sister, and wife of King Childebertus were all present; and there, by a special agreement, it was arranged between Lord Guntchramnus and Childebertus that, after Guntchramnus’ death, Childebertus would assume his kingdom.

### VIII

At that time Rauchingus and Boso, Guntchramnus’ men, and Ursio and Bertefridus, nobles of King Childebertus, were killed on the king’s orders because they had plotted to kill him. Leudefridus, duke of the Alamanni, also incurred the displeasure of the aforementioned king and went into hiding. Uncilenus the duke was appointed in his place.

In that year King Richaridus, embracing the Christian religion through divine love, was himself baptized first [Note: Boher. and others read: “he was first baptized secretly.”]. After this he ordered all the Goths who at that time held the Arian sect to assemble at Toledo [Note: On this matter see the Third Council of Toledo, in Labbe’s *Councils*, volume V, under the year 589. The king himself attended it and, together with his wife, subscribed to the profession of faith which the Goths accepted through his agency.]. He also ordered all the Arian books to be brought before him. Having them gathered in one house, he ordered them to be burned in a fire, and he caused all the Goths to be baptized into the Christian faith.

### IX

In that year the wife of the Persian emperor Anaulfus [Note: Others read *Aunulfus, Arnulfus,* or *Monaulfus*. Paul the Deacon, *On the Deeds of the Lombards*, Book IV, chapter 52, places this story in the time of Heraclius. John of Biclarum mentions in his chronicle a Persian emperor who, after making peace with Maurice, accepted the faith of Christ. Learned men interpret all these details as referring to the younger Chosroes, who, with the aid of the emperor Maurice, overthrew the tyrant Baram and recovered the kingdom from which he had been expelled. Fredegarius, Biclarensis, and even Theophylactus thought that he was a Christian because he married a Christian woman named Syra and openly professed that he had been restored to the kingdom through the aid of the holy martyr Sergius, whose church he richly endowed. See Evagrius, *History*, Book VI, chapters 19 and 20. Learned men nevertheless deny that he was a Christian. Gregory the Great praises Domitian, bishop of Melitene, in Book II, indiction 2, letter 63, because he labored, though unsuccessfully, for the conversion of the Persian emperor. John, called the Faster, bishop of Constantinople, whom Fredegarius mentions here, succeeded Eutychius in 582. He was famous for the title of “universal,” or “ecumenical,” which he arrogated to himself despite the opposition of Gregory the Great.] left her husband and came to blessed John, bishop of Constantinople, with four boys and the same number of girls. She said that she was one of the common people and asked the aforementioned blessed John for the grace of baptism. After she had been baptized by that pontiff, the empress Augusta of Maurice received her from the sacred font.

When her husband, the Persian emperor, repeatedly sought her return through embassies, and the emperor Maurice did not know that she was the emperor’s wife, the Augusta, seeing that she was extremely beautiful, suspected that she might be the woman whom the envoys were seeking. She said to them: “A certain woman has come here from Persia and said that she was one of the common people. Look at her; perhaps she is the one you seek.”

When the envoys saw her, they prostrated themselves on the ground and worshiped, saying that she was their mistress, whom they were seeking. The Augusta said to her: “Give them your answer.”

Then she replied: “I will not speak with these men; their life is like that of dogs. If they are converted and become Christians, as I am, then I will answer them.”

The envoys, however, willingly received the grace of baptism. Afterwards Caesara said to them: “If my husband is willing to become a Christian and receive the grace of baptism, I will gladly return to him. Otherwise I shall not go back to him at all.”

The envoys reported this to the Persian emperor, who immediately sent an embassy to the emperor Maurice, asking that Saint John come to Antioch, where he himself wished to receive baptism. Then the emperor Maurice ordered an immense preparation to be made at Antioch. There the Persian emperor was baptized with sixty thousand Persians, and for two weeks the Persians were baptized by John and the other bishops until the full number mentioned above [Col. 0614B] had been reached.

Gregory, bishop of Antioch [Note: He succeeded Saint Anastasius, who had been sent into exile, in 571. He is praised by Evagrius, Book VI, passim; by Theophanes; and by John Moschus, *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 140. He died in 592, after which Anastasius regained his see.], received that emperor from the font.

The emperor Anaulfus asked the emperor Maurice to provide him with bishops and sufficient clergy [Note: Boher. reads: “that he give him clergy … throughout Persia.”], whom he could establish in Persia so that all the Persians might receive the grace of baptism. Maurice granted this request willingly, and with the greatest speed all the Persians were baptized into the worship of Christ.

## AN. DLXXXIX

### X

In the twenty-ninth year of Guntchramnus, an army was sent into Spain [Note: That is, Septimania, as is evident from Book IX, chapter 31, of Gregory’s *History.]; but through the negligence of Boso, who was commander of the army, that army was severely slaughtered by the Goths.

## AN. DXC

### XI

In the thirtieth year of the reign of the aforesaid ruler, the tunic of our Lord Jesus Christ—which had been taken from him during his Passion and for which the soldiers guarding him cast lots [Col. 0614C]—was found. The prophet David speaks of it: “And upon my vesture they cast lots” (John 19:24; Psalm 21:19). It was revealed by Simon, son of Jacob, who, after suffering many tortures for two weeks, finally confessed that the tunic had been placed in a marble chest in the city of Zafad [Note: This is, as is commonly thought, Joppa, a famous city in Palestine formerly adorned with an episcopal see, now commonly called Jaffa, and by the Italians Jaffo or Zaffo. On this tunic see Book I of *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 8.], not far from Jerusalem.

Gregory of Antioch, Thomas of Jerusalem [Note: Papebrochius thinks that the name Thomas entered Fredegarius’ text by mistake, in place of Amos, whom he believes, from Greek catalogues, to have presided over the church of Jerusalem at that time. This Amos—or, as Nicephorus Callistus calls him, Neamus—is also absent from several catalogues. Aimoinus calls him Thomas, Book III of his *History*, chapter 78. Gregory and John have been discussed above.], and John, bishop of Constantinople, together with many other bishops, fasted for three days. Then, with the marble chest miraculously made light, as though it had been made of wood, they carried it on foot with the greatest devotion to Jerusalem. They set it triumphantly in the place where the Lord’s cross is worshiped.

In that year the moon was darkened. In the same year war arose between the Franks and the Britons over the river Vicinonia.

### XII

Beppelenus, duke of the Franks, was killed by the Britons through the plotting of Hebracharius, also a duke. Consequently Hebracharius was later stripped of his possessions and reduced to the utmost poverty.

## AN. DXCI

### XIII

In the thirty-first year of Guntchramnus’ reign, Theudefredus, duke beyond the Jura [Note: The region beyond the Jura is so called from the Jura mountain, between the Helvetians and the Sequani; it is commonly associated with Saint-Claude because of the famous Benedictine monastery there. It is also called Transjurane Burgundy, which had several kings toward the end of the ninth century and in the following century.], died. Wandalmarus succeeded him in the dignity of duke.

In the same year the duke Ago was raised to power in Italy over the Lombards.

## AN. DXCII

In the thirty-second year of Guntchramnus’ reign, from morning until midday the sun was so diminished that barely a third of it could be seen.

## AN. DXCIII

### XIV

In the thirty-third year of Guntchramnus’ reign, on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, the king himself died [Note: Valesius, Book XV of *Frankish Matters*, argues that Guntchramnus died in 592; hence, where it is stated below “in the second year of Childebertus,” he thinks “in the first year” should be read, and likewise thereafter. Old and recent martyrologies give Guntram’s name on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, on which day his feast is recorded in the very ancient calendar of Murbach, written about nine hundred years ago.], and was buried in the church of Saint Marcellus, in the monastery that he himself had built. Childebertus assumed his kingdom.

In the same year Quintrio [Note: Below, in chapter 18, Clar. has *Wintrio*. See the notes on Book VIII, chapter 18, of Gregory’s *History*. Paul the Deacon discusses this war in Book IV, chapter 4, of his *History of the Lombards*. Cointius distinguishes Quintrio from Wintrio, the father of Saint Glodesindis, under the year 749, number 25 and following.] the duke of Champagne entered Chlotharius’ kingdom with an army. Chlotharius went to meet him with his forces, turned Quintrio to flight, and inflicted heavy slaughter on both armies.

## AN. DXCIV

### XV

In the second year after Childebertus had received the kingdom of Burgundy, the armies of the Franks and Britons fought one another, and both sides suffered severe slaughter by the sword.

## AN. DXCV

In the third year of Childebertus’ reign in Burgundy, many signs appeared in the sky, including a comet. In that year Childebertus’ army fought vigorously against the Warnes [Note: We suspect that these were the Werini, whose laws are preserved under the title *Laws of the Angles and Wirini*, that is, the Thuringians. Procopius mentions the Warnes, whose king Radiger had married a daughter of Clovis the Great. See Cointius under the year 564 and elsewhere.], who had attempted to rebel; and the Warnes were so thoroughly slaughtered and defeated that few of them remained.

### XVI

In the fourth year after Childebertus had received Guntchramnus’ kingdom, Childebertus died [Note: If we believe Paul the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 12, he was killed by poison together with his wife; the older authors are silent on this point.], and his sons Theudebertus and Theudericus received his kingdom. Theudebertus received Austrasia, with his seat at Metz; Theudericus received Guntchramnus’ kingdom in Burgundy, with his seat at Orléans.

### XVII

In that year Fredegundis, together with her son King Chlotharius, occupied Paris and the other cities in barbarian fashion [Note: That is, by invasion and waging war before it had been declared, as barbarians are accustomed to do.], and moved an army against the sons of King Childebertus, Theudebertus and Theudericus, at a place called Latofao [Note: Some think that this place was situated in the diocese of Sens.].

The two sides set up their camps opposite one another. Chlotharius, attacking Theudebertus and Theudericus with his forces, severely slaughtered their army.

## AN. DXCVII

In the second year of Theudericus’ reign, Fredegundis died [Note: She was buried beside her husband in the basilica of Saint Vincent, or Saint-Germain-des-Prés, where her tombstone can still be seen. Perhaps no older monument of the burial of our kings, from the time they became Christians, survives anywhere. Fortunatus sings her praises in Book IX, poems 1 and following; the other authors curse her.].

## AN. DXCVIII

### XVIII

In the third year of Theudebertus’ reign, the duke Wintrio [Note: So Clar. and Ches. and others; the rest have *Quintrio*, as above.] was killed at the instigation of Brunichildis.

## AN. DXCIX

In the fourth year of Theudericus’ reign, Quolenus [Al.: Colenus], a Frank by birth, was appointed patrician. In that year a glandular plague [Note: Colb. has *Grandoraria*; several editions have “hail”; Ches. and others have *glandis* or *inguinis*.] severely ravaged Massilia and the other cities of Provence.

In that year extremely hot water in Lake Dunus, into which the river Arula [Note: Chesn. and Freh. have *Arola*, commonly the Aigre, which enters the Loir a little below Dunus—Châteaudun—almost together with Lake Dunus. Valesius, together with Labbe and the others who identify the place with the lake near the fortress of Ebrodunum—Yverdon—argues that Fredegarius’ passage cannot refer to Dunus of the Carnutes. That lake is now called Ebrodunensis, or, from the Neuchâtel region of Switzerland, Novoburgensis; together with the river Urba, it empties into the Arola—the Aar.], flows, boiled so violently that it cooked a great quantity of fish.

In that year Warnacharius [Note: Others read *Warneharius* or *Warncharius*.], mayor of the palace of Theudericus, died; he distributed all his property among the sustenance of the poor.

### XIX

In that year Brunichildis was expelled by the Austrasians, and in the Campania of Arciacum [Note: So called from the town of Arciacum on the river Aube, discussed in the *Epitome*. Cointius, under the year 599, argues that this story is fictitious, because the church of Auxerre was not vacant at that time and because Desiderius, who succeeded Aunacharius several years later, was not poor and was not such a man as is described here. Rather, he is called most noble in the *History of the Bishops of Auxerre*, chapters 19 and 20, and a relative of our kings. He died in 623 and was buried in the basilica of Saint-Germain with his predecessors. He is venerated as a saint on the sixth day before the Kalends of November.], she was found one day by a certain poor man. At her request he brought her to Theudericus. Theudericus willingly received his grandmother Brunichildis and honored her magnificently.

In return for this meritorious service, he assumed the bishopric of Auxerre through Brunichildis’ influence.

## AN. DC

### XX

In the fifth year of Theudericus’ reign, the signs that had appeared in the preceding year appeared again: fiery globes moving through the sky and, like a multitude of fiery spears, appearing toward the west.

In the same year the kings Theudebertus and Theudericus moved an army against King Chlotharius. They joined battle at the river Aroanna [Note: It is scarcely known to the local inhabitants and is commonly called the Ouaine. It runs through the territory of Sens and flows into the Loin near Moret. The place is called Dormelles, commonly Doromellum. Cointius, however, following Fauchet, says that the Aroanna rises near Troyes and flows into the Yonne near the city of Sens. In the testament of Saint Bertichramnus, bishop of Le Mans, a small river called the Aroena is mentioned; on its bank lies the town of Diablintes among the people of Le Mans.], not far from the village of Doromellum. There Chlotharius’ army was very severely slaughtered.

When Chlotharius and those who remained had been put to flight, they ravaged and devastated the districts and cities along the bank of the Sigona [Note: Ch. and others have *Sequana*, which this author generally calls *Sigona* or *Segona.] that had surrendered to Chlotharius. The cities were broken open, and a very great number of captives was carried away from there by the army of Theudericus and Theudebertus.

Overwhelmed, Chlotharius, willingly or unwillingly, confirmed by treaty that Theudericus should possess the territory between the Sigona and the Loire, extending to the Ocean and the frontier of the Britons; and that Theudebertus should receive the entire duchy of Dentelinus [Note: Below, chapter 37. Freh. and Ch. and others have *Denzelini*, and in chapter 76, *Danzileni*. It included the region lying between the Seine, the Isara—or Oise—and the Loire. The origin of the name is unknown to me.], extending along the Sigona and Isara to the Ocean. Only twelve districts between the Isara, the Sigona, and the coast of the Ocean remained to Chlotharius.

## AN. DCI

In the sixth year of Theudericus’ reign, Cautinus, duke of Theudebertus, was killed.

## AN. DCII

### XXI

In the seventh year of Theudericus’ reign [Note: The Colb. codex and Freh. read “in the sixth year,” and continue in this way with one year less through the ninth year. They, together with Boh., call this son Sigobertus.], a son was born to him by a concubine, named Sigibertus.

The patrician Aegila [Note: Colb., together with most editions, has *Agila*.], although no offenses had been established against him, was bound and killed at Brunichildis’ instigation, solely because greed prompted her to have his property taken into the fisc.

In that year Theudebertus and Theudericus sent an army against the Wascones; and, with God’s help, after defeating them, they brought them under their rule and made them tributaries. They appointed over them a duke named Genialis [Note: Colb. has *Gelianus*; most editions, *Gemialis*.], who ruled them successfully.

### XXII

In that year the body of Saint Victor, who had suffered martyrdom at Salodorum with Saint Ursus [Note: Boh. and several editions have *Ursio*. They belonged to the celebrated Theban Legion, which completed its martyrdom in these regions under Maximian Herculius. See *The Genuine Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 293, and Surius, under September 30. Salodorum, commonly Solothurn, is the capital of the eponymous district of the Catholic Swiss.], was found by the blessed bishop Aeconius of Maurienne [Note: Valesius prefers the reading *Aeonius*. He himself calls himself Hiconius in the First and Second Councils of Mâcon, which he attended. He was the first bishop of this see.].

One night, in his own city, it was revealed to him in a dream that he should rise immediately and go to the church which Queen Sedeleuba [Note: She was the sister of Chlotildis, the wife of Clovis the Great. See Gregory, *History*, Book II, chapter 28.] had built in the suburb of Geneva, to the place marked out in the middle of the church, where the holy body was present.

When he had hastened to Geneva with the blessed bishops Rusticius and Patricius [Note: Others have *Rusticus* and *Patricus*; *Rusticus* and *Patricius* is perhaps better. The bare names of both appear in the catalogue of the bishops of Geneva; nevertheless, one or the other seems to have been bishop of Octodurum, or Sion.], they fasted for three days. During the night a light appeared at the place where that glorious and splendid body lay. In silence, with tears and prayers, the three pontiffs lifted a stone and found it buried in a silver coffin. They found its face red, as though it were alive.

Prince Theudericus was present there and, contributing many possessions to this church, confirmed there the greater part of Warnacharius’ property.

From the very day on which it was found, extraordinary miracles have been continuously displayed at that holy tomb by the Lord’s favor.

In that year Aetherius, bishop of Lyon, died; Secundinus was ordained bishop in his place.

### XXIII

In that year Phocas [Note: The beginning of Phocas’ reign is assigned to this very year in a public document promulgated at Rome by Saint Gregory; this confirms the chronology followed here. The document stands at the beginning of Book XI of that pontiff’s letters.]—duke and patrician of the state, returning victorious from the Persians—killed the emperor Maurice and assumed the empire in his place.

## AN. DCIII

### XXIV

In the eighth year of Theudericus’ reign, a son was born to him by a concubine, named Childebertus. A synod was convened at Cabillonum. They deposed Desiderius, bishop of Vienne; and, at the instigation of Aridius, bishop of Lyon, and Brunichildis, Domnolus was substituted in his place in the priestly office. Desiderius, however, was confined in exile on a certain island.

In that year the sun was darkened.

At that same time Berthoaldus, a Frank by birth, was mayor of Theudericus’ palace. He was measured in character, wise and cautious, brave in battle, and faithful toward everyone.

## AN. DCIV

In the ninth year of Theudericus’ reign, a son was born to him by a concubine, named Corbus.

Since Protadius, a Roman by birth, was now greatly honored by everyone at court, and Brunichildis wished, because of sexual intercourse, to raise him to positions of honor, after Duke Wandalmarus had died Protadius was appointed patrician over the district beyond the Jura and that of the Scotingi [Note: We learn the location of the district of the Scotingi, or Scutingi, from the *Life of Saint Anatolius, Bishop and Patron of Salins*, which has *Scodinga in the Sequani*, where Salins is now situated. Salinae, commonly Salins, is a town on the river Forica in the county of Burgundy, between Dole and Besançon, and is the seat of an archdeaconry of the same name. See Valesius’ note under the word *Sculingi*.], at Brunichildis’ instigation.
