In order that Bertoaldus might perish instead, they sent him as far as the Ocean, along the bank of the Sigona and through the districts and cities, to collect the fisc’s revenues.

### XXV

Bertoaldus, sent by Theudericus [Al.: “to Theudericus”], hastened to those regions with only three hundred men. When he had reached the villa of Arelaum [Note: Most editions have *Arelaus*; Boh. and Chesn., together with Aimoinus, have *Arelaunum*. This was the name of a forest and royal villa not far from the famous monastery of Fontenelle in the diocese of Rouen, on the peninsula formed by the Seine. See Book IV of *On Diplomatic Matters*. Others may perhaps think that the distance between this place and Gennabum was too great for Bertoaldus, fleeing from there, to have taken refuge within the walls of Orléans.], and was hunting there, Chlotharius, learning this, sent his son Meroveus and Landericus [Note: Colb. has *Landricus*; others, *Landericus*.], mayor of the palace, with an army to suppress Bertoaldus.

He presumed, contrary to the treaty, to invade most of the districts and cities between the Sigona and the Loire belonging to Theudericus’ kingdom.

When Bertoaldus heard this and could not withstand them, he turned his back and entered Orléans, where he was received by the most blessed bishop Austrinus.

Landericus surrounded Orléans with his army and called upon Bertoaldus to come out for battle. Bertoaldus answered from the wall:

“In single combat, the two of us alone—if you decide to wait for me—let us join battle, while the rest of the multitude stands at a distance. Let us be judged by the Lord.”

But Landericus postponed doing this.

Bertoaldus added: “Since you do not dare to do it, at the next opportunity our lords will join battle over what you are doing. Let you and I both put on crimson garments [Note: So the manuscripts and editions read, except Chesn. and Freh., which have *vermiola*. Aimoinus has this word. Learned men nevertheless think that the color “worm-colored,” or vermilion, is intended; the term occurs frequently among authors. Hence the vernacular word *vermeil*. Thus *vermiclae* garments, that is, purple or scarlet garments (*d’écarlate*), are so called as though they were the color of the *vermiculus*, the cochineal insect. Indeed, in the *Life of Charlemagne*, where the adornment or dress of the ancient Franks is described, among the other garments are listed *fasciolae crurales vermiculatae*, vermilion-colored leg bands.], and let us go before the others wherever the battle is joined. There the advantage of both you and me will appear; and before God let us promise one another that the truth of this promise will stand.”

### XXVI

When this had taken place on the feast day of Saint Martin the bishop, and Theudericus had learned that part of his kingdom had been invaded by Chlotharius contrary to the treaty, he immediately came with an army at Christmas to Stampae [Note: Ch. has “on the river Loa.” The town of Stampae, however, lies on the river Juine, which a little farther downstream is enlarged by the greater and lesser Loa rivers.], traveling along the river Loa.

There Meroveus, son of King Chlotharius, came to meet him with Landericus and a large army.

Because the passage where the river Loa is crossed was narrow [Note: So Clar. and Boh. Colb. has: “and since that place where the river Loa is crossed was narrow.” Freh. lacks the word “place.” Others read: “since, however, the place was passable.” The chronicles of Saint Benignus and Besançon have: “since the place was steep,” and so forth.], and scarcely a third of Theudericus’ army had crossed, battle was joined.

There Bertoaldus, according to the agreement, advanced, calling out to Landericus. But Landericus did not dare, as he had promised, to enter into so great a contest.

Bertoaldus had advanced too far ahead of the others and was killed there, together with his men, by Chlotharius’ army; he did not wish to escape from there because he knew that Protadius would strip him of the honor of his rank.

There Meroveus, son of Chlotharius, was captured; Landericus was put to flight; and a very great number of Chlotharius’ army was slaughtered by the sword in that battle.

Theudericus entered Paris as victor. Theudebertus made peace with Chlotharius at the villa of Compendium, and both their armies returned unharmed to their own territories.

### A.D. 605

### XXVII

In the tenth year of King Theuderic’s reign, Protadius was appointed master of the household at Brunhild’s instigation and by Theuderic’s command. He was exceedingly shrewd and energetic in everything, but he displayed a savage injustice toward individuals, assigning far too much to the treasury [Note: Colb. and several printed editions read, “exacting far too much, and from the property…”], cleverly stripping people of their possessions in order to fill the treasury and enrich himself. Whenever he found anyone noble by birth, he tried to humble him completely, so that no one might be found capable of assuming the rank he had attained. Having harassed these and others with excessive cunning, he made almost everyone in the kingdom of Burgundy his enemy.

When Brunhild continually urged her grandson Theuderic to take up arms against Theudebert, saying, “As though Theudebert were not Childebert’s son [Note: Learned men consider this false, as seems clear from Gregory’s *History*, Book VIII, chapter 37, and Book IX, chapter 4. Both were born of Faileuba, Childebert’s legitimate wife. If she is sometimes called a concubine by certain authors, we must remember that this term was frequently used to designate legitimate wives who had been born of lowly stock.], but the son of some gardener,” and Protadius likewise supported her in this advice, the army was at last set in motion by Theuderic’s command.

When Theuderic had pitched camp with his army at a place called Caraciacum [Note: This is Carisiacum, which later became so famous among the royal palaces. Boh. has *Caraciate*.], his leudes urged him to make peace with Theudebert [Note: Manuscripts and several editions read, “he urged each of them.”]. Protadius urged each man individually that battle be joined. Theudebert was encamped nearby with his army.

Then the entire army of Theuderic, finding an opportunity, rushed upon Protadius, saying that it was better for one man to die [Note: Others read, “to be dead”; others, “to die rather than so great a…”] than for the whole army to be put in danger. Protadius was sitting in King Theuderic’s tent, playing at a board game with Peter the chief physician. When the army had already surrounded him on every side, and Theuderic’s leudes were restraining Theuderic from going there, Theuderic sent Uncilenus to announce his order to the army: that they should withdraw from the ambush against Protadius.

Uncilenus immediately announced to the army: “Thus commands our lord Theuderic: Protadius is to be killed.” They rushed upon him, cutting into the king’s tent with their swords on every side, and killed Protadius. Theuderic, confused and compelled, made peace with his brother Theudebert, and both armies returned unharmed to their own seats after Protadius’s death [Others read, “after Protadius’s slaughter”].

### A.D. 606

### XXVIII

In the eleventh year of King Theuderic’s reign, Claudius, a Roman by birth [Note: Others read *Docudius*. This author also calls those “Romans” who were not Frankish by origin but belonged to the ancient families of Gaul, which had been subject to the Romans before Frankish rule was established in Gaul.], was appointed master of the household. He was a prudent man, pleasant in conversation, energetic in everything, devoted to patience, rich in sound judgment, educated in literary studies, full of faith, and intent on cultivating friendship with everyone. Fearing the examples of his predecessors, he showed himself gentle and patient in ascending to this office [Others read, “in this ascent”]. His only impediment was that he was weighed down by the bulk of his body.

### A.D. 607

In the twelfth year of King Theuderic’s reign, Uncilenus—who had treacherously spoken in connection with Protadius’s death—was mutilated in the foot, stripped of his property, and reduced to weakness [Note: Chesne and others read, “reduced to shortness”; Boh., “to baseness”], at Brunhild’s instigation.

### XXIX

Vulf, the patrician, who likewise, at Brunhild’s instigation and on her advice, had consented to Protadius’s death, was killed at the villa of Fauriniacum [Note: This place was famous for its Benedictine monastery, first for women and later for men; it is commonly called Favernay, on the small river Lantenne in the county of Burgundy and the diocese of Besançon [Col. 0621D]. In Louis the Pious’s statute it is called *Fariniacum*, as here in Ch. and Freh. Since the time of Saint Bernard, who mentions it in Letter 347, it has commonly been called *Faberniacum* or *Faverniacum*. There is also Favernach near Freiburg in Breisgau, and Favernay, a village between Dijon and Auxonne in Burgundy.], by Theuderic’s command. Richomer, a Roman by birth, was appointed in his place as patrician.

In the same year, a son of Theuderic was born of a concubine, named Meroveus, whom Chlothar received from the holy font.

### XXX

In the same year Theuderic sent Aridius, bishop of Lyon, Roccon [Note: Most printed editions read *Rogonem et Eborinum*; Colb. reads *Rocconem et Ebronium*, adding in another hand, “counts of the stable”; Aimoinus agrees, reading “prefects of the horses.”], and Aepporinus, master of the stable, to Betteric [Note: Colb. and other editions read *Bethericum*. He was Witteric, who, after killing Liuba II, seized the kingdom of the Visigoths in 603.], king of Spain, so that they might bring back his daughter Ermenberg to be joined in marriage to Theuderic. After they had given oaths that she would never be degraded from the kingdom by Theuderic, they received her and presented her to Theuderic at Chalon. He received her gladly and with every mark of care.

By the plotting of her grandmother Brunhild, she did not know sexual intercourse with a man. Through the instigating words of her grandmother Brunhild and of her sister Theudilana [Note: So Clar., Boh., and the others; but Colb., with most printed editions, reads *Theodelinda*. Of her, see below, chapter 42.], she became hated. After a year had passed [Note: From these words some infer that what follows should be assigned to the thirteenth year of Theuderic], Theuderic, having stripped Ermenberg of her treasures, sent her back to Spain.

### XXXI

Betteric, indignant at this, sent an embassy to Chlothar. Chlothar’s envoy proceeded with Betteric’s envoy to Theudebert. Again, envoys of Theudebert, together with the envoys of Chlothar and Betteric, went to Ago [Note: This was Agilulf, king of the Lombards, also called Ago, as Paul the Deacon notes in Book IV, chapters 1 and 43; see above, the notes on Gregory’s *History*, Book X, chapter 3.], king of Italy. These four kings unanimously invaded Theuderic with an army from every side, intending to take away his kingdom and condemn him to death, because they held him in such awe.

The envoy of the Goths, however, returned from Italy to Spain by ship across the sea. But this plan, by divine providence, did not achieve its purpose. When Theuderic learned of it, he despised it most courageously.

### XXXII

That year, Theuderic, acting on the treacherous advice of Aridius, bishop of Lyon, and persuaded by his grandmother Brunhild, ordered Saint Desiderius, who had returned from exile, to be stoned [Note: Saint Desiderius, bishop of Vienne, suffered in the year 607, on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, in the territory of Lyon beside the river Chalaronne. At the place where he suffered there now stands a village bearing his own name. Cointius discusses him at greater length in volume II under this year, where he attempts to defend Aridius from the crimes attributed to him here and in the preceding chapters. The martyrdom of Saint Desiderius is to be read in Ado’s letter to the church of Vienne, over which he himself presided in the ninth century.]. At his tomb the Lord has deigned, with unbroken constancy, to display marvelous miracles from the day of his passing.

It must therefore be believed that, for this evil deed, the kingdom of Theuderic and of his sons was destroyed.

### XXXIII

That year [Note: This chapter is absent from the Colb. manuscript, which Cointius calls the Metz manuscript. Yet it cannot be called an interpolation, since it is found in an old copy of the College of Clermont, which was certainly transcribed not long after the author’s time. The author of the appendix to Marius’s *Chronicle* has almost the same account. In any case, Sisebodus—or, as the printed editions have it, Sisebutus—was appointed in place of Gundemar, Witteric’s successor, in the year 612; Fredegar’s reckoning must therefore be corrected. See Isidore’s praise of Sisebutus in his *Chronicle*, under the year 650 of the era.], after Betteric’s death, Sisebodus succeeded to the kingdom of Spain. He was a wise man, highly praised throughout all Spain, and exceedingly full of piety. For he also fought courageously against the imperial power [Note: That is, against the Romans, or the emperor. Elsewhere he often calls it “the commonwealth,” and below “the imperial portion.”]

He brought the province of Cantabria [Note: It belonged to Hispania Tarraconensis; today it is commonly called Biscay. Some ancient authors also call its inhabitants Basculi or Bascli.] under the Gothic kingdom, although the Franks had once possessed it. A duke named Francio, who had subjected Cantabria during the time of Frankish rule [Note: That is, had conquered it. The printed editions read, “had governed it.” Boh. has, “had acted in it.” Cointius therefore supposes that this Francio had been appointed governor of Cantabria by Childebert and Chlothar, who had conquered it, as he infers from Gregory’s *History*, Book III, chapter 29.], had for a long time paid tribute to the Frankish kings.

But when Cantabria had been recalled from the imperial side [Note: Some editions read, “when he had been recalled.” Moreover, “from the imperial side” means “from the emperor’s army”; or perhaps one should read “to the imperial side,” that is, “restored to the empire”], it was seized by the Goths, as stated above. Sisebodus also took many cities from the Roman Empire along the seacoast and destroyed them to their foundations.

When the Romans were being slaughtered by Sisebodus’s army, Sisebodus, full of pity, said: “Alas for me, wretched man, in whose time so great a shedding of human blood is taking place!” He saved from death everyone whom he could encounter. The Gothic kingdom in Spain was consolidated along the seacoast as far as the Pyrenees.

### XXXIV

Ago, king of the Lombards, took as his wife Theudelinda, sister of Grimoald and Gundoald, of Frankish descent [Note: Colb., in another hand, and Ch. and others read, “of Bavarian descent.” Theodelinda had first married Authari, Ago’s or Agilulf’s predecessor. See Paul the Deacon, Book III, chapter 31, and Book IV, chapters 5 and following. She is said to have been of Frankish descent not only because Bavaria was then under Frankish rule, but also because, as many think, she had as her grandmother Ragintrude, daughter of Theudebert I. Moreover, she appears to have had as her mother Ultrado, widow of King Theudebald.], whom Childebert had betrothed.

When he had set her aside on Brunhild’s advice, Gundoald brought his sister Theudelinda to Italy with all her possessions and gave her in marriage to Ago. Gundoald took as his wife a woman of noble Lombard family, by whom he had two sons, named Gundebert and Charibert [Note: Others read *Haribert*, which amounts to the same thing.].

King Ago, son of King Authari, had by Theudelinda a son named Adoald [Another: Odoald] and a daughter named Gundoberg. While Gundoald was greatly loved by the Lombards, Ago and Theudelinda, having already conceived jealousy against him, arranged for him to be killed. While he was sitting on a *fald(e)on* to relieve his bowels [Note: From this comes *faldistorium*, commonly *un fauteuil*, a word which some derive from the Saxon word *fald*. See Du Cange’s *Glossary*.], he died, wounded by an arrow.

### A.D. 608

### XXXV

In the thirteenth year of King Theuderic’s reign, while Theudebert had Bilichild as his wife [Note: Others read *Belichildis*; and below, “he might see,” but more often, “Brunhild’s envoys.”], whom Brunhild had purchased from merchants, Bilichild was useful and intensely loved by all the Austrasians. She conducted herself honorably in Theudebert’s simplicity and considered herself in no way inferior to Brunhild, but often treated Brunhild with contempt through envoys, while Brunhild reproached her for having been Brunhild’s slave.

At length, through these and other words, with envoys going back and forth, they provoked one another. An assembly was arranged between Colerense and Suentense [Note: Ch. and Freh. read *placitus*. Another copy of Ch. has *Colcunse et Soitense*, or *Segintense*. Col., Bign., Bar., Ill., and Boch. read: “It was arranged that an assembly should be held at Colecense and Solnitense.” Boh. and Colb. read *in Colerense et Sogintense*. These were neighboring districts, the first in Austrasia, the second in Burgundy, and the assembly was held on their borders. The district named Sugintensis appears to be the Suntgau, in the province of Maxima Sequanorum toward Alsace; some assign this district to Upper Alsace. The other is unknown.], so that these two queens might be brought together to confer for the sake of peace between Theuderic and Theudebert. But Bilichild, following the counsel of the Austrasians, delayed coming there.

### A.D. 609

### XXXVI

In the fourteenth year of King Theuderic’s reign, the fame of blessed Columban had already spread widely through the cities and throughout the provinces of Gaul and Germany [Note: What is contained here to the end of this chapter is found in exactly the same words in Jonas’s *Life of Saint Columban*, sections 31 and following, in the *Acta Sanctorum* of the Benedictine Order, second century, p. 17.]. He was praised by the report of everyone and revered by everyone’s devotion, so much so that King Theuderic often came to him at Luxeuil [Note: The printed editions, together with Colb., read *Luxovium*, and likewise below. Columban had founded a monastery there, which from that time onward was exceedingly famous both for holiness and for the number of its monks. It still exists, together with the town of the same name, in the county of Burgundy, commonly called Luxeuil, subject to the congregation of Saint Vitonus of the Order of Saint Benedict.].

Whenever he came to him, the man of God began to rebuke him for mingling with the adulteries of concubines rather than enjoying the consolations of a lawful marriage, so that royal offspring might come from an honorable queen and not appear to emerge from brothels.

When the king’s speech had already yielded to the man of God’s command and he promised to separate himself from every illicit relationship, Brunhild’s mind—she was a second Jezebel [Note: Colb. and Clar. read *Zezabelis*; another copy of Ch. has “diabolical”; the old edition of Boch. and the others, “according to ancient and detestable [customs].” Ill. reads “detestable.” Cointius denies that King Theuderic took unlawful wives and thinks there was no reason for this hostility except that Columban had barred secular men, including princes and Brunhild herself, from entering his monastery. This is the only cause mentioned by the contemporary author of the *Life of Saint Aile of Rebais*. Perhaps this was the first occasion of the quarrels, from which, as often happens, others later arose. It is therefore surprising to see the religious zeal of our Fathers in avoiding the company of secular people. For the great care they took to preserve this discipline of excluding secular persons from monasteries, see Mabillon, preface to the second century of the Benedictines, no. 53.], the ancient serpent—approached her and, pricking her with the goad of pride, stirred her up against the man of God, because she saw Theuderic obeying him.

She feared that, if he dismissed his concubines and placed a queen at the head of the court, he would diminish the measure of her dignity and honor.

It happened, then, that one day blessed Columban came to Brunhild. At that time she was at the villa of Brucariacum [Note: In the *Life of Saint Columban* it is called *Brocariaca*. It is a village situated between Chalon and Autun, commonly called Bourcheresse.]. When she saw him coming into the court, she brought to the man of God Theuderic’s sons, whom she had by adulterous unions. When he saw them, he asked what they wanted.

Brunhild replied: “They are the king’s sons; strengthen them with your blessing.”

But he said: “By no means. Know that these boys will not receive royal scepters; they have emerged from brothels.”

Furious, she ordered the children to leave. As the man of God was leaving the royal court [Note: Others read, “the queen’s court.” Below, “he then prepared…”] and stepping across the threshold, a crash struck him with terror, yet it did not restrain the wretched woman’s fury; thereafter she prepared to devise an ambush.

Through messengers she ordered the monastery’s neighbors to allow none of the monks to travel outside the monastery’s boundaries, and to provide neither lodging nor any kind of support to his monks [Note: Colb. and the editions read, “or to anyone any support.”].

When blessed Columban saw that royal minds had been stirred against him, he hurried to them, so that by his admonitions they might break the incentives to wretched obstinacy [Note: So Boh.; others read, “they might break the wretched woman’s fixed purpose.”]. At that time they were at the royal villa of Spinsia [Note: Elsewhere called *Spissia*, commonly Espoisse, situated between Semur and Montbard in the duchy of Burgundy, not far from the river Serene, which, after passing through the district of Auxerre, joins the Yonne.].

When he arrived there at sunset, they announced to the king that the man of God was there but did not wish to pitch his tent in the royal buildings. Theuderic then said that it was better to honor the man of God with appropriate provisions than to provoke the Lord to anger through an offense against his servants. He therefore ordered provisions to be prepared suitably in royal fashion and sent to God’s servant.

They came, and in accordance with the king’s command presented what had been offered [Another: “what had been prepared”]. When he saw the dishes and cups served with royal ceremony, he asked what these things meant. They told him: “They have been sent to you by the king.”

He rejected them, saying: “It is written: ‘The Most High rejects the gifts of the wicked’” (Proverbs 15:8). “For it is not right that the mouths of God’s servants should be polluted by his food [Note: Boh. reads, “that the prayers of God’s servants should be polluted by these things”; Freh., “it is not worthy… that he be polluted.” Some old editions read, “that God’s servants should be polluted by his gifts.”], since he denies access not only to his own dwellings but also to those of others to God’s servants.”

After he had said this, all the vessels were smashed to pieces, the wines and strong drinks were poured out on the ground, and the remaining provisions were scattered separately. The frightened servants reported to the king what had happened [Another: “the reason for what had happened”]. Struck with fear, he and his grandmother hurried at dawn to the man of God. They asked forgiveness for their offense and promised to amend their conduct in the future.

Pacified by these promises, he returned to the monastery, but the pledges of the promised guarantee were soon violated and not kept [Note: Freh. reads: “but the oath promised by the power of the devil was not long kept. It was violated.”]. The increase of their miseries followed, and the king continued his adulteries as usual.

When he heard this, blessed Columban sent him a letter full of blows [Note: The old printed editions read, “full of rebukes.”] and threatened excommunication if he did not hasten to amend. Brunhild was again aroused by this and stirred up the king’s mind against Saint Columban, striving with every effort to disturb it. She urged the courtiers and all the leading men to agitate the king’s mind against the man of God. She also began to solicit the bishops, so that by disparaging his religious life they might stain the standing of the rule which he had imposed on his monks to observe [Note: Others read, “and by disparaging his religious life and the standing of the rule…” Colb., in another hand, as also Jonas in the *Life of Saint Columban*, reads, “and by disparaging his religious life they might stain the standing…” Clar. has “might stain” below.].

The royal courtiers, therefore, obeying the persuasions of the wretched queen, disturbed the king’s mind against the man of God, compelling the king, once forced, to come and examine the religious observance [Note: Chesne reads, “having been compelled.” Jonas: “and so the king, being compelled…”]. Thus the king came to Columban at Luxeuil and complained to him that he was departing from the customs of his fellow countrymen and that access within the more secluded enclosures was not open to all Christians.

Blessed Columban, bold and strong in spirit, answered the king when he made these accusations: he did not customarily open the dwelling places of God’s servants to secular men and those alien to religion. He had, however, suitable and appropriate places prepared for this purpose, where the arrival of all guests could be received.

The king replied: “If you wish to receive the gifts of our generosity and the supplement of our support, access will be open in every place.”

The man of God answered: “If you try to violate what until now has been confined under the reins of the rule [Another: “constructed under the rule”], know that I will be sustained by neither your gifts nor any kind of support from you. And if you have come here for this reason—to destroy the monasteries of God’s servants and stain the discipline of the rule—know that your kingdom will utterly collapse and perish together with your entire royal offspring [Another: “will be overwhelmed”].”

The outcome of events later proved this true. For the rash king had already entered the refectory. Terrified by these words, he quickly went back outside.

After this the king was pressed by the harsh rebukes of the man of God [Note: We have restored the following passage, down to the words “by which he came,” with the help of the manuscripts and Jonas; it is corrupt in the printed editions.]. Theuderic said to him: “You hope to win for me the crown of martyrdom; know that I am not so insane as to commit so great a crime. Rather, know that I shall devise a better course for you, so that the man who departs from the customs of all secular people may strive to return by the road by which he came [Note: Others read, “who had departed,” or “may depart.”].”

The courtiers burst forth with one voice, saying that they did not wish to have in those places anyone who would not associate with everyone. Blessed Columban replied that he would not leave the monastery’s enclosure unless he were dragged out by force.

The king therefore departed, leaving behind a leading man named Baudulf [Note: Colb., Boh., and most editions read *Audulfum* or *Adalfum*. Ch. in another copy and Freh. read, “a leading man named Audulfum.”]. When he remained there, he expelled the man of God from the monastery and led him into exile near the town of Besançon, until the royal decision should determine what was to be done with him.

After this, the man of God saw that he was not troubled by any guards and suffered harassment from no one. Everyone saw God’s power blazing in him, and therefore all kept away from injuring him, lest they become partners in guilt. On the Lord’s day, therefore, he climbed to the summit of the lofty peak of that mountain. Such is the position of the city: the dense cluster of houses lies on the spreading, sloping side of the mountain, while the heights rise sharply into lofty summits. These are cut off on every side by the channel of the river Dova [Note: Most printed editions, together with Colb., read *Deme*; Boh., *Deviae*; Freh., *Deniae*; another copy of Ch., *Duvii*. It is the river Dubis, the Doubs, which flows past Besançon, the capital of the Sequani.], whose waters surround them and leave travelers no passage.

There he waited until midday, to see whether anyone would prevent his return by the road to the monastery. When no opposition appeared, he himself returned through the middle of the city to the monastery with his companions.

When Brunhild and Theuderic heard that he had returned from exile, they were provoked by even more savage goads of anger. They ordered Count Bertharius to search carefully for the man with an armed escort, and likewise sent Baudulf, whom I mentioned above [Note: Colb. and most editions read, “to search carefully for the man”; the one whom he had sent above.].

When they arrived, they found blessed Columban in the church, engaged with the entire congregation of the brothers in psalmody [Note: *Psallentio*, that is, in present-day language, “psalmody.” Those who introduced *psallentem* did not correct the text properly.] and prayer. They addressed the man of God as follows:

“We ask you to obey both the royal commands and ours, and to leave by the road by which you first came to these places [Note: Most editions read, “not so much the royal commands as ours.”].”

But he replied: “I do not think it pleases the Creator that one should return again to the native soil which one once left for fear of Christ.”

When they saw that the man of God would in no way obey them, Bertharius left, abandoning certain men in whom the fierceness of spirit was stronger. Those who remained urged the man of God to have pity on them, since they had unhappily been left to carry out such a deed, and to consider their danger. If they did not drag him away by force, they would incur the danger of death.

He replied that he had already declared many times that he would not depart unless dragged away by force. Surrounded by this double danger and pressed on every side by fear, they touched the cloak with which the man of God was clothed. Others fell on their knees and tearfully begged him to forgive them for the guilt of so great a crime, since they were obeying not their own wishes but the royal commands.

Seeing that danger would result if he satisfied his own severity, the man of God departed amid great lamentation and sorrow, with guards assigned to him who were not to leave him until he had been expelled from the king’s dominion. The first among them was Ragumundus [Note: In the *Life of Saint Columban*, *Ragamundus*; Freh., *Raguimundus*], who escorted him as far as Nantes.

Thus expelled from Theuderic’s kingdom, he again intended to return to the island of Ireland. But since no one can take a step on a journey unless it is granted by the Most High [Note: Colb., in another hand, reads: “But warned by the Spirit not to seek again what he had once left, he turned his steps back and sought Italy.”], the saint himself sought Italy and, building a monastery of holy observance at a place called Bobbio [Note: Bobbio is situated in a very deep valley in the Cottian Alps, beside the river of the same name, not far from the Trebia and the Apennines. It grew into a town and was given an episcopal see in the year 1014. The monastery still survives, although small, under the Cassinese congregation. For more, see Mabillon’s *Italian Journey*, p. 215. Saint Columban died in the year 615; Bede and Wandelbertus record his feast on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December, while others place it on the ninth. Paul the Deacon, Aimoinus, and the others praise him.], departed to Christ full of days.

[Note: In Colb., in another but ancient hand, the following has been added in the margin. It appears to have been taken from an anonymous author who wrote the *Deeds of the Franks* under King Theuderic, from chapter 38: “Queen Brunhild, however, did not cease daily urging Theuderic, saying: ‘Why do you neglect, and why do you not seek, your father’s treasure and his kingdom from the hand of Theudebert, when you know that he is not your brother? For he was born in adultery from your father’s concubine.’ Stirred to some degree by these and similar incitements, one began to rise up against the other. See above, chapter 27.”]

### A.D. 610

### XXXVII

In the fifteenth year of King Theuderic’s reign [Note: So the manuscripts and Freh.; Col., Bign., Bar., and Boch. erroneously read “the twelfth year.” Ch. does not give the year], while he held the Alsatians [Note: That is, Alsace, a very well-known province, where Theuderic had been brought up at Marlenheim, as Gregory of Tours reports. From this passage the learned Obrecht, in his *Prodromus of Alsatian History*, rightly rejects the opinion of those who have written that the name Alsace is nowhere found in authors before the eighth century.], which he had received from his father Childebert, Theudebert invaded them in barbarian fashion.

Accordingly, the two kings arranged an assembly at the fortress of Saloissa [Note: It is remarkable how variously the name of this place has been written. It lies on the Rhine between Saverne and Brumath and is commonly called Seltz. See Valesius’s note under *Saletio*.], so that the matter might be settled by the judgment of the Franks.

Theuderic came there with only ten thousand *scarites* [Note: The manuscripts read *utrumque*. I think that soldiers are designated by the term *scariti*, so called from *scara*, a word expressing a troop of soldiers or a battle line. From this came the French word *escarmouche*, “skirmish.” See Alteserra on this passage and Du Cange’s *Glossary*.].

Theudebert, however, with a large army of Austrasians, undertook to join battle there. When Theuderic was surrounded on every side by Theudebert’s army, Theuderic, forced and compelled, terrified by fear, confirmed the Alsatians as belonging to Theudebert’s side through a treaty. He also surrendered the Suggentians, the Turenses, and the Campanenses [Note: Above, in the note to chapter 35, we discussed the county of Sugintensis, commonly called Suntgau. The Turensis, which Aimoinus carelessly calls Turonensis, appears to be the Turgau, a district of the Helvetians between the Zürich district and Lake Constance. Cointius thinks that by the name Campanensis is meant that part of Champagne lying around the banks of the Seine, above and below the city of Troyes, which Guntram had previously held. Yet this district appears to have been not far from Sugintensis and Turensis. Another copy of Ch. and Freh. read *Campianenses*.], which he had often reclaimed, and seemed likewise to have lost.

Both kings returned to their own seats.

In those days the Alamanni also entered Upper Jura hostilely through the district of Aventicum [Note: Aventicum, once a famous city and the capital of the Helvetians, is now reduced to a village. It had as its bishop Marius, the author of the *Chronicle*, who subscribed to the Second Council of Mâcon in 585. His episcopal seat has now been transferred to Lausanne. We call the place Avenche; the inhabitants call it Wiflisburg.]. After plundering that district, Counts Abbelinus and Herpinus [Note: Some printed editions read *Appellinus et Erpinus*; others *Abbelenus*.], together with the other counts of that district, advanced with an army to meet the Alamanni.

Each side joined its battle lines [Note: So the manuscripts. Some editions read, “the ranks.” Below, “most of them”; Colb., “more of them then.”]. The Alamanni defeated the Upper Jura forces, slaughtered and overthrew most of them with the sword, and burned the greater part of the territory of Aventicum. They carried off an exceedingly large number of people into captivity, and then returned with their booty to their own country.

Because of these injuries, Theuderic thereafter continually deliberated how he might crush Theudebert. That year Bilichild [Note: Others read *Belieldis*. She was Theudebert’s wife, as stated above, in chapter 35] was killed by Theudebert. Theudebert took as his wife a girl named Theudichild.

### A.D. 611

In the sixteenth year of Theuderic’s reign, Theuderic sent an embassy to Chlothar, declaring that he wished to attack Theudebert as an enemy because he was not his brother. If Chlothar did not support Theudebert, then, should Theuderic overcome him, Chlothar was to receive under his own rule the duchy of Dentelin [Note: Others read *Denzelini*, and likewise below], which he had declared void against Theudebert. Once this agreement between Theuderic and Chlothar had been confirmed through the exchange of envoys, Theuderic set his army in motion.

## AN. 612. XXXVIII

In the seventeenth year of King Theuderic, an army was assembled at Lingones in the month of May from all the provinces of his kingdom. Advancing through Andelot, and having captured the fortress of Nasium, it proceeded to the city of Toul. There Theudebert, advancing to meet it with the Austrasian army, engaged in battle on the plain of Toul. Theuderic defeated Theudebert and routed his army. An enormous number of brave men from that army were slain in the same battle.

Theudebert, turning his back and coming through the territory of Metz, crossed the Vosges and reached Cologne in flight. Theuderic followed behind with his army. The blessed and apostolic man Leonisius, bishop of the city of Mainz, who was concerned for Theuderic’s advantage and hated Theudebert’s folly, came to Theuderic and said:

“What you have begun, complete. You ought rightly to pursue the purpose of this undertaking, since it has been so advantageous to you.”

A rustic tale is told: when a wolf had climbed a mountain and his cubs had already begun to hunt, he called them to himself on the mountain and said:

“As far as your eyes are able to see in every direction, you have no friends except the few who are of your own kind. Complete, therefore, what you have begun.”

Theuderic crossed the Ardennes with his army and reached Tolbiac. Theudebert, with the Saxons, Thuringians, and the other peoples whom he had been able to gather from beyond the Rhine and from every quarter, marched against Theuderic at Tolbiac. There battle was joined again. The Franks and the other peoples are said to have maintained that from ancient times there had never been, nor perhaps ever would be, a battle of such magnitude.

For such slaughter was inflicted by both armies that the phalanxes, fighting against one another at the beginning of the conflict, had nowhere to lay the corpses of the slain; instead, the dead stood upright among the other corpses, packed together as though they were alive.

But with the Lord once again going before him, Theuderic defeated Theudebert, and from Tolbiac to Cologne Theudebert’s army was slaughtered by the sword. The corpses covered the surface of the land, and on that very day he proceeded to Cologne, where he took possession of all Theudebert’s treasures.

Theuderic sent Bertharius, his chamberlain, across the Rhine in pursuit of Theudebert. Bertharius followed Theudebert closely and, when he was already fleeing with only a few companions, captured him and presented him to Theuderic at Cologne, stripped of his royal clothing. Theudebert was deprived of his garments, and his horse with its royal trappings, together with all this, was granted by Theuderic to Bertharius.

Theudebert was sent in chains to Chalon. His little son, Meroveus, was seized at Theuderic’s command; a certain man struck him by the foot against a stone, and, with his brain burst from his skull, he gave up his spirit.

In accordance with Theuderic’s agreement, Chlothar brought the duchy of Dentelin wholly under his own authority. Because of this, when Theuderic already ruled the whole of Austrasia, he was moved by immense indignation and marched his army against Chlothar.

## AN. 613

In the eighteenth year of his reign, Theuderic ordered an army to set out from Austrasia and Burgundy. He first sent an embassy demanding that Chlothar remove himself in every way from the aforementioned duchy of Dentelin; otherwise, he should know that Theuderic would fill Chlothar’s kingdom on every side with his army. The outcome confirmed this declaration, just as the envoys had reported it.

### XXXIX

That same year, when the army was already advancing against Chlothar, Theuderic died at Metz from a flux of the bowels. The army immediately returned to its own homes.

Brunichildis, remaining at Metz with Theuderic’s four sons—Sigibert, Childebert, Corbo, and Meroveus—attempted to establish Sigibert in his father’s kingdom.

### XL

Chlothar entered Austrasia with the support of Arnulf and Pippin, and the other nobles. When he had reached Antonnacum and Brunichildis was staying at Worms with Theuderic’s sons, she sent envoys, Chadoindus and Herpo, to Chlothar, declaring that he should withdraw from Theuderic’s kingdom, which he had left to his sons.

Chlothar replied and, through his own envoys, informed Brunichildis that he promised to fulfill whatever, with the Lord going before them, should be decided among them by the chosen judgment of the Franks.

Brunichildis sent Sigibert, Theuderic’s eldest son, into Thuringia. With him she dispatched Warnacharius, mayor of the palace, and Alboin, together with the other nobles, so that they might attract the peoples beyond the Rhine and thereby be able to resist Chlothar.

She sent a message afterward instructing Alboin to kill Warnacharius together with the others, because he wished to transfer his allegiance to Chlothar’s kingdom. Alboin, having reread the message, tore it up and threw it onto the ground. It was found by one of Warnacharius’s servants; on a wax-coated tablet it was restored and made firm again.

When Warnacharius had reread the message and realized that his life was in danger, he began thereafter to consider how Theuderic’s sons might be destroyed and Chlothar might be chosen as king. By a secret agreement he caused the peoples who had been gathered there to withdraw from supporting Brunichildis and Theuderic’s sons. They then returned with Brunichildis and Theuderic’s sons and made for Burgundy, while messengers were sent throughout Austrasia attempting to raise an army.

### XLI

The barons of Burgundy—both bishops and the other nobles—feared Brunichildis and hated her. They entered into a plan with Warnacharius and arranged that not one of Theuderic’s sons should escape; once they had all been destroyed, they would also eliminate Brunichildis and seek the kingdom of Chlothar. The outcome confirmed this plan.

When, at Brunichildis’s command and that of Sigibert, Theuderic’s son, the armies of Burgundy and Austrasia advanced against Chlothar—

### XLII

Sigibert came into the territory of Champagne in the district of Châlons, beside the river Aisne. There Chlothar came to meet him with an army, already having many Austrasians with him through the faction of Warnacharius, mayor of the palace, as he had arranged long before, with the agreement of the patrician Aletheus and the dukes Rocco, Sigoald, and Eudelanus.

When they ought to have engaged in battle, before they began to fight, the armies gave the signal; but Sigibert’s army turned its back and returned to its own homes. Chlothar gradually followed behind with his army, as had been arranged, and reached the river Saône.

After capturing Theuderic’s three sons—Sigibert, Corbo, and Meroveus, whom Chlothar himself had lifted from the baptismal font—Childebert fled on horseback and was never seen again afterward. The Austrasian army returned unharmed to its own homes.

Through the faction of Warnacharius, mayor of the palace, together with nearly all the remaining nobles of the kingdom of Burgundy, Brunichildis was brought out by Herpo, constable of the district beyond the Jura, from the estate of Orbe, together with Theudelana, Theuderic’s sister, and was presented to Chlothar at Rionava, a village on the river Vigenne.

Sigibert and Corbo, Theuderic’s sons, were killed at Chlothar’s command. Meroveus was secretly taken by Chlothar’s order to Neustria, since Chlothar cherished him with affection because he himself had received him from the sacred font. He was entrusted to Ingobodus, the count, where he lived for many years.

When Brunichildis was brought before Chlothar, and he bore immense hatred toward her, holding it against her that through her ten Frankish kings had been killed—namely, Sigibert; Meroveus and his father Chilperic; Theudebert and his son Chlothar; Meroveus, Chlothar’s son; Theuderic and his three sons, who had just then been destroyed—he first ordered her, after she had been subjected to various tortures for three days, to be led seated on a camel through the whole army. After this he ordered her hair, one foot, and one arm to be tied to the tail of a most vicious horse. There she was torn limb from limb by its kicks and the speed of its running.

Warnacharius was appointed mayor of the palace in the kingdom of Burgundy, after receiving an oath from Chlothar that he would never be degraded during his lifetime. In Austrasia, Rado likewise assumed this rank of honor.

The whole kingdom of the Franks was consolidated, as it had been ruled by the earlier Chlothar, and with all its treasures was subjected to the authority of the younger Chlothar. He held it successfully for sixteen years, maintaining peace with all the neighboring peoples.

This Chlothar was devoted to patience, learned in letters, fearful of God, a great benefactor of churches and priests, giving alms to the poor, and showing himself kind and full of piety toward everyone. He was excessively devoted to hunting wild beasts, and in the end yielded too much to the suggestions of women and girls; for this reason he was reviled by the nobles.

### XLIII

In the thirtieth year of his reign, when he had taken possession of the kingdom of Burgundy and Austrasia, he appointed Herpo, a Frank by birth, as duke in the district beyond the Jura, in place of Eudelanus. When Herpo vigorously undertook to pursue peace in that district and to restrain the frivolity of evildoers, Duke Herpo was killed by the inhabitants themselves, through the audacity of rebellion, at the instigation of the opposing party and on the advice of the patrician Aletheus, Bishop Leudemundus, and the count Herpo.

When Chlothar had gone to an estate in Alsace called Marolegia with Queen Bertethrudis, pursuing peace, he slaughtered many who were acting unjustly with the sword.

### XLIV

Bishop Leudemundus of Sion came secretly to Queen Bertethrudis and, on Aletheus’s advice, spoke disgraceful words: that Chlothar would in every way depart from this world in that same year; that she should transfer as secretly as possible to Sion, his own city, as many treasures as she could, since it was the safest place; and that Aletheus was prepared, after abandoning his own wife, to take Queen Bertethrudis as his wife, because she was of royal Burgundian descent, and that he himself could assume the kingdom after Chlothar.

When Queen Bertethrudis heard this, fearing that it might be true, she burst into tears and withdrew to her chamber. Leudemundus, realizing that these words had placed him in danger, fled by night to Sion. From there he secretly fled to Luxeuil, to the lord Abbot Eustasius.

Afterward the abbot excused him before the lord Chlothar from these accusations, and Leudemundus returned to his own city. Chlothar, staying with the nobles at the estate of Masolacum, ordered Aletheus to come to him. When his wicked counsel had been discovered, he ordered him to be killed by the sword.

## AN. 616

In the thirty-third year of Chlothar’s reign, he ordered Warnacharius, mayor of the palace, to come to him at the estate of Bonogelo, together with all the bishops and also the Burgundian barons. There he granted all their just petitions and confirmed them by royal orders.

### XLV

I shall relate how the people of the Lombards paid an annual tribute of twelve thousand solidi to the authority of the Franks; nor will I conceal by what arrangement they had ceded to the Franks the two cities of Augusta and Susa, together with their territories.

After Cleph, their prince, had died, the twelve dukes of the Lombards lived for twelve years without kings. During that period, as is written above, they broke into the kingdom of the Franks in various places. In compensation for that presumption, they handed over the cities of Augusta and Susa, with their entire territory and population, to the party of Guntram.

After this they sent an embassy to the Emperor Maurice. The twelve dukes sent twelve individual envoys, seeking the peace and protection of the empire. They also sent another twelve envoys to Guntram and Childebert, so that, possessing the protection and defense of the Franks, they might fulfill an annual tribute of twelve thousand solidi to these two kings. They ceded to Guntram’s party the valley called Ametegis, so that through these envoys they might secure his protection wherever it was more suitable.

After this they chose the protection of the Franks with complete devotion. Without delay, with the permission of Guntram and Childebert, the Lombards elevated Authari, a duke, as their king.

Another Authari, also a duke, surrendered himself and his entire duchy to the authority of the empire and remained there; and Authari the king paid annually the tribute which the Lombards had promised to the Franks. After his departure, his son Ago was elevated to the kingdom and is likewise known to have fulfilled the obligation.

## AN. 617

In the thirty-fourth year of Chlothar’s reign, three noble envoys from the Lombard people—Agiulfus, Pompegius, and Gauto—were sent by King Ago to King Chlothar. They requested that the twelve thousand solidi which they paid annually into the Frankish treasuries should be canceled.

They cunningly and secretly presented three thousand solidi, of which Warnacharius received one thousand, Gundelandus one thousand, and Chucus one thousand; to Chlothar himself they presented thirty-six thousand solidi altogether.

Therefore, on the advice of the men named above, who had secretly received these gifts, Chlothar canceled the tribute owed by the Lombards and confirmed perpetual friendship with the Lombards by oaths and treaties.

## AN. 618. XLVI

In the thirty-fifth year of Chlothar’s reign, Queen Bertethrudis died. Chlothar had loved her with unique affection, and all the nobles, seeing her goodness, had loved her exceedingly.

## AN. 622. XLVII

In the thirty-ninth year of Chlothar’s reign, he made his son Dagobert his partner in the kingdom and established him as king over the Austrasians, retaining for himself the lands toward Neustria and Burgundy that were bounded by the Ardennes and the Vosges.

## AN. 623. XLVIII

In the fortieth year of Chlothar’s reign, a certain man named Samo, a Frank by nationality and from the district of Sennonago, gathered a number of merchants around him and went among the Slavs, called Wends, to conduct business.

The Slavs had already begun to rebel against the Avars, called Huns, and their king, Gaganus. The Wends had been the Huns’ “double fighters” from ancient times. Whenever the Huns advanced with an army against any people, the Huns remained assembled in their camp, while the Wends fought. If they prevailed and won, the Huns then set about capturing the booty; but if the Wends were defeated, they regained their strength with the support of the Huns. They were therefore called “double fighters” by the Huns, because, engaging in battle twice, they fought at the front before the Huns.

The Huns came every year to the Slavs to winter. They took the wives and daughters of the Slavs to their beds, and the Slavs paid tribute to the Huns in addition to other forms of oppression.

The sons of the Huns whom they had fathered by the wives and daughters of the Wends eventually, unable to endure this wickedness and oppression, rejected Hunnic domination and, as I mentioned above, began to rebel.

When they had gone out with the Wendish army against the Huns, Samo, the merchant whom I mentioned earlier, went with them in the army. His usefulness there was so great that it was astonishing, and an enormous number of Huns were slaughtered by the swords of the Wends.

Seeing Samo’s usefulness, the Wends chose him as their king. He ruled successfully for thirty-five years. Under his leadership the Wends fought many battles against the Huns; through his counsel and usefulness the Wends always prevailed.

Samo had twelve wives from the Wendish people, by whom he had twenty-two sons and fifteen daughters.

### XLIX

That same fortieth year of Chlothar, King Adaloald, son of King Ago of the Lombards, having succeeded his father in the kingdom, kindly received Eusebius, an envoy of the Emperor Maurice, who had cunningly come to him.

While Adaloald was being anointed in a bath with certain ointments by Eusebius, Eusebius persuaded him; after this anointing he was able to do nothing except what Eusebius urged him to do.

Persuaded by Eusebius to arrange for all the leading and noblest men in the Lombard kingdom to be killed, he would, once they had been destroyed, hand himself and the entire Lombard people over to the empire of Maurice.

When he had already killed twelve of them by the sword, although they had committed no offenses, the others, seeing that their lives were in danger, unanimously conspired and chose as king to be elevated Charroaldus, duke of Turin, whose wife was Gundeberga, the sister of King Adaloald.

Adaloald died after taking poison. Charroaldus immediately seized the kingdom. Taso, one of the Lombard dukes, while governing the province of Tuscany, became puffed up with pride and began to rebel against King Charroaldus.

### LI

Queen Gundeberga was beautiful to behold, kind toward everyone, exceedingly full of piety, a Christian, generous in almsgiving, and loved by all because of her outstanding goodness.

A certain man named Adalulfus, of Lombard descent, was constantly occupied in the royal palace in the king’s service. On one occasion he came to the queen and stood in her presence. Queen Gundeberga, loving him as she did the others, said that Adalulfus had been formed with a dignified stature.

Hearing this, he secretly said to Gundeberga:

“You have deigned to praise the form of my figure; order me to be joined to your bed.”

She firmly refused him, despised him, and spat in his face.

When Adalulfus realized that his life was in danger, he immediately ran to King Charroaldus and asked permission to disclose privately what he had to report. Having obtained an opportunity, he said to the king:

“My queen, your Gundeberga, spoke secretly with Duke Taso for three days, so that he might kill you with poison and elevate him as her husband to the kingdom.”

Believing these lies as though they were true, King Charroaldus thrust Gundeberga into exile in a tower of the fortress of Caumellum.

Chlothar sent envoys to King Charroaldus, asking why he had humiliated Gundeberga, the queen and kinswoman of the Franks, and thrust her into exile. Charroaldus replied as though these lying statements had been true.

Then one of the envoys, named Ansoaldus, spoke to Charroaldus—not as though he had been instructed to do so, but on his own initiative:

“You could clear this charge of reproach. Order the man who reported such words to you to arm himself, and let another come from Queen Gundeberga’s side. Let the two armed men engage in single combat, so that by the judgment of God it may be discovered whether Gundeberga is innocent of the charge of this offense or perhaps guilty.”

When this pleased King Charroaldus and all the leading men of his palace, he ordered Adalulfus to enter the armed combat. From Gundeberga’s side her cousins and Aribertus came forward, and a man named Pitto, armed, attacked Adalulfus.

When they had fought in combat, Adalulfus was killed by Pitto. Gundeberga immediately returned from exile after three years and was restored to the kingdom.

### Editorial notes and textual apparatus

- [Cols. 0629C–0630D, Andelot.] As we have already observed elsewhere, this place retains its ancient name; it is commonly called Andelot, in the diocese of Langres, toward the fortress of Nasium of the Leuci. The latter, now situated in the duchy of Bar on the river Ornain, is commonly called Naz. Nasium was once famous, as is clear from ancient authors and from the ancient coins frequently found there. Certainly, when we were in that region in 1696, a chamber was discovered whose walls were faced with mosaic; square tesserae dug out from it were brought to us. Some have wrongly written that this place was Nancy, the capital of Lorraine.

- [Col. 0630D, Leonisius.] In Clar. and Ch. and some others, *Lesio*. He was bishop of Mainz; Cointius says that he was also called Lindegasius or Ludegastus. Bruschius calls him Saint Lindegasius in his catalogue of the bishops of Mainz.

- [Col. 0630D, battle at Tolbiac.] Others read: “that from ancient time such a battle had never been fought.”

- [Col. 0630D, phalanxes.] Codex Clar.: “where the phalanxes … fight, so that the corpses …”

- [Col. 0630D, Theudebert’s presentation.] Chesn.: “he presents [him], displayed in royal clothing,” etc. Colb. has both readings; and below, in some copies, “with the trappings.”

- [Col. 0630D, *Auster*.] Clar. consistently uses this form to designate Austrasia; the printed editions vary.

- [Col. 0631C, Sigibert.] Clar.; the edition with Boh. and Colb. reads *Sigobertus*, and does so consistently.

- [Col. 0631C, Arnulf and Pippin.] Arnulf was bishop of Metz; Pippin is discussed below.

- [Col. 0631C, Antonnacum.] Colb. and Bolier., with most editions, read *Captonacum*. But Antonnacum is intended here, commonly Andernach, a small town between Bonn and Koblenz under the authority of the archbishop of Cologne. Captonacum, by contrast, was a palace not far from Paris; its site is uncertain, unless it is the village of Chatou near Saint-Germain-en-Laye. See book IV of *De Re Diplomatica*, no. 29.

- [Col. 0631C, Worms.] A very well-known city, commonly Wormes.

- [Col. 0631D, envoys.] Some editions and Colb. read *Erbo*; Boh. reads *Caduinus*.

- [Col. 0631D, “chosen judgment of the Franks.”] Others read *electo* (“chosen”). Matters of greater importance were decided by the judgment of the Franks—that is, by the orders or estates of the realm. By that tribunal Bernard, king of Italy, who had conspired against his uncle Louis the Pious, was condemned to death; Louis mitigated the penalty, being content with the loss of his eyes. This was succeeded by the institution of the twelve Peers of France, and later of the parlements.

- [Col. 0631D, Thuringian mission.] Ch., Freh., and the others read: “she sent [him], with whom were Warnacharius,” or *Warnharius*, “and Alboin.”

- [Col. 0631D, wax tablet.] Others read: “it is again sealed after being coated.” From this Chiffletius infers, in his *Anastasis Childerici*, that our kings used wax tablets (*pugillares cerati*), to which they entrusted their orders—here called *indiculi* (“little written instructions”).

- [Col. 0631D, Burgundian *farones*.] Colb. and several printed editions read *barones* (“barons”), a word later especially used for the magnates of the realm. They were called *farones* because they had sprung from a noble *fara*. For *farae* are generations or lineages, as the Lombard law, book III, title 14, states, and as Paul the Deacon observes in *History of the Lombards*, book II, chapter 9. It should be read as one word, *Burgundaefarones*, as below in chapter 44; Boh. has *burgundefarones*. Indeed Saint Faro, bishop of Meaux, was called Burgundofarus, and his sister Burgundofara, as their Lives in the second Benedictine century show. The variant is *Chlothario* (“for Chlothar”) in place of “the kingdom of Chlothar.”

- [Cols. 0632C–D, battlefield.] Ch. reads “the territory of Champagne of Châlons”; others, “the Champagne district of Châlons.” Several printed editions, with Boh. and Colb., read *Coxonia*; some editions, erroneously, “the river Coxoma.” But the river intended is the Axona (the Aisne), a river of Champagne which, after watering Soissons, joins the Oise near Compiègne.

- [Col. 0632D, Saône.] Clar. reads *Sauconna*; Colb., *Sagonna*. All designate the same river, the Saône. Hence Freh. and Chesn. add “that is, Saogonna.”

- [Col. 0632D, Childebert.] Colb., in a second hand, reads: “beginning his flight after mounting a horse, he was never afterward seen.” This should also be connected with what Florentius, priest of Tricastin, relates in his *Life of Saint Rusticula*, abbess of Arles, in Chesnius, vol. I, p. 565: she is said to have been accused before Chlothar of secretly nursing the king. This king can be none other than the Childebert mentioned here. When the accusation was received, Chlothar, moved by anger, ordered the truth to be investigated very carefully, fearing that Childebert might be planning a return to his father’s kingdom.

- [Cols. 0633C–D, Orbe and Neustria.] Most printed editions read “from Urbana”; Clar. and another Ch. manuscript, “from Orba.” Both names, Urba and Orba, occur in authors; it is commonly called Orbe or Orbach, a fortress named from the river of the same name in the Free County of Burgundy. Colb., with most editions, reads “in New Town.” Cointius identifies Rionava with Rionne. Vincenne (la Vicenne or Vigenne) flows into the Saône near Pont-Arley. Clar. consistently reads *Neptrico*; Boh., Ch., and Freh. read *Neptria*, others *Neptrico*; Col., Bign., Bar., Boch., and Ill. read *Neustria*. All designate the same Neustria.

- [Col. 0633D, *Graffiones*.] Graffiones were the same as counts or judges of districts, as is clear from various ancient authors cited in Du Cange’s glossary. Chiffletius thinks, in his *Anastasis Childerici*, that they were so called because they guarded the king’s writing-case. They are often written *Graviones*, and the Landgraves are still held in highest nobility among the Germans.

- [Col. 0633D, Brunichildis.] Cointius argues at length that Brunichildis was falsely accused of many crimes by Jonas and Fredegar; consult him, especially under the year 613, where he writes her defence and assembles her praises from various monuments. Her punishment is also described in the appendix to Marius; the complete passage is in the appendix to this volume.

- [Col. 0633D, previous Chlothar.] Chlothar I, son of Clovis, had obtained sole rule after the deaths of his brothers and nephews.

- [Col. 0634C, duration of the rule.] Boh. reads “for sixteen years”; Freh., “after fifteen years.”

- [Col. 0634C, “reviled.”] That is, censured; French *blâmé*, as we have already observed.

- [Col. 0634C, Herpo.] Chesn. and Freh. read *Theudelanus*; another Ch. manuscript, *Eudelanus*. The variants in the text are *Herpinum* for Herponem and *Bertrude* for Bertethrude.

- [Col. 0634C, Marolegia.] Clarom. has this form, correctly. Colb. and Chesn. read *Maurolegia*; another Ch. manuscript, *Maurolegico*; most printed editions, “the estate Aurolegia.” This is the estate discussed above.

- [Cols. 0634C–D, Leudemundus and Eustasius.] Clarom. reads “bishop of Sedunum”; Colb. and Boh., with most editions, “of Sidon.” The former is intended: Sedunum, commonly Sion, in Valais, a city already discussed. Freh. and Ch. read “the patrician who … should take [her]”; several editions regularly call the queen Bertrude or Beretrude. Colb. also has “to the house of Abbot Austasius”; it and Freh. and another Ch. manuscript have *Austrasii*. He is Saint Eustasius, successor of Saint Columbanus, whose life by Jonas appears in the second Benedictine century among the *Acts of the Saints*, under the year 625.

- [Col. 0634D, Masolacum.] Clar. reads *Masolacum*. The site of this estate is unknown. See book IV of *De Re Diplomatica*.

- [Cols. 0634D–0635C, Bonogelo.] Clar. reads the thirty-third year; all the others, with Aimoin, the twenty-fourth year, that is, 617. Clar. has “with all the bishops and also the Burgundaefarones”; Colb., with the printed editions, “with the bishops of Burgundy and the farones”; Boh., “with the farones of Burgundy.” Peter Delalande reports canons from the Rheims Church manuscript in his *Supplement to the Ancient Councils of Gaul*, p. 62, under the year 618, which he considers to have been enacted in this synod. Many identify Bonegesil with places of that name, leaving the location of this royal estate uncertain; they are commonly called Boneil. Cointius wishes it to be the place in Brie near the Marne, not far from the monastery of Chelles; others identify another place in the Paris region. See book IV of *De Re Diplomatica*.

- [Cols. 0635C–D, Augusta, Susa, and Cleph.] Augusta is Augusta Praetoria of the Salassi, commonly Aosta; Susa, or Segusium, is Suze. They had formerly been reckoned in Transpadane Italy and then in Liguria; after this cession they belonged to Burgundy. See Valesius’s geographical notice. Below, editions read “to the party.” Freh. reads “after their chief Cleph”; Ch., “after the chief Cleph”; other editions, “after Prince Cleph.” Paul the Deacon writes, in book II, chapter 32, that there were thirty-five Lombard dukes.

- [Col. 0635D, Authari and Ago.] Colb. and several editions read *Chlotharium*; others, “with Chlothar.” See Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book III. Ago, or Agilulf, was not Authari’s son. Valesius therefore conjectures that this should be referred to Adaloald, son of Ago. But Fredegar thought Ago to have been Authari’s son because he succeeded him in the kingdom.

- [Cols. 0635D–0636C, Lombard embassy.] Clarom. reads the thirty-fourth year; the others, the thirty-fifth, which is 618. Others give the names as Agilulfus, Pompeius, and Guto. Ago, according to Cointius’s calculation, was then dead. If, however, as others hold, he came to the throne in 592 and reigned twenty-five years, as Paul the Deacon writes, he survived to 617; this would confirm the Claromontane reading. Other witnesses read *Hunus*, or, with Colb., *Chunus*. Warnacharius was mayor of the palace in Burgundy, Gundelandus in Neustria, and perhaps Chucus had succeeded the previously mentioned Rado in Austrasia. Freh. and Chesn. read thirty-five thousand solidi.

- [Cols. 0636C–D, Bertethrudis.] Clar. gives the thirty-fifth year; Colb. has thirty-eighth; Boh., Chesn., and Freh., with the Anonymous and Aimoin, thirty-sixth; other editions, thirtieth. Some maintain that Beretrude was buried in the church of Saint Peter, now Saint Ouen, at Rouen, where Aldetrudis, another wife of the same king, lies. But that Beretrude was buried at Saint-Germain-des-Prés is established not only by the authority of other writers but by her tomb, excavated some years ago and placed with the other royal tombs in the presbytery of that church, with a stone bearing her recently carved likeness.

- [Col. 0636D, Dagobert’s territory.] The Ardennes and the Vosges are very well-known forests: *les bois d’Ardennes* and *de Vosges*.

- [Col. 0636D, Sennonago and the Wends.] Most editions have in the margin *Sennonico*, perhaps because they thought the famous Gallic people of the Senones (Sens) was meant. Others prefer to understand the district of Senonago (Sengaw) in Hainaut, where Sonegia—French Soignies—is located. Their provinces are still called the March of the Wends, Slavonia, and Carinthia. On the Wends and similar barbarian peoples, and on their origins, read Hugo Grotius’s prolegomena to his *History of the Goths*, etc.

- [Cols. 0636D–0637D, Huns and *Befulci*.] Others read *Hunni* (“Huns”), consistently. Freh. has *Bifulci*: they were so called because they fought twice; below, as in some Chesn. witnesses, *Praefulci*. Most editions read “they engaged in battle”; then follows “the Huns,” etc. Others read: “by the wives … and daughters they fathered [children].”

- [Col. 0637D, Adaloald and Taso.] Ch. and Freh. read “having taken poison”; other editions, “poisoned.” Clar. and a Freh. variant have *auctus*; another Freh. variant, *unctus* (“anointed”). In Chesn. variants Taso is called Taro and Aso, and so below. On Taso’s death, see below, no. 69. Clar., a Freh. variant, and a Chesn. variant read “Tuscany,” that is, Tuscia; others “in Tuscan”; another variant, “held [it].” Paul the Deacon, book IV, calls Charoaldus Rodoaldus; another Ch. manuscript reads Chrodoaldus. The ancients, however, prefixed H and pronounced Chrodoaldus. Yet, if the correct chronological sequence is observed, this was Arioald, whom Rothari—called Chrotarius below by our author—succeeded, and Rodoald succeeded him. What is said here of Charoald is attributed below, chapters 70 and 71, to Chrotarius. Fredegar has, in fact, wholly confused Lombard history. For it one should read Paul the Deacon’s six books.

- [Col. 0638C, Adalulfus.] Others read “my stature.”

- [Col. 0638D, Caumellum and Gundeberga.] Others read *Camellum*. It is Laumellum, today a small village in Insubria called Lumello. According to Paul the Deacon, book IV, chapter 49, Gundeberga was daughter of King Agilulf and Theodelinda. Theodelinda was the daughter of Garibald, duke of the Bavarians, and Waldrada, widow of Theobald, king of the Franks. See above, chapter 34.

- [Col. 0638C–D, ordeal and champion.] “Reproach,” that is, *blâme*. They called single combats, tests by fire or water, and similar procedures “the judgment of God,” using them at that time to uncover hidden truth because they were convinced that God would certainly reveal the truth, even by a miracle if necessary. Du Cange discusses their types and various rites extensively in his glossary, including when they were permitted or prohibited. Colb., Ch., and Freh. read *Haribertus*, whence the printed editions have Charibertus. Paul the Deacon, in the passage cited, writes that the injury was avenged by Carellus, the queen’s own servant.

## AN. 624. LII

In the forty-first year of King Chlothar [Note: Bollandus notes in his commentary on the Life of Saint Pippin, under 21 February, that this chapter is absent from several manuscripts; nevertheless, it is found in ours.], when Dagobert was already ruling Austrasia effectively, a certain nobleman of the Ayglolfingian people [Note: Most editions have *Anglolfinga*, named Rodoaldus or Charoaldus. Bollandus, in the work cited, has *Agilolfinga*, or, as he explains it, Bavarian. The history of the Agilolfingian family—which he believes to be the source from which the origin of the Welfs and other noble families of Germany should be traced—was described at length by Bucelinus, a monk of Weingarten, in volume II of *Sacred Germany*.], named Chrodoaldus, fell into Dagobert’s displeasure. This happened at the instigation of the most blessed man and bishop Arnulf, Pippin, mayor of the palace [Note: Of these two most holy men, who are frequently mentioned below, the former was bishop of Metz and the latter a layman; from them arose the second dynasty of our kings. For Ansegisus, Saint Arnulf’s son, married Begga, Pippin’s daughter, by whom he fathered Pippin of Herstal, who was the father of Charles Martel, from whom Pippin the Short was born, the father of Charlemagne.], and also the other leading men elevated in Austrasia. Chrodoaldus himself was exceedingly wealthy, had seized the property of others out of greed, was devoted to arrogance and filled with pride; no good quality was found in him.

When Dagobert now wished to kill him for his crimes, Chrodoaldus turned his back on him and fled to Chlothar, so that Chlothar might deign to preserve his life and that of his son. When Chlothar saw Dagobert, he pleaded with him for Chrodoaldus’s life, among the other matters discussed. Dagobert promised that Chrodoaldus would not be endangered if he corrected what he had done wrong. But there was no delay: when Chrodoaldus had come with Dagobert to Trier, he was killed at Dagobert’s command. Bertharius, a man from Scarponna [Note: Scarponna is an ancient fortress of Lorraine, now reduced to a village and scarcely known, on the Moselle, a league and a half from Pont-à-Mousson toward Nancy, commonly called Sarpeigne, not far from Custodia Dei [Doulewart].], drew his sword and cut off his head at the door [Al.: rear door] of the chamber.

## AN. 625. LIII

In the forty-second year of Chlothar’s reign, Dagobert, in royal attire and honorably accompanied by his *leudes*, came by his father’s command to Clichy, not far from Paris [Note: The manuscripts have *Clippiaco procul*. In the Claromontanus, three letters have deliberately been rubbed away. What remains is *leudibus nec . . . Clippiaco procul*. The Old Edition, except Freherus, has *de Piato procul*. Clichy, commonly called Clichy, lies in the Parisian region near the Seine; Saint Ouen died there. See Book IV of *On Diplomatic Matters*, no. 36. Elsewhere, however, this event is said to have occurred at Romilly, below, chapter 58.], and there took as his wife Gomatrude, the sister of Queen Sichilde [Note: She was Chlothar himself’s wife.].

Three days after the wedding, a serious dispute arose between Chlothar and his son Dagobert. Dagobert was demanding that he be allowed to receive under his authority everything belonging to the kingdom of Austrasia, whereas Chlothar strongly refused to grant him anything on this matter. The two kings selected twelve Frankish nobles to settle the dispute by their judgment. Among them Lord Arnulf, bishop of Metz, was chosen together with the other bishops; in accordance with his holiness, he spoke with the greatest kindness between father and son in favor of peace and concord. At last, through the bishops and the wisest noblemen, the father was reconciled with his son. He restored to him the entire territory that he had regarded as belonging to the kingdom of Austrasia, retaining under his own authority only what lay on this side of the Loire or in the region of Provence.

## AN. 626. LIV

In the forty-third year of Chlothar’s reign, Warnacharius, mayor of the palace, died [Note: From this it may be inferred that he was a different man from the Warnacharius who, wishing to defend the party of Agrestius against Saint Eustasius, abbot of Luxeuil, died suddenly at the Council of Mâcon in 622.]. His son Godinus, a man of unstable character, took his stepmother Bertane as his wife that year. King Chlothar was consequently moved against him by extreme fury and ordered the duke Arnebert, who had Godinus’s sister as his wife, to kill him with an army.

Seeing that his life was in danger, Godinus fled with his wife to King Dagobert in Austrasia and, terrified by royal fear, sought refuge in the church of Saint Aper [Note: In the suburb of Toul, Saint-Evre, of which city he had been bishop; there is now a Benedictine abbey there under the congregation of Saint Vanne.]. Dagobert repeatedly pleaded with King Chlothar through envoys for his life. At last Chlothar promised that Godinus’s life would be spared, but only on condition that he abandon Bertane, whom he had taken as his wife contrary to the canonical ordinances.

When he had abandoned her and returned to the kingdom of Burgundy, Berta immediately went to Chlothar, saying that if Godinus were brought into Chlothar’s presence, he intended to kill the king. By Chlothar’s command, Godinus was led through the principal shrines of the saints—those of Lord Medard at Soissons and Lord Dionysius at Paris—to take oaths under such a pretext that he would always remain faithful to Chlothar, while a suitable place might be found where he could be separated from his companions and killed.

Chramnulfus [Note: Colbertinus has *Ramnulfus*.], one of the nobles, and Waldebertus, the chamberlain [*domesticus*], told Godinus to go to Orléans, to the church of Saint Aignan, and to Tours, to the threshold of Saint Martin, to fulfill the same oath once more. When, at Chramnulfus’s indication and under his escort, he had come at lunchtime to a certain little estate in the suburb of Chartres, Chramnulfus and Waldebertus fell upon him there with an army and killed him. They also killed some of those who had remained with him and, stripping the others, drove them into flight and left them.

That year Palladius and his son Sidocus, bishop of Eauze [Note: The Boherianus and Colbertinus manuscripts, together with several editions, have *Seducius, bishop of Toulouse*; others have *Sedocus*. Aimoinus, Book IV, chapter 14, has *Sedocus, bishop of Toulouse*. Chesnius and Cointius have *Senocus, bishop of Eauze*. He is the man who had attended the Council of Reims under Bishop Sonnatius in the preceding year. In the Claromontanus, where the first hand has *Aelosani*, a second hand, also ancient, has written *To* above the diphthong *AE*. Senocus is the last name in the catalogue of the bishops of Elusa. Nevertheless, this see continued until the ninth century, when Eauze was destroyed by the Northmen and the care of its diocese was entrusted to the bishop of Auch, who thereafter held the dignity of metropolitan of Novempopulania.], were driven into exile at the accusation of Duke Aighynan, on the ground that they had been accomplices in the rebellion of the Gascons.

Boso, son of Audolenus, from the district of Stampae, was killed by order of Chlothar at the hands of Duke Arnebert, because he was charged with adultery with Queen Sighilde.

That year Chlothar joined the nobles and *leudes* of Burgundy at Troyes [Note: Chesnius has *Trecassinis*; others, *Trecas suis*. Troyes, commonly called Troyes, lies in Champagne and is also called the city of the Tricassians. This passage shows that even then the mayors of the palace were elected by the nobles of the kingdom.], after sounding them out as to whether, now that Warnacharius was dead, they wished to raise someone else to the same rank of honor. But all unanimously refused, declaring that they by no means wished to elect a mayor of the palace; earnestly asking for the king’s favor, they reached an agreement with him.

## AN. 627. LV

In the forty-fourth year of Chlothar’s reign, when the bishops and all the nobles of his kingdom, both from Neustria and from Burgundy, had assembled at Clichy with Chlothar for the benefit of the kingdom and the safety of the country, a man named Ermenharius [Note: The Claromontanus has *Ermarius . . . Gariberto*, instead of *Chariberti*. The Boherianus has *Gariberto et filio Chlotharii . . . obtimate*.], who was governor of the palace of Charibert, Chlothar’s son, was killed by the servants of Aegyna, a nobleman of Saxon origin. Almost a great slaughter of many people followed from this, unless it had been checked by Chlothar’s patience [Note: The printed editions have *praesentia*, “presence.”], which intervened and took care of the matter.

At Chlothar’s command Aegyna took up his position on Mont Mercure [Note: This is the reading of the Claromontanus and Boherianus, *Mercoris*; the Colbertinus has *Monte Cori*; Freherus and the Chigi manuscript have *Monte Mercomire*; the other editions have *Monte Mercurii*.
