This mountain, also called Mont des Martyrs, lies near Paris and is today called Montmartre after Saint Dionysius and his fellow martyrs.]. He had a very large number of warriors with him.

Brodulfus [Note: This is the reading of the Claromontanus and Freherus. The name of this man is found written in almost as many different ways as there are manuscripts and editions: *Brunulfus, Produlfus, Rudulfus, Hradulfus*. Below, the Claromontanus has *Airiberti*, the Colbertinus *Hariberti*, and the Boherianus *Ariberti*. The same variations occur below in the following chapter.], Charibert’s uncle, gathered an army from every side and intended to fall upon him with Charibert.

Chlothar gave particular orders to the Burgundian barons [Note: The printed editions have, as above, “barons of Burgundy.”] that whichever party wished to evade its own judgment should be crushed by their efforts and strength. By this arrangement, both men were pacified through the royal command.

## AN. 628. LVI

In the forty-fifth year of his reign [Note: This is the reading of the Colbertinus, Boherianus, the Chronicle of Saint Benignus, and all the printed editions. The Claromontanus, however, has forty-six.], Chlothar died and was buried in the suburb of Paris, in the church of Saint Vincent [Note: His body now lies enclosed in a stone tomb near the high altar with the other kings buried in the same basilica.].

When Dagobert saw that his father had died, he ordered all the *leudes* whom he ruled in Austrasia to take up arms. He sent envoys into Burgundy and Austrasia [Note: Unquestionably, “Neustria” should be read.] to require them to choose his rule.

When he came to Reims and proceeded toward Soissons [Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts, except the Boherianus, which has: “When he had come to Reims, proceeding at the suggestion.” The Chigi and Freherus manuscripts have: “When he had come by suggestion.” The anonymous author who wrote the deeds of Dagobert has: “When he had come to Reims, the suggestion proceeding.” Cointius insists that the text should be read in this way. Our reading is found in the Chronicle of Saint Benignus.], all the bishops and *leudes* of the kingdom of Burgundy are known to have submitted themselves to him there.

A very large number of the Neustrian bishops and nobles also appeared to seek Dagobert’s kingdom [Note: Some editions have “the Austrasian bishops and nobles.”]. His brother Charibert was striving, if he could, to seize the kingdom, but because of his simplicity his desire achieved little. Brodulf, wishing to establish his nephew in the kingdom, began to plot against Dagobert; but the outcome showed how this matter would turn out.

## LVII

When Dagobert had occupied the kingdom of Chlothar, both Neustria [Note: The Chigi manuscript and others have *Neptricum*; the Boherianus has “Neustria . . . to Dagobert.”] and Burgundy, seizing its treasures and bringing them under his authority, he was finally moved by mercy and, following the advice of wise men, granted his brother Charibert the districts and cities on this side of the Loire and of the frontier of Spain, which lies in the region of Gascony, as well as the Pyrenean mountains [Note: Others have “and the Pyrenees.” Fredegarius calls “on this side of the Loire” what we would call “beyond Paris.” In any case, on this first occasion the younger son was excluded from his father’s kingdom; this custom gradually gained strength and eventually became law. See Valesius, Book XIX of *Frankish History*.].

He granted Charibert the counties of Toulouse, Quercy, Agen, Périgord, and Saintonge—or whatever territory extending from these regions toward the Pyrenees was included—only what would suffice for him to live in the manner of a private person [Note: The Boherianus reads: “which could have sufficed for Charibert to live on,” omitting the rest.], and bound him by a pact that Charibert would never again presume to reclaim from Dagobert any part of their father’s kingdom.

Charibert chose Toulouse as his seat and ruled part of the province of Aquitaine [Note: Chesnius and Freherus have *Equitanicae*; the other editions have *Aquitaniae*.]. Three years after he had begun to reign [Note: He died in the third year of his reign. Compare chapter 67.], he defeated all Gascony with an army and brought it under his authority, somewhat enlarging the extent of his kingdom.

## AN. 628. LVIII

When Dagobert had already reigned for seven years, he entered Burgundy and took possession of the greater part of his father’s kingdom, as I mentioned above. Such fear had shaken the bishops and nobles living in the kingdom of Burgundy, as well as the other *leudes*, at Dagobert’s arrival that the effect was astonishing to all.

He brought great joy to the poor who possessed claims of justice. When he came to the city of Langres, he judged justice among all his *leudes*, both the high and the poor [Note: From this passage Cointius infers that the word *leudes* sometimes designated all subjects; elsewhere it signifies laymen, in opposition to priests, as is clear from chapter 1 of the Chronicle of Fredegarius. Most often, however, it specifically designates the king’s vassals, who were later called barons, as we have already observed. See the glossaries of Henry Spelman and Du Cange.], with such impartiality that he was believed to have been wholly pleasing to God. No reward intervened there, nor acceptance of persons; justice alone held sway, and the Most High loved it.

Then he proceeded to Dijon and even settled at Laon [Note: It received its name from the patron of its church, Saint-Jean de Laon, above the river Saône.], remaining there for several days. He had devoted himself so earnestly to judging justice for the whole people of his kingdom [Note: Several editions have “to judge with justice”] that, filled with the desire for this kindness, he neither allowed sleep to come to his eyes nor satisfied himself with food, thinking with the utmost intensity how everyone might return joyfully from his presence after receiving justice.

On the same day on which he decided to hasten from Laon to Chalon, before daylight he entered the bath and ordered Brodulf, the uncle of his brother Charibert, to be killed. Brodulf was killed by the dukes Amalgarius [Note: He was duke of Transjurane Burgundy and founder of the monastery of Bèze near Dijon. He arranged for his son Waldalenus, a monk of Luxeuil, to be made its abbot; he also founded Donatiacum near Besançon for nuns, of which his daughter Adalfinda was the first abbess. These matters are related in the Chronicle of Bèze in volume I of Acher’s *Spicilegium*.] and Arnebert and by the patrician Willibad.

When Dagobert set out for Chalon, where he was directing himself with the intention of completing the work of justice he had begun, and then proceeded through Autun and Auxerre, he came to Paris by way of Sens. There he left Queen Gomatrude at Romilly [Note: It is now joined to the Parisian suburb of Saint-Antoine and is commonly called Reuilly. Compare chapter 53 above, where the king is said to have taken Gomatrude at Clichy.], the estate where he had married her [Note: Chesnius added “because she was barren, with the counsel of the Franks,” as the anonymous author who wrote the deeds of Dagobert relates; but this should rather be attributed to the king’s lack of self-restraint. At that time the worst custom had become prevalent, contrary to Christian law: repudiating one’s wife and taking another after divorce, as is clear from Book II, form 30, of the formulas of Marculfus. This plague was later eradicated by the sacred canons and royal authority.].

He took Nantechild, one of the girls from the household [Note: This must certainly be read as *de ministerio*, not *de monasterio*, as the printed editions have together with Aimoinus. No one has yet seen a manuscript in which *ministerio* is not read. Thus it appears in the Claromontanus, Colbertinus or Metensis, Boherianus, and Thuaneus, according to Valesius, as well as in a manuscript once belonging to Queen Christina of Sweden, formerly owned by Goldastus and cited by Bollandus; the Chronicles of the monastery of Bèze and of Saint Benignus agree with them. Dagobert would not have taken a nun as wife with the consent of the nobles of the kingdom; and the sense requires that a girl raised from the household service be said to have been elevated to queenship. In the same way Balthildis was taken from household service into the bed of Chlodovech II, as is related in her Life.], and elevated her as queen.

From the beginning of his reign until that time, using first the counsel of the most blessed Arnulf, bishop of Metz, and of Pippin, mayor of the palace, he had governed the royal administration in Austrasia with such prosperity that he received immense praise from all peoples.

He had so thoroughly shaken their fear by the force of his power that they now eagerly undertook to submit themselves to his authority. Even the peoples living around the frontier of the Avars and Slavs sought him willingly, so that he might march successfully behind them and confidently promised to bring the Avars, the Slavs, and the other nations of the peoples under his authority as far as the public hand [Note: By “the public hand” this author usually means the Roman Empire. See below, chapter 69. Thus “as far as the public hand” may mean “as far as the regions belonging to the Empire.” Several editions have “as far as the public hand” in the ablative.].

After the departure of blessed Arnulf [Note: Saint Arnulf, having abandoned his see, withdrew into the solitude of the Vosges. Saint Romaric had built there, in the fortress of Habendum, one monastery for virgins and another for monks; he received Arnulf, who lived on a neighboring mountain. A chapel and a small hermits’ dwelling can still be seen there. The monastery of Habendum, later called Mount Romaric—Remiremont—from its location and founder, was subsequently transferred into the valley below, where it still stands, together with the town of the same name beside the Moselle, inhabited by secular canonesses who have cast off the yoke of the Benedictine rule. The mountain itself, now called the Holy Mountain, is inhabited by Benedictines of the congregation of Saint Vanne. Besides the principal church, several chapels can be seen on either side, together with the ancient tombs of the saints buried there. We visited all these places in 1696. The Life of Saint Arnulf is found in the second volume of the Benedictine *Acts of the Saints*, under the year 640. His body was transferred to Metz and is preserved in the magnificent basilica dedicated to his name, possessed by Benedictine monks of the congregation of Saint Vanne.], Dagobert continued to govern, still using the counsel of Pippin, mayor of the palace, and Chunibert [Note: Others have *Hunibertus*. He attended the Council of Reims in 630. His Life is found in Surius under 12 November, the day on which his feast is celebrated.], bishop of Cologne, and strongly guided by the latter’s admonitions. He embraced all the peoples subject to him with such love of prosperity and justice that, until he reached Paris, as I have mentioned above, none of the preceding Frankish kings was believed to have surpassed him in reputation.

## AN. 629. LIX

In the eighth year of his reign [Note: Some have seven, others nine; the latter is correct in relation to these words, since Sigibert was born in 630 if the year is reckoned from January.], while he was traveling through Austrasia in royal attire, he took a certain girl named Ragnetrude [Note: The Colbertinus and some editions have *Regintruda*; several editions below have *Sygobertum*.] into his bed, and that year she bore him a son named Sigibert.

## LX

Returning to Neustria, he chose his father Chlothar’s seat as his residence and resolved to remain there continually. Having entirely forgotten the justice he had previously loved, and driven by greed, he wished, with cunning desire, to fill his new treasuries with spoils gathered from the churches and the *leudes* everywhere.

Excessively devoted to lust, he had three queens, after the manner of Solomon [Note: The phrase “after the manner of Solomon” appears only in the Colbertinus, and there in a second but ancient hand.], and a great many concubines. His queens were Nantechild, Wlfegund, and Berchild [Note: Others have *Nanthildis, Ulfigundis,* and *Berthitais*.].

Because there were many concubines, it would have been burdensome to insert their names in this Chronicle. Although his heart had become greatly estranged, as we mentioned above, and his thought had departed from God, he nevertheless later—would that it had been to his true reward—distributed alms to the poor with extraordinary generosity. Had the shrewdness prompted by greed not hindered this, he would, it is believed, have merited the eternal kingdom.

## LXI

When his *leudes* were lamenting his wickedness, Pippin saw this. He was more prudent than all, very wise in counsel, entirely faithful, and loved by everyone because of his devotion to justice—the same justice in which he had wisely instructed Dagobert while Dagobert had followed his counsel. Yet Pippin himself forgot nothing of justice and did not depart from the path of goodness. Whenever he approached Dagobert, he acted prudently in everything and showed himself cautious in all matters.

The jealousy of the Austrasians against him was repeatedly and vehemently reported to Dagobert, so that they even attempted to make him hateful to Dagobert and have him killed. But the love of justice and fear of God, which Pippin had carefully embraced, rescued him from harm.

That year Pippin himself went with Dagobert’s son Sigibert to King Charibert.

## LXII

Charibert, coming from Orléans, received Sigibert from the sacred font [Note: Baudemundus relates in the Life of Saint Amandus, bishop of Tongeren, whose disciple he was, that Sigibert was baptized by him and that a notable miracle occurred on that occasion. When the holy man was making the little boy a catechumen and no one answered the prayer, the boy replied in a clear voice, “Amen.” The same author indicates that this took place at Clichy.].

Aega, meanwhile, was constantly engaged in Dagobert’s counsels among the other Neustrians [Note: Several editions have “among the other Austrasians.” Below, the reading is “he was lying in wait”; the Boherianus has “in ambush.”].

That year Dagobert’s envoys, whom he had sent to the Emperor Heraclius—Servatus [Al.: Servatius] and Paternus by name—returned to him, announcing that they had established perpetual peace with Heraclius. I shall not omit the account of the miracle performed by Heraclius.

## LXIII

Heraclius was patrician [The Chigi manuscript: “over”] of all the provinces of Africa, while Phocas—who had murdered the Emperor Maurice by tyrannical means and seized the empire—was ruling most wickedly. In his madness he would even throw treasures into the sea, saying that he was giving gifts to Neptune.

When the senators saw that he intended through folly to destroy the empire, they seized Phocas by a conspiracy organized by Heraclius. With his hands and feet cut off and a stone tied around his neck, he was thrown into the sea by the hands of the senate. With the senate’s consent, Heraclius was elevated to the imperial throne [Note: Heraclius became emperor in 610. Chosroes captured Jerusalem in 614, and Saes, commander of his armies, captured Chalcedon, Alexandria, and all Egypt in 615 or the following year. In 623 Heraclius marched against them; after defeating Chosroes in 628, he made peace with his son Siroes, recovered the Holy Cross, which had been carried into Persia, and restored it to Jerusalem in a solemn procession. The Greek authors Theophanes, Cedrenus, and others discuss these matters at length.], after many provinces had been devastated by the attacks of the Persians during the reigns of the emperors Maurice and Phocas.

## LXIV

As usual, the emperor of the Persians again rose against Heraclius with an army. When the Persians had reached Chalcedon, a city not far from Constantinople, devastating the provinces of the state [Possibly: “the provinces”], they burst into the city and burned it with fire. After this, approaching Constantinople, the seat of the empire, they attempted to destroy it.

Heraclius went out with an army to meet them. As envoys moved between the sides, Heraclius asked Cosdroe, the Persian emperor [Note: The Old Edition and Chesnius have *Construes*, or *Costrues* and *Costrus*; the Boherianus has *Construe*, and likewise below.], that the two emperors should meet in single combat, while the great multitude of each army remained at a distance. He proposed that whichever side received victory from the Most High should take possession of the empire and people of the defeated ruler unharmed.

The Persian emperor promised by this agreement that he would come out to single combat. Emperor Heraclius took up arms, left the battle line and phalanx prepared behind him by his men [Note: The Colbertinus has “taking up the battle line”; other editions have “and the phalanx.”], and advanced to battle like a new David.

The Persian emperor Cosdroe sent against Heraclius, on his behalf and according to the terms of the agreement, a certain patrician from his own men whom he had found to be the strongest in battle.

When the two men, each on horseback, approached one another in combat, Heraclius said to the patrician, whom he supposed to be Cosdroe, the Persian emperor: “It was agreed that we should fight in single combat. Why are others following behind you?”

The patrician turned his head to see who was coming behind him. Heraclius then drove his horse forward vigorously with his heel, drew his weapon [Note: This is the reading of the Claromontanus, Palatinus, and Freherus. In the Colbertinus the first word is damaged, but *ensem*, “sword,” is written. The Chigi manuscript and other editions have *gladium*, “sword.”], and cut off the head of the Persian patrician.

The emperor Cosdroe, defeated and disgraced along with the Persians, turned his back and was killed by his own men in tyrannical fashion. The Persians fled and returned to their own lands.

Heraclius, transported by sea with his army [Note: The words following this point are placed differently in some witnesses.], entered Persia, brought all Persia under his authority, and captured many treasures. Seven Aeltiarnites [Note: This is the reading of the Claromontanus and Colbertinus, as well as Chesnius and the others. The old editions carelessly joined the numeral VII to the proper name and produced *Waltiarnitis*. The Palatinus has “four Aeltiarnites”; the Chigi and Freherus have “seven Arnites”; others have *Aeltis*. The Boherianus has *Celtiarnitis*.] were also captured. After Persia had been devastated for approximately three years, it was subjected to his authority.

After this, the Persians once again created an emperor over themselves [Note: The printed editions, together with the Colbertinus, have: “Again the emperor defeated the Persians.”].

## LXV

The Emperor Heraclius was handsome in appearance, with a beautiful face and a well-proportioned stature; he was exceedingly strong and an outstanding warrior. He often killed lions in the arena and, unarmed, killed several men by himself.

Since he was extremely learned in letters, he became an astrologer. Through astrology he perceived that, by divine will, the empire was destined to be devastated by circumcised peoples. He therefore sent to Dagobert, king of the Franks, asking him to order all the Jews in his kingdom to be baptized into the Catholic faith. Dagobert immediately carried this out [Note: Chilperic had done the same, according to Gregory, Book VI, chapter 17. John Launoy and Father John Nicolai, a Dominican, have written extensively on this matter on both sides.].

Heraclius resolved to do the same throughout all the provinces of the empire; for he did not know whence this calamity against the empire would arise.

## LXVI

The Hagarenes, also called Saracens, as the book of Orosius [Boherianus: Erosius] testifies, were a circumcised people living long ago beside Mount Caucasus, above the Caspian Sea, in a land called Ercolia [Note: The Colbertinus and several editions have *Ercolriae*; others have *Hercolei*. It is recorded in Ortelius that the lower regions of the Caucasus were called the region of Colchis.].

When they had grown to an enormous multitude, they finally took up arms and invaded the provinces of Emperor Heraclius to devastate them. Heraclius sent soldiers against them to resist. When battle began, the Saracens overcame the soldiers and slaughtered them grievously with the sword. It is said that 150,000 soldiers were killed by the Saracens in that battle.

Through envoys the Saracens offered Heraclius the spoils for him to receive. Heraclius, desiring vengeance upon the Saracens, refused to accept anything from them.

Heraclius gathered an enormous number of soldiers from all the provinces of the empire and sent an embassy to the Caspian Gates [Note: The Claromontanus and Colbertinus have *Cispias*; Freherus and others have *Cispium*. Pliny prefers to call them the Caspian Gates; they are also called the Iberian Gates—not because actual gates existed there, although the inhabitants call them the Iron Gate, but because the place is so narrow that any attack by an enemy can easily be repelled. The passage is only three hundred paces wide between the Caucasus and the Hyrcanian Sea, and a fortress on a cliff called Cumani overlooks it. There is a city there called Harmastis, which the Turks call Derbent, that is, “Narrowness,” and also Demir or Temir-kapi.]. Alexander the Great of Macedon had ordered these gates to be made of bronze and shut with bars above the Caspian Sea because of the savage nations living beyond the heights of the Caucasus. Heraclius ordered the gates opened and sent from there 150,000 fighting men hired with gold to fight the Saracens in his aid.

The Saracens, who had two leaders, numbered nearly 200,000. When both armies had established their camps not far from each other, intending to begin battle the following day, they engaged. That same night the army of Heraclius was struck by the sword of God.

In the camp, 52,000 of Heraclius’s soldiers lay dead [Note: Chesnius and Freherus have 55,000; another edition has 50,000 and 52,000.]. When they were supposed to go out to battle the next day, the soldiers of Heraclius’s army saw that most of their forces had been killed by divine judgment, and they did not dare engage the Saracens.

Heraclius’s entire army returned to its own lands. The Saracens, in the manner in which they had begun, continued continually to devastate the provinces of Emperor Heraclius.

When they had drawn near Jerusalem, Heraclius saw that he could not resist their violence. Seized by excessive bitterness and sorrow, the wretched man, already adhering to the Eutychian heresy [Note: Heraclius defended the heresy of the Monothelites, which was descended from the Eutychian heresy. The latter admitted one composite nature from two; the former, a single will. He did not hesitate to publish this in an official decree called the *Ecthesis* and propose it for universal acceptance. Constantine, a Catholic, succeeded his father Heraclius in 641. For fuller information about the disasters inflicted by the Saracens—who, having joined themselves to the disciples of Muhammad, or Mahomet, who died in 631, in the ninth year of his reign over certain Arabs, declared war no less against God than against mankind—see Theophanes, Nicephorus, and the other authors. No one is unaware how widely those barbarians later spread throughout the world.], abandoned the worship of Christ. He had as his wife the daughter of his sister and, stricken cruelly by a fever, ended his unhappy life.

His son Constantine succeeded him in the imperial office. During his reign, a large part of the state was excessively devastated by the Saracens.

## AN. 630. LXVII

In the ninth year of Dagobert’s reign [Note: Freherus has “the eighth year.”], King Charibert died, leaving a little son named Chilperic, who himself also died shortly afterward. It is said that he was killed through Dagobert’s plotting.

Dagobert immediately brought the entire kingdom of Charibert, together with Gascony, under his authority. He also sent Duke Barontus [Note: Others have *Barontum ducem*; others, “through Duke Barontus.”] to bring Charibert’s treasures and present them to him.

Barontus is known to have caused a serious loss in this matter: acting together with the treasurers [Al.: the treasures], he fraudulently withheld an excessive amount.

### LXVIII

That year, the Sclavi, also called Winidi, having killed a very large number of Frankish merchants in the kingdom of Samo and plundered their possessions, this became the beginning of the dispute between Dagobert and Samo, king of the Sclavi.[^c0066-1] Dagobert sent Sicharius as an envoy to Samo, asking that Samo justly make restitution for the merchants whom his men had killed and for the goods that they had wrongfully seized. Samo refused to see Sicharius or to allow him to come into his presence. Sicharius, therefore, dressed in garments resembling those of the Sclavi,[^c0066-2] reached Samo’s presence with his companions and announced everything that had been entrusted to him.

But, as is characteristic of paganism and the arrogance of the wicked, Samo made no restitution for what his men had done. He merely wished to establish arrangements by which justice might be done reciprocally concerning these and other matters that had arisen between the two parties.[Col. 0648C] Sicharius, like a foolish envoy, spoke insulting words that had not been entrusted to him, and uttered threats against Samo, on the ground that Samo and the people of his kingdom owed service to Dagobert.

Samo replied, already wounded—or, according to another reading, more cautiously:[^c0066-3] “The land that we possess belongs to Dagobert, and we are his people, provided that he is willing to preserve friendship with us.” Sicharius said: “It is impossible that Christian servants of God should be able to establish friendship with dogs.” Samo, on the contrary, replied: “If you are servants of God and we are God’s dogs, then, since you continually act against him, we have received permission to tear you apart with our bites.” Sicharius was expelled from Samo’s presence.[Col. 0649A]

When Dagobert had been informed of these events, he arrogantly ordered an army to move from the whole kingdom of the Austrasians against Samo and the Winidi. When the army entered against the Winidi in three divisions, the Lombards likewise, with Dagobert’s assistance—or, according to other copies, at his solicitation or in exchange for payment—advanced hostilely against the Sclavi. The Sclavi prepared for them in these and other places. The army of the Alamanni, with Duke Chrodobert, gained a victory in the region through which it had entered. The Lombards likewise gained a victory, and the Alamanni and Lombards carried away with them a very large number of captives from among the Sclavi.

The Austrasians, however, surrounded the fortress of Wogastisburc,[^c0066-4] where a great force of the bravest Winidi had taken up its position. After fighting there for three days, many men of Dagobert’s army were slain by the sword.[Col. 0649B] Then all the survivors fled, abandoning their tents and possessions, and returned to their own settlements.

After this, on many occasions, the Winidi invaded the Frankish kingdom, ravaging Thuringia and the neighboring districts. Deruanus too, duke of the people of the Urbii,[^c0066-5] who were of Sclavian origin and had long been connected with the Frankish kingdom, surrendered himself and his people to Samo’s kingdom.[^c0066-6] The victory that the Winidi won over the Franks was achieved not so much by the courage of the Sclavi as by the folly of the Austrasians, who saw that they had incurred Dagobert’s hatred while they were continually being plundered.

### 643 — LXIX

That year Charoald, king of the Lombards, secretly sent envoys to Hisacius, the patrician,[^c0066-7] asking him by whatever means he could devise to kill Taso, duke of the province of Tuscany. In return for this service, he promised that Charoald would cancel for the imperial authorities one of the three hundredweight units of gold that the Lombards annually received from the public treasury,[^c0066-8] so that only two would thereafter be paid.

When the patrician Hisacius heard this, he considered by what means he might accomplish it. He cleverly instructed Taso, who was then in Charoald’s disfavor, to cultivate friendship with Hisacius, while Hisacius himself would provide Taso with assistance against King Charoald.

Taso was trapped by this deception and went to Ravenna. Hisacius sent word to meet him, but, through fear of the emperor, did not dare admit Taso and his armed companions within the walls of Ravenna. When Taso, believing this, left his men’s weapons outside the city and entered Ravenna, those who had been prepared immediately fell upon him and killed him and all his companions who had come with him.[Col. 0650A]

King Charoald canceled one hundredweight of gold, as he had promised, for Hisacius and the imperial authorities. Thereafter only two hundredweights of gold were paid annually by the Roman patrician to the Lombard side. One hundredweight contains one hundred pounds of gold. Immediately afterward King Charoald died.

### LXX

Queen Gundeberga, because all the Lombards had confirmed their loyalty to her by oaths, ordered a certain Chrotharius,[^c0066-9] one of the dukes from the territory of Brescia, to come to her. She compelled him to abandon the wife he had and to marry her. Through her, all the Lombards raised him to the kingship.

Chrotharius willingly consented. He confirmed by oaths taken at holy places that he would never set Gundeberga aside, diminish anything of her rank or honor, or fail to love her with undivided affection and show her every fitting honor. At Gundeberga’s urging, all the Lombard nobles raised Chrotharius to the throne.

When Chrotharius began to reign, he killed many Lombard nobles whom he perceived to be rebellious toward him. Seeking peace throughout the entire Lombard kingdom, he imposed a very strict discipline and fear.

Chrotharius forgot the oath he had given Gundeberga. He shut her away in a chamber at Ticinum, in the palace hall, and forced her to live as a private person. She remained confined there for five years.[Col. 0650C] Chrotharius continually indulged in debauchery with concubines. Gundeberga, because she was a Christian, blessed almighty God throughout this tribulation and devoted herself constantly to fasting and prayer.

### LXXI

When it pleased God, Aubedo,[^c0066-10] an envoy sent by King Chlodoveus,[^c0066-11] reached Papia, also called Ticinum,[^c0066-12] a city of Italy, in the course of an embassy to Chrotharius, king of the Lombards. Seeing the queen, whom he had often encountered when coming on embassies and by whom he had always been kindly received, now imprisoned, and considering this a matter entrusted to him, he suggested among other things to King Chrotharius that he ought not to humiliate a kinswoman of the Franks whom he had held as queen, through whom he had also obtained the kingdom.

Otherwise, he said, the kings and Franks would be indignant. Chrotharius, now showing respect toward the Franks, ordered Gundeberga to be brought out. After approximately five years, she proceeded throughout the city and outside it, in royal fashion, to the holy places for prayer.

Chrotharius ordered that the estates and fiscal property that she had possessed be restored to her. She retained them until the day of her death and, enriched with many possessions and restored to her rank of dignity, continued thereafter to live happily in royal style. Aubedo, meanwhile, was richly rewarded by Queen Gundeberga.

In 645, Chrotharius advanced with an army against the coastal cities of Genava, Albinganum, Varicottim, Saona, Ubitergium, and Luna.[^c0066-13] He took them from the empire, ravaged them, breached them, burned them with fire, plundered their inhabitants, stripped them of their possessions, and condemned them to captivity. Destroying their walls down to the foundations, he ordered that these cities be called villages.

### LXXII

That year, a violent conflict arose in the kingdom of the Avari, also called the Huns,[^c0066-14] in Pannonia,[^c0066-15] because a dispute had arisen over which claimant should succeed to the kingdom: one from among the Avars and another from among the Bulgars. Each gathered a multitude and fought against the other. At length the Avars defeated the Bulgars.

After the Bulgars had been defeated, nine thousand men, with their wives and children, were expelled from Pannonia. They sought Dagobert, asking him to receive them for settlement in Frankish territory. Dagobert ordered the Bavarians to receive them for the winter, provided that he could discuss with the Franks what should afterward be done with them.

When they had been dispersed among the houses of the Bavarians for the winter, Dagobert, following the advice of the Franks, ordered the Bavarians to kill those Bulgars, with their wives and children, each household killing those assigned to it in a single night. The Bavarians immediately carried this out.

No one from among the Bulgars survived except Altioeus,[^c0066-16] with seven hundred men and their wives and children. They were saved in the March of the Winidi.[^c0066-17] Afterward he and his people lived for many years with Walluco,[^c0066-18] duke of the Winidi.

### LXXIII

That year I shall not omit what happened in the region of Spain and to its kings. After the death of Sisibud,[^c0066-19] a most merciful king, whom Sintela had succeeded in the kingdom about a year earlier, 646, Sintela was exceedingly unjust toward his subjects and incurred the hatred of all the leading men of his kingdom.

With the counsel of the others, a certain Sisenandus, one of the nobles, sought Dagobert, asking him to assist him with an army so that he might depose Sintela from the kingdom. In return for this favor he promised Dagobert a magnificent golden dish from the treasure of the Goths, which King Thursemodus had received from the patrician Aetius,[^c0066-20] weighing five hundred pounds of gold.[^c0066-21]

When Dagobert heard this, being greedy, he ordered an army to be summoned from the whole kingdom of Burgundy to assist Sisenandus. When it became known in Spain that a Frankish army was approaching in support of Sisenandus, the entire Gothic army submitted to Sisenandus’s authority.

Abundantius and Venerandus, with the army of Toulouse, advanced with Sisenandus only as far as the city of Caesaraugusta. There all the Goths of the kingdom of Spain raised Sisenandus to the throne.

Abundantius and Venerandus, honored with gifts, returned with the army of Toulouse to their own settlements.[Col. 0652B] Dagobert sent an embassy to Sisenandus, consisting of Duke Amalgarius and Venerandus, ordering him to send the promised dish. When Sisenandus the king had handed the dish over to the envoys, the Goths seized it by force[^c0066-22] and did not allow it to be carried away.

Later, when the envoys had traveled about, Dagobert received two hundred thousand solidi from Sisenandus as the price of this dish and accepted that payment in place of it.

### 631 — LXXIV

In the tenth year of Dagobert’s reign, when he had been informed that the army of the Winidi had entered Thuringia, he advanced from the city of Metz with an army from the kingdom of Austrasia. After crossing the Ardennes, he made for Magantia with a great army,[^c0066-23] intending to cross the Rhine. He had with him a *scara*,[^c0066-24] a force of chosen and brave men from Neustria and Burgundy, together with dukes and counts.

The Saxons sent envoys to Dagobert, asking him to remit the tribute that they paid to the fiscal authorities. In return, they promised, through their own initiative and for their own advantage, to resist the Winidi and to guard the Frankish frontier in those regions.

Dagobert, having obtained the advice of the Neustrian nobles, granted the request to the Saxons who had come to present this petition.[^c0066-25] According to their custom,[^c0066-26] they confirmed an oath over laid-down—or, according to another reading, prepared—weapons on behalf of all the Saxons.

But this promise achieved little. Nevertheless, by Dagobert’s order, the Saxons were released from the tribute that they had customarily paid. They had been assessed by the elder Chlothar at an annual payment of five hundred tribute-cows,[^c0066-27] and Dagobert canceled this obligation.

### 632 — LXXV

In the eleventh year of Dagobert’s reign,[^c0066-28] while the Winidi were fiercely ravaging at Samo’s command and frequently crossing their frontier to devastate the Frankish kingdom, entering Thuringia and the neighboring districts, Dagobert came to the city of Metz. With the agreement of the bishops and nobles, and with all the leading men of his kingdom consenting, he raised his son Sigibert as king in Austrasia and permitted him to have his seat in the city of Metz.

He appointed Chunibert, bishop of the city of Cologne, and Adalgisel, duke, to govern the palace and the kingdom.[^c0066-29] Giving his son a treasury sufficient for his needs, he raised him appropriately, as was fitting, to this eminence. He resolved to confirm individually by written commands whatever he had granted him.

Thereafter the Austrasians are known to have successfully defended the frontier and the Frankish kingdom against the Winidi through their own efforts.

### 633 — LXXVI

When, in the twelfth year of Dagobert’s reign, a son named Chlodoveus was born to him by Queen Nantechilde, it is known that, on the advice and at the urging of the Neustrians,[^c0066-30] he established an agreement with his son Sigibert through a formal pact.

All the leading Austrasian bishops and the other *leudes* of Sigibert, placing their hands upon the agreement, confirmed by oaths that Neustria and Burgundy, in an orderly and firmly established arrangement, should pass to Chlodoveus’s kingdom after Dagobert’s departure. Austrasia, however, being equal both in population and in extent of territory, should likewise pass in its entirety to Sigibert’s kingdom.

Whatever had formerly belonged to the kingdom of Austrasia, King Sigibert was to receive for administration under his authority and to possess forever, except for the duchy of Dentelin,[^c0066-31] which had been unjustly taken away from the Austrasians. This was to be restored to the Neustrians and subjected to Chlodoveus’s rule.

But the Austrasians appear to have confirmed these agreements under compulsion, willingly or unwillingly, through fear of Dagobert. It is clear that the arrangement was preserved later, during the reigns of Kings Sigibert and Chlodoveus.

### LXXVII

Radulf, duke of that Chamari whom Dagobert had appointed duke of Thuringia, fought against the Winidi on several occasions and, defeating them, put them to flight.

Elated by the pride of this victory and repeatedly provoking hostility against Duke Adalgisel on various pretexts, he had gradually begun to rebel against Sigibert as well. But, as has been said, he acted according to the proverb: “He who loves quarrels devises dissensions.”

### 635 — LXXVIII

In the fourteenth year of Dagobert’s reign, when the Wascones were fiercely rebelling and conducting much plundering in the Frankish kingdom formerly held by Charibert, Dagobert ordered an army to advance from the whole kingdom of Burgundy. He appointed as its commander Chadoindus, a referendary who, in the time of the former King Theuderic, had proved himself brave in many battles.

When Chadoindus had advanced into Wasconia with ten dukes and their armies—namely, Arimbertus,[^c0066-32] Amalgarius, Leudebertus, Wandalmarus, Waldericus, Ermenus, Barontus, Chairaardus, of Frankish origin, Chramnelenus, of Roman origin, Wilibadus the patrician, of Burgundian origin, and Aigyna, of Saxon origin—besides very many counts who had no duke over them,[^c0066-33] the whole land of Wasconia was filled with the Burgundian army.

The Wascones emerged from the rocky mountain passes and hurried to battle. When they began to fight, they turned their backs, as was their custom, as soon as they saw that they were being overcome. Giving themselves refuge in the jaws of the valleys and in the Pyrenees, they concealed themselves in very secure places among the rocks of those mountains.[Col. 0654C]

The army, pursuing them from behind with its dukes, overcame the Wascones, took a very large number captive, killed many of them, burned all their houses, and stripped them of their livestock and possessions.

At last, overcome or subdued, the Wascones sought pardon and peace from the aforementioned dukes. They promised that they would present themselves before the glory and presence of King Dagobert and, once delivered into his authority, would carry out everything that he ordered.

This army would have returned safely to its homeland without suffering any injury if Duke Arembertus, together with the elders and nobles of his army, had not through negligence been killed by the Wascones in the valley of Subola.[^c0066-34] The Frankish army that had come from Burgundy into Wasconia returned to its own settlements after accomplishing—or, according to another reading, securing—the victory.

Dagobert, residing at Clichy, sent messengers to Britain, ordering the Britons to make swift restitution for the wrongs they had committed and to submit themselves to his authority. Otherwise, he warned, the Burgundian army that had been in Wasconia would immediately invade Britain.

When King Judacaile[^c0066-35] of the Britons heard this, he hastened to Clichy with many gifts. There he asked Dagobert’s pardon and promised to make amends for everything that the people of his kingdom of Britain had unlawfully done against the *leudes* of the Franks. He also promised that both he himself and the kingdom of Britain that he ruled would always remain subject to the authority of Dagobert and the Frankish kings.

Nevertheless, he did not wish to recline at table or dine with Dagobert, because Judacaile was religious and greatly feared God. When Dagobert had sat down to dine, Judacaile left the palace and went to the residence of Dado the referendary,[^c0066-36] whom he knew to follow a holy way of life, and dined there. On the following day Judacaile, king of the Britons, took leave of Dagobert and returned to Britain. Dagobert nevertheless honored him suitably with gifts.

### 636

In the fifteenth year of Dagobert’s reign, all the elders of the land of the Wascones came with Duke Aiginane[^c0066-37] to Dagobert at Clichy. There, terrified by royal authority, they took refuge in the church of the lord Dionysius.

By Dagobert’s mercy they were granted their lives. There they confirmed by oaths, and simultaneously promised, that they would always remain faithful to Dagobert, his sons, and the Frankish kingdom. The outcome later proved what they had done in their customary manner, as they had often done before.[^c0066-38] With Dagobert’s permission, the Wascones returned to the land of Wasconia.

### 637 — LXXIX

In the sixteenth year of his reign,[^c0066-39] Dagobert began to suffer from a flux of the bowels at the villa of Spinogelus on the river Seine, not far from Paris.[Col. 0656A] From there his attendants carried him to the basilica of Saint Dionysius.

After a few days, when he sensed that his life was in danger, he ordered Aega to come to him quickly. He entrusted Queen Nantechilde and his son Chlodoveus to Aega’s care, feeling that he was already about to depart this life. He greatly valued Aega’s counsel, since through Aega’s energy the kingdom could be governed vigorously.

After these events, a few days later, Dagobert breathed his last. He was buried in the church of Saint Dionysius, which he himself had previously adorned suitably with gold, jewels, and many precious materials, and had ordered to be constructed appropriately all around it, seeking the precious protection of the saint.

He had bestowed such great wealth, villas, and many possessions upon that church in numerous places that many people marveled at it. He had ordered a continual office of psalmody to be established there after the manner of the monastery of the saints of Agaunum. But the laxity of Abbot Aigulf is known to have opposed this institution.[^c0066-40]

After Dagobert’s death, his son Chlodoveus, still a child, assumed his father’s kingdom. All the *leudes* of Neustria and Burgundy raised him to the kingship at the villa of Massolacum. Aega, together with Queen Nantechilde, whom Dagobert had left behind, governed the palace.

### 638–639 — LXXX

In the first year of Chlodoveus’s reign, the second, and as the third year of the same reign was approaching,[^c0066-41] Aega governed the palace and the kingdom suitably.

Among all the other leading men of Neustria, Aega acted with particular prudence and, endowed with complete patience—or, according to another reading, wisdom—was superior to them all. He was noble by birth, rich in possessions, devoted to justice, learned in speech, and ready with replies. He was, however, widely denounced because he was devoted to avarice.

The property of many people that had been unlawfully seized by Dagobert’s command in the kingdoms of Burgundy and Neustria and unjustly absorbed into the fiscal domain was restored to everyone on Aega’s advice.[Col. 0657A]

### LXXXI

That year the emperor Constantine died.[^c0066-42] His son Constans, still a child, was raised to the imperial throne by decree of the senate.

During his reign the empire was devastated most grievously by the Saracens. Jerusalem was captured by the Saracens, and the other cities were overthrown. Upper and Lower Egypt were overrun by the Saracens. Alexandria was captured and plundered. All Africa was devastated and occupied by the Saracens. Paululum [reading uncertain]; there the patrician Gregory was killed by the Saracens.

Only Constantinople, together with the province of Thrace and a few islands, as well as the Roman province,[^c0066-43] remained under imperial authority. For almost the entire empire had been severely battered by the Saracens. Finally the emperor Constans was constrained and compelled to become tributary to the Saracens, so that at least Constantinople, with a few provinces and islands, might be preserved under his authority.

For approximately three years, and it is said even longer, Constans paid one thousand gold solidi every day into the Saracen treasury.[^c0066-44] At length, having recovered his strength to some extent and regained control of the empire, Constans refused to continue paying tribute to the Saracens.

How this event came about I shall relate in its proper place, in the year in which it occurred, and I shall not cease writing until, if God permits, I complete the account of these and other matters and insert into this little book everything that I have learned with certainty.

---

[^c0066-1]: The Claromontanus manuscript reads *Sclav*, as do the others more often below; here, however, the reading is *Sclavorum*.

[^c0066-2]: From this, perhaps, the name *Sclavinia* was given to a type of garment worn by pilgrims in the twelfth century, according to Caesarius’s *Book of Miracles*, chapters 40 and 42, as Alteserra observes. He also cites *Saxonica* from Augustine, chapter 127 of the *Questions on Both Testaments*.

[^c0066-3]: The Claromontanus manuscript reads *caucius*, “more cautiously,” rather than *saucius*, “wounded.”

[^c0066-4]: The Claromontanus manuscript reads *Wogastisburc*. The Colbertinus and Boherianus manuscripts, together with the Palatinus, read *Vocastense*; others have *Vogastense* or *Vocatense*.

[^c0066-5]: The Colbertinus, Boherianus, and several printed editions read *Urbium*. Cointius says that these were the Surbi, Sorbi, or Sorabi, neighboring the Thuringians and subject to the Austrasians.

[^c0066-6]: The manuscript has *se ad regnum Samoni*; another reading is *se et regnum*, “himself and his kingdom.”

[^c0066-7]: The edition of Chesne has *Chrodoaldus*; another has *Hysacius*. Several editions read *Isacius*, and below they have *Asonem* with the Colbertinus. The history of the Lombards must chiefly be reconstructed from Paul the Deacon, since Fredegar often confuses the events. Observe that Fredegar calls Hisacius, who governed Italy in the emperor’s name, “patrician of the Romans”; Charlemagne later held supreme authority in Italy under this title.

[^c0066-8]: That is, from the empire.

[^c0066-9]: The Colbertinus reads *Rotharius*; Chesne has *Chrotacharius* in one place, as does the Boherianus. He is commonly called Rotharis.

[^c0066-10]: This was Audobald, count of the palace, according to Peraldus. He is mentioned in a charter of Chlothar III for the monastery of Saint Benignus at Dijon, issued in 664. In the chronicle of the same monastery he is called Audebedo or Audebellus.

[^c0066-11]: Compare chapter 50 above, where the same story is told. Most printed editions read “King Chlotarius”; the Colbertinus has “Chlodavius.” In the chronicles of Saint Benignus and Besançon, he is said to have been called both Chlotarius and Chlodoveus.

[^c0066-12]: Papia, now called Pavia, was the royal city of the Lombards. It was also called Flavia and Ticinum, from the river Ticinum, now the Ticino, which flows beside it. It was an episcopal see subject to no archbishop, and was distinguished by the title of duchy and by its university.

[^c0066-13]: These names are entirely corrupt in the printed editions. We have retained the readings of the Claromontanus, Chesne, and Freher. The Colbertinus has *Albingam, Novariam, Cottisam, Omavibitergio, Luna*. Other editions have *Albinga, Novaria, Cottisaonia, ubi Tergio et Luna*. The cities listed are well known except Varicottim, a corrupt name that cannot be conjecturally restored. Maritime Genava, now Genoa, is so called to distinguish it from Geneva among the Allobroges. Albenganum retains its ancient name in modern Albenga, made an episcopal see by Alexander III. Saona is Savona, now subject to Genoa; Opitergium is modern Oderzo. The ancient city of Luna was succeeded by Sarzana. Paul the Deacon mentions this expedition in book IV, chapter 47, saying that Rothari captured all the Roman cities on the sea coast from the city of Luna in Tuscany to the Frankish frontier and destroyed Opitergium.

[^c0066-14]: Other copies read *Avarorum*. Some aspirate the name as *Habarorum*. The same practice explains *Hunnorum* for *Chunorum*, as noted frequently elsewhere.

[^c0066-15]: The Colbertinus and Boherianus, together with most printed editions, read “Spain” instead of “Pannonia.”

[^c0066-16]: The Claromontanus reads *Altioeus*. The Colbertinus has *Alticcus*; Chesne and Freher have *Altiaus*; others have *Alticeus*, together with the Palatinus manuscript.

[^c0066-17]: Freher notes that this was the Windische Mark.

[^c0066-18]: The Claromontanus, Freher, and Chesne read *Walluco*; another reading is *Wallaco*, and another *Walduco*.

[^c0066-19]: Sisebut, who succeeded in 621, was followed by his son Reccared II, and after him, three months later, by Suintila—here called Sintela or Sintilla, and in some manuscripts Senzila. Isidore’s chronicle ends with him. In 631 Sisenand expelled Suintila from the throne.

[^c0066-20]: The Illyrian manuscript has *Aetio*, which was also the worn reading of the Colbertinus. The Claromontanus has *Agecio*; the others have *Ejicio*, the form under which the name of Egidius is generally written in these manuscripts. See below the fourth fragment from other books of Fredegar.

[^c0066-21]: The Boherianus reads “five hundred gold solidi” rather than “weighing five hundred pounds of gold.”

[^c0066-22]: The printed editions and the Colbertinus, together with the Boherianus, read *per viam*, “by the way.” Another reading below is *exinde abstrahere*, “to carry it away from there.”

[^c0066-23]: The Boherianus reads *Magantia ... egreditur*, “he advances from Magantia,” rather than *aggreditur*, “he attacks Magantia.”

[^c0066-24]: A *scara* is a troop of soldiers, as we have already observed. The old edition reads *Austria* instead of *Neuster*.

[^c0066-25]: The Boherianus reads *hujus*; Chesne and the others have *hujus petitionis*, “of this petition.”

[^c0066-26]: Cangius observes in his *Glossary* that this custom was familiar to all the northern peoples.

[^c0066-27]: Aimoinus, book IV, chapter 26, notes that these were called *inferendales* because they were delivered annually.

[^c0066-28]: Cointius believes that this should read “the twelfth year,” and the next chapter “the thirteenth,” but it was not permissible to alter the text without the authority of a manuscript.

[^c0066-29]: Valesius argues from the Claromontanus manuscript that the reading should be “Adalgisel, duke, to govern the palace and the kingdom.” The chronicles of Besançon and Saint Benignus, the Metz annals, the *Life of Blessed Pippin*, and others agree, as do the Boherianus and Freher, who have “duke, palace, etc.” Chesne and other editions, together with the Colbertinus, read: “Adalgisel, duke of the palace, to govern the kingdom,” and some have consequently inferred that Dagobert then instituted a new office, that of duke of the palace, among the Franks. The Boherianus has *Adalgisus*; others have *Adagysilus*.

[^c0066-30]: Several editions read “Austrasians,” perhaps because their exemplars contained *Neauster* or *Neaustrasii*.

[^c0066-31]: The Boherianus reads *ducato Dentileno*; others have *Danzileni*.

[^c0066-32]: We have followed the reading of the Claromontanus manuscript. Others read: Almagarius, Haribertus, Ermenricus, Barantus, Arialdus or Hariardus, Ramelenus or Ranlenus, Willibaldus, and Aghyno or Agino.

[^c0066-33]: From such counts, there later came to be admitted among the Peers of France as many counts as there were dukes.

[^c0066-34]: The valley of Subola lies at the foot of the Pyrenees. It formerly belonged to the diocese of Aquae, now Dax, and now to that of Elorum, or Oloron. Its chief town is Malleon, now Mauléon, watered by the Saison. Today the name is contracted to Sola or Seula, commonly La Soule.

[^c0066-35]: The Boherianus reads *Judacaule*. He is commonly called Judicael. Later, after abandoning the kingdom, he assumed monastic clothing in the monastery of Saint John of Gael, now Saint Mevennius, in the diocese of Aleth, or Saint-Malo. He is commemorated in the Benedictine Martyrology on 16 December.

[^c0066-36]: This was Saint Audoenus, later bishop of Rouen, famous under his own name; he is discussed below.

[^c0066-37]: The editions, together with the Colbertinus, read *Ainandus*; others have *Amandus*.

[^c0066-38]: Chesne adds “they deceived them, as the outcome proved.”

[^c0066-39]: These sixteen years include the years during which Dagobert reigned jointly with his father. Thus Dagobert should be said to have died in 638, on 18 January. The year may be called 637 if the year begins at Easter, as it does in Fredegar. Mabillon confirms this view, following Valesius and Cointius, with many arguments both in the preface to the second Benedictine century and in a separate dissertation published in volume III of the *Old Analecta*, against those who, believing that Dagobert reigned sixteen years after his father’s death, postpone his death until 644.

Spinogelus, the village where Dagobert fell ill, lies above the Seine, about one league from the town of Saint-Denis. It is commonly called Épinay, although, as Valesius notes, it ought to be called and written Espineuil. Dagobert was buried in the Dionysian basilica. Learned men have established with many arguments that the basilica existed at that place, together with the tomb of the holy martyrs, where it is still seen, about two leagues from the city. This is also confirmed by numerous autograph charters of the first dynasty of our kings, preserved in book VI of *On Diplomatic Matters*.

When the distinguished Sebastian Le Nain de Tillemont, illustrious no less for piety than for learning, wrote about this matter in volume IV of his *Ecclesiastical History* as though he doubted it, he later investigated it more carefully after being advised by friends. He acknowledged that the opinion of those who contend that the basilica in which the martyrs were buried, and in which Dagobert was deposited, once stood within the city cannot be supported by any certain arguments; on the contrary, the other opinion is demonstrated by the strongest evidence. He promised to correct himself in writing at the first opportunity. This is recorded here because he himself, having died a devout death on 10 January of this year, 1698, was unable to fulfill his promise.

Even today Dagobert’s tomb may be seen at Saint-Denis to the right of the high altar, although learned men do not think that the monument itself is of such great antiquity. It would be superfluous to say more here about the privileges, sacred relics, numerous possessions, jurisdictions, and other matters concerning this most noble monastery, which thereafter became the common burial place of our kings, especially those of the third dynasty.

[^c0066-40]: Freher and others read “supported” rather than “opposed.” The chronicle of Saint Benignus favors this reading, stating that Dagobert ordered the institution and that it was completed through the zeal and industry of Abbot Aigulf. Johannes Columbus believes that Aigulf later became bishop of Valence; Aimoinus, however, distinguishes Agilulf, bishop of Valence, from Aigulf, abbot of Saint-Denis. By the Agaunian psalmody is meant continuous singing of psalms, maintained day and night, such as existed among the Greek monks called *Acoemetae*, “the sleepless,” because they supposedly never slept. They carried it out in several rotating groups. Chlodoveus II restored this practice after Aigulf had neglected it, as is shown by a charter that will be printed in the appendix. The arrangement was likewise confirmed by Theuderic IV and Pippin.

[^c0066-41]: The Claromontanus and the other manuscripts read as translated. The Illyrian, Colbertinus, Bignonius, Boherianus, and Baronius agree. Chesne and Freher, however, read: “Aega, in the first year of Chlodoveus and as the second year of the same reign was approaching, governed the palace suitably,” a reading that Cointius considers preferable. Fredegar is not assigning the events narrated in these chapters to three separate years; rather, he means that Aega governed the palace during the first and second years and died as the third was approaching, as he says below in chapter 83. The chronicle of Saint Benignus agrees.

[^c0066-42]: Constantine, Heraclius’s son, succeeded his father in 641. Shortly afterward, according to report, he was killed by poison administered by his stepmother Martina. Heraclonas, another son of Heraclius by Martina, succeeded him. After six months, however, Heraclonas was deposed by a decree of the senate, his nose being cut off, while his mother’s tongue was cut out. Constans, son of Constantine and defender of the Monothelites, was substituted for him.

[^c0066-43]: The region now called Romania, comprising Thrace proper and neighboring territories. The Boherianus and old editions read “the Thracian province of the empire,” omitting “Roman,” as do the others.

[^c0066-44]: The Colbertinus, in another hand, reads “one thousand gold solidi per year” rather than “per day.”

### LXXXII

In that year King Sintela of Spain, who had succeeded Sisenand on the throne, died. His son, named Tulga, while still a child, was raised to the throne of Spain at his father’s request. The Gothic people cannot tolerate having any yoke imposed upon them. Throughout Tulga’s youth, all Spain was corrupted in the customary manner, as he committed various acts of insolence.

At last one of the nobles, named Chintasindus, having gathered a great many Gothic senators and the rest of the people, was raised to the throne of Spain. He had Tulga degraded and tonsured for the clerical order—according to others, *honus* instead of *honorem*, “honor.” After securing the whole kingdom of Spain under his authority, and recognizing the Gothic disease—the practice they had concerning the deposition of kings, about which he had often deliberated with them—he ordered all those whom he had discovered to have been openly guilty of this vice against kings expelled from the kingdom to be killed individually. He condemned others to exile and handed over their wives and daughters, together with their property, to his faithful followers.

It is said that two hundred Gothic nobles were killed in order to suppress this vice; of the lesser men he ordered five hundred to be killed. Until Chintasindus knew that this Gothic disease had been completely subdued, he did not cease slaughtering with the sword those whom he suspected. The Goths, however, having been subdued by Chintasindus, dared nothing against him, as they had formerly been accustomed to plot against their kings.

When Chintasindus was full of days, he established his son, named Richysindus, as king throughout the whole kingdom of Spain. Chintasindus, doing penance and giving abundant alms from his own property, is said to have died in extreme old age at the age of ninety.

### Notes

- **[Col. 0657D]** Others have *Sentela* or *Sintilla*. He is commonly called Cinthila, or Suinthila II. He was succeeded by Tulga, called *Tolga* in most editions and *Tholga* in Boh. The man who expelled him in 642 was Chindaswindus, who in 649 left his son Receswinthus as sole ruler.
- **[Col. 0658D]** Others have *honus*, for *honorem*, “honor.”
- **[Col. 0658D]** The same thing had been done by Leuvigildus. See Gregory, Book III of the *History*, chapter 30, and Alteserra’s notes on that chapter.

### 640—LXXXIII

In the third year of the reign of King Chlodoveus, Aega, afflicted by fever at the estate of Clippiacum, died. A few days earlier, Ermenfredus, who had married Aega’s daughter, killed Count Aenulfus at the village of Albioderus, at the *mallus*.

Because of this deed, a very severe slaughter of his people was carried out, by order and permission of Queen Nantechildis, by Aenulfus’s relatives and by the populace. Ermenfredus fled for refuge in Auster to the basilica of Saint Remedius, where he remained for many days, avoiding this persecution and fearing the royal authority.

### Notes

- **[Col. 0658D]** Clar. calls him once *Chainulfus* and elsewhere *Ainulfus*. Colb. has *Aniulfus*; in Boh.’s index, *Aginulfus* or *Agnulfo*.
- **[Col. 0658D]** The *mallus* was the assembly of an entire region, or the greater court, in which matters of greater importance were settled by the count. See Cange’s *Glossary*.

### LXXXIV

After Aega’s departure, Erchinoaldus, mayor of the palace, who was related to Dagobert through his mother—according to others, through his lineage; most have “through Dagobert’s mother”—became mayor of the palace of Chlodoveus.

He was a patient man, full of goodness. Since he was patient and prudent, humble and kindly disposed toward priests, he answered everyone patiently and benevolently. He was not swollen with pride, nor did he rage with greed. He pursued peace throughout his administration so earnestly that he was pleasing to God. He was wise, but above all marked by great simplicity; moderately enriched with possessions, he was loved by everyone.

Therefore, after the departure of King Dagobert, I shall not omit the order in which his treasures were divided among his sons; rather, I shall take care to insert the account clearly into this volume.

### Note

- **[Col. 0658D]** Others have *genere*; most have *genetrice*, or “through Dagobert’s lineage.” Erchinoaldus later ransomed Balthildis from captivity and received Saint Furseus. He gave Furseus Latiniacum for the construction of a monastery and built a church in his name at Perona. He died shortly before Saint Eligius, according to Book II, chapter 26, of Saint Eligius’s *Life*—that is, about the year 659.

### LXXXV

After Dagobert’s death, Pippin, the mayor of the palace, and the other Austrasian dukes, who until Dagobert’s death had remained under his authority, unanimously sought Sigibert. Pippin and Chunibert, who had previously been joined to one another in a bond of friendship, recently bound themselves—as before—to preserve their friendship vigorously, firmly, and perpetually.

Each of them prudently and graciously drew all the Austrasian *leudes* to himself, governing them kindly, securing their friendship, and preserving it forever.

As envoys traveled about, Sigibert demanded from Queen Nantechildis and King Chlodoveus the portion of Dagobert’s treasures owed to him, and a court was convened for its return. Chunibert, bishop of the city of Cologne, and Pippin, mayor of the palace, were sent by Sigibert with several nobles. They reached the estate of Compendium.

There, by order of Nantechildis and Chlodoveus, Dagobert’s treasure was presented through the efforts of Aega, the mayor of the palace, and divided on equal terms. Queen Nantechildis nevertheless received one-third of what Dagobert had acquired. Chunibert and Pippin had Sigibert’s share of this treasure brought to Metz; it was presented to Sigibert and inventoried.

After approximately a year—according to Colb. and Freh., “after the cycle of a year”; Boh. has simply “a cycle”—Pippin died. His death caused no small grief to everyone in Auster, because he had been loved by them for his devotion to justice and his goodness. His son Grimoaldus, being energetic, was loved by many in imitation of his father.

### Notes

- **[Col. 0659C]** Perhaps no place in France was more frequently visited by kings. It is commonly called Compiègne, situated somewhat below the confluence of the Axona and the Isara. See Book IV of *On Diplomatic Matters*. It remains a celebrated town, with a notable Benedictine abbey belonging to the Congregation of Saint Maur; it owes its origins to Charles the Bald.
- **[Col. 0659D]** Colb. and Freh. read: “After the cycle of a year.” Boh. has “a cycle.” That cycle of a year should be understood as following the division of the treasure, not Pippin’s death, since both men died in the year 640. Pippin was buried at Landis beside the Geta River, on the border of Hasbania and Brabant, now a small town not far from the monastery of Saint Trudo. See Book IV of *On Diplomatic Matters*. From that place Pippin received the surname of Landen. His body was later transferred to Nivelles and placed beside that of Saint Gertrude, his daughter. Itta, his wife, had built that monastery with Saint Gertrude. Saint Pippin’s life is presented by Chesnius in volume I and by Bollandus on 21 February, the day on which his feast is celebrated.

### LXXXVI

A certain Otto, son of Uro—Ches. has *Beronis*; others *Vronis*, *Vironis*, *Eronis*, or *Aronis*; Boh. has *Vrones*—was a member of the household. He had been Sigibert’s *bajulus* since his youth. He became swollen with pride against Grimoaldus, was jealous of him, and tried to despise him.

Grimoaldus, binding himself in friendship with Bishop Chunibert, began to consider how Otto might be expelled from the palace and Grimoaldus might assume his father’s rank.

### Note

- **[Col. 0659D–0660C]** A king’s *bajulus* was the man entrusted with his education; hence the common people called such men *monitores*, as is clear from Lupus of Ferrières, letter 64, to King Charles: “You will not admit *monitores*, whom the common people call *bajuli*, lest they divide your glory among themselves.” For this reason they possessed great authority, since for the most part everything was done according to their will. Cange discusses them extensively and learnedly in his *Glossary*.

### 640—LXXXVII

When Sigibert was reigning in his eighth year—Colb. has “ninth year”; Sigibert of Gembloux reads the same in Freh., “seventh year”—and Duke Radulfus of Thuringia was preparing to rebel vehemently against Sigibert, all the Austrasian *leudes* were summoned by Sigibert’s order to march with the army.

Sigibert crossed the Rhine with his army, and peoples from all the districts of his kingdom beyond the Rhine joined him from every direction. First, he broke the army of Faro, son of Chrodoaldus, who had been allied with Radulfus, and killed Faro himself. He assigned to captivity all of Faro’s people who had escaped the sword.

All the nobles and the army then gave one another their right hands, promising that no one would spare Radulfus’s life. But this promise did not take effect.

Sigibert next crossed Buchonia with his army and hastened toward Thuringia. Seeing this, Radulfus built a fortress of wood on a certain mountain above the river Unstrut in Thuringia. Gathering as large an army as he could, he established himself in the fortress with his wife and children in order to defend himself.

Sigibert then arrived with the army of his kingdom and surrounded the fortress on every side. Radulfus remained inside, firmly prepared for battle. But this battle was undertaken without a common plan. The youthful rashness of King Sigibert caused it: some wished to advance to battle that same day, while others wished to wait until the following day, and they had no united counsel.

The dukes Grimoaldus and Adalegiselus, seeing this and being concerned for Sigibert’s safety, guarded him continually on every side. Duke Bobo of Auvergne, with part of Adalegiselus’s army, and Count Aenovalaus of Sogiontis, with his district troops, together with the rest of the army’s many forces, went at once to fight against Radulfus at the fortress gate.

Radulfus trusted that some of Sigibert’s army commanders would not attack him with their full strength. Bursting through the gate of the fortress, he fell upon Sigibert’s army with his men. Radulfus and his followers inflicted such a slaughter upon Sigibert’s army that it was astonishing.

The Maganenses were not faithful in this battle. It is said that many thousands of men were killed there by the sword.

After winning the victory, Radulfus entered the fortress. Sigibert, seized by deep and bitter sorrow together with his faithful men, sat upon his horse, tears bursting from his eyes, and mourned those whom he had lost. Duke Bobo—or Bodo—and Count Aenovallaus, together with the other bravest noble warriors and a great part of King Sigibert’s army who had entered the engagement with them, were slaughtered in this battle before Sigibert’s eyes.

Fredulfus too, the household officer who was said to have been Radulfus’s friend, fell in this battle. That same night Sigibert remained with his army in tents not far from the fortress.

On the following day, seeing that they had achieved nothing against Radulfus, they sent messengers throughout the region so that they might cross the Rhine peacefully once more. Sigibert and his army reached an agreement with Radulfus and returned to their own settlements.

Radulfus, lifted up by pride, considered himself in Thuringia to be like a king. He strengthened his friendships with the Wends and bound the neighboring peoples whom he had around him by the obligations of friendship. In his words, however, he did not deny Sigibert’s authority; in his actions he vigorously resisted his rule.

### Notes

- **[Col. 0660D]** We have already made some observations on this word in the notes on Gregory. A *bannum* is an edict or proclamation of something. It was sometimes also used for the penalty imposed on those who had not obeyed; thus *heribannum* (*l’arrière-ban*) denoted the fine imposed on those who neglected to go to the army. The use of these terms has not entirely disappeared: today we say *convoquer le ban et l’arrière-ban* and *être mis au ban de l’empire*. We even call the customary proclamations of marriages in churches *banns*.
- **[Col. 0660D]** Most editions have: “Faro, son of Chroaldus by name, with …” Manuscripts, together with Freh., have *Faram*; below, *Farae*. Clar. has *Faram, son of Chrodoaldus*, and so forth. Colb. and several editions read “slaughtering Sigibert’s army,” which is evidently an error.
- **[Col. 0660D]** Boh. has *Sogotinsis*. Colb. and most editions have *Enovalaus Sigiotensis*—the Sundgau. Chesn. and Freh. have *Nauvalaus*; others *Innovalaus*, *Aenovalatus*, and similarly below.
- **[Col. 0661D]** Ches. and Freh. have *Freudolfus*.

### 642—LXXXVIII

In the tenth year of Sigibert’s reign, Otto, who was swollen with pride and hostility against Grimoaldus, was killed through Grimoaldus’s faction by Leutharius, duke of the Alamanni.

The rank and honor of mayor of the palace, both in Sigibert’s palace and throughout the whole Austrasian kingdom, was firmly confirmed in Grimoaldus’s hands.

### Note

- **[Col. 0661D–0662D]** Later Grimoaldus advanced to such insolence that, after Sigibert’s death and after Sigibert’s son Dagobert had been sent away to Scotland, he ordered his own son Childebert to be proclaimed king of Austrasia. The leading men of the kingdom detested this crime, expelled the tyrant, and cast Grimoaldus into chains at Paris, where he died. Then Dagobert, recalled by the nobles of the kingdom, received his father’s Austrasian kingdom. On this matter see Valesius, Books XX and XXII of *Frankish Affairs*; Henschenius, in the *Life of Saint Sigibert*, 1 February; and the Bollandists and Mabillon in the preface to volume II of the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*. Sigibert was buried in the monastery of Saint Martin that he had built near Metz on the bank of the Moselle, where his sacred relics were preserved until 1552. In that year, after Saint Martin’s abbey had been completely destroyed, they were transferred to Nancy, where they rest in the church called the primatial church, endowed from the spoils and revenues of that abbey and of other sacred places. His feast is celebrated on 1 February.

### 641—LXXXIX

In the fourth year of Chlodoveus’s reign, when Queen Nantechildis, together with her son King Chlodoveus, had come to Orléans, in the kingdom of Burgundy, after Aega’s departure, she ordered all the elders, bishops, dukes, and nobles of the kingdom of Burgundy to come to her.

There Nantechildis drew them all individually to her side, and Flaochatus, a Frank by birth, was nobly established by Queen Nantechildis as mayor of the palace in the kingdom of Burgundy, by the election of the bishops and all the dukes. She betrothed her niece, named Ragnoberta, to Flaochatus.

This betrothal was brought about by some unknown intrigue. For Flaochatus and Queen Nantechildis were secretly contriving another plan, which is believed not to have been pleasing to God and therefore did not come into effect.

When Erchinoaldus and Flaochatus, the two mayors of the palace, had apparently reached a common agreement, consenting to one another and giving mutual support, they arranged to hold this office successfully.

Flaochatus confirmed by letter, and also by oaths, to all the dukes of the kingdom of Burgundy and to the bishops that he would preserve for each of them forever his rank, dignity, and friendship.

Raised to this dignity, Flaochatus traveled throughout the kingdom of Burgundy. Continually taking counsel and recalling the former enmity that he had long concealed in the secrets of his heart, he planned to kill Willebadus the patrician.

### Notes

- **[Col. 0662D]** Others have *Flaucadus* or *Flaochadus*, and so below.
- **[Col. 0662D]** Colb. has *Regimbertam*; others *Ragimbertam*; Chesn. *Ragnobergam*.
- **[Col. 0662D]** Colb. has *Ramleni*. Several editions have *Ramneleni* or *Chramaneli*, *Chramleni*, and so below.

### XC

Willebadus, being rich in resources and having enriched himself by taking the property of many people through various devices, was famous for his wealth. He was devoted to pride because of his patrician rank and his excessive possessions. He was swollen with hostility toward Flaochatus and tried to despise him.

Flaochatus gathered the bishops and dukes of the kingdom of Burgundy around him and convened a court at Chalon in the month of May to deliberate for the benefit of the homeland. Willebadus too arrived there with a large following.

Flaochatus attempted to kill Willebadus there. Seeing this, Willebadus refused to enter the palace. Flaochatus began to fight Willebadus outside. Amalbertus, Flaochatus’s brother, intervened to make peace when they were already about to engage in combat. Willebadus kept Amalbertus with him and escaped this danger. Other intervening persons then separated them unharmed.

Afterward Flaochatus devised a vehement plan for Willebadus’s destruction.

In that year Queen Nantechildis died. In September of the same year, Flaochatus, King Chlodoveus, Erchinoaldus—also mayor of the palace—and several Austrasian nobles advanced from Paris through Sens and Auxerre and reached Autun.

There Chlodoveus ordered Willebadus the patrician to come to him. Willebadus recognized that an unjust plan for his destruction had been devised by Flaochatus and his brother Amalbertus, as well as by the dukes Amalgarius and Chramnelenus. He therefore gathered around himself a great multitude from the territory of his patriciate, including bishops, nobles, and strong men whom he had been able to assemble, and set out toward Autun.

Chlodoveus the king, Erchinoaldus the mayor of the palace, and Flaochatus sent Ermenricus, a household officer, to meet him. Willebadus was uncertain whether to approach or, avoiding danger, turn back. Ermenricus’s promises induced him to proceed to Autun, and Willebadus, believing him, honored him with suitable gifts.

He followed behind him to Autun and there pitched his tents with his men not far from the city.

On the very day he arrived there, he had sent Aigilulfus, bishop of the city of Valence, and Count Giso to Autun to observe what was happening. Flaochatus detained them in the city.

On the following day Flaochatus, Amalgarius, and Chramnelenus, who had unanimously conspired to destroy Willebadus, advanced early from the city; the other dukes of the kingdom of Burgundy joined them with their army. Erchinoaldus, taking up arms with the Neustrians whom he had with him, entered the war as well.

Willebadus, for his part, prepared the weapons of battle and gathered together everyone he could. The two battle lines joined in combat. In that fight Flaochatus, Amalgarius, Chramnelenus, and the duke Wandelbertus engaged Willebadus and fought against him.

The other dukes and the Neustrians, who ought to have surrounded them on every side, held back and watched, awaiting the outcome; they did not wish to attack Willebadus. There Willebadus was killed, and many of his followers were slaughtered with the sword.

In that conflict, Count Bertharius of the palace, a Frank from the district beyond the Jura, was the first of the others to engage Willebadus. Against him, the Burgundian Manaulfus, enraged, came out from among the rest with his men to fight Bertharius.

Because Bertharius had previously been his friend, he said to him: “Come under my shield; I shall free you from this danger.” When he had raised his shield to protect him, Manaulfus struck Bertharius in the chest with a spear.
