The others who had come with him surrounded Bertharius—because he had advanced far ahead of the rest—and wounded him severely.

Then Aubedo, Bertharius’s son, seeing his father in mortal danger, ran with the greatest speed to aid him. He struck Manaulfus in the chest with his spear and threw him to the ground. He killed all the others who had struck his father. Thus, by God’s favor, like a faithful son, he saved his father Bertharius from death.

Those dukes who had refused to attack Willebadus with their army plundered the tents of Willebadus, the bishops, and the others who had come with him, and seized a great amount of gold and silver there. The other goods and the riders—or horses—were taken by those who had refused to fight.

After these events, Flaochatus advanced from Autun on the following day and proceeded to Chalon. After he entered the city, the entire city was almost completely consumed by fire on the following day, through some unknown accident.

Struck by God’s judgment and afflicted by fever, Flaochatus was placed in a boat and carried by water along the river Arar, called the Saône—also *Sagonna*. He was hastening toward Latona, but on the journey, on the eleventh day after Willebadus’s death, he breathed his last. He was buried in the church of Saint Benignus in the suburb of Dijon.

Many believe that these two men, Flaochatus and Willebadus, were both brought to destruction by God’s judgment because they had sworn many oaths to one another at holy places concerning friendship, yet each had unjustly oppressed the peoples subject to him through greed and had stripped them of their possessions. Thus, it is believed, a great multitude was freed from their oppression by God’s judgment, and their treachery and lies caused both of them to perish.

### Notes

- **[Col. 0662D]** Colb. and several editions have *vehementer minabat consilium*; Boh. has *entinebat*; others *eliminabat*.
- **[Col. 0662D]** Nantechildis was buried in the basilica of Saint Denis.
- **[Col. 0662D]** Clar., Boh., and Colb. have *Chramneleni*; some editions have *Ramneleni*, *Chramaneli*, or *Chramleni*, and similarly below.
- **[Col. 0663C]** Several editions have *Ailulfum*; Freh. has *Aigulfum*.
- **[Col. 0663C]** Freherus suspects that *telam praelii*, “the web of battle,” should be read.
- **[Col. 0663C]** Clar. and Ch. have *Chaubedo*.
- **[Col. 0663C]** That is, “the remaining goods and riders, or horses.”
- **[Col. 0663C]** Clar., Boh., Colb., and Palat. read: “among the peoples subject to them … they oppressed [them] together with *letarebus*” [the final word is corrupt or uncertain]. Freh. has *lateribus*, “sides.” For the deaths of both men, see the *Life of Saint Eligius*, written by Saint Audoenus, and the *Life of Saint Sigiranus*, in the second Benedictine century.
- **[Col. 0663C–0664D]** Here the chronicle ends in the Clermont manuscript, which appears to have been written about that time, as we stated in the preface. The same is true of an old codex formerly belonging to Melchior Goldast, cited by Henschenius in volume I of the Bollandist February under his observations on the *Life of Saint Sigibert*. The closing formula *Explicit*, placed at the end both of the index and of the chronicle itself, prevents anyone from calling that codex incomplete. If I am not mistaken, it is the same codex that Valesius cites in Book XX of *Frankish Affairs* from the library of Christina, Queen of Sweden. Moreover, in the Boherian codex, which contains the following chronicles and all the additions, space is left blank here; then it has in large letters, “Therefore,” and so forth, while the index of chapters prefixed to the work ends at 89, with the death of Willebadus and Flaochatus. Hence it is clear that these little works are entirely distinct.
  
  Although Fredegarius ended his chronicle in the fourth year of Chlodoveus—641 or 642 according to Valesius’s reckoning—it is nevertheless clear that he lived beyond that year. In chapter 48 he states that Samo was elected king by the Wends in the fortieth year of King Chlotarius, A.D. 623, and held the kingdom for thirty-five years. He also records the death of Chindaswindus, king of Spain, and other events that occurred after Chlodoveus’s death.

**The Chronicle of Fredegarius ends here.**

## Continuation of the Chronicle of Fredegarius the Scholastic

### Part One, by an Anonymous Author (C)

### XCI

- **[Col. 0665B–0665C]** The author of this appendix appears to be the same person who collected various chronicles into a single body. He filled the gap of about thirty-nine years from the end of Fredegarius’s Chronicle to 680, when the following chronicle begins below in chapter 97, chiefly from the anonymous author who wrote the *Deeds of the Kings of the Franks* under Theuderic of Cale, and from the monk of Saint-Denis, author of the *Deeds of Dagobert* and of his son Chlodoveus. Since these authors inserted many little tales into their writings, this continuator has no great authority among learned men.

Therefore Chlodoveus, the son of Dagobert, took as his queen a woman of foreign origin named Baldechildis. He fathered by her three sons: Chlotharius, Childericus, and Theodoricus. He had as mayor of the palace a vigorous and wise man named Erchanwaldus.

Chlodoveus thus maintained peace in his kingdom without war. In the final years of his life, however, he became deranged and died. He had reigned for eighteen years.

### Notes

- **[Col. 0665C]** Balthildis was of Saxon origin—that is, from the people who, together with the Angles and Jutes, crossed into Britain in the fifth century. From captivity she was brought into the royal chamber. After her husband’s death she administered the kingdom; finally she withdrew to the monastery of Cala, which she had built, became a nun there, and died in the year 680, on 30 January, the day on which her feast is celebrated. Her life is found in the second Benedictine century, page 775. Her tomb can still be seen there in the underground crypt.
- **[Col. 0665C]** Colb. and Pal. Boh. have *Baldigilde* and *Herchonoaldo*. The others have *Erchoaldum*. This is the Erchinoaldus mentioned above.
- **[Col. 0665C]** Boh. has seventeen years. He was buried in the basilica of Saint Denis. During his reign the power of the mayors of the palace is said to have greatly increased, eventually reaching the point at which, after expelling the kings, they finally placed the crown upon themselves. Cointius, however, strongly attacks those who called the following kings incompetent.

### 656—XCII

The Franks established Chlotharius, his eldest son, as king, together with the aforementioned queen, his mother. At the same time Erchanwaldus, mayor of the palace, died. The Franks, wavering in uncertainty, took counsel and appointed Ebruinus to the care and dignity of this office.

### 660—XCIII

In those days King Chlotharius, seized by a severe fever, died in his youth. He had reigned for four years.

### Note

- **[Col. 0666B–0666C]** One should read “fourteen years.” But after four years of Chlotharius’s reign, his brother Childericus became king of Austrasia, namely in the year 660. In 669, when Chlotharius died, Theodoricus III, the brother of both, was raised to the kingdom of Neustria and Burgundy; shortly afterward he was removed from the throne, and Childericus, while Ebruinus was exiled at Luxeuil, obtained sole rule. Our author explains this in this and the following chapter. Some more recent writers say that Chlotharius was buried in the basilica of Saint Denis; but it is more likely that he was laid to rest in the monastery of Cala, where his tomb, together with a stone effigy of him carved about seven hundred years ago, can still be seen. Mabillon more fully proves that Chlotharius’s third year fell in 659 in volume III of the *Analecta*, from an old inscription in the Fossatensis manuscript, which reads: “In the hundredth year after the completion of the reckoning of Saint Victor the bishop, in the third year of our lord Clotharius, a king of noble character, by order of the princes themselves and of his exalted mother, the lady Balthildis, queen,” and so forth.

### 669

Theodoricus, his brother, succeeded him in the kingdom. His brother Childericus was raised by the Franks to the kingship in Austrasia, under Duke Wulfoaldus.

### Note

- **[Col. 0666C]** The printed editions, omitting one line, read: “Theodoricus, his brother in Austria,” which is contrary to the truth, since Childericus was already reigning in Austrasia. We have corrected this error, which had caused difficulty for learned men, with the help of the manuscripts.

### XCIV

At that time the Franks prepared an ambush against Ebruinus. They rose up against Theodoricus and expelled him from the kingdom. Cutting off the hair of his head, they tonsured him; they also tonsured Ebruinus and sent him unwillingly to the monastery of Luxeuil in Burgundy.

They sent an embassy to Childericus in Austrasia. He came together with Duke Wulfoaldus, and they received him over the entire kingdom.

### XCV

Childericus himself was a fickle and excessively impulsive king, driving the Frankish people into rebellion, scandal, and derision. Eventually no small hatred grew among them, leading to scandal and ruin.

As this hatred grew stronger, he ordered a noble Frank named Bodilo to be stretched out against a stake and beaten, contrary to law. Seeing this, the Franks were stirred to great anger. Ingolbertus, Amalbertus, and the other leading men of the Franks incited a rebellion against Childericus himself.

### 673

The aforementioned Bodilo rose up against him with many others, intending an ambush, and killed the king in the forest of Lauchonia together with his pregnant queen, named Bilihildis. It is painful to relate.

Wulfoaldus escaped by flight and returned to Austrasia. The Franks, following the counsel of the blessed Leudegarius and his companions, appointed Leudesius, the noble son of Erchonwaldus, to the dignity of mayor of the palace.

### Notes

- **[Col. 0667B–0667C]** Colb. and Boh. have: “intending an ambush against the king in the forest of Lauconis … Bilihilde.” They believe this forest to be the one lying between Cala, then a royal estate, and the town of Saint Denis; today it is called the Liberiac forest, commonly the forest of Livry, or perhaps the Bungiac forest, Bondy. We should not listen to those who think this happened near Rouen, where they say Childericus and his wife Bilechildis were buried in the church of Saint Peter, now called Saint Ouen after its patron. This must be regarded as beyond dispute since their tombs were discovered in the church of Saint-Germain-des-Prés when it was restored about forty years ago. In addition to the royal insignia in Childericus’s tomb, this inscription, written in large letters, was found: **CHILDR. REX.** See Valesius, Book XXI of *Frankish Affairs*, for a discussion of the matter.
- **[Col. 0667C]** Others have *dolus est*, “it is deceit,” rather than *dolor*, “it is painful.”

### XCVI

When Ebruinus heard of these dissensions, he took counsel and, finding the Franks divided against one another, summoned many allies and other persons to his aid. With a large force of troops, he left the monastery of Luxeuil and returned to Francia.

He advanced as far as the river Isara—the Oise. He killed the guards who were sleeping at Sainte-Maxence, crossed the river Isara, and killed the ambushers whom he found there.

Leudesius, the mayor of the palace, escaped by flight together with the king’s treasures. Fleeing from the estate of Bacivus, he ran away; when Ebruinus arrived there, he seized the treasures that he found there.

From there Ebruinus departed and came to the estate of Criscecum in the Ponthieu. He deceitfully promised Leudesius his loyalty, pretending to be sincere, and arranged a court so that, after an oath of mutual agreement had been sworn, Leudesius might depart in peace.

But Ebruinus acted deceitfully, as was his custom. Preparing an ambush for his fellow countryman, he killed Leudesius, restored King Theodoricus to the throne, and skillfully reestablished his own authority.

He ordered Saint Leudegarius, the bishop, to be killed by the sword after he had been beaten with the most cruel tortures. He killed his brother Gerinus by a different torture.

The remaining Frankish men, their companions, escaped by flight, crossed the Loire, and fled as far as the Gascons. Very many were condemned to exile and were never seen again.

### Notes

- **[Col. 0667C]** Most editions have *Issam*; others *Isaram*. The Isara is the river commonly called the Oise. The town still stands beside it, named from its bridge and Saint Maxentius, commonly Pont-Sainte-Maxence. On this occasion Ebruinus raised a certain young Chlodoveus to the kingship, pretending that he was Chlotharius’s son. Dagobert II reigned in that part of Austrasia lying on both sides of the Rhine near this river until 680. Mabillon discusses his return to Gaul, his death, and his burial at length in the preface to the fourth Benedictine century, *Acts of the Saints*, part I, §9, no. 198 and following. He is Saint Dagobert, king and martyr, venerated at Satanac, or Stenay.
- **[Col. 0668B]** He is mentioned in Queen Emma’s calendar, preserved in the Rhemigian library at Reims, on 23 December, where an ancient author says that he suffered martyrdom. Mabillon proves that this occurred in 679.
- **[Col. 0668B]** There can be no doubt that this must be read *Bacivo*, although the manuscripts commonly prefer *Abacivo*. Hence Samson of Abbéville and Cointius thought that Abbéville was intended. But Bacium was once a celebrated royal estate, situated near Corbie before it was ravaged by the Normans; its ruins can still be seen, and the village retains the name Baisiu. See Book IV of *On Diplomatic Matters*, no. 12.
- **[Col. 0668B–0668C]** Others have *Creciacum*, together with the forest of the same name in Ponthieu—Crécy in Ponthieu—not near the Alteia, as Valesius thought, but near the river Maye. See Book IV of *On Diplomatic Matters*, no. 46.
- **[Col. 0668C]** Saint Leudegarius was killed in the district of Arras on 3 October 678 and buried at Sarcinga, or Sorcin. See the two lives written by contemporary authors in the second Benedictine century. His brother Gerinus, or Guarinus, is also commemorated as a martyr in the Roman Martyrology on the same day; according to the second *Life of Saint Leodegarius*, no. 11, he was crushed beneath stones. Leudegarius himself recounts the matter more fully in a letter addressed to his mother. In the old calendar of the monastery of Murbach in Alsace, written about five hundred years ago, Saint Gerinus the martyr is commemorated on 25 August.

### Part Two, by an Anonymous Austrasian Author (C)

[Col. 0667D] 667 **IN THE YEAR 680.**—XCVII. In Austrasia also, after Duke Ulfoald’s death, Duke Martin and Pippin, son of Ansegisel, formerly a noble Frank, held power. After the kings had died—Dagobert, that is, and perhaps his son Sigibert—[Col. 0668D] the leaders Ebroin, Martin, and Pippin, having joined forces, were stirred up to war against King Theuderic. When the army had been mobilized at a place called Locofao, [Col. 0668D] they meanwhile joined battle there; fighting with great determination, a very large part of the people on both sides fell. Defeated, Martin and Pippin fled with their companions; Ebroin pursued them and ravaged most of that region. Martin therefore entered Lugdunum Clavatum, [Col. 0669C] the ancient name of that city; today it is called Laudunum (Laon), and fortified himself within its walls. Ebroin pursued him and, coming to the village of Erchreco, sent messengers to Lugdunum Clavatum—Aegilbert and Reulus, [Col. 0669D] bishop of the city of Rheims—to induce them, on the strength of a pledge given, to administer false oaths over empty reliquary chests. Believing them in this matter, he left Lugdunum Clavatum and, coming with his companions and allies to Erchrecum, was there killed together with all his men.

[Note: [Col. 0667D] This author is much more precise than the preceding one. He reveals his own period below, in chapter 109, where he indicates that he was writing in the year 735.]

[Note: [Col. 0667D] Martin mentioned here was the son of Saint Clodulf and the grandson of Saint Arnulf; Pippin, his brother, was his first cousin and likewise a grandson of Saint Arnulf through Ansegisel.]

[Note: [Col. 0667D] That is, Dagobert II, and perhaps his son Sigibert. A contemporary author of the Life of Saint Salaberga mentions the civil war that arose between Theuderic and Dagobert, in the second volume of the Benedictine collection. Another edition reads: “When the kings had died.”]

[Note: [Col. 0668D] Thus Boh.; the printed editions have Locofico. The Deeds of the Frankish Kings, chapter 46, have Lufao; other copies have Lucofao and Lucofago. Valesius did not know this place and thought it might be Loixi in the Laonnois. See Book IV of *De re diplomatica*, no. 57. Some, however, will more plausibly think that the place called Lufaus in the Toul region is meant. Hericus mentions it in his *History of the Bishops of Auxerre*; this may perhaps more plausibly be the place intended here.]

[Note: [Col. 0669C] Thus Boh., referring to the ancient name of this city; today it is called Laudunum (Laon).]

[Note: [Col. 0669C] This place is written variously in different manuscripts. Colbert has here “Extreco” and below “Erchreco”; Boh. has “Erchrego” and “Herchrego”; the printed editions have “Ertreco,” “Erereco,” and “Ercheco.” The *Deeds of the Frankish Kings* have “Erchaco,” “Ergariaco,” and “Ercherego.” Valesius considers this place to be Acheri, a village situated between Ribemont and Faram, in the Laonnois. It is more probably Escheri-Launois, closer to Laon, as stated in Book IV of *De re diplomatica*, no. 57. There is also, in the diocese of Rheims not far from Château-Porcien, a place on the Aisne called Ecry, which may perhaps be intended here.]

[Note: [Col. 0669D] Thus Boh. The editions have “Regulum”; Colbert has “Aigilbertum ac Regulfum.” The former, called Aglibertus in Boh., was, according to Valesius, Agilbert, first bishop in England and later bishop of Paris in Francia. His body was found in 1631, dressed in pontifical vestments, in the chapel of Saint Paul the Hermit at the monastery of Jouarre, as André Saussay, who was present at the discovery, frequently testifies. Reulus—or, as Frodoard calls him, and as he is called in the ancient diptychs and the litanies of the Church of Rheims, Reolus—founded the monastery of Orbacum, where he was buried and is still venerated, on 3 September. Both have a place in the sacred calendars. Cointius attempts, in his entry for 680, to vindicate them from the crime attributed to them here.]

**XCVIII.** Ebroin continued to oppress the Franks with ever greater and more excessive cruelty, until at last he made threats against Ermenfrid the Frank and resolved to seize his possessions. After consulting with his companions, he gathered a band of associates by night, rose against Ebroin during the night, and killed him.

**IN THE YEAR 681.**—After Ebroin had been killed, Ermenfrid came with his gifts to Duke Pippin in Austrasia. Thereupon the Franks, following their counsel, appointed the illustrious man Warado in his place to the office of mayor of the palace. [Col. 0670C] Accordingly, the aforesaid Warado, receiving hostages from Duke Pippin, established peace between them.

[Note: [Col. 0670C] Thus Colbert and the printed editions have *majoris domus*, “of the mayor of the palace,” and likewise below. Warado is elsewhere regularly called Warato in the manuscripts.]

**IN THE YEAR 682.**—At that time the aforementioned Warado had a son, a very capable and energetic man, well trained in counsel, named Gislemarus, who administered the palace in his father’s place. Because of his excessive cleverness and cunning, he displaced his father from his proper office. Saint Audoenus the bishop repeatedly rebuked him for this and urged him from time to time to return to peace or to his father’s favor. He refused to listen and remained hardened in his heart. Thus many disagreements and numerous civil wars arose between Pippin and the aforementioned Gislemarus. For when Gislemarus rose against the enemy of Duke Pippin at the fortress of Namugo, [Col. 0670C] that is, against Pippin’s army, he killed many of their noblemen after deceitfully giving a false oath. On his return, because of his displacement of his father or some other considerable wickedness that he had treacherously committed, the aforesaid Gislemarus was struck by God and, as he deserved, poured forth his most wicked spirit.

[Note: [Col. 0670C] Thus Boh.; other copies have “the fortress of Manucum.” The place intended is Namucum, or, as we write it today, Namurcum, commonly Namur, a city of Flanders famous by that name and endowed with an episcopal see in the preceding century.]

[Note: [Col. 0670C] Freher, the Illyrican collection, and others have “Adoinus”; others have “Audoinus.” Gislemarus is also called Gislemaris and Ghislemarus. More will be said about them below.]

**IN THE YEAR 683.**—When he had died, his father Warado recovered his former office as mayor of the palace.

**IN THE YEAR 684.**—XCIX. At that time blessed Audoenus the bishop, full of virtues, departed to the Lord. [Col. 0670B]

[Note: [Col. 0670D] He died on 24 August 684. He was buried in the monastery of Saint Peter in the suburb of Rouen, still famous in the city under the name of Saint-Ouen, belonging to the Order of Saint Benedict of the Congregation of Saint Maur. The relics of this saint were burned in the preceding century by the raging Calvinists.]

At that same time the aforementioned Warado, the mayor of the palace, died. [Col. 0670D] He had a noble and vigorous wife named Ansfledis, whose son-in-law, Bercharius, assumed the office of mayor of the palace. He was short in stature, limited in understanding, fickle and impulsive, and often disregarded the friendship and counsel of the Franks. The Franks, indignant at this—Auderamnus, Reulus, and many others—left Bercharius, joined Pippin through the exchange of hostages, formed an alliance, and stirred up opposition against Bercharius and the rest of the Franks.

[Note: [Col. 0670D] Other copies have Anfledis or Anfredis.]

[Note: [Col. 0670D] Others have Warato. In a charter of King Theuderic, in Book VI of *De re diplomatica*, no. 13, we read: “Waratune, Ebroin, and Ghistemare, formerly mayors of the palace, and Bercharius, mayor of the palace,” all of whom are frequently mentioned here. These variations, except for Bercharius, also occur in our manuscript chronicles. The printed edition has Bertharius.]

**IN THE YEAR 697.**—C. Pippin, having mobilized his army, rose in hostility from Austrasia and hastened to war against King Theuderic and Bercharius. They met in the Vermandian district, [Col. 0670D] at a place called Textricius, and fought one another there. Pippin and the Austrasians prevailed; King Theuderic and Bercharius fled, Pippin was victorious, and, pursuing them, subjugated that region to himself. Later, Bercharius was killed by false friends and flatterers, at the instigation of Ansfledis, his mother-in-law. After this, Pippin took King Theuderic with his treasures and, having arranged all matters concerning the palace, returned to Austrasia. He had a noble and extremely prudent wife named Plecthrudis, [Col. 0671C] by whom he had two sons: the elder was named Drocus, and the younger Grimoaldus.

[Note: [Col. 0670D] Boh. reads: “Rising with a hostile army … hastening to … Vermandisse.” There is disagreement among authors as to whether the chief city of the Viromandui, formerly the episcopal seat of the bishops who transferred their see to Noviomum (Noyon), was the modern Augusta Viromanduorum, commonly called Saint-Quentin after the city’s famous martyr and patron of the region, or whether it was the village that still retains the ancient name of the Veromandui, Vermands, distinguished by an abbey of the Premonstratensian Order. Not far from the latter is Textricius, on the Dalmanion River, commonly Tertri or Testri-sur-Daumignon, a village situated between Péronne and Saint-Quentin.]

[Note: [Col. 0671C] Thus Boh. and Colbert; the printed edition has Plictrudis, and likewise below. Pippin later dismissed her in order to take Alpais; but, after being rebuked by the bishops and after Alpais withdrew to the monastery of Orp, he took Plechtrudis back.]

[Note: [Col. 0671C] Thus Boh. and Colbert; the printed editions, together with most copies, have Drogo. Below they have both Drocus and Drogo.]

**IN THE YEAR 690.**—CI. King Theuderic died; he had reigned seventeen years. [Col. 0671C] They elected his young son Chlodoveus to the kingdom. But not many years later, the aforesaid King Chlodoveus fell ill and died; he had reigned four years.

[Note: [Col. 0671C] Thus Boh., Colbert, and Queen Christina’s manuscript. The printed editions have fourteen years. The author of the *Deeds of the Frankish Kings* gives nineteen years, and others eighteen. Several chronicles published by Chesne support our manuscripts. Cointius assigns him nineteen years and gives his successor, Chlodoveus III, two. This calculation does not conflict with our author’s total, who assigns seventeen years to the former and four to the latter. Theuderic was buried at Arras in the monastery of Saint Vedast (Saint-Vaast), which is said to have been built or at least endowed by him.]

**IN THE YEAR 694.**—His brother Childebert succeeded to the kingdom. [Col. 0671D] From the inscription in the manuscript of Jacobus Bongarsius it is clear that Childebert III’s fifth year coincided with the year of the common era 699, when Easter was celebrated on 23 March. The inscription is given here from Scaliger’s notes on the Eusebian chronology:

> IN THE FIFTH YEAR OF CHILDEBERT, KING OF THE FRANKS, BY ORDER OF PIPPIN, FROM ADAM THERE ARE FIVE THOUSAND NINE HUNDRED YEARS. EASTER WAS ON THE TENTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF APRIL. THE ASCENSION OF THE LORD WAS ON THE KALENDS OF MARCH [read: MAY], ACCORDING TO CYCLE NUMBER 1, YEAR 91, THE REPETITION FROM THE BEGINNING OF THE CYCLE, IN THE YEAR 1,190.

Drocus, instructed by his father Pippin, received the dukedom of Champagne.

**IN THE YEAR 695.**—Grimoald the younger was elected mayor of the palace over the Franks together with King Childebert. He was a very gentle man, filled with every goodness and mildness, generous in almsgiving and ready in prayer.

CII. Pippin and Ratbod, [Col. 0671D] the pagan duke of the Frisian people, made war against one another, fighting there at the fortress of Dorestate. [Col. 0672C] Pippin was victorious. After Duke Ratbod had been put to flight with the Frisians who escaped, Pippin returned with much spoil and booty. After this, Drocus, Pippin’s son, was seized by a severe fever and died; he was buried in the basilica of Blessed Arnulf the Confessor in the city of Metz. Grimoald also fathered a son by a certain concubine, named Theudoaldus.

[Note: [Col. 0671D] This is the Ratbod who, having recognized the truth of the Christian religion, preferred to descend into hell with the kings and princes mentioned above rather than ascend to heaven separated from them. Thus, rejecting baptism, he died a pagan, leaving the peoples free to accept the faith. See the Life of Saint Wulfram in the third volume of the Benedictine collection, under the year 720. The Frisians, an ancient people of Lower Germany, spread into Batavia and occupied a considerable part of it; from them it was called Frisia. See Mabillon’s observations on the Life of Saint Willibrord, no. 7, in the third volume of the Benedictine collection, under the year 739.]

[Note: [Col. 0672C] Boh. has Duristate, commonly Durostadium, today called Batavodurum (Wijk bij Duurstede), in the duchy of Guelders, on a channel of the Rhine.]

CIII. The aforementioned Pippin then took another wife, a noble and elegant woman named Alpheidam, by whom he fathered a son. In his native language he called him Carlus, and the handsome and excellent boy grew up.

[Note: [Col. 0672C] That is, in the vernacular, specifically in the Germanic language, Karl. He later became famous as Charles Martel, who is always called Carlus in the Boh. and Colbert manuscripts. The printed editions have Carolus, and in Boh. his mother is called Calpaida.]

CIV. In those days King Childebert died and was buried at Cauciacum, [Col. 0672C] in the basilica of Saint Stephen the Martyr. He had reigned sixteen years. [Col. 0672D]

[Note: [Col. 0672C] This was formerly a royal estate in the Noviomian district and the diocese of Soissons, not far from Compiègne and the confluence of the Aisne and Oise rivers; today it is called Choisy. It once had a famous monastery and is still subject to Saint Medard of Soissons. See Book IV of *De re diplomatica* and Valesius, Book XXIII of the *History of the Franks*.]

[Note: [Col. 0672D] Thus Boh. and Colbert; the printed editions have thirteen. The manuscript reading confirms Labbe’s view in the *Historical Miscellanies*, p. 64, and supports Cointius, although he assigns Childebert seventeen years, since he writes that Childebert himself lived only two days into his final year.]

**IN THE YEAR 710.**—Dagobert, his son, took possession of his father’s royal seat. Grimoald then married Ratbod, duke of the Frisians’ daughter. [Col. 0672D]

[Note: [Col. 0672D] Her name was Teutsinda, according to the *Deeds of the Frankish Kings* and the book concerning the mayors of the palace.]

**IN THE YEAR 714.**—When Pippin was ill at the estate of Jupille on the river Meuse, [Col. 0672B] Grimoald came to visit him. As Grimoald had gone to pray in the basilica of Saint Lambert the Martyr, he was killed by a most cruel and wicked man named Rantgarius. After this, his young son Theudoaldus was made mayor of the palace in his place, together with the aforementioned King Dagobert. [Col. 0672D] Soon afterward Duke Pippin himself fell ill and died. He had ruled the Frankish people for twenty-seven years. He left his son Carlus alive. After his death, the aforementioned matron Plechtrudis conducted everything by her own counsel and administration. At last the Franks turned against one another in revolt and, after accepting an ill-considered plan, joined battle in the forest of Coatia, [Col. 0673A] against Theudoaldus, the former retainers of Pippin, and Grimoaldus. [Col. 0673D] An enormous army fell there. Theudoaldus escaped by fleeing from his companions. Great and powerful disorder and persecution arose among the Frankish people.

[Note: [Col. 0672D] Boh. has “Job estate.” It is also called Jopila or Jopilum, commonly Jupil or Jopil, situated opposite Herstal near Liège. See Book IV of *De re diplomatica*, no. 71. The basilica of Saint Lambert is today the cathedral of Liège. This saint had been killed around the year 708. His Life is found among the Benedictine *Acts of the Saints*, volume III, part I.]

[Note: [Col. 0672D] He died in December 714, shortly after the killing of his son. He was called the younger because his maternal grandfather was Pippin of Landen; the elder was his grandson, who later obtained the kingdom.]

[Note: [Col. 0673C] Chesne has Cotia; Colbert has Gotia in the index. This is the forest of Cocia, with a village of the same name near Compiègne—the forest of Cuise—according to the *Deeds of the Franks*.]

[Note: [Col. 0673D] Thus the copies read; but Grimoaldi must be read, since Grimoaldus, like his father Pippin, had already died.]

CV. At that time they elected a certain Frank named Raganfridus to the office of mayor of the palace. [Col. 0673D] They mobilized a hostile army and hastened as far as the river Meuse, laying waste to everything. They made a treaty with Duke Radbod. In those days Duke Carlus was being held under guard by the aforementioned woman Plechtrudis, but he was freed by God’s assistance.

[Note: [Col. 0673D] The Colbert manuscript has Raginfridus, and likewise throughout what follows.]

**IN THE YEAR 715.**—CVI. At that time King Dagobert died, having reigned five years. The Franks established in the kingdom a former cleric named Danihel, whose hair had grown long, and called him Chilperic. [Col. 0673D]

[Note: [Col. 0673D] Thus Chesne. Other printed editions, together with Boh. and Colbert, read: “The Franks established a certain king, Chilperic.” Repeated.]

Again they mobilized an army and directed it against the aforementioned Carlus. On the other side, they invited Duke Radbod to come with the army of the Frisians as an enemy. The aforementioned Carlus rose against him with his own army, and they joined battle. But he suffered considerable loss there among his brave and noble men; seeing that his army was wounded, he turned his back and withdrew. After this Chilperic and Raganfridus, having gathered a hostile multitude, crossed the Ardennes forest. With Duke Radbod waiting on the other side with his army, they reached the city of Cologne on the Rhine, ravaging those regions together. They received many gifts and treasures from the aforementioned Plechtrudis and returned. [Col. 0673C] But on the way, at a place called Amblava, they suffered a great defeat at the hands of Carlus’s army. Later Carlus, having mobilized an army, marched against Chilperic and Raganfridus.

[Note: [Col. 0673D] Colbert has Blictruda. It likewise has, as does Boh., “he returned after receiving … great loss.” Among the royal estates of Austrasia, the younger Sigibert lists Amblava, situated on the river of the same name. The Amblava, today called the Amblève, flows not far from the monasteries of Stavelot and Malmedy and therefore near the borders of the dioceses of Cologne and Liège.]

**IN THE YEAR 717.**—They joined battle on Sunday in Lent, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, at a place called Vinciacum, [Col. 0673D] in the district of Cambrai, and clashed with one another in a great slaughter. Chilperic and Raganfridus were defeated; turning their backs, they escaped by flight. Carlus pursued them and hastened as far as the city of Paris.

[Note: [Col. 0673D] Boh. has Vinceco. Vinciacum is today a village which, according to Miraeus, is called la Cense de Vinci, not far from the town of Crépy (Crèvecœur). Paul the Deacon discusses this battle in Book VI, chapter 42, of his *History of the Lombards*.]

[Col. 0674A] CVII. He then returned to the city of Cologne and captured it, since its gates had been opened. The aforementioned Plechtrudis returned her father’s treasures to him and restored everything to his authority.

**IN THE YEAR 718.**—He established for himself a king named Chlotharius. Chilperic and Raganfridus therefore sent an embassy to Duke Eudo, requesting and entreating his assistance; they handed over the kingdom and gifts. [Col. 0673D] Eudo likewise, having mobilized the army of the Wascones, came to them, and together they advanced against Carlus. But he firmly and fearlessly hastened to meet them. Eudo, terrified because he could not withstand him, fled. Carlus pursued him as far as Paris, crossed the river Seine, and advanced as far as the city of Orléans. Eudo barely escaped and entered the borders of his own territory.

[Note: [Col. 0673D] Valesius thinks that by these words the kingdom was granted to Eudo, so that he might exercise supreme and royal authority in Aquitaine. Cointius, however, maintains that nothing more can be inferred from this passage than that a crown—which among medieval authors is often called a kingdom—was sent to Eudo as a mark of honor.]

[Note: [Col. 0674D] Boh. has: “He also, perhaps for *he*, having changed the enemy [for *army*], coming to them, together”; the printed editions have: “They also … coming.”]

**IN THE YEAR 719.**—He carried away King Chilperic with him, together with the treasures. King Chlotharius died that year. [Col. 0674D]

[Note: [Col. 0674D] Thus Chesne. The others, together with Colbert, have: “The dead king passed away. Through his messengers, Carolus received from Duke Eudo the aforementioned King Chilperic.”]

**IN THE YEAR 720.**—In the following year Carlus made peace with Duke Eudo through his messengers and received from him the aforementioned King Chilperic, together with many gifts. Coming to the city of Noviomum, [Col. 0674D] after not much time he lost both the course of his life and his kingdom, and died; he had reigned six years.

[Note: [Col. 0674D] This was the well-known episcopal city commonly called Noyon, under the metropolitan see of Rheims. Others write that he died at Attigny.]

**IN THE YEAR 721.**—After his death they established Theuderic as king in the royal seat; he now occupies this position on the royal throne, [Col. 0674D] for the years of life that have been allotted to him.

[Note: [Col. 0674D] Thus Boh.; others have “he then occupied this position.” Our reading is better. For Theuderic IV, called of Chelles, was reigning while the author of this chronicle was alive, as he himself testifies below, in chapter 9. Below, Labbe reads *protelatis* instead of *praestolatis*.]

**IN THE YEAR 724.**—After these events had been removed, Prince Carlus pursued the same Raganfridus, besieged the city of Angers, and, after ravaging that region, returned with much spoil.

CVIII. At the same time, when the Saxons rebelled, Prince Carlus came upon them, defeated them, and returned victorious.

**IN THE YEAR 725.**—A few days later, when the annual cycle had passed, he gathered a multitude of troops, crossed the river Rhine, traversed the territories of the Alamanni and Suebi, and advanced as far as the Danube. After crossing it, he occupied the borders of Bavaria. [Col. 0674D] Having subdued that region, he returned with many treasures, together with a certain matron named Bilitrude and her granddaughter Sonichilde.

[Note: [Col. 0674D] Thus Boh. and Colbert; Colbert nevertheless has Bajoarenses in the chapter index. The printed editions have Bajorenses.]

[Note: [Col. 0675C] Boh. has Billetrude … Sunichilde. Other writers call her Pilitrudis; she had been married to Grimoaldus—or rather to Theobaldus, duke of the Bavarians. Sonichildis later married Charles Martel and had a son by him, Grifo. After Charles’s death, Pippin and Carloman confined her at Chaumont, so that she would not cause disturbances on account of Grifo, who had been excluded from the office of mayor of the palace.]

**IN THE YEAR 731.**—At that time, when Duke Eudo withdrew from the terms of the treaty, Prince Carlus learned of it through intermediaries, mobilized an army, and crossed the river Loire. After Duke Eudo had been put to flight and much booty taken, and after it had been ravaged twice that year by these enemies, he again returned to his own lands. For Duke Eudo, seeing that he had been defeated and mocked, summoned the treacherous people of the Saracens to aid him against Prince Carlus and the Frankish people. They went out with their king, named Abdirama, crossed the Garonne, and reached the city of Bordeaux. Having burned the churches with fire and consumed the people, they advanced as far as Poitiers, where they burned the basilica of Saint Hilary and—painful to say—planned to overthrow the house of Blessed Martin.

**IN THE YEAR 733.**—Against them Prince Carlus boldly drew up his battle line and, as a warrior, charged upon them. With Christ’s help he overturned their tents, hastened to the battle to crush their ranks, killed their king, named Abdirama, overthrew their army, and, trampling them down, fought and conquered. Thus, victorious, he triumphed over the enemy.

[Note: [Col. 0675C] Eudo had already withdrawn from his alliance with the Saracens and gave Charles distinguished assistance in this battle. See Anastasius in the Life of Gregory II and Paul the Deacon, Book VI, chapter 46, of the *History of the Lombards*.]

**IN THE YEAR 732.**—CIX. In the following year, as the year advanced, the distinguished warrior Prince Carlus skillfully penetrated the region of Burgundy. He stationed his most trusted retainers, energetic men, along the borders of that kingdom to resist rebellious and unbelieving peoples. After making peace, he entrusted the city of Lyon in Gaul to his faithful men. [Col. 0675C] Having confirmed the truce agreements [alternative reading: judicial agreements], he returned as a victor, acting with confidence.

**IN THE YEAR 735.**—In those days Duke Eudo died. When the aforementioned Prince Carlus heard this, [Col. 0676A] he took counsel with his nobles, crossed the river Loire again, and, advancing as far as the Garonne, the city of Bordeaux, or the fortress of Blavia, [Col. 0675D] occupied it. He captured and subjugated that region, together with its cities and the suburbs of its fortresses. He returned victorious and in peace, with the aid of Christ, King of kings and Lord of lords.

[Note: [Col. 0675D] Thus Colbert; the printed editions have Blavium. Both forms are found in ancient writers. It is the fortress commonly called Blaye, situated on a hill above the Garonne, somewhat below the confluence of that river and the Dordogne.]

The following chronological calculations are found up to this point.

From Adam, or the beginning of the age, to the Flood: 2,242 years; from the Flood to Abraham: 942 years; from Abraham to Moses: 505 years; from Moses to Solomon: 489 years; from Solomon to the rebuilding of the Temple, in the time of Darius, king of the Persians: 512 years; from the restoration of the Temple to the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ: [Col. 0676B] 548 years.

[Note: [Col. 0675D] Boh. has 479. Freher, omitting this item, has “from Moses to the rebuilding,” and so forth.]

Certainly, from the beginning of the world to the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ: 5,538 years. [Col. 0675D] From the Passion of the Lord to the present year, which is in the cycle of Victorius: 177 years, on the Kalends of January, a Sunday, in the year 735. [Col. 0676C] And, in order for this millennium to be completed, 265 years remain.

[Note: [Col. 0675D] Boh. and Colbert have 5,228. An old manuscript of the monastery of Weingarten gives almost this number, namely one more. In it are the Angevin formulas published in volume IV of Mabillon’s *Analecta*, at the end of which the scribe added: “From the beginning of the world to the Passion of Christ there were 5,229 years. Afterward, when the reigns of Chlodoveus, Chlotharius, Theuderic, and Childeric had been completed, from the beginning of the world there were 5,880 years, in the third year of King Theuderic.” We reproduce this entire passage because it was written at the same time as the present chronicle.]

[Note: [Col. 0676C] Boher has “in order that the thousand-year period may be completed, 65 years”; Colbert has “LXLIII,” that is, 93; Chesne’s margin has another reading, 113. Although none of these figures agrees with the others, we have reproduced them as they appear in the manuscripts.]

**IN THE YEAR 733.**—Also, what we omitted above: against the very savage maritime people of the Frisians, who were rebelling with excessive cruelty, [Col. 0676C] the aforementioned prince boldly hastened by sea. Entering the sea in rivalry, after gathering a large number of ships, he penetrated the Frisian islands of Wistrachia and Austrachia. [Col. 0676D] He established a camp beside the river Burdine; he killed Poppo, their pagan duke and treacherous counselor, [Col. 0676C] overthrew the Frisian army, destroyed their shrines of idolatry, and burned them with fire. He returned victorious to the Frankish kingdom with great spoils and booty.

[Note: [Col. 0676C] People are said to rebel not only when subjects shake off their ruler’s yoke, but also when, after suffering defeat, they break a treaty that has been made. Cointius proves this with many examples, including examples from Livy, in his entry for 595, no. 19. Thus in our author the Frisians, Saracens, and others are said to have rebelled, although they had never been subject to Frankish rule.]

[Note: [Col. 0676D] We have restored this form from the Boh. manuscript. Westrachia, today Westergo, begins at Staveren, formerly the capital of the Frisians, and comprises eight administrative districts. Among the cities of this region is the famous Franeker, where there is a celebrated academy. Austrachia, or Ostergo, has twelve administrative districts and 127 villages; Leewarden, commonly Leeuwarden, is there, the chief of the other cities. See Emmius, Book I of the *History of Frisia*.]

[Note: [Col. 0676D] Boh. has Bordine, and below, like the others, Bobonem … consularium.]

**PART THREE, BY AN ANONYMOUS AUSTRASIAN AUTHOR, WHO WROTE AT THE COMMAND OF COUNT CHILDEBRAND.** (C)

[Col. 0677]

[Col. 0677A] **IN THE YEAR 733.**—Therefore the most astute man, Duke Charles, having mobilized an army, marched toward Burgundy. He brought the city of Lyon in Gaul, together with the leading men and governors of that province, under his own authority and the rule of the state. As far as the city of Marseille or Arles, he appointed his own judges. With great treasures and gifts he returned to the Frankish kingdom, to the seat of his principate.

[Note: [Col. 0677B] We say that this part of the chronicle was written at Childebrand’s command because of the heading that we shall present below, after no. 117. If anyone should maintain that the preceding part also was written at the command of the same count, we will not object, provided that he admits either that they were written by two different authors or, at least, that they are two separate works by the same author, written at different times. Boh. begins: “Therefore,” and below has *hoste* for *exercitu*, “army.”]

**IN THE YEAR 738.**—Also, when the most pagan Saxons who dwell beyond the river Rhine rebelled, the vigorous man Duke Charles mobilized the Frankish army and crossed the river at the place where the Lippe enters the Rhine, with careful purpose. He laid waste most of that exceedingly savage region and ordered that people, so fierce, to become tributary in part. [Col. 0677B] He also took many hostages from them and, with the Lord’s assistance, returned victorious to his own land.

[Note: [Col. 0677C] It is also called Lupia or Lupias, with a city of the same name in Westphalia. It flows into the Rhine near Wesel and is commonly called the Lippe. Others, however, say that Lipia is the Lahn, a river of Hesse that joins the Rhine between Boppard and Koblenz.]

**IN THE YEAR 736.**—When the exceedingly powerful people of the Ishmaelites again rebelled—people whom, by a corrupted name, they now call Saracens—and burst across the river Rhône, certain unbelieving men, under the deceit and fraud of a man named Maurontus, [Col. 0677C] who was lying in wait with his associates, the Saracens themselves entered the strongly fortified and mountainous city of Avignon after gathering their hostile forces. Since they had rebelled, that region was laid waste.

[Note: [Col. 0677C] Others have Mauronte; Boh. has Moronto. Below he is called Aux. As we infer, he had been governor of certain cities in the province and, having rebelled, summoned the Saracens to his aid, as is stated in the Chronicle of Fontenelle, chapter 11.]

### Year 737

But, on the other hand, the distinguished man Charles, duke, sent his brother, the industrious man Childebrand [Note: Some have Nonnunt, Hildebrandus, and likewise below; the meaning is the same. Cointius argues that he was the brother of Charles by both father and mother, since he is called his *germanus*, a word which the author of this third part of the Chronicle never uses elsewhere in another sense. Chiffletius, however, in his book *On the Origin of Childebrand*, confuses him with another Lombard of the same name who succeeded King Liutprand; Cointius refutes this opinion under the year 737.], duke, together with the remaining dukes and counts, with a hostile military force into those regions. They, arriving very quickly at the same city, pitched their tents. They seized the entire town and its suburbs on every side, besieged the strongly fortified city, and drew up their battle line, until the warlike man Charles, who was following them, attacked the aforesaid city, surrounded its walls, established a camp, and intensified the siege. In the manner of Jericho, with the uproar of the enemy and the sound of trumpets, they rushed upon the walls and the fortifications of the buildings with engines and ropes; entering the strongly fortified city, they set it on fire, captured their hostile enemies, killed, slaughtered, and struck them down, and effectively restored it to their own dominion.

Thus the victorious and renowned warrior Charles, undaunted, crossed the Rhône River with his army, penetrated the borders of the Goths, and advanced as far as Narbonese Gaul. He besieged their celebrated city, their metropolis; on the River Aude [Note: Commonly called the Aude. Other copies have *Atace*, and this river is properly called the Atax; it flows past Narbonne itself. Below, in Colbertinus, *Athema*.] he constructed a fortification in a circuit, in the manner of a battering ram, shut in there the king of the Saracens, named Athima, with his attendants, and encamped all around.

When the elders and leaders of the Saracens who were at that time staying in the region of Spain heard this, they assembled an enemy army with another king, named Amor [Note: Boh., *Amormagna nomine*, “named Amormagna,” against Charles. The old edition writes *machinis* as though it were a proper name. Below, in chapter 134, Amormuni is mentioned as king of the Saracens.], and, armed with engines, rose up bravely against Charles and prepared for battle. Against them the aforementioned duke Charles, the triumphant one, advanced, intending to fight at the River Birra [Note: Other copies of Chesnius and Freherus have *Birsa*, and add “and in the valley of Corbaria.” Birra, commonly Berre, flows between Narbonne and Leucate through the valley of Corbaria, and finally empties into a coastal lagoon. It rises in the mountain of the same name, *le mont de Corbière*, from which the archdeaconry of Corbaria in the diocese of Narbonne also takes its name. Baudranus calls it Cervera. What is designated by the words “the palace of Corbaria”—for this is the reading both of the manuscripts and of the editions—is uncertain. Valesius believes that a palace once stood in the valley of Corbaria and therefore should be counted among the royal estates; he includes it under that name in Book IV of *On Diplomatic Art*. Our author supports him, calling Carisiacum a palace-estate. Otto of Freising still recognizes in the twelfth century a palace in these regions famous under the name “the Palace of the Goths,” because Athaulf, the first Gothic king in Septimania, settled there, as Alteserra observes. They believe that it stood in the town of Saint-Gilles, still famous today for its monastery, which was converted into a college of secular canons. There was also the Palace of Saint Aemilianus in Levitania, succeeded by the monastery of Saint Savin near Bareges. Certainly Bishop Peter of the Palace signed the Council of Agde; some think that, in accordance with the custom of those barbarians, he had been Alaric’s court bishop. But Peter was a Catholic. Nor was he called that after the city of Pau, from *Palo*: Galactorius of Béarn and Gratus of the city of Oloron signed the same council. Finally, he was not the bishop of Limoges whom Valesius suspects was so named because he lived in his city’s palace, or at least in a palace somewhere in his diocese.], and in the valley of Corbaria Palace. When they clashed with one another, the Saracens were defeated and struck down. Seeing their king killed, they fled and turned their backs.

Those who had escaped, wishing to get away by sea, swam in the lagoon; indeed, they leapt upon one another in their effort to save themselves. Immediately the Franks, coming upon them with ships and weapons for throwing missiles, leapt upon them, suffocated them in the water, and killed them. Thus the Franks, triumphing over the enemy, seized great booty and spoils. After taking a multitude of captives, they devastated the Gothic region together with their victorious duke [Note: Chesnius and Freherus have: “together with the duke, the victor … devastates.”]. Destroying the walls and fortifications of the most famous cities—Nemausus, Agatha, and Biterrae [Note: Commonly Nîmes, Agde, and Béziers, the best-known episcopal cities of Occitania. Instead of *ac Biterris*, some editions have *his in terris*, “in these lands”; Colbertinus has *hac in terris*. Other copies have *Beteriis*. Boh., below, has “they burn … devastate … return.”]—Charles set them completely ablaze after applying fire. He devastated the suburbs and fortresses of that region. Having defeated the enemy army, with Christ presiding over all things and as the head of salvation and victory, he returned safely to his own region, to the land of the Franks and the seat of his principate.

### Year 739

Again, in the second month of the course of that year [Note: Cointius believes that this passage should be restored as follows: “Again, in the second year afterward,” that is, “in the year after the second.” Otherwise this second expedition would have to be assigned to the same year, 737, as the first, and indeed to the second month afterward; this conflicts with the Chronicle of Fontenelle and other records, from which we learn that the first expedition was undertaken in 737 and the second in 739. Paul the Deacon, Book VI of the *History of the Lombards*; Isidore of Beja; Rodrigo of Toledo; Anastasius, in the *Life of Gregory III*; and many other authors everywhere praise Charles’s expeditions against the Saracens.], he sent his aforesaid brother, with many dukes and counts, toward the region of Provence, having assembled an army. When they arrived at the city of Avignon, Charles advanced with all speed and restored the entire region, as far as the shore of the great sea, to his dominion. Having driven Duke Maurontus into impregnable and very secure rocks and coastal fortifications, the aforesaid prince Charles returned victorious, having acquired all those kingdoms for himself, with no one rebelling against him. Returning to the region of the Franks, he began to fall ill at the palace-estate of Verimbrea [Note: Colbertinus and the old edition have *Vermbrea*. Other copies of Freherus have *Vermeria*; other copies of Chesnius add “on the River Isara.” Vermeria is the proper name of this town, situated between Compiegne and Senlis, commonly Verberie. See the account of Valesius and Book IV of *On Diplomatic Art*.], on the River Isara.

### Year 741 — Chapter 110

At that time, the blessed Pope Gregory, twice from the Roman see of Saint Peter the Apostle [Note: This is Gregory III, who on the same occasion wrote two letters to Charles, which have survived to us. In them he set out for Charles, whom he calls a sub-king, the various calamities that the Roman Church was suffering at the hands of the Lombards, and implored his help against them, sending him the keys of the confession of Saint Peter. Cointius and others understand these words to mean golden keys containing some filings from Saint Peter’s chain, such as Gregory the Great had once sent to Childebert (Book V, Letter 6), so that, hung around the neck, they might protect him from every evil, and so forth. Hence they understand the words “something never before heard or seen in any age” as referring to the embassy sent to implore aid. Read the following note.], sent an embassy to the aforementioned prince bearing the keys of the venerable tomb, together with the chains of Saint Peter and great and countless gifts—something never before heard or seen in any age.

An agreement having been made, whereby, if he withdrew from the emperor’s side [Note: All printed editions have: “so that he might withdraw to the emperor’s side.” Aimoinus’s reading is difficult: “that he might free the Church from Lombard tyranny … and withdraw from the Lombard side, and that the aforesaid prince Charles might establish the Roman consulship.” Cointius therefore thinks that our author’s text should be restored as follows: “That he might join the emperor’s side, and [that Charles might establish] the Roman consulship,” arguing that Gregory wanted nothing other than that Charles, breaking peace with the Lombards, should take the emperor’s side. But, unless I am mistaken, our reading is better, and it is supported by the manuscripts. In it the author implies that Gregory promised Charles that, if he freed the Romans from Lombard tyranny, he would confer the Roman consulship upon Charles, setting aside the rule of the emperor, who was providing no assistance to Italy. Although this was left unfulfilled because Charles, and Gregory himself, died shortly afterward, it nevertheless happened later, as everyone knows. Hence I infer that the keys Gregory sent to Charles were the actual keys of the confession of Saint Peter, which he wished to give him as a pledge of the rule to be conferred upon him; this is suggested by the pope’s letter to Charles: “I adjure you … by those most sacred keys of the confession of Saint Peter, which we have sent to you as a pledge of the kingdom.” Our reading is certainly confirmed in explicit words by the *Annals of Metz*, where we read: “The aforesaid bishop Gregory had also sent him a letter, by decree of the Roman leaders, stating that the Roman people, abandoning the emperor’s rule, wished to entrust themselves to his protection and unconquered clemency.” Charles also needed no lesser incentive to break his treaty with the Lombards, by whom he had been greatly assisted in the Saracen expedition. See Paul the Deacon, Book V of the *History of the Lombards*, chapters 53 and 54.], and that he would establish the Roman consulship [Note: Boh., “and by the Roman decree.”] for the aforesaid prince Charles.

The prince therefore received the embassy with extraordinary and magnificent honor, bestowed precious gifts, and, with great rewards, sent to Rome, to the thresholds of Saint Peter and Saint Paul, Grimo, abbot of the monastery of Corbie [Note: Freherus has *Corvensis*; others have *Corbensis*. The celebrated monastery of Corbie, commonly Corbie, was so called from a nearby stream that flows there into the Somme; it was founded by Saint Balthild and her son, King Chlothar. Pomerayus, in his *History of the Archbishops of Rouen*, thinks that the Grimo praised here was later raised to the see of Rouen. Cointius disagrees, arguing that Grimo had presided over the Church of Rouen long before 741. Sigibertus—or, as the editions and Boh. have it, Sigobertus—was, as Dubletus believes, not a different person from Singibertus, who later became abbot of Saint-Denis.], and Sigibert, a recluse of the basilica of Saint Denis the martyr.

Then the aforementioned prince, having sought the advice of his nobles, divided the kingdoms among his sons [Note: The editions, except Chesnius, have “the kingdom.” France was once divided into three kingdoms: Austrasia, Neustria, and Burgundy; each had its own mayor of the palace, although sometimes two or three of these kingdoms had a single king. After Burgundy was united with Neustria, only two kingdoms remained, and Charles, after defeating Raginfred, was the sole mayor of the palace in both. These kingdoms, or all of France, comprised eight major regions: Austrasia, Swabia, Thuringia, Bavaria, Neustria, Burgundy, Provence, and Aquitaine. Septimania, which lay within Gaul, obeyed the Goths, or the kings of Spain. In the division made between Charles’s sons, Bavaria and Aquitaine are not mentioned, because Hunold, duke or governor of Aquitaine, and Odilo of Bavaria, detesting the excessive authority that Charles claimed for himself under the title of mayor of the palace, had refused to submit to him.]. Thus he gave his firstborn son, named Carloman, Austrasia [Note: Boh. and Colbertinus have “he elevated him into Thuringia.” Below, other copies and Boh. have “he granted Burgundy, Neustria, and Provence.”], Swabia, which is now called Alamannia, and Thuringia. He placed his second son, named Pippin, in charge of Burgundy, Neustria, and Provence.

That year Duke Pippin, having assembled an army, went toward Burgundy with his uncle, Duke Childebrand, and a multitude of nobles and many troops of retainers; they seized the borders of the regions in advance. Meanwhile, as sorrow and grief must be said to have brought about, ruin was impending [Alternative reading: “arousing.”] New signs appeared in the sun, moon, and stars, and even the most sacred order of Easter was disturbed.

The prince Charles [Vaticanus, *Karlus*] enriched the basilica of Saint Denis the martyr at Paris with many gifts. Then, coming to the palace-estate of Carisiacum [Note: Boh. has “the estate of Carieco.” This was a famous royal residence under the second dynasty of kings, commonly Kiersy, as is demonstrated at length in Book IV of *On Diplomatic Art*, no. 30.], on the River Isara, he was seized by a severe fever and died in peace, with all the surrounding kingdoms acquired [Note: Vaticanus has “leaving all the kingdoms acquired around him”; this addition was made by a later hand.].

He had ruled both kingdoms for twenty-five years [Note: That is, from the battle of Vinciacum, in which Raginfred was defeated; otherwise he died in the twenty-sixth or twenty-seventh year of his dukedom, as other authors report. Some also hold that he died on the Ides of October and was buried on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December in the basilica of Saint Denis, which the author says was at Paris, although it stood two leagues from the city, as learned men have observed. Other copies have “twenty-two.”]. Therefore he died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November and was buried at Paris in the basilica of Saint Denis the martyr [Note: Here the surviving manuscripts of Colbertinus, Vaticanus, and the Nazarianus from the Palatine Library, preserved by Freherus, end, as do the editions of Colbertinus, Bignonius, Baronius, Illyricus, and Boch. We would therefore have separated what follows from this part under another title, had not the heading reproduced below prevented us.].

### Year 742 — Chapter 111

His daughter Chiltrudis [Note: Others have *Hiltrudis*. We have prefixed chapter numbers from this point onward for ease of citation, although none appeared previously in the printed or manuscript copies.], acting because of the wicked counsel of her stepmother, secretly crossed the Rhine through the hands of her companions and came to Odilo [Note: Boh. and others erroneously have *Dodilo*, and below he is called *Hodilo*. This is Odilo, under whose rule the Christian faith greatly increased in Bavaria.] duke of Bavaria. He married her against the will or advice of his brothers.

Meanwhile, when the Basques rebelled in the region of Aquitaine, Carloman and Pippin, the brother-princes, with Duke Chunoald [Note: Others call him Hunald or Hunold; the Canon copy once has Chunobald.], formerly the son of Eudo, assembled an army and crossed the bed of the Loire at the city of Orléans. They crushed the Romans, advanced as far as the city of Bourges, and burned its suburbs with fire. Pursuing Duke Chunoald, they drove him to flight while devastating everything. They destroyed the fortress of Lucca [Note: Commonly Loches, in the territory of Tours, which we have mentioned elsewhere.] and overturned it completely; they captured the guards of that fortress and emerged victorious there. Dividing the booty among themselves, they led away captive with them the inhabitants of that place [Note: We restore this from Boh., which has *ejusdem locis*; the others have *eisdem locis*.].

Returning from there around the time of autumn, in the same year they again moved their army beyond the Rhine against the Alamanni. They remained there and pitched camp on the River Danube, at a place called Usquequo [Note: Chesnius has *nuncupante*. Freherus takes *usquequo* as an adverb and notes that the proper name of the place is missing.]. The inhabitants of Alamannia, seeing themselves defeated, gave hostages, promised to obey the laws, offered gifts, and, seeking peace, submitted themselves to their rule.

### Year 743 — Chapter 112

Returning from there in the second year of their reign, their kinsman Duke Odilo of Bavaria raised a rebellion against them. They were compelled to move a general army with the Franks into Bavaria. Coming to the river called the Lech [Note: It is still called the Lech or Lecx; in Latin, Lechus, Licus, and Lycias. It flows between Swabia and Bavaria and joins the Danube near Werdau.], both armies camped on the riverbank, facing one another from opposite sides for fifteen days. At last, provoked by the taunts of that people and stirred by indignation, they exposed themselves to danger through deserted and marshy places where there was no customary crossing [Note: The editions have “where there was no bridge for crossing.”]. At night they attacked, divided their forces, and caught them unprepared.

When battle had been joined, the aforementioned Duke Odilo, after his army had been cut down, barely escaped shamefully by flight beyond the River Igne [Note: This is the Aenus or Oenus, commonly the Inn, which rises in the Alps and, as is said below, flows into the Danube.]. These triumphs having been accomplished, not without the loss of many men, they nevertheless returned home as fortunate victors.

### Year 744 — Chapter 113

After three years had passed, Carloman again invaded the borderlands of the Saxons with an army, since they were in rebellion. There he captured the inhabitants who appeared to be adjacent to his kingdom and, without the hazards of war, happily brought them under his control. Many of them, with Christ as their guide, were consecrated by the sacrament of baptism.

At the same time, when Theudebald [Note: Duke of Swabia or Alamannia.] son of Duke Godfrey rebelled, Pippin, by the strength of his army, shamefully drove him out while he was fleeing from the siege of the Alps [Note: Unless I am mistaken, he calls the Vosges Mountains “the Alps”; after crossing the Rhine, Theudebald was trying to occupy them.]. Having recovered the dukedom of that place for himself, he returned home victorious.

### Year 745 — Chapter 114

Then the aforesaid brothers, in the following year, having been challenged by the warlike spirit of the Basques [Note: The Aquitanians with their duke Hunald.], again came together as far as the River Loire. When the Basques saw this, they seized the initiative, sought peace, and carried out Pippin’s wishes in everything. By entreaties they obtained from him, after giving him gifts, permission to return from their borders.

### Year 746 — Chapter 115

When these events had been completed, in the following year, after the Alamanni had broken faith with Carloman, he entered their homeland with an army in great fury and slaughtered with the sword many of those who were in rebellion against him.

### Year 747 — Chapter 116

After these events, in the course of the following years, Carloman, inflamed by religious devotion [Note: So Boh.; others have *inexstincto*, that is, “by an unextinguished impulse.” This alteration arose from the custom of pronouncing the letter *s* as though it were *es*.], entrusted the kingdom, together with his son Drogo, to the hands of his brother Pippin. He came to Rome, to the thresholds of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, intending to persevere in the monastic order [Note: He assumed the monastic habit at Rome, then withdrew to Mount Soracte and afterward to Monte Cassino. Read his eulogy in the third century of Benedictine history, Part II, under the year 755, when he died at Vienne in Gaul. Zacharias wrote to the Frankish bishops about his journey to Gaul to arrange peace between Pippin and Grifo, and also about restoring the body of Saint Benedict to the Cassinese monks.]. By this succession Pippin was strengthened in the kingdom.

### Chapter 117

In the same year the Saxons, according to their customary practice, attempted to break the faith they had promised their brother. For this reason, after assembling an army, he was compelled to forestall them [Note: The editions have “to reach them.”]. The kings of the Wends, or Frisians, also came together with one accord to help him.

When the Saxons saw this, compelled by their customary fear, after many of them had already been slaughtered and sent into captivity, and after their regions had been burned with fire, they sought peace. They submitted themselves to Frankish law, as had been customary from ancient times, and promised that from then onward they would render in full the tribute they had once paid to Chlothar [Note: They paid five hundred cows each year. See Fredegar, chapter 74.].

Among them, a very great multitude, seeing that they could not rebel against the Frankish attack, deprived of their own strength, asked that the sacraments of Christianity be conferred upon them. After this had been done, the Bavarians, at the counsel of wicked men [Note: The ancient writers report that these disturbances were stirred up by Grifo, or Grippus, Pippin’s half-brother through his mother. After being released from prison, he first drew the Saxons to his side; then, after Odilo’s death, he seized the dukedom of Bavaria. Defeated by Pippin and given a dukedom of twelve counties in Neustria, he withdrew to Aquitaine. Driven from there, he finally crossed into Italy and went to Aistulf, king of the Lombards; he was killed in the Maurienne valley, as is related in the following chapter.], again broke their faith and violated the pledge they had given to the aforesaid prince.

### Year 749

For this reason, having assembled an army and prepared a great force, he advanced into their homeland. But the Bavarians, compelled by fear, fled beyond the River Igne with their wives and children [Note: That is, the Oenus. The Oenus, commonly the Inn, descends northward from Mount Bernina in the Alps, flows through the county of Tyrol, where it gives its name to Oenipons (Innsbruck), then waters Bavaria, and finally, swollen by other rivers, joins the Danube.].

The aforesaid prince pitched camp on the bank of the Inn and prepared a naval battle, intending to pursue them to destruction. When the Bavarians saw that they could not help themselves by their own strength, they sent envoys with many gifts, submitted themselves to his rule, and gave oaths or hostages, so that they would never again rebel.

He himself, with Christ as his guide, returned happily to France and to his own seat in great triumph. The land then rested from wars for two years.

### Year 752

At that time, with the counsel and consent of all the Franks, after a report had been sent and authority had been received from the apostolic see, the exalted Pippin was raised to the throne of the kingdom by the election of all France, with the consecration of the bishops and the submission of the princes, together with Queen Bertrada, as ancient custom required [Note: These words plainly declare that the Roman pontiff, who at that time was Zacharias, intervened in Pippin’s election and that the prince was raised to kingship by the consecration of the pontiffs. Both ancient and more recent writers agree. Cointius nevertheless argues that this passage was interpolated and should be restored as follows: “The land rested from wars for two years. At that time the exalted Pippin, by the election of all France, was raised to the throne of the kingdom together with the queen,” and so forth. But he offers no reason for his conjecture, which contradicts all manuscripts and editions, except that he believes the Franks did not consult the pontiff about the king’s election and that the custom of anointing kings did not yet exist. Both claims are refuted by the conclusion of an old Dionysian codex written during Pippin’s reign, which we shall present below after Gregory’s book *On the Glory of the Confessors*.].

Up to this point the illustrious man Childebrand, count and uncle of the aforesaid King Pippin, had diligently arranged for this history, or *Deeds of the Franks*, to be written. From this point onward, authority passes to the illustrious man Nibelung, the son of Childebrand himself and likewise a count [Note: Chesnius published this heading from the Petavian manuscript, which the other codices do not contain. That manuscript, which passed from the Petavian library to Queen Christina of Sweden, is now preserved at Rome in the library of the eminent Cardinal Ottoboni. It formerly belonged to the monastery of Saint Oyend in the Jura and was offered at the tomb of Saint Eugendus at the end of the ninth century by Mannus, as we learn from the inscription prefixed to it: “The book of Mannus, of good memory, offered at the tomb of Saint Eugendus.”].

## Part Four, by an Anonymous Author Who Wrote at the Command of Nibelung (C)

### Year 753 — Chapter 118

When these events had been completed, in the following year the Saxons again, according to their usual custom, rebelled against King Pippin, contrary to the pledge of faith that they had formerly promised him. Therefore King Pippin, moved by anger, crossed the Rhine again with the entire Frankish army and came into Saxony with a great force. There he burned their homeland chiefly with fire, led away captives, both men and women, after taking much booty there, and struck down very many Saxons.

When the Saxons saw this [Note: The editions have: “when the Saxons assembled.” The place where they were defeated is called Rimi, above the River Weser, in the *Annals of Lorsch*. The conditions of peace, as recorded in the *Annals of Metz*, were that priests should have permission to preach the faith of Christ and baptize the Saxons, and that they should give the king three hundred horses each year.], moved to repentance, they sought the king’s mercy with their customary fear, asking him to grant them peace, promising to pay oaths and tributes much greater than before, and never again to rebel.

King Pippin, with Christ’s favor, returned in great triumph to the Rhine, to a fortress called Bonn [Note: Today it is the seat of the archbishop-elector of Cologne, since the city of Cologne itself is a metropolitan and Hanseatic city with its own jurisdiction. It retains its ancient name and is commonly called Bonn.].

While he was engaged in these matters, a messenger came to the aforesaid king from Burgundy, reporting that Grifo, the king’s brother, who had formerly taken refuge in Wasconia with Prince Waifarius [Note: Boh., Freherus, and Can. have *Gwasconiam*, and below repeatedly *Gwascones*. They usually call Waifarius *Waiofarius*; Can. sometimes has *Gaiofarius*.], had been killed near the city of Maurienne, on the River Arbor [Note: This river is commonly called the Arca, or l’Arche; it flows into the Isara, or Isère. For the city of Maurienne, see the notes in Book I of *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 14.], by Count Theudo of Vienne and also by Count Frederick of Transjurane, while he was making for Lombard territory and preparing an ambush against the aforesaid king. The two counts mentioned above were also killed in that battle.

### Chapter 119

As the king himself was coming through the Ardennes forest and had taken up residence at the public estate of Theudone [Note: A very strongly fortified town in the duchy of Luxembourg, between Metz and the Sier; it retains its ancient name, called Thionville by the French and Diedenhoven by the Germans.], on the Moselle, a messenger came to him and announced that Pope Stephen, from the region of Rome, with a great retinue and many gifts, had already crossed Mount Jovis [Note: Called the Great Pennine by Aethicus; commonly the Great Saint Bernard, and by others Montjou or Montjeu.] and was hastening to meet him.

Hearing this, the king ordered him to be received with joy, gladness, and great care, and ordered his son Charles to go out to meet him [Note: These words, “and he ordered his son …,” are absent from the Boherian codex.]. Charles was to escort him to the king’s presence as far as the public estate called Pont Ugone [Note: Chesnius has *Pontem Hugonis villam publicam*. This is Pontigo or Pontico, commonly Pontion, which we discussed above in Book IV of Gregory’s *History*, chapter 23. For Stephen III’s reception, see Anastasius in his *Life of Stephen*.].

### Year 754

There Pope Stephen of Rome came into the king’s presence and gave many gifts both to the king himself and to the Franks. He asked for help against the Lombard people and their king Aistulf, so that through the king’s assistance he might be freed from their oppression or treachery, and so that they would cease demanding from the Romans, contrary to the order of law, tributes and gifts that they had never previously demanded.

Then King Pippin ordered the aforesaid Pope Stephen to spend the winter, with immense care and great diligence, in the city of Paris, in the monastery of Saint Denis the martyr [Note: The pontiff wintered in the celebrated monastery of Saint Denis and, afflicted by a serious illness, recovered his health through the prayers of the holy martyr. When he departed, he left his pontifical pallium with the monks of the place as a pledge of affection; they still preserve it devoutly. On Pippin’s anointing and other events involving Stephen in Gaul, and on his return to Rome, Anastasius should be consulted.].

He sent an embassy to Aistulf, king of the Lombards, asking him, out of reverence for the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, not to move hostilely through the region of Rome and, at his request, not to undertake superstitious, impious, or unlawful actions of a kind that the Romans had never previously experienced.

### Chapter 120

When King Pippin had not obtained through his envoys what he had requested, and Aistulf had scorned to comply, after a year had passed [Note: Together with three months, according to our calculation, since he begins the year on the Kalends of March. Hence, a little above, we added “in the year 754.”], the aforesaid king ordered all the Franks, as is the Frankish custom, to come to him at the public estate of Bernacum [Note: The *Annals of Metz* have *Brennacum*.] on the Kalends of March.

After taking counsel with his nobles, at the season when kings customarily set out for war, he went with Pope Stephen [Note: Thus Boh. The editions have “Pope Stephen.”], the other peoples who lived in his kingdom, and the Frankish forces toward Lombard territory with the entire multitude. Passing through Lyon in Gaul and Vienne, they reached Maurienne.

When Aistulf, king of the Lombards, heard this, he assembled the entire Lombard army and came as far as the Clusae [Note: Chesnius has the erroneous form *Clasas*. The Clusae are the passes and narrow defiles of the mountains. The valley is called Susa, or, as Freherus and Can. have here, Swesiana; Chesnius has Suesana; it is commonly called the Susa Valley, *le Val de Suze*.], which is called the Susa Valley. There he pitched camp with his entire army and, with weapons, engines, and abundant equipment, wickedly attempted to defend what he had impiously committed against the commonwealth [That is, against the emperor] and the apostolic Roman see.
