When the aforementioned King Pippin had taken up residence at Maurienne with his army [The editions have “had returned.”], and the aforesaid king’s army could not cross because of the narrow valleys, mountains, and cliffs, a few men nevertheless broke through the mountains and narrow places and reached the Susa Valley.

Seeing this, Aistulf, king of the Lombards, ordered all the Lombards to arm themselves and came boldly against them with his whole army. When the Franks saw this, they thought that they could not free themselves by their own assistance or strength, but invoked God and asked the blessed apostle Peter for help [Note: The editions have “the assistance of blessed Peter the apostle.”].

When battle had been joined, they fought one another vigorously. Seeing his army wounded, Aistulf, king of the Lombards, turned his back and lost almost his entire army, which he had brought with him: the dukes, counts, and all the leading men of the Lombard nation. He himself barely escaped by sliding down a certain rocky mountain and came to his city of Ticinum with only a few men.

Then the exalted King Pippin, having achieved victory with God’s help [Note: Chesnius has “by God’s assistance.”], advanced with the whole army and multitude of Frankish troops as far as Ticinum. He pitched camp and devastated everything around him on every side. He burned much of Italy with fire, laid waste the entire region, plundered all the Lombard fortresses [The editions have “destroyed.”], and seized and carried off many treasures of gold and silver and very many other ornaments, as well as all their tents.

When Aistulf, king of the Lombards, saw that he could in no way escape, he asked for peace through the Frankish priests and nobles, submitting himself to the aforesaid King Pippin and promising to make full restitution for whatever he had done unlawfully against the Roman Church or the Apostolic See [Probably, “for whatever he had done.”].

He gave oaths and hostages there, promising that he would never withdraw from Frankish rule and would never again approach the Roman Apostolic See or the commonwealth in a hostile manner.

The aforesaid King Pippin, being merciful by nature, moved by compassion, granted him his life and kingdom. King Aistulf gave many gifts to the aforesaid king’s party. He also bestowed many gifts upon the Frankish nobles.

After these events, King Pippin sent the aforementioned Pope Stephen [Note: That is, the aforesaid Pope Stephen.], with his nobles and many gifts, toward Rome with great honor, and restored him safely to the Apostolic See, where he had previously been [The editions have “just as he had previously been.”].

When these events had been completed, King Pippin returned safely to his own country with his army, many treasures, and many gifts, with God’s help.

### A.D. 755—CXXI

In the following year, Aistulf, king of the Lombards, through the agency of sin, broke the faith which he had promised King Pippin. Coming once more to Rome with his army, he traversed the territories of the Romans, ravaging that region, and, arriving at the church of Saint Peter, burned with fire most of the houses which he found there.

[Note: Ed., “traversed the boundaries of the Romans.”]

[Note: Boh., “coming.” The church of Saint Peter in the Vatican was formerly outside the City; Leo IV later enclosed it within the new city, which was called Leonine after him. In these difficult circumstances Stephen wrote a letter to Pippin and all the Franks in the name of Saint Peter: “Peter, called the apostle … to Pippin, Charles, and so forth.” Cointius publishes this and other documents relating to this history in volume V of his *Annals*.]

When King Pippin heard this through messengers, he was exceedingly moved to fury and anger. He again mobilized the entire army of the Franks and, passing through Burgundy, by way of the city of Châlons and from there through Geneva, came as far as Maurienne.

[Note: Boh., “through Cavilon”; “Geneva.” These cities are Châlons-sur-Saône, Geneva, and Saint-Jean de Maurienne.]

When King Aistulf learned of this, he again sent the Lombard army to the Locks to resist King Pippin and the Franks and prevent them from entering the territory of Italy. King Pippin, having crossed Mount Cenis, arrived at the Locks, where the Lombards were striving to resist him. At once the Franks, breaking through the mountains and crags in their customary manner, as they had been trained to do, entered Aistulf’s kingdom with great anger and fury and killed the Lombards whom they found there. The rest who remained scarcely escaped by fleeing.

[Note: Commonly called Mount Cenis, in the Cottian Alps.]

King Pippin, together with his nephew Tassilo, duke of the Bavarians, again advanced into Italy as far as Ticinum. Ravaging that whole region with great force, he pitched his tents on both sides around the walls of Ticinum, so that no one could escape from there.

[Note: Then, as Anastasius relates, an envoy of the emperor met Pippin and asked him to restore the exarchate to the empire. But he refused, saying that he had undertaken this war solely out of piety, for love of Saint Peter and forgiveness of his sins, and that he could not allow himself to take away what he had once offered to blessed Peter. Hence, as that author continues, after peace had been established, he sent in writing a donation concerning the cities recovered for blessed Peter and to be possessed forever by the holy Roman Church and by all the pontiffs of the apostolic see. “It is kept to this day,” he says, “in the archive of our holy church.” An authentic monument of this same donation survives near Ravenna, engraved in Roman letters on stone, although mutilated. The missing portions can easily be supplied. It reads as follows: “PIPPIN THE PIOUS, THE FIRST, OPENED THE WAY FOR THE ENLARGEMENT OF THE CHURCH AND [GAVE] THE EXARCHATE OF RAVENNA, TOGETHER WITH THE MOST EXTENSIVE …”]

When Aistulf, king of the Lombards, saw this and no longer hoped for any possibility of escape, he came once more through the supplication of the Frankish priests and nobles. He begged peace from the aforesaid king and promised that, with full satisfaction according to the judgment of the Franks and the priests, he would make amends for the oaths which he had formerly given to that king and for the wicked deed which he had committed against the apostolic see.

[Note: Ed., “so that he who had committed the wicked deed against the apostolic see …”]

Then King Pippin, as was his custom, moved once more by mercy, granted life and kingdom to him at the request of his nobles. By judgment of the Franks and the priests, King Aistulf handed over to the aforesaid king the treasure which was at Ticinum, namely one-third of it; he also gave King Pippin’s party many other gifts, greater than those he had given before. Again he gave oaths and hostages, promising that he would never again be rebellious or defiant against King Pippin or the nobles of the Franks.

[Note: Boh. and Can., “that he must not be … nor dissolve [the obligation] toward the king …”]

He also promised that the tributes which the Lombards had long given to the king of the Franks should be paid every year through his messengers. The exalted King Pippin, victorious, with great treasures and many gifts, returned unharmed with his entire army to his own royal seat, without a battle having taken place; and the land rested from warfare for two years.

### A.D. 756—CXXII

After this, while Aistulf, king of the Lombards, was hunting in a certain forest, by divine judgment he was thrown from the horse on which he was riding against a certain tree, and cruelly lost his life and kingdom by a death he deserved. The Lombards, with the consent of the aforesaid King Pippin and on the advice of their nobles, installed Desiderius in the royal seat.

### A.D. 757—CXXIII

While these things were taking place, King Pippin sent an embassy to the emperor Constantine at Constantinople for the sake of friendship and the safety of his country. Emperor Constantine likewise sent an embassy to the aforesaid king with many gifts, and through their envoys they mutually promised one another friendship and good faith.

[Note: This was Constantine Copronymus, the destroyer of the sacred images.]

[Note: Among the gifts which Pippin received was an organ, which, according to the old annalists of those times, was then seen for the first time in Gaul.]

For some reason—who can say what caused it?—the friendship which they had mutually promised one another afterward achieved no effect.

### A.D. 758–760—CXXIV

After these events, and after the land had ceased from warfare for two years, the aforesaid King Pippin sent an embassy to Waifarius, prince of Aquitaine. Through his envoys he demanded that Waifarius return the property of the churches in his kingdom which were situated in Aquitaine, and that they should be preserved under the protection of immunity, as they had been previously. He was not to send judges or tax collectors against the aforesaid church property, as had not been done for a long time; he was also to make restitution to the aforesaid king for the Goths whom Waifarius had formerly killed contrary to law, and he was to return the men who had fled from the kingdom of the Franks to Waifarius the prince.

Waifarius contemptuously refused to do all that the aforesaid king had commanded him through his envoys. Therefore King Pippin, unwilling and constrained on every side,

[Note: Ches., “constrained.” Others, “compelled from every side.”]

gathered an army and advanced into Aquitaine through the district of Troyes as far as the city of Auxerre. From there, with the entire army of the Franks, he came to the Loire and crossed the river at the village of Masua in the district of Auxerre.

[Note: Valesius thinks this place was Massava, mentioned on the Peutinger Map. Today it is called Mesve. Below, Ches. has the erroneous form “Arutisiodorensi.”]

He advanced through the district of Berry as far as Auvergne, traversing that region and burning a very large part of Aquitaine with fire. Waifarius, prince of Aquitaine, sent envoys to beg for peace and gave oaths and hostages there, promising that he would fulfill at the appointed assembly all the obligations which the aforesaid King Pippin had communicated to him through his envoys. King Pippin returned unharmed to his own country with his entire army.

### A.D. 761—CXXV

When a year had passed—that is, in the tenth year of his reign—he ordered all the nobles of the Franks to come to him at Dura, in the district of the Ripuarians, at the Field of May, after an assembly had been established, in order to deliberate concerning the safety of the country and the welfare of the Franks.

[Note: Freh., “in the district of Riguern”; Can., “in Riguern”; Ches. explains it as “in the district of the Ripuarians.” The Ripuarians were peoples of Lower Germany, enclosed by three rivers, the Rhine, Moselle, and Meuse. Dura, or Duria, now commonly called Düren, in the duchy of Jülich on the river Rur (Roer), was called Marcomagus, or Marcodurum of the Ubii, by the ancients, as Valesius observes in his *Description of Gaul*. A royal estate, or famous palace, existed there under the second dynasty of our kings; concerning it, see book IV of *On Diplomatic Affairs*. On the Field of May, see below, the notes to chapter 130.]

While these things were taking place, Waifarius, having formed an evil plan, prepared an ambush against Pippin, king of the Franks. He sent his army, together with Hunibert, count of Berry, and Blandinus, count of Auvergne, who, shortly before, in the preceding year, had been sent to the aforesaid King Pippin with Bishop Bertellan of the city of Bourges and had excessively provoked the king’s anger, along with the remaining counts, secretly and in a hostile manner as far as Châlons.

[Note: Ches., in the margin, “Hunibert,” or “Chunibert,” as below in chapter 134; others have “Umbert.” Below, Boh. has “Biturivo”; Can. and Freh., “Bitorvio,” for “Bitorino” (Berry). With Ches., they call Blandinus “Blaudenus.”]

He sent his entire army across, and burned the whole region from Autun as far as Châlons, and they ravaged everything they found in the suburbs of the city of Châlons. They burned the royal estate of Melciacum, returned home with much plunder and booty, and met no resistance.

[Note: Ches., in the margin, “Melliacum.”]

When it was reported to King Pippin that Waifarius had ravaged a very large part of his kingdom and had broken the oaths which he had given him, the king was exceedingly angered and ordered all the Franks to come in a hostile manner, after an assembly had been convened, to the Loire. Having mobilized the army with the entire multitude, he again advanced as far as Troyes; from there he came through Auxerre to the city of Nevers. After crossing the Loire, he reached the fortress called Bourbon, in the district of Berry.

[Note: There are two fortresses of this name, famous for the healthfulness of their waters and separated from one another by about fifteen leagues, though the Loire and Allier rivers lie between them: Bourbon of Ansellus (Bourbon-Lancy), on the right bank of the Loire in the territory of the Aedui; and Bourbon of Erchembaldus, also called “at the Baths” (Bourbon-l’Archambault, or Bourbon-les-Bains), in the territory of the Bituriges, which is the one mentioned here. It gave its name to the most illustrious Bourbon family, now the royal family of France. The other cities mentioned above—Troyes, Auxerre, and Nevers—are well known.]

After he had encamped all around it, it was suddenly captured and set on fire by the Franks. The men of Waifarius whom he found there he took with him. Ravaging most of Aquitaine, he came with his entire army as far as the city of Auvergne. He captured and burned the fortress of Clermont by force of arms, and in the fire they burned a great multitude of people, both men and women, as well as many children.

[Note: Savaro observes in his *Origins of Clermont* that this is the first mention of Clermont among ancient authors. The writer clearly distinguishes it from the city of Auvergne itself, which the ancients called Augustonemetum. Hence he conjectures that a fortress or citadel once stood on a nearby mountain to guard the city and was called “Clear Mountain.” Later this name was transferred to the whole city, when, after it had been repeatedly violated by the turmoil of wars, it was moved onto the mountain. He supports this from popular tradition, according to which the inhabitants call the vineyards and lands near the city *la Cita*, while the part of the city occupying the summit of the mountain is called *Clairmont*.]

They captured and bound Blandinus, count of that city of Auvergne, and brought him into the king’s presence. Many Basques were captured and killed in that battle. Thus King Pippin, after the city had been captured and the whole region ravaged, returned once more to his own country with much booty and plunder, with God’s help and with his army unharmed. It happened, moreover, that after King Pippin had captured the city of Auvergne, he ravaged that entire region.

### A.D. 762—CXXVI

In the following year, that is, the eleventh year of his reign, he came with the entire multitude of the Frankish people to Bourges. He pitched camp all around it and ravaged everything that lay in the surrounding area. He surrounded the city with extremely strong fortifications, so that no one dared to leave it or was able to enter it. He enclosed it with a rampart, using siege engines and every kind of weapon. After many had been wounded and very many killed, and after the walls had been broken, he captured the city and restored it by right of war to his own authority.

The men whom Waifarius had left there to defend the city he released in the clemency of his mercy; once dismissed, they returned to their own homes. He brought Count Hunibert and the remaining Basques whom he found there with him after they had given oaths. He ordered their wives and children to travel into Francia, ordered the walls of the city of Bourges to be restored, and sent his counts into the city to guard it.

[Note: “Umbert” in another source.]

From there he came with the entire army of the Franks as far as the fortress called Thouars. When he had pitched camp around it, the fortress itself was captured and burned with marvelous speed.

[Note: It is situated in the territory of the Pictones, commonly called Thouars, and is still famous today, distinguished by the title of duchy and possessed by the noble family of La Trémoille. Aimoinus has “Cadurcia”; perhaps he intended Cahors? The Annals of Metz have “the fortress of Thouars,” than which there was no stronger fortress in Aquitaine.]

He brought the Basques whom he found there, together with the count himself, into Francia. King Pippin, with Christ as his guide, returned again with the entire army of the Franks, with much booty and plunder, to his own seat.

### A.D. 763–764—CXXVII

A long dispute arose between Pippin, king of the Franks, and Waifarius, prince of Aquitaine. With God’s help King Pippin grew stronger and stronger and became continually more powerful in himself; but the party of Waifarius and his tyranny diminished day by day. Waifarius continually pretended not to be preparing ambushes against the aforesaid King Pippin.

For he sent his cousin Count Mancio into the region of Narbonne with the remaining counts, against the guards whom the aforesaid king had sent to Narbonne to guard it against the Saracen people, so that the Saracens might neither enter nor, should they ever return to the country, be able to capture or kill them.

[Note: That is, into the region subject to Pippin.]

It happened that Count Australdus and Count Galemanius, together with their equals, were returning home. Mancio, together with a multitude of the Basque people, rushed upon them. While they were fighting one another fiercely, the aforesaid Galemanius and Australdus, with God’s help, killed Mancio and all his companions there.

When the Basques saw this, they turned their backs. They lost all the horsemen [that is, the horses] which they had brought there. Wandering through the mountains and valleys, only a few scarcely escaped by flight. The others, with much booty, horses, and plunder, returned home joyfully.

### CXXVIII

While the Franks and the Basques were continually disputing with one another in these and other ways, Count Chilping of Auvergne, having gathered an army from every direction, attempted to march into the district of Lyon, in the kingdom of Burgundy, to plunder.

Against him came Count Adalard of Châlons and the same Count Australdus, together with their companions. They fought fiercely with him on the river Loire. At once Count Chilping was killed in that battle by the counts mentioned above, and many who had come with him were killed there as well.

When the Basques saw this, they turned their backs; only a few, entering the woods and marshes, scarcely escaped. Count Amanugus of Poitiers, while plundering the territory of Tours after it had been attacked, was killed by the men of Wulfard, abbot of the monastery of blessed Martin. Many others who had come there with him also fell together with him. The rest who remained, turning their backs, scarcely escaped.

While these things were happening, Remistanus, Waifarius’s maternal uncle, came to the aforesaid king and promised many oaths and his good faith to King Pippin, promising that he would always be faithful both to the aforesaid king and to his sons. The king received him into his authority and enriched him by bestowing many gifts of gold and silver, precious garments, horses, and weapons.

### CXXIX

King Pippin ordered the fortress called Argentonus in the district of Berry to be restored from its foundations to its former state by marvelous workmanship. He sent his counts there to guard it and granted the fortress to Remistanus, together with half of the district of Berry as far as the Cher, so that he might resist Waifarius.

[Note: The editions read, “with them half [the district].”]

[Note: Boh., “as far as Care.” The Cher, or Caris, commonly called *le Cher*, divides the province of the Bituriges into two parts. Swollen by many small tributaries, it eventually flows into the Loire somewhat below Tours.]

When the aforesaid Waifarius, prince of Aquitaine, saw that the king had captured the fortress of Clermont by war and had taken Bourges, the capital of Aquitaine and a very strongly fortified city, with siege engines, and that he had been unable to withstand the king’s attack, he threw down to the ground all the walls of the cities in the province of Aquitaine that were under his authority: Poitiers, Limoges, Saintes, Périgueux, Angoulême, and many other cities and castles.

[Note: Boh., “Poitiers … Limoges, Saintes, Périgueux, Angoulême.” These are Poitiers, Limoges, Saintes, Périgueux, and Angoulême, the capitals of the provinces that bear their names.]

Later the exalted King Pippin ordered their walls to be repaired and left his men to guard those cities. Again in that year the aforesaid King Pippin returned with his entire army to his own seat.

### A.D. 765—CXXX

Again, in the following year, having mobilized the entire army of the Franks, he came through Troyes, then Auxerre, as far as the city of Nevers with the entire army. There, holding his assembly at the Field of May with the Franks and his nobles, he proceeded afterward, having crossed the Loire, into Aquitaine. He advanced as far as Limoges and, ravaging that entire region, ordered the royal estates belonging to Waifarius to be burned completely.

[Note: Cointius believes that the words “there, holding his assembly …” through “holding” should be deleted, because, in his view, that year the assembly of the Franks, or Field of May, was held at Attigny in the Remian Champagne. Nevertheless, they occur in all the printed and manuscript copies which he was able to see. Perhaps here “Field of May” means nothing other than an assembly of the Franks compelled to deliberate about certain difficulties connected with the expedition. Certainly, as Cointius himself observes, the Annals of Metz call a meeting held in August of the year 567 the “Field of May,” although in that same year a solemn assembly had actually been held in May.]

After almost the whole region had been ravaged and many monasteries depopulated, he came as far as Issoudun. From there he captured and ravaged a large part of Aquitaine, where there were very many vineyards. Accordingly, he ravaged and captured nearly all Aquitaine, where churches and monasteries alike, rich and poor, had been accustomed to have wine.

While these things were happening, Waifarius came against the aforesaid king with a large army and with very many Basques who lived beyond the Garonne and were anciently called the Vaceti.

[Note: Boher., “Vacceti.” Can. and Freh., “Vaoeci.” These are perhaps the Vasci, or Basques, whom we still call Basques today.]

But immediately, in their customary manner, all the Basques turned their backs, and very many of them were killed there by the Franks. When the king saw this, he ordered them to be pursued. Pursuing him until nightfall, he scarcely escaped by flight, with the few who remained.

In that battle Count Blandinus of Auvergne, whom the aforesaid king had previously captured and who had afterward fled to Waifarius, was killed. King Pippin emerged victorious with God’s help.

After victory had again been achieved with a great triumph, he came with a large army of Franks to Denegontius on the Loire. From there he returned through the district of Autun to his own seat, undefeated.

[Note: Boh., “to Digontio.” Can. and Freh., “to Degontum.” It is commonly called Digoine or Digoins. The place is a barony in the district of Charolais, at the confluence of the Arroux and the Loire.]

[Note: Boh. has this form. The edition reads, “he returned. There he was defeated.”]

Waifarius sent an embassy to the aforesaid king, asking him to return to him Bourges and the other cities of the province of Aquitaine which the king had taken from him, and promising that thereafter Waifarius would make them subject to his authority. He also promised that he would pay every year to the aforesaid King Pippin the tributes and gifts which his predecessors, the kings of the Franks, had been accustomed to exact from the province of Aquitaine. But the king, on the advice of the Franks and his nobles, refused to do this.

[Note: Freh. and Can. add here, “and of many peoples who lived in his kingdom”; these words are absent in the same sources in the following chapter.]

### A.D. 766—CXXXI

When a year had passed, therefore, having mobilized the entire army of the Franks and also many peoples who lived in his kingdom, he came as far as Orléans. There he established his assembly, the Field of May, for the welfare of the Franks. Holding it, he was enriched with many gifts by the Franks and his nobles.

[Note: Above, in chapter 125, he called it the Field of May. The Annals of Petau report that this change was made in the year 755. Hincmar, in the *Life of Saint Remigius*, says that the Field of March was so called from Mars; later the Franks began to call it the Field of May, when kings customarily set out for war.]

After crossing the Loire, he proceeded through all Aquitaine as far as Agen and ravaged the entire region. The Basques and the leading men of Aquitaine, compelled by necessity, came to him in great numbers. There they gave him oaths and made themselves subject to his authority.

Thus, after the whole province of Aquitaine had been exceedingly ravaged, he returned that year once more to Francia with all his people, through the district of Périgueux and Angoulême, when almost all Aquitaine had already been acquired, with the entire army of the Franks and with much booty and plunder.

### A.D. 767—CXXXII

Again, in the following year, having mobilized the entire army of the Franks, he came through the district of Troyes and from there to the city of Auxerre, to the fortress called Gordinus.

[Note: Cointius interprets this as a place near Sancerre, or the Sacred Fortress of Caesar, in Berry—Gordon near Sancerre.]

With his queen Bertrada, he then crossed the Loire confidently and came to Bourges, where he ordered a palace to be built for himself. Again he ordered the Field of May to be held there, as was customary. After taking counsel with his nobles, he left the aforesaid Queen Bertrada there at Bourges with the other Franks and his faithful counts.

[Note: Another source has “Bertrada”; some call her Berta.]

The aforesaid king himself proceeded with the remaining Franks and his nobles to pursue Waifarius. When the king, pursuing Waifarius, failed to find him, it was already winter. He returned with his entire army to Bourges, where he had left the aforesaid Queen Bertrada.

### CXXXIII

While these things were taking place, Remistanus, son of Eudo, broke the faith which he had formerly promised to the aforesaid King Pippin. He came again to Waifarius and made himself subject to his authority. Waifarius received him with great joy and appointed him his assistant against the Franks and the aforesaid king.

[Note: Can. and Freh., “son of Judona.” It should read “son of Eudo,” the duke of Aquitaine mentioned above, who was the father of Hunuald and Remistanus—or, as others write, Remistagnus. Thus Waifarius, the son of Hunuald, had Remistanus as his paternal uncle, although above, in chapter 128, he is called his maternal uncle.]

The aforesaid Remistanus advanced with great hostility against the aforesaid king and the Franks, and against the garrisons which the king himself had left in his cities. He ravaged the territory of Berry, or Limousin, which the king had acquired, by plundering it so thoroughly that no tenant of the land dared to work the fields or cultivate the vineyards.

The aforesaid King Pippin remained throughout the winter at Bourges in the palace with his queen Bertrada. He sent his entire army into Burgundy to spend the winter. At the city of Bourges, by the counsel of the bishops and priests, he reverently celebrated the Nativity of Our Lord Jesus Christ and the holy Epiphany.

### A.D. 768—CXXXIV

When that year had passed, while he was residing at Bourges in the middle of February, he ordered his entire army, which he had sent into Burgundy to spend the winter, to come to him. After taking counsel, he prepared an ambush against Remistanus. He secretly sent Count Hermenaldus, Beringarius, Childeradus, and Count Hunibert of Berry, together with the remaining counts and their men, to capture Remistanus.

[Note: The edition has “Chunibert”; below, “Hunibert.” See above, the note to chapter 125.]

The aforesaid King Pippin set out with the entire army of the Franks once again to pursue Waifarius.

Queen Bertrada came from Orléans and then traveled by boat along the Loire as far as the fortress of Sellus on the river Loire.

[Note: This place must be distinguished from the cell of Saint Eusicus in Berry on the Cher, commonly called Selles. Sellus stood on the Loire, if our author is to be trusted.]

After these events, it was reported to the king that his envoys, whom he had formerly sent to Amormun, king of the Saracens, had returned to Marseille after three years and had brought with them to the aforesaid king the embassy of Amormun, king of the Saracens, together with many gifts.

[Note: Other authors call him Amiramomen; Cointius and others call him Almansor. See above, the note to chapter 109.]

When this became known to the king, he sent his own envoys to receive that embassy reverently and escort it to the city of Metz to spend the winter.

[Note: The edition reads, “who should receive them.”]

Thus the counts who had been sent to capture Remistanus, by divine judgment and through the king’s good faith, captured him and brought him bound, together with his wife, into the king’s presence. The king immediately ordered Count Hunibert and Count Ghiselarius of the city of Bourges to hang Remistanus on the gallows.

The aforesaid King Pippin advanced as far as the Garonne. There the Basques who lived beyond the Garonne came into his presence and gave oaths and hostages to the aforesaid king, promising that they would always be faithful to the king’s party and to his sons Charles and Carloman. Many other peoples from Waifarius’s side also came to him and submitted themselves to his authority. King Pippin received them kindly into his dominion.

Waifarius, hiding in a forest called Edobola, in the district of Périgueux, wandered uncertainly here and there with a few companions.

[Note: As Valesius observes, it is commonly called the forest of Ver.]

The aforesaid King Pippin again prepared an ambush to capture Waifarius. From there he went to his queen at Sellus and ordered the embassy of the Saracens, which he had sent to Metz to spend the winter, to come to him at the fortress of Sellus. The Saracens presented there the gifts which Amormun had sent.

Again the king gave gifts to the Saracens who had been sent to him and ordered them to be escorted with great honor as far as Marseille. The Saracens returned home by ship across the sea.

### CXXXV

That year the exalted King Pippin again left the fortress of Sellus with a few men to pursue Waifarius. He came first, with marvelous speed, as far as Saintes and, when Waifarius heard this, he turned his back in his customary manner.

King Pippin sent his counts in four directions, together with his *scarae* (military bands) and his leudes, to search for Waifarius. While these things were happening, as they say, by the king’s counsel Waifarius, prince of Aquitaine, was killed by his own men.

The aforesaid King Pippin had now acquired all Aquitaine. All who came to him made themselves subject to his authority, as they had been in ancient times. He came with great triumph and victory to Saintes, where Queen Bertrada was residing.

### CXXXVI

When the aforesaid king had come to Saintes and was handling matters concerning the welfare of the country and the interests of the Franks, he began to fall ill, afflicted by a certain fever. He established his counts and judges there.

From there he proceeded through Poitiers to the city of Tours, to the monastery of blessed Martin the Confessor. There he bestowed a great alms offering on churches, monasteries, and the poor, and asked the help of blessed Martin, so that he might deign to pray to the Lord for mercy on account of the king’s sins.

From there he set out with the aforesaid Queen Bertrada and his sons Charles and Carloman. He came as far as Paris, to the monastery of the blessed martyr Denis, and stayed there for some time. Seeing that he could not escape the danger to his life, he ordered all his nobles, the dukes and counts of the Franks, both bishops and priests, to come to him.

There, with the consent of the Franks, his nobles, and the bishops, while he was still alive he divided the kingdom of the Franks, which he had held, equally between his aforesaid sons Charles and Carloman. That is, he established his elder son Charles as king of the kingdom of Austrasia; to his younger son Carloman he gave the kingdoms of Burgundy, Provence, Gothia, Alsace, and Alamannia.

[Note: Can. and Freh., “Alesans”; Ches., “Alexacis,” that is, Alsace, commonly called *l’Alsace*.]

He divided Aquitaine, which he himself had acquired, between them.

After these events, King Pippin, a few days later—“as grief is to say,”

[Note: Ch. and Freh., “as deceit is to say.”]

—lost his final day and his life together. The aforesaid kings Charles and Carloman, his sons, buried him in the monastery of the blessed martyr Denis, as he had wished, with great honor. He had reigned for twenty-five years.

[Note: This calculation cannot be admitted in any way. From the time Pippin was acclaimed king at the assembly of Soissons, he reigned sixteen years and six months; from the time he was crowned by Pope Stephen, almost fifteen years; but from the year in which, after his father’s death, he assumed the office of mayor of the palace, twenty-seven years. He died in September of the year 768.]

### CXXXVII

After these events, the aforesaid kings Charles and Carloman each came with his own men to his own royal seat. Having established an assembly and taken counsel with their nobles, in the month of September, on Sunday, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October, Charles at the city of Noyon and Carloman at the city of Saxones (Soissons) were jointly elevated to the kingdom on the same day by their nobles and through the consecration of the priests.

[Note: Cointius says that the words “the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October” were added by an interpolator, because according to his calculation Pippin died on the eighth day before the Kalends of that same month. Nevertheless, they occur in both the printed and manuscript copies, as well as in the Annals of Metz. Charles was inaugurated at Noyon, and his brother at Soissons, which city some ancient writers call Saxon, Session, and so forth.]

Here ends the *Chronicle of Fredegar*, together with its continuators.

[FRAGMENTS]

### NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING FRAGMENTS (C)

### [Col. 0697]

[Col. 0697B] It seemed appropriate to append to Fredegar’s *Chronicle* selected fragments by the same author pertaining to Frankish history, which we have transcribed from his other works. For although that author testifies that he is reporting material excerpted from Eusebius, Jerome, Hydatius, and others, he nevertheless occasionally includes items not found in those authors—whether he reported them from ancient traditions then circulating, or copied them from old authors unknown to us. From these we have selected only those passages relevant to our history, and present them as they are read both in the old style of the manuscript of the Parisian College of the Society of Jesus, written in the author’s lifetime, and in another manuscript from Dijon, formerly in the library of the illustrious Boherius.

[Col. 0697]

# SELECTED FRAGMENTS EXCERPTED FROM OTHER WORKS OF FREDEGAR, PERTAINING TO THE HISTORY OF THE FRANKS. (C)

[Col. 0697]

## I.—Among the Excerpts from Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, translated by Jerome.

[Col. 0697C]

**705** At that time (chapter 3), Priam abducted Helen. The ten-year Trojan War arose. The cause of the evil was that Helen was the prize of one of the three women competing in beauty, with the shepherd acting as judge making the promise [Note: [Col. 0697C] The canon manuscript reads: “with the shepherd judge making the promise.”]. Memnon and the Amazons brought aid to Priam. From this originated the Franks. At first they had Priam as king; afterward it is written in the books of the Histories [Note: [Col. 0699C] Aimoinus, book I of *The Deeds of the Franks*, praises certain authors who wrote about this origin. What we give here may perhaps be excerpted from Dares Phrygius’s *History of the Origin of the Franks*. For in the Boherian manuscript and in one of Canisius’s manuscripts several passages are inserted under this author’s name. In all the manuscripts, however, after the fragment that we have transcribed here, the following is appended: “Let us return to the order in which the race of the Hebrews came into being.” Vossius mentions Dares Phrygius in book III of his *Latin Historians*, but considers him fictitious and says that he relates fables. Certainly it was once the common opinion of the Franks that their people descended from the Trojans, as is clear from the ancient Chronicles and authors, especially those who wrote at the end of the first dynasty of our kings and afterward. See Chesnius, volume I of the *History of France*, Sigebert, and others.] how they had Friga as king; afterward they were divided into two parts. One part proceeded into Macedonia. They were called Macedonians, after the people by whom they were received, and were invited by the king of Macedonia, who was being oppressed by neighboring peoples, to provide him with aid [Can.: “and the region of Macedonia”]. Later, when they had been subjected to him and had grown into a very large population, the Macedonians, sprung from that stock, became exceedingly brave warriors. In the end, the reputation of their valor was confirmed in the days of King Philip and his son Alexander, such as it was.

For that other part, which had departed from Phrygia [Note: [Col. 0699D] Canisius reads, correctly: “from Friga”], was deceived by Ulysses through trickery [that is, by Odysseus], though it was not captured; rather, it was driven out from there and wandered through many regions with wives and children.

They chose a king for themselves, named Francio, after whom the Franks are called. Finally, because Francio himself is said to have been extremely brave in war and to have fought for a long time against many peoples, ravaging part of Asia, he turned toward Europe and settled between the Rhine and the Danube, and the sea.

After Francio died, and only a small band of them remained because of the many battles he had fought (chapter 5), they appointed leaders from among themselves. Nevertheless, always refusing the rule of another, they made agreements with their leaders long afterward, until the time of Pompey the consul. He fought against them, or against the remaining peoples who lived in Germany, and subjected all of them to Roman rule [Note: [Col. 0699D] The Claromontane manuscript reads thus. The Boherian manuscript reads: “to Roman rule.” Canisius reads: “and subjected all their territories to the Romans.”]. But immediately the Franks entered into an alliance with the Saxons and, rebelling against Pompey, rejected his authority. Pompey died in Spain while fighting against many peoples [Note: [Col. 0699D] Canisius reads: “put him to death.”]. After this, no people up to the present day has been able to overcome the Franks—although one might have subjected them to its rule [Note: [Col. 0699D] The Claromontane manuscript omits the words “although one might have subjected them to its rule” [Col. 0700C].]. In the same way, the Macedonians, who sprang from the same stock, although they had been worn down by severe wars, nevertheless always strove to live free from foreign domination.

Tradition confirms that a third people arose from the same origin, the Torci [Note: [Col. 0700C] Below: “Turci.” The Boherian and Canisian manuscripts read “Torqui” and “Thurci”; below, “Torquoto.”] (chapter 6). When the Franks, wandering through Asia, had crossed many battlefields and, entering Europe, had arrived on the bank of the Danube between the Ocean and Thrace, one part of them settled there. They chose a king for themselves, named Turquotus, from whom the people received the name of Turks. The Franks made this journey with wives and children, and there was no people that could resist them in battle. But they fought many battles, and when they settled beside the Rhine, after they had been reduced by Turquotus, only a small band of them remained. From the captivity of Troy to the first Olympiad are 406 years.

## II.—Among the same Excerpts.

Gallienus was confirmed in the imperial power (from chapter 40). The Germans came to Ravenna. The Alamanni, after devastations at Aventicum by an assault of violent harm, and after ravaging a large part of Gaul, crossed into Italy [Note: [Col. 0700D] Thus the Claromontane manuscript. The Boherian manuscript reads: “after an assault of violent harm, … of Gaul; and from there into Italy.” Canisius reads: “They arrived with immeasurable damage and ravaged a very large part of Gaul; from there they went into Italy,” and so forth.]. The Greeks occupied Pannonia. The Germans seized Spain and also invaded Syria, having the Franks as their allies.

Valentinian (from chapter 45), and so forth. The Saxons were defeated at Deusone [Note: [Col. 0700D] This is also how it is read in Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, in all the manuscripts, as Scaliger notes; he thinks that the name designates some town near the Rhine. The Boherian manuscript reads “Diosone.” Canisius reads: “The Saxons were defeated at Diovio and the survivors settled in the territory of the Franks.” Then chapter 46 begins: “At that time,” and so forth.] and settled in the territory of the Franks.

At that time approximately eighty thousand surviving Burgundians (from chapter 46), who had never previously even been mentioned by name, descended to the Rhine. They pitched their camp where they had arrived and called it, as it were, a *burgus*; from this they received the name Burgundians [Note: [Col. 0700D] See Orosius, book VII of the *History*, chapter 4.]. There they presumed to do nothing except what they were able to do, receiving their pay as a price from the Germans. After they had remained there for two years, they were invited by envoys of the Romans or Gauls, who remained in the province of Lugdunum, in Gaul Comata, Gaul Domata, and Cisalpine Gaul [Note: [Col. 0700D] The Boherian manuscript reads: “The provinces and Gaul Comata Cisalpina remained.” Canisius reads: “The province and the Gauls, conquered in Cisalpine territory, remained as public tributaries … and there, when …,” and so forth. Gaul Comata, or Transalpine Gaul, contained modern France; Cisalpine Gaul, or Togata, contained part of Italy, which we now call Lombardy.], so that they might be able to reject public tribute; there they were seen to have settled with their wives and children.

## III.—Among the Excerpts from the *Chronicle* of Hydatius.

Martianus (chapter 55 in Canisius; book III, chapter 5), and so forth. The race of the Huns, having broken the peace, rushed into Gaul. When the patrician Aetius learned that they were approaching, he sent Saint Anianus, bishop of Orléans, on an embassy to Theodoric, king of the Goths, requesting aid against the Huns: if he prevailed in resisting them, he would give half of Gaul to the Goths. When King Theodoric had agreed to this request and promised assistance, Aetius sent envoys to Attila, king of the Huns, asking aid against the Goths, who were attempting to invade Gaul: if the Huns prevailed in defending it against the Goths, they would receive half of Gaul from Aetius.

King Attila, hastening with the Huns and sparing [Note: [Col. 0701D] The Claromontane manuscript reads “dividing.” The Boherian manuscript reads “devastating.”] the cities of Germany and Gaul, fought against the Goths on the Loire, settling not far from Orléans. Two hundred thousand Goths were slain. King Theodoric fell in this battle. One hundred and fifty thousand Huns were slain. The city of Orléans was delivered through the prayers of the blessed Anianus. The Huns withdrew to Troyes [Note: [Col. 0701D] The Boherian manuscript reads: “With the Huns withdrawing to Troyes.” Canisius reads: “to the camps.”] and settled in the Mauriac plain.

Thorismod [Note: [Col. 0701D] The Boherian manuscript reads “Thorismodus.” Canisius reads “Thorsimodus.”], son of Theodoric, who succeeded him in the kingdom, gathered the Gothic army and, desiring to avenge his father, fought Attila and the Huns at Mauriac. There, for three days, both battle lines fought one another, and an immeasurable multitude of the people [Note: [Col. 0701D] The Claromontane manuscript reads “of the people”; then *-um* was added, that is, “of the peoples.”] perished.

Aetius, since he was extremely capable in counsel, came to Attila by night and said to him: “I had hoped that by your courage I might be able to rescue this region from the treacherous Goths, but this cannot be done at all. Until now you have fought with only a few warriors; tonight Theuderic, the brother of Thorismod, has arrived with an immense multitude and the bravest Gothic warriors. You will not withstand them; would that you might at least escape.”

Then Attila gave Aetius ten thousand solidi, so that by his own ingenuity he might return to Pannonia. That same night Aetius went to Thorismod and said to him something similar: that until then he had been fighting against the insignificant warriors of the Huns; for a very large multitude and the bravest warriors had come from Pannonia to Attila that very night, and he had heard that their brother Theodoric had seized the kingdom of the Goths and wanted to take the kingship, unless Thorismod hurried to return; if he did not hasten to withdraw, he would be in danger of being degraded. Thorismod likewise gave Aetius ten thousand solidi, so that the Goths, freed by his ingenuity from pursuit by the Huns, might return to their own settlements. And immediately they departed.

Aetius, however, with his own men, also having the Franks with him, marched in the rear of the Huns and followed them from a distance as far as Thuringia. He ordered his men, wherever they halted at night, to make ten fires scattered about, so that they might appear to be an immense multitude [Note: [Col. 0701D] The Boherian manuscript reads: “They made scattered fires so that they might resemble an immense multitude.” Canisius reads: “scattered … that they might pretend …”].

This battle came to an end. Through Aetius’s strategy, Gaul was freed from its enemies.

Later, when this arrangement had been reported by King Thorismod and the Goths, they demanded that Aetius fulfill his promise. When he refused, a golden dish [Note: [Col. 0701D] Fredegar himself calls it a *missorium* in the *Chronicle*, chapter 73. It is also called this in the *Chronicle of Saint Benignus*. Hence one may infer that by *missorium* this author means a basin or dish.] adorned with gems, weighing five hundred pounds, was sent by Aetius to Thorismod as a settlement, and these disputes ceased. This object is still revered and kept to the present day among the treasures of the Goths as an ornament.

In the second year of Anthemius (from chapter 58; Canisius, book III, chapter 8), in the middle of the city of Toulouse blood burst from the earth and flowed all day, signifying that Gothic domination had been removed and that the kingdom of the Franks was arriving.

## IV.—Among the same Excerpts from Hydatius.

[Col. 0702B] Once [Note: [Col. 0701D] Compare this chapter with chapter 20 of book I of Aimoinus’s *Deeds of the Franks* and book IV of Rorico.] (chapter 60; Canisius, book III, chapter 10), King Clovis of the Franks and King Alaric of the Goths, whose seat was at Toulouse, after they had fought many battles against one another, began to make peace through the intervention of envoys, on the condition that Alaric should touch Clovis’s beard and become his godfather [Note: [Col. 0702D] In place of *illi*, “to him.” In the Claromontane manuscript, in another but very ancient hand, it reads: “he would become his godfather.” Later spiritual kinship was established not only by touching but also by cutting the beard or hair. Whoever cut another’s hair became his spiritual father. See Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book IV, chapter 40, and book VI, chapter 53. Mabillon discusses this matter further in the preface to the first volume of the third century of the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*.], so that they might preserve perpetual peace with one another; and, according to the terms of this agreement [Note: [Col. 0702D] The Boherian and Canisian manuscripts read “agreement.”], neither the Franks nor the Goths should approach armed at all.

They appointed a day and a place for one another. There the envoy of Clovis, named Paternus, approached Alaric and asked whether the Goths were keeping the agreement unarmed, in the condition they had promised, or whether perhaps, as was later proved, they were obeying their customary falsehoods [Note: [Col. 0702D] That is, “whether they would prove themselves liars,” as Canisius has it.].

While Paternus was speaking with King Alaric, conveying Clovis’s greetings and carefully asking in what manner they should join together, the Goths deceitfully carried swords in their hands in place of staffs [Note: [Col. 0702D] This is how both manuscripts read, and correctly. See chapter 64 of the *Chronicle* and the *Glossary* of Du Cange.]. Paternus seized one of them and drew it out, saying: “Your agreements are lies, king, since you are attempting by deceit, together with your Goths, to trick my lord and the Franks.”

After making an agreement with Alaric, Paternus promised on behalf of the Franks that King Theodoric of Italy would settle the matter by judgment. The envoys of King Alaric and Paternus, sent by Clovis, immediately hastened to appear before Theodoric. Paternus explained in order the case of Clovis and the Franks, which Alaric’s envoy could not deny, except by asking that Theodoric’s judgment should settle the matter.

Theodoric considered within himself how the case would turn out and, not consigning to oblivion what would be necessary in future times, retained resentment against the two kings. He said to the envoys: “Tomorrow I shall be able to discuss this matter more carefully with the elders of the Palace, as the order of justice demands, for the concord of peace; and I shall not fail to communicate the result to my brothers with complete affection and abundant love.”

But while deliberating in the secret recesses of his heart, he had long concealed his desire that these two kings should always remain at odds with one another. He therefore gave them this judgment: since it would be difficult for the Goths ruled by Alaric to provide compensation for this offense, the Frankish envoy was to come mounted on a horse, holding an erect spear in his hand, before Alaric’s palace. Alaric and the Goths were then to throw solidi upon him until they had covered the envoy, the horse, and the tip of the spear with the coins.

Alaric’s envoys immediately reported that Theodoric had settled the matter by judgment. Since it was difficult for Alaric and the Goths to fulfill this condition, they wished to deceive Paternus, the Frankish envoy. He was sent to an upper chamber; during the night, the structure that had been placed beneath him gave way, and, breaking his arm, he barely escaped [Col. 0703B] alive.

The next day Alaric led him to the fortress [Canisius reads “camp”], showed him his treasures, and declared under oath that he had no more solidi than those he had displayed, filling the fortress as it then stood. At this point Paternus drew one solidus from his fist, threw it into his bosom, and said: “I shall take this solidus as earnest [Note: [Col. 0703D] The Boherian manuscript reads “these solidi.” Canisius reads: “With these solidi I shall give earnest.”] on behalf of my lord King Clovis and the Franks.”

He returned to Clovis and recounted everything in detail. Clovis took up arms against Alaric, whom he killed in the plain of Vouillé, ten miles from the city of Poitiers, and there cut down the greater part of the Gothic army with the sword. He took his kingdom from the Loire and the Rhône, by the Tyrrhenian Sea [Note: [Col. 0703D] Canisius reads “Tyrrhenian.”] and the Pyrenees, as far as the Ocean; and it remains to this day under rightful dominion [Note: [Col. 0703D] Canisius reads “under rightful rule.” The Boherian manuscript reads “rightfully subject to the dominion.”] as part of the kingdom of the Franks.

## V.—Among the same Excerpts from Hydatius.

Chrocus, king of the Vandals [Note: [Col. 0703D] Fredegar treated the Vandals in their proper place, as in Hydatius. Sigebert assigns Chrocus’s invasion to the first year of the reign of Theodosius the Younger; others customarily date it to the times of Valerian and Gallienus.], set out from his homeland with the Suebi and Alans, making for Gaul (chapter 62; Canisius, book III, chapter 12). He followed the advice of his utterly wicked mother, who had told him: “If you wish to undertake something new and acquire a reputation, destroy everything that others have built, and kill the entire population that you overcome. For you cannot build a better structure than your predecessors, nor accomplish a greater deed by which to raise your name.”

Ingeniously crossing the Rhine by a bridge at Mainz, he first ravaged the city itself and its people. Then, laying waste to all the cities of Germany, he reached Metz, where, by divine will, the city wall collapsed during the night, and the city was captured by the Vandals. The people of Trier, however, were saved in the arena of that city, which they had fortified.

After this, Chrocus wandered through all Gaul with the Vandals, Suebi, and Alans. He destroyed some cities by siege [Al.: “by blockade”] and ravaged others by breaking through them by stratagem; no city or fortress in Gaul was freed from them. While they were besieging Arles, Chrocus was captured by a certain soldier named Marius and bound in chains. He was led through all the cities he had ravaged to his punishment and ended his impious life by a death he deserved. Trasamund succeeded him in the kingdom.

The Alamanni took up arms against the Vandals. The two sides agreed to send two men to fight a single combat. The man sent by the Vandals was defeated by the Alamann. Trasamund and the Vandals, having been defeated, according to the agreement abandoned Gaul and made for Spain with the Vandals, Suebi, and Alans. There they killed many Christians for the Catholic faith.

After a short time they crossed the sea into Mauretania, I believe by divine will, led by a wild animal, and passed over with the Vandals by wading. It is said that the sea there is seven miles wide. After Trasamund died in Mauretania, the more cruel-minded Huneric succeeded him as king of the Vandals. Occupying all Mauretania [Note: [Col. 0704D] Thus the Boherian manuscript. The Claromontane manuscript reads in the first hand *auream totam* (“the whole golden [land]”); in the second, “Mauretania.” Canisius reads “the whole land.”], he inflicted an immense slaughter upon the Christians, at the urging of Cyrola, a bishop of the heretics. In this persecution a very great number of Christians were crowned with the palm of martyrdom.

In those days the bishops Eugenius, Longinus, and Vindemialis displayed wondrous powers in the name of Christ [Note: [Col. 0704D] The Boherian manuscript reads: “They displayed them among Christian invalids.”], and even raised the dead. Cyrola bribed a certain man, giving him fifty gold pieces, to pretend to be blind and cry out before King Huneric that through Cyrola’s powers he had received his sight. When Cyrola touched him, he became blind; afterward, through Eugenius’s prayer, he received his sight.

At Cyrola’s instigation, because of envy, Huneric ordered Eugenius to be beheaded. Longinus and Vindemialis, subjected to various punishments for the name of Christ, departed to eternal blessedness. Huneric, as his deserts required, tore himself apart with his own bites and ended his unworthy life by a just death. Childeric succeeded him in the kingdom. After Childeric died, Childemeris received the kingdom. Under him the patrician Belisarius fought with great courage; during his reign the kingdom of the Vandals came to an end.

[Belisarius] was defeated in Italy by a certain Frank named Buccelenus. Glorious for the renown of so great a victory, Belisarius lost both his reputation and his life when he was defeated by Buccelenus [Note: [Col. 0704D] Compare Aimoinus, book II of *The Deeds of the Franks*, chapter 23.].

[Col. 0704D] Here end the Fragments of Fredegar.

[Col. 0705]

# THE BOOKS OF SAINT GEORGE FLORENTIUS GREGORY, BISHOP OF TOURS, ON MIRACLES. (C)

[Col. 0705]

## Prologue

That one must adhere not to the fabrications of poets or the opinions of philosophers, but to evangelical truth.

**713–714** Jerome the presbyter, and after the apostle Paul a good teacher of the Church, reports that he was led before the tribunal of the eternal Judge and stretched out under punishment, severely beaten because he repeatedly read the subtleties of Cicero and the deceptions of Virgil. He confessed before the holy angels and the Ruler of all that he would never afterward read or discuss these works, except those judged worthy of God and suitable for the edification of the Church [Note: [Col. 0705A] Jerome relates this very thing in his letter to Eustochium.].

But the apostle Paul also says: “Let us pursue the things that make for peace, and the things that build one another up” (Romans 14:19). And elsewhere: “Let no corrupt speech proceed from your mouth, but only such as is good for edification, so that it may give grace to those who hear” (Ephesians 4:29).

Therefore we ought to follow, write, and speak those things that build up the Church of God and enrich impoverished minds with holy instruction for knowledge of the perfect faith. For we ought not to recall deceitful tales, nor follow the wisdom of philosophers, which is hostile to God, lest we fall under the judgment of eternal death when the Lord distinguishes between us.

Fearing this, and wishing to disclose certain miracles of the saints that have hitherto remained hidden, I do not wish either to be bound or entangled in those nets [Note: [Col. 0705A] Here the prologue ends in the Claromontane manuscript.]. I do not recall Saturn’s flight, Juno’s anger, Jupiter’s adulteries, Neptune’s wrongs, or Aeolus’s scepters; I do not recount the wars, shipwrecks, or kingdoms of the descendants of Aeneas; I am silent about Cupid’s shooting, Ascanius’s love, and Dido’s marriages, tears, and cruel destruction; I do not recall Pluto’s gloomy vestibule, Proserpina’s shameful abduction, or Cerberus’s threefold head; I do not revisit Anchises’s conversations, the schemes of Ithacan Odysseus, Achilles’ subtleties, or Sinon’s deceits; I do not bring forward Laocoön’s counsels, the strength of Amphitryon’s son, or the conflicts, flights, and disastrous death of Janus; I do not display the forms of the Eumenides and various monsters; nor do I recount the inventions of the remaining fables, which this author either fabricated with falsehood [Note: [Col. 0706A] Some manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read before the end: “fashioned by falsehood … depicted.”] or depicted in heroic verse.

But seeing all these things as placed upon sand and soon destined to collapse, let us turn instead to the divine and evangelical miracles, from which the Evangelist John began, saying: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:2–3).

And afterward he says: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us; and we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (ibid., 14).

That he was to be born in Bethlehem, the Prophet says: “And you, Bethlehem Ephrata [Note: [Col. 0706A] Several manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read “Eufrata.”], are not the least among the thousands of Judah. For from you shall come forth a King who will rule my people Israel” (Micah 5:2; Matthew 2:6; John 21:2).

Nathaniel of Cana in Galilee also said this: “Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel” (John 1:49).

He is also the salvation of the world, of whom Simeon said: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2:29).

# [BOOKS OF MIRACLES]

## BOOK ONE. ON THE GLORY OF THE BLESSED MARTYRS

### CHAPTER ONE. On the birth of Our Lord Jesus Christ in Bethlehem

[Note: [Col. 0705A] The printed editions read: “The star that the Magi saw still appears in Bethlehem to the pure of heart.” In the Colbertine manuscript the first eleven chapters are missing; there the book begins with chapter 12 [Col. 0706A]. “On Saint John the Baptist,” which in that manuscript is called the first chapter, nevertheless has a prologue.]

**721** When therefore Our Lord Jesus Christ was born according to [Col. 0705] the flesh in the town of Bethlehem (five years before the common era, 25 December), in the days of King Herod, according to the testimony of the Gospel, Magi came from the East to Jerusalem, [Col. 0707A] saying: “Where is he who has been born King of the Jews? For we saw his star in the East and have come to worship him” (Luke 2:2), and the rest.

There is [Note: [Col. 0707C] In Colbertine manuscript A, in the manner of a title and in another but ancient hand, this reads: “On the star that fell into the well.” We observe, moreover, that even now, near the Bethlehemite cave, a well or cistern is shown to pilgrims, into which popular belief holds that the star of the Magi fell [Col. 0707D].] in Bethlehem a large well, from which Mary the glorious is said to have drawn water. There a remarkable miracle is repeatedly shown to those who look into it: the star that appeared to the Magi is displayed there to those who are pure in heart.

When the devout visitors arrive and recline over the mouth of the well, their heads are covered with linen. Then the person whose merit has obtained this privilege sees the star move from one wall of the well across the water to the other, in the manner in which stars ordinarily travel across the circle of the heavens. Although many look, it is seen only by those whose minds are sounder.

I have seen some who asserted that they had seen it. Recently, however, our deacon reported that he had looked at it with five men [Note: [Col. 0707D] The Colbertine manuscript, in another hand, reads “looked into it.”], but that it appeared to only two of them.

### CHAPTER TWO. On the miracles of Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ

[Note: [Col. 0707D] This chapter and the following chapters through chapter eleven are missing from the Claromontane manuscript.]

Our Lord Jesus Christ, therefore, in the flesh he had assumed from the Virgin (year 30), deigned to display many miracles to the peoples. He changed water drawn into the taste of wine; driving away the night from the eyes of the blind, he infused light; restoring the power that had been taken away, he directed the steps of paralytics; driving out the heat, he extinguished the fevers of the sick; by compressing the swelling, he healed the dropsical man; by the power of his sacred mouth he commanded leprosy to depart; he raised up the woman bent down by a demon, despite the envious Jews. Upon the waters he walked, while the waters did not part; by the touch of his saving fringe he stopped the woman’s flow of blood [Col. 0707C].

He did many other things, which the sacred history of the Gospels recounts. Yet, after restoring many to life through a saving and heavenly command, he brought three back from infernal death and restored them to life: he raised the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue in the house; he commanded the only son of a widow to rise at the town gate; and he called Lazarus from the tomb.

### CHAPTER THREE. On his passion, resurrection, and ascension

The Jews, inflamed by fury and surrounding the Just One with false accusations, handed him over to death and condemned him to crucifixion (year 33, 3 April). God the Father raised him from the dead on the third day, having released him from the pains of death (Acts 2:24), because, as the apostle Peter says, it was impossible for him to be held in the realm of the dead.

Afterward, promising the Paraclete and filling the apostles with heavenly teachings, he ascended victoriously into heaven. He promised, with the angels bearing witness, that he would come to judge, as the history of the apostolic Acts says: “This Jesus, who has been taken up from you, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11).

### CHAPTER FOUR. On the apostles and blessed Mary

[Col. 0708B] After the wondrous glory of the Lord’s ascension (year 33, 14 May), which, having crushed the head of the devil’s wickedness, stirred the minds of the faithful to contemplate heavenly things, the holy apostles of our Lord and Savior, together with blessed Mary his mother, gathered in one house and placed everything in common. No one said that anything was his own; rather, each possessed everything in charity, as the sacred account of the apostles’ deeds relates (Acts 4:34).

Afterward they dispersed through various regions to preach the word of God (year 36). Finally, when blessed Mary had completed the course of this life and was already being called away from the world, all the apostles were gathered from their several regions at her house (year 48). When they heard that she was to be taken from the world, they kept vigil with her. And behold, the Lord Jesus came with his angels, received her soul, handed it over to the archangel Michael, and departed.

At dawn the apostles lifted her body with its bier, placed it in a tomb, and guarded it while awaiting the Lord’s coming. And behold, the Lord again appeared to them, and commanded that the holy body he had received be carried in a cloud into paradise. There, now reunited with her soul, she rejoices with his elect and enjoys the blessings of eternity, which will never come to an end [Note: [Col. 0707D] The Morin manuscript reads “will enjoy.” What Gregory relates here about the most blessed Virgin’s death and its circumstances was without doubt drawn from the book of the Pseudo-Melito, bishop of Sardes, *On the Transit of Blessed Mary*, which Pope Gelasius listed among the apocrypha; that book was published in the *Library of the Fathers*. It is the opinion of learned men that she died at Ephesus. Yet no one before Gregory of Tours is found explicitly to have asserted the resurrection of blessed Mary and the assumption of her body and soul together into heaven. Nevertheless, this opinion prevailed in Gaul not long afterward, to such an extent that it was introduced even into the liturgy. This is clear from the Gothic Missal, book III of the *Gallican Liturgy*, in the Mass of the Assumption of Saint Mary [Col. 0709D], where it is stated more than once that the body of this most blessed Virgin was carried into heaven, and indeed in the *contestatio* with the same circumstances that Gregory recounts here. See also another Gallican sacramentary, volume I of the *Italian Museum*, page 300. The Roman sacramentary of Saint Gregory contains nothing similar. This matter was discussed more fully in this century on the occasion of Usuard’s Martyrology. See the notes of the illustrious Tillemont, notes 14 and 15 on the *Life of Blessed Mary the Virgin*, volume I of his *Ecclesiastical History*; add to these the passage of Adamnanus, book I of *The Holy Places*, chapter 9, where he speaks of the tomb of blessed Mary, which was shown near Jerusalem in the Valley of Jehoshaphat, as follows: “In it,” says that author, “she once lay buried in repose. But concerning that same tomb—how, or at what time, or by what persons her holy little body was removed, or at what place it awaits resurrection—no one, as is said, can know with certainty.”].

### CHAPTER FIVE. On the cross and its miracles at Poitiers
### 725. The Lord’s Cross, Discovered by the Empress Helena at Jerusalem (in A.D. 326, 3 May)

The Lord’s cross, which the empress Helena discovered at Jerusalem (in A.D. 326, 3 May), is worshiped on Wednesday and Friday.[^c0072-1] Queen Radegund, seeking its relics with a devotion and faith worthy of Helena (in A.D. 569), reverently placed them in the monastery at Poitiers, which she had established through her own efforts.[^c0072-2] She also again sent servants to Jerusalem and throughout the whole region of the East. Going around the tombs, they brought back the relics of all the holy martyrs and confessors. When these had been placed in a silver chest together with the holy cross itself, she was granted the sight of many miracles thereafter.

Of these I shall first relate one which the Lord deigned to reveal there during the days of his Passion. On the Friday before holy Easter, while they were spending the night in vigil without light, around the third hour of the night a small light appeared before the altar, in the form of a spark. Then it grew larger, scattering locks of radiance here and there, and gradually began to rise upward. It became a great lamp and gave light to the dark night and to the praying congregation keeping vigil. When the sky began to brighten, it gradually diminished; after giving light to the earth, it vanished from the eyes of those who marveled.

I had often heard that even the lamps which were lit before these relics, boiling over through divine power, sometimes overflowed with so much oil that they frequently filled the vessel placed beneath them. Yet, in keeping with the folly of my hardened mind, I was never moved to believe these things, until the power then displayed itself reproved my brutish sluggishness. Therefore I shall explain what I saw with my own eyes.

The reason for my devotion was that, while visiting the tomb of Saint Hilary, I went to converse with this queen. Entering the monastery, I greeted the queen and prostrated myself before the cross to be worshiped and the sacred relics of the saints. At last, after praying, I rose. A lamp was burning on the right. When I saw it dripping with frequent drops, I call God to witness that I thought its vessel had been broken, for a basin had been placed beneath it into which the flowing oil fell.

Then, turning to the abbess, I said: “Does such great laziness of mind hold you back that you cannot take care of an entire lamp in which oil may be burned unless you place beneath it a broken vessel into which it can flow?”

She replied: “It is not so, my lord, but it is the power of the holy cross that you see.”

Then, coming to my senses and recalling what I had previously heard, I turned toward the lamp and saw it, like a boiling pot, overflowing in great waves. The oil swelled over its rim and poured out in waves; and, as I believe, in order to rebuke my disbelief, it increased more and more, so that within the space of one hour the little vessel—which could not hold even a quart—yielded more than a sextarius. I marveled and fell silent, and thereafter proclaimed the power of the cross to be worshiped.

A certain girl named Chrodegildis, while living in the territory of the city of Le Mans after her father’s death, was afflicted with the loss of her sight. Later, by order of King Chilperic, while the blessed Queen Radegund was still alive, she was sent to the aforesaid monastery.[^c0072-4] At the command of that most blessed woman, she prostrated herself before the holy chest. There, keeping vigil with the other holy women, she remained after morning came and the others had departed, lying prostrate on the ground in that same place.

It appeared to her in a vision that someone was opening her eyes. While one had been restored to health and she still struggled with the other, she was suddenly awakened by the sound of the opened door and recovered the sight of one eye. There is no doubt that this was granted through the power of the cross. Possessed persons, the lame, and other sick people are also very often healed in this place.

Thus far concerning this matter.[^c0072-5]

### Chapter VI. The Discovery of the Nails

The beautiful nails of the Lord’s cross, more noble than every kind of metal, which held his blessed limbs, were found by Queen Helena after the discovery of the holy cross itself (in A.D. 326). Of two of them she made the emperor’s bridle, so that, if hostile peoples resisted the emperor, they might more easily be put to flight by this power. Concerning these nails the prophet Zechariah is known to have prophesied: “It shall be what is put into the mouth of the horse, holy to the Lord” (Zechariah 14:20).

At that time the Adriatic Sea was being stirred by great waves. Shipwrecks and drownings were so frequent there that it was called the abyss of sailors. Then the provident queen, grieving over the destruction of the unfortunate, ordered one of the four nails to be lowered into the sea, trusting in the Lord’s mercy that it could easily subdue the violent agitation of the waves. When this had been done, the sea became calm, and thereafter gentle breezes were granted to sailors. Hence, to this day, sailors venerate the sanctified sea when they enter it, devoting themselves to fasting, prayer, and psalmody.[^c0072-6]

The reason, then, why there were four nails of the Lord is this: two were fastened in his palms and two in his feet. But the question arises why they were fastened in his feet, since the feet seemed to hang upon the holy cross rather than stand upon it. It is clear that a hole was made in the upright beam. A foot was inserted into this hole in a small board; upon this board the sacred feet were fastened, as though the man were standing.

It is also asked what became of these nails. Two, as we have said, were fitted into the bridle; the third was thrown into the strait; the fourth, they assert, was driven into the head of the statue of Constantine. This statue is said to rise higher than the entire city, so that the whole fortification over which it towers might somehow be crowned with a helmet of salvation.[^c0072-7]

They assert that this bridle possesses great power—a fact that can in no way be doubted, for the emperor Justin publicly experienced it and made it known to all his people. Having been deceived by a certain magician on account of money that had been lost, he disclosed the ambushes which the shadow of the demon had inflicted upon him for the course of two nights, making them unbearable.[^c0072-8] But when, on the third night, he placed the bridle upon his head, the enemy no longer had a place from which to lie in wait. He found the author of the ambushes and struck him with the sword.

For us, the power of this wood was made manifest in the following way. Someone came and showed us a very old cloth of pure silk, saying that the Lord’s cross had been wrapped in it at Jerusalem. Since this was considered incredible by our rustic minds, and since we carefully investigated how it could have acquired such favor there as to deserve this distinction—for we know that at the time when this sacred wood is worshiped, no one gains anything from it, and anyone who approaches too intrusively is driven away with blows—he replied:

“When I departed from Jerusalem, I found Abbot Futen, who enjoyed great favor with the empress Sophia, for she had entrusted the whole East to him as its governor.[^c0072-9] I placed myself under his authority, and when I returned from the East, I received from him both the relics of the saints and this cloth, in which the holy cross was wrapped at that time.[^c0072-10]

“After that man had told me this and handed me the cloth, I confess that I presumed to wash it and give the water as a drink to those suffering from fevers. Immediately, with divine power assisting, they were healed. I also frequently cut off small pieces from it and gave them to religious people as a blessing.

“I gave a portion to one abbot. When he returned to me two years later, he asserted under oath that twelve possessed persons, three blind people, and two paralytics had been healed by it. He placed the cloth itself in the mouth of a mute. When it touched his teeth and tongue, his voice and power of speech were immediately restored.

“This the Lord’s own promise permits us faithfully to believe, for he says: ‘Whatever you ask for in my name, believe that you will receive, and it will come to you’” (Mark 11:14).

### Chapter VII. The Lance, the Crown of Thorns, and the Column

Concerning the lance with which the side of our Savior was pierced, the reed, the sponge, the crown of thorns, and the column to which the Lord and Redeemer was tied while being scourged at Jerusalem, something must be said.[^c0072-11]

Many people full of faith approach this column and make woven straps, which they wrap around it; afterward they receive them back as a blessing, believing that they will be useful against various illnesses. They also say that the thorns of the crown appear almost green. Even if they seem to have withered in their leaves, nevertheless they grow green again each day through divine power.

A marvelous power also proceeds from the monument where the Lord’s body lay.[^c0072-12] The ground there is repeatedly filled with a natural radiance of white light. Water is again sprinkled over what has been removed from it; little cakes are made from this, and they are sent to various parts of the world. From them the sick often draw healing.

It is a cause for rejoicing that they very often avoid the approach of snakes. But why should I, rash man that I am, dare to speak about these things, when faith holds that everything which touched the most sacred body has been sanctified?

### Chapter VIII. Christ’s Seamless Tunic

The Gospel faith reveals that the tunic of the blessed body was not sewn but woven from above throughout, and that, in accordance with David’s prophecy, it had been assigned by lot. For it says: “They divided my garments among themselves, and for my robe they cast lots” (John 19:24).

I cannot remain silent about what I have heard from certain people concerning this tunic of the immaculate Lamb. They say that it is kept in the city of Galathea,[^c0072-13] in the basilica called that of the holy Archangels.[^c0072-14] This city is about one hundred and fifty thousand paces from Constantinople. The basilica contains a very secluded crypt, and there this garment is enclosed in a wooden chest.
