Devout and faithful people worship the chest with the greatest care, and it is deservedly worthy to preserve this garment, which the Lord’s body either merited to touch or to cover.

### Chapter IX. The Miracles of the Basilica of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Built by the Emperor Constantine

The glorious Mary, mother of Christ, is believed to have remained a virgin after childbirth just as she was before childbirth. As we said above (chapter 4), she was translated into paradise while angelic choirs sang and the Lord went before her.[^c0072-15]

Her basilica, built by the emperor Constantine with wondrous workmanship, shines resplendently. Columns were brought to it which, because of their great size, could not be raised: their circumference was sixteen feet, and the workers were exhausted each day by their futile labor.

Then the holy Virgin appeared in a vision to the craftsman and said: “Do not be sad, for I shall show you how these columns can be raised.” She showed him which machines should be fitted, how the pulleys should be suspended, and how the ropes should be arranged. She added: “Take three boys from the school to assist you, so that with their help you may complete this task.”

When he awoke and had arranged what he had been commanded, he summoned three boys from the school and raised the columns with the greatest speed. The people were granted the sight of an astonishing miracle: what a multitude of strong men had been unable to lift, three little boys, without the strength required for such a work, lifted.[^c0072-17]

This sacred feast is celebrated in the middle of the eleventh month. Her relics are contained in the oratory of the Marciac house, in the territory of Auvergne.[^c0072-19]

When this feast arrived, I went there to celebrate the vigils. As I hurried to the oratory through the dark night, I suspected from a distance that such immense brightness was shining through the windows that one might have thought a multitude of lamps and candles had been lit there.

Believing, therefore, that some devout people had already gone ahead of us to celebrate the vigils, I approached the door and knocked, but found no one. When I discovered that the door was secured by a key, I realized that everything was silent.

What more need be said? We sent to the custodian, whose duty at that time was to lock up, asking him to come with the key and open the door. While he was coming, we lit a candle outside. Meanwhile the door opened of its own accord. When we entered, the brightness we had admired outside disappeared—as I believe, because of the darkness of my sins—when our candle appeared. Nevertheless, we could see nothing whatever except the power of the glorious Virgin from which that brightness had arisen.

### Chapter X. A Highly Memorable Miracle Concerning a Jewish Boy

I shall not remain silent about what happened in the East to strengthen the Catholic faith.[^c0072-20]

The son of a certain Jewish glassmaker was being educated with Christian boys in literary studies. One day, while the feast of the Mass was being celebrated in the basilica of the blessed Mary, the Jewish child approached with the other children to partake of the glorious body and blood of the Lord.

After receiving the holy sacrament,[^c0072-21] he returned home joyfully and reported with delight to his father what he had received, while the father was at work.[^c0072-22] But the father, an enemy of Christ the Lord and of his laws, said:

“If you have communicated with these children, forgetting filial piety, I shall become a harsh murderer toward you in order to avenge the insult to the Mosaic law.”

He seized the boy and threw him into the mouth of a blazing furnace. He added wood so that the boy might burn more fiercely and persisted in the act.

But that mercy was not absent which had once sprinkled the three Hebrew boys, thrown into the Chaldean furnace, with a dew-bearing cloud. It likewise prevented this child, lying amid the flames and heaps of burning coals, from being consumed at all.

When the mother heard that the father had resolved to burn their son, she ran to free him. But when she saw the fire spraying here and there from the open mouth of the furnace, she threw her head covering to the ground and, her hair streaming loose, filled the city with cries, calling herself a wretched woman.

When the Christians learned what had happened, they all hurried to witness so wicked a spectacle. Drawing back the fire from the furnace’s mouth, they found the boy lying as though upon the softest feathers. They pulled him out, and everyone marveled that he was unharmed. The place was filled with shouting, and the whole people blessed the Lord.

They also cried out that the perpetrator of this crime should be thrown into the flames themselves. When he was thrown in, the fire consumed him entirely, leaving scarcely any recognizable trace of his bones.

The Christians asked the child what shelter he had had amid the flames. He replied:

“A woman who, in that basilica where I received the bread from the table, was sitting on a chair and holding a little child in her lap covered me with her cloak, so that the fire would not devour me.”[^c0072-23]

There is no doubt that the blessed Mary appeared to him. Once the child had recognized the Catholic faith, he believed in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. After being washed in the saving waters, he and his mother were born again. Many Jews in that city were saved by this example.

### Chapter XI. The Monastery at Jerusalem and the Miracles Worked Through the Power of the Relics of Saint Mary

There is a very large monastery in Jerusalem with a considerable community. There, not only does the devotion of the people often contribute very generously, but by order of the emperor they also receive substantial donations.[^c0072-24]

At one time, however, because of extreme poverty, the food necessary for them ran out completely. The talkative congregation of monks, after going one day and then another without receiving food at the meal, cried out to the abbot:

“Provide food, or allow each of us to depart to a place where he can sustain his life. Otherwise, without consulting you, we shall leave, lest we perish from hunger.”

When they had said this, the abbot replied:

“Let us pray, dearest brothers, and the Lord will provide food for us. For it cannot happen that grain should fail in the monastery of her who, from her womb, brought the fruit of life to the perishing world.”

They kept vigil and sang psalms throughout the entire night. At dawn they found all the storage rooms filled with grain, so full that the door could scarcely be opened. After receiving food, they gave thanks to God.

Many years later, when food again ran out, the monks cried out to the abbot. He said:

“Let us keep vigil and beseech the Lord; perhaps he will deign to send us provisions.”

They threw themselves down upon the floor of the church. Keeping vigil, they passed the night in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. When they had given themselves to sleep after the morning office, an angel of the Lord came and placed an innumerable quantity of gold upon the altar. The doors of the building had been locked.

At dawn the abbot rose with the monks to celebrate the office and saw the great quantity of gold upon the altar. The abbot said to the custodian of the building:

“Which of the officials entered here and left this?”

He replied:

“After you departed, no one came in here. I kept the key of the locked door with me until you arose to sound the signal.”[^c0072-25]

Then the abbot and the monks, astonished, understood that the gift was heavenly. Giving thanks to God, he gathered it, purchased the necessities of life, and abundantly fed the people entrusted to him.

Nor is it surprising that the blessed Virgin provided food for her servants without labor, since she conceived without intercourse with a man and remained a virgin after childbirth.

On one occasion I displayed the relics of this blessed Virgin, together with those of the holy apostles and of blessed Martin, placed upon my breast in a golden cross.[^c0072-26] As we were walking along the road, I saw not far away a little dwelling belonging to a poor man being consumed by fire. It was covered with leaves, which provide the greatest fuel for flames.

The wretched man ran about with his children and wife, carrying water, but the flames did not abate. Then I drew the cross from my breast and raised it against the fire. Immediately, at the sight of the holy relics, the entire fire became still, as though it had never been lit.

### Chapter XII. Saint John the Baptist

John the Baptist was imprisoned through Herod’s cunning, by means of Herodias, his brother’s wife (in A.D. 30). At that time a certain matron had gone from Gaul to Jerusalem solely out of devotion, so that she might be worthy to experience the presence of our Lord and Savior.

She heard that blessed John was to be beheaded (in A.D. 31 or 32). She hurried there swiftly and, having given gifts to the executioner, begged him to allow her to collect the blood as it flowed, rather than prevent her.[^c0072-27]

When he struck, the matron prepared a silver bowl. After the martyr’s head had been severed, she devoutly received the blood, carefully placed it in a small vessel,[^c0072-28] and carried it back to her homeland. At the city of Vasates, she built a church in his honor and placed it upon the holy altar.[^c0072-29]

### Chapter XIII. The Vasates Gem, Born by Divine Power

Since we have mentioned the city of Vasates, I think it worthwhile to relate the miracle which the Lord granted there.

At the time when the city was surrounded by a prolonged siege by the Chuni,[^c0072-30] the priest in charge went around it every night, singing psalms and praying. He sought help from no one except the Lord’s mercy. He urged everyone to pray and not grow faint, declaring that humble prayers penetrate the gates of heaven.

The enemy ravaged the surrounding villages, set houses on fire, and devastated fields and vineyards by letting their animals into them.[^c0072-31] But while the good priest persisted in his work, divine power quickly came to his aid.

One night the barbarian king saw, as it seemed to him, men singing psalms in white garments and carrying lighted candles as they went around the walls of the city. Indignant, he said:

“What is this perversity and foolish confidence, that the besieged, as though scorning us, should make a din with songs and praises of some sort? Truly, they deserve destruction.”

He immediately sent messengers to the city to ask what this meant. But the inhabitants denied knowing anything about it and said they had perceived nothing of the kind.

The following night he saw, as it seemed, a great ball of fire descending upon the city, and he said:

“If these besieged people act insolently against us and do not fear us, heavenly wrath will consume them.”

When he saw no fire rising from the city, he again sent to ask what the things he had seen might be. They likewise denied having seen anything at all.

Then King Gausericus said:

“If these people do not know about these things, it is clear that their God is helping them.”

He immediately departed from that place.[^c0072-32]

The priest, having summoned the citizens, celebrated vigils and conducted the feast of the Mass for the deliverance of his people.[^c0072-33] While he was doing this, he looked upward and saw above the altar, as though falling from the ceiling of the church, three drops equal in size and surpassing crystal in brightness and whiteness.[^c0072-34]

As everyone watched intently with wonder and great astonishment, no one dared touch them. A certain priest named Peter, who, as the event itself shows, was a man of great merit, brought a silver paten and tried to collect the drops. As they rolled in an erratic course across the altar and flowed into the paten, they immediately joined together and formed what seemed to be one most beautiful gem.

It then became clear that this had occurred as an evident answer to the wicked and God-hated Arian heresy, which was flourishing at that time. It was recognized that the holy Trinity, joined in the equality of one omnipotence, cannot be divided by any arguments.

The people rejoiced, understanding that a divine gift had been granted to them. Collecting gold and precious gems, they made a cross and set this gem in it. But immediately all the other gems fell away when this one was added.

Then the bishop, understanding that heavenly things do not consort with earthly things, made a cross of the purest gold, placed the gem in its middle space, and presented it to the people for worship. Without delay, the enemy was driven away, as we have said, and the city was liberated.

Even now many sick people are immediately restored to health after drinking wine or water in which the gem has been washed. Finally, when it has been worshiped, if a person is free from sin, it appears clear; but if, as most often happens, he has brought some offense upon human weakness, it appears wholly dark to him. Thus it provides a wondrous distinction between the innocent and the guilty: to one it appears black, while to the other it is shown shining.

### Chapter XIV. The Woman Who Obtained the Thumb of John the Baptist

Benedicti*, century III, part II, p. 506.

[^c0072-14]: The same tunic is said in Fredegar’s *Chronicle*, chapter 11, to have been transferred from the city of Zafad—called Zaphat by Sigebert, which we interpret as Jaffa or Joppa—to the holy city of Jerusalem in the thirtieth year of King Guntram. It was later brought into Gaul in the time of Charlemagne and deposited at Argenteuil in the Paris region, where Gisela, the emperor’s sister, and Theodrada, his daughter, were nuns. After remaining hidden for a long time because of the turmoil of wars, it was discovered around the middle of the twelfth century. In the presence of Louis the Younger and other nobles of the kingdom, it was exhibited for public veneration by Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, together with several other bishops and abbots, in the year 1156. From then onward the church at Argenteuil became famous through the great concourse of people. Even now the Benedictine monks of our Congregation of Saint Maur preserve and venerate this precious relic with the greatest devotion. See the booklet on this subject published in Paris by Dom Gabriel Gerberon in 1677.

[^c0072-15]: Adamnanus, book I, chapter 13 of *On the Holy Places*, describes a church near Jerusalem where, at that time, the tomb of the blessed Mary was shown. Since no one before the time of Juvenal, who flourished in the middle of the fifth century, had said that the blessed Virgin’s tomb existed at Jerusalem, the learned Tillemont, in his *Life of Constantine the Great*, article 68, thinks that the church mentioned here by Gregory is none other than the cathedral at Ephesus. According to the acts of the Council of Ephesus, that church had been consecrated in honor of the Virgin Mother of God, and before that time it alone is recorded by reliable authors as bearing the title of the blessed Virgin.

[^c0072-17]: The sacred feast is said to have been celebrated in the middle of the eleventh month. That is, according to one interpretation, in January, when the feast of the deposition or assumption of the most blessed Virgin was formerly celebrated in Gaul. This is certain from ancient Gallican liturgies and the oldest martyrologies, under 18 January, as Mabillon proves in book II of the *Gallican Liturgy*, no. 22, p. 118. Scaliger nevertheless holds, in book VI of *The Correction of the Times*, that Gregory begins the ecclesiastical year with April; on that reckoning, Gregory would designate February as the eleventh month. The Gallican Sacramentary, edited by Mabillon from a very ancient manuscript of the monastery of Bobbio and published at the end of volume I of the *Museum Italicum*, appears to support this view, since it places the Assumption of Saint Mary immediately after the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter and immediately before Lent. Gregory, however, usually begins the year with March.

[^c0072-19]: This apparently refers to Marciacum, or Marsac, an ancient women’s monastery still bearing the name of the Blessed Mary and subject to the monastery of Mauzac, where nuns continue to live under the direction of a prioress. It is distinct from the monastery at Marcinianum, which Peter, abbot of Cluny, mentions more than once. See Savaron on letter 119 of book II of Apollinaris Sidonius.

[^c0072-20]: A similar story is found in Evagrius, book IV, chapter 36, and Nicephorus, book XVII, chapter 25. The same event is said to have occurred at Bourges, in the church of Saint Mary, in the time of Humatus, bishop of that city, as the Monk of Saint-Sulpice relates in chapter 19 of the *Patriarchium Bituricense*. From this story he received the surname “of the Hot Furnace.”

[^c0072-21]: Several manuscripts read “when the holy thing had been received,” using the accusative instead of the ablative; this change of case is frequent in Gregory. It should be observed here that *sanctum* (“the holy thing”) is used absolutely for the Eucharist, as in many prayers of our liturgy, including the modern liturgy.

[^c0072-22]: Codex Colbertinus A reads “while he was hurrying.”

[^c0072-23]: It should first be observed that the Jewish boy received only the bread, that is, only one species of the Eucharist, although Gregory above calls it the body and blood of the Lord. Second, the ancient custom of representing the blessed Virgin seated with the infant Jesus, whom she holds in her arms, should be noted.

[^c0072-24]: Codex Romanus reads: “in which the devotion of the people often contributes very much.” Most others read: “in which place there is devotion”; the edition reads: “in a certain place.” From what follows, it is clear that this monastery was dedicated to the blessed Mary.

[^c0072-25]: This shows that responsibility for summoning the monks to divine worship—what Gregory here and elsewhere often calls the *cursus*—belonged to the abbot. Saint Benedict prescribed this in chapter 47 of his Rule, “On announcing the hour of the Work of God.” Claromontanus A nevertheless reads *surgerem* (“until I rose”).

[^c0072-26]: The pectoral cross is listed among the sacred ornaments used by the supreme pontiff for celebrating Mass by Innocent III in his book *On the Mysteries of the Mass*. Nowhere, however, is it found that this was a special privilege of the Roman pontiff, as Vicecomes maintains in book IV, chapter 30 of *On the Equipment of the Mass*. Cardinal Bona, of pious memory, concludes in book I, chapter 24, no. 10 of *Liturgical Matters* that the custom is not very ancient, since the pectoral cross is nowhere mentioned in the ancient sacramentaries. It is nevertheless an old custom to carry crosses suspended around the neck containing relics of the saints, as can also be inferred from this passage of Gregory. Gregory the Great certainly carried phylacteries filled with sacred relics suspended around his neck, as John the Deacon relates in book IV, chapter 80. Gregory himself interprets those phylacteries as a cross in book XII, letter 7, to Theodelinda. Such crosses were carried not only by bishops but also by laymen. For the same pontiff, in book II, letter 3, sent the patrician Dynamus a small cross containing something from the chains of Saint Peter and from Saint Lawrence’s gridiron, saying that it should release his neck from sins. Compare book V, letter 6, to King Childebert. It is remarkable how heavy the crosses were that the Greek emperors wore suspended around their necks. They called them *encolpia* because they hung upon the breast. Our monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés received by the testament of the most serene Princess Palatine, in 1683, an outstanding cross of this kind, reinforced by a double transverse beam and enriched with substantial particles of the life-giving cross. Two verses engraved on its reverse indicate that it was made by Manuel Comnenus, emperor of Constantinople. Today in Gaul, bishops customarily wear a pectoral cross suspended around the neck at all times; most regular abbots, except Cistercians, and abbesses are pleased to imitate them.

[^c0072-27]: The printed editions read: “to allow her to collect it”; another reading has “to allow her to collect the blood.”

[^c0072-28]: Codex Claromontanus A reads “in a cloth.”

[^c0072-29]: The cathedral church of Vasates is still dedicated to Saint John the Baptist, and it is said that some of the blood of the blessed Forerunner is still preserved there.

[^c0072-30]: Several manuscripts read “by the Huns,” which means the same thing.

[^c0072-31]: Two manuscripts read “letting in the animals,” using the accusative instead of the ablative. Colbertinus and Claromontanus B read “and letting in the animals.”

[^c0072-32]: Some ancient writers call Genseric, king of the Vandals, Gaiseric; perhaps he is meant here. Valesius’s opinion, however, seems preferable: he writes, under the year 437 in volume I of *Frankish Affairs*, that this Gausericus was king of the Chuni, or Huns, whom the Romans, through the agency of Aetius, had then summoned against the Goths, who already occupied that part of Gaul where Cossio Vasatium was situated.

[^c0072-33]: Among the ancients, the celebration of Mass was considered a kind of feast, as Mabillon concludes from this passage and canon 17 of the Second Council of Tours in the preface to book II of the *Gallican Liturgy*.

[^c0072-34]: “The ceiling,” that is, a vault, or more probably a wooden coffered ceiling. See below, chapter 47.

For (Ed., “Also”) a certain woman [Note: [Col. 0719C] Albert of Stade calls her Thecla the virgin in his *Chronicle*, where she is said to have obtained the finger of Saint John.] setting out from the city of Maurienne, sought the relics of the Forerunner and bound herself by such an oath that she would not leave the place beforehand unless she should deserve to receive something from his limbs. But when the inhabitants of the place declared that this was impossible, she prostrated herself daily before the tomb, praying that, as we have said, some portion of the holy limbs might be granted to her. In this intention she spent an entire year. In the same way she also spent a second year, always petitioning with continual prayer. But as the third year was beginning, when she saw that her prayer was not reaching fulfillment, she cast herself before the tomb and solemnly declared that she would not rise from there until this request had been obtained [Col. 0719B] from the Saint.

On the seventh day, when she was already failing from hunger, a thumb of wondrous whiteness appeared above the altar, shining with light. When the woman recognized God’s gift, she rose from the pavement, made a golden reliquary, placed in it what she had deserved to receive through the Lord’s generosity, and so returned joyfully to her own country. In her was fulfilled what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you, if he persists in knocking, even if he does not rise because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence he will rise and give him as many things as he needs” (Luke 11:8).

[Note: [Col. 0719D] Others read *pulsare*, “to knock”; and below four manuscripts read *surgit et tribuit*, “he rises and gives,” while Clar. b has *surget et tribuit*, “he will rise and give.”]

After this, three bishops came from their cities to worship at this place and wished to draw off a portion of this pledge. When it had been placed in their midst, they were completely unable to take anything away. Then, keeping watch through one night, they prayed that they might deserve to receive something from the thumb. When they placed a linen cloth beneath it and tried to remove a portion, a single drop of blood fell from it upon the linen cloth.

When they saw this, they kept watch for two further nights. Then, prostrate before the holy altar, while they begged that they might deserve to receive something greater still from the thumb, two more drops flowed from it. The bishops rejoiced and, reverently collecting what the Lord had given, divided the linen, with its drops, according to their number [Note: [Col. 0719D] Several manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read “according to the number of his servants.”] and carried it, with great wonder, to their cities.

Because that place of Maurienne formerly belonged to the city of Turin [Note: [Col. 0719D] Colb. a has *quamdam*, “a certain,” instead of *quondam*, “formerly.” That city first belonged to the diocese of Turin; then, after being occupied by the Franks under King Guntram, it obtained its own bishop, who was assigned to the metropolitan of Darentasia. Hence, in certain ancient lists among the cities of the provinces of the Graian and Pennine Alps, Maurienne is listed last. Nevertheless, Ursicinus, bishop of Turin, complained about this matter, as is clear from Letter 114 of Book VII, in the second indiction, of Gregory the Great, addressed to Syagrius, bishop of Autun, and from the following letter to Kings Theodoric and Theudebert. He obtained nothing, however, and thereafter the bishopric of Maurienne continued—and still exists today—but under the metropolitan of Vienne. Because of the fame of the miracles of Saint John’s relics, the city itself, as well as the valley, is commonly called Saint-Jean-de-Maurienne (*Saint-Jean de Maurienne*). We shall provide in an appendix an ancient document concerning the beginnings of the church of Maurienne.] at the time when Rufus was bishop, his archdeacon said to him: “It is not fitting that this pledge should be kept in an inferior place. Rather, rise, take it, and carry it to the church of Turin, which is regarded as more populous.”

He replied that he did not dare to do this. The archdeacon said: “I will carry it, if you permit me.” And the bishop replied: “Do what you wish.” Then the archdeacon approached the place and, while celebrating the vigils, put his hand to the reliquary. Immediately he became insane, was seized by fever, and died on the third day. Great fear then came upon everyone, and no one thereafter dared to move the blessed relics.

## CHAPTER XV. On the relics of blessed John placed within the monastery of Saint Martin

[Col. 0720B] At Tours [Note: [Col. 0720D] This chapter and the following one are absent from cod. Clar. a. In another Clar. manuscript, this chapter is absent together with the following six—that is, through chapter 21 inclusive. Some think that the oratory in the atrium of Saint Martin mentioned here is the one that still exists under the title of Saint John the Baptist, in which the canons of Saint Martin customarily assemble their chapter. Another ancient chapel of Saint John the Baptist stands at the very entrance of the church of Saint Martin; this may perhaps be the one designated here.] while we were placing the relics of the Forerunner in the oratory of the atrium of blessed Martin, a certain blind man, led by an attendant, received his sight. An energumen, invoking the power of blessed John and of Bishop Martin, was cleansed when the demon was expelled.

In this oratory, one of the young women whose duty it was to prepare the wicks of the lamps entered carrying a candle, in order to perform this task. Having arranged and lit the lamp, she drew the rope toward herself, raised it aloft, fastened it with intertwined knots to a nail in the wall, and departed.

When she returned, the candle that she was carrying in her hand went out. Returning quickly to the lamp, she was unable to light the candle by touching it, nor could she loosen the rope’s knot. While she remained uncertain about the cause, suddenly a flame descended from the lamp, lit the candle in her hand, and so, with the light leading her way, she went wherever she wished.

They say that oil boils up from the lamp in this oratory. For the relics of the holy cross are also kept there.

[Note: [Col. 0720D] The same thing occurred, as stated above in chapter 5, before the holy cross preserved in the monastery at Poitiers; Gregory alludes here to that account.]

## CHAPTER XVI. On the extinguishing of the burning of a certain woman’s hand

In the territory of this city, near the village of Alangavia [Note: [Col. 0720D] Cod. Mart. and Clict., together with Bell. and Colb. a, have *Langaviensis* in the index. Laud. likewise has *Lanuviensis* in the index. At the end of Book X of the *History* the village is called Alingavia; other authors call it Lingiacum or Langesium, commonly Langeais, a place still known today and quite famous in those times.], a certain local woman sprinkled flour on the Lord’s Day and shaped a loaf. After separating the embers, she covered it with hot ash to bake. As soon as she had done this, her right hand began to burn, set alight by divine fire [Col. 0721A].

Crying out and lamenting, she sought the basilica of this village, in which the relics of blessed John are kept. After pouring out a prayer, she vowed that on this day consecrated to the divine name she would perform no work, but would devote herself entirely to prayer. On the following night she made a candle as tall as herself. Then, keeping vigil through the night in prayer and holding the candle throughout the night with her own hand, she emerged unharmed, the burning having been extinguished.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the River Jordan

741 Since we have mentioned John the Baptist, it is fitting that we recall something about the Jordan. From Mount Panium two springs arise, one called Jor and the other Dan. Descending on either side of the city of Phaniada [Note: [Col. 0721D] Paneas, or Caesarea Philippi, once an episcopal city under the metropolitan of Tyre, on the borders of Coele-Syria, now destroyed. Concerning it, see Eusebius, Book VII of the *History*, chapter 17, and Rufinus, chapter 13, based on him. “At Caesarea Philippi, which the Phoenicians call Paneas, springs are seen at the foot of Mount Panium, from which the Jordan flows,” and so forth. Jerome writes in his *Questions on Genesis* that the city’s name itself was Dan, and he observes there that the two springs are called Jor and Dan; joined in reality and in name, they both produce and constitute the Jordan.]—the city formerly called Caesarea Philippi—and being joined beneath the city both in their waters [Al., “flowing waters”] and in their single name, they form the Jordan, which flows as far as the city of Jericho and beyond.

There is a place in it where the Lord was baptized. At one particular bend [Note: [Col. 0721D] Several manuscripts read *refluxu*, “backflow.” Pilgrims who visit Palestine still observe that the Jordan is curved at the place where, according to ancient tradition, our Lord is remembered to have been baptized.] the water itself turns back; lepers are now cleansed there. When they arrive, they wash themselves repeatedly in the river until they are purified from their disease. Nevertheless, while they remain there, they receive food from the public provision; once healed, they depart for their own homes.

The Jordan itself, five miles from that place, mingles with the Dead Sea and loses its name. The sea is called Dead because it was formed from the conflagration of Sodom and the other cities, and its water is mixed with asphalt [Col. 0721C]. Hence some call it the Asphalt Sea [Note: [Col. 0721D] It is commonly called the Asphalt Lake, from the bitumen that grows there. As we learn from reports, what Gregory observes here about the Dead Sea is still experienced by those who enter it in order to bathe.]. Anyone who does not know how to swim is carried upon the water there, and sulfur adheres around him.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the waters of the city of Levida

There are also at the city of Levida [Note: [Col. 0722D] Cod. Colb. tut. has *Leviadem*; but the following chapter has *Levidae*, as do the other manuscripts in the index. Clict. has *Lenidam*. The anonymous Ravennate, published by our Placidus Porcheron, calls it Leviada, from Pliny’s Livias. *Λιβίας* (*Libias*) is famous in Josephus, Eusebius, and others; it was so called by Herod in honor of Livia Augusta, and according to Saint Jerome was previously called Betharam. It once had its own bishop under the metropolitan of Caesarea, as did Jericho, a city well known from the Sacred Scriptures.] hot springs in which Jesus son of Nave was accustomed to bathe; lepers are likewise cleansed there. It is twelve miles from Jericho.

Near Jericho there are trees that produce wool. They bear fruits shaped like gourds, with hard shells all around; inside they are filled with wool. They also say that garments used to be made from these for Jesus son of Nave. Even today such trees produce wool, of which we have seen specimens brought by certain people, and we have admired either their whiteness or their fineness.

## CHAPTER XIX. On a leper cleansed at the place where the Lord was baptized, and on the relics of Blessed Mary

For I once saw a man named John who had left Gaul as a leper and said that he had remained for an entire year at the very place where, as we have said, the Lord was baptized. He washed himself continually in the river, and, restored to his former health, was healed, his skin renewed for the better.

This man, having received relics of blessed Mary from Jerusalem, was returning to his homeland; but first he had decided to travel to Rome. When he entered the deep wildernesses of Italy, however, he fell among robbers. Immediately he was stripped of his clothing, and the very chest in which he carried the blessed relics was also seized. The robbers thought that gold coins had been amassed there. Breaking open the lock, they searched everything carefully.

When they found no money in it, they took out the relics and threw them into the fire. After beating the man, they departed. But he, rising half alive, in order to gather at least the ashes of the burned relics, found the relics lying unharmed upon the glowing coals. He was astonished that the very linen in which they had been wrapped was so intact that it seemed not to have been thrown upon the embers but to have been hidden in water.

He collected everything joyfully and, entering upon the road he had been traveling, reached Gaul safely. We have also seen many who, having been immersed either in the Jordan or in the waters of the city of Levida, were cleansed of this disease.

## CHAPTER XX. On the church of Blessed Mary and the punishment of perjurers at Tours

In the city of Tours [Note: [Col. 0722D] This chapter and the following two are absent from cod. Clarom. a. The church mentioned here seems to be the one that Bishop Ommatius built, as is said in Book X, chapter 31 of the *History*. Not far from the cathedral of Saint Gatianus there once stood an oratory dedicated to Blessed Mary; it has now been destroyed. Another church in the same part of the city, under the title of Saint John, still exists. Whether one of these, or some other church now destroyed, is meant here is uncertain.] there is a church consecrated under the name of the holy Virgin Mary and Saint John the Baptist, in which divine vengeance appeared against perjurers.

A certain man entered this church in order to commit perjury. When he stood before the altar and raised his hand upward to utter a false oath, he immediately fell backward and struck his head against the pavement so violently that he could scarcely have been raised alive. When he recovered consciousness, he publicly disclosed the deceit of the perjury that he had concealed.

We ourselves also saw certain people from Tours perjure themselves in that same place. They were condemned by divine judgment in such a way that within the course of that very year they were finished with this world.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the image of the Lord at Phaniada

As we have said, at the very beginning of the Jordan’s outflow lies the city of Phaniada [Note: [Col. 0723C] Paneas, discussed above in chapter 17]. In it there is a statue made of the purest electrum, in which the likeness of our Redeemer is said to have been represented. For, as I have heard from many who had looked upon it, a wondrous brightness is contained in his face.

Lest anyone find it absurd, I shall not hesitate to relate what Eusebius of Caesarea reports about it. He says:

> “It is established that the woman whom the Gospels relate to have been healed by the Savior from an issue of blood was a citizen of this city, and her house is still shown there. Before the entrance of her house, on elevated ground, a certain base is displayed, upon which a bronze image of the woman herself appears represented as if kneeling and stretching out her palms in supplication. Beside it stands another statue, likewise cast in bronze, in the form of a man elegantly clothed in a robe and extending his right hand toward the woman.
>
> “At the foot of this statue, on the base, a plant of novel appearance grows. When it has sprung up, it usually grows until it reaches the hem of that bronze robe. When the plant, growing upward, touches its highest point, it receives power to drive away every disease and infirmity, so that whatever bodily illness there may be is removed by drinking a small quantity of the healing grass moistened with water [Col. 0723C]. But it has no power at all if it is plucked before, by growing, it has touched the top of the bronze hem.
>
> “They said that this statue had been fashioned in the likeness of Jesus’ face. It remained even down to our own time, as we ourselves saw with our own eyes. Nor is it surprising that those among the nations who believed, in return for the benefits they had received from the Savior, should seem to offer something of this kind as a gift, since even now we see images of the apostles Peter and Paul, and of the Savior himself, being represented and painted on panels.”

[Note: [Col. 0723C] This is from the translation of Rufinus, who has it in Book VII, chapter 14 of his *History*, whereas Eusebius relates this story in the same book, chapter 18. Rufinus adds these words: “The preservation of the memorials of ancient people for the memory of later generations is an indication of honor toward the former and of love toward the latter.” Furthermore, Julian the Apostate, as Sozomen reports in Book V, chapter 21, overturned this statue of Christ the Savior and substituted one of himself for it. But immediately, he says, fire fell from heaven, split open the statue’s chest and the parts near the chest, struck down its head together with its neck, and drove it face-first into the ground; from that time onward it remained blackened by the soot of the lightning. Nevertheless, the pagans dragged Christ’s statue through the city and broke it to pieces; later the Christians gathered it up and placed it in a church. The same Sozomen, who flourished under Theodosius the Younger—that is, more than a hundred years before our Gregory wrote—testifies that both statues, namely that of Christ the Lord in the church and that of the Apostate, disfigured by soot, continued to exist in his own time.]

This is what Eusebius reported.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Jew who stole and pierced an image of Christ

Even in the present time Christ is loved with such complete faith that believing people, who retain his law on the tablets of their hearts, also affix his image, painted on visible panels in memory of his power, throughout their churches and homes. But in this matter too the enemy, ever the adversary of the human race, is present.

A certain Jew had often seen an image of this kind painted on a panel and affixed to the wall in a church. He said: “Behold that deceiver who humbled us and our race.” So, coming at night, he struck the image with a weapon, knocked it from the wall, covered it with a cloth, carried it to his house, and prepared to burn it in the flames.

But a marvelous event appeared, and it cannot be doubted that it resulted from the power of God. From the wound where the image had been pierced, blood flowed [Note: [Col. 0723D] At Damascus there was a famous statue of the martyr Theodore that had shed blood when struck with a weapon by a certain Saracen, as Saint John of Damascus testifies in his third discourse on the holy images.].

The wicked striker, filled with fury, did not notice this. When he had entered his house through the darkness of night and brought in a light, he saw that he was completely stained with blood. Fearing that his crime would be exposed, he cast the panel aside and hid it in a dark place, and he did not dare touch again what he had wickedly presumed to steal.

At dawn, Christians came to the house of God but did not find the image [Note: [Col. 0724C] Others read *iconiam* or *iconam*; Bal. has *iconem*. Our reading should be retained, since it is found in the older editions and manuscripts. Those authors wrote *iconica* to designate an image, as above in the chapter title and in *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 12. From this arose the custom of calling the sacred image of Christ the *Veronica*, as though “true image” (*vera iconica*), as our Mabillon proves from numerous authors in his *Italian Journey*, pages 88–89. Later, however, some thought this word was a woman’s name and invented Veronica as a pious woman who, meeting Christ as he ascended toward Calvary, received on a small cloth the impression of his sacred face, which she had wiped. Hence the name Saint Veronica entered certain martyrologies. Baronius and other learned men opposed its admission into the Roman martyrology. It is therefore surprising that the Carmelites accused the Bollandists of wrongdoing for speaking hesitantly about Veronica as a woman. Indeed, Nicholas and several other Roman pontiffs testified that the image of Christ the Lord itself was commonly called the Veronica. See Papebroch’s response to the presentation of errors by Sebastian of Saint Paul.] and, astonished and investigating what had happened, discovered traces of blood. Following these traces, they came to the Jew’s house.

Finally, when they questioned him about the panel, they learned nothing certain. Searching for it carefully, they found the image in a corner of the Jew’s little room. After it had been returned to the church, they buried the thief beneath stones.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the crucified image at Narbonne

In the older church at the city of Narbonne, which rejoices in the relics of blessed Genesius the martyr, there is a painting that shows our Lord crucified, as though girded with a linen cloth.

While the people were continually looking at this painting, a terrifying figure appeared in a vision to a certain Basil, a priest, saying: “All of you are covered with various garments, while you continually look upon me naked. Go as quickly as possible and cover me with clothing.”

The priest did not understand the vision and, when day came, gave no further thought to it. The figure appeared to him again, but he also treated that appearance lightly. After the third day following the second vision, when he had been tortured with severe blows, it said: “Did I not tell you to cover me with clothing, so that I would not be seen naked, and yet you have done nothing about it? Go,” it said, “and cover with linen that painting in which I appear crucified, lest swift destruction overtake you.”

Moved and greatly afraid, Basil reported these things to the bishop. The bishop immediately ordered a veil to be spread over it, and so the painting is now viewed covered [Note: [Col. 0725D] Perhaps from this arose the custom of depicting Christ the Lord clothed while hanging on the cross. Certainly, I remember having seen more than once the crucified Lord dressed in a full-length garment at Rheims, in the collegiate church of Saint Balsamia, or, as they call her, Saint Nurse—for she is said to have nourished Saint Remigius. Mabillon likewise testifies that he saw similar images in the preface to the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, fourth century, part 1, no. 47, and in his *Italian Journey*, p. 133.]. For even if it is uncovered briefly for viewing, it is immediately covered again with the lowered veil, so that it may not be seen exposed.

## CHAPTER XXIV. A notable miracle concerning the springs of Spain

There is also that famous miracle concerning the springs of Spain, which the province of Lusitania produces. At Osen [Note: [Col. 0725D] This place seems to be none other than Osser, or Oset, near Seville, which Gregory himself mentions in Book VI of the *History*, chapter 43. Seville belonged to the province of Baetica and is now the capital of the kingdom of Andalusia. Similar springs existed in Gaul; see below, *Book on the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 69.] there is a pool, an ancient work, carved in the shape of a cross and constructed from various-colored marble with marvelous craftsmanship. A large and highly splendid building was also constructed above it by Christians.

When the sacred day arrived after the completion of the year’s cycle—the day on which the Lord, after confounding the betrayer, gave the mystical supper to the disciples—the citizens gathered at that place with their bishop, already sensing the fragrance of the sacred aromatic substance. After the priest had offered a prayer, they ordered the temple doors to be sealed with signs and awaited the arrival of the Lord’s power [Col. 0725C].

On the third day, which is the Sabbath, when the people gathered for baptism, the bishop arrived with his citizens. After inspecting the seals, he opened the closed doors. Marvelous to say, they found the pool that they had left empty full, and so heaped up to a greater height that it resembled wheat piled above the rim of a grain measure. You could see the waters surging here and there, yet not flowing away in any direction.

Then, after the water had been sanctified by exorcism and sprinkled with chrism, all the people drew it out in devotion and carried home a full vessel for their salvation, intending to protect their fields and vineyards by a healing sprinkling [Note: [Col. 0726D] This custom still flourishes: as is clear from this passage, we received from our fathers the practice of carrying home water sanctified by the prayers of priests at the Easter vigil, both as protection against demonic attacks and to drive away the snares of the aerial powers. See the *Life of Saint Caesarius, Bishop*, Book II, no. 13.].

Although thereafter an uncounted multitude of jars was drawn from it, its fullness was never diminished. Yet when the first infant had been immersed, the water was immediately restored; and once all had been baptized, the waters returned into themselves. In the manner in which they are first seen, I do not know; so, at the end, they are closed again in a way unknown.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the heretics who did not believe them

I shall not be silent about a certain heretic who did not fear God, showed no reverence for this holy place, and did not believe in his heart the miracle that the Lord had deigned to perform there to strengthen the faith of his people.

He came with a crowd of horses and ordered that, once their harnesses had been removed, they be placed in the basilica and that stalls be prepared there for the riders [that is, for the horses], mocking the poor people who recounted what happened at this place.

When midnight had passed, he was seized by fever and was almost lifeless. Repenting later than he should have, he shouted that the horses should be driven out of the church. Although he was subject to a king, he nevertheless possessed great authority in that region. Once the horses had been expelled from the holy basilica, he turned upon himself and began tearing his own little body with his teeth. His attendants could not restrain him at all because of the excess of his frenzy. Finally overcome, he breathed out his spirit in the hands of his attendants.

Finally, Theodegisilus [Note: [Col. 0726D] Cod. Bell. has *Teodegisilis*. Isidore calls him *Teudisculus*, in the year 586. But after reigning for one year and several months, he was killed at Seville. Perhaps the person meant here is Theudix, or Theudis, or Theodas, who ruled nearly forty-seven years before Theudisclus.] the king of this region, having seen this miracle that occurred at these springs consecrated to God, reflected within himself, saying: “It is the ingenuity of the Romans”—for they call people of our religion Romans—“that this happens in this way; it is not the power of God.”

When the following year arrived, he sealed the door with his own seals and with the bishop’s seal, and placed guards around the temple, in case he might catch someone responsible for some deception through whose ingenuity water was entering the springs [Col. 0726C]. He did the same thing the next year.

In the third year, he summoned a multitude of men and ordered trenches to be dug around the basilica, lest water perhaps be conveyed into the spring through hidden channels [Ed., “places”]. The trenches were twenty-five feet deep and fifteen feet wide. Yet nothing hidden could be found.

Nevertheless, as he came to the end of his life—and, I believe, because of the rashness of this investigation—he was not permitted to see the following year’s day on which this mystery was celebrated, since he had presumed to investigate the secret of divine power.

The relics of Saint Stephen the deacon are also kept there.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the man who could not draw water because of a theft he had committed

Since that spring, as we have said above, is filled by divine command for the purpose of baptism, and since, once it is full, the people eagerly hurry to draw water from it, a certain man took a small vessel and handed it to the priest who was distributing this water, so that he might fill it.

While the priest was filling it, the man, amid the pressing crowds, extended his hand to another man’s belt and stole a knife. He put it back into its sheath, then extended his hand to receive the jug that he had given to the priest. After receiving it and moving aside, he could not find a single drop of water in it.

Then, greatly confused, and realizing that this had happened to him because of the theft, he returned to the man the knife he had stolen. When he held out the bottle again, he received it full of water.

That people is heretical. Although it sees these great wonders, it is not moved to believe, but always craftily continues to attack the mysteries of divine commands with the most wicked babbling of interpretations. Yet the Lord’s power destroys and confounds the opposing side.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the martyrdom of James the apostle, the brother of the Lord

James [Note: [Col. 0727B] This chapter is absent from both Clarom. manuscripts.] the apostle (year 61 or 62, May 1), who was also called the brother of the Lord, is said to have been ordained bishop by our Lord Jesus Christ himself [Note: [Col. 0727C] Eusebius, Book VII; Chrysostom, on the First Epistle to the Corinthians; Jerome, in his Epistle to the Galatians; Proclus, in Oration 22; and other ancient writers state that James was appointed by Christ himself. Others—including Clement of Alexandria, indeed Eusebius himself in several passages, and Jerome in *On Illustrious Men*—report that he assumed special responsibility for the Jerusalem Church from the apostles. Perhaps he was designated by Christ but proclaimed and enthroned by the apostles. For this reason he may have worn a golden plate on his head, as Epiphanius writes in *Against Heresies*, 29, following the custom of the ancient pontiffs. Here Gregory does not distinguish James the bishop from the apostle; this seems to have been the more common opinion among ancient and modern writers, although others think differently. On this matter see the Bollandists under May 1, Tillemont in his notes to volume I of the *Ecclesiastical History*, and others.].

After the Lord’s glorious Ascension, while James was attempting to open the way of righteousness to the Jews who had gone astray, he was thrown down from the pinnacle of the Temple and struck. When a fuller’s club crushed his skull, he gave up his spirit [Note: [Col. 0727C] Hegesippus describes his martyrdom in Eusebius, Book II of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 23. See also Josephus, Book XX of the *Antiquities*, chapter 8. Read the *Genuine Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 1 and following.].

He was buried on the Mount of Olives, in the memorial that he had previously built for himself and in which he had buried Zechariah and Simeon [Note: [Col. 0727D] Many maintain that Zechariah, the father of Saint John the Baptist, was killed by Herod’s order within the precincts of the Temple itself. Adamnanus testifies that the tomb of the aged Simeon, who had received Christ in his arms, stood in a rock on the Mount of Olives.].

This is what we have to say about the apostle James.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On Saint Peter the apostle
750 **Peter**, the apostle [Note: [Col. 0727D] This chapter and the following one are absent from the Colbert manuscript], instituted the practice of having the top of his head tonsured, in order to teach humility [Note: [Col. 0727D] Medieval authors commonly attribute the origin of the clerical tonsure to Saint Peter, although they give various reasons for its institution. See Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, book V, chapter 22. Below, the Vindobonensis manuscript does not have *episcopus*. —Thomassinus, *Ecclesiastical Discipline*, part I, book II, chapter 37, strongly maintains that this passage should not at all be understood of the clerical crown, but of all Christians, who, out of modesty, ought to wear their hair short. On this occasion he cites an excellent passage of Amalarius [Col. 0728B–C], testifying that the opinion which traces the clerical tonsure to Saint Peter is not so certain that one must adhere to it. See the notes on the *Life of Saint Nicetius*, in the *Book of the Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 17], who, ordained bishop by the other apostles, established his see at Rome. Through the prayer of Peter and [Note: [Col. 0728C] The manuscripts read *vel*, “or,” which amounts to the same thing. In the same sense below, *vel detecta est vel obruta*, that is, “both exposed and overthrown,” and so frequently elsewhere] Paul, the cunning of Simon Magus was either exposed or overthrown [Note: [Col. 0728C] The victory which the apostles won over Simon Magus is confirmed by the testimonies of so many holy Fathers that it cannot be rejected without rashness, although some authors have obscured the historical truth in certain details through apocryphal narratives].

Even today, near the city of Rome, there are two hollows in the stone upon which the blessed apostles, kneeling, poured forth a prayer to the Lord against that same Simon Magus. When rainwater has collected in them, sick people seek it; and, after drinking it, they immediately receive health.

As we have already said, Saint Peter the apostle, after the battles against Nero and Simon, came to the cross. When the contest of his blessed triumph had been completed, he requested to be crucified with his feet turned upward toward heaven, loudly declaring himself unworthy to be exalted like the Lord [Note: [Col. 0728C] Ambrose, in his commentary on Psalm 118, Augustine, Theodoret, and others give the same reason. Others add different explanations, which there is no time to pursue at greater length]. Thus, directing his living spirit toward the stars, he was buried in the temple formerly called the Vatican [Note: [Col. 0728C] The apostles’ memorials, as Gaius calls them in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 25, were already famous at Rome at the beginning of the third century, at the Vatican and on the Ostian Way [Col. 0728D]—that is, in the very places where their sacred relics are still venerated. For half of each is preserved in the Vatican church, while the other half is kept in the basilica of Saint Paul, which is an abbey of the Benedictine order; their sacred heads are in the Lateran basilica], a building containing four rows of columns, ninety-six in all, of remarkable beauty. It also has four columns at the altar, making one hundred altogether, apart from those supporting the ciborium [Note: [Col. 0728D] A *ciborium* is a turreted structure, like a canopy, resting on several columns and intended to cover an altar or the tomb of a saint. See Mabillon, *Gallican Liturgy*, book I, chapter 8, no. 8].

751 For this tomb, situated beneath the altar, is considered very unusual [Note: [Col. 0728D] The Vindobonensis reads *valde ratum* (“very firm”). It is an ancient custom received in the Church to place the relics of saints in underground crypts beneath an altar; the tombs of more celebrated saints can still be seen beneath the altars of ancient basilicas. From this arose the practice of erecting altars over the tombs of pious men whom bishops wished to be regarded as saints; this was formerly the rite of canonizing saints. Gregory himself mentions relics deposited by him in a baptistery, *History*, book X, final chapter; and in book VII, chapter 31, he relates that the relics of Saint Sergius had been hidden by a certain Syrian high in the wall opposite the altar. They were never placed upon the altar, except perhaps for a very brief period, as is clear from Gregory himself, book IX, chapter 6, although others disapproved of this. See Mabillon, *Gallican Liturgy*, book I, chapter 9. Mabillon explains when the bodies of saints began to be raised and translated in the West in his preface to the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, century II, no. 42].

But anyone wishing to pray approaches the tomb after the grilles surrounding the place have been opened; then, when a small window has been opened, he puts his head inside and asks for whatever necessity demands. The result is not delayed, provided that the prayer expresses a just petition.

If someone wishes to carry away blessed tokens, he has a small cloth [Note: [Col. 0729D] Hormisdas calls such small cloths *sanctuaria*—“holy tokens”—of the blessed Peter and Paul in his letter to the emperor Justinian. The legates of that same pontiff also begged him to lower such *sanctuaria* as far as the second cataract, out of devotion to the emperor to whom they were being sent. Gregory the Great calls them *brandea*. One of these, said to have been sent to Queen Brunhild, is preserved in the treasury of our monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés and is commonly called Saint Peter’s corporal] weighed inside on a small scale [that is, a balance]. Then, keeping vigil and fasting, he prays with the greatest devotion that apostolic power may support his devotion.

Wonderful to relate! If the man’s faith prevails, the small cloth, lifted from the tomb, becomes so imbued with divine power that it weighs much more than it had previously weighed. Then the one who lifted it knows that, through the saint’s grace, he has received what he requested.

Many people also have golden keys made for opening the grilles of the blessed tomb. Those who carry them receive them first as a blessing [Col. 0729B], so that they may bring relief to the weakness of the afflicted. For steadfast faith accomplishes everything.

There are also four columns of marvelous elegance and snowy whiteness, said to support the ciborium of the tomb.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the Apostle Paul

Paul the apostle [Note: [Col. 0729D] This chapter is absent from the Claromontanus b. In Claromontanus a, the words following “after the cycle of the year had passed” are absent. Although that reading may seem closer to the truth, it is uncertain whether it is in fact more genuine. Nevertheless, from Fortunatus and from the Gallican Liturgy in Mabillon, book II, no. 63, it is clear that the opinion that Peter and Paul suffered on the same day and in the same year was more common in Gaul] (year 66, 29 June), after the cycle of the year had passed, was struck down by the sword and died near the city of Rome on the very day on which the apostle Peter had suffered. From his sacred body milk [Note: [Col. 0730D] Gregory derived this from an apocryphal work under the name of Linus, or from some similar history; the ancient writers are silent about it. See Mabillon, *Italian Journey*, p. 142] and water flowed forth.

Nor is it surprising that milk flowed from his body, since he both conceived and gave birth to unbelieving nations, and, having nourished them with spiritual milk, led them to the solid food of the holy Scriptures by opening what had been obscure.

We have heard many things about his miracles; but of the many we have chosen to relate only one.

It happened in a certain place that a man, urged on by the devil, prepared a noose for himself in order to take his own life. Having found a secluded room in which to carry this out, he passed a rope over a beam and began tying the noose, while continually invoking the name of the apostle Paul and saying, “Help me, Saint Paul.”

Suddenly a grim and dreadful shadow appeared to him, whose face resembled nothing less than the devil. It urged him on, saying, “Come, act; do not delay. Quickly finish what you have begun.” But while he was preparing this deed—that is, the taking of his own life [Col. 0730A]—he kept saying, “Most blessed Paul, be my helper.”

Finally, when the noose had been prepared and the shadow pressed him more insistently to put his neck into it, another shadow resembling it suddenly appeared. It said to the one who had been with the man, “Flee, wretched one! Here comes the apostle Paul. Invoked by this man, behold, he is present.”

Then the shadows vanished. The man came to his senses, traced the cross of the Lord’s power upon his trembling breast, and, his cheeks drenched with tears, did penance, wondering why he had attempted such a thing [Note: [Col. 0730D] The Vindobonensis reads: “Doing penance, drenched with tears, he said…”].

Thus it is clear that this same man was saved by the power of the blessed apostle from the precipice of that cruel death.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the Apostle and Evangelist John

753 John, the apostle and evangelist of God [Note: [Col. 0730D] This chapter is absent from Claromontanus a] (year 100 or 104, 27 December), after completing the course both of his legitimate struggle and of his most salutary preaching, descended alive into the tomb and ordered himself to be covered with earth.

His tomb still today emits manna [Note: [Col. 0730D] According to the second *Life of Saint Willibald*, no. 5, in part II of the Benedictine series, this manna still flowed from the apostle’s tomb in the eighth century. Many, even among the ancients, doubted the manner of his death. On this subject see Tillemont’s learned discussion, as is his custom, in volume I of his *Ecclesiastical History*, under “Saint John,” article 7. See also Augustine, *Tractate on John*, 124, and Photius, *Bibliotheca*, codex 229], in the form of flour; blessed relics from it, carried throughout the world, grant health to the sick.

This is the John whom the Lord loved more than the other apostles. He was distinguished by such great love that, reclining upon the breast of the sacred Body itself, he drank in the secrets of the heavenly mysteries. At the hour of his passion, when our Lord was placed upon the cross for the salvation of the world, he also entrusted his glorious Mother to him as to a disciple in a special manner.

Of him, indeed, the Lord said after the resurrection: “I wish him to remain thus until I come” (John 21:22).

At Ephesus there is a place where this apostle wrote the Gospel that is read in the Church under his name. On the summit of the nearby mountain there are four roofless walls. He remained there, devoting himself to prayer and constantly beseeching the Lord for the people’s sins; and he obtained that no rain should fall in that place until he had completed the Gospel. Even to this day the Lord grants this: no rain falls there, nor does a violent storm arrive.

[Col. 0731A] In that city Mary Magdalene rests [Note: [Col. 0731D] The author of the *Life of Saint Willibald*, cited in the preceding note, says the same, as does Saint Modestus, bishop of Jerusalem, at the beginning of the seventh century, in Photius, *Bibliotheca*, codex 275. Her relics are said to have been transferred to Constantinople toward the end of the ninth century under Leo the Wise. There are now other traditions in various places in Gaul concerning the tomb and relics of Blessed Magdalene, which there is no occasion to examine here. The Seven Sleepers are also discussed in the *Life of Saint Willibald*. See below, chapter 95], with no covering over her. The Seven Sleepers are also found there; concerning them we shall narrate something later, with the Lord’s permission. In that place there was also the idol of Diana, destroyed by the apostle Paul.

But let us return to what we had begun.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the Apostle Andrew

754 The apostle Andrew [Note: [Col. 0731D] This chapter is absent from Claromontanus b] (year 66 or 70, or 93, 30 November) produces a great miracle on the day of his solemnity: manna in the form of flour, or oil with a nectar-like fragrance, flows from his tomb. By this the fertility of the coming year is revealed. If only a little flows forth, the earth produces little fruit; but if it is abundant, this signifies that the fields will have a great yield of produce [Col. 0731B].

For they say that in some years so much oil flows from the tomb that the stream reaches the middle of the basilica. These things take place in the province of Achaia, in the city of Patras, where the blessed apostle and martyr, crucified for the name of the Redeemer, ended his present life by a glorious death [Note: [Col. 0731D] This is the tradition of the ancients, approved by Saints Paulinus, Gaudentius, Peter Chrysologus, and other writers. The *Acts of the Passion of this apostle*, attributed to the presbyters and deacons of the Church of Achaia, are famous; there is not, however, complete agreement concerning their authenticity. See Tillemont’s notes on Saint Andrew, volume I of his *Ecclesiastical History*. —In the Gallican Gothic Missal edited by our Mabillon from Thomasius, *Gallican Liturgy*, book III, no. 17, there is a Mass for Saint Andrew whose *contestatio*, or, as we say, preface, is for the most part composed from the words of the published *Acts* of this holy apostle].

When the oil has flowed forth, however, it gives off such a fragrance to the nostrils that one would think a heap of many spices had been scattered there. This is regarded among the people as both a miracle and a benefit. For whether applied in anointings or administered in potions, it generally brings relief to the sick.

After his glorious assumption, many miracles are said to have been displayed either at this tomb or in various places where his relics have been deposited. I have thought it worthwhile to recall a few of them, because the glory of martyrs and the power of the saints build up the Church.

At the time when, after King Chlodomer of the Franks had been killed [Note: [Col. 0732D] See above, *History*, book III, chapter 6], his army was regrouping and ravaging Burgundy, the relics of the aforesaid apostolic martyr Saturninus were being kept in a certain basilica. When the basilica had been set on fire and the mass of timbers was already collapsing, the poor and the elderly whom the barbarity had spared wept, saying:

“Woe to us, who today are deprived of the help of such great tokens; nor will any hope for this present life remain for us if these things perish.”

While they were weeping in this way, a man from Tours arrived by God’s command. Moved by their lamentations and learning of the power of the martyrs, protected by faith no less than by his shield, he entered through the midst of the flames, seized the holy relics from the altar, and carried them outside, unharmed by the fire [Col. 0732A]. But immediately he was so stricken that he could no longer take a step forward.

Then, considering himself unworthy to carry them, he chose a small, undefiled girl from the spoil, placed the small case around her neck, and thus reached his homeland safely. He then placed the relics upon the altar of the church of Novivicium [Note: [Col. 0732D] Claromontanus a reads *Noviacensis*; Colbertinus tutior reads *Novicensis*. The place is near Tours, commonly called Neuvi, where an ancient church dedicated to Blessed Andrew can still be seen], where no relics of saints had previously been kept, and every year celebrated their solemnity with the greatest devotion.

After his death, his son failed to carry this out. He suffered from quartan fever for an entire year and vowed that he would build a new basilica in their honor. When he had done so, he was cured, the fever having departed.

I also believe that it did not happen without divine providence that, on the very day when the blessed relics were transferred to another basilica, certain travelers who had lost their way while carrying the relics of Saint Vincent were brought to that very village [Col. 0732B]. At the presbyter’s request, they divided a portion of the relics with him, and he placed it upon the holy altar from which he had previously taken the others.

Mummolus, in the reign of King Theudebert, was traveling by ship toward Constantinople on his way to the Emperor Justinian. He put in at the city of Patras, where that same apostle is kept. While he remained there with his attendants, his bladder became diseased and he developed stones. Then, afflicted by various pains, he was consumed by fever. Having lost all pleasure in eating and drinking, he awaited only the arrival of death.

When he judged himself so exhausted and without hope of life, he asked that his will be written; after it had been secured with signatures and seals, he ordered an inquiry to be made as to whether anyone in the city skilled in medicine might be found who could assist a dying man.

When this was reported to the bishop who then presided there, he said:

“How long, my dearest ones, will you weary yourselves with futile labor and seek medicine among human beings, when there is here a heavenly physician who often drives away the illnesses of the sick without the aid of herbs, by the effect of his own power?”

“And who,” they asked, “is he?”

“Andrew,” he replied, “the apostle of Christ.”

When this was reported to the sick man, he asked to be carried to the blessed tomb [Note: [Col. 0732D] His sacred body was transferred to Constantinople in the year 357, under the emperor Constantius, as ancient authors report. See Philostorgius, book III, no. 2, and Theodorus Lector, book II].

As he lay prostrate upon the pavement and faithfully prayed for what his need required, sleep overcame nearly everyone who was present around midnight. Immediately the sick man felt the urge to urinate. Touching one of the boys, he asked in a weak voice that a vessel be brought. When it was brought, as he tried to urinate he expelled a large stone [Col. 0733A], so large that, when it fell, it made a sound in the very basin that had been prepared.

Then, with both the fever and all the pain removed, he was restored to health and returned safely by ship [Note: [Col. 0733C] In Claromontanus a, this chapter is followed by a chapter on the miracles of the apostle Andrew, which is chapter 79 below].

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the Apostle Thomas

Thomas the apostle [Note: [Col. 0733C] This chapter is absent from Colbertinus tutior and, together with the following two chapters, from Claromontanus a. In other manuscripts this chapter is divided into two; the title of the second part is: “On the power of the basilica to which he was later transferred.” We know of no authentic account of Saint Thomas’s passion. It nevertheless seems certain that he spread the faith of Christ among the Indians, as Gregory Nazianzen, oration 25; Jerome, letter 148; Ambrose, on Psalm 45; Paulinus; and other holy Fathers attest. Among them Gaudentius and others, together with the more ancient martyrologies, say that he ended his life there, and indeed by martyrdom, according to Nilus, Asterius, Gaudentius, and others] (after the year 66, 21 December), according to the account of his passion, is declared to have suffered in India.

After a long time, his blessed body was taken up and transferred to the city which the Syrians call Edessa [Note: [Col. 0733D] Several manuscripts and editions read “Edessa of Syria”; it is certain from Rufinus and others that Saint Thomas’s body was present there in the fourth century], where it was buried.

Thus, in the region of India where he first rested, there is a monastery and a temple of remarkable size, carefully decorated and arranged. In this temple God displays a great miracle.

A lamp placed there and lit before the site of his burial shines perpetually, day and night, by divine will. It receives fuel neither of oil nor of rushes from anyone; it is not extinguished by the wind, does not go out by accident, and is not diminished by burning. Through the apostle’s power it has an increase unknown to human beings but recognized as belonging to divine power [Note: [Col. 0733D] Several manuscripts and editions read “recognized only”].

This was explained to us by Theodorus, who visited the place.

In the aforesaid city, where we have said that his blessed limbs were buried, when the festival arrives a great crowd of people gathers. Those who come from different regions with votive offerings and merchandise [Note: [Col. 0733D] Balbius reads “and with merchants coming”; several manuscripts read “and those engaged in commerce coming.” *Negotium*, meaning merchandise or a saleable object, is sometimes used for profit or a commodity, as Bignonius notes in *Ancient Formulae*, chapter 45] are granted permission to sell and buy for thirty days without any toll being exacted.

During these days, which occur in the fifth month [Note: [Col. 0733D] According to the Syrian calendar, which began the year in November, this month is March, when the Syrians celebrated Saint Thomas’s feast, as is clear from their calendar published by Genebrard at Lyon in 1615 together with his commentary on the Psalms. The Latins, however, celebrate the feast of Saint Thomas—namely, the feast of his Translation—on 3 July, the fifth month], great and unusual benefits are provided to the people.

No disorder arises among the crowd, no fly settles upon a dead body, and water is not lacking for the thirsty. For on the other days water is drawn from wells at a depth of more than one hundred feet, whereas then, if one digs only a little, one finds water abundantly overflowing. There is no doubt that this is granted through the power of the blessed apostle.

When the festival days have passed, the public toll is restored [Note: [Col. 0733D] Others read “publicly,” or “in public”; that is, the toll is restored to the public authorities], the flies that had been absent return, and the water recedes into the depths. Then rain sent by God cleanses the entire courtyard of the temple of the filth and various uncleanness produced during the festivities, so thoroughly that one would think the place had never been trodden.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the Apostle Bartholomew

The account of his passion relates that the apostle Bartholomew suffered in India [Note: [Col. 0733D] This is the reading of the Martyrologium and of Clictonus. All other editions and manuscripts read “in Asia.” If the account of the passion cited here by Gregory is not different from the one published under the name of Abdias, our reading is preferable. In the printed editions, chapter 33 concerns Saint Stephen, and the following chapter Saint Bartholomew. It seems clear from Eusebius, book V, chapter 10; Rufinus, book III, chapter 1; Jerome, or Sophronius, *On Illustrious Men*; Socrates; and others, that Bartholomew proclaimed the faith among the Indians. It is not equally certain, however, what region those authors intended by the name India. See Tillemont, volume I of his *Ecclesiastical History*] (first century, 24 August).

After many years had passed since his passion, when persecution again arose against Christians and the pagans saw the entire people flocking to his tomb, continually bringing prayers and incense to it, they were moved by envy. They removed his body, placed it in a lead sarcophagus, and threw it into the sea, saying, “You will no longer seduce our people.”

But, with God’s providence working through the hidden operation of his power, the lead sarcophagus was lifted from that place by the waters and carried to an island called Liparis [Note: [Col. 0734C] Lipara is the principal island of the Aeolian Islands in the Tyrrhenian Sea, not far from Sicily. It once had its own bishop, but its bishopric was later joined by Boniface VIII to that of Pactum, or Patti, on the coast of Sicily. The tomb of Saint Bartholomew was violated by the Saracens in 808, and his sacred relics were transferred the following year to Benevento. From there they were brought to Rome by Otto III and deposited on the Tiber Island, where they are still preserved. Theodorus Lector, book II, writes that the relics of Saint Bartholomew were transferred around the year 508 to the city of Dara by order of the emperor Anastasius].

It was revealed to Christians that they should retrieve him. After retrieving and burying him, they built a large temple over him. In it, when invoked, he now manifests his usefulness to many peoples through numerous miracles and benefits.

## CHAPTER XXXIV [Note: [Col. 0734D] In this chapter Gregory mentions a church of Saint Stephen which he says existed near the city of Tours. He adds shortly afterward that, after many days, he returned to the city; unless these words are to be understood of another journey, they indicate that the oratory itself was situated outside the city, in some village. In any case, even today near Tours, not far from the city’s principal church, there is a church of Saint Stephen with parish status, which gives its name to the city gate and the neighboring suburb]. On Stephen the Protomartyr

Stephen, the first either deacon of the holy Church or martyr [that is, both] (year 33, 26 December), was stoned near Jerusalem for the holy name of Christ, whom he saw by spiritual contemplation at the right hand of Power, as the sacred history of the Apostles relates (Acts 6:7); and he prayed to that same Majesty for his persecutors.

There was an oratory near the city of Tours, dedicated by the ancients to his name, which we ordered to be extended somewhat. When this had been done, we moved the altar forward intact as it stood.

When we searched inside the small chamber, we found none of the holy relics that tradition reported to be there. I then sent one of the abbots to bring his relics to us from the oratory of the ecclesiastical house. I forgot, however, to give him the key to the chest, which hung from my belt.

759 When the abbot arrived, he removed the seal from the cupboard [Col. 0735B] and found the chest locked. What could he do? What should he do? He was left in uncertainty. If he returned to me, the journey there and back would take a long time. If he brought the chest itself, he knew that this would trouble me, since relics of many saints were kept there. If he did nothing, he would fail to carry out the command he had received.
