What more need be said? While he hesitated, holding the chest in his hands, the bolts sprang back with a noise, and he saw that the chest had been opened.

Then, giving thanks, he brought us the relics he had taken out, with great astonishment. After Masses had been celebrated, we planted them there by the Lord’s command.

When I returned to the city many days later, I found the chest locked again, with the bolt restored as I had left it.

A portion of the sacred blood of this blessed levite is preserved, as is widely reported, in the altar of the church of Bourges [Note: [Col. 0735D] The words following “At Bordeaux,” and so forth, are absent from Claromontanus b. Even today, in the cathedral church of Bourges, a flask filled with the blood of blessed Stephen can be seen. Tradition holds that it is the very flask mentioned here by our Gregory. It is said to have been brought to Bourges by Blessed Ursinus when he first arrived there to proclaim the faith of Christ. That the faithful diligently collected the blood of the protomartyr is clear from book I of Augustine’s *Miracles of Saint Stephen*, chapter 1, where mention is made of a flask filled with the martyr’s blood that was preserved at Uzalis in Africa. A glass flask of this kind can still be seen at Naples; Saint Gaudiosus, an exile from Africa, is said to have brought it to Italy. See our edition of the *History of the Vandal Persecution*, part II, chapter 9].

At the time of Bishop Felix [Note: [Col. 0736D] On this holy bishop, see *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 102], a certain man accused his neighbors of some offense. Since he often assailed them with insolent words and summoned them before the public court, the leading men of the city decreed that those who were accused should purge themselves of the charge by oath.

They entered the altar of the church mentioned above. As they raised their hands and pronounced the oaths, the prosecutor loudly declared that they had sworn falsely.

Immediately, with his feet lifted high, he was hurled into the air. He struck his head against the pavement and was seen by the surrounding crowd to be almost lifeless.

After nearly two hours, when he was thought to be breathing his last, he opened his eyes and confessed the crime. He declared that he had unjustly harassed the men and falsely proclaimed them guilty. Thus the innocent were released, the guilty was exposed, and the power of the Blessed One became manifest [Col. 0735D].

At Bordeaux [Col. 0736A], there was an old woman weighed down by age but strengthened by the integrity of her faith. She was accustomed to light lamps in the basilicas of the saints by adding oil. To perform this task, she entered the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter on a Sunday night.

Its altar is raised high, being set upon a platform [Note: [Col. 0736D] Nearly all the manuscripts read “the platform having been raised high.” Below, “having the girl” likewise refers to an elevated structure. Mabillon proves by many examples that altars were formerly raised and generally had a crypt beneath them where the faithful could pray, in his preface to century III, part I, no. 79, of the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order]. Its lower part is closed by a door in the form of a crypt, and it also has its own altar containing relics of saints [Note: [Col. 0736D] We have already said that the relics of saints were formerly kept beneath the altar. See Saint Paulinus, *Natale* IX, on Saint Felix].

The venerable woman descended into it devoutly to light the lamp, as we have said, accompanied only by a little girl.

While she was carrying out this task and night had covered the world in darkness, the clergy arrived, recited sections of the Psalms, closed the door of the crypt, and departed, unaware that the woman was inside.

After lighting the lamp, she hurried to the door to leave. When she realized that it was closed, she cried out and called by name for someone who could open it. But because of her advanced age her voice was not strong enough to penetrate those barriers.

When she realized that no one heard her, she lay down upon the pavement and said:

“I will pray for my sins and for the people to the Lord, the Creator of all, until the one who must open the entrance of this church arrives.”

While keeping vigil in prayer, she saw, around the middle of the night, that the doors had been opened and the entire basilica shone with immense light.

Then behold, a choir of singers entered the basilica [Note: [Col. 0736D] Visions of this kind occur frequently even in the most trustworthy acts of the saints. See the *Life of Saint Germanus of Auxerre*, written by Constantius, chapter 15]. After they had said “Glory to the Trinity” and the melody of their psalmody had ceased, she heard men complaining among themselves and saying:

“Saint Stephen the levite is delaying us. We ought already to have visited the other basilicas, but we cannot until he who is awaited arrives.”

As they repeated these words frequently, a man suddenly arrived in a white garment. The entire reverent multitude humbly greeted him, saying:

“Bless us, sacred and holy levite Stephen.”

He in turn greeted them [Note: [Col. 0736D] The Laud manuscript reads “greeting them in return”], offered a prayer, and, when they asked him why he had been delayed for a while from visiting the holy places, replied:

“A ship at sea was in danger of sinking. I was invoked there, and I came to its aid; having rescued it, behold, I am here. And so that you may know that what I say is true, you can see that the garment I am wearing is still wet, with drops of seawater dripping from it.”

The woman, trembling greatly, pressed herself against the pavement and watched intently.

When they had departed and the doors had again been closed by divine power [Col. 0736D], she approached the place where the saint had stood [Col. 0737A], carefully gathered with a cloth the drops that had fallen onto the pavement, and revealed them to Bertchramn [Note: [Col. 0737D] More about him appears throughout the books of the *History*], who at that time governed the city as its bishop.

He received them with great joy and astonishment and kept them with him. Many sick people experienced healing through this cloth; and the bishop himself, often taking small portions from it, faithfully placed them wherever he consecrated churches.

We learned these things from the report of that bishop himself.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On Clement, Bishop and Martyr

Clement the martyr, as is read in his passion, was thrown into the sea with an anchor hung around his neck (year 100, 23 November) [Note: [Col. 0737D] This chapter and the following two are absent from Colbertinus tutior. It is absent together with the following five chapters from Claromontanus b. Rufinus attributes the title “martyr” to Saint Clement, and thereafter it became common among authors generally. That the *Acts* of Clement’s passion, which Gregory cites here, were known before the sixth century cannot be demonstrated by any ancient evidence. They later became famous in Gaul, as is clear not only from Gregory but also from the Gothic Missal, where an abridgment of them is given. See Tillemont’s note 12 on the *Life of Saint Clement*, volume II of his *Ecclesiastical History*].

Now, on the day of his solemnity [Col. 0737B], the sea recedes for three miles, providing a dry path for those who enter, until they reach the martyr’s tomb. There the people fulfill their vows and pray, and then return to the shore [Note: [Col. 0737D] The author of the *Life of Saint Constantine*, or Cyril, relates that this miracle was unknown at Chersonesus in the ninth century [Col. 0738D], in the Bollandist entry for 9 March. Nevertheless, the sacred body of that holy pontiff was found there at that time and brought to Rome, as the same author describes at length; consult his account].

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the Boy Who Slept at Clement’s Tomb for the Course of a Year as Though for Only One Night
It happened that on one of the solemn festivals a woman came to the place with her little son. After the sacred rites had been completed, while she was dining, the child fell asleep. While these things were taking place [762], suddenly there arose the sound of the approaching sea. Then, forgetting her child, the woman began hastening with the rest of the people toward the shore. When the advancing sea had reached the coastline, she remembered that she had left her son behind. Then, overcome with grief and thrown to the ground [Col. 0737C], she cried out that she was wretched, filling the shores with her lamentations, and ran all around the banks, in case someone might have seen the child dead and cast up on the shore.

But when she found no sign of him, she was eventually comforted by her relatives and returned home, spending the whole year in mourning and lamentation. When the annual cycle came around again, she returned to witness the martyr’s solemn festival [Note: Most manuscripts have *expectandam* (“to await”), according to the pronunciation; as below, *exspectantibus* (“for those awaiting”) is used instead of *spectantibus* (“for those witnessing”), and so frequently elsewhere], perhaps hoping that she might find some indication concerning the little boy.

Why say more? When the sea withdrew, she anticipated everyone in entering and was the first herself to proceed to the tomb. After prostrating herself on the ground and completing her prayer, she rose up; her cheeks were drenched with abundant streams of tears. As she turned her face toward the other side [Col. 0737D], she saw her son in the very place where she had left him sleeping, still held in that same slumber. Thinking that he was dead, she approached closely, as though to gather up a lifeless corpse. But when she realized that he was asleep, she quickly awakened him and, while the people looked on, lifted him unharmed into her arms. Amid kisses she asked where he had been for the space of a year. He said that he did not know whether a whole year had passed; he thought he had slept in a pleasant slumber for the space of a single night.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the water of the spring restored through his power

There was a well-watered spring [Note: Two manuscripts read *Mons erat* (“There was a hill”)], in a certain countryside within the territory of the city of Limoges. Its water either nourished the crops of the gardens and the cultivated fields by its approach, or fertilized them by its force. It was also led through channels to the places where it was needed, so that human effort might summon it where nature did not provide it [763]. Its stream was so abundant in sweet waters [Col. 0738B] that one could see a vegetable or shrub rejoicing if it had been irrigated by it. The grace of the divine Majesty also assisted it, so that wherever the stream had been released, the shoots quickly received vigorous growth.

When the local inhabitants, as though engaged in a game, led it through each place in turn, through the envy of the adversary, I believe, it broke through beneath the ground and, as though twelve stadia away, rose in the middle of a marsh, where it could accomplish absolutely nothing, scattering its waves. At once fear seized everyone’s minds, and the inhabitants of the region awaited some new destruction coming upon their land; at the same time they lamented with continual weeping the loss of the benefit they had been accustomed to possess.

Thus one year and then another passed in this dryness. Everything in that place which the spring had been accustomed to irrigate withered from thirst [Col. 0738C]. In the third year it happened that a certain traveler displayed relics of the blessed martyr Clement, whom we have already mentioned above, and carried them to Aridius [Note: This is Saint Aridius, whom Gregory frequently mentions and whose Life we shall give below], the presbyter of that city, a man religious in every holiness.

When the sorrowful neighbors came to him day and night [Note: The manuscripts generally read *vicina moesta penderent* (“the sorrowful neighbors waited”)]., trusting in his prayer because, if he asked the Lord, he might be able to restore the spring to its former place, he said:

“Come, dearest friends. If what our bearer has asserted is true—namely, that these are relics of the martyr Clement—it will now become evident, when his power has been revealed.”

Then he approached the place of the spring with psalmody. After the psalms had been recited, he prostrated himself in prayer. Placing the holy relics at the very entrance of the spring, he asked that the one who had once opened a well-watered river in the desert for condemned men cutting marble might, through Clement’s intercession, restore to this place the waters which holy mercy had formerly bestowed.

Immediately the stream returned [Col. 0739A] to the entrance, pouring forth great waters, and, flowing onward, filled the channel which it had previously occupied. The people marveled, and thanks were given to the Lord for his immeasurable grace, because he had both revealed the martyr’s power and deigned to fulfill the prayer of his faithful servant [764].

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the martyr Chrysanthus

The martyr Chrysanthus, as the history of his passion declares [Col. 0739C] [Note: This chapter and the following two are absent in Claromontanus B. Thereafter Claromontanus A lacks most of the material; some passages are arranged differently from the other manuscripts and editions, with several chapters from the book *On the Glory of the Confessors* sometimes intermingled.] [Note: The Acts of Saints Chrysanthus and Daria, which are available today and which Gregory seems here to praise, have no authority. Indeed, they contradict themselves: they claim that these martyrs suffered under Numerian, that is, in the year 283, while also reporting that their Acts were written at the command of Pope Stephen, who died in 257. Their memory is celebrated among the Greeks on 19 March and among the Latins on various days. They are praised by Saint Aldhelm in *On the Praise of Virginity*, by Saint Damasus, the Gelasian Sacramentary, Florus, and others. See below, chapter 83. They are commemorated on 25 October], after receiving the crown of martyrdom with the virgin Daria, bestowed many benefits of healing upon the people (year 257 or 283, 25 October).

For this reason, too, a crypt was constructed over them with marvelous workmanship. Vaulted in the manner of arches, it stands with the firmest stability. Finally, when crowds of people had gathered for his festival [Col. 0739B], the most wicked emperor ordered a wall to be erected at the entrance of that crypt. After the multitude had been shut inside, he ordered the shrine to be covered with sand and stones. A great mound was made above it, and the written account of the contest itself most certainly makes this clear.

The crypt remained buried under this covering for a long time, until the Roman city abandoned its idols and submitted to Christ the Lord. As time passed, no one knew the location of his burial, until it was revealed by the Lord Jesus. In one part of the place, the tombs of the martyrs Chrysanthus and Daria were separated by an intervening wall; in the other part [Note: The printed editions read “the tombs were separated in one part,” or “in the other part,” etc.; others read *segregate* (“separated”)], the bodies of the remaining saints had been gathered together into one.

Nevertheless, the builder left a window opened in the wall placed between them, so that access for viewing the bodies of the saints might be available [Col. 0739C]. They also report that at the time when those who had come to the holy rites were shut inside, men had brought with them silver vessels made of the precious metal, containing the wine offered for the oblation of the divine sacrifice. It is evident that the silver remained there, and those who look upon it can still see it today.

But since the human mind continually longs for shameful and disgraceful desires, a certain subdeacon, having seen the silver through the window, conceived within himself the thought which avarice compelled him to fulfill the next day [Note: Almost all manuscripts read: “what avarice later filled …”].

During the night he arose and entered the basilica of the Saints. Then, entering the chamber through the window and groping with his hands in the darkness of night, he took some of the vessels. Wishing afterward to leave with his booty, he wandered around for the entire night but could never find the entrance through which he had entered.

When daylight came, wishing to conceal his deed, and mindful of the saying of the Lord’s oracle, “Everyone who does evil hates the light, so that his works may not be revealed” (John 3:20), he hid himself all day in a corner of the chamber so that he would not be seen. The following night he again sought the entrance, but could not find it. He did this for the course of three nights.

On the third day, when he was already being tormented by hunger, he went before the people to the window and, leaving the silver behind, confessed his deed [Col. 0740B]. He went out with great shame, and the crime he had committed did not remain hidden from the people who were present.

After a long time, when Damasus, bishop of the holy apostolic see, learned of this event, he ordered the window to be more carefully enclosed and adorned the place with verses [Note: Since Baronius did not include these verses in his *Annals*, we shall give them in the appendix to this volume from Sarazani’s Roman edition]. There our Lord Jesus Christ is blessed, to the praise of his name, even to this day.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the martyr Pancratius

Not far from the wall of this city [Note: This chapter is absent from Colbert T and Claromontanus A from the words “this city’s wall” [Col. 0740C].] there is also the martyr Pancratius, a powerful avenger of perjurers (year 304, 12 May) [Note: Two manuscripts read *Pancratus*. Colbert manuscript A has *Prancatius* here once and in the table of contents; this variation in the spelling of the name occurs in other ancient monuments].

At his tomb [Note: Gregory the Great preached Homily 27 on John in this basilica, at the tomb of this martyr. The same holy pontiff wished the basilica, which had been neglected by its priests, to be assigned to monks, in Book III, Letter 18, to Abbot Maurus; he also dealt with this saint in various other places. Anastasius observes that this very basilica was restored by Pope Honorius; we shall present the inscription placed on that occasion, from our Mabillon, at the end of this volume. Concerning the relics of the same saint, see below, chapter 83. The monastery of Solemniacum, near Limoges, built in honor of the blessed Pancratius and other saints, is attested by a charter of Saint Eligius, found at the end of the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, volume II, p. 1091. Gregory the Great mentions another church dedicated to him and other martyrs at Saintes in Book V, Letter 50. See more about these matters in the Bollandists, 12 May], if anyone’s deranged mind wishes to utter a false oath, before he reaches his tomb—that is, before he approaches the grating beneath the arch, where the singing clerics customarily stand—he is immediately either seized by a demon or falls to the pavement and loses his life [Col. 0740C].

For this reason, whenever someone wishes to elicit from another person proof of any matter, in order to learn the truth, he is sent nowhere else for this purpose except to the basilica of the blessed Pancratius. For they say that many people living near the basilicas of the apostles or of other martyrs, when this necessity arises, seek no other temple than that of blessed Pancratius, so that, when his severe judgment publicly distinguishes the matter, they may either hear the truth and believe it or experience the judgment of the blessed martyr for their deceit.

## CHAPTER XL. On John, bishop and martyr

There are indeed many martyrs in the city of Rome whose histories of suffering have not been handed down to us intact. Yet concerning Bishop John, since his struggle has not come down to us in written form, I could not remain silent about what I have learned from the faithful [Note: Many things about Saint John are found in the commonly published authors. Preferable to the others is the anonymous writer of the *History of Caesarea*, from the reign of Constantius Chlorus until the death of King Theodoric the Great, published by Henri Valois after the books of Ammianus Marcellinus. This author makes clear that after the edict of the emperor Justinian ordering the expulsion of heretics, John was summoned by Theodoric to Ravenna and from there sent to Constantinople, so that he might dissuade the emperor from carrying out the edict. But when the emperor persisted in his purpose, the pontiff, returning from his journey, was thrown into prison by the king’s order, and there, worn down by hardships, died. See the Bollandists, 27 May].

When he had become bishop, he denounced the heretics with the utmost zeal and consecrated their churches as Catholic churches (year 526, 27 May). When King Theodoric learned of this, he was inflamed with fury because he was devoted to the Arian sect [Col. 0741B]. He ordered gladiators to be dispatched throughout Italy to slaughter all the Catholic people they found.

When the blessed John heard this, he went to the king to beg that these things not be done. The king received him deceitfully, bound him, and placed him in prison, saying: “I will see to it that you no longer dare to mutter against our sect.”

The saint of God, once placed in prison, was worn down by such great insults that after not much time he breathed out his spirit. He died gloriously in prison near the city of Ravenna.

But the mercy of the Lord immediately inflicted vengeance upon the wicked king. Suddenly struck by God, he perished, exhausted by severe afflictions [Note: The anonymous author mentioned above says that he died from a flux of the bowels which lasted three days. A certain hermit of the island of Lipara testified that he was thrown into the cauldron of Vulcan by Pope John and the patrician Symmachus, whom he had killed; see Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, Book IV, chapter 30], and at once received the everlasting burning of Gehenna’s flames [767].

## CHAPTER XLI. On the power of faith and of the Christian name

[Note: This chapter is absent in Claromontanus A. In the other manuscripts it bears the title: “On the Christian who stood before a pagan offering sacrifice.” [Col. 0742D]]

[Col. 0741C]

Great indeed is the dignity of the Christian name if you pursue in action the things you confess by faith. For, as the Apostle says: “Faith without works is dead in itself” (James 2:17, 20, 26).

Just as it is faith, not carnal birth, that makes one a son of Abraham, so true Christians are distinguished not merely by the honor of the name but by their works. Through this name darkness is illuminated, serpents flee, idols are overthrown, the diviner falls silent, the sorcerer withers away, and the worshipers of demons are driven off, as our Prudentius recalls in his book *Against the Jews* [Note: This work is commonly called the *Apotheosis*. The following verses are taken from lines 449–502, with several omitted].

The emperor [Diocletian] proceeded to the foul sacrifice of demons. After worshiping the gods and prostrating himself before the images—that is, idols [Col. 0741D]—he watched the priests [Col. 0742A] of the statues slaughtering crowds of sheep, whose laurel-bound foreheads were cut with axes.

While the old man, with bloody hands, handled the entrails and tried to investigate something divine among the fibers of the liver and amid the vital organs and innards of the animals [Note: The Laud manuscript reads “the fibers of the entrails amid the organs”], he saw everything confused and could not confidently discern what he wished to know.

Disturbed, he exclaimed:

“Alas, alas! I do not know what is happening here, which is thought to be contrary to our gods. For I see our gods withdrawing far away and not tasting any part of the sacrifices prepared for them. Someone is here, as the event itself shows, connected with certain gods who are accustomed to oppose us. And it is no wonder if some of the worshipers of the God of the Christians—the one whom they assert was crucified—are driving our gods to flight.

“The censers of incense grow cold; the fire on the altar grows lukewarm [Note: The Laud manuscript reads, “the altar grows weak”]; even the iron thrust into the victims can be seen to grow dull. Tell me now, most sacred Augustus, who is standing here, washed and anointed with balsam, and who will immediately withdraw so that the gods whom we invoke may approach.”

Saying this, as though he saw Christ himself, the avenger of these things, he fell lifeless to the ground and cried out against the offended gods.

Then the emperor himself, laying aside his diadem, said:

“Who is this man opposed to our gods and associated with the Christian religion, who carries his forehead marked with the inscription of the chrism and worships the wood of the cross? Let him declare himself without delay.”

Then one of the emperor’s armor-bearers, standing in the midst, threw down his weapons and said:

“I am the one whose God is Christ, who have been washed in his baptism and redeemed by the cross. I always invoked his name while your priests of the demon were consecrating the things that have been set out. Your gods flee from his name and cannot remain in a place where the name of such great majesty has been invoked.”

When the young man had said this, the emperor, stunned and trembling, left the temple of the demons [Note: Colbert manuscript A reads “the temple of the idols”]. Such great fear of God seized all who were standing there that no one followed Augustus to the palace. Instead, with palms and eyes raised to heaven, they all praised the Lord Christ with one voice and one accord, and with humble cries invoked him to be their helper.

Lest this account perhaps seem unbelievable to anyone, I shall append a few verses from it:

> Yet among all the princes there was one man,
>
> whom, when I was a boy, I remember as a most valiant commander in arms,
>
> renowned as a founder of laws, adviser to his country in word and deed,
>
> but no adviser concerning the religion that must be held,
>
> loving three hundred thousand gods, to bend his Augustan head
>
> before Minerva’s feet,
>
> and to lick the soles of earthenware Juno [Note: Colbert manuscript A reads *plantas* (“soles”) instead of *plantis* (“with the feet”). The following verses are absent from the Bellov manuscript to the end of the chapter; nevertheless, *plantis* belongs with the following line. Soles are a kind of sandal, discussed in the Acts of Saints Fructuosus and others and in chapter 18 of the Life of Saint Fulgentius],
>
> to fall at Hercules’ feet,
>
> and to wax the knees of Diana [Note: Others read “to bend.” Our reading is better, as Heinsius observes. Prudentius uses the same expression in *Hamartigenia*; Juvenal also has “to wax the knees of the gods,” *Satire* 10].
>
> Perhaps, while sacrificing, he appeased Hecate [Note: Read *Hecaten*, “Hecate,” instead of *Achaten*, “Achates.” This is Diana, who was called the Moon in heaven and Proserpina in the underworld. They think she was called Hecate because she was appeased with a hundred victims, to which Prudentius seems to allude. Below she is called Persephone] with much blood,
>
> an old man crowned with fillets according to custom, and with bloody hands
>
> handling the trembling organs chilled by deadly cold,
>
> skillfully marking the final movements of the spirit
>
> in the still-warm heart, noting their number and conclusion.
>
> Suddenly, amid the sacred rites, the priest cried out,
>
> pale: “See what I am doing! Greater, O excellent king, greater
>
> is the unknown power that has intervened at our altars.
>
> I see the summoned shadows dispersing far away [Note: Several editions of Prudentius read *Ascitas video* (“I see the summoned ones”); Heinsius considers *eccitas*, for *excitas* (“aroused”), a better reading. This word was especially common among ancient writers for magical matters],
>
> and surely some Christian worshiper has crept in here.
>
> This class of men makes every fillet and every divine couch tremble:
>
> let the washed and anointed man remain far away,
>
> and let beautiful Proserpina return to the rites restored.”
>
> He spoke, and collapsed bloodless, as though he saw Christ himself
>
> threatening with his lightning bolt drawn forth.
>
> The emperor himself, lifeless, laying aside his diadem,
>
> grows pale and looks around at those standing nearby, to see whether any follower
>
> of the chrism bears temples marked with its sign [Note: Three manuscripts, together with Prudentius and Heinsius, read *signarit … ligno* (“has marked … with the wood”)],
>
> who might have disturbed the Zoroastrian murmurs on his forehead.
>
> One young armor-bearer from the troop of fair-haired youths [Note: From this Heinsius infers that this armor-bearer belonged to the praetorian soldiers, Germans, or other northern peoples, who commonly had blond and even long hair]
>
> is discovered, a guardian of the purple flank.
>
> He does not deny it, but throws down his two-javelined, gem-studded spear
>
> and admits that he bears the sign of Christ.
>
> The frightened prince, having cast down the chief priest, flees
>
> the marble shrine, with no one accompanying him;
>
> while the shaken cohort, forgetting its lord,
>
> raises its faces toward heaven and invokes Jesus [770].

I have inserted these few verses into my account as confirmation of what I have narrated [Note: Lactantius relates almost the same events as Gregory here recounts from Prudentius, in Book IV of the *Institutes* and in the valuable little book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 10, where he says that these events happened under the emperor Diocletian. This was the first occasion for the persecution of Christians, although previously Diocletian had always been well disposed toward Christians, as Eusebius relates more fully in Book VIII of his *Ecclesiastical History*. In his *Chronicle*, however, he records that the persecution against the soldiers in the East began with Veturius in the year 302.

Paul Baudri, a learned Calvinist who published Lactantius’s little book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* with notes by various authors and illustrated it with his own observations, admits, apropos of the Christian youth who disturbed the sacrifices of the gods by displaying the sign of the cross, that Christians had been accustomed from the earliest centuries of the Church to fortify themselves with Christ’s sign. He cites Tertullian’s notable passage on this subject from *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 3, where we read: “At every advance and movement, at every entrance and exit, in clothing and footwear, at baths, tables, lamps, beds, seats, and whatever activity occupies us, we mark our foreheads with the sign of the cross,” and so forth.

A little farther below he praises a passage from Theodoret’s *History*, Book III, chapter 3, where Julian the Apostate is said to have driven away demons by the sign of the cross, and he suggests that similar examples are found throughout the ancient writers. But since he should consequently have praised the Catholic religion for preserving the customs of the primitive Church, he turns the matter in another direction and argues that his own sect, which has rejected this custom, cannot be condemned because this practice of signing oneself appears nowhere in Scripture. As though it were permissible to reject what the Church, received from the apostles or their disciples, has commended to later generations.]

Thus I have included these verses in my account, showing what the Christian name and the banner of the cross benefit those who believe by faith and perfect in action the things they have believed, as was said above.

## CHAPTER XLII. On the church of blessed Lawrence

[Note: This chapter is absent in Colbert T. In Claromontanus B it is lacking together with the following four chapters. [Col. 0744D]]

[Col. 0743C]

There was a church in a certain place dedicated to blessed Lawrence, consecrated both by his relics and by his name [Col. 0744A]. Through the neglect of a long period it had become badly exposed to the elements (year 358, 10 August). When the inhabitants of the place wished to renew it, they went into the forests, cut and smoothed timber, made beams, and transported them on wagons to the site.

When they had laid them out on the ground in order to begin the work, one beam was found to be shorter. Immediately the priest in charge of the work was seized by the deepest grief. Weeping bitterly, he did not know what to do or where to turn.

Then, looking at the shorter beam, he said:

“O most blessed Lawrence, who, placed upon the fire, glorified yourself, always cherishing and refreshing the poor, consider my poverty. For our poverty has no means by which another beam can be provided here.”

Immediately, while everyone stood astonished, the beam grew to such a length that a large portion had to be cut off [Col. 0744B]. Thinking it wrong to lose the benefit through the industry of the people, and believing that the beam had been touched and lengthened by the martyr’s hand, he tore off pieces of the remaining portion and frequently drove away various illnesses with them.

The presbyter Fortunatus celebrated this in the following verses:

> Lawrence, deservedly burned in living flames,
>
> who return victorious from the fire through fervent faith,
>
> while the people renew your temple with a shorter trunk,
>
> the beams grew, and blessed faith grew too.
>
> When the trunk was shortened, it stretched itself through your favor,
>
> as much as it had first been small and afterward cut;
>
> the tree, cut down by axes, deserved to grow still more,
>
> and learned to be longer when dry,
>
> from the place where it had been cut.
>
> From it the people receive healing:
>
> if a blind man comes without fear, he receives his sight.

He wrote many more verses about this [Note: This is poem 14 of Book IX, comprising twenty-two verses], which I have omitted, writing only these as testimony to the truth [another manuscript: “to the man”] [Col. 0744C].

These things happened at Brionas, a fortress of Italy [Note: Paul the Deacon mentions the region of the Briones, where blood rained, in Book IV, chapter 4 of his *History of the Lombards*. He speaks of the same place in Book II, chapter 13, as does Fortunatus in a letter to our Gregory. Some locate the Breones in the county of Tyrol; the author of the Life of Saint Corbinian also mentions them. Ortelius places Brios near Vercelli, where, he says, the emperor Charles the Bald died. Charles did indeed die at Brios, but only after he had crossed the Alps and Mount Cenis while returning from Rome to Gaul] [Col. 0745A].

I myself saw a man who was suffering severely from toothache. After receiving from the priest a fragment of this wood, as soon as he touched the tooth with it, he was immediately free of pain.

Nor did I think I should omit the fact that his relics, rescued from the burning caused by hostile forces, were brought by a certain man into the Limousin. Although he was repeatedly warned in a vision to take them to Abbot Aridius, he failed to obey the command. He himself, his wife, and his entire household then began to fall ill. Compelled by necessity, he brought the relics to the holy man; immediately he was restored to health and departed.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On the martyr Cassianus

Cassianus, a martyr of Italy and a famous teacher of boys, was handed over, when persecution arrived, to the judgment of the persecutors by the very tender and childish flock entrusted to him (year …, 13 August) [Note: Prudentius describes his martyrdom in Book *On Crowns* (*Περὶ στεφάνων*), hymn 9. He suffered at Imola, a city otherwise called Forum Cornelii or Silla, in Romagna, under papal jurisdiction and the metropolitan see of Ravenna. His sacred body is preserved beneath the high altar in the cathedral church called Saint Cassianus after him. His feast is celebrated on 13 August, but it is uncertain in what year or under which persecution he suffered. Bede gives an abridgment of the history of his martyrdom in his authentic *Martyrology*].

Thirsting for their teacher’s blood, the boys struck wax-covered tablets against his head [Note: In Colbert A and Claromontanus A, *in* is absent. For here, as often elsewhere, the accusative is used for the ablative; hence Colbert T reads *ceratis caput inlidunt tabellis* (“they strike his head with wax-covered tablets”) [Col. 0745D]]. Cutting his flesh with the broad edges of their writing-styluses and piercing his limbs with their tiny points, they made him a martyr worthy of God. In his honor such great fear is still maintained today that absolutely no one has dared to touch anything belonging to him. If anyone does so, he is either seized by a demon or consumed by sudden death; he does not escape without punishment [772].

## CHAPTER XLIV. On the martyrs Agricola and Vitalis

Agricola and Vitalis were crucified near the Italian city of Bologna for the name of Christ (around the year 303, 4 or 29 November) [Note: This chapter and the following two are absent from Colbert manuscript T. Saint Ambrose described the passion of these martyrs at the beginning of his book *On the Exhortation to Virginity*. Their sacred bodies had been placed beneath an altar, as Paulinus relates in his Life of Ambrose. Saint Paulinus praises them in poem 24, as do others. Jovinus, military prefect in Gaul and later consul, built a splendid basilica at Reims under the name of Saint Agricola not long after their martyrdom; he himself was buried there. It still exists today, dedicated to Saint Nicasius and occupied by Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur].

We have learned through the report of the faithful that their tombs, since the history of their passion has not yet reached us, are placed above the ground. Because many people, as is customary, either touched them with their hands or kissed them with their mouths, the church custodian was warned to keep the unclean away from them.

A certain bold and criminal man removed the covering of one of the tombs in order to steal something from the sacred ashes. Having thrust his head inside, he was trapped by it and was scarcely freed by others. He withdrew in confusion and did not obtain what he had presumptuously attempted to take. From then on he approached the saints’ tombs with greater reverence.

Another man, while carrying public taxes, carelessly lost his money-bag on the road. As he approached the city, he realized that he had lost the public purse [Col. 0746A] which he was carrying. He then prostrated himself before the tombs of the blessed men and tearfully begged that, through their power, he might recover what he had lost, lest he, his wife, and his children be reduced to captivity because of it.

When he went outside into the courtyard, he encountered a man who had found the money lying on the road. After carefully questioning him, he said that he had found the purse at the very hour when this man had implored the martyrs’ aid [773].

Namacius, bishop of Clermont [Note: Gregory discusses Saint Namacius and the church he built in Book II of his *History*, chapter 16. This church, namely the cathedral, was first called that of Saints Vitalis and Agricola, then that of Saint Lawrence, and finally that of Saint Mary, the name it still retains today. See Cointius, under the year 554, section 4. There is, however, another church of Saint Lawrence at Clermont. Consult Savaron, *On the Churches of Clermont*, chapters 1 and 3], devoutly sought their relics, intending to place them in the church he had built. He sent there a presbyter who, going with the grace of God, brought back what he had requested [the printed reading *patierat* is uncertain].

When he returned with his companions, they halted at a lodging-place five miles from Clermont and sent messengers to the bishop, asking him to order what they should do. At dawn, the priest notified the citizens and hurried with the greatest devotion, carrying crosses and candles, to meet the holy relics.

When the presbyter offered to let him see the blessed relics, if he ordered it, the bishop replied:

“For me, it is better to believe these things than to see them. For thus we read in Scripture concerning the saints: The Lord himself judges blessed those who have believed in him even though they have not seen him” (John 20:29).

Through the priest’s faith, therefore, the Lord glorified his saints in power. When they were approaching, the sky suddenly became dark. Then a shadowy and dreadful rainstorm descended upon them, and so much rain poured out there that rivers could be seen running through the roads.

Nevertheless, around the sacred relics, across a full *jugerum*, not a single drop was seen to fall [Col. 0746C]. As they departed, the rain followed them from afar, as though offering its service: it refreshed the people but did not touch the bearers of the relics.

When the bishop saw this, he glorified the Lord, who, thus favoring his faith, had deigned to perform such things for the glory of the saints. Then, after the citizens had gathered with great joy and devotion, he dedicated the holy church, adorned with these relics.

## CHAPTER XLV. On Saint Victor the martyr

[774]

The renowned martyr Victor is also magnified in the city of Milan because he frequently releases those bound in prisons and permits captives to depart free (year 303, 8 May) [Note: Ambrose praises this martyr among the special patrons of Milan in Book VII on Luke. Ennodius, bishop of Pavia in the sixth century, relates in Letter 24 of Book VIII that, when he was at the point of death, he recovered his health miraculously after being anointed with oil of Blessed Victor; he repeats the account in his *Eucharistic*. The Acts of his martyrdom exist, but they have no authority. He rests in Milan in the church of Saint Victor *Ad corpus*, where Olivetan Benedictine monks replaced the former community in 1507. In 1576 Saint Charles Borromeo transferred the body of the same saint from the old church to the new one. On this matter, see Puricellus in the *Ambrosian Monuments* and the Bollandists, 8 May].

At a certain time Apollinaris went to Italy with the commander Victorius [Note: Apollinaris was the son of Saint Apollinaris Sidonius, whom Gregory discusses in Book II, chapter 37, and Book III, chapter 2. He discusses Victorius in Book II, chapters 20 and 21]. They say that Victorius was killed near the city of Rome [Note: The printed editions and several manuscripts read *quo*, “where,” instead of *quo … interfecto*, “when he had been killed”].

The local inhabitants held Apollinaris as though he were a captive, saying:

“You will not see your homeland, but as his associate you will pay the punishment you deserve.”

After making these threats, they sent him into exile near the city of Milan.

It happened that, when the festival of Saint Victor arrived and the people gathered, Apollinaris also attended the vigils. He was considered released under a loose form of custody. Prostrating himself before the sacred tomb of Saint Victor, he began to pray always, and now with even greater intensity, asking that the martyr’s power free him from this exile.

Around midnight, as he was leaving the church, he heard one poor man say to another:

“What do you think, fellow poor man, is the power of this martyr? I tell you the truth, and I am not mistaken: on this night, whoever is a captive and escapes his master by flight reaches his homeland as a free man and is never found again.”

Apollinaris received these words as though they were an omen sent by God’s will. Again and again he threw himself down before the martyr’s tomb and prayed that, aided by the martyr’s power, he might depart without hindrance.

Then he summoned a servant and ordered a horse to be saddled, saying:

“Today we shall be freed from this bond of custody.”

They mounted and crossed the passes of the Alps, which were filled with a great multitude of heaps [*congeriorum*, uncertain] [Note: This is the reading of Claromontanus A. The Martianus and Laud manuscripts read *juga, neque aliorum congeriorum*, “the mountain ridges, and not of other heaps”; Colbert A and Morenas read *neque alium*, “nor another”; the Roman edition reads *neque alium congeriosum*; Clictovius reads *atque alium congerium montem oppleta*, “and filled with another piled-up mountain”]. They were brought safely to Clermont [775], with the power of the blessed martyr preceding them, so that no one asked where they were going or from where they had come. It was manifest that they had been saved from this hardship through the protection of the blessed martyr.

# CHAPTER XLVI  
## On the Restored Crystal Chalice

There is in the same city a basilica of Saint Lawrence the deacon, whom we mentioned above. In it there was kept a crystal chalice of remarkable beauty. [Note: This chapter and the following four are absent from Clar. a. Above, however, chapter 42 dealt with the basilica of Saint Lawrence, but at Brionas. Hence I conjecture that the words “whose [basilica] above” should be referred back to Saint Lawrence himself.]

During the celebration of a certain solemn feast, while it was being carried by a deacon to be offered at the holy altar, it slipped from his hand, fell to the ground, and was smashed into fragments. But the deacon, pale and bloodless, carefully gathered the pieces of the vessel and placed them upon the altar, not doubting that the Martyr’s power could restore it. Finally, after spending the night in vigils, tears, and prayer, he found the sought-for chalice solid again upon the altar.

When this miracle was announced to the people, it kindled such devotion in their hearts that they asked the priest to celebrate new solemn rites for God in the Martyr’s honor. Then the bishop of the place, having suspended the chalice above the altar, established that from then onward the feast should be celebrated with the greatest devotion every year.

[Note: Saint Jerome, praising Saint Exsuperius in his letter to Rusticus, who had distributed everything to the poor, says: “No one is richer than he who carries the Lord’s body in a wicker basket and his blood in a glass vessel.”]

# CHAPTER XLVII  
## On Saints Gervasius and Protasius, Nazarius and Celsus

[Note: So too it begins in Colb. tut., although three chapters are omitted there, since what precedes does not concern Milan. So also Clar. b, in which, however, some later hand, having erased the earlier reading, substituted “In the Milanese [city].” The printed editions have “In this city also.”]

In this city the victorious bodies of the blessed martyrs Gervasius and Protasius are preserved (about A.D. 66, June 19). For a long time, as the history of their passion itself relates, they lay hidden beneath the earth, until the place was revealed to Saint Ambrose (A.D. 386). He found them and, after miracles had been displayed, buried them in the basilica that he himself had built through his own efforts.

[Note: We know no history of the passion of Saints Gervasius and Protasius other than a letter written under the name of Saint Ambrose to the bishops of Italy, beginning “Ambrose, servant of the servants,” and so forth. It is spurious and was therefore rejected by our scholars into the appendix, although it had previously been listed under number 53. Saint Ambrose himself narrated the story of their discovery and translation in Letter 54 to his sister Marcellina, which is Letter 22 in the new edition. On this subject one should also consult Paulinus in his Life of Saint Ambrose; Saint Augustine, *City of God*, book XXII, chapter 28; and *Confessions*, book IX, chapter 7. Besides these authors, Saint Paulinus, bishop of Nola, in Letter 12, Saint Gaudentius, and others wrote about the relics of these martyrs, which were distributed throughout almost the entire world, and about the various miracles that occurred through them. They are believed to have suffered under Nero’s persecution. They were discovered in the year 386, when the persecution of Saint Ambrose by the empress Justina and the Arians was raging at Milan, on June 17; on June 19 they were deposited beneath the principal altar of the Ambrosian basilica.]

As for their relics, the city of Tours has its older churches especially adorned by them; and, by God’s favor, they have also been spread throughout the whole of Gaul.

[Note: This passage seems corrupted through scribal error, and it could not be restored with the help of the manuscripts. Perhaps it means that the principal churches of Tours were adorned with the relics of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, by which it doubtless designates the cathedral church and the basilica of Saint Martin. For one will scarcely find elsewhere in Gregory that churches are called “older” except cathedral churches. A little below, the printed editions and almost all the manuscripts, except Colbertinus tut., read: “the relics had been so densely distributed through the various places.”]

On one occasion a discussion arose among certain religious men concerning these matters, and concerning the reason why the aforesaid relics had been distributed so densely among different places. What I heard from one who reported it, I did not think improper to insert in this account, since it is not contained in the history of their passion.

He said that when these glorious bodies had been translated into that church, and the solemn celebration of Mass was being held in honor of the martyrs, one of the roof panels fell from the ceiling [that is, from the vault] and struck the Martyrs’ heads, drawing forth a stream of blood. The blessed blood was collected in the linen cloths, coverings, or ecclesiastical veils stained by it. It is said to have flowed in such abundance that cloths capable of receiving it had to be found.

From this source their relics were collected in great quantity and carried throughout Italy and Gaul. Saint Martin also received many of them, as the letter of the most blessed Paulinus relates. [Note: On this letter, see *History*, book X, chapter 31, number 5.]

As for the holy Nazarius and Celsus, whose bodies, according to the account of their contest, were said to have suffered at Ebredunum, a city of Gaul (the date is uncertain, June 12), their bodies too were buried so secretly, because of the persecution by the pagans, that they would be forgotten by succeeding generations.

[Note: What follows is found under another chapter heading in the manuscripts and is entirely absent from Clar. b. Most people think that the Nazarius and Celsus whom Gregory here says suffered at Ebrodunum are not the same as those who completed their martyrdom at Milan under Nero. Ado and others, however, judge them to be different. The former pair was famous in the fifth century because Saint Ambrose discovered their relics in A.D. 395 or the following year, as Paulinus writes in his Life of Ambrose. Ennodius, bishop of Ticinum, in the sixth century, and an ancient author commonly published under Saint Ambrose’s name relate something about their deeds. In their commonly published Acts, Nazarius is said to have preached the Christian faith at Ebrodunum. In any case, whether the two pairs are different or identical, both are commemorated by Ado on June 12. On that same day the Roman Martyrology also commemorates another Nazarius; the Milanese Nazarius, however, is commemorated with Celsus on July 12.]

The man who had related what we have just reported about the aforesaid saints used to say that a pear tree had grown above these graves, and that a certain poor man had made a little garden there, enclosing the tree. Whenever it bore fruit at the proper season, any sick person afflicted with any disease who plucked one of its pears with his teeth immediately recovered when the illness had been removed. Thus the poor man made a considerable profit.

But when the Martyrs revealed themselves and ordered the tree to be cut down, the poor man broke into loud lamentation and would not permit it to be felled. Once he had been removed, the pear tree was cut down, and a basilica of wondrous workmanship was built. On its altar the relics of the blessed Genes­ius, martyr of Arles (see below, chapter 68), are also venerated.

The poor man was so distinguished for his faith that afterward he was deemed worthy of the priesthood in that church.

# CHAPTER XLVIII  
## On Saint Saturninus

The martyr Saturninus, as is reported, was ordained by the disciples of the apostles [Note: If Gregory truly means the apostles by this expression, he disagrees with himself in book I of the *History*, chapter 30, where, on the basis of Saturninus’ own Acts, he dates the beginning of his episcopate at Toulouse to the consulship of Decius and Gratus, that is, the year 250. Perhaps even then, as remains the case today, there was a popular tradition that Saint Saturninus had been ordained bishop by the apostles themselves and sent into Gaul, and Gregory followed it here, although his Acts, which we consider genuine, say otherwise. See *Genuine Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 109, where we made further observations about this holy bishop. His martyrdom was celebrated by Apollinaris Sidonius, book IX, letter 16, and Fortunatus, book II of the poems, poem 8.] and sent to the city of Toulouse (after A.D. 250, November 29).

At the instigation of the pagans, he was tied to the feet of a wild bull, dragged down the steps of the Capitol, and, his skull shattered, ended his present life. When certain religious men were transferring his relics to another region, the course of their journey led them past the boundary of the district of Brioude in the territory of Auvergne. As the sun was setting, they turned aside to the lodging of a poor man and asked for accommodation.

The man received them, and when they explained what they were carrying, he was moved by human kindness and admonished by the fear of God. He placed the chest containing the relics in a storeroom and set it above the grain that had been stored in a vessel. In the morning the travelers took up the sacred pledge, thanked their host, and continued the journey they had begun.

On the following night the man was warned in a vision by an old man who said to him: “Do not remain in this place, for it has been sanctified by the relics of the martyr Saturninus.” He, however, paid little attention to the vision and, as rustic people do, did nothing about what he had been warned.

Before long he fell into distress, his small resources began gradually to diminish, and his wife wasted away from another illness. Why say more? Within a year he had been reduced to such poverty that he had nothing left with which he could be fed or clothed, as human necessity requires.

At last, coming to his senses, he said to his wife: “I have sinned before God and his saints because I did not leave this little lodging, as I was warned. I know that for this reason the evils we suffer have come upon us. Now let us obey the vision we saw and remove this little house from the place, so that we may be saved.”

He then removed the hut and set up an oratory made of wooden boards. There he poured out prayers every day and implored the aid of the blessed Martyr. At last, when the afflictions ceased, he applied his hands to work and enjoyed such an abundance of produce that within a short time he recovered more than he had lost.

These events took place within our territory.

Nor will I omit the following event, which may restrain the arrogance of the wicked. In the time of King Chlothar, a certain Plato came to the monastery of Pauliacum, in whose oratory the relics of this saint are preserved. Because he had received no gift from the abbot, he is said to have declared: “I shall turn this church into a royal residence, in one corner of which his horsemen [or: his horses] will be fed.”

As he departed in anger and was preparing to go to the ruler, he was seized by a fever and breathed out his spirit on the third day. He descended swiftly into hell and left God’s house to the worship of the one in whose name it had previously been consecrated.

# CHAPTER XLIX  
## The Passion and Names of Forty-Eight Martyrs

The names of the forty-eight martyrs who are said to have suffered at Lyon (A.D. 177, June 2) are these:

[Note: These saints were the firstfruits of the Gallic martyrs, if the opinion of Eusebius, Sulpicius Severus, and other ancient writers is true: on the occasion of these martyrs of Lyon, they maintain that martyrdoms first appeared in Gaul under the emperor Marcus Aurelius. Their outstanding contests were described, as learned men think, by Saint Irenaeus, in a letter written in the name of the churches of Vienne and Lyon to the Phrygians and Asians, which Eusebius preserved for us almost entire in book V, chapter 1, of his *Ecclesiastical History*. We compared their names with the ancient Martyrologies in *Genuine Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 47.]

Vectius, Epagathus, Zacharias, Macarius, Alcibiades, Silvius, Primus, Ulpius [or Alpius], Vitalis, Comminius, October, Philominus, Geminus, Julia, Albina, Grata, Aemilia, Posthumiana, Pompeia, Rodone, Biblis, Quarta, Materna, Elpenipsa, and Stamas.

The following were handed over to the beasts: Sanctus and Maturus, Alexander, Ponticus, and Blandina.

The following died in prison: Arescius, Photinus, Cornelius, Zotimus, Titus, Zoticus, Julius, Aemilia [Note: Colb. tut. has *Aemilius*. The other manuscripts have *Aemelia*, as above.], Gamnite, Pompeia, Alumna, Mamilia, Justa, Trifime, Antonia, and the blessed Photinus, bishop.

[Note: Some manuscripts have *Photinus*, which would more correctly be written *Pothinus* from the Greek. Gregory promised the names of these forty-eight martyrs but gives only forty-five. He omits Attalus, the most famous figure in the letter of the church of Lyon. The ancient Martyrologies include Rogata, Apollonius, Geminianus, Julianus, Ausonia, and Domna. The second part of the fourth-century Benedictine *Life of Saint Bernard*, bishop of Vienne, adds Severinus, Exsuperius, and Felicianus. They suffered on various days under Marcus Aurelius.]

Their holy bodies were ordered by the unjust judge to be burned, and, after they had been consumed, their ashes were scattered into the Rhône. But after these events, when the Christians were in the deepest sorrow, as though the blessed relics had perished, they appeared by night to faithful men at the place where they had been handed over to the fire. They were standing whole and unharmed, and they said to the men:

“Let our relics be gathered from this place, for none of us has perished. From here we have been translated to the rest that Christ, the King of heaven, promised us, for whose name we suffered.”

The men reported this to the other Christians, gave thanks to God, and were strengthened in the faith. They gathered the sacred ashes and built a basilica of astonishing size in their honor. They buried the blessed relics beneath the holy altar, where they continually showed by manifest miracles that they dwelt with God.

The place where they suffered is called Athanacum [Note: Colb. a has *Athenacum* and below *Athenacenses*. This reading of the name appears more compatible with its etymology. The place was so called from Athens, because an altar was famous there among the ancients on account of contests in Greek and Latin eloquence instituted by Gaius Caligula. It later became more renowned because of the holy martyrs, and a distinguished basilica was erected there with a notable Benedictine monastery, which in our time passed to secular canons.], and for that reason some also call the martyrs Athanacenses.

# CHAPTER L  
## On Saint Photinus, Bishop of Lyon

Thus the glorious bishop Photinus, who served as priest over the city of Lyon, having consummated martyrdom, was carried into heaven through the merit of his noble contest (A.D. 177, June 2).

Irenaeus, worthy of him in merit and holiness, succeeded him as bishop. He too ended his life through martyrdom (A.D. 203, June 28). [Note: Several manuscripts have *Hereneus*. His Acts had already perished in the sixth century; he seems to have suffered about the year 203. See *Genuine Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 59. On the crypt in which Saint Irenaeus was buried with other martyrs, see the Bollandists’ June 6, in Chifflet’s *Claudian Illustrations*, chapter 4, pp. 676 and following. In 1562, after capturing Lyon, the Calvinist heretics commonly called Huguenots violated Saint Irenaeus’s tomb and scattered his sacred body. The skull of his head, accidentally rescued from their hands, is now reverently preserved at Lyon.]

He is buried beneath the altar in the crypt of the basilica of Saint John. On one side of him the martyr Epipodius is buried (A.D. 178, April 22 and 24), and on the other the martyr Alexander. [Note: We included their passion among the *Genuine Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 61. See also *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 64.]

If dust from their tombs is gathered with faith, it immediately heals the sick. Great radiance is contained in that crypt, which, as I believe, signifies the merit of the Martyrs.

# CHAPTER LI  
## On Benignus, the Glorious Martyr

Benignus, a witness to the Lord’s name, completed his martyrdom at the fortress of Dijon (A.D. 178, November 1). [Note: This chapter is absent from Colb. tut.; it is cited in the *Chronicle of Saint Benignus*. Almost all the manuscripts have “But Benignus, a witness to the Lord’s name,” and so forth. The Acts of this holy martyr survive, although they are not free from blemishes. His history, his discovery, and the notable basilica and monastery at Dijon are treated at length in the *Chronicle* of that place, published in volume I of Acher’s *Spicilegium*. We think he suffered under Marcus Aurelius, since he is called a disciple of Saint Polycarp in the older sources. See *Genuine Acts of the Martyrs*, pp. 68–69.]

Because he was placed after his martyrdom in a great sarcophagus, people of our own time—and especially the blessed bishop Gregory—thought that some pagan had been buried there. For peasants used to pay their vows at that place and quickly obtained what they asked.

Accordingly, when a certain man had received many benefits from the Blessed One’s tomb, he brought a candle and, after lighting it, returned home. A little boy who had watched this, after the man had gone away, descended to the tomb to extinguish and remove the burning candle.

As he went down, behold, a serpent of extraordinary size came from the other side and coiled itself around the candle. The boy, frightened, went back up. Twice or three times he tried to remove the candle, but the serpent prevented him.

When these and similar events were reported to the blessed bishop, he did not believe them at all; rather, he vigorously asserted that people should not worship there. At length the Martyr of God revealed himself to the blessed confessor and said:

“What are you doing? You not only despise me, but you also reject those who honor me. Please do not do this, but prepare a covering over me as quickly as possible.”

Shaken by this vision, the bishop went to the holy tomb and there, for a very long time, tearfully begged forgiveness for his ignorance. Since the crypt that had been vaulted by the ancients [Note: Gregory regularly uses this expression for the vault of a building] had fallen into ruin, the blessed bishop rebuilt it, giving it an elegant vaulted structure.

But the holy tomb, for some reason, happened to be outside. Wishing to move it inside, he summoned abbots and other religious men for this work and service. At this gathering the blessed Martyr performed a great miracle both for the people and for his confessor.

The sarcophagus was, as we said above, so massive that in our time not even three pairs of oxen could pull it. Since they spent a long time without finding a way to bring it inside, Saint Gregory lit candles with great chanting. He took hold of the sarcophagus at the Martyr’s head, while two priests moved it from the foot. They carried it with perfect ease into the crypt and set it down wherever they wished. This was a spectacle of no small wonder to the people.

A few years later, the blessed confessor received from travelers returning from Italy the history of the Martyr’s passion. From then on the holy Martyr also manifested himself to the people through many miracles. Without delay, Gregory ordered a large basilica to be built over the crypt. [Note: The *Chronicle of Saint Benignus* also relates that monks were established there by the blessed bishop under Abbot Eustadius. Paschasia is discussed below in *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 43.]

Nearby there is another basilica in which a certain religious woman named Paschasia is venerated. At that time the builders thought they saw an old woman coming out of the basilica itself, dressed in black, with white hair and a beautiful face. She addressed the builders as follows:

“Come, my beloved ones, complete this good work. Let the machines by which this structure is raised be lifted, and let the work be hastened, since it has such an executor. For if your eyes were permitted to behold what is taking place, you would certainly see that, while you labor, Benignus himself goes before you.”

After saying this, she entered the basilica from which she had emerged and appeared to no one again. The people of that time therefore believed that the blessed Paschasia had appeared there. [Note: What follows from this chapter is absent from Clar. b.]

Upon the stone on which her feet had been fastened with molten lead, small cavities were made, and many people pour wine or cider into them. If eyes afflicted with blurring or any wounds are anointed with it, the illness immediately departs and they are healed. I myself have clearly experienced this. For when my eyes were troubled by severe blurring, I was touched with this sacred ointment and was immediately freed from the pain.

When that bubonic plague came to the Auvergne region, which was driven away by the prayer of Saint Gallus the bishop [see *History*, book IV, chapter 5], and when the walls of houses and churches were suddenly marked and scratched with signs, my mother saw in a nocturnal vision what seemed to be the wine kept in our storerooms turned into blood.

As she lamented and said, “Woe is me, for my house has been marked with the plague,” a certain man said to her:

“Do you know that the day after tomorrow, which will be the Kalends of November, the passion of Benignus the martyr will be celebrated?”

“I know,” she replied.

“Go,” he said, “keep vigil the whole night in his honor, and arrange for Masses to be celebrated, and you will be freed from the plague.” [Note: That is, take care that they are celebrated. See *Gallican Liturgy*, book I, chapter 6, number 4.]

Awakening from sleep, she fulfilled what she had been commanded. Although the houses of the neighbors were marked, our house remained unharmed.

# CHAPTER LII  
## On Saint Symphorianus

The martyr Symphorianus completed his martyrdom at the city of Autun (A.D. 179, August 22). [Note: This chapter is absent from cod. Colb. tut. It is also absent, together with the following chapters through chapter 57 inclusive, from Clar. b; in another Clar. it is absent through chapter 56. We published the Acts of Saint Symphorianus among the genuine Acts of the Martyrs, p. 69, where we made further observations about him.]

At the place where he was struck with the sword and his blood flowed, a certain religious man picked up three stones together with the blood. He placed them in a silver chest and set them upon the holy altar of a church built of wooden boards at the fortress of Thigernum [see below, chapter 67], in the city of Auvergne.

At the time when King Theodoric of the Franks devastated that region [see *History*, book III, chapter 12], this fortress was burned by the enemy. When the house of God—which, as we said, had been built of wooden boards—caught fire and was consumed along with the burning of the other houses, the people lamented and said:

“If only the blessed relics had not perished!”

Meanwhile, when the fire had produced a great heap of embers, a sudden north wind blew and violently scattered in every direction the ashes left by the fire. Then behold, that silver chest appeared, shining unharmed like a brilliant star.

The clerics who were present gathered it and examined it. Finding that none of the blessed relics had been diminished, they marveled that amid such a powerful fire so delicate an object had been preserved—an object in which, so to speak, not only these relics but even a thousand pounds of silver or iron could have been melted without delay.

Truly, great power was manifested there. It strengthened the people in the worship of God and the honor of his name. They afterward built another basilica in the same place and placed the holy relics upon its altar.

# CHAPTER LIII  
## On the Blessed Marcellus of Chalon

Only a few memorials of the miracles of the blessed martyr Marcellus of Chalon have come down to us. [Note: Colb. tut. consistently has *Cabillonensis*. The published Acts of Saint Marcellus say that he belonged to the number of the martyrs of Lyon. When persecution was raging, he escaped from prison and encountered the prefect Priscus near Chalon. After being questioned and confessing that he was a Christian, he was buried in the earth up to his waist and died on the third day. King Guntram built a famous monastery at his tomb; we discussed it in the note on chapter 1 of Fredegar’s *Chronicle*.]

Although these may be considered small in what they report, they must nevertheless be attributed to the one who performs such things in each case.

An incident occurred that led Fedamius, the son of Eunomius, formerly a priest of Auvergne, to visit the city of Chalon (A.D. 179, September 4). He stayed as a guest at the basilica of the holy martyr Marcellus and received his provisions from the abbot of the place. He himself related what I am about to say.

“An argument arose between two men,” he said, “and while they were disputing, the quarrel reached the point at which they decided to settle it by oath. They entered the basilica of the holy Martyr. One of them raised his hands to swear, and when he tried to utter the Saint’s name with open mouth, his voice stuck in his throat, and his tongue could not move to perform its function.

“Nor did this seem enough to display the glory of the blessed athlete: while his hands remained raised, his entire body became stiff, as though made of bronze. A prayer was then offered for him, and he obtained release from the bonds imposed by the devil. After he had been freed, he himself confessed in his own words what he had done and corrected what he had negligently undertaken.”

# CHAPTER LIV  
## On Saint Valerianus

To this martyr is joined the blessed athlete Valerianus, his neighbor in blood and contest (A.D. 179, September 15). [Note: According to his published Acts, Valesianus escaped from the prison at Lyon in the same manner as Marcellus, was arrested at Trenorchium by the prefect Priscus, and, after various tortures, was beheaded. A very celebrated Benedictine monastery was added to the church built at his tomb, but it eventually passed to secular canons. The fortress of Trenorchium, also called Tinurtium or Tornusium, commonly Tournus, is only about twenty miles—that is, six leagues—from Chalon. See Valesius’s *Notitia*.]

He completed his contest and was buried at the fortress of Trinorcium, forty miles from the city of Chalon.

Gallus, the count of this city, was afflicted by the pain of a coeliac illness [Note: Colb. a has *caelaci*; another hand has *ciliaci*, that is, colic]. The disease had swollen his entire abdomen not merely with spasms but also with such distension that he was thought to have dropsy. He could eat nothing and take no drink, and, as a consequence of this affliction, he was wasting away from starvation.

When he was almost lifeless and saw that he was beyond hope, he asked to be carried to the tomb of the blessed Martyr. When he had been laid there, the priest Epirechius [Note: Colb. tut. has *Epiricius*], who governed that church at the time—a man of miracles and pure mind, as we ourselves saw with our own eyes—approached him and said:

“If you wish to become well, trust in the power of the glorious Martyr and vow that you will send one beam, with its fastenings, to restore the roof of this church. It will be your protection if you devoutly fulfill what you promise.”

Gallus prayed more earnestly, vowed what the priest had indicated, and immediately became well. Without anyone reminding him, he ordered the beam to be brought to the Saint’s basilica.

Behold what the Lord Jesus Christ grants on earth through the holy martyrs, whom he has glorified and received into the heavenly kingdoms. And rightly so: believing his holy name in their hearts, invoking him in their works, and confessing him in temptations, they followed the Lord not only as faithful servants but also encouraged others to follow through their example.

# CHAPTER LV  
## On the Martyrs Timothy and Apollinaris

Timothy and Apollinaris earned the heavenly kingdom after completing their martyrdom at the city of Reims (the date is uncertain, August 23). [Note: Two manuscripts have *Apollonaris*. The Acts of these martyrs relate that they suffered under Nero, together with the priest Maurus and many others, under the prefect Lampadius. This opinion is not accepted by those who admit no martyrs in Gaul before the time of Marcus Aurelius. They nevertheless seem to be earlier than the time of Maximian, for they are nowhere said to have suffered under the prefect Rictiovarus, like the other martyrs of Belgic Gaul from that period. On these saints, see Marlot, book I of *Metropolis of Reims*, chapter 21. Frodoardus gives their Acts almost in full but does not specify the date of their passion; he writes that Timothy came to Reims from the East and cites this chapter of Gregory. Eusebius, a distinguished man, built a basilica in their honor, in which, according to Frodoardus, Saint Remigius had asked to be buried. It still exists, distinguished by its chapter of canons and parish title, and is more notable because the relics of several martyrs are preserved there. Not far from it one can see an ancient cemetery commonly called the Martyrs’ cemetery. In it and in the neighboring places, bodies are found when the earth is dug up, fixed through the head and arms with large nails; they are thought to be the bodies of martyrs. They receive no public veneration, however, since they shine with no miracles and have not been claimed by the Church, as Optatus puts it.]

A devout man sought their relics and built a basilica in their honor. The bishop who was present sent them with honor through a priest.

As the priest was traveling, an importunate woman—who, I believe, was unworthy of the favor—came upon the road. After greeting the priest, she kissed the cloth in which the sacred ashes were wrapped and asked that some portion of them be given to her.

The priest hesitated for a long time and delayed giving her anything. Finally, overcome by her persistence, he divided off a small piece for her. He mounted his horse and began the journey entrusted to him. But although he struck both sides of the horse, he could not make it move. He himself was so weighed down that he could scarcely lift his head.

Understanding that he was being held by the power of the Martyrs, he was moved to a salutary repentance and took back what, through negligence, he had presumed to give away. Once he had returned it to the chest, he was allowed to depart.

# CHAPTER LVI  
## On Saint Eutropius

Eutropius, also a martyr of the city of Saintes, is said to have been sent into Gaul by the blessed Bishop Clement (second or third century, April 30). [Note: Laud., Bell., and Colb. a have *Eutropis*, and the chapter heading reads “On Eutropius the martyr.” Here too Gregory accepts a martyr from before the time of Marcus on the basis of popular tradition. The church of Saint Eutropius at Saintes, collapsing from age, was restored by Bishop Leontius, as Fortunatus sings in book I of his poems, poem 3. This is the Leontius who around the middle of the sixth century was bishop of Bordeaux. Toward the end of that century Palladius transferred the body of the same saint; it remained in the church bearing his name, together with an attached Cluniac monastery, until the immediately preceding century, when it was burned by the Calvinists. His Acts exist, but they are fabulous; for this reason Henschonius omitted them on April 30 in the Bollandists.]

Clement also consecrated him to the episcopal order. [Note: Cod. Laud. has “obtained the grace” of the episcopal order.] After he had completed the duties of this office and preached to unbelievers, the pagans rose against him—those whom the author of their envy did not permit to believe—and he victoriously fell when his head was struck.

Because, during the persecution then raging, he was neither buried in a worthy place nor honored as was proper by Christians, it was very nearly consigned to oblivion that he had been a martyr. This is said to have been revealed in the following manner.

After many years, a basilica was built in his honor. When the work was complete, Palladius [Note: He is famous in Gregory’s *History*, books VII and VIII, for appointing Faustus bishop of Aire in Novempopulania. He attended the fourth Council of Paris and the second Council of Mâcon. He received letters and holy relics from Gregory the Great.]—who at that time governed the episcopal see—summoned the abbots and arranged for the sacred ashes to be transferred to the place he had prepared.

When this had been done, two of the abbots opened the covering, saw the holy body, and examined the scar on its head where the edge of an axe had been driven in. But lest the physical vision be dismissed as meaningless, a spiritual instruction also followed. When the priests had lain down to rest the next night, the Martyr appeared in a vision to these two men and said:

“Know that the scar you saw on my head is the means by which I completed my martyrdom.”

Thus it became known to the people that he had been a martyr, because there was no history of his passion. [Note: A history of his passion does exist today, or rather a patchwork of fables, as we have said, entirely unworthy of belief. His book of Miracles, written in the twelfth century and published by the Bollandists under April 30, is nevertheless not without value.]

# CHAPTER LVII  
## On Saint Amarandus
Amarandus [Note: [Col. 0757D] Amarandus, or Amaranthus, is said to have completed his martyrdom in the time of Decius. He was buried near the village of Viancium, not far from the city of Albi, and there his sacred body remained until 1404, when it was transferred by Louis de Ambesta to the cathedral church of Saint Cecilia in the city [Col. 0758C].
