Concerning the church and monastery of Viancium, see our *History of the Vandal Persecution*, chapter 8, no. 8. We have nowhere seen the history of Saint Amarandus’s passion [Col. 0758D] that Gregory praises, or any other version.] who, having faithfully completed the course of his contest, lives buried in glory as a martyr near the city of Albi (A.D. 250, 7 November). As the history of his passion declares, his tomb long lay hidden beneath brambles and thorn bushes [Ed., [Col. 0757C] hedges], but, at the Lord’s command, it was revealed to the Christian people, and the crypt in which he rested was exposed and shone brightly.

But when, under pressure from hostile circumstances, that place had been abandoned by its inhabitants, people coming from far away sought to pay honor to the blessed Martyr as their own guardian. Accordingly, since Christian devotion frequently brought candles there, it happened one day that someone, because of the length of the journey, had brought no supply of fire with which to light his candle. He seized a flint and struck it with iron, as though he intended to draw out fire. Although he did this repeatedly, striking the stone with frequent blows, he could not bring forth any spark [Col. 0758A]; nevertheless, the candle that had already been fastened to the blessed tomb was kindled by a heavenly lamp. Thus what human industry had not accomplished was performed by the majesty of the divine power. When human effort ceased, heavenly service was supplied, and the candle was made radiant by the brilliance of the new light with which it was kindled.

When this had been made known to the people, no one afterward dared to bring a supply of fire for lighting the lamp. But after that place began once more to be continually inhabited by people, and houses in which fire could be kindled were present there, this miracle was no longer granted to the common people, although the place was more frequently made illustrious by other miracles.

## CHAPTER LVIII. Concerning Saint Eugenius

[Col. 0758B] Associated with this crypt is also that martyr of the [so-called] Honorifician persecution, Eugenius [Note: [Col. 0758D] One should read *Hunerician*. Here is celebrated Saint Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, who in the time of Huneric, king of the Vandals in Africa, vigorously defended the Catholic faith against the Arians by word, writings, and miracles. At length, however, by order of Trasamund, he was banished to Gaul, died at Albi, and was buried near Saint Amarandus; with him, as we said in the preceding chapter, he was transferred to the cathedral church. He is commemorated at Albi on 6 September, and in the commonly used martyrologies on 13 July. Gregory reproduced his letter in full in *History*, book II, chapter 3. For more about him, see Victor Vitensis, bishop, and the *History of the Vandal Persecution* appended to that work, chapter 8.]—the supreme ornament of the priestly dignity—whom the account of his own or his companions’ passion relates to have been driven into exile in this city (A.D. 505, 13 July).

Since he had shone with great virtues in the world and had already emerged victorious from the torments of martyrdom and exile, he learned through the Lord’s revelation the time of his calling, when he would be summoned to glory. In particular, he came to know what was hidden from the people: that he was to become the companion of the martyr Amarandus. He was directed to Amarandus’s tomb, and, prostrating himself on the ground, poured out a lengthy prayer to the Lord. Then, stretching his arms upon the pavement, he directed his spirit toward heaven. The Christians gathered it up and committed it to burial in the very crypt we have mentioned [Col. 0758C].

Once, when countless people had assembled for his festival, they brought many goods into the courtyard for sale. A young girl, one of the local inhabitants, approached a stall as though she intended to buy something. Seeing an item suitable for herself, she received it from the merchant. Immediately—sooner than words can say—she denied to another person that she had received what had been handed to her.

The merchant insisted: “I brought it to you with my own hand, and you carefully took it in order to examine it.” When she continued to deny this, the merchant said: “If, driven by greed, you are so obstinate in denying it, let the blessed martyr Eugenius judge the matter. If, at his tomb, after taking an oath, you declare that you did not receive it, I shall regard as no loss to me whatever I have lost.”

She promised that she could free herself from this oath and hurried to the tomb. But when she raised her hands to swear, her limbs suddenly failed and she became rigid; her feet were fixed to the pavement, and her voice stuck in her throat; only her open mouth gaped, deprived of speech.

When the merchant and the rest of the people saw this, he said: “May the article you took from me benefit you, girl. The punishment given through the Martyr is sufficient for me.” Saying this, he departed.

She remained in this torment for a very long time. At last, by the Martyr’s command, she spoke and openly confessed what she had wished to conceal.

“What are you doing, wretched greed? Why do you, a woman’s mind rather than a man’s, yield to the pursuit of things belonging to others? Why do you strike a strong breastplate of the mind with the little arrow of desire [Col. 0759B]? Why do you gather, O human being, talents of rusting gold, when you will burn with them in Gehenna? What good are profits that perish, which produce the loss of eternal life? In accordance with the Lord’s saying: ‘What does it profit a person to gain the whole world but suffer the loss of his soul? Or what exchange will a person give for his soul?’” (Matthew 16:26).

## CHAPTER LIX. Concerning the punishment of a certain thief

790 There is a church in the village of Icidiorum [Note: [Col. 0759D] This chapter is absent from Clar. a, and together with the following chapter from Clar. b. Colb. a has “Icioderensis.” We discussed this passage in the notes to book VI, chapter 12 of the *History*.], within the territory of the city of Tours. It is often made illustrious by sacred miracles and, as is customary, has windows closed by glass set into wood, so that they might supply the consecrated building with as much light as the world deserved.

A nocturnal and persistent thief attacked this church. Entering it at night and seeing that everything was carefully guarded by the custodians, and finding none of the sacred furnishings that he could carry away, he said to himself: “If I can find nothing else, I will at least take these very glass panes that I see and, having melted down the metal, obtain some gold for myself.”

He therefore removed and smashed the panes, took away the metal, and carried it into a village in the territory of Bourges. He placed the glass in a furnace and boiled it for three days, but could produce no object from it. Overcome by his crime and recognizing the divine judgment against him, he nevertheless did not turn away from his wickedness.

He sold the glass removed from the cauldron, which had been changed into certain little pellets [Col. 0760A], to merchants who came there, so that, having received the money, he might, like a new Gehazi, acquire perpetual leprosy. For on the day that completed a year after he had committed this theft [Al., “on the day on which”], his head was given over to swelling; his eyes too became so inflamed that they seemed ready to burst from their sockets. This happened to him every year on the day when he had committed the theft. The wretched man lamented the glass, which he could not recover from the journey on which he had sent it [Al., “which he could not recover because of the journey”].

## CHAPTER XL. Concerning the martyrs Rogatianus and Donatianus, and Similinus the confessor

Near the city of Nantes two martyrs were slain in the name of Christ (A.D. 290, 24 May). One was called Rogatianus, the other Donatianus [Note: [Col. 0759D] So Clar. a; the other manuscripts and the old printed editions have “Donatus.” We have given the account of these martyrs’ passion among the *Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 295, and Henschenius published it under 24 May in the Bollandists. Baronius postpones their martyrdom until the year 303.].

There is also there Similinus [Note: [Col. 0759D] Bell. has “Similianus,” commonly Saint Sambin. He is listed third among the bishops of Nantes in the commonly used catalogues, but we have no certain information about his date.] 791, a great confessor (A.D. 310, 16 June).

When the aforesaid city was surrounded by a barbarian siege in the time of King Clovis [Note: [Col. 0759D] Cointius assigns this siege to the final years of Clovis I, that is, to 510 or the following year, although the city of Nantes was under his authority in 511. For Epiphanius of Nantes subscribed that year to the First Council of Orléans.] (about A.D. 510), and sixty days had already passed in this distress, at about midnight men in white garments, carrying shining candles, appeared to the people as they came out from the basilica of the blessed Martyrs [Note: [Col. 0759D] This basilica still exists today, bearing a parish title, as does the basilica of Saint Similinus, whose titular priest is named by one of the canons of the cathedral church and is therefore called “of Saint Similinus.” It is distinct from the abbey of Saints Rogatianus and Donatianus in the territory of Nantes, mentioned in a charter of King Odo dated 893 [Col. 0760D], book VI of *De Re Diplomatica*, no. 121.]. And behold, another choir resembling it came forth from the basilica of Bishop Similinus.

When they joined one another, exchanged greetings, and devoted themselves to prayer, each group returned to the place from which it had come. Immediately the entire hostile army, terrified by immense fear, withdrew from the place in such sudden flight that, when daylight came, none of them could be found.

This power mentioned above appeared to a certain Chillonius [Clar. a: Chillinus], who was then in command of that army. He had not yet been reborn from water and the Holy Spirit. Immediately cut to the heart, he turned to the Lord, was begotten through a second birth, and testified in a loud voice that Christ is the Son of the living God.

## CHAPTER LXI. Concerning the relics of Blessed Nazarius

In the territory of the city of Nantes [Note: [Col. 0760D] Several manuscripts, including Clar. b, in which the preceding chapter is absent, read: “In the territory also of that city itself, in …” Here, too, the final marginal note reads: “near the city of Nantes.” The place below Nantes still bears the name Saint-Nazaire. Besides a parish church, it has a priory subject to the monastery of Saint-Albin of Angers; from this passage I infer that, in Gregory’s time, an abbot presided over a community of men there. Which Nazarius this was cannot be determined, since three men named Nazarius are commemorated on 12 June: the first at Milan with the boy Celsus, discovered by Saint Ambrose of Milan; also two martyrs bearing the same name, if indeed they were distinct; one at Embrun; and a third at Rome, whose body was brought from Rome to Gaul in 765 by Chrodegang, bishop of Metz. This led to the foundation of the celebrated abbey of Lorsch in the diocese of Worms.], in a certain village above the channel of the Loire, the relics of Blessed Nazarius are preserved (A.D. …, 12 June).

At one time [Col. 0761A] a devout man placed upon the altar of that basilica a belt of the purest gold, carefully fashioned with all its fittings [Note: [Col. 0761C] It was customary at that time to place objects offered to God upon the altar [Col. 0761D]. See Bignon, book I of the *Formulas of Marculf*, formula 1.], praying that the Martyr’s power might deign to assist him in his affairs.

After he departed, a certain Britto, one of the retainers of Waroch, count of the Britons [Note: [Col. 0761D] They think this happened during the war begun in 590, concerning which see Gregory, *History*, book X, chapter 9.], who had arrived there first with him, violently removed the belt’s fittings and demanded the belt itself as well (A.D. 590).

The presbyter resisted, saying: “These things belong to God and have been given to the holy Martyr for the relief of the poor, so that those who serve this church with faithful devotion may not suffer the worst hunger. Therefore you ought rather to bring something here than to take something away.”

The abbot’s preaching did not soften the greedy man’s heart. Instead, becoming more inflamed, he began to threaten him and say: “Unless you immediately hand over the belt, you will be killed by my hand.”

[Col. 0761B] Then the abbot, overcome, placed the item upon the altar where the sacred relics are covered, saying: “Here is the little mesh-work item you seek; if you have no fear of the Martyr’s power, take it. For, as we trust, he will be the judge at once if you dare to take it.”

Fearing nothing, the man took it and ordered that his horse be prepared before the very entrance of the basilica. The priest said to him: “No one has ever dared to mount a horse in this place. I beg you, give glory to God and honor the Martyr, lest you suffer some evil.”

But he disregarded the priest’s orders. Having mounted his horse in the sacred courtyard, when he came to leave [Note: [Col. 0761D] Others read, “having mounted the horse,” etc.; the manuscripts have “when he came to leave.” Clar. a, Colb. a, and Clar. b, in another hand, read “he wished to leave.”], he struck his head against the upper threshold of the gate, fell to the ground with his skull shattered, and was carried by his men into the hut of a poor man nearby. There he immediately breathed out his spirit.

When Waroch heard this, he restored the things that the man had taken and, terrified with fear, contributed much from his own possessions.

## CHAPTER LXII. Concerning the fifty Theban martyrs

There is near the city of Cologne a basilica in which fifty men from that sacred Theban legion are said to have completed their martyrdom in the name of Christ (A.D. 286, 10 October) [Note: [Col. 0761D] What follows through the words of chapter 69, “They also report,” is absent from Clar. b. It is an old tradition that many martyrs from the Theban legion suffered at Cologne and in neighboring places. Helinandus, or whoever the author may be, gathers much concerning them in a sermon published by Surius under 10 October. He interprets the “Golden Saints” praised here as Saint Gereon and his companions, although they are said to have been considerably more than fifty. He thinks their basilica was built by Helena, mother of Constantine the Great, and that ministers were assigned to it to sing the divine praises [Col. 0762C]. He calls it the monastery of Saint Gereon [Col. 0762D], which today is a distinguished collegiate church.].

Because it shines with an admirable work made somehow golden by mosaic, the inhabitants chose to call the basilica itself the Golden Saints.

At one time, when the head of Bishop Eberegisilus [Note: [Col. 0762D] He was appointed by King Childebert in 590 to suppress disturbances in the monastery of Poitiers, as Gregory writes in book X of the *History*, chapter 15.]—who was then bishop of this city—was shaken by severe pains, he was staying in a country estate near the town, greatly weakened by the illness, as we have said. He sent his deacon to the basilica of the Saints.

Since there is said to be a well in the middle of that church into which the Saints were collectively thrown after their martyrdom, the deacon brought the bishop some dust collected from it. But when he touched his head with it, all the pain immediately disappeared.

## CHAPTER LXIII. Concerning Saint Mallosus

The body of the holy martyr Mallosus was discovered by this same bishop in the following manner (A.D. 286, 10 October).

Rumor had it that he had completed his martyrdom at the town of Bertunum [Note: [Col. 0762D] Cod. Colb. a has “Bertinensem”; Colb. tut. has “Bertunensem.”], but the people did not know where he rested. There was nevertheless an oratory there in which his name was invoked.

The aforesaid bishop built a basilica in his honor, intending that, if he should receive some revelation concerning the Martyr, he might, with the Lord’s consent, transfer his blessed limbs there.

Finally, at the side of the basilica—that is, in the wall that stood on the side of the oratory—he constructed an apse [Note: [Col. 0762D] Clar. b reads “he gathered the apse”], awaiting the mercy of the Lord to reveal what he should order concerning the Martyr.

Afterward, a certain deacon from Metz was led in a vision to learn where the Martyr rested. A short time later he came to the bishop and, as though recounting sure signs that he had seen in the vision, although he had never previously been there, said to the bishop: “Dig here, and you will find the body of the Saint—in the middle of the apse.”

He dug down about seven feet [Col. 0762C]. Immediately the scent of an immense fragrance reached his nostrils, and he said: “I believe in Christ, who has shown me his Martyr, since this sweetness has surrounded me.” As he continued digging, he found the holy body unharmed. He raised a loud cry, “Glory to God in the highest,” and caused the entire clergy to sing with him.

After the hymn had been sung, he transferred the holy body to the basilica and buried it with due praise.

They also report that the martyr Victor was buried there [Note: [Col. 0762D] In Colb. a the word “martyr” is absent. If it is true, as some believe, that this martyr belonged to the Theban legion and that, at the place where he suffered with many others, he gave the place the name “Saints”—from which the common people formed “Xantum,” a town in the territory of Cleves—we can determine the location of the town of Bertunum. For Victor and Mallosus are said to have rested in the same place, and certain ancient martyrologies celebrate them together.], but we have not yet learned through revelation who he was.

## CHAPTER LXIV. Concerning the martyr Patroclus

Patroclus [Note: [Col. 0762D] This chapter is absent from Colb. tut.; everything through chapter 74 is likewise absent from Clar. a.] too, a martyr buried near the city of Troyes, frequently showed himself to be God’s friend through many miracles (A.D. 259 or 273, 21 January).

There was a small oratory over him, served by only one cleric. The people of the place rendered the Martyr only limited service because an account of his passion was not readily available. For it was customary among country people to venerate more attentively those saints whose contests they read about.

A man therefore came from a distant journey and brought a little book containing this contest. He handed it to the reader whom, as we have said, we know to have served at that place. After reading it through, the reader was very glad and, by lamplight during the night, quickly copied it.

When the people had departed, he presented to his bishop what he had found, thinking that by this he would win the priest’s favor. But the bishop did not believe him and judged that the text had been fabricated. He rebuked the cleric, who had been beaten, and ordered him to leave, saying: “It is clear that you composed these things according to your own wishes, for you never found them with anyone.”

795 Much later, so that the Martyr’s power would not remain hidden, an army went into Italy and brought back the history of this passion [Note: [Col. 0763C] In those times there were Frankish expeditions into Italy, on account of which someone may have brought the Acts of Saint Patroclus from Italy to Gaul. It is uncertain whether they are the Acts that have survived to us, in which Patroclus is said to have been beheaded by order of Aurelian. Aurelian came into Gaul in 273 and the following years [Col. 0763D]. Others, however, more plausibly think that the name Aurelian designates the governor. Bruno, bishop of Cologne and brother of the emperor Otto the Great, obtained the relics of this holy Martyr from Ansegisus, bishop of Troyes, and deposited them at Soest, a town of Westphalia in the diocese of Münster, where they are still preserved. See the Bollandists, 21 January. Camuzat transcribed the history of the translation from Rotger, a monk, in the *Promptuarium*, fol. 434.], just as it had been written down by the cleric.

Then the bishop, greatly ashamed, recognized that what the cleric had said was true. From that time the people began to honor the Martyr more greatly. They built a basilica over him and devoutly celebrated his festival every year.

## CHAPTER LXV. Concerning the basilica of Saint Antolianus the martyr

Antolianus [Note: [Col. 0763D] Gregory discussed Antolianus in book I of the *History*, chapter 31, where, among the other martyrs said to have suffered during the invasion of Gaul by Chrocus, king of the Alamanni, in the time of the emperors Valerian and Gallienus, he seems to list Antolianus and other martyrs of Auvergne. In the book *On the Churches of Clermont*, Saint Antolianus is said to rest in the church of Saint Gallus; but after that church was destroyed, his sacred body was transferred to the church of Saint Illidius. Others nevertheless maintain that, after the church of Saint Gallus was destroyed in the tenth century, the relics of Saint Antolianus were transferred to the Benedictine monastery of Cantogil [Col. 0764C], in the modern diocese of Saint-Flour, where they are still said to be kept with many other relics of the saints that make the place illustrious.] completed his martyrdom near the city of Clermont (A.D. 255, 6 February).

Alchima, the sister, and Placidina, the wife of Bishop Apollinaris, wishing to build a church in his honor, removed many bodies of saints while laying the foundations [Note: [Col. 0764C] Sirmond thinks this should be restored in this way in his notes to Apollinaris Sidonius, book III, letter 13; the truth of the matter requires it [Col. 0764D]. See the notes above on books III, chapters 2 and 12 of the *History*. I do not deny, however, that I have found this reading nowhere in the printed or manuscript editions. The printed editions of Badius and others read: “Alchima and Placidina’s sister and wife … wishing.” The Roman and Colb. tut. read: “Alchima, the sister and wife of Placidina … wishing”; Laud., Bec., and Colb. a read “wishing.”], not knowing the merit of those whose tombs they had discovered.

Since they could not bury them individually because of the multitude of other tombs that had long filled the place, they threw the gathered mass of bones into a single pit and covered it with earth. This deed, which was not pleasing to God or the holy Martyr [Note: [Col. 0764D] Let those consider what sacrilege they commit who, setting aside all religion, do not hesitate so easily to dig up the bodies of the dead according to their own will.], was revealed in a vision to someone.

The man saw the blessed Antolianus complaining with the other saints and saying: “Woe to me, because on my account many of my brothers have been dishonored. Nevertheless I say that those who began this work cannot bring it to completion.”

And so it happened.

After they had raised the walls over the altar of that building, they erected a tower with columns, pharos, and Heraclean figures supporting crossing arches [Note: [Col. 0764D] Most manuscripts read this way; others, together with the printed editions, have “from columns.” Below, most manuscripts read *eraclis* or *heraclis*. The Bollandist explains the passage as referring to arches supported by telamons or atlantes, whom Gregory calls “Heracles,” as if “Hercules.” Pharos, he thinks, are beams that rose like a lighthouse.], adding a remarkable painted design to the vault, fashioned with varied colors.

The work was so elegant and delicate that, after a long period in which it had been divided by frequent cracks, it seemed almost to hang in ruin. When Bishop Avitus [Note: [Col. 0764D] The bishop of Clermont, frequently mentioned by Gregory.] saw the danger and anticipated the future collapse of the columns, he ordered the beams, planks, and tiles to be removed.

When these had been taken away and no supports had been placed beneath the columns, the builders left the structure to eat, by God’s will. As the others also withdrew from the basilica, the column, burdened by its immense weight, fell with a great crash upon and around the altar. The building was filled with a cloud of dust from the shattered mortar.

The priest, pale with fear and sighing over the possibility of two disasters—both that the marble might have been broken and that someone from the people might have perished—could not determine what damage had occurred. No one could approach because of the cloud of dust.

After two hours, when the cloud had cleared, they entered either to gather the bodies of the dead or to examine the fragments of the columns. They discovered that no one had perished. They also marveled that the altar was unharmed: although the columns had struck it from such a height, they had caused it no damage.

What more is there to say? They found everything intact and saw that all had been preserved. They glorified the Martyr and perceived the power of God, who had thus kept the altar and the columns unharmed.

In the territory of this city, the martyr Julianus (A.D. 304, 28 August) also earned the palm of the contest by legitimately fighting the struggle [Col. 0765A]. We have explained the miracles concerning him that have come down to us in the book that we specifically undertook to write about his miracles [Note: [Col. 0765C] This is the second book, which you have below.].

## CHAPTER LXVI. Concerning a theft committed in the church of Saint Saturninus

In the same territory, at the time when Chramnus [Note: [Col. 0765C] Colb. a has “Condramnos.” For Chramnus’s crimes, see book IV of the *History*, chapters 13 and 16.] went to Clermont (after A.D. 250, 29 November), while various crimes were being committed by his agents, five men secretly attacked the sacred oratory of the house at Iciacum [Note: [Col. 0765C] The same manuscript has in the margin, in an ancient second hand: “Of the oratory at Iciodorum” [Col. 0765D]. The town of Iciodorum—Issoire—is well known among the people of Auvergne. It once had a monastery famous for its schools, where Saint Praejectus learned his letters; it is mentioned below. The title in the index of Bell. and Laud. supports this: “Concerning the oratory at Iciodorum in Auvergne, where Saint Saturninus rests.” Colb. a has: “Concerning … Iciodorum … where Saint Symphorianus …” It is more plausible to retain the word *Iciacensis*. The village apparently designated here is Issac, commonly so called, one Gallic league from Ricomagus, where the parish church still recognizes Saint Saturninus of Toulouse as its patron.].

The relics of Saint Saturninus were kept there. Breaking in, they removed little cloaks and the other ornaments used in the ministry and departed under cover of night.

The presbyter recognized the theft and searched among the neighbors, but could find no clue concerning what had been taken. The robbers immediately moved into the territory of Orléans. After dividing the goods, each took his share.

Soon, however, divine vengeance pursued them: four were killed in riots. The fifth survived and claimed the entire inheritance of this theft for himself. But when he carried the stolen goods into his house, his eyes were immediately covered with blood and he was blinded.

Then, overcome both by suffering and by divine inspiration, he made a vow, saying: “If God regards my misery and restores my sight, I will return to that holy place what I have taken.”

When he prayed this with tears, he recovered his sight. As he approached the town of Orléans, by God’s providence he met a deacon from Auvergne. After handing the goods over to him, he earnestly begged him to return them to the oratory. The devout deacon fulfilled his request.

## CHAPTER LXVII. Concerning Saint Genesius of Auvergne

In very recent times (A.D. …, 28 October), in the territory of the city of Clermont, which adjoins the castle of Thiers, Saint Genesius [Note: [Col. 0765D] In Colb. tut., here and in the index, he is called a bishop, mistakenly, as is clear from the context, for he completed his martyrdom *in white garments*, that is, within the first week after his baptism. Another Genesius was bishop of Auvergne toward the end of the seventh century and is commemorated on 3 June. His Acts exist, but deserve little credence. [Col. 0766C] He is said to have arrived at Arles from Greece with his mother Genesia while fleeing persecution, and to have been baptized there by Saint Trophimus. Coming from there to Auvergne, he found Austremonius there, who sent him to Saint Serenatus. Near Thiers he was seized and killed by pagans in the eighteenth year of his age. He is commonly called Genesius the Child (*saint Genez l’enfant*), so that he may more easily be distinguished from other saints of the same name.] revealed himself in the following manner.

A certain poor man lost the oxen he used for plowing when they accidentally slipped from his sight. Although he searched for them anxiously, he could not find them. The following night a certain man appeared to him in a vision and said: “Go along the road that leads to the forest, and you will find the oxen you are diligently seeking, near a marble stone, pulling up an abundance of grass. Yoke them to the cart, bring the marble, and set it upon the tomb near the road. For I am Genesius, who speak these things to you. That mound is mine; clothed in white garments, I departed from this world through martyrdom.”

The man arose at dawn, found the oxen beside the stone, and did as he had been instructed in the vision. A miracle was not lacking here either: the immense stone, which many pairs of oxen could scarcely have moved, was carried by only two oxen.

Because of this, many sick people come there, fulfilling the promises they made in their vows, and receive health.

When Avitus, bishop of that city, heard this, he built a large basilica over the Saint’s tomb [Note: [Col. 0766D] A monastery was attached to the basilica. After the middle of the eighth century it was governed by Joseph, an abbot who is said to have been King Pepin’s representative in the account of the translation of Saint Austremonius, which took place at that time. It was later united to the Cluniac order while retaining the title of abbey, and it still exists today, commonly called Thiern or Thiers, in lower Auvergne.], consecrated it, and ordered his festival to be celebrated there [Col. 0766B]. Now, as we have said, a great multitude of people comes there with vows and returns with health. He also made this basilica illustrious with relics of Saint Genesius of Arles.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. Concerning Genesius of Arles the martyr, or, Concerning the reviving mulberry tree

This martyr Genesius completed his contest by the severing of his neck in the name of Christ, at Arles—that is, in the same city—through the fervor of his powerful faith (A.D. …, 25 August) [Note: [Col. 0766D] We have included his passion, attributed to Saint Paulinus, among the *Genuine Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 603. The time of his suffering is uncertain. His feast is celebrated on 25 August. He is praised by Prudentius, Eucherius, bishop of Lyon, or by the so-called Gallican Eusebius, by Fortunatus, and by others.].

There is a tree there, said to be the one at which he was beheaded. It is a mulberry tree, from which, through the Martyr’s intervention, many benefits have often been granted to the sick. But as time passed, and many people removed its branches and bark for the sake of healing, it dried up.

Nevertheless, it still lives for those who faithfully ask, providing similar remedies from what remains of the trunk.

## CHAPTER LXIX. Concerning the miracles performed through Blessed Genesius

There was once a bridge over the river Rhône at the place where Blessed Genesius is said to have swum. On the day of his solemnity, because it had been set upon boats, it began to sway after its chains broke. As the boats themselves split apart under the excessive weight of the people, they submerged the crowd in the river channel [Col. 0767A].

Then, with everyone placed in danger, they all cried out with one voice: “Most blessed Genesius, rescue us through the power of your holiness, lest the people perish who have faithfully come to celebrate your solemn festival with devotion.”

Immediately, when the wind blew, the entire crowd was brought back to the shore, and they marveled that they had been saved through the Martyr’s power [Note: [Col. 0767D] For this miracle, see the homily of Saint Hilary, bishop of Arles, in Surius.].

The railings of the blessed tomb were also frequently smashed by the Lombards or other enemies. But men seized by demons, or gripped by madness and raging, or tearing themselves with their own teeth, took away nothing of what they had violently seized.

They also report that in this city [Note: [Col. 0767D] Clar. b likewise has this, although the preceding material is omitted.] there was a woman who had been accused by her husband of a crime, but against whom it had not been proved at all. A judge decided that she should be immersed in water [Note: [Col. 0767D] Perhaps as a test of the crime, as in the following chapter; this examination was called the judgment of water. Medieval authors mention it frequently. See Bignon on title 55 of the Salic Law.].

When an immense stone had been tied to her neck with ropes [Col. 0767B], she was thrown from a boat into the Rhône. But she prayed for the help of the blessed Martyr and, invoking his name, said: “Holy Genesius, glorious Martyr, who sanctified these waters by swimming through them [Note: [Col. 0767D] He crossed the Rhône by swimming while being pursued by officers, as the author of his passion and Gallican Eusebius relate], rescue me according to my innocence.”

Immediately she began to be carried upon the water. When the people saw this, they received her into a boat and brought her unharmed to the Saint’s basilica. Neither her husband nor the judge ever questioned her again.

## CHAPTER LXX. Concerning a certain woman unjustly accused of adultery by her husband
800 O how greatly innocence prevails, how much a pure mind deserves! For another woman likewise received from her husband a charge of adultery. After denying it for a very long time before the judge, and since she could not be overcome by her own confession, she was sentenced to be submerged. Then, as the people flocked together to watch, she was led to the bridge of the river Arar. A millstone was fastened to her neck with a rope, and they hurled her into the river, while her husband shouted down at her:

“Wash away now in the abundant waters your fornications and impurities, with which you have often stained my bed.”

But the mercy of the Lord, who does not permit the innocent to perish, had provided a stake beneath the waters, which no human being could see. Receiving the rope, it supported the woman so that she did not reach the bottom of the river. Thus both were beneath the waters: the woman, and the stone balanced upon that stake as upon a lance.

When the sun was already approaching sunset, the woman’s relatives begged the judge for permission to search the riverbed for the corpse of their kinswoman. Having received permission, they descended to the place where the woman had been thrown. They saw her hanging there with the stone and, having cast a hook, drew her out. Understanding that she was alive, they quickly carried her to the basilica, which was near the river; for they feared that the judge might order her to be submerged again.

They asked the woman how she had been able to live beneath the water. She replied:

“It seemed to me no otherwise than a dream. I felt the water no further, except when I was thrown into it and descended, or when I was taken up from it again and rose.”

Everyone marveled that she had been unable to die in such peril. The faith of her pure [another reading: “own”] conscience had saved her, and the Lord, whom she had continually implored. Afterwards, when she had been restored to her parents, she was questioned no further either by the judge or by her husband. But let us return to the virtues of the martyrs.

## CHAPTER LXXI. On Ferreolus and Ferrucio

The city of the Vesontians [Note: This chapter and the three following are absent from Clermont manuscript B.], also illuminated by its own martyrs, rejoices in many present miracles. In a hidden crypt there are buried two martyrs, Ferreolus and Ferrucio, as their Passion [Note: Surius published the Acts of these martyrs. Their feast, with a proper Mass, is found in the Gothic Missal edited by Thomas and Mabillon, *Gallican Liturgy*, book III, no. 53. Learned men consider that their martyrdom occurred at the beginning of the reign of Antoninus Caracalla. They had been sent to Vesontio, where they suffered, by Saint Irenaeus for the purpose of preaching the faith.] relates (A.D. 211, 16 June).

Now it happened at a certain time that my sister’s husband fell gravely ill as his fever grew stronger. When he had already lain gasping on his bed for the space of four months, so that his grieving wife thought of nothing except what was necessary for his burial, she went weeping and sorrowful to the basilica of the Saints. Falling prostrate before the tombs, with her palms and face stiffened by grief, she pressed herself against the pavement.

By chance, as she stretched out the palm of her right hand, it covered a leaf of sage that had been scattered in the crypt in honor of the Martyrs. After she had risen from the tombs with tears and prolonged prayer, thinking that she had grasped in her hand a piece of the linen with which she was clothed—as commonly happens—she kept her palm closed. When she had left the basilica and opened her hand, she marveled at the leaf of the herb. Astonished at what it could be, she recognized it as a heavenly gift divinely granted to her, so that through it the Martyrs’ power might come to the aid of the sick man.

Returning home therefore now more joyful, she diluted the leaf in water and gave it to her husband to drink. As soon as he drank it with complete faith, he immediately deserved to regain perfect health.

## CHAPTER LXXII. On Saint Dionysius, Bishop of Paris

802 Dionysius, bishop given to the city of Paris, became a martyr [Note: From what Gregory wrote in *History*, book I, chapter 30, Dionysius suffered after A.D. 250. If credence is given to other records, which attest that he was sent into Gaul by Saint Clement, his Passion must be assigned to the second century. This was the opinion of the fathers of the Council of Paris concerning sacred images in A.D. 825. See Mabillon, volume I of the *Analecta*, p. 63, and King Theodoric IV’s decree in the appendix to this work.] (A.D. 250, 9 October).

When King Sigibert came with his army to that city and burned a very large part of its suburbs [Note: From this passage Launoius and his followers tried to infer that the basilica of Dionysius and the martyrs’ tombs then stood within the city of Paris. But if this passage is compared with book IV of the *History*, chapter 44, where the suburbs around the city are said to have been burned by Sigibert’s army, the difficulty disappears—especially since Gregory and other authors of his age often understood by the city’s “suburbs” places situated at a considerable distance from the city itself. Cointius proves this decisively at A.D. 574, no. 6, and Hadrian Valesius discusses it at length in part II of his *Defense* against Launoius, where he treats the location, monastic status, and other matters concerning the basilica of Dionysius. See above, column 651, in the notes to chapter 79 of the *Chronicle of Fredegar*.], one of his leading men hurried to the basilica of the aforesaid martyr—not out of devotion to prayer, but merely to steal something from the church. When he found the doors opened and the temple empty of its custodians, he boldly seized and carried away a silk cloth, adorned with gold and gems, which covered the holy tomb.

When he reached the camp, he had to travel by boat. His servant-boy, whom he then held in trust, boarded the vessel with him, two hundred gold pieces hanging around his neck. Suddenly, touched by no one, he fell from the boat, was overwhelmed by the waters, and could never be found. The other man, seeing God’s judgment upon himself through the loss of the boy and the gold, quickly returned to the shore from which he had departed and restored the cloth to the tomb with the utmost haste. Yet although he had done this, he did not reach the day on which he had committed these acts when the year had come around again.

Another man, who did not fear trampling upon the holy tomb, was trying to strike down a golden dove with a spear. His feet slipped on either side, because the tomb was turreted [Note: That is, pointed like a pyramid—not because a large tower had ever been erected above the tomb. See Valesius, *Defense against Launoius*, part I, final chapter.]. His testicles were crushed, and, with the spear fixed in his side, he was found lifeless. No one should doubt that this happened not by chance but by God’s judgment.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. On Saint Quintinus of the Viromandenses

803 At the town of the Viromandenses in Gaul rests the martyr Quintinus [Note: Saint Quintinus is recorded in the published Acts as having suffered under Rictiovarus and therefore during the persecution of Maximian. He gave his name to the city of the Viromandenses, now famous under the name of Saint-Quentin, where there is an important collegiate church that was once the seat of the bishops of the Viromandenses, before Saint Medard transferred the episcopal see to Noyon. Learned men nevertheless dispute whether Augusta Viromanduorum stood where Quintinopolis is now seen on the Somme River, or where a Premonstratensian abbey and the village called Viromandus—still known as Vermand—survive. See Cointius at A.D. 531; Valesius in his *Notitia*; Samson; Hemeraeus; Vassorius; and others.] (A.D. 287, 31 October). His blessed body was discovered by a certain religious woman who had long been blind [Note: In the published Acts she is called Eusebia, a noble Roman matron. Saint Audoenus describes another discovery of Saint Quintinus, made by Saint Eligius, in the *Life* of that saint, book II, chapter 6.].

But as soon as the body had been lifted from the bottom of the river (A.D. 342), it produced a miracle: when it first came to light, it restored sight to the blinded eyes of the woman’s face [Note: Several manuscripts read *faciem* (“face”); *faciei* (“of the face”) should be read].

In this same city one of the thieves secretly stole a presbyter’s horse. The presbyter found him and reported him to the judge. Without delay he was seized, bound, and subjected to punishment; indicating his deed with his own mouth, he was condemned to the gallows.

But the presbyter feared that the man’s soul might be taken away because of the loss he had suffered. He begged the judge to spare his life and release the guilty man from punishment, saying that it was enough for him that, through so many kinds of torture, the thief had declared what he had done. But the judge’s severity could not be softened by any prayers, and he condemned the guilty man to the gallows.

Then the presbyter fell prostrate in tears at the tomb of the blessed Martyr and prayed earnestly:

“I beg you, most glorious athlete of Christ, to rescue this poor man from the hand of unjust death, lest it become a reproach to me if this man dies because of my accusation. Show, I beg you, your power, so that the man whom human harshness cannot release [Note: Two manuscripts read: “whom human wickedness cannot release.” Colbert manuscript A reads: “whom it refused to release.”] you may free by the moderating force of gentle mercy.”

While the priest was making this tearful prayer, the gallows’ bonds broke apart, and the condemned man fell to the ground. When the judge heard this, he was terrified by fear and, astonished at the divine power, dared to harm him no further.

## CHAPTER LXXIV. On Genesius, Martyr of Bigorre

[Note: We found this chapter in the Floriacensis manuscript, written approximately six hundred years ago. Not only does its title, as in the other manuscripts, read “On Genesius, martyr of Bigorre,” but the martyr’s name—absent from the others—also appears in the text of the chapter itself, in these words: “There is another martyr within the territory of the city of Bigorre,” and so forth.]

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read: “On another certain martyr.” But who that Genesius was, it has not been possible to discover.]

804 There is another martyr within the territory of the city of Bigorre [Note: That is, the territory of Bigorre, where the city of Tarbes stands. See the notes to *History*, book IX, chapter 6.], possessing the dignity of the priesthood, whose history of martyrdom is read among the inhabitants of the place.

While he was still alive in the body (A.D. . . .), by his prayers he obtained that a long-dried chestnut tree should return to greenness. Since marvelous things are often displayed in his basilica over the sick, this is more remarkable than the others: a lily that had long before been picked and dried blossoms again on his feast, so that on that day the people see fresh flowers which they had previously seen withered.

At his tomb, too, a false oath often brought forward by the faithless is refuted by the Martyr’s power, so that one who had arrived lifted up by presumption departs corrected.

## CHAPTER LXXV. On Saint Sigismund, King

The Lord often weakens the arrogance of a stubborn mind with the rod of correction, in order to restore it through reverence for the worship of God [Note: Thus Colbert manuscript A and Clermont manuscript A. The other manuscripts read “reverence.” The printed editions read “generation.”], as manifest faith once reports in the case of King Sigismund [Note: Laude, Bellovacensis, and Colbert manuscript A read “Sigimund.” He is discussed at greater length in *History*, books III, chapters 5 and 6, where the monastery of Agaunum and the perpetual psalmody are also treated in the notes.] (A.D. 523, 1 May).

After his son had been killed at the instigation of his wicked wife, Sigismund, pierced with remorse, went to Agaunum. There, prostrate before the tombs of the most blessed martyrs of the happy legion [Note: That is, Maurice and the other martyrs discussed in the following chapter. We discussed this name in the observations on their Acts, among the *Sincere Acts of the Martyrs*, chapter 286.], he performed penance [Note: Valesius had written that Sigismund then assumed the monastic habit, in book VII of his *Frankish History*. He says this occurred toward the end of the preface to volume II, in the year 523, when, under the consulship of Maximus, according to the Chronicle of Marius of Avenches, Sigismund was handed over by his own people, brought into Gaul in monastic dress, and killed.].

He prayed that, whatever offenses he had committed, divine vengeance might repay him in this world, so that he might be acquitted at the judgment if the evils he had done were requited to him before he departed from the world. There he also established daily psalmody [Note: Colbert manuscript A reads “a choir of daily psalmody,” and does so consistently. The other reading is nevertheless preferable, as we have already noted.] and enriched the place most abundantly both in lands and in other possessions.

Afterwards he was captured with his sons by King Chlodomer and killed at Chlodomer’s command. He was brought back to the same place and buried there. That he was admitted into the company of the Saints is manifested by what now occurs: for if those who are now afflicted with chills devoutly celebrate Masses in his honor and offer an oblation to God for his repose [Note: This Mass is found in the ancient Gallican Sacramentary of the monastery of Bobbio, edited by Mabillon; we shall give it in the appendix. The oblation “for the repose of Saint Sigismund” is here said in order to give thanks to God for his repose, or in his honor, as Gregory puts it here. Thus in the Mozarabic Missal an offering is made “for the spirits of the departed,” that is, confessors.], their trembling is immediately suppressed, their fevers extinguished, and they are restored to their former health.

## CHAPTER LXXVI. On the Saints of Agaunum, or On Saint Maurice and His Companions

There is also great power at the tombs of the aforesaid martyrs, of whom, leaving aside many things, I have chosen to touch upon a few [Note: Their Passion, written by Saint Eucherius, bishop of Lyon, was published among the *Sincere Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 289, where we made several observations concerning these same holy martyrs and the Happy Legion, p. 286. See also Brouwer on Fortunatus, book II, poem 14.].

A certain woman brought her only son to this monastery and handed him over to the abbot to be educated, so that, when he had become a cleric, he might be devoted to the holy offices (A.D. 286, 22 September). When he had been instructed in spiritual learning and was singing psalms with the other clerics in the choir, he was struck by a slight fever and breathed out his spirit.

His bereaved mother ran weeping to attend the funeral and buried her son. Yet the tears shed at the funeral were not enough for her grief. Every day she came and wailed over her son’s tomb, uttering loud cries.

At last blessed Maurice appeared to her in a nocturnal vision and said:

“Why, woman, do you continually mourn your son’s death? Do you never cease grieving?”

She replied:

“The days of my life do not exhaust this mourning. As long as I live, I shall always grieve for my only son, and I shall never be relieved of tears until the appointed death closes the eyes of this body.”

He said to her:

“Do not mourn him as though he were dead, but act with equanimity, for know that he lives with us and enjoys, while seated [Note: Colbert manuscript A reads “seat”; others read “sitting.”], our fellowship in eternal life. And so that you may truly believe that what I say is certain, rise tomorrow for matins, and you will hear his voice among the choirs of the monks singing psalms [Note: Above he called them “clerics.” Observe from this that Gregory called monks who were accustomed to devote themselves to singing God’s praises in the choir “clerics.” Gregory did this not only here, but elsewhere often calls the same men sometimes monks and sometimes clerics. Similar examples frequently occur in other authors as well, as our Mabillon demonstrates more fully in the preface to the second Benedictine century, no. 27. See Hadrian Valesius in his discussion of basilicas and in his defense, and Thomassin, *Ecclesiastical Discipline*, part I, book III.]. And not only tomorrow, but on every day of your life, whenever you come to the psalmody, you will hear his voice. Therefore do not weep, since you ought rather to rejoice than to mourn.”

The woman rose and drew long sighs. She did not fall asleep in her bed until the monks gave the signal to rise. When the signal had been given, she went to the church, intending to test something of the vision she had seen.

Nothing of the holy promise failed, but what had been announced divinely was immediately fulfilled. When the cantor had sung the responsory [another reading: “when the response had been sung”] and the company of monks had taken up the antiphon, the mother heard and recognized the child’s voice, and gave thanks to God.

The promise made by the Martyr’s mouth was also completely fulfilled: every day of her life, whenever the woman came to the psalmody, she heard the voice of this little child among the other melodies of the voices.

When King Guntram had devoted himself so fully to spiritual works that, abandoning the splendors of the world, he distributed his treasures to churches and the poor, it happened that he sent a presbyter to convey gifts, as he had vowed, to the brothers who served the Saints of Agaunum. He instructed the presbyter, on his return, to bring him relics of the Saints.

After carrying out the king’s command, the presbyter returned with these relics and reached the Lake of Geneva, through which the Rhône flows, seeking a boat. The lake extends for approximately four hundred stades in length and one hundred fifty stades in breadth [Note: Marius of Avenches writes in his *Chronicle* that it is sixty miles long and twenty miles wide. It is commonly called Lake Geneva, after the famous city situated upon it.].

807 Finally, when the presbyter, as we have said, had boarded this vessel, a storm suddenly arose and raised the waves. Mountains of water rose to the stars. Now, with the boat’s stern lifted and its prow gaping open, the vessel was carried upward; then again, with the stern submerged, the prow was raised on high.

The sailors were thrown into confusion, and nothing except death itself was expected in this danger. When the presbyter saw that he was being overwhelmed by the waves and heavily covered by their foam, he drew from his neck the capsule containing the relics of the Saints, cast it faithfully into the swelling waters, and invoked the protection of the Saints in a loud voice:

“Lest I perish in these waves, I beg your power, glorious martyrs. Rather, since you continually offer aid to those who are perishing, please deign to extend to me the right hand of salvation. Restrain the waves and, through the help of your aid, bring us back to the desired shore.”

As he said this, the wind ceased, the waves subsided, and they were carried to shore. I learned this from the presbyter himself.

They also say that in this lake trout are found weighing as much as one hundred pounds.

## CHAPTER LXXVII. On Saint Victor of Marseille

There is also wondrous power at the tomb of Saint Victor, martyr of Marseille [Note: The Colbert manuscript lacks this chapter and the two following. In Clermont manuscript A, the material extending through chapter 88 is absent. Saint Victor suffered at Marseille during the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian. We have given his Acts among the *Sincere Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 292. His feast is celebrated in the Martyrologies on 21 July, while Fortunatus praises him in book VIII, poem 4. Our Gregory discusses his basilica in *History*, book IX, chapter 22. It remains famous, together with the important Benedictine monastery whose origin is owed to John Cassian, who flourished in the fifth century. Guesnay published the history of this place under the title *Cassianus Illustratus*.] (A.D. 290 or 303, 21 July). Although the sick who frequently come to him are otherwise healed, the possessed, after violently struggling and shouting against the Martyr, are freed when the demons are expelled.

A servant of the patrician Aurelian, seized by a demon, was tormented by a grievous affliction, so that he often tore himself with his own teeth. But when he was brought to the Saint’s basilica and confessed that he was being burned by the Martyr’s power, he raved throughout the entire church and departed cleansed on the third day.

He was strengthened so greatly through the merit of his faith that thereafter, with his hair cut short, he was appointed abbot and placed in charge of a monastery.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. On the Glorious Martyr Baudillius

At the town of the city of Nîmes is the glorious tomb of the blessed martyr Baudillius [Note: Colbert manuscript A reads “Baudelius,” and does so throughout. His Acts are found under 20 May in the Bollandists, but they are not sufficiently ancient to deserve complete credence. After the persecutions of the pagans had subsided, Christians built a church over the tomb of this saint, which is said later to have been honored with the title of an abbey. Toward the end of the eleventh century it was reduced to a priory and placed under the abbot of La Chaise-Dieu, who restored monks there. But around the year 1561 it was burned to ashes by Calvinist heretics, together with the regular houses; since then the blessed Martyr’s tomb has lain beneath the ruins and has not yet been discovered. Indeed, when no hope appeared of restoring the old monastery, the monks of La Chaise-Dieu purchased the old episcopal palace, where a new monastery was erected under the protection of Saint Baudillius. With the support of the illustrious bishop of Nîmes, Esprit Fléchier, Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur were brought into it from the monastery of La Chaise-Dieu on 23 September 1689, and they remain there. On whether the relics of this saint were transferred to Orléans, see the Bollandists.] From it many miracles are frequently manifested (A.D. . . ., 20 May).

From this tomb a laurel tree arose and passed through the wall, becoming outside a tree flourishing with a health-giving crown. The inhabitants of the place often experienced it as a heavenly remedy in various illnesses.

Because of these benefits of its miraculous powers, it was often stripped of its leaves and even became, as it were, dry in its bark. Since we have said that diseases from many illnesses were driven away by it, it would take too long to recall each one individually. I therefore thought it sufficient to say that, by distributing those medicines, it became dry.

It is also reported that a certain merchant carried to the East a celebrated relic made from these leaves. But before the merchant reached port, a possessed man in the church, to the amazement of the people, cried out that the martyr Baudillius was going toward the eastern region. The blessed Martyr also displayed his power in other matters.

Aram, a commander of the Italian King Theodoric, while residing in the city of Arles, had a certain archpriest of the parish of Nîmes in his disfavour. Burning with anger, he sent servants against him, saying:

“Go as quickly as possible, bind him hand and foot, and bring him here by force, so that he may learn that I am lord of this region.”

But they did not understand that he meant the archpriest and thought that he had ordered them to bring the archdeacon. Mounting their horses, they came to the city and asked about the archdeacon; he was pointed out to them.

His name was John. He was highly religious and, in his archdeaconate, devoted himself diligently to teaching children [Note: Saint Isidore describes the duties and prerogatives of archdeacons excellently in his letter to Leudefredus, bishop of Córdoba. See also book I of the *Decretals*, chapter 2, in the Bollandists, 18 March, in the eulogy of Saint Braulio.].

The duke’s servants seized him, bound his hands and feet, and brought him beneath the belly of a horse.

Yet the Martyr’s power did not cease to aid his own protégé. The servants lodged with him near the very gate, because, since the gates had been closed for the night, they could not enter. During that night, while the duke was sleeping, the archdeacon appeared to him in a vision and said:

“What wrong have I done you, O man, that you ordered me to be summoned with such insult and reduced to this humiliation? I tell you truly: you will not escape God’s judgment.”

When he awoke, terrified and shaken by fear, he cried out to his men:

“Inquire whether the servants whom we sent to Nîmes have yet arrived.”

They asked those stationed on the city wall, who replied that the servants were there with a man. The messengers reported what they had heard.

Immediately the duke said:

“Bring to me the man whom you have brought.”

When this had been done, the duke looked at him and, overcome with fear, said:

“I ordered the archpriest to be brought, not the archdeacon.”

He fell at the archdeacon’s feet and said:

“Please forgive the injury of this offense, for it was not in my intention that you should have suffered these things.”

He immediately sent him back to the city, honoring him with gifts worthy of him. Thereafter, out of reverence for the Martyr, he loved him with such affection that, when the bishop of that city died, he ordered John himself to be appointed bishop [Note: It is remarkable that this John is absent from the catalogues of the bishops of Nîmes. He should be placed between Sedatus, who attended the Council of Agde in 506, and Pelagius, who attended the Council of Narbonne in 589 and, in the preceding year, the Council of Toledo.].

Nor did he order the archpriest to be sought any further.

O great power of the Martyr, which, through the injury done to an innocent man, freed the guilty from punishment! The Apostle’s saying was fulfilled: “For those who love God, all things work together for good” (Romans 8:28). This injury built for him the step by which he would ascend to govern the Church of God.

## CHAPTER LXXIX. On the Miracles of the Blessed Apostle Andrew in the Church of Agde

The church of the city of Agde, which rejoices in the relics of Saint Andrew the Apostle [Note: Saint Severus built a monastery beside this church, where he presided over three hundred brothers, as recorded in his Life in the appendix to the first Benedictine century. This monastery later passed to secular canons. The Council of Agde was held there in A.D. 506, as appears from its preface.], is also frequently illuminated by glorious miracles and often reproves those who seize its property.

When Count Gomacharius [Note: The Laude manuscript reads “Comacharius.”] was seizing the land of that church, Bishop Leo [Note: Leo governed the church of Agde between Sophronius, who attended the Council of Agde in 506, and Tigridius, who subscribed to the Council of Narbonne in 589.] came to him in great sorrow and said:

“Leave, my son, the property of the poor, which the Lord has entrusted to our administration, lest it become harmful to you and you perish through the tears of the needy who were accustomed to be fed by its produce.”

But because he was a heretic, he paid little attention to what the bishop said and retained the property under his control.

Meanwhile, as the day advanced, he was seized by a fever. Since he was afflicted not only by bodily heat but also by distress of soul, he sent messengers to the bishop, saying:

“May the priest deign to pour out a prayer to the Lord for me, and I will relinquish his land.”

When the bishop prayed, the man recovered from the illness that had oppressed him. Once he was well, he said to his men:

“What do you think those Romans will say now? They say that I was afflicted with fever because I took their land, whereas what happened to me was in accordance with the ordinary condition of the human body. Nevertheless, they shall not have it while I am alive.”

No sooner had he spoken than he sent men to seize it again.

When the bishop learned of this, he came to him and said:

“Do you regret having done good before, that you are now trying to overturn it? Please do not do so, lest you be subjected to divine vengeance.”

The man said to the bishop:

“Be silent, be silent, you old ruin! I will have you bound with ropes, led around the city on a donkey, and made a laughingstock to everyone who sees you.”

But the bishop, remaining silent, returned to his familiar protections. He prostrated himself in prayer, kept vigils, and spent the entire night in tears and psalmody.

When morning came, he approached the lamps hanging from the church chamber. Extending the staff he held in his hand, he broke them all and said:

“Let no light be kindled here until God takes vengeance on his enemies and restores the property of his household.”

As soon as he had said this, the heretic fell again into a fever. When he was at the point of death, he sent to the bishop, saying:

“Let the priest pray to the Lord for me, that I may live; I will restore the land and confer an equal amount upon its lordship.”

The bishop replied:

“I have already prayed to the Lord, and he has heard me.”

He sent other messengers, and then a third group. But the priest, persisting in his one answer, was not moved to offer prayer to the Lord for him.

When the heretic saw this, he ordered them to place him in a wagon and carry him to the bishop, so that he could beg him in person, saying:

“I will restore the land that I unjustly seized, with double compensation, if only your holiness will pray for me.”

When the bishop again refused, he compelled him by force to go to the church. As soon as the bishop had departed and entered the church, the heretic breathed out his spirit. Immediately the church recovered its property.

## CHAPTER LXXXI. On the Confirmation of the Christian Faith through a Miracle

Heresy is always the enemy of Catholics, and wherever it can set an ambush, it does not fail to do so. Such is the famous event that, according to widespread report, occurred in a certain place.

There was a certain Catholic woman who had a heretical husband. When a very Catholic presbyter of our religion came to her, the woman said to her husband:

“I ask your kindness that, in honor of this priest’s arrival—he has deigned to visit me—there may be joy in our house, and that we may dine with him at a meal prepared with worthy expense.”

Her husband promised that he would do as she requested. Then another presbyter of the heretics arrived, and the husband said to his wife:

“Today’s joy is doubled, because priests of both religions are in our house.”

When they were reclining at the banquet, the husband occupied the place on the right-hand side with the presbyter of his party [Note: Savaro adduces many examples from sacred and profane authors on both sides in his notes to book I, letter 2, of Apollinaris Sidonius, concerning the more honorable place at table and whether it should be reckoned on the right or the left. This diversity of opinion may perhaps arise from the fact that different people understood the right and left sides differently. Gregory here calls the right the more honorable side. Ancient images represent Saint Paul on the right and Saint Peter on the left. Lambecius discusses reclining at table at length in volume IV of the *Imperial Library*, supplement 8, where ancient paintings on the subject are reproduced. See Sirmond’s notes on book I, letter 2, of Apollinaris Sidonius, and two letters of Sidonius on this matter in volume V of the new edition.], while placing the Catholic on the left and setting a small chair beside him on the left for his wife.

The husband said to the heretical presbyter:

“If you agree to my proposal, let us make sport of this Roman presbyter today. When a dish has been set before us, you should hasten to make the sign first; when he has not laid his hand upon it, we shall eat the food cheerfully while he is saddened.”

The other replied:

“I will do as you command.”

Then a dish of vegetables arrived. The heretic made the sign and was the first to place his hand upon it. When the woman saw this, she said:

“Do not do this, for I deeply resent the injury done to the priest.”

Another dish was served, and the Catholic partook of it. The heretic acted similarly with the second and third dishes.

When the fourth dish was brought, a hot frying pan was placed in the middle. In it was a food customarily prepared from beaten eggs mixed with a little flour and decorated with pieces of dates and rounded olives. The heretic hurried, and before the dish had even touched the table, he raised his hand to meet it and made the sign. Then, taking up a spoon at once, without realizing whether it was hot, he quickly swallowed the boiling food.

Immediately his chest began to burn. With an enormous sigh and a rumbling of the belly, he breathed out his wicked spirit. He was removed from the banquet, placed in a tomb, and covered with a mound of earth [another reading: “of earthly matter”].

Then the presbyter of our religion rejoiced and said:

“Truly God has avenged his servants.”

Turning to the man whose banquet it was, he said:

“The memory of this man has perished with a sound, but the Lord remains forever” (Psalm 9:7). “Now set before me what I may eat.”

The terrified man, when the meal had ended, fell at the presbyter’s feet and was converted to the Catholic faith. He and his entire household, who had been held in this false belief, came to faith, and joy was multiplied, just as the woman had first requested.

## CHAPTER LXXXI. On the Dispute of a Catholic Deacon with a Heretical Presbyter
An Arian presbyter was having a dispute with a deacon of our religion, bringing forward, as is customary for that people, poisonous assertions against the Son of God and the Holy Spirit. But after the deacon had argued at length and in great detail about certain matters concerning our faith, and the heretic, blinded by the darkness of his faithlessness, rejected what was true—according to the saying, “Wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul” (Wisdom 1:4)—he added:

“Why do we weary ourselves with the extended efforts of speeches? Let the truth of the matter be demonstrated by deeds: let a bronze vessel be heated over a fire, and let someone’s ring be thrown into boiling water. Whoever lifts it out of the boiling water will be proved to have justice on his side. Once this has been done, let the opposing party submit to recognition of this justice. Understand, then, heretic, that if our side, with the help of the Holy Spirit, accomplishes this, you must confess that there is nothing discordant, nothing unlike, in the Holy Trinity.”

The heretic agreed to this arrangement, and after they had made an appointment to meet in the morning, they departed. But the fervor of faith by which the deacon had first proposed this began to grow lukewarm as the enemy lay in wait. At daybreak he arose, anointed his arm with oil, and smeared it with ointment. Nevertheless, he went around the holy places and prayed to the Lord.

What more need be said? Around the third hour they met in the forum. The people rushed together for the spectacle. A fire was kindled, the bronze vessel was placed upon it, and it became extremely hot. The ring was thrown into the boiling water. The deacon first invited the heretic to remove it himself from the heat. But he immediately refused, saying: “You who proposed this decision must remove it.”

The deacon, although trembling, nevertheless bared his arm. When the heretical presbyter saw that it was smeared with ointments, he exclaimed: “You thought that you could protect yourself by magical arts by applying these ointments; but these things you are doing will be of no use.”

While they were arguing in this way, a deacon from the city of Ravenna arrived, named Jacinctus [Col. 0778B], and, asking what this dispute was about, learned the truth. Without delay, he pulled his arm out from his clothing and plunged his right hand into the bronze vessel. The ring that had been thrown in was very light and small; it was borne by the water no less readily than a straw can be carried by the wind. After searching for it for a long time and with great effort, he found it within the space of an hour.

Meanwhile, the fire beneath the vessel was being stoked with great force, so that, as the vessel boiled more fiercely, the ring would not easily be reached by the hand of the man searching for it. At last he drew it out, yet the deacon felt nothing in his flesh. Rather, he testified that the bronze was cold at the bottom but contained only a moderate warmth at the top.

When the heretic saw this, he was greatly confounded. He boldly thrust his hand into the bronze vessel, saying: “My faith will secure this for me.” As soon as his hand was inserted, all the flesh between the joints, down to the very bones, immediately melted and flowed away. Thus the dispute came to an end.

[Note: [Col. 0777D] See the notes on chapter 14 of the book *On the Glory of the Confessors*.]

## CHAPTER LXXXII. Concerning a cleric beaten in Spain for confessing the Lord.

In our own time also, when unbelief and the wicked sect of the Arians had been spread through the regions of Spain by the most evil assertions, a certain cleric was arrested. He confessed that he was a Christian, affirming that the Son and the Holy Spirit are equal to the Father.

The king who ruled there [Note: [Col. 0777] I think this was Leovigild, who began a persecution against the Catholics.], after offering him gifts, entreated him as though he were a superior, asking him to suppress his confession concerning the equality of the Holy Trinity and to acknowledge that the Son, together with the Holy Spirit, was less than the Father. If he did so, he would be enriched with possessions and held in high esteem among the people.

When the cleric avoided this counsel as though it were a viper’s bite and rejected the deadly poison of the evil serpent, the king added: “I see the harsh resolve of an unsound mind; but I know your temperament, so that, since gifts do not bend you, tortures may easily do so.”

The cleric replied: “Would that I might be considered worthy to have my throat cut for this confession; for I loathe your gifts as dung.”

Then the angry king ordered him to be stretched upon the rack and severely beaten, asking: “What do you believe?”

He answered: [Col. 0779A] “I have already told you: I believe in God the almighty Father and in his Son Jesus Christ.”

After this he was beaten severely, but he remained constant in his confession, and the torture could never turn him from the line of faith. For at the beginning, when he was being beaten, he felt only three blows of the whip, which, as he later related, penetrated his very soul. He felt the remaining lashes no more than if some covering had been placed over his back, and, while undergoing the torments, he proclaimed the faith he had begun to confess even more boldly.

Thus, when the king was satisfied with his punishment, he was released, after the king had ordered him never again to be found within the borders of Spain. The cleric departed joyfully and returned to Gaul [Al., “went out”]. But, so that credence may be given to this account, I saw the man who narrated these events as he had heard them from the cleric’s own mouth.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII. Concerning the relics of several martyrs—namely Paul, Laurence, Pancratius, Chrysanthus, the virgin Daria, and John and Paul his brother.

Through this confession, the glorious martyrs have always merited unspeakable benefits of saving gifts, and have granted by their power what those who ask them have requested—power bestowed upon them by the Lord the Creator. We have learned that the following event occurred, as it was recently reported to us by our deacon.

This deacon [Note: [Col. 0779D] Concerning him, see Book X, chapter 1 of the *History*. From this we infer that this translation of the relics should be assigned to approximately the year 590.] had received from Pelagius, pope of the city of Rome (A.D. 590), relics of certain martyrs and confessors. With great psalm-singing, the attendance of the clergy, and the escort of an immense crowd, he was conducted as far as the harbor.

He entered the ship, raised the sails, and, with the rigging of the mast—which bears an arrangement in the form of a cross—extended, they took to the deep sea as the wind blew. While sailing toward the harbor of the city of Marseilles, they began to approach a certain place where, rising from the seashore, a rocky mountain extends gradually outward and stretches beneath the surface of the sea.

As the keel, driven by the wind, was carried headlong with great force and was about to be shattered against the rock, and the sailors, seeing the danger, cried out for help, the deacon lifted up the chest containing the holy relics and began, with groans and a loud voice, to invoke the names of each of the saints, begging that by their power they might be rescued from the danger in which they were about to perish.

The ship was already approaching the rock, as we have said. Immediately, as the holy relics were contemplated, a wind of greater violence, stirred up at that very spot and contrary to the existing wind, struck the wave and drove back the opposing wind. The ship was recalled into the deep sea, and everyone was rescued from the danger of death. Thus, after the mass of danger had been turned aside, they reached the harbor they desired through the mercy of the Lord and the protection of the saints.

The relics were those of saints whose sacred footprints had been washed by the hands of the Lord [Col. 0780A] [Note: [Col. 0779D] That is, the apostles, whose feet Christ washed], together with the relics of Paul, Laurence, Pancratius, Chrysanthus, the virgin Daria, John, and another Paul, his brother [Note: [Col. 0780D] These are the famous biological brothers, eunuchs of Constantia, who are said to have suffered at Rome under Julian the Apostate]. The city of Rome, itself the head of the world, devoutly celebrates their contests and palms of victory.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV. Concerning the relics that my father possessed.

What, then, shall I say about what happened with those relics that my father once carried with him?

At the time when Theudebert ordered the sons of the Auvergnats to be taken as hostages, my father, who had recently married, wished to strengthen himself with the relics of the saints. He asked a certain priest to give him something of them, so that, setting out on a long journey, he might be protected by such a safeguard.

The priest then placed the sacred ashes, enclosed in a golden container, around him. Since the man did not know the names of the blessed, he was accustomed to relate that he had then been rescued from many dangers. He testified that by their power he had often escaped the violence of robbers, the dangers of rivers, the outrages of rioters, and assaults of swords [Note: [Col. 0780D] Colbert 2 reads *assultus ensuum*; should it perhaps be read *assultus ensium*, “assaults of swords”?].

What I myself saw concerning these relics I will not keep silent. After my father’s death, my mother kept these sacred objects upon her person. The time for cutting the crops had arrived, and great heaps of grain had been gathered on the threshing floors. In those days, when the seeds were already being threshed and the region, like Lemane [Note: [Col. 0780D] Other manuscripts have *Lemmane*, that is, Arvernian Limagne], clothed with grain but stripped of its forests, lay under frost, they had no material with which to light a fire except the very straw. The threshers therefore made fires for themselves from it.

Meanwhile, everyone went away to take food. And behold, among the heaps, the fire began gradually to spread through the straw. Soon, with the south wind blowing, the heaps were caught by the fire. A great conflagration arose, followed by the shouting of the men, the uproar of the women, and the wailing of the children.

This was happening in our field. When my mother perceived it—she was wearing these relics suspended around her neck—she sprang up from the meal and raised the sacred objects toward the globes of fire. At once the entire fire died down, so quickly that scarcely even a spark could be found among the masses of burned straw. Yet it had done no harm to the grain it had seized.
