Many years later I received these relics from my mother. As we were traveling from Burgundy to Auvergne, a great storm arose against us. The sky began to flash with repeated fires of lightning and resound with powerful crashes of thunder.

I then drew the blessed relics from my bosom and raised my hand toward the cloud. Immediately the cloud divided into two parts and passed by on the right and left; thereafter it harmed neither us nor anyone else.

But then, as youthful fervor commonly does, I began to swell with pride in vain glory. I silently thought that this had not been granted so much through the merits of the saints as specifically to me, and I boasted to my companions, proclaiming what God had granted to my innocence, so that I might deserve such a favor.

No sooner had I done this than my horse suddenly slipped beneath me and threw me to the ground. In that fall I was so severely injured that I could scarcely rise. I understood that this had happened to me because of my vanity, and thereafter it was enough for me to take care that the goad of vain glory should not spur me further.

For if it happened that I later deserved to behold some manifestation of the saints’ powers, I proclaimed that these were gifts of God bestowed through faith in the saints [Laud., *munere* (“gift”), for *munera* (“gifts”)].

## CHAPTER LXXXV. Concerning the man who washed his feet in a paten.

No rashness is useful, since no one should seek to do what he is not permitted to do. Thus, when the count of the Britons was being gravely afflicted by pains in his feet and had spent his resources on physicians without obtaining any improvement, one of his attendants said to him:

“If some vessel used in the church, one of those placed upon the altar, were brought to you from the church, so that you could wash your feet in it, this might bring you relief.”

Such people were foolish and senseless, not recognizing that vessels consecrated to God must not be adapted to human uses.

The count quickly sent to the church and took from the sacristy a silver paten from the most holy altar. There he washed his feet [Note: [Col. 0781D] From this passage Mabillon correctly concludes, *Gallican Liturgy*, Book I, chapter 7, that patens at that time were very capacious. Compare chapter 8 of the book *On the Virtues of Saint Julian*]. But immediately his pains increased, and he became completely disabled; afterward he was never able to walk again. I have also learned that the duke of the Lombards did the same thing.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI. Concerning the deacon from whose hands a tower escaped.

We lament and bewail our sins when we do not know ourselves to be clean and, approaching the very altar of the Lord, boldly receive his holy body and blood while polluted by our actions—receiving them for judgment rather than obtaining forgiveness.

For I recall what I heard had happened in my youth. It was the day of the passion of the great martyr Polycarp, and his solemn observance was being celebrated in the village of Ricomagus in the city of Auvergne. After the Passion had been read [Note: [Col. 0781D] We have shown in the preface to the *Acts of the Sincere Martyrs*, p. 14, that the Acts of the martyrs were once read publicly in church. They were also recited during Mass, as is confirmed by this passage, by Hilduin in the letter prefixed to his *Areopagitic*, by Braulio in the *Life of Saint Aemilianus*, and by others], together with the other readings introduced by the priestly canon, the time came to offer the sacrifice.

The deacon took the tower in which the mystery of the Lord’s body was kept [Note: [Col. 0781D] All the manuscripts that I was able to consult, together with Cl. have this reading, whereas some later printed editions have “ministry.” Our reading is confirmed by Saint Odo, who, citing this passage of Gregory in Book II, chapter 32 of the *Collations*, interprets the words as “a chest containing the Lord’s body.” Indeed, Bishop Felix of Bourges is praised by Fortunatus, Book III, poem 23, for having arranged for such a tower to be made:

“Where well-joined ornaments adorn the sacred Lamb’s body,  
And bear a great pearl and gifts of gold.”

This splendidly confirms the opinion of our Mabillon, in the *Gallican Liturgy* and in his commentary on the *Roman Order*, §20: formerly, he writes, it was customary in the church for the Eucharist to be carried before the bishop as he proceeded to the altar. As this passage shows, the custom was received not only at Rome but also in Gaul. See below in the appendix for the blessing of such a tower.]

He began to carry it toward the entrance. When he entered the church to place it upon the altar, it slipped from his hand and was carried through the air. As he approached the altar in this way, the deacon’s hands could never reach it [Col. 0781D]. We believe that this happened for no other reason than that he was polluted in conscience.

For it was frequently reported that he had committed adultery. Only one presbyter and three women were permitted to see this; one of the women was my mother. The others did not see it. I myself was present at that festival, I confess, but I was not worthy to see these things.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII. Concerning Epachius, who dared to celebrate after eating breakfast.

Similarly, the presbyter Epachius, when he rashly presumed to perform what he was unworthy to do, fell to the ground and died by divine judgment.

When he had gone to the church to celebrate the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, he went out of God’s temple at each successive hour and in his own house drained cups of revelry from foaming bowls [Col. 0782B]. Many people asserted that they had seen him drinking there during that very night, after cockcrow.

But since he was of senatorial stock and no one in that aforementioned village of Ricomagus was considered nobler according to worldly rank, he was requested to celebrate the solemn Mass. The wretched man, soaked in wine, did not hesitate to undertake what no fasting person can perform without fear, with conscience trembling.

When the sacred words had been completed, the sacrament of the Lord’s body broken, and he himself had received it and distributed it to others to eat, he immediately emitted a sound like the neighing of a horse, fell to the ground, and expelled from his mouth foam together with the portion of the sacred mystery that he had been unable to crush with his teeth. He was carried out of the church in the hands of his attendants.

He was not thereafter free from this illness of epilepsy. During each lunar cycle, with its increase and decrease, he always suffered it, because the unhappy man did not abstain at all from excessive drinking of wine.

The present example therefore teaches with what honor and reverence this night ought to be celebrated.

On one occasion, when I had left the vigil of this solemnity and had fallen asleep for a little while, a certain man came to me and said: “Rise and return to the church.” I awoke and, making the sign of the cross, went back to sleep.

He did not desist, but the same person repeated the earlier words [Note: [Col. 0782D] Printed editions and some manuscripts read *eademque personat*, “and he utters the same things.”]. But when I still did not rise after being admonished a second time and again fell asleep, he came a third time, slapped me on the cheek, and said: “You ought to awaken the others for the vigils, and yet you are still overcome by sleep?”

Then, terrified with fear, I returned to the church with great haste. Let these remarks about the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity suffice. Let us return to the rash.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII. Concerning the Jordan fleeing before a sinful woman.

There was an adulterous woman from the city of Jericho whose most dreadful custom was this: whenever she conceived a child by a fornicator and gave birth, she immediately suffocated it and buried it in the earth, so that what was hidden from human beings might nevertheless not be hidden from God and his angels.

When the holy day of the Epiphany arrived and everyone went down into the Jordan to wash both the wounds of the body (see above, chapter 17) and the scars of the soul, she approached the riverbank with the rest of the people.

When she lifted her garments as far as her knees in order to enter the river—wondrous to relate!—the water fled before her feet. As she pursued it, the river was forced back toward the opposite bank [Note: [Col. 0783D] In nearly the same way, Mary of Egypt was divinely prevented from entering a church until she had promised to undertake repentance. See her Life on 2 April in the Bollandists].

When the people saw this, they were astonished that such an event had occurred on so celebrated a day. Recognizing that the woman was a criminal, they asked what evil she had committed, so that this had happened to her amid such a gathering of people.

She turned toward the people and confessed her crime, saying: “I have already given birth to and killed seven little children. I conceived them through incest and feared to make them public. Only yesterday I battered an eighth. I therefore beg you to pour out prayers to the Lord for me, so that, my iniquity being forgiven, I may cease from sinning, lest heavenly wrath consume me.”

While she was saying this, the entire people fell prostrate upon the ground and offered prayer to the Lord, asking him mercifully to forgive her for the sin she had committed through the aid of sloth.

After the prayer, the woman stretched out her arms upon the ground and breathed out her spirit. I think this happened so that she would not repeat her forgiven crime thereafter.

The people understood why the waters of the river had withdrawn before the woman’s face. The proverb of Solomon was fulfilled: “The Spirit of the Lord flees from deceit” (Wisdom 1:5).

I learned of this miracle from the mouth of the deacon John (see above, chapter 19); for he asserted that he had been present at the time.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX. Concerning the inability of the corpse of the wicked Antoninus to rest in the church of Saint Vincent.

Near the city of Toulouse, they say, there was a certain man named Antoninus [Note: [Col. 0783D] Colbert 2 and Claromontanus a have “Antonius”], wicked toward God and hateful to all human beings because he committed many crimes.

When his days had been completed and he departed from this world, he was buried in the basilica of blessed Vincent, in which he had deposited a vessel for himself while still alive [Col. 0783D].

But when deep night had taken hold of everyone and all had given their limbs to rest under the caress of sleep, that sarcophagus was thrown from the holy basilica through a window and set down in the middle of the courtyard.

When morning came, it was found there with its covering broken open above it. His relatives, not understanding the power of God and not perceiving the insult done to the saint in whose church they had rashly buried an unworthy man, again placed the sarcophagus in the spot where it had previously been and dug the grave deeper.

When the next day dawned, however, they found it again cast outside in the middle of the courtyard. Thus they understood the great works of God. From then on, untouched by anyone, it has been preserved to this day at the place where it was thrown out, as a testimony [Note: [Col. 0783D] A similar miracle happened to a monk who died while visiting his parents, in Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, Book II, chapter 24. See also Book IV, chapter 53, where Valentinus, buried in the church of Saint Syrus at Milan, was shamefully thrown out the following night].

Let these remarks about the rash suffice.

## CHAPTER XC. Concerning Vincent, the glorious martyr.

Vincent, a deacon or levite and a Spanish martyr [Note: [Col. 0783D] Claromontanus a, Colbert a, and most printed editions have “of Spain”; others have “Spanish.” It would be superfluous to collect more about this celebrated martyr. See the *Acts of the Sincere Martyrs*, p. 387], completed his martyrdom (A.D. 304, 22 January).

Near the territory of Poitiers there is a village in the district of Arbatilicus [Note: [Col. 0784D] Arbatilicus, or the district of Herbatilicus, lay on the boundary between the territories of Nantes and Poitiers. It took its name from the city of Herbadilla, which is said to have been swallowed by a fissure in the earth around the year 580. The district nevertheless retained its ancient name for a long time afterward, together with the title of county (*le Comté d’Herbauge*). See Valesius’s notice and Mabillon’s notes on the *Life of Saint Amandus*, Benedictine century II, under the year 679], named Becciacum, where his relics are kept.

His solemnity is celebrated on the twelfth day before the Kalends of the eleventh month [Note: [Col. 0784D] Here Gregory plainly calls January the eleventh month, contrary to Scaliger’s opinion. See also the following chapter, Book II, chapter 29, and Book IV, *On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 4. Below, however, in Book II, chapter 35, he seems to count differently].

But the inhabitants of the place, and especially the archpresbyter, having fallen into some error of which I know nothing, wished to celebrate it one day early. After Mass had been said, while they were sitting at the meal, behold, one of the possessed began to cry out and say:

“Run, citizens! Leave the village! Go out to meet blessed Vincent! Behold, he is coming to the vigil; behold, tomorrow you will celebrate his feast.”

When he said this, they renewed the solemn observances and kept vigil throughout the entire night. In the morning, while the mysteries of the Mass were being celebrated, this possessed man who had foretold the saint’s arrival, and two others with him, were cleansed. Two paralytics were also restored that very day, and the people departed from the feast with joy.

When some pilgrims were carrying his relics, they came to the village of Ceratensis in the territory of the city of Tours [Note: [Col. 0784D] This place and Orbaniacum are discussed in the notes to the final chapter of Book X of the *History*.]. They carried them to the hut of a poor man and were received there. On the following day, two paralytics received the power to walk through these relics, and one blind man recovered his sight.

Not far from that village there is another called Orbaniacum, in whose church relics of this saint are kept. When they had been stolen and the man who had taken them had left them with an abbot at Bourges in exchange for a price, it was revealed to the abbot that he should restore them to the place from which they had been removed [Al., “taken away”].

The same thing was also revealed in a vision to the archpresbyter of a monastery near that place, so that he should not delay at all in restoring them. As he carried them back with psalm-singing, a certain man who had lain bedridden for a full year, crushed by a grave illness, was carried in the hands of his attendants. As soon as he reverently worshiped and kissed the cloth with which the sacred ashes [Al., “relics”] were covered, his illness was immediately checked and he was healed. He followed the others in the martyr’s funeral rites [Note: [Col. 0785D] Claromontanus a and Colbert a emend this to *exsequias martyriales*, “the martyr’s funeral rites.”].

## CHAPTER XCI. Concerning Saint Eulalia.

Eulalia, the glorious woman who suffered at the city of Emerita [Col. 0785B] (A.D. 304, 10 December), displays a great miracle to the people on the day of her sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0785D] Since the commonly circulated Acts of Eulalia are not especially reliable, we related the history of her martyrdom from Prudentius in the *Acts of the Sincere Martyrs*, p. 497, where we made several further observations. See the Mass for her feast in Book III of the *Gallican Liturgy*, no. 18 of the Gothic Missal. Emerita, once the metropolis of Lusitania, now lies ruined in Extremadura, its episcopal seat having been transferred to Compostela].

Before her altar, beneath which her holy remains are covered, stand three trees, though I do not know what kind they are. When, by the middle of the tenth month, in which her passion is celebrated, they have been stripped of all the beauty of their leaves, at dawn on that day they produce sweet flowers in the form of a dove’s wing. This signifies that her holy spirit entered heaven in the form of a dove, and that, after her blessed little body had become lifeless and been stripped of its clothing, falling snow from heaven had covered it with a soft fleece [Note: [Col. 0785D] Prudentius has this miracle, and the following one concerning snow, in hymn 3 of *On the Crowns* (Περὶ στεφάνων)].

If the trees produce this miracle at their customary time, the people know that the coming year will be either free from hardships or abundant in crops. If the flowers appear later than usual, the people recognize that this occurs because of their fault. Before the flowers emerge, the people lie complaining and sorrowful at the martyr’s tomb, praying that they may deserve to behold her customary favor.

Nor do they proceed with psalm-singing if these signs have not been revealed. If the martyr is appeased by the tears of the people, jewel-like flowers immediately emerge from the trees. Breathing forth a nectarous fragrance, they gladden the sorrowful spirit by their arrival and refresh it with their sweetness.

Then they are carefully gathered and carried to the priest in the basilica, and the procession is celebrated with joy. For we have often learned that these flowers benefit the sick.

## CHAPTER XCII. Concerning the basilica of Saint Felix.

At a certain time the basilica of the martyr Felix was broken into by thieves [Col. 0786A] (A.D. 304, 1 August). This martyr suffered in the city of Gerunda in Spain.

The thief seized silk garments woven with gold, ornaments decorated with necklaces, and the remaining furnishings, and departed. As he went, an unknown man joined him and asked where he was going.

The thief answered: “If my secret were safe with you, I would show you a great treasure.”

The man replied: “Show me whatever you wish; I will conceal it entirely by my efforts.”

The thief showed him the objects and said: “If these are sold in other regions, they will bring great profit to both of us.”

The man answered: “I am someone who has many friends in various regions, and I have a large, secret house. If you place these things there, you can sell them later whenever you wish.”

The man carrying the bundle went ahead, believing that he was being led to another city. God had closed his eyes, and he did not recognize that he was returning by the road on which he had come.

What more need be said? They reached the basilica of the saint, and the man said to him: “Here is the house of which I spoke to you. Enter and put down your bundle.”

He entered. But when he had put down the bundle and began to look around, he came to himself and recognized the saint’s basilica from which he had stolen the objects. The other man, however, had already withdrawn from him.

Thus he related to the people everything he had done with that man. There is no doubt, therefore, that the blessed martyr himself had appeared to him.

His relics are kept at the basilica of Narbonne. But because the height of this church prevented Liguria—a most pleasant place—from being seen from the king’s palace, King Alaric discussed the matter with his counselor Leo [Note: [Col. 0786D] Some manuscripts read *non cerneretur*, “might not be seen”; Martinus has *altitudine Liguria … non cerneretur*. The place was later called Livoria, commonly *la plaine de Livière*, as Valesius notes. The present situation of the sites also confirms the truth of this history. Although the basilica of Saint Felix was demolished under King Louis XII because it endangered the city’s fortifications, a chapel replacing it remains under Saint Felix’s name, with the status of a priory. It lies between Livoria (*la plaine de Livière*) and the place where the palace once stood. The latter was once called the Capitol and is still commonly called *le Capdueil*.] [Note: [Col. 0786D] This is the same Leo to whom Apollinaris Sidonius, then counselor or treasurer of King Euric, wrote in Letter 3 of Book VIII and Letter 22 of Book IV. Ennodius also praises him in the *Life of Epiphanius*.].

Leo said: “Let one structural part of the building’s machinery be removed, and the king will be able to view whatever he wishes more freely” [Note: [Col. 0786D] Other manuscripts and printed editions have “one structure of the machinery.”].

Immediately the workmen were summoned, and this counselor lowered the basilica of the saint, without diminishing its merits. But he immediately lost the light of his eyes.

## CHAPTER XCIII. Concerning the martyrs Hemeterius and Chelidonius.

The city of Calagurris in Spain bears the martyrs Hemeterius and Chelidonius [Note: [Col. 0786D] This chapter and the following one are absent from Claromontanus a. Some manuscripts have “Emeterius and Celedonius.” Their Acts had already perished in Prudentius’s time. They suffered at Calagurris, now called Calahorra, an episcopal city of Old Castile. See the Bollandists, 3 March], and, frequently witnessing miracles through their power, receives remedies for various illnesses.

These martyrs were seized by the persecutor and dragged away to punishment (A.D. …, 3 March). While they were being afflicted with various torments for confessing the divine name, they were led to be beheaded after the sentence of ultimate condemnation had been pronounced.

When the executioner cut off their heads, a great miracle appeared to the people. One man’s ring and the other’s handkerchief were received by a cloud and carried up into heaven. Everyone who was present saw this, and as far as the range of their eyes could extend, they followed the gleam of the gold and the whiteness of the linen in astonishment [Al., “in astonishment” plural].

Aurelius Clemens [Note: [Col. 0787D] Prudentius, hymn 4 of *On the Crowns*] bears witness to this event in the book of the *Crowns*, saying in these verses:

That glory is not hidden,  
Nor does it grow old with time:  
For the gifts sent upward  
Flew through the air,  
Showing beforehand  
The way open to heaven.  

Figuring his faith,  
The ring is borne by a cloud;  
The handkerchief, as they say,  
Gives a token of its border.  

Carried away by a heavenly breeze,  
They enter the innermost light;  
Along the axis of the liquid sky  
The gleam of gold is hidden.  

And for a long time the pursuing gaze  
The whiteness of the fabric eludes;  
They are carried up to the stars  
And are seen no more.

## CHAPTER XCIV. Concerning the most blessed Cyprian.

Cyprian, the most blessed bishop and martyr of Carthage (A.D. 258, 13 September) [Note: [Col. 0787D] This chapter is absent from Colbert 2, although it is included in the table of contents. Concerning Saint Cyprian, it is best to say only a little. We have given his Acts and the Life written by Pontius, among other materials, in the *Acts of the Sincere Martyrs*, under the year 258], frequently grants healing to the sick who beseech him.

In his basilica there is said to be a remarkably fashioned reading desk (*analogium*), on which the book placed above it is sung or read. It is said to have been sculpted entirely from a single block of marble. It consists of a table above, approached by four steps; a surrounding railing; columns beneath; and a platform under which eight persons can be accommodated.

No one has ever been able to produce anything of this kind there by any human skill, unless the martyr’s power had provided it.

## CHAPTER XCV. Concerning the Seven Sleepers at Ephesus.

Seven brothers who rest near the city of Ephesus (A.D. 250, July 27)—this is their story. During the reign of the emperor Decius, when persecution was being waged against Christians, seven men were arrested and brought before the ruler. Their names were: Maximian, Malchus, Martinianus, Constantinus, Dionysius, [Col. 0787D] John, and Serapion [Note: Their names are reported somewhat differently by the Greeks. The first writer known to us who celebrated these martyrs was our Gregory. Concerning them, see Photius, *Bibliotheca*, codex 253; Constantine Manasses and others. See [Col. 0788D] Baronius, under July 27.].

They were tested with various arguments to make them yield, but they did not consent in the least. Because of their distinction, however, the emperor granted them time for deliberation, so that they might not perish immediately. They shut themselves up in a single [Col. 0788A] cave, and lived there for many days. One of them nevertheless went out, procured food, and supplied whatever was necessary.

When the emperor returned to the same city, they asked the Lord to deem them worthy of being rescued from this danger. After praying, they fell prostrate on the ground and fell asleep. When the emperor learned that they were staying in this cavern, by God’s command he ordered the mouth of the cave to be blocked with large stones, saying: “Let those who refused to sacrifice to our gods perish there.”

While this was being done, a certain Christian wrote their names and martyrdom on a lead tablet and secretly enclosed it at the entrance of the cavern before it was sealed. After many years had passed, when peace had been granted to the Churches and the Christian Theodosius had obtained the empire (A.D. 447), [Col. 0788B] the impure heresy of the Sadducees arose—those who deny that there will be a resurrection.

At that time, a citizen of Ephesus decided to make sheepfolds beside that very mountain. As he rolled away stones to fit together the walls of the folds, unaware of what lay within, he opened the entrance to the cave, though he did not discover the secret that it contained. The Lord then breathed the spirit of life into the seven men, and they rose, thinking that they had slept only one night. They sent one of their number to buy food.

When he reached the city gate and saw the sign of the glorious cross, and heard the people swear by the name of Christ, he was astonished. When he produced the coins he had possessed since the time of Decius, a merchant seized him, saying: “You must have found ancient hidden treasures.” But he denied this, and was led [Col. 0788C] before the bishop [Note: Photius calls him Marus or Marinus; Stephen the Metaphrast, in Surius, calls him Stephen. The former is otherwise unknown, while the latter had driven Bassianus from his see in A.D. 448 and was himself deposed in the Council of Chalcedon in A.D. 451. In one manuscript Marinus the bishop and Antipatus the proconsul are named.], and before the city judge.

When they questioned him, necessity compelled him to reveal the hidden mystery, and he led them to the cave where the men were. When the bishop entered, he found the lead tablet on which everything they had suffered was written. After speaking with them, they reported these events with swift dispatch to the emperor Theodosius.

He came and prostrated himself on the ground before them. They addressed the ruler in these words:

“Glorious Augustus, a heresy has arisen that strives to overthrow the Christian people from the promises of God, so that they may say that there is no resurrection of the dead. Therefore, so that you may know that, in accordance with the apostle Paul, we shall all be brought before the tribunal of Christ, the Lord has commanded us to be raised and to speak these things to you. See, then, that you are not led astray and excluded from the kingdom of God.”

When the emperor Theodosius heard this, he glorified the Lord, who had not permitted his people to perish. The men then again fell prostrate on the ground and fell asleep. When the emperor Theodosius wished to construct tombs for them of gold, he was forbidden to do so in a vision. The men remain there to this day, covered with little cloaks of silk or linen. Their passion—which we translated into Latin from a certain Syrian interpreter—sets this out more fully [Note: It is found in Simeon the Metaphrast, in Surius, under July 27; but it is different from the account translated into Latin by Gregory, as is evident from the fact alone that the names are listed there differently from those given by Gregory. We found another account in manuscripts in which the names are given as Gregory lists them here; but since it is uncertain whether it is the very account translated by Gregory, and since it contains nothing new, it would have been superfluous to publish it.].

## CHAPTER XCVI. On the Forty-Eight Martyrs of Armenia

It is said [Note: This chapter and the following one are absent from Colb. tut. Here, as also in Book X, chapter 24 of the *History*, the martyrs are called forty-eight, although it seems certain that they were no more than forty. They suffered at Sebaste in Armenia during the persecution of Licinius, and the holy Fathers celebrated their martyrdom at length. We discussed them in the *Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 580. See also the Bollandists, under March 10.] that there were forty-eight men in Armenia (A.D. 320, March 9) who suffered on the very mountains of Armenia, where, because of their extraordinary height, water and earth are bound by severe cold. The Lawgiver indicates that these mountains are of considerable height when he says that Noah’s ark, built by him, rested upon them [Col. 0789B] (Genesis 8:4).

There the persecutor dug out the earth and ordered a great cistern to be made and filled with water. He commanded that the men, stripped naked and their hands bound behind their backs, be placed in a pool chained by ice [Note: It is more likely that this pool already existed, according to the testimony of the holy Fathers, and it still exists today. Gregory, moreover, like certain other ancient writers, says that the holy martyrs were killed by the freezing cold in the pool itself; but Basil testifies that they suffered not in a pool but in the middle of the city. Vossius, however, says that he saw a very ancient Greek manuscript in the monastery of Grottaferrata in which, instead of ἐν μέσῃ τῇ πόλει (“in the middle of the city”), one reads ἐν μέσῃ τῇ λίμνῃ (“in the middle of the pool”). See the Bollandists.].

He had a bathhouse heated opposite them and said: “Choose one of two alternatives. Either confess your Christ in this cold and perish, or deny him, sacrifice to the gods, and hurry to the bathhouse, so that you may live and not die miserably on account of a crucified man.”

When all of them refused to sacrifice to demons, their guard saw forty-eight most precious crowns descending from heaven and settling upon the men’s heads. One of the crowns, however, was called back, for the faith of one man had failed. He immediately abandoned his companions and hurried to the bathhouse. After sacrificing victims, he was honored by the governor and washed in the warm bath, only to receive thereafter the punishment of everlasting fire.

When that guard, as we have said, saw this, he proclaimed in a loud voice that he was a Christian, saying: “I wish to die with them.” Without delay he was subjected to various punishments, stripped of his clothing but not of his faith, and placed in the pool to suffer the cold with the others and obtain the crown that the wretched man had lost.

By then the men’s little bodies were deadened by the cold, and as their teeth chattered against one another, even the sound of their voices was stifled. Only a murmur of prayer rose from their secret hearts into heaven, known to God alone, who knows the hidden things of the heart. Their exhausted limbs trembled from both hunger and frost; their hope was directed toward heaven, while their flesh was already half dead.

Meanwhile the wicked judge ordered the water removed and the bathhouse heated seven times over, so that, obviously, those whom the cold had not loosened might be destroyed by savage flames. [Col. 0790A] The men who had confessed Christ were brought out of the pool and cast amid the burning vapors of the fires. They patiently endured the punishments inflicted upon them, so that they might receive a greater palm of victory.

At last, leaving their bodies behind and entrusting their souls to Christ, they completed their martyrdom in peace. Then the governor, seeing himself overcome by their steadfastness and thinking that he might conquer them dead, since he had been unable to overcome them alive, ordered their little bodies to be burned and thrown into a nearby river.

When this had been done, a new miracle appeared to the weeping Christians. The current stopped and did not swallow the half-burned bones, but held them up upon itself as though they had been entrusted to it. Thus the Christians gathered them with rejoicing and buried them with the highest honor.

## CHAPTER XCVII. On the Glorious Martyr Sergius

Sergius [Note: This chapter and the following two are absent from Clar. b. Sergius is said to have died a martyr with Bacchus under Maximian. Surius gives his *Acts* under October 7, on which day his feast is celebrated. Concerning him, see the notes on Book VII of the *History*, chapter 31. There is also a famous ancient abbey of the Order of Saint Benedict in the suburb of Angers, belonging to the congregation of Saint Maur, under the name of Saint Sergius.] also, a martyr (A.D. 303, October 7), performs many signs among the people, faithfully curing the illnesses and healing the ailments of those who pray to him. Consequently, enormous votive offerings are either promised to his basilica or brought to it, and it is not permitted to take away or remove anything whatsoever from them. If anyone does so, he soon incurs judgment, punishment [Alternative manuscripts: *noxae*, “harm,” or *notae*, “disgrace”], or death.

For this protection, many dedicate their possessions to the Saint, so that, fortified by his power, they may not be plundered by evil men. In the end, there was a small old woman—I believe she resembled that poor woman in the Gospel who once, having nothing else, devoutly cast two small coins into the treasury (Mark 12:11; Luke 21:1). This woman had a few chickens, which she had placed under the basilica’s jurisdiction by a vow, intending to give them to the household there whenever necessity demanded it.

When many people had come for the Saint’s feast, two men who had once seen these chickens made an agreement and secretly stole one. They cut off its head, plucked its feathers, and chopped off its feet; then they placed it in a vessel of water over the fire and heated it vigorously.

The liquid boiled violently, but the stolen flesh did not cook. Even while boiling, the water was consumed, and the chicken did not soften at all. They repeatedly tested it with their hands and tried to pierce it with a fingernail, but found it harder than when they had put it in.

Meanwhile the guests invited to the banquet arrived, but could not in any way partake of the preparations. A table stood covered with white cloths and adorned with embroidered work. [Col. 0790D] Although the food had been transformed into a new hardness, the dish was repeatedly rinsed with water, but nothing cooked could be found in it. Thus, through a new miracle, the banquet having been turned to stone, the hosts were confounded and the guests were embarrassed; they departed from the meal in shame.

## CHAPTER XCVIII. On Cosmas and Damian

The twin brothers Cosmas and Damian [Note: Various accounts of these martyrs circulate, but they are doubtful. More reliable are the things that ancient writers commonly record about their cult and miracles. Concerning them, see the Seventh General Council, act 4. A Mass for their feast is found in the Gregorian Sacramentary. Saint Sabas is said to have converted his paternal house into a church dedicated to their memory. Justinian built two churches for them, according to Procopius, and Felix IV, the ancestor of Saint Gregory, built one at Rome. The Greeks call them ἀνάργυροι, “without silver,” because they are said to have practiced medicine without payment.], physicians by profession, after becoming Christians (A.D. 303, September 27), drove away the illnesses of the sick solely through the merit of their virtues and the intervention of their prayers. Having been brought to perfection through various torments, they were united in heaven, displaying many miracles to the inhabitants.

For if any sick person prayed to them with faith at their tomb, he immediately obtained healing. Many also report that they appear in visions to the sick and tell them what they should do; when they have done it, they depart healed. I heard many such accounts, which I thought it too lengthy to pursue, believing that what I have said could suffice. All who prayed faithfully departed healed.

## CHAPTER XCIX. On the Renowned Martyr Phocas

Phocas [Note: This chapter is absent from Colb. tut. The common Martyrologies celebrate the feast of this martyr Phocas near Antioch on March 5. Whether he is the same as the gardener who lived at Sinope and was praised by Saint Asterius of Amasea is not entirely certain. See the *Sincere Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 627, and the Bollandists, under March 5.] also, himself a martyr and regionally connected with these martyrs, rests in Syria (A.D. . . ., March 5). After suffering many insults for the name of the Redeemer, he is still declared to the people as one who triumphed over that ancient serpent.

Indeed, if a snake bites anyone in these places and injects its venom by tightening its jaws, as soon as the wounded person touches the door of the courtyard where the Martyr rests, the swelling subsides, the poison’s power is removed, and he is saved. Several people, as the famous report has it, already swollen from the bite of the evil beast, their whole bodies bloated with venom and inflated to the point of expelling their breath, were carried in the hands of others and placed in the courtyard, where they were healed. No one is ever permitted to die from this poison if he touches the sacred threshold full of faith.

## CHAPTER C. On the Outstanding Martyr Domitius

There is indeed another martyr, Domitius, in this region [Note: Thus also Clar. b, in which the preceding chapters are absent; hence someone has substituted “in Syria.” The Latin Martyrologies mention Domitius as having suffered in Syria, and Baronius, for I know not what reason, distinguishes him from the one whom Gregory praises here. The Greeks celebrate Dometius, or Dometion, as a martyr in Phrygia under Julian the Apostate, on March 23.]. Since he grants many benefits to the inhabitants, he nevertheless cures sufferers from sciatica with swift power (A.D. . . ., July 5).

For it is said that this Saint himself was afflicted by the pain while he was still in the body. Since he cured many, as we have said, who suffered from this condition, a certain Jew, himself struck by the same illness, devoutly sought the Saint’s basilica, although he did not believe in Christ. He ordered himself to be laid at the door of the courtyard, loudly declaring himself unworthy to enter the sacred threshold.

For he said:

“I know, glorious martyr, that I am blinded by the veil of the Law, and that you may perhaps disdain to show me mercy. But now I flee to you and humbly ask your mercy: first turn away the bodily illness, and then remove the sickness of unbelief.”

While he was confessing these things before the entrance of the hall, night came and he fell asleep. But the blessed Martyr did not delay long in showing mercy. That night he visited the sick man in a dream and commanded him to depart healed.

When the man awoke, he felt that his health had been restored. He confessed that Christ was the Son of God and the Savior of the world, and departed healed.

When the Christians who were suffering from the same illness saw this, they brought complaints against the Saint, saying: “Look, we have confessed God rightly, yet we have not deserved to be freed, while this unbeliever in Christ the King, circumcised in flesh but not in heart, departs healed.”

As they said these things in anger, they began to smash the basilica’s lamps, which hung from the ceiling. But even they were not denied the mercy they requested. On that very day they were healed and returned to their homes.

## CHAPTER CI. On the Distinguished and Glorious Martyr George

We have learned of many miracles performed by the martyr George (A.D. 284, April 23), of which I shall say a few things [Note: This chapter is absent from Colb. tut. and, together with the following chapter, from Clar. b. Published authors report many more things about Saint George, but his *Acts* are plainly fictitious. Fortunatus recounts the various torments he endured in Book II, poem 15. Numerous basilicas built in his honor as early as the sixth century, together with many writers of that period, prove that his memory was celebrated in both East and West; concerning these, see the Bollandists at length under April 23. We assign his martyrdom to A.D. 284, when he is said to have suffered under the consuls Carinus II and Numerianus, according to the Alexandrian or Paschal Chronicle. Others maintain that he suffered under Decius.].

The relics of this man were being carried along with those of other saints. When the bearers reached a place on the borders of the Limousin, where a few clerics had already constructed an oratory from wooden boards and were constantly praying to the Lord, they asked for lodging. They were kindly received and spent the night with the other brothers singing psalms.

In the morning, however, they were completely unable to lift the small chest they had taken up. Since they could not possibly continue their journey without the holy pledge, and great grief had settled upon their hearts, they understood—by God’s inspiration [Alternative: “by God’s command”]—that they ought to leave something of the relics at that place.

They then opened the bindings and divided the particles, giving a portion to the elder who presided over the cell. They left behind part of the protection and obtained permission to depart wherever they wished.

His relics are also kept in a certain village in the region of Le Mans, where many miracles are regularly displayed. The blind, the lame, those suffering from chills, and other sick people often receive the gift of health there.

## CHAPTER CII. On Isidore, Most Holy Martyr

Isidore [Note: The manuscripts Mart. and Colb. a read “Isidorus.” He is a celebrated martyr among Greeks and Latins, although the *Acts* attributed to him are full of blemishes, including the Greek account published by the Bollandists under May 15. He is said to have completed his martyrdom under Decius in A.D. 252, but Decius had already died by then; hence the Bollandists preferred to assign his martyrdom to A.D. 250. They mention that they found an older life in their supplements, which they promise to publish. They also include there certain accounts of the translation of this saint’s relics by the Venetians. Chios is a celebrated island in the Aegean Sea, situated between Samos and Lesbos.] the martyr rests on the island of Chios (A.D. 250, May 15)—such is the name of the island. In the Saint’s basilica there is a well into which he is also said to have been thrown. The possessed, those suffering from fever, and other sick people are often saved after drinking its water.

It is also said that the faithful frequently see a light there, like a burning candle. I myself saw a presbyter who affirmed that he had often observed this light issuing from the mouth of the well. [Col. 0793B] On this island, too, the seed of the mastic tree is gathered in abundance; such trees, they say, are not found in other regions.

## CHAPTER CIII. On the Holy Martyr Polyeuctus

At Constantinople, the martyr Polyeuctus [Note: He suffered at Melitene in Armenia, where his *Acts* are preserved, though they are not so genuine that they can be called free of blemishes. They assert that he suffered under Decius and Valerian, which creates difficulty concerning the date of his martyrdom, since these two emperors did not reign jointly. See the Bollandists under February 13 and Tillemont, volume III of the *Ecclesiastical History*. A basilica of Saint Polyeuctus was famous at Melitene in the fifth century, as is clear from the *Life of Euthymius the Great*, whose parents had obtained him from God through the prayers of that same martyr.], is honored with great devotion (A.D. 250 or 252, February 13), especially because, although he possesses great virtues, he is a present avenger of perjurers [Note: For this reason he was also famous among the Franks. See above, Book VII of the *History*, chapter 6.].

For whoever, as often happens, has committed a hidden crime and is brought to the temple under suspicion of it either immediately confesses what he has done, terrified by the Martyr’s power, or, if he swears falsely, is at once struck by divine vengeance.

A certain matron of that city, Juliana [Note: Perhaps the passage of Codinus in the *Origins of Constantinople* should be referred here. He relates that Juliana, the daughter of Valentinian and sister of the wife of Theodosius the Great, spent four years and more constructing the basilica of Saint Polyeuctus at Constantinople, even summoning craftsmen from the city of Rome. See Du Cange’s description of Constantinople, Book IV.], covered the ceiling of this basilica with pure gold in the following manner.

When reports of her wealth reached the emperor Justinian through the accounts of many people, he hastened without delay to meet her, saying:

“I do not think it is hidden from you, venerable mother, how the public treasuries have been drained of their gold, while we seek to keep you at peace, strive to defend our fatherlands, appease foreign peoples, and acquire the support of various groups by granting them benefits.

“Therefore, since the power of the divine Majesty has bestowed so much gold upon you, I ask you to extend your hand to us and lend us some money, so that, when the total of the public taxes has been delivered, what you have lent may immediately be returned to you; and in the future, with the title of your praise preceding it, let it be sung that Constantinople was relieved of its financial burdens by the money of the matron Juliana.”

But she, understanding the emperor’s character, wisely concealed what she had vowed to God, saying:

“The smallness of my income, both from taxes and from what is expected from my estates, still remains tied up in those very houses. If, therefore, your Glory grants time for receiving it, once it has been collected it will be presented to your sight. When you have examined everything with your own eyes, you may leave what pleases you and take away what you wish. Whatever your heart’s will decrees will be acceptable to me.”

Thus deceived by these words, the emperor returned joyfully to the palace, thinking that he already held this money in the public treasuries. But she summoned the craftsmen and secretly handed over to them as much gold as she could find in her storerooms, saying:

“Go and, having made boards according to the measure of the beams, adorn the ceiling of the blessed martyr Polyeuctus, so that the hands of the greedy emperor may not reach it.”

When they had completed everything the matron had ordered, they fixed it to the ceiling and covered it with the purest gold.

When the work was finished, the woman summoned the emperor, saying: “The small sum of money that I have been able to assemble is here. Come and look at it, and do whatever you please.”

The emperor rose joyfully from his throne, expecting to receive the gold. He went to the woman’s house, thinking that he would carry abundant treasures away to the palace. When the woman humbly came to meet him, she invited him to pray in the Martyr’s church, which was near her house; she had dedicated to that holy place everything she had been able to obtain.

The emperor took the woman by the hand, since she was elderly, entered the building, and prostrated himself in prayer. When the prayer was finished, the woman said:

“Look, I ask you, most glorious Augustus, at the ceiling of this building, and know that my poverty is contained in this work. Do with it whatever you wish; I will not oppose you.”

When he looked up and admired it, he blushed. So that his embarrassment might not become apparent, he praised the work highly and gave thanks, then began to withdraw.

But so that he would not return empty-handed, the woman drew a ring from her finger, enclosing its gemstone in her palm; it contained no more than half an ounce of gold. She offered it to him, saying:

“Receive, most sacred emperor, this little gift from my hand, which is considered more valuable than the price of this gold.”

It contained a Neronian stone [Note: That is, an emerald. According to Epiphanius, Book XII, *On Gems*, chapter 3, in Bollandus, the Neronian emerald is small, exceedingly green, translucent, and shining. The same author says that it was so called because Nero used to make the color of this stone more vivid with the help of a certain oil—or else because of a craftsman named Nero who especially recommended its use. That Nero delighted in emeralds is clear from Pliny, Book XXXVII, chapter 5, where he is said to have watched gladiatorial combats through an emerald. Marbodeus says the same in Book *On Precious Stones*, chapter 54.], of extraordinary greenness [Col. 0795A] and brilliance. When it was displayed, all the gold seemed, by the beauty of the gemstone, to have been transformed into green.

The emperor accepted it, repeatedly gave thanks, praised the matron highly, and returned to the palace. There is no doubt, therefore, that the Martyr’s power intervened even in this matter, so that the wealth dedicated to holy places and the poor would not be transferred into the possession of one whose efforts had not gathered it.

## CHAPTER CIV. On Felix of Nola, the Distinguished Martyr

Concerning Felix of Nola, the martyr (A.D. 269, January 14), since the history of his passion is not at hand, I shall insert a few things into this reading, following what blessed Paulinus composed in verse [Note: This chapter is absent from Colb. tut. Blessed Paulinus celebrated Saint Felix’s praises in fifteen poems, which have been published more than once; but he especially pursued the events of his life in poems 4 and 5. The year of his death is uncertain. The church built at Nola by Saint Paulinus himself in honor of Saint Felix still survives today. See the *Sincere Acts*, p. 255, and the Bollandists under January 14.].

Felix, endowed with the honor of the presbyterate by Maximus [Note: Laud., Rom., and Clar. b read “Maximianus”; this variation also occurs in the Martyrologies. He is venerated at Nola on February 7; see the Bollandists under that date.], bishop of the aforesaid city, possessed wisdom and learning of such a kind that they could not be concealed not only from Christians but even from the pagans themselves. When the decrees of the emperors ordered Christians to be persecuted, the bishop Maximus, already weighed down by old age and thinking that he could not endure the punishments, went into the forest wilderness. As he wandered through it in agitation over the persecution, he was overcome by hunger, battered by frost, and collapsed half alive upon the ground.

But the presbyter Felix was arrested. After arguing at length that the portents of the gods were nothing, he was subjected to various kinds of punishment and condemned to prison, where he was held fast in no ordinary chains.

At midnight an angel of the Lord came to him, broke his chains, and tore apart the beam in which his feet had been confined. The angel said: “Rise and follow me.”

Felix rose and went out with him through the prison door. The angel of the Lord said to him: “Climb into the mountains and seek your bishop. When you have found him and restored his strength, bring him back to the city and hide him in a secret place, lest he perish from hunger and cold before the persecution against the Christians ends.”

Having received this command, Felix went toward a place he did not know. But, by God’s providence, he found the bishop lying prostrate on the ground, his eyes closed and his teeth clenched. Nothing but a faint breath entered him. Felix called to him but could draw no speech from him. When he touched him, he felt that his limbs were rigid with winter and almost dead, without any living warmth.

Anxious because he had no food to offer the man in danger, nor anything with which to kindle a fire, Felix stood astonished. Then he beheld an angelic gift descending, as it were, from the heavenly dwellings—and so it was.

For look: he saw a bunch of grapes hanging from a nearby thornbush. He squeezed the berries into the confessor’s mouth, and the old man was somewhat restored and rose. Felix placed him on his shoulders and carried him with such speed that it seemed rather that the man was being carried than that Felix was carrying him.

He entrusted him to the care of a certain widow in a hut and supplied him with food until the persecution against the Christians had passed. After the bishop’s departure, the people elected Felix to be placed over the ecclesiastical see, but he refused to consent. A presbyter named Quintus [Note: Ughellus gives him the title of saint in his catalogue of the bishops of Nola.] was ordained bishop.

When persecution of the Catholics arose, Felix the presbyter was admonishing the people in the street not to stray from the right path. A persecutor sent to arrest him arrived, but did not know Felix the presbyter. He began anxiously asking who Felix was.

Felix pointed with his right hand and said: “He went in this direction.”

When the man had departed, Felix sought a hiding place. He entered for a short distance among ruined walls and wanted to conceal himself there. Immediately the persecutor followed, but God frustrated the vigilance of the searcher.

For by divine command, spiders stretched threads of web across the passage through which the Martyr had entered. Following the tracks, the persecutors tried to inspect the place. When they saw the beginnings of the web, they said to one another: “Do you suppose that a man passed through these threads, which even the delicacy of flies repeatedly breaks through?” Deceived by God’s providence, they departed.

Blessed Felix also withdrew that night to another place, where for three months he received food from a certain woman. When peace was granted, he was restored to his church and people. Yet he never saw the face of the woman who ministered to him, nor did she suspect who he was while he remained in hiding.

After resting in peace, he was buried near the city, displaying many virtues among the people. I shall touch briefly upon a few of them [Note: The remainder of this chapter is omitted in Clar. b, and consequently the sense is deliberately interrupted.].

There was a poor man who had two oxen with which to cultivate his land. He possessed nothing else except what he could earn by splitting the earth with the plow. One day, tired from this work, he returned home, left the oxen, and withdrew into his little lodging.

Without delay a rapacious thief appeared, secretly seized the animals, and led them away. When the poor man went out the next day, he found nothing. He searched the byways, went around the forests, and climbed the heights of the mountains, but could not detect even a trace of them.

He returned home, cried aloud in grief, and mourned with his wife and children, saying: “Woe is me! Since the young oxen have been lost [Rome manuscript: “defrauded”], you will die of hunger this year.”

What more need be said? Mourning, he approached the tomb of blessed Felix the martyr, groaned with tears, and begged that the Martyr’s power might obtain from the Lord the return of what he had lost.

When he came out of the church, he recognized his oxen before the very door of the courtyard and said: “O great power of the Martyr, which has caused what I lost to be restored to me so quickly!”

He entered again, prostrated himself on the pavement, and, giving thanks, returned with his possessions. The Martyr’s power also restored sight to this man, who had been blind in one eye.

Against the wall of this cell, where the blessed body rests buried in its tomb, there is an attached portico. A lamp suspended by a rope was accustomed to provide light for the place. The man whose duty it was to attend to its arrangement approached, loosened the rope, and departed, as though to fetch oil.

When everything was covered by the darkness of night and the rope, with its little hooks, hung down lower in the middle of the portico, someone attending the Saint’s vigil, wearied by the smoke of the cell that had risen from burned papyrus, went outside.

As he passed through that portico, one of the little hooks on the rope caught the approaching man’s face and, thrusting its sharp point in, pierced his eye. Feeling the pain, he quickly spread his hands and covered his endangered face and eyes. He cried out with no small lamentation, saying:

“Come to my aid, I beg you, holy priest, and draw near to one who is perishing, since you stand near this place. Send forth your sacred hands through hidden remedies and pull out the evil that threatens my sight, lest I depart deprived of light, since I came to see the light of your miracles.”

At this lamentable cry, those present brought a light and saw the man hanging from the rope by his pierced eye. Since the blood was flowing and no one dared to put out a hand to remove the hook, the immense power of the blessed Martyr came to his aid. It pulled out the hook in such a way that it neither tore out the eye nor penetrated the sight, and it stopped the stream of blood that was running down.

When the iron had been removed from the eye and the pain in the eyelids had subsided, the power of the holy Martyr was made manifest among the people. This author has also frequently written that possessed persons were tested and cleansed at the sacred shrine of this athlete of Christ. But let us return to the martyrs of Gaul.

## CHAPTER CV. On Vincent of Agen
Vincent [Note: Clarendon manuscript B: this chapter is absent.] of the city of Agen, himself also a martyr (A.D. 257, 9 June), whose history of the Passion [Note: This seems to be the history published by François Bosquet, *Ecclesiastical History of Gaul*, book V. The memory of this blessed martyr was once celebrated, though it seems to have been somewhat overshadowed by the fame of another bearing the same name, namely the deacon Vincent of Zaragoza. Thus, if we are to believe several learned men, most of the basilicas that today honor Vincent of Zaragoza as their patron were originally consecrated under the title of Vincent of Agen. See Tillemont, volume IV of his *Ecclesiastical History*, p. 546, and in the notes, p. 753, where he also discusses the burial place, tomb, and other matters relating to this martyr; and Brower’s notes on Fortunatus, book I, poems 8 and 9, concerning the basilicas of this saint embellished by Leontius, bishop of Bordeaux.] is preserved by the inhabitants, shining in the Church of Christ with the brightness of the Levitical robe, and very often gleaming with great miracles; he is generally a severe avenger against those who seize his possessions.

At the time when the army, aroused against Gundobald [Col. 0797D], was directed toward the city of Convenae, his basilica was entirely surrounded by the multitude of that hostile force. Within it was a population relying upon all the protection of their possessions [Note: Thus the Colbertine manuscript. The others read: “the population, with all the protection of their possessions.” Gregory recounts the same story in *History*, book VII, chapter 35, where we spoke of Saint Vincent and his basilica.], confident in the reverence due to the Martyr, since no one would dare to touch them in such reckless presumption. Having barred the doors, they enclosed themselves inside with their belongings.

But when the besieging enemies [Manuscripts 3: “doorposts”] could find no entrance by which they might get in, they set fire beneath the doors of the church. They burned them for a long time, yet the gates did not catch fire, until, having smashed them with blows of axes, they entered, plundering the possessions and slaughtering the people enclosed there at sword-point. But this deed did not long remain unpunished. Some were seized by a demon; several were killed in the river Garonne; many were also attacked by “cold” [that is, fever], and in different places were afflicted by various kinds of disease.

I myself saw many of them in the territory of Tours, men who had been involved in this crime, being grievously tortured and tormented by unbearable pains even to the loss of their present life. Many of them confessed that, by God’s judgment, they had been destined for a most wretched death because of the injury done to the Martyr.

Behold how much God grants to his martyrs; behold with what praises Christ the Lord, overseer of the battles of the faithful, honors them; behold how much the dignity of the very name “Christian” accomplishes, if we do not, after the manner of the pagans, either gape after greed [variant: “vain desire”] or serve luxury.

## CHAPTER CVI. A Wonderful Miracle Concerning the Greedy [Note: Printed editions: “Also.” The manuscripts entitle this chapter: “Concerning the woman who hid money.”]

For I heard of something that happened in Gaul in years gone by. A certain woman, under the guise of religion, devoted herself to fasts and persisted in prayers; she kept vigil obstinately and regularly visited holy places with feigned devotion. While she maintained this appearance of a righteous life, she received immense wealth from many people. Every day she gathered gold, and what Christian devotion offered for the redemption of captives was hidden away in secret little boxes; what was given to benefit the needs of the poor was concealed in wicked purses.

The woman dug up the ground in the middle of her little cell, placed there an enormous jar, and whenever anything was given to her, carefully hid it inside. She then covered it with a stone so that the secret might be disclosed to no one.

O greed, thrice and four times and in every way accursed, which, depriving human beings of the light, plunges them into darkness! What more need be said? When the jar had been filled with coins, the woman’s time of dissolution arrived. She died to God and, departing this life, was buried in hell.

After her funeral, the priests who were present asked her attendant girl what she had done with so much money, or whether she had allowed herself time to distribute it. She replied that she had never seen her extend the hand of mercy to any poor person, and confessed that she did not know what had become of the money given to her.

“I know only one thing,” she said: “whatever was carried into the cell, I never saw brought back out again.”

When the clergy heard this, they were astonished and carefully investigated what had happened. As they repeatedly struck the pavement with blows [Note: Colbertine manuscript A: “and when the pavement had been beaten with repeated blows, the spot where the hidden money lay …”], the spot where the hidden money lay gave off a ringing sound; resounding over the hollow beneath, it revealed what had been concealed. At once, when the stone was removed, a heap of gold was found.

And the clergy, astonished at such subtle perversity, reported what had happened to the bishop. He, moved by the matter, ordered the tomb to be opened and the money thrown over the lifeless body, saying:

“Let what you gathered remain yours. The poor of Christ will not lack the means by which they may be sustained.” [Note: Thus Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 55: he ordered the body of a property-owning monk to be thrown onto a dung-heap together with his silver.]

No sooner had the first period of nighttime rest begun than voices were heard from the tomb—immense weeping and wailing. Among these voices the following words were heard most clearly: “Wretched me! Unhappy me! I am being consumed by the fire of gold.”

Finally, when these voices had resounded at nightfall for three days and the people could bear it no longer, they went to the priest. He approached and ordered the covering of the tomb to be removed. When it had been taken away, he saw gold, as though melted in a furnace, entering the woman’s mouth together with sulphurous flame [Note: A flame was likewise seen issuing for several days from the tomb of a certain criminal member of the curial class, as Gregory the Great relates in *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 32. See also chapters 51 and 15 below, in the book concerning Saint Julian.].

Then the priest prayed to the Lord that, since her wickedness had been revealed to the people, the Lord would finally order the punishment to cease from her body. He covered the tomb and departed, and the woman’s voice was heard no more [Note: Here the chapter and the first book end in the Colbertine manuscript. That manuscript then omits the book concerning the Miracles of Saint Julian and continues, as stated there: “Book II, Concerning the Miracles of the Holy Confessors,” etc.].

You therefore see how great is the difference between heavenly conduct and worldly wealth; how great the difference between the riches of the martyrs and the pomp of the world; you see what rewards have been granted to the martyrs as an aid toward the religious life.

And you, mortal human being, do not turn away from crimes; you do not cease from vices; you do not struggle against savage desires! Your eye entices you when you gaze upon what belongs to another, although the holy martyr was not turned aside by the lavish offering of riches. You waver amid wicked thoughts and yield, although that martyr did not yield to flames and claws. A single dart of your most evil desire wounds you, although neither the storm of blows nor the rack prevailed in driving Christ’s martyr from the path of righteousness!

He endured these things with a visible body, as you do, yet you do not restrain the invisible movements of the body. And although, according to the Apostle, “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, and these oppose one another, so that you do not do what you wish” (Gal. 5:17), nevertheless see what the same teacher says:

“I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin” (Rom. 7:23).

Therefore, if you should feel yourself being led away captive under the law of sin, immediately mark your forehead with the saving sign [Laudunensis manuscript: “the Savior’s sign”] of the cross, by which you may repel the dart of this ambush, because, as Prudentius says [Note: *Cath. Hymns*, poem 6, line 133]:

> The cross drives away every crime;  
> Darknesses flee the cross.  
> To a mind dedicated  
> To such a sign, wavering is unknown.

For I shall unfold what recently happened, so that the strength of this most holy standard may be understood.

## CHAPTER CVII. Concerning the Priest Pannichius [Note: Bellarmine and others: “Concerning the persistence of a fly, turned away by the bishop’s sign.”]

Pannichius, a priest in the territory of Poitiers, was sitting at dinner with friends whom he had invited and asked for a cup. When it had been handed to him, an exceedingly troublesome fly flew around, attempting to contaminate the cup. The priest repeatedly drove it away with his hand, but when it rose a little and tried to return again, he recognized the enemy’s ambush. Taking the cup in his left hand, he made the sign of the cross over it with his right. Immediately the liquid it contained divided into four parts; its wave rose high and was poured out upon the ground [Note: Thus, as Saint Gregory relates in *Dialogues*, book II, chapter 3, a vessel containing a poisonous drink could not withstand the sign of the cross made by Blessed Benedict.].

Thus it became unmistakably clear that this had been an ambush of the enemy. Therefore, if you too, bravely and not lukewarmly, place the saving sign upon your forehead or breast, then, by resisting vices, you will be considered a martyr. For the martyrs themselves accomplished the things they conquered not by their own strength but by God’s assistance, through the sign of the cross; in them, as we have often said, the Lord himself both fights and triumphs.

Hence we too ought to seek their protection, so that we may deserve to be aided by their intercessions; or, what we are not worthy to obtain by our own merits, may be acquired through their intercession. Thus, using the assistance of the sacred Trinity, may we deserve to become martyrs of Christ, renouncing carnal desires, as he himself says [Note: The Colbertine manuscript, by another hand: “as he himself, the leader, who …”]. May he, who crowns those who faithfully fight for him with precious stones in heaven, deign to protect in this world the pupils and worshipers of his friends; and may he grant that the martyrs, invoked by their own people, may stand beside them—martyrs whom the paradise of blessedness holds immortal after their victory.

Then, at that time of judgment, when eternal glory surrounds them, may either forgiving mercy intercede for us or a light punishment pass over us [Note: Namely, in purgatorial fire, or by whatever other means appointed for cleansing the slight stains of the dead]; and may he not condemn forever, because of their criminal deeds, those whom he redeemed through the commerce of his precious blood.

Amen.

**The first book ends.**

# BOOK TWO. CONCERNING THE PASSION, MIRACLES, AND GLORY OF SAINT JULIAN THE MARTYR

[Note: He suffered in A.D. 304, on 28 August.]

[Col. 0801]

## GREGORY’S PREFACE BEGINS

Divine mercy kindles within us, in a certain manner, a great little flame for attaining the path of his righteousness, when it says: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayers” [Bellarmine: “to their prayer”] (Ps. 33:16). It shows that whoever has loved righteousness with all his heart will be heard by the Lord when he prays.

Would that each one of us, when he begins to sing these words [Note: The printed editions read “attempts.” The Colbertine manuscript C reads “sings”], would immediately reject the scandals of the world, disregard empty desires, abandon crooked paths, and strive to enter the way of righteousness unencumbered and without the hindrance of worldly affairs.

Through this way righteous Abel is received, blessed Enoch is taken up, Noah is preserved, Abraham is chosen, Isaac is blessed, Jacob is enlarged, Joseph is guarded, Moses is sanctified, David is predestined, Solomon is enriched, and the three boys prophesy amid the dew-filled flames. Daniel is fed among savage beasts [Note: Thus the Colbertine manuscript A; the others, together with the printed editions, read “harmless beasts”].

Through this way the apostles are directed and the blessed martyrs are glorified. And how, you ask? Certainly, while they heal the weak, raise the dead [Note: Thus two of the Mainz manuscripts, the German and the Gembloux manuscripts; others read “the dead things”], despise present things, desire future things, scorn their torturers, feel no pains, and hasten toward the heavenly kingdom [Laud: “ascend”]. Without doubt they would not have obtained this by their own strength unless, walking most rightly along the way of righteousness, they had been heard by the Lord.

## CHAPTER I. Concerning the Passion of Saint Julian the Martyr

Thus the renowned martyr Julian, who was born in the city of Vienne and given as a martyr to Auvergne, kindled by this fire, desired these things and longed for them with all his heart [Note: In two Mainz manuscripts, the Colbertine manuscript T, the German manuscript, and the Gembloux manuscript, a brief preface is placed here, followed by the complete Passion of the blessed martyr. Some may perhaps think that Gregory inserted it into this book. The title of the chapter or book supports this view, since all printed editions and manuscripts have “Concerning the Passion,” etc. Since, however, that Passion is absent from the other copies, it seemed preferable to present it at the end of this volume.].

For while he was staying with the most blessed Ferreolus, he was already burning with the fragrance of martyrdom. He abandoned riches and relatives and came to Auvergne solely out of love for martyrdom. Yet he did not do this without divine command, since persecution was then raging in the city of Vienne. For he had read that the Lord had foretold: “If they persecute you in this city, flee into another” (Matt. 10:23).

Therefore he came here into the territory of Auvergne, not from fear of death, but so that, by abandoning what was his, he might more easily reach the palm of victory. He feared that his relatives might meet him if he began this contest among them, and that the soldier of Christ might lose the crown of glory if he did not fight lawfully.

As the persecution intensified, he arrived at the village of Brioude, where funeral songs of pagan error were being celebrated. When he perceived by God’s will that his enemies were pursuing him, he begged a certain widow to conceal him. She hid him, but immediately, at the Martyr’s request, she revealed him. He addressed his pursuers as follows:

“I do not wish to remain longer in this world, because with the whole desire of my soul I already thirst for Christ.”

Then, with his right hand brandishing a sword, they cut off his head and, so to speak, divided the glorious Martyr into three parts. His head was carried to Vienne, while his limbs were buried at Brioude [Note: No one denies that the martyr Julian suffered martyrdom and was buried at Brioude. But since there are two villages bearing this name—Old Brioude and New Brioude—there is disagreement about where the holy Martyr was first laid. Savaro, Sirmond, and others believe that he was buried at Old Brioude, now called Vieille-Brioude, which they think was the place meant by Gregory, Fortunatus, Apollinaris Sidonius in his *Propempticon* or poem 24, and other ancient writers. Others understand these references as concerning New Brioude, where the body of Saint Julian is still preserved in a very famous basilica, distinguished by a noble college of canons called counts. The relics of Saints Ilpidius and Arconius are also kept there; these are said to have been the two old men discussed below and in chapter 4.].

His blessed soul was received by Christ the Creator. The two old men who had committed his sacred body to burial were restored so completely that, although placed in extreme old age, they were regarded as young men. The martyr Ferreolus also received his head, and when the contest was complete, both Ferreolus’s limbs and Julian’s head were placed in the receptacle of a single tomb.

So that this account may not perhaps seem incredible to anyone, I shall faithfully report what I heard had happened [Laud: “I shall reveal.”]

## CHAPTER II. Concerning the Discovery of His Head

Once, when I had gone as far as Lyon to meet the blessed bishop Nicetius, I felt inclined to travel to Vienne—not for any other reason than prayer—and especially to visit the tomb of the glorious martyr Ferreolus (A.D. 304, 18 September). Because of my ancient affection for them, the thought had taken hold of my mind that I was as much his pupil as Julian’s.

After praying, I raised my eyes toward the tribunal [Note: Cyprian calls this the pulpit from which the deacon read the Gospel in church. Today we call it the ambo], and saw verses written there as follows:

> This hall contains two heroes of Christ:  
> Julian in head, Ferreolus in body.

As I read these words and asked the sacristan why they had been written in this way, he replied:

“The basilica of Saint Ferreolus had formerly been built directly on the bank of the Rhône. Eventually, when the portico situated on that side collapsed under the violent force of the river, a prudent priest named Mamertus, who then governed the Church of Vienne, anticipated the coming ruin and constructed another basilica with elegant workmanship and with exactly the same dimensions, applying careful thought to the project. He wished to transfer the body of the holy Martyr there.

“A great number of abbots and monks came for this work. After keeping vigil through the night, they took up mattocks and began to dig. As they descended into the depths, they discovered three tombs, and immediately astonishment seized the minds of those looking on. No one knew which tomb belonged to the blessed Martyr.

“While they all stood there stunned and dull with bewilderment [Note: Most manuscripts and printed editions read *hebitate*, or *hebetate*], one of those standing nearby, inspired, as I believe, by the Divinity, cried out:

“‘It was formerly customary to relate, and it was widely known among the people, that the head of the martyr Julian was kept in the tomb of the martyr Ferreolus. If the covering is removed and each body is examined, it will immediately be possible to determine which members belong to the martyr Ferreolus.’

“When the priest heard this, he ordered everyone to prostrate themselves in prayer. When the prayer had been completed, he went to the tombs. Two having been opened, he found a single man resting in each. When he opened the third, he found a man lying there with his body unharmed and his clothing intact. Though his head had been severed, he held another head clasped against himself in his arm.

“He appeared as though he had only recently been buried: his face had not changed color, his hair had not been disfigured by cutting, and no corruption had dissolved him. He was so whole and unharmed that one would have thought he was still held in bodily sleep.

“Then the bishop, filled with great joy, said: ‘There can be no doubt that this is the body of Ferreolus and that this is the head of the martyr Julian.’

“Then, with great psalm-singing and the applause of the people, it was carried, with the Lord’s assent, to the place where it is now worshiped” [Note: The memory of this translation is celebrated at Vienne on 13 December.].

I learned these things from the sacristan himself at the martyr’s tomb and have reported them faithfully. Our Sollius also bears witness to this account [Note: The Gembloux manuscript erroneously reads “Solilius.” This is Gaius Sollius Apollinaris Sidonius, who records the words quoted here in letter 1 of book VII, writing to Mamertus himself, bishop of Vienne. He compares him with Ambrose: just as Ambrose had transferred the bodies of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius, so Mamertus had been granted the translation of Ferreolus whole—that is, with his entire body—and of Julian’s head. The basilica of Saint Ferreolus, which Mamertus had built, was burned by the Saracens. Bishop Wilicarius, as Ado reports in his *Chronicle*, transferred the relics of the same martyrs into the city. On this occasion the people of Brioude say that they received Saint Julian’s head together with Blessed Ferreolus’s arm.
