Concerning Mamertus and the Litanies instituted by him, see above, *History*, book II, chapter 34, and Avitus’s homily on the Rogation ceremonies, etc. Concerning the same matter, see more in the Bollandists under 11 May.] He wrote to Mamertus in these words:

> “To you alone in the regions of the Western world has the complete translation of the martyr Ferreolus been granted, together with the head of our Julian. Therefore, in return, we ask that a portion of his protection come to us from there, since from here a portion of the patron has returned to you.”

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the Power of the Spring Where His Head Was Washed

[Note: The manuscripts that contain Saint Julian’s complete Passion do not have this chapter; in them it is inserted into the narrative of the Passion. The place where the blessed Martyr fell, formerly called Vincella and situated not far from both Brioudes, is now called Saint-Ferreol. The spring famous for miracles is still seen there, and Saint Julian’s head is said to have been washed in it before it was carried to Vienne.]

In that place where the blessed Martyr was struck down there is a bright spring, gentle and abundant in sweet waters. In it the head, severed by the persecutors, was washed, and many cures are attributed to those waters.

Often the eyes of the blind have been touched by them and restored to sight. Those afflicted by the heat of tertian or quartan fevers, when they drink the water, become calm. If anyone suffering from a serious illness, inspired by the Martyr, desires to draw from it, as soon as he has drunk, he recovers. The power of the fever is extinguished as swiftly as if one saw all the flames of an immense pyre quenched by water poured over it.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning the Old Men and the Matron Whose Husband Was Held in Prison

After the blessed Martyr’s Passion, when the fame had spread of the old men who, while committing the sacred limbs to burial, had been restored to their former strength, many people came there seeking benefits and obtained them through the Martyr’s mercy.

As I briefly relate a few of these events, I beg pardon, since I recognize that I am neither sufficiently capable nor sufficiently skilled to tell such things, being neither trained in grammatical arts nor educated in the liberal disciplines. But what can I do? The love of my patron urges me so strongly that I cannot remain silent about them.

A certain prisoner from Spain, who had been handed over to prison under the emperor at Trier, was being held under sentence of death [Note: Although, from the time when barbarians arising from the northern regions attacked Gaul, many emperors often stayed at Trier, I think that the expression “the emperor at Trier” here specifically means the tyrant Maximus, who had his royal residence at Trier.].

When his wife learned of this, she hastened to bury her husband’s remains and came to the village of Brioude. There she found some men and, while carefully investigating various matters, learned what had happened in that place concerning the Martyr and the old men. Trusting their faithful account, she decided to hurry to the blessed Martyr’s tomb, to present her reasons, disclose her misfortune, and lay before him the whole burden of her grief.

The people further assured her:

“Without doubt, mistress, we promise you that the Martyr will restore joy to you. He once restored the stiffened limbs of old men in decrepit age to their former strength.”

After making this prayer, she promised that, if she received her husband back safe, she would cover the Martyr’s tomb with cement, as far as she could, with faithful devotion [Note: The Gembloux manuscript reads, “with cement, as far as she could, and with complete faith.”].

Full of faith and confident in the Martyr’s mercy, she entered Trier. She found that her husband had been restored through imperial favor, and she returned joyfully. The time at which her husband was released from prison was investigated, and it was precisely the hour of his liberation at which she had implored the Martyr’s help. Afterwards she fulfilled her promise with immense gifts.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning the Man Who Tried to Kill Another in the Basilica

Not far from the small chapel that this matron had built over the Martyr’s tomb there was a great pagan shrine. On a very tall column an image of Mars and Mercury was worshiped there.

When the pagans were celebrating the festivals of that shrine and the dead were carrying incense to the dead, two young men from the crowd were provoked into a quarrel. One drew his sword and attacked the other in order to kill him.

When the second saw that no mercy was being offered to him and that he was not being defended by his gods, he sought the protection of our religion, the pardon of our confession, and the remedy of our participation in it: he fled to the chapel of the glorious Martyr.

The pursuer could not reach him with a sword in the attack. When the fugitive opened the door above him, the other seized both doorposts and tried to break the door down. Immediately his hands, clinging to the boards, were shaken by the most severe pain, and the wretch was tormented by such anguish that the tears flowing abundantly outward revealed what pain he felt within.

Meanwhile, while the crowd stood amazed, the man who had been shut inside came out free. The parents of the man who had been restrained by the Saint’s power, recognizing the Martyr’s burial place, prayed for their son with many devout gifts.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the Conversion of the Inhabitants

While these events were taking place, a certain priest happened to be coming down that road. When he learned what had happened, he promised the parents that, if they abandoned paganism, they would receive their son back unharmed.

The priest himself also saw in a dream the following night those images worshiped by the pagans crushed by divine power and thrown down upon the ground, reduced to dust.

On the fourth day, when the pagans wished once more to offer libations to their gods, the sorrowful priest prostrated himself at the Saint’s tomb. With tears he prayed that the splendor of divine power might at last visit this pagan people lying in darkness, and that the blessed Martyr would not allow his own followers to remain any longer in such blindness, while he himself possessed the joys of everlasting brightness.

Immediately, in response to his prayer, thunder was stirred up, lightning flashed, and rain mixed with fire and hail descended; everything was thrown into confusion.

The crowd ran to the chapel. The whole assembly of pagans prostrated themselves before the priest, and with wailing mingled with tears they all implored the Lord’s mercy. They promised the priest that, if the hail withdrew, they would seek the Martyr as their patron and, abandoning the worship of images, turn to his God with an undivided heart.

The priest poured out his prayer and deserved to obtain everything he had asked. When the storm withdrew, the boy, believing together with his parents, was freed from his pains that same day. The pagans were baptized in the name of the Trinity. They smashed the statues they had worshiped and threw them into the lake nearest the village and river.

From that time onward, both the Catholic faith and the Martyr’s power were more fully manifested in that place.

## CHAPTER VII. How Hillidius Delivered the People from Their Enemies

After this, certain Burgundians came to the village of Brioude and surrounded it with a great multitude of armed men. Having captured the people and plundered the sacred vessels, they crossed beyond the river. They prepared to kill the men with the sword and divide the rest of the population by lot.

Then a certain Hillidius, coming from Velay, and, as they say, stirred up by the prompting of a winged dove, rushed upon them [Note: Some manuscripts, and below as well, read “Illidius.” By Velay the region of the Vellavi is meant—Le Velay. Another Mainz manuscript ends here; the remaining leaves have been torn away.]. He encouraged his companions and struck down the enemies to destruction. After the captives had been released, he crossed the river in triumph, praising the Martyr, and returned to the blessed chapel with the whole people, singing like a new Moses.

Nor, I think, was the rejoicing of those who had been rescued less than that once felt by the Israelites when the Egyptians were drowned.

So that no one may doubt that this victory belonged to the blessed Martyr, the dove’s prompting is believed to have been some ministry of divine power [Note: Thus the German and Colbertine manuscripts C. The Colbertine manuscript A, the Martian manuscripts, and others read “some mystery.” Some read “the bird’s mystery.”].

When Hillidius was coming, the dove came to meet him. When he paused, as people commonly do, it flew around him; when he moved forward, it went ahead of him and returned to meet him, as though urging him to hasten his journey. While this was happening, a boy arrived and announced the captivity, and Hillidius then hastened his way. Even while he was fighting, the dove was always seen moving about him.

Let no one, therefore, begrudge the story of the dove or think it fabricated for the benefit of a Christian man, since Orosius (*History*, book III, chapter 6) records that a Roman consul—namely Marcus Valerius—was aided by a raven [Note: Some read “of the Romans.” This man, who was thereafter called Corvinus, was then fighting against a Gaul, one of the Senones. He is famous among the historians of Rome.].

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the Destruction of Those Who Carried Away the Basilica’s Sacred Vessels

After Hillidius had overthrown the enemies, four of them escaped and carried away a paten and a pitcher, called an *anax*, to their homeland. They divided the paten into as many portions as there were of them and presented both the paten and the pitcher to King Gundobald, seeking his favor.

The queen’s vigilance discovered the remaining silver. She added many gifts and restored it to the holy place, faithfully explaining to the king that he ought not to lose the favor of the holy Martyr because of the small amount of silver [Note: This was Caretena, who died in 506 and was buried at Lyon in the basilica of Saint Michael, which she had built. See Valesius, book VI of *Frankish Affairs*. Gundobald is sufficiently well known from other sources.].

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning Fedamia the Paralytic

For these and similar adornments of miraculous power, a great basilica was built there by the faithful. As we have said, it shines with the miracles of the blessed Martyr, and remedies are frequently sought there for paralytics, the lame, the blind, and sufferers from other diseases.

A certain woman named Fedamia, constricted by paralytic illness so that no limb of her body functioned without pain, was carried by her relatives to the blessed basilica, so that she might at least deserve a charitable handout from those who gave.

While she lay in the portico adjoining the holy basilica, during the Lord’s night, when the people’s devoted faith was celebrating the sacred vigils together [Note: The Colbertine manuscript A reads: “when the people, in devoted faith, were celebrating the sacred vigils.” Colbertine C and the German manuscript read: “on the Lord’s night,” etc. Certainly in those times not only clergy but also all the laity took part in the nighttime vigils, as is easily proved from this and many other passages. See Thomassin, *Ecclesiastical Discipline*, part I, book II, chapter 79], she fell into a brief sleep on her little bed.

In a vision she was seized and rebuked by a certain man, who asked why, while the others were offering nighttime vigils to God, she alone was absent. She replied that she was weak in every part of her limbs and could not take even a single step.

Then, as though supported by the man who was speaking to her and led as far as the tomb, while she poured out a prayer in her sleep, it seemed to her that a multitude of chains fell from her limbs onto the ground. Awakened by the sound, she perceived that complete health had returned to all her limbs.

She immediately rose from her bed and, while everyone stood amazed, entered the holy basilica, crying out with thanksgiving.

Some also report that she used to describe the appearance of the man who had spoken to her. She said that he was tall in stature, splendid in clothing, outstanding in elegance, cheerful in countenance, blond-haired with gray hairs mixed in, swift in movement, free in speech, and exceedingly gentle in conversation. The brightness of his skin shone beyond the radiance of a lily, so that, although she had often seen many thousands of people, she had never seen anyone like him.

For this reason many reasonably think that the blessed Martyr appeared to her. The woman was healed after eighteen years.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning the Man Who Tried to Drag His Assailant from the Basilica

A certain man had lost an eye during a riot that he himself had caused. He tried to drag from the basilica the man who had struck him. While doing so, he not only failed to recover the sight of the lost eye but also felt the other eye, which had been sound, becoming blind.

When he confessed his sins, saying, “It is deservedly that a judgment without mercy has come upon me, since I showed no mercy,” he prostrated himself before the holy tomb together with the people who had come for the festival. He forgave the man who had injured him and recovered both his sight and the Saint’s favor.

Thus it came about that the man who had sought the Saint’s help was protected, while the one who did not believe was reproved; and both departed joyful and corrected.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the Cripple Who Yoked Oxen on the Lord’s Day

Another man, acting with reckless presumption, began to yoke oxen and plow a field on the Lord’s Day. He took up an axe to repair something on the plowshare, but immediately his fingers contracted and the handle clung to his right hand.

As he was tormented by immense pain, he came to the blessed Martyr’s basilica after two years and faithfully celebrated the vigils. Immediately, on that very Lord’s Day, his hand opened, and he lost the piece of wood that he had been holding against his will. This gave the people a great lesson: what had been committed on the Lord’s Day was cleansed on that same Lord’s Day.

The man glorified the Martyr’s power and departed unharmed. From then on, he no longer dared to do any work on the Lord’s Day of the Resurrection [Note: Here and frequently elsewhere, any Sunday is plainly called “the day of the Lord’s Resurrection.”].

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning Anagildus, Who Was Mute, Deaf, and Blind
858 Thus Anagildus also [Note: Laud. with Clict. and Sur. has Anagilus; Gem. has “Sed et,” etc.], a certain mute, deaf, and blind man, or one weakened in the structure of all his limbs, was cast down at the sacred threshold—clearly so that he might at least be fed by the alms of the devout [Note: Here Gregory and elsewhere commonly understands *devoti* to mean pious persons who, although living in the world, devoted themselves to good works more diligently than others. This manner of speaking still exists today. In the same sense Augustine calls them *devoti*, Sermon 52, no. 5; Cassiodorus frequently; Hincmar, *On Predestination*, chapter 2, and in his letter to Pope Nicholas; Frodoardus, and others]—since he could not work with his own hands to obtain food. After he had lain there for a full year before the holy building, he was at last visited by the power of blessed the Martyr and healed of every illness.

### CHAPTER XIII. Concerning those who broke into the basilica in the time of King Theoderic

It seems to me that, just as illnesses cured by the Saint’s power are related, so the depravity of unbelievers, confuted by his prayer, should also be made known for the correction of others, lest they desire similar deeds. For each aspect of the Saint’s glory is beneficial: it restores the former to health, so that they may no longer suffer, and reproves the latter, so that they may not be condemned at the future judgment.

And since I believe that no one is unaware of the hostility of King Theoderic [Note: This chapter is cited in the *Life of Saint Stremonius*, volume II of Labbe’s *Bibliotheca*, p. 498. Gregory himself narrates Theoderic’s expedition against the Arverni in *Histories* III.12. Here the same author also seems to praise our Gregory’s *History*, or at least some work excerpted from it, which he calls the *Deeds of the Germans*. From this source he relates Theoderic’s expedition into Arvernia, though not very accurately] and of the illnesses that befell Sigivald while he was stationed in Arvernia, nevertheless, on account of the blessed Martyr’s power, these matters must be set forth more carefully, so that faith may more readily be given to what is said.

When the aforementioned king was hastening to plunder the Arverni (A.D. 525), and, entering the territory, was subjecting everything to devastation, a section separated from the army rushed hostilely toward the village of Brioude, since rumor had spread that the inhabitants, together with many treasures, were gathered in the basilica. When they reached the place, they found a multitude of both sexes residing in the church itself with their possessions, the doors having been barred. Since they could not enter, one of them, like a thief, entered through a glass window broken in the holy altar [Note: Thus Germ., Gem., and Colb. c—that is, “in the presbytery,” as we have already observed; the others have *altari*, “the altar”]. For “the one who does not enter by the door is a thief.” Then, having opened the doors of that building, he admitted the army.

They divided outside the village all the poor people’s belongings that they had plundered, together with the furnishings [Note: Beyond doubt, *ministeriis* should be read] of the basilica itself, as well as the rest of the people who had been brought out from within. When this was reported to the king, he condemned some of those captured among them to various deaths. But the man who, after breaking into the building, had been the leader of this crime fled and was consumed by fire falling from heaven. When many people had piled up a heap of stones over him, thunder and flashes of lightning exposed him, and he was denied burial in the earth.

Those of his accomplices who had hidden and returned to their homeland without the king’s knowledge were seized by a demon and cruelly ended their lives by various deaths. When the king heard this, he restored everything that had been taken from that place. For he had ordered that no one should inflict violence within seven miles of the basilica.

### CHAPTER XIV. Concerning Sigivald the Usurper

At that time Sigivald, powerful with the king, migrated with his entire household into the region of Arvernia at the king’s command [Note: Gregory has the same account in *Histories* III.13, where Sigivald is said to have been one of the king’s relatives. His administration is discussed in book III, chapter 16]. While he was unjustly laying claim to the property of many people, he greedily seized, under the pretext of a disguised exchange, a certain estate that Tetradius of glorious memory [Note: He took part in the Council of Agde in 507 and the First Council of Orléans in 511. Bollandus discusses him on 16 February], bishop of Bourges, had left to the basilica of Saint Julian. But in the third month after he had undertaken this, he was struck by a fever, lost consciousness, and bent his head down onto his bed.

While his wife was grieving over this outcome, she was warned by a certain priest that, if she wished to see him restored to health, she should remove him from the estate. On hearing this, she prepared wagons and arranged a cart to carry him away. As soon as they had left the estate, both were immediately rewarded by divine grace: he received health [Read *sospitatem*], and she earned joy from his recovery.

It is also reported that a religious man was shown Saint Julian the Martyr speaking with Bishop Tetradius in the estate’s oratory, promising that he would recover for the bishop the estate that Tetradius had left to him for the remedy of his soul. He also related that the blessed Martyr appeared in the same condition as the paralytic woman had formerly described [see above, chapter 9].

### CHAPTER XV. Concerning Pastor’s wickedness

There was a certain Pastor, Ingenuus by name rather than by energy. While he was acting unjustly against the basilica of the holy Martyr in many matters, his frivolity grew stronger as the enemy fattened it, until he did not fear to seize the basilica’s *colonicae*—that is, its tenant-farms—which lay nearest to his own fields [Note: Most medieval authors wrote *colonias* for *colonicas*. A *colonica* is an estate with as much land as one tenant can cultivate. The terms *colonica*, *mansus*, and *villa* mean nearly the same thing; among the Germans, *hoba* and *hobunna*. See Bignon’s notes on book I, formula 30, of Marculf].

The priest of the place sent some clerics to him as envoys, so that, after the matter had been explained, he might relinquish what he had wrongly seized. But Pastor sprang upon them as though against an unjust enemy, taking up weapons; and, after driving the clerics away with arrows, he retained the Saint’s property under his own control.

Now it happened that the day of the glorious Martyr’s passion was approaching. Forgetful of his seizure and of the injury he had inflicted upon the clerics, Pastor came to the village of Brioude five days before the solemnity. While he was enjoying a banquet in his lodging with happiness and rejoicing, suddenly lightning flashed and thunder sounded. Then again, after another flash, a fiery dart slipped down from heaven and struck him, although none of the others perished. Thereafter, as an example to all, he was gradually consumed like a blazing, flaming pyre (see above, book I, chapter 106).

The people who had gathered for the Blessed One’s festival witnessed this miracle and were terrified with amazement. It was sufficient warning to him, so that nothing further might happen concerning the Saint’s possessions. And lest anyone should think that this had happened by chance, let him observe that, among many unharmed people, one sacrilegious man perished.

### CHAPTER XVI. Concerning Beccho’s Defiance

I shall unfold what the blessed Martyr did to confound the pride of Count Beccho [Note: *Actiones* here denotes an office. Thus Marculf, book I, formula 8, speaks of the offices of countship, dukedom, and patriciate. Huneric, in Victor of Vita, book II, forbade any Catholic to serve in the palace or hold public offices. See Bignon’s notes on book I, chapter 11 of Marculf].

While Beccho was holding public office and, swollen with arrogance, oppressing many people contrary to justice, it happened by chance that he lost a falcon he had released, after it had wandered for a long time through various places. Similarly, one of the servants of the basilica of Saint Julian found another falcon while walking along the road, as though it were a stray. The boy was a cupbearer in the basilica’s household.

When Beccho learned that the boy was holding a falcon he had found, he began to bring an accusation, saying: “That falcon was mine, and this boy stole it.” Then, as greed increased, he had the boy bound and put in prison, intending to condemn him to the gallows on the following day.

The priest, greatly distressed, hurried to the Saint’s tomb. Opening the reliquaries with a sigh, he took ten gold pieces and offered them to Beccho through faithful friends. Beccho rejected them as worthless and swore that he would never release the boy unless he received thirty gold pieces. The priest took this message from above the Saint’s tomb and sent the thirty pieces to Beccho. After receiving them, and with his greedy desire satisfied, Beccho restored the boy unharmed [Note: Germ. reads *avari*, “of the greedy man”; the others have *auri*, “of gold”; Mart. and Gem. have *auro*, “with gold”].

But almighty God, who remains before the sun, humbled the false accuser according to the riches of his goodness. When a year had passed, Beccho came to the Saint’s festival with a crowd of attendants and entered the sacred threshold. As a lector came forward to recite the account of the blessed passion, he opened the book and, at the beginning of the reading, pronounced the name of Saint Julian. At once Beccho collapsed to the ground with some exceedingly dreadful cry. Foaming bloodily, he began to utter various sounds. He was then lifted from the basilica in the hands of his attendants and taken home.

His servants had no doubt that this had happened to him because of the injury inflicted upon the basilica’s servant. He gave the basilica all the adornment he was then wearing, both gold and clothing, and thereafter sent many gifts; but he remained senseless until the day of his death.

### CHAPTER XVII. Concerning the Deacon who Took Away the Basilica’s Sheep

There was also a certain deacon who, having abandoned the church, joined himself to the public treasury [Note: Germ. has *relicta ecclesia*, “having abandoned the church,” but Gregory frequently uses the accusative in place of the sixth case]. Having received authority from the patrons, he committed such great crimes that he could scarcely be endured by the surrounding neighbors.

On one occasion he happened to be going around the mountain pastures where the sheep had gone for the summer and investigating the grazing taxes owed to the treasury [Note: *Pascuarium* is a tax levied on animal pasturing, just as *agrarium* is imposed on fields. On these matters see Bignon’s notes on Marculf, book I, formula 35]. While he was unjustly stripping various people, he saw in the distance flocks that were then being protected under the name of the Martyr. He flew toward them at a light run and, like a ravenous wolf, seized the rams.

The shepherds, troubled and frightened, said to him: “Please do not touch these rams, for they have been placed under the authority of blessed Julian the Martyr.” He is said to have mocked them and replied: “Do you suppose that Julian eats rams?” Then, after beating them, he took whatever he wished. The wretch did not know that whoever takes anything from the houses of the saints insults the saints themselves, as the Lord himself testifies: “Whoever rejects you rejects me” (Luke 10:16), and, “Whoever receives a righteous person will receive a righteous person’s reward” (Matthew 10:41).

After many days, it happened that he went to the village of Brioude—not through religious devotion, but by chance. He threw himself on the ground before the tomb and was immediately seized by a fever. He was overwhelmed by such intense heat that he could neither rise nor call for a boy.

When his servants saw that he was lying there longer than usual, they approached and said: “Why are you being overcome for such a long time? It was not your custom to pray for so long, nor was your devotion so prolonged” [Note: Most manuscripts read: “It was not your custom to pray for so long, nor was your devotion so prolonged”]. It was reported of him that whenever he entered the church, he would mutter briefly and return without even bowing his head [Another reading: “and not bowing his head”].

Then, when the boys questioned him and he was unable to answer, they carried him away in their arms and placed him in a cell near the bed. As the fever grew stronger, the wretched man cried out that he was being burned by the Martyr. What he had initially kept silent about, when the torches of judgment were brought close to his soul, he confessed: his crimes. He begged them, in whatever voice he could muster, to throw water over him.

When water was brought in a vessel and repeatedly poured over him, smoke came from his body as though from a furnace. Meanwhile his miserable limbs, as if burned, turned black, and such a stench came from him that scarcely any of those standing nearby could endure it. Then, signaling with his hand, he indicated that he was feeling lighter. Soon, when they withdrew, he breathed out his spirit.

There can be no doubt what sort of place he occupies there, having departed from here under such a judgment.

### CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the Man who Stole a Horse during the Saint’s [Note: Laud., with Clict., Bal., and Mor., reads “Saint Peter’s.”] Vigil

Another man, during the vigil of the festival, stole someone’s horse—someone who happened then to have come to the same solemnity—and quickly mounted it and hurried away. The man who had lost the light of truth was thereby prevented from being found by the light, and the darkness of night concealed the fraudulent theft of one whose heart had been occupied by the darkness of greed. For the Lord said of such people in the Gospel: “Everyone who does evil hates the light” (John 3:20).

When the sky began to grow white, he said: “Now I am safe, for I am thirty leagues away from the Saint’s basilica. Surely I now believe this place to be my own home.” While he silently turned these thoughts over within himself, the darkness having been removed from the heavens, he realized that he was wandering among crowds near the very village. Fearing that his crime might become publicly known, he took great care to return the horse to the place from which he had departed.

Thus the wretched man was held throughout the entire night in a circuit around the village by the Martyr’s power—and, as I believe, was deceived by the author who had possessed him, so that he could not reach the road he had intended to take. O wicked greed, what are you doing? You always plunge your lovers into disgrace.

### CHAPTER XIX. Concerning the Man who Perjured Himself over a Triant

One man had lent another a *triant*, which he recovered after a few days. A year later, in the Saint’s courtyard, after meeting the other man, he demanded that the object be returned to him as though he had not received it. The other man, indignant, insisted that he had returned what he had received.

After they had argued for a very long time, the man who had returned it said to his companion: “How long shall we both contend? Let us place this matter under the judgment of almighty God. Let us go to the Martyr’s tomb, and let the holy power of the Patron decide what you say under oath.”

The other man, without hesitation, entered the tomb. As he boldly raised his hands to swear falsely [Another reading: “to perjure himself”], miserable wretch that he was, he suddenly became rigid. His voice stuck in his throat, his tongue was constricted in his gullet, and his lips moved without speech. He was entirely unable to draw back the arms that he had raised to support his false oath.

As the crowd marveled at this and the crime became publicly known, the entire multitude of people burst out with one voice, imploring the Lord’s mercy and the aid of the blessed Martyr. After four hours or somewhat more, he returned to consciousness, publicly confessed what he had unjustly demanded again, and departed healed.

### CHAPTER XX. Concerning the Man who Robbed the Holy Basilica

The man who had committed violence against the holy basilica had often heard these things, but goodness could not soften a wicked mind once possessed by vice, as Solomon testifies: “Wisdom does not enter a malicious soul” (Wisdom 1:4).

The Saint’s festival had arrived, and a certain man from the crowd saw the blessed basilica shining with immense ornaments. With an evil mind he desired what he could not conceal once he obtained it. After the people had left the basilica following the evening service, he hid himself in a corner of the basilica. When silence had been given to all by the night’s rest, and shadowy darkness covered the world, he rose from his corner.

Without hesitation—certainly because Satan’s accomplice was driving him—he leapt rapidly over the railing of the blessed tomb. He tore down from the top a cross glittering with gems [Note: A cross was placed at the summit of the *ciborium* that was customarily built above altars or the tombs of saints. Mabillon discusses this at greater length in *Gallican Liturgy* I.8.7]. He threw it to the ground, gathered the small curtains and cloaks hanging around the walls, made one bundle of them, and placed it upon his shoulders. Holding the cross raised in his hand, he returned toward the place from which he had come. He set the bundle beside his head and, overcome by the sleep of sin, fell asleep.

At midnight the guards, making their rounds of the holy basilica, saw a single jewel of the cross shining in a corner like a heavenly ray. Stunned, they approached fearfully. Bringing a candle near, they found a man lying there with the stolen objects that he had been unable to carry away.

They kept him under guard for the rest of the night. At dawn he disclosed everything he had done, asserting that he had fallen asleep from exhaustion because, after circling the basilica for a very long time with the bundle [Another reading: “with a torch”], he had been unable to find the door through which to leave.

### CHAPTER XXI. Concerning the Man who Lost his Horse at the Festival

The Saint displayed many other things of this kind among transgressors, but these examples are sufficient to restrain their negligence. Let us now return to the joyful benefits that he bestows upon the people in his abundant compassion.

First, however, I do not think we should pass over what we have learned by direct experience: what faithful prayer obtains from this Patron in matters that have been lost. I shall recall only one example.

A devout poor man had come to the festival of the blessed Martyr. He left his horse untethered, entered the sacred building, and, remaining steadfast at the vigils, spent the night praying with the others. When the sky began to brighten, he returned to his lodging but did not find the horse he had left there. After searching for it for a very long time, he could not even discover any sign of the direction in which it had gone.

After two days had passed, he went again through the woods, questioning the inhabitants of the area to see whether anyone had captured it or had seen it captured by someone else. Finding no indication of any kind, anxious and sorrowful, he returned to the Saint’s tomb. There he explained the causes of his pain and grief, saying:

“I came to your threshold, Saint, bringing nothing except the prayers of my poverty. I have taken nothing unjustly; I have done nothing unworthy of your solemnity. Why, then, have I lost my property? I ask you to restore what has been lost, to return what I need.”

After saying this with tears, he left the church and saw in the distance a certain man holding his horse. Approaching him, he questioned him about where the horse was from, where it had come from, and how long he had possessed it. He learned that it had been found at precisely the hour when he had implored the aid of the blessed Martyr.

### CHAPTER XXII. Concerning the Blind Man who Received Sight

When a certain man had lost an eye through a demonic attack and sat miserably in his little lodging deprived of light, unable to work with his own hands and having no hope of obtaining food, a man appeared to him in a nighttime vision and instructed him to go to the basilica of the blessed one. He promised that, if the man made his request devoutly, aid would be found there.

Without delay, the man seized his staff and, assisted by a boy, entered the holy place. After completing his prayer, he approached the archpriest who then governed the place, named Publianus [Note: Archpriests already existed in villages at that time. Thomassinus discusses their duties at length in *Ecclesiastical Discipline* I.II.3 and following], begging him to place Christ’s cross upon his blind eyes. Publianus was highly religious.

While Publianus tried to avoid this, wishing to escape any appearance of ostentation, the blind man seized him and would not release him at all until he fulfilled what was requested. Then Publianus prostrated himself before the Martyr’s tomb and prayed for his aid for a very long time. Afterward he brought his hand close to the blind man’s eyes and, as soon as he made the sign of the cross, the man recovered his sight.

Marvel, I ask you, at the Martyr’s power: although it is little for him to perform miracles by himself, he now also works publicly through the hands of his disciples, with the favor of his power bearing witness. Nor was the disciple’s merit insignificant, since these things are seen to have been granted through him.

### CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning the Healed Foot of Gallus, Later Bishop

At that time my uncle, Bishop Gallus, was in the city of Arvernia [see *Life of the Fathers*, chapter 6]. It should not be omitted how he was assisted in his youth by the Saint’s power.

Since I have often mentioned what devastation King Theoderic inflicted upon the region of Arvernia—when nothing of their own property was left either to the older or to the younger people, except the empty land that the barbarians could not carry away with them—during those times my uncle of glorious memory, who later, as I have said, governed the Church of Arvernia with the priestly office, was an orphan. His possessions had been so thoroughly plundered by the army that absolutely nothing remained available.

He himself, with only one boy, often traveled on foot as far as the village of Brioude. On one occasion, while he was making this journey, he loosened his sandals because of the heat of the sun and walked barefoot. He stepped on a thorny stake which, perhaps recently cut and still fixed in the earth, lay hidden among the green grasses with its sharp point upright.

The stake was driven into the sole and protruded above it. When it broke off below, it could not be extracted. As a stream of blood flowed and he could not walk, he implored the aid of the blessed Martyr. When the pain had been somewhat restrained, he nevertheless completed the journey he had begun, though limping.

On the third night the wound began to rot, and the pain grew extremely severe. He fled to the aid he had previously experienced and prostrated himself before the glorious tomb. After completing the vigils, he returned to his bed. While awaiting the Martyr’s power, he was overcome by sleep.

Then he arose and felt no injury from the pain. Looking at the sole of his foot, he could not see the part of the stake that had entered it, although he felt that it had been pulled out of his foot. Carefully searching for the piece of wood, he found it in his bedding, marveling at how it had emerged.

For he was accustomed, during his episcopate, to show the place of the wound, where a large depression was still visible, declaring that the blessed Martyr’s power had been at work in this.

### CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning the Fever of my Brother Peter

A long time afterward the festival of the blessed Martyr arrived, and my father was hurrying with his entire household to the joys of this solemnity. As we traveled, my elder brother Peter was seized by the heat of a fever and was so gravely ill [Note: Colb. a, Germ., and the others have *agitur*; some editions have *angitur*, “was distressed, so that he could not even drink.” Gregory narrates the death of his brother Peter, then a deacon, in *Histories* V.5.] that he could neither be well nor take food. The entire journey was thus spent in great sorrow, and the matter reached the point of uncertainty whether he would recover or perish.

At last, with this difficulty, we reached the place. We entered the basilica and worshiped at the sacred burial place of the Martyr. The sick man also lay prostrate on the pavement, imploring healing from the glorious Martyr.

After completing his prayer, he returned to the lodging, and the fever subsided somewhat. When night came and we were hurrying to the vigils, he asked to be carried there as well. Lying before the tomb, he prayed throughout the entire night for the Martyr’s aid.

After the nighttime watch had ended, he asked them either to give him for drinking some dust gathered around the blessed tomb or to hang it around his neck. When this had been done, all the fever’s heat subsided so completely that on that very day he was able to eat safely and walk wherever his desire led him.

### CHAPTER XXV. Concerning the Pain in my Head

At the festival that followed, while we were again hurrying with great joy to the holy basilica, my head began to ache severely after being struck by the sun. As the pain increased, it generated an internal fever, so that it would not allow me either to eat or to speak.

After I had been consumed by this pain for two days, on the third day we arrived at the basilica of Saint Ferreolus, adjoining the spring mentioned above (chapter 3). The basilica is about ten stadia from the village of Brioude.

When we had reached that place, I wished to proceed as far as the spring, trusting in the Martyr’s power: if its gentle water washed over me, I would immediately be healed. When I arrived, I offered a prayer, drew water, cooled my mouth, and immersed my head. As the water flowed down, the pain immediately fled, and I departed healed. I entered joyfully as far as the tomb of the glorious Martyr, marveling and giving thanks to the Martyr because he had deigned to visit me with his power before I had deserved to see his tomb.

### CHAPTER XXVI. Concerning a Man with Fever Healed at the Spring

At this spring there is an extraordinary power [Note: Thus Colb. a with Sur. and Clict. Colb. c and Germ. have: “For the power of the spring is extraordinary, because …” Mart. and most editions read corruptly: “And indeed at Hunoron.” Laud. and Bell. have “Unoronem.” Germ. has: “For at the spring where the head of the most blessed Julian was washed there is extraordinary power, because the Martyr was struck there.” Some …], since the Martyr was struck there.

A certain man, seized by a fever and already in extremis, desired to drink water from the spring. He earnestly begged to be carried there. His people took him in their arms and set him down at the place. As soon as he drank the water and washed his face and head with it, he deserved to recover his health. Carried there by others, he returned on his own feet.

He had been an inhabitant of this village, but his name has been forgotten.

### CHAPTER XXVII. Concerning the Thunder and Lightning that Occurred in the Basilica

One day a storm arose and rapidly descended upon the village of Brioude with a great blast of wind. Lightning flashed from the clouds, and thunder gave forth terrible sounds. The earth shook with the crash, and almost everything seemed likely to be burned by the lightning. The only expectation was in the power of the glorious Martyr.

Without delay, after a heavy clap of thunder accompanied by lightning, a fiery dart entered through the opening from which the rope of the bell hung. It struck two columns and knocked off fragments. Then, rebounding, it went out through the window above the holy tomb, yet, under the Blessed One’s protection, it harmed no one from the crowd.

O how great is the blessed Martyr’s love for his own dependents! He allowed the columns to be struck but did not permit the people to be struck; he allowed the glass to be shattered but not the crowd; he permitted the lightning to pass over his own tomb so that the entire multitude would not perish. The fiery dart expelled from the basilica of the holy Martyr burned heaps of hay, killed livestock, and destroyed pack animals.

If anyone thinks these things happened by chance, let him admire and be astonished still more at the power of the renowned Martyr: the fire passed through the midst of the people and harmed no one, but fulfilled its purpose only where it recognized that it had permission.

### CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning the Man who Could Not Approach the Tomb because of the Crowd

A certain cleric of Aridius, abbot of Limoges, came to the festival. Because of the crowd, he could not merely approach the holy tomb—he could not even enter the basilica itself.

Sorrowfully returning to his lodging, he lay down on his bed and fell asleep. Immediately a man stood beside him in a vision and said: “Why are you being weighed down by sleep? Go quickly to the Martyr’s church, and you will find everything opened.”

Terrified by fear, the man rose. Trusting the words, he hurried to discover whether what had been announced to him was true. When he reached the door, he found that the people had been removed on every side [Note: Editions have “the people having been removed.” Germ. has “the people and everything …” and “no one resisting”], and that a path had been opened all the way to the holy altar and the tomb itself, with no one obstructing him. Approaching without any pressure from the crowd, he poured out his prayer and returned joyfully.

Lest anyone doubt this, I call almighty God to witness that I learned these things from the abbot’s own mouth, among whose monks the event had occurred [Note: Observe that Gregory here calls a monk one whom he had previously called a cleric; the same usage is found frequently among other authors of his age. See the notes above, book I, *Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 76].

### CHAPTER XXIX. Concerning his Festival

The ignorant populace waited sadly for the time of this festival, not knowing on what day the blessed Martyr ought to be honored for the glory of his power and passion. This ignorance continued until the blessed Germanus, bishop of Auxerre.

It happened that the aforementioned bishop came to Brioude. When he asked the inhabitants when they celebrated this holy festival, they replied that they did not know. Then he said: “Let us pray, and perhaps the power of the Lord will reveal this to us.”

When they had done so, at daybreak he summoned the elders of the place and said that the festival should be celebrated on the fifth day before the Kalends of the seventh month [Note: Here too Gregory begins the year in March, calling September the seventh month].

From that time onward, the devout people who come, presenting their vows to the bishop, receive healing for both soul and body.

### CHAPTER XXX. Concerning the Possessed

When the possessed arrive, they commonly vomit insults against God’s Saint, asking why he summons other saints to his festivals and, naming them individually, confessing their powers and merits.

They say: “Let it be enough for you, Julian, to torment us by your own power. Why do you summon the others? Why do you invite outsiders? Look, there is Martin the Pannonian, our continual enemy, who drove three dead men from our caves. Privatus from Gabalum is here, who refused to hand over his sheep to the barbarians, stirred up by our instigation. Ferreolus, your colleague from Vienne, has arrived, who sent us punishment through you and protection to the inhabitants. Why do you call Symphorianus the Aeduan, or Saturninus the Tolosan? You have assembled a council to inflict infernal torment upon us.”

As they said these and similar things, they represented God’s saints to human minds so vividly that no one could doubt that the saints were dwelling there. Nevertheless, many of the sick were healed by them and departed in health.

### CHAPTER XXXI. Concerning the Gentleness of the Animals

But there is another matter most worthy of remembrance: the gentleness of the animals dedicated as offerings in this basilica [Note: Animals offered to God or the saints were called *votiva*; some also called them *sacriva*, because among the pagans animals of this kind had been destined for sacrifices. On these matters see title 2 of the Salic Law, with Bignon’s notes on that passage. Suetonius, book I, no. 81, mentions horses consecrated by Julius Caesar while crossing the Rubicon and therefore released without guards].

Reckless calves, kicking horses, and grunting swine [Another reading: “pigs,”] become quiet when they enter the sacred threshold. We have often seen horned bulls, tied by fifteen men or more and led by ropes, charge at people with such force that one would think they might even break the ropes themselves. But when they entered the holy building, they became so quiet that one might suppose they were being kept as gentle as lambs.

We have also seen many of them enter through the middle of the crowds, pushing the people aside with lowered heads and their snouts, not with their horns. It was as though, approaching a judge’s tribunal, they possessed some awareness of fear: they did not kick, charge anyone with their horns, or look with savage eyes. In complete gentleness they proceeded to the holy altar, kissed it, and then walked back with the same patience with which they had entered.

So too the unruliness of the other beasts, whenever they come there [Perhaps read: “whenever they have come there,”] lays aside all its fury and grows mild, so that you may observe with great amazement the gentleness of doves in creatures that are naturally untamed.

No one is permitted to take away anything at all from these animals offered as votive gifts. No one presumes, before bringing them to the basilica, either to exchange them or to sell them. Those who do so are often severely shaken by divine vengeance. Either fever threatens, or some evil steals upon them, or serious loss follows, or illness takes away what they have taken. It is difficult for the matter to pass without immediate punishment.

### CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning his Relics Transferred to Campania
Of these matters [Note: [Col. 0819D] Frodoardus praises this chapter in Book I, chapter 23 of his *History of Rheims*, where he discusses the basilica mentioned here. Atolus, a distinguished man and, as is believed, its founder, was buried there. His epitaph—which the author here calls the “inscription”—was carved on the highest pinnacle of the church; it praises him for having built twelve hospices in honor of Saint Remigius. Moreover, the basilica of Saint Julian at Rheims still survives, subject to the Remigian archmonastery and retaining its parish title.] It is enough to have spoken of the miracles that have occurred or are occurring around the holy basilica. Now, prompted by devotion, I wish to bring this little book to an end by discussing briefly the places where his relics are kept [Col. 0819C].

A certain man in the province of Belgica Secunda, that is, in the suburb of the city of Rheims, diligently built a basilica in honor of the blessed Martyr; after completing the building, he faithfully and devoutly sought his relics. Having received them, he returned on foot, singing psalms along the way, and entered the Rheims district of Champagne.

Not far from the road there was a field belonging to a certain wealthy Campanian, toward which a great crowd had gathered to plow. When the traveler with these relics drew near, one of the plowmen began to suffer terribly and, as though out of his mind, said: “Look! The most blessed Julian is approaching; behold his power, behold his glory. Run, men! Leave the oxen, release the plows; let the whole crowd go to meet him.”

They stood amazed, not knowing what he was saying [Al., “ignorant of what he was saying”], and, stupefied, marveled both at the man’s cries and at his words. At once the wretched man abandoned the plowshare in the fields, threw himself to the ground, and beat his hands together. Then he was carried swiftly toward the place where the man bearing the blessed Martyr was coming, crying: “Why do you torment me so, Saint? Why do you set me aflame, glorious Martyr? Why do you attack a region that does not belong to you? Why do you inspect our dwellings?”

As he was saying these things, he came in turmoil to the place where the priest had already erected a tent. He fell prostrate before the Saint’s relics and lay upon the ground for a very long time [Al., “the man lay upon the ground”]. Then, when the priest placed the holy reliquary upon him, blood immediately burst from his mouth, and he was cleansed from the assault of diabolical delusion. From then on he proclaimed the Saint’s power and became a companion of this journey.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Of his relics displayed in the East.

[Col. 0820B] I shall relate what the report of faithful brothers records concerning his relics in the East. In a certain city of the East, while a man was being tormented by a demon in a church, he declared that relics of the blessed Martyr were aboard a ship. When the ship had reached the harbor, he leapt toward it, fell forward on the ground before the vessel, and, with corruption bursting from his mouth and nostrils, was cleansed.

When this was reported to the bishop, he stirred up the people [Note: [Col. 0819D] Others read *commonet* or *commonuit*.] to proceed as far as the harbor with lighted candles. The shipmaster, hearing this and weeping for joy, hurried to meet the bishop, declaring that he had taken nothing else from the Blessed One’s basilica except a little dust lying around the holy tomb. But Almighty God, confirming the man’s faith, did not allow the Martyr’s power to remain hidden [Col. 0820C].

Afterward the bishop carried the relics that had been taken away to the holy church with great honor. The merchant, seeing such wonders, built a basilica in honor of the Martyr. There he placed the blessed relics, and afterward witnessed many miracles being performed.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. How his relics were placed in a basilica at Tours.

I myself experienced this some time ago [Note: [Col. 0820D] Mart. and Colb. a read: “I experienced these things long ago,” for “these things experienced,” as Pithoeus reads. Germ., Gem., and Colb. c read: “having experienced these things.”]. It happened that, after my ordination, I went to Clermont. Having set out, I visited the basilica of the blessed man. When the feast had been completed, I tore off some fringes from the cloth covering the holy tomb, believing that they would bring me protection, and, after completing my prayer, departed.

At the city of Tours, monks had built a basilica in honor of this Martyr, as far as their means permitted, desiring that it should be consecrated by his powers [Note: [Col. 0820D] The monastery of Saint Julian at Tours, formerly called “of the Scalari,” was destroyed by the Northmen and restored around the year 938 by Archbishop Tetolo, who entrusted its reform to Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny. While laboring at this work, the holy man died there and was buried near Tetolo himself. See his eulogy in the fifth-century volume of the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, numbers 23, 41, and following. The monastery of Saint Julian still exists, attached to the Benedictine rule under the Congregation of Saint Maur.]. When they heard that I had brought these relics, they asked that the church, once dedicated, might be enriched by the same remains.

But I secretly took up the reliquary and, as night began, hurried to the basilica of blessed Martin. A faithful man who was standing some distance away told me that, when we entered the basilica, he had seen a beacon of immense light descend from heaven upon the blessed basilica and afterward enter it, as it seemed.

When faithful people reported these things to us the following day, we concluded that the light had proceeded from the power of the blessed Martyr. After placing the sacred relics upon the altar [Al., “upon the altar”], and keeping vigil through the night with abundant psalm-singing, they were carried to the aforementioned basilica. And behold, one of the possessed, striking his hands against himself, mouth open and spitting bloody saliva [Note: [Col. 0821D] Mart., Rom., Germ., and Colb. 2 read “bloody spits”], was saying:

“Why have you joined yourself, Martin, to Julian? Why do you provoke him in these places? Your presence alone was punishment enough for us; you have summoned one like yourself to increase our torments. Why are you doing this? Why do you torment us so with Julian?”

While the wretched man continued declaiming these and other words, and after the solemnities of the Mass had been completed, he battered himself for a very long time before the holy altar. As foul matter poured from his mouth, he was freed from the assault of diabolical madness.

## CHAPTER XXXV. How the wine increased that night.

Nor do I think I should keep silent about what happened that night, before the holy relics were placed there [Note: [Col. 0821D] Others read *sileri*, “to be kept silent.” The printed editions read *silendum*, “that it should be kept silent.”].

A monk of that place, rejoicing at the arrival of the feast and most eagerly inviting everyone individually to the basilica’s small cellar, urged them all to keep faithful vigil in the basilica. Drawing wine from a vessel, he began to serve it joyfully to them as an act of devotion, saying: “Divine mercy grants us great protection in the blessed Martyr. Therefore I ask your charity to keep vigil with me in unity, for tomorrow his holy relics are to be placed here.”

After the night had passed with sacred hymns and heavenly melodies, and after the solemnities of the Mass had also been celebrated, the cleric, rejoicing in the feast [Note: [Col. 0821D] Gem. reads “monk,” and likewise below; the sense is the same], again began to invite those whom he had previously invited to a meal, saying: “I thank you for standing so steadfastly in keeping vigil. But the Martyr did not delay long in rewarding your good will through the power of his virtue.”

The cleric entered the storeroom and found that the cask, which he had left almost half full, was overflowing through its upper opening, so abundantly that a stream of flowing wine ran across the ground all the way to the doorway. Astonished, he placed a vessel beneath it and repeatedly drew it out full. Even after a sufficient and abundant quantity had been used from it, nothing at all was lacking; rather, to the amazement of everyone, it remained full until the following day.

It was the third day before the Kalends of the fifth month [Note: [Col. 0821D] Here Gregory seems, contrary to his usual practice, to call the fifth month May, and therefore to begin the year in January. See above the notes to Book I, chapter 90, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*].

O wondrous power of the Martyr! From a vessel he produced a vintage without blossoms. Normally, gathered wines are stored in vessels, but he brought forth a vat of new wine, in which not grapes [Note: [Col. 0821D] Several manuscripts, with the printed editions, read “not wines”; below [Col. 0822D], “with the liquid by which the fruit …” Germ. reads “in which there was fruit”], but power alone flowed down. The vessel swells with liquid; no fruit was brought into it, but was created.

The Lord does this to glorify the Martyr: he who filled the Virgin’s womb without seed and granted that she should remain a mother in chastity. Yet here the fruit is more wonderfully abundant, when he offers Falernian wine for drinking without vines [Note: [Col. 0822D] Gem. reads *majus*, “greater,” perhaps instead of *Maius*, “May”]. In other vineyards the buds are scarcely yet bursting forth, but from this vessel wine flows. Through this power May is made equal to October, when it offers new cups; indeed, it possesses more than October, since no vineyard appears in the open, while Falernian wine is produced in a house.

For an unworked vintage comes forth without a winepress, found not on vine-branches but in hidden mysteries. A heap of grapes is not crushed by a tree, yet waves of wine flow down. Falernian wine is drawn, though no grapes are seen pressed in a winepress. Behold, no vine is visible, yet cups are filled generously.

But why do I speak thus? That heavenly power is not lacking among the faithful. He who once changed water into wine at the wedding feast now freely offers the same to his own people without the nature of any element; and he who fed five thousand men with two fish now returns multiplied gifts to good will.

At the time of his birth an angelic voice bore witness, saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14). But now let us proceed to the following works of his power.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Of the cripple healed in the same place.

A servant of that monastery had long been crippled and was dragged along miserably [Note: [Col. 0822D] Germ. reads “a servant.” The printed editions read “a servant of this place,” and so forth]. Coming to the Saint’s own basilica, he kept vigil. When the vigil had ended, as he returned to his bed in the morning, his tendons were released and he was healed between the hands of those carrying him.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Of the girl with diseased eyes [Note: [Col. 0822D] Most manuscripts read: “Of the blind man given sight.”].

A certain girl suffered from diseased eyes and, because of the excessive flow of tears, was nearly blind. Her father, having heard of the glorious Martyr’s power, hurried with her to the holy basilica. After they had kept vigil, in the morning he brought food and drink to the poor who were at the *matricula* [the charitable institution attached to the church] [Col. 0822D].

While they were eating, the girl suddenly declared that she was tormented by a headache and begged to be allowed to sleep briefly. While she rested and the guests were finishing their meal [Note: [Col. 0822D] Thus Germ. and Colb. c. Others read “were drawing near”], she rose and asked to be led to the holy altar. Before she had even prostrated herself on the bare ground and earnestly prayed for the Lord’s mercy, her tears ceased, her eyes were cleansed of their disease [Col. 0823A], and she rose joyfully. Then, while her father rejoiced, she was returned home [Note: [Col. 0823D] The same manuscripts read “was led back.” Rom. reads “returned”] healed.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Of another cripple.

There was another very small boy whose parents lived not far from the basilica. In the second year of his life he became crippled in all his limbs and was raised without hope of any good. He was so contracted that his knees could not be separated from his mouth.

His parents kept vigil at the holy basilica and laid the infant before the most sacred relics. After a short while they found him sitting with all his limbs straightened. Then, having poured out a prayer, they returned home rejoicing.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Of perjurers.

There is also a village in the territory of Tours called Gaudiacum [Note: [Col. 0823D] Near Tours, on the River Cher, there is a place called Joyacum, commonly Joué or Jouay, which may perhaps be intended here. In Book V, chapter 14 of the *History*, the Jocundiac estate is mentioned; some think this is the same place, called Jouay, Gaudiacum, or Joyacum. Ursinus mentions Gaudiacum in chapter 22 of the *Life of Saint Leodegar*, but in the diocese of Chartres.], in which the relics of the blessed Martyr are preserved. Though the place is frequently made illustrious by great miracles, it usually exacts vengeance upon perjurers.

For whenever someone there, persuaded by the enemy of the human race, commits perjury, divine vengeance follows in such a way that it soon becomes clearly manifest either in a succession of losses, in the loss of a close relative, or in the wasting power of disease. The Martyr does not permit the offense to remain unavenged; nor does the crude rusticity of the barbarians there dare to commit perjury with such reckless boldness [Al., “already dare”]. Let this suffice concerning the matter, since it would be lengthy to recall individually in order all that has happened regarding it.

## CHAPTER XL. Of the relics of the Martyr taken by the presbyter Aridius.

When the presbyter Aridius came to me from the Limousin—a very religious man, whom I also mentioned in Book II of *The Miracles of Saint Martin* (chapter 39)—I carefully investigated his life and began asking what deeds the most blessed Julian had manifested there through miracles. Aridius had built a basilica in honor of the blessed Martyr and had also adorned it with his relics.

Since he was extremely modest, he hesitated for a long time and finally, very unwillingly, disclosed the following:

“When I first visited the basilica of the blessed Julian, I took a little wax from the tomb. From there I came to the spring in which the Martyr’s blood had been shed. After washing my face with its water, I filled a small flask from it as a blessing. I call Almighty God to witness that, before I reached home, it had changed in color, thickness, and scent into balsam.

“When the priest came to dedicate the church, and I had told him these things, he was unwilling to place anything else as a relic upon the holy altar except the vessel whose water had been changed into balsam. He said: ‘These are genuine relics, which the Martyr has illumined with the powers of paradise.’”

## CHAPTER XLI. Of the paralytic who was healed.

There are many other matters, of which I omit most and disclose a few. A certain sick man, weak in all his limbs, was brought by wagon to the Martyr’s monastery. As he lay in this vehicle before the basilica during the night [Note: [Col. 0823D] In Colb. a, “during the night” is absent], he suddenly saw it shining with great splendor [Col. 0824B] and heard within it voices singing psalms, as though they were those of many people.

While these things were happening and he poured out a prayer, he became, as it were, stunned and no longer remembered his pains. As the hour of his approach drew near, the splendor he had seen passed before his eyes. When the radiance had disappeared, he came to himself and realized that he had been restored to his former health.

## CHAPTER XLII. Of the blind man given sight.

A blind man, led by an attendant, approached the most sacred altar. When he touched his eyes to the cloth covering the holy relics, he received his sight. Possessed persons covered with this cloth were also often cleansed; and whenever the power of the judges acted excessively in that place, it departed in confusion.

## CHAPTER XLIII. Of the stolen altar cross.

A cross of solid gold hung above the altar itself [Note: [Col. 0823D] Mabillon discusses the cross placed at the top of the altar in Book I, chapter 8, no. 8, and chapter 9, no. 24 of the *Gallican Liturgy*. There he cites an important passage on the subject from Saint Paulinus, bishop, writing to Severus, which we append:

> The venerable altars cover the divine covenant,  
> and, with the martyrs arranged together beneath the sacred cross,  
> all the insignia of saving Christ unite:  
> the cross, the body, the blood, and God himself, the Martyr.

Some light on this matter also seems to come from canon 3 of the Second Council of Tours, which decrees: “That the Lord’s body should be placed upon the altar not in an imaginary arrangement, but under the title of the cross.” See Mabillon, Book I of the *Gallican Liturgy*, chapter 9.], made with elegant workmanship. It was so splendid in appearance that one would have thought it made of the purest gold.

When barbarians arrived, one of them judged it to be gold, seized it, and hid it in his bosom. But the man who had taken it was suddenly weighed down by such a great burden that he could not bear it at all. Immediately pierced with remorse by the Martyr’s power and moved to repentance, he returned it from the road to the holy place.

## CHAPTER XLIV. How his relics were sought.

After these things had occurred, Aridius sent his cleric [Note: [Col. 0824D] Germ., Gem., and Colb. c read: “The aforesaid Aridius sent his cleric.”], saying:

“Go to the basilica of the blessed Julian. Pour out your prayer, and beg the custodians to grant you some wax or dust from the tomb that lies there, so that what is brought to me may be received with a blessing.”

The cleric came and requested and received what had been commanded. When he wished to carry away what he had received, he was weighed down by such a burden that he could scarcely raise his neck. Shaken by great trembling, he fell prostrate upon the pavement. Then, once again pouring out a prayer with tears, he rose unharmed and felt that he had been granted freedom to depart.

He therefore set out. As the sun became excessively hot, he was seized by thirst. Coming to a village near the road, he approached a small hut and asked for water. As he was leaving, a young man came out to give him an answer; when he saw the cleric, he fell to the ground and became like a dead man.

His parents rushed together and accused the men, asserting that their relative had been killed by their magical arts. They seized their son and lifted him up, half alive. But he slipped from their hands, struck his palms together, and began shouting wildly or declaring that he was being burned by the power of the martyr Julian.

When the cleric heard this, he placed the reliquary containing the holy relics upon the boy’s head and, full of faith, began to pray more earnestly. The boy himself expelled both blood and the demon by vomiting, and, cleansed, departed.

The bearer of the relics, strengthened in faith, then traveled the entire way with psalms and thanksgivings and, under the Martyr’s guidance, reached the desired place. From that time onward, as time passed, so many possessed persons, fever sufferers, and people afflicted by various illnesses were healed there by the Martyr’s power that neither their names could be retained nor their number counted.

## CHAPTER XLV. Of a boy taken to diviners, and another healed by the Saint’s power.

Among the other notable miracles that should be received, we include this one as well, so that it may correct the foolish and strengthen the wise.

In the time of Bishop Cautinus, when the sins of the people had provoked the plague called the bubonic plague and the Auvergne region was being devastated by it (see *History*, Book IV, chapter 31), I went to the village of Brioude, so that, since I could not protect myself by my own merits, I might be saved by the protection of the blessed martyr Julian.

While I was staying in that village, one of our boys was seized by this disease. He laid his head upon his little bed and began to suffer severely. He had a persistent fever accompanied by stomach phlegm, so that, if he took anything, he immediately rejected it. Food was not a source of strength for him, but rather seemed to lead to death.

Finally, when my people saw him suffering at the point of death, they summoned a certain diviner. He did not delay in coming, but approached the sick boy and attempted to practice his art. He muttered incantations, cast lots, hung amulets around the boy’s neck, and promised life to one whom he himself had handed over to death.

These things were done without my knowledge. When they were reported to me, I became deeply distressed, and with a heavy sigh recalled what the Lord declared through the prophet Elijah to King Ahaziah:

“Because you have abandoned the Lord God of Israel and consulted the god Acharon, therefore you shall not rise from the bed to which you have gone up, but shall surely die” (2 Kings 1:16).

For after the diviner’s arrival this boy was inflamed by a more severe fever and breathed out his spirit. A few days after his death, another boy began to suffer from a similar illness.

Then I said to them: “Go to the Martyr’s tomb, take something from there to the sick boy, and you will see the mighty works of God. You will learn what difference there is between the just and the unjust, and between one who fears God and one who does not serve him.”

They went and took a little dust lying around the tomb. When the sick boy drank some of it with water, he immediately obtained a cure; his strength returned, the fever subsided, and he recovered.

Understand now, therefore, all you who are foolish among the people. After considering these things, know that the works the devil performs to deceive the human race are nothing. Therefore I warn you: if anyone is signed with the banner of the cross; if anyone has been cleansed by the washing of baptism; if anyone, having put off the old self, now lives in the new person—let him put aside and neglect such practices. Let him seek the protection of the martyrs, through whom miracles of healing are celebrated; let him ask the assistance of confessors, who rightly are called the Lord’s friends. Whatever he desires, he will obtain.

## CHAPTER XLVI. Of the roses divinely displayed at his tomb.

At that time, after the death of Proserius, the *martyrarius* [Note: [Col. 0825D] We have already discussed the *martyrarius*. Here it seems to be the custodian or keeper of the basilica, or even its rector. Hence abbots sometimes called themselves *martyrarii* and custodians.], Urbanus the deacon was appointed custodian of this basilica [Col. 0826C]. A wondrous event appeared at the Saint’s tomb.

While the deacon was keeping vigil in his little bed, he heard a sound as though the basilica door were being opened. After many hours had passed, he heard it being closed again. Then he rose from his bed and, with a light going before him, approached the Saint’s tomb. Wonderful to relate, he saw the pavement strewn with gleaming roses!

They were extremely large and possessed an immense fragrance. He also saw roses within the carved latticework of the screen [Note: [Col. 0826D] The passage from “These” through “month” is absent from Colb. 2, Germ., Gem., Laud., and Bell.]. It was the ninth month, yet they were so green that one would have thought they had been plucked from green branches at that very moment [Note: [Col. 0826D] The printed editions read “at the same hour and moment.”].

He gathered them with great reverence and secretly put them away, distributing medicines made from them to many sick people. For a certain possessed man who came from the territory of Tours drank a potion infused with them [Col. 0826C] and, after the demon had been expelled, departed cleansed.

## CHAPTER XLVII. Of the woman given sight.

There was a woman blind from birth who begged her parents to have her taken to the tomb of blessed Martin. When she arrived there, she lay prostrate for three days at the grating situated outside before the tomb of the holy bishop. In a dream she received an answer from the holy man, who said to her:

“If you desire to receive light, seek the basilica of Saint Julian. When you seek the Martyr’s protection there, he, joined with Martin, will restore to you the sight you need, together with the help of their prayers.”

The woman rose, and, not knowing that this Martyr’s relics were kept in the territory of Tours, set out for the city of Saintes.

A certain noblewoman named Victorina [Note: [Col. 0827C] Colb. a reads “Victuriana”; Laud. reads “Victurina.”], born of a distinguished family, had built a basilica in honor of the Martyr within the territory of her estate and had placed the blessed Martyr’s relics there.

The woman therefore approached this church and prayed for three days. On the third day the feast of the Lord’s Baptizer arrived. While the people stood listening to the teachings of the readings, a great murmur suddenly arose.

The presbyter celebrating the solemn rites, wishing to silence the voices, asked what was happening. One of those standing there answered him:

“The murmuring cannot be quieted, because the Lord’s power has revealed a miracle. Behold, the woman who testified that she had been born blind has received her sight, with blood bursting from her eyes.”

Then everyone blessed God, recognizing together what had occurred.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. Of the relics brought by the presbyter Nanninus.

The presbyter Nanninus [Note: [Col. 0827C] Others read “Manninus” or “Naninus.” Savaro, in his *Origins of Clermont*, thinks that the name Vibriacum here designates Old Brioude, commonly Vieille-Brioude; a basilica in honor of Saint Ferreolus stands not far from Old Brioude. But Nanninus, carrying the relics of Saint Julian from New Brioude to Old Brioude, could not have encountered the church of Saint Ferreolus on the way, since New Brioude lies between Old Brioude and the church of Saint Ferreolus. Perhaps “Vibriacum” here refers to the estate called Vibrac or Vibrat, a village in the diocese of Clermont, or certainly to Vebret in the same diocese.]—the presbyter of the Vibriacum estate—sought the relics of this glorious Martyr. Having taken them by order of blessed Bishop Avitus, he carried them with psalm-singing to the basilica of Saint Ferreolus, which is not far from that village. When he reached it, one of the possessed was cleansed.

Proceeding while singing psalms, and having reached midday [Note: [Col. 0828C] Thus Germ. and Colb. c. Gem. reads “having reached the midday hour.” The others, with the printed editions, read “when he had arrived, before the enemy.” Sur. reads “openly before the enemy.”], he drove away the wicked enemy through the Saint’s power, and another girl departed cleansed [Col. 0827C].

## CHAPTER XLIX. How many sick people were healed by his relics.

When he came to the place where he had built an oratory in honor of the Saint, he placed these relics upon the holy altar [Col. 0828A]. One man approached him having lost the use of his eyes, and another was weak in one hand [Note: [Col. 0828C] Gem. reads: “And one came to him having lost the use of his eyes.”]. After the prayer had been completed, the first received light after darkness, while the other recovered the use of his hand after a long period of inactivity.

A woman named Aeterna [Gem. “Acerna”], whose daughter was tormented by the wicked enemy, was also healed at this altar and departed safely with her child. Several people suffering from fevers were likewise saved in that place.

## CHAPTER L. Of another blind man given sight.

It is not absurd that blessed Julian should grant gifts of healing together with John or Martin, with whom the Victor of the world rejoices in heaven. I shall therefore relate further how he flourished with similar power together with Nicetius of Lyon.

Within the boundaries of the territory of Tours, a certain man built a basilica in honor of the holy Martyr at Litomeris [Col. 0828B]. We were summoned there according to custom to give a blessing, and we placed the relics of the martyr Julian together with those of Nicetius of Lyon.

Not long afterward, a blind man came, and, having faithfully poured out his prayer, deserved to receive his sight [886–890]. I remember this blind man from the *Life of Saint Nicetius* (the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 8), because it is fitting that the written account of the common power of both saints should be joined together [Laud. reads “writing”].

Let the reader who attends to these miracles understand that he can be saved only through the assistance of the martyrs and of the other friends of God.

For my part, I implore the Lord’s mercy through the protection of the blessed martyr Julian: may he, acting as advocate in the affairs of his own disciple and standing before the Lord, obtain that I may complete the course of this life without the impediment of any stain, and that I may hold irreproachably what I confessed in baptism, practice it faithfully, and guard it manfully until the completion of this life. Amen.

The second book, *On the Glory of the Holy Martyr Julian, Our Special Patron*, ends here.

[Col. 0827]
