# THE BOOK OF SAINT GEORGE FLORENTIUS GREGORY, BISHOP OF TOURS, ON THE GLORY OF THE BLESSED CONFESSORS. (C)*

[Col. 0827]

## Preface.

I am ashamed, foolish, blameworthy, unskilled, and inept to undertake what I cannot complete. But what am I to do? I cannot conceal what I have seen repeatedly myself concerning the powers of the blessed, or what I have clearly learned through the reports of good and trustworthy men to have taken place.

Yet I fear that, when I begin to write, because I lack rhetorical learning and grammatical art, someone may say to me [Al., “another”]:

“By rustic and ignorant boldness, why do you suppose that your name should be numbered among writers? Or do you think that this work will be accepted by the learned, when your intellect does not provide the skill of the art, nor any knowledge of letters supply what is lacking? You possess no useful argument in writing; you do not know how to distinguish the genders of nouns. You frequently exchange feminine forms for masculine, neuter for feminine, and masculine for neuter. Even the prepositions—which the authority of distinguished writers has decreed must be observed—you generally do not place in their proper position. You put accusatives where ablatives belong, and again ablatives where accusatives belong” [Note: [Col. 0829A] Most manuscripts read: “For you place … ablatives … and again place ablatives before accusatives.”].

Do you think this sluggish person will be seen exercising in the games of the wrestling school, or that a sluggish ass will dart swiftly through the ranks of ball players [Note: [Col. 0829A] This was the name given to those who played with a ball. See Apollinaris Sidonius, Book II, letter 9, and Book V, letter 17. This game required agility, which an ass lacks; hence the proverb cited here by Gregory.]? Or could a black crow cover its blackness with the feathers of white doves, or could the darkness of pitch be changed into the color of milky liquid?

Just as these things are impossible, so you too will never be numbered among other writers.

Nevertheless, I shall answer them and say: “I am doing your work, and through my rusticity I shall exercise your wisdom.” For, as I think, these writings will offer you one benefit: namely, that what I describe crudely and briefly with an unpolished pen, you will be able to expand clearly and splendidly in a sustained style across more extensive pages [Note: [Col. 0829A] Clar. a and Colb. a, with the printed editions, read “this writing will offer.”].

In the first little book we inserted certain accounts of the miracles of the Lord, the holy apostles, and the other martyrs—things that had hitherto remained hidden, but that God daily deigns to increase in order to strengthen the faith of the faithful—for it was very troubling that they should be handed over to oblivion.

In the second we set down the miracles of the holy martyr Julian. Then there are four little books on the miracles of Saint Martin; a seventh on the life of certain religious men [Note: [Col. 0829A] Laud. and Bell., with Bal., read “religious men”]; and this eighth book, which we write about the miracles of confessors [Note: [Col. 0830A] Here Gregory lists the book *On the Glory of the Confessors* as eighth, because, although it was written before the fourth book on Saint Martin and before some chapters of the *Lives of the Fathers*, he revised it after the others; hence in the oldest manuscripts it occupies the final place. Gregory himself certainly praises the book on confessors in the prologue to the *Lives of the Fathers*. It therefore seemed preferable to follow the order already adopted in the printed editions.].

We ask those who read it with particular attention to grant indulgence freely to our presumption, because, as we have often testified, neither the talent of an art nor eloquence of speech is available to us. It is not worldly vainglory that raises us up to write, but shame weighs us down into silence, while love and fear of Christ compel us to relate these things.

And since I began the first little book with the miracles of the Lord, I wish to give this little book its beginning from the powers of the holy angels as well.

## CHAPTER I. [Col. 0829B] Of the powers of the angels.

While I was staying in the territory of Auvergne, a faithful man told me—and I know that he told the truth, because I clearly learned that the events he described had taken place:

“An order was given that a drink should be prepared for the harvesters from grain soaked in water and then boiled.”

Orosius reported that this preparation is called *ceria*, from *coquere*, “to cook” [Note: [Col. 0829C] Thus Laud. Most manuscripts, with Bad., read *coelia*. Other printed editions read *coctia*. *Ceria* is a kind of drink made from grain, used by the Spaniards, as Passeratius observes from Pliny.].

When it had been prepared and stored in a vessel, while the master was delayed near the city, the servants, following their custom, drank most of it and left only a small quantity for their master’s use. That faithful man ordered the harvesters to be invited, so that, when he returned from the city, he might find them cutting the grain.

This was done, and when about seventy workers had been placed in the grainfield [Col. 0829C], the owner of the estate arrived. He examined the quality and quantity of the drink and found very little. Then, overcome with shame and considering the matter a disgrace to himself, he feared that the drink would run out for the workers. As he reckoned, there was not more than five *modii* [a measure of capacity] remaining. He did not know what to do or where to turn.

At last, inspired by the Lord, he turned to the vessel and devoutly invoked over its opening the names of the holy angels taught by the sacred Scriptures. He prayed that their power would deign to turn this small quantity into abundance, so that the workers might not lack what they could drink.

Wonderful to relate! Throughout the whole day, as it was drawn from the vessel, it never failed those who drank. Until night brought the work to an end, it was served abundantly to everyone.

## CHAPTER II. Of Saint Hilary, bishop of Poitiers.

Hilary [Note: [Col. 0829C] Saint Hilary is praised by Gregory, Book I of the *History*, chapter 36. His *Life*, mentioned below, is said to have been written by Fortunatus, who also published another book on the miracles of the same saint. Our Peter Coutant prefixed a fuller life of the same saint, compiled from his own writings, to the new edition of his works, which appeared in 1693; there are also found there numerous testimonies by the holy Fathers and other writers concerning the writings and virtues of that saint. — In the *Missal of the Franks*, no. 14, there are prayers and petitions for the feast of Saint Hilary, as they were then said at Mass and perhaps in other offices.] the most blessed man returned to his own city in the fourth year of his exile, and, having completed the course of his good work, departed to the Lord (Ann. 368, 13 January). Many miracles are said to have been displayed at his blessed tomb, which the book of his Life contains. Nevertheless, two lepers were cleansed in that same place.

[Col. 0831A] There was a mountain in the territory of Gévaudan, called Helanus [Note: [Col. 0831C] Colb. 2: *Hilarius*. Clar. a: *Elarum*; Bad.: *Helarum*. The word is worn away in Laud.], having a large lake. At a certain season a crowd of peasants used to come to it, offering what were, as it were, libations to the lake: they threw in linen cloths, garments suitable for men’s clothing, some fleeces of wool, and many also forms of cheese, wax, or bread, together with various other things, each according to his means—items which I consider too lengthy to enumerate. They came with wagons, bringing drink and food, slaughtering animals, and feasting for three days.

On the fourth day, when they ought to depart, a storm came upon them with thunder and powerful flashes of lightning. Such a violent rain descended, accompanied by a pelting of stones, that scarcely anyone thought he would escape. This happened every year, and the foolish people were ensnared in error.

After a long time, a certain priest from the city [Note: [Col. 0831D] That is, the bishop of Gévaudan, now of Mende.] itself, having been appointed to the episcopate, came to the place and preached to the crowds that they should desist from these practices, lest they be consumed by heavenly wrath. But his preaching was in no way received by their crude rusticity.

Then, by divine inspiration, the priest of God built a basilica in honor of blessed Hilary of Poitiers [Note: [Col. 0831D] Some suspect that Gregory was mistaken in this narrative, confusing Hilary of Gévaudan with Hilary of Poitiers. But they offer no reason for this except that there really was a bishop of Gévaudan named Hilary, who is venerated as a saint; and it would seem more probable that the relics of that saint were present among the people of Gévaudan than those of the bishop of Poitiers. Yet if some relics of Saint Hilary of Poitiers were then kept among the Lemovices, as is certain from the *Life of Saint Aredius*, why could the bishop of Gévaudan not have obtained some of them and opposed them, as belonging to a most zealous defender of the faith, to the superstitious rites of unbelievers? Relics, moreover, at that time generally meant not bones but garments, dust scraped from a tomb, lamp oil, or something similar.], at some distance from the edge of the lake, and placed his relics in it. He said to the people:

“Do not, my little children, do not sin before the Lord, for there is no religion in the lake. Do not defile your souls with these empty rites, but rather acknowledge God and render veneration to his friends. Worship Saint Hilary, God’s bishop, whose relics are buried here; for he can stand as an intercessor for you before the mercy of God.”

Then the people, pierced in heart, were converted. Abandoning the lake, they brought to the holy basilica everything that they had been accustomed to throw there, and thus they were released from the error by which they had been bound. From that time onward the storm was also kept away from that place; nor did it ever again harm them during this solemnity, which belonged to God, after the relics of the blessed Confessor had been placed there.

## CHAPTER III. Saint Eusebius, Bishop of Vercelli

Eusebius, Bishop of Vercelli [Note: [Col. 0831D] Among those who fought against the Arians in the fourth century, Saint Eusebius was renowned for steadfastness of spirit, gentleness of character, and the immense labors that he endured in defense of the faith. Some call him a martyr, others a confessor; he rightly obtained both titles, although the more common opinion among the ancients seems to be that, after a long martyrdom, he rested in peace. Nevertheless, the author of his *Life*, which is found in ancient manuscripts and whom most writers have followed—especially more recent ones—reports that he was overwhelmed with stones and killed by the Arians. Several sermons circulated under the name of Saint Ambrose say the same, and the account is supported by the ancient tradition of the Church of Vercelli. On these matters see Ferrerius, Bishop of Vercelli, who discusses them fully and learnedly and collected much material about Saint Eusebius and his successors. He was buried in the church of Saint Theonestus the martyr, which thereafter, because of the frequency of miracles, was called Saint Eusebius’s church. His feast is commemorated by Bede’s *Martyrology* and others on 1 August.] (Ann. 370, 1 August) was a great assistance to this Hilary against heresies, and after his burial he shows by present miracles that he lives.

For on the day of his feast, when many sick people are healed, those possessed by demons nevertheless rage through the entire church in violent spinning, loudly confessing that they are tormented by excessive suffering. Lifted into the air, they strike and shatter with their hands the lamps that are kindled for the service of light. When they are drenched with the liquid from these lamps, the demon immediately departs and the persons are cleansed. The people then know that as many sick persons have been cleansed as they have seen lamps shattered.

He also preserves with such pious protection everything held under the authority of his basilica that nothing is taken away from it by anyone. For you may see, amid hostile and wicked people, herds of cattle, beasts of burden, and sheep, yet no one touches them at all when the voice has sounded. These are the works of the Confessor Eusebius.

My mother placed relics of this saint in the chapel of her house. One winter day, while she was sitting for a long time before the hearth, which had been arranged with a great pile of wood, engaged in cheerful conversation because of the length of the night, and the household was already asleep, she arose and placed herself on a small bed not far from the fire. While everyone slept, sparks from the flames climbed as far as the beams. One of them caught hold there and began to scatter flames violently. But, I believe, by the power of that saint whose relics were nearby, the flame, contrary to nature, bent downward and turned back. It did not spread toward the roof, as is customary, but flowed downward, so that you would have thought not a flame but a fleece of wool was hanging from the beam. Nor did it consume the beam, except that it burned as it wandered along it, [Col. 0832C] until the mistress of the household awoke, summoned the servants, and extinguished the fire by pouring water over it. The whole house could easily have burned while everyone slept, if the power of the Blessed One had been absent.

## CHAPTER IV. Saint Martin, Bishop of Tours, and the Tomb of Saint Gatianus

We have learned from tradition that Gatianus [Note: [Col. 0832D] Colb. tut., Vict., and Clar. m.: *Gratianum*. Colb. a, Clar. b, and Bad.: *Catianum*. Clar. a: *Gazianum*. Laud., Bell., and Colb. a in the index: *Catiani*.] was sent by the Roman bishops to the city of Tours and was given as the first bishop to the people of Tours (after 250, 18 December).

When blessed Martin came to his tomb to pray, after pouring out his prayers and reciting the little chapter, he said: “Bless me, man of God.” As he said this, a voice was heard coming down to him, saying: “I also beg you, servant of the Lord, to bless me.” After praying again, he departed. Those who were present at the time were amazed and said that he then dwelt in Martin, who once called Lazarus from the tomb.

## CHAPTER V. The Same Saint and the Tomb of the Virgin Vitalina

I have often heard old men relate a similar event at Arthiona [Note: [Col. 0833D] Others: *Archtona*. It still retains its ancient name, commonly Artonne, where there is a college of canons in honor of Saint Martin. Labbeus reports the charter of its foundation, dated 1048, in volume I of the *Bibliotheca nova*. Fortunatus discusses the chapel of this place, dedicated to Saint Gabriel, in Book X, poems 1 and 13, although the printed editions there have *Artanensi* instead of *Artonensi*. Vitalina, called Vitaliana in several manuscripts, is honored on 25 May. See Bollandus under 5 February.] in the territory of Auvergne (Ann. 390, 25 May).

A certain religious woman named Vitalina rests in this place. When blessed Martin came to her tomb, he gave her a greeting, and she begged him to deign to bless her. After they had completed their prayer, the blessed man turned to her and said: “Tell me, most holy virgin, have you now merited the presence of the Lord?”

She replied: “One matter stood in my way, although it seemed easy in the world. On the sixth day of the week, when we know that the Redeemer of the world suffered, I washed my head with water.”

As the blessed Confessor withdrew from the Virgin’s tomb, he said to his companions: “Woe to us who live in this world! If this virgin, consecrated to Christ, incurred offense through the fact that she washed her head on the sixth day, what shall we do, whom the deceptive world persuades to sin every day?”

The blessed man also performed many other works in that village, which I considered too lengthy to recount. Leaving the village of Artonne, the man of God directed his steps toward the city of Auvergne.

When the senators of the city heard that the holy man was approaching—senators who at that time shone in that place with the nobility of Roman lineage—they went out to meet him with horsemen and wagons, with carts and carriages. But he was mounted on a little donkey and sat upon a very shabby covering. When he had reached the summit of Mount Belenatensis [Note: [Col. 0833D] The location of this mountain is sufficiently understood from this passage of Gregory; otherwise it is scarcely known, and today is entirely unknown to the inhabitants. It was so called from the god Belenus, that is, Apollo, whom the Gauls especially worshiped together with Mercury and Mars. We have spoken elsewhere of Ricomagus, commonly Riom.], from which the position of the village of Ricomagus can be seen, he saw them approaching him with this display and said:

“What do these men want, who are approaching us with such pomp?”

One who had arrived first replied: “The senators of Auvergne are coming to meet you.”

He said to them: “It is not fitting for me to enter their city with such ostentation.”

Immediately he turned the donkey’s bridle back and began to retrace the road by which he had come. But they followed him and humbly begged him to proceed to the city, saying: “We have heard of your holiness; there are many sick people whom you ought to visit.”

When they could not persuade him, he laid his hands on the sick who had come and restored them to health, then returned to the village of Artonne. A railing still stands there, at which the Saint is said to have stood.

After this he approached the Virgin’s tomb and said: “Rejoice now, most blessed sister Vitalina, for after three days you will be presented to the divine Majesty.” Then he departed from that place.

Afterward the Virgin appeared to many in visions, granted the benefits they requested, and declared the day of her death on which her commemoration was to be celebrated. This must be understood only in the sense that, through the intercession of the blessed bishop, she had merited the presence of the divine Majesty, so that she could thereafter perform these things.

At a certain time, when vigils had been celebrated in her honor, the archpriest of the place, Eulalius, invited the clergy to a banquet, while another priest, Edatius, was preparing food for widows and the poor. The former lacked fish, and the latter good wine.

A fisherman was warned in a vision by the Virgin to bring a supply of fish to the archpriest. He rose from his bed and found an enormous salmon [Note: [Col. 0834D] Most printed editions have *piscem*, “fish.” The same word occurs in Severus Sulpicius and denotes the well-known salmon (*un saumon*) among our Britons or Armoricans. See Du Cange’s *Glossary*. The error arose from *Alteserra*, a bend of a river into which fish seem to collect as if they had slipped there. In medieval authors nets are called this, as we have already observed. See the *Lives of the Fathers* below, chapter 17.] in his fish-trap, which he presented when commanded.

Edatius the priest likewise saw the Virgin in a vision, who said: “Go, and beneath one of the trees of the courtyard you will find a *triens*; give it, and you will buy wine suitable for the feasts of the poor.”

He told no one what he had seen. He went, searched, found it, bought wine, and refreshed Christ’s poor. Thus the power of the Virgin, appearing to both men, enriched each of them with the provisions that had been lacking.

## CHAPTER VI. The Stone on Which the Saint Sat

[Col. 0834C] He did many things in this world, of which the writers of his *Life* passed over much, while striving to ward off the weariness of detractors, lest those who so often attack the holiness of good men with poisonous tongues refuse to believe them.

But we, who daily—though unworthy—see his miracles at the tomb, since a physician is not needed by the healthy but by those who are ill, have considered it absurd to keep silent about things that we know were plainly accomplished by him in former times. If anyone is still unbelieving and hostile and does not believe these things, let him come to the basilica; he will see daily both new miracles being performed and those that happened long ago being repeated.

And because we have written a third little book about his deeds [Note: [Col. 0834D] Bal., with Vict. and Clar. m.: “four . . . little books.”], so that this book too might not be devoid of his miracles, we have undertaken to write in it some of those things that have plainly come to our knowledge, for there are many matters—as we have often testified—that have remained hidden until now.

In the very basilica mentioned above, which the faithful built in his honor, there still stands a stone on which the blessed man is said to have sat. After a long time, a certain priest named Leo moved the holy stone from its place in order to make himself a tomb. Without delay, returning home trembling, he was seized by a fever and died on the third day. It became known that he had offended the Bishop.

We recall that this happened in our own time.

## CHAPTER VII. The Erected Tree

In the district of Nobiliacum belonging to the city of Tours there was a tree which, having fallen under the force of the wind, blocked the public road [Note: [Col. 0835D] On Nobiliacum, see the notes to Book X of the *History*, final chapter, no. 15.].

When the blessed man was traveling along that road, moved by compassion for travelers, he made the sign of the cross over the tree and raised it. It has been seen standing upright beside the road down to the present day, even though it was already dead. For although it had been stripped of its bark, [Col. 0835B] it nevertheless lived through the honor paid to the man of God [Note: [Col. 0835D] Laud., Bell., and the others: *viri*, “of the man”; others: *viridi*, “green.”]. Many people faithfully scraped off pieces of its bark, diluted them in water, and drank them; immediately they received remedies.

We too saw this tree standing upright.

## CHAPTER VIII. The Chapel of the Estate of Martiniacum

There was a chapel near the town of Tours, situated in the village of Martiniacum [Note: [Col. 0835D] It still retains its ancient name, commonly Martigny, three or four leagues from the city.], where Martin was frequently reputed to have prayed.

When Guntharius the abbot [Note: [Col. 0836D] Gregory speaks of him in Book IV of the *History*, chapters 4 and 11, and in Book X, the final chapter.] was governing the monastic community, whenever he happened by chance to travel along the road that runs not far from the chapel, he would cross over after praying. After he had been made bishop, as he passed along the same embankment, he came before the chapel but postponed dismounting there to pray. Immediately the horse, with its head turned toward the chapel, stopped in the middle of the road.

Then he was beaten with heels, driven with reins, and urged with spurs, but remained motionless as though made of bronze. The priest then realized that he was being held by divine power. He dismounted, prayed, remounted, and passed on.

I wish, O noble steed, that the Lord would open your mouth, as he once did the donkey’s, so that you might say what you saw that was worthy of wonder, so that you would not proceed; what was lovely, so that you might gaze upon the door of the little chapel; what was fearful, so that you compelled your rider to pray. Surely you would cry out in a louder voice that, seeing Martin’s glory, you did not dare to move until your master had placed the proper encounter before you.

## CHAPTER IX. The Oil of His Tomb

Aredius [Note: [Col. 0836D] This chapter and the following one are absent from Clar. a.] the priest from the territory of Limoges, a man of supreme goodness and holiness, was once sitting with me in my cell. I began to be concerned about whether any miracles were being displayed in the chapel where he had placed the relics of the blessed bishop.

He related the following. At the time when blessed Euphronius was bishop, he came to the city of Tours. After staying there for a long time, he took away a small bottle filled with oil from the tomb of the holy bishop.

When he had returned home and, wearied by the journey, was sitting and telling his mother about the hardships of the road, he was suddenly struck by such a severe illness that he could not even recover his breath. He turned toward the chapel in which the relics of the blessed bishop were kept, spent the night in vigils, and in the morning anointed the place of his illness with the oil he had brought. The pain subsided, and he recovered.

After this, someone brought a hand swollen from being pierced by a thorn. As soon as it was touched with the oil, the person was restored to health. A woman who had lost her senses and was thought for several hours to be possessed by a demon was touched with this oil and healed.

Another abbot [Note: [Col. 0836D] The word *abbas* is absent from Colb. a.], who lived near the same cell, touched the eyes of a blind man with this oil, and the man immediately recovered his sight.

After he had restored many possessed persons to health through it, he placed oil upon the head of one who, as I believe, had a more savage demon. Immediately the man expelled the demon through a discharge of the bowels. In another person the demon descended into the nail of the thumb. When the priest saw this, he poured oil on the finger; soon the skin burst open, and as blood flowed out, the demon departed.

This is what he related about the oil.

## CHAPTER X. The Grape from the Vine He Planted, and the Wax of His Tomb

He also added an account of a grape from the vine that the Saint had planted. He took the grape and placed it in a small bottle, which he filled with water.

Not long afterward, a man came to him whose mouth was swollen by a malignant pustule, while his head and eyes were so swollen from excessive poison that they were closed. The priest poured into his mouth water from the bottle containing the grape [Bal.: “from the mouth”]; with each drop, all the swelling and pain departed [Col. 0836C] and disappeared.

He also asserted that the seeds of that grape remained green in the same water even after four years.

Concerning wax that he had taken from the tomb, he added the following. A deaf and mute woman who, as I believe, had a demon, came to him. He placed some of that wax in her ear. When she came the following day, she gave thanks to the priest for the health she had received.

## CHAPTER XI. His Miracles Displayed at Ternodorum

Within the territory of the fortress of Ternodorum, which belongs to the city of Langres, there was a priest who was weak in his gait. As he was traveling along the road leading to the church of God, he met an old man with a boy.

Both were clerics. After they exchanged greetings, the old man said to the priest: “Do you wish to become well?”

He replied: “What more does the human race desire than to live safe and sound in body?”

The old man made the sign of the blessed cross over his knee and said to the priest: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, stretch out your foot.”

The priest immediately stretched it out and drew it back sound. Giving thanks, he began to continue along the road on which he had been traveling.

The boy who was with the old man called him back and said: “Do you know, priest, who restored you to health?”

“I do not know,” he replied.

The boy said to him: “It was Saint Martin, bishop of the city of Tours. He himself restored you to health by his power. At the place where you saw the Saint standing, build a chapel without delay. It will bring healing to the people if you do what I tell you.”

The priest did not delay. He built a chapel at that very spot, in which, recently, many paralytics have deserved to recover the use of their legs and blind people their sight [Note: [Col. 0837D] Some hold that the place mentioned in this chapter was Chablis, a town of Burgundy, where there is still a collegiate church under the jurisdiction of Saint Martin of Tours.]

## CHAPTER XII. His Monastery in Spain

I have recently learned of the following event in Spain (Ann. 583).

When King Leovigild was marching against his son, and his army, as is customary, was violently disturbing the holy places, there was a monastery of Saint Martin between Saguntum and Carthago Spartaria [Note: [Col. 0837D] Saguntum was a city of Tarraconian Spain, famous for the destruction it suffered at Hannibal’s hands. In the same province is New Carthage, or Spartaria, commonly Cartagena, still famous for its very large harbor.].

When the monks heard that this army was going to approach the place, they fled and, leaving behind their aged abbot, hid themselves on an island in the sea. When the Goths arrived [Note: [Col. 0837D] This alludes to a similar story that happened to Cyrola, an Arian bishop in Africa, which he related in Book II of the *History*, chapter 3. Compare chapter 15 of Book IX.] and plundered the monastery’s possessions, which had been left without a guardian, they encountered the abbot, bent with old age but upright in holiness.

One of them drew his sword, as though to cut off the old man’s neck, but fell backward and breathed out his spirit. When the others saw this, they fled in terror.

When the matter was reported to the king, he gave orders, with an attestation, that everything taken away should be restored to the monastery.

## CHAPTER XIII. The Heretic Who Tried to Give a Man Sight but Blinded Him

When the aforementioned king saw so many miracles being performed through servants of God who belonged to our religion, he summoned one of his bishops and said to him privately:

“Why do you not display signs among the people according to your faith, as these men who call themselves Christians do?”

The bishop said to him: “I have often restored light to the blind and hearing to the deaf. Now I can do what you say.”

He summoned one of the heretics and secretly said to him:

“Take forty gold pieces and sit with your eyes closed in the place through which we are to pass. When I go by with the king, cry out, so that by my faith I may restore to you the sight you have lost.”

When this man, having received the money, had done what he had been commanded, a new Cyrola [Note: [Col. 0838D] Bignonius made further observations about such judgments in his notes to title 55 of the Salic Law. Later they were prohibited by various civil and ecclesiastical laws. See above, Book I of *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 81.] advanced at the king’s right hand, surrounded by a crowd of heretics. The man blinded by money also cried out, asking that he receive his eyes through the bishop’s faith.

The bishop, placing his hands upon his eyes with no small arrogance, said: “According to my faith, let it be done to you.”

As he said this, the man’s eyes were so firmly sealed shut and with such pain that he not only lost his sight but also exposed the deception that he had contrived under the impulse of avarice.

## CHAPTER XIV. The Dispute between a Heretic and a Catholic

Another faithful man reported that he had seen a Christian contending with a heretic on behalf of our faith.

After they had disputed for a long time about the divine Scriptures, and the heretic could not be persuaded to acknowledge the truth, the Christian said:

“If the practice of our religion and the testimonies of the sacred Scriptures do not move you at all to believe, at least test the power of the indivisible Trinity by miracles. I have a gold ring on my finger. I will throw it into the fire; you must take it out while it is glowing.”

He threw the ring among the embers and allowed it to become so hot that it could be seen to resemble them. Then he turned to the heretic and said:

“If your argument is true, take it from the fire.”

When the heretic resisted, the man said:

“Immense Trinity, God, if I believe anything unworthy of you, show it. But if my faith is correct, may these savage flames have no power over me.”

He took the ring from the fire and held it for a very long time in the palm of his hand without being harmed at all. Rather, the heretic was put to shame, and the other Catholics were strengthened in the fervor of their faith [Note: [Col. 0838D] Bignonius made further observations about such judgments in his notes to title 55 of the Salic Law. Later they were prohibited by various civil and ecclesiastical laws. See above, Book I of *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 81.].

Thus far concerning this matter.

## CHAPTER XV. Abbot Venantius

Not far from the basilica of blessed Martin, Abbot Venantius rests (late fifth century, 13 October) [Note: [Col. 0838D] This chapter is absent from Clar. a and Colb. tut.], a man of magnificent holiness who brought assistance to many who were sick in body. After completing his time and departing from this world, he continually shows through his own miracles that he lives forever.

For if anyone, seized by intermittent chills, spends one night in prayer and vigil at his tomb, he soon obtains a remedy, the onset of the illness being suppressed. Among the other things that happened there, whether seen or heard by us, we saw a woman healed who had been seized by a quartan fever [Note: [Col. 0838D] Laud.: “the things we saw performed, a woman.”].

Held by this disease for a long time, she could take neither food nor sleep, but had wasted away throughout her body so completely that scarcely any breath of life remained in her. She spent the night at his tomb in groaning and prayer, remaining motionless until the coming of daylight. In the morning she lay down to sleep; when she awoke, she felt no illness and departed healed.

We have written the life of this saint (*Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 16).

## CHAPTER XVI. Saint Papula

There was also the blessed Papula [Note: [Col. 0838D] Clar. a with the printed editions: *Pappula*. Others: *Pappola*. Nothing certain is known about her acts. The virgin and martyr Eugenia, however, is famous; she too is said to have lived in a monastery of men under male clothing. See her *Life* in Rosweyde, Book I of the *Lives of the Fathers*. Avitus also commends her at length in Book VI of *On Virginity*, verses 503–534.] (Ann. 500, 31 January), a very religious woman. Since she repeatedly begged her parents to place her in a monastery for women, because she could not serve God in her parents’ house, being hindered by worldly cares, and they, out of affection, were unwilling to separate her from themselves, she cut off the hair of her head, put on men’s clothing, went to the diocese of Tours, and joined a community of monks. Living there in fasting and prayer, she subsequently shone forth in many virtues.

She was like a man among men, and no one knew her sex. Her parents searched for her but could never find her. Meanwhile, when the abbot of the monastery to which she had come died, the monks chose her as abbot because of her continual virtues, not knowing her sex; but she refused this with all her strength.

She spent thirty years in the monastery without anyone knowing what she was. Three days before she departed from this world, she revealed the matter to the monks. After her death she was washed and buried by other women, and thereafter manifested through many miracles that she was a handmaid of God. For those suffering from intermittent fevers and from other diseases are often restored to health at her tomb.

## CHAPTER XVII. The Covering of a Certain Tomb

In another district of Tours there was a tomb situated among thorns and brambles (Ann. . . . . 28 June). It was said that a bishop had been buried in it, but his name was unknown [Note: [Col. 0839D] Colb. a: “yet they were ignorant of the name.” The same is found in Colb. tut. and Clar. a, but they do not have *tamen*.].

It happened that the son of a certain poor man died. After he had been buried, the father, unable to find a covering for the sarcophagus, came to this place. He removed the cover from this tomb—it was so enormous that it required three pairs of oxen to transport it—and covered his son’s little body with the stolen covering of another tomb.

After he had done this, he became deaf, mute, blind, and weak, and remained in this punishment for almost an entire year. Then a certain priest appeared to him in a vision and said:

“What violence have I inflicted upon you and your people, man, since you uncovered me by removing the covering of my tomb? Go now, and if you wish to become well, order it to be returned quickly. If you are unwilling, you will immediately die. For I am Bishop Benignus [Note: [Col. 0839D] Baronius believes this to be Benignus, the bishop mentioned in the Roman *Martyrology* on 28 June, whose sacred relics were later transferred to Utrecht on the Rhine [Col. 0840D]. Some more recent writers hold that he was a bishop of Chartres, but the ancient catalogues oppose this, making no mention of any Benignus. There is another Benignus known among the people of Tours, the son of Saint Maura; but he was a martyr, not a bishop.], who came as a stranger to this city.”

The man signaled to his family, approached his son’s tomb, lifted the stone, placed it on a cart, transported it back, and restored it to the sarcophagus. Immediately he was made well.

On the return journey, the stone was so light that although three pairs of oxen had carried it away, two oxen afterward brought it back [Note: [Col. 0840D] Colb. a and Clar. a: “when returning.”].

## CHAPTER XVIII. The Tombs of Two Virgins
Within the very boundary of the territory of Tours there was also a small hill [Col. 0840A], filled with thorns, brambles, and wild vines, and so densely overgrown with wild grapevines that scarcely anyone could force his way inside (An. . . . 27 Jan.). For rumor had it that two virgins consecrated to God rested in that place. Indeed [Note: [Col. 0840D] Colb. a has *hilicet*; Clar. a, *hilico*. Colb. tut. has *qui cum in . . . luminibus accensus*.], when the faithful repeatedly saw a divinely kindled light burning there during the vigils of feast days, one man, bolder than the rest and relying on his courage, did not fear to approach the place in the darkness of night. Seeing a candle blazing with an immense light of extraordinary brightness, he gazed at it in amazement for a long time, then departed and reported to others what he had seen.

Then the Virgins appeared to one of the inhabitants of the place in a dream. They explained that they were buried there and could not endure for long the injury caused by the rains without a roof; but if he wished to provide for them, he should cut down the brambles and place a covering over the tombs [Col. 0840B]. When he awoke, however, other thoughts intervened, and he consigned what he had seen to oblivion. The next night they appeared to him again, threatening him terribly with menacing faces: unless he covered the place, he would depart from this world in the present year.

Terrified by the vision, the man therefore took an axe, cut away the vegetation, and uncovered the tombs. He found thick drops from candles exuding a nectarous fragrance, as though from frankincense. He then assigned oxen and a cart to the work, gathered stones, and, when summer came, built an oratory over the place. When the work was completed, he invited blessed Euphronius, who at that time governed the church of Tours (An. 572), to bless it.

But the bishop, already exhausted by old age, excused himself from going, saying: “You see, my son, that I have grown old and that winter is approaching with greater severity than usual. Rains are falling and winds are driving everything before their tempest; the rivers are swollen [Col. 0840C], and even the roads, washed out by the continual rains, have almost dissolved into mud. It is not now appropriate to my age to hasten along such roads.”

Hearing this, the man withdrew from the priest’s presence and went away in great sorrow. But when the bishop had relaxed his limbs in sleep, he saw two Virgins standing before him. The elder of them, with a sorrowful expression, began as follows: “What have we done to make ourselves ungrateful to you, most blessed bishop? What trouble have we brought upon the region entrusted to you by God? Why do you despise us? Why do you pretend not to come and consecrate the place which a faithful man has built for us? Come now, we beseech you, in the name of almighty God, whose handmaids we are.” Having said this, she wetted her cheeks with the tears that welled forth.

When the old man awoke, he summoned the head of the ecclesiastical household and said: “I have sinned by not going with the man. For I saw two virgins reproaching me for this very reason, and I fear incurring God’s displeasure if I delay going there.” He immediately set out upon the road. As he went, the rain ceased and the fierce violence of the south winds subsided. He himself completed the journey successfully, blessed the place, and returned in peace.

For he often described the Virgins’ appearance and manner of walking. He said that one was taller and the other shorter in stature, though not in merit, and that both were whiter than snow. He called one Maura and the other Britta [Note: [Col. 0841B] Even today they are venerated under these names among the people of Tours, on 28 January; but in the town named after them, Sainte-Maure, on the preceding day. Whether they are to be distinguished from the holy Maura and Brigitta, who are famous in the diocese of Beauvais, is clear from what follows.—In the territory of Beauvais there are two famous virgins and martyrs, Maura and Brigitta. According to their Life in a manuscript of the collegiate church of Crisolium, they were born in Scotland of royal parents. After the death of their father and mother, they renounced the kingdom in their desire to preserve their virginity and went to Rome with Hispadius, their brother. After various pilgrimages, they were joined by Ursicinus at Rome and by John, together with his mother, from a village in the territory of Angers. At last they arrived in Belgica Secunda, where, near Baligniacum, a village of the diocese of Beauvais, they were robbed by brigands. After the robbers had long tried in vain to violate the most blessed virgins, they killed them and their companions, except Ursicinus.

The most devout queen Bathildis attempted to transfer the bodies of these virgins to the monastery of Chelles, but was prevented by a miracle. They were therefore deposited at Nogent, which was named after them Nogent-des-Vierges. They are said still to rest there in a church subject, under the title of a priory, to the monastery of Fécamp, not far from the town of Crisolium on the river Oise.

When certain pious and learned men at Beauvais observed that this Life was full of blemishes and sprinkled with chronological errors which there is no time to pursue, they conceived the idea that these two virgins were none other than Maura and Britta, whom our Gregory records as having been found in his diocese of Tours. This opinion did not displease Saussay in the Gallican Martyrology, nor was it entirely rejected by Bollandus on 15 January.

It therefore seemed worthwhile to examine the matter somewhat more carefully. To do so, I wrote once and again to Tours. I was informed that Maura and Britta were regarded as famous virgins in the diocese of Tours and that their feast was celebrated on 28 January. There was also a small town, about seven leagues from the city, bearing the name of Saints Maura and Britta. It stood on a hill whose situation corresponded to the place described by Gregory. In the parish church of the town, a large and ornamented reliquary was religiously preserved. When it was opened in 1666, with the permission of Victor Buticularius, archbishop of Tours, by his vicar general, twenty-five large bones, together with several smaller ones, were found within it, decently wrapped in linen and silk. Various documents written on parchment and bearing seals had been placed above them; these documents certified that the reliquary contained the sacred relics of the blessed Maura and Britta.

From these documents, as I learned from a letter written by the venerable parish priest of that place to our Dom Charles Lopin, one was by Vincent, archbishop of Tours. In it he testified that in 1267, after the Sunday called *Reminiscere*, he had opened the reliquary of Saints Maura and Britta and, at the request of William, lord of Sainte-Maure, had removed their heads, leaving the other bones in the chest.

Another document establishes that the relics of the same saints were visited by Archbishop John in the presence of Richard, bishop of Coutances, the abbot of Noyers, John, lord of the place, and many other distinguished men, on 30 June 1454.

All this, it seems to me, proves sufficiently and more than sufficiently that the virgins Maura and Brigitta of Beauvais are to be distinguished from the women of Tours whom our Gregory praises, as is also another Maura who is said to have suffered martyrdom with her seven sons at the hands of the Goths in the territory of Tours, likewise in the time of Saint Martin. We received their Life, though a corrupted one, from a manuscript of the monastery of Marmoutier.], saying that she had learned these names from their own lips.

## CHAPTER XIX. What Saint Euphronius foretold about King Charibert

[Note: [Col. 0842D] This chapter, together with the following two, is absent from Clar. a.]

The bishop himself, when many people repeatedly urged him to go to meet King Charibert and delayed his departure by making excuses, was at last moved by those around him and said: “Go and prepare the journey, so that we may go to meet the king, whom we shall not see.”

They therefore loaded the carts with what was necessary and prepared the horses for the journey. When everything was ready and he was about to set out, he said: “Let the carts return and let the horses be unharnessed; we are not going on this journey.”

When his attendants asked what this sudden change meant—why he had ordered preparations to be made so urgently and then dismissed them so easily—he said to them more privately: “The prince to whom you are compelling us to go has died; if we depart, we shall not find him alive.”

Struck with amazement, they noted the day and silently preserved the saint’s words. When men arrived from the city of Paris, they announced that the king had died at the very hour when the priest had ordered the carts to be brought back from the road [Note: [Col. 0842D] From this passage it may be inferred that Charibert died at Paris and was also buried there. For I fear that those who, together with the author of the *Deeds of the Franks*, maintain that he was buried at the fortress of Blavia in Aquitaine confuse him with another Charibert, the brother of Dagobert.].

## CHAPTER XX. On the dedication of our oratory

Concerning our oratory, in which the relics of Saint Saturninus the martyr and of Martin the bishop, together with those of Illidius the confessor and other saints, have been placed, it will not be burdensome to recount something for the instruction of believers: namely, how the power of blessed Martin manifested itself through a revelation, so that the terrifying fiery globe which had once appeared to only a few during the celebration of the solemn rites was seen by many, bursting forth from the crown of his head [Note: [Col. 0842D] So Bad. Other printed editions have *a capite arcae*; the manuscripts have *arce*. Sulpicius Severus recounts the miracle in *Dialogue* 2.].

For, inspired by an impulse of divine compassion, my mind conceived the plan of faithfully dedicating to prayer a very elegant cell which Saint Euphronius had used as a storeroom [Col. 0842B]. After it had been carefully arranged and an altar had been placed according to custom, we spent one night keeping vigil in the holy basilica [Note: [Col. 0842D] Observe the rites already used at that time in the dedication of churches in the Gallican Church. Compare Menard’s *Gregorian Sacramentary*, pp. 155–156 and elsewhere. The abundant lights used in the carrying of relics are also frequently found among ancient authors. See Evodius’s books on the miracles of Saint Stephen in Augustine.]. In the morning we came to the cell and consecrated the altar we had erected.

Returning to the basilica, we solemnly brought his holy relics, together with those of the martyrs Saturninus and Julian, and also those of blessed Illidius, with shining candles and crosses. There was a considerable choir of priests and Levites in white garments [Col. 0843B] [Note: See Book II of the *History*, chapter 23; Jerome, Book I *Against the Pelagians*; and others. That ministers, not only the greater but also the lesser, wore white garments when assisting at divine services is proved by canon 12 of the Council of Narbonne (589), which provides that a priest or deacon must not leave the altar, and that a subdeacon and lector must not remove their white garment before the completion of Mass. From the following canon it appears that the subdeacon, doorkeeper, and others raised curtains for their superiors at the doors.], as well as a distinguished company of honored citizens and a large gathering of people of lower rank who followed.

When we carried the sacred relics, adorned with cloaks and *naufae* [Note: [Col. 0843C] Thus Colb. a, Colb. tut., and Bell. The printed edition has *mappis*. Pithoeus, in his *Glossary* to the Salic Law, title 17, understands by *naufa* in the words “a man buried in a *naufa* or in stone” a wooden sarcophagus. From this arose the common word *nau* or *noue.], on high, we reached the entrance of the oratory.

As we entered, a sudden and terrifying radiance filled the cell, so that the eyes of those standing there closed from fear and excessive brightness. It moved throughout the entire cell like lightning, causing us no little fear. No one could determine what it was, and all, overcome with terror, lay prostrate on the ground.

Then I said: “Do not be afraid. It is the power of the saints that you see. In particular, remember the *Life* of blessed Martin and recall how, when he uttered sacred words, a globe of fire came forth from his head and was seen to rise to the heavens. Therefore do not be terrified; believe that it has visited us together with the holy relics.”

Then, setting fear aside, we glorified God, saying: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. The Lord is God, and he has shone upon us” (Psalm 117:26–27).

The earlier miracle, however, was seen by only a few, whereas this one appeared to the entire people. In the former there was a sign of power; in the latter an increase of grace. The former was then hidden because of vainglory; the latter was made manifest to all for glory. There, deeds faithfully performed for the Lord are proclaimed with festive utterance [Note: [Col. 0843C] So Laud. and Beil. Printed editions have *ibi de more festiva*. Colb. tut. has *ibidem morae festiva*. Pith., *festivo*.]; here the new oratory, which would advance the praise of the Lord, is consecrated through the illumination of the holy relics.

Therefore we must faithfully seek and pray to him, as is fitting, that he may visit this people—the one who has often lifted the vows of prayer on high through this sacred fire. I believe that this fire, whether when I recounted the fire that came forth from a monk at prayer [Note: [Col. 0843C] This is found only in chapter 38 of this book, while chapter 39 speaks of Brachio. Has the order of the chapters perhaps been changed in the revision of the book?—Gregory speaks of the same fire in the *Life of Saint Brachio*, chapter 12 of the *Lives of the Fathers*. Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, praises both passages in his sermon *That Saint Martin Could Be Called Equal to the Apostles*, where he says: “In like manner, when Gregory of Tours was bringing his relics into a new basilica, it appeared to him; and Brachio, whenever he entered an oratory, was accustomed to see a globe of fire moving through the upper parts of the church.”], or when I explained that Abbot Brachio had seen fire coming forth from the saints’ relics, is mystical, because it does not burn but gives light. Yet it is not without the grace of divine majesty, which can either reveal itself [Note: [Col. 0843C] So SB.; Bell. and Colb. 2 have *quam vel prodere*. Laud. has *qui*. Col. and other editions read: “Nor, I think, is it without the grace of divine majesty, which can either reveal itself [Col. 0843D] or appear.” Bad. has *qui vel se*, and so forth.] or appear to certain people.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the tomb of Saint Solemnis

Although we have already written something about the city of Tours, nevertheless, since we recently saw the tomb of Saint Solemnis [Note: [Col. 0843D] Other copies have *Solennis*; he is commonly called Saint Soulein. Sigebert praises him under the sixth year of Clovis in these words: “Solemnus, bishop of Chartres, is renowned; in preaching he earnestly persisted in instructing the Franks in Christ.”], we could not remain silent about what happened at the monastery of Malliacum, which was built on the summit of a mountain [Note: [Col. 0843D] So Colb. a. The printed edition reads: “We could not remain silent about what we discovered at the monastery of Malliacum, which . . . was established.” The two Colbertine manuscripts do not have *comperimus, quod*. There were two places called Malliacum near Tours: one on the river Vienne, commonly called Maillé-Lallier; the other three leagues below Tours, above the Loire, now known by the altered name of Luynes and distinguished by the title of a duchy and by its collegiate chapter. A few years ago it was converted into a monastery of regular canonesses called the Holy Sepulchre.

Saint Solemnis lived and died there, in the monastery which, now reduced to a priory, is subject to Marmoutier. Attached to the priory church, which is dedicated to Saint Venantius, is a parish title. The body of Saint Solemnis was transferred from there to Blois and deposited in the church of Saint Peter, which thereafter took from him the name of Saint Solemnis, together with its parish title, until it was raised this year to cathedral status and, its name being changed, began to be called Saint Louis.

His sacred body, except for a few bones, was burned by the Calvinists in the preceding century. We have seen his Life, the account of his discovery by our Gregory, the history of its translation, and the miracles in a manuscript of the royal library.

In this Life Saint Solemnis is said to have succeeded Flavius as bishop of Chartres in the time of Clovis, whom he is said to have made a catechumen when the king was setting out against the Goths. According to the same author, he accompanied Clovis on a second expedition against the Goths as far as Tours. When the bishop fell ill there, the king left him at the fortress of Malliacum; he died and was buried in the ancient basilica of Saint Mary, situated on the summit of the mountain. After that church was destroyed by pagans, the body of the bishop remained unknown until the time of our Gregory. When his body was being carried to Chartres, it was deposited at Blois in the church of Saint Peter, but on the following day it could never be removed. From then onward it was glorified by many miracles, which the same author wrote down toward the end of the eleventh century.

What he says about our Gregory seemed worth reproducing here:

“Blessed Gregory, then bishop of Tours, having learned of the miracles that were taking place at the tomb of the saint, went to the place to see for himself what he had already heard from many people. Seeing the wondrous and continual works of the Lord being performed through the man of God, he praised God, because such is the glory of all the saints, and returned joyfully to his own people.

Among the other miracles concerning the praise of the holy confessors that he wrote, he spoke of blessed Solemnis, bishop of Chartres, as follows:

‘Although we have already written something about the city of Tours, nevertheless, since we recently saw the venerable tomb of Saint Solemnis, we could not remain silent about what we learned concerning it. The fortress anciently called Malliacum lies about twelve miles west of the city of Tours. Near it, toward the rising sun, a mountain bearing the same name rises beyond the hollow of an intervening valley. On its summit the ancient devotion of Christians built a monastery [Col. 0845C].

There the most blessed Solemnis ended his present life while King Clovis was waging war against King Alaric. Because divine mercy, in accordance with his merits, performed many miracles at his tomb, the inhabitants of the place built an honorable sepulcher for him over his venerable ashes, with marvelous structures. But after a considerable period had passed, it was so devastated by the most impious pagan people that not even a sign could then be seen that a building had ever stood there.

For the natives of the same fortress say that, while the crypt of his burial was still hidden and no Christian knew the secret of that place with certainty, they nevertheless suspected and truthfully maintained that something sacred was being kept there—until, through God’s mercy, the revelation became manifest. The mausoleum of Saint Solemnis, bishop of Chartres, was indeed there; through the many cures of the sick, with the Lord’s favor, it has become known to faithful people.

Thus the saint spoke of the saint in testimony.’”

The same author records that Saint Solemnis died on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, although his feast is celebrated on the following day in various martyrologies.

The monastery, surrounded by ancient buildings that had by then been excavated, stood there (An. 519, 25 Sept.) [Col. 0845A]. For they say that while the crypt remained hidden and the place had not been revealed to any Christian, the inhabitants saw a light burning there every night before the Sunday solemnities. Yet no one knew what this mysterious sign meant. People retained only the suspicion that something divine was being kept there.

Meanwhile, two possessed men came from the basilica of Saint Martin. Striking their hands together, they began to cry out, saying: “Here, in a hidden crypt, the most blessed Solemnis rests. Open, therefore, the tomb of the friend of God. When you have found it, cover it with veils, light a lamp, and offer it the worship that is due. It will benefit this region if you fulfill what we are saying.”

As they said this, they tried with loud cries to dig up the earth with their fingernails [Col. 0845B]. When the inhabitants saw what was happening, they took a mattock, dug, and opened the crypt. Descending through a succession of steps, they found a large tomb. The two men, who were still mentally disturbed, testified that it was the tomb of the most blessed Solemnis; immediately afterward they recovered their senses.

After this, the sick began to flock to him from various diseases and returned healed. A native of the city of Lithomerus [Note: [Col. 0845D] Thus the manuscripts and Bad. Other printed editions and SB. have *Litthomerus*, a city of Poitiers.] was also afflicted by a fever of the quartan type. Taking candles from his lodging, he rose with only one boy and went to the place. After offering a prayer, lighting the candles, and holding them in his own hand throughout the night, he kept vigil [Col. 0845C]. He suffered no further severity from this illness of chills [Note: [Col. 0845D] Colb. tut. has *frigoris*; Colb. a and Bell. have *frigorae*. *Frigoritio* is an attack of fever, so called because it begins with cold; *confractio* is the remission of the same fever, because it appears as though the fever were being broken.], or from any kind of intermittent fever.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Abbot Maximus

There was a certain religious man, Maximus both in name and in virtue (An. 400 . . . 20 Aug.). As the book of his Life teaches [Note: [Col. 0845D] We have never seen this Life. We do possess another, from a manuscript of Marmoutier, collected by a certain monk or cleric of Chinon; but it contains little beyond what Gregory relates here.—The learned Stephen Baluzius thinks that the Maximus mentioned here was Maximinus, whom Leidrad, in his letter to the emperor Charlemagne, lists among the abbots of the Island of Barbara, to whom the bishops of Lyon entrusted their responsibilities.

Eucherius, in a letter to Philo, which the same Baluzius published in an appendix to the works of Agobard, asks this presbyter to go to the monastery of the Island of Barbara, to see and encourage “our brother Maximus, the abbot who presides over that monastery, because word has reached us that he wishes to leave it and abandon his brothers, since many, through fear of the nations, have withdrawn their offerings, which they had been accustomed to give for the sake of God. . . . Let him prepare for us the raised house which we ordered to be built, and the parchment, because, if God permits, we plan to spend Lent with him on the Island,” and so forth. The bishop then orders three hundred measures of grain and other necessities for food to be conveyed to the monastery, promising to offer more after his return.], which we have read written in verse, he was a disciple of our Martin.

Desiring to conceal what he was, he wished to make a pilgrimage to the monastery of Lyon on the Island of Barbara [Note: [Col. 0846D] The Island of Barbara is a very ancient monastery of the territory of Lyon, situated in the middle of the river Saône above the city of Lyon. After belonging to the Benedictine order for many centuries, it passed to secular canons in 1549. Dom Le Laboureur wrote its history in French under the title *Ruins of the Island of Barbara*.]. But when he was recognized there as well, he decided to return to his homeland.

Finally, as he wished to cross the river Saône, the boat, filled with water, sank, and the priest himself was covered by the waves. Around his neck he had his daily ministry together with the book of the Gospels [Note: [Col. 0846D] The meaning of this word is clear here, as we have often already explained. See the notes of our Menard on the *Gregorian Sacramentary*, p. 155.], that is, a small paten with a chalice.

But divine mercy, unwilling to allow what belonged to God to perish, restored him from this danger to the shore at the Lord’s command, so that he suffered neither loss of life nor the loss of his possessions. What the Psalmist sang under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit was fulfilled: “When the righteous man falls, he will not be shattered, because the Lord supports his hand” (Psalm 36:21). And again: “The Lord does not kill the soul of the righteous” (Proverbs 10:3).

He then came to the fortress of Chinon in the territory of Tours and established a monastery there. When that fortress was besieged by Aegidius [Note: [Col. 0846D] They think this occurred around the year 463, when Aegidius, or Gillo, commander of the Roman army, was forced to raise the siege of Chinon.], and the people of that district were enclosed within it, the enemy blocked a well that had been dug out from the side of the mountain and which the besieged used for drinking.

When the aforementioned servant of God, who at that time was shut inside the fortification with the others, saw this and saw the people being consumed by the hardship of thirst, he prayed to the Lord throughout the entire night [Col. 0846C], asking him to look upon the people, drive away the wicked enemy, and not allow them to be destroyed by the burning of thirst.

Then, by revelation from the Holy Spirit, he said to the people: “Whoever has a vessel, set it out in the street and beseech the Lord. For today his generosity will give you water in abundance, so that neither you nor your children will fail.”

As he spoke, clouds suddenly covered the sky, and a great rain descended from heaven upon the fortress, accompanied by thunder and flashes of lightning. The rain provided the people with the double benefit of relieving their thirst and driving away the enemy by its crashing sounds. Everyone’s vessels were filled, and all were satisfied.

Thus, through the intercession of the priest, the adversaries were driven away and the people were saved from the fortress. In the monastery [Note: [Col. 0847D] This monastery still exists at Chinon, though it was long ago converted into a collegiate church. The relics of Saint Maximus, commonly called Saint Mexme, were preserved there until 1563, when they were burned by the Calvinist heretics. The canons of Saint Maximus, Saint Maxe, at Bar-le-Duc in the diocese of Toul nevertheless claim that the body of Saint Maximus was somehow rescued from the fury of the heretics at Chinon and brought to them; they recognize the same saint as their patron.], after reaching an advanced age, he died and was buried there. At his tomb the sick are frequently healed.

A little boy from the household of the church of Tours fell ill. As he lay gasping and was thought to be at the point of breathing his last, he was carried to the saint’s basilica; immediately the fever went out of him and he was restored to health.

A girl among the female slaves was likewise suffering from fever. When she had been laid before the railings of the tomb, she was restored to health that very day.

When news of these events reached us, we assigned the boy, with his hair cut short, to this monastery; but we ordered the girl, after changing her clothing, to be joined to the community of nuns, there to serve God [Note: [Col. 0847D] These words are absent at the end of the chapter in Colb. a.].

## CHAPTER XXIII. On John the Recluse

Not far from this basilica rests a certain presbyter named John [Note: [Col. 0847D] He is called John the Recluse in Baudonivia’s *Life of Saint Radegund*, section 4, where he is said to have confirmed the blessed queen in her purpose. The oratory mentioned in this chapter still exists under the title of Saint Radegund; the tomb of blessed John is visible there, though empty of relics, for the Calvinists burned them in the same year, 1563.] (An. 400 . . . 5 May), a Briton by birth, who lived in the highest degree of religious devotion. Through his hands the Lord graciously performed many signs of healing.

Because of his love for God, he restrained himself from the sight of human beings and had a small oratory cell in front of the church of the village of Chinon. There, in a little garden which he cultivated with his own hands, he had planted laurel trees. Their trunks are now enormous, and they extend in the beauty of their pleasant foliage. Beneath their shade the holy man would sit, either reading or writing.

After his death, when those trees had spread out their broad branches and shaded the garden, one of them, growing old with age, withered. The caretaker of the place dug up the trunk with its roots, cut off its branches, and fashioned it into a bench. He used it sometimes to sit on when tired, or to place something safely upon it when necessity required.

After he had used the bench for this purpose for two years or somewhat longer, he was touched, as I believe, by divine inspiration and said in the sorrow of his heart: “Woe to me, for I have sinned in using for various needs the tree which such a priest planted with his own hands.” [Manuscripts: *incisiones*, “cuttings.”]

Having said this, he took a mattock, dug up the earth, cut off the legs of the bench, and placed it beneath the soil; then he filled the hole with earth.

Wonderful to relate! When spring arrived, just as the other trees blossomed, so too did this trunk, which had, so to speak, been buried by the man’s hand. Revived and flourishing in health, it sent forth new leaves. Even today shoots from it remain, five or six feet high or somewhat more; each year they increase in size and are raised up by the Lord.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Religious Woman Monegundis

In the city of Tours itself the blessed Monegundis died (An. 570, 2 July) [Note: [Col. 0848D] This chapter and the two following are absent from Clar. a.]. She came from the territory of Chartres. Leaving both her homeland and her parents, she sought Tours for this one purpose: to devote herself to prayer. Through her God frequently deigned to display miracles.

If anyone contracted a malignant pustule [Note: [Col. 0848D] Colb. and others have *pustulam*, and so throughout the manuscripts and printed editions. Others have *pusulam*; still others, *pustulam*.], and came to her to ask for prayer, she immediately prostrated herself to implore the Lord. Gathering a leaf from any vegetable or fruit, she smeared it with saliva, made the sign of the cross over the ulcer, and placed the leaf upon it. At once all the poison disappeared, so that the sick person suffered no further injury deserving death.

She also frequently healed sufferers from quartan fever and those with sore throats by giving them blessed water. Even now the sick continually flock to her tomb and are healed. How many people afflicted with chills, how many nearly overcome by malignant pustules as poison thickened within them, and how many cured there of dysentery, cannot be recounted individually.

But since we recorded many of these things in the book we wrote about her Life (*Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 19), we could not remain silent about what happened afterward. A female servant of our esteemed archdeacon was severely shaken by quartan fever and had been ill with it for almost a year. When she was laid upon the holy tomb in the hands of her parents, she was carried home in good health.

## CHAPTER XXV. On Abbot Senoch

We wrote the Life of Abbot Senoch some time ago [Note: [Col. 0848D] In the book *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 15. He also dealt with him in Book V of the *History*, chapter 7.] (An. 576, 24 Nov.). In that little work, after recording many of his virtues, we brought it to an end. But since power appeared at his tomb, it would have been absurd for us to remain silent.

A boy named Nantulfus was afflicted with extreme blindness. He continually lamented that even the first years of his youth were disfigured by this affliction. He sought the tomb of this saint and, prostrate and supported by humble prayer, begged that through the saint’s intercession the light he had lost might be restored to him.

He persevered in this prayer for four days, then departed illuminated, his eyes opened. Even now many suffering from chills and other illnesses are healed as soon as they either tear off a fringe of his cloak or touch it.

Thus far concerning the people of Tours.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On Saint Simeon of the Column

Simeon the confessor, who is said to have stood upon a column in the district of Antioch, frequently grants healing to the inhabitants (An. 460 or 463, 5 Jan.) [Note: [Col. 0849C] This chapter and the two following are absent from Colb. tut. The memory of Simeon Stylites is famous among both Greeks and Latins; Theodoret, Evagrius, Theodore the Lector, and others celebrated it. His Life is found in Rosweyde’s *Lives of the Fathers*, Book I, and among the Bollandists on 5 January.].

For, as is written in the book of his Life, after his conversion he never looked attentively upon any woman [Col. 0849B]. Once he had fervently entered upon a higher holiness on the column, he did not permit himself to be seen not only by a strange woman but even by his own mother. Even now he protects that place from the approach of this sex.

For they say that a certain woman put on men’s clothing and wished to enter the basilica of the column. In her misery she reasoned that she could do what she wished by means of clothing that might conceal her from the Most High, not knowing the Apostle’s saying: “God is not mocked” (Galatians 6:7).

As soon as she came to the temple, she raised her foot to enter the holy threshold; nevertheless, she immediately fell backward and died [Note: [Col. 0849D] Pith. has *Ilico ubi*. The printed edition has *Et licet*. In the manuscripts below, *tamen* is absent.]. This punishment was sufficient for the people, so that no woman would thereafter dare attempt such a thing, when she saw the terrible vengeance inflicted upon this one.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Tombs of the Presbyters in the Basilica of Saint Martial
Thus Saint Martial, bishop sent by the Roman bishops (A.D. 250, 30 June), began to preach in the city of Limoges, and, after overthrowing the rites of the idols, when the city was already filled with belief in God, departed from this world. At that time there were with him two presbyters whom he had brought with him from the East into Gaul.

[Note: These words, up to “true,” are lacking in Colb. a; but above, after “sent by the bishops,” another hand has added “with two presbyters.” Those two presbyters are called Alpinianus and Stratoclianus in Bell., by a different but nearly equivalent hand; in the Roman Martyrology on 30 June, Albinianus and Austriclinianus. See Bernard Gui’s *Sanctorale*, in Labbe, vol. II of the *Bibliotheca nova*, p. 265. There is no opportunity here to discuss at greater length the time of Saint Martial’s mission to Gaul. Gregory writes in Book I, chapter 28 of his *History* that it occurred during the consulship of Decius and Gratus, that is, in A.D. 250. Here he says that Martial was sent by the Roman bishops, while a little farther below he suggests that he came to Gaul from the East. See Bosquet’s history. The *Acts* of Martial that circulate seem to have no authority, nor do the letters attributed to him deserve greater esteem. Concerning his apostleship, his disciples, and the famous monastery in his name near Limoges—which the Cluniacs obtained in the eleventh century and which eventually passed to secular canons—more is found throughout volume II of Labbe’s *Bibliotheca nova*. In Paris, moreover, he already had a church in the seventh century, which Saint Eligius endowed.]

When their days were completed and they too were called from this world, their sarcophagi were joined together, and they were buried in the same crypt in which the holy bishop was buried. One was next to the wall, and the other was adjoining it. Both, however, stood above ground; but because of the one that was first, honor could not be shown to the other: that is, no cloth could be spread there and no lamp could be lit.

[Note: Clar. a reads “not for himself”; the editions, “not except.”]

When the local inhabitants were troubled by this, they came to the crypt one morning and found that the graves had been placed against different walls. Thus free access to both graves was opened, and it became evident in what manner the blessed bishop, as a worshiper of God, was to be venerated.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Miracles performed at his tomb

A certain girl, whose one hand had become stiff through some sin—I do not know what—and whose fingers had been fixed into her palm, came to his tomb, trusting in the power of the Confessor: his intercession, she believed, could release her withered hand, just as his preaching had released a people entangled in the empty rites of superstition.

After vigils had been celebrated on the very night of the feast, while she was praying attentively beside the tomb, she was astonished to discover, in the presence of the people, that her hand had been healed and her fingers straightened.

[Note: This chapter and the following two are absent from Clar. a.]

## CHAPTER XXIX. Concerning the man who received speech from a priest

[Note: In Colb. tut. the title is “Concerning Saint Martial, bishop of Limoges”; Bell. and Laud. have no title.]

A certain man regained his speech in the following manner. For, as the unrefined rusticity of the people sometimes does, he uttered a false oath in a church. Immediately his tongue stiffened and he became mute, so that he seemed to imitate not a human voice but the bellowing of a two-year-old sheep.

Coming to the tomb of this Confessor, he prostrated himself in prayer and, as he later asserted, felt as though someone were touching his throat. This, I believe, was the power of the Lord’s Confessor. When he came out, he implored by a gesture the priest who was present to make the sign of the cross over his closed throat.

When the priest had done this, he again prostrated himself in prayer. At once he rose, his faculty of speech restored, and in his own voice disclosed everything that he had suffered.

## CHAPTER XXX. Concerning Saint Stremonius, bishop of Clermont

Through Saint Stremonius, who was also sent by the Roman bishops with the most blessed Gatianus [Mss.: Catianus] and the others whom we have mentioned, the city of Auvergne first received the word of salvation, and, as he preached, began to believe in Christ, the Son of God, the Savior of the world and Redeemer of all (A.D. 250, 1 November).

[Note: Colb. tut. has “Austremonius.” He is commonly called Saint Austremoine. Our Gregory places his arrival in Gaul in the time of Decius, Book I of the *History*, chapter 28. Some wish him to have been one of Christ’s seventy disciples, or at least to have been sent by Saint Peter. Having taken Urbicus as his successor, he withdrew to Issoire, where he was buried. Labbe published his Life, though it is full of fables, in volume II of the *Bibliotheca nova*, p. 482. At Issoire—where Saint Praejectus, later bishop and martyr of Auvergne, learned letters and the principles of monastic life, as his Life relates—there is still a celebrated Benedictine monastery of the Congregation of Saint-Maur dedicated to Saint Stremonius. His relics, however, were transferred from there to Volvic and then to Mozac, places distinguished for their Benedictine monasteries, as is reported more fully in Labbe, at the cited place, pp. 500 and following.]

His tomb is at the village of Issoire. Although the unrefined rustic population knew that he rested there, it nevertheless offered him no honor or cult. After a long succession of years, Cautinus, who had been appointed bishop of the city of Auvergne, governed the church of that village during his diaconate.

One night, while he was lying in the little bed of his cell, which adjoined this basilica, he heard psalm-singing, as though with faint voices. Rising, he saw the church shining with a great light. Astonished, he looked inside—for that cell was above, opposite the church windows—and he saw a multitude of men in white garments around the tomb, holding candles and singing psalms.

He watched this for a very long time. When they had departed, he immediately ordered, as soon as morning came, that the tomb be enclosed with a railing and covered with gleaming cloths; and he commanded that reverence be shown to that place. From then on prayer has been poured out over the tomb, and the bishop’s aid has been obtained.

I heard this from the bishop’s own mouth.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Concerning the man who received a blessing from a priest

Great indeed is the grace bestowed when the priesthood is worthily preserved in practice.
