If priesthood granted so much to an unjust man and persecutor of righteousness that he deserved prophecy—namely, Caiaphas, who prophesied that one man must die for the people lest the whole nation perish (John 11:50)—how much more may divine majesty grant to those who fear God and preserve their priesthood in holiness and purity that, as James says, the priest’s visit, together with prayer, may benefit the sick (James 5:15), and that even the mere offering from his hand of blessed bread may often provide protection.

This is illustrated by an event that occurred among the people of Auvergne and that I learned of truthfully in my youth. A solitary presbyter, traveling along the road, sought lodging at the home of a poor man of Limagne. Having received it, he rose from his bed during the night, according to the custom of priests, and devoted himself to prayer.

[Note: The piety of our fathers is noteworthy in their performance, even privately, of the night office at the appointed hours. See the notes on Book IX of the *History*, chapter 6.]

The man, however, whom necessity compelled to haul wood from the forest, also rose very early. As is the custom of country people, before daylight had begun he asked his wife for food, and she immediately brought it. Having received the bread, the man did not eat it until it had been blessed by the priest or received eulogiae (blessed bread) from him. Having received them, he took it and departed.

When he had reached a river before dawn, he loaded his cart and oxen onto a bridge that had been built over a boat and began to cross to the farther bank. But when he reached the middle of the river, he heard a voice saying:

“Sink, sink; do not delay.”

Another voice answered:

“Without your prompting I would have done what you command, if a sacred thing did not obstruct my efforts. Know that he is protected by the priest’s blessing; therefore I cannot harm him.”

Hearing the voices, seeing no person, and realizing that they were speaking about him, the man marked himself with the Lord’s cross and gave thanks to God that the opposing side had not been able to prevail against him. Then he proceeded to the farther bank and returned home safely with his desired load.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning the Two Lovers

Ancient tradition reports that there were two people in Auvergne, namely a man and a girl, who were joined in marriage but not in intercourse. They rested in one bed, yet were not defiled by one another through carnal pleasure (A.D. 500, … 25 May).

After they had lived in the greatest chastity for many years, by mutual agreement the man was tonsured for the clerical state, while the girl put on a religious habit. It happened that, when her days were completed, the girl departed from this world. Her husband prepared a grave and brought her little body for burial.

As he was placing her in the grave, he revealed the secret that had been agreed between them, raising his hands toward heaven and saying:

“I give you thanks, maker of all things, because, just as you deigned to entrust her to me, so I have returned her to you undefiled by every contamination of pleasure.”

But she smiled and said:

“Be silent, be silent, man of God, for there is no need for you to confess our secret when no one has asked.”

After this, he covered her with the burial cloth and departed. Not long afterward he too departed from this world and was buried in his own place.

Their graves were in one basilica, but they were situated against different walls: one toward the south and the other toward the north. In the morning, however, the graves were found to be together, and they have remained so up to the present day.

For this reason the inhabitants now call them the Two Lovers and venerate them with the highest honor.

[Note: Concerning these two, see Book I of the *History*, chapter 42, and what we observed there. Tertullian, in his book *On the Soul*, mentions a certain body placed in a cemetery that left space for another to be placed beside it. See also the Life of Saint John the Almsgiver, chapter 50, in Book I of the *Lives of the Fathers*.]

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Concerning Amabilis the presbyter

There was also in the aforementioned city of Auvergne a certain Amabilis, a presbyter of the village of Riom, of admirable holiness. Distinguished by great virtues, he is often said to have commanded serpents (fifth century, 19 October).

When Duke Victorius had disdained to pray at his tomb and had tethered his horse opposite it, he could by no means move the animal away. Although he urged it with whips and spurs, it stood motionless, as if made of bronze. At last the duke was admonished by his men—for, so to speak, he had become like the beast itself—and descended to pray. When he had prayed faithfully, the horse went wherever he wished.

At this tomb I saw a man possessed by an evil spirit cleansed; I saw a perjurer stiffen like iron, confess his crime, and immediately be absolved.

[Note: It is read in Savaron’s edition of the book *On the Churches of Clermont*, chapter 12: “In the church of Saint Hilary … where Saint Amabilis rests in body.” His tomb is seen in the church of Saint Mary Magdalene of Croso in the suburb of Clermont. As may be conjectured, this is the same church that was once called Saint Hilary’s and is now subject to the church of Saint Amabilis of Riom. Nevertheless, many centuries ago the body of this holy man was transferred to Riom, where he has a church of notable abbey status dedicated to his name; in 1548 it passed from regular canons to secular canons. In the reliquary where his sacred remains are kept, the following old inscription was found some years ago, carved on a marble tablet: “Here lies the body of Saint Amabilis the Confessor, who died while … was reigning …” At Riom he is honored as the town’s chief patron on 19 October, the day on which his feast is recorded in various Martyrologies. On the same day Surius presents his Life, though it is filled with numerous errors.]

## CHAPTER XXXIV

[Note *: Since in this chapter and those that follow Gregory discusses ancient monuments that stood in his time near the basilica of Saint Illidius, it seemed appropriate to discuss them somewhat more fully. Some of them still survive in our Illidian monastery, situated near the city of Clermont.

Gregory testifies in Book I of the *History*, chapter 31, that many martyrs suffered at Auvergne and were buried near the city; hence not only the city’s bishops but other Christians as well wished to be buried in the same place. Certainly, already in the time of Sidonius Apollinaris—that is, in the fifth century—the place had been filled with a multitude of graves containing many bodies of saints. When Alcimus and Placidina rashly moved these from the site in order to lay the foundations of a church, Saint Antolianus, for whom that new church was being prepared, was greatly displeased, as Gregory relates in Book I of the *Miracles*, chapter 65.

If we may trust the old tradition of the people of Auvergne, Austremonius, their first bishop, built a church there in honor of the Virgin Mother of God. It was called Saint Mary among the Saints because, situated in the middle of a cemetery, it was surrounded by many graves of saints. They hold that a new church in honor of Saint Clement was joined to it by Saint Illidius, who, later buried there himself, gave it his name. Others added other churches nearby.

It is certain that in Gregory’s time three basilicas existed there, with many graves of saints—some inside those basilicas and others outside them—as he relates below, chapter 36. Those three basilicas still survive. The first two bear the names given by Gregory: Saint Illidius, which is the principal church of the monastery, and Saint Venerandus, in the monastery’s present gardens. The third, whose name Gregory does not mention, is called Saint Cassius; it stands not far from the others and also serves as a parish church.

In these churches one can see ancient tombs of saints, or at least of Christians, of the sort Gregory describes. They are especially numerous in the church of Saint Venerandus, where several display the preaching of Christ the Lord, the multiplication of loaves and fish performed by him, and other sacred histories, represented in the manner of those ancient times, as may be seen in the *Roma subterranea* and in other ancient monuments of the Church.

No tombs now remain outside those churches, either because they were transferred into the churches or because they were buried beneath the ruins of the ancient buildings that the people of Auvergne suffered under the Normans.

In the church of Saint Cassius there is still, beside the Gospel side, a stone chest that contained the body of Saint Georgia, with the following verses carved on a marble slab. We reproduce them exactly as they appear in the inscription, without regard to meter or verse division:]

> HERE LIES IN THE TOMB THE CONSECRATED GEORGIA OF CHRIST,  
> DEVOTED TO GOODNESS IN MIND AND FAITH, RIGHTLY.  
> BECAUSE HER FATHER WAS GREATLY PRESSED BY A CROWD OF SUITORS,  
> SHE CHOSE GOD UPON A MORE BLESSED BED.

In the church of Saint Venerandus no inscription is visible except one carved below the martyrs’ graves. I conjecture that it belonged to someone who, in order to secure the patronage of the saints, asked to be buried near them. Because the letters are fading and half destroyed, only the following could be read:

> [lacuna] `ETVM NATVRE QVIDEM CO...` — “... by nature indeed ...” [uncertain].  
> [lacuna] `FRAGELE VMEDA TERRA SVMIT NON TENIT AD...` — “the frail, moist earth receives ... does not hold ...” [uncertain].  
> `HIC ANTRA SEPVLCRI SED HACELOS QVEM JVSTA...` — “here [the] recesses of the tomb, but ... whom the just ...” [uncertain].  
> `FELICEM CONDETVM HOC TOMOLO LEVITA DNI...` — “the blessed one buried in this tomb, the deacon of the Lord ...” [uncertain].  
> `...HEM INNOCENCIVS ILLI NOMEN AB AVO PROTRA...` — “... Innocentius; his name derived from his grandfather ...” [uncertain].  
> `...BEATVS IN MOREBVS VITAM BENIGNA T...` — “... blessed in character, he led a kindly life ...” [uncertain].  
> `...VIX GESSERAT ANNVS CVM S...` — “... he had lived ... years when ...” [uncertain].  
> `...CO... NEPOTINS. CEDASPEC... R... X KL ABRILIS` — “... Nepotianus ... the tenth day before the Kalends of April” [uncertain].

In the oratory that has retained the name Saint Mary among the Saints there is a marble altar. Beneath it one sees a cross carved in white marble, at whose feet are two inscriptions, which we reproduce here:

> + + IN THIS PART OF THIS TOMB REST THE BODIES OF THE SAINTS, WHOSE NAMES GOD KNOWS, WITH WHOM THE BODY OF CORVUS, THE FATHER OF SAINT ILLIDIUS, RESTS.  
> + IN THIS OTHER PART OF THIS TOMB REST THE BODIES OF SEVEN INNOCENT SAINTS, WHOSE NAMES ARE WITH GOD.

In the chapel of the Illidian church, now dedicated to Saint Benedict, marble tablets are displayed representing the miracle of Christ the Lord multiplying the bread. On one of them is the following inscription:

> HERE REST THE BODIES OF SAINTS WHOSE NAMES GOD KNOWS.

In the chapel of Saint Justus there is a similar marble tablet with various figures and this inscription:

> HERE RESTS SAINT JUSTUS, BISHOP OF THE CITY OF AUVERGNE.

This Justus should be a different person from Justus, the archdeacon of Saint Illidius, whom Gregory mentions in Book I of the *History*, chapter 40. Besides the title of bishop, which is attributed here to Justus, this is suggested by the history of the translation of Saint Illidius, carried out in 1311. There Bishop Arbert is said, after raising the relics of Saints Illidius and Venerandus, to have left the bodies of the other saints—especially Blessed Nepotianus the bishop and Justus the archdeacon and disciple of Saint Illidius—in their places because of the difficulty of searching for them.

Certainly the booklet *On the Churches of Clermont* has two Justuses. Hence Savaron, and after him Sirmond, in Book IV, letter 11 of Sidonius Apollinaris, assigned Justus a place among the bishops of Clermont between Avolus and Caesarius.

### Concerning Georgia the religious woman

It is also said that there was in that city a certain girl, religious and devoted to God, who lived in the countryside so that, removed from the crowds of the city, she might more freely offer God worthy sacrifices of praise. Every day she devoted herself to fasting and prayer (A.D. 500, 15 February).

It happened that, when she departed from this world, she was carried to the basilica of the town for burial. But when the bier had been raised and her body began to be carried along the road, a large flock of doves arrived and began to fly over her, following wherever she was carried by those accompanying her.

When she had been brought into the basilica, the whole flock was seen to settle upon the roof of the building. After she had been buried, the doves flew up to heaven. Therefore she was rightly called Georgia: she exercised her mind in spiritual worship, and, having attained the sixtyfold fruit of virginity, departed from this world and was honored with a heavenly funeral.

[Note: She was buried in the church of Saint Cassius, according to Savaron’s edition of the booklet *On the Churches of Clermont*, chapter 9. Her sacred body rested there until our own age in a stone chest bearing the old inscription that we gave above, note *. First, in 1531, her sacred head was taken from there and given by Guillaume du Prat, bishop, to the monks of Saint Illidius. Then, in 1653, the entire body was brought into the same church of Saint Illidius by Louis de Stein, bishop of Clermont, where it is reverently preserved.]

## CHAPTER XXXV. Concerning the tomb broken open in the basilica of Saint Venerandus

[Note: The basilica of Saint Venerandus, about twenty paces from that of Saint Illidius and a little farther from the church of Saint Cassius, still survives in the gardens of the Illidian monastery. It is discussed in the book *On the Churches of Clermont*, chapter 10, where the bodies of several thousand saints are said to rest in it. See above. Gregory praises Venerandus from Paulinus in Book II of the *History*, chapter 13.]

In the basilica of Saint Venerandus, which is close to Saint Illidius, there was on the western side a vaulted chamber [that is, equipped with a vault] containing many sarcophagi carved from Parian marble. In them rest certain holy men and religious women. There is therefore no doubt that they were Christians, because the histories displayed on the tombs concern the miracles of the Lord and his apostles.

At the time when Georgius, a citizen of Velay, held the office of count of the city of Auvergne (around A.D. 569), part of that vaulted structure, which through long neglect had been soaked by rain, collapsed upon one of those sarcophagi and shattered its cover into pieces.

A girl was revealed lying inside, with all her limbs so firm that she seemed to have been taken from this world only recently. Her face and hands, together with her other limbs, were intact, with an enormous length of hair; but I believe that she had been embalmed with spices. The garment covering her lifeless limbs was of lambskin; it was undamaged, had not been dissolved by any decay, and was darkened by no blackness whatsoever.

[Note: This is the reading of all the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “it was unharmed by the force of the waters, and by no …,” etc.]

What more can be said? She appeared so intact that she seemed sleeping rather than dead. Some of our people maintained that, because of the whiteness of her silk garment, she had passed away in white garments. They said that gold rings and necklaces had been found around her and secretly removed so that the bishop would not learn of them. Yet no one of our own time knew, either by report or by reading, what her rank, family, or name had been.

While this little body lay exposed for a year, and no one, out of human compassion, provided a covering for the tomb, it happened that the wife of the aforementioned count fell gravely ill after her husband’s death. After suffering a prolonged illness, she was deprived of the light of her eyes.

When she had been released from the fever, she summoned physicians, tried various treatments, and offered generous rewards. Yet she could obtain no remedy from them, until at last the Lord’s compassion was moved to look upon her.

A certain figure appeared to her in a vision of the night and said:

“If you wish to be restored to your former sight, go as quickly as possible and seek a clean stone. Cover the sarcophagus of the resting girl, which is exposed in the basilica of Saint Venerandus. As soon as you have covered it, the sight of your eyes will be opened and you will see everything clearly.”

When she had done this and closed the vessel with its cover, she immediately received her sight in full.

There is therefore no doubt that she was a woman of noble merit, since she was able to accomplish such things for a sick woman.

[Note: Her name is still unknown.]

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Concerning other tombs of saints in the same basilica

[Note: This chapter and the following one are absent from Clar. a.]

There are in this place many tombs which, as we have said, are proved to belong to the faithful.

There is there a tomb adjoining this one on the left, similar in length, breadth, height, and every other arrangement. On the upper front of it is written:

> OF HOLY MEMORY: GALLA

(A.D. …, 31 May.)

There is also a sculpted tomb glorified by merits, situated on a raised place between the exit from the basilica of Saint Illidius and the entrance to the church of Blessed Venerandus. They say that a certain religious man named Alexander was buried in it. The frequent needs of the sick are immediately relieved there: after scraping off dust and drinking it mixed with water, they at once obtain health. So much medicine is continually taken from it that, because of its constant benefits, it can be seen by observers to be pierced through.

[Note: So SB. has it. Colb. a, Bad., Mor., and Chol. have *sculpti*; others, *sculptis*. Bal. has *multis*. In any case, no tombs now remain among these basilicas. See chapter 34, note *. Baronius confuses this Galla in his notes on 5 October with Galla, the wife of Saint Eucherius, whose feast Ado commemorates on 16 November.]

[Variant: others read “they pursue” (*exsequitur*) in place of “is obtained” (*exigitur*).]

Opposite this tomb, if you enter the basilica of Saint Venerandus through the door, you will see on the right a small tomb situated above ground, formed from a rather crude stone. No one knows who rests in it.

That something divine is present there is revealed by the event I am about to relate. A beggar, as we ourselves saw with our own eyes, was accustomed to sit upon it. I believe that he had become involved in some unworthy deed, as human frailty sometimes does; for, by the power of the one resting there, he was suddenly hurled far away with a great noise. The middle of the tomb split open, and it can still be seen in that condition.

The buried person judged that it was unworthy for a man to sit upon those limbs.

[Note: The printed editions have this reading. Laud. has “judging, I think, that it was unworthy for a man to sit upon him”; Colb. 2 has “as though upon a man … with these limbs.”]

The blessed martyr Liminius is also buried in this basilica (around A.D. 258, 29 March).

[Note: Gregory discusses him in Book I of the *History*, chapter 31. See also Savaron’s notes on chapter 10 of the book *On the Churches of Clermont*. He is believed to have suffered during the invasion of Chrocus, which Gregory places in the time of Valerian and Gallienus, while others place it at the beginning of the fifth century.]

Although the inhabitants preserve the story of his martyrdom, no cult of veneration is offered to him. There are, as we have said, men of distinguished merits whose names are unknown to the inhabitants, but are nevertheless, as we believe, retained in writing in heaven.

[Note: This is indicated by an old inscription cited by Savaron. See chapter 34, note *.]

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Concerning the tombs of the holy bishops Venerandus and Nepotianus

There is also there the tomb of Saint Venerandus himself, the bishop from whom this building received its name (A.D. 400, 18 January). It is arranged beneath a reading stand, and above it is an opening through which anyone who wishes may insert his head. Whatever necessity compels him to ask, he obtains immediately, provided that he asks justly.

[Note: Gregory discussed Saint Venerandus in Book II of the *History*, chapter 13. In 1311 his sacred relics were transferred by Bishop Arbert into a chest together with the body of Saint Illidius, at the request of Guido Scotus, abbot of the Illidian monastery. The feast of the Translation is commemorated on 22 December. Bollandus discusses the same saint on 18 January.]

Saint Nepotianus the bishop also rests there (A.D. 388, 22 October). In this world he was a man of the highest holiness, and now, with the power of the Lord, he obtains what is implored of him.

Often, when prayer is poured out over these tombs by sufferers from fever, it obtains the desired cure.

[Note: The body of Saint Nepotianus could not be found, although Bishop Arbert searched for it in vain for a long time. His sacred ashes are therefore believed to have remained in the place of his burial. Nevertheless, the old catalogues of relics of the Illidian church list the body of Saint Nepotianus. According to Gregory’s *History*, Book I, chapters 40 and 41, he had succeeded Blessed Illidius.]

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Concerning the monk whom the abbot watched while he prayed

There were once great lights of the world who, like the sun with its rays, illuminated the world with their virtues.

They say, therefore, that there was in a certain monastery a monk who, while among the others he devoted himself according to the monastic rules to prayer and reading, nevertheless offered the Almighty God the sacrifices of his prayers more secretly and in a more singular manner.

After completing the appointed office in the oratory, he would secretly slip away from the presence of the brothers. Going among dense brambles, box trees, and holm oaks, where he hoped that no one except God alone would see him, he would prostrate himself in prayer.

After lying there and imploring the Lord for a very long time, he would rise from the ground, stretch his hands and eyes toward heaven, and silently recite the sequence of the psalms. He was so intent upon heaven and so deeply contrite that streams of tears flowed violently from his eyes.

One of the brothers, who had cautiously followed him and observed this, did not keep silent before the abbot. The abbot carefully watched when he would go to perform these things, followed him from a distance, and, lying on the ground, watched what the faithful disciple was doing.

From a distance he saw a great miracle. For a flame proceeded from both sides of the monk’s mouth and, extending gradually upward, rose above him like a little column of smoke. The two flames joined together and formed a great torch, which seemed to climb all the way to heaven.

Although a plume grew upward and lengthened, it did not harm his head.

[Note: Colb. a reads: “although the hair, extended aloft, grew longer.”]

[Note: Colb. 2, Clar. a, and Mor. have *funiculus* (“cord”); compare chapter 20 above.]

The abbot, astonished by the sight, drew back somewhat. After completing his prayer, the monk returned to the monastery. The abbot followed by another route and later rebuked the monk with many reproaches in order to restrain him from vainglory.

[Note: Compare Book IV of the *History*, chapter 34.]

He did not, however, reveal what he had seen.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Concerning the fire that often burst forth from the relics of saints

This fire, as I think, contains a mystical sacrament, and the darkness of my understanding cannot grasp how, while appearing as light, it gives light without burning anything. I know only that such things appear to the just or over the just.

For it appeared to Moses in the bush and to the other fathers in the burnt offering. It also burst from the crown of blessed Martin’s head and penetrated the heights of heaven.

[Note: Sulpicius Severus relates this in *Dialogue* 2.]

I often heard Abbot Brachio relate that, as we wrote in the book of his Life (*Lives of the Fathers*, ch. 15), while he was celebrating the nightly vigils in the basilica of the aforementioned bishop, and the relics of saints brought by pilgrims were placed upon the altar, suddenly a globe of fire emerged from them and was seen to rise as far as the ceiling of the church. But, as he himself said, it was not shown to many.

The same thing appeared at the dedication of our oratory, as we mentioned above (chapter 20).

## CHAPTER XL. Concerning the visions experienced on account of my father’s illness

[Note: This chapter and the following one are absent from Clar. a.]

Nor is it absurd to believe that the Lord often deigns to reveal through visions how the saints are to be honored or how the sick may obtain remedies.

I remember an event from my childhood. My father was suffering from an illness caused by gouty humors. Wasted by the heat of fevers and by many pains, he lay in bed. In a vision of the night I saw a figure who said to me:

“Have you read,” he said, “the book of Joshua?”

I answered:

“I have recognized nothing in literature except the letters, whose study now binds and afflicts me. I do not even know whether this book exists.”

He said:

“Go and make a little tablet from wood that can receive this name. Write it in ink and place it beneath the support of your father’s head; it will be a protection for him if you carry out what I say.”

When morning came, I told my mother what I had seen, and she ordered the instructions of the vision to be fulfilled. When I had done this, my father immediately recovered from his illness.

After the course of another year, he was again seized by the same affliction. The fever grew hot, his feet swelled, and his nerves were twisted by terrible pain. While he was enduring these things and lying in bed with great groaning, I again saw in a vision the figure asking me whether I now knew the book of Tobit. [Variant: some read “while I lay in bed.”]

I answered that I had not read it.

He said:

“You should know that Tobit had been blind. His son, while traveling with an angel as his companion, caught a fish in a river. At the angel’s instruction he removed its heart and liver and smoked his father’s eyes with them; immediately, when the darkness had been driven away, he regained his sight.

“Go, then, and do likewise, and your father will receive relief from his pains.”

When I reported this to my mother, she immediately sent servants to the river. The fish was caught; what had been ordered was removed from its entrails and placed on the coals.

[Note: Colb. a has “and, after removing them from …, he placed them.”]

As soon as the fragrant smoke reached my father, the swelling and pain immediately departed.

## CHAPTER XLI. Concerning Saint Germanus of Auxerre

[The supplied source ends here.]

## Germanus

Germanus, the glorious confessor, died in the city of Rome [Note: [Col. 0859C] This chapter is absent from your Colbert manuscript. Yet Hericus, in *On the Miracles of Saint Germanus*, chapters 29 and 30, reports it and the following chapter in full under the name of our Gregory. In Colb. *Ravenna* has been corrected by an ancient hand. Bad. likewise reads this, together with Hericus; and indeed Saint Germanus died at Ravenna.] (A.D. 448, July 31). He was then taken up sixty days later, brought to the city of Auxerre, and committed to burial [Note: In the celebrated monastery which still exists at Auxerre under his name. His sacred body was burned by Calvinist heretics in the previous century. A stone sarcophagus remains, with several bones, as well as the cloth-of-gold vestment decorated with imperial eagles in which that blessed pontiff had been buried by the Empress Placidia. His Life was written by Constantius, a priest and his disciple, which may be found in Surius. Most of his successors in that see wished to be buried beside his tomb; their graves, together with their sacred relics, may still be seen in the underground crypt. Germanus’s Mass is found first in the *Missale Gallicanum*, in Mabillon, book III of *Gallic Liturgy*.].

In the time of Queen Teudechilda [Note: See the notes on book IV, chapter 26], a certain tribune named Nunninus [Al., Numnius], returning from Auvergne in Gaul after paying tribute to the queen, visited the city of Auxerre solely for religious reasons. Having thrown himself down before the blessed man’s tomb and prayed for a very long time, he drew a sword from its sheath [Note: Bad. has *ense*, “sword.” In Bell., another, but ancient, hand has corrected the text as follows: “and having drawn the sword from its sheath, he struck,” etc. He uses the fourth case instead of the sixth.] and, without anyone seeing him, struck the stone that lay over the venerable tomb.

A small fragment was knocked from it, and he stiffened like bronze, so that he could move no limb at all or utter a sound. When the boys saw him lying there in this condition, they did not know what had happened to him. One of them approached and, when he questioned him, received no answer [Note: Laud., Bell., and Ed. read: “and received no answer from him.”].

Then, remaining rigid as he was, he understood in his heart that he had been condemned and made this vow: “I know that I have acted presumptuously, most blessed Confessor, but devotion compelled me to presume. Therefore, if you deign to absolve me and permit me to return home with your favor, I shall place these relics in the basilica and take care to celebrate your feast with the utmost devotion every year.”

The holy man understood his muffled prayer, absolved him, and allowed him to depart unharmed. He returned, placed those relics in the church, and faithfully celebrated the Saint’s feast every year for 929 years.

Once, we came with Bishop Avitus to the basilica mentioned above, where the relics had been deposited. When the holy pontiff entered it fasting at about the tenth hour, all of us who were with him breathed in through our nostrils the fragrance of lilies and roses. We do not doubt that this was granted to us through the merits of the blessed pontiff. It was the ninth month.

This occurred in the village of Musiacas [Note: Hericus, *On the Miracles of Saint Germanus*, chapter 30, has this form. But Laud. and Bel., together with Hericus in the Vindocinensis manuscript, read *Musciacas*. It seems to be a place still highly renowned for its notable Benedictine abbey, founded by the senator Calminius, as Savaro writes, and restored by King Pippin. It is commonly called Mauzac or Mozac, situated in the district of Riom; later it was subjected to the Cluniac order and still exists, distinguished by the body of Saint Austremonius.].

## CHAPTER XLII. On Hilary, senator of Dijon

At the fortress of Dijon a certain Hilary [Note: Laud., Bell., and Colb. a have *Helarius*, and likewise throughout, or *Elarius*. This chapter is cited by the Chronicle of Saint Benignus of Dijon from Gregory’s book *On Illustrious Men*, where Hilary’s wife is called Quitta; there they are also said to have been saints and the parents of Saint John, abbot of Réome, mentioned below, chapter 87. This is expressly transmitted in the Life of that same saint, written by a contemporary author, in the second Benedictine century, under the year 539. Cointius nevertheless denies, under the year 534, that John was born of these parents. Their translation is mentioned in the manuscript Martyrology on July 1.

In chapter 42 and the two following chapters, certain saints celebrated at Dijon are mentioned, buried in various basilicas near the city. A cemetery originally existed there, where Saint Benignus had been buried. Although a crypt had been built over his tomb, the place was unknown to the inhabitants, and even to Bishop Saint Gregory himself. By divine revelation he learned that the blessed martyr lay there; as Gregory relates in book I of *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 51, this gave occasion for the construction of a great basilica over the crypt, in which the blessed bishop is said to have established monks under the rule of Abbot Eustadius.

Near this basilica stood another under the patronage of Saint Paschasia, where she herself lay. Not far away was a baptistery under the patronage of both Saint Johns, the Baptist and the Evangelist, said to have been consecrated by Benignus himself; the author of the Benignian Chronicle also affirms that a community of nuns existed there. Saint Urban and several other bishops of Langres were buried in this church, among them the celebrated Gregory himself and Tetricus, his son and successor.

Gregory does not state in which church Hilary and his wife Quitta, or Saint Florida, were originally buried. He called all these churches basilicas by one name in book IV of the *Histories*, chapter 16. Into these churches Chramnus was admitted by Bishop Tetricus, although, fleeing from fear of his father Chlothar, he had not previously been permitted to enter within the walls of Dijon.

Two or three of these basilicas still survive, though enclosed within the city walls. The chief of them, and of the city’s other churches, is the basilica of Saint Benignus, with its attached Benedictine monastery of the Congregation of Saint Maur. Another is dedicated to Saint John and bears a parish title; so does a third, now known under the name of Saint Philibert, nearer to the Benignian basilica, though its origin is uncertain.

The Benignian basilica was restored in the year 1003 by William, a most devout abbot; a description of it may be found in the often-cited Chronicle of that place. In its eastern section there is a crypt with an oratory of Saint John the Baptist, supported by three rows of columns. Above it rises an octagonal chapel dedicated to the Blessed Mary, resting on sixty-eight columns.

From the same Chronicle we learn the order in which the saints’ bodies were arranged in that basilica in the eleventh century. There we read:

“Eustadius … was granted burial beside the body of Saint Benignus the martyr. Tranquillus succeeded him and was buried on the right side of the tomb of Saint Benignus the martyr, beside Saint Paschasia; and Saint Florida was placed beside him. On the other side, beside the tomb of Saint Eustadius, was the tomb of Saint Hilary the senator and of his wife, Saint Quitta.”

Today, in the same lower crypt, the stone tomb of Saint Benignus may be seen, with other tombs surrounding it, though their occupants are unknown. The body of the holy martyr is preserved in an exceedingly rich reliquary. The relics of the other saints, except for the head of Saint Paschasia, either still lie buried in the earth or have been mixed with those of other unknown persons in two wooden chests lined with gold, kept in the monastery’s sacristy.]

He was one of the senators [Col. 0861A] and lived there with a wife, by whom he is said to have had children (fifth century, November 28). Yet he cultivated his entire household in such chastity and complete purity, both of soul and body, that no one there dared commit adultery. Thus was fulfilled in that household what the Apostle, long ago filled with the Holy Spirit, proclaimed: “Marriage is honorable, and the marriage bed undefiled” [Note: Colb. a reads: “to honor … and undefiled marriage beds.”] (Hebrews 13:4).

This man, whose chastity prevailed among both masters and servants, died. What sort of person he was, and how great according to worldly rank, is shown today by his tomb, which gleams sculpted from Parian marble.

After his death, and after he had been committed to burial according to human custom, the woman fell ill at the completion of a year, died, and was washed. Since that tomb was so immense that it could receive her beside her husband, its cover was removed. As she was being placed in the tomb, suddenly the man’s right arm [Al., “the right arm”] was raised and embraced his wife’s neck. The people marveled, replaced the cover, and learned what chastity, what fear of God, and what love between them had existed in this world, since they had embraced one another so in the tomb.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On Saints Florida and Paschasia

In this basilica Saint Florida also rests [Note: The author of the Chronicle of Saint Benignus testifies that her body lay near Saint Benignus’s tomb. No office is celebrated for her. See chapter 42, note o.] (A.D. …, January 10). According to the inhabitants, she had been exceedingly religious after changing her clothing.

There is also another basilica not far away, in which Saint Paschasia rests [Note: Gregory likewise has this above, book I of *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 51. In the Chronicle of Saint Benignus she is called a virgin and martyr, having completed her martyrdom by fire after being instructed and baptized by Saint Benignus. Blessed William, abbot of Saint Benignus, built an altar in her honor in the eleventh century. Her translation is recorded on July 1 in the manuscript Martyrology, where her feast is also mentioned on January 9, the day on which she is honored in various churches of Burgundy.] (A.D. 177, January 9).

She is said to have appeared to the builders of the basilica of Saint Benignus the martyr, exhorting them to persevere in the work they had begun and assuring them that they were being aided by the martyr’s help. After returning to her own basilica, she disappeared completely.

## CHAPTER XLIV. On Saint Tranquillus, bishop [Col. 0862A]

In this place Saint Tranquillus the blessed confessor also rests. His tomb stands above the ground, and from it great benefit is granted to those who ask [Note: This chapter is absent from Clar. a. Nevertheless, it is praised in the Chronicle of Saint Benignus, where Tranquillus is said to have succeeded Eustadius as the first abbot of the Benignian monastery. His feast is celebrated nowhere, nor was he a bishop. On his burial, see chapter 42, at the end of note i.] (sixth century, March 15).

For from the mosses [Note: Bel. has *musulis*; Bad. and below *museo*; commonly we say *de la mousse*.] that grow upon it, the people obtain medicines, and I myself have had abundant experience of this. When my hands had erupted in small pustules and I was suffering severe pain because of them, I touched them with this moss; the moisture immediately subsided, and I found them healed.

## CHAPTER XLV. On Severinus, bishop of Bordeaux

The city of Bordeaux also has venerable patrons [Note: This chapter and the following four are absent from Clar. a.] (A.D. 400, October 23). It honors Saint Severinus, the bishop, with the greatest faith outside its walls, for he frequently manifests himself through miracles.

Although I said in the prologue of this book that I would write only what God had deigned to accomplish through His saints after their deaths, I do not think it absurd to recall something of the lives of those about whom we know nothing to have been written.

Thus, according to the faithful account of the clerics of Bordeaux, Saint Severinus was sent to that city from the regions of the East [Note: Nevertheless, some think that this is the same Severinus who presided over the church of Cologne in the time of Saint Martin. Although absent, he is said to have learned his death by divine revelation, book I of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 4. All this is described at length in a sermon published by an ancient author in Surius on October 23, where more is found concerning his death, tomb, and translations. Others maintain that the Severinus mentioned here transferred from the see of Trier to the see of Bordeaux; Cointius refutes them under the year 597, no. 9. See Lopes’s *History*.].

While he was traveling, and Bishop Amandus was governing the church of Bordeaux [Note: Gregory praises him among the holiest bishops on the basis of a letter of Paulinus, book II of the *Histories*, chapter 13. Paulinus also wrote several extant letters to him. His relics rest in the church of Saint Severinus.] (A.D. 400, June 18), the Lord appeared to Amandus in a nocturnal vision and said:

“Rise and go out to meet my servant Severinus, and honor him as Holy Scripture teaches that a friend of the Divine Majesty should be honored; for he is better than you and higher in merits.”

Bishop Amandus rose, took his staff in his hand, and went to meet him, knowing nothing about the holy man except what the Lord had revealed. And behold, Saint Severinus was coming as though to meet him.

When they approached one another, they greeted each other by name, fell together into one another’s arms, kissed, and entered the church with abundant prayer and great psalmody.

From then onward Bishop Amandus loved and honored him so greatly that he appointed him as his successor, while he himself was regarded as the junior. Finally, after a few years, the most blessed Severinus died. After he had been buried, Bishop Amandus resumed his office, which there is no doubt was restored to him because of the obedience he had shown toward God’s saint.

From that time, once the inhabitants had learned of his holiness, they adopted him as their patron. They were confident that whenever disease invaded the city, hostility besieged it, or any trouble struck, the people would immediately gather at the Saint’s basilica [Note: It still exists near Bordeaux, decorated with the title of abbey. Formerly it was held by Augustinian Canons Regular; today it is held by secular clergy.], proclaim fasts, celebrate vigils, and pour forth prayers most devoutly; and soon they were saved from the impending calamity.

After we had written these things, however, we learned that his Life had been written by the priest Fortunatus [Note: Brouverus says that this Life has been lost, in chapter 5 of Fortunatus’s Life.].

## CHAPTER XLVI. On Romanus, a priest of the same city

In this region there is also Saint Romanus the priest, whom, as the written accounts of his Life teach, our Martin committed to burial (A.D. 382, November 24). His tomb is adjacent to the fortress of Blaye [Note: An abbey of Saint Romanus may still be seen there; it is held by Augustinian Canons Regular. Concerning the fortress of Blaye, commonly called Blaye, below the confluence of the Garonne and Dordogne, in the diocese of Bordeaux, see Valesius’s *Description of Gaul*. Under the year 385, which he says was the penultimate year of the Emperor Gratian and therefore the year 382, Sigebert writes: “In Gaul Saint Romanus of Blaye died …”], on the bank of the river Garonne.

There, by the intervention of his power, he often saves those about to perish in shipwreck. Amid the waves of the rushing torrent they cry out: “Have mercy on us, Saint Romanus, confessor of God.” But immediately the storm subsides, and they reach the desired shore.

Yet no one who has been granted the sight of his basilica from the middle of the river can rightly perish in shipwreck. We too experienced this very power in a grave emergency.

For when exceedingly heavy rain had poured down for many days, forcing the Garonne beyond its banks, and when, driven by the wind, it surged in powerful waves, enormous mountains of water rose up and inspired no small fear in those who watched them, the blessed Confessor, as we believe, obtained through the support of his power that the roaring should be restrained and the riverbed made smooth. Thus we entered a boat and were carried safely to the opposite bank.

## CHAPTER XLVII. On two priests who sing psalms

In a village of the same territory two priests are also buried [A.D. …], men of outstanding holiness, as the event itself demonstrates. For the miracle that takes place most clearly teaches that they live after burial.

They are buried in one basilica, but at opposite walls. One of their tombs is on the southern side, the other on the northern.

Whenever the clergy begin to perform the office of singing psalms, and the crowd sings to the Lord in choirs formed by them, the public voice mingles with the psalmody of both. One choir is aided by the voice of one of them, while the other grows stronger through the melody of the other’s voice.

Their harmony is so sweet that it often delights the attentive ears of those who hear it. It is also proved that many benefits are granted along with these things if faithful prayer precedes them.

This occurs in the village of Vodollacum [Note: Could this be the village of Bouliac, or, as its inhabitants pronounce it, Vouliac, commonly said to lie between the two seas—that is, the Garonne and the Dordogne?].

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On the church of Reontium

Likewise, at Reontium [Note: It is a fortress still known today, commonly called Riuntium or Rions, situated on the Garonne above Bordeaux], there is a village in which, when there was a Catholic church, the Goths arrived and transferred it to the impurity of their sect.

Beside it stands a large house. When the vigil of Easter arrived, they baptized little children here in our church together with the heretics’ priests [Mss., “baptized”], so that, by denying the Catholic priest access to baptize them, the people might more easily be entangled in that sect.

But, with shrewd intention, while they were in our church, he prepared the necessary ministry in their house and began to baptize there, while they were baptizing in the church. Divine vengeance, however, overtook the infants whom the heretics had baptized there—namely, twice ten of them—and none of them was able to reach the Closed Feast [Note: Bal. has *claustrum*, incorrectly. The “Closed Easter,” that is, Low Sunday, is intended here, the octave of Easter] alive.

When the heretics saw this, and feared that their house would become a church, they returned their church to the priest. Of those whom he baptized, no one died at that time except one whom the Lord deigned to call after he had reached the proper age.

## CHAPTER XLIX. On the priests Justinus and Misilinus [Al., Similinus]

Within the territory of the city of Bigorre, in the village of Sexciacum, the priest Saint Justinus rests [Note: Bel. has *Justissimus*. Laud., Col. a, and Bell. call the other *Similinus* in the index. The ancient Martyrologies celebrate Saint Justinus the bishop with three companions at the city of Bigorre on May 1. Labbe, volume II of the *New Library*, page 579, also gives a Life—though a fabulous one—of Justinus the confessor, whose body is preserved at the village of Partiniacum in Gascony. His feast is said to be celebrated there on May 3; Papebrochius, under May 1 in the Bollandists, considers him the same as the man from Bigorre.

Ferrarius praises Justinus and Similinus on September 17, from Molanus’s additions, writing that they were celebrated in the territory of Tours according to our Gregory. Saussayus followed him in the supplement to the *Gallican Martyrology*, where he also commemorates on May 24 Missolinus, who is honored in the church of Tarbes.

The marble tomb of this Misselinus, commonly Saint Mesclin, may be seen behind the high altar of the parish church of Saint John at Tarbes. When it had been opened two years ago by the vicars-general of the illustrious bishop, it was found entirely empty. A general procession of the entire clergy is held on his feast, May 24.

Concerning Justinus and the village of Sexciacum, we learned the following after publishing our observations on the book *On the Glory of the Confessors*. Not far from the parish church of the village of Serciacum or Sexciacum, as Gregory calls it, commonly Sers, an old, nearly ruined oratory with two cells may be seen on a high hill. It is dedicated to God under the name of Justinus; perhaps the same saint was resting there in Gregory’s time.

I do not know the village of Talua. Sersiacum, however, lies in the valley of Barèges, in the county of Bigorre, about six leagues from the city of Tarbes.] (A.D. …, May 1).

Since he is endowed with many virtues, possessed persons who cry out at his tomb are frequently cleansed. His neighbor Misilinus is close to him in merits and holiness. He held the office of the same order in the Church and rests in the village of Talua in this territory, flourishing with similar virtues.

## CHAPTER L. On Saint Severus the priest

Associated with this city and territory [Note: In Clar. a, after the earlier writing had worn away, this was substituted by the same hand: “within the territory of the city of Bigorre.” It seems that the words “associated with this city,” etc., had been omitted deliberately. It is nevertheless clear that the preceding chapter had itself been omitted; otherwise there would be no sense.] is Saint Severus [Note: Bal. has *Severinus*. Following Rosweydus, some think that this was Severus Sulpicius, the disciple of blessed Martin, who, besides his *Sacred History* and other short works, also wrote the Life of that same saint.

In the diocese of Tarbes, Tarbes in Bigorre, there is a monastery of Saint Severus called Rostagno, which some think was named after the Saint Severus mentioned here. The inhabitants of the place demonstrate the miracle of the lily that grew green again there, not only from ancient tradition but also because it was carved above an old basin in which the sacred body of the blessed man was deposited, after its first elevation, seven hundred years ago.

The Calvinists burned this same body of Saint Severus, together with other relics, in 1573. The monastery still exists, belonging to the Benedictine order under the Congregation of Saint Maur, and Saint Severus’s feast is celebrated there on August 1.

One of our associates informed me that the miracle of the tree which withered at Saint Severus’s prayers and was later restored to its former state when he prayed again appears represented on the tomb of the saint mentioned above.] He too was ordained a priest and was born of noble lineage (A.D. 500, August 1).

In the countryside, on an estate of Sexciacum that belonged to his benefice, he built a church. Then, in another village, he built another temple of God, fortifying both with relics of the saints [Note: Bell. and Colb. 2 read as above; the other editions, however, read: “he built two churches, a temple of God of the saints,” etc.].

When Sunday came [Note: This note observes that one priest said two Masses every Sunday], after celebrating the Masses in one place, he went to the other. There was a distance between the two churches of about twenty miles. This was his task every Sunday.

One Sunday, while making this journey and hurrying faster by striking his swift horse with his heel, a branch of a medlar tree struck his head [Note: Bad. has *mespuli*. The other printed editions have *mespili*, which is in fact the name of this tree].

Feeling the injury, he said: “May God cause you to wither, you who have grown from the earth by His will.” Immediately the tree withered down to the very roots of its strength.

He continued to the place where he was going, celebrated the solemn rites, and remained there for three days. On the fourth day, when he returned and saw the tree dry, he said: “Woe is me, because in the bitterness of my heart I cursed this tree. Behold how it has withered.”

He dismounted, prostrated himself at its roots, and said to the Lord:

“Almighty God, by whose will all things are governed, by whose command things not yet born are created, created things live, and dead things are restored; whose life-giving command we obey, believing that we shall live after the death of this body through the future resurrection: command this tree to grow green again and to be as it was before.”

Immediately, as though through some arrangement of its veins, moisture rose from the earth and spread through all the branches of the spreading tree in abundant irrigation. Loosening the withered knots, it burst forth in leaves, and those standing by marveled that it had come back to life.

His power and almsgiving were indeed great. As was said above, he made churches from his own houses and distributed his possessions as food to the poor. In one of these churches he placed his tomb, and in it he was buried.

He was accustomed to gather lily blossoms during the season when they appear and hang them along the walls of this building [Note: It was customary in the early centuries of the Church to adorn sacred buildings and martyrs’ tombs with flowers. Jerome praises Nepotianus for this in his epitaph, and Fortunatus praises Radegund in book VIII of his *Epigrams*, poem 9. Paulinus invites the faithful to do the same in poem 14, and Augustine recounts miracles performed through such flowers placed near the relics of Saint Stephen, book XXII of *The City of God*, chapter 8.].

## CHAPTER LI. On the lily of his tomb

Thus, through the cooperation of the Lord, the kind of life he lived in this world becomes so clear that it is now demonstrated by evident prodigies.

The lily that, as we said, he had gathered and placed in the basilica of his tomb gradually withers as time passes. Its flower petals loosen downward and its crown dries up. It appears so completely dried that, if touched by hand, it would seem likely to crumble instantly into dust, and it remains in this dryness for the entire year.

But when the day arrives on which the Confessor departed from the body, it rises again in renewed greenness. One may see the leaves gradually growing green, the flowers themselves rising, and the plant being restored, without any moisture from water or earth, to the form in which it had once been.

Thus the blessed Confessor produces new flowers from his tomb; with the relics of the saints, it flourishes like a palm in heaven.

## CHAPTER LII. On tombs that rise

Within the territory of the village of Julius, three priests are also buried, according to an ancient report (A.D. …). They were not related by any bond of blood, but were companions solely in the love of God, made brothers in heaven. By their tombs, placed side by side in one small area, they glorify the place through the continual occurrence of miracles.

After they had rested for many years in the little tombs where they were buried, the pavement—which had been poured as hard as flint from lime and crushed pottery—recently split, and the top of one tomb appeared. When it had been raised slightly, the split earth revealed the summit of a second. When that one emerged, a third mound followed. These now rise gradually above the ground, in proportion to the beginning of their manifestation [Note: In former times canonization took place through the elevation of a dead person’s body from the earth, over which an altar was erected. Hence it was a great sign of holiness if a tomb rose from the earth without human intervention through a miracle. This happened to Saint Droctoveus, the first abbot of Saint Germanus of the Meadows, according to his Life, no. 18, in volume I of the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, page 257: “His tomb-urn, moved for several years, gradually rose above the earth and demanded an altar. For he had obtained a dwelling in the land of the living and ought not to remain entirely within the boundary of the earth of the dying.”].

But now the first is free from the earthly mass and presents itself openly to human eyes. The other two still follow, but each year they advance toward emergence.

O admirable mystery of the Godhead, which reveals to the world the purity of buried limbs, as it brings them forth from the pavement and prepares them for resurrection—not [the text is uncertain] to be given to the undying worm, but to be made equal to the brightness of the sun’s light and glorified in conformity with the Lord’s body [Note: Clar. a, with Ed., reads: “not to be given to the dying worm.”].

These tombs are within the territory mentioned above, near the village of Atroa [Note: Perhaps it should be read *Atora* or *Atura*, from which the name of the village of Julius may have derived; the place still retains it, commonly called Aire.].

## CHAPTER LIII. On the tomb of Thaumastus, bishop

Thaumastus [Note: Clar. a lacks this chapter and the following five. All manuscripts, with Bad., have *Theomastus*, except the Antwerp manuscript, which has *Thomastus*. The etymology of the name given by Gregory requires our reading. It is strange that this saint is not celebrated even in the church of Saint Hilary of Poitiers, nor in the Poitevin litanies of Louis Castanaeus, where he is mentioned only among the additions on the basis of this passage of Gregory.

His tomb, however, may be seen in the oratory of Saint Bartholomew near the basilica of Saint Hilary, and it is famous for the colic pains which it is said to relieve in children.

Concerning the city of Momociacum, we spoke in book IX of the *Histories*, chapter 29. Most consider it to be Mainz; Labbe and Castanaeus consider it Mende. On maps of ancient Gaul it appears above the River Meuse, within the territory of the Remi, as Momociacum, at the place where the town of Mosomagus, commonly Mousson, is situated—a town already famous at that time. Yet nowhere is it read that a bishop was seated there.] was also, in accordance with the interpretation of his name, a man of admirable holiness. He is said to have been bishop of the city of Momociacum. For some reason removed from that city, he went to the town of Poitiers, where he ended his present life, persevering in a good confession (A.D. …, January 1).

What reward he possesses in heaven is displayed at his tomb; the power proceeding from the tomb reveals that he inhabits paradise. It truly demonstrates in him what the Lord Jesus Christ says in the Gospel to Martha: “Whoever believes in me, even if he dies, lives” [Note: Ed. reads: “If he has died, he will live.”]; “and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die” (John 13:25–26).

He has his tomb above the ground before the atrium of blessed Hilary. Many people scrape dust from this mound and drink it; it cures toothache and fevers so effectively that whoever drinks it marvels at the result. This blessing is sought so constantly that the sarcophagus now appears pierced in one place.

## CHAPTER LIV. On Lupianus the confessor

Within the territory of Poitiers, adjoining the city of Nantes—that is, in the village of Ratiatum [Note: This place was once famous and gave its name to the district; some bishops of the Poitevins consequently bore the title “bishop of Ratiatum.” Opinions differ concerning the location of this place. See Valesius’s *Description of Gaul*. Several Martyrologies celebrate Lupianus’s feast on January 1 and his translation at Clermont on July 1. For this reason some suspect that he was an Auvergnian and different from the disciple of Saint Hilary.]—a certain Lupianus rests, having departed this life in white garments (fourth century, October 11).

He is said to have received the gift of baptism from blessed Bishop Hilary; but soon afterward, as we have said, he departed from the body. God, the giver of every good, has granted him such grace that at his tomb the blind receive sight, the paralytic the ability to walk, and the mute the power of speech.

## CHAPTER LV. On Melanius, bishop of Rennes

Melanius [Note: This chapter is absent from Colb. tut. Saint Melanius subscribed to the First Council of Orléans in 511. He died in 530, on November 6, the day on which he is honored at Rennes; or certainly in the following year, if the true date of his death is the one assigned in the Roman Martyrology, January 6. See Cointius under the year 530, nos. 7 and following, and Bollandus under January 6, where his Life is presented.

His sacred body is preserved in the monastery dedicated to his name, belonging to the Order of Saint Benedict and the Congregation of Saint Maur. Its abbot seems to have been Bertulfus, who subscribed to the Council of Chalon in 650 on behalf of Durioterus, bishop of Rennes.] bishop of the city of Rennes, after countless signs of his virtues, continually intent upon heaven, shone forth in the world. Over his tomb the Christians had raised a marvelous structure of great height (A.D. 530, November 6).

But through the instigation of the Evil One, who always opposes good works, it was at one time seized by fire. There was a linen cloth [Ed. “wooden”] covering the Confessor’s holy tomb. Immediately, when the mass of beams was cut down by the dominant flames, the tiles fell with their fastenings and the rest of the roof’s fittings.

One of the beams, however, driven forward by the force of the collapse with its head aflame, fell upon the Saint’s tomb. It could not merely have set the cloth on fire; it could also have crushed it against the stone of the tomb. An immense mass of burning coals fell upon it as well.

Other coverings hanging from the walls or doors were consumed at the first breath of flame. But this cloth was not burned; indeed, it was not even discolored by the fire to the slightest degree [Note: Laud., with Ed., reads: “was not even disfigured.”].

When the fire had ended, the people entered with great wailing and hurried to the bishop’s tomb, expecting new joy amid weeping and tears. They removed the wood and flames from above the tomb, seized the tomb-covering, shook off the embers, and all marveled that it had remained unharmed.

## CHAPTER LVI. On Victorius, bishop of the Cenomanienses
Victorius [Note: [Col. 0869C] He succeeded his father Victurus and was ordained by Saint Martin, whose disciple he had been. He occupied the see for forty-one years, six months, and ten days. He was renowned for miracles both before and after his death, as the author of the *Deeds of the Bishops of Le Mans*, chapter 6, published by Mabillon in volume III of the old *Analecta*, testifies; this author praises an ancient *Life* of the same holy man written by himself. He took part in the Council of Angers concerning the ordination of Talasius in 453, and in the First Council of Tours in 461. Together with Leo and Eustochius, he wrote a letter to the bishops of the province of Lyon III, which is extant. He died on the Kalends of September, during the second consulship of Faustus the Younger and the consulship of Longinus. —His father, however, died on 25 August. Both were buried in the church of Prato, which is still a famous monastery of Benedictine nuns. There, in the underground crypt—blocked off by a wall several years ago—the tombs of many of the ancient bishops of Le Mans could be seen, those who rested there around the tomb of Saint Julian. Saint Bertramnus, bishop of Le Mans, calls Saint Victurius his special patron in his *Testament*, in volume III of Mabillon’s *Analecta*, p. 142; there he also mentions the basilica of Saint Victurius, which, unless I am mistaken, is the very one still visible not far from the abbey of Prato, now endowed with parochial status. —Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, praises this chapter in a sermon, using the following words concerning the possibility that Martin might be called equal to the apostles: “Hence it is that Saint Martin was shown in the fire to Saint Trojan, bishop of Saintes.”] bishop of Le Mans repeatedly displayed himself through great miracles (Annals 490, 1 September). For they say that once, while the city itself was burning and the wind drove great balls of flame here and there, he, like a good shepherd unable to endure the ecclesiastical folds being ravaged by Satan’s attacks, set himself against the whirlwind. Raising his hand and making the sign of the cross against it, he immediately caused the entire fire to cease [Col. 0869B], and the city, having been delivered, gave thanks to its Shepherd because he had not permitted its possessions to be devoured by the threatening fire. The sick are also frequently healed at his tomb.

## CHAPTER LVII. On Martin, abbot of Saintes

Martin, abbot of the city of Saintes and, as they say, a disciple of our Martin, rests in peace (Annals 400, 7 December) near the town of that city, in the monastery [Note: [Col. 0870C] Cointius calls it Saliginense, under the year 752.] that he himself built after receiving his master’s teachings. At his tomb a certain countryman, bringing hands contracted, took them back healed [Ed., *a certain woman*]. Another man, whose nerves had been burned by fever, whose knees were twisted, and who had lost the ability to walk, was carried to the holy tomb. As soon as he had prostrated himself there, he received new strength; the stiffness disappeared, and he was carried away sound, afterward serving there for many years. The bishop Palladius, unable to move this man’s tomb together with many others, moved it with the help of the Confessor’s aid, together with five abbots, and set it where he wished.

## CHAPTER LVIII. On Bibianus, bishop of the same city [Col. 0870A]

Bibianus, the bishop of this city, also rests in its suburb [Note: [Col. 0870C] The feast of Saint Bibianus, also called Vivianus or Vibianus, is celebrated on 28 July. Fortunatus, *Book I, Poem 12*, praises Leontius of Bordeaux for completing the basilica of this same saint, which had been begun by Eusebius and then by Emerius, bishops of Saintes. In it stood the tomb of Saint Bibianus, which the same author testifies had been covered with silver and gold at the expense of Leontius and Placidina. The church of Saint Vivianus, with the suburb bearing the same name [Col. 0870D], still exists. In an old manuscript of Saint Peter of Chartres there is a letter attributed to Saint Augustine and addressed to Bibianus, bishop of Saintes; Mabillon published it in his appendix to the *Gallican Liturgy*. There Augustine replies to a letter that Bibianus had sent him through his deacon Trojanus. Bibianus is listed second in the commonly circulated catalogues of the bishops of Saintes.] (Annals . . . 28 July). A book already written about his life recounts the mass of his virtues; now, when entreated, he frequently grants health to the sick. Therefore I shall dare to relate at least one of so many miracles.

A woman whose hands had withered, and whose fingernails had already become wounded, had lost the ability to work because her tendons were contracted [Colb. 2: *had become wounded*]. She devoutly prostrated herself at the Blessed One’s tomb. After praying, she was granted the restoration of her hands; the cords of her fingers were loosened, and she was able to raise them in order to give thanks to the Lord.

## CHAPTER LIX. On Trojanus, bishop of that city [Col. 0870B]

Trojanus, likewise the bishop of that city, lies near the tomb of this man, joined to him in heaven [Note: [Col. 0870D] Ed.: “of Saint Bibianus of that city of Saintes, joined to him.” In the Colbert manuscript he is called *Trofianus* and *Trophianus*. He seems to be the man who wrote to Eumerius, bishop of Nantes, concerning a boy who did not know whether he had been baptized. From this Cointius concludes, under the year 508, that Trojanus did not meet Clovis when he was returning from the battle of Vouillé, as some say, since Peter, Trojanus’s predecessor, signed the First Council of Orléans in 511. He is different from the deacon Trojanus of Saint Bibianus mentioned in the preceding note.] (Annals 532, 30 November). This priest is said to have possessed great virtue.

Once, during the darkness of night, while he was making the rounds of the holy places then situated around the city with only one subdeacon as his companion, a great globe of light appeared to him, as though descending from heaven. When the man of God understood what had happened, he said to his companion: “Do not follow at all until I call you.” The subdeacon, however, having thrown himself to the ground, watched from not far away to see what miracle the servant of God would perform. It was a public field in which he had stopped.

As the light drew near, the priest ran to meet it, and, humbling himself to the ground, said: “Bless me, I beg you, blessed bishop.” The one who had arrived replied: “You bless me, Trojanus, priest of God.” After they had exchanged a kiss and prayed, they spoke together for a very long time. The astonished subdeacon watched and saw the light that had appeared return by the same route along which it had come.

Calling the subdeacon to him, Trojanus said: “Come now, so that we may complete the journey we have begun to visit the holy places.” Trembling, the subdeacon replied: “I beg you, lord, do not despise my humility, but tell me what you have seen. I perceived that something divine had occurred.” He answered: “I shall tell you, but you must tell no one. For know that on whatever day you make this public, you will depart from this world.”

“I saw Saint Martin of Tours,” he continued, “and he himself spoke with me. Therefore beware of daring to divulge the mysteries of God to anyone.”

The priest, having completed the course of this life, died. The subdeacon, however, having reached an advanced age and being distressed that the virtue of Saint Trojanus remained concealed, summoned the bishop, clergy, citizens, and certain elders. He disclosed in order everything that he had heard from the Saint and how he had seen the mystery of the light—something that most clearly revealed the faith of Trojanus and the glory of Martin [Col. 0871B]. He concealed nothing, adding:

“And so that you may prove that what I am saying is true, I shall end my speech by ending my life.”

With these words he closed his eyes and died, to the astonishment of those present [Note: [Col. 0871D] John the Deacon relates a similar event in Book IV, chapter 69, of the *Life of Saint Gregory the Great*. When the deacon Peter saw that envious men wished to obscure the memory of the holy bishop, and that, at their instigation, some of the bishop’s books had already been burned while the remainder were soon to suffer the same fate, he publicly testified in church that he had often seen the Holy Spirit, in the form of a dove, sitting upon the head of the blessed man while he wrote his books. To prove that this was true, he said that he would immediately breathe out his soul as testimony to the matter; and this actually happened. For scarcely had he finished speaking when he died without any pain on the very ambo.]

As we have said, the blessed bishop Trojanus possessed great virtue and was honored among all the citizens of his city.

It is said that, while he was still in the body, whenever he had put on a new *amphibalus* [Note: [Col. 0872D] An *amphibalus*, or *birrus*, was a shaggy garment with a hood sewn onto it. See Du Cange’s *Glossary*. Saint Martin, indeed, gave his tunic to a poor man while retaining his *amphibalus*, that is, his outer garment, in Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* 1.], as was customary, and went out to travel through the diocese, people of various kinds would tear pieces from the fringe of this garment, everyone considering whatever he could snatch from him to be beneficial.

Buried in the earth, he demonstrates through many miracles that he lives in heaven. For the possessed, those suffering from chills, and other sick people commonly depart from his tomb after obtaining health through their prayers.

## CHAPTER LX. On the tomb divinely moved in the same city [Col. 0871C]

[942] Not far from the church of this confessor there was a small oratory [Note: [Col. 0872D] This chapter is absent from Clar. a.]. In the corner from which the arch rose stood a large sarcophagus, in which, it was said, two people—a bridegroom and a bride—had been buried [Note: [Col. 0872D] There is no memory of them among the people of Saintes, and the location of the oratory is likewise unknown, as is that of the church of Saint Trojanus, of which no trace remains.]. They had departed from the world after baptism, dressed in white garments. Antiquity also maintained that they belonged to the family of Saint Hilary of Poitiers.

This tomb, situated in such a place, not only obstructed the passage of those entering, but also prevented the repair of the wall beside it, which had been soaked by dripping water. For this reason Palladius, bishop of the city and a descendant of the formerly wealthy Palladius, made every effort to remove it from the place (Annals 580). More than three hundred men joined together, trying to pull it with ropes and push it with levers, after stones had already been laid on which the sarcophagus was to be placed.

At last the entire strength of the men pulling was expended, but they could not move the tomb. Everyone’s brow was drenched with sweat, but the difficult task was not completed. Voices were raised by those encouraging the work and saying: “Come on, pull the rope!” Yet the tomb did not move at all.

What more need be said? Everyone grew weary from the labor, and, as night intervened, they all asked to rest. But as soon as the darkness of night had passed and a new morning dawned, the priest, troubled in thought, asked his men to return to the oratory. He went ahead of them all and found the sarcophagus standing firmly upon the very stones he had arranged.

Amazed, he glorified the Lord, who by his powerful might had accomplished what human hands could not. Yet the names of these two people have been revealed to no one.

## CHAPTER LXI. On Saint Nicetius, bishop of Lyon [Col. 0872B]

[943] Nicetius, also a confessor in the city of Lyon, a man of complete holiness, most chaste conduct, and outstanding charity, completed his life (Annals 573, 2 April). His almsgiving and acts of kindness [Ed.: *humility*] cannot be sufficiently investigated or recounted by us.

After he had sent his blessed spirit ahead to heaven, he was placed in a bier and carried to the basilica in which he was buried. And behold, a little boy afflicted by long-standing blindness followed with the others, weeping and supported by someone’s assistance.

As he proceeded, a voice reached his ear, speaking secretly: “Draw near to the bier, and when you have entered beneath it, you will immediately receive your sight.”

He asked the man who was dragging him who it was that was conveying these words to his ears. The man denied seeing anyone speaking to him. When the voice had struck his ears a second and a third time, the boy understood that something extraordinary was about to happen and asked to be led to the bier.

Approaching it, he slipped through the crowd of white-robed deacons and entered where he had been commanded. As soon as he began to invoke the Saint’s name, his eyes opened and he immediately recovered the light of sight.

Afterward the boy remained constantly in the basilica, serving at the Saint’s tomb and lighting lamps. But certain leading citizens oppressed and harassed him, so that he could not obtain even the food necessary for life. When he repeatedly implored the blessed man at his tomb, the Saint appeared to him in a vision and said:

“Go to King Guntram and carefully tell him what you are suffering. He will provide you with clothing and food and will rescue you from the hands of your enemies.”

Strengthened by this admonition, the boy approached the king and obtained what the Saint had instructed him to seek [Col. 0873A].

Even now many miracles are attributed to the tomb of the blessed Confessor, through Christ’s favor. There the chains of the unfortunate are broken, the blind are given sight, demons are driven away, paralytics are restored to health, and those suffering the attacks of fevers are released. Miracles are displayed there so frequently that it would take too long to record them all in order.

Nevertheless, a faithful man reported to me that four blind people had been given sight there only a few days earlier, and that he had recently seen in good health a man whom he had formerly known as lame.

## CHAPTER LXII. On the tomb of Helius, bishop of the same city

Once, while I was walking to meet the aforementioned bishop and making the rounds of the holy places of the town of Lyon [Col. 0873B], the man who was leading us invited us to pray at the crypt of the blessed Helius [Note: [Col. 0873D] Laud. and Clar. a have *Heliae*. Colb. has *Elii*, and below *Helias*. In the commonly circulated catalogues he occupies a place before Faustinus, whom Saint Cyprian praises in Letter 67, or 68 in the new edition, written in 254 to Pope Stephen against Marcianus of Arles, who had joined himself to Novatian. Severus, in his *Chronology of the Bishops of Lyon*, conflates Helius and Faustinus.], saying that a great priest rested in that place (Annals 248).

After I had prayed and was admiring the Saint’s tomb, silently considering whether I might learn something about his merits, I saw written at the entrance how a violator of the tomb had stripped the dead body.

When I asked about the matter, wondering whether the things depicted at the entrance were true, the man related the following to me:

“Saint Helius was bishop in this city during the time of the pagans. When he died, the faithful buried him. On the following night a certain pagan came, rolled away the stone that covered the sarcophagus, and, having raised the body upright before him, tried to strip the Saint.

“But the Saint, extending his arms, firmly embraced the man and held the wretched one in his arms until morning, as the people watched [Col. 0873C] [Note: [Col. 0873D] Most editions have *exspectantibus*, “while they awaited”; the present reading is *spectantibus*, “while they watched.” John Moschus relates a similar miracle in *The Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 78: a thief who had stripped a dead virgin was not released until he promised to embrace monastic life. In chapter 77 of the same work, another violator of a tomb was struck with blindness. See also Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, Book III, chapter 22.], as though he had been bound fast with straps.”

The local judge then ordered the violator of the tomb to be dragged away and condemned according to the sentence of the legal penalty [Note: [Col. 0873D] Colb. a and Clar. b have *legalis*, “legal.” Civil laws commonly declare violators of tombs liable to capital punishment. See numerous examples of this matter in the *Theodosian Code*.]. But the Saint did not release him.

Then, understanding the will of the deceased, the judge made a promise concerning the man’s life. The Saint released him, and he was restored unharmed.

O truly holy vengeance mingled with mercy! He retained the man in order to rebuke him, but did not permit him to be handed over to punishment—he whom he had already made repentant.

## CHAPTER LXIII. On the daughter of the emperor Leo

The daughter of the Roman emperor Leo [Note: [Col. 0874D] Among the emperors who ruled at Rome, none was called Leo. It is impossible to determine whether this was the Leo who ruled Constantinople after the middle of the fifth century or someone else.] was being tormented by an unclean spirit and was being led around to the holy places. The wicked spirit continually shouted:

“I shall not go out from here unless the archdeacon of Lyon comes; and unless he himself drives me out of this little vessel that I have acquired, I shall in no way depart from here.”

When the emperor heard this, he sent his men into Gaul. When they found the archdeacon, they earnestly entreated him to consent to go with them to Rome to visit the girl.
