He refused, protesting loudly that he was unworthy to be the instrument through whom Christ should display miracles. But, instructed by the advice of his bishop, he set out with the envoys [Note: [Col. 0874D] Colb. a has *missis dirigit*; Clar. and Colb. tut. have *dirigitur*.] and, when he came to the emperor, was received with honor.

When he heard of the girl’s illness, he went to the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter. There, after completing a three-day fast accompanied by vigils and prayers, on the fourth day, through the invocation of our Lord Jesus Christ and the standard of the cross, he drove the unclean spirit from the girl’s body.

After she was healed, the emperor offered him three hundred pounds of gold. But that man, whose spirit was set on higher things, rejected perishable riches as worthless, saying:

“If you wish to enrich me with your gifts, give what will benefit the entire city. Forgo, I say, the tax levied from the people at the third milestone around the walls; this will be a beneficial gift to both souls. I have no need of your gold. Distribute it to the poor for the welfare of yourself and your people.”

The emperor did not refuse. He distributed the gold to the poor and granted the city the requested exemption from the tax. Consequently, to this day taxes are not publicly collected at the third milestone around the walls of that city.

After the blessed archdeacon’s departure, the emperor said to his men:

“If this man loves God more than money, then the church served by such a minister deserves to be adorned with our gifts.”

He then ordered a chest for enclosing the holy Gospels, together with a paten and chalice, to be made of pure gold and precious stones. When the work had been completed with remarkable craftsmanship, he sent it to the church through a trusted man [Col. 0874C].

But the messenger, while crossing the Alps and carrying these objects, turned aside to the house of a certain goldsmith. When the craftsman asked him what business he was conducting, the messenger disclosed the matter secretly and straightforwardly.

“If you will agree to follow my advice,” said the goldsmith, “this arrangement can bring us considerable profit.”

The messenger was seduced by the devil’s prompting. As the common saying among country people goes, minds are often joined together by a craving for gold and by the deceitful schemes that serve it; so the messenger immediately consented to this plan.

The deceiver then made similar objects out of silver, so that they would appear to be nothing other than the purest gold. He most carefully fastened with nails the work that had been superimposed with gems and gold threads [Col. 0874D].

Nevertheless, he did not break up the chalice, because its *cataclyza* had been solidly affixed to it [Note: [Col. 0874D] Clar. b has *Cataclipha*. The passage should be understood in this way: the precious stones had been set solidly into the vessel. Likewise, garments made *ex cataclysis*, or rather *cataclistis*, were so called because gems and stones had been woven into them, or because they had been adorned with embroidery. See Du Cange’s *Glossary*.].

At last the carrier arrived at Lyon with this fraud. After presenting the gifts, he received a gift from the bishop in return. When he returned to his associate, he demanded that he be given the gold represented in the objects.

The craftsman declared that the work was not yet entirely finished, but promised to complete it during that very night.

After supper, while the two were sitting together in the room where the work was being done, the room was suddenly shaken by an earthquake and collapsed upon them. The ground split beneath their feet and swallowed both men, together with the money. They descended alive and crying out into Tartarus. God had swiftly avenged the fraud perpetrated against his Church.

I myself have very often seen these objects in the church of Lyon. Let this be a warning to the people, so that no one may attempt either to covet or to defraud the property of the Church. Otherwise, he will see God’s judgment swiftly threatening him [Col. 0875B].

## CHAPTER LXIV. On the woman who collected the shoe of the martyr Epipodius

[947] In the suburb outside the walls of that city there rests a woman (Annals 178) who is said to have collected the shoe of the blessed martyr Epipodius [Note: [Col. 0875C] Gregory treated Epipodius in *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, Book I, chapter 50. We have given his Acts among the authentic acts of the martyrs under approximately the year 178. In them the woman mentioned here [Col. 0875D] is called Lucia.]. It had fallen from his foot as he was being led to martyrdom.

At her tomb those suffering from chills and other illnesses are frequently healed. They scrape up dust from the tomb itself, swallow it, and depart unharmed.

## CHAPTER LXV. On another woman, to whom her husband appeared because of an offering

They say that there were two people in this city, a man and his wife, distinguished by senatorial lineage. They died without children and left the Church as their heir. The husband died first and was buried in the basilica of Saint Mary.

The woman, however, lived for an entire year at this church, devoting herself constantly to prayer, celebrating the solemn rites of the Mass every day and offering a gift in memory of her husband. She did not doubt the Lord’s mercy, believing that the dead man would receive rest on the day when she made an offering to the Lord for his soul. She always supplied a sextarius of Gaza wine as a sacrifice for the holy basilica [Note: [Col. 0875D] Observe the manner of expression by which a Mass is said to have been celebrated even by a woman. Also note this important passage as evidence for the offering of sacrifice to obtain rest for the deceased. Finally, this passage shows that not everyone who made offerings or attended sacrifices necessarily received the holy Eucharist at that Mass. Hence Mabillon rightly criticizes, in Book I, chapter 6, of the *Gallican Liturgy*, an observation by the Oxford editor in his treatise on Saint Cyprian’s *Lord’s Prayer*. The editor had claimed that the communion of a solitary priest was formerly unknown, on the basis of Saint Cyprian’s words: “When we assemble together with the brethren and celebrate the divine sacrifices with God’s priest,” and so forth. For even a layperson may be said to celebrate Mass if he merely attends it, as is clear from this and other passages of our Gregory.].

But a wicked subdeacon, keeping the Gaza wine for his own appetite [Note: [Col. 0875D] That is, “with the Gaza wine kept back.” See the notes on Book VII, chapter 29, of the *History*.], offered exceedingly strong vinegar in the chalice, since she did not always approach to receive communion.

When God decided to reveal this fraud, the husband appeared to the woman and said:

“Alas, alas, sweetest wife, into what [Note: [Col. 0876C] Colb. a and Clar. b read *inquit* (“he says”); Colb. tut. reads *in quo* (“into what”). In the edition and several manuscripts, *defluxit* stands absolutely.] has my labor in the world come, that I should now make an offering of vinegar?”

She replied: “Indeed, for I have not forgotten your love. I have always offered the strongest Gaza wine for your repose in the sanctuary of my God.”

She awoke, astonished at the vision, and, without consigning it to forgetfulness, rose at the customary hour for Matins. When these had been completed and the Masses celebrated, she approached the chalice of salvation. She drank vinegar so hot that she thought her teeth would be knocked out if she swallowed the draught too slowly.

She then rebuked the subdeacon, and the things that had been wickedly defrauded were corrected [Note: [Col. 0876C] Clar. a, together with the editions, reads *excuti, quae nequiter fuerat* (“to be knocked out, which had been wickedly …”), with the singular *fuerat*.].

I do not think, however, that this miracle occurred without the merit of a good work.

## CHAPTER LXVI. On Memmius, bishop of Châlons [Col. 0876D]

The city of Châlons also possesses as its particular patron the bishop Memmius [Note: [Col. 0876D] This chapter is absent from Clar. a. Frodoardus is the authority for the claim that Memmius was sent into Gaul by Saint Peter together with Saint Sixtus, the first bishop of Reims. An ancient author of his *Life*, said to have flourished in the seventh century, likewise attributes this mission to Saint Peter. Almamus, however, a monk of Hautvillers in the diocese of Reims who flourished in the ninth century, thought it sufficient to trace the mission back to Saint Clement. See Mabillon, *Analecta*, vol. II, pp. 86 ff.; the same place also discusses the discovery of his relics under Charles the Bald in 868. The abbey of Saint Memmius, commonly called Saint-Menge, still stands near the walls of Châlons. It was first inhabited by monks and later by regular canons.] who, while he still remained in mortal flesh, is said to have raised a dead man to life (second or third century, 5 August).

At his tomb we have often seen the broken chains and fetters of the unfortunate. We ourselves also experienced his power directly.

Once, while we were staying in that city, one of our boys was seized by a fever, tormented by vomiting, and so repelled by food and drink alike that he could not tolerate either. We were greatly distressed because the boy’s illness delayed our journey.

Without delay I approached the basilica of the Saint and prostrated myself at the tomb on behalf of the boy. Pouring out tears, I prayed that he who had often shown compassion to those suffering in bondage, breaking their fetters, would grant this feverish boy relief and the refreshment of healing [Col. 0876C].

Wonderful to relate: during that very night the sick boy was visited by the Saint’s power, and at daybreak rose healthy from his bed [949].

## CHAPTER LXVII. On Lupus, bishop of Troyes [Col. 0876D]

No one is unaware of Lupus, the bishop buried in the city of Troyes in Champagne (Annals 479, 29 July) [Note: [Col. 0876D] Lupus, formerly a monk of Lérins and later bishop of Troyes, crossed into Britain with Saint Germanus of Auxerre to combat the Pelagians, and took part there in the synod of Verulamium. He delivered his city, which Attila, king of the Huns, was threatening with destruction. Sidonius wrote him several letters, and more than once calls him “bishop of bishops,” “easily the foremost of the bishops of Gaul,” “a holy man,” and so forth. He praises him in Letter 1 of Book VI for having completed nine five-year periods in the apostolate. Surius gives his *Life* under 29 July. He was buried in the suburban church of Saint Mary, later called Saint Lupus because of the frequent miracles that occurred at his tomb. —As this church was destroyed by the Normans toward the end of the ninth century, a new one was soon built within the city under the name of the same Saint Lupus, and the blessed bishop’s relics were deposited there. A few clerics were appointed to the chapel of Saint Martin, which had survived from the first church; in 1104 they adopted the institute of regular canons, and in 1135 the canons of the new church of Saint Lupus in the city followed their example, since the monks there had by then died out. This was the origin of both abbeys of regular canons in the city of Troyes. See Camuzat’s *Promptuarium*. Moreover, the final year of the blessed Lupus is not clear.].

A certain slave of Maurus [Note: [Col. 0877D] The manuscripts and Bad. read *Mauri*; the other editions, *Maurus*.], having committed an offense, fled to his basilica. His master, raging, pursued him at once and entered the basilica. Without prostrating himself in prayer, he began to pour forth blasphemies against the Saint and to say:

“Here you are, Lupus! You will take away my slave, and because of you I shall not be allowed to exact the punishment he deserves?”

He seized the slave and began to drag him away, saying:

“Lupus will not put out his hand from the tomb today to rescue you from my hands.”

As the wretched man spoke, the tongue that had uttered blasphemies against the Saint was immediately bound by divine power. The man, now changed—or mute [variant]—began to rave throughout the entire church, bellowing like an animal and unable to produce human speech.

When this was reported to his people, they seized him and took him home. His wife placed many gifts in the basilica, but on the third day he died in great torment. After his death, the woman who had made the offering took it back; the slave, however, remained free.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. On Aventinus, his minister [Col. 0877D]

A certain religious man named Aventinus served this bishop (Annals 537, 4 February) [Note: [Col. 0877D] Camuzat published his *Life* in the *Troyes Promptuarium*, and the Bollandists under 4 February. There he is said to have flourished under Saint Camelianus, the successor of the blessed Lupus, who appointed him superintendent of the church’s stores. Aventinus later withdrew outside the city in order to devote himself more freely to his way of life. He then went to a place called Insula, because it was surrounded by the river Oza, and there served as abbot. At last, after substituting Saint Fidolus for himself, he withdrew around 534 into a solitude near Verrières, where he died in 537. —The location of the monastery of Insula is so uncertain that it was not well known even to Camuzat or to other learned men who investigated the places. Nevertheless, it was once famous, as is clear from the *Life of Saint Leo, abbot of Moutier-en-Der*, and Saint Melanius, bishop of Troyes, was buried there. The view seems preferable of those who think it was the small town about two leagues from the city still called Insula (*l’Ile*), where a priory of the monastery of Molesme can be seen today. As for the body of Saint Aventinus, the blessed Vincentius, then bishop of Troyes, deposited it in a suburban church he had built at the place where the holy man had lived for some time; Vincentius himself was later buried there. Today the church bears the title of the parish of Saint Aventinus and possesses his relics, although others maintain that they are preserved in the cathedral church. See Cointius under the years 486 and 537.].

After Aventinus’s death, captives took refuge with him, and he offered their price to their master. But the master bound himself by an oath and said:

“I shall never accept this except in my own village.”

The master gave his right hand as a pledge that, if the money were sent there, he would immediately release the captives from the bond of slavery.

The price was therefore sent. But the master, forgetting his pledge and pretending that he would not release the captives, became bound himself.

For immediately the tip of the finger of the hand that had given the pledge began to suffer severe pain. Then, as the pain gradually increased, it spread through the entire hand and arm. What more need be said? His arm was severed at the very joint of the elbow and fell away [the text reads *eum*, apparently corrupt], and he breathed out his spirit.

After this his wife wished to return the captives to servitude, but she was struck with pain in her head and followed her husband in death. Thus the captives remained permanently free, without the protection of any written document.

## CHAPTER LXIX. On Bishop Marcellinus [Col. 0878C]

The city of Embrun also has as its own patron the bishop Marcellinus [Note: [Col. 0878C] This chapter is absent from Colb. tut. The Bollandists published the Acts of Saint Marcellinus, after Mombritius, under 20 May. There he is said to have been consecrated bishop by Saint Eusebius of Vercelli and to have established the church of Embrun, which is the metropolitan church of the Maritime Alps. His companions were Domninus and Vincentius, who rest at Digne. Wandelbertus joins them together in his Martyrology, although they are celebrated on different days in other sources.], through whom, while he still dwelt in the body, Christ performed many miracles (fourth century, 20 April).

He is said to have made a baptismal font in which water is said to rise miraculously at the Nativity of the Lord and at the Lord’s Supper [Note: [Col. 0878C] The editions read *Domini et dominicae* (“of the Lord and of the Lord’s”). Pithoeus reads *Natale dominicae coenae* [Col. 0878D], that is, “at the solemnity of the Lord’s Supper.” The manuscript against which he collated his edition, however, like the others, has *Domini, dominicae*. I therefore suspect that Pithoeus corrected this solely by conjecture.]

Water is also carried from that spring to another bath in which the ancient custom of baptism had been established. It is not, however, increased in volume, as we related above concerning the springs of Spain (Chapter 24, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*).

At this holy man’s tomb a lamp constantly provides light. Once lit, it continues for many nights without any addition, and it often happens that, after being extinguished by the wind, it is lit again by divine power. From this oil the sick frequently receive remedies.

## CHAPTER LXX. On Marcellus, bishop of Die

There was also Marcellus, bishop of the city of Die [Note: [Col. 0878D] Colb. 2, Clar. a, and Bad. have *Dien­sis*. Both readings are sound. The city is today called Die, in the Dauphiné, under the metropolitan see of Vienne. Its see was long united with that of Valence, but a few years ago they were separated, and each city was given its own bishop. Marcellus flourished around the beginning of the sixth century. His basilica, together with the monastery attached to it, stood outside the city and was destroyed by Calvinist heretics in the last century. The monks were then transferred into the city, where they still remain. Saint Ulfinus, who governed the church of Die at the beginning of the eighth century, is said to have written the *Life of Saint Marcellus* in prose. He is mentioned in the Roman Martyrology and by the Bollandists under 9 April.], a bishop of magnificent holiness [Col. 0879A]. Nevertheless, at his tomb a lit lamp customarily shines for a long period; from its oil the power of the Lord provides medicine for the sick (Annals 500, 9 April).

## CHAPTER LXXI. On Metria, confessor of Aix-en-Provence
From Aquae (commonly Aix), there was also granted the celebrated athlete Metrias [Note: [Col. 0879C] Others have Mitrias; Clar. b has Menas, and below Metrii.], a man in the flesh and, according to the account of his deeds (13 November), of magnificent holiness. Although a slave by status, he was nevertheless free in righteousness. As those who read the account of his contest relate, after completing the course of good works he departed from the world victorious, often demonstrating by manifest miracles that he dwelt in heaven.

At a certain time, when Franco governed the church of this town as bishop (A.D. 566), Childeric, who then held first place with King Sigibert, occupied his estate [Note: [Col. 0879D] *Competere* means to seize another’s property. Hence Gregory, book IV, final chapter, calls one who invaded alien possessions an *alienarum rerum competitor*.], saying that it was being unjustly retained by the church of Aquae. The bishop was summoned immediately, and, having furnished sureties, appeared before the king, crying out and imploring that the king turn his presence away from hearing this case [Note: [Col. 0879D] Colb. *tut.* and several editions read: “turn his presence away from hearing …”; Bal. reads “turn his attention away.”], lest he be condemned by heavenly judgment. He added:

“For I know the power of the blessed man Metrias, and that he swiftly inflicts vengeance upon the one who has seized his property.”

At last the assembled hearers [Note: [Col. 0879D] Thus Colb. 2 and Clar. b; the others read *adjutores*, “supporters.”] examined the case. Childeric rose up and, reproaching the bishop as laden with crimes [Note: [Col. 0879D] Colb. a and Clar. a read “aggravated by crimes”; Bell. reads “aggravated by crimes as well.”], alleging that he unjustly retained property owed to the royal treasury, ordered him to be dragged by force from the court; and, after he had been seized, he condemned him to pay three hundred gold pieces, the estate having been taken from him by legal judgment. Everyone favored the king, and no one dared decide anything against his will, except according to what pleased him.

At last the condemned and dispossessed priest returned to the city. Prostrate in prayer before the Saint’s tomb, after uttering the opening verse of a psalm, he said:

“Here no lamp shall be lit, nor shall the melody of psalms be sung, most glorious Saint, unless you first avenge your servants upon their enemies and restore to the holy Church the things violently taken from you.” [Note: [Col. 0879D] Saint Eligius did the same, according to his *Life* by Saint Audoenus, book I, chapter 30. Evodius mentions candles lit before the relics of Saint Stephen in the books *On the Miracles of Saint Stephen* found in Augustine.]

Having spoken these words with tears, he threw thorn branches with sharp spines upon the tomb; and, after leaving and closing the doors, he placed others similarly at the entrance. Immediately the usurper was seized by a fever. He took to his bed, loathed food, detested drink, and continually uttered a burning sigh. [Col. 0880A] Even if thirst sometimes came upon him from the heat of the fever, he drank only water and nothing else.

Why say more? During this illness he passed an entire year, yet his evil mind was not bent. Meanwhile all his hair fell out, together with his beard, and his entire head remained so bald that one might have thought him formerly buried and recently cast out of a tomb after the funeral.

Afflicted by these and similar miseries, the wretched man at last reflected, saying:

“I have sinned, because I stripped the Church of God and inflicted injury upon a holy bishop. Now go immediately, restore the estate, and place six hundred gold pieces upon the Saint’s tomb; for I hope that the restored property will grant healing to the sick man.”

When his men heard this, they took the money and did as they had been ordered. They restored the field and placed the solidi upon the tomb of the servant of God. But when they had done this, the man immediately breathed his last where he was; and by obtaining his unjust gain he secured the loss of his soul.

The bishop, however, obtained the vengeance upon the enemy of the Church which he had promised would come through the power of God’s Athlete.

## CHAPTER LXXII. On Saint Arvatius, Bishop of Tongeren-Maastricht

Arvatius [Note: [Col. 0879D] This is the reading of the manuscripts and editions that I have seen, except for Clar. a, which has Servatius. The Codex of Saint Lawrence of Liège agrees with that reading; it was presented to this church at its dedication by Reginard, bishop of Liège, in A.D. 1034, as Henschenius observes in his *Exegesis on the Bishopric of Tongeren-Maastricht*, where he argues at length that the name Servatius should be retained. Yet the Codex of Saint-Denis, written in the eighth century and formerly in his possession, gives Aravatius, as the distinguished Daniel Papebrochius informed me. So too does the Codex of Fleury in its table of chapters: “On Aravatius, Bishop of the Tongeren people.” See what we observed concerning this at chapter 5 of book II of the *History* and at chapter 1 of Fredegar’s *Epitome*. Valesius further observes that on this first occasion the bishop of Tongeren was called “of Tongeren-Maastricht”; nevertheless Bad. and Clar. a, in another hand, read “of Tongeren.”] was bishop of Tongeren-Maastricht during the time of the Huns, when they were bursting into Gaul to ravage it (A.D. 450, 13 May). He is also reported to have been buried beside the very bridge of the public embankment [Note: [Col. 0880D] That “public embankment” designates a public or military road paved with stone or flint is demonstrated by Alterserra in chapter 5 of book II of the *History*, from books 4 and 5 of the Theodosian Code. Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogue* 2, chapter 4, says: “Along the public embankment a fiscal wagon came, filled with military men.” *Agger* also denotes a kind of dike placed along public roads or rivers to contain the banks. For Servius it is the middle portion of a road, slightly raised and paved with stone. Hence military roads were called *stratae*, “paved roads.”]

Although snow melted around his tomb, it never moistened the marble placed above it. Even when those regions are bound by the frost of extreme cold and snow covers the earth to a thickness of three or four feet, it does not touch the mound at all. For this gives it to be understood that he was a true Israelite. For them [Note: *Perhaps: for those.*] the waters among the walls of the waters are not for destruction but for salvation; and the snow falling around this righteous man’s tomb is not a sign of moisture but of honor. You may see snowy mountains rising all around, yet not touching the boundary of the monument. We do not marvel that the earth is covered with snow; we marvel that it has not dared to touch the place of the blessed man’s tomb.

Often the devotion and zeal of the faithful built a small oratory from smoothed wooden boards; but immediately these were either carried away by the wind or collapsed of their own accord. [Col. 0881A] I believe that these things happened until one should come who would build a worthy structure in honor of the glorious Bishop.

As time passed, the bishop Monulfus [Note: [Col. 0881D] He held the see between Saints Domitian and Gundulf, concerning whom Herigerus, Aegidius of the Vale of Gold, and others provide further information. See Henschenius in the preliminary material to volume VII of the Bollandists for May, and Cointius under the year 550.] arrived in this city (A.D. 550) and built, arranged, and adorned a great church in his honor. The body was transferred there with great devotion and reverence, and now displays many miracles.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. On the Cemetery of the City of Augustodunum

The cemetery near the city of Augustodunum was called in the Gallic language [Note: [Col. 0881D] The word is nevertheless derived from the Greek *koimētērion* (κοιμητήριον), meaning approximately “dormitory.” The manuscripts have *cimiterium*. Even today, not far from the city of the Aedui, a cemetery is visited where a great number of stone tombs remain, together with a church—or rather the walls, without a roof, of the church of Saint Stephen. Peter Ladoneus writes that the tombs of the saints Rheticius, Cassianus, Simplicius, and other bishops of Augustodunum stand there. See the notes on the following chapters.] because the corpses of many people had been buried there. Among them, that there are tombs of certain faithful souls worthy of God is shown by the frequent mystery of hidden psalmody: for they often appear to many, giving due thanks to almighty God in the proclamation of their voices.

I heard that two inhabitants of the place, while preparing to go around the holy sites for the sake of prayer, heard in the basilica of Saint Stephen, which adjoins this cemetery, the sound of psalmody. Admiring the sweetness of the melody, they approached the door of the church, supposing that certain religious people were keeping a vigil. Entering, and devoting themselves to prayer for a very long time, they rose and saw a choir singing psalms; yet nothing shone through the church except that, by its own radiance, everything appeared bright. They recognized none of the persons.

Finally, while they were astonished and struck with wonder, one of the singers approached them and said:

“You have done an accursed thing by presuming to be present while we render to God the mysteries of prayer. Depart, therefore, and withdraw from our dwellings [Note: [Col. 0881D] Thus Colb. *tut.*; but Colb. a and Clar. a have “from your dwellings.” The other manuscripts and editions read “to your dwellings.”], or you will depart from this world.”

One of the two departed and went away; but the other, who remained in that place, departed from this world a few days later.

## CHAPTER LXXIV. On the Tomb of Bishop Cassianus

In this cemetery I saw the tomb of the blessed priest Cassianus, a great man, worn away by many sick people. At that time it was thought to have been almost pierced through (fourth century, 5 August). For the sick are washed with dust from it, and immediately perceive the greatness of its power.

There also, they say, is buried Simplicius (see chapter 76), bishop of that city, against whom the savage madness of the people brought the charge of adultery. [Note: [Col. 0881D] Saint Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, also saw it. When Saint Cassianus revealed his glory to him, the blessed Bishop commended himself and his people to Cassianus’s prayers, as Constantius recounts in book II, chapter 6, of his *Life*. Even today the tomb of Saint Cassianus is kept in this cemetery, in an oratory dedicated to his name. There is no memorial there, however, of Saint Simplicius; perhaps his tomb has been mixed together with the others.]

## CHAPTER LXXV. On Bishop Rheticius

Since it is useful to say something about these matters, we must first speak of Saint Rheticius [Note: [Col. 0882D] Colb. *tut.* has Aricius, and below Aricius. Rheticius is well known in ecclesiastical history: Constantine the Great appointed him judge in the case of the Donatists. He subscribed to the First Council of Arles in A.D. 314. Jerome, Augustine, Optatus, and others frequently praise him and his works.], because he died first.

He was born to very noble parents and was distinguished for his sharpness of intellect and learning (A.D. 314, 19 July). After passing through adolescence, he married a woman equally renowned for the propriety of her conduct. They were joined not by lust but by the fellowship of spiritual love. Almsgiving flourished among them, vigils were celebrated, and the work of God was continually practiced by them.

After a long time, the woman inclined her head toward her bed and spoke her final words into the ears of the blessed man:

“I beg you, most devout brother, that after my departure, when the appointed span of life has passed, you be placed in the tomb where I am laid, so that those whom the love of a single chastity preserved in one marriage bed may be united in the fellowship of one tomb.”

Having spoken these words, she breathed out her spirit amid tears, to heaven.

When the people of Augustodunum chose Rheticius as bishop, he accepted the episcopate. [Col. 0882B] He displayed such religious devotion that the goodness of his character equaled the grace of his pontificate, and he reached the day of his death in the fullness and perfection of spiritual graces.

After his body had been washed and placed upon the bier, the attendants could not move it. Then, fixed in astonishment of mind, they heard from an old man that the husband had bound the woman by oath to receive them within the spaciousness of a single tomb. [Col. 0882C] When the old man had finished speaking, the bier was immediately lifted. Once it had been brought near the tomb, the priest recovered his spirit.

He addressed his companion, saying:

“Remember, dearest wife, what you had asked for us. Now receive the brother whom you have long awaited, and join yourself to these undefiled limbs, which lust did not stain but true chastity cleansed.”

As he spoke, the tomb was moved in a wondrous manner, and the virgin’s bones were gathered together in one place. The blessed priest, received into the sleep of peace, was covered by the covering of this tomb. [Note: [Col. 0882D] Near the cemetery mentioned in the preceding chapters stands the parish church of Saint Peter of the Road, called *de l’Etrier*. There the tomb of the blessed Bishop may be seen, hollowed out beneath a small arch in the church wall, with this recent inscription: “Saint Rheticius, Bishop of the Aedui, 314.”]

Cassianus, whom we mentioned above, succeeded him. After him, Egemonius assumed the episcopal chair. [Note: [Col. 0882D] In ancient manuscript codices we possess a *Life of Saint Cassianus*, written both in prose and in metrical form, in which Rheticius is said to have been succeeded by Egemonius, and Egemonius by Simplicius. Cassianus was born in Egypt and became bishop of Orta there during the reign of the emperor Jovian. After leaving his see, he came to Gaul, where he was received by Simplicius, bishop of the Aedui, and succeeded him. He died toward the end of the fourth century. Therefore Gregory seems to require correction here, since he places Cassianus before Egemonius and Simplicius. Indeed, Simplicius is listed among the bishops who are said to have attended the Council of Cologne in A.D. 346 against Euphratas, bishop of that city; consequently he was already seated before Cassianus’s arrival, since Cassianus became bishop during the time of Jovian, that is, in A.D. 363. If anyone should nevertheless prefer to emend the *Life of Cassianus* in accordance with Gregory, I will not oppose him.]

## CHAPTER LXXVI. [Col. 0883A] On Bishop Simplicius

When Egemonius died, blessed Simplicius was placed over that same church. [Note: [Col. 0883D] Constantius calls him a man of supreme simplicity and charity in the *Life of Saint Germanus of Auxerre*, book I, chapter 3.] (A.D. 364, 24 June).

He was of noble lineage, very rich in the resources of this world, and joined to a wife of the highest nobility. Their life was most chaste, hidden from the world and known only to God, though unknown to mortals. Both were righteous and extremely prompt in sowing the seeds of almsgiving and enduring vigils.

Meanwhile, because of that worldly dignity, as we have said, Simplicius was chosen by the people when Egemonius died, but was appointed by God for the glory of chastity and holiness.

After he had received the rank of bishop, his blessed sister—who had previously been joined to her husband not by lust but by chastity—did not consent to be removed from the bishop’s bed. Rather, in the same purity of chastity with which she had formerly approached the bed of her most chaste husband, secure in the conscience of her holy mind, she knew that she could not be burned by the heat of the kindling fire.

But the cruel envy of the devil stirred shameful wars against the saints of God; what it could not destroy by its own prompting, it tried to defame by deceitful words.

Why say more? On the day of the Lord’s Nativity, the citizens were stirred to scandal and rushed swiftly to the blessed Virgin, saying:

“It is unbelievable that a woman joined to a man cannot be defiled; nor will a man joined to a woman’s limbs be able to abstain from intercourse. Thus Solomon’s proverbs say: ‘No one who touches pitch can remain clean’ (Sirach 13:1). Surely anyone carrying fire in his bosom will be burned. We see you reclining together on one bed, and we can suspect nothing else except that you mingle with one another.”

The most holy Virgin, moved by these words, approached the Bishop, who likewise shone with chastity. She repeated before the entire people the words she had heard, and summoned a young girl who was then, as is customary during the hardship of winter, holding a small brazier filled with coals. [Note: [Col. 0884D] Thus Colb. 2 and Bell. The editions read: “having heard, she calls the girl, who was then holding a small brazier …”]

Spreading out her cloak, she received the burning coals and held them for nearly an hour. Then she summoned the priest, saying:

“Receive a fire gentler than usual, which will in no way harm your garments, so that these flames may show that the flames of lust have been extinguished in us.”

When the Bishop received them, the fire did no harm whatsoever to his garment.

By this miracle the people, who had previously been unbelieving, believed in God; and within seven days more than a thousand people were reborn through the renewal of the sacred washing. The Church received them and joyfully joined them to the heavenly kingdom as its soldiers.

## CHAPTER LXXVII. On the Image of Berecynthia

They also report that there was in this city an image of Berecynthia, as the account of the passion of the holy martyr Symphorianus makes clear. [Note: [Col. 0884D] We included this among the genuine acts of the martyrs, under approximately A.D. 180, where this passage is cited in section 2. Sulpicius Severus observes in the *Life of Saint Martin* that it was the custom of the ancient Gauls to carry images of the gods through the fields. Examples of this practice also occur frequently in the Roman historians.]

They were carrying it in a cart, according to the wretched pagan custom, for the protection of their fields and vineyards. The aforementioned Bishop Simplicius happened to be there, watching from some distance as they sang and danced before the image. [Note: [Col. 0884D] Thus Clar. a, SB, and Pith. Bell. and Colb. 2 have “singing psalms”; the edition has “singing.”]

He uttered a groan to God over the people’s folly and said:

“Enlighten, I beg you, Lord, the eyes of this people, so that it may recognize that the image of Berecynthia is nothing.”

He then made the sign of the cross against it, and immediately the image fell to the ground. The animals fixed to the earth that were pulling the wagon on which it was being carried could not move.

The countless crowd was struck with amazement, and the entire company cried out that the goddess had been injured. Victims were sacrificed; the animals were beaten, but they could not be moved.

Then four hundred men from that foolish multitude joined together and said to one another:

“If there is any power in the deity, let her rise of her own accord and command the oxen fixed to the earth to move forward. Certainly, if she cannot move, it is clear that there is no divinity in her.”

They then approached and sacrificed one of the animals. When they saw that their goddess could in no way be moved, they abandoned their pagan error, sought out the bishop of the place, and, converted to the unity of the Church, came to know the greatness of the true God and were consecrated in holy baptism.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. On the Bishop upon Whose Breast a Lamb Appeared

Since in the preceding chapter we explained how chastity adorns those who love God, I remember what I heard Felix [Note: [Col. 0884D] Gregory frequently discusses Felix, bishop of Nantes, in his *History*. See book V, chapter 5.] of Nantes relate while we were discussing these matters.

He said that there had been a bishop in his city who lived with his wife. But when he attained the honor of the priesthood, he separated his bed in accordance with the rule established by the Catholic Church. [Note: [Col. 0884D] This had been established by several canons. See book I of the *History*, chapter 39, and Gregory the Great, *Dialogues* IV, chapter 20. From this arose the terms *episcopa*, “female bishop’s companion,” *presbytera*, and *diacona*.]

The woman found this very distressing. Each day she urged him to rest in one bed with her, but the Bishop refused to comply with such an improper request, which the decrees of the canons did not permit.

One day, inflamed with anger, she said within herself:

“I do not think my husband is without some hidden motive for rejecting me from his embrace in this way. I will go and see whether perhaps another woman is sleeping with him, for whose love he despises me.”

Immediately she entered the Bishop’s bedroom and found him sleeping in the afternoon. Approaching his bed, she saw a lamb of immense brightness resting upon his breast.

Then, terrified by fear, she quickly withdrew from the holy man’s bed and never again attempted to discover what the man full of God did in secret. She recognized most clearly that what the Lord himself graciously promised to his faithful was fulfilled in the servants of God:

“Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20). [Note: [Col. 0885C] Others, together with the editions, read: “For behold, I am with you,” and so forth.]

## CHAPTER LXXIX. [Col. 0885B] On Remigius, Bishop of the People of Rheims

Remigius, bishop of the city of Rheims [Note: [Col. 0885C] Frodoardus inserted almost this entire chapter into his *History*, book I, chapters 19 and 20. Gregory says more about Saint Remigius in the *History*, especially book II, chapter 31. Hincmarus, his ninth-century successor in that see, wrote his *Life*, which may be found in Surius. He died on the Ides of January, though most martyrologies commemorate him on 1 October. Saint Leo IX, supreme pontiff, decreed that his feast be celebrated under the title “Apostle of the Franks”; the Gallican clergy renewed that decree in a general assembly in 1657.] (A.D. 533, 13 January), is said to have completed seventy years or more in the episcopate. By his prayer he obtained the resurrection of a dead girl’s body; he often bestowed the grace of healing upon the sick and very frequently became an avenger against those who seized property.

Not far from the basilica [Note: [Col. 0885D] The Basilica of Remigius still exists, though for several centuries it has been enclosed within the city walls. It has been granted the title and privileges of an archmonastery because the blessed Bishop’s body is preserved there incorrupt in a magnificent mausoleum. Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur inhabit it.] there was a field of fertile soil. The inhabitants call such fields *olcae* [Note: [Col. 0885D] Commonly *une ousche* or *osche*, a particular portion of land. See Du Cange’s *Glossary*.], and this field had been given to the holy basilica.

One of the citizens seized it, despising the man who had donated it to the holy place. Although the Bishop and the abbot of the place repeatedly summoned him to restore what he had unjustly seized, he paid little attention to their words and defended what he had taken with stubborn determination.

At last an occasion, rather than devotion, brought him to the city of Rheims. He hurried to the Saint’s basilica. The abbot again rebuked him for the seizure of the field, but he gave no reasonable response.

When his business was finished, he mounted his horse and prepared to return home. But the injury done to the priest obstructed his attempt. Struck by a stroke [Note: [Col. 0885D] That is, seized by apoplexy; see book V of the *History*, chapter 5.], he fell to the ground. His tongue, which had spoken of taking the field, was bound; his eyes, which had coveted it, were closed; his hands, which had grasped it, were contracted. [Col. 0886A]

Then, stammering and scarcely able to make his speech understood, he said:

“Carry me to the Saint’s basilica, and throw upon his tomb whatever gold is upon me. For I have sinned by taking away his property.”

When the man who had given the field saw him coming with gifts, he said:

“Do not accept, I beg you, Saint of God, his gifts, which you have never been accustomed to accept. Do not, I implore you, become the helper of one who, inflamed by desire, has become the wicked possessor of your property.”

The Saint did not delay in hearing the voice of his poor man. For although that person had given gifts, when he returned home he breathed out his spirit [Note: [Col. 0885D] Clar. a, Colb. *tut.*, and Frodoardus read “lost his spirit.”], and the Church recovered its property.

Nor should we omit what happened at the time when bubonic plague was devastating the people of First Germany [Note: [Col. 0885D] This was the name they gave to the province subject to the metropolitan of Mainz.] (A.D. 546).

When everyone was terrified by news of this disaster, the people of Rheims rushed to the Saint’s tomb and demanded an appropriate remedy for the affliction. After lighting many candles and lamps, they kept vigil throughout the night with heavenly hymns and psalms.

When morning came, they considered what might still be lacking in their prayer. For God revealed to them how, after the preceding prayer, they might fortify the city’s defenses with an even greater rampart. [Note: [Col. 0885D] The Remigian Codex adds: “He who wished his saint to be glorified among human beings, whom he had glorified with himself.”]

They therefore took the pallium [Note: [Col. 0886C] Not only does that pallium still survive, reverently preserved in the Basilica of Remigius and commonly called Saint Remigius’s shroud, but the pious custom also continues of arranging it in the form of a bier and carrying it through the city streets whenever some necessity arises. Several ancient monuments prove that this custom was not interrupted from the age of our Gregory. Among them is a manuscript codex given by Hincmarus to the library of Remigius, in which such a procession is represented in an image. Another description of the same rite appears in ancient tapestries depicting a similar procession.]

from the Blessed man’s tomb and arranged it in the form of a bier. They lit candles upon crosses and upon candlesticks [Note: [Col. 0886D] Bell. reads “upon the cross … and upon the candle-bearers”; Rem. reads “and above the candle-bearers.” From this passage Menardus, in his notes on Saint Gregory’s *Sacramentary*, p. 202, concludes that in ancient public processions burning candles were attached to the crosses themselves; he proves that this was instituted by Saint John Chrysostom from Socrates, book VI, and Sozomen, book VIII.], raised their voices in song, and went around the city through its streets. They did not pass a single lodging without including it in this circuit.

Why say more? In a few days the plague mentioned above attacked the boundaries of this city. [Col. 0886C] Yet when it approached the place where the relic of the Blessed man had come, as though it saw a boundary fixed there, it not only dared not enter but, driven back by the relic’s power, abandoned the places it had first invaded.

## CHAPTER LXXX. On Saint Ursinus, Bishop of the People of Bourges

The city of Bourges first received the word of salvation from Saint Ursinus [Note: [Col. 0886D] Various writers assign Saint Ursinus’s mission to different periods. Gregory here says that he was sent by the disciples of the apostles, which some understand of Saint Clement. On that account, the disciple who established the church among the people of Bourges during the time of Decius, as Gregory relates in book I of the *History*, chapter 29, would be someone other than blessed Ursinus—perhaps Senicianus, who is said to have been the second bishop of Bourges.], who, ordained bishop by the disciples of the apostles and sent into Gaul, first established and governed the church of Bourges. When he departed from the world, he was buried in a field [Note: [Col. 0887C] The custom of burying people outside cities, in fields and open country, is extremely ancient. It was often confirmed and renewed by legal authority, even by Christian emperors. The Gauls practiced it especially devoutly, as is clear from canon 36 of the First Council of Braga and elsewhere. See Savaron’s notes on letter 12 of book III of Apollinaris Sidonius.] among the other graves of the people (second century, 9 November or 29 December).

For that people did not yet understand that the priests of the Lord should be venerated and given their due reverence. Consequently, as the soil increased and a vineyard was planted above it, all memory of the city’s first priest was uprooted, and no mention of him was made until the time when Bishop Probianus [Note: [Col. 0887D] He is praised by Fortunatus in the *Life of Saint Germanus of Paris*, where this very account of the translation is found. A boy was freed from a serious illness through the merits of Saint Hilary, according to book II of the *Miracles of Saint Hilary*. Having become a priest, he subscribed under the name of Bishop Arcadius to the Fourth Council of Orléans in A.D. 541. After Desideratus, he became his successor; he attended the Second Council of Paris in A.D. 555 and the Third in A.D. 557. He went to Rome, where he died and was buried.] was appointed to the city’s see.

There was a certain man named Augustus, from the household of Desideratus [Note: [Col. 0887D] Desideratus was Probianus’s predecessor; his *Life* is said to have been written by the abbot of Beze. But it is actually the *Life of Saint Audoenus* written by Fridegodus, which some scoundrel in the patriarchal church of Bourges attributed to Desideratus by changing Audoenus’s name to Desideratus. Cointius proves this by comparing the two works under the year 549, no. 70 and following. Desideratus subscribed to the Fifth Council of Orléans and the Second Council of Clermont in A.D. 549. [Col. 0888C] He died on 8 May 550, the day on which his feast is celebrated. Augustus, who later became an abbot, is honored as a saint in Molanus’s additions to Usuard, under 7 October.], a former bishop. His hands and feet had contracted so severely that, if he wished to go anywhere, he could move only by supporting himself on his knees and elbows.

Inspired by God, he built, from the alms of the devout, an oratory at the village of Brivas [Note: [Col. 0888C] Laud., together with the editions, has *Brias*. In the archpresbyterate of Issoudun there is a place called Brives, where, together with a parish church, there is a priory formerly subject to the monastery of Déols; this may perhaps be the place intended here.] in honor of the holy and most blessed Bishop Martin. When he had brought Martin’s relics into it, his limbs were immediately straightened and he was restored to health.

Afterward, gathering a few monks around him and living under the monastery’s rule, he devoted himself continually to prayer. Consequently, when summoned by the Bishop, he was ordained abbot in the basilica of Saint Symphorian, which the aforementioned Bishop had built before the walls of Bourges.

He did not, however, abandon the monks whom he had previously gathered. Instead, appointing a superior over them, he himself governed both communities.

At last, while he was staying at this basilica, Saint Ursinus appeared to him in a nighttime vision and said:

“Dig up the earth and seek my little body” (A.D. 560). “For I am Ursinus, the first bishop of this city.”

He replied:

“Where shall I go, or where shall I seek your tomb, since I do not know the place where you were laid?”

Then Ursinus took his hand, led him to the place, and said:

“My body lies beneath the roots of these vines.”

When he awoke, the abbot related this to his priest. But the priest paid little attention to what the presbyter said [Col. 0888A] and made no effort to investigate.

Meanwhile, blessed Germanus, bishop of Paris, arrived. After being received by the Bishop, he went to sleep after dinner in the ecclesiastical residence. Saint Ursinus appeared in a vision to both men—the bishop and the abbot together—and led them to the place of the tomb, asking them to remove him from that spot.

They awoke and came together for the vigils in the very basilica of Saint Symphorian. When the morning offices had been completed, the Bishop told the abbot what he had seen, and confessed that he too had seen the same thing.

The following night they went there with only one cleric carrying a candle. They dug deeply into the indicated place and found a tomb. When it had been uncovered and its covering removed, they saw the holy body like that of a sleeping man, not dissolved by any corruption.

They marveled at this, replaced the covering, and informed the Bishop by day of what they had seen. Then he summoned the abbots and clergy, and with honor and psalmody they lifted the blessed tomb.

Because the poles on which it was being carried were very long, when they reached the portico they could not turn them through the entrance so as to approach the door of the church without difficulty.

Then blessed Germanus raised his voice and said:

“Holy priest of God, if it is your will to enter this basilica, let us feel the relief of your assistance.”

Immediately, when its weight was removed, the sarcophagus became so light that, leaving the poles behind, a few men carried with their hands the one that many had brought to that place.

Thus, after Masses had been celebrated, and while the people rejoiced, he was buried beside the altar. [Note: [Col. 0888D] It is still preserved there. See the *Patriarchium of Bourges*. This church now lies within the city walls, bears the changed name of Saint Ursinus, and is distinguished by a college of canons and the status of a parish.] Thereafter he manifested himself through many miracles.

## CHAPTER LXXXI. On Marianus the Recluse
964 Now, in that very period [Note: Colb. a reads “at that very time.” He is commemorated in the Roman Martyrology on 19 August. Nevertheless, his feast is celebrated on 19 September in the church of Bourges; Labbe published his life from a very ancient Breviary in volume II of the *Bibliotheca nova*, p. 432, where it is said that he lived for six years in the monastery of Princay under Abbot Faterius, then withdrew to the village of Spinolaium and spent forty-four years there in the life of a hermit. Nothing is said about his death. Tetradius, bishop of Bourges, who is said to have dedicated his church, attended the Council of Agde in 506 and the First Council of Orléans in 511. Hence we infer that Marian flourished during the reign of Clovis I. He had as a nephew the blessed Animius, and Terentia, his abbess, preserved his beard for a long time as a relic.] there was a certain hermit named Marian (A.D. 513, 19 August), who had no other food than wild apples. If some people occasionally brought him honey, or if he himself managed to find it in the woods, that was his food.

Since he was usually visited by many people, at one time he could not be found by those who sought him. At length, the men who had come to look for him followed his tracks and found the place where, kneeling, he had drawn water from the river. Proceeding from there, they found him lying dead beneath an apple tree. Accordingly, it was widely reported among the people that he had been struck by the tree and breathed out his spirit; but this was not clearly known, since no one reported having seen it.

The men who had arrived then lifted him up and carried him to the village of Evaunus [Note: This is a village in the diocese of Limoges, commonly called Evaux, where Marian was buried. He had been found dead in the neighboring forest—the forest of Antraigues in Combrailles. His sacred body had been placed in the very wall of the church, now occupied by Canons Regular of Saint Augustine; it was later transferred to a silver reliquary by Reginald de la Porte, bishop of Limoges, in 1300, as Bernard Gui reports in Labbe, volume I of the *Bibliotheca nova*, p. 635.], washed him, clothed him in suitable garments, and buried him in the church, celebrating the anniversary of his death every year. Crowds gathered for these celebrations and were frequently healed of their illnesses [Note: Thus Colb. a, in a later hand; the others read “and to these.”].

One of the neighboring inhabitants had long-infected grain, mixed with water and sprouted grain, prepared. Having kindled a fire, he was about to roast it on a woven framework in order to make a drink. One of his neighbors approached him and said: “What are you doing, man, that you are occupied with this work? Do you not know that it is the feast of blessed Marian?”

He replied angrily: “Do you suppose, you who say these things, that a man struck down from a tree for the sake of satisfying his stomach has been admitted into the company of angels, so that he ought to be venerated as a saint? It is better to carry out necessary work in the household than to honor such a saint.”

Hearing this, the other man went away and proceeded with the rest to the saint’s basilica, leaving his neighbor at home laboring at his task. Immediately, however, as the wind blew, the house caught fire and was entirely consumed by the flames; nothing of the man’s property remained. Then globes of flame rose above the little dwellings that stood around it and leapt across them [Note: The word “leaping across” occurs only in Colb. a, in a later hand; there, and below, it reads “they set fire to the threshing-floor.”]. The fire burned this man’s threshing-floor, fences, little huts for pigs and other animals, and everything else belonging to him. Nothing remained for the wretched man that had not been consumed by fire.

If anyone thinks that this happened by chance, let him marvel that it harmed none of the neighboring inhabitants who lived around the place. What are you doing now, crude rusticity, which always murmur against God and his friends, so that you may thereby acquire misfortune for yourself?

A thief, through his wickedness, had stolen another man’s oxen. Following the tracks, but losing them among roads flooded with water and deep chasms of mud, he hastened to the Saint’s tomb. After pouring out a prayer, when he had left the basilica, he noticed a man coming along the public road, driving those oxen before him with a horse exhausted from the journey.

The thief had been bewildered by the road and, becoming almost deranged, had returned with confused mind toward the place from which he had departed. The man recognized the oxen he had lost. Taking them back, he allowed the other man to return without accusation, because he understood that this had been granted to him through the power of Saint Marian: at the very hour when he had approached his tomb full of faith, he had found what was lost.

After these events, the people of Bourges began to honor God’s Confessor with even greater devotion.

## CHAPTER LXXXII. On Eusitius the Recluse

In this territory there was also Eusitius [Note: Others read *Eusicius*. Bell, in the title, has *Usichius*. The edition has *Eutichius, a man of many virtues*. He first lived in the monastery of Patriciacum; later, withdrawing into the wilderness, he founded the celebrated monastery now called, after him, the Cell of Saint Eusic(i)us—Selles in Berry. Labbe published the Life and Observances of Eusitius in volume II of the *Bibliotheca nova*, p. 371, and the miracles on p. 463. Chesne also presents fragments of another Life in volume I of his *History of the Franks*. Cointius explains how these accounts should be reconciled both with Gregory’s text and with one another, under the year 531. The year of his death is uncertain. He was already an old man in 531, when Childebert made war against the Visigoths.], a man of miracles (A.D. 532, 27 November), who, like a hermit, had withdrawn from human society into the dense thickets of thorns [Col. 0890B], and who detested gold and the riches of this world as dung.

When different people flocked to him because of various illnesses, infants whose throats had swollen were often brought to him. He would touch them with the gentlest touch and say, as though taking spiritual delight in jesting: “It is only right that this throat should be shaken by pains, since it does not permit swallowing” [Note: Bell reads, “which will not permit anything in the throat.”]. Then, making the sign of the cross in the name of the Trinity, he freed their diseased throats from pain and swelling.

For those suffering from quartan fever, his help was so immediate that, by merely giving them blessed water to drink, he restored them at once to health.

His clerics had two beehives. When one of his neighbors was tormented by the heat of quartan fever, he came to Eusitius, received from him the customary medicine, and was restored to health. As he wished to return home, he saw the hives from a distance in a tree. Inflamed immediately by desire—the desire which is described as the root of all evils—he considered stealing them. Finding an accomplice like himself, he went to the tree at night.

When he had climbed it and was lowering the hives by handing them to his companion, the old man suddenly arrived from the other side. At the sight of him, the man who was on the ground fled, without telling his companion what to beware of.

The old man stood beneath the tree and received from the thief one hive as he handed it down. When the thief wished to take away the second also, the Priest said: “This one is enough for now, my son; reserve the other for the man who worked for it.”

Terrified by these words, the thief threw himself down. The old man caught him, led him to his cell, and said: “Why, my son, do you follow the devil, who goes before you? Did you not come to me yesterday and receive the Lord’s blessing?”

“If you took pleasure in honey,” he continued, “you should have asked me, and I would have given it to you without any reproach or hindrance, as much as you wished.”

Then, rebuking him with many other words, he gave him a honeycomb and allowed him to depart unharmed, saying: “Take care not to repeat this, because theft is Satan’s money.”

King Childebert, on his way to Spain, came to this old man (A.D. 531). When he offered him fifty gold pieces, the old man said: “Why do you bring these to me? Give them to those who will distribute them to the poor. I have no need of them. It is enough for me if I may deserve to pray to the Lord for my sins.”

He added: “Go, and you will obtain victory; you will accomplish whatever you wish.”

The king then distributed the gold among the poor and vowed that, if the Lord brought him back from that journey with his favor, he would build a basilica in God’s honor at that place, in which the old man’s remains would rest. He later fulfilled this vow.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII. On Maximus, Bishop of Riez

Maximus, bishop and confessor of Riez [Note: He became bishop of Riez, under the metropolitan authority of Aix, after being abbot of Lérins, in 433. He attended the Council of Riez in 439, the First Council of Orange in 441, and the Third Council of Arles, concerning the jurisdiction of the monastery of Lérins, around 455. Faustus succeeded him first in the governance of the abbey of Lérins and then in the episcopate, as Sidonius sings in the *Eucharisticus*. He was renowned for miracles both before and after his death. Writers of those times praised him greatly. Dynamius Patricius wrote his Life, which Vincentius Barralis records in his *Chronology of the Saints of Lérins*. Surius also has his Life under 27 November, the day on which he departed to heaven. He was buried in the church of Saint Peter, which he had built. He wrote several homilies, which are included among those published under the name of Eusebius of Emesa, or of Gaul, or Eucherius of Lyon.] (A.D. 460, 27 November), frequently reveals himself to the inhabitants through many miracles. At his tomb not only are the blind given sight, but other kinds of illness are also driven away through his powers.

I shall relate a recent event that I learned about. There was a little boy, about three years old, still dependent on his mother’s breast. Seized by fever, while he was being carried in his mother’s arms, he became so afflicted that he could take neither the breast nor any other food.

For three days he grew steadily worse while being carried in the arms of those who loved him. Then one of the servants said: “If only this little child were carried to the tomb of blessed Maximus! We trust in his merits that he can restore him to his former health.”

While he was being carried in the arms of those who loved him, he breathed out his spirit. When his parents saw this, weeping and crying aloud, they threw him before the tomb of blessed Maximus the Confessor. They closed the doors and left the lifeless body there.

After the night had been spent in lamentation, another day dawned and was given back to the earth. When the doors of the sacred church were opened, they saw the little boy standing upright, pulling himself along the rails of the tomb and trying to walk. He was not yet old enough to walk properly.

His parents marveled and rejoiced. His sorrowful mother received him with joy and restored him to his home in good health. I myself saw the boy when he had grown older; he related these things to us.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV. On Valerius the Bishop

Blessed Valerius the Confessor, the first bishop of the people of Couserans [Note: The period in which Saint Valerius lived is uncertain. Glycerius, his successor in the commonly circulated lists, subscribed to the Council of Agde in 506. The city of Couserans takes its name from Licerius, its fifth bishop: Saint-Lizier of Couserans in Gascony, under the metropolitan see of Auch.] (A.D. . . . . . , 5 July), revealed himself in the following way.

He had previously possessed an oratory built over him, but when it collapsed through neglect, the place where he rested was forgotten. The inhabitants remembered only that he had been buried before the holy altar.

Bishop Theodorus arrived [Note: Eleutherius, archdeacon, sent by Theodorus, bishop of the church of Couserans, subscribed to the Fifth Council of Orléans in 549.]. Enlarging the oratory itself to a greater size, he made it into a large basilica. Then, searching for the body of the holy man, he found two tombs, but did not know which of the two was that of the priest.

He therefore summoned the clergy and celebrated vigils throughout the night, praying that the blessed Confessor would reveal to him where he lay. He filled two small flasks with wine and placed one on each tomb, saying: “Whichever one is found to have increased its Falernian wine, let that be shown to be the burial place of Valerius the bishop.”

When daylight came, he left the basilica, sealed the doors, and gave his limbs over to sleep. Rising at the third hour, he came to the holy basilica with the clergy and people. When the doors had been opened, he found that one flask contained a little wine, while the other was overflowing so abundantly through its open mouth that it had washed the entire monument of the blessed Pontiff.

By this the priest learned which tomb belonged to Bishop Valerius. Yet wishing to know still more certainly, he uncovered the monument and, after removing its cover, found the venerable body very much intact. No hair had fallen away, no beard had diminished, and nothing on the skin appeared corrupted or foul [Col. 0892C]. Everything was unharmed, as though it had only recently been placed there. Such a fragrance of sweetness rose from the tomb that there could be no doubt that God’s friend rested there.

Laurel leaves had also been spread beneath him. The bishop took some of them and provided medicine to many sick people. He then took relics from his garments, covered the tomb again, and continued to honor the venerable Bishop, witnessing many miracles from these relics thereafter.

## CHAPTER LXXXV. On Silvester, Bishop of Chalon

The most blessed Silvester governed the Church of Chalon [Note: This chapter and the following six are absent from Clar. a. Nevertheless, it is preserved in full, together with the following chapter, in the history of the elevation of Saints Silvester and others, which the Bollandists published from an old manuscript after Perrius and Cussetus under 17 March. From this history we learn that the Lives of Saints Silvester, Agricola, and Desideratus had long been lost, if they had ever been written. The author of that history attempts to repair this loss from the chapters of our Gregory cited above and from the history of the discovery of their relics, which he describes as having occurred in his own time. This was arranged by Girbaldus, or Girboldus, bishop of Chalon toward the end of the ninth century. After the body of Saint Lupus, bishop of Chalon, had been raised from the earth in 877 in the suburban basilica of Saint Peter, he conceived the plan of transferring Saints Silvester, Agricola, and Desideratus, who lay at Saint-Marcel. He carried this out in 878 or the following year, on the day before the Nones of May. Pope John VIII, who came to Chalon shortly afterward, established an annual solemnity in honor of these same saints.], who, after serving in the priesthood for forty-two years [Note: Laud., Colb. tut., and Bell., in a later hand, read “in the forty-second year.” Silvester subscribed to the Council of Épaone in 509 and the First Council of Lyon in 517. His feast is observed on 20 November.], full of days and virtues, departed to the Lord (A.D. 514, 20 November).

He had a little bed woven with fine cords. When the sick—whether suffering from quartan fever or oppressed by various fevers—were placed beneath it once or twice, they were immediately healed by the power divinely imparted to it.

For this reason the bed was carried into the church sacristy, where it still shines with the same power. Many people, as I have seen with my own eyes, cut off pieces of those cords and carried them to distant places; when the pieces were placed upon the sick, they saw the benefit of health arrive.

My mother had a piece cut from it and made a little girl suffering from chills and fever hang it around her neck. The illness immediately subsided, and she saw the girl restored to health.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI. On Desideratus, a Recluse of the Same Territory

970 In this city there was also the priest Desideratus, whom I saw at the monastery of Gourdon [Note: In the history of the discovery mentioned above, the name is *Guerdonensis*. Today it is called Gourdon, a village in the district of Charolais.] (A.D. 570, 30 April), a man illustrious for holiness, who often brought an end through prayer to chills, toothache, and other illnesses.

He was completely a recluse [Note: Most manuscripts read, “For he was not entirely a recluse.”], that is, he did not leave his cell; nevertheless, whoever wished to see him could see him in the cell. As we have said, he shone in the world, distinguished by outstanding virtues.

When the blessed Bishop Agricola heard this [Note: Gregory speaks of Saint Agricola, bishop of Chalon, in *History* V.46, where we have said more about him. He wrote to Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, to obtain the health of his chamberlain, as related in chapter 1 of the Life of Saint Germanus. On the word “blessed,” see the notes to chapter 16 of Book III of the *Histories*.], he sent his archdeacon to bring the blessed man to the city cemetery. But, because the monks resisted, the archdeacon did not carry out what he had been ordered to do.

Afterward, when a hospice for lepers had been built by the priest outside the city, he gathered the abbots and all the clergy and transferred the blessed body to its basilica [Note: The history of the discovery mentioned above says that the body of Saint Desideratus was sought in the basilica of Saint Marcel, but nowhere says that it was found there.]. He buried it with the greatest care in the basilica mentioned above. He now manifests through great miracles that he lives with Christ.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII. On John the Abbot

There was [Note: This chapter is absent from the manuscripts. An anonymous monk of Réomay, his contemporary, wrote the Life of Saint John; Jonas interpolated it and added a book of his miracles. On these matters see Mabillon, *Acta sanctorum Ordinis sancti Benedicti*, century I, under the year 539; Bollandus under 28 January; and Cointius under the year 539, no. 18. The monastery of Réomay, which he founded, still exists under his name, commonly called Moutier-Saint-Jean, under the Order of Saint Benedict and the Congregation of Saint Maur, in the district of Tonnerre. Its history was published by Petrus Roverius.] in the district of Tonnerre, in the parish of Langres, an abbot named John, outstanding in holiness and, in accordance with the etymology of his name, preceded by divine grace (A.D. 539, 28 January).

It is said that, when he wished to build the monastery called Réomay and the brothers were suffering from an extreme lack of water, he found a well of immense depth in which a deadly basilisk serpent lived. Having killed the serpent by invoking God and cleansed the well, he made the well’s water drinkable for the brothers. When we were traveling to Lyon and were kindly received by the brothers of that monastery, we too drank from this water as a testimony to the miracle; many people suffering from chills are also cured by drinking it.

The following miracle is also told of this man. A certain fratricide, bound with iron rings because of the enormity of his crime [Note: This form of penance frequently occurs in books about the miracles of the saints and was customarily imposed by bishops and penitentiary priests for more serious crimes. It was prohibited in Book I of Charlemagne’s Capitularies. Nevertheless, several examples of it occur in later centuries, as Mabillon observes. See Roverius’s note 75 or the Bollandists, volume II of January, p. 866.], had been commanded to travel around visiting the shrines of the saints for seven years.

When he reached Rome, he learned through a divine revelation that he could not be absolved unless he reached the relics of the body of Saint John, abbot of Réomay. Thus, after visiting various places, he finally came to the basilica where the most sacred body of the saint was laid, not far from the monastery [Note: This basilica is now the parish church of the village that received its name from it, Saint-Corps, not far from the monastery itself. The authors cited above mention several translations of the saint; consult them if desired. His stone tomb is still visited there.].

There, devoting himself to prayers and vigils, he was released from all his bonds.

This just and religious man lived, like the lawgiver Moses, for one hundred and twenty years. His eye did not grow dim, nor was his tooth moved. He was also the teacher of a memorable man [Possibly Saint Sequanus, the subject of the next chapter], about whom we shall speak in his proper place.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII. On Sequanus the Abbot

That Sequanus too was a man of great virtue [Note: The Life of Saint Sequanus is found in century I of the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*. The monastery of Segestrum, founded by him, is now commonly called Saint-Seine, together with the neighboring town, five leagues below Dijon. It still exists under the Order of Saint Benedict and the Congregation of Saint Maur, where his sacred relics are preserved.]—an abbot of the territory of Langres [Col. 0895A]—who during his life often released people from the bondage of demonic entanglement, and after his death allowed those bound with prison chains to depart free through his merits (A.D. 580, 19 September).

King Guntram had lost a horn [Note: Valesius observes in his defense against Launoy, part I, that kings always used horns in hunting, but trumpets in battle. See Rigord in the *Deeds of Philip Augustus*.], by whose sound he was accustomed either to gather his mastiffs or to drive away those herds of wild woodland animals [Col. 0895B]. It had been stolen, and the theft threw many people into chains and deprived some of their possessions.

Three men from among these sought the tomb of the aforesaid Confessor. When the king learned of this, he ordered them to be bound with chains and fetters. This was done.

At midnight a light brighter than human light arose in the basilica. The iron barriers of their feet burst apart, and, when the links of their chains had broken [Note: All the manuscripts read *bacis*. Fortunatus uses this word in the same sense in the *Life of Saint Germanus*, chapter 30.], the prisoners were released.

When the king heard this, he was terrified and promptly granted them the freedom of their own will.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX. On Marcellus, Bishop of Paris

Marcellus, bishop of the city of Paris, who once, as is read in his Life [Note: Surius gives the Life of Saint Marcellus, written by the priest Fortunatus, under 1 November. He was buried in a suburban church, which Launoy maintained was at that time the cathedral, though Valesius and others objected. No one will deny that it was already famous under the first dynasty of our kings. For many centuries it has enjoyed an illustrious college of canons; nevertheless, the body of the holy Bishop was transferred from there to the larger church, where it is preserved in a very rich shrine.], drove an enormous serpent from the town, now rests in a village of that city (fourth century, 1 November).

Ragnimodus the priest, who is now regarded as the priest of that town [Note: That is, the bishop of Paris. He is frequently mentioned in Gregory’s *History*], came to his tomb suffering from quartan fever and lay there. After spending the whole day fasting and praying, he fell asleep when evening had already come. Shortly afterward he awoke from sleep and rose from the tomb in good health.

## CHAPTER XC. On Germanus, Bishop of the Same City

When King Chilperic entered the city of Paris, on the day after the king had entered the city (A.D. 576, 28 May), a paralytic who was sitting in the portico of the basilica of Saint Vincent, in which blessed Germanus rests bodily [Note: Our Gregory frequently praises Saint Germanus in the books of the *History*. Having become bishop after serving as abbot of Autun, he subscribed to the Third Council of Paris in 557, the Third Council of Tours in 567, and the Fourth Council of Paris in 573. We shall give his letter to Brunhild in the appendix. He was renowned for miracles both before and after his death, so that ancient authors commonly designated him “Most Holy” and “Most Blessed.” Shortly after his death, Bertramnus built a church and monastery in his name; Saint Eligius adorned his tomb with gold, silver, and gems, as Saint Audoin reports in Book I, chapter 32. Bede says of him in the authentic Martyrology: “He was of such virtue that he healed the causes of illnesses by touching them.” He was buried in the oratory of Saint Symphorian, attached to the principal basilica of the monastery that King Childebert had built at his urging. His tomb is still seen there, although the sacred body was transferred to the larger church in the eighth century. It is preserved in a shrine made of gold and silver and decorated with gems. Surius, Mabillon in Benedictine century I, and the Bollandists under 28 May published his Life by Fortunatus. The latter, in Benedictine century III, also include more about the translation of this saint, his miracles, and the monastery, which, together with its entire suburb—equal to the greatest cities—is still called Saint-Germain-des-Prés after him. The epitaph said to have been composed by King Chilperic is likewise given by these authors from Aimoinus.], was healed. At daybreak, while the people waited, he was giving thanks to the blessed Bishop.

For often in that place the steps of paralytics and the sight of the blind are restored by the Saint’s power, and scarcely does his feast ever arrive without his power being displayed there.

## CHAPTER XCI. On the Most Holy Virgin Genovefa [Note: Laud., Bell., and Colb. a read: “On Genovefa the Religious.”]

There is also Saint Genovefa [Note: Gregory calls her “Most Blessed” in Book IV, chapter 1. Surius and Bollandus give her Life under 3 January. The Life published by Chiffletius is interpolated. Constantius praises her virtues in the Life of Saint Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, by whom the most blessed Virgin was consecrated to God.
