That her memory was already famous shortly after her death is shown not only by ancient Martyrologies but also by a proper Mass preserved in the old Gallican liturgy in Mabillon, Book II, no. 16. Sigebert, in his *Chronicle* under the year 512—the twentieth year of Theodosius the Younger, which he calls the twenty-eighth of Clovis, that is, 509, and to which he assigns the First Council of Orléans in 511—writes: “Genovefa, a Parisian virgin, aged eighty, departed to the Lord.” Clovis built a basilica at the very place where she was buried. After various fortunes, it was granted in the twelfth century to the Canons Regular of Saint Augustine by Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis. They still remain there under a regular abbot, the general superior of the entire Gallican congregation of stricter observance. R. P. Gerard Dubois discusses at length the various translations of Saint Genovefa, whose Acts Bollandus records, in his *History of Paris*, Book I, chapter 9. Her sacred body, which is customarily carried solemnly through the city during public disasters, is devoutly preserved in the same monastery in a very rich shrine, which that author describes.] buried in the basilica of the holy apostles (A.D. 509, 3 January). While still bodily present, she had such power that she raised a dead person. At her tomb, petitions frequently obtain assistance, and through her power the fevers of those suffering from chills are very often extinguished.

## CHAPTER XCII. On the Tomb of Blessed Lusor

In the village of Dol, in the territory of Bourges, blessed Lusor, once the son of the senator Leocadius, rests (A.D. 255, 4 November). He is said to have departed from the world in white garments. Placed in a crypt above the pavement, he has a tomb wonderfully carved from Parian marble [Note: Even now, in the underground crypt of the church of Saints Stephen and Saturninus at Dol, commonly Bourg-Deols, near Bourges, two very ancient tombs decorated with various figures can be seen. Saint Lusor is said to have been buried in the marble one, and his father Leocadius in the stone one. Gregory writes in Book I of the *History*, chapter 29, that Leocadius descended from the line of Vettius Epagathus, the martyr of Lyon. The feast of Lusor, commonly Saint Ludre, who died “in white,” that is, during the first week after his baptism, is commemorated not only by more recent Martyrologies but also by the Martyrology of Florus, on 4 November. It is therefore surprising that his name was removed from the Breviary of Bourges several years ago. See Labbe’s *Bibliotheca nova*, volume II, pp. 426–427. The period in which Saint Lusor lived is unknown. Gregory says in the cited passage that Leocadius granted his house to the first Christians of Bourges so that it might be converted into a church. He writes that these Christians had been instructed in the faith by the disciples of the seven bishops whom he thinks arrived under Decius. Hence we infer that Leocadius and Lusor lived toward the end of the third century.].

It happened once that Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris [Col. 0897A], was celebrating vigils at this tomb. Nearby he had a small form on which he bent his knees whenever necessity required.

During one night of vigils, while they were singing psalms from the reading of David, the clerics, tired from standing, leaned for relief upon the Saint’s tomb, supporting themselves on their interlocked arms. Immediately the tomb of the blessed Confessor trembled and, by its visible shaking, declared that an injury was being inflicted upon it.

Bishop Germanus, terrified with fear, ordered the sleepy men to be removed from it, saying: “Go away, you sluggish men, far from the tomb, lest trouble be inflicted upon God’s saint.” After they had been removed, they no longer felt that trembling.

Nor should the following be passed over. Blessed Lusor appeared in a dream to a certain poor man and ordered him to clean a cell in which, they say, he had uttered the cries of infancy. When the poor man delayed carrying out the command after being warned twice, Lusor appeared to him a third time and said: “If you do what I command, you will receive one triens for your obedient service.”

The man rose, swept the cell with brooms, washed it with water, and sprinkled it with herbs. He then stood astonished, waiting for the promised reward, until by God’s providence he noticed a triens shining on the floor. He picked it up and departed joyfully.

## CHAPTER XCIII. On Maximinus, Bishop of Trier

At the outskirts of the city of Trier there is also Saint Maximinus [Note: Saint Maximinus is famous for receiving Athanasius, an exile, at Trier; Athanasius praises his faith in his *Apology to Constantius* and in Book I *Against the Arians*. I omit Jerome in the *Chronicle*, our Gregory in Book I of the *History*, chapter 35, and others. Surius published his Life, written by Lupus, a bishop of the ninth century. The Bollandists published another Life, thought to be two hundred years older, under 29 May. He is listed among those who attended the Council of Sardica in 347, and, as Henschenius maintains, the Council of Cologne in the preceding year against Euphratas or his predecessor. He died on 12 September in Aquitania and was brought back to Trier and buried on 29 May in the suburban monastery of Saint John, which was thereafter called Saint Maximinus. It still flourishes under that name as a famous Benedictine monastery, where he rests in an underground crypt beneath the high altar with Saints Agroecius and Nicetius, bishops of the same city.], a great advocate with the Lord for that people. Glorious miracles are often seen at his tomb (A.D. 349, 29 May).

In the time of King Theodobert, a certain priest named Arboastes [Note: Most manuscripts read *Arboastis*. Colb. throughout has *Arbogastis*.] was engaged in a lawsuit with a Frank in the king’s presence. While these proceedings were taking place, the king was visiting the holy places of the city, situated in the suburbs, for the sake of prayer.

When the king saw that the priest’s case was craftily presented, he turned to him and said: “If the claims you are pursuing are true, confirm them by an oath over the tomb of Bishop Maximinus.”

“I dare,” said the priest, “to fulfill what you command.”

Immediately he placed his hands upon the holy tomb and said: “May I be struck down by the power of this saint if I speak anything false about what I am asserting in my case against this Frank.”

The barbarian, growling and raging as though against God’s saint, and the priest left the basilica. As they traveled together along the road, the priest suddenly slipped, fell headlong to the ground, and died.

Afterward the barbarian praised the Saint’s power, which he had previously disparaged.

Similarly, the city’s archdeacon, when Bishop Nicetius accused him of adultery, requested to be cleared by an oath at this saint’s tomb. He entered the first threshold of the crypt and stopped as though stunned. Then, descending by the steps, he came to another doorway. When he wished to approach the third, he was immediately seized by fever and, no longer daring to take another step, confessed the crime with which he had been charged, placed in danger of death. He begged the people to seek on his behalf the assistance either of the holy Bishop or of his own bishop.

As soon as he had confessed, however, he was freed from the attack of fever and received back into the affection of his bishop.

## CHAPTER XCIV. On Nicetius, Bishop of the Same City

As we said above, Nicetius [Note: His Life is found below among the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 17], bishop of that city, shone with the merit of almsgiving, charity, and every holiness while he dwelt in the body (around A.D. 566, 5 December).

When he departed from the world, he was buried in the basilica of his predecessor, Saint Maximinus. At his tomb now the chains of prisoners are broken; those suffering the force of a demonic assault are freed when the demons are driven out [Col. 0898C]; the eyes of the blind are often filled with light when the darkness is removed.

What shall I say about perjurers [Note: Several manuscripts and the edition read “perjuries”]? If anyone dares to utter a false oath there, he is immediately corrected by divine vengeance. No one even dares to speak of such a thing if, tormented by conscience, he recognizes himself as guilty and presumes to pronounce an oath there.

## CHAPTER XCV. On Medardus, Bishop of Noyon [or of Soissons]

Medardus, the glorious confessor, rests near the city of Soissons [Note: [Col. 0898D] Other manuscripts have *Sessionis* and *Sessionas*. The edition has *Suessionicam*. Saint Medard was bishop of Vermandois and transferred his see to Noyon, where it has remained to the present, adorned with the title of a county of the city and a peerage of France [Col. 0899C]. We spoke of Saint Medard’s death and monastery in chapter 19 of Book IV of the *History*. He is called “Soissonian” [Col. 0899D] in the chapter heading because his tomb and church are near Soissons. The author of the second Life of Saint Medard, in volume VIII of the *Spicilegium*, incorporated this entire chapter into his work.] (around A.D. 560, 8 June). At his tomb we have often seen the fetters of wretched prisoners broken. After I had written a book about his miracles, a woman whose hand was disabled devoutly sought the aid of the blessed Priest. Finally, she kept vigil with the others in complete faith, trusting that, through his power, the bonds that held her hand rigid could be loosened by the one whose power freed the chains of the unfortunate. It happened that, while Mass was being celebrated, the dry sinews’ bonds were relaxed. Giving thanks to the Confessor and approaching the holy altar, she received the grace of blessing, restored to health.

Since, before the church was built, there had been above the Saint’s tomb a small cell made of slender branches, and since this was removed when the church was consecrated, it is fitting to relate something remarkable about the frailty of that wood. For small pointed sticks made from it have often brought relief from toothache [Col. 0899B]. When Charimeris [Note: [Col. 0899D] He succeeded Saint Ageric in the bishopric of Verdun, concerning whom see above, Book IX of the *History*, chapter 23. The author of the Life of Saint Medard cited above, however, says: “He was then regarded as King Childebert’s *referendarius*.” From this statement Cointius inferred that this book was written before Gregory wrote his *History*. But perhaps this author adapted Gregory’s text to his own time.]—who at that time was regarded as King Childebert’s *referendarius*—was suffering from this pain, he went to the Saint’s basilica, hoping to receive healing from the Saint’s power through a piece of the wood. When he arrived, however, he found the door locked. Trusting, therefore, that the Blessed One’s power was present everywhere, he drew his knife and cut a small stick from the door. As soon as he touched his teeth with it, the painful affliction disappeared. We also possess his staff, from which the sick have often experienced remedies.

## CHAPTER XCVI. On Albinus, bishop of Angers

The confessor Albinus (A.D. 550, 1 March), whose Life was recently written by Fortunatus the presbyter [Note: [Col. 0899D] This book was published in the first century of the *Acta Sanctorum* of the Benedictine Order, as also by Surius and the Bollandists, on 1 March. Albinus, formerly abbot of Trincillacum or Cincillacum, became bishop of Angers and signed the acts of the Third Council of Orléans in A.D. 538 and, through Abbot Sapaudus, those of the Fourth Council of Orléans in A.D. 549. To celebrate his feast, Fortunatus, at the invitation of Bishop Domitianus, went to Angers; he described this journey in verse, *Poem* 24 of Book II. He rests in the abbey dedicated to his name, which is still famous under the Rule of Saint Benedict and the Congregation of Saint Maur. Other churches, nevertheless, also claim to possess relics of this holy man. See Geoffrey of Vigeois, *Chronicle*, chapter 15, and the Bollandists for 1 March.] likewise obtains, through his merits, that miracles be displayed at his tomb. There was, then, a day of solemn celebration on which a paralytic, powerless in all his limbs, had been carried in a wagon and sat before the glass window of the apse where the sacred remains were enclosed. Falling asleep, he saw a man approach him and say: “How long will you sleep, and do you not desire to become well?” He replied: “Would that I might deserve to become well.” The man said to him: “When you hear the signal for the beginning of the third hour ring out, rise immediately and enter the basilica to which you have come. For at that very hour blessed Martin, together with Albinus, his fellow tribesman, will enter the basilica, so that, after prayer has been offered, he may proceed to Tours for Albinus’s solemnity. If you are present at that moment, you will be made well.”

Without delay, when the signal rang, the man approached the Saint’s tomb. As the clergy began to sing the praise of David’s psalm, a fragrance of sweetness filled the Saint’s basilica, and the man rose healed, his legs straightened. This was witnessed not by a few but by many, as the region’s foster-child testifies.

Likewise, in the village of Crovium [Note: [Col. 0900D] So read all the manuscripts, and likewise more than once below in the miracles of Saint Martin, although the printed editions generally have *Croniensis vicus*. They suppose this to be Craon, a town of Anjou, where there is a conventual Benedictine priory of the Congregation of Saint Maur. In a charter of a certain Adalberga for the monastery of Saint Sergius at Angers, in volume IV of *Gallia Christiana*, the village of Nubiliacus is mentioned in the pagus of Angers, in the *vicaria* of Croniacum.] a woman who had been blind from birth invoked the Saint’s name and was given sight on that very day.

## CHAPTER XCVII. On Hospitius, the confessor

In the region of Nice there was Hospitius [Note: [Col. 0900D] See Book VI of the *History*, chapter 6, and the Bollandists for 21 May.] (A.D. 581, 21 May), a great servant of God, endowed with many virtues [Col. 0900B], who departed from this world. When he was being buried, someone placed his hand beside the tomb, lifted a little dust, wrapped it in a linen cloth, and carried it away with him. Proceeding on the following day [Note: [Col. 0900D] Manuscript Clar. a has “after three days.” It would be superfluous to speak of the monastery of Lérins. It still exists and is possessed by the Benedictines of the Cassinese Congregation. The island is commonly called Saint-Honorat; today, together with the neighboring islands, it belongs to the diocese of Grasse.] he encountered on the shore a ship preparing to sail to Marseille. But he wished to visit the monastery of Lérins. The men who owned the ship were of Jewish descent. For this reason, the man did not wish to tell the sailors what he was carrying. At last, after they had set out and reached a point opposite the monastery of Lérins, the ship stopped in the middle of the sea. Though the winds were blowing, it moved in no direction.

The Jews were astonished and asked what this meant. The man revealed the truth, saying: “I have the relics of blessed Hospitius with me, and now I desire to go to Lérins, but I was afraid to tell you. Now I know that your ship is being held back by his power; it will certainly not be able to move from here unless you agree to let me go where I have decided to travel.” When the men heard this, they were overcome with amazement. They changed the sails, and, with a favorable wind, freely departed wherever they wished after putting the man ashore on the island of Lérins.

## CHAPTER XCVIII. On the hermit whose cooking pot was wooden

See what great and what kind of riches the poverty of the world gathers for its own, so that the Redeemer, who created all things from nothing, not only gives them whatever they wish, but even commands the elements themselves to serve them.

For I remember hearing some years ago that there was a certain man in the wilderness of a particular region. When a brother came from nearby with eager devotion to seek him, the hermit welcomed him with complete affection. They then entered a small hut of sorts and, after praying, sat down. While they discussed many matters concerning the word of God, the old man rose from his little chair [Edition: *cellula*, “cell”]. He entered the garden and gathered vegetables for food. After lighting a fire, he placed a wooden cooking pot filled with water and vegetables over it [Note: [Col. 0901D] Manuscripts Colb. 2 and Bad. have “a wooden cauldron … began to boil.”], and drove the fire so forcefully that the pot seemed to be bronze. When the visitor saw this, he was astonished and asked what it meant.

The old man replied: “I have lived in this wilderness for many years, but in this cooking pot, at the Lord’s command, I have always prepared food to restore my frail little body.” When the food was cooked and the hymns owed to God had been sung, both men were refreshed by the service of this little vessel.

“I heard this long ago. But recently I saw an abbot who called him Ingenuus [Colb. a: *Ingenium*], asserting that he had lived within the territory of Autun and had often eaten with him from this vessel vegetables or porridge that had been cooked in it. He confirmed under oath that he had seen the cooking pot placed over the flames and boiling violently, while its bottom always remained so moist that it seemed continually to be kept wet by someone.”

## CHAPTER XCIX. On Avitus, the confessor of Orléans

Avitus, abbot of the district of Chartres, which is called Perche [Note: [Col. 0901D] Cointius believes this Avitus to be the same as Saint Avitus, abbot of Micy, who foretold the death of Chlodomer. Baronius, however, thinks that they should be distinguished, a view that Mabillon considers more than probable in the *Acta Sanctorum* of the Benedictine Order, first century, p. 613. They are distinguished in Ado’s *Martyrology*: the abbot of Micy is commemorated on 19 December, the other on 17 June. In the heading of this chapter, manuscript Colb. has “of Chartres.”], repeatedly foretold, by revelation of the Holy Spirit, that the dissolution of his body was approaching [Col. 0901C] (A.D. 530, 17 June). When he departed from the body, he was honorably buried near the city of Orléans. Over him the Christian faithful built a church [Note: [Col. 0901D] We discussed this church in the notes to Book VIII of the *History*, chapter 2.]

After his death, when the anniversary of his assumption was being celebrated with the greatest honor, one of the townsmen, while the others were going to attend the solemnities of Mass, took a hoe and went to dig over his vineyard. Many rebuked him for being absent from the feast, but he refused to return, saying: “The man you are honoring was also a worker.” But when he entered the vineyard and opened the earth with the first stroke, his neck was immediately twisted back and his face turned toward his back [Note: [Col. 0901D] Colb. tut. has: “His face fell toward the ground.”].

Then, trembling and watched by the people, he entered the Saint’s basilica with great weeping. After a few days, as he prayed constantly in the same place, his neck straightened and he recovered.

## CHAPTER C. On Cyprian, abbot of Périgueux

Cyprian, abbot of the town of Périgueux, was a man of magnificent holiness [Note: [Col. 0901D] He is said to have lived the monastic life in the monastery of Genoliacum, in the diocese of Périgueux, under Abbot Savolus, during the reign of King Chlothar. From there he withdrew to a place near the Dordogne River, where a village still exists under the name of Saint Cyprian. He flourished during the time of Charterius, bishop of Périgueux, who attended the Second Council of Mâcon in A.D. 585. Labbe, in volume II of the *Bibliotheca nova*, published the Life of Saint Sorus and a fragment of the Life of Saint Amandus, who were companions of Saint Cyprian.] through whom God deigned to perform many miracles in this world (A.D. 580, 9 December). For he frequently restored strength to disabled hands, returned the use of their legs to paralytics, and restored sight to the blind; he also returned three lepers, after they had been anointed with oil, to their former health. Even now he frequently displays healings over the sick if they faithfully seek his tomb or entreat him.

## CHAPTER CI. On Eparchius, the recluse of Angoulême

The sick are often healed at the tomb of Eparchius, a recluse of the city of Angoulême [Note: [Col. 0902D] Others have *Equolenensis*, *Engolismensis*, and so forth. On Saint Eparchius see Book VI of the *History*, chapter 8, and the notes.] (A.D. 581, 1 July). For through his merits the fevers of those suffering from chills and other ailments are extinguished. A blind man from the territory of Périgueux threw himself upon his grave, poured out a prayer, and deserved to receive his sight.

The count of the aforesaid city of Angoulême ordered a thief who had been discovered and subjected to torture to be condemned to the gallows. As he was being led to his death, however, he began to invoke the name of this saint. When he had been brought to the stake and had poured out a prayer upon the ground, he was left hanging from the gallows.

When the monks learned of this, they immediately threw themselves down before the Saint’s tomb and began to pray, saying: “O holy Confessor, if you still had life in this world, you could rescue this poor man from the hand of death, just as you have often freed those condemned to such punishment. But now we do not doubt your prayer: what you did while living in this world, you can renew when exalted in heaven.”

When night came, the abbot sent someone to the gallows. As the monk approached, the bonds immediately broke, and the man fell to the ground. Thus supported by the monk, he was brought alive to the monastery. After drinking a little wine, he recovered; and, having obtained his life from the judge, he departed free.

## CHAPTER CII. On Felix, bishop of Bourges

After the death of Felix, bishop of Bourges [Note: [Col. 0902D] He was ordained by Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, in A.D. 568, and attended the Fourth Council of Paris in A.D. 573. Fortunatus praises him in Book III, poem 23, for a tower he built to preserve the Eucharist, expressing it in these words:

> How fittingly all things adorn the consecrated Body of the Lamb,  
> that a mighty jewel should bear gifts of gold.  
> Let Solomon’s vessels of metal yield to chrysoliths;  
> art and faith make these more pleasing.

He is said to rest in the collegiate church of Saint Austregisilus at Château, in the suburb of Bourges, but is not celebrated with public worship.] (A.D. 575, 1 January), when a certain blind man received the light of his eyes after the darkness had been driven away at his tomb, which had been carved from Parian marble and placed above the ground, the people recognized the friend of God whom, while he was still in the body, they had not been fully able to know because worldly darkness stood in the way. They began to visit his resting place continually in prayer.

But because, as we have said, the marble sarcophagus was covered with an inferior stone, the citizens, and especially the bishop [Note: [Col. 0903C] This was Sulpicius Severus, Felix’s successor after Remigius. He was already bishop in A.D. 585, when he signed the acts of the Second Council of Mâcon, twelve years after the Fourth Council of Paris, which Felix had attended.], with greater insight covered the sarcophagus with a better casing, namely, one of Heraclean marble.

After the inferior stone had been removed, nearly twelve years later, they found the body of the blessed Confessor so unharmed that there was no dissolution in the body and no decay in the clothing. Everything was so intact that, so to speak, it seemed to have been placed in the tomb at that very hour [Col. 0903B]. Nor was the Lord’s mercy absent there, so that the removed stone would not remain without honor. For they say that many people, scraping off and drinking a small amount of its powder, are quickly freed from quartan, tertian, and quotidian fevers.

## CHAPTER CIII. On Junianus, the recluse of Limoges

There was also Junianus [Note: [Col. 0903C] His Life is reported by Gononus in Book IV of the *Lives of the Western Fathers*, but he did not distinguish him from Junianus, abbot of Mairé [Col. 0903D], who flourished among the Poitevins and is still honored there in the monastery of Nobiliacum, to which he was transferred in A.D. 830, according to the *Chronicle of Saint-Maixent*. The other man whom Gregory praises here flourished in the diocese of Limoges. We learn the location from the *Chronicle* of Geoffrey, prior of Vigeois, chapter 15, concerning the more illustrious saints of Limoges, where it says: “The people of Comodoliacum rejoice in Junianus together with Amandus, his teacher; for Josfredus, once treasurer, fraudulently took that monastery, together with the church of Saint Peter at the Crossroads, from the jurisdiction of Saint Martial.” He repeats this in chapter 59. The church in which Junianus was buried had been built by Ruricius the Younger, bishop of Limoges, whom the holy man had freed from a demon. Junianus flourished with Saint Amandus the hermit under Clovis I and his sons. See Bernard Gui, volume II of Labbe’s *Bibliotheca*, p. 277, in the historical works, where he records his feast on 16 October. The monastery of Comodoliacum [Col. 0904C] has been converted into a college of secular canons; together with the town surrounding it, it is commonly called Saint-Junien.] a recluse within the territory of the city of Limoges (A.D. 530, 16 November), who during his lifetime displayed many miracles to the people. Even now illnesses are often cured at his tomb.

For I have seen many—counting them all would be tedious—who, brought there with blind eyes [Note: [Col. 0904C] The edition has “brought there,” *eo perducti*], received their sight, and paralytics whose limbs were straightened. The people themselves bear witness to this even today: when they recover their health, they immediately make themselves tributaries of that place and, as the yearly cycle returns, pay their dues in gratitude for the health restored to them. Among these are many who seem to belong to the basilica of Saint Martin, our bishop.

## CHAPTER CIV. On Pelagia of Limoges

Pelagia, the mother of blessed Aredius the abbot [Note: [Col. 0904C] Gregory frequently speaks of Saint Aredius; his Life is given below after the *Lives of the Fathers*. In the *Chronicle* of Geoffrey, prior of Vigeois, chapter 15, concerning the illustrious saints of Limoges, we read: “At Saint Aredius, his holy mother Pelagia.” It is therefore clear that she was buried in the monastery of Attane, as Bernard Gui explicitly states in his historical works, in Labbe, volume I of the *Bibliotheca nova*, p. 631. Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, praises this chapter in his sermon “That Saint Martin Is Equal to the Apostles,” where he says: “At the funeral of Pelagia, mother of blessed Aredius the abbot, a globe of fire illuminating the whole church came from heaven, while the possessed cried out that Martin had come to the funeral of the dead woman.”], whom we mentioned above (A.D. 570, 26 August), was a woman of great devotion.

When she was afflicted by fever and was at the point of death, she summoned her son and said: “I beg you, dearest son, do not bury me before the fourth day, so that all the servants, male and female, may come and see my little body, and so that none of those whom I diligently nourished may be deprived of my funeral rites.” Having said this, she gave up her spirit.

After being washed according to custom, she was placed in a bier and carried into the church. On the fourth day, before she was buried, such a great fragrance of sweetness arose from her body that everyone marveled. During the night, a great globe of fire appeared. Rising in the east and traveling around the circle of heaven, it came to rest above the church in which the dead woman’s body lay. Suddenly, such a brightness covered the entire building that they thought they were looking upon midday.

Many possessed persons immediately cried out, saying that Martin had come for Pelagia’s passing. On the following Sunday, after she had been buried, they placed a candle at her head and said: “We have little wax, and the night is already growing longer. When we rise for Matins, let this candle be lit.” Then they closed the door and departed.

After they had slept, they entered the basilica and found the candle burning, although they had left it extinguished. Healings of the sick are also frequently performed at the tomb of this devout woman.

## CHAPTER CV. On the tomb of Crescentia of Paris

There was a tomb in a village of the Parisians, not far from the place that, as they say, is now called the Elder Church. It was covered by no protection, and on the stone there was written [Col. 0904C]:

> HERE RESTS CRESCENTIA, A MAIDEN CONSECRATED TO GOD.

But no generation could recall what her merit had been or what she had done in the world [Note: [Col. 0904D] The memory of this Crescentia has been so completely obliterated that absolutely nothing is known about her, nor is it known where her tomb was.].

Recently, however, this epitaph was read by a certain cleric. Moved by faith, some people suspected that the Virgin might have obtained something from the divine majesty. While they remained in this state of suspicion, a man whom the heat of a tertian fever afflicted with severe trembling scraped a little dust from the tomb and swallowed it. Immediately the trembling ceased, and he recovered. The report spread and often benefited many who were suffering from this illness.

Later, the city’s moneyer fell seriously ill. In a vision, the maiden appeared to him and said: “Go at once and cover the tomb of the virgin Crescentia. This will be your aid, so that you may not be tormented longer by the disease with which you are afflicted.” Trusting her, he sought tiles, built an oratory over the tomb, and was immediately released from his illness.

But so that the Virgin’s power might be honored even more greatly, a certain man in the city suffered from a toothache so severe that, when his jaw swelled, he could scarcely take even a little thin food. Full of faith, he went to the tomb. Having made a small pointed stick, as is customary for human use in cleaning the teeth, he placed it upon the maiden’s tomb. As soon as he touched the aching tooth with it [Col. 0905B], all the pain was stopped.

After this experience became known, those afflicted by this pain sought the Virgin’s help and were immediately healed.

## CHAPTER CVI. On blessed Radegund of Poitiers

Blessed Radegund [Note: [Col. 0905D] This chapter is absent from manuscript Colb. tut. Gregory praises Saint Radegund in many places. See the notes to Book III of the *History*, chapter 7, and Book IX, chapter 2.], whom we mentioned at the beginning of the book (A.D. 587, 13 August), departed from this world after completing the labors of her life (chapter 5). When we received news of her passing, we went to the monastery in the city of Poitiers, which she herself had founded.

We found her lying in a bier. Her holy face shone so brightly that it surpassed the beauty of lilies and roses. An immense multitude of nuns stood around the bier, about two hundred in number. Converted through her preaching, they lived holy lives. According to the rank they had held in the world, some came not merely from senatorial families but even from the royal lineage; all flourished in this form of religious life.

They stood weeping and saying: “To whom are you leaving us as orphans, mother? To whom do you entrust us in our desolation? We have left our parents, our possessions, and our homeland, and followed you. To whom are you leaving us, except to perpetual tears and grief that will never end?

“Until now, this monastery was greater to us than the spaces of villages or cities. Wherever we went, when we looked upon your glorious face, there we found gold, there silver; there we gazed upon flourishing vineyards and waving fields; there were meadows green with flowers of every kind. From you we gathered violets; you were our glowing rose and shining lily. Your words shone for us like the sun, and like the moon they kindled for us, amid the darkness of our conscience, the bright lamp of truth.

“But now the whole earth has been darkened for us, and the space of this place has narrowed, since we are no longer worthy to look upon your face. Alas for us, abandoned by our holy mother! Happy are those who, while you were still alive, departed from this world!

“We know indeed that you have been joined to the choirs of holy virgins and to the paradise of God. But although this consoles us, it is still grievous to us that we cannot behold you with bodily eyes.”

While they were saying these and other things amid their lamentation, and while we could not restrain our tears, I turned to the abbess [Note: [Col. 0905D] Agnes, the first abbess, was still alive; Gregory mentions her in many places. Her feast is celebrated on 13 May.] and said: “Refrain for a little from these tears and attend instead to what is necessary. Our brother Maroveus, bishop of this city, is not here, because the duty of visiting the parishes has taken him away. Now take counsel, lest the holy little body suffer injury and the grace that God has granted to the blessed limbs be taken away while burial is delayed. Hasten the rites due to her, so that she may be honorably committed to the tomb.”

The abbess replied: “What shall we do if the bishop of the city does not arrive? The place where she is to be buried has not been consecrated by a priestly blessing.”

Then the citizens and the other honored men who had gathered for the funeral of the blessed queen ordered my insignificance, saying: “Rely upon the affection of your brother and bless that altar [Note: [Col. 0906D] From this we infer that in ancient times cemeteries had to be consecrated not only by priestly blessing but also were never without an altar, where the sacred rites for the dead could be performed. In Book II of the Life of Radegund, section 27, she is said to have been buried in the church of Saint Mary, which, as we have already observed, is now possessed by secular canons, under the title of blessed Radegund.]. We trust in his goodwill: he will not regard it as troublesome if you do this, but will rather give thanks for the favor. We beg you to rely upon him, so that the holy flesh may be given to burial.”

Thus, instructed by them, I consecrated the altar in that very cell. But when we lifted the holy body and began to escort it with psalmody, the possessed immediately cried out, confessing the holy woman of God and declaring that they were being tortured by her.

As we passed beneath the wall, another crowd of virgins began to raise their voices and lament from the windows [Note: [Col. 0906D] The nuns could not leave the monastery according to the rule of Saint Caesarius.] of the towers and even from the wall’s battlements. Amid the sound of weeping and the striking of hands, no one could restrain his tears. Even the clergy, whose duty it was to sing the psalms, could scarcely complete the antiphon through their sobs and tears.

Then we approached the tomb. The abbess, with foresight, had made a wooden chest in which she had enclosed the body, embalmed with spices. For this reason, the burial pit was wider, so that, after the individual side slabs of two tombs had been removed, the chest containing the holy limbs could be placed alongside them [Col. 0906C–0907A].

After prayer had been offered, we departed, leaving it to the bishop of the place that, after he had celebrated Mass, the tomb should be covered with its lid.

When we returned to the monastery, the abbess led us with the virgins through the various places where the Saint had been accustomed either to read or to pray, mourning and saying:

“Here we enter the cell, and we do not find our mother whom we have lost. Here is the place where, bending her knees with tears, she used to implore the mercy of almighty God, and she is not seen by us. Here is the book in which she read, but her voice, seasoned with spiritual salt, does not strike our ears. Here are the distaffs with which she used to spin through long fasts and abundant tears, but her holy fingers are not seen.”

As they said these things, the tears were renewed, sighs were uttered, and the very inward parts of those who mourned dissolved into weeping. Such grief had occupied my heart that I would not have ceased from tears, had I not known that blessed Radegund had been taken from the monastery in body, not in virtue; taken from the world and placed in heaven.

## CHAPTER CVII. On Bishop Tetricus

Although all the manuscripts include these three chapters in their tables of contents, I have been unable to find any that presents anything beyond the bare titles [Col. 0907B]. Nevertheless, so that some knowledge might be had of the saints whom they indicate, I have thought it worthwhile to bring here the little that we have observed concerning them.

[Saint Tetricus, bishop of Langres, succeeded his father, Saint Gregory (A.D. 572, 18 March). Gregory speaks of him in many places. We have observed more about him in the notes to Book IV, chapter 16, but there is no need to repeat it here.]

## CHAPTER CVIII. On Saint Orientius, bishop

Two Lives of Saint Orientius are found among the Bollandists, on 1 May. From the earlier and more ancient one we infer that he governed the church of Auch around the middle of the fifth century (A.D. 450, 1 May), at the time when Littorius, the Roman commander, was captured and killed by the Goths. In the later Life he is said to have succeeded Saint Ursinianus.

His body is preserved in a church consecrated to his name, together with a celebrated monastery of the Cluniac order, in the city of Auch itself [Col. 0907C–0908].

## CHAPTER CIX. On the virgin Quiteria

The Acts of Quiteria exist, but they are entirely fabulous. She is especially honored at Aire in Gascony (A.D. …, 22 May). Its church, situated at Manso of Saint Quiteria near the city, enjoys the privilege of being a co-cathedral and bears the title of an abbey; its abbot is also the bishop.

Her bones, which were kept in the monastery of Saint-Sever, in the headland of Gascony, under the Rule of Saint Benedict and the Congregation of Saint Maur, were thrown into a fire by the Calvinists. The Catholics rescued them from the flames, half burned, as best they could. She is honored on 22 May; for that day see the Bollandists and Gononus, Book III [Col. 0907D]. Tamayus, however, gives many fables about her.

## CHAPTER CX [Alternative numbering: CVII]. On Saint Paulinus, bishop of Nola
The life of the venerable Paulinus, bishop of the city of Nola [Note: [Col. 0907D] The word “bishop” occurs only in Colb. a, and there in another hand. Jerome, Ambrose, Augustine, Gregory the Great, and many of the Fathers celebrated Paulinus’s praises; their testimonies, together with the Blessed Man’s writings, Life, and other works, were published with the greatest diligence at Paris in 1685 by the distinguished Le Brun. See also Chifflet’s *Paulinus Illustrated* [Col. 0908D]. He was buried at Nola in the church of Saint Felix, which he had built. He is said to have been transferred from there to Rome, where he is displayed in the church of Saint Bartholomew.] (431, 22 June), was born of noble lineage. He married Tarasia, a woman like himself, possessed great wealth, and was very rich and prosperous both in landed possessions and in the resources of his household. [Col. 0908A] But as soon as that Gospel reading penetrated his ears in which the Lord rebukes a young man on account of his riches, saying, “Go, sell everything that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matthew 19:21), and also, “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God” (ibid., 24), he immediately sold everything that he possessed and distributed it to the poor.

Freed from every desire, he follows the Master unencumbered, thinking that by this means he would become rich in the riches of paradise if he were seen to possess nothing transitory. The divine Majesty granted him that what He had declared impossible through the Gospel this man might merit to fulfill in practice as something possible.

One day a man came to him seeking alms, and he said to his wife: “Go and give him what he needs.” She replied: “We have nothing more than one loaf of bread.” He answered her: “Go, I say, and offer it to him. The Lord will provide food for us.” But she, wishing—as though with commendable prudence—to keep something in reserve lest anything be lacking, refused to offer it. Meanwhile some men arrived saying that their masters had sent them to deliver a supply of grain and wine to him, but that they had been delayed because a storm had carried away one of their ships with its wheat.

Then the man of God turned to the woman and said: “Understand that you have now stolen one loaf from the poor man, and for that reason this ship has been sunk.”

He therefore set out with his wife, as though traveling to another region, possessing nothing except his own person. After a long time, when the inhabitants of his region were searching for him and he could nowhere be found, a merchant from that city came to the town [Col. 0908C] in which the blessed man was serving the heavenly Lord. When he saw him, he immediately threw himself to the ground and embraced the saint’s feet, saying: “This is the blessed Paulinus, renowned throughout the whole world, whom his fellow citizens sought for a long time but could not find at all.” As he recounted all his deeds, those who heard were struck with amazement.

Nor was there delay: when the priest died in the city of Nola, Paulinus himself was appointed in his place as bishop. That church possessed many riches, and the Lord fulfilled in him what He had deigned to promise through the Gospel: “Whoever has left everything for my sake will receive a hundredfold in this age, and in the age to come will possess eternal life” (Matthew 19:29).

Yet after accepting the episcopate he always presented himself as humble, because he knew that he would be exalted before God if he pursued humility. Whatever money from the revenues of the church came into his hands was immediately distributed to the poor. His most chaste wife did not leave him.

The holy man was also of extraordinary prudence and learned in rhetorical literature. His work made this very evident when it reached us. For when he wrote on various subjects both in verse and in prose, he composed six books in verse on the virtues of blessed Martin [Note: [Col. 0908D] All this was composed not by Paulinus of Nola but by another man, who in some manuscripts is called Paulinus of Périgueux; his little works have been published more than once.]; he also wrote other verses in [Col. 0909A] his praise.

He saw him while he was still in the body and received from him the restoration of his own eye. He shone with such a multiplication of spiritual gifts of grace [Note: [Col. 0909D] The fourth case is used instead of the sixth.] that, before his death, he beheld with bodily eyes Saint Martin himself and Januarius of Italy [Note: [Col. 0909D] The manuscripts have “Genuarius.” Florus copied this in his Martyrology under 22 June. The celebrated Januarius meant here is the bishop of Benevento, who suffered at Pozzuoli with other martyrs during the persecution of Diocletian on 19 September. His body was transferred to Naples. Uranius the presbyter recounts this vision in the letter that he wrote to Pacatus concerning the death of blessed Paulinus [Col. 0910D].], before he gave up his spirit. They had departed from this world before him.

And because we had read nothing about the life of this blessed man, we have therefore recalled what we learned through the report of the faithful when we wished to speak about almsgiving. Concerning his passing, however, we have among us an extensive reading [Note: [Col. 0910D] The letter of Uranius concerning Saint Paulinus’s passing is extant and has been published more than once.], and for that reason we have not followed him systematically.

Behold what almsgiving bestows; behold what treasures God grants to His saints who love Him in the poor. Conversely, from those who gape after the evil of avarice and wickedly desire, He takes away what they covet, in accordance with that saying of the holy Gospel: “To the one who has, more will be given, and he will abound; but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away” (Matthew 13:12; 25:29).

## CHAPTER CXI [Al., CVIII]. Concerning a merchant who did not give alms

Likewise, the report of many people confirms that the following occurred somewhere in a seaport. A certain poor old man, weighed down with purses, came to the seashore. Approaching the harbor, he began to ask the sailors for alms, and he persistently importuned the man who was first aboard the ship, saying: “Give me something.”

Then the sailor, angered, said: “Go away, you decrepit old man, please, and do not ask us for anything. We have nothing here except stones.”

But the old man replied: “If you say that what this ship contains in your possession is stones, may everything be turned into stones.”

Immediately the entire cargo of the ship—everything that could be eaten—was turned into stone. For I myself saw among it dates and olives harder than marble. Once they had been changed into the hardness of stone, they nevertheless never lost the color they had possessed: they retained the same shape and the same appearance.

The ship’s owner, moved to repentance, could nowhere find the old man whom he sought. And, as they say, he sent the transformed goods through many cities to be seen, so that they might serve as an example to everyone, lest they commit similar offenses.

Behold what you do, shameless avarice: you made a poor man poor who, by not giving to a poor man, thought he could become richer.

## CHAPTER CXII [Al., CIX]. Concerning another man who adulterated wine

I will not be silent about what also happened to another man who attempted to multiply his earthly profits by adulteration. A certain man near the city of Lyon worked so hard that he could scarcely possess a single *triens*. Inflamed by that accursed hunger for gold—“for hunger for gold is acquired through gold once obtained,” according to that verse of our Prudentius—

he therefore bought wine with this one *triens* [Note: [Col. 0910D] Here Colb. a ends, its remaining leaves having been torn away.], mixed it with water, and sold it again for silver coins, doubling his money. He did this again and again, and became such a follower of shameful profit that eventually he earned one hundred *solidi* from that single *triens*.

But God’s judgment confounded the devil’s profits. For when the avaricious merchant had gathered his gold into a purse, intending to possess the money for only a moment, he went to another merchant’s market. Having taken out the *triens*, as though he intended to make some purchase, he began conversing with his associate. His purse was made of Phoenician leather [Note: [Col. 0910D] Jerome mentions Babylonian skins for decorating books in his letter to Laeta.], such as people customarily carry by hand.

And suddenly a kite arrived, seized it with its feet, and attempted to tear it apart, thinking from its color that part of it was flesh. But when it felt no fat in it, it flew over the bed of the Arar, from which the man had drawn water and mixed it with the wine, and dropped the loosened purse into the river.

The merchant tore his hair, threw himself to the ground, and scattered dust over his head, saying: “Woe to me! I have been crushed by God’s judgment and have lost the money that had been amassed unjustly, for from one *triens* I raised up one hundred *solidi*. Now that I have lost one hundred *solidi*, only one *triens* remains to me. Woe to me: as I did, so I have received; and I see that what I acquired from nothing has returned to nothing.”

“Such money, devil, is yours; by such profit you lead those who obey you [Note: [Col. 0910D] The printed edition reads: “you led the disobedient to God.”] into Tartarus. Such commerce both brings the mark of loss in the present and produces various kinds of punishment in the future.

“Keep away from these things, I beg you who read this; keep away, and do not become participants in such deeds. Let your profits be the grace of the divine Majesty; let your pursuits be the teaching of Holy Scripture. Let your accumulation take place in the purses of the poor, whose burning fire may extinguish the flames of eternal Gehenna. This too must be sought from the Lord’s mercy, not pursued by our own strength. May He deign to grant it to us through the holy intercession of those whose sacred miracles this book reveals, so that, having rendered a good account not only of earthly riches but also of the talents of His word, and having received the reward of increase, we may merit to hear from Him: ‘Well done, good servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your Lord’” (Matthew 25:21). Amen.

Here ends the book *On the Glory of the Confessors*.

In a parchment codex that formerly belonged to the monastery of Saint-Denis near Paris and is now at Antwerp in the possession of the Reverend Fathers Bollandists, there is found at the end of Gregory of Tours’s book *On the Glory of the Confessors* a closing statement concerning Pippin, in whose time the codex was written, and his consecration as king of the Franks. This took place after the abdication of Childeric, the last king of the Merovingian family [Col. 0911]. We have thought it worthwhile to reproduce the statement here, copied from the codex itself and published by those scholars, in order to confirm what we observed above, column 685, in the notes to the third continuator of Fredegar concerning this matter.

If you wish to know, reader, in what period this little book appears to have been written and published for the precious praise of the holy martyrs, you will find that it was in the year 767 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the time of the most fortunate, peaceful, and Catholic Pippin, king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, son of the blessed-memory, late Prince Charles; in the sixteenth year of his most fortunate reign, in the name of God, in the fifth indiction; and in the thirteenth year of his sons, the same kings of the Franks, Charles and Carloman.

They were consecrated by the hands of the man of holy memory, the most blessed lord Pope Stephen, together with their aforesaid father, the glorious lord Pippin, king, with sacred chrism, by divine providence and through the intercession of Saints Peter and Paul. For the aforesaid most flourishing lord Pippin, pious king, had been elevated to the royal throne three years earlier, by the authority and command of the lord Pope Zacharias, of holy memory, through the anointing with sacred chrism by the hands of the blessed priests of Gaul and through the election of all the Franks.

Afterward, by the hands of that same pontiff Stephen, on a single day, in the church of the aforesaid blessed martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius—where the venerable man Folradus is known to be archpresbyter and abbot—he was anointed and blessed as king and patrician, together with his aforesaid sons Charles and Carloman, in the name of the Holy Trinity.

In that same church of the blessed martyrs, on one and the same day, the aforesaid venerable pontiff also blessed Bertrada, the most noble and devout wife of the aforementioned flourishing king, who was dressed in royal garments, with the sevenfold grace of the Spirit. At the same time he confirmed the princes of the Franks with the blessing and grace of the Holy Spirit, and bound them all by such a prohibition and law of excommunication that they should never dare to choose as king one sprung from another’s loins, but only one from among those whom divine piety had deigned to exalt and whom, through the intercession of the holy apostles, it had determined to confirm and consecrate through the hands of their vicar, the most blessed pontiff.

For this reason we have briefly inserted these matters in the final little page of this book for your charity, so that the posterity of later ages may be able to know it through the succession of times and the report of the people.

## [ON MIRACLES]

[Col. 0911]

## [ON THE MIRACLES OF SAINT MARTIN, BISHOP (C)*]

[Col. 0911]

## LETTER OF SAINT GREGORY, BISHOP OF TOURS, IN FOUR BOOKS ON THE VIRTUES OF SAINT MARTIN, BISHOP

993–994 To the holy lords and sweetest brothers and sons in Christ’s love [Note: [Col. 0911A] Germ., with the printed editions, has “most beloved.”], of the Church of Tours entrusted to me by God: Gregory, a sinner.

Those miracles [Note: [Col. 0911A] Most manuscripts have “the miracles that.” Here Codex Beccensis begins.] which our Lord God has deigned to perform through blessed Martin, His bishop, while he was still in the body, He continues daily to confirm in order to strengthen the faith of believers. He now adorns [Al., “adorns”] his tomb with the virtues that He worked through him when he was in the world; and He grants benefits to Christians through him who formerly sent that bishop to the perishing nations.

Let no one therefore doubt the virtues of the past when he sees the gifts of present signs being dispensed, when he sees the lame raised up, the blind given sight, demons driven away, and every other kind of illness cured by him as physician [Note: [Col. 0911A] The printed editions, together with some manuscripts, have “through him as mediator.” Bell., “by healing.”].

I, for my part, relying on the credibility of that book [Note: [Col. 0911A] So the manuscripts Mart., Colb. a, Germ., Rom., Laud., Bell., and most others. Colb. b has “repeating.” [Col. 0912A] The printed editions have “relying on the credibility of this book.”] which was written by those who came before us concerning his Life, shall, as far as I recall [Al., *de quanto*], commit his present virtues to the memory of posterity, with the Lord’s command.

I would not have presumed to do this unless I had been admonished twice and a third time through a vision. Yet I call almighty God as witness: once, in a dream [Note: [Col. 0912A] Several manuscripts have “in sleep.” And below, “from different persons … and I saw these things.”], at midday, I saw in the basilica of the lord Martin many weak people oppressed by various illnesses being healed, and I saw them while my mother watched [Note: [Col. 0912A] Bec. has: “I saw my mother waiting.”]. She said to me: “Why are you slow to write down the things that you see?”

I replied: “Are you unaware [Note: [Col. 0912A] Clar. and other manuscripts: “Are you unaware … that I am poor in letters.”] that I am ignorant of letters, and that, being foolish and uneducated, I do not dare to proclaim such marvelous virtues? If only Severus or Paulinus were alive, or at least Fortunatus were present, to write these things down! For if I attempt to record them, I immediately incur disgrace in this matter.”

She said to me: “And do you not know that, for the understanding of the people among whom we live, if someone speaks as you are able to speak, that makes him all the more distinguished? Therefore do not hesitate, and do not cease doing these things, because it will be a crime for you if you remain silent about them.”

I, however, eager to undertake the work, am afflicted by the torment of a double weariness: grief and terror alike. Grief, because the many virtues performed under our predecessors have not been written down; terror, because I, a rustic, am undertaking a distinguished work.

Yet drawn on by hope in divine mercy, I shall undertake what I am commanded. For, as I believe, He who, bringing forth water from a dry rock [Al., “stone”] in the wilderness, quenched the thirst of the people may bring these things forth through the barrenness of my tongue [Al., “service”]. Or certainly He will once again cause the mouth of an ass to speak, if, opening my lips, He deigns through me, an unlearned man [The printed edition has “unworthy”], to unfold these things.

But why should I fear my rusticity, when our Lord, Redeemer, and God, in order to destroy the vanity of worldly wisdom, chose not orators but fishermen, and not philosophers but rustics?

I therefore trust in your prayers [Note: [Col. 0912A] The printed editions have “in your prayers.” Bec. has “let us therefore believe,” and so forth.], because, even if unpolished speech cannot adorn the page, the glorious Bishop will nevertheless make it shine with distinguished virtues.

## THE FOUR BOOKS OF SAINT GEORGE FLORENTIUS GREGORY, BISHOP OF TOURS, ON THE MIRACLES OF SAINT MARTIN, BISHOP

[Col. 0913]

# BOOK ONE

## CHAPTER ONE. That Severus composed the Life of Saint Martin

999 There are many who have set down the virtues of Saint Martin, either in sustained verse or in prose style. Of these, the first was Severus Sulpicius [Note: [Col. 0913B] So too Gennadius in his *Catalogue*, chapter 29: “Severus, surnamed Sulpicius.” Others, however, prefer to write “Sulpicius Severus.” In the manuscripts, indeed, the name Sulpicius is sometimes placed before the other, sometimes after it, as we observed in a codex of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, no. 652, written about eight hundred years ago. Some think that this man was the same as Sulpicius Severus, bishop of Bourges; conversely, others maintain that the name of Sulpicius of Bourges was introduced into the Roman Martyrology in place of our Sulpicius. See the Bollandists under 29 January, and above the notes to chapter 50 of *The Glory of the Confessors*.], whose love for the Saint of God burned so fiercely that, while Martin was still living in the world, he wrote one book on the marvels of his life. After the blessed man’s passing, he wrote two further books, which he wished to be called *Dialogues* [Note: [Col. 0913B] Severus wrote three dialogues, but the title *On the Virtues of Saint Martin* is prefixed only to the latter two, although he also deals with him in the first. [Col. 0913C].].

In them, reporting through Posthumianus, he inserted several matters concerning the virtues of hermits and anchorites. Yet in no respect could he find our Martin inferior, and he equated him with the earlier apostles [Note: [Col. 0913C] The printed editions have “with the apostles and holy martyrs, and holy men,” and so forth. Below they have “the apostle Paul.” Severus does not have the word “Paul” at the end of Dialogue 3, from which this passage is taken.], so that he even said: “Fortunate indeed is Greece, which deserved to hear an Apostle preaching; but neither did Christ abandon Gaul, to which the Lord granted the possession of Martin.”

## CHAPTER II. That blessed Paulinus composed the same Life in verse

Blessed Paulinus too, bishop of the city of Nola [Note: [Col. 0913C] So all the manuscripts and printed editions have it here and in book *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 110. Yet that Paulinus must be distinguished from the bishop of Nola. The Nolanus was a contemporary of Saint Martin; but the man whose works are praised here had received, as Gregory himself writes a little later, a catalogue of miracles from Perpetuus, bishop of Tours, and at the beginning and end of book six he praises Perpetuus for having related to him certain and indisputable miracles. This Perpetuus was the sixth bishop to preside over the church of Tours after Martin’s death.

Moreover, the same author repeatedly praises Paulinus, bishop of Nola. In manuscript codices he is called Paulinus of Périgueux, a name by which the city of the Petrocorii, commonly Périgueux, is sometimes designated. Perhaps Severus’s passage in Dialogue 3 misled Gregory: there Posthumianus is instructed to visit Paulinus of Nola and communicate to him what he has heard, so that, just as he had already done with the earlier little book, he might disseminate other works throughout Italy and Illyricum. Fortunatus, in book 1 of *The Life of Saint Martin*, also seems to have fallen into the same error as Gregory. Nevertheless, since Saint Paulinus wrote frequently in praise of Saint Martin, Fortunatus’s words may be referred to him. The books of Paulinus praised by Gregory were reprinted many times, generally under the name of Paulinus of Nola.], after composing verses [Al., “in verse”] on his virtues, which Severus had gathered together in prose, included in five books those miracles that occurred after Martin’s death—that is, in the sixth book of his work.

He says: “When demoniacs were being carried through the grilles of the basilica by an aerial flight, and were often hurled by the demon’s force into the well located within the same basilica, they were afterward recovered unharmed before the eyes of the people. We too have seen this happen in that same well in our own time.

“Another demon dragged a vessel that had been taken possession of headlong toward the river, as though it were carrying off and about to drown prey that it had captured [The printed edition has “released.”]. But the aid of the blessed Confessor was not absent from the one about to perish. For when he entered the river and made for the farther bank, he suffered no harm and emerged even with his clothes dry [Note: [Col. 0914C] Nearly all manuscripts have “without harm, with dry clothes.”]. When he reached the cell of the Greater Monastery, he appeared cleansed.

“This man also testified [Note: [Col. 0915C] Several manuscripts, together with the printed editions, have “they testified.” But Gregory is speaking of Paulinus, who had expressed this very thing in verse.] that the demoniac was accustomed to utter many voices, to speak very often in the languages of unknown peoples, to disclose future events, and to confess crimes. But, as we have said, after he touched the Saint’s threshold [Note: [Col. 0915D] Most manuscripts have “the holy threshold.”], he departed healed.

“Egidius [Note: [Col. 0915D] He was the master of the army in Gaul, later said to have been replaced by Childeric, king of the Franks. He was shut up at Arles when, after invoking the aid of Saint Martin, he burst out of the city and routed the Visigoths. This victory brought security to the emperor Majorian and peace to Gaul. Valesius, book 4 of *Frankish History*, states that it occurred in 459.] too, when he was besieged by enemies and, deprived of assistance, was being attacked in confusion, was freed through the invocation of the blessed Man, when the enemies were put to flight. At the very hour when it happened, a demoniac in the middle of the basilica declared that this had been granted through Saint Martin’s favor.

“A certain girl, afflicted with paralytic fluid and, worse still, entangled in the error of fanatical worship, sought the Blessed One’s tomb. After keeping vigil, she was restored to health. But when she was again recalled to the vomit of idolatry, she once more contracted the illness from which she had been free through the favor of the blessed Bishop.

“A certain madman named Chunus [Note: [Col. 0915D] It is certain from Paulinus that this should be read *Chunus*, to which nearly all manuscripts agree. Some have, erroneously, *scimus*, and the printed editions have *Thimus*. Several manuscripts also have *rapidus* instead of *rabidus*.], driven by demonic inspiration, violently seized the crown of the tomb that proclaimed the Saint’s merit. Immediately deprived of sight, he returned the plunder under the compulsion of pain and recovered the sight he had lost.

“Another man [Note: [Col. 0915D] He belonged to the same race of Chuni, or Huns, who had then burst into Gaul, as Paulinus says.], moved by the tempter, drew his sword and attempted to strike someone in the Confessor’s atrium. At once his anger was turned back upon himself, and, as God’s swift judgment pursued him, he pierced himself with the very blade.

“Finally, when the people joyfully wished to transport columns for the adornment of the Blessed One’s church, a certain man who was envious and opposed to this work threatened his wife with many things because she provided assistance to those asking for help with the wagons [Note: [Col. 0915D] This passage is corrupt in the manuscripts and printed editions. Most have “he would provide to those asking.” From Paulinus’s text I think it should be restored as follows: “He was opposed and threatened his wife with many things because he would provide assistance—that is, help—to those asking for help in transporting the wagons.” Below: “choked by his blows,” since, as Paulinus has it, he would scarcely have been choked by pressing upon the sand while there was only water in the stream. This entire section is absent from Codex Gat.].

“When, in his pride, he struck the horse, he was thrown into a small stream and died, suffocated in the basin of the watery whirlpool by his own blows. Then, with a young man [Note: [Col. 0916D] So most manuscripts. Others have “with the people.” The printed editions have “with the young people.”] leading the way, the columns were carried as far as the Blessed One’s church.

“They also report that whenever oil had been placed at the blessed tomb, they saw it increased. The holy Bishop Perpetuus, worthy to be proclaimed the Blessed One’s disciple, carried a flask of oil to the holy tomb so that the infused virtue of the righteous man might sanctify it [“*eum*” means “it”; the printed editions have “*eam*”]. He scraped dust from the marble covering the holy limbs and mixed it into the liquid; from this so much oil overflowed that the priest’s garment, fragrant with nectar-like scent, was drenched with an olive-colored stream. Many sick people experienced healing from it [Note: [Col. 0916D] The printed edition has: “They obtained health … when sanctified.”]. Storms were also often kept away from fields purified by this liquid.

“When a certain devout man, full of faith, had approached the holy church and, thirsting for the Saint’s grace, was considering what he might take from the blessed shrine for his healing, he came near the tomb and begged the sacristan to give him a little blessed wax from the tomb. He received it and departed joyfully; he confidently placed it upon the field in which he had sown grain.

“A very violent storm then arrived, one that had often devastated the neighborhood in previous years, but it was kept away by this blessing and did no further harm there, as it had been accustomed to do [Note: [Col. 0916D] So Gat., Vinc., and Bec. Most other manuscripts have “the neighborhood.” Some have “the neighboring area.” The printed editions have “everything.”].

“When the magnificent and desirable festival of Easter approached, the people devoutly came to the Blessed One’s cell, where he had often lived among angels. Kissing each place in turn or watering it with tears—where the holy man had sat before, or prayed, or taken food, or granted rest to his body after many labors—they prepared a fleet of ships and set out to cross the river, so that they might approach the blessed tomb and, pleading for forgiveness with tears, prostrate themselves before the Confessor.

“While they were sailing, however, the wind was stirred up by the tempter’s impulse, the fleet [Note: [Col. 0916D] Rom. has “the ship.” Below the printed edition has “and the people everywhere from the river.”] sank in the deep, and both sexes were carried away by the river. As they were tossed amid the storms of the waves, and every hope of escape had vanished, one voice from all was raised in a cry, saying: ‘Merciful Martin, rescue your servants and handmaids from this present destruction!’

“When these words had been spoken, behold, a gentle breeze arose, carrying the bodies of the submerged from the waves unharmed, and, with the wave serving them, restored them all to the shore that they desired. No one perished; rather, all were saved and celebrated the Easter festival with the greatest rejoicing. For there was not absent that power which, splitting the Jordan, led the people across beneath the masses of water along a dry bank, when Joshua consecrated on the shore to which he had come the twelve stones taken from the riverbed, bearing the signs of the apostles; nor that power which, with a merciful right hand, embraced Peter as he was perishing and rescued him lest he perish; nor that which drew a sailor about to drown, invoking Martin’s Lord [Note: [Col. 0916D] Pith. has “with the sailor invoking the Lord through Martin.” But, together with the other manuscripts, Paulinus contradicts this: he records that a sailor, placed in danger, invoked the God whom Martin worshiped and escaped unharmed …], from the depths of the sea to the shore that he desired.

“A certain man, asking to take something from the holy church as a blessing, received a little wax [The printed edition has “a small amount of wax.”] from the Saint’s tomb and stored it within the inner rooms of his house as a heavenly treasure. It happened that, through the envy of the tempter, a fire was set, and the house was surrounded by devouring flame, which spread across the dry timbers and destroyed everything.

“Meanwhile a cry was raised to heaven and the aid of blessed Martin was implored. He also remembered the piece of wax brought from the Saint’s church [Note: [Col. 0917D] Most manuscripts have “and he remembered the piece of wax.” Others have simply “the wax.”]. When it was found and thrown into the fire, it immediately extinguished the entire blaze. In a new miracle, the wax, which was accustomed to feed fire, overcame the violence of the fire by the power of holiness.

“Paulinus wrote this in verse in the sixth book of his work, having received a catalogue of these events from Saint Perpetuus, bishop. But when the written account of this catalogue came to him, his nephew was suffering from a serious illness. Trusting in the Saint’s power, he said: ‘If it pleases you, blessed Martin, that I should write something in your praise, let yourself appear over this sick man.’ When the written account was placed upon the sick man’s chest, the fever immediately withdrew and he was healed [Note: [Col. 0917D] Paulinus himself also relates this miracle in verses that he published in thanksgiving for it.].

“But the presbyter Fortunatus also composed the whole work of his Life in four books of verse. Encouraged by these examples, we too, although inexperienced, shall nevertheless attempt to recall to memory something of the virtues of the holy and most blessed Martin that was performed after his death, insofar as we can discover it. For this will be a subject for writing that is not found inserted in the work of Severus or Paulinus.”

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the ordination and passing of blessed Martin

Radiant and glorious lord Martin, resplendent throughout the whole world, like a new sun rising while the old world was passing away [Note: [Col. 0917D] Others have “while the sun was already setting over the world.”], was born at Savaria in Pannonia, as the earlier History relates, and was sent, with God’s help, for the salvation of Gaul. Having illuminated it with virtues and signs, he reluctantly accepted the honor of the episcopate in the city of Tours, compelled by the people. There he lived a glorious and almost inimitable life, and, after five periods of five years, with two additional months and ten days, in the eighty-first year of his age, during the consulship of Caesarius and Atticus, he rested in peace at midnight.

It is therefore perfectly clear that his glorious and praiseworthy passing occurred on a Sunday; we shall establish this in the following chapter through reliable testimony. It is considered a matter of no small merit that the Lord received him into paradise on that day on which the same Lord and Redeemer, victorious over the underworld, rose again; and that he who had always celebrated the solemnities of Sunday without stain should, after the tribulations of the world, be placed in rest on a Sunday.

## CHAPTER IV. How the singing concerning the passing of Saint Martin was revealed to Saint Severinus, bishop

Blessed Severinus [Note: [Col. 0917D] This chapter and the next are absent from Colb. b, Vinc., Bec., and Germ. In the Claromontane and Colb. tut. codices, only their beginnings occur, directing the reader to seek them elsewhere in the same codex, where they are copied out of order under the title of sermons, lessons, or a letter, because they were read under that title in the divine offices. They are in fact copied thus also in Bec., Vinc., Colb. b, and another Germ. manuscript written about the year 700. In the Corbie codex written about the year 900, they occur under the title *Versicolus on the Passing of Saint Martin*, and Severinus is there called bishop of Colossae. The entire history of this vision is also related in the *Life of Saint Severinus, Bishop of Cologne*, printed in Surius under 23 October.], bishop of the city of Cologne, a man of upright life and praiseworthy in all respects, was making his customary round of the holy places with his clerics on Sunday after the morning hymns [Note: [Col. 0918D] In the manuscripts Laud., Bell., Gat., Mart., and Colb. a, the words “after the morning hymns” are absent. Others have “after matins” or “after the morning offices.”]. At the hour when the Blessed One died, he heard a choir singing on high.

He summoned the archdeacon and asked whether his ears were struck by voices that the bishop himself heard attentively. He replied: “Not at all.” Then the bishop said: “Listen more carefully.”

The archdeacon began to stretch his neck upward, raise his ears, and stand on tiptoe, supported by his staff. But I believe that he was not of equal merit, since he was not worthy to hear these things [Col. 0918B]. Then he and the blessed bishop alike prostrated themselves on the ground and prayed to the Lord that divine mercy might permit the archdeacon to hear it.

When they had risen, the old man again asked: “What do you hear?”

He replied: “I hear the voices of singers as though they were in heaven, but I do not know at all what it is.”

The bishop said to him: “I will tell you what it is. My lord Martin, the bishop, has departed from this world, and now the angels are carrying him upward while singing. And, to delay him for a little while so that these things might be heard, the devil attempted to hold him back with the wicked angels; but, finding nothing of his own in him, he departed in confusion.

“What then will become of us sinners, if the hostile [Al., “wicked”] party wished to harm so great a priest?”

While the priest was speaking, the archdeacon marked the time and quickly sent men to Tours to investigate these things carefully. When they arrived, they learned with complete certainty that blessed Martin had passed away on that very day and at that very hour when Saint Severinus had heard the singing choir.

And if we return to the History of Severus [Note: [Col. 0918D] Codex Mart. has “of Severinus.” Gregory is referring, I believe, to the vision that Sulpicius Severus says was revealed to him in the letter to the deacon Aurelius.], he wrote in his book of Life that Martin’s passing had been revealed to him at that same hour.

## CHAPTER V. How the same passing was shown to blessed Ambrose
At that time the blessed Ambrose, whose eloquence even today sheds its fragrance throughout the whole Church, was bishop over the city of Milan. His custom in celebrating the feasts of the Lord’s day was this: when the reader came with his book, he would not presume to begin reading until the saint had given a sign.

It happened that on that Sunday, after the prophetic reading had been recited, while the reader was already standing before the altar [Note: Corb. reads this way; others have “when the reading had already been read, before the altar,” and some “before the altars.” If Gregory’s account is accurate, either Ambrose’s death must be placed later than the year 397—for he died in April—or it is not true that Martin died in November of that same year. This story has moreover been depicted in mosaic for about nine hundred years on the altar of the Ambrosian Basilica at Milan; an image of it may be found in Puricellus, vol. I, p. 133.], preparing to deliver the reading from blessed Paul, the most blessed bishop Ambrose fell asleep above the holy altar.

When many people saw this, and no one at all dared to wake him, after nearly two or three hours had passed they awakened him, saying: “The hour is already passing. Let the lord order the reader to read the lesson, for the people, already very tired, are waiting.”

But blessed Ambrose replied: “Do not be troubled. It is of great benefit to me that I have fallen asleep in this way, since the Lord has deigned to show me such a miracle. For you should know that my brother, the priest Martin, has departed from the body, and that I have attended his funeral. After the customary service had been completed, I had not finished even the brief chapter when you awakened me.”

Then, astonished and filled with wonder, they noted the day and hour and carefully made inquiries. They discovered that the day and hour were precisely those of the saint’s passing, at which blessed Ambrose had said that he had attended his funeral rites.

O blessed man, at whose passing the company of the saints sings, the choir of angels rejoices, and the army of all the heavenly powers comes forth: the devil is confounded in his presumption, the Church is strengthened by power, and priests are glorified by a revelation. Michael took him up with the angels; Mary welcomed him with choirs of virgins; paradise holds him joyful among the saints!

But why do we attempt his praise, when we are not sufficient to complete it? He himself is his praise, whose praise never departed from his mouth. Would that we could at least explain his story in simple form [Note: In Corb. this conclusion is added: “The verse of Saint Ambrose concerning the passing of Saint Martin, bishop and confessor, is finished.” Bec. has: “Our Lord Jesus Christ departed, who lives with the Father and the Holy Spirit,” etc.].

## CHAPTER VI. The Translation of the Blessed Body of Saint Martin

[Note: This chapter is absent from Colb. b. In Vinc. and Bec. it appears out of order, and in Vinc. under the title of a sermon on the translation, etc. In Clar. and Corb. tut. only the opening words are present.]

It is worthwhile also to insert into the reading how, with an angel’s assent, his holy body was transferred to the place where it is now worshiped [Note: So most manuscripts, as also below. Others, along with the printed editions, read “venerated.” The difference is immaterial. Gregory often used the word “worship” to express the reverence with which we handle sacred things, or the honor with which we attend holy men.].
