In the sixty-fourth year after the passing of the glorious lord Martin, blessed Perpetuus obtained the honorable chair of the see of Tours. Having attained this dignity, and with the great agreement of the devout [Note: Several manuscripts, along with the printed editions, read “with the great agreement of the vows.”], he resolved to place the foundations of a larger church above the blessed remains than the one that had previously stood there; and, applying himself to this undertaking with keen diligence, he brought it wonderfully to completion. There would be much to say about this construction, but since it still exists, we have thought it better to be silent about it [Note: On this, see Book II, chapter 14, and Book X, chapter 31 of the *History*. The Malleacense Chronicle says that it was burned in the year 903 and restored by Hervaeus the treasurer. See also the note at column 211, editor’s note.].

When the desired time came for the priest to dedicate the church and transfer the holy body from the place where it had been buried, blessed Perpetuus summoned for the feast day the neighboring bishops, as well as a considerable multitude of abbots and various clerics. Since he wished to carry this out on the Kalends of July, after keeping vigil for one night, at daybreak they took a mattock and began to dig up the earth that lay above the holy tomb.

When it had been uncovered, they laid hands upon it in order to move it, and although the entire multitude labored there, they achieved absolutely nothing throughout the whole day. After keeping vigil for another night, they tried again in the morning, but could accomplish nothing at all. Then, troubled and terrified, they did not know what to do.

One of the clerics said to them: “You know [Al.: “you know”] that after three days the anniversary of his episcopate [Note: That is, the anniversary of his ordination as bishop. It is still commemorated in the martyrologies together with the feast of his translation on 4 July. See Mabillon, *Gallican Liturgy*, Book II, no. 72. Bede, in his authentic *Martyrology*, commemorates all three feasts together.] was accustomed to occur; perhaps he is warning you that he ought to be transferred on that day.”

Then, devoting themselves to fasts, prayers, and unceasing psalmody [Ed.: silence] day and night, they passed the intervening three days without interruption. On the fourth day they approached and laid their hands upon the tomb, but were utterly unable to move it.

As they all stood there terrified by fear, now intending to cover with earth the little vessel they had uncovered, an old man of venerable whiteness appeared to them, his hair shining like snow. He said that he was an abbot and spoke to them:

“How long will you remain troubled and delay? Do you not see the lord Martin standing there, ready to help you if you lay your hands upon him?”

Then, casting aside the cloak that he wore, he placed his hand upon the sarcophagus with the other priests. Crosses had been prepared and candles were lit; an antiphon was begun, and all together they raised the voices of those singing psalms [Note: The printed editions read “singing.” Gat. reads “all the voices of those singing psalms.”] on high.

At the old man’s effort the sarcophagus was immediately moved with the greatest ease, and, with the Lord’s assent, it was brought to the place where it is now worshiped. When it had been arranged according to the priest’s desire [Al.: vow], and Masses had also been said, they came to the meal [Note: Concerning such banquets celebrated on the birthdays of saints—which were later prohibited because of abuses—Savaro collects much material in his commentary on Letter 15 of Book IV of Apollinaris Sidonius; consult him. See also Augustine’s Letters 22 and 29.].

They carefully searched for the old man, but could not find him at all. Nor was there even a person who had seen him leave the basilica. I believe that he was an angelic power, which declared that it had seen the blessed man and afterward appeared to no one.

From that day many miracles occurred in that place, but through negligence they were not written down. We, however, have been unable to remain silent about as much as we either saw happen in our own time or certainly learned had happened.

## CHAPTER VII. The Mute Theodemund

A certain young man named Theodemund [Note: Laud., Vinc., Rom., Bec., and the two Colb. manuscripts read: “A certain Theodomund came.” Gat. has “Theodmundus.”], with the passage to hearing and speech obstructed, used to return daily to the holy basilica. Bending himself in prayer, he moved only his lips. For although his understanding was sound, he could emit no voice; he had been deprived of the faculty of speech.

He seemed to pray so earnestly that he was often seen weeping in the midst of his silent words. If anyone, out of regard for his reward, gave him some alms, he immediately distributed it to poor people like himself; and, asking others for a gift by gestures, he handed the proceeds to those in need.

After he had spent three years [Bel.: “hours”] in that holy place in this devotion, one day, warned by divine mercy, he came before the holy altar. Standing there with his eyes and hands raised toward heaven, a stream of blood mixed with corruption burst from his mouth. Spitting upon the ground, he began to groan bitterly and to cough up—I do not know what parts—with blood, so that it seemed that someone was cutting his throat with a blade. Corruption also hung from his mouth like blood-red threads.

Then, when the bonds of his ears and throat had burst, he rose, again [Gat.: “meanwhile”] lifting his eyes and hands toward heaven, and, with his mouth still bloody, first broke into these words:

“I give you great thanks, most blessed lord Martin, because, by opening my mouth, you have caused me, after a long time, to release words in your praises.”

While all the people marveled and were astonished at such a miracle, they asked whether he had recovered his hearing as well. In the presence of the people he replied freely that he heard everything [Note: So Bec., Gat., and Rom. Others read “with the people as witnesses.” The printed editions have “he testified before the people.” What follows appears in the printed editions as follows: “After his recovery, therefore, he returned to Queen Chrodechild,” etc. Bal. reads “Throdechildem.” Chrodechild was the widow of Clovis the Great; after her husband’s death she withdrew to Tours, where she also died, as Gregory relates in Book IV, chapter 1 of the *History*. There was a school in each church where clerics were instructed in singing and other disciplines. Hence in pontifical and ritual books the term “school” designates whatever is to be sung collectively by the clergy. See Menard’s notes on the *Gregorian Sacramentary*.].

Thus restored to health, he was taken in by Queen Chrodechild out of reverence for the power of Saint Martin, and was placed in the school, where he committed the entire sequence of the psalms to memory. God perfected him as a cleric and allowed him to remain for many years thereafter in the service of the Church.

## CHAPTER VIII. The Blind Woman Chainemunda

A certain woman named Chainemunda [Note: Colb. tut. and Gat., together with the printed editions, have “Chamemunda.” Clar. has “Chanemunda.” Colb. b and Bec. have “Camemunda.”], deprived of the light of her eyes and unable to keep to the road unless led by someone else, very devout and full of faith, came to the venerable church of blessed Martin the bishop.

As we have said, she was not only blind but also covered over her entire body with ulcers [Al.: wounds]. Corruption with pustules had taken possession of all her limbs, and her face was miserable and horrible to behold, so that the people thought her a leper.

Every day she hurried by touch to the church of the glorious bishop [Note: So nearly all the manuscripts. The printed edition has: “She stood with faith before the same glorious bishop.” Mart. reads “stood.”]. After nearly three years, while she was standing before the tomb, her eyes were opened, so that she could see everything clearly. All the sickness of her limbs was removed, and the fluid that had flowed from her body dried up. New skin grew over her, and she was restored to her former health so completely that not even a sign of illness remained on her body.

She lived for many years thereafter, continually giving thanks to almighty God because, through his blessed Confessor, he had restored her in such complete health.

## CHAPTER IX. Blessed Bishop Baudinus

I shall not omit how the immediate invocation of his name calmed a stormy sea [Note: The printed editions read “which.” Clar. has “how great.”].

When blessed Baudinus [Note: He is also called this in Book X, the final chapter of the *History*, where he is listed in section 16. Gat. nevertheless has “Baudoenus,” Colb. b “Bladenus,” Bec. “Blandenus,” and the printed editions “Baudenus.”], bishop of the city of Tours, was being carried by ship to a village [Note: All the manuscripts read this, except Mart., which has “from village to village.” The printed editions have “from city to city.” Below, Rom. reads “was moved”; Bec. “of the river”; the edition “of the waves.”], suddenly a dreadful storm-cloud arose with violent wind. The calm sea was stirred by the force of the blast, and the ship was tossed by the mass of the waves.

One wave lifted its head first into the breakers; another dipped down among the gaps between the waves. Some hung down on the outer face of a watery mountain; others, with the waves opened, yawned into the depths [Note: Gat. has “these before the scene”; Colb. tut. “these in the scene”; Colb. a “these into the scene”; Bec. “these in the meal.” The word *scena* should be retained. It designates the exterior face of something, by comparison with the stage of a theater, and is used in this sense by Tertullian in *On the Soul*, by Apollinaris Sidonius in Book VII, Letter 1, by Apuleius in Books II and V, by Eumenius, and others.]. Nor did the mast remain upright, although it bore the sign of the blessed cross [Note: The Laud. and Colb. a manuscripts read “which bore the sign of the blessed king.” A sign of the holy cross was evidently painted on the sail attached to the mast, or the mast itself represented a cross.].

Then, with their limbs weakened by fear and everyone already prepared to die without hope of life, the old man fell prostrate in prayer with tears. Stretching both hands toward the stars, he implored the aid of blessed Martin and cried out, asking him to deign to come swiftly to his assistance.

But one of the unbelievers said: “That Martin whom you invoke has already abandoned you and does not come to your aid in this necessity” [Al.: “will come to your aid”]. I truly believe that this speech was uttered by the tempter in order to disturb the blessed priest in his prayer.

But he repelled that dart with the breastplate of faith and demanded the holy man’s protection more and more insistently, while at the same time urging everyone to pray.

While this was happening, a most sweet fragrance, like balsam, suddenly filled the ship. It was as though someone were walking around with a censer, and the scent of incense spread through the air. At the arrival of this fragrance, the violence of the savage winds subsided; the masses of water that stood around them broke apart, and the sea became calm.

All marveled at the peace of the waves, since they had already given themselves up for dead, and, as soon as calm weather was granted, they were brought safely to shore. No one should doubt that this storm was calmed by the arrival of the blessed man.

Then all together they gave thanks to the Lord because he had deigned, through the invocation of his bishop, to free them from this danger.

## CHAPTER X. The Man Who Carried the Relics of the Saint to Cambrai

During his lifetime, a certain man from the church of Cambrai requested relics of blessed Martin. Having received them in the evening, he set out singing psalms. After he had crossed the River Loire [Note: The edition has “crosses.” Several manuscripts read “was crossing, and when it had grown late, suddenly,” etc.], it became late, and suddenly the sky was darkened. Great flashes of lightning and great thunder descended.

While this was happening, two lances of the boys, emitting fiery torches, provided light for the travelers [Note: Other manuscripts read “with flames emitted, they provided light.”]. The flashing spears went before them, offering the travelers no less a marvel than a benefit [Note: Mart. reads “carrying them before the travelers”], and displaying the power of the blessed bishop.

## CHAPTER XI. The Conversion of the King of Galicia and His People, or, Concerning the Suevi

A sterile tongue fails while attempting to recount such great miracles.

The son of a certain Galician king named Charraric [Note: Most manuscripts have “Chararic.” There was no king of Galicia by that name. But this is evidently the same man whom others call Theodemir or Ariamir. Under him the Suevi, who had occupied Galicia from the beginning of the fifth century, renounced the Arian heresy and joined the Catholic Church. The son of the king mentioned here was, as is clear from Book IV, chapter 7 below, Miro, who succeeded his father in the kingdom in the year 570.], fell gravely ill. He was so afflicted that he merely trembled with the breath of life.

His father had subjected himself, together with the inhabitants of that region, to the foul Arian sect. That region also was more soiled than the other provinces by leprosy [Note: Colb. a reads “was soiled by leprosy.” This gave Pithoeus occasion to add to his manuscript “with this leprosy,” so that the term “leprosy” would designate the Arian heresy. But Gregory is speaking of bodily leprosy, as is clear from the conclusion of this chapter.].

When the king saw that his son was in extremity, he said to his attendants: “That Martin whom they say in Gaul shines with many miracles—what religion did he belong to? Please tell me.”

They replied: “He governed the people of the Catholic faith with pastoral care while he was in the body, affirming that the Son ought to be worshiped together with the Father and the Holy Spirit as equal in substance and omnipotence. Even now, established in the seat of heaven, he does not cease to care for his own people by continual benefits.”

The king said: “If what you say is true, let my faithful friends hasten to his church, carrying many gifts. If they obtain healing for my little son, I will believe the Catholic faith and believe what he believed.”

He therefore weighed out gold and silver equal to the weight of his son [Note: Those of lesser means were accustomed, when seeking the aid of the saints, to offer a candle equal in weight to the sick person, or measured according to his height.], and sent it to the venerable place of the tomb. When they had brought it there [Note: Bec. has “when it had been brought there.” The printed edition has “when those who had set out”], they offered the gifts and prayed at the Blessed One’s tomb for the sick man.

But because the sect still occupied his father’s heart, the son did not immediately deserve to receive complete healing. The messengers returned and told the king that they had seen many miracles at the Blessed One’s tomb, adding: “We do not know why your son was not healed.”

The king understood that his son could not be healed until he believed that Christ was equal to the Father. In honor of blessed Martin, therefore, he built a church. When it had been completed with marvelous workmanship, he cried out:

“If I am deemed worthy to receive the relics of the just man, I will believe whatever the priests preach” [Note: Bec. has “If I should be deemed worthy to receive,” etc.].

Thus he sent his men again with a greater gift. When they came to the holy place, they requested relics. When the usual cloths were offered to them [Note: That is, linen cloths or pieces of fabric that had been placed for a time upon the blessed man’s tomb. This was done at Rome at the tombs of the Apostles, as is known from the letters of Gregory the Great; he called such cloths *brandea*.

Mariana is mistaken in Book V, chapter 9 of his *History of Spain*, where, apparently from Gregory’s account alone, he writes that the envoys of Theodemir obtained from the people of Tours a portion of the cloak Martin had worn while alive. I think that the famous cloak of Saint Martin, which our kings arranged to have clerics carry with them from the tomb of the holy bishop on journeys, especially military expeditions, was nothing other than such a cloak or linen cloth; from this the clerics were called chaplains. Gregory also mentions here a church of Saint Martin built in Galicia. Some, as Mariana observes in the cited passage, hold that it was established at the hot springs, now Orense, or Auria, but without stronger evidence than the fact that the chief church of that city bears the name of Saint Martin.], they said: “We will not do it in this way. Please grant us permission to place something there, which we may afterward take up again.”

Then they placed a measured portion of a silk cloak upon the holy tomb and said:

“If we find favor before the patron whom we seek, what we have placed here will weigh more on the following day; it will be placed with us as a blessing, sought through faith” [Note: Most manuscripts read: “and it will be for us a blessing sought.” Compare Book I, chapter 28, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*.].

After keeping vigil for one night, at daybreak they weighed what they had placed there. So great was the grace of the blessed man infused into it that they lifted the bronze scales into the air as high as the scales could rise by their own momentary movement.

When the relics had been raised with great triumph, they heard the voices of people singing psalms who had been confined in prison in the city. Amazed at the sweetness of the sounds, they asked the guards what this meant. The guards replied: “The relics of the lord Martin are being sent to Galicia, and therefore psalms are being sung in this way.”

Then the prisoners, weeping, invoked Saint Martin, asking him to free them from the prison of their confinement by his visitation.

The guards were terrified and fled. The barriers and restraining fastenings were broken, and the freed people rose from their bondage. They came as far as the holy relics while the crowd looked on [Note: Manuscripts have “while the people waited”; others, “while the people watched.”]. Weeping, they kissed the blessed relics and at the same time gave thanks to blessed Martin for their release, because he had deigned in his mercy to save them.

Then, through the priest’s intervention with the judge [Note: That is, the bishop, namely the bishop of Tours, where these events occurred.], they obtained pardon for their offenses and were released unharmed.

When the bearers of the relics saw this, they rejoiced greatly, saying: “Now we know that the blessed bishop deigns to show himself favorable to us sinners.”

Giving thanks in this way, and with the protection of their patron accompanying them, they reached the harbor of Galicia swiftly by a prosperous voyage: on gentle waves, with moderate winds, a hanging sail, and a calm sea.

Then a certain man named Martin, from a distant region, who is now regarded there as a priest, was warned by God and came to them. I do not believe that this happened without divine providence either: on the day when the blessed relics were lifted from their place, he was moved to depart from his homeland, and thus entered the harbor of Galicia together with the relics themselves.

The people received these relics with the greatest reverence and confirmed their faith by miracles. The king’s son, freed from all illness, hurried forth in good health to meet them.

Blessed Martin received the rank of priestly grace [Note: First he was bishop of the monastery of Dumium, which he had founded under the Benedictine rule; afterward he was raised to the metropolitan see of Braga. Fortunatus attributes the conversion of the Suevi to both Martins in the letter prefixed to Book V of his poems, addressed to this same Martin together with Poems 1 and following; he also praises him elsewhere more than once.].

The king confessed the unity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit and was anointed with chrism together with his entire household. The people were cleansed of the foulness of leprosy, and all the sick were healed. From that time until now the disease of leprosy has never appeared among them.

The Lord granted such grace at the arrival of the relics of the blessed patron that it would take far too long to recount the miracles performed there on that day. For that people is now so eager in the love of Christ that, if a time of persecution should arise, they would all willingly embrace martyrdom.

## CHAPTER XII. Queen Ultrogotha

Queen Ultrogotha as well [Note: Nearly all manuscripts have “Ultrogotho.” She is also called this by Fortunatus and in canon 15 of the Fifth Council of Orléans. Bec. has “Ultrogodis.” She was the wife of Childebert I. Gregory speaks of her and her two daughters in Book IV, chapter 20 of the *History*, and Fortunatus in Book VI, poem 8. She was buried in the basilica of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. The author of the *Life of Saint Balthildis* praises her among holy queens in these words: “It is said of Queen Ultrogotha, wife of the most Christian king Childebert, that she was the nurse of orphans, the comforter of the fatherless, the support of the poor and servants of God, and the helper of faithful monks.”], having heard of the miracles performed at the place where the holy remains rest, desired with devout heart to behold them, as though she had come to hear Solomon’s wisdom [Note: Nearly all manuscripts read “as though she had heard Solomon’s wisdom.” Gregory alludes to the Queen of Sheba, who came to Jerusalem in order to hear Solomon.].

Abstaining from food and sleep, and sending generous alms ahead of her, she reached the holy place. Entering the basilica, she was afraid and trembled and did not dare approach the blessed tomb. She proclaimed herself unworthy and unable to draw near because her sins stood in the way.

Nevertheless, after spending one night in vigils, prayers, and abundant tears, she offered many gifts in honor of the blessed Confessor and requested that Masses be recalled [Note: The printed editions, together with Clar., read “celebrated.” The reading of all the other manuscripts should be retained, for Gregory uses this expression elsewhere. See Book I, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 51. Fortunatus also used it more than once, as our learned Mabillon observed in Book I, chapter 6 of the *Gallican Liturgy*. There he retracts what he had previously written about a recalled Mass, explaining that the expression means nothing other than a Mass celebrated. This passage also confirms that interpretation.].

While these were being celebrated, three blind men who had long sat at the feet of the blessed bishop deprived of sight were suddenly surrounded by an immense radiance and received back the light they had once lost.

When this had happened, a shout of praise was raised to heaven, glorifying God. At this miracle the queen ran forward, and the people also gathered. All marveled at the woman’s faith and at the glory of the Confessor; above all, however, they praised our God, who grants such power to his saints that he deigns to perform such deeds through them, assigning to this world, among its other lights, the blessed Martin as an immense star, through whom its darkness might shine again [Al.: “might shine”].

For truly, like a fruitful olive tree, he offers fruit to the Lord every day from the conversions of the wretched [Note: All manuscripts read this except Clar., which has “from the conduct of the wretched.” The printed editions instead have: “every day he displays glory to the Lord through deeds and through the conversions of the just.”].

## CHAPTER XIII. The Man Who Was Suffering from a Pustule in Extremity [Note: Most manuscripts read “who was stationed in the army.”]

Nor should I pass over what I recall was reported by my venerable fellow-servant, the presbyter Fortunatus.

A certain man in Italy was so afflicted, when the poison of a pustule [Note: Most manuscripts, especially the older ones, have *pusulae*, and nearly always use this spelling whenever the word recurs.] had spread through him, that he was in danger and all hope of life had been abandoned. He asked some bystanders who had gone to the church of blessed Martin [Note: That is, who had visited it. The verb *esse* often occurs in Gregory with this meaning.].

One of those present said that he had been there. The sick man asked what he had brought away from there as a blessing. The man denied that he had taken anything. The sick man then asked what clothing he had been wearing when he had gone to the saint’s church. He replied that it was the clothing he was wearing at that very moment.

The sick man faithfully cut off a piece of the garment and placed it upon the pustule. As soon as it touched the sick man’s limbs, the wound of the poisonous pustule lost its force. Through this remedy, the power of the saint was manifested, and the sick man was restored to health.

He asserted that a special healing power prevailed among the Italians: if anyone were struck by the wound of a pustule, he should seek refuge at the nearest oratory of blessed Martin [Al.: “should go”]. If whatever was first snatched from the veil [Note: Jerome praises Nepotian for his care of churches, among other things mentioning the veils that hung at the doors. Our Gregory mentions the veil of the sanctuary in Book IV, chapter 31 of the *History*. The Council of Narbonne also speaks of it in canon 13. Anastasius frequently mentions such veils in his *Lives of the Popes*. In the larger churches of Gaul even today, on certain days a veil stretched across the church separates the choir from the sanctuary, or the place where the high altar stands; veils around the altar, commonly called curtains, are also hung. Walls too were covered with veils, which Gregory here calls *palliola*; sacred stories were usually depicted on them for the instruction of the uneducated.] of the door, or from the small hangings suspended from the walls, were placed upon the sick person and adhered to him, it became a source of healing.

He asserted that this remedy had delivered his own natural father from death by the pustule.

## CHAPTER XIV. The Italian Fortress Called Tertium

The same man reported the following:

On the summit of a fortress in the region of Italy called Tertium, an oratory of blessed Martin has been founded. Beside the neighboring tower, whenever the enemy approached by night through treacherous attacks during an invasion by barbarians, if any of the guards in the tower drew from its sheath a lance, sword, knife, or stylus, the entire weapon gave off such a light for nearly an hour [Note: Five manuscripts have “for more than an hour”] as though the iron had been turned into a candle.

At once the guards, warned by this sign, became more attentive to their watch and drove out the enemies lurking nearby with stones. This is rightly attributed to the help of Saint Martin, who by his proximity showed himself a diligent and present guardian to the peoples devoted to him.

We learned of this miracle from the Fortunatus mentioned above.

## CHAPTER XV. The Lamp Oil over the Saint’s Painted Image

He also confessed that at Ravenna, while he and his companion Felix were studying rhetoric [Note: This chapter is absent from Colb. b and Bec. We have retained the reading of Gat., Clar., and Vinc. Other manuscripts have: “At Ravenna, with Felix, his companion.” The printed editions read: “and with Felix and Rhetoricius, his companions.”

This passage can easily be clarified from Paul the Deacon, who in chapter 13 of Book II of his *History of the Lombards* recounts the same miracle. He says it occurred at Ravenna, when Fortunatus was studying rhetoric there with Felix, later bishop of Treviso, as Paul had said in the preceding chapter:

“While this man was suffering the most severe pain in his eyes, and Felix, his companion, was likewise suffering from pain in his eyes, both went to the basilica of the blessed Paul and John, which is situated within the same city. There is also an altar there, built in honor of blessed Martin the Confessor, with a nearby window in which a lamp had been placed to give light. Fortunatus and Felix immediately touched their afflicted eyes with its oil. At once the pain departed, and they obtained the health they desired.”

As Paul continues, this was the occasion that led Fortunatus—who was born at Duplavilla, not far from the fortress of Cenita, or the city of Treviso, and was educated at Ravenna—to travel to Gaul to the tomb of Saint Martin. From there he went to Poitiers, where he was first ordained presbyter and then made bishop of that city.], he and his companion Felix touched their eyes with oil that was burning in a lamp beneath the painted image of blessed Martin, and confessed that sight had returned to them [perhaps: “had been given to them”].

## CHAPTER XVI. The Steward Placidus

Similarly, in the aforementioned city, when the steward Placidus, given up by the physicians, fled to another nearby oratory of the girls [Note: Most manuscripts have “to another.” Mart. has “to an arium.” The printed edition has “to that.” There was an old monastery at Ravenna dedicated to Saint Martin, said to have been built by King Theodoric and later called Saint Apollinaris Nuovo. Perhaps in Gregory’s time religious women lived there, succeeded by monks of our order, who possessed the place for a long period. Finally, in 1514, the place passed to the Franciscans, while the abbey’s revenues were assigned to Saint Paul’s in Rome.] and lay down in the courtyard, blessed Martin came to the abbess in a dream during the night.

When she asked him what he was doing, he said that he was resting. The saint said to her:

“I had already intended to return to Gaul, but because of this man who lies outside in the courtyard, I declare that I have been delayed.”

The abbess then rose and reported the vision. She gave the man assurance that he would be freed from danger, which he certainly did obtain.

But [perhaps: “and”], as the aforementioned presbyter relates, it is much more desirable to venerate the glory of Martin in the regions of Italy than—if one may say so—in the place where his own remains lie buried [Note: The printed editions have: “in the regions of Italy where he is venerated, than where his own remains lie.”], to such an extent that the frequent miracles cannot be gathered together in words, nor can such infinite numbers be contained in books.

## CHAPTER XVII. Events That Took Place at Amiens
1019 At the gate of Amiens, where once the blessed man covered a shivering poor man with a cut cloak, the faithful built an oratory. [Note: [Col. 0928D] Severus Sulpicius recounts this deed as exceedingly famous throughout the Church in the *Life of blessed Martin*. The place where it occurred is now occupied by the Reverend Fathers Celestines; in the middle of their church choir stands a column bearing an inscription that sets out the event. Ambianum is a very well-known city, commonly called Amiens, the capital of Picardy, under the metropolitan see of Rheims.] Religious girls now serve there in honor of the holy Bishop, possessing little means, except that the devotion of the devout often feeds them.

At one time, however, they had a few beehives that had been given to them. When a certain envious man saw them, he said to himself: “If only I could take something from these vessels.” On the following night, prompted by the devil, he took away three hives and loaded them onto a boat, intending that, once he had crossed the river, he might more easily secure what he had stolen. But, I believe, this theft became an impediment to him, as was afterward clearly proved. Accordingly, when people were hurrying toward the river-port at sunrise in order to cross, they saw the boat at the bank, the bees emerging in swarms from the hives, and the man lying prostrate apart from them. Thinking that he was overcome by sleep—for they had already learned from the girls that a theft had been committed—they hurried to bind him. But when they approached, they found him dead. At once they informed the girls of what had happened and restored to the little cell what had been taken by theft [Al.: stolen], marveling that the sentence of divine vengeance had so quickly overtaken the man.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Oratory of Siroialum

So also at the oratory of Siroialum [Note: [Col. 0929D] Thus the manuscripts, except Colb., which has *Sirmalense*. Bec. has *Sirmalensim*, and Victor. *Sirogalense*; this reading is also found in Bell., Colb. a, and Colb. tut. in the list of chapters prefixed to the book, where Gat. has *Sirolialensi* and Mart. *Sirojarensi*. The printed editions here have *Sirojabense*. Marollius thinks this place is Siran-la-Late, not far from Severiacum and Bellismum near Tours; others, however, think it is Saint-Ciran-du-Sambot, a village on the Anger between Châtillon and Luçay.]—whose altar was consecrated by the holy Confessor’s gracious hand—while many were obtaining the benefits they sought, a certain paralytic came and kept watch through the entire night, holding a candle as tall as his own stature. When morning came and light was restored to the world, he himself leaped up sound and whole, walking with unhindered steps before the testimony of the people. 1020

## CHAPTER XIX. On Bella, the Blind Woman

Nor will I be silent about what he accomplished for blindness, when a devout woman sought the blessed man’s tomb. A certain woman from the territory of Tours, named Bella, was suffering grievously after losing the light of her eyes. When she was tormented day and night by unremitting pains, she said to her family: “If only I were taken to the basilica of the lord Martin, I would immediately recover my health. For I trust that he can pour light into my eyes, since he was able to heal the leprosy of a poor man by touching him with a kiss.” [Note: [Col. 0929D] Severus Sulpicius testifies in the *Life of the holy man* that this happened at the gate of the city of Paris. [Col. 0930D] That miracle afterward provided the occasion for the construction of an oratory in his honor, which has been mentioned elsewhere.]

Then, led by assistance, she came to the holy place. There, persisting in fasts and frequent prayers, she deserved to recover the sight she had lost. She was healed in such a way that, although she had come blind and was led by another, she returned with sight, destined to become a plentiful guide for the blind. Later she took a husband and bore children, and, sound and well, gave thanks to her Restorer.

## CHAPTER XX. On Ammonius, Who Fell from a Height

Since we have already narrated twice or three times how virtues were performed and dangers dispelled merely through invocation of the glorious name, I shall unfold how the blessed Bishop, when invoked at the very brink of death, provided support to a certain man who was perishing. A certain Ammonius, an agent of the holy basilica [Note: [Col. 0930D] The printed editions have *vices agens*, “acting in place of.” But the manuscript reading is better. Gregory frequently mentions *agentes*, meaning those who, as they are also called today, were appointed to conduct the affairs of the Church or of distinguished men.], was returning from supper, soaked with wine, when, with the enemy driving him on, he fell from a high cliff adjoining the road. The depth of that place was nearly two hundred feet. As he rolled down the depth of that precipice and flew downward without the rowing of wings, he cried out for the help of Saint Martin at every moment of his descent. [Col. 0930A] Then, as though shaken from his mount by the hands of others, he was thrown onto trees growing in the valley. Thus descending gradually from branch to branch, he reached the ground without danger of death. Yet, so that the work begun by the ambusher would not appear wholly frustrated, it slightly injured one of his feet. But when he came to the temple of the glorious lord Martin and devoted himself to prayer, he lost all force of pain.

## CHAPTER XXI. On Another Man Who Was Hanged

I do not think it superfluous to insert into this account how invocation of his name gave life to a dying man. In a certain place, a man was seized because of the crime of theft, beaten severely, and led to the gallows to be condemned to hanging. When he had reached this end, with death already approaching, he asked for time to pray. Then, with his hands bound behind his back, he threw himself face down upon the ground and began with tears to invoke the name of blessed Martin, asking that, even if he did not come to his aid in that necessity, he would at least excuse him from his sins thereafter.

When his prayer was complete, he was hanged, and the soldiers [Gat.: attendants] withdrew from the place. He, however, with his mouth half open and moving his lips a little, continued striving to implore the help of Saint Martin. After they had departed, his hands and feet were immediately released. Thus, while he hung there for two days, it was revealed to a certain religious woman [Note: [Col. 0930D] Several manuscripts, together with the printed editions, have “to a certain religious man . . . who.”] that she should take him down. When she came, she found him still alive. Then, with the help of blessed Martin, she took him down from the gallows and brought him unharmed to the church. Those who saw him there were astonished and wondered, saying: “How is he alive?” They asked him how he had been delivered.

He replied: “Blessed Martin rescued me from present death and brought me this far.” Truly, according to the understanding of my judgment, I consider the virtue displayed in this man no less than that displayed in a dead man raised to life: for the blessed Confessor, having broken—as I may say—the chasm of death and drawn him back from its mouth, restored him to life. He is still alive in the world to this day as a testimony to the power of the holy man.

## CHAPTER XXII. On Leomeris, the Cripple

I will not pass over what was done in the diocese of Condatensis. [Note: [Col. 0930D] That is, in a village. Gregory often uses this word to designate a *pagus*, or small district.] That place is illuminated by frequent miracles. For from there the blessed man, casting off the burden of the flesh, departed to the Lord.

A certain man named Leomeris, a servant of a man from Angers, had been struck by a stroke [Col. 0931A] [Note: [Col. 0931D] Thus all the manuscripts; that is, seized by apoplexy. The printed editions, however, have “struck by a serpent.”]. His hand was contracted and his tongue bound, and he remained rigid. Held in this weakness for a long time, he performed no work either for himself or for his master. Instructed by faith, he kept vigil at the basilica of the blessed man. His hand was restored and his tongue, freed from every impediment, became articulate. He testified to the miracle of Saint Martin before the people, saying: “Behold what the holy man of God has done this night. I am the witness; test it.”

When he returned to his master, he told him everything that had happened. But his master, by no means believing in the power of the glorious Bishop, assigned him again to his usual service. When he began to work, he was reduced once more to weakness. His master, understanding that this was a mystery of God, sent him again to the holy place to which he had previously gone. There he spent the night with the greatest devotion, and when day came he was restored to the health he had previously obtained.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Wiliacharius, Freed from Chains

I considered it worthy not to omit from my account what I heard from the priest Wiliacharius himself. At the time when Wiliacharius, through the treachery of Chramn, incurred the anger of King Chlotar [Note: [Col. 0931D] We have restored this passage from Gat., Mart., Bec., Colb. tut., and others. The printed editions, together with Clar. and several others, have: “At the time when Chramnus, or Chranius, incurred the anger of King Chlotar because of treachery,” and in the chapter title: “On Chramnus, or Chranius,” and so forth. Some codices call Wiliacharius *Wilicharius* or *Vihatharius*; others call him *Miliatharius*.], he fled to the basilica of Saint Martin and was kept there under guard in chains. But through the power of the blessed Bishop, the battered chains could not remain intact.

I do not know through what impending negligence he was captured outside the atrium. Loaded with iron and with his hands bound behind his back, he was being led to the king. Then he began to cry out in a loud voice and to pray that blessed Martin would have mercy on him and would not allow him to depart as a captive, since he had devoutly sought the saint’s temple. Immediately, while Bishop Euphronius was praying from the city wall toward the basilica, his hands were released and all the links of the chains broke and fell.

When he had been brought before the king, he was again held bound in fetters and chains. But when he invoked the name of the aforementioned patron, all the iron upon him was so crushed that one would have thought it had been potter’s clay. This alone delayed his release: he was not freed from the bond until he had invoked that most sacred name; once he had invoked it, everything was loosened.

Then the king, a man of superior understanding, seeing the power of Saint Martin working there, released him from the burden of his bonds and restored him to his former freedom. I learned from the mouth of the priest Wiliacharius himself, in the presence of many witnesses, that these things had happened. Would that the blessed Confessor deign to manifest himself to me in such power, so that he might loosen the bonds of my sins just as he crushed the massive weights of chains upon that man.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On Count Alpinus, Who Was Afflicted

Count Alpinus of the city of Tours, having been grievously consumed for a whole year by pain in one foot, had no rest day or night. Amid the very cries of his torment, he continually implored the help of Saint Martin. One night the blessed Confessor appeared to him in a vision, smiling with a cheerful face and bearing his customary weapons. When he imposed the blessed sign of the holy cross upon the afflicted foot, all pain immediately fled, and Alpinus rose healthy from his bed.

## CHAPTER XXV. On Charigisilus, the Cripple

After these events, Charigisilus [Note: [Col. 0931D] Bec. has *Charigilius*; the printed editions have *Charigisitus*.], the referendary of King Chlotar, whose hands and feet had become contracted by an excess of moisture [Note: [Col. 0931D] Several manuscripts have *contraxerant*, “had contracted.” This word frequently occurs in authors of the later age in place of “had become contracted.”], came to the holy basilica. Devoting himself to prayer for two or three months, he was visited by the holy Bishop and deserved to obtain health for his weakened limbs. He afterward became a member of the household of the aforementioned king [Note: [Col. 0931D] From this passage Labbeus proves in his *Historical Miscellanies* that the offices of *domesticus* and *referendarius* were entirely different.], and administered many benefits to the people of Tours and to those serving the blessed basilica.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On Aquilinus, the Madman

I shall also relate how the madness produced by demonic art was exposed at the saint’s basilica. A certain man named Aquilinus, while hunting with his father in the forests of Gaul, was seized by a terrible fear, the enemy lying in wait for him. His heart trembled, and meanwhile he appeared to be *exsensus* [Note: [Col. 0932D] That is, mad, as though “outside his senses.” Since the editors of the earlier editions did not notice this, here and often elsewhere, wherever the word recurs, they printed *extensus*.].

His parents, understanding that he was being disturbed by a demonic attack, brought him, according to the custom of country people, charms and potions from fortune-tellers and diviners. But when these customary remedies accomplished nothing [Note: [Col. 0932D] Other manuscripts, together with the printed edition, have “when that custom was of no avail.”], they urgently sought the help of Saint Martin, driven by their distress, saying: “He can uncover the malice of these ambushes who, as we have heard, exposed a great shadow worshiped under the false name of religion.” [Note: [Col. 0932D] This alludes to the story that Severus Sulpicius relates in the *Life of the holy man*. There he is said to have exposed the mask of a false martyr who had been a robber and had ended his life after being punished for his crimes, yet was regarded by the people as a martyr. Overcome by the holy man’s prayer, he appeared under the form of a foul and savage shadow and was forced to confess the imposture. In most manuscripts the word *multum* is absent.]

They sent Aquilinus from the region to the holy basilica. There he kept himself with the greatest austerity while at prayer and continually sought the Saint’s help. After he had remained there for a long time in this faith, all fear was removed, and he recovered the understanding he had previously possessed. Forgetting his parents, he has remained in that place to this day, serving there in return for the benefit he received.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On Charivaldus, Who Was Afflicted

A certain Charivaldus also encountered similar ambushes while hunting and lost the use of one side, his hand and foot having been weakened. Carried by the hands of servants to the glorious temple, he devoted himself to continual fasts and prayers for nearly a whole year. When he had done this, he recovered the health of all his limbs and joyfully returned home.

Therefore we warn that no one should be troubled by diviners, since they will never benefit the sick. A little dust from the basilica is more powerful than they are [Al.: a thousand of them] with their insane medicines.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the Severed Cord

Who could ever investigate or know how many miracles are continually performed, or have been performed, through the dust, the wax, or anything else that someone has been able to take from that place or from the tomb? Yet I thought it a crime to keep silent about one manifest miracle that I learned from the faithful.

A man full of faith sought to carry away secretly some token from the Saint’s basilica. Though he tried many times, he could never do so while he dared not act publicly. When he wished to return, he came by night to the cord from which the signal is moved and cut off a piece of it with a knife, carrying it away with him.

When he returned home, he brought healing through it to many sick people, so that there could be no doubt that a sick person would escape illness if he faithfully deserved to kiss that token. Behold what you grant, Holy One, to the faithful who devoutly seek your walls [Note: [Col. 0933D] Almost all manuscripts have *proprie*, “properly.”]. Through you those who have carried away votive tokens are saved, and with your subsequent aid they are delivered. But faith, steadfast faith, accomplishes all these things, as the Lord says: “Your faith has saved you” (Luke 18:42).

## CHAPTER XXIX. On King Charibert, Who Seized Church Property

It seems that this too should not be passed over in silence: how the holy man everywhere provides assistance to his servants for defending their property.

When King Charibert, hating the clergy, neglected the churches of God and, despising priests, had turned more toward luxury, it was brought to his ears that a certain place, which the basilica of Saint Martin had held for a long time, should be restored to the rights of his treasury. That place had been given the name Navicellae by ancient usage. [Note: [Col. 0933D] The place lies on the river Sicer, or Cisse, commonly called Nazelles.]

After receiving this wicked counsel, he quickly sent servants to bring that little estate under his own dominion. Since he appeared to possess it without possessing it lawfully, he ordered stablemen with horses [That is, with mounts] to be sent to the place and commanded that the horses be fed there without regard for justice.

The servants therefore approached and took the hay that had been piled up for the horses’ provisions. While the assigned service was being diligently carried out and the horses had begun to consume the hay supplied, they were seized by madness. Snorting at one another, they broke their reins, rushed across the open ground, and turned to flight. Thus, scattered disastrously, some were blinded [Bec.: killed], some were hurled from cliffs, and others, thrusting themselves into hedges, were pierced through by the sharp points of stakes.

At last the stablemen, understanding the anger of God, drove outside the boundary of the place the few horses they were able to catch, and received them back sound; they reported to the king that the property was being held most unjustly. After suffering these things, they said: “Release it, and there will be peace for you.”

The king, filled with fury, is said to have replied: “Whether it ought to be returned justly or unjustly [Note: [Col. 0934D] Bell., Clar., and Laud. have “whether it should be restored”; Bec., three Colb. manuscripts, Victor., and the others have “whether it should be retained.”], while I reign this basilica shall not have it.”

Immediately afterward, receiving his passage by divine command, he died. When the most glorious King Sigibert came into his kingdom, at the request of blessed Bishop Euphronius, he restored this property to the dominion of Saint Martin, and it remains possessed by his basilica to this day.

Hear this, all who possess power. Clothe some in such a way that you do not strip others; add to your riches what will not inflict harm upon the churches. For God is a swift avenger of his servants. Therefore we warn anyone in authority who reads this not to become angry. For if he becomes angry, he will acknowledge that it has been said about him.

## CHAPTER XXX. On Eustochius of Poitiers

In a similar manner the blessed Confessor appeared in matters unjustly taken from him. A certain Eustochius repeatedly brought a case against Saint Bishop Euphronius concerning the inheritance of his kinsman Baudulf, who had appointed the basilica of Saint Martin as his heir. Moved by Eustochius’s continual insults, the blessed Bishop returned to him something from those possessions.

But when Eustochius carried this to his house, his only son immediately fell into a fever. After burning with fever grievously for one day and one night, he died. The arrival of death was as immediate for the son as the father’s becoming master of property not rightfully due to him had been swift.

Like Gehazi, he possessed gold and silver, but he lost what was more precious to him: having acquired leprosy of the soul, he lost his son and never afterward deserved to obtain another.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On Him Who Swore Falsely in the Holy Portico

I will not be silent about how immediate divine vengeance came upon another man who had sworn falsely in the holy portico, so as to restrain the audacity of the treacherous.

Since the faithful provide necessities for that community of enrolled poor (*matricula*) which the Saint daily sustains through his beneficence from the alms of the devout, the blessed poor have the custom that, when many of them have dispersed to various places, they leave behind a guardian to receive whatever is offered.

Accordingly, a certain devout man brought one triant, with a view to a reward. The guardian of the place did not fear to conceal the coin he had collected from the brothers. [Col. 0935A] When the poor assembled at the sixth hour, they asked the aforementioned guardian what the blessed Shepherd, looking upon them with his customary kindness, had sent them; for they had heard that something had been given there.

He replied under oath: “By this holy place and by the powers of the lord Martin, no more than one silver coin came here.” He had not yet finished speaking—the words were still hanging in his mouth—when he suddenly fell trembling to the ground and, carried back to his little bed by the hands of others, began to sob violently.

When those standing around asked what was wrong with him, he replied: “I swore falsely about that triant which the poor were seeking, and therefore this immediate vengeance is scourging me. But I ask you to take it and return it to the poorhouse.” When it had been returned, he immediately gave up his spirit.

O unhappy man [Col. 0935B] [Note: [Col. 0935D] What follows to the end of the chapter is absent from Colb. b.], who, overtaken by wicked greed, perished in such a way that he both lost the profit of life and failed to retain the money he had gained.

But to what will accursed greed not drive mortal hearts? You who once, in your envy, caused the widow to purchase the heavenly kingdom with two small coins [Note: [Col. 0935D] The printed editions, together with several manuscripts, have “you had been for the purpose of selling,” and so forth.], now plunge this man into the depths for a single triant. You who hanged Judas by a noose for the price of the Master, now sink this man into Tartarus for a small coin. Let this, then, suffice to restrain the rashness of the wicked.

## CHAPTER XXXII. How His Power Restored Me Sound from Illness

Having completed the events that occurred in the case of others, I shall now undertake what the power of the present patron accomplished for me, unworthy as I am.

In the year 163 after the assumption of the holy and renowned man, blessed Bishop Martin, while Saint Bishop Euphronius was governing the church of Tours in his seventh year, and in the second year of the most glorious King Sigibert [Note: [Col. 0935D] The second year of King Sigibert is the common era year 563, and according to this calculation the year 400 was the last year of blessed Martin’s life. There is no variation in the reading here in either the printed editions or the manuscripts; hence Cointius considers that one should read above: “in the year 166 after the assumption,” and so forth.], I fell ill with malignant pustules and fever. Deprived of the use of drink and food, I was so distressed that, having abandoned all hope of present life, I thought only about what was necessary for burial.

For a persistent fever besieged my limbs with heat, seeking to drive my soul from my body. Then, already almost lifeless, I invoked the name of blessed Bishop Martin and recovered a little. Still making slow efforts, I began to prepare for a journey; for the thought had taken hold of my mind that I ought to visit the place of the venerable tomb. I was affected by such longing that I would not wish to remain alive [Note: [Col. 0935D] Cod. Laud. has “that it would be necessary”; Pith., in a later hand, has “I would think.”] if I were to set out too late. Although I had scarcely escaped the heat of my illness, I began again to burn with the fever of longing.

Without delay, though still scarcely strong, I undertook the journey with my companions. After traveling two or three stages, we entered the forests. I fell again into fever and began to suffer so severely that everyone thought I was about to die.

Then my friends approached me and, seeing that I was extremely exhausted, said: “Let us return home. If God wishes to call you, die in your own house; but if you recover, you will more easily complete your vowed journey. It is better to return home than to die in the wilderness.”

Hearing this, I wept bitterly. Mourning my misfortune, I said to them: “I adjure you by almighty God and by the judgment day feared by all the guilty, consent to what I ask. Do not abandon the journey we have begun. If I deserve to see the basilica of Saint Martin, I give thanks to my God; if not, carry my lifeless body there and bury it, for I have resolved not to return home unless I deserve to be brought before his tomb.”

Then, all weeping together, we undertook the journey we had begun. With the protection of the glorious lord going before us, we arrived at his basilica.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On Our Cleric Who Was Mad

At that time one of my clerics, named Armentarius, was very well educated in the spiritual Scriptures. He grasped musical melodies so easily that you would not have thought he was practicing them but writing them down. He was exceptionally diligent in service and faithful in what had been entrusted to him.

But when the poison spread, he lost all his senses through malignant pustules and had been reduced to such a state that he could neither understand nor do anything at all. [Col. 0936C] On the third night after we arrived at the holy basilica, we decided to keep vigil, and we did so.

When morning came and the signal for Matins was given [Note: [Col. 0936D] The manuscripts Gath. and Colb. tut. have: “When the signal was given at the hours of Matins.” Laud., Bel., and Colb. a have *commonito*, “having been announced.” Bec. has *commorato*, “having been delayed.” Note here that Matins is distinguished from the nocturnal Vigils. Today we call the Vigils “Matins,” but call Matins “Lauds.” Saint Benedict likewise distinguishes them in his Rule, as Gregory does here.], we returned to our lodging [Ed.: to sleep]. Resting on our beds, we slept until nearly the second hour.

When I awoke, with all languor and bitterness of heart removed, I felt that I had recovered my former health. Rejoicing, I called for a young household servant to attend me.

Armentarius rose and quickly stood before me, saying: “Master, I will prepare whatever you command.” But, thinking that he was still *exsensus* [Note: [Col. 0936D] Several manuscripts have *exsensim*, and so whenever the word recurs.], I said: “Go, if you can, and call the boy.”

He replied: “I will carry out whatever you command.”

Astonished, I asked what this meant. He said: “I understand that I am completely well, but there is one error in my mind: I do not know from which direction I came here.”

He then began to serve me just as he had been accustomed to before his illness [Note: [Col. 0936D] The printed editions have “for three days.” Cod. Clar. has “as he had been accustomed before. Then.”].

Then, exulting and weeping for joy, I gave thanks to almighty God both for myself and for him: through the intercession of the patron, God had restored me sound in body and him sound in mind. One encounter, proceeding from faith, had granted healing even to another madman who did not know how to ask.

Nor will I pass over the fact that, after forty days, on that very first day, I took pleasure in drinking wine, whereas, because of my illness, I had regarded it with aversion until then.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. How His Power Prevented a Storm from Reaching Our Field

When we returned, we carried three little candles as a blessing from the blessed tomb. It would take too long to recount how many miracles have been performed through that wax upon those suffering from chills and other illnesses. But I shall relate one miracle among many.

A certain field of our estate was accustomed to be ravaged by hail every year. The storm raged so fiercely that, whenever it came, it left nothing there. I therefore chose in those vineyards a tree that was taller than the others and placed holy wax upon it.

From that day until the present, no storm has ever fallen there. Whenever one came, it passed by that place as though afraid of it.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the Wood of the Blessed Lattice Brought to Us

Prompted by faith, one of our men had brought, without my knowledge, a venerable piece of wood from the lattice of the tomb, which is at the monastery of Saint Domnus. [Note: [Col. 0937D] Germanus has: “Then one of our men.” Mabillon observes in book I of *Gallican Liturgy*, chapter 8, no. 11, that the word *lectuli* here designates a tomb. It sometimes signifies an altar, in the same work, no. 3.] He kept it in his guesthouse for protection.

But, I believe, because it was not honored or cherished as it ought to have been [Note: [Col. 0937D] The printed editions have “was adorned as it ought to have been.”], his entire household began to fall seriously ill. Since no one at all knew what this meant, and nothing was corrected, but matters grew worse each day [Note: [Col. 0937D] Several codices, together with the printed editions, have “and the evil increased daily.”], he saw in a night vision a terrifying figure saying to him: “Why is this happening to you?”

He replied: “I have no idea at all where this has come from.”

The figure said to him: “You brought here the piece of wood from the tomb of the lord Martin, and you keep it carelessly with you. That is why these things have befallen you. But go now, carry it to the deacon Gregory, and let him keep it with him.”

Without delay he brought it to me. I received it with the greatest reverence and placed it in a worthy location. Thus his entire household was healed, and no one there afterward suffered any misfortune.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. How His Power Restrained Our Enemies

It happened once that, wishing to visit my venerable mother, I was traveling into Burgundy. As I was passing through the forests situated beyond the river Berber [Note: [Col. 0937D] Several manuscripts have *Verberem*; others *Berberim*. Some call it the Barberus, commonly le Barberon, which flows into the Rhône on its left bank below Vienne, as Cointius observes from Chorier’s description of the rivers of Dauphiné. See the notes on the final chapter of book III below.], we encountered robbers.

They surrounded us, intending to strip and kill us. Then I fled to my customary aid and implored the protection of Saint Martin. He immediately graciously stood by me and so terrified them that they could do nothing against us. Those who had come to be feared began instead to fear and fled at the fastest possible pace.

But, mindful of the Apostle’s saying that our enemies ought to be fed with food and drink (Rom. 12:20), I ordered drink to be offered them. They did not wait for it at all, but fled as fast as they could. You would have thought that they were being driven by clubs, or forced against their will to run beyond their horses’ capacity. Thus, through the Lord’s granting and the patron’s help, we arrived where we were traveling [Note: [Col. 0938D] Thus most manuscripts. This word occurs frequently in writers of the Middle Ages in this form. Others have “where we were being directed.” Mart. has “where we were loved.”].

How many tribulations and hardships he has rescued me from, in how many necessities his mercy has stood by me, and how much bitterness he has restrained in me by his power—it would take far too long not only to write but even to recount.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On Those Suffering from Dysentery

What shall I say about those suffering from dysentery, when healing is found as quickly as it has been sought faithfully? I saw a woman who had suffered severely from dysentery for five months, so that whenever necessity moved her, she had to be carried in the hands of others to the required places. Through excessive discharge she had lost both the nourishment of food and the strength of her little body.

With me as witness, I learned that she kept vigil at the basilica. When day was restored after the darkness of night, she scraped away dust from the blessed tomb [Note: [Col. 0938D] Most manuscripts have: “having scraped away the dust.” Colb. b adds: “they say that she also drank the remedy,” and so forth.] and drank it together with a potion [Col. 0938C]. She was then restored to her home on her own feet, although when she came she had been supported by others.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the Possessed and Those Suffering from Chills

1033 What shall I say about the possessed or those suffering from chills, when, if austerity and faith are truly joined together, all the enemy’s snares [Ed.: *mente*, “in mind”] are immediately removed with the patron’s assistance? Thus many of those suffering from chills, while being terribly shaken by the force of fever, lie all day between the altar and the holy tomb [Al.: rave], and in the evening, after drinking dust from the blessed tomb, immediately obtain the benefit of health.

For Paul, a man possessed, who was said to have a legion of demons, climbed, at the enemy’s urging, onto a structure near the holy chamber and is said to have cried out: “Perish the vessel which, burned, I inhabit.” [Note: [Col. 0938D] Thus most manuscripts. The printed editions have: “Let the vessel be spared, which, stripped, I inhabit.” Codices Colb. a, Laud., and the others simply have: “He is said to have spoken: ‘The vessel which, burned, I inhabit.’” Then, throwing himself down.] Burning with agitation, he threw himself downward. But by the power of the blessed man he was placed lightly upon the pavement, so that no limb of his condemned little body was struck.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On Leomeria, the Blind Woman

A certain Leomeria [Bec.: Deomena], blind and crippled, lived miserably for a long time. She repeatedly traveled that road by the hands of others, the road by which people go to the basilica of the Blessed One. At last, regarded with mercy by him, she lay at the holy door and received both light and the power to walk.

O, if everything were made public that each person secretly receives when asking faithfully—and what many consciences keep hidden, namely, that health sought secretly through faithful prayer has been obtained! If all these things, as we have said, were made public, I think that not only books, but not even the world itself, as the Evangelist says concerning the Lord, could contain them (John 21:25).

## CHAPTER XL. On Secûrus, the Cripple
And since the discourse is approaching its conclusion, I shall first relate to you one more remarkable miracle, before the book comes to an end. A certain youth named Securus, as he emerged from his mother’s womb, had put forth a withered hand and a foot; and the framework of all his limbs had so dried and stiffened that he resembled some kind of monster. He was also bound by the yoke of servitude. When his masters saw that for seven years he had been entirely incapable of doing anything useful, they carried him in their arms and placed him before the blessed tomb, so that at least passers-by might feed him, since he could not support himself by his own labor. After he had lain in that place for many days, the foot that had been disabled was straightened, and his withered hand, its veins suffused with blood, was healed. Thus, having received the aid of the blessed Confessor, his whole body was restored, so that one would have thought he had been born again. The boy was then redeemed by Count Justinus and released as a free man. Later he received baptism, and to this day he remains unharmed under the protection of the holy Church. Who could ever investigate or relate such things in proper order, so as to praise them adequately? Nevertheless, we have faithfully endeavored to write down as much as we could discover, hoping to receive this reward: that while these things are read in praise of the most holy Bishop, we may perhaps be granted relief from our sins [Note: [Col. 0939] The German manuscript adds: “For our sins, through the agency of him who is to judge the living and the dead on the throne of his heavenly majesty. Amen.” The manuscript ends here.], as the poet says:

> Perhaps one day it will be pleasing to remember even these things.

The first book ends.

# BOOK TWO. ON THE MIRACLES THAT OCCURRED AFTER WE CAME HERE

[Col. 0939]

## Prologue

[Col. 0939] 1037 Since we had written down the miracles of Saint Martin that we ourselves witnessed, or that we were able to discover from faithful men concerning earlier times, and were burning with great thirst that what the Lord had deigned to perform in praise of his Bishop should not be consigned to oblivion, we completed the first little book [Note: [Col. 0939C] Colb. b reads: “It remains to relate those things which occurred in our time.” Most other manuscripts read “his Bishop,” followed by “to relate,” and so on, as in the printed editions.]. We also wish to relate the things that we marvel to see happening in our own time, leaving no small subject matter for more eloquent writers, while gathering together the great works of miracles in our own composition, so that what skill does not enlarge upon the pages may be extended by the multitude of miracles in their abundance.

## CHAPTER ONE. How I Was Delivered from Fever and Dysentery

In the year 572 after the passing of the blessed Bishop Martin, in the twelfth year of the reign of the most glorious King Sigibert [Note: [Col. 0939C] All manuscripts and printed editions give all these figures. Sigibert’s twelfth year, however, was in the common era 573. The clerics of Tours—or rather Abbot Odo in the Life of Saint Gregory—followed these calculations. Cointius, nevertheless, holds that Sigibert’s twelfth year should be associated with the year 176 after the passing of Saint Martin [Col. 0940C].], after the death of Bishop Eufronius, I received the burden of the episcopate—not through any merit of mine, since my conscience is utterly vile and I am enveloped in sins, but through the gift of the faithful God, who calls things that are not as though they were. I was unworthy of it.

In the second month of my ordination, while I was in the countryside [Note: [Col. 0940C] All manuscripts without exception read this way. The printed editions, however, read “while I was going into the city.” The conclusion of this chapter indeed makes it clear that Mass was celebrated in the same place by a rural priest.], I contracted dysentery together with a violent fever, and began to suffer in such a way that, with death approaching, I completely despaired of living. I was continually discharging the products of digestion, which could not be received without expense, and I had a horror of food. As the strength of my stomach failed from hunger, the fever alone was sustenance for my body [Note: [Col. 0940C] Several manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read “the strength of the body.”]. For no restorative nourishment approached me [Col. 0941A]; there was also a severe pain penetrating my entire abdomen and descending to my loins, consuming me by its torment no less than the fever had exhausted me.

When I was in such a state that no hope of life remained, and everything was being prepared for my funeral, and the physician’s antidote was utterly ineffective—though death had made him its servant for my destruction—I myself, despairing of my condition, called Armentarius, the chief physician, and said to him: “You have devoted all the ingenuity of your art; you have already tested the power of every medicinal preparation, but the affairs of this world do nothing for one who is dying. One thing remains for me to do: I shall show you a great remedy. Bring out some powder from the most sacred tomb of my lord Martin, and prepare a potion for me from it. If this does not help, every means of escape has been lost.”

Then, sending a deacon to the aforesaid tomb of the blessed Bishop [Col. 0941B], he brought out some of the sacred powder, diluted it, and offered it to me to drink. As soon as I had swallowed it, all pain immediately subsided, and I recovered my health from the tomb. The benefit was so immediate that, although this took place at the third hour, I came safely to the meal that same day at the sixth hour [Note: [Col. 0941D] Almost all manuscripts read “that same day at the sixth hour.” According to our method of reckoning, at the equinox the third hour corresponds to what we call the ninth hour of the morning, while the sixth is midday.].

I thought it should also be inserted into this collection, how God admonished me not to permit foolish and undiscerning people to disparage the solemn rites of the saints before me [Note: [Col. 0941D] The printed edition lacks *de*, “of.” Bec. reads “of the solemn rites of the Blessed.”]. On the following day, after I had recovered, which was Sunday, I came to Mass. Since I did not wish to tire myself, I ordered one of the priests to celebrate the glorious solemn rites. But when that priest uttered certain festive words in a rustic manner [Note: [Col. 0941D] Bec. reads: “He uttered some festive words in a rustic manner.”], many of our people began to mock him [Ed.: “rebuke him”], saying: “It would have been better to remain silent than to speak so uncultivatedly.” [Col. 0941C]

During the night that followed, I saw a man saying to me: “The mysteries of God must by no means be debated.” For I call God to witness that I have not composed this myself, but have reported to you the very words that I heard. Therefore, beloved, let no one presume to debate this mystery [Mart.: “ministry”], even if it seems to be expressed in a rustic manner, because before the majesty of God pure simplicity has greater power than the subtlety of philosophers.

## CHAPTER TWO. On the Illness of Justinus

I thought it fitting not to omit something else that escaped me in the earlier book. I had related there how I took from the tomb of the blessed Bishop those little candles [Note: [Col. 0941D] In the preceding book, chapter 34.], by which I said that storms had been calmed and other illnesses prevented. While I was keeping these with me, Justinus, my sister’s husband, was suddenly struck by illness. As the fever grew stronger, together with pains in all his limbs, his condition began to worsen greatly and approach its end [Note: [Col. 0941D] Several manuscripts read: “his illness began to be at the point of death”; others, “began to verge toward the end.”].

A messenger brought me this news, urgently asking that, if I could find any medicine, I should send it to the dying man, lest he perish. But I, trusting in the power of the blessed Bishop, sent one of the little candles by a boy [Col. 0942A], saying: “Light it before him, and let him pour out a prayer to the Lord while contemplating the light; let him beseech the Bishop’s omnipotence [Rom.: “power”] to come to his aid.”

The boy carried away what I had given him. After it had been lit before the sick man’s bed, they scraped off with a knife the ash of the rushwick that the fire had already consumed, diluted it in water, and offered it to the sick man to drink. As soon as he swallowed it, he immediately recovered and was restored to health.

Later he explained to us how the power of the blessed Bishop had come to his aid. He was accustomed to relate that as soon as the radiance of light proceeding from the candle drove away the darkness of night before his eyes, the fever immediately withdrew from his body in the contemplation of the flame. His stomach, which had long languished from hunger, began to demand nourishing food; and he, who had been accustomed to drink only pure water to extinguish the fever’s burning, now desired wine. Such is the power of the Bishop, which often grants aid to the afflicted through abundant compassion and bestows remedies upon the sick.

## CHAPTER THREE. On Maurusa, Afflicted with Gout of the Hands

I fear that, by presuming to go on too long, a more rustic discourse may make the page grow stale. A certain Maurusa had been severely afflicted by the pain of a gout-like humor in the hands, so that, with her feet twisted back toward her legs, she could not rise at all. She had also been deprived of the light of her eyes. Suffering grievously for a long time, she was regarded as alive but as good as dead, and she had no hope of sustenance unless someone extended to her a hand of mercy. Every day, looking toward the devoted people who visited her, she begged for the necessities of life.

It happened that at one time she suffered more severely than usual and could not move any of her limbs; only the breath of life moved within her breast [Note: [Col. 0942D] All manuscripts read this way. The printed editions instead have: “She could in no way be helped by the function of her limbs, except that … it moved.” A little later *judicare* likewise means “to move” or “to raise,” and is used in this way elsewhere.]. By now almost lifeless, she asked to be carried to the feet of Saint Martin. When she had been brought to that place in the arms of the faithful, crying out under the pressure of pain, she prayed that the blessed Man would help her and have mercy on her.

At last that compassion looked upon her which had never been accustomed to send the poor away empty-handed. On his feast day the cords of her withered nerves were loosened, and thus, making the sign of the blessed cross toward her mouth with her right hand—which she had not moved for six years [Note: [Col. 0942D] That is, “had not raised,” as in the printed editions. Colb. b: “had not straightened.” Pith.: “had not moved.” Bec.: “had not dedicated.”]—she was restored to her feet, so that she returned to her little lodging without anyone’s assistance, though she had not recovered the light of her eyes.

After two years she came again to the tomb of the blessed patron and began to pray more attentively, as was appropriate. Immediately her eyes opened, and she rose in renewed light. We have written this miracle here because she was enlightened after we came here; previously she had been healed of her physical weakness.

## CHAPTER FOUR. On the Servant of the Priest Simon

The servant of our most faithful fellow priest Simon, named Veranus, who had been approved for the stores entrusted to him [Note: [Col. 0943D] The printed editions and several manuscripts read *praelibatus*, “previously mentioned.” Bec. reads “of the storeroom.” Observe that here Simon the priest is called “fellow priest” by Bishop Gregory. See the Second Council of Tours, canon 7.], was sitting at the post assigned to his keeping [Note: [Col. 0943D] Most manuscripts, together with the printed edition, read “deposited.” Bec. and Colb. b read “entrusted.”] when an attack of gout came upon him and deprived him of the use of his feet. After he had been tormented by such pains for an entire year, so that he even disturbed the neighboring community nearby, his tendons suddenly contracted and he was completely disabled.

When his master saw this, grieving over the fate of his faithful servant, he ordered him to be carried to the feet of the blessed Bishop, making a vow and saying: “If you restore him to health, most merciful lord Martin, then on that day, released from the bond of my service, with his hair cut short [Ed.: “with his hair shorn”], he shall be assigned to your service.”

He was therefore placed at the feet of the most precious Lord. After he had lain there immobile for five days, on the sixth day he was overcome by sleep.
