While asleep, he seemed to see, as though a man were accustomed to stretch out his foot on his usual little bed [Note: [Col. 0943D] All manuscripts read this way except Colb. b, which has: “It seemed to him that, as a man was accustomed to stretch out his foot on his little bed, he stretched it out.” The printed editions read: “It seemed to him that he stretched out his feet on his usual bed.”].

When he awoke, he rose healthy and free from all disability. His head was shaved, and after receiving his freedom he now serves the needs of the blessed Lord in that same place. O marvelous redemption by the blessed man! Who has ever effected such a redemption for a thousand talents as this present advocate for our sins? With one stroke and in a single moment, without a coin of gold, he freed both the body from disability and the man’s condition from its burden.

## CHAPTER FIVE. On the Paralytic from Auxerre

A certain man from the town of Auxerre, named Manlulfus [Note: [Col. 0943D] Laud. and Bell. read “Malulfus”; others, “Mallulfus.”], was brought in the arms of those carrying him to the tomb of Saint Martin. Persisting in constant prayer and fasting, he returned the feet that he had presented twisted to their customary use, straightened by a sudden restoration of health. Thus, through the power of the Saint, he was somehow remade: he had been carried in the hands of others, but in the presence of us all he rose up sound, firmly supported on his own feet.

## CHAPTER SIX. On the Paralytic from Orléans

Another paralytic from the territory of Orléans was brought in a wagon and came to the holy basilica. After lying for many days at the door beside the baptistery, which opens onto the way out toward midday [Al.: “midday”], he implored the aid of the blessed Bishop. It happened that one day, while lying there, he was tormented more severely than usual, so that the neighbors nearby ran together at his cries [Note: [Col. 0943D] Several manuscripts read: “so that the neighborhood … ran together.”].

The bindings of his tendons were coming undone and being straightened; for that reason the pain was unbearable. Thus, through the gift of the patron, he rose upright on the soles of his feet, weeping for joy, with the people as witnesses [Col. 0944A]. He immediately became a cleric and, firmly restored to health, returned home.

## CHAPTER SEVEN. On the Paralytic from Bourges

There was also another man weak in his gait, named Leuboveus. He came already as a cleric, dragging himself over the ground because, owing to his poverty, he had no one to carry him. Day after day he sought the threshold of Saint Martin. One day, while weeping outside at the Saint’s feet, he received his health in the sight of the people, his knees and feet having been straightened.

It is established that these three miracles occurred on the very day when the most glorious King Sigibert, crossing the Seine, made peace with his brothers without any clash [Note: [Col. 0943D] Bec. reads “without counsel”; both readings are possible. Gregory himself relates this story in Book IV of the Histories, chapter [Col. 0944D] 50, where he also records these three miracles and attributes this peace to the protection of Saint Martin.] of armies (A.D. 574). Let no one doubt that this too was a victory of the blessed Bishop [Ed.: “the third victory”].

## CHAPTER EIGHT. On a Blind Man Who Was Given Sight

At that same time a certain blind man, begging alms from those who gave charity—for he had no other means of livelihood unless someone extended a hand to him out of compassion, and he had no support at home except the mercy of the devoted—was standing one day with his feet fixed before the holy tomb. Suddenly pain seized him in his eyes. As he was consumed by the severity of this pain, his eyes began to emit foam. Then, as blood burst from his eyelids, he was reborn into renewed light and was granted sight of the light he had once lost.

## CHAPTER NINE. On Another Blind Woman

1044 A certain Gunthedrudis [Note: [Col. 0944D] Others read “Gundetrudis” or “Gunthetrudis.”], from the territory of the Viromandui [Note: [Col. 0944D] The Viromandui, once a prominent people of Belgica, occupied part of modern Picardy, commonly called le Vermandois; their chief city was Augusta Viromanduorum, commonly called Saint-Quentin. See *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 73. Elsewhere Martin, together with Clichtoveus, reads “in the village of Mandense,” and Chol. “in the village of Madense.” Bign. has “Vicomadensi.” But this is a scribal error.], had lost the light of her eyes. Leaving home and country, prompted by faith, she came to the holy basilica. After serving there for many days, she was deemed worthy to recover the sight of one eye. Soon afterward, forgetting her husband and children, and changing her clothing, she entered the religious life of the Church, inspired by the Lord.

## CHAPTER TEN. On a Woman Delivered from a Flow of Blood

Nor will I be silent about how, as though from the garment of our Redeemer [Col. 0944D], a flow of blood was dried up at the blessed tomb [Note: [Col. 0944D] He alludes to the woman with the hemorrhage who was healed by touching the garment of our Lord, as Matthew relates in chapter 9 and the other Evangelists also recount.].

A certain woman who had come from Auvergne [Col. 0945A] with her husband, from the district of Transaliensis [Note: [Col. 0945D] So the older manuscripts write it. Several have “Trasaliensis.” The printed editions, with Clar., have “Transiliensis.” Victor. has “Trasalerensis.”], was suffering from a flow of blood. She had a lodging near the basilica’s courtyard. Every day she lay at the threshold of the holy Confessor, prostrate and begging for the help of healing.

It happened that one day she approached the holy tomb, praying and kissing it. From the cloth spread over it she touched her ears and eyes. Immediately the stream of blood dried up, and she was so completely healed that she thought she had touched the fringe of the Redeemer’s garment. Her husband, seized by illness, was carried by the hands of others to the door of the basilica. Praying faithfully, he recovered when his fever subsided. Thus, he healed of his illness and she of her flow, they returned together to their own home, glorifying God.

## CHAPTER ELEVEN. On a Lame Woman

The wife of the tribune Animus [Note: [Col. 0945D] So all manuscripts except Bell. and Clar., which read “Animii.” The printed editions nevertheless have “Aniani.”], named Mummola [Note: [Col. 0945D] So all manuscripts. Bec. and Colb. b have “Nummela”; Vinc., “Nummola”; Clar., “Nummula.” The printed editions read “Unimola.”], terrified by fear during the night, had lost the use of one foot. She had fallen into such weakness that she could stand only when supported by the hands of others, whenever she intended to move forward [Note: [Col. 0945D] Two printed editions read: “whenever she proposed to go somewhere.”].

She was laid down at the feet of Saint Martin and held a candle in her hand throughout the night as a votive offering, while we kept vigil in the basilica. When morning came and the signal for Matins was sounded, she stood upon the weakened foot. Once all her disability had subsided, she returned freely to her lodging on her own feet, with no one supporting her.

## CHAPTER TWELVE. On a Man Healed of Dysentery

At one time, when Saint Germanus, bishop of the city of Paris, was coming to the feast of the glorious Bishop [Col. 0945C], Ragnimodus [Note: [Col. 0945D] The printed editions read “Ragnimundus” or “Ragiamundus.” He is the same man who succeeded Saint Germanus in the see of Paris.], then a deacon and now a bishop, accompanied him in his service, suffering severely from dysentery.

Saint Germanus first went to a villa of his church [Note: [Col. 0945D] This was, as it seems to me, Severiacum, commonly Sevray in Touraine. Fortunatus mentions it in the Life of Saint Germanus, chapter 65. There, instead of “to the villa of the holy Church,” I think one should read: “When he returned from the basilica of Saint Martin to the villa of his Church at Severiacum.” Bal. reads “to his city,” and others “to remain in the city.”], situated in this territory. When he began to arrive at Tours before the night of the vigil of the feast, he ordered the deacon to remain at the villa, saying: “You might become fatigued by traveling and something worse might happen to you.”

But he replied: “It is God’s power that commands us to suffer according to our deserts. I shall not leave by any other route than to go to the basilica of the blessed Bishop; for I trust that if I touch his tomb, I shall be saved.” Immediately, having mounted a horse [i.e. *equo*], he came to the basilica. In the morning, after drinking a potion made from the powder of the tomb, his illness immediately subsided and he recovered.

## CHAPTER THIRTEEN. On a Blind Man Who Was Given Sight

A certain Ursulfus [Note: [Col. 0945D] Clar. reads “Orsulfus.” Vinc., Bec., and Colb. b read “Arnulfus.”] from the city of Tours, from the district beyond the Loire, was blind and devoutly sought the aid of Saint Martin. He served at the Saint’s shrine continuously for two months, persevering in fasting and prayers.

It happened one day, on the Lord’s Resurrection [Note: [Col. 0946D] The authors of that age frequently called all Sundays, as we call them, “days of the Resurrection,” evidently because they were named after the principal Sunday on which the feast of the Resurrection is celebrated in the Church.], while he was at the feet of the Lord and watching the solemn celebration of Mass with the rest of the people [Note: [Col. 0946D] Several manuscripts read “awaiting.” But this results from the manner of pronouncing *s* as though it were *es*. Elsewhere Gregory frequently writes *spectare missas* for “to attend Mass.” Thus it makes no difference that the man was blind.], his eyes suddenly opened and he began to see everything clearly. He came to the holy altar to receive Communion without anyone leading him.

I shall explain the cause of his blindness. On the first day of Easter his master ordered him to walk around a field and close the entrance through which the animals entered. While he was trying to close it, he was struck blind. Then, as we have said, he came to the tomb, weeping and lamenting, and begged for the sight he had lost.

On that day, while the grace of the Lord’s Body was being given to the people, the blessed Bishop deigned to restore his light; and when the sun of his eyes shone forth, the stars of his eyes gleamed. Who, I ask, could ever be found as such a physician, one who bestowed two cures for a single illness? Behold, two miracles were displayed in one blind man: first he opened his bodily eyes to contemplate earthly things, and now he illumined the eyes of his heart so that he would not desire them. He also deigned to dedicate to his service the man whom, so to speak, he caused to be born again into the world.

## CHAPTER FOURTEEN. On a Paralytic Girl

Nor will I keep silent about what this patron accomplished on his feast day. A certain girl from the Palatinate, struck by paralytic fluid, had lost the use of her legs and had been reduced to a miserable condition, so that, with the tendons contracted behind her knees, she drew her heels up to her legs. Her father carried her to Tours and devoutly placed her before the feet of Saint Martin. She lay there for three months, begging alms from passers-by.

It happened on the day of the blessed Man’s distinguished feast that, while we were saying Mass, she faithfully prayed in the place mentioned above. As we were properly celebrating the sacred solemn rites, we began to recount the miracles of the holy Lord [Note: [Col. 0946D] This was otherwise called the *illatio* or *immolatio*; today we call it the Preface. In former times each feast had its own, in which the notable deeds of the saint whose feast was being celebrated were recounted. A remnant of this practice still survives in the Prefaces of the greater feasts, in which the mysteries being celebrated are briefly explained. We shall give the *contestatio* praised here by Gregory in an appendix.], when she suddenly began to cry out and weep, indicating that she was being tortured.

But when, after the *contestatio* had been completed [Col. 0947A], all the people proclaimed “Holy” in praise of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0947D] The Council of Valence II established this in the year 529, canon 3.], the tendons that had been bound were immediately loosened. She stood upon her feet before the eyes of the entire people and, with the Lord’s favor, reached the holy altar to receive Communion on her own feet, without anyone supporting her. She has remained in good health to this day.

## CHAPTER FIFTEEN. On a Blind Man Who Was Given Sight

A certain Merobaudus [Note: [Col. 0947D] Several manuscripts read “Merobaudis.” Colb. b, “Geroblandus.” Clar., “Gerobaudus.” Bec., “Meroblandus.”] from the district of Poitiers was working when he was struck by an exceedingly severe blindness, inflicted by the enemy. After enduring this illness painfully for six years, he came to the holy church of Saint Martin. There he devoted himself constantly to prayer.

On the day after the holy feast, while he stood at the feet of Saint Martin, it suddenly seemed to him that a flash of light was shining around him. Immediately, when his eyes opened, he saw everything. He at once became a cleric in that same place and departed healed.

## CHAPTER SIXTEEN. On What a Sailor Reported

There was also that remarkable miracle when, on the day of the Epiphany, the Lord, through the intercession of the blessed Bishop, brought Falernian wine out of the waters and drew wine from the bottom of the riverbed for a poor man—he who once changed water into wine.

At one time, therefore, while we were traveling [Note: [Col. 0947D] Most manuscripts express this and what follows in the singular person.] through the district of Balbiacum [Note: [Col. 0947D] All manuscripts read this; the printed editions have “Belvacum.” It may be the place called Beauvau, not far from Chinon and the Loire. Savaro, in his commentary on Sidonius, Book II, letter 14, quotes from the black charter of Saint Martin: “Beluacus for the footwear of the brothers,” in exchange for which the brothers, deceptively induced, gave the villa of Martiacum [Col. 0948D] in the territory of Auvergne.], we reached the Loire River.

When we carefully asked the sailor who was to ferry us to the opposite bank about the places where we should go fishing [Col. 0947C], he pointed one out, saying: “May blessed Martin be your help.” Our people received this ungratefully, saying that no catch had ever been seen to occur in his name.

But the sailor replied: “There can be no doubt, because his power provides this. I shall tell you what happened to me this year, and how, through invocation of his name, with the Lord’s help, I obtained what I desired.

“It was the day of the Epiphany. I entered the storeroom and found nothing to drink that I could draw out. I went outside and prayed, saying: ‘Most holy Martin, send me some wine on this sacred feast, lest, while others feast, I remain fasting.’

“While I was praying these words silently, I heard a voice on the farther bank calling me to bring a boat to a man who was traveling. But when I took up my poles and began to cut through the water in that direction [Note: [Col. 0948D] Most manuscripts read: “with the poles, and also with the force of the oars, to cut through the waves.”], and when I reached the middle of the river, suddenly a great fish was thrown from the whirlpool into the boat. I immediately killed it, ferried the people across, and returned home. After selling the fish for a measure of wine, I was refreshed with the others.

“Know, therefore, how quickly he will appear in response to whatever is invoked, if it is requested faithfully.” I call God to witness that I learned these things from the sailor’s own mouth.

## CHAPTER SEVENTEEN. On Duke Gunthramnus

One day, while Gunthramnus Boso was crossing the Loire River opposite the village of Ambasiacum [Note: [Col. 0948D] Most manuscripts read “Ambiacum,” commonly Amboise. Gregory says more about Gunthramnus Boso in his *History*, where we have also spoken about the town of Ambasiacum.], and dreadful night was already holding the world as darkness descended, the sailors were suddenly thrown into confusion by an opposing wind on the open water. The ships supporting that bridge became separated, and, filling with water to the very top, they all sank into the depths up to their waists together with the ships, though the ships were not drawn away from beneath their feet.

When everyone was terrified, Boso cried out loudly for the aid of Saint Martin and prayed that he might come quickly to rescue them. He confidently said to his men: “Do not be afraid. I know that the right hand of the holy Man is especially ready to extend aid in times of need.”

As he said this, God set the ships straight, and the contrary wind changed into a favorable one. No one perished, and they reached the shore. There the aid of the blessed Confessor appeared so immediately that even the silver they had lost when the river carried it away was restored to them when the river itself finally returned it to the bank.

## CHAPTER EIGHTEEN. On Landulfus, Possessed by Lunacy

A certain man named Landulfus from the territory of Vienne [Note: [Col. 0948D] The printed editions read “Laudulphus from the territory of Vienne.” Bec. reads “Laudulfus.”] was grievously tormented by the assault of a lunatic demon. He often thought that he was being surrounded by an enemy and fell to the ground, emitting bloody foam from his mouth, so that he was regarded as though dead.

The learned physicians called this kind of illness epileptic [Note: [Col. 0948D] Most manuscripts read “ephileptic.”]; the peasants called it *cadivum* [Note: [Col. 0948D] This is the reading of the manuscripts. The printed editions have *caducum*, as we say today.], because the sufferer fell.

When the aforesaid man saw himself afflicted in this state, he heard of the fame of the blessed Bishop and went to his holy basilica, so that the aid present there for all might come to his assistance. But when he came to the same place full of faith, the savage demon attacked him with even greater ferocity. Because of the public assault of the demons, he was not permitted to leave the courtyard; yet within the courtyard he was unharmed.

For demons visibly came with a great clashing of weapons and tried to pierce him with the points of their *cassistela* [Col. 0948D]. If he threw himself to the ground, a horrifying multitude of frogs seemed to leap upon him. Voices were also heard publicly from him, reproaching and saying: “Martin, whom you have sought, will be able to do nothing to help you, because you are enslaved to our dominion.”

But he confidently and steadfastly opposed them with the sign of the cross [Col. 0949A] and drove them away terribly through the thin air [Note: [Col. 0949D] Colb. a reads this way; others have “through the tenuous air.”].

After these empty and futile assaults, when the enemy saw that he could not claim the man for himself, he tried to deceive him by trickery. Taking on the appearance of a veteran soldier [Note: [Col. 0949D] That is, a soldier. Perhaps even then the blessed man was depicted, as is now done, in the military cloak in which he was shown dividing his cloak with a poor man, because of the fame of that glorious deed.], he came to him, saying: “I am Martin, whom you invoke. Rise and worship before me if you wish to recover your health.”

The man replied: “If you are Lord Martin, make the sign of the cross over me, and I shall believe.” But when the demon heard the name of the sign that was always opposed to him, he vanished like smoke.

After this, while standing at the feet of the glorious Lord, the man fell into a trance of mind and saw the blessed basilica shining with a new light. The Saint came out of it and said to him: “Your prayer has been heard, and behold, you shall be healed of the illness you suffer.” Making the sign of the blessed cross over his head [Col. 0949B], he departed.

The man came to himself and, all the attacks having been removed, perceived that he had received complete health. Nevertheless, after recovering his health, he began to use wine excessively, and his body, long deprived of moisture, became drenched by rain [Note: [Col. 0949D] This is the reading of the manuscripts Gat., Rom., Colb. tut., and Vinc. Mart. and Clar. read “while rain was absent for a long time.” Bell., Laud., and Colb. a read “his body, abstaining from rain, was drenched by rain.” Vict. reads “his body, having abstained, was drenched.” Colb. b reads “his body, long weakened, was drenched by rain.” The printed editions of Chol., Clict., and Col. read “while rain was absent for a long time, it was nourished”; Balesd. reads “washed.”]. His side contracted, together with one foot and one hand. But once again devoting himself to moderation and having his head tonsured, he was restored to health by the power of the Blessed One.

## CHAPTER NINETEEN. On Theudomerus, the Blind Deacon

As we write down each of the miracles of the blessed Man briefly, without expanding them into a more extensive discourse, we proceed on the path we have begun with great reverence and fear [Note: [Col. 0949D] These words through “Theudomerus the deacon,” etc., are absent from Bec. and Colb. b.], lest wiser people perhaps say: “A skilled writer could have expanded these considerably” [Note: [Col. 0950D] The printed editions read: “This could have been expanded more skillfully.”].

But to us, who are engaged in ecclesiastical doctrine, it seems that a history contributing to the edification of the Church should be woven, with verbosity set aside, in a brief and simple style, so that it may reveal the virtue of the blessed Bishop without imposing boredom upon the wise. By this means the reader is encouraged in reading, and the Saint is displayed in his deeds.

The deacon Theudomerus [Note: [Col. 0950D] Elsewhere, “Theodomerus” or “Theudomerus.”], because of an ailment of the head, had the passages of his eyes severely blocked for four years by descending cataracts [Al.: “closing cataracts.”]. He came to the cell at Condat, in which the blessed man had died. Prostrate before his bed, he spent the entire night in tears and prayers. Lying motionless, he soaked the ground with his weeping, and his sighs warmed the venerable wood of the screen.

When day dawned, the cataracts of his eyes were opened, and he was granted the sight of light. What have physicians ever accomplished with their instruments, when they cause more pain than healing, when, by stretching and piercing the eye with their little probes, they produce the torments of death before opening the light? If caution fails in this procedure, it prepares eternal blindness for the wretched man. But for this blessed Confessor, will is the instrument, and power alone is the ointment.

## CHAPTER TWENTY. On Desiderius, the Possessed Man

In that cell, when Desiderius, a possessed man who had come from Auvergne, had raved throughout the entire night, at daybreak he began to declare that blessed Martin was burning him. While uttering these cries, he vomited some substance—I do not know what—mixed with blood. Once the demon had been expelled, he was cleansed; leaving behind dust stained with pus, he departed the cell healed.

## CHAPTER TWENTY-ONE. On a Man with a Contracted Hand

A certain man brought to the same place a weak hand with contracted fingers, so that his fingernails were embedded in his palm and, as blood sometimes ran down, caused him great pain. Throwing himself before the bed of the aforesaid glorious Lord, weeping and praying, impelled both by pain and by faith, he recovered the use of his hand the following day, his fingers having been straightened.

## CHAPTER TWENTY-TWO. On the Matron Remigia
1052. When the matron Remigia contracted a similar affliction, she came with great devotion to the blessed cell. Applying herself to vigils and prayers, and feeding the enrolled poor who had gathered there, she raised her withered arm, with its contracted fingers, restored to health, so that she could serve [Note: [Col. 0950D] That is, to provide draughts of wine; for this is what the word *miscere* signifies, as is more fully demonstrated in the preface to the first part of the fourth century of the Benedictine *Acta Sanctorum*.] [Col. 0950C] [to the poor]. And thus, serving the blessed poor throughout the entire day, she returned home in good health. In the years that followed, she supplied the aforesaid brothers with sufficient nourishment each year.

It happened, however, that on one occasion one of her daughters was grievously afflicted by quartan fever. When, as usual, she came and provided food for those poor people, she implored the holy Man’s help. For four days she lay at the blessed cell in continuous prayer and fasting [Note: [Col. 0950D] The printed editions, together with several manuscripts, read “to continuous prayer and fasting.” Colb. b and Bec. read “in continuous prayer amid fasts.”]. The girl was cured of every fever and returned home with her household [Note: [Col. 0950D] Most manuscripts read: “the girl, once healed, returned with her servant, glorifying God.”], glorifying God.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning Vinastus the Blind

A certain man who practiced such works, named Vinastus [Note: [Col. 0950D] Thus the older manuscripts; others have *Vivastus* or *Vinastus*.], received his sight while he supplied those poor people with the necessities of life. He had been oppressed by very severe blindness for many years and had made it his custom to come from his own region to the aforementioned cell of the Saint, provide those poor people with abundant food, and, after devoutly keeping vigils, refresh them with food until they were satisfied. He himself served them, as far as he was able, like a servant.

When, as we have said, he had continued this for many years, on one occasion, having fulfilled both his vow and his service, he prostrated himself at the railing of the holy bed. After praying and saying farewell, he wished to return. When he rose after completing his prayer, he opened his eyes a little and saw a silk curtain hanging from the railing. He said: “I see something like a silk cloak hanging here.”

1053. His companions said to him: “We recognize that you truly see.” But he began once more to weep and pray that the blessed Confessor would graciously complete the work he had begun. While he prayed more intently, he fell asleep. A man appeared to him in a vision and said: [Col. 0951B] “Go to the basilica of Lord Martin, and there you will obtain complete health.” Without delay, he was led by the hands of servants. As soon as he reached the threshold of the blessed Confessor, he received full sight through the help of faith.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning a Man Whose Entire Body Was Contracted

At Bourges there was also a woman who conceived and gave birth to a son whose knees had contracted toward his stomach and whose heels had drawn up toward his legs [Note: [Col. 0951D] The printed editions read: “had been contracted.”]. His hands, moreover, were attached to his chest, and his eyes were closed. He resembled more some kind of monster than a human being.

When many people looked upon him with derision and his mother was reproached for having produced such a son, she confessed with tears that he had been conceived on a Sunday night [Col. 0951C]. Not daring to kill him, as mothers commonly do [Note: [Col. 0951D] Bal. reads: “as a monster,” or “as though he were one.”], she raised him as though he were a healthy child. When he grew up, she handed him over to beggars. They took him, placed him in a cart, and dragged him around for people to see, earning a considerable livelihood through him.

After this had continued for a long time, in the eleventh year of his life [Bec. reads: “in his fortieth year”], he came to the festival of blessed Martin. Thrown out before the tomb, he lay there miserably. When the festival had ended, he recovered his sight and hearing. He was then taken back to his customary life and begged for alms.

About a year later, or somewhat more, he came again to the solemn festival. He was placed in the spot where he had previously lain, and when the festival days had passed, all his limbs were straightened and he obtained complete health. [Col. 0951D] Lest this perhaps seem incredible, I myself saw him in good health; and I learned these things not from someone else’s report, but from his own mouth [Note: [Col. 0951D] Here Colb. b has: “The Second Book of the Miracles of Saint Martin ends”; it does not contain what follows, but proceeds with the *Life of Pelagia the Penitent*.].

1054. But since I have said that this happened to his parents because of their sin, through violating the Sunday night, beware, men who are joined in marriage. It is enough to devote yourselves to pleasure on other days; spend this day undefiled in the praises of God. For those married couples who come together on that day subsequently have children who are either contracted in their limbs, epileptic, or leprous [Note: [Col. 0951D] Vict., Colb. *tut.*, and others read: “for it often happens that from this there arise,” and so forth.]. Let what we have said serve as a warning, lest an evil committed in a single night be endured through the course of many years [Note: [Col. 0951D] Here Bec., as also Vinc., ends with this clause: “The account of the miracles of Saint Martin, bishop and Confessor, ends.”].

## CHAPTER XXV. Concerning a Paralytic Who Was Healed

I shall relate to you as you pray [Note: [Col. 0952D] Ed. reads: “to us,” and so forth. Rom. reads: “to you in prayer.”] that miracle which ought to be admired above all others. After an immense accumulation of sorrow, it revealed great joy to us: it displayed the power of the Blessed One, raised up what was tottering [Note: [Col. 0952D] Gat. reads: “and turned aside what was feared.”], and fortified the wavering hearts of the people with an abundant firmness of stability.

For when, on the venerable night of the Lord’s Nativity, the sacred vigils had been completed and we were preparing to proceed from the church [Col. 0952B] to the basilica of the Saint [Note: [Col. 0952D] That is, from the principal or cathedral church, where, according to the arrangement of Perpetuus—as is said in Book X, at the end of the *History*—the vigils were celebrated, to the basilica of Saint Martin.], one of the possessed, more violent than the others, began to rave terribly. Tearing and striking himself, he cried out:

“You seek the threshold of Martin in vain; you approach his house to no purpose, because he has abandoned you on account of your many crimes. Behold, abhorring you, he performs wonders at Rome. There he gives sight to the eyes of the blind; there he directs the steps of paralytics; and by his power he also brings an end to other illnesses.”

At the devil’s words the entire people were thrown into confusion. Not only were the hearts of the lesser people overwhelmed [Note: [Col. 0952D] Most manuscripts omit *membrorum*. Several read: “Not only the brutish hearts of the lesser people,” and so forth.], but we ourselves were also shaken with fear.

When we entered the basilica amid great weeping, we all prostrated ourselves on the pavement, praying that we might be found worthy of the holy Man’s presence [Col. 0952C]. And behold, a man named Bonulfus, whose two hands and one foot had contracted three years earlier because of an excessive fever [Note: [Col. 0952D] Rom. reads: “because of excessive illness-induced fever.”], and who, although his hands had been straightened at the blessed Man’s festival, still limped on his weak foot, lay down before the holy altar. He prayed that the one who had restored his withered hands would likewise straighten his contracted foot by a similar power.

During this prayer he was suddenly surrounded by an intense fever and, as though stretched upon a rack, was tortured by pain in his sinews. Meanwhile, pain provoked insolence in the suppliant, and the man who had come to seek a cure began to utter reproaches. He said:

“O Lord Martin, I sought health from you, not torments. If I am not worthy of health, at least do not afflict me with pains.”

As we stood around in tears awaiting the blessed one’s arrival, and while the sacred rites were being performed, the holy offerings were placed upon the altar and the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood was customarily covered with a cloth. The contractions of the sinews relaxed; and when the skin behind the sick man’s knee burst open, a stream of blood flowed out, and he extended his foot [Col. 0953A] sound and unharmed.

When I saw this, I gave thanks to almighty God and moistened the threshold with my tears [Note: [Col. 0953D] Several manuscripts read: “the lamps were moistened,” instead of “the thresholds,” or “the lamps or thresholds were moistened.”]. Then I cried out to the people:

“Let all fear depart from your hearts, because the blessed Confessor dwells among us. Do not believe the devil at all, for he has never spoken anything true. He is a liar from the beginning and has not stood in the truth” (John 8:44).

When I had said this, the grief of everyone was released into joy. The sick man himself rose up before us and stood on his feet, freed from his affliction. Seeing this, the whole people raised a cry to heaven and applauded, saying:

“Glory to God in the highest, who has glorified us today by the presence of the blessed Confessor, just as once he glorified the shepherds by angelic light, and has shown by his present power that he is with us.”

Thus all were rescued from the enemy’s fear [Col. 0953B] and strengthened by the protection of Christ.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Concerning Piolus the Mute

The blessed man appeared with no lesser power on the holy day of Epiphany, when he opened before the people the closed mouth of a certain mute man.

A certain Piolus, a cleric from Condat [Note: [Col. 0953D] All manuscripts have *Piolus* except Clar., which has *Piolius*. The printed editions have *Paulus*, and likewise in the title.], came from birth with closed hands, useless for the labor of the world. Whether this happened because he or his parents had sinned, so that he was born maimed, is not ours to determine (John 9:2). We know only one thing: in him, as in the other sick, the grace of the Priest was revealed.

When he was ten years old and his growing nails caused him severe pain in his hands, which he could no longer endure [Col. 0953C], he went to the threshold of the blessed Confessor. After staying there many days with the utmost frugality, he returned with straightened fingers and healthy hands.

About five years later he suffered a grievous affliction. While he was weakened by the force of a severe fever, he lost the power of speech. After being rescued from the fever, he remained without the faculty of language. The passage of his mouth had been so obstructed that he could not produce even the slightest grunt. He carried three boards fastened together with a strap in his hand; striking them against one another, he produced with the boards the sound he could not produce with his mouth.

This device is useful to vine-growers when they attempt to defend the vineyards from flocks of destructive birds.

When the aforementioned man came to the Saint’s basilica on the night when our Lord Jesus Christ, drawing streams of water, provided Falernian wine [Col. 0953D], he resolved to keep vigil at the Blessed One’s feet. After some time had passed beyond midnight, he fell asleep. While he was seeing some danger in a vision, he was terrified by fear and, for the first time, opened his previously closed mouth with these words:

“Lord Martin, deliver me!”

Thus, as blood burst from his mouth and throat, he recovered both hearing and speech.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Concerning a Paralytic Woman

After King Sigibert had been killed (A.D. 575), Chilperic, having escaped imminent death, had taken possession of the kingdom. Ruccolenus, together with the men of Le Mans, was grievously oppressing the city of Tours [Col. 0954A] [Note: [Col. 0954D] See what Gregory relates more fully in Book V of his *History*, chapters 2 and 4.], devastating everything so completely that he left no hope of sustenance in the houses of the church or in the shelters of the poor.

The next day he sent messengers to the city ordering that the men who, for a reason not unknown to us, were staying at the Saint’s basilica should be dragged out by the clerics. If this were delayed, he promised to burn everything in a conflagration.

When we heard this, we were exceedingly sorrowful. We went to the holy basilica and implored the Blessed One’s aid. Immediately a paralytic woman who had been contracted for twelve years was straightened.

Ruccolenus himself, however, having attacked the farther bank, was immediately stricken by the royal disease. Afflicted by Herodian maladies [Col. 0954B]—which would take too long to recount—and battered by them, he wasted away, dropping away piece by piece like wax melting before fire. Swollen with dropsy, he died on the fiftieth day.

Nor will I omit this: at that time, by God’s command or [that is, and] by the power of the holy Man, the bed of the river was filled without any inundation of rain, preventing the enemy from crossing and harming the city.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning a Blind Woman

On the day of the returning solemnity when the Lord, soon to suffer for the salvation of the world, served a meal to the apostles after the treacherous disciple had been confounded [Note: [Col. 0954D] Thus the manuscripts Colb. *tut.* and Vict. Others read “having suffered”; the printed editions read “more willingly.”], everyone was hurrying to the church to fulfill their desired vows to the Lord.

A certain woman, burdened by long-standing blindness, was in the countryside. She began to weep and say [Col. 0954C]:

“Woe is me, for having been blinded because of my sins, I am not worthy to behold this festival with the rest of the people.”

Then, prostrating herself alone amid great weeping, she invoked the name of the blessed Confessor. When her prayer was completed, she was restored to her former light. After recovering her sight, she came to the blessed basilica to give thanks to God, with her eyes possessing marvelous clarity. One of the possessed was also cured by the Saint’s power on that day.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Concerning Two Blind Men

Two blind men came from Bourges. Their eyelids had dried up and were joined together with adhesive matter. They lay praying at the feet of the blessed Lord.

On the day of his festival, while the people were present and the miracles from his life were being read [See below, chapter 49], a radiance like a flash of lightning appeared over them. The bonds that had closed their eyelids broke apart, blood flowed from their eyes, and their sight opened widely, so that they were found worthy to see everything.

## CHAPTER XXX. Concerning a Mute Woman

A certain woman’s open mouth had been bound by excessive moisture [Ed. reads: “pain”] together with fever, so that she could not control her tongue. She could emit only a grunt like an animal, not a human voice.

Moved by faith [Col. 0955A] and with great confidence of spirit, she approached the atrium of the blessed Confessor. Remaining there for many days, asking both for alms and for the opening of her mouth, she was at last regarded by the Saint’s power.

One Sunday, while the solemn Masses were being celebrated, she stood in the holy basilica with the rest of the people. When the Lord’s Prayer was being recited, she opened her mouth and began to sing the holy prayer together with the others [Note: [Col. 0955D] Among the Greeks also everyone sang the Lord’s Prayer together; this rite differed from the Roman one, as Gregory the Great testifies in Book VII, Indiction 2, Letter 64. See the *Gallican Liturgy*, Book I, chapter 5, no. 22.].

Since she had been bound under the yoke of servitude, she was redeemed from the property of the blessed Confessor; and now she remains free, possessing the use of her voice.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Concerning Another Disabled Woman

By no less a miracle, the blessed Man also showed that he was present when invoked.

A certain religious woman named Apra [Al. *Abra*], oppressed by a violent fever, had lost the use of all her limbs, with only her tongue still serving her. Lying with both hands and feet contracted, she begged the Blessed One’s help day and night.

One night it seemed to her that an old man had come to her and was gently stroking all her limbs. When she awoke in the morning, she felt that her feet and one hand had been restored to health. Astonished, she did not know what occurrence had brought this about.

On another day, having been warned in sleep, she proceeded without delay to the blessed basilica. That night was the vigil of the Confessor’s passing. After midnight had passed, she was awake when she was shaken by some kind of terror; suddenly her contracted hand was straightened.

While the people marveled, she recounted everything she had previously suffered [Col. 0955C], recognizing that it was the same power of the Saint that had earlier appeared in the straightening of her feet and now shone forth in the straightening of her hand.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning the Oil That Increased at the Saint’s Tomb

Since we see such miracles as those we have written about every day, what will those wretched men say who declare that Severus lied in the *Life of the Holy Bishop*? For I heard a certain man, filled—as I believe—with an evil spirit, declaring that it could not have happened that oil increased under Martin’s blessing. Nor did he believe that, when a flask slipped and fell onto the marble pavement, it could have remained unbroken [Note: [Col. 0956D] Severus Sulpicius relates these two miracles together at the beginning of Dialogue 3, concerning the virtues of blessed Martin.].

What happened recently, however, I shall explain, presenting many witnesses. One of our deacons was suffering severely from quartan fever. I often reproached him for not hastening to the Saint’s basilica and for not praying from his heart that the Pontiff’s power might come to his aid. At last, moved by our exhortations, he tremblingly threw himself before the blessed tomb.

Then, when the fever’s fire had subsided for a little while, he asked that a flask half full of rose oil be brought to him. He had already used much of it for the fever, although it had helped him only a little, and very little remained. Anointing his forehead and temples with this liquid, he asked that the vessel also be placed beside the Blessed One’s tomb [Col. 0956A].

On the fourth day, when the fever again oppressed him, he went to the basilica and prayed for a very long time while prostrate. Taking up the flask he had left half full, he found it full. Astonished at the power of the blessed Bishop, he carried it home with fear and reverence. After he had been anointed again with it, all the heat of the illness immediately subsided, and he was never again weakened by that disease.

We also recall, not without a deep sigh and a sense of wonder, what happened to the same flask afterward. It was hanging on the wall in the lodging of the aforementioned deacon when, through the enemy’s ambush, it was struck and shattered into pieces. The oil poured out and was quickly absorbed by the ground.

A boy who was present, seeing what had happened, took a small vessel and, squeezing the earth, extracted a little oil. Gathering up the rose oil that had been spilled together with the broken glass, he brought it to us. I took it and carefully transferred it into another vessel. There was approximately enough oil to fill half a small cup, yet in the vessel it reached a height of only two fingers.

On the following day, when I looked at it, the oil stood at a height of about four fingers. Astonished at the power of the holy liquid, I left it secured and covered with my seal. Seven days later, when I looked again, I found there more than one sextary.

I summoned the deacon and showed it to him, marveling. He declared under oath that as much had been lost from the shattered flask as could then be seen in the new one. To this day it grants benefits, in God’s name, to those who seek them.

Later, he himself anointed another sick person with this ointment. As the oil increased, the man was healed, and afterward many others were restored to health through it.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Concerning Allomer, Who Was Contracted

Let the region of Angers also produce its miracle. From there came a certain man named Altomeris [Note: [Col. 0956D] Some manuscripts, together with the printed editions, have *Alomeris*, *Elomeris*, or *Leomeris*, and likewise in the table of contents.], with contracted feet and hands and a weak tongue. He sought the temple of the blessed Confessor.

After remaining there throughout Lent, praying and imploring continually that the power of the holy Bishop might visit him, he reached the Sunday before Holy Easter on which our Lord Jesus, walking along roads strewn with branches stripped from the trees [Ed. reads: “leaves”], came to Jerusalem while the crowd followed and cried out: “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matthew 21:9).

On that day, when evening had already come and he alone was lying outside before the tomb, he suddenly fell into ecstasy and lay there terrified by fear as though dead. As he himself relates, after being overwhelmed for two hours or more, he returned suddenly to his senses as though awakening from sleep. Raised up, he was astonished to find himself well.

He kept vigil there throughout the night and in the morning revealed to us with his own mouth what had happened. He became a cleric and returned unharmed to his lodging [Col. 0957A].

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Concerning a Blind Cleric

Finally, in that same year, when the festival celebrated in summer [Note: [Col. 0957D] On July 4, when his ordination and translation are celebrated together with the dedication of the basilica.] had arrived, a festival eagerly desired by the people, a certain cleric whose eye was covered by a dreadful cloud that prevented him from seeing the light went to the house of the blessed Confessor.

After keeping vigil through the night with the others, when the sky began to brighten and he was leaving the basilica, he was found worthy to recover the sight he had once lost.

At the same festival, three possessed men repeatedly struck themselves, called upon the holy Bishop, confessed their crimes, and begged the Saint to restore peace to them [Note: [Col. 0957D] Colb. a reads thus; the others, together with the printed editions, read “to spare them.”]. At last they cast from their mouths some kind of foul matter [Col. 0957B] and were thus cleansed by the Saint’s power.

## CHAPTER XXXV. Concerning Prisoners Who Were Released

Soon afterward—that is, on the third day after the festival—four men were bound in prison. The judge’s cruelty confined them so harshly that no one was permitted to provide them even the necessities of food. They prayed with pure hearts for the protection of the blessed Bishop.

While they were devoutly engaged in this, at midday the beam enclosing and constraining their feet suddenly split. When their chains broke, they realized that they were free. Without delay they made for the door; when it was opened, they entered the Saint’s church, with no one preventing them.

The guards were so astonished that they did not even dare to rebuke them in words [Col. 0957C]. Indeed, they followed them and hid with them in the church. The prisoners, marveling, offered the greatest thanks to God, because he had deigned to free them through the intercession of the Bishop.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Concerning the Relics Brought by Bishop Leodovaldus

Many people, filled with faith and carrying relics of the blessed Man, experience many miracles. Leodovaldus, bishop of the city of Avranches [Note: [Col. 0957D] He governed the Church of Avranches, in Second Lyonnaise, which we today call Normandy, between Sinerius, or Senator, and Childoaldus, according to Cointius.], devoutly sought the relics of the holy Lord through his priest.

After receiving them, when he had entered the territory of the aforementioned city, he encountered a paralytic still lying in a deserted place, carried in the hands of those bearing him. He faithfully kissed the veil covering the chest of the holy relics [Col. 0957D], and immediately stood upon his feet and returned home on his own legs.

For you do these things, most blessed Confessor; nor is it enough for you to adorn your own house with wonders, unless you also illuminate by awesome powers various regions that you did not visit on foot [Col. 0958A].

Afterward, a certain blind man also hastened rapidly to meet the relics, led by an attendant. When he arrived as the Blessed One’s relics were being placed upon the holy altar, he was found worthy, once the solemn rite was completed, to recover the sight of his eyes. Another woman, who had long been mute, likewise recovered the use of speech.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Concerning a Possessed Man Who Was Healed

In those days, a certain possessed man came to the basilica of the blessed Man. He loudly declared that he was suffering many torments from demons [Note: [Col. 0957D] Several manuscripts read: “that he was suffering many torments from a demon,” and so forth.], and confessed that, through the holy Bishop, the demon was being forcibly expelled from the vessel it had seized.

Thrown to the ground [Note: [Col. 0957D] Nearly all manuscripts read: “having rolled upon the ground.”], he began to eject foul blood through his mouth [Col. 0958B]. After lying there for about two hours, he was cleansed and raised up once the demon had been expelled.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Concerning a Mute Girl

1063. A small girl, a native of the city of Tours, was born mute from her mother’s womb. Her mouth was so tightly closed that she could not utter even the sounds produced during infancy [Note: [Col. 0957D] Most manuscripts read: “the sounds that infancy requires.”].

Her mother, distressed by such a grievous offspring and continually mourning, was warned in a vision to visit the tomb of the blessed Bishop. Awakened, she went fearlessly to the temple of the Saint with the little girl [Note: [Col. 0957D] The manuscripts read: “taking the girl with her, she went fearlessly.”]. After laying her before the Saint’s tomb and praying for a very long time, she took her up again.

Then, having lit incense and holding the girl above it, she asked whether it gave her a pleasant smell [Col. 0958C]. The girl replied: “Good.” The sorrowful mother recognized this as her daughter’s first word.

She then placed upon the girl’s mouth water that she had once taken from blessed springs and again asked what taste it gave her. The girl replied: “Good.”

Then the mother joyfully carried home the daughter whom, in faithful trust, she had sorrowfully brought to the Blessed One’s tomb (*See* Book II, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 26).

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Concerning What the Priest Aredius Carried Away as a Blessing

Aredius [Note: [Col. 0958D] Several manuscripts have *Aridius*. The printed editions have *Aridus*. This is the holy Aredius whom Gregory frequently mentions. We shall provide his Life from Gregory, as well as another version in the first Benedictine volume.] was a religious man from Limousin who came to Tours solely out of devotion. After kissing the blessed tomb in prayer, he crossed the river and arrived at the holy monastery [Note: [Col. 0958D] Today it is called the Greater Monastery, commonly Marmoutier; we have discussed it elsewhere. Besides the cell cut into the rock, which is still visible within the walls of the greater basilica, where Saint Martin is said to have rested, there is not far away, in a hollow of the rock, a spring that tradition says was dug out by the holy man. I readily believe that this is the very spring mentioned here by Gregory.].

As he visited each place where the blessed Man had either humbled himself in prayer or sanctified it by singing psalms, and where he had provided sleep for his tired body or food for himself when weakened by fasting; as he went around and visited everything, he came to the well that the Saint of God had opened by his own labor.

After pouring out a prayer, he drew water and placed it in a small flask, carrying it home on his return. When he subsequently gave it to many sick people, it brought them healing.

On one occasion his brother Renosindus [Note: [Col. 0959D] Thus Colb. two, Laud., Bell., Vict. SB., and Clar. The printed editions read *Rinoscindus*, “his father,” incorrectly, for in both Lives of Saint Aredius his father is called Jocundus, as also in the Chronicle of Geoffrey of Vigeois, chapter 15.] was struck down by the violence of a fever and lay in bed.

On the eighth day, when he lay there with his eyes closed, apparently about to breathe out his spirit, and the whole household was lamenting the death of their patron or preparing what was necessary for the funeral, it occurred to the priest to place a drop of water from the blessed well in the mouth of the dying man.

As soon as the water touched his mouth, the sick man opened his eyes. His tongue was also freed, and he asked that more of it be administered. When he received a cup and drank, the fever immediately fled. Thus, while the household marveled, he rose healthy from the bed on which he had lain.

## CHAPTER XL. Concerning Sisulfus the Maimed

What can my littleness say about these miracles, when the Saint of God, though taken from the world, is still regarded as a preacher in the world? Although he cannot display himself openly to the people, he continually reveals himself through manifest powers: he gives sight to the blind, heals paralytics, and restores the other sick to their former health.

But, as I have often testified, I consider myself unworthy to recount the signs of so great a man. Nevertheless, because I dare to be bold, I ask pardon from the reader. Since love for my patron impels me [Col. 0959C], and since I have declared that he is still a preacher, I shall relate what happened recently.

Sisulfus, a poor man from the region of Le Mans, had fallen asleep at midday in his little garden and suffered some unknown evil. Leaping up from sleep, he raised his weak hands with his fingers contracted into his palms and, overcome by great pain, soon sank again into sleep.

In a vision he saw a man standing before him, dressed in black and with gray hair. Turning toward him, the man said:

“Why are you so agitated with tears?”

Sisulfus replied:

“Behold, venerable lord, when I fell asleep for a little while, I awoke in pain and lost the use of my hands, the work of my hands. I do not know what crime I may have committed.”

Then that man, as the Lord said to his disciples concerning the man born blind—that neither he nor his parents had sinned, but that the work of God might be revealed in him (John 9:2)—said:

“Your weakness indicates the torment of a sinful people. Go now through the villages and fortified towns, and proceed as far as the city. Preach that everyone should abstain from thefts, perjuries, and usury, and that on Sunday no one should perform any work apart from the solemn mystical rites.

“For behold, we shall lie before the Lord in tears, imploring pardon for the people, and there is still hope of obtaining it if reformation follows among the people. For the hostilities, illnesses, and many other evils that the people suffer are stirred up by the Lord’s indignation [Note: [Col. 0960D] Several manuscripts and printed editions read: “stir up the Lord’s indignation.”].

“Therefore announce this quickly, so that they may strive to reform, lest they perish cruelly in their wickedness. When you have done what I command, hurry to my basilica at Tours. There, visiting you, I shall obtain from the Lord that you be healed.”

Sisulfus said to him:

“Tell me, I beg you, lord, who are you, or what is your name?”

The man replied:

“I am Martin, priest of Tours.”

At these words of the Saint, the poor man rose from sleep. Taking hold of a staff, he undertook the journey commanded of him and announced to the people what he had been ordered to announce.

Seven months after these events, he came to the blessed basilica. There he lay prostrate for three days and on the fourth day was visited by the Saint’s power. The flesh of his palms had already putrefied where they had been held closed [Note: [Col. 0960D] The printed editions read: “the flesh or sinews of his palms, by which he was confined.”]. When his fingers were straightened, blood burst from them. After all these wounds had been treated, he recounted what we have related with his own mouth.

## CHAPTER XLI. Concerning a Blind Man Who Was Given Sight

Thus, most blessed Confessor, according to your custom, you show mercy to the people’s sins and heal the illnesses of all. You illuminate with your remedies all who faithfully invoke you, and you do not deny outsiders what you willingly grant to your own.

A man, therefore, a resident of the territory of Tours, about twenty-five years old [Note: [Col. 0960D] Rom. reads: “about five years old.” Below, Bell. and Colb. a read: “for five years.”], was afflicted by a feverish eye disease. His cataracts descended [Col. 0960C], his eyelids became tightly closed, and he was rendered completely blind. To this misfortune was added the fact that, after being struck by a club and his sight being shattered, one of his eyes burst.

He had already lived in this blindness for twenty-five years. Warned in a vision, he came to the Blessed One’s tomb. There he devoted himself to prayer and on the third day recovered the sight of one eye.

Encouraged by this remedy, he began to pray more earnestly. On the fourth day the eye that had burst opened, its sight restored. Although it did not see as clearly as the other [Al. “although he does not see as clearly”], it nevertheless supplied the benefit of light.

## CHAPTER XLII. Concerning a Man’s Contracted Hand

A certain disabled man whose contracted hand had stiffened prayed attentively in the atrium before the Blessed One’s tomb [Col. 0960D]. During the Saint’s holy vigil he was visited; his fingers were straightened, and his hand was restored to its former use and recovered strength.

## CHAPTER XLIII. Concerning a Little Boy Who Was Raised from the Dead

How often we marvel here that the powers of the prophets and exalted men, whose deeds we once read about, are renewed! But what am I saying? What many men did while living in the world, this one alone renews every day, even after the tomb.

What, then, are we doing? Why are we silent? Why do we conceal what the many people proclaim, though we are few? Let us not remain longer in this hesitation. Let us bring forth for our age a new Elisha, who sent the corpse of a dead man alive from the tomb (2 Kings 13:21). The blessed Confessor also performed this deed in our presence.

What the circumstances were, I shall explain while imploring the aid of the undivided Trinity.

A boy was born and, when his mother’s milk failed, was given to a nurse to be fed. Since she, being barren of this fluid, did not provide milk in sufficient abundance for the needs of his tender age, the child who ought to have been growing began, as the days passed, to waste away [Col. 0961B]. He diminished so greatly that nothing more remained of him than thin skin covering his little bones.

His mother had died, and he had passed almost a year in this condition. He was his father’s only child and a kind of memorial of his wife’s love [Note: [Col. 0961D] Several manuscripts read: “his father’s only child, born of his wife’s love,” and so forth.]. As his nourishment diminished, fever came upon him when he was already weakened by starvation.

When this heat touched him, his father hurried to the church, lest his child die without the rebirth of baptism. The boy was baptized, but, not strengthened in body beyond that spiritual remedy, he was laid upon the holy tomb. His eyes were sunken, his eyelids loose and drooping, and he no longer had any breath of life. His father lamented loudly.

Nor was that heavenly power absent which once restored a little boy to life in the hands of the blessed Confessor [Note: [Col. 0961D] Severus Sulpicius relates this miracle at the beginning of Dialogue 2, which concerns the virtues of Saint Martin. It occurred on a journey that the blessed man made to Chartres.].

As soon as the boy’s clothing touched the covering of the tomb [Col. 0961C], the little boy immediately breathed. A wondrous miracle! You would have seen his pale cheeks gradually redden as divine power took effect, and his sleeping eyes open to renewed light.

Then, revived by the Saint and received by his father, he has remained alive to this day as a testimony to the power.

## CHAPTER XLIV. Of another blind man who was given sight

There was also a certain blind man from Poitiers who had been deprived of light for six years. After praying for three days prostrate before the blessed tomb, he received the sight that he had long lacked, through the working of the customary power. This occurred during the feast of the holy patron, at which Maroveus, bishop of Poitiers, was present—a man who deservedly should be proclaimed a most blessed disciple of Hilary. When the solemnity had ended, he returned joyfully to his own city with his fellow citizen who had been given sight.

[Note: The printed editions have *Meroveus* or *Meroneus*. He is known because at that time he was present when the crowds were stirred up in the monastery at Poitiers of Saint Radegund; Gregory discusses them in Books IX and X of the *History*.]

## CHAPTER XLV. Of two little boys who were healed

At Vultaconnum, a village of Poitou, while two little boys were sleeping together in one bed on the Lord’s Day night, they seemed to see or hear something like the sign that is customarily sounded at Matins. Rising from their bed, they set out for the church. When they had reached the church’s courtyard, they found there choirs of women singing. Terrified, and recognizing that the crowd was a band of demons, they fell to the ground without shielding themselves with the sign of salvation, as is appropriate to the weakness of their age. One was deprived of his sight, and the other of both sight and the ability to walk.

When they had been afflicted by these infirmities for many years, the one who had lost only his sight came devoutly to the basilica of blessed Martin. As soon as he had completed his prayer, he immediately recovered his sight. The other, having recovered his sight in the same holy place, returned home but still limped, being weak. Coming to the cell at Condat, where the bed of the blessed Man is kept, he found that a vigil was being celebrated there on the Lord’s Day night. Suddenly, as the people prayed, he felt the divine power present.

With the crowd looking on, he dragged himself across the ground and raised himself against the wall in which there is a window that was once the entrance through which the Blessed Man’s body had been carried. As he prayed and wept for joy, he was restored to complete health, and thereafter suffered no further severity from his infirmities.

[Note: The *Gat.* manuscript has *Multaconnum*; *Vict.* has *Multacomium*. Valesius cites, in his notice of a coin of Theudomer, the reverse of which reads *Wultaconno*.]

## CHAPTER XLVI. Of the lame man who was straightened

A certain little boy named Leodulfus, weak in his left foot, came to Tours while going about with the other beggars in search of alms. After remaining there for a short time, he tried to complete the journey he had begun. Proceeding with his companions while limping, he was overcome by the severity of the pain at the tenth mile from the city. Abandoned by his companions, he lamented alone on the bank of the river, calling out to the many who were hastening to the feast and saying:

“Woe is me, because I did not wish to behold the solemnity of the glorious Man; therefore his power has struck me down. For this reason I beg you, most faithful Christians who fear God: help my ignorance; help one who is oppressed and weak. And if the fear of God remains [Another reading: *moves*] in you, carry me to the holy place.”

While he was imploring this from the many passers-by, someone placed him on his cart and carried him to the holy basilica. There, continuing in prayer for three days, he departed unharmed, his feet restored.

[Note: Most manuscripts read “after remaining there for a short time.” The printed editions read “after delaying only a little.”]

## CHAPTER XLVII. Of the cripple whom an ox drew

There was a certain cripple who, after the manner of the hermit to whom an ox once provided assistance, owned a single ox. The ox was yoked to a cart, and he was drawn through the houses while asking alms from the devout.

When, therefore, he had come to Tours as the bishop’s feast approached, he prostrated himself before the tomb and devoted himself to prayer, earnestly imploring the help of the blessed Bishop. He was then carried again by his companions and placed before the holy apse of the tomb. When the Masses had ended and the people had begun to receive the most holy body of the Redeemer, the knots that bound his knees suddenly came undone, and he rose to his feet.

While everyone marveled, he gave thanks and proceeded on his own feet to the blessed altar, with no one supporting him. Thereafter he lived in good health.

[Note: The Mass was considered finished before Communion was offered to those present. See the notes on Book IX of the *History*, chapter 3.]

## CHAPTER XLVIII. Of the man who had contracted hands and feet

From the district of Carnon, which is situated in the territory of Anjou, a certain man named Floridus, whose hands and feet were contracted, was brought to the holy cell at Condat, from which the blessed Confessor had departed to Christ. While he devoted himself there for several days to vigils and prayer, every illness was driven from his body and departed. Thus, with his limbs straightened, he returned home in good health.

[Note: Bell., Laud., Colb., and the printed *Clict.* edition have *Carnonensi*. Gat., Mart., Colb. *tut.*, and Clar., together with Balesd., have *Carnotensi*; Chol. and Col. have *Carnoensi*; finally SB. has *Croviensi*, as in Book IV below, chapters 17 and 23, where the printed editions have *Croniensi*. This place is thought to be Credo, commonly Craon. See what we said in the notes to *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 96.]

## CHAPTER XLIX. Of the man who brought a contracted arm

The feast day of the solemnity had arrived, and large crowds of people had gathered. Then behold, a certain weak man appeared with a contracted arm. As he kissed the blessed tomb with his lips, watered it with his tears, and implored the help of the blessed Confessor’s voice, he did not lose faith but awaited the customary aid.

Finally, as the priests who had come proceeded to conduct the solemn rites, and the lector whose duty it was to read arrived, took up the book, and began to read the life of the holy Confessor—see above, chapter 29—the man’s arm was immediately straightened, and he rose healed. In the sight of everyone, he obtained the assistance that he had faithfully sought.

## CHAPTER L. Of a blind man who was given sight

So also, during the same feast, a blind man humbly implored the restoration of his sight. As soon as he touched the little cloth that hangs from the wall outside down to the feet of the Saint, blood burst from his eyelids, and, with the people witnessing it, he recovered his sight.

## CHAPTER LI. Of those suffering from dysentery

When that dysenteric disease, accompanied by hidden pustules, was ravaging many cities, and the city of Tours was suffering more severely than other places, many were healed after scraping dust from the blessed tomb and drinking it. Many were freed after being anointed with the oil kept there. For some, the water with which the tomb was washed before Easter was also a remedy.

[Note: That is, on the day of the Lord’s Supper, when—even now, as is customary in certain Gallican churches—the altars are solemnly washed by the priests after the principal Mass with water and wine. See Menard’s notes on the *Gregorian Sacramentary*, p. 88, and below, Book III, chapter 34.]

Since many benefits were being granted to many people, I saw a man lying in despair from dysentery. He was brought to the basilica, and while the others celebrated the vigils, he passed an uncomfortable night. At dawn he approached the tomb, drank dust mixed with wine, and returned from the tomb healthy.

## CHAPTER LII. Of another man healed of a severe bodily discharge

Another man, seized by a violent fever, vomiting poison from his mouth and suffering excessive looseness through the lower part of his body, lay on a small bed. As the poison spread, a wound arose in his groin, and in an astonishing manner visibly moved all the way to the sole of his foot. It was as large as a goose’s egg.

Then, returning upward, it spread with extreme pain through his sides and arms and advanced as far as his neck. From there it descended along the other side all the way to his foot. Then, turning back, it returned to the place from which it had first arisen.

As it wandered in this way through the sick man’s limbs, he did not know where the miserable thing was heading or what it was doing; he could only utter cries amid his weeping. The pain demanded groans, since so many sufferings assailed a single little body.

At last, when this had been reported to us, I declared that the customary antidote was being sought from the true physician, through whom a dying man might regain life. I confidently advised that dust from the tomb be taken. The attendants immediately ran with great haste, carried away dust from the monument, and brought it to the sick man, offering it to him to drink mixed with wine. When he had drunk it, all the pain was driven away so completely that he was restored to health at that very hour.

## CHAPTER LIII. Of a deranged man restored

Countless people, hearing such things, seek the aid of the blessed Confessor from distant regions. Among these events, one thing is especially astonishing: how human senses, deceived by the devil’s art, are restored.

A certain citizen of Bayeux, while walking along the road confused from drinking too much wine, suddenly saw dust from the field stirred up by winds blowing from different directions. Mixed, as it usually is, with stubble, it was lifted high into the air, and the whole atmosphere became a single cloud of dust. Covered by it, the man lost his senses and was thrown from his horse.

A little later, his people found him and brought him home in a state of agitation. From then on he became uncontrollable and tried to flee, although no one was pursuing him. What more need be said? He was confined with bonds, loaded with chains, and kept under guard. Grinding his teeth because he was denied the freedom to escape, he tore himself with his own bites.

While this was happening, his parents were advised to take him to the basilica of the Blessed Man. After a long period of prayer there, he departed healed, promising that he would come every year and fulfill his vows to the holy Confessor.

Then he withdrew to the monastery nearest to him, having had his hair cut in humility.

[Note: This is how the printed editions read, together with the manuscripts, except Colb. *tut.* and Victor., which have: “for the sake of humility he cut off his hair, and was ordained a priest.” Our reading is familiar from Gregory, and we do not think it follows from it that this man was given monastic clothing. The things reported about him below do not permit us to say this; they show that he remained legally his own master. He therefore withdrew to a monastery in order to be instructed in clerical duties and to devote himself for a time to spiritual exercises, as Gregory says of Meroveus in Book V of the *History*, chapter 14.]

After being ordained a priest, he began zealously to serve God, but he did not fulfill what he had promised to the blessed Bishop. Therefore, in the fourth year, when—as I believe—the enemy was again granted power over him, he fell once more into his former madness. Bound with chains as before, he was brought back to the holy church. There, remaining for six days and longer in vigils and prayers, and fulfilling what he had previously deceitfully and negligently withheld, he returned home healed.

[Note: The manuscripts Colb. *tut.* and Clar. Vict. have “for six months or so”; Laud., Bell., and Colb. *a* have “for six months or days.”]

But because of his sins, after again repeatedly soaking himself in wine, he died in the same affliction.

## CHAPTER LIV. Of a blind girl from Lisieux

If we were to pursue each and every thing that is happening or has happened, we would pile up a great mass of the Confessor’s miracles. A girl from Lexovium, already grown, had lost the light of her eyes.

[Note: Laud., Gat., and Colb. *a* have “Paula, however.” Further below Laud. has *Lesoensi*, whence the printed editions have *Lesuensi*; Vict. has *Luxoviensi*. All designate the same episcopal city in the Second Lyonnaise, or Normandy, commonly called Lisieux.]

She came devoutly to the Saint’s threshold and spent the entire period of the feast praying prostrate on the ground. On the third day after the holy feast, when her people were urging her to return, she asked to be led to the Blessed One’s tomb. There she again and again prostrated herself, wiped her eyes with the cloth covering the holy tomb, and departed after saying farewell.

When she had already boarded the boat, she said: “I thank you, blessed Confessor, because, although I was not worthy to see your holy threshold, I at least perceived it by touch.”

After she had uttered these words with tears, she wiped her eyes and recovered her sight. Turning around, she said: “Perhaps this is the Blessed One’s basilica?” Those who were nearby told her that it was.

Then she said: “I will not return unless I give thanks to my patron for the health I have received.” Many saw her returning and proclaiming the Bishop’s praise. After completing her prayer, she departed joyfully.

## CHAPTER LV. Of a little boy with a contracted hand

At the same feast, another boy from Sens brought a withered hand. On the fourth day after the blessed solemnity, while he was standing and praying at the Saint’s feet, his fingers were straightened in the sight of the people. The entire assembly saw the greatness of God: how the hand was suffused with blood, which rose gradually through the dry veins, and how the hand was so absorbent that one might have thought a sponge long dried out was greedily drinking in liquid when immersed in water.

When the veins had been filled, the nerves strengthened, and the skin had reddened, he raised the pale hand, healed.

## CHAPTER LVI. Of the woman who came with her fingers contracted into her palm

A woman from Poitiers likewise deserved to obtain healing in a similar manner. Her fingers were contracted into her palm, with the nails fixed, so to speak, into the very bones; her entire hand had already rotted. She came devoutly to the Saint’s feast, seeking the desired cure.

After witnessing the solemn rites according to custom,

[Note: Some manuscripts, together with the printed edition, have “the solemn days of the Saint,” and say that she spoke to her own people.]

she said to her companions: “We have come with a whole heart to ask for the Blessed One’s help, but because of the obstacles presented by our sins, we have not deserved to receive what we sought. Now, therefore, after completing our prayer, let us return to our homeland, trusting in the goodness of the Bishop, that the prayer of a faithful soul may benefit a weak body.”

After saying this and similar things, and as though bidding farewell to the Saint, she departed. As the day was turning toward evening, she found lodging near the bank of the river Cher.

[Note: Some manuscripts, together with the printed edition of Bales, have *Cari*. It is a river that flows into the Loire somewhat below Tours, commonly called the Cher.]

Awakened near midnight, she gave thanks to God that she existed, that she lived, that she was strong, and that she had touched the tomb of the blessed Bishop. After speaking these words amid much weeping, she fell asleep again.

And behold, a man with swan-white hair and purple clothing, carrying a cross in his hand, stood before her and said: “Now you will be healed in the name of Christ our Redeemer.” He took her hand, inserted his finger between the fingers that had closed over her palm, and, moving them for a little while, straightened them.

When she awoke and saw this vision, with blood still flowing, she raised her healed hand in praise of God. At dawn she returned to the basilica, completed her thanksgiving, and went back joyfully.

## CHAPTER LVII. Of the woman who was weakened while working on the feast of Saint John

On the feast of blessed John, while the people were gathering for the solemn Masses, a certain woman took a hoe and went into the field, intending to pull up the weeds of bad seed and clear the crop by herself. She could not have been surrounded by divine assistance, out of reverence for the Lord’s Forerunner.

[Note: This is how the Victor manuscript reads; SB. has “human assistance”; the other manuscripts have “surrounded by assistance.”]

As soon as she began to work, her hands were immediately seized by a divine fire. Her face also seemed to emit flames, and her whole body boiled with blisters and pustules. The wretched woman burned no less with the pain of shame than with that of her body, since against her will she was revealing what she had done secretly.

Then, crying out and lamenting, she quickly sought the basilica of blessed Martin. She remained prostrate before his tomb in this torment for four months; when all the heat had been extinguished, her body was restored and made sound.

She was the servant of a certain citizen of Tours, who, after granting half the price, sought another servant.

## CHAPTER LVIII. Of a blind and crippled man

A boy from Paris whose trade was making clothing, as melancholy increased in him—that is, the dregs of congealed blood—became a quartan fever patient. As the humor boiled, his entire body became so constricted by tiny pustules that some people thought him a leper. He also suffered the worst pains throughout all his limbs and was deprived of the light of both eyes.

Having heard the fame of the blessed Bishop and of the miracles proclaimed everywhere, he sought the city of Tours. Coming to the Saint’s basilica, fasting and praying for many days, he recovered his sight and was restored to his former health.

[Note: The accusative case is used instead of the ablative, as often elsewhere.]

He was of free birth. When Leodastis, who at that time held the office of count of Tours, heard that he was such a craftsman,
