[Note: This is Leudastes, who had accused Gregory before Chilperic. More about him is found in Book V of the *History*, chapters 48 and following. His unhappy death is reported in the following book, chapter 32.]

he began to slander him, saying: “You are a deserter from your masters, and you will no longer be permitted to wander about in different places.” He sent him bound to his own house to be held in custody.

But even there the power of the angelic Confessor was not absent. For as soon as the man had been seized, he was immediately afflicted by the illness from which he had been free. When he became extremely ill, the count saw that he could accomplish nothing against him and ordered him released from his bonds and allowed to depart freely. He returned to the basilica and was healed again.

## CHAPTER LIX. Of another woman who was sold after gaining her freedom

A similar event is this: after a woman had won her freedom, she was again sold by the barbarous sons of her former patron. But through the Saint’s power, so that she might be defended more easily, her limbs became completely disabled. The tendons behind her knees were so twisted that they touched the calves of her legs.

[Another reading: “below, the legs.”]

Abandoned by the masters to whom she had been unjustly sold, she sought the protection of the blessed Confessor. After spending no great length of time at his church, she was granted both freedom and health.

## CHAPTER LX. Of the pain in my eyes and head

Since the earlier little book was begun at the time when Paulinus departed

[Note: The first chapter concerns Severus, but no miracle is narrated there. Therefore the second book, in which the miracles described by Paulinus are discussed, may be regarded as the beginning of the Book of Miracles.]

and consisted of forty chapters when completed, I resolved to complete this book, once begun, with sixty. The intention was that blessed Martin,

[Note: Through the three levels of fruit produced from the seed in the Gospel parable of Matthew 13:23, Saint Augustine wished the crowns of widows, virgins, and martyrs to be signified. Gregory, persuaded that all these were found in Martin, tried to indicate them by the number of chapters in his work. The earlier little book has forty chapters, corresponding to the crown of widows; the second book has sixty chapters, expressing the fruit of virgins. Joined together, they make one hundred, that is, the crown of martyrdom. As Gregory says, Martin was widowed from this world and acquired the merits of widows; through continence he earned the honor of virginity; and he obtained the palm of martyrdom by enduring public injuries and being assailed by hidden plots.]

who, widowed from this world, preserved the honor of virginity intact and triumphantly fulfilled martyrdom, whether through hidden plots or public injuries, and to whom also belonged the crown of the thirtieth, sixtieth, or hundredfold fruit, might have that crown increased through these hundred virtues.

[Note: The printed editions have “the sixtieth; the fruit of the hundredfold is increased in these.”]

I hoped that I would not be defrauded of my vow, which, by the Lord’s command, I completed in eight years. In this very book, begun through the power that had been worked upon me, I have returned again to myself.

[Note: The printed editions have: “the very book, begun in me, to finish again.” The events narrated throughout this Book II took place during the first eight years of Gregory’s episcopate, that is, up to the year 581.]

I consider that this happened not without divine providence, so that it might be brought to an end by the one by whom it is read to have been begun.

After I had described fifty-nine virtues in it and was awaiting the sixtieth with still greater attention, suddenly the left side of my head was constricted by pains. As my veins throbbed and tears flowed, such torment threatened me that I forcibly closed my eye lest it burst.

I endured this severely for a day and a night. In the morning I came to the Saint’s basilica and prostrated myself in prayer. After completing it, I touched the place of pain with the cloth that hung before the blessed tomb. As soon as I touched it, both the throbbing of my veins and the flow of my tears stopped.

After three days, a similar pain seized the right side of my head. My veins throbbed, and tears flowed abundantly. Again I rose in the morning and, having touched the cloth in the same way as before, departed healed in my head.

After ten days had passed, it seemed to me that I should reduce my blood. On the third day after the bloodletting, a thought entered my mind—and, as I believe, was injected by the one lying in wait—that what I had suffered had arisen from my blood, and that if a vein had immediately been cut, these symptoms would have ceased at once.

As I considered and turned this over in my mind, the veins at both temples burst out. The pain that had been there returned, and now seized not one part of my head but my entire head.

[Note: Laud. has “it seizes my entire body.”]

Agitated by the pains, I hurried to the basilica, begging forgiveness for my wicked thought. I touched my head with the cloth that covers the blessed tomb, and immediately, when the pain had been calmed, I departed from the tomb healed.

There are indeed many other things that the blessed Man performs every day, but it would take too long to pursue them. Nevertheless, if we still deserve to see miracles, I am pleased that they should be joined to another little book. For, as we have said, let these two little books be counted in this number.

I also give the greatest thanks to the Lord’s mercy, because through the intercession of the glorious Bishop I have been granted the ability to carry through to the end what I undertook at the beginning.

[Note: The printed editions have: “what I promised at the beginning, to be able to carry through to the end.”]

I pray that what the Confessor often grants to the people, he may bestow more abundantly upon me, a sinner; that he may cleanse me from the errors

[Note: Most manuscripts have “from my diseases.” The printed editions have “diseases from me.”]

which he often sees and observes; that he may restore to me the light of truth; rescue me from the fall of unbelief; cleanse my heart and mind from the filthy leprosy of lust; purify my thoughts from wicked desires; and wash away and cast down from me the entire burden of crimes.

Thus, when I have been placed on the left side at the judgment, may he deign with his holy right hand to draw me away from the midst of the goats, and, keeping me reserved behind him, await the Judge’s sentence.

And when, at his judgment, I have been assigned to the infernal flames, may he cover me with the holy cloak with which he himself is covered in glory, and excuse me from punishment, while the angels say to the King what they once said concerning the monk who had been raised from the dead: “This is the one for whom Martin is praying.”

[Note: The blessed man raised this man, who was still a catechumen, at the monastery located near Poitiers, before he was appointed to the episcopate. Severus Sulpicius tells this story in his book on the life of blessed Martin.]

May it happen that, since I am not worthy to be clothed in that brightness, I may at least deserve to be delivered from the ministers of Tartarus as they rush upon me. May guilt not prevail over me so greatly that I am separated from the kingdom of the one whom I faithfully confessed in this world.

The second book ends.

# BOOK THREE

## Prologue

As, by Christ’s ordinance, we begin to write a third little book concerning the miracles of blessed Martin, we give thanks to almighty God, who has deigned to grant us such a physician—one who would cleanse our infirmities, wash away our wounds, and provide health-giving medicines.

For if the mind is humbled before his blessed tomb and prayer is lifted up; if tears flow and true compunction follows; if sighs are sent forth from the depths of the heart and sinful breasts are beaten; then lamentation finds joy, guilt finds pardon, and the sorrow of the heart reaches healing.

For the touch of the blessed tomb has often commanded fluxes to stop, the blind to see, the paralyzed to rise, and even the bitterness of the heart to depart far away.

Although I have often experienced this myself, I consider myself unworthy to insert here, amid the mass of such great miracles, those things that he has deigned to perform upon me. Yet again I fear that I may appear harmful if, like a fraud, I conceal them.

For I call God to witness, and the hope that I have placed in his power, trusting that I will not be disappointed in his mercy: whenever a headache has attacked me, or throbbing has struck my temples, or my ears have been burdened by impaired hearing, or darkness has obscured the sharpness of my eyes, or pain has settled in other limbs, as soon as I touched the painful place either to the tomb or to the hanging cloth, I immediately recovered my health. I silently marveled that, in the very act of touching, the pain had withdrawn with its course.

## CHAPTER I. Of the pain in my throat

I shall first insert into this little book the miracle of what I suffered recently. While we were seated at a meal after fasting—for we were eating—fish was brought on a dish. As we ate it after signing it with the Lord’s cross, one of the fish’s bones lodged most painfully in my throat.

It caused severe pain, cutting into my throat with its sharpness and blocking the gullet itself along its length. It impeded the sound of my voice and did not allow even the liquid of saliva, which often flows down from the palate, to pass.

On the third day, when I was unable to expel it by coughing or spitting, I resorted to familiar remedies. I approached the tomb, threw myself down on the pavement, and with tears poured out amid groans begged the Confessor for help.

Then, rising, I touched my throat, my pharynx, and the rest of my head to the cloth that hung there. There was no delay: I recovered my health. Before I left the holy threshold, I felt no fatigue.

Yet I do not know what became of the evil splinter. I did not expel it by vomiting, nor did I feel it pass into my bowels. I know only this: I felt myself healed so swiftly that I thought someone had reached in with a hand and removed the things that had injured my throat.

## CHAPTER II. Of a weak girl who was healed

A twelve-year-old girl, weak in all her limbs, had lain for six years on a bed in her parents’ house as if dead. She could not walk, perform any work with her hands, see the light, speak, or hear anyone speaking.

Her parents poured out prayers for their daughter at the Blessed One’s tomb, offered gifts, and continued to make vows. The people gathered for the solemn rites, and the holy festival was celebrated with joy.

On the third day of the feast, the girl called her father and said: “I am thirsty.” Rejoicing that he had been found worthy to hear his daughter’s voice, which he had never heard before, he ran quickly and brought the girl a little water to drink.

After she had drunk it, she said: “Give me your hand.” Her father took her right hand and raised her up. Standing on her own feet, she lifted her hands and eyes toward heaven and said:

“I give you thanks, almighty God, who, looking upon my humility, have deigned to save me through your holy Bishop.”

Thus, with her limbs restored, she recovered her sight and hearing and returned home joyfully.

## CHAPTER III. Of the man in whose hand a stick adhered

Two years before these events occurred, a certain man, fearing neither nor honoring the holy day of the Lord’s resurrection, took some grain and went to the mill. After putting the wheat in place, he began turning the mill with his hand.

When the work was finished, he could not open his palm. Instead, amid severe pain, he unwillingly held the stick that he had grasped. Afterwards, seeing that he could not release it, he cut the stick on both sides and came to the Saint’s basilica. After making his prayer and celebrating vigils, his fingers loosened and his hand was restored to its former use.

The following year, on this same holy day, he undertook again the work for which he had previously been rebuked by God, and once more the wood adhered to his hand. Weeping in pain, he returned to the basilica of the holy Confessor, but he did not immediately deserve to be heard.

Two years later, at the same feast at which we reported the healing of the girl, he too was freed from the burden of the wood.

## CHAPTER IV. Of a cripple who was healed

A cripple came from the region of Limoges. He could neither walk nor see the light of day. Carried in the hands of devout people, he was set down before the holy tomb. After imploring the mercy of the blessed Bishop, his disabled limbs were straightened, and he was restored to health.

## CHAPTER V. Of a blind man who was given sight

A certain blind man who had long lacked the light of his eyes came to the same feast. After making his prayer, as he stood before the holy tomb, his eyes suddenly opened. Rejoicing, he recovered his sight.

## CHAPTER VI. Of a weak man who was healed

A boy who lived in the city of Tours was being consumed by a severe and prolonged illness. All his limbs became weak, and the fever left him without hope of walking; his shins were twisted like ropes and could not be separated.

After the fever had departed, he asked his parents to carry him to the holy basilica. They brought him there and set him down at the Saint’s feet, praying that the customary power might assist him.

On the third day, while he or his parents continued in prayer and fasting, the light of mercy arose. His twisted shins were straightened, and his parents took him home unharmed.

## CHAPTER VII. Of the man who made a key on the Lord’s Day

So also, another man named Senator, from the Angevin village of Cracatonnum,

[Note: All the manuscripts have *Cracatonno*, except Colb. *a*, which has *Cratonno*. The second printed edition has *Cracotonno*. Clict. has *Cratotonno*.]

was making a key on the Lord’s Day when the fingers of both his hands contracted, with the nails fixed into his palms. Although he had wished to open a door, he could not open his hands.

After four months had passed, with the nails already embedded in the flesh and the palm putrefying, he sought the Confessor’s help. He devoted himself to prayer and fasting for four days, then raised his healthy hands and returned unharmed, praising the Bishop’s power and proclaiming that no one should undertake what he himself had presumed to do.

## CHAPTER VIII. Of a dead man raised

At the time when such things were occurring in the city of Tours, envoys from Spain—namely Florentius and Exsuperius—were coming to King Chilperic.

[Note: This embassy is discussed in Book VI of the *History*, chapter 18.]

I received them at the church for a meal. While we were dining, since they professed to be Catholics, Florentius, who was older in years, earnestly asked to learn something about the power of the blessed Man.

Giving thanks to God, I asked whether his name was even heard in those regions or whether anyone read his Life. In response to my question, he said that the Man’s name was greatly honored in those places. He also declared that he was a special protégé of the Bishop, saying that the Bishop’s great power had been displayed upon him.

“My grandfather,” he said, “built a basilica many years ago in honor of blessed Martin the Bishop. After it had been completed and adorned with elegant workmanship, he sent devout clerics to Tours,

[Note: Up to this point, the Martinian manuscript is the only witness; the remainder is eaten away by decay and corruption in the others.]

seeking relics of the Bishop, so that the place he had built in his name might be consecrated by his relics.

“After he had done this, he came every day and, prostrate on the ground with his wife, implored the help of the holy Bishop. After a long time, a child was born to them.

“When he was three months old, he was struck by a fever and so utterly wasted away that he could neither suck the breast nor take any nourishment. Meanwhile, as the illness continued and food was refused, with only his breath fluttering, he awaited death alone. Before long, his breath itself departed.

“Then the sorrowful mother, or grandmother, grieving the death of her only and firstborn child, took the lifeless little body in her arms and laid it before the altar of blessed Martin with no uncertain hope. As though they were seeing the Saint with their visible eyes, the old woman

[Another reading: “the grandfather”]

addressed him, saying:

“‘We had the greatest hope, most blessed Confessor, when we brought your pledge here, by which diseases might be driven away, fevers extinguished, the darkness of blindness dispelled, and other infirmities cleansed—for many things are read about you, things that you did either while alive or that you perform after your passing.

“‘For we have heard that you raised the dead by prayer, drove away leprosy by a kiss, cured the possessed by a word, restrained poison with a finger, and performed many other deeds. Your power will appear here if you now raise this little child according to our faith.

“‘But if you do not do so, we will no longer bow our necks here, light lamps, or offer you any mark of honor.’”

Having said this, she left the little child before the altar and departed with those who were with her.

[Note: In several manuscripts the words “she herself, and those who were with her” are absent.]

When morning came, they returned and found him turned toward the altar. While they marveled, his mother took him in her arms. Recognizing that he had recovered his breath, she brought him to the breast. He immediately drank milk and was strengthened.

Then his mother, together with his father and the entire household, raised their voices to heaven and blessed God, saying:

“Now we know that you are a great God and that you alone perform wonders, for by the prayer of your Confessor you have restored our little child to us.”

From then on they showed that place greater reverence than before.

I learned from Florentius’s own lips that these things had happened in this way.

## CHAPTER IX. Of the man who had a weak foot
A cleric from the city of Poitiers lived on an estate in that region belonging to the holy basilica. He had the use of one foot only with difficulty, which, as he himself maintained, he had lost through an attack by the noonday demon (see below, Book IV, chapter 36). Having cut a staff to the length of his knee and placed a hide over that same knee, he extended the impaired limb backward and completed the step he was attempting to make with his foot, using the staff for support. After nine years he came to the aforementioned basilica. Having poured out a prayer for three days, he rose on the third day before the festival, with his knee straightened. When the people arrived for the Saint’s solemnities, he explained how he had been healed through his power.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning the healing of my mother’s shin

The Saint’s power came to my mother’s assistance in the following manner. At the time when, after the pains of childbirth had passed, she gave birth to me, she suffered pain in one of the muscles of her shin. It was sudden, as though a nail had been driven into it, and it inflicted such a severe, fixed pain [Note: See the notes in Book 5 of the *History*, chapter V, column 209.] that it often caused her to faint. Nothing could relieve it except when, after being held for a very long time against the fire, it became numb from the heat of the hearth; and if some ointment was applied, it would also subside for a little while. What more need I say? [Column 0973D] After my ordination she came to Tours, either to meet the holy Bishop or because of her longing for me. When she had remained there for two or three months and had continually sought the help of the blessed Bishop, at last, as his customary compassion looked upon her, the pain departed from her shin—the pain that had wearied the woman for thirty-four years [Note: From this it may be inferred that Gregory was at least thirty-four years old when he was ordained. His mother had incurred this pain at the beginning of her labor, in which she gave birth to him.].

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the healing of a woman’s hand

Another woman from the territory of Angers had her fingers fixed into her palm. When she poured out prayers at the holy place, her fingers straightened, and she departed with her hand healed.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning a boy healed of illness

A boy in our household was seized by a severe fever and was burning with it. His limbs were burning externally, while internally he suffered intense thirst; and if he took any drink, he immediately vomited it back from his stomach, while taking no food at all. When he had been exhausted by this suffering on the fourth or fifth day [Others: year], he asked that a little powder from the tomb be given him to drink. When it had been given to him and diluted with wine, he drank it faithfully and recovered his health and strength.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning the healing of Theoda’s foot

Theoda, daughter of the former priest Wiliacharius, frequently suffered from an excess of fluid in her feet. She lost the use of one foot, which had been reduced to weakness. Afterward she came to the blessed basilica, where, while she poured out repeated prayers, the weakness was removed and she was restored to health.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning a bent man

At that time there was in a village [Edition: city] that was held under the protection of the holy mother church [Note: Thus the Gatian manuscript. The printed editions do not have *holy*. Bell., Laud., two Colbert manuscripts, and Clar. read “holy mother-church.” “Mother church” means the cathedral church; I think that is more likely what is designated here than a “mother-church” in the narrower sense.], a certain man who walked bent over, as though his lower back had been broken. Like the woman in the Gospel narrative (Luke 13:11), he was bent downward and utterly unable to straighten himself upward; with two sticks placed beneath his armpits, he moved along in a stooped posture. When he came to the festival, he was standing upright on the third day after the solemnities had been celebrated, cleansed of every demonic attack, and departed healed.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning the infirm Gundulf

A certain Gundulf, a citizen of that city, had lived from his childhood with Guntharius, son of King Chlothar [Note: He was the eldest son of Chlothar the Great by Queen Ingund; he died while his father was still alive, as Gregory himself testifies in Book IV of the *History*, chapter 3.]. While he was in Guntharius’s service and, at the king’s command, was climbing a tree to pick ripe apples, a branch broke and he fell. His foot struck against a stone, and he was left disabled.

Many years later [Column 0974D], while he remained in this condition, he mounted a horse and urged it rapidly forward. When his gait slipped, he was thrown down and severely injured the other foot—the one that had been sound—by crushing it. He then asked to be carried to the holy basilica. Thrown down upon the pavement, he poured out a faithful prayer. The divine compassion, which is always accustomed to help those in distress, did not delay [Note: Roman manuscript: “nor did the effect that…”]; immediately all pain was removed, and he rose unharmed from the pavement.

Thus for about thirty years he had continually limped on the other foot, as we said above. At last, having examined the offenses of his own conscience, he resolved to convert—namely, by cutting his hair and serving the holy Bishop himself. First, however, he obtained from the king an order that, while still alive, he should hand over all his possessions to the basilica. When this had been done, his head shaved, and the resolve of his good intention fulfilled, the foot that had been shortened by broken bones was lengthened. Whereas previously he had gone supported by two boys, he now goes wherever he wishes without anyone’s assistance and without any hindrance from his disability.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning a blind man whose sight was restored

After this a little boy from the Limousin, who was blind, came and received the light of his eyes in the following manner. In the third year of his life, when he was beginning to set his feet in walking and, as his tongue broke into speech, was loosening his lips into words, he was fondly playing with his mother, drinking her kisses, clinging to her neck, and being carried in her arms. Then, when a wind was stirred up by a demonic assault, dust from the ground, mixed with straw, rose and was carried in a great whirlwind over the boy and his mother. But the rustic and careless woman did not take care to protect herself and her son with the banner of the Savior [Note: Most manuscripts read *salutari*, “with the saving sign”—that is, the sign of the cross, which the faithful had used from the earliest centuries of the Church to ward off the assaults of demons.]. Therefore, when the ambush prevailed, the young boy’s eyes were filled with dust and sealed shut.

After crying out for a long time, he was eventually quieted by his mother, but remained blind. When he grew older, he was given to beggars, so that by walking about with them he might receive some sort of support. His parents were extremely poor. In the twelfth year of his blindness [Note: Clar. reads “of his birth.” The printed editions read “of his age.”], he came to Tours before the day of the solemnity on which God the Father, joining the Word to flesh, brought salvation to the world. When the vigil of the festival had passed [Laud.: “on the day”], while the others were departing and he lay motionless at the Saint’s feet, he suddenly felt as though someone had pricked his eyes with a thorn. At once blood began to flow from them down his cheeks. Turning his face upward, he saw a candle shining above him, and he cried out in a loud voice:

“I give you thanks, holy Confessor of God, because through your power I have deserved to receive the light. O wondrous grace! O immense power! [Note: The printed editions read: “for by many effects.”] In many ways you scatter your gifts among the peoples. The man who had asked for alms has received sight, and for a long time deprived of external light, he is now adorned with the light of your power. If only the darkness of your many crimes did not keep you away from our sight, surely you would come visibly and say to the sick in Peter’s voice: ‘I have no gold or silver, but what I have I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ, depart healed’” (Acts 3:6).

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning the ear of Siggo the Referendary

There had been a reason for our going to the town of Reims. After we had been kindly received by Bishop Aegidius, who then governed the Church, we went to the church on Sunday morning and, sitting in the sacristy, awaited the Bishop’s arrival. At that time I had the relics of Saint Martin with me, although I possessed them in a rash manner. Then Siggo [Note: Some manuscripts read *Sigo*. See above, Book V of the *History*, chapter 3. Frodoard praises this passage of Gregory in Book II of the *History of Reims*, chapter 2, and Book IV, chapter 50.] the former referendary of Sigibert came to meet us. I asked him to sit beside me after he had exchanged a kiss with me.

[Note: The Roman manuscript omits the passage from “But” to “Indeed.”] But he had one ear blocked and could scarcely understand what we were saying with the other. After we had conversed sufficiently, he was summoned into the church’s house. As soon as he had left me, the obstruction of his deaf ear was broken open. Feeling as though a great wind were escaping from it, he recovered his hearing. He immediately returned and began to give me thanks, saying:

“It was already the third day since I had lost the hearing of this ear; but while I was speaking with you, I felt it quickly opened.”

Then I, confessing [Others: confused], lest this be attributed to me, said:

“My dearest son, do not give me any thanks, but give them to him whose power restored your hearing. For you should know that I have with me the relics of blessed Martin, by whose power the heaviness of your hearing has been removed.”

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the disease of livestock

At a certain time a savage plague raged so fiercely among the livestock that it seemed unlikely that any of the breed would remain to recover. One of our people went to the holy basilica and took oil from the lamps that hung from the ceiling, together with the water, placing them in a small vessel. He carried it home and, dipping his finger into the liquid, marked with the Lord’s cross the foreheads and backs of the animals that the disease had not yet touched [Note: The sense seems to be the same as if one read: “…and, after carrying the oil home, he marked the animals that the disease had not touched, dipping his finger…”]. He then poured some of this oil, full of faith, into the mouths of the animals after they had been thrown to the ground and turned onto their backs. Immediately, faster than words can tell, the hidden plague was driven away and the livestock were delivered.

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning a blind man whose sight was restored

An inhabitant of Avranches [Note: Clar. reads *Cebrincatinus*. He was from the city of Avranches, in Normandy], who had been denied the use of sight for six years, sought to be saved by the protection of the blessed Confessor. Coming to his basilica and devoting a long time to fasts and prayers, he implored the help of the blessed Bishop. Finally, when the most holy festival arrived and the people were watching the solemnities of the Mass, sight was restored to him. He returned to his homeland seeing, though he had arrived at the holy basilica being led by another. In gratitude for such great compassion, he vowed to be tonsured there. He later returned devoutly and fulfilled this vow.

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning another blind man whose sight was restored

A certain man came from overseas regions. While he was working in a field, a violent wind suddenly arose over him with dust, and he lost the light of his eyes. He who for a long time had guided the blind was himself led home by another. He remained in this blindness for three years. Afterward he sought the basilica of the blessed Confessor and, after devoting himself to prayer there for four years, was visited by divine power. His eyes were opened, and he deserved to see the light.

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning Julian, a cripple

As we have often said, this fame spread widely not only through our own city but also through other cities and almost throughout the whole world. A certain Julian came from Spain with weak hands and feet. Devoutly entering this physician’s presence, he said:

“For I unshakably believe, most holy Bishop, that you will be able to offer me the remedies of healing which you are not accustomed to withhold from others who hope in you.” [Note: Most manuscripts read: “weak in hand and foot … he addressed him, saying: ‘For I believe, most holy one,’” and so forth.]

Persisting continually in prayer with this faith and not doubting the Lord’s compassion, he was restored unharmed, with his feet and hands straightened.

## CHAPTER XXII. Concerning a woman whose sight was restored at the holy bed

In the preceding books we have often said that many miracles are performed in that place from which he departed to heaven. I shall now disclose what happened recently.

A native woman of the city of Tours, deprived of the clarity of sight, sought the cell of Condat, where the little bed of the blessed Bishop is kept. She thought that she would have protection if she touched the rails of that bed. The “bed” is said to be nothing other than the place where, on that pavement, with ashes spread beneath him and a stone placed under his head, the Israel of our time lay with bent neck [Note: Victor, with the editions of Baluze and Choler: “The bed is said to be nothing other than ashes spread on that pavement and a stone placed beneath the head, on which he would lie at night with bent neck.”].

The woman was therefore led to this shrine with the support of a man, and there she poured out a contrite prayer for many days. At last, compassion, which is often poured out to show mercy, looked upon her and restored the sight she had lost. Thereafter such great faith inflamed the woman that she never departed from that place until the day of her death.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning a mute whose brothers deprived him of his property

An inhabitant of the city of Angers, his bodily members disordered by illness, turned his head toward the little bed. Then, as the fever grew stronger day by day, he became deprived of all use of his limbs and lost both hearing and speech. After a few days, when he had recovered from the fever but remained without a voice, his brothers deprived him of his share of the property and expelled him from his father’s house, saying:

“This man has become insane. May God not allow him either to cling to our property or to acquire a share of the inheritance.”

They were free men living on their own property [Note: Three printed editions read: “They were tenants and occupied themselves with their own property, but they thought unjustly,” and so forth.]; but, thinking nothing of the things that belonged to God, they expelled the mute and deaf man whom they ought rather to have supported. Although he lacked these faculties, he nevertheless retained understanding in his heart. He took wooden tablets in his hands and struck them together, imitating the voice of someone asking for something.

With this device he came to the aforementioned village, where he joined others who were begging for alms. Six years had now passed during which this poor man had lived on the generosity of the holy cell. It happened that one Sunday night, while he was lying in the house of his host, that place was suddenly filled with immense light. Terrified with fear, he fell prostrate on the ground. Immediately a certain man appeared to him, dressed in priestly attire. He touched him, placed the cross of Christ on his forehead, and said:

“The Lord has made you well. Rise, hasten to the church, and give thanks to your God.”

He himself raised his voice in thanksgiving and filled the neighborhood with his cries. Everyone immediately ran together to see the spectacle and marveled at the man speaking whom they had seen mute the day before. Meanwhile the signal was given at the morning hour; the people gathered, and after the vigils had been celebrated, the Saint’s power was gloriously revealed. During those days two possessed persons were cleansed in that place when the demon was expelled.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning the increase of oil

But let us return to our Aredius [Note: Here too the printed editions read *Aridus*. See the preceding book, chapter 39], indeed, as I may say, the special fosterling of the blessed Confessor, who is often granted to behold miracles through his relics.

He came to the Saint’s festival with the kindness, humility, and charity that were customary in him. On his return he carried with him a small flask filled with oil from the holy tomb, saying:

“Perhaps there is some sick person along the road who desires, with a contrite heart, to receive a blessing from the church of blessed Martin.”

At length, in a certain place, a devout woman approached him, offering another flask with oil and saying:

“I ask you, servant of Christ, to sanctify this oil with your blessing.”

But he, lest he seem subject to vanity, said:

“My power is small. But, if you wish, I have oil from the tomb of blessed Martin, with which this oil may be infused. If you believe that his power is great, you will draw healing from it.”

The woman, rejoicing, asked that what the priest had said be carried out. The vessel was half full. When the liquid taken from the Saint’s basilica was poured into it, the oil immediately began to boil and filled the flask to the very top. When the matron saw this, she marveled at the power of the blessed Confessor and returned home rejoicing.

## CHAPTER XXV. Concerning a woman whose fingers were straightened

Another woman, whose fingers were contracted and fixed into her palm, sought the basilica of the blessed Bishop Martin. After a few days had passed, while she poured out a prayer and implored the Saint’s help, her fingers were straightened and she recovered the use of her hand.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Concerning a crippled woman

Some years ago a girl fell into a very serious illness. All her limbs were weakened and contracted. When she heard of the miracles that the glorious Bishop performed for individuals, she devoutly invoked his name. After a few days she asked to be carried to his basilica. Lying in its courtyard for many days and repeatedly pouring out prayers with tears, she was visited by the Bishop’s power. Thus, through the assistance of divine mercy, she departed healed.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Concerning a crippled boy

A boy from the territory of Angers was staying in his parents’ house when, as he himself maintained, through the assault of magical demonic art he lost the use of his hands and feet. His fingers contracted inward so that his nails were fixed into his palms, while the tendons [Others: sinews] behind his knees dried up and twisted his heels toward his legs. For six years his parents carried him about in this pitiable condition, and then he was taken to the temple of the holy Bishop.

But he persevered in prayer, and when his limbs were restored, he blossomed forth like a new Floridus, in accordance with the meaning of his name.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning a blind man whose sight was restored

A cleric who had been a slave from birth and belonged to the holy basilica had been deprived of sight through an attack by an ambusher. Unable to do any work there, he remained sick in his own little lodging. He endured this blindness for nearly three years. Then he sought the church of the blessed priest, prayed there for the customary mercy, and returned home with his sight restored.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Concerning a man whose hand adhered to a staff

A slave belonging to someone in the territory of Tours was repairing a hedge on Sunday when his hand began to adhere to the wood itself. He quickly pulled away his right hand, and, while he stared at the event in amazement, the hand contracted with great pain; his nails also became fixed into his palm. With all the fingers of his right hand contracted, he returned sorrowfully to his lodging.

After four years he came to the Saint’s basilica, and, after praying, was healed. He proclaimed to the people that no one should imitate his deed, lest a greedy farmer stain the solemnity of so great a day, and lest weak humanity, engaged in earthly work, destroy the heavenly mystery of the holy Resurrection and our redemption [Note: Roman manuscript: “lest weak humanity, engaged in earthly work, destroy the heavenly mystery of our holy redemption and resurrection.”].

## CHAPTER XXX. Concerning a boy whose stomach was diseased

A little boy from Albi, whose stomach was wasting away from various illnesses, loathed food and drink. Even what he seemed able to take he vomited back with bitter anguish. When he had been tormented by this suffering for many days [Edition: illness], he was filled with faith and desired to come to the basilica of the blessed Confessor.

There he fasted and prayed for three days. On the fourth day he began to desire food, and after tasting wine with his mouth he was strengthened. Then, giving thanks, he departed healed.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Concerning a woman’s withered right hand

A certain woman, also said to have come from Angers, was withered in all her limbs, but especially carried a right hand more withered than her other joints, together with withered fingers. She prostrated herself at the Saint’s tomb. Afterward she went out and remained for a short time in the courtyard.

When the intervention of the glorious Bishop came to her aid, her vein received blood, her skin its color, and the rest of her body its strength; she was restored to solidity. The cause of her suffering was this: on the Sabbath after sunset, which bordered on the Lord’s Day, she had wished to shape bread [Note: This pious custom still persisted in the ninth century: from Saturday evening onward the faithful refrained from manual labor out of reverence for the following Sunday, as is evident from the *Miracles of Saint Theodoric, Abbot of Reims*, in the first volume of the Benedictine series, p. 621.].

## CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning a woman whose hands had adhered to each other

Another woman suffered something similar. Her hands were contracted inward and joined together so that they adhered to one another. Tormented by the greatest pains, she set out on the road, saying:

“If I go to the basilica of Saint Martin, this illness will immediately depart. For I trust that he will also come to my aid, since he has often taken pity on those suffering such things.”

As she said this and began the journey as best she could, her hands immediately separated, though the fingers were not straightened. But when she reached the holy place and poured out a prayer, all pain was immediately removed. Her fingers became firm, and she returned with her hands free, giving thanks.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Concerning the disease of horses

That year there was a severe disease of horses in the region of Bordeaux. Near the village [Edition: city] of Marciac, which lies within this district and is subject to the authority of blessed Martin, there is an oratory consecrated both by his name and by his powers.

When the aforementioned calamity arrived, people came to the oratory and made vows for their horses, promising that, if the animals survived, they would offer tithes from them to that place. Since this seemed to help them, they added that they would take the iron key that locked the door of the oratory and impress its marks upon the horses.

When this had been done, the Saint’s power prevailed so greatly that those who had fallen ill were healed, while those who had not contracted the disease suffered from it no further.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Concerning a plague accompanied by blisters

The previous year the people of Tours were being devastated by a very severe pestilential illness. The sickness was of such a kind that when a man was seized by a powerful fever, his whole body erupted in blisters and small pustules. The blisters were white and hard, possessing no softness, but causing immense pain. When, having reached maturity, they began to crackle and discharge, the pain increased still more as the clothing adhered to the body. In this illness no medical skill could help unless the Lord’s aid intervened.

Many who sought a blessing from the holy basilica deserved assistance. But why is it necessary to speak of many, when the others received what we saw one woman receive?

The wife of Count Eborinus was suffering from this plague. She was so covered with blisters that neither her hands, nor the soles of her feet, nor any part of her body remained free of them; even her eyes themselves were covered and obscured by them. When she was already considered to be in danger of death, she sought the blessing of the holy tomb.

Water was sent to her, the water with which the tomb of the blessed man had been washed on the Lord’s Pascha (see above, Book II, chapter 51). After she had anointed her wounds with it, she also drank some of it. Immediately the fever was extinguished, the blisters ran off without pain, and she was healed.

## CHAPTER XXXV. Concerning two paralytics and one blind man who were healed

There are many miracles that the whole world experiences, of which, as I think, not even the smallest part reaches us. Let us nevertheless report those that occur in our vicinity [Column 0981C].

Badegisilus, bishop of Le Mans [Note: Concerning his election, see Book VI of the *History*, chapter 9], was invited to a certain place in his diocese to consecrate a basilica of the blessed man, both in name and in relics. After the solemnities had been celebrated [Note: Thus the manuscripts, with a change of case familiar to Gregory. Clar. reads “after the solemnities had been celebrated,” and so forth. Colbert manuscript: “when the solemnities had been celebrated,” and so forth. The printed editions read: “when he had celebrated the solemnities.”], two paralytics recovered the use of their legs and one blind man received his sight when the name of Saint Martin was invoked.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Concerning the crippled Augustus

A certain Augustus [Note: The manuscripts read *Agustus*, in accordance with the spelling customary in those times], a citizen of the city of Tours, was suffering from excessive pain in his loins. His feet were contracted and drawn almost up to his loins, and he was gravely debilitated. He suffered from this illness for two years.

Then, at the urging of his relatives, he sought the Saint’s basilica. There, fasting and praying for seven days, he was freed from pain, his feet were straightened, and he departed healed.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Concerning a mute girl

At this time, when the other women had departed and one woman alone remained at the loom, a most terrifying shadow appeared to her as she sat. It seized her [Others: “the little girl”] and began to drag her away. Crying out and weeping, and seeing no help, she nevertheless tried courageously to resist.

After two or three hours had passed, the other women returned and found her lying half-dead on the ground, utterly unable to speak. She gestured with her hand, but since they understood nothing, she remained mute. The shadow that had appeared to her so greatly harassed the people in that house that they abandoned the place and moved elsewhere.

Later, after two or three months had passed, the girl came to the basilica and deserved to recover the power of speech. She then recounted with her own mouth everything that she had suffered.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Concerning a deacon from Châlons

Meanwhile a deacon from Châlons, as was customary among that people, was drinking while others were celebrating the morning thanksgiving when he was deprived of his sight. Recognizing his fault and realizing that he had acted unworthily of his calling, he abstained from food and drink, spending the night in vigils and devoting himself to prayer.

As he was doing this, the report that had spread throughout the world reached his ears: namely, that Martin the Bishop was at Tours, and that at his tomb the devastation of such illnesses was often driven away and brought to rest. The deacon did not delay. He immediately ordered the journey to be undertaken and came without doubting the power of the blessed man. Prostrate on the ground and supported by prayer, he received the light on the third day when his eyes were opened.

As I carefully sought to discover the truth of why this had happened to him, I learned the following from him:

“Seven months ago,” he said, “when I was going to church after the morning signal had been sounded, I met one of my friends. I rushed into his embrace and kisses and began to ask whether he had left everything prosperous at home. Then, having been called back from the road, I began to drink with him. When it seemed that we had fulfilled our friendship over cups, he said farewell and departed. After he had gone, my eyes were so firmly joined by the adhesion of my eyelids that I could not open them at all.

“Finally, as I departed sadly in this condition, I desired to visit the tomb of the blessed Bishop. On the third day after I arrived, while I was standing beside his tomb, a sudden great fever seized my eyes. I began to groan bitterly and earnestly implore the Saint’s help. Immediately blood burst from my eyes, drove away the night, and brought back the day.”

After the deacon had told us this, he returned home unharmed.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Concerning a woman who was crippled and blind

There was also a certain blind woman whose hands and feet were contracted backward. With the support of her parents, she came to celebrate the blessed festival of the glorious Bishop. On the third day after the festival had ended, when she wished to return home, she fell prostrate in the holy basilica and began to pray that the Lord might deign to show her the customary help of his mercy.

As she asked this with tears, her hands were immediately straightened and her feet made firm. She was brought to the holy tomb and gave thanks for the health she had received. After this she asked to be led to the door. There she again fell prostrate and said to her companions:

“I will not rise from here unless he who restored the use of my feet and hands first gives me back the light of my eyes.”

As she said this, some possessed persons suddenly began to cry out that they were being tormented and confessed that Martin was present. But since the devil, who is a liar from the beginning (John 8:44), is not admitted as a witness, the presence of the blessed man was nevertheless made clear by the events themselves. For this woman, who shortly before had been straightened, now also received sight and proved that the blessed Bishop was present.

## CHAPTER XL. Concerning a paralytic who was healed

A short time afterward, a paralytic lay on a bed. He had been brought from Bourges on a cart. He too was visited in the same way by the power of the blessed Bishop, rose unharmed, and, restored to the use of his legs, was received in health while a crowd of his parents [Note: Two printed editions: “relatives”] looked on.

## CHAPTER XLI. Concerning chains broken from a girl

During these days a certain girl, born of parents who had once been slaves [Note: Some manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read “born of free parents.” Our reading is better and belongs to the older manuscripts. The girl’s parents were not free by birth, but slaves who had been granted freedom; such people were called *liberti*, as though “freed.” This is clear from the fact that the patron’s sons—that is, the sons of the man who had granted the parents their freedom—were attempting to reduce the girl to slavery again.], was condemned to the yoke of servitude by the patron’s sons, her freedom having been broken.

Since she would not consent to perform any work for her unjust masters, she was bound with chains and fetters. While she remained in this custody, weeping and lamenting because she could not attend the blessed festival as others were doing, the beam in which her feet were confined suddenly split. Thus, as though already free, though still bound by chains, she escaped and sought the blessed basilica.

As soon as her feet touched the sacred threshold, the broken chains immediately fell from her neck. Thus she was granted both health and freedom.

## CHAPTER XLII. Concerning the book of his Life preserved amid flames

What if I turn to the very writings of the blessed Life? Will it not be remarkable that the sacred book of this history, surrounded by flames, was neither scorched nor consumed?

A monk of the Monastery of Marmoutier, sent by order of his abbot to another cell [Note: That is, a country estate, or, as we would say today, a priory or provostry], as though to carry out some task, took with him the book of the blessed Bishop’s Life for the salvation of his soul and the correction of his life. When night came, he placed himself on a little bed filled with old straw and put the book beneath his head.

As he slept, a man appeared to him in a dream and said:

“Do not sleep on this straw, for it has been sprinkled with blood.”

I believe that, as human mortality allows, some crime had been committed in that place, and that for this reason the blessed man would not permit the words of his praise to be tossed about there. The first vision seemed trivial [Note: That is, futile or empty, as is clear from many other passages of Gregory], and the second warning had no effect. But the third shook the monk terribly.

He arose and went out at dawn to his work. He ordered a boy to remove the straw from the bed and consume it in the fire, saying nothing about the book. The ignorant boy, finding the book among the straw, carried it outside and lit the fire.

When everything had been reduced to ashes and nothing remained but cinders, the book appeared unharmed. Not a letter [Colbert manuscript: “not a page,”]—indeed, not even a single leaf, as the truth requires—had been consumed. Thus divine power deigned to guard the praises of its fosterling, so to speak: the flame did not burn his book, whom the goad of desire had not scorched in this world.

But lest this seem incredible to anyone, the book itself is still preserved with us [Note: Roman manuscript: “with us.” Edition: “the book itself is with us.”].

## CHAPTER XLIII. Concerning two boys who were healed

Once, as we were traveling, two boys among the keepers of the horses began to fall ill. One suffered from an illness, the other from dysentery. A strong fever nevertheless afflicted them both, and they were so exhausted that they could not be kept sitting even when placed on the backs of horses.

I took out some powder that I had removed from the Saint’s tomb and kept in a little box, mixed it with water, and ordered them to drink it. Immediately their fever was subdued and their pain extinguished, and both recovered.

## CHAPTER XLIV. Concerning the crippled Malulf

The miracles that the Lord daily deigns to perform for the praise of his Bishop are renowned. As I have often testified, I am unable to recount them adequately in my ignorance; nevertheless, precisely because of this ignorance, I shall labor over them, lest they appear to be concealed [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “lest they appear to be despised or consigned to oblivion.”].

A certain Malulf [Note: Gatian manuscript: *Palulfus*. The editions: *Madulphus*], a citizen of the territory of Tours, was overcome by a savage illness and lay gasping on his little bed. As he wasted away under this affliction, his hands and feet became contracted. He endured this weakness for five years.

Finally, in the sixth year, he asked to be carried to the Saint’s basilica. There, lying in prayer, he lost his disability and deserved to obtain health.

## CHAPTER XLV. Concerning the straightening of another woman’s hands
And so, lest what is related here seem incredible to anyone because the names of individuals are not recorded beforehand in the pages, the reason is this: when they have been restored to health by the Saint of God, they immediately depart; and sometimes they return so secretly that, if one may say so, no one sees them. When word spreads that the power of the blessed Bishop has appeared, we summon the custodians of the church and learn what has happened; yet we do not always learn the names from them. We generally write down by name those whom we have been able to see, or those whom we ourselves have investigated.

A certain man from Bourges came to the festival with disabled hands. His fingers were fixed into his palms so deeply that he was thought to be swarming with worms. But after the solemnity had been celebrated, the fingers of both hands were straightened, and he was restored to health; the entire people saw him return sound. The cause of his disability was that he had wished to repair a grain-field hedge on the Lord’s Day.

## CHAPTER XLVI. Of the woman whose arm had contracted

There was a woman from the territory of Poitiers whose arm had withered after the sinews contracted. Coming to the tomb of the blessed Man, she spent the night in prayer and vigils and returned with her arm healthy. But immediately afterward she was seized by her masters and reduced to servitude, and the same affliction returned. She came back again and was healed. Then her masters came, intending to take her away; but after accepting payment from the Saint’s possessions, they ceased their efforts, and thus she was granted her freedom.

## CHAPTER XLVII. Of the man who was held for debt

In those days, when a certain man was being pressed to discharge a debt that he had incurred in his necessities, and had neither the means nor the ability to repay what he had borrowed, he was confined in prison. Finally, when the creditor saw that he could extort nothing from him because he had nothing and no one extended to him a hand of mercy, he bound him more tightly and, denying him food and drink, said:

“I shall make you waste away from hunger as an example to everyone, until you repay everything.”

While these things were taking place, the relics of the holy Bishop, which were being carried to the district of Soissons, were passing along the street. When the prisoner heard the voices of those singing psalms, he prayed that the power of the holy Bishop might visit him. Immediately his bonds were loosed, and with no one restraining him, he entered the holy basilica. Thereafter he was ransomed by devout persons and released from the bond of his debt.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. Of the blind woman who was given sight

1105 It also happened at one of the festivals that a woman who had lost her sight and remained in blindness, having heard of the miracles of the holy Man, eagerly sought his basilica with devoted faith. She prostrated herself on the bare ground before the tomb, and as soon as she had poured out her prayer, she was deemed worthy to receive her sight.

## CHAPTER XLIX. Of the paralytic whose entire body was disabled

At this solemnity there came a little boy whose eyes were closed, whose ears were blocked, whose mouth was obstructed, whose hands had lost their use, and whose feet were incapable of walking. What more need be said? He was so utterly dead, as regards the use of all his limbs, that he merely trembled with the breath of life. But as soon as he reached the holy place, all his disability was completely removed, and he departed healthy, giving thanks.

## CHAPTER L. Of the presbyter healed of the chills

Lupus, a presbyter of the city of Bordeaux, was once severely afflicted by quartan fever, so that whenever the fever came upon him he could take neither food nor drink. Meanwhile the festival of Saint Martin the Bishop arrived. After keeping vigil with the rest of the clergy [Ed., “the people”], he went ahead of everyone in the morning and hastened to the Saint’s basilica.

As he hurried along, he met a Jew. When the Jew asked where he was going, he replied:

“I have contracted quartan fever, and now I am hurrying to the Saint’s basilica, so that his power may drive this illness from me.”

The Jew said:

“Martin will be of no help to you. Earth has crushed him and made him earthly, and you are seeking his church in vain. A dead man cannot give healing to the living.”

But Lupus, disregarding the words of the ancient serpent, continued on his way. Prostrated before the holy relics, he poured out a prayer and found there two little candles made of wax and papyrus. Taking them, he brought them home. After lighting them, he drank the ash of the papyrus with clean water, and immediately recovered his health.

But the Jew was struck by this illness and was shaken by it for a whole year; yet his wicked mind could never be changed, even by torments.

## CHAPTER LI. Of the healing of the little son of Cardegisilus

Cardegisilus [Note: Laud., Chadegisilus; others, Chardegysilus], a citizen of the city of Saintes, surnamed Gyso, received us into his house and invited us to the oratory which his mother had built and consecrated with relics of blessed Martin.

When our prayer had been completed, we were concerned to know whether the power of the holy Bishop had been manifested there. He replied:

“Less than three years ago, this little boy, my son, whom you see before you, while he was still hanging at his mother’s breast, began to be seriously ill. For thirty days or more he was carried from hand to hand with great difficulty, until he became so debilitated that he could no longer suck the breast, much less take any other food. When he was failing, on the sixth day after he had begun to grow worse, we laid him before the altar in tears, awaiting his death.

“I could not bear the grief and left the house, instructing the woman that, when he died, she should immediately place him in the grave. While his mother wept, the infant lay there until evening. When the sun was setting, he raised his voice and said: ‘Dearest sister, where are you?’ For he was accustomed to call his mother this, as infants do when they use terms of endearment.

“She ran up and said: ‘Here I am, my dearest son.’ She took him in her arms and immediately offered him her breast. As soon as he had drunk the milk, he recovered.”

## CHAPTER LII. Of the cleric with dysentery

When these matters were reported to us, one of our clerics contracted diarrhea of the bowels with fever and extreme stomach weakness; and most of what he discharged from below was blood. His condition was made worse by the fact that, as his nausea increased, he immediately rejected the food he took. But as soon as he drank from the dust of the tomb, he was freed from every illness and regained his strength.

## CHAPTER LIII. Of the hanged man who was released; also of another

I have decided not to remain silent about this either: more than once the extended right hand of mercy has lifted men who were rushing headlong toward death.

A servant of Genitor, one of our citizens [Ed., “our servant”], was seized by a judge for the crime of theft and condemned to the gallows. As he was being led away, he invoked the name of the blessed Bishop, saying:

“Deliver me, holy confessor Martin, from the danger that threatens me.”

He was hanged and left there alone. Suddenly a wind arose, and he heard a voice saying: “Let us set him free.” Then the stake supporting the man was shaken from the four quarters of the heavens, torn from the earth with an immense clod of soil like an uprooted tree. Thus the man condemned to death was raised alive again.

Another man [Note: Gat. divides the chapter here, and consequently the chapter numbers thereafter do not agree, although the same narratives are given], who had committed many crimes and, moved by God, was doing penance for the evils he had perpetrated, was arrested without cause and condemned to a similar death. He continually invoked the aid of the holy Confessor. After he had been hanged, the bonds broke, and he fell unharmed to the ground.

But the evil minds of men hanged again the man whom God had rescued. When the abbot of the monastery nearest the place heard this, he ran to the count to plead for him. The monastery was about three miles away. Having obtained the man’s life from the count, he returned and found him alive. After taking him down from the gallows, he brought him to the monastery, where the man confessed and said:

“I experienced the power of Saint Martin, who rescued me.”

## CHAPTER LIV. Of the man who was healed of muteness

There was a man within the territory of the city of Tours, from the village of Mount Laudiacensis [Note: Perpetuus built there a church in honor of Saint Laurence. See the notes on the final chapter of Book X of the *History*]. He was a simple man by nature and bound in marriage.

One night, while he was sleeping with his wife, terror suddenly arose. Frightened, he leapt from his bed, and as he wandered anxiously through his little dwelling, he lost the service of his voice. Without delay, he indicated by signs to his wife that she should bring him to the Saint’s basilica.

When he arrived and then lay continually in prayer before the blessed tomb for six months, his tongue was released, and by the power of the blessed Bishop he was deemed worthy to recover speech as he had possessed it before.

## CHAPTER LV. Of the woman whose hand had contracted

A woman from the territory of Transligeria was working on the Lord’s Day at a task which the authority of the Fathers forbids being performed on that day. Her hand contracted and became rigid, and her fingers were fixed into her palm.

While she was tormented by pain, she went to the holy church of the Confessor. She vowed that, if she were healed of this illness, she would thereafter perform no work on the day of the Lord’s resurrection that was inappropriate to that day. Immediately her fingers were removed from her palm, and her hand was straightened; she departed healed.

## CHAPTER LVI. Of the woman who was contracted and blinded

Great is the mercy of the Confessor, which rebukes the foolish in such a way that, by placing the fault before their eyes, it makes them corrected thereafter.

For this reason another woman was afflicted. On Saturday, after sunset, during the night adjoining the Lord’s resurrection, she placed bread in the oven. Her arm was shaken by pain. After she had put in a second and a third loaf, her hand unwillingly began to tighten around the piece of wood she was holding. Understanding that she was being condemned by the judgment of divine power, the woman quickly threw away the peel she held. Nevertheless, she could not escape the punishment. Her hands contracted with such severe pain that her nails were driven into her palms.

Believing that no physician’s remedy could heal her, she sought the Basilica of the Blessed One. There, praying faithfully, she departed healed with her hands straightened. She vowed that, every month, she would come for one week to the holy church and serve God and the blessed Bishop [Note: Laud., Colb. *tut.*, and others, “she must serve”]. It was clearly learned that she observed this for one year.

After a year, however, she omitted the week of one month and did not come to the holy basilica. While she was sitting in her little lodging, one of her eyes was pierced by pain. Pressing it, she lost the eye, and immediately the other also began to hurt. Thus, within the space of one hour, she became blind in both eyes.

Without delay, she confessed her fault and fled to the familiar refuge. There she poured out a humble prayer and penitently performed penance for her negligence. On the eighth day, with blood flowing from her eyes, she was given sight.

## CHAPTER LVII. Of the blind man who was given sight

The eyes of a certain man had been covered by a thick cloud of darkness. His eyelids had been sealed together by some sort of glue, and what remained of the man was held by great pains.

What more need be said? With the others, he devoutly sought the Saint’s festival, earnestly praying that he might be deemed worthy to be visited by the power of the blessed Bishop on the day of the solemnity.

But the power of the Confessor anticipated the sacred ceremonies, showing the people that he was present when it drove away the darkness and restored the light. Therefore, three days before the festival, while this man was praying in the courtyard that surrounds the body’s apse, his eyes suddenly opened, and he was enabled to see as he looked upon the light.

When he related this with thanksgiving to those who were present, he was told that he should instead remain silent and pour out his prayer, so that the blessed Bishop might more quickly complete the power he had begun. Then he prostrated himself on the ground and burst into tears. When his eyes had been strengthened, he rose unharmed from the ground.

## CHAPTER LVIII. Of a paralytic and two blind men healed, and two possessed persons cleansed

After the third day of this solemnity, a certain paralytic was praying in this place. As he himself related, his disability had come about in the following way.

When he was a little boy and was tending livestock in the field with the other shepherds, he fell asleep beside a certain spring. When the others withdrew at midday, he alone remained. Finally, waking from sleep and trying to rise, he was seized by pains. His limbs immediately contracted; his arms were twisted outward; the sinews behind his knees contracted; and his heels were drawn up toward his legs. Since he had no strength to walk, immense tears poured from him amid loud cries.

When his companions returned to look after the animals, they found him lamenting. His parents then carried him home in their arms. After a few days, when his pains had eased somewhat, he was assigned to certain beggars. With them he traveled around regions and cities for ten years or more. Coming also to this festival, he was strengthened in all his limbs.

On the same day two blind men were given sight, and two possessed persons were cleansed at the Bishop’s tomb.

## CHAPTER LIX. Of the feverish boy

A certain young man from among our people was afflicted by nightly fevers so severely that, from the eighth hour of the day until the second hour of the following day, he could find no relief from the burning fever. Every kind of food was horrible to him, and he took nothing by which he might be strengthened. Severe pain also shook all his limbs, and pallor covered his cheeks.

While he was being carried sick in the arms of his parents, I could scarcely manage [Note: Thus all the manuscripts except Clar., which, with the printed editions, reads “he could scarcely manage”] to have him brought to the tomb of the blessed Bishop. At last he was brought there. As soon as he drank from the holy dust of the tomb, diluted in water, the entire illness fled through this blessing, the fever was extinguished, and he recovered.

Without delay, the boy sought the private place used for bodily evacuation, and he was led aside to relieve his bowels. But when he discharged the contents of his intestines, propelled by gas, two worms immediately emerged from him in the form of snakes. They appeared to move before human eyes in such a way that they were thought to be alive. After he had expelled them, he was immediately completely healed, and he took food and drink as he was accustomed to do. The redness returned to his cheeks when the pallor had fled, and all his limbs were strengthened.

## CHAPTER LX. Of the things that happened during my journey

Recently an opportunity arose for me to go to the territory of the city of Cavillonensis [Note: This is how all the manuscripts read, except the single manuscript of Clermont, which, with the printed editions, has *Cabillonensis*. Hence some have thought that the city of Cabillonum in Burgundy, commonly called Châlons-sur-Saône, is meant here. Yet it is absolutely certain that Gregory is speaking here of the city of Cavellionensis, or Cavellicensis, or Cabellicensis, commonly called Cavaillon, which was formerly subject to the metropolitan of Arles and is now subject to the metropolitan of Avignon. Indeed, Veranus, the bishop whom Gregory praises below, was bishop of Cabellicum, not of Cabillonum [Col. 0990D]. At that time both cities belonged to the kingdom of Burgundy. See Cointius’s discussion of this matter, and compare what we observed on Book VIII, chapter 31, and Book IX, chapter 4 of the *History*, where we confirmed learned men’s arguments by the authority of the manuscript codices].

I was going to visit my mother. But fearing that illnesses might overtake us, I ventured to take with me some of this dust—that is, dust from the tomb of the blessed Bishop—so that, if some illness attacked one of our people, the Saint’s power might come to his aid in its customary manner.

When I reached my mother, a fever immediately seized one of the boys, together with dysentery; it weakened and consumed him so completely that, deprived of the ability to eat, he was nourished only by the fevers. On the third day, when these things were happening and the matter had been reported to me, I gave the dying boy the dust, moistened, to drink. Immediately, when the fever had been driven away and the pain quieted, he recovered [Note: Thus Rom.; others, “when I had heard these things, the dust, diluted”; Bal., “moistened”].

During these days I heard from Bishop Veranus [Note: He was bishop of Cabellicum, as we said above] that once, when he was burning with quartan fever, he sought the basilica of blessed Martin that stood in that place and was healed after keeping vigil.

As we came from this journey to Auvergne, we found Bishop Avitus being so severely shaken by tertian fever that, even if he took any food, he immediately rejected it. But after drinking from this relic, he was strengthened, the fever having been trampled down.

A debilitating fever attacked two of our boys, and severe pain seized all their joints, as commonly happens with this infection. But after they drank from this blessing, they were healed.

I myself, during this journey, was suffering severe toothache [Rom., “felt severe toothache”]. Not only the teeth themselves but my entire head was pierced by the throbbing of the veins and by stabbing pains, and my temples throbbed violently. I sought this remedy and immediately recovered when the pain was suppressed.

O indescribable theriac! O ineffable medicine! O praiseworthy antidote! O, so to speak, heavenly purgative, which surpasses the physicians’ skill, exceeds the sweetness of spices, and rises above the strength of every ointment! It cleanses the belly like agrimony, the lungs like hyssop, and purifies the head like pellitory. It not only strengthens weakened limbs, but—greater than all these things—it wipes away and smooths the very stains of the conscience.

Let what has been inserted into this little book suffice, then. Yet if we are still deemed worthy to witness miracles, I would like them to be inserted into another little book, so that what is displayed may not be hidden but may rather be proclaimed aloud.

For the rest, we ask for his power: may he who grants such things from the tomb deign to raise us, dead to God through sins, from the sepulchre of this death, so that at the time of the resurrection of our flesh he may obtain forgiveness for us, when he is advanced to the crown.

[Col. 0991] Here ends the third book.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0991]

## Prologue

1115 The Prophet exhorts us with most salutary advice, saying: “Your friends, O God, are worthy of honor” (Psalm 138:17). Likewise, in another psalm: “Those who magnify those who fear the Lord” (Psalm 14:4) are joined to the blessedness of the eternal house.

Thus it is plainly evident to human understanding that everyone is admonished to render reverent worship to God’s friends—not only those free from wrongdoing, but also those devoted to the evil of culpable sin. This matter not only grants benefit in the present age but also provides refreshment in the age to come.

For when we often see signs of power proceeding from the tombs of the blessed, we are rightly reminded to offer them the reverence of honor that is their due, since we never cease to ask them for remedies for our infirmities. Through their prayers we do not doubt that we may obtain even the remission of sins—and not only merit this remission, but also be saved from infernal punishments through their intervention.

For we trust that, just as here they cut away kinds of diseases, so there they may turn aside the savage penalties of torments; and just as here they mitigate bodily fevers, so there they may extinguish eternal ones; and just as here they cleanse the foul, disfiguring sores of leprosy, so there they may obtain, through their intervention, the cleansing of the stains of wrongdoing; and just as here they raise the corpses of the dead to life, so there they may restore to eternal life those buried in sin, rescuing them with an outstretched hand from the pools of Acheron.

Therefore, while each person rejoices in his own joy under his patron, he renders the honor that is due all the more fervently when he has felt himself cleansed by that patron’s power from the infirmity by which he was held. Both we and countless peoples have now experienced this through the blessed Bishop Martin, the special patron of the whole world. If only the sloth of our mind permitted us to venerate him as befits a friend of God, who so often restores us to health when we are oppressed by so many kinds of illness.

[Note: Here the manuscript of Colbertinus Tutelensis ends; the remainder has been torn away from the other codices. Nevertheless, it contains the table of contents of the chapters of this book.]

## CHAPTER I. Of the pain in my belly

Only recently I suffered pain in my belly. Although it did not entirely cause looseness, the evil of the pain nevertheless wandered through those winding recesses of the entrails. I often applied baths, I confess, and had hot things bound over the very twists of my bowels, but they could do nothing to heal the illness.

The sixth day had dawned, and the pain was growing stronger and stronger, when I remembered that a few years earlier, as is written in the second book of this work (chapter 1), I had been healed of this pain by the Saint’s power.

I rashly approached the place of the tomb [Note: The two printed editions read, “I approached, not rashly”]. I threw myself on the ground and poured out a prayer. Then, more secretly, I took a thread hanging from the curtains, inserted it beneath my clothing, and drew upon my belly with it the sign of the cross. Immediately the pain was quieted, and I departed healed.

## CHAPTER II. Of my tongue and lips

At one time my tongue had swollen severely, so that whenever I wished to speak it often made me stammer, which was not without embarrassment to me. I approached the Saint’s tomb and drew my obstructed tongue along the wood of the screen. Immediately, when the swelling was compressed, I recovered.

For it had swollen greatly and filled the entire cavity of the palate. Then, three days later, my lip began to protrude painfully. I again approached the tomb to seek health. When I touched my lip to the hanging curtains [Note: Thus Clar.; others have “and when I touched,” or “having touched”], the throbbing of the vein immediately ceased.

I believe that this happened to me because of an excess of blood. Nevertheless, I did not try to reduce the blood on account of the Saint’s power. This condition caused me no further trouble.

## CHAPTER III. Of the boy healed of fever

Finally, a little boy was weighed down by fever. His limbs had been wasted away, and, since he took no food, he was at the point of breathing out his spirit. His father ran to me in tears. I instructed him to bring the boy to the basilica and keep vigil over him there throughout the night. When he had done this, he received his son back healthy immediately through the power of the holy Bishop.

## CHAPTER IV. Of the contracted man, the blind woman, and three possessed persons

1118 A certain man came to the festival celebrated in the fifth month, his fingers contracted into his palm. After praying, he departed with his fingers straightened.

A blind woman, after eight years, prostrated herself on the ground before the Saint’s tomb and returned to her home with her eyes illuminated.

At that time three possessed persons were cleansed by the Saint’s power.

## CHAPTER V. Of Theodulf’s servant

In that year (A.D. 588), the thirteenth year of King Childebert, a servant of Theodulf, a citizen of Tours, came to the festival celebrated for the blessed Bishop’s passing.
