He was keeper of a herd of swine [Note: Thus Gat., Rom., Laud., Colb., and Clar., that is, “of a herd of pigs”; two other manuscripts, “of the estate.” The printed editions, “of the sheepfold”].

While he kept watch at night over the herd entrusted to him, lest either a beast carry off anything from it or a thief’s fraud steal it away, his eyes were suddenly covered with darkness and he lost his sight. He remained blind for six years and came to this festival. On the third day, however, he was given sight through the Saint’s power and was released by his master as a free man.

## CHAPTER VI. Of many infirmities healed

In the fourteenth year of the aforementioned king (A.D. 589), when the Saint’s solemnity arrived, twelve paralytics were straightened, three blind persons were given sight, and five possessed persons were cleansed.

Aredius, abbot of the city of Limoges, whom we mentioned in the earlier books [Note: Book II, chapter 39, and Book III, chapter 24], was also present at this festival. Through him the Lord restored a certain paralytic woman, who for eight years had lain in the courtyard of the blessed Confessor, placed upon a cart, by straightening her feet.

For this man of God declared that he had felt what was like the hand of blessed Martin when, after applying the sign of the cross, he touched the woman’s infirm limbs with healing contact.

Florentianus the major also came to this festival with Romulfus, the count of the palace [Note: Thus all the manuscripts, and correctly, as is clear from Book IX of the *History*, chapter 3, where these two men are said to have come to Tours in this same year to collect taxes. Hence the reading in most printed editions is corrupt, where “Temulphus, count of the palace” appears. Florentianus was, moreover, steward of the royal household, as stated in the cited passage of the *History*].

They were greatly astonished at the glory of the Confessor, through whom the Lord has now deigned to perform such miracles.

## CHAPTER VII. Of the grape in Galicia

Since we have mentioned Florentianus the major, I consider it wrong to remain silent about what I learned from him.

Once, on a diplomatic mission, he went to Galicia. Approaching King Miro, he disclosed the business entrusted to him. At that time King Miro was in the city where his predecessor had built a basilica of Saint Martin, as we explained in the first book of this work [Note: Namely, in chapter 11, where Miro’s father, who then ruled the Sueves in Galicia, is called Chararic].

Before the portico of this church, a vine stretched across a trellis, blooming as if painted, with clusters of grapes hanging down. Beneath it ran a path that led pedestrians to the doors of the sacred church.

As the king passed beneath it on his way to enter this church for prayer, he said to his attendants:

“Take care not to touch any of these clusters, lest you perhaps incur the displeasure of the holy Bishop. For everything contained in this courtyard has been consecrated to him.”

Hearing this, one of the boys said to himself:

“I do not know whether these things have been consecrated to this Saint or not. I know one thing: it is my intention to eat from them.”

Immediately he put out his hand and began to cut off the stem of a cluster. At once his right hand adhered to the trellis; his arm dried up and became rigid.

He was the king’s jester, accustomed to arousing the king’s amusement with humorous words. But no laughter or trick of his art helped him. Overcome by pain, he began to cry out and say:

“Come to the aid of a wretched man! Help the oppressed! Bring relief to the hanged man [Note: Two codices have “be relieved, hanged man.” Clar., with the printed editions, “relieve the hanged man”], and implore the power of the holy Bishop Martin on my behalf. For I am tormented by such an outcome, afflicted by such a wound, and severed by such a cutting.”

The king came out, and when he learned what had happened, he was so enraged against the boy that he wanted to cut off his hand, had his attendants not restrained him. They also said:

“Do not, O king, add your vengeance to God’s judgment, lest perhaps you turn against yourself the injury you threaten against the boy.”

Then, moved in his heart, the king entered the basilica and prostrated himself before the holy altar. With tears he poured out prayers to the Lord, nor did he rise from the pavement before the river of his eyes had washed away the page of this offense.

When the boy had been released from the bond by which he was held and had entered the basilica, the king raised him from the ground. Thus, receiving his servant unharmed, he returned to the palace.

The aforementioned major testified that he had learned these things from the king’s own account, just as we have related them.

Thus the glorious Bishop so illuminates his own city with miracles that he is not felt to be absent in foreign places.

## CHAPTER VIII. Of the Saint’s basilica near the city of Saintes

In the present year, Palladius, bishop of the city of Saintes, requested relics of this holy Confessor. He had built a basilica in his honor and consecrated it with these relics. There he was deemed worthy to receive miracles such as the city itself has often experienced.

For after two or three months had passed, I received a letter from him in which he reported that three paralytics with contracted legs had arrived. As soon as they entered the basilica and poured out their prayers, their feet were straightened and they were restored to health.

Two blind persons at that place were deemed worthy to receive sight after praying, and more than twelve who had been held by fever with chills recovered when the trembling was driven away.

## CHAPTER IX. Of two persons with dysentery

Two of our boys—a cleric named Dagobaldus and a layman named Theodorus—were suffering from dysentery with fever. They were so weakened by the illness [Gat., “relaxed”] that, whenever the need for evacuation arose, they could be lifted from their bed only by the hands of others. But after drinking dust from the tomb, they immediately recovered.

## CHAPTER X. Of the patens that the Saint provided

We have among us a sapphire-colored paten, which is said to have been brought by the Saint from the treasury of the Emperor Maximus [Note: That is, the Maximus who rebelled against Valentinian II, called the Younger, and whom Saint Martin visited at Trier, where Maximus had his royal residence. See Sulpicius Severus for more on this matter]. From it the Saint’s power often proceeds against fever with chills.

When someone is undergoing a fever attack, which ordinarily occurs with trembling, if he comes [Note: Thus Clar.; Vict. has, “if he comes with trembling, as ordinarily happens”; the others, with the printed editions, “when someone undergoing a fever attack, which ordinarily occurs with trembling, comes,” etc.] and drinks water from it, he is immediately healed.

There is also at the village of Condat another paten displayed by the Saint, made of crystal-like metal [Note: The printed editions, “entirely of crystal”], providing a similar benefit to the sick if it is sought with faith.

Bodillo, one of our notaries, was once troubled in spirit by weakness of the stomach, so that he could neither write according to his custom [Note: Others, with the printed editions, “according to his custom, nor take down what was dictated”] nor even scarcely transcribe what was dictated to him. After being repeatedly rebuked in words, he poured water over this paten of the blessed Man, which we said was with us, and transferred it into his mouth. Immediately restored to his senses, he carried out the work of his office more skillfully than usual.

## CHAPTER XI. Of Blidericus, to whom no children had been given

But why should it be surprising if he restores a mind disturbed by adversity to human beings, when he has often turned barrenness into fertility?

A certain Blidericus [Note: The printed editions, with Clar., Bledericus; Vict., Belidericus], a citizen of the territory of Chartres, took a wife and prayed that, by God’s gift, he might be enriched with offspring from her. But he received no fruit from her [Note: The printed edition adds, “namely, because she bore nothing”].

Thirty years had passed, his wife remaining barren, when the man, thinking most wisely about the welfare of his soul, said to his wife:

“Behold, the age in which we live is passing away, and no offspring is born between us to possess, when we are gone, the accumulation of our labor. I shall go,” he said, “to the basilica of Saint Martin and make it my heir, so that, since children have been denied us, I may at least possess in the future with him whatever I am able to possess here.”

The wise woman consented to the prudent counsel of her husband. Without delay they went to the Saint’s basilica. After pouring out a prayer, he invited the abbot to come home with him. When the abbot came, he handed over all his property to him, saying:

“Let all these things that I seem to possess be under the dominion of Saint Martin. Let me use only this much of them: that, while I live, I may be nourished by them.”

After drawing up the deed of transfer, he compelled the abbot to remain there.

Wonderful to say, after the thirty years had passed, as we have said, on the very night when he handed over his property to the basilica, he had intercourse with his wife. She conceived and bore a son. Thereafter she had other children as well.

There is no doubt that this was granted to the man through the Saint’s power. Nevertheless, when children had been given to him, the man did not violate his promise. He assigned other places to them and confirmed what he had first bestowed upon the Saint.

## CHAPTER XII. Of the blind woman at the village of Turnacum

At the village of Turnacum in the territory of Le Mans [Note: Three printed editions, with Clar., have *Tornacensem*; Clict., *Turonicensem*; Colb. *tut.*, in the table of contents, *Tornacesim*. Absolutely all the manuscripts have *villam*, “village.” Here, and frequently elsewhere in Gregory, where the manuscripts have “village,” the printed editions have supplied “city.” This place, as Valesius conjectures in his *Description of Gaul*, is a village commonly called Tornes, situated between Lavarzinum and the fortress of Carcer, across the river Lidericus or Lidus, at the extreme boundary of the territory of the Cenomani [Col. 0996C–D]. Chiffletius rightly criticizes John Cognatus in his *Anastasius Childericus*, chapter 21, for thinking that Gregory was speaking here of a donation made by Chilperic to the church of Tournai in Belgica Secunda. Yet Chiffletius himself was no less mistaken when he substituted Toronensem; for how could he place Tours in the territory of the Cenomani?], a woman who had been afflicted by prolonged blindness and weighed down by old age sat at the village oratory, seeking alms and constantly invoking the name of Saint Martin.

One Sunday night her eyes began to be pierced by pain. Then she prostrated herself before the holy altar, and, as blood burst forth, she received her sight.

Nevertheless, relics of the most blessed Apostles, Peter and Paul, are kept in that same place. Yet she maintained that she had been healed by the power of the holy Bishop.

Our faith, however, holds that one Lord works through the powers of many saints. Nor does he separate those whom, equal in heaven, he makes equal in miracles on earth.

## CHAPTER XIII. Of the restoration of a withered hand
At that festival, however, which Aunacharius [Note: Others have Annacharius. Colbert and Victor have Aunarius, and this is likewise read in the Deeds of the Bishops of Auxerre, in Labbe, volume I of the Library. He worked to settle the disturbance among the nuns of Poitiers, as Gregory reports in Book IX, chapter 41 of the *History*. He attended several synods and held one at Auxerre with his priests, whose canons are extant. He died in 605, as Cointius observes, and was buried at Saint-Germain with his predecessors. Counted among the saints, he is commemorated on 25 September.] the bishop of Auxerre, attended, a man brought a withered and contracted hand, but on the third day after the festival he carried it home restored.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the crippled Baudegisilus. [Col. 0997A]

A certain Baudegisilus, son of Baudulfus, from the territory of Angers and an inhabitant of the village of Geinensis [Note: Thus in Colbert and Laudianus. Bellovacensis and Claromontanus have *Geniensis*. The printed editions have *Gennensis*.], was struck by the dart of a grievous disease and, weakened, collapsed. Since his poor father supported him without the benefit of his labor, the son begged him with tears to kiss the threshold of Saint Martin’s basilica [Note: The custom of kissing the thresholds of churches was received from the earliest centuries of the Church in both East and West. See Chrysostom, *Homily 30 on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians*; Prudentius, in the hymn on Saint Lawrence; Saint Paulinus, in the sixth poem on Saint Felix; Fortunatus, Book IV of the *Life of Saint Martin*, and elsewhere.]. Without delay the father placed him in a boat, since he could not travel by any other means of transport, and devoutly set his son down before the feet of the Saint—that is, outside the tomb. After devoting several days to prayer and asking the Saint’s aid, he was restored to health, his weakness having been removed, and so he returned home unharmed with his father.

## CHAPTER XV. On the man who sent the wax. [Col. 0997B]

In the territory of Auch [Note: Thus Claromontanus. The others have *Ausciensi*; Bignonius has *Ansciensi*. Here, without doubt, Asiacum is meant, commonly called Asay, [Col. 0998D] of which name there are several villages in Touraine, as Valesius observes in his *Description of Gaul*.] there was also a man named Coelestis who possessed many beehives. When a swarm emerged from them and rose high into the air, going far beyond his reach, and when he followed it without obtaining any opportunity at all of catching it, he fell prostrate on the ground and invoked the name of Saint Martin, saying:

“If your power, most blessed Confessor, wishes to retain this swarm and return it to my possession, I will take for my own use whatever honey is produced from it hereafter, but I will send the wax, in its entirety, to the lamps of your basilica.”

After saying this, while he still lay upon the ground, the swarm of bees immediately fell upon and settled in a little tree close to the man. He gathered it, put it into a hive, and carried it home. From it he collected a great quantity over the course of two or three years. When he had already accumulated more than two hundred pounds of wax, a rumor of hostile activity arose. But so that he would not see his vow perish, he covered the wax in a pit in the ground.

When peace had been restored, he summoned our deacon to retrieve it. A boy was then with him who suffered from an extremely severe pain in the kidneys. The boy approached the man and, learning from his mouth what had happened, ordered that the wax hidden in the earth be uncovered. The boy who suffered the pain I have mentioned took a hoe to dig the ground and said:

“If you are favorable, Saint Martin, to looking upon this man’s offering, may your power touch my kidneys, and may I be healed when I have uncovered this wax.”

When he struck the earth with the hoe, his kidney-bone rang, and immediately all the pain was removed. Thus he was brought, unharmed, together with this wax, to the blessed basilica.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the release of a prisoner. [Col. 0997D]

A certain man was found guilty by the judge of the city of Tours [Col. 0998A], who ordered him bound and held in custody. When the holy days of the Lord’s Resurrection approached, the judge ordered him to be thrust into another prison on the farther bank of the Loire. He was led away with his neck bound not only by chains but also with his hands tied behind his back. When they had reached the bank of the river in question and were awaiting the vessel by which they were to cross, while he continually implored the aid of Saint Martin, the guards suddenly seemed to themselves to have been struck on the head by someone. At once they fell to the ground, the chains holding the prisoner broke, and the loosened straps fell away from his hands.

Feeling himself free, while the men still lay upon the ground, he withdrew from them and entered the threshold of the holy church [Col. 0998B]. Thus he was released by the judge. For some people reported that during those same days prisoners at the city of Poitiers had also been freed from the prison-house. This cannot be doubted, because the power of one Confessor [Note: Thus the Gallican manuscript. Most of the other manuscripts have “because the power of both Confessors.” The remaining manuscripts, with the printed editions, have “because the power of the Confessor.”] was able to illumine both cities with sacred miracles.

## CHAPTER XVII. On a blind boy. [Col. 0998B]

A very small boy named Leudovaldus [Note: Colbert, Tutilanus, and Claromontanus have *Leodowaldus*. The printed editions have *Lendonaldus*.], a slave belonging to a certain Baudeleifus from a village in the territory of Angers, which antiquity called Crovium [Note: Thus in all the manuscripts. The printed editions have *Cronium*. See below, chapter 23, and the notes above on Book II, chapter 43], was running about here and there with the other children, playing in the street as that age permits, after being reborn from water and the Holy Spirit with the other infants. Suddenly a violent wind arose and, lifting dust, filled the child’s eyes. As he was tormented by pains caused by the blow of blindness, a certain man appeared to his grandmother in a dream and instructed her in these words:

“Go,” he said, “to the basilica of Saint Martin, and this boy will recover his sight.”

The woman did not delay. Full of faith, she came to the festival of the blessed Man and received her grandson back, illumined by the power of the Bishop.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On a blind girl. [Col. 0998C]

A girl from the territory of this city, named Viliogundis [Note: The Gallican manuscript has *Juliogundis*. The printed edition has *Vigiogundis*, and below, “the streets of the city.”], was blinded in a similar manner. While she was running about with the other little girls, playing in the streets of the village, dust lifted by the violence of the wind filled her eyes. Immediately afflicted by pain, she asked her parents to lead her to the basilica of Saint Martin. When this had been done, as soon as they had offered prayer for her, she was illumined.

As we too were leaving the sacred solemnities of the Mass, the boy and the girl mentioned above met us together, saying that at that very hour they had received light through the power of the blessed Bishop. This gave us great joy, because we believed that the power of the blessed Confessor had deigned to visit us.

## CHAPTER XIX. On a cripple who was also blind. [Col. 0999A]

A certain Litoveus [Note: The printed editions, with Claromontanus, have *Litoneus*.], weak in his limbs from childhood, became blind when fever supervened. He came to the preceding festival and departed with his limbs restored, though his sight was still removed. But when he had returned again for this solemnity, the darkness was taken away and clear light arose for him [Note: Several manuscripts have “light was given to him and arose.”].

## CHAPTER XX. Likewise, on another blind man. [Col. 0999D]

At this festival Leudardus [Note: The printed editions have “Lendaidus, the slave of Emnerius.” Colbert and Claromontanus have “of Eumerius.”], the slave of Emnerius, a deacon of the city of Nantes, came to the basilica. He had been bound by the chain of blindness for six years, but through the power of the blessed Confessor he was illumined. For he had been admonished in a dream-vision to implore the aid of this holy Bishop [Col. 0999B].

## CHAPTER XXI. On the blessed gifts that Motharius, a citizen of Tours, took away. [Col. 0999C]

A certain citizen of Tours, while hastening to meet the king, placed at the tomb a vessel of wine and a single loaf of bread to remain there together for one night, so that, when he was on his journey, he might have these as a safeguard of health. Afterward he took them up and began his journey.

It happened that, while looking for lodging, he entered the house of a certain man. After he had set down his baggage, a woman who possessed an unclean spirit began to announce the arrival of blessed Martin in loud cries and to say:

“Why do you persecute us, Saint? Why do you torment us, servant of God?”

Then the visitor took a cup and removed a little wine from that vessel; he broke off a piece of the blessed bread [Note: Victor has “a broken crust”; others have “broken pieces.”] and placed it in the cup. As soon as the raging woman received it, the demon was expelled with blood, and she was immediately healed.

Another woman in the same place had long been ill with the chill of fevers [Alternative: “with chills of fever.”]. She received a little of this blessing, and as soon as she took it, she was healed.

## CHAPTER XXII. On a cripple restored. [Col. 0999D]

Silluvius [Note: The Gallican manuscript has *Sillimius*. Claromontanus has *Hicluvius*. The printed editions have *Simillimius*.], a resident of the territory of Bayeux, was working in the countryside when a wind arose. Struck by fear, he began to tremble, to lose the use of all his limbs, and even to cry out, declaring that death threatened him. Meanwhile, as his neighbors ran together to witness such a spectacle [Note: The printed edition has “a spectacle; he himself, on the way.”], he became completely crippled amid cries and howls, his sinews contracted. Not only was the use of his ears denied him, but he also lost the light of his eyes.

After spending fifteen years in this misery, he came to the festival of Saint Martin and departed with his limbs strengthened and his eyes restored.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On a blind woman and a cripple who were healed. [Col. 1000A]

With no different power, a woman named Ermegundis, a citizen of Angers and an inhabitant of the village of Croviensis [Note: Bignonius has *Eroniensis*. Others have *Croniensis*. See above, chapter 17.], who was crippled and blind, came to this festival and departed restored and illumined.

Charimundus too, coming in a weakened state from Bricilonnum [Note: The name is written differently in various manuscripts. Thus in Laudianus and Colbert. Bellovacensis and Claromontanus have *Bricillonno*; Victor has *Briciolonno*; the Gallican manuscript has *Bricilomno*; Saint-Benoît has *Brisciconno*. Finally, the printed editions have *Briscillamo* or *Briscillami*.], was restored through the power of the blessed Bishop.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On many blind persons and possessed people who were healed. [Col. 1000B]

On the day of this solemnity also, several people experienced this power, with Christ’s grace cooperating. For Leodemundus, blind for seven years, came to the basilica of the aforesaid Bishop and recovered his sight. Three other blind persons also recovered their sight at this festival through the Bishop’s aid [Note: Laudianus, Bellovacensis, Claromontanus, and Colbert have: “Leodemundus, blind for seven years; Domnitta, after three; and three other blind persons at this festival, etc.”]. Many possessed people were cleansed as well.

## CHAPTER XXV. On a girl healed of fever. [Col. 1000D]

A female servant of our presbyter Leo had withdrawn after being carried in her parents’ arms to a little estate near the city. She was overcome by the violence of a fever and, violently agitated day and night, was seen to be in danger of death.

When the presbyter saw her being exhausted by the force of the disease, he mounted a horse at night [The printed edition has “a mount”] and went to the basilica of the holy Confessor. He knocked at the door of the little cell where the sacristan was resting, but could not rouse the man. Since he was unable to enter the holy basilica, he offered prayer before the apse of the tomb. He gathered a little of the earthy dust [Col. 1000C], carried it away with him full of faith, diluted it, and offered it to the little girl to drink. Immediately the fever departed.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On prisoners set free. [Col. 1000C]

We had some matter that required us to visit King Childebert. As we proceeded, we set out through the district of Rheims and encountered a certain man who told us, according to his own account, that the prison of this city—where, among the other prisoners, a servant of the king was being held—had been opened through the power of Martin. He said that the prisoners had been released from the prison-house and had gone away free.

The prison was constructed in such a way that strong planks had been laid above a framework of beams and projected like the sloping roof [Note: Others have “strong boards ... trembled.” Our reading is better, since *pulpitum* is the ridge or sloping structure of a roof.]. Large stones had been placed above them to crush the prisoners [Col. 1000D]. Moreover, the prison door was secured by an iron bar and locked with a key inserted into the bolt. But, as the narrator himself asserted, the Bishop’s power displaced the stones, scattered the roof timbers, broke the chains, and opened the beam that confined the prisoners’ feet. Without the door even being unlocked, it lifted the men through the air and brought them outside through the opening in the roof, saying:

“I am Martin, the soldier of Christ, your liberator. Depart in peace, and go away without fear.”

When we approached the king and spread abroad the report of this miracle, the king affirmed that some of those who had been released had come to him and that he had remitted to the accused the composition owed to the treasury, which they call the *fredum* [Note: Most manuscripts have *fretum*. The meaning of this word is sufficiently explained here. They derive it from the Germanic word *frid*, meaning peace. See Bignonius, Book I of Marculf’s *Formulas*, formula 3. According to an old Glossary, *freda* is also a wooden covering placed behind the altar over the bodies of saints. See Du Cange’s *Glossary* concerning both words.].

This happened four days before the festival, in the sixteenth year of the aforesaid king [A.D. 591].

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the slave of Bishop Nonnichius healed of weakness. [Col. 1001A]

When the feast of blessed Martin arrived, Nonnichius [Note: The printed editions have *Monnichius*. See Book VIII of the *History*, chapter 43.], bishop of Nantes, came to the Saint’s basilica, bringing with him a boy whose limbs were slack, named Baudegisillus. After celebrating the Saint’s solemnities, he took the boy back with him unharmed, his limbs restored [Col. 1001B].

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the fever of Claudius, the royal chancellor. [Col. 1001B]

While we were also staying with the king, a certain Claudius, one of the royal chancellors [Note: Bellovacensis has “one of our royal chancellors,” and the word *regalis* is absent from the chapter heading. Chancellors wrote and authenticated diplomas of lesser importance. On their name and offices, see Gothofredus, *Theodosian Code*, Book I, title 12, and Mabillon, *On Diplomatic Matters*, Book II, chapter 11. Certainly, this passage of Gregory shows that there were then several chancellors, from which the title of archchancellor was later introduced. The archbishop of Rheims held this dignity in France for a long time, just as three archbishops later became electors in the Empire.], was seized by a fever.

When, overcome by the excessive fever, he had developed an aversion to food and drink, he complained to us of what he was suffering. As soon as he drank the diluted dust that we had taken from the tomb of the holy and blessed man for healing, the fever was suppressed and he was immediately cured.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On what Agnes, abbess of Poitiers, reported about a certain sailor. [Col. 1001C]

The venerable Agnes, abbess of the holy women of Poitiers [Note: She was the first abbess of the monastery of the Holy Cross, established through the efforts of Saint Radegund. Fortunatus celebrated her at length in Book XI and also treats of her in Book VIII, poem 4.], reported as follows a miraculous event told to her by the very man to whom it had happened, namely Trevericus, a merchant:

“When I had arrived at Metz,” he said, “a certain merchant asked me where I came from. I said, ‘From Poitiers.’ He asked whether I had ever gone to the basilica of blessed Martin at Tours. I said that, while traveling through Austrasia [Note: The Colbert manuscript has: “I said that, while I was traveling in Neustria, I had presented myself there in this way.” The printed editions have: “While I was traveling through Austrasia ... to the city ...,” etc. Below they have “and my little boys ... with the little boys.”], I had presented myself there in that manner.

“He asked me what benefit I had experienced from Lord Martin. When I had been trading in salt at Metz and had reached the bridge of Metz [Note: The Roman manuscript has “the bridge of death.” Indeed, near Metz there is still a bridge called the Bridge of Death.], I said: ‘Lord Martin, I commend to you myself, the little children I have, and my little boat.’

“Meanwhile we lay down in the boat, and all fell asleep. In the morning, when I awoke with the little children who were with me, we found ourselves before the gate of Trier, not knowing how we had come there; for we still believed that we were at Metz [Col. 1002A]. By what means we had sailed or flown, we did not know. Through the sole commendation of blessed Martin, we had not felt the river and had escaped the shipwrecking waves of the Moselle, which was then raging [Alternative: swelling]. And—what is especially marvelous—how had we passed unharmed among the rocks at night, when no sailor was awake, no wind was blowing, and no oar was pulling?”

## CHAPTER XXX. On the miracles of the monastery of Ligugé. [Col. 1002A]

Some time afterward, when we had reached the city of Poitiers, we wished, simply for the sake of prayer, to visit the monastery of Ligugé [Note: Most manuscripts have *Locodiacense* in the table of chapters, but here *Locotigiagense*. It is commonly called Ligugé; see the notes to Book I of the *History*, at the end of the book.], where the blessed Man had established a gathered community of monks. There, it is said, he first raised a dead man [Note: Namely, in his Life by Severus Sulpicius, where his election—or rather his abduction—to the episcopate is also described. Fortunatus rendered all these events in verse in Book I of his Life of the same holy Man.], and from there he was led to the episcopate.

Therefore, desiring the place I had longed for, I prostrated myself before the screen of the corner where he was said to have restored the dead man’s spirit. After pouring out tears with my prayer and solemnly celebrating Masses, I asked the abbot whether the Lord had displayed any miracle there. In the presence of the brothers who were there, he asserted that the blind were often illumined there and the weak restored.

“But what has happened recently,” he said, “since you inquire so carefully, lord, I shall disclose to you.”

A certain woman living near this place, struck by paralytic fluid, had completely lost the function of all her limbs. Placed upon a cart drawn by oxen, she went around the houses of the wealthy to satisfy the needs of her poverty [Note: Balbus has “the houses by daily alms, to satisfy her poverty.”].

When she had been carried to this place and was laid upon the pavement, she approached slowly and devoutly kissed the veil covering the sacred screen, saying:

“Here, blessed Confessor, I believe that you are present; here, I testify that you raised a dead man. For I trust that, if you wish, you can save me and restore me to health, just as once, after breaking open the jaws of hell, you brought back the soul of the dead man.”

After saying this, she drenched her cheeks abundantly with tears. Immediately, when her prayer was fulfilled, whatever in the woman’s body had been dry, contracted, or slack was restored through the power of the blessed Bishop.

A second paralytic likewise came to this monastery, and as soon as he touched the veil of the screen, all weakness was removed and he departed healthy. The monastery is approximately forty stadia from the city of Poitiers.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the spring that the Saint obtained by prayer. [Col. 1003A]

From there we departed and entered the territory of Saintes. While we were speaking at a certain banquet about the miracles of blessed Martin, one of the citizens faithfully related the following to me, while the others affirmed that it was true.

There is a village called Najogialo situated in this territory. When Saint Martin, while still alive in the body, came to it, he met a man carrying water in a small vessel. The well from which he had drawn the water was situated in a valley nearly one thousand paces from the village, and the inhabitants carried water drawn from it.

Then the Man of God said to the man carrying the water:

“Please, my dearest friend, hold out your hand and give a little water to drink to this little donkey on which I am sitting.”

He replied:

“If you consider it necessary to water your animal, go to the well, draw water, and give it to him. I will not provide what I brought with difficulty.”

With these words he passed by.

As he departed, a woman immediately came, herself carrying water in a jar [Manuscripts: “in her arm”]. The Man of God said the same thing to her. She immediately replied to him, as if she were Rebecca once hearing the messenger of God (Genesis 24):

“I will give drink both to you and to your donkey. Nor is it any trouble for me to draw water again. Only let your will be done, since you are traveling and suffering need.”

She set down the little vessel from her arms and gave the donkey his drink. After doing this, she drew water again, filled the vessel, and returned to the village.

The Saint followed her and said:

“I will repay you with a benefit as your reward, because you watered my donkey.”

Then he knelt upon the ground and prayed to the Lord that he would show a spring of water in that place. Immediately, when the prayer was finished, the earth burst open and revealed an immense spring to the astonishment of the people. It continues to provide a benefit to the people who live in that countryside to this day. At the mouth of that spring there is a stone as a testimony, retaining the footprint of the donkey on which the holy Bishop sat.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the burning of the city of Poitiers. [Col. 1003C]

I do not think that the following should be passed over in silence. At the time when Plato [Note: Thus in all the manuscripts. He became bishop in 592, according to our Gregory, who was present when Plato entered his church, as Fortunatus sings in verse in Book X, chapter 20. When Plato died in 599, Fortunatus himself succeeded him. Some, however, substitute Placidus for Plato, but incorrectly, as Cointius observes. Indeed, this very passage of Gregory proves that Placidus was not a different person from Plato, since the printed editions here read *Placidus* for *Plato*, and, as the Sammarthani admit, there is no other known Placidus. Gregory praises Plato, his archdeacon, in Book V of the *History*, chapter 50; in my opinion, he should not be distinguished from this man.] obtained the episcopate of the city of Poitiers, the Saint’s power was displayed.

A house adjoining the ecclesiastical residence was being consumed by a great fire, and sparks together with burning embers, driven by the wind, were falling upon the roof of the church. But the bishop had with him dust from the blessed tomb. When he raised the *chrismarium* [Note: A *chrismarium* was a vessel for holding holy chrism. Medieval authors also used the name for vessels enclosing holy relics, as Fortunatus does in the *Life of Saint Germanus, Bishop of Paris*, and Eddius in the *Life of Saint Wilfrid*. A *chrismale*, however, was a vessel in which the body of Christ was kept; indeed, Ralph Glaber says that a *chrismale* was the same as a corporal.], he held it against the fire. Suddenly a wind arose contrary to the first wind, defending the church roof from the flames and driving the fire in another direction [Col. 1004A]. Thus the church building was saved.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On a boy healed of fever. [Col. 1004A]

When his boy was lying in bed, burned by a very severe fever and already regarded as almost lifeless, he offered the sick child some of this diluted dust. Immediately the fever was driven away, and the boy recovered from his illness.

But let us return to the Saint’s basilica.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the deranged and crippled Leodulfus. [Col. 1004B]

When, some years ago, a great earthquake shook the earth and everything was violently moved, as though about to fall in a single moment, a certain Leodulfus [Note: Some manuscripts have *Leudulfus*, whence the printed editions have *Lendulfus*.] was violently thrown about by it. He was not only deprived of his senses but also became weak in all his limbs.

Coming to the Saint’s basilica at Tours, devoting himself to prayer for several days, he was restored to his voice and his senses, and was returned healthy, as though restored to life, with all his limbs sound.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On an innocent man accused by slander and set free. [Col. 1004B]

Nor do I think the following should be omitted: an innocent man, accused through the slanders of evil people, was being led to the city bound with a leather strap, so that he might be thrust into prison. When he had reached the public embankment before the basilica of the holy apostle Peter, his hands were released, and he said to the guards:

“By this it is shown that I am free from the guilt you allege, since my hands have been released by divine power.”

Then, in anger, they bound him more tightly and, adding another leather strap to the binding, so to speak, bound the bonds themselves.

It happened at that time that we were coming through the street from the basilica of Saint Martin. As these men approached us to meet us, the moment the bound man saw the Saint’s basilica, his hands were immediately released. He leapt from the horse on which he was riding, seized our feet, and explained that he was being unjustly condemned.

Thus, after we had spoken with the judge, he departed without difficulty.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On a woman who lost her speech and was healed. [Col. 1004C]

The wife of Serenatus, one of our men, was returning from the fields, her husband having gone ahead, when suddenly she slipped from the hands of her companions and fell to the ground. Her tongue was bound, and she became mute, unable to utter any word from her mouth [Col. 1004D].

Meanwhile, diviners approached and said that she was suffering an attack of the noonday demon [Note: Concerning this, see the Passion of Saint Symphorianus among the authentic *Acts of the Martyrs*, p. 72, where it is said: “The diligence of the saints discovered that Diana was a demon of the noonday.” See the *Life of Saint Rusticula*, second age of the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, where, on the basis of this passage of Gregory and other saints’ lives, Mabillon observes that the “noonday demon,” or its attack, was what the ancients called the sudden and overt onset of a violent illness, by which a person seemed suddenly deprived of the faculties of the senses or mind. It was so called because people believed it was inflicted by a demon and because it usually occurred at midday. Cardinal Bona also discusses this in *On Divine Psalmody*, chapter 3, section 3.]. They produced bindings of herbs [Col. 1005A] and words of incantation, but according to their custom they could provide no medicinal benefit to the woman, who was on the point of death.

While the household resounded with combined howling, her son ran breathlessly to our niece Eustenia [Note: The Gallican manuscript has *Extenia*; Claromontanus has *Eustena*], announcing that his mother had reached the end of her life. She came to the sick woman, visited her, removed the bindings that the fools had put on her, poured oil from the blessed tomb into her mouth, and smoked her with wax [Note: That is, burned wax beneath her, as the Claromontanus manuscript reads.].

Immediately her speech returned; the deceit of the evil was broken, and the sick woman recovered.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On people suffering from intermittent fever who were healed. [Col. 1005B]

At the time when, after the death of the most glorious King Guntram, King Childebert visited the city of Orléans [A.D. 593], one of the court boys was severely shaken by a tertian fever, with the fevers coming and going and a tremor supervening.

When he had complained to us of this, we offered him a drink made from the dust of the holy tomb. As he drank it, the tremor was suppressed and he recovered.

On the following night, when the day had arrived on which the fever usually abated [Note: That is, the day on which the intermittent fever ceases. See the Book *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 21.], he saw in a vision a very hideous figure approaching and saying to him:

“Look, the time of your tremor has now arrived. Why are you delaying? Do what you are accustomed to do.”

While this figure was speaking, a certain man appeared, splendid in face, snow-white in hair, and handsome in appearance. He said to him:

“Do not tremble, but make the sign of the venerable cross upon your forehead, and you will immediately be healed.”

Awakening from this vision, and fortified by the sign with which he had been ordered to mark himself, he never again suffered what he had been accustomed to endure.

A girl of the queen, worn down by this fever, was healed after drinking this holy medicine [Col. 1005C].

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On blind people, possessed people, and paralytics. [Col. 1005C]

Not many days later, when the annual day of the holy solemnity returned, we came back from the king and attended the festival. At it, four blind people returned with their sight restored; two possessed people were cleansed; and two paralytics, their limbs restored and their steps made firm, returned home unharmed.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On prisoners who were released. [Col. 1005C]

A few days later, when the judgment of the judge had shut certain guilty men from the city of Tours into the prison-house, and the prisoners were lamenting, the power of the blessed Confessor appeared. It broke the fetters of those bound and allowed them to go free into the basilica. Thus these men too were released by the judge and returned to their homes.

## CHAPTER XL. On Mauranus, who was mute. [Col. 1005D]

A certain man named Mauranus [Note: Here all the manuscripts begin the fortieth chapter, and we have followed them, although in the printed editions what follows is placed under the thirty-ninth chapter. Today we call Cantabria Biscay, a province of Spain situated between Navarre, Old Castile, and the sea.] in the region of Cantabria rose from his bed one morning. As he went out of the house, it seemed to him that someone had struck him on the neck. He immediately fell to the ground and became like a dead man. For three days he lived only by his breath and was considered dead.

On the fourth day, when he opened his eyes, he could say nothing, for the power of speech had been taken from him. Having heard of the miracles of blessed Martin, he offered a single *triens* to some sailors, indicating with supplication that they should carry him to the temple of the blessed Bishop.

After they departed, he returned to his house and saw before his feet a piece of gold in the shape of a *triens*. When he picked it up and weighed it, it was found to have the weight of one solidus. Seeing this, he said within himself:

“The power of blessed Martin has repaid me with a reward for the loan that I sent to his temple.”

Burning with desire, he wished to board one ship and then another [Col. 1006B], but his parents restrained him. When a third ship was found, he could not be held back at all. Once he had boarded it, and they had entered the open sea driven by the wind, the power of the holy Bishop opened his mouth. He stretched out his hands toward heaven and spoke, saying:

“I give thanks to you, almighty God, who ordered me to cross this route. Even before I see the temple of your Saint, I am already filled with his benefits.”

They reached the city of Bordeaux by sea. Leaving the ship, he approached the basilica of the holy man of God and fulfilled his vow. We learned what we have written from his own mouth.

## CHAPTER XLI [Alternative: XL]. On a cripple and prisoners who were freed. [Col. 1006B]

When another festival arrived, celebrated in winter, a certain Maurellus from the household of Ponticon [Pontion], the slave of Duke Aginus, who in March had lost the use of one knee through some kind of attack, came to attend it. Unable to plant his foot, he used a stick at his knee, as lame people do.

After offering prayer to the Lord for three days, on the fourth day—the day after the festival—he departed healthy, his knee restored.

A few days later, some men who were being held in the chains of a prison were divinely released. They entered the Saint’s basilica and were freed by the judge without penalty.

## CHAPTER XLII [Alternative: XLI]. On another cripple. [Col. 1006C]

A certain boy whose feet and hands were contracted came from the estate of Themellus, in the district of the city of Tours, in the village of Ambiacum [Col. 1006D] [Note: Saint-Benoît has *Ambaciensis*—Amboise—which we have already mentioned more than once.]. He came to the Saint’s basilica and, while asking among the other beggars for alms to live on, was visited by the Saint’s power and departed restored.

## CHAPTER XLIII [Alternative: XLII]. On boys suffering from fever who were healed. [Col. 1007A]

Another little boy belonging to our presbyter Euthymius [The Gallican manuscript has *Euchenius*], fell ill with an excessive fever and was thought to be dying from it. The presbyter took up some dust from the holy tomb, tore off the fringes of the cloth laid over it, and carried them away with him. He gave the dust to the boy to drink and tied the fringes around his neck. Immediately the fever was extinguished and he was healed.

In a similar manner, the presbyter Ulfaricus came to the aid of another boy suffering from fever, and through the power of the Saint the boy immediately recovered, free from the fever.

## CHAPTER XLIV [Alternative: XLIII]. On Principius, who was deranged. [Col. 1007B]

A certain good man named Principius [Note: The printed editions, with the Gallican manuscript, have *Praecipuus*.], a citizen of the city of Périgueux [Note: Périgueux, commonly called Périgueux, is a city of Aquitaine in Gaul, on the river Isle.], was thought to have fallen into some kind of madness. At times he was so severely affected that he seemed to lose his senses.

After enduring this for many months, he sought the basilica of the blessed Bishop. There, as I believe, he remained for four months, abstaining from meat and wine. Aided by the protection of the blessed Confessor, he was restored unharmed to his home.

## CHAPTER XLV [Alternative: XLIV]. On Leodulfus, who was blind and was healed. [Col. 1007C]

Since the rusticity of men, when it follows priestly preaching too little, prepares itself for offense against God, I shall report what happened recently.

A certain Leodulfus, a man of the city of Bourges, had cut hay. Fearing that the arrival of rain would soak it and cause him to lose his labor, he yoked his oxen on Sunday morning and drove them to the meadow. He began to heap the hay upon the wagon. Immediately one of his feet seemed to him to be burning, and he returned to his lodging [Col. 1007C], where he ceased from his work.

After the solemn celebration of Mass, he again yoked the oxen and continued to complete the work he had begun. When the wagon had been filled with hay, his eyes immediately seemed to be pierced by some kind of goads, causing him the greatest pain. After they closed, he could never open them again.

Thus he remained blind for an entire year and devoutly came to the festival of the holy Bishop. On the third day afterward, through the gift of the light he had lost, he was restored [Col. 1008A].

## CHAPTER XLVI [Alternative: XLV]. On two other cripples.

At that time [Note: [Col. 1007C] The following two chapters do not occur in the older manuscripts in the table of contents prefixed to the books, and yet they are found in full in their proper place in the codex], another crippled man also came, directed by the Saint’s power, and returned to his own city on his own feet. A certain man from Britain, named Paternianus, had been rendered blind, mute, deaf, and crippled in his hands by some contagion; and, all his limbs having been exhausted by the disease, only his feet offered the man support. He sought the basilica of the mighty Patron, poured out his prayer, saw the lost light when his eyes were opened, and recovered the use of his hands. Astonished that he had been saved through the power of the blessed Bishop, he declared the grace of his restoration to the people. From many he received gifts in gratitude for this miracle, and by means of them he has already freed several from the yoke of captivity. [Col. 1008B]

## CHAPTER XLVII [Elsewhere, XLVI]. On the Fire Extinguished through His Aid

At the present time also, in the city of Bordeaux, one house, seized by flames, began to burn violently. As the flames spread in every direction and other houses were exposed to the same danger, with no doubt that they too would be consumed by the heat of this fuel, the people gathered around began to invoke the name of blessed Martin with particular earnestness and to beseech him with tears not to permit his power to burn the neighboring houses. Thus, at the raised cry of the mourners, the crackling of the flame began to subside. And while they cried out to heaven, aid suddenly arrived through the Bishop’s intercession; the crowd extinguished the fire, subdued by humble prayer, through its tears—something it had been unable to overcome with water. At that time, when our boy Laudovaldus [Note: [Col. 1008C] Colbert, Claromontanus, Romanus, and Bellovacensis read *Launovaldus*.] was being severely worn down by dysentery, as soon as he received some dust from the tomb, he was immediately freed from the illness.

Here ends the fourth book concerning the virtues and miracles of Saint Martin the Confessor.

[Col. 1007]

# PROSE ON SAINT MARTIN

[Col. 1007]

## [NOTE]

[Col. 1007C] In the manuscript codex of Saint Victor of Paris, which contains Gregory’s books on the Miracles of Saint Martin and several chapters of the book on the Glory of the Confessors, there are a prose piece—as it is called there—and a prayer in honor of Saint Martin. I would judge these little works rather to be a testimony and a collection extracted from ancient Missals. It has nevertheless seemed appropriate to reproduce them here, since some readers may perhaps think that such pieces could have a place among the works of our Gregory.

# PROSE ON SAINT MARTIN

[Col. 1007]

[Col. 1007D] Let the whole Catholic Church of peace throughout the world sing of Martin, the priest of Christ, and let every heretic flee his name in fear. Let Pannonia rejoice as the mother of such a son; let Italy, nurse of so great a youth, exult; and let the threefold division of Gaul contend in sacred rivalry over which part should possess the bishop. But let all rejoice that they share him equally as a father; let only the people of Tours shelter his body. From this let all the people of the Franks and of Germany applaud, [Note: [Col. 1007D] Something appears to be missing here. EDIT.] for whom he saw the Lord in his own garment.

He is celebrated in the regions of Egypt, and likewise among all the learned of Greece, who recognize themselves as unequal to Martin’s merits and to his healing power. For he calms fevers, drives away demons, joins together paralytic limbs, and by his prayer restores to their former life the bodies of three dead people. He destroys sacrilegious rites and gives idols to the flames for the glory of Christ. Performing the mysteries with bare arms, he is endowed with heavenly light; with eyes and hands he is lifted with all his strength toward heaven, rejecting all earthly things. Christ was never absent from his mouth, whether in justice or in whatever pertains to true life.

Therefore we all beseech you, O Martin: since you displayed many wonders here, pour out for us from heaven, through your intercession, the grace of Christ forever, and so forth.

Almighty and everlasting God, source and origin of every good thing, who are glorified in the blessed Bishop Martin: you are the praise of his virtue, the strength of his courage, the glory of his holiness, and the beauty of his form; the love of his heart and the suspension of his soul; the light of his mind and the guide of his journey. In him you marvelously restored the likeness of your image, and through him displayed to us, in a manner almost tangible, the form of your purity. When, by your inspiration, he loved justice and hated iniquity, you anointed him with the oil of gladness—not above your fellow participants, but among the greatest participants in your Only-Begotten Son.

Through his intercession, hear our prayers, pressed down beneath the heavy burden of sins, and grant that his prayers before your mercy may erase the stains of my crimes; that his examples may call me toward higher works of pious action; that his miracles may terrify me away from evil; and that the ardor of his spiritual gifts may draw me to run after you in the fragrance of your ointments. May the rain of his teaching penetrate the hardness of my heart, and may every grace that he received from you, the author of goodness, contribute to the increase of my devotion and salvation. Through the same Christ.

[Col. 1009]

# THE LIVES OF THE FATHERS BY SAINT GEORGE FLORENTIUS GREGORY, BISHOP OF TOURS, OR, THE BOOK ON THE LIFE OF CERTAIN BLESSED MEN [Note: [Col. 1009C] Elsewhere, “religious men.”]. (C)*

[Col. 1009]

## Prologue

1143 I had indeed determined to write only about those things divinely accomplished at the tombs of the most blessed martyrs and confessors. But since I recently discovered certain accounts of men whom the merit of a blessed way of life raised to heaven, and whose course of life I have learned through reliable reports and judged worthy of edifying the Church, I do not postpone speaking of some of them when circumstances require it. For the life of the saints not only reveals their purpose; it also incites the minds of their hearers to advance.

Some ask whether we ought to say *the Life of the Saints* or *the Lives of the Saints*. Agellius [Note: [Col. 1009C] Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions have “Aulus Gellius”; the same variation occurs in other authors. See Augustine, *City of God*, book IX, chapter 4, of the new edition. He is the author of the *Attic Nights*, who flourished in the second century, around the time of Marcus Aurelius.] and several other philosophers preferred to say *Lives*. For Pliny [Note: [Col. 1009C] This is Pliny the Elder, who lived in Nero’s time and wrote the *Natural History*, whose prologue praises books on the art of grammar. He was the uncle of Pliny the Younger.] states in the third book of the *Art of Grammar*: “The ancients called the life of any one of us *Lives*”; but grammarians do not think that *life* has a plural. Hence it is clear that *The Life of the Fathers* is better than *The Lives*, because although there is a diversity of merits and virtues, one life of the body nevertheless sustains them all in the world.

I confess that in my earlier book on the Confessors I wrote briefly about the lives of certain men and about what they accomplished in the body. For although great works are judged to have been performed through God’s power, they are nevertheless rendered small in writing. In this book, which we have chosen to call *The Life of the Saints*, we presume, as unskilled and ignorant men, to disclose more extensive accounts, praying the Lord to deign to place a word in our mouth. He has often opened the mouths of the mute to their former use, so that my lips may report things beneficial to hearers and readers and worthy of the holy Fathers; and may he regard what he commands to be written about the saints as proclaimed in his own praises.

[Note: [Col. 1009C] Laudunensis and the editions read *Vita* … *Vitae*.]

[Note: [Col. 1009C] The editors read *superiore*, “earlier.” Above, he does indeed praise the book *On the Glory of the Confessors*. But, as we have already noted, Gregory wrote the books *On the Glory of the Confessors* after most of the *Lives of the Fathers*, although he revised the *Lives of the Fathers* after the book *On the Glory of the Confessors*. Thus both readings are sound here. Gregory himself lists the book *On the Lives of the Fathers* after the seven books of Miracles at the end of his *History*; elsewhere, however, he places it before the book *On the Glory of the Confessors*, as is clear from its prologue.]

[Note: [Col. 1010C] The Badian manuscript reads *quem Vita*, “whom the Life”; other editions read *quem de Vita*, “whom concerning the Life.” The prologue to the book *On the Glory of the Confessors* says: “Of the life of certain blessed men,” or, as other codices have it, “of certain religious men.”]

[Note: [Col. 1011] The following words through *referant* are absent from the manuscripts.]

# [LIVES OF THE FATHERS]

## CHAPTER I. [Col. 1011A] On the Abbots Lupicinus and Romanus

The sequence of evangelical teaching admonishes us (Matthew 25:27) that the money of the Lord’s generosity, lent at interest to the bankers, should, through the Lord’s administration, be restored with a worthy profit of increase, and not be buried in deep pits to our detriment. Instead, being distributed through rational stewardship, it should increase toward the gain of eternal life. Thus, when the Lord of recompense begins to demand what he lent, he may say, with the interest received and the talents doubled in repayment of his loan: “Well done, good servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord” (Matthew 25:21).

For these are the predestined, who accomplish such things with God’s aid. From the very cries of their cradles—as we often read of many—they have deserved to know the Lord; and, once they have come to know him, they have never departed from his commands. After the sacrament of baptism, they have not defiled that white and shining robe of regeneration by shameful deeds. Rightly they follow the Lamb wherever he goes; the splendid whiteness of the Lamb himself has crowned them with lilies of beauty that do not wither under the heat of any temptation.

With such garlands, the right hand of glorious dominion extended, he urges those beginning, helps those who are conquering, and adorns the victorious. Raising those marked beforehand with the title of his name from earthly groans, he carries them gloriously into the joys of heaven.

Among this number, white with the whiteness of election, I have no doubt that those men also belong who, exploring the shadowy places of the Jura wilderness, deserved not only to make themselves a temple of God but also to prepare, in many minds, tabernacles for the grace of the Holy Spirit: namely, Lupicinus and his brother Romanus. [Col. 1011C]

[Note: [Col. 1011D] A certain anonymous author, a disciple of Saint Eugendus and himself living at the beginning of the sixth century, wrote the lives of both these men and of Saint Eugendus. See them in the Bollandists and in the first volume of the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*.]

### I

Lupicinus (Christian year 480, 21 March), seeking God with all his heart from the beginning of his life and educated in letters, had reached the proper age when, compelled by his father, he was bound by a marriage contract, although his mind did not consent. Romanus, however, still younger (year 460, 28 February), and himself wishing to devote his mind to God’s work, refused marriage.

When their parents abandoned the world, the two, by common agreement, sought the wilderness. Coming together into the secluded places of that Jura desert, which lie between Burgundy and Alemannia and adjoin the city of Aventicum, they pitched their tents. Prostrate on the ground, they prayed daily to the Lord with the melody of psalmody, seeking their food from the roots of plants. [Col. 1012A]

[Note: [Col. 1012D] The settlements of the Alemanni were in Swabia beyond the Rhine; but later, having crossed the Rhine, they occupied the region that then belonged to Maxima Sequanorum, from that river to Mount Jura. They also gave it the name Alemannia, of which Gregory speaks here. See Sirmond on poem 7 of Apollinaris Sidonius.]

[Note: [Col. 1011D] This region is called after Mount Jura, which even today is famous under this name or that of Saint Claude. It lies between the Helvetii and the Sequani. We have already spoken of the city of Aventicum, whose episcopal see was transferred to Lausanne. In my opinion, the person who recently thought he had discovered the ruins of the city of Aventicum not far from the Jura monastery is mistaken.]

But because the envy of the one who fell from heaven has always been accustomed to set snares for the human race, he armed himself against these servants of God and tried through his agents to turn them back from the path they had begun. For demons did not cease pelting them with stones every day; and whenever they bent their knees to pray to the Lord, the demons immediately rained stones down upon them, so that they were often wounded and tormented by immense anguish.

Meanwhile, their still immature age began to fear the daily insults of the enemy and, unable to endure the pain any longer, they decided to leave the wilderness and return to their own country. But what will the enemy’s envy not compel? When they had left the dwelling they had sought and returned to the villages of those who remained, they entered the house of a poor woman.

The woman asked from what journey the soldiers of Christ had come. They answered, not without embarrassment, that they had left the wilderness, and explained in order the reason that had delayed them from their undertaking.

But she said: “You ought, men of God, to fight manfully against the devil’s snares and not fear the enmity of one who has often been defeated and overthrown by God’s friends. For he is jealous of holiness, fearing that from the place where he fell through his treachery, the human race, ennobled by faith, might rise.”

Then, pierced in heart and withdrawing apart from the woman, they said: “Woe to us, for we have sinned against God by abandoning our purpose. Look: now we are rebuked by a woman for our cowardice. And what kind of life will be ours in the future if we do not return to the place from which the enemy’s fury drove us?”

### II

Then, armed with the banner of the cross and taking staffs in their hands, they returned to the wilderness. When they arrived, the devil’s snares again began to assail them with stones. But by persisting in prayer, they obtained from the Lord’s mercy that, the temptation having been removed, they might remain free and unimpeded in his divine service.

While they were thus occupied in prayer [the editions read “persisting”], crowds of brothers began to flock to them from every side and to hear the word of preaching from them. When the blessed hermits had become publicly known among the people, as we have said, they built for themselves a monastery which they wished to be called Condatiscone. [Col. 1012D]

[Note: [Col. 1012D] It is commonly called Condatescense, later Saint Eugendus (Saint-Oyan), who was abbot of that place, and finally Saint Claude; the name was given because he withdrew there after resigning the bishopric of Besançon. The name remains to this day, and the monastery continues to be famous under the Order of Saint Benedict. The second monastery, called Lauconne, was destroyed long ago; only a church remains, which is a parish church. Finally, the third monastery, situated in the Waldensian county of the diocese of Lausanne or Aventicum, was entrusted, toward the end of the ninth century, to the rule of Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, as appears from the letters of Adelaide, published in the fifth volume of the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, page 135. The monastery of Romanus is mentioned in the Cluniac library; under this name it is still commonly known as Romain-Môtier, in the Bernese region—the canton of Bern—in Helvetia, near Neuchâtel.]

Having cut down the forests and made the land level, they sought their food from the labor of their own hands. Such fervor for the love of God had kindled the neighboring inhabitants that the multitude gathered for the service of God could not live together in one place. So they built another monastery, in which they established a happy swarm like that of a beehive.

As these communities later increased with God’s help, they founded a third monastery within the borders of Alemannia. The two fathers went back and forth, seeking their sons, whom they might imbue with divine disciplines, preaching in each monastery those things that pertained to the formation of the soul.

Lupicinus, however, as abbot [the editions read “of the abbot”], exercised sole authority over them. He was extremely sober and abstained from food and drink, so that he generally refreshed himself only every third day. When thirst seized him, as the necessity of the human body demands, he had a vessel of water brought to him, in which he kept his immersed hands for a long time.

Wonderful to tell! His flesh absorbed the water that had been placed before him so completely that one would have thought it was being taken in through his mouth, and thus the burning of his thirst was extinguished.

He was exceedingly strict in disciplining the brothers. He allowed no one not only to act perversely but even to speak. He also carefully avoided both conversation with women and encounters with them.

Romanus, by contrast, was so simple that he took none of these matters deeply to heart; instead, he bestowed equally on all, men and women alike, the requested blessing, invoking the name of the Divinity.

### III

Since Abbot Lupicinus did not have enough resources to support so large a community, God revealed to him a place in the wilderness where treasures had been hidden in ancient times. Going there alone, he brought to the monastery as much gold and silver as he could carry, and with it he bought food to refresh the multitudes of brothers whom he had gathered for God’s service.

He did this every year. Yet he revealed to none of the brothers the place that the Lord had deigned to disclose to him.

It happened at a certain time that he visited the brothers whom, as we have said, he had gathered in those regions of Alemannia. Arriving at midday while the brothers were still in the fields, he entered the house where food was being cooked for their refreshment. He saw a great array of various dishes and a large quantity of fish assembled, and said in his heart:

“It is not fitting that monks, whose life is solitary, should use such extravagant provisions.”

Immediately he ordered a large bronze vessel to be prepared. When it had been placed over the fire and had begun to boil, he put into it all the food they had prepared at once—fish, vegetables, legumes, and whatever else had been intended for the monks to eat—and said: “Let the brothers now refresh themselves with this porridge. Let them not occupy themselves with delicacies that impede them from divine work.”

When the brothers learned of this, they took it very badly. Then twelve men, having taken counsel and inflamed with anger, left the place and wandered through the wilderness, seeking the pleasurable things of the world.

This was immediately revealed to Romanus in a vision, and divine mercy did not wish to conceal from him what had happened. When the abbot returned to the monastery, Romanus said to him:

“If you were going to go to them only to disperse the brothers, I wish you had not gone to them at all.”

He replied: “Do not take badly, dearest brother, what has happened. Know that the Lord’s threshing floor has been cleansed: the wheat alone has been stored in the granary, while the chaff has been cast outside.”

Romanus answered: “Would that none of them had departed! But now, I beg you, tell me how many left.”

He replied: “Twelve men, wearing high boots and puffed up with pride, in whom God does not dwell.”

Then Romanus said with tears: “I believe, in view of that divine mercy, that he will not separate even them from his treasure, but will gather them together and make them a gain for him who deigned to suffer for them.”

After praying for them, he obtained that they should return to the grace of almighty God. For the Lord caused their hearts to be pierced with remorse. Doing penance for their offense, they each gathered communities of their own and built monasteries for themselves, which endure to this day in the praises of God.

Romanus, meanwhile, continued in simplicity and good works, visiting the sick and saving them by his prayer.

### IV

It happened once, while he was traveling to visit the brothers, that, when twilight came on, he turned aside to a small hospice of lepers. There were nine men. They received him, and immediately, filled with the charity of God, he ordered hot water to be prepared. With his own hands he washed all their feet and ordered a spacious bed to be made so that they might all rest on one couch, showing no aversion to the livid stain of leprosy.

When this had been done and the lepers had fallen asleep, Romanus remained awake reciting psalms. He extended his hand and touched the side of one sick man, and immediately the man was cleansed. Touching another again with a healing touch, he too was immediately cleansed.

When they realized that they had been restored to health, each one touched his neighbor, so that, when they awoke, they might ask the Saint to cleanse them. But after they had touched one another, they themselves too were cleansed.

When morning came, Romanus saw them all shining with radiant skin. He gave thanks to God, bade them farewell, kissed each one, and departed, charging them always to retain in their hearts the things that belonged to God and to practice them in their deeds.

### V

When Lupicinus had grown old, he went to Chilperic [Note: [Col. 1014D] This was Chilperic, son of Gundioc, king of the Burgundians, and father of Clotilde, wife of Clovis the Great, king of the Franks. His brother Gundobad killed him together with his wife, as Gregory recounts in *History*, book II, chapter 28, and Fredegar, *Epitome*, chapter 17. He had a royal residence at Geneva, which Gregory here calls Januba; Balbus mistakenly calls it Lanuba. See Apollinaris Sidonius, book V, letters 6 and 7, and the notes of Savaro and Sirmond.] the king, who then ruled Burgundy.

He had heard that the king was living near the city of Januba. When Lupicinus entered the gate, the king’s throne shook, while the king was seated there at that hour for a banquet. Terrified, he said to his attendants: “An earthquake has occurred.”

Those present replied that they had felt no movement. He said: “Go immediately to the gate, lest perhaps someone wishing to oppose our kingdom has arrived, intending to harm us. This chair did not tremble without cause.”

They hurried out and encountered an old man dressed in a sheepskin. They told the king about him, and he said: “Go and bring him before me, so that I may learn what sort of man he is.”

When he had been brought in, Lupicinus stood before the king, as Jacob once stood before Pharaoh. The king said to him:

“Who are you, and where have you come from? What is your work? What necessity do you lack—or, as the editions read, what necessity do you have—that you have come to us? Tell me.”

He replied: “I am the father of the Lord’s sheep. Although the Lord continually refreshes them with spiritual food, they sometimes lack bodily nourishment. Therefore we ask your power to grant something for the necessities of food and clothing.”

Hearing this, the king said: “Take fields and vineyards from which you can live and satisfy your needs.”

Lupicinus replied: “We will not accept fields and vineyards. But, if it pleases your authority, assign us something from their produce. It is not fitting for monks to be exalted by worldly possessions; rather, in humility of heart they should seek the kingdom of God and his justice.”

When the king heard these words, he gave them an order that every year they should receive three hundred *modii* of wheat and the same measure of wine, as well as one hundred gold pieces for purchasing clothing for the brothers. It is reported that they continue to receive this from the resources of the treasury. [Col. 1015C]

### VI

After this, when the two had grown old and reached an advanced age [the editions read “when he was an old man and of advanced age”], Lupicinus the abbot said to his brother Romanus:

“Tell me, in which monastery do you wish a tomb to be prepared for you, so that we may rest together?”

Romanus replied: “It cannot be that I should have a tomb in a monastery from which women are barred. For you know that the Lord my God, although I am unworthy and undeserving, has granted me the grace of healings, and that many have been freed from various illnesses through the laying on of my hand and the power of the Lord’s cross.

“There will be a gathering at my tomb if I depart from this light. Therefore I ask to rest at a distance from the monastery.”

For this reason, when he died, he was buried ten miles from the monastery, on a small mountain. A great church was later built over his tomb, and a vast crowd of people runs there every day. Many miracles are now displayed there in the name of God; the blind often recover their sight, the deaf their hearing, and the paralytic their ability to walk.

Abbot Lupicinus, however, died and was buried inside the monastery basilica. He left to the Lord the talents of the entrusted money multiplied: namely, blessed communities of monks devoted to his praise.

[Note: [Col. 1015D] In many places women were not even admitted into the monks’ church, as our Mabillon proves in the preface to the first volume of the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*. The Cistercians renewed this practice at their beginning.]

[Note: [Col. 1015D] The anonymous author of the *Life of Saint Romanus* calls this place the monastery of Balm, of which today, under its ancient name of Balma, only a church remains, situated among rocks and crags. There is another monastery of the same name for virgins, which still continues under the Benedictine rule between Besançon and Montbéliard, as well as a third monastery of the Cluniac order in the same diocese of Besançon.]

## CHAPTER II. On Saint Illidius, Bishop

Among the other seeds of eternal life which the heavenly Sower, from that fountain of divinity, either watered by instruction or made fruitful by doctrine in the untilled field of the mind, he said:

“Whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:38).

And elsewhere:

“Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the ground, dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it produces much fruit. He who loves his life will lose it; and he who hates his life in this world preserves it for eternal life” (John 12:24–25).

But blessed Paul the Apostle, nevertheless a vessel of election, says:

“Always carrying in your body the death of Christ, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in your mortal heart” [two manuscripts read “body”] (2 Corinthians 4:10).

Therefore the Confessors of Christ, whom the time of persecution did not summon to martyrdom, made themselves their own persecutors. In order to be considered worthy of God, they adopted various crosses of abstinence; and, so that they might live only for him after their limbs had been mortified, they did so of whom the same Apostle said:

“Now it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” [Note: [Col. 1016D] These words are absent from three manuscripts through *slaughter*. The text of Psalm 118 and of Mark 16, quoted below, is likewise absent.] (Galatians 2:20).

And elsewhere, citing that passage from the forty-third Psalm:

“For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are reckoned as sheep for slaughter” (Romans 8:36).

With the inward eyes of the mind they saw the Lord of heaven descend to earth—not cast down into humiliation, but mercifully humbled for the redemption of the world. They saw him hanging on the cross—not the glory of divinity, but the pure offering of the assumed body, of which John had shortly before foretold:

“Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of this world” (John 1:29).

They also possessed within themselves the fastening of the nails: pierced by fear of him and terrified by divine judgments, they did nothing unworthy of his omnipotence in the dwelling of their bodies, according to what is written in Psalm 118:

“Pierce my flesh with your fear, for I have feared your judgments” (Psalm 118:120).

In them shone also that distinguished light of the resurrection, with which the angel gleamed when he rolled away the stone of the tomb, as we read in Mark 16:

“And entering into the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right, clothed in a white robe, and they were astonished” (Mark 16:5).

With that same light Jesus shone when he entered amid the closed doors and stood unexpectedly in the midst of the apostolic assembly. The same Lord instructed them in words of life and raised them with his company into the heavenly citadel.

Among them, blessed Illidius the Confessor placed all these things in the tabernacle of his heart, so that he too might deserve to become a temple of the Holy Spirit. As I am about to write something about his life, I ask pardon from my readers. For I was not trained by study of the art of grammar, nor did polished reading of secular authors educate me. Only the devotion of blessed Father Avitus, bishop of Arvernia, drew me toward ecclesiastical writings. [Col. 1017C]

[Note: [Col. 1016D] These words are absent from three manuscripts through “but he.”]

[Note: [Col. 1016D] Colbert reads “in the manner of his persecutor, so that”; Laudunensis and the editions read “so that,” but omit *modo*.]

[Note: [Col. 1016D] The editions read “for Christ.”]

[Note: [Col. 1017C] Bolandus reads: “the study of ecclesiastical Scripture drew him,” by which wording Henschenius thinks that Saint Avitus’s letter is being praised, containing the scriptural passages mentioned above. But Gregory means nothing other than that he was educated by blessed Avitus and trained in ecclesiastical letters. This is how the passage is explained in Gregory’s own Life prefixed to this volume. See also Fortunatus, book V, poem 4.]
