If what I heard from him when he preached, or was compelled to read again, had not come before me for judgment—for I am unable to observe it—he was the one who led me from the reeds of David’s song [Molsheim reads “songs”] to those sayings of evangelical preaching and to the histories and letters of apostolic virtue. From him I was able to grasp only enough to recognize that Jesus Christ, the Son of God, came for the salvation of the world, and to honor his friends, who, having taken up the cross, followed the Bridegroom in austere observance, with worthy acts of service.

Therefore, displaying the rashness of my unformed rusticity, I shall set forth in whatever style I can what I have learned about the blessed Illidius.

### I

Saint Illidius, distinguished by the holiness of a perfect life (year 385, 5 June), had accumulated within himself, through the Lord’s generosity, the gifts of various graces. What was still lacking from the summit of holiness was supplied when, by God’s inspiration and the people’s choice, he was selected as priest of the church of Arvernia and shepherd of the Lord’s sheep.

As the fame of his holiness rose through various advances of grace, it reached not only the boundaries of the territory of Arvernia but also the borders of neighboring cities. Hence it happened that this renown reached the ears of the emperor Trevericus, whose daughter, when she was severely afflicted by an unclean spirit and no one could be found who could free her, learned of the blessed Illidius through his reputation.

The emperor’s servants were sent and, sooner than one could say it, brought the holy old man, found in the aforesaid city, swiftly before the royal authority. The emperor received him reverently and complained of the fate of his unfortunate daughter.

Illidius, trusting in the Lord, prostrated himself in prayer. After passing the night with sacred hymns and spiritual songs, he placed his fingers in the girl’s mouth and drove the wicked spirit from the body of the possessed girl.

When the emperor saw this miracle, he offered the holy priest immense heaps of gold and silver. Illidius rejected and condemned the offer, but obtained this instead: the city of Arvernia, which had been paying its tribute in wheat and wine, should pay it in gold, since the produce was brought into the imperial treasury only with great labor.

The Saint, they say, having completed the period of his present life, departed to Christ in the very course of his journey. His people carried him back and buried him in his own city. [Col. 1018A]

[Note: [Col. 1018D] He was buried in the church that he himself had built, still famous under his name (Saint-Allire), with an attached monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict and the Congregation of Saint Maur, which has a regular abbot. The Bollandists have another Life of Saint Illidius for 5 June, but it abounds in fables. More reliable is the appendix there concerning the translation of the saint’s body in 1311 by Bishop Arbertus. The Roman Martyrology commemorates his feast on 5 July, but among the Arverni it is celebrated on 5 June.]

[Note: [Col. 1017D] Gregory says the same in *History*, book I, chapter 40, where Illidius is listed as the fourth bishop of Arvernia. The emperor, called Trevericus in both places, is none other than the usurper Maximus, who stayed for a long time at Trier. According to an ancient inscription, the Arvernians hold that his daughter, said to have been freed from a demon, was buried among them.

Gregory also relates here and in book I, chapter 40 of the *History*, that the daughter of the emperor Trevericus was freed from a demon by Saint Illidius. But he says nothing about her coming to Arvernia, nor does the author of the second Life. Nevertheless, her tomb is still visited today in the church of Illidius.

Indeed, in the year 1311, as is related in the history of the translation of Saint Illidius, on 5 June, among the Bollandists, Albert, bishop of Clermont, after the translation of the bodies of other saints, opened a lead coffin fixed in the wall of the church of the monastery of Illidius near the altar of Blessed Mary. In it were found the bones of the emperor’s daughter, whom Saint Illidius had freed from the demon.

As that author says, the same coffin appeared to contain beneath it a certain lead memorial tablet. This memorial, which was then engraved in bronze, bears the following inscription, as Savaro reports:

“Daughter of the Alemannic Emperor, whom Saint Illidius freed. Buried on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April.”]

## II

And perhaps, as people often are accustomed to grumble, someone may chatter [Note: Colb. reads *gratulatur* (“congratulates”); Ed. *garrulabit* (“will chatter”).], saying: “He cannot be counted among the saints on account of the performance of only one miracle.” For if one considers what the Lord says in the Gospel—“Many will say to me on that day: ‘Lord, Lord, did we not cast out demons in your name and perform many mighty works?’” and [Bell. adds *et non*, “and I will not”] “I will answer them, saying: ‘I do not know you’” (Matthew 7:22–23)—one will certainly understand that the power which proceeds from a tomb contributes more to praise than that which someone performed while living in the world. The latter could have been stained by the continual hindrances of worldly involvement, whereas the former was wholly free from every stain.

Therefore, because those deeds which Saint Illidius performed before this time have, as we believe, been consigned to oblivion and have not come to our knowledge, we shall declare what we have seen with our own eyes and experienced ourselves, or what we have learned from the testimony of the faithful.

At the time when Bishop Gallus governed the church of Arverna (see below, chapter 6), the writer of this account, then still an adolescent, was seriously ill. Gallus frequently visited him with singular affection, because he was his uncle. His illness consisted of an excessive quantity of stomach phlegm together with a severe fever. Meanwhile the boy conceived a desire—and, I believe, by God’s inspiration—to be carried to the basilica of blessed Illidius. When he had been carried by the hands of boys to the saint’s tomb, and had poured out a prayer with tears, he felt himself lighter than when he had arrived. Returning home, however, he was again seized by fever.

One day, when he had begun to grow worse and the fever was oppressing him more severely than usual, while it remained uncertain whether he would survive, his mother approached him and said: “Today, dear son, I shall have a sorrowful day, since such a fever has overtaken you.”

He replied: “Please, do not grieve at all. Send me to the tomb of blessed Bishop Illidius. For I believe—and my faith assures me—that his power will grant you joy and me health.”

He was then carried to the saint’s tomb and poured out a prayer to the Lord [Note: Ed. reads: “he poured out a prayer … if the power of his bishop …”]. Prostrating himself voluntarily, he promised that, if through the intercession of his bishop the Lord freed him from this illness, he would become a cleric; nor would he delay at all if his entreaty obtained its effect.

After saying this, he immediately felt the fever depart [Col. 1019B]. He summoned the boy and asked to be carried home. When he had been brought to the dining room, where they were then eating, a great quantity of blood burst from his nostrils; fever and blood flowed away together. This is regarded as a proven cure accomplished through the merits of the blessed Confessor.

Recently also, a servant of Count Venerandus, who had remained blind for a long time, departed restored to health after vigils had been celebrated.

## III

Concerning his relics, the writer mentioned above personally witnessed the following, just as it happened. In the first year of his priesthood he had dedicated an oratory within the episcopal residence of the city of Tours (see *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 20), and had placed there, among the relics of other saints, the relics of this bishop.

Many days after the dedication, the abbot reminded him to inspect the relics that he had placed on the altar itself, lest moisture from the new building should have dampened them and caused some rot to settle in them. When he searched for them and found them affected by dampness, he removed them from the altar and began drying them before a fire.

When he had arranged the bindings one by one, he came to the relics of blessed Bishop Illidius. Holding them before the fire, he allowed the thread with which they were bound—because it was extremely long—to fall upon the burning coals. It became glowing with the heat of the fire, as though it were bronze or iron. He paid little attention to what would happen to the thread with which the holy relics were bound, supposing that it had already been reduced to ashes; yet he found it still whole and uncorrupted, since shortly before it had been the bond and fastening of this glorious bishop [Note: Laud., Bell., and Bal. read as above. Colb. and the other editions: “It happened that the holy relics were merely dried. But, supposing the thread itself…” Bollandus: “What would happen to the thread, taking care only that the holy relics should not be damaged; then follows: ‘and the thread unharmed.’”].

## IV

[A small child, about ten months old, who, as the truth of the matter revealed, was regarded as the blessed man’s great-grandson, was afflicted by the onset of an extremely grave illness [Note: The material that follows through the clause “Many indeed…” is found only in the Molsheim manuscript and in the Bollandists under 5 June. That manuscript was written more than eight hundred years ago in the monastery of Saint-Denis near Paris.]. His mother wept no less over the child’s death than because he had not yet been washed in the divine sacrament.

After taking counsel, she went to the tomb of the blessed Confessor. She laid the sick child on the pavement; he was no more than faintly breathing. She kept vigil before the Bishop’s tomb in prayers and supplications. When that winged herald of light [that is, the cock], beating its wings, had uttered its cry more loudly, the child, who had been thrown down almost lifeless, recovered. Revealing the joy of his heart with a preceding laugh, and opening his mouth by divine intervention, he called for his mother, saying: “Come here.”

She approached trembling and rejoicing. Since she had never yet heard her son’s voice, she asked in astonishment: “What do you want, dearest son?”

He replied: “Run as quickly as you can and bring me cups of water.”

She remained motionless in prayer until daylight, giving thanks to the holy Bishop and dedicating her child to him, and then returned home. When water was offered to him, the infant drank; freed from every bond of illness, he fully recovered.

Afterward he returned to his former infant cries and could not speak again until he had grown to that stage of life at which an infant’s tongue ordinarily becomes capable of speech.

Nor do I think I should be silent about what happened once, when the kiln for baking the basilica’s lime was being fired. The beam that very firmly secured the mouth of the furnace broke while those present, including the abbot of the place, were asleep.

Thereupon a figure appeared suddenly to the priest in a vision, seemingly a priest, saying: “Hurry quickly and awaken the sleepers, lest the collapse that is about to occur overtake them. For the beam that supports the entire mass of stones is already prepared to fall together with the fire.”

When the priest awoke, he removed everyone from the mouth of the furnace. Immediately the heap of stones assembled on both sides fell, injuring none of those standing nearby. I believe this was accomplished through the Bishop’s intercession [Col. 1020C].

The priest mentioned above then prayed at the Saint’s tomb. After the beams had been repaired and the stones replaced, he resumed the work begun in the kiln and completed it with the Bishop’s assistance.

The blessed body of this Confessor had been buried by the ancients in a crypt. But because the building was cramped and its entrance difficult, the holy Bishop Avitus of the city constructed around it an apse of remarkable workmanship. He sought out the blessed remains, found them in a chest made of wooden boards, and, according to custom, enclosed them in a sarcophagus.

In this place Justus rests, both in name and in merit [Note: Concerning him, see above, *History*, book 1, chapter 40; see also the note at chapter 34 and following of *On the Glory of the Confessors*, above, column 853. Editor’s note.]. He is said to have been the archdeacon of this glorious bishop.]

## V

Many other miracles of this saint have indeed been reported, but I have thought it tedious to write them down, judging that what has been said is sufficient for perfect faith. For those whom a few things do not satisfy will gain no benefit from many.

At his tomb the blind are given sight, demons are driven away, the deaf receive hearing, and the lame recover their ability to walk, through the agency of our Lord Jesus Christ, who promised believers that he would grant without hesitation what they asked of him.

# CHAPTER III  
## On Abraham, the Abbot

I do not think it is unknown to any Catholic what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you: if you have complete faith and do not hesitate, if you say to this mountain, ‘Move yourself,’ it will move itself; and whatever you ask in my name, believe that you will receive it, and it will come to you” (Matthew 21:21; Mark 11:23).

Therefore there can be no doubt that the saints can obtain from the Lord what they ask, since, established upon that foundation of faith [Note: Laud. and Colb. read: “in him faith … having been placed.” Ed. and Bell.: “in them, faith having been placed upon the foundation … it falters.”], they do not waver amid the waves of doubt. For the sake of this faith they not only became exiles within the boundaries of their own country while desiring to lead a heavenly life, but also sought transmarine and foreign places, so that they might please more fully the one to whom they had devoted themselves.

So it was with blessed Abraham the abbot, who, after many worldly trials, entered the borders of the territory of Arverna. He is rightly compared with that aged Abraham because of the greatness of his faith, to whom God once said: “Go out from your land and from your kindred, and go to the land that I shall show you” (Genesis 12:1).

This Abraham left behind not only his native land but also the conduct of the old human being, and put on the new human being, who has been formed according to God in justice, holiness, and truth. Therefore, when he saw himself perfected in God’s work, he did not hesitate in faith to ask for what, trusting in a holy life, he believed he would obtain. Through him the maker of heaven, sea, and earth deigned to perform miracles few in number but marvelous.

## I

This Abraham was born on the bank of the Euphrates River (480, 15 June). As he advanced in the work of God, he desired to visit the hermits and to go to the deserts of Egypt. While he was making that journey, he was captured by pagans [Note: That is, Persians, as is evident from his epitaph, where their king is called the king of the Susian region, from Susa, the famous Persian city]. He was beaten severely for Christ’s name and thrown into chains. After rejoicing in those chains for five years, he was released when an angel loosed them.

Desiring also to visit the western region, he came to Arverna and established a monastery beside the basilica of Saint Cyricus [Note: The same account appears in *History*, book 2, chapter 21, where he praises the Life of Abraham written by himself. The church of Saint Cyricus, where Saint Abraham and others rest, is mentioned by the author of *The Churches of Clermont*, chapter 14. It still exists today, commonly called Saint-Cirgues. The monastery was destroyed long ago, but the church remains distinguished by the title of parish church; beside it flows a spring named after Saint Abraham].

He possessed remarkable power: he drove out demons, gave sight to the blind, and was an exceedingly powerful healer of other illnesses as well.

When the festival of the aforementioned basilica arrived, he summoned the provost and told him to arrange, according to custom, vessels full of wine in the courtyard for the refreshment of the people attending the celebration.

The monk protested: “Look, you have invited the bishop with the duke and the citizens, and scarcely four amphorae of wine remain for us. How will you fill all these vessels?”

He replied: “Open the storeroom for me.”

When it had been opened, he entered. He offered a prayer, and, like a new Elijah, raising his hands to heaven and lifting tear-filled eyes, he said: “I beg you, Lord, let the wine in this vessel not fail until it has been served abundantly to everyone.”

When the Holy Spirit came upon him, he said: “Thus says the Lord” (1 Kings 17:14): “The wine in the vessel will not fail, but it will be given abundantly to all who ask, and it will overflow.”

In fact, the wine was served to the entire people in abundance, exactly as he had said and with the joyful generosity of that distribution, and some remained.

The provost, however, had previously measured the fifty-measure vessel carefully and found it to contain four palms’ measure. When he saw what had happened, he measured it again the next day and found as much wine in the vessel as had remained in it the preceding day.

Through this the saint’s power was made manifest among the people. He died full of days in that monastery and was buried there with honor.

At that time Saint Sidonius was bishop, and Victorius was duke. By the favor of Euric, king of the Goths, Victorius had received authority over seven cities. Blessed Sidonius wrote this saint’s epitaph [Note: We shall provide it in the appendix. Gregory frequently speaks of Apollinaris Sidonius and Duke Victorius], in which he prefaced some of the matters I have mentioned.

At the tomb of this blessed Abraham, those lying sick with quartan fever are frequently raised up by the aid of heavenly medicine.

# CHAPTER IV  
## On Quintianus, the Bishop

Everyone who recognizes that he bears a body made of earthly matter ought to take care not to sink into those things known to be earthly and friendly to this flesh. For, according to the Apostle Paul: “The works of the flesh are manifest” (Galatians 5:19). They are full of impurity and iniquity; they make the person who pursues them polluted and foul, and finally consign him to eternal weeping.

The fruit of the Spirit, however, is everything that flourishes and shines in God. In this world, when the flesh has been put to death, it causes the soul to rejoice; in the future, it grants eternal joys.

Therefore we who are now placed in the body ought to look upon what God has accomplished in his saints. In them, as though residing in a splendid, bright, polished tabernacle adorned with various flowers of virtue [Ed. reads *intra*, “within,” rather than *in*, “in”], he has deigned, extending the majesty of his right hand, to accomplish through his own mercy what they asked. So now, through blessed Quintianus, who shone with the nobility of an excellent mind, he often completed the work of justice.

Let us not, then, allow the pursuit of the flesh, like the behavior of beasts, to plunge and bury us in earthly things. Rather, attracted by the examples of the saints and wisely understanding the things that belong to God, may spiritual works lift us to heavenly and eternal things. Let the mind within us not be conquered by shameless deeds and luxuriate in them; instead, as wisdom claims the throne of eternity on the basis of merit, let it reign victorious.

## I

The most blessed Quintianus, an African by birth (527, 13 November), and, as some maintain, the nephew of Bishop Faustus [Note: At that time Faustus, bishop of Praesidium, was famous. During the exile imposed by Huneric for the sake of the faith, he built a monastery in the place of exile, as is clear from the Life of Saint Fulgentius. Victor of Vita praises Blessed Faustus, bishop of Buronitanum, book 1, no. 11. Saint Quintianus may perhaps have been the nephew of one of these two], who is said to have raised his mother from the dead, was endowed with holiness, radiant with the gift of virtues, ardent with the flame of charity, and distinguished by the flower of chastity. He was chosen, sought out, and ordained bishop of the church of Rodez [Note: He subscribed to the Council of Agde in 506 and to the First Council of Orléans in 511].

In that episcopate, while he continued to grow in God’s works and his virtues were still increasing, he transferred the holy body of blessed Bishop Amantius into the enlarged basilica [Note: Some read: “he enlarged the basilica.” Labbeus prints a Life of Saint Amantius in volume 2 of the *Bibliotheca nova*, including an account of his translation. The pious abbot Richard pawned the abbey of Saint Amantius of Rodez, which was subject to the monastery of Saint-Viton of Verdun, to the count of Rodez, in order to help the poor during a public calamity, as Hugh of Flavigny reports in his *Chronicle*. The records of the visitation of the diocese of Rodez conducted by Simon, archbishop of Bourges, in 1286 mention the priory of Saint Amantius in the suburb of Rodez].

But this deed was not acceptable to the Saint. Therefore he appeared to Quintianus in a vision and said: “Because you have rashly dared to remove remains resting in peace, behold, I shall remove you from this city, and you shall be an exile in another region; nevertheless, you shall not be deprived of the honor that you now enjoy.”

Not long afterward, when a quarrel arose between the citizens and the bishop, the Goths who were then living in that city became suspicious that the bishop wished to subject himself to the authority of the Franks. After taking counsel, they planned to run him through with a sword [Note: Compare *History*, book 2, chapter 36].

When this was reported to the holy man, he rose during the night and, leaving that city with his most faithful attendants, came to Arverna. There he was received by Bishop Eufrasius, who had succeeded Bishop Aprunculus. Eufrasius—or the man who governed the city of Lyon—provided him with houses, fields, and vineyards, and they both cared for him with the greatest diligence [Note: Ed. reads: “both he and the man who governed,” with the same meaning].

He was already an old man and a true worshiper of God. When Saint Eufrasius departed from this world, Apollinaris served as bishop for three months and then died [Note: Compare *History*, book 3, chapter 2].

When this was reported to King Theoderic, he ordered Saint Quintianus to be installed there and all authority over the church to be entrusted to him, saying: “He was expelled from his own city because of his zeal for our love.”

After Saint Quintianus had assumed the episcopate in that city, a certain Proculus, a presbyter appointed from the treasury, inflicted many injuries upon him. He deprived him of all authority over church property and ordered that barely enough daily sustenance be provided to him. But through Quintianus’s prayer, Proculus was rebuked by the wiser citizens; after all authority had been restored to the bishop, he withdrew from his plots against him.

Nevertheless, the aforementioned priest, not forgetting the injury, used to sing of Proculus, just as the Apostle Paul once did of Alexander (2 Timothy 4:14): “Proculus the treasurer did me much harm; the Lord will repay him according to his works.” It is clear that this later happened to him.

## II

The blessed man was constant in prayer and loved his people so greatly that, when Theoderic arrived and surrounded the city with his army, the Saint of God went around its walls at night singing psalms. He prayed fervently, afflicted by fasts and vigils, that the Lord might quickly come to the aid of the region and its people.

King Theoderic was then considering destroying even the city walls (525). But the mercy of the Lord softened him, as did the prayer of his priest, whom he had been planning to drive into exile [Note: Ed. reads: “he was softened … by the prayer of his priest”].

For one night, terrified by fear, he leaped from his bed and tried to flee alone along the public road. He had lost his senses and did not know what he was doing. His attendants noticed this and, trying to restrain him, could scarcely do so; they urged him to protect himself with the saving sign.

Then his duke, Hilpingus, approached the king more closely and said: “Hear, most glorious king, the advice of my insignificance. Behold, the walls of this city are extremely strong, and enormous fortifications surround it. So that your magnificence may understand this more fully, I speak of the saints whose basilicas encircle the city walls; but the bishop of this place is held in great esteem with God.

“Do not do what you are contemplating. Do not injure the bishop or destroy the city.”

The king graciously accepted his advice and issued an order that no one was to be harmed within eight miles of the city.

No one should doubt that this was accomplished through the intercession of the Priest.

At that time the priest Proculus was also torn to pieces by sword blows before the altar of the church, after the walls of the fortress of Lovolautra [Note: Thus the manuscripts read, as also in *History*, book 3, chapter 13, where the same story is told. The printed editions here read *Utrense*] had been breached and the invading enemy had entered. Thus the Lord repaid him, as the Priest was accustomed to sing, according to his works.

## III

After the slaughter and disaster inflicted upon Arverna had been completed, Hortensius, one of the senators who governed that city, ordered one of the Saint’s relatives, a man named Honoratus, to be held wickedly in the city square.

This was quickly reported to the blessed man. Through his friends he began asking Hortensius to grant the man a hearing and order his release. Hortensius did not do so in any way.

Then the blessed old man ordered that he be carried into the square where Honoratus was being held. Once brought there, he asked the soldiers to release the prisoner. They were afraid and did not dare obey the Bishop.

The Priest then said: “Carry me quickly to the house of Hortensius.”

He was very old and could not walk on his own feet. His attendants carried him into Hortensius’s house. There he shook the dust from his shoes into the house and said: “Cursed be this house, and cursed be its inhabitants forever. Let it become desolate, and let no one dwell in it.”

All the people said: “Amen.”

He added: “I beg you, Lord, may no one from this generation ever be advanced to the episcopal priesthood who does not obey a bishop” [Note: It is said that Saturninus, the first bishop of Toulouse, uttered a similar imprecation above, *History*, book 1, chapter 28: that no citizen of Toulouse should ever be chosen bishop there].

When the Priest had left the house, all the members of the household within it were immediately seized by fever. After groaning for a short time, they breathed out their spirits.

When this had continued into the third day, Hortensius saw that none of his servants would be left to him. Fearing that he too might perish, he went sorrowfully to the holy man, threw himself at his feet, and begged forgiveness with tears.

The Saint most graciously granted it and sent blessed water to the house. When it had been sprinkled over the walls, all the sickness was immediately driven away, and a great miracle appeared there: those who had fallen ill were healed, and those who had been healthy did not subsequently fall ill [Al. reads “those who had been healed”].

## IV

This priest was considered learned in ecclesiastical writings, and he was also generous in almsgiving.

When he saw some poor person crying out, he would say: “Help, please help, and provide the poor man with what he needs for sustenance. You are ignorant, you idle people. Perhaps he himself is the one who, throughout the Gospel reading, commanded that he be refreshed in the least of the poor” (Matthew 25:40).

He also expelled demons that confessed their presence.

When he came to the monastery of Canbidobrinum [Note: Thus Colb., Laud., and most editions. Bell., with Bal., reads *Candidobrinum*. Today it is commonly called Combronde; its priory is subject to the monastery of Menat of the Order of Saint Benedict], and found a possessed man raging with exceptional violence, he sent priests to lay hands upon him. But when the apparition had not been expelled by their exorcism, the Saint of God approached closely, inserted his fingers into the man’s mouth, and restored him, freed from the possessing spirit.

The blessed man performed many other miracles and, after praying, frequently obtained from the Lord what he asked.

Once, when severe drought was consuming the fields of Arverna, and when the grasses had dried up so completely that no fodder at all remained for the animals, the Saint of God was devoutly celebrating those litanies that are performed before the Lord’s Ascension. On the third day, when they were already approaching the city gates, the people suggested that he himself should deign to begin the antiphon. They said: “If you, blessed Bishop, devoutly begin the antiphon, we trust in your holiness that the Lord will immediately deign, in his gracious mercy, to grant us rain.”

He prostrated himself upon his hair shirt in the middle of the square and prayed for a very long time with tears.

Then he rose and began the antiphon they had requested, as his power permitted. Its words, drawn from Solomon’s prayer, were these:

“If the heavens are closed and there is no rain because of the sins of the people, and they turn and plead before you, hear, Lord, and forgive the sins of your people, and give rain to the land that you gave your people to possess” (2 Chronicles 6:26–27).

When they began to sing psalms with the greatest devotion, the humble prayer of the Confessor reached the ears of the exalted Power. And behold, the sky grew dark and was covered with clouds. Before they reached the city gate, heavy rain descended upon the whole region, so that everyone marveled and said that it had been granted in response to the prayers of the blessed man.

## V

The Priest of God grew old and advanced so far in years that he could no longer spit the saliva from his mouth onto the ground. Instead, having a little vessel brought to his lips [Note: Laud., with the editions, reads *trudione*], he deposited his saliva in it.

His eye did not grow dim, nor was his heart changed from the ways of God. He did not turn away the face of the poor, nor did he fear the person of the powerful. The same holy freedom governed him toward everyone, so that he received the cloak of a poor man as though he were honoring the toga of a famous senator.

He died perfected in holiness and was buried in the basilica of Saint Stephen [Note: This church is said to have been built by the wife of Saint Namatius; see above, *History*, book 2, chapter 17, where we discussed it. A short work, *The Churches of Clermont*, chapter 13, mentions Saint Quintianus resting there, and his tomb can still be seen there. But his sacred body was later transferred to the church of Saints Symphorianus and Genesius in the city, where it still rests], on the left side of the altar. At his tomb, quartan fevers are now often extinguished and melancholy suppressed.

# CHAPTER V  
## On Portianus, the Abbot

How much the almighty God grants to those dedicated to his name, and how greatly he repays their faithful service through the aid of his goodness!

He promises that he will give them great things in heaven, but he often reveals in this world what they are going to receive. For he frequently makes slaves free, and the free glorious, according to the Psalmist’s saying: “He raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dungheap, to place him with the princes of his people” (Psalm 112:7–8).

Anna, the wife of Elkanah, also said concerning this: “Those who were full hired themselves out for bread, and the hungry were filled” (1 Samuel 2:5).

For this reason the Virgin Mary, mother of our Redeemer, herself said: “He has cast down the powerful from their throne and exalted the humble” (Luke 1:52).

The Lord himself likewise says in the Gospel: “The first will be last, and the last first” (Matthew 20:16).

[Note: SB reads *illucet* (“shines upon”); Colb. *licet … misericordia inopum* (“it is permitted … the mercy of the poor”); Bell. and Laud. *inlicet* (probably *illicet*, “immediately”); Bad. and the editions except Bal. *illi cet* (an uncertain reading).]

Therefore let divine mercy shine through its love upon the needy, so that it may make the lowly great and make the weak co-heirs of his Only-Begotten Son. For from this world’s poverty he has appointed them in heaven, where earthly power could not ascend, so that the peasant may enter where the man clad in purple did not deserve to enter.

So it was with blessed Portianus the abbot. He not only freed him from the burden of worldly service but also raised him up through great virtues. After the world [Ed. reads “movement”] and the pressures of this age, he established him in eternal rest and placed him among the choirs of angels, from which that earthly lord had been expelled.

## I

From the beginning of his life, the most blessed Portianus (527, 24 November) always sought the God of heaven, even amid earthly servitude.

He is said to have been the servant of a certain barbarian [Note: That is, a Frank. Some call him Malfangus, a name that appears to have been invented]. He frequently fled to the monastery, so that the abbot might excuse him to his master.

At last, when he fled once again, his master followed him closely. He began to accuse the abbot, believing that the abbot himself was seducing the servant so that he would no longer serve his master.

When the master continued, as was his custom, to harass the abbot with accusations and demand that the servant be returned, the abbot said to him: “What do you want me to do?”

The master replied: “Return him to me with an excuse.”

When the servant had been returned with the abbot’s excuse and his master wished to take him home, the master was suddenly struck blind, so that he could recognize absolutely nothing.

Seeing himself afflicted by severe suffering, he summoned the abbot and said: “Please, pray to the Lord for me, and accept this servant for his service. Perhaps I shall deserve to receive the sight I have lost.”

Then the abbot called the blessed man and said: “Please place your hands upon his eyes” [Note: Here, as elsewhere, Gregory uses the accusative case instead of the ablative].

When Portianus refused, he was finally overcome by the abbot’s prayers and placed the sign of the blessed cross upon his master’s eyes. Immediately the darkness was broken, the pain subsided, and the man was restored to his former health.

Afterward blessed Portianus became a cleric and was distinguished by such an abundance of virtue that, when the abbot died, he succeeded him [Note: This monastery, which gave its name to the neighboring town, still exists in the territory of the Arverni toward Bourbonnais. The title of abbey was lost eight hundred years ago and it was reduced to a priory subject to the monastery of Tournus. When the monks of Tournus were given secular dress in 1627, the monastery of Saint Porcianus remained under the regular order; in 1645 it was entrusted to the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint-Maur for reform].

He is said to have done the following in summer, when the heat of the sun consumed everything by the force of its burning and wearied even bodies strengthened by food and drink. After fasting had exhausted all moisture from his mouth, he would chew salt while burning with heat, so that, when moisture returned, he might for a short time moisten his parched gums.

Although this moistened his dry palate, it added still greater torment to the thirst of his body. For, as no one fails to understand, salt intensifies the heat of thirst more than it extinguishes it. Yet, by the Lord’s gift, this effect was kept from him.

## II

In those days Theoderic entered the territory of Arverna (525), destroying and devastating everything.

When he had pitched his camp in the meadows of the village of Arthon [Note: Most editions, with Laud., read *Archonensi*. But this passage refers to Artona, a village very well known among the Arverni. Theoderic’s expedition is related in *History*, book 2, chapters 12 and following, where Sigivald is also discussed. See the preceding chapter, on Saint Quintianus], the aforementioned old man hurried out to meet him, as though he intended to plead on behalf of the people.

He entered the camp in the morning, while the king was still sleeping in his tents, and approached the pavilion of Sigivald, who was then regarded as the king’s chief man. While Portianus complained about the captivity of the people, Sigivald begged him, after washing his hands in water, to accept unmixed wine. He said: “Divine mercy grants me great joy and benefit today if, after offering a prayer within the enclosure of my tent, you deign to accept a drink.”

He had heard of the Saint’s reputation for holiness and therefore showed him honor out of reverence for God.

Portianus excused himself in various ways and insisted that it could not be done: “For,” he said, “the proper hour has not arrived, I have not offered the king a fitting greeting, and, more important than all these things, I have not yet rendered to the Lord the psalmody that is his due.”

But Sigivald set these objections aside and compelled him by force. When the vessel containing the drink had been brought, he asked the Saint to sanctify it by placing his hand upon it first.

Portianus raised his right hand and made the sign of the cross. Immediately the vessel split in two, and the wine contained within it poured onto the ground together with an enormous serpent.

Those present saw this, were terrified, fell at the blessed man’s feet, licked his footprints, and kissed his feet. Everyone marveled at the old man’s power, and they marveled that they had been divinely saved from the venom of the wicked serpent.

At this miracle the entire army ran together. The whole multitude surrounded the blessed man, longing to touch his garments with their hands, since they could not honor him with a kiss.

The king leaped from his bed and hurried to meet the blessed Confessor. Without a word from the Saint, the king released all the captives whom he was demanding and thereafter recovered the rest as he wished.

With the Lord’s cooperation, he bestowed a double benefit there: he rescued some from death and freed others from the yoke of captivity [Note: Ed. reads “and thus he received a double benefit,” omitting *largitus* (“bestowed”). Colb. reads “he received; thus, a double [benefit].”].

Truly, as I believe and as my faith assures me, it is certain that those saved from this danger were, as it were, raised from the dead.

III. Nor did I wish to pass over the fact that, when the devil attempted to mock him by various devices and saw that he could do him no harm, he attacked him with visible assaults. For one night, while he had surrendered himself to sleep, he suddenly awoke and saw his cell as though it were being consumed by fire [Col. 1028C]. Rising in terror, he made for the door. When he was unable to open it, he prostrated himself in prayer; and, making the saving sign before him and around himself, he immediately caused the apparition of flames that had appeared to vanish. Thus he recognized that this had been a deception of the devil.

This was immediately revealed to the blessed Protasius, who at that time was living as a recluse in the monastery at Canbidobrium [Note: [Col. 1028D] This monastery was mentioned in the preceding chapter. Saussaius lists Protasius in the appendix to the *Gallican Martyrology* among those whose feast day is uncertain. Branchus records him in the *Lives of the Saints of Auvergne* under 24 November. He is known from this passage of Gregory alone.]. He, with the greatest haste, sent a monk from his cell to the brother and exhorted him, saying:

“Most beloved brother, you must resist the devil’s snares manfully and fear nothing of his deceitfulness, but overcome by continual prayer everything that he brings against you, opposing to it the sign of the cross [1168], because he always strives to conquer the servants of God by such temptations.”

The blessed man grew old and, having completed the course of a good work [Col. 1028D], departed to the Lord. His tomb is now repeatedly glorified by divine miracles [Note: [Col. 1028D] He was buried in his own monastery. Toward the end of the tenth century his sacred body was raised from the earth; thereafter his head and some bones, stolen by certain Normans [Col. 1029C], were carried to a Norman fortress commonly called Aquila, or L’Aigle [Col. 1029D]. The remaining relics of his sacred body still rest in the monastery of Saint Portianus.

The sacred head of the blessed Portianus was secretly taken by certain Normans toward the end of the tenth century and carried to their homeland, where it is still venerated in the church of Saint Martin at the town called Aquila. In 1673, on 26 November, with the permission of Henri de Maupas, bishop of Évreux and diocesan ordinary of the place, the chest called Saint Portianus’s was opened. The head of the blessed man was found in it, cut into various pieces, with this inscription: “The head of Saint Portianus, which was broken by the heretics in the church of Saint Martin at Aquila in the year 1567, on 18 March.” In another chest his arm was found.].

These are the only things we have learned about the holy man; we do not judge those who learned greater things about him, should they wish to write anything in his praise [Col. 1029A].

## CHAPTER VI. On Saint Gallus, Bishop

The summit of worldly nobility always longs after desires, rejoices in honors, is puffed up by encounters, pounds at the forum with lawsuits, feeds on plunder, delights in slanders, and desires talents of tarnished gold. And while it seems to possess little, it is inflamed all the more to accumulate much; the heap of gold imposes upon it an arduous thirst for possession, as Prudentius says:

> For the hunger for gold grows greater from gold.

[Note: [Col. 1029D] Another reading: “gives birth.”]

Thus it happens that, while it rejoices in the pageantry of the world and delights in empty honors [Col. 1029B] [Note: [Col. 1029D] Bal.: “is delighted.”], nothing recalls to it the enduring dignities. Nor does it look toward things that are not seen, so long as it may greedily possess those things by which it thinks the soul can be satisfied.

Yet there are some who have freed themselves from these bonds, like birds flying out of snares, and, reaching toward higher things, have released themselves through the vigor of a more eager mind. Having abandoned and come to hate earthly possessions, they have applied all their strength to heavenly things. Such was Saint Gallus, a native of the city of Auvergne, whom neither the splendor of his family, nor the eminence of senatorial rank, nor wealth of possessions could draw away from the worship of God. Nor could the love of his father, his mother’s caresses, the affection of his nurses, or the attentions of his attendants separate him from the love of God. He regarded all these things as worthless and hated them as dung [Col. 1029C]; he devoted himself to the love of God and to God’s service, and subjected himself to monastic discipline.

For he knew that the flames of youthful ardor could not otherwise be subdued unless he submitted to canonical restraint and the strictest discipline. He knew that he would be raised from the low estate of the world to higher things, and that through patient endurance he would be lifted to the glory of that exalted summit. The outcome later proved this.

### I

Saint Gallus (554, 1 July) began from his youth to be devoted to God. Loving the Lord with his whole soul, he loved whatever he knew to be dear to God. His father was named Georgius [Note: [Col. 1030C] He was the grandfather of our Gregory, namely, the father of Saint Gallus [Col. 1030D] and of the senator Florentius. Vectius Epagathus was one of the martyrs of Lyon; his eulogy is found in the celebrated letter that Eusebius inserted in Book V, chapter 1, of his *History*.]. His mother, Leocadia, descended from the family of Vectius Epagathus, whom Eusebius’s *History* records as having suffered martyrdom at Lyon. They were of such rank among the leading senators that nothing more distinguished or noble could be found in Gaul.

When his father wished to seek for him the daughter of a certain senator, Gallus took a young servant with him and went to the monastery of Cromon [Note: [Col. 1030D] Thus the editions and Colbertinus; Laudunensis has “Crononinsim”; Bellovacensis, “Cronosensim”; commonly Cournon. See *History*, Book IV, chapter 40.], situated six miles from the city of Auvergne. There he humbly begged the abbot to deign to cut the hair of his head.

But the abbot, seeing the boy’s prudence and elegance, asked his name and inquired about his family and homeland. He replied that he was called Gallus, a citizen of Auvergne, and the son of the senator Georgius. When the abbot learned that he had been born of the first nobility, he said:

“You desire well, my son; but first this must be brought to your father’s attention. If he wishes it, I shall do what you request.”

The abbot therefore sent messengers to the father, asking what he ordered them to do concerning the boy [Col. 1030B]. The father, saddened for a while, said:

“He was my firstborn, and therefore I wished to unite him in marriage. But if the Lord deigns to call him to His service, let His will rather than ours be done.”

He added: “Whatever the child, under God’s inspiration, tells you, fulfill.”

### II

When the abbot learned this from the messengers, he made the boy a cleric [Note: [Col. 1030D] From this and other passages of Gregory, Ludovicus Thomassinus infers that abbots formerly used to confer the clerical tonsure, that the tonsure of monks and clerics was once the same, and that monks were often designated by the name “clerics.” We too have frequently observed this. On the matter, see Thomassinus, *Ecclesiastical Discipline*, Latin edition, Part I, Book II, chapter 39. Cointius agrees, under the year 518. See also Mabillon’s notes on the Life of Saint Sequanus, *Benedictine Century I*, p. 264.].

He was of remarkable chastity and, like an elder, desired nothing perversely. He restrained himself even from youthful amusements. He had a voice of extraordinary sweetness with a pleasing modulation; he devoted himself constantly to reading, delighted in fasts, and abstained greatly from food.

When the blessed Bishop Quintianus came to that same monastery and heard him singing [Col. 1030C], he did not allow him to remain there any longer, but brought him with him to the city and nourished him as a heavenly father in spiritual sweetness.

After his father’s death, as his voice became more and more composed with each passing day [Two manuscripts: *componeret*], and as he enjoyed the greatest popularity among the people, these things were reported to King Theuderic. Gallus was summoned with all speed, and the king honored him with such affection that he loved him more than his own son. The queen also loved him with a similar affection, not only because of the excellence of his voice but also because of the chastity of his body.

At that time King Theuderic took many clerics from among the citizens of Auvergne and ordered them to serve the Lord in the church of Trier. But he would not allow the blessed Gallus to be separated from him [Col. 1031A]. Thus, when the king went to the city of Agrippina [Note: [Col. 1031D] This is Cologne, a city celebrated under that name.], Gallus went there with him.

There was a certain shrine there filled with various ornaments. The neighboring barbarian people, offering lavish libations [The edition reads “rich libations”], filled themselves with food and drink to the point of vomiting. There they also worshiped idols as gods and carved in wood the limbs corresponding to whatever part of the body had afflicted each person with pain.

When Saint Gallus heard this, he hurried there with only one cleric. After lighting a fire, and when none of the foolish pagans was present, he approached the shrine and set it ablaze. When they saw the smoke of the sanctuary rising all the way to heaven, they sought the author of the fire. Upon finding him, they pursued him with drawn swords.

He fled and hid himself in the royal palace. But when the king learned what had happened, while the pagans were threatening, he calmed them with gentle words and so mitigated their wicked fury.

The blessed man often used to recount these things with tears, saying:

“Woe to me, who did not persist so that I might have been finished in this cause.”

At that time he was performing the office of deacon [1171].

### III

Finally, when the blessed Bishop Quintianus, at the Lord’s command, had departed from this world, Saint Gallus was staying at that time near the city of Auvergne. The citizens of Auvergne gathered at the house of the priest Impetratus, his uncle, lamenting the death of the bishop and asking who should be appointed in his place.

After they had discussed the matter for a very long time, each returned to his own home. After their departure, Saint Gallus summoned one of the clerics and, as the Holy Spirit came upon him [Col. 1031C], said:

“What are these men muttering? Why are they running about? What are they reconsidering? Their work is empty. I shall be bishop; the Lord will deign to bestow this honor upon me. But when you hear that I have returned from the king’s presence, take my predecessor’s saddled horse, go out, and present yourself to meet me. If you disdain to obey this command, beware lest you later regret it.”

As he said these things, he was lying on a bed. The cleric became angry with him and reproached him at length; then, in his agitation, he struck his side against the bedframe [Note: [Col. 1031D] That is, the side of the bed, from the Greek word σπονδή, “treaty.”] and departed.

After he had gone, the priest Impetratus said to Saint Gallus:

“Listen, my son, to my advice. Do not delay at all, but go to the king and report to him what has happened here. If the Lord inspires him to bestow this priesthood upon you, we shall give great thanks to God; otherwise, you will be commended to the one who is ordained.”

Gallus went away and reported to the king what had happened concerning the blessed Quintianus. At that time Aprunculus, Bishop of Trier, also died [Note: [Col. 1031D] He died around 527. His feast is celebrated on 22 April.]. The clerics of that city gathered before King Theuderic and requested Saint Gallus as their bishop.

The king said to them:

“Go away and seek another, for I have destined the deacon Gallus elsewhere.”

They then chose and received Saint Nicetius as bishop [Col. 1032A].

But the clerics of Auvergne, having made an agreement with the consent of foolish men [Note: [Col. 1032D] That is, by means of an instrument of election.], and bringing many gifts, came to the king. By then that wicked shoot had begun to bear fruit [The edition reads “to sprout”], so that priesthoods were either sold by kings or purchased by clerics.

They then heard from the king that they would have Saint Gallus as their bishop. The king ordered that he first be ordained priest, and that, at public expense, the citizens be invited to a banquet and rejoice over Gallus’s future episcopate. This was done. For he used to say that he had given no more for the episcopate than one *triens* to the cook who had served the meal.

Afterward the king gave him two bishops for his consolation and sent him to Auvergne. The cleric who had struck his side against the bedframe, a man named Viventius [Col. 1032B], hurried to meet the Pontiff as he had commanded, not without great embarrassment. He presented himself, together with the horse that Gallus had ordered him to bring.

When both had entered the bath, Gallus mildly reproached him for the pain in his side that he had suffered from the cleric’s proud assault, thereby causing him great shame. Yet he did so not in anger, but taking pleasure merely in a spiritual jest.

From that point onward Gallus was received into the city with much psalmody and was ordained bishop in his own church.

### IV

After he had assumed the episcopate, he conducted himself toward everyone with such humility and charity that he was loved by all. He possessed patience beyond ordinary human measure, so that, if it is permissible to say so, he might be compared with Moses in bearing various injuries.

Thus, when he was struck on the head at a banquet by one of his own priests, he remained so calm that he did not even answer with a harsh word. Patiently enduring everything that happened to him, he attributed it to the judgment of God, from whom he sought to be nourished.

A certain senator named Evodius [Note: [Col. 1032D] The edition has “Ennodius,” as below.] was a priest. At a banquet of the church he had provoked Gallus with many accusations and insults. The Priest rose and went around the sites of the holy basilicas. When this was reported to Evodius, he hurried after him, threw himself at his feet in the street, and begged forgiveness, asking that Gallus’s prayer not condemn him before the omnipotent Judge.

Gallus kindly lifted him up and mercifully forgave everything he had said. He admonished him never again to dare to direct such words against the priests of the Lord, because he himself would never deserve to receive the episcopate [1173].

The outcome later proved this. For when he had already been elected bishop in the region of Gévaudan [Note: [Col. 1032D] After the death of Saint Hilary, whose successor was Evanthius, who subscribed to the Fourth Council of Orléans.], had already taken his seat, and everything was prepared for his episcopal consecration, the whole people suddenly rose against him so violently that he barely escaped alive. He later died as a priest.

### V

At the city of Orléans, after Bishop Marcus had been accused by wicked men and driven into exile [Col. 1033A], a great assembly of bishops was convened by order of King Childebert. At that synod [Note: [Col. 1033D] This is the Fifth Council of Orléans, which is said in its preface to have been convened by order of Childebert. Marcus had taken part in the Fourth Council of Orléans in 547.], the bishops recognized that the charge which had been whispered against him was baseless and restored him to his city and his see.

At that time Valentinianus [Note: [Col. 1033D] Thus Colbertinus. Others, with the edition, have “Valentianus.” Below all have “Valentinianus.” He was a *vocalis*, that is, a cantor, according to Cangius’s Glossary. Below he is explicitly called a cantor.] the deacon, now regarded as a priest and cantor, was serving Saint Gallus.

When another bishop was celebrating Mass and that deacon wished to sing out of ostentation rather than fear of God, Saint Gallus forbade him, saying:

“Wait, my son. When, at the Lord’s command, we celebrate the solemn rites, then you too should sing. For now, let the clerics of the one who consecrates the Mass sing.”

But Valentinianus declared that he could sing then as well. The Priest said to him:

“Do as you please, for you will not accomplish what you wish.”

Neglecting the Pontiff’s command, he went away and sang so disgracefully that everyone mocked him.

When another Sunday arrived and the aforementioned Pontiff was celebrating Mass, he ordered him to go forward:

“Now,” he said, “in the name of the Lord you shall accomplish what you wish.”

When he did so, his voice became so splendid that everyone praised him.

O blessed man, to whom such grace was granted that, just as human souls were subject to him, so also human voices were under his authority: when he wished, he prevented them from singing, and when he wished, he permitted them to sing.

### VI

God also performed other great miracles through him. When Julianus Defensor [Note: [Col. 1033D] *Defensores* were those to whom the care and defense of the church’s affairs and business were entrusted. See Thomassinus, *Ecclesiastical Discipline*, Part I, Book II, chapter 98 and following.], later a priest and a man of exceedingly gentle disposition, was severely tormented by a quartan fever, he sought the bed of the holy Priest. Lying upon it, and covered by the bedclothes, he slept for a short while and was so completely healed that afterward not even a trace of contact with the illness remained.

When the city of Auvergne was being consumed by a great fire and the Saint learned of it, he entered the church and for a very long time entreated the Lord with tears before the holy altar. Then he rose, took up and opened the Gospels, and set himself against the fire. With this countermeasure prepared [Note: [Col. 1033D] The edition reads: “having taken up and opened the Gospels … and when it had obeyed.” Our reading is more authentic, although more obscure, since Gregory characteristically uses the fourth case for the sixth.], the whole fire was immediately extinguished at the sight of them, so that not even an ember remained in it.

During his time the city of Auvergne was shaken by a great earthquake, but we do not know why this happened. We do know, however, that it injured no one among the people.

When that plague called the inguinal plague [Note: [Col. 1033D] Gregory discusses the same plague in *History*, Book IV, chapter 5, and in *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, Book I, chapter 51. It occurred in 545 or the following year.] was raging through various regions and was then devastating the province of Arles above all, Saint Gallus was anxious not so much for himself as for his people.

As he prayed to the Lord day and night that, while alive, he might not see his people ravaged, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a nighttime vision. The angel’s hair and clothing were brilliant white, like snow, and he said to him:

“For divine mercy looks favorably upon you, Priest, as you pray for your people. Therefore do not be afraid, for your prayer has been heard. Behold, you will be delivered from this illness together with your people; and while you live, no one in this region shall perish in this slaughter.

“Now do not fear. But after eight complete years you will depart from this world.”

This was later made manifest.

When he awoke, he gave thanks to God for this consolation, because God had deigned to strengthen him through a heavenly messenger [Col. 1034B]. He then instituted those processions in which, in the middle of Lent, the people came on foot, singing psalms, to the basilica of the blessed martyr Julianus. The journey is about 360 stadia.

When, as we have said, that plague was consuming those regions [1175], it did not reach the city of Auvergne, through the intercession of Saint Gallus’s prayer. I therefore consider no small the grace of the man who merited that, while set as shepherd over his sheep, he should not see them devoured, because the Lord defended them.

### VII

But let us come to the time when the Lord commanded him to be taken from this world. As he lay weighed down by illness, an internal fever so ravaged all his limbs that he lost his hair and beard at the same time.

Knowing through the Lord’s revelation that he would depart after three days, he summoned the people and, after breaking bread for all, distributed Communion [Note: [Col. 1033D] Was it *eulogiae*, or Communion under one species?] with holy and devout intention.

When the third day arrived, which was a Sunday and brought immense grief to the citizens of Auvergne, the sky was already growing light. He asked what they were singing in the church. They replied that they were singing the blessing.

After Psalm 50 and the blessing had been sung, and the alleluiatic psalm with its short concluding section had been completed, he finished Matins [Note: [Col. 1034D] Thus the manuscripts; that is, he completed the office we call Lauds. In it we still sing the same psalms designated here, namely Psalm 50, the *Benedicite*, and Psalm 148 with the two following psalms, which are called alleluiatic from their title. The editions instead have: “He completed the entire office of the morning hour. Having now performed this final duty,” and so forth. From this passage it is clear that *decantare* means the same as “recite.”].

When he had completed the office, he said:

“We bid you farewell, brothers.”

As he said this, he stretched out his limbs and sent his spirit, intent upon heaven, before him to the Lord.

He died in the sixty-fifth year of his life and the twenty-seventh year of his episcopate [Note: [Col. 1034D] Fortunatus gives a slightly lower number in his epitaph, which is poem 4 of Book IV, perhaps constrained by the laws of meter. He died around 554, though not on 1 July, despite the celebration of his feast on that day. See Cointius and Mabillon, *Benedictine Century I*, p. 119. Gallus subscribed to the Council of Auvergne in 535, the Fourth Council of Orléans in 541, and the Fifth in 549. Through the priest Laurentius he was present at the Second Council of Orléans in 533, and through Optardenu(s) at the Third in 538.].

Then, after being washed and clothed, he was carried into the church until the bishops of the neighboring provinces [Note: [Col. 1034D] That is, neighboring bishops, who customarily gathered for the funerals of deceased bishops just as they gathered for the ordination of new ones.] could assemble to bury him.

A great miracle was shown to the people there: Saint Gallus, drawing up his right foot while lying in the bier, moved himself onto the other side, which faced the altar.

While these things were taking place, those processions that are held everywhere each year at Easter [Note: [Col. 1035D] Colbertinus and Laudunensis read “which take place after Easter”; Colbertinus also has “were celebrated.” This reading supports Mabillon’s interpretation in *Gallican Liturgy*, Book II, no. 57, where he explains the passage as referring to the entire period extending from the Resurrection to the Ascension, and even to Pentecost.] were being celebrated.

He lay in the church for three days, amid continual psalmody [Note: [Col. 1035D] Observe the uninterrupted prayers around the body of the deceased.], with a great crowd of people present.

On the fourth day, when the bishops arrived, they lifted him from the church and carried him to the basilica of Saint Lawrence [Note: [Col. 1035D] The same is stated in the little book *On the Churches of Clermont*, chapter 3. Another Gallus is said there to rest in a church bearing his name, in chapters 8 and 11. Yet another Gallus is said to have been buried in the church of Saint Illidius, but he is unknown. The basilica of Saint Lawrence was built by the commander Victorius, according to Gregory, *History*, Book II, chapter 20. Savaro and Cointius warn that it must be distinguished from the cathedral.], where they buried him.

The extent of the mourning at his funeral and the number of people who attended can scarcely be described. Women came in mourning garments, as though they had lost their husbands. The men likewise covered their heads [Note: [Col. 1035D] Mabillon observes that even today, at the funerals of kings, the deceased’s male officials attend the funeral with their heads covered.], as is customary at the funerals of wives. The Jews themselves followed the procession, lamenting with lamps lit.

All the people said with one voice:

“Woe to us, for after this day we shall never again be granted a pontiff like him.”

Because, as we have said, the bishops of the province lived far away and could not come more quickly, the faithful placed a clod of earth over the blessed body, as is the custom of country people, so that it would not swell from the heat.

After the funeral, a certain woman, truly—as I carefully investigated—a most pure virgin devoted to God, named Meratina [Bal.: “Meretina”], collected that clod after others had thrown it away, placed it in her garden, and, repeatedly pouring water over it, caused it to live, with the Lord granting it growth.

From that clod the sick were healed, not only when they removed and drank the grass, but also when a faithful prayer was offered over it and obtained help. Later, when the virgin died, it perished through neglect.

Finally, many miracles were displayed at his tomb. Those suffering from quartan fever and from various fevers, as soon as they faithfully touched the blessed tomb, immediately drew healing from it.

Valentinianus the cantor, whom we mentioned above and who is now regarded as a priest [Note: [Col. 1036D] Thus the manuscripts and the editions, except Bal., which reads: “who was then regarded as a priest.” From this, however, Thomassinus inferred in Book II, Part I, chapter 31, that in the sixth century cantors were no longer, as formerly, boys or minor clerics, but priests, and so forth.], was serving in the office of deacon when he was seized by quartan fever and suffered for many days from severe weakness [1177].

It happened that, on the day when this fever recurred, he resolved to visit the holy places in prayer. When he came to the tomb of this saint, he prostrated himself and said:

“Remember me, most blessed and holy priest. For I was raised, taught, and encouraged by you. Remember your own pupil, whom you loved with unique affection, and rescue me from this fever by which I am held.”

After saying this, he gathered the little herbs that had been scattered by the devout in honor of the Priest’s tomb. Because they were green, he applied them to his mouth, plucked them with his teeth [Col. 1035D], and swallowed their juice [Col. 1036A].

That day passed, and he was not struck by the illness. From then on he was restored to such health that he no longer suffered even the attacks commonly called “breaks” [Note: [Col. 1036D] Several manuscripts and editions have “frictions.” A *fractio* is an interruption of fever, by which the fever seems, as it were, to be broken.].

I learned that this happened from the priest’s own mouth. For there is no doubt that, through the power of the one who called Lazarus from the tomb, miracles proceed from the tombs of his servants.

## CHAPTER VII. On Saint Gregory, Bishop of Langres

The men of outstanding holiness whom the palm of perfect blessedness raises from earth, where they were born, to heaven are those whom either the bond of unfeigned charity binds, or the fruit of almsgiving enriches, or the flower of chastity adorns, or the assured struggle of martyrdom crowns.

In these men, the first effort toward beginning the work of perfect justice was to prepare a spotless body as a dwelling for the Holy Spirit, and thus strive toward the heights of the remaining virtues. Becoming persecutors of themselves, as they destroyed their own vices within themselves, they proved themselves martyrs and, having completed the course of the lawful contest, triumphed.

No one can accomplish this without God’s help, unless he is protected by the shield or helmet of the Lord’s assistance. Whatever he accomplishes, he must attribute not to himself but to the glory of the divine name, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Whoever boasts, let him boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31).

In this way blessed Gregory placed all his glory. From the exalted power of senatorial rank he subjected himself to such humility that, casting aside every concern of the world, he devoted himself solely to God in his works [Col. 1036C], whom he kept in his heart [1178].

### I

Saint Gregory, born of the leading senators and well trained in letters, sought the countship of the city of Augustodunum (539, 4 January). Once in office, he governed that region for forty years with justice as his companion [Another reading: “ruled it”]. He was so severe and strict toward wrongdoers that scarcely any accused person could escape him.

He had a wife of senatorial family, named Armentaria, whom he is said to have known only for the purpose of producing offspring. By her, through the Lord’s generosity, he had children. He did not become inflamed with desire for another woman, as youthful ardor commonly causes.

### II

After the death of his wife, he turned to the Lord. Chosen by the people of Langres [Note: [Col. 1036D] A very famous city, commonly called Langres, whose bishop is a duke and peer of France.], he was ordained bishop.

He practiced great abstinence. But so that it would not be thought ostentatious, he secretly placed other thin barley loaves beneath wheat loaves [Note: [Col. 1036D] Thus the manuscripts, instead of “beneath wheat loaves.” Those who edited Gregory’s works without noticing the change of case corrupted the passage by substituting: “He placed wheat beneath barley loaves baked under the ashes, which were thinner.”]. Breaking the wheat bread, he distributed it to others; he himself secretly ate the barley, without anyone realizing.

He did the same with wine. When the cupbearer brought him water, he ordered water to be poured over it from above in order to conceal it, choosing a kind of glass that obscured the water’s clarity.

In fasts, almsgiving, prayers, and vigils he was so effective and devoted that, placed in the midst of the world, he shone like a new hermit [Note: [Col. 1037C] The material below concerning the possessed and other matters is related in Bollandus’s edition to the death of the blessed man.].

For he stayed continually near the fortress of Dijon, and his house adjoined a baptistery [Note: [Col. 1037C] The author of the Life of the second abbot Garnerius, written in the twelfth century, thinks this baptistery was the oratory of Saint Vincent [Col. 1037D], which still survives near and beneath the basilica of Saint Stephen, without any title. Yet in the Benignian Chronicle the church of Saint John is said to have been the baptistery; many holy relics were kept there.], in which the relics of many saints were preserved.

At night, without anyone noticing, he rose from his bed and went to pray, with God alone as witness. The door was opened by divine agency, and he attentively chanted psalms in the baptistery.

After he had done this for a long time, the matter was finally discovered and made known by a deacon. When the deacon learned what was happening, he followed from a distance so that the holy man would not notice him, and watched what he did.

The deacon said that when God’s Saint came to the door of the baptistery and knocked with his own hand, the door opened without anyone appearing. After he entered, there was silence for a very long time; afterward psalmody, as though from many voices, was heard for three hours and even longer [1179].

I believe that, because the relics of great saints were kept in that place, they revealed themselves to the holy man and together rendered psalmody to the Lord.

When he had completed the course [Note: [Col. 1037D] We have already observed more than once how diligently clerics formerly performed the divine offices. Saint Audoenus calls it the canonical course in the Life of Saint Eligius, Book I, no. 11, where he praises the saint and his clerics, who “day and night in his chamber strove with every devotion solemnly to complete the canonical course.” Below he explains the word *course*: “When he visited his diocese, as bishops customarily do, for some reason he forbade the course—that is, the canonical prayers and sacrifice—to be celebrated in a certain basilica until he himself gave the order.”], he returned to his little bed and lay down so quietly upon it that no one noticed him at all.

The observers, finding the baptistery door locked, opened it in the customary manner with their key. When the signal was sounded, God’s Saint, like the others, rose anew for the Lord’s service.

On the first day of his episcopate [Note: [Col. 1037D] Bollandus: “at the beginning”; the edition: “at first.”], possessed persons acknowledged him, and the priests asked him to deign to bless them.

But the holy man manfully avoided this, lest he incur empty glory, crying out that he was unworthy to be a minister for revealing the Lord’s miracles. Nevertheless, since he could not conceal this for long, he ordered them to be brought before him. Without touching them, but merely making the sign of the cross against them, he commanded the demons by his word to depart [Col. 1038A].

As soon as they heard this, the demons released the bodies that they had bound by their wickedness [Note: [Col. 1038C] Several editions have “tormented”; another reading is “carried away.”]. In his absence, many people would drive out possessed persons who had been suspended from and marked with the staff that he was accustomed to carry.

Moreover, if a sick person took anything from his bed, it served as an immediate remedy.

At one time his niece Armentaria [Note: [Col. 1038C] She was the mother of our Gregory. She was called by this name and was the granddaughter, through a daughter, of Saint Gregory.] was severely afflicted in her youth by quartan fever. Although she was often treated by the efforts of physicians, she could find no relief. The blessed Confessor repeatedly urged her to devote herself to prayer.

One day she sought his bed. When she lay upon it, the fever was so completely extinguished that she never afterward fell ill from it [1180] [Note: [Col. 1038C] In Bollandus’s edition a brief narrative is inserted here [Col. 1038D] concerning the translation of Saint Benignus by Saint Gregory, discussed in *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 51, and concerning the basilica of Benignus, built by Gregory, with monks established there. These matters are related at length in the Benignian Chronicle, volume I of Acher’s *Spicilegium*.].

### III.

When Saint Gregory had walked to the city of Langres because of the holy day of the Epiphany [Note: [Col. 1038D] Throughout Gregory, the word *per* is sometimes used in the sense of “because of,” which is how it must be understood here; otherwise he could not be said elsewhere to have died on 4 January.], struck by a slight fever, he departed from this world to Christ. After his passing, his blessed face was so glorified that it appeared rose-colored. For it was seen to be red, while the rest of his body shone like a gleaming lily, so that one would think he had already then been prepared for the glory of the future resurrection.

As they were carrying him to the fortress of Dijon, where he had ordered himself to be buried [Note: [Col. 1038D] The Bollandist interpolator has: “where, out of devotion to Saint Benignus, he had asked to be buried.”], in that open country which lies to the north, not far from the fortress, the bearers were overcome [Note: [Col. 1038D] So Laud., Bell., and Colb., instead of *aggravatur* (“is weighed down”). The editions read *aggravati gestatores* (“the burdened bearers”); Max. has *fatigati* (“wearied”).] and, unable to support the bier, set it down upon the ground. There they recovered their strength for a little while; then, after a short time, they lifted it and carried him into the church within the walls [Note: [Col. 1038D] This is the church of Saint Stephen, later possessed by Regular Canons, who became secular in 1613. Its history was recently published by the distinguished Claudius Fiot, abbot and restorer of that place.].

When the bishops arrived on the fifth day, he was being carried from the church to the basilica of blessed John [Note: [Col. 1038D] The interpolator has: “to the anciently constructed basilica, renowned as the burial place of the bishops of Langres.”]. And behold, the prisoners in the jail began to cry out to the blessed body, saying:

“Have mercy on us, most merciful lord, so that those whom, while living in this world, you did not release, you may at least, now dead and possessing the heavenly kingdom, deign to absolve. Visit us, we beseech you, and have mercy on us.”

As they cried out these and other words, the body became so heavy that they could no longer support it at all. Then, placing the bier upon the ground, they awaited the power of the blessed Bishop. While they were waiting, the doors of the prison suddenly opened; the beam that held the prisoners’ feet tight was split in the middle after the bolts had been forced back, and when their chains had been broken, they were all released together. They came to the blessed body, with no one holding them back. Then the bearers lifted the bier, and these men joined the others in the procession; afterward the judge dismissed them without any penalty.

### IV.

After these events, the blessed Confessor manifested himself among the people through many miracles. For a certain religious man said that he had seen the heavens opened on the day of his burial; nor can there be any doubt that, after his angelic deeds, he was gathered among the celestial companies.

A certain prisoner was being led along the road by which the blessed body had been brought from Langres to the aforementioned fortress. The soldiers and horsemen who went ahead were dragging the prisoner behind them. When they reached the place where the limbs of the blessed Confessor had rested, the prisoner, invoking the name of the blessed Bishop, asked him to free him through his mercy. As he prayed, the ropes fell loose from his hands. Feeling himself released, he became quiet; but because he covered his hands, he was still thought to be bound. When they had entered the gate of the fortress and reached the forecourt of the church, he sprang up, took hold of the strap by which those dragging him had been pulling him, and, with the help of almighty God and through the favor of the blessed Pontiff, was freed.

But this other miracle is also remarkable: when his blessed body was transferred after many years, it appeared glorious. The blessed Bishop had been buried in a corner of the basilica, but the place was small, and the people could not approach there as devotion required. Saint Tetricus [Note: [Col. 1039D] We spoke of this Saint in *History*, Book IV, chapter 16. He was buried beside his father in the church of Saint John, where Saint Urban also lay, according to the Benignian Chronicle. Their bodies were transferred to the basilica of Benignus, where the entire body of Saint Urban still remains; the church of Langres possesses half of Saint Gregory’s relics. The body of Saint Tetricus, however, has been mixed with the relics of other unknown saints.], his son and successor, seeing this and observing that miracles were constantly being performed there, laid the foundations before the altar of the basilica. He erected an apse, constructed it with marvelous workmanship, and vaulted it; after it had been vaulted and the wall broken through, he built an arch.
