When this work had been completed and adorned [Note: [Col. 1039D] That is, “when the work had been completed,” etc. Laud. has: “he dug out the place.”], he excavated a small chamber in the middle of the apse. Wishing to transfer the body of the blessed father there, he summoned priests and abbots for this service. They kept vigil and prayed that the blessed Confessor would permit himself to be transferred to this prepared dwelling.

When morning came, amid choirs of psalm-singers, they took up the sarcophagus and carried it before the altar into the apse that the blessed bishop had built [Note: [Col. 1040D] The feast of this Translation is celebrated on 6 November in the *Gallican Martyrology*.]. While they were carefully arranging the tomb, suddenly—and, as I believe, by God’s command—the lid of the sarcophagus moved on one side. And behold, his blessed face appeared so complete and unharmed that one would think he was not dead but sleeping. Nor was any part of the garment that had been placed with him found diminished [Bal., “damaged”]. Thus he rightly appeared glorious after his passing, since his flesh was not subjected to corruption’s mockery.

Great is the integrity of body and heart, which both grants grace in the present world and bestows eternal life in the future. Concerning this the Apostle Paul says: “Pursue peace and sanctification [Note: [Col. 1040D] Colb. has “holiness.”], without which no one will see the kingdom of God” (Hebrews 12:14).

### V.

A certain girl, while arranging her hair on the Lord’s Day, grasped a comb which, I believe because of the offense against the holy day, stuck to her hands. Its teeth were fixed in both her fingers and her palms, causing her great pain. As she went about the basilicas of the saints, weeping and pleading, she threw herself down at the tomb of blessed Gregory the Bishop, trusting in his power. After she had long implored the protection of the blessed Confessor, her hand was restored to its former use when the comb fell away [Col. 1040B].

Energhumens who confessed him were also often cleansed at his tomb. For after his passing we frequently saw them so firmly fixed to the walls by the little rod mentioned above, which he used to carry in his hand, that one would think they were held there by strong and extremely sharp stakes.

### VI.

We have learned many other things concerning him, but, lest they become wearisome, we have briefly touched upon a few of the many. He died in the thirty-third year of his episcopate, at the age of ninety, having repeatedly manifested himself through evident miracles [Note: [Col. 1040D] The Bollandist interpolator adds an epitaph published by Fortunatus, which is Book IV, poem 2. Saint Gregory attended the Councils of Epaon in 517; Lyon I in 535; Clermont I; and, through the priest Evantius, Orléans III in 538. Gregory praises him in *History*, Book III, chapters 15 and 19.].

## CHAPTER VIII. On Saint Nicetius, Bishop of Lyon

The goodness of the divine presence [Note: [Col. 1040D] Laud. has *praescientiae* (“foreknowledge”).], which often provides for its kingdom those whom it is to admit, is frequently attested by the oracles of sacred Scripture. Thus, from the heavenly mouth, mystical words were conveyed to Jeremiah, that outstanding prophet, saying: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you, and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you” (Jeremiah 1:5).

And the Lord himself, creator of both Testaments, when he places at his right hand those whom his generous gift has clothed with the fleece of the Lamb, what does he say? “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34) [Note: [Col. 1040D] In Colb. and Bell., “of my Father” is absent.].

The blessed Apostle, that vessel of election, says likewise: “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Romans 8:29). For concerning Isaac (Genesis 17) and John (Luke 1), he foretold how they would be born, what they would do, their name, their work, and their merit.

So now, concerning blessed Nicetius, that same ancient mercy of divine compassion—which enriches the undeserving, sanctifies the unborn, and disposes and orders all things before they come into being—wished first to reveal to his mother with what priestly insignia of grace he would flourish on earth. A little book concerning his Life is indeed preserved with us [Note: [Col. 1041D] Chifflet published this little book from a manuscript of the monastery of Jura in *Pauline Illustrated*, and the Bollandists published it under 2 April. It was written at the command of Bishop Aetherius, as the author himself testifies.]. I do not know by whom it was composed. It discloses many of his miracles, but does not clearly set out either the beginning of his birth and conversion or the sequence of his miracles. Although we too have not investigated all the miracles that the Lord deigned to perform through him, whether secretly or publicly, we have nevertheless taken care to relate in a rather rustic style those that did not reach the earlier author.

### I.

A certain Florentius [Al., Florentinus], one of the senators, had married Artemia. When he already had two children, he was being sought for the episcopate of the city of Janubus (Geneva) (2 April 583), and, once the matter had been settled with the prince [that is, by the king], he returned home and told his wife what he had done.

When she heard this, she replied to her husband:

“Cease, I beg you, dearest husband, from this undertaking, and do not seek the episcopate of the city, because I am carrying in my womb a bishop conceived by you.”

The wise man fell silent after hearing his wife, remembering what the divine voice had once commanded blessed Abraham, the founder of our faith: “Whatever Sarah says to you, listen to her voice” (Genesis 21:12).

When the days of childbirth had been fulfilled, the woman gave birth to a boy. Since he would be a victor of the world, she named him Nicetius at baptism [Note: [Col. 1041D] “Victor” is called *nikētēs* (νικητής) in Greek.], and, having raised him with the utmost care, entrusted him to be instructed in ecclesiastical letters.

After his father’s death, while he was already a cleric and lived with his mother in the paternal house, he worked with his own hands alongside the other servants, understanding that bodily passions can be suppressed only through labors and hardships.

At a certain time, while he was still living in that house, a grievous pustule arose on his face. As the poison grew and ripened, it brought the boy to the point of despair. But his mother continually invoked, among the names of many saints, the name of blessed Martin especially for his recovery.

When the boy had lain in bed for two days with his eyes closed, uttering no word of consolation to his grieving mother—while his mother herself, wavering between hope and fear, was preparing the necessities of the funeral according to the custom of burial—on the second day toward evening he opened his eyes and said:

“Where has my mother gone?”

She immediately came and said:

“Here I am. What do you want, my son?”

He replied:

“Do not be afraid, mother. Blessed Martin made the sign of Christ over me and ordered me to rise healthy.”

After saying this, he immediately rose from his bed. Divine power doubled the grace of this miracle, so that Martin’s merit might be revealed and that Nicetius, who was destined to become a bishop, might be saved from the disease. The scar visible on his face was a witness to this event.

### II.

Even when he was already thirty years old and endowed with the honor of the priesthood [Note: [Col. 1041D] As is said in another Life, he was ordained by Saint Agricola, Bishop of Chalon, concerning whom see *History*, Book V, chapter 46.] (543), he did not abstain from the labor of the work he had previously undertaken. Rather, he always worked with his own hands alongside the servants, fulfilling the Apostle’s command: “Work with your hands, so that you may have something to give to those in need” (Ephesians 4:28).

He made it his particular concern that all the boys born in his household, as soon as they had left behind the infant’s first cry and begun to speak, should immediately be taught letters and steeped in the psalms. Thus, at the beginning of their entrance [Note: [Col. 1041D] Manuscripts: “so that the beginning of the entrance.” Boll. and Sur.: “at the first entrance.”] they might be joined to a choir of psalm-singers and, through both antiphons and various meditations, fulfill what devotion of the soul required [Note: [Col. 1042D] So Colb., Bad., and other editions. Laud., Bell., and Bal. have: “what devotion required, their mind.” Bol. and Sur. have: “what devotion required, so that they might be able to serve God in their souls.”].

He carefully guarded chastity in himself, and continually preached to others the grace of guarding it. He taught them to abstain from polluted touch and obscene speech.

For I remember that in my adolescence, when I had just begun to recognize the elements of learning and was about eight years old, he ordered that I, though unworthy, be placed upon a bed. With the tenderness of paternal affection he took me upon his arm, but, grasping the edge of his garment between his fingers, he wrapped himself in his *colobium* so that none of my limbs would touch his blessed members.

Consider, I beg you, and observe the caution of the man of God! If he abstained so carefully lest he be touched by the limbs of an infant, in whom there could as yet be no impulses of desire or incitements of lust, how did he flee from a place where suspicion of lust might exist? For, as we have said, he was chaste in body, pure in heart, speaking no words of buffoonery but always speaking of the things of God.

Although he loved all people in the bond of heavenly charity, he was nevertheless so subject to his mother that he obeyed her like one of the household servants.

### III.

When the Bishop of Lyon was ill in the city of Paris [Note: [Col. 1042D] His feast is celebrated on 12 September. He attended the Fifth Council of Orléans in 549 and died in 551.], and was greatly loved by the elder Childebert, the king wished to travel to the bishop’s bedside and visit the sick man.

When he arrived, the bishop said:

“You know very well, most devout king, that I have faithfully served you in all your needs and have devoutly carried out whatever you commanded. Now I beg you: since the time of my departure is at hand, do not let me leave this world in sorrow, but kindly grant one request that I make.”

He replied:

“Ask whatever you wish, and you shall obtain it.”

The bishop said:

“I ask that Nicetius the priest, my nephew, be appointed bishop in succession to me in the Church of Lyon. For, as the words of my testimony declare, he is a lover of chastity, a devoted supporter of churches, extremely generous in almsgiving, and in works and conduct he possesses whatever befits servants of God.”

The king replied:

“Let the will of God be done.”

And thus, with the full consent of the king and people, he was ordained bishop of Lyon. For he was an outstanding lover of harmony and peace: if anyone injured him, he immediately either forgave the person himself or sent word through another asking that forgiveness be sought.

For I myself once saw Basil the priest sent by him to the count Armentarius [Note: [Col. 1043D] Bell. has “Ermentarius.”], who at that time governed the city of Lyon with judicial authority. Basil said to him:

“Our Bishop has brought this case, which is being reopened, to an end by his judgment; therefore he warns you not to presume to renew it.”

Inflamed with fury, the count replied to the priest:

“Go and tell him that many cases have been brought before him which will have to be settled by another judgment.”

The priest returned and simply reported what he had heard. Saint Nicetius, angered against the count, said:

“Truly, I say that you will not receive blessings from my hand, because you have brought to my ears words provoked by anger.”

He was reclining at a banquet, and I, while still serving in the office of deacon, had taken a place near his left hand. He said to me privately:

“Tell the priests to pray for him.”

When I had spoken, they did not understand the Saint’s intention and remained silent. Seeing this, he said:

“You rise and pray for him.”

I rose trembling, kissed his holy knees, and prayed for the priest. When he had forgiven him and offered him the blessings, he said:

“I ask you, dearest brothers, not to let useless words, muttered in cowardice, strike my ears, for it is not fitting that rational men receive the insolent words of irrational men. You should devote yourselves only to ensuring that those who wish to contrive something against the welfare of the Church are confounded by your arguments. I desire not only not to admire irrational words, but not even to hear them.”

O blessed man, who sought with complete dedication to avoid scandal!

Let those who, when offended, refuse to forgive hear this. They summon the whole city to their vengeance and do not fear even to call witnesses who will say with criminal words: “We heard this and this man speaking these things about you.” Thus the poor of Christ are oppressed by such accusations, with mercy set aside.

### IV.

One morning, when Saint Nicetius had risen for matins [Note: [Col. 1043D] The author of the little book mentioned above praises his diligence in celebrating matins. He explains that he performed it with devotion of heart and mouth as follows: “The courses of the night and day, which the ancient institution of sacred religion established by fixed limits and a definite rule in the divine offices, he doubled through constant zeal for psalm-singing, so that meditation on the divine law was never absent from his mouth or heart.”], after two antiphons had been awaited, he entered the sacristy. While he was sitting there, the deacon began to sing the responsorial psalm [Note: [Col. 1043D] Gregory mentions responsorial psalms sung at Mass in *History*, Book VIII, chapter 3. We noted there that they were so called because, when one person recited each verse of the psalm, the others added an antiphon or response, as Augustine seems to indicate in *Confessions*, Book IX, chapter 12. But the very learned J. Carus, or Thomasus, says in the preface to the Psalter that in responsorial psalms the entire verses, as they were spoken by the cantor, were repeated by the whole congregation.].

The Saint, angered, said:

“Let him be silent, let him be silent! Let the enemy of righteousness not presume to sing.”

And immediately, with his mouth closed, the deacon fell silent. The Saint ordered him to be brought before him and said:

“Had I not commanded you not to enter the church of God? Why, then, did you presume to enter with reckless boldness? Or why did you dare to raise your voice in the Lord’s songs?”

While all who were present stood astonished, knowing nothing evil about the deacon, a demon cried out from within him and confessed that he was being tormented by the Saint with immense sufferings. The deacon had dared to sing in the church; the Saint recognized the voice, although the people did not. He cursed it—the demon—in the harshest terms, not the deacon [Note: [Col. 1044D] The editions read “not to say,” words omitted by Sur. and Boll.].

Then the Saint laid his hands upon the deacon, expelled the demon, and restored him to a sound mind [Col. 1044B].

### V.

Having been made known among the people through these and other signs, he departed to Christ in the twenty-second year of his episcopate, at the age of sixty.

As he was being carried for burial, a certain blind man asked to be brought beneath the bier. As soon as he entered, his face, long deprived of the light, was adorned when his eyes were opened [Note: See *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 61, which concerns his miracles.]. Divine mercy did not delay to glorify with signs the blessed limbs of one whose blessed soul it was receiving among the stars with angelic choirs.

After the number of days established by Roman law had passed, so that the will of a deceased person might be publicly read, the testament of this Bishop was brought into the forum. With the crowd standing around, it was opened and read aloud by the judge.

The priest of the basilica, swelling with anger because he had left nothing to the place where he had been buried, said:

“Many people always used to say that Nicetius was foolish. Now it is plainly evident that this is true, since he left nothing to the basilica in which he was buried.”

On the following night he appeared to the priest with two bishops, namely Justus and Eucherius [Note: [Col. 1044D] Both were bishops of Lyon. Saint Justus is commemorated on 2 September, and Eucherius on 16 November. Nicetius was buried in the church of the Apostles, which was afterward called Saint Nicetius and still exists today, adorned with a collegiate chapter and parish title, where his holy relics are preserved. Stevertius records his epitaph. Gregory calls him a patriarch in *History*, Book V, chapter 29. He subscribed to the Second Council of Lyon in 567.], clothed in shining garments, and said to them:

“This priest, most holy brothers, has covered me with blasphemies, saying that I left no property to this church in which I rest. He does not know that whatever I possessed that was more precious, I left there—that is, the mass of my body.”

They replied:

“He acted unjustly by slandering the servant of God.”

Then the Saint turned to the priest and struck his throat with his fists and palms, saying:

“Wretched sinner, fit to be crushed, stop speaking foolishly.”

When the priest awoke, his throat was swollen and he was so constricted by pain that he could scarcely swallow even his own saliva without the greatest effort. As a result, he lay suffering severely in bed for forty days. But after invoking the name of the Confessor, he was restored to health and never again dared to chatter the words he had previously presumed to utter.

Since we know that Bishop Priscus [Note: [Col. 1045D] He succeeded blessed Nicetius. Concerning him see above, *History*, Book IV, chapter 36. He attended and subscribed to numerous councils from 573 to 585, when the Second Synod of Mâcon was held.] had always been hostile to this Saint, he gave a deacon this Saint’s *casula* [Note: [Col. 1045D] Colb. has *infra casubulam*; Bell. *casublam*; Laud. *cabsulam*.]. It was sturdy, since the man of God himself had also been robust in body.

The hood [Note: [Col. 1045D] Laud. and most editions have *capsa*. The garment had a hood, as is clear below; ancient cloaks did indeed have hoods. See Mabillon, *Gallican Liturgy*, Book I, chapter 7, no. 2.] of this garment was so broad and so sewn as hoods are customarily made on those white vestments placed upon the shoulders of priests during the Paschal festivals [Note: [Col. 1045D] Caesarius of Arles, in Book I of his Life, is said to have given the poor a processional *casula* and a Paschal alb. Saint Remigius, Bishop of Reims, bequeathed a white Paschal *amphibalus* to his successor in his Testament.].

The deacon went about in this garment and thought little of whose possession it had been. He kept it on his bed and used it in the forum; and, if reliable faith had been present, the sick could have received health from its fringes.

Someone said to him:

“O deacon, if you knew the power of God and whose garment you are using, you ought to treat it with greater caution.”

He replied:

“I tell you truly: I wear this *casula* on my back, and I will cut off the wider part of its hood to make a covering for my feet.”

The wretched man immediately did what he had promised, and was soon to receive the punishment of divine judgment. But when, after cutting off the hood and fitting foot-coverings, he had covered his feet with them, he was at once seized by a demon and fell to the floor.

He was alone in the house, and there was no one to help the unfortunate man. As he spewed bloody foam from his mouth, he stretched his feet toward the hearth, and the fire consumed both his feet and the foot-coverings.

Thus far concerning punishments.

### VI.

Our deacon Agiulfus [Ed., Aigulfus], returning from Rome, was bringing us blessed relics of the saints. He visited the place where the Saint rests solely for the sake of prayer. When he entered the church and considered the remarkable works of various miracles, he saw an immense crowd streaming in ranks to his tomb, like swarms of fortunate bees flowing to their accustomed hive.

Some, with the priest who was present ministering, took pieces of wax as a blessing; others took a little dust; still others took fragments torn from his covering. They departed carrying these things, and through them received the one grace of healing for different illnesses.

When he saw this, pierced by faith and weeping, he said:

“If devotion to my Priest caused me to plow through the vast masses of the sea with oars [Note: [Col. 1046D] So all the manuscripts and editions except Sur. and Boll., which omit the words *tonsis actum*], so that, after visiting the tombs of the Eastern martyrs [Note: [Col. 1046D] That is, “after visiting … the tombs.”], I ought to bring away some relic from them, why should I not take relics of my Gallican Confessor, through which complete health might be restored to me and to my own?”

Immediately approaching, he took, with a hand covered with linen, some herbs [Note: [Col. 1046D] See *History*, Book VII, chapter 12, and *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 50. Nepotianus is praised by Jerome, in his letter to Heliodorus, for adorning the basilicas of the church and the assemblies of martyrs with various flowers and leafy branches of trees, and for shading the glass with vine tendrils.] that the devotion of the people had placed upon the sacred tomb, with the priest handing them to him. He carefully carried them home.

The efficacy of the miracle immediately confirmed the man’s faith. For when leaves had been torn from them and given to those suffering from chills with water to drink, they immediately brought health with the draught, and afterward did the same for many others. When he reported these things to us, he said that four people had already been cured of this illness.

Our priest John, while returning from the city of Massilia with the merchandise of his trade, prostrated himself in prayer at this Saint’s tomb. When he rose from prayer, he saw broken fetters and shattered pieces of chains that had either bound the necks of the guilty or bruised their shins. He was astonished, but this sight was not without miracles.

For when the priest returned to us, he solemnly asserted that three blind people had been restored to sight there in his presence and had returned home healed.

When his relics were carried with the honor of psalm-singing through the Gallic city of Genabum [Note: [Col. 1046D] Bal. has *Genebum*. There can be no doubt that the city of Orléans is meant by Genabum, for Gregory regularly calls Geneva Januba.], the Lord deigned to grant such great grace there that those who devoutly worshiped received both their sight, if blind, and the use of their legs, if lame. No one could doubt that the Confessor was present when they saw such gifts of healing being administered to the sick.

### VII.

A riot broke out in a certain place. As the populace raged, stones and torches flew about, and fury supplied weapons in no small measure. One man, raising the point of his sword, struck another with a violent attack.

A few days later, the killer was found by the brother of the murdered man and was slaughtered in a similar manner. When the judge of that place learned of this, he ordered the bound man to be thrown into prison, saying:

“This criminal deserves to die, since, acting according to his own will and without awaiting a judge, he rashly dared to avenge his brother’s death.”

While he was being held in custody, he invoked the names of many saints and prayed for mercy. Then, turning specifically to the Saint of God, he said:

“I have heard of you, holy Nicetius, that you are powerful in the work of mercy and compassionate in releasing weeping prisoners. I now beg you to deign to visit me with that surpassing mercy through which you have so often been glorified in releasing other prisoners.”

Afterward, as he fell asleep, the blessed man appeared to him and said:

“Who are you, who invoke the name of Nicetius? Or how do you know who he was, since you do not cease to beseech him?”

The prisoner explained the circumstances of his crime in order and added:

“Have mercy, I beg you, if you are the man of God whom I invoke.”

The Saint said to him:

“Rise in the name of Christ and walk free; no one will seize you.”

Awakening at these words, the man was astonished to find himself released, the chains shattered and the beam broken. Without delay, and with no one restraining him, he proceeded fearlessly to the Saint’s tomb. Then, when the judge had granted him remission of the penalty for his crime, he was released and went away to his own home.

### VIII.

It is worthwhile to add to the miracles what happened when a lamp was lit [Note: [Col. 1047D] So the manuscripts, and correctly: by the term *cicindilis* he means a lamp, mentioned below under the name *lychnus*, which lasted forty days without fuel. The editions have “when lamps were lit.”] beside his bed, for great are the things this Saint, dwelling in heaven, accomplishes on earth.

The little bed on which the Saint had been accustomed to rest is often adorned with remarkable miracles. It was constructed with great care by Aetherius [Note: [Col. 1047D] He succeeded Priscus. He subscribed to the bishops’ rescript on behalf of the monastery of Poitiers in Gregory, *History*, Book IX, chapter 41. See also Book X, chapter 28.]—now the bishop—and is rightly worshiped with the greatest devotion. Those suffering from chills are often placed beneath it and saved when their feverish heat and cold are compressed, while other sick people, laid there, are immediately relieved.

It is covered with a beautiful cloth, and lamps are continually lit upon it. One of these, as the sacristan himself asserted, continued to shine for forty days and as many nights without the aid of any fuel. No papyrus [Note: [Col. 1047D] Ancient authors frequently attest that papyrus was used in place of a wick. Hence in some glossaries *papyrus* is explained as though it meant “providing fire.” See Gregory the Great, *Dialogues*, Book I, chapter 5.] was added, nor a drop of dripping oil, but it remained in the light in the very arrangement in which it had first been set [Note: [Col. 1047D] Colb. and Laud. have: “in which it was first set.”].

Gallomagnus, Bishop of Troyes, devoutly requested relics of this Saint [Note: [Col. 1047D] Gallomagnus, Bishop of Troyes, subscribed to the Council of Paris IV in 573 and Mâcon I in 581. The relics of Saint Nicetius mentioned here are still preserved, as Camusatus observes in his *Catalogue of the Bishops of Troyes*, in a church dedicated to him, which is a parish church in the city of Troyes.]. When they were carried away with psalm-singing [Al., “while psalms were being sung”], the power of the relics illuminated the eyes of the blind, and people suffering from other kinds of disease were granted healing.

A *facitergium* (face-cloth), woven with hanging tufts [Note: [Col. 1048D] Apollinaris Sidonius mentions a linen cloth loaded with tufts in Letter 17 of Book V; Savaro has further material on tufted cloths in his commentary.], which the Saint had worn upon his head on the day of his death, was also brought to us [Col. 1047C]. We received it as a heavenly gift.

After many days had passed, we were invited to dedicate a church in the parish of Paternacum [Note: [Col. 1048D] It still exists today and is commonly called Perrenay or Pernay.] in the city of Tours. I went there, I confess; I consecrated the altar, tore threads from the linen, and placed them in the church. After the Masses had been celebrated and prayer had been offered, I departed.

A few days later, the man who had invited us came to us and said:

“Rejoice in the name of the Lord, priest of God, because of the power of blessed Nicetius the Bishop. Know that he has displayed a great miracle in the church you consecrated.

“There was a blind man in our village who had long been held in the night of blindness and the darkness of his eyes. A certain man appeared to him in a nocturnal vision and said: ‘If you wish to become well, prostrate yourself in prayer before the altar of the basilica of Saint Nicetius, and you will receive your sight.’ When he had done this, the darkness was broken apart and divine power opened the light to him.”

I confess that I placed some of these relics on the altars of other basilicas as well. There, too, energumens confess the Saint, and faithful prayer frequently obtains its effect.

A servant of Phrominius [Note: [Col. 1048D] So Boll., and correctly—not *Phronimius*, as the other editions and manuscripts have; below the bishop himself is called *Phronimius*. Gregory describes his varied fortunes in *History*, Book IX, chapter 24.], Bishop of Agde, was afflicted by attacks of epilepsy. He would often fall and foam at the mouth, tearing his tongue with his own teeth. Although the physicians did much for him, the disease would sometimes leave him untouched for several months; then, falling again into a renewed torment [Note: [Col. 1048D] Laud. and Colb. have “into a returning torment.”], he suffered worse than before.

When his master saw that such great miracles were being performed at the tomb of blessed Nicetius, he said to him:

“Go and prostrate yourself before the Saint’s tomb, praying that he may deign to help you.”

When the servant had carried out this command, he returned healthy, and the disease never again touched him. For it was the seventh year since the boy’s recovery when the bishop presented him to us.

1193 IX. A certain poor man, while the Saint was still alive, obtained from him a letter bearing his own signature, by which he might solicit alms from the houses of the devout. After the Saint’s death, he continued going about with that same letter and received no small amount from those who gave alms in memory of the Saint. Everyone wished that whoever saw the Saint’s signature would give something to the needy man.

Seeing this, a certain Burgundian, who neither honored nor venerated the Saint, began watching the poor man from a distance. When he saw him enter the woods, he rushed upon him, stole six gold pieces from him together with the letter, and left him beaten with kicks and apparently lifeless. But amid the kicks and other blows the poor man cried out:

“I adjure you by the living God and the power of Saint Nicetius to have his letter returned to me, for I shall have no life left if I lose it.”

The other threw it on the ground and went away. The poor man picked it up and came to the city, for at that time Bishop Phronimius, whom we mentioned above, was there. Approaching him, the poor man said:

“Here is the man who severely beat and robbed me; he took the six gold pieces which I had received out of regard for Saint Nicetius’s letter.”

The bishop reported this to the count. The judge summoned the Burgundian and began asking him what he had to say about the matter. But he denied everything before them all, saying:

“I have never seen this man, nor have I taken away his property.”

The bishop, however, looked at the letter, saw the Saint’s signature, and turned to the Burgundian:

“Here, in this letter, is the signature of Saint Nicetius. If you are innocent, come closer and, touching the writing which he himself wrote, swear to it with your hand. For we believe in the power of that man that either today it will prove you guilty of this crime, or certainly allow you to depart innocent.”

Without hesitation he approached the hands of the bishop, who was holding the letter extended. Raising his hands to take the oath, he fell backward on his back; with his eyes closed, he cast foam from his mouth and was thought to be dead. After the passage of about two hours, he opened his eyes and said:

“Woe is me, for I sinned by taking away this poor man’s property!”

Immediately he recounted in order how he had injured that man. Then the bishop, together with the judge [Note: That is, by the judge, or count.], having obtained his confession, returned to the poor man only what he had stolen, and added two solidi for the beating. Thus both men departed from the judge’s presence.

X. How many people bound in the prison-house have been released through this Saint, and how many prisoners’ chains or fetters have been broken, is testified today by that mass of iron, assembled from the punishments mentioned above, which is seen in his basilica.

Recently, in the presence of King Guntram, I heard Syagrius, bishop of Autun, reporting to the king that on a single night the blessed Man had appeared in seven prison-cities, released the prisoners from confinement, and allowed them to depart free; and afterward the judges did not dare to do anything against them.

If someone suffering from fever, chills, or various illnesses takes some dust from his tomb and drinks it dissolved in water, he immediately recovers his health. There is no doubt that this is accomplished by him who says to his saints: “Whatever you ask in my name, believe that you will receive it, and it will come to you” (Mark 11:24).

XI. At the village of Prisciniacus, in the territory of the city of Tours [Note: There are still two villages of this name in the Touraine district, close to one another, and both under the jurisdiction of Luçay. The first is called Greater Prisciniacus (Le Grand-Précigni), on the river Claise; the second, Lesser Prisciniacus (Le Petit-Précigni), on the small river Brenonne (Brignon).], a church had long stood without the relics of saints. Since the inhabitants of the place frequently asked that we consecrate it with the ashes of some saints, we placed some of the relics mentioned above upon the holy altar [Note: Colbert has “we consecrated it.”]. In that church the power of the Lord is frequently manifested through the blessed bishop.

Very recently, three women afflicted by a demon, coming from the territory of Bourges, were being led to the basilica of Saint Martin. They entered this church, and immediately, striking their palms together, they confessed that they were tormented by the powers of Saint Nicetius. Casting from their mouths something purulent mixed with blood, they were at once cleansed of the spirits possessing them [Another reading: “from unclean spirits.”].

A certain Dado, one of the country people, had gone out on that hostile expedition which took place near Comminges [Note: That is, on the expedition against Gundobald Ballomer, during which the city of Comminges was destroyed, as related in Book VII of the *History*, chapter 38.]. Since he repeatedly found himself in mortal danger, he vowed that, if he returned home unharmed, he would donate to adorn the church remembered above, in honor of blessed Nicetius, something from what he acquired. On his return he carried two silver chalices, and while still on the journey he again vowed that he would give them to the church if he reached his own home safely.

When he approached his house, he gave only one and contrived to defraud the other, offering a Sarmatian covering with which the Lord’s altar and the offerings were to be covered. But the blessed Man appeared to him in a dream and said:

“How long will you hesitate and delay fulfilling your vow? Go,” he said, “and return to the church the other chalice which you vowed to give, lest you and your household perish. But the covering, because it is thin [Note: That is, transparent because of its thinness.], must not be placed over the altar’s gifts, since the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood is not fully covered by it.”

Terrified, he delayed no longer and quickly fulfilled the vow he had made.

This man’s brother came for the vigils of the Lord’s Nativity and urged the priest, saying:

“Let us keep vigil together in the church of God and devoutly implore the power of blessed Nicetius, so that through his intercession we may pass the course of this year in peace.”

When the priest heard this, he rejoiced and ordered the signal for the vigil to be sounded. When it had sounded, and the priest arrived with the clergy and the rest of the people, this man, intent on his appetite, kept delaying his arrival. The priest repeatedly sent for him. He replied:

“Wait a little, and I am coming.”

What more need be said? When the vigils had ended and daylight had come, the man who had earlier issued the invitation did not attend the vigil. The priest, having completed the service, became angry with him and hurried to his lodging, as though he were going to suspend him from communion. But the man had been seized by a fever and was being consumed by a divine fire just as by wine. At once, when he saw the priest, he cried out with tears and begged that penance be given to him.

When the priest rebuked him, saying, “You are rightly consumed by the power of Saint Nicetius, to whose church you neglected to come for the vigil,” he breathed out his spirit in the midst of their conversation.

When the third hour had come and the people were gathering for the solemn celebration of Mass [Note: Here there is mention of only one Mass on the Nativity of the Lord, which was the custom of the Gallican Church. Three are assigned in the Gelasian and Gregorian Sacramentaries, because at Rome there were three stations on that same day, where Mass was celebrated by three different priests. From this, however, arose the custom of celebrating three Masses on that day. See Mabillon, Book II of *Gallican Liturgy*, no. 7.], the dead man was carried into the church.

No one can doubt that this happened through the power of the holy bishop. The priest himself explained these things to us. We have personally experienced many such events, or learned of them through reports of the faithful, but we have thought it too lengthy to recount them.

XII. Since it has pleased us to bring this little book to a close, I shall mention one further remarkable miracle from the book of his Life, which, as we stated above, was written by a certain man. The divine power proceeding from it did not leave the miracle without glory; rather, to confirm the power of what was written, it showed it to be glorious to many.

A deacon of Autun, afflicted with severe blindness of the eyes, heard of the things which God, the glorifier of his saints, performed at the Saint’s tomb. He said to his companions:

“If I were to visit his tomb, or take something from his holy relics, or at least deserve to touch the cloak with which the Saint’s limbs are covered, I would become well.”

While he was discussing these and similar matters with his companions, a certain cleric suddenly appeared and said:

“You believe rightly. But if you wish to strengthen your mind concerning these same miracles, here is a book written about them, so that you may more easily believe what has reached your ears.”

Before he attempted to read it, the deacon, moved by the inspiration of divine mercy, said:

“I believe that God is powerful enough to work extraordinary deeds through his servants.”

Immediately he placed the volume over his eyes. At once the pain fled and the cloudiness was dispersed; through the power of the book he was granted the recovery of sight. He obtained such clarity [Note: Colbert reads “with such clarity”; the other editions read “placed in such great clarity.”] that, reading with his own eyes, he learned the accounts of the miracles.

These things are performed by one and the same Lord, who glories in his saints and makes those whom he has exalted through illustrious miracles glorious [Note: The printed editions read: “who made them glorious.”]. To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

# CHAPTER IX. Saint Patroclus, Abbot

1197 When the outstandingly prudent prophet Moses was preparing to construct the tabernacle of the divine descent, according to the command of the Lord’s mouth, and, having been ordered to gather for this purpose a great quantity of materials [Note: Baudi and Surius read “and of the same,” while Baluzius and Laudunensis read “for this same purpose.” Below: “shown to him.”], he did not have readily at hand in the storehouse all the things which the Lord himself had shown him upon the summit of the lofty mountain, he ordered the people to be summoned so that each person might offer God some gift according to his means—and not under compulsion, but willingly (Exodus 25).

They therefore offered gifts of gold, silver, bronze, and iron; the beauties of gleaming gems; threads of doubled byssus and twice-twisted scarlet; and some offered dyed skins of rams and goats’ hair. But when the teachers of the churches had taught that all these things were allegorical and had shown in the remaining gifts the various kinds of graces [Baluzius: “had declared”], they compared words of praise with the goats’ hair.

So now, although we do not offer gold, silver, gems, or doubled and twisted threads, at least we present in the holy Church goats’ hair—that is, words which reveal the miracles of the saints and friends of God—so that those who read may be stirred to the zeal by which the saints deserved to ascend to heaven.

Therefore, because a certain report recently given to us has disclosed some things about the Life of blessed Patroclus, I have taken care not to omit them but to make them known. Though barren in understanding, unskilled in zeal, and shabby in action, and though my language is rustic, I did not think that what God accomplished through his servant should be concealed.

I. The most blessed Patroclus was an inhabitant of the territory of Bourges, born of a father named Aetherius. When he was ten years old (A.D. 376, 19 November), he was assigned to be a shepherd of sheep, while his brother Antonius was given over to the study of letters. They were not indeed exalted by nobility, but they were freeborn [Note: Freeborn people stood between nobles and slaves, being born free.].

One midday, the former returning from school and the latter from the flock entrusted to him, they met at their father’s lodging to eat. Antonius said to his brother:

“Go farther away, rustic. Your work is to tend sheep, mine to study letters. The care of my own occupation makes me nobler, while the servitude of guarding these animals makes you low.”

When he heard this and thought that the rebuke had been sent to him by God, Patroclus left the sheep on the plain of the field and hastened to the boys’ school with energetic determination and swift running. After learning his letters and then the things necessary to a boy’s studies, he was so quickly instructed, with memory assisting him, that he either surpassed his brother in knowledge or, with the help of divine power, outstripped him in liveliness of understanding.

After this he was entrusted for training to Nunnio [The edition reads “Mumioni”], who had once been held in high esteem as a great official of Childebert, king of the Parisians. Since Nunnio raised him with the greatest care and affection, Patroclus showed himself so humble and submissive toward everyone that all loved him as though he were their own parent, in the highest goodness.

Returning home after his father’s death, he found that his mother was still alive. She said to him:

“Behold, my sweetest son, your father has died, while I live without consolation. I shall seek a beautiful and freeborn girl, so that, joined to her, you may provide consolation for your widowed mother.”

But he replied:

“I shall not join myself to a worldly wife; rather, I shall accomplish what my mind has conceived with the Lord’s will.”

When his mother, not understanding, asked what this meant, he refused to disclose it. Instead, he went to Arcadius, bishop of the city of Bourges [Note: Arcadius signed the Third Council of Orléans in 538 and, through the priest Probianus, the Fourth Council of Orléans in 541.], and asked that the hair of his head be cut and that he be enrolled among the clergy. The bishop, by the Lord’s will, accomplished this without delay.

Not long afterward, having undertaken the office of deacon, Patroclus devoted himself to fasting, delighted in vigils, exercised himself in reading, and poured himself out eagerly in continual prayer, so that he did not even join the other clerics at the canonical meal.

When the archdeacon heard this [Note: Archdeacons were, as it were, superintendents of the other clerics. Thomassin discusses their offices and prerogatives in *Ecclesiastical Discipline*, Part I, Book II, chapter 12. Note that at that time clerics lived at a common table.], he growled against him:

“Either eat with the other brothers, or else leave us. It is not right that you should pretend to share a livelihood with those with whom you are thought to fulfill an ecclesiastical office.”

II. The servant of God was not inwardly shaken by these words, for he already thirsted to enter the solitude of the desert. Leaving the city mentioned above, he came to the village of Nereus [Note: Baluzius reads “Mereus,” and likewise below. At Bourges there is a Meriacum above the river Cher (Mery-sur-Cher). But our reading, found in the other editions and manuscripts, is preferable. Here the reference is evidently to a place once famous, called the Waters of Neri in the Peutinger Tables, which still retains its ancient name in the Bourbonnais, commonly called Neris—a pleasant town where a priory can be seen, although not even ruins of a monastery of virgins remain.].

There he built an oratory consecrated with relics of Saint Martin and began to instruct boys in the study of letters. The sick came to him and were healed; those possessed by demons were cleansed when they confessed his name. His solitude was not therefore as he had wished, for the power revealed through him made it public everywhere.

Then, as an indication of what he should do, he wrote something on small slips [Note: The edition reads: “Then, as a lodging, he placed something.” Hence Surius reads: “Then, having written brief notes for choosing a lodging,” and so forth.] and placed it upon the altar. He kept vigil and prayed for three nights, asking that the Lord graciously and clearly reveal what he should do.

But the renowned mercy of divine compassion, which had foreknown and determined that he should become a hermit, commanded him to take that brief note and hasten to the desert. In the little cell where he lived, he gathered virgins and established a monastery for girls. When he departed, he took nothing of all his labor that he had accumulated there except one rake and one double-headed axe. Entering the deep solitudes of the forests, he came to a place called Mediocantus.

There he built a cell and devoted himself to God in the work mentioned above. After restoring many possessed persons to soundness of mind by laying on his hand and driving out the demons through the sign of the cross, a madman was brought to him. With gaping jaws and bloody teeth, the man tore with his own teeth whatever he could reach.

For him Patroclus lay prostrate in prayer for three days. He obtained such power from the mercy of God that, when the man’s fury had been calmed, the man was cleansed though threatened by death. Patroclus placed his fingers in the man’s mouth, drove out the spirit of savage violence, and restored him to health.

Before Patroclus, the illusion of wicked persuasion could have no power. Just as he cleansed those who were afflicted, so through the most sacred power of the cross he repelled the atrocious things which the author of evil secretly inflicted.

When a certain woman named Leubella was afflicted with that groin disease, the devil, disguising himself as Martin, wickedly offered oblations through which, as though by them, the people might be saved. When these offerings were brought to the Saint, they vanished—not only because the Holy Spirit revealed their nature, but also because the very instigator of evil, appearing in a most dreadful form to the Saint, confessed what he had wickedly done.

For the devil often transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14), so that by this deception he may mislead the innocent.

When he laid many snares for Patroclus, lest he should ascend to the place from which the devil had fallen, he injected into him the thought that he should abandon the desert and return to the world. But when the Saint perceived the poison at work in the sinner, he prostrated himself in prayer and asked that he might do nothing except what was pleasing to God.

Then an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a vision and said:

“If you wish to see the world, behold this column. Climb it and contemplate all that takes place in the world.”

A column of astonishing height had been placed before him in the vision. When he climbed it, he saw murders, thefts, slaughters, adulteries, fornications, and all the wicked things committed in the world.

When he descended, he said:

“No, I beg you, Lord; let me not return to these wickednesses, which, after confessing you, I had earlier forgotten.”

Then the angel who was speaking with him said:

“Cease, therefore, seeking the world, lest you perish with it. Instead, go to the oratory, where you may pray to the Lord; and whatever you find there will be your consolation during your pilgrimage.”

Entering the cell of the oratory, he found a baked tile on which the sign of the Lord’s cross had been impressed. Recognizing the divine gift, he understood that this was an impregnable defense against every incitement of worldly persuasion.

III. After this, Saint Patroclus built the monastery of Columbaris [Note: Commonly Columbiers, in the archpriesthood of Montluçon, in the territory of Bourges, where there was a Cluniac priory subject to the monastery of Silviniacum. This is distinct from the monastery of Columbaris mentioned in Book I, *On the Churches of Clermont*, chapter 30.] five miles from the desert cell in which he lived. He gathered monks there and, so that he might exercise his authority more freely in solitude, appointed an abbot to preside over the monastic flock.

He had completed his eighteenth year in that desert place. Then, having gathered the brothers and announced his departure, he died in a good old age [Note: He died at the age of eighty, as stated in Book V of the *History*, chapter 10.], distinguished by exceptional holiness.

After his body had been washed and placed upon a bier, it was carried to his monastery, where while still alive he had ordered himself to be buried. Then the archpriest of the village of Nereus, gathering a company of clerics, wished to seize the holy body by force, intending to bury it in his own village, from which Patroclus had originally departed.

But when he came in fury and saw from a distance the pall covering the holy limbs shining with extraordinary brightness, he was so terrified by fear at God’s command that he quickly recalled from his mind the rash plan he had wickedly conceived. Joining the singing at the Saint’s funeral, he proceeded with the others and buried him, together with the brothers who were present, in the monastery of Columbaris.

At his holy tomb, a blind woman named Prudentia and another girl from Limoges, likewise deprived of sight, kissed the holy tomb in prayer and deserved to receive their sight. Maxonidius, after the fifth year of his blindness, visited this holy burial place and received his sight.

Those possessed by demons—Lupus, Theodulfus, Rucco, Scopilia, Nectariola, and Tacihildis—were cleansed at the Saint’s tomb. Two girls from the territory of Limoges also came and, after being anointed with oil blessed by the Saint himself, were cleansed of the wickedness by which they were possessed.

Every day the Lord works there to strengthen the faith of the nations—he who continually glorifies his saints.

# CHAPTER X. Saint Friardus, Recluse

There are many and various steps by which one ascends to the kingdom of heaven. Of these, I think, David also says that he has arranged ascents in his heart (Psalm 83:6). These steps are understood as the progress of various works toward divine worship, and no one can set foot upon them unless, as we have often testified, he is moved by God’s help.

Thus the Psalmist speaks on that middle step of progress:

“Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Psalm 126:1).

The martyrs continually sought this help, as did also those whom the authority of holy life strengthened [The edition reads “honored”]. Through it they eagerly attained that to which the thirst of spiritual desire urged them.

If the mind was inflamed for martyrdom, the martyr sought the assistance of this help so that he might conquer. If someone wished to practice fasting, he afflicted himself so that he might be strengthened by it. If he wished to preserve his limbs undefiled in chastity, he prayed to be guarded by it. If, after ignorance, he desired to turn back through repentance, he begged for it with tears so that he might likewise be lifted up by it. And if anyone meditated on performing some good work, he sought this help so that it might assist him.

Through these ascents of the ladder—so difficult, lofty, and arduous, though varied—one ascends to the one Lord through the aid of this help. Therefore he must always be asked, sought, and invoked, so that he himself may perfect by his help what the mind conceives as good. Of him we must say without end:

“Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Psalm 123:8).

So too did that most blessed man of whom we are now to speak. Amid the various temptations and crosses of the world, he always sought the protection of this help.

I. On the island of Vindunitta, in the territory of the city of Nantes [Note: Most editions read “Vindimitta.” Colbert and Bellovacensis read “of Vindonitus” below.], there lived a man of outstanding holiness named Friardus, a recluse. He died in 576 or 577, on August 1. It pleases me to say a little about his life for the edification of the Church, since I do not know whether it has been written down by anyone else.

From infancy he was always devoted to God and chaste. Once he became a man, he spent all his time in the praises of God, in prayer, and in vigils. He obtained the necessities of life from the earth by his own hands, and even when he hurried to work with the others, he never ceased praying.

To neighbors and strangers this seemed ridiculous, as is the custom among country people. One day, while he was gathering sheaves with the others in a field of cut grain, they came upon a swarm of wretched and savage flies, commonly called wasps. When the insects tore the reapers most fiercely with their stings, the men went around the field, leaping over the place where the swarm had gathered. Mocking blessed Friardus, they addressed him deceitfully:

“Let the blessed man come; let the religious man come, who never ceases praying, who always places the cross before his ears and eyes, who sends salutary standards ahead along the roads he travels. Let him reap over the swarm; let him calm it by his prayer.”

Receiving these words as though they were intended to shame the power of the Lord, Friardus fell prostrate on the ground and poured out a prayer to the Lord. Then he approached, made the sign of the cross over them, and said:

“Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

At his prayer all the wasps immediately hid themselves inside the hollow from which they had emerged. Then, in full view of everyone, he went over the swarm unharmed.

For those who had mocked him this was unmistakably a miracle, since the Lord had deigned to strengthen the man who trusted in him, to their shame.

Afterward, when Friardus had climbed a tree for some necessity, a branch suddenly broke beneath his feet and he began to fall. As he fell downward, invoking the most blessed name of Christ at each branch that struck him, he said:

“Christ almighty, save me.”

When he reached the ground, he was not harmed at all. He continued to say:

“Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

II. Strengthened by these and other miracles, he began silently to consider in his heart:

“If the cross of Christ, the invocation of his name, and the help sought from him have such power that they overcome every harsh thing in the world, crush dangers, drive away the darkness of temptations, and make all the delights of this age seem worthless and contemptible, what have I to do with the world, except that, abandoning everything belonging to it, I should devote myself solely to the service of him whose name has saved me from wicked dangers?”

He left his little lodging and, forgetting his parents and homeland, sought the desert, lest, while living in the world, worldly concern should bring him some impediment to prayer.

He and the abbot Sabaudus [Colbert: “Baudus”], who had once been a minister of King Chlothar, accepted a life of penance and entered the island of Vindunitta in the territory of Nantes. They had with them also the deacon Secundellus.

But the abbot, removing his hand from the Lord’s plow, left the island and returned to the monastery [Note: Baluzius reads “left the monastery.”]. Not long afterward, for reasons kept hidden, he was killed by the sword.

Saint Friardus, however, remained steadfast on the island with the deacon Secundellus. Each of them had his own cell, although they were located far apart. While they were persevering earnestly in prayer, the tempter appeared by night to the deacon Secundellus in the form of the Lord and said:

“I am Christ, whom you pray to every day. You have already become holy, and I have entered your name in the book of life with my other saints. Now leave this island and go, performing healings among the people.”

Deceived by these enticements, Secundellus left the island without informing his companion. Yet when he laid hands on the sick in the name of Christ, they were healed.

After a long time he returned to the island and came to his companion with empty glory, saying:

“I went outside the island and performed many miracles among the people.”

The elder, terrified, asked what this meant. Secundellus simply disclosed everything he had done. The elder was stunned, sighed, and wept:

“Woe to us! From what I hear, you have been deceived by the tempter. Go and do penance, lest his deceits prevail over you again.”

When Secundellus understood this and feared that he was lost, he fell weeping at his feet and begged him to pray to the Lord for him.

“Go,” Friardus said, “and together let us ask his almighty power for the salvation of your soul. The Lord is not slow to show mercy to those who confess their sins, since he himself says through the prophet: ‘I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live’” (Ezekiel 33:11).

While they were praying, the tempter again came to the deacon Secundellus in a similar form and said:

“Did I not command you, because my sheep were sick and needed a shepherd, to go out, visit them, and provide them with the help of healing?”

But Secundellus replied:

“I have truly discovered that you are a deceiver, and I do not believe you are God, though you pretend to have his appearance. Nevertheless, if you are Christ, show me the cross you left behind, and I will believe you.”

When the tempter did not show it, the deacon made the sign of the Lord’s cross over his mouth. The tempter was confounded and vanished.

Again he came against him with a multitude of demons and beat him so severely that he was scarcely thought capable of escaping. Then he departed and never appeared again.

The same deacon afterward persevered in the highest holiness and died on the appointed day [Note: He is venerated together with Saint Friardus at Nantes on August 2, since August 1, Saint Friardus’s feast day, is occupied by the feast of Saint Peter in Chains. Albert of Montmorillon says that Saint Secundellus died on April 29.].

III. Blessed Friardus, shining with great virtues, once found a branch broken from a tree by the wind—one which, as they say, he himself had grafted. He collected it and made from it a staff which he carried in his hand.

After a long time, he planted the now-dried stick in the ground. By repeatedly pouring water upon it, he caused the staff to put forth leaves and fruit; within two or three years it grew and spread to the great height of a tree.

When the people considered this a great miracle and a huge crowd gathered daily to see it—so that the power revealed by the event even made the remoteness of the island publicly known—the Saint of God, lest he be overthrown by the stain of empty glory, cut down the tree with an axe.

Again, when the Saint saw another tree toppled by the violence of the wind and lying full of flowers, he was moved by compassion and prayed:

“Do not let the fruit of this little tree perish, I beg you, Lord, since at your command it produced the adornment of flowers. Rather, may it deserve from you the effect of restoration, granted through renewed growth” [Note: That is, “through growth granted anew.”].

With these words he took an axe, cut off the trunk of the tree, sharpened it like a stake above the roots that still clung to the ground, and fixed the trunk into the earth. Then, binding the branches to it without roots, he restored it to its former condition. The flowers that had withered became green again, and in that same year the tree returned fruit to its cultivator.

I believe that the present miracle compelled us to speak of God’s mercy, for through his prayer Friardus was able to obtain from the Lord life for the dead, since he obtained that dry trees should put forth leaves again in renewed greenness.

IV. Since Friardus often announced his departure to the brothers, one day, when he had been struck by a fever, he said to his companions:

“Go to Bishop Felix and announce my departure to him, saying: ‘Your brother Friardus has said: Behold, when the course of this life has been completed, I am being released from this world. And so that you may be more certain of this word, I shall depart on Sunday and go to the rest which God, the eternal King, has promised me. Come, I beg you, so that I may see you before I die.’”

When Felix was detained by some circumstance unknown to us, he sent a message:

“I ask you, if it can be done, to wait for me a little, until, after the business of public proceedings has been concluded [Note: That is, legal hearings (*les plaids*). Baluzius reads “the members of official business.”], I can reach you.”

When the messengers returned and reported this, Friardus was already lying on his little bed. He said:

“Let us rise, then, and wait for our brother” [Note: Baronius rejects the letter of Saint Benedict to Saint Remigius because in it the holy Father calls the blessed bishop “brother.”].

O man beyond expression in holiness! Although he hastened to be released and to be with Christ, he did not forget charity. He obtained from the Lord that, while he was still in this world, he should behold his brother with spiritual sight.

Nor do I think that Felix was of lesser merit, since by his coming the Lord deigned to prolong the days of this holy man. When news arrived of the delay, the fever immediately subsided, and Friardus rose healthy from his bed.

After a long time, when the bishop arrived, Friardus was seized by fever. He welcomed him as he entered and kissed him, saying:

“You cause me great delays in the journey that is owed me, holy priest!”

While they remained awake, dawn came upon the night that was Sunday, and Friardus surrendered his spirit. When it departed, the whole cell immediately trembled, completely filled with a sweet fragrance. It was therefore certain that an angelic power had been present there, marking the Saint’s merit and making the cell fragrant with divine aromas.

The priest washed his glorious body and placed it in a tomb [Note: A parish church now stands there under the title of Saints Friardus and Secundellus, as Cointius observes from the Breviary of Nantes. Gregory frequently mentions Bishop Felix; we have noted several things about him in their proper places. The same Gregory praised Friardus in Book IV of the *History*, chapter 37. For the year of his death, see Cointius under the year 577, no. 49, and compare it with the passage of Gregory cited immediately above.]. Christ received his soul into heaven, leaving examples of virtue for those born on earth.

# CHAPTER XI. Saint Caluppas, Recluse

Worldly poverty always opens the royal [Note: That is, the door. The editions read “kingdom”; below Baluzius reads “and, while they live, not only…”] door of heaven. It prepares those who practice it not only for heaven but also declares them, glorified by miracles, to be distinguished in the world. Thus, while that prison-like bond of affliction [Note: Several editions read “bond of confinement.”] opens the door of paradise, the soul, joined to the angelic choirs, rejoices in everlasting rest.

So it is with blessed Caluppas the recluse. We cannot remain entirely silent about what we have learned to be true.

### I

From early youth (3 March 578) he always sought and found the good of ecclesiastical religion. Having converted at the monastery of Meletum, in the territory of Auvergne, he presented himself to the brothers in great humility. He was exceedingly abstemious, so much so that, excessively weakened by hunger, he could not complete the daily work with the other brothers. Therefore, as is the custom of monks, they brought him great reproach, especially the provost saying to him: “He who is unwilling to work undeservedly asks to eat.”

While he was continually tormented by these words of reproach, he saw not far from the monastery a valley, [Col. 1059B] from whose middle a stone, rising by nature’s provision, climbed to a height of about five hundred feet or more. It had absolutely no connection with the other mountains surrounding it. A river washed through the middle of the valley; touching this mountain gently, it flowed away.

Into a fissure in this stone—which in ancient times had once served as a refuge during the passage of enemies—the holy hermit entered. Having hewn out the stone, he established dwellings there, which are now reached by a very difficult ladder. For that place is so difficult to traverse that even wild beasts find it laborious to approach.

In this place he made, in a manner of speaking, a little oratory. While he was praying there, as he himself was accustomed to tell us with tears, serpents often fell upon his head; [Col. 1059C] wrapping themselves around his neck, they caused him no small horror. But since the devil is regarded as appearing in the form of a crafty serpent, there is no doubt that this was his snare and assault.

When the saint remained unmoved by these things and was not disturbed by the bites of the lesser snakes, one day two dragons of immense size entered and stood at a distance. One of them, as I suppose, the stronger and leader of the temptation, raised his breast and lifted his mouth toward the mouth of the blessed man, as though about to mutter something. But the saint, terrified with fear, became utterly rigid like bronze, unable to move any limb at all or even raise his hand to oppose the sign of the blessed cross.

After both had stood for a very long time in silence, it came to the saint’s mind through the Spirit that he should cry out the Lord’s Prayer, even if he could not move his lips, at least in his heart. While he silently recited it, his limbs, which had been bound by the enemy’s art, gradually began to loosen. Sensing that his right hand was now free, he placed the sign of the blessed cross upon his mouth. Then, turning again toward the serpent, he once more traced Christ’s cross against it, saying:

“Are you that one who cast the first-formed man from the dwelling of paradise, who stained a brother’s right hand with murder, who armed Pharaoh to persecute the people of God, who finally stirred up the Hebrew people to persecute the Lord when envy was inflamed? Depart from the servants of God, from whom you have so often departed in confusion after being defeated. You were cast out in Cain, supplanted in Esau, struck down in Goliath, and hanged in Judas the betrayer; and on that very cross of the Lord’s power you were triumphed over and crushed, together with your powers and dominions. Now hide your head, enemy of God, and humble yourself beneath the sign of the divine cross, for you have no share with the servants of God, whose inheritance is the kingdom of Christ.”

As the saint spoke these and similar words, making the sign of the cross at each point, the dragon, confounded by the power of this standard, humbled himself in turn and sank down upon the earth. While this was happening, the other dragon coiled in ambush around the saint’s feet and shins. When the holy hermit saw it lying confused at his feet, he prayed and ordered it to depart, saying: “Go behind me, Satan; in the name of my Christ you can no longer harm me.”

It went out as far as the threshold of the cell and emitted a powerful sound from its lower part, filling the cell with such a stench that it could be believed to be nothing other than the devil. After that, neither serpent nor dragon appeared again before the saint.

### Note

[Col. 1059D] Others read *conversatus* (“having lived” or “having dwelt”) instead of *conversus* (“having converted”). Bal. reads *territorii* (“of the territory”) rather than *termini* (“of the boundary”). The monastery of Meletum is otherwise unknown. In the present-day diocese of Saint-Flour there is a village called Melet, and another in the Clermont region named Mialet, but no memory of Saint Caluppas or of his monastery survives there. [Col. 1060D]

### Note

[Col. 1059B] Others read *uteretur* (“was occupied”) for *ureretur* (“was tormented”).

### Note

[Col. 1060D] A few editions read *aheneus* (“bronze”) instead of *aeneus*; below, they also read “could move.”

### Note

[Col. 1060D] Colbertinus and Bellovacensis read: “Are you that one … you are crushed. Hide [yourself].”

### II

He was assiduous in the work of God and had no leisure for anything else unless he was reading or praying. Even when he took a little food, he prayed continually. Sometimes he took a fish from the river—rarely, indeed, but whenever he wished, one immediately appeared with the Lord’s assistance. He received no bread for food from elsewhere except what was sent from the monastery.

If any devout person brought bread or wine, it was assigned as food for the needy—specifically for those who sought from him either the saving sign or remedies for their illnesses—so that those whom he restored to health through prayer might also be strengthened by nourishment. He remembered what the Lord said in the Gospel concerning the crowds whom he had healed from the contagion of various diseases: “I do not want to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way” (Matthew 15:32).

Nor do I think that the benefit which divine mercy bestowed upon him in that place should be concealed. Since water had to be carried from the depths of that valley for about ten stadia, he prayed to the Lord to show him a spring within the dwelling of his cell. The heavenly power was not lacking which once brought forth water from the rock for thirsty peoples. Immediately, in response to his prayer, a drop of liquid burst from the rock and began to wet the ground with frequent trickles.

Rejoicing in the heavenly gift, he hollowed out a small cavity in the stone in the form of a cistern, holding nearly two *congia* [a liquid measure; Ed. reads *condia*]. He received the waters divinely granted to him, from which each day only as much was supplied as sufficed for him and for the boy who had been assigned to serve him.

### III

We too came to the place with the blessed bishop Avitus, [Col. 1061A] and learned that some of the things we have narrated were reported by him and that we ourselves observed others with our own eyes. From the aforementioned pontiff he received the rank of deacon and priest, and he brought many remedies to people afflicted by various illnesses.

Yet he never allowed anyone to see him outside his cell. He merely extended his hand through a little window to impose the saving sign. If anyone came to visit him, he approached this opening and offered prayer and conversation. Finally, completing the course of his life in this religious manner, he departed to the Lord at the age of fifty, as I suppose. [Col. 1061D]

### Note

Gregory narrates Avitus’s election in Book IV, chapter 35 of our edition; an anonymous author copied the whole account six hundred years ago into the Life of the same Avitus, which Savaro frequently cites. On this matter, see the notes to the aforementioned chapter 35 of Book IV.

### Note

He is commemorated in various Martyrologies on 3 March. We learn the year of his death from Book V of the *Histories*, chapter 9.

## CHAPTER XII  
### On Saint Aemilianus the Hermit and Brachio the Abbot

[Col. 1061B] How much heavenly discipline offers to those who guard it, and how much it must impose upon those who negligently fail to guard it, the Holy Spirit reveals through the mouth of the Psalmist: “Take hold of discipline,” he says, “lest the Lord become angry and you perish from the righteous way” (Psalm 2:12). Concerning good things Solomon says: “The discipline of peace” [Col. 1061D]—so Colbertinus reads; others have “the discipline of the Father”—“shall be upon him” (Isaiah 53:5).

This discipline therefore produces fear of the Lord, and fear of the Lord provides the beginning of wisdom. Wisdom teaches one to love God; the love of God lifts a person above earthly things, summons him to heaven, and places him in paradise, where the souls of the blessed feast in the kingdom of God on the new wine drawn from that life-giving vine.

People ought therefore to desire to drink in the mystery of this vine, so that they may be able to approach that most beautiful place of such delightful habitation. If the vines that we now see, stretched along trellises and interwoven with leaves through their spreading branches, delight us with their pleasing appearance while producing an abundance of fruit and protecting us with a timely shade from the heat of the burning sun—vines that, once their appointed fruit has been gathered, we know become like dry things when their leaves fall—how much more ought we to desire that vine which never fails, which withers under no heat of temptation, where, once hope has passed, the thing hoped for is both possessed and enjoyed.

Many who desired this not only abandoned their own possessions but also undertook deserted and uncultivated places, so that, through the support [or comfort] of solitary and more remote prayer and through a stream of tears, they might quench the thirst of this desire. Thus, as is now shown, the blessed Aemilianus, a hermit new to our times, acted.

### I

He therefore abandoned his parents and personal property and sought the deserts of the wilderness. He hid himself within the secluded forests of Ponticiacum in the territory of Auvergne, [Col. 1061D] clearing a small plot in the felled woodland, digging the soil with a mattock, and drawing from it the nourishment of life.

He also had a small garden, which he watered when water came to it, and from which he took vegetables for refreshment, without adding any fat. He had no comfort apart from God’s help. For his companions were the beasts and birds, which came to him every day as to a servant of God. He devoted himself to fasting and prayer, and no occasion of worldly concern could obstruct him in this purpose, because he possessed nothing besides God.

### Note

[Col. 1061D] Bal. reads *Pontivacensium*. Branchus translates it in the *Lives of the Saints of Auvergne* as “the forest of Pont-Gibaud.” Pont-Gibaud is a town in lower Auvergne on the Cicaula River (the Sioule). Ruins of an old church are visible there, and the populace thinks that a Benedictine monastery was once attached to it. But there is no memory there of Saint Brachio or Aemilianus. One of our scholars’ conjecture is not implausible: he interprets Ponticiacum as the village of Punsat in Combraille, whose patron is Saint Bravy, abbot of Menat, whom he considers identical with Saint Brachio. The former, however, is commemorated on a day in February, the latter on 15 September; perhaps one of these is the feast of a translation. Not far away stands the priory of Saint Saturninus of Vensat, which he likewise considers to be the place later called the house of Vindiciacum.

### II

At that time Sigivaldus, [Col. 1062B] a man of great power, was residing in the city of Auvergne. [Col. 1062D]

### Note

Colbertinus and Laudunensis read *Sigiuvaldus*. On him see Gregory, *Histories*, Book III, chapter 13, and elsewhere.

A certain young man named Bracchio was in his service; in their language the name means “bear cub.”

### Note

The same manuscripts that here and elsewhere have *Bracchio* sometimes give *Brachio*. He was a Thuringian by origin, as is stated in Book V of the *Histories*, chapter 12. [Col. 1062D] This man had chosen him to undertake the hunting of wild boars. Bracchio went about the forests with a great troop of Molossian hounds, and whatever he captured he brought to his master.

One day, while he was pursuing a boar of immense size with this barking pack, the boar entered the enclosure surrounding the saint’s cell.

### Note

Bal. reads *canum allatrantium* (“of barking dogs”); others read *cum allatrantium*. The pack of dogs followed with barking as far as the entrance of the vestibule, but immediately stopped in its tracks and was not permitted to enter after the boar.

When Bracchio saw this and marveled that it had happened by heavenly agency, he went to the saint’s cell. He saw the boar standing before the door, utterly unafraid. The old man greeted and kissed him and invited him to sit down.

When they had sat together, the old man said:

“I see you, dearest son, adorned with great elegance, yet following pursuits that prepare greater ruin for the soul than salvation. Leave your earthly lord, I beg you, and follow the true God, maker of heaven and earth, by whose will all things are governed, at whose command everything is subjected, and by whose majesty the very beast that you see stands here fearless.

“Let not the power of your master make you proud or lift you up; it is nothing. For the apostle Paul says: ‘Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord’ (1 Corinthians 1:31). And elsewhere: ‘If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ’ (Galatians 1:10).

“Submit yourself to the service of him who says: ‘Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you’ (Matthew 11:28). He is the Lord whose burden is light and whose yoke is easy (ibid., 30), whose worship both grants present blessings and bestows eternal life.
