“For he says: ‘If anyone renounces all that he possesses, he will receive a hundredfold and, in addition, will possess eternal life’ (Matthew 19:29).”

While the old man vigorously discoursed on these and similar matters, the boar unharmed returned to the forest, and the young man departed in profound amazement because he had seen the wild boar which he had begun to pursue stand meekly before the old man like a lamb.

Bracchio therefore pondered many things in his mind and turned over much within himself: what he should do, whether he should abandon the world or serve the world. At last, pierced by divine mercy—and, I believe, by the prayer of Saint Aemilianus—he began secretly to seek a way by which he might become a cleric, since publicly he did not dare to do so because of his earthly master.

While he was still a layman, he would rise from his bed two or three times during the night, throw himself upon the ground, and pour out prayer to the Lord. He did not know what he was singing, because he was ignorant of letters. But when he repeatedly saw letters written above the icons [Col. 1063D] of the apostles and the other saints in the oratory, he copied them into a book.

Whenever clerics or abbots regularly came to visit his master, Bracchio would secretly question whichever of the younger men he could first summon about the names of the letters, and thus he began to understand them. Through the Lord’s inspiration, he had learned to read and write before he had come to know the sequence of letters.

After Sigivaldus died, he hastened to the aforementioned old man and, living with him for two or three years, committed the Psalter to memory. His own brother often wanted to kill him because he refused to marry. Subsequently monks were added to them.

### Note

[Col. 1063D] This is what they called images that represented their subjects vividly. Hence a true image of the Savior was called an *iconic* image, as we explained in the notes to Book I, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 22.

### III

When the blessed Aemilianus had completed the days of his life and departed from the body at approximately ninety years of age, he left Brachio as his heir (538). After establishing a monastery, Brachio obtained from Ranichilde, the daughter of the aforementioned Sigivaldus, a considerable extent of land, which she left to this monastery. It was a woodland belonging to the house of Vindiacum. [Col. 1063D]

### Note

Colbertinus reads *Ranihilde*; Badensis, Gontranus, and the other manuscripts have *Ranichilde*; Bellovacensis likewise has *Ranihilde*; Bal. has *Rachinilde*; Laudunensis, *Rahinilde*. Sidonius, Book IV, letter 8, mentions Queen Ragnahild, whom Sirmondus considers to have been the wife of King Euric. Savaro writes, however, that she married Theodoric, Euric’s brother and predecessor; but Sigivaldus’s daughter was much younger than that queen.

Colbertinus reads *Vindiciacense*.

He then left this monastery and came to Tours. There, after building oratories, he gathered together two monasteries. At one time some travelers arrived bringing relics of saints with them. They placed them upon the altar of the basilica of Saint Martin at Tours, intending, as it seemed, to depart the next day.

Abbot Bracchio was present. While keeping vigil in the basilica, around the middle of the night he saw what appeared to be an immense globe of fire flash from the holy relics and rise with a great light as far as the roof of the church. There is no doubt that this was something divine, yet it was shown to none of the others who were present, but only to him.

### Note

Compare chapter 20 of *On the Glory of the Confessors*.

Afterward he returned to Auvergne, to his former monastery. Having lived there for five years, he came to Tours, established abbots in the monasteries mentioned above, and returned to Auvergne. While he was staying at his former cell, he was appointed to the monastery of Menat, [Col. 1063D] which had grown lukewarm through the negligence of its abbot, so that under his leadership the community itself might be governed according to rule.

### Note

The monastery of Menat, commonly Menat, still exists among the Arvernians and belongs to the Benedictine Order. Saints Carilefus, Avitus, and others who later became renowned, and fathers of other monasteries, lived there.

He lived with the greatest chastity and vigorously compelled others also to lead chaste lives. He was pleasant in conversation and gentle in affection [Bell. reads “in conduct”; Ed. “in speech”]. Toward transgressors of the rule [that is, toward transgressors; others read “toward transgressions”], however, he was considered so severe that he was sometimes thought cruel. Through fasts, vigils, and charity he had rendered the man perfect.

When the time of his departure drew near, he saw in a vision—as he himself related to the blessed bishop Avitus—that he was led into the heavens into the presence of the Lord.

### Note

Bellovacensis reads simply “as he related to the blessed bishop.” What follows appears corrupt in the editions and manuscripts. Colbertinus reads: *Domini et cherubin ac serafin obumbrare majestatem. Isayam prophetam extenso volumine verba quae vaticinaturus erat clamare. Et dum attonitus* (“the Lord’s majesty, and cherubim and seraphim overshadowing [it]; the prophet Isaiah, with an unrolled scroll, crying out the words he was about to prophesy; and while astonished”). Bellovacensis: *Domini aethereos et in hac serafin obumbraret . . . clamare turba, dum attonitus* (“of the Lord, heavenly [beings], and here seraphim overshadowing . . . a crowd crying out, while astonished”). The printed editions read: *Ibique serafin obumbrare majestatem Domini et Isayae prophetae verba, quae vaticinaturus erat, intimare, turba circumstante angelorum, in laudem Dei voce sedentes aetheras et in hac seraphim obumbrare majestatem. Esayam prophetam extenso volumine verba quae vaticinaturus erat clamare dum*, etc. Bal. has: *Dei sedentis super aethera et ibi seraphim obumbrare majestatem* (“of God seated above heaven, and there seraphim overshadowing [his] majesty”). There the cherubim and seraphim overshadowed the majesty of the Lord, and the prophet Isaiah, with an extended scroll, proclaimed the words he was about to prophesy, while a surrounding host of angels cried out in praise of God seated above the heavens.

As he gazed at this in astonishment, he awoke. Carefully considering his dream so that he might recognize, through the Lord’s revelation, the end of his life, he said to the abbot whom he had appointed over the monastery:

“That place beside the river, where I had planned to build an oratory, is very pleasant. Therefore I ask you to complete what I intended and not to refuse to transfer my bones there.”

After he had departed (9 February 576) and had been buried in the oratory of his former cell, the abbot, wishing to carry out the assigned work, found by God’s will both anciently baked bricks and a foundation of the dimensions he himself had planned to establish. When the building was completed, he uncovered the abbot’s grave. Once it had been opened, he found the little body intact, so that it seemed he had died only the day before. Thus, amid rejoicing and accompanied by the crowd of monks whom he himself had instructed, he was transferred to that place after two years.

## CHAPTER XIII  
### On Saint Lupicinus

[Col. 1064D] The athletes of Christ and triumphers over the world, desiring to treat the loss of this fleeting life as nothing, wished to press onward to that life which remains in everlasting rejoicing, which no groaning disturbs and no boundary encloses; whose light will never be extinguished and whose serenity no darkness of cloud will cover.

Therefore they always regarded the insults of present sufferings as nothing, knowing that they were afflicted in a few things but would be well ordered in many. For this reason, whoever contends in this contest is not terrified by fear, unstrung by punishment, or broken by pain, provided that he may deserve to enjoy with God’s elect the beauty of that eternal delight. We know that many holy men have done this, whose lives are now recounted or read.

### I

A certain Lupicinus, of great holiness and exceedingly strong in the works of God (500, … 24 June), first went from house to house among the devout asking for alms, and whatever he was able to acquire he distributed to people like himself.

Finally, when he had reached middle age, he came to the village of Berber, now called Lipidiacum [Col. 1065D]—we do not know this place under either name. There he found ancient walls and shut himself in, preventing himself from being seen by anyone. Receiving a little bread or water through a small window, he sometimes made even that very small provision last until the third day.

Water was brought in through a little channel, while the window was covered with a veil. The access to both things was so concealed that no one could see the blessed man’s face.

As he delighted day and night in the praise of God through the melodies of the Psalms, he imposed upon himself a torment that weighed more heavily upon his little body, remembering the apostle’s saying: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18).

He placed upon his neck a large stone which two men could scarcely lift and carried it around the cell all day while singing to God. At night, to add to his affliction, he fixed two stakes into the staff he carried in his hand, preparing points above him, which he placed beneath his chin so that he would not fall asleep.

At last, near the end of his life, his chest corrupted by the weight of the stone, he began to expel blood through his mouth, spitting it onto the nearby walls. Often, when faithful men secretly approached the cell at night, a sound like the voice of a great choir resounded.

He also restored many sick people to health, especially those oppressed by attacks of chills or by malignant pustules, merely by touching them or imposing the saving sign.

### Note

[Col. 1065D] The edition reads *multorum psallentium* (“of many singers”) rather than *multi psallentii* (“of much singing”).

### II

When he had already grown old, he summoned his attendant and said:

“The time for concealment has passed; the time for revelation has come. Know, therefore, that after three days I shall be released from this world. Now call the faithful brothers and sons to whom I am to say farewell, so that they may come to visit us.”

When the third day dawned and the brothers had gathered, he opened the door that had been closed. As they entered, he greeted and kissed everyone who was present, then poured out a prayer to the Lord, saying:

“I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, who commanded me to be saved from the impediments of this world and deigned to sustain me in this age in such a way that the author of crime found nothing of his own in me.”

Then, turning to the people, he said:

“I beg you, dearest ones, magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together (Psalm 33:3), him who raised me from the dung, rescued me from the work of darkness, and made me a companion of his friends; who sent his angel to summon me from this worldly station and promised to lead me into everlasting rest, so that, made a fellow of his friends, I might deserve to be enrolled in his kingdom.”

O blessed man, who deserved to be consoled in this body in such a way that, before he departed from the world, he already knew what he was going to enjoy in heaven! He deserved to obtain here, through divine power, what David so often sang: “Make known to me, Lord, my end and the number of my days, so that I may know what I lack” (Psalm 38:5–6).

Then, leaning upon the ground, he sent his spirit, directed toward heaven, to the Lord.

All then fell prostrate in tears. Some kissed his feet; others tore away the hems of his clothing; others, competing among themselves, scraped from the wall the blessed blood that had been expelled from his mouth. Each person called himself wretched if he departed without a relic of him.

The wall itself still bears witness today, pierced by as many little hollows as it received spittle from the mouth of the blessed Confessor. The channel from which the holy man drew water also bears witness; those who faithfully kiss it draw healing from it for themselves. I myself saw many people who, having taken from the wall the spittle of his sacred mouth, deserved to receive healing when afflicted by various illnesses.

### III

After his death, as we have said, a certain matron arrived. She clothed the washed body in suitable garments and wished to carry it to the village of Transaliscum. [Col. 1065D] But the people of the district of Lipidiacum resisted her, saying:

“He alone nourished this man; the earth of his body is owed to us.”

The matron replied:

“If you reproach me with some necessity of his food, I often sent him both wheat and barley, which he either consumed himself or distributed to others.”

But they said:

“He became a man of our race, drank the waters of our river, and our earth sent him to heaven. Is it right, then, that you, coming from foreign soil, should snatch him from our hands? Know that none of us will endure this; he will be buried here.”

The matron replied:

“If you seek the shoot of his lineage, he came here from other regions. If you bring forward the waters of your river, they scarcely relieved his thirst; rather, that spring flowing from heaven quenched it.”

While they exchanged these and similar words, and the people of Lipidiacum were trying to bury him after digging the earth and placing the sarcophagus, the matron summoned assistance, drove away the country people, seized the holy body, and began to carry it in a bier toward the village of Transaliacum.

Along the route she arranged groups of singers with crosses and candles, together with the fragrance of burning incense. When the people saw this, moved by penitence, they sent after the matron, saying:

“We sinned by resisting you. We certainly recognize that this is the Lord’s will. Now we ask that we not be excluded from the rites of this funeral, but that we be admitted to perform its offices.”

When she allowed them to follow, both peoples joined together. Thus, coming together to the village of Transaliacum, they celebrated Masses and buried the blessed body with the greatest honor and joy.

In that village the most blessed man often revealed himself through miracles. At Lipidiacum also, as we stated above, his holy work is frequently displayed. Both places are protected by the guardianship of the one saint.

And if the barking of certain unbelievers attempts to drown out these matters, let them know that I saw the priest Deodatus, a man of eighty years, who conveyed these things to me as they have been written and confirmed by oath that he had related nothing false among them.

### Note

[Col. 1065D] Colbertinus has *Transiliensem* here and *Transaliacensem* twice below. Laudunensis and Baturicensis read *Transaliensem* here and *Transaliacensem* below. Bellovacensis has *Transsaliensem*. Surius consistently has *Transaliacensem*, and Gontranus *Transiliensem*.

Above, in Book II, *On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, a village called Transaliensis is mentioned as situated in the district of Auvergne. If our conjecture is sound, there was a church there called Treselliacum (Trézay or Trésel), mentioned in the old catalogue of benefices of the diocese of Clermont. Fulco of Jaligny subjected this church to the monastery of Tournus in 1056, where William, Fulco’s brother, established monks as abbot of Tournus. Hence, in 1059, among the possessions which Henry I confirmed to that monastery, there appears the monastery of Tresal in the county of Auvergne.

There is also a place among the Bituriges called Transaulx. Whether one of these places, or neither, is meant here is uncertain.

## CHAPTER XIV  
### On Saint Martius the Abbot

Divine mercy grants us a great increase when it has commanded that, despite our sins, a refuge of forgiveness be made available—if we forgive the negligent, pardon those who harm us, and, in return, grant the benefit of blessing to those who hate us. The Lord Jesus Christ says:

“Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who slander and persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:44–45).

See what a great treasure is amassed by the rejection of anger, the reconciliation of one condemned, and the forgiveness of one judged! It makes you a son of God the Father, enrolls you as a coheir of Christ, and establishes you as an inhabitant of the heavenly kingdoms. Thus it is clear that the sins of the one who grants the benefit of pardon to a sinner are erased in heaven.

For the sentence spoken by the Lord’s mouth testifies:

“If you forgive people their sins,” he says, “your heavenly Father will also forgive your sins” (Matthew 6:14).

And when he teaches his suppliant servants to pray, he says:

“This is how you shall say to the Father: Forgive us our debts, just as we also forgive our debtors” (ibid., 12).

This holy Martius, therefore, a blessed abbot renowned for holiness and instructed in divine studies, kept the goodness of this teaching in his heart, so that he willingly forgave the offender. He not only pardoned the offense but also bestowed a gift [Col. 1067D]—or, according to Colbertinus, “gifts … graciously”—so that he would not in any way make the guilty person’s status seem contemptible. But before approaching this benefit of grace, we shall first say a little about his way of life.

### I

The most blessed Martius, abbot of the city of Auvergne (13 April 525), is said to have been a native of that same territory. From childhood he led a religious life and dedicated himself wholly to the works of God.

He was frugal in food, generous in alms, prompt in vigils, and exceedingly devoted to prayers. With all his strength he restrained luxury by the bridle of abstinence and the contest of frugality, lest anything steal upon him.

He was not inappropriately called Martius, for with the sword of the Holy Spirit, as in a martial triumph, he cut down at the very beginning of their emergence the thoughts that give rise to mortal actions. He was not a deaf hearer of the apostolic exhortation, recalling its words:

“Gird yourselves with the armor of God and the sword of the Holy Spirit, so that you may be able to despise the flaming darts of the devil” (Ephesians 6:11, 16).

When he had reached the proper maturity of age and shone in this city like a distinguished star, he nevertheless thought that something was still lacking. He withdrew not far from it, took a mattock, and began to cut into a rocky mountain. Carving out little cells there, he made small dwellings for himself, so that, bound more tightly by the chain of sobriety, he might more easily offer to almighty God the incense of prayers and the holocausts of praise upon the altar of a pure heart.

He remembered that the Lord said through the Gospel:

“Enter into your room, shut the door, and pray to your Father; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matthew 6:6).

He knew that the consolation of angelic visitation would also come to him if he withdrew farther from human eyes.

In this hollowed rock, therefore, he prepared the necessities of habitation as we have said. In the caves he shaped from the stone itself a bench and a little seat—or a bed—on which, after much labor, he could grant rest to his weary little body. These were immovable, however, because they remained attached to the very mass of stone from which they had been cut.

When he rested, he spread nothing upon them. He lay down only in the garment with which he was clothed, having no other carpets, cushions, or blankets with which to cover them, except when he himself sat upon them. He possessed nothing of his own except the worship of God, in which he remained unwavering. Sometimes the generosity of the devout supplied him with food.

### Notes

[Col. 1067D] Colbertinus reads *munera … grata* (“gracious gifts”); Bal. reads *pro munere … nec aliquis vilem velit reddere* (“as a gift … and let no one wish to make [the person] contemptible”).

[Col. 1067D] Ed. reads *cellulam* (“little cell”) instead of *sellulam* (“little seat”). Below, Boll. reads *fesso corpusculo* (“for the weary little body”).

[Col. 1068D] So Colbertinus; Boll. and most editions read *incisae massae ipsi petrae* (“cut into the mass itself of the stone”). Bal. reads *incisa malleo* (“cut with a hammer”), and so forth.

## II. Finally, the eternal Lord, who continually glorifies his saints, began to make the heavenly merit of his servant known to earthly people, and to show what sort of worshiper he was of his divinity, when he graciously granted him the gift of healing. For he drove demons from possessed bodies by a word, in the name of Jesus Christ [Col. 1069A]; he suppressed the poison of the malignant pustule by the sign of the cross; he expelled quartan and tertian fevers by administering blessed oil [Ed., “he cured them”]; and, with the Lord, giver of all good things, consenting, he bestowed many other benefits upon the people.

As the fame of so great a man spread, certain people began to flock to him, rejoicing to be instructed in his disciplines. What more need be said? He gathered men, formed monks, and made them perfect for the work of God. For he possessed great patience and had acquired such goodness in enduring the weapons of injury that you would have thought him enclosed in a breastplate of gentleness.

For the monks he had a garden abundantly filled with various vegetables and fruit-bearing trees, pleasing to the eye and delightful in its fertility. Beneath the shade of these trees, whose leaves whispered as the breeze rustled through them [Col. 1069B], the blessed old man often sat.

But a certain shameless man without fear of God, ensnared by an appetite for gluttony, broke through the garden fence and entered stealthily [Note: [Col. 1069D] Most copies read “by climbing.” Bal., “a stealthy … ascent.”], just as the Lord reproaches in the Gospel those who do not enter through the door: “He who does not enter through the door is a thief and a robber” (John 10:1). It was, moreover, nighttime—for such deeds could only be carried out at night—because “everyone who does evil hates the light” (John 3:20).

After gathering vegetables, onions, garlic, and fruit, he loaded himself with a burden of wicked theft and made for the entrance by which he had entered. But he could not find a way out. The burden weighed him down, his conscience terrified him [Note: [Col. 1069D] Bol., “weighed down by the burden.” Others, “weighed down … by conscience.”], and amid the labor of carrying the weight he uttered deep sighs. At times he supported himself against the trunks of the trees. Again and again he went around the entire extent of the garden [Col. 1069C]; yet he found not only no door, but could not even recognize the very entrance through which he had opened his way amid the darkness of night.

He was tormented by a double anguish: lest he be detained by the monks or captured by the judge. Amid these burning thoughts, the night was prolonged for him, and the radiance of the undesired daylight returned. The abbot, meanwhile, passed the night in psalmody and, as I believe, God revealing what was happening, understood it.

For when the sky was already growing pale, he summoned the superior and said: “Hurry more quickly to the garden, for a wanton ox has entered it, but it has harmed nothing there. Go now, load upon it what is necessary, and let it go. For it is written: ‘You shall not muzzle the ox while it is treading out the grain’” (1 Corinthians 9:9).

The superior, not understanding what he meant, went to fulfill the command. When the man saw him approaching, he threw to the ground what he had taken [Col. 1069D] and began to flee. He thrust his head among the thorns and brambles and, like a pig, tried with an easy blow to open the passage through which he might escape.

The monk seized him and said: “Do not be afraid, my son, for our elder has sent me to lead you out of this place.” Then the monk gathered up what the man had thrown down, both fruit and vegetables, loaded it upon his shoulders [Col. 1070A], opened the door, and dismissed him, saying: “Go in peace, and do not again repeat what you have done while idleness was your companion.”

## III. The Priest himself, shining throughout the world like the radiance of the true light, continually drove away the diseased afflictions of illness through the efficacy of his virtues.

A certain Nivardus, held by a prolonged fever, continually drank water while burning with heat. He became swollen with dropsy, so that both his belly and his stomach appeared distended like a bladder. Having therefore been placed in despair because of such an illness, he requested that he be carried to the Saint in a cart, for healing.

At last he was lifted from his bed, placed upon the vehicle, and brought to the cell of Saint Martius. He humbly begged that the Priest of God would lay hands upon him. The Saint, having prostrated himself in prayer before the Lord [Col. 1070B], turned toward the sick man and, touching his limbs with the gentlest contact, restored him to health before the eyes of those standing by.

For it is said that the entire swelling fled from the afflicted body before his fingers, so that no trace of this illness remained in him thereafter. I learned this from the report of my father, because this Nivardus had been bound to him by a friendship. He also asserted that he himself had seen the Saint, in these words:

“When he was still a boy, about eleven years old, he was seized by an attack of tertian fever. His friends took hold of the boy and led him to the Man of God. The latter was already old and near the day of his dissolution, and his eyes were growing dim.

“He placed his hand upon the boy and said: ‘Who is this, or whose son is he?’ They replied: ‘He is your servant, the boy Florentius, son of the former senator Georgius.’

“And he said: ‘May the Lord God bless you, my son, and may he deign to heal your illnesses.’ The boy kissed his hand, gave thanks, and departed healed.” He asserted that thereafter, throughout his entire life, he was never again afflicted by this contagion.

## IV. When he was already ninety years old, laboring in the good struggle, having completed the course of life and keeping his faith in God, he departed for that crown of righteousness which the Lord will give him on the day of recompense.

Afterward, having been washed with the greatest honor and clothed in suitable garments, he was buried within the monastery’s oratory [Note: [Col. 1069D] Since the monastery of Saint Martius was destroyed long ago, there remains a small oratory belonging to the abbey of Saint Illidius, subject to it under the title of a priory. Saint Martius’s body is believed to lie there, but the location of his tomb is unknown. This is the very church of Saint Martius mentioned in Book II, *On the Churches of Clermont*, chapter 16, where the same saint is said to rest. It lies, Savaro says, not far from the city, at the foot of the castle of Waifer, between the monastery of Rubiacum and the church of Saint Victor. Among the Arverni, the feast of Saint Martius is celebrated on 13 April. He is praised by Trithemius and in various indexes of the saints.].

That his blessed tomb is illuminated by divine powers, the very crowd that was present can testify: when they send the sick to the tomb, it immediately sends them home unharmed. For when people flock there from different regions, bringing various kinds of diseases, and receive healing in that place, the limbs of those suffering from chills—shaking violently with tremors—are nevertheless very often restored to complete strength. This is granted by our Lord Jesus Christ, who now glorifies the tombs of the saints with illustrious miracles, bringing back from their tombs those who were once dead [Col. 1071A]. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.

# CHAPTER XV. On Saint Senoch, Abbot

“Vanity of the vain,” says Ecclesiastes, “and all is vanity” (Ecclesiastes 1:2) [Note: [Col. 1071D] Thus in two manuscripts, and thus Augustine reads it. Others have “vanity of vanities.”]. Is it true, then, that everything done in the world is altogether vanity? Hence it happens that the saints of God—whom no heat of lust has burned, whom no goad of desire has driven, whom no filth of luxury has tempted even in thought, so to speak—carried away by the tempter’s cunning, have seemed righteous to themselves and, inflated with the proud arrogance of boastfulness, have often fallen.

Thus it came about that those whom the sword of greater crimes could not slaughter were easily ruined when enslaved by the light smoke of vanity [Col. 1071B]. So too the very man about whom we are now to speak, although he had flourished with many virtues, would almost have perished, overwhelmed in that abyss of arrogance, had not the attentive exhortation of faithful brothers restored him.

## I.

The blessed Senoch, by race a Tiphalian, was born in the territory of Poitiers, in the district they call Tiphala [Note: [Col. 1071D] See the notes on Book IV of the *History*, chapter 18, and chapter 25 of the book *On the Glory of the Confessors*] (Year 576, 24 October). Converted to the Lord, he became a cleric and established a monastery for himself.

For within the boundaries of the territory of Tours he found ancient walls. After clearing them of their ruins, he fitted them out as suitable dwellings. There he also found an oratory in which our famous Martin was said to have prayed. He carefully restored it, erected an altar, and prepared within it a small repository for receiving the relics of the saints [Col. 1071C]. Then he invited the bishop to bless it.

The blessed bishop Euphronius attended. After consecrating the altar, he bestowed upon Senoch the dignity of the diaconate. When the Masses had been celebrated, and they wished to place the reliquary in the repository, the chest proved too long and could not be received within it.

Then the deacon, prostrate with the Priest in prayer, poured forth tears mingled with his petitions and obtained what he asked. Wonderful to relate! The repository was divinely enlarged and the chest constricted, so that it was received within it with ample room and not without astonishment.

In this place [Note: [Col. 1071D] A village bearing his name still exists not far from the town of Lucca [Col. 1072D], commonly called Saint-Senou. He is believed to have lived there, but no ruins of the monastery are visible, since it was destroyed long ago.], he gathered three monks and continually served the Lord. Above all, he walked the narrow path of life, taking scant food and thin drink. During the days of holy Lent, his abstinence was increased by a further reduction of food [Col. 1071D].

His food consisted only of barley bread and water, taking one pound of each element each day. He was content to endure the severity of winter without any covering for his feet [Note: [Col. 1072D] The editions add “to endure …,” and also “around his neck.” Surius and Gontier have “he was content to endure.” The same sources below have “withdrawn.”], while his hands and feet, and even his neck, were bound with an iron chain.

Afterward, withdrawing from the company of the brothers, he shut himself away alone in a cell, praying constantly and continuing day and night without interruption in vigils and prayers.

The devotion of the faithful often brought him money, but he stored it not in hidden chests [Col. 1072A], but in the purses of the poor, frequently recalling the oracle of the Lord’s words: “Do not store up treasure for yourselves on earth” (Matthew 6:19), “for where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (ibid., 21). He gave away for God’s sake what he received, in response to the various needs of the needy. Consequently, during his lifetime he freed more than two hundred people from the bond of slavery and the burden of debt.

## II.

When we came to Tours, he came out of his cell and visited us. After greeting and kissing us, he returned again. As we have said, he was exceedingly abstinent and healed the illnesses of the sick. But just as holiness had arisen from abstinence, so vanity began to creep in from holiness.

For he left his cell and, with the proud arrogance of boastfulness, went to seek out and visit his relatives in the district of Poitiers, which we mentioned above [Col. 1072B]. Upon returning, swollen with arrogance, he strove to please himself alone. But after we rebuked him and explained that the proud are far from the kingdom of God, he purged himself of boastfulness and made himself so humble that no root of pride remained in him at all.

Indeed, he openly confessed, saying: “Now I have learned that what the blessed Apostle proclaims in the utterance of his holy mouth is true: ‘Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord’” (1 Corinthians 1:31).

But since the Lord performed many miracles through him for the sick, and he had enclosed himself so strictly that he never appeared to human eyes, we advised him not to bind himself perpetually by this confinement, except on those days that fall between the deposition of Saint Martin and the solemnity of the Lord’s Nativity, or likewise during those forty days before the Paschal festivals in which the authority of the Fathers established that the greatest abstinence should be practiced [Col. 1072C]. On the remaining days, he should make himself available to the people for the sake of the sick.

When he heard our advice, he willingly accepted what had been said and carried it out without hesitation.

## III.

Since we have spoken briefly about his manner of life, let us now turn to the miracles that the healing right hand of divine power deigned to perform through him.

A certain blind man named Popusitus came to him. At that time the blessed Senoch had already been ordained a priest. When the man asked for some food, the Saintly Priest touched his eyes with his hand and, as he received the saving sign, he immediately recovered his sight.

Another boy from Poitiers, suffering from a similar illness, heard of this confessor’s deeds and prayed to receive back the light he had lost. Senoch did not delay: invoking the name of Christ, he placed the cross upon the blind man’s eyes. Immediately, as a stream of blood flowed forth, light entered, and after the passage of twenty years the radiance of twin stars shone upon the forehead deprived of sight.

Two boys, weak in all their limbs and contracted into a round shape like a sphere, were brought before him. When he laid hands upon them, their joints were restored, and within the moment of a single hour he returned both to full health. He then doubled the benefit of his twofold power.

A boy and a girl stood before him with their hands contracted. It was then the middle of the solemn Easter festival. They begged the servant of God for healing and he delayed attending to the matter because of the crowd that had gathered in the church, declaring himself unworthy to be the one through whom God deigned to grant benefits to the sick. At the repeated entreaties of everyone, he took their hands in his own, touched them, and, their fingers straightened, ordered them to depart healed.

Likewise, a woman named Benaia came carrying her eyes closed. Blessed by the touch of the saving right hand, she departed enlightened.

Nor, I think, should I conceal that his prayer often succeeded in draining the venom of serpents [Col. 1073B]. Two men swollen from the bite of a viper fell at his feet, begging him by his power to drive out the poison that the tooth of the evil beast had injected into their dying limbs.

He poured out a prayer to the Lord, saying: “Lord Jesus Christ, who in the beginning created all the elements of the world and decreed that that serpent, rival of human dignity, should be under a curse (Genesis 3), drive away from these your servants the evil of this poison, so that it may not be the serpent that triumphs over them, but they who triumph over the serpent.”

When he had said this, he stroked every joint of their bodies. Immediately the swelling subsided, and the deadly poison lost its power to do harm.

The day of the Lord’s Resurrection had arrived. As a certain man was going to church, he saw a multitude of his livestock grazing on his crop [Col. 1073C]. He groaned and said: “Woe is me, for the fruit of my year’s labor is perishing so completely that nothing at all will remain of it.”

Taking an axe, he cut off branches and began to close the opening in the fence. At once his contracted hand unwillingly held fast what he had voluntarily grasped. Driven also by pain, he went sorrowfully to the holy Confessor, dragging behind him the branch that his hand had clutched, and related everything as it had happened.

Then Senoch anointed his hand with sanctified oil, pulled away the branch, and restored the hand to health. Thereafter too he restored him to health. Thereafter also he restored many people to health from the bites of serpents and the poison of the malignant pustule by placing the sign of the cross over them.

When he laid hands upon certain people possessed by demons and disfigured by the malice of a savage spirit [Note: [Col. 1073D] That is, “upon certain people possessed …”], the demons immediately fled and he restored their minds, disturbed by the evil spirit, to sound understanding [Col. 1073D].

For all whom the divine hand saved through him from various illnesses, if they were poor, he himself gladly supplied with food and clothing. He cared so greatly for the needy that he even carefully built bridges over riverbeds, so that no one would mourn a cruel shipwreck when the waters flooded.

## IV.

Famous among the people through these and similar great virtues, when he was about forty years old, he was struck by a slight fever. He lay in bed for three days, and it was announced to me that his passing was near.

I hurried there more quickly and approached his bedside [Col. 1074A], but I could elicit no conversation from him, for he was extremely exhausted. Then, after an interval of about an hour, he breathed out his spirit.

That multitude of redeemed people gathered for his funeral—those whom, as we said above, he had freed either from the yoke of slavery or from various debts, and whom he had either fed with food or clothed. They mourned, saying: “To whom do you leave us, holy Father?”

After he had been placed in the tomb, he frequently manifested himself through evident miracles. For on the thirtieth day after his death, while Mass was being celebrated at his tomb, a certain cripple named Chaidulfus [Ed., Caidulphus], who had come to his burial place to ask for alms, venerated by kisses the cloth spread over it. The bonds of his limbs were loosened, and he was straightened.

I learned of many other things that happened there, but I have committed only these to memory as worthy of being recorded.

# CHAPTER XVI. On Saint Venantius, Abbot

The heavenly power grants a singular yet manifold gift to churches and to earthly peoples when it continually bestows upon the world not only intercessors for sinners but also teachers of eternal life. This gift is seen to be one when granted by the divine majesty, yet manifold because it is generously offered to all who wish to seek it, according to the saying: “Ask, and you will receive” (John 16:24), and what follows [Note: [Col. 1073D] The prologue is absent from the Mainz manuscript.].

Therefore the human mind ought vigilantly and unceasingly to investigate the lives of the saints, so that, stirred by such zeal and kindled by their example, it may always extend itself toward those things that it knows are pleasing to God [Col. 1074C], in order that it may either deserve to be rescued by him or be heard by him.

The saints sought to receive these things from his majesty, continually asking that he himself would instill them in the heart, accomplish them in action, and speak through the mouth, so that the mind, purified in thought, speech, and deed, might think holy thoughts, speak what is just, and perform what is honorable.

Thus it came about that, while they served in those things that please the Divinity, they obtained remission of the debt of sin, were rescued from contact with filthy mire, and were invited, according to their merits, to the heavenly kingdom.

They also placed the examples of their predecessors before their eyes and, in accordance with their devotion, praised the omnipotent Lord, whose examples, as we have said, they were preparing to follow.

Therefore, as we strive to proclaim the devoted servant of God, Venantius the abbot, we attribute his gifts rather to the Divinity, since it is manifest that the divine hand accomplished through him what the saints are known to have done [Note: [Col. 1074D] The editions read, “what they are known to have done.” Two manuscripts read, “what the saints are known to have done.”]. We pray that he may open the mouth of the mute to make known the works of his Bishop, because just as we recognize that we are weak in knowledge, so we know ourselves to be sinners in conscience.

## I.

Saint Venantius was a native of the territory of Bourges, born to parents who were free and Catholic according to the dignity of the world (Year 400 … 13 October). When he was flourishing in youthful age, his parents bound him by a betrothal. And since, as is fitting for that age, he made himself agreeable to the girl in love, and even brought her footwear along with frequent cups [Note: [Col. 1075D] Gontier reads, “and besides frequent cups, he also dressed luxuriously.” In his notes, however, he praises our reading and says that formerly a betrothed man and woman gave shoes to each other as a sign of mutual love and fidelity: the bridegroom would remove his own shoes and give them to the bride, and she would do the same in turn for the bridegroom. He thinks that the “cups” mentioned here were small gold or silver chains fashioned in the shape of cups. See below, chapter 20, on Saint Leobard, and Alteserra on chapter 42 of Book I of our Gregory’s *History*.], it happened that, inspired by the Lord, he came to the city of Tours.

At that time there was a monastery near the basilica of Saint Martin [Note: [Col. 1075D] It still exists today under the jurisdiction of the chapter of Saint Martin [Col. 1076D], having long ago been converted into a college of canons under the title of Saint Venantius.], in which Abbot Silvinus governed a flock devoted to God with the rule’s scepter.

This devoted man approached it and, seeing the virtues of blessed Martin, said within himself: “As I judge, it is better to serve Christ undefiled than to become entangled in worldly contamination through the marriage bond. I shall leave the bride of the territory of Bourges and attach myself by faith to the Catholic Church, so that what I believe in my heart, I may also deserve to bring to effect in deed.””

Turning these thoughts over in his heart, he came to the abbot mentioned above, fell at his feet, and tearfully disclosed what he carried in his inmost heart. The abbot gave thanks to God for the boy’s faith, added priestly instruction, tonsured the young man, and enrolled him among the monastic flock [Col. 1075B].

From then on he displayed humility toward the brothers and loved everyone with charity. He is said to have risen to such a height of holiness that all honored him with the greatest devotion as their nearest parent. Consequently, when the abbot died, the brothers chose him to take the abbot’s place in the monastery [the transmitted text is corrupt].

## II.

One Sunday he was invited to celebrate the solemn Masses. He said to the brothers: “My eyes are now covered with darkness, and I cannot read the little book. Therefore entrust these duties to another priest.”

When the priest was speaking, Venantius himself stood nearby. The time came for the holy offering to be blessed, according to Catholic custom, by placing the sign of the cross over it [Note: [Col. 1076D] “Catholic custom,” that is, the practice received throughout the universal Church of blessing the sacred offerings with the sign of the cross.] [Col. 1075C].

As he looked, he saw what appeared to be a ladder placed at the window of the apse, and an old man descending by it, venerable in the dignity of the clerical office, extending his right hand and blessing the sacrifice offered upon the altar.

These things were taking place in the basilica of Saint Martin. No one deserved to see them except Venantius himself; why the others did not see them, we do not know. He later reported them to the brothers. There is no doubt that the Lord showed these things to his faithful servant, to whom he also deigned to reveal the secrets of heavenly mysteries.

For once, when he was returning from the basilicas of the saints after completing his Sunday prayer, supported by a staff, he stood motionless in the middle of the atrium of the blessed Confessor, with his ears raised and his eyes fixed intently upon heaven for a long time. Then, moved from the place, he began to groan and utter prolonged sighs.

When his attendants asked what this meant, or whether he had seen something divine and would tell them about it, he replied: “Woe to us, sluggish and lazy men! Look: the solemn Masses are already being completed in heaven, while we, sluggish as we are, have not even begun the sacramental mystery.

“Truly I tell you, I heard the voices of angels in heaven proclaiming, ‘Holy, Holy,’ in praise of the Lord.”

Immediately afterward, he ordered the solemn Masses to be completed in the monastery.

Nor will I pass over the following. On one occasion, when, as we said above, he was returning from the basilicas he had visited for the sake of prayer, and the words of the Lord’s Prayer were being sung in the basilica during Mass, when they said, “Deliver us from evil,” he heard from someone’s tomb a voice saying the same thing: “Deliver us from evil.”

It is judged to be a mark of no small perfection that he deserved to hear this. He also came to the tomb of the priest Passivus [Note: [Col. 1076D] The printed editions and two Mainz manuscripts have “Passinus.” Surius and Gontier have “Bassinus.”], and, with the deceased himself as his teacher, learned the quality of his merit and the extent of his refreshment [Col. 1076B].

## III.

Although these things are great, let us nevertheless turn to the gift of healings that the Lord brought to the sick through him. For there is no doubt that the hand of God worked through him, as we said above, and that God wished to reveal through him the great things we have mentioned [Note: [Col. 1076D] Two Mainz manuscripts read, “wished to reveal such great things.”].

A little boy named Paulus, afflicted by severe pain in his legs and knees, came to the Saint. Falling upon his knees, he began to implore him to obtain healing for him from the mercy of the Lord through his prayer.

After praying, the Saint immediately touched the sick boy’s limbs with blessed oil [Note: [Col. 1076D] Thus the manuscripts, instead of “touching the limbs.” The editions read, “touching.”] and made him rest upon his own bed. After he had rested for a little while, the Saint ordered him to rise after the passage of an hour. The boy rose and was restored healthy to his mother by the hands of the Saint [Col. 1076C].

A certain servant of Faretrius [Note: [Col. 1076D] The editions read “Pharetrius.” The German edition has “Raretrius.”], hostile to his master, sought the oratory of this Priest. But, swollen with pride and while the blessed Man was absent, he seized the servant and fell down. Soon afterward, however, he was seized by a fever and breathed out his spirit.

By prayer he frequently mitigated attacks of quartan, tertian, and other fevers [Note: [Col. 1076D] Most manuscripts read “outbreaks.” Baddeley, as the manuscripts often have elsewhere, reads “kindled.”]. By placing the saving sign upon it, he extinguished the poison of the malignant pustule; invoking the name of the Trinity, he cleansed those possessed by demons.

For he himself was often assailed by the demons, but remained victorious in the struggle. One night, when he rose from his bed to perform his duty, he saw two great rams standing at his doors, as though awaiting his arrival. When they saw him, they charged furiously at him.

But he opposed the sign of the cross to them. They vanished, and without fear he entered the oratory.

On another night, returning from the oratory, he found his cell full of demons and said to them: “Where do you come from?” They replied: “From Rome. We departed yesterday and came to this place” [Col. 1077A].

He said to them: “Depart, detestable creatures, and do not approach the place where the name of the Lord is invoked.”

As he said this, they vanished like smoke [Col. 1077A].

## IV.

Powerful through these and similar great virtues [Note: [Col. 1077C] Both Mainz manuscripts read, “powerful through privileges.”], having completed the course of his present life, he departed this world to receive eternal life [Note: [Col. 1077C] The German edition reads, “he departed,” and ends the *Life* with these words: [Col. 1077D] “is rendered glorious.” On his holy tomb, see the book *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 15. Today, in the church of Saint Venantius situated in the cloister of Saint Martin, a crypt beneath the church choir can be seen. It contains three stone sarcophagi raised above the ground: one in the middle, upon which an altar has been placed and which is believed to be that of Saint Venantius, and two others situated on either side. His sacred relics, however, were transferred from there—probably at the time when the Normans were devastating everything—and deposited in the village of Cuvinium in the district of Lomacum near Namur, where, according to the author of the *Life of Saint Gerard of Brogne*, monks of Saint-Germain-des-Prés were keeping watch over the holy abbot Venantius at the beginning of the tenth century. At the end of that same century, the monks of Saint-Germain were forced to leave Cuvinium and returned to Paris, carrying with them the relics of the blessed abbot, which are still preserved in the basilica of Saint-Germain.], and his blessed tomb is often rendered glorious by the effect of illustrious miracles.

An unjust demon had seized the mind of Mascarpio, a servant of that monastery. After becoming possessed for three years, he raged at the tomb of the blessed man. At last, as we believe, the demon was expelled through the Saint’s prayer, and Mascarpio was cleansed, living thereafter many years with a sound mind.

The wife of Julian, suffering from a quartan fever, touched the tomb of the blessed man and immediately departed healed, the heat and bodily trembling having been suppressed.

Baudimundus’s wife likewise suffered from this fever. But when she prostrated herself and poured out a prayer at the holy man’s bedside, she soon recovered and was restored to health.

We have heard many other things about him, but we think that these written accounts are sufficient for the belief of Catholics [Note: [Col. 1077D] In one Mainz manuscript there follows chapter 15 of the book *On the Glory of the Confessors* [Col. 1078C], which concerns the same Saint Venantius. At the end it adds: “Gregory, bishop of the see of Tours, speaks about himself in this passage.”].

# CHAPTER XVII. On Saint Nicetius, Bishop of Trier

If credence is given to testimony, I think that those who report holy works ought to be believed faithfully in proportion to the merit of their faith. For not everything that is read in the Scriptures could have been seen with one’s own eyes: some things are confirmed by the account of Scripture itself, some are established by the testimony of other authors [Col. 1077C], and some are believed on the authority of personal observation.

Yet there are people—what is worse—who, with perverse judgment, do not believe written accounts and therefore criticize the things testified to; they disdain things seen as though they had been fabricated. They do not possess in their faith what the Apostle Thomas carried in his heart when he said: “Unless I see, I will not believe” (John 20). “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (ibid., 29) [1232].

But this man, when he saw, immediately believed. For, as we have said, many people, even when they see, not only do not believe but also mock [Note: [Col. 1078D] Colbert and Laude read, “those who see do not believe.” Hence the edition reads, “one and I.”].

Therefore, as I prepare to write something about the virtues, courage, greatness of spirit, and holiness of Saint Nicetius, Bishop of Trier, I fear that some may criticize me, saying: “Since you are younger, how can you know the deeds of your elders? How did their actions come to you? Surely these things that you have written are judged to be nothing but inventions of your own.”

For this reason it is necessary to place the reporter of this work before the reader, so that those who detract from the truth may be put to shame. Let them know, then, that I heard the following from the blessed Aredius [Note: [Col. 1078D] He was educated by Saint Nicetius, as Gregory himself testifies in Book X of the *History*, chapter 29. See also his *Life* below.], abbot of the city of Limoges, who had been brought up by Nicetius himself and had received the clerical order.

I do not believe that Aredius deceived me in this matter, since through him God, at the time when he related these things to me, both gave sight to the blind and granted movement to the paralytics, and restored demoniacs to sound minds after expelling the demons.

Nor should we believe that he could be darkened by a cloud of falsehood, since God often protected him from the cloud of rain in such a way that, although his companions were soaked, he himself was not wet from a single falling drop [Col. 1078B].

Finally, if such a reporter is doubted, the benefits of God are distrusted.

The priest mentioned above therefore said concerning the bishop already named:

“I have certainly learned many things about Saint Nicetius through the testimony of good men, dearest brother, but I have seen still more with my own eyes, and I have also learned things that I scarcely managed to elicit from him himself.

“When he explained to me some of the things that God had performed through him, he did not swell with the high boots of boastfulness. Rather, moved in his heart, he would say with tears: ‘I seem to disclose these things to you, dearest son [Ed., “I wish to disclose them”], so that you too, living with the utmost innocence of heart, may meditate upon similar things.

“‘For no one can strive toward the heights of God’s virtues unless he is innocent in his hands and pure in heart’ (Psalm 23:4), as the pipe of David’s song sings [Note: [Col. 1078D] Here *canna* denotes a pipe or flute.]’”

Thus the reporter, having prefaced his account with these words, began his narrative about him.

I. Therefore the most blessed bishop Nicetius was designated a cleric from the very time of his birth (An. 566, 5 December). For when he had been brought forth from the womb, his entire head was seen to be bare of hair, as is customary with newborn infants; but around it appeared a circle of short hairs, so that you might think that a cleric’s crown had been marked out by them.

[Note: This is, if we believe Thomassinus, the oldest testimony by which it can be demonstrated that the tonsure of clerics was made in the form of a crown in earlier centuries. For previously, as he discusses at greater length, clerics were indeed tonsured, like monks, as is evident from numerous conciliar canons and sayings of the Fathers, but without any configuration in the shape of a crown. Consult him in Part I, *Ecclesiastical Discipline*, Book II, chapter 39; and see in Bosius’s or Aringhi’s *Roma subterranea*, in Ciampini’s mosaics, and in other ancient monuments, the old images of priests.]

From that time he was brought up by highly devout parents and instructed in letters. He was entrusted to a certain abbot in a monastery, where he showed himself so devoted to God that, when the abbot died, he succeeded him.

Now, having assumed the office of abbot, he conducted himself with such discipline and such concern for the instruction and correction of the brothers that he permitted no one not only to act, but even to speak, perversely, saying:

“Scurrility, dearest brothers, and every idle word must be avoided, so that, just as we ought to present our whole body pure to God, so also we may not open our mouths for anything except the praise of God. For there are three things in which the human race goes astray: it either thinks, speaks, or acts. Therefore, dearest brothers, you must avoid scurrility, wickedness, and every evil deed.”

He exhorted the brothers in many other ways also, so that he might present them worthy and pure before the Lord.

King Theoderic, too, revered him with great honor, because Nicetius frequently exposed his vices and crimes, and, once chastised, the king became more corrected. Accordingly, when the bishop of the city of Trier died, Theoderic ordered Nicetius to be summoned to the episcopate.

[Note: Two manuscripts, Bad. and the others, read *arceri*. Sur., and others, read *acciri*. Examples of the agreement of the citizens and the royal decree are found in the appendix.]

When, with the consent of the people and by the king’s decree, he was being brought for ordination by men greatly honored with the king [that is, in the king’s presence], then, as they approached the city at sunset, they pitched their tents and prepared a lodging. They then turned their horses loose [Note: That is, horses. The edition reads, “the horses having been released.”] into the grainfields of the poor.

When blessed Nicetius saw this, moved by compassion, he said: “Drive your horses out of the poor man’s grain as quickly as possible, or I shall remove you from my communion.”

But they, indignant, said: “What is this charge you are making? You have not yet attained the episcopal dignity, and already you threaten excommunication?”

And he replied: “I tell you truly: the king has determined that, after removing me from the monastery, he will order me to be consecrated to this burden. God’s will shall indeed be done, for the king’s will [Sur. reads “anyone’s will”] will not be fulfilled in everything evil while I resist it.”

Then he went away at a swift pace, drove the horses out of the grainfield, and was thus escorted into the city to the astonishment of those men. For he did not honor the person of the powerful man, but feared God alone, both in his heart and in his deeds.

When he had been placed upon the episcopal chair and was listening to the sequence of readings, he felt something heavy upon his neck. Twice or three times he secretly raised his hand to examine it, but could find no object that might have caused such a weight. Turning his head to the right and left, he perceived a fragrant odor. He also understood that this burden was the dignity of the priesthood itself.

[Col. 1079D]

II. After he had assumed the episcopate (An. 527), he made himself so terrible to all who failed to observe God’s commandments that, through the herald’s proclamation [Others read *praeconia*, “proclamations”], he testified that imminent death was near.

For these reasons I think it worthwhile to say a little, both to strengthen the discipline of priests, to instruct the people, and also to correct the kings of the present time.

When, after Theoderic’s death, his son Theodebert had taken possession of the kingdom and was committing many injustices, Nicetius frequently reproved him, whether for what the king himself perpetrated [Note: Nevertheless, Gregory praises him highly in Book III, chapter 25 of his *History*] or for failing to rebuke those who perpetrated such acts.

The Lord’s Day arrived, and behold, the king entered the church with those whom this priest had ordered to be excluded from communion. When the readings prescribed by the ancient canon had been read [Note: This passage refutes the opinion of those who assert that the Gallican Order derived from the Hispanic Mozarabic rite, since here an ancient canon is mentioned before the Mozarabic rite published by Saint Isidore had appeared], and offerings had been presented upon God’s altar, the priest said:

“Today the solemnities of the Mass shall not be completed here unless those deprived of communion first depart.”

While the king resisted, one of the people, a young boy seized by a demon, suddenly cried out. Amid the tortures of his possession, he began with a loud voice to confess both the saint’s virtues and the king’s crimes.

He said that the bishop was chaste, but the king adulterous; that the former was humble through fear of Christ, while the latter was proud through the glory of kingship; that the priest, undefiled, was destined by God to be preferred in the future, while the king was destined swiftly to be struck down by the author of his crime.

When the terrified king asked that the possessed man be expelled from the church, the bishop said: “First let those who followed you—incestuous men, murderers, and adulterers—be driven from this church, and then God will command this man to be silent.”

Immediately the king ordered all those who had been condemned by the priest’s judgment to leave the church. After they had been expelled, the priest ordered the demoniac to be taken outside.

But when he had seized a column, and ten men were unable to pull him away, the saint of God, making the sign of Christ’s cross secretly beneath his garment so as to avoid ostentation, commanded the demon to release him.

At once the man collapsed together with those who were trying to drag him away, and shortly afterward he rose healed. Then, after the solemn rites had been completed, he was sought everywhere but could never be found, and no one knew where he had come from or where he had gone.

Many nevertheless conjectured that he had been sent by God so that he might not leave unspoken the deeds of the king and the priest. Thus it came about that, while the priest prayed, the king became more merciful, and that the shepherd, whom the Lord would worthily reward, heard that prophetic saying: “Whoever brings forth the precious from the vile shall be as my mouth” (Jeremiah 15:19).

Every day the priest preached to the people, exposing the crimes of each individual and continually praying for the forgiveness of those who confessed. Consequently, the venom of hatred frequently flared against him, because he disclosed the crimes of so many with such truthfulness.

Often he voluntarily presented himself to his persecutors and offered his neck to the drawn sword, but the Lord did not permit them to harm him. He wished to die for justice, had the persecutor been more violent.

For he said: “I shall gladly die for justice.”

He also repeatedly excommunicated King Chlothar for his unjust deeds [Note: That is, he did not permit him to approach Holy Communion, or he denied him the *eulogiae*, as I conjecture. I do not think that Chlothar was separated by Nicetius from the society of the faithful by the greater excommunication. Mapinius, bishop of Reims, carefully distinguishes these two kinds of excommunication in the letter to Nicetius that we shall give in the appendix], and he was never terrified when Chlothar threatened him with exile.

[Col. 1081A]

III. At a certain time, when he had already been led into exile and was being abandoned by the other bishops, who had become flatterers of the king, and when all his own people had deserted him, he said to one deacon who still remained steadfast in the faith:

“What are you doing now? Why do you not follow your brothers, so that you may go wherever you wish, as they have done?”

The deacon replied: “As the Lord my God lives, so long as my spirit remains within these limbs, I shall never abandon you.”

And he said: “Because you have spoken thus, I shall tell you what I have learned through the Lord’s revelation. Tomorrow at this hour I shall receive my honor and be restored to my church; but those who have abandoned me will flee to me in great shame.”

The deacon therefore awaited the promised event in amazement, and afterward experienced it. At dawn on the following day, a messenger of King Sigibert suddenly arrived with letters, announcing that King Chlothar had died, and that Sigibert ought to receive both the kingdom owed to him and the bishop’s affection.

When Nicetius heard this, he returned to the church and was restored to his authority. Those who had abandoned him, now confounded, he received back into charity.

Who could adequately recount how courageous he was in preaching, how fearsome in correcting, how steadfast in enduring, and how prudent in teaching? He always displayed the same firmness in prosperity and adversity. He feared neither the man who threatened him nor was he deceived by the one who flattered him.

For truly, as that aforementioned narrator, Saint Aredius, used to say, it was little short of his suffering, like the Apostle Paul (2 Corinthians 11:26), “perils of rivers, perils of robbers, perils in the city, perils among false brothers,” and the rest.

One day, while crossing the river Moselle by boat, he was driven by the force of the waves between the piers of a bridge. He clung to a pier with his hands alone, while holding the boat with his foot, and was rescued by those watching him when he was already thought to be on the point of drowning. He used to say that he had undergone this experience not without the snares of the Tempter.

The author of the crime himself also frequently appeared before his eyes as though intending to harm him. One day, while traveling, Nicetius descended from his horse and entered a dense thicket to relieve his bowels. Behold, an exceedingly dreadful shadow stood beside him: tall in stature, massive in bulk, hideous in color, with enormous glittering eyes like those of a raging bull, and with open jaws, as though ready to swallow the man of God.

But when Nicetius made the sign of the cross against it [Others read “when the sign was made”], it vanished like rising smoke. There is no doubt that the prince of wickedness himself had been shown to him in this form.

IV. As we have said, he was exceedingly steadfast in fasting. While others were taking nourishment, he often went about the basilicas of the saints with only one boy, having covered his head with a hood so that he would not be recognized in public.

God also granted him the gift of healing. While, as we have said above, he was visiting the holy shrines in this disguise, he came to the church of Saint Maximinus the bishop. In its atrium, three possessed men, exhausted after many fits, were resting in sleep. When he saw them given over to sleep, he made the sign of the cross against them. Immediately they awoke, raised their voices on high, and, compelled to vomit, were cleansed.

When the bubonic plague was devastating the people of Trier throughout the surrounding area, and the priest of God was continually imploring the Lord’s mercy for the sheep entrusted to him, a great sound arose at night above the river bridge, like a mighty thunderclap, so that it seemed that the city itself was splitting open.

The entire population, terrified, remained in its beds awaiting a deadly end. Then, amid the tumult, one voice was heard louder than the others, saying:

“And what shall we do here, companions? At one gate the priest Eucharius keeps watch; at another Maximinus stands guard; Nicetius is in the midst. We can prevail no further here unless we leave this city to their protection.”

When this voice had been heard, the disease immediately subsided, and no one afterward died from it. Thus there is no doubt that the city was defended by the power of the aforementioned bishop.

At a certain time, when the priest had been invited by the king, he said to his men:

“Seek for us an abundance of fish, so that when we go to meet the king, our needs may be fulfilled and our friends supplied generously.”

They said to him: “Our fish-trap [*Labsus*; Note: Colb. and the edition read *lapsus*. Below, two manuscripts read *materiae*. Although *lapsus* usually designates a net, here it seems to refer to a place into which fish gather and are more easily caught, or a receptacle in which those already caught are kept]—where fish usually fall—is entirely deserted. Moreover, the very embankments are known to have been torn from their places by the force of the river. Your command cannot be fulfilled, since there is no convenient means of catching what you order.”

When he heard this, he entered his cell, summoned a boy, and said: “Go and tell the master of the cooks to bring fish from the river.”

The boy, reporting the order, was mocked by the man. When he returned, the priest said: “I know that you told them what I ordered, but they refused to listen. Go and tell them to go.”

When they had received this order harshly a second and a third time, they were finally moved to go to the fish-trap. They found it so filled with fish that ten men could scarcely have carried away what they had discovered.

The power of God frequently showed him what was necessary for him.

V. I do not think it should be left unmentioned that the Lord showed him something concerning the kings of the Franks.

In a nighttime vision he saw a great tower of such height that it seemed to approach the heavens. It had many windows, and the Lord stood upon its summit, while God’s angels were stationed at those lookout windows.

One of them held a great book in his hand and said: “That king and this king shall live so long in the world.”

He named them all individually, both those who existed at that time and those who were born afterward. He also declared the character of their reigns and the length of their lives. After each person’s name, however, the other angels always responded, “Amen.”

Thus these things were fulfilled in the future just as the saint had announced through the revelation mentioned above.

After returning from the king by boat, he fell asleep. Behold, the river, stirred by the wind, began to raise its waves high, so that it seemed that the boat itself would sink.

The priest, as we have said, was asleep in some kind of sleep and, as often happens to those who sleep, seemed to be oppressed by someone. When his companions awakened him, he made the sign of the cross over the water, and the storm ceased.

Then, sighing repeatedly, he was asked by his companions what he had seen. He replied:

“I had resolved to keep silent, but nevertheless I shall speak. I saw myself stretching nets across almost the whole world for the purpose of catching, and I had no helper except this boy Aredius. The Lord rightly wished to show him as a net-maker [or fisher], since every day he caught peoples for divine worship.”

A certain man then came to him, wearing long hair and a long beard. Falling at his feet, he said:

“I am the man, lord, who, placed in danger at sea, was saved by your help.”

But Nicetius rebuked him for attributing the glory of this praise to him and said:

“Tell how God rescued you from this danger, for my power can help no one.”

He replied:

“Very recently, when I boarded a ship bound for Italy, a multitude of pagans entered with me. Among that whole crowd of rustic people, I alone was a Christian.

“When a storm arose, I began to invoke the name of the Lord and to beg that your intercession might rescue me. But the pagans invoked their gods: one called upon Jupiter, another Mercury, another begged the help of Minerva, and another that of Venus.

“When we were already in mortal danger, I said to them: ‘Men, do not invoke these gods, for they are not gods but demons. If you wish to be rescued from this present destruction, invoke Saint Nicetius, so that he may obtain for you, through the Lord’s mercy, that you be saved.’

“When they had all raised their voices together in a cry of this kind, saying, ‘God of Nicetius, rescue us,’ the sea immediately became calm, the wind fell, and, the sun having returned, the ship reached the place where we wished to go.

“I vowed that I would not cut the hair of my head before presenting myself to your sight.”

Then, by the bishop’s order, the man was tonsured and went to Auvergne, where he confessed that he was from there.

We also learned countless other things concerning this man from the aforementioned abbot, but I think the little book should now be brought to an end.

VI. When he learned that the time of his departure and migration was near, he told the brothers:

“I saw the Apostle Paul and John the Baptist inviting me to eternal rest and presenting me with a crown adorned with heavenly pearls. They said to me: ‘You shall enjoy such things in the kingdom of God.’”

After reporting this to certain faithful people, he was struck a few days later by a slight fever and sent his spirit before the Lord. He was buried in the basilica of Saint Maximinus the bishop, whose tomb is now frequently illuminated by divine miracles.

[Note: These matters are discussed in Book I of *The Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 94. Concerning the church and monastery of Saint Maximinus, where the body of Saint Nicetius is still preserved, we have spoken in the notes to chapter 93 of that same book. Nicetius was present at the First Council of Clermont in 535, the Fifth Council of Orléans in 549, and the Second Council of Clermont in the same year. The Council of Toul was convened on his account in 550; Mapinius, bishop of Reims, refused to attend because it had been assembled without consulting him, as is clear from his letter to Nicetius. Fortunatus praises him in Book III, poem 9, and in the following poem praises his fortress above the Moselle. In poem 11, Magnericus is called his successor and disciple. Nicetius wrote to the emperor Justinian to recall him from heresy, and to Chlothsind to promote the conversion of the Lombards.

Some learned men have written, on the basis of a manuscript codex, that Nicetius the bishop was the author of the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*, but they were uncertain whether it was the work of Nicetius of Lyon or of Nicetius of Trier. It is explicitly attributed to the Nicetius of Trier in a martyrology written six hundred years ago, which we saw in the monastery of Vallis Gregoriana in Alsace. In truth, however, this hymn is older than either Nicetius, for it is mentioned in chapter 11 of the Rule of Saint Benedict.]

CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the Abbots Urso and Leobatius

When the oracle of the law-bearing prophet had begun his account of the beginning with the Beginning, and had declared that the Lord stretched out the heavens with the right hand of his majesty, he said:

“And God made two great lights and the stars, and placed them in the firmament of heaven, to rule the day and the night, and to shine in the firmament of heaven” (Genesis 1:16–17).

So now, in that heaven of the human mind, as the authority of those who came before has established, he gave great lights—namely, Christ and his Church—to shine in the darkness of ignorance and illuminate the understanding of our humility, just as John the Evangelist says of the Lord himself: “This is the light of the world, which illuminates every person coming into this world” (John 1:9).

He also placed stars in it: patriarchs, prophets, and apostles, who either teach us through their doctrines or enlighten us through their miracles, as he says in the Gospel: “You are the light of this world” (Matthew 5:14); and: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (ibid., 16).

These apostles are rightly taken as representing the whole Church, which remains undefiled, without wrinkle or stain, as the Apostle says: “He presented the Church to himself clean, without stain or wrinkle or anything of that kind” (Ephesians 5:27).

[Note: Labb., from the Codex of Saint-Albinus, reads: *usque in nostris fuerunt fratribus, qui in hoc*—“down to among our brothers there were those who in this …” (the reading is incomplete or corrupt).]

From the teaching of these men down to our own times there have likewise been those who, like the splendor of the stars in this world, have shone not only with the radiance of their merits but also with the brilliance of their doctrines, illuminating the entire world with the ray of their preaching. They went everywhere preaching, established monasteries for divine worship, and taught people to abstain from worldly cares and, abandoning the darkness of desire, to follow the true God through whom all things were made.

Such is what the account of the faithful brothers records concerning the abbots Urso and Leobatius.

I. Abbot Urso was a native of the city of Cahors [Col. 1085A] (An. 500 . . . . 28 July), religious and devoted to the love of God from his earliest age.

Leaving that place, he entered the territory of Bourges. After founding monasteries at Tausiriacum, Onia, and Pontiniacum [Note: Colb. reads *Tausiriaco, Onia,* and *Pontiniaco*. It also has *Pontiviacum*. Labb. reads *Saysiriacum, Onia*, and so forth. Tausiriacum is perhaps the place called *Tausiliacum*, now Toiselay, where a priory still stands beside the town walls under the title of Saint Theobald, subject to the abbey of Bourgueil. Onia is a forest with a village of the same name among the Bituriges, now called the forest of Heugne, where the monastery of Onia may once have stood. I was unable to discover anything about Pontiniacum. In the diocese of Bourges there is a place called Montiniacum, dependent upon the chapter of Sancerre], and having appointed superiors distinguished for holiness [Labb. reads “distinguished for his honor”], he entered the territory of Tours.

He came to the place which ancient authority established should be called Senaparia [Note: This is a village of the Touraine, situated between the rivers Andria, or Anger, and Andresium, now called Sénevière. It still recognizes Saint Leubatius as its patron, and is commonly called Saint-Leubasse or Saint-Libesse. Valesius, in his *Notice of Gaul*, holds that this place received its name from mustard, and therefore thinks that it was first called Sinaparia].

After building an oratory, he established a monastery. Entrusting the full rule to Leobatius as superior, he founded another monastery, now called Loccis [Note: Laud. and most editions read *Locis*. Bal. reads *Locias* . . . the river Loire, and likewise below. Labb. reads *Lucas*. But this is a known place, now called Loches. The monastery itself disappeared long ago; nothing remains of it except the church, which is now a parish church, together with the title of a priory subject to the nearby Benedictine monastery of Beaulieu, of the congregation of Saint Maur], situated on the river Anger in a recess of the mountain, above which a castle now rises; the monastery itself was called by that same name.
