When a community had been joined to him there, he resolved in his heart not to go elsewhere, but to work there with the whole community with his own hands and obtain his food from the earth by the sweat of his brow. Among his other gifts of preaching, he commended to the brothers what the Apostle Paul says:

“Let him labor with his hands, so that he may have something with which he can repay those suffering need” (Ephesians 4:28).

And also: “For whoever does not work, let him not eat” (2 Thessalonians 3:10).

The Lord also gave him the grace of healing, so that when he breathed upon possessed persons, the demons were immediately driven from the bodies they had occupied.

The Lord also deigned to perform other miracles through him. He abstained from food and drink and instructed the monks continually to turn their eyes and thoughts away from every form of luxury [Note: The editions read *indicens*, “imposing,” and below Bal. reads “without necessity”].

II. While he was doing these things, and the brothers were turning a hand-mill and grinding wheat for the necessities of their food, it seemed good to him, for the sake of relieving the brothers’ labor, to establish a mill in the bed of the river Anger itself.

Having fixed stakes across the river, he built barriers from great heaps of stones and gathered the water into a channel. By the force of the current he caused the wheel of the structure to turn with great speed. By this work the monks’ labor was eased, and, after the task had been entrusted to one of the brothers, the necessary work was carried out.

A certain Goth named Sichlarius [Note: Colb. and Bel. read *Silarius*. The same name appears in the book on the castle of Amboise and the deeds of its lords, chapter 3, volume X of Acheri’s *Spicilegium*, p. 522, where he is called a close associate and friend of Alaric. It is there also reported that a monastery stood in a mountain retreat near the castle of Loches, on the river Anger, where many religious men lived under Abbot Urso. It calls that monastery Angeris and describes the history of the mills which Gregory narrates below], who was greatly loved by King Alaric and was hostile to the monastery, coveted this construction and said to the abbot:

“Give me this mill [Note: Colb. and Laud. read “this mill,” and likewise below], so that it may be under my control, and I will repay you whatever you wish.”

He replied: “Our poverty established it through great labor, and now we cannot give it away, lest my brothers perish from hunger.”

The Goth said: “If you are willing to give it freely, I thank you; otherwise I shall take it away by force. Or at least I shall build another, turn the water of your barrier backward, and prevent it from turning your wheel any longer.”

The abbot replied: “You will not do what God does not wish, for you will not take it from us at all.”

Then Sichlarius, burning with anger, built a similar structure beside it. When the water, turned backward beneath the wheel of this construction, flooded it and formed a whirlpool, the wheel stopped completely and could not turn at all as it had before.

Its keeper came to the abbot in the middle of the night, as they say, while he was keeping vigil with the brothers in the oratory, and said:

“Rise, abbot, and beseech the Lord more earnestly. The mill wheel has stopped because of the flooding from the channel built by Sichlarius.”

When he heard this, the abbot immediately sent individual brothers to the monasteries he had established, saying:

“Prostrate yourselves in prayer, and let nothing else occupy you until I send for you again.”

He himself also did not leave the oratory, but prayed earnestly to the Lord and awaited the coming of his mercy. He did this for two entire days and as many nights.

When the third day was dawning, the monk who had been the keeper came again, announcing that the wheel of his structure was turning at full speed according to its former custom.

The abbot then left the oratory with the brothers and went to the riverbank. When he looked for the mill that Sichlarius had built, he did not find it. He approached the bank and examined the riverbed, but found no trace of it.

No sign of wood, stone, iron, or any other material could ever be shown, except that it could be conjectured that, at the very place where it had been built, it had split open through divine power and been removed from human sight.

Then he sent messengers to the brothers, saying:

“Rest now from your labor, for God has avenged the injury done to our brothers.”

III. Endowed with these and similar powers, and having completed the course of his life, he departed to the Lord.

[Note: His tomb is still visited in the church of Loches mentioned above, beside the high altar. A few years ago the most illustrious Victor Buticularius, bishop of Tours, elevated the relics of Blessed Urso. We have assigned his death to about the year 500 because he is said to have lived under Alaric, king of the Visigoths.]

At his tomb, possessed persons were afterward healed and the blind were given sight. After his death, the superiors who were in charge of the monasteries assumed the office of abbots, with the bishops’ permission.

Leobatius [Note: All the manuscripts here read *Leopatius*. The editions read *Leubatius*] was also appointed abbot of the monastery at Senaparia, which lay within the territory of Tours. He persevered in the greatest holiness and old age, and died and was buried there.

CHAPTER XIX. Concerning Monegundis the Religious Woman

The remarkable gifts of divine benefits bestowed from heaven upon the human race can neither be grasped by the understanding, expressed in words, nor contained in writings.

The Savior of the world, from that earliest and still-unformed beginning of the age, allowed himself to be seen by the patriarchs and announced by the prophets; finally, he deigned to be received in the womb of the ever-virgin and undefiled Mary. The all-powerful and immortal Creator suffered himself to be clothed in mortal flesh, underwent death for the restoration of humanity dead through sin, and rose again victorious.

He led us—wounded by the darts of grave crimes and afflicted by the wounds inflicted by lurking robbers—after pouring in the liquid of pure wine and oil, to the inn of heavenly medicine—that is, the holy Church.

He continually encourages us, through the gift of his instruction, to live by the examples of the saints. He offers us as examples not only men but also the lesser sex, struggling not sluggishly but courageously. He grants the heavenly kingdoms not only to men who contend lawfully, but also to women who labor favorably and zealously in these battles.

So now, the blessed Monegundis, who left her native land, like the prudent queen who went to hear Solomon’s wisdom (1 Kings 10), sought out the basilica of blessed Martin so that she might marvel at the miracles granted there at every moment and draw from the priestly fountain whatever might open the entrance to the paradisiacal grove.

## I

Thus the most blessed Monegundis, a native of the city of Chartres (A.D. 530, 2 July), married at her parents’ wish, had two daughters, over whom she rejoiced greatly, saying: “God has propagated my offspring, so that two daughters were born to me.” But this worldly joy was overtaken by the bitterness of this age, when the two girls, struck by a slight fever, completed the span allotted to nature. At this, the grieving mother, lamenting and mourning that she had been bereaved, ceased neither by day nor by night from weeping; neither her husband, nor a friend, nor any of her relatives could console her [Note: [Col. 1087D] Mai m. reads *amici … potuit … in se reversa* (“friends … could … having come to herself”).].

At last, coming to herself, she said: “If I receive no consolation from the death of my daughters, I fear that on this account I may offend my Lord Jesus Christ. But now, abandoning these lamentations, let me sing in consolation with blessed Job: ‘The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord’ (Job 1:21).”

And saying this, she removed her mourning garment and ordered a small cell to be prepared for her. She instructed that only one little window be fitted into it, through which she might see a small amount of light. There, despising the world’s splendor and rejecting the companionship of her husband, she devoted herself to God alone, in whom she had placed her trust, pouring out prayer for her own sins and those of the people. She had one young girl, whose service supplied her with whatever necessity required.

She also received barley flour and ashes infused with water; carefully straining them, she made from the water a mixture for dough, formed loaves with her own hands, and baked them herself [Note: [Col. 1087D] Bal. reads “and she herself baked it.” Mai m. and other editions read “and she herself baked it.”]. After long fasts she refreshed herself with them; the remaining food from her household she distributed to the poor.

It happened one day that the girl just mentioned, who had been accustomed to serve her, seduced, I believe, by the craft of the enemy—whose constant practice it is to inflict injuries upon the good—withdrew herself from her service, saying: “I cannot remain with this woman, who lives in such abstinence. I would rather enjoy the world and take food and drink in abundance.”

The fifth day of her departure had already passed. The religious woman had received neither her customary flour nor water, but remained steadfast and immovable, fixed in Christ, in whom no one established [Note: [Col. 1088D] The editions add “or founded.” Mai m. has “no one founded.”] is swept away either by the violence of wind or by the force of waves. Nor did she think that life was to be sustained for her by mortal food, but by the word of God, as it is written (Deut. 8:3; Matt. 4:4). She recalled that Solomonic proverb of Wisdom: “The Lord does not kill the soul of the righteous by famine” (Prov. 10:3), and also this: “The righteous lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17).

But since the human body cannot be sustained without earthly food, she prostrated herself in prayer and asked that he who had given manna from heaven to the hungry people (Exod. 16), and brought forth water from the rock for the thirsty (Num. 20:11), might likewise deign to grant nourishment by which her weary little body might for a short while be strengthened.

Immediately, in answer to her prayer, snow fell from heaven and covered the ground. Seeing this with thanksgiving, she stretched her hand through the window and gathered some of the snow that lay around the wall. Squeezing water from it, she formed bread as usual [Note: [Col. 1088D] Mai m. reads: “she gathers … she squeezed it out and formed the bread as usual, which …”], and thus supplied bodily nourishment for another five days.

[Col. 1088D] She had a small garden adjoining the cell. She was accustomed to go out into it for a certain revelation [Note: [Col. 1088D] Bal. reads “recreation.” Below, Mai m. has: “In which, having entered, while she walked about … of the place, a woman … wheat … to dry … forgetful of her cares … was deprived of light.”]. Having entered it, she was looking at the plants of the place and walking about when a woman who had placed wheat on the roof of her house to dry looked down upon her importunately, as though from a higher place, weighed down by worldly cares. At once she lost the light of her eyes.

Recognizing her guilt, she approached her and disclosed what had happened. Then the woman cast herself down in prayer and said: “Woe is me, because, on account of my sinful insignificance, the eyes of another have been closed.”

When she had finished praying, she laid her hand upon the woman. As soon as she had made the sign of the cross, the woman immediately recovered her sight.

A certain man from that village, who had formerly lost his hearing, devoutly came to her cell. His parents begged her to deign to lay her hand upon him. But she protested that she was unworthy to be the one through whom Christ should perform such things. Prostrating herself on the ground, and as though she were kissing the very footprints of the Lord’s feet, she humbly implored divine mercy for him. While the deaf man was still lying on the ground, his ears were opened, and he returned to his own home, his grief removed and joy restored.

## II

Having been glorified among her relatives by these signs, and fearing that she might fall into vain glory, she faithfully sought the basilica of Saint Martin, leaving her husband, her household, and all her domestic establishment.

As she began the journey, she came to a village of the city of Tours named Evena [Note: [Col. 1089D] Perpetuus built a church there, according to Book 10, chapter 31, of the *History*.], in which the relics of blessed Medard, confessor of Soissons, are kept. His vigil was being celebrated that night. She kept watch attentively in prayer and, at the appointed hour, went with the rest of the people to the solemn Mass.

While these rites were being celebrated by the priests of God, a certain girl arrived, covered with a malignant pustule formed from poison, and proceeded to her feet, saying: “Help me, because an unjust death is trying to take my life.”

Then, as usual, Monegundis prostrated herself in prayer, made supplication to God, the creator of all, on the girl’s behalf, and, rising, placed upon her the sign of the cross. As the wound burst apart in four places, and pus flowed freely [Note: [Col. 1089D] Mai m. reads: “The pustule bursting in four places, the girl, with the corruption flowing away …”], the unwelcome death abandoned the girl.

After this, the blessed Monegundis arrived at the basilica of Saint Martin. There she prostrated herself before the tomb and gave thanks that she had been worthy to behold the holy burial place with her own eyes. Settling in a small cell, she devoted herself daily to prayer, fasting, and vigils.

Nor was that place without glory from her power. A certain widow brought her daughter, whose hands were contracted. When Monegundis had been entreated and laid upon them the sign of salvation, she began to touch the girl’s fingers with her own hands. The fingers were extended, the sinews straightened, and she loosened the girl’s palms, sound and unharmed.

While these things were taking place, her husband, having heard of the blessed woman’s fame [Al.: “that man, having heard”], summoned his friends and neighbors, went after her, brought her back to her own home, and placed her in the cell where she had previously lived.

But she did not cease from the work to which she had been accustomed. She continued in fasting and supplications, so that at last she might obtain the place in which she desired to live.

She began the desired journey again, imploring the help of blessed Martin, so that he who had given her the desire might also grant the fulfillment of reaching the basilica [Note: [Col. 1089D] Mai m. reads: “the fulfillment. She reached … and from this she remained steadfast.”].

She returned to the cell in which she had previously lived and remained there steadfastly. She was no longer sought by her husband. There, gathering a few nuns [Note: [Col. 1089D] This monastery was called Saint Peter Puellaris. It still retains that name, although it has been converted into a college of secular canons under the jurisdiction of the chapter of Saint Martin.], she lived in complete faith and prayer.

She ate no bread except barley bread, and no wine except a little on feast days, and even that was diluted with a great deal of water [Note: [Col. 1089D] Bal. reads “moderately.” Mai m. reads “and this too with much vinegar.”]. She had no bed of hay or soft covering of straw, except only that which is customarily made from interwoven slender rods, commonly called mats. She placed this upon a frame [Note: [Col. 1090D] Mai m. reads “the servant of Christ placing this upon …” A mat is assigned as a bed to monks by Saint Benedict and the other fathers of monastic life. Here *formula* means a seat or bench.], and spread nothing else over it. This was her daily bench, her mattress, her pillow, her blanket—this was the whole equipment of her little bed. Thus she taught those whom she had gathered to live as she did.

There, living in the praises of God, she bestowed salutary remedies upon many sick people after praying for them.

## III

A certain woman brought her daughter, who was covered with wounds. As some call it, the girl had contracted this condition from a potion [Note: [Col. 1090D] All manuscripts read this way. The edition reads “the same pus had produced it”; others read “they had produced it.”].

Then Monegundis prayed, took saliva from her mouth, and anointed the savage wounds. She restored the girl to health, aided by the power of him who formed the eyes of the man born blind with spittle [Note: [Col. 1090D] Bal. reads “restored.” Mai m. reads “opened … applied [spittle], and from it he was healed.”].

A boy who lived in the place drank a magical poison in a potion. Having been enchanted, as they say, he had serpents generated in his entrails, and these aroused great pain by their bites, so that no opportunity for rest, not even for a brief moment, was granted him. He could neither take food nor drink. If, after a long interval, he took anything, he immediately vomited it back.

He was brought to the blessed woman and asked to be cleansed by her power. When she protested that she was unworthy to perform such things, she was constrained by the entreaties of the parents [Note: [Col. 1090D] Mai m. reads “nevertheless, prevailed upon by the parents’ prayer.”]. She felt the boy’s abdomen and soothed it with her palm, sensing that the wickedness of poisonous snakes lay concealed there.

Then, taking a green vine leaf, she anointed it with saliva and impressed upon it the sign of the blessed cross. When she placed it upon the boy’s belly, his pain was somewhat calmed, and he fell asleep on the bench—he who had previously been deprived of sleep because of the continual attacks of pain.

After about an hour he rose and went out to empty his bowels. He expelled the germ of the pestilential growth, gave thanks to the handmaid of God, and departed healed.

Another boy, disabled by paralysis, was carried before her in the arms of others [Col. 1090D], begging to be healed by the blessed woman. She prostrated herself in prayer and poured out a prayer for him to the Lord. When she had finished praying, she rose, took the boy’s hand, lifted him up, and allowed him to depart in good health.

There was a blind woman who was brought to her and begged her to lay hands upon her.

But Monegundis replied: “What have you and I to do, people of God? Is not Saint Martin dwelling here, who shines daily through the work of illustrious miracles? Go there and entreat him, so that he himself may deign to visit you. For what can I, a sinner, do?”

But the woman persisted in her request and said: “God performs his excellent work daily through all who fear his name. Therefore I, a suppliant, flee to you, to whom the grace of healings has been divinely granted.”

Then the handmaid of God was moved. She laid her hands upon the buried eyes, and at once, when the cataracts were opened, the woman who had been blind looked upon the broad, open light of the world [Note: [Col. 1091D] Mai m. reads “the open light of the world.”].

Many possessed persons also came to her. When she laid hands upon them, the wicked enemy was driven out and health was restored. Those whom the Saint allowed to approach her were not delayed in being healed.

## IV

Now the time of her summons was approaching, and, exhausted in body, she was being released from it.

When the religious women who lived with her saw this, they wept bitterly, saying: “To whom, holy mother, are you leaving us? To whom do you entrust the daughters whom, for the sake of God, you gathered into this place?”

She wept for a little while and said: “If you pursue peace and holiness, God will be your protection, and you will have Saint Martin the bishop as a great shepherd. For I shall not leave you, but, when invoked, I shall be present in the midst of your love.”

They replied, asking: “Many sick people will come to us, begging to receive a blessing from you. What shall we do when they do not see you surviving? We shall send them away confused, since we shall not behold your face. But we ask that, since you are being hidden from our eyes [Note: [Col. 1091D] Mai m. reads “since you have been hidden from our eyes”], you would at least deign to bless oil and salt, so that we may administer them as a blessing to the sick who request it.”

Then she blessed the oil and salt and handed them to the women, who received and carefully preserved them.

Thus the most blessed woman died in peace and was buried in that same cell [Note: [Col. 1091D] She was buried in the church of Saint Peter Puellaris mentioned above, where her sacred remains were preserved in a precious reliquary until 1562, when raging Calvinists plundered it. Most of her bones, however, escaped the fire; partly burned, they were hidden in the earth together with the Saint’s hair. They remained there until 1657, when on 9 July they were raised from the earth and exposed for the veneration of the faithful. Her feast is celebrated on 2 July in various Martyrologies. Some manuscripts of Usuard call her a Virgin; in our exemplar, which appears to be an autograph, she is called consecrated to God [Col. 1092D].], showing herself afterward through many miracles.

For after her passing, many sick people experienced the benefits of health through the blessing mentioned above.

Finally, one foot of the deacon Boson [Note: [Col. 1092D] Mai m. reads “the deacon Basenus”] had been inflamed by a malignant pustule, so that he could not walk. He was carried to her tomb and poured out a prayer. The girls took some of the oil mentioned above, which the Saint had left, and placed it upon his foot. Immediately the wound burst and the poison flowed away, and he was healed.

[Col. 1091D] A certain blind man was brought to her tomb and prostrated himself in prayer. When sleep suddenly overcame him, he fell asleep, and the blessed woman appeared to him, saying: “I judge myself unworthy to be equated with the saints [Note: [Col. 1092D] Mai m. reads “I judge myself indeed to be unworthy to equal …”], but nevertheless you will recover the sight of one eye. Then hurry as quickly as possible to the feet of blessed Martin and prostrate yourself before him in heartfelt contrition. For he will restore to you the sight of the other eye” [Note: [Col. 1092D] The editions read “sight.” Mai m. reads “the other eye.” “Awakening from the vision.”].

The man awoke, having recovered the light of one eye, and went where the command of the one who had ordered him sent him. There, again entreating the power of the blessed Confessor, the night of the blind eye was driven away, and he departed seeing.

A mute man also prostrated himself at the tomb of the blessed woman and lay there. He was so moved by faith that he soaked the floor of the cell with streams of tears. Rising, he returned with his speech restored by divine power.

Finally, another mute man came and lay in prayer. In his heart alone he implored the help of the blessed woman, not with a voice capable of being released [Note: [Col. 1092D] Mai m. reads “and not with a voice, he implored for himself only the help of the blessed woman.”]. A portion of the aforementioned blessing was poured into his mouth, and, when blood mixed with pus burst forth, he was deemed worthy to recover the use of his voice.

A feverish man [Note: [Col. 1092D] The same source reads “febriticus,” and so below: “a certain man came to this tomb for this purpose.”] also came to this monument and touched the cloth covering it. The fever of the disease was extinguished, and he recovered.

A cripple named Marcus was carried by others on their hands to the tomb of the blessed woman and prayed for a very long time. At the ninth hour he stood on his own feet and returned home.

When the boy Leodinus had fallen into severe illness and had been sick for four months, he had lost not only the ability to walk but also the use of food, since the fever continued with great force. He was carried to her tomb, apparently already dead; having received health, he rose from the tomb restored to life.

Why should I speak of the remaining feverish sufferers, when this remedy benefited many, whenever they faithfully kissed the cloth of her tomb? Why speak also of the possessed, who, when brought to the blessed woman’s cell and having entered the holy threshold, are restored to a sound mind? The spirit does not delay in leaving the body when it has felt the power of this Saint present, through the working of our Lord Jesus Christ, who grants eternal rewards to those who fear his name.

# CHAPTER XX  
## Concerning Saint Leobard, a Recluse at Marmoutier near Tours

The faithful Church is built up whenever the deeds of the saints are devoutly rehearsed. Although she derives the greatest joy from those who, leading a religious life from the beginning of their years, have been worthy to reach the harbor of perfection, she also rejoices, at the Lord’s command, over those who, converted from the world, have been able, with the help of divine mercy, to bring a work once begun to completion.

## I

Thus the most blessed Leobard was a native of the territory of Auvergne [Col. 1093A] (born 593, 18 January). He was not of senatorial birth, but was freeborn; and although he did not flourish through noble ancestry, he shone forth in glorious merits, keeping God in his heart from the beginning.

At the proper time he was sent to school with the other boys. He committed some portion of the Psalms to memory [Al.: “someone”], and, without knowing that he would become a cleric, was already being prepared for innocent service to the Lord.

But when he reached the proper age, his parents, compelling him according to human custom, urged him to give a pledge to a girl, as though he were going to take her as his wife.

When he refused, his father said: “Why, dearest son, do you reject your father’s will, and why do you not wish to join yourself in marriage, so that you may raise up offspring from our family to benefit future generations? We labor in vain to produce things if there will be no possessor to enjoy them. Why then do we fill the house with wealth if no one from our family will arise to use it? Why do we subjugate slaves purchased at a price to our authority if in turn they are destined to come under the domination of others? The divine Scriptures testify that children ought to obey the voice of their parents (Eph. 6:1). And since you are shown to be disobedient to your parents, take care lest you be unable to rescue yourself from heavenly offenses.”

Although he had another son [Note: [Col. 1093D] Comp. reads “other sons.” See below.], the father easily persuaded one so young to oppose his own wishes.

At last Leobard gave the bride a ring, offered her a kiss, and presented her with a shoe [Note: [Col. 1093D] Compare the notes above in chapter 16. The ring and shoes were offered to the bride, says Marollius, as a sign of entering into possession. In this way, the bride’s feet and hands were symbolically bound into submission to the husband.], and he celebrated the day of the betrothal [Ed.: “the day of the betrothal rites”].

Meanwhile his father and mother, overcome by the sleep of death, departed from the world, having completed the course of the present life.

After he had completed the period of mourning with his brother [Note: [Col. 1093D] Comp. reads “with one brother … of another brother.”], he went, burdened with wedding gifts, to his brother’s house. He found him so drenched with wine that he neither recognized nor received his own brother into the house.

Leobard, sighing and weeping, withdrew to one side and came to a hut in which hay had been piled up. There, having tied up and supplied fodder to the horse [Ed.: “having tied up the horse and supplied it with fodder”], he lay down upon the hay to rest.

Awakening in the middle of the night, he rose from his bed and, raising his hands toward heaven, began to give thanks to almighty God that he existed, that he lived, and that he was nourished by God’s gifts, and he continued with other thoughts of this kind.

As he prolonged his deep sighs and copiously wet his cheeks with frequent tears, almighty God—who foreknew and predestined those whom he would make conformable to the image of his Son (Rom. 8:29)—pierced his heart with compunction, so that, abandoning the world, he might devote himself to divine worship.

## II

Then, as though already a priest and guardian of his own soul, he began to preach to himself, saying: “What are you doing, soul? Why do you remain suspended in uncertainty? The world is vain, its desires are vain, the glory of the world is vain, and everything that is in it is vanity. It is therefore better to leave it and follow the Lord than to give consent to its works [Al.: “its appetites”].”

When he had spoken these words and daylight began to restore the day to the earth, he mounted the horse [Ed.: “horse”] and began to return to his lodging.

As he proceeded joyfully along the road, he began to turn over within himself what he should do and where he should go. He said: “I shall seek the tomb of blessed Martin, from which healing power proceeds upon the sick. For I believe that his prayer will open a path for me to God, since, when entreated, he restored the dead from hell.”

Thus, taking the road with prayer as his companion, he entered the basilica of Saint Martin. After staying nearby for a few days, he crossed the river and devoutly came to a cell near Marmoutier, from which a certain Alaric had departed. There he prepared himself for writing, making parchment with his own hands [Note: [Col. 1093D] This was the only craft practiced by the monks of Marmoutier, as Severus Sulpicius testifies in the *Life of Saint Martin*. See his praises in Cassiodorus, *Institutions*, Book 2, chapter 7, and in Peter the Venerable, Book 1, letter 29.].

There he devoted himself to understanding the Holy Scriptures and to retaining the Psalms of David, which had long since escaped his memory [Al.: “to the Psalms of David”]. Thus instructed by readings from the divine Scriptures, he recognized that what the Lord had previously inspired in his heart was true.

But, lest what we have related seem fabulous to anyone, I testify before God that I learned these things from the mouth of blessed Leobard himself [Note: [Col. 1094D] Here this book ends in the Beauvais manuscript. The name Leobard occurs only in Comp. Manuscript III has: “But he himself, after an interval …”].

After a short interval of time, he showed himself so humble and so great [the text is uncertain] that he was honored by everyone. Taking a mattock, he enlarged the cell into which he had entered by cutting away a stone [Col. 1094C].

In that cell he delighted in fasts, prayer, psalmody [Note: [Col. 1094D] Comp., Sur., Gon., and Rip. read “silence.”], and reading. He never ceased from the divine offices or from prayer. At times he wrote, so that he might drive away harmful thoughts.

## III

Meanwhile, when the tempter wished to reveal himself as always hostile and envious toward the servants of God, after one of Leobard’s little monks [Note: [Col. 1094D] So the Laudunensis manuscript. The edition reads “when someone …” Colbertinus has “when some matter concerning the monastic clothing of that little monk …” Comp. reads “when someone had a dispute about that monastic habit …” Sur. and Boll. read “when one of the holy monks …”] had had a dispute with his neighbors, the tempter injected into him the thought of leaving that cell and moving elsewhere.

When we had arrived there for prayer as usual [Note: [Col. 1094D] Compare the *Life of Gregory* itself. These books were the *Lives of the Fathers* and the works of Cassian, which Saint Benedict the holy father commended to monks in nearly the same words.], he disclosed to us the trick of the advancing poison.

I, sighing with no little grief, began to rebuke the man, asserting that this was the devil’s cunning. I sent him books, the *Lives of the Fathers*, and the *Institutes of the Monks*, showing what those who become recluses ought to be and with what caution monks ought to live [Col. 1094D; the text is defective].

After these books had been left with him, he not only drove away the wicked thought but also cultivated his understanding with such sharpness that we marveled at the eloquence of his speech.

He was sweet in conversation, gentle in exhortation, and concerned for peoples, attentive to kings, and constant in prayer for all who feared God among the clergy.

Nevertheless, unlike some, he did not boast by letting his hair fall in strands or by wearing a barbarous beard [Note: [Col. 1095C] Sur. and Boll. read “yet he did not … or by letting his beard grow.”]. He cut his hair and beard at the proper time.

Having lived in this cell for twenty-two years in this way, he was so strengthened by the grace of the Lord that, when malignant pustules were anointed with the saliva of his mouth, he suppressed the force of the raging poison [Al.: “restrained it”]. For feverish sufferers, by means of a drink sanctified with the sign of the blessed cross, he extinguished the advancing chill and heat. Not without reason did he drive harmful fevers from others, since in himself he had extinguished the incentives of sinful evil.

At one time a blind man came to him, humbly lamenting the misery of his suffering [Note: [Col. 1095C] Comp. reads “lamenting, imploring …”], and begged the Saint to touch his closed eyes with his right hand.

Leobard refused for a very long time. At last, overcome by the man’s tears and moved by compassion, he poured out prayer to the Lord for him for three days. On the fourth day, placing his hand upon the man’s eyes, he said:

“Almighty Lord, only-begotten Son of God the Father, who reign with him and the Holy Spirit forever, you who restored light to the man blind from birth (John 9:6) by the spittle of your blessed mouth: restore the sight of light to this servant of yours, so that he may know that you are the almighty Lord.”

And saying this, as soon as he traced a cross over the blind man’s eyes, the darkness was driven away and he immediately restored light to him in the present life.

Eustachius [Note: [Col. 1095C] Several editions read “Eustathius.” He is thought to have been abbot of Marmoutier. He is called Eustochius in the anonymous work of Bochellus, *On the Deeds of the Bishops of Tours*, etc. He does not appear in *Gallia Christiana*. Marmoutier was attached to the rock that is still near it; there were several caves in it, as Severus Sulpicius relates, habitations of holy men, which were for the most part destroyed when the rock was cut away or fell of its own accord. The cell said to have been inhabited by Saint Martin was carefully preserved, together with another lower cell in which Briccius, his successor, is said to have done penance. Both, out of reverence for those holy men, were enclosed within the walls of the larger basilica and converted into an oratory, with altars built there. Not far away, in caves cut into the rock itself, is seen the fountain of Saint Martin, mentioned above, as is also the oratory of the Seven Sleepers. Not far from the monastery there remains an ancient church of the present parish village, dedicated to Saint Radegund, who is said to have stayed there and frequently devoted herself to prayer in the oratories cut into the rock beside which the basilica itself stands. [Col. 1096C] Nearby is another chapel dedicated to Saint Clarus, whose martyrdom can be seen painted in the window glass for more than four hundred years. We do not doubt that all these are traces of the dwellings of the holy monks and hermits who, as Severus Sulpicius testifies, lived there under the discipline of blessed Martin, and of those who succeeded them. Leobard, however, has an oratory dedicated to his name by the walls of the city, beside the fortress located there, which those suffering from fevers commonly visit.] stood by as a supporting witness.

## IV

Finally, broken down by the labor of quarrying the stone beneath the mountain, which he cut constantly, worn out by the severity of fasting, and strengthened by unceasing prayer, he gradually began to be deprived of bodily strength [Note: [Col. 1096C] The editions read “weakened by uninterrupted prayer … to be deprived of strength.”].

One day, when he was extremely exhausted, he ordered us to be summoned. When we approached him, after he had lamented the necessity of his death, he asked us sinners for eulogiae (blessed bread). Having received them and having drunk wine, he said:

“My time is already being fulfilled. The Lord commands that I be released from the bonds of this body, but there will still be an interval of a few days. Nevertheless, I shall be summoned before the holy day of Easter [Al.: “the second day of Easter”].”

O blessed man, who served the Creator of all in such a way that he knew his death beforehand through divine revelation!

It was the tenth month when he spoke these words. In the twelfth month [Note: [Col. 1096C] If Leobard truly died on 18 January, as the Martyrologies suggest, Gregory here appears to count the year from January and to call December the twelfth month [Col. 1096D].] he began to fall seriously ill again.

Sunday arrived. He called his servant and said: “Prepare some food for me to take, because I feel extremely exhausted.”

When the servant replied, “It is ready, lord,” Leobard said to him: “Go outside and see whether, now that the solemn rites have been celebrated, the people are leaving Mass.”

He said this not because he wished to take food, but so that no one might be present as a witness to his passing.

The servant went out and returned. When he had entered the cell, he found the man of God stretched out, having closed his eyes and breathed out his spirit.

Thus it became clear that he had been received by angels, since the sacred hero did not wish the man to be present at his passing.

Seeing this, the servant raised his voice in lamentation. Then, when the other brothers had assembled, Leobard was washed, clothed in suitable garments, and placed in the tomb that he himself had carved for himself in the aforementioned cell. That he was admitted into the company of the saints, I think no believer can regard as uncertain [Note: [Col. 1096D] Comp. reads: “Admitted, with repeated miracles making it clear that no one of the faithful should consider it uncertain,” through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and is glorified as God through endless ages of ages. Amen.].

**Here ends the book on the Lives of the Fathers.**

[Col. 1097]

# Fragments of a Commentary on the Psalms by Saint Gregory, Bishop of Tours (C, S)

## Here begins the explanation by Florentius Georgius Gregory of the titles of the Psalms

(Recovered from Vatican manuscripts by the distinguished Joseph Thomas.)

[Col. 01097A]

Finally, the psalms that explain David’s flight and persecution indicate the Lord’s persecution and passion. Those, however, that are entitled “For the End” indicate the perfection of good works, because this end is unlike other ends: while those have a limit, this one has fulfillment. “For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4).

“Of the winepresses” is a hymn concerning the fruits of eternal gifts. “For those who will inherit” teaches the recompense of the saints, or of the Church, which is the body of Christ, so that they may receive the inheritance and the kingdoms of heaven.

“On the Eighth.” Some assign this number to the Gospels, because they contain the eight beatitudes through which one comes into the kingdom of God; or to the eight souls of that ark.

“In the consummation,” or “at the dedication of the tabernacle,” signifies the perfection of the Church.

“For those who will be changed” foretells the change of the Jewish people into the Gentile people, or of the Synagogue into the Church.

“For hidden things” speaks of the coming of the Son of God, who was hidden from the Jews.

“A song of resurrection,” that is, of the truth of the Lord’s own resurrection.

“The prayer of Moses, the man of God.” It returns to the Law, because the Law itself declares that we are joined to the resurrection of the Redeemer.

“A Psalm of Solomon.” This is understood to have been sung of the peaceful one, Christ, who is our peace.

“In confession” it teaches that a person should continually confess God both with voice and with heart.

Those who narrate the deeds according to the truth of the letter are nevertheless understood to possess spiritual understanding.

“A Psalm of the sons of Korah” prefigured the people to be redeemed through the passion of Christ, because *Korah* is interpreted as “baldness,” just as our Lord Jesus Christ was crucified at the place of Calvary.

“For the words of Cush the son of Jemini.” This refers to the fact that Cush, having abandoned David, went over to Absalom, who was an enemy of his father, just as Judas was of Christ.

“On the morning assumption,” because the Lord, rising in the morning, led back from the underworld the captivity he had taken captive.

“On the first day of the week,” in the resurrection itself.

“Before he was anointed,” before he was glorified by the resurrection.

“Upon remembrance of sins,” namely, his own.

“A Song of Ascents,” for it designates the heavenly ascent. Therefore the Psalm that stands in the middle of the Songs of Ascents is placed like a most beautiful tower.

But I do not think it is without mystery that this book is written in three groups of fifty, and I believe that their meaning is this. The first grants remission of sins; the second invites us to hope for the heavenly kingdom; the third sends us into the city, toward the kingdom of eternal blessedness.

The *diapsalmoi*, which are always interpreted, teach that the faithful mind should always exercise itself in these matters.

# Two Fragments from a Commentary on the Psalms

(Recovered by D. J. Mabillon from a very ancient collection on virtues and vices in a manuscript of Saint Martin of Tournai.)

## I. In the chapter on compunction

Gregory of Tours, *Commentary on Psalm* [1260]: “For if the bonds of our sins have been broken, and our mind has rejoiced in Christ, then we offer ourselves to God as a living and holy sacrifice, remaining with him in the heavenly Jerusalem.”

## II. In the final chapter on the recompense of the righteous

Gregory, *In the Exposition of the Psalms*: “Therefore, if we do not harden our ears against the commandments of God; if we carry out the admonitions of the saints with innocence; if we are not afflicted by the thorns of our crimes; if, together with the innocent, we wash hands free from all blood—our Lord God will honor us with worthy rewards, with which the saints rejoice eternally together with him. To him be glory with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit forever. Amen.”

# Works Attributed to Saint Gregory, Bishop of Tours

[Col. 1099]

# Preface of Saint Gregory, Bishop of Tours, to the Book of the Miracles of Blessed Andrew the Apostle

(From a manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.) (C, S)

[Col. 1099A] 1261 I believe that the renowned trophies of the holy apostles are hidden from none of the faithful, since some of them teach evangelical doctrines, while others recount apostolic deeds. Of certain apostles, books exist in which their own actions are recorded; for most, however, we have received nothing other than accounts of their sufferings. For I came upon a book about the miracles of the holy apostle Andrew, which some called apocryphal because of its excessive verbosity. It seemed best, after reviewing and extracting only the miracles, to omit whatever produced weariness and to confine the remarkable miracles in a single small volume—one that would both offer grace to its readers and remove the envy of detractors. For unviolated faith is not demanded by a multitude of words, but by sound reasoning and purity of [Col. 1099B] mind.

## HERE BEGINS THE TEXT OF THE MIRACLES THEMSELVES

Accordingly, after that noble and glorious triumph of the Lord’s Ascension, when the blessed apostles had been dispersed through various regions to preach the word of God, the apostle Andrew began to announce the Lord Jesus Christ in the province of Achaea. The apostle Matthew, who was also an evangelist, announced the word of salvation to the city of Mirmidona, and so forth, almost as in the commonly circulated Book III of the *Apostolic History* by Abdias. For this reason it did not seem appropriate to reproduce that book here in full. It will be sufficient to present here the list of chapters as it appears in the manuscript, together with the two final chapters in full. In the first of these, he briefly presents the Apostle’s death, which is narrated somewhat more fully by Abdias; in the other, [Col. 1099C] he speaks of oil flowing from the tomb of that same saint, which Abdias does not mention. All these matters are brought to a close by Gregory’s brief epilogue.

## HERE BEGIN THE CHAPTERS OF THE BOOK OF THE MIRACLES OF THE BLESSED APOSTLE ANDREW

**CHAPTER I.** On the apostle Matthew and what took place in [1262] Mirmidonia. “Accordingly, after that…” and so forth, as above.

**CHAPTER II.** On a blind man restored to sight. “But Andrew, departing from that place, came into his own region, and while he was walking…” and so forth.

**CHAPTER III.** On a boy restored to life. “Now Demetrius, the chief man of the city of the Amaseans…” and so forth.

**CHAPTER IV.** On the boy Sustratus, whom his mother accused of a crime. “A certain boy named Sustratus [the Colbertine manuscript and the editions read: ‘named Sostratus’]…” and so forth.

**CHAPTER V.** On Gratianus, his son, and his wife. “Gratianus of Sinope also had a son…” [Colbertine manuscript: *Gratinus*; edition: *Cratinus … filius*] and so forth.

**CHAPTER VI.** On seven demons expelled from Nicaea. “After this he proceeded to Nicaea, where there were…” [Col. 1100B] [Edition: “he proceeded to Nicaea in Asia, where there were…”]. “There he appointed as bishop a man named Coelestis.” [Colbertine manuscript and editions: *Callistus*.]

**CHAPTER VII.** On a dead man restored to life. “Finally, as he approached the gate of Nicomedia…”

**CHAPTER VIII.** On the calming of a troubled sea. “From there the Apostle departed and, entering the Hellespont, sailed to come to Byzantium…” and so forth.

**CHAPTER IX.** On robbers struck with astonishment. “From there they proceeded to come to Thrace…” and so forth.

**CHAPTER X.** On those who believed while aboard a ship. “The holy Apostle came to Berintum, a city of Thrace, and found there a ship that was making for Macedonia…” [Col. 1100C] [Colbertine manuscript: *Berintum*; the editions: “to Perinthus, a maritime city of Thrace, in order to cross by ship to Macedonia…”] and so forth.

**CHAPTER XI.** On the marriage of boys. “There were two men in Philippi, brothers…”

**CHAPTER XII.** On Exiio [thus] and his parents. “There was a certain young man in Thessalonica named Exohus…” [Colbertine manuscript: *Exuus*; edition: *Exoos*] and so forth.

**CHAPTER XIII.** On the disabled son of Carpianus. “The young man asked the blessed Apostle to go with him to Thessalonica…” [Col. 1101A] [Edition: “Now when he had remained for a long time in the vicinity of Thessalonica…”] and so forth.

**CHAPTER XIV.** On a dead man restored to life. “One of the townsmen…” [Edition: “Another of the townsmen came forward…”] and so forth.

**CHAPTER XV.** On the son of Medias, his children, and other sick people who were healed. “A certain man named Medias came to him from Philippi…” and so forth.

**CHAPTER XVI.** On the disabled daughter of a certain man who was healed. “Finally, a certain Nicolaus…” and so forth.

**CHAPTER XVII.** On a demon expelled. “On the following day…” and so forth.

**CHAPTER XVIII.** On the proconsul Virinus, his son, and a woman restored to life. “While these things were taking place…” [Col. 1101B] [The Colbertine manuscript calls the proconsul *Virinus*, as does our German manuscript; the editions read *Quirinus*.]

**CHAPTER XIX.** On a serpent killed and a dead man restored to life. “When these things had taken place…” and so forth.

**CHAPTER XX.** On the revelation of the blessed Apostle’s passion. “On the following night…” and so forth.

**CHAPTER XXI.** On the man who fell into the sea. “Many people from Macedonia arrived, having landed at Patras, a city of Achaea…” and so forth.

**CHAPTER XXII.** On the proconsul Lisbius and his faith. “Finally, when many were asking him…” and so forth.

**CHAPTER XXIII.** On Trophima and the proconsul’s wife. “Accordingly, Trophima, who…” and so forth.

**CHAPTER XXIV.** On many dead people restored to life. “Afterward, while he was walking about…” and so forth.

[Col. 1101C]

**CHAPTER XXV.** On a certain woman’s difficult childbirth. “There was a woman named Caliopa, who had conceived unlawfully after becoming involved with a murderer … and could not give birth…” and so forth.

**CHAPTER XXVI.** On Sustratus and his servant. [The Colbertine manuscript and the editions read *Sostratus*.] “Now while he was performing many signs … in Corinth…” and so forth.

**CHAPTER XXVII.** On demoniacs healed at a bath. “A few days later…”

**CHAPTER XXVIII.** On the old man Nicolaus. “While these things were taking place, behold, a certain man…” and so forth.

**CHAPTER XXIX.** On Antiphanus, his wife, and his servants. “While he was staying in that place, Antiphanus, a citizen of Megara, came to him.” [Colbertine manuscript: “Antiphanus … of Megara.” Edition: “While these things were taking place at Corinth, [Col. 1101D] Antiphanes, a citizen of Megara…”]

**CHAPTER XXX.** On Maximilla, the wife of the proconsul of Aegeae. “The blessed Apostle came to Patras…” and so forth.

**CHAPTER XXXI.** On a disabled man who was healed. “From there, descending…” [Colbertine manuscript: “Departing from there.” Edition: “And leaving the house…”] and so forth.

**CHAPTER XXXII.** On three blind men restored to sight. “But having gone on to another place…” and so forth.

**CHAPTER XXXIII.** On a withered man restored to health. “When a certain man saw these signs…” [Col. 1102A] [Edition: “While these things were taking place at Patras…”] and so forth.

**CHAPTER XXXIV.** On Stratocles, the brother of the proconsul. “While such things were being done at Patras through the blessed Apostle, Stratocles came…” [Colbertine manuscript: *Stratocles*. Edition: “Stratocles came from Italy…”] and so forth.

**CHAPTER XXXV.** [1264] On the proconsul who returned from his journey. “For every day…” and so forth.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. ON THE PASSION OF THE HOLY APOSTLE

After this, the blessed Apostle was arrested by the proconsul Aegeas [Note: The commonly circulated Abdias recounts the passion of Saint Andrew from the commonly circulated Acts, and concludes his book with it.] and placed in prison. Everyone came to him to hear the word of salvation. But he did not cease preaching the word of God night and day. After a few days had passed, he was brought out of prison, severely [Col. 1102B] beaten, and hung upon a cross. While he remained alive upon it for three days, he did not cease preaching the Lord the Savior, until on the third day, as the crowds flocked in, he breathed out his spirit. The reading of his passion also sets this forth fully. Maximilla received his blessed body, embalmed it with spices, and placed it in a tomb; and she continually prayed over it, beseeching the Lord that His blessed Apostle might remember her.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. ON THE POWER OF HIS TOMB

From that tomb manna, in the form of flour, and oil with a most pleasing fragrance flow forth. By these, the fertility of the present year is shown to the inhabitants of that region. [Col. 1102C] If only a little flows forth, the earth produces little; but if it flows abundantly, a great abundance of fruits is supplied. For they say that this oil runs as far as the middle of the holy basilica, as we wrote in the first book of the *Miracles* (chapter 31). We have not pursued the sequence of his passion, because we found it had been written very usefully and elegantly by someone else.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. THE WRITER’S EPILOGUE, BRINGING THE WORK TO AN END

These, nevertheless, are the things that I, unworthy in speech, rustic in language, and depraved in conscience, have dared to make known concerning the miracles of the blessed Apostle. I beseech his mercy that, just as on his birthday I came forth from my mother’s [Col. 1102D] womb, so through his intercession I may be rescued from hell; and that, just as on the day of his passion I took up the beginning of this life, so he may deign to claim me as his own disciple. And because a great part of our wrongdoing turns us back from greater merits, I dare to ask this much: when, after the judgment, he shines in glory, conformed to the Lord’s body, may he at least obtain that, despite my immense crimes, forgiveness not be denied me.

Here ends Gregory, bishop of Tours, his book on the miracles and virtues of the blessed apostle Andrew.

[Col. 1103]

# THE BOOK OF SAINT GREGORY, BISHOP OF TOURS, ON THE PASSION, MIRACLES, AND GLORY OF SAINT JULIAN THE MARTYR

(From manuscript codices.) (C, G, S)

[Col. 1103]

## Here begins the preface of Gregory, bishop of Tours, on the passion of Saint Julian the martyr

[Col. 1103A] 1265. “Great in us…” and so forth, as above, col. 847, “might be heard.” In the same way, the renowned martyr Julian, born in the city of Vienne and given as a martyr to the Arverni, was kindled by this fire and desired these things with his whole mind. It is pleasing to explain a few matters about his deeds and miracles in the style of a historian. But since a concise discourse undertakes the abundant subject of an outstanding contest, I beg that forgiveness be granted to me for touching briefly, as I have said, upon only a few matters, since I recognize that I am less than competent or skilled to relate them, neither trained in grammatical arts nor educated in the liberal disciplines. But what of it? I do what [Note: Two major manuscripts read: “what love of my patron impels me to do.”] the love of my patron urges me to do, so that I cannot remain silent about these things. I shall therefore begin as I am able, because I do not think that God requires more concerning the struggles of the saints than that they have conquered—not that they have run exceedingly far, but that they have completed the course [Col. 1103B] they undertook. For although He recognizes the struggles and victories of those who persevere as belonging to His own praise, He nevertheless prepares crowns alike for those who conquer in a short or a long battle. Therefore it makes no difference by what memorials the brave deeds of conquerors are revealed, or by what order venerable events are committed to memory, provided that it is established that, just as heavenly history depicts in perpetual letters the contest of the heavenly athlete for proclamation under the gaze of the divine Rewarder, so a faithful discourse should pass through that same contest for the sake of imitation by posterity, so that they may follow the faith of the Christian religion [Note: In the Gembloux manuscript the following appears here: “The preface ends,” followed by the list of chapters and then: “Here begins the passion of Saint Julian, the outstanding martyr. Chapter I: The saint…”].

## HERE BEGINS THE PASSION OF SAINT JULIAN THE MARTYR

1266. Saint Julian, born in the city of Vienne, was given as a martyr to the Arverni: illustrious indeed in lineage and adorned to no small degree by the uprightness of his character, but—what is greater—fervently kindled by the fire of heavenly love. The blessed Ferreolus, already a soldier of Christ in the time of Crispinus the consular, before he was exposed, was serving in the aforesaid city in the office of tribune, in outward rank but not in heart, in appearance but not in disposition. The holy Julian, now grown to manhood and soon to become his companion in heaven, by divine providence offered him consolation in this world. Though they had been placed together in the fellowship of temporal military service, they loved one another more through the zeal of faith than through military affection; and amid public labors, holy love had bound them together with faithful bonds in the fellowship of the saints.

Moreover, when the savage fury of the pagans had armed itself through continual persecutions against the race of Christians beloved by God, and, resisting the immortal husbandman, the hostile hand strove to uproot completely the vine of the new plantation as it sprouted; and when the rage of the impious was ranging through various parts of the world with the sword of cunning, insatiable savagery, it was nevertheless announced by common report that it was drawing near the city of Vienne.

Therefore, since there was no doubt that the eminent worshiper of Christ, Julian, burning with love for martyrdom, would in no way allow himself to remain hidden, Saint Ferreolus began to act by every means [Note: Several manuscripts read: “with every urgency”] so that, before the persecutors’ rage reached that place, the aforementioned man of God might secretly depart and, surviving for the consolation of the remaining Christians, himself as a survivor might evade the attack of the mad fury for a little while. This he urged by counsel and entreated by prayers. But Julian, because he possessed the virtue of self-control, although he had long thirsted for the contest of martyrdom with the whole desire of his heart, nevertheless did not delay obeying his friend’s affectionate advice. For he saw that he would not have done this without a divine command, since persecution was then raging in the city of Vienne. For he had read that the Lord had commanded: “If they persecute you in this city, flee into another” (Matthew 10:23).

He feared that his relatives might oppose him if he entered this contest among them, and that the soldier of Christ might lose the crown of glory if he did not fight lawfully. Having weighed all these matters within himself, he left behind everything of his own, thought little of carnal attachments, being inflamed solely by love of Christ, and secretly departed according to the counsel of the blessed Ferreolus. Turning aside into the territory of the city of Auvergne, [Col. 1104C] he resolved to hide nowhere except at the village of Brioude, where the songs of pagan error were being honored. Thus it is clear that he had not fled secretly from the city of Vienne out of fear of death, but rather so that, by fleeing from city to city, he might fulfill Christ’s command and, having nevertheless spurned both his possessions and his relatives, might run more freely the course of the desired contest.

Now when the consul Crispinus learned that the holy man was hiding in the territory of the city of Auvergne after fleeing secretly, he immediately issued this deadly order: wherever he was found, the persecutor was to pursue and kill him. In keeping with the madness of his rage, by which he rushed headlong, wholly intent upon the blood of the saints, he indeed ordered the death of the blessed Julian. But by God’s hidden dispensation this was happening so that he might heap up for himself a greater accumulation of condemnation, while the glorious martyr might quickly reach Christ, as he had long desired.

The executioner, hastening on, caught sight of Saint Julian at a place called Vinicella. As he watched him, Julian entered the hut of certain old men, as though to be concealed. But because he felt, by God’s command, that his adversaries were pursuing him, and because he could no longer delay when God was calling him—God who had prepared his ascent to heaven—he immediately asked to be exposed, even though the old men were eagerly trying to hide him. When they hesitated and held him back, while he was being sought with the threatening terror of those breaking in, lest any danger threaten those attempting to excuse themselves, he sprang outside at once and said:

“Whom do you seek? Whom are you looking for? Here I am before you. Turn your sword against me; now inflict upon me the punishment I desire; exact from me the penalty you have been commanded to impose. Let not the shedding of innocent blood permit the guilt of your apostasy in any way to be imputed to its patient suffering.”

But when they stood stupefied and hesitating before such steadfastness in the blessed martyr, he added still more firmly:

“I do not wish to remain any longer in this world, because I thirst for Christ with the whole eagerness of my soul. Behold, I come forward to meet you; fearlessly I offer my head. You have what you sought with your whole mind. Only strike, and fulfill both your devotion [Note: Two major manuscripts and the Gembloux manuscript read *devotationem*, an orthographic variant] and my desire.”

As the most blessed man sought to consecrate his soul to martyrdom with this confession, he also commended himself to Christ in the religious prayer that followed. But neither the steadfastness of his devout purpose nor such extraordinary confidence in offering himself turned the barbarous savagery and the bloodstained minds of the raging men away from the shedding of innocent blood. They drew the sword and, brandishing it in their right hand, struck his neck. After his throat had been cut, the executioners washed his severed holy head in a spring which, perhaps because of the place where the blood had been poured out, was flowing there. And because the minds of the persecutors, burning with insatiable fury, did not know how to show mercy even after the murder had been committed, they left the headless body behind and carried to Saint Ferreolus the head that their murderous hands had washed, so that he could not doubt that the man he saw severed by the sword had been killed, and might recognize that in death he himself would undergo what he saw in Julian’s body through his passion.

The executioners did all this without knowing it, according to the divine will, so that the spring, sprinkled with sacred blood, might become future salvation for many, and so that it might retain there in burial an even more precious union of the saints of God whom military fellowship had joined together. For just as Julian is in no way inferior to Ferreolus in heaven, so he is joined to him in the tomb by the greatest and principal part of his body.

O how happily the most blessed man, and with what swift a step, deserved to reach the highest summit! How quickly, fighting eagerly for Christ, the raw recruit became a veteran of accomplished service! The reward that courageous comrades in arms scarcely obtain after a long time and much labor, the brave warrior gained through a brief struggle, destined to receive the wages of immortality. By the authority of his victory, he made his untrained beginnings equal to the renowned ends of the saints. [Col. 1106B]

Thus, just as the martyr’s patience was consecrated in matters deserving proclamation, so the persecutors’ profane savagery was carried out; and the glorious soldier was divided, so to speak, among three places. His head was carried to Vienne, his body was taken to Brioude from the place where he had been struck, and his blessed soul was received by Christ the Creator.

But the most blessed old men, who, inflamed by spiritual grace, had committed the sacred body to burial, were so renewed that, although placed in extreme old age, they were strengthened with the vigor of youth and were regarded as young men. This martyr and witness of Christ, carefully buried there, is daily venerated with the joyful devotion of the faithful. There such great benefits and miracles are continually performed that no human tongue is sufficient to recount them.

[Note: The text from “In that place” through “for ever and ever” is absent from the German manuscripts b and u; in the other manuscripts and the editions it is chapter 3.]

At the place where the blessed [Col. 1106C] martyr was struck there is a bright spring, gentle and abundant in sweet waters, in which the head severed by the persecutors was washed. From these waters many healings are granted to the sick. Often the eyes of the blind have been touched by them and restored to sight. Those afflicted by the burning fevers of the third or fourth day find relief when they have drunk them. If someone suffering from a serious illness, inspired by the martyr, desires to draw water, as soon as he has drunk it he recovers; and the force of the fever is extinguished so swiftly that it is as if one were to see all the flames of an immense pyre quenched by waters poured upon them. For the people always rejoice in the grace of so great a patron, with the devotion of prayer granted [Note: “Effect” may perhaps be the correct reading instead of “devotion”]. And those whom that place receives in sorrow, it sends away joyful, while our Lord Jesus Christ reigns, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, belong honor, power, and glory forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1105]

# HISTORY OF THE SEVEN SLEEPERS (C)

## LETTER OF SAINT GREGORY, BISHOP OF TOURS, TO THE BLESSED SULPICIUS, ARCHBISHOP OF BOURGES, ON THE LIFE OF THE SEVEN SLEEPERS

[Col. 1105D] To the most blessed father Sulpicius, archbishop of Bourges by the grace of God, Gregory, unworthy priest of the people of Tours, sends perpetual greetings in God our Savior.

Among poets, the virtue and prudence of bees are praised under an allegory, when he says:

> The more exhausted they have become, the more keenly all  
> Labor to mend the ruins of their fallen race.  
> (Virgil, *Georgics* IV)

Most blessed Father, it was permissible to place this at the beginning of the letter, when one considers with how much prudence and care you strive to strengthen the condition of the tottering Church and repair its ruins. You do not cease to accomplish this especially through shining examples, through the honey-sweet words of your exhorting [Note: The Victor manuscript reads “exhortations”] sermons, and finally through bringing before the public the deeds of the saints who came before us.

This is why, among the other tasks that your eminence commanded my smallness to undertake, your pressing command—namely, the admonition of a friend—urged me to write down the deeds, life, and end of the Seven Sleepers, who are said to be resting at the monastery of Majus and whose fame is spread far and wide, if I could find them anywhere. Then, according to that poetic line, as is my custom and out of reverence for you, I replied:

> It is your task, gracious father, to explain what you desire;  
> It is my right to undertake what you command.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* I)

And immediately, as they say, with obedient step, following your command, I searched the chests of the churches and turned over the libraries. At last, at the aforementioned monastery of Majus, I found what I was seeking. I have therefore sent to Your Paternity, as you requested, a transcript preserving the Church’s account. For the rest, it is your task both to bring it forth and, for the sake of Christ’s grace, to seek and build churches and to obtain the grace of Christ the Lord for your friend—or rather, your obedient servant.

## HERE BEGINS THE LIFE, OR CONDUCT, AND ALSO THE DEATH OF THE SEVEN HOLY SLEEPERS [Note: The Claromontane manuscript adds “kinsmen of Saint Martin”], WHOSE BODIES ARE KEPT AT THE MONASTERY OF MAJUS AND WHOSE NAMES ARE INSCRIBED HERE: CLEMENS, PRIMUS, LAETUS, THEODORUS, GAUDENS, QUIRIACUS, INNOCENTIUS

[Col. 1107]

### I

[Col. 1107A] In the time of Diocletian and Maximian, as their cruelty demanded, almost the whole world began to withdraw and secede from Roman power. Among many peoples, the kingdom of the Huns seceded [Note: The Claromontane manuscript reads “of the Hungarians,” but below it calls them Huns, like the others], under the rule of Florus, a most vigorous king. When Florus’s father, named Amnarus [Note: The same codex reads *Aumarus* here and below; Victorinus generally reads *Ainarus*. Alberic, who wrote his chronicle in the thirteenth century, copied the genealogy of Saint Martin from this Life of the Seven Sleepers, which he attributes to our Gregory], had recently entered upon the way of all flesh, Florus acquired the kingdom when he was twenty years old.

The same Florus had two younger brothers, Martin and Amnarus. The aforementioned Florus took as his wife a very beautiful girl named Brichild, daughter of Chut, king of the Saxons. By her he fathered three sons: Florus the firstborn, father of the blessed Martin of Tours; Hilgrinus the second; and Amnarus the third. Hilgrinus, the second, fathered four sons: Clemens, Primus, [Col. 1107B] Laetus, and Theodorus. Amnarus, the third, fathered three: Gaudens, Quiriacus, and Innocentius.

Florus therefore enjoyed his kingdom prosperously for nearly ten years, until Maximian attacked him. After struggling for nearly three years, Maximian scarcely and with the greatest difficulty entered the first parts of Florus’s kingdom, and not without the death and blood of his own warriors. For Florus fought him two or three times and shamefully defeated and drove him away. But through the treachery of his own men, Maximian seized a certain fortress and fortified it against Florus and his kingdom; he did the same with a second and a third. Finally, he besieged Florus in a very strongly fortified castle, together with almost all the nobility of the Huns. After being besieged for half a year, Florus was compelled to surrender, on the condition that his life and limbs, and those of his people, would be spared.

Maximian took the captives with him to Rome. Among them were the two brothers of King Florus, Martin and Amnarus. Florus had not yet fathered any sons except his firstborn, Florus, who was three years old; he fathered the other two after returning from captivity. When the captives were presented to Diocletian, he sent them to prison. After about a year and a half, Diocletian remembered Florus’s uprightness and ordered him to be brought before him. Seeing that his beauty had withered from the filth and hardship of prison, he was moved by pity. He released Florus and sent him back to his own country, allowing him during his lifetime to retain his kingdom and its revenues, while the fortifications were removed or seized [Edition: “broken down”]. He permitted him to reign on this condition: after his death, his son would not be elevated to the kingship or the consulship, but would exist only as a tribune. When this agreement had been confirmed by both sides, Florus departed with all his people.

### II

After returning, he fathered two twin sons in that same year, Hilgrinus and Amnarus. [The following passage, enclosed in brackets, is replaced in the Victor manuscript and the editions by this text:

> “Diocletian, however, not long afterward, choosing a private life, ended his days at Milan. Maximian, when he plotted the death of his son-in-law Constantine, who at that time held the kingdom, by laying an ambush, was discovered through his deceit. He was captured at Massilia and, not long afterward, strangled in prison by demons, thus ending his impious life with a fitting death.”]

God, however, who does not show partiality to rulers, rejects their counsels, hardens whom He wills, delivers them over to a depraved mind, and brings them into confusion, permitted the emperors themselves, who had long afflicted the Church with the gravest persecutions, to undergo such a transformation of madness and vanity that Diocletian at Nicomedia and Maximian at Milan, on the same day laying aside the insignia of empire, lived as private citizens after their reign, like commoners.

But Maximian, repenting not long afterward of what he had done, plotted the death of his son-in-law Constantine, who already held the kingdom, by preparing an ambush. His treachery was discovered, and he was captured at Massilia; not long afterward he was strangled in prison, his neck broken by a noose. Or, as some assert, he was suffocated by demons and ended his impious life with a death he deserved. Diocletian, understanding that Constantine likewise regarded him as suspect for the same reason, became the impious punisher of himself by drinking poison, and ended the final day of his life at his villa near the town of Salona. When these men had thus been punished with both temporal and eternal death, and after the foul and dreadful darkness of wars and persecutions, the tranquility of the long-desired peace began, by divine command, to shine throughout the world, [Col. 1109B] Florus entrusted his firstborn son Florus to Constantine. Constantine had succeeded those same emperors, Diocletian and Maximian, after the very brief intervening joint reign only of his father Constantius and Galerius Maximian [Note: The editions, together with the Victor manuscript, read: “after a brief interval, with Auxentius as intermediary”]. [1273]

Constantine always held this Florus dear and beloved. When he had reached adulthood and become a soldier, Constantine gave him his niece as wife, the daughter of his sister, appointed him tribune, and sent him back to his father. By this wife he fathered a son while his own father was still alive, and ordered that he be called Florus. He [was indeed born in Constantine’s seventeenth year, but] afterward, in the time of [his son] Constantius, by the providence of God, became a catechumen and was baptized by the blessed Paul, bishop of Constantinople, and was named Martin [Note: The editions, together with the Victor manuscript, read “was named.” He was born in the eleventh year of Constantine. Florus, etc.].

[The venerable Paul, his baptizer and the same patriarch, was driven into exile by that same Constantius, who had succeeded his father in the empire and had turned toward the Arian heresy. He was exiled to a certain little town in Cappadocia called Cucusus because of the Catholic faith, and, cruelly strangled through the plotting of the Arians, he departed victoriously to the heavenly kingdoms [Note: The material concerning Saint Paul found here in the Claromontane codex is placed by the other manuscripts in the following section. Saint Athanasius likewise records his martyrdom. His feast is celebrated on June 7].]

The elder Florus, worn out by old age, ended his days, left his land to his firstborn son, and entrusted his two young brothers to him. After their father’s death, the son ruled the land bravely and married his brothers to the daughters of the noblest men of the Hunnish people. From these marriages his firstborn, namely Hilgrinus, as stated above, fathered four sons, while the second, Amnarus, fathered three.

### III

Thus Florus the tribune, son of King Florus, came to Constantinople after Constantine’s death, during the reign of Constantius, with his young son Florus [Note: That is, Martin. They wish him to have been called this at that time.], whom he commended to the emperor. The emperor kept him with him and made him a soldier [Note: So the Claromontanus manuscript. Others read: “he made him a soldier”; he also kept him with him after Constantius’s death, but the holy man, etc.].

[Julian Caesar also, while Martin was still a young man, brought him with him from that same Constantius, his paternal uncle, into Gaul against the barbarians who were ravaging Roman territory. Unaware of what had been ordained for Martin, Julian kept him in his entourage to provide military support and trained him in warfare for as long as he prevailed.]

But the holy man chose rather to serve the heavenly God than to serve as a soldier under an earthly emperor. [For [Note: We give within brackets what is found in the Claromontanus Codex; what the printed editions together with the Victoriacus have is placed here in the notes. “For it was specially ordained that the banner of the holy cross should be carried into the western regions of the world, and that the military oath should be exchanged for evangelical commands. He, as we have said, was first made a catechumen by the blessed Paul, bishop of Constantinople, in the time of Constantius, with God as his teacher, and was baptized not long afterward. This blessed bishop was driven into exile by the emperor Constantine because of the Catholic faith, at a certain city of Cappadocia called Cuthusa, and was cruelly strangled by the plots of the Arians; he departed to the heavenly kingdom. After the mystery of holy baptism, blessed Martin became renowned throughout the world for great miracles and shone far and wide throughout the earth with Catholic teachings. He first spent the flower of his youth in the city of Milan, but afterward, expelled by the ferocity of the Arian rulers, withdrew into the regions of Gaul and joined the venerable bishop Hilary of Poitiers. After laying aside his military belt, holy Martin attached himself to that bishop’s instruction. From there, warned by a divine oracle, the holy man converted his parents, who had abandoned error, to the profession of the holy faith; and the mother who had given him birth in the world he himself begot in Christ. He followed the example of his grandfathers Martin and Amnarus, who were most Christian, and of the cities, etc.”]

For this purpose in particular he was destined: that the triumphant banner of the holy cross should be carried into the western parts of the world, there to be raised and worshiped, and that the military oath should be exchanged for evangelical commands. Illustrious by his ancestors, but more illustrious by his merits, holy from infancy, devoted from childhood, perfect in adolescence, he advanced perpetually from day to day and from virtue to virtue; he became renowned in the world for great miracles and shone far and wide with Catholic teachings.

For one who had begun at the outset of his ways in God with such virtue and so great and astonishing a miracle, what wonder if he always had prosperous progress and blessed outcomes in them? Indeed, would it not be astonishing if, after such a remarkable conversion—by which God drew him to himself—a conversion lofty in virtue, glorious in the brightness of miracles, and splendid in the beauty of religious devotion, he did not continue that way of life unceasingly until the end of his life?

Who would not consider it more marvelous than almost every virtue and miracle that a child scarcely ten years old, as one might say still at his mother’s breast, should abhor the fanatic superstition of error imbibed with his mother’s milk, and, despite his parents, guardians, and attendants trying to dissuade him—now by threats, now by blows, now by blandishments—take refuge in the faith of Christ and in fellowship with the Church, whose sacraments he had not yet received?
