Who would not raise to the highest praise a twelve-year-old boy who, like a prudent and courageous man, disregarding the weakness of his age, desired the harshness of the desert and everything he might have to endure there as though they were delights; and what he could not yet accomplish because of bodily weakness, but was later to fulfill, began already to perform before God by meditating and desiring it—for God sometimes counts willingness as action?

Who would not judge an adolescent worthy of distinguished praise who, raised amid the greatest luxuries and bound by his father’s authority to secular military service, nevertheless conducted himself like a solitary or monk, restraining himself not only from evil deeds but from every wicked desire, and preserving himself undefiled in the midst of a Babylonian furnace burning with sulfur and pitch? While others plundered what belonged to others and mocked him, he gave to the poor not only his surplus possessions but even what was necessary for himself—and, indeed, went beyond the command [the syntax requires *transcendisse*, “went beyond”], as is evident from what he did with the divided cloak.

We have a command to give one of two garments for Christ, not to divide one garment; this is what he did, for his heart was ready to expend both his possessions and himself for Christ and, for Christ’s sake, for his brothers. Who would not also receive with amazement this fact about him: that, although he was placed among exceedingly wealthy and illustrious parents, descended as he was from royal ancestors, and was compelled in his youth to follow and serve first King Constantius and then Julian Caesar, now one and now the other, in different parts of the world—being their maternal uncles’ sons—although one was an Arian and the other an apostate, and both persecutors of the orthodox, nevertheless, amid such a conflict of circumstances opposed to him, he preserved an uncorrupted faith, always embraced earthly poverty, and maintained perfect humility?

Who would pass over without reflection this further fact about him? When he saw Christ clothed in the portion of the cloak with which he had covered a poor man, and saw that portion as though it were displaying itself and glorying before the angels, he himself did not glory in so great and glorious a vision, a vision in which another might have gloried. Rather, he was humbled. With eager longing, like a thirsty deer seeking springs of water, he returned to Constantinople and received from the blessed Paul, patriarch of that city, the sacrament of baptism, as we have said. He had diligently revolved this in his heart and had long labored to bring it to birth; now, as though it were ripe for natural delivery, he eagerly resolved to bring it forth into the fruit of life.

What was this, then? That, having trampled underfoot all the delights of the seductive world, he might freely devote himself to God and, without interruption from external cares, raise a heavenly way of life, tasting more frequently and seeing how sweet the Lord is. Since he regarded this one thing as supremely necessary according to the Lord’s command and burned with intense desire to attain it alone, who would not delight to contemplate, who would not try to imitate, how with such simple and genuine love he postponed it for the salvation of his brother?

O truly marvelous kindness of the holy youth! Although he knew that he could obtain this best portion, which is taken from no one who follows it, only in the cleft of the rock and the hollow of the wall—where there is one protection and a unique refreshment for those who flee into shelter from the heat of day, and safety and concealment from storm and rain—nevertheless, because of his resolve to save his companion, he endured the world’s hardships against his own desire for two years. He stood outside, as though without a roof, amid storms, showers, and hailstones, in deep mud and on the slippery ground of the world, where his foot could find no rest; where he was afflicted not only by injuries but also pressed by innumerable dangers.

What would he do—or rather, what would he not do—for the salvation of many, who endured so much weariness and bore so prolonged a loss of his own repose for the devotion of one person? What crosses, punishments, or injuries, if inflicted for the Savior, would he not prefer to every kind of banquet, however luxurious, when for the love of a mortal man he postponed for so long the one desire of his unique joy, the delay of which tormented him severely?

But surely the patience of the holy youth was being exercised, his courage tested, and his experience formed. Through spontaneous love he was foreshadowing in himself what he would later have to do, at the proper time, for many, when placed as a bishop over souls. Thus instructed in his youth, he did this very thing in old age, beyond almost all other people and more than could rightly have been demanded of him.

In the days of the emperor Maximus, when he walked according to the love that does not seek its own, he not only desired to become like Paul, but almost made himself accursed from Christ for the sake of brothers belonging to a harmful communion—not by his own will but under compulsion, entering into the assembly so that he might provide for the churches of Spain, over whose necks the sword of a savage king hung.

Yet he knew without doubt that, to fulfill the law, the burdens of others must be borne by others; he knew that love is the fullness of the law, that love is the bond of perfection and the beginning of spiritual fruits; he knew that through it people must serve one another, that love never fails, and that one who walks in it neither goes astray nor falls away. Relying on the support of so great a virtue, he confidently presumed that whatever loss he might at some time incur for preserving it could easily be restored or made good through that same love, which covers a multitude of sins.

And I beg no one to judge this digression burdensome or pointless merely because it concerns the contemplation of the merits of Martin while he was still a young man. The whole purpose of this little work looks toward him, and we have moved our sluggish pen not less to display the abundance of his love, with which he was always filled, and the nobility of his origin—which Severus, the first writer of his life, omitted—than to make known to posterity the venerable conduct and death of the relatives mentioned above.

### IV

But now let us return from these matters to the sequence of the narrative we have undertaken. Martin, stripped of the old man and clothed through baptism in the new [man], remained in the retinue of his tribune, whom he was so eager to win for Christ. When the period of his tribuneship had elapsed, the tribune had promised that he would change his life and manner and serve God. Overcome by Martin’s entreaties and bound, as it were, by affection, Martin remained with him for two years, occupied not with plunder but with holy works, as he had begun.

When the period of waiting—which he bore most grievously—had ended, he did not immediately agree to remain, but renounced flesh and blood. Although Caesar resisted and was indignant, he renounced secular military service and abandoned his parents, estates, and homeland, where he had been born and was known, and where he could have been regarded as wealthy, illustrious, and therefore honored and distinguished. Since God was appointing him for us as a patron, he fled into these foreign regions, where he would be considered unknown and without distinction, an exiled and praiseworthy poor man. As evidence of his great humility, he submitted himself to be instructed by the teaching and example of Hilary, a man of outstanding distinction and renown, who in those days appeared as the singular light and pillar of the Gallican Church. He did this so that, if he followed only his own judgment and made himself his own teacher, he would not run in vain or dangerously; and so that he would not fall among those of whom it is said: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight” (Isaiah 5:21).

While he was laboring in the school of virtue, his teacher ordered him to ascend to a higher rank in the Levitical order. But, to advance in his progress, he settled instead in the lowest office of exorcist, all the more securely because it was more humble. At length, with the same teacher both granting and admiring it, he remained there.

What, then, would become of a man established upon such humility? Would it not be that, according to the Scriptures, glory would receive the humble in spirit; that he who had humbled himself would be exalted by the supreme teacher of humility, whom he almost followed; and that he would make known to others the ways of life which, while submissively silent, he had investigated, being powerful in deed and word and worthy of apostolic ministry?

But how could he approach ministry unless he were appointed? And how could he preach unless he were sent? Therefore, while he lived with his teacher in complete submission and was quietly instructed, thinking nothing great of himself and planning nothing lofty, he was commanded by the Lord—who observed and highly valued the heart of his little servant—to perform the work of an evangelist by revelation. He was also instructed to visit his parents, who were still held by the error of paganism, in order to disclose to them the faith of Christ.

Relying, then, upon the divine oracle and with the permission of the blessed Hilary—for he had not yet been sent into exile by Augustus Constantius in defense of the faith—he obediently departed for the place to which he had been ordered. Scattering the word of God everywhere, he strove to bring a rich harvest from the conversion of unbelievers into Christ’s granary. With heavenly grace cooperating, he converted his parents to the profession of the Christian faith. Only his father remained, by the inscrutable judgment of God, in the image and error of the earthly man, defending the superstition of fanatic worship solely by the authority of an old custom wrongly imbibed from infancy.

His mother also, who had given him birth in the world, he himself regenerated in Christ: he became the spiritual father of her whose fleshly son he was. He granted her to be the beginning of a new creation for the world, from whom he himself, after God, had received his beginning as a human being.

He also brought it about that she and the others whom he had gathered for salvation were reborn in Christ through the hands of his father’s paternal uncles—that is, his great-uncles Martin and Aumarius—who were most Christian and, in the cities assigned to them, exercised the office of bishop. Among those baptized were also his paternal uncles Hilgrinus and Amnarus, together with their seven sons: namely Clement, Primus, Laetus, Theodorus, Gaudentius, Quiriacus, and Innocentius.

Their fathers, Hilgrinus and Amnarus, did not divide their paternal inheritance like other brothers. Rather, just as they had been born twins from one birth, so they remained content with one household, one estate, and one common possession, together with their wives and sons. In the same year in which they were baptized, they entered upon the way of all flesh.

The seven sons named above therefore sold all their estates and distributed the proceeds to the poor; they also set their slaves free. They themselves shut themselves away in a certain place, devoting themselves to reading, prayer, and psalmody, content with only two little servants to provide them with assistance and comfort.

They lived together in an upper room, without complaint and pleasing both God and human beings. They lacked the agreeable companionship of wives and children and strove to lead a celibate life. From the remains of their food, wherever they were carried or by whatever sick persons they were consumed, those who suffered from any illness were immediately healed.

For this reason, at first from the neighboring province and afterward from almost the entire region, people came to them and venerated them like prophets of God. Many of these, imitating their faith through their preaching, submitted themselves to Christianity; stripping off the old man, they put on the new, who has been created according to God.

Finally, everyone honored them with acts of service and many gifts [Note: The Claromontanus reads: “they honored them with presents.”]. Christian princes, tribunes, and soldiers, as well as Jews and pagans, visited, revered, and honored them.

Moved by this, the servants of God, fearing subjection to the empty glory and ambition of this world, resolved to seek a hiding place in flight and to leave their homeland. For they had the example of Abraham in this matter, as well as many other righteous men of more recent times, and, most recently, their cousin, the most blessed Martin [Note: Printed editions with the Victoriacus read: “And many other righteous men, and above all their cousin, the blessed Martin.” But on hearing the report of his holiness, etc.]. [Who, just as he obediently heard both the commands and the counsels of Christ and placed nothing before his love, but left everything, took up his cross, denied himself, followed Christ as his leader, and entrusted himself to Christ’s will, rejecting the ruinous freedom of doing whatever he pleased, so Christ also generously fulfilled in him the promise he had made. He had glorified him, though he fled these things, with the glory of miracles, the honor of the episcopate, and an abundance of riches; he had already repaid him a hundredfold even in this life, reserving for the future the fullness of everlasting recompense.

When he alone had gone out from his land and kindred for Christ’s sake, Christ his leader glorified him in the land of his pilgrimage and performed wonders at the word of his mouth. Wonderful to relate, he raised up children of Abraham from stones, changed human hearts, led the erring and unbelieving to the paths of righteousness and to the prudence of the just. He overturned shrines, founded monasteries, and built churches; and so, gradually increasing, he had become a great nation.]

### V

When the aforesaid men heard of his sanctity and the fame of his name, and that he had been appointed to the episcopate of the city of Tours, they took counsel together. After making a short provision of money and gathering a few belongings, they determined to go to him and live according to his counsel [page 1279]—and so it happened.

When they came as far as the city of Tours, they found the blessed Martin, as was his custom, celebrating the solemn Mass on the Lord’s Day in his episcopal church. Like pilgrims, they asked for his blessing.

When the divine solemnities of the Mass had been completed [Others: “when the rites had been completed”], the most blessed Martin recognized them as his kinsmen and cousins. He wept over each of them and kissed them. He led them across the river with him, to the place where a multitude of brothers lived, and invited them to dine together with the brothers.

On the following day they recounted the whole course of their pilgrimage and said that it was their intention to visit the thresholds of the apostles Peter and Paul, to go also to Jerusalem to visit the Lord’s tomb and worship the Lord’s cross, and to travel by way of the tomb of blessed James, and then return to Martin.

With the blessing of the blessed Martin, they undertook this journey barefoot, wearing woolen garments and living on bread, water, and raw herbs. They completed it over five years.

When they returned safe and unharmed, they presented themselves to the blessed Martin with many relics: from the Lord’s tomb and his most holy cross; from the tomb of holy Mary, the Lord’s mother, and from her garments; from the relics of the apostles Peter and Paul and of holy James, the Lord’s brother; and many others. The blessed Martin reverently received them and placed them with reverence in the apse of the principal church.

The seven brothers themselves, surrendering both soul and body to the blessed Martin and to the brothers living there, vowed that they would not leave that place. At once the blessed Martin gladly received them, clothed them in the monastic habit, and confirmed them with his own blessing. He placed them beside a hollowed mountain, in a certain cave. He also made an oratory for them in the rock itself [Note: They say that this is the place still seen today near the basilica of the Major Monastery, hollowed out in the overhanging rock, where their tombs—or rather, representations of their tombs—are carved in stone]. He blessed the altar and deposited there with his own hand the relics they had brought.

He ordained Clement and Primus priests; Laetus and Theodorus, deacons; and Gaudentius, Quiriacus, and Innocentius, subdeacons. They remained in the same cell or oratory, delighting in fasting, prayer, silence, and reading, for as long as the blessed Martin lived.

Martin himself, foreseeing his death long beforehand through a revelation, decided to go to the village of Condat, in order to restore peace among the clergy of that church who were divided against one another. Knowing also through the Spirit that he would not return, he summoned all the brothers of the monastery, kissed each of them, blessed them, and appointed one of the brothers in his place, named Gualbert. He made him abbot and confirmed him with his blessing. He also commended to him the seven brothers mentioned above, his cousins, and Gualbert received them. He loved them individually among the other brothers and visited and strengthened them spiritually.

### VI

After his death, the blessed Martin very often appeared to them in visions until the day of their departure, consoling and strengthening them [Note: So the Claromontanus manuscript; this resolves Marollius’s difficulty, since in the printed editions he read: “They lived twenty-five years after the death of blessed Martin, sixteen years during the lifetime of blessed Martin, and thirty years under Gualbert, the first abbot after blessed Martin, and two years under Aicard, the second abbot. During the time of Aicard, etc.”].

They lived with him in their holy calling for sixteen years and, after his departure, for twenty-five: namely, twenty-three years under Gualbert, the first abbot, and two years under Aicard, the second abbot.

During the time of this Aicard, the second abbot, it happened that the feast of blessed Martin’s departure fell on a Saturday. On the following day, when we celebrate the Lord’s Day, after the solemn office of Matins had been completed, blessed Martin appeared to them at midnight and announced the day of their death, saying:

“Tomorrow, very early in the morning, call Aicard the abbot here to you. When he is present, tell him one by one the whole course of your lives and your deeds, confessing all your sins. Say to him from me that he should celebrate a Mass in honor of the holy Trinity, commemorating me and placing upon the present altar, consecrated by me, the saints whose relics it contains. Let him offer individual hosts for each of you, to be sacrificed [Others: “to be offered”], and, when they have been consecrated, let each of you communicate.

“When communion has been completed and you have received as viaticum the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, and when the Mass has ended, you shall prostrate yourselves in prayer and enter upon the way of all flesh. You shall be strangers both to the pain of death and to the corruption of the flesh. Thus you shall be received by the angels and led upward by me myself, until we present you before the tribunal of Christ.”

All this took place as the blessed Martin had commanded. When they had received communion [Others: “the viaticum”] from the hand of Aicard the abbot, and the Mass had ended, they knelt down, healthy and unharmed, and, prostrate in prayer, entered upon the way of all flesh, just as Martin had foretold. They had been strangers both to the pain of death and to the corruption of the flesh.

At once that cell was filled with such a fragrance that it seemed as though a mass of many spices had been scattered there. Aicard the abbot, together with the brothers, received them not as dead but as though from prayer, and considered them sleeping, since their faces were red like roses and their flesh shone like snow.

Therefore he arranged them on seats as they had been accustomed to sit in their cell and placed them where all could see them. Only the necessary barriers were set between them and those entering, to protect them from the violence of the crowds.

The doors also stood open so that all who came might see the faces of the saints, not like those of the dead but like those of the sleeping; for although they were dead to human beings, they slept in God, to whom all things live.

For the seven days during which they remained above the earth, that most sweet fragrance did not disappear. The number of visitors was as great as the place allowed and the roads and paths could contain.

All those suffering from fever or chills who came returned healthy. Many lepers, deaf people, mute people, and lame people were healed. Those who could not come were carried in beds and pallets, and through the fragrance they returned in good health.

Finally, on the seventh day after their departure, Aicard the abbot gathered the brothers of the holy monastery and attended the funeral. He also sent for and summoned the most holy old man, the bishop of the city of the see of Tours [Note: So the Claromontanus; others read “archbishop.” Bishops in the West were not given this title in Gregory’s age, nor did Gregory elsewhere use it], the blessed Brictius, together with the clergy and people.

After taking counsel, they buried them as they were clothed, in that same cell or oratory, before the altar of the oratory, which had been consecrated by the blessed Martin with the relics of the saints.

They departed on the day before the Ides of November, the second day after the feast on which the departure of Saint Martin is celebrated, and were laid to rest [Note: So the Claromontanus; others read “were buried.” From this one may infer that the name of the day of deposition does not always mean the day of death. Their sacred bodies are preserved in coffers behind the principal high altar of the basilica of the Major Monastery].

On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December [Note: Besides these Seven Sleepers, there are others likewise famous at Ephesus, whom Gregory discusses in chapter 95 of Book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*. Paul the Deacon also praises seven Sleepers in Germany in Book I, chapter 4, of *The Deeds of the Lombards*; after Baronius, Marollius does not appear to regard them as the same as these].

Although buried in the earth, they show by their virtues and miracles that they live in Christ, through the favor of that same Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1117] Here ends the life and death of the Seven Sleepers.

### Prologue of Saint Gregory, Archbishop of Tours, to the Life [Note: It would more properly be said, “to the lives of the blessed Maurilius and Albinus.” If you wish to know why Ruinart did not reprint these lives here, although they are elsewhere published under the name of Fortunatus, consult the preface, no. 80, column 65. Editor.] of the Blessed Maurilius, Bishop and Confessor

(From several manuscript codices.) (C)

To the most holy lord Germanus, bishop of the holy mother Church of Paris, Gregory, humble bishop of the metropolitan church of Tours, sends greetings.

You indeed asked that we correct, by the competence of our authority, the lives and miracles which the Lord graciously performed through the blessed Maurilius and Albinus, bishops of Angers, and which the priest Fortunatus had described in polished language but which had by now been almost corrupted by the faults of scribes; and that we send them to your Devotion, since you desire to advance through the examples of those who came before.

But when we recall that, if we undertake this, we shall be torn apart by the barking and bites of the treacherous—people who do not know how to seek instruction but only to envy—we are shaken by the sorrow of a double weariness, fearing both to disobey your commands and to displease them.

Nevertheless, trusting in the promises of the Almighty, who, speaking through his prophet, made known that “those who sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Psalm 125:6), we shall satisfy your will.

For we know that if someone arranges and corrects with his pen the lives and virtues of the most holy confessors of Christ—things worthy of imitation and capable of benefiting another age—even if in a rustic style, he will gain a reward for himself and confer salvation upon those who wish to imitate them.

Therefore, considering it a crime not to speak of or correct the very great virtues of the most precious confessors of Christ, Maurilius and Albinus, because they are worthy of remembrance, we shall, as you requested, use a plebeian pen, which may benefit ordinary people more readily. Of the many matters, we shall correct a few, but, with God as our witness, the truest ones, omitting many things published by Fortunatus that might perhaps appear incredible to unbelievers.

What we have corrected we have thought proper to offer more worthily to your Holiness’s request, so that you, who rejoice to imitate them, may advance by being instructed through their virtues.

### The Life of Saint Maurilius Begins

Thus Maurilius was a native of the town of Milan, born to most illustrious parents, etc.

(In the Patriciacian Codex of Percy, in Burgundy, written approximately eight hundred years ago, after the Life of Saint Albinus, which is usually attributed to Fortunatus, this conclusion is found: “Here ends the Life of the blessed Albinus, composed by the blessed Gregory, bishop of the city of Tours.”)

### Antiphon of Saint Gregory, Bishop of Tours, on Saints Medard and Gildard, Bishops and Brothers

(From a manuscript codex in Surius, under 8 June.) (C, S)

Hail, great bishops throughout the whole world, twin in birth, equal in holiness, consecrated together, crowned alike, joined together—you have proclaimed one feast day. Holy Medard, together with illustrious Gildard, always bring aid to the people who ask for help.

### The Life of Saint Aridius, Abbot

[Note: This little work is entirely corrupt, as will be evident to the reader, and abounds in incomplete phrases. Editor.]

(Extracted by Dom J. Mabillon from an ancient manuscript codex of Saint Gall.) (C, S)

#### In the Name of Our Lord Jesus Christ, the Prologue of Saint Gregory, Bishop of Tours, on the Life of the Blessed Aridius, Abbot of Limoges, Begins

#### I

Whenever we narrate the deeds of the saints and fix our minds upon their actions and examples, or desire to be their imitators, we do so lest we be held captive in the misery of this exile by its snare.

We are illuminated by heavenly grace to the degree that, with humbled heart, we are able to ascend to the heights through contemplation of God. Therefore we do not freely dare, although we could, to unfold for the people in speech, however modest, a history that might edify—especially since apostolic authority admonishes us to recall certain matters concerning the life or virtues of the saints, as it is written: “Let us praise glorious men, who conquered the kingdoms of the world, so that their memory may be in blessing and their name may endure forever” (Ecclesiasticus 44:1); and again: “The memory of the saints is with praises” (Proverbs 10:7).

Therefore, when in the yearly cycle we celebrate the solemn feasts of the saints, we ought to recount some of their deeds for the edification of Christians gathered together in the praises of Christ.

Since the miracles of almost all the confessors and the manifold victories of the martyrs have already been committed to written memorials, we have now attempted, according to the quality of our talent, to compose even this small book. In it, with the help of Christ’s grace, we undertake to explain the birth, life, and glorious death of the holy and most blessed confessor Aridius, so that the one whose life is with Christ may have his memory celebrated in the world with glory.

Our holy fathers strove to love nothing in this world so that they might love their neighbors lawfully and perfectly, and, gathered together in one love, become Christ’s co-heirs and participants.

Many, fighting from earliest age; some in adolescence or youth; many in old age, tried to cling to the Lord, so that those who had long endured the world’s temptations might at last return to Christ without stain.

The example of a good work, with the simplicity of strength, edifies more than much preaching accompanied by the swelling of empty glory. The excellent preacher, the teacher of the nations, bears witness, saying: “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Corinthians 1:27); and again: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Corinthians 3:19).

The elect are not lifted up by the prosperity of the world, so that they may be able to grasp the crown after triumph. For if we consider what and how much is promised to us in heaven, the things seen on earth become worthless in our minds.

#### II

Thus the most blessed Aridius [Note: A shorter life of this saint, which appears to be an epitome of this one, is found among the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, first century, p. 349. Moreover, chapter 29 of Book X of our Gregory of Tours’ *History* presents in a few words almost everything narrated here at greater length.] was born of noble family in the province of Aquitaine, in farther Gaul, which faces toward the western region. He was a native of the city of Limoges, destined, by the Lord’s gift to his soldiers, to be a lamp for all the faithful.

His father was named Jucundus [Note: He is called Roscindus in the common printed editions of Gregory, Book II of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, but we have removed that error from the manuscript codices. The same Gregory praises Pelagia, especially in *The Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 104. Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, writes in the Life of Gerald that Caesarius, bishop of Arles, and Aridius [Note: His name is written this way as well. Editor.] the abbot came from the same stock, from which Saint Gerald, count of Aurillac, later arose.], while his blessed mother was called Pelagia.

Their way of life testified that they were religious, walking in the commandments of God so as to be without blame, like Zachariah and Elizabeth (Luke 1:16), except that John was not among them.

Aridius was therefore born and raised in the true faith. Finally, having been instructed in the Catholic religion by Christian parents, he passed beyond the years of childhood and entered adolescence with great diligence.

When his parents saw that, in adolescence, their son had taken up the wholesome path and was adorned with devotion to religion, they entrusted him to be educated in letters.

He was immediately so illuminated by divine grace that many marveled at his eloquence in speech, for his discourse, sweet and flowing from a honeyed mouth, delighted everyone.

Carrying an old man’s heart, he gave his spirit to no pleasure, lest he be captured and held subject to the misery of the world.

### III

Meanwhile, he was commended to the most illustrious King Theudebert, so that he might educate him in the learning of the palace. Thus Aridius found favor before God and before the king, and his reputation was borne by everyone, to such an extent that he served as the king’s chief chancellor. His honor increased with great favor from day to day; approved on every side, he flourished at court. The king treated him with such familiarity that his great good fortune aroused intense hatred in many.

For he hated pride and loved truth; yet the good held him in admiration. He therefore pursued charity, gentleness, and humility without ceasing. He loved the Lord with all his heart, with all his soul, and with all his mind. He was serene in appearance and tranquil in manner; he always displayed good works more through deeds than words, continually entrusting his hope to Christ, frequently devoting himself to prayer, and preferring nothing to the love of Christ. His mind was always meditating on the heavenly commandments.

### IV

When these things had taken place, not long afterward, as he was already living in manhood and desired to offer himself to the Lord as a sanctified vessel, fearing the future and dreadful judgments lest any sins should stain his heart, he confessed all the deeds of his youth before the blessed Bishop Nicetius.

Thereafter, having been divinely admonished through the aforesaid Nicetius, bishop of the city of Trier, he fled the pomp of the world, avoided worldly pleasures, the vain superstitions of the royal palace, and the undisciplined stories of his companions, and submitted himself to the discipline of a rule in order to contemplate the palm of the heavenly homeland. Imposing upon himself a severe penance, he began manfully to resist the struggle of the flesh with the fervor of the spirit.

For the future fires of punishment he set before himself against the present fires of the flesh: “in labors,” as the Apostle says, “in vigils, in fastings, in purity, in gentleness, in great patience, and in sincere love” (2 Corinthians 6:6). He therefore prayed to the Lord for heavenly gifts and prayed to Christ by day and by night. He deprived himself of satiety from bread, so that he might merit for himself the bread of heaven. His face grew pale through fasting, and his body withered, becoming exceedingly dry; but his mind burned with desire for eternal things.

Always contemplating the end of the present life and the Lord’s future sentence, he feared the judgments that were to be dreaded, knowing what is written: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful” (Proverbs 28:14). He also remembered what was said by Job: “I have always feared the Lord, as though waves swelling against me” (Job 31:23); and the Apostle’s words: “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling” (Philippians 2:12).

Before the sight of God he lay at night, beating his breast with his hands, wetting his cheeks with tears, and raising his eyes toward heaven. He always looked toward Him whom he feared he might have offended by sinning even in the smallest matters. With tears, and with David’s voice, he earnestly prayed these words: “Against you alone have I sinned; have mercy on me, Lord, according to your great mercy” (Psalm 50:6–7). He was always striving toward what the Apostle said: “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart—what the Lord has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9).

Meditating on these things, the more he advanced, the more he humbled himself, according to what Truth says in the Gospel: “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted, and whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 18:14). The more he had been humbled, the more he advanced; and, so that the measure of his sorrow might also become the measure of his pardon—O profound goodness of the Lord! O simple penance!—by frequent fasting he obtained from the Lord the mercy he sought.

For concerning such people the Lord says through the prophet: “I gave him fear, and he feared me, and he trembled before the face of my name” (Malachi 2:5). Again it is written: “He who fears the Lord will fear nothing and will not tremble, for he is himself” (Ecclesiasticus 34:16). And again: “The fear of the Lord drives out sin” (Ecclesiasticus 1:27).

Amid these practices he prayed to the Lord with all his strength, so that his penance might be acceptable before the presence of Christ. Then, equipped with these weapons and binding himself more tightly within Christ’s militia, he conformed himself to the rule of the Church.

### V

One day, as he was maintaining the course of a most pure conscience, a dove descended from the chamber, settled upon his head, and accompanied him as he proceeded through the street. The man of God Aridius could not remove it from himself until he entered the cell of his bishop. When the day declined toward evening, the dove returned by the way it had come.

When morning arrived and the clergy were returning to the church, it descended upon his head again, just as it had done before. For thirty days, as he himself secretly related, the man of God endured this embarrassment without the dove ceasing. He perceived in it a sign of heavenly grace, so that it might plainly be understood that the Spirit would then descend upon him once and for all through divine generosity.

Therefore Truth also testifies to the disciples, saying: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him; and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23). For it was fitting that, since he had guarded the innocence of his mind, the visitation of the Holy Spirit should be present with him.

### VI

When the blessed man heard of his father’s death, he returned to Limoges to console his mother. The blessed Pelagia then exchanged her worldly clothing for the dress of a holy woman and became religious in the love of God. She urged her son, who was living a good life, toward his reward.

The blessed man immediately sought the wilderness. He withdrew into a hollow rock and there, day and night without ceasing, prayed to the Lord, continually striving to repel the invisible enemy through prayers and supplications, fighting with his mouth rather than with a sword, with prayers rather than with iron, with petitions rather than with a weapon. At every hour and every moment he begged God’s protection, so that after the labor of the world he might be found worthy to reach the prize.

After he had remained there for several days with great abstinence, his mother heard of this and fell at her son’s feet. She asked him to come out and build a monastic cell in a pleasant rural place where he could look upon it with satisfaction.

Then the man of God Aridius found a pleasant site, nearly three miles from the same rock into which he had withdrawn, and there he began with great diligence to build a monastic cell. This monastery was called Atano.

> **Note:** It still exists today among the people of Limoges, although it has been converted into a college of canons under the jurisdiction of the chapter of Saint Martin of Tours. The town received the name by which it is commonly called, Saint-Irier.

There, intent upon prayer and devoted to reading whenever he had leisure, while his venerable mother labored in the fields and sought food for his body: but what life she lived after her conversion [lacuna].

The blessed man grew ever stronger in vigils, fastings, prayers, and charity. His fame began to spread, and religious men—strangers and monks—flocked to him from everywhere. A multitude of poor people also gathered around him like bees to a hive. Indeed, however many poor people came to him, no one departed from him empty-handed.

Why say more? Whatever he possessed from the property of his noble parents, he distributed entirely among the poor or among monasteries—especially to the church of blessed Martin of Tours and that of Saint Hilary of Poitiers—as well as among various churches and his own monastery. He scattered his gold and silver among the poor, mindful of the Apostle’s command: “Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content” (1 Timothy 6:8); and: “Those who desire to become rich in this world fall into temptation and the devil’s snare” (1 Timothy 6:9); and: “Many useless and harmful desires, which plunge a person into destruction and perdition” (ibid.).

Considering what is written—“Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41)—and what Truth says: “He will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life” (Matthew 19:29), and what is written elsewhere: “Almsgiving delivers from death, and whoever practices it will not enter darkness” (Tobit 12:9), he fulfilled these things daily. He was always generous in almsgiving, diligent in vigils, devoted in prayer, abundant in humility, and perfect in charity.

He never gave himself over to idleness without either devoting himself to reading, completing Christ’s work, working with his hands, or finally copying sacred books. Above all, he had resolved to distribute among neighboring dioceses the sacred books that he himself had written with his own hands, remembering what the Apostle said: “Idleness is the enemy of the soul.”

In these activities, therefore, he never ceased at any time. When he had built the monastic cell and completed the work he had begun, it is necessary, with Christ’s help, to explain something of his miracles. We shall gladly publish the miracles that are to be proclaimed concerning the way in which this servant of God devoted himself to almsgiving, vigils, and prayers; of these many miracles, we believe that a few may be briefly related.

### VII

It happened that the man of God Aridius was traveling in Auvergne. When night overtook him, he could find no water or place where he might take shelter. While his attendants searched here and there without finding any, Aridius thrust his staff into the sand. When he pulled it out, an abundant spring leapt forth from a fissure in the earth, so that its surging waters were sufficient and later irrigated the place to such an extent that cattle drank there.

Thus this great man was remarkable in miracles, bearing the type of Moses, who struck the rock and provided water for the people in the wilderness.

He then took care to choose companions for his journey, men whom religious devotion made distinguished. After gathering the group, he requested the support of everyone’s prayers, so that the Giver of mercy might grant comfort for the journey ahead. Under Christ’s leadership, he then approached with them the place where the sacred remains of Saint Julian the martyr had been buried, recognizing those who were present with him by the will of the merciful Judge.

When they reached the place, he asked that he himself might merit to receive the relics of the holy martyr with a devout heart. But the guardian of the basilica of the most blessed martyr refused his request.

After remaining there for a short while and searching without finding anything at all, he proceeded onward and came to the place where the venerable martyr had been beheaded by his persecutors long before. With the fullest devotion, he cheerfully placed in the reliquary that he wore around his neck a very small quantity of the stones from that place—what is commonly called sand—as sacred relics of the holy martyr.

When he began to return from that province, such a multitude of people tormented by evil spirits followed in his footsteps with great cries that scarcely could all their names be recorded.

The fame of the blessed man therefore reached the ears of the bishop of that city.

> **Note:** That is, the bishop of Auvergne, in whose diocese the church of Brioude then stood.

He immediately followed the holy man’s footsteps with his own people and, falling at his feet, began to ask him to return at last to the tomb of the holy martyr and bring away his sacred relics.

Then he said: “This gift that almighty God has bestowed upon me I shall carry with me, proceeding with it as my companion. For the Lord, Creator of all, has deigned to display two miracles of power at the same place.”

When the man of God opened his reliquary, he found various precious stones among the stones that he had taken from the spring, so that the wonderful power of the holy martyr might be proclaimed in different regions of the earth, the faith of the man of God might be proved, and the matter might be shown to many.

When he reached the place where the man of God had built an oratory, he deposited the sacred gift there with great joy. There also almighty God deigned to reveal many signs and wonders.

### VIII

Nor should what was granted to Christ’s servant be omitted. One day, while the traveler was proceeding along the road he had undertaken, a violent wind was blowing and such rain roared around Aridius that the downpour flowed in streams; yet not a single drop wet him or his attendants. The storm parted, the whirlwind turned elsewhere, and the clouds fled through the air, fearing the traveler.

If, then, the sea and the winds obeyed the Creator of all things amid the waves, and “a great calm” came to pass, he likewise commanded this power to be displayed before all who saw it in his faithful servant.

On another occasion, when the crops had armed themselves with ripe ears and, already heavy, demanded to be cut by the farmer, an enormous rainstorm broke out, preventing anyone from gathering the harvest, so that the grains hidden in their ears might sprout.

Meanwhile, the people appealed to him, and the intercessor held vigils. On the following day, he took up the relics of the saints, carefully and reverently covered with a little silk cloak. The deacons came out in white garments for the procession, while the people cried out because of the assault of the storm clouds.

The holy man replied to them: “He who commanded water to be created is powerful enough to calm this rain.”

Then, as they immediately proceeded from the church, the clouds were suddenly cut apart, the sun returned in brightness, the sky’s serenity was restored to the world, the farmer was drawn back to his work, and the reaper was summoned to the crops to gather the sheaves.

Nor should what happened in a similar circumstance be passed over. While he was building an oratory at his estate at Noniac in honor of blessed Julian the martyr—

> **Note:** Compare the Book of the Miracles of Saint Julian, chapter 40.

—and a heavy rainstorm was breaking in, while he was reciting the Lord’s Prayer, the cloud diverted its assault, the storm drove away the whirlwind, and the rain withdrew. Not a drop touched either the place or the holy man Aridius as it fell.

### IX

Let this be added to the account, by which the miracles of these events are increased. One day, while the same holy man was praying in the oratory, a young man named Arctardus, son of Nivardus, was carried in lifeless and laid by his parents before the sacred altar in the oratory of Saint Julian the martyr. They begged that he be restored alive by the Lord.

Then the most reverent man, moved by compassion, forcing strength into his tears, looked toward heaven and prayed to the Lord. He next called to the little boy, but the body lay lifeless. After about an hour had passed, the boy was awakened, opened his closed eyes, and began to speak, restored to life.

Thus the faithful soldier, endowed with such great powers and girded with divine grace, was able through his prayers to obtain before the Lord that the young man should be restored to life, just as the Creator of all things raised the widow’s son from his bier and returned him unharmed to his mother.

A certain woman with a large wound on her face came to Saint Aridius and begged to be healed. When she had been marked with the banner of the cross, immediately, in the presence of the surrounding people, the swelling of the wound opened, and something resembling a small stone, about the size of a lesser nut, emerged from it. Without delay she returned home healed.

### X

Let another deed be added to the work, joined to its mysteries. A certain man named Ingratius, son of Dulcissimus, lay on a bier and was presented by his father for burial. He was so swollen that it seemed his eyes had been drawn back within him.

Then the man of the Lord, Aridius, after offering a prayer for him, anointed his eyes with blessed oil. When he applied it in faith, whatever disease there had been immediately fled at the touch of the ointment.

### XI

Since they raise themselves as far as they can toward the advancement of the holy man and toward the lofty contemplation of God, it must be believed that they were divinely moved to do so.

At one time, coming to the city of Limoges out of compassionate concern, he heard that several men recently condemned to death were being held in chains in prison. Aridius, mindful of the Lord’s words—“I was in prison and you came to me” (Matthew 25:36), and “As often as you did it for one of the least of mine, you did it for me” (ibid., 40)—considered whether he might somehow free them.

When he approached the prison to seek out the prisoners, immediately, by divine command, as though struck by a great blow, the bars were broken, the hinges were scattered, the prison doors opened, and all the bonds of the shackled prisoners were loosed. That same night a brightness like the sun appeared inside, and light flashed in the darkness. The guards were overcome by sleep, and all the prisoners fled from the prison to the most sacred tomb of Saint Martial the bishop.

> **Note:** See Gregory, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, book, chapter 28.

Thus, through the prayers of the blessed man, they were freed both from prison and from death.

### XII

What benefited the light of the eyes should benefit the ears of God’s people. Nivardus’s aforementioned daughter, named Actefledis, had lost the light of her eyes, so that she could not see at all.

One day her parents brought her to the man of God Aridius and begged that she be given sight. When they prostrated themselves at the priest’s feet, the holy man marked her eyes with the sign of the cross and prayed inwardly to the Lord. She was immediately restored unharmed; she who had been led there as a blind woman returned to her homeland as one who could lead others.

### XIII

The examples of the righteous also instruct their followers more eagerly than the preaching of many. Once, when the man of God was hastening to Burgundy to visit the king on a matter of compassion, the duke Antestius earnestly invited him to turn aside to his house, where his half-dead daughter lay on a bed.

> **Note:** This may be the Antestius whom Gregory says was sent by Guntram to Angers in his *History*, book 8, chapter 43.

When the girl was breathing her last, the man of God Aridius entered the house. After offering a prayer for her, he restored joy to the household by obtaining a remedy, and the girl returned from death to life.

For he who commanded the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue to be raised within the chamber granted this to his petitioner, so that she might return from death to life.

A woman named Bessa, weakened by illness in her limbs, with drawn fingers and bent joints, unable to walk on her own feet, prayed prostrate to be healed. She was a devout suppliant, wasted away by affliction. At once Aridius touched her legs with the holy sign of the cross; her nerves relaxed into their proper functions, and the limbs that had long awaited it were finally permitted to recognize themselves. Thus she was made well through the prayers of the holy man.

Let the praises that are justly reported for the palm of victory be recorded.

A woman who was already considered near death carried a wound on her neck. She approached the holy man, begging him to arm the wound with the banner of the holy cross, for she feared dying. When he pressed the sign of Christ upon the wound, the worms suddenly died, and the woman returned unharmed.

### XIV

As we behold the greater miracles of the saints, we are turned more earnestly and more fully toward the love of God. A girl from the city of Périgueux came to the man of God so contracted that, with her heels joined to her body, she touched her legs; for a long time she had been condemned to move about in this manner.

The most sacred man did not release her until the illness released her and she walked on her feet, although previously she had walked on her hands. He carefully asked whether she had hope in Christ and whether she believed that she would one day be healed.

When she affirmed her faith in all things, Aridius fixed his knees upon the ground and prayed at length. Then, raising both his eyes and his hands toward heaven, he reminded the Lord Jesus Christ with the fullest faith of his promise, which says: “Whatever you ask in faith will be done for you” (Mark 11:23); and: “If you have faith, you will not only do these signs, but you will do greater ones than these” (John 14:12).

When he had requested these things with all his strength and devotion, he turned to the girl and said: “If you believe faithfully, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ rise and stand upon your feet.”

Immediately she rose. Her feet and limbs were strengthened, and from that hour she was healed.

Again, another woman from the same city, afflicted with a similar illness, came to him. When the holy man had touched her with his hand, she returned home upright; and the old woman ran along the road that the young girl had not crossed.

### XV

Whenever we raise our minds toward the heights of almighty God, the things we see on earth become worthless in our estimation, so that, once divine grace has been received, we may enter the heavenly homeland. Such was this man, adorned with so many virtues and not darkened by earthly contamination.

A certain man named Addo, son of a man named Proculus, came into the presence of the most blessed man so weak that his heel had become attached to his foot, and the unhappily fused limb could not be separated. He sought remedies from Saint Aridius.

But when the sign of the cross had been placed upon him, the man who had come crawling on his knees departed walking on straightened feet, his heel restored to its proper place.

### XVI

Let the virtues of his works be added, by which they are believed to be genuine. A certain man from the territory of Périgueux, with contracted nerves and weakened feet, came in haste to the monastery and begged the holy man’s assistance.

The man of God Aridius undertook his cause for the sake of reward. After prayer had been poured out for him together with a blessing, he returned unharmed; the holy hand had touched him.

### XVII

Let a page be gained by what grace accomplishes. A certain man named Leonacter had been made so deranged by bodily madness that he seemed to be nothing but fury. His dreadful rage could scarcely be endured. Although he was heavily bound hand and foot, and, overcome by violence, was still fettered with chains, the added pain of punishment crushed him. Thus, raging savagely, he was finally brought to Saint Aridius.

Without delay, the sign of the cross having been made upon his forehead, he was freed in an instant from the ancient enemy and from his bonds at the same time. He later became a cleric and, devoting himself to better works with song, rendered service to Christ.

But by the wondrous disposition of almighty God it comes about that those whom divine rewards do not invite to better things are instructed by temporal scourges.

### XVIII

At the same time when the soldier of Christ lived on earth, the venerable Bishop Ferreolus was present in the city of Limoges to govern the people entrusted to him. Whenever the bishop himself was oppressed by fevers or worn down by severe pain from some illness, he sent messengers to the man of God Aridius, asking him to intercede more fully with the Lord on his behalf.

The holy man held vigils for him and obtained healing for the shepherd: the venerable abbot for the bishop, the rejected and humble man for the exalted one.

Since a growing account conceals greater miracles, let a wondrous event concerning a certain blind man be brought forward. A man who had long ago lost the light of his eyes, oppressed by darkness and clouded by thick blindness, was led on foot to the cell of the blessed man. When the holy man saw him, he took pity on him, restored his sight through prayer, and he returned to his own region illuminated by clear light.

### XIX

It is pleasant to relate what became a glorious memory. A certain man named Witrimundus, surnamed Atto, suffered such cruel toothache—

> **Note:** Gregory calls him Wistrimundus, surnamed Tatto, a citizen of Tours, in book 10, chapter 29; the author of another Life calls him Guiestremondus.

—that no respite whatsoever could relieve the pain pressing upon him.

He came to the holy man while devoutly going to meet blessed Martin. When asked why one side of his face appeared more swollen, he replied that he was being tortured by severe toothache. Then the man of God gently stroked his swollen face and said: “You will be healed by the Lord, through the intercession of Martin, God’s most faithful servant.”

Thus, as the words begun by Justus were immediately fulfilled, health was restored to the tooth, and the pain was cured together with the swelling.

### XX

A certain woman named Ricovera, wife of a moneyer of Tours, had faithfully offered the holy man half a flask of oil to be blessed. Aridius then made the sign of the cross and brought forth from his reliquary another flask containing oil from blessed Martin.

> **Note:** Compare chapter 39 of book 2 of the *Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 24 of book 3, and chapter 9 of the *Book on the Glory of the Confessors*.

When he poured a drop into the half-filled flask, the power of the oil burst forth in such abundance that the flask became full and the oil overflowed elsewhere; none of the surplus blessing was lost.

The blessing of both flasks benefited each in equal measure: the one who gave it to the petitioner and the petitioner who received what she had merited.

### XXI

This too is granted to only a few: that Christ’s soldier should be loved through such great miracles. The most reverent man had resolved that, in order to gain the palm of the heavenly homeland, he would go to Tours for the feast of the blessed bishop.

At one time, therefore, it happened that the holy man was hastening toward that city. While the bishop of the city, together with the clergy, was earnestly performing the nocturnal office of psalmody in the church, his deacon, while singing in the church, was overcome by sleep. When the bishop saw him sleeping, he said to him: “Why are you falling asleep, brother?”

Awakening from sleep, he replied: “My lord, I saw you going out of the church and hastening to meet the blessed man Aridius.”

Hardly had the deacon finished speaking when an evil spirit in a certain man immediately cried out that he could not endure the presence of Saint Aridius. Hearing this, the bishop realized that the man of God Aridius was approaching.

The bishop then went out to meet the abbot before the doors of the church, with lighted candles. With great joy and rejoicing they entered the church, and they continued in divine services for almost the entire night. For many sick people, afflicted with various illnesses, returned home in sound health through his prayers and intercession.

At another time, when he had again gone to Tours for the same feast, the man of God Aridius gently touched the legs of a paralytic.

> **Note:** Gregory relates this same miracle of a paralytic in book 4 of the *Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 6.

The paralytic testified that he had seen the hand of Saint Martin directing his weak limbs, and thus, when the saint’s right hand touched him, the paralytic was immediately restored to walking on his own feet.

The power of healing granted to him by divine grace shone forth so greatly that every sick person who came to him departed healed and unharmed. The possessed, too, were restored so quickly that the names of such a great multitude could not be recorded.

### XXII

If the miracles are recounted one by one, it is by no means inappropriate that the words of such great power should be believed. One time, after the man of God had left the basilica following the completion of the nocturnal vigils, he saw a globe of light descend from heaven upon his cell.

Believing that the radiance was being produced by a human being, the man of God asked his disciple who it was that was walking through the garden with a torch at such an hour. While he was marveling, the globe that had appeared above the cell immediately rolled back toward the stars.

He himself, with fear and trembling and his hands extended, offered thanks to the divine power for the gift of the light.

The monk who had seen this together with him asked what this miracle was: a vision of such great brightness, through which the mysteries of the most blessed bishop had been revealed in this way.

The holy man replied: “Be silent, be silent, foolish one. Know that the most blessed Martin is visiting this cell with exceptional favor, and that he returns to heaven with the glory of shining light.”

But since divine grace protected him, it was fitting that he should receive a visitation as the Holy Spirit illumined him. Yet the friend of God, guarding against the vice of boasting, ordered his disciple to tell no one of this vision until he had departed to the Lord.

Thus this faithful soldier observed the rule of the Master and Mediator of God, who, transfigured on the mountain, commanded his disciples to tell no one of the vision they had seen until the Son of Man had risen from the dead.

Consider, then, with how great a fire of love for God and neighbor this man was aflame, since, when the Spirit revealed it, he was deemed worthy to receive such a divine gift. For “God is a consuming fire” (Deuteronomy 4:24; Hebrews 12:29), as James bears witness, saying: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1:17).

### XXIII

When these things had taken place, the holy man remained continually devoted to the divine offices. The enemy of the human race could find in him neither anything by which to deceive him through fraud nor anything by which to stain him through pretense.

He was generous in almsgiving, devoted in prayer, diligent in vigils, abundant in humility, distinguished in teaching, peaceful in speech, cautious in conversation, most holy in conduct, strong in harsh sufferings, joyful in good works, safest in temptation, exceedingly generous in hospitality, beneficent amid hatred, and always intent upon heaven in prosperity and adversity alike. In charity, which is “the bond of perfection” in Christ (Colossians 3:14), he was perfect.

He displayed the sincerity of his mind through the serenity of his face and showed the compassion of his heart in the gentleness of his speech. Nothing was more serious than his laughter, nothing sweeter than his sadness, nothing more merciful than his spirit, and nothing gentler toward the humble.

If he saw a poor person, he supported him; if a rich person, he encouraged him to act well, calling God as witness that he did all these things for His name’s sake. He constantly remembered what Truth says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5:7); and also: “Nevertheless, give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41); and elsewhere: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclesiasticus 3:33).

Constantly remembering these commandments, he fulfilled them with great zeal. He was the foot of the lame and the eye of the blind, the father of orphans, and the consoler of widows.

What blind person did he not call his heir, or what weak person did his hand not support? He continually went about accompanied by this army. In them he desired to embrace Christ, whom he saw in them; and when he gave them clothing, he believed that he was clothing Christ’s members beneath the garments of the poor.

For this reason, dividing his money with his Lord, he rejoiced to share his possessions with Christ, so that Christ might make him a co-heir of the heavenly kingdoms, knowing what is written: that a good inheritance is preserved under the Lord’s protection.

Among his people, his admonitions were nothing other than divine teachings and foundations of the sacred Scriptures. It is fitting that the good should love and imitate him, while the harmful should fear him—him whom divine power illumined, so that the gift received from God might be joined with honey-sweet teaching, seasoned by the Holy Spirit, made savory by longing for Christ, and always solicitous for eternal blessedness.

### XXIV

If we consider what and how many things almighty God accomplished through his bishop, a longer account is proclaimed by the pen. The wicked often subvert the hearts of earthly kings through their evil and flattering counsels, according to Solomon’s saying: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Corinthians 15:33).

At one time it happened that taxes or censuses had been assessed by the kings upon the people. This measure was imposed with the greatest severity throughout all the cities established in Gaul.

Moved by compassion on this account, the most reverent man hastened into the king’s presence to make a petition on behalf of the citizens who had been enrolled by royal decree under a heavy public tax. But since it is written, “The king’s heart is in the hand of the Lord” (Proverbs 21:1), whatever the holy man requested, he obtained from the devout king.

It happened that, as he was returning from this journey and coming through a certain village called Catuliacum, on the very day when the sacred mysteries of the Lord’s resurrection were being celebrated, he was invited by the people and began to devote himself to the holy offices.

While he was celebrating the divine solemnities, a certain girl who was being grievously tormented by demons cried out that she could not endure the presence of the holy man, although she invoked his name without knowing it.

Following his customary practice of works of compassion, and having completed the divine mysteries, he fled to the harbor of prayer so that the girl might no longer be tormented by the ancient enemy, and he stood forth as her intercessor.

There were seven most wicked spirits in her. While he devoted himself to prayer, he immediately expelled five demons through his supplication. Since two still remained, the most blessed man commanded the girl’s parents not to leave the church until what remained of the malign affliction had been driven from her body.

The holy man therefore came to the church where he had ordered her to remain. Taking his monks with him, he prostrated himself in prayer and obtained from the Lord that the two demons who remained should be expelled, so that she might return home with a sincere mind and a sound understanding.

## XXV

At another time, when the man of God was seeking the king’s presence on account of such a circumstance, as though the king’s arrival were concealed, he hastened on his journey. When he had entered the gates of the city of Paris, the people of that city were suffering from a severe fever, dysentery, and a dreadful disease, so that, because of the multitude dying each day—especially the crowds of infants—not even the number of bodies could be reckoned.

One day, while he was being deservedly honored with affection by the bishop of that city, the bishop asked him to remain with him for a few days in the service of charity, so that he might stand before the Lord as an intercessor for the people. Accordingly, when the man of God, Aridius, wished to comply with his request, it happened that some of his companions fell gravely ill with that same terrible disease. The most blessed man, secure in the Lord through the strength of his confidence, prayed with his customary prayer for the people of that city. He did not cease to console them with gentle exhortation and his own words, so that no one would despair of the mercy of the Lord’s compassion.

He ordered blessed oil to be brought to him, and with the sign of the cross he personally anointed the mouths and noses of each one, saying to them: “Take comfort in the Lord, and exhort one another, brothers. The right hand of Christ restores you all safely.” And he spoke thus to his companions: “Do not, I beg you, my brothers, do not grieve; rather, strengthen yourselves manfully and trust more earnestly in the mercy of the Lord, because divine power will restore you all unharmed to your own land.” Meanwhile, he considered in his mind where he knew the king to be, since he ought to seek him out.

Leaving the brothers in that city, he hastened onward with a few companions and made his way as far as a place called Brinnacum [*]. While the traveler was still on the road, he said to those following him: “Know that the king is being hard pressed by a severe fever, and that the end of his life is almost at hand; but, in the Lord’s mercy, because of his regard for the poor, he will deliver him safely when we visit him. Keep this more secretly among yourselves. After these few days, however, his offspring, who now appear to be still alive, will depart from this world.”

Through the Spirit of prophecy, the man of God Aridius knew what events afterward confirmed. When the holy servant of God had reached the place mentioned, the king, learning of his arrival, ordered him to be brought into his chamber, believing that through his prayers he would be helped by the Lord. When Aridius had entered and offered the customary greeting, he began to touch the king with his hands, while inwardly asking the Lord in prayer to incline the king to his requests. As the king began to feel some relief from the distress of his illness under the sacred hands of the blessed man, he explained the reason for his visit. But, with God favoring him—God who rules all things and arranges everything gently—whatever the priest of God asked of the king, he obtained readily.

The king also handed over to him, for the sake of the holy man and for his own security, the books in which the people of his kingdom were recorded as burdened by a grievous levy, so that Aridius might burn them by his own authority. Then Aridius, having received the books, ordered that coals be prepared. When this had been done, he took the books in his own hands and burned them in the fire while many people stood around. Having obtained what he had requested, he took leave of the prince on the third day.

[*Note: See Gregory, Book V of the *History*, chapter 35, where he discusses this dysentery, the illnesses of the king and his children, the burning of the books of assessments, and related matters. He says nothing there, however, about Saint Aredius.]

## XXVI

One day, before he reached Paris, the event confirmed there what he had told his companions not long before. The man of God undoubtedly learned from a messenger that the king’s sons had died, as he himself had previously foretold, and that they were being carried to Paris amid a great funeral procession.

When he had returned and reached the aforementioned city, he found that its people had already been freed from the disease of dysentery by divine aid. He also found one of his companions, named Constantine, lying in grave danger of death. Some others whom he discovered to have died he restored to life through his prayers.

Then his companions urged him to entrust the man who had succumbed to the dreadful illness to someone in a suitable place, so that, when he departed this life, he might be enclosed in a grave of earth; for he was already so near death. But the most blessed man, moved by compassion and ready in his customary kindness, lifted him onto the vehicle on which he himself was accustomed to sit, and had him carried under another’s direction.

When he had been on the road for three days, weakened by illness, he was struck by the blow of death and collapsed lifeless upon the ground. When the blessed man saw this, he began, with a stricken heart, groaning and weeping, to devote himself most earnestly to prayer. When he rose from prayer and turned toward the body, touching the man with his hands, the man began to open his eyes. Before many hours had passed, having conquered death’s prey, he was restored unharmed to his former life. He who had been given up as lost was restored to uninterrupted health.

Then, in a feeble voice, he asked that water be given him. All the others anxiously searched here and there, but could not find any, since that place was unquestionably without water. The holy priest of God, however, withdrawing a little and striking the ground with his staff, caused abundant water to spring forth. They immediately carried it in a vessel to the one who had asked for it. Thus the burning thirst was subdued, the pallor fled from his face, his countenance took on its color, and he rose to his feet. He who had been condemned to the onset of death was presented alive and well to his homeland. He afterward lived through many years.

## XXVII

It must be added to the miracles of his virtues that the hearts of those who hear them may be enlightened by his example. When he was already approaching his homeland and was joining a certain village called Argentomagus, one of the monks, Artemius, opportunely suggested that food should be prepared for the brothers.

He replied: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you” (Luke 12:31); and also the Psalmist’s words: “Those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing” (Psalm 33:10). “But receive this word from me, dearest brother: when you have crossed the bed of this river, raise your eyes toward the right-hand side. You will find a suitable place where we can relieve the hunger of ourselves and of our vehicle.”

When they came to the place he had indicated, they found there two fish of extraordinary size, still very much alive. After they had been roasted, the man of God Aridius took a portion of them for food, and many of the company appeared to have eaten until satisfied. But he in whose name the apostles cast their nets into the waves, and were unable to haul them in because of the multitude of fish, distributed food also to the hungry.

[*Note: This appears to be a village among the Bituriges, still called Argenton, situated not far from the monastery of Selles (Saint-Benoît-du-Sault), where Marcellus and Anastasius are said to have suffered for Christ, according to Usuard on 3 Kalends of July.]

## XXVIII

As the virtues of the saints are recounted, the minds of the faithful, like thirsty people, desire to be satisfied with the depths of God’s mysteries. Once, while he was traveling along the road, approaching a village called Argentomagus, he addressed those following him and said: “Let us pass through silently, lest a delay be imposed upon our journey.”

This was a profane place, consecrated to the worship of demons by ancient superstition. The Christian people who lived there could not endure their misery, for they were afflicted by various illnesses or were continually harassed by the demons themselves.

When the man of God Aridius wished to slip away secretly from the people and was praying in private, the multitude of the sick was stirred up, invoking his name. For the insolent crowd of demons could not conceal itself from the arrival of the holy man.

When a multitude of sick people followed him, he looked back and stopped. Immediately he prostrated himself on the ground and devoted himself to prayer, asking the Lord that they might be saved according to their faith. When he had risen from prayer, he at once impressed the sign of the cross upon each one. Then those afflicted by various illnesses, as well as those tormented by unclean spirits, were freed from their diseases and demons. Adding oil with a blessing, he caused them to return to their former health, and they gave thanks to the Lord.

## XXIX

Those whom God chose before the foundation of the world are despised by the greatness of the reprobate. This holy man was rejected among men and least in the eyes of the world, but he was exalted as the greatest among the ranks of the saints.

Once, while traveling, as evening approached one day and he was not far from a village called Moeno, he ordered that the journey be ended and that the packs carried by the beasts be unloaded in a suitable place. When they had seen a pleasant spot, beautiful to look upon, where they could stay, the most blessed man, knowing through the spirit of prophecy what would afterward happen there, addressed his companions in fatherly speech. He knew that a great injury threatened them, and he said:

“Men, brothers, and sons, believe that we shall suffer great harm here tonight. But take courage and trust that we shall be delivered by heavenly aid.”

There was no delay. Although the sky appeared perfectly clear, serene with the brilliance of the stars, suddenly the earth was shaken by thunder. Because of the tremendous sound, it seemed to be turned from its stability into trembling. The clouds in the air were thrown into confusion and appeared dark among the stars. Those that had been brilliantly white were driven into rain, lightning flashed repeatedly from the darkened sky, and thunder resounded.

Not far from them were three idols dedicated to pagan worship. As the air was assailed by flashes of light, they were so overturned from heaven in the violence of the thunderclap that by the following day no foundations of the idols could be found. With the same flash of fire-bright lightning, a huge fire consumed part of a forest visible at a distance from them, while the force of the winds tore up and laid low the trees.

Those who were with the man of God were so terrified that none believed he could escape, fearing that God’s punishment would descend upon them. For this reason he repeatedly urged them to persist in prayer and to continue throughout the whole night in the duty of singing psalms.

The place where the man of God Aridius had turned aside to stay appeared lower than the place where the others had fixed their tents. Consequently, they were all so drenched by the enormous quantity of water that no part of their clothing remained untouched by the rushing rain. But the holy priest of God—[the text is syntactically defective]—wore around his neck a small reliquary containing sacred relics; looking about at his companions, with a little cloak and bedding laid over the place where he was to rest, it was as though that place, touched by the sun’s heat, had felt no moisture.

## XXX

Nor should we pass over an event that accords with his virtue. Once, when war had arisen between two princes, the people of the region of Limoges feared that the walls of their city would be breached, and that the city would be laid waste and destroyed. A messenger was sent to them by the king, under whose rule the people were to be placed, and the already devastated city was under siege.

One of the men, named Domaricus, who had come with the others to seize the city, approached the holy man of God and earnestly questioned him, asking him to foretell the future—whatever he had learned through the spirit of revelation. He spoke to them in silence:

“Although I know that you fear King Theudebert, know this: his kingdom is recently taken from him, but he himself will soon be killed. Your king, moreover, will stir up the forces of many peoples against him, and victory will be granted to your king. Once victory in battle has been obtained, however, he will be deceitfully deceived, and his kingdom will be handed over to be governed by his sons and grandsons.
