“As for the other kings, whose kingdoms appear to stand securely, when the moment of death intervenes, they will be seized from this world in dishonor.”

The aforementioned Domaricus then returned to the warriors. What the man of God Aridius had foretold was afterward confirmed by events.

Among his other virtues, he had also been abundantly endowed with wisdom and knowledge. Above all, he possessed charity and humility. He did not oppress his servants as slaves but loved them with kindly affection. Why should I delay with more? Throughout his entire way of life he shone like the morning star among the stars of heaven, like a great lamp. He always strove toward the good and always set the virtues of others before himself as an example. He was slow to speak and quick to listen; rich in almsgiving, patient in charity, exalted in humility, subtle in speech, alert in understanding, ready in eloquence, ardent in zeal—in truth, a useful vessel in the house of Christ.

[*Note: This is Theudebert, son of Chilperic. After the defeat of the leader Gundobald, he plundered Limoges and the neighboring provinces, as Gregory relates in Book V of the *History*, chapter 48. He was eventually killed by the army of Sigibert, chapter 51.]

## XXXI

It is fitting to believe that, in the case of many saints, those who prophesy future events through the Spirit of prophecy recount, with clear understanding, things divinely accomplished. Thus this man of God also, when heavenly grace enlightened him, announced through the revelation of the Holy Spirit what was going to happen to men.

A certain man from among the citizens of Limoges, named Nectarius, was not poor in possessions but wealthy in riches. He had one son, and the blessed servant of God perceived that a sudden attack of death was threatening the boy. Therefore the most reverent man sent a messenger to the boy’s parents, ordering them to present him before his sight before death overtook him.

When the mother heard the message, she burst into tears over the destruction of her child. Meanwhile, accompanied by a few servants, she obeyed the blessed man’s command. As she set out on the road, so that the truth of the prophecy might be confirmed, the force of a violent fever attacked the boy’s limbs, which became limp. With his head lowered and his eyes closed, he appeared almost dead.

While the holy man awaited the outcome, the servants saw that the youth was lifeless. They immediately burst into tears and cries and hurried with all speed to the man of God. Moved by compassion, he received the lifeless boy and ordered him to be laid before the sacred relics of the blessed bishop Hilary. He commended him to the Lord with great prayers and supplications, asking that He who had restored the four-day-old Lazarus alive from the tomb might mercifully help this boy as well.

When the prayer had been completed, the one who had appeared lifeless was immediately restored unharmed to his mother. He whom he had believed dead and was taking to burial returned home with his mother amid great joy and exultation.

## XXXII

The Lord’s man Aridius, adorned with the grace of prophecy, foretold these events and many others like them, which it would be tedious to recount individually. For the almighty God revealed many works of virtue through the most blessed man; when these are recalled again and again, the wonders perceived in them continually increase. Yet the foregoing accounts comprise only a few of the many.

Having lived on earth as a pilgrim, after gaining the heavenly palm and returning to Christ, freed from the snare of the world, he left us a considerable example of what he had been able to accomplish while living in the world. But now it would take too long to relate in words each miracle of his virtues, especially since this book, already filled beyond measure and demanding an end, rejects further speech, while the dryness of our discourse, weakened and almost exhausted by the length of the road, begins to fail.

This is not because we have explained everything that ought to be told about him. We could not even reach a hundredth part of his works of virtue, nor recount how many and how great ornaments of good works the supreme privilege of heavenly reward bestowed upon the blessed man.

It remains, therefore, that we should be able to reach the end of our course. O truly imitable man! O example to be preferred above all others! O blessed seed according to Abraham! Abraham’s blessing merited a son, while blessed Aridius is transferred into the heavenly kingdom. Abraham hands over an heir, and this man likewise an inheritance. Finally, Abraham presented what he possessed as a pledge, while Aridius entrusted everything he was able to possess in the world to the judgment and authority of the Lord.

Let this, then, suffice to have been said. Now, as I hope, although I have drawn out a lengthy discourse in an unpolished style, even though I would in no way have been sufficient to narrate praises worthy of his merits, I think it fitting for the edification both of those who hear and of those who read to explain briefly how he departed from this life to the Lord, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns in the unity of the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# HERE BEGINS THE ACCOUNT OF THE DEATH OF THE HOLY AND MOST BLESSED ARIDIUS, ABBOT AND CONFESSOR

## XXXIII

When the man of God had already reached old age, when he had patiently endured all the adversities and labors of the world, after he had accumulated on every side the merits of the most faithful stewardship entrusted to him, after his many works of mercy, after his service to monasteries and monastic communities, after the sweet examples of his life, and after the works and miracles of all his goodness and virtues had been made manifest—when his age was already declining and he was more than eighty years old—he knew that the dissolution of his body was near and said to his monks:

“Know, dearest brothers, that the Lord will soon deem me worthy of release from the snare of this world.”

When they heard this, they were all weakened by his words and turned to anguish. In mourning they began to say: “May it not be granted, lord, that your servants should see this; rather, may Christ permit your blessedness to flourish here for many years as an adornment of the Church.”

But he said to them with tears and long sighs: “In this matter, let not our will but rather the Lord’s be done.”

Then, while they were all grieving, he said: “Do not, I beg you, my brothers, do not grieve; rather rejoice and exult, because I have long desired this time and have wished to receive this release.”

As they were thus overcome with anguish and sighing, and were also held back by uncertainty about the matter, the conversation came to an end. Soon afterward, a very slight fever entered his body, and he began to feel ill.

Then he summoned a certain boy and ordered him, saying: “Hurry, my son; go quickly to the illustrious man Astidius and tell him to come at a swift pace, because after the days of my death he himself will assume responsibility for governing this monastery.” He added: “For if he delays at all, he will no longer see my face in this life.”

The messenger fulfilled the command, but the aforementioned Astidius arrived late for the journey. When he reached the place, he did not find the man of God still alive in this world. Thus, just as the man of God had foretold, events afterward confirmed it.

Meanwhile, as I began to say, when the blessed man was lying in his final illness, he still did not cease from the work of God, considering it the good completion of his virtues if he brought it to the end. Through the night he continued in prayers and vigils. Although his limbs were failing, he compelled his spirit and mind to serve God, and with great joy awaited the journey he desired.

When he sensed that the day was near, he gathered his disciples on the ninth day before the Kalends of September [24 August]—disciples whom he was beginning to leave in body but not in spirit—and said to them:

“If you will, dearest brothers, hear the counsel of my lowliness. If you truly love me, love Christ’s admonitions; continually fear God’s awesome judgments. Take careful thought to avoid being found unworthy on the day of judgment. For I am now going my way; I long to be dissolved and, if the Lord permits, to be at rest.”

When he had said this, and all were weeping and lamenting, he said to them:

“Behold, today I commend the salvation of your souls into your hands. Remember my admonition, therefore, and let each of you reflect upon himself. Practice continually what I say; understand and repeat these things, and always retain my memory with you. Aridius will no longer be with you in this world.”

When all who stood around heard this, they raised a great groan and wept together with one voice, saying:

“Why do you abandon us, father, or why do you wish to depart from us so quickly? We know that you desire Christ, but your rewards are secure. Have mercy also on us whom you are abandoning. We cannot endure your absence, because we shall never afterward have one like you. Have pity on us, father; do not leave us orphans so quickly.”

As they lamented these things, that most compassionate shepherd drenched his face abundantly with tears. Since he was loving and could neither abandon them nor remain separated from Christ any longer, he finally resumed his speech amid bitter tears and said:

“Do not grieve over my departure, and, I beg you, do not distress yourselves any longer with weeping. You ought rather to rejoice than to mourn, because even if I am absent in body, I shall be present in spirit. If I was able to accomplish anything, I served your progress; and although I am wretched, the Lord is always Lord. I commend you to Him and entrust your care to Him. I know that, as a useless servant, I have not done what I ought; but the Lord knows how I wished to do it.”

After these words, as the day was already declining, he suddenly fell upon the pavement. Raising his eyes to heaven, he prayed humbly, groaning and sighing:

“I commend to you, Lord Jesus, the sheep whom you entrusted to me.”

Thus commending to the Lord, with increase, the talent he had received from Him, and now lying at the point of death, he called his disciples to him, embraced each one, and, weeping and bidding farewell to them all, said:

“I shall no longer speak with you; you will see my face no more. Therefore, farewell in peace, and know that I am at rest.”

Those standing around could not in any way restrain their weeping. Yet amid bitter tears they could scarcely utter anything but these words:

“We grieve for our own sake, father, because you deprive us of the comfort of your presence. But for your sake, best of fathers, we rejoice, because after the labor of this world you are going to eternal rest.”

Then, raising his eyes to heaven, he poured out a silent prayer. Afterward, with tears, he said:

“Remember me, Lord, who alone are without sin, Redeemer of the world. Lead me out from this body of death and save me into your heavenly kingdom. You are my protector, Lord; into your hands I commend my spirit. Receive me according to your great mercy, and do not put me to shame in my expectation. Help me and assist the departure of my soul. Open for me, Lord, as I hasten, the door of your kingdom. Let not the princes of darkness meet me, but may your mercy protect and defend me, and may your hand lead me into a place of refreshment and consolation, or at least into the final dwelling that you have prepared for those who fear your holy name.”

During this he also added:

“Now, Lord, let your servant depart in peace, according to your word.”

Having said this, he gave up his spirit amid the words of his prayer (Luke 2:29).

## XXXIV

When that holy soul had cast off the burden of the flesh, at the second hour of the night a globe shining with extraordinary brightness appeared to descend from heaven over his cell and suddenly to penetrate upward toward the stars.

In this manner his holy soul, freed from earthly contamination and conducted by holy angels, joyfully flew back to its creator. The man had indeed given up his spirit, while mourning and weeping resounded toward heaven. His body was arranged according to custom and placed upon a bier, and there they spent the entire night keeping vigil with psalms and hymns.

When daylight had appeared, a multitude of people gathered. When the matter also came to the attention of the bishop of the city of Limoges, he heard it, came running with great weeping and haste, and wept for a long time over the body of the holy man, because he had not found him alive in this world.

Then, wishing to carry him to the church of the holy martyr Julian, which the holy man had built and where the sacred body lay, they were completely unable to lift the bier even slightly. The man of God Aridius, however, had determined that his body should be committed to burial in the church of the bishop Saint Hilary, which he himself had built through his own labor.

The bishop Ferreolus was then deeply saddened and ordered a three-day fast to be observed with psalm-singing. When this had begun, he himself and his people observed the fast continuously throughout those three days.

When the fast had been completed, he said: “If it is the Lord’s will, or that of this saint, that he should go there where I and this people desire, let him be lifted without any delay.”

The place was in a more secluded part. When they approached the bier and tried to lift it, it was immediately raised with such ease that two men could carry it, although previously not even a great many people had been able to move it.

When all who were present saw this with the bishop, they magnified Christ’s glory with great exultation, saying: “Great and wonderful are your works, Lord God almighty.”

When the body had been carried to the tomb, all who were present could not restrain their weeping. They cried out that they had lost their father, and amid tears and sobs could scarcely utter these words:

“Why do you abandon us, father, and to whom do you entrust your foster-children to be governed?”

The body was then committed to burial according to custom. The aforementioned bishop, showing reverence, returned to his own [the text here is corrupt].

Let the empty glory of the world, if you please, be compared with the funeral rites—not funerary rites, but rather the triumph—of this holy man. Let the pomp of wealthy men also be compared, if it can be made equal, with this dead priest.

The madness of crowds honors them with confused applause; angels, with heavenly praises, carry Aridius, freed from the world’s distress, into everlasting kingdoms. After the pomp of this age they are thrust into Tartarus; after the adversities of the world, Aridius is joyfully received into Abraham’s bosom. Overwhelmed by the wealth of riches, they are hurled dead into Gehenna; Aridius, exalted by almsgiving, will rise with the saints in glory. They mourn at the end, condemned in hell; Aridius, crowned with laurel, rejoices in the Church with all the saints who have departed from this world.

We give you thanks, our God, who have repaid him greatly for little, made him rest in everlasting glory, and granted him the evangelical promise in which you said: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you were faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things” (Matthew 25:21). Here he merited hearing: “Enter into the joy of your Lord.”

And as it is written of such men through Solomon: “The righteous man is delivered from distress” (Proverbs 11:8). And through Jeremiah it is written: “Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord will be his confidence” (Jeremiah 17:7). David also says: “His delight is in the law of the Lord,” and “he shall be like a tree planted beside running waters” (Psalm 1:2–3).

The Lord also says through the prophet Isaiah: “I have called him and blessed him, and his way has been made straight” (Isaiah 48:15). In the book of Ecclesiasticus it is likewise said: “It will be well with one who fears the Lord at the end, and on the day of his death he will be blessed” (Ecclesiasticus 1:13).

Elsewhere it is written: “The fruit of his good labors will be glorious” (Wisdom 3:15), and “his crown triumphs forever” (Wisdom 4:2).

Let this suffice as our account of the death of the holy man, lest I weary those who read. When his life comes to an end, let our discourse also come to an end.

# HERE BEGIN THE MIRACLES OF SAINT ARIDIUS, ABBOT

## XXXV

Now I shall undertake, for the benefit of those who read, to relate a few of the many miracles that the Lord continually performs through his merits at his most sacred body, and that Jesus Christ manifested there at the conclusion of his death. The human mind cannot break forth in words adequate to the mysteries by which heavenly grace enlightens its soldiers.

One of the monks from the cell of the most sacred man, named Baudenus, did not delay to travel to the region of Burgundy with documents by which the monastery’s possession was secured. He sought out the venerable and distinguished bishop Syagrius, bishop of the Aedui, and implored him with his prayers—since he was held in greater honor than all others in the king’s palace—to protect the cell through his patronage from the plots of various rivals.

The bishop, agreeing to the requests of the aforementioned monk, did not refuse what the most reverent man had asked. He also secured the documents with royal authority and granted him freedom to return to his region.

After many days had passed, and after obtaining what he had requested, Baudenus hurried on his way and entered a town in the region of Limoges. One day, in a village called Ricomagus, he found there the illustrious man Nectarius and revealed to him everything that the outcome of his requests had brought about.

Meanwhile, when Nectarius questioned him, Baudenus began to falter in his speech and to lose control of his mind. With a furious expression, he suddenly burst into speech and could not keep silent about the reason for his behavior: he had been shamefully polluted by the crime of adultery.

Gnashing his teeth and tearing himself with his own bites, he violently shook off and threw to the ground the reliquary that the blessed Aridius customarily carried and that contained relics of the saints. Since his great fury could in no way be calmed, he was bound and handed over to custody.

Meanwhile, one of the aforementioned man’s servants picked up the reliquary he had thrown down and, not knowing what it was, placed it among the clothing. While this was happening, they gathered the belongings together and began loading a beast. When the load had been lifted onto it, the beast, weighed down by the sacred burden, fell to the ground and could move no farther.

What more need be said? It was placed upon another beast, but that one, having received the burden, likewise fell to the ground in the same condition. Although it was driven with many bloodied goads, it could not be made to rise until the reason for the crime that had been understood had been revealed.

When he was driven more violently by the rage of his madness, Baudenus cried out that the reliquary, which he confessed he had carried unworthily, was fastened among his clothing, and that therefore the vehicle would not move until it was removed, since the fault lay in their negligence.

They immediately found it when they searched the pouch. Out of reverence and devotion, the noble Nectarius placed it respectfully upon the innocent boy. At once the passage of the hours was released [or: the delay immediately came to an end].

The aforementioned Baudenus, before his spirit was disturbed—for it is impossible to judge him otherwise, since he was not in control of his senses—fled in full view of everyone. In the space of one hour he ran almost twelve miles swiftly on his feet, then, exhausted in body, fell half-dead to the ground. When the guards caught up with him, he was taken to a lodging.

At dawn, after the night had passed, he rose and, compelled by the unclean spirit, presented himself at the most sacred tomb of Saint Martial. There, when he revealed the confession of his deed, the evil spirit was expelled and he merited receiving the remedy of health.

## XXXVI

There are many other things that the almighty God accomplished after the death of the holy man. While the people were awaiting such an outcome, one of the household servants reached the aforementioned illustrious man with the greatest speed and announced that his wife was being held in grave danger of death. He warned him to come quickly if he wished to find her alive.

Trusting meanwhile in the Lord’s compassion, Nectarius ordered the boy who had brought the holy man’s reliquary with him to hurry on ahead. When he entered the house, the whole household was occupied with mourning and lamentation, because she was subject to so sudden and imminent a danger of death.

With her eyes closed, the sign of one about to die appeared in her throat, where a very severe swelling had arisen. Her power of speech had also been blocked, her eyes were clouded, and she could no longer recognize her husband.

But when the holy man’s reliquary was hung around the dying woman’s neck, death immediately fled. At once her eyes opened to the light, and the breath of her spirit was restored to her former health. Forcefully belching, she brought up the obstruction in her throat, which she had not taken in through eating, and she was restored to life while death stood at the door.

The reliquary itself was then reverently carried to the holy man’s monastery after priests had been summoned.

### XXXVII

But who could recount individually all the miracles that the Lord Jesus Christ continually performs at the holy man’s tomb? [Col. 1141B] One day a woman had resolved to be seen in the presence of the holy man, so that she might offer thanks. While the monks were celebrating the night vigils, a certain Dabolenus, who had a son named Babolenus afflicted with a grievous disease of the limbs, had the boy carried by his parents and laid before the holy man’s tomb. While he was lying on the pavement, almost at midnight the boy suddenly cried out and felt the joints of his limbs being restored to the places from which they had been dislocated. Then, raising himself from the pavement, with his limbs strengthened, he stood upon his feet. He who had been carried to the tomb in his parents’ arms returned to his own home on his own feet, rejoicing with his father and giving thanks to Christ.

### XXXVIII

One must carefully consider how many gifts of His grace almighty God bestowed upon His saints in this present 1307 life, so that after their triumph they might be rewarded in the heavenly homeland with a greater accumulation of glory. Thus a certain monk named Gaudomeres, from the monastery of Ambiacum, situated not far from the city, was himself held by an evil spirit, to such an extent that he wished to tear apart by biting whatever he saw; and he was led about bound in two chains, as though guilty before a judge. One day he was brought to the holy man’s tomb, and there he was restored to his former health and rescued from the hostile adversary by whom he was tormented. He converted many to the service of almighty God.

For the chains by which the wretched man was bound came apart of their own accord, so that by a double miracle it might be revealed that, in a single moment, the tightly fastened chains were shattered and divine grace released the man possessed by the demon, [Col. 1141D] so that he might serve God in freedom, to whom every creature groans. Indeed, if anyone, for whatever reason, has been bound for some offense or fettered with chains, and it happens that he is led in bonds across the public road near the basilica itself, as soon as he comes opposite that church all his bonds are immediately broken and the prisoner is released; he cannot thereafter remain held in chains.

### XXXIX

Even more marvelous things follow upon the marvelous events. One day two mute men came to the holy man’s tomb. Although they could not ask with their tongues, they asked by faith. After they had been anointed with oil, at the Lord’s command the tongues of the mute were immediately released, and they began to speak as they worshiped. Those who had been rendered speechless at once addressed the people. For the elect have received this gift: that the more they excel in virtues, the more they should judge themselves unworthy, lest they be carried away into empty glory and be deprived of the heavenly gift.

Four men, then, came from different provinces, all afflicted with blindness. Prostrate in the oratory, they awaited light, seeking the holy man’s remedy through the outcome. While they offered prayers at the sacred tomb, all asking with one accord, he immediately opened the eyes of the blind, which had long been closed. Having received clear light, they sought the thresholds of the church.

### XL

Many other signs and miracles are likewise performed there at the command of heavenly grace through his merits. Among them, a lamp is also filled and overflowed with an abundant supply of oil. From this sacred liquid [Col. 1142B] many who are anointed there are healed of various illnesses, and the name of the Lord, the eternal God, is continually blessed there.

Likewise, many miracles are displayed at his bed, which is situated on the estate of his monastery. Throughout various places also, wherever his sacred relics are carried, or wherever they have been brought, very many signs of miracles are accomplished, as the glory of Christ reveals his merits. We have thought it burdensome to pursue all these events in order, and therefore have gathered them into these very few words, because we are now hastening to cease our discourse.

If we were now 1308 to undertake to explain each event individually, as the facts establish them, we would exceed the limits of this very short volume and, because of its very length, perhaps impose weariness upon our readers. Yet what we have narrated less fully gives clear testimony to everyone who sees the many chains of the fettered, which are displayed and hung at his tomb as evidence of these events. Of these we have mentioned either only a few or almost none, simply because they are set before everyone’s eyes; just as we know the place, so, we assume, do all others know it.

All these events are recorded as having occurred within a short time. But who can now comprehend by estimation what kinds and how many miracles will be performed in the long stretches of time yet to come, since even today miracles never cease to be performed at the bishop’s tomb? Every day the sick come to the holy man’s tomb and, keeping vigil there, are made well; the blind come and are given sight; the demon-possessed come and are freed; perjurers come, [Col. 1142D] and either die or are tormented by the devil; those bound in iron flee there and are released; the lame, carried in carts, return safely to their homes with their steps restored.

Many healings are accomplished through the liquid of the oil that grows there. Again, how many people held by chills or various illnesses have been freed after the passing of the most blessed man—people who had been captives of the enemy? The page of a small book cannot attach each event individually, lest it prepare weariness for those weaker in faith and a more extended account be published for those who doubt.

Let it therefore suffice to have spoken of these few among the many, so that, as though from different flowers fragrant in the bosom of holy Church, the hearts of many believers may be filled, enabling them to gather perfect fruits that worldly pleasure does not defile. For one cannot rejoice here with the world and reign there with Christ, nor serve two masters, namely God and mammon. Therefore, laying aside the works of darkness, let us put on the weapons of light, because the Creator of all is the true light, which enlightens every human being who comes into this world, through our Lord Jesus Christ, His Son, who as God lives and reigns in perfect Trinity and unity of the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 1143A] Although the Testament of Saint Aredius is not found in the manuscript Codex of Saint Gall, it has nevertheless seemed preferable to include it here rather than in the appendix, as we promised in the notes to chapter 29 of Book X of the History, where Gregory praises him. It is now given in full for the first time from the archive of Saint Martin of Tours.]

## Testament of Saint Aredius, Abbot of Attanum

[Col. 1143B]

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. On the day before the Kalends of November, in the eleventh year [Note: [Col. 1143D] Others read “seventeenth,” but incorrectly, for Sigibert did not reign for so many years. That the Limoges region belonged to his kingdom, that is, to Austrasia, is proved not only by this passage but also by both Lives of this saint and by Gregory himself, Book X of the History, chapter 29, where Aredius is said to have been raised at the court of King Theudebert. The same is also clear from the agreement fully reported in Book IX, chapter 20.] 1309 of the reign of our lord King Sigibert, I, Aredius the presbyter, and Pelagia, being of sound mind and complete judgment, fearing the accidents of human frailty lest the occasion of sudden death overtake us unexpectedly, seated as judges and arbiters of our affairs, drew up our testament. I, Aredius himself, wrote it in my own hand and delivered it to a sufficient number of witnesses for subscription.

If, by chance, our testament should not be valid under civil or praetorian law, or under the wording of any new or old law, we order it to have the force of codicils and of every written instrument [Col. 1143C] that is declared to have legal validity [Note: [Col. 1143D] Mabillon reads: “that firmly possess validity, we order.” Martin, manuscript B: “reciprocally, which are ordered by the strength of the seals.”]. Let it be produced, granted, and preserved unimpaired in every respect, according to the tenor written below, which, with the help of Christ the Lord, we have established.

Accordingly, we appoint you, holy Martin of Tours, as judge [Note: [Col. 1143D] Mosheim reads: “declaring you heir.” Below Mabillon reads: “that your basilica may be duly ordered …” From this passage and what follows, the origin of the subjection of the monastery of Attanum—which is today a college of secular canons—to the basilica of Saint [Col. 1144D] Martin is evident.] in such a way that this may be carried out through the provost of the holy order of your basilica. Whatever we have given to you, or to anyone else, or whatever we have asked to be done, we beseech you, by your authority and holy dominion, to ensure that all these things be done and remain so after our death.

Therefore, holy Martin, by this page of our testament we give you half of Griciensis [Note: [Col. 1144D] Manuscript B of Martin reads: “Griciensis with all its rights; the other [half] is situated at Attanum.” In manuscript A of Martin, “at Attanum” is absent.], while the other half, with its buildings and all its rights, situated at Attanum, let our monks possess forever, with you, holy Martin, as their defender. This is on the condition that we commend to you, Lord Martin, for appointment the monastery which, with the Lord inspiring and helping us, we established, and the monks whom God has ordained through us sinners to be there, or whom God may later command to be appointed—both those from among our free persons and those from among our slaves.

If thereafter, which God forbid, anyone should wish to withdraw from your authority anything that has been built for you, holy Martin, at the holy places out of love for Christ and in your honor or that of the saints, by some evil and wicked contrivance—which God avert—and if the person considered worthy to govern and administer it should neglect to appoint or subordinate it without the administration of your holy basilica [Note: [Col. 1144D] Manuscripts read: “considered worthy”; and “if the provost of your pious holy administration should neglect to appoint or undertake the administration of your holy basilica.”], let him be accursed by your powers.

Our portion of the estate of Sisciacum [Note: [Col. 1144D] Mosheim consistently reads Fisciacum.], namely the house and oratory with the remaining buildings, fields, woods, meadows, pastures, and inhabitants [Editor: small fields], with all its rights, as it is possessed by us at present, let your holy basilica, Lord Martin, and also the monks of Attanum entrusted to you 1310 [Col. 1144B] possess it. We decree that they live under your protection, and that you may have God propitious. From this estate of Sisciacum we have given you, Lord Martin, and your monks, for the portion of your basilica, three plowmen—Parminius, Talasius, and Claudius—and our other slaves, or whatever persons owe us servile service, except those who are already free, namely Clara and Marcia.

We likewise give Ursacius, with his wife and children, to you for service, on the condition that they cultivate four arpents of vineyard each.

Let our monks of Attanum also possess, with you, Lord Martin, as their defender, our cell dedicated in honor of Saint Medard, which seems to be situated under Gaudomarus [Alternative: Gandomarus] and is commonly called Exidolium. [Col. 1144C] [Note: [Col. 1144D] This clause is absent in manuscript A of Martin. Exidolium, commonly Exideuil, is a fortress near the monastery of Attanum, frequently mentioned by Geoffrey, prior of Vigeois, in his Chronicle.]

We wish our monks of Attanum to have, through you, holy Martin, our house at Nonniacum [Note: [Col. 1144D] So the manuscripts; Mosheim reads Homacum, Mabillon Memacum. Meimac is a place made famous by a Benedictine monastery.], with its buildings, vineyards, woods, meadows, pastures, and all its rights, and likewise Luciacum and Marcomont, with their vineyards and all their rights, according to what we have possessed by God’s favor. We ask that, with you as their defender, they possess these places, together with the following slaves: Parminius, with his wife and children; Leomere, with his wife and children; Armedius, with his wife and children; Rusticus, with his wife and children; Claudius; and Silvius, with his wife and children.

These people shall likewise cultivate four arpents of vineyard for the monks, while their wives shall pay ten silver pieces each year to the monks of Attanum named above. No one at any time shall presume to demand anything more from them. They shall possess their personal property—small fields and little vineyards—without anyone disturbing them, but on the condition that they presume neither to sell nor alienate it.

As for Scauriniacum, our house, which is called our portion [Alternative: “is owed to us,”] apart from what we have given and what we have sold, with its vineyards, meadows, woods, and pastures, let your basilica, Lord Martin, retain half as its heir [Note: [Col. 1145D] Mabillon reads: “Lord Martin, let it possess [as] is recalled in this instrument.”], and we humbly request that our monks of Attanum possess the other half through you.

We have assigned Eufrasius and Meroaldus as vine-growers of your [Col. 1145B] vineyard, Lord Martin, on the condition that they cultivate and tend four arpents of vineyard.

We likewise assign Valentinian to the monks named above, so that he too may cultivate four arpents of vineyard for the monks and nothing more. His wife Subfronia, and any children they may have, shall remain 1311 free.

We have given to the basilica of Saint Lord Martin our portion of the estate of Rofiace [Note: [Col. 1145D] Mosheim reads Rosiacum. This seems to designate Moutier-Rouseil, where a monastery existed wholly subject to the jurisdiction of Saint Martin, as it still does today, although it has been converted into a college of canons and recently transferred to Albussonium.], namely a house called Juliacum [Note: [Col. 1145D] So Martin and Mosheim; others read Viliacum. Mosheim below reads Gemiliacum.], with all its rights. Likewise, we wish Genuliacum, with its buildings, meadows, woods, pastures, and all its rights, to be given to Saint Martial.

From Scauriniacum, five arpents of cultivated vineyard which Provincianus the vine-grower cultivated, and at Negiacum the cultivated vineyard arpents which we give as our offering, shall be received by those serving Saint Martial or his matricula through our holy heir.

The enclosed plot with our house within the walls of the city of Limoges, together with its entrance and exit, shall be possessed in equal succession by your basilica, holy Martin, and our monks of Attanum. Likewise, at the fortress of Issandon [Note: [Col. 1145D] This fortress is situated on the Vienne, commonly called Issaudon.], let them possess the enclosed plot within the walls, with our house, in equal measure [Alternative: “possess it.”].

We wish our portion of Eustriacum to be given to Florentia and her children. Our freedpersons, whose names are listed below, shall remain under your protection, holy lord Martin: Castorius with his wife Limphasia; Octardus with his wife Exsuperia; Aquilinus and Pascentius with their wives and children; Mallostus with his wife; Antedia with her son; Leotcardus with his wife Gaudiosa; Gariabaudus with his wife; Faustinus with his wife Ermentaria; John with his wife and children; Marometus with his wife Sanctonidia; Frontuinus with his [Col. 1145D] wife and children; Antonia [Note: [Col. 1145D] Others read: “and Antonia’s children”]; Nimasus with his wife Maria; Majorianus with his wife Gerontia; Leonetus with his wife Bajola; Basulus with his wife [Col. 1146A] Avencia; Mauricius with his wife Margaridia; Sanieldus with his wife Marcella; Leontius with his wife Euminia; Urretia; Eulia [Note: [Col. 1145D] Others read: “with their wives Cumina, Urasecia, and Lucia”], whom we redeemed from captivity; Romana with her children; the children of Burgonerus; and Frontasius with his children.

We order Hildemodus, with his wife and children, to be free, together with their small fields and little vineyards and whatever personal property they have or may later acquire. They shall have it granted on the condition, however, that they have no power to sell or give away any of their small fields or vineyards.

We likewise order Procula and Macedonia to continue serving there. We also order our slaves listed below, together with their lineage [Note: [Col. 1146D] “Lineage” is likewise written for *agnatio* in the Visigothic laws.], to be declared slaves: Solemius with his wife and children; Maurencianus with his wife Valeriana; Aligilius with his wife Basilia; Aliasonius [Col. 1146B] with his wife Florentina; Specia with his wife Eugeria [Alternative: Eugenia]; Lupicinus with his wife Hoctorecia and children; Francardus with his wife 1312 Orogia and children; Amaretus with his wife Savina; Frangomeres with his wife Leoboda; Parthenius with his wife Mariosa; and Sonulfus [Alternative: Ronulfus] with his wife Animia and children.

We have spoken of their lineage, but we have also made some of them free. We decree that they may have their small fields and little vineyards, or whatever they appear to possess or may hereafter acquire, on the condition that each year they bring three pounds of something called *carra* to our [Note: [Col. 1146D] Others read: “three pounds of earth, bring it to our [monastery]”; and that each month they bring individual *condoma* in turn and recall our Masses. Mabillon suspects that the reading should be: “they shall bring to the monastery, or to the monastery’s treasury, a pound of wax for each measure of land.”] and that each month they recall our Masses in turn with eulogiae (blessed offerings), and place five silver pieces upon the altar, and give a gift according to what their poverty is able to provide.

Nothing more shall be demanded from them, or from the basilica of Saint Martin, or from our monks, than what is written; they must fulfill it.

These free men and free women of ours, whom our father of blessed memory, Jucundus, commended to us by his testament [Note: [Col. 1146D] He is buried in the church of Saint Michael of Poitiers, in the suburb of Limoges; that church is still subject to the jurisdiction of Saint Martin.], and likewise those whom we made free for the salvation of the soul of our brother Eustadius of blessed memory [Alternative: “our son”], we commend to you, holy Martin, for protection. If anyone wishes to disturb or dominate them in any way beyond what has been imposed upon them, you, holy Martin, defend them.

We also order the women listed below to serve there: Baudonidia [Note: [Col. 1146D] Others read Lindonidia … Abenda.] with her children; Habenda; Allovera; Fraterna; Amasonia; Artemia; Susanna; Proba; Probatia; and Frotania. They shall each pay one tremissis annually to our monks, and no one shall presume to demand more from them, lest he incur what has been set forth above.

Our horses and little draft animals, or cows, sheep, oxen, and pigs; bedding; household equipment; and whatever the administrator of Saint Martin finds in our storerooms or enclosed plots after our death—let him distribute half to the poor, and let our monks named above receive the other half.

We also add the slaves called tenant-farmers, who are said to be tributary to us [Alternative: “are owed to us.”]. Let half benefit your basilica, Lord Martin, and the other half our monks, and let them all pay one tremissis each year. These are: Eulodius with the children who are owed to us; Renchardus with his children; Friardus with his children; Amanda with her children; Gundemerus without [Editor: with] children; and Dominica with her daughter. For this reason we have given the aforesaid slaves to these holy places, so that [Col. 1147B] their merits may free us sinners.

We have judged it right to insert a statement of the ministry that each holy place established there is to possess 1313 [Note: [Col. 1147D] That is, sacred furnishings.]: four towers, three silk coverings, and four silver chalices. Two are handled vessels, bought for thirty solidi each. The middle one, made with gold, is worth thirty solidi, and the fourth is worth thirteen solidi. A silver paten worth seventy-two solidi.

Four silk coverings: one is worth thirty solidi, another sixteen solidi, the third fifteen solidi, and the fourth forty-five solidi. Two of these are made with gold. Also, an ornamented linen covering worth four solidi; four corporal cloths; three silk coverings; five smaller ones; and [Col. 1147C] altar cloths—tribunals [Alternative: tribunae] in the basilica worth twelve solidi; other ordinary ones worth six solidi; and other ordinary ones before the altar worth five solidi.

Ornamented veils for the great doorway worth three solidi. Other veils for that doorway worth three solidi. Also a veil for the smaller doorway worth two solidi. Also a painted veil worth five solidi.

Likewise, in the oratory of Saint Hilary, a crown with a gilded silver cross and precious gems, filled with relics of the holy lords, with its ornaments, valued at one hundred solidi. That crown has hanging from it eight leaves made of gold and gems; on that cross are two similar [ornaments], and large imitation gems set around it in gold; beneath it is a little cross of gold and eight small gems.

A silk altar cloth with its ornamentation, worth twelve solidi. Also an altar cloth over the little altar of Saint Hilary, overlaid with gold and made with pearls, worth thirty solidi. Three silk wall hangings ornamented throughout the oratory, worth eight solidi. Also an ordinary altar cloth on the altar of Lord Hilary, worth two solidi. Also a veil in the house of Hilary, made of *dramiosericum*, worth [Col. 1148A] forty solidi.

Also, at the shrine of Lord Maximinus, three little veils: one before the altar, crimson, worth two solidi, and the other two worth three solidi. Also a crimson altar cloth at the shrine of Lord Julianus, worth one solidus. An ordinary silk altar cloth, ornamented, at the shrine of Lord Maximinus; corporal cloths at the shrine of Lord Hilary; and ordinary doorway veils.

Also, two silk cloths over the holy tomb [Note: [Col. 1147D] So Mosheim; the manuscript reads “our tomb.” Below Mosheim reads “five ornamented with gold.” Aredius counted Saint Maximinus among his patrons because he had spent a long time at Trier.], worth sixty solidi. Also five altar cloths ornamented in the Achaian manner over the tombs, worth fifteen solidi. Also a *profedata* cloth [Alternative: *proserica*], worth two solidi. Another *profedata*, worth one solidus. Two veils before those tombs, worth five solidi.

All these things and the ornaments of the saints, and whatever is over the tombs of the holy martyrs of Attanum, namely [Col. 1148B] the deacon Scipio and Aventiolus, whom we appointed to guard them and minister before the saints, we have entrusted to our lord Nicetius, deacon of Saint Martin. Likewise, from Sisciacum, two tribunals in the oratory, worth four solidi; three doorway veils, worth six solidi; towers, chalices, altar cloths, and 1314 coverings, we have handed over to the aforesaid martyr-shrines for safekeeping.

We further adjure the provost of Saint Martin and our monks of Attanum, by the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ and by the merits of all the saints, that in the oratory of Saint Hilary [Note: [Col. 1147D] According to chapter 34 of his Life, Aredius had asked to be buried in the oratory of Saint Hilary.], in my cell, every Thursday, at all times, the morning office and the Mass of the holy lords be celebrated there by the monks at an early hour.

And when necessary, order the roofs of the holy places to be repaired, namely at Attanum and Sisciacum, admonishing our monks, free persons, slaves, and inhabitants that these holy places remain fortified at all times. Let what has been arranged here be preserved in the Lord Jesus Christ as we have left it, just as it ought to be.

Those, however, who do not wish to serve us, or our monastery and community, shall be considered strangers to all our property, both while we are alive and after our death.

If the Attanenses [Note: [Col. 1147D] The manuscripts read: “While we are alive, the Attanenses monks have provided the Vigeois monks with comforts as they have pleased.” The passage is entirely corrupt. In the Vigeois exemplar several things are inserted that were given by Aredius and Pelagia to the monastery of Vigeois; see Mabillon, *Analecta*, vol. II, p. 66. The monastery of Vigeois, commonly Vigeois, on the Vienne among the Limoges people, was formerly an abbey and later a priory of Saint Martial of Limoges, whose prior was Geoffrey, author of the Chronicle of Vigeois.] provide comforts to the monks of Vigeois during our lifetime, as seems appropriate, we willingly give them our portion of Fexitoialum and one hundred arpents of land at Sisciacum. But if they refuse to provide the comforts, reclaim, holy Martin, for your basilica and the monks of Attanum, for perpetual possession, everything entrusted to you that was given to them by us. [Col. 1148D]

Whatever, perhaps, has not been included in this testament of ours, or has gone beyond what ought to have been set down—if a small piece of land or any movable property is found, let our heir, Lord Martin, reclaim everything for himself. If little slaves remain and are found [Col. 1149A] outside the testament, both those who have had documents of freedom drawn up and those who have not shall remain free, with Saint Martin as their defender. Whatever we have given by documents confirmed with the subscription of our hand, we order to be entirely valid.

If anyone wishes to act against this testament of ours, or attempts to proceed in any way other than what is established by this our deliberation, both here and forever, by the powers of the holy and blessed lord Martin, let him be excommunicated and anathematized, and let the curse contained in Psalm 108 against Judas Iscariot come upon him.

If any letters or erasures are found, we ourselves made them while repeatedly rereading our testament and deciding to correct it. [Col. 1149B]

[Col. 1150A] Aredius, presbyter and sinner in the name of Christ, wrote, reread, and signed our testament on the day and in the year stated above.

Pelagia reread and subscribed our testament on the day and in the year stated above.

Alstidius, at the request of my lord Aredius and Pelagia, subscribed the testament made by them.

Calpurnus, at the request of my lord Aredius and Pelagia, subscribed this testament 1315 on the day and in the year stated above.

Leo, requested by Lord Aredius and Pelagia, confirmed this testament on the day and in the year stated above.

Nectarius 1316 confirmed this testament at the request of Lord Aredius and Pelagia.

Sign. + Aidelfus, subdeacon. [Col. 1150B] Sign. + Nectarius, witness.

[Col. 1149]

## Appendix to the Works of Saint Gregory of Tours, Containing Ancient Documents Praised by Him or Illustrating His Works

[Note: [Col. 1149D] We have not hesitated to reprint this appendix in its entirety, although it contains some material already published or soon to be published elsewhere in the *Patrologia*. We have judged that it will be especially welcome to the reader to have Gregory’s works and their necessary supplement before his eyes in a single continuous sequence. Editor.]

[Col. 1149]

## Poem of Saint Damasus the Pope on the Holy Martyrs Chrysanthus and Daria

[Note: [Col. 1149D] See Book I, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 38, at the end. Editor.]

(From Sarazanius.) (C)*

[Col. 1149B]

By equal votive offerings two names preserve the tomb:

[Col. 1149C] Chrysanthus and Daria, now an honor to be revered.

Savage madness, disregarding the law of burial,

made the tombs of the saints the prey of raging violence.

Now these things rise more splendidly from the resources of the poor,

but are more pleasing to God through rich devotion.

Weep, cruel race, for your crime: your frenzies have perished;

in these shrines honor has increased through your losses.

## Inscription in the Apse of Saint Pancratius

[Note: [Col. 1149D] See Book I, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 39, note h, column 74. Editor.]

(From Mabillon, *Analecta*, vol. IV.)

On account of the outstanding merit and singular benefit of the blessed martyr Pancratius, Honorius, bishop and servant of God, stripped away the weight of age and, when ruin threatened, newly built from the foundations for God’s people the basilica, worn out by age, which had been erected beside the martyr’s body and neglected in antiquity [Note: [Col. 1150D] Perhaps: “in ancient times.”]. He also placed the martyr’s body, which had lain obliquely in the hall, in its proper place at an altar adorned with distinguished metals. [Col. 1149D]

## Testament of Perpetuus, Bishop of Tours

[Note: [Col. 1150D] See Book X of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 31, at the end, number 6, column 567. Editor.]

(From D’Achery, *Spicilegium*, vol. V.)

[Col. 1150A] 1317

In the name of Jesus Christ. Amen. I, Perpetuus, a sinner and priest of the Church of Tours, did not wish to depart without a testament, lest the poor be defrauded of those things which heavenly grace, not because I deserved it but generously and lovingly, bestowed upon me, and lest, God forbid, the goods of a priest pass to anyone other than the Church.

To the presbyters, deacons, and clerics of my church I give and bequeath the peace of the Lord Jesus Christ. Amen. Confirm, Lord, what you have wrought in us; let them know no schisms; let them remain steadfast in the faith. Whoever follows the rule of the Gospel, let him be blessed with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places through Christ Jesus. Amen.

And may the Lord Jesus slay the wicked one with the breath of His mouth. Amen, amen. Peace to the Church; peace to the people, in the city and in the countryside, from God and the Father of the Lord Jesus Christ. Amen. Come, Lord, and do not delay. Amen.

Therefore, presbyters, deacons, and clerics of my church, with the counsel of Count Agilo, I permit you to choose wherever you wish to bury this corpse of death. I know that my Redeemer does not die, and that in the flesh I shall see my Deliverer. Amen. Yet if you should show me the mercy I humbly request, I would wish to rest at the feet of Lord Martin until the day of judgment. You will see, judge, and choose. I wish and decree it. I order whatever pleases you, my lords and brothers, to be valid.

First, therefore, I, Perpetuus, wish all the men and women whom I possess at the estate of Saponaria, whom I bought with my own money, to be free, and likewise the children whom I do not manumit in the Church on the day of my departure. They shall nevertheless serve freely as long as they live 1318 for my Church, but without servitude transmissible to heirs or tied to the soil.

I also give and bequeath to my Church the field that Aligarius sold me at the said estate of Saponaria, with its pond. Likewise the mills above the Carus near the said estate, as well as the grazing lands and meadows, I give and bequeath to my Church.

I likewise give and bequeath to my Church the estate of Bertiniacum, with its wood and all its revenue, under the same condition on which it was sold to me by the deacon Daniel: that oil be prepared from its produce to keep the tomb of Lord Martin continually illuminated. But if this is neglected, and my will, which I do not expect, is made void, let the said estate of Bertiniacum with its dependencies immediately pass to my heirs, who will be named below. I wish, decree, and order it. [Col. 1151A]

Whatever is owed to me, in whatever place and by whatever person, on the day of my departure I give and bequeath to the debtors themselves. No one shall presume to collect what I remit. I wish and decree it.

To you, my most beloved brother and fellow priest Eufronius, I give and bequeath a silver reliquary containing relics of the saints. I mean the one I used to carry. As for the other, gilded one, which is in my reliquary chest together with two golden chalices and a cross likewise of gold, made by Mabuinus, I give and bequeath to my Church.

At the same time, I give and bequeath to my Church all my books, except the Gospel book written by Hilary, once priest of Poitiers [Note: [Col. 1151D] Recently we saw in the library of the cathedral church of Tours a codex written in Saxon letters a thousand years ago. It is said, as one may conjecture from the circumstances, to have been written by the hand of Saint Hilary. But that it is not of so great an antiquity, apart from the form of its script, is proved by the inscription prefixed to the codex, which seems to indicate the date of the book. In it the discovery of Saint Innocentius, a martyr from the Theban Legion, is praised. As is clear from Surius under 22 September, this discovery occurred in the time of Protasius, bishop of Octodurum or Sion, who took part in the Council of Chalon around the year 650. Moreover, at the end of the codex the scribe reveals his name. The first inscription, written in capital letters, reads: “God, the true lover of innocence, long after the passion of the most sacred legion of Innocentius, with the waters of the Rhône River serving, revealed the illustrious limbs of the martyr Innocentius.” At the end it reads: “I, Holaindus—may the Trinity have mercy on me—amen. I beg all you Christians to pray the Lord’s communion for me, a sinner,” and so forth. From this codex it is evident that Protasius of Sion, Domitianus of Geneva, and Gratus of Aosta, who are said to have taken part in the discovery of Saint Innocentius, have been placed out of their proper order in the commonly circulated lists of the bishops of those sees.] which I give and bequeath, wish, and decree to you, my most beloved brother and fellow priest Eufronius, together with the aforementioned reliquary. Remember me. Amen.

To the church of Saint Dionysius at Ambasciacum [Note: [Col. 1152D] This church of Ambacia, dedicated to Saint Dionysius, still exists today, with a parish title and a priory, subject to the monastery of Saint Julian of Tours.], I give and bequeath a silver chalice and likewise a silver cross, in whose handle there is a relic of that same Saint Dionysius. [Col. 1151B]

To the church of Proillium I likewise give and bequeath a silver chalice and silver ewers [Perhaps: “pitchers”]. Likewise, to Amalarius, the presbyter there, I give one ordinary silk reliquary 1319, and also a silver *peristerium* and a silver dove for the repository, unless my Church should prefer to transfer to Amalarius the one it uses and retain mine. I leave the choice to my Church. I wish and decree it.

To my sister Julia Perpetua I give and bequeath a small gold cross, made of embossed work, containing relics of the Lord. Yet I earnestly ask her that, if—should the Lord so will—it should happen that she departs this life before the virgin Dadolena, she leave it to my Church for its possession. You also, sister Dadolena, I ask that, when dying, you assign it to whichever Church you please, lest it come into unworthy hands. But if Dadolena should pass away before you, it shall be entirely free for you, dearest sister Fidia Julia Perpetua, to leave the aforesaid cross to whatever Church you wish. I will and ordain this. Remember me, dearest, amen.

To you, Count Agilo, on account of your outstanding services to my Church and to my poor children, and so that you may continue firmly to undertake their defense as you have begun, I give and bequeath my serviceable horse and whichever mule you choose. Remember me, dearest son, amen.

To the Church of Saint Peter I give and bequeath outright the hangings which I have often granted it for use on the birthday feast of that same saint. To you, dearest brother and fellow priest, whom the Lord will provide to govern the Church after my departure—the Church that is now mine, then yours, or rather neither mine nor yours, but Christ’s—I give permission to choose from my possessions in the chamber and the adjoining treasury whatever you wish for episcopal use. Whatever you do not want shall belong to my heirs, who are to be named.

Never restore the priest from Malleio or the one from Orbona to the ranks from which they were deservedly deposed. Nevertheless, let them receive an allowance throughout their lives from a share of my revenues from Preslaio. Whatever remains, together with the share that I have granted them to use and enjoy, I leave for you to use and enjoy after they have died; after your departure, I give and bequeath it to my Church. But you, dearest brother and fellow priest, love my priests, deacons, clerics, and virgins—your own as well as mine; help them by your example and anticipate them with goodwill. See to it that they know themselves to be your children, not your slaves, and that you are their father, not their master. I ask, will, and ordain this.

But you, my very inmost being, dearest brothers, my crown, my joy, my lords, my children, Christ’s poor, the needy, beggars, the sick, widows, and orphans: you, I say, I name, declare, and establish as my heirs. After the things mentioned above have been deducted, whatever I possess in property—whether fields, pastures, meadows, woods, vineyards, homesteads, gardens, waters, or mills; or gold, silver, clothing, and other possessions whose disposition will not be found to have been settled—I order that you be the heirs.

And so that everything may be administered with discretion, I wish that, as soon as I have died and as soon as it can be done, these things be sold and converted into money, which shall be divided into three parts. Two parts are to be distributed among needy men, as the priest Agrarius and Count Agilo shall determine; the third is to be distributed among widows and poor women, as the virgin Dadolena shall determine [1320; Col. 1152B]. I will, ask, and ordain this.

I, Perpetuus, reread and subscribed this testament, written in my own hand, on the Kalends of May, after the consulship of Leo the Younger, Augustus. You, Delmatius, my son, keep this deposited with you, and, together with another similar document written and subscribed by my own hand, which I deposited with Dadolena, deliver it to Count Agilo to be opened and read before my brothers, the priests, deacons, and clerics. In the name of the Lord, I will, ask, and ordain that it be fixed and confirmed. Bless, Lord; come, Jesus Christ. I, Perpetuus, in your name. Amen.

### Epitaph of the same man

The peaks whose lofty summit raises crests,  
the distinguished Perpetuus had bestowed  
upon Lord Martin, beneath whose marble rest  
his bones, revered in prayer by the devout people.

He named Christ his heir, and many golden vessels,  
consecrating them with the Lord’s blood, he gave.  
He sent to heaven abundant gifts, which he gave to the needy,  
and he made his riches ascend before his own ascent.

Renowned through ancestors and mighty forebears, he was also a senator;  
more renowned still when he distributed his wealth to the poor.

Yet he did not build so great a tomb for Martin alone:  
he made the burial mound his own as well.

And although he lies buried before Martin’s feet,  
each rejoices in heaven in a like dwelling.

Look down from above upon this flock, good shepherd,  
and make Perpetuus’ homeland perpetual.

### Epitaph of Saint Abraham

[Note: [Col. 1152D] See Gregory, *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 3, at the end. Ed.]

From Apollinaris Sidonius, Book VII, Letter 17.

Abraham, rightly to be joined to the holy patrons,  
whose companion I would not hesitate to call you:

for they go before, so that you yourself may soon follow;  
the portion of martyrdom grants a share in the kingdom.

Born beside the Euphrates, you endured prison for Christ,  
and endured chains, loosened only after five years of hunger.

Escaping the savage king of the region of Susa  
[Note: [Col. 1153D] That is, Persia.],  
you alone hasten all the way to the western land.

But signs of virtue follow the confessor,  
and, fugitive, you drive evil spirits into flight.

Wherever you come, a crowd of ghosts proclaims that it is yielding;  
you command demons to go, an exile into exile.

You are sought from every quarter, and no region contains you;  
the honor conferred on you is more burdensome than any weight.

You shun the Roman and Byzantine tumult,  
and the walls shattered by the arrow-bearing Titus.

The wall of Alexandria does not hold you, nor that of Antioch;  
you disdain the Carthaginian roofs of the house of Elissa.

You reject the populous countryside of marshy Ravenna,  
and the places that derive their name from the wool-bearing sow  
[Note: [Col. 1153D] Milan.].

This corner pleases you, this poor retreat,  
and the hut whose roof was pressed down with thatch.

Here you yourself build a venerable temple to God,  
you who had first become God’s temple in body.

Here the course of life and the journey of life are finished;  
a double crown remains for your toil.

Now the thousands of sacred Paradise surround you:  
now Abraham has you as a fellow pilgrim.

Now you enter your homeland—the homeland from which Adam fell—  
and now you can go to the spring of your river  
[Note: [Col. 1153D] The Euphrates flows from the paradise of Eden.].

### Letter of King Theodoric to Clovis: congratulating him on the victory won over the Alemanni

[Note: [Col. 1153D–1154D] See Saint Gregory, *History of the Franks*, Book II, chapter 30. Ed.]

(Cassiodorus, Book II, Letter 41.)

Theodoric, king of Italy, to Luduin, king of the Franks. We indeed congratulate you upon the glorious kinship of your valour, because you have successfully roused the Frankish nation, inactive in former times, to new wars, and have subjected by your victorious right hand the peoples of the Alemanni, overcome by stronger claims. But since excess seems always deserving of curtailment in the authors of treachery, and since the punishable fault of the foremost men ought to be a vengeance upon all, moderate your anger against the exhausted remnant; for those whom you see to have fled for refuge to the protection of your forefathers deserve by right to escape through grace. Be merciful to those who, terrified, are concealed within our borders [Col. 1153C]. It is a memorable triumph that the fiercely warlike Alemann has been so frightened that you compel him to beg you for the gift of life. Let it suffice that their king has fallen together with his people's pride; let it suffice that an innumerable nation has been subdued, partly by the sword and partly by servitude. For if you contend with the survivors, you will not yet be thought to have conquered them all. In such matters accept a maxim frequently proved by experience: those wars have turned out prosperously for me which were concluded with a moderate end. For he wins continually who knows how to moderate everything, since pleasant prosperity rather favours those who do not become rigid through excessive harshness. Yield therefore graciously to our inclination what the nations have customarily granted it by common precedent. Thus you will seem also to have satisfied my requests, and you need not be anxious about that part which you know belongs to us. Therefore, greeting you with the grace, honour, and affection due to your rank, we have sent our envoys, this man and that man, to your Excellence with our customary goodwill, through whom we may receive both assurance of your welfare and the fulfilment of our hoped-for request [Col. 1153D]. We have entrusted to the bearers of this letter certain matters which have come to us for your advantage, to communicate orally, so that, made more cautious, you may steadfastly attain the victory you desire. For your safety is our glory; and as often as we learn joyful news concerning you, we judge that the kingdom of Italy has advanced. We have also sent with them, at your request, a cithara-player trained in his art, who by singing with voice and hands in harmony may delight the glory of your power; and we believe he will be welcome for this reason, that you judged him especially worth sending to you.

### Extracts from the letter of Avitus, bishop of Vienne, to King Clovis

[Note: [Col. 1154D] See the same work, chapter 31. Ed.]

(From Sirmond.)

[Col. 1154A]

[1322] “The keenness of your discernment, of whatever kind, etc. For even in the western regions the light of a new sun rises in a king who is not new; and fittingly the birth of our Redeemer began his splendour, so that it may seem appropriate that on the day on which the world received the Lord of heaven, born for its redemption, you too should be reborn from water unto salvation. Therefore, let the Lord’s birthday, which is celebrated, be yours also: the day on which you were consecrated to Christ, as Christ was born for the world; on which you consecrated your soul to God, your life to the present generation, and your fame to posterity. What can now be said of the most glorious solemnity of your rebirth itself? Although I was not bodily present at its rites, I was not absent from the sharing of its joys. For divine mercy added this further cause for congratulation to our regions: before your baptism, news of your most exalted humility reached us. Hence, after this expectation, the sacred night found us already assured concerning you [Col. 1154B]. For we were comparing and considering among ourselves what it was like when the assembled company of bishops, in the holy eagerness of service, cherished the royal limbs with life-giving waters; when the head feared by nations bowed itself to the servants of God; when hair grown beneath a helmet was clothed with the saving helmet of sacred anointing; when, the covering of armour laid aside, spotless limbs shone with the same brightness of white garments, etc. Therefore shine perpetually upon those present by your diadem and upon those absent by your majesty. All celebrate the successes of the happy triumphs which that realm achieves through you. The good fortune reaches us too: whenever you fight there, we conquer. Yet amid these things, concern for mercy preserves in you the affection of the Catholic religion; and on the summit that holds the helm of all affairs, holiness stands out no less than power. It was doubtless from this that you commanded, by a princely decree, that the son of your servant, the illustrious man Laurentius, be sent to you; and I report that I obtained this from my lord, indeed the king of his own nation, but your soldier [Col. 1154C]. For there is nothing in which he cannot serve. He commends the man sent. I rejoice with him on being sent, and envy him because he will see you. To him it is less to be counted as an advantage to be restored to his own parent than to be presented to the father of all.”

On this occasion Anastasius, bishop of Rome, also congratulated King Clovis; his letter has been published. At that time too, as learned men suppose, he appointed his blessed Remigius his vicar in the kingdom of the Franks, although the letter on that matter reported by Hincmar bears the name of Hormisdas.

### Extracts from the conference of bishops before King Gundobad

[Note: [Col. 1154D] See the same work, chapter 34, col. 230, note h. Ed.]

(From *Spicilegium*, vol. V.)

Since the Lord provided for his Church and inspired the heart of lord Remigius for the salvation of the whole nation—Remigius who everywhere destroyed altars of idols and powerfully spread the true faith with a multitude of signs—it came about that several bishops assembled, the king not opposing, in the hope that the Arians, who were dividing the Christian religion, might return to unity [1323; Col. 1154D]. So that this might be done more successfully and appear to have happened by occasion rather than design, lord Stephen wrote to many bishops and invited them to the approaching feast of Saint Justus, at which, because of the abundance of miracles, a very great concourse of people gathered. Thus Avitus came from Vienne, Aeonius from Arles, from Valence [lacuna], from Marseilles [lacuna]ius, and many others besides, all of Catholic confession and praiseworthy life in the Lord. All these, with lord Stephen, went to Sarbiniacum, where the king then was, to greet him [Col. 1155A]. Certain of the more powerful Arians were there with him; had they been able, they would have prevented our people's access to the king, but, with the Lord's help, they accomplished nothing.

After the greeting had been made, lord Avitus—who, although neither in rank nor age the senior, was nevertheless greatly deferred to—said to the king: “If your Excellence were willing to procure peace for the Church, we are ready to demonstrate our faith so clearly to be according to the Gospel and the apostles that no one will doubt that the faith which you maintain is not according to God and the Church. You have here men of your own who are trained in every learning: command them to confer with us and see whether they can answer our arguments, as we are ready to answer theirs.” To this the king replied: “If your faith is true, why do not your bishops restrain the king of the Franks, who has declared war on me and allied himself with my enemies in order to destroy me? For there is no faith where there is coveting of another's property and thirst for the blood of peoples. Let him show his faith by his deeds.” Then lord Avitus humbly replied, with a face and speech like an angel's: “We do not know, O king, by what counsel or for what cause the king of the Franks does what you say; but Scripture teaches us that because of abandonment of God's law kingdoms are often overthrown and enemies raised up on every side against those who set themselves as enemies against God. But return with your people to God's law, and he himself will give peace within your borders. For if you have peace with him, you will have it with the rest also, and your enemies will not prevail.” The king said to him: “Do I not profess God's law? Yet because I refuse three gods, you say that I do not profess God's law. In Holy Scripture I have not read that there are several gods, but one,” etc. [Note: [Col. 1155] See Saint Gregory, *History of the Franks*, Book II, chapter 32. Ed.]

The following day it happened. For as the king was returning by the Saône to the city, he sent for lords Stephen and Avitus to come to him. When they had come, the king said: “You have what you ask. For my priests are ready to show you that none can be coeternal and consubstantial with God. But I do not wish this to be done before all the people, lest disturbances arise; only before my senators and others whom I shall choose, as you shall choose whom you wish from among your own, though not in a large number. This shall be done tomorrow in this place.” Having said this, the bishops greeted the king, departed, and returned to report everything to the other bishops [Col. 1155C]. It was the vigil of the solemnity of Saint Justus. Though they had wished the matter to take place on the day after the feast, they did not wish to delay longer for so great a good. Instead, they unanimously resolved to keep vigil at Saint Justus's tomb, that through his intercession they might obtain from the Lord the petitions of their hearts. It happened that night, when the reader according to custom began the reading from Moses, that he came upon these words of the Lord: “But I will harden his heart, and multiply my signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, and he will not hear you” (Exod. 7). Then, after the psalms had been sung, when he read from the prophets, he came upon the Lord's words to Isaiah: “Go and say to this people: Hear indeed, but do not understand; and see the vision, but do not know it. Blind the heart of this people, make their ears heavy, and close their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand in their heart, be converted, and I heal them” (Isa. 6) [Col. 1155D]. When psalms had again been sung and he read from the Gospel, he came upon the words in which the Saviour reproaches the Jews for unbelief: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the miracles done among you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have done penance in sackcloth and ashes” (Matt. 11). Finally, when a reading was made from the Apostle, these words were pronounced: “Do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering? Do you not know that God's forbearance leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you store up wrath for yourself in the time of wrath” (Rom. 2).

When this had been noticed by all the bishops, they understood that those readings had occurred thus by the Lord's will, so that they might know the king's heart had been hardened and that God was leaving him in his impenitence to display the riches of his justice. They became very sorrowful and spent the night in tears [Col. 1156A]. Yet they did not cease to maintain the truth of our religion against the Arians. Therefore, at the time commanded by the king, all the bishops assembled and went together to the king with many priests and deacons and some Catholics, among whom were Placidus and Lucanus, who were among the leading officers of the king's service. The Arians too came with their party. When they had therefore taken their seats before the king, lord Avitus spoke for the Catholics and Boniface for the Arians. But after lord Avitus had set forth our faith with testimonies from Holy Scripture, being another Tully, and the Lord inspired grace into all that he said, such consternation fell upon the Arians that Boniface, who had listened quite amicably, could make absolutely no answer to lord Avitus's arguments [Col. 1156B]. He merely raised difficult questions, by which he seemed to wish to weary the king. But when Avitus pressed him to answer what had been said before, promising that he himself would also answer the questions Boniface had raised, Boniface could not answer a single argument proposed by lord Avitus, nor allege anything in defence of his own side. He only opened his mouth in abuse, calling the Catholics deceivers and worshippers of a multitude of gods. When he said only this and the king saw the confusion of his sect, he rose from his seat, saying that Boniface would answer on the following day. All the bishops therefore departed; and because the day had not yet declined, they went together with the other Catholics to the basilica of lord Justus, confessing that the Lord is good and praising him who had granted them such a victory over their enemies.

On the following day they again set out for the palace with those who had been present on the preceding day. When they entered, they found Aredius, who was trying to persuade them to return, etc. [Col. 1156C]

When they had taken their seats, lord Avitus proved so clearly that the Catholics did not worship several gods that both Catholics and opponents marvelled in astonishment at his wisdom. He did this in answer to the abuse Boniface had cast upon our faith. After he was silent, in order to give place to Boniface's answers, the latter could say nothing other than he had done the day before; adding abuse to abuse, he shouted with such violence that through hoarseness he could speak no further and seemed almost to be suffocated. When the king saw this and had waited long enough, he finally rose, showing indignation in his expression against Boniface. Then lord Avitus said to the king: “If your Sublimity would command these men to answer our propositions, you could judge which faith ought to be retained.” But neither the king nor the other Arians with him answered, so astonished were they at lord Avitus's teaching and wisdom [Col. 1156D]. Seeing their silence, he added: “If your men cannot answer our arguments, what prevents us all from coming together in the same faith?” Then, while they murmured, confident of his faith in the Lord, he added: “If our arguments cannot convince them, I do not doubt that God will confirm our faith by a miracle. Let your Sublimity command that both they and we go to the tomb of Justus, the man of God, and inquire of him concerning our faith, and let Boniface likewise inquire concerning his; and the Lord will declare through the mouth of his servant in which he is pleased.” The astonished king seemed to assent, but the Arians began to cry out, saying that for the manifestation of their faith they did not wish to do as Saul had done and was therefore cursed, or resort to incantations and unlawful practices; that Scripture, which was stronger than all sorceries, was sufficient for them [Col. 1157A]. Repeating this continually and bellowing rather than shouting, the king, who had already risen, took lord Stephen and lord Avitus by the hands and led them to his chamber. On entering, he embraced them and asked them to pray for him. They indeed recognized the perplexity and anguish of his heart; but because the Father had not drawn him, he could not come to the Son, so that the truth might be fulfilled: “It is not of one who wills nor of one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9) [1326].
