From that day very many Arians came to repentance and, after some days, were baptized. And the Lord magnified our faith through the intercession of lord Justus in the sight of all.

### Letter of Saint Remigius to King Clovis

[Note: [Col. 1157D] See Saint Gregory, *History of the Franks*, Book II, chapter 31, at the end. Ed.] (C)

Remigius, bishop, to the lord Clovis, illustrious in merits, king. Your cause of sorrow distresses me, and distresses me greatly: your sister Albochledis, of glorious memory, has died. Yet we can be consoled because she so departed from this light that she ought rather to be received in remembrance than mourned [Col. 1157B]. For such was her life that she is believed to have been taken up by the Lord, she who, chosen by God, passed to heaven. She lives in your faith, though she has been withdrawn from the sight you desire. Christ fulfilled her desire to receive the blessing of virginity. She who has been consecrated is not to be mourned, she who breathes forth before the Lord the flower of virginity and is, of course, adorned with the crown she received for virginity. Far be it that she should be mourned by the faithful who deserved to be the good fragrance of Christ, so that through him whom she pleases she may be able to bring help to those who ask. My lord, drive sorrow from your heart. With your mind duly composed, govern the kingdom more wisely, taking more exalted counsels through zeal for serenity; strengthen your limbs with a joyful heart, cast off the body of grief, and you will watch more keenly for salvation. The kingdom remains for you to administer and, with God as your auspice, to govern. You are the head of peoples and bear their rule. Let not those accustomed to see happy things through you see you afflicted by the bitterness of mourning. Be yourself the comforter of your soul, maintaining the vigour of that inborn prudence, lest sorrow take brightness from your mind [Col. 1157C]. At her present departure, she who, as I believe, is joined to virgin choirs, the king rejoices in heaven. Greeting your glory, I commend my friend, the priest Maccolus, whom I have sent. I ask that you pardon such presumption: I who ought to have come in person have presumed to send words of exhortation. Yet through the bearer of this letter, if you command me to come, disregarding winter's severity, neglecting the cold, and trampling down the labour of the journey, I shall strive, with the Lord's help, to reach you.

### Another letter to the same

[Note: [Col. 1157D] The same work, chapter 37. Ed.] (C)

Remigius, bishop, to the lord Clovis, king illustrious and magnificent in merits. A great report has reached us that you have undertaken a successful administration of military affairs. It is no novelty that you have begun to be as your parents always were. This must first be done: that the Lord's judgment may not fail in you, a man of such merit, who through the industry of your humility has reached the summit of eminence; for, as the common saying has it, a man's deed is tested by its end [1327; Col. 1157D]. You ought to employ counsellors able to adorn your reputation; your beneficence ought to be chaste and honourable; you ought to show honour to your priests and always have recourse to their counsels. If you agree well with them, your province can prosper better. Raise up your citizens, relieve the afflicted, cherish widows, nourish orphans—or rather educate them—so that all may love and fear you. Let justice proceed from your mouth. Let nothing be expected from poor people or strangers, lest you should wish rather to receive gifts or anything else. Let your tribunal be open to all, so that no one departs from it sad. Whatever paternal wealth you possess, use it to free captives and release them from the yoke of slavery. If anyone comes into your presence, let him not feel himself a stranger [Col. 1158A]. Converse playfully with the young, deliberate with the old, if you wish to reign and be judged noble.

### Letter of King Clovis to the bishops

[Note: [Col. 1158D] The same work. Ed.]

(From the edition and the Corbie manuscript.)

Clovis, king, to the holy lords and bishops most worthy of the apostolic see. The report of what has been done or commanded to our whole army before we entered the land of the Goths could not have escaped your Blessedness. First, concerning the servants of all Churches, we commanded that no one should attempt to seize anything; nor any religious women, nor widows who proved themselves devoted to the Lord's religion. The same condition applies to clerics and to the children of the aforesaid clerics and widows who appeared to live with them in their houses. It was also commanded to be observed concerning Church slaves who, having been taken from churches, are proved by the bishops' oaths to be such, that none of them should suffer any violence or harm [Col. 1158B]. Thus it is to be understood in full that, if any of the persons mentioned above had suffered forcible captivity, whether in churches or outside the Church, we command that they be restored entirely without any delay. As for the other lay captives who have been captured outside the peace [i.e. protected territory] and have been identified, apostolic men, it is not to be denied to whichever of you it may please, at your discretion. But concerning those, clerics as well as laymen, who had been seized within our peace, if you truly recognize your letters as sealed below with your ring, let them in every case be sent to us, and know that an order issued on our part is to be confirmed. Yet our people ask that, to whomsoever you have deigned to give your letters, you do not delay in declaring under oath by God and by your blessing that what is requested to be remitted is true; because many variations or falsehoods have been found, so that, as it is written, “the just man perishes with the wicked.” Pray for me, holy lords and popes most worthy of the apostolic see.

### Diploma of Clovis the Great concerning the status of the monastery of Micy at Orléans

(From *Spicilegium*, vol. V.)

[Col. 1158C]

Clovis, illustrious man and king of the Franks. To you, venerable elder Euspicius, and to your Maximinus, so that you and those who succeed you in the holy profession may obtain by your prayers divine mercy for the welfare of ourselves, our beloved wife, and our sons, we grant Micy; and whatever belongs to our fisc within the river channels we transfer without exception by sacred *confarreatio* and ring, and grant for bodily possession free from tribute, ferry-toll, and exaction, both on this side and beyond the Loire and the Loiret, with Quercetum and Salictum and both mills. But you, holy Eusebius, bishop of the Catholic religion, support the old age of Euspicius, favour Maximinus, and keep both them and their possessions within your parish free from every calumny and injury. For those whom royal affection supports ought not to be harmed. Do likewise, all you bishops of the holy Catholic religion [Col. 1158D]. Therefore you, Euspicius and Maximinus, cease to be strangers among the Franks, and let the possessions which we give in the name of the holy, indivisible, equal, and consubstantial Trinity be to you in place of a homeland forever. So be it, as I, Clovis, have willed. I, Eusebius, bishop, have confirmed it.

### Letter of Leo, bishop of Sens, to King Childebert, that a new bishopric not be created at Melun, in a parish of his diocese where one has never existed

[Note: [Col. 1158D] The same work, Book VI, chapter 31, note c, col. 397. Ed.]

(From the edition and the Corbie manuscript.)

Leo, bishop, to the illustrious lord, most glorious lord, and son in Christ, King Childebert. I acknowledge that I have received the letter of your Highness with the honour due to it, in which you deem it proper that either our presence or our consent should be available for ordaining a bishop at Melun [Col. 1159A]. Let your Glory know that we are greatly astonished at this: first, because, without an order from our most glorious lord and prince, your son King Theudebert, under whose royal administration we are subject, you command that matters not done in past times should now be begun by our presence or consent. Above all, we could never even suspect or believe that you would wish such an injury to be done either to our order or to your own times: that we should permit our diocese, entrusted to us by God and guarded until now, by God's favour, in pontifical order, to pass, as though we were negligent and idle, to another's authority or to have its pastoral care transferred by an irrational decision. Therefore, greeting you with the fitting and due affection of charity in God, we ask and solemnly entreat that no bishop dare act against the decrees of the Fathers, whereby he may be convicted by synodal examination and blamed for unlawful presumption. Rather, let those things be done in your times, by God's inspiration, through which peace may exist among the priests and the people may not be torn from the care of their own pastor by a novel and unlawful ordination [Col. 1159B]. Keep, I pray, the decrees of the Fathers; bound by the severity of the canons, do not permit, as you write, another bishop to be ordained at the request of that people while their own bishop lives. For if they request this—which it is impious to believe—they ought to be judged deserters rather than faithful. Nor should the prince readily hear the prayers of men whose petitions produce scandals rather than preserve the peace beloved of God. For as blessed are the feet that bring peace, so woe is declared to those through whom scandal comes. If perhaps they ask that another bishop be made for them because, with the roads blocked, we can neither send them a visitor nor come ourselves, that fault does not concern us. For if the route on your side, as you know very well, had not been blocked for so long, we could, though old or infirm, have visited the people committed to us by ecclesiastical discipline, or at least have sent a visitor, as the canons prescribe [Col. 1159C]. For your Glory ought very well both to believe and know that, if any bishop contrary to the decrees of the canons should wish to ordain a bishop at Melun without our consent, then, until the matter comes to the pope's knowledge or a synodal hearing, both those who ordain and the man ordained will be separated from our communion. I, Leo, servant of Christ, have subscribed.

### Here begins the letter of our most merciful and blessed King Childebert, issued through the Churches to the priests and to all the people

[Note: [Col. 1159D] See Saint Gregory, *History of the Franks*, Book IV, chapter 20. Ed.]

(From the edition and the Corbie manuscript.)

We believe, with God propitious, that it pertains to our reward and to the salvation of the people that the Christian people, having abandoned the worship of idols, should serve purely, insofar as he deigns to inspire us, God to whom we have promised an undivided faith [Col. 1159D]. And because it is necessary that the populace, which does not observe a priest's command as it ought, should also be corrected by our authority, we have decreed that this charter be issued generally through all places. We command that whoever, after being warned, does not immediately cast down from his land, wherever they may be, images erected or idols made by men and dedicated to demons, or prevents priests from destroying them, shall not depart after giving sureties unless he is presented before us. How God's injury is to be avenged upon sacrilegious persons is for us to determine. Since our faith requires that, when a priest from the altar announces whatever is from the Gospel, prophets, or Apostle, insofar as God grants understanding, many complaints have come to us that sacrileges are committed among the people by which God is offended [Col. 1160A] and the people decline through sin toward death: all-night vigils with drunkenness, buffoonery, or songs; even on the holy days themselves—Easter, the Lord's Nativity, and the other festivals—and the wandering of dancing women through the villages on the approach of Sunday. We permit none of these things, by which God is known to be offended, to be done. Whoever, after the warning of priests or our command, presumes to perpetrate these sacrileges, if he is of servile condition, we command that he receive one hundred lashes. But if he is freeborn or perhaps of more honourable rank, he is deserving of strict confinement. Such persons are to be brought to repentance, so that those who despise wholesome words that call them back from the danger of death may at least be able, through bodily suffering, to be brought back to desire for the health of the mind.

The enactments made by subsequent kings are found in volume I of the *Capitularies of Kings* by the most distinguished man Stephen Baluze.

### Ancient Formulae

(From volume IV of Mabillon's *Analecta*.)

[Col. 1160B]

## Solemn Formula concerning a Dowry

This is the document made by the agent Chestantus in the fourth year of the reign of our lord King Childebert.

When, according to the custom of the city of Angers, the public court was sitting in the forum, the magnificent man So-and-so, prosecutor, said:

“I ask you, praiseworthy man So-and-so, defender; So-and-so, curator; So-and-so, master of the soldiery; and the rest of the public court—in short, I ask you to order the public records to be opened, because I have a matter that I must prosecute before the proceedings.”

The principal defender and the entire public court said:

“The public records are open to you; prosecute what you wish.”

“That document, by her mandate, enjoined upon me that I should act as prosecutor: namely, that, in accordance with the mandate which my sweetest beloved, So-and-so, made concerning all her legal actions, both in the county and at the palace, or wherever they may arise, her portions—which legally came, or ought to come, to her from the inheritance of my parents, or which are most justly due back to her—should be pursued, summoned before court, or litigated against her parents or against any person whatsoever. Having inspected that mandate, which my sweetest beloved, So-and-so, made, I must enter it in the municipal records.”

The court then said:

“Let the venerable man So-and-so, deacon and record-keeper, receive the mandate that you say you possess.”

The prosecutor So-and-so said:

“I ask all my public lords that, just as you have read this mandate and recognized that it was made, you order the dowry that I hold in my hands to be read aloud here before you in the public forum.”

The court then said:

“Let the deacon and record-keeper So-and-so receive for rereading, here in the city of Angers and in our presence, the dowry which you say you retain in your hands.”

Having received it, he said:

### Mandate

“To my sweetest beloved, my lord So-and-so: I ask and earnestly entreat your sweetest grace that, in my place, you cause all our legal actions, both in the county and at the palace, or wherever they may arise, to be pursued; and that you cause our portions—which legally came to me, or ought to have come to me, from the inheritance of my parents, or which have been most justly restored to us—to be pursued, summoned before court, or litigated against my parents or against any person whatsoever. Whatever you shall thereafter have done, made, or carried out in our place, know that I shall regard as rightfully done.”

Sworn mandate, in the city of Angers, before the public court.

### Cession

“My sweetest bride, to be loved with complete affection, daughter of So-and-so, named So-and-so: I, So-and-so. Since, with the Lord’s favor and according to custom, with the consent of your parents, I have betrothed you, therefore I cede to you from my property, both as a betrothal-gift and as a gift to you, namely: a house with an enclosed courtyard; movable and immovable property; woods; meadows; pastures; waters and watercourses; adjoining and dependent properties; and everything named above.

“To you, my sweetest bride, on the most fortunate day of the wedding, I give and transfer these things by this cession, so that you may receive them as your right.

“I cede to you a bracelet worth so many solidi; so many *toneneae* [term uncertain]; furnishings for a made bed worth so many solidi; golden earrings worth so many solidi; and a ring worth so many solidi.

“I cede to you a horse with its saddle and all its trappings; so many oxen; so many cows with their offspring; so many sheep; and so many solidi.

“You ought to receive all these things written below as your right and possession, or leave them to your descendants, if any should be born between us, saving the right of Saint So-and-so, whose land this appears to be.

“And if at any time anyone should arise against this cession, which I have asked to be written for you of my own good will—whether I myself, or any of my heirs or relatives, or any person or outsider—or should presume to bring an action or make a claim, before entering litigation he shall pay you double the amount, and another amount equal to whatever this cession contains, or to whatever it may have been improved to at that time; and his claim shall not obtain effect.

“This cession and our will shall remain firm at all times.”

After this the court said:

“If you still have anything further to say or do concerning this matter, say it now in the presence of all.”

The prosecutor So-and-so said:

“We give thanks to your greatness, because I have produced in the municipal records the written dowry which I am prosecuting, as your charity [*caretas*; reading uncertain] has [lacuna] caused to be drawn up for you according to custom.”

### Another Cession

**2.** May this be good and auspicious. The law of felicity approves it sufficiently, Roman law teaches it, the custom of the county agrees with it, and the principal authority does not prohibit it: namely, that both in the case of an intervening benefit and on the most fortunate day of the wedding, something desirable may take place.

Therefore I, in the name of God, So-and-so, named So-and-so, write beforehand to my bride, So-and-so, daughter of So-and-so, and transfer to her by this letter and cession, namely: a house with a courtyard, and so forth.

### Another Cession

**3.** “My sweetest bride, and so forth. I, So-and-so, son of So-and-so: since it is not unknown that I appear to have betrothed you according to Roman law, and so forth, you shall have what has been granted to you for as long as you live, perpetually, for usufruct and possession, and so forth.”

### Judgment

**4.** A man named So-and-so came before the venerable man So-and-so, abbot, and the other venerable and magnificent men whose names are inserted below. He brought a complaint against a certain man named So-and-so, as though the latter owed him service. The other man was present and firmly denied that he had ever owed him service.

The man So-and-so was questioned whether, through his kinship, he had other men in his service or not. He spoke as follows: he did not owe this service, since the man So-and-so did not owe him service; rather, concerning kinship or purchase, they maintained among themselves that, because the other man did not owe service through his kinship, he himself likewise did not owe it.

It therefore seemed proper to the abbot and to those who were with him that this man should swear, with twelve men and with his own hand making thirteen, in the basilica of the lady So-and-so, during such-and-such a night, that for thirty years or more he had never owed him service. If he could do this, the man So-and-so ought to be acquitted from this matter; but if he could not, he should strive to make amends.

### Oath

Record of the oath: how and in whose presence So-and-so entered before so many free men, upon the altar of So-and-so, in the city of Angers, because a man named So-and-so had brought a complaint against him for service, in the name of his father and mother.

He swore and said:

“By this holy place and by all the divine things that are performed here: for thirty years or more I have remained here in freedom, under the name of So-and-so. Nor have I rendered, nor shall I render, service to the aforementioned man, out of reverence for this place.”

Those are the persons in whose presence this occurred.

### 5. Another

Likewise, record of the oath … The sworn man said:

“By this holy place and by all the patronage of the saints who rest here,” and so forth.

### 6. Another

Brief record of the oath … in the basilica of the lady So-and-so. The sworn man said:

“By this holy place and by all the divine things that are performed here, which are offered here fully to God: the man named So-and-so brought a complaint against me because I had stolen his horse,” and so forth.

### 7. *Solsadia*

Record of the *solsadia*: how and in whose presence the man So-and-so attended his hearing in the city of Angers, on the Kalends of So-and-so, by judgment of the illustrious count So-and-so and his assessors, against the men named So-and-so and So-and-so, and against their mother, named So-and-so, together with their uncle So-and-so.

They said that a certain woman named So-and-so had killed their father, named So-and-so, by an evil deed. The men named above [Note: [Col. 1161D] See the same work, book VII, chapter 23.] were seen to have attended their hearing lawfully from morning until evening. The woman herself neither came to the hearing nor sent a representative who could have rendered the judicial excuse (*sonia*) due.

Therefore it was necessary for the aforesaid men to prosecute this record, confirmed by the hands of good men, as they were seen to have done.

### 8. *Appennis*

Whoever suffers violence or loss in any province at the hands of brigands, criminals, seditious persons, or incendiaries ought openly to report this to the governors of the cities or to the *curiales* of the province in which the deed is said to have been committed, and to make it known by public denunciation.

Accordingly, when, for the benefit of the Church or in a matter belonging to the fisc, the apostolic man, Bishop So-and-so, together with the illustrious man, Count So-and-so, and the other venerable and magnificent men of the state, was sitting in the city of Angers, a man named So-and-so came and publicly reported that, at a place called So-and-so, men had come and broken open his doors, and had carried away his property—gold, silver, valuable articles, clothing, his manufactured goods, bronze vessels, and many other things—as well as documents of sale, security, cession, donation, dowry, composition, conferral, exchange, agreements, covenants, guarantees, releases, judgments, records, and other documents too numerous to list individually, for the purposes of theft.

He further stated that, by means of those documents, they claimed that many lands had been sold after him, and that on the following day an accessorial document, together with good outsiders living as neighbors in that place, had been brought forward and confirmed by their hands.

When the matter had been reported, they presented the documents to the aforesaid lords for rereading. From them the lords learned that the matter had been carried out and perpetrated in this way. When a careful inquiry was then made, the good outsiders living nearby—who were well and fully informed about the matter—were required to recount truthfully what they knew of it. The men gave testimony as follows: after examining the letter that he had presented, they agreed truthfully with his denunciation.

When everything had thus become publicly known, the aforesaid bishop and count, and those who were with them, declared to that man that whatever he had rightly and lawfully possessed during the years from that time until now, he and his heirs should henceforth hold and possess, free of the royal claim, by the straight course of attested law.

For the present and future, it was agreed that he should receive and confirm this document, called an *appennis*, validated by the hands of the aforesaid lords and the other citizens. He did so, receiving two equal copies of the *appennis*: one to retain with himself, and the other to be displayed in the public forum.

The *appennis* having been made.

### 9. Here begins the letter that a father and mother make for their son

Although everyone is permitted to improve, for holy places or for parents, the property which he appears to possess in the present age, and although the law remains and longstanding custom continues, each person may do what he wishes with it, therefore I, in the name of God, So-and-so, and my wife, that sweetest woman So-and-so, and our son So-and-so, whom we love with complete affection—

Since in all things and through all things, and above all, you have appeared to serve us faithfully, and for our needs have endured many hardships and injuries in various places, and have served in hostile order for the benefit of our lords in the regions of Brittany and Gascony, it is therefore fitting that we should improve something of our property for you.

And so they did. Therefore we transfer to you, and so forth.

### 10. Record [concerning the Marriage of Slaves]

Record of how So-and-so and So-and-so—

It is not unknown that a male slave named So-and-so and a female slave belonging to So-and-so, named So-and-so, joined themselves in marriage against the wishes of their owners. But now we have agreed in a single concord of peace that, from the offspring born of them, So-and-so is to receive two shares for her female slave, and I and So-and-so a third for the male slave So-and-so; and that, of whatever they acquire while the marriage lasts, So-and-so is to receive two shares from that peculium for his male slave, and she likewise a third for her female slave.

Therefore, so that no dispute should arise between us later, we ought to make two letters of one wording with our hands concerning this matter. This we have done, and for the security of the entire matter we have now confirmed them, so that neither we ourselves nor any of our heirs or relatives, nor any outside person in service, may come against these letters; whoever wishes to do so shall be liable for double the sum, and so that his claim shall not obtain effect, and so that these agreements shall retain firm, unshaken, and unaltered validity.

# On the Laws of the Franks

*(From Baluze’s Capitularies.)*

King Theodoric of the Franks, while he was at Châlons, chose wise men who had been instructed in the ancient laws within his kingdom. At his own dictation, he ordered them to write down the law of the Franks, Alamanni, and Bavarians, for each people that was under his authority, according to its own custom.

He added what needed to be added and cut away what was improvised and disorderly. Whatever followed the custom of the pagans he changed in accordance with the law of the Christians.

Whatever King Theodoric was unable to correct because of the very ancient custom of the pagans, King Childebert began to correct afterward, but King Chlothar completed the work.

The most glorious King Dagobert renewed all these things through the illustrious men Claudius, Chaudus, Indomagnus, and Agilulf. He transformed all the old laws for the better and delivered written laws to each people, which have endured to this day.

This was decreed before the king, his princes, and the entire Christian people who dwell within the kingdom of the Merovingians.

# Letter of the Synod of Auvergne to King Theudebert

That clerics and others subject to the authority of other kings should not be deprived of possessions which they lawfully hold in his kingdom.

To the illustrious, most excellent lord and son, King Theudebert: Honoratus and the other bishops.

While your servants, the bishops of your churches, were sitting together in the city of Auvergne to review the provisions of the canons and to clarify ecclesiastical law for those who were perhaps burdened by uncertainty about the ordering of their own lives, a crowd of people came to us, requesting a remedy for their despair.

They hoped that our humility would implore your piety no less for the prosperity of your kingdom than for their own consolation, and that through our petition the justice and piety of your ears would be informed that your piety should not permit anyone to be deprived of his own property or small holdings; and that, while each person is subject to the power and dominion of one king, he should not lose property situated in another’s jurisdiction through anyone’s accusation, as commonly happens.

Trusting in the justice and piety of your highness, we do not believe that this request will be denied. While we attend, as we believe rightly and in a manner pleasing to God, to the needs of many, may you increase the prosperity of your kingdom and the presence of the heavenly Lord through the grace of piety granted to you.

Therefore, most reverently, as is fitting, we beseech you that, with divine regard, your piety not deny this request of ours. Do not permit either the governors of churches or all clerics, or even laymen living under the condition of your kingdom, nor those belonging to the dominion of your royal fathers, to become strangers to what is in your share, or to what they have always appeared to possess as their own.

Rather, let anyone securely possess his property and pay the due taxes to the lord into whose jurisdiction his possession has come.

We also judge this to be altogether more useful to your treasuries, if property preserved through your piety provides its customary revenue. And your clemency will console us especially if, through the granting of this petition, your Highness causes us also to rejoice.

# Extracts from a Letter of Aurelian, Bishop of Arles, to King Theudebert

[Note: [Col. 1163] See Saint Gregory’s *History of the Franks*, book III, chapter 25, and note f, col. 261. Editor.]

*(From Freher and Chesne.)*

To the illustrious, everywhere most glorious, and in Christ most devout lord and son, King Theudebert: Bishop Aurelian.

Although the service of writing is most justly accompanied by hesitation when it is so late, nevertheless I do not at all think that speech will be judged to have escaped offense if, in the presence of the ears of clemency, it is weighed solely according to the devotion of the mind.

This is especially so because, while everyone presses around your Highness, they neither draw fear from the privilege of your eminence nor fear rejection because of the disadvantage of delay. Your exalted position is so solemn that it touches even the love of the humble, and the summits burdened with a mass of dignities are still claimed by the primitive services of scarcely trained attendants.

For now we are being formed by new efforts for the service of a religious prince, and with testimony to our perfect devotion we are admitted into the presence of a consecrated mind.

Therefore, best of princes, measure from this part of our love the confidence with which we approach you: in your services we are neither frightened away by delay nor deprived, through embarrassment at our poor abilities, of the opportunity to speak.

Receive, then, with kindness, the beginnings of your servants’ devotion, and open the folds of more abundant forgiveness to those who implore it.

For although all generally enjoy the goodness of your illustrious heart, we, even though a small portion of your service, claim for ourselves in full the abundance of princely indulgence.

Indeed, when we speak of you, grace is present even if eloquence is lacking; and the subject alone is sufficient to adorn our discourse, although learning may be absent.

Since this is so, I shall celebrate your distinguished character and glory more through my prayers and wishes than through writing. For what is greatest always requires conscience rather than tongue, and is more worth entrusting to the judgment of the heart than to speech.

Accordingly, it is not what the times celebrate that I wish to mention, but what eternity approves, and so forth.

# Letter of King Theudebert to the Emperor Justinian

*(From Freher and Chesne.)*

To the illustrious and most excellent lord and father, Emperor Justinian: King Theudebert.

When the distinguished man Theodorus came to us from Solon together with the letters which the clemency of your empire had sent, we received them with complete affection and devotion of mind. Since you care for us, we thereby spread more widely among various peoples and provinces the friendship beloved by God.

As for what you deign to ask concerning the provinces in which we dwell, or the peoples who are subject to our rule, with God’s help our dominion extends over the Thuringians, happily subdued by the mercy of our God and their provinces acquired, their kings at that time having been destroyed.

The reconciled people of the Norsavi have submitted their necks to our majesty. With God’s favor and protection, our dominion extends from the Visigoths who inhabit the northern region of Gaul, through Pannonia with the Saxons and Eucii—who voluntarily submitted themselves to us—along the Danube and the frontier of Pannonia, as far as the shores of the Ocean.

Since we know, as your letters also attest, that your august Highness rejoices with complete gladness of heart at the progress of Catholics, we therefore report plainly, according to your wish, whatever God has granted us.

With eager hearts we desire that your glory may prosper so happily that you preserve the friendship of former princes and that, through the favor which you so often promise, we may be joined in common utility.

# Letter of King Theudebald to the Same

*(From Freher and Chesne.)*

To the illustrious, renowned, triumphant, and ever-August Emperor Justinian: King Theudebald.

When your envoys, John and Missarius, came to us, we received them with no small joy, learning from their report that the prosperity of your empire, founded by divine power, was increasing and would remain unshaken.

We therefore greet your serenity as is due and inform you that we received your gifts from the aforementioned bearers with the same disposition with which it is clear that they were sent by you.

For this reason, both for the generosity of the gift and for the delight of spirit which you indicated had been shown to you, and because heavenly power ordered you to sit, as was fitting, upon the throne of your father, we offer an unbreakable thanksgiving.

Among all things, however, this caused great distress to our minds: that, after the death of so great and such a prince, and conqueror of diverse peoples, you appear, as the letter proceeds, to be tearing him apart. While alive, he preserved unblemished faith toward emperors, kings, and all peoples, and kept friendships once promised under firm conditions.

Nor, out of regard for the Christian religion, did he abandon, as you write, the holy places; rather, after they had been consumed by the destruction of the pagans, he restored them, with Christ as author, to a better condition in his own times.

For the faith which the aforementioned prince—against whom you have said so many things to his disgrace—kept toward all peoples is demonstrated by innumerable triumphs and victories, God willing.

We ask that you take care to preserve firmly the friendships which you so gladly seek, and that, so that they may remain all the more securely under an inviolable treaty, no intervening causes impede them in your hearts.

# Letter of Mapinius, Bishop of Rheims, to Nicetius of Trier

[Note: [Col. 1165D] See Saint Gregory’s *Book on the Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 17, at the end, and note e, col. 1080. Editor.]

*(From the same sources.)*

To the holy and most blessed brother in Christ, Nicetius the bishop: Bishop Mapinius.

The teaching of the Gospel reading testifies that a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand. If this is rightly and deservedly believed concerning lovers of the world who remain in earthly desire, it is unquestionably even more rightly held concerning the persons of priests, if they are shown to be divided among themselves by conflicting wishes and efforts.

With what confidence shall we offer prayers to our Creator, who commanded us to live in the unity of the structure which is the body of his Divinity, if we in turn separate ourselves from one another in mutual love?

As the divine word teaches in one place, we ought to strive so that brother helping brother may stand upon an unshaken foundation, like a fortified and strong city.

That is, all of us should participate with equal-minded sympathy in the sorrow of one brother and support one another through mutual efforts.

For this reason, most devout and dearly beloved lord and brother, we inform you that we received a letter from our son, Lord King Theudebald, ordering us to be present in the city of Toul on the Kalends of June.

Since he disclosed no reason for the summons, we replied by return letter that we ought not to go there, because we were known to be ignorant of the reason and circumstances.

In repeated letters your Blessedness informed us that, while rebuking certain Franks out of zeal for divine fear and removing them from ecclesiastical communion because of incestuous circumstances, you were suffering many scandals and anxieties.

We greatly grieve over this matter, because you have not informed us through your report whether they are condemned according to canonical teaching or corrected for lesser offenses through pastoral diligence.

Although we know that you can discover nothing new concerning these matters which the skill of the ancient Fathers could not discover, nevertheless it seems absurd that we should receive those whom you reject with ecclesiastical severity according to the order of the canons.

For we know that, if we do this knowingly, we become involved in the crimes of others; if unknowingly, we are not subjected to guilt.

Therefore, greeting you with the charity that is owed, we inform you and at the same time urge you to make us participants in every respect both in the troubles and hardships of your tribulations and in the benefits of your prosperity.

For, through our head, who is Christ, no adversities tear us away from your anxiety, and no hardships divide us from your charity.

If we are not so presumptuous, we nevertheless presume to say this: it would have been fitting for your consolation concerning such circumstances, rather than a royal summons, to bring us together. For if something similar—which we think may happen in the future—had happened to us, we would immediately have sent a letter to your fraternity, so that, at a suitable time and place, we might see one another face to face.

Although it is both fitting and pleasing for us to obey royal commands in good matters, nevertheless let them be directed by your letters no less, through the effort of charity, and not with the penalty [perhaps: haughtiness] of contempt. For your bitterness cannot become our sweetness, nor can your rejection exist without our humiliation; and the reverence owed to you is not seen to be far removed from what we offer.

Would that, as we have said, with charity advising and the letter proceeding, your matters might become open to us. You have determined the distress of our hearts; we should know whether we sympathize with your troubles or rejoice in them.

For, as you yourselves know, when the divine voice is silent, humanity can understand only what a human being says.

Let your perfection know this more fully: if the repeated letter of our lord the king had reached us five or six days before the Kalends of June, you would have found our humble presence appointed for the day in question.

# Extract from a Letter of Nicetius, Bishop of Trier, to Chlodosinda

[Note: [Col. 1166D] See Saint Gregory, *History of the Franks*, book IV, chapter 3. Editor.]

*(From the same sources.)*

To the most merciful lady, Queen Chlodosinda, daughter in Christ: Nicetius, a sinner.

When we see envoys traveling among the Frankish kings, your brothers, we are concerned for your prosperity. But we hear this about you—and we confess that we always hear it repeated—how great, how exalted, how praiseworthy, how useful, how humane, and how generous you are; how concerned for the poor, how shrewd concerning the realm, and how splendid in pious conduct among the entire people.

May he grant this who has already given you the spirit of wisdom and understanding.

We rejoice in this; may Christ grant that we rejoice in King Alboin, whom you have, and exult in his prosperity.

We are astonished when peoples tremble before him, when kings offer him reverence, when rulers praise him without ceasing, and when even the emperor himself places him before his own commands [Note: [Col. 1166D] Gallandus reads: “the emperor himself before his own.” Editor.], because he does not hasten to seek the remedy of his soul.

We read in Scripture: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all good things will be added.” Since his reputation shines in this way, I marvel that he does not strive to investigate the kingdom of God and the salvation of his soul; rather, he receives and listens to those who would sooner destroy the soul in hell than lead it to the way of salvation.

They proclaim that there are two gods: one, the Father in the Godhead; the other, the Son in the Godhead, but as a creature—although Scripture says: “I am the Savior, and there is no other besides me.”

I adjure you, Lady Chlodosinda, by the fearful day of judgment, to read this letter carefully, to strive to explain it carefully and frequently to him, and to ask him: “Who is the Savior?” Do they say that the Father is the Savior, or the Son? For they declare that there are two, although there is one and there is no other.

If they say “the Son,” then the Father is not Savior, and so forth.

Why is it necessary for us to go through each point? Let us come to the twelve disciples whom he had, since these Goths today offer them reverence and secretly take away their relics … [Note: [Col. 1167D] Gallandus reads continuously: “secretly take away their relics.” Editor.] But they have nothing there, because they presume to annul their faith.

Why is it that they do not enter the basilicas in which their bodies are now venerated? Why is it that they dare presume nothing there except secretly, like dogs outside, deceiving souls?

Let King Alboin send his faithful men and have them led to the thresholds of Lord Peter, Paul, John, and the other saints [Note: [Col. 1167B] Gallandus: “have them led there.” Editor.]. Let them decide to celebrate Mass there, if they dare. But they do not dare, because the disciples of Lord Peter do not appear, and they are shown to be adversaries of Christ, since the wretched are found destroying what he himself redeemed through the cross.

Why does such a king, and such an age, receive their poisons?

If he wishes, let him send them to Lord Martin for his festival, which he celebrates on the eleventh day of November. Let them presume anything there, if they dare, where today we see the blind receive sight [Note: [Col. 1167D] Gallandus: “be made to see.” Editor.], where the deaf receive hearing and the mute receive healing.

For what shall I say about the lepers, or about the many others who, struck by whatever degree of weakness, are healed there year after year, different persons in turn?

Perhaps they say: “They pretend,” or that the blind appear to be blind from birth. What shall I say when we see those who have received sight there and behold them return home healthy, by God’s mercy?

What more shall I say about Lord Germanus, Hilary, or Bishop Lupus? There so many miracles appear today that I cannot express them in words: sufferers—that is, those possessed by demons—are suspended in the air and tormented, and confess that the lords whom I have named exist.

Do they do such things in their churches? They do not, because they do not perceive that God and the holy lords dwell there. A demon does not exorcize a demon.

Where the saints dwell, a demon is not permitted to wander; therefore it happens that the place where God is may be revealed.

What shall I say about Bishops Lord Remigius and Lord Medardus, whom I believe you have seen? We cannot explain the many miracles which we see God perform through them.

You heard from your grandmother, Lady Clothilde, of blessed memory, how she came to Francia and how she brought Lord Clovis to the Catholic faith. Although he was an extremely shrewd man, he refused to yield until he recognized the truth.

When he learned that the things I have mentioned above had been proved, he fell humbly at the threshold of Lord Martin and allowed himself to be baptized without delay.

You have heard how many things he did after his baptism against the heretical kings Alaric and Gundobad, and you do not fail to know what good things he himself and his sons possessed in this world.

Such is the adornment, such the man, such the reputation attributed to King Alboin, whom the world sets above others in this way. Why does he not convert, or why does he appear slow to seek the way of salvation?

Good God, who are the glory of the saints and the salvation of all, send yourself into him.

And you, Lady Chlodosinda, when you speak, give consolation, so that we may all rejoice in such a star and such a jewel in a manner pleasing to God.

I greet you as much as I am able; I ask that you not be idle. Cry out without ceasing; sing without ceasing.

You have heard the saying: “An unbelieving man will be healed through a faithful woman.” For know this: the first salvation and the first remission is to turn a sinner back from his error.

Keep watch, keep watch, because you have God favorable to you.

I ask you to act in such a way that you may make the strong people of the Lombards strong against their enemies and permit us to rejoice in the salvation of you and your husband.

# On the Bishopric of Dunum

[Note: [Col. 1168D] See Saint Gregory, *History of the Franks*, book VII, chapter 17. Editor.]

*(From the editions and Corbie manuscripts.)*

## Substance of the petition submitted to the synod by Bishop Pappolus

To all my lords, always to be honored for their apostolic dignity, the bishops who have now assembled at Paris in the holy synod: Pappolus, bishop of the city of Chartres, your humble servant.

Canonical institution admonishes us that whenever certain matters arise in the Church, they ought to be made public in a synodal assembly.

Therefore, most devout lords, we have undertaken to bring to the notice of your piety, through the substance of this present petition, the matters that have been done against us.

Some time ago, when the will of the clergy and citizens of the city of Chartres had chosen me as bishop by common agreement, with the concurrence also of my metropolitan, and this had been done with the Lord’s consent, a few days later a certain presbyter from the territory of that city of Chartres, named Promotus, who had left his own cell without a letter from my predecessor, appeared to have invaded my parish, called Dunum, by unlawful presumption, as though under the title of a bishopric.

He also invaded, under a similar pretext, the small property of the church over which I appear to preside, insofar as it is known to lie within that county, I do not know by whose authorization.

For this reason, as your suppliant, I make this complaint to your Holiness. By the Holy Spirit who dwells in you, by the day of the future judgment, and by the remission of sins, I adjure you, my lords, to order this to be corrected in the manner in which you yourselves would not wish it to be done to you.

Let no one thereafter dare, through crafty presumption and the swelling of pride, to perpetrate similar acts; and, through your care and ordering, let the rivalry of the churches now, by Christ’s favor, come to rest.

In response to this petition, the holy synod, replying with spiritual favor and according to canonical rite, wrote the following against the rash persons.

### Synodal Letter to Egidius

[The supplied source ends here.]

To his lord, most blessed and apostolic brother in merit, Bishop Egidius, Philippus, etc., and the bishops.

While we were staying in Paris on public business and private complaints, our apostolic brother, Lord Bishop Pappolus, brought before our modesty a complaint that, in the fortress of Dunum, and therefore in the parish of Chartres—a fortress which plainly belongs neither to the territory of your city nor to your province—you had consecrated a bishop contrary to every rule and to canonical discipline. Although, according to the ancient decrees of the most blessed Fathers, such an excess could have been restrained more harshly to your injury, we nevertheless, observing the laws of charity, inform Your Beatitude that you should summon to yourselves, or retain with you, the presbyter Promotus, who, it is said, was so rashly consecrated by you in disregard of canonical severity that he ought justly to be deposed from the dignity of his order, as the canonical statutes have decreed. Thus he must no longer inflict injury either upon the Church or upon his own bishop.

And since he had been summoned by your brother, Lord Bishop Germanus, at the request of Lord Constitutus, the metropolitan, and had been warned by an immediate invitation to come to the synod—and since it is also established that Lord Constitutus and Lord Germanus reported this matter to the synod, while he delayed coming to the synod—therefore let Your Beatitude know that the present council has established the following for all time: if the aforesaid presbyter, whether through his own contumacy or through the support of any power, should presume to remain any longer in the aforementioned church of Dunum under the pretext of this usurped honor, or to seize the property of that church, or to bless altars, confirm infants, or perform ordinations in any parishes whatsoever, or should presume with evil intent to resist his bishop, your brother Lord Pappolus, let him be struck by perpetual anathema and excluded from every assembly of bishops and from communion.

And let our brother Lord Bishop Pappolus, or the church of Chartres, govern under his authority, with the Lord’s help, the parishes that it has possessed up to this time. We further decree that whoever among that people, after this edict has been made known or published, either requests the blessing of the aforesaid presbyter Promotus or is content to receive it, shall be barred from communion and from the thresholds of the church.

This decree was issued on the third day before the Ides of September, in the twelfth year of the reigns of our lords, in the sixth indiction, at Paris. I, Philippus, bishop of the Church of Vienne, have subscribed this decree of ours in the name of Christ, etc. The decree was subscribed in the basilica of Lord Peter, in the aforementioned indiction, at Paris.

## Another letter to King Sigibert

To the most glorious lord and son of the holy Catholic Church, King Sigibert, Sapaudus, etc., and the bishops.

As great as the ineffable joy announced to a synodal council is when a new undertaking is conceived by a Catholic ruler out of love for Christ, so lamentable and execrable is it when dissension is generated in the holy Church against God and against canonical discipline.

Recently, having been summoned to Paris—as we believe, not without the connivance of Your Glory—and having come there, we learned that a new and unheard-of ordination had been carried out in the fortress of Dunum, which belongs to the parish of Chartres. Although we can scarcely believe that this matter could have been done with the consent of Your Glory, nevertheless, if you were forestalled by someone’s evil suggestion and consented to so obscene an act, contrary to the whole Church, cleanse the conscience of your sincerity from the defense of such a scandal. For it is better that the man who, driven by ambition, sought this utterly wicked matter through deceitful ambition should be compelled to wash away his guilt through penitential satisfaction than that your purity—God forbid—should be stained by the contagion of this crime.

And because it was necessary for us, in accordance with the canonical statutes, to restrain the presumption of this rash person, we offer you the service of salvation with the fitting devotion and reverence due in Christ. We ask that you, whom God has ordained to be distinguished both by exalted rank and by sincerity, do not involve yourselves, through the rash counsel of anyone or of any group, in defending such scandals. God knows that we in no way desire divine wrath to be stirred up against you.

May divine power preserve the glory of your kingdom for many years with complete happiness, most glorious and most excellent lord. I, your venerator, Bishop Sapaudus, presume to offer greetings, etc.

This letter was given on the third day before the Ides of September, in the twelfth year of the reigns of our lords, at Paris.

## Evidence that from ancient times the Church of Morinensis [Maurienne] was subject to the metropolitan Church of Vienne

[Note: See the book *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 14, and note d at column 719. Editor.]

*(From the edition.)*

In the days of the most excellent King Guntram, there was a woman named Tygris, born in the territory of Maurienne, in the town called Volacis. Nobly born and educated in the sacred writings, she did not consider the care of priests and visiting pilgrims unimportant; rather, insofar as her means allowed, she took care to provide hospitality and to supply the necessities of life to those in need.

She had as her companion a sister named Pimenia, who had been married but remained devoted in widowhood. Together with the aforementioned sister, they diligently and constantly devoted themselves to all divine services: fasting, vigils, prayers, and visiting the places of the saints night and day.

It happened that a religious company of good monks was traveling from the regions of Jerusalem toward Scotland. By God’s will, these men remained with these servants of God for the sake of hospitality, stayed there for three days, and rejoiced together in the service of God while persevering in vigils and fasts.

From them the venerable Tygris heard about blessed John the Baptist, whose relics she eagerly sought: his remains, they said, had been buried in the city of Samaria, now called Sebaste; later, at an earlier time, they had been sent to Alexandria, while his head had been carried to Phoenicia. Instructed by this account, the servant of God applied herself until she found the venerable relics. In accordance with her desire to honor blessed John the Baptist, she resolved to build a church at Maurienne.

When the glorious King Guntram heard about the relics of blessed John and the miracles that the Lord had displayed there, he sent his legates to Maurienne to construct a church there, together with the neighboring bishops and counts, in which the relics of blessed John the Baptist might be deposited. He ordered that, once it was completed, it should be consecrated by the Bishop of Vienne, Saint Isychius, since the place belonged to his diocese.

Afterward he caused a synod of holy bishops to assemble in the city of Chalon. There he first established Saint Felmasius as bishop of Maurienne, ordained by the Bishop of Vienne, and, with the consent of the bishops, subjected that church of Maurienne to the city of Vienne.

To that church of Maurienne, where he had placed the relics of blessed John the Baptist, he subjected the city of Seusium, which had long before been received from the Italians, together with all the inhabitants of that place. With the consent also of the Roman pontiff, he decreed that the bishop of the city and district of Maurienne should remain subject by perpetual right to the Church of Vienne.

[Column 1170C]

To the most merciful and most excellent lady, and always most devoted to us, etc.
