## Letters of King Childebert II concerning Italian affairs, etc., to the emperor and others

[Note: See Book X of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 2, note a at column 531. Editor.]

*(From Freher and Chesn.)*

### 1

To the glorious, pious, perpetual, illustrious, triumphant, and ever august father, Emperor Mauricius, Childebert, king.

We have chosen to unite ourselves to Your Most Merciful Serenity by treaties and to offer you the affection pleasing to the Lord: an expeditious peace, arising from the bond of a peaceful people, which will benefit both sides alike. Therefore, confidently offering services of greeting to Your Most Merciful Tranquillity, with the honor owed to your supreme rank, we have resolved, with God’s favor, to fulfill what we previously promised to your envoys: that we would send our letters.

Accordingly, we have sent the illustrious man Sennodius, a nobleman; Grippo, the sword-bearer; Radan, the chamberlain; and Eusebius, the notary. We entrusted them with certain matters to report verbally to your principate. When they have fully disclosed these matters and safely returned to us, give them such words as, with the Lord’s inspiration, may advance the common interest.

### 2

To the glorious lord, ineffably desirable and beloved nephew, King Athanagild, Queen Brunichild.

A welcome occasion of great happiness has come to me, dear nephew, by which I am partly relieved of the fervent longing with which I desire to see you: through letters sent to me, I behold you represented before those beloved eyes. In you, my sweetest daughter, whom my sins have taken from me, is restored to me—not entirely forgiven [perhaps, I think: “not entirely lost”]—if, by the Lord’s favor, the child born to me is preserved.

Therefore, greeting Your sweetest Highness, we render our services with the deepest devotion, and we earnestly pray that divine Clemency may command me to rejoice and be refreshed by your innocence. Through our envoys I have informed the most pious emperor that I have instructed them to communicate certain matters verbally. Through them you will be able to learn what is to be arranged, if Christ in his favor should graciously command its fulfillment.

### 3

To the most glorious and everywhere most exalted lord, my sweetest nephew, King Athanagild, King Hildebert.

We are relieved by the convenience of the present opportunity, through which we can at least express in the language of letters the affection we owe to our relative. Therefore, by right of kinship, we desirably offer Your Exalted Glory the services of our greeting, confidently hoping that he who knows the desires of all and the secrets of hidden things may command us to rejoice in your safety.

We have taken care to inform the most serene ruler that, with Christ’s favor, we have sent the bearer of this letter as an envoy for the common good. When you have presented him to the aforesaid Augustus—or, with the Lord happily governing you—you will be able, by carefully inquiring, to learn what we have resolved and desire to do concerning your circumstances. May he who governs human counsels and the foundations of affairs grant that the parties be reconciled [variant: “that the reconciled party”].

Other letters of Childebert and Brunichild concerning the same matter are extant; see them in Freher or Chesnius, volume I.

### 4. In the name of Lord Childebert, to Patriarch Laurentius

Extending everywhere the course of your blessed reputation through your merits, and striving to equal the blessed martyr both in name and in reward, so that through you the whole of that man whose name you have obtained may return—he who so scattered the coinage of the holy Church that, through its distribution among the poor, he increased the talents of its treasury—we give thanks to the heavenly Clemency, which has bestowed upon you what for many is a gift, and which, in the time of future glory, may uniquely profit you as a reward.

Therefore, having rendered the services of greeting to your holy Apostolate, with the foregoing commendation, and confidently beseeching you to deign to remember us in your sacred intercessions, we hope that, since divine Clemency strengthens us at such an age that our Catholic cause is not without assistance [that is, support], we have sent forces into Italy, at the request of the Roman state and of our most sacred father the emperor, against the Lombard nation, which is utterly hostile to religion and faith.

Through your diligence, order the exalted man Smaragdus at Ravenna to be informed quickly, so that the Roman state may hasten to bring whatever armed support it can against the enemy, and so that he may not delay doing in the present whatever the Lord has commanded and what can be done.

As for what remains, if it pleases Christ, when the coming year arrives we intend to send an army for this purpose, so that the hand of the Lord, in response to your prayers, may deign to destroy that execrable nation, which has armed the hands of its cruelty through injury to the saints and the death of its faithful, with the shedding of blood.

We also hope that you will order the exalted Smaragdus to be informed by our envoys, so that, under both your direction and his, they may hasten to reach the appointed place in the imperial city. After reporting to us, under Christ’s protection, what instructions have been given, let them quickly bring to completion, with divine favor, whatever remains in the interest of peace.

### 5

To the most excellent and most exalted lord Childebert, king of the Franks, Romanus.

As much as the Christianity of your kingdom daily asks what must be offered to appease God, so much do we trust that Your Excellence thinks and acts concerning the liberation of Christians. We believe that it is pleasing to you that prosperity has been granted by divine favor for their relief, so that such and so great promises, made with God as their author, and such manifest divine mercy, may invite Your Excellence to share in the reward and acquire the greatest praise.

We believe that long ago you heard of the cities of Montena, Altinum, and Mantua, because they have been restored to the holy Roman state. In our earlier letters, we remember informing you that, while we were setting out to besiege the cities of Parma, Reggio, and Piacenza, the Lombard dukes stationed there came with all haste to us at Mantua to submit themselves to the holy Roman state.

We afterward received them into the service of the holy Roman state, taking their sons as hostages. On our return to Ravenna, we resolved to march into the province of Istria against the enemy Grasoulfus. When we arrived in that province, the magnificent man Gisoulfus, duke and son of Grasoulfus, wishing to show himself better than his father while still young, came to us so that, with complete devotion, he might submit himself, his leading men, and his entire army to the holy Roman state, as he had been.

The glorious patrician Nordoultus likewise, coming into *talia* [perhaps, “Italy”] with the favor of our lords, gathered all his men to serve our most serene lords, and, together with the glorious man Ossus and his Roman army, restored various cities with our counsel.

Since we do not doubt that Your Excellence remains in the same promise and devotion which you once promised to your most pious fathers, our lords—especially since it is established that you were displeased when, without fulfilling your commands, the dukes returned and thereby placed themselves under your anger—may Your Excellence command with all speed that the promises you made to your fathers, our most pious lords, be fulfilled. Thus, through the fulfillment of your promise, you may be increased by worthy grace, and let the forces be sent at such a time that they find all the crops outside the enemies’ territory.

Order us also to be informed by which routes and at what time they should be expected by us. Above all, we hope that, when the Frankish army has happily descended, the Romans, for whom we request your aid, will not be led into plunder and captivity. Rather, command that those whom they carried away at an earlier time be released and restored to the province, so that, by correcting the past, you may show what they ought to preserve in the future.

Nor should you command the buildings to be burned, so that it may be recognized that we have received the aid of a Christian people for the defense of Italy.

### 6

In the name of our Lord God Jesus Christ, emperor and Caesar, Flavius Mauricius Tiberius, faithful in Christ, mild, great, beneficent, peaceful, Alamannic, Gothic, Antic, Alanic, Vandalic, Herulic, Gepidic, African, pious, fortunate, illustrious, victorious and triumphant, ever Augustus, to the glorious man Childebert, king of the Franks.

The letters of Your Glory, sent to us through Jucundus the bishop and Cothro the chamberlain, indicate that you preserve toward us and toward our most sacred state a friendly will and paternal affection. We find the same thing written to our piety in many words through other envoys.

It seems astonishing to us that, while affirming that you possess a sound mind and declaring that the ancient unity of the Frankish people with Roman dominion has been confirmed, Your Eminence has so far appeared to display no deed corresponding to friendship. Your promises in writing, confirmed through priests and strengthened by terrible oaths, have passed such a long time without producing any result.

And if this is so, why do you uselessly tire your envoys over such great stretches of land and sea without a necessary response, boasting in youthful speech of things that have produced no benefit?

Nevertheless, following imperial benevolence, we received your aforementioned envoys, although we learned that they had not truly been sent by you. We listened with peaceful ears to what they announced and gave them a suitable reply; Your Glory has already learned this through your other envoys.

If you desire and wish to seek our friendship, we want you to discuss everything firmly and without hesitation—not merely to recount matters in words, but to carry out what you have recounted manfully, as a king ought, and likewise to await our pious goodwill.

Your Glory should therefore also bring to completion whatever has been agreed between us in writing, so that on this occasion the unity of your people and of our most fortunate state may be established ever more firmly and no dispute may arise between us. These agreements were not made out of hostility, but so that friendship might remain firm and unimpaired.

May the Divinity preserve you for many years, most Christian and beloved father.

Given on the Kalends of September at Constantinople, under the emperor, the divine Mauricius Tiberius, perpetual Augustus, and after his consulship, in the year … [the remainder is lost].

### 7. Letter sent concerning the emperor to Lord Childebert, king

Since all good things are conferred through worthy deeds, just as much as has been granted to you by right of your merits for the love of orthodox faith, so much has been granted for the rescue you undertake in order to save Christian blood. Thus, from the throne from which others receive the highest honor, Your Glory has supplied ornaments to the kingdom itself—not only through your ineffable plans, but through your sons and grandsons.

Knowing that the Divinity has summoned Your Highness to worship him through the greatest benefits, we believe that we increase our zeal by which the stability of your kingdom may receive stronger foundations, so that the lives of your sons and grandsons may be preserved and the glory of the kingdom—which appears doubled in you through your son and tripled by the reign of your grandsons—may be fortified by fulfilling God’s commands.

When the magnificent man Andreas arrived, we learned from his report that the opinion concerning your Christianity which had been brought to us was true, and that the reality was even greater. As though we were present and seeing what he described, we began to rejoice even more than before in venerating you.

Therefore, you do not wait to be asked for what concerns the reward of your soul; rather, we believe that you anticipate the will of those who ask. He explained to us with what ready spirit and complete devotion Your Glory had sent the flourishing army of the Franks for the liberation of Italy.

All this concerning your devotion and most Christian will, and concerning the urgency with which you desire Italy to be liberated, I reported specially to my most merciful lord, the emperor, and to your sister, the most serene Augusta, just as the aforesaid magnificent man Andreas reported it to us.

Before your dukes entered the boundaries of Italy, God, in his mercy and in response to your prayers, enabled us to enter the city of Mutina by battle. Likewise, by fighting and breaking through the walls, we entered the cities of Altinum and Mantua, so that the army of the Franks might see us, with God’s help.

We hurried lest the most wicked Lombard nation be allowed to unite against the Frankish army. A magnificent man was stationed with nearly twenty thousand men near the city of Verona; we considered it necessary to send to him without delay, hoping that we might meet him face to face and, by common counsel, arrange what would be useful for destroying the treacherous nation.

But, as we learned, he had already sent his embassy to Autharit the king, and had already negotiated some form of peace with him before your dukes came to me.

Nevertheless, they sent Leufredus, Olfigandus, and Raudingus, magnificent men and dukes, to us. As was fitting, I received them with every honor for the sake of Your Glory, and we also treated them generously.

We had planned the following: Autharit had shut himself inside Ticinum, while the other dukes and his entire army had shut themselves up in various forts. We, with the Roman army and the dromons, together with Cheno, who, as we have said, was stationed nearby with twenty thousand men, were to come to besiege Autharit. Once he had been captured, the greater part of the victory would have been secured. Only then, if there were anything to say or do with the others, would everything first be reported to your knowledge.

We believe that the flourishing Frankish army also wished to do this. Your glorious Christianity will be able to learn from copies of the letters in what ways we begged and urged them to proceed. We did not dare to say or do anything against the enemies of God and our common enemies without the counsel of your dukes.

But they, as we have said, had dealings with those men from the beginning. Leaving us aside in every matter, they made peace with them for ten months. Although they had abundant plunder and safety, they suddenly withdrew, with the army already following the will of their duke.

We believe that you consider and regret what praise and reward this matter has taken away from you. For if they had been willing to endure or listen for only a little longer, Italy would today have been found free from the most wicked Lombard nation, and all the possessions of the most wicked King Autharit would have been brought to Your Excellence.

Your promise would truly have been fulfilled, even if somewhat later, since the Lombards did not think themselves safe within their walls and did not dare resist the Franks.

Therefore, offering you the services of greeting with the highest honor, we hope that even now, in accordance with the Christianity of your kingdom, you will command that worthy dukes and an army be sent at the proper time for the rescue of Christian blood and for the reopening of the churches, so that the priests who were able to escape their slaughter may be rescued.

Thus the promise you made to your father may be fulfilled before that most wicked nation can gather its crops. God has restored not only the cities mentioned above but also others—namely Parma, Reggio, and Piacenza—with their dukes and many Lombards, to the holy Roman state. In so great a reward, Your Glory may obtain the greatest share, as it has begun to do.

Beyond what Your Glory habitually does on its own, we ask that you command the Romans whom the Frankish army plundered to be released, for the sake of your reward and that of your sons and grandsons. Other provisions have also been established in the agreements: captives are to be released. This is likewise the intention of your most Christian father, so that he may daily acquire reward with you through the liberation of souls.

## Appendix to the Chronicle of Marius: On the death of Brunichild

[Note: See Fredegar’s *Chronicle*, chapter 42, and note f at column 633. Editor.]

*(From Chesnius.)*

During the reign of this emperor Heraclius, up to the fourteenth year of his empire, and during the fortieth year of the reign of the most glorious Frankish ruler Chlothachar, many losses were inflicted upon the Roman state almost everywhere by various peoples.

In his time the Persians reached as far as Chalcedon. The Huns, breaking through the Long Wall and approaching the walls of Constantinople, spoke with the aforesaid emperor while he stood upon the wall with them. Having received the price of peace from him, they withdrew for a time.

During the same period, Francia, formerly divided among three kingdoms, was united into one kingdom by the aforesaid king of the Franks. King Theuderic pursued his brother, Theudebert, king of the Austrasians. The Franks defeated the Austrasians and moved into Burgundy, finally killing Theudebert himself.

Soon afterward, when the victorious Theuderic had died at Metz, he left the kingdom, wrongly usurped, to his young son Sigibert together with his grandmother Brunihild. While his brother was still alive, Theuderic ordered his own nephew to be dashed against the rock at Albis.

At the same time his sons were defeated and captured by the aforesaid King Chlothachar. The aforementioned queen, grandmother of those men, was captured by him and afflicted with various kinds of punishment. Then, placed upon a camel, she was made a spectacle to many of her own people. Finally, bound by her feet to the back of a very fierce horse, she breathed her last.

Afterward the people burned her little body, and fire became her tomb. The paternal judgment once delivered without mercy against her brother and grandson rebounded upon her sons. After they had been killed, as some report, the king who had been proclaimed obtained the monarchy of the three kingdoms, and now, governing it happily and religiously, he continues to live in the fortieth year of his reign, together with the earlier years of his kingdom.

From the beginning of the world to the present era—that is, the fourteenth year of Heraclius and the fortieth of King Chlothachar—there are 4,822 years.

## Letter of Sigibert III to Desiderius, Bishop of Cahors

*(From the edition.)*

To the holy and apostolic lord, Father in Christ, Desiderius, Sigibert, king.

While rumor was circulating among many, and we learned from our faithful men, that you had apparently been summoned by Bishop Wlfoledus, our same father, to a synodal council on the Kalends of September in our kingdom, we do not know where you and the rest of your provincial brothers are supposed to assemble.

Although we wish to preserve the canonical statutes and ecclesiastical rules just as our parents preserved them in God’s name, nevertheless, since this matter had not previously been brought to our attention, we and our nobles have agreed that no synodal council should be held in our kingdom without our knowledge.

Nor should any gathering of priests belonging to our dominion take place on the said Kalends of September. Later, at a suitable time, if it is announced to us beforehand whether the gathering is intended for the condition of the Church, for the advantage of the kingdom, or for any reasonable purpose whatsoever, we do not object—provided, as we have said, that the matter is first brought to our knowledge.

Accordingly, we have taken care to send this letter to Your Sanctity. Through it we ask you to deign to pray for us and not to attend this gathering in any way before you know our will. To make you certain, we have subscribed this little notice with our own hand.

I, Sigibert, king, have subscribed.

## Erchambert’s Brief History of the Kings of the Franks and of the Mayors of the Palace

*(From Freher and Chesnius.)*

King Chlodharius of Austrasia, after the kings and brothers Theoderic and Theodebert had died, received their kingdom through the counsel and assistance of Pippin the Elder, who was then mayor of the palace. The aforesaid king obtained the monarchy of the three kingdoms for sixteen years, just as the abbot Saint Columbanus had previously foretold to him in a prophetic spirit, because King Theoderic, at the instigation of his grandmother Brunihild, expelled him from his monastery. As soon as Chlodharius captured her, he caused her to end her life shamefully.

At that time Gundolandus, an outstanding man, was mayor of the palace. Not long afterward, the king sent the aforesaid Pippin to Austrasia with his already grown son Dagobert, to establish him there as king; he appointed Pippin as his mayor of the palace and tutor.

King Dagobert reigned for sixteen years after his father’s death. He was a magnificent giver and distributor of gifts to the churches of God. His mayor of the palace was Erchanoldus [variant: Erchanbaldus], an illustrious man, while Pippin was duke in Austrasia; Pippin died not long afterward.

After the death of King Dagobert, his son King Chlodoveus reigned for sixteen years. He was devoted to every kind of filth. The mayor of the palace was the same as above.

King Chlodharius, the son of Chlodoveus, died while still in the youthful age of childhood and reigned for four years. His mayor of the palace was Ebroinus.

King Theoderic, son of Chlodoveus and brother of Chlodharius, reigned for nineteen years. His mayor of the palace was Bertharius. After Bertharius was killed, Pippin the Younger, son of Ansegisil [variant: Ansgil], came from Austrasia and succeeded to the principate of the mayors of the palace.

From this point the kings began to possess the name but not the honor. Nevertheless, wherever they were established, abundant food was provided for them, and constant guard was maintained over them so that they could not exercise anything by right of their power.

In those times and afterward, Gotefridus, duke of the Alamanni, and the other dukes throughout the surrounding regions refused to obey the dukes of the Franks, because they could not serve the Merovingian kings as they had formerly been accustomed to do. Each therefore held apart with his own people, until eventually, after the death of Duke Gotefridus, Carlus and the other Frankish leaders gradually made efforts to recall them to themselves by whatever means they could.

They established Chlodoveus, the young son of Theoderic, as king; he reigned for only two years. His mayor of the palace was the aforementioned Pippin.

They established Childebert, the son of Theoderic and brother of Chlodoveus, as king. He reigned for seventeen years. Grimoaldus, son of Pippin, was appointed mayor of the palace, because Pippin himself had begun to fall ill; he died from that illness, and in the meantime Grimoaldus was killed.

They established Dagobert, son of Childebert, as king; he reigned for five years. His mayor of the palace was Theodoaldus, after whom came Regnifredus [variant: Raginfredus].

At that time Carlus, son of Pippin by a concubine, was held in custody by Plectrude, the wife of that same Pippin. With the Lord’s help, he scarcely escaped. The Franks made Daniel, formerly a cleric, king, allowing his hair to grow on his head; they called him Chilperic. Since the royal line was failing, they established the man whom they could find who was closest to the Merovingians, because the Merovingians, as they say, like the ancient Nazirites, did not cut the hair of their heads. He reigned for six years.

Meanwhile, the aforementioned prince Carlus fled to the Austrasians, to his ancestral seats. There he seized the principate and established for himself a king named Chlodharius. He waged many wars against King Chilperic and his mayor of the palace, Reganfredus, defeated them as he wished, and recovered his father’s treasure from Plectrude. His king Chlodharius died not long afterward.

The Franks established Theoderic, the son of the younger Dagobert, as king for themselves. He had been raised in the monastery of Cala and reigned for six years. His mayor of the palace and prince was Carolus, who now governed both kingdoms manfully, continually waging wars throughout the surrounding regions with kings and dukes and always achieving victory, until it was established that he had overcome all who appeared likely to oppose him.

## Documents of Episcopal Elections

### Agreement of the citizens concerning a bishopric

*(Marculf, Book I, no. 7.)*

To the most pious and most excellent lord, that king or senior, a common petition from his servants, whose subscriptions or seals are inserted below. To Your Princely Authority, etc.

Since that apostolic man of blessed memory, the bishop of that city, has departed from this light as the time appointed by nature approached its completion, we humbly ask that you deign to appoint that illustrious man, or that venerable man, as successor to his chair. In him are found exalted insight, the nobility of his nation, radiant elegance, diligence in chastity, abundant charity, and an unshakable will. We have decided to strengthen this agreement with our own hands.

### The king’s appointment concerning a bishopric

*(From the edition and manuscripts.)*
## 2. King Dagobert to the bishops and dukes, and to the whole people established within the boundaries of Gaul

It befits princely clemency to pursue matters with careful investigation and to consider them with ever-watchful concern, so that our election or appointment may accord with the will of God and of men. Since, by the Lord’s generosity, regions and kingdoms are known to have been entrusted to us for governance, the privileges of dignities should be assigned to those whom a praiseworthy life and upright conduct, or noble lineage, have commended. And since we have learned that the illustrious man Desiderius, our treasurer, has from the very time of his boyhood observed the practice of religion in all things, borne the service of Christ under secular dress, and possessed angelic conduct and priestly manners—and since the fame of his goodness has spread and grown not only in neighboring but also in distant regions—we therefore believe that he ought deservedly to be advanced to the priesthood, seeing that, as we have said, we constantly observe him aspiring toward the heavenly homeland with an adorned character.

And since the agreement of the citizens and abbots of Cahors demands in every way that they have him as bishop, and our devotion likewise consents, we undoubtedly believe that this is being done by the will of God: although he is sufficiently necessary to us in our palace, we should in a certain sense do violence to ourselves and, for your benefit, arrange for him to depart from our residence. But while, as we have said, we remove him from our household—although we, to whom regions and kingdoms have been entrusted by God, thereby incur a loss—we ought to provide such shepherds as will govern, according to God and the apostolic teachings, the peoples entrusted to them by us, so that a greater reward may accrue to us.

Therefore, in accordance with the petition of the citizens, and with our will, which agrees with it in every respect, we decree and command that, with the clergy and people assisting and acclaiming his praise, the illustrious man and true worshiper of God, Desiderius, is to be consecrated bishop in the city of Cahors; and that what our will and that of the citizens has decreed shall in every respect be accomplished in the name of God. Raised to the episcopal dignity, since, with Christ’s favor, we truly and religiously profess that his life and conduct are regarded by all as worthy and approved, he shall pray for us and for all the orders of the Church, and shall strive to offer sacrifices acceptable to God. For on this account we believe that, by the Lord’s authority, our life will be prolonged to a greater age, if the man is chosen and elevated to the priesthood who, on our behalf and on behalf of you entrusted to him, may confidently offer prayers before the tribunal of Christ and stand at the future judgment to excuse the sins of sinners.

For this reason, by the present authority we decree that the aforesaid Desiderius shall presently receive the episcopate in the city of Cahors and, with Christ’s favor, hold it throughout his lifetime. And so that this decision of our will may be held more firmly, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the subscription of our hand.

Chrodobert presented it. King Dagobert subscribed.

Given on the Ides of April, in the eighth year of King Dagobert.

## Letter to the metropolitan

### 3. King Dagobert to the holy and apostolic lord, Father Sulpicius

We believe that it is known to God and to Your Holiness how our faithful servant, the truly illustrious Desiderius, our treasurer, faithfully served us during the time of our youth. We are well acquainted with his deeply devout and monastic way of life. Therefore, know that we have decided as follows: in the city of Cahors, where his brother, the lord Rusticus, preceded him, he is to receive, in the name of God, the dignity of the episcopate in his brother’s place.

For, by divine inspiration, our devotion remains such that those whom we perceive to be adorned with good conduct and devoted to holy works—as is this most faithful servant of God and of ours, Desiderius—we ought to advance to the episcopal summit. For it befits royal majesty that those whom it knows to conduct themselves in the fear of God, to preserve the Catholic faith intact, and to observe the evangelical commandments, it should strive in every way to promote to pontifical office.

Since we know that you hold the metropolitan citadel [or, according to another reading: “we know that you, arch-metropolitan,”] we have taken pains to send these present letters to Your Eminence with the proper duty of greeting. We ask that you hasten to bless him and send letters to your provincial brothers, so that they too may be present and, canonically and according to apostolic institution, he may be consecrated in your presence with pontifical blessing during the holy Paschal solemnity.

We also earnestly ask above all that you commend us to the Lord in your holy and God-pleasing prayers, and that you cause no delay in completing this matter. As for this letter, we have decreed that it be strengthened, as is customary, by the subscription of our hand.

King Dagobert subscribed.

## Election: how a bishop is elected by the clergy and people in his own see, with the consent of the king, the archbishop, and the entire people

*(From Morin and the Corbie manuscript.)*

### 4. To the lord N., father equal in merit to the Franks, father of fathers, supreme prelate, the entire clergy and all the people of the holy church of N. wish abundant salvation in the Lord

Accordingly, whenever any people subject to your authority has been deprived of its own shepherd, help must be sought nowhere other than from you. The divine Majesty ordained you for this purpose, not only that you might specially feed your own sons, but also that you might provide shepherds to those who lack rulers and need spiritual nourishment.

Therefore, with confidence we pour out our prayers before the fatherhood of your holiness, asking you, namely, to deign to ordain this man N., of the highest uprightness and your humble servant, as our bishop. Insofar as we have come to know his conduct and character, we praise them and testify that he is suitable for so worthy a work. And so long as we remain free from episcopal blessing, strengthened by his teaching and example and, by the Lord’s mercy, returning to the way of salvation like a lost and recovered sheep [the text reads *onus*, “burden”; read *ovis*, “sheep”], we believe that we shall return.

We have decided to send you this decree, strengthened by our hands, for your church of N. Year of the Incarnation of the Lord and of your episcopate, and year N. of King N., in such-and-such indiction, dated such-and-such.

## The ancient statutes of the Church concerning the man who is to be ordained bishop

*(From the Colbert manuscript.)*

First, it must be examined whether he is naturally prudent, teachable, temperate in conduct, chaste in life, sober, attentive to his own affairs, humble, approachable, merciful, learned, grounded in the law of the Lord, cautious in understanding the Scriptures, and trained in ecclesiastical doctrines.

Above all, it must be examined whether he asserts the articles of the faith in simple words: namely, affirming that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God; proclaiming the entire Godhead in the Trinity to be of one essence, consubstantial, coeternal, and co-omnipotent; and confessing each individual person in the Trinity to be fully God, while the three persons as a whole are one God.

He must confess that the divine incarnation did not take place in the Father or in the Holy Spirit, but in the Son alone: he who was, in divinity, the Son of God the Father became, in humanity, the son of a human mother—true God from the Father and true man from his mother, possessing flesh from his mother’s womb [read: “from the womb of his mother”] and a rational human soul. Both natures exist together in him: the same man and God, one Son, one Christ, one Lord, creator and author of all that exists, and Lord and creator, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, of all creatures.

He must confess that Christ suffered with a true suffering of the flesh, died with the true death of his body, rose with the true resurrection of his flesh and truly with the resurrection of his soul, and will come to judge the living and the dead.

He must be asked whether he believes that the God of the New and Old Testaments—that is, of the Law, the Prophets, and the Apostles—is one and the same author. Whether the devil became evil not by his created nature but by his own choice. He must also be asked whether he believes in the resurrection of this flesh that we bear, and not of another; whether he believes that a judgment will come and that each person will receive either punishments or rewards for what he has done in this flesh.

Whether he does not disapprove of marriage; whether he does not condemn second marriages; whether he does not criticize the eating of meat; whether he communicates with penitents after their reconciliation; whether in baptism all sins are forgiven—that is, both the original sin contracted and those voluntarily committed; and whether no one is saved outside the Catholic Church.

When he has been examined in all these matters and found fully instructed, he is to be ordained bishop with the consent of the clergy and laity, at the assembly of the entire people, and especially with the authority or presence of the bishops of the province and of the metropolitan.

Having received the episcopate in the name of Christ, he must submit not to his own pleasure or to his own customs, but to these definitions of the Fathers.

**The statement ends.**

# A Specimen of Gallican Liturgy from Ancient Monuments

Our Mabillon has fully set out the order of the Gallican liturgy in a special treatise on the subject, which he published in 1635 on the occasion of the Gallican Lectionary discovered by him in the monastery of Luxeuil. There he also presents three sacramentaries that were in use under the first dynasty of our kings. A fourth is found in the Bobbio manuscript, brought to light by the same scholar in the appendix to volume I of the *Museum Italicum*. From these sources we select the more notable passages in order to compose this specimen of the Gallican Mass; we shall supplement some items from Gregory and other monuments of the same period.

## Antiphon, or Introit

In all liturgies the Mass begins with an antiphon. The Council of Agde indicates this concerning the Gallican rite in canon 30. What that antiphon was, however, is unknown, since no Gallican antiphonary has yet been found. We supply one from the Mozarabic rite.

> Alleluia. Blessed is he who comes, alleluia, in the name of the Lord, alleluia, alleluia.
>
> God is the Lord, and he has shone upon us. In the name of the Lord, alleluia, alleluia.
>
> Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, from Gregory’s Book VI, chapter 40. As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end. Amen. From the Second Council of Vaison, canon 5. In the name of the Lord, alleluia, alleluia.

## Kyrie eleison

“Lord, have mercy.” It is to be repeated frequently, according to the Second Council of Vaison, canon 3.

## Reading of the Prophet Isaiah

*(Gallican Liturgy, Mabillon, p. 107.)*

> At that time the Lord spoke to Ahaz, saying: “Ask for a sign for yourself,” etc.

From chapter VII, verse 10, through verse 8 of the following chapter, but with many verses omitted throughout. On the feasts of the saints, the passion of the saint whose feast was being celebrated, or his Life, was read in place of the prophecy, as we said in our preface.

## Collect after the prophecy

*(Liturgy, p. 190.)*

> You have risen for us, true Sun of justice, Jesus Christ. You came from heaven as the Redeemer of the human race. You raised up for us the horn of salvation; and, eternal Offspring of the exalted Father, begotten in the house of David because of the ancient prophecies of the seers, wishing to set your own people free and to erase the record of the ancient crime, you opened the triumph of eternal life.
>
> Therefore we now ask you to appear to our minds, O eternal salvation, in the depths of your mercy; and, rescuing us from the wicked enemy, make us worshipers of justice. Rejecting every error of death, and walking by the straight path along the way of peace, may we be able to serve you rightly, Savior of the world. You who live, rule, and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever.

## Daniel with the blessing

*(Liturgy, pp. 107, 139.)*

> Bless the Lord, all the works of the Lord. Sing a hymn to him and exalt him above all forever.
>
> Bless the Lord, angels of the Lord. Sing a hymn to him and exalt him above all forever, etc.
>
> Let us bless the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, the Lord. Let us sing a hymn and exalt him above all forever.

## Collect after the prayer

*(Liturgy, p. 190.)*

> Hear, O Lord, the family dedicated to you and gathered in the embrace of your Church on this present solemnity of your Nativity, so that it may proclaim your praises. Grant redemption to captives, sight to the blind, and forgiveness to sinners, because you came to save us. Look down from your holy heaven and enlighten your people, whose spirit trusts in you with complete devotion, Savior of the world, who live forever.

## Epistle of the Apostle Paul to the Hebrews

*(Liturgy, p. 107.)*

> Brothers, in many and various ways, etc.

Hebrews 1:1–13.

Here, as we conjecture, a responsorial psalm was sung, concerning which Gregory speaks in Book VIII, chapter 3; meanwhile the deacon proceeded to the place where the Gospel was customarily read.

## Reading of the holy Gospel according to Luke

> Glory to almighty God.

This was answered by the entire people, according to Book VIII of the *History*, chapter 4.

*(Liturgy, p. 108.)*

> It happened in those days that a decree went out from Caesar Augustus, etc.

From Luke 2:1–19.

If a homily was to be delivered to the people, it was then given, as appears from the *Life of Saint Eligius* by Saint Audoen, Book II, chapter 22.

## The Priest’s Apology

*(Liturgy, p. 251.)*

> Before the sight of your immensity, and before the eyes of your ineffability, O wondrous Majesty—namely, before your holy countenance, great God, almighty Father of supreme mercy and power—I, a very lowly petitioner, approach, though not without due reverence, yet without any dignity of office, and I stand before you as a witness against my conscience.
>
> What shall I ask for that I do not deserve? But is it not piously said—may this be said without offending God—that one who ought to be an intercessor for sins is rather their accuser? I therefore accuse myself to you and do not excuse myself; and before witnesses I confess my injustice to you, Lord my God.
>
> I confess, I say, I confess before witnesses the injustice of my ungodliness, so that you may forgive the ungodliness of my sin. I confess that, unless you forgive me, you justly punish me. You have me confessing my guilt, but—I know it—not correcting it except in words. For in words I appease you, but in deeds I offend. I feel my fault, but postpone amendment.
>
> Help, therefore, help, ineffable mercy. Forgive, forgive me, wondrous Trinity. Spare, spare, spare me, I beseech you, O appeasable Godhead. Hear, hear, hear me, I ask, crying out in these words of your Son:
>
> “Eternal Father God, I have sinned against heaven and before you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants.”
>
> And now, merciful Father, with Christ’s favor I ask for the one refuge of your mercy: grant that what is made vile through me may be accepted through him, who lives and reigns with you forever.

The deacon called for silence so that the Mass might be heard, according to Gregory, Book VII of the *History*, chapter 8.

## Preface of the Mass

*(Liturgy, p. 190.)*

> Let us venerate with rejoicing, as we desired in our prayers, the most holy day of the blessed Nativity, on which, when the Lord was born, the mysteries of the virginal womb were opened and the burden of the incorruptible birth poured forth as a relief for the world.
>
> This birth is indeed more splendid than day and more radiant than light. On this day, most beloved brothers, let us humbly entreat almighty God, who for the sake of our redemption assumed earthly and fragile matter, so that he may preserve under perpetual devotion those whom by the birth of his body he visited, by fellowship of life taught, by the command of preaching instructed, by tasting death redeemed, by embracing death received, and by the infusion of the divine Spirit enriched; and grant that we may remain in these works of blessed service.
>
> He who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever.

## Collect, or Mass, or prayer before the names

*(Liturgy, pp. 191, 323.)*

> O God, who are rich in mercy, by which you made us, dead in sins, alive together with Christ your Son, so that he might receive the form of a servant, he who formed all things; so that he who was in divinity might be born in the flesh; so that he who was adored among the stars might be wrapped in swaddling clothes; so that he who reigned in heaven might lie in a manger: mercifully incline the ear of your majesty to us who call upon you.
>
> Grant this through the ineffable love of your mercy: that we who rejoice in the nativity of your Son, who was either born from the Virgin or regenerated from the Holy Spirit, may obey his commandments, by which he taught us for salvation.
>
> Grant this through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives with you.

After this collect, the excommunicated having been expelled from the church, on every Sunday—as the Second Council of Mâcon states in canon 4—the offering of bread and wine was made by all men and women, both bread and wine, whereas on other days this was left to the will of the faithful, as we gather from Gregory.

Meanwhile, while the deacon brought from the sacristy the tower in which the mystery of the Lord’s body was kept, psalms were sung, as may reasonably be conjectured. We still retain the antiphon preceding such psalms under the name “Offertory.”

After the offering had been made, the gifts placed on the altar were covered with a veil or cloth, which Gregory commonly calls a *palla*. The name of the lord pope then presiding over the apostolic see was recited, according to canon 4 of the Second Council of Vaison; afterward, the names of those making offerings, and then those of the dead, whose names were written on a list and, as appears from a letter concerning the association between the canons of Laon and the monks of Saint-Remi, remained deposited on the holy altar at the time of the sacrifice, at least in some churches.

The sacred diptychs were read—that is, the catalogue of bishops who had died in Catholic communion—such as our Mabillon published from the church of Arles in volume III of the *Analecta*. In the church of Reims this was performed by a subdeacon, according to Folcuin in the *Chronicle of Lobbes*.

We found the diptychs of that same church in two manuscript codices, one in the metropolitan library and the other in the archmonastery of Saint-Remi. The following verses are prefixed to them:

> Here behold the names of every bishop of Reims,
>
> Among whom the middle one is like the sun: Remigius.
>
> For while the sacred offering of the table is sanctified,
>
> These names of the bishops are spoken.
>
> Sixtus, Sinicius, Amantius, etc.

The memory of others was also commemorated, namely benefactors and friends, as is evident from the formula found at the end of the rule of Saint Aurelian in the *Book of Rules* published by our Mabillon.

> At the same time, while praying, we also pray, O Lord, for the souls of your servants, our fathers and founders, Aurelian, Peter, etc., Childebert, Ultrogotha, and all our brothers whom you have deigned to call to yourself from this place; and for all the faithful of this place, and likewise for our parents and those serving in this place; and for the souls of all the faithful who have died in the peace of the Church.
>
> Grant them, O Lord our God, forgiveness of sins and bestow eternal rest, through the merits and intercessions of your saints: Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ; John the Baptist and forerunner of our Lord Jesus Christ; Stephen, Peter, Paul, etc.; Matthias, Genesius, etc.; Hilary, bishop and confessor, etc.; and Caesarius, bishop. In your mercy, deign to grant and hear these prayers, you who live and reign, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

## Collect after the names, or over the offerings

*(Liturgy, p. 299.)*

> After the names of those making offerings have been recited, most beloved brothers, let us beseech the Lord to receive their offering among the gifts of the saints, whose commemoration we are to make, so that they too may deign to remember us.
>
> Let us also ask for those who have gone before us in the peace of the Lord, that the Almighty may deign to raise them from the terror of Tartarus and place them in Abraham’s bosom, in his first resurrection, which he will bring about. Through him.

Then the faithful gave one another the kiss of peace, and the following was said:

## Collect for peace

*(Liturgy, p. 255.)*

> O God, through whose mouth it was proclaimed that you would give peace to all and leave ordinances of peace, pour into our hearts the pursuit of peace and the affection of a devout will. Thus, cleansed from every stain of vice, may we hold with pure hearts the peace that we pursue with the lips of our mouths. Through him.

## Contestation, or offering of the Mass

We have selected this prayer because Gregory praises it in chapter 14 of Book II of the *Miracles of Saint Martin*. We have supplied its conclusion from the prayer for Saints James and John.

*(Liturgy, p. 295.)*

> It is truly worthy and just, almighty God, to honor you in praising your Martin, who, kindled by the gift of your Holy Spirit, was found so perfect in the very training of faith that he clothed Christ in a poor man, and the Lord of the world put on the garment that the needy man had received.
>
> O happy generosity by which the Godhead is clothed! O glorious division of the cloak, which clothed both the soldier and the King! It is an immeasurable gift that deserved to clothe God with a garment of divinity.
>
> Worthily did you entrust him with the reward of this confession; worthily did he not submit to the savagery of the Arians; worthily did Martin, secure because such was the glorification of his suffering, not fear the tortures of the persecutor out of such great love, since through the measure of the small garment he both deserved to clothe Christ and to see him.
>
> O kindness of soul worthy of imitation! O venerable power of virtues! He fulfilled the office of the episcopate he had received in such a way that, through the pattern of a blameless life, he exacted the observance of discipline. By apostolic virtue he brought healing to those who hoped in him, saving some through his prayers and others by his appearance.
>
> This is your venerable power, O Lord. Since our tongue is insufficient to entreat you with merits, may we, with your help, deserve to imitate Saint Martin’s works through Christ our Lord [your Son (Liturgy, p. 198), who is the strength and glory of all the saints, the victory of martyrs and their crown, the shepherd of the sheep and the sacrifice of priests, the redemption of the nations and the propitiation of sins. Before his most sacred throne stand angels and archangels, and without ceasing they proclaim, saying: Holy, holy, holy.]
>
> The Second Council of Vaison, canon 3, likewise prescribes this.

## Collect after the Sanctus

*(Liturgy, p. 198.)*

> Hosanna in the highest. Truly holy, truly blessed is our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who, holy among the holy, has deigned to grant life in place of death, glory in place of punishment, and victory in place of confession. For on the day before he suffered, etc.

In the Frankish Missal, edited by Thomasius and Mabillon, the following is found at the end: “Here begins the canon of the action. Lift up your hearts, etc. It is truly worthy and just, etc. Therefore, most merciful Father, etc.,” as in the Roman Liturgy. All these items are found at the beginning of the Gallican Sacramentary, which the same Mabillon extracted from the Bobbio manuscript, but under this title: “Daily Roman Mass.”

Hence in the individual Masses nothing appears after the contestation. Perhaps already at that time the canon of the Mass was recited according to Roman custom, at least in some churches. In the Gothic Gallican and Old Gallican Missals, however, published by Mabillon, which present the pure rite of the Gallican Church, the canon varies according to the diversity of solemnities, but everywhere it is brief, as we have represented it here.

Gregory calls the sacred words this in chapter 87 of Book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*. From the same author, in chapter 16 of the *Lives of the Fathers*, we also learn that the holy gift was blessed according to Catholic custom—that is, according to what was observed in the universal Church—with the sign of the cross placed over it.

We infer that all these things were done and said secretly and in a lowered voice from the following prayer, which everywhere is called “after the secret,” or “after the mystery.” In the Mozarabic rite, indeed, it is prescribed that the consecration be said in silence. In the Gothic rite, however, it is prescribed that during the Rogation Days, at three Masses, after the Sanctus the words “This offering, therefore, etc.” be said.

## After the secret

*(Liturgy, p. 192.)*

> We believe in your coming, O Lord; we recall your passion. Your body was broken for the forgiveness of our sins; your holy blood was poured out as the price of our redemption. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

The same prayer is said elsewhere under the following title:

## After the mystery

*(Liturgy, p. 195.)*

> This, therefore, we do, O Lord; these commandments we observe; this passion of the sacred body we proclaim in sacred solemnities. We ask you, almighty God, that just as we now carry out the truth of the heavenly sacrament, so we may cling to the very truth of the Lord’s body and blood. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son.

## Before the Lord’s Prayer

*(Liturgy, p. 192.)*

> Not presuming upon our own merit, holy Father, but obedient to the command of our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, we dare to say: Our Father, who are in heaven, etc.

## After the Lord’s Prayer

*(The same.)*

> Deliver us, almighty God, from every evil and from every danger, and preserve us in every good work, perfect Truth and true Freedom, God, who reign forever and ever.

## Blessing of the people

*(Liturgy, p. 200.)*

> O God, who consecrated to yourself the firstfruits of the martyrs through the innocence of little children. Amen.
>
> And you first joined infancy to yourself in confession, before the tongue was loosened into words. Amen.
>
> Grant your people innocence through grace, even if there are no martyrdoms through the shedding of blood in their time. Amen.
>
> May this people, purified by baptism, be preserved: you made innocence pleasing to yourself through blood. Amen.
>
> Thus may the flock approach there through the washing, where the blessed little ones, drenched with the dew of blood, rejoice. Amen.
>
> Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you.

## Collect at the breaking of the bread

*(Liturgy, p. 251.)*

> Look upon this offering, almighty God, which we offer to you in honor of your name, for the salvation of kings and their armies, and of all who stand around us. Grant that those who partake of it may receive health of mind, integrity of body, protection of salvation, understanding of the mind of Christ, security of hope, strengthening of faith, and the eternity of the Holy Spirit. Grant this through him who lives and reigns with you.

Then those who were about to communicate approached the altar, while eulogiae were given to the others who remained, as we said from Gregory in our preface. Aurelianus suggests that psalms were sung at that time, since he prescribed in his rule that all should communicate while singing psalms. Indeed, we still sing the antiphon prefixed to such psalms under the name “Communion.”

## After Communion; elsewhere, after the Eucharist, or Preface after the Eucharist

*(Liturgy, p. 190.)*

> Strengthened by heavenly food and drink, most beloved brothers, let us offer praise and thanks to almighty God, asking that he who judged us worthy to share in the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son, may also reckon us worthy of heavenly reward. Through the same Lord Jesus Christ, his Son.

## The following collect; elsewhere, “Conclusion of the Mass”

*(The same.)*

> May we grasp with our minds what we have received with our mouths, and may what is temporal in the gift become for us an everlasting remedy.

In the Frankish Missal this prayer bears the title “For the People,” and in it the priest repeatedly asks that the people be blessed by God. In the Mass provided in the Gothic Missal for the beginning of Lent, and in the Gallican Missal in the second Mass of Advent, the blessing of the people is given after the collect, or conclusion, of the Mass.

# Mass for Saint Sigismund for Those Suffering from Fever

[Note: See the book *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 75, and note f, column 771. Editor.]

From the Gallican Sacramentary in the Bobbio manuscript.

## Epistle of the Apostle John to the Nations

> Brothers, do not love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him, because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life.

*(From Mabillon’s *Museum Italicum*.)*

## Reading of the holy Gospel according to Matthew

> In those days the Lord Jesus went throughout all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues, preaching the Gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every sickness among the people. His reputation spread throughout all Syria, and they brought to him all who were suffering, seized by various diseases and torments, and he healed them.

## Mass of Saint Sigismund the King

> Most beloved brothers, let us beseech the almighty Lord, who through his apostles and martyrs bestows various gifts of healing, that he may mercifully come to the aid of this servant of his, N., who is afflicted by the distress of quartan fever, through the prayers of his faithful servant Sigismund; and, while he makes the merits of that saint known to us, may he grant healing to this man.

## Secret

> Incline, O Lord, [your ears, perhaps; the printed text reads “merciful prayers”] to the desires of those who entreat you, and graciously accept what we ask with devout heart, so that you may mercifully come to the aid, through the prayers of your faithful servant Sigismund, of your servant N., who is afflicted by the distress of quartan fever. Make his merits known to us and grant healing to the present sick man.

## Contestation

> It is truly worthy and just, almighty God, to praise your name. We are the more bound to your majesty in proportion to what we owe him because of the humility of our body that he assumed, leaving us an example so that we might follow his footsteps, who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.
>
> Who in this world could follow him in such a way that neither deceit were found in his mouth nor sin in his work? Yet the divine majesty commends the patience that God loves.
>
> Now, therefore, by the gift of your majesty we recognize that relics belong to a peaceful man. You, therefore, O Lord our God, who amid the tumult of wars granted your chosen one Sigismund the triumph of martyrdom, not through the testing of a persecutor; you who, in distributing alms to the poor, deigned to open to the one who knocked, following grace and attaining mercy, so that after death you might display in power the one whom before death you had strengthened in faith:
>
> For your gifts, O Lord, are such that, in the name of your chosen one Sigismund, through communion in the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, you may drive away from your servant N. the chills of the illness and the heat of fevers, and deign to restore him to his former health. Grant this through him whom all the angels praise in the Trinity, etc.

## From the same Sacramentary

## Blessing of the chalice, paten, and tower

[Note: See Book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 86, and note a, column 781. Editor.]

> Almighty God, when with Moses your servant on Mount Horeb you arranged the commandments to be kept by your people, you instructed them how your holy temple was to be built. We beseech you, Lord: sanctify and bless this chalice, paten, and tower, in which we are to celebrate the most holy mysteries, with heavenly blessing, so that it may render acceptable service with your holy vessels. Through him.

## From the Frankish Missal

## Preface of the Chrism

[Note: See Book IV, chapter 32, of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*. Editor.]

*(Liturgy, p. 316.)*

> Let us pray, most beloved brothers, that almighty God may deign, as we pray, to endow this vessel, which bears the ministry of the body of his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, with blessing, the protection of sanctification, and the power of defense. Through him.

> Almighty God, Trinity, pour the help of your blessing into our hands, so that through our blessing this vessel may be sanctified and, by the grace of the Holy Spirit, become a new tomb of Christ’s body. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives with you.

Other prayers for consecrating the paten, chalice, etc., are found in the same place.

## Prayer over a vessel found in an ancient site

> Almighty and everlasting God, join yourself to our offices, and by the power of your majesty deign so to cleanse these vessels, fashioned by the art of pagans, that, with every impurity driven away, they may be used by your faithful in a time of peace and tranquility. Through him.

## Prayer for testing relics

*(From the manuscript of Saint-Remi of Reims.)*

> O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise.

Three times.

> O God, come to my assistance; O Lord, hasten to help me, with “Glory to the Father,” and with “Alleluia,”

three times.

Psalm: “Let God arise,” through “Sing a psalm and speak praise to God,” three times with “Glory to the Father.”

Hymn: “Come, Creator,” etc.

Prayer: “O God, who gave the Holy Spirit to the hearts of the faithful.”

Psalm: “In the Lord I trust.”

Antiphon: “For the saints who are on earth.”

Psalm: “Preserve me, O Lord.”

Antiphon: “You have tested me with fire.”

Psalm: “Hear, O God.”

Psalm: “It is fitting for you.”

Psalm: the same.
