> The Lord be with you.

Beginning of the holy Gospel according to John:

> In the beginning was the Word.

Then the litany, through:

> All holy ones, pray for us.

“Kyrie eleison,” three times; “Christe eleison,” three times; “Kyrie eleison,” three times.

> Our Father.

> And lead us not into temptation.

> Show us, O Lord, your mercy.

> And your salvation.

## Prayer

> Lord God Jesus Christ, who are King of kings and Lord of lords, and lover of all who believe in you; who are a just judge, strong and powerful; who revealed your holy mysteries to your priests; and who calmed the flames of fire for the three youths: grant to us, your unworthy servants, and hear our prayers, so that if this cloth or this thread in which these bodies of the saints have been wrapped is not genuine, it may be consumed by this fire; but if it is genuine, may it escape, so that injustice may not rule over justice and falsehood may be subjected to truth.
>
> Thus may your truth be declared to you and manifested to us who all believe in you, so that we may know that you are God, blessed forever and ever. Amen.

Our Father. Then the antiphon: “You have tested me by fire.” And when it is begun, let the relics be placed in the fire, and remain there until the antiphon itself has been completed three times, together with the psalm “You have proved my heart, O Lord,” and with the Gloria Patri. By doing this, you will discover whether the relics are genuine or false.

From the Second Council of Zaragoza, in the era 630 [that is, A.D. 592], in the seventh year of King Reccared, under Gregory the Great.

### Canon 2

[Col. 1186B] The holy synod decreed that relics found in any places belonging to the Arian heresy should be brought forth by the priests in whose churches they are found, presented to the bishops, and tested by fire. But if any have been concealed and are discovered, they are to be separated from the assembly of the sacred Catholic Church.

## THE LANGUAGE PROPERLY USED BY THE ANCIENT KINGS OF THE FRANKS

From the distinguished scholar Marquard Freher.

(Chesne, vol. II, p. 385.)

Since it has been noted [on the occasion of the treaty between the sons of Louis the Pious] that each of the two languages [the Roman and the German] was equally known and familiar to both brothers, [although each language was spoken for the peoples of each king], it is not irrelevant to ask what, then, was the proper and native speech of the Frankish kings who possessed Gaul. For, apart from Latin—which they themselves, no less than we today, had to learn with laborious effort—there is no reason to doubt that they possessed a particular ancestral and native language; a single passage of Fortunatus concerning King Charibert is enough to establish this:

> Though you are sprung from the illustrious race of the Sicambri,  
> Your Latin tongue flourishes in eloquence.  
> How excellent you are in the learned speech of your own tongue,  
> You who surpass us Romans in eloquence.

And Thegan, writing about Louis the Pious, says that he was highly learned in Greek and Latin, but could understand Greek better than he could speak it; Latin, however, he could speak as naturally and equally as his native tongue.

Besides that genuinely pure and unadulterated Ausonian language—which at that time was declining together with the Empire—there had also arisen a certain provincial language, much more polluted Latin, or rather a Gallo-Latin language, which Sidonius, with his customary wit, calls in one place the “scale” of the Latin language and elsewhere the “rust of commonplace barbarisms.” The Franks themselves called it nothing other than rustic Latin. It was more or less the language which Nithard here dignifies with the name “Roman,” because it was spoken, in however rough a fashion, throughout the Roman provinces, which the Franks called Romania. Fortunatus gives the same testimony in his poem to Chilperic:

> Hence barbarism for you, while Romania applauds you there.

It was also used by the provincials who, mingling with the victorious Franks, are repeatedly called “Romans” in the old laws.

But since the kings themselves were by origin Sicambri, although those remnants of Latin speech existed in conquered Gaul, I could establish with countless arguments that they used their own ancestral and original language, brought by their forefathers from Sicambria, or Francia, rather than that popular and rustic semi-Latin; and, finally, that they used their own victorious language, as is credible, rather than the captive language of their subjects. They retained it consistently for a long time, while the Merovingian and Carolingian dynasties flourished. It is pleasing to confirm this with a few more notable sayings of kings from both lines.

Concerning Clovis, then, who was the first to receive the saving faith through baptism from blessed Remigius, there is a passage in his Testament:

> “With two estates which King Louis, of illustrious memory and most pious prince, who had received holy baptism from me, gave me out of love for my name—estates called in his own language Piscofesheim—he entrusted them to me.”

Throughout central Germany there are several estates called Bischofsheim by this name; and, in the same form, the castle of blessed Nicetius built above the Moselle and celebrated in the verses of Fortunatus is still called Bischofstein.

Moreover, in four places in the Turonian author we read of a certain Gundobald, who had come from Greece and falsely claimed to be the son of King Chlothar. King Guntram, whether out of indignation or contempt, called him Ballomer—a term without doubt bitter and grave in its reproach, though not requiring fuller explanation here. It is enough to know that it signifies a pseudo-king, as *Balmond* signifies a false and wicked guardian.

[Col. 1187B] I come now to the Carolingians. Concerning the first of them, the Continuator of the Turonian History, chapter 103, says:

> “Thereafter the aforementioned Pippin took another wife, noble and elegant, named Alpheid, by whom he fathered a son; and he called his name, in his own language, Charles.”

I could prove immediately, and with complete certainty, that this name has nothing at all in common with *Caro* or *Carinus*, but is thoroughly Germanic, if I were not cautious about even lightly plucking a flower from my *Onomathotera*—the title we gave to our book specifically on German proper names.

Who, moreover, does not know the names which Charles himself gave to the months and winds? His son and successor, Louis the Pious, when at the point of death he repelled the malign spirits that appeared before him by the power of faith, repeatedly exclaimed, “Huz, huz”; the writer of his Life tells us that this meant “Out, out.”

I shall conclude with a notable passage from Frodoard concerning the synod held at Ingelheim in A.D. 949:

> “After the reading of these letters, and their interpretation for the kings in the Theotisc language,” etc.

What could anyone ask for clearer than this? Therefore the more sensible Frenchmen do rightly when they acknowledge that the German language—which the foolish common people insultingly call *baragouin*, a word more than barbarous, as though it were barbaric and uncouth—was the gentile and vernacular language of their ancestors and of their earliest and most distinguished kings. If they do not themselves learn and willingly use it, they certainly admire it for its antiquity, abundance, and majesty; and they hold Germany in the same reverence in which the Romans once held Ilium.

## From canon 17 of the Third Council of Tours

It seemed good to our unanimity that every bishop should have homilies . . . and that each should take care to translate them openly into the rustic Roman language or into the Theotisc language, so that all might more easily understand what is being said.

## CONCERNING THE ROYAL ABBEY OF SAINT-GERMAIN-DES-PRÉS NEAR PARIS

[Col. 1187D]

As I gathered every ancient monument useful for illustrating Gregory’s History, I could not omit those that are present in the celebrated Abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. Founded by King Childebert, the son of the great Clovis, and honored by succeeding kings and by their tombs, it is frequently praised and mentioned by our Gregory.

The antiquity of the times and the vicissitudes of human affairs have caused only a few monuments of those ancient ages to survive from among the many. Nevertheless, since more remains of the first royal line of our kings are visible there than in any other place in Gaul, it seemed necessary to linger a little in order to elucidate them.

The fame of the site and the majesty of its founders persuade us that the basilica was magnificent. Begun after the year 542, it was completed in 559 and consecrated by blessed Germanus himself, bishop of Paris. The occasion for its construction was Childebert’s victory over the Visigoths, so that he might deposit in a fitting place the sacred objects, especially the stole of blessed Vincent, which he had brought from Spain.

An old author of the Life of Saint Droctoveus teaches that the church was built in the form of a cross under the direction of Saint Germanus, consecrated with five altars, and filled with various relics of the saints. Hence it is probable that it was distinguished by both the name of the Holy Cross and that of Saint Vincent. That it bore both names from the beginning is established by Venantius Fortunatus, the Testament of Ermentrude, and other sources.

The author of the Life of Saint Bathildis counts the basilica of Saint Germanus among the older foundations of the kingdom. In his Testament, Saint Bertramnus, illustrious bishop of Le Mans, asks the abbot of that renowned place to have his own name recited in the book of the Life—that is, among the monastery’s benefactors—having given for this purpose the estate of Bobane.

We learn how magnificent it was from the aforementioned author of the Life of Saint Droctoveus, who wrote at the end of the ninth century, when this basilica had already been violated once and again by the fury of the Normans, though it had not yet been destroyed. It would therefore not be unreasonable to say that he described it as it had originally been constructed:

> “It seems superfluous for us to describe the wondrous workmanship of this basilica: how it was distinguished by windows; by what precious marble columns it was supported; in what manner its curving vault was adorned with gilded coffers; and with what beauty the walls, as befitted Christ’s hall, shone with paintings of golden color, while the floor below was spread with a beautiful mosaic pavement. The roof of the basilica itself, covered completely with gilded copper [that is, Cyprian bronze], reflected the sun’s fiery rays and gleamed with such brilliance that it dazzled the eyes of those who looked upon it. Hence, on account of its excessive beauty, the house itself was not improperly called, metaphorically, in the speech of the common people, ‘the Hall of Gilded Germanus.’”

A double oratory was attached to the lower part of this basilica. In one of them, facing north and long since violated, blessed Droctoveus was buried. He was the first abbot of the place, appointed by Germanus himself. Later, after miracles had become frequent, he was removed from there and transferred to the greater basilica, where he is still preserved in a reliquary.

In the opposite oratory, facing south, was deposited the most blessed bishop himself. His tomb, already renowned for miracles in the time of King Chilperic, as Gregory relates, was honored by that king with a poem, if we trust the commonly circulated account of Aimoin. Shortly afterward, Saint Eligius adorned it with gold, silver, and the most precious gems, as blessed Audoenus, the author of his Life, testifies.

Even today the faithful visit the place of the burial of so great a bishop, although his sacred body was transferred from there more than nine hundred years ago into the greater basilica, under Abbot Lantfrid. Only a stone was left as a memorial of the first burial, on which, several centuries later, this inscription was carved:

> **HERE BLESSED GERMANUS WAS FIRST BURIED.**

[Col. 1188D] Another square stone is also seen there, bearing a figure of the cross and an old inscription around it, carved in the eighth century. It records the generosity of King Pippin when he was present at the translation of the sacred body, in these words. The letters are for the most part Roman and square, but interwoven with one another, with large and small letters mixed together, so that some were enclosed within others and occupied less space. Since the forms of type did not permit us to reproduce them, we represent them in ordinary letters:

> **WHEN SAINT GERMANUS WAS RESTING, ON THE DAY OF THE TRANSLATION, KING PIPPIN GAVE HIM THE ESTATE OF PALATIOLUS WITH ALL ITS APPURTENANCES.**

This oratory was subsequently violated several times, but was reconciled just as many times. Its altar, repaired at the beginning of the present century, was consecrated in 1619 by Saint Francis de Sales, bishop of Geneva.

But since the entire building, weakened by age, was believed soon to be about to collapse, it was almost entirely restored and repaired from its foundations a few years ago. The tomb of the holy bishop was also embellished, as it is seen today, with an inscription carved in marble indicating the day and year of the blessed pontiff’s death.

Between the two oratories there is a tower displaying such great antiquity to those who look upon it that some have thought it older than the monastery itself. Not far away stood an ancient idol which common authors say belonged to Isis. In the immediately preceding century the monks broke it to pieces because it seemed to provide an occasion for idolatry to certain little women who prayed before it.

Under that tower are the main doors of the greater basilica, with a portico in which several stone statues of kings and queens can be seen, set beside the doorposts. Learned men who have examined them most carefully think that they were placed there when the basilica was first built, or certainly shortly thereafter. The matter itself indeed speaks plainly.

Above the upper lintel of the doorway is a representation of the Lord’s Supper, in which the Lord sits at table with his apostles in the customary manner. The statues we have said stand on either side of the doors are exactly eight in number, nearly life-size and of the form in which figures could be represented in that barbarous age.

Besides a bishop, we long suspected from the appearance alone that they represented King Clovis with Clotilde and four sons, together with Ultrogotha, the wife of Childebert, the founder. More careful observation has made this entirely certain. For, examining more closely the scrolls which some of them hold in their hands, we discovered traces of letters on two of them. These showed that one was Clodomir and the other Chlothar.

Although these letters may seem to have been substituted for the original ones, the form of the characters and the almost completely worn-away green color prove that they are extremely ancient. We infer that they were painted when the church itself was restored, from Childebert’s tomb, which was then, as we shall say below, sculpted. It too had been painted in a similar color, as several surviving traces of its painting indicate.

The first statue encountered by those entering on the left represents a bishop clothed in pontifical vestments and holding a pastoral staff in his left hand. Its upper part is broken off, so that it is impossible to determine the form of its crook. He wears a maniple on his left arm, in the manner and form in which priests and bishops still wear it.

He has a mitre on his head, not pointed, as is customary today, but low, like those formerly worn. He is clothed in a chasuble, whose outer edges are raised slightly by his partly lifted arms, enough for the lower edge of the dalmatic to be visible beneath it. Below this, the lower portions of the stole hang down on either side almost to the feet, over a white alb whose lower border, ornamented with various figures, shows that it was magnificent.

Some think this is Saint Germanus, the second founder of the place. I would rather believe it to be Saint Remigius, to whom this honor was given because he brought King Clovis and the entire Frankish people to faith in Christ. [Col. 1189B] The figure of a snarling devil, which he tramples underfoot, persuades me of this. By that symbol, the extirpation of idolatry by the same holy man is represented.

The statue next to this represents a king dressed in broad and magnificent garments and wearing a crown on his head. In his left hand he holds a scroll, whose writing, if it ever existed, has been completely worn away. In his right hand, instead of a scepter, he holds a consular staff with an eagle mounted upon it, such as Roman consuls used.

There can therefore be no doubt that Clovis, father of the Augusti, is represented here, adorned with a purple cloak and tunic, as our Gregory describes him. After receiving from the Emperor Anastasius the documents concerning the consulship, Clovis entered the city of Tours in triumph as Augustus and consul, after a diadem had been placed upon his head in the basilica of Saint Martin.

This monument ought to be considered all the more precious because it greatly illuminates an important passage of our Gregory. Beside Clovis stands a queen whom I have no doubt was his wife. She wears a crown on her head, and her curls extend almost to her knees. What she held in her right hand, however, we have been unable to determine.

The form of her garments, though crude, was exceedingly magnificent, as is especially clear from the clasp of her mantle, which consisted of precious stones. She also has a belt fashioned in the ancient manner. Certainly, from the Life of Saint Eligius we learn that queens at that time were accustomed to wear ornaments of gold and gems—a practice which the holy bishop, even after his death, rebuked in the widowed Queen Bathildis.

Finally, the last statue on that side is a king. Several surviving letters painted on the scroll he holds identify him as Clodomir, Clovis’s firstborn son by Clotilde, after Ingomer had died in infancy:

> **CLODOMRIUS**

On the other side of the doors there are an equal number of statues. The one nearest the doorway seems to represent Theodoric. Childebert, the founder of the place, gave him that position of honor because he was Clovis’s firstborn. Like the others, he holds a scroll in his hand, but no letters appear on it.

We infer that the statue next to him is that of Childebert the founder because he holds writing tablets in his hands, containing the documents of the monastery he founded. He is not only crowned, like the other brothers, but also carries a scepter in his right hand. Perhaps, since he reigned at Paris, he alone among them was entitled to use the royal rod.

Beside him stands his wife Ultrogotha, likewise distinguished by royal dress, but without the belt and clasp which we observed on Clotilde’s statue. At her left side, Chlothar, the younger of the brothers, occupies the eighth place, as we discovered from the remnants of letters painted on his scroll:

> **CHLO . . . . . VS**

He has curls flowing over his shoulders, such as Gregory and other authors repeatedly observe that the sons of our kings were accustomed to wear.

Although all those kings and queens have crowns, each adorned with four flowers, the flowers are not formed in the same manner on all the crowns. Some appear almost like the present-day French lilies, while others are entirely different. All this will be shown more fully in the engraved copperplate.

Within the basilica itself, many noble men were formerly buried; even if we remained silent, the stones that are continually excavated would cry it out plainly. Indeed, one might reasonably say that it was once the common burial place of the kings and princes of the first royal line.

Gregory himself records that Childebert and Chilperic were buried there; later authors testify that others were buried in the same place. Moreover, although Chlodoveus and Meroveus, Chilperic’s sons by Audovera, had been buried elsewhere, after several years King Guntram arranged for their bodies to be brought to the royal basilica of Saint Vincent.

Then, if any kings had met a violent death and had consequently made no provision concerning their place of burial, they were buried in the Vincentian basilica. Such were Chilperic and Childeric, as everyone knows.

Of all the tombs of so many kings and princes, only six were known to have been brought up from the earth before our own time. Childebert and his wife Ultrogotha, the founders of the place, lay between the morning altar and the place where Saint Germanus’s body was kept, in the apse of the choir, in separate tombs.

Four others had been deposited in four arches hollowed out of the wall of the towers adjoining the choir, in the lower part of the choir as it was then arranged: Chilperic with Fredegund to the north, and on the other side Chlothar II, their son, with his wife Bertrude.

Each tomb had a tablet attached to it indicating the name and rank of the person buried there. Only Chilperic’s tomb bore an inscription, carved in large and ancient letters around it, in these words:

[Col. 1191A]

> **+ KING CHILPERIC IS COVERED BY THIS STONE.**

The tombs were of stone, low, wholly simple, and without any ornament, except for three on which the likenesses of the deceased were still sculpted.

The first represents Childebert carrying a scepter in one hand and the church he had founded in the other. This was the customary manner of representing the founder of the place.

Chilperic is represented on another stone with a scepter in his right hand and his left hand placed against his beard. Some have believed this to indicate a murdered man bringing his hand to his throat. But the learned Jacobus Brolius, a monk of this monastery of Saint-Germain, writes that he saw, in the possession of Philippe Lauter, then superintendent of the mint at Paris, the seal of King Chilperic, on which Chilperic was represented in exactly the same manner as on his tomb.

The matter is of little importance, since learned men agree that the figures of Childebert and Chilperic were sculpted many centuries after their deaths; they consider them no more than six hundred or somewhat more years old. We therefore conjecture that these royal tombs were arranged in this way when, after the Norman incursions had been brought to an end—the Normans having violated the monastery by fire two or three times—Abbot Morard restored the basilica with the time and assistance of King Robert; or certainly in the following century, when the same basilica was repaired in better form under the care of Abbot Hugh III and consecrated by Pope Alexander III, accompanied by a large number of cardinals and bishops.

But the stone placed over the tomb of Queen Fredegund is of far greater importance, both because of its magnificence and because of its antiquity. It is the very stone originally placed over the queen’s tomb and preserved down to our time. Fredegund is represented on it wearing a fleur-de-lis crown on her head, holding a royal scepter in her hand, and dressed in very broad and magnificent garments. These garments, as well as her belt of singular design, are decorated with almost countless circles representing gems.

No likeness of her face, however, is shown; and in place of her hands and feet the stone has been left flat. The entire surface of the tomb, moreover, is covered with fragments of marble, jasper, and similar precious stones, joined in mosaic work and scattered with thin bronze wires. All this shows that the monument was fashioned with great care and skill, considerable for that age.

That this tomb is Fredegund’s is proved, besides the tablet formerly placed upon it, as we have said, and the continuous tradition of our fathers handed down to us, by other considerations.

The appearance of the tomb itself proves that it is a queen’s tomb, and it cannot more properly be assigned to any other queen lying in the Vincentian basilica than to Fredegund. It cannot be Ultrogotha, the wife of Childebert, since her tomb, different from this one, was always displayed in the church of Saint Germanus; nor will anyone easily persuade himself that the monks of the place placed the monument of their foundress over the tomb of another woman hated by all.

Still less can it be Bertrude, who, as we have seen, had her own tomb distinct from the others. Furthermore, the magnificence of this tomb suits Fredegund better than any other queen.

Ultrogotha, driven into exile after her husband’s death, although later recalled, is said to have devoted herself entirely to pious works, leaving no one behind who would have wished to construct such a magnificent tomb for her.

Fredegund, however, died at the time when King Chlothar, her son, was at the height of his power. Shortly before, after defeating the other kings, he had seized Paris and many other cities through Fredegund’s counsel and assistance.

Moreover, Chlothar owed everything to his mother Fredegund. He was about four months old when he lost his father and was abandoned by everyone; yet she never abandoned him amid dangers, disgrace, and varied fortunes. She asserted his royal birth, which some attempted to call into question; secured for him the friendship of his uncle Guntram; obtained from Guntram for him a portion of the kingdom from which he had been excluded; and, finally, after placing him upon the royal throne, arranged for the restoration of the cities he had lost and acquired others by force and stratagem.

She left him, at her death, triumphing over other kings and enriched with glory and wealth. It should therefore surprise no one that her son gave her such a mausoleum. For this reason, it seemed appropriate to reproduce it here in an engraving.

[Col. 1193A] This was the arrangement of the royal tombs in the basilica of Saint Germanus until the middle of the present century. In 1656, however, when the choir was remodeled, it became necessary to move those tombs from their places.

The body of Saint Germanus, which had long been kept in the apse of the choir above four columns, in a reliquary made of gold and silver, was taken to the sacristy, where it awaits a new mausoleum. The stone coffin in which the blessed bishop had first been buried was placed beneath the main altar and, together with the altar itself, was transferred to the place where it is now seen.

The bodies of Eleutherius and Eusebia, the parents of the blessed pontiff, which are said to have been brought into the choir from the oratory of Saint Symphorianus on the occasion of the translation, were left in their own graves.

The tombs of the kings and queens which, as we said, had been deposited in the arches of the towers were transferred to the presbytery. There they were enclosed in stone tombs made and decorated in the more recent style and arranged on either side as before.

The stones by which they had previously been covered were placed individually upon the respective tombs, with an inscription added to each so that in future one would not be confused with another. Even on those in which no figure had existed, simple outline representations of the kings or queens whom they covered were carved with a knife, for greater distinction.

But so that Childebert, as founder of the place, might receive greater honor than the others, a tomb was constructed in the middle of the choir, as it is still seen today, large enough to contain him and his wife.

The bodies of both were therefore lifted from the place where we said they had lain and enclosed in a lead coffin divided into two compartments. Above Childebert’s bones was placed a bronze plate with this inscription:

> **Here rest the bones and ashes of Childebert, most Christian king of the Franks; their resting place was restored in the year of Our Lord 1656, on December 23, the anniversary of that king’s death.**

Above the queen’s remains was placed another:

> **Here rests Ultrogotha, queen, wife of King Childebert; she was reinterred in the year of Our Lord 1656, on December 23.**

A lead tablet common to both, filled with innumerable lilies, covers the entire coffin; the names of the king and queen are inscribed upon it. After all these remains had been placed together in the common tomb, the old stone representing Childebert, as described above, was set over it. Previously it had covered only the king’s tomb.

Marble panels were added to the sides of the tomb to receive inscriptions. The one facing north displays the epitaph of King Childebert formerly inscribed on his tomb, as the commonly circulated Aimoinus reports. It is written in golden letters:

> **TO THE KING OF THE AGES**
>
> Renowned ruler of the Franks, illustrious leader of the host,  
> Whom the Allobroges feared to disobey,  
> And the Dacian, the Arvernian, the king of the Britons, the Goth,  
> The Iberian—  
> Here lies the honorable king called Childebert.  
>
> He founded this hall, renowned under Vincent’s name;  
> A man distinguished by piety and rich in the gift of righteousness,  
> He enriched God’s temples and rejoiced in repaying gifts;  
> He gave thousands of solidi to beggars and the needy,  
> And diligently sought to store up heaps of treasures in heaven.

[Col. 1193D] On the other side is written Ultrogotha’s eulogy, excerpted from the Life of Saint Bathildis, as follows:

> **TO ETERNITY**
>
> Ultrogotha, wife of Childebert, most Christian king; nurse of orphans; comforter of the afflicted; supporter of the poor and servants of God; and helper of faithful monks.

This inscription is added:

> Here she awaits, with her most beloved husband, that day when their works will praise them in the gates. For these two excellent founders, transferred from their humble resting place together with their tombstone, the faithful pupils of this Royal Abbey, Benedictine ascetics, after restoring the basilica and choir to a better form, erected a more splendid monument in the year of Our Lord 1656, on December 23, the anniversary of their repose.

The royal maidens Crodesindis and Croberga are absent from their parents’ tomb. They rest in the same basilica, but in unknown graves. Yet, so that oblivion may not bury those whom incorruption has made immortal, let the august name and everlasting memory of these dearest daughters live here also with their most pious parents.

While the workmen were laboring over the adornment of the choir, turning the pavements upside down and inside out, countless fragments of precious and variegated stones were found, cut into various shapes. These suggest that the pavement of our church had been laid in mosaic work of the kind still seen in some of the larger basilicas.

The author of the Life of Saint Droctoveus, whose entire passage we cited above, expressly states this. On the same occasion, several stone tombs were discovered. Some had been inserted into the very foundations of the church; others had been arranged in the church’s area around the altar.

When some had been accidentally broken open, bodies were seen wrapped in silk and other precious cloths. Remains of boots, belts or girdles, and other ornaments were also found, indicating that eminent men had been buried there.

They were left in their places, except for King Childeric and his wife Bilihild, who were lifted from the earth and placed here and there in the presbytery among the other kings, each with an inscription added.

Since this discovery was famous—for some had previously maintained that Childeric and his wife were buried at Rouen—it seemed worthwhile to describe it somewhat more carefully, according to what we learned from those who were present at the time and from the surviving notes of others.

In 1646, two large sarcophagi or stone chests were first discovered. In them the bodies of the king and queen lay buried, entirely intact and clothed in royal garments that had not yet completely decayed. Since the monks were absent, the workmen are believed to have taken away many of the ornaments. They denied the theft, however, and could never be persuaded to return them, except for part of a diadem made of woven gold, with which they claimed the king’s head had been encircled.

When the tombs were opened again in 1656, the garments were found to have been almost entirely disturbed, and the bones had been moved from their places. In the king’s tomb only a glass flask remained, containing a dry but not wholly faded perfume.

There were also several fragments of swords and a dagger almost consumed by rust, together with remains of the royal belt or girdle: namely, a clasp of the purest gold weighing more than eight ounces, several silver bosses representing *amphisbaenae*, or two-headed serpents, and other ornaments.

Remains of a staff were also found, which some thought to be parts of his scepter. The form of the clasp is almost exactly like the one represented by Chifflet in *Anastasis Childerici I*, chapter 16, in the lower corner toward the outer margin of the illustration on page 236.

The ornaments at the end of the belt were similar to those described in the same work, chapter 14, p. 204. Two of this kind were found in the tomb of our Childeric, one slightly larger than the other.

In the queen’s tomb nothing was found except bones and garments, which, as soon as the tomb was opened, vanished into dust. Above the queen’s tomb was a small stone chest containing the bones of an infant. We have no doubt that this was her son, the young Dagobert.

Nevertheless, uncertainty remained in our minds as to whose tombs these were, until, after the earth had been removed so that the bones could be arranged more decently, the following inscription appeared at the bottom of the royal tomb. It was written in uncial letters occupying the entire width:

> **CHILD. REX.**

From this, everyone immediately adopted the opinion that these were the tombs of Childeric II and his wife. Accordingly, they were rightly granted a place in the presbytery among the other kings and queens.

This would have been enough concerning the royal tombs, had not the discovery of other tombs in 1643 required us to write something about them as well.

It occurred by chance. On Good Friday, while sand was being removed from the cloister beside the gate that provides access from there to the dormitory and the church, two stone tombs were found. One contained the body of a man; the other, as is believed, that of a woman.

The latter had no inscription, but on the stone covering the first, externally, there was an inscription carved in Roman letters, irregularly abbreviated for the sake of concision, with some letters growing out of others and joined together. Since the type does not permit us to reproduce them here, they formed these words:

> **AT NO TIME DO I WISH THE BONES (*ozza*) OF HILPERIC (*Hilperici*) TO BE REMOVED FROM HERE.**

On the inside, however, on the reverse side of the stone, the buried man made the same request: namely, that no one remove his coffin, or at least transfer his bones elsewhere. The letters were similar, but painted only in vermilion:

> **I, ILPERICUS (*Ilpericvs*), BESEECH YOU: LET MY BONES (*ozza*) NOT BE REMOVED FROM HERE.**
[p. 1380; Col. 1195B] The tombstones were ordinary and of the usual shape. Their feet faced east, as in all the other tombs that are excavated here and there. Their heads were raised much higher than their feet. In Chilperic’s tomb, together with the bones, each properly arranged in its place, there was found a small bronze lamp, equal in size to a walnut; also a bronze cross about half a palm in length, to which an image of Christ hanging on the cross was attached.

Valesius, in Book XI of his *Frankish History*, thought that those two tombs belonged to King Chilperic and his wife Fredegund, because the name Hilpericus was engraved on one of them. But it can easily be demonstrated that the learned man was mistaken—not only from what we reported above concerning the tombs of Chilperic and Fredegund, but also from the very discovery of these tombs, which Valesius himself inserted into his history.

First, it is certain that no indication of Chilperic’s wife was found there. The sutures of the skull might indeed indicate a woman, although even this is emphatically denied by skilled physicians; but nothing determines that she was Fredegund rather than some other woman, except her proximity to Hilpericus. As for that Hilpericus, I would readily believe him to have been a man of distinction, as one may infer from the name alone, but not a king. For the title “king” is absent; it would certainly not have been omitted from the inscription.

Nor is there any reason to agree with Valesius that, after death, Christian princes—who make great and small equal—would not wish to glory in such titles, or at least that Chilperic was killed and buried hastily. Both claims are refuted by the example of King Childeric. He was killed by a conspiracy of nobles whom he had provoked by violating the rights of the Franks; nevertheless, as we have said, he was buried with his wife and little son in royal attire, and the title “king” was not omitted.

Furthermore, Chilperic was buried in the basilica of Saint Vincent, whereas this man was buried outside the doors. For our church was rebuilt on that site after the Norman incursions had been brought to an end, in the place where it had first been constructed. This is proved by the ancient statues affixed to the great gate, by the remains of pavements excavated there, and by the monuments of Childeric and other illustrious men, which, as we have mentioned, were found in the presbytery.

Add to this the inscription placed both outside and inside the tomb. It indicates a man who thoughtfully and carefully considered his own burial, and who, out of humility, wished to be laid in that place so that he would be trodden underfoot by those entering the church; or at least so that the monks, who frequently passed that way, might more easily be moved to pray to God for him. The same man’s piety is indicated by the image of the Crucified One enclosed with him in the tomb.

All these things are plainly incompatible with the character of King Chilperic and with the manner of his death. One must also add the inscription carved approximately six hundred years ago on King Chilperic’s tomb, which cannot be rejected without the gravest reason. For no one will easily persuade himself that this inscription, like the tablets that had been placed on other tombs before the choir was altered, was rashly written here by someone.

We infer that those tablets had been borrowed from older monuments from the booklet of Peter of Corbeil, abbot of Saint-Germain, *On the Deeds of the Kings Who Rest in the Basilica of Saint-Germain or Conferred Certain Benefits upon It*. In that book, published in 1330, he reports, among other things, the epitaphs that had been attached to the kings’ tombs.

Nor is it surprising that the monks of Saint-Germain thought about adorning Chilperic’s tomb, since he himself—as is clear from the testament of Saint Bertram—built a new church, made known the miracles of Saint Germain, and bestowed certain estates upon the monastery.

The ancient monuments of the kings that are displayed in the basilica of Saint-Germain may be joined by the remarkable Book of Psalms commonly called the Psalter of Saint-Germain. Some have written that it was given to Saint Childebert, bishop, and they maintain that the king brought it from Spain into Gaul together with other ecclesiastical spoils mentioned by Gregory in Book III, chapter 10.

Whatever the truth may be, it is certain that this codex deserves a place among precious treasures and that it is not later than the time of Saint Germain. It is altogether similar to the codices that Jerome describes in the preface to the Book of Job: written on purple parchment in uncial letters of gold and silver.

For a long time it was preserved in the basilica’s treasury among the other relics of the saints; later it was placed in a cupboard in the library, where it can still be seen. Anyone may examine the form of its script in Mabillon’s book *On Diplomatic Science*, p. 357, where a specimen of it is engraved on copper. Its variant readings from the Vulgate edition are reported in volume V of the works of Saint Augustine, in the new edition prepared by our own scholars.

A somewhat later codex is the Greek-Latin manuscript of the letters of Saint Paul, a specimen of which is likewise found in the same book, *On Diplomatic Science*, p. 347.

Of no lesser antiquity is the large linen cloth commonly called the corporale of Saint Peter. It is said to have been sent by Gregory the Great, Roman pontiff, to Queen Brunhild and then granted to our church. Gregory speaks more than once of such linens, which he calls *brandea*, especially in Book III, Letter 30. There he replies to the empress Constantina, who had begged him for relics of the blessed Paul, that it was not customary among the Romans, when they gave relics of the saints, to presume to touch anything belonging to the body; instead, they placed only a *brandeum* in a small reliquary, and, after it had lain for some time near the most sacred bodies of the saints, it was regarded as a relic.

We also possess the arm of Saint George and relics of the Innocents, which are believed to have been given to this basilica by Saint Germain and are still preserved in the treasury with the other treasures.

I omit the stole of Saint Vincent, which had provided the occasion for founding the monastery, and that incomparable cross, in workmanship and weight, adorned with the most exquisite gems and brought from Spain. An ancient charter of our monastery, after the anonymous author of the *Life of Saint Droctoveus*, testifies that it was given to the basilica of Saint Vincent. The charter also praises the treasures of the church, many of which King Childebert had gathered there for the adornment of the house of God.

Time has consumed all these things. Yet, with God’s favor, no age will ever erase from our minds the memory of so many benefactions. What our fathers received from their fathers and transmitted to us, we too shall commend to those who come after us, so that they may commend it in turn to generations yet to come.

It was certainly an ancient custom preserved in this monastery that, in the notices of the dead—which they called rolls and which were customarily sent each year to other places for the commemoration of the deceased—the name of our founder Childebert and of the other kings should be mentioned.

Recently we saw such an original document in the library of Saint-Aubin at Angers, copied more than five hundred years ago. It reads as follows:

> Title of Saint-Germain of Paris. The soul of Abbot Robert, etc. Pray for our deceased, for Lord King Childebert and the other kings and queens, and for all the benefactors of our church.

Our fathers were always particularly careful that the solemn memory of Childebert, our founder, should be maintained in this royal basilica. Usuard, the celebrated monk of this place in the ninth century, entered his deposition in the Martyrology.

Among the principal solemnities of the year, the anniversary of King Childebert is listed in the charter of Charles the Bald concerning the division of the possessions of the monastery of Saint-Germain, by which the abbot was irrevocably obliged to provide meals for the monks.

In the *Book of Benefactors* of this monastery, compiled in 1270, the following is read among other entries:

> On the day of the anniversary of our lord King Childebert, the provision is to be made by the abbot … all the more generously because he for whom it is made was more munificent in distributing the possessions and goods assigned for the support of the church.

In the old books the abbot was ordered to celebrate solemnly on this day, or, if he could not do so himself, to entrust his duties to his vicar.

From the ancient constitutions of the monastery, which the most devout Abbot William gathered into a single body, we learn with what solemnity this anniversary—namely, on 23 December—was celebrated. On the preceding day all the monks without exception were required to assemble in the chapter house. There, after the anniversary commemoration of the most devout founder had been announced from the Martyrology, prayers were offered in common for the granting of rest to him. Then all the bells of all the towers were rung solemnly for so great a patron.

Afterward the king’s tomb was decorated with cloths and surrounded with many candles. One of these, much larger than the others, burned continuously from that hour until Compline on the following day.

Vespers for the dead and then the vigils were celebrated, followed on the next day by the principal Mass, in addition to the private Masses that each monk was instructed to celebrate for the founder, just as on the more solemn feasts Masses were celebrated by the abbot. During these services the altars and then the king’s tomb were incensed. The vestments of the celebrant and the sacred ministers, as well as those of the other officials, were more splendid than usual and were purple.

When the service was completed, bread, wine, and other provisions were distributed at the dais in the refectory. All this concluded with alms distributed to thirty poor people.

We still celebrate this anniversary today, although it has been altered in certain respects.

## Royal Charters

[Note: See Fredegarius Scholasticus, *Chronicle*, chapter 79, and note f, column 656; likewise the book *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 72, and note h, column 768. —Editor.]

[Column 1197C] Concerning the location, perpetual psalmody, and other matters of the royal basilica of Saint-Denis near Paris.

## Charter of Chlothar II

*(From the original charter.)*

… illustrious men, Chrodegarius … journeying through the basilicas, wished legally to assign from his own possessions by the document of his testament … by our authority … our Abbot Dodo of the basilica of our lord Saint Dionysius, our special patron, [received] the document of the testament from John, formerly a merchant … [that] he should assign some of his possessions to the basilica of that same Saint Dionysius or to the other holy places within the city of Paris, and also to some of his relatives, and that this should be confirmed generally by us.

Your Greatness will recognize that, just as we do not deny a just request to anyone, and for the sake of the benefit of our reward, we have not refused this favor … the aforesaid John is rightly recognized as having assigned to the aforesaid basilica of Saint Dionysius, or to the other holy places, or to his relatives, namely, lands, houses, slaves, [lacuna], or some other property. By this authority of ours, this general benefaction, confirmed for those basilicas or for his relatives, shall benefit them forever … Likewise, by this decree, they shall remain secure and established, so that this authority, through the expansion of our titles and in future times, may remain undisturbed in law …

I, Chlothar, king in the name of Christ, have subscribed this decree. Ursinus presented it … of our [estate] at Stirpiniachum, happily in the Lord.

## From a Charter

*From a charter of Chlodoveus II. On Diplomatic Science, p. 466.*

Chlodoveus … for whose love and desire, among the other glorious triumphs, the blessed martyrs Dionysius, Eleutherius, and Rusticus deserved to win the palm of victory and receive a glorious crown. In their basilica, where they appear to rest, Christ is seen to perform no small number of miracles through them over many generations. In that same place our parents, our lord Dagobert and our lady Nanthechild, also appear to rest …

And because that holy place appears to have been enriched by those princes, by other ancient kings, and also by God-fearing Christian people … [we decree] that, just as in the time of our lord and father psalmody had there been established by groups, and just as it is maintained day and night at the monastery of Saint Maurice of Agaunum, so it should likewise be celebrated in that place, etc.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, in the sixteenth year [that is, A.D. 633] of our reign.

## From a Judgment

*From the judgment of Childebert III concerning the market of Saint-Denis. Ibid., p. 482.*

King Childebert, etc.

The agents of the venerable man Dalfinus, abbot of the basilica of our special patron Saint Dionysius, where the precious lord rests bodily, came forward and asserted … that long ago Chlodoveus, formerly our grandfather, and afterward our maternal uncle Childeric, and our lord and father Theuderic, and also our brother Chlothar, by their decrees had granted in full to the basilica of Saint Dionysius whatever toll was due from all merchants, Saxons, or people of any nation whatsoever who came to that holy feast of Saint Dionysius and to that market, etc.

And because, in former times, after a calamity had occurred, that market had been moved from the village of Saint-Denis and established at the city of Paris, between the basilicas of Saint Martin and Saint Laurent, they had there received decrees from the aforesaid princes that, in that place … the aforesaid basilica of Saint Dionysius should receive its portion in full, etc.

Given on 13 December, in the sixteenth year [that is, A.D. 710] of our reign, happily at Mamaccas.

## From the Charter of Theuderic of Châlons

*Ibid., p. 488.*

Theuderic, king of the Franks, illustrious man.

It is fitting, etc. For whose love and desire, among the other glorious triumphs, the blessed martyr Dionysius, together with his companions Rusticus and Eleutherius, who were the first after the apostles to come into this province of Gaul under the direction of the blessed Clement, successor of the apostle Peter, deserved to win the palm of martyrdom and receive glorious crowns.

There they preached the baptism of repentance and the remission of sins. While they were striving in this manner, they deserved the palm of martyrdom and received glorious crowns. In their basilica, where their precious bodies appear to rest, Christ has for many generations, and down to the present, deigned to perform through them no small number of miracles by his power.

In that same place our glorious parents, and Dagobert, our forefather of blessed memory and formerly king, appear to rest. May we too, through the intercession of those saints, deserve to share with all the saints in the heavenly kingdoms and receive eternal life.

Therefore our venerable and faithful man Berthoaldus, by God’s favor abbot of that basilica of our special patron, our lord Dionysius, submitted a petition through the illustrious man Charles, our mayor of the palace, to the clemency of our royal power. They represented that, from ancient times, the bishops of the city of Paris had granted an undiminished privilege to the basilica of our lord Dionysius, and that it had been confirmed by our former royal parents from that time down to the present. They assert that they have the privilege itself, as well as the decrees and confirmations, in their possession.

But for complete security the man Charles and the abbot themselves petitioned our Highness that we too should confirm this by a renewed decree. Let your Greatness know that we received their most religious petition with the greatest willingness and confirmed it in every respect.

And it pleased us to insert into this privilege of our serenity the following provision: when the abbot of that house of God has been summoned from this world by divine will, the holy congregation of that monastery may elect from among themselves the man whom they find to be good and worthy, one who can rule and govern the office of abbot according to holy order. If they agree unanimously, he shall, by authority granted by us or by our successors, be installed as abbot in that house of God, so that, for the stability of our kingdom, for all our people, and for the welfare of the country, they may be able to implore the mercy of the Lord.

At the most gracious request and with the wholehearted devotion of our illustrious nobles and leading men, we have been pleased to grant and concede this, namely: just as psalmody by groups had been instituted in that holy basilica in the time of the former kings, our parents, so, as holy order teaches, it should be celebrated there perpetually by day and night.

This arrangement, etc.

Given on the Kalends of March, in the third year of our reign, at Valenciennes, happily in the name of God. Amen.

## From a Judgment under King Pippin

Pippin, king, etc.

In the eighth year of our reign [that is, A.D. 759] … the agents of Saint-Denis and Abbot Folleradus came forward … They presented and produced the decree of King Dagobert, showing how he had established that market in the district and afterward assigned and confirmed it, together with all the tolls, to the estate of Saint Dionysius.

And the lord King Pippin affirmed that from his childhood he had always seen those tolls belong to and be collected for the estate of Saint Dionysius, etc.

Childebertus I, king, 162, 284, 577, 582. He sits at Paris, 563, 569. He plots the murder of his nephews, 123. What the plot was, 124, 565. Later he repents, ibid., 125. He divides Chlodomer’s kingdom, 125. His expedition into Spain, 113, 566, 966. From there he brings back booty, 114. His expedition into Burgundy, 114, which he subjects to himself, 564. A second expedition into Spain, 130. He threatens Theodatus, king of Italy, with destruction, 133. He receives money from him, 566. He possesses Bourges, 115. His treaty with Theodoricus, 118, and peace, 565. They arm against Chlotarius, 565. He invades Auvergne, 115, 564. He attempts to exclude Theodebertus from the kingdom, 128. Then he gives him gifts, ibid. He takes up arms against Chlotarius, 129, against whom he plots, 568. He joins Chramnus, who conspires against Chlotarius, 156. He incites the Saxons against Chlotarius and devastates the Champagne of Rheims, 158. He receives Gundovaldus, 297. He attempts to establish a bishopric at Melodunum, 304 n., 1328. He founds the monastery of Saint Vincent, or Saint Germanus, at Paris, 131 n., and the church of Saint Eusitius, 967. He summons the Fifth Council of Orléans, 1173. He visits a sick priest-bishop, 1185. He purges the laws of the Franks of paganism, 1334. A constitution concerning this, 1329. Forms written under him, 1330. He buries Saint Chlotildis, 141. He dies, 568. He is buried in the church of Saint Vincent, 160, where his tomb, statue, celebrated memory, and other things are found, 1372–1382. His praises, 160 n., 379. His daughters, 160 n. His courtier Nunnio, 1198. Sigibertus acquires his kingdom, 194.

Childebertus II, king of Austrasia, 595–681, and of Burgundy, 601, 226, 259, 260, 268, 274, 299, 300, 323, 423 n., 425, 442, 444, 521, 575, 578, 1118. He succeeds his father, 196. He is brought to Metz, 576. Rescued, he is established as king, 201, 209. Favorable omens, 379. Guntramnus Boso joins him, 235, as do many others, 204. His embassy to Chilpericus, 322. He joins him, 271, 581, by treaty, 273, 304, and by peace, 286. He receives Marseilles, 288, 308. He receives part of Marseilles, etc., 583, and the city of Albi, 415. He receives Sigibertus’s treasures, 396, and part of Gundovaldus’s treasures, 367. He loses cities, [Col. 1218] 339. He is declared of age, 359. His register, 513. He joins Guntramnus, 318, and is called his nephew and son, 385. He is greatly loved by him, 446, and presented with the kingdom, 358. He is instructed, 359. He is adopted, 221, 378, 577.

He comes to Paris and sends ambassadors to Guntramnus, 335, 336, 340, 341, 439. A copy of their agreement, ibid., 440. He receives Guntramnus’s embassy, 384. There is peace between them, 598, which is broken, 289. His leading men seek Gundovaldus, 358, 360, 363. His army, 300 n. A conspiracy against him, 426, 511. It is discovered, 427. Ursio and others prepare to resist him, 428. His conference with Guntramnus, 429, 430. He pursues Ursio and the others, 431. He is unjustly suspected by Guntramnus, 455. He wishes to send Theodobertus to Soissons, 455. He complains that Guntramnus received Chlotarius from the sacred font, 522.

He becomes king of Burgundy, 601. His kingdom extends beyond the Garonne, 391. He goes to Orléans, 1135; remains at Meaux, 334; at Metz, 409; at Strasbourg, 460; in the villa of Bolsonacum, 393. There he holds an assembly, 394, and another, 349. His letters to Maurice, etc., 485 n., 1346 ff.; to Athanagildus, ibid. He receives from the emperor the Carthaginian ambassadors’ murderers, 488. He prepares against the Lombards, 452, 1347. He unsuccessfully asks Guntramnus for aid, 445. His Italian expedition, 319, 390, 485, 583. He receives gold from the emperor Maurice, 584. Peace with the Lombards, 319. He deceives the Lombards, 449, but is defeated by them, 450. They seek his protection, 449, 625, and he receives their embassy, 488. He possesses part of Italy, 487. He defeats the Varni, 601. He dies, 601.

His Spanish expedition, 319, 397. Leuvigildus fears him, 315. He receives an embassy, 294, 409, and another from Reccaredus, 420, 435. Gregory is at his court, 1129. He confirms the immunity of Tours, 454. He exempts the clergy of Auvergne, etc., from taxes, 490. He consoles Agericus, 432. He spares Egidius, bishop of Rheims, 433. He harasses Theodorus, bishop of Marseilles, 384, then protects him, 385, 447. He grants Berthegundis’s petition, 496. He commits the case of the Poitiers monastery to a tribunal, 476. For this reason he summons a synod, 504, and issues an authoritative order, 470. His order subjecting the monastery to the bishop, 468.

He demands Fredegundis back, 336, 397, who plots against him, 397, 398, 510, 511. His mother and grandmother, 419. Theodelinda had been betrothed to him, 610. His sons, 411. They are driven out by Chlotarius II, 602. His son Theodebertus, 409, 597, whose legitimacy Brunichildis denies, 607. His other son Theodoricus, 421, 598, to whom he had assigned Alsace, 616. His ancestors, 298. His tutor Wandelinus, 395. His referendaries Otto, 512, and Charimeris, 977. His sister is the wife of Hermenigildus, 316.

Childebertus, son of Theuderic II, 604, 620. He flees, 622 and n.

Childebertus III, king, 670. He dies, 671. The years of his reign are corrected, 672 n. His age, 337, 1353. His epoch, 1397. His diploma, 1384.

Childebertus, intruded into the kingdom, 657 n.

Childebrandus, count, arranges for the Chronicle to be written, preface, 142, 677, 686. Brother of Charles Martel, duke, 678, 680. Uncle of Pippin, 681.

Childemeris, king of the Vandals, 712.

Childeradus, 701.

Childericus, king of the Franks, 63–78. He is deposed, 66, 551. He lives in Thuringia, 552, and at Constantinople, 553. He is restored, 66, 553. He fights against Aegidius and the Romans, 553. He takes Basina as his wife, 554. His battles, 555. He drives away Odovacrus, king of the Saxons, 554, 555. [Col. 1219] He dies, 78, 555.

Childericus II, son of Chlodoveus II, 663. King, 664. He becomes monarch, 665. He is killed, 665. The discovery of his tomb, 1378. His epoch, 675 n.

Childericus III, 683.

Childericus, king of the Vandals, 50, 712.

Childericus, son of Chlotarius I, 142, 143, 567. He kills Amalricus, 563.

Childericus, chief of Sigibertus’s court, 951.

Childericus the Saxon, 334. He takes refuge in the basilica of Saint Martin, 391. He becomes duke, etc., 391. He dies, 515.

Chillo, commander of the army, 791.

Chilpericus, son of King Gundeuchus, 80. King of the Burgundians, 1150. He is killed by his brother, 557, 559. He consents to Chlotildis’s marriage, 558, then unsuccessfully withdraws, 559.

Chilpericus, king of the Franks, 142, 236–326, 357, 392, 423, 442, 567, 726. He invades the kingdom of Paris and is expelled, 162, 569. He becomes king at Soissons, 162, 163, 569. He invades Tours and other places, 187, 261, and loses them, 188, 574. He drives away the Campani, 576. He invades Rheims, 163, 569. He prepares against Sigibertus, 192, 194. War with Sigibertus, 190; the war is renewed, 193. He flees to Cameracum, 318, 583. A son is born to him, 319. He is besieged at Tournai, 235, where the Franks abandon him, 194. After losing everything, he is restored, 575. After Sigibertus is killed, he takes his kingdom, 1056. He buries his brother, 195. He resides at Paris, 277.

He attacks Guntramnus, 214, 289, and conspires against him, 335. He invades his cities, 295. He occupies Poitiers, 235, 252. He places guards at the bridge of Urbs, 294, who are driven away, 295. His army is routed, 305. He swears peace with his brothers, 575, and with Guntramnus, 305. Childebertus II joins him, 271. They make peace, 286, and a treaty, 273, 304. His ambassadors go to the emperor Tiberius, 272, 581, from whom he receives coins, 273. He unsuccessfully attempts the conversion of the Jew Priscus, 274.

His embassy to Spain, 293, 308, from which he also receives an embassy, 253, 294, 315, 318, 321. The son of the king of Spain seeks his daughter in marriage, 309, and she is betrothed, 179, 484.

He comes to Paris, 201, 300, 301, 583, 972. He dissolves the marriage of Meroveus, 202, and pursues him, 215, 219, 228, 229. He attacks Brittany, 237. His illness, the death of his sons, the burning of the census books, etc., 1296. He recovers, 243. He repents and benefits the churches, 244.

His wives, 169, 571. Having several, he marries Galsuinta, 168, whom he kills and for whose sake he is expelled from the kingdom, 169. His sons, ibid.: Chlodoveus, 573, whom he persecutes, 230, though he does not mourn his death, 451; another son, Samson, 235, whose death he mourns, 578; likewise Theodobertus, 569; Theodoricus, 301; another son is born, 297, 582. He dies, 309. Two die together, 243, 245; three, 580. His other sons also die, 268, 362, 1297. His son Chlotarius, 404, 412, 413, is left alone, 381, 382, and becomes king, 336.

Chilpericus’s daughter Basina, 463, 514, etc.; the other, Rigunthis, 358, etc., whose wedding he celebrates, 322.

He removes Leudastes, 259. He rejects him—the same man who accused Gregory—260, 262, and receives him again, 307. He orders the man who is killed to be reserved for punishment, 308. Many abandon his kingdom, 204. His friend is Egidius, bishop of Rheims, 512. He assembles the Council of Brennacum, 264. Gregory visits him, 272. Because of his rash accusation, the bishops threaten him with excommunication, 265.

He is hostile to Praetextatus, [Col. 1219] 577, whom he accuses, 222, 223, 226. He deceives and seduces Praetextatus, 227, but unsuccessfully attempts to influence Gregory, 224. He builds circuses, 222. He teaches doctrine, 256, and is opposed by Gregory, 257. He invents new letters, 238. He writes unsuccessfully to Saint Martin, 218. He violates the immunities of clerics and churches, 287. He afflicts the people with surveys and tax assessments, 238, 239, 379. He repairs the church of Saint Germanus and is praised by Saint Bertramnus, 326 n. He compels the Jews to baptism, 292. His favorable disposition toward a bishop, 313. He restores church property to the bishop, 241. He shows moderation toward those accused of offenses against the archdeacon, etc., 263.

Chilpericus’s vision concerning him, 217, 379, 380. His death, 324, 333, 337, 339, 584, 587, 597; by whom, 583 n. It is attributed to Brunichildis, 623. Sunnigisilus is accused, 511. Should “Childebertus” be read here? ibid. n. He dies because of a violated oath, 335. Childebertus possesses his treasures, 334, and his register, 513.

Gregory exaggerates his vices, 324. He composes verses, etc., 321. He is buried, 326. His tomb, 1373. Fortunatus praises him, 257 n. He was more uxorious than cruel, preface, 115. He was a liar, 571. His prudence, 265; goodness, 296; vices, etc., 216; crimes, 512. Guntramnus corrects his evil deeds, 336, 337, 344. Guntramnus wishes to avenge his death, 379. His master of the horse, Cuppa, 489. His physician, Marileifus, 350.

Chilpericus, son of Charibertus II, 641.

Chilpericus, formerly called Daniel, becomes king, 672, 1353. He is defeated by Charles, 673. He dies, 674.

Chilpingus, count of Auvergne, 697.

Chiltrudis, daughter of Charles Martel, marries Duke Odilo, 682.

Chinstasindus, king of Spain, 653. He represses the Goths who were killing kings, 654.

The island of Chios, 834.

Chlodericus, son of Sigibertus Claudus, 93. He kills his father, 96. He himself is killed, 97, 562.

Chlodio, king of the Franks, 60 n.; or Chlogio, 62, 63, 64 n., 550. He resides on the borders of Thuringia, captures Cameracum, advances to the Somme, and routs the Romans, 551.

Chlodoaldus, son of Chlodomeris, 110, 564. He escapes death and becomes a priest, 125, then a monk, 125 n. His monastery and church, ibid., 1392. He is renowned for miracles, 565.

Chlodobergis, daughter of Guntramnus, 222 n., 441 n.

Chlodobertus, son of Chilpericus, falls ill, 243. He dies, 244.

Chlodomeris, king of the Franks, 754. He is born, 81, 561. His kingdom, 162. His seat is at Orléans, 563, 569. At his command Ommatius becomes bishop of Tours, 123. His mother incites him against the Burgundians, 108. He kills Sigismundus, 805. He defeats the Burgundians, 109, 464. He is killed, 110, 223, 464. His wife and sons, ibid. Chlotarius seizes his treasures, 133. His sons are raised by Chlotildis, 123. They are killed, 124, 565, and buried, 125. His kingdom is divided, 125.

Chlodomeris, son of King Guntramnus, 164, 221, 570.

Chlodosinda, queen of the Lombards, 182. Daughter of Chlotarius I, 142, 567. She marries King Alboin, 143, 573. Saint Nicetius of Trier writes to her, 1338.

Chlodosvinda, daughter of Sigibertus, 368, 441. She is sought in marriage by Reccaredus, 436, 444, 445. Whether she married him, 449 n., 452.

Chlodoveus I, king, 62–102, 555. Omens concerning him, 554. His birth, 66. He drives away and kills Syagrius, 78, 556. He reigns in Gaul, 532. He punishes the insolence of a soldier, 78, 79. He returns a church vessel to Saint Remigius, 78 n., 79. He subdues the Thuringians, 79. He seeks Chlotildis in marriage, 557, 558, and receives her, 559. Chlodoveus disregards her counsels, 80, 81. He invokes Christ, defeats and subjugates the Alamanni, 82, 560. Saint Remigius instructs him in the faith, 83. He himself urges the Franks to the faith, ibid. He is baptized, 1340, at Rheims, 560, on Christmas Day, 1322. He is compared with Constantine at his baptism, 83. He is confirmed, 84. Was the ampulla then brought from heaven? 83 n. He had invited bishops to his baptism, 83 n. Avitus of Vienne congratulates him, 1322, as does Theodoricus of Italy on the defeat of the Alamanni, 1321.

He joins Godegiselus against Gundobadus, 85, 561. He besieges Gundobadus at Avignon, 86. He makes him tributary, 87, 561. He returns to Gaul, 562. His conference with Alaric, 90. His expedition against him, 92, 709, 710, 1327. His hatred of the Arians, 91. He honors the basilica of Saint Martin and endows it with gifts, 92, 95, and that of Saint Hilary, 93. He receives a letter from Saint Remigius, 1326. He discovers the ford of the Vienne by a miracle, 93. He kills Alaric and defeats the Goths, 94, 533. He enlarges his kingdom, 711. He seizes their treasures, 95, 562. By a miracle he captures Angoulême, 95. He winters at Bordeaux, 95. He returns to Tours, 95, 96. His prosperity because of his confession of the Trinity, 104. His religious observance on the expedition against the Goths, 95 n. His letter to the bishops for the protection of the churches, 95 n., 1327. His diploma concerning the monastery of Miciacum, 95, 1328.

He subjugates the Britons, 144. He orders Chlodericus to be killed and acquires his kingdom, 562; likewise King Chararicus, 97, 98, 562, and others, 562. He drives away and captures Ragnacharius, 98, and acquires his kingdom, 563. He kills Regnomerus and other kings and his own relatives, and subjugates all Gaul, 99. He is called consul and Augustus, 95. His statue, 1372. He establishes his seat at Paris, 95, 96. He causes the death of Sigibertus Claudus, 96, and occupies his kingdom, 97. His severity, 556. He preserves the right of asylum for churches, 422. The extent of his kingdom, 562, 563. He gave the kingdom its beginning, 199. He makes Rheims the capital of Theodoricus’s kingdom, 163 n. His death, 138, 196, 576, at Paris, 100, and his burial, 100, 563. Chlotildis is buried beside him, 141.

Chlotildis, their daughter, 114. After his death the kingdom of Gaul is divided, 105, 563. The Goths invade what they had previously lost, 127. Was Theodechildis his daughter? 168 n. His sister marries Theodoricus the Great, 131.

Chlodoveus, or Chlodio, 550 n.

Chlodoveus II, king, 1353. Son of Dagobertus, 648. He is designated king of Neustria, 649. He goes into Burgundy, 658. He holds an assembly at Autun, 659, 660. His diploma, 1383. His wife, sons, madness, and death, 663. His epoch, 675 n. The mayor of his palace, Erchinoaldus, 654.

Chlodoveus Chlotarius, king of the Franks, 644 n.

Chlodoveus III, king, 1353. He dies, 670.

Chlodoveus, a fictitious king produced by Ebroinus, 665 n.

Chlodoveus, son of King Sigibertus, at Cologne, 562.

Chlodoveus, son of Chilpericus, 169, 188, 190, 202, 214, 249, 571, 574, 577. He did not plot his father’s death, 266 and n. His death, 250, 251, 581. His body is discovered, 382. He is buried in the church of Saint Vincent at Paris, 383.

Chlotarius I, king, 244, 284, 362, 443, 778. King of Soissons, 563. His brothers arm against him, 129, 565. He is divinely delivered, 130. He is thwarted by Theodatus’s money, 566. His expedition into Spain, 130, 566. His threats against the king of Italy, 133. His expedition into Thuringia, 110, 111. He discovers Theodoricus’s plot, 112. He attempts to exclude Theodebertus from the kingdom, 128.

Chlotarius succeeds Theodebaldus, 148, 567. He defeats the Saxons and punishes Thuringia, 567. His expedition into Burgundy, 114, which he subjugates, 564. He marries his brother’s wife, 110, 564. His expedition against the Saxons, 153, 154, 157, 158. A great slaughter takes place, 155. He suppresses the rebellious Saxons, 148, and devastates Thuringia, ibid. He possesses something in Italy, 148 n. He returns to the kingdom, 159. He is defeated by the Saxons, 568. He receives tribute from them, 647, 684. He grants certain regions to Suavis, 219. He comes to Paris, 123.

He kills Chlodomeris’s sons and divides their kingdom, 124, 125, 565. He also seizes their treasures, 133. He buries Saint Chlotildis, 141. He sends his son Guntharius against the Goths, 127. He imposes tribute on the churches, 567. Saint Injuriosus reproves him, 141. He repents, 142. He becomes monarch, 160, 340, 568, 623. He sends against Chramnus, 156, and pursues him, 1022; into Brittany, 161. Under him Provence is divided in two, 413 n. He purges the laws of paganism, 1334. In his time the monastery at Poitiers is founded, 467, which he favors, 472, 473. He had ordered a bishop to be ordained without a metropolitan, 165, which Charibertus defends, 166. Saint Nicetius excommunicates him, 1236. He condemns Bishop Cautinus, 151, 152. He buries Saint Medardus and builds a church, 160. He assists the church of Saint Martin, 536. He repairs it and covers it with tin, 161. He exempts Tours from the census, 453. He visits the tomb of Saint Martin, 162, 285. He dies repentant at Compiègne, 162, 569. Signs precede his death, 194. He is buried at Soissons, 195. After his death the Huns invade Gaul, 163. Under his sons the Britons are subjected, 437.

He had Radegundis as his wife, 112. His sons and wives, 567. His wives and children, 142, 143. His incontinent conduct, ibid. His daughter Chlotosinda, 182. His son Guntharius, 1089. Rauchingus claims to be his son, 427, as does Gundovaldus, 297, 357, 358, 582. His minister, later Abbot Sabaudus, 1203. His referendary Baudinus, 535. His referendary, later domesticus, Charigisilus, 1024. Chlotarius I and II were monarchs, 522 n.

Chlotarius II, king, from 336 to 538, 404. Son of Chilpericus, 413, 426. Guntramnus administers his kingdom, 391. His birth, 319. As an infant, 335, 337, 362. Guntramnus does not acknowledge him, 359 n. Guntramnus calls his birth into question, 446. His legitimacy is proved, 382. His baptism is delayed, 381, 382. He is baptized, 375, 522, 597. He becomes king, 336, 597, 651, of Neustria, 597. His cities, 412.

He remits tribute to the Lombards, 626. He vindicates his relative, the queen of the Lombards, 629. He permits the leading men to elect a mayor of the palace, 632. He receives Meroveus from the sacred font, 608. He drives out Quintrio, 601, and the sons of Childebertus II, 602. He makes peace with them, 603, then violates it, 605. He is defeated and makes peace with Theodebertus, 606. He is defeated by Theodebertus and Theodoricus, 603. He joins other kings against Theodoricus II, 609. He receives the duchy of Dentelinus, 619. His war with Theodoricus II, 620, whom he joins against Theodebertus, 617, 618. He attempts to occupy Austrasia, 620. He attacks Sigibertus II, 621. He orders Theodoricus’s sons killed, 622, and Brunichildis, 623. He becomes monarch, 623, 1351, 1353. He quarrels with his son Dagobertus, [Col. 1221] 630, 631. He falls ill, 495. He dies and is buried, 633.

His wife Sichilda, 630 n. His son Meroveus, 605. His diploma, 1383.

Chlotarius, also called Chlodoveus, king of the Franks, 644.

Chlothar III, son of Chlodovech II, king, 663, 1383. Dies, 664. Proclaimed mayor, 359, n. Dies, 664. Chlothar IV becomes king, 673. Dies, 674, 675, n. Chlothar, whether king of the Lombards, 625, n. Chlothar, son of King Guntram, 164, 222, 570. Chlothar, son of Theudebert II, 623.

Chlothildis, queen, 105, n., 533, 1009, A. Chlodovech seeks her in marriage, 557, 558. Obtains her, 80. Labors for her conversion, ibid., 81, 82, 550. She comes into Francia on horseback and marries Chlodovech, 559. Incites her sons to avenge their parents, 564. Against the Burgundians, 108. Raises the sons of Chlodomer, 110, 123. Her virtues, 125. Resides at Paris, 565. Civil war is brought to an end by her prayers, 129, 565. Secures the bishopric of Tours for Theodore and Proculus, 123. Builds the basilica of the Apostles at Paris, 141. Pious practices among the people of Tours, 563. Her charters, 150, 151. Dies, 141, 534, 567.

Chlothildis, daughter of Chlodovech, badly treated by Amalaric; her steadfastness in the faith, 113. Dies, 114.

Chlothildis, daughter of Guntram, 222, n. Her inheritance, 441.

Chochilaicus, king of the Danes, ravages Gaul and is killed, 106.

Chonober, count of the Britons, 160. Perishes in battle, 161.

Chonoo, count of the Britons, 161, n., 1392.

The sons of Chore in the Psalms, 1258.

Chorepiscopi, 207, n.

Psalmody performed by divided choirs, 933.

Chosroes, king of the Persians, 355, n. Deceives Heraclius, 638. Defeated, he is killed by his own men, 639.

Chosroes the Younger, king of the Persians, 598, n.

Chramnelus, duke, 649, 659, 660.

Chramnisindus, 371, 372.

Chramnisindus, a citizen of Tours, 437. Hated by Brunichildis, 438.

Chramnulfus, 632.

Chramnus, 536. Son of Chlothar I, 142, 143, 567. Is called king, 153. His evil character, 152, 155. Sent by his father to the Arverni, 148. Favors Cato’s party, 149. Harasses Bishop Cautinus, 153. The crimes of his ministers among the Arverni, 797. Falls ill, 155. Conspires against his father, 156. Deceives his brothers, 157. Hostile to his father, 1022. Takes the daughter of Willacharius, 158. Comes to Paris, ibid. Is presented to his father, 160. Inquires by lot into the future from Holy Scripture, 157. Is not admitted at Dijon, 158. Rebels against his father and flees to Britain, 568. Fights against his father and is captured, 161. Is burned with his wife, etc., 162, 568.

Chrasmarus, bishop of Tournai, 235, n.

What is the chrismal? 1131, n. Its blessing, 1365.

Chrismarium, 1133, 1288, 1292, 1305, 1306.

Anointing with chrism used in receiving Arians, 85, n., 88, 168, 248, 434.

The blessing of chrism by the bishop, 392. In the blessing of the fonts, 747.

Anointing with chrism, 46. Anointing after baptism, 84.

Christians have their foreheads marked with the inscription of chrism, [Col. 1222] 768, 769.

Crispus, son of Constantine, 27.

When Christians first appeared at Rome, 20. The first schisms and heresies among them, 21. They celebrate Easter on a different day from the Jews, 516. Washed, anointed with balsam, and marked with the inscription of chrism, 768, 769.

The dignity of the Christian name, 841. It must be adorned with good works, 767. The name “Christian” given to Catholics in preference to heretics, 113, 215, 903. Converts to Arianism are said to become Christians, 598. Why they were hated by the Senate, 20.

The Christians’ quarter, 25.

Christophorus, merchant, 369.

Christ is our end, 7. Our peace, 1258. His nativity, 16, 17, 721. Adoration by the Magi, ibid. His baptism, 317. His Transfiguration, 318. The place of his baptism, 741. His preaching, miracles, death, etc., 18. His miracles, 722, 723. His Passion, resurrection, and ascension, ibid., 19. He freed the fathers from the underworld, 498. He ordained Saint James bishop, 749. His coming, resurrection, Passion, etc., in the Psalms, 1257, 1258. He receives the soul of blessed Mary and leads it with her body into paradise, 724, 730. Crucified on Mount Calvary, where the victim was substituted for Isaac, 11, and n. His cross, 725 ff. The nails, 727. The lance, reed, sponge, crown of thorns, column, and tomb, 729. The seamless tunic, 730. His tunic is found, 600.

God, 17, 18, 19. His divinity, 28, 49, 316, 317. His mission, 316. His equality with the Father, 253, 254. The Son of God: what must be believed concerning him, 6, 7. In him God created all things, 8. The Son of Man: whether he was ignorant of the day of judgment, 7, and n. So that a woman might see him, she went from Gaul to Jerusalem, 735. His age, 676. Sacred objects are consecrated by the touch of his body, 730. Christians bear his sign, 769. Oaths are sworn in his name, 827. When he is invoked, the sacred rites of the pagans are disturbed and their gods driven away, 767 ff. Chlodovech invokes him and defeats the Alamanni, 82.

The infant Jesus depicted in Mary’s arms in a church, 733. An image of him crucified, 745. A statue, 743. Images, 744. A type of him in Adam, 8; in Noah, 9; in Joseph, 12; in Zerubbabel, 16.

Chrocus, king of the Alamanni, ravages Gaul, 25. When, ibid., n. His death, 26. He is called king of the Vandals, 711. He is captured by Marius, 711. He is killed, 712.

Chrodegildis, religious woman, 726.

Chrodieldis, 515. Regulates the affairs of the monastery, 470. Stirs up disturbances, 463. Goes to the king, 468. Returns, 469. Her obstinacy, 466. Is questioned in the council, 506, 508. Genesius, Saint, martyr, 745. Church of Saint Genesius at Clermont, 74 n. Genesius, martyr of Arles, 777, 798. The feast of his miracle and his basilica, 799. Genesius, Saint, of Auvergne, 797.
